name: .sav file structure and metadata
origin: SPSS Inc. system file format; open readers such as ReadStat (Evan Miller) and pyreadstat
summary: Understanding and using the metadata stored in SPSS .sav files, such as variable labels, value labels, missing-value codes and measurement levels, so survey data move between tools without losing meaning.
description: A .sav file holds more than a data matrix: it stores variable names, variable labels (the question text), value labels (e.g. 1 = 'Strongly disagree'), user-defined missing values (e.g. 98 = 'Don't know', 99 = 'Refused'), measurement levels, formats and weights. Survey platforms export to .sav precisely because this metadata functions as a codebook. Losing it, for example by exporting to CSV, causes classic errors: 'Don't know' codes averaged as scale points, reversed value orders, and unlabelled variables. Rigour comes from inspecting the dictionary before analysis, using tools such as pyreadstat that read metadata into Python, converting user-missing codes explicitly, and producing a codebook from the file itself.
steps: Import the .sav with metadata (in SPSS, DISPLAY DICTIONARY; in Python, pyreadstat.read_sav returning data and meta).
Review variable labels, value labels and declared missing codes for every analysis variable.
Convert user-defined missing codes (e.g. 98, 99, -1) to system missing before computing statistics.
Verify value label direction for each scale, especially items that will be reverse-coded.
Generate a codebook from the metadata and store it with the project.
When writing back to .sav, preserve or add labels so the processed file is self-documenting.
outputs: A verified data dictionary, a generated codebook and analysis-ready data with missing codes handled.
useWhen: Any project receiving survey data from Qualtrics, Alchemer, panel providers or partners as .sav, or moving data between SPSS and Python or R.
avoidWhen: Not relevant for purely qualitative or log data; for CSV-only sources, build a separate codebook.
whyLost: Metadata handling is taught in social science data management, but UX teams often export CSV and lose labels without noticing.
whereToUse: Survey-heavy UX programmes, market research handovers and longitudinal tracking.
example: A SaaS team's satisfaction average looks implausibly high. Inspecting the .sav metadata shows 'Not applicable' was coded 9 on a 1-7 scale; once declared missing, the mean falls from 5.9 to 5.2.
sources: Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
reference: IBM SPSS Statistics Command Syntax Reference

name: 5-Second Test
origin: Christine Perfetti, User Interface Engineering, around 2005
summary: Participants see a design for five seconds and then recall what they noticed, measuring first impressions, visual hierarchy and clarity of the value proposition.
description: The five-second test shows a participant a screen, often a landing page or key view, for about five seconds, then hides it and asks what they remember, what the page was about, who it was for or what they could do there. The short exposure approximates the first glance many users give before deciding whether to stay. It assesses whether the core message, primary call to action and visual hierarchy communicate immediately. Rigour comes from a single clear question focus per test, consistent exposure times, recruiting people unfamiliar with the design, enough participants (around 20 to 50) to quantify recall, coding open-ended answers against intended messages, and comparing variants rather than interpreting one result in isolation.
steps: Define what the design should communicate at a glance, such as purpose, audience and main action.
Prepare a static screenshot at the size it will be seen.
Write 3 to 5 recall questions, starting with an open question about what the page was about.
Show the design for 5 seconds to each participant who has not seen it before.
Collect responses from 20 to 50 participants, usually remotely.
Code answers against the intended messages and compute the proportion who recalled each.
Compare variants and iterate on hierarchy or copy.
outputs: Recall rates for key messages, coded first impressions, and comparisons of variants on clarity.
useWhen: For landing pages, home screens, onboarding screens and ads where the first impression and value proposition must land immediately.
avoidWhen: Avoid for assessing task flows or interaction; use usability testing. Not suited to dense screens meant for study, such as dashboards.
whyLost: Still in use: Quick first-impression test; useful remotely; low friction for participants.
whereToUse: Landing pages; onboarding screens; any design where first impression is critical.
example: An AI writing tool tests two landing pages with 40 participants each. Only 30 percent recall the product's purpose from version A versus 70 percent from version B, which leads with a concrete example.
reference: Perfetti, C. (2005). 5-second tests: Measuring your site's content pages. User Interface Engineering.

name: A/A test
origin: Industry practice; Kohavi, Longbotham and colleagues, 2009 (Crook et al., KDD 2009)
summary: Randomise users into two identical experiences to check that the experimentation platform yields false positives at the nominal rate and to estimate metric variance.
description: In an A/A test, users from the same population are randomised into two groups that receive the same unchanged experience. Because there is no true difference, the comparison tests the experimentation system itself: randomisation, logging, metric pipelines and variance estimates. At alpha 0.05, about 5 per cent of metrics or runs should be significant; more frequent rejections signal a biased split, broken logging or wrong variance estimation. Kohavi and colleagues recommend simulating many A/A tests by replaying stored data with fresh randomisation seeds, plotting p-value histograms per metric and testing them for uniformity. Skewed histograms suggest variance errors, a spike near 0.32 a dominant outlier, and point masses rare non-zero values. A/A tests also check sample ratio against the intended split and supply variance for power calculations. Replay cannot catch performance or caching issues, so live A/A tests should continue alongside A/B tests.
steps: Set up two randomised groups with identical experiences, using the same splits (including unequal ones) as planned A/B tests.
Run for a normal test duration and collect all planned metrics.
Check sample sizes in each arm against the intended split.
Test each metric for a difference and record p-values.
Repeat many times, live or by replaying stored data with new randomisation seeds, and plot p-value histograms per metric.
Test histograms for uniformity (for example Kolmogorov-Smirnov or Anderson-Darling) and expect about 5 per cent rejections at alpha 0.05.
Investigate failing metrics, fix variance, capping or instrumentation, and distrust results produced before the fix.
outputs: Validation of the platform and metrics, sample ratio checks, and metric variance estimates for power analysis.
useWhen: Before relying on a new or changed experimentation platform, metric or randomisation unit, and periodically as ongoing quality control.
avoidWhen: Do not judge a platform from a single A/A run, which can be significant by chance. It does not test whether your treatment is valid or your metrics meaningful.
whyLost: It survived because large experimentation programmes found many platform bugs through it, and it is standard in mature A/B testing practice.
whereToUse: Any online experimentation programme: e-commerce, SaaS, media, mobile apps, marketplaces.
example: An e-commerce team replays a week of traffic 1,000 times with new seeds. Revenue per user shows far more than 5 per cent significant results because of a few huge orders, so the team caps the metric before running real tests.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D., & Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Cambridge University Press; Crook, T., Frasca, B., Kohavi, R., & Longbotham, R. (2009). Seven pitfalls to avoid when running controlled experiments on the web. Proceedings of KDD 2009.

name: A/B result decision rules and triage
aka: Launch decision by statistical versus practical significance
donor: Online experimentation; statistics and decision analysis
origin: Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020); King, Churchill and Tan (2017); Harris (Quant UX Con 2022)
summary: A pre-agreed decision procedure that maps an experiment's result, confidence interval and practical-significance threshold to ship, iterate, abandon or rerun, before anyone sees the data.
description: Most teams run A/B tests but decide ad hoc once results arrive. This method fixes the decision rule first. The team chooses the decision type (superiority, bias to ship or non-inferiority, agnostic, measurement, or lean-startup exploration), the key metric and the smallest change worth acting on, and translates verbal certainty into numbers (for example 'almost certainly' as 95%, 'quite likely' as 80%). After the planned sample, the confidence interval is compared with both zero and the practical boundary, giving six cases from clear launch to rerun with more power. Results are then triaged as expected, unexpected or flat, each with its own questions: user disruption and maintenance cost for winners, execution faults and secondary metrics for losers, and power, duration and cell differentiation for flat results. Rigour comes from pre-commitment and from separating statistical from practical significance.
steps: Before launch, agree the decision type with stakeholders: superiority, bias to ship (non-inferiority), agnostic, measurement or lean-startup exploration.

Choose one key metric and fix the practical significance boundary, the smallest change worth acting on (for example 1% relative), plus the certainty levels in agreed phrases mapped to numbers (95% 'almost certainly', 80% 'quite likely').
Run a power analysis for that rule, start the test, validate the data (sample ratio, logging) and wait for the planned sample without peeking.

Compute the confidence interval of the delta and classify it: not significant with a narrow interval (iterate or abandon); statistically and practically significant (launch); significant but below the practical boundary (launch only if cheap); or an interval spanning the practical boundary (rerun with more power).
For an expected result, weigh user disruption, retraining, support and maintenance costs and any shortcuts taken in the test before shipping.

For an unexpected (negative) result, question assumptions about use and motivation, read the secondary metrics, add qualitative research and check for execution faults; rework the hypothesis rather than polishing the failed design.
For a flat result, check sample, duration, business cycles, external events, how different the cells really were and upstream flow effects; retest only with other supporting evidence.
Record the decision in the agreed phrases: roll out to 100%, widen exposure, or keep the existing experience, and plan communication for global changes.
outputs: A pre-registered decision memo, a classified result (one of six statistical cases and expected/unexpected/flat) and a documented ship, iterate, abandon or rerun decision.
useWhen: Any team running product experiments that needs consistent, defensible launch decisions, especially when stakeholders disagree about what a result means or when flat results are common.
avoidWhen: Exploratory tests run purely to learn rather than decide, or when the effect is too small to power at available traffic; then use qualitative research or Bayesian expected-loss decisions instead. Stakeholders who drift from agreed thresholds defeat it.
whyLost: Experiment platforms report p-values and lift but not decision rules, so the practical-significance boundary and pre-commitment are usually skipped and results are read post hoc.
whereToUse: Growth and checkout experiments in e-commerce, pricing and onboarding tests in SaaS, ranking changes in marketplaces, any organisation building an experimentation culture.
example: A fintech team agrees that a new transfer flow must lift completion by at least 1% to justify migration costs. The result is significant at +0.4%, so by the pre-agreed rule it ships only because the code is already built and maintenance is unchanged, and the write-up says 'quite likely a small improvement'.
sources: Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Cambridge University Press.

name: A/B Test Design Beyond Conversion Rates
origin: Kohavi et al. on overall evaluation criteria and guardrails (2007 onwards); King, Churchill and Tan (2017)
summary: Designs online experiments around a pre-specified hierarchy of primary, secondary and guardrail metrics, with power analysis, so decisions reflect user experience and long-term value, not conversion alone.
description: Many A/B tests optimise a single short-term conversion metric, which can reward dark patterns and miss harm to retention, trust or support load. Rigorous experiment design pre-registers a metric hierarchy: a primary decision metric (or overall evaluation criterion) that predicts long-term value, secondary metrics that explain the mechanism, and guardrail metrics that must not degrade, such as latency, error rates, unsubscribes, complaints or retention. A power analysis sets sample size and duration for the primary metric's minimum detectable effect, and the analysis plan specifies decision rules before data arrive. King, Churchill and Tan add the UX perspective: grounding hypotheses in qualitative insight and treating experiments as part of a learning agenda. Holdout groups and longer-term follow-ups detect novelty effects and delayed harm.
steps: Before any A/B test:
Primary metric — what single metric determines ship/no-ship?
(2) Secondary metrics — what additional signals support the decision?
(3) Guardrails — what metrics must not worsen (latency, error rate, NPS)?
(4) Power calculation for primary metric. Run the test. Report: did primary metric move? Did guardrails hold? Did secondary metrics tell a consistent story?
outputs: Pre-registered experiment plan with metric hierarchy, power calculation, guardrail results, decision record and a learning log linked to hypotheses.
useWhen: Any product experiment, especially changes that could trade short-term conversion against retention, trust or wellbeing (pricing, notifications, onboarding nudges).
avoidWhen: When traffic is too low to power the primary metric (use qualitative testing or Bayesian or sequential designs), or when randomisation is impossible (use quasi-experimental methods).
whyLost: Experimentation platforms made it trivial to launch tests on a single conversion metric, and teams under growth pressure skipped pre-registration and guardrails.
whereToUse: All A/B testing. Particularly important for any test where short-term conversion and long-term retention may trade off (dark pattern detection).
example: A subscription news app tests a more aggressive paywall prompt. Conversion rises 9%, but the pre-registered guardrail of 28-day reader retention drops 4%, so the variant is rejected and a softer metered version is tested next.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: King R, Churchill EF & Tan C (2017) Designing with Data: Improving the User Experience with A/B Testing. O'Reilly Media

name: A/B Testing
origin: R. A. Fisher's experimental design, 1920s to 1930s; online controlled experiments popularised by Kohavi and colleagues, 2000s
summary: Randomly assigns users to design variants and compares behavioural outcomes, giving causal evidence of a change's effect at scale.
description: A/B testing is a randomised controlled experiment in a live product. Users are randomly assigned to a control and one or more variants, and a predefined outcome metric, such as conversion, retention or task completion, is compared between groups. Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders, so differences can be attributed to the change. Rigour comes from a pre-registered primary metric and minimum detectable effect, a sample size calculated from power analysis, a fixed duration covering full weekly cycles, checks for sample ratio mismatch, guardrail metrics to catch harm, and avoiding repeated peeking without sequential correction. A/B tests show what changed behaviour, not why, so they pair well with qualitative research.
steps: Write a hypothesis and choose one primary metric, plus guardrail metrics.
Set the minimum detectable effect and compute the required sample size with a power analysis (typically 80 percent power, alpha 0.05).
Implement random assignment at the appropriate unit (user, account or session) and validate with an A/A test if new to the platform.
Run for the precomputed duration, at least one full weekly cycle, without stopping early unless using sequential methods.
Check sample ratio mismatch and data quality before analysis.
Analyse the primary metric with confidence intervals and review guardrails and pre-planned segments.
Decide, document and share results, including null results.
outputs: Effect estimates with confidence intervals for primary and guardrail metrics, and a documented ship or no-ship decision.
useWhen: When you have enough traffic to detect meaningful effects and need causal evidence about whether a design change improves behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid with low traffic, when outcomes take months to observe, for exploring why users behave as they do, or for ethically sensitive manipulations; use usability testing, interviews or quasi-experiments.
whyLost: Still in use: Gold standard for validating design changes at scale; widely supported by product analytics tools.
whereToUse: High-traffic digital products where behavioral metrics are trackable; conversion optimization.
example: A food-delivery app tests showing total delivery fees earlier in checkout. With 400,000 users per arm, conversion falls 0.3 percent but refund requests fall 12 percent, and the team ships the change on net value.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi, Tang & Xu)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)

name: Abductive Reasoning in Research Synthesis
origin: Charles Sanders Peirce, 1870s-1900s; abductive analysis by Timmermans and Tavory, 2012
summary: Makes the leap from surprising observations to the most plausible explanation explicit, generating and testing competing hypotheses during synthesis.
description: Peirce identified abduction as the form of inference that generates hypotheses: a surprising fact C is observed; if A were true, C would follow; so there is reason to suspect A. Research synthesis is largely abductive, yet it usually happens implicitly. Timmermans and Tavory's abductive analysis turns it into a method: researchers deliberately look for surprising findings relative to existing theory and assumptions, generate several candidate explanations, and revisit the data to test which best explains the evidence, using variation across cases and over time. Rigour comes from documenting surprises, writing rival hypotheses explicitly, specifying what evidence would distinguish them, and seeking disconfirming cases. This guards against the common failure of jumping to a single convenient insight.
steps: List the team's prior assumptions and expectations before analysis begins.
During analysis, log surprising observations that contradict those expectations.
For each surprise, write at least three rival explanations.
Specify what evidence in the existing data or new research would distinguish between them.
Revisit the data and, if needed, run targeted follow-up research to test the rivals, actively seeking disconfirming cases.
Report the best-supported explanation with its rivals and the evidence that ruled them out.
outputs: Surprise log, rival hypothesis tables, evidence matrix, explained findings with confidence levels.
useWhen: Discovery synthesis, interpreting unexpected analytics results, and any study where findings may be shaped by team assumptions.
avoidWhen: Purely confirmatory evaluation with predefined measures; use hypothesis-driven experimental designs.
whyLost: Latent: Epistemological foundation for design research; rarely made explicit; valuable for teaching research reasoning.
whereToUse: Research synthesis; design thinking; hypothesis generation in discovery research.
example: A fintech team was surprised that users with high balances ignored a savings feature. Rival explanations were distrust, existing savings elsewhere and confusion; targeted interviews showed most already held savings at another bank, redirecting the feature toward account consolidation.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess
Collected Papers of Charles Sanders Peirce
Timmermans & Tavory, Theory construction in qualitative research: From grounded theory to abductive analysis (2012), Sociological Theory
Tavory & Timmermans, Abductive Analysis: Theorizing Qualitative Research (2014)
reference: Timmermans, S., & Tavory, I. (2012). Theory construction in qualitative research: From grounded theory to abductive analysis. Sociological Theory, 30(3), 167-186.

name: Accelerated Failure Time Duration Model
aka: Accelerated lifetime (accelerated failure time) duration model
origin: Reliability engineering and duration econometrics; presented for marketing by Philip Hans Franses and Richard Paap, 2001
summary: Survival model in which covariates speed up or slow down time to an event by a multiplicative factor, with a chosen baseline distribution and censored cases handled in the likelihood.
description: Durations (time between purchases, time to cancel, time to respond) are positive and often censored, so they need hazard-based models. In the proportional hazards model covariates multiply the hazard; in the accelerated failure time model they stretch or shrink time itself through a factor of exp(-X beta), so coefficients read as percentage changes in expected duration, which stakeholders often find more intuitive. The two coincide only for the Weibull distribution. Baselines include exponential (memoryless), Weibull (monotone rising or falling hazard), and loglogistic or lognormal (hazards that rise then fall). Censored spells contribute their survival probability to the likelihood, and time-varying covariates can be included if they change a limited number of times. Fit is checked with generalised residuals, which should be unit exponential: plot their empirical integrated hazard against a 45-degree line and run conditional moment tests. Unobserved heterogeneity can be added but is hard to separate from duration dependence.
steps: Define the spell (start and end), the event and a censoring indicator for each case.
Choose a baseline distribution (Weibull, loglogistic, lognormal) and the accelerated failure time or proportional hazards form.
Estimate by maximum likelihood with density terms for completed spells and survival terms for censored ones.
Compute generalised residuals, plot their empirical integrated hazard against the 45-degree line and run moment tests; move to a more flexible baseline if rejected.
Compare models with likelihood ratio tests and AIC or BIC.
Interpret coefficients as percentage changes in expected duration and forecast durations or the number of events per period on a hold-out sample.
outputs: Covariate effects as time ratios, the hazard shape, expected durations and hold-out forecasts.
useWhen: Time-to-event questions such as time to repurchase, time to churn or time to first key action, where you want effects expressed as speeding up or slowing down time and the hazard shape matters.
avoidWhen: You want to avoid assuming a baseline distribution (use Cox proportional hazards); time is coarse with many ties (use discrete-time hazard models); events recur frequently (use count or recurrent-event models). The diagnostic tests shown apply cleanly only to uncensored observations.
whyLost: Product analytics teams that do survival analysis default to Kaplan-Meier and Cox models; parametric AFT models remain in reliability engineering and econometrics.
whereToUse: Repurchase and replenishment timing in e-commerce, subscription lifetime, time to adoption of a new feature, time between support contacts.
example: A pet-food subscription models days between orders for 20,000 households with a loglogistic AFT model. Households with two or more pets reorder 22% sooner and a price increase stretches intervals by 9%; the non-monotone hazard supports a reminder sent just before the typical reorder peak.
sources: Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
reference: Franses, P. H., & Paap, R. (2001). Quantitative Models in Marketing Research. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

name: Accessibility Evaluation
summary: Systematic assessment of conformance with accessibility standards and real usability for disabled people, combining automated scans, expert audit and testing with disabled users.
description: Accessibility evaluation assesses whether a product can be perceived, operated, understood and used robustly by people with disabilities, including those using assistive technologies such as screen readers, switch devices, magnifiers and voice control. It combines automated scanning, which detects only a minority of issues, manual expert audit against WCAG success criteria, assistive-technology testing, and usability testing with disabled participants. Conformance is necessary but not sufficient: a product can pass criteria and still be hard to use. Rigour comes from defining scope and target conformance level, sampling representative pages and flows, testing with multiple assistive technologies, documenting each failure against its criterion with evidence, and including disabled people in evaluation rather than relying solely on simulations.
steps: Define scope, target standard and level (for example WCAG 2.2 AA) and sample representative pages and flows.
Run automated scanning tools to catch detectable issues.
Conduct a manual audit against each applicable success criterion, including keyboard-only navigation and colour contrast.
Check colour palettes and finished data visualisations with a colour-deficiency simulator (protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia), for example Coblis or ColorBrewer's colour-blind-safe flag.
Test key flows with screen readers and other assistive technologies on target platforms.
Run usability sessions with 5 or more disabled participants across disability types.
Document issues with criterion, location, severity and remediation advice.
Retest fixes and track conformance over time.
outputs: A conformance report with failures mapped to criteria, severity and remediation guidance, plus usability findings from disabled users.
useWhen: For all digital products, especially government, healthcare, education and finance, and before procurement or legal conformance claims.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying only on automated tools or simulations; they miss most real barriers. Use expert audit plus testing with disabled users.
whyLost: Still in use: Legal and ethical imperative; growing regulatory pressure worldwide.
whereToUse: All digital products; particularly critical for government, healthcare, and education.
example: A university learning platform audits its exam submission flow. Screen-reader testing reveals that a countdown timer steals focus every minute, making submission nearly impossible, and it is fixed before exams.
sources: Rhyne, T.-M., The Process of Colorizing a Data Visualization (keynote, 2021)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
A Practical Guide to Designing with Data (Suda, 2010)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
The Process of Colorizing a Data Visualization (Rhyne, 2021)

name: AcciMap Analysis
origin: Jens Rasmussen's risk management framework (1997); later applied by Salmon, Cornelissen and Trotter (2012) and others
summary: Map an accident's contributory factors onto six system tiers, from government policy down to equipment, and link them by cause and effect to find where intervention is needed.
description: AcciMap extends Rasmussen's risk management framework into a graphical analysis of the failures, decisions and actions behind an accident or incident. Contributory factors are placed on six hierarchical tiers: government policy and budgeting; regulatory bodies and associations; local area government planning and budgeting; technical and operational management; physical processes and actor activities; and equipment and surroundings. Cause-effect links are drawn within and across tiers, so a frontline error is traced back to the management, regulatory and policy conditions that shaped it. A hierarchical evaluation then identifies the significant factors and the levels where intervention is needed. Unlike Swiss Cheese or HFACS, which classify failure types, or STAMP/STPA, which models control structures, AcciMap is a free-form systemic causal map whose value lies in drawing attention away from blaming the last person to act. It has been applied in aviation, road transport and mining.
steps: Collect data on the accident, incident or failure from reports, logs, interviews and documents.
Identify contributory factors: failures, decisions, actions and conditions.
Place each factor on one of the six tiers, from government policy to equipment and surroundings.
Draw cause-effect links between factors within and across tiers.
Evaluate the map hierarchically to identify the significant factors and the tiers where interventions would have most effect.
Translate findings into recommendations aimed at each relevant tier, not only the frontline.
outputs: A multi-tier causal map of the accident and a list of key systemic factors with recommended interventions by tier.
useWhen: Post-incident analysis of serious failures involving people, technology and organisations, such as harmful product incidents, safety-critical errors or major outages with user harm.
avoidWhen: Prospective hazard analysis of a new design (use STAMP / STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis) or HAZOP); routine bug triage; when only frontline data are available.
whyLost: It lives in safety science and accident investigation; product teams run blameless post-mortems without a structured multi-level causal map.
whereToUse: Health tech and medical device incidents, fintech failures harming customers, trust and safety incidents, autonomous system failures.
example: After a medication app double-doses users, an AcciMap links the user action to a confusing confirmation screen, a release process that skipped clinical review, a deadline set by management, and an unclear regulatory classification, producing fixes at four tiers.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Rasmussen, J. (1997). Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem. Safety Science, 27(2-3), 183-213.

name: Achievement Goal Orientation and Motivational Climate Assessment
aka: Task and Ego Orientation in Sport Questionnaire
donor: Educational and sport psychology (achievement goal theory)
origin: Nicholls (1984, 1989) and Ames (1992); TEOSQ by Duda and Nicholls (1992); POSQ by Roberts and colleagues (1998); reviewed by Roberts, Treasure and Conroy in Chapter 1 of the Handbook
summary: Measures whether people judge success by their own improvement (task orientation) or by beating others (ego orientation), and whether an environment is perceived to promote mastery or comparison.
description: Achievement goal theory holds that people define competence in two ways: self-referenced (task orientation, success means learning and improving) and other-referenced (ego orientation, success means outperforming others). Following Nicholls, measures ask about the criteria that make someone feel successful. The TEOSQ (13 items, two dimensions) and POSQ treat the two orientations as independent rather than opposite. Ames's motivational climate concept describes the environment instead: a mastery climate stresses effort, cooperation and learning, while a performance climate stresses normative comparison, rivalry and punishment of mistakes. The Handbook reviews evidence that mastery climates relate to more self-determined motivation, that ego involvement with doubt about ability links to dropout and burnout, and that a Rasch analysis found TEOSQ task items poorly discriminating because almost everyone endorses them. For UX, orientation measures help segment users of learning, fitness and competitive products, and adapted climate measures show whether a product's design, through leaderboards, rankings, badges or feedback wording, is perceived as a mastery or a performance climate.
steps: Adapt orientation items to the product domain, keeping the 'I feel most successful when...' stem.
Write climate items describing what the product emphasises, for example 'This app rewards improving on my own past results' or 'This app makes me compare myself with others'.
Pilot and check factor structure and item discrimination.
Survey users and segment them by task and ego orientation scores.
Compare perceived climate across design variants or features such as leaderboards.
Relate orientation and climate to persistence, churn and satisfaction in product data.
outputs: Task and ego orientation scores per user, perceived mastery and performance climate scores per design, and their links with persistence.
useWhen: The product involves learning, practice or competition and you are deciding on social comparison features, feedback framing or progress displays.
avoidWhen: The product has no achievement element, or you cannot adapt and validate items for your context.
whyLost: Gamification practice borrowed points and leaderboards without the measurement tradition from education and sport that checks what climate they create.
whereToUse: Learning platforms, fitness and running apps, coding practice sites, language apps, competitive games, sales and performance dashboards.
example: A coding-practice platform surveys users after adding a global leaderboard. Ego-oriented users rate the climate as more motivating, while task-oriented beginners perceive a stronger performance climate and churn more; the team makes the leaderboard opt-in and adds personal-best tracking.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Roberts, G. C., Treasure, D. C. and Conroy, D. E. (2007) 'Understanding the dynamics of motivation in sport and physical activity: an achievement goal interpretation', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 1.

name: ACSI (American Customer Satisfaction Index)
origin: Claes Fornell, Ross School of Business, University of Michigan (1994)
summary: A national satisfaction index model linking expectations, perceived quality and value to satisfaction, loyalty and complaints, with a website survey version.
description: The ACSI publishes 0 to 100 satisfaction indexes for hundreds of companies, industries and government services. Its model treats customer expectations, perceived quality and perceived value as drivers of satisfaction, which in turn drives loyalty and complaints, estimated with structural modelling. For websites, a core survey of 14 to 20 ten-point questions covers quality and freshness of information, clarity of organisation, overall satisfaction and loyalty. Sauro and Lewis note there is little published psychometric data, but it is widely used for tracking, especially by US government sites, which makes it a common external benchmark.
steps: Use the ACSI website or e-government question set, usually through a licensed provider.
Survey site visitors with the core 10-point items plus custom questions.
Compute the satisfaction index and driver scores.
Compare with published ACSI scores for the sector.
Use driver impacts to prioritise improvements.
outputs: A satisfaction index comparable with published sector scores, plus driver estimates.
useWhen: Public-sector or large consumer sites that need comparison with published national benchmarks.
avoidWhen: Task-level diagnosis is needed, or the cost of a licensed provider is not justified.
whyLost: It lives in marketing and government reporting rather than UX research.
whereToUse: Government websites, utilities, retail and financial services.
example: A federal benefits site scores 68 against a 74 e-government average; the driver model points to search as the largest gap.
reference: Fornell, C. et al. (1996). The American Customer Satisfaction Index: Nature, purpose, and findings. Journal of Marketing 60(4).

name: ACT-R Cognitive Modelling
origin: John R. Anderson, Carnegie Mellon, 1993 onward; perceptual-motor extension by Michael Byrne (2001); CogTool by Bonnie John et al. (2004)
summary: Builds executable simulations of users from a validated cognitive architecture to predict task time, errors and learning on interface designs.
description: ACT-R is a cognitive architecture with modules for declarative memory, procedural rules, vision, motor and goals, each with parameters fitted across decades of experiments. Modelling a user means writing production rules for a task and running the model against a simulated interface; the architecture constrains timing, memory retrieval (with activation and decay), visual attention and motor movement. Predictions include task time distributions, memory errors and learning curves. CogTool made the approach accessible by generating ACT-R KLM-style models from storyboards. ACT-R is the most rigorous way to answer 'how will a skilled user perform on this design?' without testing, and to explain why.
steps: Specify the task, user expertise and interface precisely, including screen layouts and timings.
Use CogTool for keystroke-level prediction from storyboards, or write ACT-R productions for more complex cognition.
Set architecture parameters to defaults and avoid fitting free parameters to the data you will predict.
Run the model many times (e.g. 100+) to get time and error distributions.
Validate against a small sample of human data; aim for predictions within about 10-20% of observed means.
Use the model to compare design variants and inspect which modules (visual search, retrieval, motor) drive differences.
outputs: Predicted task time distributions, error and learning predictions, and module-level explanations of performance differences.
useWhen: Skilled, repetitive tasks where small time differences matter at scale, or where testing is expensive (safety-critical, specialised users).
avoidWhen: Novel creative tasks or attitudes and preferences; the architecture does not model motivation well.
whyLost: Modelling expertise is rare and slow to acquire; CogTool stopped being maintained, and product cycles favour A/B tests.
whereToUse: Call centre and back-office tools, in-vehicle interfaces, medical order entry, high-frequency trading screens.
example: An airline's check-in kiosk redesign is modelled in CogTool. The model predicts a 4-second saving per passenger from reordering fields; validation with 10 users confirms 3.5 seconds, worth thousands of agent hours annually.
sources: Anderson et al., An integrated theory of the mind (2004), Psychological Review
Byrne, ACT-R/PM and menu selection (2001), IJHCS
John et al., Predictive human performance modeling made easy (2004), CHI
reference: Anderson, J. R., et al. (2004). An integrated theory of the mind. Psychological Review, 111(4), 1036-1060.

name: Active Inference (Free Energy) Models
origin: Karl Friston, 2005-2010 onward; Active Inference textbook by Parr, Pezzulo and Friston (2022)
summary: Models users as agents minimising expected free energy, balancing goal-seeking (pragmatic value) with uncertainty-reducing exploration (epistemic value).
description: Active inference frames perception and action as minimising variational free energy, a bound on surprise under an internal generative model. Agents act to fulfil preferred observations and to reduce uncertainty, which naturally explains curiosity, information-seeking and exploration-exploitation trade-offs. Formally, models are partially observable Markov decision processes in which policies are scored by expected free energy, decomposed into epistemic and pragmatic value. For UX, it offers a single principled account of why users explore new interfaces, check status, seek confirmation and abandon when predictions fail. Applications remain experimental, but simulation studies can test whether a design reduces users' uncertainty where it matters.
steps: Specify the user's generative model: hidden states, observations the interface provides, and actions available.
Define preferences as prior beliefs about desired observations (e.g. task completed, no error message).
Implement the model with a discrete-state active inference toolkit (e.g. SPM DEM routines or pymdp).
Simulate behaviour under design variants, separating epistemic actions (checking, exploring) from pragmatic ones.
Compare simulated with observed behaviour, for example frequency of status-checking actions.
Use the model to identify where interfaces leave users uncertain and add observations that resolve it.
outputs: A generative model of the user, simulated policies, epistemic versus pragmatic action predictions and design implications.
useWhen: Research teams exploring theory-driven explanations of exploration, checking behaviour and uncertainty in interfaces.
avoidWhen: Applied product decisions on tight timelines; simpler usability or analytics methods answer most questions.
whyLost: The mathematics is demanding and the framework is young and contested; it has hardly been applied to HCI beyond a few papers.
whereToUse: Status and progress design, onboarding exploration, AI agents that communicate uncertainty, health self-monitoring apps.
example: A delivery app's users repeatedly refresh order status. An active inference simulation predicts this checking as epistemic action driven by uncertainty about arrival time; adding a confidence band to the ETA reduces refreshes in a field test.
sources: Friston, The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory? (2010), Nature Reviews Neuroscience
Parr, Pezzulo & Friston, Active Inference: The Free Energy Principle in Mind, Brain, and Behavior (2022)
reference: Parr, T., Pezzulo, G., & Friston, K. J. (2022). Active Inference. MIT Press.

name: Active Intervention
origin: Described by Joseph Dumas and Janice Redish, 1993 (revised 1999)
summary: A tester sits with the participant and probes their understanding at planned points during tasks, revealing how their mental model develops.
description: In active intervention a member of the test team sits in the room and deliberately probes the participant throughout the session rather than waiting for spontaneous think-aloud or a closing interview. Typical probes ask what the participant would do next and why, or, on choosing a menu option, how they understand the menu structure at that moment. Because probes recur across tasks, the method shows how the participant's mental model forms and changes, and gives diagnostic insight into the causes of problems. It is especially productive early in design and with prototypes. Its rigour depends on planning probe questions and points in advance and phrasing them neutrally. It deliberately trades away timing and independence: time-on-task and assistance counts are invalid.
steps: Define the test goals and the mental-model questions you need answered.
Plan probe questions and the points in each task where they will be asked.
Seat a test team member next to the participant and explain that questions will be asked during tasks.
Probe at the planned points (next step and why, current understanding of structure or terms), avoiding leading questions.
Record answers alongside behaviour, noting how explanations change across tasks.
Analyse answers for mental-model gaps and causes of problems.
outputs: Diagnostic data on users' evolving mental model and the causes of observed problems.
useWhen: Formative testing of early prototypes, new concepts or navigation structures where understanding why matters more than measuring performance.
avoidWhen: Summative or benchmark tests that need time on task, success rates or help-desk counts; use Think-Aloud Protocol or unprobed Moderated Usability Testing instead.
whyLost: It survives as ad hoc probing in moderated sessions, usually unplanned, and the original name and its explicit trade-offs are rarely cited.
whereToUse: Early concept tests, IA and navigation prototypes, complex B2B tools and AI features whose behaviour users must model.
example: Testing a new budgeting app prototype, the moderator asks after each categorisation step how the participant thinks categories and accounts relate. By task three, the answers reveal users believe categories are separate accounts.
sources: A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish, 1999)
reference: Dumas, J.S. and Redish, J.C. (1999) A Practical Guide to Usability Testing, revised edition. Exeter: Intellect.

name: Active Learning for Annotation
origin: Angluin (1988) on learning with queries; survey by Settles (2010)
summary: Let a model choose the unlabelled items it is least sure about, have people label those, retrain and repeat, so each costly label improves the model most.
description: Labelling data is expensive, and random samples waste effort on easy cases. In active learning a model trained on a small labelled set scores the unlabelled pool by how informative each item would be: uncertainty sampling picks items whose predicted class has the lowest probability or lie near the decision boundary; query-by-committee picks items on which models trained with different settings or data slices disagree; other heuristics estimate expected loss reduction. The chosen items go to annotators, labels are added and the model is retrained, repeating until performance is sufficient. Candidates can come from a stored pool or a live stream, which lets models adapt to changing data. Settles' toy example reached 90 per cent accuracy with 30 actively chosen labels against 70 per cent with 30 random ones. For UX research, it reduces the effort of coding large qualitative corpora with a classifier.
steps: Hand-label a small seed set and train an initial model.
Score unlabelled items by uncertainty, committee disagreement or expected loss reduction.
Send the highest-scoring items to annotators, with clear coding guidance.
Add the new labels and retrain the model.
Track performance on a fixed, randomly sampled validation set.
Repeat until performance plateaus or the labelling budget is spent.
outputs: A smaller, more informative labelled set and a trained classifier, with a learning curve against labelling effort.
useWhen: Coding large volumes of feedback, support tickets, reviews or interaction logs with a classifier when labelling budget or expert time is limited.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the codebook is still emerging; settle categories qualitatively first. Actively chosen sets are biased towards hard cases, so do not use them to estimate prevalence; for that use random samples and Ground-truth labelling from qualitative review.
whyLost: It is routine in machine-learning operations but UX researchers seldom build classifiers, so qualitative coding at scale is done by hand or with generic topic models.
whereToUse: App-store and NPS comment coding, support ticket triage, content moderation queues, intent labelling for conversational AI.
example: A research team needs 40,000 support tickets classified into 12 friction categories. After 300 seed labels, three rounds of uncertainty sampling of 200 tickets each lift classifier F1 from 0.61 to 0.82, far beyond what 900 random labels achieved.
reference: Settles, B. (2010). Active Learning Literature Survey. Computer Sciences Technical Report 1648, University of Wisconsin-Madison; Huyen, C. (2022). Designing Machine Learning Systems. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly, pp. 101-102.

name: Active UX Surveillance
origin: Active surveillance and population health surveys; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Periodically assesses representative user populations with standard task batteries, exposure measures and harm reports to estimate UX harm missed by logs.
description: Active surveillance collects data specifically for monitoring, through surveys, structured observations and periodic studies of representative samples, and captures conditions passive systems miss: behavioural risk factors and diffuse harms not tied to clinical records. The treatise proposes active UX surveillance: periodic structured assessment of representative populations, measuring failure rates on standard task batteries, exposure to specific patterns and reported harms. It argues this is expensive but no more so than routine national health surveys. Representative sampling, standardised instruments and repeated waves allow prevalence estimates, trends and demographic distributions comparable across products and over time.
steps: Define the population and draw a representative sample (probability panel or weighted quota).
Develop a standard task battery and validated harm and exposure questionnaires.
Administer in waves (for example annually) with consistent protocols.
Weight data to the population and estimate prevalence with CIs.
Analyse distribution by demographics and trends over time.
Publish findings and feed into interventions and regulation.
outputs: Population prevalence estimates, trend series, demographic distributions, benchmark task performance.
useWhen: Measuring harms spanning many products, cross-industry benchmarking, regulatory monitoring.
avoidWhen: Single-product questions answerable with that product's logs.
whyLost: No institution owns cross-product UX health; UX research is funded per product.
whereToUse: Regulators, consumer groups, national digital service agencies, industry consortia.
example: An annual panel of 5,000 adults attempts standard tasks (cancel a subscription, change consent) on top apps; cancellation failure prevalence falls from 22% to 11% after new rules.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) methodology
Groves RM et al. (2009) Survey Methodology. 2nd ed
reference: Groves RM et al. (2009) Survey Methodology. 2nd ed. Wiley.

name: Active-User Definition and DAU/MAU Stickiness
aka: Active-user definition and DAU/MAU stickiness ratio
origin: Consumer software and social media analytics practice; procedure described by Christian Crumlish (2022)
summary: Define 'active' by a basket of meaningful events rather than presence, add a stricter engaged tier, and track DAU, WAU, MAU and their ratios as stickiness.
description: Analytics tools often count anyone who appears on a day as active, which inflates activity with people who bounce or are churning. The rigorous version defines a basket of qualifying events, so a user is active in a period only if they trigger at least one, and optionally a smaller, stricter basket for engaged users. Periods are chosen to match the product's natural cadence. A user active on four days of one week counts four times in DAU, once in WAU and once in MAU. DAU/MAU then shows the average share of days a monthly user is active: 20% is about six days a month. Crumlish cites a rule of thumb of about 40% as good and above 50% as excellent, varying by industry. The engaged-to-active ratio identifies casual users who could become participants.
steps: Choose the period that matches the product's natural usage cadence (daily, weekly or monthly).
Define a basket of events that count as meaningful activity, excluding mere sessions or page views; a user is active if they trigger any of them.
Optionally define a stricter engaged-user basket and track engaged users separately from active users.
Compute DAU, WAU and MAU, then ratios such as DAU/MAU, read as the share of days in a month a typical user is active.
Compare engaged with active users to size the pool of casual users who could be converted.
Track the ratios over time and check them against retention curves and qualitative research before calling growth real.
outputs: Active and engaged user counts per period, DAU/WAU/MAU and stickiness ratios, and trends over time.
useWhen: Defining a product's core engagement metric, judging whether growth is real, and comparing stickiness across features, segments or releases.
avoidWhen: Avoid DAU/MAU for products with naturally infrequent use (tax, travel booking), where WAU or MAU and retention are better; do not use presence-based counts as success metrics. For a full metric system use the HEART Framework or startup metric frameworks.
whyLost: The acronyms are ubiquitous, but the careful definition of qualifying events is often skipped, leaving presence counts that work as vanity metrics.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, SaaS products, communities, AI assistants and any subscription product reporting engagement to leadership.
example: A note-taking app's DAU/MAU is 35% when any app open counts, but 14% when only creating or editing a note counts. The team adopts the stricter basket and finds that most 'active' users only open shared links.
reference: Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People: From Designing to Thriving in a Product World. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media, pp. 98-99.

name: Activity Score (Media-by-Time Coordination Chart)
origin: Edwin Hutchins (1995), from fieldwork aboard US Navy ships in the 1980s
summary: A chart with representational media as rows and time as columns showing when each medium is in coordination during a team task, revealing parallel work, interference and delays.
description: Hutchins devised the activity score to show how a navigation team computes a ship's position across people and artefacts. Representational media are listed as rows, ordered from sensors at the bottom to higher-level media such as the chart at the top; time runs along the columns in small fixed intervals (two seconds in his example); and each interval is shaded when that medium is in coordination with another, with one fill pattern per item being processed. Read like a musical score, it shows parallel activity across team members, why overlapping speech causes no interference when different media are involved, how a rushed signal propagated a delay, and how small functional systems join into larger ones. It is a notation within Distributed Cognition Analysis, built from synchronised recordings rather than interviews.
steps: Record a complete task cycle with synchronised video and audio, plus field notes for off-camera events.
List the representational media involved (screens, documents, spoken channels, sensors), ordered from raw inputs to higher-level representations.
Divide time into small fixed intervals suited to the task pace (for example two seconds).
Shade each interval in which a medium is in coordination with another, using one pattern per item being processed.
Read the chart for parallelism, interference, delays, bottlenecks and hand-offs.
Compare charts across cycles or designs to see where a new tool changes coordination.
outputs: A score-like timeline of coordination events per medium for each task cycle.
useWhen: Analysing fast team work across several tools and channels, such as incident response or clinical handover, where the problem lies in coordination timing rather than any single interface.
avoidWhen: Avoid for individual, single-tool tasks; use the Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) or Hierarchical Task Analysis. Without synchronised recordings the chart cannot be built reliably.
whyLost: Distributed cognition is cited widely in HCI, but its charting notations are rarely used because they require detailed recording and coding.
whereToUse: Incident response and on-call tooling, operating theatres and emergency departments, live broadcast and esports production, collaborative design tools.
example: An emergency dispatch centre records ten calls. The activity score shows the call-taker's CAD entry and radio channel never overlap, so units are dispatched only after typing ends, which supports a design that pushes partial location data to the radio operator.
reference: Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, pp. 186-195.

name: Activity Theory Analysis
origin: Lev Vygotsky (1930s), Alexei Leont'ev (1978); Yrjö Engeström's activity system model, 1987; brought to HCI by Bødker, Kuutti and Nardi in the 1990s
summary: Analysing work as a mediated activity system and its activity-action-operation levels, using contradictions between elements as drivers of breakdown and design opportunity.
description: Activity theory analyses human activity as purposeful and mediated by tools within a social context. Leont'ev's hierarchy distinguishes activity (motive-driven, such as patient care), action (conscious goal-directed steps, such as entering a medication record) and operation (automated routines like typing that break when conditions change). Engeström's activity system extends the unit of analysis to subject, object, tools, rules, community and division of labour. Contradictions between these elements, for example a tool designed for billing used within a care activity, show up as frustration, workarounds and non-standard behaviour, and are treated as sources of change. The framework helps explain why technically usable systems fail in practice.
steps: Define the activity under study and its object (the motive the activity serves), drawing on fieldwork data.
Map the activity system: subject, object, mediating tools, rules, community, division of labour and outcome.
Classify observed behaviour into activity, action and operation levels, noting where operations break down into conscious actions.
Identify contradictions within and between system elements, evidenced by frustration, workarounds or rule-breaking.
Trace each contradiction historically: how did the tool, rule or role come to conflict with the object?
Translate priority contradictions into design opportunities and test them with participants.
outputs: Activity system diagrams, level analyses, a catalogue of evidenced contradictions, and design opportunities linked to them.
useWhen: Organisational or professional settings where tools are embedded in complex social practice and adoption fails despite adequate usability.
avoidWhen: Narrow interface optimisation questions; use usability testing or task analysis.
whyLost: Its vocabulary is dense and was eclipsed in HCI by more lightweight frameworks, leaving it in Scandinavian HCI, education and CSCW research.
whereToUse: Clinical information systems, education technology, public sector digital transformation, and enterprise tool rollouts.
example: Teachers resist a grading platform that is fast to use. Activity analysis shows a contradiction between the tool's numeric rubrics and the school's object of formative feedback, leading to narrative feedback fields.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nardi BA (Ed) (1996) Context and Consciousness: Activity Theory and Human-Computer Interaction
Kaptelinin V & Nardi BA (2006) Acting with Technology: Activity Theory and Interaction Design
reference: Engeström, Y. (1987). Learning by Expanding: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Developmental Research. Orienta-Konsultit.

extra.The Three Levels: Activity: The motive-level of behaviour — why is this person doing anything at all? What is the broader social and personal objective? (A nurse enters patient data because her activity is patient care, not data entry.) Action: Goal-directed behaviour — what specific goal is the person pursuing right now? Actions are conscious and deliberate. (Entering a specific patient's medication record.) Operation: Automatised behavior that was once an action but has become unconscious through practice. (Touch-typing, mouse movement.) Operations fail when conditions change unexpectedly.
extra.Contradiction Analysis: Contradictions are the engine of change in activity systems. They arise when one component of the system (tool, subject, rules, community, division of labor, object, outcome) conflicts with another. The most common UX contradiction: a tool designed for one activity is used in the context of a different activity. Identify contradictions by: observing where participants express frustration, develop workarounds, or engage in non-standard behavior. Each contradiction is a design opportunity.

name: Actor-Network Theory Tracing
origin: Michel Callon, Bruno Latour and John Law, 1980s (Callon's scallops study, 1986; Latour, Reassembling the Social, 2005)
summary: Follows how human and non-human actors (people, devices, documents, algorithms) are enrolled into networks that make a technology work or fail, without assuming a priori who acts.
description: ANT treats humans and non-humans symmetrically as actants that mediate action. Researchers 'follow the actors', tracing associations and the work of translation by which actors are enrolled: problematisation, interessement, enrolment and mobilisation (Callon). Stable networks become black boxes; controversies reveal how they are assembled. For UX, ANT is useful when products only work because many elements align (regulations, data standards, partner apps, informal intermediaries, devices) and when failures arise because a non-human actor (a PDF form, an API, a fax machine) quietly holds a network together. It shifts analysis from user-interface to socio-material assemblage.
steps: Choose a controversy, failure or innovation where the network is visible.
Follow actors through observation, documents and interviews, recording all human and non-human participants.
Map associations and translations: who or what enrols whom, through what devices and inscriptions.
Identify obligatory passage points and black boxes that hold the network together.
Analyse where translations fail or betrayals occur, causing the network to destabilise.
Derive design and strategy implications for enrolling or re-arranging actors.
outputs: Actor-network maps, accounts of translation and failure points, and strategic implications.
useWhen: Adoption or failure of products embedded in complex socio-technical ecosystems, platform strategies and infrastructures.
avoidWhen: Narrow usability questions where interface-level analysis suffices.
whyLost: ANT is known in STS and some CSCW work, but its theoretical vocabulary and lack of a step-by-step protocol limit practitioner use.
whereToUse: Health information exchange, open banking, smart city deployments, AI in professional workflows, B2B platforms.
example: An e-prescribing rollout stalls. ANT tracing reveals the paper prescription pad was an obligatory passage point for pharmacy reimbursement; the network re-stabilises only after the insurer accepts digital records.
sources: Latour, Reassembling the Social: An Introduction to Actor-Network-Theory (2005)
Callon, Some elements of a sociology of translation (1986), in Law (ed.), Power, Action and Belief
Law, After Method: Mess in Social Science Research (2004)
reference: Latour, B. (2005). Reassembling the Social. Oxford University Press.

name: Actuarial versus clinical prediction
donor: Clinical psychology; judgement and decision making
origin: Sarbin (1940s); Meehl (1954); Goldberg (1965); Dawes and Corrigan (1974); Dawes, Faust and Meehl (1989)
summary: Compare expert holistic judgement with a simple statistical rule built on the same cues, including equal-weight rules, and adopt whichever predicts outcomes more accurately.
description: In clinical prediction a judge combines information in their head; in actuarial prediction a rule combines it mechanically. Across about a hundred comparative studies the rule equalled or beat experts, and a meta-analysis of 136 comparisons found it at least as good in all but eight. Goldberg's simple MMPI rule was 70 per cent correct on 861 new cases, beating all 29 judges, and thousands of practice judgements with feedback did not close the gap. Dawes showed that improper linear models, with equal or even random positive weights on expert-chosen variables, matched or beat judges and fitted regressions and transferred better across settings. The expert's value lies in choosing variables, not combining them. Rules must be cross-validated, monitored and revalidated in each new setting.
steps: Define the decision, the criterion outcome and a set of past cases with known outcomes.
Elicit from experts the cues they consider relevant.
Collect experts' holistic predictions for a sample of cases.
Build a simple rule on the same cues: a fitted regression, an equal-weight sum of standardised cues, or a tally.
Cross-validate the rule on fresh cases not used to build it.
Compare rule and expert accuracy on the same cases.
Deploy the better approach and monitor accuracy, revalidating whenever the setting or population changes.
outputs: A validated decision rule, an accuracy comparison between rule and experts, and a list of cues that matter.
useWhen: Teams repeatedly make the same kind of judgement from the same information, such as triaging research findings, scoring leads, prioritising support tickets or screening participants.
avoidWhen: Avoid when outcomes are never observed or cases are unique, since a rule cannot be validated; use structured expert judgement such as the Delphi method. Rules are local and fallible and must not be transferred blindly.
whyLost: It is a classic of clinical and decision psychology but UX teams seldom track outcomes of their own judgements, so the comparison is never run.
whereToUse: Feature prioritisation and opportunity scoring, research participant screening, churn-risk flags for customer success, content moderation triage and evaluating whether AI recommendations beat expert intuition.
example: A SaaS customer-success team predicts churn by gut feel at quarterly reviews. An equal-weight score of five cues the managers named (logins, seats used, tickets, champion departure, contract age) predicts the next quarter's churn better than the managers did, and becomes the triage list.
reference: Dawes, R. M., Faust, D. & Meehl, P. E. (1989). Clinical versus actuarial judgment. Science 243, 1668-1674; Dawes, R. M. (1979). The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making. American Psychologist 34, 571-582.

name: Adapting Sessions for Participants with Cognitive Disabilities
origin: Compiled by Lazar, Feng and Hochheiser (2017) from Kumin et al. (2012), Yaneva et al. (2015), Morris et al. (2015) and others
summary: Adjust accounts, passwords, scales, environment, pacing and tasks so people with cognitive disabilities can take part meaningfully in research sessions.
description: Standard usability protocols can exclude people with cognitive disabilities or produce misleading data. Studies with people with Down syndrome, autism, aphasia and other conditions show a set of practical adaptations. Use real accounts and data, since participants may refuse to work in someone else's account; ask for passwords to be brought on paper; give printed confirmations; replace numeric scales with a visual Likert scale to point to; reduce sensory distractions such as bright lights, noise, smells and notifications; allow breaks, reminders and extra time; follow specialist advice for the specific condition (for example avoiding items on the far right of questionnaires for some people with aphasia); allow slight task changes when participants object to unrealistic scenarios, recording them; and plan for augmentative and alternative communication or written responses. Focusing each study on one specific disability improves validity.
steps: Focus the study on one specific cognitive disability and consult specialists or advocates in it.
Arrange real accounts and data, ask participants to bring passwords on paper, and provide printed confirmations.
Prepare a visual Likert scale and simplified layouts for any questionnaires.
Control the sensory environment: lighting, noise, smells and device notifications.
Schedule breaks, reminders and extra time in the session plan.
Allow minor task modifications when participants object to realism, and record each change.
Plan alternative communication channels such as AAC devices or written responses.
outputs: Valid participation and data from people with cognitive disabilities, with documented adaptations.
useWhen: Usability and interview studies that include people with intellectual disability, autism, aphasia, dementia or acquired brain injury.
avoidWhen: Avoid generic 'accessibility' adaptations across mixed disabilities; tailor to the condition. Where capacity to consent is in doubt, add consent-capacity assessment first.
whyLost: It sits in accessibility research; mainstream UX recruiting still rarely includes people with cognitive disabilities.
whereToUse: Public services, banking, health portals, workplace tools and any product claiming inclusive design.
example: A bank tests its mobile app with adults with Down syndrome using their own accounts, a pictorial satisfaction scale and a quiet room. Participants complete tasks they had refused in a pilot that used demo accounts.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. and Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 511-513.

name: Adaptive Choice-Based Conjoint (ACBC)
origin: Developed by Sawtooth Software (Johnson and Orme, 2007; released 2009)
summary: A conjoint survey that adapts to each respondent: they configure their ideal product, rule out unacceptable options, then make choices among tailored alternatives.
description: Standard choice-based conjoint shows everyone the same kind of randomised product profiles, many of which a given person would never consider. ACBC runs in three stages. In a build-your-own section the respondent picks their preferred level of each attribute. A screening section then shows near-variations of that product and asks whether each is a possibility, which reveals must-have and unacceptable levels. Finally a choice tournament asks them to pick between the products that survived screening. Because every task is close to what the respondent actually wants, the data is more engaging and gives better predictions with fewer respondents, and it captures non-compensatory rules ('anything without offline mode is out') that ordinary conjoint models struggle with. The cost is a longer survey and specialist software for design and estimation.
steps: Define attributes and levels from qualitative research, keeping them concrete and mutually exclusive.
Set up the build-your-own, screening and choice tournament sections in ACBC-capable software.
Pilot with a few respondents to check length (often 15 to 20 minutes) and comprehension.
Field to the target sample, typically 150 to 300 per segment.
Estimate part-worth utilities, usually with hierarchical Bayes, and identify must-haves and unacceptables.
Run market or tier simulations to compare candidate products, bundles or prices.
outputs: Part-worth utilities per respondent, lists of must-have and unacceptable features, and a simulator for product and pricing scenarios.
useWhen: High-stakes product, tier or pricing decisions with many attributes, especially where some features are deal-breakers.
avoidWhen: Flat lists of features with no attribute structure (use MaxDiff), early discovery, or teams without access to conjoint software.
whyLost: ACBC lives in commercial market research tools. UX teams that use conjoint usually stop at standard CBC, and many do not know the adaptive version exists.
whereToUse: Subscription tier design, hardware configuration, SaaS packaging and pricing, B2B feature bundles.
example: For a project-management tool, ACBC shows that single sign-on is a must-have for 70% of enterprise respondents, so it moves from the top tier to every business plan.
sources: Orme, B., Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (2014)
reference: Johnson, R. M., & Orme, B. K. (2007). A new approach to adaptive CBC. Sawtooth Software Conference Proceedings. Orme, B. (2014). Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (3rd ed.). Research Publishers.

name: Additive Similarity Tree Analysis (ADDTREE)
origin: Sattath and Tversky (1977)
summary: Fit a tree to pairwise similarity data in which item distance equals path length, revealing distinct groups and items typical of many others.
description: Unlike hierarchical clustering, which forces all items to the same depth (an ultrametric), an additive tree lets branch lengths vary, so distance between two items is the length of the path joining them. Long internal branches show distinct clusters; short leaf branches mark items close to many others. Sattath and Tversky build the tree from quadruples: for every four items they find which pairs are neighbours, merge the pair that wins most often, and repeat, then estimate arc lengths by least squares. On animals, letters and an occupation sort by 154 people, trees matched or beat two- and three-dimensional spatial solutions on fit and were easier to read; structure survived noise of a third of each distance. Skewness of the distances helps choose between a tree and a spatial map, and where the root is placed is an interpretive choice.
steps: Collect a symmetric proximity matrix: similarity ratings, card-sort co-occurrence counts or confusion data.
Check whether the data look tree-like or space-like using the skewness of distances (tree distances bunch at the top of the range, spatial distances at the bottom).
Fit the additive tree, estimate arc lengths and set negative arcs to zero.
Report stress and the correlation with the data, and compare with hierarchical clustering and a two-dimensional map.
Try more than one root and label clusters only where other evidence supports the grouping.
outputs: An additive tree with arc lengths, fit statistics and a comparison with ultrametric and spatial solutions.
useWhen: Analysing open card sorts or similarity judgements where some items belong loosely to several groups, or when dendrograms hide how distinct clusters really are.
avoidWhen: Data are clearly dimensional (for example perceived price and quality); use a spatial map. Software support is thinner than for hierarchical clustering, and labels depend on rooting.
whyLost: Hierarchical clustering became the default in card-sort tools, and additive trees remained in mathematical psychology.
whereToUse: Information architecture, content taxonomies, product catalogue structure, concept similarity studies.
example: An open card sort of 40 help articles shows 'billing' as a tight branch with a long stem, while 'account settings' sits on a short leaf near many groups and becomes a candidate for cross-linking.
reference: Sattath, S., & Tversky, A. (1977). Additive similarity trees. Psychometrika, 42(3), 319-345.

name: Adjusted-Wald Confidence Interval for Completion Rates
origin: Agresti & Coull (1998); recommended for small-sample usability data by Sauro & Lewis (2005)
summary: A confidence interval for a task success rate that stays accurate with the tiny samples typical of usability tests.
description: Completion rates from usability tests are binomial proportions measured on 5 to 20 people. The textbook Wald interval (p plus or minus z times the standard error) collapses at these sizes: it can run below 0% or above 100% and covers the true rate far less often than its nominal 95%. The adjusted-Wald interval fixes this by adding z²/2 successes and z² trials (about two successes and four attempts at 95%) before computing the interval. Sauro and Lewis showed it has the best average coverage of the common options for usability data, beating the exact Clopper-Pearson interval, which is too conservative. It turns "4 of 5 users succeeded" into an honest statement such as "between 36% and 98% of all users would likely succeed".
steps: Count successes x and attempts n for the task, using a pre-agreed success rule.
Choose the confidence level (90% is common for formative work, 95% for summative claims) and look up z.
Compute the adjusted proportion p_adj = (x + z²/2) / (n + z²).
Compute the margin z × sqrt(p_adj(1 − p_adj) / (n + z²)) and form p_adj ± margin, truncating at 0 and 100%.
Report the observed rate, the interval and n together, and plot intervals as error bars when comparing tasks.
outputs: A completion rate with a defensible lower and upper bound for the whole user population.
useWhen: Reporting any success, conversion or agreement proportion from a sample under about 100, especially formative tests with 5 to 15 users.
avoidWhen: Very large analytics samples, where any interval method gives the same answer, or when you need a one-sided test against a goal (use a binomial test against the benchmark).
whyLost: UX inherited the habit of reporting raw percentages from small tests and either skipped intervals entirely or used the Wald interval from introductory statistics, which fails at small n. The fix is a two-line formula, but it lives mainly in quantitative UX books.
whereToUse: Any usability test report, unmoderated task studies, tree tests and first-click tests where success rates drive decisions.
example: Seven of eight participants complete a new checkout. The adjusted-Wald 95% interval is roughly 52% to 99%, so the team can say most users will succeed but cannot yet claim the 95% target was met.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
Predicting User Behavior: The Must-Know Distributions for UX & HF Researchers (carousel, n.d.)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2005). Estimating completion rates from small samples using binomial confidence intervals. Proceedings of HFES 49.

name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect Measurement
origin: Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura (1995); replicated by Noam Tractinsky (1997, 2000)
summary: Measures how much visual appeal inflates perceived usability by separating aesthetic ratings from objective performance, controlling for aesthetics as a confound in evaluations.
