description: The aesthetic-usability effect is the finding that people rate attractive interfaces as easier to use, even when objective performance is equal or worse. Kurosu and Kashimura found apparent usability correlated more with aesthetics than with inherent usability, and Tractinsky replicated the effect across cultures and found it persisted after use. For research this is a confound: polished prototypes can mask usability problems in satisfaction scores, and comparisons between a polished and a rough variant are biased. Measurement involves collecting aesthetic ratings, subjective usability (for example SUS) and objective performance (success, time, errors) for the same interface, then estimating how much aesthetics predicts perceived usability after controlling for performance. Controlled studies vary visual polish while holding interaction constant.
steps: Two-condition study: same functional design with aesthetic enhancement (improved visual design) vs. baseline.
Before usability testing, collect aesthetic rating.
After testing, collect perceived usability.
Compare: does aesthetic rating predict perceived usability beyond actual performance?
Measure: aesthetic rating × task performance correlation.
Large positive correlation = halo effect present.
Partial out aesthetics from perceived usability measures.
outputs: Correlations or regression estimates of aesthetics on perceived usability controlling for performance, gap between perceived and objective usability, and fidelity-matching guidance.
useWhen: Comparing designs of differing visual fidelity, interpreting satisfaction scores, testing visual redesigns, and studies of emotional design.
avoidWhen: When you only measure objective performance and do not rely on subjective ratings; then the confound does not affect conclusions.
whyLost: The effect is widely cited as a design principle but seldom measured; most teams treat subjective ratings at face value and do not control for visual fidelity.
whereToUse: UX evaluation design (control for aesthetics), A/B testing interpretation (aesthetic changes confound usability changes), design ROI research.
example: A SaaS team finds its redesigned dashboard scores 12 points higher on SUS but task completion is unchanged. Regressing SUS on aesthetic ratings and performance shows the gain is almost entirely visual appeal, so usability work continues.
sources: Universal Principles of Design — William Lidwell
Tractinsky, Katz & Ikar, What is beautiful is usable (Interacting with Computers, 2000)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 36 — Emotional Design Hierarchies & the Aesthetic-Usability Effect
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Kurosu M & Kashimura K (1995) Apparent usability vs. inherent usability: Experimental analysis on the determinants of the apparent usability. CHI 1995 Conference Companion

name: Affective imagery word-association elicitation
donor: Judgement and decision making; social psychology
origin: Slovic et al. (1991), Decision Research; developed further in work on the affect heuristic (Slovic, Finucane, Peters and MacGregor, 2002)
summary: Collect the first images a stimulus word evokes, have respondents rate each image's valence, and sum the ratings into an affect index that predicts preference and behaviour.
description: Self-reports of future behaviour are often unreliable, so this method measures the feeling attached to a concept indirectly. Respondents see a target word or short phrase and write the first thought or image that comes to mind, repeated three to six times or until none come. They then rate each image from very positive (+2) to very negative (-2), and ratings are summed or averaged into an affect index for the stimulus. The index has predicted preferences for cities and states as places to visit or live, support for technologies, investment in new companies and adolescents' smoking and exercise. Unlike open projective techniques, it yields a number per stimulus that can be compared and correlated with choices, while the images themselves can be content-analysed for meaning.
steps: Choose target words or short phrases, such as brand names, product categories or feature concepts.
For each, ask for the first thought or image that comes to mind; repeat three to six times or until no more come.
Have respondents rate each of their images from +2 (very positive) to -2 (very negative).
Sum or average the ratings per stimulus to form the affect index.
Compare indices across stimuli and segments, and test whether they predict stated or observed choices.
Optionally content-analyse the images to explain what drives positive or negative affect.
outputs: Image lists per stimulus, an affect index per stimulus and respondent, and themes from content analysis.
useWhen: You need a quick, indirect measure of the feelings attached to brands, concepts or technologies, especially to predict preference or adoption.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need detailed reasons or usability evidence; use interviews or testing. Indices depend on the stimulus wording, and images can be shaped by recent news.
whyLost: It is established in risk perception and decision research but was never packaged for UX, where brand and concept testing rely on rating scales.
whereToUse: Concept and naming tests, brand perception, emerging technology adoption such as AI features or biometrics, and health behaviour products.
example: A bank tests names for a new AI assistant. Image associations for one name include 'robot', 'cold' and 'spying', giving a negative index, while another evokes 'helpful' and 'friend'; the second predicts higher stated willingness to try the assistant.
reference: Slovic, P., Finucane, M., Peters, E. & MacGregor, D. G. (2002). The affect heuristic. In Gilovich, T., Griffin, D. & Kahneman, D. (eds) Heuristics and Biases: The Psychology of Intuitive Judgment. Cambridge University Press.

name: Affective State Induction in User Testing
aka: Induced frustration with rigged system delays
Functional user state induction in usability testing
donor: Affective computing; Russian applied and occupational psychology
origin: Scheirer, Fernandez, Klein and Picard (2002), MIT Media Lab; functional states theory (A. B. Leonova) applied by Yakunin and Bodrunova (2022)
summary: Deliberately induce frustration, anxiety or monotony with rigged delays, goal changes or repetitive tasks, and measure physiological and self-rated responses at known moments.
description: Instead of waiting for emotions to occur, the researcher engineers them at logged moments. In the MIT frustration paradigm, participants play a timed, incentivised puzzle game under a cover story while the software randomly becomes unresponsive; synchronised skin conductance and blood-volume pressure are labelled by episode to train models distinguishing frustrated from non-frustrated states. The functional states variant induces anxiety (a ten-minute search task whose goal changes after three minutes, with time cut to five and then two minutes) or monotony (copying a whole website 'within an hour', stopped unannounced at 35 minutes). Attention-switching lability (Gorbov-Schulte table) and four 1-10 self-ratings (calm-anxious, energetic-fatigued, excited-depressed, confident-helpless) are taken before and after. Crossing these with product aesthetics and individual versus group testing shows how test conditions themselves distort usability results. Deception requires ethical approval and full debriefing.
steps: Choose the state to induce (frustration, anxiety, monotony) and the measures: physiological sensors, attention-switching tests or self-rating scales.
Obtain ethical approval for deception, and prepare a plausible cover story.
Take baseline measures before the task.

Run the induction: random logged unresponsive episodes under time pressure and an incentive; or goal changes with time cuts (10 to 5 to 2 minutes); or a long repetitive task with an unannounced stop at about 35 minutes.
Record synchronised physiological data or repeat the attention and self-rating measures after the task.
Debrief every participant on the deception and offer to withdraw their data.
Compare pre-post changes across conditions (for example design variants by individual or group testing), or train classifiers on episode-labelled data.
outputs: Episode-labelled physiological data and affect classifiers; pre-post changes in attention lability and self-rated state per condition; evidence of test-condition distortion.
useWhen: You need ground-truth emotional episodes to validate affect sensing, or want to know how a design holds up under stress, time pressure or fatigue.
avoidWhen: You cannot obtain ethics approval for deception, or participants are vulnerable; use naturally occurring frustration in field logs or retrospective emotion ratings instead. Small cells (eight per group) limit conclusions.
whyLost: Deception, ethics overhead and sensor set-up keep it in affective computing labs, while usability testing aims to make sessions comfortable rather than stressful.
whereToUse: Affect-aware and adaptive interfaces, safety-critical and time-pressured workflows, customer support tools, and validating emotion-detection models.
example: A trading platform team times traders on order entry while injecting logged two-second freezes. Skin conductance spikes and self-rated anxiety are far higher with the dense layout, supporting a calmer default for volatile markets.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Scheirer, J., Fernandez, R., Klein, J., & Picard, R. W. (2002). Frustrating the user on purpose: A step toward building an affective computer. Interacting with Computers, 14(2), 93-118.

name: Affective State Measurement
origin: Rosalind Picard, 1997; James Russell, 1980
summary: Measures users' emotional states during interaction by combining self-report on valence and arousal with physiological and behavioural signals such as skin conductance and facial expression.
description: Grounded in Picard's affective computing and Russell's circumplex model, which locates emotions on dimensions of valence (pleasant to unpleasant) and arousal (calm to activated), this method measures emotional responses during interaction. It triangulates three channels: self-report (e.g. Self-Assessment Manikin or moment-by-moment ratings), physiological signals (electrodermal activity, heart rate variability) and expressive behaviour (facial expression, voice). Signals are time-aligned with interaction logs so peaks can be attributed to specific events. Rigour requires baselines per participant, artefact handling, awareness that physiological arousal does not indicate valence alone, validation of automated classifiers against human coding, and careful ethics given the intimacy of emotional data.
steps: Multi-channel affect measurement protocol:
Physiological: EDA (electrodermal activity) = arousal level. HRV = cognitive load and stress.
(2) Facial: FACs (facial action coding system) or automated tools (Affectiva, Microsoft FER).
(3) Voice: pitch, rate, and energy features from audio.

(4) Self-report: SAM (Self-Assessment Manikin — valence and arousal). Triangulate: agreement across channels = high confidence. Disagreement = the most interesting data (which channel is wrong, and why?).
outputs: Time-aligned valence and arousal traces, emotional peaks linked to interface events, triangulated self-report and sensor data.
useWhen: Experiences where emotion is central or risky: games, health, finance stress, onboarding anxiety, error recovery and AI interactions.
avoidWhen: Avoid when inferences from sensors cannot be validated, when consent and privacy cannot be assured, or when simple post-task ratings will do; use SAM or interviews instead.
whyLost: Sensors, signal processing and validity problems kept affective computing in labs; UX settled for satisfaction ratings.
whereToUse: Emotion-informed UX design, accessibility for emotional expression, health and wellbeing product research, affective gaming UX.
example: A loan application flow is tested with 20 participants wearing skin-conductance sensors; arousal spikes cluster at the credit check consent step, and adding a plain-language explanation reduces spikes and abandonment.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Picard RW (1997) Affective Computing. MIT Press

name: Affective state taxonomy
origin: Rosalind Picard, Affective Computing (1997); dimensional models from Russell's circumplex (1980) and Mehrabian and Russell's PAD model (1974); learning-centred states from D'Mello and Graesser (2012)
summary: Defines the set of affective states that matter in a product context, with dimensional coordinates and observable indicators, so emotion can be measured consistently across channels.
description: Emotion measurement fails when teams do not define what they are measuring. Basic emotion categories such as anger, fear and joy rarely occur during product use; states such as confusion, frustration, boredom, engagement, anxiety and relief are far more frequent, as D'Mello and Graesser showed in learning technologies. An affective state taxonomy specifies the states relevant to the domain, locates each on dimensions such as valence and arousal (and sometimes dominance), and defines the indicators expected in each channel: self-report wording, facial action units, physiological markers and behavioural signals. It also defines which states are desirable, which are acceptable and which are failure signals. Rigour comes from grounding the taxonomy in observation of the domain, operational definitions, and checking inter-rater agreement when coding states.
steps: Collect candidate states from domain observation, interviews and literature, aiming for 6 to 12 states relevant to the product (for example confusion, frustration, anxiety, relief, confidence, boredom).
Define each state operationally, and place it on valence and arousal dimensions (and dominance if control matters, as in financial decisions).

For each state, specify expected indicators per channel: self-report items, facial cues, physiological signals such as heart rate variability or electrodermal activity, and behaviours such as hesitation or rage clicks.
Classify states as target, acceptable or failure states for each journey stage, for example anxiety acceptable at loan submission but a failure state after approval.
Pilot the taxonomy by having 2 coders label 30 to 50 video segments, aiming for Cohen's kappa of 0.60 or above, and refine definitions.
Use the taxonomy to structure multi-channel affective studies and to report results consistently over time.
outputs: A defined set of affective states with dimensional coordinates, channel-specific indicators, journey-stage targets, and coder agreement statistics.
useWhen: Planning emotion measurement, comparing affective data across studies, or designing emotionally sensitive flows such as finance, health or education.
avoidWhen: You only need a single satisfaction rating, or affect is not relevant to the decision; avoid inventing taxonomies without domain observation.
whyLost: It is standard in affective computing and learning sciences research, but UX emotion work often jumps to tools such as facial coding without defining the states that matter.
whereToUse: Loan and insurance applications, health diagnostics, learning platforms, customer support, AI assistant interactions, games.
example: Before a study of a high-stakes loan application, the team defined 8 states, including anxiety, confusion, relief and distrust, with indicators across facial, heart rate variability and verbal channels. Coders reached kappa 0.71, and relief at approval became a target state to design for.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 37 — Picard's Affective Framework — Multi-Channel Emotion Measurement
reference: Picard, R. W. (1997). Affective Computing. MIT Press; Russell, J. A. (1980). A circumplex model of affect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 39(6), 1161–1178; D'Mello, S., & Graesser, A. (2012). Dynamics of affective states during complex learning. Learning and Instruction, 22(2), 145–157.

name: Affinity Diagramming
origin: Jiro Kawakita, 1960s (KJ method); adapted for UX in Contextual Design by Beyer & Holtzblatt
summary: A bottom-up synthesis method in which individual observations are clustered by affinity into labelled groups, revealing themes from raw qualitative data.
description: Affinity diagramming organises large numbers of individual observations, quotes or interpretation notes into groups based on their natural affinity, building a hierarchy from the bottom up. It derives from Jiro Kawakita's KJ method, developed to make sense of anthropological field data, and was adapted in Contextual Design to synthesise contextual inquiry notes. Notes are grouped without predefined categories, and each group receives a label written as a first-person statement of the insight it contains, then groups are clustered into higher-level themes. Rigour comes from writing atomic notes that each carry one idea with a source code, resisting pre-set categories, writing insight labels rather than topic labels, and keeping a traceable link from every theme back to participants.
steps: Write each observation, quote or interpretation as an atomic note tagged with a participant code.
Clear a large wall or digital board and place notes one at a time, grouping those that share an underlying meaning.
Keep groups small (about 4 to 6 notes) and split larger ones.
Label each group with an insight statement written in the user's voice, not a topic heading.
Cluster groups into higher-level themes and label those.
Walk the wall to check coverage and identify gaps or contradictions.
Derive design implications and questions from each top-level theme.
outputs: A hierarchical affinity diagram with labelled insight groups, top-level themes and traceable links to source data.
useWhen: After interviews, contextual inquiries or workshops, when a team needs to synthesise many observations and build shared understanding.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for systematic coding when findings must be defended rigorously; use thematic analysis or grounded theory. Not suitable for quantitative data.
whyLost: Still in use: Collaborative synthesis staple; surfaces team consensus; democratizes analysis across disciplines.
whereToUse: After any qualitative fieldwork; workshop synthesis; cross-functional alignment sessions.
example: After 12 contextual inquiries with warehouse supervisors, a logistics SaaS team builds an affinity diagram of 400 notes. A top-level theme, 'I trust my own whiteboard more than the system', drives a new shift-planning view.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Beyer H & Holtzblatt K (1998) Contextual Design
Scupin R (1997) The KJ method: a technique for analyzing data derived from Japanese ethnology. Human Organization
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Kawakita, J. (1975). The KJ Method: A Scientific Approach to Problem Solving. Kawakita Research Institute; Beyer, H. & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual Design.

name: Affordance Analysis
origin: James J. Gibson, 1977/1979; adapted for design by Donald Norman, 1988
summary: Maps the action possibilities an interface offers against those users actually perceive, separating real affordances from signifiers to find hidden and false affordances.
description: Gibson defined affordances as action possibilities that exist in the relation between an actor and an environment. Norman brought the idea into design and later clarified that what designers control are signifiers: perceivable cues that communicate an affordance. Affordance analysis operationalises this distinction. For each element the analyst records what actions are actually possible, what actions are signalled, and what actions users perceive. Gaver's taxonomy then classifies the result as a perceptible affordance, a hidden affordance (possible but not signalled, such as an undiscovered swipe) or a false affordance (signalled but not possible, such as decorative text styled like a link). Rigour comes from checking perception empirically, through first-click tests, prediction prompts or observation, rather than relying on designer intuition, and from considering the actor's capabilities, including motor and sensory impairments.
steps: Inventory interactive and non-interactive elements on the screens or physical product under review.
For each element record actual possible actions and the signifiers that communicate them.
Ask 5-8 users to predict what each element does or where they would act to achieve a goal, without instruction.
Classify each element as perceptible, hidden or false affordance using Gaver's taxonomy.
Prioritise hidden affordances on critical paths and false affordances that cause wasted actions.
Redesign signifiers and re-test predictions, including users with different motor and sensory capabilities.
outputs: Affordance inventory, classification of perceptible, hidden and false affordances, signifier redesign recommendations.
useWhen: Gesture, touch, AR/VR and novel interaction designs where discoverability is uncertain, or flat visual styles that may have removed cues.
avoidWhen: When the issue is content comprehension or navigation structure; use tree testing or content testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Foundational HCI concept; but widely misunderstood — real vs. perceived affordances conflated.
whereToUse: Interaction design; product design; AR/VR interaction.
example: A banking app hid account actions behind a left swipe. Affordance analysis showed only 2 of 8 participants predicted the gesture; adding a visible overflow menu as a signifier removed the hidden affordance on the critical path.
sources: The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
The Design of Everyday Things (Don Norman)
Goldstein, E. B., Sensation and Perception
Gibson, J. J., The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979)
Whalen, J., Design for How People Think (2019)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (Gibson, 2015)
reference: Gaver, W. W. (1991). Technology affordances. Proceedings of CHI '91, 79-84.

name: After-Action Review
origin: US Army, mid-1970s at the National Training Center; TC 25-20 (1993)
summary: A short, structured debrief asking what was planned, what actually happened, why there was a difference, and what to sustain or improve.
description: The AAR was developed by the US Army to learn from training exercises. Its four questions (What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we sustain or improve?) are answered by participants themselves, facilitated rather than judged, immediately after the event. Ground truth from instrumentation is used to correct memory. Its rigour comes from comparing intent with observed outcome, from rank-free participation, and from repetition across many events, which allows patterns to be aggregated. In UX it suits research operations (after each study), design sprints and launches, and also field studies with users who perform team activities.
steps: Schedule the AAR immediately after the event, within hours, with all participants present.
Restate the objectives and plan (what was supposed to happen) using written records.
Reconstruct what actually happened using data, recordings and logs, letting participants add their perspectives.
Discuss causes of differences, focusing on the system and decisions rather than individuals.
Agree 2-3 items to sustain and 2-3 to improve, with owners.
Store AARs in a searchable log and review trends quarterly.
outputs: Brief AAR records with plan-versus-actual comparisons and sustain/improve actions; a longitudinal lessons log.
useWhen: After research studies, launches, sprints or team exercises, and in field research on teams performing coordinated tasks.
avoidWhen: Major incidents with harm, where a formal blameless postmortem is more appropriate.
whyLost: Retrospectives in agile replaced AARs with looser 'what went well' formats that lack the plan-versus-actual comparison and ground truth.
whereToUse: Research operations, launch reviews, incident drills, game days, customer onboarding programmes.
example: After each usability study, a research team runs a 20-minute AAR. Over six months the log shows recurring recruitment mismatches, prompting a screener redesign that cuts no-shows by half.
sources: US Army, TC 25-20: A Leader's Guide to After-Action Reviews (1993)
Darling, Parry & Moore, Learning in the thick of it (2005), Harvard Business Review
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: US Army (1993). TC 25-20: A Leader's Guide to After-Action Reviews.

name: After-Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ)
origin: James R. Lewis, IBM (1991)
summary: A three-item post-task questionnaire covering ease, time taken and quality of support information.
description: The ASQ is asked straight after each task scenario. Its three seven-point items cover satisfaction with ease of completion, with the time it took, and with the support information (help, messages, documentation). It predates the Single Ease Question and covers slightly more ground, at the cost of two extra items per task. Sauro and Lewis's comparisons of post-task questionnaires found the ASQ, SEQ and SMEQ all correlate well with task performance, so the choice comes down to whether separate time and support ratings are useful.
steps: Ask the three items immediately after each task.
Average the items into a task score (lower is better on the original scale).
Compare tasks and designs using means and confidence intervals.
Inspect the support item separately when help or messages are part of the design.
outputs: A post-task satisfaction score per task with a separate read on support materials.
useWhen: Tasks where help content or system messages are under evaluation.
avoidWhen: Long studies with many tasks, where the single-item SEQ reduces fatigue.
whyLost: Superseded in practice by the one-item SEQ.
whereToUse: Enterprise software tests, documentation and help-centre evaluations.
example: A tax tool's "claim a deduction" task scores fine on ease but poorly on the support item, pointing to inline help.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Lewis, J. R. (1991). Psychometric evaluation of an after-scenario questionnaire for computer usability studies: the ASQ. SIGCHI Bulletin 23.

name: Age-Period-Cohort Analysis
origin: Lexis diagrams (Wilhelm Lexis, 1875); Mason, Mason, Winsborough and Poole (1973); Yang and Land (2013)
summary: Separates whether changes in a metric come from user tenure (age), calendar events (period) or sign-up cohort, despite their linear dependence.
description: In products, a user's tenure (age), the calendar date (period) and sign-up cohort are linked (period = cohort + age), so ordinary regression cannot separate them. Yet the distinction matters: falling engagement could be because users tire with tenure, because of a seasonal or competitive period effect, or because recent cohorts are lower quality. APC methods use Lexis diagrams for visual decomposition, constrained models, intrinsic estimators, or hierarchical APC models (cross-classified random effects) with explicit, stated identifying assumptions. Done carefully, APC prevents misattributing acquisition-mix effects to product changes.
steps: Build a dataset of outcomes by tenure interval and calendar period (e.g. weeks), with cohort implied.
Visualise with Lexis surfaces or heat maps of rates by age and period.
Choose an APC approach and state its identifying assumption (e.g. hierarchical APC with random period and cohort effects).
Estimate age, period and cohort effects with uncertainty.
Check robustness across alternative specifications.
Interpret effects in light of known events (launches, seasonality, acquisition campaigns).
outputs: Lexis visualisations, estimated age, period and cohort effects with uncertainty and robustness checks.
useWhen: Long-running products with changing acquisition and many calendar events, where retention or engagement trends are debated.
avoidWhen: Short histories or when one of the three effects can be ruled out by design.
whyLost: Cohort tables in analytics tools show the data but no method to decompose it; demographic methods are rarely known.
whereToUse: Subscription retention, gaming engagement, marketplace activity, learning platforms.
example: A meditation app's engagement decline is decomposed: tenure effects are stable, but cohorts acquired via a 2025 influencer campaign have much lower engagement, a cohort effect, not product decay.
sources: Yang & Land, Age-Period-Cohort Analysis: New Models, Methods, and Empirical Applications (2013)
Mason et al., Some methodological issues in cohort analysis of archival data (1973), American Sociological Review
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Yang, Y., & Land, K. C. (2013). Age-Period-Cohort Analysis. CRC Press.

name: Agent Decomposition (Society of Mind)
origin: Marvin Minsky, 1986
summary: Decomposes complex user behaviour into many simple interacting 'agents' (sub-processes with goals), revealing conflicts and coordination failures that explain behaviour.
description: Minsky's Society of Mind proposed that intelligence arises from the interaction of many simple, mindless agents, each performing a narrow function, organised into agencies with conflicting and cooperating goals. As an analytic method, agent decomposition models a user's behaviour in a complex situation as a set of such agents (for example, a goal to save, a habit to browse, a need for social approval) and maps how they compete, which wins in which context, and what arbitrates between them. This makes inconsistent behaviour explicable and suggests interventions that strengthen, weaken or coordinate specific agents. Rigour comes from grounding each agent in observed evidence, specifying activation conditions, and testing predictions against behaviour.
steps: Agent-level error analysis: for any UX error, decompose into agent-level failures:
Attention agent: was the relevant information in the attentional field?
(2) Recognition agent: was the stimulus correctly identified?
(3) Memory agent: was the correct action retrieved?
(4) Execution agent: was the action performed correctly?
(5) Goal agent: was the current action aligned with the active goal? Each agent failure type maps to a specific design intervention.
outputs: An agent map of competing sub-goals and processes, identified conflicts and arbitration points, and design interventions targeting specific agents.
useWhen: Analysing apparently irrational or inconsistent behaviour, such as self-control conflicts and multitasking, and designing multi-agent AI systems and their interfaces.
avoidWhen: Avoid when standard task analysis suffices; the framework is metaphorical and should not be presented as a validated cognitive model.
whyLost: Minsky's theory was influential in AI but never operationalised as an HCI method; behavioural economics now explains similar conflicts with dual-process models.
whereToUse: Complex error analysis, multi-step task design, expert system interface design.
example: A budgeting app models users as a 'saver' agent and an 'impulse' agent plus a 'social' agent responding to friends' spending; designing a commitment device for the saver at payday reduces overspending.
sources: The Society of Mind — Marvin Minsky
reference: Minsky M (1986) The Society of Mind. Simon & Schuster

name: Agent-Based Modelling
donor: Complexity science, ecology and computational social science
origin: Thomas Schelling's segregation model (1971); Joshua Epstein and Robert Axtell (Growing Artificial Societies, 1996); ODD protocol by Volker Grimm et al. (2006, 2020)
summary: Simulates many heterogeneous agents following behavioural rules to see how collective patterns such as adoption, congestion or polarisation emerge.
description: Agent-based models represent individual users (or sellers, bots, moderators) with their own attributes and decision rules, interacting with each other and an environment. Macro patterns emerge from micro rules, often in surprising ways, as Schelling showed with mild preferences producing strong segregation. ABMs suit questions where heterogeneity, networks and local interaction matter. Rigour comes from grounding rules in empirical research (including qualitative), documenting with the ODD protocol, validating against multiple observed patterns (pattern-oriented modelling) and exploring parameter space systematically rather than presenting single runs.
steps: Define the question and the emergent pattern to explain or predict.
Specify agent types, attributes, decision rules and interactions, grounded in research data.
Document the model using the ODD protocol and implement it (NetLogo, Mesa, AnyLogic).
Calibrate and validate against several observed patterns at different levels.
Run parameter sweeps and sensitivity analysis with many replications.
Test interventions in simulation and design field experiments to confirm key predictions.
outputs: A documented ABM, validation evidence, emergent pattern explanations and intervention scenarios.
useWhen: Two-sided markets, social features, communities, multiplayer systems and policies where interactions drive outcomes.
avoidWhen: Individual usability problems or when behaviour rules cannot be grounded in evidence.
whyLost: ABM requires programming and sits in complexity science; UX research rarely builds simulations.
whereToUse: Marketplace pricing and matching, social network feeds, moderation policies, crowd and venue experiences, game economies.
example: A dating app models how changes to swipe limits affect match distribution. The ABM shows limits reduce inequality of matches without lowering total matches, a prediction later confirmed in an experiment.
sources: Grimm et al., The ODD protocol for describing agent-based and other simulation models: A second update (2020), JASSS
Wilensky & Rand, An Introduction to Agent-Based Modeling (2015)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Wilensky, U., & Rand, W. (2015). An Introduction to Agent-Based Modeling. MIT Press.

name: Agent-Host-Environment Analysis of UX Harm
origin: Classical epidemiological triad (19th-20th c.); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Decomposes a UX harm into agent (pattern), host (user susceptibility), environment (platform, context) and mechanism to target interventions at each.
description: The epidemiological triad holds that disease results from interaction of an agent, a susceptible host and an environment that brings them together. The treatise uses this structure throughout: a dark pattern is the agent, the user the host, the platform and situation the environment, with cognitive bias exploitation as the mechanism of action and modifying factors altering susceptibility. Structuring a harm this way prevents single-cause thinking ('users should read more carefully') and maps interventions to each vertex: remove or weaken the agent (redesign), protect the host (literacy, defaults, accessibility) and change the environment (platform rules, regulation, timing). The roach motel case study in the treatise is an exemplar of this analysis.
steps: Define the harm outcome precisely with a case definition.
Characterise the agent: pattern features and the cognitive or structural mechanism it exploits.
Characterise hosts: which users are susceptible and why (literacy, stress, age, disability).
Characterise the environment: platform, context, incentives, time pressure.
Gather evidence for each element from research, logs and literature.
List interventions per vertex and estimate feasibility and impact.
outputs: Triad map of the harm, evidence summary, intervention matrix by vertex.
useWhen: Analysing dark patterns, persistent harms, or failures whose causes span design, users and context.
avoidWhen: Simple defects with a single obvious cause.
whyLost: Epidemiological reasoning never migrated into UX analysis.
whereToUse: Trust and safety, dark pattern audits, financial harm reviews, accessibility harm analysis.
example: Triad analysis of 'accidental international roaming charges' identifies the agent (buried toggle default on), hosts (infrequent travellers) and environment (arrival stress), leading to arrival-time prompts plus default-off.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rothman KJ, Greenland S & Lash TL (2008) Modern Epidemiology
reference: Gordis L (2014) Epidemiology. 5th ed. Elsevier Saunders.

name: AI as instrument, not analyst
aka: Instrumental stance on AI in research
origin: Epistemological position developed in qualitative methods debates from 2023; draws on the idea of the researcher as instrument in qualitative inquiry (Lincoln and Guba, 1985)
summary: An epistemological stance that treats AI as a measurement and processing instrument to be calibrated and validated, while interpretation, judgement and accountability for findings remain with researchers.
description: In qualitative research the researcher is traditionally the primary instrument, bringing reflexivity and accountability to interpretation. Framing AI as an analyst blurs responsibility and invites unexamined authority for fluent outputs. Framing it as an instrument means it is specified (model, version, prompts), calibrated (validated against human judgement on samples), scoped (used for tasks like transcription, segmentation and deductive tagging), and reported like any instrument, with its error characteristics. Interpretive moves such as abstraction, theorising, judging significance and recommending action stay with people who can be accountable. The stance is a governance principle that shapes pipeline design, checkpoints and reporting.
steps: Write a short statement of AI's role for the project, listing tasks delegated and tasks reserved for researchers.
Specify the AI instrument fully: tool, model version, prompts, parameters.
Calibrate against human judgement on samples and report its error characteristics.
Reserve interpretive decisions (themes, theory, significance, recommendations) for researchers and record who made them.
Maintain reflexive memos on how AI outputs may have shaped researchers' thinking.
Report AI's role as an instrument in methods sections and stakeholder briefings.
outputs: A role statement, instrument specification, calibration results and documented human interpretive decisions.
useWhen: Setting governance for any AI-assisted research practice, and when stakeholders treat AI summaries as findings.
avoidWhen: Not a rejection of AI assistance; avoid using the stance to justify unvalidated automation by calling it an 'instrument' without calibration.
whyLost: A new framing; tool marketing presents AI as an analyst or 'insight generator', so the instrumental stance must be argued for actively.
whereToUse: Research operations policies, academic UX, regulated research and leadership education about AI insight tools.
example: A product leadership team asks for 'AI insights' from a vendor tool. The research lead reframes it as an instrument, calibrates its tagging against researcher coding (kappa 0.62, below threshold) and limits its use to search and retrieval until it improves.
sources: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985) Naturalistic Inquiry
Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2022) Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide
The Inquiry Series, C14 — Ethical Constraints & Epistemological Limits of AI-Assisted Qualitative Research
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985) Naturalistic Inquiry

name: AI Explainability Auditing for UX
donor: Machine learning interpretability and human-AI interaction
origin: Explainable AI techniques such as LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016) and SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017); human-centred XAI by Liao et al. (2020)
summary: Audits whether AI explanations help users understand, calibrate trust in and correct AI outputs, testing explanation types against users' actual questions and decisions.
description: Machine learning teams generate explanations such as feature importance, SHAP values, LIME local explanations, saliency maps and counterfactuals mainly for developers. An explainability audit asks whether these serve users. It starts by eliciting users' explanation needs, for example why this output, why not another, what would change it, and how confident the system is, using Liao's XAI question bank. It then evaluates candidate explanations on comprehension, decision accuracy, trust calibration (do users rely on the AI when it is right and override it when wrong), time and perceived usefulness, ideally in controlled studies with known correct and incorrect AI outputs. Explanations that increase trust without improving calibration are flagged as harmful. Regulatory requirements, such as the right to explanation under GDPR and the EU AI Act, add urgency.
steps: Explainability UX audit:
Identify every AI decision point visible to users.
(2) For each, apply: a SHAP or LIME explanation (which features drove this decision?).
(3) Translate the technical explanation into user-facing language.
(4) Test: do users understand the explanation? Can they predict how to change the outcome? User explainability score = % who can accurately predict what change would change the AI's output.
outputs: Inventory of user explanation needs, evaluation of explanation types on comprehension and calibration, flagged misleading explanations, and recommended explanation designs.
useWhen: AI products making consequential recommendations: credit, hiring, healthcare, insurance, content moderation and enterprise decision support.
avoidWhen: When the AI's outputs are low-stakes and easily verified by users, or when no model access exists to generate faithful explanations; then focus on error recovery design.
whyLost: Explainability is studied by ML researchers and a small human-AI interaction community; product UX teams rarely have model access or methods to evaluate explanations with users.
whereToUse: AI product UX research, recommendation system design, automated decision UX (credit, content moderation, medical AI), LLM interface design.
example: A lender's credit-limit model shows SHAP-based reasons to applicants. An audit with 60 participants finds the explanations raise trust but not understanding, while a counterfactual explanation ('a limit of £2,000 would be possible with 6 more months of history') improves both.
sources: Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin, 'Why should I trust you?' Explaining the predictions of any classifier (KDD 2016)
Liao, Gruen & Miller, Questioning the AI: Informing design practices for explainable AI user experiences (CHI 2020)
Lundberg & Lee, A unified approach to interpreting model predictions (NeurIPS 2017)
reference: Liao QV, Gruen D & Miller S (2020) Questioning the AI: Informing design practices for explainable AI user experiences. CHI 2020

name: AI objective function audit
origin: Goodhart's law (Charles Goodhart, 1975); Raji et al.'s internal algorithmic auditing framework, 2020; alignment literature (Christian, 2020)
summary: Examines what an AI system is actually optimised for, compares it with user and business values, and identifies where optimising the proxy harms the intended outcome.
description: Every recommender, ranking or personalisation system optimises an objective: clicks, engagement time, trades or conversions. These are proxies for what users and the business actually value, and Goodhart's law predicts divergence when they are optimised hard. An objective function audit documents the objective, training labels, reward signals and constraints; maps them against stated values (user wellbeing, financial health, informed decisions); and tests for divergence using behavioural and attitudinal data. It draws on algorithmic auditing frameworks and alignment research. Rigour comes from tracing objectives in code and documentation, interviewing model owners, gathering user evidence on outcomes, and proposing measurable alternative objectives or constraints.
steps: Document the system's objective, loss function, reward signals, training labels and constraints by interviewing model owners and reviewing documentation.
Articulate intended user and business values explicitly, drawing on research and policy.
Map each objective component to the values it is assumed to proxy and note where links are weak.
Gather evidence of divergence: compare optimised metrics with wellbeing, satisfaction or long-term outcomes for affected users.
Identify failure modes, such as engagement driven by anxiety or churn hidden behind short-term clicks.
Recommend revised objectives, constraints or guardrail metrics and a monitoring plan.
outputs: An audit report mapping objectives to values, evidence of divergence, failure modes and recommended objective changes and guardrails.
useWhen: Before launching or scaling AI-driven ranking, recommendation or nudging, and when metrics improve but user outcomes or sentiment worsen.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple rule-based features with no optimisation, or where model owners cannot share objective details; use external behavioural audits instead.
whyLost: Responsible AI work is often siloed in policy or ML teams, and UX researchers are rarely asked what systems optimise.
whereToUse: Investment and trading recommendations, social and content feeds, health engagement nudges, AI assistants with engagement metrics.
example: An investment AI optimised for engagement increases logins by 20%, but interviews and surveys show rising anxiety and impulsive trades. The audit recommends a confidence-weighted objective and a wellbeing guardrail.
sources: Raji et al. (2020) Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
The Inquiry Series, Ch 58 — AI Explainability & Value Alignment Audit
reference: Raji, I. D. et al. (2020) Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing. FAT* '20, 33-44.

name: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
origin: Emerging practice with large language models, 2023 onward; builds on computer-assisted qualitative data analysis and content analysis reliability norms
summary: Applying a human-built codebook to large transcript corpora with an LLM, validated against human coding with kappa thresholds and human review of low-confidence output.
description: Large language models can apply qualitative codes at a scale no team can match, but they also produce plausible yet wrong labels. This method keeps theory and interpretation human. Researchers first build a codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules and examples, then human-code 20 to 25 percent of the corpus as a test set. The model is prompted to return structured output (code, supporting quote, confidence, rationale) for each segment, and human-AI agreement is computed; deployment proceeds only above a threshold such as kappa 0.70, with low agreement treated as evidence of codebook ambiguity. The model codes the rest, with periodic human spot checks and review of low-confidence segments. Humans produce the themes and conclusions.
steps: Develop the coding manual first: Code definitions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and worked examples — exactly as for human coding.
Structured JSON output schema: {'{'}code_name, supporting_quote, confidence_score, rationale{'}'}. Enables systematic comparison with human codes.
Human baseline coding first: Human coders code 20–25% of the corpus. This becomes the IRR test set.
Calculate IRR human vs. AI: κ > 0.70 before deploying the AI on the remaining corpus. If κ < 0.70, revise coding instructions — the failure reveals ambiguity in your scheme.
AI codes remaining corpus with human spot-checking every 10th transcript. Flag segments with confidence < 0.7 for human review.
Human interpretation: The AI produces labelled segments. Humans produce themes, propositions, and the final analysis.
outputs: A validated codebook, human-AI agreement statistics, coded corpus with quotes and confidence scores, review logs, and human-authored themes.
useWhen: Large corpora (hundreds of interviews, thousands of tickets or open-ended responses) where a stable codebook exists or can be built.
avoidWhen: Small studies where human coding is quick, interpretive approaches such as IPA, or sensitive data that cannot be processed by external models without consent and safeguards.
whyLost: It is rapidly being adopted because LLMs make scale cheap; the risk is skipping human baselines and reliability checks.
whereToUse: Support ticket and review analysis, open-ended survey coding, research repositories, and large multi-market interview programmes.
example: A telecom codes 5,000 complaint transcripts. After human-AI kappa reaches 0.74 on 1,000 double-coded segments, the model codes the remainder and humans review the 8% flagged low-confidence before synthesis.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology (Krippendorff)
reference: Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Alarm Flood Analysis (EEMUA 191 / ISA-18.2)
origin: EEMUA Publication 191 (1999) after the 1994 Texaco Milford Haven explosion; ANSI/ISA-18.2 (2009)
summary: Measures alarm and notification rates against benchmarks, identifies floods, chattering and stale alarms, and rationalises each alarm against a required operator response.
description: Process industries learned that operators drown when alarms exceed what a human can process. EEMUA 191 set benchmarks: an average of about one alarm per 10 minutes per operator is acceptable, more than 10 alarms in 10 minutes constitutes a flood, and every alarm must require a defined operator action. Analysis uses alarm logs to compute rates, top-ten 'bad actors', chattering alarms (repeated within seconds), standing alarms and priority distributions (recommended roughly 80% low, 15% medium, 5% high). Rationalisation then reviews each alarm's cause, consequence, required response and time available. Notifications, badges and AI alerts in digital products suffer exactly the same pathologies, and this is a ready-made quantitative method. The same problem appears in clinical products: in paediatric intensive care, over 90% of alarms have been reported as clinically insignificant, a driver of alarm fatigue (Case and Day, 2018).
steps: Export notification or alert logs per user or operator with timestamps, type and priority.
Compute average rates per 10 minutes and per hour, peak 10-minute counts and the percentage of time in flood (>10 per 10 minutes).
Identify bad actors: the top 10 sources by volume, chattering alerts (repeats within 60 seconds) and standing alerts never cleared.
Check priority distribution against roughly 80/15/5 low/medium/high and look for priority inflation.
Rationalise each alert in a workshop: what action is required, how quickly, what happens if ignored; delete or demote alerts with no required action.
Re-measure rates and user response times after changes, and set ongoing monitoring targets.
outputs: Alarm/notification performance metrics, a bad-actor list, a rationalised alert catalogue with required actions and priorities.
useWhen: Users ignore or disable notifications, operators miss critical alerts, or a product sends many automated alerts.
avoidWhen: Products with very few notifications; standard usability testing suffices.
whyLost: Alarm management is an industrial discipline with standards UX designers never read. Product teams measure notification engagement rather than overload.
whereToUse: Observability and incident tools, security operations, clinical monitoring, fintech fraud queues, mobile push strategy.
example: An observability platform finds on-call engineers average 34 alerts per hour during incidents, with 60% from five chattering sources. Rationalisation removes alerts with no required action and adds hysteresis, reducing incident alert load by 70%.
sources: EEMUA Publication 191, Alarm Systems: A Guide to Design, Management and Procurement (3rd ed., 2013)
ANSI/ISA-18.2, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries (2009/2016)
Case, A. & Day, A., Designing with Sound: Fundamentals for Products and Services (O'Reilly, 2018)
reference: EEMUA (2013). Publication 191: Alarm Systems. Engineering Equipment and Materials Users Association.

name: Algorithmic Experience Research
donor: Science and technology studies and social computing
origin: Algorithm awareness studies by Eslami et al. (2015); 'algorithmic experience' framing by Alvarado and Waern (2018)
summary: Longitudinal study of how people perceive, theorise about and are affected by recommendation feeds and automated decisions, combining log data with interviews.
description: Algorithmic experience research investigates the user side of algorithmic systems: whether people know an algorithm is shaping what they see, the folk theories they hold about it, how they try to steer it, and how its outputs affect behaviour, mood and wellbeing over time. Because effects accumulate slowly and are personalised, single-session usability tests miss them. Rigorous designs combine longitudinal diaries or experience sampling with logged exposure data, folk-theory elicitation interviews, and, where possible, controlled variation of the algorithm (for example a chronological feed holdout). Analysis links what people believe about the system to what it actually does, revealing misattribution, learned helplessness or gaming. The approach is well developed in social computing research but rarely operationalised in product UX teams.
steps: Define the algorithmic surface (feed ranking, recommendations, pricing, moderation) and the experience outcomes of interest (control, trust, wellbeing, diversity).
Recruit 15-30 participants and obtain consent to pair their exposure logs with self-reports.
Run baseline interviews eliciting folk theories: what the participant thinks drives what they see, and how they try to influence it.
Collect 2-6 weeks of diary or experience-sampling entries tied to specific algorithmic moments, alongside logged exposure.
Where feasible, introduce a controlled variation (for example a holdout with reduced personalisation) and compare experience measures.
Analyse gaps between folk theories and actual system behaviour, and link exposure patterns to experience outcomes.
Translate findings into transparency, control and ranking-objective recommendations.
outputs: Folk-theory taxonomy, longitudinal experience trajectories, exposure-outcome associations, and design recommendations for control and transparency.
useWhen: Products driven by feeds, recommendations or automated decisions where long-term wellbeing, trust or perceived control matter: social media, streaming, gig-work platforms, news.
avoidWhen: When you only need to tune ranking metrics (use online experiments) or when you cannot access logs, in which case limit claims to perceptions.
whyLost: Latent: Critical and growing area; limited standardized methods; primarily academic.
whereToUse: Social platforms; content recommendation; AI-driven personalization.
example: A food-delivery platform studies 20 couriers over four weeks pairing their dispatch logs with diaries. Couriers believe acceptance rate drives job allocation, which it does not, leading to unsafe acceptance of distant jobs; the team publishes allocation factors in-app.
sources: Eslami et al., 'I always assumed that I wasn't really that close to [her]' (CHI 2015)
reference: Eslami M et al. (2015) 'I always assumed that I wasn't really that close to [her]': Reasoning about invisible algorithms in news feeds. CHI 2015

name: Analogical Reasoning Analysis for Onboarding
origin: Dedre Gentner's structure-mapping theory (1983); developmental work by Usha Goswami
summary: Analyses interface metaphors as structure mappings from a known source domain, identifying correct, missing and misleading relational correspondences to design onboarding that transfers knowledge.
description: Gentner's structure-mapping theory explains analogy as mapping relational structure, not surface features, from a familiar source to a new target. Goswami showed that even young children reason analogically when they know the source domain's relations. Interface metaphors (desktop, folders, wallet, cart, inbox) work the same way: users import the source's relations, and the analogy succeeds when relations hold and misleads when they do not. The method lists the source's key relations, maps each to the target system, and classifies them as valid, absent or misleading. Onboarding and design then reinforce valid mappings, explicitly flag misleading ones, and use worked comparisons that make relational similarity salient, which research shows improves transfer. Testing checks whether users predict system behaviour from the metaphor correctly.
steps: Test analogical transfer for any new interface concept: teach users the concept in one interface context (source).
Present an unfamiliar but structurally analogous interface (target).
Measure: how much does source learning transfer to target performance?
High transfer (> 70% performance improvement vs. control) = the analogy is structurally sound.
Low transfer = the analogy's structure doesn't match the target domain.
outputs: Source-to-target relation mapping table with valid, absent and misleading correspondences; prediction-test results; onboarding content built on comparisons.
useWhen: Introducing new product categories, naming features with metaphors, onboarding novices, and diagnosing errors caused by inappropriate metaphors.
avoidWhen: When users are already experts in the target domain, or the interface uses no metaphor; use task analysis or usability testing.
whyLost: Analogy research flourished in cognitive and developmental psychology, but UX treats metaphors as copywriting or visual choices rather than testable structure mappings.
whereToUse: Onboarding design, tutorial design, cross-product migration, help documentation, AI interface explanation design.
example: A crypto wallet app uses a 'wallet' metaphor, but mapping shows the misleading relation that losing the wallet means losing only its contents, not access to funds held elsewhere. Onboarding adds a comparison to a house key to correct recovery-phrase expectations.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development — Usha Goswami
Gentner, Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy (Cognitive Science, 1983)
reference: Gentner D (1983) Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science 7(2):155-170

name: Analogical transfer test
origin: Dedre Gentner's structure-mapping theory (1983) and Gick and Holyoak's analogical problem solving studies (1980, 1983)
summary: Tests which relational inferences users carry from a source domain metaphor into a product, revealing correct transfer, missing transfer and harmful over-transfer.
description: When a product borrows a metaphor (wallet, folder, cart, inbox, assistant), users infer how it behaves by mapping relations from the familiar source domain onto the new target. Structure-mapping theory predicts that people transfer relational structure, not surface features, and that they may also transfer relations the designer never intended. An analogical transfer test presents the metaphor and asks users to predict system behaviour in scenarios that probe specific relations: is money in the wallet insured, can someone take it, does it disappear if the phone is lost? Answers are scored against the system's actual behaviour. Rigour comes from deriving probes systematically from the source-domain relational structure, including probes for intended, unintended and absent mappings, and from comparing alternative metaphors on the same probe set.
steps: Map the source domain's key relations (for a wallet: carried on the person, can be lost or stolen, holds cash, no interest, no institution behind it) and the target system's actual relations.
Classify each relation as intended transfer, harmful transfer (true in source, false in system) or missing transfer (true in system, absent in source).
Write 8 to 15 scenario probes, each targeting one relation, phrased as predictions: 'Your phone is stolen. What happens to the money?'
Present the metaphor in context to 15 to 30 participants per segment and collect predictions and confidence ratings (1 to 5) for each probe.
Score each prediction as correct or incorrect against system behaviour and compute per-relation transfer rates, flagging harmful transfers held by more than 20% of participants with high confidence.

Repeat with one or two alternative metaphors on the same probes and choose the metaphor with the highest correct transfer and lowest confident harmful transfer, or plan explicit explanation for the remaining gaps.
outputs: A relational mapping table, per-probe transfer and confidence rates for each candidate metaphor, and a list of harmful over-transfers requiring design or onboarding fixes.
useWhen: Choosing or defending a core product metaphor; users hold wrong expectations about security, reversibility or ownership; introducing novel concepts such as AI agents or digital assets.
avoidWhen: The concept is already well understood without metaphor, or you only need label findability; use tree testing or comprehension testing instead.
whyLost: Analogical reasoning research stayed in cognitive science and education, while UX metaphor critique (for example of the desktop) remained rhetorical rather than experimental.
whereToUse: Digital money and crypto products, cloud storage, AI agent and assistant design, health records, smart-home automations.
example: Users of a 'digital wallet' predicted that a lost phone meant lost money (67%) and that balances earned no protection. The system was account-based and recoverable; the team kept the term but added a recovery explanation at onboarding, and the harmful transfer fell to 18%.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
reference: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155–170.

name: Analogous Situations
donor: Cognitive science of analogy; design ideation
origin: Jon Kolko (2014), drawing on Douglas Hofstadter and Alan Cooper
summary: An ideation practice that finds an unrelated situation sharing the interactions and emotions of users' goals, then borrows the artefacts that support people there as feature ideas.
description: Analogous situations turns research insights into ideas by deliberate analogy. The team lists the human interactions and emotions involved in pursuing a user goal, strips out domain vocabulary, and asks where else in life all of those conditions hold at once: training for a marathon, tending a garden, completing an executive MBA. One analogue is chosen and its timeline sketched, with the artefacts, rituals and supports that help people succeed in it (trackers, coach calendars, peer groups, magazines). For each, the team asks why it works there, then repurposes it liberally for the product. The discipline lies in generalising the list before searching, so the analogue matches on structure rather than surface, and in grounding the starting goals in research rather than opinion. Kolko grounds the technique in Hofstadter's view that analogy is central to cognition.
steps: Start from synthesised research insights and two to four high-level user goals.
For each goal, list the interactions and emotions typical of pursuing it (for example checking in with an expert, feeling progress, fearing failure).
Rewrite the list without domain terms so it describes a generic human situation.
Brainstorm other situations where every item on the list holds, aiming for at least five candidates from unrelated fields.
Choose one analogue and sketch its timeline, listing the artefacts, roles and rituals that support people through it.
For each artefact ask why it works in the analogue, then translate it into a candidate feature or service element.
Cluster the candidates and carry the strongest into concept sketches or a design studio.
outputs: A chosen analogous situation, its timeline and supporting artefacts, and a list of candidate features traced back to them.
useWhen: Use when research has produced clear goals but ideation keeps returning to category conventions, or when designing for long, effortful behaviours (adherence, saving, learning) where other domains have mature support systems.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the user goals themselves are unknown or contested: run Contextual Inquiry or Jobs-to-be-Done Research first. The practice needs a broad worldview; teams with narrow experience produce shallow analogues. It generates ideas, it does not test them, so follow with Prototype Testing.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, needs no special materials and reliably breaks category fixation; design consultancies teach analogous inspiration as a standard ideation move.
whereToUse: Health adherence apps, financial wellbeing products, onboarding and learning products, B2B tools with long adoption curves.
example: A medication-adherence team lists taking a daily pill, feeling progress, checking in with a professional and feeling in control, and finds marathon training matches all four. Training plans, pace trackers and running clubs become a dose calendar, a symptom trend view and a peer check-in group.
reference: Kolko, J. (2014). Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press. pp. 126-128.

name: Analysis of Competing Hypotheses
origin: Richards Heuer, CIA, 1970s; Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (1999)
summary: Evaluates evidence against all plausible hypotheses in a matrix, focusing on disconfirmation, to counter confirmation bias in explaining what is happening.
description: Analysts, like researchers, tend to pick a favoured explanation and collect supporting evidence. ACH lists all reasonable hypotheses, lists significant evidence and arguments, and marks in a matrix whether each item is consistent, inconsistent or not applicable to each hypothesis. The key insight is that evidence consistent with all hypotheses has no diagnostic value; hypotheses are ranked by how much evidence is inconsistent with them, not consistent. Analysts then assess sensitivity to critical evidence, identify missing evidence that would discriminate, and report conclusions with milestones for re-evaluation. It is a rigorous structure for UX synthesis questions like 'why did activation drop?'.
steps: Brainstorm all plausible hypotheses with a diverse group, including unpopular ones.
List evidence and assumptions: data, findings, logs, absence of expected evidence.
Build the matrix and rate each item's consistency with each hypothesis; note diagnosticity.
Refine the matrix: delete non-diagnostic evidence, add hypotheses if needed.
Rank hypotheses by inconsistent evidence; test sensitivity to a few critical items and their reliability.
Report conclusions with relative likelihoods and define indicators that would change the judgement.
outputs: An ACH matrix, ranked hypotheses, diagnostic evidence, evidence gaps and monitoring indicators.
useWhen: Explaining ambiguous phenomena (metric drops, puzzling behaviour, mixed research results) where several explanations compete.
avoidWhen: Questions with a single obvious explanation, or purely generative exploration.
whyLost: Structured analytic techniques remained in intelligence agencies; UX synthesis relies on affinity mapping and narrative.
whereToUse: Root cause investigations, competitive analysis, research synthesis disputes, AI behaviour investigations.
example: Activation fell 9%. ACH across five hypotheses shows most evidence is consistent with all of them, but the timing of the decline in one acquisition channel is inconsistent with a UX cause, pointing to traffic mix change.
sources: Heuer, Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (1999), CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
Heuer & Pherson, Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis (2nd ed., 2014)
reference: Heuer, R. J. (1999). Psychology of Intelligence Analysis. CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence.

name: Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
origin: R. A. Fisher's covariance analysis; Johnson-Neyman technique (1936); Lord's paradox (1967)
summary: Compare group means while adjusting for a pre-measured covariate such as a baseline score, increasing precision and reducing bias, after checking that slopes are parallel.
description: ANCOVA combines ANOVA and regression: group effects are estimated after statistically controlling a continuous covariate that predicts the outcome, usually a pretest or baseline. In randomised designs this shrinks error variance and raises power, sometimes turning a non-significant ANOVA significant. Assumptions are linearity, equal slopes across groups, a covariate measured before treatment and unaffected by it, and constant error variance; measurement error in the covariate biases non-randomised comparisons. Covariates should be chosen at design time from prior evidence, not by screening current data. When slopes differ, the heterogeneity-of-regression model tests the treatment effect at chosen covariate values and Johnson-Neyman regions show where it is significant. Lord's paradox shows gain scores and ANCOVA answer different questions in intact groups. Online experimentation's CUPED is the same regression adjustment under a new name.
steps: Choose covariates at design time from prior evidence (often a pre-period or pretest measure) and measure them before treatment.
Run the plain ANOVA, then fit the ANCOVA with the covariate and request adjusted (marginal) means.
Test homogeneity of slopes by temporarily adding a group-by-covariate interaction; if it is clearly significant, use a separate-slopes model.
With unequal slopes, estimate treatment effects at chosen covariate values and compute Johnson-Neyman regions of significance.
Check linearity and residual variance, then run post hoc comparisons on adjusted means.
Report F tests for covariate and group with effect sizes (such as omega squared); in non-randomised studies, treat adjustment as imperfect and consider whether a gain-score question is the real one.
outputs: Adjusted group means, F tests, effect sizes, post hoc comparisons and, where slopes differ, conditional effects and regions of significance.
useWhen: Comparing designs or treatments where a baseline measure (prior usage, pretest skill, pre-period spend) explains much outcome variance, especially with small samples or noisy metrics.
avoidWhen: The covariate is affected by treatment, slopes differ strongly and are ignored, or groups are non-randomised and the covariate is measured with error; ANCOVA does not substitute for randomisation.
whyLost: Classic ANCOVA is rare in UX reports, but its logic survives in online experimentation as CUPED and regression adjustment, with its origin and slope checks often forgotten.
whereToUse: A/B tests with pre-period data, learnability and training studies with pretests, small-sample lab comparisons.
example: A learning app compares two lesson designs, using each user's placement-test score as covariate. Adjusted means show a clear effect the raw comparison missed, and a slope check shows the gain is larger for low scorers.
sources: Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2018). Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data: A Model Comparison Perspective (3rd ed.). Routledge, chs. 9-10.

name: Analyst Debiasing Procedures
donor: Judgement and decision making; social psychology
origin: Wilson and Brekke (1994); Lerner and Tetlock (1999); Lord, Lepper and Preston (1984); Koriat, Lichtenstein and Fischhoff (1980)
summary: Protect evaluators' judgements by blinding them to contaminants first, announcing accountability before evidence is seen, and prompting a few reasons they could be wrong.
description: Researchers rating severity, coding data or judging designs are vulnerable to unwanted influences they cannot detect. Wilson and Brekke's model orders defences: exposure control, preparation, resistance, remediation and behaviour control. People over-trust resistance and remediation, which usually fail because contamination is invisible and its size unknown, so blinding comes first. When blinding is impossible, rate items twice under different circumstances and re-examine disagreements, and check whether judgements covary with a suspected contaminant. Tetlock's work adds pre-decisional accountability: telling analysts before they see evidence that they must justify conclusions to an informed audience whose views are unknown prompts self-critical thinking and reduces primacy, anchoring and overconfidence, though it amplifies dilution and safe-option choices. Consider-the-opposite prompts, asking for a small number of reasons a judgement might be wrong, reduce overconfidence; asking for many backfires.
steps: List potential contaminants of the judgement (participant identity, brand, segment, condition, order, the stakeholder's preferred answer).
Blind evaluators to these wherever feasible, for example by masking condition labels during coding or severity rating.
Before evidence is seen, tell analysts they will justify conclusions to an informed reviewer whose views are unknown; do not reveal stakeholders' preferred conclusions.
Where blinding is impossible, rate each item twice at different times or settings and re-examine items whose ratings differ.
Compare ratings across subgroups defined by a suspected contaminant to detect covariation.
After initial judgements, ask for two or three reasons each could be wrong, then re-elicit the judgement; avoid asking for many reasons.
outputs: Less contaminated ratings and codes, flags on suspect judgements, and a record of the debiasing steps used.
useWhen: Severity rating, qualitative coding, design reviews, heuristic evaluation and any study where the analyst knows the hypothesis or the client's preference.
avoidWhen: Avoid over-blinding where context is essential to judgement, and avoid accountability after commitment, which produces bolstering. For bias in participants rather than analysts, use design controls such as randomisation.
whyLost: It is established in judgement and decision-making research but UX quality assurance rarely addresses the analyst's own bias systematically.
whereToUse: A/B test interpretation, research repositories, regulated or high-stakes evaluations, AI model output review, competitive benchmarking.
example: Two researchers rate usability issue severity with prototype versions masked as A and B and re-rate a sample a week later. Covariation analysis shows they rated issues harsher on the competitor version until masking was applied.
sources: Mental Contamination and Mental Correction (Wilson & Brekke, 1994)
Accounting for the Effects of Accountability (Lerner & Tetlock, 1999)
reference: Wilson, T. D., Centerbar, D. B. and Brekke, N. (2002). Mental contamination and the debiasing problem. In T. Gilovich, D. Griffin and D. Kahneman (Eds.), Heuristics and Biases: The Psychology of Intuitive Judgment. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

name: Analytic Bracketing (Gubrium and Holstein)
aka: Interplay of discursive practice and discourses-in-practice
origin: Jaber Gubrium and James Holstein (1997); Holstein
summary: Alternate during analysis between how people build meaning in talk and which institutional discourses and resources shape that building, documenting each against the other.
description: Analytic bracketing is not phenomenological bracketing of the researcher's assumptions. It is a constructionist analytic move that alternates between two foci. First the analyst sets aside the 'whats' of everyday life to document the 'hows': the discursive practice by which participants build accounts, categories and identities in interaction. Then the analyst brackets those 'hows' to document discourses-in-practice: the institutional categories, rules and resources locally available, and how they are distributed and regulated. Each is referred to while documenting the other, and unlike ethnomethodological bracketing the alternation continues throughout analysis rather than only at the start. Later work extends it to narrative reality, distinguishing narrative work from narrative environments. There are no mechanical rules; the risk is collapsing one side into the other.
steps: Collect naturally occurring talk, interviews or documents from an institutional setting.
Document how participants build their accounts: categories used, identities claimed, how descriptions are made to count (discursive practice).
Bracket that and document the discourses, categories, rules and constraints available in the setting (discourses-in-practice).
Move back and forth, linking each finding about talk to its institutional conditions and vice versa.
Write up both the constitutive and the contextual picture and show where they shape each other.
outputs: An account of interpretive practice in context: how people make sense of things and what institutional resources make that sense available.
useWhen: Studying how users or staff talk about a system inside an institution (insurance, health care, HR, government services) where official categories shape what they can say.
avoidWhen: When you need user needs or usability issues quickly; use Thematic Analysis. Do not confuse with Phenomenological Reduction (Epoché).
whyLost: It belongs to constructionist sociology and is described in theory-heavy texts; UX discourse work usually stops at content or framing.
whereToUse: Service design in institutions, claims and benefits systems, clinical documentation tools, internal enterprise platforms.
example: Analysing calls in a benefits helpline, a researcher shows how callers reframe their circumstances to fit eligibility categories, and how the script and system fields make some accounts sayable and others not.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Gubrium, J. F. and Holstein, J. A. (1997). The New Language of Qualitative Method. New York: Oxford University Press.

name: Analytic Generalisation
donor: Case study and qualitative social science methodology
origin: Robert K. Yin, developed in his case study writing and restated in Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016); contrasted with statistical generalisation by Bromley, Burawoy, Mitchell, Small and others
