summary: A two-step argument that generalises findings from a small qualitative study to concepts and theory, and then from those concepts to other similar situations, instead of to a population.
description: Yin argues that every study, including a laboratory experiment, is a single study, and that the way findings travel beyond it is usually not statistical. Analytic generalisation is a two-step process. First, the researcher makes a conceptual claim: the findings are shown to inform a particular set of concepts, theoretical constructs or a hypothesised sequence of events, ideally ones already present in the literature. Second, the same concepts are applied to argue that other similar situations are implicated. The claim is an argument, not a proof, so it has to be built carefully and be resistant to logical challenge, and it is much stronger when plausible rival explanations have been actively tested and rejected. Yin distinguishes it from transferability, which makes a more modest claim that depends on how similar the sending and receiving contexts are. For UX teams this addresses the recurring objection that eight interviews cannot generalise: the answer is to state which mechanism or concept the study supports or challenges, show the evidence, and say which other products, segments or flows share that mechanism, rather than implying population percentages.
steps: Before fieldwork, name the concepts, theories or hypothesised sequence of events the study could inform
Identify plausible rival explanations and plan to collect evidence that could support them
After analysis, state whether and how the findings supported or challenged each concept, citing the evidence
Test and document the rivals; reject them only where diligent search found no supporting evidence
Raise the claim to the conceptual level and write it as a mechanism, not a frequency
Name the other situations (products, segments, flows) that share the mechanism and argue why the concept applies there
Treat the generalised claim as a working hypothesis to be checked by later studies
outputs: A written generalisation argument linking findings to named concepts, the rivals tested, and a list of other situations to which the concepts are claimed to apply.
useWhen: Small-sample qualitative or single-case studies whose findings need to inform decisions beyond the specific participants, product or site studied.
avoidWhen: The decision needs a population estimate such as prevalence or market size; use a sample survey or analytics instead.
whyLost: UX reporting tends to borrow survey language (most users, 6 of 8) and so either overclaims or apologises for sample size; the theoretical framing analytic generalisation needs is seldom taught in practitioner training.
whereToUse: Discovery research reports, single-customer or single-market case studies, research that must justify reuse across product lines.
example: Interviews with ten clinic administrators show that a scheduling tool is abandoned when it shifts accountability for double bookings onto front-desk staff. The team frames this as a blame-shifting mechanism, rules out the rival that the interface was simply hard to learn, and argues the same mechanism will apply to the company's rota and shift-swap products.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Analytic Hierarchy Process
origin: Thomas Saaty, 1970s (The Analytic Hierarchy Process, 1980)
summary: Structures a decision into a hierarchy of criteria, derives weights from pairwise comparisons and checks the consistency of judgements.
description: AHP decomposes a complex decision (choosing among design directions, vendors or roadmap items) into goal, criteria, sub-criteria and alternatives. Stakeholders compare elements pairwise on Saaty's 1-9 scale; the principal eigenvector of each comparison matrix gives weights, and the consistency ratio (target below 0.10) flags incoherent judgements. Weights combine to rank alternatives. Group judgements can be aggregated by geometric mean. AHP has known criticisms (rank reversal) but makes stakeholder priorities explicit, auditable and testable, a strong upgrade on informal prioritisation meetings.
steps: Define the decision goal, criteria (e.g. user value, effort, risk, strategic fit) and alternatives.
Build the hierarchy and confirm criteria are independent and complete.
Collect pairwise comparisons from stakeholders using the 1-9 scale.
Compute weights (eigenvector) and the consistency ratio; revisit judgements above 0.10.
Score alternatives on each criterion (pairwise or rated), synthesise and rank.
Run sensitivity analysis on weights and share the rationale transparently.
outputs: Criteria weights, consistency ratios, ranked alternatives and sensitivity analyses.
useWhen: Multi-stakeholder prioritisation or design direction decisions with several competing criteria.
avoidWhen: Many alternatives (pairwise burden grows quickly) or decisions dominated by a single criterion.
whyLost: Product teams use simple scoring frameworks (RICE, effort-impact) without weighting rigour or consistency checks.
whereToUse: Roadmap prioritisation, vendor and tool selection, design concept selection, research portfolio planning.
example: A health platform's leadership weights patient safety, clinician time and revenue via AHP. Consistency checks expose contradictory judgements from one executive, and the final ranking moves a safety feature to the top.
sources: Saaty, Decision making with the analytic hierarchy process (2008), International Journal of Services Sciences
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Saaty, T. L. (1980). The Analytic Hierarchy Process. McGraw-Hill.

name: Analytic Induction
origin: Florian Znaniecki, 1934; developed by Alfred Lindesmith (1947) and Donald Cressey (1953)
summary: Iteratively revising a hypothesis or redefining the phenomenon case by case until a proposition holds for every examined case without exception.
description: Analytic induction is a case-by-case logic for testing explanations with qualitative data. The researcher defines the phenomenon, states a working hypothesis about its causes, and examines cases one at a time. Each case that does not fit forces either reformulation of the hypothesis or a justified redefinition of the phenomenon to exclude it; negative cases are never discarded silently. The process continues until a universal statement holds for all cases examined, and the final report documents the trajectory of reformulations and the scope conditions. Classic studies (Lindesmith on opiate addiction, Cressey on embezzlement) showed that small samples can support strong causal propositions when every exception is confronted.
steps: Formulate a provisional definition of the phenomenon to be explained and a working hypothesis about its causes or conditions.
Examine a case. Does the case fit the hypothesis? If yes: proceed to next case.

If the case does not fit: either (a) reformulate the hypothesis to accommodate the case, or (b) redefine the phenomenon to exclude the case (and justify this exclusion). Do not discard the negative case.
Continue until a universal proposition is reached: a statement that holds for all examined cases without exception.
Report: state the final hypothesis, document the trajectory of reformulation, and specify the scope conditions (for what kinds of cases does the hypothesis hold?).
outputs: A final hypothesis that holds for all cases, a documented reformulation history, and explicit scope conditions.
useWhen: When you have a sharply defined outcome (adopted, abandoned, made a critical error) and want a necessary-condition explanation from a modest number of rich cases.
avoidWhen: When outcomes are probabilistic or multi-causal at scale; use regression, qualitative comparative analysis or cross-case analysis instead.
whyLost: Criticised in sociology for seeking universal laws and largely displaced by grounded theory, it never entered UX curricula.
whereToUse: Root-cause investigation of critical failures, safety incidents, and conversion or adoption outcomes in B2B products with small numbers of high-value accounts.
example: A SaaS team studies 14 enterprise accounts that churned. The first hypothesis (no executive sponsor) fails on two cases; reformulating to 'no sponsor and no admin who completed onboarding' holds across all 14, giving a clear intervention target.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Polish Peasant / The Method of Sociology (Znaniecki)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Znaniecki, F. (1934). The Method of Sociology. Farrar & Rinehart.

name: Analytic Memo Writing
origin: Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Strauss, 1987 (Qualitative Analysis for Social Scientists)
summary: Writing dated, code-linked memos throughout analysis as the primary act of theorising, also creating an audit trail of interpretive decisions.
description: Memoing treats writing as thinking. Instead of documenting conclusions reached elsewhere, the analyst writes continuously: a code memo for every new code (scope, properties, illustrative incidents), category memos during axial coding, free-form theoretical memos about surprises and contradictions, and methodological memos recording sampling and procedural decisions. Memos are dated and tagged to the codes they discuss, so they can be sorted later into the skeleton of a report or theory. The practice slows premature closure, captures fleeting insights before they are lost, and makes interpretation traceable. Methodological memos also satisfy Lincoln and Guba's dependability criterion by forming part of the audit trail.
steps: Write a memo every time a new code is created. Every time.
Write a memo every time you notice a connection between two codes.
Write a memo every time you encounter data that surprises you or challenges your expectation.
Date every memo and tag it with the codes it relates to.
Treat memo-writing as primary analysis, not documentation of analysis done elsewhere.
outputs: A searchable corpus of code, category, theoretical and methodological memos that can be sorted into report structure and serve as an audit trail.
useWhen: Any qualitative analysis beyond a quick debrief, especially multi-week studies, team analysis, or work that must be audited or reused later.
avoidWhen: Very rapid evaluative tests where findings are logged directly as issues; even then, a short methodological memo is advisable.
whyLost: Analysis moved into collaborative whiteboards where only clusters survive, and the reflective writing that produced them is rarely kept or valued.
whereToUse: Research repositories, long-running discovery programmes, AI-assisted analysis workflows (to record human interpretive decisions), and regulated research needing audit trails.
example: While coding interviews about an insurance claims app, a researcher writes a memo noting that 'waiting' is described as active monitoring, not passivity. Sorting memos later shows this idea anchors the final model of claim anxiety.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 26 — Grounded Theory — Generating Theory from Data
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing Grounded Theory (2nd ed.). Sage.

extra.Types of Memo: Code memo: Written for a specific code. Describes: what the code covers, its properties and dimensions, incidents that illustrate it, and how it relates to other codes. Written every time a new code is created. Category memo: Written for an emerging category during axial coding. Explores the category's properties (what makes something an instance of this category?) and its relationship to causal conditions, contexts, and consequences. Theoretical memo: Free-form thinking about theoretical connections, surprises, contradictions, and emerging propositions. The most analytically valuable memos. No format requirements — the goal is to think in writing. Methodological memo: Documents decisions about sampling, analysis procedures, and deviations from plan. Creates the audit trail that Lincoln & Guba's dependability criterion requires.

name: Analytics Data Quality Assessment
aka: Data quality assessment for analytics datasets
origin: Pipino, Lee and Wang (2002); Batini et al. (2009); Maydanchik (2007)
summary: Judge whether an analytics dataset is fit for use by counting records that fail completeness, consistency, validity, accuracy and timeliness, before drawing conclusions.
description: Data quality assessment asks whether data are fit for a specific use, not whether they are perfect. Five aspects are checked: completeness (required data present), consistency (no contradictions across sources, such as spelling variants), validity (conformance to rules, such as legal dates), accuracy (agreement with real-world facts) and timeliness (current and delivered on time). Methods include profiling for missing values, outliers and type mismatches; cleansing; validation against predefined rules; governance policies; and auditing against reality or regulation. Each aspect gets a simple count-based metric, such as the share of records missing, invalid or older than a threshold. Metrics are chosen per data type and goal and themselves reviewed, and decisions about exclusions are documented so later analysts can follow them.
steps: Define the intended use of the dataset and the questions it must answer.
Profile the data for missing values, outliers, duplicates and type mismatches.
Validate records against rules (allowed values, date ranges, event sequences).
Count records failing each aspect: completeness, consistency, validity, accuracy and timeliness.
Cleanse or flag failing records and document each exclusion decision.
Audit a sample against reality, for example comparing tracked events with a manual test session.
Repeat the assessment whenever data are refreshed or tracking changes.
outputs: A quality scorecard per aspect, a cleaned or flagged dataset, and documented exclusions.
useWhen: Before analysing product analytics, survey exports, CRM data or social media data, especially after tracking changes or when merging sources.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating a passing scorecard as proof the metric measures the construct; that needs a validity argument. Do not over-cleanse in ways that remove real but unusual behaviour.
whyLost: It belongs to data engineering and governance; UX researchers using analytics often assume the data are sound.
whereToUse: Product analytics, experimentation platforms, research repositories, dashboards feeding UX metrics.
example: Before reporting a fall in checkout completion, a researcher profiles event data and finds 18% of sessions after an app release lack a 'payment_submitted' event. The drop is a tracking fault, not a UX problem.
sources: Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Pipino, L. L., Lee, Y. W. and Wang, R. Y. (2002). Data quality assessment. Communications of the ACM, 45(4), 211-218.

name: Analytics-Driven Playtest
donor: Games user research and game analytics
origin: Described by Graham McAllister and Sebastian Long of Player Research (chapter 8) as one of their eight core services
summary: A usability playtest whose focus is chosen by analytics, so the session reproduces a known drop-off or problem and reveals why it happens.
description: Analytics tell a team where players drop out, fail or stop spending, but not why. An analytics-driven playtest follows the same procedure as a normal observed usability playtest, except that the sections of the game to watch are picked from the data. The narrower the analytics can pin the problem down, for example to one screen or one encounter rather than 'drop-off on Day 3', the better the chance that the issue is reproduced in the lab. Researchers observe players at those points and interview them afterwards, then present the underlying causes and possible fixes, with video of all sessions. Player Research use it in soft launch or after launch, once gameplay is polished, and report that it strengthens understanding and usability insight most, with secondary value for appeal, experience and monetisation (for example why a store or purchase flow underperforms). The method is a simple, structured way to join quantitative and qualitative evidence and applies to any live product with event data.
steps: Review analytics to locate a specific problem point such as a drop-off, failure spike or underused feature.
Narrow the location as far as possible (screen, level section, flow step).
Write a playtest plan and tasks that bring players to that point naturally.
Recruit target players and run observed one-to-one sessions, recording video.
Interview each player about what happened at the focus points.
Synthesise causes, propose fixes, and agree metrics to check whether the fix works after release.
outputs: A report of causes behind the analytics signal with proposed solutions, plus session recordings.
useWhen: A live or soft-launched product shows a clear metric problem whose cause is unknown.
avoidWhen: There is no instrumentation, or the problem cannot be narrowed enough to reproduce in a session.
whyLost: The idea of triangulating analytics with observation is common, but few teams formalise it as a distinct study type with its own planning step.
whereToUse: Free-to-play and live-service games, mobile apps, SaaS onboarding and checkout flows.
example: Data show many players quit at the first boss of a mobile game; eight players are observed reaching that boss and reveal they never noticed the dodge mechanic taught earlier.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 8 (McAllister and Long).

name: Anchoring check for survey questions
aka: Anchoring check for numeric and bracketed survey questions
donor: Judgement and decision making; social psychology
origin: Tversky and Kahneman (1974); later work by Chapman and Johnson, Epley and Gilovich, Strack and Mussweiler
summary: Audits and counterbalances numbers shown before numeric answers, such as example values, default slider positions and starting price brackets, because they anchor responses.
description: In the classic paradigm a random number from a wheel of fortune preceded a higher-or-lower question and an estimate; median estimates of the share of African countries in the UN were 25 and 45 for anchors of 10 and 65, and paying for accuracy did not help. Anchors act even when extreme, unattended or known to be irrelevant, and have most effect when expressed on the response scale and dimension. Survey instruments create anchors routinely: example values in placeholders, default slider positions, the first bracket in an unfolding sequence, prices in willingness-to-pay ladders, or earlier numeric questions. Warnings and incentives do not remove anchoring; prompting people to consider the opposite reduces it. The check audits instruments for such numbers, removes or randomises them, or deliberately splits samples across high and low starting points to measure sensitivity.
steps: Audit questionnaires, pricing questions and moderator scripts for any number that precedes a numeric judgement: examples, defaults, slider start points, first brackets.
Remove anchors that serve no purpose, or replace defaults with blank or neutral starting states.
Where an anchor is unavoidable, split the sample and counterbalance high and low starting values across versions.
Compare median estimates between versions to quantify anchor sensitivity.
Report the difference alongside results, and add a consider-the-opposite prompt where anchors must remain.
outputs: A list of anchors in the instrument, an estimate of anchor sensitivity from split samples, and revised numeric questions.
useWhen: Surveys and interviews with willingness-to-pay, frequency, time or quantity estimates, slider inputs, or bracketed price questions.
avoidWhen: Questions without numeric judgements. Sometimes an anchor is used on purpose to stabilise wild estimates; then document and keep it constant.
whyLost: Anchoring is widely known as a bias, but survey practice in UX seldom audits or split-tests for it, and slider and placeholder defaults are set by designers without measurement in mind.
whereToUse: Pricing research, Van Westendorp and Gabor-Granger studies, usage-frequency questions, onboarding forms that ask for estimates, conversational surveys.
example: A pricing survey shows a slider starting at $20. A split test with sliders starting at $5 and $40 shifts median willingness to pay from $12 to $26, so the team switches to an unanchored text entry and reports the anchor sensitivity.
sources: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974 paper) (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
reference: Tversky, A. and Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131.

name: Anchoring Vignettes
donor: Political science and health survey research
origin: Gary King, Christopher Murray, Joshua Salomon and Ajay Tandon, 2004
summary: Respondents rate short fixed scenarios on the same scale as themselves, allowing correction for groups using the response scale differently.
description: When users in different countries or segments rate 'ease of use' on a 1-5 scale, differences may reflect different interpretations of the scale (differential item functioning), not experiences. Anchoring vignettes describe hypothetical people or situations at fixed levels of the construct. Because the vignettes are identical for everyone, differences in how they are rated reveal each group's response scale. Nonparametric methods recode self-ratings relative to vignette ratings; parametric models (CHOPIT) estimate thresholds. This is the leading solution for cross-cultural and cross-segment comparability of self-report scales.
steps: Write 3-5 vignettes describing fixed levels of the construct (e.g. users with varying difficulty completing a task).
Ask respondents to rate themselves and each vignette on the same scale, randomising vignette order.
Check vignette equivalence and response consistency (vignettes rated in expected order).
Recode self-ratings relative to vignettes (nonparametric C-scores) or fit a CHOPIT model.
Compare groups on corrected scores and report how conclusions change.
Retain vignettes for future waves to monitor scale-use drift.
outputs: DIF-corrected comparisons across groups, threshold estimates and vignette diagnostics.
useWhen: Comparing self-reported experience across countries, cultures, age groups or professions.
avoidWhen: Within-group comparisons over time with stable populations, or when objective measures exist.
whyLost: It is published in political science and health metrics, and global UX programmes rarely address scale-use differences.
whereToUse: Global satisfaction programmes, cross-market benchmarks, international health app outcomes, B2B surveys across roles.
example: A global CSAT programme shows Japan lowest. Anchoring vignettes reveal Japanese respondents rate identical vignettes lower; after correction Japan ranks mid-table, redirecting investment.
sources: King, Murray, Salomon & Tandon, Enhancing the validity and cross-cultural comparability of measurement in survey research (2004), American Political Science Review
King & Wand, Comparing incomparable survey responses (2007), Political Analysis
reference: King, G., et al. (2004). American Political Science Review, 98(1), 191-207.

name: ANOVA for Multi-Design Comparisons (One-Way and Two-Way)
summary: Tests whether three or more designs differ on a continuous measure, and whether two factors interact.
description: When comparing more than two designs, running every pairwise t-test inflates false positives. ANOVA tests all groups at once by comparing variation between groups to variation within them (the F-statistic). Two-way ANOVA adds a second factor, such as device or experience level, and tests their interaction: does the new design help novices more than experts? Significant results are followed by planned contrasts or corrected post-hoc comparisons. Bruce and Bruce also show a resampling (permutation) version that avoids distributional assumptions.
steps: Define factors and levels (for example, design A/B/C by device desktop/mobile).
Log-transform task times; check group variances are not wildly different.
Run one-way or two-way ANOVA and read the F tests for main effects and interactions.
Follow significant effects with corrected pairwise comparisons (Tukey, Holm, Bonferroni).
Report effect sizes (partial eta squared) and plots of group means with intervals.
outputs: Tests of differences among several designs and of interactions between factors.
useWhen: Three or more design variants, or two crossed factors.
avoidWhen: Binary outcomes (use logistic regression or chi-square) or only two groups (a t-test is simpler).
whyLost: Not lost, but UX teams often avoid multi-arm studies or analyse them with multiple t-tests.
whereToUse: Design explorations with several prototypes, multi-variant tests, device-by-design studies.
example: Three navigation prototypes on two devices: the two-way ANOVA shows no overall design effect but a strong interaction, as the mega-menu fails only on mobile.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)

Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Applied Statistics and Probability for Engineers: Student Solutions Manual (Montgomery & Runger, 2002)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)

name: Answering Objections to Research (Rebuttal Table and Mock Buyer Interview)
aka: Objections to research and the real reasons behind them
Mock buyer interview with a stakeholder role-playing the buyer
Answering the 'we know our buyers' objection
donor: Design research practice; B2B marketing research
origin: Erika Hall / Mule Design practice (2013); Adele Revella (2015) for the mock buyer interview
summary: Buy-in tactics that prepare replies to standard objections to research and let a sceptical stakeholder role-play a buyer in a mock interview to expose what they do not know.
description: Teams proposing research meet a predictable set of objections: no time, no budget or expertise, the CEO decides anyway, we already know, we will find out in beta, it gets in the way of innovation. Hall lists them with rebuttals and names the real reasons often behind them: inertia, fear of being wrong and discomfort talking to people. Preparing a rebuttal table in advance turns an argument into a routine reply. Revella adds a sharper tactic for the 'we already know our buyers' objection: accept the stakeholder's offer of expertise and interview them, using normal interview technique, first in role as a buyer who chose the product and then as one who chose a competitor. Interrupting marketing-speak and pressing on stock answers such as 'too expensive' makes the gaps visible to the stakeholder themselves. The exercise ends with a proposal for a small study, not with the role-play data, which is biased by construction.
steps: List the objections you expect (time, budget, expertise, executive decides, we already know, find out in beta, too slow, stifles innovation) and write a short rebuttal for each.
For each objection, note the likely underlying reason (fear of being wrong, discomfort with users, inertia) and how to address it.
When a stakeholder claims to know buyers already, agree a 45-60 minute session in which you interview them.
Interview them in role as a recent buyer who chose your product, interrupting whenever answers slip into sales or marketing language.
Repeat with them in role as a buyer who chose a competitor, pressing stock reasons such as price with questions about perceived value.
Debrief on the questions they could not answer and propose a small interview study (for example 6-10 buyers) tied to one business goal.
Record the role-play answers as hypotheses only, to be checked in the real study.
outputs: A rebuttal table for common objections, stakeholder agreement to a small study, and an initial set of hypotheses from the role-play.
useWhen: Use when research is being blocked by scepticism rather than by a real constraint, especially in sales-led or founder-led organisations that believe they already know their customers.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the role-play as evidence: the answers are the stakeholder's beliefs. Use Buyer Persona interviews or Jobs-to-be-Done Switch Interviews for real buyer data. Handle it tactfully; a stakeholder who feels exposed will resist further.
whyLost: It survived because every in-house researcher faces the same objections; Hall's list is widely taught, though the mock buyer interview is less known outside B2B marketing.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS, sales-led start-ups, agencies pitching discovery work, new research teams establishing a mandate.
example: A VP of sales insists research is unnecessary. The researcher interviews him as a buyer who chose a rival and asks why, if buyers think as he says, the company is not winning every deal; he agrees to eight win-loss interviews.
reference: Hall, E. (2013). Just Enough Research. New York: A Book Apart, pp. 18-22; Revella, A. (2015). Buyer Personas. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Anthropometric Analysis
origin: Military human engineering, 1940s-1970s; Pheasant (1986)
summary: Uses population body-dimension data and percentile limits to size reach, grip, touch targets and viewing geometry for the intended user range.
description: Anthropometric analysis designs for the range of human bodies using population databases of dimensions such as finger breadth, hand length, reach envelope and eye height. Designers set design limits (often 5th to 95th percentile of the target population) and check that clearances, reaches and target sizes accommodate them. The treatise lists anthropometric databases among the rigorous human factors methods UX abandoned. In digital products it governs touch target sizing, thumb reach zones on large phones, wearable fit, kiosk height and XR interaction volumes. Rigour comes from using data for the actual target population (age, sex, nationality, disability) rather than designing for an imaginary average user.
steps: Define the user population, including age range, regions and disability groups.
Identify the body dimensions that constrain the design (for example fingertip width, thumb reach, standing eye height).
Obtain percentile data from a relevant anthropometric database or measure a sample.
Set accommodation targets, commonly 5th-95th percentile, or wider for safety-critical products.
Check designs with digital human models or physical mock-ups at the boundary percentiles.
Document accommodation achieved and residual exclusion.
outputs: Design limits table, reach and target-size specifications, accommodation percentage.
useWhen: Touch, wearable, kiosk, automotive and XR products where body dimensions constrain use.
avoidWhen: Purely cognitive or content problems; screen-only desktop software rarely needs it.
whyLost: UX grew from graphic design and software, not ergonomics engineering, and assumed screens removed the body from the problem.
whereToUse: Large-phone thumb zones, smartwatches, ticket kiosks, in-car touchscreens, VR controllers, accessible public terminals.
example: A transit agency's kiosk places the payment slot at a height that only 60% of wheelchair users can reach; percentile analysis sets a new range accommodating 95%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Pheasant S & Haslegrave CM (2006) Bodyspace: Anthropometry, Ergonomics and the Design of Work
Parkinson MB et al. on design for human variability
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Pheasant S & Haslegrave CM (2006) Bodyspace: Anthropometry, Ergonomics and the Design of Work. 3rd ed. CRC Press.

name: Anthropometric Percentile Accommodation Analysis
origin: Military anthropometric surveys (1940s-1960s); codified by Stephen Pheasant (Bodyspace, 1986)
summary: Uses population body-dimension data to design for a target percentage of users, typically the 5th to 95th percentile, and checks combined accommodation.
description: Anthropometry provides distributions of body dimensions such as hand length, finger breadth, reach and eye height for defined populations. Designers choose the limiting user for each dimension (smallest for reach, largest for clearance) and design for a target range. A key subtlety is that accommodating 90% on each of several dimensions accommodates far fewer people on all of them simultaneously, so multivariate methods or digital human models are needed. For digital products, the method applies to touch target size, thumb reach zones, wearable fit, kiosk heights and VR headset adjustment, and it forces explicit decisions about who is excluded, an inclusive design question with numbers.
steps: Identify the target population and source matching anthropometric data (age, sex, nationality, disability).
List the design-relevant dimensions and the limiting user for each (e.g. 5th percentile thumb reach, 95th percentile finger pad width).
Calculate percentile values with appropriate clothing or posture corrections.
Assess multivariate accommodation by simulation or boundary manikins, as univariate 5-95 limits exclude more than 10% combined.
Prototype at the limiting dimensions and test with participants recruited at the extremes.
Document the percentage accommodated and who remains excluded, with adjustable or alternative options for them.
outputs: Design dimension specifications, accommodation percentages, a list of excluded groups and mitigation options.
useWhen: Physical products, wearables, kiosks, automotive HMIs, touch-target sizing and one-handed reach zones.
avoidWhen: Purely software decisions without physical dimensions.
whyLost: Digital UX treats bodies as interchangeable cursor operators and adopts platform guidelines without knowing their anthropometric basis.
whereToUse: Mobile thumb zones for large phones, smartwatch UIs, ATMs and kiosks, VR and AR devices, accessible hardware.
example: A bank sizes its new ATM screen and keypad height using wheelchair-user reach data, accommodating 95% of seated users instead of the previous design that excluded most of them.
sources: Pheasant & Haslegrave, Bodyspace: Anthropometry, Ergonomics and the Design of Work (3rd ed., 2006)
ISO 7250-1:2017 Basic human body measurements for technological design
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
reference: Pheasant, S., & Haslegrave, C. M. (2006). Bodyspace (3rd ed.). CRC Press.

name: Anticipatory Failure Determination (AFD)
donor: Systems engineering / TRIZ inventive problem solving
origin: Boris Zlotin, Alla Zusman and colleagues (Ideation International), 1990s, based on Altshuller's TRIZ
summary: Inverts failure analysis by asking how one could deliberately make the system fail, then uses resource analysis to find and block those routes.
description: Listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix for systems engineering, AFD applies TRIZ to failure. Instead of asking 'what might go wrong?', which is limited by imagination and optimism, analysts take a subversion stance: 'how could we make this fail?' They then search for the resources (substances, fields, time, user behaviours, system states) in the system that would enable that failure, and design out the routes. For UX, the subversive question becomes 'how would we design this flow to make users lose money, leak data or give up?', a stance that surfaces dark-pattern-like risks and abuse cases that conventional reviews miss.
steps: Define the undesired outcome (for example user unknowingly shares location).
Reformulate as an invention problem: how could we deliberately cause it?
Brainstorm subversion scenarios using existing system resources and user behaviours.
Check which scenarios are already possible in the current design.
Design countermeasures that remove the enabling resources.
Re-run subversion on the revised design.
outputs: Subversion scenarios, resource inventory, countermeasures.
useWhen: Anticipating misuse, abuse, privacy and safety failures; red-teaming designs and AI features.
avoidWhen: Mature, well-characterised failures already covered by FMEA data.
whyLost: TRIZ is niche even in engineering; UX never adopted structured inventive methods.
whereToUse: Trust and safety, privacy-by-design, AI red-teaming, child safety features, fraud prevention.
example: Asked 'how could we make users accidentally publish private notes?', a team finds a share link inherited by duplicated notes, and fixes it before launch.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kaplan S, Visnepolschi S, Zlotin B & Zusman A (1999) New Tools for Failure and Risk Analysis: Anticipatory Failure Determination and the Theory of Scenario Structuring. Ideation International
Altshuller G (1984) Creativity as an Exact Science
Kaplan, Visnepolschi, Zlotin & Zusman, New Tools for Failure and Risk Analysis: Anticipatory Failure Determination and the Theory of Scenario Structuring (1999), Ideation International
reference: Kaplan S et al. (1999) New Tools for Failure and Risk Analysis: Anticipatory Failure Determination (AFD). Ideation International.

name: Anxiety Intensity and Direction Rating (CSAI-2 Directional)
donor: Sport psychology and test anxiety research
origin: CSAI-2 by Martens and colleagues (1990); direction modification by Jones (1995), following Alpert and Haber's (1960) facilitating and debilitating test anxiety scales; critically reviewed by Hanin in the Handbook
summary: Measures cognitive and somatic anxiety and self-confidence before a performance, and adds a rating of whether each symptom is felt to help or hinder.
description: The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 measures state cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety and self-confidence just before a performance. Jones's directional modification adds a second rating to each item, from -3 (very debilitative) to +3 (very facilitative), so each subscale yields both an intensity score and a direction score (from -27 to +27). The Handbook traces the idea back to Alpert and Haber's test-anxiety work and notes that elite performers often report anxiety as more facilitative. It also sets out limits: direction is not well defined, ratings do not say how anxiety helps or hurts, and studies often do not check direction against actual performance. In UX, the pairing of intensity and perceived effect is useful wherever users perform under evaluation: online exams and proctoring, job-interview video platforms, presentation tools, live coding interviews, and the usability test session itself. Two users with the same anxiety level can see it very differently, and the direction score separates challenge from threat. Because the original items are sport-worded, they need careful adaptation and validation.
steps: Adapt item wording to the product context and pilot it for comprehension.
Administer intensity items shortly before the evaluated task, then the direction item for each symptom.
Score cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety and self-confidence for both intensity and direction.
Measure task performance so that direction ratings can be checked against outcomes.
Compare conditions (for example practice mode on and off) on intensity and direction separately.
Interview high-intensity, negative-direction users to find the design triggers.
outputs: Intensity and direction scores for cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety and self-confidence, linked to task performance.
useWhen: Users carry out evaluated, high-stakes tasks through the product and you want to separate how anxious they are from whether that anxiety hurts.
avoidWhen: Tasks carry no evaluative pressure, or you cannot validate adapted items in your population.
whyLost: UX anxiety measurement rarely goes beyond general state-anxiety items; competitive anxiety instruments are sport-specific and the directional idea has not crossed over.
whereToUse: Online assessment and exam platforms, interview and hiring tools, presentation and public-speaking apps, competitive games, driving-test simulators.
example: An online exam provider tests a new countdown timer. Intensity of cognitive anxiety rises similarly with both timer designs, but the direction score turns negative only with the flashing red timer, and those students score lower; the team adopts the calmer design.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Hanin, Y. L. (2007) 'Emotions in sport: current issues and perspectives', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 2.

name: App Usage Analytics as Qualitative Trace Data
origin: Trace ethnography (Geiger and Ribes, 2011) and qualitative web analytics practice
summary: Reads behavioural logs, session paths, errors and abandonment points as qualitative evidence of intent and struggle, reconstructing session narratives rather than only counting events.
description: Digital trace data — logs, clicks, navigation paths, search queries, error patterns, abandonment points — is usually treated as quantitative. But trace data can also be analysed qualitatively: as evidence of users' intentions, confusions, mental models, and strategies. The key shift is from counting events to interpreting patterns of events as evidence of underlying experience. This is 'qualitative in spirit even when the data is structured' — the analyst is asking 'what does this pattern mean?' rather than 'how often does this occur?'
steps: Session narrative reading: For a sample of individual sessions, reconstruct a narrative of what the user was trying to do: what problem were they solving? Where did they encounter difficulty? How did they respond to difficulty?

Path analysis as intention mapping: What navigation paths do users take? Which paths suggest clear intention? Which suggest confusion, search, or guessing? The shape of a path is evidence of a mental model.
Error pattern analysis: Which errors recur across users? What do they reveal about shared misunderstandings or failed affordances? Errors are qualitative data about the user-interface mismatch.

Abandonment context analysis: For sessions that end in abandonment: what was the user trying to do? At what point did they give up? What preceded the abandonment? This sequence is the qualitative story of a failed experience.

Triangulate with interview data: Use the patterns identified in trace data as prompts for qualitative interviews: 'I can see that lots of users do X at this point — does that match your experience? What were you thinking when you did that?'
outputs: Reconstructed session narratives, path-based intention hypotheses, recurring error and abandonment contexts, and interview probes grounded in observed behaviour.
useWhen: You have rich event or session data and need to understand what users were trying to do when metrics change, or to generate grounded hypotheses before interviews.
avoidWhen: You need to quantify prevalence or test causal impact; use product analytics or A/B testing. Logs cannot reveal motivations alone, so do not substitute this for talking to users.
whyLost: Analytics and qualitative research sit in different teams and tools, so logs are aggregated into funnels while the individual session stories they contain are rarely read.
whereToUse: SaaS onboarding, e-commerce checkout, search and navigation, AI assistant conversation logs, and churn investigations.
example: A SaaS team reads 40 session replays and event sequences from users who abandoned setup. Narratives show users repeatedly toggling between pricing and integrations, suggesting doubt about whether their tool is supported, which interviews confirm.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley)
reference: Geiger, R. S. & Ribes, D. (2011). Trace ethnography: Following coordination through documentary practices. Proceedings of HICSS-44.

name: Appeal / Enhance / Awaken Profiling
origin: John Whalen (2019)
summary: A framing practice that sorts research findings into what attracts people now, what would improve their lives in months, and what serves their deepest goals and fears.
description: Whalen's framework asks a team to read user value on three planes. Appeal is what people say they want and what draws them in, inferred from their attention, language and framing of the problem. Enhance is what would actually solve their problem over the coming months, inferred from how they decide, outdated frames of reference and pain points. Awaken is what would help them reach life goals and allay fears, inferred from emotion, what success means to them and the steps they believe lead there. Findings from deep interviews are sorted into the three tiers and summarised as a persona table with one column per tier for each segment. The tiers then steer different work: Appeal feeds positioning and promotion, Enhance feeds product and service design, Awaken feeds long-term resonance. The quality of the output depends entirely on interviews reaching goals and fears, not just feature wishes.
steps: Plan interviews that move from innocuous questions to deep ones about goals, success and fears.
Record each participant's life stage, major fears and how much is at stake in the decision.
After synthesis, sort findings into Appeal (stated wants, language), Enhance (real near-term problems) and Awaken (life goals and fears).
Build a persona table per segment with three columns, one per tier.
Map Appeal to messaging and acquisition, Enhance to product and service features, Awaken to long-term engagement and progress cues.
Check where Appeal and Enhance diverge and plan how to attract people with what they want and then educate them towards what helps.
outputs: A three-tier persona or psychographic profile per segment, with positioning and design priorities for each tier.
useWhen: Use after in-depth interviews when a team needs to separate what will attract users from what will help them, for example in financial, health or career products where stated wants and real benefit differ.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for research: without interviews that reach goals and fears the Awaken column is invented. For measuring how strongly segments hold these values use Laddering (Means-End Chain Analysis) or a survey; for building personas from data use Latent Class Analysis for Personas.
whyLost: It is a recent, single-author framework presented within a broader cognitive model; few teams have adopted it outside Whalen's consultancy, though the underlying idea of layered value is familiar.
whereToUse: Wealth management, insurance, health coaching, B2B products where buyers and users fear losing standing.
example: A pensions app finds that savers are drawn by a simple balance view (Appeal), need help consolidating old pots (Enhance) and fear running out of money in old age (Awaken). The team sells the balance view, builds consolidation, and adds a retirement-readiness progress view.
reference: Whalen, J. (2019). Design for How People Think: Using Brain Science to Build Better Products. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Applicability-Domain Check for Predictive Models
origin: Applicability domain concept from QSAR (Netzeva et al., 2005); classifier approach adapted from Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman by Kuhn and Johnson (2013)
summary: Train a classifier to tell real training rows from a permuted copy of them, then use its membership probability to flag new cases whose predictions are likely extrapolations.
description: Predictive models assume new cases come from the same data-generating process as the training set. Extrapolation includes values outside training ranges and also empty interior regions of a high-dimensional predictor space. Knowing how both data sets were produced is the first defence. A quick global check projects training and new data onto principal components and looks for overlap, but two-dimensional projections can hide sparse pockets. For a case-level check Kuhn and Johnson adapt Hastie and colleagues: rather than sampling uniformly across predictor ranges, they permute each predictor independently, which spreads points across the space while keeping only allowable values, and they restrict this to the top 20 or so important predictors. A classifier trained to separate real from permuted rows then scores each new case by its probability of resembling the training data. Low scores mark predictions to treat with caution.
steps: Fit the predictive model, compute variable importance and keep the top predictors (for example 20).
Create a random version of the training set by permuting each of those predictors independently.
Stack the real and permuted rows and label them training versus random.
Train a classifier (for example bagged trees) to separate the two.
Predict the probability of training-set membership for each new case, and overlay training and new data on principal components as a global check.
Flag low-probability cases as extrapolations, and route them to fallback behaviour or human review.
outputs: A similarity-to-training probability for each new case and overlay plots of training and new data.
useWhen: Deploying a predictive feature (risk score, recommendation, triage, estimate) to new users, markets or contexts and needing to know which individual predictions rest on unfamiliar inputs.
avoidWhen: It says nothing about whether the outcome relationship itself has changed, and results depend on the predictors and classifier chosen. For population-level shift over time use distribution or drift monitoring such as Mixed-Methods Behavioral Drift Detection Framework.
whyLost: It is standard in cheminformatics model governance but uncommon in product ML, where monitoring focuses on aggregate drift rather than per-case trust.
whereToUse: Credit and insurance scoring UIs, clinical prediction tools, AI features launched in new markets, confidence cues and fallbacks in AI products.
example: A lending app's affordability model is trained on salaried applicants. The membership classifier gives gig-economy applicants low scores, so the interface shows those estimates as provisional and offers a call with an adviser.
reference: Kuhn, M. and Johnson, K. (2013). Applied Predictive Modeling. New York: Springer, pp. 34-35, 534-541; Netzeva, T. I. et al. (2005). Current status of methods for defining the applicability domain of (quantitative) structure-activity relationships. ATLA 33(2).

name: Applied Cognitive Work Analysis (ACWA)
origin: Elm, Potter, Gualtieri, Easter and Roth (2003); case studies by Potter, Gualtieri and Elm (2003)
summary: An engineering form of cognitive work analysis that carries domain analysis through to display concepts via five linked, traceable artefacts, from a functional abstraction network to presentation designs.
description: ACWA was built to close the gap between cognitive analysis and design. It produces a chain of five artefacts: a Functional Abstraction Network of domain goals, processes and means; cognitive work requirements (the decisions and monitoring each node demands); information and relationship requirements; representation design requirements, which also serve as test specifications; and presentation design concepts as storyboards or prototypes. Each artefact links back to the previous one, so every display element can be traced to a domain function and decision. The work proceeds in expanding spirals, with knowledge elicitation used to bootstrap the network, and a quality worksheet checks the functional network. Worked applications include military command and control decision support. Its rigour lies in traceability; its cost is heavy documentation and the need for skilled modellers.
steps: Bootstrap a Functional Abstraction Network of goals, processes and means from documents and expert elicitation, and check it with the quality worksheet.
Overlay the cognitive work requirements (decisions, monitoring, planning) at each network node.
Derive the information and relationship requirements each decision needs.
Write representation design requirements that state how each relationship should be shown; these double as evaluation criteria.
Produce presentation design concepts as storyboards or prototypes.
Iterate in expanding spirals across the domain, preserving links between all five artefacts.
outputs: Five linked artefacts (FAN, cognitive work requirements, information requirements, representation requirements, presentation concepts) with traceability from display to domain function.
useWhen: Designing decision-support displays for complex, high-consequence domains where every element must be justified by a domain function and requirements must be testable.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple or consumer products where the documentation overhead outweighs the benefit; use Hierarchical Task Analysis or Cognitive Task Analysis. For constraint-based analysis without a design thread, use Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA).
whyLost: It stayed in defence and process-control engineering because it is documentation-heavy and needs specialist modellers.
whereToUse: Operations and monitoring dashboards, grid and energy control, clinical decision support, cybersecurity consoles.
example: A grid operator's alarm console is redesigned by building a functional network from 'keep frequency stable' down to generators and interconnectors. Each new display element traces to a decision such as 'is reserve sufficient for the next hour', and those requirements become the test script.
reference: Elm, W. C., Potter, S. S., Gualtieri, J. W., Easter, J. R. and Roth, E. M. (2003). Applied cognitive work analysis: a pragmatic methodology for designing revolutionary cognitive affordances. In E. Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (pp. 357-382). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Appraisal Theory Analysis (Martin and White)
origin: James Martin and Peter White, 2005 (The Language of Evaluation), building on Michael Halliday's systemic functional linguistics
summary: Codes evaluative language into attitude (affect, judgement, appreciation), engagement and graduation to analyse how users express feelings and stance far more precisely than sentiment scores.
description: Sentiment analysis reduces evaluation to positive or negative. Appraisal theory distinguishes Attitude: Affect (emotions: 'I was furious'), Judgement (evaluating people's behaviour: 'they were dishonest') and Appreciation (evaluating things: 'the app is clunky'); Engagement (how voices are positioned: acknowledging, denying, conceding); and Graduation (force and focus: 'really', 'kind of'). This reveals, for example, whether complaints target the product (appreciation) or the company's integrity (judgement), which have different implications. Systematic coding with defined categories and reliability checks provides rigorous evaluative analysis of interviews, reviews and support conversations.
steps: Select texts and define the evaluative targets of interest (product, company, self, others).
Code instances of Affect, Judgement and Appreciation with polarity and target.
Code Engagement (monoglossic vs heteroglossic resources) and Graduation (force, focus).
Check inter-coder reliability on a subset and refine coding guidelines.
Aggregate patterns by target, segment and context; read examples in context.
Translate findings into design or communication actions (e.g. integrity concerns need trust repair, not UI polish).
outputs: Appraisal-coded corpus, distributions of attitude types by target, engagement patterns and interpretations.
useWhen: Analysing complaints, reviews, interviews or social media where the type of evaluation matters.
avoidWhen: When only broad positive or negative polarity is needed at large scale with no time for coding.
whyLost: Systemic functional linguistics is specialised and largely confined to linguistics and education research.
whereToUse: Complaint analysis, brand trust research, AI response tone evaluation, employee feedback.
example: Appraisal coding of 500 app reviews after a pricing change shows a shift from Appreciation of the app to negative Judgement of the company ('greedy', 'sneaky'), signalling a trust issue rather than a usability one.
sources: Martin & White, The Language of Evaluation: Appraisal in English (2005)
Halliday & Matthiessen, Halliday's Introduction to Functional Grammar (4th ed., 2014)
reference: Martin, J. R., & White, P. R. R. (2005). The Language of Evaluation. Palgrave Macmillan.

name: Appreciative Inquiry
origin: David Cooperrider and Suresh Srivastva, Case Western Reserve University, 1987
summary: Participants interview each other about peak experiences and strengths, then analyse the stories together for themes to build on, rather than starting from problems.
description: Appreciative inquiry starts from what works rather than what is broken. Participants are trained briefly and interview one another in pairs using a small set of positive questions, for example a time they felt most alive and engaged; what they value about themselves, their work and the organisation; the core factors that give life to the organisation; and three wishes for its future. The resulting stories, examples and metaphors are analysed together in groups to find shared themes, which become the foundation for development plans. Data collection, analysis and change are blended in one participatory process, usually framed as discovery, dream, design and destiny phases. The positive framing builds energy and ownership, but can suppress real problems, so it works best alongside methods that surface pain points.
steps: Agree the focus of inquiry with sponsors and frame it positively (for example 'exceptional customer moments' rather than 'complaints').
Train participants briefly in paired interviewing.
Have pairs interview each other with four or five appreciative questions about peak experiences, values, core strengths and wishes.
Collect the stories, examples and metaphors of the organisation or product at its best.
In groups, analyse the interviews for common themes and the conditions that made peak experiences possible.
Turn themes into shared aspirations and concrete design or development commitments, and review them later.
outputs: Stories of peak experiences, shared themes of strengths, and aspirations and plans owned by participants.
useWhen: You want to engage a team, service organisation or community in change, or to find what already works in a service so it can be extended, especially where morale is low.
avoidWhen: You need a balanced diagnosis of failures or usability problems; pair with problem-focused research or use journey mapping, interviews or usability testing.
whyLost: It is a mainstream organisational development method, but UX research rarely uses strength-based inquiry and treats it as facilitation rather than research.
whereToUse: Service design with frontline staff, internal tools adoption, research operations and design-team culture, and community or public-sector projects.
example: A hospital service design team runs appreciative interviews among nurses about shifts that went exceptionally well. Themes of 'protected handover time' and 'visible bed status' become requirements for the new ward dashboard.
reference: Cooperrider, D. L., & Srivastva, S. (1987). Appreciative inquiry in organizational life. Research in Organizational Change and Development, 1, 129-169.

name: Appropriateness assessment for AI-assisted coding
aka: When AI coding is appropriate vs. inappropriate
origin: Emerging methodological debate from 2023 (e.g. Braun and Clarke's position on reflexive TA; Morgan, 2023)
summary: A structured judgement of whether AI coding fits a given study, based on epistemology, data sensitivity, task type and validation capacity, before any automation is used.
description: Not all qualitative work suits AI assistance. Deductive coding against a clear codebook, large corpora, and descriptive content analysis are better fits; reflexive thematic analysis, interpretative phenomenological analysis and work where researcher positionality is central are poor fits, because coding there is the researcher's own interpretive engagement. Data sensitivity, consent terms, participant vulnerability and language also matter, as does whether the team can validate outputs. A structured assessment makes the decision explicit and defensible, rather than defaulting to automation because tools are available. Rigour comes from documenting criteria, the decision and its rationale, and revisiting it if validation results are poor.
steps: Identify the analytic approach and its epistemology (e.g. deductive content analysis, codebook TA, reflexive TA, IPA).
Classify the task: deductive application of codes, inductive suggestion, summarisation or interpretation.
Assess data sensitivity, consent terms and participant vulnerability, and whether local processing is required.
Assess validation capacity: can humans code a 10-20% sample to measure agreement?
Decide: AI not used, AI as suggester only, or AI as primary coder with validation; document the rationale.
Revisit the decision if agreement falls below the pre-set threshold (e.g. kappa below 0.70) or new risks emerge.
outputs: A documented appropriateness decision with criteria, rationale and conditions for revisiting.
useWhen: Before any AI-assisted qualitative study, especially those to be published or involving sensitive data.
avoidWhen: Not needed for non-research uses such as meeting notes, but any output presented as research findings should go through it.
whyLost: Methodological guidance has lagged behind tool adoption, so most teams adopt AI coding without explicit fitness judgements.
whereToUse: Academic UX research, health and public-sector research, and research operations policies.
example: A team planning an IPA study of people living with chronic pain decides AI will only transcribe, not code, because interpretation is the method and data are sensitive. A parallel deductive analysis of 5,000 app reviews uses AI coding with validation.
sources: Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2022) Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide
Morgan, D. L. (2023) Exploring the use of artificial intelligence for qualitative data analysis: The case of ChatGPT. International Journal of Qualitative Methods
The Inquiry Series, C14 — Ethical Constraints & Epistemological Limits of AI-Assisted Qualitative Research
reference: Morgan, D. L. (2023) Exploring the use of artificial intelligence for qualitative data analysis: The case of ChatGPT. International Journal of Qualitative Methods 22

name: Argument-Based Validation of Archival and Secondary-Data Measures
aka: Messick validity facets for secondary data
donor: Psychometrics, applied in management and economics research
origin: Messick (1995); Kane (1992, 2013); Cook and Beckman (2006); applied to archival data by Miller (2023)
summary: Justify interpreting an existing metric as a construct with evidence on content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables and consequences, iterating on weak assumptions.
description: Validity belongs to an interpretation and use, not to a measure. Argument-based validation, from Messick and Kane, builds a case for using an existing metric as evidence of something. Content evidence asks whether the measure covers the construct and excludes unwanted variance, for example aggregates that mix unrelated components. Response-process evidence asks whether the data were generated by a stable process: incentives to misreport, policy changes that altered recording, independent raters, units based on few records (weight by the square root of record counts), and imputation by the source. Internal structure checks factor patterns among multiple indicators. Relations to other variables test whether correlations match theory, ideally across sources. Consequences ask what happens when the metric is used, for example in rankings. Kane's procedure is to state the interpretation, gather evidence on the weakest assumptions, and iterate.
steps: State the intended interpretation and use of the measure (for example 'support tickets per user indicate task difficulty').
Gather content evidence: does the measure cover the construct, and what unrelated variance does it include? Check definitions with the data owner.
Examine the response process: incentives, policy or tracking changes, rater independence, small-count units and source imputation.
Check internal structure where several indicators exist, watching for near-perfect correlations or group differences.
Test relations to other variables against theory, preferably using independent sources.
Consider the consequences of using the measure, such as gaming once it becomes a target.
Collect further evidence on the weakest assumptions and iterate, documenting the argument.
outputs: A documented validity argument for each metric, identifying its weakest assumptions and the evidence for and against.
useWhen: Using existing operational data (analytics events, support tickets, CRM fields, app-store ratings) as UX metrics or KPIs, especially for decisions or public reporting.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you can design a purpose-built measure and validate it psychometrically; for survey instruments use standard reliability and factor analysis.
whyLost: Validity theory lives in psychometrics and education; product teams adopt proxy metrics without asking what they mean.
whereToUse: UX KPI programmes, north-star metric selection, HEART metric definitions, dashboards used in performance reviews.
example: A team wants 'time in app' as an engagement KPI. The validity argument finds that a background-sync change inflated it and that it correlates negatively with task success, so it is dropped for completed-task rate.
sources: Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Validating the Interpretations and Uses of Test Scores (Kane, 2013)
reference: Kane, M. T. (2013). Validating the interpretations and uses of test scores. Journal of Educational Measurement, 50(1), 1-73; Miller, J. (2023). Archival data. In A. L. Nichols and J. E. Edlund (Eds.), The Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods and Statistics for the Social and Behavioral Sciences, Vol. 1 (pp. 400-419). Cambridge University Press.

name: Arts-Based Research
origin: Elliot Eisner, 1990s; Patricia Leavy, 2009
summary: Uses art-making (drawing, collage, poetry, performance) as a means of eliciting and representing experience that participants struggle to put into words.
description: Arts-based research treats artistic practice as a legitimate mode of inquiry: participants (and sometimes researchers) create drawings, collages, poems, photographs or performances that express experiences, and these artefacts are analysed together with the participant's account of them. The premise is that some knowledge is tacit, emotional or embodied and is distorted when forced into propositional speech. ABR is rigorous when the art-making prompt is carefully framed, the participant's own interpretation is captured rather than the researcher reading meaning into images, analysis is systematic across artefacts, and the study is explicit about what claims it can make. It also offers evocative ways to represent findings to stakeholders, strengthening empathy without sacrificing traceability to the data.
steps: Choose ABR form appropriate to the research question and population:
Visual narrative — participants draw or collage their experience of using a product.
(2) Photovoice — participants photograph their usage context and caption the photos.
(3) Drama/role-play — participants enact future use scenarios.

(4) Musical mapping — participants select music that represents their emotional experience of the product. Analyze: what does the form of the artifact (not just its content) reveal about the experience?
outputs: Participant-made artefacts with their own interpretations, thematic analysis of artefacts and talk, evocative representations for stakeholder communication.
useWhen: Exploring emotional, embodied, or tacit experiences (illness, grief, money anxiety, identity), with participants for whom verbal interviews are limiting, or when findings must move stakeholders emotionally.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need measurable or generalisable answers, when participants would find art-making patronising or exposing, or when time is very short; use interviews or surveys instead.
whyLost: ABR lives in education and health social science; UX borrowed fragments (collage in generative sessions) without the analytic framework that treats art as data.
whereToUse: Designing for non-verbal populations, emotional experience research, health and wellbeing product research, cross-cultural UX research.
example: A mental health app team asks young adults to make collages of 'a bad week with my phone'; the artefacts reveal notification shame that never surfaced in interviews, reshaping the notification strategy.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 33
The Inquiry Series, Ch 33 — Participatory & Arts-Based Methods
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Leavy P (2015) Method Meets Art: Arts-Based Research Practice. 2nd ed. Guilford Press

extra.When to Use ABR: ABR is appropriate when: (1) the phenomenon involves emotional or embodied experience that participants cannot easily verbalise, (2) participants are from cultures or groups for whom verbal interview is not the natural mode of expression, (3) the research question concerns aesthetic, sensory, or creative aspects of experience. ABR is not a softer alternative to "real" research — it accesses a qualitatively different kind of knowledge that verbal methods cannot.
extra.Four ABR Forms: Collage: Participants create a collage representing their experience of [phenomenon] using provided materials (magazine images, coloured paper, markers). Analysis: spatial composition (what is central? what is peripheral? what is overlapping?), colour use, text, and participant narration of the collage. Visual narrative / comics: Participants draw a sequence of panels showing their experience with a product or task. Particularly powerful for process-oriented research — the panel sequence reveals participants' understanding of causality and temporal structure. Role play / drama: Participants enact future use scenarios, past frustrating experiences, or imagined interactions. The bodily enactment surfaces tacit knowledge about spatial, temporal, and social dimensions of experience that description cannot. Musical mapping: Participants select music that represents their emotional experience of different stages of a product interaction, or of using the product overall. Analysis: emotional mapping from music characteristics (tempo, key, instrumentation, lyrics) to product experience dimensions.

name: ASPIRE Risk-Weighted Quality Review of Recurring Surveys
aka: A System for Product Improvement, Review and Evaluation
origin: Statistics Sweden with Paul Biemer and colleagues, used annually since 2010 (Biemer et al., 2014)
summary: A structured review that rates each error source of a recurring survey on five criteria, weights it by risk and produces a quality score tracked across cycles.
description: ASPIRE operationalises the total survey error paradigm as a repeatable audit for survey products that run every cycle. Total error is decomposed into sources (sampling, frame, nonresponse, measurement, data processing, modelling and estimation). Reviewers gather evidence from documentation, self-assessments and a quality interview with programme staff and users, then rate each source on five criteria: knowledge of the risk, communication with providers and users, compliance with best practice, available expertise, and progress on mitigation plans. Ratings use defined levels from poor to excellent, are weighted by each source's intrinsic risk (low, medium, high) and roll up into source and product scores. Product owners comment before scores are fixed, and the review repeats so improvement can be tracked. Its weakness is subjectivity: scores depend on raters and do not capture all of total survey error.
steps: List the error sources relevant to the recurring survey (sampling, frame, nonresponse, measurement, processing, estimation).
Gather evidence: documentation, quality declarations, self-assessments and a structured interview with the survey owners and main users.
Rate each source on five criteria (knowledge of risk, communication, compliance with best practice, expertise, achievement of mitigation plans) using defined levels from poor to excellent.
Assign each source an intrinsic risk weight (low, medium, high) and compute source and overall product scores.
Let product owners review and comment before finalising.
Produce a prioritised improvement list and repeat the review each cycle to track change.
outputs: Per-source and overall quality scores, a risk-weighted improvement list and a time series of quality ratings.
useWhen: Governing long-running survey programmes such as quarterly satisfaction trackers, HaTS-type surveys or employee and customer panels whose numbers inform executive decisions.
avoidWhen: One-off surveys, where a single total survey error review is enough. Do not present scores as objective measurements; they are structured expert judgements.
whyLost: UX research programmes rarely have a quality-governance function, and the framework is published in official-statistics literature rather than practitioner channels.
whereToUse: Enterprise research operations teams managing several trackers, regulated sectors reporting customer outcomes, platform teams maintaining in-product survey infrastructure.
example: A research operations lead reviews three in-product trackers. ASPIRE scoring rates nonresponse as high risk with poor knowledge (no nonresponse analysis exists), so the next quarter funds a nonresponse bias study before improving wording.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Biemer, P. P. (2016). Total survey error paradigm: theory and practice. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 122-141). London: SAGE.

name: Assignment mechanism reconstruction
origin: Donald Rubin's potential outcomes framework, 1974-1978; propensity scores by Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983
summary: Reconstructs how users actually came to receive a feature or treatment in observational data, so that the assignment can be modelled and adjusted for.
description: In an RCT the assignment mechanism is known: a coin flip. In product logs, exposure results from user choice, targeting rules, rollout schedules, eligibility logic and algorithms. Rubin argued that causal inference from observational data rests on understanding this mechanism. Reconstruction means documenting the actual rules (feature flags, ranking algorithms, marketing targeting), interviewing engineers and product managers, and modelling the probability of treatment given pre-treatment covariates as a propensity score. Rigour comes from checking overlap (every type of user had a chance of either treatment), covariate balance after weighting or matching, and identifying any deterministic rules that can be exploited as natural experiments.
steps: Collect documentation on feature flags, rollout schedules, targeting rules and recommendation logic in force during the study window.
Interview the engineers and product managers responsible to confirm how exposure was decided.
Model treatment probability with logistic regression or gradient boosting on pre-treatment covariates to estimate propensity scores.
Check overlap: trim or flag users with propensity below 0.05 or above 0.95.
Apply weighting or matching and verify balance with standardised mean differences below 0.1 for all covariates.
Note any random or arbitrary elements (hash-based rollouts, thresholds) that can be used as instruments or discontinuities.
outputs: A documented assignment mechanism, propensity scores, overlap and balance diagnostics, and identified natural experiments.
useWhen: Before estimating effects of features that users chose or were targeted for, especially in target trial emulation.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on propensity models when assignment depended on unmeasured factors such as offline sales conversations; seek an instrument or experiment.
whyLost: UX analysts rarely look upstream at how exposure was generated, and the potential outcomes framework is taught in statistics rather than design research.
whereToUse: Evaluating personalised features, targeted campaigns, opt-in tools and algorithmic recommendations in fintech, e-commerce and health.
example: Investigating a portfolio insights feature, the team learns from engineering that it was shown only to users with over 5,000 in assets after a certain app version. They model this explicitly and find a version-based rollout window usable as a natural experiment.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983) The central role of the propensity score
The Inquiry Series, Ch 48 — Target Trial Emulation — Causal Evidence from Log Data
reference: Rosenbaum, P. R. & Rubin, D. B. (1983) The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika, 70(1), 41-55.

name: Assistive Technology Testing
origin: Emerged with Section 508 (1998) and WCAG 1.0 (1999); formalised in W3C WAI evaluation guidance
summary: Usability testing with disabled participants using their own screen readers, switch access, magnification or voice control to find barriers automated checkers miss.
description: Assistive technology testing evaluates a product as experienced through NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack, switch devices, screen magnifiers, voice control and alternative keyboards.
