Automated tools catch roughly a third of accessibility issues at best; the remainder concern focus order, meaningful announcements, live region behaviour, gesture alternatives and cognitive load that only emerge when an experienced AT user attempts real tasks. Rigour comes from testing with habitual AT users on their own configurations (not sighted testers switching a screen reader on), from covering the browser and AT combinations your audience actually uses, and from separating code-level defects from interaction-level usability problems. Sessions record task success, time, and the specific announcement or interaction that failed, so engineers can reproduce each issue.
steps: Identify the AT and browser combinations your users rely on (for example JAWS with Chrome, NVDA with Firefox, VoiceOver with Safari on iOS) from analytics, support data or WebAIM survey benchmarks.
Run an automated scan and an expert manual audit first so participant time is spent on issues tools cannot find.
Recruit 5-8 experienced AT users per major technology, testing remotely on their own devices and settings where possible.
Give realistic end-to-end tasks and ask participants to think aloud, capturing screen-reader speech output and screen recording.
Log each failure with the AT, browser, element, what was announced or required, and whether the participant recovered.
Rate severity by task blocking versus friction, map issues to WCAG success criteria, and retest fixes with the same AT combination.
outputs: Task success by AT combination, reproducible defect log with WCAG mapping, severity ratings and announcement transcripts.
useWhen: Before launch of public-facing or regulated digital services, after major UI framework changes, and when complaints or legal risk indicate AT users are blocked.
avoidWhen: When the product has not yet passed a basic automated and manual audit (fix the obvious first), or when you need to understand broader inclusion beyond AT use (use inclusive design research).
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for accessibility validation; cannot be replaced by automated scanning alone.
whereToUse: Any digital product; critical for government, health, education, and enterprise.
example: A healthcare booking portal passes an automated audit, yet VoiceOver users cannot tell which appointment slot is selected because the state is conveyed only by colour. Three of six participants book the wrong time; adding aria-pressed and a spoken confirmation resolves it.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (2023) Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

name: Association Rule Mining
origin: Retail transaction mining; set out step by step as 'associative rules' by Glenn Myatt (2007)
summary: Finds IF-THEN rules about which categorical values tend to occur together in records, and ranks them by support, confidence and lift.
description: Association rule mining is an unsupervised grouping method that groups records by combinations of categorical values and turns each group into IF-THEN rules, for example IF a user has used search AND saved a filter THEN they export a report. Every candidate rule is scored against the whole data set. Support is the share of all records covered by the full group. Confidence is the group support divided by the support of the IF-part, so it says how predictable the THEN-part is once the IF-part holds. Lift divides confidence by the support of the THEN-part alone, so it corrects for outcomes that are common anyway: values above 1 indicate a positive association and below 1 a negative one. A minimum group size keeps the search tractable but hides rules based on few records. Continuous variables must first be binned. For product teams the method turns feature-usage or event logs into readable statements about co-use, bundles and paths to an outcome, which are easier to discuss with stakeholders than cluster centroids. Rules describe co-occurrence, not cause, and the method can produce many rules that need prioritising and checking with domain knowledge or hypothesis tests.
steps: Build a table with one row per user, session or transaction and categorical columns (for example features used, plan, platform); bin any continuous variables.
Set a minimum group size (support threshold) using what you learnt when characterising the data.
Generate groups of value combinations that meet the threshold.
Extract every possible IF-THEN rule from each group, putting one value in the THEN-part at a time.
Calculate support, confidence and lift for each rule against the whole data set.
Rank rules by confidence and lift, discard rules with lift near or below 1, and review the remainder with subject matter experts.
Test promising rules with a hypothesis test or a controlled experiment before acting on them.
outputs: A ranked list of IF-THEN rules with support, confidence and lift for each.
useWhen: You have many records described by categorical attributes or binary feature-use flags and want readable statements about what goes with what.
avoidWhen: Data are mainly continuous and cannot sensibly be binned, samples are small, or you need causal claims rather than co-occurrence.
whyLost: It is a retail and data-mining staple, but UX analysts tend to reach for funnels, clustering or regression and rarely frame feature co-use as rule mining.
whereToUse: SaaS feature adoption, e-commerce bundles and recommendations, onboarding checklists, help content cross-linking, survey multi-select answers.
example: An analytics team mines 40,000 accounts with flags for 25 features. The rule IF uses dashboards AND invites a teammate THEN uses scheduled reports has confidence 0.71 and lift 2.4, so the team tests surfacing scheduled reports right after a teammate invite.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Myatt, G. J. (2007). Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Assumption Surfacing and Knowledge Audit
origin: Mason & Mitroff, 1981 (strategic assumption surfacing); David Travis, 2019
summary: Makes the team's unstated assumptions explicit and sorts them by what is known, believed and unknown, before they shape research design and product decisions.
description: Assumption surfacing and knowledge audit, drawing on Mason and Mitroff's strategic assumption surfacing and on David Travis's advice to research practitioners, makes the beliefs that underlie a product plan explicit before they silently shape research. The team writes down assumptions about users, problems, behaviour, value and feasibility, then classifies each by evidence strength (known with evidence, believed, unknown) and by the consequence of being wrong. A knowledge audit then checks existing research, analytics and support data to see what is already known, preventing duplicate studies. High-risk, low-evidence assumptions become research questions. Rigour comes from writing assumptions as testable statements, requiring evidence references for anything marked 'known', and revisiting the inventory as research reports.
steps: Team workshop — 30 minutes: Each participant writes 20–30 statements on sticky notes starting with "Users…" or "We know that users…" No filtering. All assumptions included, however obvious they seem.

Evidence audit: Researcher leads evidence audit for each statement. For each: "What's the evidence?" Possible answers: (a) strong evidence from prior research, (b) weak evidence from anecdote, (c) no evidence — assumption only.

Categorise: (1) High confidence / high importance → monitor but don't research. (2) Low confidence / high importance → priority research question. (3) Low confidence / low importance → deprioritise. (4) Contradicted by evidence → immediate action.
Convert to research questions: Each category-2 assumption becomes a research question. The research plan follows from this audit, not from a predetermined method preference.
outputs: An assumption inventory classified by evidence strength and risk, a knowledge audit of existing research, and a prioritised list of assumptions to test.
useWhen: Project kick-offs, before planning research, when a team is confident without evidence, and when inherited research may already answer some questions.
avoidWhen: Avoid letting the workshop become a substitute for research; it identifies what to test, not answers. For well-evidenced, low-risk work, keep it brief.
whyLost: Assumption mapping survives as a sticky-note exercise, but the knowledge audit step (checking existing evidence) and the rigour of classification are usually skipped.
whereToUse: Kick-offs for new products or major features; research planning in organisations with large but scattered research repositories; strategy work in regulated sectors (fintech, health) where wrong assumptions are expensive to reverse; aligning stakeholders before discovery.
example: A neobank team lists 34 assumptions about freelancers; a knowledge audit finds prior research already answers nine, while 'freelancers want automatic tax pots' has no evidence and high risk, so it becomes the first study.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher (David Travis)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Travis D & Hodgson P (2019) Think Like a UX Researcher: How to Observe Users, Influence Design, and Shape Business Strategy. CRC Press

name: Assumption Surfacing Through Pre-Study Interview
donor: UX research practice and strategic planning
origin: David Travis and Philip Hodgson (Think Like a UX Researcher, 2019); related to Mason and Mitroff's strategic assumption surfacing (1981)
summary: Before research, the team writes what it believes about users and the researcher interrogates the evidence behind each belief, turning unevidenced assumptions into research questions.
description: Many studies answer questions the team already thinks it knows, or skip the beliefs that actually drive decisions. Assumption surfacing makes those beliefs explicit. In pre-study interviews or a workshop, stakeholders list what they believe about users, their needs, behaviours and the product's value. The researcher then probes the evidence for each: is it based on data, anecdote or opinion, how recent and representative is it? Travis distinguishes knowledge (supported by evidence) from assumptions and opinions. Each assumption is rated for the risk of being wrong and the impact on decisions, and high-risk, low-evidence items become the research questions. The approach mirrors Mason and Mitroff's strategic assumption surfacing and testing in management science. It sharpens study focus and makes subsequent findings harder to dismiss.
steps: Pre-study workshop: team writes 20–30 statements about users starting with 'Users...' or 'We know that...'. Researcher leads evidence audit: for each statement, asks 'what's the evidence?' Statements with no evidence are candidate research questions. Categorize:
high confidence/high importance → monitor,
low confidence/high importance → research first,
low importance → deprioritize.
outputs: Assumption register with evidence grade, risk and impact ratings, prioritised research questions, and a baseline of stakeholder beliefs to compare with findings.
useWhen: At the start of any study or discovery phase, when stakeholders hold strong beliefs, or when research previously failed to change decisions.
avoidWhen: When the team has no prior beliefs to examine (purely exploratory new territory) or when the research question is already tightly specified and agreed.
whyLost: Research planning in UX is often reduced to a brief and a discussion guide; eliciting and grading stakeholder beliefs is seen as politics rather than method, so it rarely appears in toolkits.
whereToUse: Research planning, sprint zero, product discovery, cross-functional alignment. Complements Sharon's assumption mapping with a team interrogation protocol.
example: Before research on a B2B invoicing product, the PM states 'finance teams want automation above all'. The researcher finds this rests on two sales calls; it becomes a research question, and interviews show auditability matters more than automation.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher — David Travis
Mason & Mitroff, Challenging Strategic Planning Assumptions (1981)
reference: Travis D & Hodgson P (2019) Think Like a UX Researcher: How to Observe Users, Influence Design, and Shape Business Strategy. CRC Press

name: Asynchronous Online Focus Groups (Bulletin Boards)
donor: Market research and qualitative social research
origin: Market research bulletin-board practice; Williams et al. (2012); Stewart and Shamdasani (2017)
summary: A moderated online discussion run over several days in which questions and stimuli are posted at intervals and participants contribute when they log in.
description: Unlike synchronous online groups held by video or chat, asynchronous focus groups run over several days on a secure discussion platform. The moderator posts questions and stimuli at intervals; participants log in at their convenience to answer, read others' posts and respond to them. The moderator need not be online throughout but reviews contributions periodically and probes with follow-up questions. The aim is to understand attitudes, perceptions and reactions to stimuli rather than to reach consensus. The format allows reflective, longer answers, includes people in different time zones or with care duties, and produces ready-made transcripts. It can stand alone or help develop a questionnaire or explain survey results. Weaknesses are weaker commitment and drop-out, emotive written exchanges, and the need for moderators skilled in online group dynamics.
steps: Choose a secure, password-protected platform and decide whether responses are visible to others before or after posting.
Recruit and over-recruit by 20 to 30 per cent, considering incentives tied to daily participation and access for those without devices.
Authenticate participants and set a code of conduct.
Post questions and stimuli at planned intervals over several days, typically one to two activities per day.
Review contributions at least daily, probe individuals and the group, and nudge quiet participants.
Export transcripts and analyse with thematic, content or discourse analysis.
outputs: Multi-day discussion transcripts with media responses, and an analysis of attitudes and reactions.
useWhen: Reflective topics, distributed or time-poor participants, stimulus reactions over several days, or sensitive topics where writing feels safer than speaking.
avoidWhen: When spontaneous interaction or observation of behaviour is needed; use synchronous groups, interviews or usability testing.
whyLost: It survived because commercial platforms made it cheap and it fits distributed teams and participants.
whereToUse: Concept reactions for B2B audiences across time zones, healthcare professionals, parents, sensitive financial topics.
example: A pension provider runs a five-day bulletin board with 18 people near retirement, posting a new drawdown dashboard concept on day two. Overnight reflection produces detailed worries about running out of money that a one-hour group had not surfaced.
reference: Dawson, C. (2020). A-Z of Digital Research Methods. Abingdon: Routledge.

name: Attention Management in Data Visualisation (Knaflic Method)
origin: Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, 2015
summary: Designs research and analytics charts by removing clutter and using preattentive attributes such as colour and size to direct the audience to the key finding.
description: Knaflic's method treats a chart as an argument. The designer first defines the audience, the action wanted and the single big idea, then chooses an appropriate visual form, removes clutter (borders, gridlines, redundant labels, unnecessary colour) and uses preattentive attributes such as colour, intensity, size and position to direct attention to the data that matters. Text does work: action titles state the finding and annotations explain anomalies. Finally, a sequence of visuals builds a narrative. Grounded in perception research on preattentive processing and cognitive load, the method is rigorous when emphasis reflects real findings rather than preferences, when charts are checked by a colleague who must state the takeaway unaided, and when exploratory and explanatory visuals are kept distinct.
steps: For every visualization in a UX report:
Identify the single most important message.
(2) Apply pre-attentive highlighting to the data supporting that message (bright color, larger size, bold text).
(3) De-emphasize all other data elements (grey, smaller, light).
(4) Remove all non-data ink: gridlines, backgrounds, unnecessary axes.
(5) Write the insight directly on the chart as a title, not as a caption. Measure: can a reader identify the key point in < 5 seconds?
outputs: Decluttered charts with deliberate emphasis, action titles, a narrative sequence and before/after comparisons of communication effectiveness.
useWhen: Presenting research findings, dashboards and metrics to stakeholders, where the goal is that the audience sees and acts on one point quickly.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the audience needs to explore data openly (exploratory dashboards), where heavy emphasis can bias interpretation; then use neutral, filterable views.
whyLost: Researchers rarely receive training in visual communication; findings reach stakeholders as default spreadsheet charts or dense slides.
whereToUse: UX research reporting, stakeholder presentations, analytics dashboards, usability findings communication.
example: A researcher presents SUS results across five releases as a grey line chart with the latest drop highlighted in orange and the title 'Usability fell after the navigation change'; leadership approves a fix in the meeting.
sources: A Practical Guide to Designing with Data (Suda, 2010)
reference: Knaflic CN (2015) Storytelling with Data: A Data Visualization Guide for Business Professionals. Wiley

name: Attention Network Analysis for Interface Design
origin: Posner & Petersen, 1990
summary: Applies the three attention networks (alerting, orienting, executive control) to audit whether an interface captures, directs and sustains attention appropriately.
description: This method translates Posner and Petersen's model of three anatomically distinct attention networks into a design audit. The alerting network maintains readiness and responds to warning signals; the orienting network shifts attention to locations or objects, driven by salient cues or by expectation; the executive network resolves conflict between competing responses. For each critical element of an interface, the analyst asks which network it relies on, whether cues are calibrated to priority, whether orienting cues compete, and how much conflict resolution the user must do under load. Rigour comes from grounding judgments in established findings (cue validity effects, inhibition of return, conflict costs) and from verifying high-stakes conclusions empirically with detection or eye-tracking studies.
steps: Map design goals to attention networks:
Alerting (need user to be alert) → use novelty, motion, bright colors, sounds (RAS activation).
(2) Orienting (need user to focus on specific element) → use high salience features at target, reduce salience of competitors.

(3) Executive control (need user to resolve ambiguity or make decisions) → minimize competing demands on ACC by removing non-essential choices. Measure: does the design engage the intended network (EEG or behavioral proxies)?
outputs: An attention audit mapping interface elements to alerting, orienting and executive demands, a list of conflicts and overload points, and design recommendations.
useWhen: Designing alerts, dashboards, notifications and multitasking interfaces; diagnosing missed signals or attention fatigue in monitoring or clinical systems.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for measuring attention empirically; when stakes are high, follow with eye tracking, detection tasks or performance testing.
whyLost: Neuroscience of attention is taught as theory in psychology but rarely translated into actionable audits; UX reduced it to 'visual hierarchy' heuristics.
whereToUse: Alert design, dashboard attention management, decision flow design, safety-critical interface design.
example: An ICU monitoring team audits its alarm screen and finds that low-priority alerts trigger the same orienting cues as critical ones, exhausting the alerting network; tiering the cues reduces missed critical alarms in simulation.
sources: Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
reference: Posner MI & Petersen SE (1990) The attention system of the human brain. Annual Review of Neuroscience 13:25-42

name: Attention network mapping (Alerting/Orienting/Executive)
origin: Michael Posner and Steven Petersen, 1990; Attention Network Test by Fan et al., 2002
summary: Maps interface demands onto Posner's three attention networks, alerting, orienting and executive control, to diagnose which kind of attention a design fails to support.
description: Posner and Petersen proposed that attention comprises three anatomically and functionally distinct networks: alerting (achieving and maintaining readiness, linked to noradrenergic systems), orienting (selecting a location or modality, linked to parietal and frontal eye field regions), and executive control (resolving conflict between responses, linked to anterior cingulate and lateral prefrontal cortex). The Attention Network Test measures each via cue and flanker conditions. In UX, mapping each interface element and failure to the network it taxes clarifies remedies: alerting failures need warning cues and vigilance management; orienting failures need spatial cues and layout changes; executive failures need conflict reduction, such as removing competing response options. Rigour comes from coding failures against operational definitions of each network and, where feasible, measuring network efficiency in users.
steps: Inventory attention-dependent moments in the workflow (alerts, scanning, decision points with competing options).
Classify each moment by the network it primarily loads, using definitions: alerting for readiness and vigilance, orienting for where to look, executive for conflict resolution.
Code observed failures from tests or incidents into the same categories; use two coders and require kappa of at least 0.7.
Optionally run the Attention Network Test (about 20 minutes) with representative users, especially under fatigue, to estimate network efficiency.
Match remedies to networks: temporal warning cues for alerting, spatial or modality cues for orienting, reducing incongruent options for executive control.
Re-test critical moments and compare failure counts per network.
outputs: An attention demand map by network, coded failure distribution, optional ANT scores, and targeted design remedies.
useWhen: When attention failures are frequent but poorly understood, in long-shift or vigilance-heavy work, or when alert redesigns have not worked.
avoidWhen: For general visual hierarchy questions; use a saliency model or pre-attentive audit. For workload overall, use NASA-TLX.
whyLost: The model is foundational in cognitive neuroscience, but it has not been translated into a practitioner protocol, so UX treats attention as a single resource.
whereToUse: Surgical and ICU interfaces, air traffic control, security operations, driver monitoring, and attention-heavy AI supervision tasks.
example: Coding 64 missed surgical alerts shows most are orienting failures (alerts appear outside the surgeon's foveal area during instrument work), not alerting failures. Moving alerts into the endoscope view fixes more misses than making them louder.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Posner, M. I. & Petersen, S. E. (1990). The attention system of the human brain. Annual Review of Neuroscience, 13, 25-42.

name: Attention Restoration Assessment (Kaplan / Ulrich)
origin: Rachel and Stephen Kaplan (1989, 1995); Roger Ulrich (1984, 1991)
summary: Evaluates whether an environment restores directed attention through being away, fascination, extent and compatibility, measured by attention tasks and restorativeness scales.
description: Attention restoration theory proposes that directed attention is a limited resource depleted by effortful focus, and that environments with four properties restore it: being away, soft fascination, extent (coherent scope) and compatibility with intentions. Ulrich's stress recovery theory adds rapid affective recovery from natural scenes. The treatise suggests ART provides a theoretical framework for understanding cognitive load in complex interfaces. As a method, it measures directed attention (for example backwards digit span, sustained attention to response task) before and after exposure, along with perceived restorativeness scales, to compare designs that aim to reduce depletion, such as break screens, calm modes or ambient displays.
steps: Deplete or measure baseline directed attention with a standard task.
Expose participants to the interface condition (for example a calm mode versus standard).
Re-measure attention with the same task and collect a perceived restorativeness rating.
Include a control condition and randomise order or assignment.
Analyse change scores between conditions with appropriate statistics.
Translate restorative properties into design guidance.
outputs: Attention change scores, restorativeness ratings, evidence on restorative design features.
useWhen: Designing for long sessions, high cognitive load, wellbeing products, breaks and ambient interfaces.
avoidWhen: Short transactional tasks where attention depletion is negligible.
whyLost: Never crossed from environmental psychology into UX, which framed load in terms of task difficulty rather than restoration.
whereToUse: Control room break screens, clinician EHR fatigue, meditation and focus apps, VR, long-form reading apps.
example: A trading platform tests a two-minute 'nature pause' screen after market close; backwards digit span recovers significantly more than with a news feed, supporting a default break feature.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kaplan R & Kaplan S (1989) The Experience of Nature
Kaplan S (1995) The restorative benefits of nature. J Environmental Psychology 15
Ulrich RS et al. (1991) Stress recovery during exposure to natural and urban environments. J Environmental Psychology
reference: Kaplan S (1995) The restorative benefits of nature: toward an integrative framework. Journal of Environmental Psychology 15(3):169-182.

name: Attentional Blink Timing Analysis
origin: Raymond, Shapiro and Arnell, 1992
summary: Uses the attentional blink finding, that a second target 200-500 ms after a first is often missed, to time sequential alerts and UI events so critical information is not lost.
description: The attentional blink is a robust laboratory phenomenon: when people identify a first target in a rapid stream, their ability to detect a second target presented roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds later drops sharply, then recovers. The original paradigm uses rapid serial visual presentation. Its UX implication is that tightly sequenced events, such as a toast appearing just after a confirmation animation or two alarms firing in quick succession, can render the second event effectively invisible even though it was on screen. As a research method it involves auditing event timelines for second critical items inside the blink window and, where stakes justify it, running a small detection experiment that varies the onset gap between events. Rigour comes from controlled timing, detection rates per lag, and enough trials per participant to estimate the dip reliably.
steps: Log the timeline of sequential UI events in the flow, noting onset times to the nearest 50 ms.
Flag any pair where a critical second event begins 150-600 ms after a salient first event that demands attention.
For high-stakes cases, build a test harness that varies the lag between the two events (e.g. 100, 300, 500, 800 ms).
Run 12-24 participants with at least 20 trials per lag and record detection or response to the second event.
Plot detection by lag; a dip of 20 percentage points or more at 200-500 ms confirms a blink effect.
Reschedule critical events outside the window, merge them into one event, or make the second event persistent.
outputs: Event timing audit, lag-by-detection curve, revised notification and alert schedule.
useWhen: Designing alarm sequences, rapid notifications, games, in-car and cockpit displays, or onboarding flows with chained animations.
avoidWhen: Static interfaces or events separated by more than about a second; standard usability testing will suffice.
whyLost: Latent: Laboratory phenomenon with clear UX implications for notification timing and sequential UI events.
whereToUse: Notification design; sequential task design; alert timing in safety-critical interfaces.
example: An ICU monitoring app fired a 'battery low' toast 300 ms after a high-priority arrhythmia alarm. A timing test showed nurses missed the toast on 45% of trials at that lag; delaying it to 1 second after acknowledgement fixed detection.
reference: Raymond, J. E., Shapiro, K. L., & Arnell, K. M. (1992). Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: An attentional blink? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 18(3), 849-860.

name: AttrakDiff
origin: Marc Hassenzahl, Michael Burmester and Franz Koller, 2003
summary: A semantic differential questionnaire measuring pragmatic quality, hedonic quality (stimulation and identity) and attractiveness of an interactive product.
description: AttrakDiff operationalises Hassenzahl's model of user experience, which separates pragmatic quality (usefulness and usability in achieving goals) from hedonic quality, itself split into stimulation (novelty, challenge) and identification (what the product communicates about its owner), with attractiveness as an overall judgement. The questionnaire has 28 seven-point word pairs (a 10-item short form exists) grouped into these four scales. Its value is showing that products can be usable but dull, or exciting but impractical, and plotting products in a portfolio of pragmatic against hedonic quality. Rigour comes from using the validated item set, checking scale reliability in the sample, and comparing products or versions rather than interpreting absolute values alone. It is freely available online in German and English.
steps: Select the full 28-item version or the 10-item short version depending on respondent burden.
Administer after meaningful use of the product, ideally after realistic tasks or a period of real use.
Collect responses from at least 20-30 participants per product or version.
Compute scale means for pragmatic quality, hedonic stimulation, hedonic identity and attractiveness, and check reliability.
Plot products in the pragmatic-hedonic portfolio with confidence intervals.
Compare versions or competitors and interpret differences alongside qualitative feedback.
outputs: Scale scores for PQ, HQ-S, HQ-I and ATT, word-pair profiles, pragmatic-hedonic portfolio chart.
useWhen: Evaluating experience quality beyond usability, comparing branded or consumer products, and assessing redesigns aimed at appeal.
avoidWhen: Purely functional enterprise evaluations where SUS suffices, or when you need diagnostic detail about problems.
whyLost: Siloed: Academic origins; used in academic UX research and German-speaking industry; less known in English-speaking product teams.
whereToUse: Product experience evaluation; hedonic quality assessment; brand experience research.
example: A car-maker compared two infotainment concepts. Both had similar pragmatic quality, but concept B scored much higher on hedonic stimulation, supporting its selection for a premium trim line.
sources: AttrakDiff: Ein Fragebogen zur Messung wahrgenommener hedonischer und pragmatischer Qualität (Hassenzahl, Burmester & Koller)
Measuring and Improving User Experience Through Artificial Intelligence-Aided Design (Yang et al., 2020)
reference: Hassenzahl, M., Burmester, M., & Koller, F. (2003). AttrakDiff: Ein Fragebogen zur Messung wahrgenommener hedonischer und pragmatischer Qualität. In Mensch & Computer 2003 (pp. 187-196). Teubner.

name: Attributed Peer-Claim Probe
aka: 'We are hearing from other buyers that...' probe
origin: Adele Revella (2015), Buyer Personas
summary: Late in a buyer interview, present a prepared claim as something other buyers have said and ask for reactions, testing a differentiator or concept without sounding like a pitch.
description: Revella's buyer interviews are retrospective stories of a recent purchase decision. Once the story is complete, the interviewer can test a specific claim by attributing it to peers: other buyers say they pay more because of capability X; what are your thoughts? Attribution makes the statement neutral, so the participant reacts to the idea rather than defending against a sales message. Revella gives four uses: testing a differentiator after asking what a dearer option offered, testing whether a workaround meets the intended outcome when a feature is missing, testing a new capability with recent buyers of competing products (several statements are allowed), and, for strategic foresight, opening with a deliberately provocative peer-attributed claim about a trend to provoke an emotional response. The interviewer stays neutral, records awareness, importance and emotion, and never argues or sells.
steps: Prepare one or two claim statements with product managers, worded as what other buyers or role-holders report.
Complete the participant's own buying story first, without introducing the claims.
Pose a statement as what other buyers or people in their role are saying.
Ask an open question such as 'What are your thoughts?' and let them answer fully.
Record awareness of the claim, its importance and the emotional reaction; do not argue, correct or pitch.
Swap or reword statements if buyers consistently react poorly to the framing rather than the idea.
outputs: Evidence on whether buyers already knew of a claim or concept, how much they value it and how they react emotionally.
useWhen: Testing positioning claims, differentiators, workarounds or early concepts inside B2B buyer or win-loss interviews, where direct questions would sound like selling.
avoidWhen: Wording easily turns it into a sales pitch, and the provocative-trend version is easy to bias and needs an experienced interviewer; attributing invented claims to peers can mislead, so base statements on real evidence. For broader concept evaluation use concept testing or Projective Techniques.
whyLost: It belongs to product marketing's buyer persona practice and is little known among UX researchers, who test concepts directly.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS positioning, pricing justification, feature gap decisions, foresight interviews with industry buyers.
example: After a buyer recounts choosing a competitor's analytics platform, the interviewer says other data leads value scheduled exports as a workaround for missing integrations and asks what they think. The buyer says exports were never considered, which reframes the gap as a messaging problem.
reference: Revella, A. (2015). Buyer Personas: How to Gain Insight into Your Customer's Expectations, Align Your Marketing Strategies, and Win More Business. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Attrition Management in Longitudinal Studies
origin: Panel survey and clinical trial methodology; missing data framework from Donald Rubin, 1976
summary: Planning for dropout from the start, testing whether it is non-random, interviewing leavers and reporting attrition to protect longitudinal validity.
description: Every longitudinal study loses participants, and those who leave usually differ from those who stay, for example the least engaged or most frustrated users. Ignoring this biases findings toward positive trajectories. Attrition management treats dropout as a design and analysis concern: oversample at baseline (20 to 40 percent loss over six months is common), use retention strategies such as check-ins, flexible timing and fair compensation, compare dropouts with stayers on baseline measures at each wave, and conduct short exit interviews, since reasons for leaving are often substantive findings. Rubin's missing data categories (missing completely at random, at random, not at random) guide whether analysis can be corrected or results must be qualified.
steps: Oversample at baseline: Expect 20–40% attrition over a 6-month study. Recruit proportionally more.
Test for non-random dropout at each wave: Compare dropouts to continuing participants on key baseline measures. Systematic differences = biased results.
Dropout interview: When participants withdraw, conduct a brief 10-minute interview: 'What made it difficult to continue?' Reasons are often substantive findings, not just logistical failures.
Retention strategies: Regular check-ins between waves, acknowledgement of contributions, flexible wave timing, appropriate compensation.
Document attrition fully: Report how many dropped out, when, and why (where known). Discuss potential impact on trustworthiness.
outputs: Retention plan, wave-by-wave attrition statistics, dropout-versus-stayer comparisons, exit interview findings and an attrition statement in reporting.
useWhen: Any multi-wave diary, panel, learning or longitudinal interview study, and beta or pilot programmes measured over time.
avoidWhen: Single-session studies; there, focus on recruitment no-show management instead.
whyLost: UX longitudinal work is usually short and informal, so dropout is handled operationally (rerecruiting) rather than analysed as bias.
whereToUse: Diary studies, beta programmes, health app trials, longitudinal panels and education technology evaluations.
example: In a 12-week study of a sleep app, 35% drop out. Comparing baselines shows leavers had worse sleep at week 1, and exit interviews reveal the alarm feature woke partners, an important finding rather than an inconvenience.
sources: Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
A Practical Guide to Experience-Sampling Procedures (Conner Christensen et al., 2003)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Rubin, D. B. (1976). Inference and missing data. Biometrika, 63(3), 581-592.

name: Auction Mechanics Analysis
origin: William Vickrey, 1961; Milgrom and Wilson (Nobel 2020)
summary: Applies auction theory to evaluate and design bidding and allocation interfaces, testing whether users understand the format and bid as the mechanism intends.
description: Auction theory analyses how formats such as English (ascending), Dutch (descending), first-price sealed-bid, Vickrey (second-price) and combinatorial auctions allocate goods and set prices, and how bidders should behave in each. Formats that are theoretically efficient can fail in practice if users misunderstand them; second-price auctions, for example, reward truthful bidding but are poorly understood. The UX method combines theoretical analysis of the format with behavioural study of bidders: checking comprehension of the rules, observing whether bids follow the intended strategy, and measuring outcomes such as revenue, efficiency and perceived fairness. Rigour comes from comparing observed bidding against theoretical benchmarks, using controlled experiments or replay of real auction logs, and adjusting the interface (proxy bidding, clear feedback, explanation of what the winner pays) to bring behaviour closer to the intended equilibrium.
steps: Identify the auction format and the bidding strategy the theory predicts is optimal.
Test rule comprehension with 8-12 users through explanation and prediction tasks.
Analyse historical bid logs for deviations such as overbidding, sniping or bid shading.
Design interface interventions (proxy bidding, clearer payment rules, timers) to support the intended strategy.
Run controlled experiments or staged rollouts comparing formats or interface variants.
Measure revenue, allocation efficiency, bidder satisfaction and perceived fairness.
outputs: Comprehension findings, bid deviation analysis, interface recommendations, format comparison metrics.
useWhen: Ad platforms, ticketing, procurement, resale marketplaces and any product where prices are set through bidding.
avoidWhen: Fixed-price commerce; use pricing research such as Van Westendorp or conjoint instead.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives in platform economics; occasionally applied in ad tech and marketplace UX.
whereToUse: Ad platforms; marketplace matching; ticket/pricing systems.
example: A ticket resale platform used a second-price auction but users bid low and lost. Comprehension tests showed users thought they paid their own bid; adding 'You pay just above the next highest bid' raised truthful bidding and seller revenue.
sources: Putting Auction Theory to Work (Paul Milgrom)
reference: Vickrey, W. (1961). Counterspeculation, auctions, and competitive sealed tenders. Journal of Finance, 16(1), 8-37.

name: Audio Map and Deliverable Table
origin: Amber Case and Aaron Day (2018), from Day's sound design practice
summary: A table of every product state with its sound, light and haptic response, used to audit current feedback and specify the sounds to be designed.
description: The audio map breaks a product into its states (actions, status, programming states) and records for each the audio, light and haptic response with type and length. For an existing product two maps are drawn, current and desired, so the map doubles as an audit showing where senses are overloaded, missing or inconsistent. Each new sound starts from an intended connotation and style described with dichotomous descriptors (for example resolution rather than tension for power off), which later becomes the test target. The map then feeds a simpler deliverable table listing use case, filename, what the user hears when, frequency of occurrence and style. That table is kept as the master reference through prototyping and testing, with sounds grouped into classes and lengths set by frequency: frequent sounds short and quiet, rare ones allowed more character.
steps: Break the product's interactions into functions and states: actions, status changes and programming or settings states.
For each state record the audio, light and haptic response with its type and length.
For an existing product draw a current-state map and a desired-state map side by side.
State the intended connotation and style of each new sound using dichotomous descriptors (natural or synthetic, resolved or tense, short or long).
List the use cases where sound must be added, changed or removed.

Build the deliverable table with use case, filename, what the user hears when, frequency of occurrence and style; group use cases into classes and set lengths, keeping frequent sounds short and less intense.
Keep the table as the master reference through prototyping and testing, ticking off finished sounds and tracking changes across senses.
outputs: Current and desired audio maps, a sound deliverable table, and inputs to the sound design brief and test plan.
useWhen: Use when a connected device, appliance, vehicle or app relies on sound, light or haptic feedback and the team needs a complete inventory before commissioning or revising sounds.
avoidWhen: Avoid using the map to judge whether sounds are understood or annoying: that needs listener evaluation such as the MUSHRA Listening Test (ITU-R BS.1534) or a Semantic Differential with users. It is a specification tool, not a study.
whyLost: It lives in the sound design and audio branding trade; mainstream UX teams rarely specify sound systematically, so the inventory practice has not crossed over.
whereToUse: Smart home devices, robot vacuums, medical devices, in-car systems, payment terminals, mobile notifications.
example: A home-robot team maps 24 states and finds that six share one beep while low battery has no sound at all. The deliverable table assigns short, quiet confirmations to frequent states and a distinct, longer sound to the stuck state.
reference: Case, A. and Day, A. (2018). Designing with Sound: Fundamentals for Products and Services. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 124-129.

name: Audio-haptic synchronisation measurement
origin: Case and Day (2018), from Aaron Day's sound design practice
summary: Record a device with two microphones to measure delays between a touch, its haptic pulse and its sound, so feedback either fuses into one event or is deliberately separated.
description: When sound, vibration and visual events that should be simultaneous drift apart, users must work to match them and the interaction feels broken, as with a coin sound arriving late in a game. Events within a millisecond or two are perceived as one. The bench method attaches one microphone to the device body to pick up the touch bump and haptic motor, and a second over the speaker; an audio editor then shows the touch, haptic pulse and sound on the waveforms so intervals can be measured against targets. Where fusion cannot be achieved, the parts should be decorrelated so each has a distinct transient. Testing is repeated under heavy processor load, alongside checks that every state plays its mapped sound and haptic, rapid-press stress tests and overlapping-sound tests.
steps: Attach one microphone to the device with rubber bands, near the haptic motor if known.
Rest the device on thick foam or cloth with the speaker facing up, and place a second microphone on a stand over the speaker.
Perform each interaction to be tested several times.
In audio-editing software, identify the touch bump, the haptic pulse and the sound on the waveforms.
Measure touch-to-haptic and touch-to-sound intervals and compare with target synchronisation times; aim for fusion or clear separation.
Repeat with the processor under heavy load, and run rapid button-press and overlapping-sound stress tests.
After any change, retest every sound and haptic mapping.
outputs: Measured touch-to-haptic and touch-to-sound delays per interaction, and a list of out-of-sync states.
useWhen: Shipping a device or app with combined audio and haptic feedback, such as keyboards, payment confirmations, game events or wearables.
avoidWhen: Avoid for interfaces with no time-critical multimodal feedback; it assumes you want sound and vibration to fuse, which is not always the design intent.
whyLost: It is an audio-engineering bench check that lives with device and sound teams rather than UX research.
whereToUse: Mobile keyboards and controls, payment terminals, game feel, automotive controls, wearables and accessibility feedback.
example: A payment terminal's success chime lags its vibration by 80 ms under load, and customers tap again thinking it failed. Two-microphone recordings locate the delay in the audio pipeline, and the team moves the chime to a pre-loaded buffer.
reference: Case, A. & Day, A. (2018). Designing with Sound: Fundamentals for Products and Services. O'Reilly Media, pp. 164-167.

name: Audit (correspondence) study
origin: Turner, Fix and Struyk (1991); Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004); Pager (2007)
summary: A field experiment that submits matched profiles differing in one signal to real decision makers or systems and compares responses, isolating discrimination by that signal.
description: Audit studies measure discrimination in real decisions rather than self-report. Researchers build sets of applications, accounts or profiles that are identical in every relevant respect except one signal, such as a name implying ethnicity, an age or a postcode, and submit them to the same real opportunities in randomised order. Differences in callbacks, prices, rankings or moderation decisions can then be attributed to the varied signal. In labour economics, matched CVs answering the same job adverts revealed large callback gaps by name. The design transfers directly to algorithm audits: sock-puppet accounts let researchers test whether recommendation, pricing, ad-delivery or moderation systems treat equivalent users differently. Rigour comes from tight matching, randomised submission order and enough pairs to estimate differential response rates.
steps: Define the attribute to test (for example name-implied ethnicity, gender or location) and the outcome (callback, price, rank, approval).
Build sets of profiles identical on all relevant characteristics except the test attribute, and pre-test that the signal is perceived as intended.
Submit each set to the same real opportunities or system queries, randomising which version goes first.
Record responses systematically (callbacks, quoted prices, ranking positions, moderation outcomes).
Compare response rates between versions with paired analysis and report the differential with its uncertainty.
Review ethics: minimise burden on real decision makers and consider whether the signal carries more than one meaning.
outputs: Differential response rates or outcome gaps attributable to the varied attribute, with paired statistics.
useWhen: Testing whether a marketplace, recommender, pricing engine or moderation system treats equivalent users differently by a protected or proxy attribute.
avoidWhen: When deceiving real human decision makers cannot be justified, or when the attribute cannot be varied cleanly (names carry class as well as ethnicity signals); use observational disparity analysis or internal logs instead.
whyLost: It lives in labour economics and sociology; UX rarely frames fairness as an experimental question, and the ethics of deceiving real decision makers deter product teams.
whereToUse: Algorithmic fairness audits of hiring platforms, lending and insurance quotes, ride-hailing, rental marketplaces, ad delivery and AI content moderation.
example: A rental marketplace team creates paired guest accounts identical except for profile names and sends identical booking requests to the same hosts. Acceptance rates differ by eight points, which motivates hiding names until after booking.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Bertrand, M. and Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? American Economic Review, 94(4), 991-1013.

name: Audit Attribute Sampling
origin: Acceptance sampling by Dodge and Romig (Bell Labs, 1920s-1940s); audit sampling standards (AICPA, ISA 530)
summary: Samples records to estimate the deviation rate of a control or quality attribute with a stated confidence and tolerable rate, then accepts or rejects.
description: Auditors cannot inspect every transaction, so they sample statistically. In attribute sampling, the auditor sets a tolerable deviation rate (e.g. 5%), an expected rate and a confidence level (e.g. 95%), derives the sample size from tables or the binomial distribution, selects randomly, inspects each item against the attribute, and computes an upper deviation limit. If the upper limit exceeds the tolerable rate, the control is not relied upon. Discovery sampling is designed to find at least one instance if the rate exceeds a threshold. These methods suit UX quality audits: accessibility compliance of content, accuracy of AI responses, policy compliance of moderation decisions, data quality of research repositories.
steps: Define the population, sampling unit and the attribute (what counts as a deviation).
Set tolerable deviation rate, expected rate and confidence level.
Compute sample size (e.g. about 59 items for zero expected deviations, 5% tolerable, 95% confidence).
Select items randomly and inspect them with clear criteria, ideally with two reviewers on a subset.
Compute the sample deviation rate and the upper deviation limit.
Accept or reject the control or quality claim, and investigate the nature of deviations.
outputs: Sample-based deviation rate with upper limit, accept/reject decision and deviation analysis.
useWhen: Auditing quality or compliance of large sets of items: content, AI outputs, moderation decisions, data records.
avoidWhen: Exploratory research where attributes are not yet defined.
whyLost: Audit methods live in accounting and quality control; UX content and AI audits often inspect convenience samples.
whereToUse: AI response quality assurance, accessibility of CMS content, help article accuracy, moderation decision quality.
example: A support AI's answers are audited monthly: 59 random conversations are inspected for factual errors; 2 deviations give an upper limit of 9.8%, above the 5% tolerable rate, so the release is held.
reference: IAASB. International Standard on Auditing 530: Audit Sampling.

name: Autobiographical Design
origin: Carman Neustaedter and Phoebe Sengers (2012) definition of autobiographical design
summary: Design research based on long, genuine use of a system by the people who build it, documented continuously and reflected on to produce experiential design knowledge.
description: Autobiographical design requires a genuine need, building the system oneself, and living with it for an extended period, often months or years. Unlike autoethnography it involves making a system, and unlike research through design it requires genuine self-use. Researchers document continuously through photos, time-lapse video, tutorials, diary logs and boundary objects, iterate as frictions arise, and periodically step back for retrospective analysis, ideally with a second researcher who did not live with the system. Other household or team members are acknowledged as participants with their own consent. Neustaedter and Desjardins draw lessons from two multi-year projects, a family video system used for two years and a self-built camper van studied since 2013, on participation, documentation, reflection and deciding when to end. Its knowledge is deep but personal: generalisability is limited, and personal and research life blur.
steps: Start from a genuine personal, household or team need that the researchers themselves have.
Build the system and commit to living with it for months or years.
Document use continuously with photos, time-lapse video, diary logs, tutorials and boundary objects.
Iterate the design as frictions arise, recording each change and its trigger.
Periodically step back for retrospective analysis with a second researcher who provides distance.
Treat other household or team members as participants, with consent and the right to opt out.
Decide when to end, considering both research aims and personal needs, and write up insights with their limits.
outputs: Experiential knowledge of a design space, a documented design history and transferable design insights.
useWhen: Exploring long-term, intimate or domestic technologies where real-life use over time cannot be simulated, or early design spaces with no existing users.
avoidWhen: Evaluating a product for a population unlike the designers, or when results must generalise; use field deployments with recruited participants.
whyLost: It is legitimate in HCI academia but resembles uncritical dogfooding in industry, so product teams rarely adopt the documentation and reflection discipline that makes it research.
whereToUse: Smart home and family technology, personal informatics, maker and DIY tools, internal developer tools, AI assistants used daily by their builders.
example: A small team building a household AI assistant uses it in their own homes for nine months, keeping diary logs and time-lapse video of placement changes. Quarterly retrospectives with an external researcher surface how routines and family members' tolerance changed, informing which features to test with recruited families.
sources: Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
reference: Lucero, A., Desjardins, A. and Neustaedter, C. (2021). Longitudinal first-person HCI research methods. In E. Karapanos, J. Gerken, J. Kjeldskov and M. B. Skov (eds.), Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research. Cham: Springer.

name: Autoethnography
origin: Term by Karl Heider (1975) and David Hayano (1979); developed by Carolyn Ellis & Arthur Bochner, 1990s; analytic form by Leon Anderson, 2006
summary: The researcher's own experience as a member of a community becomes primary data, connected through systematic reflection to wider cultural and social processes.
description: Autoethnography positions the researcher's personal experience as a legitimate and primary source of data about a cultural phenomenon. It is appropriate when: the researcher is a member of the community under study and has access to insider knowledge that outsider observation cannot provide. It requires rigorous reflexivity — the researcher must continuously question how their particular insider position shapes what they see and report.
steps: Field diary: Keep a daily diary of your own experience with the phenomenon under study. Write as a researcher, not as a user — note your own reactions, expectations, and interpretations alongside the experience itself.

Layered account: Alternate between first-person experience description and third-person analytical commentary. "I found myself clicking back and looking for a cancel button (description). This suggests the interface had produced a sense of irreversibility that I was uncertain was intended (analysis)."
Peer debrief: Share your accounts regularly with a peer who is outside the phenomenon. Their external perspective surfaces insider assumptions you cannot see yourself.
Member check with community: Share interpretations with other community members. Do they recognise the experience you describe? Where do they diverge from your account?
outputs: Field diaries, layered first- and third-person accounts, peer debrief notes, member-checked interpretations and insights about insider experience.
useWhen: When the researcher is genuinely a member of the community studied, for long-term or sensitive experiences that are hard to observe, or to complement other research with insider insight.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for research with other users, or when the researcher is not a genuine insider; use interviews, diary studies or ethnography. Not suited to generalisation.
whyLost: Siloed: autoethnography lives mainly in academic qualitative research and is often dismissed in industry as anecdote, although researchers who are also users can use it as a disciplined way to surface insider assumptions.
whereToUse: Niche community products; researchers who are also users; sensitive cultural contexts.
example: A researcher with type 1 diabetes keeps a six-week autoethnographic diary using a new insulin dosing app, layering experience with analysis. Peer debriefs and member checks with other users confirm a pattern of distrust after night-time alerts.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection
The Inquiry Series, Ch 33 — Participatory & Arts-Based Methods
Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Ellis, C., Adams, T. E. & Bochner, A. P. (2011). Autoethnography: An overview. Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung, 12(1); Anderson, L. (2006). Analytic autoethnography. Journal of Contemporary Ethnography, 35(4), 373-395.

name: Automated facial expression analysis
donor: Psychology (facial expression research) and computer vision
origin: Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen's Facial Action Coding System (1978); automated detection from the 2000s (for example CERT, Affectiva, Noldus FaceReader, OpenFace)
summary: Uses computer vision to detect facial action units and estimated expressions from video during product use, providing time-stamped indicators of affective response.
description: FACS decomposes facial movements into action units, such as AU4 brow lowerer and AU12 lip corner puller, which human coders score after about 100 hours of training. Automated systems detect action units and often infer emotion categories from video at frame level. In UX this yields continuous, time-aligned signals during tasks without interrupting participants. However, Barrett and colleagues' 2019 review concluded that facial movements do not reliably map to specific emotions across people and contexts; confusion often shows as AU4, and many users show little expression while using screens. Rigour therefore means using action units as signals rather than emotion labels, controlling lighting and camera angle, using within-person baselines, and triangulating with self-report and behaviour.
steps: Set up recording with a frontal camera at face height, even lighting and at least 720p at 30 frames per second, and check detection quality in a pilot with 2 to 3 people of varied skin tones, ages and with or without glasses.
Record a neutral baseline of 1 to 2 minutes per participant, then record task sessions with time stamps for task events.
Run automated detection and export action unit intensities per frame, excluding frames with poor tracking confidence (for example below 0.8).
Compute within-person changes from baseline around task events, focusing on interpretable signals such as AU4 (effort or confusion) and AU12 (smiling).
Validate a sample of automated detections against manual FACS coding or careful human review, and report agreement.
Triangulate facial signals with self-report and behaviour, and report them as indicators of response at specific moments rather than definitive emotions.
outputs: Time series of action unit intensities aligned to tasks, event-locked changes from baseline, validation statistics and triangulated interpretations.
useWhen: Studying moment-level responses to content, advertising, onboarding or high-stakes moments, alongside other measures in a controlled setting.
avoidWhen: Making claims about specific emotions from faces alone, studying populations underrepresented in training data without validation, or contexts where filming faces raises consent or legal concerns (for example under GDPR biometric rules); use self-report and behavioural measures instead.
whyLost: Market research and neuromarketing vendors use it widely, but UX research largely avoids it due to cost, validity criticism and privacy concerns, so it stays niche.
whereToUse: Media and advertising testing, game research, high-stakes financial and health moments, automotive driver monitoring research.
example: In a loan approval study, the team expected AU12 smiles at approval but found instead brief AU4 and AU1 activity followed by relaxation, which participants described in retrospection as 'checking it was real'. The design added a clear confirmation of terms after approval.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 38 — FACS, Micro-Expression Analysis & Psychophysiology
User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
reference: Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1978). Facial Action Coding System. Consulting Psychologists Press; Barrett, L. F., Adolphs, R., Marsella, S., Martinez, A. M., & Pollak, S. D. (2019). Emotional expressions reconsidered. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 20(1), 1–68.

name: Automated Usability Evaluation
aka: Automated usability testing with manual checks
origin: Surveyed by Melody Ivory and Marti Hearst, 2001
summary: Software checks interface code against coded guidelines, flags items that need human manual checks, and reports compliance and interface statistics at scale.
description: Automated evaluation tools read interface code quickly and report conformance with coded guidelines, often suggesting fixes, along with statistics such as number of fonts, average font size, button size, menu depth and image load time. They cannot judge meaning: a tool can confirm an image has alternative text but not whether the text is meaningful, so where a criterion needs judgement the tool flags a manual check for a human reviewer. Tools suit large page sets with little time, and also high-level surveys across many sites, such as comparing accessibility features across government agencies. Rigour comes from combining the automated pass with systematic completion of the flagged manual checks and recording which guideline version was applied. Typical tools include WAVE, AChecker and Deque products.
steps: Choose the tool and guideline set (for example WCAG 2.x level AA) and define the pages or screens in scope.
Run the automated tool across the full set.
Review the summary report, interface statistics and any suggested fixes.
Carry out every manual check the tool flags, such as meaningfulness of alt text and labels.
Fix failures, then rerun the tool to confirm.
Optionally aggregate results across many sites or releases for a high-level picture.
outputs: A guideline compliance report, interface statistics and a list of resolved manual checks.
useWhen: Large sites or apps, regression checks in CI, accessibility compliance audits and cross-site surveys.
avoidWhen: When you need to know how people actually use the product; automated checks miss most usability and many accessibility problems. Follow with Accessibility Evaluation, Assistive Technology Testing or Usability Testing.
whyLost: It survived because accessibility law and continuous integration made cheap, repeatable checks valuable; the manual-check discipline is the part often skipped.
whereToUse: Public-sector and regulated websites, design-system component libraries, e-commerce at scale, and release pipelines.
example: A retailer runs an accessibility checker on 4,000 product pages in its build pipeline. It flags missing labels automatically and queues 300 alt-text manual checks for content editors each week.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Ivory, M.Y. and Hearst, M.A. (2001) The state of the art in automating usability evaluation of user interfaces. ACM Computing Surveys 33(4), 470-516.

name: Automatic Persona Generation (APG)
aka: Automatic persona generation and persona analytics
origin: Salminen, Jansen, An, Kwak and Jung, Qatar Computing Research Institute, 2016 onwards
summary: Generate and periodically refresh personas from aggregated platform analytics by matrix factorisation, then enrich them with names, photos and quotes and track how stakeholders use them.
description: APG builds personas from audience interaction data collected through YouTube, Facebook and Google Analytics APIs, keyed by gender, age group and country. A demographic-group by content matrix is decomposed with non-negative matrix factorisation to find latent interaction patterns. The most impactful demographic group for each pattern becomes a skeletal persona, enriched with a census-based name, photo, description, topics, quotes from comments, content and reach. Personas regenerate as data change, keeping them linked to underlying numbers. Design principles include consistency, relevance, non-offensiveness, authenticity and context. Persona analytics extends this by logging stakeholders' mouse movements and webcam gaze on persona profiles to see which elements are used. Limitations: aggregates can hide minorities, demographic buckets drive the results, and automatically chosen text and images need filtering.
steps: Collect aggregated interaction data through platform or analytics APIs.
Build a demographic-group by content (or behaviour) matrix.
Apply non-negative matrix factorisation to extract latent interaction patterns; choose the number of patterns by interpretability and fit.
Select the most impactful demographic group for each pattern to create skeletal personas.
Enrich each persona with a name, photo, description, topics, quotes, content and reach, filtering offensive or inauthentic items.
Regenerate personas on a schedule as data change.
Optionally log stakeholders' interaction with persona profiles (mouse, gaze) to learn which elements they use.
outputs: An interactive persona set linked to underlying numbers and content; engagement data on persona profile elements.
useWhen: You have large audience analytics, need personas that stay current, and want them traceable to data, for example in media or content businesses.
avoidWhen: Your concern is motivations and context rather than content consumption; use qualitative persona methods. Aggregates hide minorities, platform biases carry through, and webcam gaze is imprecise.
whyLost: It is used mainly through the research team's own system and academic deployments; most product teams still build personas by hand.
whereToUse: Media publishers, content platforms, marketing analytics, social media audiences, large e-commerce catalogues.
example: A news publisher generates eight personas from YouTube analytics, refreshed monthly. Editors notice an emerging persona of young viewers in one region watching explainers, and commission a series for them.
sources: Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: An, J., Kwak, H., Jung, S.-G., Salminen, J., & Jansen, B. J. (2018). Customer segmentation using online platforms: Isolating behavioral and demographic segments for persona creation via aggregated user data. Social Network Analysis and Mining, 8, 54; Jansen, B. J., Salminen, J., Jung, S.-G., & Guan, K. (2021). Data-Driven Personas. Morgan & Claypool.

name: Autopoiesis and Structural Coupling in HCI
origin: Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela (1972, 1987); introduced to HCI by Winograd and Flores (1986)
summary: Analyses interaction as structural coupling: interfaces perturb users rather than instruct them, so responses depend on users' history and structure, observed through breakdowns over time.
description: Maturana and Varela described living systems as autopoietic, continuously producing themselves, and coupled to their environments through recurrent interactions that trigger, but do not determine, internal changes. Winograd and Flores brought this view into HCI in Understanding Computers and Cognition, arguing that systems cannot transmit meaning to users and that design should attend to breakdowns, moments when ready-to-hand use fails and becomes visible. As an analytic stance, it focuses research on the history of interactions between a person and a system: how repeated use changes what a cue triggers, how different users respond differently to the same signal, and where breakdowns reveal mismatched structure. Practically, this means longitudinal observation of breakdowns and recovery rather than single-session tests.
steps: Reframe interaction analysis from information transmission to structural coupling: instead of 'the interface communicated X to the user', ask 'what internal state was triggered by this interface perturbation, given this user's existing structure?' This shifts error analysis from 'the interface failed to communicate' to 'the interface produced a perturbation that triggered an undesired internal state in this user'.
outputs: Longitudinal breakdown log, analysis of how responses to the same cues change with history, and design recommendations that support recurrent coupling and recovery.
useWhen: Long-term use of complex tools, habits and adaptation, AI systems that adapt to users (mutual coupling), and theory-driven reframing of design problems.
avoidWhen: Short-term evaluative questions or teams needing concrete metrics quickly; use usability testing or analytics.
whyLost: Winograd and Flores' work was influential in the 1980s but the autopoietic vocabulary proved hard to operationalise, and HCI theory moved on to activity theory and embodied interaction.
whereToUse: Error analysis reframing, cross-cultural UX research (where the 'same' interface produces entirely different responses in different structural histories), AI interaction design.
example: A design team studying a personalised fitness app over eight weeks logs breakdowns where users stop responding to streak notifications. Responses change with history, so the team designs notifications that vary with the user's coupling stage rather than a fixed schedule.
sources: The Tree of Knowledge — Humberto R. Maturana
Understanding Computers and Cognition (Terry Winograd & Fernando Flores)
reference: Maturana HR & Varela FJ (1987) The Tree of Knowledge: The Biological Roots of Human Understanding. Shambhala

name: Awareness-usefulness gap analysis
origin: Practice described by William Albert and Thomas Tullis in Measuring the User Experience (since the first edition)
summary: Asks whether users knew of each feature, lets them try it, then rates its usefulness; features with high usefulness but low awareness need promotion or more prominent design.
description: The method needs two metrics per feature. Participants first answer a yes/no question on whether they were aware of each feature, asked before the feature is shown so the question does not create awareness. They then explore the feature for a couple of minutes and rate its usefulness on a 1-5 scale. Ratings are converted to top-2-box percentages and plotted beside the awareness percentages for each feature. Features with the largest gap between usefulness and awareness are useful but little known, and are candidates for better promotion, onboarding or more prominent placement. Features with high awareness and low usefulness are candidates for redesign or removal. The analysis is simple, but ordering the questions correctly and giving every participant the same brief exposure keep it honest.
steps: List the features of interest, typically 5-15.
Before showing any feature, ask 'Were you aware of this feature?' (yes/no) for each.
Let the participant explore each feature for a couple of minutes with a consistent prompt.
Ask for a usefulness rating on a 1-5 scale after each exploration.
Compute percentage aware and top-2-box percentage useful per feature, with confidence intervals.
Plot the two percentages side by side, rank features by gap, and flag high-usefulness, low-awareness features.
outputs: Per-feature awareness percentage, usefulness top-2-box percentage and a ranked gap chart.
useWhen: Mature products with many features where adoption is lower than expected and the question is whether features are unknown or unwanted.
avoidWhen: Very new products where few features exist, or when real usage data are available to measure discoverability directly (combine the survey with analytics). Usefulness judged after a short trial may not match real use.
whyLost: It survived as a simple survey analysis in UX metrics practice and is common in feature-adoption research, though the question-order safeguard is often missed.
whereToUse: Feature adoption studies, release planning, onboarding redesign, enterprise software with deep feature sets, mobile banking and productivity apps.
example: In a study of an email client, 'scheduled send' is rated useful by 82% after a two-minute trial but only 25% knew about it. It is promoted in the compose window and its adoption is then tracked in analytics.
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience: Collecting, Analyzing, and Presenting UX Metrics (3rd ed.). Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 5, p. 150.

name: Axial Coding
origin: Anselm Strauss & Juliet Corbin, 1990 (Basics of Qualitative Research)
summary: Reassembling open codes around central categories by mapping causal conditions, context, strategies and consequences, moving analysis from description to explanation.
description: Axial coding is the second stage of Strauss & Corbin's Grounded Theory. Having fractured data into open codes, you now reassemble it by identifying the relationships between codes. You work around an "axis" — a central code or category — and map what causes it, what conditions it occurs under, what actions or strategies it involves, and what its consequences are. This is the stage where your analysis moves from description to explanation.
steps: Take your full open code list and group codes by similarity. Each group becomes a candidate category. Name categories at a conceptual level, not descriptively.
For each major category: map it using the coding paradigm above. Write a memo for each mapping.
Draw a diagram showing categories and relationships. This is your emerging theory.
Return to your data: are there incidents that don't fit the diagram? These are negative cases — the most analytically valuable data you have.
outputs: Candidate categories with properties and dimensions, paradigm-model memos, a relationship diagram, and a list of negative cases.
useWhen: After open coding, when you need to explain why and under what conditions a behaviour occurs, for example why trust collapses or why a workaround persists.
avoidWhen: When the team only needs descriptive themes or a prioritised issue list; when the data are too thin (fewer than about eight rich sessions) to support relational claims. Use thematic analysis or framework analysis instead.
whyLost: The Strauss-Corbin paradigm was criticised in sociology as overly prescriptive, and UX rarely gets beyond descriptive themes, so explanatory category-relating is seldom operationalised.
whereToUse: Explaining abandonment, trust breakdowns, and adoption barriers in high-stakes products; building causal hypotheses for later quantitative testing.
example: In a study of a crypto wallet, the category 'transaction anxiety' is mapped: causal condition is irreversible transfers, context is first large transfer, strategies are sending test amounts, consequences are delayed adoption. The paradigm model directly informs a 'test transfer' feature.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick ed.)
reference: Strauss, A. & Corbin, J. (1990). Basics of Qualitative Research: Grounded Theory Procedures and Techniques. Sage.

extra.The Coding Paradigm (Strauss & Corbin): Causal conditions: What events, incidents, or happenings lead to or influence the category? (What causes trust collapse?) Phenomenon: The central idea or event around which action is directed. (Trust collapse itself.) Context: The specific set of properties — spatial, temporal, cultural — within which the phenomenon occurs. (First-time use of a high-stakes financial feature.) Intervening conditions: The broader contextual factors that bear on action/interaction strategies. (User's prior experience with similar products; organisational norms.) Action/interaction strategies: The purposive, goal-oriented behaviors participants engage in to respond to the phenomenon. (Workarounds; seeking external confirmation; abandonment.) Consequences: The outcomes, intended and unintended, of the strategies. (Product abandonment; increased anxiety; developing compensatory ritual.)

name: Axial coding agent
origin: Axial coding from Strauss and Corbin, 1990; LLM implementation emerging from 2023
summary: Using an LLM agent to propose relationships between open codes, such as conditions, actions and consequences, around central categories, for researchers to evaluate and refine.
