The five stages are Signal Framing, Spectral Decomposition, Contextual Annotation, Modeling and Visualization, and Validation and Iteration. It explicitly names where translation fails (stationarity, irregular sampling, semantic noise, label scarcity, non-equivalence of energy and meaning, intentionality, ethics) and redesigns around them: recurrence over strict periodicity, Lomb-Scargle for uneven events, noise retained as emotion, wavelets as a behavioural microscope, metadata context anchors and a human-in-the-loop quant → qual → quant loop. The integration equation states: meaningful behavioural insight = spectral precision × contextual anchoring × interpretive dialogue. It is presented as a conceptual playbook; the case is hypothetical.
steps: Signal Framing: choose the behavioural signal (e.g. interaction density per minute), align time resolution to the hypothesised rhythm, capture context variables and secure informed consent.
Pre-process: normalise timestamps, interpolate small gaps (< 30 seconds) and retain longer gaps as disengagement indicators.

Spectral Decomposition: apply Fourier for global periodicity, CWT or STFT for temporal localisation and Lomb-Scargle for irregular events; extract dominant frequencies, power distribution, spectral entropy and phase coherence.
Contextual Annotation: align spectral peaks and bursts with transcripts, logs or video, open-code each event (frustration, curiosity, learning, boredom) and build a Spectral Annotation Matrix.
Modeling and Visualization: train interpretable models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM) on spectral features and produce spectrograms, entropy drift plots and coherence maps.
Validation and Iteration: correlate spectral metrics with SUS, NPS or TLX, verify interpretations in post-analysis participant interviews, and re-analyse with updated codes.
Run an ethical check: use insights to improve design, not to infer private cognition without consent or to manipulate behaviour.
outputs: Per-user or per-session rhythm signatures, a Spectral Annotation Matrix, spectrograms, entropy drift and coherence maps, a behavioural resonance map and validated interpretations.
useWhen: When dense, time-stamped behavioural or physiological data exist and you suspect rhythm, bursts or drift carry meaning (onboarding overload, habit formation, human-AI turn-taking).
avoidWhen: When data are sparse, labels absent and no qualitative follow-up is possible; spectral output without narrative validation risks false precision. Use standard funnel analytics instead.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; signal-processing methods remain siloed in physics, engineering and neuroscience.
whereToUse: Fintech onboarding, emotional journey mapping, agentic AI interaction, longitudinal habit formation, multimodal biometric studies.
example: In a hypothetical fintech onboarding study, high-frequency bursts (0.8–1.2 Hz) cluster at KYC and form-filling, spectral entropy falls from 0.89 to 0.62 by session three, and a Random Forest separates stable from volatile sessions with 82% accuracy.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
Matteo Paz (2024), A Sub-Millisecond Fourier and Wavelet Based Model to Extract Variable Candidates from the NEOWISE Single-Exposure Database
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology.

name: Behaviour Coding for Questionnaire Pretesting
origin: Charles Cannell, Floyd Fowler and Lois Oksenberg; Fowler (2011)
summary: Coding recorded pretest interviews for interviewer and respondent behaviours, then flagging questions whose problem-code rate exceeds about 15 per cent for revision.
description: A quantitative pretest for interviewer-administered questionnaires. Pretest interviews are recorded and every administration of every question is coded with a standard set: interviewer codes (exact reading, minor change, major change, wrong skip) and respondent codes (interruption, request for clarification, inadequate answer, don't know, refusal, adequate answer). Problem-code rates are computed per question, and items above roughly 15 per cent, or high relative to the rest, are flagged once each has at least about ten administrations. Its strength is objectivity and scale: it shows where questions break in real interaction without relying on respondents' introspection. Its limit is that it shows where problems occur, not why, so flagged items are interpreted with coders and interviewers and usually paired with cognitive interviews.
steps: Record 50 to 100 pretest interviews, with consent.
Code each question administration for interviewer behaviour (exact reading, minor change, major change, wrong skip).
Code respondent behaviour (interruption, request for clarification, inadequate answer, don't know, refusal, adequate answer).
Compute problem-code rates per question.
Flag questions above about 15 per cent problem codes, or clearly high relative to others, with at least about ten administrations each.
Debrief coders and interviewers to interpret flagged items, then revise and, where needed, probe them in cognitive interviews.
outputs: Per-question problem rates by code, a ranked list of problem items and revision notes.
useWhen: Pretesting scripted interviews, phone or voice surveys, moderated screeners and structured interview guides that will be used at scale.
avoidWhen: Self-administered web surveys with no interviewer interaction; use web probing or paradata. Do not use alone to decide how to fix an item; pair with cognitive interviewing.
whyLost: UX rarely runs interviewer-administered surveys, and qualitative interviews are not scripted tightly enough for coding to apply.
whereToUse: Voice assistant and IVR dialogue scripts, call-centre satisfaction surveys, structured intake interviews in health and financial services, conversational AI survey agents.
example: A bank's phone-based onboarding survey is behaviour coded across 60 calls. One item about 'linked accounts' draws clarification requests in 28% of administrations and is reworded, while a skip error rate reveals a scripting fault in the agent prompt.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Willis, G. B. (2016). Questionnaire pretesting. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 359-381). London: SAGE.

name: Behaviour Setting Survey (Barker)
origin: Roger Barker and Herbert Wright, Midwest Psychological Field Station, Oskaloosa, Kansas, 1947-1972 (Ecological Psychology, 1968)
summary: Identifies standing patterns of behaviour bound to particular places and times (behaviour settings) and analyses how settings, not individuals, shape behaviour.
description: Barker found that behaviour was better predicted by setting (a classroom, a drugstore, a church service) than by individual personality. A behaviour setting has a standing pattern of behaviour, a physical milieu, synomorphy (fit between them), and boundaries in time and space. Barker's team surveyed every setting in a town, with explicit criteria for distinguishing settings (the K-21 index of interdependence) and measuring them by occupancy, penetration (roles from onlooker to leader) and action patterns. Manning theory showed that undermanned settings pull people into more active roles. For UX, settings explain why the same product is used differently in a clinic, home or commute, and digital spaces (channels, rooms) can be analysed as settings.
steps: Define the community or system and inventory candidate behaviour settings (physical and digital).
Apply criteria for distinct settings (interdependence in behaviour, people, time and place).
Document each setting's standing pattern, milieu, programme, time boundaries and occupants.
Measure occupancy time, penetration levels (roles) and action patterns.
Analyse synomorphy and manning (under- or over-staffed) and how they shape behaviour.
Design products to fit settings or create new settings with appropriate programmes.
outputs: A behaviour setting inventory with standing patterns, occupancy, penetration and design implications.
useWhen: Understanding how contexts govern behaviour, designing for multiple use settings, or designing community and workplace spaces (physical or digital).
avoidWhen: Narrow interface evaluations detached from context.
whyLost: Barker's exhaustive surveys were enormously labour-intensive and ecological psychology declined after the 1970s.
whereToUse: Workplace collaboration tools, online community design, retail, schools and edtech, healthcare environments.
example: A team messaging platform treats each channel as a behaviour setting. Analysis shows undermanned project channels pull members into leadership roles, while overmanned company-wide channels produce onlookers, guiding defaults for channel size and roles.
sources: Barker, Ecological Psychology: Concepts and Methods for Studying the Environment of Human Behavior (1968)
Wicker, An Introduction to Ecological Psychology (1979)
reference: Barker, R. G. (1968). Ecological Psychology. Stanford University Press.

name: Behavioural Causal Map
origin: Stephen Wendel (2014)
summary: A flowchart of every main route to a target outcome, separating the product's ideal path, other in-product routes and external causes, annotated with data.
description: The causal map places a behaviour-change product's ideal path inside a fuller picture of why people reach or miss the target outcome. Boxes are distinguished by type: the ideal path through the product, other in-product actions that also affect the outcome, and external actions the company cannot claim credit for. In-product boxes must be measurable; external causes are drawn only to their last measurable footprint, so the map does not sprawl. Each box is annotated with analytics or rough research estimates. The finished map shows where outside forces block action, reveals unplanned routes worth supporting, supplies control variables for non-experimental impact models, and lets the team make rough forecasts of what a change to one step would do to the outcome. It is a design artefact that disciplines later measurement rather than a formal causal model.
steps: Write the ideal path from the behavioural plan, ending in the target outcome.
Add other in-product actions that can lead to the outcome.
Add external causes, drawing each only as far as its last measurable footprint.
Distinguish the three route types visually (colour or shape).
Annotate each box with measured conversion or volume data, or with research estimates where data are missing.
Identify hindering forces and productive unplanned routes, and list external factors as controls for impact models.
Estimate the effect of proposed changes, such as removing a module or raising one step's completion rate.
outputs: An annotated causal flowchart, a list of candidate control variables, and rough forecasts of the effect of design changes.
useWhen: Use when a product aims at a real-world outcome (saving, exercising, adherence) and the team needs to see which routes the product controls before choosing what to design or measure.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the map as causal proof: to estimate effects use A/B Testing or, for observational data, Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) with proper adjustment. Do not try to map every external possibility.
whyLost: Wendel presented it as novel in product design, and behaviour-change teams usually stop at the behavioural plan or funnel; formal causal diagrams sit with data scientists rather than designers.
whereToUse: Personal finance, health behaviour change, sustainability apps, employee benefits products.
example: An emergency-savings product maps two feature paths, budgeting as an in-product alternative, and windfalls and income shocks as external causes. The map shows most new savings come from tax refunds, so the team designs a refund-time prompt.
reference: Wendel, S. (2014). Designing for Behavior Change: Applying Psychology and Behavioral Economics (1st ed.). Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 238-242.

name: Behavioural Discovery (Outcome, Actor, Action)
origin: Stephen Wendel (2014), from product work at HelloWallet; builds on Ries's Minimum Viable Product (2011)
summary: A staged planning procedure that fixes a product's measurable real-world outcome, its target actors and the single action they should take, before any design.
description: Behavioural discovery makes a behaviour-change product's intent concrete and exposes hidden assumptions. The team writes a vision, turns it into a measurable outcome refined by which, where, what and when (avoiding states of mind), and lists hard constraints. It then brainstorms at least five very different physical actions that would directly cause the outcome, pushes each to the action closest to the outcome, and cuts each to a Minimum Viable Action: one-off before repeated, smaller, without risky parts. After user research, actions blocked by known impediments are dropped and the rest are rated low, medium or high on impact, user motivation, ease and company cost. One action, or two to test in the field, are selected and written as a success statement naming actor, action and outcome. Keeping outcome and action separate is the key safeguard against unexamined assumptions.
steps: Write the product vision, then state the target outcome refined by which, where, what and when, with a metric.
Reject states of mind as outcomes, using prompts such as 'what happens next?' and 'what would a stranger see?'; if outcomes compete, drop any the product could succeed without.
List hard constraints: channel, time frame, resources, tone and mandated audience.
Generate at least five very different candidate actions, each naming who acts, what they physically do and how it causes the outcome.
Push each action to the one that directly causes the outcome and cut it to its Minimum Viable Action.
Research the target users, remove actions blocked by known impediments, and rate the rest low, medium or high on impact, motivation, ease and company cost.
Select one action, or two to compare in the field, and write a success statement naming actor, action, outcome and company objective.
outputs: A defined outcome and metric, a list of actors and candidate actions, a selected target action, and a success statement that later drives impact metrics.
useWhen: Use at the start of a behaviour-change product, or when retrofitting an existing one, when stakeholders talk about awareness or engagement but cannot say what users should actually do.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the team does not yet understand users' context: run Contextual Inquiry or Jobs-to-be-Done Research first. If stakeholders cannot agree on an outcome, the product should not proceed. The ratings are judgements; to confirm that an action changes the outcome use A/B Testing.
whyLost: It is practised by behavioural design teams influenced by Wendel's book but not in mainstream UX, where outcome definition tends to be folded into OKRs and product strategy without the action-selection discipline.
whereToUse: Fintech savings and debt products, health and fitness, civic participation, workplace wellbeing, sustainability.
example: A savings app replaces 'raise financial awareness' with 'members hold one month of expenses in cash within a year'. Of six candidate actions, setting up an automatic transfer scores highest on impact and ease and becomes the target action.
reference: Wendel, S. (2014). Designing for Behavior Change: Applying Psychology and Behavioral Economics (1st ed.). Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 73-109, 257-258.

name: Behavioural Economics Analysis
origin: Kahneman and Tversky, 1970s; Thaler, 1980s
summary: Diagnoses decision points in a product using documented biases such as loss aversion, present bias and status quo bias, and tests interventions to change behaviour.
description: Behavioural economics documents systematic departures from rational choice: loss aversion, present bias, status quo bias, anchoring, mental accounting and others. In UX the method is to map the behaviour a product wants to support, identify the decision points along the journey, diagnose which biases and frictions are operating at each, and design interventions that work with them. A rigorous practice uses a behavioural diagnosis framework (such as COM-B or the BIT EAST model), states each intervention as a falsifiable hypothesis tied to a specific mechanism, and tests it with randomised experiments rather than assuming effects from the literature. Many published effects are small or fail to replicate in new contexts, so local testing and ethical review are part of the method, not optional extras.
steps: Define the target behaviour precisely, including who, what, when and the measurable outcome.
Map the user journey and mark every decision point and friction point.
Diagnose the barriers at each point using a framework such as COM-B, citing the specific bias or mechanism suspected.
Generate interventions (defaults, framing, commitment devices, timely prompts) each linked to one mechanism.
Review interventions for manipulation risk and user benefit before testing.
Test with randomised A/B experiments powered to detect realistic effect sizes, typically 1-5 percentage points.
outputs: Behavioural journey map, bias diagnosis per decision point, intervention hypotheses, experimental results.
useWhen: Products whose success depends on users taking beneficial actions: saving, adhering to medication, completing onboarding, choosing plans.
avoidWhen: When the barrier is capability or usability rather than motivation or choice; fix usability first. Avoid when interventions would serve the business against user interests.
whyLost: Still in use: High industry interest; supports engagement and behavior change design.
whereToUse: E-commerce; health apps; financial products; any behavior-change design.
example: A pension app found few users raised contributions. Diagnosis identified present bias; a 'save more tomorrow' option committing future pay rises lifted contribution increases from 4% to 11% in a randomised test.
reference: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness. Yale University Press.

name: Behavioural Mapping
origin: William Ittelson, Leanne Rivlin and Harold Proshansky, 1970
summary: Systematically records who does what, where and when on a floor plan at timed intervals, producing quantitative maps of how spaces and services are used.
description: Behavioural mapping, developed for psychiatric ward design, records behaviour on a plan of the setting at scheduled intervals. Place-centred mapping observes a fixed area and notes all activities; person-centred mapping follows individuals through space. Coding categories are defined in advance and observers are trained to reliability. GIS-based versions allow spatial statistics. The output reveals use intensity, conflicts, unused zones and flows. For UX and service design, it applies to physical-digital touchpoints: stores with self-service, clinics with check-in kiosks, offices with booking systems, and transit with ticketing. It complements journey maps with real spatial data.
steps: Obtain a scaled plan of the space and define zones.
Define behaviour categories and observer characteristics to record (e.g. age group, alone or group).
Set the observation schedule (e.g. every 15 minutes across representative days and times).
Train observers and check reliability before main data collection.
Record behaviours on the plan (paper, tablet or GIS) and aggregate into density and activity maps.
Interpret patterns, combine with interviews and identify design changes.
outputs: Spatial maps of activity density and type, temporal patterns, and identified conflicts or underused areas.
useWhen: Services delivered in physical spaces with digital touchpoints, or physical product deployment in environments.
avoidWhen: Purely digital experiences without physical context.
whyLost: It remains in architecture and environmental psychology; UX field research seldom quantifies spatial behaviour.
whereToUse: Retail stores, hospital waiting rooms, airports, libraries, co-working spaces, museums.
example: Behavioural mapping in a bank branch shows the self-service kiosks are used mainly to wait for staff, as they sit near the queue; relocating them and adding appointment check-in cuts staff-assisted transactions by a fifth.
sources: Ittelson, Rivlin & Proshansky, The use of behavioral maps in environmental psychology (1970), in Proshansky et al. (eds.), Environmental Psychology
Sommer & Sommer, A Practical Guide to Behavioral Research (5th ed., 2002)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Ittelson, W. H., Rivlin, L. G., & Proshansky, H. M. (1970). The use of behavioral maps in environmental psychology. In Environmental Psychology. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.

name: Behavioural Testing of ML Models
aka: Behavioural testing of ML models (perturbation, invariance, directional expectation tests)
origin: ML engineering practice as described by Chip Huyen (2022); systematised for NLP by Ribeiro et al. (2020, CheckList)
summary: Check a model by perturbing test inputs, swapping sensitive attributes and making changes with known expected effects, to see whether outputs behave robustly, fairly and sensibly before launch.
description: Aggregate accuracy on a held-out set says little about how a model will behave with real users. Behavioural testing probes specific expectations. Perturbation tests add realistic noise to test inputs, such as background noise, clipped audio, typos or poor lighting, and favour the model that degrades least. Invariance tests change only sensitive information, such as name, race or gender, while holding everything else fixed; outputs should not change, and if they do, the sensitive features or their proxies should be removed. Directional expectation tests apply changes whose effect direction is known, such as a larger lot size raising a predicted house price, and investigate any reversal. The tests are written from domain and user knowledge, which is where UX researchers contribute: they know which real-world variations, user groups and expectations matter. A model sensitive to small perturbations is hard to maintain and open to adversarial attack.
steps: List the real-world input variations users will produce (accents, noise, typos, device cameras, phrasing) and create perturbed copies of the test set that mimic them.
Compare candidate models on the perturbed data as well as the clean test set.
For sensitive attributes, swap values while holding other inputs constant and check that outputs do not change.
Define input changes with known expected output directions and check that predictions move accordingly.
Log and investigate every violation, fixing data, features or model before deployment.
Keep the test suite and rerun it on every model update.
outputs: Robustness and bias evidence for each candidate model, with a catalogue of failing cases.
useWhen: Before launching or updating ML-driven features (voice, vision, ranking, credit and risk scoring, LLM features) where real inputs differ from training data or fairness matters.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for testing with users in context; for open-ended generative output quality use Large Language Model Evaluation; for explaining individual predictions use SHAP values for feature attribution.
whyLost: It is ML engineering practice owned by data science teams; UX researchers rarely contribute the expectations and user variations the tests depend on.
whereToUse: Speech and vision features, recommendation and ranking, lending and insurance decisions, health classifiers, chatbots.
example: A cough-screening app scored well on clinic recordings but near chance on users' phone recordings. A perturbation suite with phone microphones, background television and clipped audio would have exposed this before launch, and now runs on every model release.
reference: Huyen, C. (2022). Designing Machine Learning Systems. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 181-183; Ribeiro, M. T., Wu, T., Guestrin, C. and Singh, S. (2020). Beyond accuracy: behavioral testing of NLP models with CheckList. ACL 2020.

name: Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS)
origin: Patricia Cain Smith and Lorne Kendall, 1963
summary: Rating scales whose points are defined by concrete behavioural examples derived from critical incidents, improving rater agreement and meaning.
description: BARS were developed for performance appraisal. Critical incidents of effective and ineffective behaviour are collected from experts, grouped into dimensions, retranslated by a second group to confirm dimension membership, then scaled by experts so each incident anchors a scale point. Raters then judge observed behaviour against concrete descriptions rather than vague adjectives. Agreement improves and ratings are more defensible. For UX, BARS suit observer ratings of task performance, severity of usability problems, quality of AI outputs, or rubric-based design critique, where adjectives like 'good' and 'poor' produce inconsistent ratings.
steps: Collect critical incidents of good and poor performance or quality from experts (e.g. 50-200).
Group incidents into dimensions and define each dimension.
Retranslation: have a second group assign incidents to dimensions; keep those with at least 60-80% agreement.
Have experts rate each retained incident's level; keep incidents with low variance as anchors.
Build scales with behavioural anchors at key points and train raters with examples.
Measure inter-rater reliability in a pilot and revise anchors with poor agreement.
outputs: Behaviourally anchored scales with documented development and reliability estimates.
useWhen: Observer or expert ratings of performance or quality that need consistency, such as AI response quality or usability severity.
avoidWhen: Self-report attitudinal measurement, or when a quick rating is enough.
whyLost: It is an HR and organisational psychology tool; UX rubrics are usually ad hoc.
whereToUse: LLM output evaluation rubrics, support agent quality, usability severity rating, design review rubrics.
example: An AI team replaces a 1-5 'helpfulness' rating with BARS anchored by concrete response behaviours. Inter-rater ICC rises from 0.52 to 0.81.
sources: Smith & Kendall, Retranslation of expectations (1963), Journal of Applied Psychology
Schwab, Heneman & DeCotiis, Behaviorally anchored rating scales: A review of the literature (1975), Personnel Psychology
reference: Smith, P. C., & Kendall, L. M. (1963). Journal of Applied Psychology, 47(2), 149-155.

name: Belief-bias syllogism evaluation
donor: Psychology of reasoning; judgement and decision making
origin: Evans, Barston and Pollard, 1983
summary: People judge whether conclusions follow logically from premises, with logical validity crossed with believability, to measure how far plausible conclusions override sound reasoning.
description: The task presents syllogisms in a 2 x 2 design: valid or invalid form, crossed with a believable or unbelievable conclusion. Participants say whether each conclusion follows. The textbook pattern is that valid syllogisms are accepted about 80 percent of the time with believable conclusions but only 56 percent with unbelievable ones, while invalid ones with believable conclusions are still accepted about 71 percent of the time. Time pressure strengthens the effect. The design separates form (validity) from content (truth), which is exactly the confusion that affects how people read explanations, arguments and justifications. Rigour comes from the full crossing, matched content, and a time-pressure manipulation that shows whether people are relying on intuitive plausibility.
steps: Write syllogisms in four cells: valid-believable, valid-unbelievable, invalid-believable and invalid-unbelievable, with at least four items per cell.
Match items across cells for length and structure, varying only form and conclusion content.
Instruct participants to accept a conclusion only if it follows necessarily, assuming the premises are true.
Present items in random order; optionally add a time-limited condition (for example 10 seconds per item) to increase reliance on intuition.
Compute acceptance rates per cell and the belief effect (believable minus unbelievable) and logic effect (valid minus invalid).
Test the interaction and check whether restating an invalid argument with neutral content exposes its form.
outputs: Acceptance rates in the 2 x 2 design, belief, logic and interaction indices, and the effect of time pressure.
useWhen: Testing whether users, reviewers or stakeholders accept AI explanations, recommendation reasons or persuasive copy because the conclusion sounds right rather than because the reasoning holds.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a general measure of reasoning skill, since abstract syllogisms have low ecological validity and people vary widely in strategy; for real decisions use scenario-based judgement tasks.
whyLost: It belongs to the psychology of reasoning, and UX rarely measures how people evaluate arguments as opposed to whether they like content.
whereToUse: Explainable AI, health and financial advice copy, fact-checking and misinformation labels, research readouts to executives.
example: An AI assistant's explanations are rewritten so that sound and flawed reasoning lead to plausible or implausible conclusions; users accept flawed explanations with plausible conclusions almost as often as sound ones, so the team adds visible evidence links.
reference: Evans, J. St. B. T., Barston, J. L., & Pollard, P. (1983). On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning. Memory & Cognition, 11, 295-306.

name: Believed-Cause versus Logged-Data Covariation Check
origin: Donald Redelmeier and Amos Tversky (1996)
summary: Elicit exactly which factor people believe drives an outcome and at what delay, then correlate their own logged data at that lag and others to test the belief.
description: People confidently report causal links that their own records do not support. Redelmeier and Tversky asked 18 arthritis patients which weather variable affected their pain and at what lag, then analysed 15 months of fortnightly measures. The mean correlation at each patient's stated variable and lag was about .02, and across nine lags only 6% of correlations were significant, close to chance, yet nearly all patients believed in a strong effect. A second task found that people correctly identified correlated pairs of random-walk graphs about 90% of the time but saw unrelated pairs as related up to 87% of the time. The mechanism is selective matching: memorable coincidences count, non-matches are ignored, and freedom to pick variables and lags helps. The method pairs belief elicitation with an analysis of the believer's own data.
steps: Elicit the belief precisely: the outcome, the causal factor, the direction and the lag.
Pull the relevant logs for the same people or system covering the outcome and the factor over a long enough period.
Correlate at the stated lag and at a grid of other lags, adjusting for multiple comparisons.
Optionally run a classification task with correlated and uncorrelated series pairs to estimate the group's rate of illusory perception.
Feed both results back to the team or users, noting the limits of coarse logs.
outputs: Correlations at the believed and alternative lags for each belief, and an estimate of how often the group perceives relations in unrelated series.
useWhen: Testing stakeholder or user folk theories ('tickets spike after every release', 'this notification causes churn') against existing telemetry, and studies of self-tracking users' beliefs.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating one null correlation on coarse data as disproof. For causal claims, run an experiment or a proper causal analysis of observational data.
whyLost: It comes from medical judgement research and has not been packaged as a UX method, though UX teams are full of untested causal beliefs.
whereToUse: Self-tracking and health apps, product teams' operational beliefs, support and incident analysis, personal finance insights.
example: Support leads believe tickets rise the day after each release. Correlating two years of queue logs with release dates at lags of -2 to +2 days shows no consistent relation, redirecting attention to a weekly billing run.
sources: On the Belief that Arthritis Pain Is Related to the Weather (Redelmeier & Tversky, 1996)
reference: Redelmeier, D. A. and Tversky, A. (1996). On the belief that arthritis pain is related to the weather. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 93(7), 2895-2896.

name: Bellotti's Five Questions for Sensing Systems
origin: Victoria Bellotti, Maribeth Back, Keith Edwards, Rebecca Grinter, Austin Henderson and Cristina Lopes, CHI 2002
summary: Inspect a sensing or gestural design by asking how users address it, how it shows attention, what actions exist, how it responds and how accidents are handled.
description: Bellotti and colleagues argued that sensing systems lose the communicative cues that GUIs take for granted, so designers must answer five questions explicitly. Address: how does the user direct input to the system and not to something else? Attention: how does the system show that it is ready and attending? Action: what can be done and how are targets and operations specified? Alignment: how does the system respond and show that it is doing the right thing? Accident: how are errors avoided, and how can they be corrected or undone? Saffer recommends the questions as a completeness check on gestural interface documentation, alongside movement notation, because notation alone ignores the interplay between person and system. Used as an inspection, any question the design cannot answer marks a likely failure point.
steps: Assemble the design or specification of the sensing, voice or gestural system.
Answer Address: how does the user direct input to this system rather than to others or to nothing?
Answer Attention: how does the system signal that it is ready and attending?
Answer Action: what can the user do, and how are targets and operations specified?
Answer Alignment: how does the system respond and show that it understood?
Answer Accident: how are errors avoided, detected and recovered from?
Flag any question the design or documentation cannot answer and resolve it before testing.
outputs: A completeness check of a sensing-system design or specification, with flagged gaps.
useWhen: Specifying or reviewing gesture, voice, proximity, camera or wearable interfaces, and any always-listening or ambient system.
avoidWhen: Conventional GUIs, where Heuristic Evaluation covers similar ground. It is a question set, not a test; follow with Usability Testing or Wizard of Oz Prototyping.
whyLost: It is cited mainly in ubiquitous computing research and rarely appears in practitioner toolkits, despite the growth of voice and gesture products.
whereToUse: Smart speakers, in-car gesture control, AR and VR input, camera-based kiosks and wearables.
example: Reviewing a smart speaker's wake-word design, a team finds no good answer to Accident: accidental activations during TV dialogue cannot be noticed or undone. They add an audible earcon and a voice 'cancel that' command.
reference: Bellotti, V., Back, M., Edwards, W.K., Grinter, R.E., Henderson, A. and Lopes, C. (2002) Making sense of sensing systems: five questions for designers and researchers. Proceedings of CHI 2002, 415-422.

name: Benchmarking
origin: Summative usability testing tradition; Common Industry Format, ANSI/ISO, 2001 to 2006
summary: Measures a product's usability with standardised metrics against past versions, competitors or targets, providing a quantitative baseline to track improvement.
description: UX benchmarking measures a product's experience with a fixed set of tasks and standardised metrics, such as task success, time on task, errors, SUS or SUPR-Q, so results can be compared over time or with competitors. Unlike formative testing, its purpose is measurement, not problem discovery, so the protocol must stay stable across rounds. Rigour comes from representative tasks with clear success criteria, sample sizes that give useful precision (often 30 to 100 or more per product), consistent recruitment and environment, validated questionnaires, reporting confidence intervals, and statistical comparisons rather than raw differences. Benchmarks are most valuable when repeated at regular intervals and tied to business outcomes.
steps: Select 5 to 10 key tasks that represent core value and define success criteria.
Choose metrics: task success, time, errors, task ease (SEQ) and a validated questionnaire such as SUS.
Calculate the sample size needed for target precision and recruit consistently across rounds.
Run the study with a fixed protocol, usually unmoderated for scale.
Analyse metrics with confidence intervals and compare against baseline or competitors using appropriate tests.
Create a scorecard and repeat at regular intervals, such as every release or year.
outputs: A benchmark scorecard with metrics and confidence intervals, competitor comparisons and trends over time.
useWhen: For establishing a baseline before redesign, demonstrating UX improvement or ROI, competitive comparison and tracking product maturity.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the goal is discovering why problems occur; use moderated testing. Avoid comparing results collected with different tasks or protocols.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for demonstrating UX ROI and tracking improvement over time.
whereToUse: Product maturity assessment; competitive analysis; before/after redesign evaluation.
example: A HR software vendor benchmarks five tasks against two competitors with 60 users each. Its expense submission success is 15 points lower, which justifies the next quarter's redesign; a year later the gap has closed.
sources: Building a Quant UXR Practice from Inception to Integration (Bakhshi, 2024)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld & Morville, 2006)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience. MeasuringU Press.

name: Benford's Law Data Integrity Testing
origin: Simon Newcomb (1881); Frank Benford (1938); forensic accounting application by Mark Nigrini (1990s)
summary: Checks whether naturally occurring numbers in data follow the expected first-digit distribution, flagging fabricated, manipulated or erroneous entries.
description: In many naturally occurring datasets spanning several orders of magnitude, the leading digit d appears with probability log10(1 + 1/d): about 30% start with 1 and under 5% with 9. Fabricated numbers usually deviate. Forensic accountants use first-digit, first-two-digit and last-digit tests with mean absolute deviation thresholds to flag suspicious records. For UX research and product data, Benford tests can flag fraudulent survey responses (numeric answers), fake reviews with numeric claims, manipulated self-reported metrics, or data pipeline errors. It is a screening tool, not proof, and requires data that should follow Benford.
steps: Confirm the dataset is suitable: naturally occurring, spanning multiple orders of magnitude, not bounded or assigned.
Extract first digits (and optionally first two digits) of the values.
Compare observed with Benford frequencies using MAD with Nigrini's conformity thresholds, plus chi-square for large samples.
Drill into subsets (by respondent, panel source, seller) that deviate most.
Investigate flagged records with other evidence (timing, IP, consistency checks).
Document and exclude confirmed problematic records, reporting the procedure.
outputs: Conformity statistics, deviating subsets and investigated suspicious records.
useWhen: Screening survey panels, self-reported numeric data, marketplace listings or financial data for fabrication or errors.
avoidWhen: Data that should not follow Benford (prices set at thresholds, assigned IDs, narrow ranges).
whyLost: Data quality checks in UX research focus on attention checks and speeders; forensic accounting methods are unknown.
whereToUse: Online survey panels, expense and invoicing tools, fitness and health self-reports, seller-provided data.
example: A UX survey asking monthly spend shows one panel vendor's responses deviating strongly from Benford (MAD 0.031), along with straight-lining; their 400 responses are removed after investigation.
sources: Nigrini, Benford's Law: Applications for Forensic Accounting, Auditing, and Fraud Detection (2012)
Benford, The law of anomalous numbers (1938), Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Nigrini, M. J. (2012). Benford's Law. Wiley.

name: BERTopic (transformer-based topic clustering)
origin: Maarten Grootendorst, 2020 (library), 2022 (paper)
summary: Clustering sentence embeddings of feedback or transcript passages into topics, which handles short texts and semantic similarity better than word-count topic models.
description: BERTopic encodes each document with a sentence transformer, reduces dimensionality with UMAP, clusters with HDBSCAN and describes each cluster with class-based TF-IDF keywords. Because embeddings capture meaning, it groups semantically similar texts that share few words, which suits short app reviews, survey comments and chat messages. HDBSCAN also labels outliers rather than forcing every document into a topic. Rigour comes from fixing seeds (UMAP is stochastic), tuning min_cluster_size, checking how many documents are outliers, evaluating topics by reading representative documents, checking stability across runs, and avoiding over-interpretation of small clusters.
steps: Prepare documents as passages or responses, removing moderator speech and boilerplate.
Encode with a pinned sentence-transformer (e.g. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for speed or a larger model for quality).
Configure UMAP (n_neighbors about 15, n_components about 5, fixed seed) and HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size scaled to corpus size, e.g. 10-50).
Fit BERTopic and inspect topic sizes and the proportion of outliers (investigate if above about 30%).
Read representative documents for each topic, merge redundant topics and label them.
Re-run with 3 or more seeds and keep topics that recur; report prevalence by segment and over time.
outputs: Topic clusters with keywords and representative documents, outlier list, topic-over-time and per-segment distributions.
useWhen: Short-text corpora (reviews, chat logs, survey comments, AI prompts) and multilingual corpora with multilingual embeddings.
avoidWhen: Avoid on small corpora (under a few hundred documents) and where interpretive depth is needed; use thematic analysis there. Be wary when documents mix many topics.
whyLost: It is recent and requires machine learning tooling; UX teams increasingly encounter it via vendor tools but rarely run it with validation.
whereToUse: App review analysis, in-product feedback, AI assistant prompt analysis and support conversation mining.
example: An AI writing tool clusters 60,000 thumbs-down comments with BERTopic. Stable topics include 'ignored my tone instructions' and 'too long', and topic-over-time shows the first rising after a model update.
sources: Grootendorst, M. (2022) BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure. arXiv:2203.05794
McInnes, L., Healy, J. & Astels, S. (2017) hdbscan: Hierarchical density based clustering. JOSS
Reimers, N. & Gurevych, I. (2019) Sentence-BERT. EMNLP
The Inquiry Series, C11 — Topic Modelling at Scale — LDA, BERTopic & Semantic Clustering
reference: Grootendorst, M. (2022) BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure. arXiv:2203.05794

name: BERTopic Topic Modelling
origin: Maarten Grootendorst, 2020-2022 (BERTopic)
summary: Discovering semantically coherent topics in thousands of text segments using sentence embeddings, UMAP, HDBSCAN and class-based TF-IDF, then interpreting them qualitatively.
description: BERTopic improves on bag-of-words topic models such as LDA by clustering meaning rather than word co-occurrence. Text is chunked into semantic units, embedded with a sentence-transformer model, reduced in dimension with UMAP and clustered with HDBSCAN, which also identifies outliers. Class-based TF-IDF then extracts representative terms per cluster. Parameters are tuned until topics are interpretable, and each topic is named after reading representative excerpts rather than from its keyword list. In qualitative research it serves as a map of large corpora, showing what is talked about and where human attention should go, not as a replacement for interpretive coding.
steps: Prepare corpus: Chunk transcripts into semantic units (50–200 words). Remove filler words, researcher turns, timestamps.
Generate sentence embeddings: sentence-transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sufficient for most UX research corpora).
Run BERTopic: UMAP for dimensionality reduction, HDBSCAN for clustering, c-TF-IDF for topic word extraction.
Evaluate coherence: Review top 10 words per topic. Adjust UMAP/HDBSCAN parameters until topics are interpretable.
Interpret qualitatively: For each topic, retrieve 5–10 representative excerpts. Name the topic based on meaning, not keyword list.
Use as sampling guide: Topics identify where to focus human qualitative analysis — not to replace it.
outputs: Topic clusters with keywords and representative excerpts, topic size and trend charts, outlier lists, and a sampling guide for human analysis.
useWhen: Thousands of open-ended responses, reviews, tickets or transcript segments where you need an overview of themes before deep analysis.
avoidWhen: Small corpora (under a few hundred segments), or when you need explanatory or causal insight; use human coding.
whyLost: It spread rapidly in data science and customer insight teams because it is open source and produces readable topics with little tuning.
whereToUse: App store and product review mining, support ticket triage, open-ended NPS comments, and large research repository exploration.
example: A travel booking site runs BERTopic on 12,000 post-trip comments. A small but growing topic on 'hidden resort fees' is spotted, and researchers then read its 50 most representative comments to scope a pricing transparency study.
sources: BERTopic: Neural Topic Modeling with a Class-based TF-IDF Procedure (Grootendorst)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Grootendorst, M. (2022). BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure. arXiv:2203.05794.

name: Beta-Binomial conjugate model
origin: Thomas Bayes (1763) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1774); conjugate prior analysis formalised by Raiffa and Schlaifer (1961)
summary: Estimates success rates, such as task completion or conversion, as a Beta distribution updated with observed successes and failures, giving full uncertainty with simple arithmetic.
description: For binary outcomes the Beta distribution is the conjugate prior of the binomial likelihood: if the prior is Beta(a, b) and you observe s successes and f failures, the posterior is Beta(a + s, b + f). This makes Bayesian estimation of completion rates, conversion rates or error rates trivial to compute and easy to explain. The posterior gives credible intervals and direct probability statements, such as the probability that the completion rate exceeds 80%, or that variant B beats A. Small-sample usability studies benefit especially, because the posterior remains well behaved at 0 or 100% success, where Wald intervals fail. Rigour comes from stating and justifying the prior, checking sensitivity to it, and using posterior simulation for comparisons.
steps: Define the binary outcome precisely, such as task success under defined criteria or conversion within a session.

Choose a prior: Beta(1, 1) for uniform ignorance, Beta(0.5, 0.5) for the Jeffreys prior, or an informative Beta based on past studies with prior strength equivalent to a stated number of observations.
Update with data: posterior is Beta(a + successes, b + failures).
Report the posterior mean and 95% credible interval, and answer decision questions directly, such as P(rate > 0.8).
To compare variants, draw 10,000 or more samples from each posterior and compute P(B > A) and the distribution of the difference or ratio.
Check prior sensitivity by repeating with a weak prior and report whether conclusions change.
outputs: Posterior distributions, credible intervals, probabilities of exceeding thresholds or beating alternatives, and prior sensitivity checks.
useWhen: Estimating proportions from small usability samples, communicating uncertainty in probability terms, comparing conversion rates, or combining evidence across studies.
avoidWhen: Outcomes are not binary or trials are not exchangeable (for example strong clustering by user); use hierarchical or regression models. Avoid informative priors that cannot be defended to stakeholders.
whyLost: Bayesian methods are standard in statistics and some experimentation platforms, but UX research training emphasises frequentist tests, so the model is rarely used directly.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks with 5 to 20 participants, fintech conversion tests, feature adoption estimates, A/B tests with low traffic.
example: In a test with 9 of 10 participants completing a transfer, a Beta(1, 1) prior gave a posterior of Beta(10, 2), with a 95% credible interval of about 0.59 to 0.98 and P(rate > 0.7) about 0.91, which the team reported instead of '90% success'.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design
Predicting User Behavior: The Must-Know Distributions for UX & HF Researchers (carousel, n.d.)
Bayesian Methods in Engineering Design Problems (Swiler, 2006)
reference: McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking (2nd ed.). CRC Press; Gelman, A., et al. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd ed.). CRC Press.

name: Beta-Binomial Problem Discovery Model
origin: Schmettow (2008, 2009), building on Ennis & Bi (1998)
summary: Models variation in how often different problems occur, so estimates of how many problems remain are not overly optimistic.
description: The classic 1 − (1 − p)^n model assumes every problem has the same chance of being found. In reality some problems hit almost everyone and some very few, and this heterogeneity (overdispersion) makes the simple model overestimate how much has been found: you think you are done when you are not. The beta-binomial model lets p itself vary according to a beta distribution, with a mean and a spread parameter. Schmettow's simulations found it fitted real discovery curves better in three of five datasets. His advice, reported by Sauro and Lewis: use Lewis's adjusted binomial for small studies (n under 6), switch to the beta-binomial once you have 10 or more participants, and keep a generous safety margin when usability is mission-critical. A zero-truncated logit-normal binomial is a related alternative.
steps: Record a participant-by-problem matrix from a formative study of at least about 10 participants.
Fit a beta-binomial (or zero-truncated logit-normal binomial) to the problem frequencies.
Estimate the mean and variability of p.
Project the discovery curve and the expected number of unseen problems.
Compare with the simple adjusted binomial; if they differ, plan more sessions.
outputs: A more realistic estimate of undiscovered problems and of the sample needed.
useWhen: Safety-critical or large formative programmes where stopping too early is costly.
avoidWhen: Very small studies (under about 6 participants), where there is too little data to estimate variability.
whyLost: It requires statistical fitting beyond spreadsheet formulas, and the five-user debate was settled in public with the simpler model.
whereToUse: Medical device formative evaluation, aviation and automotive HMI, large research programmes.
example: After 12 sessions the simple model says 91% of problems are found; the beta-binomial says 74%, so the team schedules another round.
reference: Schmettow, M. (2008). Heterogeneity in the usability evaluation process. Proceedings of HCI 2008.

name: Between-Subjects vs Within-Subjects Design Selection
origin: Classical experimental design (Fisher, 1935); practical treatment in Schweigert (2012)
summary: A decision procedure for choosing within-subjects, between-subjects or mixed designs in UX studies, weighing error variance, carryover effects and sample size.
description: In a within-subjects design every participant experiences all conditions, which removes between-person variability and typically needs far fewer participants, but introduces order, practice, fatigue and carryover effects that must be controlled through counterbalancing such as Latin squares. In a between-subjects design each participant sees one condition, avoiding carryover but requiring larger samples and random assignment. Many UX comparisons are run without considering this choice, for example letting participants try both prototypes in the same order, or running unmoderated between-subjects tests underpowered by a factor of three. The method makes the choice explicit: assess whether exposure to one condition changes the response to another, estimate required samples for each design from expected effect size and variability, and specify counterbalancing or randomisation.
steps: Design selection decision tree:
Is carryover possible (learning, fatigue, practice effects)? YES → between-subjects or counterbalanced within-subjects. NO → within-subjects (60% fewer participants needed).
(2) If within-subjects: counterbalance condition order using Latin square.
(3) For preference studies: always within-subjects (between-subjects preference studies are severely underpowered).
(4) Compute required N using G*Power for the chosen design.
outputs: Documented design choice with rationale, sample size estimates for each option, counterbalancing or randomisation scheme, and analysis plan matched to the design.
useWhen: Any comparative UX study: prototype comparisons, preference tests, benchmark studies and lab experiments.
avoidWhen: When learning or one-time experiences are the point (first impressions, onboarding), carryover makes within-subjects invalid; when only observational data exist, use quasi-experimental methods.
whyLost: UX borrowed experiments without the methodological training around them, so design choice is often made by convenience and its consequences are invisible in small studies.
whereToUse: All UX study design. The most consequential methodological decision for study efficiency and validity.
example: Comparing two navigation prototypes, a team realises participants who learn the information structure in one will be faster in the other. They choose a between-subjects design for first-use task time, and a within-subjects counterbalanced design for preference.
sources: Research Methods in Psychology — Wendy A. Schweigert
Research Methods in Psychology: A Handbook (Wendy Schweigert)
Quantifying the User Experience (Jeff Sauro & James Lewis)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Schweigert WA (2012) Research Methods in Psychology: A Handbook. 3rd ed. Waveland Press

name: Between-Viewer Gaze Dispersion on Video
aka: Between-viewer gaze dispersion on dynamic video
origin: Stelmach, Tam and Hearty (1991); Goldstein, Woods and Peli (2007); Mital et al. (2010); Kirkorian, Anderson and Keen (2012)
summary: Eye-track many viewers watching the same video and measure frame by frame how spread out their gaze is, showing when attention converges and how cuts disrupt it.
description: For each video frame, the gaze points of all viewers are clustered or enclosed in an ellipse holding most of them. Low dispersion means viewers look at the same place at the same time, called attentional synchrony, which indicates attention driven by the narrative or by strong salience. Adults converge strongly on edited video; infants are more dispersed, especially just after a camera cut, and converge over the course of a shot, suggesting they need more time to process each scene. Plotting dispersion against time since each cut gives recovery curves. Because strong bottom-up features such as motion also produce convergence, results should be compared with a saliency model. For UX, the metric turns eye-tracking of videos, animations, tutorials or dynamic dashboards into a time series showing which moments hold shared attention and which scatter it.
steps: Eye-track a group of viewers (for example 20 or more) watching the same video or animated sequence.
Align gaze samples to video frames.
For each frame compute dispersion, such as the area of the ellipse covering most gaze points or the number of gaze clusters.
Mark events such as cuts, scene changes, captions or calls to action on the timeline.
Plot dispersion against time since each event and compare viewer groups or video versions.
Compare with a computational saliency model to separate story-driven from motion-driven convergence.
outputs: Dispersion time series per group or version, recovery curves after cuts, and moments of high and low shared attention.
useWhen: You are evaluating video, animation or motion-heavy content (tutorials, ads, onboarding videos, game cutscenes) and need to know where viewers' attention converges or scatters over time.
avoidWhen: Content is static, or you need individual comprehension rather than group attention; use standard eye-tracking metrics, recall tests or interviews instead.
whyLost: It needs many eye-tracked viewers and frame-level processing, and UX eye-tracking has focused on static pages and heatmaps.
whereToUse: Product videos and tutorials, children's media, advertising, streaming interfaces, game cutscenes and animated data stories.
example: An edtech company eye-tracks 30 learners on a tutorial video. Dispersion spikes for four seconds after each fast cut and stays high during on-screen text, so the team slows editing and moves key text away from motion.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Anderson, D. R., & Kirkorian, H. L. (2015). Media and cognitive development. In L. S. Liben & U. Müller (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 2, pp. 949-994. Wiley.

name: Bias and Gaming Audit for Incentivised Customer-Feedback Scores
origin: Reichheld and Markey, 2011, drawing on Enterprise Rent-A-Car, Philips Healthcare and KPMG practice
summary: Anticipate and audit four biases in customer-feedback scores (fear of retribution, bribery, sample bias, grade inflation) and validate scores against behaviour before tying them to pay.
description: Once feedback scores affect rankings or pay, staff have reason to manipulate them: begging for top scores, sending surveys only to happy customers, altering contact details of unhappy ones. Reichheld and Markey name four bias sources (fear of retribution, bribery, sample bias, grade inflation) and pair countermeasures with audits. Countermeasures include confidentiality (account averages in B2B), educating customers and staff, ranking teams so peers police each other, unpredictable request timing, third-party collection soon after the event, very high response rates from the right sample, imputing non-respondents and asking relative questions. Audits track failed survey contacts per unit and inspect outliers, have executives call random customers, monitor survey calls, keep methods consistent with footnoted reports, and commission external audits of lists, calls, verbatims and calculations. Scores are regularly validated against referrals, purchases and retention, and linked to pay only after several cycles of published rankings.
steps: List how each of the four bias sources (retribution, bribery, sample bias, grade inflation) could arise in your setting.
Choose countermeasures for each, such as third-party collection, unpredictable timing and confidentiality.
Track contact-failure and response rates by unit and investigate outliers.
Spot-check by calling random customers and detractors and monitoring survey calls.
Keep the collection method consistent and document it in report footnotes; consider an external audit.
Validate scores against later customer behaviour (referrals, purchases, retention).
Delay linking scores to pay until they have proved stable and valid over several cycles.
outputs: An audited, trustworthy score series, a list of detected manipulations, and validation evidence linking scores to behaviour.
useWhen: Any NPS, CSAT or review score that feeds team targets, bonuses, partner rankings or public claims.
avoidWhen: Purely diagnostic research scores with no incentives attached, where a lighter data-quality check is enough. Even paying on response rate can bias who is surveyed.
whyLost: Organisations adopt score targets quickly but rarely budget for auditing them; Goodhart-style gaming is widely acknowledged yet seldom checked systematically.
whereToUse: Customer success and support teams with CSAT targets, marketplaces ranking sellers or drivers, franchise networks and B2B account scores.
example: A ride-hailing firm notices one city's driver ratings rising while complaints also rise. Contact-failure tracking shows riders with cancelled trips rarely receive surveys there, so collection moves to an automatic post-trip trigger before ratings are used in driver incentives.
reference: Reichheld, F., with Markey, R. (2011). The Ultimate Question 2.0: How Net Promoter Companies Thrive in a Customer-Driven World (rev. and expanded ed.). Boston: Harvard Business Review Press.

name: Biased assimilation of evidence
donor: Social psychology; judgement and decision making
origin: Lord, Ross and Lepper, 1979
summary: People with opposing prior views rate the same mixed evidence; each side finds supportive studies convincing and opposing ones weak, measuring myside bias in evaluating evidence.
description: A questionnaire first classifies participants by their position on an issue. Everyone then reads descriptions of studies that support and oppose that position, matched in quality and method, and rates how convincing each is. In the original study on capital punishment, each side rated the studies that agreed with them as convincing and the others as flawed, and exposure to mixed evidence polarised rather than moderated views. The design is a clean way to measure selective acceptance of evidence: the same material is evaluated differently depending on prior commitment. Rigour depends on balanced, quality-matched study descriptions, counterbalanced order and an attitude measure taken before and after.
steps: Measure each participant's prior position on the issue with a short questionnaire, and select or stratify for clear supporters and opponents.
Prepare paired evidence descriptions that support and oppose the position, matched for method, sample size and quality.
Counterbalance which design (for example cross-sectional or longitudinal) is attached to which conclusion.
Have participants rate each piece of evidence for convincingness and methodological quality.
Re-measure attitude after reading to test for polarisation.
Analyse ratings by prior position and evidence direction; the interaction is the bias.
outputs: Convincingness ratings by prior attitude and evidence direction, a myside bias index, and pre-post attitude change.
useWhen: Auditing how stakeholders receive research findings that support or contradict their roadmap, or how users react to fact-checks and corrective information.
avoidWhen: Avoid when evidence descriptions cannot be matched in quality, since differences will be legitimate; for broader stakeholder bias reviews use a cognitive bias audit.
whyLost: It is a social psychology demonstration, not a packaged research method, and UX rarely studies how its own audiences evaluate evidence.
whereToUse: Research operations and readout design, news and fact-checking products, health misinformation, AI-generated summaries of contested topics.
example: Before a pricing decision, product leads rate anonymised study summaries that favour or oppose the proposed change; each camp rates the opposing studies as weaker, so the team agrees quality criteria before seeing results.
reference: Lord, C. G., Ross, L., & Lepper, M. R. (1979). Biased assimilation and attitude polarization. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37, 2098-2109.

name: Bibliometric Knowledge Mapping
origin: CiteSpace by Chaomei Chen; applied to UX literature by Xia and Liu (2022)
summary: Retrieve a field's literature and map publication trends, keyword co-occurrence clusters, central keywords and bursts to identify research hotspots and trends.
description: Bibliometric knowledge mapping treats a body of literature as data. Records are retrieved from a database with a defined query and source tiers, irrelevant items are removed by hand, and software such as CiteSpace builds keyword co-occurrence networks ranked by frequency and betweenness centrality. Keywords are clustered, with modularity Q above 0.3 taken as a significant structure and mean silhouette S above 0.5 reasonable and above 0.7 convincing. Burst detection finds keywords that surged in particular periods, and a timezone view divides the field into stages. Descriptive statistics on publications per year, journals and institutional co-operation complete the picture. In the example study, 510 of 1,069 records on UX in China yielded ten clusters with Q = 0.80 and S = 0.98. Results depend heavily on search terms and filtering.
steps: Define the search: theme, keywords, database and source tiers, and the date range.
Retrieve records and manually exclude irrelevant items such as notices and reports.
Chart publications per year, journals, disciplines and institutional co-operation.
Build the keyword co-occurrence network and rank keywords by frequency and betweenness centrality.
Cluster keywords and check modularity Q (above 0.3) and silhouette S (above 0.5, ideally above 0.7).
Run burst detection and a timezone view to identify surging topics and stages, then synthesise hotspots and trends.
outputs: Publication trend charts, co-occurrence and cluster maps, a burst keyword list, and a staged history with trend predictions.
useWhen: Scoping a research programme, entering an unfamiliar domain, or positioning a research team's agenda against the literature.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for reading key papers or for a systematic review of evidence on a specific question. Results are sensitive to database coverage and search terms.
whyLost: It is standard in information science but UX practitioners rarely analyse literature quantitatively.
whereToUse: Research strategy, academic-industry partnerships, emerging areas such as AI UX or accessibility, research operations.
example: A research lead maps 2,000 papers on conversational AI and trust. Burst detection shows 'explainability' surging after 2020, informing which questions the team should treat as settled and which remain open.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Xia, W. and Liu, Z. (2022). User experience research in China: A 15-year bibliometric analysis. In M. M. Soares, E. Rosenzweig and A. Marcus (Eds.), Design, User Experience, and Usability: DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321 (pp. 295-313). Cham: Springer.

name: BIC model selection (K=2..10)
origin: Gideon Schwarz, 1978
summary: Chooses the number of clusters or model complexity by balancing fit against parameter count, favouring the K that minimises the Bayesian information criterion.
description: BIC equals minus twice the log-likelihood plus the number of parameters times the log of sample size. Adding clusters always improves likelihood, but BIC's penalty grows with parameters, so the minimum indicates the best trade-off and approximates the model with the highest posterior probability. For Gaussian mixture segmentation, fitting K = 2 to 10 and comparing BIC across covariance structures gives a principled number of segments rather than one chosen to fit a slide. Differences in BIC above 10 are conventionally treated as very strong evidence. Rigour requires stable fits (multiple initialisations), checking the BIC curve rather than just its minimum, and judging whether extra clusters are substantively meaningful.
steps: Fit candidate models for K = 2 to 10, each with multiple random initialisations (e.g. 10) and several covariance types.
Compute BIC for each and plot BIC against K by covariance type.
Identify the minimum; treat BIC differences below 2 as negligible, 2-6 as positive, 6-10 as strong, above 10 as very strong evidence.
If the curve flattens, prefer the simpler model or use an elbow in BIC improvement.
Confirm the chosen K with stability and validation indices and qualitative interpretability.
outputs: A BIC curve across K and covariance options, a recommended number of segments and supporting evidence strength.
useWhen: Selecting the number of segments in mixture models, latent class analysis or other likelihood-based models.
avoidWhen: Avoid for k-means (no likelihood; use silhouette or gap statistic), for very large samples where BIC may favour many small clusters with trivial differences, or when the goal is prediction (use cross-validation).
whyLost: UX teams often fix the number of personas in advance or choose it visually; information criteria come from statistics training few UX researchers have.
whereToUse: Behavioural segmentation in fintech, SaaS and e-commerce; latent class analysis of survey attitudes.
example: Fitting GMMs to investor behaviour, BIC drops sharply to K = 4 and then flattens, with K = 5 only 3 points lower. The team selects four archetypes as both statistically supported and interpretable.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Schwarz (1978) Estimating the dimension of a model
The Inquiry Series, Ch 51 — Behavioral Clustering & Probabilistic Segmentation
Mixed Models: A Flexible Approach to Correlated Data (Seltman, n.d.)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Schwarz, G. (1978) Estimating the dimension of a model. Annals of Statistics, 6(2), 461-464.

name: Bifurcation and Phase-Plane Analysis
origin: Standard tool of nonlinear dynamical systems theory; the book teaches it with the Grind (de Boer) and deBif (de Roos) R tools, applied to models such as the spruce budworm, panic (Robinaugh et al. 2019) and van Geert growth models.
summary: Writing a verbal theory of behaviour as a few differential equations, then numerically finding its stable and unstable equilibria and how they appear, disappear or switch as a parameter changes.
description: Many behaviour change theories describe feedback loops in words: anxiety raises arousal which raises perceived threat, use builds skill which builds use. The book shows how to turn such theories into small systems of differential equations, simulate them, and analyse them rather than only run them. Phase-plane plots show the direction of change for two variables at once and locate fixed points; a Newton search finds equilibria from different starting states, and parameter continuation traces how each equilibrium moves as a parameter varies, producing a bifurcation diagram that reveals bistability, hysteresis and tipping points. Adding stochastic noise shows spontaneous jumps between states. The book separates dynamic noise, which changes the trajectory, from measurement error, which does not, and warns that fitting such models to data is sensitive to starting values and model choices; seemingly small changes in a term can transform the qualitative behaviour. For UX, the main value is formalising a theory of a habit loop, engagement spiral or abandonment so that its assumptions, time scales and tipping points become explicit and testable, even before data are collected.
steps: State the phenomena to be explained and the verbal mechanism, naming the variables and the feedback loops between them.
Write each loop as a differential (or difference) equation term, choosing functional forms such as linear, logistic or saturating and justifying each.
Simulate the model from several starting states, with and without noise, and draw phase-plane plots for pairs of variables.
Find equilibria and classify them as stable or unstable, then continue them across a key parameter to draw a bifurcation diagram.
Identify tipping points, bistable regions and hysteresis, and derive qualitative predictions that data could falsify.
Where time-series data exist, fit parameters and check sensitivity to start values and to the distinction between dynamic and measurement noise.
outputs: A formal model of the behaviour, phase portraits, bifurcation diagrams showing where the system tips, and a list of testable qualitative predictions.
useWhen: A team relies on a feedback-loop theory (habit loops, network effects, burnout or engagement spirals) and needs to know what it really predicts, including where interventions would or would not work.
avoidWhen: No one on the team can scrutinise the mathematics, or the goal is a quick descriptive answer that does not depend on mechanism.
whyLost: UX training rarely includes differential equations, and system dynamics tools favour running simulations over analysing equilibria; the book notes that building useful models is hard even for experts.
whereToUse: Habit and engagement models, onboarding drop-off, workload and burnout in productivity tools, two-sided marketplace dynamics, persuasive technology.
example: A wellbeing app team writes its 'motivation fuels practice, practice fuels motivation' theory as two coupled equations with a saturating effect. The bifurcation diagram shows that below a certain reminder strength users settle in a low-use state and above it in a high-use state, with a range where both are possible, implying that a temporary boost can move users permanently while a small permanent nudge cannot.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Big Five Personality Inventory
origin: Adapted for UX from personality psychology: lexical work by Allport and Odbert (1936) and Cattell; Five-Factor Model by Goldberg and by Costa and McCrae (1992)
summary: A validated self-report questionnaire scoring people on openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, for use as a covariate or segmenting variable.
description: The trait approach searched the roughly 18,000 English person-describing words for core traits; Allport reduced them to about 4,500, Cattell factor-analysed them into 16 source traits, and the Five-Factor Model holds that five dimensions are stable over time, shared across cultures and predictive of behaviour in aggregate. Inventories present first-person statements such as 'I am always prepared' rated for self-accuracy; the public-domain 120-item IPIP-NEO short form takes 15 to 20 minutes, and shorter validated forms exist. Use depends on reliability (stability over time) and construct validity (relation to other measures and behaviour). Mischel's critique applies: trait-behaviour correlations in any single situation are low, so traits predict aggregates of behaviour, not one interaction. Typologies such as the MBTI, though popular, lack reliability and validity and are suitable only as icebreakers.
steps: Decide why personality matters to the research question (covariate, moderator or segmenting variable) and state the hypothesis in advance.
Administer a validated inventory, for example the 120-item IPIP-NEO or a validated short form, rather than an ad hoc or typological instrument such as the MBTI.
Score responses on the five dimensions using the published keys, reversing negatively keyed items.
Check internal consistency in your sample and compare with published norms.
Relate scores to aggregated behaviour or attitudes across many observations rather than single events, since single-situation correlations are low.
Report effect sizes and avoid labelling individuals as types.
outputs: Scores on five dimensions per respondent, with reliability estimates, ready for use as covariates or moderators.
useWhen: Studies where individual differences plausibly moderate experience: adoption of novel features, response to gamification, AI assistant tone, risk-taking in finance apps, or persona validation research.
avoidWhen: Designing personas from personality types, predicting a single user's behaviour, or when only a few participants are available. Do not use MBTI-style typologies.
whyLost: Personality measures belong to psychology and HR; UX segmentation favours behaviour and goals, and long inventories are costly in product surveys.
whereToUse: Academic HCI, game and gamification research, conversational AI personalisation studies, wellbeing and health apps.
example: A language-learning app tests whether streak reminders help or annoy. A 30-item short form collected with consent shows reminder opt-outs rise with neuroticism, so reminders become user-configurable rather than personality-targeted.
reference: Costa, P. T. and McCrae, R. R. (1992). Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI-R) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI) professional manual. Odessa, FL: PAR.

name: Bimodal population identification
origin: Finite mixture models from Pearson (1894); Hartigan and Hartigan's dip test (1985); Gaussian mixture modelling with information criteria (for example Fraley and Raftery, 2002)
summary: Detects whether a metric's distribution conceals two or more distinct user populations, then estimates their sizes and characteristics instead of reporting one misleading average.
description: An average of a bimodal distribution describes nobody: if novice investors take 3 minutes and experts 40 seconds, a 'typical' 1 minute 50 seconds is a fiction. Bimodal population identification tests for multiple modes and models the data as a mixture of component distributions. Hartigan's dip test checks for unimodality; Gaussian mixture models fitted to log-transformed values, compared via BIC across 1 to 4 components, estimate how many groups exist, their proportions and parameters. Each user's probability of belonging to each component can then be linked to behavioural and demographic attributes to identify who the groups are. Rigour comes from requiring both statistical support and substantive interpretation, checking stability across samples, and avoiding over-fitting components that reflect noise.
