steps: Plot a histogram and kernel density of the metric (log-transformed if skewed), with several bandwidths to avoid artefacts.
Run Hartigan's dip test; p below 0.05 indicates departure from unimodality, though with very large samples small dips may be significant.
Fit Gaussian mixture models with 1 to 4 components to the (log) values and select the model with the lowest BIC, requiring a BIC improvement of about 10 or more for strong support.
Assign users to components by posterior probability, keeping only confident assignments (for example above 0.8) for profiling.
Profile components by joining with attributes such as tenure, device, region and feature use, and interview 5 to 8 users from each component to interpret them.
Replicate on a different time window or sample, then report components separately with their sizes and characteristics.
outputs: Density plots, dip test and BIC results, component proportions and parameters, profiles of each user group, and segmented reporting.
useWhen: Metrics show wide spread or multiple humps; averages contradict qualitative experience; suspecting novice and expert or different-purpose groups.
avoidWhen: Samples are small (below roughly 100 observations), where mixtures are unstable; segment by known attributes instead.
whyLost: Mixture modelling is standard in statistics and data science but rarely used by UX researchers, who report single averages or segment only by predefined attributes.
whereToUse: Investment and trading platforms, onboarding time, B2B tools with admin and casual users, health apps with clinicians and patients, AI tool usage patterns.
example: An investment platform's order time was bimodal: a GMM on log times favoured two components (BIC difference 46), 62% fast at a median of 35 seconds and 38% slow at 3.4 minutes. The slow group was mostly first-year users researching each trade, which led to a separate guided flow.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 39 — The Distribution of Human Performance — Why Averages Lie
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Hartigan, J. A., & Hartigan, P. M. (1985). The dip test of unimodality. Annals of Statistics, 13(1), 70–84; Fraley, C., & Raftery, A. E. (2002). Model-based clustering, discriminant analysis, and density estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 97(458), 611–631.

name: Biographical Narrative Interpretive Method
origin: Gabriele Rosenthal and Wolfram Fischer-Rosenthal, 1990s, building on Fritz Schütze's narrative interview; anglicised by Tom Wengraf (2001)
summary: A three-subsession biographical interview opened by a single narrative-inducing question, followed by separate analysis of the lived life and the told story.
description: BNIM begins with a single question aimed at inducing narrative (SQUIN), such as 'Please tell me the story of your life, all the events and experiences that were important for you personally', after which the interviewer does not interrupt. A second subsession probes only topics the participant raised, in their order and words, asking for particular incidents. A third, optional subsession addresses researcher topics. Analysis separates the lived life (the chronology of biographical data) from the told story (how and in what order the participant narrates it), using panels that hypothesise future-blind, event by event. Comparing the two reveals how people make sense of their history. Rigour comes from the strict non-directive structure and panel-based hypothesis testing.
steps: Initial narrative prompt (SQUIN): Single Question aimed at inducing Narrative: 'I'd like to understand your experience of [domain]. Please start wherever seems right and tell me about all the experiences and events that have been important.' Do not interrupt.
Internal narrative questioning: After the free narrative, probe only topics raised by the participant: 'You mentioned [X] — could you tell me more about that?'
External questioning (if needed): Only after the first two phases: probe topics not yet addressed that are necessary for the research question.
Biographical data analysis: Reconstruct the chronological life history from the narrative. What did the participant experience?
Narrative analysis: How did the participant narrate the history? Compare chronological biography to the told narrative — gaps, reorderings, and emphases are the analytic data.
outputs: Recorded biographical narratives, a biographical data chronology, a text structure sequentialisation, panel hypotheses, and a case structure explaining how past experience shapes current practice.
useWhen: Current behaviour is strongly shaped by life history, such as financial habits, health management, migration, career change or caring, and you need deep understanding of a small number of people.
avoidWhen: You need answers to specific product questions quickly or have more than a handful of cases to analyse; use semi-structured interviews or Narrative Inquiry. Avoid where recounting life stories could cause harm without support in place.
whyLost: The panel-based analysis takes many hours per interview and its sociological framing has no obvious product deliverable, so it never crossed into UX practice.
whereToUse: Financial wellbeing and debt products, chronic illness management, migrant and refugee services, later-life technology adoption, and foundational strategy research for new markets.
example: A pensions provider conducts 8 BNIM interviews with people in their fifties. Analysis shows avoidance of retirement planning traces back to witnessing a parent's pension loss, informing a reassurance-led engagement strategy rather than more calculators.
reference: Wengraf, T. (2001). Qualitative Research Interviewing: Biographic Narrative and Semi-Structured Methods. Sage.

name: Biometric Storyboards
origin: Pejman Mirza-Babaei and colleagues (Mirza-Babaei et al., 2012, 2013); presented as an experience graph reporting style in chapter 18
summary: A visual report that plots players' moment-to-moment experience, based on physiological arousal and observation, against the sequence of a level or game, annotated with the events and issues behind each peak or dip.
description: Biometric storyboards combine physiological data, usually electrodermal arousal, with observation and player comments, and draw them as a graph over the structure of a level or session. Each notable rise or fall is annotated with the game event that caused it and with any usability issue, quote or designer intention, so the team can compare the experience they meant to create with what players actually went through. Mirza-Babaei's chapter on reporting places it among 'experience graph' reports: the graph can also be drawn by players themselves, recalling how they felt across the session (Thomsen et al., 2016), or generated from gathered metrics. These graphs show where players were most engaged or frustrated and help researchers convey the impact of issues, which motivates teams to act on them. They are usually delivered with another report. For UX research outside games, the same idea suits any time-structured experience, such as onboarding, a checkout journey or a training module, where showing intended versus experienced intensity over time is more persuasive than a list of issues.
steps: Agree with designers the intended experience curve for the level or flow.
Record arousal (for example skin conductance) synchronised with gameplay video, plus observation notes.
Interview players after play, using the video to cue recall of key moments.
Identify significant rises and falls in each player's signal and link them to game events.
Aggregate across players and draw a graph over the level timeline, annotating causes, quotes and usability issues.
Overlay or compare the designer's intended curve and present the gaps to the team.
outputs: Annotated graphs of experienced intensity over the level or session, compared with the intended experience.
useWhen: Communicating how an experience unfolds over time and where it diverges from the design intent.
avoidWhen: You cannot collect synchronised physiological or detailed observational data, or the experience has no meaningful time structure.
whyLost: Requires physiological recording and manual annotation; known mainly in academic games research and a few studios.
whereToUse: Games levels, trailers, onboarding flows, training and learning modules, theme park and media experiences.
example: A storyboard for a shooter level shows a long flat stretch where designers intended rising tension; annotations reveal players were lost looking for a door.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 18 (Mirza-Babaei). Mirza-Babaei, P., Nacke, L. E., Gregory, J., Collins, N. and Fitzpatrick, G. (2013). How does it play better? Exploring user testing and biometric storyboards in games user research. CHI 2013, 1499-1508.

name: Biometric Trailer Testing
donor: Games user research and consumer neuroscience
origin: Montreal User Research Lab at Ubisoft; case study on Far Cry 4 E3 2014 trailer described by Pierre Chalfoun and Jonathan Dankoff in chapter 17
summary: Players watch a trailer or linear sequence while skin conductance is recorded, then comment on it in a think-after protocol; arousal upswings and downswings and comments are combined per short segment to guide edits across iterations.
description: In the Ubisoft procedure, eight players per iteration hold an electrodermal activity bracelet at their fingertips, read a neutral text for about two minutes to provide a baseline, then watch the in-game trailer. A retrospective think-aloud follows, and on a second individual viewing players stop the video whenever they wish to give impressions. The trailer is divided into 'beats' of a few seconds. Skin conductance responses significantly above baseline are coded as upswings and significant drops as downswings; downswings are not judged good or bad, simply as falls in arousal. Moderators code comments for each beat as positive or negative. A single chart plots upswings, downswings and positive and negative comments per beat, which shows the team where interest drops and which moments land. Iterating over several versions, the Far Cry team strengthened the co-op introduction and packed salient sequences. The authors chose in-game rather than pre-rendered footage because it can still be changed and is less noisy early on. For UX research, the approach suits any linear content such as onboarding videos, adverts or product demos.
steps: Divide the trailer or sequence into short beats and prepare event timestamps.
Recruit a small group per iteration and fit EDA sensors.
Record a neutral baseline (for example reading unrelated text).
Play the sequence while recording EDA, then run a think-after on a second viewing with free pausing.
Detect significant phasic upswings and downswings per beat and code comments as positive or negative.
Plot both per beat, share with the team, revise the content and repeat with new participants.
outputs: A per-beat chart of arousal changes and comment valence, with recommended edits for each iteration.
useWhen: Iterating on short linear content where the team wants to know which moments engage and where interest drops.
avoidWhen: The content cannot be changed between iterations, or you lack physiological recording and analysis capacity.
whyLost: Lives inside a few large studios' labs; biometric methods remain costly and specialised.
whereToUse: Game trailers and cut-scenes, adverts, onboarding and product videos, keynote demos.
example: An onboarding video shows a downswing and two negative comments during a 20-second settings walkthrough; the team cuts it to five seconds and the dip disappears in the next round.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 17 (Chalfoun and Dankoff).

name: Blameless Postmortem and M&M Review
donor: Surgery and medicine; site reliability engineering
origin: Ernest Codman's end-result system (1910s) and surgical M&M conferences; blameless postmortems popularised by John Allspaw at Etsy (2012) and Google SRE (2016)
summary: A structured, non-punitive review of an adverse event that reconstructs what people knew and why their actions made sense, to improve systems rather than assign blame.
description: Medicine's morbidity and mortality conference has reviewed adverse outcomes for over a century. Software engineering adopted the blameless postmortem, grounded in Sidney Dekker's 'new view' of human error: people's actions made sense to them at the time given their goals, knowledge and focus of attention. A rigorous review reconstructs a timeline, explores local rationality through interviews, identifies contributing factors (including interface and process design), and produces specific action items with owners. For UX, user-facing incidents (a confusing change causing data loss, a dark pattern complaint, a support surge) deserve the same treatment, with users' experiences reconstructed alongside internal decisions.
steps: Declare a review for any user-impacting incident above an agreed threshold, and set a blameless ground rule.
Reconstruct a detailed timeline from logs, support tickets, chat records and user reports.
Interview involved staff and, where possible, affected users, using questions about what they saw, expected and were trying to do.
Identify contributing factors across design, process, tooling, communication and organisational pressure, avoiding 'human error' as a conclusion.
Write the review using a standard template and agree action items with owners and dates.
Track actions to completion and periodically analyse reviews in aggregate for recurring themes.
outputs: A written review with timeline, contributing factors, local rationality narratives, action items and a cross-incident theme log.
useWhen: After user-facing incidents, failed launches, or research misses that led to poor decisions.
avoidWhen: Routine issues better handled by normal bug triage; or where psychological safety cannot be guaranteed.
whyLost: UX research rarely owns incident review; engineering does, and it focuses on system reliability rather than user experience. Design failures seldom get formal reviews.
whereToUse: Product launches, migrations, pricing changes, AI feature failures, accessibility regressions.
example: After a redesign leads to thousands of accidental subscription cancellations, a blameless review reveals the button swap was tested only on desktop. Actions include a mobile-first test gate and a release checklist for destructive actions.
sources: Dekker, The Field Guide to Understanding 'Human Error' (3rd ed., 2014)
Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (2016), chapter on postmortem culture
Allspaw, Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture (2012), Code as Craft blog
Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Dekker, S. (2014). The Field Guide to Understanding 'Human Error'. Ashgate.

name: Bland-Altman Agreement Analysis
origin: J. Martin Bland and Douglas Altman, 1983 and 1986 (The Lancet)
summary: Assesses whether two measurement methods agree well enough to be interchangeable by plotting differences against means and computing limits of agreement.
description: Correlation is the wrong statistic for comparing measurement methods: two methods can correlate at 0.95 yet differ systematically by a large amount. Bland and Altman proposed plotting the difference between methods against their mean for each subject, computing the mean difference (bias) and the 95% limits of agreement (bias plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations of differences), and judging whether those limits are acceptable for practical use. Proportional bias appears as a slope. In UX this applies whenever a cheaper measure is proposed to replace a gold standard: unmoderated versus moderated task time, webcam versus lab eye tracking, AI-generated ratings versus human ratings, short versus long scales.
steps: Measure the same participants or items with both methods.
Compute differences and means for each pair.
Plot differences against means; calculate bias and 95% limits of agreement with confidence intervals.
Check for proportional bias (regress differences on means) and heteroscedasticity; use log transformation or ratio-based limits if needed.
Compare limits with a pre-specified acceptable range based on practical decision impact.
Conclude interchangeability only if limits fall within the acceptable range.
outputs: Bland-Altman plots, bias and limits of agreement with confidence intervals, and an interchangeability judgement.
useWhen: Validating a new, cheaper or automated measurement against an established one.
avoidWhen: Comparing categorical classifications (use kappa) or when no reference method exists.
whyLost: It is standard in clinical measurement but UX validation studies report correlations.
whereToUse: AI-assisted coding and rating, remote versus lab measurement, short-form scales, webcam eye tracking, wearables.
example: An LLM rates usability severity of 300 issues alongside human experts. Correlation is 0.82, but limits of agreement span plus or minus 1.6 points on a 4-point scale, so the LLM cannot replace experts for prioritisation.
sources: Bland & Altman, Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement (1986), The Lancet
Altman & Bland, Measurement in medicine: the analysis of method comparison studies (1983), The Statistician
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Bland, J. M., & Altman, D. G. (1986). The Lancet, 327(8476), 307-310.

name: Blind Walking as an Action Measure of Perceived Distance
origin: Jack Loomis and colleagues (1992); Philbeck, Loomis and Beall (1997)
summary: Participants view a target, close their eyes and walk to where they think it is; the stopping point measures perceived distance without verbal estimates.
description: Blind walking measures distance perception through action rather than words. A participant views a target up to about 12 metres away, then, without vision, walks to where they believe it is. In the angled or triangulated version they first walk off to one side and, on a cue, turn and continue towards the remembered target, which rules out simply counting steps along a rehearsed line. People in real environments typically stop within a fraction of a metre, combining knowledge of their own movement with memory of the layout. Because verbal estimates are biased and compressed, action measures give a more direct reading of perceived space; this is why blind walking became the standard measure in virtual and augmented reality distance studies, where distances are commonly underestimated.
steps: Place a target at a known distance, typically 2-12 m, in a real or virtual environment.
Have the participant view it, then close their eyes or occlude the display.
Ask them to walk to the target without vision; in the angled version, first walk in another direction and turn on a cue.
Record the stopping point and path, using tracking where available.
Compute walked distance and end-point error relative to the true position, and compare across conditions such as real versus virtual.
outputs: Walked distance, end-point error and path records per trial and condition.
useWhen: Evaluating whether a VR or AR display conveys correct scale and distance, and comparing rendering, field-of-view or headset conditions.
avoidWhen: Avoid where participants cannot walk safely without vision or space is limited; use verbal estimates or bisection tasks. It measures egocentric distance only, not judgements of size or layout.
whyLost: It is standard in perception and VR research labs, but product teams building spatial interfaces rarely run perceptual calibration studies.
whereToUse: VR training simulators, AR navigation and placement apps, architectural visualisation, automotive head-up displays.
example: An AR furniture app tests whether virtual sofas appear at the right distance. Blind-walking errors show users underestimate virtual distances by about 15% beyond 3 m, so the team adds ground-contact shadows and retests until error matches real objects.
reference: Loomis, J. M., Da Silva, J. A., Fujita, N. and Fukusima, S. S. (1992). Visual space perception and visually directed action. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 18(4), 906-921; Goldstein, E. B. and Cacciamani, L. (2021). Sensation and Perception (11th ed.). Cengage, pp. 154-155.

name: Bluebells Method (Children as Design Informants)
aka: I-Spy, Hide and Seek, Tig and Blind Man's Bluff design activities
origin: Kelly, Mazzone, Horton and Read (2006)
summary: Adults draft requirements and sketches, take them to children for four playground-game activities that fill in vocabulary, navigation and look and feel, then fold the results back in.
description: Bluebells treats children as informants rather than full design partners and is built for technology projects that need input from many children, each usually attending a single session. It sandwiches children's activity between two adult-only stages. First, designers write a requirements list, technical specification and rough sketches. Second, they take the design to children through four activities named after playground games: I-Spy, in which designers observe children doing activities that match the design aim; Hide and Seek, in which children generate words they associate with the product and place them on wireframes; Tig, for navigation and wayfinding; and Blind Man's Bluff, for look and feel. Third, the design team collates and incorporates the outputs. Its strength is the structure that separates information, navigation and graphics so young children without design background can contribute concrete details, with the design moving back and forth between adults and children.
steps: Adults draft a requirements list, technical specification and initial sketches of the product.
Run I-Spy: observe children doing everyday activities that match the design aim (for example how they chat with friends when designing a chat app).
Run Hide and Seek: children list words they associate with the product and place them on wireframe prototypes.
Run Tig for navigation and wayfinding, and Blind Man's Bluff for look and feel.
Collate the outputs by layer (vocabulary, navigation, visual design) and revise the design.
Return the revised design to children in further single sessions as needed, with consent from parents and assent from the children.
outputs: Child-sourced vocabulary, navigation and visual design inputs mapped onto wireframes, and a revised specification.
useWhen: Designing apps, games or learning products for children when many children can each give one session and adults retain overall design direction.
avoidWhen: When children should shape the overall concept or work as long-term partners (use cooperative inquiry); when evaluating a finished product (use Usability Testing with Children and Teens).
whyLost: It is known within child-computer interaction research but rarely adopted by commercial teams, who rely on testing with children rather than structured informant sessions.
whereToUse: Edtech, children's games and media apps, kid-safe messaging, museum and library digital experiences.
example: A reading app for 7 to 9-year-olds runs Hide and Seek in a school: children place words such as 'my books' and 'treasure' on wireframes, and the team renames 'Library' to 'My Books'. Tig sessions show children expect a back arrow at top left on every screen.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Kelly, S. R., Mazzone, E., Horton, M. and Read, J. C. (2006). Bluebells: a design method for child-centred product development. NordiCHI '06.

name: Body Mapping
origin: Jane Solomon and the Memory Box Project, Cape Town, around 2002, with people living with HIV
summary: Participants draw and collage their experiences onto a life-size outline of their own body, externalising embodied, emotional and social knowledge that is hard to verbalise.
description: Body mapping (developed in community health research, particularly with HIV/AIDS communities) involves participants drawing or collaging on a life-size outline of their own body to represent their experiences, feelings, relationships, and significant life events. The body as canvas makes visible the embodied, situated nature of experience in a way that abstract verbal description cannot. Applied to UX and health technology research: body mapping is particularly powerful for understanding how people experience their bodies in relation to digital health products, wearables, or medical technology.
steps: Materials: Large paper (body-length), markers, collage materials, paint. Create a life-size outline by tracing the participant's body, or provide a pre-drawn outline.

Guided prompts: Rather than open-ended 'draw your experience,' provide structured prompts for different body zones. 'Where in your body do you feel [the product]?' 'Mark on the body where you carry stress when using [service].' 'Where do you feel the impact of [condition/experience]?'
Story-telling around the map: After completing the map, the participant narrates it. The narration is as analytically important as the visual content.
Collective body mapping: Groups can work on body maps together, stimulating collective discussion and shared meaning-making.

Analysis: Analyse both the visual (what is placed where, what symbols are used, what colours) and the narrative (what the participant says about their map). The relationship between visual and verbal is itself data.
outputs: Completed body maps, participant narratives and keys, recorded group discussions, and analysis of where and how experiences are located in the body.
useWhen: Experiences are embodied, emotional or stigmatised, such as chronic illness, pain, stress, disability or body-worn technology, and participants benefit from a creative, participant-led format.
avoidWhen: You need quick or structured comparable data, or participants may find body-focused activity distressing without support; use interviews with trauma-informed practices or Photo Elicitation.
whyLost: It developed in community health and arts-based research, takes several hours per participant, and produces artefacts UX teams find hard to translate into requirements.
whereToUse: Wearables and medical devices, chronic pain and mental-health products, disability and accessibility research, femtech, and workplace wellbeing.
example: A wearable glucose-monitor team runs body-mapping sessions with 8 teenagers with diabetes. Maps show the sensor site linked to social exposure and shame more than pain, prioritising discreet placement and covers.
reference: Gastaldo, D., Magalhães, L., Carrasco, C. & Davy, C. (2012). Body-Map Storytelling as Research. Toronto.

name: Bootstrap methods for confidence intervals
origin: Bradley Efron, 1979
summary: Estimates the uncertainty of any UX metric by resampling the observed data with replacement thousands of times, giving confidence intervals without strong distributional assumptions.
description: The bootstrap treats the sample as a stand-in for the population: drawing many resamples of the same size with replacement and recomputing the statistic gives its sampling distribution. Intervals can then be formed for medians of task time, differences in SUS scores, ratios of conversion rates or model coefficients, all of which lack simple formulas or violate normality. The BCa (bias-corrected and accelerated) interval generally performs best. For UX, the bootstrap makes honest uncertainty reporting accessible even for small usability samples, though with very small n (under about 10-15) intervals are unreliable. Rigour requires resampling at the right unit (participants, not individual tasks, when tasks are nested) and enough resamples. The jackknife, an older relative, recomputes the statistic leaving out one case at a time and is used mainly to estimate bias and standard error; it is less suitable than the bootstrap for non-smooth statistics such as the median.
steps: Identify the statistic of interest (e.g. median task time or the difference in completion rates).
Identify the independent resampling unit, usually the participant or user, and resample at that level.
Draw at least 2,000 resamples (10,000 for percentile tails or BCa) with replacement.
Recompute the statistic for each resample and build the BCa or percentile 95% interval.
Report the point estimate with the interval and note sample size limitations, especially below around 15 participants.
outputs: Confidence intervals for arbitrary metrics, bootstrap distributions and an honest statement of uncertainty.
useWhen: Reporting uncertainty for skewed metrics (task time), complex statistics (ratios, medians, model outputs) or small-to-moderate samples.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it with very small samples or highly dependent data (time series need block bootstrap); for simple proportions, adjusted Wald intervals suffice.
whyLost: Most UX reports omit intervals altogether; the bootstrap is well known in statistics but rarely part of UX training.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks, A/B test reporting for non-standard metrics, survey scores, model coefficients and mediation effects.
example: Comparing median task times between two checkout prototypes with 20 participants each, a BCa bootstrap gives a difference of 18 s (95% CI 4-35 s), which supports choosing the faster design while showing the effect could be modest.
sources: Monte Carlo Methods with R (Christian Robert & George Casella)
Efron (1979) Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife
An Introduction to the Bootstrap (Bradley Efron & Robert Tibshirani)
Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 56 — Monte Carlo Simulation & Predictive Forecasting
The Inquiry Series, C2 — Quantitative UX Analysis in Python — Descriptive to Inferential
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella, 2010)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Efron, B. & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993) An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall.

name: Bootstrapped indirect effects
aka: Percentile bootstrap CI for indirect effects
origin: Bradley Efron, 1979 (bootstrap); Shrout and Bolger, 2002, and Preacher and Hayes, 2004 and 2008 (application to mediation)
summary: Testing a mediated (indirect) effect by resampling the data thousands of times to build a confidence interval for the product of paths, without assuming normality.
description: An indirect effect is the product of the X to M path (a) and the M to Y path controlling for X (b). The sampling distribution of a times b is usually skewed, so the older Sobel test, which assumes normality, is underpowered and inaccurate. The bootstrap resamples cases with replacement (typically 5,000-10,000 times), re-estimates a and b in each sample and uses the percentiles of the resulting a times b distribution as a confidence interval. If the 95% interval excludes zero, the indirect effect is supported. Rigour comes from adequate resamples, a fixed seed, reporting the point estimate with CI, completely standardised effects where helpful, and remembering that a significant indirect effect does not prove causal mediation.
steps: Estimate path a (X predicting M) and path b (M predicting Y controlling for X) in the full sample.
Draw at least 5,000 bootstrap resamples of cases with replacement, with a recorded random seed.
Re-estimate a times b in each resample and store the distribution.
Form the 95% percentile confidence interval (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles); bias-corrected intervals are an option but can inflate Type I error.
Conclude that mediation is supported if the CI excludes zero, and report the effect with CI and the proportion of the total effect.
Discuss assumptions: temporal order, no unmeasured M-Y confounding and measurement reliability of M.
outputs: An indirect effect estimate with bootstrap CI, its distribution plot and an assessment of causal assumptions.
useWhen: Any mediation hypothesis in UX survey or experimental data, especially with moderate samples where normal-theory tests are unreliable.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it with very small samples (under about 50) or when M-Y confounding is likely and unaddressed; consider causal mediation analysis with sensitivity analysis.
whyLost: The approach is standard in academic psychology but UX rarely tests mechanisms statistically.
whereToUse: Experiments on onboarding, trust and explanation design, health behaviour apps and satisfaction driver models.
example: A fintech experiment shows a simplified fee display increases conversion. A 10,000-sample bootstrap shows an indirect effect via perceived transparency of 0.11 (95% CI 0.05-0.18), around 40% of the total effect.
sources: LOGISTIC REGRESSION procedures; Hayes PROCESS macro v4
Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed.
Efron, B. & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993) An Introduction to the Bootstrap
Shrout, P. E. & Bolger, N. (2002) Mediation in experimental and nonexperimental studies. Psychological Methods
The Inquiry Series, C8 — SPSS for Regression, Moderation & Mediation
reference: Preacher, K. J. & Hayes, A. F. (2008) Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models. Behavior Research Methods 40(3)

name: Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale
origin: Gunnar Borg, early 1960s; 15-point graded category scale (Borg, 1971) and the Category Ratio CR-10 scale; reviewed by Tenenbaum and Hutchinson in the Handbook
summary: A single-item scale on which people rate how hard physical work feels, anchored so that ratings track physiological strain.
description: Borg's RPE scale asks people to rate the intensity of physical effort on a 15-point graded category scale (6 to 20) whose numbers were designed to parallel heart rate in a healthy adult (rating times ten roughly equals heart rate). The later Category Ratio CR-10 scale uses verbal anchors with ratio properties and is also used for other sensations. The Handbook describes RPE as well validated, reliable and widely used for monitoring exercise intensity, but warns that a single item cannot capture the whole range of sensations, that psychological factors explain around a third of the variance, and that effort tolerance (how long effort can be sustained) is a separate construct. A many-facet Rasch analysis suggested the scale tracks cumulative exertion over a bout. For UX, RPE fills a gap: workload instruments such as NASA-TLX focus on mental demand, while products for VR, AR, mid-air gesture, touch walls, exergames, wearables and physical work tools also impose bodily effort. Repeated RPE ratings during a session show when interaction becomes physically fatiguing, for example arm fatigue in mid-air input.
steps: Choose the 6-20 scale for whole-body effort or the CR-10 for localised sensations such as arm or neck strain.
Train participants on the anchors before the session, using a standard instruction.
Collect ratings at fixed intervals or after each task block, not only at the end.
Record task duration and, if possible, heart rate or task performance alongside ratings.
Plot ratings over time for each design to see how quickly perceived effort accumulates.
Add questions or interviews on effort tolerance and coping, since RPE alone does not capture them.
outputs: Perceived exertion ratings per task block and over time, showing which interaction designs become physically tiring and how fast.
useWhen: Interaction involves sustained bodily effort or posture: VR and AR, gesture input, large touchscreens, exergames, wearables, warehouse or field devices.
avoidWhen: Tasks are purely cognitive and seated, where a mental workload measure is more appropriate.
whyLost: UX workload measurement grew from aviation human factors with a cognitive focus; physical effort was left to ergonomics, so RPE rarely appears in UX toolkits.
whereToUse: VR and AR headsets, gesture and mid-air interfaces, kiosks and large displays, fitness and exergame apps, handheld industrial devices.
example: A VR design team compares a raised-arm menu with a wrist-anchored menu. Participants give CR-10 ratings for arm effort every two minutes during a 15-minute task; the raised-arm design reaches 'strong' within six minutes, so the team moves frequent actions to the wrist.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Tenenbaum, G. and Hutchinson, J. C. (2007) 'A social-cognitive perspective of perceived and sustained effort', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 25.

name: Bottom-up vs. top-down perceptual flow
donor: Cognitive psychology and neuroscience of perception
origin: Neisser's analysis-by-synthesis, 1967; Gregory's perception as hypotheses, 1970; Corbetta and Shulman's dorsal and ventral attention systems, 2002
summary: Analyses how much users' perception of a screen is driven by the stimulus itself versus by their goals and expectations, and designs for both pathways.
description: Bottom-up processing is stimulus-driven: salient features capture attention regardless of goals. Top-down processing is driven by goals, knowledge and expectations, determining what users look for and how they interpret ambiguous information. Corbetta and Shulman linked these to dorsal (goal-directed) and ventral (stimulus-driven) attention networks. In interfaces, novices rely more on bottom-up cues while experts scan according to goals; unexpected critical events must break through top-down focus. This analysis compares where design puts bottom-up salience with where users' tasks direct top-down attention, using saliency maps and goal-driven eye-tracking data. Conflicts reveal where critical information is invisible to goal-driven users or where salient decoration hijacks attention.
steps: Generate bottom-up predictions with a saliency model or pre-attentive audit for key screens.
Define user goals per task and the information each goal should lead users to.
Run eye tracking with 10-15 participants in free-viewing and task-driven conditions on the same screens.
Compare fixation patterns with saliency predictions; low correlation in task conditions indicates top-down dominance.
Identify conflicts: critical but non-salient items missed in free viewing, and salient irrelevant items capturing fixations during tasks.
Redesign so critical items are both salient and placed where goal-driven search expects them, then re-test.
outputs: Saliency versus fixation comparisons by condition, a conflict list, and redesign recommendations balancing both pathways.
useWhen: For mixed-expertise products, monitoring displays, and alerts that must interrupt focused work.
avoidWhen: When eye tracking or saliency modelling is impossible and stakes are low; use a heuristic visual hierarchy review.
whyLost: The distinction is textbook cognitive psychology but rarely structured as a design analysis; UX uses 'visual hierarchy' as a catch-all.
whereToUse: Clinical displays, cockpits, retail product pages, dashboards, and AR overlays.
example: Experienced surgeons' fixations on a console correlate weakly (r = 0.2) with the saliency map; they look where their task tells them. Critical alerts placed in salient but task-irrelevant regions are missed, so alerts are moved to goal-driven scan paths.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Sensation and Perception
Gibson, J. J., The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979)
Whalen, J., Design for How People Think (2019)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
reference: Corbetta, M. & Shulman, G. L. (2002). Control of goal-directed and stimulus-driven attention in the brain. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 3(3), 201-215.

name: Boundary critique
origin: C. West Churchman, 1970s; Werner Ulrich's Critical Systems Heuristics, 1983; Midgley, 2000
summary: Systematically questions who and what is included in or excluded from a system's design, revealing the value judgements behind boundaries and whose interests are served.
description: Every system design draws boundaries: who counts as a user, what problems are in scope, what knowledge counts. Ulrich's Critical Systems Heuristics provides 12 boundary questions grouped into four sources of influence (motivation, control, knowledge, legitimacy), each asked in 'is' and 'ought' modes: who is the beneficiary, who should be? Who decides? What expertise is relied on? Who represents those affected but not involved? Midgley adds analysis of marginalised groups and conflicting boundaries. In UX, boundary critique exposes stakeholders and harms outside the design scope, such as people affected by AI decisions who never use the product. Rigour comes from structured use of all 12 questions and including affected stakeholders in answering them.
steps: Define the system under consideration and its current stated purpose.
Answer Ulrich's 12 boundary questions in 'is' mode, based on documentation and interviews.
Answer the same 12 questions in 'ought' mode with diverse stakeholders, including those affected but not involved.
Compare 'is' and 'ought' answers to identify contested boundaries and marginalised groups.
Decide which boundaries to change, documenting the rationale and trade-offs.
Feed revised boundaries into research recruitment, requirements and evaluation criteria.
outputs: A 12-question boundary analysis in two modes, contested boundaries and marginalised stakeholders, and revised scope decisions.
useWhen: When designing systems affecting people beyond direct users, in public services, healthcare, AI and platform governance, or when ethics and equity matter.
avoidWhen: For narrow interface optimisation where scope is not contested; standard stakeholder mapping is enough.
whyLost: Boundary critique is established in operational research and critical systems thinking but rarely crosses into UX, which defines scope as 'users'.
whereToUse: AI decision systems, public services, healthcare, workplace monitoring, and platform policy.
example: Boundary critique of a surgical robot programme finds patients and theatre cleaning staff have no voice in design, although sterilisation workflows affect turnaround. Including cleaning staff surfaces a docking design that adds 12 minutes per case.
sources: PACT analysis (Dix; Benyon, Designing Interactive Systems)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
reference: Ulrich, W. (1983). Critical Heuristics of Social Planning: A New Approach to Practical Philosophy. Haupt.

name: Bradford Hill Criteria
aka: Bradford Hill Criteria for UX Causation
Bradford Hill Criteria for Causal Assessment
origin: Austin Bradford Hill, 1965
summary: A structured checklist of viewpoints (strength, consistency, temporality, plausibility and others) for building confidence that an observed association reflects causation when experiments are impossible.
description: Hill proposed nine viewpoints for judging whether an association is causal: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. They are not proof but a disciplined way to weigh observational evidence. Vivek Gopinath's playbook applies them as a narrative check in UX when randomisation is not possible: temporality (the change preceded the effect), strength (a 19-point lift), consistency (replicated across segments) and plausibility (aligns with mental-model evidence). The value is in forcing explicit reasoning about alternative explanations rather than declaring causality from correlation.
steps: Write the causal claim and the observational evidence for it.
Check temporality: did the design change precede the outcome shift?
Assess strength and dose-response (e.g. size of lift, more exposure giving more effect).
Check consistency across segments, platforms and time periods.
Assess plausibility and coherence with qualitative mechanism evidence.
Summarise which viewpoints are met and state the residual uncertainty.
outputs: A criterion-by-criterion assessment of causal confidence.
useWhen: When only observational data exist and stakeholders need a principled confidence statement.
avoidWhen: When an experiment is feasible; run it instead. Do not present the checklist as proof.
whyLost: A staple of epidemiology that never entered UX training, where observational analytics are read causally without structure.
whereToUse: Post-launch analyses, regulatory or policy changes, platform migrations, retrospective reviews.
example: After a navigation change without an A/B test, the team shows the lift followed the release, was large, repeated across iOS and Android, and matched interview evidence, stating moderate confidence in causation.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Hill AB (1965) The environment and disease: association or causation? Proc R Soc Med 58:295-300
Rothman KJ & Greenland S (2005) Causation and causal inference in epidemiology. AJPH
Hill, The environment and disease: association or causation? (1965), Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine
Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology (3rd ed., 2008)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Hill, A. B. (1965). The environment and disease: Association or causation? Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine, 58(5), 295–300.

name: Bradley-Terry Paired Comparison Scaling
origin: Ralph Bradley and Milton Terry, 1952 (anticipated by Zermelo, 1929)
summary: Estimates a latent strength for each item from many pairwise choices, handling incomplete designs, ties and covariates with uncertainty.
description: The Bradley-Terry model sets the probability that item i beats item j as pi_i / (pi_i + pi_j), equivalent to a logistic model on strength differences. It accommodates incomplete comparison designs (not every pair compared), allows home-advantage or position effects, and extends to ties, covariates and random effects. It underpins comparative judgement in educational assessment and human preference modelling for language models (RLHF reward models). For UX, it lets you scale many design variants, AI outputs or content items from simple pairwise preferences collected adaptively, with confidence intervals rather than raw win rates.
steps: Define items and the comparison question (e.g. 'Which response is more helpful?').
Design comparisons: random or adaptive pairing so the comparison graph is connected; randomise left/right.
Collect judgements from raters, recording rater and position.
Fit a Bradley-Terry model (BradleyTerry2, choix) with position effects and optional rater random effects.
Report strengths with confidence intervals and check model fit and intransitivities.
Use adaptive pairing to refine estimates among close competitors.
outputs: Latent strength scores with intervals, position-bias estimates and rankings.
useWhen: Comparing many alternatives where absolute ratings are unreliable: AI outputs, designs, copy, images.
avoidWhen: When attribute-level trade-offs are needed (use conjoint) or with very few items.
whyLost: UX uses rating scales and simple preference counts; paired comparison models are known mainly in sports, education and ML.
whereToUse: LLM response evaluation, design variant preference, icon sets, voice selection, content headline testing.
example: An AI writing tool evaluates 12 prompt strategies with 3,000 pairwise human judgements. Bradley-Terry estimates show two strategies statistically tied at the top and reveal a strong left-position bias of 6 points.
sources: Bradley & Terry, Rank analysis of incomplete block designs: I. The method of paired comparisons (1952), Biometrika
Turner & Firth, Bradley-Terry models in R: the BradleyTerry2 package (2012), Journal of Statistical Software
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Bradley, R. A., & Terry, M. E. (1952). Biometrika, 39(3/4), 324-345.

name: Brainstorming
origin: Alex Osborn (1953); brainwriting after VanGundy (1984); mind mapping after Buzan (1974)
summary: Structured idea generation under deferred judgement, run aloud, in silent written rounds (brainwriting) or into a visual structure such as a mind map, web or tree.
description: Osborn's brainstorming asks a group to state any idea that comes to mind, build on others' ideas and suspend criticism, favouring quantity. Research summarised by Goldstein shows interactive groups produce fewer ideas than the same number of people working alone and pooling, because of dominance, fear of judgement and production blocking; idea counts are also not idea quality. Variants address this. Brainwriting has each person write a one or two sentence solution to a plain problem statement, pass the sheet on and build on what is written, so quiet people get an equal voice and no strong leader is needed; it can be run with users. Graphic organisers capture ideas in a structure chosen for the job: a web around a central question, a tree for hierarchies, a flow diagram for sequences and cause and effect; a mind map puts the problem at the stem and solutions on branches.
steps: Write a focused problem statement or central question in plain language without jargon.
State the rules: defer judgement, aim for quantity, build on others' ideas, welcome odd ideas.
Start with silent individual generation (3-5 minutes) before any group sharing, to reduce production blocking.
For brainwriting, each person writes one idea on a sheet or numbered shared document, passes it on and builds on what is there, for as many rounds as there are participants.
Alternatively capture ideas into a chosen structure: a web, a tree diagram for hierarchies or a flow diagram for sequences and actors.
Review the whole set for gaps and unexpected links, then cluster related ideas.
Screen ideas separately against user fit, technical feasibility, resources and company goals.
outputs: A large set of ideas, sheets of collaboratively developed solutions or a visual map of the idea space, and a shortlist for development.
useWhen: Use when a team needs many options for a well-framed problem, when quiet or junior voices must be heard (brainwriting), or when users can co-create ideas in a session.
avoidWhen: Avoid open interactive brainstorming when a few people dominate; use brainwriting or the Nominal Group Technique. Do not use it to learn what users need: that requires Interviews or Contextual Inquiry. Adapt brainwriting for people who find writing difficult.
whyLost: It survived as the default ideation ritual because it is simple and social; the evidence against interactive groups has mostly been absorbed through silent-first variants rather than abandonment.
whereToUse: Any product team ideation, co-design sessions with users, hackathons, service redesign.
example: A cancer-care team runs online brainwriting with adolescent patients using one numbered shared document each; after six rounds the sheets converge on a peer forum, an information library and a symptom tracker.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Osborn, A. F. (1953). Applied Imagination. New York: Scribner.
reference: Osborn, A. F. (1953). Applied Imagination. New York: Scribner.

name: Brand Audit for Interactive Products
origin: Erika Hall / Mule Design practice (2013)
summary: Audit how an interactive product's existing brand, name and logo signal intended attributes in every context users meet them, compared with competitors.
description: For many interactive products the brand experience is the user experience: the interface's visual design is the identity and its language the voice. A brand audit, run alongside competitive research, makes the existing brand explicit and checks it. The team lists the attributes the brand should and should not carry, states the value proposition, and gathers customers' associations from interviews. It then judges how much branding matters in this market (more with wide audiences, strong competition and premium pricing) and chooses comparable competitors. The name is assessed for uniqueness in the field, ambiguity and ease of spelling and saying; the logo is checked in every context users will meet it, beside competitors' logos in the same contexts. The audit ends with a judgement of how well name and identity express the intended attributes and avoid the unwanted ones.
steps: List the attributes the brand should be associated with and those it should avoid, gathered from people inside and outside the company.
State the value proposition and how the brand currently communicates it.
Collect customers' brand associations during ethnographic or stakeholder interviews.
Judge how important branding is in this market and choose three to six comparable competitors.
Assess the name for uniqueness in the competitive field, ambiguity, ease of spelling and pronunciation, and fit with the domain.
List every context where users meet the logo (app icon, notification, card, signage) and compare competitors' logos in the same contexts.
Rate how well name, identity and interface language express the intended attributes and avoid the negative ones, and list fixes.
outputs: A brand attribute list, a value proposition statement and an assessment of name, logo and interface identity against competitors.
useWhen: Use before a redesign, rebrand or market entry, or when the product's look and voice seem at odds with what it claims to stand for.
avoidWhen: Avoid overinvesting where branding matters little or the logo rarely stands alone. The audit reflects the team's judgement; to measure how users actually perceive the brand use Brand Lift and Drag Measurement or a Semantic Differential survey.
whyLost: It survived because brand and product design have converged in digital products and competitive reviews routinely include brand signals.
whereToUse: Fintech and other trust-sensitive products, consumer apps entering crowded categories, rebrands, mergers of product lines.
example: A personal finance start-up audits its name and app icon against five rivals on the phone home screen and in bank-connection screens. Its playful name scores well on memorability but poorly on trust, so the redesign leans the interface tone towards calm and precise.
reference: Hall, E. (2013). Just Enough Research. New York: A Book Apart, pp. 98-101.

name: Brand Awareness, Attitude and Usage Survey
origin: Hierarchy-of-effects tradition in marketing research; procedure as given by Jeff Sauro (2015)
summary: Survey prospects on unaided then aided brand awareness, with fake distractor brands, followed by product knowledge, attitude, brand associations, usage and intent, then model the drivers.
description: Framed on the hierarchy of effects: people become aware of a brand, form an attitude through use, then become loyal. Unaided awareness is asked first with open questions (name the rental car companies you know); answers are coded and reported as percentages with confidence intervals as a top-of-mind benchmark. Aided awareness follows as a multi-select list that includes distractor brands, a fake brand and a real brand outside the category, whose selection rate shows how much recognition is false. Product knowledge is probed open then closed, with where respondents heard of it so awareness can be attributed to campaigns. Attitude is rated for own and competitor brands and on brand pillars such as value, quality and trust, with reasons. Brand affinity asks for free word associations, then picks from positive and negative terms. Usage and intent close the survey, and drivers come from coded comments and multiple regression, analysed by segment.
steps: Screen qualified respondents and collect segmenting demographics.
Ask unaided awareness as an open list; code, count and report percentages with confidence intervals.
Ask aided awareness as a multi-select list with an Other option and at least one fake and one out-of-category distractor brand.
Ask favourability for brands known, own and competitors, and probe product knowledge open first, then from a feature list, including where they heard of it.
Ask brand affinity: free-listed words, then a choice of positive and negative terms tied to brand pillars, and rate the product on pillar attributes with a reason.
Ask past usage and future intent (which brand would you buy today, likelihood to continue or recommend).
Analyse drivers with coded comments and multiple regression, and compare segments.
outputs: Unaided and aided awareness with confidence intervals, false-recognition rate, attitude and pillar scores, word-association profile, usage and intent, and key drivers.
useWhen: Benchmarking awareness and perception before a launch, rebrand or campaign, or understanding why prospects who know the product do not choose it.
avoidWhen: Always ask unaided before aided and open before closed, or answers are primed; aided awareness measures familiarity, not salience. For measuring a campaign's effect use Brand Lift and Drag Measurement with a control group.
whyLost: Brand tracking is owned by marketing and agencies, so UX teams rarely run it even though perception and expectations shape product experience.
whereToUse: Market entry and positioning decisions, rebrands, competitive analysis for consumer apps, B2B category awareness.
example: A survey of 120 laptop buyers finds unaided awareness of 60 percent for the leader and 20 percent (CI 14 to 28) for a challenger; 4 percent claim to know the fake brand 'Prionsonic', which sets the noise floor for aided figures.
reference: Sauro, J. (2015). Customer Analytics For Dummies. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, pp. 103-112, 259.

name: Brand Experience Workshop
aka: Who we are and are not continuum
origin: UX and brand strategy practice (as described in Universal Methods of Design)
summary: A half-day stakeholder workshop using about 100 brand and product images, dot reactions and a who-we-are continuum to agree four or five experience attributes.
description: The workshop makes a product team's brand ambitions explicit and shared before visual and interaction design begins. About 100 printed images of well-known brands and products, including competitors and familiar categories, are displayed. Participants place green and red dots to record gut reactions for 15-20 minutes. The facilitator then picks images that drew strong or split reactions and asks people to explain them, placing each on a continuum from 'who we do not want to be' to 'who we want to be' and recording the adjectives people use. Adjectives can be card sorted into clusters. Synthesis yields four or five distinctive attributes for the experience that later guide design and critique. The output reflects stakeholder aspiration, not user perception, and the image set strongly shapes what is said.
steps: Print about 100 images of brands and products across familiar categories, including direct competitors.
Give each participant 10-25 green and red dots.
Let participants mark gut reactions in silence for 15-20 minutes.
Discuss images with strong or split reactions and place each on a continuum from who we do not want to be to who we want to be.
Record every adjective used; optionally card sort them into clusters.
Synthesise four or five distinctive experience attributes and share them as design principles.
outputs: A brand continuum wall, an adjective list and four or five agreed experience attributes.
useWhen: Use at the start of a new product or rebrand when stakeholders hold different, unspoken views of how the experience should feel.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the attributes as evidence of what users value: test perception with users through a Semantic Differential or Brand Lift and Drag Measurement. Image choice biases the outcome, so curate it across styles.
whyLost: It survives because it turns vague brand talk into concrete attributes quickly and gives designers criteria for later critique.
whereToUse: New digital products, rebrands, design systems, mergers that combine two product identities.
example: A new banking app team places an airline image under 'not us' and a chocolate brand under 'us', and settles on warm, candid and quick as the experience attributes used in later design reviews.
reference: Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Beverly, MA: Rockport Publishers. Method 12, Brand Experience Workshop.

name: Brand Lift and Drag Measurement
origin: Advertising effectiveness research; applied to UX benchmarks by Sauro (2018)
summary: Measures how using a product changes how people feel about the brand, by asking before and after the experience.
description: A good experience should improve brand perception and a bad one should damage it. Brand lift measurement asks participants to rate the brand (favourability, trust or likelihood to use) before they attempt tasks and again afterwards. The change, analysed as paired data, is the experience's effect on the brand: lift if positive, drag if negative. Breaking results down by task success and prior experience shows which failures hurt the brand most, connecting UX metrics to outcomes marketing and leadership care about.
steps: Ask a brand attitude question before any task (for example, a 7-point favourability rating).
Run the tasks and standard metrics as usual.
Ask the identical brand question at the end.
Compute the paired change per participant and test it with a paired t-test or sign test.
Cross-tabulate lift against task success, product and prior experience.
outputs: A measured brand effect of the experience, linked to the tasks that caused it.
useWhen: Benchmarks and competitive studies where you need to connect UX to brand value.
avoidWhen: Unbranded prototypes, or short studies where asking twice will feel repetitive.
whyLost: Brand belongs to marketing and UX rarely borrows its measures, so experience effects on brand go unreported.
whereToUse: Consumer brands, retail, travel and financial services websites.
example: Participants who failed the "find opening hours" task showed a 0.8-point brand drag, double that of any other task failure.
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapter 11.

name: Brier Score and Calibration Analysis
origin: Glenn Brier, 1950 (weather forecast verification); Murphy decomposition (1973); Tetlock's Good Judgment Project (2011-2015)
summary: Scores probabilistic predictions against outcomes and decomposes accuracy into calibration and resolution, applicable to researchers, users and AI systems.
description: The Brier score is the mean squared difference between forecast probabilities and outcomes (0 or 1); lower is better. Murphy's decomposition separates reliability (calibration: do 70% forecasts happen 70% of the time?), resolution (do forecasts discriminate?) and uncertainty. Calibration curves plot predicted against observed frequency. Weather forecasters became well calibrated through feedback. In UX this applies three ways: calibrating researchers' and teams' predictions about tests and launches; evaluating AI confidence displays shown to users; and measuring whether users' own confidence judgements are calibrated.
steps: Collect probabilistic forecasts (e.g. teams predict the probability each A/B test wins, or an AI model gives confidence scores).
Record outcomes once known.
Compute Brier scores and Murphy decomposition; plot calibration curves with binned or smoothed estimates.
Compare forecasters or models, and against base-rate forecasts (Brier skill score).
Feed results back to forecasters regularly to improve calibration.
For AI products, recalibrate model confidence (e.g. temperature scaling) before displaying it to users.
outputs: Brier scores, skill scores, calibration curves and recalibration recommendations.
useWhen: Evaluating predictions by people or models, especially confidence shown to users or used in decisions.
avoidWhen: When forecasts are not probabilistic and cannot be made so.
whyLost: Forecast verification lives in meteorology and intelligence; UX teams rarely track the accuracy of their own predictions.
whereToUse: AI confidence displays, research team prediction markets, risk scores, health predictions, recommendation confidence.
example: A product team logs probabilities for 80 A/B tests. Their Brier score is worse than always predicting the 30% base win rate, revealing overconfidence; quarterly calibration feedback improves it.
sources: Brier, Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability (1950), Monthly Weather Review
Murphy, A new vector partition of the probability score (1973), Journal of Applied Meteorology
Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974 paper) (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
reference: Brier, G. W. (1950). Monthly Weather Review, 78(1), 1-3.

name: Brown-Peterson distractor task and release from proactive interference
origin: Brown, 1958; Peterson and Peterson, 1959; Wickens, 1970s
summary: Briefly present items, block rehearsal with a counting task, then test recall; switching item category across trials shows how strongly people code that dimension.
description: Three consonants are presented, followed by a three-digit number from which the participant counts backwards by threes aloud to prevent rehearsal; after 3 to 18 seconds the letters are recalled. Peterson and Peterson found about 80 percent recall after 3 seconds and about 12 percent after 18. Later work showed much of this loss is proactive interference from earlier trials. In the release-from-PI extension, four trials each present three words, a 15-second counting interval and recall: when all trials use one category, recall falls trial by trial; when the fourth trial switches category, recall jumps back. Because release depends on the change in meaning, its size indexes how strongly people encode a given dimension, even over seconds.
steps: Prepare item sets (three letters or three words per trial) and three-digit start numbers for counting.
On each trial present the items, then have participants count backwards by threes aloud for the retention interval.
For forgetting curves, vary the interval (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 seconds) and record recall.
For release from PI, run four trials from one category, then switch category on the final trial for the experimental group only.
Keep a no-switch control group and counterbalance which categories come first.
Compare recall by interval, and by trial for switch versus control groups.
outputs: Recall accuracy by retention interval, trial-by-trial recall curves, and the size of the release from interference.
useWhen: Testing whether users can hold codes, labels or values across a short interruption, or whether a category distinction in an interface is strongly encoded.
avoidWhen: Avoid as evidence of pure decay, since interference explains much of the loss; for realistic interruption effects use task-based interruption studies.
whyLost: Short-term memory paradigms moved into memory theory and working-memory span tasks, leaving little applied use in UX.
whereToUse: One-time passcodes and verification flows, form fields that require copying values, multi-step wizards with interruptions, label distinctiveness.
example: A banking app tests one-time passcode entry after a forced screen switch: recall drops sharply after 15 seconds of distraction, so the app adds autofill and keeps the code visible.
sources: Peterson, L. R., & Peterson, M. J. (1959). Short-term retention of individual verbal items. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 58
reference: Peterson, L. R., & Peterson, M. J. (1959). Short-term retention of individual verbal items. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 58, 193-198.

name: Brunswik Lens Model Analysis
origin: Egon Brunswik, 1952-1956; operationalised by Kenneth Hammond (1955) and the lens model equation of Tucker (1964)
summary: Compares how cues relate to a true criterion with how people actually weight those cues, quantifying judgement accuracy, consistency and cue misuse.
description: The lens model places a distal criterion (e.g. actual trustworthiness of a seller) on one side and a person's judgement on the other, connected through a set of proximal cues (ratings, photos, response time). Regressing the criterion on cues gives ecological validities; regressing judgements on cues gives cue utilisation. The lens model equation decomposes achievement (the correlation between judgement and criterion) into environmental predictability, judge consistency and matching of cue weights. For UX, this precisely diagnoses whether users misjudge because the interface presents weak cues, because they weight cues wrongly, or because they are inconsistent, and so tells you whether to change the cues or help users use them.
steps: Define the criterion users are judging and obtain ground-truth values for a set of cases (e.g. 50-100 profiles, products or messages).
Identify the cues available in the interface and code their values for each case.
Have participants judge each case; include repeated cases to estimate consistency.
Regress criterion on cues (environment side) and each participant's judgements on cues (judge side).
Compute the lens model equation components: achievement, environmental predictability, judge consistency (Rs) and knowledge (G).
Redesign: add or strengthen valid cues, de-emphasise invalid but salient ones, and retest achievement.
outputs: Cue validity and utilisation weights, lens model statistics, and a diagnosis of judgement failure sources.
useWhen: Users judge quality, risk, authenticity or relevance from interface cues: reviews, phishing, listings, AI answers, medical images.
avoidWhen: Tasks without a measurable criterion, or with very few cases.
whyLost: The method lives in judgement and decision-making research and requires regression across many cases per judge, which UX studies rarely design for.
whereToUse: Marketplaces (seller trust), security warnings, misinformation labels, recruiting platforms, AI answer credibility.
example: A rental marketplace studies how renters judge listing quality. Renters heavily weight photo count, which has near-zero validity, and ignore host response rate, which predicts satisfaction; the listing page is redesigned to make response rate prominent.
sources: Brunswik, Perception and the Representative Design of Psychological Experiments (1956)
Cooksey, Judgment Analysis: Theory, Methods, and Applications (1996)
reference: Cooksey, R. W. (1996). Judgment Analysis. Academic Press.

name: BSF Stage 1 — Wavelet Decomposition
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Decomposes user behaviour time series into components at multiple temporal scales, separating session-level activity from weekly routines and lifecycle trends.
description: Wavelet decomposition is the first stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook. User activity is represented as a time series, for example events per hour or per day for each user, and decomposed into components at several temporal resolutions, analogous to a discrete wavelet transform. Unlike a single Fourier transform, wavelets localise patterns in time, so a weekly routine that begins in month two or a burst of activity around a billing event can be detected where it occurs. The stage turns undifferentiated activity counts into separate layers that later stages map, filter and model. Its rigour depends on consistent time binning, sufficient series length relative to the slowest scale studied, handling of missing periods, and checking that the components sum back to the original signal.
steps: Choose the unit of analysis (user, account or cohort) and a consistent time bin such as hourly or daily event counts.
Ensure each series spans at least three to four cycles of the slowest rhythm to be studied.
Handle gaps explicitly, distinguishing true inactivity from missing data.
Apply a multi-level wavelet decomposition (for example a discrete wavelet transform with a Haar or Daubechies basis).
Verify that reconstructed components sum to the original series within tolerance.
Store components per scale for each unit for use in frequency mapping.
outputs: Multi-scale behavioural components per user or cohort, with energy per scale and time localisation of patterns.
useWhen: When analysing long behavioural logs where micro and macro rhythms are mixed and averages hide when patterns start or stop.
avoidWhen: Avoid with short or sparse series, or when the team lacks signal-processing skills; use simpler cohort retention curves instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Novel analytical approach within BSF; enables pattern detection across micro and macro behavioral timescales.
whereToUse: Longitudinal behavioral data analysis; session-level vs. lifecycle-level behavior separation.
example: A language-learning app decomposes 120 days of daily practice counts per learner and finds a strong 7-day component emerging only after week three, which pinpoints when habit forms.
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 2 — Frequency Mapping
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Assigns decomposed behavioural components to high, mid and low frequency bands and labels each band with concrete behaviours to inform prioritisation.
description: Frequency mapping is the second stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Components produced by wavelet decomposition are placed on a frequency axis: high-frequency bands represent repeated micro-habits such as checking or scrolling, mid-frequency bands represent routines such as weekly planning, and low-frequency bands represent milestone events such as renewals or annual reporting. Each band is then labelled with the specific features and behaviours that contribute most energy to it. The result is a spectrum showing which rhythms dominate a product and which features serve each rhythm. Its rigour comes from defining band boundaries before analysis, attributing energy to features using event-level data, and comparing spectra across segments rather than relying on a single global picture.
steps: Define band boundaries in advance, for example under 1 day, 1 to 14 days and over 14 days.
Aggregate the energy of decomposed components into each band per user and segment.
Attribute band energy to features by recomputing spectra on feature-specific event streams.
Label each band with its dominant behaviours and features.
Compare spectra between retained and churned users or between segments.
Translate dominant and missing rhythms into feature prioritisation hypotheses.
outputs: A behavioural spectrum per segment, feature-to-band attribution and prioritisation hypotheses tied to rhythms.
useWhen: When deciding which features to invest in for habit-forming or engagement-loop products; when segments differ in how they use a product over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid if wavelet decomposition has not been done or event data cannot be attributed to features; use feature adoption funnels instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Part of BSF playbook; provides quantifiable metaphor for behavior regularity.
whereToUse: Feature usage analytics; habit-formation product design; engagement loop design.
example: A project-management SaaS maps its spectrum and finds retained teams concentrate energy in a weekly band driven by sprint review features, while trial teams show only high-frequency task edits. The team prioritises weekly review onboarding.
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 3 — Noise Filtering
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Removes accidental, exploratory and outlier interactions from the behavioural spectrum with explicit thresholds so design decisions rest on genuine usage patterns.
description: Noise filtering is the third stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Not every logged interaction represents a meaningful behaviour: accidental taps, one-off exploration, bot or test traffic, and extreme outlier users all add energy to the spectrum without reflecting stable patterns. This stage applies threshold-based filtering analogous to wavelet denoising, removing components whose energy falls below a defined level and excluding units that meet explicit outlier rules. Its purpose is to prevent teams from over-engineering for edge-case behaviour. Rigour comes from writing filtering rules before seeing results, reporting how much data each rule removes, running sensitivity checks with alternative thresholds, and keeping excluded data available so that genuinely important minority behaviours are not silently discarded.
steps: Write filtering rules in advance, covering bots and internal accounts, accidental interactions (for example sessions under 3 seconds) and outlier users.
Apply energy thresholds to each band to suppress low-energy components.
Report the proportion of events and users removed by each rule.
Run a sensitivity analysis with stricter and looser thresholds and check that conclusions hold.
Review excluded data for meaningful minority patterns, such as accessibility-related usage, before discarding.
Pass the filtered spectrum to pattern reconstruction.
outputs: A filtered behavioural spectrum, an exclusion log with removal rates and a sensitivity report.
useWhen: When usage analytics or A/B test results are distorted by accidental or outlier behaviour; before building personas or models from logs.
avoidWhen: Avoid when edge cases are the research focus, as in accessibility or error research; analyse those directly with critical incident or error studies.
whyLost: Still in use: Critical BSF stage; prevents over-engineering for edge-case behaviors.
whereToUse: Usage analytics cleanup; A/B test interpretation; longitudinal study data processing.
example: An e-commerce team finds that a feature's apparent daily usage is driven by accidental taps on a sticky banner. Filtering sessions under 2 seconds removes 40 percent of its events and changes the prioritisation decision.
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 4 — Pattern Reconstruction
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Rebuilds clean, representative behavioural trajectories from filtered signals, producing data-grounded archetypes for each frequency band.
description: Pattern reconstruction is the synthesis stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework.
