Gilmore's catastrophe flags are a set of phenomena that a cusp (two stable states with an unstable region between) predicts and a smooth process does not. No single flag is decisive, but combinations are: the book singles out inaccessibility plus hysteresis as convincing. Some flags need only cross-sectional data (multimodality, divergence of the distribution as a splitting variable such as involvement increases), others need repeated measures (sudden jumps, critical slowing down) or experimental control of a variable (hysteresis, inaccessibility). For UX research the flags give a disciplined way to test claims such as 'adoption tips once a team reaches a critical mass' or 'trust collapses suddenly after errors', instead of reading tipping points into any steep curve. The choice of which flags to test depends on what you can measure and manipulate.
steps: Define the behavioural variable and state the two hypothesised stable modes, the unstable middle and the candidate control variables (one shifting the balance, one splitting the modes, such as involvement).
Start with cross-sectional data: test the distribution of the behavioural variable for multimodality with a mixture model; if it is unimodal, reconsider the hypothesis.
Test divergence: check whether the distribution becomes bimodal only at high values of the proposed splitting variable.
Where you have dense repeated measures, test for sudden jumps with change-point methods and look for rising variance, autocorrelation or slower recovery before transitions.
Where you can manipulate the normal variable, run an ascending and descending sweep to test hysteresis, and try to hold participants in the middle state to test inaccessibility.
Tabulate which flags were found and judge the combined evidence; then consider fitting the cusp model directly.
outputs: A flag-by-flag evidence table stating which signatures of a tipping point are present, absent or untested, with a judgement on whether the change is discontinuous.
useWhen: You suspect a behaviour, attitude or adoption state flips between two states and want evidence stronger than a steep curve, especially before designing interventions that assume a tipping point.
avoidWhen: The behaviour is naturally continuous with no plausible stable alternative states, or you have neither dense time series, large cross-sectional samples nor any experimental control.
whyLost: Catastrophe theory suffered a backlash in the late 1970s and its testing programme stayed inside developmental and mathematical psychology; UX tipping-point talk usually relies on curve shape alone.
whereToUse: Habit formation, churn and reactivation, trust collapse after failures, team adoption of collaboration tools, opinion shifts about features or brands.
example: A team-chat product believes teams 'tip' into daily use. Researchers check whether the distribution of weekly active-days per team is bimodal, whether bimodality appears only in teams with high manager involvement, and whether churned-and-returned teams show hysteresis (they need more colleagues active to re-adopt than they had when they dropped off).
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Category structure paradigms: typicality, family resemblance and basic level
aka: Attribute listing for family resemblance and category level
origin: Berlin and Kay, 1969; Eleanor Rosch, 1973-1976; Rosch and Mervis, 1975
summary: A set of procedures (typicality ratings, attribute listing, best-example and boundary marking, basic-level naming) that reveal category prototypes and the level at which people naturally name things.
description: Rosch's programme showed that categories have graded structure. In typicality rating, people rate about 50 members of a category on a 7-point scale from very good to poor example (sparrow 1.18, penguin 4.53); typicality predicts verification speed, order of mention and priming. Attribute listing (about a minute per item) measures family resemblance through shared features, and shows the basic level carries most information: roughly 3 shared features for 'furniture', 9 for 'table', 10 for 'kitchen table'. Basic-level naming and speeded verification confirm the preferred level, which expertise shifts downwards. Best-example and boundary marking on a standard array, from Berlin and Kay's colour work, shows wide disagreement about boundaries but strong agreement on best examples. Hedge acceptability ('technically speaking', 'loosely speaking') reveals beliefs about category membership. Together these are the empirical basis for label and taxonomy decisions.
steps: Assemble the domain items (product images, terms, icons) and candidate category names at several levels.
Typicality: ask participants to rate each member on a 7-point scale from very good to poor example, and compute mean gradients.
Attribute listing: give about one minute per item to list features; compute overlap within and between categories and features per level.
Best example and boundaries: for each category, ask participants to mark all members and the single best example on a standard array; compute agreement.
Basic level: compare levels on naming preference, speeded verification and shared shape or actions; check expert and novice groups separately.
Optionally rate hedged statements ('technically', 'loosely speaking') to see how firmly membership is held.
Use best examples and basic-level terms for labels, icons and top-level navigation.
outputs: Typicality gradients, family-resemblance scores, best-example agreement, boundary maps, and the basic level of a taxonomy for each user group.
useWhen: Choosing navigation labels, category names, icons and illustrative examples, or deciding which level of a taxonomy to expose first.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing crisp category edges from fuzzy boundary data, and do not assume novices and experts share a basic level. For grouping structure use card sorting; for findability use tree testing.
whyLost: Its findings survive in IA folklore ('use the words users use', 'basic-level labels') and in card sorting, but the measurement procedures and their origin in Rosch's work are rarely used directly.
whereToUse: E-commerce category design, navigation labelling, icon and illustration selection, search query suggestions, content taxonomies.
example: A home-goods retailer runs typicality and naming tasks: shoppers name products 'sofa' and 'lamp' rather than 'seating' or 'lighting', and a velvet sofa is the agreed best example, so top navigation and hero images are changed accordingly.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Rosch, E., Mervis, C. B., Gray, W. D., Johnson, D. M., & Boyes-Braem, P. (1976). Basic objects in natural categories. Cognitive Psychology, 8
reference: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104, 192-233.

name: Category-based induction argument-strength rating
origin: Osherson, Smith, Wilkie, Lopez and Shafir, 1990
summary: People rate how convincing it is that a property of some categories also holds for another, revealing how similarity, coverage and causal knowledge drive generalisation.
description: Participants rate arguments that project a novel property from premise categories to a conclusion category, such as 'cows have sesamoid bones, so dogs do'. The similarity-coverage model predicts strength from the similarity of premises to conclusion plus coverage: how well the premises span the smallest superordinate that contains them all. Diverse premises give more coverage, atypical premises little. The type of property changes which similarity counts (anatomical versus behavioural), causal links in the premises raise strength, and adding a distant premise can lower it. Experts often reason from causal knowledge and ignore diversity. The method is rigorous because ratings are compared against quantitative model predictions under systematic manipulations of similarity, typicality, diversity and causal links.
steps: Choose premise and conclusion categories with known similarity and typicality (from prior ratings).
Attach a blank property (unfamiliar to participants) or a domain-specific one, depending on the question.
Build argument sets that vary premise diversity, typicality and causal relations while holding the conclusion constant.
Present arguments in random order and collect strength or likelihood ratings on a fixed scale.
Compare ratings with similarity and coverage predictions, and test diversity, typicality and nonmonotonicity effects.
Repeat with expert and novice groups to see whether causal knowledge overrides similarity.
outputs: Argument strength ratings, estimated effects of similarity, typicality, diversity and causal links, and model fit.
useWhen: Studying how users generalise from examples, for instance which reviews, case studies or sample items make a claim about a product range convincing, or how people extrapolate model behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid blank properties when the real question involves domain knowledge; experts may reason causally. For category membership itself use typicality and basic-level paradigms.
whyLost: It remains an academic tool for modelling induction and has no packaged UX application.
whereToUse: Example selection in marketing and onboarding, social proof design, AI capability communication, recommendation explanations.
example: A SaaS landing page tests which combination of customer case studies (two banks versus a bank and a retailer) makes visitors more confident the tool will work for their own sector; diverse cases raise ratings more than similar ones.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Osherson, D. N., Smith, E. E., Wilkie, O., Lopez, A., & Shafir, E. (1990). Category-based induction. Psychological Review, 97
reference: Osherson, D. N., Smith, E. E., Wilkie, O., Lopez, A., & Shafir, E. (1990). Category-based induction. Psychological Review, 97, 185-200.

name: Category-Theoretic Design System Modelling
origin: Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, 1945
summary: Uses category theory's objects, morphisms and composition to model how design-system components and transformations compose, exposing inconsistencies in component APIs.
description: Category theory describes mathematical structures in terms of objects and the arrows (morphisms) between them, with an emphasis on composition: if arrows compose associatively and have identities, the system behaves predictably when assembled. Applied to design systems, components, tokens and states can be modelled as objects, and transformations such as theming, responsive resizing or state transitions as morphisms. The question becomes whether these transformations compose consistently: does applying dark mode then compact density give the same result as the reverse? Do component variants form well-defined structures? The method is formal and largely analytical, drawing on functional programming practice where these ideas are already embedded. Its rigour comes from specifying composition laws explicitly and testing them, often by property-based testing in code, so that design systems scale without combinatorial surprises.
steps: Identify the objects to model: components, tokens, themes, states and layouts.
Specify transformations between them (theming, density, responsive breakpoints, state changes) as morphisms.
State the composition laws the system should obey, such as order independence of theme and density.
Check laws against the design system, using property-based tests in code or systematic visual comparison.
Log violations where composition produces inconsistent or undefined results.
Refactor component APIs and token structures so transformations compose predictably.
outputs: Formal model of design-system objects and transformations, stated composition laws, violation log, API refactoring recommendations.
useWhen: Large, multi-brand or multi-platform design systems with many interacting variants, especially in functional UI codebases.
avoidWhen: Small component libraries or teams without mathematical or functional programming expertise; use a design-system audit instead.
whyLost: Latent: Theoretical; growing interest in functional programming UI (e.g. Elm, Haskell ecosystems).
whereToUse: Design system architecture; component API design; functional UI frameworks.
example: A multi-brand banking design system had 4 brands, 2 modes and 3 densities. Modelling transformations as composable maps exposed 37 components where brand-then-dark differed from dark-then-brand, which the team fixed by restructuring token layers.
sources: Category Theory for the Sciences (David Spivak)
reference: Spivak, D. I. (2014). Category Theory for the Sciences. MIT Press.

name: Causal Chain and Antecedents Matrix
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 8, sections E and F.
summary: Linear chains of what leads to what, and a matrix ordered by an outcome showing which antecedent variables act as immediate or remote causes in each case.
description: Early in causal modelling it helps to make simplifying assumptions and lay causes and effects out as a linear chain, for example individualisation, then pupil self-pacing, then inability to monitor, then development of trust, then 'letting go', then a changed self-image. Chains are quick to communicate and can also explain decline (initial difficulties, annoyance, resignation, guilt, futility), though they must later be elaborated into networks. In cross-case causal networking, the analyst isolates for each case the stream of variables leading to an outcome and compares streams across cases. The antecedents matrix gives the big picture without getting lost in stream-by-stream matching: it is ordered by the outcome variable and shows all variables that seem to be at work in producing it, clustered conceptually. Each cell records whether the variable is an immediate cause (no more than two steps from the outcome) or a remote cause, with its strength (high, moderate, low), or is left blank. Reading column by column yields statements such as 'user commitment is a remote cause in high-impact cases and absent in low ones'. Families of cases sharing a scenario are then sought and verified. For UX it turns many interview-based explanations into a structured comparison of what drives an outcome like retention.
steps: Write simple causal chains for key processes in each case, from the field notes.
For each case, trace the stream of variables leading to the outcome and mark immediate (within two steps) and remote causes.
List variables that appear in at least a third of the case streams, plus conceptually important ones, clustered under headings.
Build a matrix with cases ordered by outcome as rows and these variables as columns; enter cause type and strength.
Read each column and write a summary statement of its role across cases.
Group cases with similar streams into families and check them against the original networks.
outputs: Causal chains per case, an outcome-ordered antecedents matrix, and summary statements of which antecedents matter.
useWhen: You have causal networks or rich explanations for several cases and want to see which antecedents recur.
avoidWhen: You have only one or two cases or no explicit causal reasoning in the data.
whyLost: UX rarely builds explicit qualitative causal models; root-cause work tends to use five whys or fishbone diagrams for a single incident.
whereToUse: Churn and retention research, adoption studies, incident pattern analysis across accounts.
example: Researchers interview 10 churned and 10 retained teams of a scheduling app. A chain for one churned team reads: no admin owner, then calendar sync errors unresolved, then double bookings, then manager loses trust, then team reverts to spreadsheet. The antecedents matrix shows 'no admin owner' as a remote cause in 8 of 10 churned teams and absent in retained ones.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Causal effect estimation from observational data
origin: Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983; Robins's g-methods, 1986 onward
summary: Estimates the effect of a feature or intervention from logs or surveys by adjusting for confounding with methods such as weighting, matching, g-computation or doubly robust estimation.
description: When experiments are impossible, causal effects can still be estimated under the assumptions of exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding given covariates), positivity (every user could have received each treatment) and consistency (a well-defined treatment). Estimators include outcome regression (g-computation), inverse probability of treatment weighting, matching, and doubly robust methods such as augmented IPW or targeted maximum likelihood, which remain consistent if either the treatment or outcome model is correct. For time-varying treatments, marginal structural models handle confounders affected by earlier treatment. Rigour requires a DAG-justified adjustment set, balance and overlap diagnostics, bootstrapped intervals and sensitivity analysis such as E-values for unmeasured confounding.
steps: Specify the causal question and target trial, then select covariates from a DAG.
Estimate propensity scores and an outcome model; inspect overlap and trim extreme weights (e.g. truncate at the 1st and 99th percentiles).
Estimate the effect with a doubly robust estimator (AIPW or TMLE) and compare with IPW and g-computation estimates.
Verify covariate balance after weighting with standardised mean differences below 0.1.
Compute bootstrap confidence intervals with at least 1,000 resamples.
Report an E-value or similar sensitivity analysis showing how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain away the effect.
outputs: Adjusted causal effect estimates with intervals, diagnostics, comparisons across estimators and a sensitivity analysis.
useWhen: Questions about feature or policy effects where randomisation was not done, especially with rich logs of pre-treatment behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when assignment is driven by unmeasured factors, when positivity fails (some segments never get treatment), or when an experiment is feasible.
whyLost: These methods are routine in epidemiology and economics, but product analytics typically reports raw differences between users and non-users.
whereToUse: Retrospective feature evaluation, health app engagement effects, fintech product impact where regulation limits experiments.
example: An investment platform estimates the effect of price alerts on panic selling during volatility. AIPW adjusting for portfolio size, experience and prior trading shows alerts reduce panic sells by 18%, robust to an E-value of 1.9.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
VanderWeele & Ding (2017) Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value
The Inquiry Series, Ch 48 — Target Trial Emulation — Causal Evidence from Log Data
reference: Hernán, M. A. & Robins, J. M. (2020) Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC.

name: Causal Forests for Heterogeneous Effects
origin: Stefan Wager and Susan Athey (2018); Athey, Tibshirani and Wager, generalised random forests (2019)
summary: Uses honest random forests to estimate how treatment effects vary across users, with valid confidence intervals and tests for heterogeneity.
description: Causal forests adapt random forests to estimate conditional average treatment effects. Splits are chosen to maximise treatment effect heterogeneity, and 'honesty' uses separate subsamples for choosing splits and estimating effects, yielding asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Built-in diagnostics include calibration tests for heterogeneity and best linear projections of effects onto covariates. Compared with ad hoc segment slicing of A/B results, which inflates false discoveries, causal forests provide disciplined discovery of who benefits and who is harmed, and can work with observational data under unconfoundedness with orthogonalisation.
steps: Start with randomised experiment data (preferred) or observational data with plausible unconfoundedness.
Select pre-treatment covariates that might moderate effects, e.g. tenure, device, prior usage.
Fit a causal forest (grf package) with honest splitting and sufficient trees (e.g. 2,000+).
Run the calibration test for heterogeneity and compute the average treatment effect with confidence interval.
Summarise heterogeneity with best linear projection and by ranking users into quantiles of predicted effect (RATE or TOC curves).
Validate key subgroups in a follow-up experiment before acting.
outputs: Conditional effect estimates, heterogeneity tests, variable importance for moderation, and targeting evidence.
useWhen: Large experiments where you suspect effects differ across users and want principled subgroup discovery.
avoidWhen: Small experiments (under a few thousand users) or when averages suffice for the decision.
whyLost: It is recent and computational, sitting in econometrics and data science rather than UX research.
whereToUse: Feature launches across diverse user bases, personalisation, health and finance interventions, accessibility features.
example: A language-learning app's new review schedule has a small average effect. A causal forest shows strong benefit for learners with irregular study habits and slight harm for daily learners, leading to adaptive scheduling.
sources: Wager & Athey, Estimation and inference of heterogeneous treatment effects using random forests (2018), JASA
Athey, Tibshirani & Wager, Generalized random forests (2019), Annals of Statistics
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)

name: Causal Inference Methods
origin: Donald Rubin, 1974 (potential outcomes); Judea Pearl, 2000; Hernán and Robins, 2020
summary: Estimates causal effects from observational data using designs such as difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables and matching when randomised tests are impossible.
description: The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we never observe the same user both with and without a treatment. Randomised experiments solve this by design; when they are not possible, quasi-experimental methods approximate them. Difference-in-differences compares changes over time between affected and unaffected groups, assuming parallel trends. Regression discontinuity exploits thresholds that assign treatment. Instrumental variables use a factor that affects treatment but not outcome directly. Propensity score matching balances observed confounders. Synthetic control builds a weighted comparison from untreated units. Rigour comes from stating the causal question and assumptions explicitly (ideally with a DAG), choosing a design whose assumptions are plausible, testing them where possible (pre-trend checks, balance diagnostics), and running sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
steps: State the causal question precisely, including treatment, outcome, population and time frame.
Draw a DAG of plausible causes to identify confounders and choose an identification strategy.
Select a design (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables, matching or synthetic control) whose assumptions fit the situation.
Prepare data and test assumptions, such as parallel pre-trends or covariate balance after matching.
Estimate the effect with confidence intervals.
Run sensitivity and placebo analyses and report limitations alongside the estimate.
outputs: Causal effect estimates with intervals, assumption diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, documented identification strategy.
useWhen: Evaluating features launched without experiments, policy or pricing changes, regional rollouts and situations where randomisation is unethical or impossible.
avoidWhen: When an A/B test is feasible, since randomisation is more reliable; or when data lack a credible comparison group.
whyLost: Latent: Growing in data science; rarely used in UX research; powerful for evaluating natural experiments.
whereToUse: Feature impact evaluation; policy evaluation; retrospective study design.
example: A retention lift after a feature launch coincided with a competitor's outage. Difference-in-differences using markets without the outage showed the feature's true effect was near zero, preventing a misguided expansion.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 45 — The Causal Revolution — Pearl's Ladder & the Fundamental Problem
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Hernán, M. A., & Robins, J. M. (2020). Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC.

name: Causal Layered Analysis
origin: Sohail Inayatullah, 1998
summary: Analyses an issue at four layers (litany, systemic causes, worldview/discourse, myth/metaphor) to uncover deep assumptions and reframe problems and futures.
description: CLA examines issues at increasing depth. The litany is the public, quantitative view (headlines, metrics). The systemic layer covers social, economic and technical causes. The worldview layer examines discourses and paradigms that make those systems seem natural. The myth/metaphor layer captures deep, often emotional stories. Alternative futures are created by changing the metaphor and rebuilding upward. It is a rigorous way to move beyond surface metrics in UX strategy: for example, the litany 'low engagement' may rest on a worldview that 'more use equals value' and a metaphor of 'capturing attention'.
steps: Choose the issue and collect material: data, documents, interviews, media.
Describe the litany: common statements, metrics and visible problems.
Identify systemic causes: structures, incentives, technical and economic factors.
Surface worldviews and discourses that legitimise the system, including stakeholder differences.
Identify myths and metaphors underlying the worldviews, from interviews and language.
Construct alternative metaphors and rebuild new worldviews, systems and litanies; derive strategic options.
outputs: A four-layer analysis, alternative metaphors and reconstructed futures with strategic implications.
useWhen: Stuck strategic problems, reframing product purpose, or exploring cultural assumptions.
avoidWhen: Operational problems with clear technical causes.
whyLost: It belongs to critical futures studies and its poststructuralist framing feels abstract to product teams.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing, social platforms, AI product purpose, healthcare and education reform.
example: A fitness app's CLA moves from the litany 'users quit after 3 weeks' to the metaphor 'body as machine to optimise'. A new metaphor, 'body as companion', leads to features centred on enjoyment and recovery.
sources: Inayatullah, Causal layered analysis: Poststructuralism as method (1998), Futures
Inayatullah (ed.), The Causal Layered Analysis Reader (2004)
reference: Inayatullah, S. (1998). Causal layered analysis. Futures, 30(8), 815-829.

name: Causal Loop Diagram from Qualitative Data
origin: Jay Forrester's system dynamics (1960s); causal loop diagrams popularised by Peter Senge, 1990; qualitative-data methods by Kim & Andersen, 2012
summary: Translating causal claims from qualitative data into variables and signed links, exposing reinforcing and balancing loops and evidence-backed leverage points.
description: Causal loop diagrams come from system dynamics, where problems are explained by feedback structure rather than single causes. Building them from qualitative data starts by extracting causal claims from transcripts or codes ('when X rises, Y falls'), turning them into variables, and drawing signed arrows. Tracing closed paths reveals reinforcing loops (vicious or virtuous cycles) and balancing loops (self-correction). An evidence audit marks every arrow with its supporting data, and unsupported links are labelled as hypotheses. Leverage points are variables central to several loops. Kim and Andersen's method for purposive text data emphasises traceability from text to diagram, guarding against analysts imposing their own model.
steps: List all causal claims emerging from your analysis: 'when X increases/decreases, Y increases/decreases.'
Draw nodes for each variable. Draw arrows for causal relationships with direction and sign (+/−).
Identify feedback loops: Trace paths returning to their starting node. Label reinforcing loops (R) and balancing loops (B).
Evidence audit: Every arrow must correspond to evidence in your data. Arrows without evidence are hypotheses — label [HYPOTHESIS].
Leverage points: Where would a design intervention have the largest systemic effect? Variables in multiple loops with high centrality.
outputs: A causal loop diagram with signed links and labelled loops, an evidence table per arrow, hypothesised links, and candidate leverage points.
useWhen: Problems with circular causality and unintended consequences, such as marketplace dynamics, trust spirals, support load or habit loops.
avoidWhen: Linear task problems or simple usability issues; use task analysis or usability testing. For quantified dynamics, move to stock-and-flow simulation.
whyLost: System dynamics is taught in management and policy schools, and UX synthesis rarely represents feedback loops explicitly.
whereToUse: Two-sided marketplaces, social platforms and content moderation, healthcare service systems, and organisational adoption of tools.
example: Interviews with ride-hail drivers yield claims linking surge pricing, driver positioning and rider wait times. The diagram reveals a reinforcing loop where drivers chase surges and leave suburbs underserved, pointing to a leverage point in positioning incentives.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Creating System Dynamics Models from Qualitative Data (Kim & Andersen)
reference: Kim, H. & Andersen, D. F. (2012). Building confidence in causal maps generated from purposive text data. System Dynamics Review, 28(4), 311-328.

name: Causal Loop Diagrams (System Dynamics)
origin: Jay Forrester (1961); John Sterman (2000); Donella Meadows (2008)
summary: Maps reinforcing and balancing feedback loops, stocks and flows in a product ecosystem to anticipate second-order effects of design changes.
description: Causal loop diagrams represent variables linked by arrows marked with polarity; loops are reinforcing (amplifying) or balancing (stabilising), and delays are marked. Stock-and-flow models allow simulation. The treatise's transfer: model product feedback loops (engagement increases network effects, which increase retention, which increases engagement). A locally optimal change can set off a reinforcing loop that degrades experience over time, and CLDs make second-order effects visible before they occur. Dark pattern analysis particularly benefits: a dark pattern's short-term gain may initiate a trust-erosion loop that produces long-term harm. Rigour comes from grounding links in evidence and testing dynamic hypotheses with simulation.
steps: Define the problem behaviour over time (for example declining trust despite rising engagement).
Identify key variables and draw causal links with polarities, from data and stakeholder workshops.
Identify loops, mark delays and label them reinforcing or balancing.
Locate leverage points and likely unintended consequences of planned changes.
Optionally build a stock-and-flow simulation and calibrate with historical data.
Use the model in decision reviews and monitor indicators for each loop.
outputs: Causal loop diagrams, identified loops and leverage points, optional simulation results.
useWhen: Platform, marketplace and social features; engagement strategies; ethics reviews.
avoidWhen: Isolated interface details with no feedback effects.
whyLost: System dynamics stayed in management science and policy; UX focused on single interactions.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, social networks, recommendation systems, subscription businesses, dark pattern assessment.
example: A CLD of a dating app shows that boosting notifications increases short-term activity but feeds a 'match fatigue' loop that reduces reply rates after 3 weeks; the team caps notifications.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Sterman JD (2000) Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Sterman JD (2000) Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World. McGraw-Hill.

name: Causal networks
origin: Miles and Huberman, Qualitative Data Analysis (1984; 2nd ed. 1994)
summary: Builds evidence-backed diagrams of the variables and causal links that explain an outcome within each case, then compares networks across cases to find recurring causal streams.
description: Miles and Huberman argued that qualitative data can support causal explanation because field research observes local mechanisms directly: who did what, under which conditions, with what result. A causal network is a display of the most important variables in a case, drawn as boxes, with arrows showing directional influence, accompanied by a narrative that explains each link with evidence. Variables are rated (for example high, moderate or low) and links are justified from coded data. Cross-case analysis then compares networks to identify causal streams, chains of variables that recur across cases leading to the same outcome. Rigour comes from explicit evidence for every arrow, inclusion of antecedent and intervening variables, informant review of the network, and predictions that can be checked later.
steps: Choose the outcome to explain (for example sustained digital record use at 6 months) and list candidate antecedent and intervening variables from coded data and memos, typically 10 to 25 per case.
Rate each variable for the case on a simple scale (high, moderate, low) using documented decision rules and evidence.
Draw directional links between variables only where field evidence supports them, and annotate each link with its evidence source and strength.
Write an accompanying narrative that walks through the network causally, citing excerpts for each link.
Have one or two key informants review the network and narrative, and revise links they convincingly dispute.
Compare networks across cases to identify causal streams that recur, and mark streams specific to subsets of cases.
Derive predictions from the cross-case streams and check them against new cases or later outcomes.
outputs: Per-case causal network diagrams with evidence-annotated links and narratives, cross-case causal streams, and testable predictions.
useWhen: Explaining why outcomes differ across sites, accounts or users; building theory of change for interventions; designing quantitative studies to test mechanisms.
avoidWhen: You need to estimate effect sizes or prove causation statistically (use experiments or causal inference on logs); or data are too thin to evidence links.
whyLost: Causal claims from qualitative data are often discouraged in UX ('qual is for why, not cause'), so the causal network technique never crossed from evaluation research into practice.
whereToUse: Multi-site rollouts, enterprise adoption, health system digitisation, service design evaluation, churn explanation in B2B accounts.
example: Causal networks for 12 clinics showed a recurring stream: power outages led to data loss, which led to supervisor distrust, then paper audit requirements, then duplicate entry, then non-adoption. Fixing offline sync alone was predicted insufficient unless audit policy changed, which later data confirmed.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage.

name: Causal Structure Discovery from Correlational Data (IC*, PC/TETRAD)
donor: Computer science and philosophy of causation
origin: Judea Pearl, IC* algorithm (2000); Peter Spirtes, Clark Glymour and Richard Scheines, TETRAD and the PC algorithm, Carnegie Mellon (1993 onwards)
summary: Uses patterns of conditional independence among observed variables to build a partially directed causal graph showing definite, possibly confounded and ambiguous links, as a hypothesis generator.
description: Constraint-based causal discovery reads causal structure from which variables become independent when others are held constant. The core inference: if A and C are each associated with B but independent of each other, and become dependent once B is conditioned on, then A and C both point into B (an unshielded collider). Starting from all associated pairs, the algorithm removes links between variables that some conditioning set renders independent, orients colliders, and propagates further arrowheads by rule. Pearl's IC* allows for latent common causes, so its output distinguishes genuine causal links, links that may reflect hidden confounders, and fully ambiguous links. The result is not one model but a class of equivalent models; known temporal order fixes many directions and speeds the search. Loehlin and Beaujean compare it to exploratory factor analysis: valuable for generating and constraining hypotheses, not a replacement for confirmatory modelling or experiments.
steps: Select variables measured on the same units, ideally with known temporal order (for example signup attributes before early usage before retention).
Test conditional independence for each pair given subsets of the other variables, and connect only pairs that no conditioning set makes independent.
Find unshielded triples (A and C linked to B but not to each other) where A and C are dependent given B, and orient both arrows into B.
Apply propagation rules to add further arrowheads, using temporal order as background knowledge.
Read the output as definite causes, possible latent confounding and ambiguous links, and list the equivalent models it implies.
Treat the graph as hypotheses: check stability across subsamples and test key links with experiments or quasi-experiments.
outputs: A partially directed graph (pattern or PAG) encoding a class of equivalent causal models, with flagged ambiguous and possibly confounded links.
useWhen: Many candidate drivers exist in product analytics or survey data, no experiment is yet possible, and you want principled hypotheses about direction and confounding to prioritise tests or to inform a DAG.
avoidWhen: You need a causal estimate for a decision (run an experiment or a designed observational analysis); key confounders are unmeasured and temporal order unknown; samples are small, so independence tests are unreliable. It assumes faithfulness and correct tests; many links stay ambiguous.
whyLost: It sits in computer science and philosophy of science; UX causal work is either experimental or hand-drawn DAGs, and algorithmic discovery looks like a black box to stakeholders.
whereToUse: Retention and engagement driver exploration; generating hypotheses from large surveys linked to logs; checking whether a hand-drawn DAG is consistent with the data's independencies.
example: A B2B SaaS team runs the PC algorithm on 40 onboarding and usage variables for 30,000 accounts, with time order as background knowledge. The graph suggests integration setup drives seat expansion only through weekly active admins and flags a possible hidden confounder between plan type and support contacts, so the team designs an experiment on admin activation.
reference: Spirtes, P., Glymour, C., & Scheines, R. (1993). Causation, Prediction, and Search. New York: Springer.

name: Causal thinking audit for research reports
donor: Epidemiology / research methodology, adapted for UX
origin: Adapted from reporting standards (e.g. Hernán's causal language guidance, 2018) in Vivek Gopinath's DAGs+SEM Playbook
summary: A structured review of a research report that checks every causal claim against its design, flags confounds and rewrites overclaims before decisions are made.
description: The causal thinking audit treats a research report as data to be tested. Each sentence implying cause (drives, leads to, because of, improves) is extracted, matched to the evidence and design behind it, and checked for the threats that could produce the same pattern: confounding (such as a market rally lifting retention), selection, reverse causation, regression to the mean and collider bias. The audit then asks what counterfactual the claim implies and whether the data could distinguish it. It draws on Hernán's argument that hiding causal intent behind associational language is worse than stating it with explicit assumptions. Rigour comes from a fixed checklist, independent auditors and a documented verdict per claim.
steps: Extract every explicit or implied causal claim from the report into a table.
For each claim record the design behind it (experiment, quasi-experiment, observational log, survey, qualitative) and its rung on Pearl's ladder.
Check each claim against a fixed threat list: confounding, selection bias, reverse causation, regression to the mean, collider bias, seasonality or market events.
Sketch a minimal DAG for contested claims and identify any open backdoor paths.
Assign a verdict per claim (supported, supported with stated assumptions, overclaimed, unsupported) and propose reworded language or a follow-up design.
Have a second auditor review independently and reconcile disagreements before the report is circulated.
outputs: An annotated claims table with verdicts, threat analysis, revised wording and a list of follow-up studies needed for key decisions.
useWhen: Before research findings feed strategy, roadmaps or board decks; when a metric moved and the team is ready to credit a feature.
avoidWhen: Avoid for purely exploratory reports with no causal intent, or when time-critical decisions are low-stakes and easily reversed.
whyLost: UX critique traditions focus on method execution, not causal logic, and few teams have the epidemiological vocabulary to run such a review.
whereToUse: Research ops quality gates, growth team post-mortems, fintech and health products under regulatory scrutiny, and executive readouts.
example: An investment app attributes a 15% retention lift to a new dashboard. The audit notes the launch coincided with a market rally; comparing against a non-exposed cohort shows the lift is almost entirely market-driven, and the claim is withdrawn.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 45 — The Causal Revolution — Pearl's Ladder & the Fundamental Problem
reference: Hernán, M. A. (2018) The C-word: scientific euphemisms do not improve causal inference from observational data. American Journal of Public Health, 108(5), 616-619.

name: Censored and Truncated Regression (Type-1 Tobit)
origin: James Tobin, 1958; named Tobit by Arthur Goldberger, 1964
summary: Regression for a continuous outcome piled up at a limit, such as many zero spends or a ceiling, or observed only beyond a threshold, where ordinary regression would be biased.
description: Two data problems look similar but differ. Truncation means cases beyond a limit are never sampled, for example spend recorded only for orders over a minimum. Censoring means those cases are present but recorded at the limit, for example many users with zero spend or ratings stuck at the scale maximum. Simulations show ordinary least squares on such data inflates the intercept and attenuates slopes towards zero. The truncated regression model conditions the normal density on being past the threshold. The Type-1 Tobit treats the limit value as a latent variable at or beyond the threshold and combines a probit-like part for the probability of a non-limit outcome with the density of observed values. A predictor therefore moves the chance of a positive outcome and its size in the same direction. Effects must be read through marginal effects on the probability, the conditional mean and the unconditional mean, not from the latent coefficients alone.
steps: Inspect the outcome distribution for a spike at a limit (zeros, a ceiling) or a cut-off below which nothing is observed.
Decide whether the data are truncated (limit cases absent) or censored (limit cases present but uninformative about the latent amount).
Specify the latent regression with normal errors and the threshold (zero or any constant, from above or below) and estimate by maximum likelihood.
Check residuals and assumptions: generalised residuals and conditional moment tests for heteroskedasticity and normality, since violations make Tobit estimates inconsistent.
Compare models with likelihood ratio tests, pseudo-R-squared and AIC or BIC.
Interpret marginal effects on the probability of exceeding the limit and on the conditional and unconditional expected amount, and validate forecasts on a hold-out sample.
outputs: Coefficients on the latent scale, marginal effects on the probability of a non-limit outcome and on expected amounts, and hold-out forecasts.
useWhen: Outcomes such as spend, time in a feature, number of items added or satisfaction scores with ceiling effects, where a large share of users sit exactly at a limit.
avoidWhen: Different factors plausibly drive whether users participate and how much they do (use a Type-2 Tobit or two-part model); the outcome is a count (use count models); errors are clearly non-normal or heteroskedastic. Zeros that reflect a separate decision rather than censoring call for a selection or hurdle model.
whyLost: UX and product analysts usually run OLS on all users or on non-zero users only, unaware of the bias, because limited-dependent-variable models are taught in econometrics.
whereToUse: In-app purchase and donation amounts, time spent in optional features, credit or loan amounts in fintech, rating scales with ceiling effects.
example: A charity app analyses 4,000 users' donations after an appeal, 59% of whom gave nothing. OLS on all users understates the effect of recent engagement; a Tobit model shows each recent session raises both the chance of giving and the expected gift, which changes the targeting rule.
sources: Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
reference: Tobin, J. (1958). Estimation of relationships for limited dependent variables. Econometrica, 26, 24-36.

name: Centrality analysis
donor: Social network analysis and graph theory
origin: Linton Freeman's centrality measures, 1977-1978; PageRank, Brin and Page, 1998
summary: Ranks nodes in an information architecture by structural importance, identifying hubs, bottlenecks and peripheral content, and compares structural with intended importance.
description: Centrality metrics quantify how important a node is in a network. Degree centrality counts links; closeness centrality measures average distance to all other nodes; betweenness centrality counts how often a node lies on shortest paths between others, identifying bottlenecks; eigenvector centrality and PageRank weight links from important nodes more heavily. In an IA, these show which pages carry structural load and which important content is marginal. High-betweenness nodes are single points of failure: if they are confusing or broken, many journeys fail. Comparing the centrality ranking with business or user priority reveals misalignment. Rigour comes from a complete graph, using directed versions where links are one-way, and weighting by transition data where available.
steps: Extract the IA graph with directed edges and, optionally, transition weights from analytics.
Compute degree, closeness, betweenness and PageRank for all nodes in a tool such as NetworkX or Gephi.
Rank nodes and list the top 5% by betweenness as potential bottlenecks.
Compare centrality ranks with a priority ranking of content or tasks (from stakeholder input or top-tasks surveys) using Spearman's rank correlation.
Inspect high-betweenness nodes for usability quality and resilience; inspect high-priority, low-centrality nodes for missing links.
Propose link changes and recompute centrality to check alignment improves.
outputs: Centrality rankings, bottleneck list, priority-centrality alignment score, and recommended structural changes.
useWhen: For large IAs, knowledge graphs, intranets and documentation; when priority content is hard to reach; for resilience planning.
avoidWhen: For small or linear structures; use a simple sitemap review. For user mental models, use card sorting.
whyLost: Centrality is central in network science and SEO but has not entered UX research methods practice, where IA work is mostly qualitative.
whereToUse: Documentation portals, enterprise knowledge bases, medical device menus, e-commerce category structures, and AI retrieval corpora.
example: Centrality analysis of a 3,000-page help centre shows 'Account settings' has the highest betweenness while 'Cancel subscription', a top task, ranks in the bottom 20%. Adding links from billing and profile pages raises its closeness and halves related support contacts.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 7 — Graph Theory & the Architecture of Information
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Freeman, L. C. (1978). Centrality in social networks: conceptual clarification. Social Networks, 1(3), 215-239.

name: CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis)
origin: Karl Jöreskog, 1969
summary: Tests whether survey items measure a pre-specified set of latent constructs as theorised, giving fit indices, loadings and evidence of construct validity.
description: Confirmatory factor analysis specifies in advance which items load on which latent factors (e.g. five trust items on Interface Trust, four on Institutional Trust) and tests how well this structure reproduces the observed covariance matrix. Unlike EFA, items are not allowed to load freely on all factors. CFA provides standardised loadings, factor correlations and global fit, and it is the measurement model underlying any SEM. Rigour comes from theory-led specification, adequate sample size (commonly 200 or more), appropriate estimators for ordinal Likert data (WLSMV), reporting multiple fit indices, examining convergent and discriminant validity, and testing measurement invariance before comparing groups.
steps: Specify the measurement model from theory or a prior EFA on a separate sample: which items load on which factors.
Collect data from at least 200 respondents (more for complex models) and inspect item distributions.
Fit the model with an estimator suited to the data (WLSMV for ordinal items, MLR for continuous-like items).
Evaluate fit with CFI and TLI at or above 0.95, RMSEA at or below 0.06, and SRMR at or below 0.08.
Check standardised loadings (ideally above 0.5, preferably 0.7), average variance extracted above 0.5 and discriminant validity (HTMT below 0.85).
Test measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar) before comparing groups, and avoid purely data-driven modification indices.
outputs: A validated measurement model with loadings, fit indices, reliability, convergent and discriminant validity evidence and invariance results.
useWhen: Validating a UX questionnaire's structure, confirming a scale works in a new population or language, and as the measurement step before SEM.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you have no prior structure (use EFA), with samples under about 150, or for single-item measures.
whyLost: CFA is routine in psychology and marketing research, but UX teams usually adopt or invent questionnaires without testing their structure.
whereToUse: Trust, perceived usefulness and AI-reliance scales, localisation of standard questionnaires, enterprise satisfaction instruments.
example: A fintech team confirms that its 12-item digital trust scale has three factors in a new sample of 420 users, with CFI 0.97 and RMSEA 0.045, before using the scale to compare markets.
sources: Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (Rex Kline)
A Primer on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (Joseph Hair et al.)
Quantitative User Experience Research (Chris Chapman & Kerry Rodden)
Confirmatory Factor Analysis for Applied Research (Timothy Brown)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 49 — Structural Equation Modeling — From Quotes to Coefficients
The Inquiry Series, Ch 50 — Factor Analysis — Discovering the Latent Structure of Experience
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Brown, T. A. (2015) Confirmatory Factor Analysis for Applied Research, 2nd ed. Guilford Press.

name: Change Blindness Testing
origin: Rensink, O'Regan and Clark, 1997; Simons and Levin, 1997
summary: Tests whether users notice changes to a screen that occur during transitions, reloads or interruptions, revealing state changes that go unseen.
description: Change blindness is the striking failure to notice large changes in a visual scene when the change coincides with a disruption such as a blink, saccade, screen flash, page reload or interruption. Because visual memory retains little detail, people rely on attention to detect change, and without a transient motion signal changes are often missed. In UX this explains why updated totals, validation messages, reordered lists or silently refreshed data go unnoticed. As a method, researchers present the before and after states with realistic transitions and measure whether and how quickly participants detect the change, adapting the flicker paradigm. Rigour comes from controlling the transition type, measuring detection rates and latency, and comparing techniques such as animation, highlighting or persistent change markers that restore the missing transient signal.
steps: Identify state changes in the product that users must notice (totals, errors, reordering, live data updates).
Build prototypes that reproduce the real transition (full reload, fade, instant swap) and variants with change cues such as motion or highlighting.
Give 10-20 participants a primary task, then trigger the change without warning.
Record whether each participant reports the change and the latency to detection.
Compare detection rates across transition variants; treat detection under 80% for safety or money-critical changes as a defect.
Adopt the cue design that maximises detection and verify it does not create excessive distraction.
outputs: Detection rates and latencies by transition type, list of unseen state changes, recommended change-signalling patterns.
useWhen: Single-page apps, live dashboards, checkout totals, form validation and any interface where content updates without a full navigation.
avoidWhen: When the problem is comprehension of a change users did notice; use think-aloud usability testing.
whyLost: Siloed: Well-documented in perception psychology; rarely applied deliberately in UX practice.
whereToUse: Animation and transition design; onboarding change communication; screen reader design.
example: An e-commerce checkout recalculated shipping silently after an address change. Only 6 of 15 participants noticed the new total; animating the price change and briefly highlighting it raised detection to 14 of 15.
sources: Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
reference: Simons, D. J., & Levin, D. T. (1997). Change blindness. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 1(7), 261-267.

name: Change-Point Detection
donor: Statistical quality control and signal processing
origin: E. S. Page (1954, CUSUM); PELT by Killick, Fearnhead and Eckley (2012); Bayesian online change-point detection by Adams and MacKay (2007)
summary: Statistically locates the points in a time series where its mean, variance or trend changes, distinguishing real shifts from noise.
description: Metric dashboards invite people to see changes in noise. Change-point methods formalise detection: CUSUM accumulates deviations from a target and signals when they exceed a threshold; offline methods such as PELT or binary segmentation find the optimal set of change locations with a penalty for complexity; Bayesian online methods give a running probability that a change has just occurred. Applied to UX metrics (task success, satisfaction, error rates, support contacts), they identify when behaviour shifted, which can then be linked to releases or external events, and they support alerting on real regressions.
steps: Choose the metric series and its time resolution; consider seasonality and remove it if needed.
Specify the type of change to detect (mean, variance, slope) and an appropriate cost function.
Run offline detection (e.g. PELT with a BIC-like penalty) on historical data to find past changes.
Check sensitivity of detected points to the penalty and validate against known events.
For monitoring, configure CUSUM or Bayesian online detection with an acceptable false alarm rate.
Investigate each detected change with release notes, segment breakdowns and qualitative data.
outputs: Detected change points with magnitudes and confidence, and a monitoring configuration.
useWhen: Monitoring UX metrics over time, investigating when a problem started, or annotating long-term trends.
avoidWhen: Very short or highly irregular series; or when the change date is known (use ITS).
whyLost: Product dashboards rely on eyeballing and simple thresholds; change-point methods remain in statistics and engineering.
whereToUse: Experience metrics programmes, app performance, support volumes, review ratings, AI quality monitoring.
example: PELT on daily app rating data finds a mean shift on 14 March, two days after an SDK upgrade, rather than at the redesign date the team suspected.
sources: Killick, Fearnhead & Eckley, Optimal detection of changepoints with a linear computational cost (2012), JASA
Adams & MacKay, Bayesian online changepoint detection (2007), arXiv
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Killick, R., Fearnhead, P., & Eckley, I. A. (2012). JASA, 107(500), 1590-1598.

name: Channel Capacity Analysis
donor: Information theory and early human factors
origin: Shannon and Weaver, 1949; George Miller, 1956
summary: Treats human perception and response as limited-bandwidth channels, estimating transmitted information in bits to compare display codes and modalities.
description: Early human factors researchers applied Shannon's communication model to people, measuring how many bits per second or how many distinguishable levels a perceptual channel could carry. Miller's 'magical number seven' paper summarised findings that absolute judgement of a single dimension saturates at about 2.5 bits, roughly seven categories, while multidimensional stimuli carry more. The method computes transmitted information from stimulus-response confusion matrices, revealing how many levels of colour, size, pitch or vibration users can reliably distinguish. This gives a rigorous basis for coding decisions: how many alert tones, colour categories or haptic patterns can be used before confusion rises. It faded as cognitive models and usability testing took over, but remains valuable for designing multimodal codes.
steps: Define the coding dimension(s) to evaluate (e.g. tones, colours, vibration patterns) and candidate levels.
Run an absolute identification task in which 10-20 participants identify randomly presented levels, with many trials per level.
Build stimulus-response confusion matrices.
Compute transmitted information in bits and the effective number of distinguishable levels (2^bits).
Compare codes and modalities, and test combinations of dimensions for added capacity.
Set the number of levels to stay within capacity with a safety margin for real-world conditions.
outputs: Confusion matrices, transmitted information per code, maximum reliable number of levels per channel, coding recommendations.
useWhen: Designing alert tones, haptic vocabularies, colour coding in dense displays and multimodal signals in vehicles, medical devices or wearables.
avoidWhen: General screen usability questions; use usability testing or cognitive load assessment.
whyLost: Extinct: Grounded early HCI but supplanted by cognitive load frameworks and more applied usability methods.
whereToUse: Multimodal design; information display; notification channel design.
example: A smartwatch team planned eight distinct vibration patterns for notification types. Identification testing showed transmitted information of 1.9 bits, about four reliable levels, so they reduced to four patterns plus a visual glance.
sources: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two (George Miller)
The Mathematical Theory of Communication (Shannon & Weaver)
Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81-97.

name: Chatbot Introduction Social-Cue Audit
aka: Social cues in chatbot introductions codebook
Social cue framework and content analysis of chatbot introductions
origin: Charlotte van Hooijdonk, Gabriëlla Martijn and Christine Liebrecht, 2023, building on CASA (Nass, Reeves), MASA (Lombard and Xu) and Feine et al.'s chatbot social cue taxonomy
summary: Systematically sample live chatbot introductions and code identity, competence, conversational, communication and proactive cues with a reliability-tested codebook.
description: A chatbot's opening screen sets users' expectations of what it is and what it can do. This audit applies content analysis to that moment across a sector. The framework groups cues into identity (disclosure label, avatar type, name type), competence (claims of expertise or admissions of limits), conversational (greeting, self-introduction, giving the turn), communication (explaining purpose and how to interact) and, added during coding, proactive cues (privacy disclaimers, proactive information, handover to a human). Introductions are sampled by listing sectors and competing organisations, screenshotting the first screen without interacting, and coding header, welcome messages and response options. Coders train on a joint set, revise the codebook, then a subset is double-coded for Krippendorff's alpha. The original study of 88 introductions found humanlike avatars common, but purpose explained in only 12.5 percent and handover offered in 18 percent. Codebook and sample are on OSF.
steps: List sectors, the organisations in each and their competitors, and locate each customer-service chatbot on home, contact or support pages.
Screenshot the first screen without interacting (interact only to confirm an unlabelled agent is a bot) and stop at saturation.

Code header, welcome messages and response options with the codebook: avatar and type, name and type, disclosure, greeting, self-introduction, competence or limitation, purpose, interaction instructions, turn-giving, handover, privacy disclaimer, proactive information, response option type, number of buttons and character limits.
Train coders on examples and a jointly coded set of about 10 introductions, resolving differences and revising the codebook.
Split the sample among coders and have an independent coder double-code a subset (about 25) to compute Krippendorff's alpha per cue.
Report cue prevalence and describe how organisations combine cues, noting cues with low alpha.
outputs: A per-cue reliability table, a prevalence table across the sample, an updated cue framework, and a qualitative account of cue combinations.
useWhen: Benchmarking competitors' or a portfolio's chatbot introductions, setting a baseline before redesigning a bot's opening, or building a sector-wide picture of conversational agent conventions.
avoidWhen: When the question is how users respond to an introduction (run an experiment or Conversation Analysis for Chatbot Evaluation instead); or for a single bot, where an expert review against the framework is enough.
whyLost: It is a recent academic method; industry conversation designers review competitors informally rather than with sampled, reliability-tested coding.
whereToUse: Customer-service and banking bots, public-sector assistants, AI assistant onboarding, competitive analysis for conversational products.
example: An insurer audits 40 competitor bots before relaunching its own. Only 6 explain what the bot can do and 9 mention handover, so the new introduction leads with purpose and an explicit route to an agent.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: van Hooijdonk, C., Martijn, G., & Liebrecht, C. (2023). A framework and content analysis of social cues in the introductions of customer service chatbots. In Følstad et al. (Eds.), Chatbot Research and Design (LNCS 13815). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-25581-6_8

name: Chatbot Miscommunication Repair Responses
aka: Chatbot miscommunication repair responses with capability hints
origin: Common conversation-design practice; described by Christine Liebrecht, Naomi Kamoen and Celine Aerts (2023), citing earlier chatbot recovery-strategy studies
summary: Design escalating responses for input the bot does not understand: notify, ask the user to rephrase, then reveal what the bot can help with, and measure breakdowns in logs.
description: Every conversational agent misunderstands some input, and how it recovers shapes whether users persist. The escalating repair pattern has three tiers. The first response notifies the user that the bot did not understand. Paired with it is a repair request asking the user to rephrase. If the failure repeats, the bot tells the user what kinds of information or actions it can provide, a capability hint that earlier chatbot studies found effective. Liebrecht, Kamoen and Aerts used this set in voting-advice chatbots and also randomised connective sentences (acknowledging, restating, confirming) so conversation felt varied. Coding chat logs then showed far more miscommunication with voice input than with text. The practice is only half design: repair responses need log-based measurement of how often each tier fires and whether users recover.
steps: List the fallback situations: no intent matched, low confidence, out-of-scope request, and repeated failure.
Write a short error notification for the first failure, avoiding blame.
Pair it with a repair request asking the user to rephrase, ideally with an example phrasing.
On a second consecutive failure, list the types of information or actions the bot supports, as buttons where possible.
On a third failure, offer handover to a human or another channel.
Write several variants of each response and of connective sentences, and rotate them so the bot does not repeat itself.
Instrument each tier and review logs for how often it fires and whether users recover, per modality.
outputs: A tiered repair response set with variants, a handover rule, and log metrics for miscommunication and recovery per tier.
useWhen: Building or tuning any chatbot or voice assistant, especially with free-text or voice input where recognition errors are frequent.
avoidWhen: When the team does not yet know why breakdowns happen; read transcripts first with Conversation Log Review and Tuning, or test dialogue paths with Dialog Traversal Testing. Repair design cannot compensate for a bot whose scope does not match what users ask.
whyLost: It survived because every conversational platform needs fallback handling and vendors ship default reprompt patterns; the capability-hint tier is the part teams most often skip.
whereToUse: Customer-service bots, voice assistants, in-car and smart-speaker interfaces, civic information bots, AI assistants with constrained tools.
example: A utility's voice bot fails often on account numbers. After adding a rephrase example on the first failure and a spoken menu of four options on the second, logs show users recovering from 61 percent of breakdowns, up from 38 percent.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Liebrecht, C., Kamoen, N., & Aerts, C. (2023). In Følstad et al. (Eds.), Chatbot Research and Design (LNCS 13815). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-25581-6_3

name: Chatbot Self-Introduction Design
aka: Chatbot self-introduction design for expectation management
origin: Charlotte van Hooijdonk, Gabriëlla Martijn and Christine Liebrecht (2023), drawing on Go and Sundar, Mozafari et al., Khadpe et al. and Kull et al.
summary: Design a chatbot's header, welcome messages and response options so identity cues are consistent, warmth is shown, purpose and interaction are explained, and handover is offered.
description: A bot's introduction is where users form expectations of what it is and can do, and mismatched expectations drive later frustration. The practice treats the introduction as three designed parts (header, welcome messages, response options) across five cue types. Identity: decide whether to mark or mask the artificial identity and keep disclosure, avatar and name consistent, since a humanlike avatar with a machine disclosure caused expectancy violation in Go and Sundar's study. Competence: prefer warmth or honest statements of limits over boasts of capability. Conversation: greet, introduce, and hand the turn to the user. Communication: explain the bot's purpose and how to talk to it, and mention handover to a human. Proactive cues: consider privacy disclaimers. Where intent recognition is weak, constrain free text with buttons or character limits. Most live introductions omit purpose and interaction guidance.
steps: Decide whether to mark or mask the bot's artificial identity, then choose a disclosure label, avatar and name that send the same signal.
Write a greeting and short self-introduction, preferring warmth or an honest statement of limits over claims of expertise.
State the bot's purpose in one sentence and explain how to interact (keywords, buttons, example questions).
Mention how to reach a human and add a privacy note if personal data will be collected.
End the welcome by explicitly giving the turn to the user.
Choose response options: buttons, a text field or both, constraining free text where intent recognition is weak.
Benchmark the result against competitors' introductions and test comprehension of purpose with users.
outputs: An introduction specification covering header, welcome message sequence and response options, with the chosen cue for each category.
useWhen: Launching or redesigning a customer-service bot or AI assistant, especially when users misjudge its scope or treat it as a human.
avoidWhen: When the team lacks evidence on what users expect or misunderstand; run usability tests or Conversation Analysis for Chatbot Evaluation first, or audit the market with a Chatbot Introduction Social-Cue Audit.
whyLost: It survived because every deployed bot needs an opening message; what is often lost is the deliberate, cue-by-cue design, so purpose and handover go unstated.
whereToUse: Customer service, banking and insurance bots, public-sector assistants, AI copilots inside SaaS products.
example: A bank replaces its bot's opening 'Hi, I'm Eva!' with a robot icon, the label 'digital assistant', one line on the five things it can do, buttons for each, and 'type agent to reach a person'. Out-of-scope questions in the first turn fall by half.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: van Hooijdonk, C., Martijn, G., & Liebrecht, C. (2023). A framework and content analysis of social cues in the introductions of customer service chatbots. In Følstad et al. (Eds.), Chatbot Research and Design (LNCS 13815). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-25581-6_8

name: CHECk Ethical Checklists
origin: Read, Horton and colleagues in the ChiCI group, University of Central Lancashire (2013); applied in Chapter 1
summary: Two short checklists that make researchers question their own values before a study with children, and plan how children can give genuinely informed consent.
description: CHECk is an ethics tool for design and evaluation work with children. Its premise is that ethics is more than a signed consent form: in a school, teachers consent on behalf of a class, and a child may find it hard to refuse. CHECk1 asks six questions before any activity, pushing the team to be honest about why they are building the technology, why children are involved, and what values drive the work. CHECk2 looks before and beyond the activity from the child's side: what the children will be told about the activity, how their contributions will be used and disseminated, and who will get credit for their ideas. The aim is 'ethical symmetry', where children consent in their own right rather than adults consenting for them. Completing the checklists also surfaces weaknesses in study design and forces the team to work out how to explain the study in words children understand. The chapter also varied how much ethical information children received, showing that the briefing itself can be studied. For UX teams working with minors or other groups with unequal power, CHECk is a practical way to move beyond compliance.
steps: Before planning sessions, have the team answer the six CHECk1 questions in writing about the purpose of the technology and of involving children.
Revisit the study design in light of the answers, dropping or changing activities that cannot be justified.
Work through CHECk2: decide what children will be told, how their data and ideas will be used and credited, and how this will be explained.
Write a child-friendly script for the briefing and for asking assent, and make it easy for a child to decline.
Run the study, giving every child the same briefing, and debrief afterwards on how their contribution will be used.
Keep the completed checklists with the study records and review them after the study.
outputs: Completed CHECk1 and CHECk2 forms, a revised study plan and a child-appropriate briefing and assent script.
useWhen: Planning research or co-design with children, especially in schools where institutional consent can mask a child's reluctance.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for formal ethics review or legal safeguarding requirements, which still apply.
whyLost: It is known mainly within child-computer interaction; mainstream UX ethics practice focuses on consent forms and data protection rather than values reflection.
whereToUse: Children's products, edtech, school-based studies, research with other dependent groups.
example: Before testing a reading game in a primary school, the team completes CHECk1 and realises the main reason for involving children is to publish a paper; they add a feedback session in which children see how their comments changed the game and learn who will be credited.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Sim, G., Read, J. C. and Horton, M. (2016). Practical and ethical concerns in usability testing with children. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 1. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Checklist Matrix
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 5, section B, illustrated with 'preparedness' for implementing a school innovation.
summary: A matrix that breaks one important variable into its components as rows and rates and quotes each component for different people, combining judgements with supporting evidence.
description: Sometimes field researchers want comparable data on one conceptually important variable that can be unbundled into indicators, especially across several cases or alongside survey measures. The checklist matrix lists the components of that variable as rows (for preparedness: commitment, understanding, materials, skills, training, time, organisational support, and later 'relevant prior experience') and puts people or roles as columns. The analyst retrieves coded material, forms a judgement of the level of each component (absent, sketchy, basic, adequate, present, strong) and enters it in the cell together with a short supporting quote, so another analyst can check the rating. Decision rules are written down, for example not forcing a general judgement when two users hold different roles. Conclusions come from scanning columns, then going back to the notes to ask why patterns appear; in the book's example, weak training turned out to stem from administrators minimising new users' needs, and a missing row (support from other teachers) emerged. The book notes that a matrix like this can be assembled and analysed in a few hours. For UX it is a tidy way to assess readiness, adoption conditions or the components of a construct such as trust across user roles.
steps: Choose a single variable that matters to the research question and can be broken into components.
List the components as rows; add roles, people or time points as columns.
Write decision rules for ratings and for when to split or merge respondents.
For each cell retrieve coded notes, rate the level and add a short supporting quote.
Scan down columns and across rows for patterns, then return to the notes to explain them.
Add rows for components the data show are missing, and transpose or split the matrix if needed.
outputs: A component-by-role grid of ratings with evidence quotes, and a short analytic text.
useWhen: One construct is central, it has clear components, and you need comparable judgements across people or cases.
avoidWhen: The domain is still poorly understood and fixing components would be premature.
whyLost: UX uses readiness checklists and heuristic scorecards, but rarely ties each rating to a quote from field data in one display.
whereToUse: Enterprise rollout research, onboarding readiness, change management, adoption studies of internal tools.
example: Before rolling out a new design system, researchers interview product teams and build a checklist matrix of 'readiness to adopt': rows for understanding of tokens, available components, engineering time, design lead sponsorship, training received; columns for designers, front-end engineers and product managers. Cells read 'sketchy: "we've seen the Figma file once"', making clear that engineers lack time while designers lack training.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Chi-Square and Fisher's Exact Tests
