origin: Karl Pearson (1900); R. A. Fisher (1922, 1935)
summary: Tests whether categorical outcomes differ across groups, such as preference by device or success by design.
description: The chi-square test compares observed counts in a contingency table with the counts expected if the variables were unrelated. Fisher's exact test computes the exact probability for small tables. Bruce and Bruce present a resampling approach that shuffles labels to build the null distribution directly, which makes the logic intuitive. For 2×2 tables Sauro and Lewis recommend the N-1 chi-square over both the classic test and Fisher's test; for larger tables the standard chi-square applies when expected counts are adequate.
steps: Build the contingency table of counts.
Check expected counts; for small 2×2 tables use the N-1 variant, for tiny tables use Fisher's exact test.
Compute the statistic and p-value (or simulate by permutation).
Inspect standardised residuals to see which cells drive the result.
Report counts, percentages and an effect size such as Cramér's V.
outputs: A test of association between categorical variables.
useWhen: Comparing preferences, choices or success across several groups.
avoidWhen: Paired data (use McNemar) or ordinal outcomes where order matters (use ordinal regression).
whyLost: Not lost; frequently misapplied to small samples or paired data.
whereToUse: Preference tests, card-sort agreement, survey categorical items.
example: Preference for three icon sets differs by age band (χ² = 14.2, p = 0.007); residuals show older users strongly favour labelled icons.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Performance Analysis of the CHAID Algorithm for Accuracy (Yang et al., 2023)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 3; Sauro & Lewis (2016), chapter 5.

name: Child Comprehension Tasks: Act-Out, Direction-Following and Picture-Choice
origin: Adapted for UX from developmental psycholinguistics, as reviewed by McDaniel et al. (1996) and presented in Berko Gleason and Bernstein Ratner, The Development of Language
summary: Test whether a child understands a spoken expression by having them act it out with toys, carry it out as an instruction, or choose the matching picture.
description: Three classic ways to measure what children understand rather than what they say. In act-out tasks the child uses toys to enact a sentence, such as making the girl kiss the duck; in direction tasks the child carries out an instruction or answers a question; in picture-choice tasks the child selects, from an array including foils, the picture that best matches an expression (the select-or-point method for single words). Sentences are written to contrast the structure of interest, including reversible ones where world knowledge cannot give the answer, and each response is scored as correct or as a specific error, giving accuracy per structure and an error profile. Limitations are well known: action verbs and relations are hard to picture, and very young children often do not point reliably even when their looking shows recognition, which led to preferential-looking methods. For product teams it offers a disciplined way to check children's understanding of spoken prompts and instructions.
steps: Write target sentences or prompts that contrast the structure or wording of interest, including reversible items.
Prepare toys or picture arrays containing the target and plausible foils.
Present each item in random order and ask the child to act it out, carry it out, or choose a picture.
Score each response as correct or as a specific error type.
Compute accuracy per structure or wording and inspect error patterns by age group.
For children too young to point reliably, switch to looking-time measures.
outputs: Accuracy per sentence structure or prompt wording, and a profile of error types by age.
useWhen: Checking whether children understand spoken instructions, voice-assistant prompts, game tutorials or educational content at a target age.
avoidWhen: Infants and toddlers who do not point reliably (use Looking-time paradigms (preferential looking, habituation, violation of expectation)); content that is hard to picture, such as abstract verbs and relations.
whyLost: It belongs to child language research; children's product teams test whole experiences rather than isolating comprehension of specific wording.
whereToUse: Children's voice assistants and smart toys, edtech instructions, game onboarding, health information for children.
example: A reading game's voice prompt 'Tap the bear before the rabbit' is misread by many 5-year-olds in a picture-choice task as an order of animals, not of actions. Rewording to 'First tap the bear. Then tap the rabbit' raises accuracy markedly.
reference: Berko Gleason, J. and Bernstein Ratner, N. (Eds.). The Development of Language (10th ed.). Plural Publishing; McDaniel, D., McKee, C. and Cairns, H. S. (Eds.) (1996). Methods for Assessing Children's Syntax. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.

name: Choice Architecture Optimisation for Option Sets
origin: Iyengar & Lepper, 2000; Schwartz, 2004; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008
summary: Designs the number, structure, ordering and defaults of options shown to users, testing how choice overload and decision stakes affect choice quality and satisfaction.
description: Schwartz documents the choice overload effect (Iyengar & Lepper 2000) and provides practical guidance: more options reliably reduce decision quality, increase regret, and reduce satisfaction — especially for maximizers (who always want the best) vs. satisficers (who accept 'good enough'). Applied to UX: the optimal number of options is not a universal constant but depends on user type and decision stakes.
steps: Measure choice-induced regret: after task completion with N options, ask 'How confident are you that you made the best choice?' (1–7).
Run across 3, 6, 12, and 24 options.
Plot confidence as a function of N.
The option count at which confidence peaks = the optimal set size for this user and decision type.
Also measure: did users check back or reconsider?
High reconsideration rate = choice overload signal.
outputs: Recommended option counts and groupings per context, default and ordering decisions, experimental evidence on choice quality, regret and conversion.
useWhen: Plan pickers, product catalogues, configuration screens, investment or insurance choices, and clinical option sets where too many or poorly structured options harm decisions.
avoidWhen: Avoid when options are few and familiar, or when ethical risk of steering is high without transparency; use neutral presentation and decision aids instead.
whyLost: Choice overload became a slogan ('fewer options') rather than a tested design variable, and replication debates made teams wary of applying it rigorously.
whereToUse: Pricing tier design, settings page organization, filter and facet design, onboarding option sets, feature comparison tables.
example: An insurer tests showing 3, 6 or 12 health plans with a recommended default; 6 grouped plans with a comparison table produce the highest satisfaction and lowest switching in the following year.
sources: The Paradox of Choice — Barry Schwartz
The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Schwartz B (2004) The Paradox of Choice: Why More Is Less. Ecco

name: Choice paralysis detection
origin: Iyengar and Lepper's jam study (2000) and Schwartz's The Paradox of Choice (2004); moderated by Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd's meta-analysis (2010)
summary: Detects whether the number or complexity of options is causing users to defer, abandon or regret decisions, using behavioural deferral signals and controlled set-size variation.
description: Iyengar and Lepper found shoppers were about ten times more likely to buy jam from a display of 6 than of 24 flavours, but Scheibehenne and colleagues' 2010 meta-analysis of 63 conditions found a mean effect near zero with large variance. Choice overload is real only under certain moderators: no clear prior preference, options hard to compare, high complexity, time pressure and a goal of choosing quickly. Choice paralysis detection therefore does not assume overload; it tests for it. It combines log signals (deferral, dwell without selection, back-and-forth comparison, abandonment) with controlled variation of set size or structure, and checks moderators. Rigour lies in treating overload as a conditional hypothesis and measuring deferral and post-choice satisfaction, not just conversion.
steps: Define deferral behaviours in logs: leaving a choice screen without selecting, repeated toggling between options, dwell times above the 90th percentile without action, and returns to the same screen.
Plot deferral and abandonment rates against the number of options shown and option similarity across existing sessions to spot dose-response patterns.
Assess known moderators for your context: preference uncertainty, comparability of options, decision complexity and time pressure, using 5 to 8 interviews or a short survey.
Run a controlled test that varies set size (for example 4 versus 12 options) or structure (categorised versus flat, with versus without a recommendation) with random assignment.
Compare selection rate, time to decision, post-choice satisfaction and regret (a short 3 to 5 item scale) across arms.
Conclude overload only if the larger or flatter set reliably increases deferral or regret; otherwise look for other causes such as missing information or trust.
outputs: Deferral metrics by set size and structure, experimental effect sizes, moderator assessment, and recommendations on set size, categorisation and recommended defaults.
useWhen: Users stall on plan pickers, catalogues, configuration screens or clinical option lists; teams debate cutting options without evidence.
avoidWhen: Users are experts with strong preferences who benefit from breadth, or traffic is too low for controlled variation; use moderated observation and interviews instead.
whyLost: The jam study became a design platitude ('fewer options are better') while the failed replications and moderator findings never reached practice, so overload is asserted rather than detected.
whereToUse: E-commerce category pages, pension and investment fund menus, insurance plan selection, triage and clinical decision support, AI model or template pickers.
example: A pension app offered 38 funds and saw 62% of new members defer the investment choice. A test of a 5-option tiered menu with a recommended default reduced deferral to 21% without lowering satisfaction, confirming overload under high preference uncertainty.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Scheibehenne, B., Greifeneder, R., & Todd, P. M. (2010). Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409–425; Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995–1006.

name: Choking Under Pressure Paradigm
donor: Cognitive and sport psychology (skill and attention research)
origin: Baumeister (1984); Beilock and Carr (2001); Beilock, Carr, MacMahon and Starkes (2002); Gray (2004); Masters's reinvestment theory (1992); reviewed by Beilock and Gray in Chapter 19 of the Handbook
summary: Induces realistic performance pressure and compares performance under a skill-focused secondary task with an unrelated dual task, to find out whether a skill is automated and how pressure breaks it.
description: Laboratory choking studies build pressure from several sources at once: a monetary incentive, peer pressure (a partner's reward depends on you, and the partner has supposedly already succeeded) and social evaluation (being filmed for experts to review). Manipulation checks confirm that pressure was felt, using state anxiety, rated importance and reported thoughts. To find the mechanism, the paradigm compares two secondary tasks. In the skill-focused condition the person attends to a part of their own execution (for example, which side of the foot last touched the ball). In the dual-task condition they monitor something unrelated, such as tones. Experts are harmed by skill focus but not by the distraction, while novices show the opposite, because expert skill runs as proceduralised units that break down when attended to. Under pressure, experts shift attention inward. For UX this matters in two ways. It tests whether expert users' fast interactions (keyboard shortcuts, game controls, clinical order entry) are automated and fragile under pressure. It also warns that asking experts to narrate step by step during testing can itself degrade their performance.
steps: Choose a well-practised interaction and recruit novices and experienced users.
Establish baseline performance under low pressure.
Run a skill-focused condition (attend to a component of one's own actions) and an unrelated dual-task condition, counterbalanced.
Introduce a combined pressure manipulation (incentive, partner dependence, being recorded for review) for a randomised group.
Check the manipulation with anxiety, importance and thought reports.
Compare performance by expertise, attention condition and pressure, and inspect fine-grained timing or error data.
Use findings to shape interfaces and training for high-stakes moments, and to choose think-aloud or silent protocols for expert testing.
outputs: Performance and error changes under pressure and attention manipulations by expertise level, showing whether skills are automated and how pressure degrades them.
useWhen: Expert users perform fast, practised interactions in high-stakes moments, or you need to decide whether concurrent verbalisation will distort expert performance in a study.
avoidWhen: Users are all novices on new tasks, or ethical limits rule out inducing pressure.
whyLost: HCI studies pressure mainly as time limits and workload; the attention-focus and pressure-induction designs from skill research are little known outside psychology.
whereToUse: Clinical order entry, air traffic and dispatch tools, trading terminals, competitive games, professional keyboard-driven software, live production tools.
example: A trading platform tests its order ticket with veteran traders. Under a recorded, incentive-linked session, traders asked to monitor their own keystrokes make more entry errors, while an unrelated tone task has little effect; the team avoids adding confirmation steps that force step-by-step attention and instead adds a post-entry review panel.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Beilock, S. L. and Gray, R. (2007) 'Why do athletes choke under pressure?', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 19. Also Chapter 11 (Abernethy, Maxwell, Masters, van der Kamp and Jackson).

name: Choosing a Resemblance Coefficient for Clustering
aka: Choosing a resemblance coefficient by sensitivity to profile shifts and toy-matrix calibration
Euclidean, cosine, correlation, Canberra, Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, simple matching
origin: H. Charles Romesburg (1984); coefficients from Sneath and Sokal (1973), Penrose (1953), Jaccard and others
summary: Select the similarity or distance measure for clustering by deciding which profile differences should count, then confirm the choice on small toy matrices whose right answer you can judge.
description: Distance and similarity coefficients differ in what they ignore. Euclidean distance ignores nothing; Penrose's shape difference ignores additive shifts; cosine ignores proportional shifts; Pearson correlation ignores both but treats mirror images as opposites; Canberra weights attributes equally; Bray-Curtis is dominated by large values. For binary data the decision is whether shared absences (0-0 matches) are evidence of similarity: Jaccard and Sorensen exclude them, simple matching includes them. Romesburg's procedure is to decide from the research goal whether level and size differences matter, shortlist coefficients with the right sensitivities, build small made-up matrices representing plausible outcomes, judge by intuition which objects should group, and keep the coefficient that agrees. He warns that several coefficients are monotonically related, so obtaining the same tree from them is no confirmation.
steps: State whether differences in overall level or size between profiles are meaningful for the research goal.
For binary data, decide whether shared absence of a feature should count as similarity.
Shortlist coefficients with the required sensitivities (for example cosine to ignore proportional shifts, Jaccard to exclude 0-0 matches).
Drop attributes that never vary and use Jaccard-type coefficients for dummy-coded multistate attributes.
Build several small toy matrices of plausible outcomes and decide by intuition which objects belong together.
Compute each shortlisted coefficient on the toy matrices and keep the one whose grouping matches; use average Euclidean distance when values are missing.
outputs: A justified choice of resemblance coefficient with its rationale and toy-matrix evidence.
useWhen: Before clustering card-sort co-occurrences, feature-usage profiles, survey responses or behavioural segments, when software defaults would otherwise decide the outcome.
avoidWhen: Avoid agonising when variables are standardised and coefficients are monotonic transforms of each other. For mixed numeric and categorical data use Gower's Distance for Mixed-Data Clustering; for checking the resulting clusters use Silhouette scores and gap statistic validation.
whyLost: Clustering in UX is run through tools with fixed defaults, so the choice of coefficient is invisible and rarely argued.
whereToUse: Behavioural segmentation, card sort analysis, persona clustering from survey data, feature co-usage analysis.
example: A SaaS team clusters accounts by feature usage counts. Heavy and light users of the same features should group together, so a toy matrix shows Euclidean distance splits them by volume while cosine groups them by mix; the team adopts cosine.
reference: Romesburg, H. C. (1984). Cluster Analysis for Researchers. Belmont, CA: Lifetime Learning Publications, pp. 93-118, 141-169.

name: Chunking effectiveness measurement
origin: George Miller (1956) and Nelson Cowan (2001) on memory capacity; codified for design in Lidwell, Holden and Butler (2003)
summary: Designs and tests information grouping and staged disclosure based on working-memory evidence, adjusting chunk size and disclosure depth to users' expertise.
description: Chunking is the grouping of information into meaningful units so that more can be held and processed; progressive disclosure staggers information so only what is needed now is shown. In UX both survive as slogans, notably the misapplied '7 plus or minus 2' rule for menus. The empirical application restores what the evidence says: working memory holds about four chunks (Cowan) rather than seven, chunk size depends on expertise because experts recognise larger meaningful units, and chunking matters for material that must be remembered, not for visible items users can scan. The method analyses which information users must hold in mind, groups it into meaningful units, defines disclosure levels by task frequency, and tests recall, error rate and time across variants for novices and experts separately.
steps: Audit every multi-item display: how many items are in each visual group?
Measure chunking effectiveness: test recall of chunked vs. non-chunked versions (target: chunked version produces ≥30% better recall at 5 minutes).
For expert users: increase chunk size — experts' larger schemas allow larger chunks.
For novices: reduce chunk size and increase visual separation.
outputs: Memory-load analysis of tasks, chunking scheme and disclosure levels, comparative recall, error and time data by expertise group.
useWhen: Complex forms, configuration screens, onboarding, data-dense dashboards and any interface where users must retain information across steps.
avoidWhen: When applied to scannable menus and lists where everything stays visible (memory limits do not apply), or as a reason to arbitrarily cap items at seven.
whyLost: Miller's 7 plus or minus 2 became a design myth, applied to visible menus rather than memory, while the newer evidence on four-chunk capacity and expertise effects never replaced it in practice.
whereToUse: Navigation design, settings page organization, dashboard layout, onboarding flow segmentation.
example: A broker's account-opening flow asks users to remember a 16-digit reference across screens. Chunking it as 4-4-4-4 and carrying it forward visibly cuts transcription errors from 9% to 2% among novice investors.
sources: Universal Principles of Design — William Lidwell
Miller, The magical number seven, plus or minus two (Psychological Review, 1956)
Cowan, The magical number 4 in short-term memory (Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2001)
Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience

name: Claims Analysis
donor: HCI design rationale and cognitive psychology
origin: John M. Carroll & Mary Beth Rosson, 1992
summary: Identifies the psychological claims, the upsides and downsides, that a design feature makes about users, and traces them to outcomes in usage scenarios.
description: Claims analysis is a design rationale technique from scenario-based design. For each key feature of a design, the analyst writes a claim describing the feature together with its hypothesised positive and negative psychological consequences for users, for example 'animated tutorial: + shows the task in context, - may be hard to follow at the user's own pace'. Claims are derived by walking through usage scenarios and asking questions grounded in Norman's stages of action. They make design trade-offs explicit, connect design decisions to psychological theory, and can be reused across projects as a body of design knowledge. Rigour comes from grounding claims in specific scenarios, stating both upsides and downsides, linking claims to evidence or theory, and testing important claims with users.
steps: Write usage scenarios that describe realistic user goals and activities with the design.
Walk through each scenario, identifying the features that most affect user experience.
For each feature, write a claim stating its hypothesised upsides and downsides for users.
Ground each claim in theory or evidence, such as Norman's stages of action or prior studies.
Review claims as a team to identify trade-offs and design alternatives.
Test the most consequential claims in usability sessions and update the claims library.
outputs: A set of claims with upsides and downsides per feature, documented design trade-offs and a reusable claims library.
useWhen: For scenario-based design, making trade-offs explicit in early design, documenting design rationale and teaching design reasoning.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need empirical evidence of user behaviour; claims are hypotheses. Use usability testing or experiments to confirm them.
whyLost: Extinct: Academic origin; complex to apply; practitioner knowledge base has largely dissolved.
whereToUse: Scenario-based design research; evaluating design tradeoffs with psychological grounding.
example: An AI assistant team writes a claim for 'auto-applied suggestions': it saves effort but may reduce user awareness of changes. Testing confirms users miss edits, so suggestions become reviewable diffs.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Carroll JM & Rosson MB (1992) Getting around the task-artifact cycle. ACM TOIS 10(2)

reference: Carroll, J. M. & Rosson, M. B. (1992). Getting around the task-artifact cycle: How to make claims and design by scenario. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 10(2), 181-212.

name: Classical Item Analysis: Difficulty and Discrimination Indices
origin: Truman Kelley, 1939; Robert Ebel, 1966; Anne Anastasi
summary: Try out a draft test or scale, compute each item's difficulty and its power to separate high and low total scorers, and keep the items that discriminate best.
description: Classical item analysis prunes a surplus pool of draft items using tryout data. After expert review, the preliminary form goes to a representative tryout sample, respondents are ranked by total score, and upper and lower groups are formed: the top and bottom 27% (Kelley), or thirds or quarters (Ebel). Difficulty is the percentage answering correctly; in achievement tests items answered correctly by under about 33% or over about 67% are usually dropped. Discrimination is (U - L) divided by the size of one group, where U and L are the numbers in each group answering correctly or endorsing the item. Items above a critical value are retained (.40 is often cited as very good, though thresholds vary). Item-total correlations serve the same purpose for rating scales. Qualitative review, reliability, validity and norms follow before the final form is assembled. Small samples give unstable indices, and difficulty is rarely relevant for attitude scales.
steps: Draft surplus items and review them with experts.
Administer the preliminary form to a representative tryout sample.
Score and rank respondents by total score.
Form upper and lower groups (top and bottom 27%, or thirds or quarters).
Compute each item's difficulty (proportion correct or endorsing) and discrimination index (U - L)/n, or item-total correlations for rating items.
Rank items and reject those below the critical discrimination level or outside the target difficulty range.
Review retained items qualitatively, assemble the final form, and establish reliability, validity and norms.
outputs: An item statistics table (difficulty, discrimination) and a pruned final form.
useWhen: Building knowledge checks, comprehension tests, competency assessments or new rating scales where you start with more items than you need.
avoidWhen: Small tryout samples (under about 100), where indices are unstable; validated standard scales that must not be altered. For adaptive or calibrated item banks, use item response theory.
whyLost: UX researchers usually adopt existing questionnaires or write a few items without tryout, so item pruning by discrimination is rarely done outside education.
whereToUse: Onboarding knowledge checks, security awareness quizzes, AI literacy measures, product comprehension tests and new UX attitude scales.
example: A health app drafts 30 items testing understanding of medication instructions and tries them on 200 users. Twelve items with discrimination below .30 are dropped, including two that nearly everyone answers correctly, leaving an 18-item comprehension check.
sources: Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
How to Develop a Good Survey Scale in Quantitative UX Research? (Zhaoyang, 2024)
reference: Mangal, S. K., & Mangal, S. (2013). Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences. New Delhi: PHI Learning.

name: Classifier Evaluation (Confusion Matrix, Precision, Recall, ROC, Lift)
origin: Signal detection theory (1950s) and information retrieval (1960s); standard in machine learning
summary: Measures how well a classifier, human coder or AI feature sorts things correctly, and what kinds of mistakes it makes.
description: Accuracy alone hides the errors that matter. A confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives. Precision says how many flagged items were right; recall says how many of the real items were caught; specificity covers the negatives. The ROC curve shows the trade-off across thresholds and AUC summarises it. Lift shows how much better than random the top-ranked cases are. For UX researchers these are essential when evaluating AI features (does the spam filter or recommendation help users?), auto-coding tools, and screening questions in recruitment.
steps: Collect ground-truth labels for a test set.
Build the confusion matrix at the chosen threshold.
Compute precision, recall, specificity and F1.
Plot ROC and precision-recall curves and compute AUC.
Choose thresholds based on the user cost of each error type, not on accuracy.
outputs: A profile of a classifier's errors and a justified operating threshold.
useWhen: Evaluating AI features, automated coding, fraud and spam filters, or screener questions.
avoidWhen: There is no reliable ground truth.
whyLost: UX evaluates AI features by satisfaction and task success but rarely by error profile, even though error types drive trust.
whereToUse: AI product evaluation, research ops tooling, content moderation UX.
example: An AI meeting-notes feature has 92% precision but 61% recall for action items; users trust what it shows but miss many tasks, so the UI adds a "check for missed items" prompt.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
Methods for Applying Predictive Modeling to Survey Data (Yih, 2024)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)

Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 5.

name: Clinical Decision Analysis (Decision Trees)
origin: Howard Raiffa (Decision Analysis, 1968); Milton Weinstein and Harvey Fineberg (Clinical Decision Analysis, 1980)
summary: Models a decision as a tree of choices, chance events with probabilities and outcomes with values, and computes expected values with sensitivity analysis.
description: Decision trees make uncertainty explicit: decision nodes, chance nodes with probabilities (from data or calibrated judgement) and terminal outcomes with values or utilities. Folding back the tree computes expected values; one- and two-way sensitivity analyses and threshold analysis show which parameters could change the decision; probabilistic sensitivity analysis via Monte Carlo propagates uncertainty. Clinical medicine uses this for test-or-treat decisions, which map neatly onto UX questions like whether to add a confirmation step (test) versus allow and offer undo (treat), or whether to show an AI warning given false-positive rates.
steps: Frame the decision, alternatives, time horizon and outcome metric.
Draw the tree with decision and chance nodes, using realistic event sequences.
Estimate probabilities from logs, research or calibrated experts, and values for outcomes.
Fold back to compute expected values for each alternative.
Run one-way, threshold and probabilistic sensitivity analyses.
Present the decision, its robustness and the parameters worth researching further.
outputs: Decision tree, expected values, sensitivity and threshold analyses and recommended choice.
useWhen: Design decisions under uncertainty with identifiable probabilities and consequences, such as safeguards, warnings and verification steps.
avoidWhen: Decisions with poorly defined alternatives or outcomes; start with VFT or qualitative research.
whyLost: UX debates such choices qualitatively; decision modelling is taught in medicine and business schools.
whereToUse: Fraud and security friction, AI warning thresholds, confirmation dialogs, health app triage.
example: A bank models whether to add a step-up verification for new payees. With fraud probability 0.3%, loss $2,000 and abandonment cost of $1.20 per prompted user, the threshold analysis shows verification pays only for transfers above $400.
sources: Hunink et al., Decision Making in Health and Medicine (2nd ed., 2014)
Raiffa, Decision Analysis: Introductory Lectures on Choices under Uncertainty (1968)
Four Ways to do Project Analysis (Crawford, n.d.)
Scenario Analysis, Decision Trees and Simulation for Cost Benefit Analysis of Cargo Screening Processes (Sherman et al., 2010)
reference: Hunink, M. G. M., et al. (2014). Decision Making in Health and Medicine (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

name: Closed-Loop Customer Feedback
origin: Enterprise Rent-A-Car ESQi process from 1994 (Andy Taylor); generalised by Fred Reichheld, Bain and the NPS Loyalty Forum
summary: Route each identified survey response to the person who served the customer, call detractors quickly to diagnose and fix the cause, and escalate recurring causes to process and product owners.
description: The operating core of the Net Promoter system. Short identified surveys follow transactions; dissatisfied customers are asked for permission to call (over 90% agree at Enterprise). Alerts with transaction and customer details go to the responsible branch or team, and managers call, apologise, probe the root cause and resolve, aiming to reach every detractor within 24 hours. The survey vendor should not diagnose root causes. Feedback sets the agenda of the next morning's team huddle and weekly meetings; recorded calls and verbatims are played back to staff; patterns go to middle managers for process redesign and to executives for strategy. Low-scoring firms can phase it in, celebrating 10s first and calling zeros before other detractors. The return can be measured: contacted detractors at Apple bought substantially more over two years. Later practice calls these the inner and outer loops, terms the book does not use.
steps: Define transactional triggers and sampling rules for identified surveys.
Ask the recommend question, the reason for the score, and permission to call back.
Route alerts with transaction context to the responsible manager, including alerts on drops of 2 or more points.
Call detractors within 24-48 hours: apologise, diagnose the root cause and resolve it; record cause and action.
Review feedback at daily huddles and weekly meetings, playing back customer voices.
Escalate recurring causes to process, product, policy and strategy owners, and report back to customers what changed.
Measure the loop's return, for example later purchases of contacted versus uncontacted detractors.
outputs: Resolved cases, root-cause records, coaching material, a prioritised list of systemic fixes, and evidence of the loop's financial return.
useWhen: Products with transactional touchpoints (support, delivery, onboarding, purchases) where front-line teams can act on individual feedback and patterns can feed the roadmap.
avoidWhen: Anonymous research where identification would bias answers, or when no one can act on alerts; survey fatigue follows if nothing changes. Identified surveys trade candour for follow-up.
whyLost: Widely practised in customer experience and support teams, usually through feedback platforms; it survives because it ties feedback to visible action, though often reduced to alert routing without root-cause escalation.
whereToUse: SaaS customer success, e-commerce delivery, fintech support, healthcare patient experience and B2B account management.
example: A SaaS company routes every detractor response from post-ticket surveys to the support lead, who calls within a day. A monthly review finds 30% of detractor calls trace to one billing export bug, which the product team fixes and announces to the affected customers.
reference: Reichheld, F., with Markey, R. (2011). The Ultimate Question 2.0: How Net Promoter Companies Thrive in a Customer-Driven World (rev. and expanded ed.). Boston: Harvard Business Review Press.

name: Cloze Probability Norming
aka: Cloze probability norming of word and note predictability
Cloze norming of sentence constraint and word predictability
origin: Wilson Taylor (1953) cloze procedure; predictability norming in ERP and eye-movement research (Kutas and Hillyard, 1984)
summary: A norming sample completes text fragments with the next word; the share giving each word is its cloze probability, quantifying what people expect next.
description: Cloze probability is the proportion of people who supply a given word as the continuation of a fragment; the top answer's share defines how constraining the context is. Psycholinguists use it to build and control stimuli: predictable targets are skipped more often and fixated more briefly in eye-tracked reading, and low-cloze continuations produce a larger N400 brain response, for which cloze is the best single predictor. Contexts are commonly split into high and low constraint at around 40%. The same logic extends to music, where listeners sing the expected next note. The rigour lies in a separate norming sample from the test sample and in population-specific norms. For UX, cloze norming offers a quantitative way to measure what label, word or next step users expect in microcopy, menus, autocomplete, search suggestions or voice replies.
steps: Write context fragments ending just before the target word or step, including predictable and unpredictable versions where you are building stimuli.
Give the fragments to a norming sample, each person supplying the first word or option that comes to mind.
Tabulate completions, normalising spelling and obvious synonyms by a stated rule.
Compute each continuation's cloze probability as the proportion of respondents giving it, and each fragment's constraint as the top answer's share.
Classify fragments as high or low constraint (for example at a 40% threshold).
Use the normed items with a different sample for reading, eye-tracking or interface tests, and compare behaviour by predictability.
outputs: Cloze probabilities per candidate word, constraint levels per fragment, and normed stimuli or expected labels.
useWhen: You need to quantify which word, label or next action users expect in a given context, or to control predictability in a reading or language experiment.
avoidWhen: You need to know whether users understand or prefer a label in real use; follow with tree testing, first-click tests or A/B tests. Norms do not transfer across populations.
whyLost: It is a stimulus-control tool in psycholinguistics, and UX measures label expectations with card sorting and surveys instead.
whereToUse: Microcopy and button labels, navigation terms, search autocomplete, conversational AI responses and localisation.
example: A banking app team gives 200 users the fragment 'To move money between your own accounts, tap ...'. 'Transfer' reaches a cloze probability of 0.68 while the current label 'Move' gets 0.05, supporting a rename.
reference: Taylor, W. L. (1953). 'Cloze procedure': A new tool for measuring readability. Journalism Quarterly, 30(4), 415-433.

name: Cluster Analysis
origin: Robert Tryon, 1939; k-means by MacQueen, 1967; Ward's method, 1963
summary: Groups users or observations into homogeneous segments based on similarity across variables, used for behavioural segmentation and data-driven personas.
description: Cluster analysis is a family of unsupervised techniques that partition observations into groups whose members are more similar to each other than to members of other groups. Common methods include k-means, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture models and density-based approaches. In UX it supports segmentation from behavioural logs or survey responses and provides quantitative grounding for personas. Results depend heavily on choices: which variables, how they are scaled, the distance measure, the algorithm and the number of clusters. Rigour comes from theory-driven variable selection, standardisation, comparing solutions with internal validity indices such as silhouette scores, testing stability with resampling or split halves, and checking that clusters differ meaningfully on external variables not used in clustering.
steps: Define the purpose of segmentation and select variables that relate to it.
Clean data, handle missing values and standardise variables.
Reduce dimensionality or remove highly correlated variables if needed.
Run one or more algorithms and compare solutions with different numbers of clusters using silhouette, elbow or information criteria.
Test stability by re-running on random subsamples or split halves.
Profile clusters on clustering and external variables and name them.
Validate usefulness with stakeholders and qualitative research before building personas or targeting.
outputs: Cluster assignments, cluster profiles, validity and stability metrics, and segment descriptions for personas or targeting.
useWhen: For user segmentation from behavioural or survey data, data-driven persona development and identifying distinct usage patterns.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you have predefined groups to compare (use group comparisons) or very few observations; avoid treating clusters as real types without stability checks.
whyLost: Still in use: Core data science technique; widely used in product analytics for segmentation.
whereToUse: User segmentation; behavioral clustering; persona generation from data.
example: A music streaming service clusters 200,000 users on listening behaviour and finds five stable segments, including 'background workers' who stream long sessions with skips disabled. Interviews confirm the segment and inspire a focus mode.
sources: Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
