avoidWhen: Usability problems with no behavioural target, where standard usability methods are better.
whyLost: UX imported behavioural design via popular nudge books and the Fogg model, while the more systematic implementation-science framework stayed in health research.
whereToUse: Digital health and therapeutics, savings apps, sustainability features, workplace safety tools.
example: A medication adherence app diagnoses that missed doses stem from automatic motivation and physical opportunity (pills not visible), not knowledge. It drops educational content and adds habit-stacking prompts (BCT 8.3) and refill logistics.
sources: Michie, van Stralen & West, The behaviour change wheel (2011), Implementation Science
Michie, Atkins & West, The Behaviour Change Wheel: A Guide to Designing Interventions (2014)
Michie et al., The behavior change technique taxonomy (v1) of 93 hierarchically clustered techniques (2013), Annals of Behavioral Medicine
reference: Michie, S., van Stralen, M. M., & West, R. (2011). Implementation Science, 6, 42.

name: Common Industry Format (CIF) Usability Report
origin: US NIST Industry Usability Reporting project, from 1997; ANSI/INCITS 354-2001; ISO/IEC 25062:2006
summary: A standard format for summative usability test reports, covering product, participants, context, tasks and effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction results, so purchasers can compare products.
description: In 1997 NIST convened software makers and large purchasers to agree how summative usability results should be reported so customers could compare products. The resulting Common Industry Format became ANSI/INCITS 354 and then ISO/IEC 25062. A CIF report describes the product, test objectives, participants (numbers and characteristics), context of use and environment, tasks and procedure in enough detail for replication, and reports effectiveness (completion rates, errors), efficiency (task time and its ratio to completion) and satisfaction (a standard questionnaire) with variability. The format turns usability from opinion into evidence that contracts and procurement can rely on. A separate effort produced guidance for formative reports. The authors stress the general principles behind it: know who will read the report and keep it concrete.
steps: Run a summative test with defined tasks and representative participants, typically at least 8 per user group.
Describe the product, test objectives, participants, context of use and test environment.
Describe tasks, procedure, instructions and measures in replicable detail.
Report effectiveness (completion rate, errors), efficiency (time on task, completion per unit time) and satisfaction (standard questionnaire) per task, with variability.
Add an executive summary written for purchasers and managers, keeping all statements concrete.
Archive raw data so results can be audited or compared with later releases.
outputs: A standard-format summative report comparable across products, vendors and releases.
useWhen: Procurement, regulatory submissions, vendor comparisons and formal acceptance testing where results must be auditable and comparable.
avoidWhen: Formative, iterative testing where a short problem-focused report serves better; the CIF is summative only.
whyLost: Agile product teams rarely run formal summative tests; the format survives in regulated domains such as electronic health record certification and government procurement.
whereToUse: Health IT safety-enhanced design submissions, medical devices, public-sector procurement and enterprise vendor selection.
example: A hospital group comparing two e-prescribing systems requires each vendor to submit a CIF report on ten core tasks. The standard reporting exposes that one vendor used only internal staff as participants.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: ISO/IEC 25062:2006 Software engineering: Software product Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE): Common Industry Format (CIF) for usability test reports. Geneva: ISO.

name: Communalities interpretation
origin: Thurstone's multiple factor analysis, 1930s-1947
summary: Reading how much of each survey item's variance is explained by the retained factors, to identify weak items and judge whether the factor solution is adequate.
description: An item's communality (h squared) is the proportion of its variance accounted for by the common factors; the remainder is unique variance (specific variance plus error). Initial communalities in principal axis factoring are squared multiple correlations; extraction communalities reflect the final solution. Low communalities (commonly below about 0.40, and certainly below 0.20) suggest the item is unrelated to the other items, poorly worded or measuring something else. Communalities above 1 (Heywood cases) signal a misspecified solution. MacCallum et al. (1999) showed that high communalities reduce the sample size needed for stable solutions, so they also inform design. Rigour comes from reading communalities alongside loadings and content, not mechanically deleting items.
steps: Request initial and extraction communalities in the EFA output.
Flag items with extraction communalities below about 0.40 and treat those below 0.20 as strong candidates for removal.
Investigate any communality at or above 1.0 as a Heywood case and revisit the number of factors or extraction method.
Review flagged items' wording and content coverage before deleting; a low communality can mean a unique but important facet.
Remove items one at a time and re-run, monitoring changes in other communalities and loadings.
Report mean communality; with averages above about 0.60, smaller samples (around 100-200) can give stable solutions.
outputs: Item communality table, a list of weak items with decisions and an assessment of solution adequacy.
useWhen: During EFA of UX attitude scales and when trimming long questionnaires.
avoidWhen: Not used for formative indices (where items are not expected to correlate) or for single-item measures.
whyLost: A technical step of factor analysis that is invisible to those who never run EFA, which describes most UX practice.
whereToUse: Scale development and adaptation for AI trust, financial confidence and satisfaction instruments.
example: In a 20-item AI assistant trust scale, the item 'The assistant is fun to use' has a communality of 0.14. On review it measures enjoyment rather than trust, so it moves to a separate engagement scale.
sources: RELIABILITY procedures; syntax automation; parallel analysis via Python plugin
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
MacCallum, R. C. et al. (1999) Sample size in factor analysis. Psychological Methods
Fabrigar, L. R. & Wegener, D. T. (2012) Exploratory Factor Analysis
The Inquiry Series, C7 — SPSS for Survey Analysis — EFA, Reliability & Scale Validation
reference: MacCallum, R. C., Widaman, K. F., Zhang, S. & Hong, S. (1999) Sample size in factor analysis. Psychological Methods 4(1)

name: Communicative Temptation Task
aka: Structured elicitation of requests and rejections
origin: Casby and Cumpata (1986) for requests; Olswang, Kriegsmann and Mastergeorge (1982-1983) for rejection
summary: Stage a situation that tempts a participant to communicate, such as a desirable item they cannot reach, and observe how they signal requests or refusals.
description: This is structured observation: the situation is arranged so that the behaviour of interest becomes likely, in contrast to low-structured observation of natural play. In the request version an attractive toy is sealed in a transparent container the child cannot open. A child not yet communicating intentionally bangs and fusses; a preverbal communicator hands it to the adult, makes eye contact, points or vocalises, and persists. Rejection is elicited by offering a less-desirable item while preferred ones are visible but out of reach. Coding adult-directed behaviours (giving, eye contact, pointing, vocalising, persistence) reveals whether and how a participant communicates intent before or without speech. It is used in research and in clinical evaluation, and suits product research with users who cannot be interviewed.
steps: Decide which communicative act to elicit: request, rejection or both.
Set up the temptation: a desirable item in a container the participant cannot open, or an unwanted item offered while preferred ones are visible but out of reach.
Brief the adult partner to wait and not anticipate the participant's needs.
Observe live or record on video from an angle that captures gaze and gestures.
Code adult-directed behaviours: giving, eye contact, pointing, vocalising and persistence, with two coders for reliability.
Summarise the forms of intentional communication observed for each participant.
outputs: Presence, frequency and form of intentional communicative acts for each participant.
useWhen: Research with pre-verbal toddlers or non-speaking users, including people using augmentative and alternative communication, where interviews and think-aloud are impossible.
avoidWhen: Avoid with verbal participants who can be interviewed or tested directly; for open-ended observation of natural behaviour use ethogram-based focal sampling. Ensure the provocation is gentle and ethically approved.
whyLost: It belongs to speech-language pathology and child development research, and UX teams designing for these groups rarely know structured elicitation procedures.
whereToUse: AAC devices and apps, toys and early-learning products, assistive technology for autistic or non-speaking users.
example: Designers of an AAC tablet place a favourite snack in a clear box and record how six non-speaking children request it. Most reach for the adult's hand rather than the device, so the team tests a mode where touching the device near the adult triggers speech.
reference: Casby, M. W. and Cumpata, J. F. (1986). A protocol for the assessment of prelinguistic intentional communication. Journal of Communication Disorders, 19, 251-260; Gleason, J. B. and Ratner, N. B. (Eds.) (2022). The Development of Language (10th ed.). San Diego: Plural, ch. 2.

name: Community Attribute 2x2 Mapping
origin: Jon Kolko (2014)
summary: A team diagramming practice that plots user communities on 2x2 grids of factual and emotional attributes to find white space and gaps in research.
description: After research has identified user communities or segments, the team lists factual attributes (population size, cost, equipment, time commitment, age) and emotional attributes (stigma of joining, perceived ease, introspection, anxiety, body image) by asking what differentiates one group from another. A blank 2x2 is drawn with one attribute per axis and communities are placed approximately relative to one another. White space may signal an opportunity or simply a space with no upside, and uncertainty about where to place a community is itself a finding that calls for research. The team repeats the exercise with other attribute pairs and discusses what each diagram means. Kolko frames these as thinking tools, not answers.
steps: List the community segments identified in research.
List factual and emotional attributes that differentiate them.
Draw a blank 2x2 and assign one attribute to each axis.
Place communities relative to one another, marking any whose position is uncertain as a research question.
Read white space as a possible opportunity or as no market upside, and discuss which.
Repeat with three to five other attribute pairs and compare what each diagram suggests.
outputs: Several 2x2 diagrams of communities, candidate opportunity spaces and a list of research questions.
useWhen: Use when a team has identified segments or communities and needs to see where its product could sit and what it does not yet know.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting placements as measurements: to position segments on evidence use a survey with Semantic Differential items or Correspondence analysis. Do not race through every combination of attributes.
whyLost: Positioning 2x2s are a staple of design and product strategy because they are fast, visual and provoke discussion.
whereToUse: Health and wellness, community products, marketplaces, new-category strategy.
example: A fitness start-up plots sixteen wellness communities by size against introspection and finds no large, highly introspective group served, prompting interviews with people who journal about their training.
sources: A Practical Guide to Designing with Data (Suda, 2010)
reference: Kolko, J. (2014). Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press. pp. 53-56.

name: Comparative Segmentation Study
aka: Comparative design study of alternative user segmentations
Segmentation utility test with designer pairs
origin: Janna Lynn Dupree, Richard DeVries, Daniel Berry and Edward Lank, CHI 2016
summary: Give matched designer pairs different user segmentations for the same design task and compare how each segmentation shapes their reasoning and ideas.
description: Segmentations and persona sets are usually judged by statistical fit, not by whether they help design. This study design tests their utility directly. Practitioners work in pairs on a realistic, time-boxed design task; each pair receives one of the competing segmentations, presented as the team's own research. Sessions are audio-recorded and observed, and the analysis focuses on discourse rather than design quality: whether designers identify with segments, which segments they keep or drop, and whether they propose segment-specific features. A post-task questionnaire asks pairs to assess their segmentation, then shows the alternative and asks them to compare. In the original study, pairs given Westin's privacy categories designed for one undifferentiated majority, while pairs given five behavioural clusters proposed features for specific segments.
steps: Define the competing segmentations or persona sets and prepare equivalent presentation materials for each.
Recruit practitioners with design-discussion experience and form pairs, assigning pairs to segmentations.
Set a realistic redesign task with a fixed time limit, such as 30 minutes.
Audio-record sessions and take field notes on design attributes and references to segments.
Give a post-task questionnaire on the segmentation used, then show the alternative and ask for a comparison.
Transcribe and code discourse: self-identification, segments kept or dropped, and segment-specific design ideas.
Compare conditions and report which segmentation better supports differentiated design reasoning.
outputs: A qualitative comparison of how each segmentation is used in design reasoning, plus participants' stated preferences.
useWhen: Choosing between persona sets or segmentations before rollout, or demonstrating to stakeholders that a new segmentation changes design decisions.
avoidWhen: When statistical validity of segments is the question (use Cluster Validation or Persona Validation Against Behavioural Data). Samples are tiny, so treat results as formative.
whyLost: Persona and segmentation work is rarely evaluated for downstream use at all; this design exists as a single research study.
whereToUse: Persona programmes, privacy and security settings design, marketing-to-UX segmentation handovers.
example: A health app team compares a demographic segmentation with a motivation-based one using four designer pairs each. Only the motivation-based pairs propose distinct onboarding paths, which settles the choice.
reference: Dupree, J.L., DeVries, R., Berry, D.M. and Lank, E. (2016) Privacy personas: clustering users via attitudes and behaviors toward security practices. Proceedings of CHI 2016, 5228-5239.

name: Comparative Usability Evaluation (CUE) Studies
origin: Rolf Molich and colleagues, CUE-1 to CUE-10 (from 1998); Hertzum, Molich and Jacobsen (2014)
summary: Have independent professional teams evaluate the same product or session videos and report issues, then measure how much their findings overlap.
description: CUE studies test the reproducibility of usability evaluation itself. Several teams independently evaluate one product with their usual methods, or, as in CUE-9, all watch the same session recordings, and report issues in a common format. Reports are merged into a master list of unique issues and the overlap is computed. Results have been sobering: in CUE-1 only 1 of 141 issues was found by all four teams; in CUE-2, 75% of issues were found by only one of nine teams; in CUE-9, 35 professionals watching the same five 30-minute videos reported 223 unique issues, only four reported by at least 75% of them, with 40% reported by one evaluator alone. Hertzum, Molich and Jacobsen traced this evaluator effect to human judgement in detecting, rating and reporting issues. The same design can audit an organisation's own evaluators.
steps: Recruit several independent evaluators or teams.
Give all the same product and scenario, or the same session recordings to remove differences in test sessions.
Have each report issues independently in a common format with severity ratings.
Merge reports into a master list of unique issues, matching duplicates with explicit rules.
Compute how many evaluators reported each issue and the share found by only one.
Analyse reasons for disagreement and set policies, such as using multiple evaluators for critical studies.
outputs: Overlap statistics between evaluators, lists of commonly versus singly found issues, and causes of the evaluator effect.
useWhen: Auditing the reliability of a research team's usability findings, calibrating evaluators, or deciding how many evaluators critical studies need.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a way to evaluate a product; it is expensive and measures the evaluators. For routine reliability checks on heuristic evaluation, use inter-evaluator agreement statistics.
whyLost: It is a research programme in HCI methodology; few organisations audit their own evaluators' reproducibility.
whereToUse: Large research teams, agencies, regulated domains such as medical devices where missed issues carry risk, research operations quality programmes.
example: A medical-device company has four researchers analyse the same eight summative test videos independently. Only 30% of issues overlap, so the company requires two independent analysts for every use-error review.
reference: Molich, R. (2018). Are usability evaluations reproducible? Interactions, 25(6), 82-86; Hertzum, M., Molich, R. and Jacobsen, N. E. (2014), as cited in Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience (3rd ed.), pp. 169-170.

name: Competitive Sonic Brandscape Mapping
origin: Amber Case and Aaron Day (2018), framed as standard brand practice
summary: Plotting competitors' audio logos and product sounds on two-axis matrices of dichotomous sound attributes to find positioning gaps before designing a sonic identity.
description: Before designing an audio logo or product sound set, the designer collects competitors' and reference brands' sounds and plots them on several two-axis matrices built from dichotomous descriptors: spacious or closed, resolution or tension, natural or synthetic, simple or complex, short or long, obtrusive or discreet. Plotting the same set on different pairs shows clusters and empty spaces. The team then decides whether to sit near a competitor to borrow its associations or to claim open space, and carries that position into the design brief. Competitive interview questions add context: who uses sound and why, whether those sounds are loved or hated, and whether competitors use too much or too loud sound. In the book placements are made by expert judgement; listener ratings are not part of the method.
steps: Collect competitors' and reference brands' audio logos and product sounds.
Choose two or more pairs of dichotomous attributes (for example obtrusive-discreet, natural-synthetic, simple-complex, short-long).
Place each sound on each two-axis matrix.
Read the matrices for clusters and empty spaces.
Decide whether to sit near a competitor or move into open space, noting the reasons.
Write the chosen position and descriptors into the sound design brief.
outputs: Attribute matrices of the competitive sound landscape and a positioning decision for the design brief.
useWhen: Use before commissioning an audio logo, notification set or product sound palette, when a brand needs sounds distinct from rivals.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating expert placements as how listeners hear the sounds: validate with listeners through a Semantic Differential or the MUSHRA Listening Test (ITU-R BS.1534).
whyLost: It lives in sound branding agencies and marketing; UX teams rarely own sound identity, so the practice has not crossed into mainstream UX.
whereToUse: Fintech payment confirmations, automotive, voice assistants, consumer devices, streaming and media brands.
example: A payments app plots six rival confirmation sounds on natural-synthetic by simple-complex and finds them all short, synthetic and simple, so it briefs a warmer, natural-sounding confirmation.
reference: Case, A. and Day, A. (2018). Designing with Sound: Fundamentals for Products and Services. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 86-90, 102-103.

name: Competitive UX Benchmarking
origin: Sauro, Benchmarking the User Experience (2018); MeasuringU practice
summary: Measures your product and competitors on the same tasks and metrics so you know where you stand.
description: A competitive benchmark runs identical tasks and questionnaires on two or more products. Key design choices are within-subjects (each person uses every product, which is efficient and allows direct preference questions but introduces carryover) versus between-subjects (cleaner but needing more people), and the mixed design where each participant uses their current product plus one competitor. Sauro's ten best practices include counterbalancing order, controlling for prior experience (prior users always rate a product higher), choosing tasks every product supports, and adjusting for brand attitudes. Results are reported as task and study metrics with confidence intervals and significance markers.
steps: Pick competitors and tasks that every product supports equivalently.
Choose within, between or mixed design based on sample, carryover and task length.
Counterbalance product order and record prior experience with each brand.
Collect task metrics, SUPR-Q or SUS, preference and brand attitude before and after.
Analyse with appropriate within or between tests, control for prior experience (for example weighted t-tests), and report gaps with intervals.
outputs: A scorecard showing where you lead and lag competitors, task by task.
useWhen: Setting strategy, making a business case for redesign, or after a competitor launch.
avoidWhen: Products are not truly comparable, or you cannot get legitimate access to competitor flows.
whyLost: Not lost, but frequently run informally by expert review rather than with users and statistics.
whereToUse: Travel, banking, insurance, retail, SaaS categories with a few strong rivals.
example: Four hotel booking sites are tested with 200 people each; one competitor completes "change dates" 30 points better, and its flow becomes the redesign reference.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld & Morville, 2006)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapters 2 and 13.

name: Complete UX Practitioner Curriculum
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: A proposed core curriculum restoring human factors, cognitive science, causal inference, field methods, rigorous qualitative and quantitative analysis, cross-domain methods and UX Epidemiology.
description: The treatise argues UX education has narrowed to design thinking, interviews, usability testing, IA, interaction and visual design and prototyping tools, a small fraction of the field's heritage, partly because educators teach what they know. Its proposed curriculum covers: human factors foundations (task analysis, GOMS, KLM, CPM-GOMS, anthropometrics, environmental ergonomics, UFMEA); cognitive science (full verbal protocol analysis, predictive models, repertory grid, concept mapping, SDT, NDM); causal inference (Bradford Hill, Rubin, DAGs, DiD, RDD, PSM); ethnographic and field methods (full contextual inquiry, thick description, ethnomethodology, participatory design); rigorous qualitative analysis (grounded theory, Braun and Clarke, Miles and Huberman, phenomenography, micro-phenomenology, discourse analysis); quantitative methods (multilevel modelling, Bayesian inference, IRT/Rasch, scale construction, lag sequential analysis, experimental design beyond A/B); history and theory of HCI; cross-domain methods; and UX Epidemiology.
steps: Audit the current curriculum against the proposed areas.
Prioritise areas using the Method Recovery Priority Index and programme goals.
Design modules pairing primary readings with applied exercises.
Recruit instructors from donor disciplines where needed.
Assess students on applying methods to real questions.
Review content periodically against the canon.
outputs: Curriculum map, module designs, assessment plan.
useWhen: Designing UX degrees, bootcamps, in-house academies and researcher career frameworks.
avoidWhen: Single-method training needs.
whyLost: Original proposal of the treatise.
whereToUse: Universities, corporate research academies, professional certification bodies.
example: An in-house academy adds a causal inference module and a qualitative rigour module; within a year research reports cite estimands and audit trails routinely.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lost Methods in UX treatise, Chapter 33
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 33 (A Curriculum for the Complete UX Practitioner).

name: Component and Analogous Prototyping for Physical Products
origin: Kathryn McElroy (2016), from physical computing practice
summary: Prototype each part of an electronic product separately or with a cheaper analogous part, then combine them in a series of prototypes each testing one assumption in context.
description: Smart objects and wearables fail in many places at once, so this practice breaks prototyping into controllable pieces. Before buying parts the designer writes the user flow, an if-this-then-that story of inputs and outputs and pseudocode, and draws a circuit diagram checked by someone who reads circuits. Each component (sensor, output, control) is prototyped and debugged alone before being combined, so troubleshooting is limited to the joins. Where real parts are large or costly, an analogous prototype tests the interaction first: a small dial and one LED for a wall-sized installation, or a screen mock of an LED array. Each subsequent prototype has one goal, such as whether haptic pulses are acceptable on the arm, pacing rates in daily wear, user control, materials for sport or long-term use, and is tested where and how the product will be used. Spare copies are built because fragile wiring breaks mid-session.
steps: Write the user flow and an if-this-then-that story of inputs and outputs, and turn it into pseudocode.
Draw a circuit diagram and have someone with electronics knowledge check it before buying parts.
Prototype each component (sensor, output, control) separately until it works reliably.
Where components are costly or large, test the interaction with an analogous cheaper part or a screen mock.
Combine components and debug only the transitions between them.
Give each further prototype one goal (acceptability, settings, control, materials, long-term use) and test it with users in the real environment and body position.
Build spare copies and reinforce joints before user sessions.
Carry findings into the next prototype until a full-function prototype is reached.
outputs: A series of working component and integrated prototypes, each with a stated goal and test findings.
useWhen: Use when designing connected devices, wearables, installations or any product where hardware, software and the body interact.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the question is whether the product is wanted at all; explore need first with Contextual Inquiry or Experience Prototyping. Materials and placement can only be judged in context, so pair late prototypes with Field Usability Testing or Living labs.
whyLost: It survived because physical computing platforms made component prototyping cheap, and staged, single-goal prototypes are standard in hardware product teams.
whereToUse: Wearables, smart-home devices, medical and assistive devices, interactive installations, automotive controls.
example: A haptic pacing arm-band goes through six prototypes: circuit, pulse acceptability, pacing in daily wear, user control, sports materials and long-term use. Tests show one pulse rate feels like a phone ringing and that users wear it on ankles, widening the use cases to music and therapy.
reference: McElroy, K. (2016). Prototyping for Designers: Developing the Best Digital and Physical Products. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 179-187, 202-216, 228.

name: Composite Experience Scores (qxScore, Bentley Scorecard)
origin: UserZoom qxScore (Kuldeep Kelkar and colleagues); Bentley University User Experience Center scorecard (Bill Albert and Heather Wright Karlson), reported 2022
summary: Combine behavioural task results and attitudinal ratings into a single 0-100 experience score per product, used to rank competitors and track against targets.
description: Executives want to know who won; composite scores answer with one number while keeping components visible. The qxScore gives 50% weight to task success and 50% to top-2-box percentages on the eight SUPR-Q items (ease, trust, appearance, loyalty), producing a 0-100 score per site and a colour-banded scorecard of success and attitude by task. The Bentley Experience Scorecard takes a broader view: participants choose tasks relevant to them from a short list, rate usability, design and content, brand and emotion, and weight the four attributes by personal importance, giving a weighted overall score compared with a target. Plotting average weight against average rating for each attribute shows priorities. Rigour requires fixed tasks and samples across products, confidence intervals on differences, and always reporting components alongside the composite.
steps: Define the products or versions to compare and a common task set (or, for the Bentley approach, a short list from which participants pick relevant tasks).
Run a benchmark study with adequate samples per product, for example 50 or more per site in a between-subjects unmoderated design.
Compute task success per product and attitudinal components (for qxScore, top-2-box on the eight SUPR-Q items; for Bentley, ratings on usability, design and content, brand and emotion).
For the Bentley approach, collect each participant's importance weights and compute weighted scores.
Combine components into the composite (qxScore: mean of behavioural and attitudinal components) and calculate confidence intervals.
Present the ranking with a component scorecard and, where relevant, an importance-by-rating priority plot against a target.
outputs: A composite score per product, component scorecards, rankings against competitors or targets, and an attribute priority plot.
useWhen: Competitive benchmarks, executive reporting, and tracking experience quality across releases where one headline figure is needed.
avoidWhen: Diagnosing why problems occur, or when samples are too small to separate products; weights are conventions, so pair with Single Usability Metric (SUM) or report components separately.
whyLost: It survives because benchmarking vendors and agencies sell scorecards to executives; the risk is that the fixed weightings go unquestioned.
whereToUse: Competitive e-commerce and insurance benchmarks, quarterly UX health reporting, and agency evaluations.
example: Four regional health insurer sites are benchmarked with 50 participants each on three tasks. qxScores of 76, 63, 56 and 48 give executives a ranking, while the scorecard shows the lowest site fails mainly on finding a doctor.
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022) Measuring the User Experience: Collecting, Analyzing, and Presenting UX Metrics, 3rd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 235-236 and 302-311.

name: Composite Sequence Analysis
origin: A. Michael Huberman, 1989 and 1993; described by Miles and Huberman, 1994
summary: Find the shared 'stories' in many narrated sequences by grouping cases phase by phase on theme and features, preserving order, to yield a few modal scenarios with their coverage.
description: A way to compare many individual trajectories without reducing them to variables. Informants divide their own history into phases and name them, rather than choosing from a list. Each case is condensed to a protocol of identical format and mapped as a sequence of themes with features. Within each phase, cases are grouped when the theme is identical in meaning and at least two features are shared, overlaying individual trajectories into a branching network per subgroup. Reviewing the subgroup charts yields a few modal sequences and the share of the sample each covers, with diverging cases noted. The grouping rule grows stricter phase by phase. In Huberman's study of 160 Swiss teachers in 16 subgroups, four modal sequences covered 65% of the sample. The method links case-oriented and variable-oriented analysis; condensation loses texture, and analysts may stop at the charts rather than force scenarios.
steps: Collect informant-named phases and their features for each case.
Condense each case to a protocol of identical format.
Map each trajectory as an ordered sequence of themes with features.
Within each phase, group cases whose theme matches in meaning and who share at least two features.
Draw a branching chart per subgroup showing groups and their common features.
Across charts, extract modal sequences, report the share of cases each covers, and note cases that diverge.
outputs: Composite sequence charts and named modal scenarios with their coverage of the sample.
useWhen: Many participants describe a process over time (adoption, career, illness, product use over years) and you want typical paths without losing order.
avoidWhen: Logged behavioural sequences at scale; use sequence alignment of behavioural paths instead. Small samples cannot support coverage claims.
whyLost: UX journey mapping usually produces one idealised journey rather than overlaying many narrated trajectories with explicit grouping rules and coverage figures.
whereToUse: Longitudinal adoption studies, patient journeys, professional tool careers (for example designers moving between tools), and life-event research.
example: Forty freelancers describe their history with accounting software in self-named phases. Overlay yields three modal paths, such as 'spreadsheet chaos to accountant-led setup to self-service' (35%), which become journey variants instead of a single journey map.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Compositional Data Regression via Log-Ratio Transform
aka: Compositional data regression via log-ratio transform (multivariate t)
origin: John Aitchison, 1986 (log-ratio analysis); Jonathan Katz and Gary King, 1999 (multivariate t model)
summary: Turns each observation's shares into log-ratios against a reference part, regresses them jointly, then maps predictions back to shares that respect the sum-to-one constraint.
description: Many outcomes are compositions: non-negative parts that sum to one, such as how a user's time splits across features, how a budget splits across categories, or vote shares across parties. Ordinary regression on each share separately ignores the constraint, can predict impossible values and produces spurious negative correlations. Aitchison's log-ratio approach transforms each composition into J - 1 log-ratios against a reference part (additive log-ratio) or against the geometric mean (centred log-ratio), which are unconstrained and can be modelled with multivariate regression. Katz and King found electoral log-ratios heavier tailed than a normal distribution even after covariates, so they used a multivariate t regression with estimated degrees of freedom; Jackman fits it by Bayesian MCMC. Coefficients describe effects on log-ratios, so results are interpreted by simulating predicted log-ratios and back-transforming them into shares with uncertainty. Zero parts must be handled before transforming, and results are relative to the reference part.
steps: Confirm the outcome is a composition (non-negative parts summing to one) and choose a reference part or use centred log-ratios.
Handle zero parts (replacement, amalgamation of categories, or a separate model for presence) and compute the J - 1 log-ratios.
Specify a multivariate regression for the log-ratios, using a multivariate t error if residuals are heavy tailed.
Fit by maximum likelihood or MCMC (several chains from dispersed starting values) and check convergence.
Interpret coefficients by simulating predicted log-ratios for chosen profiles and back-transforming them to shares with intervals.
Note cases excluded because a part was absent and consider how that might bias the results.
outputs: Coefficients on each log-ratio, residual scale and correlation, and predicted shares with uncertainty for chosen user profiles.
useWhen: Outcomes are shares of a whole: time allocation across app sections, spend across categories, task-time breakdowns, attention split across screen regions, or distribution of support contacts across channels.
avoidWhen: Many parts are often zero (use a hurdle or Dirichlet-multinomial approach); you care about one part alone and can model it directly; the totals, not the shares, are the outcome. Results are always relative to the reference part.
whyLost: Compositional data analysis is known in geology, ecology and political science; UX analysts usually model each share separately or ignore the constraint.
whereToUse: Time-use and attention allocation within products, budget-allocation exercises, channel mix in support or acquisition, engagement mix across features after a redesign.
example: A productivity suite models how each user's weekly time splits across email, calendar and documents. After transforming to log-ratios against email, regression shows the new calendar integration shifts about five percentage points from email to calendar for team accounts, with documents unchanged.
sources: Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
reference: Aitchison, J. (1986). The Statistical Analysis of Compositional Data. London: Chapman and Hall.

name: Compositionality audit for UI copy
donor: Philosophy of language and formal semantics
origin: Principle of compositionality attributed to Frege; Fodor's language of thought, 1975; Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988
summary: Checks whether UI labels and messages combine predictably, so that the meaning of a compound phrase follows from its parts and users can generalise across the interface.
description: Compositionality holds that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by its parts and how they are combined. Fodor argued thought itself is compositional, and systematic: anyone who understands 'save draft' and 'delete file' should understand 'delete draft'. Interface language can violate this when the same verb means different things in different contexts ('Save' commits to a record for one role but stores locally for another), when compound labels have idiosyncratic meanings, or when combinations are missing. A compositionality audit inventories verbs, objects and modifiers, builds a grid of their combinations, and checks each for consistent meaning and behaviour. Rigour comes from mapping each label to its actual system effect, not its dictionary meaning.
steps: Extract all action labels, menu items and messages and decompose them into verbs, objects and modifiers.
For each verb, list every system effect it triggers across contexts and roles.
Build a verb-by-object grid and mark combinations as consistent, inconsistent or missing.
Flag verbs with more than one distinct effect and compounds whose meaning does not follow from parts.
Test predictions with 6-10 users: show novel combinations and ask what will happen; target at least 80% correct predictions.
Define a compositional vocabulary with one effect per verb and apply it across the product.
outputs: A verb-object grid, an inconsistency list, prediction accuracy data, and a compositional UI vocabulary.
useWhen: For large products with many actions, multi-role systems, design system content guidelines, and command languages.
avoidWhen: For small, single-purpose interfaces; standard content review suffices.
whyLost: Compositionality is foundational in semantics and cognitive science but has not been framed as a UX content method.
whereToUse: Enterprise software, clinical systems, developer tools, voice commands, and AI agent instructions.
example: In a surgical system 'Save' stores a preset for surgeons, commits the record for nurses and exports logs for admins. The audit splits it into 'Save preset', 'Sign record' and 'Export logs', and novel-combination predictions rise from 55% to 90%.
sources: Fodor, J., The Language of Thought (1975)
Lakoff, G., Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 17 — Mentalese, Compositionality & the Language of Thought
reference: Fodor, J. A. & Pylyshyn, Z. W. (1988). Connectionism and cognitive architecture: a critical analysis. Cognition, 28(1-2), 3-71.

name: Comprehensive Literature Search for a Research Synthesis
origin: Patrick Wilson, 1992 (five retrieval modes); Cooper, 1985; Reed and Baxter; Rothstein and Hopewell, 2009
summary: A recall-oriented, documented search across all five retrieval modes and grey-literature sources, stopped when further searching stops yielding new relevant studies.
description: Recall and precision vary inversely, and a synthesis needs high recall. Wilson's five retrieval modes are footnote chasing, consultation, subject-index searching (natural language versus controlled vocabulary), browsing, and citation searching, including related records ranked by bibliographic coupling. Least-effort strategies are biased toward central researchers and cannot be replicated. Reed and Baxter give six steps from topic definition to final searches, with Boolean search profiles, author and forward-citation searches, and a stopping rule. Rothstein and Hopewell list grey-literature sources (dissertation and report databases, hand-searching journals and proceedings, reference lists, contacting researchers, research registers, the internet) and show that published trials report larger effects than unpublished ones, which is why grey literature matters. Every source is biased, vocabularies differ across disciplines and decades, and consultation finds unpublished work but favours insiders' views, so the search mixes modes and documents everything.
steps: Define the topic as a sentence or question after preliminary reading, and set scope, population, methods and inclusion criteria.
Harvest subject terms from known relevant papers, adding synonyms and thesaurus terms; for interventions combine problem, intervention and design concepts.
Write a search profile with Boolean AND, OR, NOT, proximity operators and truncation, and run it in several complementary databases.
Evaluate retrieved records for relevance, revise terms and run final searches, adding searches on the most prolific authors and forward citation searches.
Footnote-chase reference lists and use related-records (bibliographic coupling) features.
Search grey literature: dissertation and report databases, hand-search key journals and conference proceedings, research registers, contact researchers, and the web.
Stop when the last searches yield under about 1% new unique relevant citations, or ten hours of searching yield nothing new.
Document every source, query, date and count in a search log.
outputs: A documented set of candidate studies and a reproducible search log.
useWhen: Systematic reviews or meta-analyses of UX and HCI evidence, evidence reviews for policy or design guidance, and any desk research where missing studies would bias the conclusion.
avoidWhen: Quick orientation reading or scoping where recall is not critical; a rapid review with stated limits is cheaper.
whyLost: UX desk research is usually a least-effort search of a few sources; systematic search methods stayed with librarians and evidence-based medicine.
whereToUse: Evidence reviews on accessibility, dark patterns, AI explanation effects, health app engagement, and internal research repositories.
example: A team reviewing evidence on onboarding checklists searches ACM DL, Scopus and PsycINFO with harvested terms, chases references, hand-searches CHI and CSCW proceedings and asks vendors for unpublished experiments. It stops after two rounds add under 1% new studies and publishes the search log.
sources: The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
reference: White, H. D. Ch. 4; Reed, J. G. & Baxter, P. M. Ch. 5; Rothstein, H. R. & Hopewell, S. Ch. 6. In Cooper, H., Hedges, L. V., & Valentine, J. C. (Eds.) (2009). The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Russell Sage Foundation.

name: Computational Cognitive Modelling for UX Prediction
origin: Newell, 1990 (unified theories); O'Reilly & Munakata, 2000
summary: Builds runnable simulations of the cognitive processes users employ, predicting performance, errors and learning on a design before testing with people.
description: Computational cognitive modelling expresses hypotheses about perception, memory, attention and decision-making as runnable programs (symbolic architectures such as ACT-R and EPIC, or connectionist networks) and simulates users interacting with a design. Because the model is explicit, it yields quantitative predictions of task times, error likelihoods and learning trajectories, and it explains why a design performs as it does. In UX the method allows many variants to be screened before recruiting participants and supports decisions in domains where testing is expensive or risky. Rigour depends on grounding the model in established architecture parameters, validating predictions against at least some human data, and reporting where the model's assumptions are likely to break down, such as novel strategies or emotional states.
steps: Select the cognitive phenomenon relevant to the interface and the published or pilot human data the model must reproduce.

Choose a model class: for example spreading activation to predict which labels users will associate during navigation, drift-diffusion to predict decision time and errors across option-set sizes, reinforcement learning to predict which interaction sequences users will learn, or an architecture such as ACT-R.
Encode stimuli as feature patterns or task states, simplifying deliberately and documenting each simplification.
Fix one parameter set across all simulations, taken from prior research or found by limited search, and check that qualitative behaviour is robust to parameter changes.
Map model output to behaviour, for example activations to response probabilities with the Luce choice rule and cycles to criterion as latency.
Rerun the human study's conditions as a simulation experiment and compare the pattern of results, not exact numbers, with the human data.
Model group or design differences by changing a single parameter, and use the model's predictions to set hypotheses for the empirical study.
outputs: An executable model, predicted task times, error rates and learning curves per design variant, and a mechanistic explanation of why one design outperforms another.
useWhen: Safety-critical or high-volume interfaces where small performance differences matter, comparing many design variants cheaply, or explaining a puzzling performance pattern mechanistically.
avoidWhen: Avoid for exploratory or attitudinal questions, novel domains where cognitive processes are unknown, or teams without modelling expertise; use KLM/GOMS for simple predictions or empirical testing.
whyLost: HCI's cognitive modelling tradition (GOMS, ACT-R, EPIC) peaked in the 1990s; modelling expertise was scarce and rapid empirical testing became cheaper than building models.
whereToUse: Theoretically grounded UX research, pre-study prediction (Forward-Thinking Playbook Stage 1), cognitive modeling for safety-critical interface design.
example: An air-traffic tool team uses an ACT-R model to compare two alert-handling layouts, predicting a 400 ms advantage and fewer missed alerts for one variant before a costly simulator study confirms it.
sources: Computational Experiments in Cognitive Neuroscience — Yuko Munakata
McClelland JL, Rumelhart DE & PDP Research Group (1986) Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition, Vol. 2: Psychological and Biological Models. MIT Press
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
Computational Experiments in Cognitive Neuroscience (O'Reilly & Munakata, 2000)
reference: Munakata Y (2004) Computational cognitive neuroscience: Modelling the brain. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 8(3)

name: Computational phenotyping by model inversion
aka: Model-based data analysis and computational phenotyping by meta-Bayesian model inversion
origin: Daunizeau et al., 2010; Schwartenbeck and Friston, 2016; set out by Parr, Pezzulo and Friston, 2022
summary: Fit a generative model of decision-making to each participant's choices or eye movements to estimate personal model parameters (a computational phenotype) and compare rival explanations of behaviour.
description: The participant is assumed to act on a subjective generative model of the task. The scientist builds an objective model whose likelihood is the probability of the participant's observed actions when that subjective model, set with candidate parameters, is solved on the same stimuli, with a softmax temperature for unexplained randomness. Inverting it gives posterior estimates of each person's priors and preferences (their computational phenotype) and the evidence for alternative models. Individual estimates go to a second level with parametric empirical Bayes and Bayesian model reduction, or to association tests such as canonical variates analysis against questionnaires. Face validity is checked by simulating fictive data and identifiability by parameter recovery. Any normative model, such as reinforcement learning, can supply the likelihood. Asking whether behaviour is optimal is meaningless, since some prior always makes it so; the model is a hypothesis to compare.
steps: Collect trial-level behaviour (choices, saccades, response times) together with the exact stimuli available at each choice, plus between-person variables.
Formulate a task model (for example a POMDP or reinforcement-learning model) as a function from parameters to predicted action probabilities.
Specify the likelihood by solving the model on the real stimuli and computing the probability of the observed actions with a softmax temperature, and set priors over plausible parameter ranges.
Before real data, simulate fictive participants to check face validity and run parameter recovery to confirm parameters are identifiable.
Invert the model per participant (for example variational Laplace) to obtain posterior parameters and model evidence for rival models.
Analyse at group level with parametric empirical Bayes and Bayesian model reduction, or relate parameters to questionnaires and outcomes with association tests.
outputs: Per-person posterior parameter estimates (computational phenotypes), model evidence for rival explanations and group-level effects with credible intervals.
useWhen: When you want to explain individual differences in decision behaviour mechanistically, such as exploration versus exploitation, sensitivity to reward or uncertainty, and you have rich trial-level data.
avoidWhen: Avoid without trial-level stimulus logs, enough trials per person (often 100 or more) or modelling expertise. For descriptive segmentation use clustering; for simpler decision timing use Drift Diffusion Modelling of Decisions.
whyLost: It is new and specialist, living in computational psychiatry and neuroscience labs, and UX rarely collects trial-level data or writes generative models.
whereToUse: Recommendation and feed interaction, game design, adaptive learning, behavioural segmentation for personalisation, AI-assisted decision tools.
example: An investing app logs 200 sequential buy-or-explore decisions per beta user. A reinforcement-learning model fitted per person separates high-exploration from loss-averse users, and onboarding nudges are tailored to each parameter profile.
reference: Schwartenbeck, P., & Friston, K. (2016). Computational phenotyping in psychiatry: A worked example. eNeuro, 3(4); Parr, T., Pezzulo, G., & Friston, K. J. (2022). Active Inference. MIT Press, ch. 9.

name: Computational player modelling
aka: Computational player modelling (model-based, model-free and hybrid)
origin: Yannakakis and Togelius, 2011; Yannakakis, Spronck, Loiacono and Andre, 2013
summary: Build computational models of players' cognitive, affective and behavioural states from gameplay metrics, body signals and context, using theory-driven, data-driven or hybrid approaches.
description: Player modelling is the computational modelling of a player's cognitive, behavioural and affective states from interaction data, distinct from static profiling. Model-based (top-down) approaches start from a theory such as arousal and valence, Russell's circumplex, OCC, flow or Koster's fun, and test fit to observations. Model-free (bottom-up) approaches learn the mapping from data to annotated states by classification, regression or preference learning, or cluster when labels are absent; most practice is hybrid. Inputs include gameplay metrics, physiological signals (ECG, GSR, EEG, EMG, pupillometry, gaze, posture, face), game context and profile. Outputs come from self-report, third-person annotation or unsupervised learning. Context fusion is essential: a GSR rise after a death and after level completion mean different things. Applications are adaptive difficulty, personalised content, believable agents, playtest analysis and monetisation.
steps: Decide which player states to model: cognitive, affective or behavioural.
Choose a model-based, model-free or hybrid approach.
Collect inputs: gameplay metrics, objective bodily signals, game context and any static profile.
Obtain outputs through self-report, third-person annotation (ratings, classes or preferences) or, without labels, unsupervised clustering.
Fuse game context with signals so that states are interpreted correctly.
Train or fit the model (classification, regression, preference learning) and evaluate it on held-out players.
Use the model to adapt or analyse the game, monitoring players' responses to adaptations and correcting misjudged states.
outputs: A predictive model of player states, behavioural clusters, and inputs for adaptation or playtest analysis.
useWhen: You need to infer experience at scale from interaction data in games or other interactive systems, for adaptation or playtest analysis.
avoidWhen: You need individual-level certainty; metrics observe experience indirectly and suit populations. Physiological sensors are invasive, model-free methods find meaningless relationships, model-based ones miss features, and in-game behaviour need not reflect real-life personality.
whyLost: It is mature in game AI and affective computing research, but non-game UX rarely models user states computationally and relies on surveys.
whereToUse: Games and serious games, adaptive learning, fitness and wellbeing apps, adaptive interfaces, VR training.
example: A puzzle game trains a preference-learning model on players' pairwise rankings of levels plus gameplay metrics. The model predicts frustration and the game adapts hint timing, with a hold-out check that players' reported enjoyment rises.
reference: Yannakakis, G. N., Spronck, P., Loiacono, D., & Andre, E. (2013). Player modeling. In Artificial and Computational Intelligence in Games (Dagstuhl Follow-Ups 6, pp. 45-59).

name: Computational Thing Analysis
origin: Janlert & Stolterman, 2017
summary: Analyses interactive artefacts in terms of their 'thingness' and interactivity (states, faces, expressions) to understand how they demand attention and shape engagement.
description: Janlert and Stolterman analyse what it means for a thing to be interactive. They distinguish an artefact's internal states from its outward faces and expressions, and examine how interactivity introduces demands: interactive things invite, require and sometimes compete for attention, keeping people busy. Computational thing analysis applies this vocabulary to a product, inventorying its states and how they are expressed, the modes of interaction it supports (from operating to conversing to coexisting) and the cumulative attention load it places on users within an ecology of devices. The analysis informs choices about how much interaction a thing should demand. Rigour comes from systematic inventory and comparison of alternatives, ideally grounded with field observation of use.
steps: Character analysis of interface elements: for each significant interface element, measure:
Interactional richness — how many distinct ways can this be interacted with?
(2) Behavioral consistency — does it behave consistently across all interaction modes?
(3) Character coherence — does it have a consistent 'personality' across states?
(4) Addressability — can users directly address it, or only access it indirectly? High interactional complexity + consistent character = 'thing-ness' that feels solid and reliable.
outputs: An analysis of an artefact's states, faces and interaction modes, its demands on attention, and design alternatives with different interaction characters.
useWhen: Designing ambient, IoT, wearable and AI devices where the character of interaction and attention demands matter more than screen usability.
avoidWhen: Avoid for routine screen-based usability questions; it is an analytical framework, not an evaluative method, so pair it with field studies.
whyLost: It is recent interaction design theory read mainly in academic HCI; practice lacks time for theoretical analysis of interaction character.
whereToUse: Interface element design, design system component character design, interactive data visualization design.
example: A smart thermostat team analyses how often the device 'calls' for attention and in what states; reducing its expressive states and moving adjustments to a quiet mode lowers user irritation in a field trial.
sources: Things That Keep Us Busy — Janlert & Stolterman
User Experience (UX) meets Artificial Intelligence (AI) (Wiberg & Stolterman Bergqvist, 2022)
Things That Keep Us Busy (Janlert & Stolterman, 2017)
reference: Janlert L-E & Stolterman E (2017) Things That Keep Us Busy: The Elements of Interaction. MIT Press

name: Computerised Adaptive Testing (CAT)
origin: Frederic Lord, 1970 (tailored testing); Howard Wainer, 2000; David Thissen and Maria Orlando, 2001
summary: Selects each next question from a calibrated item bank to be most informative at the respondent's current estimated level, stopping at a fixed length or target precision.
description: A fixed questionnaire wastes items that are far from a respondent's level: people with very high satisfaction learn little from items that only discriminate at the low end. A computerised adaptive test needs five components: a calibrated IRT item bank, a starting rule, an item selection rule, a stopping rule and a scoring method. Item information is additive and roughly the inverse of the squared standard error, so precision at a level depends on how many items target it. Maximum-information selection picks the item most informative at the provisional estimate; before responses vary, MAP or EAP estimation with a prior keeps that estimate finite. Fixed-length stopping gives uniform length; precision-based stopping gives shorter questionnaires for most people and suits cut-score decisions, but is limited by bank coverage. Health outcome systems such as PROMIS use CAT to measure constructs precisely with four to eight items.
steps: Build and calibrate an item bank with an IRT model on a large, representative sample (typically several hundred to over a thousand respondents), checking unidimensionality and fit.
Choose a starting item or starting estimate (for example the population mean).
After each response, update the provisional trait estimate with EAP or MAP.
Select the next item with maximum information at that estimate, subject to any content-balance or exposure constraints.
Stop at a fixed number of items or when the standard error falls below a target (for example 0.3 on the theta scale).
Report the final IRT score and standard error, and monitor item exposure and bank drift over time.
outputs: Individual trait estimates with standard errors from fewer items, item exposure statistics and bank information curves.
useWhen: You repeatedly measure the same construct (satisfaction, self-efficacy, digital literacy, workload) at scale and survey length or in-product interruption is the binding constraint.
avoidWhen: No calibrated bank exists and you cannot afford to build one (use a validated short form); the construct is multidimensional; items must be identical for all respondents for comparability or legal reasons. Maximum-information selection can overuse a few items without exposure control.
whyLost: Building and calibrating an item bank is costly and needs psychometric skills UX teams rarely have; adaptive surveys in UX usually mean simple skip logic instead.
whereToUse: Short in-product surveys, health and wellbeing apps using patient-reported outcome banks, onboarding assessments of skill or literacy, and large research panels measured repeatedly.
example: A digital health app replaces a 28-item fatigue questionnaire with a CAT drawing on a calibrated bank. Most users answer five to seven items to reach a standard error of 0.3, cutting completion time by 75% while matching full-form scores at r = .95.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Wainer, H. (Ed.) (2000). Computerized Adaptive Testing: A Primer (2nd ed.). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Computers-as-social-actors (CASA) experiment
origin: Nass, Reeves, Fogg and colleagues, Stanford, 1990s (Reeves and Nass, 1996; Fogg and Nass, 1997)
summary: Take a human-human social psychology finding, substitute the computer for one person, and run a controlled experiment varying only the social cue to see if users respond socially.
description: The CASA paradigm tests whether people apply human social rules to interfaces. A well-established social effect (similarity attraction, in-group favouritism, response to praise, reciprocity, politeness) is replicated with a computer in place of one person. Conditions differ in a single social cue, such as dominant versus submissive text style, a 'teammate' label with matching colours, sincere versus random praise, or helpful versus unhelpful prior results, while information content and function stay identical. Stanford studies used samples of around 48 to 76 participants, pre-screened moderators such as personality, and controls such as an identical but different machine. Measures combine questionnaire ratings (competence, liking, credibility) with a behavioural outcome such as adopting the computer's ranking or effort spent on a favour. Today it is the natural way to test personas and social framing in chatbots, voice assistants and AI agents.
steps: Choose an established human-human social effect and state the prediction for the interface or agent.
Pick a task that gives the computer a believable role and a measurable behaviour, such as a ranking task where users can adopt or reject its advice, or an open-ended favour task.
Create conditions that differ in one social cue only (text style, labels, colours, praise, helpfulness) while holding information and functionality constant.
Pilot the stimuli so manipulations land as intended and messages do not repeat; pre-screen or measure moderators such as personality and cross them with interface type.
Add controls that rule out other explanations, such as an identical but different machine or praise disclosed as random.
Randomly assign participants (the classic studies used 48 to 76) and run sessions with a consistent cover story and minimal experimenter influence.
Measure attitudes (competence, liking, credibility) by questionnaire and at least one behavioural outcome (recommendations adopted, effort, cooperation).
Analyse condition differences and debrief participants about any cover story.
outputs: Effect estimates of whether a social cue changes perception of and behaviour toward an interface or agent, informing decisions on persona, praise, team framing or personality matching.
useWhen: Deciding whether to give a chatbot, voice assistant or AI agent a persona, flattery, team framing or matched personality, and measuring the behavioural consequences.
avoidWhen: Efficiency tools where social cues may irritate, or when only attitudes (not behaviour) can be measured; early studies used students and 1990s text interfaces, so do not assume transfer without replication. Insincere flattery working as well as sincere praise is an ethical warning.
whyLost: It remained in communication research; UX teams test personas with preference surveys rather than controlled single-cue experiments, despite renewed relevance for conversational AI.
whereToUse: Conversational AI, voice assistants, AI copilots, health coaching apps, persuasive and educational technology.
example: An AI writing assistant team tests whether framing the assistant as 'your teammate' with matching workspace colours changes acceptance of its suggestions. Output is identical across arms; acceptance rises, prompting a review of whether the framing is ethically appropriate.
reference: Reeves, B. and Nass, C. (1996). The Media Equation: How People Treat Computers, Television, and New Media Like Real People and Places. Cambridge University Press.

name: Concentration Curve and Concentration Index
origin: Adam Wagstaff, Pierella Paci and Eddy van Doorslaer, 1991, in health-equity research
summary: Shows whether an outcome is concentrated among people who rank low or high on another variable, and summarises the gradient in one signed index from -1 to +1.
description: The concentration curve ranks people by one variable (in health economics, living standard from poorest to richest) and plots the cumulative share of people against the cumulative share of an outcome such as illness or subsidy received. If the curve lies on the diagonal, the outcome is spread evenly across the ranking; above the diagonal it is concentrated among those ranked low, below it among those ranked high. The concentration index is twice the area between the curve and the diagonal, ranging from -1 to +1, and is zero when there is no rank-related inequality. Unlike the Gini coefficient, which measures how unequally one quantity is spread by ranking on that quantity itself, the concentration index is bivariate: it asks whether a good or bad lands disproportionately on one end of another ranking. It says nothing about the average level of the outcome, so it is read alongside means.
steps: Choose the ranking variable (for example device age, plan tier, income band or digital-skills score) and the outcome whose distribution matters (errors, support contacts, feature benefit).
Rank all cases by the ranking variable from lowest to highest, breaking ties consistently.
Plot the cumulative share of cases against the cumulative share of the outcome, with the line of equality.
Compute the index as twice the area between the curve and the diagonal, signed negative when the curve lies above the diagonal.
Attach bootstrap confidence intervals and compare indices across products, releases or time points.
Interpret the sign according to whether the outcome is a good or a bad, and report it with the outcome's mean.
outputs: Concentration curve plot and a signed concentration index with interval, comparable across groups or releases.
useWhen: Equity questions: whether failures, friction, benefits or support burden fall disproportionately on users with less money, older devices, lower skills or less-served regions.
avoidWhen: You only need to know how concentrated one quantity is (use the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient); the ranking variable is unordered; you need the size of the gap in natural units (report group means or a regression). Avoid comparing indices across outcomes with different sign conventions.
whyLost: It belongs to health-equity economics and has not been picked up by UX, where inclusion work relies on segment comparisons rather than a gradient summary.
whereToUse: Inclusive design and accessibility programmes; public-sector digital services; fintech and health products monitoring whether improvements reach lower-income or lower-literacy users.
example: A government benefits portal ranks applicants by an area deprivation score and plots the cumulative share of failed submissions. The concentration index of -0.21 shows failures are concentrated among the most deprived; after a form redesign it moves to -0.08, while the overall failure rate also falls.
reference: Wagstaff, A., Paci, P., & van Doorslaer, E. (1991). On the measurement of inequalities in health. Social Science & Medicine, 33, 545-557.

name: Concept Mapping
origin: Joseph Novak, 1972 (concept maps); cognitive mapping from Edward Tolman (1948) and Robert Axelrod (1976)
summary: Participants generate and link concepts into a network, externalising how they understand a domain; maps are analysed and aggregated to reveal shared and divergent mental models.
description: Concept mapping asks people to externalise their understanding of a domain as nodes (concepts) and labelled links (relationships). In Novak's hierarchical form, a focus concept sits at the top with progressively specific concepts below and cross-links connecting branches; in cognitive mapping, arrows often represent causal beliefs. Participants generate 10 to 15 concepts, arrange them, and label the relationships while thinking aloud. Analysis counts nodes, links and cross-links, compares structures between groups such as novices and experts, and aggregates individual maps into a group map of frequently shared links. The method is rigorous when the elicitation prompt is standardised, structure is scored consistently, and individual maps are kept separate from the analyst's interpretation.
steps: Concept elicitation: Ask participants to generate 10–15 concepts associated with a domain. Write each on a card.
Relationship mapping: Participants arrange cards spatially and draw arrows between related concepts. For each arrow: label the relationship ('causes', 'is part of', 'prevents', 'requires').
Hierarchical variant (Novak concept maps): Root concept at the top; subordinate concepts below; cross-links between branches.
Analysis: Count nodes, links, and cross-links across participants. High cross-link density = rich, well-integrated understanding. Low = fragmented understanding.
Group concept map: Aggregate individual maps into a group map showing the most frequently appearing concepts and relationships — your population-level mental model.
outputs: Individual concept maps, structural metrics (nodes, links, cross-links, hierarchy depth), an aggregated group map, and a comparison of mental models across segments.
useWhen: You need to understand how users mentally organise a complex domain (insurance, investing, data permissions, ML systems) to inform IA, onboarding or explanations, or to compare novice and expert understanding.
avoidWhen: You only need labels and groupings for navigation; card sorting is faster. If you need to find usability problems, use usability testing.
whyLost: Mental model research in UX shifted to Indi Young's task-based mental model diagrams and card sorting, while scored concept mapping remained in education research.
whereToUse: Financial literacy and investing products, AI explainability, enterprise domain modelling, healthcare self-management, and onboarding design.
example: An investing app asks 12 new investors to map 'how my money grows'. Most maps omit fees and link 'risk' only to 'loss', never to 'return'. Onboarding is redesigned to make the risk-return link and fee drag explicit.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Novak JD & Gowin DB (1984) Learning How to Learn
Novak JD & Cañas AJ (2008) The theory underlying concept maps and how to construct and use them. IHMC
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
reference: Novak, J. D. & Gowin, D. B. (1984). Learning How to Learn. Cambridge University Press.

name: Conceptual Blockbusting
origin: James L. Adams, Conceptual Blockbusting (Stanford, 1974); chapter by Stacie Rohrbach
summary: Diagnose the perceptual block a team is suffering and run a matched exercise to break it, before or during ideation.
description: Adams identified recurring perceptual blocks that narrow problem solving. Universal Methods of Design pairs six with remedies: sketching first impressions exposes stereotyping; changing the scale of the prompt counters poor scoping; prototyping without the 'essential' features breaks a limiting frame; role-playing other stakeholders counters singular viewing; doing a task from memory exposes poor recall of detail; and designing for a different sense each round breaks sight-only thinking. A facilitator runs a quick first-sketch or recall task, diagnoses which blocks appear, applies the matching exercises and has the team regenerate concepts after each, then compares early and later concepts. The value lies in naming the block, so the team becomes aware of its own assumptions rather than merely producing more ideas.
steps: Run a quick first-impression sketch or recall task on the design subject (for example 'draw a refrigerator').
Compare outputs and identify which of the six blocks appear: stereotyping, poor scoping, limiting frame, singular viewing, poor recall, single-sense thinking.
Apply the matching exercise, such as rescaling the prompt or role-playing another stakeholder.
Regenerate concepts after each exercise.
Compare early and later concepts and discuss which assumptions were dropped.
outputs: A wider set of concepts and a team that can name its own assumptions.
useWhen: Use when ideation keeps converging on the familiar form of a product, or before a design studio to loosen a team that knows the domain too well.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the block is a lack of knowledge about users rather than a perceptual habit: do Contextual Inquiry or Field Studies. It takes workshop time and needs a facilitator who can diagnose blocks.
whyLost: Adams's book is widely cited in design education, but its diagnostic exercises are seldom run in product teams, which jump straight to generic brainstorming.
whereToUse: Industrial and IoT design, service redesign, mature product categories facing disruption.
example: In a food-storage workshop every participant draws a closed refrigerator with a power cord. After a scale change ('store food for one meal') and a different-sense round, concepts include open shelving that signals freshness by smell.
sources: Adams, J. L. (1974). Conceptual Blockbusting: A Guide to Better Ideas. San Francisco: W. H. Freeman.
reference: Adams, J. L. (1974). Conceptual Blockbusting: A Guide to Better Ideas. San Francisco: W. H. Freeman.

name: Conceptual Model Design (Objects and Operations)
origin: Jeff Johnson and Austin Henderson (2002, expanded 2011); objects/operations analysis after the Xerox Star team (1989), Newman and Sproull (1973) and Card (1996); task mapping after Moran's ETIT (1983)
summary: Turn user and task research into an explicit, interface-free model of the objects, attributes, operations and relationships an application exposes, with vocabulary and task mappings, tested before UI design.
description: A conceptual model describes an application in task terms: its purpose, every concept users meet (objects, attributes with value types, operations) and their relationships (specialisation, containment, whole and part, source and result), plus a mapping of domain tasks onto those concepts as task scenarios. It is distinct from users' mental models, metaphors, the UI and the implementation. The aims are simplicity, the fewest concepts that deliver the function, and task focus, concepts that map directly onto the domain. Draft concepts come from research transcripts (nouns suggest objects, verbs operations), then modelling rules are applied: every operation belongs to an object, implementation concepts are excluded, near-identical objects share a type attribute. The model, with a vocabulary and an issues log, acts as a contract: the UI may expose only what the model contains. It takes a team one week to a month. Object-oriented UX (OOUX) is a current revival under a new name.
steps: Gather user profiles and task analysis (use cases, task hierarchy, task sequences) from observing and interviewing people at work.
Write the application's purpose and high-level functionality.
Draft objects, operations and attributes from transcripts (nouns as objects, verbs as operations, adjectives as attribute values) and correct mis-voiced concepts.
Build the objects/operations analysis, applying the rules: every operation belongs to an object; exclude implementation concepts; admit new concepts sparingly; settle containment and inheritance.
Compile the vocabulary list with agreed user-visible names and definitions.
Write task scenarios using only model terms and redesign if common tasks need complex plans.
Log resolved and open conceptual issues; one person drives drafts, the whole team reviews, and any change is a team decision.
Test the model early with users or domain experts through concept and terminology sessions or low-fidelity prototypes, and keep it current through releases.
outputs: A conceptual model document (purpose, concepts and vocabulary, object-operation hierarchy, task mapping, issues log), a product vocabulary and conceptual task scenarios.
