Define 3 to 5 tone dimensions with anchored endpoints (for example NN/g's funny-serious, formal-casual, respectful-irreverent, enthusiastic-matter-of-fact) and set a target position on each for every situation row.

Write 2 to 3 exemplar strings per cell and run a Gricean maxim audit on each, flagging any string that over- or under-informs, asserts something not guaranteed, is irrelevant to the user's goal, or is ambiguous.

Test the highest-stakes cells (errors, money, health, security) with 5 to 10 users using a comprehension and implicature probe: 'What is this message telling you? Whose fault is it? What will you do next?'

Revise cells where more than 1 in 5 participants draw an unintended implicature (for example self-blame or false reassurance), then publish the matrix in the design system with do and do-not examples.
Re-audit quarterly or whenever new message types ship, sampling live strings against the matrix.
outputs: A situation-by-tone matrix with target positions per dimension, exemplar and counter-example strings per cell, a maxim-audit log of violations, and implicature test results for high-stakes messages.
useWhen: A product speaks in many contexts with varying stakes; error, payment or health messages are generating confusion, blame or distrust; multiple writers or LLM-generated strings need a shared, checkable tone standard.
avoidWhen: The product has only a handful of messages (just write and test them directly), or the problem is information architecture or task flow rather than wording; use a usability test or cognitive walkthrough instead.
whyLost: It survived because content design became a profession and design systems needed shareable tone rules. What was largely lost is the pragmatic grounding: many matrices encode brand personality without testing what users infer.
whereToUse: Fintech error and decline messaging, health and insurance notifications, conversational and LLM-driven interfaces needing tone guardrails, localisation into cultures with different politeness norms.
example: A lending app's playful 'Oops! Something went wrong' appeared on declined applications. A tone matrix placed 'application declined' at serious, respectful, matter-of-fact, and the maxim audit flagged the Quantity violation of giving no reason; the rewritten message stated the reason category and next step, and complaint volume on that screen fell.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 18 — Pragmatics — What Language Actually Does
reference: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and Conversation. In Cole & Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts; Moran, K. (2016). The Four Dimensions of Tone of Voice. Nielsen Norman Group.

name: Context Chart
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1984; expanded 1994
summary: A one-page network of the roles and groups around the behaviour studied, showing each person's attitude and influence and the quality of relationships, governed by explicit data-entry rules.
description: A context chart shows formal authority and division of labour together with study-relevant properties, so individual statements can be read in their social context. Each person's box carries a job title, whether they use the innovation or product, their attitude (+, ±, 0), and symbols for advocates and high-influence actors; lines between boxes show the character of relationships. What makes it rigorous is its decision rules: 'DK' where information is unknown or ambiguous; no relationship rating that the other party would disconfirm; advocate and influence ratings need at least one confirmation. Variants draw assistance flows as arrows, informal influence as dotted lines, informal groups as circles, successive charts over time, or physical maps. It is not an organisation chart and never exhaustive. A chart takes about an hour and is redrawn as the setting changes.
steps: Draw the formal authority structure and division of labour at the levels relevant to the study.
Add per-person properties: title, user status, attitude (+, ±, 0), and advocate and influence symbols.
Mark the character of relationships between boxes, adding informal influence as dotted lines and informal groups as circles where relevant.
Apply the entry rules: DK when unknown; no rating contradicted by the other party; influence ratings confirmed at least once.
Use the chart to interpret individual statements and to list questions for the next visit.
Redraw at intervals as the organisation changes, keeping earlier versions.
outputs: A one-page context chart, with dated versions if the setting changes.
useWhen: B2B, enterprise and service research where adoption depends on who influences whom, and where a participant's comments only make sense given their role and relationships.
avoidWhen: Consumer research with isolated individual users; use a simpler stakeholder map when no data on attitudes and relationships has been collected. Keep early versions simple.
whyLost: UX stakeholder maps and ecosystem maps took over the visual form but usually without per-person attitude coding or the rules that prevent unconfirmed ratings.
whereToUse: Enterprise software rollouts, clinical workflow studies, procurement and buying-committee research.
example: In a study of a hospital e-prescribing rollout, the chart shows the pharmacy lead as a high-influence advocate with a strained link to ward managers. That explains why ward nurses describe the tool as 'imposed', and it sets the next visit's questions.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Context Map
origin: Based on The Grove Consultants International's Context Map Graphic Guide (1996-2010); described in Gamestorming
summary: A facilitated six-panel wall chart on which a group maps the political, economic, technological, customer, trend and uncertainty forces around an organisation.
description: The context map helps a group see the external factors surrounding its organisation so it can respond proactively. Six flip-chart sheets are hung in two rows. The organisation sits top middle under political factors and economic climate; two 'trends' panels with inward arrows sit at top left and right with blank qualifiers; technology factors, customer needs and uncertainties fill the bottom row. The group chooses which category to start with, the facilitator scribes, and the trend qualifiers (for example online, demographic) are agreed by poll or dot vote. The facilitator notes where the group starts and where it generates most content, as signals of where its attention lies, and steers away from internal issues. The map is only as good as the group's knowledge, so prior research or employee interviews help.
steps: Hang six flip-chart sheets in two rows of three.
Top middle: draw the organisation and label political factors and economic climate above it; top left and right: inward arrows labelled '____ trends'.
Bottom row: technology factors, customer needs (with an image of the customer) and uncertainties.
Introduce the map and let the group choose a non-trend category to begin; scribe comments and work through all non-trend panels.
Agree qualifiers for the two trend panels by poll or dot vote and fill them.
Summarise and ask for observations, insights and concerns, noting where the group's energy concentrated.
outputs: A populated external-context map and notes on where the group's attention concentrates.
useWhen: Use at the start of strategy or product planning to give a team a shared picture of external forces, especially customer needs and uncertainties.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the customer-needs panel as research: it records what the group believes. Feed it with Interviews or Field Studies, and use Three Horizons Framework or Scenario generation under uncertainty for deeper futures work.
whyLost: It belongs to graphic facilitation and strategy consulting; UX teams seldom run environment-scanning sessions themselves.
whereToUse: Product strategy offsites, digital transformation programmes, public-sector service planning.
example: A health-insurer product team fills the map in 90 minutes; the uncertainties panel fills fastest with regulation and AI triage, prompting a research plan on member trust in automated advice.
reference: Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010). Gamestorming: A Playbook for Innovators, Rulebreakers, and Changemakers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Context of Use Description (ISO/IEC 25063)
aka: Common Industry Format context of use
origin: ISO/IEC 25063:2014, Common Industry Format for usability: context of use description; presented by Peissner, Pollmann and Fronemann (2021)
summary: A structured, factual document of user groups, their goals and tasks, and their technical, physical and social environments, serving as the evidence base for requirements.
description: In human-centred design, user requirements documents serve different purposes. The context of use description records insights; design principles and How Might We questions guide design; the user requirements specification (ISO/IEC 25065) gives an evaluation baseline. The context of use description records factual current or expected conditions: user and stakeholder groups and their characteristics, their goals and tasks, and the technical, physical, social and organisational environments, including predecessor and competitor systems. It also records user needs, meaning prerequisites for achieving an outcome in context, rather than features. It deliberately contains no interpretations about required system capabilities, which belong in a separate specification. It starts from existing knowledge and is extended by interviews, contextual inquiry and observation.
steps: Gather existing knowledge about users, tasks and environments as a starting point.
Run user research (interviews, contextual inquiry, observation) to fill the gaps.
Describe each user and stakeholder group and its relevant characteristics.
Describe goals and tasks for each group, including frequency and criticality.
Describe the technical, physical, social and organisational environments, including current and competing systems.
Record user needs separately from any system features and remove interpretations; derive requirements later in a user requirements specification.
outputs: A context of use description that feeds personas, scenarios, use cases and the user requirements specification.
useWhen: Regulated or procurement-driven projects that need standard-conformant documentation, and any project where research findings must be kept separate from design decisions.
avoidWhen: Avoid in fast product discovery where a lightweight canvas is enough; use PACT analysis or personas. Do not let it drift into requirements; use a user requirements specification for those.
whyLost: Standard documents are used in public-sector, medical and procurement contexts, but product teams prefer personas and journey maps and rarely know the ISO format.
whereToUse: Medical devices, public-sector digital services, defence and transport systems, enterprise procurement, accessibility compliance work.
example: For a hospital ward tablet system, the team documents nurses, porters and patients, their tasks, shift patterns, glove use, noise and Wi-Fi blackspots, without proposing features. The procurement team then derives testable requirements from it.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: ISO/IEC 25063:2014. Systems and software engineering: Common Industry Format (CIF) for usability: Context of use description. Geneva: ISO; Peissner, Pollmann and Fronemann in Salvendy, G. and Karwowski, W. (Eds.) (2021). Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.). Wiley, ch. 37, pp. 961-965.

name: Context-match design (encoding specificity, state dependence)
aka: Context-match design (encoding specificity, state dependence, transfer-appropriate processing)
origin: Godden and Baddeley, 1975; Tulving and Thomson, 1973; Morris, Bransford and Franks, 1977
summary: A crossed design in which people learn in one context and are tested in the same or a different one, measuring how much recall depends on matching conditions.
description: Participants learn material in context A or B and are tested in A or B, so half test in a matching context. Godden and Baddeley's divers learned 40 words on shore or 20 feet underwater and recalled best where they had learned. Variants match background noise (reading with cafeteria noise or silence), mood (induced until ratings reach very pleasant or unpleasant, retested two days later) or drug state. Transfer-appropriate processing extends the logic to processing type: people who encoded words by rhyme did better on a rhyming test than those who encoded by meaning, reversing the usual depth advantage. The rigour lies in the full 2 x 2 crossing, which separates the match effect from main effects of either context.
steps: Define the two contexts that matter (environment, device, noise, mood, processing type).
Randomly assign participants to learn in context A or B.
After a delay, test half of each group in the same context and half in the other.
Use the same materials and test format across cells; for mood, induce and verify mood by rating before learning and testing.
Analyse the study-by-test interaction; the match advantage is the effect of interest.
Debrief and restore mood after any negative induction.
outputs: The interaction of learning and test context, with recall or performance in matched versus mismatched cells.
useWhen: Testing whether training, onboarding or practice transfers to the context where the skill is used (a different device, a noisy ward, a stressful moment).
avoidWhen: Avoid partial designs without the full crossing; for skill transfer across tasks rather than contexts use an analogical transfer test.
whyLost: Memory research keeps it, but training and onboarding studies in UX rarely vary the test context deliberately.
whereToUse: Clinical and safety training, emergency procedures, mobile versus desktop learning, onboarding, password and recovery flows.
example: Hospital staff learn a new infusion-pump procedure in a quiet room or with recorded ward noise and are tested in either. Those trained in quiet perform worst on the ward, so training moves into simulated noise.
sources: Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1975). Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: On land and underwater. British Journal of Psychology, 66
reference: Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1975). Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: On land and underwater. British Journal of Psychology, 66, 325-331.

name: Contextual Design Visioning
origin: Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt (1997; evolved 2014)
summary: A facilitated team workshop that invents, as quickly drawn stories, how users will live and work with a new product, then evaluates the stories and extracts coherent concepts.
description: Visioning is the point in Contextual Design where the team stops describing users and invents the solution, driven by consolidated field data. Starting from a 'hot idea' from the wall walk, one person narrates what a persona does in the new world, inventing features as they go; others build on it, and one person acts as the pen, drawing a pictorial story on a flip chart. Nobody criticises; problems are met with fixes. Teams are capped at eight, with parallel teams for more people. A vision takes 20-40 minutes and four to six are typical. Evaluation is a separate step allowing only three kinds of issue: poor fit to user practice, technical difficulty and conflict with the business mission, with positives listed first. Finally the team identifies coherent product concepts, drawn separately, borrowing the best parts of every vision. Storytelling forces the invented life to hang together.
steps: Review the consolidated data (affinity, work models, personas) and list hot ideas during a wall walk.
Start from one hot idea; one person narrates a persona's new day with the product while others add ideas and the pen draws it on a flip chart.
Allow no criticism; continue until ideas run out or the story ends (20-40 minutes).
Pick the next uncovered hot idea and repeat, usually for four to six visions, with no more than eight people per team.
Evaluate each vision: list what works, then issues of user fit, technical difficulty or business fit, each with a design fix.
Identify coherent product concepts and draw each separately, combining the best parts of all visions; share with management and carry into storyboards.
outputs: Flip-chart vision drawings, evaluation lists and a set of product concept drawings.
useWhen: Use after field research has been consolidated, when a team must move from understanding to a coherent product direction that covers system, delivery and support.
avoidWhen: Avoid without grounding data: visioning on assumptions produces fiction, so run Contextual Inquiry first. To test concepts with users afterwards use Prototype Testing or Mock-up and Trial Sessions (Cooperative Prototyping).
whyLost: It is used mainly by teams trained in the full Contextual Design process; most UX teams replaced it with lighter ideation and rarely keep its separation of storytelling and evaluation.
whereToUse: Enterprise and workplace tools, travel and life-management apps, any product redesign after substantial field research.
example: A travel team runs five visions from field data and extracts three concepts: a trip research tool for collecting ideas, a planning tool, and an in-trip app for recording and sharing events.
sources: Beyer, H. and Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems. San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann.
reference: Holtzblatt, K. and Beyer, H. (2014). Contextual Design: Evolved. Synthesis Lectures on Human-Centered Informatics #24. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool. doi:10.2200/S00597ED1V01Y201409HCI024, pp. 44-49.

name: Contextual Inquiry
donor: Anthropology and ethnography, adapted for systems design
origin: Karen Holtzblatt & Hugh Beyer, late 1980s (Contextual Design, 1998)
summary: An in-situ interview where the researcher observes and questions users as they do real work, revealing practices, workarounds and context invisible in the lab.
description: Contextual inquiry combines observation and interviewing in the user's own environment while they carry out their actual work. The researcher adopts the stance of an apprentice learning from a master, guided by four principles: context (go where the work happens), partnership (interpret jointly with the user), interpretation (share and check meanings as you go) and focus (a clear research scope that steers attention). Because users demonstrate rather than describe, contextual inquiry exposes tacit knowledge, workarounds, artefacts and interruptions that people omit in conventional interviews. Rigour comes from observing ongoing work rather than demos, interpreting with the participant in the moment, holding interpretation sessions within 48 hours, and capturing findings in structured work models and affinity diagrams.
steps: Define a project focus that states which work practices you need to understand.
Recruit 6 to 12 participants across key roles and sites, and arrange to visit during real work.
Open with a brief conventional interview to understand role and context (about 15 minutes).
Transition to observing ongoing work, asking about actions as they happen and sharing interpretations for the user to confirm or correct.
Collect or photograph artefacts such as notes, printouts and spreadsheets.
Wrap up by summarising your understanding and checking it with the participant.
Hold a team interpretation session within 48 hours and capture notes, work models and affinity notes.
outputs: Interpretation notes, work models (flow, sequence, artefact, cultural, physical), artefact collections and an affinity diagram of insights.
useWhen: When designing tools embedded in complex real-world work, when users cannot articulate tacit practices, or when workarounds and environment matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need statistical generalisation or when work cannot be observed for privacy or safety reasons; use surveys, diaries or retrospective critical incident interviews instead.
whyLost: Vestigial: the label is widely used, but most teams now run a remote interview with screen-share and call it contextual inquiry, losing the in-situ observation, joint interpretation and work modelling that gave the method its power.
whereToUse: Workplace tools; healthcare systems; any product embedded in complex real-world workflows.
example: A clinical informatics team shadows ward nurses during medication rounds. They observe nurses writing doses on gloves because the EHR session times out, a workaround never mentioned in interviews, which reshapes the barcode scanning design.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Beyer H & Holtzblatt K (1998) Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems
Holtzblatt K & Beyer H (2017) Contextual Design: Design for Life. 2nd ed
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Beyer, H. & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems. Morgan Kaufmann.

extra.Four Principles (Holtzblatt & Beyer): Context: Conduct the interview where the work happens. Not in a conference room. Not remotely. At the desk, on the floor, in the vehicle, in the field. The environment contains information that the participant cannot verbalise because they no longer notice it. Partnership: The researcher takes the role of apprentice — genuinely curious, asking the participant (master) to explain their work. Not expert evaluator; not passive observer. Engaged learner. Interpretation: Share your interpretations with the participant in real time. "I notice you always copy that data to a spreadsheet before you enter it — is that a workaround for something?" This surfaces tacit knowledge that pure observation misses. Focus: Stay focused on the work that matters to your research question. When the participant goes off-topic, return gently: "I'm curious to understand more about how you handle [the specific task] — can we go back to that?"
extra.Work Artifact Analysis: During CI, collect all artifacts the participant has created or modified: post-it notes, custom spreadsheets, printed manuals with annotations, physical workarounds. Photograph and catalog. Analyse for: (1) information the interface failed to surface (filled gaps); (2) actions the interface failed to afford (physical workarounds); (3) mental models embedded in artifact structure (how they organised their workaround reveals how they think about the underlying task).

name: Contextual Inquiry with Work Artefact Analysis
origin: Contextual inquiry by Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt (1990s), artefact models in Contextual Design (1998); catalogued by Martin and Hanington (2012)
summary: Contextual inquiry that systematically collects and analyses the notes, printouts, spreadsheets and workarounds people create, revealing tacit needs and shadow systems interviews miss.
description: Contextual inquiry pairs observation and interview in the user's own setting under a master-apprentice model. Artefact analysis extends it by treating the physical and digital things people create or use as data in their own right: sticky notes on monitors, annotated printouts, personal spreadsheets, cheat sheets, renamed folders and custom tools. Each artefact is photographed or collected, and analysed for its structure, the information it carries, who creates and uses it, and the breakdowns it compensates for. Workarounds often form a shadow information system that reveals what the official product fails to support. Holtzblatt and Beyer's artefact model formalises this analysis. In contemporary practice contextual inquiry survives in shortened forms, and the systematic artefact component is usually dropped.
steps: During field observation, collect all artifacts users have created or modified: post-it notes, custom spreadsheets, printed manuals with annotations, physical workarounds. Photograph and catalog. Analyze artifact content for:
information the interface failed to surface (filled gaps),
actions the interface failed to afford (physical workarounds),
mental models embedded in artifact structure.
outputs: Artefact inventory with photographs, artefact models (structure, content, usage, breakdowns), workaround catalogue and design requirements derived from shadow systems.
useWhen: Workplace and professional tools, healthcare, logistics, finance operations, and any setting where people supplement official systems with their own records.
avoidWhen: When access to the work setting is impossible or artefacts are confidential and cannot be recorded; use diary studies or remote contextual interviews with screen sharing instead.
whyLost: Time-boxed research cut field visits short and remote research removed the opportunity to see artefacts, so the artefact model from Contextual Design became the first part dropped.
whereToUse: Enterprise software redesign, complex professional tool research, any context where workarounds and adaptations are common. Connects to niche construction theory — workarounds are niche construction.
example: At a primary-care clinic, researchers photograph post-it notes stuck to a shared tablet listing patients awaiting callbacks. The notes form a shadow triage queue, leading the EHR vendor to add a visible callback list.
sources: Universal Methods of Design — Bella Martin
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Martin B & Hanington B (2012) Universal Methods of Design: 100 Ways to Research Complex Problems. Rockport Publishers

name: Contextual Simulation Lab Prototyping
aka: Contextual prototyping in a simulated environment
origin: Steve Gill and colleagues, Cardiff Metropolitan University, 2010s
summary: Recreate the target environment's sights, sounds, climate, smells and people in a lab so device prototypes can be tested in context under lab control.
description: When the real context is unsuitable for testing (ethical limits, confidentiality, or a prototype tethered to lab equipment), the context itself is prototyped. The Perceptual Experience Laboratory combines a 180-degree wrap-around screen, surround sound, controlled temperature and air movement, scents, actors and props, with eye-tracked perspective correction planned. The aim is to mimic an environment in under a day while keeping lab advantages: observation, recording, technical support and confidentiality. The same principle underlies driving simulators and hospital simulation suites. Rigour depends on choosing which contextual cues matter for the device and checking that the simulation produces the behaviours seen in the field.
steps: Identify the contextual factors likely to affect use of the device: noise, light, temperature, smell, other people, interruptions.
Build or adapt the device prototype for lab use.
Recreate the target environment with imagery, sound, climate, scent, actors and props.
Run trials with representative users performing realistic tasks, with observation and recording.
Compare behaviour with any available field observations to check the simulation's fidelity.
Iterate device and scenario.
outputs: In-context trial observations and problem lists gathered under lab conditions.
useWhen: Devices for environments that are hard to access or risky to test in (hospitals, vehicles, factories, emergency settings), or confidential pre-release hardware.
avoidWhen: When the real setting is accessible and safe (use Field Usability Testing), or when budgets cannot support the build; the reported lab had no validation data.
whyLost: Building simulated environments is expensive, so it remains in automotive, aviation, healthcare simulation and a few design research labs.
whereToUse: Medical devices, in-car systems, retail kiosks, smart-home products and public-space installations.
example: A ward-monitoring device is tested in a lab mock-up with alarms from other beds, disinfectant smell and an actor playing a distressed relative. Nurses miss a low-priority alert that went unnoticed in quiet lab tests.
reference: Dix, A., Gill, S., Ramduny-Ellis, D. and Hare, J. (2022) TouchIT: Understanding Design in a Physical-Digital World. Oxford: Oxford University Press, pp. 441-443.

name: Contextual Sound Testing
aka: Sound testing at distances and in enclosures
origin: Amber Case and Aaron Day, 2018
summary: Test product sounds in real places, at a ladder of distances, inside bags and across social settings to see whether they are heard, ignored or intrusive.
description: Whether a sound is welcomed, ignored or intrusive depends on time, place, noise, ability, culture and season, so lab listening misleads. Case and Day set out a structured series of contexts. Testers ideally live with the product at home. Sounds are checked inside a purse, backpack or pocket (where high frequencies are lost), across a distance ladder from in hand to behind a solid door and in large open spaces, on public transport with a colleague in busy and quiet conditions, on flights, and against cultural norms of politeness in each market. Social contexts (alone, coworkers, crowd, friends and family, school) each come with questions about disruption, and inclusive design cards prompt situational, temporary and permanent limitations. The result is a list of contextual failures and the settings users will need.
steps: Where possible, give testers the product to use daily at home.
Test audibility inside a purse, backpack and pocket, noting loss of high frequencies.
Test at a distance ladder: in hand, on a table, across the room, next room with door open, behind a hollow door, behind a solid door, and in a large open space; note disturbance to others.
Test on public transport with a colleague, seated together and apart, in busy and quiet conditions, and on a flight if possible.
Review cultural expectations of loudness, length and politeness for each target market.
Check each social context (alone, coworkers, crowd, friends and family, school) and situational, temporary and permanent limitations with inclusive design prompts.
Record failures and the user settings required (volume, alert style by sender, silent mode).
outputs: A list of contextual sound failures (inaudible, intrusive, ill-timed) and required sound settings.
useWhen: Designing alerts, earcons, voice prompts and notification sounds for devices used across homes, workplaces and public spaces.
avoidWhen: Products without sound output, or when precise perceptual thresholds are needed (use Psychophysical Threshold Methods (JND)).
whyLost: Sound is rarely a UX research focus and is usually signed off in the studio rather than tested in the world.
whereToUse: Wearables, smart speakers, kitchen appliances, medical alarms, cars and mobile notification design.
example: A portable speaker's low-battery voice prompt plays at 3 a.m. and is mistaken for an intruder. Contextual testing in bedrooms leads to a quiet-hours rule and a softer tone.
reference: Case, A. and Day, A. (2018) Designing with Sound: Fundamentals for Products and Services. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 172-179.

name: Continuous Discovery Infrastructure
origin: Teresa Torres, 2021 (Continuous Discovery Habits)
summary: A standing weekly interview cadence run by product trios and fed into a living opportunity solution tree linking evidence to decisions.
description: Continuous discovery reframes research from episodic projects into an ongoing team habit. Torres recommends that the product trio (product manager, designer, engineer) talk to customers at least weekly, supported by automated recruitment such as in-product intercepts and customer success referrals. Short interviews collect specific recent stories rather than opinions. Insights are mapped onto an opportunity solution tree: a desired outcome at the top, opportunities (needs, pain points) beneath, then candidate solutions and the assumption tests that evaluate them. The tree is updated after each session and replaces static reports. Its strength is sustained exposure and traceability from evidence to decisions; its risk is shallow, unsystematic synthesis when no trained researcher supports it.
steps: Standing recruitment pipeline: In-product banners, email lists, customer success referrals. Maintain a pool of willing participants contactable for a 20-minute conversation with 24-hour notice.

Interview structure (20 min): 5 min — how has the product been part of your life since we last spoke? 10 min — follow the story of one specific recent moment. 5 min — what's coming up that will involve the product?
Living Opportunity Solution Tree: Outcome → opportunities (unmet needs from interviews) → solutions → experiments. Update after every session. Replaces the traditional research report.
Team involvement: Engineers and PMs attend at least every 4th session. Direct exposure changes how teams interpret research.
Cadence: Weekly, not only when there's a 'big question.' Consistency is the point.
outputs: A standing recruitment pipeline, weekly interview snapshots, a living opportunity solution tree, and assumption test results.
useWhen: Product teams making frequent decisions who need steady contact with customers and a traceable link between evidence and roadmap.
avoidWhen: Deep foundational questions, sensitive populations, or rigorous measurement; use dedicated studies by trained researchers.
whyLost: It spread rapidly through product management, because it fits agile cadences and gives teams direct ownership of discovery.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS, consumer subscription apps, marketplaces and fintech product teams with direct customer access.
example: A payroll SaaS trio runs three 20-minute calls each week from an in-app intercept. After six weeks, the tree shows 'year-end filing anxiety' as the largest opportunity, reshaping the next quarter's roadmap.
reference: Torres, T. (2021). Continuous Discovery Habits. Product Talk LLC.

name: Continuous Wavelet Transform (Scalograms)
origin: Jean Morlet & Alex Grossmann, 1984
summary: Localises frequency content in time by sliding scaled wavelets across a signal, revealing when bursts, transitions and slow drifts occur in behaviour.
description: Where Fourier reveals global rhythm, wavelets reveal local story. The continuous wavelet transform correlates the signal with a wavelet at many scales and positions, producing a time-frequency scalogram. In the Behavioral Spectral Framework, short-scale bursts are read as spikes of cognitive load, surprise or momentary confusion, long-scale drifts as slow learning, sustained focus, fatigue or attention decay, and coexisting scales as multitasking or conflicting goals. Recommended adaptations include adaptive scales, wavelet energy envelopes to estimate task load and recovery time after failures, and scalograms aligned with qualitative annotations. The synthesis method extracts dominant bands with FFT, then localises them in time with CWT or STFT and aligns them with coded moments. In the fintech case, Frustration-coded moments consistently coincided with transient high-frequency spikes in the wavelet energy map.
steps: Choose a mother wavelet and a range of scales matched to the behaviours of interest.
Compute the CWT of the behavioural signal and plot the scalogram.
Compute wavelet energy envelopes to estimate load and recovery time after failure events.
Detect bursts and drifts and export their timestamps.
Align bursts with qualitative annotations (video, transcript, sentiment) in a Spectral Annotation Matrix.
Report scalograms with annotation overlays.
outputs: Scalograms, burst timestamps, energy envelopes and annotated overlays.
useWhen: When you need to know when within a session or journey rhythm changes, not just which rhythms exist.
avoidWhen: When signals are too short or sparse to resolve scales, or no qualitative alignment is possible.
whyLost: Standard in geophysics, EEG and engineering, absent from UX training.
whereToUse: Micro-frustration detection, recovery-time measurement, emotional journey mapping, biometric UX.
example: A scalogram of a checkout session shows a short-scale burst at the OTP step followed by a slow rebound, quantifying recovery time after the failure.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
Matteo Paz (2024), A Sub-Millisecond Fourier and Wavelet Based Model to Extract Variable Candidates from the NEOWISE Single-Exposure Database
reference: Torrence, C., & Compo, G. P. (1998). A practical guide to wavelet analysis. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 79(1), 61–78.

name: Contradiction identification
origin: Yrjö Engeström, Learning by Expanding, 1987, building on Vygotsky and Leont'ev
summary: Identifies systemic tensions within and between elements of an activity system, such as tools, rules and division of labour, that explain recurring breakdowns and workarounds.
description: Engeström's activity system model includes subject, object, tools, rules, community and division of labour. Contradictions are historically accumulating structural tensions: primary (within an element, such as a tool being both a commodity and an instrument), secondary (between elements, such as a new tool clashing with existing rules), tertiary (between old and new forms of the activity) and quaternary (between neighbouring activity systems). Contradictions surface as disturbances, breakdowns, workarounds and complaints. Identifying them shifts analysis from individual usability problems to systemic causes, and Engeström argues they are the engine of change. Rigour comes from tracing disturbances in data to specific element pairs, distinguishing contradictions from one-off problems, and validating with participants.
steps: Model the activity system: subject, object, tools, rules, community, division of labour and outcome.
Collect disturbance data from observation, interviews and incident logs: breakdowns, workarounds, conflicts and complaints.
Code each disturbance against the element pairs involved, recording evidence.
Classify recurring tensions as primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary contradictions.
Validate with participants in a workshop (for example a Change Laboratory session) to confirm and prioritise contradictions.
Generate design and organisational interventions that address the contradiction, not just the disturbance.
outputs: An activity system model, a coded disturbance set, a contradiction map by type, and intervention ideas.
useWhen: When products are adopted in complex workplaces with persistent workarounds, and when design goals clash with actual use.
avoidWhen: For simple consumer tasks where social and organisational structures are not relevant; use usability testing.
whyLost: Activity theory was prominent in 1990s HCI (Kuutti, Nardi, Bødker) but its vocabulary proved heavy for practitioners, and it retreated to academic and workplace studies.
whereToUse: Hospital technology adoption, enterprise software rollouts, education technology, and AI tools in professional work.
example: Surgeons use a robot's camera auto-follow feature far less than designed. Contradiction analysis traces this to a secondary contradiction between the tool and hospital rules requiring the assistant to control the camera for training.
sources: Newell, A., Unified Theories of Cognition (1990)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
reference: Engeström, Y. (1987). Learning by Expanding: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Developmental Research. Orienta-Konsultit.

name: Contrast Table of Exemplary Cases
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1994
summary: Unpack what an outcome is made of by setting a few exemplary high, low and negative cases side by side on several aspects of that outcome.
description: An exploratory display for understanding a general outcome variable before trying to predict it. After reading all or most case reports, the analyst picks two to four exemplary cases where the outcome is high, low or negative. Aspects of the outcome noticed in the reports become rows (for example start-up discrepancy, pervasiveness, technical mastery, energy invested, negative changes, feeling stretched), and each cell holds a short characterisation per case. Comparing columns shows how the outcome actually works and what distinguishes its levels, and promising aspects are carried forward as predictors into a predictor-outcome matrix. In the source example the negative case looked like the high case at first and then regressed, which a single outcome score would have hidden. The tables also teach readers what the outcome means. Exemplars can only be chosen after reading the cases, and three cases cannot test anything.
steps: Read all or most case reports before choosing exemplars.
Choose two to four exemplary cases spanning high, low and negative forms of the outcome.
List the aspects of the outcome noticed in the case reports as rows.
Fill each cell with a short characterisation for that case and aspect.
Compare columns to see what distinguishes the levels of the outcome.
Carry promising aspects forward as candidate predictors for a cross-case predictor-outcome analysis.
outputs: A small contrast table and a list of candidate predictor variables.
useWhen: When an outcome such as 'successful adoption' or 'churned' is used loosely and you need to know what it consists of before explaining it across cases.
avoidWhen: Testing hypotheses or estimating prevalence; use a case-ordered predictor-outcome matrix or quantitative analysis instead.
whyLost: UX synthesis tends to jump from cases to themes or personas, skipping the step of decomposing the outcome itself with deliberately contrasting cases.
whereToUse: Churn and retention research, onboarding success studies, and B2B account health investigations.
example: A fintech team contrasts one thriving, one dormant and one churned small-business account on setup speed, breadth of features used, who owns the tool, and workarounds. The churned account resembled the thriving one in month one, which shifts attention from onboarding to month-three ownership changes.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Control Theory and Feedback Loop Analysis
origin: Norbert Wiener (Cybernetics, 1948); Duane McRuer and Henry Jex (1967, crossover model); William Powers (Behavior: The Control of Perception, 1973)
summary: Models users and systems as closed feedback loops with gain, delay and noise, predicting oscillation, overshoot and instability in interaction.
description: Control theory analyses closed loops: a controller compares a reference with feedback and acts to reduce error. Delays and high gain cause oscillation and instability. In manual control, McRuer's crossover model showed humans adapt their dynamics so the combined human-machine system behaves like an integrator near crossover frequency, with effective time delay of roughly 0.1-0.3 seconds. Perceptual control theory frames behaviour as controlling perception. For UX, loops are everywhere: scrolling with inertia, sliders with lag, thermostats, recommendation feedback, algorithmic pricing. Analysing gain, latency and feedback quality predicts overshoot (users scrolling past), hunting (repeatedly adjusting) and runaway loops (filter bubbles).
steps: Draw the loop: user goal (reference), action, system dynamics, feedback display, perception.
Measure system parameters: latency, gain (output per input), noise and feedback resolution.
Collect interaction traces (e.g. cursor, scroll, setting adjustments) and identify overshoot and oscillation.
Fit simple models (e.g. first-order plus delay) or apply crossover model reasoning.
Adjust gain, damping, latency or feedback (e.g. preview, rate-aided control) and predict effects.
Test changes with tracking or adjustment tasks, measuring settling time and overshoot.
outputs: Loop diagrams, measured gain and delay, overshoot and settling metrics, and tuned interaction parameters.
useWhen: Continuous control interactions, adjustable settings with lag, and algorithmic feedback loops affecting users.
avoidWhen: Discrete form-filling or content questions without dynamic feedback.
whyLost: Manual control research declined with the shift from vehicles to GUIs, and design rarely uses engineering dynamics.
whereToUse: Scrolling and zoom physics, smart thermostats, drone and robot control, audio mixing, recommender feedback loops.
example: A smart thermostat app shows users repeatedly overshooting set points because heating response is delayed 20 minutes; adding a predicted temperature curve (feedback of future state) reduces adjustment cycles by 60%.
sources: McRuer & Jex, A review of quasi-linear pilot models (1967), IEEE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics
Jagacinski & Flach, Control Theory for Humans (2003)
Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973)
reference: Jagacinski, R. J., & Flach, J. M. (2003). Control Theory for Humans. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Control-Location Expectation Probing
origin: Population stereotype research in human factors; case study from the Ford SYNC 3 team (Parrish Hanna), 2015
summary: Give participants only a goal and record where they first look or reach for the control, revealing population stereotypes for control placement.
description: People hold stereotyped expectations about where controls live and what form they take: seat adjustment under the seat, temperature on a knob. Control-location expectation probing elicits these directly. Participants are given a goal without any hint of the interface ('make it warmer', 'play music') and the researcher records the first place they look or reach, the gesture used and the control type they expect. Aggregated across participants, the results show dominant stereotypes and how consistent they are; repeated over product generations, they show expectations shifting, for example from physical Play buttons to screens. Ford used it within observational research on prototypes in simulators and on the road, triangulated with clinics, surveys and large-sample validation. It is related to first-click testing but works in physical space.
steps: Choose core tasks and phrase each as a goal without naming any control.
Present the goal to each participant in a realistic setting (vehicle, simulator, device mock-up).
Record the first search location, gaze or reach, the gesture and the expected control type.
Ask briefly why they looked there, after the first response.
Aggregate locations and types across participants to identify dominant stereotypes and their strength.
Repeat over time or product generations to track shifting expectations.
outputs: Expected control locations and types per task, with agreement levels and trends over time.
useWhen: Placing physical or on-screen controls in vehicles, appliances, devices or dense interfaces, and deciding whether to move a function between physical and digital control.
avoidWhen: When users have learned a specific product deeply (expectations reflect that product); for screen-only layouts a first-click test is cheaper.
whyLost: Population stereotype studies are standard in automotive and industrial human factors but seldom framed as a UX method elsewhere.
whereToUse: In-car controls, smart appliances, VR and AR interfaces, medical devices and kiosks.
example: Asked to 'make it cooler', 18 of 24 drivers reach for a physical knob rather than the touchscreen. The team keeps a physical temperature control despite pressure to move climate to the screen.
reference: Rowland, C., Goodman, E., Charlier, M., Light, A. and Lui, A. (2015) Designing Connected Products: UX for the Consumer Internet of Things. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 332-333.

name: Controlled Experiments with Groups (Groupware Evaluation)
origin: Dix, Finlay, Abowd and Beale (2004), drawing on CSCW experiments such as the York Conferencer and ARKola at Xerox PARC
summary: Plan controlled evaluations of collaborative systems around tasks that force cooperation, with per-participant recording and analysis strategies that survive large group-to-group variation.
description: Evaluating a collaborative system means the unit of analysis is the group, not the person, which multiplies participant numbers and session length so only a few groups can be run. The method is a set of design rules for such experiments. Tasks must require consensus or distributed information and control, and must use the channels under test: shared report writing, design on a shared pinboard, ranking games such as desert survival, or time-critical simulated process control. Each participant's view, sound, keystrokes and video are recorded so their experience can be relived, with only rough synchronisation across people. Because groups vary so much, even a clean result needs at least four groups per condition to reach 5 percent significance, so analysts use within-group designs, micro-analysis of measures such as gaps between utterances, or incident analysis of breakdowns. Unlike group task analysis, which models the work, this compares system conditions experimentally.
steps: Estimate participant numbers in groups rather than individuals, and allow session time for the group to build rapport.
Choose a task that requires consensus or distributed information and control, and that exercises the communication channels the system provides.
Record, for each participant, what they saw and heard plus their own input and video, synchronising roughly across participants.

Decide the analysis strategy in advance: within-group comparison of conditions, micro-analysis of fine-grained measures (for example gaps between utterances) suited to parametric tests, or critical-incident analysis of breakdowns using conversation analysis.
Plan for at least four groups per condition if a between-groups significance test is intended, or switch to a within-group design.
Spend groups on conditions likely to be informative rather than strict controls, and consider a field study of an existing team where group formation would distort the result.
outputs: Per-participant records of each session and quantitative or incident-based comparisons between system conditions.
useWhen: Comparing designs of collaborative tools (shared canvases, co-editing, video meeting features, multiplayer coordination) where the question is how the group performs, not how individuals use the interface.
avoidWhen: When only a handful of groups can be recruited and a statistical claim is needed; when the real question is how existing teams work (use field studies, Distributed Cognition Analysis or Group Task Analysis instead).
whyLost: Group experiments are slow and costly and rarely reach significance; CSCW moved towards field studies, and product teams test collaborative features with individuals or analytics.
whereToUse: Shared whiteboards and design tools, co-authoring, incident-response and trading consoles, multiplayer games, AI assistants in meetings.
example: A team testing two presence indicators for a co-editing tool runs eight triads on a shared brief, each triad using both designs in counterbalanced order. Per-person screen and audio recordings let them count overwrite collisions and repair talk within each group.
reference: Dix, A., Finlay, J., Abowd, G. D. and Beale, R. (2004). Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed.). Harlow: Pearson.

name: Controlling for Prior Experience (Weighted t-Test)
origin: Post-stratification weighting from survey statistics; applied to UX benchmarks by Sauro (2018)
summary: Adjusts competitive comparisons so a product is not rewarded just because more of its testers already used it.
description: People who already use a product rate it higher and perform better on it. If one product's sample contains more existing users than another's, comparisons are biased. Sauro's approach weights each group so that the proportion of experienced and new users matches across products (or a target mix), then runs a weighted t-test. This is a simple form of post-stratification. It is especially important in competitive benchmarks recruited from general panels, where a market leader will naturally have more prior users.
steps: Record prior experience with each product (for example: never, under a year, over a year).
Choose a target mix of experience levels, such as the overall sample proportions.
Compute weights for each participant so each product's sample matches the target mix.
Run a weighted t-test or weighted regression on the metric of interest.
Report unweighted and weighted results side by side.
outputs: Comparisons fair to products with different user bases.
useWhen: Competitive and retrospective benchmarks where samples differ in familiarity.
avoidWhen: Experience groups are tiny, which makes weights unstable.
whyLost: Weighting is routine in survey research but almost unheard of in usability reports.
whereToUse: Competitive benchmarks, multi-brand customer surveys.
example: A market leader's SUS lead of 9 points shrinks to 3 after weighting for its much larger share of existing customers.
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapter 11.

name: Convergent and Discriminant Validity (CR, AVE, Fornell-Larcker, HTMT)
origin: Claes Fornell & David Larcker, 1981; HTMT by Henseler, Ringle & Sarstedt, 2015
summary: Checks from CFA loadings that each construct's items converge (CR, AVE ≥ 0.50) and that constructs are distinct (Fornell-Larcker criterion or HTMT < 0.85).
description: Before interpreting structural paths, the measurement model must show that indicators measure their construct well and that constructs are not redundant. With standardised loadings λi and error variances θi = 1 − λi², composite reliability CR = (Σλi)² / ((Σλi)² + Σθi) and average variance extracted AVE = Σλi² / (Σλi² + Σθi). Convergent validity requires AVE ≥ 0.50; discriminant validity requires each construct's √AVE to exceed its correlations with other constructs (Fornell-Larcker) or the heterotrait-monotrait ratio to be below 0.85. Vivek Gopinath's payments case reports Trust CR 0.87/AVE 0.69, Fraud Risk 0.82/0.61, Slowness 0.81/0.57 and Support 0.83/0.62, with Cronbach's α of 0.86 (TR) and 0.79 (SL), and drops indicators loading below 0.60 unless theory demands.
steps: Run CFA and obtain standardised loadings for each construct.
Compute θi = 1 − λi² for each indicator.
Compute CR and AVE per construct; require AVE ≥ 0.50.
Compute √AVE and compare with inter-construct correlations (Fornell-Larcker), or compute HTMT and require < 0.85.
Drop or revise indicators with loadings < 0.60 unless theory demands them, and re-run.
Report CR, AVE, α and the discriminant test in the measurement table.
outputs: A measurement validity table with CR, AVE, α and discriminant tests.
useWhen: Whenever latent constructs measured by multi-item scales feed an SEM or regression.
avoidWhen: With single-item measures or purely observed variables.
whyLost: Routine in marketing and IS research, but UX surveys rarely report construct validity beyond α.
whereToUse: Trust, security, ease and satisfaction scales in fintech and SaaS research.
example: Before modelling tap-to-pay adoption, the researcher confirms that Trust (AVE 0.69) and Fraud Risk (AVE 0.61) are distinct constructs with HTMT below 0.85.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Campbell & Fiske, Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix (1959), Psychological Bulletin
Eid & Diener (eds.), Handbook of Multimethod Measurement in Psychology (2006)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Fornell, C., & Larcker, D. F. (1981). Evaluating structural equation models with unobservable variables and measurement error. Journal of Marketing Research, 18(1), 39–50.

name: Convergent Mixed Methods Design
origin: John Creswell and Vicki Plano Clark (2003 onwards), renamed from concurrent triangulation; roots in Campbell and Fiske (1959) multitrait-multimethod logic
summary: Collect and analyse quantitative and qualitative data on parallel questions in one phase, then merge the results and deliberately follow up any divergence.
description: One of the three core mixed methods designs, renamed from 'concurrent triangulation' to stress the intent of integration rather than timing. Both strands address parallel concepts, usually in the same period and often with a qualitative sample nested in the larger quantitative one. Each dataset is analysed separately with its own procedures, then merged: side by side in a discussion, by transforming qualitative codes into variables, or in a joint display. Fit between results is judged as concordance, expansion, complementarity or discordance (Fetters, 2020), leading to meta-inferences. The rigour lies in two requirements often skipped: questions must be genuinely parallel so results can be compared, and divergence must be pursued by re-analysis, more data or questioning one database, not simply noted as a limitation. Unequal sample sizes are handled by equalising, weighting or justifying the difference.
steps: Write parallel quantitative and qualitative questions about the same concepts.
Collect both datasets in the same phase, deciding whether the qualitative sample is nested in, overlaps with or is separate from the quantitative one.
Analyse each dataset separately with its own procedures.
Merge the results side by side, through data transformation, or in a joint display organised by concept.
Judge fit for each concept as concordance, expansion, complementarity or discordance.
Follow up discordance by re-analysing, collecting more data or questioning the quality of one source.
State meta-inferences and how each strand contributed.
outputs: A joint display, an assessment of fit per concept, follow-up of divergences and integrated meta-inferences.
useWhen: When a decision needs both breadth and depth on the same question at the same time, such as a release evaluation combining a survey and interviews.
avoidWhen: When one strand should inform the other's design or sampling; use a sequential explanatory or exploratory design. Avoid if the strands cannot address parallel questions.
whyLost: UX teams routinely run surveys and interviews together and call it triangulation, but rarely align questions or follow up divergence, so the integration that defines the design is lost.
whereToUse: Post-launch evaluations, annual customer research programmes, AI feature adoption studies combining telemetry, surveys and interviews.
example: A project management tool runs a 1,500-person survey and 15 interviews on a new timeline view in the same month. The joint display shows high satisfaction scores but interviews describe workarounds; the discordance prompts a log analysis confirming that heavy users export to spreadsheets.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Creswell, J. W. and Plano Clark, V. L. (2018). Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (3rd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Conversation Analysis
origin: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson, 1974 (turn-taking paper, Language)
summary: Micro-analyses naturally occurring talk, including talk with machines, for turn-taking, sequence structure and repair, revealing the implicit rules users bring to interaction.
description: Conversation Analysis studies the sequential organisation of real talk: how turns are allocated, how adjacency pairs (question and answer, offer and acceptance) structure exchanges, how trouble is repaired, and how dispreferred responses are delayed and mitigated. It works from recordings transcribed in Jefferson notation, capturing pauses to a tenth of a second, overlaps and intonation. Because CA treats interaction as orderly at the finest level, it is unusually powerful for conversational interfaces: it shows exactly where a voice assistant or chatbot breaks users' expectations of how the next turn should go. Rigour comes from using naturally occurring rather than elicited data, detailed transcription, and grounding every claim in participants' own displayed orientations in the next turn.
steps: Collect naturally occurring interaction data: CA requires authentic data — actual user-chatbot logs, voice assistant recordings, or customer service chat transcripts.
Jefferson transcription notation: Capture overlapping speech ([ ]), latency ((0.5)), elongated sounds (::), cut-off words (-). The transcript is an analytic document.
Identify sequential structure: What adjacency pairs exist (question-answer, greeting-greeting)? Where do sequences complete normally and where do they break? Breakdowns are your design data.
Repair sequences: When non-understanding is signalled (explicit question, repetition, silence), how is repair initiated? Failure to achieve repair is the UX problem.
Preferred vs. dispreferred responses: Dispreferred responses (disagreement, rejection) are typically delayed, prefaced, or mitigated. CA reveals the social logic of how users phrase requests.
outputs: Jefferson-notated transcripts, a collection of sequence types and repair patterns, documented breakdown points in human-machine dialogue, and design rules for turn design.
useWhen: Designing or evaluating chatbots, voice assistants, LLM agents, call-centre scripts or any product where interaction is turn-based talk, and you have real conversation logs or recordings.
avoidWhen: You only have interview data about conversations rather than the conversations themselves, or you need fast directional feedback; use usability testing of the conversational flow instead.
whyLost: Transcription is slow and the notation intimidating, and CA's refusal to speculate about intentions frustrates teams wanting quick insight, so it stayed in sociology and academic HCI.
whereToUse: Conversational AI and LLM assistants, voice interfaces, customer support chat, telehealth consultations, and multi-party collaboration tools.
example: Analysing 200 logged exchanges with a banking chatbot, a researcher finds users repeat their question with added detail when the bot answers after a long latency, treating the delay as non-understanding. Adding a brief acknowledgement turn cuts repetition.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Moore, R. J. & Arar, R. (2019) Conversational UX Design
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Sacks, H., Schegloff, E. A. & Jefferson, G. (1974). A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language, 50(4), 696-735.

name: Conversation Analysis Applied to UI
origin: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson (1974); Suchman (1987); Moore and Arar (2019)
summary: Micro-analyses turn-taking, adjacency pairs, repair and preference organisation in human-system dialogue to pinpoint where conversational interfaces break down.
description: Conversation analysis studies the sequential organisation of talk: turn-taking, adjacency pairs (question-answer), repair sequences and preference organisation. Suchman applied it to HCI, showing that plan-based models miss the situated, moment-by-moment character of interaction. The treatise's transfer: analyse chatbot and voice transcripts for repair sequences (retries, corrections, clarifications), system misattributions (treating the wrong prior turn as relevant) and failed adjacency pairs (responding to the wrong question). CA offers a principled vocabulary for diagnosing exactly where breakdowns occur, and Moore and Arar's Natural Conversation Framework operationalises CA patterns for conversational design.
steps: Collect real interaction transcripts or recordings, with consent.
Transcribe in CA detail where needed (timing, overlaps, pauses for voice).
Identify sequences: adjacency pairs, insertion sequences, repairs and closings.
Locate breakdowns: failed pairs, misattributions, repair loops and abandonment.
Build a collection of instances for each breakdown type.
Design conversational patterns (clarification, confirmation, repair) and re-analyse after release.
outputs: Annotated transcripts, breakdown collections, conversational pattern library.
useWhen: Chatbots, voice assistants, IVR, LLM chat interfaces, multi-turn agents.
avoidWhen: Non-conversational GUIs; use other evaluation methods.
whyLost: Requires specialist transcription and analysis skills; conversational UX revived but mostly with intent-accuracy metrics.
whereToUse: Customer service bots, LLM assistants, voice in cars, healthcare triage bots.
example: CA of 300 bank chatbot transcripts finds 22% of breakdowns occur when users answer the bot's question with a question; adding insertion-sequence handling halves escalations at that point.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Sacks H, Schegloff EA & Jefferson G (1974) A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language 50:696-735
Suchman L (1987) Plans and Situated Actions
Moore RJ & Arar R (2019) Conversational UX Design
reference: Sacks H, Schegloff EA & Jefferson G (1974) A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language 50(4):696-735.

name: Conversation Analysis for Chatbot Evaluation
origin: Sacks, Schegloff & Jefferson, 1974; applied by Erika Hall, 2018
summary: Analyses chatbot or voice assistant transcripts turn by turn using conversation analysis concepts such as adjacency pairs, repair and preference organisation.
description: Conversation analysis (CA) studies how people organise talk-in-interaction: turn-taking, adjacency pairs such as question and answer, repair of misunderstandings, and preference for certain responses over others. Applied to chatbots and voice assistants, CA examines real transcripts turn by turn to see where the system violates conversational expectations, for example by failing to recognise repair initiations, answering a question that was not asked, or producing dispreferred responses without mitigation. Because breakdowns are located precisely in the sequence, the findings map directly onto dialogue design changes. Rigour comes from systematic transcription, analysing sequences rather than isolated utterances, building collections of comparable cases, and checking interpretations against what the next turn reveals about how the user understood the system.
steps: Collect 50+ chatbot conversation transcripts. Code each turn for:
adjacency pair completion (does the bot's response constitute an appropriate second pair part?),
repair (does the bot handle user corrections?),

topic closure (does the conversation reach a coherent ending?). Compute violation rates per category. Target: adjacency pair completion > 85%, repair success > 70%. Violations are redesign priorities.
outputs: Annotated transcripts, a catalogue of breakdown types (failed repair, misaligned turns, dispreferred responses), frequency counts and design recommendations for dialogue flows.
useWhen: Evaluating chatbots, voice assistants and LLM-based agents where conversational breakdowns, not screen layouts, drive the experience.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need large-scale quantitative evaluation alone (use automated metrics and log analytics), or when transcripts are unavailable or cannot be ethically used.
whyLost: Conversation analysis is a demanding academic discipline; conversational UX grew fast from engineering, evaluated with intent accuracy and CSAT rather than interaction structure.
whereToUse: Chatbot and voice assistant UX, LLM interface evaluation, IVR system design, customer service bot testing.
example: A bank reviews 200 transcripts of its AI assistant and finds users repeatedly attempt self-repair ('no, I meant...') that the bot treats as new intents; adding repair handling cuts escalations by a fifth.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Sacks H, Schegloff EA & Jefferson G (1974) A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language 50(4):696-735

name: Conversation Log Review and Tuning
donor: Speech technology (IVR tuning); conversational product practice
origin: IVR industry practice (Balentine and Morgan 2001; Cohen, Giangola and Balogh 2004); bot-builder practice reported by Shevat (2017) and Pearl (2017)
summary: Reads and classifies chatbot or voice-interface logs turn by turn, locating where conversations fail, then tunes prompts, models and thresholds and regression-tests the changes.
description: Conversational interfaces leave a complete transcript of every session, a direct record of what users try to do. The rigorous form comes from IVR tuning: log every turn by design, including recognition result and confidence, N-best list, audio, state name, no-speech timeouts, no-matches, latency and barge-in. Humans transcribe a sample of utterances because the recogniser cannot measure its own accuracy. In-grammar utterances are classified as correct accept, false accept or false reject, out-of-grammar ones as correct reject or false accept, separating out-of-domain from in-domain failures. Per-state indicators (dropout, silence, repeats, back, modality) locate problems; thresholds, timeouts, vocabularies and prompt wording are tuned; and recorded audio is rerun to confirm improvement. Chatbot practice adds routing unmatched inputs to editors and logging success and failure events with their place in the dialogue.
steps: Specify logging of every turn with developers from the start: input, recognised intent or result, confidence, state or node, errors, latency and outcome; anonymise transcripts and audio.
Start by reading raw transcripts end to end to learn how users actually phrase requests.
Hand-transcribe or label a sample of utterances and classify each as correct accept, false accept, false reject or correct reject, separating in-domain from out-of-domain inputs.
Review per-state indicators such as dropout, no-match and timeout rates, repeats, back and help requests, and escalation to a human.
Route unmatched inputs to a shared queue where editors review them weekly and extend intents or flows, prioritising frequent signals over fringe requests.
Tune confidence thresholds, timeouts, vocabularies, intents and prompt wording; in pilots, set a goal such as 75% of utterances handled.
Regression-test by rerunning recorded inputs through the tuned system to confirm error rates fall without new breakage; repeat continuously.
outputs: Recognition and intent accuracy breakdowns by state, recurring failure points, unmatched-input lists, tuned parameters and prompts, and regression results.
useWhen: Any live chatbot, voice assistant, IVR or LLM-based conversational product that needs to find and fix failures after launch.
avoidWhen: When logs cannot be anonymised or shared lawfully. Accuracy alone is a poor success measure, and human transcription is costly at large scale; failures may lie in recognition, understanding or back end, so diagnose before tuning. For interactional quality use Conversation Analysis for Chatbot Evaluation.
whyLost: The disciplined IVR tuning cycle was largely forgotten when chatbot teams moved to dashboards of containment and intent counts.
whereToUse: Customer service bots, voice assistants, LLM copilots, healthcare triage bots, banking IVR.
example: A bank's support bot logs show 18% of 'card' utterances falling to the fallback node; labelling 500 of them reveals users saying 'freeze' rather than 'block', so the team adds the intent phrasing and reruns the logged set, cutting fallbacks to 6%.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Pearl, C. (2017). Designing Voice User Interfaces. O'Reilly Media, pp. 198-216; Cohen, M. H., Giangola, J. P. and Balogh, J. (2004). Voice User Interface Design. Addison-Wesley.

name: Conversational implicature audit
origin: H. P. Grice, 1975; Levinson's theory of generalised conversational implicature, 2000
summary: Identifies what users are likely to infer beyond the literal content of interface messages, checking for unintended implications that mislead decisions.
description: Implicature is meaning communicated beyond what is literally said, inferred from the assumption that the speaker is cooperative. 'Some of your files were backed up' implies not all; 'Your password was changed recently' may imply a security problem. Levinson identified generalised implicatures that arise by default, such as scalar inferences. Interfaces generate implicatures constantly, often unintended: an error message that blames a component implies the user did nothing wrong; a confirmation without a warning implies there are no consequences. An implicature audit lists each message's literal content and probable inferences, checks them against truth and intent, and tests with users. Rigour comes from eliciting inferences from users, not only expert judgement, and focusing on decision-relevant implications.
steps: Select messages that inform decisions: errors, warnings, status, confirmations, recommendations and AI answers.
For each, write the literal content and expert-predicted implicatures (scalar, relevance, manner-based).
Elicit actual inferences from 10-20 users with questions such as 'What does this tell you?' and 'What would you do next?'
Code inferences as intended, unintended but harmless, or unintended and harmful; flag any harmful inference held by more than 20% of users.
Rewrite to cancel harmful implicatures explicitly or change what is said.
Re-test rewritten messages with new participants.
outputs: A message inventory with literal content, intended and actual inferences, harmful implicature list, and rewrites.
useWhen: When messages influence safety, financial or health decisions; for AI outputs; when users act on misread messages.
avoidWhen: For simple, low-stakes messages where inference cannot cause harm; a style guide review is enough.
whyLost: Implicature is core pragmatics but UX writing focuses on clarity and tone, not on systematically checking what is implied.
whereToUse: Clinical alerts, banking notifications, security messages, AI assistants, and legal consent.
example: After a surgical robot error, the message 'Arm 2 recovered successfully' leads 60% of surgeons to infer the procedure can continue as normal, although calibration was lost. The message is revised to state recalibration is required.
sources: Gleason, J. B., The Development of Language
The Inquiry Series, Ch 18 — Pragmatics — What Language Actually Does
reference: Levinson, S. C. (2000). Presumptive Meanings: The Theory of Generalized Conversational Implicature. MIT Press.

name: Conversational Survey (Chatbot-Administered Questionnaire)
aka: Chatbot-administered questionnaires with multimodal sentiment capture
origin: Chatbot survey studies from the late 2010s; the multimodal version described by Chira, Mathioudis and colleagues (ALAMEDA project, 2023)
summary: Deliver a standard questionnaire as a branching chatbot conversation with button or free-text answers, optionally capturing sentiment, while watching for mode effects against web forms.
description: A conversational survey turns each questionnaire item into a turn in a chat flow, with question, answer and follow-up branches. Respondents answer by buttons or free text, with entity recognition for dates and numbers, and optional open conversations collect context a form would miss. The ALAMEDA project modelled patient-reported-outcome questionnaires for stroke, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's patients this way, choosing with clinicians and patient groups which questionnaires suited conversation, and fused text sentiment with camera-based facial emotion recognition into a session sentiment that could steer the dialogue. Because a validated instrument changes when its mode changes, the conversational version must be checked for mode effects (item wording, response scale presentation, social presence) against the form it replaces. The ALAMEDA evaluation was preliminary: text sentiment F1 of 0.56 to 0.76 and no ground truth for the fused estimate.
steps: Gather requirements with representative respondents and domain experts, and choose which questionnaires suit a conversational format.
Model each questionnaire as a conversation flow with question, answer and follow-up branches, keeping validated item wording and response options intact.
Offer button and free-text answers, with entity recognition for dates and numbers and confirmation of parsed values.
Optionally add open conversational prompts for context, and sentiment capture only with explicit consent.
Pilot against the original form with the same respondents or randomised groups to check for mode effects on scores and completion.
Store responses and transcripts in a structured form that analysts can link back to the original instrument scoring.
outputs: Questionnaire responses scored as in the original instrument, dialogue transcripts, completion data, and optional per-session sentiment estimates.
useWhen: Repeated self-report from users who find forms burdensome, such as patients, older adults or mobile-only populations, or when follow-up probing of answers adds value.
avoidWhen: When strict comparability with historical form-based data is required and mode effects cannot be tested (see Mode Effects Analysis in Survey Administration); long batteries where chat adds time; or sensitive topics where a bot's social presence may change disclosure.
whyLost: It is growing in health research and survey tooling but remains niche in UX practice, where most surveys are still forms and mode effects of chat delivery are seldom tested.
whereToUse: Patient-reported outcomes in digital health, in-product micro-surveys, longitudinal check-ins in coaching or wellbeing apps, research with low-literacy users.
example: A rehabilitation app delivers a weekly fatigue scale as a chat. A two-week crossover against the web form shows equivalent scores but 18 percent higher completion, so the chat becomes the default with periodic form checks.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Chira, C., Mathioudis, E., Michailidou, C., Agathangelou, P., Christodoulou, G., Katakis, I., Kontopoulos, E., & Avgerinakis, K. (2023).
