An affective multi-modal conversational agent for non intrusive data collection from patients with brain diseases. In Følstad et al. (Eds.), Chatbot Research and Design (LNCS 13815). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-25581-6_9

name: Cool Drilldown
origin: Karen Holtzblatt and Hugh Beyer, Cool Project (InContext), Contextual Design evolved (2013-2014)
summary: A three-to-four-day workshop in which sub-teams each enrich the same product concept using the design principles of one Cool Concept, then reconcile them into one design.
description: Visioning is too fast to reflect on how a product supports motives, identity and fit to the day, so once product concepts exist the team works through them one at a time. For each of four to six concepts, the team splits into sub-teams, each assigned one Cool Concept (Accomplishment, Connection, Identity, Sensation, Direct into Action, The Hassle Factor, The Learning Delta) with its eight to ten design principles. Each sub-team returns to the affinity and models for relevant data, then brainstorms and sketches additions that strengthen that Cool Concept. A full-team review reconciles the independent enhancements into a single revised concept. Sub-teams rotate Cool Concepts across product concepts so everyone learns all of them. A Cool Drilldown review is also recommended after two rounds of mock-up testing, to restore a structural view.
steps: Select four to six product concepts from visioning.
For one concept, form sub-teams and give each one Cool Concept with its design principles.
Each sub-team reviews the relevant field data, then brainstorms and sketches enhancements for its Cool Concept.
The full team reviews and reconciles all enhancements into one revised concept.
Repeat for each product concept, rotating Cool Concepts among sub-teams.
After two rounds of mock-up testing, rerun a shorter drilldown review on the evolving design.
outputs: Enriched product concept sketches and shared understanding of the Cool Concept design principles.
useWhen: Use after visioning when concepts are functional but emotionally thin, and the team has field data on motives, identity and daily life.
avoidWhen: Avoid without field data on the Cool Concepts; the principles are not listed in the 2014 lecture and need Holtzblatt's other sources. To check the emotional effect on users use Think-Aloud with Emotional Annotation or Prototype Testing.
whyLost: It is a proprietary step of a heavy process, published briefly, and needs several days of a full team; few organisations outside InContext's clients have run it.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, workplace tools needing adoption, products competing on experience rather than features.
example: A team's trip-planning concept gains shared itineraries from the Connection sub-team, a progress view from Accomplishment and one-tap booking from Direct into Action, merged in a single review.
reference: Holtzblatt, K. and Beyer, H. (2014). Contextual Design: Evolved. Synthesis Lectures on Human-Centered Informatics #24. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool. doi:10.2200/S00597ED1V01Y201409HCI024, pp. 22, 49-51, 70.

name: Cooper's Magic Principle
origin: Alan Cooper, Interaction Design Practicum course (as cited by Scott and Neil, 2009)
summary: Imagine the user could complete a task by magic, then compare with the current steps to expose which steps are artefacts of technology rather than parts of the goal.
description: The magic principle is a thought experiment for escaping technology-driven design. The team decomposes a current task into its concrete steps, then describes how the user's goal would be met if magic were available. Comparing the two marks the steps that vanish as artefacts of the technology rather than of the goal. Taking magic to the extreme (no camera at all) is unhelpful; keeping some real elements makes the artefactual steps stand out. In Scott and Neil's example, sharing photos meant finding a cable, importing, uploading with a second program, copying a link and emailing; with magic, the camera would know it was a birthday and share the photos itself. Wi-Fi memory cards later removed the cable. The same lens exposes artefactual pages in multi-step web flows.
steps: Decompose the current task into its concrete steps, ideally from observation.
Describe how the user's goal would be met if magic were available, keeping the key real objects in place.
Compare the two lists and mark the steps that disappear as technology artefacts.
Rank artefactual steps by frequency and effort.
Design to remove, automate or merge the artefactual steps, and check the result against the user's goal.
outputs: A list of artefactual steps and design opportunities to remove or automate them.
useWhen: Use when redesigning a multi-step flow that grew around system constraints, or when a team needs to separate user goals from current tooling.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on the team's own picture of the steps: observe them with Contextual Inquiry or Hierarchical Task Analysis. Scott and Neil give only a one-page illustration, so it is closer to ideation than research.
whyLost: It circulated in Cooper's teaching and a few practitioner books rather than as a documented method, and its goal-directed spirit was absorbed into Jobs-to-be-Done language.
whereToUse: Checkout and onboarding flows, document workflows, IoT set-up, AI assistants that can automate steps.
example: An expense app lists eleven steps from receipt to reimbursement; in the magic version the card transaction becomes the expense. Photographing, typing amounts and choosing categories are marked as artefacts and replaced by automatic matching.
reference: Scott, B. and Neil, T. (2009). Designing Web Interfaces: Principles and Patterns for Rich Interactions. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 158-159.

name: Cooper-Harper Rating Scale
origin: George Cooper and Robert Harper, NASA, 1969 (NASA TN D-5153); modified for workload by Wierwille and Casali, 1983
summary: A decision-tree rating scale in which evaluators answer sequential yes/no questions about controllability and adequacy before assigning a 1-10 rating.
description: Cooper-Harper was designed for test pilots to rate aircraft handling qualities. Instead of asking for a number directly, the scale leads raters through a decision tree: Is it controllable? Is adequate performance attainable with tolerable workload? Is it satisfactory without improvement? Only then do they choose among three descriptors in the relevant branch. This anchoring produces highly consistent ratings and clear thresholds, with ratings of 4 and above indicating deficiencies that warrant improvement and 7 and above major deficiencies. The Modified Cooper-Harper version adapts it to cognitive workload for non-control tasks. The decision-tree structure is a valuable model for any UX rating that needs reliable, actionable categories.
steps: Define the task, performance standards (desired and adequate) and the conditions under which it is rated.
Have expert or trained raters perform the task under each design condition.
Administer the decision tree immediately after each trial, following the yes/no questions in order.
Record the final 1-10 rating and the rater's comments explaining deficiencies.
Compare designs by median rating and by the proportion of ratings falling in 'deficiency warrants improvement' (4-6) or 'major deficiencies' (7-9).
Use comments to diagnose the specific causes of poor ratings.
outputs: Anchored ratings per condition, proportions in each deficiency band, and qualitative diagnostic comments.
useWhen: Expert evaluation of control-intensive interactions (gestures, game controllers, drones, vehicle HMIs) where consistent go/no-go thresholds matter.
avoidWhen: General satisfaction or attitudinal research; use SUS or UEQ.
whyLost: It belongs to flight test culture and requires trained raters. UX favours numeric Likert scales without decision-tree anchoring.
whereToUse: Drone and robotics control apps, game controllers, in-car touch controls, accessibility switch control.
example: Evaluating a remote drone inspection app, trained pilots rate precision hover with on-screen sticks at 6 (moderate compensation required) and with physical controller at 3, justifying controller support.
sources: Cooper & Harper, The use of pilot rating in the evaluation of aircraft handling qualities (1969), NASA TN D-5153
Wierwille & Casali, A validated rating scale for global mental workload measurement applications (1983), Human Factors Society
reference: Cooper, G. E., & Harper, R. P. (1969). NASA Technical Note D-5153.

name: Cooperative Evaluation
origin: Andrew Monk, Peter Wright, Jeanne Haber and Lora Davenport, Improving Your Human-Computer Interface: A Practical Technique (1993)
summary: A relaxed think-aloud variant in which the participant acts as a collaborator who criticises the system, while evaluator and participant may question each other during tasks.
description: In standard think-aloud the participant is a subject and the evaluator stays silent. Cooperative evaluation reframes the participant as a co-evaluator of the system: they think aloud from the start and are invited to criticise. The evaluator may ask 'why' or 'what if' questions when behaviour is unclear, and the participant may ask the evaluator for clarification when stuck. Dix and colleagues list its advantages: the process is less constrained and easier for evaluators to learn, users are encouraged to criticise, and confusion is clarified the moment it occurs, which maximises the number of problems found. Its value rests on recording the session and analysing the resulting protocol, optionally with a post-task walkthrough. It was designed as a practical technique for designers without psychology training.
steps: Prepare realistic tasks and brief the participant that they are a collaborator evaluating the system, not the person being tested, and that criticism is wanted.
Ask the participant to think aloud while doing each task.
When behaviour is unclear, ask why or what-if questions rather than waiting silently.
Answer the participant's requests for clarification when a problem arises, noting each point of confusion.
Record audio, video and screen so the session forms a protocol.
Analyse the protocol for problem areas and the user's explanations, adding a post-task walkthrough of the recording if needed.
outputs: A recorded protocol and a list of problem areas with users' explanations and criticisms.
useWhen: Formative evaluation of prototypes by designers or small teams who want many problems and their reasons quickly, especially when evaluators are not trained in strict think-aloud.
avoidWhen: Avoid for time-on-task or other performance measures, because questioning alters how tasks are done; use a summative usability test or classic concurrent think-aloud instead. Reports are subjective and selective.
whyLost: Its features were absorbed into ordinary moderated think-aloud practice, which now routinely allows probing, so the name and the explicit collaborator framing are largely forgotten.
whereToUse: Early prototype rounds, internal tools with expert users who enjoy critiquing, co-design sessions that shade into evaluation.
example: A designer tests a clinic booking prototype with receptionists framed as co-evaluators. When one hesitates over 'hold slot', the designer asks what she expected, and she explains the term means something else in her practice, leading to a relabel.
reference: Monk, A., Wright, P., Haber, J. and Davenport, L. (1993). Improving Your Human-Computer Interface: A Practical Technique. Prentice Hall; described in Dix, A., Finlay, J., Abowd, G. D. and Beale, R. (2004). Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed.). Harlow: Pearson, p. 344.

name: Cooperative Inquiry (Intergenerational Co-Design with Children)
origin: Allison Druin and colleagues, University of Maryland (Druin et al., 1997; Druin, 1999)
summary: A small standing team of children and adults works as equal design partners over many sessions, jointly examining requirements and iterating one design towards a specification.
description: Cooperative inquiry places children closer to equal partners than informants. A small group of children, often a standing KidsTeam recruited from out-of-school groups, meets an adult research and design team over several sessions across weeks. Together they examine requirements, make low-fidelity prototypes and elaborate one another's ideas, converging on a single design; the Children's Digital Library came from this work. Sessions are deliberately informal and playful, with shared snack time. Markopoulos, Read and Giannakos place it mid-way between child-as-informant and child-as-partner and closer to technology specification than to ideation, in contrast with one-off workshop approaches that involve more children and fewer adults. Its rigour comes from continuity: children build expertise in the techniques across projects, and power is consciously balanced between adults and children. Variants include distributed co-design and layered elaboration.
steps: Recruit a small group of children (often six to eight, ideally a standing KidsTeam) and an adult research and design team.
Obtain parental consent and the children's own assent, and plan the ethical case for involving them.
Plan a series of sessions across weeks, each informal and playful, with a shared snack time.
In each session, have adults and children jointly examine requirements and build or elaborate low-fidelity prototypes.
Carry ideas forward across sessions, converging on one design, while keeping adults from dominating decisions.
Retain the team across projects so children build expertise in the techniques.
outputs: Iterated design ideas, prototypes and requirements converging on a specification, plus a team with growing co-design expertise.
useWhen: Designing technology for children where their perspective must shape the concept and specification over time, not just validate adult ideas.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need breadth of children's views quickly; a one-off workshop or Research Interviews with Children suits that. Avoid with highly vulnerable groups unless the ethical case is strong. For evaluating a finished product use Usability Testing with Children and Teens.
whyLost: It is the standard method in child-computer interaction research but needs a standing team and weeks of sessions, which product schedules rarely allow.
whereToUse: Educational technology, children's media and games, family safety and parental-control tools, children's health apps.
example: An edtech company runs a KidsTeam of seven 8-11-year-olds for six weekly sessions on a reading app. The children's paper prototypes reshape the reward system from badges into a shared class story, which becomes the core of the specification.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Druin, A. (1999). Cooperative inquiry: developing new technologies for children with children. Proceedings of CHI '99, 592-599. ACM.

name: Cophenetic and Matrix Correlation Checks for Hierarchical Clustering
origin: Adapted for UX from numerical taxonomy as presented by Romesburg (1984); linkage comparison after Hughes (1979)
summary: Correlate pairwise resemblances with tree-implied distances, and compare matrices or opposite linkage methods, to check whether a hierarchical clustering distorts the data or produces artefactual clusters.
description: A family of checks on whether a dendrogram faithfully represents its data. Tracing each pair of objects to the level where they first join gives the cophenetic matrix; unstringing it and the original resemblance matrix into lists and computing Pearson's r gives the cophenetic correlation, with about 0.8 or more commonly accepted (UPGMA tends to score highest). The same matrix-correlation move compares any two resemblance matrices over the same objects: two measures, two user groups, two coefficients, or a hypothesis-predicted tree against the observed one; many analyses can themselves be clustered to see which agree. A third check clusters the same matrix with single linkage, which chains, and complete linkage, which resists chaining: if the opposite methods give much the same tree the clusters are well defined, and if not they may be artefacts. These checks turn card-sort or similarity dendrograms from pictures into evidence.
steps: Compute the resemblance matrix and cluster it with the chosen method (for example UPGMA).
Derive the cophenetic matrix by recording, for every pair, the level at which they first join in the tree.
Unstring the lower triangles of the resemblance and cophenetic matrices into two lists, plot them, and compute Pearson's r; treat about 0.8 or above as acceptable distortion.

Re-cluster the same matrix with single linkage and complete linkage and compare the trees visually or by correlating their cophenetic matrices; treat groups stable across both as real and investigate groups found in only one.
To compare two measures, groups or coefficients, correlate their resemblance matrices (preferred over cophenetic matrices) against a tolerance set in advance.
Report the coefficients with scatter plots, noting that pairs are not independent so no ordinary significance test applies.
outputs: Cophenetic correlation, matrix correlations between analyses, and a judgement on cluster definition and chaining.
useWhen: Interpreting dendrograms from open card sorts, similarity judgements or behavioural clustering, or checking whether two user groups or two methods produce the same similarity structure.
avoidWhen: Partitioning methods such as k-means without a tree (use silhouette or gap statistics); when inferential tests of matrix association are required (use a permutation-based Mantel test). Agreement is evidence, not proof.
whyLost: UX tools draw dendrograms automatically with no fit statistic, and numerical-taxonomy literature never reached practitioners.
whereToUse: Card sorting and tree-test preparation, similarity-based persona or segment clustering, comparing IA mental models across audiences.
example: An open card sort of 60 banking features gives a UPGMA tree with cophenetic r of 0.71, below the 0.8 rule, and the single-linkage tree chains most cards together. The team reports only the three groups stable across both linkages and reruns with more participants.
reference: Romesburg, H. C. (1984). Cluster Analysis for Researchers. Belmont, CA: Lifetime Learning Publications.

name: Corpus Keyness Analysis
origin: Mike Scott (WordSmith Tools, 1996-1997); Paul Rayson and Roger Garside (log-likelihood comparison, 2000); Paul Baker (Using Corpora in Discourse Analysis, 2006)
summary: Statistically compares word frequencies between a target corpus and a reference corpus to find words and collocations that are unusually frequent, revealing distinctive concerns.
description: Corpus linguistics provides robust statistics for comparing language across groups. Keyness compares each word's frequency in a target corpus (e.g. churned users' feedback) with a reference corpus (e.g. retained users' feedback) using log-likelihood or chi-square, with effect sizes such as log ratio. Collocation analysis (MI, t-score, log-Dice) shows which words co-occur, and concordance lines show words in context so interpretation stays grounded. Unlike word clouds or sentiment scores, keyness gives significance and effect size for differences and links back to actual utterances. It sits between qualitative reading and topic modelling, and works well with small to mid-size corpora.
steps: Assemble a target corpus and an appropriate reference corpus, with comparable text types.
Tokenise and lemmatise consistently; decide on handling of case and stop words.
Compute keyness (log-likelihood) and effect size (log ratio) for each word, applying minimum frequency and dispersion thresholds.
Examine collocates of key words and read concordance lines to interpret usage.
Group key words into semantic fields and relate them to user concerns.
Report keyness tables with statistics and illustrative concordances.
outputs: Ranked keyword lists with significance and effect sizes, collocation networks, concordances and interpreted semantic fields.
useWhen: Comparing feedback, reviews, tickets or interview transcripts across groups, versions or time.
avoidWhen: Very small text samples (a few interviews) where close reading suffices.
whyLost: UX text analysis jumped from manual coding to sentiment tools and topic models, skipping corpus linguistics' statistical comparison methods.
whereToUse: Churn feedback, app store reviews before and after releases, support chat logs, community forums.
example: Comparing reviews of the old and new app versions, keyness shows 'buried', 'hunt' and 'used to' as top keywords in the new corpus; concordances reveal frustration about relocated features.
sources: Baker, Using Corpora in Discourse Analysis (2006)
Rayson & Garside, Comparing corpora using frequency profiling (2000), Workshop on Comparing Corpora
Scott & Tribble, Textual Patterns: Key Words and Corpus Analysis in Language Education (2006)
reference: Baker, P. (2006). Using Corpora in Discourse Analysis. Continuum.

name: Correlation Analysis with Confidence Intervals
origin: Galton and Pearson (1890s); Fisher z transformation for intervals (1915)
summary: Measures how strongly two UX measures move together, with an interval showing how sure you can be.
description: Correlation quantifies association: does SUS track completion, does NPS rise with ease ratings, do two tasks share difficulty. Pearson r suits continuous measures, Spearman ranks suit skewed or ordinal data, and phi suits two binary variables. Sauro and Lewis emphasise reporting confidence intervals (via the Fisher z transformation) because small-sample correlations are very unstable: r = 0.5 from 20 people could plausibly be anywhere from about 0.07 to 0.77. They also give sample size formulas for detecting a correlation of a given size and benchmarks for magnitude in UX data. A partial correlation applies the same logic while holding a third variable constant, for example ease and satisfaction controlling for tenure.
steps: Plot the two variables in a scatterplot first to check for non-linearity and outliers.
Choose Pearson, Spearman or phi to fit the data types.
Compute r and its p-value.
Transform to Fisher z, form the interval and transform back.
Interpret magnitude in context and avoid causal language.
outputs: A correlation coefficient with its interval and significance.
useWhen: Checking whether metrics agree, validating questionnaires, exploring drivers before regression.
avoidWhen: You need to know cause or the effect of one variable holding others fixed (use experiments or regression).
whyLost: Commonly reported without intervals or scatterplots, so weak relationships from small samples get over-read.
whereToUse: Questionnaire validation, metrics programmes, survey analysis.
example: Across 30 tasks, SEQ and completion rate correlate at r = 0.62 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.80), supporting SEQ as a quick proxy.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)

name: Correspondence Analysis
origin: Jean-Paul Benzécri and the French analyse des données school (1960s-70s); MCA in Greenacre and Blasius (2006)
summary: Turn a cross-tabulation of categorical variables into a map on which associated row and column categories sit close together, with inertia showing how much association the map retains.
description: Correspondence analysis is the categorical counterpart of principal components analysis. Counts in a contingency table are converted to row and column profiles and masses and chi-square based association measures; dimensions are extracted with the same matrix algebra as PCA, and row and column categories are plotted in one space. Total inertia (chi-square divided by n) measures how much association there is; Mazzocchi suggests above 0.20 for a useful map, and each dimension's share of inertia shows how much the plot keeps. Normalisation (row principal, column principal, symmetrical) decides which distances can be compared, and row-to-column distances are not direct association measures. Rare or irrelevant categories can be made supplementary. Multiple correspondence analysis extends the method to three or more variables via an indicator or Burt matrix. Axis units have no intuitive meaning: the value is in seeing which categories cluster.
steps: Build a contingency table of counts for two categorical variables, categorising continuous ones first.
Compute row and column profiles, masses and chi-square association measures, and extract dimensions (for example with ca in R or prince in Python).
Check total inertia (ideally above 0.20) and the share of inertia on the first two dimensions.
Choose a normalisation: row principal to compare rows, column principal to compare columns, symmetrical otherwise.
Mark sparse or irrelevant categories as supplementary points.
Read the contributions of points to dimensions and of dimensions to points, and name the dimensions.
Plot rows and columns together and interpret proximities within each set; for three or more variables run multiple correspondence analysis.
outputs: A joint map of categories with the inertia explained per dimension, category scores and contribution statistics.
useWhen: Exploring associations between categorical variables such as segment by feature used, plan type by churn reason, or coded interview themes by participant group.
avoidWhen: It gives no formal tests of individual associations (use log-linear models or Chi-Square and Fisher's Exact Tests); rare categories distort the solution; it is a graphical exploration tool, not a dimension-reduction step for large data.
whyLost: It is standard in French and European market research and social science but rarely taught in UX, where PCA and clustering dominate.
whereToUse: Survey cross-tabs, coded open-ended responses, persona and segment profiling, brand and feature perception maps.
example: Cross-tabulating eight churn reasons by four subscription plans for 3,000 exit surveys gives inertia 0.31 with 88 percent on two dimensions. Annual-plan churners sit near 'price' and 'moved to competitor', monthly-plan churners near 'didn't use it enough'.
sources: Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: Greenacre, M. and Blasius, J. (Eds.) (2006). Multiple Correspondence Analysis and Related Methods. Chapman and Hall/CRC; Mazzocchi, M. (2008). Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research. London: SAGE, ch. 14, pp. 300-315.

name: Cortisol Sampling and the Trier Social Stress Test
origin: Kirschbaum, Pirke and Hellhammer (1993) TSST; hair cortisol after Stalder and Kirschbaum (2012)
summary: Measure the stress hormone cortisol in saliva or hair, as reactivity to a standard stressor, as a daily rhythm, or as months of accumulated load.
description: The body has a fast stress system (indexed by skin conductance or salivary alpha-amylase) and a slower one indexed by cortisol, which peaks about 20 to 25 minutes after a stressor, so sampling must be timed. The Trier Social Stress Test, a filmed public speech and mental arithmetic before an unresponsive panel, is the most reliable laboratory stressor, usable from about age seven. Saliva samples give reactivity, the awakening response or diurnal slope; hair samples give an integrated record over months and avoid adherence problems. Results are sensitive to many confounds: food, dairy, medication, time of day, waking and napping. Good practice includes testing at the same clock time, controlling diet, using logged sample containers at home, freezing samples and assaying in batches. Some studies add immune markers and mood scales. For UX, cortisol offers an objective index of stress from high-stakes workflows or sustained tool overload.
steps: Decide what is needed: acute reactivity to a task, diurnal rhythm, or long-term load (hair).
For reactivity, schedule all sessions at the same clock time, take a baseline saliva sample, and ask participants to avoid food, especially dairy, for 30 minutes beforehand.
Apply the stressor or task (the TSST or a demanding product workflow), then sample at about 20-25 and 40 minutes after onset.
Record covariates: medication, waking time, naps, recent food; for home sampling use containers that log opening times.
Freeze samples and assay them in batches with the same antibody lot within 6 to 12 months.
Analyse change from baseline or area under the curve, and relate it to behaviour, task performance and self-report.
outputs: Cortisol reactivity and recovery, diurnal slopes, awakening response, hair cortisol concentration, and their relation to conditions and self-report.
useWhen: You need an objective, hard-to-fake index of physiological stress, for example comparing high-stakes workflow designs or studying chronic overload from work tools.
avoidWhen: You need moment-to-moment emotion or cannot control timing and confounds; use skin conductance, heart rate variability or self-report scales instead. Laboratory stressors raise ethical issues.
whyLost: It requires biological sampling, lab assays, ethics approval and careful timing, which sit outside UX budgets and skills.
whereToUse: Clinical and emergency software, air traffic and control rooms, financial trading, call centres and workplace wellbeing research.
example: A hospital trial compares two medication-ordering systems during simulated night shifts. Saliva taken 25 minutes after each scenario shows lower cortisol rises with the redesigned system, matching fewer self-reported interruptions.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Kirschbaum, C., Pirke, K.-M., & Hellhammer, D. H. (1993). The 'Trier Social Stress Test': A tool for investigating psychobiological stress responses in a laboratory setting. Neuropsychobiology, 28(1-2), 76-81.

name: Cost-Importance Analysis
aka: Cost-importance analysis with priority ratio and line of affordability
origin: Rex Hartson and Pardha Pyla, 2012; frequency adjustment after Karat, Campbell and Fiegel, 1992
summary: Rate each UX problem's importance and cost to fix, rank by their ratio, accumulate costs, and fix everything above the iteration's line of affordability.
description: A cost-importance table lists each UX problem or problem group with an importance rating (M for must fix, then 5, 3 or 1, adjusted up for frequency and learnability impact), a proposed design solution, the cost to fix in person-hours including redesign, and a priority ratio of importance divided by cost multiplied by 1000. Problems are sorted by ratio, cumulative cost is computed down the list, and a line of affordability is drawn where cumulative cost exceeds the resources available for the iteration. Problems above the line are fixed; those below are deferred or accepted. Must-fix items stay above the line regardless of ratio. Variants handle problem groups, ties, multiple candidate solutions, extra weight for safety-critical problems, and a rapid team bubble sort without numbers. Recording actual costs calibrates future estimates.
steps: List UX problems and group related ones that share a fix.
Rate importance to fix as M, 5, 3 or 1, raising it for high frequency or learnability impact and weighting safety-critical problems more.
Propose a design solution for each (not training or documentation).
Estimate cost to fix in person-hours, including redesign effort.
Compute priority ratio = importance / cost x 1000 (M stays M), sort and rank.
Compute cumulative cost down the ranked list and draw the line of affordability at the iteration's resource limit.
Resolve each problem: fix above the line, defer or accept below; record actual costs to calibrate later estimates.
outputs: A ranked, costed fix list for the iteration with an explicit cut-off and rationale.
useWhen: After a usability test or review produces more problems than the team can fix, and the team needs a defensible, transparent cut-off.
avoidWhen: When problems cannot be costed with any confidence or when strategic bets, not fixes, are being prioritised (use Kano Analysis or Research Question Prioritisation Matrix).
whyLost: Effort-impact grids kept the idea but dropped the explicit ratio, cumulative cost and affordability line that make the cut-off auditable.
whereToUse: Agile sprint planning after testing, enterprise software backlogs and regulated products with fixed release budgets.
example: After testing a parking kiosk, a 'Submit' label confusion rated importance 3 is raised to 4 for frequency. Relabelling costs one person-hour, giving a high ratio, and it falls well above a 16 person-hour line.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019) The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience, 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, section 26.4.

name: Cost-sensitive decision thresholds and expected-loss rules
origin: Bayesian decision theory; presented by Ridgeway, 2003 and Bishop, 2006
summary: Set a classifier's decision threshold from the costs of misses and false alarms, not 0.5, and choose models by expected cost, deferring uncertain cases to humans.
description: Inference (estimating class probabilities) is separated from decision. Stakeholders specify a loss matrix of costs for each true versus assigned class. For two classes, if a miss costs c1 and a false alarm c0, expected cost is minimised by acting whenever the predicted probability exceeds c0/(c0+c1), not 0.5. Models are compared by expected cost on held-out data, including trivial rules (flag none, flag all), alongside calibration checks such as the Brier score. A reject option defers cases whose largest posterior falls below a threshold to another process, such as human review. When a model is trained on rebalanced data, posteriors are rescaled by population over training priors. Keeping posteriors allows the loss matrix to change without retraining. Ridgeway's school-dropout example judged a miss 20 times worse than a false flag, giving a threshold of 0.047.
steps: Agree with stakeholders the cost of each error type (and of deferral), and record the reasoning.
Fit probability models and check calibration with a calibration plot and Brier score.
If trained on rebalanced data, rescale posteriors by population priors over training priors and renormalise.
Set the threshold at c0/(c0+c1) for two classes, or assign each case to the class with minimum expected loss.
Optionally set a reject threshold and route uncertain cases to human review, tracking the reject fraction.
Compute expected cost on test data for each model and for the trivial rules, and choose the lowest.
outputs: A decision threshold or rule, reject fraction, and an expected-cost comparison of models.
useWhen: A model drives user-facing actions with asymmetric error costs: fraud flags, churn interventions, content moderation, alerting, triage.
avoidWhen: Probabilities are poorly calibrated, or costs cannot be agreed; costs are judgements and must be stated openly. For ranking tasks where no action threshold exists, use ranking metrics.
whyLost: UX and product teams inherit default 0.5 thresholds and accuracy metrics from data science, and costs of errors to users are seldom elicited.
whereToUse: Fraud and risk alerts, AI-assisted moderation, health triage apps, spam filtering, human-in-the-loop AI products.
example: A fintech app's fraud model blocks payments at 0.5. Research with support teams shows a false block costs about one-tenth of a missed fraud, so the threshold drops to 0.09 with uncertain cases sent to a step-up verification screen.
sources: Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
reference: Bishop, C. M. (2006). Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, section 1.5. Springer; Ridgeway, G. (2003). Strategies and methods for prediction. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining.

name: Counterfactual Probing
origin: Operationalised for UX in Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Interview probes asking participants to contrast before and after a change, or an alternative design, to explain the mechanism behind a measured effect.
description: Quantitative evidence can show that risk fell but not why. Counterfactual probing asks participants to reason about the alternative world: 'If we labelled it Price Alerts at top level, would you choose differently? Why?', or, after a change, how the old and new experiences differ. In the playbook, quotes such as 'Before, I always checked Notifications first' and 'Now Alerts is right where I expect it under Markets' explain the mechanism behind a hazard ratio of 0.68: fewer mistakes and better mental-model alignment. Responses are written into mechanism memos linking minimised QCA paths, quotes and HRs. Rigour comes from pairing probes with measured effects rather than relying on stated preference alone, since participants' counterfactual predictions are fallible.
steps: Identify the measured effect or design change whose mechanism needs explaining.
After the task, ask participants what they expected and whether an alternative label or structure would change their choice.
For post-change sessions, ask participants to contrast the old and new experience in their own words.
Code answers for mechanism (e.g. mental-model alignment, reduced time pressure, increased confidence).
Write mechanism memos linking codes to the quantitative effect.
Treat stated counterfactuals as supporting evidence, not proof, and confirm with behavioural data.
outputs: Mechanism quotes and memos explaining why a measured effect occurred.
useWhen: Alongside A/B or survival results, or in moderated sessions testing label or structure alternatives.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for behavioural evidence; people are poor predictors of their own future behaviour.
whyLost: Counterfactual reasoning is central to causal inference but rarely structured as an interview technique in UX.
whereToUse: IA and labelling changes, onboarding redesigns, pricing page changes, AI feature explanations.
example: After a relabelling lowers abandonment, participants say 'Now Alerts is right where I expect it', confirming the mental-model mechanism behind the hazard ratio.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Section 4.4.

name: Counterfactual simulation from a fitted causal model
origin: Pearl's do-calculus; Bayesian workflow as taught by McElreath (2020)
summary: Use a model fitted to an assumed causal graph to simulate what happens to an outcome when a variable is set to new values, including effects through mediators.
description: Regression coefficients answer predictive questions; product teams usually ask 'what if we changed X?'. This method answers that by simulation. Given a directed acyclic graph, a model is fitted for every variable on the path from the intervention to the outcome. The intervention variable is then set to chosen values, which cuts all arrows entering it, and each downstream variable is simulated in causal order from the posterior samples, carrying parameter and outcome uncertainty. Plotting simulated outcomes against set values gives a counterfactual plot of the total effect, and contrasts between two set values give a causal estimate. Rigour depends entirely on the DAG being right and the effect identified; implausibly large counterfactuals are a warning that linear models are extrapolating.
steps: Take the DAG as given and fit a model for every variable on the path from the intervention to the outcome (a joint model, for example of mediator on cause and outcome on both).
Choose the intervention variable and the range of values to set it to, for example from 2 standard deviations below to 2 above the mean.
Remove all arrows entering the intervention variable, so its usual causes no longer act on it.
For each posterior sample and each set value, simulate downstream variables in causal order, carrying parameter and outcome uncertainty.
Summarise and plot the distribution of simulated outcomes against the set values.
Compute contrasts, such as the expected change in outcome between two set values, and check whether they are plausible given the data range.
outputs: Counterfactual plots of total effect with uncertainty and numerical causal contrasts.
useWhen: An experiment is impossible or slow and you have an explicit causal model of how a design variable affects an outcome through intermediate behaviours.
avoidWhen: When the DAG is contested, the effect is not identified, or the variable cannot be manipulated without changing others; run an experiment or use backdoor adjustment with sensitivity analysis instead.
whyLost: It requires Bayesian modelling and explicit causal graphs, which most UX analytics teams do not maintain; tools report coefficients, not simulated interventions.
whereToUse: Onboarding length and retention, notification frequency and engagement, pricing and churn in SaaS, where mediators such as feature exposure carry part of the effect.
example: A product analyst builds a DAG where onboarding length affects feature exposure and both affect 30-day retention. Simulating onboarding set from 3 to 7 steps shows the total effect, including the indirect path, is small and uncertain, so the team runs a test rather than a redesign.
reference: McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan (2nd ed.). CRC Press, pp. 140-144.

name: Course-of-Action Analysis with Self-Confrontation Interviews
donor: French-language ergonomics and cognitive systems engineering
origin: Jacques Theureau, as presented in Hollnagel (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
summary: Record work continuously, then have people watch video of their own activity to describe what they perceived, intended and felt, modelling their lived course of action for redesign.
description: A French ergonomics approach that treats activity as embodied, situated and cultured (enaction). Its 'observatory' combines continuous recording of behaviour, provoked verbalisation during work where feasible, self-confrontation interviews in which each person watches video of their own activity and describes what they perceived, intended, felt and knew at each moment, explicitation interviews for what video misses, and second-degree self-confrontation in which participants become co-analysts of their own activity. The observation period is sized to the natural unit of activity, such as one call, a traffic period, an incident or a season. Analysis models the course of experience as a chain of meaningful units and shows how individual courses of action interlink collectively. Unlike a single stimulated recall interview, it is a full research programme that feeds redesign of tools, training and organisation together.
steps: Agree a collaboration contract with the people studied and spend time becoming familiar with their work.
Size the observation period to the natural unit of activity (one call, a traffic period, a whole incident, a season).
Record behaviour continuously, with provoked or interruptive verbalisations where they will not disrupt the work.
Run self-confrontation interviews in which each person watches video of their own activity and describes what they perceived, intended and felt moment by moment.
Add explicitation interviews for what the video does not capture, and second-degree self-confrontation with participants as co-analysts.
Model each course of experience as a chain of meaningful units and map how individual courses interlink.
Iterate analysis with redesign of the situation, tools, training and work culture.
outputs: Course-of-action models per person and their collective articulation, plus redesign proposals for tools, training and organisation.
useWhen: Complex, time-critical or skilled work (control rooms, dispatch, clinical teams, sport coaching) where you need participants' own account of moment-to-moment experience tied to recorded behaviour.
avoidWhen: Short product studies or when trust and a long engagement are not possible; it is labour-intensive. For a single session's reasoning use Stimulated Recall Interview; for fine-grained experience without video use Micro-Phenomenological Interviewing.
whyLost: It developed in French-language ergonomics and is little translated; its demands on time and trust exceed typical UX project cycles.
whereToUse: Air traffic and rail control, emergency dispatch, hospital handovers, trading floors, professional tools where experts' lived activity shapes design.
example: A dispatch software team records a full night shift. Each dispatcher later watches their own video and explains what they noticed before reallocating ambulances; the models reveal reliance on a radio cue the new software would remove, so it is kept and visualised.
reference: Theureau, J. (2003). Course-of-action analysis and course-of-action centered design, in Hollnagel, E. (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum, pp. 55-82.

name: Covariate matching (nearest-neighbour, Mahalanobis, CEM)
origin: Abadie and Imbens (2006, 2011); Iacus, King and Porro (2012)
summary: Estimate a treatment effect from observational data by pairing treated units with control units closest on confounders, directly or via coarsened bins, then checking balance.
description: Where propensity score matching collapses confounders into one score, covariate matching matches on the covariates themselves. Nearest-neighbour matching imputes each treated unit's counterfactual from the M closest controls under a scale-invariant distance (normalised Euclidean or Mahalanobis), with replacement; because matching discrepancies bias the estimate and shrink slowly as covariates multiply, Abadie and Imbens' bias correction adjusts each matched difference using a regression fitted on controls, and variance comes from matching formulas, not the bootstrap. Coarsened exact matching (CEM) instead bins covariates on substantive cutpoints, exactly matches on the bins, drops strata lacking either group and weights the rest; the coarsening bounds imbalance in advance and balance is reported with the multivariate L1 statistic (0 perfect, 1 maximal). Both rest on untestable conditional independence.
steps: Choose covariates that satisfy the backdoor criterion from a credible DAG.
Inspect imbalance by comparing means and full distributions of covariates between treated and control groups.
For nearest-neighbour matching, define a distance (normalised Euclidean or Mahalanobis), match with replacement using a small M (often 1 to 4), and inspect matching discrepancies.
Apply bias correction: fit the outcome on covariates among controls and adjust each matched difference by the fitted-value difference.
For CEM, coarsen a copy of the covariates into meaningful bins, form strata, drop strata without both a treated and a control unit, and weight the rest by stratum size.
Estimate the ATT (or ATE) with matching variance formulas or weighted regression on uncoarsened data; do not bootstrap matching estimators.
Report balance in the matched sample (standardised differences or L1 per covariate and overall) and state how pruning changed the estimand.
outputs: A matched or weighted sample, balance diagnostics (including L1 imbalance), and an ATT or ATE with a standard error.
useWhen: Estimating the effect of a self-selected feature, programme or behaviour from logs when randomisation is impossible and you have rich pre-treatment covariates and a large control pool.
avoidWhen: When important confounders are unmeasured, covariates are many and continuous with a small donor pool, or a randomised test is feasible; consider difference-in-differences, instrumental variables or an A/B test.
whyLost: UX analytics knows propensity scores but rarely the matching variants, bias correction or CEM, which remain in econometrics and political science toolkits.
whereToUse: Effects of opting into premium features, training programmes, community participation or support contact on retention and spend in SaaS and consumer apps.
example: A SaaS team wants the effect of attending onboarding webinars on 90-day retention. Using CEM on plan, company size band, signup month and first-week activity, they drop unmatched strata, reach L1 near zero and estimate a 4-point retention effect among attendees.
reference: Abadie, A. and Imbens, G. W. (2006). Large sample properties of matching estimators for average treatment effects. Econometrica, 74(1), 235-267; Iacus, S. M., King, G. and Porro, G. (2012). Causal inference without balance checking: coarsened exact matching. Political Analysis, 20(1), 1-24.

name: Cox Proportional Hazards Survival Analysis
origin: David R. Cox, 1972
summary: Models when users abandon or complete a task, estimating hazard ratios for design variants and covariates such as SNR and mistake rate rather than only whether they finish.
description: Survival analysis models time to an event while handling censoring. The Cox model, h(t|X) = h0(t)·exp(βX), leaves the baseline hazard unspecified and estimates hazard ratios (HR): the relative risk of the event per unit time. In Vivek Gopinath's playbook the event is abandonment of a task, and the model includes design variant, SNR and mistake rate: in a 600-participant prototype A/B, the new IA had HR 0.68 [0.59, 0.77] (32% lower abandonment risk), each +0.10 SNR HR 0.92, and each extra mistake per minute HR 1.28. The playbook stresses that reporting only completion rates ignores when users abandon, and that the proportional hazards assumption must be tested with Schoenfeld residuals. HRs become decision bars (HR ≤ 0.80) and are re-checked in production during validation (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.63–0.82).
steps: Define the event (abandonment) and time origin (task start), and log time to completion or abandonment per participant with censoring.
Choose covariates from earlier stages (variant, SNR, mistake rate, segment).
Fit h(t|X) = h0(t)·exp(β1·Variant + β2·SNR + β3·Mistake rate).
Report HRs with 95% CIs and p-values, interpreting HR < 1 as reduced risk.
Test the proportional hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residuals.
Compare HRs with the decision bar (e.g. HR ≤ 0.80) and re-estimate in production.
outputs: A hazard ratio table with intervals, survival curves per variant, and a verdict against the bar.
useWhen: When timing matters: when users drop off in a multi-step flow, onboarding or trial, not only whether.
avoidWhen: When there is no time-to-event structure or very few events; use logistic regression or descriptive funnels.
whyLost: Latent: survival analysis is standard in medicine and widely used in data science for churn, but it is almost absent from UX research literature and training, where retention is still reported as simple percentages that ignore censoring.
whereToUse: Onboarding, KYC, checkout, free-trial conversion, feature adoption timing.
example: A trading app's new IA cuts abandonment hazard by 32% (HR 0.68), and every extra mistake per minute raises it by 28%, supporting a bundled labelling and error-proofing fix.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
The Inquiry Series, Vol III, Ch 44
The Inquiry Series, C4 — Behavioural Log Analysis — From Clickstreams to Personas
Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 44 — Survival Analysis, Longitudinal Design & Behavioral Drift
Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
reference: Cox, D. R. (1972). Regression models and life-tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 34(2), 187–220.

name: CPM-GOMS
donor: Cognitive psychology and operations research (critical path method)
origin: Bonnie E. John, 1990; validated in Project Ernestine by Gray, John & Atwood, 1993
summary: A GOMS variant modelling skilled performance as parallel cognitive, perceptual and motor operators in a schedule chart, whose critical path predicts total task time for design alternatives.
description: GOMS analyses skilled performance in terms of Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules. Traditional GOMS treats perceptual, cognitive and motor activities as sequential; CPM-GOMS expresses tasks with parallel activities (listening to a customer while visually searching while typing) as a schedule chart. Each activity is a box with a duration, dependencies are lines between boxes, and the critical path, the longest dependent sequence, determines total task time. Large models are built from small building-block schedule charts for system response time, perception of sounds and visual information, conversation and hand movements, then used for what-if evaluation of alternative designs. In Project Ernestine it predicted that a new telephone operator workstation would be slower, saving an organisation millions of dollars. Vivek Gopinath's forward-thinking playbook uses it in Stage 1 with operator estimates of about 1.2s cognitive, 0.4s perceptual and 0.2–0.3s motor to set predicted-time benchmarks and decision bars.
steps: Decompose the task into goals and methods with a detailed understanding of the work.
Represent each perceptual, cognitive and motor operator as a box with an estimated duration (the playbook uses cognitive ≈ 1.2s, perceptual ≈ 0.4s, motor ≈ 0.2–0.3s).
Draw dependency lines between boxes using goal decomposition and operator-placement heuristics (e.g. the 'collect' key cannot be pressed until the word 'collect' is perceived and verified).
Assemble the full task model from building-block schedule charts for system response, perception, conversation and hand movements, using project management software.
Identify the critical path, the longest dependent sequence, which predicts total task time.
Run what-if evaluations by swapping building blocks for alternative designs and compare predicted times.
Set decision bars from the prediction (e.g. predicted ideal 6s; observed median > 15s indicates breakdown) and compare with observed data.
outputs: A schedule chart, critical path, predicted task time per design alternative, and benchmarks for later testing.
useWhen: Routine, skilled, high-frequency tasks with parallel activity where seconds matter (call centres, trading, data entry, operator consoles).
avoidWhen: Creative, exploratory or novice tasks where performance is not skilled and routine; use usability testing or cognitive walkthrough.
whyLost: Building models is laborious and requires cognitive psychology expertise; agile UX shifted to observe-first testing, leaving predictive modelling in academic niches.
whereToUse: Contact centre tooling, trading terminals, clinical order entry, logistics scanners, any flow where seconds translate to cost.
example: Before redesigning a trading app's alert creation, a researcher models scan, decide, move and type operators and predicts a 5.5–6.0s ideal, with two wrong tabs adding 6–10s, giving a benchmark for the tree test.
sources: Bonnie E. John & Wayne D. Gray (1995), CPM-GOMS: An Analysis Method for Tasks with Parallel Activities, CHI '95 Conference Companion
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Gray WD, John BE & Atwood ME (1993) Project Ernestine. Human-Computer Interaction 8(3)
John BE (1990) Extensions of GOMS analyses to expert performance requiring perception of dynamic visual and auditory information. CHI
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 16 — Cognitive Task Modeling — GOMS, KLM & CPM-GOMS
The GOMS Family of User Interface Analysis Techniques (John & Kieras, 1996)
GOMS Models: Simplified Cognitive Architectures (Kieras, n.d.)

name: Crab Canon Walkthrough
origin: Adapted for UX from the 'Crab Canon' dialogue in Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), modelled on the crab canon in Bach's Musical Offering, which reads the same forwards and backwards
summary: Walk a flow backwards from its end state, checking at each step that the user can undo it, can tell where they are, and would make sense of the screen arriving from the other direction.
description: A crab canon is a piece of music that works played forwards or backwards. Hofstadter uses it, and a dialogue written the same way, to show structures that hold up when reversed. Most walkthroughs only go forwards, along the path designers intended, so they miss what happens when people change their mind, press back, cancel half-way or arrive at a middle step from a link or notification. The crab canon walkthrough starts at the end of a flow and moves backwards one step at a time. At each step the reviewer asks four questions: can this step be undone, and does undoing it restore what was there before; can the user tell what the previous step was; does the screen make sense if you arrive here from the step after it; and what happens to data entered on later steps. The result is a list of one-way doors and broken return paths that forward testing seldom finds.
steps: Choose a flow and write down its steps in forward order, including the end state.
Start at the end state and move back one step at a time, using the product's own back, cancel and undo controls where they exist.
At each step answer: can it be undone; does undo restore the previous state exactly; can the user tell where they came from; does the screen make sense when reached from the following step.
Record what happens to data entered later in the flow when the user goes back.
Mark one-way doors (steps that cannot be undone) and check each is intentional and clearly signalled before the user takes it.
Repeat with entry points in the middle of the flow, such as deep links and notifications.
outputs: A reversed step list with undo, orientation and data-loss findings for each step, and a register of one-way doors with whether each is signalled.
useWhen: Checkout, onboarding, booking and configuration flows; anything with irreversible actions; flows that users often abandon and return to.
avoidWhen: Single-screen tasks, or flows already covered by thorough exploratory testing of back and cancel paths.
whyLost: Cognitive walkthroughs and heuristic reviews follow the intended path forwards. 'User control and freedom' is a heuristic, but there is no standard procedure that systematically walks the reverse path.
whereToUse: E-commerce checkout, insurance and loan applications, account deletion, device setup, admin configuration.
example: Walking back from a booking confirmation shows that 'Back' from the payment step clears the passenger names, and that the seat map makes no sense when reached from a reminder email. Neither appeared in forward testing.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Dialogue 'Crab Canon'.

name: CREAM (Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method)
origin: Erik Hollnagel, 1998
summary: Assesses how working conditions set a person's control mode (scrambled, opportunistic, tactical, strategic) and uses this to predict or retrospectively explain cognitive failures.
description: CREAM is a second-generation HRA method that rejects context-free error probabilities. It uses nine Common Performance Conditions, including adequacy of the human-machine interface, available time, time of day, training and crew collaboration, rated as improving, not significant or reducing performance. The count of improving versus reducing conditions places the operator in one of four contextual control modes, each with an error probability interval. CREAM also offers a retrospective analysis with classification groups linking observed error modes (phenotypes) to causes (genotypes) through cause-consequence tables. For UX, it formalises the idea that the same interface yields very different reliability under different contexts, and it gives a structured way to analyse failures in terms of observation, interpretation, planning and execution.
steps: Describe the task and its context; perform a task analysis down to cognitive activities (observe, interpret, plan, execute).
Rate the nine Common Performance Conditions using field observation, interviews and log evidence.
Count improving and reducing conditions and determine the expected control mode from the CREAM diagram.
For predictive use, identify likely cognitive function failures per step and adjust estimates by control mode.
For retrospective use, trace observed error modes back through antecedent-consequent tables to plausible root causes.
Recommend design changes that shift conditions from reducing to improving, especially interface adequacy and time available.
outputs: Common Performance Condition profile, predicted control mode, error probability interval, and causal chains for observed errors.
useWhen: Tasks performed under highly variable conditions (night shifts, emergencies, mobile use on the move) where context dominates reliability.
avoidWhen: Lightweight consumer usability questions; use usability testing or heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Developed for nuclear and process control, with a dense vocabulary of phenotypes and genotypes. UX rarely separates context-driven reliability from interface quality.
whereToUse: On-call incident tooling, emergency services dispatch, field service apps, clinical night-shift software.
example: An on-call alerting app is evaluated with CREAM for 3 a.m. pages. Most conditions are reducing, predicting an opportunistic control mode; the team simplifies the first-response screen to a single recommended action with a runbook link.
sources: Hollnagel, Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method: CREAM (1998)
The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Hollnagel, E. (1998). Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method (CREAM). Elsevier.

name: CREATE action funnel diagnostic
aka: CREATE Action Funnel Review and Debugging
origin: Stephen Wendel, 2013, building on the Fogg Behavior Model (2009)
summary: A step-by-step review checking that each action in a design has a cue, positive reaction, favourable evaluation, ability and timing, and a hypothesis generator for drop-offs.
description: The CREATE funnel holds that five events must precede any action: a Cue, an intuitive Reaction, a conscious Evaluation of costs and benefits, the Ability to act, and a reason to act now (Timing). People leak out at every stage, and each stage is judged against competing alternatives. Used as a design review, every click and form entry in a wireframe is checked against the five conditions, with question sets for structuring the action, shaping the environment and preparing the user, and tactics chosen per stage. Used for debugging a live product, once a drop-off is located the team writes at least one hypothesis per stage, each with a quick, cheap test, including tests of a hypothesis's logical implications. The discipline is forcing a hypothesis at every stage rather than jumping to the most obvious one.
steps: Treat the design as a behavioural plan and list every small step (click, field, decision) the user must take.
For each step, check whether cue, reaction, evaluation, ability and timing are all in place; fix small obvious problems such as unclear actions or competing cues.
For large gaps, work through question sets on structuring the action, constructing the environment and preparing the user, and pick stage-specific tactics.
For a live product, locate the drop-off from analytics and observation, and first try removing the step or common-sense fixes.
Write at least one hypothesis for each of the five stages explaining the drop-off.
Pair each hypothesis with a quick test: check existing data, prototype a fix, or test a logical implication of the hypothesis.
Discard clearly wrong explanations before investing engineering effort, and re-measure after changes.
outputs: Annotated wireframes with stage-by-stage gaps, a list of hypotheses and cheap tests for each drop-off, and recommended design changes.
useWhen: Reviewing onboarding, habit-forming or conversion flows before build, or explaining why users stop at a known step in a live funnel.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating it as a solution generator or a strict sequence; stages compensate for each other. For population-level behaviour change programmes use COM-B; for locating drop-offs in the first place use funnel analysis.
whyLost: It is known among behavioural designers but overshadowed by the simpler Fogg model, and rarely taught in UX research courses.
whereToUse: Health and savings apps, onboarding, form completion, notification design, feature adoption.
example: A task-management app loses users at first sync. The team writes stage hypotheses: no connectivity on the commute (ability), tested by logging failed offline attempts; low trust (evaluation), tested by skipped optional questions and privacy-policy clicks.
reference: Wendel, S. (2013). Designing for Behavior Change: Applying Psychology and Behavioral Economics. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Creative Matrix
origin: Design consultancy practice (Jump Associates)
summary: An ideation grid crossing people-related categories (personas, pain points, segments) with enablers (technologies, spaces, policies), filled silently with ideas in every cell.
description: The creative matrix forces ideas at the intersections of who the design serves and what could enable change. Columns hold people-related categories such as personas, pain points, segments or How Might We questions; rows hold enablers such as technologies, spaces, policies and activities, plus a wild-card row. Teams of four to six fill every cell with ideas on sticky notes in silence for 15-20 minutes, review the matrix silently, mark favourites and then discuss and cluster the chosen ideas. Adding unrelated categories or imagined worlds jolts thinking. The grid guarantees coverage of combinations a free brainstorm would skip, though many ideas are shallow and the categories chosen limit the range.
steps: Choose four to six column categories (personas, pain points or How Might We questions) and four to six enabler rows plus a wild-card row.
Draw the grid on a wall or digital board.
Ideate silently into the cells for 15-20 minutes, aiming for at least one idea per cell.
Review the matrix silently and mark favourites with dots.
Discuss and cluster the chosen ideas into a shortlist for development.
outputs: A dense matrix of ideas across combinations and a shortlist for development.
useWhen: Use when a team has research-based personas or pain points and wants systematic coverage of solution spaces, or when brainstorms keep circling the same ideas.
avoidWhen: Avoid when columns would be guesses about users: build them from Personas or Journey Mapping grounded in research. For ranking the shortlist with users use Kano Analysis or concept testing.
whyLost: Its simple grid and silent working make it easy to run in person or remotely, so it remains a standard ideation tool.
whereToUse: Hospitality, retail, SaaS feature planning, public services, sustainability innovation.
example: A hotel team crosses 'more comfortable than a five-star hotel' with 'sustainable technologies' and generates a wind-powered spa idea among 60 others.
reference: Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Beverly, MA: Rockport Publishers. Method 27, Creative Matrix.

name: Credibility audit
aka: Prolonged engagement, triangulation and member checking
origin: Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba, Naturalistic Inquiry (1985)
summary: Checks whether qualitative findings credibly represent participants' realities using prolonged engagement, persistent observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative case analysis and member checking.
description: Lincoln and Guba proposed credibility as the qualitative parallel to internal validity: confidence that findings are a plausible representation of participants' realities. They specified techniques: prolonged engagement (enough time to understand the culture and build trust), persistent observation (depth on the most relevant elements), triangulation across sources, methods, investigators and theories, peer debriefing, negative case analysis, referential adequacy and member checking with participants. A credibility audit applies these as a checklist with evidence, so that each finding's support is visible. Later critiques note that member checking can be problematic when participants disagree with analytical interpretations, so the audit treats participant feedback as data rather than a veto. Rigour lies in planning these techniques into the study design, not adding them after analysis.
steps: At design stage, plan which credibility techniques apply and their scale, for example at least 2 site visits per location, 3 data sources and 2 analysts.
Ensure prolonged engagement: spend enough time in context to see routine and exceptional days, and log time in the field.
Triangulate each key finding across at least two of: data sources (interviews, observation, logs, documents), methods, investigators and theoretical lenses, and record convergence or divergence.
Conduct negative case analysis: search for cases that contradict each finding and revise the finding until it accounts for them or explicitly bounds its scope.
Run peer debriefing with a researcher outside the project who challenges interpretations, logging questions and responses.
Member check by sharing synthesised findings (not transcripts) with 3 to 6 participants or community representatives, and record agreement, corrections and disagreements as additional data.
Produce a finding-by-technique matrix showing the credibility evidence for each major finding.
outputs: A credibility matrix linking each finding to triangulation, negative cases, peer debriefing and member-check evidence, plus field-time logs and revised findings.
useWhen: Qualitative findings will drive costly or high-stakes decisions, face sceptical stakeholders, or describe groups the team is distant from.
avoidWhen: Quick tactical studies where findings are low stakes and easily reversible; a lighter peer review is proportionate. Avoid member checking as validation of complex theoretical interpretations participants were never asked to hold.
whyLost: The trustworthiness criteria are standard in academic qualitative research but rarely enter industry UX, where speed is prioritised and credibility is asserted through quotes and video clips.
whereToUse: Healthcare and public-sector research, strategic discovery, research informing regulation or policy, multi-country studies.
example: A study claimed rural health workers distrusted sync. The audit triangulated interviews with sync logs and observations, found two negative cases at a clinic with reliable power, and narrowed the finding to 'distrust where outages had previously caused data loss', which member checks confirmed.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Credibility Techniques (Lincoln and Guba)
origin: Yvonna Lincoln & Egon Guba, 1985 (Naturalistic Inquiry)
summary: A set of six techniques establishing that qualitative findings faithfully represent participants' realities: engagement, observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative cases and member checks.
description: Credibility is Lincoln and Guba's naturalistic counterpart to internal validity. Rather than claiming objectivity, it asks whether the researcher's reconstruction of participants' realities is plausible to them and defensible to others. Six techniques support it: prolonged engagement (enough time in context to learn culture and spot misinformation), persistent observation (depth on the most relevant elements), triangulation across methods, sources, investigators or theories, peer debriefing with an outsider who challenges interpretations, negative case analysis, and member checking. Each is planned in advance and documented so a reader can judge how far the findings can be trusted. Together they make qualitative trust an evidenced property rather than an assertion.
steps: Plan which credibility techniques the study will use and how they will be documented, before fieldwork begins.
Build prolonged engagement and persistent observation into the schedule, for example repeat visits or multi-day immersion rather than single sessions.
Triangulate at least two methods or sources for each major finding and record convergence and divergence.
Hold regular peer debriefs with a researcher outside the study and minute the challenges raised and how they were resolved.
Conduct negative case analysis on each emerging finding and member-check key interpretations with a diverse subsample.
Report the techniques used, their outcomes and their limits in the methods section.
outputs: A credibility plan and log: engagement time, triangulation matrix, peer debrief notes, negative case record and member-check outcomes.
useWhen: When qualitative findings will drive major decisions or be challenged, in regulated or public-sector contexts, and in academic-industry work.
avoidWhen: Rapid tactical usability rounds where findings are low-stakes and quickly retested; a light peer review suffices.
whyLost: Industry research reports rarely include methods sections, so trustworthiness criteria were reduced to the occasional mention of triangulation.
whereToUse: Health, government and financial services research; foundational studies feeding strategy; research quality frameworks in research operations.
example: A public-benefits portal team spends two weeks embedded in welfare offices, triangulates interviews with case-file review, and runs weekly peer debriefs. The credibility log lets policy leads accept a counterintuitive finding about form abandonment.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
Analysing and Presenting Qualitative Data (Burnard et al., 2008)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
Qualitative Methods in Information Retrieval Research (Fidel, 1993)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

extra.Six Credibility Techniques: Prolonged engagement: Spending sufficient time in the field to learn the culture, test for misinformation, and build trust. No prescribed duration — sufficient time is when you stop being surprised by what you see. Document your engagement time in methods reporting. Persistent observation: Identifying the characteristics and elements most relevant to the problem and focusing on them in depth. Breadth of observation is produced by prolonged engagement; depth by persistent observation of key elements. Triangulation: Using multiple methods, multiple sources, multiple investigators, or multiple theories to check the consistency of findings. Method triangulation (interview + observation + document analysis) is the most common. Note: triangulation does not require convergence — divergence is equally informative. Peer debriefing: Regular sessions with a peer who is outside the study. The peer's role: ask hard questions, probe for bias, challenge interpretations that seem too convenient. Document these sessions. Negative case analysis: Actively seeking and accounting for cases that disconfirm emerging findings. A study that reports no negative cases has not looked hard enough. Member checking: Systematically soliciting participants' feedback on the researcher's interpretation of their data. This is the most important credibility technique and the most commonly done poorly. See Method 25.

name: Crisp-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA)
origin: Charles C. Ragin, 1987
summary: Set-theoretic analysis of small-N cases that identifies which combinations of binary conditions are sufficient or necessary for an outcome such as abandonment.
description: QCA treats cases as configurations of conditions and uses Boolean minimisation to find combinations sufficient for an outcome, reasoning with necessity and sufficiency rather than correlation. It suits small moderated samples where statistics are weak. In Vivek Gopinath's playbook, conditions are calibrated to binary membership (Low SNR = 1 if element SNR < 0.50; High Mistakes = 1 if ≥ 1/min; High TLX = 1 if frustration > 60; Timed OTP), a truth table is built from interview and usability cases, and minimisation (Quine-McCluskey, e.g. the QCA package in R) yields solutions such as Low SNR * High Mistakes ⇒ Abandon. A light necessity check asks whether Low SNR appears in nearly all abandonment cases; if so it becomes a hard guardrail (element SNR ≥ 0.60). Sufficient paths are used to bundle prescriptions and the truth table is rebuilt on a fresh sample during validation.
steps: Choose the outcome (e.g. Abandon) and 3–5 candidate conditions from earlier evidence.
Calibrate each condition to crisp membership with explicit thresholds (Low SNR if element SNR < 0.50; High Mistakes if ≥ 1/min; High TLX if frustration > 60).
Build a truth table with one row per case from interviews and usability sessions.
Minimise configurations with Quine-McCluskey or QCA software to derive sufficient paths.
Run a necessity check on key conditions.
Link solutions to quotes and hazard ratios in mechanism memos, bundle fixes accordingly, and re-run on a fresh sample after the fix.
outputs: Minimised sufficient paths, necessity results and mechanism memos.
useWhen: Small-N studies (10–40 cases) where you suspect conjunctural causation: failure needs several conditions together.
avoidWhen: Large samples where regression is feasible, or when conditions cannot be calibrated meaningfully.
whyLost: Established in comparative social science but almost unknown in UX, where small-N work is treated as purely descriptive.
whereToUse: Moderated usability studies, enterprise deployments with few accounts, B2B churn case reviews, service design pilots.
example: Across usability cases, QCA shows Low SNR combined with High Mistakes is sufficient for abandonment, so the team ships labelling and clutter reduction together rather than one alone.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
