reference: Ragin, C. C. (1987). The Comparative Method: Moving Beyond Qualitative and Quantitative Strategies. University of California Press.

name: Critic-Proofing
origin: Livingston, Mandryk and Stanley (2010); described by Ian Livingston in chapter 4
summary: A heuristic evaluation in which the severity of each issue is adjusted according to how strongly that kind of issue affects critics' review scores, so fixes are prioritised by likely impact on reception.
description: Critic-proofing builds on the classic heuristic analysis process but changes how problems are prioritised. Before evaluating the game, the researcher conducts a baseline analysis of a set of video game reviews to learn which types of problem, mapped to the heuristics, critics mention and how strongly they are associated with lower scores. During the evaluation, each issue found against a heuristic is then given a severity that reflects not only its effect on the player but the effect that kind of issue tends to have on a critic's review. The aim is to make sure that problems most likely to hurt reception are fixed first. Livingston notes that the process can be extended to any set of heuristics, provided the researcher is willing to do the baseline review analysis. For UX teams beyond games, the same principle applies wherever public ratings matter, for example app store reviews or analyst evaluations: severity can be weighted by evidence of what reviewers penalise rather than by expert judgement alone.
steps: Choose the heuristic set to be used for evaluation.
Collect a baseline sample of reviews for comparable products and code which heuristic categories they criticise.
Estimate how strongly each category of problem is associated with lower review scores.
Carry out the heuristic evaluation of your product in the usual way.
Adjust each issue's severity using the review-based weighting for its heuristic category.
Prioritise and report fixes by the adjusted severity.
outputs: A heuristic issue list prioritised by severity weighted for likely impact on reviews.
useWhen: Public reviews strongly influence success and the team must decide which known issues to fix before launch.
avoidWhen: No comparable review corpus exists, or review scores are not an important outcome.
whyLost: Published as an academic method and rarely adopted; most teams prioritise by expert severity scales.
whereToUse: Games before launch, consumer apps where store ratings matter, products reviewed by trade press.
example: Camera problems are frequently penalised in reviews of platform games, so a minor camera issue found in evaluation is upgraded to high priority before release.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 4 (Livingston). Livingston, I. J., Mandryk, R. L. and Stanley, K. G. (2010). Critic-proofing: how using critic reviews and game genres can refine heuristic evaluations. Future Play 2010.

name: Critical Analysis Walkthrough
origin: Ben Light, Jean Burgess and Stefanie Duguay, 2018
summary: A researcher maps an app's purpose, business model and governance, then uses it step by step from sign-up to exit to expose the values and exclusions built into its design.
description: The walkthrough method treats an app as a cultural artefact. Like a heuristic evaluation it needs no participants, but its aim is critical rather than diagnostic: to understand how the interface guides users, what ideal user it assumes, whose needs it privileges, and what that means for access and inclusion. The researcher first maps the environment of expected use: vision (purpose and target audience), operating model (business strategy and revenue) and modes of governance (terms of service and rules). They then walk through every button, menu and screen as a typical user across registration, everyday use and leaving, recording UI arrangement, functions, branding and wording, and interpreting each feature against prior research and social norms. It is distinct from the cognitive walkthrough, which predicts learnability problems.
steps: Map the environment of expected use: the app's stated vision and audience, its business and revenue model, and its governance (terms of service, community rules).
Create an account and walk through registration and entry, noting every field, option and default.
Walk through everyday use screen by screen, recording UI arrangement, functions, features, wording, branding and colours.
Walk through suspension, deletion or leaving, noting obstacles and retention tactics.
Record everything with notes, screenshots or screen recording.
Analyse critically: which actions are encouraged, how users are constrained, what ideal user is assumed, and whose needs are privileged or excluded.
Pair the findings with interviews or usability tests to add users' own perceptions.
outputs: Annotated screenshots and an interpretive account of embedded values, assumptions, biases and exclusions.
useWhen: You need to audit an app, your own or a competitor's, for the values, business incentives and exclusions encoded in its flows, for example in inclusion or ethics reviews.
avoidWhen: You need to predict usability problems or know how real users experience the app; use cognitive walkthrough, heuristic evaluation or usability testing instead.
whyLost: It belongs to academic app studies and is published in media journals, so UX teams know the cognitive walkthrough but not this critical counterpart.
whereToUse: Inclusion and equity audits, dating and social apps, gig-economy and fintech onboarding, dark pattern reviews and AI product governance.
example: A team walks through a competitor's sign-up and finds gender options ordered male, female, non-binary, and account deletion buried four levels deep. They use the findings to set inclusive defaults and a one-step exit.
sources: UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
reference: Light, B., Burgess, J., & Duguay, S. (2018). The walkthrough method: An approach to the study of apps. New Media & Society, 20(3), 881-900.

name: Critical Facet Playtest
origin: Named in Michael C. Medlock's overview of GUR methods (chapter 7), drawing on publisher playtesting practice
summary: A survey-based playtest that measures players' attitudes to one specific core mechanic, such as aiming, camera or steering, rather than the whole game.
description: A critical facet playtest isolates one core experience that the game depends on and quantifies how players perceive it. Medlock gives examples such as the aiming model on vertical levels, the camera in a 3D platformer, or steering through turns in a racing game. Players play a slice of the game that exercises the facet, then answer rating questions focused only on it, so the team learns whether the mechanic feels right and can compare alternative tunings or later builds. Because the facet is narrow, the build can be early and the questionnaire short, and results can feed directly into tuning. The method shares the limits of other self-report playtests: it does not say why players felt the way they did, and it does not show whether the facet matters to overall enjoyment, so it is often paired with observation, interviews or telemetry. For UX research outside games, the idea transfers to any product with one interaction that carries the experience, such as a drawing tool's brush feel or a camera app's focus behaviour.
steps: Identify the core facet the experience depends on and the decisions the team must make about it.
Build or select a short play slice that exercises the facet repeatedly.
Write focused rating items (for example feel, control, precision, satisfaction) plus one or two open questions.
Recruit target players and have them play the slice, optionally across two or more tunings in counterbalanced order.
Collect ratings immediately after each slice.
Compare ratings between tunings or against earlier builds and follow up on outliers with observation or interview.
outputs: Quantified ratings of one mechanic, comparisons between tunings, and a short list of follow-up questions.
useWhen: One mechanic or control scheme is central to the experience and the team needs evidence on how it feels before committing.
avoidWhen: You need to understand overall enjoyment or the reasons behind ratings.
whyLost: Mainly an internal publisher technique; outside games teams rarely separate the 'feel' of one interaction from overall satisfaction.
whereToUse: Games, creative tools, input devices, camera and gesture interactions.
example: Two steering sensitivity settings for a kart racer are rated by 30 players on control and precision after three laps each, and the team ships the higher-rated setting.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 7 (Medlock).

name: Critical Incident Technique
origin: John C. Flanagan, 1954
summary: Collects detailed accounts of specific events that were exceptionally good or bad, then classifies them to reveal what determines success or failure in an experience.
description: The Critical Incident Technique, developed by John Flanagan from aviation psychology work during the Second World War, collects detailed accounts of specific incidents in which behaviour or experience was notably effective or ineffective. Asking about concrete events rather than general opinions reduces vague answers and gives behaviourally specific data. Each incident is captured with its situation, actions, outcome and feelings, and incidents are then content-analysed and classified into categories that reveal the critical factors driving good and bad experiences. In UX, CIT works in interviews, surveys and diaries, and in reviews of support data. Rigour comes from a clear definition of what counts as critical, structured probes for each incident, collecting enough incidents for categories to stabilise (often 50 to 100 or more), and checking classification reliability.
steps: Define "critical": Incidents that were either significantly more positive or more negative than the participant's baseline expectation. Not typical experiences — threshold-crossing events.

Collection: "Think about the last [time period]. Tell me about a time when using [product] was particularly [difficult / helpful / frustrating / satisfying]." The temporal framing matters — recent incidents are more accessible and more accurately recalled.
Structured probe: For each incident: (a) What was the situation? (b) What did you do? (c) What was the outcome? (d) How did you feel? (e) What would you have done differently?

Diary integration: Deploy CIT as a diary trigger: "Tonight, if you had an experience with [product] that you would call particularly [good/bad], write it down using this template." This captures incidents in near-real-time rather than in retrospective interviews.

Analysis: Code incidents for: type of event, trigger, participant action, outcome, and emotional response. Frequency analysis: which types of critical incidents are most common? Impact analysis: which types have the largest effect on overall satisfaction?
outputs: A categorised set of positive and negative incidents with frequencies, critical factors driving experience, and impact estimates on satisfaction.
useWhen: When you need concrete, behaviourally specific evidence of what makes experiences succeed or fail, for error analysis, service quality or rare but important events.
avoidWhen: Avoid for routine, unremarkable behaviour, which participants do not remember as incidents; use observation, diaries or analytics.
whyLost: Renamed: the term itself has faded in UX, but the method lives on as 'tell me about the last time...' interviewing, incident-triggered diaries and structured story collection, usually without Flanagan's classification and reliability steps.
whereToUse: Error analysis; training design; understanding exceptional and problematic use cases.
example: A health insurer collects 120 critical incidents about claims from interviews and diaries. Negative incidents cluster around 'no status update after submission', which becomes the top fix ahead of form redesign.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Flanagan JC (1954) The critical incident technique. Psychological Bulletin 51(4):327-358
Butterfield LD et al. (2005) Fifty years of the critical incident technique. Qualitative Research
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Flanagan, J. C. (1954). The critical incident technique. Psychological Bulletin, 51(4), 327-358.

name: Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω
origin: Lee Cronbach, 1951; Roderick McDonald, 1970/1999
summary: Coefficients estimating how consistently a set of items measures one construct; omega is the modern, less restrictive alternative to alpha.
description: Cronbach's alpha estimates reliability from item inter-correlations, but assumes all items contribute equally to the construct (tau-equivalence) and a single factor, which rarely holds; when violated it typically underestimates reliability, and it rises simply with more items. McDonald's omega uses factor loadings from a fitted model, allowing items to differ in strength, and omega hierarchical indicates how much variance is due to a general factor in multidimensional scales. Rigour means checking unidimensionality before computing either, reporting omega (with alpha for comparability), reporting confidence intervals, and not treating high values as proof of validity. Values above 0.95 often signal redundant items.
steps: Confirm the scale or subscale is unidimensional with a factor analysis before computing reliability.
Compute omega total from a one-factor model and alpha for comparison, each with 95% confidence intervals (e.g. via pingouin or psych).
Interpret values: 0.70 is a minimum for group research, 0.80 or above is good, and above 0.90 is needed for individual-level decisions.
Inspect item-total correlations (flag below 0.3) and alpha-if-item-deleted to find weak items.
For multidimensional scales, compute omega hierarchical and subscale omegas rather than a single overall alpha.
outputs: Reliability coefficients with intervals for each scale and subscale, item diagnostics and recommendations on item removal.
useWhen: Whenever a multi-item scale score is used, including adopting an existing questionnaire in a new context.
avoidWhen: Avoid for single-item measures, formative indices (where items need not correlate), or as a substitute for validity evidence.
whyLost: Alpha is reported routinely and uncritically as a stamp of quality; omega and the assumptions behind alpha are seldom understood in UX.
whereToUse: Survey programmes, benchmark questionnaires, trust and satisfaction indices, academic-industry studies.
example: A team's 6-item trust subscale has alpha 0.71 but omega 0.79 because one item loads weakly; removing the item raises omega to 0.83 and sharpens the scale's correlation with retention.
sources: Quantitative User Experience Research (Chris Chapman & Kerry Rodden)
Cronbach (1951) Coefficient alpha and the internal structure of tests
McDonald (1999) Test Theory: A Unified Treatment
The Inquiry Series, Ch 50 — Factor Analysis — Discovering the Latent Structure of Experience
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
reference: McNeish, D. (2018) Thanks coefficient alpha, we'll take it from here. Psychological Methods, 23(3), 412-433.

name: Cross-Case Analysis
origin: Robert Yin, 1984 (Case Study Research); Miles & Huberman, 1984
summary: Comparing fully analysed cases on theoretically motivated dimensions to find patterns, explanations and scope conditions that transcend individual cases.
description: Cross-case analysis compares multiple participants, sites or accounts after each has been analysed in its own right. Premature comparison flattens within-case detail, so within-case analysis comes first. The analyst then defines comparison dimensions grounded in theory or the research question, rather than comparing everything with everything, and looks for informative contrasts: similar cases with different outcomes, and different cases with the same outcome. Yin's pattern matching and replication logic treat each case like an experiment that should confirm or contradict a proposition. The result is an explanation of the pattern plus scope conditions stating where it holds. Displays such as case-ordered matrices make the comparison transparent.
steps: Within-case analysis first: Fully analyse each case before cross-case comparison. Premature cross-case comparison collapses important within-case variation.
Define comparison dimensions: Theoretically motivated dimensions — not everything versus everything.
Pattern matching: Similar cases producing different outcomes, or different cases producing the same outcome — these are the analytically richest comparisons.
Build the explanation: What explains the pattern of similarities and differences? This is your theoretical contribution.
Specify scope conditions: For what types of cases does this pattern hold? This is the boundary of your theory.
outputs: Within-case summaries, cross-case comparison matrices, explanatory propositions, and scope conditions.
useWhen: Multi-site, multi-account or multi-segment studies where you need to explain why outcomes differ across cases.
avoidWhen: Single-case deep dives or when cases are too few and too similar to compare; use within-case analysis or IPA.
whyLost: Synthesis in UX often pools all data into one affinity wall, losing case boundaries and the comparative logic.
whereToUse: Enterprise customer studies, multi-country research, service evaluations across locations, and B2B churn or success analyses.
example: Comparing eight hospitals adopting an e-prescribing system, two similar hospitals show opposite outcomes. Cross-case analysis attributes the difference to whether pharmacists were involved in configuration.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Case Study Research: Design and Methods (Yin)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2018). Case Study Research and Applications (6th ed.). Sage.

name: Cross-Cultural Survey Equivalence Testing
origin: Harkness, 2003 (TRAPD); Vandenberg & Lance, 2000 (invariance)
summary: Ensures a UX survey measures the same constructs in the same way across languages and cultures, through team translation and measurement invariance testing.
description: Cross-cultural survey equivalence testing addresses whether scores from different language or cultural groups can be compared. It has two parts. First, translation and adaptation follow a team approach such as TRAPD (translation, review, adjudication, pretesting, documentation), with cognitive interviews in each locale to check that items are understood as intended. Second, multi-group confirmatory factor analysis tests measurement invariance in steps: configural (same factor structure), metric (equal loadings, allowing comparison of relationships) and scalar (equal intercepts, allowing comparison of means). Partial invariance can sometimes be accepted with justification. Rigour comes from documenting adaptation decisions, adequate samples per group, and limiting claims to the level of invariance achieved.
steps: International UX survey protocol:
Translation: forward translation, back-translation, cognitive interview in each language.
(2) Functional equivalence: focus groups in each culture to confirm the construct is relevant.
(3) Metric equivalence: run measurement invariance testing (configural → metric → scalar CFA) before computing cross-cultural means.
(4) If scalar invariance fails: report country-specific results separately, do not aggregate.
(5) Use MACS (mean and covariance structures) analysis to identify which items lack equivalence.
outputs: Translated instruments with documented adaptation decisions, invariance test results (configural, metric, scalar), and a judgement on which cross-country comparisons are valid.
useWhen: Global products comparing satisfaction, trust or usability scores across markets; multilingual benchmarking; and instruments launched in new regions.
avoidWhen: Avoid comparing scores across countries without it; when invariance fails, compare within-country patterns or use qualitative research instead.
whyLost: Global UX teams machine-translate surveys and compare means directly; equivalence testing lives in cross-cultural psychology and international survey programmes.
whereToUse: International UX benchmark programs, global product research, multi-country satisfaction surveys.
example: A ride-hailing app compares trust scores across Japan, Brazil and Germany; scalar invariance fails for one item because 'reliable' translates differently, so comparisons use a reduced set of invariant items.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Harkness JA, van de Vijver FJR & Mohler PPh (Eds.) (2003) Cross-Cultural Survey Methods. Wiley

name: Cross-Cultural UX Research
origin: Cross-cultural usability work by Nielsen, del Galdo and Fernandes in the 1990s; methods consolidated by Quesenbery and Szuc (Global UX, 2011)
summary: Planning, running and interpreting research across cultures so that instruments, moderation and analysis are equivalent, and culture-specific behaviours and signs are correctly read.
description: Cross-cultural UX research adapts the whole research process for multiple cultural contexts. Instruments must achieve conceptual and linguistic equivalence through translation and back-translation, not literal word swaps. Moderation styles must account for differences in politeness norms, criticism avoidance and the effect of the moderator's status, which can mask problems in think-aloud sessions. Local researchers or cultural brokers help recruit, moderate and interpret. A related technique is the cross-cultural sign audit, which tests whether icons, colours, metaphors and gestures carry the intended meaning in each locale. Rigour comes from piloting instruments in every locale, using same-culture moderators where possible, checking response-style biases (such as acquiescence or extreme responding) before comparing scores, and analysing findings jointly with local team members.
steps: Define which comparisons matter and whether you need cross-locale comparability or deep local understanding.
Partner with local researchers or cultural brokers in each market for recruitment, moderation and interpretation.
Translate instruments with forward and back-translation, cognitively pretest them with 3-5 participants per locale, and adapt examples.
Adjust moderation: use same-culture moderators, indirect probing where direct criticism is unusual, and suitable session settings.
Run a sign and icon audit testing whether key symbols, colours and metaphors are interpreted as intended in each locale.
Check survey data for response-style differences before comparing means, and analyse qualitative data jointly with local partners.
outputs: Locale-validated instruments, culture-specific findings and shared patterns, sign-failure inventory and market-specific design recommendations.
useWhen: Launching or adapting products in new markets, global products with diverse user bases, and comparative studies across regions.
avoidWhen: When you only need to check translation and formatting (use localization testing) or when comparisons across cultures are not needed for the decision.
whyLost: Still in use: Critical for global products; growing body of methodology.
whereToUse: Global product teams; market entry research; localisation validation.
example: A payments app expanding to India and Indonesia finds rural users interpret the trash-can icon as 'save for later' and that participants in moderated sessions praise designs they later abandon. Switching to local moderators and a text label surfaces the real issues.
sources: Global UX: Design and Research in a Connected World (Whitney Quesenbery & Daniel Szuc)
Usability and Internationalization of Information Technology (Nuray Aykin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Quesenbery W & Szuc D (2011) Global UX: Design and Research in a Connected World. Morgan Kaufmann

name: Cross-Domain Borrowing Matrix
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Maps each donor discipline to the UX problem it addresses, its key methods, the transfer mechanism and the main training barrier to adoption.
description: Appendix C of the extended treatise maps 13 donor disciplines (epidemiology, econometrics, cognitive science, linguistics, social science, machine learning, statistics, psychophysics, systems engineering, clinical research, anthropology, philosophy, network science) against the UX problem addressed, key methods, transfer mechanism and training barrier. Transfer mechanisms are classified as direct transplant, direct structural transplant, conceptual reframe, measurement upgrade or level-of-analysis shift. For example, econometrics addresses quasi-experimental causal inference via DiD, RDD, IV and PSM by direct transplant, with econometrics training as the barrier; network science addresses system-level dynamics by a level-of-analysis shift. The matrix turns 'borrow from other fields' into a structured adoption plan.
steps: Identify the UX problem class you cannot address well with current methods.
Locate donor disciplines that solve structurally equivalent problems.
List candidate methods and classify the transfer mechanism.
Identify the training barrier and the collaborators or courses that would remove it.
Pilot one method on a real question with a donor-discipline expert.
Document adaptations and add the method to the team's library.
outputs: Borrowing matrix tailored to the organisation, pilot plans, adaptation notes.
useWhen: Expanding a research team's methodological range; curriculum and hiring plans.
avoidWhen: When existing UX methods already answer the question well.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research strategy, cross-functional collaboration with data science, academic partnerships.
example: A research lead uses the matrix to pair UX researchers with economists on DiD analyses of regional launches, with a short training to cross the barrier.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lost Methods in UX treatise, Appendix C
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Appendix C (The Cross-Domain Borrowing Matrix).

name: Cross-Impact Analysis
donor: Futures research (RAND and Institute for the Future)
origin: Theodore Gordon and Olaf Helmer, 1966 (Kaiser Aluminum 'Future' game); cross-impact balances by Wolfgang Weimer-Jehle (2006)
summary: Systematically assesses how the occurrence of one future event or trend changes the likelihood of others, producing consistent scenarios from interacting factors.
description: Delphi gives independent estimates for future events, but events interact. Cross-impact analysis builds a matrix in which experts judge how each event's occurrence would change the probability of each other event. Monte Carlo simulation then generates consistent scenario sets and adjusted probabilities. Cross-impact balance analysis (CIB) uses qualitative influence judgements between descriptor states to find internally consistent scenarios. For product strategy, it structures how trends such as regulation, AI capability, user trust and competitor moves interact, producing scenarios that are consistent rather than arbitrary combinations.
steps: Select key events or descriptors (e.g. regulation passes, AI cost falls, trust scandal occurs) with defined states.
Estimate initial probabilities or state plausibilities with experts (e.g. via Delphi).
Fill the cross-impact matrix: how each event or state influences each other one.
Run Monte Carlo simulation (probabilistic CIA) or consistency analysis (CIB) to derive scenarios.
Review resulting scenarios for plausibility and robustness.
Use scenarios to stress-test product strategy and research priorities.
outputs: Cross-impact matrix, adjusted probabilities, consistent scenario sets and strategy stress tests.
useWhen: Strategic planning with multiple interacting uncertainties.
avoidWhen: Few uncertainties or short horizons; simple scenario 2x2s may suffice.
whyLost: It is a specialist futures method; product strategy uses informal scenario discussions.
whereToUse: AI product strategy, fintech regulation, healthcare policy, platform ecosystems.
example: A health AI firm uses CIB with 8 descriptors; consistent scenarios show that strict liability regulation combined with clinician shortages favours assistive over autonomous products, reshaping roadmap bets.
sources: Gordon & Hayward, Initial experiments with the cross impact matrix method of forecasting (1968), Futures
Weimer-Jehle, Cross-impact balances: A system-theoretical approach to cross-impact analysis (2006), Technological Forecasting and Social Change
Gordon, Cross-impact method (2009), Futures Research Methodology 3.0
reference: Weimer-Jehle, W. (2006). Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 73(4), 334-361.

name: Cross-modal interference measurement
origin: Multisensory interference paradigms (for example McGurk and MacDonald, 1976; crossmodal Stroop tasks); applied in human factors by Wickens and Spence
summary: Measures performance costs when information arrives through two senses at once, revealing when audio, visual and haptic channels help or hinder each other.
description: Multiple resource theory predicts less interference across modalities, but cross-modal interference still occurs, especially when signals conflict in meaning or spatial location, compete for central processing, or capture attention involuntarily (auditory onsets are particularly hard to ignore). Spence and colleagues showed spatial co-location of cues across modalities improves performance while mismatched locations impair it. Measurement uses controlled paradigms in which participants perform a primary task in one modality while signals arrive in another under congruent, incongruent and neutral conditions, recording response time and error costs. In UX this answers practical questions such as whether spoken alerts disrupt reading or whether haptic feedback conflicts with visual cues.
steps: Define the primary task and modality and the secondary signals in other modalities.
Construct congruent, incongruent and neutral conditions (for example spoken 'left' with a left versus right visual cue; co-located versus separated sound sources).
Run a within-subjects study with 16-24 participants, counterbalanced, with at least 30 trials per condition.
Compute interference cost as performance in incongruent minus congruent or neutral conditions for response time and accuracy.
Test whether costs exceed acceptable limits (for example more than 100 ms or a 5% error increase on safety-critical responses).
Adjust timing, spatial location or content of cross-modal signals and re-test.
outputs: Interference costs per condition, response time and accuracy comparisons, and design rules for combining modalities.
useWhen: When adding sound, voice or haptic channels to visual interfaces, designing alerts in multitasking contexts, or building AR/VR.
avoidWhen: When tasks are not concurrent; use a single-modality usability test.
whyLost: Cross-modal research is extensive in psychology but UX designers add sound and haptics by intuition and do not measure interference.
whereToUse: Automotive HMIs, surgical consoles, wearables, AR glasses, and voice assistants combined with screens.
example: A surgical robot plays spoken instrument names while showing icons. When the spoken and displayed instruments differ, response time increases by 240 ms and errors double, so the voice channel is restricted to alerts that confirm the visual cue.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: Spence, C. & Driver, J. (Eds.) (2004). Crossmodal Space and Crossmodal Attention. Oxford University Press.

name: Cross-Product Interface Coordination and Synergy Review
aka: Coordinating authority for the total interface
origin: Jakob Nielsen (1993; synergy review added in the 1994 printing), drawing on Perlman (1989), Poltrock (1994) and Bellantone and Lanzetta (1991)
summary: Give one person or committee authority over the whole user interface across screens, documentation, training and releases, and hold early cross-project reviews to find shareable elements.
description: Nielsen's 'total interface' covers application screens, documentation, online help, tutorials, training and successive releases, and consistency should hold across all of them and across product families. His recommended means is a coordinating authority for each project (one person, or a committee for large or corporate efforts), supported by standards, a project terminology dictionary, early prototypes as reference exemplars, and shared code or constraining toolkits. The synergy review extends this across projects: a panel with one representative from each of several projects in early design reviews each concept in turn, not for detail but to list interface elements and features likely to be shared by two or more projects, which then become candidates for joint design, testing and code. In Nielsen's 1992 survey specialists rated total-interface coordination 4.1 of 5 for impact, but only 38 percent of projects did it.
steps: Name a coordinating person, or a committee for large or corporate efforts, for each project.
List every component of the total interface: screens, manuals, help, tutorials, training, installation and later releases.
Adopt relevant standards and write a project terminology dictionary used by every component.
Share an early prototype as the reference statement of the intended interface, and provide shared code or constraining toolkits.
Hold a synergy review while several projects are still in early design: one representative per project presents its concept in turn.
For each concept, note functions and interface elements that overlap with other projects, and compile those shared by two or more.
Assign owners for joint design, testing and code of shared elements, and check training and documentation whenever the interface is redesigned.
outputs: A coordinator role, terminology dictionary, list of shared interface elements with owners, and consistent behaviour and language across user-facing materials and releases.
useWhen: Use it when several teams or products share users, or when documentation, training and support content risk drifting from the shipped interface.
avoidWhen: It works only before designs diverge. To audit consistency of interfaces that already exist use Guidelines Review and Consistency Inspection. Consistency is not the only goal; do not force bad design in its name.
whyLost: The idea survives as design-system teams, DesignOps and content governance, but Nielsen's specific coordinator role and synergy review are rarely named.
whereToUse: Product suites, platform companies, enterprise software families, and organisations merging products after acquisitions.
example: A bank's mobile, web and branch-tablet teams hold a synergy review and find all three are designing payee selection from long lists. One shared component is designed and tested once, and the help centre is updated in the same release.
reference: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering. Boston: AP Professional. pp. 90-91, 112-113, 235-236.

name: Cross-Tabulation of UX Metrics
origin: Pearson (1904) contingency tables; staple of market research tabulation
summary: Breaks metrics down by participant groups in a table to see where experiences differ.
description: Cross-tabulation lays one variable against another, for example task success by device, or NPS category by customer tenure, to show how outcomes vary across segments. It is the first step in "why" analysis for benchmarks. Sauro advises collapsing sparse categories (such as merging 7-point responses into top-box and the rest) so cells have enough data, then testing differences with chi-square or N-1 tests. Done carelessly, slicing by many variables generates false positives, so pre-planned comparisons and multiple-comparison corrections matter.
steps: Choose the outcome and the grouping variables you planned to examine.
Collapse sparse categories so each cell has adequate counts.
Build tables with row or column percentages as appropriate.
Test differences with chi-square, N-1 or Fisher tests, correcting for multiple comparisons.
Present only meaningful splits, with counts shown.
outputs: Tables showing which groups differ on key metrics.
useWhen: Exploring differences across devices, segments, tenure or regions in survey and benchmark data.
avoidWhen: Small samples sliced many ways, which manufactures spurious findings.
whyLost: Not lost, but rarely done with significance testing and multiplicity control in UX reporting.
whereToUse: Benchmark reports, survey analysis, analytics segment reviews.
example: Task success on a tablet is 22 points lower than on desktop, significant after correction, prompting a tablet-specific review.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapter 11.

name: Cross-Tool Log Sessionisation with Diary Validation
aka: Log-derived time metrics validated by diaries
origin: Ciera Jaspan, Collin Green and colleagues, Google engineering productivity research, 2020-2022
summary: Joins logs from many tools into task sessions, derives time-spent metrics, and validates them against participant diaries before using them to evaluate interventions.
description: Work spread across many tools cannot be measured from any single product's analytics. This method normalises logs from all tools into events, tags artefacts as task-identifying (such as a code change) or informational, and groups events into sessions with explicit rules: same day, gaps under 10 minutes, same task artefact. Sessions are mapped to a small set of time metrics; at Google these were coding, reviewing, shepherding, investigation, development, email and meetings. Crucially, the metrics are validated: 25 engineers kept one-day diaries, and agreement with the logs was computed per metric with prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK), benchmarked against well-understood measures such as meetings. Only validated metrics were used in mixed models with person random effects, for example showing readability certification associated with 4.5% shorter review time.
steps: Inventory log sources and prioritise those covering most of the work.
Normalise logs into events and tag artefacts as task-identifying or informational.
Group events into sessions with explicit rules, for example same day, gap under 10 minutes and same task artefact.
Map sessions to a small set of time metrics tied to recognisable activities.
Collect diaries from a sample of participants (for example 25) for the same days and compute agreement per metric with PABAK, comparing against well-understood metrics such as meetings.
Enrich sources where agreement is weak (for example add window-focus events) and set up automated monitoring of data quality.
Apply privacy rules: no individual reporting without consent, limited retention.
Use validated metrics in models such as mixed models with person random effects to evaluate interventions.
outputs: Validated per-person time metrics, documented sessionisation rules and agreement statistics, and intervention effect estimates.
useWhen: Measuring time-on-task across a multi-tool workflow, especially developer, knowledge-worker or internal-tool productivity.
avoidWhen: When work is largely offline or unlogged; logs miss it and gap thresholds are arbitrary. Employee telemetry raises serious privacy and trust issues; without consent and governance use Time-Use Survey or Diary Studies instead.
whyLost: It is a recent engineering-productivity practice; most UX analytics stay within one product and rarely validate log metrics against self-report.
whereToUse: Developer tools, enterprise suites, internal platforms, clinical systems where staff move between applications.
example: A design-tools company joins editor, chat and ticket logs into sessions, validates 'time in review' against diaries from 30 designers (PABAK 0.7), then shows that a new commenting feature cut review time by 8%.
sources: Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Jaspan, C. et al. (2020). Enabling the study of software development behavior with cross-tool logs. IEEE Software, 37(6), 44-51; Egelman, C. et al. (2022). In Chapman, C. N. et al. (eds) Proceedings of Quant UX Con 2022, pp. 142-148.

name: Cross-Use Prototype Evaluation
aka: Cross-cultural usability user evaluation in context
Culture-targeted prototype evaluation with design markers
origin: Jasem Alostath and Abdulwahed Khalfan, 2007
summary: Participants from several cultures each use alternative prototypes built for each target culture, and discriminant analysis shows which design markers drive preference and usability.
description: Cross-Use tests whether culture-specific design actually helps. One prototype is built per target culture, each maximising that culture's design markers (colour, layout, imagery, language, trust cues), with swappable content. Equal samples per culture use all prototypes in counterbalanced Latin-square order on real tasks, giving a mixed design of culture by prototype by task complexity. Sessions run through consent, a pre-interaction questionnaire illustrated with design-marker images, simple and complex tasks with comparison questions after each group (usefulness, ease, frustration, satisfaction, cultural fit, trust), a post-interaction ranking of cultural design claims, and demographics. Discriminant analysis and chi-square tests then identify the markers that separate preferences and performance by culture, producing separate preference and usability models, which may diverge.
steps: Derive cultural design claims and concrete design markers from prior cultural analysis.
Build one prototype per target culture with swappable culturally appropriate content.
Recruit equal samples per culture (the original used 21 per culture).
Counterbalance prototype order with a Latin square and include simple and complex tasks.
Collect pre-interaction expectations, task performance, per-task comparison ratings and post-interaction rankings of design claims.
Analyse with discriminant analysis and chi-square to find the markers that drive preference and usability per culture.
outputs: A cultural preferences model and a cultural usability model, each listing the influential design markers.
useWhen: Deciding whether to localise design beyond translation for specific markets, especially for trust-sensitive services.
avoidWhen: When budgets cannot support several full prototypes, or when participants (for example English-speaking urban users) would not represent the wider culture; consider Cultural Dimension Analysis for Global UX as a cheaper start.
whyLost: It was a single academic study design; building multiple full prototypes is costly and localisation is usually decided by market teams.
whereToUse: Banking, government and e-commerce services launching in several regions, and global design systems with regional variants.
example: UK, Egyptian and Kuwaiti participants each use three e-banking prototypes. Analysis shows trust markers drive preference in Kuwait while layout drives task performance everywhere, so only trust cues are localised.
reference: Alostath, J.M. and Khalfan, A.M. (2007) Cross-Use: cross-cultural usability user evaluation-in-context. In Aykin, N. (ed.) Usability and Internationalization: HCI and Culture, LNCS 4559. Berlin: Springer, pp. 225-234.

name: Cross-volume method chaining (DSRP to ethnography to DAG to SEM to GMM)
donor: Mixed-methods research design; systems thinking; causal inference; psychometrics; machine learning
origin: Vivek Gopinath, The Inquiry Series, building on Cabrera's DSRP, Pearl's DAGs and latent-variable modelling
summary: A deliberate sequence in which each method's output becomes the next method's input, moving from systems framing to ethnographic mechanism to causal graph, measurement model and segmentation.
description: Method chaining makes the hand-offs between methods explicit and testable. DSRP (Distinctions, Systems, Relationships, Perspectives) frames the problem space and surfaces candidate constructs. Ethnography grounds those constructs in observed practice and mechanisms. The mechanisms are formalised as a directed acyclic graph that states which variables cause which, and which are confounders. The DAG's latent constructs are then measured with a validated survey and estimated in a structural equation model, and the resulting factor scores or behavioural features feed a Gaussian mixture model that segments users probabilistically. The rigour lies in traceability: every SEM path should trace back to an ethnographic observation, every segment should be interpretable through the SEM constructs, and each link carries its own validity check rather than inheriting confidence from the previous stage.
steps: Map the problem with DSRP, listing distinctions, part-whole systems, relationships and stakeholder perspectives, and extract 5-12 candidate constructs.
Run ethnographic fieldwork (typically 10-20 participants) to confirm, discard or refine each construct and to describe causal mechanisms in participants' terms.
Translate mechanisms into a DAG, mark confounders, mediators and colliders, and check it with domain experts before measurement.
Develop or adopt multi-item scales (at least 3 items per construct) and collect survey data large enough for SEM (commonly N of 200 or more).
Fit a CFA then SEM, accepting the measurement model only at acceptable fit (e.g. CFI of 0.95 or above, RMSEA of 0.06 or below, SRMR of 0.08 or below).
Fit GMMs on factor scores or behavioural features, choose the number of components by BIC and interpretability, and require each segment to be at least about 5% of the sample.
Write a traceability matrix linking each segment and path back to field evidence, and flag links supported by only one stage.
outputs: A construct inventory, field-grounded mechanism descriptions, a validated DAG, a fitted measurement and structural model, probabilistic user segments and a traceability matrix.
useWhen: When a programme must move from an ill-defined problem to quantified, segment-level decisions while keeping qualitative grounding, and when the team has the skills and sample to support SEM and mixture modelling.
avoidWhen: Avoid when samples are small (under about 200), when constructs are already well established, or when a simple experiment can answer the question directly; then use a focused A/B test or a single validated survey.
whyLost: An original integrative framework; in most organisations these methods sit in different teams (qual researchers, data scientists, survey specialists), so the hand-offs are never designed.
whereToUse: Fintech segmentation, health behaviour programmes, B2B SaaS adoption strategy, and any product where personas need to be both statistically defensible and ethnographically grounded.
example: An investment app maps the trust problem with DSRP, observes 16 investors at home, and finds that perceived control mediates trust. A DAG and SEM on 600 survey responses confirm the path, and GMM on factor scores yields four trust segments that drive differentiated onboarding.
sources: Cabrera, D. & Cabrera, L. (2015) Systems Thinking Made Simple
Pearl, J., Glymour, M. & Jewell, N. P. (2016) Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer
Kline, R. B. (2023) Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling, 5th ed.
The Inquiry Series, Ch 60 — The Forward-Thinking Research Loop — Predict → Diagnose → Prove → Forecast → Prescribe → Validate
reference: Gopinath, V. Forward-Thinking Playbook (The Inquiry Series)

name: Crowdsourced Tagging of Qualitative Data
origin: Crowdsourcing practice (Amazon Mechanical Turk); described for UX by Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015)
summary: Have colleagues or crowd workers tag thousands of short entries against a taxonomy, with a 'none of the above' option and double coding to measure agreement.
description: Large diary studies, feedback channels and open-ended surveys can produce thousands of short entries that no single researcher can code in time. This method distributes the coding. If a taxonomy exists (for a travel app, its features such as flight search or account settings), volunteers inside the organisation or paid crowd workers tag each entry with one label. If not, a provisional taxonomy is built by affinity diagramming a random subset, and taggers can choose 'none of the above' and propose a label, which reveals missing categories. Rigour comes from clear instructions with examples, assigning at least two taggers per item, computing inter-rater reliability such as Cohen's kappa, resolving disagreements and revising the taxonomy. It works only when entries stand alone and the domain is easy to grasp.
steps: Define a taxonomy, or derive a provisional one by affinity diagramming a random subset of entries.
Write tagging instructions with worked examples for each label.
Distribute entries to internal volunteers or crowd workers after checking privacy and consent allow it.
Offer a 'none of the above' option with a field for a suggested label.
Assign at least two taggers to each entry and compute agreement, for example Cohen's kappa.
Resolve disagreements and revise the taxonomy from suggested labels, then re-tag affected items.
outputs: A labelled dataset ready for counting and comparison, an agreement score, and a revised taxonomy.
useWhen: Diary studies, app-store reviews, support tickets or survey verbatims with thousands of short, self-contained entries and a reasonably clear category scheme.
avoidWhen: Avoid for specialist domains, long or context-dependent entries, or data that cannot be shared outside the research team. Consider AI-assisted coding with human checks, or a researcher-led content analysis instead.
whyLost: Privacy concerns and the rise of automated text classification left it little used, though the quality controls remain relevant for AI-assisted coding.
whereToUse: Large diary studies, feedback programmes, voice-of-customer pipelines and creating labelled training data for classifiers.
example: A travel app collects 6,000 diary entries. Twenty colleagues tag them against the feature taxonomy, two per entry; kappa is 0.72 and 'none of the above' suggestions add a 'refunds' category.
sources: Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Baxter, K., Courage, C. and Caine, K. (2015). Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Research Methods (2nd ed.). Waltham, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 206-207.

name: Cultural Commentators
origin: William Gaver, Interaction Research Studio, 2007
summary: Documentary filmmakers or journalists are commissioned to make their own accounts of people living with a deployed design, adding outside voices to evaluation.
description: Gaver's group developed cultural commentators to evaluate ludic and research-through-design prototypes for which usability metrics make little sense. After a design is deployed in people's homes or communities, independent commentators such as documentary filmmakers and journalists are hired to observe and interview the people involved and produce their own personal, interpretive accounts. Because they are not designers or HCI researchers, their non-native interpretations bring new perspectives and resist the designers' own framing, producing a polyphonic assessment in which several voices sit side by side rather than being reduced to a single verdict. The method sits alongside cultural probes as a dialogical, interpretive approach. Its rigour lies in commentators' independence and in triangulating their accounts with designers' and participants' own views.
steps: Deploy the design with people in their everyday setting for a substantial period.
Commission independent commentators (documentary filmmakers, journalists) with no stake in the design.
Brief them on access and ethics but not on what to conclude.
Let them observe, interview and produce films or articles in their own style.
Set their accounts alongside designers' observations and participants' own views.
Discuss agreements and tensions among the voices to inform the next design.
outputs: Films or articles about people's experience with the design, used as evaluation material alongside other accounts.
useWhen: Evaluating exploratory, playful or provocative designs and long-term deployments where experience and meaning matter more than task performance.
avoidWhen: Usability problem finding or decisions needing measured comparison; use Field Usability Testing or Diary Studies.
whyLost: It is costly and suited to research-through-design labs; commercial teams rarely commission outside storytellers for evaluation.
whereToUse: Research prototypes in homes and communities, civic technology pilots and cultural sector products.
example: A smart-home prototype that reads local weather poetically is deployed for three months. A documentary maker's film shows one family treating it as a companion, a reading the designers had not considered.
reference: Gaver, W.W. (2007) Cultural commentators: non-native interpretations as resources for polyphonic assessment. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 65(4), 292-305.

name: Cultural Consensus Analysis
origin: A. Kimball Romney, Susan Weller and William Batchelder, 1986
summary: Estimates whether a group shares a single body of knowledge, each person's competence in it, and the culturally correct answers, without knowing the answers in advance.
description: The cultural consensus model treats agreement among informants as evidence of shared knowledge. Factor analysis of the respondent-by-respondent agreement matrix tests whether a single dominant factor exists (first-to-second eigenvalue ratio above about 3), estimates each informant's cultural competence, and weights their answers to derive the 'culturally correct' answer key. Residual agreement analysis reveals subcultures. In UX, consensus analysis tells you whether a user group shares a mental model or vocabulary (e.g. what counts as 'urgent'), who the most knowledgeable informants are, and whether different groups hold different models, all with modest samples of 20-30.
steps: Develop items about the domain (true/false, multiple choice, or rankings), often derived from free lists or interviews.
Administer to informants from the target group(s).
Compute the agreement matrix corrected for guessing and factor it (e.g. with UCINET or the CCTpack/AnthroTools packages).
Check the eigenvalue ratio for a single culture and that competences are positive.
Estimate the culturally correct answers and informant competences; examine residuals for subgroups.
Use results to define shared models for design and to select expert informants for deeper interviews.
outputs: Evidence for or against shared knowledge, competence scores, consensus answer key and subgroup patterns.
useWhen: Checking whether users share a mental model, vocabulary or norms before designing for 'the user'.
avoidWhen: Preference or attitude questions where there is no 'correct' cultural answer to estimate.
whyLost: It is known only in anthropology and some public health research; UX assumes or asserts shared models.
whereToUse: Clinical terminology, enterprise workflows across sites, community norms on platforms, financial literacy.
example: Consensus analysis of nurses' triage priority judgements finds two subcultures (ICU and ward nurses) with different answer keys, so the alerting tool supports configurable priorities per unit.
sources: Romney, Weller & Batchelder, Culture as consensus: A theory of culture and informant accuracy (1986), American Anthropologist
Weller, Cultural consensus theory: Applications and frequently asked questions (2007), Field Methods
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
reference: Romney, A. K., Weller, S. C., & Batchelder, W. H. (1986). American Anthropologist, 88(2), 313-338.

name: Cultural Dimensions Analysis
aka: Cultural Dimension Analysis for Global UX
origin: Geert Hofstede (Culture's Consequences, 1980); Fons Trompenaars (1993); applied to web design by Aaron Marcus and Emilie Gould (2000)
summary: Using national cultural dimensions such as power distance, individualism and uncertainty avoidance to generate hypotheses about how design should differ between markets.
description: Cultural dimensions analysis applies frameworks such as Hofstede's six dimensions (power distance, individualism, masculinity, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation, indulgence) or Trompenaars' seven to anticipate how users in different markets may respond to design choices. For instance, high uncertainty-avoidance cultures may want more explicit guidance and reassurance, and high power-distance cultures may respond to authority cues. Used rigorously, dimension scores are hypothesis generators, not conclusions: they describe national averages, are partly dated, and can stereotype individuals. Good practice uses the dimensions to design specific comparative studies, measures individual-level cultural values within the actual user sample, and checks whether predicted differences appear in behaviour. Marcus and Gould showed how website conventions vary along these dimensions, but few teams follow through with empirical validation.
steps: Select the markets to compare and retrieve dimension scores for each from published sources.
Identify design decisions plausibly sensitive to the dimensions with the largest gaps (for example onboarding guidance and uncertainty avoidance).
Write explicit, testable hypotheses linking each dimension gap to an expected difference in preference or behaviour.
Measure individual-level values in your own sample with a validated short scale rather than assuming national scores apply.
Test the hypotheses with comparative studies such as A/B tests per market or matched usability sessions.
Report which predicted differences held, which did not, and avoid generalising to individuals.
outputs: Dimension gap profile across markets, testable design hypotheses, individual-level value measures and validated or refuted localisation decisions.
useWhen: Early planning for multi-market products to decide where localisation beyond language may matter and what to test.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for research with actual users in each market; never use national scores to stereotype individuals or justify untested design changes.
whyLost: Popular in international business, it was criticised for essentialism and remains rarely used rigorously in UX beyond localisation checklists.
whereToUse: Global product design; localization strategy; international IA.
example: An e-commerce platform entering Japan and Germany hypothesises that high uncertainty avoidance calls for more detailed return policies at checkout. A market-level A/B test confirms a 6% conversion lift in Japan but none in Germany.
sources: Marcus & Gould, Crosscurrents: cultural dimensions and global web user-interface design (Interactions, 2000)
reference: Marcus A & Gould EW (2000) Crosscurrents: Cultural dimensions and global Web user-interface design. Interactions 7(4):32-46

extra.The Six Dimensions Applied to UX: Power Distance: High PD cultures expect authority and hierarchy to be visible. Low PD cultures prefer egalitarian interfaces. Research implication: in high PD contexts, interfaces that position the system as an expert or authority may be trusted more; peer-recommendation features work better in low PD contexts. Individualism vs. Collectivism: Individualist cultures: personal benefit, privacy, individual control. Collectivist cultures: group benefit, shared visibility, social approval. Research implication: sharing features, privacy controls, and default settings should differ by cultural context. Uncertainty Avoidance: High UA cultures: prefer explicit rules, formal processes, complete information before action. Low UA cultures: comfortable with ambiguity and experimentation. Research implication: onboarding, help systems, and error messages should be more comprehensive in high UA contexts. Long-term vs. Short-term Orientation: Long-term: patience, persistence, investment in the future. Short-term: tradition, social obligation, quick results. Research implication: progress indication, savings features, and reward systems should calibrate to temporal orientation.

name: Cultural Probes
donor: Interaction design and critical design (Royal College of Art)
origin: William Gaver, Anthony Dunne and Elena Pacenti, 1999
summary: Deliberately ambiguous kits of cameras, postcards, maps and diaries that provoke participants' self-documentation, yielding inspiration for design rather than comparable data.
description: Cultural probes (Gaver, Dunne & Pacenti, 1999) are deliberately incomplete research instruments — packages of materials given to participants that are designed to be provocative and ambiguous rather than systematic. Unlike diary studies, probes are not designed to collect comparable data across participants. They are designed to evoke unexpected, personal, and creative responses that inspire designers rather than generate findings. Probes are a research inspiration tool, not an analysis tool.
steps: Define the inspirational territory you want to open up (not hypotheses to test) and the population, often one hard to observe directly.
Design a probe kit of 5-8 open-ended items, such as a disposable camera with 10-15 printed prompts, a map to annotate, postcards with provocative questions and a small diary.
Make the materials crafted and personal so participants feel invited to play rather than report, and pilot the kit with one or two people.
Hand over kits in person with a brief explanation and leave them with participants for 1-4 weeks, with a light-touch reminder midway.
Collect the returns and review them as a team, treating ambiguous responses as prompts for design thinking rather than coding them for frequency.
Follow up with interviews or design responses that reflect the returns back to participants, and keep the probes' fragments visible during ideation.
outputs: Returned artefacts (photos, annotated maps, postcards, diaries), team reflections, design provocations and follow-up interview prompts.
useWhen: Early, open-ended exploration of intimate, domestic or remote contexts where direct observation is intrusive or impossible, and when the goal is design inspiration.
avoidWhen: When you need systematic, comparable or quantifiable data (use a diary study or experience sampling) or when stakeholders will treat probe returns as evidence of prevalence.
whyLost: Vestigial: Creative and valuable for hard-to-reach populations; time-intensive; rarely applied rigorously.
whereToUse: Cross-cultural design; marginalized populations; distant communities.
example: A smart-home start-up mails probe kits to 12 multi-generational households asking them to photograph 'something in your home that only one person knows how to work'. The returns reveal informal gatekeepers of household technology, reframing the product around shared control.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection
Gaver, Dunne & Pacenti, Design: Cultural Probes (Interactions, 1999)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 33 — Participatory & Arts-Based Methods
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Gaver B, Dunne T & Pacenti E (1999) Design: Cultural probes. Interactions 6(1):21-29

extra.Probe Package Design: Disposable camera: With 10–15 printed prompts attached — questions like "photograph something that represents your relationship with this software," "photograph the moment you feel most frustrated today," "photograph something that doesn't belong." Diary: Open sentence completions rather than closed questions. "Today I felt… when I tried to…" "The most unexpected thing that happened with my [product] today was…" "If this product could speak, it would say…" Map: A large-format map of the participant's environment with instructions: "Mark where you use this product most. Mark where you never use it. Mark where you wish you could." Postcards: Addressed back to the research team. Prompts on the back: "The one thing I wish the product understood is…" "If I could change one thing tomorrow, it would be…"

name: Cumulative Risk Index
aka: Cumulative risk index and cumulative protective index
origin: Sameroff and colleagues (Sameroff, Gutman and Peck, 2003; Sameroff and Rosenblum, 2006)
summary: Score each known risk factor a person is exposed to as one, sum to a cumulative risk score, optionally balance it against a protective index, and target the highest-risk groups.
description: Exposure to several risks predicts poor outcomes better than any single risk, so the index counts them. Each empirically supported risk factor, spanning individual, family, neighbourhood and wider levels, is dichotomised and scored 1 if present; the sum is the cumulative risk score. A parallel cumulative protective index can be built from validated protective factors, and the balance between them examined. The index represents simultaneous risks on a common metric, is easy for decision-makers to read, works with existing data and improves power by reducing many variables to one. Interventions can aim to reduce the number of risks, starting with the factor that covaries most with others. The drawback is that the index cannot say which specific factor matters for which outcome, and dichotomising discards detail.
steps: List empirically supported risk factors for the outcome across levels (individual, context, product exposure).
Dichotomise each factor with a justified threshold and score exposure as 1.
Sum to a cumulative risk score per person or group.
Optionally build a cumulative protective index from validated protective factors and examine the balance.
Check that outcomes rise with the score, then identify high-risk groups and target the factor that covaries most with the others.
outputs: Per-person or per-group cumulative risk and protective scores, and a risk-protection balance.
useWhen: Predicting which users are likely to churn, fail, be harmed or need support when many weak risk factors each matter a little, and when stakeholders need an easily understood score.
avoidWhen: You need to know which factor drives the outcome, or factors have very different weights; use regression or key-driver analysis instead.
whyLost: It is a tool of developmental and public-health research; product analytics jumped to predictive models without passing through simple, transparent risk counts.
whereToUse: Customer health scores, digital inclusion and vulnerability screening, financial hardship detection, patient engagement programmes.
example: A utilities app counts six risk factors for missed payments (prepayment meter, recent move, no autopay and so on). Customers with four or more get a proactive support flow, and the protective factor of a saved contact number is promoted.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Wachs, T. D. (2015). Assessing bioecological influences. In R. M. Lerner (Ed.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 4, pp. 811-846. Wiley.

name: CUPED Variance Reduction
origin: Alex Deng, Ya Xu, Ron Kohavi and Toby Walker, Microsoft, 2013
summary: Uses each user's pre-experiment metric as a covariate to remove predictable variance from A/B test outcomes, shrinking confidence intervals substantially.
description: CUPED adjusts each user's outcome Y by subtracting theta times (X minus mean X), where X is a pre-period covariate (often the same metric before the experiment) and theta is cov(X,Y)/var(X). Because X is measured before assignment, it is independent of treatment, so the estimate remains unbiased while variance falls by a factor of 1 - rho squared. With typical correlations of 0.5-0.7 this cuts required sample sizes by 25-50%. It is a control-variate technique well known in Monte Carlo and survey sampling. UX-led experiments, which are often underpowered, benefit greatly, yet many teams compare raw means.
steps: Choose a pre-period covariate strongly correlated with the outcome (e.g. same metric over the prior 2-4 weeks).
Ensure the covariate is measured strictly before randomisation; handle new users without history (impute or use other covariates).
Compute theta from pooled data across both arms.
Compute adjusted outcomes and estimate the treatment effect and its standard error.
Report variance reduction achieved and compare with the unadjusted estimate as a sanity check.
Use the expected variance reduction in power calculations for future tests.
outputs: Variance-reduced effect estimates with tighter confidence intervals, and realised variance reduction.
useWhen: A/B tests on metrics with stable per-user history, especially when traffic is limited.
avoidWhen: Tests mostly on new users without history, or with covariates possibly affected by treatment.
whyLost: It is known inside large experimentation platforms but not in UX training, and smaller teams use naive calculators.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS with modest traffic, engagement metrics, revenue per user, task time in repeated-use tools.
example: A B2B app with 6,000 weekly users tests a new editor. Adjusting by pre-period edit counts (rho = 0.7) halves variance, detecting a 4% improvement in two weeks instead of four.
sources: Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker, Improving the sensitivity of online controlled experiments by utilizing pre-experiment data (2013), WSDM
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella, 2010)
reference: Deng, A., Xu, Y., Kohavi, R., & Walker, T. (2013). WSDM '13, 123-132.

name: Cusp Catastrophe Model Fitting
origin: Maximum likelihood approach by Loren Cobb and colleagues (Cobb 1978; Cobb and Zacks 1985), implemented in the cusp R package by Grasman, van der Maas and Wagenmakers (2009).
summary: A maximum likelihood model, fitted like a regression, that tests whether a behavioural outcome is better described by a cusp with two stable states controlled by a 'normal' and a 'splitting' variable than by a linear model.
description: The cusp catastrophe describes a behaviour that changes smoothly when a splitting variable is low but jumps between two stable states, with hysteresis, when it is high. Cobb made this deterministic model statistical by adding stochastic noise to the dynamics, which yields a probability distribution that can be unimodal or bimodal depending on the control variables. As in regression, the behavioural state is a weighted sum of measured outcome items, and the normal (alpha) and splitting (beta) controls are each linear functions of measured predictors. Estimation gives coefficients, standard errors and fit indices, and the cusp is compared with linear and logistic alternatives using AIC and BIC. A classic example in the book is attitude data where intensity of feeling loads only on the splitting axis: low-involvement respondents are spread around the middle, high-involvement respondents polarise. The book's rules are to simulate data from the model first to understand power, to use independent cross-sectional observations (the method is not valid for time series), and to remember that a better cusp fit is evidence, not proof. For UX this turns claims about polarised attitudes or all-or-nothing adoption into testable models.
steps: Specify the behavioural outcome and candidate predictors for the normal axis (pushes the outcome up or down) and the splitting axis (amplifies polarisation, such as involvement).
Simulate data from a cusp with plausible parameters and fit it, to check that your sample size can recover the effects.
Inspect the data descriptively: histograms overall and at high levels of the splitting predictor, and pairwise plots.
Fit the full cusp model with each predictor allowed on both axes, then reduced models that drop non-significant paths.
Compare the cusp with linear and logistic models using AIC and BIC, and check how many observations lie inside the bifurcation set.
Interpret which predictors act on which axis and report the result alongside other catastrophe flags.
outputs: Estimated normal and splitting coefficients, model comparison indices against linear alternatives, and a plot of cases located in the cusp's control plane.
useWhen: You have a large cross-sectional sample with a continuous outcome and theory that some factor (involvement, experience, stakes) makes responses polarise rather than shift.
avoidWhen: Data are repeated measures from the same people (observations must be independent), the sample is small, or there is no theoretical candidate for a splitting variable.
whyLost: It requires comfort with nonlinear likelihood models and catastrophe theory, which carried a poor reputation after early overclaiming; UX surveys are usually analysed with linear models.
whereToUse: Attitude and trust surveys, adoption intent studies, satisfaction data where involvement may polarise responses, privacy concern research.
example: A survey of 3,000 users rates a controversial AI feature. Researchers fit a cusp with perceived usefulness on the normal axis and personal involvement with the topic on the splitting axis, and find that highly involved users split into enthusiasts and rejecters while low-involvement users sit near neutral, a pattern a linear model misses.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Custom component creation (spaCy)
origin: spaCy v3 component API (Explosion, 2021)
summary: Writing bespoke processing steps for an NLP pipeline, such as speaker filters, codebook taggers or anonymisers, so research-specific logic runs consistently over every transcript.
description: spaCy lets researchers register custom components that run inside the pipeline and add extension attributes to documents, sentences and tokens (e.g. doc._.participant_id, sent._.speaker, sent._.code_candidates). This turns study-specific rules into reusable, testable code: removing moderator turns, tagging sentences that match codebook definitions, redacting personal data, or attaching interview metadata. Rigour comes from unit tests for each component, clear documentation of rules, versioning components with the pipeline, and evaluating outputs on annotated samples just as for statistical components. Keeping such logic inside the pipeline, rather than in scattered post-processing scripts, also ensures every transcript receives identical treatment.
steps: Specify the component's job, inputs and outputs (e.g. add sent._.speaker from diarisation data).
Register extension attributes and implement the component with @Language.component or a factory.
Insert it at the correct pipeline position (e.g. after the parser and before downstream taggers).
Write unit tests on small example texts covering normal and edge cases.
Evaluate on a sample of real transcripts and record precision and recall where applicable.
Package and version components with the pipeline configuration so others can reproduce runs.
outputs: Tested, versioned custom components and enriched documents with research-specific attributes.
useWhen: When research-specific logic must be applied consistently across large corpora, such as speaker filtering, codebook tagging or anonymisation.
avoidWhen: Avoid for one-off analyses where a short script suffices; avoid encoding interpretive judgements as rigid rules.
whyLost: Building components needs software engineering skills uncommon among qualitative researchers.
whereToUse: Research operations pipelines, anonymisation of transcripts, codebook pre-tagging and multi-study repositories.
example: A health research team writes an anonymiser component that replaces names, dates of birth and clinic names with tags. Tested on 50 annotated transcripts it achieves 0.98 recall, and it is reused across five studies.
sources: spaCy documentation: Processing pipelines and custom components (spacy.io)
The Inquiry Series, C10 — spaCy — Building NLP Pipelines for Qualitative Research
reference: Honnibal, M., Montani, I., Van Landeghem, S. & Boyd, A. (2020) spaCy: Industrial-strength Natural Language Processing in Python. Zenodo

name: Custom NLP pipeline construction (spaCy)
origin: spaCy library, Matthew Honnibal and Ines Montani (Explosion), 2015; transformer pipelines from spaCy v3 (2021)
summary: Assembling a sequence of language processing components that turns interview transcripts into structured, analysable data such as entities, sentences, phrases and quotes.
description: spaCy processes text through an ordered pipeline: tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, named entity recognition and any custom components. For qualitative UX research a pipeline might segment transcripts into sentences, remove moderator turns, tag product features and emotions, extract candidate quotes and attach metadata (participant, segment, timestamp).
