The rigour comes from designing the pipeline around research questions rather than generic NLP, evaluating each component against a hand-annotated sample (precision, recall, F1), pinning model versions, and keeping the pipeline as a pre-processing instrument that supports, rather than replaces, interpretive analysis.
steps: Define the research questions and the structured outputs the pipeline must produce (e.g. feature mentions, pain-point sentences, quotes).
Start from a pinned pre-trained model (e.g. en_core_web_trf for accuracy, en_core_web_sm for speed).
Add components in order: sentence segmentation, speaker filtering, entity ruler for domain terms, custom attribute extractors.
Hand-annotate 100-200 sentences as a gold standard and measure precision, recall and F1 per component.
Iterate until key components reach agreed thresholds (e.g. F1 of 0.80 or above), then freeze and version the pipeline.
Export results to a table linked back to transcript IDs and timestamps for analysts to verify.
outputs: A versioned pipeline, per-component evaluation scores and a structured dataset of sentences, entities and quotes linked to transcripts.
useWhen: Large qualitative corpora (dozens to hundreds of transcripts, open-ended survey responses, support tickets) needing consistent structure before analysis.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small studies (under about 15 interviews) where manual coding is faster and richer, and never as a replacement for interpretive analysis.
whyLost: NLP pipelines are standard in computational linguistics and industry text analytics, but qualitative UX researchers rarely have programming support.
whereToUse: Interview repositories, voice-of-customer programmes, support ticket analysis and AI-assisted coding pipelines.
example: A SaaS company processes 300 customer interviews through a spaCy pipeline that removes moderator speech, tags 40 product feature names and extracts complaint sentences, producing a feature-by-complaint table that analysts then read and code.
sources: Honnibal, M. & Montani, I. spaCy documentation (spacy.io)
Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft
The Inquiry Series, C10 — spaCy — Building NLP Pipelines for Qualitative Research
reference: Honnibal, M., Montani, I., Van Landeghem, S. & Boyd, A. (2020) spaCy: Industrial-strength Natural Language Processing in Python. Zenodo

name: Customer Co-Innovation Partnership
origin: Janaki Kumar and Mario Herger (2013), from SAP practice
summary: A standing, NDA-backed partnership with three to six customer organisations that gives trusted access, customer-nominated participants and repeated short validation rounds for innovative enterprise products.
description: Enterprise vendors building standard software for new processes cannot rely on normal recruitment: customers distrust sharing process details with a vendor who also serves their competitors, suitable participants are scarce, and innovation needs many quick iterations. Kumar and Herger describe a co-innovation partnership as the answer. A mutual non-disclosure agreement commits the vendor to use insights only for design and the customer to keep early designs confidential. Each customer nominates suitable employees, who take part in early discovery and then return for periodic, shorter validation rounds, and the trust built allows generative sessions such as gamestorming. Customers gain early influence, early adoption and lower implementation and training costs. Three to six partners is the recommended range: fewer risks building custom software for one customer, more becomes hard to administer.
steps: Recruit three to six customer organisations as partners.
Sign a mutual non-disclosure agreement: the vendor uses insights only for design and the customer keeps early designs and prototypes confidential.
Ask each customer to nominate employees who match the target roles.
Run early discovery (observation and interviews) on their current work practices.
Return to the same participants for periodic, shorter validation rounds on each iteration.
Use the established trust to run generative sessions, such as gamestorming, together.
Give partners early influence and early adoption in return, and review the partner mix if one customer starts to dominate.
outputs: Ongoing access to vetted participants, iterative validation findings across several organisations, and partner buy-in for adoption.
useWhen: B2B and enterprise products where target users sit inside customer organisations, processes are confidential and the product needs many rapid iterations with the same people.
avoidWhen: Fewer than three partners turns it into custom development for one customer; for broad market evidence use Surveys or recruitment from a panel, and for finding extreme needs use Lead User Method.
whyLost: It survives as 'design partner' and customer advisory programmes in B2B SaaS, usually run by sales or product management without the explicit research protocol and partner-count rule.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS, vertical software for regulated industries, early-stage B2B start-ups seeking design partners, internal platform teams serving several business units.
example: A procurement software vendor signs four mid-size manufacturers as partners. Nominated buyers join discovery visits, then 45-minute validation sessions every three weeks, and the vendor avoids overfitting by requiring each change to hold for at least three partners.
reference: Kumar, J. M. and Herger, M. (2013). Gamification at Work: Designing Engaging Business Software. Interaction Design Foundation, ch. 4 and 11, pp. 51, 143-145.

name: Customer Feedback and Support Log Analysis
origin: Practitioner method described by Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed (2012); feedback typology from Thor Muller (Get Satisfaction)
summary: Systematically mines support requests, feedback forms, forums and front-line staff for pain points and clues, reading with explicit rules and tracking topics over time.
description: Support and feedback channels are a continuous, free stream of user evidence, but they are biased and easily misread. The method starts by listing every channel, including informal ones such as salespeople, and examining how each channel's design (tone of invitation, follow-up, auto-responses, difficulty of reaching you) shapes what arrives. Analysts read a broad sample of actual comments with their context, sort them into Muller's three types (actionable suggestions, statements of the obvious, and clues, usually the richest), and code for who users are, what they are trying to do, how they approach problems and what problems they have. Five reading rules apply: take the user's perspective, facts first, no jumping to conclusions, complaints point to problems rather than describe them, and remember the silent majority. Trends are tracked over time and compared with behavioural data.
steps: List every feedback channel, including informal ones such as sales and account managers, and note how each channel's process biases what arrives.
With help-desk software, review historical data on who comments and how often, then focus on recent weeks or a specific problem; without it, interview support staff and collect their stock answers.
Read a broad sample of actual comments, not only answered ones, keeping context such as the feature or path the commenter was on.
Sort feedback into actionable suggestions, statements of the obvious and clues, and code for who, goal, approach and problem.
Apply the reading rules: user's perspective, facts first, no premature conclusions, complaints as pointers not specifications, remember the silent majority.
Use topic and sentiment clustering to compare groups and track change over time; interpret a doubling of complaints after a release as a change for the worse, not twice as many unhappy users.
Set a regular review slot, share findings with front-line staff, and compare perceived problems with usage data.
outputs: Coded themes, trending topics, quotations, questions for the research plan, and early warnings after releases.
useWhen: Continuous discovery for a live product, prioritising pain points, and spotting regressions after releases.
avoidWhen: When you need representative prevalence: feedback is overwhelmingly negative and from a vocal subset, and channel design biases it. Pair with surveys or analytics; for structured review mining use Review Analysis Methodology (RVA).
whyLost: Most teams now glance at ticket dashboards or auto-tagged sentiment, losing the disciplined reading rules and bias analysis.
whereToUse: SaaS, fintech, e-commerce, any product with a support desk, community forum or in-app feedback.
example: A payroll SaaS team codes 400 recent tickets and finds most 'how do I' questions about tax codes come from first-time employers, prompting an onboarding interview study rather than a help-article rewrite.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. and Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience: A Practitioner's Guide to User Research (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 468-475.

name: Customer Hierarchy of Needs Workshop
origin: Paige Dysert and Sasanka Prabhala, Crown Equipment Corporation (2022), inspired by Maslow
summary: A team workshop that places features on a four-level pyramid (functional, operational, value, efficiency needs) to define a product vision and triage scope.
description: Dysert and Prabhala adapt Maslow's hierarchy into a product facilitation tool. Level 1 holds functional needs (what the solution must do), level 2 operational needs (routine obligations and efficiency), level 3 value needs (higher benefits such as time or cost savings) and level 4 efficiency needs (peak performance, the team's north star). After preliminary research, a Jobs-to-be-Done workshop produces job statements; a second workshop has the development team fill the template with features at each level. The pyramid sets MVP scope and becomes a checkpoint: incoming requests are first checked against the vision, dropped if they do not move towards it, and otherwise placed at a level and scheduled. After release, the team checks whether expected value is delivered. The authors stress it is a discussion tool, not a specification, and it can be built top-down when the vision already exists.
steps: Complete preliminary research so the customer's problem and perceived value are understood.
Run a Jobs-to-be-Done workshop with the product team to write job statements from past field research and customer requests.
In a second workshop, fill the four levels with features: functional, operational, value, efficiency.
Design and critique each level to decide how its features will be built.
Triage new requests: drop those that do not move towards the vision; place the rest at a level and schedule them.
After release, measure whether the expected value at each level is delivered.
outputs: A four-level feature hierarchy, a product vision, and a basis for prioritisation and progress tracking.
useWhen: Use in agile teams that need a shared, customer-framed way to set MVP scope and triage a stream of feature requests.
avoidWhen: Avoid using the levels as evidence of what customers value: classify needs with users through Kano Analysis or Outcome-Driven Innovation. It will not say exactly what to build.
whyLost: It is a single conference paper from one company's design research team and has not been taken up widely.
whereToUse: B2B platforms, industrial and fleet software, API products, internal tools with many stakeholders.
example: A fleet-management API team places on-demand CSV reports at level 1, scheduled reports at level 2, APIs at level 3 and an integration platform at level 4, and declines a dashboard request that serves none of them.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Dysert, P. and Prabhala, S. (2022). Customer Hierarchy of Needs: Customer Centric Approach to Agile Product Development. In M. M. Soares, E. Rosenzweig and A. Marcus (eds), Design, User Experience, and Usability: UX Research, Design, and Assessment. DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, pp. 3-11. Cham: Springer. doi:10.1007/978-3-031-05897-4_1

name: Customer Journey Mapping Game
origin: Christophe Tallec (We Design Services) and Paul Kahn
summary: A board-game workshop in which mixed stakeholders choose a persona and goal and lay touchpoint cards on a swim-lane board to build and compare journeys.
description: The game gives participants with very different perspectives a common language for a service. A blank journey board with swim lanes for the relevant touchpoint and information types is prepared, with a deck of touchpoint cards for the domain. Players choose a persona, define the persona's goal, and as a team place touchpoints in the order the persona would meet them. They reflect on patterns, gaps, emotional highs and lows and opportunities, then repeat with other personas or goals, including extreme users, and compare journeys. Piloted with a major French city on reinventing urban transport, with car makers, transit companies, unions and users, it produced a shared language and better alignment. An online version exists. Journeys reflect participants' assumptions unless users take part or research feeds the cards.
steps: Prepare a blank journey board with swim lanes and a deck of touchpoint cards for the domain, based on research where possible.
Participants select a persona.
Define the persona's goal or job.
As a team, place touchpoint cards in the order the persona would meet them.
Reflect on patterns, gaps, emotional highs and lows, and opportunities.
Repeat with another persona or goal, including extreme users, and compare the journeys.
outputs: Co-created journey boards per persona and a list of shared opportunities.
useWhen: Use when many organisations or departments share a service and need a common picture of it before redesign.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the boards as evidence of real journeys: build those through Journey Mapping from Interviews, Diary Studies or Field Studies, and include users or research-based cards in the game.
whyLost: It is known in service design and multi-stakeholder co-creation but seldom used by product UX teams, who make journey maps themselves rather than as a game.
whereToUse: Urban mobility, public services, healthcare pathways, multi-party ecosystems such as travel or utilities.
example: Transit operators, car makers, unions and riders build journeys for a commuter and a wheelchair user; comparing boards shows no operator owns the transfer between modes, which becomes the redesign focus.
reference: Kalbach, J. (2016). Mapping Experiences: A Complete Guide to Creating Value through Journeys, Blueprints, and Diagrams. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 218-221.

name: Customer Language Listening
aka: Noun and verb extraction from user talk
origin: Erika Hall (2018), Conversational Design
summary: Interview customers about their typical day, extract the nouns and verbs they use, and catalogue real-world voice samples to ground an interface's vocabulary and voice.
description: Hall treats research on how people talk as a precondition for defining an interface's voice. The aim is not to mimic users but to be intelligible, to replace internal jargon with words people actually use, and to understand their emotional states, including negative ones. Beyond eavesdropping on how customers discuss the service, the researcher interviews about six representative customers about their typical day, saying little and letting them talk, then pulls every noun and verb from the notes as a vocabulary reference for labels and action phrases. For inspiration on voice, the team goes where customers go and listens to people in relevant roles, noting word choice, sentence structure and tone, and collects good and bad voice samples in a shared, annotated catalogue. Existing digital products are a poor model and spread cliché.
steps: Eavesdrop on how target customers talk about the service and their problems, in person and in their own online spaces.
Interview representative customers about their typical day, staying quiet and letting them speak.
Repeat with about six customers.
Go back through the notes and extract every noun and verb they used.
Use the list as the reference for interface vocabulary, labels and action phrases, replacing internal jargon.
Visit places customers frequent and listen to people in relevant roles, noting word choice, sentence structure and tone.
Collect and annotate good and bad voice samples in a shared space, noting what makes each work; optionally send the team out to eavesdrop and report back.
outputs: A customer noun and verb vocabulary list and an annotated catalogue of voice samples.
useWhen: Before writing labels, navigation, microcopy or a conversational interface's voice, especially when the team's internal vocabulary differs from customers'.
avoidWhen: The interface is not the customer's peer: aim to be meaningful, not to imitate. For validating labels at scale use Tree Testing or Card Sorting; for formal vocabulary control use Thesaurus and Controlled Vocabulary Construction (ISO 25964).
whyLost: 'Use the customer's language' is a common slogan, but the systematic extraction of nouns and verbs and the curated voice catalogue are usually skipped in favour of writer intuition.
whereToUse: Chatbots and voice assistants, onboarding copy, navigation labels, help content, AI assistant persona and tone.
example: Before designing a pension app's assistant, six savers describe their typical week. Nobody says 'contributions' or 'drawdown'; they say 'putting money in' and 'taking it out', which become the default button labels.
reference: Hall, E. (2018). Conversational Design. New York: A Book Apart, pp. 83-85, 98-99.

name: Customer problem interviews
origin: Steve Blank's customer development; Ash Maurya, Running Lean (2012); Rob Fitzpatrick, The Mom Test (2013); scoring by Croll and Yoskovitz (2013)
summary: Interview prospects about concrete past behaviour and current workarounds to test whether a problem is painful and widespread, using a fixed script and, optionally, a scoring rubric.
description: People are polite and will praise ideas, so problem interviews avoid opinions and hypotheticals and ask about the most recent concrete instance: not 'how often do you go to the gym?' but 'when did you last go?'. Maurya's script sets the stage, collects demographics to test the segment, tells the story of the problems, has the subject rank them, explores how they solve each today, and asks for a follow-up and referrals. Divergent interviews let subjects name problems, counting unprompted mentions; convergent ones present problems to rank. Interview at least 15 prospects per stage. Croll and Yoskovitz score each convergent interview on six weighted items (ranked problem, actively solving, engagement, follow-up, referrals, willingness to pay) out of 43, treating 31 or more as good.
steps: Recruit at least 15 prospects per stage, ideally meeting face to face in a neutral setting with a fixed script.
Rewrite questions that invite opinions, frequencies or hypotheticals into questions about the most recent concrete instance.
Set the stage and collect demographics to test the segment hypothesis.
Start divergent (let subjects name their problems), then with new people run convergent interviews in which subjects rank the problems you present.
For each problem ask how they solve it today and let them talk; dig with 'why' and pauses, and do not reveal your preferred answer.
Close by asking for a follow-up session and referrals, and note any offer to pay.

Score each interview immediately (ranked problem 10, actively solving 10, engaged 8, follow-up 8, referrals 4, offered to pay 3; good at 31 or more), then compare high and low scorers and sum first-place rankings to choose the problem and segment.
outputs: Ranked problems, current workarounds, segment evidence, interview scores, and follow-up leads for solution interviews.
useWhen: Validating whether a problem is worth solving and for whom, before building, in a new product or market.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to understand complex work practice in depth; use contextual inquiry. Convergent interviews can steer past adjacent needs, divergent ones can be diffuse, and the scoring rubric is the authors' own and debated.
whyLost: It thrives in startup and product management culture because it is fast, cheap and directly tied to go or no-go decisions.
whereToUse: Early-stage startups, new B2B and B2C products, internal innovation teams, and feature discovery in established SaaS.
example: A team exploring invoicing for freelancers runs 20 interviews asking about the last invoice each person chased. Fourteen describe spreadsheet reminders and three offer to pay for automation; scores cluster above 31 among designers, so the first segment is design freelancers.
reference: Fitzpatrick, R. (2013). The Mom Test; Maurya, A. (2012). Running Lean (2nd ed.). O'Reilly Media; Croll, A. & Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics. O'Reilly Media.

name: Customer Problem Stack Ranking (CPSR)
aka: Customer Problem Stack Ranking from app reviews
origin: Shreyas Doshi (CPSR); review-mining adaptation by S. White, 2022
summary: Mines low-rated app reviews for pain points, rewrites them as first-person problem statements, and has users select and rank those affecting them over repeated small rounds.
description: Customer problem stack ranking asks users to rank problems, not features. White's adaptation seeds the problem list from online reviews: reviews rated 3 or below in a recent window, with sentiment below the median, are split into sentences, pricing and bug sentences are dropped, and pain-point sentences are clustered and rewritten as first-person statements ('I cannot...'). A short survey (3-6 minutes) asks users to select the problems that affected them, add missing ones, sort them by importance and explain. Rounds of about 20 users are repeated, keeping the top five and adding new statements from write-ins, so the list converges on the problems that matter most. Results feed problem or system mapping and follow-up interviews.
steps: Pull app or product reviews and filter to ratings of 3 or below in a recent window, with sentiment below the median, dropping pricing and bug sentences.
Cluster pain-point sentences and rewrite each cluster as a first-person problem statement.
Survey about 20 users: select the problems that affected them, add missing ones, sort by importance and explain why.
Keep the top five problems, add new candidates from write-ins, and run further rounds until the ranking stabilises.
Follow up with problem or system mapping and interviews on the top-ranked problems.
outputs: A ranked list of customer problems with explanations, and a pool of user-worded problem statements.
useWhen: Prioritising which problems to solve for an existing product with a body of reviews, before committing to solutions.
avoidWhen: When reviewers are unrepresentative of your users or review volume is low; small rounds give unstable ranks. For larger, statistically robust ranking use MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling); for problem discovery use interviews.
whyLost: It is a recent practitioner technique; most teams rank features or read reviews without converting them into a ranked problem set.
whereToUse: Gig-economy and marketplace apps, consumer mobile apps, SaaS with active review sites.
example: A delivery-courier app mines 1,200 low-rated reviews into 24 problem statements; three rounds of 20 couriers converge on 'I cannot see the full route before accepting' as the top problem.
sources: Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: White, S. (2022). Surfacing user pain points with online reviews and problem stack ranking. In Chapman, C. N. et al. (eds) Proceedings of the 2022 Quantitative User Experience Conference, pp. 488-493.

name: Customer Unit Economics (Churn, CLV, CAC, Repurchase Mode)
donor: Lean startup and product analytics; direct marketing
origin: Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz (2013); churn formula credited to Steven H. Noble; repurchase modes from Kevin Hillstrom; magic number from Josh James
summary: Calculates churn, customer lifetime value, acquisition cost, payback and repurchase mode to judge whether a product's customer relationships are economically sustainable.
description: Unit economics links user behaviour to business viability. Churn is the share of customers who leave in a fixed period: churns in the period divided by customers at its start, with average lifetime equal to 100 divided by monthly churn percentage; because churns accumulate while the denominator is a snapshot, fast growth distorts it, so churn should be computed by cohort or daily. Customer lifetime value (CLV) is lifetime times average revenue per user, compared with customer acquisition cost (CAC) per channel; healthy businesses keep CAC well below CLV, roughly under a third, and track months to breakeven. SaaS firms use the magic number (quarterly recurring revenue change over prior quarter sales and marketing spend). Hillstrom's repurchase test classifies e-commerce businesses by the share of last year's buyers who buy again: under 40% acquisition mode, 40-60% hybrid, over 60% loyalty.
steps: Define an inactive or churned customer (for example no login within 90 days) and fix the measurement period; track free and paid users separately.

Compute churn as churns in the period divided by customers at its start; if growth is fast or uneven, compute it per signup cohort or per day; for apps, check 1-day, 1-week and 1-month churn separately.
Compute average revenue per user and lifetime (100 divided by monthly churn %), and derive CLV.
Compute CAC per acquisition channel and compare with CLV, aiming for CAC under about a third of CLV, and compute months to customer breakeven.
For SaaS, compute the magic number: below 0.75 indicates a flawed model, above 1 a self-funding one.
For commerce, compute the annual repurchase rate (or 90-day rate: 1-15% acquisition, 15-30% hybrid, over 30% loyalty) and classify the business mode.
Set product and marketing priorities for the mode and stage, and recheck before scaling.
outputs: Churn rate and lifetime, CLV, CAC, CLV:CAC ratio, payback months, magic number and repurchase mode classification.
useWhen: Product strategy decisions where retention, onboarding or engagement work must be justified in business terms, or when deciding whether to invest in loyalty versus acquisition.
avoidWhen: When samples are tiny or the product is too young for stable rates. Inflated active-user definitions lower ARPU; averaging start and end counts fails with hockey-stick growth. For behavioural detail behind churn use Cohort Analysis and interviews.
whyLost: It lives with finance and growth teams; UX researchers rarely compute or connect to it, so experience work is not tied to economic outcomes.
whereToUse: Subscription SaaS, consumer apps, e-commerce, fintech, marketplaces.
example: A meal-kit app computes 9% monthly churn (11-month lifetime) and CLV of $27 against CAC of $14, giving 5.7 months to breakeven; its 90-day repurchase rate of 22% puts it in hybrid mode, so the team prioritises second-order onboarding over a loyalty scheme.
reference: Croll, A. and Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics: Use Data to Build a Better Startup Faster. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: CxPi (Forrester Customer Experience Index)
origin: Forrester Research, annual report since 2007
summary: Three questions on how well a company meets needs, how easy it is to deal with and how enjoyable it is, each scored as top-two minus bottom-two.
description: Forrester's CxPi asks consumers about their interactions with a firm over the past 90 days: how well it met their needs (usefulness), how easy it was to do business with (usability) and how enjoyable it was (enjoyability). Each uses a five-point scale from very negative to very positive and is scored like NPS as a net percentage: top two boxes minus bottom two. The index is the average of the three. Sauro and Lewis note it has no published psychometric data but is a common industry tracking metric. For UX teams it is a quick way to place the usability of an experience alongside usefulness and emotion in terms executives already recognise.
steps: Ask the three questions about recent interactions on five-point scales.
For each, compute the percentage in the top two boxes minus the bottom two.
Average the three net scores for the index.
Track over time and compare with Forrester's published industry results where relevant.
outputs: Net scores for usefulness, ease and enjoyment, and an overall index.
useWhen: Executive-level tracking that needs to sit alongside industry reports.
avoidWhen: Diagnostic research or small samples; net scores need large samples to be stable.
whyLost: Market research ownership and proprietary benchmarks.
whereToUse: Banks, airlines, insurers, telecoms and retailers.
example: A telecom scores well on usefulness but its ease score is net negative, building the case for a self-service redesign.
reference: Forrester Research (2011). The Customer Experience Index, 2011.

name: Cyberball social exclusion paradigm
aka: Cyberball social exclusion with ego-network density
origin: Williams, Cheung and Choi (2000), Cyberball; reviewed by Somerville (2013)
summary: Lead participants to believe they are interacting with online peers, then manipulate inclusion or evaluative feedback and measure mood, belonging and physiological response.
description: Participants believe they are playing an on-screen game of catch with two other people. After a period of fair passing, the computer-controlled players stop throwing to the participant, who typically reports feeling rejected, with lowered belonging, control and self-esteem. The paradigm is a standard, replicable way to induce ostracism and compare it with inclusion. Variants manipulate who excludes, for how long, and with what cues; one variant relates neural responses to the density of the participant's real friendship network, finding stronger mentalising-network responses for people with sparse networks. Rigour comes from the fixed inclusion and exclusion schedule, an inclusion control, standard need-threat questionnaires and careful debriefing. Related paradigms follow the same logic: in the chat-room task supposed peers select or reject the participant for a conversation, and in the social-feedback task peers rate the participant's photo for likeability. With adolescents and other sensitive groups, ethical review and a full debrief are essential.
steps: Present a cover story of online interaction with other participants.
Run an inclusion phase, then an exclusion or negative-feedback phase, counterbalanced with inclusion or positive conditions across participants.
Record self-report measures (mood, belonging, need satisfaction) and, where relevant, gaze, pupil or other physiological measures.
Compare responses between inclusion and exclusion conditions.
Debrief fully, explaining the deception and checking participants' wellbeing before they leave.
outputs: Effect of exclusion versus inclusion, or negative versus positive feedback, on mood, belonging and physiological response.
useWhen: Testing how social features (read receipts, reaction counts, group invitations, algorithmic visibility) affect felt exclusion, in a controlled lab analogue with ethics approval.
avoidWhen: Without ethics review, with vulnerable groups lacking safeguards, or when real platform data can answer the question; use diary studies or log analysis instead.
whyLost: It belongs to social psychology and neuroscience; UX rarely runs deception paradigms and measures social harm through surveys instead.
whereToUse: Social media, messaging, multiplayer games, community platforms and youth-focused products.
example: A messaging app studies whether showing 'seen by 5 of 8' in group chats increases felt exclusion. In a Cyberball-style analogue, participants whose messages are visibly unanswered report lower belonging, so the team tests hiding partial read counts.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
Williams, K. D., Cheung, C. K. T., & Choi, W. (2000). Cyberostracism: Effects of being ignored over the Internet. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79
reference: Williams, K. D., Cheung, C. K. T. and Choi, W. (2000). Cyberostracism: effects of being ignored over the Internet. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(5), 748-762.

name: Cycle-by-Cycle Reconstruction of an Emergent Division of Labour
origin: Adapted for UX from Edwin Hutchins, Cognition in the Wild (1995), based on fieldwork aboard US Navy ships in the 1980s
summary: From recordings, reconstruct each repetition of a team computation, the order of steps and who did each, then segment the series to show how a division of labour emerged.
description: A micro-analytic procedure for watching a team reorganise itself. After a ship's gyrocompass failed, two navigation team members corrected 66 lines of position with no procedure for sharing the work. Hutchins reconstructed each repetition by fitting known values to the numbers spoken on tape, notating calculator groupings and spoken intermediate sums, and coding who began, structured and completed each computation. Thirteen computational structures appeared before a stable one emerged, and the series fell into four regions, from data-driven improvisation to a stable division with a coined term for the shared step. The analysis shows that change came through local adaptation and local design, not a global designer, and that the final configuration may not be represented in any one person's head. It extends Distributed Cognition Analysis from describing a system to tracing how it learned.
steps: Identify a computation or task cycle that a team repeats many times, ideally after a disruption.
Record the values and resources available in the setting (reports, constants, tools) alongside audio and video.
For each repetition, fit the available values to what was said or entered to recover the order of operations.
Notate groupings and intermediate results, and code who began, structured and completed each repetition.
Plot the sequence of configurations and partition it into regions by organising principle.
Explain each transition as local adaptation, local design or global design, and identify the stable configuration.
outputs: A repetition-by-repetition chart of computational structure and social configuration, with regions of organisational change explained.
useWhen: Studying how teams adapt workflows after a tool change or failure, how collaborative practices emerge in new software, or why a workaround stabilised.
avoidWhen: When the task is not repeated enough times to show change, or recordings are too coarse to recover the order of operations. For a static description of a socio-technical system use Distributed Cognition Analysis.
whyLost: It requires dense recordings and painstaking reconstruction; it is cited as a classic of cognitive anthropology but rarely repeated outside academic CSCW.
whereToUse: Incident response and on-call teams, clinical teams adopting new devices, operations centres after migration, pair and mob work with AI coding tools.
example: After an outage disables a ticket router, a support team triages manually for a week. Reconstructing 200 triage cycles from chat logs shows the split between reading and assigning stabilised after day three around an improvised tag, which the redesigned router adopts.
reference: Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, Chapter 8.

name: Cynefin Sense-Making Framework
origin: Dave Snowden, IBM Institute for Knowledge Management, 1999-2003; Kurtz and Snowden (2003); Snowden and Boone (2007)
summary: Classifies situations as clear, complicated, complex, chaotic or confused, each calling for different research and decision approaches.
description: Cynefin distinguishes ordered domains, where cause and effect are knowable (clear: sense-categorise-respond; complicated: sense-analyse-respond, needing expertise), from unordered domains (complex: probe-sense-respond via safe-to-fail experiments; chaotic: act-sense-respond). A central zone of confusion (aporetic) covers not knowing which applies. Properly used, Cynefin is constructed by groups through contextualisation exercises, placing their own situations onto the framework from narrative data, rather than assigning domains top-down. For UX, it guides methodological choice: complicated problems call for expert analysis and rigorous evaluation, complex ones for portfolios of small probes and narrative sensing (e.g. SenseMaker).
steps: Collect situations or decisions as short narratives from teams or users.
Run a contextualisation workshop: place items relative to each other, then draw domain boundaries emergently.
For each domain, agree appropriate approaches: best practice, expert analysis, safe-to-fail probes or rapid action.
For complex items, design a portfolio of parallel probes with amplification and dampening criteria.
Monitor through narrative sensing and indicators, and re-assess domain placement over time.
Watch for complacency moving clear items toward chaos.
outputs: Domain classification of situations, matched research and decision approaches and probe portfolios.
useWhen: Choosing research strategy under uncertainty, especially for new markets, AI products and organisational change.
avoidWhen: Well-defined evaluation questions where the method choice is already clear.
whyLost: Widely shown as a 2x2-like slide, with domains assigned top-down and the contextualisation and narrative practices dropped.
whereToUse: Product strategy for emerging technologies, research portfolio planning, incident response, organisational change.
example: A team building an AI tutor contextualises its open questions: model accuracy is complicated (expert evaluation), but how students integrate the tutor into study habits is complex, so it runs five small classroom probes instead of one large study.
sources: Kurtz & Snowden, The new dynamics of strategy: Sense-making in a complex and complicated world (2003), IBM Systems Journal
Snowden & Boone, A leader's framework for decision making (2007), Harvard Business Review
Snowden et al., Cynefin: Weaving Sense-Making into the Fabric of Our World (2020)
reference: Kurtz, C. F., & Snowden, D. J. (2003). IBM Systems Journal, 42(3), 462-483.

name: D-prime calculation
origin: Tanner and Swets, 1954; Green and Swets, Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics, 1966
summary: Separates a user's true ability to detect a signal (d') from their willingness to respond (criterion), using hit and false-alarm rates.
description: Signal detection theory models any yes/no detection, such as noticing an alert or spotting a fraudulent transaction, as a decision between overlapping noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. Sensitivity d' = z(hit rate) - z(false alarm rate) measures how far apart those distributions are, independent of response bias; criterion c = -0.5[z(H) + z(F)] captures how liberal or conservative the observer is. This matters because raw accuracy confounds the two: an operator who responds to everything has a perfect hit rate and poor discrimination. In UX, d' tells you whether a design change made signals genuinely more discriminable or merely shifted users' thresholds. Rigour requires a design with both signal and noise trials, enough trials per cell, and corrections for perfect rates.
steps: Define the detection task with explicit signal-present and signal-absent trials, for example true alerts versus benign events, in a realistic ratio.
Run each participant through at least 50 signal and 50 noise trials per condition (more if rates are near ceiling) and record hits, misses, false alarms and correct rejections.
Correct rates of 0 or 1 with the log-linear correction (add 0.5 to each cell count and 1 to each trial total).
Compute d' = z(H) - z(F) and criterion c for each participant and condition.
Compare conditions with a within-subjects test on d' (for example paired t-test across 12-20 participants); interpret d' near 1 as weak, 2 as good, and above 3 as excellent discrimination.
Report d' and c separately and recommend design changes for sensitivity (signal salience) versus bias (cost of misses, instructions, alarm credibility).
outputs: d' and criterion per participant and condition, statistical comparison across designs, and a diagnosis of whether failures are perceptual or decisional.
useWhen: When users must detect rare events (alerts, anomalies, fraud flags, AI hallucinations) and you need to know whether a design improves discrimination or just shifts bias.
avoidWhen: When there is no meaningful 'noise' condition or the task is not a binary judgement; use task success or ROC analysis with confidence ratings for graded responses.
whyLost: d' is standard in psychophysics, radiology and aviation but UX reports accuracy and conversion, which hide bias; few UX researchers are trained in SDT.
whereToUse: Alarm and alert design, content moderation tools, security warnings, fraud review queues, and human review of AI outputs.
example: A clinical decision-support vendor tests two alert designs. Hit rate rises from 80% to 92% with the red banner, but false alarms rise too; d' is unchanged at 1.9, showing the banner only made clinicians more trigger-happy. A redesign that adds patient-specific context raises d' to 2.6.
sources: Van Drongelen, W., Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent
reference: Green, D. M. & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

name: D-separation
origin: Judea Pearl, 1988
summary: A graphical rule that reads off a DAG which variables should be statistically independent given others, enabling tests of causal assumptions against data.
description: D-separation determines whether a set of variables blocks every path between two other variables in a DAG. A path is blocked if it contains a non-collider that is conditioned on, or a collider that is not conditioned on (nor any of its descendants). If all paths are blocked, the two variables are d-separated and must be conditionally independent in any data generated by that graph. This gives two uses for UX research: checking a proposed causal model by testing its implied independencies against survey or log data, and understanding why controlling for a variable opens or closes bias. Rigour comes from computing implications mechanically with software and testing them with appropriate conditional independence tests.
steps: Encode the DAG in a tool such as DAGitty or the Python package pgmpy.
List all implied conditional independencies the graph makes, which the tool generates automatically.
Test each implication in data with partial correlations or conditional independence tests, correcting for multiple tests.
Treat strong violations (e.g. partial correlation above 0.1 with a tight interval) as evidence the graph is missing an edge or variable.
Revise the DAG and repeat, documenting every change and its evidential basis.
outputs: A list of testable implications, test results, a revised and better-supported causal graph, and clear explanations of adjustment choices.
useWhen: Validating a causal model built from qualitative work or expert judgement before using it for adjustment or SEM.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the graph has few implied independencies (dense graphs) or when data is too small for reliable conditional independence tests.
whyLost: It is a technical result in graphical models, rarely taught outside CS and epidemiology, and UX teams seldom formalise causal models to the point of needing it.
whereToUse: Mixed-methods trust and adoption research, survey-based SEM in fintech, model checking for causal analysis of product logs.
example: A DAG implies that app-store rating is independent of feature usage once satisfaction is conditioned on. Survey data shows a strong residual association, revealing a missing path from usage to rating via in-app prompts.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems (Judea Pearl)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 46 — Directed Acyclic Graphs — Making Assumptions Explicit
reference: Pearl, J. (1988) Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: DAG + SEM Mixed-Methods Protocol
aka: DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX
donor: Causal inference (DAGs) and psychometrics (SEM) joined with qualitative research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Turns qualitative themes into a causal DAG, tests it with CFA and SEM, and binds each estimated path to a quote and a design prescription.
description: Reports usually end with themes or dashboards; what is missing is a mechanism showing how a perception change propagates through behaviour to outcomes. In this protocol the DAG expresses the mechanism and SEM estimates its strength. Qualitative discovery yields a codebook of constructs; the DAG makes causal assumptions and confounders explicit and identifies mediators and colliders; a CFA measurement model validates latent constructs; the structural model estimates DAG paths with direct, indirect and total effects; and a joint display maps qual mechanism → quant evidence → prescribed change. In the tap-to-pay case (n = 520, MLR), FR → TR −0.45, SR → TR +0.31, TR → DC −0.50, DC → SL +0.42, SL → AD −0.28 and TR → AD +0.26, with indirect effect ≈ +0.059 and total TR → AD ≈ +0.32. Robustness checks include multi-group invariance, common method bias, sensitivity to confounders and out-of-sample validation. Qual arrays and the DAG are kept under version control.
steps: Run qualitative discovery (interviews, think-aloud) and build a codebook of constructs, marking each as latent or observed (e.g. Trust, Fraud Risk, Double-Checking, Slowness, Support, Adoption).
Draw the DAG from qual: write causal assumptions, confounders to adjust (past fraud, device type, tenure) and colliders not to control.
Design 3-item Likert batteries per latent construct; screen missingness < 10% (FIML), check Cronbach's α ≥ 0.70 and run CFA, dropping loadings < 0.60 unless theory demands.
Check convergent validity (AVE ≥ 0.50, CR) and discriminant validity (Fornell-Larcker or HTMT < 0.85).
Estimate the structural model per the DAG with robust ML (MLR) and report CFI, TLI (≥ 0.95), RMSEA (≤ 0.06) and SRMR (≤ 0.08).
Decompose direct, indirect and total effects (|β| ≈ 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large) and never interpret paths without quotes beside them.
Run robustness checks: multi-group invariance (iOS/Android, new/veteran), common method bias via behavioural covariates, confounder sensitivity and split-sample or time-based validation.
Bind paths to prescriptions in a joint display and validate with A/B tests, guardrails and brief qual follow-ups (e.g. decision bar +5–8 points adoption in 4 weeks; 5 post-launch sessions).
outputs: A versioned DAG, CFA table with loadings, CR and AVE, SEM path diagram with fit indices and effect decomposition, a joint display and a reporting template.
useWhen: When latent constructs (trust, perceived security, ease) matter, when multiple mediators exist and indirect effects matter, and when qual narratives must be aligned with quantitative tests.
avoidWhen: When samples are small (SEM typically needs several hundred cases), constructs are not yet understood, or the question is purely descriptive; use interviews or simple regression instead.
whyLost: Original protocol by Vivek Gopinath; DAGs and SEM are standard in epidemiology and psychology but rarely joined to UX qualitative work.
whereToUse: Banking and payments adoption, trust and security features, AI feature adoption, healthcare apps.
example: A bank's tap-to-pay adoption lags despite a bug-free flow; interviews reveal double-checking from low trust; SEM confirms trust reduces double-checking (−0.50), which raises perceived slowness (+0.42), which suppresses adoption (−0.28), so the team ships a trust explainer, one-tap verification and adaptive 2FA together.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments.

name: DAG construction from qual themes
donor: Epidemiology / causal inference with qualitative research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, DAGs+SEM Playbook; building on Pearl (1995) and participatory causal mapping
summary: Translates themes and mechanisms from qualitative research into an explicit directed acyclic graph that can guide measurement and causal analysis.
description: Qualitative research produces rich mechanism stories but rarely commits them to a testable structure. This method converts coded themes into nodes and stated mechanisms into directed edges, producing a DAG that encodes assumptions about what causes what. Each edge must be traceable to evidence (quotes, observations) or labelled as an assumption. The resulting graph identifies which variables must be measured, which are confounders, mediators or colliders, and what quantitative design could test the story. Rigour comes from evidence tracing per edge, deliberately adding plausible unmeasured common causes, checking acyclicity, and testing the graph's implied conditional independencies against data where available.
steps: List candidate variables from the theme codebook, phrasing each as a measurable quantity (e.g. perceived interface trust, frequency of double-checking).
For each causal statement in the data, add a directed edge and log the supporting excerpts; mark edges without direct evidence as assumptions.
Add plausible unmeasured common causes (e.g. financial literacy, market conditions) as latent nodes, even if not mentioned by participants.
Check acyclicity; represent feedback loops by time-indexing variables (trust at t1 to behaviour at t2).
Review the DAG with researchers and domain experts in a workshop, recording disagreements as alternative graphs.
Derive testable implications (conditional independencies) with DAGitty and plan the measures and design needed to test key paths.
outputs: An evidence-linked causal DAG, alternative graphs, a list of variables to measure and testable implications for quantitative follow-up.
useWhen: After qualitative discovery when the team wants to test a mechanism quantitatively, design a survey or SEM, or analyse logs causally.
avoidWhen: Avoid when qualitative data is thin or purely descriptive, or when the question is exploratory and premature formalisation would close down inquiry.
whyLost: Qualitative and quantitative UX work are usually run by different people, and DAGs are taught in epidemiology rather than design research, so the bridge is rarely built.
whereToUse: Mixed-methods programmes in fintech, health and AI products; designing surveys for SEM; framing log analyses and experiments.
example: Field interviews with traders reveal that distrust of the payment interface leads to double-checking, which delays Tap to Pay adoption. The team encodes this as a DAG with financial literacy as a confounder, then measures each node in a survey for path analysis.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 46 — Directed Acyclic Graphs — Making Assumptions Explicit
reference: Pearl, J. (2009) Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.

name: DAG-informed covariate selection
origin: Greenland, Pearl & Robins, 1999; VanderWeele's disjunctive cause criterion, 2019
summary: Chooses which variables to include as controls in a model by reading them off a causal diagram, rather than by significance tests or data availability.
description: Covariate selection by stepwise regression or 'include everything' can introduce bias by adjusting for mediators or colliders, or leave confounding by omitting unmeasured causes. DAG-informed selection uses the backdoor criterion to pick a minimal sufficient set, adds precision variables that predict the outcome only, and excludes instruments, mediators and colliders. When the full DAG is uncertain, VanderWeele's disjunctive cause criterion offers a practical rule: adjust for any pre-treatment variable that causes the treatment, the outcome or both, excluding known instruments. Rigour comes from deciding covariates before seeing outcome data and showing robustness across plausible adjustment sets.
steps: List all available pre-treatment variables and place them in the DAG.
Derive minimal sufficient adjustment sets for the effect of interest using DAGitty.
Add outcome-only predictors for precision, and remove variables affected by treatment, colliders and pure instruments.
Where the DAG is uncertain, apply the disjunctive cause criterion and record which variables were included on that basis.
Pre-register or time-stamp the covariate list before running outcome models.
Run the analysis with two or three plausible adjustment sets and report how much the estimate changes.
outputs: A justified covariate list, the DAG used, estimates under alternative adjustment sets and a robustness statement.
useWhen: Any observational analysis, quasi-experiment or covariate-adjusted A/B test where the choice of controls affects conclusions.
avoidWhen: Avoid for purely predictive models, where covariates should be chosen by out-of-sample performance rather than causal role.
whyLost: UX statistics training focuses on model fitting, and covariate choice is treated as a technical detail rather than a causal decision.
whereToUse: Feature impact analysis, adjusted retention comparisons, CUPED-style variance reduction choices and survey driver models.
example: Evaluating a goal-setting feature, the team avoids controlling for post-launch engagement (a mediator) and instead adjusts for pre-launch activity and account age. The estimated retention effect is 4 points, versus near zero in the 'control for everything' model.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 46 — Directed Acyclic Graphs — Making Assumptions Explicit
Cinelli, C., Forney, A. & Pearl, J., A Crash Course in Good and Bad Controls (2022)
reference: VanderWeele, T. J. (2019) Principles of confounder selection. European Journal of Epidemiology, 34, 211-219.

name: Data Adequacy Model Set
origin: Dorian Pyle (2003)
summary: Build many small random models on training, test and evaluation splits and compare their behaviour; if performance differs across splits, the data are not adequate for modelling.
description: Before investing in a predictive model, Pyle checks whether the data are sufficient and representative. The data are split into training, test and evaluation sets. A set of quick models is built, each on a random group of about 11 inputs with one randomly chosen variable as the output, trained on the training set and scored on all three sets. If the models behave similarly across sets, the splits represent the same population and hold enough data; marked differences mean the data are insufficient or unrepresentative and more data or a new sample is needed. It is a rough, model-agnostic sanity check, and Pyle gives no threshold for 'dissimilar'.
steps: Split the data into training, test and evaluation sets.
Draw random groups of about 11 variables, each with one randomly chosen output variable.
Train a quick model for each group on the training set.
Score every model on all three sets and compare performance distributions.
Treat consistently dissimilar performance as a sign of inadequate or unrepresentative data and collect more or resample.
outputs: A judgement of whether the data support modelling, with the comparison of model performance across splits.
useWhen: Starting a churn, propensity or segmentation model on product data of uncertain size or quality.
avoidWhen: You need a formal sample-size calculation or have strong prior knowledge of data sufficiency; use learning curves or cross-validation instead. Thresholds are not defined.
whyLost: It was a practitioner heuristic of early data mining and was superseded by cross-validation and learning-curve diagnostics.
whereToUse: Product analytics and data science teams building models from logs, small B2B datasets.
example: Before building a churn model on 3,000 accounts, an analyst runs 50 random mini-models; performance on the evaluation split is consistently much lower, so the team waits for another quarter of data.
reference: Pyle, D. (2003). Data collection, preparation, quality, and visualization. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 365-392). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Data display (matrices, networks, flowcharts)
origin: Miles and Huberman, Qualitative Data Analysis (1984; 2nd ed. 1994)
summary: Organises reduced qualitative data into structured matrices and networks so patterns, comparisons and explanations can be seen and verified, rather than inferred from narrative text.
description: Miles and Huberman argued that extended narrative text is a weak display for analysis: it is sequential, bulky and lets analysts jump to vivid but unrepresentative conclusions. Displays, defined as organised, compressed assemblies of information, allow conclusion drawing. Matrices cross two dimensions (for example cases by variables, time periods by roles), and networks show nodes and links (flows, causes, relationships). Their sourcebook catalogues dozens of display types, including checklist matrices, time-ordered matrices, role-ordered matrices, conceptually ordered displays, effects matrices and causal networks. Rigour comes from explicit decision rules for what enters each cell, and from verification tactics such as counting, noting patterns, checking extreme cases and following up surprises applied to the display.
steps: Choose a display type to suit the analytic question: time-ordered for process, role-ordered for perspectives, case-by-variable for comparison, network for causation or flow.
Define rows, columns or node types precisely, and write decision rules for cell entries, such as what counts as evidence, how to rate strength and how to cite sources.
Populate the display from reduced data, citing case and excerpt identifiers for each entry and marking missing data explicitly.
Read the display using verification tactics: count, note patterns and clusters, make contrasts, check outliers and extreme cases, and look for negative evidence.
Write a short analytic text for each display summarising patterns and the conclusions drawn, and keep the display and text together.
Revise or build follow-up displays when conclusions raise new questions, iterating between reduction, display and conclusions.
outputs: A set of matrices or networks with documented entry rules, analytic text for each, and verified conclusions with traceable evidence.
useWhen: Comparing across multiple cases, roles or time periods; testing explanations against all the data; presenting rigorous qualitative analysis to decision-makers.
avoidWhen: Very small samples where displays add overhead without insight, or highly interpretive phenomenological work where categorising into cells distorts meaning.
whyLost: UX inherited the affinity wall and journey map but not the broader display catalogue, so systematic comparison across cases is replaced by memorable anecdotes.
whereToUse: Multi-segment research, multi-market studies, account-based B2B research, service blueprint evidence, longitudinal studies.
example: A role-ordered matrix with health workers, supervisors and district managers as rows and adoption barriers as columns showed that supervisors alone cited audit requirements, revealing the real blocker sat in the supervisory role.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage; Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Data Distribution Shift Detection and ML Monitoring
origin: Chip Huyen (2022); tests from Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Gretton et al. (2012, MMD), Bu et al. (2018, LSDD) and Rabanser et al. (2019)
summary: Compare production inputs and predictions with a reference window using schema checks, summary statistics and two-sample tests, to catch data shifts that silently degrade a model-driven feature.
description: Models degrade when production data drift from training data. Shifts may be covariate (inputs change), label (outcome rates change) or concept (the input-outcome relation changes). Where labels or user feedback arrive, accuracy can be monitored directly; otherwise one monitors predictions, features and raw inputs. Feature validation checks values against expected schemas (ranges, formats, allowed sets). Summary statistics are a start, but two-sample tests between a reference and a current window are better: Kolmogorov-Smirnov for one-dimensional quantities such as prediction scores, and MMD or LSDD for multivariate features after dimensionality reduction. Window choice matters: cycles shorter than the window are missed, short windows raise false alarms, and cumulative metrics hide dips that sliding metrics reveal. Statistical significance is not practical importance, and KS in particular raises many false positives on large samples.
steps: Log user feedback, predictions, input features and raw inputs with timestamps.
Validate features against expected schemas: ranges, formats, allowed values and relations between fields.
Compare summary statistics of the current window with a reference window.
Run two-sample tests on predictions (for example Kolmogorov-Smirnov) and on dimension-reduced features (MMD or LSDD).
Choose windows that respect daily and weekly cycles, use sliding rather than cumulative statistics, and merge short windows for longer views.
Alert on shifts that are both significant and practically large, then decide whether to retrain, adapt or investigate the product change behind them.
outputs: Shift alerts, monitoring dashboards and decisions to retrain or investigate.
useWhen: Running recommendation, ranking, search, fraud or AI assistant features whose quality depends on models that can silently degrade as user behaviour or upstream data change.
avoidWhen: Avoid alerting on every significant test, which causes alert fatigue. For shifts in user behaviour patterns rather than model inputs, see Mixed-Methods Behavioral Drift Detection Framework; for metric guardrails during launches use Guardrail metric monitoring.
whyLost: It is standard practice in ML operations but rarely shared with UX, even though drift often originates in product or audience changes that researchers can explain.
whereToUse: Recommendation and personalisation, search ranking, fraud and risk scoring, LLM-based assistants, any model-driven UX feature.
example: A grocery app's substitution model degrades after a marketing campaign brings in many first-time users. A KS test on prediction scores flags the shift within two days, and the researcher links it to new users lacking purchase history, prompting a cold-start fallback.
reference: Huyen, C. (2022). Designing Machine Learning Systems. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 237-259; Rabanser, S., Günnemann, S. and Lipton, Z. C. (2019). Failing loudly: an empirical study of methods for detecting dataset shift. NeurIPS 2019.

name: Data Mining Project Process (Define, Prepare, Implement, Deploy)
origin: Glenn Myatt (2007), in the tradition of data mining process models such as CRISP-DM
summary: A four-stage plan for analytics projects: define the problem and deliverables, prepare the data, select and optimise analyses, then deploy and measure the results.
description: Myatt frames every exploratory analysis or data mining project as four linked steps, with iteration between them. Problem definition breaks a headline goal into questions the data can answer, sets specific measurable success criteria tied to a business objective, states deliverables (report, rules, embedded model, new workflow), the accuracy needed and the relative cost of the two kinds of wrong prediction, checks the data represent the target population, and assigns roles: project leader, subject matter expert, analyst, IT expert and consumer of the results. A plan adds timetable, constraints, privacy issues, risks and a cost-benefit case. Data preparation characterises, cleans, transforms and segments the data. Implementation selects among summary tables, graphs, statistics, grouping and prediction methods according to whether the task is summarising, finding hidden relationships or predicting, and optimises them. Deployment delivers a report or integrated model, plans change management and training, measures business impact, ideally with a randomised field comparison of users with and without the model, monitors models as data age, and ends with a project review. For UX analytics it gives a scoping discipline that ties exploratory work to decisions.
steps: Write the headline objective and break it into answerable data questions with measurable success criteria.
Define deliverables, required accuracy, speed constraints and the consequences of each type of error.
Assemble a cross-disciplinary team, agree roles and share a glossary of terms.
Plan: data sources, privacy and legal issues, timetable with review points, risks and cost-benefit.
Prepare the data, then select, run and optimise the analysis methods that fit the questions.
Deploy results as a report, rules or integrated model, with training and change management.
Measure impact against the success criteria (ideally with a randomised comparison), monitor over time and run a project review.
outputs: A project plan with success criteria, a prepared data set, analysis results and a deployment and evaluation plan.
useWhen: Starting an analytics or data mining project on product data that must lead to a decision or a deployed model.
avoidWhen: A quick one-off query or a small qualitative study where the overhead of formal planning outweighs the benefit.
whyLost: UX teams borrow agile research plans and rarely adopt data mining process models, which stay in data science and BI groups.
whereToUse: Churn analysis, personalisation, segmentation projects, survey analytics, analytics programmes run jointly by UX and data teams.
example: Asked to 'improve web sales', a team defines three data questions (which visitor groups buy, how usage patterns group, how usage relates to buying), sets a target of a 10% lift in conversion for a targeted segment, agrees that missing a likely buyer costs more than a wasted prompt, and plans an A/B rollout to measure the model's impact.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Myatt, G. J. (2007). Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Data Physicalisation
origin: Information visualisation research (Jansen et al., 2015; Huron et al.); emotion workshop by Pamela Pavliscak (2018)
summary: Representing data as physical objects, using material, texture, weight and scale as encodings, to explore patterns, communicate findings or let participants reflect.
description: Data physicalisation turns quantitative or qualitative data into objects: 3D charts, sculptures, installations or hand-held mementos. Material, texture, weight and scale act as extra channels and make data accessible to people with visual impairments. Teams use it to explore patterns, to communicate findings memorably, or as a probe in which participants build physicalisations of their own tracked data. Pavliscak's emotion workshop bridges research and design: activity cards (discover, cope, remember, anticipate), data cards summarising emotion findings with topic, source and visual, and materials with contrasting properties (rigid, flexible, binding, translucent) are provided; participants choose cards, pick at most three materials and build and document a representation, then discuss what it reveals about emotional goals. Encodings are imprecise, so the aim is reflection and conversation, not exact reading.
steps: Choose the data and decide what should be felt or seen.
Map variables to physical properties (height, colour, texture, weight, transparency).
For a workshop, prepare activity cards, data cards (topic, source, description, visual) and materials with contrasting properties.
Let individuals or groups choose cards and at most three materials.
Build the physical representation with simple materials and document the process.
Use the object in team analysis, presentation or discussion with participants, and capture the reflections it prompts.
outputs: Physical data artefacts and documented reflections linking material qualities to patterns or emotional goals.
useWhen: Use when findings must be made tangible for stakeholders, when participants should reflect on their own data, or when moving emotion research into material design qualities.
avoidWhen: Avoid when precise comparison of values matters: use a standard chart built with Data display (matrices, networks, flowcharts). It is time-consuming; keep within participants' comfort when the data are personal.
whyLost: It is an active research topic in information visualisation and art and design but rare in UX practice, where screen visualisation is the default.
whereToUse: Self-tracking and wellbeing products, research readouts, museum and public engagement, accessibility.
example: An e-sports research team turns emotion findings into a paper chain of linked figures behind colour-coded translucent windows, which stakeholders use to discuss belonging and tension in team play.
sources: Jansen, Y., Dragicevic, P., Isenberg, P., Alexander, J., Karnik, A., Kildal, J., Subramanian, S. and Hornbæk, K. (2015). Opportunities and Challenges for Data Physicalization. Proceedings of CHI 2015.
reference: Jansen, Y., Dragicevic, P., Isenberg, P., Alexander, J., Karnik, A., Kildal, J., Subramanian, S. and Hornbæk, K. (2015). Opportunities and Challenges for Data Physicalization. Proceedings of CHI 2015.

name: Data Preparation and Transformation for Analysis
aka: Normalisation, value mapping, discretisation and aggregation
origin: Standard data mining practice, codified as a six-step preparation table by Glenn Myatt (2007)
summary: A structured sequence for turning raw, multi-source data into a clean analysis table: characterise, clean, remove, transform and segment, while recording every change.
description: Analyses of product data usually start with data collected for another purpose, and Myatt argues this step is often the most time-consuming and decides the quality of everything after it. The procedure first builds a single data table and characterises each variable (continuous or discrete, scale of measurement, role, frequency distribution). Cleaning then consolidates inconsistent category labels, inspects outliers with histograms, box plots and z-scores, converts or removes non-numeric entries in numeric fields, puts measurements on a single unit, handles missing values and removes duplicate records. Variables that are constant, mostly missing or redundant with others are dropped. Transformations follow: normalisation (min-max, z-score, decimal scaling) so variables with large ranges do not dominate distance-based methods; log, exponential or Box-Cox transforms towards normality; value mapping of ordinal text to numbers and nominal values to dummy variables; discretisation (binning) of continuous values or generalising many categories into fewer; and aggregation into derived variables. Finally the table may be segmented into subsets. Each transformation is recorded so results can be translated back to original units before presentation.
steps: Assemble data from all sources into one table with one row per observation (user, session, account).
Characterise every variable: type, scale of measurement, role (descriptor or response) and frequency distribution.
Clean: merge inconsistent labels, review outliers with subject experts, fix or remove non-numeric values, unify units, deal with missing values and remove duplicates.
Remove constants, mostly-missing variables and variables that add no information beyond highly correlated ones.
Transform as needed: normalise, apply log or Box-Cox transforms, map ordinal and nominal values to numbers or dummy variables, bin continuous values, and derive aggregate variables.
Segment the table into random or problem-driven subsets, noting the criteria used.
Document every step and keep the inverse of each transformation for reporting results.
outputs: A prepared, documented analysis table plus a log of cleaning rules and transformations.
useWhen: Before clustering, prediction, association rules or any analysis of logs, CRM exports, survey exports or joined data sets.
avoidWhen: The data are already a curated, documented analysis table, or a tiny study where each record can be checked by hand.
whyLost: UX researchers often receive analytics dashboards rather than raw tables, so preparation is left to data teams and rarely taught as a research method.
whereToUse: Product analytics, survey analysis, CRM and support data, joined behavioural and attitudinal data sets.
example: Before clustering trial users, a researcher merges event logs with signup survey answers, consolidates 14 spellings of job titles into six roles, converts sessions-per-week and minutes-per-session to a 0 to 1 range, dummy-codes acquisition channel and drops a constant 'region' column.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Myatt, G. J. (2007). Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Data privacy in AI processing (local vs. cloud)
donor: Information privacy law; research ethics; security engineering
origin: Data protection principles (GDPR, 2016/2018; data minimisation and privacy by design, Cavoukian, 2009)
summary: Deciding where participant data are processed, on local hardware or with cloud AI providers, based on consent, sensitivity, legal obligations and provider terms, and minimising what leaves controlled systems.
description: Interview audio and transcripts contain personal and often special-category data (health, finances, ethnicity). Sending them to cloud transcription or LLM APIs creates processing by third parties, possibly across borders, with retention and training implications. Local processing (whisper.cpp, local NLP and open-weight models) keeps data in controlled systems at the cost of setup and sometimes accuracy; cloud processing offers capability under contractual safeguards such as zero-retention terms and data processing agreements. Rigour comes from a data protection impact assessment, consent wording that matches actual processing, anonymisation or pseudonymisation before any external processing, data minimisation, and documentation of the decision.
steps: Classify data sensitivity (e.g. special-category, financial, children's data) and check consent terms for AI and third-party processing.
Conduct or update a data protection impact assessment for the pipeline.
Default to local processing for raw audio and identifiable transcripts where feasible.
Before any cloud call, pseudonymise names, places, organisations and identifiers, and verify redaction recall on a sample (aim for 0.95 or above).
Use providers with data processing agreements, no-training and limited-retention terms, and approved data residency.
Document the decision, data flows and retention, and delete intermediate data according to schedule.
outputs: A data flow map, DPIA, processing decision record, redaction validation and retention schedule.
useWhen: Every AI-assisted research pipeline, especially in health, finance, children's services, the public sector or the EU and UK.
avoidWhen: Not a reason to avoid AI entirely; with proper safeguards cloud processing is often acceptable. Purely public data (e.g. app store reviews) needs lighter treatment, though terms of service still apply.
whyLost: Privacy review traditionally focused on recruitment and storage; AI processing pathways are new and researchers often assume tool terms cover them.
whereToUse: Health research, fintech, public services, enterprise customer research and research operations policies.
example: A mental health app team transcribes locally with whisper.cpp, runs a spaCy anonymiser validated at 0.97 recall, and only then sends pseudonymised segments to a cloud LLM under a zero-retention agreement, as described in the participant consent form.
sources: Cavoukian, A. (2009) Privacy by Design: The 7 Foundational Principles
The Inquiry Series, C14 — Ethical Constraints & Epistemological Limits of AI-Assisted Qualitative Research
reference: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, General Data Protection Regulation

name: Data provenance logging
donor: Database research; scientific workflow systems; archival science
origin: Buneman, Khanna and Tan (2001) on data provenance; W3C PROV standard (2013)
summary: Recording where every dataset came from, when and how it was obtained, and every transformation applied, so findings can be traced back to source data.
description: Provenance answers the question 'where did this number come from?'. For UX research this means logging the origin of each raw file (survey platform export, analytics query, recording batch), its retrieval date, query or filter used, consent basis and checksum, then logging every transformation step (exclusions, recoding, imputation, model runs) with inputs, outputs and code version. Rigour comes from automatic rather than manual logging, from hashing raw inputs so silent changes are detected, and from keeping a machine-readable lineage that connects each reported figure to its inputs. This is particularly important when analytics data are re-queried later and return different results, or when participant data must be deleted on request.
steps: Create a data manifest recording source, retrieval date, query or export settings, row count, checksum and consent basis for each raw file.
Log each processing step automatically (function, input files, output files, parameters, code commit, timestamp) to a provenance log.
Record exclusion counts at each stage (e.g. 1,240 started, 1,102 completed, 1,031 after attention checks) as a flow table.
Re-verify raw file checksums before each full rerun and stop if any have changed.
