Link each figure and table in reports to the provenance entries and code commit that produced it.
Maintain a deletion register so data subject requests can be traced through all derived files.
outputs: A data manifest, a processing log, a participant flow table and a figure-to-source traceability record.
useWhen: Studies combining multiple sources, analytics re-queried over time, regulated domains and any pipeline with automated transformations or AI-assisted analysis.
avoidWhen: Excessive for a single small usability study with notes only; a dated study log is enough there.
whyLost: UX research treated data as disposable inputs to insight rather than as evidence needing a chain of custody, so lineage practices stayed in data engineering and archives.
whereToUse: Research repositories, health and finance research, GDPR-sensitive studies, analytics-heavy product teams and agentic AI pipelines.
example: A health app reports a 9% fall in task completion. The provenance log shows the analytics query had been changed to include a new user cohort, and the like-for-like rerun shows no real change.
sources: Buneman, P., Khanna, S. & Tan, W.-C. (2001) Why and where: A characterization of data provenance. ICDT
W3C (2013) PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Buneman, P., Khanna, S. & Tan, W.-C. (2001) Why and where: A characterization of data provenance. ICDT 2001

name: Data reduction (coding, memoing, pattern noting)
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, Qualitative Data Analysis (1984; 2nd ed. 1994); renamed 'data condensation' by Miles, Huberman and Saldaña (2014)
summary: The systematic selection, focusing, simplifying and transforming of raw qualitative data through coding, memoing and pattern noting, as the first of Miles and Huberman's three concurrent analysis flows.
description: Miles and Huberman described qualitative analysis as three concurrent flows: data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. Data reduction is not summarising for convenience; it is a sequence of analytical choices about what to code, how to cluster codes and which patterns to pursue. It includes first-cycle coding (descriptive, in vivo, process or other codes), second-cycle pattern coding that groups codes into smaller sets of themes or explanations, jotting and memoing, and contact summary sheets written after each fieldwork contact. Because reduction starts before data collection (through framework and question choices), the method asks researchers to make these choices explicit. Rigour comes from a documented start list of codes, clear code definitions, and memos linking codes to emerging patterns.
steps: Before fieldwork, create a provisional start list of 15 to 40 codes derived from the research questions and conceptual framework, each with a definition.
After each contact, complete a one-page contact summary sheet: main themes, information relevant to each research question, salient points and new questions.
First-cycle code transcripts and field notes, revising the start list and adding inductive codes, and keep a code definition log.
Second-cycle pattern code, grouping first-cycle codes into themes, causes or explanations, relationships among people, or theoretical constructs.
Write memos whenever a pattern, contradiction or explanation appears, linking each memo to the codes and cases it draws on.
Check intercoder agreement on a sample of 10% to 20% of the data, aiming for about 80% agreement or kappa of 0.70 or more, and refine definitions.
Feed reduced data into displays for analysis rather than treating reduction as the final product.
outputs: A start list and evolving codebook, contact summary sheets, coded data, pattern codes and analytic memos.
useWhen: Medium to large qualitative datasets (for example 15 or more interviews or several sites) where structured, auditable analysis is needed.
avoidWhen: Very small, quick studies where a findings grid suffices; or purely inductive theory-building where a start list could bias analysis (consider grounded theory).
whyLost: The concept survived under the label 'data condensation' and inside generic 'coding' advice, but the contact summary sheets and explicit start lists are rarely used in UX practice.
whereToUse: Multi-site field studies, longitudinal diary studies, continuous discovery repositories, B2B account research.
example: A team studying adoption across 20 clinics used contact summary sheets after every visit and a 30-code start list. Pattern coding grouped codes into five adoption barriers, which then fed a cross-case matrix.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage; Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Data structure diagram construction
origin: Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013); in use since Corley and Gioia (2004)
summary: Builds a left-to-right diagram showing how informant-level concepts aggregate into themes and theoretical dimensions, making qualitative analysis traceable at a glance.
description: The data structure diagram is the visual centrepiece of Gioia-style analysis. First-order concepts are listed on the left, second-order themes in the middle and aggregate dimensions on the right, with lines or brackets showing which concepts form which themes. It is accompanied by a table of representative quotes. Its value is evidentiary: a reader can see the full chain from informants' words to theory, judge whether groupings are plausible, and see how much data underlies each theme. It is not a causal model; relationships among dimensions belong in the separate grounded theoretical model. Rigour comes from including every retained concept, ensuring each theme has several supporting concepts, and having the structure challenged by a second researcher.
steps: Finalise first-order concepts, phrased close to informant language, and remove duplicates or concepts supported by only one informant unless theoretically important.
Confirm each second-order theme has at least 2 to 3 first-order concepts and each aggregate dimension has at least 2 themes.
Lay out three columns (concepts, themes, dimensions) and connect them with brackets or arrows, ordering items so related ones sit together.
Build an accompanying table with 2 to 4 representative quotes per first-order concept, each tagged with an informant identifier.
Ask a colleague to test the diagram by trying to reassign concepts; groupings that are frequently contested should be revisited in the data.
Present the diagram with the quote table in reports, and keep a separate model figure for relationships among dimensions.
outputs: A three-column data structure diagram and a representative quotes table supporting each concept.
useWhen: Communicating qualitative analysis to sceptical or analytically minded audiences; demonstrating rigour in published or regulated research; handing analysis to other researchers.
avoidWhen: The audience needs actionable design implications quickly, where a findings summary is better; or the analysis was deductive with a fixed framework, where a framework matrix fits better.
whyLost: UX synthesis outputs evolved toward affinity walls, journey maps and insight statements, which hide the chain of evidence the diagram makes visible.
whereToUse: Research repositories, stakeholder readouts for strategic studies, academic-industry collaborations, audit-ready research in finance and health.
example: A fintech research readout presented a data structure linking 28 first-order concepts to 7 themes and 3 dimensions of informal lending identity. Risk analysts challenged one grouping, the team returned to the quotes, and the revised diagram strengthened trust in the findings.
sources: Gioia (Administrative Science Quarterly) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 28 — The Gioia Methodology — Identity-First Systematic Analysis
reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31.

name: Data Visualisation Design (LATCH)
origin: Richard Saul Wurman's LATCH; Nathan Yau; Cleveland and McGill's ranking of visual cues
summary: A stepwise practice for building a visualisation: choose organisation (LATCH), coordinate system, scales and one visual cue per data type, keeping form fitted to content.
description: The practice treats a chart as a sequence of explicit design decisions. First decide which relationships matter. Then choose an organising principle from Wurman's LATCH (location, alphabet, time, category, hierarchy), a coordinate system (Cartesian, polar, geographic) and scales (linear, categorical, percentage, logarithmic, ordinal, time). Finally assign one visual cue per variable from the set position, length, angle, direction, shape, area, volume, saturation and hue, preferring the cues Cleveland and McGill found people judge most accurately (position and length) for the most important comparisons. Layering one cue per variable lets relationships show without clutter. Decorative choices can mislead, and area and volume are hard to judge, so the result should be tested by having others read it.
steps: Decide which relationships in the data the viewer must see.
Pick an organising principle (location, alphabet, time, category or hierarchy) and a coordinate system.
Set scales appropriate to each variable.
Assign one visual cue per variable, using position or length for the key comparison and avoiding area and volume for precise values.
Remove decoration that does not encode data.
Test readability by asking two or three people to say what they see first and what the main message is, then revise.
outputs: A visualisation of research or usage data whose encodings are chosen and justified.
useWhen: Use when presenting survey, analytics or synthesis results and the choice of chart form will shape what stakeholders conclude.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the task is analysis rather than presentation: explore with Exploratory Data Analysis for Behavioural UX Data first. For checking how an audience actually reads a chart, run Fresh-eyes feedback as in Design Critique or a quick Think-Aloud Protocol.
whyLost: Visualisation craft is widely taught and practised; LATCH and perceptual cue rankings remain the standard vocabulary for chart decisions.
whereToUse: Research readouts, product analytics dashboards, executive reporting, public data stories.
example: A team reports satisfaction by region on a map coloured by saturation, then switches to a sorted bar chart when colleagues misjudge the differences, keeping the map only as an index.
sources: Wurman, R. S. (1989). Information Anxiety. New York: Doubleday.

Cleveland, W. S. and McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531-554.
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
A Practical Guide to Designing with Data (Suda, 2010)
reference: Cleveland, W. S. and McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531-554.

name: Data-Frame Analysis
origin: Gary Klein, Brian Moon and Robert Hoffman, 2006
summary: Models how experts fit data into frames, then elaborate, question, preserve or replace those frames, to design tools that support reframing when anomalies appear.
description: Klein's data-frame theory describes sensemaking as a reciprocal process: people use frames (stories, scripts, mental models) to decide which data matter, and data in turn confirm, elaborate or challenge frames. Key activities include elaborating a frame, questioning it when anomalies appear, preserving it by explaining anomalies away, comparing alternatives and reframing. Fixation, failing to reframe despite contrary evidence, is a major source of expert error. As a research method, analysts use cognitive task analysis interviews, often the Critical Decision Method, to reconstruct incidents and code when frames formed, which data triggered questioning and how long reframing took. Rigour comes from grounding analysis in real incidents, coding sensemaking functions explicitly, and designing tools that surface anomalies and alternative frames rather than reinforcing the first interpretation.
steps: Select challenging incidents where experts had to interpret ambiguous or changing data.
Conduct Critical Decision Method interviews with 6-12 experts, sweeping each incident multiple times for detail.
Code each incident for frame formation, elaboration, questioning, preservation and reframing events.
Identify anomalies that should have triggered reframing and the cues that were missed or explained away.
Derive requirements for surfacing anomalies, showing alternative hypotheses and tracking frame confidence.
Test prototypes in scenario-based evaluations that include frame-breaking events.
outputs: Coded incident timelines, catalogue of fixation risks and missed cues, decision-support requirements.
useWhen: Expert decision support in medicine, security, operations, intelligence and diagnosis tools, including AI assistants that propose interpretations.
avoidWhen: Novice or routine tasks without diagnostic ambiguity; standard task analysis is sufficient.
whyLost: Siloed: NDM research literature; powerful for expert system design; rarely applied in UX.
whereToUse: Expert decision support; medical/military UI; complex monitoring systems.
example: A radiology AI flagged likely diagnoses. Data-frame analysis of clinician incidents showed early AI suggestions anchored frames; the team redesigned the tool to show differentials and highlight findings inconsistent with the top suggestion.
sources: Making Sense of Sensemaking 2: A Macrocognitive Model (Klein, Moon & Hoffman)
reference: Klein, G., Moon, B., & Hoffman, R. R. (2006). Making sense of sensemaking 2: A macrocognitive model. IEEE Intelligent Systems, 21(5), 88-92.

name: Day Reconstruction Method
origin: Daniel Kahneman, Alan Krueger, David Schkade, Norbert Schwarz and Arthur Stone, 2004
summary: Participants reconstruct the previous day as a sequence of episodes, then report context and feelings for each, approximating experience sampling with less burden.
description: Experience sampling is accurate but intrusive. The DRM asks people to recall yesterday in a structured diary: first listing episodes like scenes in a film (what, when, where, with whom), then rating feelings during each episode on affect scales. The episodic reconstruction reduces retrospective biases compared with global questions, and validation studies show DRM results correlate well with experience sampling. Time-weighted affect (U-index: proportion of time in which the strongest feeling is negative) quantifies experienced wellbeing. For UX, DRM shows how product use fits into daily life, which episodes involve the product and how they feel.
steps: Have participants complete the DRM in one sitting (45-75 minutes), ideally the day after the target day.
Ask for a diary of the previous day divided into episodes with start and end times.
For each episode, collect activity, location, companions and technology use.
Rate affect for each episode on adjective scales (e.g. happy, frustrated, tired, competent) and, following Dolan (2014), add purpose items rating how worthwhile or meaningful the episode felt (0-6).
Compute duration-weighted affect, U-index and comparisons between episodes with and without product use.
Follow up with interviews on notable episodes.
outputs: Episode-level time use and affect data, U-index, comparisons of experiences across activities and product use.
useWhen: Understanding how products fit into daily life and affect experienced wellbeing at scale.
avoidWhen: Momentary micro-interactions where in-the-moment sampling is needed, or very short-term evaluations.
whyLost: It stayed in wellbeing economics, while UX used diary studies with looser structure.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing, social media, productivity tools, health and caregiving apps, commuting apps.
example: A social app runs DRM with 500 users. Episodes involving passive scrolling have a U-index of 0.31, versus 0.12 for messaging episodes, informing a redesign emphasising messaging.
sources: Kahneman et al., A survey method for characterizing daily life experience: The day reconstruction method (2004), Science
Kahneman & Krueger, Developments in the measurement of subjective well-being (2006), Journal of Economic Perspectives
Dolan, P., Happiness by Design: Change What You Do, Not How You Think (2014)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)

name: DBSCAN density-based clustering
origin: Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu, 1996
summary: Cluster points by local density, finding clusters of any shape and number while labelling sparse points as noise, with parameters set from a k-distance plot.
description: Density at a point is the number of points within radius Eps. Points with at least MinPts neighbours are core points; points within Eps of a core point are border points; the rest are noise. Core points within Eps of each other are linked into clusters, border points join a neighbouring core cluster, and noise is discarded. The algorithm therefore finds the number of clusters itself and produces a partial clustering, which suits behavioural data with many unrepresentative users. Parameters come from a sorted plot of each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour: Eps is set at the knee and MinPts equals k (k = 4 in the original two-dimensional work). DBSCAN fails when cluster densities differ widely, struggles in high dimensions, and is sensitive to k: small k turns noise clumps into clusters, large k swallows small clusters.
steps: Prepare and scale features, reducing dimensionality first if there are many (for example with PCA or UMAP).
Choose k; compute each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour.
Sort and plot these distances; set Eps at the knee and MinPts equal to k.
Label points core, border or noise and remove noise points.
Connect core points within Eps into clusters and assign border points to an associated core cluster.
Inspect cluster sizes and noise share, then profile clusters and check robustness to nearby Eps values.
outputs: Clusters of arbitrary shape and number, plus a set of noise points.
useWhen: Behavioural or spatial data contain irregular groups and many outliers, and you do not want to force every user into a segment, for example location data or session embeddings.
avoidWhen: Clusters differ widely in density or data are high-dimensional; use HDBSCAN, GMM or k-means after reduction. Do not use when every user must be assigned a segment.
whyLost: It is standard in data mining and spatial analytics, but UX segmentation workflows default to k-means and latent class analysis.
whereToUse: Location and mobility apps, session embedding clusters, anomaly detection in usage, fraud patterns, retail footfall.
example: A ride-hailing team clusters pickup locations with DBSCAN and finds irregular hotspots outside stations that k-means split arbitrarily. Noise points show one-off trips, and hotspots inform suggested pickup pins.
sources: Cluster Analysis: Basic Concepts and Algorithms (Tan et al., 2006)
7 Clustering Methods for UX Researchers (carousel, n.d.)
8 Clustering Algorithms in Machine Learning that All Data Scientists Should Know (McGregor, 2020)
reference: Ester, M., Kriegel, H.-P., Sander, J., & Xu, X. (1996). A density-based algorithm for discovering clusters in large spatial databases with noise. Proceedings of KDD-96, 226-231.

name: Dead-end identification
origin: Sink and orphan node detection from graph theory; web IA practice since the late 1990s
summary: Identifies pages, states or results that offer users no meaningful next step, using structural analysis and behavioural evidence of exits and back-tracking.
description: A dead end is a node with no outgoing path towards the user's goal: a page with no links, an empty search result with no suggestions, an error screen with only 'OK', or a confirmation page that does not lead onward. In graph terms, dead ends are sinks or near-sinks. Structural identification lists nodes with zero or only trivial outgoing edges; behavioural identification finds pages with high exit or back-button rates relative to expectations. Combining both separates pages that are genuinely terminal (task complete) from those where users are stranded. The method is common in content audits but often reduced to a crawler report; the rigorous version asks whether exits lead towards the goal, not merely whether links exist.
steps: Crawl or export the site or app graph, including dynamic states such as empty results and error screens.
List nodes with no outgoing navigation edges and nodes whose only edges are global navigation.
Join analytics to find pages with exit rates or back-navigation rates more than 2 standard deviations above site median for their template.
Classify each candidate as intended terminal, stranded user, or broken, checking against task goals.
Design next steps for stranded nodes: related actions, suggestions, recovery options or contact paths.
Monitor exit and back-navigation rates after changes.
outputs: A dead-end inventory with classification, analytics evidence, and next-step recommendations per node.
useWhen: In content audits, after migrations, for search and error states, and when funnels show unexplained drop-off.
avoidWhen: When the problem is labelling or wayfinding within reachable paths; use tree testing or first-click tests.
whyLost: It survived because crawlers and analytics make it cheap, though the goal-directed classification step is often skipped.
whereToUse: Content-heavy websites, help centres, e-commerce search, SaaS onboarding, and error states.
example: An e-commerce site finds 12% of searches return zero results with no suggestions; these pages have an 81% exit rate. Adding spelling correction and category suggestions halves the exit rate.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 6 — Strange Loops, Recursive Failures & Navigation Traps
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J. (2015). Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (4th ed.). O'Reilly.

name: Deception with Funnel Debriefing
aka: Deception with debriefing in HCI studies
origin: Psychology research tradition; Orne (1962) on demand characteristics; Blackhart et al. (2012); Boynton, Portnoy and Johnson (2013)
summary: Use a cover story only when disclosure would change the behaviour studied, then debrief with general-to-specific questions that detect suspicion and restore participants' trust.
description: Some behaviour cannot be studied if participants know the hypothesis, for example security behaviour: in one HCI study, people role-playing with test accounts behaved less securely than those using their own. Deception is justified only when disclosure would invalidate results, risk is minimal, and ethics approval is obtained. The funnel debriefing closes the study. A standard prompt invites honest, negative feedback with no penalty; questions move from general (how did the study go, anything odd?) to specific (what was it about, did you suspect anything?), and participants cannot return to edit earlier answers. Anonymous self-administered forms and graded suspicion scales draw more admissions than face-to-face yes/no questions; fewer than one in five deliberately informed participants admit it otherwise. The deception is then revealed, explained and discussed, and participants may withdraw their data. Evidence shows a full funnel debriefing removes negative effects on mood and trust.
steps: Establish that disclosure would invalidate results and that no non-deceptive design would work.
Design the cover story to minimise risk and distress, and obtain ethics approval, working with the board if prior consent is impossible.
Run the study, then deliver a standard opening prompt inviting honest, negative feedback with no effect on payment.
Ask general then increasingly specific questions about purpose and suspicion, preferably on an anonymous form with graded ratings, without allowing earlier answers to be edited.
Reveal and explain the deception and why it was needed, and offer withdrawal of data.
Pre-set exclusion thresholds for suspicion, and analyse and report results with and without aware participants.
outputs: Behavioural data uncontaminated by knowledge of the hypothesis, suspicion ratings per participant, a sensitivity analysis, and debriefed participants.
useWhen: Studies of security, privacy, persuasion, trust or social influence where knowing the purpose would change behaviour, such as phishing susceptibility or dark-pattern effects.
avoidWhen: Avoid when an honest design (own accounts, field data, naturalistic observation) can answer the question; avoid online deception where debriefing cannot be guaranteed. Excluding aware participants can bias the sample.
whyLost: It is routine in social psychology; HCI uses deception occasionally but seldom with structured suspicion probes and sensitivity analyses.
whereToUse: Security and fraud UX, persuasive design ethics, AI disclosure studies, trust and compliance research.
example: A bank tests whether a warning screen stops scam transfers, telling participants the study is about payment speed. A funnel debriefing finds 15% suspected a security focus; results hold with and without them, and all participants leave understanding why the cover was needed.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Exploring the Ethics and Psychological Impact of Deception in Psychological Research (Boynton et al., 2013)
reference: Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. and Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann; Boynton, M. H., Portnoy, D. B. and Johnson, B. T. (2013). Exploring the ethics and psychological impact of deception in psychological research. IRB: Ethics & Human Research, 35(2), 7-13.

name: Deceptive Pattern Analysis
origin: Harry Brignull, 2010; taxonomy extended by Gray et al. (2018) and Mathur et al. (2019)
summary: Identifies and classifies interface designs that steer users against their interests, using established taxonomies, to support ethical review and regulatory compliance.
description: Deceptive patterns are interface designs that trick or pressure users into actions they would not otherwise take, such as roach-motel cancellation, confirmshaming, hidden costs, sneak-into-basket and disguised ads. Harry Brignull coined the term and catalogue; academic work by Gray and colleagues and by Mathur and colleagues produced more rigorous taxonomies and showed prevalence at scale through automated crawls. As a method, an auditor walks key journeys, especially sign-up, purchase, consent and cancellation, captures each screen and codes instances against a taxonomy. Rigour comes from using a published taxonomy with definitions, having two coders independently classify instances, counting steps and asymmetries (for example clicks to subscribe versus to cancel), and mapping findings to regulations such as the EU Digital Services Act, GDPR consent rules and FTC guidance.
steps: Select journeys most prone to deception: sign-up, checkout, consent, upgrade and cancellation.
Walk each journey and capture every screen and step, including on mobile and web.
Code instances against a published taxonomy (e.g. Gray et al. or Mathur et al.), with two coders working independently.
Measure asymmetries such as steps to opt in versus opt out and default states of consent toggles.
Rate each instance by harm and regulatory exposure, referencing applicable law.
Recommend fair alternatives and re-audit after changes.
outputs: Coded pattern inventory with screenshots, asymmetry metrics, harm and compliance ratings, remediation list.
useWhen: Ethics and compliance reviews, competitor audits, before regulatory scrutiny, and when retention or conversion tactics are under debate.
avoidWhen: When you need to understand users' actual experience of a pattern; pair with interviews or usability testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Growing regulatory and ethical imperative; widely referenced in industry and academia.
whereToUse: UX audits; ethical design review; regulatory compliance; competitive analysis.
example: A streaming service audit found sign-up took 3 steps while cancellation took 9 including a guilt-framed retention screen. Mapping this to FTC click-to-cancel guidance justified a one-page cancellation flow.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Mathur, A. et al. (2019). Dark patterns at scale: Findings from a crawl of 11K shopping websites. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), 81.

name: Decision Bars
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Explicit success and failure thresholds set before a study or change, so every finding and fix resolves to a clear pass, fail or iterate decision.
description: Decision bars recur throughout Vivek Gopinath's playbooks as the device that turns research into decisions. A bar is a numeric threshold stated before data collection, tied to a specific task and metric, often with guardrails. Examples include: predicted ideal 6s with breakdown declared if the observed median exceeds 15s; tree direct success ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0, first-click ≥ 75–80%; element SNR ≥ 0.60 and behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70; completion ≥ 80% and HR ≤ 0.80; OTP success ≥ 80% within 3 attempts; TLX frustration ≤ 40/100; +5–8 points adoption in 4 weeks; entropy > 2.0 for 70% of active users within 4 weeks; act if DriftScore ≥ 0.50 for 2 consecutive weeks. Bars make findings falsifiable, prevent post-hoc rationalisation and let qualitative and quantitative evidence converge on the same verdict.
steps: Name the decision the study informs and the primary metric that will decide it.
Set the threshold before data collection, anchored on a baseline or a prediction (e.g. GOMS ideal time or Monte Carlo forecast).
Add secondary bars and guardrails (e.g. misroute ≤ 10%, no increase in errors, declines or chargebacks).
Specify the time window and population (e.g. within 4 weeks, 70% of active users, 2 consecutive weeks).
Record the bars in the study plan or joint display alongside the prescribed fix.
After data collection, issue a verdict per bar (met, missed, guardrail breached) and decide ship, iterate or stop.
outputs: A table of pre-set thresholds per metric and a pass/fail verdict per study.
useWhen: In any evaluative or experimental study where results must drive a decision.
avoidWhen: In open exploratory discovery where no outcome is yet defined; bars set without a baseline become arbitrary.
whyLost: Original framing by Vivek Gopinath, generalising pre-registration and acceptance criteria into everyday UX research.
whereToUse: Experiment plans, research briefs, design reviews, post-launch reviews.
example: Before redesigning a payments flow the team commits to +5–8 points tap adoption in 4 weeks with declines and chargebacks as guardrails, so the readout is a verdict rather than a debate.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook.

name: Decision Memo Format
origin: Practitioner format in UX research operations, drawing on policy-brief and management decision-memo traditions
summary: Converts research findings into a one-page, decision-oriented brief with insight sentences, recommendations, guardrail metrics and an effort-impact view, so research is acted on rather than archived.
description: Long research decks are read once and archived. The decision memo is built around the decision a stakeholder must make, not the study that was run. A single page states what the team was trying to understand, what was learned (as insight sentences of the form 'finding, which means implication, which suggests action'), the confidence and evidence behind each claim, and specific recommendations. Each recommendation names a guardrail metric that would show whether acting on it worked or caused harm, and recommendations are placed on an effort-by-impact grid to support sequencing. Supporting evidence is linked rather than embedded. The format's rigour lies in forcing explicit links between evidence, implication and action, and in making uncertainty and success criteria visible to decision-makers.
steps: One-page structure: (1) What we were trying to understand (2 sentences). (2) What we found — 3–5 findings, each a single declarative sentence. (3) What this means for the decision — one recommendation per finding. (4) What we need to know before acting with full confidence.
The insight sentence pattern: '[Finding], which means [implication], which suggests we should [action].' Forces the analyst to complete the chain from observation to recommendation.
Guardrail monitoring: For each recommendation: what metric to monitor to know whether the recommendation was correct? What threshold triggers reassessment?
Effort × impact grid: Plot each recommendation on effort × impact. High-impact, low-effort quadrant = starting point.
outputs: A one-page decision memo, insight sentences with evidence and confidence, prioritised recommendations, guardrail metrics, and an effort-impact grid.
useWhen: Research must inform a specific product, design or strategy decision, stakeholders are time-poor, or previous research has gone unused.
avoidWhen: The goal is exploratory sense-making with the team, or findings are too early for recommendations; use a synthesis workshop or a narrative report. Do not compress findings whose nuance is the point, such as ethnographic accounts.
whyLost: It survives because product organisations reward actionability, though the guardrail-metric and evidence-confidence parts are often dropped in favour of bullet-point recommendations.
whereToUse: Roadmap and prioritisation meetings, executive reviews, launch decisions, research repositories, and research operations templates.
example: After 12 interviews on a SaaS billing page, the researcher writes a one-page memo: 'Admins cannot predict next month's invoice, which means they delay seat expansion, which suggests showing a projected invoice.' The guardrail is support tickets about billing; the change ships within the sprint.
reference: Knaflic, C. N. (2015). Storytelling with Data. Wiley.

name: Decision memo template (one-page)
donor: Military and executive staff work / management practice
origin: Military staff memo and Amazon narrative traditions; structured briefing (e.g. bottom line up front)
summary: A single-page document that states a decision to be made, the recommendation, the evidence and its confidence, options, risks and the ask, linking research directly to action.
description: Research often fails to influence decisions because it is reported as findings rather than as recommendations tied to choices. The one-page decision memo leads with the decision and recommendation (bottom line up front), followed by the key evidence with explicit confidence levels, the options considered and their trade-offs, risks and mitigations, and the specific ask and deadline. The constraint of one page forces prioritisation. Rigour comes from separating evidence from interpretation, stating uncertainty quantitatively where possible, citing the underlying research for traceability, and recording the decision and its outcome for later learning.
steps: State the decision needed, the decision owner and the deadline in the first line.
Write the recommendation in one or two sentences.
Summarise 3-5 key pieces of evidence, each with its source and a confidence level (e.g. high, medium, low or a posterior probability).
Lay out 2-3 options with expected impact, cost and risk.
List key risks, assumptions and what would change the recommendation.
Close with the explicit ask and link to full research; afterwards record the decision taken and revisit the outcome.
outputs: A one-page memo, a recorded decision, and a traceable link from evidence to action.
useWhen: When research must inform a specific decision by leaders or cross-functional teams with limited time.
avoidWhen: Avoid for exploratory findings with no pending decision (use an insight report) or for very complex decisions needing a full strategic brief.
whyLost: It survives because decision-makers prefer concise, action-oriented documents; UX has adopted it unevenly.
whereToUse: Product leadership reviews, roadmap decisions, launch go/no-go, board briefings.
example: After a pricing study, the researcher writes a one-page memo recommending tiered pricing, citing a conjoint analysis with 90% posterior confidence that it maximises revenue without lowering satisfaction. The VP approves in the same meeting.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief
reference: Minto, B. (2009) The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking. Pearson.

name: Decision Trees and Random Forests for Behaviour Prediction
origin: Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone (1984) CART; Breiman (2001) random forests
summary: Builds readable if-then rules (trees) or robust ensembles (forests) that predict outcomes like churn or task failure.
description: A decision tree repeatedly splits users on the variable that best separates outcomes, yielding rules such as "users who skipped onboarding and have fewer than three projects churn at 62%". Trees are easy to explain but unstable; random forests average hundreds of trees built on bootstrap samples and random subsets of variables, trading readability for accuracy, and provide variable importance scores. Bruce and Bruce cover growing, pruning and tuning. For UX, a shallow tree is a powerful communication tool for showing which behaviours separate successful and struggling users.
steps: Define the outcome (churn, task failure, conversion) and candidate behavioural predictors.
Fit a shallow tree with limits on depth and minimum leaf size for interpretability.
Fit a random forest for accuracy and variable importance, tuning by cross-validation.
Evaluate on held-out data with a confusion matrix and AUC.
Translate top splits into hypotheses for qualitative follow-up.
outputs: Interpretable rules and ranked behavioural predictors of an outcome.
useWhen: You have behavioural data on many users and want to know which behaviours separate outcomes.
avoidWhen: Small samples (trees overfit badly) or when causal claims are needed.
whyLost: UX analytics stops at funnels and dashboards; predictive modelling stays with data science teams.
whereToUse: SaaS onboarding, subscription churn, feature adoption studies.
example: A shallow tree shows that trial users who never invite a teammate convert at 4% versus 29% for those who do, reframing onboarding around collaboration.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Kass GV (1980) An exploratory technique for investigating large quantities of categorical data. Applied Statistics 29(2):119-127
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Performance Analysis of the CHAID Algorithm for Accuracy (Yang et al., 2023)
Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 6.

name: Decision-Centered Design with Decision Requirements Tables
donor: Cognitive systems engineering / naturalistic decision making
origin: Hutton, Miller and Thordsen, in Hollnagel (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
summary: Centre design on a job's critical, difficult judgements: elicit them by cognitive task analysis, tabulate cues and strategies in decision requirements tables, storyboard concepts and evaluate with decision-stressing scenarios.
description: Decision-Centered Design is an end-to-end design process built on cognitive task analysis, whereas CTA alone stops at elicitation. It assumes that a system's value lies in supporting the few critical, difficult decisions and judgements a role involves. After domain familiarisation, experts are interviewed with the Knowledge Audit and Critical Decision Method and observed at work. Findings are compiled into decision requirements tables that list, for each key decision, why it is difficult, the cues and information used, common errors, and the strategies experts apply. These tables are transformed into design concepts and storyboards, and evaluated with scenarios built specifically to stress those decisions, against real-world outcome criteria rather than generic usability. The process has been applied to air campaign plan evaluation and a Navy landing signal officer display.
steps: Prepare: familiarise yourself with the domain, roles and documentation.
Elicit with cognitive task analysis: Knowledge Audit, Critical Decision Method interviews and observation of experts.
Build decision requirements tables listing each critical decision, why it is difficult, cues and information used, typical errors and expert strategies.
Transform the requirements into design concepts and storyboards that support each decision.
Build evaluation scenarios that deliberately stress those decisions and test the concepts with practitioners.
Set real-world outcome criteria and iterate design and evaluation.
outputs: Decision requirements tables, storyboards and design concepts, and scenario-based evaluation results.
useWhen: Designing decision-support tools, dashboards and displays for expert, high-stakes roles where judgement under uncertainty matters more than routine task flow.
avoidWhen: Simple transactional or consumer tasks with few hard judgements; when genuine experts and skilled interviewers are unavailable. For elicitation alone use Cognitive Task Analysis.
whyLost: It sits in defence and naturalistic decision-making consultancies; mainstream UX adopted journey and task flows rather than decision-centred requirements.
whereToUse: Clinical decision support, fraud and risk analyst tools, operations dashboards, AI recommendation interfaces for professionals.
example: For a fraud analyst console, CDM interviews identify 'escalate or release a flagged payment' as the critical decision. The decision requirements table lists cues analysts actually use, such as device history and payee age, and the redesign puts them in one panel, tested with scenarios built around ambiguous cases.
reference: Hutton, R. J. B., Miller, T. E. and Thordsen, M. L. (2003). Decision-centered design: leveraging cognitive task analysis in design, in Hollnagel, E. (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum, pp. 383-416.

name: Decision-Maker Self-Test
aka: User sensitivity boot camp for decision makers
origin: Louis Rosenfeld and Peter Morville, 2006; phrase credited to Steve Toub
summary: Decision makers attempt three or four common tasks on their own site while thinking aloud, and the problems they hit are listed and classified with them.
description: Return-on-investment arguments rarely persuade executives as well as feeling the pain themselves. In this boot camp, decision makers who are not web-savvy sit at a browser and attempt three or four basic, common tasks on their own site, or a competitor's if theirs does not yet exist. As in a think-aloud test they talk through what they are doing, while a facilitator writes each problem on a whiteboard as it occurs. The group then reviews the list together and classifies each problem as caused by information architecture or by other design issues. The output is a problem list the stakeholders generated themselves, which builds buy-in and a shared basis for prioritising work.
steps: Recruit decision makers who do not know the site's inner workings.
Choose three or four basic, common user tasks on their own site, or on a competitor's.
Have each decision maker attempt the tasks while thinking aloud.
Write each problem on a whiteboard as it occurs.
Review the list together, classifying problems as information architecture or other design.
Use the agreed list as the basis for prioritising work.
outputs: A stakeholder-generated, classified problem list and stronger stakeholder buy-in.
useWhen: Securing executive support for research or redesign, and aligning leaders on the most visible problems.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for testing with real users; executives are not representative. Follow with Usability Testing.
whyLost: Teams more often invite executives to watch user sessions; the self-test is a little-documented stakeholder tactic.
whereToUse: Intranets, public-sector websites, enterprise portals and early stages of a redesign programme.
example: Before an intranet redesign, five directors try to find the parental leave policy and book a meeting room. Four fail at the first task, and the classified list makes navigation the agreed priority.
sources: Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld & Morville, 2006)
reference: Rosenfeld, L. and Morville, P. (2006) Information Architecture for the World Wide Web, 3rd edn. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Decoy effect measurement
origin: Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto (1982), 'Adding asymmetrically dominated alternatives'
summary: Measures how adding an inferior, asymmetrically dominated option shifts choice share towards the option it makes look better.
description: The decoy or attraction effect violates the regularity principle of rational choice: adding an option should never increase the share of an existing one, yet adding a decoy that is clearly worse than target A but not clearly worse than competitor B raises A's share. Decoy effect measurement quantifies this in a product's real option sets, typically pricing tiers, plans or bundles, by comparing choice shares between a core set and the same set plus a candidate decoy. Effects in laboratory studies are often 5 to 15 percentage points but are fragile: they shrink when attributes are not numerically comparable or when options are presented pictorially. Rigour therefore requires between-subjects randomisation, attribute-level dominance checks, and testing in the real presentation format rather than abstract tables.
steps: Map the option set on its two or three decisive attributes (for example price and coverage) and identify the target option you want to make more attractive and its main competitor.
Design a decoy that is dominated by the target on all decisive attributes but not by the competitor, typically 10% to 25% worse than the target on one attribute at a similar price.

Randomise users between the core set and the core-plus-decoy set in the real interface; plan for several hundred choices per arm, since effects of 5 to 10 points need roughly 400 to 1,500 per arm for 80% power.
Measure the target's share among choices of target and competitor, the decoy's own share (which should be small, under about 5%), and downstream outcomes such as refunds or churn.
Test for regularity violation with a two-proportion test or logistic regression and report the effect size with a confidence interval.
Assess ethics and robustness: confirm the target genuinely suits most choosers, and replicate on a second segment or format before rollout.
outputs: Choice shares with and without the decoy, effect size and confidence interval, decoy selection rate, and downstream satisfaction or churn data.
useWhen: Designing or reviewing pricing pages, plan tiers, insurance packages or any option set where relative evaluation drives choice.
avoidWhen: Traffic is too low to detect effects of a few percentage points, or the goal is to steer users to options that serve the business rather than them; use qualitative choice interviews or remove the manipulation.
whyLost: Decoy effects are standard knowledge in pricing consultancies and marketing science, but UX researchers rarely run controlled tests, relying on the textbook anecdote rather than measuring their own sets.
whereToUse: SaaS pricing tiers, telecom and insurance plans, subscription bundles, e-commerce product ranges, clinical option menus where a recommended option must stand out.
example: A health insurer added a mid-tier plan with lower coverage than the 'Standard' plan at nearly the same price. Standard's share rose from 41% to 49% of Standard-or-Basic choices, while the decoy took only 3%; complaint and switching rates were monitored for 90 days before keeping it.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Huber, J., Payne, J. W., & Puto, C. (1982). Adding asymmetrically dominated alternatives: Violations of regularity and the similarity hypothesis. Journal of Consumer Research, 9(1), 90–98.

name: Deep hanging out (ten-foci structured immersion)
origin: Phrase from anthropology (Geertz; Clifford, 1997); structured version from Intel People and Practices research (Teague and Bell, 2001)
summary: A team immerses itself in a public setting as users of the place, each member owning standard focal points, then debriefs focus by focus to compare sites systematically.
description: Anthropologists use 'deep hanging out' for informal immersion in a community. Intel's People and Practices group turned it into a structured team method for public settings. Researchers become users of the place, from arrival to departure, and divide ten standard focal points between them: family and kids, food and drink, built environment, possessions, media, tools and technology, demographics, traffic, information and communication access, and overall experience. Sampling different days and times, they observe discreetly, sketch and collect maps, and read the signs. The fixed foci keep novices looking broadly, stop parallel observers returning with identical findings, and allow comparison across sites. Debriefs start with a one-sentence summary per focal point, followed by standard questions on surprises, norms and implications. It reveals context but not motives, since there is no interaction.
steps: Choose the setting (for example an airport, market or hospital lobby) and a sampling plan across days and times.
Assign the ten focal points among team members, typically two per person.
Use the setting yourself from arrival to departure, keeping a low profile and taking discreet notes.
Sketch maps of hot spots and flows, collect site maps and signage, and photograph where permitted.
Debrief with a one-sentence summary per focal point, then answer standard questions about surprises, norms and what to do differently.
Organise themes, compare across sites, and list questions for follow-up interviews.
outputs: Notes per focal area, annotated maps of hot spots and flows, cross-site comparisons and questions for follow-up research.
useWhen: Early discovery in public or semi-public places where a product will be used, especially with novice field researchers or multi-site comparisons.
avoidWhen: When you need motives, private contexts or specific workflows; use contextual inquiry or interviews. Researchers must not mistake their own experience for users', and deliberately breaking norms needs ethical care.
whyLost: Intel's structured version faded with its research group; immersion survives under looser names (safaris, field visits) without the fixed foci and debrief protocol.
whereToUse: Travel and transport apps, retail and payments, healthcare waiting environments, smart city and public kiosk design.
example: A team designing an airport travel app spends a week in two airports, each member owning two foci. Maps show queues forming at self-service kiosks near security, not at check-in, which reshapes the app's mobile boarding pass flow.
reference: Teague, R. and Bell, G. (2001). Getting out of the box: ethnography meets life. Intel People and Practices research, as described in Baxter, K., Courage, C. and Caine, K. (2015). Understanding Your Users (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 13.

name: Deese-Roediger-McDermott false recall
origin: Deese, 1959; Roediger and McDermott, 1995
summary: People study lists of words associated with an unpresented critical word, then recall; frequent recall of that word measures schema-driven false memory.
description: Lists of words all associated with a non-presented critical word (bed, rest, awake, tired, dream for 'sleep') are read at about one word a second, then recalled freely or tested by recognition. Many people recall or recognise the critical word with high confidence even though it was never shown. The effect shows that memory is constructive: the same associative and schema processes that support true memory generate false ones. Note that the acronym DRM also refers to the Day Reconstruction Method, so the full name should be used. As an applied method, the logic can test whether users 'remember' an expected label, feature or step that was never there because it fits the category.
steps: Build study lists of 12 to 15 words, each strongly associated with a critical lure that is not presented.
Present each list at about one word per second, followed by free recall or a later recognition test.
Include studied items, critical lures and unrelated new items in recognition tests.
Optionally collect confidence or remember-know judgements.
Compute false recall or recognition of critical lures and compare with true recall and unrelated false alarms.
For applied versions, build lists of interface elements or steps around an expected but absent item.
outputs: Rates of false recall or recognition of critical lures compared with true recall, and confidence in false memories.
useWhen: Checking how far users' recall of a flow, menu or policy is reconstructed from expectations, and therefore how much to trust recall-based interviews and surveys.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating it as a measure of deliberate error or dishonesty; for real-world recall accuracy compare reports with logs.
whyLost: It is a staple of memory research but no applied UX form has been packaged.
whereToUse: Recall-based interviews and surveys, terms and consent comprehension, onboarding retention tests, eyewitness-style incident reporting.
example: After a checkout task, users are asked which steps they saw. Many 'remember' an address confirmation step that does not exist, which shows that recall-based post-task surveys overstate what users noticed.
sources: Roediger, H. L., & McDermott, K. B. (1995). Creating false memories: Remembering words not presented in lists. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 21
reference: Roediger, H. L., & McDermott, K. B. (1995). Creating false memories: Remembering words not presented in lists. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 21, 803-814.

name: Defamiliarisation as Fieldwork Mindset
origin: Viktor Shklovsky, 1917; Jay Hasbrouck, 2018
summary: Trains researchers to observe familiar practices as if foreign, surfacing taken-for-granted behaviours, workarounds and meanings that experts no longer see.
description: Defamiliarisation, from Shklovsky's concept of ostranenie and central to anthropology, is the practice of rendering the familiar strange so that it can be seen. Jay Hasbrouck presents it as the mindset at the heart of ethnographic thinking: researchers who already 'know' a context stop noticing its practices, workarounds and meanings. Techniques include describing activities as an outsider or an alien would, questioning the purpose of every object and step, attending to what people treat as obvious, and comparing practices across contexts. Rigour lies in making this stance systematic in field notes and debriefs, recording observations before interpretations, and checking emergent interpretations against participants' own accounts so that strangeness generates questions rather than exoticism.
steps: Before any observation session: defamiliarization exercise.
(1) Describe the interface as if explaining it to an alien who has never seen a computer.
(2) List 10 things you assume users will understand.
(3) For each assumption, bracket it: 'I will not assume users understand X'.
(4) During observation: when a user does something unexpected, resist the impulse to explain it away. Record it first, interpret it later.
(5) Post-session: what did users treat as strange that you had treated as obvious?
outputs: Field notes that question assumptions, lists of taken-for-granted practices, reframed problem statements and new observational hypotheses.
useWhen: Research in domains the team knows too well (its own product, its own culture or industry), and any ethnographic fieldwork at risk of confirming assumptions.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a standalone method when the goal is evaluating a specific design; pair with structured observation or usability testing for that.
whyLost: Defamiliarisation is a core competence in anthropology training but invisible in UX, where research is framed as technique (interviews, tests) rather than ways of seeing.
whereToUse: Usability testing moderation, field research, expert review (combating evaluator familiarity bias), cross-cultural UX research.
example: A bank's researchers study how customers pay a plumber, writing up 'cash' as if never seen before; they notice cash is used to negotiate and signal trust, not merely transfer value.
reference: Hasbrouck J (2018) Ethnographic Thinking: From Method to Mindset. Routledge

name: Defamiliarisation Protocol
origin: Viktor Shklovsky, 1917; Jay Hasbrouck, 2018
summary: A structured set of exercises for treating familiar products, practices and settings as strange, so observers notice what familiarity hides.
description: Defamiliarisation (from the Russian Formalist concept of ostranenie) is the deliberate act of perceiving familiar things as if encountering them for the first time. In qualitative research, familiarity is the enemy of observation: experienced researchers stop seeing what is in front of them because they already "know" what it means. Defamiliarisation is the technique that restores genuine observation. Hasbrouck identifies it as the core competence of ethnographic fieldwork — not note-taking or interviewing, but the ability to actually see.
steps: The Alien Exercise (before fieldwork): Write a description of your research environment as if you are a being from another planet encountering it for the first time. Every object, gesture, and routine requires explanation. What do you actually not know? This surfaces your hidden assumptions.

The Novice Constraint (during observation): Impose a rule: you may not use any insider vocabulary in your field notes. You cannot write "the user clicked the Save button" — you must write "she moved her index finger to a rectangular element bearing a diskette symbol and applied pressure." This forces genuine description over interpretation.

The Question-Before-Assumption Protocol: Every time you catch yourself thinking "I know why they're doing that," write the assumption down and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Return to these at the end of the day and generate at least three alternative explanations for each.

Photography-first field entry: Before taking any notes, photograph 10 things in the environment that you would not normally photograph. This forces attention to background, ambient, and taken-for-granted elements that interviews never surface.
outputs: Defamiliarised field notes, lists of taken-for-granted practices and assumptions, reframed questions, and new observational hypotheses.
useWhen: Fieldwork in familiar contexts (your own product, workplace or culture), mature products with entrenched assumptions, and teams stuck in incremental thinking.
avoidWhen: Avoid for evaluative studies with fixed questions; avoid when it would come across as condescending to participants. Pair with structured observation for measurement.
whyLost: Defamiliarisation is taught as an anthropological sensibility, not a protocol, so it was not carried into UX method toolkits.
whereToUse: Mature products and established industries (banking, healthcare, enterprise software) where teams know the domain too well; in-house research on employees and internal tools; innovation and strategy work seeking reframing; training observers before contextual inquiry.
example: Researchers at a hospital arrive pretending they have never seen a tablet and describe nurses 'carrying a glowing slab that they speak to sideways'; the exercise reveals that nurses angle screens to keep patients from seeing, prompting a privacy view.
reference: Hasbrouck J (2018) Ethnographic Thinking: From Method to Mindset. Routledge

name: Defamiliarization exercise
origin: Viktor Shklovsky's 'Art as Device' (1917), Husserl's epoché, and anthropology's 'making the familiar strange'; introduced to HCI by Bell, Blythe and Sengers (2005)
summary: Deliberately estranges researchers from familiar technologies and practices so taken-for-granted assumptions become visible and questionable.
description: Familiarity hides structure: researchers who use smartphones daily no longer see the assumptions embedded in swipes, notifications or passwords. Shklovsky described art's function as making the familiar strange so it can be perceived afresh; anthropologists practise the same move at home. Bell, Blythe and Sengers showed how defamiliarisation exposes cultural assumptions in domestic technology. A defamiliarisation exercise uses structured techniques: describing a device as if seeing it for the first time, adopting the stance of an outsider or historical observer, inverting roles, or translating actions into literal physical terms. Rigour comes from doing it before and during fieldwork, writing the descriptions down, and turning each estranged observation into an explicit assumption that can be tested with participants.
steps: Choose the technology or practice to estrange, such as a tablet, a login flow or a form-filling routine, and the team members who will take part (3 to 8 is workable).
Each person writes a 300 to 500 word literal description of using it as if they had never encountered any similar object, avoiding jargon such as 'app', 'tap' or 'menu'.
Apply at least two further lenses: a historical lens (how would someone in 1980 interpret this?) and a cultural or role inversion lens (how would a participant from the field site describe it?).
Extract every assumption the descriptions expose, such as 'the user has private ownership of the device' or 'the user knows that the grey colour means disabled', and list them.
Convert assumptions into fieldwork questions and observation targets, and check them with participants rather than treating the exercise as a substitute for fieldwork.
Repeat the exercise midway through fieldwork to catch familiarity that develops as the team becomes immersed.
outputs: Written estranged descriptions, an assumption inventory, and a set of fieldwork questions and observation targets derived from it.
useWhen: Teams are deeply familiar with the technology and may be blind to its conventions; preparing for fieldwork with first-time or very different users; reframing a stale problem.
avoidWhen: You need empirical evidence about users' interpretations; the exercise generates hypotheses, not findings. Do not use it to speak for participants.
whyLost: Defamiliarisation stayed in critical design and HCI theory papers, while practice adopted 'beginner's mind' as a slogan without the structured writing and assumption extraction.
whereToUse: First-time digital users, new-to-market research, redesigning mature products, AI interaction paradigms, workshop kick-offs.
example: Before visiting rural clinics, a researcher described the tablet as an object 'that gives no sign of being on, that must be stroked to wake, and that hides its functions behind small pictures'. This surfaced the assumption that users knew sleep mode, which fieldwork confirmed was a major confusion.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 25 — The Philosophy of Seeing — Epistemological Foundations of Qualitative Inquiry
reference: Bell, G., Blythe, M., & Sengers, P. (2005). Making by making strange: Defamiliarization and the design of domestic technologies. ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 12(2), 149–173.

name: Default effect analysis
origin: Samuelson and Zeckhauser's status quo bias (1988), Madrian and Shea's 401(k) auto-enrolment study (2001) and Johnson and Goldstein's organ donation defaults (2003); popularised by Thaler and Sunstein's Nudge (2008)
summary: Measures how much a pre-selected option drives choice, and why, by comparing outcomes under different defaults or active choice.
description: Defaults are among the most powerful levers in choice architecture: Madrian and Shea found 401(k) participation rose from about 49% to 86% under automatic enrolment, and organ donor consent differs dramatically between opt-in and opt-out countries. Default effect analysis treats every pre-selected setting as an intervention and measures its effect, using randomised comparison of defaults or active choice where possible, or regression discontinuity and before-after designs where not. It also decomposes the mechanism: inertia and effort, implied endorsement by the designer, and reference-point shifts. Rigour comes from randomisation, measuring long-run outcomes rather than just initial selection, and checking whether people stuck with a default that harms them, which raises an ethical as well as a statistical question.
steps: Inventory all pre-selected options, pre-filled fields and pre-ticked choices in the flow, and record each one's current uptake rate from logs.
Select defaults with material consequences for users (money, privacy, safety, workload) and state for each the hypothesised mechanism: effort, endorsement or reference point.

Design arms: current default, alternative default and enforced active choice; calculate sample size for the expected difference (default effects are often 20 to 40 percentage points, so a few hundred users per arm frequently suffices).
Randomise users to arms and measure initial selection, later switching, and downstream outcomes over a pre-registered window of at least 30 to 90 days.
Probe mechanism with a short follow-up survey or 6 to 10 interviews asking whether users noticed the default and whether they read it as a recommendation.
Evaluate welfare: check whether outcomes for defaulted users are good for them, choose the default that best serves the majority, and preserve easy opt-out.
outputs: Default effect sizes per setting, switching rates, downstream outcome comparisons, mechanism evidence and an ethical rationale for the chosen default.
useWhen: Configuring settings, plans, consent, notification preferences or clinical options where many users will not change what they are given.
avoidWhen: The choice is highly personal with no defensible majority option (use active choice), or the default would serve the business against users' interests; that is a dark pattern, not a design decision.
whyLost: Default testing thrives in behavioural insights teams and policy units, but in product teams defaults are usually set by engineering or growth convenience and rarely evaluated as interventions.
whereToUse: Pensions and savings, privacy and consent settings, clinical order sets, notification settings, subscription plans, AI assistant settings.
example: In a clinic triage app, the urgency field defaulted to 'routine'. A randomised comparison with an enforced active choice found that the default led to 23% fewer urgent flags for cases later confirmed as urgent; the team moved to active choice for that field.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Johnson, E. J., & Goldstein, D. (2003). Do defaults save lives? Science, 302(5649), 1338–1339; Madrian, B. C., & Shea, D. F. (2001). The power of suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 116(4), 1149–1187.

name: Degenerate Feedback Loop Audit (Popularity Bias)
origin: Jiang et al. (2019); diversity metrics from Brynjolfsson et al. (2011), Fleder and Hosanagar (2009) and Abdollahpouri et al. (2019); position modelling after Schnabel et al. (2016); as presented by Huyen (2022)
summary: Check whether a ranking or recommendation system's outputs are narrowing because users' reactions to them feed back into training, and correct it with randomised exposure or position modelling.
description: A degenerate feedback loop arises when a system's predictions shape the feedback later used to train it, so items shown more get clicked more and are shown more still. Popularity bias and filter bubbles are the visible symptoms, and the same dynamic can entrench a proxy feature in screening systems. Detection uses diversity measures such as aggregate diversity and average coverage of long-tail items, hit rate computed separately for popularity buckets, and, in production, rising homogeneity of outputs over time. Corrections include giving some exposure at random (as with a random initial traffic pool for each new item), intelligent exploration with contextual bandits, small randomisation analysed with causal inference, and modelling position explicitly, either as a feature or with two models separating the chance an item is seen from the chance it is clicked once seen. Randomisation improves diversity but can harm the experience, so its dose is a design decision.
steps: Measure the popularity diversity of outputs (aggregate diversity, long-tail coverage).
Bucket items by past interaction counts and compare accuracy or hit rate across buckets.
Track output homogeneity over time in production.
Introduce limited randomisation or bandit-based exploration to gather less biased feedback, choosing the dose with experience costs in mind.
Model presentation position explicitly, with positional features or a seen-then-click two-model approach.
Re-measure diversity and bucket accuracy after the correction.
outputs: Diversity and popularity-bucket metrics over time, evidence of a feedback loop, and a corrected ranking or exploration policy.
useWhen: Auditing feeds, search ranking, recommendations or AI-curated content where users complain of sameness, new items never surface, or fairness to creators or sellers matters.
avoidWhen: Exploration has a real experience cost; where a system has little user-driven retraining, look first at Classifier Evaluation (Confusion Matrix, Precision, Recall, ROC, Lift) or Algorithmic Experience Research to understand user perception.
whyLost: It is handled inside ML and ranking teams as a modelling concern, while UX researchers study the felt sameness of feeds without the measurement tools.
whereToUse: Content feeds, marketplaces with new sellers, music and video recommendation, job and candidate matching, AI assistants that personalise over time.
example: A marketplace finds hit rate for items with under ten past sales is a third of that for best-sellers, and catalogue coverage has fallen each quarter. Giving each new listing a small random exposure pool raises long-tail coverage with a measured 1 percent dip in click-through.
reference: Jiang, R. et al. (2019). Degenerate feedback loops in recommender systems. Proc. AAAI/ACM AIES; Huyen, C. (2022). Designing Machine Learning Systems. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly, pp. 233-236.

name: Delphi Method
origin: Olaf Helmer and Norman Dalkey, RAND Corporation, 1950s to 1960s
summary: Runs anonymous, multi-round expert questionnaires with statistical feedback between rounds to converge on consensus or map the structure of expert disagreement.
description: The Delphi Method, developed at the RAND Corporation for technological forecasting, structures expert judgement to avoid the distortions of face-to-face groups: dominance, conformity and halo effects. A panel of typically 10 to 25 experts answers an open first-round questionnaire. Responses are synthesised into rated items for round two, and after each round participants receive the group's median and interquartile range alongside their own previous rating, then re-rate and justify outlying positions. Anonymity is maintained throughout. Iteration stops at a pre-defined consensus criterion, such as an IQR of 2 or less on a 9-point scale, or when ratings stabilise. Items that never converge are reported as genuine disagreement. Rigour comes from pre-registered consensus thresholds, careful panel selection and controlled feedback.
steps: Round 1 — Open elicitation: Open-ended questionnaire to 10–25 experts. Ask them to generate criteria, factors, or estimates. Analyse responses using thematic analysis.
Prepare Round 2 instrument: Compile Round 1 responses into a structured questionnaire. Participants rate or rank each item.
Round 2 — Structured rating: Compute median, range, and IQR for each item. These statistics are the controlled feedback.
Feedback and Round 3: Return statistics with participants' own previous rating highlighted. Ask them to reconsider in light of the group's distribution.
Consensus criterion: IQR ≤ 2 on a 9-point scale. Items not reaching consensus are reported with the distribution of expert views — the disagreement structure is itself a finding.
outputs: A list of items rated by experts, round-by-round medians and interquartile ranges, items reaching and failing consensus, and a documented rationale for dissent.
useWhen: You need structured expert judgement where evidence is thin: forecasting, defining standards or heuristics, prioritising risks, or building consensus among geographically dispersed specialists.
avoidWhen: The question can be answered with user data, or you need rich discussion and co-creation; use workshops or Nominal Group Technique. Avoid with fewer than about 8 genuine experts.
whyLost: It takes weeks of multiple rounds and careful panel management, and product teams prefer quick stakeholder workshops, so Delphi stayed in health policy, forecasting and academia.
whereToUse: Defining accessibility or clinical safety heuristics, AI risk assessment, roadmap foresight, research question prioritisation, and domain standards for regulated products.
example: A medical-device team runs a three-round Delphi with 18 clinicians to agree on which alarm-design principles are essential. Fourteen of 30 items reach consensus (IQR of 2 or less on a 9-point scale) and become design requirements.
sources: Preparing, Conducting, and Analyzing Delphi Surveys (PMC 2021)
Applying the Delphi Method in Design Research (designorate.com)
The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Dalkey, N. & Helmer, O. (1963). An experimental application of the Delphi method to the use of experts. Management Science, 9(3), 458-467.

name: Delta-method variance for ratio metrics
aka: Delta-method variance for ratio and percent-change metrics
origin: Classical delta method; applied to online experiments by Tang et al. (2010) and Deng, Lu and Litz (2017)
summary: Corrects the variance of ratio metrics such as click-through rate, and of percent changes, when the analysis unit is finer than the randomisation unit.
description: When an experiment randomises users but the metric is computed per page view, session or click, observations from the same user are correlated and the naive binomial variance is too small. Confidence intervals are then too narrow and false positives rise well above the nominal rate. The fix is to express the metric as a ratio of two per-user averages (for example clicks per user over page views per user) and apply the delta method, a first-order Taylor approximation that combines the variances and covariance of numerator and denominator. Percent-change results need the same treatment because the Control mean in the denominator is itself random. Where no ratio form exists, such as percentiles, the bootstrap or density estimation is used. The rigour lies in matching the variance estimator to the randomisation unit and confirming the correction with A/A tests whose p-values should be uniform.
steps: List every metric whose analysis unit (page, session, click) differs from the randomisation unit (usually the user or device).
Rewrite each such metric as a ratio of two per-user means, aggregating raw events to one row per randomisation unit.
Compute the delta-method variance from the variances of numerator and denominator and their covariance, and build the confidence interval from it.
For percent-change estimates, apply the delta method to the ratio of Treatment to Control means rather than treating the Control mean as fixed.
Use the bootstrap, resampling whole users, for statistics with no ratio form such as medians or 90th percentiles.
Run A/A tests and check that p-values are uniform and that about 5% fall below 0.05; a higher rate means the variance is still understated.
outputs: Correct standard errors and confidence intervals for ratio and percent-change metrics, plus A/A evidence that false-positive rates are at nominal level.
useWhen: Any A/B test that randomises by user but reports per-page, per-session or per-click rates, or reports relative lifts; whenever A/A tests fail more often than expected.
avoidWhen: Metrics already defined per randomisation unit (per-user conversion) need no correction. Per-user aggregation is a prerequisite, and bootstrapping very large experiments is computationally expensive; use the delta method or CUPED-style variance reduction instead.
whyLost: It is standard inside large experimentation platforms but rarely taught in UX statistics, so teams running their own tests often use naive binomial intervals on correlated data.
whereToUse: Experimentation platforms, search and recommendation ranking tests, content feeds, e-commerce click-through and add-to-basket rates, any dashboard reporting relative lift.
example: A news app tests a new card layout, randomising by user and measuring click-through per impression. A/A runs show 'significant' differences in 15% of tests.
