Recomputing the variance with the delta method on per-user clicks and impressions brings the A/A failure rate back to about 5%, and the layout's apparent win disappears.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

name: Demand Characteristics and Experimenter Effects Control
aka: Social desirability control in usability tests
origin: Martin Orne (1962); Robert Rosenthal on experimenter expectancy (1966)
summary: Identifies and controls cues that let participants guess what researchers want and researcher behaviours that shift responses, reducing positive bias in usability findings.
description: Demand characteristics are the cues in a study that tell participants what the hypothesis is, leading them to behave as 'good subjects'. Experimenter effects are the ways researchers' expectations and behaviour influence responses. In UX both inflate positive findings: participants know a designer may be present, praise prototypes, persist longer than they would at home, and rate satisfaction higher when the moderator built the design. Dumas and Loring and others have documented these moderator effects. Control techniques include neutral, scripted instructions; moderators who are not the designers; disclosing that the team wants to find problems; testing competitor or multiple versions so the 'favoured' one is unclear; behavioural rather than attitudinal measures; post-session suspicion probes; and anonymous ratings collected away from the moderator. These are standard in experimental psychology but rare in UX.
steps: Control strategies:
Use cover stories or task framing that doesn't reveal the study's hypothesis ('we're testing the navigation' not 'we're testing whether the new design is better').
(2) Remote unmoderated testing eliminates experimenter presence.
(3) Counterbalance: evaluator knowledge of design condition should be blind.
(4) Measure suspicion: post-session ask 'what do you think we were testing?' Participants who correctly identify the hypothesis are excluded or analyzed separately.
outputs: Audit of study materials and procedures for demand cues, controls implemented, suspicion-probe results, and estimates of bias in attitudinal measures.
useWhen: Usability tests, concept tests and any study relying on satisfaction or preference ratings, especially when designers moderate their own work.
avoidWhen: When measuring purely objective behaviour in naturalistic logs, where participants are unaware of the study; then reactivity is minimal.
whyLost: Speed and the designer-as-researcher model made neutral moderation hard, and UX training rarely covers the social psychology of experiments.
whereToUse: Usability study design, A/B testing methodology, any study where the researcher's knowledge of condition may influence facilitation.
example: A health app's designer moderates sessions and gets an average satisfaction of 6.3 of 7. Repeating with a neutral moderator, three design variants and ratings submitted privately yields 4.9, with the same usability problems now reported openly.
sources: Orne, On the social psychology of the psychological experiment (American Psychologist, 1962)
Rosenthal, Experimenter Effects in Behavioral Research (1966)
Moderating Usability Tests (Joseph Dumas & Beth Loring)
Designing an Experience Sampling Study (Dejonckheere & Erbas, 2021)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Exploring the Ethics and Psychological Impact of Deception in Psychological Research (Boynton et al., 2013)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Orne MT (1962) On the social psychology of the psychological experiment: With particular reference to demand characteristics and their implications. American Psychologist 17(11):776-783

name: Dependability Audit Trail
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985, building on Edward Halpern's audit trail categories (1983)
summary: Maintaining a structured audit trail so an external reviewer can reconstruct every methodological and analytic decision in a qualitative study.
description: Dependability is the naturalistic counterpart to reliability. Because qualitative designs legitimately evolve, consistency is shown not by identical repetition but by a traceable record of how and why the study changed. Halpern's six audit trail categories, adopted by Lincoln and Guba, structure that record: raw data; data reduction and analysis products (codes, memos, versions); reconstruction and synthesis products (themes, models and how they were reached); process notes on decisions; materials on intentions and dispositions (proposal, reflexivity journal); and instrument development information (guides and their revisions). An inquiry auditor can then examine the process and judge whether it was sound. The trail also makes research reusable and defensible long after the team has moved on.
steps: Set up a versioned study folder at kickoff with sections for each of the six audit trail categories.
Store raw data as collected, with consent records and session metadata, and never overwrite originals.
Version codebooks, memos and synthesis artefacts with dates, noting what changed and why.
Keep process notes for every sampling, guide or analysis decision, including deviations from plan.
Maintain a reflexivity journal recording assumptions and positionality throughout the study.
Invite an independent reviewer to audit a sample of decisions and record their judgement in the final report.
outputs: A structured audit trail folder, versioned codebooks and guides, decision log, reflexivity journal and an audit statement.
useWhen: Regulated or high-stakes research, long programmes with staff turnover, research to be reused or challenged, and studies combining human and AI coding.
avoidWhen: Throwaway tactical tests; even then, a minimal decision log is cheap insurance.
whyLost: Research ops focuses on storing findings, not decisions, and few organisations ever audit a qualitative study, so the practice has no visible payoff.
whereToUse: Medical device and health product research, financial services compliance contexts, research repositories, and AI-assisted analysis pipelines needing provenance.
example: A medical device team's formative studies are versioned with guides, codebooks and decision logs. When regulators ask why a use error category was reclassified, the team retrieves the dated rationale within minutes.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
A Worked Example of Braun and Clarke's Approach to Reflexive Thematic Analysis (Byrne, 2022)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

extra.The Audit Trail — Six Document Types: Raw data: Original recordings, transcripts, field notes, photographs, documents. Everything collected, preserved as collected. Data reduction and analysis products: Codes, categories, memos, working hypotheses, interpretations — with dates and version numbers. Data reconstruction and synthesis products: The final structures (themes, theory, causal network) that emerge from analysis — with documentation of how they were reached. Process notes: Methodological notes describing procedural decisions: why a particular sampling decision was made, why a code was revised, why a negative case was handled as it was. Materials relating to intentions and dispositions: Research proposal, study design, reflexivity journal. Instrument development information: Interview guides, observation protocols, and any revisions with rationale.

name: Dependency management
origin: Package managers such as pip (2008) and conda (2012); lockfile tools such as pip-tools, Poetry and uv
summary: Declaring and pinning every software library an analysis depends on, so the computational instrument can be rebuilt identically and results do not drift between runs.
description: In computational research the software is part of the instrument. Statistical and machine learning libraries change defaults between versions (for example a change in a clustering initialisation or a factor rotation algorithm), which can change results without any change in data. Dependency management records direct dependencies in a specification file and resolves them into a lockfile that pins every transitive package to an exact version and hash. Rigour comes from separating the human-edited specification from the machine-generated lock, updating dependencies deliberately rather than incidentally, and rerunning key analyses after any upgrade to check that results are stable. For models such as Whisper or spaCy pipelines, the model version and weights must be pinned too.
steps: List direct dependencies with compatible ranges in pyproject.toml or environment.yml.
Generate a lockfile (e.g. pip-compile, poetry lock or uv lock) that pins exact versions and hashes, and commit it.
Pin model artefacts separately by name and version (e.g. en_core_web_trf 3.7.x, Whisper large-v3) and record checksums.
Set random seeds and record them alongside library versions for any stochastic method (UMAP, GMM, LDA, bootstrap).
Upgrade dependencies on a branch, rerun the full analysis and compare key outputs before merging.
Record the full environment (pip freeze or conda env export) in the report appendix.
outputs: A specification file, a lockfile, pinned model versions, seed records and an environment appendix for reports.
useWhen: Any analysis using statistical, NLP, machine learning or transcription libraries, and any analysis that will be rerun over time.
avoidWhen: Not needed for GUI-only analysis; document the SPSS or tool version and saved syntax instead.
whyLost: UX research rarely treated software as part of the research instrument, so version drift was never recognised as a validity threat.
whereToUse: Tracking studies, computational qualitative pipelines, AI-assisted coding, and causal or survey modelling in Python.
example: An e-commerce team's quarterly topic model suddenly reports a new 'delivery' theme. Comparing lockfiles shows a library upgrade changed tokenisation, and pinning the earlier version confirms the theme was an artefact.
sources: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology 13(6)

name: Dependency parsing for quote extraction
origin: Dependency grammar, Lucien Tesnière, 1959; statistical dependency parsing (Nivre, 2003 and later); spaCy parser
summary: Using sentence grammar to find statements with specific structures, such as first-person evaluations of features or negated intentions, and extract them as candidate quotes.
description: A dependency parser links each word to its grammatical head (subject, object, modifier, negation). This lets a researcher search for structures rather than keywords: sentences where 'I' is the subject of an evaluative verb whose object is a product feature, statements with negated modal verbs ('I wouldn't trust'), or comparisons ('better than'). spaCy's DependencyMatcher implements these patterns. Compared with keyword search, structural matching captures who did what to what and handles negation properly. Rigour comes from testing patterns on annotated samples, measuring precision of extracted quotes, and always presenting extractions as candidates that analysts verify in context.
steps: Define the statement types you need (e.g. first-person evaluations, negated intentions, comparisons, requests).
Inspect example sentences with displacy to see their dependency structures.
Write DependencyMatcher patterns for each statement type, including negation handling.
Run patterns on 200 or more held-out sentences and measure precision (aim for 0.80 or above) and estimated recall.
Extract matches with speaker, transcript ID and timestamp, and surrounding context of 1-2 sentences.
Have an analyst verify each candidate quote against its context before it enters a report.
outputs: A library of structural patterns, a table of candidate quotes with context and provenance, and precision estimates.
useWhen: Mining large interview or feedback corpora for specific statement types, such as evaluations, intentions or comparisons, at scale.
avoidWhen: Avoid with disfluent, fragmentary transcripts where parse accuracy drops, and for nuanced meaning that needs interpretive reading.
whyLost: Syntactic analysis is a computational linguistics technique and remained there; UX teams use keyword search or manual tagging.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer programmes, large interview repositories, competitor comparison mining and AI trust research.
example: An AI assistant team extracts all first-person negated-trust statements ('I don't trust it to...') from 400 interviews. The 180 candidates reveal trust concerns cluster around calendar actions and email sending.
sources: Tesnière, L. (1959) Éléments de syntaxe structurale
Nivre, J. (2008) Algorithms for deterministic incremental dependency parsing. Computational Linguistics
Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft
The Inquiry Series, C10 — spaCy — Building NLP Pipelines for Qualitative Research
reference: Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft, chapter on dependency parsing

name: Depth-of-processing orienting tasks
aka: Depth-of-processing orienting questions and the self-reference effect
origin: Craik and Lockhart, 1972; Craik and Tulving, 1975; Rogers, Kuiper and Kirker, 1977
summary: Each item comes with a question forcing physical, sound-based, semantic or self-referential processing, followed by a surprise memory test that shows how processing type affects retention.
description: Words are shown one at a time, each preceded by a question that forces a given depth of processing: physical (is it in capital letters?), phonemic (does it rhyme with 'pain'?) or semantic (does it fit 'He saw a ___ on the street'?). An unexpected memory test follows. Recall rises from physical to phonemic to semantic questions. Self-referential questions ('does this describe you?') produce the highest recall, and survival-scenario processing also helps. The test must be incidental, so participants do not deliberately memorise. Transfer-appropriate processing qualifies the result: deep processing wins only when the test also taps meaning, so depth is not an absolute property. The design lets teams test whether an interaction makes people process content in a way that supports later recall.
steps: Select items (words, product facts, safety messages) and write orienting questions at each level: physical, phonemic, semantic and self-referential.
Assign items to question types, counterbalancing across participants.
Present each question then the item, and record the yes or no answer.
Give an unexpected recall or recognition test after a filler task.
Compare memory by question type.
Optionally add a test that matches shallow processing (for example rhyme recognition) to check transfer-appropriate effects.
outputs: Recall or recognition rates by orienting condition, and evidence of whether self-reference or semantic processing improves retention.
useWhen: Designing onboarding, learning content, safety messages or consent flows where later recall matters and different interaction prompts can be compared.
avoidWhen: Avoid if participants know a memory test is coming, and do not assume 'deeper' always wins; for overall learning outcomes use a pre-post knowledge test.
whyLost: Levels of processing is a well-known theory, but its orienting-task procedure is rarely used to evaluate interface prompts.
whereToUse: Edtech, onboarding tutorials, security and privacy notices, health instructions, financial disclosures.
example: A pension app compares three ways of presenting fee information: plain text, a quiz on wording, and a prompt asking how the fee affects 'your' retirement. A surprise recall test a week later favours the self-referential prompt.
sources: Craik, F. I. M., & Tulving, E. (1975). Depth of processing and the retention of words in episodic memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104
reference: Craik, F. I. M., & Tulving, E. (1975). Depth of processing and the retention of words in episodic memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104, 268-294.

name: Descriptive Experience Sampling
origin: Russell T. Hurlburt, 1970s onwards (formalised 1990s)
summary: Random beeps prompt participants to note their inner experience at that moment; expositional interviews within 24 hours then build faithful descriptions of pristine inner experience.
description: Descriptive Experience Sampling (Russell Hurlburt, 1990s) is a rigorous method for studying naturally-occurring inner experience. Participants carry a random beeper in their natural environments. When the beep sounds, they freeze and capture exactly what was happening in their awareness at the moment of the beep — inner speech, visual imagery, sensory awareness, emotional feeling, unsymbolised thinking — and report it in a subsequent expositional interview. DES is explicitly designed to study pristine inner experience — the naturally occurring phenomena of consciousness before they are distorted by retrospective reconstruction, self-presentation, or theory. A recurring finding: people's preconceptions about their inner experience (as measured by questionnaires) frequently diverge from their actual inner experience as captured by DES.
steps: Equipment and setup: Participants carry a random beeper (or smartphone with randomised notification app) during normal daily activities for several days. The beeper sounds at unpredictable intervals averaging 30–90 minutes.

At each beep: Participants immediately pause and attend to whatever was happening in their awareness at the instant of the beep — not what happened after the beep. They jot brief notes before memory fades.

Expositional interview: Within 24 hours of each sampling day, meet with the participant and explore each sampled moment together. The interviewer's goal is to help the participant describe the experience faithfully — not interpret it, explain it, or fit it to categories. The joint interview is an exploration, not an elicitation.

Discipline of apprehension: Rigorously distinguish what was in the participant's awareness at the sampled moment from: (a) what happened immediately after, (b) what the participant believes typically happens, (c) what makes narrative sense.

Idiographic first, nomothetic second: Build a faithful description of this individual's inner experience. Only after multiple sessions of high-quality individual description aggregate across individuals to identify group patterns.
outputs: Beep-by-beep descriptions of inner experience, frequencies of forms such as inner speech, images and feelings, and an idiographic profile of each participant's experience.
useWhen: You need to understand what is actually in people's minds during everyday use, such as attention, inner speech or feelings when notifications arrive, rather than their generalised beliefs about it.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural or attitudinal data at scale; use ecological momentary assessment or diary studies. Avoid if you cannot run skilled expositional interviews within a day.
whyLost: It requires extensive interviewer training and is slow, and UX adopted lighter experience sampling (EMA) that asks fixed questions rather than describing pristine experience.
whereToUse: Attention and notification design, wellbeing and mental-health apps, media and content consumption, voice and ambient interfaces, and research on distraction.
example: A focus app team runs DES with 6 participants for 4 days. Beep descriptions show that during 'focus mode' people often experience inner speech rehearsing unread messages, prompting a feature that summarises pending messages before focus starts.
sources: Descriptive Experience Sampling (Hurlburt & Akhter, Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 2006)
Describing Inner Experience? (Hurlburt & Schwitzgebel, MIT Press)
reference: Hurlburt, R. T. & Akhter, S. A. (2006). The Descriptive Experience Sampling method. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 5, 271-301.

name: Descriptive phenomenology (Giorgi)
origin: Amedeo Giorgi, Duquesne University, 1970 onwards
summary: A rigorous, bracketed analysis of first-person descriptions that breaks them into meaning units, transforms them into psychological language and derives the essential structure of a type of experience.
description: Amedeo Giorgi's Descriptive Phenomenological Psychological Method (Duquesne tradition) is a rigorous empirical approach to studying the structure of experience. Unlike IPA (which is interpretive and hermeneutic), Giorgi's method is explicitly descriptive — the goal is to bracket all theoretical frameworks and describe the invariant psychological structure of the phenomenon as it appears in participants' accounts. It is stricter than most phenomenological methods in its demand for epoché (suspension of prior knowledge) and its focus on the psychological dimension of experience specifically.
steps: Data collection: Written descriptions or semi-structured interviews. Participants describe a specific experience of the phenomenon as completely as possible. The researcher asks minimal questions — only to prompt further description if the account is too brief.
Reading for sense of the whole: Read the entire description to get a general sense before any analysis.
Discrimination of meaning units: Re-read the description slowly. Wherever a shift in meaning is detected, mark it. These are meaning units — not syntactically defined, but phenomenologically defined.

Transformation into psychologically sensitive language: Transform each meaning unit from the participant's everyday language into psychological language that makes the psychological meaning explicit. This transformation stays close to what the participant said — it does not interpret beyond what is given.

Synthesis of the essential structure: From all transformed meaning units, identify the essential (invariant) features — those that must be present for the experience to be what it is. Write a synthesis describing the essential psychological structure.
outputs: Meaning units, psychologically transformed statements, a general structure of the experience with its constituents, and illustrative variations.
useWhen: You want to describe the essential structure of a type of experience, such as feeling deceived by a product, waiting for test results or trusting an automated decision, as a foundation for design principles.
avoidWhen: You want interpretive, contextual or political accounts (use IPA or Critical Discourse Analysis) or tactical usability findings (use usability testing).
whyLost: Phenomenology reached UX mainly as a loose synonym for 'lived experience', and Giorgi's detailed procedures stayed in psychology and nursing research.
whereToUse: Health experiences, trust and betrayal in digital services, waiting and uncertainty in fintech and logistics, grief and legacy products, and AI interaction experiences.
example: Analysing 10 written descriptions of 'waiting for a loan decision', a researcher derives an essential structure in which uncertainty is felt as loss of agency. Design principles focus on giving users meaningful actions during the wait.
sources: Phenomenological Method in Qualitative Psychology and Psychiatry (PMC 2016)
Five Ways of Doing Qualitative Analysis (Wertz et al.)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Giorgi, A. (2009). The Descriptive Phenomenological Method in Psychology. Duquesne University Press.

name: Design Bakeoff
origin: Consulting practice described by Bill Albert and Tom Tullis
summary: Several teams build semi-functional alternatives; participants use them in a counterbalanced design and the designs are compared on issues, ratings and forced-choice preference.
description: Early in a project, rival design directions are best settled with evidence. In a design bakeoff, two or more teams build semi-functional prototypes of alternatives for the same tasks. With a large sample, a between-subjects design can compare them directly. More often each participant works mainly with one primary design, counterbalanced across participants, and is then shown the other designs briefly and asked for a forced-choice preference and ratings. Results compare the number and severity of issues found per design together with preference shares and ratings. Because the primary design receives far more use, conclusions about briefly seen designs must be cautious, and small samples support issue comparisons better than statistical preference claims. A common outcome is merging the best elements rather than choosing one design wholesale.
steps: Have two or more teams build semi-functional prototypes of alternative designs for the same core tasks.
Choose between-subjects comparison if the sample is large; otherwise assign each participant one primary design, counterbalancing which design is primary.
Run the core tasks on the primary design, recording issues and their severity.
Show the other designs briefly and ask for a forced-choice preference and ratings of each.
Compare issue frequency and severity by design, preference counts and mean ratings, with confidence intervals where samples allow.
Decide which design, or which elements of each, to carry forward.
outputs: Issue counts by severity per design, preference shares, mean ratings and a recommendation on what to carry forward.
useWhen: Choosing among competing design directions early, settling team disputes with evidence, and design sprints that produce parallel concepts.
avoidWhen: When designs differ only in small details (use A/B Testing on live traffic) or when prototypes are at very different fidelity, which biases results.
whyLost: The practice continues as comparative usability or preference testing, but the counterbalanced structure and the term have faded.
whereToUse: Navigation and IA concepts, onboarding variants, dashboard layouts and early AI interaction patterns.
example: Three teams build navigation concepts for a SaaS analytics tool. Each concept is primary for a third of 18 participants, and the team merges the winning search pattern with another concept's menu structure.
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022) Measuring the User Experience: Collecting, Analyzing, and Presenting UX Metrics, 3rd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, p. 60.

name: Design Critique
aka: Six Thinking Hats as lens-based critique
I like, I have questions, I'd suggest
origin: Studio critique tradition; Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process; ritual dissent (Snowden, Cognitive Edge); Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry (2015); Edward de Bono's Six Thinking Hats; Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic (2015, 2020)
summary: A structured, facilitated conversation that analyses work in progress against agreed objectives, producing observations and actions rather than reactions or a change list.
description: Connor and Irizarry distinguish three kinds of feedback: reaction, direction and critique. Only critique, which names an element, relates it to an objective or best practice and explains why it does or does not support it, helps a team iterate. Four questions form a critique: what is the objective, which elements relate to it, are they effective, why or why not. Sessions are scoped and prepared, run under four rules (everyone is equal, everyone is a critic, no problem solving, no rushed decisions), and facilitated with round robins, quotas, direct inquiry and public notes. Other formats change the structure: Lerman's Critical Response Process puts meaning first and opinions only with permission; ritual dissent has a presenter turn away while a panel attacks the idea; Six Thinking Hats has everyone use one lens at a time. Knaflic's fresh-eyes feedback applies the same discipline to charts and decks: a reviewer thinks aloud while the author listens without defending.
steps: Agree the foundation: personas, scenarios, goals and principles the work must serve.
Choose about six or fewer cross-functional participants and define the scope (components and objectives) and the decisions needed afterwards.
Send designs, focus notes and rules a couple of days ahead rather than revealing work in the session.
Open by restating rules and objectives; present briefly from the user's perspective.

Have participants critique with the four questions, using round robin, quotas or a single shared lens (a thinking hat or persona) at a time; one person takes public notes and problem solving is parked.
For charts or readouts, have a reviewer think aloud about where their eyes go first and what the main message is, then recall it after it is put away.
Within a day share notes, sort feedback into accept, reject or consider, reframe notes as actions with owners, and record what will not be addressed and why.
outputs: Observations on which elements support or undermine objectives, a prioritised action list, open questions and assumptions, and items deliberately not addressed.
useWhen: Use regularly during design and before readouts, when a team needs useful feedback from colleagues and stakeholders on whether work meets agreed objectives.
avoidWhen: Avoid using critique to learn whether users can use the design: run Usability Testing or a Cognitive Walkthrough. Do not confuse it with approval (design review) or with problem solving, and do not run it so often it stalls progress. Colleagues are not the audience.
whyLost: It survived because studio education carries it into practice and every design team needs a feedback ritual; structured formats spread as unstructured crits proved personal and unproductive.
whereToUse: Any design team cadence, design systems governance, research readout preparation, distributed teams with asynchronous critique.
example: An insurer's team scopes a critique of a claim photo-upload screen to the objective 'users submit usable photos first time'. Critics note the guidance text sits below the camera button and is missed; the team moves it before the next usability study.
reference: Connor, A. and Irizarry, A. (2015). Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Design Document / RFC
aka: Design document / RFC (request for comments) with template and review
origin: Engineering practice with no single originator; described by Tanya Reilly (2022)
summary: Write a short structured proposal (context, goals, design, security and privacy, alternatives) and circulate it for comment before building, using a template and a pitfalls checklist.
description: Many people cannot share an understanding of a feature, product plan, API or process until it is written down. A design document, often called an RFC, does this before work starts. Reilly's minimum headings are context (title, author, dates, status), goals stated without implementation detail, the design in enough detail to judge whether it will work (diagrams, data models, wireframes, process steps), security, privacy and compliance, and alternatives considered including prior art and in-house options. Optional sections cover background, trade-offs, risks, dependencies and operations. Authors self-check against pitfalls such as 'every user just needs to', postponing the hard part, or a disguised rewrite, and write concretely: being wrong is better than being vague. Reviewers match depth to the stage, explain their reasoning, label importance and ask whether the work should exist at all, whether it solves the problem and whether it fails safely.
steps: Use the organisation's template if one exists; otherwise include the minimum headings.
Context: title, author, created and updated dates, and status (idea, open for review, superseded, implementing, done, on hold).
Goals: the problem or opportunity and why it matters, with no implementation detail.
Design: how the goal will be met, with whatever readers need (flows, wireframes, diagrams, data models, dependencies, costs).
Security, privacy and compliance: what needs protecting and what user data is touched, or why the section does not apply.
Alternatives and prior art, including off-the-shelf and in-house options; send the document to owners of any in-house option not chosen.
Self-check against the pitfalls list, then circulate for comment with a deadline; reviewers label the importance of each comment.
Record decisions and update the status as work proceeds.
outputs: A reviewed, dated design document recording goals, design and alternatives, with reviewer comments and decisions.
useWhen: Use before building anything that crosses team boundaries or is costly to reverse, including design system changes, new interaction patterns and service flows.
avoidWhen: Avoid turning it into a heavyweight approval gate. Its 'every user just needs to' assumptions need checking with users through Usability Testing or Cognitive Walkthrough; for recording the reasoning behind design options use Design Rationale (QOC and IBIS).
whyLost: It survived because asynchronous written review scales across distributed teams and leaves a record of decisions.
whereToUse: Engineering-led product teams, design system governance, platform changes, cross-team service design.
example: A designer writes an RFC proposing a new date-picker pattern for the design system, listing three alternatives and accessibility implications. Reviewers from two product teams flag a keyboard-entry case, which is fixed before any component is built.
reference: Reilly, T. (2022). The Staff Engineer's Path: A Guide for Individual Contributors Navigating Growth and Change. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 174-183, 265-271.

name: Design Drawing as Research
aka: Sketching to examine, explore and explain
origin: Design practice; Andrew Causey, Drawn to See: Drawing as an Ethnographic Method (2016)
summary: Using drawing in three ways: to examine settings in the field, to explore many design variants quickly, and to explain ideas through concept sketches and storyboards.
description: Drawing is so familiar in design that it is rarely recognised as a method. Universal Methods of Design separates three uses. Drawing to examine means sketching settings, artefacts and interactions in the field; because the hand must render what the eye sees, it forces closer attention than photography and reveals layout, flow and use. Drawing to explore means iterative sketching of many variants as the cheapest form of prototyping. Drawing to explain means concept sketches, storyboards and technical drawings that communicate ideas and invite feedback. Annotation turns each sketch into a record of reasoning. Skill anxiety is the main obstacle: stick figures suffice. Drawing is selective, so what is left out is as telling as what is drawn.
steps: Decide whether you are drawing to examine, explore or explain.
To examine, sketch the setting, artefacts and movements in the field, timing short observation periods (for example 10 minutes per sketch).
To explore, sketch many variants quickly, aiming for quantity before refinement.
Annotate sketches with observations, questions and reasoning.
To explain, produce concept sketches or storyboards and share them for feedback.
outputs: Field sketches, variant sketches, and concept sketches or storyboards with annotations.
useWhen: Use when observation needs closer attention than a camera gives (spatial layouts, workstations, flows of people), and throughout early design for fast exploration and explanation.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on sketches as the only field record when detail matters: combine with Structured Observation or Behavioural Mapping. When the aim is to test ideas with users, move to Prototype Testing.
whyLost: Sketching survives as ideation, but drawing as a field method has been largely displaced by phone photography and video, losing the attention it once forced.
whereToUse: Hospital and workplace observation, retail and spatial design, early concept work in any product.
example: A researcher sketches a ward nurses' station across three shifts and notices nurses repeatedly walk past the screen to reach the medication cart, which leads to a proposal for a mobile medication checklist.
sources: Causey, A. (2016). Drawn to See: Drawing as an Ethnographic Method. Toronto: University of Toronto Press.
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Causey, A. (2016). Drawn to See: Drawing as an Ethnographic Method. Toronto: University of Toronto Press.

name: Design Effects and Design-Based Analysis of Complex Samples
origin: Leslie Kish, Survey Sampling (1965); European Social Survey sampling practice
summary: Planning sample sizes with design effects for weighting and clustering, then analysing data with strata, clusters and weights declared so standard errors are correct.
description: Clustering and unequal weights make a sample less informative than its nominal size. The design effect (Deff) quantifies this: the weighting component Deffp comes from variation in selection probabilities, and the clustering component is Deffc = 1 + (b - 1) x rho, where b is mean cluster size and rho the intraclass correlation. Their product gives the overall Deff, and the nominal sample needed is the effective sample size multiplied by Deff. The European Social Survey plans equal effective sample sizes across countries this way, with Deffp typically 1.20 to 1.25. At analysis, the design is declared to software (strata, clusters, weights) and standard errors come from Taylor linearisation or replicate weights (jackknife, balanced repeated replication, bootstrap). Subgroups are analysed with subpopulation options rather than by deleting cases. Ignoring the design understates standard errors and overstates significance.
steps: Estimate the weighting design effect from expected variation in selection probabilities or weights.
Estimate the clustering design effect as 1 + (b - 1) x rho from mean cluster size b and an intraclass correlation rho from prior data.
Multiply to get the overall Deff and set the nominal sample size as effective sample size times Deff.
Prefer more clusters (for example more accounts or sites) over larger clusters when budgets allow.
At analysis, declare strata, clusters and weights in survey software (R survey, Stata svy).
Estimate standard errors with Taylor linearisation or replicate weights.
Analyse subgroups with subpopulation options instead of subsetting the data.
outputs: A sample size plan expressed as effective n, and estimates with design-correct standard errors and confidence intervals.
useWhen: Surveys that sample several users per account, organisation, school or site, weighted surveys, and any analysis where respondents are clustered.
avoidWhen: Simple random samples of independent users without weights, where ordinary formulas apply. For regression on clustered behavioural data, cluster-robust standard errors may be simpler.
whyLost: UX analysts compute confidence intervals with textbook formulas that assume independent observations; design-based analysis is taught only in survey statistics.
whereToUse: B2B surveys with many respondents per account, education and health products sampled by institution, weighted trackers.
example: A B2B collaboration tool surveys 1,200 users from 60 customer accounts. With mean cluster size 20 and rho 0.08 the clustering Deff is 2.5, so the effective sample is about 480; declaring accounts as clusters widens the satisfaction difference interval enough that a planned 'win' is reported as inconclusive.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Beyond t Test and ANOVA (Yu et al., 2022)
reference: Gabler, S. and Häder, S. (2016). Special challenges of sampling for comparative surveys; and Eckman, S. and West, B. T. (2016). Analysis of data from stratified and clustered surveys. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology. London: SAGE.

name: Design fixation example-exposure test
donor: Cognitive psychology of creativity; design research
origin: Jansson and Smith, 1991; Smith, Ward and Schumacher, 1993
summary: One group sees example designs before generating ideas and a control group does not; copied example features in the outputs measure how much examples constrain ideation.
description: Participants invent, sketch, label and describe new things, such as toys or imaginary creatures. One group first sees three examples that share features (in the classic study, creatures that all had four legs, antennae and a tail); a control group sees none. The example group's designs include those features far more often, showing that examples narrow idea generation, a creative form of functional fixedness. In design research the same logic was used with engineers shown a flawed example design, who reproduced its flaws. The test is simple and controlled: the dependent measure is the proportion of outputs containing example features, scored by raters blind to condition, with originality and quality scored separately.
steps: Define a design brief and prepare two or three examples that share distinctive features.
Randomly assign participants or teams to see the examples or no examples (optionally add an instruction to avoid the example features).
Give a fixed time to generate and sketch ideas.
Code each output for the presence of example features, with two raters blind to condition.
Score originality and quality separately from conformity.
Compare the proportion of example features across conditions.
outputs: Proportion of designs containing example features by condition, plus separate originality and quality scores.
useWhen: Deciding when to show competitor screens, templates, mood boards or AI-generated concepts in workshops and design sprints.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating conformity as failure in itself; examples can raise quality. For measuring idea quantity and variety use divergent thinking tests.
whyLost: Design fixation is studied in engineering design research but rarely tested inside UX teams' own ideation practice.
whereToUse: Design sprints, ideation workshops, generative AI design tools, design education.
example: Two sprint teams ideate a new onboarding flow; one first reviews three competitor flows. Ten of twelve of its concepts reuse the competitors' carousel pattern, against two of twelve in the other team, so references are moved after first-round ideation.
sources: Jansson, D. G., & Smith, S. M. (1991). Design fixation. Design Studies, 12
reference: Smith, S. M., Ward, T. B., & Schumacher, J. S. (1993). Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task. Memory & Cognition, 21, 837-845.

name: Design Games (Scandinavian PD)
origin: Pelle Ehn and Morten Kyng (1980s); Ehn and Sjögren (1991); Brandt (2006)
summary: Structured, rule-based games with cards and boards that let users and designers jointly explore work and design options using a shared vocabulary.
description: Design games are among the Scandinavian methods the treatise lists for equalising power between designers and users. Grounded in Ehn's reading of Wittgenstein, design is seen as participation in 'language games': users and designers need shared, tangible means of expression. Games provide rules, game pieces (cards representing tasks, actors, tools or events) and boards (workflows, maps) so participants can articulate current practice and explore alternatives. Examples include the Specification Game, organisational kit games and later Brandt's exploratory design games. The game format makes participation less dependent on verbal fluency and technical knowledge and keeps the conversation anchored to concrete situations.
steps: Define the game's purpose (understanding practice, exploring scenarios, specifying requirements).
Design game materials: cards for actors, tasks, tools and events, and a board representing work or space.
Write simple rules that structure turns and move from current to future practice.
Play with mixed groups of users and designers, documenting moves and discussions.
Debrief to capture insights, disagreements and design options.
Translate outcomes into scenarios, requirements or prototypes.
outputs: Game boards and records of play, shared vocabulary, scenarios and requirements.
useWhen: Engaging users with limited technical or verbal confidence; complex organisational redesign.
avoidWhen: When participants need detailed interface critique; use paper prototyping.
whyLost: Commercial co-design adopted lighter ideation templates; the theory and game design craft stayed academic.
whereToUse: Organisational change programmes, care services, factory digitalisation, community planning.
example: Home-care workers play a card game mapping a typical shift with cards for visits, travel and paperwork; the board reveals documentation clusters at the end of shifts, leading to voice notes between visits.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Ehn P & Sjögren D (1991) From system descriptions to scripts for action. In Design at Work
Brandt E (2006) Designing exploratory design games. PDC
Muller MJ (1991) PICTIVE: an exploration in participatory design. CHI
reference: Brandt E (2006) Designing exploratory design games: a framework for participation in participatory design? Proceedings of PDC 2006:57-66.

name: Design Literacy Inoculation (UX Vaccination)
origin: William McGuire (1961); applied to misinformation by van der Linden and Roozenbeek; to UX by the treatise
summary: Confers resistance to manipulative patterns by pre-exposing users to weakened examples and explanations, evaluated by population-level susceptibility.
description: The treatise frames digital design literacy as a vaccine: knowledge and skills that let users recognise and resist manipulative patterns without being harmed first. Inoculation theory (McGuire) holds that exposure to a weakened form of a persuasive attack, with refutation, builds resistance; recent work applies it to misinformation through prebunking games and videos. A UX vaccination programme would identify the highest-morbidity dark patterns, develop inoculation materials explaining how they work and how to spot them, deploy them through education, consumer organisations and literacy programmes, and evaluate effectiveness through population susceptibility measures. Research shows users aware of specific patterns resist them substantially better. Evaluation needs randomised designs and follow-up for decay of immunity ('booster' needs).
steps: Select high-burden patterns using morbidity and prevalence data.
Develop inoculation materials: forewarning, weakened example, refutation and recognition cues.
Test in a randomised experiment measuring susceptibility (for example falling for a simulated pattern).
Measure decay of effect at follow-up (for example 1 and 3 months).
Deploy through schools, consumer bodies and in-product education.
Monitor population susceptibility and add boosters.
outputs: Inoculation materials, efficacy and durability estimates, deployment plan.
useWhen: Where design fixes are slow or impossible ecosystem-wide and user protection is needed now.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for fixing harmful patterns you control; shifting burden to users is not a remedy.
whyLost: Inoculation research stayed in persuasion and misinformation fields; UX focuses on design, not user resistance.
whereToUse: Consumer education, banking scam awareness, older adult programmes, schools, browser and OS onboarding.
example: A randomised trial of a 3-minute 'spot the fake countdown' game reduces later purchases under fake urgency by 25%, with half the effect remaining at three months.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
McGuire WJ (1961) Resistance to persuasion conferred by active and passive prior refutation. J Abnorm Soc Psychol
Roozenbeek J & van der Linden S (2019) Fake news game confers psychological resistance against online misinformation. Palgrave Communications
Bongard-Blanchy K et al. (2021) 'I am definitely manipulated, even when I am aware of it'. DIS
reference: McGuire WJ (1961) Resistance to persuasion conferred by active and passive prior refutation of the same and alternative counterarguments. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 63(2):326-332.

name: Design prescription binding protocol
donor: Original framework drawing on evidence-based medicine and requirements traceability
origin: Vivek Gopinath, The Inquiry Series (research communication chapter)
summary: A protocol that binds each design recommendation to its evidence, expected effect, success metric and validation plan, so prescriptions are accountable and testable.
description: Research recommendations often lose their link to evidence once handed over, and design changes ship without any check that they worked. The binding protocol formalises each prescription as a record: the problem, the evidence (with source and confidence), the specific design change, the mechanism expected, the metric that should move and by how much, guardrails, the validation method and the owner. Borrowing from evidence-based medicine's link between diagnosis, treatment and outcome measures, and from requirements traceability, it makes prescriptions falsifiable. Rigour comes from requiring every field before acceptance, quantified expected effects, pre-registered validation, and closing the loop by recording observed outcomes.
steps: For each recommendation, record the problem statement and the evidence supporting it, with sources and confidence.
Specify the design prescription precisely enough to be implemented and tested.
State the expected mechanism and a quantified expected effect on a named metric (e.g. +3 points completion within 30 days).
Define guardrail metrics and the validation method (A/B test, quasi-experiment, follow-up usability study).
Assign an owner and review date, and have product and design leads sign off the binding.
After launch, record observed results against the expected effect and update the evidence base.
outputs: A binding record per prescription with evidence, expected effects, validation plans, ownership and recorded outcomes.
useWhen: When research outputs must become accountable design changes, especially in high-stakes or regulated products.
avoidWhen: Avoid for exploratory concept work with no definite prescriptions, or for trivial changes where the overhead outweighs the value.
whyLost: It is an original framework rather than a lost method, formalising the traceability that research handovers usually lack.
whereToUse: Fintech and health product teams, design systems governance, research ops quality processes, board-level research programmes.
example: Following a trust study, the team binds the prescription 'show settlement timing on the confirmation screen' to interview evidence, an expected 20% drop in status-query tickets and an A/B validation. Results show a 17% drop, confirming the mechanism.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief

name: Design Rationale (QOC and IBIS)
origin: IBIS by Werner Kunz and Horst Rittel (1970); QOC by Allan MacLean, Richard Young, Victoria Bellotti and Thomas Moran (1991); dialogue mapping by Jeff Conklin (2005)
summary: Explicitly records design questions, alternative options, evaluation criteria and arguments, making the reasons behind design decisions inspectable and reusable.
description: Rittel created IBIS to structure deliberation on wicked problems: issues (questions), positions (responses) and arguments (pros and cons). MacLean and colleagues proposed QOC for design space analysis: questions identify key design issues, options are possible answers, and criteria are the bases for evaluating options, with assessments linking options to criteria. Recording rationale makes alternatives and trade-offs explicit, supports new team members, and prevents re-litigating decisions. It lost favour because capturing rationale felt costly, yet modern teams repeatedly lose the reasoning behind design choices. Lightweight QOC or IBIS maps (e.g. in decision records) restore it, and research findings can be linked directly as criteria evidence.
steps: Identify key design questions during design reviews or research synthesis.
Record options for each question, including rejected ones.
State criteria explicitly, ideally linked to user research and business goals.
Assess each option against criteria (positive or negative links) with evidence references.
Record the decision and its justification, and link to related questions.
Maintain the rationale map in a shared repository and revisit when criteria or evidence change.
outputs: QOC or IBIS maps linking questions, options, criteria and evidence; decision records.
useWhen: Complex, long-lived products with recurring design debates, team turnover or regulatory documentation needs.
avoidWhen: Throwaway prototypes or trivial decisions.
whyLost: Rationale capture was seen as overhead in fast-paced design; tools were clunky.
whereToUse: Design systems, medical device design history files, platform architecture, AI policy decisions.
example: A design system team uses QOC for 'how should destructive actions be confirmed?', documenting options (modal, undo, typed confirmation) and criteria (error rate, speed, accessibility) with test evidence; the record ends a recurring debate.
sources: MacLean, Young, Bellotti & Moran, Questions, options, and criteria: Elements of design space analysis (1991), Human-Computer Interaction
Kunz & Rittel, Issues as Elements of Information Systems (1970), Working Paper 131, UC Berkeley
Conklin, Dialogue Mapping: Building Shared Understanding of Wicked Problems (2005)
reference: MacLean, A., Young, R. M., Bellotti, V. M. E., & Moran, T. P. (1991). Human-Computer Interaction, 6(3-4), 201-250.

name: Design Review Stakeholder Handling
origin: Tom Greever (2015)
summary: A set of routines for design reviews: predict and rehearse stakeholder objections, answer feedback with a structured IDEAL response, and record decisions with notes and a fast follow-up.
description: Greever treats stakeholder meetings as a design problem. Before the review, remove known distractions (placeholder content, disliked legacy elements), note what each attendee cares about and has objected to before, write expected objections by screen with planned responses, prepare alternatives and data held in reserve, brief allies openly, and rehearse aloud. During the meeting, answer feedback by thanking, repeating the point back and preparing the listener, then giving an IDEAL response: Identify the problem, Describe the solution, Empathise with the user through one concrete story, Appeal to the business ('this design will affect this goal because'), Lock in agreement by asking directly. Tactics include side-by-side comparison and exposing trade-offs. A note-taker records who suggested and agreed to what, marks decisions as final or uncertain and assigns owners; a recap goes out within an hour, creating a decision record.
steps: Remove distractions known to derail particular attendees, such as placeholder text and rough alignment.
For each attendee note goals, likes, dislikes and past reactions; write expected objections by screen with a planned response.
Prepare alternatives (including rejected versions) for side-by-side comparison and supporting data held in reserve.
Brief allies openly, write an agenda and rehearse the meeting aloud with mock questions.
In the meeting, respond to feedback with thank, repeat, prepare, then identify the problem, describe the solution, empathise with the user, appeal to the business and lock in agreement.
Have a colleague take shared notes recording who suggested and agreed to what, with decisions marked final or uncertain and owners assigned.
Within an hour (at most a day) send a recap of decisions, actions with owners and dates, and open questions.
outputs: An agenda, objection list with answers, alternative designs, an agreed decision record and a follow-up email.
useWhen: Use when design decisions are reviewed by executives or clients whose feedback can reverse work, and the team needs decisions made and recorded.
avoidWhen: Avoid using it to settle questions of user behaviour by persuasion: bring evidence from Usability Testing or A/B Testing. Do not recite the response mechanically or cite data you cannot produce.
whyLost: It survives because stakeholder management is a daily need of design teams and Greever's book became a standard reference for it.
whereToUse: Agency and client work, enterprise product reviews, design leadership, regulated products with sign-off chains.
example: Before a checkout review the designer predicts the CFO will ask for the phone-number field back, prepares a side-by-side with completion data, and answers with a user story about abandoned orders, locking in agreement before moving on.
reference: Greever, T. (2015). Articulating Design Decisions: Communicate with Stakeholders, Keep Your Sanity, and Deliver the Best User Experience. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Design Science Research
origin: Hevner, March, Park and Ram (2004); Kuechler and Vaishnavi (2008) for the five phases; Hevner (2007) for the three-cycle view; Peffers et al. (2007) for DSRM
summary: Build and evaluate an artefact in iterative cycles of problem awareness, suggestion, development, evaluation and conclusion, so that the design principles themselves are tested.
description: Design science research treats an artefact as the vehicle for knowledge: the contribution is not only a working system but validated, prescriptive design principles. Kuechler and Vaishnavi's five phases run from awareness of the problem (interviews, literature) through suggestion (design requirements translated into principles, each mapped to requirements), development (instantiating the principles, usually alongside a baseline), evaluation (from light formative checks to controlled comparisons) and conclusion. Hevner's three-cycle view links a relevance cycle with the application context, a rigour cycle with the knowledge base, and a central design cycle. Iteration is explicit: if an interim evaluation shows the problem is understood but the principles need changing, the next cycle restarts at suggestion. In the chatbot example, principles for a context-aware product-configuration bot were refined after an unmoderated test, then compared with a step-by-step baseline, though with only six participants per group.
steps: Problem awareness: interview people close to the problem and review the literature; label and cluster findings into a problem statement.
Suggestion: derive design requirements and translate them into prescriptive design principles, mapping each requirement to the principles that address it.
Development: instantiate the principles in a prototype and build a baseline for comparison.
Evaluation: run an interim light evaluation (for example an unmoderated remote usability test), then a controlled comparison with subjective and log-based measures.
Conclusion: refine the principles; if the problem framing holds but principles need change, restart the next cycle at suggestion.
Report requirements, principles, artefact and evaluation evidence together so the principles can be reused and challenged.
outputs: Design requirements, validated design principles, an instantiated artefact and evaluation evidence across cycles.
useWhen: Research-led product teams or academic-industry projects that need generalisable, evidence-backed design principles from building something, not only a shipped feature.
avoidWhen: Pure discovery with no artefact in view (use field methods); when inquiry through making is more exploratory and principles are not the goal (Research through Design); or when only a feature decision is needed (A/B Testing).
whyLost: It is the dominant design-oriented paradigm in information systems academia, while UX practice runs similar build-test cycles without stating or validating principles.
whereToUse: Conversational agents, decision-support tools, enterprise systems, AI features where reusable principles matter across products.
example: A B2B team derives five principles for a configuration chatbot from sales interviews, builds it with a step-by-step baseline, and finds in an interim test that users need process cues. Cycle two adds them before a controlled comparison.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Hevner, A. R., March, S. T., Park, J., & Ram, S. (2004). Design science in information systems research. MIS Quarterly, 28(1), 75-105; Niederer, T., Schloss, D., & Christensen, N. (2023). Designing context-aware chatbots for product configuration. In Følstad et al. (Eds.), Chatbot Research and Design (LNCS 13815). Springer.

name: Design Studio
donor: Architecture and design education; urban planning
origin: Architecture studio and planning charrettes; adapted to digital design by Todd Zaki Warfel (2009); Jeff White and Jim Unger (credited by Patton); Connor and Irizarry (2015)
summary: A time-boxed workshop in which cross-functional participants sketch alone, present and critique in rounds, and converge on team concepts and open questions.
description: Design studio applies a divergent-convergent structure to group sketching. Participants receive the problem statement, goals, personas and scenarios in advance. Each charrette runs sketch, present, critique: there are at least two and usually three, and the first is always individual. Black markers on 6-up grid paper stop over-detailing; critique addresses fit to the problem and objectives, not liking, and red and green pens mark weak and strong elements. Later rounds iterate towards one concept per person, then one per team. Teams are three to six people, with facilitators holding an agenda and timetable as external authority. Planning charrettes run the same loop over several generations, likened to genetic algorithms. The output is several rough concepts, shared themes and open questions which the design team then synthesises: the studio does not produce the final solution, and someone must still make the call.
steps: Circulate the problem statement, business goals, personas and scenarios in advance; say little about existing solution ideas to avoid anchoring.
Form cross-functional teams of three to six (8-12 people in total works well) and brief the rules and timetable.
Charrette 1: 8 minutes of individual sketching of as many concepts as possible on 6-up paper; 3 minutes to present each; 4-5 minutes of critique against the objectives.
Charrette 2: 8 minutes to iterate into one concept per person, then present and critique again.
Charrette 3: 20 minutes for each team to merge into one concept; present to other teams for 3 minutes and critique for 7.
Discuss common themes; document open questions and assumptions to validate.
Afterwards the design team synthesises a consolidated concept and plans testing.
outputs: Many rough sketches, several team concepts marked for strengths and weaknesses, shared themes, open questions and greater team consensus.
useWhen: Use when a framed problem would benefit from many ideas and broad buy-in, with developers, stakeholders and sometimes users sketching together.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the problem is unframed or framing is not agreed, when the team must stay close to an existing concept, or with unbalanced remote set-ups. Its concepts are untested drafts: follow with Prototype Testing or Usability Testing.
whyLost: It survives because it is fast, inclusive and builds shared ownership; Crazy 8s and sprint sketching are its widespread descendants.
whereToUse: Product sprints, agile teams starting an epic, civic planning, co-design with users and stakeholders.
example: Twelve people from product, engineering and support run three charrettes on a failed-payment screen; the merged concepts all add a retry option and plain-language reasons, which the designer consolidates and tests the next week.
sources: User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
reference: Connor, A. and Irizarry, A. (2015). Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 92-104.

name: Design System and Pattern Library Governance
aka: UI guidelines framework and reusable pattern library governance
donor: Management and organisational practice; front-end design
origin: Lund (2011), from Bell Labs, Ameritech and Microsoft IT; Hogan (2014), with examples from Yelp, Starbucks and Etsy
summary: Document reusable patterns with usage rules and code, apply common requirements to every product, and govern changes so teams reuse consistent, already-optimised assets.
description: Lund sees standards and reuse as the biggest long-term lever on a UX team's productivity. His approach combines a guidelines framework that indexes general guidelines and specific style guides, a pattern framework documenting each pattern with description, supporting code and a sample, common user requirements (accessibility, localisation, responsiveness) that apply to every solution, and a change process letting anyone in engineering file bugs against guidelines and patterns. Standards should grow from successful designs on real projects rather than being written in advance. Hogan adds the front-end view: a living style guide lists colours and when to use them, button and icon classes (including deprecated ones), typography and standard components, each with copyable markup. Her colour normalisation audit collects every colour in the CSS, condenses near-duplicates and assigns each a meaning, which cut one stylesheet by 6%.
steps: Audit existing patterns, for example collecting every colour value, button style and font weight from the codebase.
Condense near-duplicates and assign each kept value or pattern a meaning and usage rule.
Ground the first guidelines and patterns in designs that succeeded on real strategic projects.
Document each pattern with description, usage rules, code sample and implementation notes, and mark deprecated patterns.
Define common user requirements (accessibility, localisation, responsiveness) that every solution must meet.
Open a bug-filing and change process to all design and engineering staff, and connect prototyping tools to the library.
Replace legacy values with normalised ones and keep guidance and training current as the library changes.
outputs: A guidelines index, a pattern library or living style guide with code, common requirements and a change log.
useWhen: Use it when several teams build on the same product or brand and inconsistency, duplicated effort or page weight is growing.
avoidWhen: A library tells you what is consistent, not what works for users; validate patterns with Usability Testing and audit adherence with Guidelines Review and Consistency Inspection. Standards written before real designs tend to be ignored.
whyLost: It thrived and became the modern design system, because reuse saves time, code and page weight at scale.
whereToUse: Multi-product companies, enterprise IT, platform teams, government design systems and e-commerce sites with many contributors.
example: An e-commerce team finds 43 greys in its CSS, condenses them to six with named roles and documents them alongside button classes. A public issue tracker lets product engineers propose changes, and a new checkout uses only library components.
reference: Lund, A. (2011). User Experience Management. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 246-249. Hogan, L. C. (2014). Designing for Performance: Weighing Aesthetics and Speed. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 82-87.

name: Design Thinking
origin: Herbert Simon, 1969; popularised by IDEO and Stanford d.school, 2000s
summary: A human-centred problem-solving process (empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test) that structures cross-functional teams to iterate from user understanding to tested concepts.
description: Design thinking packages designerly ways of working into a teachable process: build empathy with users through research, define a focused problem statement, ideate broadly, prototype quickly and test with users, iterating as learning accumulates. Its roots lie in Simon's view of design as a science of the artificial, Rittel's wicked problems and Rowe's study of designers' reasoning. In its rigorous form it relies on genuine field research, explicit problem framing ('How might we...'), divergent idea generation before convergence, and evidence from tests deciding which concepts proceed. Popularisation has often reduced it to workshop rituals with little research and no testing, which is why critics describe it as theatre. Used properly, it is a framework for sequencing methods and aligning stakeholders rather than a method in itself.
steps: Conduct real user research (interviews, observation) with at least 5-10 people affected by the problem.
Synthesise findings and write a focused problem statement or point-of-view statement grounded in evidence.
Run divergent ideation producing many concepts before any evaluation.
Converge on a small number of concepts using explicit criteria such as desirability, feasibility and viability.
Build low-fidelity prototypes and test them with 5-8 users per round.
Iterate or pivot based on test evidence, documenting what was learnt at each cycle.
outputs: Research synthesis, problem statement, concept set, tested prototypes, learning log.
useWhen: Ill-defined problems needing cross-functional alignment, early innovation and service problems where the solution space is open.
avoidWhen: Well-defined optimisation problems or when stakeholders want a workshop instead of research; use targeted evaluative methods.
whyLost: Widely adopted, but popular practice often strips out the research and testing phases, leaving sticky-note workshops whose 'empathy' is assumed rather than gathered.
whereToUse: Cross-functional innovation; product development; organizational problem-solving.
example: A council redesigning parking permits ran a two-week design thinking sprint with resident interviews, three prototype concepts and testing with 8 residents. The tested concept, automatic renewal by number plate, replaced a planned new web form.
sources: The Sciences of the Artificial (Herbert Simon)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Brown, T. (2008). Design thinking. Harvard Business Review, 86(6), 84-92.

name: Design Walkthrough
origin: Rex Hartson and Pardha Pyla, 2012 (2nd edn 2019)
summary: A leader drives stakeholders and users through scenarios on early sketches or click-through wireframes, narrating the user's story, while a note-taker logs anticipated UX problems.
description: Walkthroughs are informal early sessions on scenarios, storyboards and sketches; design reviews use click-through wireframes and are often the main evaluation of task-level designs late in the design funnel. Preparation matters: the prototype is self-tested for completeness and glitches, user and work role descriptions and driving scenarios are prepared and rehearsed, sessions have fixed start and end times, and roles are assigned (leader, prototype driver, note-taker). In the session the leader tours the main workflows and navigation first, then edge cases, errors and recovery, narrating the user's intentions and context so the group can judge the design from the user's point of view. Participants comment freely and the note-taker logs problems referenced to wireframe numbers. It simulates use rather than observing it, so it is fast but less valid than testing.
steps: Self-test the prototype for completeness and glitches.
Prepare storyboards, user and work role descriptions and driving scenarios, and rehearse the tour.
Schedule users and stakeholders with fixed start and end times and assign leader, prototype driver and note-taker.
Introduce the purpose, users and context.
Tour the main workflows and navigation, then edge cases, errors and recovery, narrating the user's thoughts and situation.
Invite comments and record each problem against its wireframe number.
End on time and feed the problem list into analysis and redesign.
outputs: A UX problem list referenced to screens, and agreed changes.
useWhen: Early design stages when sketches or wireframes need fast feedback from stakeholders and users, and as a late check of task-level designs before build.
avoidWhen: When you need evidence of actual user behaviour; designers drive and narrate, so problems are anticipated rather than observed. Use Usability Testing.
whyLost: It survives as the ubiquitous design review or critique, though the scenario narration, role assignment and problem logging are often skipped.
whereToUse: Agile design reviews, enterprise workflow design with subject-matter experts, and stakeholder sign-off sessions.
example: A claims-processing redesign is walked through with four adjusters using a scenario of a disputed water-damage claim. The note-taker logs eleven anticipated problems, including no path to attach a second assessor's report.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019) The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience, 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, section 25.2.

name: Designer versus Observed Task Model Comparison
aka: Designer versus observed user task model in field evaluation
origin: Tselios and Avouris, in Hollnagel (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
summary: Compare the designer's expected task model with task models inferred from logged field use, annotate errors and unforeseen tasks, and classify deviations to drive redesign.
description: Exploratory software such as open learning environments supports many strategies, so a single expected task flow is a poor yardstick. This method writes down the designer's task model of expected strategies, then reconstructs each real user's task model from keystroke-level logs and video gathered in the field. Observed models are annotated with plan operators and markers for errors, repetitions and tasks the designer never foresaw, and every deviation is classified into one of five categories of unexpected behaviour. Comparing designer and observed models shows where the design's assumptions break, which unforeseen strategies deserve support and which errors are systematic. A prior heuristic evaluation focuses the field study, and the cycle repeats in a spiral of redesign. Its rigour comes from making both models explicit in the same notation, so mismatches are traceable rather than impressionistic.
steps: Write the designer's task model of expected strategies, for example as a hierarchical task model with plan operators.
Run a heuristic evaluation to identify likely problem areas and focus the field study.
Log keystroke-level interaction and record video of users in their real setting.
Infer each user's actual task model from the logs and video, annotating errors, repetitions and unforeseen tasks.
Classify each deviation from the designer's model into the five categories of unexpected behaviour.
Compare designer and observed models, revise the design and repeat the cycle.
outputs: Annotated observed task models, a classification of deviations from the designer's model, and a prioritised redesign list.
useWhen: Open-ended or exploratory tools (learning environments, creative and analytical software) where users take many paths and you need to know which deviations are errors and which are legitimate strategies.
avoidWhen: Linear transactional flows where funnel analysis or Log File Analysis is enough; when you cannot capture fine-grained logs; inference from logs needs tooling and care.
whyLost: Formal task models fell out of everyday UX practice, and analytics replaced hand-built observed models; the comparison step is rarely done explicitly.
whereToUse: Educational software, data-analysis and design tools, AI-assisted workflows where designers assume one way of working.
example: A spreadsheet-modelling course tool assumes students build formulas cell by cell. Reconstructed task models from logs show many copy whole sheets and edit, an unforeseen strategy that causes reference errors, so the team adds a template-duplication feature with reference checks.
reference: Tselios, N. and Avouris, N., in Hollnagel, E. (Ed.) (2003). Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum, pp. 307-331.

name: Desk Research (Secondary and Internal Sources)
origin: UX practice; Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed (2012); Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015); Kalbach (2016)
summary: Before primary research, review the product, past studies, internal teams' data and published sources, consolidating each into evidence, interpretation and implications to set the research agenda.
description: Desk research gathers what is already known so primary research asks better questions. Internally, researchers use the product end to end and log pain points, collect previous research, interview help writers and trainers about what is hard to document or teach, read support logs for recurring problems, ask marketing how and from whom their data were collected, and gather early-adopter feedback while noting its bias. Externally, sources include analyst reports, traffic and demographic panels, reviews and app-store ratings, publications and forums, each read for how it was collected and whom it misses. Kalbach's consolidation format adds rigour: for each source, a table of evidence noted without judgement, possible interpretations, and implications for the person's experience; implications are pooled, grouped by topic, and split into those ready for a draft map and those needing research. It is broader and shallower than primary research and never replaces it.
steps: Define what you need to know and list available internal and external sources.
Use the product end to end, collect previous research reports, and interview writers, trainers, support and marketing staff.
Sample each source, for example a month of support logs, recent reviews, past surveys and analyst reports, splitting sources across the team.
