For each source fill a table of evidence (quotes, data points), interpretation (several possible causes) and implications for the user's experience.
Check how each dataset was collected and whom it misses (for example panels that under-represent locked-down work machines).
Pool implications, group them by topic, and mark which can go into a draft map or profile and which need primary research.
Turn open issues into the agenda for stakeholder interviews and field research, usually within a day or two.
outputs: A briefing on known issues, users and competitors, per-source consolidation tables, grouped implications, and a list of research questions.
useWhen: At the start of any project, before journey mapping or primary research, when entering a new domain, or when budget for primary research is limited.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating secondary data as findings about your users; support and marketing data are filtered, early adopters are unrepresentative, and interpretations are hypotheses. Follow up with primary research.
whyLost: It survives as standard practice, though often done informally without source critique or a consolidation format.
whereToUse: Project kick-offs, journey and service mapping, B2B and specialist domains, competitive analysis.
example: Before mapping a software onboarding journey, a team reviews a month of support emails, app-store reviews and a past survey in one day. Tables show installation abandonment tied to admin rights, which becomes the first question for field interviews.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: Kalbach, J. (2016). Mapping Experiences: A Complete Guide to Creating Value through Journeys, Blueprints, and Diagrams. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 108-111; Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. and Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience (2nd ed.). Waltham, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 405-410.

name: Developing Propositions (Team Proposition Cards)
origin: Stearns, Greene, David and associates, 1980; Kell, 1990; described by Miles and Huberman, 1994
summary: Turn what field researchers know into explicit propositions on cards, sort and condense them, then have each researcher rate every proposition against their own sites.
description: A team procedure for moving from many site visits to a small set of defensible claims. Each field researcher writes every statement they would like to see in the final report on a separate card, adding statements from documents and meetings. Cards are de-duplicated, specific instances are set aside as evidence, and general statements are sorted into assumptions, findings and conclusions under about 30 categories displayed on a wall. Analysts draft propositions; each field researcher then rates every proposition's validity for their own sites, or marks it 'don't know' or 'doesn't apply'. Findings are written only from sites with valid data, and non-fitting cases are re-examined. In Kell's variant propositions are rated per case as strong, qualified, neutral or contradictory and revisited after the next wave of data. The site-level rating is what separates this from an affinity exercise: a proposition must survive case-by-case verification.
steps: Each researcher writes candidate report statements, one per card, plus statements drawn from documents and meetings.
Sort the cards and remove duplicates.
Keep general statements and set specific instances aside as supporting evidence.
Sort into assumptions, findings and conclusions and into topic categories; display on a wall and draft a report outline.
Write a draft list of propositions under each heading.
Have each researcher rate each proposition as strong, qualified, neutral or contradictory for each of their sites, or 'don't know' or 'doesn't apply'.
Write findings per topic only from sites with valid data, re-examine non-fitting cases, and revisit ratings after the next data wave.
outputs: A verified set of propositions with site-by-site ratings and a report outline.
useWhen: Multi-site or multi-researcher qualitative studies where each person holds knowledge of different cases and findings must be traceable to the cases that support them.
avoidWhen: Single-researcher studies of a few participants, where a simpler matrix display suffices. Card volumes grow large (1,500 in the original study), so budget time; without site-level rating the propositions become opinion.
whyLost: UX teams adopted the card-sorting and wall-display half of the procedure as affinity mapping but dropped the explicit case-by-case rating that verifies each claim.
whereToUse: Multi-market discovery studies, research programmes run by several researchers, and synthesis sessions feeding strategy decisions.
example: After 18 retailer site visits by four researchers, the team condenses 600 cards into 25 propositions about point-of-sale adoption. One proposition ('owners delegate setup to staff') is rated contradictory at five sites, so it is rewritten as conditional on store size.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Developmental Range Assessment (Functional vs Optimal Level)
aka: Developmental range: functional versus optimal level assessment
origin: Kurt Fischer and colleagues (Fischer and Bidell; Fischer and Heikkinen, 2010)
summary: Assess the same person with and without contextual support to measure the range between everyday unaided performance and best supported performance on one scale.
description: Dynamic skill theory holds that competence is not a single level but a range. Functional level is what a person does with low support; optimal level is what they reach immediately after high support such as a model, rubric or prime; scaffolded performance with direct help sits higher still. The method plans this contrast as a design: the same task domain, the same person, assessed under graded support and scored on one common complexity scale (in the source, a 13-level scale validated with Rasch scaling). The optimal-functional gap usually exceeds one level, so any single assessment misstates capability. Its rigour comes from the common scale and the planned manipulation of support rather than an incidental comparison. For UX it reframes questions such as 'can users do this?' into 'what can they do alone, and what can they do with an example or guide beside them?'.
steps: Define the task domain and a complexity scoring scale that can be applied to all responses, ideally checked with Rasch or similar scaling.
Assess each participant under low-support conditions to establish the functional level.
Provide high support, such as a worked example, template or rubric, and reassess immediately to establish the optimal level.
Optionally assess again with direct scaffolding from the researcher to obtain a scaffolded ceiling.
Score all responses on the common scale and report the range per person; expect the optimal-functional gap to exceed one level.
Record emotional state and context at each assessment, since both shift the level reached.
outputs: Functional, optimal and scaffolded levels per person and the size of each person's developmental range.
useWhen: You need to know how much in-product support (examples, templates, guided modes) raises what users can achieve, or when evaluating learning tools, onboarding or AI assistance where unaided and aided performance differ.
avoidWhen: You need only a pass/fail usability verdict, or cannot build a credible common complexity scale; emotional shifts between conditions confound the comparison. Use standard task-based usability testing or a learnability study instead.
whyLost: It lives inside developmental psychology and education research and has never been packaged as a UX technique; UX tends to test either aided or unaided use, not the planned range between them.
whereToUse: Onboarding and template design, AI copilots and writing assistants, educational technology, complex professional tools where examples and guides are part of the product.
example: A spreadsheet tool tests how complex a financial model users can build alone, then again straight after seeing a worked template. The gap shows how much value templates add and which users never reach the template level unaided.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Mascolo, M. F., & Fischer, K. W. (2015). Dynamic development of thinking, feeling, and acting. In R. M. Lerner (Ed.), Handbook of child psychology and developmental science (7th ed.), Vol. 1, pp. 113-161. Wiley.

name: Developmental trajectory analysis
aka: Developmental trajectory analysis versus chronological-age and mental-age matching
origin: Michael Thomas and colleagues (2009), building on Annette Karmiloff-Smith's neuroconstructivist programme
summary: Compares groups by fitting performance as a function of age, experience or ability in each group, instead of matching participants to controls at one point.
description: The traditional comparison of an atypical group matches it to controls of the same chronological age and, separately, of the same mental age: a deficit against both suggests deviance, a deficit only against age-matched controls suggests delay. Matching removes the developmental variable by design and so hides how performance changes with it. Trajectory analysis instead recruits each group across a wide range of the developmental variable and fits performance as a function of it. Groups are then compared on intercept (onset), slope (rate) and shape of their functions, and on how performance on one task predicts another within each group. The approach turns a single-point comparison into a comparison of functions and exposes groups that reach similar levels by different routes. Cross-sectional trajectories describe group-level change, not individual change, so longitudinal follow-up is needed for claims about individuals.
steps: Choose the developmental or experience variable (age, months of product use, skill score) that the comparison should be expressed over.
Recruit each group across a wide, evenly spread range of that variable rather than at a single matched level.
Fit performance against the variable separately for each group, starting with a linear function and testing curvature where theory suggests it.
Compare groups on intercepts, slopes and shapes using interaction terms in a single regression or mixed model.
Relate performance on one task to another within each group to see whether skills are linked in the same way.
Report where trajectories diverge and, if claims about individuals are needed, plan longitudinal follow-up.
outputs: Fitted trajectories per group with tests of differences in onset, rate and shape, plus cross-task relations within groups.
useWhen: Comparing a specific user group (assistive-technology users, older adults, novices) with a reference group where performance depends on experience, and a single matched comparison would hide differences in learning rate.
avoidWhen: Samples that are narrow or bunched on the developmental variable cannot support trajectories. For individual change over time use growth curve modelling on longitudinal data instead.
whyLost: It was developed for developmental disorders research and has not been translated into UX, where group comparisons are usually made at one matched experience level or not matched at all.
whereToUse: Accessibility research, learnability studies across experience bands, onboarding evaluation, comparing professional and lay users of the same tool.
example: A team compares how task success grows with months of use for screen-reader users and sighted users of a banking app, recruiting both groups from first-week to two-year users. Sighted users plateau after three months while screen-reader users keep improving slowly, showing a learnability gap rather than a fixed deficit.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
reference: Westermann, G., Thomas, M. S. C. and Karmiloff-Smith, A., ch. 28 in Goswami, U. (Ed.) (2011). The Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (2nd ed.). Wiley-Blackwell.

name: Deviation Utility Model (ΔU)
donor: Game theory and behavioural economics applied to design adoption
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A deviation-utility equation combining signal clarity, new and habitual utility, effort, trust, reward and norm pressure to predict whether users abandon a stabilised design form.
description: The Deviation Utility model operationalises Nash equilibrium for design adoption. Un is perceived utility of the new form, Uh the utility of the habitual form (safety, familiarity, symbolic capital), E the effort of transition, T trust in the new form, R the reward of transition, P the pressure of norms, and SNR the clarity with which the new form presents its value. SNR multiplies Un: if users cannot perceive value, its utility is effectively zero. The decision rule is ΔU < 0, the current form is stable; ΔU ≥ 0, transition becomes viable. Each term has paired instruments: Un and Uh on 0–10 Likert, E on 0–5 normalised (task time, error rate, NASA-TLX effort), T, R and P on 0–3 scales, and SNR as a 0–1 first-encounter recognition proportion. The model yields both a verdict and a diagnostic profile of dominant negative contributors. Limitations: components treated as independent and additive, and time dynamics not yet modelled.
steps: Define the habitual form and the proposed new form, and the population whose adoption decision you are studying.
Measure Un (usefulness ranking, semantic differential, 0–10) and Uh (old versus new preference tasks, 0–10), with think-aloud and interview probes ('Why do you return to the familiar form?').
Measure E with task time, error rate and the NASA-TLX effort subscale (0–5 normalised), and T with a 3–5 item trust-in-artefact scale (0–3).
Measure R as objective gain in time, cost or steps (0–3, with diary probes) and P with a reverse-scored social norm scale (0–3, 'What would your peers say if you changed?').
Measure SNR as the proportion correctly identifying what the new form does on first encounter (0–1), optionally with eye-tracking dwell.
Compute ΔU = (SNR × Un) − Uh − E + T + R − P and read the verdict (ΔU < 0 stable; ΔU ≥ 0 viable).
Identify the dominant negative contributors, target interventions at them, and re-measure to test whether ΔU shifts toward positive.
outputs: A ΔU score, a component profile showing which forces hold the equilibrium, and targeted intervention hypotheses.
useWhen: When a demonstrably better design fails to displace an incumbent, or before investing in a redesign that requires users to switch.
avoidWhen: When there is no incumbent habit to overcome (a genuinely new category), or when you need a precise adoption forecast; ΔU is a structuring device, not a calibrated predictor.
whyLost: This is an original framework from The Inquiry Series, so it has no history of loss; it combines game theory and prospect theory, which UX research usually treats separately.
whereToUse: Feature migrations, payment method switching, enterprise tool replacement, craft and product redesign, new narrative or interaction paradigms.
example: A bank wants users to move from card entry to tap-to-pay; ΔU shows low SNR (few users recognise the protection it offers) and high P, so the team invests in a risk-coverage explainer rather than speed improvements.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Equilibrium and the Design Object, Section 4.

name: Devil's Advocate Debriefing
origin: Jeffrey Rubin and Dana Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing (2008)
summary: After the tasks, the moderator deliberately takes the opposite position to test how firmly a participant holds a stated view and draw out fuller reasons.
description: Participants often praise a product they visibly struggled with, out of politeness or self-blame. In this debriefing technique the moderator abandons neutrality, but only after all performance tasks are finished, and challenges the participant's stated view: expressing surprise at the gap between their difficulty and their comments, asking for specific reasons, saying they sense reluctance to criticise, or claiming that other participants felt the opposite. Most participants restate their view with fuller reasons; some admit they were holding back. The point is to reveal how robust an opinion is, not to change it, so a positive view that survives challenge is strong evidence. It is distinct from analyst-side red teaming, which challenges the team's conclusions rather than the participant's. Observers must be warned beforehand, and the moderator backs off if the participant seems intimidated.
steps: Warn observers and team members beforehand that the moderator will deliberately argue.
Complete all performance tasks and standard debrief questions first.
State surprise at the discrepancy between the participant's observed difficulty and their positive comments, and ask for specific reasons.
Say you sense reluctance to criticise and want to be sure they are not just being kind.
Optionally claim that other participants felt the opposite, and ask again.
Back off if the participant seems intimidated, and weight their answers accordingly when analysing.
outputs: A judgement of how robust each participant's opinion is, plus fuller rationales and admissions of withheld criticism.
useWhen: Participants seem reluctant to criticise despite visible difficulty, or a contentious feature may decide a release and the team needs to know whether acceptance is real.
avoidWhen: With very young or some very old participants, ingratiating participants, or those who see the session as a job opportunity; never before tasks are complete. For challenging the team's own interpretations use Red Teaming.
whyLost: Modern moderation training stresses neutrality and rapport, so deliberate confrontation feels risky; the technique is little taught outside Rubin and Chisnell's handbook.
whereToUse: Pricing and fee changes, consent and privacy flows, controversial AI features, B2B products where customers defer to vendors.
example: Participants rate a new subscription pause flow highly despite repeated errors. Under challenge, two admit they disliked hunting for the option but did not want to seem slow; the others defend the flow with clear reasons, so the team fixes discoverability only.
reference: Rubin, J. and Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of Usability Testing (2nd ed.). Indianapolis: Wiley, pp. 238-241.

name: Diagnose Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 2: Diagnose with Tree Testing, Error Taxonomy, and SNR
donor: Information architecture research and human error analysis
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 2 of the forward-thinking loop: combine tree testing (where), Slip/Lapse/Mistake error taxonomy (why) and signal-to-noise ratio (clarity) into a joint display with decision bars.
description: Diagnosis locates breakdowns and explains them using three lenses the playbook calls map (tree test), mechanism (taxonomy) and clarity meter (SNR). An unmoderated tree test quantifies findability; moderated think-alouds on the same tasks code each breakdown as Slip, Lapse or Mistake with two coders and Cohen's κ; and an SNR audit measures how much of the screen and of user attention goes to essential elements. Results are synthesised in a joint display linking numbers to quotes and fixes, and judged against diagnosis decision bars: tree direct success ≥ 85%, top misroute ≤ 10%, first-click accuracy ≥ 75%, element SNR ≥ 0.60 and behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70. Qual rigour comes from a participant × episode evidence array sorted by first misroute and error type, and recursive relationship mapping that exposes cascades such as Mistake → extra clicks → frustration → later lapse.
steps: Prepare 6–10 realistic tasks with no label leakage ('Set a price alert for ABC', not 'Go to Price Alerts').
Build current and proposed text-only trees of depth ≤ 3 and run an unmoderated tree test with N = 80–150, randomising task order.
Run 10–15 moderated think-aloud sessions on the same tasks and code each breakdown as Slip, Lapse or Mistake; double-code 30–40% and require κ ≥ 0.70.
Audit SNR on key screens: count essential versus total elements, and compute behavioural SNR from eye, click or cursor dwell if available.
Build an evidence array (rows participants, columns first click, path nodes, error code, quote, time to first click, SNR snapshot) sorted by first misroute then error type.
Synthesise a joint display (quant signal → qual mechanism → prescribed fix) and check against the bars: direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, first-click ≥ 75%, element SNR ≥ 0.60, behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70.
Write a mini joint assertion for Stage 3, e.g. 'Because Mistakes at Notifications co-occur with low SNR and drive extra clicks, moving Price Alerts to top level will reduce abandonment hazard.'
outputs: Misroute heatmap and tree metrics, taxonomy-by-step table with κ, element and behavioural SNR baselines, a one-page joint display and diagnosis decision bars.
useWhen: When findability or clarity is suspected (high extra clicks, low first-click accuracy) and you need both the where and the why.
avoidWhen: When the problem is not navigational or perceptual (e.g. pricing or motivation); use interviews or experiments instead. Do not run interviews alone without quant.
whyLost: Original combination by Vivek Gopinath; each component exists but they are rarely run together with reliability statistics in UX.
whereToUse: Navigation redesigns, IA migrations, fintech alert and settings flows, enterprise menus.
example: In the trading app, the current IA yields 59% direct success with 31% misrouting to Notifications; coded think-alouds show Mistakes dominate (39 per 100 sessions) and element SNR is 0.45, so the joint display prescribes moving Price Alerts under Markets.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 2.

name: Diagram Framing (Scope, Scale, Timescale, Rhetoric)
origin: Abby Covert (2014)
summary: Before drawing a diagram, fix its scope, scale, timescale (then, now, when) and rhetorical aim, then build it from movable boxes and arrows, tidy but unpolished.
description: Covert treats diagrams, maps, prototypes and lists as objects that let people compare mental models, which otherwise exist only in their heads. Before making one, the maker decides its scope (purpose and edges, including what is not diagrammed), its scale (relative size and where it will be seen), its timescale (then, now or when; diagramming then or now is often easier before proposing change) and its rhetoric: reflection, options, improvements, identification or plan. The diagram is built from boxes for things, arrows for one- or two-way relationships and diamonds for decisions, arranging boxes several ways before adding arrows. It should be tidy enough to be trusted but simple enough to change, because people judge legitimacy by tidiness and early polish discourages feedback. It is shared with the team and users rather than drawn alone.
steps: Scope: state the purpose, what people need to understand, the edges and what you are not diagramming.
Scale: decide the relative size and where the diagram will be seen (wall, slide, paper).
Timescale: choose Then, Now or When; draw the current state before proposing a future one.
Rhetoric: choose the aim: reflection, options, improvements, identification or plan.
Make a box for each concept, content item and process; try a few arrangements before adding arrows; use diamonds for decisions.
Keep it tidy but unpolished and easy to change; share it with stakeholders and users for feedback.
outputs: A purposeful diagram of a past, present or future state, ready for discussion.
useWhen: Use whenever a team must align on a messy system, flow or information structure and a diagram is the medium of discussion.
avoidWhen: Avoid assuming the diagram reflects users' understanding: elicit that with a Mental Model Diagram or Card Sorting. Over-simplified schematics can introduce ambiguity.
whyLost: Diagramming is a core skill of information architects and designers; Covert's framing questions are widely taught and reused.
whereToUse: Information architecture, service and system mapping, stakeholder alignment, strategy presentations.
example: A healthcare team draws the referral process three times: as it was ten years ago, as it is now and as intended; the 'when' diagram exposes a decision point no team owns.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert, 2014)
reference: Covert, A. (2014). How to Make Sense of Any Mess: Information Architecture for Everybody. CreateSpace.

name: Dialog Traversal Testing
origin: IVR industry practice, described by Michael Cohen, James Giangola and Jennifer Balogh, 2004
summary: Systematically drive a live voice system through every dialog state, universal command and error condition to verify it matches the dialog specification.
description: In voice design a dialog is one state in the conversational flow, usually a question and the user's reply, with all its transitions, error prompts and help prompts. Dialog traversal testing runs a script against the live system (over the phone for IVRs) that visits every state and checks that the correct action is taken and the correct prompt played. Within each state every universal command (help, repeat, go back, goodbye) and every error condition is exercised: out-of-grammar speech to trigger a reject, silence to trigger the no-speech timeout, and several successive errors to check escalation. Testers annotate a printed flow diagram as they go. Coverage is adapted to the system: every state for deep fixed trees, every function reachable from the top-level prompt for wide assistants, and best paths plus common error paths when full traversal is too costly.
steps: Take the dialog specification and flow diagram as the oracle.
Write a test script that visits every dialog state.
At each state, check the action taken and the prompt played against the specification.
Exercise every universal command (help, repeat, back, goodbye) in each state.
Trigger each error condition: out-of-grammar input, silence, and successive errors to test escalation prompts.
Mark results on the printed flow diagram and log every divergence.
For broad assistants confirm every function is reachable from the top level; for very large systems prioritise best paths and common error paths.
outputs: A list of divergences between implemented behaviour and the dialog specification, marked on the flow diagram.
useWhen: Before launching or after changing an IVR, voice assistant skill or chatbot with a defined dialog flow.
avoidWhen: Testing whether real users understand prompts or how they phrase requests; it checks conformance, not usability. Use Usability Testing or Conversation Analysis for Chatbot Evaluation.
whyLost: It is standard in the voice and telephony industry but rarely appears in UX research toolkits, where it is seen as QA.
whereToUse: Banking and utility IVRs, voice assistant skills, in-car voice systems and scripted chatbots.
example: Before launch of a pharmacy refill IVR, testers traverse all 42 states. They find that two consecutive silences at the date-of-birth prompt hang up instead of offering an agent.
reference: Cohen, M.H., Giangola, J.P. and Balogh, J. (2004) Voice User Interface Design. Boston: Addison-Wesley.

name: Diary Studies
donor: Psychology and sociology (diary methods); time-use research
origin: Diary methods in social science from the 1920s onward; adapted for HCI by Rieman (1993)
summary: Participants record experiences, behaviours and context in their own environment over days or weeks, capturing in-the-moment data that interviews and lab studies miss.
description: A diary study asks participants to log their experiences, actions and thoughts as they occur over an extended period, typically one to four weeks, in their natural environment. Entries may be interval-contingent (at fixed times), signal-contingent (in response to a prompt) or event-contingent (whenever a defined event occurs). Because entries are close in time to the experience, diaries reduce recall bias and capture infrequent, context-dependent or private behaviour. Rigour comes from a clear entry protocol and triggers, structured prompts that balance ease with richness, active monitoring and reminders to sustain compliance, incentives tied to participation, and pre- and post-study interviews that help interpret entries. Analysis treats entries as time-ordered data, not just quotes.
steps: Define the behaviours or events of interest and choose interval, signal or event-contingent entry.
Design a short structured entry template with 3 to 6 prompts and optional photo or screenshot.
Recruit 10 to 20 participants and run a kickoff session to train them on the protocol.
Run the study for 1 to 4 weeks, monitoring entries daily and sending reminders or follow-up probes.
Conduct a debrief interview with each participant using their entries as prompts.
Code entries by time, context and theme, and analyse change over time.
outputs: Time-stamped entries with context, behavioural patterns over time, longitudinal themes and debrief insights.
useWhen: When behaviour unfolds over time, is infrequent, is context-dependent or private, or when you need to see how experience changes after onboarding.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need quick answers or observation of fine-grained interaction details; use usability testing. For momentary affect with random sampling, use the experience sampling method.
whyLost: Vestigial: Demanding for participants; rarely done at full rigor. Digital diary apps revived interest but depth is often reduced.
whereToUse: Long-duration product use; health behaviors; products used infrequently but importantly.
example: A diabetes management app runs a three-week diary study with 15 newly diagnosed users who log every meal-time glucose decision. Entries show users skip logging when eating out, leading to a quick-estimate feature.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Dichotic listening with shadowing
aka: Dichotic listening with shadowing and the attenuation demonstration
origin: Colin Cherry, 1953; Donald Broadbent, 1958; Anne Treisman, 1960s
summary: Two different audio messages play, one to each ear; people repeat one aloud and are tested on the other, measuring what breaks through competing audio.
description: Two different messages go to the two ears through headphones, and the participant repeats (shadows) the attended one, which locks attention on it. Afterwards they are tested on the unattended ear. Cherry found people knew whether the unattended voice was male or female but not what it said; a word repeated 35 times went unnoticed, yet about a third of people caught their own name. Treisman's variants showed attention following meaning across ears, and an unnoticed biasing word could shift interpretation of an ambiguous sentence. Broadbent developed the method from air traffic control, where operators received several radio messages at once, and argued design should account for these limits before use. Whether selection is early or late depends on the task and stimuli.
steps: Prepare two audio streams (speech, digits, alerts) of matched length and level.
Screen participants for hearing differences and ear dominance.
Present one stream to each ear through headphones and ask participants to shadow one aloud.
Embed target items (names, alerts, keywords) in the unattended channel.
Test recall, detection or indirect influence of unattended content during or after the task.
Vary what distinguishes channels (voice, pitch, location, meaning) and compare accuracy for attended and unattended content.
outputs: Shadowing accuracy, recall or detection rates per channel, and evidence of which cues let important messages break through.
useWhen: Designing voice assistants, in-car announcements, cockpit or control-room audio, and alerts that must be heard over speech or music.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on headphone results alone for real rooms and vehicles; follow up with in-situ or simulator tests and multiple resource analysis.
whyLost: It shaped attention theory and aviation human factors but was superseded in UX by broader dual-task and workload methods.
whereToUse: Automotive voice interfaces, aviation and control rooms, hearing aids and audio products, smart speakers, accessibility.
example: A car maker tests whether navigation prompts are noticed while drivers follow a podcast: spoken prompts with a distinct voice and a preceding chime are detected far more often than prompts in the podcast's voice.
sources: Cherry, E. C. (1953). Some experiments on the recognition of speech, with one and with two ears. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 25
reference: Cherry, E. C. (1953). Some experiments on the recognition of speech, with one and with two ears. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 25, 975-979.

name: Dichotomous-Choice Contingent Valuation
origin: Cameron and James (1987); Cameron (1988); Hanemann, Loomis and Kanninen (1991) double-bounded format
summary: Each respondent answers yes or no to paying one randomly assigned amount, optionally followed by a higher or lower amount, and the population WTP distribution is estimated by maximum likelihood.
description: Respondents are asked whether they would pay a stated amount, with the amount randomised across respondents. In the double-bounded version a yes is followed by a higher amount and a no by a lower one. True willingness to pay is assumed to follow a distribution, such as normal, lognormal if strictly positive, or a spike at zero plus a lognormal for non-payers. The probability of each answer pattern is the share of that distribution falling in the interval it implies, and the mean and spread are estimated by maximum likelihood, which is ordered-probit logic with cut-offs set by the questionnaire. Because each person answers one simple question, it mimics a real purchase or referendum decision better than open-ended price questions. The method is contested (Hausman, 1993), and double-bounded answers of yes-yes or no-no remain only one-sided.
steps: Choose 4-8 bid amounts spanning the plausible WTP range and randomise them across respondents.
Ask whether the respondent would pay the assigned bid for a clearly described product or change (single-bounded).
Optionally follow a yes with a higher bid and a no with a lower bid (double-bounded).
Assume a WTP distribution: normal, lognormal, or a spike at zero plus lognormal.
Write each answer pattern's probability as the WTP probability mass in the interval it implies.
Maximise the log likelihood to estimate mean and spread of WTP and report confidence intervals.
outputs: An estimated population distribution of willingness to pay (mean, median, spread) and demand at each price.
useWhen: Valuing a new feature, service tier or public digital service where no market price exists and a simple yes/no purchase question is realistic.
avoidWhen: Avoid when real purchase data or experiments are possible (use price tests or BDM auctions), or when you need range-of-acceptable-price questions (Van Westendorp) or attribute trade-offs (conjoint). Hypothetical bias is substantial.
whyLost: It is standard in environmental and health economics, while pricing research in product teams adopted Gabor-Granger, Van Westendorp and conjoint instead.
whereToUse: Pricing new subscription add-ons, public-sector digital services, accessibility or privacy features, premium AI features.
example: A note app asks 2,000 users whether they would pay one of £2, £4, £6 or £8 a month for AI summaries, then a higher or lower follow-up. The lognormal model gives a median WTP of £3.40 and shows that half of users would pay nothing.
reference: Hanemann, M., Loomis, J. and Kanninen, B. (1991). Statistical efficiency of double-bounded dichotomous choice contingent valuation. American Journal of Agricultural Economics, 73(4), 1255-1263; Train, K. E. (2009). Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press, pp. 164-166.

name: Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
origin: John Snow (1855) precursor; Card and Krueger, 1994
summary: Estimates a change's effect by comparing the before-after change in a treated group with that in an untreated group, under a parallel-trends assumption.
description: DiD compares the change over time in outcomes for a treated group with the change for a control group that did not receive treatment. Differencing removes stable unobserved differences between groups and common time trends. The key identifying assumption is parallel trends: absent treatment, both groups would have changed at the same rate, which is assessed with pre-period data and event-study plots. The treatise applies it to product launches and redesigns with a natural control: users in a region without the rollout, or cohorts joining before versus after a change. It separates the change's effect from secular trends and selection differences. Modern staggered-adoption estimators (for example Callaway and Sant'Anna) fix biases of naive two-way fixed effects. Rated HIGH priority.
steps: Identify treated and comparison groups and pre- and post-periods (several pre-periods if possible).
Plot pre-period trends and test for parallel trends with an event-study specification.
Estimate the DiD effect with group and time fixed effects and clustered standard errors.
Use staggered-adoption estimators if rollout timing varies across groups.
Run placebo tests (fake treatment dates or unaffected outcomes).
Report the effect with assumptions and robustness checks.
outputs: Effect estimate with CI, event-study plot, parallel-trends evidence, robustness checks.
useWhen: Staged rollouts, regional launches, policy or pricing changes where randomisation was not done.
avoidWhen: When groups clearly had diverging pre-trends or treatment spilled over to controls; consider synthetic control.
whyLost: Econometrics training rarely reaches UX; teams compare before and after without a control group.
whereToUse: Feature rollouts by market, redesign impact, regulatory changes such as consent rules, cohort benchmarking.
example: A delivery app launches a new checkout in Spain only; DiD against Portugal shows a 2.1-point conversion uplift, versus a naive before-after estimate of 5 points inflated by a seasonal rise.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Card D & Krueger AB (1994) Minimum wages and employment. AER 84(4):772-793
Angrist JD & Pischke J-S (2008) Mostly Harmless Econometrics
Callaway B & Sant'Anna PHC (2021) Difference-in-differences with multiple time periods. J Econometrics
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Scott Maxwell & Harold Delaney)

name: Differential Item Functioning (DIF) Analysis
origin: Paul Holland and Howard Wainer, 1993; David Thissen, Lynne Steinberg and Howard Wainer, 1993 (likelihood-ratio approach); Nambury Raju, 1990 (DFIT); Hariharan Swaminathan and H. Jane Rogers, 1990 (logistic regression)
summary: Tests whether respondents from different groups with the same level of the measured trait answer an item differently, so biased items can be found, modelled or removed before comparing groups.
description: An item shows DIF when two people from different groups at the same trait level have different probabilities of each response. DIF items distort group differences and correlations, so a gap between countries, devices or segments may come from wording or translation rather than real differences. Classical methods (Mantel-Haenszel, logistic or ordinal logistic regression conditioning on total score) are easy but sample specific. IRT methods give results that generalise, graphical diagnostics (group trace lines, expected item and test scores) and DIF-adjusted scores for sensitivity analysis. The illustrated IRT route calibrates both groups simultaneously and compares nested models with likelihood-ratio tests, first for any DIF and then for slope and threshold differences. Groups are linked through anchor items assumed DIF-free; one can suffice but three or more is better, chosen from prior knowledge, random assignment or iterative purification.
steps: Confirm the scale is suitable for unidimensional IRT (or choose a classical method if samples are small).
Start with all other items as a temporary anchor and test each item in turn at a liberal alpha (.05) so that the final anchor set is conservative.
For each studied item, compare a model with its parameters free across groups against one with them constrained equal; a chi-square difference above 3.84 (1 df) flags DIF.
For flagged items, test slope equality and then threshold equality to locate the type of DIF.
Purify the anchor set by removing DIF items and retest the remaining items.
Plot group trace lines and expected scores, compute DIF-adjusted scale scores and compare them with raw scores to judge practical impact before deciding to drop, rewrite or model the items.
outputs: List of DIF items with the parameter affected, group trace lines, and the impact of DIF on scale-level comparisons.
useWhen: Comparing questionnaire scores across languages, cultures, devices, age groups or user segments, or validating a translated or adapted UX instrument.
avoidWhen: You need whole-scale structural equivalence (use multi-group CFA measurement invariance); groups are small (classical methods are the fallback, with caution); the scale is not unidimensional. Statistical DIF may have trivial impact on scale scores, so always check practical impact.
whyLost: UX teams compare segment means on translated or adapted surveys without testing item equivalence, and DIF methods live in educational testing and health outcomes measurement.
whereToUse: Global satisfaction and NPS programmes, localised UX questionnaires, accessibility research comparing assistive-technology users with others, AI product trust scales used across markets.
example: A global SaaS company finds Japanese users score 0.4 SD lower on a trust scale. DIF analysis shows two items translated with stronger wording have higher thresholds in Japanese; DIF-adjusted scores halve the gap, so the team rewrites those items rather than launching a trust campaign.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Holland, P. W., & Wainer, H. (Eds.) (1993). Differential Item Functioning. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Differential Susceptibility (Host Factor) Analysis
aka: Effect modification analysis for UX harm
origin: Epidemiological effect modification; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Measures how harm from a UX pathogen varies by host factors (literacy, age, stress, disability, language, device) to target protection and expose inequity.
description: Epidemiology recognises that disease does not affect all hosts equally. The treatise lists UX host factors: digital literacy, cognitive load at interaction, emotional state and stress, time pressure, prior experience with the product or category, age and generational familiarity, language and culture, disability and accessibility needs, and socioeconomic factors affecting device and connectivity. Analysis estimates harm rates within strata and tests effect modification (interaction terms, stratified risk ratios), showing which groups bear disproportionate harm. In the roach motel case, susceptibility rose with time pressure and low literacy and fell after prior victimisation. The equity implication is central: UX pathogens inflict greater harm on users with less literacy, more pressure, minority backgrounds and disabilities.
steps: Define the harm outcome and candidate host factors from theory and research.
Collect outcome and host-factor data (surveys linked to logs, panel studies, experiments).
Estimate harm rates by stratum with confidence intervals.
Test effect modification with interaction models or stratified ratios.
Identify high-susceptibility groups and mechanisms through qualitative follow-up.
Design targeted protections and monitor their effect on disparities.
outputs: Stratified harm rates, effect modification estimates, susceptibility profiles, targeted protections.
useWhen: Assessing who is harmed by patterns, accessibility and inclusion work, duty-of-care obligations.
avoidWhen: Very small samples where strata estimates are meaningless; use qualitative inclusive research.
whyLost: UX averages across users and rarely collects host-factor data linked to outcomes.
whereToUse: Financial services vulnerable customer duties, healthcare portals, government services, AI assistants.
example: An energy supplier finds bill-payment errors are 3.2 times higher among customers over 75 using small phones, motivating a large-text mode and phone fallback.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rothman KJ, Greenland S & Lash TL (2008) Modern Epidemiology (effect modification)
Financial Conduct Authority (2021) FG21/1 Guidance on the fair treatment of vulnerable customers
reference: Rothman KJ, Greenland S & Lash TL (2008) Modern Epidemiology. 3rd ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

name: Digital Storytelling (StoryCenter Workshop Method)
origin: Center for Digital Storytelling (now StoryCenter), Berkeley; Lambert and Hessler (2018)
summary: Participants are trained in a workshop to make their own short multimedia story about lived experience, which researchers then analyse alongside the participants' framing.
description: A participatory method in which people communicate their lived realities from their own perspective through short digital stories combining photographs, narration, text, music and sound. Dawson separates the broad sense (any personal narrative shared online) from the narrow workshop technique of the Center for Digital Storytelling, which trains participants over a workshop to write, record and edit their own two-to-five-minute story, while addressing confidentiality and ownership. Story types range from personal narratives and accounts of events to retold stories and instructional pieces. Stories are analysed thematically or through discourse, content, frame or comparative analysis, together with video and audio analysis. Its strength is voice: participants choose what matters and how to show it. Criticisms include sentimentality, editing that shapes authenticity, and unequal storytelling and technical confidence; harrowing stories require a duty of care.
steps: Decide the purpose, the story type and the level of researcher and participant collaboration.
Settle permissions, consent, privacy, ownership and withdrawal, including for people who appear in stories.
Run a workshop (typically over several days) that trains participants in story circles, scripting, recording narration and editing.
Participants produce their stories individually or in groups, with facilitator support.
Hold a screening and discussion where participants present and frame their own stories.
Analyse the stories thematically or through discourse, content or frame analysis, attending to images and audio as well as words.
outputs: Short participant-made multimedia stories and analyses of themes, framings and lived experience.
useWhen: Understanding lived experience in communities whose voice is under-represented, especially for services in health, public sector and social impact.
avoidWhen: Quick product feedback or usability questions; use interviews or directed storytelling. Avoid when facilitators lack skills for sensitive disclosures.
whyLost: Workshops take days and trained facilitators; UX borrowed the word 'storytelling' for presenting findings rather than for participant-made data.
whereToUse: Public services, digital health for chronic conditions, inclusion research, community-centred design.
example: A diabetes care service runs a three-day workshop in which eight young adults make two-minute stories about managing insulin at work. Analysis reveals stigma around visible devices, shaping a discreet-mode feature for the companion app.
reference: Lambert, J. and Hessler, B. (2018). Digital Storytelling: Capturing Lives, Creating Community (5th ed.). New York: Routledge.

name: Direct and Indirect Standardisation
origin: William Farr and 19th-century vital statistics; formalised in demographic and epidemiological practice
summary: Adjusts rates for differences in population composition (e.g. tenure, device, plan mix) so that groups, markets or periods can be fairly compared.
description: Comparing raw conversion or churn rates across markets, versions or time periods is misleading if the mix of users differs; this is the root of Simpson's paradox. Direct standardisation applies each group's stratum-specific rates to a common standard population; indirect standardisation applies standard rates to each group's composition to get expected counts, then reports observed/expected ratios (like standardised mortality ratios). Hospitals use case-mix adjustment to compare outcomes. In product analytics this enables fair comparisons of support teams, regions, releases or cohorts with different user mixes, and reveals when apparent improvements are composition shifts.
steps: Choose stratification variables that affect the outcome and differ in distribution (e.g. tenure band, device, plan).
Compute stratum-specific rates for each group being compared.
For direct standardisation, apply rates to a chosen standard population and compute standardised rates.
For indirect standardisation, compute expected events using reference rates and report observed/expected ratios with intervals.
Compare crude and standardised results to show composition effects.
Document the standard population and strata used.
outputs: Standardised rates or observed/expected ratios with confidence intervals and crude-versus-adjusted comparisons.
useWhen: Comparing metrics across groups or periods with different user compositions.
avoidWhen: Randomised comparisons where composition is balanced, or when strata are too sparse.
whyLost: Product analytics compares raw rates; demographic methods are unfamiliar.
whereToUse: Market comparisons, support agent performance, release health comparisons, retention trends with changing acquisition mix.
example: Version 8 appears to have higher crash-related churn than version 7. Standardising by device age shows version 8's users skew to older phones; the standardised ratio is 1.02, so the release is not worse.
sources: Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology (3rd ed., 2008)
Preston, Heuveline & Guillot, Demography: Measuring and Modeling Population Processes (2001)
reference: Preston, S. H., Heuveline, P., & Guillot, M. (2001). Demography. Blackwell.

name: Direct Manipulation Interface Evaluation
origin: Ben Shneiderman, 1983; theoretical analysis by Hutchins, Hollan and Norman (1985)
summary: Scores an interface against the four criteria of direct manipulation, continuous representation, physical actions, rapid reversible incremental operations and immediate feedback, to locate breaks in directness.
description: Shneiderman defined direct manipulation by four properties: continuous visible representation of the objects of interest; physical actions or labelled button presses instead of complex syntax; rapid, incremental, reversible operations whose effect on the object is immediately visible; and layered learning so novices can start with a small set of actions. Hutchins, Hollan and Norman explained why it works in terms of narrowing the gulfs of execution and evaluation. The evaluation method treats each criterion as measurable: for example, the proportion of operations whose result is visible within 100 milliseconds, the proportion reversible without dialogs, and whether objects remain visible during manipulation. Profiling an interface this way locates exactly where directness breaks, which is valuable for canvas tools, visual editors, dashboards and spatial or touch interfaces.
steps: Rate each principle (0–2): continuous representation (0=no visible state, 1=visible but static, 2=live representation); physical actions (0=typed commands, 1=menu-based, 2=direct drag/gesture); rapid reversibility (measure time to undo any action); immediate feedback (measure time from action to visible response — target < 100ms for continuous, < 1000ms for bounded tasks).
outputs: Per-criterion directness scores, inventory of operations with latency and reversibility, and a map of breaks in directness with redesign options.
useWhen: Evaluating design tools, editors, data visualisation and dashboards, drag-and-drop interfaces, maps and touch interfaces.
avoidWhen: For form-based, conversational or batch workflows where direct manipulation is not the intended paradigm; use task analysis or heuristic evaluation instead.
whyLost: Direct manipulation became the default GUI style, so evaluating against its criteria seemed unnecessary, and the measurable criteria were absorbed into general heuristics.
whereToUse: Touch interface design, data visualization interaction design, professional creative tool design, spatial computing UX.
example: A BI dashboard's filters apply only after clicking 'Run', with a 4-second delay and no preview. Scoring shows 30% of operations give immediate feedback; live-updating filters with undo raise exploration depth in a follow-up test.
sources: Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines — Ben Shneiderman
Hutchins, Hollan & Norman, Direct manipulation interfaces (Human-Computer Interaction, 1985)
reference: Shneiderman B (1983) Direct manipulation: A step beyond programming languages. IEEE Computer 16(8):57-69

name: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
aka: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) for Causal Reasoning
origin: Judea Pearl, 1995–2000; Greenland, Pearl & Robins, 1999
summary: Graphs of variables and one-way causal arrows that make assumptions explicit and show which confounders to adjust for, which colliders to avoid and which mediators to estimate.
description: A DAG encodes assumed causal relations as arrows with no cycles. It does not estimate anything; it determines identification: which variables must be measured and adjusted to estimate an effect without bias, and which must not be controlled (colliders) to avoid inducing bias. In Vivek Gopinath's payments protocol the DAG is drawn from qualitative themes before estimation: users double-check because they do not fully trust tap-to-pay, double-checking makes paying feel slow, and slowness suppresses adoption. The DAG links Prior Fraud Exposure and Support Responsiveness to Trust, Trust to Double-Checking and Adoption, Double-Checking to Perceived Slowness, and Slowness to Adoption, with confounders such as risk tolerance, device type and prior bank relationship. Benefits named are transparency for peer critique, identification, and an analysis plan pointing to mediators. The DAG and qual arrays are kept under version control so every assumption change is traceable before re-estimation.
steps: Extract candidate causes, mediators and outcomes from qualitative themes.
Draw arrows for assumed causal directions, ensuring no cycles.
Add confounders that affect both exposure and outcome (e.g. past fraud experience, device, tenure).
Identify colliders and avoid adjusting for them, and mark mediators whose indirect effects you will estimate.
Derive the measurement and adjustment plan from the graph.
Version-control the DAG and update it before any re-estimation.
outputs: A causal diagram, adjustment set and analysis plan.
useWhen: Before any observational analysis or SEM, especially to avoid 'control-for-everything' traps.
avoidWhen: When relationships are genuinely cyclic or feedback-driven over short time scales; use dynamic or systems models.
whyLost: Mainstream in epidemiology and causal inference, but UX analytics rarely writes assumptions down before modelling.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption studies, payments and security features, retention analyses, AI feature impact studies.
example: Interviews about tap-to-pay become a DAG showing trust affects adoption directly and via double-checking and slowness, telling the team to measure past fraud experience as a confounder.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Causal diagrams for epidemiologic research (Greenland, Pearl & Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Vol III, Ch 46
The Inquiry Series, C5 — Causal Inference in Python — DAGs, Target Trial Emulation & Sensitivity Analysis

Hernán MA & Robins JM (2020) Causal Inference: What If
Greenland S, Pearl J & Robins JM (1999) Causal diagrams for epidemiologic research. Epidemiology 10(1)

name: Directed storytelling
origin: Carnegie Mellon School of Design (Shelley Evenson); movie-making variant by Pavliscak (2018)
summary: Ask participants to tell the story of a specific recent experience, steering gently with who, what, when, where and how prompts, then cluster stories into themes when observation is impractical.
description: Directed storytelling is a quick, low-cost substitute for fieldwork when observation is impractical, for example rare, private or past events. The researcher opens with a prompt about a specific recent experience and keeps the narrative flowing, probing gently with who, what, when, where and how, while a second researcher documents. Central ideas are identified from what the teller emphasises, then clustered across stories, for example by affinity, and modelled as a framework or map. A film-based variant asks participants to frame crucial moments with a product as a movie, then replay it: noting the sequence, pausing on key events, muting dialogue to focus on actions, fast-forwarding to consequences, and summarising it as a trailer. The framing reaches emotion indirectly and helps people sequence events.
steps: Write an opening prompt about a specific, recent experience, such as 'tell me about the last time you...'.
Start the story and keep it flowing; let the participant choose what matters.
Probe gently with who, what, when, where and how questions without steering the plot.
Optionally use the movie framing: replay the story, pause on key events, mute dialogue to focus on actions, fast-forward to consequences, and ask for a one-line trailer.
Have a second researcher document the story, emphasis and emotional peaks.
Identify each story's central ideas, cluster them across participants by affinity, and model the themes as a framework or journey map.
outputs: Experience stories with key moments and emotions, a themed framework or map, and optional summary trailers.
useWhen: The experience is rare, private, past or spread over time, so observation is impossible, and you need rich, sequenced accounts quickly.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need accurate behaviour data; recall is biased and reconstructed. Use observation, diaries or logs instead. Moderators can over-steer the plot.
whyLost: It survives because it is cheap, needs no special setting and is taught in design schools and methods collections.
whereToUse: Healthcare journeys, financial life events, travel disruptions, onboarding and cancellation experiences, and emotionally significant moments with technology.
example: A hospital asks discharged patients to tell the story of their last admission. Clustering the stories shows confusion clustered at hand-offs between ward and pharmacy, which becomes the focus of a service redesign.
reference: Hanington, B. & Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design (expanded and revised). Rockport, Method 42; Pavliscak, P. (2018). Emotionally Intelligent Design. O'Reilly Media.

name: Disclosure-Risk Review of Released Results
aka: Disclosure-risk review of mined results before release
origin: Statistical database and census practice; set out for data mining by Clifton (2003)
summary: Before sharing aggregates, patterns or segments, check whether any could single out a person or be combined to reveal private values, then suppress, coarsen or perturb them.
description: Harmless-looking outputs can identify people. A rule or segment covering one customer reveals that person's behaviour, and two permitted totals can be differenced to expose an individual value (total salary minus everyone except the president gives the president's salary). Statistical agencies defend against this with minimum cell sizes, ranges instead of exact values, restrictions on overlapping queries, perturbation of data or outputs, and release of small samples so fine-grained results are unreliable. The review treats every output as a potential inference channel and checks coverage, combinability and proxy discrimination before release. In UX it applies to research repositories, analytics dashboards, segment reports and quotes, where small segments and rich filters make re-identification easy.
steps: List every output to be released: tables, segment profiles, mined rules, dashboards and quotes.
Check each output's coverage and flag any that describe very few people; census practice uses minimum group sizes, for example releases covering at least 300 people.
Check whether outputs can be combined or differenced (overlapping filters, totals with and without a subgroup) to reveal an individual.
Apply defences: minimum cell sizes, ranges or banding, suppression, perturbation or release of a sample only.
Check use restrictions and whether released variables act as proxies that could lead to unfair treatment.
Record what was suppressed or altered and why, and re-review when new outputs are added.
outputs: A cleared set of outputs and a log of suppressed or coarsened items with reasons.
useWhen: Sharing analytics, research findings or segment data beyond the immediate team, publishing dashboards with drill-down filters, or building research repositories that combine many studies.
avoidWhen: Only aggregate results on very large groups are released and no filtering is possible. It does not replace data-protection review of raw data handling; perturbation can be undone as more is learned, so pair it with access control.
whyLost: It is standard in official statistics and privacy engineering but UX teams rarely treat findings and dashboards as disclosure risks.
whereToUse: Research repositories, B2B analytics with small customer counts, health and fintech research readouts, internal dashboards with fine filters.
example: A health app's research dashboard lets anyone filter by clinic, age band and condition. A review finds some filter combinations return two patients, so cells under ten are suppressed and age is banded more coarsely.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Clifton, C. (2003). Security and privacy. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 441-452). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Discount Usability Engineering (Nielsen's Original)
origin: Jakob Nielsen, 1989-1994
summary: An economic framework combining simplified think-aloud tests, scenarios and heuristic evaluation, with attention to detection rates, evaluator reliability and severity.
description: Nielsen's discount usability argument was that simple, cheap methods capture most major usability problems, so practitioners should not wait for resources to run perfect studies. It combined scenarios, simplified thinking aloud and heuristic evaluation. The treatise argues the economic argument survived but the rest of the framework was lost: Nielsen's careful analysis of what each method can and cannot detect (problem discovery curves, the 1-(1-p)^n model), attention to evaluator reliability (aggregating 3-5 evaluators), the severity rating scale and the insistence that even discount methods apply theory-based heuristics systematically. Contemporary quick tests often lack all of these, producing unprioritised and unsystematic findings.
steps: Write task scenarios representing core user goals.
Run simplified think-aloud tests with about 5 users per user group, iterating designs between rounds.
Conduct heuristic evaluation with 3-5 independent evaluators and aggregate findings.
Estimate problem discovery coverage given observed problem frequencies.
Rate every problem with the severity scale (0-4) using independent raters.
Fix the highest-severity problems and iterate.
outputs: Aggregated problem list with severity ratings, coverage estimate, iteration log.
useWhen: Resource-constrained teams needing systematic, prioritised usability findings quickly.
avoidWhen: Summative benchmarking or statistically powered comparisons; use quantitative usability testing.
whyLost: The slogan 'test with five users' spread without the surrounding framework of detection analysis, reliability and severity.
whereToUse: Startups, agencies, internal tools, iterative design sprints.
example: A health insurer's two-person UX team runs three rounds of five-user tests plus a three-evaluator heuristic review per release, rating severity independently; release defects of severity 3-4 fall by 60% over a year.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J (1993) Usability Engineering. Academic Press
Nielsen J (1989) Usability engineering at a discount
Nielsen J & Landauer TK (1993) A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems. INTERCHI
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Nielsen J (1993) Usability Engineering. Academic Press, pp. 16-20 and 112.

name: Discourse Analysis
origin: Zellig Harris, 1952; conversation analysis by Sacks, Schegloff & Jefferson, 1974; critical discourse analysis by Fairclough, 1989
summary: Analyses how language in talk and text constructs meaning, identities and social action, revealing what users accomplish with words, not just what they say.
description: Discourse analysis studies language in use: how people construct meaning, identities, relationships and actions through talk and text. It includes conversation analysis, which examines the fine-grained sequential organisation of interaction such as turn-taking, repair and preference structure; discursive psychology, which treats attitudes and accounts as actions performed in talk; and critical discourse analysis, which links language to power and ideology. In UX it is especially valuable for conversational interfaces, customer service, community content and organisational communication. Rigour comes from detailed transcription conventions (for example Jefferson notation for conversation analysis), attention to sequence and context, grounding claims in specific excerpts, and testing interpretations against deviant cases.
steps: Define the research question and the type of discourse, such as chatbot logs, support calls or forum posts.
Collect naturally occurring data where possible, with consent and privacy protections.
Transcribe with a convention appropriate to the approach, such as Jefferson notation for conversation analysis.
Select and examine segments in detail, attending to sequence, word choice, framing and the action each turn performs.
Build a collection of similar instances and examine deviant cases.
Relate findings to design implications, such as dialogue flows or tone guidelines.
outputs: Annotated transcripts, collections of interactional patterns, analyses of framing and repair, and design implications for conversation and content.
useWhen: For conversational UI and voice assistants, customer service interactions, content tone and framing, and community or policy language.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the goal is simply to summarise what people want; use thematic analysis. Requires linguistic training to do well.
whyLost: It is explicitly political and theory-heavy, uses linguistic terminology unfamiliar to product teams, and its findings challenge business framing, which makes it hard to sell inside companies.
whereToUse: Conversational UI research; customer service analysis; cultural/political communication.
example: A bank's chatbot logs are analysed with conversation analysis. Users repeatedly rephrase after the bot's open question 'How can I help?', and repair sequences show they expect a menu, leading to a hybrid prompt design.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
reference: Sacks, H., Schegloff, E. A. & Jefferson, G. (1974). A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language, 50(4), 696-735; Fairclough, N. (1989). Language and Power. Longman.

name: Discourse Analysis of UX Data
origin: Potter and Wetherell (1987); Fairclough (1989)
summary: Analyses how language in interviews, reviews and product copy constructs identities, responsibilities and power, rather than treating talk as a transparent window.
description: Listed in the treatise's curriculum, discourse analysis treats language as action: what talk and text do, which versions of reality they construct and which interests they serve. Discursive psychology examines interpretative repertoires and accountability in talk (for example how users blame themselves for errors), while critical discourse analysis examines how texts reproduce power relations (for example how terms of service position the user). Applied to UX data, it reveals how users account for failures, how product copy frames responsibility and how marketing language constructs 'ideal users'. Rigour comes from close reading of transcribed extracts with explicit analytic claims tied to linguistic features.
steps: Assemble a corpus: interview transcripts, reviews, support chats or product copy.
Transcribe talk in sufficient detail (hesitations, emphasis, repairs).
Identify recurring repertoires, positions and rhetorical devices.
Analyse what each discursive move accomplishes (blame, legitimacy, identity).
Ground every claim in quoted extracts with line references.
Translate findings into implications for copy, framing and policy.
outputs: Annotated extracts, repertoires and positioning analysis, implications for language and framing.
useWhen: Understanding self-blame, trust, stigma, or how product language positions users; content strategy audits.
avoidWhen: Usability defect detection or quantitative estimates.
whyLost: Requires linguistic training and produces findings that look abstract to product teams.
whereToUse: Error and consent copy, terms of service, AI assistant tone, financial hardship communication.
example: Analysis of 200 support chats shows users repeatedly say 'I must have done something wrong' about failed transfers; the bank rewrites error messages to locate responsibility with the system when it is at fault.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Potter J & Wetherell M (1987) Discourse and Social Psychology
Gee JP (2014) An Introduction to Discourse Analysis
reference: Potter J & Wetherell M (1987) Discourse and Social Psychology: Beyond Attitudes and Behaviour. Sage.

name: Discovery Series
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Studio Aghora (uxguy.in)
summary: A staged discovery methodology, from problem framing to opportunity sizing, where each stage produces a defined artefact before the next begins, preventing premature convergence.
description: The Discovery Series structures generative research into five sequential stages: problem framing, landscape mapping, user archaeology, assumption inventory and opportunity sizing. Problem framing states the question and its boundaries. Landscape mapping surveys competitors, adjacent products and existing evidence. User archaeology digs into past research, support data and the history of how users have solved the problem so far. The assumption inventory lists what the team believes without evidence. Opportunity sizing estimates the value of each opportunity. Each stage must produce a specific artefact before moving on, which acts as a gate against jumping to solutions. Its rigour comes from making discovery auditable: stakeholders can see what was examined, what was assumed and why particular opportunities were chosen.
steps: Write a problem framing brief that states the question, scope, constraints and decision it will inform.
Produce a landscape map of competitors, workarounds and existing evidence.
Conduct user archaeology by reviewing prior research, support logs and 6 to 12 interviews about past behaviour.
Compile an assumption inventory ranked by risk and lack of evidence.
Size each opportunity using reach, frequency of need and estimated value.
Hold a gate review after each stage and only proceed when its artefact is complete.
outputs: A framing brief, landscape map, user archaeology report, ranked assumption inventory and sized opportunity list.
useWhen: For 0-to-1 product work, entry into unfamiliar domains, or any discovery effort at risk of converging on a solution too early.
avoidWhen: Avoid for narrow evaluative questions about an existing design; use usability testing. Too heavy for a one-week sprint question.
whyLost: Still in use: Vivek's structured alternative to unstructured generative research; prevents premature convergence.
whereToUse: New product development; 0-to-1 research; entering unfamiliar domains.
example: A health insurer exploring a caregiver product runs the Discovery Series. User archaeology reveals caregivers already rely on shared spreadsheets, and opportunity sizing favours a coordination tool over the planned symptom checker.
reference: Gopinath, V. Discovery Series (uxguy.in).

name: Discrete Choice Modeling
origin: Daniel McFadden, 1970s (Nobel Prize 2000); random utility theory from Thurstone (1927) and Marschak (1960)
summary: Statistical models of choice among alternatives, based on random utility theory, that estimate how attributes drive decisions in stated or revealed choice data.
description: Discrete choice modelling explains and predicts choices among a finite set of alternatives using random utility theory: each alternative has a utility made of observed attributes and an unobserved random component, and people choose the alternative with the highest utility. Models range from multinomial logit to nested logit, probit and mixed logit, which allows preferences to vary across people. McFadden's work on transport choices made it central to econometrics. Unlike conjoint, it applies equally to revealed preference data, such as observed choices in logs, so it can model how users choose among navigation paths, plans or options. Rigour comes from correct specification of the choice set, attention to violations such as independence of irrelevant alternatives, handling preference heterogeneity, and validating out of sample.
steps: Define the choice situation, the set of alternatives and the attributes that vary.
Collect stated choice data from designed experiments or revealed choices from logs, recording the full choice set.
Specify utility functions for each alternative with attributes and user characteristics.
Estimate a baseline multinomial logit, then test nested or mixed logit to address IIA violations and heterogeneity.
Assess fit and validate predictions on held-out choices.
Compute elasticities, willingness to pay or predicted shares under design scenarios.
outputs: Estimated utility parameters, preference heterogeneity, elasticities, willingness-to-pay estimates and scenario predictions of choice shares.
useWhen: When modelling how users choose among plans, options, paths or defaults, especially with revealed choice data from logs, and for policy or pricing scenarios.
avoidWhen: Avoid when choice sets are unclear or not recorded, or for open-ended exploration; use interviews or analytics. For simple stated trade-offs, conjoint software may suffice.
whyLost: Latent: Powerful for UX decision research; largely confined to academic and specialized quant UX.
whereToUse: Navigation choice modeling; feature adoption; accessibility option design.
example: A mobility app models 1.2 million logged trip choices among bike, scooter and transit options. Mixed logit shows high sensitivity to walking distance to vehicles among older users, informing dock placement and default suggestions.
sources: Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
Analyzing Decision Making: Metric Conjoint Analysis (Louviere, 1988)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Train, K. E. (2009). Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press; McFadden, D. (1974). Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behavior.

name: Discrete-Event Simulation
origin: Keith Tocher's General Simulation Program (1960); GPSS by Geoffrey Gordon at IBM (1961)
summary: Simulates a service as entities moving through activities and queues over time, to test design and staffing changes before implementation.
description: Discrete-event simulation represents a process as a series of events that change system state: arrivals, service starts and ends, routing decisions. Entities (users, tickets, orders) flow through activities with stochastic durations and resource constraints. Unlike queueing formulas, DES handles complex routing, priorities, time-varying demand, abandonment and human behaviour rules. Rigour comes from validating the model against current performance, running multiple replications for confidence intervals, and documenting assumptions. Service designers can use DES to test new service blueprints, triage rules or self-service options before costly pilots.
steps: Map the process with a service blueprint or process mining output.
Collect input distributions: arrival patterns, task durations, routing probabilities, abandonment.
Build the model in a DES tool (e.g. SimPy, AnyLogic, Simul8) and verify logic.
Validate against historical performance metrics (waits, throughput) before experimenting.
Run scenarios with multiple replications, warm-up periods and confidence intervals.
Communicate results with animations and key metrics; pilot the best scenario.
outputs: A validated simulation model, scenario comparisons with confidence intervals and recommendations.
useWhen: Redesigning multi-step services with resource constraints and variability, where pilots are costly.
avoidWhen: Simple systems where analytic queueing formulas suffice, or where data for inputs is unavailable.
whyLost: Simulation is an engineering skill; service design works with qualitative blueprints rather than quantitative models.
whereToUse: Hospital patient flow, contact centres, claims processing, airport and venue experiences, logistics.
example: An airport simulates a new biometric boarding process; the model shows queue lengths would increase at peak unless two self-service gates remain for passengers who fail face matching, a finding confirmed in the pilot.
