sources: Law, Simulation Modeling and Analysis (5th ed., 2015)
Robinson, Simulation: The Practice of Model Development and Use (2nd ed., 2014)
Scenario Analysis, Decision Trees and Simulation for Cost Benefit Analysis of Cargo Screening Processes (Sherman et al., 2010)
reference: Law, A. M. (2015). Simulation Modeling and Analysis (5th ed.). McGraw-Hill.

name: Discrete-Time Event History (Hazard) Analysis
origin: Paul Allison, 1982; Judith Singer and John Willett, 2003
summary: Models the probability that an event such as churn happens in each week, session or step, given it has not happened yet, with logistic regression on person-period data.
description: Ordinary regression on whether an event occurred within a fixed window wastes information and mishandles censoring. Event history analysis models time to an event while respecting users still at risk when observation stops. When time is measured coarsely (weeks, billing cycles, sessions, funnel steps) or is intrinsically discrete, the natural quantity is the discrete-time hazard: the conditional probability of the event in period t given survival to t. Data are expanded to one row per user per period at risk, and a logistic regression with a separate intercept per period (or a smooth function of time) plus covariates is fitted with standard software; time-varying covariates enter naturally. If an underlying continuous proportional hazards process is assumed, a complementary log-log link is used instead. When per-period probabilities are below about .1, discrete and continuous results nearly coincide. Unobserved heterogeneity makes hazards appear to decline over time, so frailty or mixture extensions are worth checking.
steps: Define the state, the event (for example cancellation), the time origin, the period unit, the risk set and how censoring arises.
Expand the data to a person-period file with one record per user per period at risk, ending at the event or censoring.
Code the event indicator for each period and attach time-varying covariates (usage that week, price changes, support contacts).
Fit a logistic regression with period dummies or a smooth time function plus covariates; use a complementary log-log link if a continuous-time proportional hazards interpretation is wanted.
Interpret the baseline hazard shape and covariate odds or hazard ratios, and derive survival curves from the fitted hazards.
Check for unobserved heterogeneity with a frailty or mixture term and test sensitivity to period definitions.
outputs: Period-specific hazard estimates, covariate effects (odds or hazard ratios), and survival curves derived from the hazards.
useWhen: Churn, adoption, conversion or abandonment recorded per week, billing cycle, session or funnel step, especially with time-varying covariates and many ties.
avoidWhen: Time is measured precisely and continuously with few ties (use Cox proportional hazards); the event can recur many times (use count or recurrent-event models); censoring is informative. Logit and cloglog results diverge when per-period hazards are large.
whyLost: Product teams compute retention curves and fixed-window churn rates; the person-period approach from sociology and education research is rarely taught in product analytics.
whereToUse: Subscription churn by billing cycle, trial-to-paid conversion by day, step-by-step abandonment in onboarding or checkout, adoption timing of a new feature.
example: A meal-kit subscription builds a person-week file for 50,000 customers over 26 weeks. The hazard of cancelling peaks at weeks 2 and 5, and a skipped delivery in the previous week doubles the odds of cancelling, so the team targets interventions after skips in the first five weeks.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Singer, J. D., & Willett, J. B. (2003). Applied Longitudinal Data Analysis: Modeling Change and Event Occurrence. New York: Oxford University Press.

name: Discriminant loadings interpretation
origin: Fisher, 1936; structure coefficient interpretation in multivariate psychology (e.g. Huberty, 1994)
summary: Interprets which behavioural features drive a discriminant classifier by examining correlations between features and discriminant functions.
description: Discriminant analysis produces standardised coefficients (weights) and structure coefficients (correlations between each original variable and the discriminant function). Weights indicate unique contributions given other variables and are unstable under collinearity, while structure coefficients show how strongly each variable aligns with the separating dimension and are more robust for naming what the function represents. Interpreting both, alongside group centroids on each function, translates the model into a behavioural description of what distinguishes, for example, frustrated from calm sessions. Rigour involves bootstrapping loadings for stability, using a threshold such as absolute 0.3 for meaningful structure coefficients, and validating interpretations with qualitative review.
steps: Extract standardised discriminant coefficients and structure coefficients from the fitted LDA.
Treat structure coefficients with absolute values of 0.3 or more as meaningful contributors and rank them.
Compare weights with structure coefficients to spot suppression or collinearity effects.
Bootstrap loadings (e.g. 1,000 resamples) and report confidence intervals to assess stability.
Plot group centroids on discriminant functions and describe what high and low scores mean behaviourally.
Validate the interpretation by reviewing sessions with extreme discriminant scores.
outputs: A ranked, stability-checked description of the behaviours that separate groups and a behavioural interpretation of each discriminant function.
useWhen: After fitting a discriminant model, when design teams need to know which behaviours signal a state in order to act on them.
avoidWhen: Avoid over-interpreting weights under heavy collinearity, or loadings from models with poor cross-validated accuracy. Rencher (2002) cautions that structure coefficients are proportional to each variable's univariate F or t statistic, so they say nothing about a variable's contribution in the presence of the others; he recommends interpreting standardised discriminant coefficients (with partial F values) instead, so do not rank variables on structure coefficients alone.
whyLost: Discriminant analysis itself is rarely used in UX, and structure coefficient interpretation is a niche psychometric skill.
whereToUse: Frustration and confusion detection, churn-signal identification, explaining classifier logic to designers and compliance teams.
example: Structure coefficients for a frustration classifier show repeated order edits at 0.71 and back-navigation at 0.58, while time-on-screen is near zero. The design team targets the order editing flow rather than shortening screens.
sources: Pattern Classification (Richard Duda, Peter Hart & David Stork)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Peter Bruce, Andrew Bruce & Peter Gedeck)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 54 — Linear Discriminant Analysis & Behavioral Classification
reference: Huberty, C. J. (1994) Applied Discriminant Analysis. Wiley.

name: Discursive Psychology
origin: Jonathan Potter and Margaret Wetherell, 1987; Derek Edwards and Jonathan Potter, 1992
summary: Treats attitudes, emotions, memories and intentions as things people do in talk, analysing how psychological claims are constructed to accomplish actions rather than as reports of inner states.
description: Discursive Psychology (Potter & Wetherell; Edwards & Potter) applies discourse analytic methods to psychological topics. Its central move: treat psychological concepts — attitudes, emotions, intentions, memories, cognitive states — not as inner mental states that talk describes, but as constructions that talk performs. 'Being confused' is not a mental state that users experience and then report — it is something produced and managed in interaction. Applied to UX: discursive psychology reveals how users construct and manage the expression of confusion, frustration, satisfaction, and trust in interaction with researchers — and how these constructions are interactionally produced rather than simply reported.
steps: Collect naturally-occurring interaction data: Like CA, discursive psychology favours naturally-occurring talk over interview data, because interview data is already shaped by the interview interaction.

Action orientation analysis: For any psychological construction in the data ('I was confused'; 'It made me feel frustrated'), ask: what social action does this construction perform? It is not merely describing an inner state — it is doing something in the interaction.

Variability and consistency analysis: People are inconsistent in how they describe their attitudes and experiences across different contexts. This variability is not error — it is evidence that talk is action-oriented rather than state-reporting.

Accountability analysis: How do participants construct actions and events to be accountable — to make them understandable, justifiable, or defensible? These constructions reveal social norms about what counts as reasonable behaviour.
Avoid the lure of mentalism: The analyst's job is not to get behind the words to the 'real' inner state. The words, in their interactional context, are the data.
outputs: Analyses of how psychological claims function in talk, variability and accountability patterns, and implications for interpreting interview and feedback data.
useWhen: You need to understand how users construct complaints, praise, blame or attitudes in feedback, interviews and support conversations, or to critically interpret stated attitudes.
avoidWhen: You want to measure attitudes as stable traits; use validated scales. For turn-by-turn interaction structure, use Conversation Analysis.
whyLost: Its anti-cognitivist stance contradicts UX's assumption that interviews reveal inner needs and attitudes, so it remains a specialist approach in social psychology.
whereToUse: Support conversation analysis, complaint handling, interview data critique, community moderation, and AI assistant dialogue design.
example: Analysing support chats, a researcher shows that customers say 'I'm not angry, just disappointed' to construct themselves as reasonable before escalating. Agent scripts that acknowledge reasonableness de-escalate better than generic empathy lines.
sources: Mapping the Language of Racism (Wetherell & Potter)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Edwards, D. & Potter, J. (1992). Discursive Psychology. Sage.

name: Disjunction-effect triad test
aka: Disjunction-effect triad test (known versus unknown outcome)
origin: Tversky and Shafir (1992); Shafir and Tversky (1992)
summary: Pose one decision three ways (outcome known one way, known the other, still unknown) to show whether uncertainty itself, not the outcome, drives deferral or choice.
description: The sure-thing principle says that if you would take an action whatever an uncertain event's outcome, you should take it while the outcome is unknown. Tversky and Shafir showed people violate it. Students bought a discounted holiday whether they had passed or failed an exam, but when the result was pending most paid a fee to defer. A second gamble was accepted by 69% after a win and 59% after a loss, but only 36% when the first result was unknown. The triad test operationalises this: the same decision is presented under known-A, known-not-A and unknown versions, between subjects or within subjects spaced among fillers. A disjunction pattern (same action under both known outcomes, a different one when unknown) and paying for non-instrumental information show that uncertainty is driving behaviour, which points to design responses that resolve or reframe the pending event.
steps: Write the decision and the pending uncertain event that precedes it.
Create three versions: outcome known to be A, known to be not-A, and unknown.
Administer them between subjects, or within subjects spaced among filler items with the unknown version first.
Optionally offer a small fee or delay option to wait for or learn the outcome first.
Classify each person's triad and compare action shares across versions; count disjunction patterns and the rate of paying for information that does not change the choice.
Interpret with care: some deferral is rational when the outcome genuinely matters.
outputs: Action shares per version, the share of disjunction patterns, and the rate of paying for non-instrumental information.
useWhen: Users stall or defer at a decision point while something is pending (a price announcement, an approval, a delivery estimate) and you want to know whether the uncertainty itself causes the stall.
avoidWhen: When the pending outcome genuinely changes the best action, or the known versions are not credible to participants; then study the information need directly through interviews.
whyLost: It remains a classic paradigm in decision research; UX treats deferral as friction to be removed rather than testing its cause.
whereToUse: E-commerce purchase deferral, loan and insurance applications awaiting decisions, subscription upgrades before announcements, health decisions pending test results.
example: An electronics retailer suspects customers abandon laptop purchases before a rumoured price drop. A survey triad shows most would buy whether or not the drop happens, yet most click 'notify me' while it is pending, so the team adds a price-protection guarantee.
reference: Tversky, A. and Shafir, E. (1992). The disjunction effect in choice under uncertainty. Psychological Science, 3(5), 305-309.

name: Distributed Cognition Analysis
aka: Distributed Cognition Analysis for Collaborative Tools
origin: Edwin Hutchins, 1995
summary: Analyses how cognitive work is spread across people, artefacts and representations in a setting, revealing how information propagates and where it breaks.
description: Distributed cognition treats a socio-technical system, such as a ship's bridge, cockpit or ward, as the unit of cognitive analysis. Hutchins showed that tasks like navigation are accomplished by representations moving across people, instruments and paper, being transformed at each step. The method is cognitive ethnography: observing work in situ and tracing how information is represented, transformed and coordinated. Furniss and Blandford's DiCoT (Distributed Cognition for Teamwork) structures the analysis into models of information flow, physical layout and artefacts, each with principles such as subtle bodily supports or situation awareness. Rigour comes from tracing concrete representational states rather than generic tasks, grounding claims in observed episodes, and validating models with practitioners. It exposes why replacing a paper whiteboard with software can silently remove coordination functions.
steps: Define the functional system: the goal, the people, the artefacts and the space involved.
Conduct cognitive ethnography, observing at least several full shifts or work cycles and collecting artefacts.
Trace representational states as information moves between people and tools, noting each transformation.
Build DiCoT models: information flow, physical layout, artefact and social structure.
Identify breakdowns, workarounds and implicit coordination functions served by existing artefacts.
Validate models with practitioners and derive requirements that preserve or improve those functions in new designs.
outputs: Information flow, physical layout and artefact models; catalogue of coordination functions and breakdowns; design requirements.
useWhen: Redesigning team-based, safety-critical or collaborative work where information is shared across people and tools (control rooms, hospitals, trading floors, ops teams).
avoidWhen: Single-user consumer tasks with little coordination; contextual inquiry or task analysis is lighter.
whyLost: It is cited in HCI theory courses but demands long fieldwork and conceptual training, so it stays in academic CSCW and safety research.
whereToUse: Collaborative tools; cockpit/hospital UI; any multi-person workflow system.
example: A hospital replacing a ward whiteboard with a digital bed board ran a DiCoT analysis. It revealed nurses used the board's physical position for passing glances during handover, so the new system included a large wall display rather than desktop-only access.
sources: Cognition in the Wild — Edwin Hutchins (MIT Press)
Blandford & Furniss, DiCoT: a methodology for applying Distributed Cognition to the design of teamworking systems (2006)
Distributed Cognition: Toward a New Foundation for HCI (Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 14 — Distributed Cognition & Cognitive Ecosystems
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. MIT Press.

name: Divergent thinking tests (Alternative Uses, Torrance)
aka: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking and divergent production
Alternate uses task with originality scoring
Incubation design with the alternate uses task
origin: J. P. Guilford, 1950s-1967; E. Paul Torrance, 1966
summary: People list as many uses as they can for an everyday object, scored for fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration, giving a behavioural measure of idea generation.
description: Guilford argued that intelligence tests reward convergent thinking and miss divergent thinking. His Alternative Uses Test asks people to list uses for a common object (brick, paper clip, toothpick); the Consequences Test asks what would follow from an unlikely event. Responses are scored for fluency (number of valid ideas), flexibility (number of categories), originality (statistical rarity) and elaboration (detail). In one scoring scheme, a use given by only 5 percent of the sample scores 1 point and by only 1 percent scores 2. Torrance's tests added figural tasks and became the standard battery. The task is widely used as an outcome measure: in incubation designs, a baseline task, a 12-minute break with an easy or hard filler, then a repeat showed about 40 percent improvement after the easy filler; walking also raised output.
steps: Pick two or three everyday objects of similar familiarity, or a consequences prompt.
Give a fixed time per object (2 minutes is common) and ask for as many different uses as possible.
Score fluency as the count of valid, non-duplicate responses.
Score flexibility by grouping responses into use categories and counting categories.
Score originality by rarity in the sample (for example 1 point for uses given by 5 percent or fewer, 2 for 1 percent or fewer) and elaboration by detail, with two raters.
For incubation or tool comparisons, run a baseline, the manipulation (for example a 12-minute break or an AI assistant), then a repeat on the same or matched objects.
Report the four scores separately and compare conditions.
outputs: Fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration scores per participant and condition, and change scores for incubation designs.
useWhen: Testing whether a tool, workshop format, prompt, break structure or AI assistant helps people produce more and more varied ideas, instead of relying on self-rated creativity.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating divergent thinking as all of creativity, which also needs usefulness; fluency dominates the other scores, and originality depends on the reference sample. For idea quality use expert rating.
whyLost: It is entrenched in creativity psychometrics and education but almost never used to evaluate design tools or workshop formats.
whereToUse: Generative AI writing and design tools, brainstorming software, workshop facilitation, edtech.
example: An ideation board is tested with and without AI suggestions: two groups run the uses task on the same objects, and the AI group scores higher on fluency but lower on originality, as ideas converge on the model's suggestions.
sources: Guilford, J. P. (1967). The Nature of Human Intelligence. McGraw-Hill
reference: Guilford, J. P. (1967). The Nature of Human Intelligence. New York: McGraw-Hill.

name: Dix Usability Principles Review (Learnability, Flexibility, Robustness)
aka: Usability principles: learnability, flexibility and robustness
origin: Dix, Finlay, Abowd and Beale (1993; 3rd ed. 2004), drawing partly on Thimbleby's principles
summary: Use an extendable catalogue of usability principles grouped as learnability, flexibility and robustness to write usability specifications and to inspect designs, recording findings by principle.
description: Dix and colleagues organise usability principles into three groups. Learnability covers predictability, synthesizability, familiarity, generalisability and consistency. Flexibility covers dialogue initiative, multi-threading, task migratability between user and system, substitutivity and customisability (adaptability and adaptivity). Robustness covers observability, recoverability, responsiveness and task conformance. The catalogue is used in three ways: to turn selected principles into usability specification attributes with now, worst, planned and best levels; as criteria in design rationale (for example QOC); and as inspection criteria for a design or prototype. Its value is that each principle has defined sub-properties and theoretical grounding, so conflicts between principles can be reasoned about rather than resolved by taste, unlike a flat heuristic list.
steps: Identify the tasks the product must support.
Select from the three groups the principles that matter for those tasks.
State each selected principle as a usability specification attribute (measuring concept, method, now, worst, planned and best levels) or as a criterion in a QOC design rationale.
Inspect the design or evaluate a prototype against the selected principles, recording each violation under its principle.
Where principles conflict, use the theory behind each to decide the trade-off and record the reasoning.
outputs: Usability requirements and specification attributes, a design-rationale criteria set, or inspection findings classed by principle.
useWhen: Early in design when detail is thin and you need principled requirements, or when an inspection should be organised around learnability, flexibility and robustness rather than a generic heuristic list.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for testing with users; the principles are abstract and often conflict, and specifications derived from them can set unrealistic targets. For a quick, widely understood inspection use Heuristic Evaluation; for measurable targets use Usability Specification and UX Targets.
whyLost: It lives in HCI textbooks and teaching, while practice settled on Nielsen's heuristics and Shneiderman's golden rules, so the catalogue is seldom applied as a working tool.
whereToUse: Complex productivity tools, configurable enterprise software, adaptive and AI-driven interfaces where task migratability and customisability matter.
example: A team designing an AI scheduling assistant writes a task migratability attribute for setting up a weekly meeting: now, the user enters it every week; planned, no more than 1.5 times a single entry; best, one entry delegated to the assistant. The inspection then logs two recoverability violations in the undo flow.
reference: Dix, A., Finlay, J., Abowd, G. D. and Beale, R. (2004). Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed.). Harlow: Pearson Education, pp. 259-274.

name: Document Analysis Protocol
donor: Sociology, history and case study research
origin: Established in social research methods; systematised by Glenn Bowen (2009) and in case study research (Yin)
summary: Systematically catalogues and analyses organisational documents for provenance, completeness and contradictions, revealing official process and the gaps between documents and practice.
description: Documents such as policies, procedures, training manuals, forms, tickets and internal wikis are evidence of how an organisation says work should happen and of the assumptions behind it. Document analysis treats them as data, not background reading. The protocol inventories all relevant documents, distinguishing primary from secondary sources, and assesses provenance: who wrote each document, when, for whom and for what purpose. It checks completeness by asking which documents should exist but do not, compares documents to find contradictions, and applies content analysis to key texts. Documents are then triangulated with interviews and observation. Its rigour lies in source criticism: no document is taken at face value, and silences are as informative as content.
steps: Document inventory: Catalogue all relevant documents. Distinguish primary (created by participants in the phenomenon) from secondary (created by observers). Each type requires different analytical treatment.
Provenance analysis: For each document: who created it, when, for what purpose, for what audience? Provenance shapes what can and cannot be concluded.
Completeness assessment: What documents should exist based on the processes you are studying? Which are missing? Missing documents are often as informative as present ones.
Cross-document comparison: Where do different documents contradict each other? Contradictions mark where official accounts diverge from practical reality.
Language analysis: Apply manifest and latent content analysis to key documents.
outputs: A document inventory with provenance notes, a completeness assessment, a cross-document contradiction log, coded content, and questions to pursue in fieldwork.
useWhen: Starting research in an enterprise, government or regulated domain, preparing for contextual inquiry, auditing a service, or reconstructing how a process is supposed to work.
avoidWhen: Documents are sparse or the question concerns individual experience; use interviews. Never use document analysis alone to describe actual practice; pair it with observation.
whyLost: Desk research in UX became a quick skim of competitor sites and analytics, and systematic source criticism remained a historian's and sociologist's skill.
whereToUse: Public sector service design, healthcare and financial compliance processes, enterprise software replacements, policy-driven products, and research repository audits.
example: Before redesigning a benefits application, researchers analyse 27 policy documents, guidance notes and form versions. They find three contradictory definitions of 'household', explaining why caseworkers and applicants report inconsistent outcomes.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
reference: Bowen, G. A. (2009). Document analysis as a qualitative research method. Qualitative Research Journal, 9(2), 27-40.

name: Documentary Method of Interpretation
origin: Karl Mannheim, 1920s; developed as an empirical method by Ralf Bohnsack, 1980s to 1990s
summary: Distinguishes what participants explicitly say from the implicit, taken-for-granted orientations their way of talking reveals, using formulating and reflecting interpretation plus systematic comparison.
description: The Documentary Method of Interpretation (Ralf Bohnsack, developed from Karl Mannheim's sociology of knowledge) distinguishes between two levels of meaning: the communicative meaning (what is explicitly said or shown) and the documentary meaning (the implicit orientations, habitual practices, and taken-for-granted frameworks that are enacted in communication without being directly said). The method has been applied to interview data, group discussions, and visual data. It is particularly valuable for UX research where the explicit content of what users say differs systematically from what their behaviour and interaction reveals about their underlying orientations.
steps: Formulaic interpretation: Identify the topic — what is explicitly communicated? Paraphrase without interpretation.

Reflective interpretation: How is the topic addressed? What is the mode of discussion — narrative, argumentation, description, evaluation? What does the form of expression reveal about the speaker's implicit orientation?

Comparative analysis: Compare how different participants, groups, or interviews address the same topic. Where the topic is the same but the mode of addressing it differs, the difference reveals different orientations.

Sinusoid of experience: Identify the arc of a topic discussion — when does it become animated? When does it go flat? Heightened engagement reveals what matters to participants at the level of orientation, not just stated preference.

Validation through contrast: Validate your interpretation of a group's orientation by identifying contrast cases — groups or individuals who do not share that orientation. The contrast makes the orientation visible.
outputs: Formulating and reflecting interpretations, comparative case analyses, reconstructed orientation frameworks, and typologies of implicit orientations across groups.
useWhen: Explicit statements and actual practice diverge, or you need to understand implicit orientations shared within groups, such as teams, households or professions, especially from group discussions.
avoidWhen: You need quick thematic summaries or explicit opinions; use thematic analysis. It requires training and time, so avoid on tight timelines.
whyLost: It is taught mainly in German-language sociology and education research, with limited English-language guidance until recently.
whereToUse: Team and workplace tool adoption, household technology use, professional cultures (clinicians, engineers), and group discussions in strategy research.
example: In group discussions with finance teams, everyone explicitly endorses automation, but the way they recount month-end close emphasises personal checking. The reconstructed orientation of 'accountability through touch' explains low trust in auto-reconciliation.
sources: How to Analyse Interviews: A Documentary Method of Interpretation (arxiv)
reference: Bohnsack, R., Pfaff, N. & Weller, W. (eds.) (2010). Qualitative Analysis and Documentary Method in International Educational Research. Barbara Budrich.

name: Documentation Usability Testing
origin: Joseph Dumas and Janice Redish, 1993 (revised 1999)
summary: Test documentation either by instructing participants to use it, to judge its quality, or by merely making it available, to see whether and when it is used.
description: When manuals, tutorials or online help are part of a usability test, the team must first decide which question it is asking, because one session cannot answer both. To learn how well documentation works, participants are instructed to go through the tutorial or use the manual, which yields findings on design, content, organisation and language but is unrealistic. To learn whether people use documentation, participants are given tasks and only told it is available; if few use it, little is learned about revising it. A third option mirrors real delivery, for example omitting a manual few customers would receive and providing a help-desk number, then observing where people get stuck and when they seek help. Findings about the product will always emerge and must be reported, since documentation and software problems are inseparable.
steps: Decide whether the question is the quality of the documentation or whether people use it.
For quality: instruct participants to work through the tutorial or use the manual for set tasks.
For use: give tasks and only mention that documentation is available.
Alternatively mirror real delivery (omit material users would not get; provide help-desk or chat access).
Observe where people get stuck, what they consult and when they seek assistance.
Report findings on both documentation and product, noting which question the set-up answered.
outputs: Problems in documentation content, organisation and language, or data on whether and when users consult help, plus product problems.
useWhen: Products whose success depends on tutorials, help centres, manuals or in-app guidance, and redesigns of help content.
avoidWhen: When you need to evaluate the product alone; documentation in the room changes behaviour. For document comprehension without tasks, use Protocol-Aided Document Evaluation (Schriver).
whyLost: Technical communication and UX drifted apart, and help content is now often measured through analytics rather than tested.
whereToUse: Developer documentation, SaaS help centres, onboarding tours, medical device instructions for use and assembly instructions.
example: A developer platform tests its quick-start guide by instructing eight developers to follow it. Six stall at authentication, and a separate session with docs merely available shows most never open the guide at all.
sources: A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish, 1999)
reference: Dumas, J.S. and Redish, J.C. (1999) A Practical Guide to Usability Testing, revised edition. Exeter: Intellect.

name: Dominance Analysis for the Relative Importance of Predictors
origin: David Budescu, 1993; Razia Azen and David Budescu, 2003; related to Lindeman, Merenda and Gold, 1980
summary: Ranks predictors by comparing their added contribution to R-squared across all subset models, giving complete, conditional and general dominance that sums to the full-model R-squared.
description: Key-driver questions ask which attributes matter most, yet standardised regression weights are not importance measures: with correlated predictors, suppressor effects can make an important driver look trivial or even negative. Budescu defined importance by contribution to fit, compared directly between pairs of predictors across all subset models. Predictor X completely dominates Y if it adds more to R-squared in every subset model containing neither. Because complete dominance can leave pairs unranked, Azen and Budescu added conditional dominance (mean added contribution within each model size) and general dominance (the average of those means across sizes). General dominance values partition the full-model R-squared, which makes them easy to report as shares of explained variance, and they coincide with the Lindeman, Merenda and Gold (Shapley-value) decomposition. In exploratory work, criticality analysis complements this by bootstrapping how often a predictor appears in the best subset models.
steps: Fit all 2^p - 1 subset regressions of the outcome on the p candidate drivers and record each R-squared (practical up to about 15-20 predictors).
For each predictor and each subset not containing it, compute its added contribution to R-squared.
Compare every pair across all subsets that contain neither to establish complete dominance where it holds.
Average contributions within each model size for conditional dominance, then across sizes for general dominance; check general dominance sums to the full R-squared.
Bootstrap the analysis (for example 1,000 resamples) to show how often each dominance relation and rank reproduces.
Report the dominance matrix and the R-squared shares, stating that importance is relative to this predictor set.
outputs: Pairwise dominance matrix (complete, conditional, general), an R-squared decomposition across predictors, and bootstrap reproducibility of ranks.
useWhen: Key-driver analysis of satisfaction, NPS or adoption on correlated attribute ratings where you need a defensible ranking of drivers rather than raw regression weights.
avoidWhen: Many predictors (computation grows as 2^p; use random forest or SHAP-based importance); non-linear or interaction-heavy relationships; when you need causal effects rather than shares of explained variance. Results change if the predictor set changes.
whyLost: Market-research tools offer it as relative weights or Shapley regression, but UX driver analyses usually stop at standardised betas or correlations.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and loyalty driver studies, feature importance for prioritisation, NPS verbatim-coded drivers, and checking whether a driver ranking is stable before a roadmap decision.
example: A telecom app regresses overall satisfaction on ratings of speed, billing clarity, support and design. Betas suggest design is irrelevant, but dominance analysis gives design 18% of R-squared because it overlaps with speed; billing clarity completely dominates support in every subset model.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Budescu, D. V. (1993). Dominance analysis: A new approach to the problem of relative importance of predictors in multiple regression. Psychological Bulletin, 114, 542-551.

name: Double Diamond
origin: UK Design Council, 2005
summary: A process model that alternates divergent and convergent phases, first on the problem (discover, define) then on the solution (develop, deliver), to plan and communicate research.
description: The Double Diamond, published by the UK Design Council in 2005 after studying design processes in leading companies, describes design as two diamonds. In the first, teams diverge to discover the problem space through research, then converge to define a clear problem. In the second, they diverge to develop multiple solutions, then converge to deliver a tested solution. The 2019 update framed it within a wider 'framework for innovation' with principles and methods. As a research planning tool, its value lies in making explicit which phase a project is in and which methods suit it: generative research in Discover, synthesis in Define, ideation and prototyping in Develop, evaluation in Deliver. Rigour comes from defined exit criteria for each phase, so teams do not skip problem definition.
steps: Map the project onto the four phases and agree what evidence is needed to leave each one.
In Discover, run generative research (interviews, observation, data review) to widen understanding.
In Define, synthesise findings into a clear problem statement and success criteria.
In Develop, generate and prototype multiple solution concepts.
In Deliver, test, refine and launch the chosen solution, measuring against the success criteria.
Loop back to earlier phases when evidence shows the problem was mis-defined.
outputs: Phased research plan, problem definition, concept portfolio, tested solution, shared process vocabulary for stakeholders.
useWhen: Scoping projects, planning research across a programme, and aligning stakeholders on when to explore versus decide.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for actual methods; it structures work but does not tell you how to do research.
whyLost: Still in use: Intuitive visualization of design process; useful for stakeholder communication.
whereToUse: Design process communication; project scoping; team alignment.
example: A fintech research lead used the Double Diamond to show executives that a requested feature build had skipped Define. Two weeks of discovery reframed the problem from 'add budgeting' to 'reduce overdraft surprises', changing the roadmap.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
From Hype to Practice (Jylkäs et al., 2019)
reference: Design Council (2005). The 'double diamond' design process model. Design Council, London.

name: Double Machine Learning
origin: Victor Chernozhukov, Denis Chetverikov, Mert Demirer, Esther Duflo, Christian Hansen, Whitney Newey and James Robins (2018)
summary: Estimates a causal effect from observational data with many confounders by using flexible ML to partial out confounding, with valid inference via cross-fitting.
description: With rich observational data, analysts often regress outcomes on treatment plus many controls, or use ML predictions naively, both of which bias estimates. DML fits ML models for the outcome given covariates and for the treatment given covariates, then regresses the residualised outcome on the residualised treatment. Neyman orthogonality makes the estimate insensitive to small errors in the ML models, and cross-fitting avoids overfitting bias, so standard errors are valid. It still relies on no unmeasured confounding, so it pairs with DAG reasoning and sensitivity analysis. For UX analytics with hundreds of behavioural features, it is a principled upgrade on 'controlled for everything' regressions.
steps: Draw a DAG and choose covariates that block backdoor paths; exclude mediators and colliders.
Split data into K folds (typically 5) for cross-fitting.
In each fold, fit flexible models (e.g. gradient boosting) for outcome and treatment on covariates using the other folds.
Compute residuals and regress outcome residuals on treatment residuals to estimate the effect.
Aggregate across folds and compute robust standard errors.
Run sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding and compare with simpler estimators.
outputs: A debiased causal effect estimate with confidence interval and sensitivity analysis.
useWhen: Observational analysis with many potential confounders and enough data, such as feature usage effects on retention.
avoidWhen: Small samples, unmeasured key confounders, or when an experiment can be run.
whyLost: It is new and technically demanding, and UX analytics often stops at correlation.
whereToUse: Product analytics, marketplace analytics, health app engagement effects, support channel effects.
example: A marketplace estimates the effect of seller response time on sales. DML with 300 behavioural covariates reduces the naive estimate by half, informing a realistic target for seller tools.
sources: Chernozhukov et al., Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters (2018), Econometrics Journal
reference: Chernozhukov, V., et al. (2018). The Econometrics Journal, 21(1), C1-C68.

name: Doubly robust estimation
origin: James Robins, Andrea Rotnitzky and Lue Ping Zhao, 1994; Bang and Robins, 2005
summary: Combining an outcome model with a propensity model so the causal effect estimate is consistent if either model is correctly specified.
description: Doubly robust estimators such as AIPW combine regression adjustment (modelling the outcome) with inverse probability weighting (modelling treatment assignment). If either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct, the estimate is consistent, giving two chances to get it right. Modern versions use machine learning for both nuisance models with cross-fitting (double/debiased machine learning, Chernozhukov et al., 2018) to avoid overfitting bias, and allow heterogeneous effect estimation by segment. Rigour comes from a DAG-based covariate set, overlap checks and weight trimming, cross-fitting, and reporting the estimate alongside simpler estimators and a sensitivity analysis. It cannot fix unmeasured confounding.
steps: Specify the causal question, time zero and DAG-based confounder set.
Fit a propensity model and an outcome model, using flexible learners (e.g. gradient boosting) where appropriate.
Use 5-fold cross-fitting so each unit's nuisance predictions come from models not trained on it (econml or causalml).
Check overlap and trim or truncate propensity scores outside about 0.01 to 0.99.
Compute the AIPW or DML estimate with robust or bootstrap confidence intervals.
Compare with regression-only and weighting-only estimates, examine heterogeneity by segment, and add an E-value sensitivity analysis.
outputs: An average treatment effect with CI, comparisons with single-model estimators, optional segment-level effects and sensitivity results.
useWhen: High-stakes observational effect estimation with many covariates and large logs, where modelling mistakes are likely and an experiment was not run.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small samples (under a few hundred per arm), poor overlap or unmeasured key confounders; use experiments or simpler, transparent methods.
whyLost: Used by causal data scientists in large tech and health organisations but not by UX researchers, who lack the statistical training and data access.
whereToUse: Large-scale SaaS and marketplace feature evaluation, fintech risk features, health programme impact and personalisation effect heterogeneity.
example: A marketplace estimates the effect of a seller analytics dashboard on sales. With 60 covariates and 25,000 sellers, a cross-fitted AIPW estimate shows a 6% lift (CI 3-9%), consistent with matching but with tighter intervals, and larger for new sellers.
sources: Robins, J. M., Rotnitzky, A. & Zhao, L. P. (1994) Estimation of regression coefficients when some regressors are not always observed. JASA
Chernozhukov, V. et al. (2018) Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. Econometrics Journal
Hernán, M. A. & Robins, J. M. (2020) Causal Inference: What If
The Inquiry Series, C5 — Causal Inference in Python — DAGs, Target Trial Emulation & Sensitivity Analysis
reference: Bang, H. & Robins, J. M. (2005) Doubly robust estimation in missing data and causal inference models. Biometrics 61(4)

name: Draw-a-Scientist / Draw-an-Engineer Test
origin: Child study drawings (Ricci 1887, Barnes 1892); Draw-a-Scientist Test (Chambers 1983); Draw-an-Engineer Test (Cunningham and Knight 2004); applied by Ganesh
summary: Ask people to imagine and draw a person in a role at work, answer short written prompts, and code drawings and answers together to reveal conceptions and stereotypes.
description: A structured drawing elicitation from science education. Participants close their eyes, imagine a person in a role (scientist, engineer) at work, then draw what they imagined and answer short prompts: what the person is doing, three words that come to mind, and three things they do on a typical day. Staff avoid discussing the role beforehand. The drawing and written answers are coded as one unit, starting from broad categories such as gender of the figure, whether it is in action and what tools appear, then building cross-cutting concepts with open and axial coding. Repeating the task before, during and after an intervention shows whether conceptions shift, and image-elicitation interviews check interpretations. Adapted as draw-a-user or draw-a-role, it surfaces how customers or teams picture a role, a user or an AI system. Coders' own backgrounds and media imagery shape readings.
steps: Allow 20-30 minutes and avoid discussing the role beforehand; staff only clarify instructions.
Prompt: close your eyes and imagine a [role] at work; open your eyes and draw what you imagined.
Ask for written answers: what the person is doing (two or more sentences), three words or phrases that come to mind, three things they do on a typical day.
Repeat at several points (before, during, after) if change is of interest.
Code drawing and text as one unit, starting with broad categories (gender of figure, action, tools, setting), then memo and build axial codes.
Confirm interpretations with short image-elicitation interviews and compare across time points.
outputs: Categories of how people picture a role and how these shift, with frequencies and illustrative drawings.
useWhen: You want to surface tacit images and stereotypes of a role, a typical user or a technology, especially with children or where verbal answers would be socially desirable.
avoidWhen: When you need people's model of how a system works rather than who uses it; use Icon-based mental model drawing survey. Avoid over-reading individual drawings without the written answers and follow-up.
whyLost: It is a staple of science education research but has rarely been described as a UX method.
whereToUse: Persona and audience assumptions inside teams, perceptions of AI assistants, STEM and education products, recruitment and careers products.
example: Before redesigning an AI assistant's persona, a team asks 60 users to draw 'the assistant helping you'; most draw a human secretary at a desk, which reshapes the assistant's tone and onboarding.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Ganesh, T. G. 'Children-produced drawings: an interpretive and analytical tool for researchers', in Margolis, E. and Pauwels, L. (eds.) (2011) The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods. London: SAGE.

name: Drift Diffusion Modelling of Decisions
origin: Roger Ratcliff, 1978
summary: Fits choice and full response-time distributions to separate the quality of evidence, caution, bias and non-decision time behind users' decisions.
description: The drift diffusion model treats a two-choice decision as noisy evidence accumulating toward one of two boundaries. Its parameters have psychological meaning: drift rate (how clear the evidence is), boundary separation (how cautious the user is), starting point (prior bias toward one option) and non-decision time (perception and motor). Fitting the model to accuracy and the full RT distributions, rather than mean RT, disentangles explanations that look identical in averages. For UX, it answers whether a design makes information clearer (higher drift), makes users more careful (wider boundary), or biases them (starting point), which is directly relevant to defaults, warnings and dark-pattern assessment.
steps: Design a two-choice task representing the real decision (e.g. accept/reject a suggestion, safe/phishing).
Collect many trials per participant (ideally 100+ per condition) with precise RT logging.
Clean data by removing implausibly fast responses (e.g. < 200 ms) and extreme slow outliers.
Fit the DDM with established tools (e.g. HDDM, fast-dm, or EZ-diffusion for quick estimates).
Compare parameters across design conditions using hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
Interpret: drift changes imply clearer information, boundary changes imply caution, starting-point shifts imply bias or nudging.
outputs: Estimated drift, boundary, bias and non-decision parameters per condition, with posterior comparisons.
useWhen: Evaluating how warnings, defaults, layouts or AI suggestions change rapid binary decisions, and distinguishing clarity from bias.
avoidWhen: Slow deliberative decisions or multi-option choices without adaptations; too few trials per person.
whyLost: It requires many trials and mathematical psychology expertise. UX reports mean task time or conversion, which conflates mechanisms.
whereToUse: Security warnings, content moderation tools, AI suggestion acceptance, cookie consent and default design.
example: A phishing warning redesign speeds decisions. DDM shows the speedup comes from higher drift (clearer evidence) rather than lower boundary (carelessness), supporting the redesign as genuinely better.
sources: Ratcliff, A theory of memory retrieval (1978), Psychological Review
Ratcliff & McKoon, The diffusion decision model: theory and data for two-choice decision tasks (2008), Neural Computation
Wiecki, Sofer & Frank, HDDM (2013), Frontiers in Neuroinformatics
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
reference: Ratcliff, R., & McKoon, G. (2008). The diffusion decision model. Neural Computation, 20(4), 873-922.

name: DriftScore (Behavioral Drift Score)
donor: Product analytics and composite index construction
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A 0–1 composite of normalised entropy, CTR, diversity and attention-decay signals, weighted by regression, where higher values mean greater risk that a user is drifting.
description: The DriftScore combines normalised telemetry signals into a single risk index: DriftScore = w1(1 − entropy_norm) + w2(1 − ctr_norm) + w3(1 − diversity_norm) + w4(attention_decay). Signals are normalised to [0,1] with higher meaning more engagement, then inverted where needed so higher scores mean more drift risk. Weights are set by regression or optimisation. In the e-commerce case with weights [0.4, 0.3, 0.3], P1 (entropy 1.0, CTR 0.18, 2 categories) scores 0.72 and P3 (0.9, 0.12, 1 category) 0.81, both drifting, while P2 (2.2, 0.44, 5 categories) scores 0.38. An action threshold is suggested, such as Score ≥ 0.50 for 2 consecutive weeks. The score's rigour comes from transparent components that map back to Honeycomb dimensions, and it is the objective that adaptive interventions and Thompson Sampling try to reduce.
steps: Select drift signals from telemetry: interaction entropy, recommendation or promo CTR, category or feature diversity, and attention decay (scroll depth, dwell).
Normalise each signal to [0,1] with higher meaning more engagement, then convert to risk (1 − entropy_norm, 1 − ctr_norm, 1 − diversity_norm, attention_decay).
Estimate weights via regression or optimisation against a later outcome such as churn or disengagement (examples use [0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.25] or [0.4, 0.3, 0.3]).
Compute the weighted sum per user per period.
Apply an action threshold, e.g. intervene if Score ≥ 0.50 for 2 consecutive weeks.
Use the score as the objective for adaptive interventions and A/B validation, and pair high scorers with interviews or diaries to confirm the mechanism.
outputs: Per-user drift risk scores, a ranked list of drifting users, and a trackable objective for interventions.
useWhen: When you need an operational early-warning metric for engagement erosion that product teams can monitor and act on.
avoidWhen: When signals are sparse or weights cannot be estimated; a hand-tuned score without validation can mislabel engaged but focused users.
whyLost: Original metric by Vivek Gopinath; most engagement scores reward frequency and miss narrowing behaviour.
whereToUse: E-commerce and OTT personalisation, CRM triggers, subscription retention, in-app re-onboarding.
example: An e-commerce team flags users whose DriftScore exceeds 0.50 for two weeks and routes them to a short tour of neglected categories, then tracks score reduction in an A/B test.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 44 — Survival Analysis, Longitudinal Design & Behavioral Drift
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Detecting Behavioral Drift, Section 5.3 and Appendix Worked Example B.

name: Dual-task performance testing
origin: Dual-task methods from Kahneman, Attention and Effort, 1973; secondary-task workload measurement in aviation human factors (Ogden et al., 1979)
summary: Measures the mental workload of a primary task by how much performance on a concurrent secondary task drops, giving an objective index of spare capacity.
description: If a primary task consumes most available capacity, performance on a secondary task, such as responding to a tone or a peripheral light, will degrade. Dual-task testing exploits this: it measures secondary task response time or accuracy while users perform the primary task under different designs, and compares against a single-task baseline. The difference indexes workload; designs that leave more spare capacity are less demanding. A detection response task (DRT, ISO 17488) standardises this for driving. The method can also test whether two real tasks can be performed together. Rigour requires choosing a secondary task that draws on the relevant resources, checking that primary task performance is maintained, and counterbalancing.
steps: Define the primary task and design variants to compare.
Choose a secondary task matched to the resources in question, such as a detection response task (respond to a vibration or light every 3-5 s).
Measure single-task baselines for both tasks for each participant.
Run dual-task conditions with 12-24 participants, counterbalanced, instructing them to prioritise the primary task.
Compute dual-task costs (secondary response time increase and miss rate) and check primary task performance did not drop.
Compare designs and set workload thresholds; for example, ISO 17488 DRT results are interpreted relative to reference tasks.
outputs: Single and dual-task performance data, dual-task cost per design, and a workload comparison between designs.
useWhen: When comparing designs for workload in demanding contexts like driving, surgery or control rooms, or when subjective workload scales seem insensitive.
avoidWhen: When tasks are low workload or a secondary task would be unsafe; use NASA-TLX or physiological measures instead.
whyLost: Well established in automotive and aviation human factors but largely absent in mainstream UX, which relies on self-report.
whereToUse: In-vehicle infotainment, surgical consoles, AR headsets, voice interfaces, and cockpits.
example: During simulated suturing, surgeons respond to a vibrotactile detection task with a 380 ms baseline. Using the current alert panel raises it to 720 ms; a simplified panel brings it to 480 ms, indicating substantially more spare capacity.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
reference: International Organization for Standardization (2016). ISO 17488: Road vehicles, transport information and control systems, detection-response task (DRT) for assessing attentional effects of cognitive load in driving.

name: Dynamic assessment
aka: Dynamic assessment: aided versus unaided performance in the zone of proximal development
origin: Lev Vygotsky, 1978 (zone of proximal development); Lidz and Elliott, 2000
summary: Measure performance alone, then with graded help, and treat the gap and the help needed as evidence of learning potential, not just current level.
description: Static tests measure what someone can do unaided. Dynamic assessment, built on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, also measures what they can do with graduated help: hints, prompts or collaboration given in a fixed sequence from least to most explicit. Two people with the same unaided score can reach very different levels with help, and the amount and kind of help needed says how close they are to independent mastery. The method measures process as well as product. In UX terms it turns 'did they complete the task?' into 'how much help did they need, of what kind, and did they then manage alone?', which is a direct measure of learnability and of what support an interface should give.
steps: Measure unaided performance on a set of tasks.
Define a graded hint sequence for each task, from general prompts to explicit demonstration (for example four levels).
Repeat or continue the tasks, giving hints one level at a time only when the participant is stuck.
Record the highest level reached and the number and level of hints needed.
Test transfer: give a related task unaided to see whether the help was internalised.
Report the gap between aided and unaided performance alongside the unaided score.
outputs: Unaided scores, hint counts and levels per task, aided-unaided gap, and transfer performance.
useWhen: Evaluating learnability, onboarding and in-product help, or deciding what level of guidance different users need, especially for complex or professional tools.
avoidWhen: Avoid when only completion rates are needed for benchmarking; standard moderated usability testing is cheaper. Hints change behaviour, so do not mix aided data with unaided benchmarks.
whyLost: It is established in special education and psychological assessment but rarely appears in UX, where moderators are trained not to help.
whereToUse: Professional and expert tools, edtech, accessibility and cognitive-impairment research, onboarding and help-system design, AI copilots.
example: Analysts using a new query builder are tested unaided, then with four graded hints. Most need only the second hint to succeed and then manage the next task alone, so the team builds that hint into contextual help.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in Society. Harvard University Press
reference: Lidz, C. S., & Elliott, J. G. (Eds.) (2000). Dynamic Assessment: Prevailing Models and Applications. Amsterdam: JAI/Elsevier.

name: Early-Warning Signals of Critical Transitions
origin: Marten Scheffer, Stephen Carpenter and colleagues (2009, Nature); Vasilis Dakos et al. (2012)
summary: Detects rising autocorrelation, variance and slower recovery in a time series as signs that a system is approaching a tipping point, such as collapse of engagement.
description: Ecologists found that systems near a bifurcation recover more slowly from small perturbations, a phenomenon called critical slowing down. This appears in time series as rising lag-1 autocorrelation, rising variance and sometimes skewness or flickering, before a regime shift such as a lake turning turbid or a fishery collapsing. Rolling-window analysis with trend tests (Kendall's tau) and surrogate data provides statistical evidence. Applied at the level of individual users or communities, these indicators may warn that engagement, community health or a habit is losing resilience before it collapses, giving a theory-grounded alternative to opaque churn prediction.
steps: Select time series that represent system state (e.g. daily activity of a community, a user's weekly usage).
Detrend or filter the series (e.g. Gaussian kernel) to remove long-term trends.
Compute rolling-window indicators: lag-1 autocorrelation, variance, skewness.
Test for rising trends with Kendall's tau and compare with surrogate series to assess significance.
Validate on historical cases: do indicators rise before known collapses (churn, community death)?
Use validated indicators for monitoring and target resilience-building interventions.
outputs: Rolling indicator trends, statistical tests of early warnings, validation results and monitoring rules.
useWhen: Monitoring systems that can tip, such as online communities, habits, marketplaces, or individual engagement.
avoidWhen: Short, noisy series or systems driven by abrupt external shocks without approach to a tipping point.
whyLost: The method is recent and confined to ecology, climate and psychiatry research.
whereToUse: Community platforms, multiplayer games, habit-based apps, mental health apps, marketplaces.
example: A forum platform finds that in subreddits which later died, lag-1 autocorrelation of daily posts rose for 8 weeks before decline. A moderator alert based on this indicator enables early intervention.
sources: Scheffer et al., Early-warning signals for critical transitions (2009), Nature
Dakos et al., Methods for detecting early warnings of critical transitions in time series (2012), PLoS ONE
Scheffer, Critical Transitions in Nature and Society (2009)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Scheffer, M., et al. (2009). Nature, 461(7260), 53-59.

name: Ease-of-retrieval check
donor: Judgement and decision making; social psychology
origin: Schwarz, Bless, Strack and colleagues (1991); Schwarz and Vaughn (2002)
summary: Checks whether asking respondents to recall few or many examples changes their later global judgements, because people use the felt difficulty of recall as information.
description: A recall task yields two things: the recalled content and the experience of how easy or hard recall was. Listing many examples is hard, so people infer that the behaviour or attitude is rarer or weaker, reversing what content alone would predict: people asked for twelve examples of their own assertiveness rate themselves less assertive than those asked for six. The effect is discounted when the experience is attributed to something else, and is used more for judgements of low personal relevance. The same mechanism undermines debiasing: listing ten alternative outcomes raised hindsight bias (68.0%) compared with listing two (54.3%). In questionnaires and interviews, prompts such as 'list the problems you had' before a global satisfaction rating can therefore shift that rating. The check identifies such sequences and tests them with split samples or reordering.
steps: Identify prompts that ask for examples, reasons or incidents before a global rating, in surveys, interviews or diary studies.
Where the order cannot be avoided, split the sample by the number of examples requested (for example two versus ten).
Alternatively place the global rating before the recall prompt in one version.
Compare global ratings across versions; a difference indicates an ease-of-retrieval effect.
Keep debiasing and reflection prompts short (few reasons) to avoid backfire, and fix the safer order for future waves.
outputs: Evidence of context effects on global ratings and a safer question order.
useWhen: Survey and interview guides that combine incident recall or 'list your frustrations' with satisfaction, trust or frequency ratings, and debiasing prompts in decision tools.
avoidWhen: Instruments without recall prompts before judgements. It is a check, not a fix, and effects depend on how difficult recall actually feels.
whyLost: The finding is well known in social cognition but survey design in UX seldom tests question order against it.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and NPS surveys, post-study questionnaires after critical-incident questions, diary-study prompts, reflective features in wellbeing apps.
example: A post-usability questionnaire asks participants to list every problem before rating overall ease. A split test asking for two versus all problems shows ratings are lower in the 'two problems' version, so the team moves the global rating before the problem list.
reference: Schwarz, N. and Vaughn, L. A. (2002). The availability heuristic revisited: Ease of recall and content of recall as distinct sources of information. In T. Gilovich, D. Griffin and D. Kahneman (Eds.), Heuristics and Biases: The Psychology of Intuitive Judgment. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

name: Ecological Interface Analysis
donor: Ecological psychology and cognitive systems engineering
origin: James J. Gibson, 1979; Vicente and Rasmussen, 1992 (EID)
summary: Applies Gibson's direct perception to make a domain's constraints and invariants directly visible, so users perceive system state instead of computing it.
description: Gibson argued that perception directly picks up information specified in the environment, such as invariants in the optic array, without elaborate inference. Ecological Interface Design (Vicente and Rasmussen) carried this into complex systems: rather than displaying raw variables, the interface should make the work domain's functional relationships and constraints perceptually obvious, so that operators can see when the system is heading out of bounds. The analytical method starts with an abstraction hierarchy of the work domain, from purpose to physical form, then designs displays whose geometry maps those relationships, such as configural graphics where a shape distorts when a constraint is violated. Rigour comes from deriving display elements from a formal domain analysis and testing fault detection, particularly for unanticipated events, against conventional displays.
steps: Build an abstraction hierarchy of the work domain from functional purpose down to physical form.
Identify key constraints and invariants operators must monitor, especially those violated in faults.
Design configural or emergent-feature displays where constraint violations produce visible changes in shape or pattern.
Prepare scenarios including routine, anticipated-fault and unanticipated-fault conditions.
Test with 8-16 domain users comparing detection time and diagnosis accuracy against the existing display.
Iterate on mappings that fail to support perception of the relevant constraint.
outputs: Abstraction hierarchy, constraint inventory, ecological display concepts, fault detection performance comparison.
useWhen: Process control, medical monitoring, energy, aviation and complex dashboards where operators must detect abnormal states quickly.
avoidWhen: Simple consumer interfaces without rich domain constraints; standard visual design and usability testing are enough.
whyLost: Latent: Theoretical basis for affordance concepts; ecological interface design; increasingly relevant for AR/VR.
whereToUse: Ecological interface design; AR/VR; ambient computing.
example: A grid-battery operator dashboard listed 40 numeric readings. An ecological redesign mapped charge balance to a polygon that skewed visibly when cells diverged; operators detected an injected imbalance fault in 8 seconds rather than 47.
sources: The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Vicente KJ & Rasmussen J (1992) Ecological interface design: theoretical foundations. IEEE SMC 22(4):589-606
Burns CM & Hajdukiewicz J (2004) Ecological Interface Design
Vicente & Rasmussen, Ecological interface design: Theoretical foundations (1992), IEEE Transactions on SMC
reference: Vicente, K. J., & Rasmussen, J. (1992). Ecological interface design: Theoretical foundations. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, 22(4), 589-606.

name: Ecological Momentary Interventions and Micro-Randomised Trials
donor: Clinical and health psychology; mobile health
origin: Heron and Smyth, 2010; Klasnja et al., 2015; Myin-Germeys et al., 2016; Nahum-Shani et al., 2018
summary: Deliver brief interventions on mobile devices in daily life, tailored by in-the-moment data, and test their components by randomising them repeatedly within each person.
description: Ecological momentary interventions (EMIs) are brief psychological interventions delivered through mobile technology, stand-alone or blended with therapy. Carter's three levels are low interaction (the same prompts and content for all), interactive (content triggered by reported scores) and integrative (learning systems tailored to each person, such as just-in-time adaptive interventions using sensor and response history). Designers decide when to deliver (fixed, random or after events), what data feed tailoring and how complex the system should be. The micro-randomised trial is a sequential factorial design: at each decision point each participant is randomised to receive a component or not, giving estimates of proximal effects and how they vary by context. Evaluation follows the WHO digital health life cycle (prototype, pilot, demonstration, scale-up, integration). Most studies stop at early phases, engagement drops quickly, and high-quality trials are few.
steps: Define the target moments and the decision rule for when to intervene.
Choose the complexity level and the data (self-report, sensors, history) that feed tailoring.
Involve clinicians or domain experts and end users qualitatively in early design.
Prototype and test functionality, stability and usability.
Run a micro-randomised trial: at each decision point randomise each participant to a component or no intervention, typically with fixed probabilities.
Estimate proximal effects and their moderators (time, context, prior response), then run larger trials with longer follow-up.
outputs: Proximal effect estimates per component and context, moderators of effect, and usability and engagement data.
useWhen: Designing and optimising notifications, nudges or coaching delivered in the moment, where the right timing and content are unknown.
avoidWhen: Interventions delivered once or on a fixed course; use a standard A/B test or RCT. Avoid where repeated prompting would cause harm or fatigue without monitoring.
whyLost: Product teams run A/B tests between users but rarely randomise repeatedly within users; the micro-randomised design grew up in mobile health research.
whereToUse: Habit, fitness and mental-health apps, financial nudges, learning reminders and proactive AI assistant suggestions.
example: A savings app randomises at each payday, with 50% probability, whether a user receives a 'move money now' prompt. Proximal effects show the prompt works on weekday mornings but not evenings, and fades after week four.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Ecological optics display experiments
aka: Layout perception testing with structured optical displays and open-field judgments
Optical event and self-motion display testing
origin: James J. Gibson and colleagues, 1947-1979; Lishman and Lee, 1973
summary: Add, remove or isolate one kind of optical information (texture, contours, looming, occlusion, flow) in a display and record what layout, event or self-motion observers perceive.
description: Gibson's strategy was to display information rather than apply stimuli. For layout, removing optical structure produces a fog, while adding discontinuities produces a surface; in the optical tunnel the share of observers seeing a solid tunnel rose with the number of contours (a third at 7, all at 36). Outdoors, observers matched sizes of distant stakes and bisected stretches of grass accurately, explained by texture gradients and the horizon ratio. For events, magnifying a silhouette is seen as approach and triggers blinking or ducking; progressive deletion of texture is always seen as one surface passing behind another; differing texture speeds split one surface into two. For self-motion, a moving room induces felt sway when floor contact is hidden. The method varies one optical variable at a time against controls and compares reports with geometric prediction.
steps: Choose the property or event to test (surface presence, distance, size, slant, approach, occlusion, self-motion) and the optical information that should specify it.
Build a display that varies only that information (texture density, contours, magnification, accretion and deletion, global flow), on screen, in VR or on real textured ground.
Include control changes such as minification, uniform dimming or a stationary display.
Allow or restrict head movement and binocular viewing as conditions.
Record reports (proportion seeing a surface or event), matches (size, bisection, slant settings), judgements (aiming point, time to contact) or protective responses.
Compare across conditions and against geometric prediction, reporting variability.
outputs: Proportions of report types, matched sizes, bisection points, slant and aiming-point judgements, avoidance responses and felt self-motion.
useWhen: Designing VR, AR, simulators, 3D and motion interfaces, where depth, approach, occlusion or self-motion must be perceived correctly.
avoidWhen: Avoid inferring everyday perception from monocular fixed-head viewing; non-rigid distortions of virtual layout often cause nausea. For general VR comfort use simulator sickness testing.
whyLost: Ecological psychology remains a perception-science niche; UX inherited the word 'affordance' but not the experimental method.
whereToUse: VR and AR products, driving and flight simulators, automotive head-up displays, games, motion design and transitions.
example: A VR training app tests how floor texture density affects distance judgements: with a sparse texture, users under-reach targets, and adding a fine ground texture brings bisection judgements close to true.
sources: The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (Gibson, 2015)
reference: Gibson, J. J. (1979). The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception. Boston: Houghton Mifflin.

name: Economic Games (Prisoner's Dilemma, Public Goods, Trust and Ultimatum)
donor: Experimental economics and behavioural game theory
origin: Prisoner's dilemma (Flood and Dresher, RAND, 1950); ultimatum game (Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze, 1982); trust game (Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe, 1995); public goods with punishment (Fehr and Gächter, 2000)
summary: Incentivised interactive games that measure cooperation, trust, reciprocity and fairness, used to test how design features change social behaviour.
description: Economic games put participants in standardised strategic situations with real money. The prisoner's dilemma and public goods game measure cooperation when individual and group interests conflict; the trust game measures how much one sends to another who may return it; the ultimatum game measures fairness norms and rejection of unfair offers. Repeated versions, communication and punishment options test institutions. Because they have known equilibria and large comparative literatures, deviations are interpretable. For UX of social, collaborative and marketplace products, games embedded in prototypes test how reputation systems, anonymity, visibility or AI mediators change cooperative behaviour, beyond what users say.
steps: Choose the game that matches the social dilemma in the product (e.g. trust game for marketplace transactions).
Implement the game with real, meaningful incentives (e.g. oTree), and design conditions varying product features (reputation display, anonymity).
Recruit participants and run sessions with clear instructions, comprehension checks and random matching.
Record decisions over multiple rounds and post-game beliefs.
Analyse contributions, trust and reciprocity with mixed models accounting for groups and rounds.
Translate behavioural differences into design implications and validate in field data.
outputs: Cooperation, trust and fairness measures by design condition, with dynamics over rounds.
useWhen: Designing reputation, review, collaboration, sharing-economy or community features where social behaviour determines outcomes.
avoidWhen: Individual tasks without strategic interdependence.
whyLost: Experimental economics labs and UX research teams rarely overlap; games feel artificial to practitioners.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, peer-to-peer lending, open-source and community platforms, team tools, multiplayer games.
example: A P2P rental platform tests reputation badges in a trust game; showing transaction history raises amounts sent by 28% and reciprocation by 15%, while star ratings alone do not differ from control.
sources: Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe, Trust, reciprocity, and social history (1995), Games and Economic Behavior
Fehr & Gächter, Cooperation and punishment in public goods experiments (2000), American Economic Review
Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
reference: Camerer, C. F. (2003). Behavioral Game Theory. Princeton University Press.

name: EEG in UX Research
origin: Hans Berger, 1924 (EEG); applied in HCI and neuroergonomics from the 1990s-2000s
summary: Records electrical brain activity during interaction to estimate workload, attention and engagement continuously, without interrupting the task.
description: Electroencephalography measures voltage fluctuations from neural activity via electrodes on the scalp, with millisecond temporal resolution but poor spatial resolution. In HCI, frequency-band measures (for example frontal theta increases and parietal alpha decreases with workload) and event-related potentials (such as the P300 to unexpected or task-relevant events) provide continuous indices of cognitive state.
