Modern dry-electrode and mobile headsets make field studies possible but reduce signal quality. Rigour is demanding: controlling artefacts from movement, blinks and muscle tension; using baselines and within-subject designs; time-locking events precisely; using sufficient trials; and validating indices against behavioural and subjective measures. Claims about specific emotions or 'engagement' from consumer headsets should be treated cautiously, since many proprietary metrics lack peer-reviewed validation.
steps: Define the cognitive state of interest (e.g. workload) and the EEG index that has evidence for it.
Choose equipment suited to the setting (research-grade lab system or validated mobile headset).
Design within-subject tasks with baselines and precisely time-stamped events, with enough repetitions per condition.
Record from 15-30 participants, monitoring signal quality during sessions.
Pre-process: filter, remove artefacts (e.g. with ICA) and extract band power or ERP components.
Analyse condition differences and validate against NASA-TLX, performance or other measures.
outputs: Workload, attention or ERP indices by condition and over time, validated against behavioural and subjective measures.
useWhen: High-stakes or high-workload interfaces (aviation, driving, clinical), adaptive interfaces, gaming and VR studies needing continuous measures.
avoidWhen: Routine product questions answerable by usability testing or questionnaires; most teams lack the expertise and the effect on design decisions is small. The neural generators of scalp waveforms are only partly understood, so treat EEG indices as correlates of processing, not readouts of a specific mental state.
whyLost: Siloed: Specialist equipment; interpretation expertise required; mostly academic and specialized neuromarketing.
whereToUse: High-stakes interface evaluation; gaming; immersive/VR experience research.
example: An automotive HMI team compared two touchscreen menu designs while participants drove in a simulator. Frontal theta indicated higher workload for the deeper menu, consistent with more lane deviations, supporting the flatter design.
sources: Neuroergonomics: The Brain at Work (Parasuraman & Rizzo)
Churchland, P. S., Neurophilosophy: Toward a Unified Science of the Mind-Brain (1986)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain (Bear et al., 2016)
reference: Parasuraman, R., & Rizzo, M. (Eds.) (2007). Neuroergonomics: The Brain at Work. Oxford University Press.

name: Effect size calculation
origin: Jacob Cohen (1962; 1988); eta squared from Pearson (1905); omega squared from Hays (1963)
summary: Quantifies how large a difference or relationship is, independent of sample size, so UX decisions rest on magnitude rather than on statistical significance alone.
description: Statistical significance depends heavily on sample size; effect size measures magnitude. Cohen's d expresses a mean difference in standard deviation units, with conventional benchmarks of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large, which Cohen himself cautioned were a last resort. Eta squared (η²) is the proportion of variance explained in ANOVA but is positively biased in samples; omega squared (ω²) corrects this bias and is preferred for population inference. For proportions, absolute differences, relative risk and odds ratios are often more meaningful to stakeholders. In UX, raw unstandardised effects such as seconds saved or percentage points of conversion are frequently the most interpretable. Rigour comes from reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals, choosing the measure that fits the design, and interpreting magnitude against practical criteria.
steps: Before analysis, state the smallest effect size of interest in product terms (e.g. 5 percentage points in completion, 10 seconds in task time).
Choose the effect size matching the design: Hedges' g for independent small samples, d_z or d_av for paired data, odds ratio for binary outcomes, rank-biserial for ordinal tests.
Compute it with a confidence interval (pingouin.compute_effsize with bootstrap CIs, or analytical intervals).

Report the unstandardised difference alongside the standardised value whenever units are meaningful; for non-specialist audiences, consider the common-language effect size (probability of superiority) or the binomial effect size display.
Interpret against the pre-stated threshold and prior benchmarks, using Cohen's 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 only as a last resort.
Use the observed effect and its interval to plan the sample size for follow-up studies.
outputs: Standardised and raw effect sizes with confidence intervals, interpreted against practical significance thresholds.
useWhen: Reporting any comparison or relationship, planning studies, comparing results across studies, and judging whether a significant difference matters.
avoidWhen: Purely descriptive qualitative work; for highly skewed or ordinal data, use rank-based effect sizes such as Cliff's delta or rank-biserial correlation instead of d.
whyLost: Effect sizes are routinely required in academic psychology but UX reports and A/B dashboards often show only p-values or 'significant' flags.
whereToUse: A/B test readouts, usability benchmark comparisons, survey segment differences, research meta-analysis across studies.
example: Two onboarding designs differed in SEQ ratings with p = 0.003 across 1,200 users, but Cohen's d was 0.17 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.28), equivalent to 0.2 scale points. The team judged the difference too small to justify the costlier design.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
Cohen, J. (1988) Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed.
Cumming, G. (2012) Understanding the New Statistics
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016) Quantifying the User Experience, 2nd ed.
The Inquiry Series, C2 — Quantitative UX Analysis in Python — Descriptive to Inferential
Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D. & Kelley, K., Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data, 3rd ed. (2018)
The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
Dangerous Statistical Mistakes in UX & Human Factors Research (carousel, n.d.)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
reference: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum; Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 863.

name: Effects Matrix and Explanatory Effects Matrix
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 5, section E (effects matrix) and chapter 6, section B (explanatory effects matrix).
summary: Matrices that set out the outcomes of a programme or change, split by type and time, and then trace them back to who did what and why.
description: An effects matrix focuses on dependent variables: the outcomes of something. Because qualitative outcomes are hard to pin down, the analyst first decides what makes up the outcome. In the book's example 'organisational change' was split into structural, procedural and relational or climate changes (rows), each shown for early and later use (columns) and divided into primary changes, which follow directly from the innovation's requirements, and spin-offs, which are secondary effects not fully anticipated. Reading it shows how effects ripple out over time. The explanatory effects matrix asks why. Rows are sources (for example superintendent, building administrator, developers, peer users, materials); columns show the user's assessment of each source, what was provided, short-run effects in users' words, longer-run consequences, and a researcher explanation. It is a first step towards causal explanation, but each row is read as a separate sequence, so interactions between rows need case dynamics matrices or causal networks. For UX, these matrices organise the consequences of a launch, migration or policy change, including unintended side-effects, and connect them to what different support channels actually did.
steps: Define the outcome of interest and break it into types (for example workflow, team structure, attitudes).
Choose time columns (early versus later use) and, if useful, split each into primary changes and spin-offs.
Enter outcomes from coded notes as short phrases.
For explanation, build a second matrix with sources of influence as rows and columns for what was provided, short-run effects, long-run consequences and an analyst explanation.
Fill cells with quotes and paraphrases, then compare rows to see which sources produced which effects.
Note interactions the matrix cannot show and move to a case dynamics matrix or causal network if needed.
outputs: An outcome-by-time matrix including side-effects, and a source-by-effect explanatory matrix.
useWhen: Evaluating what a launch, programme or change actually did, especially when indirect effects are likely.
avoidWhen: Outcomes are already well measured quantitatively, or the interest is in process rather than results.
whyLost: UX evaluation leans on metrics and A/B tests for outcomes, and qualitative outcome mapping with spin-off effects is seldom formalised.
whereToUse: Post-launch reviews, enterprise migrations, internal tool rollouts, service changes, programme evaluation.
example: Six months after a bank moved branch staff to a new CRM, researchers build an effects matrix: structural primary change 'all notes in one system', spin-off 'team leads now audit notes'; relational spin-off 'less informal handover chat'. The explanatory matrix shows that floor-walkers gave the most useful help ('they showed me shortcuts') while e-learning had no visible effect.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Effects-Driven IT Development
origin: Morten Hertzum and Jesper Simonsen, 2011, drawing on Ward and Daniel's benefits management
summary: Specifies the concrete usage effects a system should achieve at several levels, measures them before and after go-live, and loops back to renewed realisation or revised effects.
description: Effects are the realised benefits of using a system, as distinct from its functionality. They are specified early in workshops, ideally separately for managers (higher-level effects) and users (middle and lower levels), and arranged in a hierarchy from environment and business strategy through work tasks and processes to IT configuration. Each effect gets a template entry: description, realisation plan, follow-up measure, status, barriers, stakeholders and priority, maintained as a living document. Before measurements are taken while the old system is still in use; after measurements start a couple of months after go-live, using system data, user ratings or purpose-made measures such as record audits or location tracking. Unattained effects trigger renewed realisation activities; side effects or new benefits trigger revision of the specification, a loop akin to single- and double-loop learning.
steps: Take high-level effects from the business case and hold effects-specification workshops, separately for management and users.
Arrange effects in a hierarchy from environment and strategy through work tasks and processes to IT systems, keeping their number modest.
Fill an effects template per effect: description, plan for obtaining it, follow-up measure, current status, barriers, stakeholders and priority.
Take before measurements during preparation, while the old system is still used and before expectations bias perceptions.
Start after measurements a couple of months after go-live (earlier for cheap measures, to track recovery from the productivity dip).
Compare before and after; where an effect is not attained, run renewed realisation activities, such as training or reminders, and measure again.
Revise the specification when follow-up reveals side effects or new desirable effects; repeat until each effect is attained or abandoned.
outputs: An effects hierarchy, per-effect specification sheets, before/after measurement series, and decisions to renew, revise or abandon effects.
useWhen: Organisational implementations of enterprise, clinical or public-sector systems where the value lies in changed work practice rather than shipped features.
avoidWhen: When there is no stable before state or the organisation will not sustain follow-up. Retrospective before-versus-after staff judgements suffer forgetting and wishful thinking; keep follow-up non-blaming. For consumer feature launches use UX KPIs with Baselines and Pre-Set Success Thresholds or Interrupted Time Series (ITS).
whyLost: It is established in Scandinavian information systems research, but UX practice measures usability of systems rather than organisational effects of their use.
whereToUse: Electronic health records, enterprise resource planning, case management, workplace collaboration rollouts.
example: A hospital introducing an electronic medication record specifies that nurses record all medication electronically; six audits of 28 patients' records (two baseline, four after go-live) track violations, and a pocket guide is added when compliance stalls.
reference: Hertzum, M. and Simonsen, J. (2011). Effects-driven IT development: specifying, realizing, and assessing usage effects. Scandinavian Journal of Information Systems, 23(1), 3-28.

name: Efficiency Metrics
aka: Efficiency metrics: action counts and task success per unit time
origin: Usability practice; ratio from the Common Industry Format, ISO/IEC 25062:2006
summary: Measure efficiency as meaningful actions per successful task, or as task completion rate divided by mean time, to compare designs on effort per unit of success.
description: Efficiency combines the effort spent with the outcome achieved. Action counting follows five rules: identify which actions to count (clicks, page views, keystrokes, screens); define where each action starts and ends; count with a logger, tool or video; make sure each counted action is a meaningful step towards the goal; and count only successful tasks. Results are reported as mean actions per task with confidence intervals, or as the share of participants exceeding the minimum path. The Common Industry Format's core efficiency measure divides task completion rate by mean time per task, with a time unit chosen so most values fall between 1% and 100%; a per-participant variant divides tasks completed successfully by total time on all tasks. Because a ratio hides whether low efficiency comes from failure or slowness, both components should be reported.
steps: Choose the effort unit (clicks, page views, keystrokes, screens) or use time.
Define the start and end of each action and each task.
Record actions with a logger, an unmoderated testing tool or video.
For action counts, keep successful tasks only and compute mean actions per task with confidence intervals, or the percentage exceeding the minimum path.
For the CIF ratio, compute completion rate divided by mean time per task, or per participant tasks completed divided by total time, choosing a time unit that keeps values between 1% and 100%.
Compare designs with t-tests or ANOVA on per-participant values and report success and time alongside the ratio.
outputs: Actions per task with confidence intervals, the percentage of participants above the optimal path, and efficiency ratios per task or participant.
useWhen: Comparing designs or releases on effort, benchmarking expert workflows, and summative tests where efficiency is a stated requirement.
avoidWhen: Formative tests with few participants, or when counted actions are not meaningful steps; for predicted expert time without users use GOMS / KLM.
whyLost: Click counts are widely quoted but usually without the counting rules, success filtering or confidence intervals, and the CIF ratio is seldom used.
whereToUse: Enterprise data entry, checkout flows, navigation redesigns and productivity tools.
example: Four navigation prototypes are tested between-subjects with over 200 participants each on 20 tasks. Tasks completed per minute shows one prototype significantly more efficient than another, while success rates alone did not separate them.
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022) Measuring the User Experience: Collecting, Analyzing, and Presenting UX Metrics, 3rd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 96-101.

name: Effort × impact grid
donor: Management consulting and lean product practice
origin: Practitioner tool, widely used in product management
summary: A 2×2 grid placing evidence-based fixes by effort and impact so low-effort, high-impact changes ship first and high-effort, low-impact ones are deferred.
description: The grid sorts prescriptions into four quadrants: low effort/high impact (prioritise immediately, e.g. relabel Notifications), high effort/high impact (schedule for roadmap, e.g. redesign the OTP flow), low effort/low impact (opportunistic, e.g. tweak copy) and high effort/low impact (avoid or defer). In Vivek Gopinath's Prescribe stage the impact rating is grounded in quantitative drivers (hazard ratios, SHAP importance, Monte Carlo lifts) rather than opinion, and each fix also carries a decision bar. The playbook warns that not quantifying effort leads teams to miss low-effort, high-impact fixes that should leapfrog others.
steps: List candidate fixes from the evidence ⇒ prescription table.
Rate impact from quantitative drivers (HR, SHAP rank, forecast lift).
Rate effort with design and engineering partners.
Place each fix in one of the four quadrants.
Sequence: low effort/high impact now, high effort/high impact on roadmap, defer high effort/low impact.
Attach decision bars to each fix and revisit after validation.
outputs: A prioritised quadrant chart and sequenced fix list.
useWhen: When a study produces several recommendations and the team must sequence them.
avoidWhen: When impact cannot be estimated from evidence; the grid then becomes guesswork. Use an experiment or forecast first.
whyLost: Survives because it is simple and fits product planning rituals; rigour depends on evidence-based impact ratings.
whereToUse: Research readouts, sprint planning, roadmap reviews.
example: Relabelling Notifications lands in low effort/high impact and ships this sprint, while redesigning the OTP flow is high effort/high impact and goes on the quarterly roadmap.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Rubin & Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing (severity rating)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief

name: Eidetic variation
origin: Edmund Husserl (Ideas, 1913; Experience and Judgment, 1939); adapted for empirical psychology by Amedeo Giorgi and for qualitative research by Moustakas (1994)
summary: Identifies the essential structure of an experience by imaginatively varying its features and noting which changes would make it no longer the same kind of experience.
description: Husserl proposed that the essence of a phenomenon can be found by freely varying its features in imagination: if a feature can be removed or changed and the experience remains the same kind of experience, it is contingent; if changing it destroys the experience, it is essential. In empirical phenomenology, the researcher applies this to participants' descriptions. For example, in the experience of 'submitting a claim and waiting', is uncertainty about receipt essential, or would a confirmed receipt leave the experience intact? This distinguishes invariant structures from incidental details of particular cases. For UX it offers a disciplined way to decide what a design must address and what can vary. Rigour comes from systematic variation of each constituent, documented reasoning, and checking variations against actual participant accounts.
steps: Start from a set of rich first-person descriptions of the experience, typically 5 to 15 participants, already broken into meaning units.
List candidate constituents of the experience, such as waiting, uncertainty, being judged, effort, and dependence on others.
For each constituent, imagine it removed or radically altered and ask whether the experience would still be the same kind of experience, recording the reasoning.
Check imagined variations against actual cases: do any participants' accounts lack the constituent while remaining the same experience?
Classify constituents as essential (invariant) or contingent (variable), and describe how essential constituents relate to one another.
Translate the essential structure into design requirements and the contingent features into acceptable design variation.
outputs: A documented set of variation analyses, a list of essential and contingent constituents, and an essential structure statement with design implications.
useWhen: Understanding the core of an experience across varied contexts; deciding which aspects of a service must be preserved when redesigning or digitising it.
avoidWhen: Questions are about frequency, preference or usability defects; use surveys or usability testing. Not appropriate without rich first-person descriptions.
whyLost: Phenomenological philosophy is rarely taught in UX, and 'phenomenology' in practice often means only open-ended interviews, without the analytic operations such as variation.
whereToUse: Health and insurance claims, bereavement and life-event services, financial stress experiences, AI-mediated service experiences, high-anxiety moments.
example: Analysing accounts of submitting digital health insurance claims, researchers varied 'confirmation of receipt'. Imagining it removed turned the experience into anxious limbo, and two participants who lacked it described exactly that, so confirmation was classified as essential and prioritised over speed.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
reference: Giorgi, A. (2009). The Descriptive Phenomenological Method in Psychology: A Modified Husserlian Approach. Duquesne University Press; Husserl, E. (1913/1983). Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology. Nijhoff.

name: Elaboration Model (Lazarsfeld Paradigm)
origin: Paul Lazarsfeld and Patricia Kendall, re-analysing Stouffer's 'The American Soldier' (1949-1950), Columbia University
summary: Explain a two-variable relationship by recomputing it within categories of a third variable and reading the partial relationships as replication, explanation, interpretation or specification.
description: The elaboration model is a logic for multivariate analysis of survey data that predates and underlies today's stratified analysis, confounding and mediation checks and moderation. Starting from an observed zero-order relationship between two variables, the analyst introduces a test variable and recomputes the relationship within each of its categories, producing partial tables. The outcome is classified by two things: whether the test variable is antecedent to both variables or intervenes between them, and how the partials compare with the original. If the relationship holds in all partials it is replicated; if it vanishes with an antecedent variable it is explained away as spurious; if it vanishes with an intervening variable it is interpreted through a mechanism; if it holds in some partials and not others it is specified. Suppressor and distorter variables can hide or reverse a relationship. Ex post facto hypotheses must be tested on new data.
steps: Establish the zero-order relationship between the independent and dependent variable in the whole sample.
Choose a test variable and justify whether it is antecedent to both or intervening between them.
Split the sample by the test variable and recompute the relationship within each subgroup (partial tables).

Classify: same in all partials is replication; reduced or vanished with an antecedent variable is explanation (spurious); reduced or vanished with an intervening variable is interpretation (mechanism).
Classify as specification when the relationship is the same or stronger in one partial and weaker in another, and state the conditions.
Check for suppressor or distorter variables that hide or reverse the relationship.
Test any after-the-fact hypotheses with further data rather than resting on the observed tables.
outputs: Partial tables and a classification of how a third variable bears on the relationship (replication, explanation, interpretation, specification).
useWhen: A survey or analytics cross-tab shows an association (for example feature use and retention) and you need a disciplined first pass at whether it is spurious, mediated or conditional.
avoidWhen: Small samples where partial tables become sparse, or when many variables must be controlled at once; use regression, causal diagrams or experiments instead.
whyLost: Its logic survived inside regression, mediation and moderation analysis and causal diagrams, while the name and the simple partial-table procedure fell out of teaching.
whereToUse: Survey analysis, product analytics cross-tabs, explaining segment differences, teaching causal caution to stakeholders.
example: Users of a budgeting feature churn less; splitting by account age shows the gap disappears within each tenure band, so tenure explains the association and the feature is not credited with retention.
reference: Kendall, P. L. and Lazarsfeld, P. F. (1950). 'Problems of survey analysis', in Merton, R. K. and Lazarsfeld, P. F. (eds.) Continuities in Social Research. Glencoe, IL: Free Press.

name: Elastic trajectory similarity (DTW, LCSS)
origin: Sakoe and Chiba, 1978 (DTW); Vlachos, Kollios and Gunopulos, 2002 (LCSS trajectories); reviewed by Das and Gunopulos, 2003
summary: Compare behavioural time series or trajectories that differ in speed, phase or outliers by elastic alignment, producing distances for clustering or retrieval of similar user traces.
description: Euclidean distance fails when series differ in baseline, scale, phase or speed. Das and Gunopulos recommend z-normalising series first, then using dynamic time warping, which finds the best monotone alignment between two series within a warping window, or longest common subsequence similarity, which matches points within a tolerance and skips unmatched outliers, giving a dissimilarity based on matched length. LCSS can also fit a global scaling and shift using matched points only. DTW is distorted by outliers; on video-tracked trajectories LCSS produced intuitive clusters where DTW failed. Non-metric measures can be closer to human judgement, relevance feedback can learn a user's notion of similarity, and lower-bounding indexes allow fast retrieval without false dismissals. In UX the measures apply to mouse paths, scroll traces, gaze sequences, sensor data and engagement curves.
steps: Extract each trace as a time series or trajectory (for example cursor path, daily usage curve, gaze path).
Z-normalise each series to remove baseline and scale differences.
Choose a warping window for DTW (for example 10 per cent of length) or a matching tolerance for LCSS.
Compute pairwise DTW distances or LCSS dissimilarities.
Cluster (for example hierarchical) or retrieve nearest neighbours on the distance matrix.
Inspect clusters against examples and intuition; prefer LCSS when traces contain outliers and test sensitivity to window or tolerance.
outputs: A distance matrix between traces, clusters of similar behaviour, and nearest-neighbour retrieval.
useWhen: You want to group or compare behavioural traces that unfold at different speeds, such as engagement curves, mouse movements or wearable data.
avoidWhen: Sequences are categorical events rather than numeric series; use sequence alignment. Settings change results, and DTW is distorted by outliers.
whyLost: It sits in time-series data mining; UX analytics usually summarises traces into aggregate features and loses their shape.
whereToUse: Wearables and fitness, engagement curves for retention, mouse tracking, gaze paths, VR motion, handwriting and gesture input.
example: A fitness app clusters users' 90-day activity curves with LCSS. One cluster shows a mid-month dip and rebound across varying start dates, which a fixed-calendar analysis missed, prompting timed nudges.
reference: Das, G., & Gunopulos, D. (2003). Time series similarity and indexing. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 279-304). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Elicited Imitation (Sentence Repetition)
origin: Long-standing technique in child language research; no single originator
summary: Ask participants to repeat sentences exactly and analyse omissions, substitutions and simplifications to locate the limits of their command of a language or structure.
description: People, like children, generally cannot repeat accurately sentences whose structure lies beyond their language system; they drop, substitute or simplify the parts they do not control. Elicited imitation exploits this: the researcher says a sentence, the participant repeats it, and errors reveal which structures are not yet available, much as an adult struggles to repeat a sentence in an unfamiliar language. Sentences are built to vary the structure of interest, such as clause embedding or negation. The book gives no standard scoring scheme and cautions that production can underestimate comprehension. In UX the technique is a rough probe of whether particular phrasings, such as instructions, legal wording or voice prompts, exceed what a target audience can process and hold, especially second-language and low-literacy users.
steps: Prepare sentences that vary systematically in the structure of interest (length, embedding, negation, terminology).
Say or play each sentence and ask the participant to repeat it exactly.
Record the repetitions.
Code omissions, substitutions, reorderings and simplifications.
Compare accuracy by structure to find which forms exceed participants' processing.
outputs: Repetition accuracy by sentence type and a list of structures that are dropped or simplified.
useWhen: Checking whether voice prompts, instructions or plain-language rewrites are within the processing capacity of second-language, low-literacy or cognitively impaired users.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a comprehension test, since repetition can underestimate understanding; use Cognitive Interviewing for Questionnaire Design or Teach-Back Mental Model Elicitation for comprehension, and Cloze Probability Norming for predictability.
whyLost: It belongs to language acquisition and second-language assessment and has no tradition in UX.
whereToUse: Voice assistants and IVR prompts, plain-language programmes, multilingual products, accessibility research.
example: A voice banking assistant's prompts are tested with 12 second-language English speakers. Prompts with embedded conditionals ('If you want to..., unless...') are repeated with the condition dropped, so they are split into two short prompts.
reference: Berko Gleason, J. and Bernstein Ratner, N. (Eds.) (2022). The Development of Language (10th ed.). San Diego: Plural Publishing, ch. 1.

name: Elicited Production Tasks (Wug Test)
origin: Jean Berko (1958) wug test; Hamburger and Crain (1982) relative-clause elicitation
summary: Set up a context in which the participant must produce a target linguistic form, often on invented words, to reveal whether they have internalised a productive rule.
description: Elicited production is used when one form is the target: the researcher supplies everything except the answer. In Berko's wug test a child sees an invented creature named with a nonsense word, then two of them, and completes the frame 'There are two ...'; other items target possessives and verb endings. Correct endings on words the child has never heard show an internalised rule rather than rote learning. For rare structures the context forces the form: the child describes one of two identical figures to a listener who cannot see them, so only a relative clause will identify it. A puppet that talks only to children can be prompted by whispered cues to elicit questions. The method controls which forms are produced and tests participants to their limits, complementing spontaneous samples. In UX it can test whether users generalise naming, command or gesture patterns to new items.
steps: Choose the target form, such as a plural, past tense, question type, or in UX a command or naming pattern.
Create invented words, items or scenes so the answer cannot have been memorised.
Present the context, for example one item then two, or two near-identical items differing in one event or property.
Give a sentence frame or situation that requires the target form, supplying everything except the form itself.
Where social framing helps, use an intermediary (a puppet for children, a fictional colleague for adults) and prompt the participant to address it.
Record whether and how the target form is produced and classify errors.
outputs: Accuracy and error patterns for each target form, showing which rules participants apply productively.
useWhen: Testing whether users have learned a productive pattern, such as voice command grammar, naming conventions or gesture vocabularies, and will apply it to new cases.
avoidWhen: Artificial conditions can underestimate competence in natural use; for natural usage collect spontaneous samples or use Gesture Elicitation Study for open-ended proposals.
whyLost: It is a staple of child language research but has no tradition in UX, where pattern learnability is inferred from task success.
whereToUse: Voice assistants and command languages, query syntax, keyboard shortcut and gesture systems, product naming schemes.
example: After training on three voice commands for a smart-home app, participants see a new device called a 'flimp' and are asked how they would turn two of them off. Most say 'turn off the flimps', but few apply the room prefix, showing which rule has not generalised.
reference: Berko, J. (1958). The child's learning of English morphology. Word, 14; Berko Gleason, J. and Bernstein Ratner, N. (Eds.) (2022). The Development of Language (10th ed.). Plural Publishing.

name: Eligibility criteria definition
origin: Clinical trial methodology, mid-20th century; target trial framing by Hernán & Robins, 2016
summary: Defines precisely which users enter an analysis or study, using criteria measurable at time zero, so the population matches the decision and avoids selection bias.
description: In clinical trials, eligibility criteria define who could be randomised; in target trial emulation they must be applied using only information available at time zero. UX analyses frequently violate this, for example by restricting to users who remained active for 30 days, which conditions on the future and builds survivorship bias into the comparison. Good criteria are explicit, measurable, tied to the population a decision will affect, and documented with a participant flow diagram showing how many were excluded at each step. The same discipline improves recruitment screeners for qualitative studies, where vague criteria produce unrepresentative samples.
steps: State the decision and the population it will affect (e.g. new retail investors in their first 90 days).
Write inclusion and exclusion criteria using only variables known at or before time zero.
Check every criterion for dependence on post-baseline information (activity after time zero, survival, later purchases) and remove such criteria.
Apply criteria sequentially to the data and record counts excluded at each step in a CONSORT-style flow diagram.
Compare included and excluded users on key characteristics to describe generalisability.
outputs: Explicit criteria, a participant flow diagram with counts, and a statement of the population the results apply to.
useWhen: Every observational log analysis, target trial emulation, experiment population definition and recruitment screener.
avoidWhen: Rarely wrong to apply; it is lighter-weight in early exploratory qualitative work where breadth matters more than a precise population.
whyLost: Clinical research mandates it, but UX analyses define populations ad hoc in queries, and filters conditioning on the future go unnoticed.
whereToUse: Retention and feature-effect analyses, experiment targeting, regulated fintech and health studies, research recruitment.
example: An analysis of a savings nudge restricts to users with at least 3 deposits in month one. Rewriting criteria to use only information at sign-up removes a survivorship bias that had doubled the apparent effect.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 48 — Target Trial Emulation — Causal Evidence from Log Data
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Schulz, K. F., Altman, D. G. & Moher, D. (2010) CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340, c332.

name: Elim-First attribute identification
donor: Mathematical psychology and consumer decision research
origin: Amos Tversky's elimination by aspects model (1972); non-compensatory choice research by Payne, Bettman and Johnson (1993)
summary: Identifies the attributes users apply first to eliminate options before any trade-off, so designs surface and satisfy these screening criteria.
description: Tversky's elimination by aspects model describes choice as sequential: people pick an important attribute, discard all options that fail it, and repeat until one option remains. It is non-compensatory, so excellence on other attributes cannot rescue an option eliminated early. Elim-First attribute identification finds which attributes users eliminate on first and the cut-offs they use. In UX this explains why a technically superior option is never considered: it failed a screening aspect such as 'works offline', 'in my language' or 'no upfront fee' before comparison began. Rigour comes from process-tracing methods (information display boards, think-aloud, eye tracking or click-stream order) rather than stated importance ratings, which systematically confuse screening and trade-off attributes.
steps: List 8 to 20 candidate attributes for the decision from interviews and competitor analysis, defining each with clear levels.
Build an information display board or mock comparison interface where attribute values are hidden until clicked, so search order and stopping can be logged.
Run 15 to 40 participants through 3 to 6 realistic choice tasks while thinking aloud, logging which attribute they open first, which options they discard and why.
Classify each attribute by whether it was used to eliminate options, the order of use, and the stated cut-off (for example 'more than 2% fee, gone').

Rank attributes by elimination frequency and median position in the search sequence; attributes used for elimination by more than about 40% of participants in the first two steps are screening attributes.
Validate with a larger survey using a screening question format (for example 'Would you consider an option that...?') and check the design surfaces screening attributes early and visibly.
outputs: A ranked list of screening attributes with typical cut-offs, search-order patterns by segment, and design recommendations for what must appear first in listings, comparison tables and onboarding.
useWhen: Users face many alternatives (plans, providers, products, clinical options) and conversion is low even though your option is strong on paper; you need to design filters, comparison tables or recommendation logic.
avoidWhen: Decisions are genuinely compensatory and low in number of options; conjoint analysis or MaxDiff better quantifies trade-offs.
whyLost: Choice process tracing stayed in decision science and marketing academia; UX and product research adopted stated-importance surveys and conjoint, which assume compensatory trade-offs.
whereToUse: Fintech and insurance comparison, marketplace search and filters, health plan selection, B2B vendor evaluation, AI recommendation explanations.
example: A savings product with the best rate saw few sign-ups. Process tracing showed 55% of rural participants first eliminated any option without withdrawal at local agents; once agent withdrawal was surfaced as the first filter and badge, consideration rose sharply.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 21 — Heuristics, Biases & the Architecture of Judgment
reference: Tversky, A. (1972). Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice. Psychological Review, 79(4), 281–299.

name: Elimination by Aspects in Interface Choice Design
donor: Mathematical psychology and consumer decision research
origin: Amos Tversky, 1972
summary: Models how users choose by eliminating options that fail on the most important attribute in turn, guiding design of comparison, filtering and plan-selection interfaces.
description: Elimination by aspects is a non-compensatory choice model: rather than weighing all attributes, decision makers select an attribute (with probability proportional to its importance), eliminate options lacking it, and repeat until one option remains. Strengths on other attributes cannot compensate for failing an early cut. Consumer research uses it to explain filtering behaviour and choice overload. For interface design, the model predicts that users facing many options will screen on a few key aspects, so comparison tables, filters and pricing pages should expose the aspects people eliminate on first and in the right order. The method elicits elimination sequences through process tracing (think-aloud, information boards, filter logs) and fits attribute weights, distinguishing compensatory from lexicographic strategies.
steps: Identify first-elimination attributes through interview: 'What would make you immediately reject this option?' Surface that attribute first and most prominently.
outputs: Ranked elimination aspects, observed screening sequences, proportion of users using non-compensatory strategies, and recommendations for filter order and comparison design.
useWhen: Designing plan pickers, product listings, filters, comparison tables and any interface where users choose among many options with multiple attributes.
avoidWhen: When choices involve few options or genuine trade-offs that users weigh carefully (use conjoint analysis), or when you lack process data on how people screen.
whyLost: It is standard in consumer behaviour and choice modelling but did not migrate to UX, where choice interfaces are usually tested only for conversion rather than decision strategy.
whereToUse: Pricing pages, feature comparison tables, filter UI design.
example: A mobile carrier's plan page lists 14 plans with 9 attributes. Filter logs and think-aloud sessions show users eliminate first on data allowance, then contract length, so the page leads with those two filters and conversion rises with fewer plan-comparison exits.
sources: Preference, Belief, and Similarity — Amos Tversky
Tversky, Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice (Psychological Review, 1972)
Payne, Bettman & Johnson, The Adaptive Decision Maker (1993)
reference: Tversky A (1972) Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice. Psychological Review 79(4):281-299

name: Eliminative Materialism Critique of Mental Model Constructs
aka: Construct validity audit of mental-model terms
origin: Paul and Patricia Churchland (1981, 1986)
summary: Interrogates whether folk-psychological constructs such as user intention, goal and mental model are valid units of analysis, prompting operational definitions and behavioural evidence.
description: Eliminative materialism argues that folk psychology, the everyday vocabulary of beliefs, desires and intentions, is a theory that may be false and could be replaced by a mature neuroscience. Whatever its philosophical merits, it raises a practical question for UX research: constructs such as 'user intention', 'goal' and 'mental model' are folk concepts that researchers often treat as directly observable. The method is a construct audit. For each such construct in a study, the researcher states its operational definition, what evidence would indicate it (verbal reports, choices, eye movements, errors), and whether different measures converge. Where they do not, findings are reframed in terms of observed behaviour and predictions. This improves construct validity and guards against reifying participants' after-the-fact explanations as causes.
steps: Apply eliminative skepticism to UX research constructs: for each construct used in research ('the user intended to...', 'the user's mental model is...'), ask:
is this construct operationalized in behavior, or inferred?

(2) would different explanatory constructs (neural, computational, behavioral) better predict the phenomenon? Use behavioral measures (response time, error pattern, eye movement) alongside inferential mental-model constructs.
outputs: Construct inventory with operational definitions, convergent evidence assessment, and reframed findings that distinguish observed behaviour from inferred mental states.
useWhen: Research that leans on inferred mental states: mental-model studies, intent modelling, AI 'understanding' claims and theory-building in research programmes.
avoidWhen: Routine evaluative studies where folk terms are used loosely without affecting decisions; the audit adds little there.
whyLost: It is a philosophical position confined to philosophy of mind and cognitive science; UX research has little tradition of auditing the validity of its own constructs.
whereToUse: Research construct validity analysis, theory-driven UX research, neuroscience-informed user modeling, AI behavior explanation research.
example: A team claims users 'intend' to save articles for later because they say so in interviews. A construct audit shows save actions are rarely followed by returns, so the team reframes the feature as bookmarking-as-closure and measures it accordingly.
sources: Churchland PM, Eliminative materialism and the propositional attitudes (Journal of Philosophy, 1981)
reference: Churchland PS (1986) Neurophilosophy: Toward a Unified Science of the Mind-Brain. MIT Press

name: Elito Method
origin: Institute of Design, Illinois Institute of Technology (2002); described by Trysh Wahlig
summary: A team synthesis practice that writes logic lines from observation to judgement, value, concept and metaphor, linking each design idea to evidence.
description: In a projected spreadsheet the team writes logic lines across five columns: observation (a fact from research), judgement (why it matters), value (the human value at stake), concept or sketch (what to do about it) and key metaphor (a memorable tag). Lines can be filled non-linearly, starting from a concept and working back to the evidence. They are then printed, sorted and clustered into themes, which become design arguments tying ideas to evidence and business goals. The method bridges the gap between analysis and synthesis and builds shared vocabulary. It depends on observations being facts rather than opinions, and without clustering it degrades into a long list.
steps: Gather the team after research with observations from field notes and transcripts.
In a shared spreadsheet, write each observation as a fact.
For each, add the judgement, the human value, a concept or sketch, and a key metaphor, filling columns in any order.
Check that every concept traces back to at least one observation.
Print each logic line and sort and cluster them into themes.
Write each theme as a design argument linking concepts to evidence and business goals.
outputs: A spreadsheet of logic lines and themed design arguments.
useWhen: Use straight after research when a team needs to move from observations to concepts while keeping a traceable chain of reasoning.
avoidWhen: Avoid when observations are opinions or second-hand: collect primary data through Contextual Inquiry or Ethnographic Research first. For analysing the data itself use Affinity Diagramming or thematic coding.
whyLost: It is taught at IIT's Institute of Design and used by its alumni, but has not spread far beyond that community.
whereToUse: Retail and service innovation, consultancy synthesis, any project where concepts must be defended with evidence.
example: Observation: shoppers photograph price tags. Judgement: they cannot remember prices across stores. Value: confidence. Concept: a price-memory feature. Metaphor: 'a shopping notebook'.
reference: Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Beverly, MA: Rockport Publishers. Method 44, Elito Method.

name: EM algorithm for missing session data
origin: Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird and Donald Rubin, 1977
summary: Estimates models from behavioural or survey data with missing values by iterating expectation and maximisation steps, avoiding the bias of deleting incomplete users.
description: Behavioural and survey data in UX are routinely incomplete: users drop out of diary studies, abandon multi-step surveys or sessions end early. Deleting incomplete cases (listwise deletion) or filling gaps with means biases results whenever missingness relates to the outcome, such as frustrated users quitting. The expectation-maximisation algorithm estimates parameters by alternating an E-step, computing expected values of the missing or latent quantities given current parameters, and an M-step, updating parameters to maximise likelihood given those expectations, until convergence. It provides maximum-likelihood estimates under the missing-at-random assumption and underpins mixture models and latent variable models. Good practice diagnoses missingness patterns, states the assumption, compares results with complete-case analysis and, where uncertainty must be propagated, uses multiple imputation alongside.
steps: Frame incomplete session data as a latent variable problem: complete session outcome is the latent variable; observed partial session data is the observation.
Apply EM: E-step estimates the probability of each possible complete session given the partial data; M-step updates model parameters.
Compare: EM-estimated completion rates vs. naïve complete-case analysis.
Large differences indicate non-random missingness (MNAR — missing not at random).
outputs: Missingness diagnostics, maximum-likelihood parameter estimates, comparison with complete-case results, and documented assumptions about the missing-data mechanism.
useWhen: Longitudinal and diary studies with dropout, partial survey responses, sessions with incomplete event logs, and fitting mixture or latent variable models.
avoidWhen: When missingness is clearly not at random (data missing because of the unobserved value itself) without a model for it; use sensitivity analysis or pattern-mixture models, and avoid it when only a trivial fraction is missing.
whyLost: UX analysis tools default to deleting incomplete records, and EM sits inside statistical software rather than in UX training, so it vanished from practitioner awareness.
whereToUse: Onboarding completion rate estimation, task completion analysis with partial sessions, churn modeling with incomplete histories.
example: A 12-week wellbeing app diary study loses 35% of participants by week 8, mostly those reporting low mood. EM estimates of the mood trajectory show a smaller improvement than the complete-case analysis, preventing an overstated efficacy claim.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning — Bishop
Little & Rubin, Statistical Analysis with Missing Data
Dempster, Laird & Rubin, Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm (JRSS B, 1977)
Deep Learning (Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville)
Dempster, Laird & Rubin (1977) Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm
Statistical Analysis with Missing Data (Roderick Little & Donald Rubin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 53 — Generative Models & Synthetic User Testing
Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella, 2010)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Dempster AP, Laird NM & Rubin DB (1977) Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 39(1):1-38

name: Embodied Cognition Research
origin: Varela, Thompson and Rosch, 1991; Dourish, 2001 (embodied interaction)
summary: Studies how bodily action, posture, gesture and physical setting shape users' thinking, to design and evaluate spatial, gestural and tangible interactions.
description: Embodied cognition rejects the view that thinking is purely symbolic manipulation in the head. Perception, action and environment are treated as constitutive of cognition: people think with gestures, use spatial arrangement to reason and offload memory onto objects. Paul Dourish brought this into HCI as embodied interaction, arguing that meaning arises through engaged action. As a research approach it combines observation of bodily behaviour (gesture coding, posture, movement traces), manipulation of physical conditions (sitting vs standing, hands free vs encumbered) and measures of task performance and comprehension. Rigour comes from treating the body and setting as variables rather than noise, coding movement systematically, and testing whether interaction designs that align with natural action, such as spatial mappings or physical metaphors, improve learning and accuracy compared with abstract alternatives.
steps: Specify which bodily dimensions matter for the product: gesture, posture, reach, locomotion, tool use or spatial layout.
Observe 6-12 users performing tasks in realistic physical settings, recording video from at least two angles.
Code gestures, body movements and environmental offloading using a predefined scheme, double-coding at least 20% of footage.
Introduce controlled manipulations (e.g. encumbered hands, different spatial mappings) to test embodied hypotheses.
Compare performance, errors and comprehension across conditions and relate them to coded behaviour.
Translate findings into interaction mappings, gesture vocabularies and spatial layouts aligned with natural action.
outputs: Gesture and movement codebook, behaviour-performance analysis, embodied interaction design principles for the product.
useWhen: AR/VR, gesture and voice-plus-gesture interfaces, wearables, tangible and in-vehicle interfaces where the body is part of the interaction.
avoidWhen: Standard desktop or mobile screen flows with conventional input; conventional usability testing is more efficient.
whyLost: Latent: Strong in academic cognitive science; slowly entering UX for embodied/spatial computing design.
whereToUse: AR/VR design; gesture interfaces; physical-digital interaction; tangible computing.
example: A VR training product for warehouse pickers tested abstract menu selection against reaching to virtual shelves. Coding showed users mimed real reaching anyway; the spatial mapping cut training errors by a third.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Dourish, P. (2001). Where the Action Is: The Foundations of Embodied Interaction. MIT Press.

name: Embodied Experience Research
origin: Draws on Varela, Thompson & Rosch (1991) and Christopher Noessel's work on multi-sensory interaction design
summary: Investigates how bodily and multi-sensory experience (sound, touch, haptics, motion) shapes product perception, through a sensory channel audit and embodied-metaphor interviews.
description: Most UX research assumes experience is visual and verbal. Embodied cognition argues that understanding is grounded in bodily experience, so people describe and judge products through physical metaphors: something feels 'heavy', 'sticky' or 'smooth'. This approach first audits every sensory channel a product engages (visual, auditory, haptic, motion, even temperature or smell for physical products) and checks for cross-sensory incoherence, such as a playful sound on a serious error. It then uses embodied interview prompts that ask participants to describe the feel of using the product in physical terms, and maps those metaphors to specific interaction moments. Rigour comes from systematic channel coverage and from analysing metaphors across participants rather than collecting colourful quotes.
steps: Sensory channel audit: List all sensory channels your product engages: visual, auditory, haptic, proprioceptive. Most UX research studies only visual.

Cross-sensory coherence check: Conflicting sensory signals? Visual communicates 'calm/trustworthy' while audio communicates 'urgent'? Incoherence produces users reporting something 'feels wrong' without specifying why.

Embodied interview technique: 'If you had to describe the feeling of using this in physical terms — texture, weight, temperature — what would you say?' Embodied metaphors reveal non-verbal experience.
Analysis: Map embodied metaphors to product moments. Clusters at specific interaction points reveal tacit reactions participants cannot articulate functionally.
outputs: A sensory channel inventory, a cross-sensory coherence report, coded embodied metaphors mapped to product moments, and recommendations for sound, haptic and motion design.
useWhen: Products with significant non-visual channels: wearables, voice and in-car interfaces, haptic mobile interactions, connected devices, or brands where 'feel' is a differentiator.
avoidWhen: The product is a primarily textual or data-entry interface where sensory design is not a lever; standard usability testing is more efficient. For measuring arousal use Multi-Channel Affective Measurement.
whyLost: UX research developed in screen-based, visual-first contexts and lacks vocabulary and tools for non-visual channels, so embodiment stayed in academic HCI and industrial design.
whereToUse: Wearables and health devices, automotive HMI, voice assistants, haptics on mobile, smart home products, and premium consumer brands.
example: A smartwatch team audits notification feedback and finds the same strong vibration for a calendar nudge and a heart-rate alert. Embodied interviews show users describe the watch as 'nagging'; distinct haptic patterns by urgency follow.
reference: Varela, F. J., Thompson, E. & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind. MIT Press.

name: Embodied Simulation and Interface Metaphor Grounding
origin: Lawrence Barsalou (1999); Glenberg and Kaschak's action-sentence compatibility effect (2002); Benjamin Bergen (2012)
summary: Tests whether interface labels, gestures and metaphors evoke mental simulations compatible with the required action, using response-time compatibility effects and comprehension measures.
description: Embodied simulation theory holds that understanding language involves partially re-enacting the perceptual and motor experiences it describes. Glenberg and Kaschak's action-sentence compatibility effect showed that people respond faster when the response direction matches the motion implied by a sentence. Bergen summarises evidence that people simulate orientation, direction, shape and effort. For interfaces, labels and metaphors such as 'swipe up to archive' or 'pull to refresh' are understood partly by simulation, so mismatches between the implied and the required action slow responses and cause errors. The method identifies the action or spatial content each label implies, measures response times and errors when required actions match or conflict with it, and favours wording and gesture mappings that evoke compatible simulations.
steps: Test simulation ease of interface labels: present labels in isolation, ask users to describe the action the label refers to and mime the motion (if applicable). Measure:
response latency (faster = easier simulation),
action consistency across participants (% agreement on the described action),
simulation accuracy (does the simulated action match the actual afforded action?). Labels with latency > 1.5s or accuracy < 70% are redesign candidates.
outputs: Inventory of implied actions in labels and gestures, compatibility test results (response time and error differences), and revised mappings.
useWhen: Gesture-based interfaces, spatial and direction labels, AR and VR controls, automotive controls and any label tied to a physical action.
avoidWhen: For abstract labels with no spatial or motor content, or when you lack the ability to measure response times precisely; use comprehension testing.
whyLost: Embodied cognition remained in psycholinguistics labs, and its reaction-time paradigms were never translated into practical UX test protocols.
whereToUse: Feature naming, CTA design, gesture interface label design, voice assistant command design. Bergen's book provides the most accessible empirical grounding for embodied interface metaphor research.
example: A photo app labels a gesture 'push back to dismiss' while requiring an upward swipe. A compatibility test shows 120 ms slower responses and 8% more errors than with the label 'swipe up to dismiss', so the copy is changed.
sources: Louder Than Words — Benjamin K. Bergen
Glenberg & Kaschak, Grounding language in action (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2002)
Barsalou, Perceptual symbol systems (Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1999)
reference: Bergen BK (2012) Louder Than Words: The New Science of How the Mind Makes Meaning. Basic Books

name: Emergent Mixed Methods Design (Following a Thread)
origin: De Allegri and Lohmann; follow-the-thread from Moran-Ellis et al. (2006) and Pluye and Granikov (2022)
summary: Let the design change substantially during a study when one strand produces discordant or surprising results, and pursue the surprise with new data or analysis in the other strand.
description: A mixed methods design is emergent when iterative dialogue between strands leads to substantial changes in conceptualisation, sampling, data collection or analysis. It may be planned as emergent, with flexibility agreed upfront, or become so. Triggers include new questions, new data sources, unexpected findings in the other strand and stakeholder requests. Following a thread, from Moran-Ellis and colleagues, is the core move: take a discordant finding from one strand and pursue it with new hypotheses and analyses in the other, rather than reporting it as a limitation. In a Malawi maternal health evaluation, a survey showed no rise in service use while health workers reported more work; the team added facility records and followed the thread to referral patterns and maternal mortality. Only substantial changes count, not tweaks, and each change is documented with its rationale. The risk is sprawl, so budgets and approvals must allow flexibility.
steps: Plan for possible emergence and explain it to sponsors, ethics boards and stakeholders upfront.
At each stage, watch for triggers: new questions, new data sources, unexpected findings in the other strand, stakeholder requests.
When strands disagree, select the discordant result as a thread to follow.
Add a component, data source or sample, or change the analysis or integration point, to pursue it.
Document each change, its trigger and its rationale.
Integrate the findings and report how the design evolved and why.
outputs: An evolving design with a documented change log, resolved or explained discrepancies and integrated findings.
useWhen: Exploratory or evaluative programmes where surprises are likely and decisions depend on understanding them, such as post-launch evaluations with conflicting signals.
avoidWhen: Confirmatory studies with pre-registered hypotheses or fixed regulatory protocols; keep emergent analyses clearly labelled as exploratory.
whyLost: UX teams often adapt studies informally but do not frame divergence as a thread to follow or document design changes, so the logic is invisible and unrepeatable.
whereToUse: Product launch evaluations, metric-versus-feedback conflicts, AI feature studies where telemetry and user reports disagree.
example: Telemetry shows an AI summarisation feature is used heavily, yet a survey reports low trust. The team follows the thread by adding session replays and short interviews with heavy users, finding they use summaries only to triage and then read originals.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Moran-Ellis, J., Alexander, V. D., Cronin, A., Dickinson, M., Fielding, J., Sleney, J. and Thomas, H. (2006). Triangulation and integration: processes, claims and implications. Qualitative Research, 6(1), 45-59.

name: EMO questionnaire (Emotional Metric Outcomes)
origin: James R. Lewis and Desiree K. Mayes (2014), International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
summary: A 16-item questionnaire measuring the user's own emotions in four factors: positive and negative relationship affect, and positive and negative personal affect.
description: The EMO measures the emotions a person experiences in a relationship with a company or product, not the product's emotional qualities. Its 16 items form four factors of four items each: positive relationship affect, negative relationship affect, positive personal affect and negative personal affect. Factor scores are the mean of their items. Lewis and Mayes developed it with standard psychometric methods, and Albert and Tullis report it as a stronger predictor of overall user experience, likelihood to recommend and loyalty than some alternatives. Separating relationship affect (how the person feels about the company) from personal affect (how the person feels in themselves) helps distinguish brand-level from experience-level emotion. Item wording is in the original paper and should be taken from there.
steps: Obtain the 16 items and scoring instructions from Lewis and Mayes (2014).
Administer the items after the experience being evaluated, such as a task set, service episode or period of use.
Score each of the four factors as the mean of its four items.
Report factors separately and compare across products, versions or segments with confidence intervals.
Relate factor scores to outcomes such as likelihood to recommend, retention or task success.
outputs: Four affect factor scores per respondent, and comparisons and relations to outcomes.
useWhen: Measuring emotional outcomes of customer experiences or product use alongside usability metrics, especially in service-heavy domains where relationship with the company matters.
avoidWhen: Measuring moment-to-moment emotion during a task (use physiological or experience-sampling measures), or when a very short instrument is required; then use a single-item or brief affect scale.
whyLost: It appeared as UX questionnaires proliferated; SUS, NPS and UEQ occupy most survey space and the EMO is rarely chosen despite its validation.
whereToUse: Customer experience surveys, banking and insurance, telecom and support journeys, benchmarking experience after redesigns.
example: An insurer adds the EMO to its post-claim survey. Negative relationship affect falls after a redesign of claim status updates while personal affect is unchanged, and the drop in negative relationship affect predicts renewal better than CSAT does.
reference: Lewis, J. R. and Mayes, D. K. (2014). Development and psychometric evaluation of the Emotional Metric Outcomes (EMO) questionnaire. International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, 30(9), 685-702.

name: Emotion detection from mouse and keyboard logs
aka: Emotion detection from mouse and keyboard interaction logs
origin: Zimmermann et al., 2003; Desolda, Esposito, Lanzilotti and Costabile, 2021
summary: Train classifiers to infer users' emotions from mouse and keyboard features, using webcam-based labels during training, so emotion can later be estimated without a camera.
description: Desolda and colleagues collected in-the-wild data with a browser plug-in that logged mouse and keyboard events during ordinary web use for weeks and captured a webcam face image every two seconds. Facial expression analysis provided emotion labels. Features derived from interaction logs were used to train classifiers (decision trees, random forests, AdaBoost and a multilayer perceptron), with forward feature selection per model. Once trained, the model can run in a page script to infer visitors' emotions in real time from interaction alone. With 12 participants over 30 days, the best average accuracy was 47 per cent (random forest), so the approach remains exploratory. Labels inherit the error of face-based emotion recognition, test reliability cannot be tracked, and continuous webcam capture needs strong consent and data protection.
steps: Recruit volunteers and obtain explicit consent for interaction logging and periodic webcam capture.
Have participants install a logging plug-in and use the web normally for several weeks.
Label emotional state from face images at short intervals (every 2 seconds in the study).
Derive features from interaction logs (speed, pauses, clicks, typing rhythm) aligned with labels.
Train and compare classifiers with forward feature selection, validating on held-out participants rather than held-out samples.
Deploy the best model only if accuracy is well above chance, and validate its signal against self-report before use.
outputs: A trained emotion classifier driven by interaction data and a labelled in-the-wild dataset of emotions and interactions.
useWhen: You are researching passive, camera-free affect signals at scale, with ethics approval and enough participants to validate a model.
avoidWhen: You need reliable emotion measurement now; accuracy is low (47 per cent in the reported study). Use self-report, experience sampling or multi-channel affective measurement instead. Avoid where covert inference would be unethical.
whyLost: Accuracy has stayed modest since early work, and privacy concerns about inferring emotion without awareness limit deployment.
whereToUse: Affective computing research, stress detection in e-learning, frustration signals in analytics, accessibility research.
example: An e-learning platform pilots a keystroke-based frustration model with consenting students. Its predictions correlate weakly with self-reports, so the team uses it only to flag sessions for review, not to adapt content.
sources: User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
reference: Desolda, G., Esposito, A., Lanzilotti, R., & Costabile, M. F. (2021), as reviewed in Abbas, A. M. H., Ghauth, K. I., & Ting, C.-Y. (2022). User experience design using machine learning: A systematic review. IEEE Access, 10, 51501-51514.

name: Emotional Brand Attachment Scale
aka: Emotional brand attachment scale (connection, passion, affection)
origin: Thomson, MacInnis and Park (2005)
summary: Rate ten emotion adjectives about a brand on seven-point agreement scales and average them into connection, passion and affection subscores and an overall attachment score.
description: Emotional attachment shapes loyalty beyond satisfaction. Thomson, MacInnis and Park's scale has ten adjectives in three dimensions: connection (connected, bonded, attached), passion (passionate, delighted, captivated) and affection (affectionate, friendly, loved, peaceful). Respondents rate agreement that each describes their feelings towards the brand on a seven-point scale. Averaging within a dimension gives subscores, and averaging all items gives an overall attachment score that can be compared across competing brands or tracked over time. Sauro presents it as part of customer analytics alongside loyalty measures, with an example of airlines scoring around 4 and 5 out of 7. Its rigour comes from its published validation in consumer psychology; in UX it complements usability and satisfaction measures when the question is whether a product inspires attachment.
steps: Present the ten adjectives for the brand or product being studied.
Have respondents rate agreement with each on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
Average the items within connection, passion and affection to form subscores.
Average all ten items for an overall attachment score.
Compare scores with competitors or across releases, reporting confidence intervals.
Relate attachment to loyalty or retention data where available.
outputs: Connection, passion and affection subscores and an overall attachment score per brand.
useWhen: Comparing emotional attachment across competing products or tracking it after major changes, especially in consumer products where loyalty is emotional as much as functional.
avoidWhen: Avoid for enterprise or utility products where attachment is not a sensible goal, and do not treat it as a usability measure; use SUPR-Q or Net Promoter Score for broader loyalty benchmarks.
whyLost: It is established in marketing research but UX teams rarely measure brand attachment, leaving it to brand teams.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, travel and hospitality, retail, media and subscription services, post-redesign brand impact checks.
example: After a redesign of a travel app, the team compares attachment against two competitors. Overall scores are similar, but the passion subscore drops from 4.9 to 4.3, prompting a look at removed inspiration features.
reference: Thomson, M., MacInnis, D. J. and Park, C. W. (2005). The ties that bind: measuring the strength of consumers' emotional attachments to brands. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 15(1), 77-91.

name: Emotional Design Audit (Walter Hierarchy)
donor: Interaction design, adapted from Maslow's hierarchy of needs
origin: Aarron Walter, 2011 (Designing for Emotion), adapting Maslow's hierarchy of needs; Walter gives the hierarchy as a model, and the scored audit is the atlas's own operationalisation
summary: Scores a product against Walter's functional, reliable, usable and pleasurable tiers to show where design investment will pay off before pursuing delight.
description: Aarron Walter adapted Maslow's hierarchy to products: a design must first be functional, then reliable, then usable, and only then can it be pleasurable. The audit scores each tier from 1 to 5 using evidence (defect and outage data for reliability, usability findings for usability, affective measures for pleasure) rather than opinion. The hierarchy is treated as strict: investment in personality, micro-interactions or brand moments is wasted while a lower tier sits below 4. The audit then identifies a small number of peak emotional moments in the journey (first use, success, recovery from error) where pleasure work should concentrate. Its value is as a prioritisation discipline that stops teams polishing delight on top of unreliable foundations. Walter presents the hierarchy as a model illustrated with examples, not as an audit procedure, and uses it to check that emotional design does not erode the lower tiers; the 1 to 5 scores and the threshold of 4 are the atlas's own operationalisation.
steps: Name the key flows to audit and gather evidence for each tier: defect and outage data for functional and reliable, usability findings for usable, affect measures for pleasurable.

Score each flow from 1 to 5 at each tier: functional (does it work?), reliable (does it work consistently?), usable (can people use it without frustration?) and pleasurable (does it give genuine positive emotion?).
Treat the hierarchy as strict: direct effort to the lowest tier scoring below 4 before investing in the tiers above it.
Once the lower tiers are secure, choose a few peak moments in the journey (first use, first success, recovery from error) and design each for a specific positive emotion.
Re-score after changes and check that the emotional design work has not weakened the lower tiers.
outputs: A tier scorecard with evidence for each score, the lowest failing tier flagged as the investment priority, and a shortlist of peak moments for emotional design work.
useWhen: Teams are debating whether to invest in delight, brand or personality versus fixing reliability and usability, or you need a simple frame to communicate design priorities to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: You need a validated measurement of emotional experience; this is a heuristic prioritisation tool. Use Multi-Channel Affective Measurement or a validated scale such as AttrakDiff or UEQ instead.
whyLost: It is remembered as a pyramid diagram on slides rather than run as an evidence-based scoring exercise, so the strict ordering and the evidence requirement are usually dropped.
whereToUse: Product roadmap reviews, design-system and brand refreshes, mature SaaS products considering 'delight' initiatives, and consumer apps with high churn.
example: A budgeting app team wants animated celebrations for savings goals. The audit scores reliability at 2 because bank syncs fail weekly, so the celebrations are deferred and sync failures fixed first; pleasure work then focuses on the first successful sync.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 36 — Emotional Design Hierarchies & the Aesthetic-Usability Effect
Maslow, A theory of human motivation (Psychological Review, 1943)
reference: Walter, A. (2011). Designing for Emotion. A Book Apart.

name: Emotionally Intelligent Design Checklists
aka: Checklist for designing with emotion AI
donor: Technology ethics; affective computing; positive psychology
origin: Pamela Pavliscak, 2018; botification checklist after Frischmann and Selinger, 2018
summary: Three linked reviews for emotionally aware products: a go/no-go checklist for emotion AI, a six-question botification test, and a six-category emotional intelligence rating profile.
description: Pavliscak offers three instruments. The emotion AI checklist asks fourteen questions in three groups: understand the emotional dimension (is emotion crucial, does sensing add value to people and not only the business, is the emotion actually detectable, can the product handle complex or changing feelings); define what matters (minimal collection and retention, anonymised aggregate defaults, short unbundled consent, plans for failure and misuse, legal review starting from GDPR); and design with emotional intelligence (social norms, diverse training data tested with scenarios, multiple inputs as failsafe, user control, broad participation). The botification checklist asks six yes/no questions, such as whether human communication is replaced by machines or people are unsure whether they are talking to a bot; any yes is a flag. The intervention rating scores a product negative, neutral or positive on six emotional intelligence categories using catalogues of patterns and antipatterns, plotted as a profile.
steps: Ask whether emotion is crucial to the experience and whether emotion data would add value to individuals and at collective scale, not only to the business.
Assess detectability through voice, face, words or gesture, and state what the system cannot capture.
Set data defaults (minimum collection, shortest retention, anonymised aggregates), draft short unbundled consent, and plan for failure, misuse and legal obligations.
