Review social norms, dataset diversity (tested with scenarios), multiple inputs and user controls such as opt-out and adjustable sensitivity; decide go or no-go.
Run the six botification questions before release and redesign or justify any yes.

Rate each emotional intelligence category (self-awareness, self-management, self-catalysing, social awareness, social skills, self-transcendence) as negative, neutral or positive against the pattern catalogue.
Plot the profile, remove negatives first, then plan positive interventions.
outputs: A documented go/no-go decision with design requirements, a botification flag list, and an emotional intelligence profile with patterns to remove or add.
useWhen: Products that sense, infer or respond to emotion, conversational agents and companions, and engagement-driven features that may harm well-being.
avoidWhen: When measured evidence is required; these are unvalidated checklists. Pair with Value-Sensitive Design, Affective State Measurement or user research with affected people.
whyLost: They come from one practitioner book, and emotion AI reviews are usually absorbed into generic privacy or AI ethics processes.
whereToUse: Mental health and wellness apps, AI companions, customer service bots, automotive driver monitoring and social platforms.
example: A bank considering voice-stress detection in its call centre runs the emotion AI checklist and finds detectability poor and customer value unclear. The feature is dropped in favour of an opt-in callback option.
reference: Pavliscak, P. (2018) Emotionally Intelligent Design: Rethinking How We Create Products. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Empathic design (Leonard and Rayport)
origin: Dorothy Leonard and Jeffrey Rayport (1997), Harvard Business Review
summary: A multidisciplinary team observes people using products in their real settings to surface latent needs and workarounds, then brainstorms and prototypes solutions from what it saw.
description: Customers get used to current products and stop noticing their problems, so asking them yields incremental requests. Leonard and Rayport argued that observing people in the product's real operating environment reveals usage errors, home-made fixes and unarticulated, latent needs that can lead to breakthrough products. Their five-step process sends a multidisciplinary team (marketers, engineers, designers, usability specialists), because each observer's training shapes what they notice. The team observes chosen people doing a task in a real or artificial setting, capturing mainly visual and auditory data (often video) with a few open-ended questions; members then review each other's data and list possible problems, needs and motivations; brainstorm and visualise many solutions; and build quick prototypes to gather feedback and iterate. It is a direct ancestor of the 'empathise' phase of design thinking.
steps: Design the research: decide whom to observe, which behaviour, in which setting (preferably real use), and form a multidisciplinary observation team.
Capture data mainly from visual and auditory cues, often on video, adding a few open-ended questions to interpret actions.
Analyse and reflect: team members review each other's data and list the target group's possible problems, needs, motivations and workarounds.
Brainstorm solutions, turning observations into many visual representations.
Build quick prototypes of possible solutions, gather customer feedback and iterate.
outputs: Lists of latent needs, problems and workarounds; solution sketches; iterated prototypes.
useWhen: Front-end innovation where customers cannot articulate needs because they are habituated to current products.
avoidWhen: When you need to measure prevalence or validate a specific design; use surveys, analytics or usability tests. Observer background biases what is seen, so a single-discipline team weakens it.
whyLost: It was absorbed into design thinking as 'empathy', often reduced to interviews and persona workshops, with the original emphasis on multidisciplinary observation of real use and workarounds forgotten.
whereToUse: Consumer products, medical devices, home technology, B2B equipment and service innovation.
example: A kitchen appliance firm sends an engineer, a designer and a marketer to watch ten households cook. They see people propping recipe tablets against kettles away from splashes, which leads to a prototype splash-proof stand integrated into a smart scale.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Leonard, D. and Rayport, J. F. (1997). Spark innovation through empathic design. Harvard Business Review, 75(6), 102-113.

name: Empathic Modelling (Impairment Simulation)
aka: Empathy simulation through impairment and role-play
origin: Patricia Moore's ageing simulations (1979-1982); Ford Third Age Suit; Nicolle and Maguire (2003)
summary: Designers wear simple simulations of impairment or ageing (smeared glasses, earplugs, splints, ageing suits) while doing everyday tasks, to surface barriers and build empathy.
description: Empathic modelling puts designers physically closer to the experience of disabled or older users. Kits range from cheap props (glasses smeared with petroleum jelly for cataracts, a blindfold, earplugs, elastic bands, splints or taped knuckles for limited dexterity) to full ageing suits such as Ford's Third Age Suit or MIT AgeLab's AGNES, or simulated environments. Designers perform everyday or product tasks, such as reading a statement, entering a car or using a phone, record difficulties and translate them into requirements. Graded variants add role-play and accompanying a real person through the activity. It was first used to elicit requirements for visually impaired people in buildings. It is informal with no validation, and disability scholars criticise it for misrepresenting lived experience and reinforcing stereotypes, since a temporary impairment lacks adaptation and expertise. It should complement, never replace, research with disabled and older people.
steps: Choose the impairments or age-related changes relevant to the target users and product tasks.
Prepare simulations: smeared or blurred glasses, blindfolds, earplugs or hearing filters, gloves, splints or bands, or an ageing suit.
Have designers carry out everyday and product tasks under the simulation, ideally after role-play or accompanying a real person.
Record barriers, workarounds and feelings as they occur, using video or notes.
Translate barriers into concrete design requirements and accessibility checks.
Validate requirements with disabled or older participants before acting on them.
outputs: Lists of experienced barriers and design implications, designer empathy, and time-based media (video, comics) conveying the experience.
useWhen: You want to sensitise a design team quickly to physical and sensory barriers, or generate early hypotheses about accessibility issues for ageing or impaired users.
avoidWhen: You need valid evidence about disabled people's experience or are tempted to replace them as participants; use inclusive design research and accessibility evaluation with disabled people instead.
whyLost: It survives because it is cheap and memorable, though the critique from disability communities has made many teams treat it as a warm-up rather than research.
whereToUse: Automotive interiors, packaging, banking and health apps for older users, public kiosks and built environments.
example: A bank's mobile team uses blurred glasses and taped fingers to complete a payment on small targets and finds the confirmation button unusable. They raise target sizes and then confirm the fix with older customers.
reference: Nicolle, C., & Maguire, M. (2003). Empathic modelling in teaching design for all. Proceedings of HCI International 2003.

name: Empathy Map
origin: Scott Matthews and Dave Gray, XPLANE; later revisions add goals, Says/Does and pains and gains
summary: A team canvas summarising what one type of user sees, says, does, hears, thinks and feels, used to build shared understanding and expose knowledge gaps before ideation.
description: The empathy map externalises what a team knows about one user type. In Gamestorming's original form a large head is drawn and named, and the areas around it are labelled Thinking, Seeing, Hearing and Feeling; in about 15 minutes the group describes the person's experience, then synthesises what they want, what motivates them and what the team can do for them. Later forms use four quadrants (Says, Thinks, Feels, Does) or begin with goals and add pains and gains. Universal Methods of Design insists on order (goals, then observable see, say, do and hear from research, then inferred thoughts and feelings) and on research-based content; empty or speculative areas become research questions. One map is made per persona. Gray et al. contrast it with personas: quick and focusing, but not rigorous. The Pain-Gain Map is a sibling for decision-makers.
steps: Choose one user type or persona and state who they are and what they need to do (one map per type).
Draw the canvas: a head with areas or four quadrants.
Fill observable areas (see, say, do, hear) from research data, citing sources where possible.
Fill inferred areas (think, feel, pains, gains) and mark which are evidence-based and which are assumptions.
Synthesise what the person wants, what motivates them and what the team can do for them (about 15 minutes for a quick version).
List knowledge gaps as research questions and keep the map visible during ideation.
outputs: A completed empathy map per user type, a short synthesis of wants and motivations, and a list of knowledge gaps.
useWhen: Use early in ideation to align a team around research findings about one user type, or as a quick check on what the team actually knows.
avoidWhen: Avoid using it in place of research or personas: it is easily filled with assumptions and flattens differences between users. Build evidence with Interviews or Contextual Inquiry and use Personas for durable, research-based archetypes.
whyLost: It survived because it is fast, needs no training and fits design thinking workshops; its widespread use often drops the requirement that content come from research.
whereToUse: Design thinking workshops, onboarding new team members, sales and value proposition work.
example: After eight interviews a team maps a first-time renter and finds the Feels area full of guesses about deposits, so it adds deposit fears to the next interview guide.
reference: Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010). Gamestorming: A Playbook for Innovators, Rulebreakers, and Changemakers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 65-66.

name: Empirical Criterion Keying
origin: Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (1940s); MMPI-2 restructured scales by Tellegen et al. (2003)
summary: Build a scale by keeping the items whose answers best separate known criterion groups, and add validity items that flag lying, faking or careless answering.
description: Empirical criterion keying selects items by what they predict rather than what they appear to measure. The MMPI was built by writing more than 1,000 true-false statements, giving them to people with known disorders and to comparison groups, and keeping the items that best differentiated the groups. Kept items were combined into subscales (the MMPI-2 has more than 500 items, with clinical scales such as depression at 57 items and social introversion at 69), and interpretation rests on the respondent's profile across subscales. The inventory also includes validity items designed to detect lying, faking and non-response. Because items are chosen statistically, their content may not obviously match the construct, which makes them harder to fake but also harder to explain. It is a distinct strategy from factor-analytic scale development, which groups items by their intercorrelations.
steps: Write a large pool of candidate items.
Administer them to people known to belong to each criterion group (for example churned versus retained customers) and to a comparison group.
Keep the items whose answers best differentiate the groups, and cross-validate the selection on a fresh sample.
Combine kept items into subscales.
Add validity items to detect lying, faking, inattention and non-response.
Interpret respondents by their profile across subscales, together with their validity flags.
outputs: Subscale scores, a respondent profile and validity flags, with evidence of discrimination between criterion groups.
useWhen: Building a short screener or predictive questionnaire where the goal is to classify people into known outcome groups, such as likely churners or expert versus novice users.
avoidWhen: It relies on conscious self-report and on a trustworthy criterion; items can capitalise on chance without cross-validation. When you need a construct with interpretable dimensions, use Validated Scale Construction or Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA).
whyLost: Clinical psychology moved towards construct-based and factor-analytic scales, and UX survey work borrows those, so criterion keying is little known outside clinical assessment.
whereToUse: Churn-risk and readiness questionnaires, recruitment screeners that must identify real experts, fraud or careless-respondent detection in panels.
example: A SaaS team writes 80 statements about work habits, gives them to 300 retained and 300 churned trial users, and keeps the 12 that best separate the groups on a holdout sample, plus two attention-check items, as a churn-risk screener.
reference: Tellegen, A. et al. (2003). MMPI-2 Restructured Clinical (RC) Scales. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press; as described in Stangor, C. (2012). Introduction to Psychology, pp. 551-552.

name: Empirical touch target derivation
origin: Parhi, Karlson and Bederson, 2006; Holz and Baudisch, 2010; Henze et al., 2011 large-scale touch studies
summary: Derives minimum touch target sizes from measured touch-offset distributions for a specific device, posture and population, rather than relying on generic guidelines.
description: Platform guidelines (44 pt on iOS, 48 dp on Android, 9-10 mm physical) are averages from particular populations and conditions. Empirical derivation measures where real users actually touch when aiming at targets, under the real conditions of use: gloves, motion, one-handed grip, tremor or screen angle. Touch points form a roughly bivariate normal distribution around the intended centre, often systematically offset. The target size needed for a given hit rate follows from the distribution's spread: covering about plus or minus 2 standard deviations gives roughly 95% accuracy in each dimension. Rigour comes from realistic conditions, enough taps per location to estimate offsets across the screen, and reporting sizes for the accuracy required by the task's risk level.
steps: Define the conditions of use (device, mount angle, gloves, posture, motion, user population) and the required accuracy (for example 99% for irreversible actions, 95% for routine).
Build a calibration task presenting crosshair targets at a grid of at least 9-25 screen locations.
Collect at least 20 taps per location per participant from 12-20 participants under realistic conditions.
Compute mean offset vectors and standard deviations in x and y for each location.
Derive target size as the width covering the required proportion of the distribution (about 4 SD for 95%, 5.2 SD for 99%) and apply location-specific offset correction where offsets exceed 1 mm.
Validate derived sizes in a task-level test with fresh participants and compare error rates against guideline sizes.
outputs: Touch offset maps, spread statistics, derived minimum target sizes per accuracy level and screen region, and offset-correction parameters.
useWhen: When users operate under unusual constraints (gloves, vibration, tremor, kiosks at odd angles, children, older adults) or when touch errors are costly.
avoidWhen: For standard consumer apps used in ordinary conditions where platform guidelines are adequate; use guideline audits instead.
whyLost: Platform guidelines made calibration feel unnecessary, so teams cite them uncritically; calibration studies survive mainly in academic HCI and specialist device makers.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial touchscreens, automotive displays, field service tablets, accessibility for motor impairments, and public kiosks.
example: Theatre nurses wearing double sterile gloves showed touch spreads of 3.1 mm SD and a 2 mm downward offset on a tilted console. Derived 99% targets were 16 mm, far above the 9 mm guideline, and the redesign cut mis-taps from 7% to under 1%.
sources: Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 3 — The Ballistics of the Human Body — Fitts' Law & Motor Control
reference: Holz, C. & Baudisch, P. (2010). The generalized perceived input point model and how to double touch accuracy by extracting fingerprints. Proceedings of CHI 2010.

name: End-to-end research pipeline orchestration
origin: Workflow management tools such as Make (1976), Apache Airflow (Airbnb, 2014) and Prefect (2018)
summary: Defining the whole research data flow, from audio to transcripts, NLP, AI coding and synthesis, as orchestrated, logged tasks so it runs reliably, resumes after failure and can be reproduced.
description: An orchestrator (Prefect, Airflow, or a Makefile for small projects) represents each stage as a task with inputs, outputs and dependencies: convert audio, transcribe, diarise, run the NLP pipeline, run AI coding passes, aggregate and produce reports. It handles retries, caching of completed steps, parallelism and logging. For research this gives reproducibility (one command reruns everything), auditability (logs show what ran on which data with which versions) and robustness for hundreds of files. Rigour comes from idempotent tasks, versioned configuration, explicit quality gates between stages, and storing intermediate outputs so any result can be traced back.
steps: Map the pipeline as a dependency graph of stages with defined inputs and outputs.
Implement each stage as an idempotent task that can be rerun safely and skips already-processed files.
Configure retries (e.g. 3 with backoff) for API and transcription failures, and log errors per file.
Place quality gates between stages that halt or flag runs failing thresholds.
Store configuration (model versions, prompts, thresholds) in version-controlled files and record them with each run.
Run end to end on a pilot batch of 5-10 files before full scale, then schedule or trigger runs as new data arrive.
outputs: An orchestrated pipeline, run logs, cached intermediate outputs and reproducible final datasets and reports.
useWhen: Programmes processing many recordings or documents repeatedly, such as continuous interviewing, multi-country studies or ongoing feedback analysis.
avoidWhen: Avoid for one-off small studies; a script or notebook is enough. Orchestration overhead only pays off with repetition or scale.
whyLost: Orchestration is a data engineering discipline; research teams rarely run pipelines large or repeated enough to need it, until AI-assisted analysis.
whereToUse: Research operations, continuous discovery, voice-of-customer programmes and research repositories.
example: A research operations team processes 40 new interviews weekly. A Prefect flow converts, transcribes, diarises, codes and aggregates them overnight, with failed files retried and a summary report waiting each morning.
sources: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C13 — The Full Agentic Research Pipeline — Whisper → spaCy → AI Coder → Synthesis
reference: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology 13(6)

name: Endowment effect test
origin: Richard Thaler (1980) and Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler's mug experiments (1990)
summary: Measures how much more users value something once they own it, by comparing willingness to accept giving it up with willingness to pay to acquire it.
description: In Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler's experiments, owners of a coffee mug demanded roughly twice what non-owners would pay for it. The endowment effect explains why users resist giving up configured settings, saved data, legacy plans or familiar workflows, and why trials, customisation and early ownership cues raise retention. The test randomly endows some participants with an item (a plan, a feature, a data asset, a design they built) and compares the price or effort they require to give it up with what non-endowed participants would pay or do to get it. A ratio of willingness to accept to willingness to pay well above 1 indicates endowment. Rigour comes from random assignment of ownership, incentive-compatible elicitation such as the Becker-DeGroot-Marschak mechanism, and controls for information differences.
steps: Choose the good to test: a feature, plan, saved configuration, content library or self-made artefact, and define how ownership is created (granted, trialled or self-built).
Randomly assign 40 to 100 participants per condition to owner and non-owner conditions, ensuring both groups receive identical information about the good.

Elicit willingness to accept from owners and willingness to pay from non-owners using an incentive-compatible method such as Becker-DeGroot-Marschak, or a realistic equivalent like choosing between keeping the good and a credit amount.
Compute the median WTA/WTP ratio with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval and test the difference with a Mann-Whitney U test.
Add a variant that varies ownership duration or effort invested (for example 1 day versus 14 days of trial, or a template versus a self-built item) to estimate how endowment grows.
Apply results to design decisions about trials, migration paths, downgrades and customisation, and check them against observed retention.
outputs: WTA/WTP ratios with confidence intervals, the effect of ownership duration or effort, and implications for trials, migrations and pricing.
useWhen: Designing free trials, onboarding personalisation, plan downgrades, data migrations or feature sunsets, where ownership may shape value.
avoidWhen: You cannot create genuine ownership in the study, or the decision is simple enough to test directly with a retention A/B test of trial length.
whyLost: UX speaks loosely of 'investment' and the IKEA effect in growth design, but the experimental WTA/WTP protocol remained in economics labs.
whereToUse: SaaS trials and freemium, data portability and migration, legacy plan grandfathering, creator tools, subscription cancellation flows (ethically).
example: A note-taking app tested whether users who had built their own templates for 14 days valued premium templates more. Owners demanded a credit 2.4 times higher than non-owners would pay, and the team moved the template builder into the trial's first session.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. H. (1990). Experimental tests of the endowment effect and the Coase theorem. Journal of Political Economy, 98(6), 1325–1348.

name: Endowment-contrast decomposition of satisfaction ratings
origin: Tversky and Griffin (1991)
summary: Cross the quality of a prior experience with its relatedness to the current one to separate how past experiences raise satisfaction (endowment) or lower it (contrast).
description: A past experience affects satisfaction with the present in two opposing ways: a good memory adds to well-being (endowment), but a related good experience also raises the standard against which the present is judged (contrast). Tversky and Griffin separated them with a 2 x 2 design: prior experience good or poor, and related or unrelated to the current one, with the current experience held constant. Endowment is the rating difference after good versus poor unrelated priors; contrast is how much a related prior shifts ratings relative to an unrelated one. Vignettes on a 1 to 10 scale gave endowment around 2.2 and contrast around 0.9; a real-money game gave 2.3 and 2.1, with negative contrast larger than positive. The same work shows choices and satisfaction judgements can diverge.
steps: Fix the current experience to be evaluated so it is identical for everyone.
Create good and poor prior experiences, each in a related version (same domain or style) and an unrelated version.
Randomly assign participants to the four cells and add a filler task between the prior and current experiences.
Collect satisfaction ratings on the current experience (for example on a 1 to 10 scale).
Compute endowment E = S(unrelated good) minus S(unrelated poor) and the two contrast terms from related versus unrelated cells.
Report the asymmetry between positive and negative contrast, and check whether choices diverge from ratings.
outputs: Separate estimates of endowment and contrast effects on satisfaction, including their asymmetry.
useWhen: Sequencing experiences (onboarding before core tasks, premium trials before downgrade, a polished demo before the real product) where an earlier experience may raise or lower satisfaction with a later one.
avoidWhen: When relatedness cannot be manipulated cleanly or only choices (not ratings) matter; use a standard A/B test on the downstream behaviour instead.
whyLost: It is a hedonic psychology paradigm rarely taught outside judgement research; UX measures satisfaction without decomposing what earlier experiences contribute.
whereToUse: Free-trial to paid transitions, onboarding design, premium-tier downgrades, sequencing of product tours and demos in SaaS and games.
example: A productivity app tests whether a polished onboarding lowers satisfaction with an ordinary core editor. An unrelated onboarding raises editor ratings, but a related tutorial in the same visual style lowers them, so the team aligns the tutorial's polish with the real editor.
reference: Tversky, A. and Griffin, D. (1991). Endowment and contrast in judgments of well-being. In F. Strack, M. Argyle and N. Schwarz (eds), Subjective Well-Being. Pergamon.

name: Enhanced Cognitive Interview (Forensic)
origin: Ronald Fisher and Edward Geiselman, 1984-1992 (Memory-Enhancing Techniques for Investigative Interviewing, 1992)
summary: A memory-retrieval interview protocol that uses context reinstatement, report-everything instructions, varied retrieval orders and perspectives to elicit more accurate recall of past events.
description: Developed to improve eyewitness interviews, the cognitive interview applies memory research: mentally reinstating the physical and emotional context of the event, asking witnesses to report everything without editing, recalling events in different orders (e.g. reverse), and from different perspectives. The enhanced version adds rapport building, transferring control to the witness, open-ended questioning, witness-compatible questioning and avoidance of interruption. Meta-analyses show substantial increases in correct details with little increase in errors. Not to be confused with cognitive interviewing for questionnaire pretesting, it is ideal for UX interviews about past incidents, purchases or experiences where memory quality matters.
steps: Build rapport and explain that the participant is the expert and should report everything, even trivial details.
Guide context reinstatement: ask them to picture the place, time, device, mood and what they were trying to do.
Elicit a free narrative without interruption; take notes for later probes.
Probe with open, participant-compatible questions about images and details they mentioned.
Use varied retrieval: reverse order, different perspectives, focusing on specific senses or screens.
Summarise back, invite corrections and close with neutral, non-leading questions.
outputs: Richer, more accurate accounts of past experiences with fewer leading-question distortions.
useWhen: Interviewing about specific past events: incidents, fraud experiences, purchase decisions, errors, switching moments.
avoidWhen: Questions about general attitudes or hypothetical futures, where episodic recall is not the goal.
whyLost: Forensic psychology is far from UX training, and the name collides with survey 'cognitive interviewing'.
whereToUse: Fraud and scam victim research, incident investigations, JTBD switch interviews, healthcare adverse events.
example: Interviewing scam victims, researchers use context reinstatement and reverse-order recall; participants recall the exact screen where a fake banking notification appeared, details absent from standard interviews, informing a warning redesign.
sources: Fisher & Geiselman, Memory-Enhancing Techniques for Investigative Interviewing: The Cognitive Interview (1992)
Memon, Meissner & Fraser, The cognitive interview: A meta-analytic review and study space analysis of the past 25 years (2010), Psychology, Public Policy, and Law
reference: Fisher, R. P., & Geiselman, R. E. (1992). Memory-Enhancing Techniques for Investigative Interviewing. Charles C. Thomas.

name: Entity Co-occurrence Networks and Trend Graphs
origin: Ronen Feldman and colleagues' text-mining systems; Feldman (2003)
summary: Draw networks of entities mentioned in the same sentence, cluster dense groups, and step through time to watch links appear and vanish, drilling down to source sentences.
description: Entities and categories are first extracted from a text corpus. Each becomes a node, and an edge links two entities that appear in the same sentence, weighted by frequency. Category connection maps place chosen categories around a circle; relationship maps add a context node; spring layouts handle larger sets. Dense groups are found by iterating a neighbour-based weight (Feldman uses five iterations), keeping the top 10% of edges and taking connected components. Trend graphs add a time slider so the analyst can see links strengthen, appear or disappear across periods. Every edge can be opened to the documents and sentences behind it, which is what keeps the method honest: co-occurrence is only a candidate relationship until the text confirms it.
steps: Extract entities and categories (products, features, organisations, issues) from the corpus.
Count same-sentence co-occurrences for every entity pair.
Choose categories of interest and draw a connection map or spring layout.
Filter weak edges (for example keep the top 10%) and cluster dense subgraphs.
Step through time windows to see which links appear, strengthen or disappear.
Open the supporting sentences for each important edge and confirm the relationship before reporting it.
outputs: Interactive co-occurrence maps, clusters of related entities, and time trends with links to source text.
useWhen: Exploring large volumes of reviews, support tickets, forum posts or open-ended responses to see which features, problems and competitors are discussed together and how that changes over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the corpus is small enough to read, or when you need sentiment or causal claims. Co-occurrence is not a relationship; use topic modelling or close reading for meaning.
whyLost: It belongs to text-mining and intelligence analysis; UX teams moved straight to sentiment and topic models without network views.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer analytics, app-review mining, community forums, competitive intelligence, incident reports.
example: A fintech team maps app reviews by month and sees 'login' and 'face ID' become strongly linked after an OS update. Drilling into the sentences confirms a biometric failure that support had not yet escalated.
reference: Feldman, R. (2003). Mining text data. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 481-518). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Entity-level aggregation
origin: Aspect-based opinion mining, Hu and Liu, 2004
summary: Rolling up extracted entities and their associated sentiment, context and speakers across a corpus to see which features, competitors or workflows matter to whom.
description: After entities are extracted, aggregation turns mentions into analysable summaries: how many participants (not mentions) referred to each feature, with what sentiment or evaluation, in which segments, and alongside which other entities. The participant-level count matters because one talkative participant can dominate mention counts. Aspect-based analysis (Hu and Liu, 2004) links opinions to the entity they target rather than to the whole document. Rigour comes from normalising entity variants (lemmatisation, alias tables), counting at the participant level, reporting co-occurrence carefully, and treating counts as pointers back to transcripts rather than as prevalence estimates for the user population.
steps: Normalise entity mentions to canonical names using an alias table (e.g. 'auto-pay', 'autopay', 'recurring payments').
Attach to each mention its speaker, participant attributes, sentence-level sentiment or evaluation and context.
Aggregate at participant level: number and percentage of participants mentioning each entity, by segment.
Compute entity co-occurrence within participants or passages and visualise as a matrix or network.
Link every aggregate cell back to its underlying quotes so analysts can read the evidence.
State clearly that counts describe the sample, not population prevalence, unless sampling supports inference.
outputs: Entity-by-segment tables, sentiment summaries, co-occurrence matrices and drill-down links to quotes.
useWhen: Summarising large interview, feedback or ticket corpora by feature or topic, and comparing segments.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting mention counts as importance in small qualitative samples; importance should come from analysis of meaning and consequence.
whyLost: Aspect-based analysis lives in commercial text analytics and NLP research; UX researchers rarely have entity-extracted data to aggregate.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer dashboards, support ticket analysis, competitive research and research repositories.
example: Across 150 interviews, aggregation shows 62% of enterprise participants but only 18% of SMB participants mention 'permissions', mostly negatively, and it co-occurs with 'admin onboarding'. Analysts read the linked quotes before prioritising.
sources: Hu, M. & Liu, B. (2004) Mining and summarizing customer reviews. KDD
Liu, B. (2020) Sentiment Analysis: Mining Opinions, Sentiments, and Emotions, 2nd ed.
The Inquiry Series, C10 — spaCy — Building NLP Pipelines for Qualitative Research
reference: Hu, M. & Liu, B. (2004) Mining and summarizing customer reviews. KDD 2004

name: Environmental Ergonomics Assessment
origin: Human factors engineering, post-WWII; ISO 11064 and related standards
summary: Measures the physical conditions of use (lighting, glare, noise, temperature, vibration, posture) and their effect on interaction performance.
description: Environmental ergonomics studies how ambient conditions affect human performance. The treatise names environmental analysis as one of the rigorous human factors methods UX left behind. An assessment measures luminance and glare, ambient noise, vibration, temperature, gloves or protective equipment, and posture at the actual point of use, then tests whether display legibility, audio cues, touch accuracy and attention hold up. Its rigour lies in instrumented measurement (lux meter, sound level meter) and in testing interfaces under representative conditions rather than in a quiet lab. For mobile, field and industrial software, environmental conditions often explain failures that lab testing cannot reproduce.
steps: List the environments where the product is used and select representative sites.
Measure illumination, glare, noise, vibration, temperature and equipment constraints at each site.
Observe posture, grip, gloves and interruptions during real use.
Test legibility, audio cue detection and touch accuracy under the measured conditions or a lab simulation.
Identify mismatches between interface specifications and environmental limits.
Set environmental design requirements such as contrast ratios, cue loudness and target size for gloved use.
outputs: Environmental measurement log, failure list under conditions, environment-adjusted design requirements.
useWhen: Field, industrial, outdoor, vehicle and clinical products; any case where lab results do not match field complaints.
avoidWhen: Products used only in controlled office settings; standard usability testing suffices.
whyLost: UX matured around desktop office software where environment seemed constant, and lost contact with the ergonomics community.
whereToUse: Outdoor mobile apps, factory HMIs, delivery-driver apps, ambulance and ICU software, in-car UX.
example: Delivery drivers miss order notifications; site measurements show 85 dB cab noise and direct sunlight on the screen. The team adds haptic alerts and a high-contrast outdoor mode.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Parsons KC (2000) Environmental ergonomics: a review of principles, methods and models. Applied Ergonomics
Salvendy G (Ed) Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
reference: Parsons KC (2000) Environmental ergonomics: a review of principles, methods and models. Applied Ergonomics 31(6):581-594.

name: Environmental Legibility Analysis (Lynch)
origin: Kevin Lynch, 1960
summary: Uses sketch maps and Lynch's five elements (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks) to assess how easily users form a cognitive map of a space or information architecture.
description: Lynch's The Image of the City asked residents to draw maps and describe journeys, revealing that legible cities are structured by paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. The treatise notes that environmental legibility, how easily a user builds a cognitive map of a space, translates directly to information architecture. Applied to digital products, participants sketch the structure of a site or app from memory, describe how they would get somewhere, and the analyst codes the sketches for Lynch elements, distortions and omissions. The result shows which sections function as districts, which pages act as landmarks and where users lack a coherent map, complementing tree tests that measure findability without revealing the mental map.
steps: Recruit users with varying exposure to the product (new, regular, expert).
Ask each to sketch the product's structure from memory and describe routes to key destinations.
Code sketches for paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks, plus omissions and distortions.
Aggregate into a composite image showing commonly recalled elements.
Compare with the actual IA to locate illegible regions.
Strengthen landmarks, districts and edges in the design and re-test.
outputs: Coded sketch maps, composite cognitive map, legibility gaps, IA recommendations.
useWhen: Large sites, apps with deep navigation, VR worlds, multi-product suites.
avoidWhen: Single-screen tools or when only findability metrics are needed (use tree testing).
whyLost: Spatial metaphors for information faded after the 1990s; IA adopted card sorting and tree testing instead.
whereToUse: Enterprise suites, documentation sites, e-commerce category structures, VR and game worlds.
example: Sketch maps of a cloud console show users recall only three 'districts' out of nine; services not near a remembered landmark are rarely found, so the team introduces persistent service-group landmarks.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lynch K (1960) The Image of the City
Kitchin R (1994) Cognitive maps: what are they and why study them? J Environmental Psychology
Dillon A & Vaughan M (1997) 'It's the journey and the destination': shape and the emergent property of genre. Interacting with Computers
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Lynch K (1960) The Image of the City. MIT Press.

name: Environmental Psychology Assessment
origin: Roger Ulrich (1984), Rachel and Stephen Kaplan (1989), Kevin Lynch (1960)
summary: Applies environmental psychology instruments (legibility, restorativeness, preference, wayfinding) to digital and spatial environments to assess their psychological effects.
description: Environmental psychology studies how designed environments affect behaviour, emotion and cognition. The treatise cites Ulrich's restorative environments research, the Kaplans' attention restoration theory and Lynch's environmental legibility as sources of methods for assessing the psychological effects of spaces that apply directly to digital environments. In the 1990s these informed work on information spaces and virtual environments; with VR and AR, the treatise argues, they are more relevant than ever. Typical instruments include preference ratings, perceived restorativeness scales, sketch maps, wayfinding tasks and physiological stress measures. The priority index rates the area HIGH (evidence 5, impact 5).
steps: Specify the environment (virtual, physical-digital or information space) and outcomes (stress, legibility, wayfinding, preference).
Select validated instruments such as perceived restorativeness scales, sketch maps or wayfinding tasks.
Expose participants to the environment or controlled variants, in situ or in VR.
Measure behavioural, self-report and where feasible physiological responses.
Compare variants and relate spatial features to outcomes.
Derive design guidance for spatial structure, landmarks and restorative qualities.
outputs: Environment ratings, wayfinding performance, legibility maps, design guidance.
useWhen: VR/AR environments, large information spaces, physical-digital services such as hospitals and stations.
avoidWhen: Small, task-bound interfaces with no spatial or environmental character.
whyLost: 1990s information-space work faded with the web's page paradigm; few UX researchers train in environmental psychology.
whereToUse: Metaverse and XR apps, wellbeing apps, hospital wayfinding apps, smart buildings, games.
example: A VR meditation app compares three environments on the Perceived Restorativeness Scale and a post-session attention task; the forest scene improves attention scores while the abstract scene does not.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Ulrich RS (1984) View through a window may influence recovery from surgery. Science 224
Kaplan R & Kaplan S (1989) The Experience of Nature
Lynch K (1960) The Image of the City
Gifford R (2014) Environmental Psychology: Principles and Practice
reference: Gifford R (2014) Environmental Psychology: Principles and Practice. 5th ed. Optimal Books.

name: Epidemic Models (SIR/SEIR) for Adoption and Virality
origin: William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick, 1927
summary: Models users moving between compartments (susceptible, exposed, infected/active, recovered/churned) to estimate spread rates, reproduction numbers and saturation.
description: Compartmental models describe populations moving between states via rates: in SIR, susceptible people become infected through contact (rate beta) and recover (rate gamma). The basic reproduction number R0 = beta/gamma determines whether spread grows. SEIR adds an exposed (latent) stage; SIRS allows reinfection. Fitted to adoption or referral data, these models describe viral growth, word-of-mouth, feature adoption within organisations and even spread of misinformation or abusive behaviour on platforms. They distinguish contact rate from 'stickiness' (recovery) and quantify interventions, much more precisely than a 'viral coefficient' computed from a single cohort.
steps: Define compartments relevant to the product (e.g. unaware, aware, active, lapsed) and transitions.
Collect time series of counts in each compartment, or referral chains if available.
Fit model parameters by maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods, with uncertainty.
Estimate effective reproduction number over time and check fit to observed curves.
Simulate interventions: increasing contact (sharing), reducing churn (recovery), seeding.
Validate predictions on new cohorts or markets.
outputs: Fitted transmission and churn rates, reproduction numbers, projected adoption curves and intervention scenarios.
useWhen: Products growing by word-of-mouth or referrals, internal spread within organisations, or harmful content spreading on platforms.
avoidWhen: Growth driven mainly by paid acquisition or one-off external events.
whyLost: Growth teams use simple viral coefficients; epidemiological modelling skills are rare in product teams.
whereToUse: Referral programmes, collaboration tool spread within enterprises, social features, misinformation dynamics.
example: A note-taking app fits an SEIR model to team-level adoption and finds R below 1 in teams under 10 people because of a long latent period; a shared template launch shortens latency and lifts R above 1.
sources: Kermack & McKendrick, A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics (1927), Proceedings of the Royal Society A
Anderson & May, Infectious Diseases of Humans (1991)
Keeling & Rohani, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals (2008)
reference: Kermack, W. O., & McKendrick, A. G. (1927). Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115(772), 700-721.

name: Epistemic (Socratic) Interviewing
donor: Psychology and philosophy of qualitative interviewing
origin: Steinar Brinkmann (2007); Roulston (2010); after Plato's dialogues
summary: Interview people as accountable reasoners: ask what shared concepts mean, respectfully challenge their answers and test whether their reasons hold.
description: Most qualitative interviewing treats the participant as a holder of experiences or opinions to be recorded without challenge. Epistemic interviewing positions the interviewee as someone giving reasons who can be held to them. The interviewer asks about concepts and norms rather than lived experience (what counts as fair, as trustworthy, as a good tool), offers counter-cases, points out tensions and asks for justification. The interviewer may talk as much as the interviewee, and biography is of little interest. The aim is articulated and tested justifications, and the conversation may well end unresolved; knowledge emerges from the dialogue itself, in the spirit of phronetic social science. Rigour rests on respectful, transparent challenge and on reporting the exchange, not only the participant's final position. It can feel adversarial and is unsuitable for sensitive personal topics.
steps: Choose a concept or norm of shared concern, such as fairness, privacy or quality, relevant to the decision at hand.
Ask the interviewee to state what it is or how it should be applied in their work.
Offer counter-cases or edge cases that test the stated view.
Ask for reasons and examine with them whether those reasons hold or conflict.
Keep the tone respectful, make the challenging stance explicit up front, and let the exchange end unresolved if necessary.
Analyse transcripts for the justifications offered, how they shifted under challenge and which held.
outputs: Articulated and stress-tested justifications for stakeholder or user rules, criteria and norms.
useWhen: Stakeholders or expert users state rules, policies or quality criteria (for content moderation, risk scoring, AI behaviour) and you need to know whether their reasons are coherent.
avoidWhen: Exploring personal experience, emotions or sensitive topics; use Interviews or Micro-Phenomenological Interviewing. Avoid with participants in vulnerable or low-power positions.
whyLost: UX interviewing doctrine stresses neutrality and avoiding leading questions, so deliberate challenge looks like bad practice; the approach remains in qualitative methodology debates.
whereToUse: Defining AI policy and guardrails, moderation rules, expert-system criteria, internal stakeholder requirements, value-sensitive design.
example: Defining what an AI writing assistant should refuse, a researcher asks compliance leads what 'misleading' means, then presents edge cases such as satire and optimistic sales copy until the criteria that survive challenge are clear.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Denzin, N. K. and Lincoln, Y. S. (Eds.) (2017). The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (5th ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Epistemic action analysis
aka: Epistemic action in Tetris, with hazard-function measurement of its benefit
origin: Kirsh and Maglio, 1994; Kirsh, 1995; Maglio, Wenger and Copeland, 2003
summary: Classify observed actions as pragmatic (advancing the goal) or epistemic (changing the world to ease thinking), and inventory how people arrange space to simplify choice, perception and computation.
description: Kirsh and Maglio distinguished pragmatic actions, which move a person towards a physical goal, from epistemic actions, which change the world mainly to make their own information processing easier, faster or more reliable. Expert Tetris players physically rotate falling pieces because screen rotation beats mental rotation; Scrabble players shuffle tiles to prompt word recall. Kirsh's 'intelligent use of space' adds that people arrange workspaces to simplify choice, perception or internal computation, for example laying out a dismantled part's pieces in order or separating heavy and fragile groceries. Clark argues such actions are far more common than planning models assume, showing brain and world working as one system. Maglio, Wenger and Copeland quantified the benefit by comparing processing capacity (hazard function of response time) with and without the information an extra action provides against its time cost; gains grew with memory load and outweighed costs.
steps: Observe the task as actually performed in its real setting, recording video and interaction logs rather than reconstructing an idealised procedure.
List actions that do not advance the goal directly but reveal information, prompt memory, reduce options or reduce later computation.
Classify each action as pragmatic or epistemic, and each spatial arrangement as simplifying choice, perception or internal computation.
Where quantification matters, time the cost of each extra action per participant and compare response-time hazard functions with and without the information it yields, across memory-load levels.
Explain performance as a joint person-plus-environment system and identify which epistemic actions the interface supports, blocks or forces.
Turn findings into design: make cheap the actions people already use to think, and avoid 'tidying' away arrangements that carry information.
outputs: An inventory of epistemic actions and workspace structures, their classification, and where measured, their cost and capacity benefit.
useWhen: When users appear to take 'unnecessary' steps (rearranging, toggling, re-sorting, hovering), when designing workspaces, canvases or dashboards, or when automation might remove actions that support thinking.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the task is fully proceduralised with no room for user arrangement. Coding is interpretive; take procedures from Kirsh and Maglio and Kirsh. For workload overall use NASA-TLX; for system-level cognition use Distributed Cognition Analysis.
whyLost: It is cited in embodied cognition and HCI theory, but practitioners treat 'extra' actions as inefficiency to remove rather than as data about thinking.
whereToUse: Whiteboard and canvas tools, spreadsheets, IDEs, trading and control-room interfaces, games, file and tab management, AI-assisted workspaces.
example: In a design-tool study, users repeatedly drag variants side by side before choosing one. Classing this as epistemic action, the team adds a compare mode instead of auto-arranging layers, and decision time falls.
reference: Kirsh, D., & Maglio, P. (1994). On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science, 18(4), 513-549; Kirsh, D. (1995). The intelligent use of space. Artificial Intelligence, 73(1-2), 31-68.

name: Equivalence testing (TOST)
origin: Donald Schuirmann (1987), developed for bioequivalence trials; popularised in psychology by Daniël Lakens (2017)
summary: Tests whether an effect is small enough to be considered practically equivalent to zero, allowing teams to conclude 'no meaningful difference' rather than merely 'not significant'.
description: A non-significant result does not show that two designs are equivalent; it may reflect low power. Equivalence testing reverses the logic: you set equivalence bounds, the smallest effect that matters (for example ±2 percentage points of conversion or ±0.3 SEQ points), and run two one-sided tests to check whether the effect is significantly above the lower bound and significantly below the upper bound. If both are significant, you conclude equivalence. Equivalently, the 90% confidence interval lies entirely within the bounds. Non-inferiority tests use only one bound, asking whether a new design is not meaningfully worse. In UX this supports decisions like simplifying a flow, migrating platforms or adding a guardrail without harming a metric. Rigour comes from pre-specifying bounds based on practical relevance and powering the test for equivalence.
steps: Set equivalence bounds based on the smallest effect of interest, justified by business or user impact, for example ±0.25 standard deviations or ±1.5 percentage points.
Plan the sample for equivalence power (often larger than for a difference test), using tools such as the TOSTER package or G*Power-like calculators.
Collect data and run two one-sided tests at alpha 0.05: H01 effect ≤ lower bound and H02 effect ≥ upper bound.
Conclude equivalence if both nulls are rejected, which corresponds to the 90% confidence interval lying within the bounds.
Report the TOST p-values, the 90% and 95% intervals, and the ordinary difference test so readers see both perspectives.
For one-sided questions such as 'the new flow is not worse', run a non-inferiority test with a single margin.
outputs: Equivalence or non-inferiority conclusions with TOST p-values, confidence intervals relative to pre-set bounds, and documented bound justifications.
useWhen: Showing that a redesign, migration, cost-saving simplification, accessibility change or guardrail metric did not meaningfully harm outcomes.
avoidWhen: No defensible smallest effect of interest can be agreed, or samples are too small to achieve narrow intervals; report estimates with intervals and acknowledge uncertainty.
whyLost: Equivalence testing is routine in pharmaceutical regulation but almost absent from UX, where non-significant results are routinely misread as proof of no effect.
whereToUse: Platform migrations, design system rollouts, accessibility improvements, removing steps from flows, guardrail metrics in A/B tests, AI model replacements.
example: After replacing a three-step checkout with a two-step one, the team needed to show conversion did not fall. With bounds of ±1 percentage point, the 90% CI for the difference was -0.4 to +0.7, so TOST supported equivalence (p = 0.008), allowing rollout.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
The Inquiry Series, C2 — Quantitative UX Analysis in Python — Descriptive to Inferential
reference: Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). A comparison of the two one-sided tests procedure and the power approach for assessing the equivalence of average bioavailability. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 15(6), 657–680; Lakens, D. (2017). Equivalence tests: A practical primer for t tests, correlations, and meta-analyses. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(4), 355–362.

name: Equivalent-Model Generation and Justification in SEM
origin: Ingeborg Stelzl, 1986; Sik-Yum Lee and Scott Hershberger, 1990; Robert MacCallum and colleagues, 1993
summary: Generates the alternative path models that fit the data exactly as well as yours, then argues on design and theory grounds why the chosen model is preferred.
description: Equivalent models imply the same covariance matrix (or the same d-separation statements) with different paths, so they have identical fit and no amount of data can separate them; near-equivalent models fit almost as well. MacCallum and colleagues found equivalent models in over 80% of published applications, almost never acknowledged, a pervasive form of confirmation bias. Stelzl's and the Lee-Hershberger replacing rules generate equivalents: within a saturated block, a direct effect can be replaced by a reversed effect or a disturbance covariance, and a direct effect between two variables with the same causes can be reversed or replaced. Because these rules can break d-separation equivalence, candidates should be checked in a tool such as dagitty. CFA models have infinitely many equivalents, and a three-variable mediation model has 18. The defence is argument, not fit: temporal order, experimental manipulation, variables that cannot be effects, and design features planned before data collection.
steps: Fit the target model and confirm it is identified and fits acceptably.
Apply the replacing rules (reverse a path, replace it with a disturbance covariance) to generate equivalent and near-equivalent alternatives, starting with the paths most central to the claims.
Check each candidate's d-separation equivalence in a tool such as dagitty and fit near-equivalents to see how close they come.
Discard alternatives contradicted by temporal order, experimental manipulation, fixed attributes such as demographics, or clear implausibility.
Where possible, plan design features before data collection (measurement timing, instruments, manipulated variables) that break the equivalence.
Report the remaining plausible alternatives and the arguments for preferring the retained model; never reverse arrows post hoc simply to pick a winner.
outputs: A list of equivalent and near-equivalent models with the reasons each is rejected or retained.
useWhen: Before making directional claims from any path model, SEM or mediation analysis of cross-sectional UX survey data, such as 'ease of use drives trust, which drives adoption'.
avoidWhen: The direction of every path is fixed by experimental manipulation or strict time ordering; the analysis is purely predictive with no causal claims. It does not rescue a model with poor fit; diagnose misfit first with specification search.
whyLost: UX teams treat good fit as proof of the arrows drawn, and SEM software does not flag equivalent models, so the check is almost never run outside methodology circles.
whereToUse: Technology acceptance and trust models for AI and fintech products; satisfaction and loyalty driver models; mediation claims from cross-sectional surveys.
example: A team's SEM says perceived usefulness drives satisfaction, which drives intention to renew. Generating equivalents shows a model where satisfaction drives perceived usefulness fits identically; because both were measured in one survey, the team adds a design change before the next wave to separate the directions.
sources: A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
reference: Lee, S., & Hershberger, S. L. (1990). A simple rule for generating equivalent models in covariance structure modeling. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 25, 313-334.

name: Error Consequence and Recovery Coding
aka: Error consequence and recovery-strategy coding during user testing
origin: Dimitri van der Linden and colleagues, 2001 (error consequences); Kang and Yoon, 2008 (strategies); compiled by Susan Weinschenk, 2011
summary: Code each error in a user test by consequence (positive, negative, neutral), type and the user's recovery strategy, then prioritise redesign by negative consequences.
description: Counting errors treats them all alike; this scheme codes what they cost and how users respond. Each error is classed by consequence: positive (fails the aim but yields useful knowledge), negative (dead end, lost progress, a return to the start, or irreversible effect) or neutral (no effect). It is also typed as a commission, omission or wrong-action error, or a motor-control error. The participant's recovery strategy is coded as systematic exploration, trial and error, or rigid repetition of a failed action. Categories are fixed before testing, applied during observation, and used afterwards to remove negative-consequence errors first and to anticipate which users will struggle. Research behind it found strategy differences track device experience more than age. In safety-critical settings a formal scheme such as HFACS should be used instead.
steps: Before testing, list expected errors and fix the coding categories for consequence, type and strategy.
Recruit actual target users rather than colleagues.
During sessions, log each error with its consequence: positive, negative or neutral.
Code its type: commission, omission, wrong action or motor control.
Code the participant's recovery strategy: systematic exploration, trial and error, or rigid repetition.
After testing, prioritise redesign by removing negative-consequence errors first and use strategy profiles to anticipate problems for similar users.
outputs: An error log coded by consequence, type and recovery strategy, and a prioritised redesign list.
useWhen: Formative tests of complex devices or software where errors are frequent, and when comparing user groups with different experience levels.
avoidWhen: Safety-critical analysis needing formal taxonomies (use SHERPA or Error Taxonomy (Slips, Lapses, Mistakes)) or tests too small to code reliably.
whyLost: UX practice records errors as tallies or notes; coding consequence and recovery strategy remained in cognitive ergonomics research.
whereToUse: Consumer electronics, medical and home health devices, complex SaaS settings and products for mixed-experience audiences.
example: On a tablet prototype, choosing the brightness slider instead of volume is coded positive (the user learns the panel), deleting a file instead of moving it negative, and tapping an unavailable item neutral. Only the delete error drives an urgent redesign.
sources: 100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
reference: van der Linden, D., Sonnentag, S., Frese, M. and van Dyck, C. (2001) Exploration strategies, performance, and error consequences when learning a complex computer task. Behaviour & Information Technology.

name: Error Taxonomy (Slips, Lapses, Mistakes)
aka: Error Taxonomy (Reason's Slips, Lapses and Mistakes)
origin: Donald Norman, 1981 (action slips); James Reason, 1990 (Human Error)
summary: A coding scheme classifying each breakdown as a Slip (right intention, wrong execution), Lapse (attention or memory failure) or Mistake (wrong mental model), each implying a distinct fix.
description: Derived from Norman's analysis of action slips and Reason's Generic Error Modelling System, the taxonomy explains why users fail. In Vivek Gopinath's operationalisation: Slip, correct goal but wrong execution (mis-tap adjacent row); Lapse, attention or memory failure (forgot OTP digits after switching apps, timed out); Mistake, wrong mental model or decision (looked under Notifications for price alerts). Each maps to a design lever: slips to motor and affordance fixes (hit areas, spacing, error prevention), lapses to memory and attention support (progress save, copy/paste, timer messaging), mistakes to IA, labelling or conceptual change. Sessions are moderated think-alouds (n = 10–15, 30–40 minutes) on the same tasks as the tree test, with a short example-rich codebook and two coders on 30–40% of sessions (κ ≥ 0.70). Results are tabulated by step per 100 sessions.
steps: Write a one-page codebook defining Slip, Lapse and Mistake with product-specific examples.
Run 10–15 moderated think-aloud sessions of 30–40 minutes on the target tasks, recording screen and audio.
Code every breakdown with step, error code, coder ID and quote.
Double-code 30–40% of sessions and compute Cohen's κ; if below 0.70, refine definitions and examples, retrain and re-code.
Tabulate codes by step per 100 sessions (e.g. Find Alerts: 12 slips, 18 lapses, 39 mistakes; OTP: 6, 22, 5).
Map each dominant error type to its fix family and enter it in a joint display.
outputs: A coded error table by step with κ, representative quotes and fix families.
useWhen: When you need to explain why errors occur and turn findings into specific design levers.
avoidWhen: When there are too few observable breakdowns to code, or for attitudinal questions; use interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Rigorous in aviation, medicine and nuclear safety, but UX usually reports generic 'errors' without mechanism or reliability.
whereToUse: Fintech flows, OTP and verification steps, medical devices, enterprise forms, AI-assisted workflows.
example: Coding trading-app sessions shows Mistakes dominate navigation and rule definition while Lapses dominate the timed OTP step, leading to relabelling for the former and an extended OTP window with reassurance copy for the latter.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Reason J (1990) Human Error. Cambridge University Press
Rasmussen J (1983) Skills, rules, and knowledge. IEEE SMC
Norman DA (1981) Categorization of action slips. Psychological Review
The Design of Everyday Things (Don Norman)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
reference: Reason, J. (1990). Human Error. Cambridge University Press.

name: Essential use cases
aka: Essential use case task sequence model
Essential use cases and detailed use cases with alternative courses
Use cases with sunny-day and rainy-day cases
Sunny day / rainy day use cases
origin: Larry Constantine and Lucy Lockwood, 1993-1999, after McMenamin and Palmer's essential modelling (1984)
summary: Describe each task as a short, technology-free dialogue of user intentions and system responsibilities for one goal, then add numbered alternative courses for errors and exceptions.
description: An essential use case (or task case) captures one discrete intention of a user in a role as a two-column narrative: user intentions on one side, system responsibilities on the other, in domain language and free of interface or technology assumptions. It is named with a continuing verb and qualified object ('paying for a ticket'), keeps only essential steps and states what and why but not how, leaving room for design. Constantine adds a task case map, a check that every role is supported and every task needed, and ranking by frequency and importance so focal tasks are fully defined; Siemens STEP 7 Lite had 25 roles and 342 task cases. Detailed use cases write the normal course as numbered steps and list alternative courses numbered to the step they replace. Reiss adds the Pareto view: about 20% of cases (sunny-day paths) cover 80% of use; rainy-day cases are many.
steps: Derive task cases from user roles and requirements, each tied to a single user intention and named with a continuing verb and object.
Write the normal (sunny-day) case first as alternating user intentions and system responsibilities, abstract and technology-free.
Strip any step that names an interface element or action; keep only essential purposes.
List alternative (rainy-day) courses for errors, missing data and exceptions, each numbered to the step it replaces and stating where the flow resumes.
Draw a task case map and check coverage against the role model so every role is supported and every task is needed.
Rank cases by frequency and importance, fully define the focal ones, and walk existing flows against them to find detours or odd steps.
outputs: A set of essential use cases with alternative courses, a task case map, coverage checks against roles, and a prioritised list of focal tasks.
useWhen: When translating research into interaction requirements without prematurely fixing the interface, especially for complex or regulated systems with many roles.
avoidWhen: Avoid if teams will treat the abstract steps as screens, or when outcome-level user stories suffice. Abstraction must not slip into interface actions; cards derived from detailed use cases can lock in a WIMP model too early.
whyLost: Use cases survive in software engineering and agile backlogs, but the essential, technology-free discipline and role coverage checks have largely been lost to UI-specific flows and user stories.
whereToUse: Enterprise and regulated systems, conversational and voice interfaces (where the abstraction fits naturally), AI agent task design, service redesign across channels.
example: Designing an AI travel assistant, a team writes 'retrieving visa requirements' as an essential use case before choosing chat, form or voice. Alternative courses for unknown nationality and conflicting sources become explicit requirements.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Constantine, L. L., & Lockwood, L. A. D. (1999). Software for Use: A Practical Guide to the Models and Methods of Usage-Centered Design. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley.

name: Ethical Reporting
origin: Social science research ethics; codified in professional codes such as the British Sociological Association and AAA ethics guidelines
summary: Protects participants in published findings through anonymisation, composite cases, renewed consent and harm assessment, guarding against identification, stigma and misrepresentation.
description: Harm to participants often happens after the interview, when findings circulate. Ethical reporting treats the report itself as a risk. Names are replaced with consistent pseudonyms and indirect identifiers (role, location, rare conditions, distinctive phrases) are removed or generalised, since in small organisations or niche user groups a job title plus a quote can identify someone. Where identifiable detail is analytically necessary, researchers may construct composite cases and must say so. Consent is revisited when findings will be published more widely than originally agreed. Before release, a harm assessment asks how participants would be affected if their manager, community or insurer read the report, and whether the framing stigmatises a group. Rigour lies in anticipating secondary audiences and documenting each protective decision.
steps: Anonymisation protocol: Replace all names with pseudonyms consistently. Remove identifying details: job titles, locations, specific dates. Check: could someone reading this identify this participant?
Composite cases: When direct quotes could identify a participant, construct composite cases preserving the analytical insight. Disclose compositing in the methods section.
Consent for publication: Original consent may not cover all subsequent publication contexts. Confirm with participants before each new publication context.
Harm assessment: Could any participant be harmed by this report being read by their employer, family, or government? If yes: what further steps are required?
outputs: An anonymisation log, de-identified quotes and cases, composite case disclosures, consent records for publication, and a documented harm assessment.
useWhen: Reporting research with employees, patients, vulnerable or small populations, B2B customers who could be recognised, or when findings will be shared externally, published or stored in a widely accessible repository.
avoidWhen: It always applies when data comes from people; only its intensity varies. For data governance before analysis, see Ethics of AI-Assisted Qualitative Analysis and consent procedures.
whyLost: UX teams focus ethics on recruitment and consent forms and treat internal reports as safe, while repositories and screenshots spread identifiable data far beyond the original audience.
whereToUse: Internal enterprise research, healthcare and fintech studies, research repositories and highlight reels, conference talks and case studies, and employee experience research.
example: Research with 9 nurses on a ward system includes quotes criticising a named manager. The researcher removes ward identifiers, generalises roles, merges two accounts into a disclosed composite, and confirms consent before the findings go to hospital leadership.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Wiles, R. (2013). What Are Qualitative Research Ethics? Bloomsbury.

name: Ethics of AI-Assisted Qualitative Analysis
origin: Emerging practice, 2023 onwards, following LLM adoption in qualitative data analysis software
summary: A governance protocol for using AI in qualitative analysis, covering disclosure, data privacy, reliability checks against human coders, and human authority over interpretation.
description: Generative AI can now segment, code and summarise interview transcripts in minutes, but it does not interpret. This protocol treats AI as a junior coder whose work must be disclosed, validated and overruled where necessary. It specifies what to report (model, version, prompts, tasks delegated), how to protect participant data (local or contractually bounded models, de-identification before upload, consent wording that covers machine processing), and how to establish reliability: AI-applied codes are compared with an independent human coder using Cohen's kappa before the AI output is trusted at scale. Interpretation, theme construction and claims about meaning remain human work. Its rigour lies in treating AI output as a measurement instrument with error that must be quantified, rather than as an oracle, and in an audit trail that lets reviewers see exactly where machine judgement entered the analysis.
steps: Disclosure in reporting: Report which AI system, for which coding tasks, with what IRR validation. Non-disclosure is an ethical violation.
Data privacy: Cloud-based AI processes data on external servers. Use local models for sensitive participant data where consent does not cover external processing.
IRR requirement: AI-assisted coding without IRR validation is not rigorous. κ must be calculated and reported.
Human final authority: AI produces coded segments. Humans produce analysis, themes, and theoretical propositions.
outputs: An AI-use disclosure statement, a data-handling plan, human-AI agreement statistics (kappa per code), a log of overruled AI codes, and an audit trail separating machine coding from human interpretation.
useWhen: Your team is using LLMs or AI features in qualitative tools to code, cluster or summarise research data, especially with sensitive participants or findings that will inform consequential decisions.
avoidWhen: No AI is involved in the analysis, or the AI is used only for transcription with human verification. If you need to analyse data rigorously by hand, use Reflexive Thematic Analysis or Template Analysis directly.
whyLost: It is too new to be lost: the practice is known in principle but rarely operationalised, because AI coding features shipped faster than the governance norms around them and speed is the selling point.
whereToUse: Research repositories with AI tagging, synthesis of large interview sets, regulated domains (health, finance, government) where participant data cannot leave controlled infrastructure, and any research ops function setting policy for AI tooling.
example: A health-tech team uses an LLM to code 60 patient interviews. They run it on a locally hosted model, have a researcher independently code 15% of transcripts, find kappa of 0.58 on the 'medication anxiety' code, rewrite the code definition, retest to 0.76, and disclose the whole process in the report.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
reference: Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2022). Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide. Sage.

name: Ethno-Mining
origin: First discussed by Aipperspach et al. (2006) and developed by Ken Anderson and colleagues at Intel (2009)
summary: Mine the digital traces people produce in everyday life for patterns, then explore and check those patterns with the same people through ethnographic methods.
description: Ethno-mining combines data mining's search for hidden patterns with ethnography's long-term, participant-centred interpretation, as a hybrid rather than two methods run side by side. Data come from everyday technology: phones and apps, web activity, social media, sensors, wearables and location trackers. Mining techniques such as classification, clustering, anomaly detection, regression and summarisation identify important variables and relationships. These patterns are then taken back to the same individuals and groups through interviews, focus groups and participant observation, where people interpret them, and self-reports are cross-referenced with the mined data. Each side corrects the other: the data show what people do not notice or report, and the ethnography explains what the patterns mean. Anderson and colleagues argue it extends the social, spatial and temporal scope of research. It needs an explicit plan for integrating positivist and interpretive standpoints, and careful consent for trace data.
steps: Obtain consent to collect everyday digital traces (app logs, sensors, location, social media) from a defined group.
Apply data mining (clustering, classification, anomaly detection, regression, summarisation) to find salient variables, patterns and outliers.
Take the patterns back to the same participants through interviews, focus groups or observation, showing them their own data.
Cross-check self-reported behaviour against the mined data and explore the discrepancies.
Iterate: refine the mining with what participants explain, then return to them.
Integrate both into one interpretation of the behaviour or culture.
outputs: An integrated account of behaviour combining mined patterns with participants' interpretations, including where self-report and traces diverge.
useWhen: Products with rich behavioural data where the team needs to understand what patterns mean, or where self-reports are known to be unreliable.
avoidWhen: When participants cannot be re-contacted or have not consented to trace collection; use anonymised analytics alone or ethnography alone.
whyLost: In companies, analytics and ethnographic teams sit apart and rarely share participants, so the hybrid that requires the same people in both is seldom organised.
whereToUse: Wearables and health tracking, smart home sensing, mobile app usage, gaming communities, financial behaviour apps.
example: A fitness wearable clusters a consenting panel's activity data and finds an 'evening collapse' pattern. Interviews walking participants through their own timelines reveal it reflects childcare handovers, not motivation loss, redirecting the reminder strategy.
reference: Dawson, C. (2020). A-Z of Digital Research Methods. Abingdon: Routledge.

name: Ethnographic Decision Models (Gladwin)
origin: Christina Gladwin, 1970s-1989 (Ethnographic Decision Tree Modeling, 1989)
summary: Elicits the decision criteria people actually use from interviews, builds them into explicit decision trees, and tests their predictive accuracy on a new sample.
description: Gladwin studied why farmers chose particular crops or practices.
