She elicited decision criteria from informants, structured them as hierarchical decision trees with elimination by aspects and constraints, and then tested the trees on a separate sample of decision-makers, typically achieving 85-95% prediction accuracy. Errors were examined to refine the model. The method combines qualitative elicitation with quantitative validation, producing an explicit, testable model of real decision processes rather than assumed rational choice. For UX, it suits choices like which plan to buy, whether to switch providers, or whether to use a feature, producing models that can guide design and messaging.
steps: Choose a specific, recurrent decision (e.g. choosing a mobile money provider) and a sample of decision-makers.
Interview 20-30 informants about recent decisions, eliciting criteria, constraints and alternatives in their own terms.
Build a composite decision tree with ordered criteria, aspects and constraints.
Test the model on a new sample of 20-60 decision-makers by predicting their actual choices.
Analyse errors, revise the model and re-test where feasible.
Translate the model into design: support key criteria, remove constraints, and match messaging to decision order.
outputs: A validated decision tree model, prediction accuracy and an error analysis.
useWhen: Understanding and predicting real-world choices with a handful of key criteria, particularly in unfamiliar contexts.
avoidWhen: Highly impulsive or habitual choices without deliberation, or very complex trade-offs better modelled with conjoint.
whyLost: It belongs to economic anthropology and lost visibility as discrete choice models dominated decision research.
whereToUse: Financial inclusion products, B2B purchasing, health service choices, agritech, energy tariff switching.
example: A study of 30 street vendors in Nairobi yields a decision tree for accepting digital payments: the first criterion is whether customers expect it, then settlement speed. Tested on 50 vendors, it predicts 88% of choices.
sources: Gladwin, Ethnographic Decision Tree Modeling (1989), Sage Qualitative Research Methods Series 19
Bernard, Research Methods in Anthropology (6th ed., 2017)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Gladwin, C. H. (1989). Ethnographic Decision Tree Modeling. Sage.

name: Ethnographic Filmmaking
origin: David MacDougall; tradition of Mead and Bateson, Jean Rouch and observational cinema
summary: The researcher makes a film as a way of doing fieldwork, so that filming generates understanding through image, sound and duration rather than illustrating findings.
description: In ethnographic filmmaking the camera is an instrument of inquiry, not a recording of results. MacDougall describes a range of relations between film and research: plain records, rule-based records, illustrations of texts and interpretive accounts of experience, agency and performance. He advises beginning to film early, as part of exploration, so that fresh observations are captured and the camera does not later disrupt established relationships; avoiding a prefabricated script so that discoveries can redirect the work; and resisting the pull to force events into a conventional dramatic story. The relationship with the people filmed must be negotiated continuously, consent can change over the long period between shooting and release, and the analytical honesty of a film has to be weighed against distress or danger to individuals. It differs from participatory video, where participants hold the camera, and from highlight reels made for stakeholders.
steps: Decide the film's relation to the research: record, rule-based record, illustration or interpretive account.
Begin filming early in fieldwork as part of exploration rather than only after findings are known.
Work without a fixed script and let what is learned while filming redirect the work.
Negotiate and keep renegotiating the relationship and consent with the people filmed; do not overstay.
Edit to respect the duration and texture of events rather than forcing a dramatic arc.
Before release, weigh analytical honesty against possible distress or harm and omit material where harm outweighs value.
outputs: An ethnographic film that conveys knowledge through image, sound and duration, plus field footage as a research record.
useWhen: Practices are embodied, tacit or spatial and hard to convey in text, and a team needs a sustained, observational sense of a setting.
avoidWhen: Quick evidence for a decision, or when filming would endanger participants; use Video Highlight Reels for stakeholder communication or Participatory Video when participants should author the footage.
whyLost: It demands film craft, long fieldwork and careful ethics; corporate ethnography kept short video clips but rarely the filmmaking practice itself.
whereToUse: Industrial, clinical and craft work settings; emerging-market research; strategic research where leaders need to experience a context.
example: A medical device team embeds a researcher-filmmaker in an intensive care unit for four weeks; the resulting observational film shows how nurses improvise around alarm fatigue in ways interviews never surfaced.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: MacDougall, D. 'Anthropological filmmaking: an empirical art', in Margolis, E. and Pauwels, L. (eds.) (2011) The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods. London: SAGE.

name: Ethnographic Futures Research
origin: Robert Textor, c. 1980; Domaingue (1989); Minnesota Extension Project Future
summary: Builds alternative future scenarios from interviews about people's hopes, fears and expectations, written as if they were field reports from the future system.
description: Ethnographic futures research treats the future as something people already carry around in their expectations. Teams interview stakeholders about their visions, hopes, fears and expectations, analyse the interviews for themes and diverging trajectories, and then write alternative scenarios in the form of a qualitative study of the future: interview findings, observations and descriptions as though fieldwork had been done there. The scenarios go back to the community, which revises them and chooses a preferred future to work towards. Patton links it to the US General Accounting Office's prospective studies, which interviewed key knowledgeables and fed findings back for a second round. Its rigour comes from grounding every scenario in coded interview data rather than in designers' speculation, and from the explicit review loop with the people whose futures are described.
steps: Form a stakeholder or community team and agree the system or service whose future is being explored.
Interview a varied sample of people about their visions, expectations, hopes and fears for that future, probing for optimistic, pessimistic and most-likely versions.
Analyse the interviews for themes and for alternative trajectories that different groups expect.
Write two to four alternative scenarios as if they were qualitative field reports from the future system, citing the kinds of evidence a fieldworker would.
Return the scenarios to participants in a review session, revising them where people do not recognise their own views.
Have the group select a preferred future and derive the actions needed to move towards it; optionally run a second interview round on the revised scenarios.
outputs: Alternative narrative scenarios grounded in interview data, a selected preferred future and an action list.
useWhen: When a team needs futures thinking rooted in what real stakeholders expect and fear, for example long-horizon service strategy or community-facing systems.
avoidWhen: When you need a forecast: scenarios are easily mistaken for predictions. For trend-driven exploration use Horizon Scanning or the Three Horizons Framework; for rapid ideation use Future Workshop. The source treatment is brief, so read Textor before running it at scale.
whyLost: It sat in applied anthropology and extension evaluation, and design futures work later favoured designer-led speculative artefacts over interview-grounded scenarios.
whereToUse: Public services, health and education platforms, community technology, and strategy work where stakeholder legitimacy of a future vision matters.
example: A city transport authority interviews riders, drivers and planners about mobility in 2040, writes three 'field reports' from that year, and holds a review where residents rewrite the pessimistic one and choose a preferred scenario to guide its app roadmap.
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2002). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (3rd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage, pp. 200-201.

name: Ethnographic Research
origin: Bronisław Malinowski, 1922 (participant observation); brought into HCI by Lucy Suchman and colleagues at Xerox PARC, 1980s
summary: Extended immersion in people's settings to understand the culture, practices, values and meanings that shape behaviour and technology use.
description: Ethnographic research is a long-form, immersive approach from anthropology in which the researcher spends extended time in a community or setting, participating in and observing everyday life. The aim is a 'thick description' of practices, beliefs, social relations and meanings from the participants' perspective, including the tacit and taken-for-granted. In HCI, ethnography has shown how work and technology use are socially organised and situated. Rigour comes from prolonged engagement, detailed field notes written promptly, reflexivity about the researcher's influence, triangulation across observation, conversation and artefacts, and an iterative movement between fieldwork and analysis. Rapid or focused ethnography compresses the timeline but must still preserve immersion and reflexivity.
steps: Define a broad research question and negotiate access to the setting with gatekeepers and consent.
Spend extended time in the field, from several days for focused ethnography to weeks or months for full studies.
Combine participant observation, informal conversations and artefact collection.
Write detailed field notes the same day, separating observation from interpretation.
Keep a reflexive journal on your own position and influence.
Analyse iteratively, returning to the field to test emerging interpretations.
Produce thick descriptions and translate them into design implications.
outputs: Field notes, thick descriptions, cultural models of practice, artefacts and design implications grounded in context.
useWhen: For new market entry, unfamiliar cultures, underserved populations, or when social and cultural context strongly shapes behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when questions are narrow, time is short or results must be statistically generalised; use contextual inquiry, interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives mainly in academic HCI and specialized agency work; rarely done in product teams due to time and cost.
whereToUse: New market entry; complex cultural contexts; designing for underserved populations.
example: A mobile money provider sends researchers to spend three weeks in market towns in East Africa. They find that phones are often shared within households and that agents act as trusted advisers, reshaping PIN and account-recovery design.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Hammersley, M. & Atkinson, P. (2007). Ethnography: Principles in Practice (3rd ed.). Routledge.

name: Ethnographic Thick Description
origin: Clifford Geertz (1973); in technology research Xerox PARC (Suchman, Nardi, O'Day) and Intel (Bell, Salvador), 1980s-2000s
summary: Sustained fieldwork producing interpretive accounts that give full weight to context, meaning and participants' own categories rather than lists of needs.
description: Thick description is Geertz's term for accounts that interpret behaviour within its web of meaning, distinguishing a wink from a twitch. The ethnographic tradition in technology research brought trained anthropologists into product companies, spending extended time in the field, building sustained relationships and producing accounts both specific and theoretically rich. The treatise stresses that the difference from brief interview research is not only depth but epistemological orientation: what kinds of claims can be made, on what basis and with what confidence. Ethnographers did not arrive with questions and leave with needs; they let the participants' categories reorganise the research question. Thick description ethnography is in the treatise's curriculum.
steps: Negotiate access and define a field site and an open research question.
Spend extended time in the field (weeks to months), using participant observation and informal interviews.
Write detailed fieldnotes daily, separating description from interpretation.
Collect artefacts, photos and documents, and follow emerging threads.
Analyse iteratively, building interpretations grounded in members' categories.
Write a narrative account with implications for design and strategy, including reflexive notes.
outputs: Fieldnotes, interpretive ethnographic account, cultural models, strategic implications.
useWhen: Entering unfamiliar cultures, markets or practices; strategic questions about meaning and adoption.
avoidWhen: Narrow evaluation questions or tight timelines; use usability testing or rapid contextual interviews.
whyLost: Expensive, slow and hard to justify against sprint timelines; corporate ethnography teams were cut after the 2000s.
whereToUse: Emerging markets, financial inclusion, healthcare at home, family technology use, AI adoption in professions.
example: A remittance company embeds researchers with migrant families in two countries for six weeks; thick description reveals money transfers function as obligations negotiated in group chats, leading to a shared-request feature.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Geertz C (1973) The Interpretation of Cultures
Blomberg J et al. (1993) Ethnographic field methods and their relation to design. In Participatory Design
Nardi BA & O'Day VL (1999) Information Ecologies
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
reference: Geertz C (1973) Thick description: toward an interpretive theory of culture. In The Interpretation of Cultures. Basic Books.

name: Ethnomethodology
origin: Harold Garfinkel, 1967 (Studies in Ethnomethodology); brought to HCI by Lucy Suchman (1987) and workplace studies
summary: Studies the practical methods people use to produce and recognise orderly social activity, showing how interaction with technology is accomplished moment by moment.
description: Ethnomethodology, founded by Harold Garfinkel, studies the methods members of a society use to make sense of and produce everyday social order. It treats rules, plans and categories not as causes of action but as resources people use and account for in situated activity. Lucy Suchman's Plans and Situated Actions applied it to show that users of a photocopier help system improvised in ways the system's plan-based model could not follow, a foundational insight for HCI. Ethnomethodological studies of work examine how coordination is achieved in settings like control rooms. Rigour comes from detailed analysis of recorded naturally occurring activity, focus on members' own categories and practices rather than analysts' theories, and close attention to sequence and embodied action.
steps: Select a setting where practical activity with technology can be recorded naturally, such as a control room or shared workspace.
Obtain consent and record video and audio of ongoing activity.
Transcribe selected episodes in detail, including talk, gesture and screen activity.
Analyse how participants make actions recognisable and accountable to each other, using their own categories.
Identify the practical methods that produce order, coordination and repair.
Translate findings into design implications for supporting situated action.
outputs: Detailed analyses of situated practices, descriptions of how coordination and sense-making are accomplished, and design implications.
useWhen: For collaborative and coordination-intensive tools, voice and conversational interfaces, and understanding how users make sense of system behaviour in practice.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need fast, broad answers or quantified results; use contextual inquiry or analytics. Requires specialist sociological training.
whyLost: Extinct in UX: Deep sociological foundations make practical application rare outside academic HCI.
whereToUse: Voice UI; social platforms; collaborative tool design.
example: A voice assistant team records families using a smart speaker at dinner. Analysis shows children treat the device's silence as a turn for someone else, so families talk over its responses, informing turn-taking cues.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Suchman L (1987) Plans and Situated Actions
Dourish P & Button G (1998) On 'technomethodology'. Human-Computer Interaction 13(4)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Garfinkel, H. (1967). Studies in Ethnomethodology. Prentice-Hall; Suchman, L. A. (1987). Plans and Situated Actions. Cambridge University Press.

name: Ethnomethodology and Breaching Experiments
origin: Harold Garfinkel, 1967 (Studies in Ethnomethodology)
summary: Reveals the taken-for-granted methods people use to produce order by observing sense-making and, ethically, introducing small breaches that make tacit expectations visible.
description: Ethnomethodology (Garfinkel, 1967) studies how people practically produce and sustain the sense of orderly social life in everyday interaction. Its central insight: the rules and methods people use to make sense of their social world are so taken-for-granted that they are invisible — until they are broken. Garfinkel's 'breaching experiments' deliberately violated ordinary conversational and social rules to expose the tacit normative structure that ordinarily makes interaction seamless. Applied to UX: breaching reveals the implicit interaction contracts users bring to interfaces — contracts that, when violated, produce confusion, frustration, or the specific error type known as 'violation of expectation.'
steps: Naturalistic observation of sense-making: Observe how people handle moments of ambiguity, confusion, or breakdown in digital interactions. Focus on the repair work they do to restore sense — what assumptions do they invoke?

Indexicality analysis: Identify all the things that are left unsaid, pointed to, or taken for granted in a user's verbal account of their experience. These are the tacit background expectations that must be in place for interaction to work.

Breaching experiment design (applied): Deliberately introduce a small, controlled violation of a design convention — a non-standard icon placement, an unexpected response, a missing affordance. Observe the recovery work users do. What assumptions are they repairing from?

Documentary method: Analyse how users interpret ambiguous interface elements by treating their interpretation as 'documents of a pattern.' What underlying pattern are they reading the element against?
Analysis: Code repair sequences for: (a) what rule was assumed, (b) how the violation was detected, (c) what repair strategy was used, (d) whether repair succeeded or failed.
outputs: Documented sense-making practices, indexical expressions and assumed rules, breach-response records, repair sequence codes, and design implications about users' tacit expectations.
useWhen: You need to surface tacit conventions users rely on but cannot articulate, such as expectations of conversational agents, collaborative tools or interface conventions, or to understand why small changes cause disproportionate disruption.
avoidWhen: Breaches could cause distress, financial loss or deception without debriefing; use naturalistic observation of existing breakdowns instead. For broad attitude data, use interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Ethnomethodology influenced early HCI through Lucy Suchman and CSCW but its dense theory and the ethical difficulty of breaching meant it stayed in academic sociology.
whereToUse: Conversational AI, collaborative and real-time tools, interface conventions in redesigns, automation hand-offs, and multi-party workflows.
example: Testing an AI meeting assistant, researchers deliberately have it respond slightly out of turn in a lab session. Participants' repairs ('sorry, were you talking to me?') reveal the tacit turn-taking rules the assistant must respect.
sources: Sage Research Methods — Understanding Qualitative Research and Ethnomethodology (ten Have)
reference: Garfinkel, H. (1967). Studies in Ethnomethodology. Prentice-Hall.

name: Ethogram and Focal Sampling (Altmann)
origin: Ethograms from classical ethology (Tinbergen, Lorenz); sampling methods formalised by Jeanne Altmann (1974)
summary: Uses a defined catalogue of behaviours and explicit sampling rules (focal, scan, ad libitum, continuous or instantaneous) to observe behaviour systematically and quantifiably.
description: Ethologists build an ethogram: a complete, mutually exclusive catalogue of behaviours with operational definitions. Altmann's landmark paper showed how sampling choices bias results: ad libitum notes over-represent conspicuous behaviour; focal sampling follows one individual for a set period; scan sampling records all individuals' behaviour at intervals; continuous recording captures true frequencies and durations, while instantaneous (point) sampling estimates time budgets. Inter-observer reliability is tested. UX field observation is usually ad libitum, biased toward the memorable. Applying ethological rules yields defensible quantitative observation in stores, clinics, homes and offices.
steps: Conduct preliminary observation to draft an ethogram of relevant behaviours with operational definitions.
Choose sampling rules (focal or scan) and recording rules (continuous or instantaneous at set intervals, e.g. 30 s).
Train observers and test inter-observer agreement (kappa above 0.7) before data collection.
Collect observations according to a schedule that samples times, places and individuals representatively.
Compute frequencies, durations, time budgets and transitions, with appropriate statistics.
Combine with interviews to interpret patterns.
outputs: An ethogram, time budgets, behaviour frequencies and durations, transition data and reliability statistics.
useWhen: Observing behaviour in physical or social settings where quantitative description matters, such as retail, clinics, classrooms or homes.
avoidWhen: When the research question is about meaning and experience rather than behaviour frequency.
whyLost: UX inherited ethnography from anthropology rather than ethology, so systematic behaviour sampling never arrived.
whereToUse: Retail self-service, hospital wards, smart home use, classroom technology, warehouse work, public kiosks.
example: Observing self-checkout with 10-minute scan sampling across 40 hours, researchers find staff intervention occupies 38% of attendant time, mostly for age verification, informing a digital ID feature.
sources: Altmann, Observational study of behavior: sampling methods (1974), Behaviour
Martin & Bateson, Measuring Behaviour: An Introductory Guide (4th ed., 2021)
reference: Altmann, J. (1974). Observational study of behavior: sampling methods. Behaviour, 49(3-4), 227-267.

name: Evaluability Assessment
origin: Joseph Wholey (1979, 1994); Smith (1989)
summary: A short qualitative pre-study that judges whether a programme or product initiative is defined and implemented clearly enough for a formal evaluation to be meaningful.
description: Before spending on outcome evaluation, the assessor uses interviews, document review and observation to check three things: that the treatment (the intervention, feature or service) is identifiable and logical, that intended outcomes are clear, specific and measurable, and that what is actually implemented links plausibly to those outcomes. If any fails, a formal evaluation would measure noise. Patton notes that the process often clarifies the logic model and frequently changes the programme before any outcome evaluation is done, which is a benefit in itself. In UX it is the missing gate before an expensive impact study or A/B test of a loosely defined initiative.
steps: Interview managers and staff about goals, activities and expected outcomes.
Review documents such as proposals, roadmaps, specifications and success metrics.
Observe the initiative in operation to see what is actually delivered.
Judge whether the treatment is identifiable, outcomes are specific and measurable, and implementation links logically to outcomes.
Report whether formal evaluation is warranted now and list what must be clarified or fixed first.
outputs: A judgement of evaluability, a clarified programme or logic model and a list of preconditions for evaluation.
useWhen: Before commissioning an impact evaluation, a large experiment or a measurement framework for an initiative whose goals or delivery may be vague.
avoidWhen: The intervention and success metric are already crisp (a well-specified A/B test). It may expose an initiative as unready, which has political consequences; prepare sponsors for that.
whyLost: It belongs to public-sector programme evaluation; UX teams usually jump straight to measuring outcomes.
whereToUse: Service design programmes, internal tooling rollouts, digital transformation initiatives, measurement of design-system adoption.
example: Leadership asks for proof that a new customer-success programme improves retention. An evaluability assessment finds three teams delivering different interventions and no agreed outcome metric, so the evaluation is deferred until the treatment is standardised.
reference: Wholey, J. S. (1979). Evaluation: Promise and Performance. Urban Institute.

name: Evaluative Conditioning of Product Preference
origin: Gerald Gorn (1982); Schemer, Matthes, Wirth and Textor (2008)
summary: Pair otherwise-equivalent options with pleasant or unpleasant stimuli, then measure which option people later choose or prefer.
description: Evaluative conditioning explains part of advertising: a product repeatedly paired with something that already evokes good feelings, such as liked music or a favourite team, comes to evoke those feelings itself. In Gorn's study participants saw pens differing only in colour, one shown with pleasant music and the other with unpleasant music; offered a free pen afterwards, more chose the colour paired with pleasant music. Schemer and colleagues found more interest in products placed in music videos by liked artists. Fear appeals are the negative counterpart. The test isolates the effect by keeping options equivalent except for the neutral feature paired with the stimulus, and by measuring a behavioural choice rather than only stated liking. Effects are strongest when people know little about the product, options differ little and choices are not thought through.
steps: Choose two options that differ only on a neutral feature such as colour or name.
Counterbalance which option is paired with the pleasant stimulus (for example liked music or imagery) and which with the unpleasant or neutral one.
Present the pairings in a realistic exposure, such as an ad, onboarding screen or video.
Afterwards offer participants one option as a free gift or choice, or collect interest ratings.
Compare choice shares or ratings between the pleasantly and unpleasantly paired options with a chi-square or proportion test.
outputs: Choice share or interest rating for the pleasantly paired versus unpleasantly paired option.
useWhen: Testing whether brand imagery, sound, mascots or celebratory animations shift preference for features, plans or products independently of their merits.
avoidWhen: Avoid for high-involvement, well-understood choices where effects are small; use conjoint or A/B tests of real offers. For pure familiarity effects use the mere exposure test.
whyLost: It is a standard consumer-psychology paradigm, but UX teams test aesthetics through liking ratings rather than conditioned choice.
whereToUse: Onboarding animations and sounds, plan-selection pages, game cosmetics, marketing landing pages, sonic branding.
example: A meditation app pairs one of two otherwise identical courses with an uplifting chime during onboarding, counterbalanced across users. The chime-paired course is chosen 58% of the time versus 42%, raising questions about neutral presentation of options.
reference: Gorn, G. J. (1982). The effects of music in advertising on choice behavior: A classical conditioning approach. Journal of Marketing, 46(1), 94-101; Schemer, C., Matthes, J., Wirth, W. and Textor, S. (2008). Does 'passing the Courvoisier' always pay off? Psychology & Marketing, 25(10), 923-943.

name: Event Analysis of Systemic Teamwork (EAST)
aka: Task, social and information network analysis
origin: Neville Stanton, Guy Walker and colleagues (Stanton, Baber and Harris, 2008); presented by Holman, Walker et al. in Salvendy and Karwowski (2021)
summary: Model a work system as three linked networks of tasks, communications and information, built from observation, interviews and task analysis, to locate bottlenecks and how situation awareness is distributed.
description: EAST describes complex work as a network of networks. The task network captures goals and tasks and their dependencies; the social network captures who communicates with whom and how often; the information network captures the knowledge elements actors use and share, which is how EAST represents distributed situation awareness. The networks are built from observation, interviews, the Critical Decision Method, task analysis, social network analysis and operational sequence diagrams, so the same data are read from several perspectives and then combined into a composite. Network metrics such as centrality and density reveal overloaded actors, critical information elements and fragile links. Holman and Walker's critique is that EAST, like FRAM, CWA and STAMP, produces static snapshots at a coarse grain, insensitive to emergence and uncertain inputs, and they propose feeding it live data to make the networks dynamic.
steps: Collect data on the work system through observation, interviews, Critical Decision Method sessions and documents.
Build the task network of goals and tasks with their sequence and dependencies.
Build the social network from who communicates with whom and how often.
Build the information network from the knowledge elements used and shared by each actor.
Link the three networks into a composite and compute metrics such as centrality and density to find bottlenecks and how awareness is distributed.
Optionally drive the networks with live data to track change over time, and compare alternative team designs.
outputs: Task, social and information networks and their composite, with metrics on communication load, critical nodes and information sharing.
useWhen: Analysing or redesigning team-based work where coordination and shared awareness matter, such as incident response, clinical teams, logistics or multi-agent human-AI workflows.
avoidWhen: Snapshots may misrepresent a dynamic system and repeated analyses can disagree; for single-user tasks use Hierarchical Task Analysis, and for communication patterns alone Social Network Analysis (SNA) for Collaborative Tool UX.
whyLost: It was developed for military command and control and lives in human factors research, with no lightweight version that fits product timelines.
whereToUse: Incident management and on-call tooling, hospital team workflows, emergency dispatch, collaboration platforms, orchestration of AI agents with human supervisors.
example: Analysing a payments company's incident response, the composite network shows one on-call engineer central to both communication and the key status information. A shared status page and incident commander role reduce that node's centrality.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Stanton, N. A., Baber, C. and Harris, D. (2008). Modelling Command and Control: Event Analysis of Systemic Teamwork. Aldershot: Ashgate; Holman, Walker et al. (2021). In Salvendy, G. and Karwowski, W. (Eds.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.). Wiley, ch. 51, pp. 1380-1382.

name: Event Listing and Event-State Network
donor: Qualitative field research and process studies
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 5, section C; the critical incident chart is credited to Stiegelbauer, Goldstein and Huling (1982).
summary: A matrix of concrete events sorted by time period and level, turned into a network of events (boxes) and longer-lasting states (bubbles) linked by arrows to show what led to what.
description: Narratives drawn straight from field notes can be partial, biased or simply wrong while still sounding plausible. An event listing guards against false chronologies. Columns are successive time periods, defined arbitrarily or as empirically derived phases; rows are domains or locales of events (for example local, organisational and wider context). Each cell holds brief phrases describing specific events reported by any respondent and not contradicted, and 'barometric' events that pushed the process into a new phase are marked. A critical incident chart restricts the listing to a few critical events per period and boxes those with strong catalytic effect. The event-state network then distinguishes events (boxes: specific, short) from states or conditions (round bubbles: more diffuse, longer lasting, often the links between events) and connects them with arrows. Built on cards on a large sheet, it takes about an hour once the listing exists and makes implicit causal understandings explicit and checkable. For UX, it reconstructs how a decision, adoption or incident actually unfolded across teams, more rigorously than a recalled timeline.
steps: Ask participants for the history of the process and code chronological material.
Define time periods as columns (dates or phases) and event domains as rows.
Enter each concrete event mentioned by any respondent and not disputed, in a short phrase.
Mark critical or barometric events that moved the process on; optionally reduce to a critical incident chart.
Write each event on a card, add 'state' cards for conditions found in the notes, and arrange them on a large sheet with arrows.
Check each link against the field notes, then write a short narrative explaining the network.
outputs: A time-by-domain event matrix and an event-state network diagram with a short explanatory text.
useWhen: You need to understand a process over time (adoption, a migration, a purchase decision, an outage) from several people's accounts.
avoidWhen: The process is short and directly observed, or event logs already give a reliable sequence.
whyLost: UX has timelines and journey maps, but these are usually idealised journeys rather than evidence-based listings of what happened, and the event versus state distinction is rarely drawn.
whereToUse: B2B buying and adoption research, post-incident reviews, migration studies, organisational change around tools.
example: To learn why a hospital group abandoned a rostering app after six months, researchers list events by month across ward, IT department and executive levels: 'pilot on ward 3', 'union complaint', 'IT freezes integrations'. The network shows a state bubble 'nurses distrust auto-generated rosters' linking the pilot to the complaint, and marks the integration freeze as the barometric event.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Evidence-Graded Guideline Development
aka: Evidence-Graded Guideline Development (Relative Importance and Strength of Evidence Ratings)
donor: Evidence-based medicine and health information dissemination
origin: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services with GSA, begun 2000; editions 2004 and 2006
summary: Build a design guideline set from research and practice, then have expert panels rate each guideline's importance and the strength of its supporting evidence on defined scales.
description: HHS argued that most guideline sets rest on a few experts' opinions, without references, consensus or any sign of relative importance. Its procedure borrowed evidence grading from medicine. More than 500 candidate guidelines were culled by internal review, rated for importance by 16 external reviewers (half designers, half usability specialists), and rated for strength of evidence by eight doctoral-level researchers who first defined a five-point scale running from strong research support (5) to weak expert opinion (1). Guidelines were illustrated, organised into chapters by a 20-person card sort and the print layout was usability tested. The 2006 update re-surveyed importance and re-rated evidence (Cronbach's alpha .92). Ratings let managers mandate the top guidelines and show researchers where evidence is thin, and low-evidence guidelines indicate where testing effort should go.
steps: Gather candidate guidelines from style guides, published research, public usability reports and in-house test lessons.
Review internally: merge duplicates, resolve conflicts and reword unclear guidelines.
Have external reviewers (about half designers, half usability specialists) rate each guideline's importance to the product's success; drop low-importance items.
Have a panel of research-qualified raters agree evidence criteria, form a 5-point strength-of-evidence scale (5 strong research support to 1 weak expert opinion) and rate each guideline.
Illustrate each guideline with examples and organise the set, for example by card sort, then usability test the published format.
Update continuously: search the literature, revise guidelines, re-rate importance and evidence, and check inter-rater agreement (e.g. Cronbach's alpha).
outputs: A ranked guideline set, each with sources, an importance rating and a strength-of-evidence rating; rankings by each scale.
useWhen: Building or auditing a design system's guidance, accessibility or content standards, where teams need to know which rules are evidence-based and which are opinion.
avoidWhen: You need guidance quickly for one product; the panel process is heavy. Low evidence ratings often mean missing research rather than bad advice, so do not discard low-rated guidance automatically.
whyLost: The HHS guidelines were last updated in 2006 and the rating procedure was not adopted by design-system or pattern-library practice, which relies on team consensus.
whereToUse: Design systems, public-sector design standards, accessibility guidance, regulated health or finance interfaces.
example: A bank's design-system team grades its 120 component guidelines for importance and evidence. Twenty high-importance rules with only expert-opinion support become the research backlog for the next quarter.
reference: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2006). Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines. Washington, DC: U.S. Government Printing Office.

name: Evocative Stimuli for Empathic Design
origin: Jayne Wallace, 2007 (Wallace et al. 2007; Wright, Wallace and McCarthy 2008)
summary: A designer gives one participant crafted, evocative objects to respond to, uses the responses in conversation, and makes a personal artefact that is discussed as they live with it.
description: Developed by Jayne Wallace from craft jewellery practice and the Cultural Probes tradition, the method is one-to-one and dialogical rather than a probe pack. The designer makes beautifully crafted stimuli that gently invite an imaginative response: pressing something dear into a pot of clay, telling the story of a treasured lost object, writing a dream on fabric folding out of a small pillow. The responses become resources for conversation. The designer then immerses herself in the materials and talk, looking for ordinary and standout moments and threads she can empathise with, treating them as a puzzle to enter into rather than solve. A personal artefact is made from this dialogue and further conversations follow while the person lives with it. Open, projective tasks are used because they surface tacit meaning and avoid rehearsed self-accounts.
steps: Make a small set of carefully crafted evocative stimuli, each inviting a creative, open response (for example clay impression, lost-object story, dream pillow).
Give them to the participant and allow time for them to respond at home in their own way.
Hold conversations using the responses as resources, letting the participant lead the meaning.
Immerse yourself in the materials and transcripts, noting connections, ordinary and standout moments and threads you can empathise with; optionally make a book of images of your own reactions.
Design and make a personal artefact, letting the dialogue shape choices of material and behaviour.
Hold several further conversations while the participant lives with the artefact, recording how its meaning develops.
outputs: Deep empathic understanding of one person, a personal artefact and reflective accounts of living with it.
useWhen: Experience-centred design for intimate, emotional or memory-laden products where depth with a few people matters more than breadth.
avoidWhen: When you need generalisable findings or quick turnaround. Responses are shaped by the participant's relationship with the designer and self-presentation, and interpretation by the designer's interests; it needs long-developed fieldwork sensibility. For broader exploration use Cultural Probes or diary methods.
whyLost: It depends on craft skill and long, trusting relationships, which do not fit sprint-based product research.
whereToUse: Memorial and bereavement products, wearables, assistive and dementia care technology, connected heirlooms.
example: Designing a connected keepsake for people separated from family, a designer sends a lost-object box and a dream pillow, talks through the responses, and builds a pendant that lights when a relative abroad touches theirs, then revisits after three months of use.
reference: Wright, P., Wallace, J. and McCarthy, J. (2008). Aesthetics and experience-centred design. ACM TOCHI, 15(4), 1-21; Wallace, J., Dearden, A. and Fisher, T. (2007). The significant other. AI and Society, 22, 53-62.

name: Evolutionary Operation (EVOP)
origin: George Box, 1957; Box and Draper, Evolutionary Operation (1969)
summary: Improve a running process by repeatedly running small factorial changes around current settings and moving the operating point towards better conditions.
description: EVOP is a hybrid of monitoring and experimentation: small designed experiments run on the live process, by its own operators, as part of normal work. A two-level factorial in two or three factors is run around a centre point at current settings, with changes small enough not to harm output. Because the signal is weak against process noise, cycles are repeated until effects stand out; the operating point then moves to the better conditions and a new design is centred there, continuing until no further gain appears. Its design properties are attractive, but the small region and few factors risk confounded effects and missed interactions, and it demands a long, ideally permanent programme with management commitment. In spirit it anticipates continuous online experimentation and hill-climbing on product parameters.
steps: Choose two or three parameters that can be varied slightly without harming the user experience or business results.
Run a two-level factorial with a centre point at current settings as part of normal operation.
Repeat cycles, accumulating data until effects exceed their error limits.
Move the operating point to the better conditions and centre a new design there.
Continue until no further improvement is found, and log each move so the path can be audited.
Review factors periodically so interactions outside the small region are not missed.
outputs: A documented path of operating settings moving towards better performance, with effect estimates for each cycle.
useWhen: Tuning continuous parameters of a live system (ranking weights, timeouts, thresholds, notification timing) where large changes are risky but small ones can run indefinitely.
avoidWhen: Discrete design choices (use A/B Testing); when many factors or large changes are needed (Response Surface Methodology or Fractional Factorial Experiments); or when traffic is high enough for adaptive allocation (Multi-Armed Bandit Testing for Adaptive UX).
whyLost: It belonged to mid-century chemical manufacturing and faded with automation; online product teams reinvented continuous tuning as A/B and bandit testing without the factorial structure.
whereToUse: Recommendation and search tuning, pricing and promotion parameters, ops-heavy services such as delivery time estimates, infrastructure performance settings.
example: A delivery app nudges its ETA buffer and batching window by small amounts in a 2^2 design with a centre point, cycling weekly. After six cycles the operating point moves twice, cutting late-delivery complaints without any visible change to users.
sources: Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Box, G. E. P. (1957). Evolutionary operation: a method for increasing industrial productivity. Applied Statistics, 6(2), 81-101; Box, G. E. P., & Draper, N. R. (1969). Evolutionary Operation. New York: Wiley.

name: EXAMINE for distributional assumptions
origin: SPSS EXAMINE (Explore) procedure; exploratory data analysis, John Tukey, 1977
summary: Using SPSS EXAMINE to inspect distributions, normality, outliers and homogeneity of variance by group before choosing parametric or non-parametric tests.
description: EXAMINE produces box plots, stem-and-leaf plots, Q-Q plots, normality tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov with Lilliefors correction, Shapiro-Wilk), extreme values and Levene's test for homogeneity of variance, overall or split by group. Its purpose is to decide whether assumptions of t-tests, ANOVA or regression are plausible. Rigour comes from interpreting plots rather than relying on significance tests of normality, which are underpowered in small samples and over-sensitive in large ones, checking assumptions within groups rather than overall, and choosing robust alternatives (Welch's test, rank tests, bootstrapping, log transforms) when assumptions fail.
steps: Run EXAMINE with the outcome as the dependent list and the grouping variable as the factor, requesting plots, normality tests and Levene's test.
Inspect Q-Q plots and box plots within each group, giving more weight to plots than to normality p-values.
Note extreme values flagged by box plots (beyond 1.5 or 3 interquartile ranges) and trace them back to raw data.
Check homogeneity of variance; if the largest group variance is more than about 4 times the smallest or Levene's test is significant, use Welch-type tests.
For skewed task times, log-transform and re-examine, or switch to non-parametric or bootstrap methods.
Document the assumption decisions in the analysis log.
outputs: Distribution plots, normality and variance diagnostics, a list of extreme values and a justified test choice.
useWhen: Before comparing groups or fitting linear models, especially with small UX samples, task times and satisfaction scores.
avoidWhen: Do not use normality test p-values as a gate for large samples; with N in the thousands, focus on effect sizes and robust methods.
whyLost: Assumption checking is taught but often skipped in UX because dashboards and A/B tools hide the statistical machinery.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarking, survey group comparisons and pre-post evaluations.
example: Before comparing onboarding completion times across three app versions, EXAMINE shows heavy right skew and a variance ratio of 6 between groups, so the team uses Welch's ANOVA on log times.
sources: Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
Tukey, J. W. (1977) Exploratory Data Analysis
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016) Quantifying the User Experience, 2nd ed.
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Dangerous Statistical Mistakes in UX & Human Factors Research (carousel, n.d.)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Tukey, J. W. (1977) Exploratory Data Analysis

name: Expectancy betting paradigm
origin: David Huron's expectation research, 2000s
summary: As a sequence unfolds, participants distribute bets over possible next elements; the spread of bets at each position measures moment-by-moment uncertainty and expectation.
description: The sequence (a melody in the original work) is stopped at each position, and participants spread a fixed number of betting chips over the possible next elements. Concentrated bets mean strong expectation; spread bets mean uncertainty. Comparing groups shows how familiarity shapes expectation: American and Balinese musicians bet on the next note of a Balinese melody, and the Americans spread their bets far more, especially early on. The procedure turns the vague notion of predictability into a quantitative uncertainty profile per position, which can be compared between groups or design variants. Huron's framework links such expectations to the emotional responses of tension and surprise.
steps: Choose the sequence and define the set of possible next elements at each stopping point.
Stop the sequence at each position and give participants a fixed budget of bets (for example 10 chips).
Ask them to distribute bets over the possible next elements.
Reveal the actual next element and continue.
Compute uncertainty per position (for example entropy of the bet distribution) and accuracy.
Compare uncertainty profiles between groups (novice versus expert) or between design variants.
outputs: Uncertainty profiles across positions, compared between groups or variants, and the share of bets on the actual next element.
useWhen: Measuring how predictable the next step of a flow, conversation or sequence is for different users, or comparing the predictability of design variants.
avoidWhen: Avoid for sequences with too many possible next steps to list; the book gives only an outline, so take design details from the original work. For navigation predictability use first-click testing.
whyLost: It is confined to music cognition, and UX measures predictability indirectly through errors and hesitation.
whereToUse: Onboarding and multi-step flows, conversational AI turn design, game level design, notification sequences, music and audio products.
example: Novice and expert users of an accounting tool bet on which screen comes next at each step of the month-end close. Novices spread bets widely at the reconciliation step, which becomes the focus of redesign.
sources: The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
Huron, D. (2006). Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation. MIT Press
reference: Huron, D. (2006). Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.

name: Expectation Ratings (Expected vs Experienced Difficulty)
origin: Albert & Dixon (2003); quadrant analysis in Tullis & Albert (2008)
summary: Compares how hard users expect each task to be with how hard it turns out, mapping tasks into fix-it-fast, promote-it, big-opportunity and leave-alone quadrants.
description: Before doing any tasks, participants rate how difficult they expect each one to be. After each task, they rate how difficult it actually was, using the same 7-point scale. Plotting expectation against experience separates four groups: tasks expected to be easy that turned out hard ("fix it fast", the main source of dissatisfaction); tasks expected to be hard that were easy ("promote it"); tasks hard before and after ("big opportunity"); and tasks easy before and after ("don't touch it"). The method adds context a single post-task rating lacks, because the same difficulty score means something different if users expected it. Sauro reports that users predict task-level usability fairly well, which makes the gaps meaningful.
steps: List the study tasks and show them all to participants before testing.
Collect an expectation rating for each task on a 7-point difficulty scale.
Run the tasks, collecting the experience rating after each one on the same scale.
Average both ratings per task and plot expectation on one axis and experience on the other.
Prioritise the quadrant where tasks were expected to be easy but were hard.
outputs: A quadrant chart prioritising tasks by the gap between expectation and experience.
useWhen: Prioritising fixes across many tasks, or finding features worth marketing.
avoidWhen: Participants cannot understand tasks before attempting them, or there are only one or two tasks.
whyLost: Most teams collect only a post-task rating; the extra pre-task step seems like overhead.
whereToUse: Benchmark studies, onboarding evaluations, feature prioritisation.
example: Users expect "change delivery address" to be trivial but rate it 2.8 after trying, placing it in fix-it-fast ahead of harder-looking tasks.
reference: Albert, W. & Dixon, E. (2003). Is this what you expected? The use of expectation measures in usability testing. UPA 2003.

name: Expected Value of Information Analysis
donor: Bayesian decision theory and health economics
origin: Howard Raiffa and Robert Schlaifer (1961); Ronald Howard (1966, information value theory); widely used in health economics
summary: Calculates how much a piece of research is worth by estimating how likely it is to change a decision and how much that change would gain.
description: Research has value only if it might change a decision. The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected gain from knowing the true state before deciding, an upper bound on what any study is worth. The expected value of sample information (EVSI) estimates the gain from a specific study design with its sample size and noise. Health technology assessment uses VOI to prioritise trials. For UX research operations, VOI provides a principled way to prioritise studies, size them and decide when to stop researching and ship, using rough distributions of uncertainty and decision payoffs, as Hubbard advocates.
steps: Define the decision, alternatives and the outcome metric in value terms (revenue, retention, harm).
Quantify current uncertainty about key parameters with calibrated estimates (e.g. 90% intervals).
Model payoffs of each alternative as a function of uncertain parameters.
Compute EVPI by simulation: expected payoff with perfect information minus expected payoff of the best current choice.
For candidate studies, compute EVSI given sample size and measurement error, and compare with research cost.
Prioritise studies with highest net value and identify parameters worth measuring (partial EVPI).
outputs: EVPI and EVSI estimates, ranked research options by net value, and parameters that matter most.
useWhen: Prioritising research, deciding study size, or justifying research investment to leadership.
avoidWhen: Exploratory generative research whose value is in reframing the decision itself.
whyLost: UX research rarely quantifies decisions or uncertainty, and decision theory was never part of its training.
whereToUse: Research roadmaps, pricing decisions, large redesigns, regulated launches, AI investment decisions.
example: A team debates a $40,000 study on a checkout redesign. VOI shows EVPI of $25,000 because the redesign wins in nearly all plausible scenarios; the study is replaced by a cheap monitoring plan.
sources: Raiffa & Schlaifer, Applied Statistical Decision Theory (1961)
Howard, Information value theory (1966), IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics
Hubbard, How to Measure Anything (3rd ed., 2014)
Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: Howard, R. A. (1966). Information value theory. IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics, 2(1), 22-26.

name: Expected versus experienced emotion ratings (affective forecasting)
origin: Wilson and Gilbert, affective forecasting, 1990s-2000s; Kermer and colleagues, 2006
summary: People predict how they will feel after an outcome, then rate how they actually feel once it happens, exposing systematic overestimates of emotional impact.
description: Participants rate baseline happiness, predict their feelings under each possible outcome, experience one outcome, then rate how they actually feel after a short delay. In the textbook study, people given $5 predicted that losing $3 on a coin flip would hurt more than winning $5 would please, yet the actual pain of losing was much smaller than forecast, while winning was only slightly overpredicted; losers coped by focusing on what they still had. The gap between forecast and experience (the impact bias) shows that predicted reactions are poor guides to real ones, particularly for losses. The design is rigorous because the same people supply both predictions and experiences under a randomised outcome, with a filler interval before the experienced rating.
steps: Define two or more outcomes that will be randomly assigned (for example a feature removed or kept, a fee charged or waived).
Collect baseline ratings of mood or satisfaction.
Ask each participant to predict their rating under every outcome.
Randomly assign and deliver one outcome.
After a filler interval (10 minutes in the classic study; days or weeks for product changes), collect the experienced rating.
Compare predicted and experienced ratings by outcome, separately for gains and losses.
outputs: Predicted versus experienced affect by outcome, an impact-bias estimate for gains and losses, and evidence of coping.
useWhen: Before relying on pre-launch surveys of how users will feel about a price rise, removed feature, redesign or failed payment.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the outcome cannot be delivered for real; with tiny stakes the gap may not generalise. For continuous tracking of affect after launch use experience sampling.
whyLost: UX routinely asks people to predict reactions but rarely follows up with the matched experienced measure, so the forecasting gap goes unmeasured.
whereToUse: Pricing and plan changes, feature deprecation, redesign launches, health and wellbeing products, change-aversion studies.
example: Before retiring a legacy dashboard, a SaaS team asks users how upset they would be, then measures satisfaction two weeks after migration; the drop is far smaller than predicted, which recalibrates how much weight pre-launch objections get.
sources: Kermer, D. A., Driver-Linn, E., Wilson, T. D., & Gilbert, D. T. (2006). Loss aversion is an affective forecasting error. Psychological Science, 17
reference: Kermer, D. A., Driver-Linn, E., Wilson, T. D., & Gilbert, D. T. (2006). Loss aversion is an affective forecasting error. Psychological Science, 17, 649-653.

name: Expected-Sensed-Desired analysis
origin: Benford et al. (2005), Equator project
summary: Compare what users will expect to do, what sensors can detect and what functions are wanted, to find undiscoverable functions and spare inputs in sensor-based interfaces.
description: Sensor-based and tangible interfaces have no fixed buttons, so mismatches between user actions, sensing and functions are easy to create. ESD lists three sets: expected actions (what people will naturally do with the device), sensed actions (what the sensors can detect) and desired actions (what the designer wants to support). Placing each item in the seven regions of a Venn diagram shows where design work is needed. The centre, where all three overlap, works well. Sensed and desired but not expected means a hidden function users will not discover. Expected and sensed but not desired is spare input that could carry an unsupported desired function. Expected but not sensed means actions the system will ignore, a source of frustration.
steps: List the actions users are likely to perform with the device in context.
List everything the sensors can detect.
List the functions the design should support.
Place each item in the seven-region Venn diagram.
Flag hidden functions (sensed and desired but not expected) and ignored actions (expected but not sensed).
Reassign spare expected-and-sensed actions to unsupported desired functions, then test discoverability.
outputs: A gap and opportunity map of sensor, action and function mappings.
useWhen: Designing tangible, gestural, motion-sensing or ambient interfaces where the input vocabulary is open.
avoidWhen: Avoid for conventional GUI designs with explicit controls; use cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation. Expected actions must come from observation, not designer guesses.
whyLost: It is an academic ubicomp framework known in HCI research and rarely taught in UX practice.
whereToUse: Wearables, smart home devices, AR and VR controllers, automotive gesture controls and interactive museum exhibits.
example: A smart speaker team finds that users naturally tap the top to stop an alarm, which the device senses but maps to nothing, while a press-and-hold volume function goes undiscovered. They map tap to stop and drop the hidden gesture.
reference: Benford, S. et al. (2005). Expected, sensed, and desired: a framework for designing sensing-based interaction. ACM TOCHI 12(1), 3-30.

name: Experience annotation formats (rating, class, preference)
aka: Experience annotation formats: rating, class and preference (rank) based
origin: Yannakakis and Hallam (2011) comparison of rating and preference self-reports; Yannakakis, Spronck, Loiacono and Andre (2013)
summary: Labels experience by players or observers as a rating, a class choice or a preference between variants, preferring ranked comparisons because ratings suffer order and inconsistency effects.
description: Player-experience models need ground-truth labels of experience. Annotations come either from the player (free response during play, or forced questionnaire items) or from third parties (experts, designers, crowd workers) who triangulate behaviour, head pose and context using schemes such as FACS. Three formats exist. Rating gives a scalar or vector on a scale, as in the Game Experience Questionnaire. Class asks for a choice of state, from a yes/no question to a position on the Geneva Emotion Wheel. Preference asks which of two or more variants or sessions was more engaging, frustrating or fun. Yannakakis and Hallam found ratings prone to order-of-play and inconsistency effects that ranked comparisons avoid, because people judge relative differences more reliably than absolute levels. The choice of format therefore shapes the reliability of any model trained on the labels.
steps: Decide who annotates: the user (self-report) or trained observers or crowd workers (third person), with shared guidelines for the latter.
Choose free response or forced items.
Choose the format: rating scale, class label, or preference between variants or sessions.
For preference, present two or more variants in counterbalanced order and ask which was more engaging, frustrating or enjoyable.
Check consistency (for example intransitive choices) and inter-annotator agreement for third-person labels.
Use the annotations as outputs for experience models or as comparison data, modelling ranks with preference-learning methods.
outputs: Ratings, class labels or pairwise preference data suitable for training or validating experience models.
useWhen: Comparing game levels, AI responses, recommendation sets or other variants on subjective qualities, or building models that predict experience from behaviour.
avoidWhen: Absolute benchmarks against a norm are needed (ratings are required), or there are too many variants for pairwise comparison without an adaptive design. Free response is rich but hard to model.
whyLost: The rating-versus-ranking evidence lives in affective computing and game AI; UX research still defaults to absolute rating scales for subjective comparisons.
whereToUse: Game design, evaluation of generative AI outputs, music and content recommendation, personalisation tuning, emotion-aware interfaces.
example: A team tuning an AI writing assistant shows users pairs of responses and asks which was more helpful rather than rating each on a 7-point scale. Pairwise preferences are more consistent across sessions and feed a Bradley-Terry model of response quality.
reference: Yannakakis, G. N., Spronck, P., Loiacono, D. and Andre, E. (2013). Player Modeling. In Artificial and Computational Intelligence in Games, Dagstuhl Follow-Ups 6 (pp. 45-59). Schloss Dagstuhl, Leibniz-Zentrum fuer Informatik.

name: Experience Curve and Learning Study
origin: Power law of practice (Newell & Rosenbloom, 1981); learning curves from T. P. Wright, 1936
summary: Multi-session study tracking task time, errors, strategies and mental models as users progress from novice to expert, fitted to learning curves.
description: Most usability tests capture first-use performance only. A learning study brings participants back over six to ten sessions across weeks, using a standard task battery plus novel transfer tasks. Task time is fitted to the power law of practice (T = a n^-b), giving estimates of initial difficulty and learning rate; errors, verbalisation (which falls as skills automate) and strategy shifts are tracked alongside. Mental models are probed at intervals by asking participants to explain how the system works. The result distinguishes products that are hard at first but efficient for experts from those that plateau, identifies early struggles that predict abandonment, and reveals expert strategies novices never discover.
steps: Multi-session design: 6–10 sessions per participant over 2–4 weeks. Standardised task battery + novel transfer tasks per session.
Track across sessions: Task time (model as power function T=a·n^−b), error rate, strategy shifts, verbalisation rate (automatisation decreases verbalisation).
Mental model probing: After sessions 1, 3, 6, and 10: 'How would you explain how this works to someone new?' Track model evolution.
Strategy transition documentation: Note when participants shift from novice strategies (exploratory, high-verification) to expert strategies (direct, minimal checking).
Analysis: Fit learning curves. Identify early struggles predicting abandonment; habituation speed for key workflows; expert strategies novices never develop without explicit support.
outputs: Fitted learning curves per task, error and verbalisation trends, strategy transition records, mental model evolution notes, and plateau diagnoses.
useWhen: Professional and high-frequency tools where expert efficiency matters, comparing designs on learnability, or deciding on onboarding and training investments.
avoidWhen: Walk-up-and-use products used once or rarely; use first-use usability testing.
whyLost: Repeated sessions are expensive and slow, so industry relies on single-session tests and rarely fits learning curves.
whereToUse: Creative and developer tools, clinical systems, trading platforms, keyboard-driven productivity software, and enterprise migrations.
example: Comparing two layouts for a call-centre CRM over eight sessions, one is 20% slower at session one but reaches a 30% faster plateau by session six, reversing the decision a first-use test would have produced.
sources: Mechanisms of Skill Acquisition and the Law of Practice (Newell & Rosenbloom)
Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
reference: Newell, A. & Rosenbloom, P. S. (1981). Mechanisms of skill acquisition and the law of practice. In J. R. Anderson (Ed.), Cognitive Skills and Their Acquisition. Erlbaum.

name: Experience Deconstruction and Reconstruction
origin: Alan Dix and colleagues' design of virtual Christmas crackers, reported in Dix et al. (2004)
summary: Carry an experience into a new medium by listing its surface elements, felt effects and cultural connotations, then recreating each one rather than copying the physical form.
description: When a familiar experience moves into a digital medium, the temptation is to copy its look. Deconstruction and reconstruction instead breaks the original into three layers: surface elements (design, play, dressing up), experienced effects (sharing, suspense, surprise, hiddenness) and cultural connotations. For each aspect the designer notes how the original produces it and then finds a way to produce the same effect in the new medium, accepting a different mechanism where needed. Dix's virtual cracker was sent by email so it is still offered to someone, hid its contents from the sender, used a blank first page and a slow page change for suspense, a sound for the bang, and a printable mask instead of a pictured paper hat, because the point of the hat is that you can wear it. The discipline is to judge each candidate against the effect, not the surface.
steps: Choose the existing experience (ritual, object or service) to carry into the new medium.
List its aspects in three layers: surface elements, experienced effects and cultural connotations.
For each aspect, write how the original produces it.
Generate at least one way to produce each aspect in the new medium, allowing a different mechanism.
Review candidates against the experienced effects and reject any that keep the surface but lose the effect.
Record the result as a two-column table of original aspect against new mechanism, and prototype the riskiest rows.
outputs: A translation table mapping each aspect of the original experience to its reconstruction, plus prototypes of key rows.
useWhen: Use when digitising a physical ritual, object or service (gifting, ceremonies, paper workflows, in-store service) and the team risks skeuomorphic copying that loses what made the original work.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you do not yet know what makes the original experience meaningful to people: study it first with Contextual Inquiry or Experience Sampling. It depends on a perceptive reading and has been reported in a single case, so test the reconstruction with Experience Prototyping.
whyLost: It appeared as one case study in an HCI textbook and was never named or taught as a general method, although service designers do similar translation informally.
whereToUse: Digital gifting and greetings, remote rituals and events, paper-to-digital public services, retail-to-online experiences.
example: A bank digitising a child's first savings book lists the stamped entries, the pride of showing a parent and the ritual branch visit. The app keeps a visible stamp for each deposit, a share-to-grandparent moment and a yearly in-branch milestone.
reference: Dix, A., Finlay, J., Abowd, G. D. and Beale, R. (2004). Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed.). Harlow: Pearson Education, pp. 157-158.

name: Experience Goals Mapping
origin: Anna Dahlström (2019), from a Sony Ericsson website project
summary: Write user-voiced experience goals and statements for each life-cycle stage and plot them on hygiene, feel-good and delight levels to shape the intended emotional journey.
description: Three to five overarching experience goals, phrased as a user would describe the experience, are derived from objectives and success factors. Each is broken into experience statements for every life-cycle stage (for example awareness, consideration, purchase, use) and placed on three levels: hygiene (qualifiers that must be present), feel good (differentiators) and delight (unexpected, energising touches). The resulting pattern shows the intended emotional shape of the experience, which Dahlström compares to story shapes described by Vonnegut, Booker and Duarte. Review checks whether the journey is realistic, whether there are too many delights, and whether it reflects key barriers and competitive differentiators. The map aligns teams and clients on a vision and helps prioritise requirements; it is most valuable before any wireframing.
steps: Brainstorm experience goals from objectives and success factors, one per sticky note, phrased in user language.
Cluster the notes and write keywords for each cluster.
Formulate three to five overarching goals in user language and give each a colour.
Write detailed experience statements per goal for each life-cycle stage and place them on hygiene, feel-good or delight levels.
Review: is the emotional journey realistic, are there too many delights, does it address key barriers and differentiators?
Digitise, share and post the map as a reference for requirements and design.
outputs: Overarching experience goals and a stage-by-level map of experience statements showing the intended emotional shape.
useWhen: Use at project start to align a team or client on how the experience should feel across stages, before wireframes and feature lists.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting the map as users' actual experience: that needs Journey Mapping from research or Experience Sampling Method. To learn which features are basic or delighting to users, run Kano Analysis.
whyLost: It is one practitioner's technique in a storytelling book; most teams express experience goals as principles without the stage-by-level mapping.
whereToUse: Multidevice consumer products, e-commerce, brand websites, onboarding journeys.
example: A phone maker's website goal '.com knows me and what I want' becomes the consideration-stage statement '.com gives me relevant recommendations', placed at feel good, while accurate stock information sits at hygiene.
reference: Dahlström, A. (2019). Storytelling in Design: Defining, Designing, and Selling Multidevice Products. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 259-263.

name: Experience Prototyping
origin: Marion Buchenau and Jane Fulton Suri, IDEO, 2000 (DIS conference paper)
summary: Simulates the intended experience, not the artefact, using role play, repurposed objects, staged environments or video, to test experience qualities before any functional prototype exists.
description: Experience prototyping (Buchenau & Suri, IDEO) simulates the designed experience — not the designed artefact — using any available means: role play, existing products repurposed, environments physically modified, videos showing the experience as it would unfold. The goal is to enable stakeholders (researchers, designers, users) to experience and evaluate the quality of a designed experience before investing in its technical realisation. Unlike paper prototyping (which tests interface logic) and concept testing (which collects opinions), experience prototyping tests whether a designed experience feels right when embodied.
steps: Experience specification: Define the experience qualities you are testing — not the features or functions, but the experiential qualities: 'trust at first use,' 'feeling of control,' 'sense of being understood.' These are your evaluation criteria.

Prototype the experience: Assemble any combination of available materials that can simulate the experience. This might include: a role-play scenario, a video of the experience unfolding, physical materials representing key moments, or a wizard-of-oz simulation.

Participant enactment: Have participants experience the prototype, ideally in a realistic context. Their experience of the prototype — their emotional, embodied, and cognitive responses — is the research data.
Debrief: Immediately after the experience: 'What did you feel during that?' 'What moments felt right?' 'What moments felt off?' 'What did you find yourself wanting that wasn't there?'
Iteration: Revise the experience specification or the design based on the debrief. Re-prototype. Experience prototyping is intrinsically iterative.
outputs: Experience specifications, enacted prototypes, debrief findings about felt experience, and iterated experience qualities guiding design.
useWhen: The quality of an experience over time and in context matters more than interface details, such as services, physical-digital products, AI interactions or emotionally significant moments.
avoidWhen: You need to test interface usability or detailed interactions; use prototype usability testing. Avoid if the context cannot be credibly simulated.
whyLost: It survives under names such as bodystorming, service walkthroughs and Wizard of Oz, but its focus on specifying and testing experience qualities is often lost.
whereToUse: Service design, connected and in-car devices, AI assistants, healthcare encounters, retail and hospitality experiences.
example: Before building a voice assistant for hospital porters, designers role-play the assistant in a ward corridor with a researcher speaking responses. Porters find unprompted announcements intrusive near patients, so a proximity-aware quiet mode is designed.
reference: Buchenau, M. & Suri, J. F. (2000). Experience prototyping. Proceedings of DIS 2000, 424-433.

name: Experience Sampling Method
origin: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi & Reed Larson, 1970s to 1987; EMA by Stone & Shiffman, 1994
summary: Participants report momentary experience in real time when prompted at random or event-based moments, minimising recall bias and capturing experience in context.
description: The Experience Sampling Method, developed by Csikszentmihalyi and Larson, and the closely related Ecological Momentary Assessment from behavioural medicine, prompt participants several times a day to report what they are doing, feeling and experiencing at that moment. Prompts may be random within time windows, at fixed intervals or triggered by events, such as app use or location. Because reports are immediate and in situ, ESM reduces recall bias and captures variation within people across contexts. Data form many short, repeated measures per person and require multilevel analysis. Rigour comes from a sampling schedule matched to the phenomenon, very short questionnaires (under about two minutes), compliance monitoring (aiming for at least 70 to 80 percent), and analysis that separates within-person from between-person variation.
steps: Define the momentary experiences and contexts of interest.
Choose signal-, interval- or event-contingent sampling and set the schedule, for example 5 to 8 random prompts per day for 7 to 14 days.
Design a short questionnaire of validated momentary items that takes under two minutes.
Pilot on the target platform and adjust burden.
