Recruit 20 to 50 or more participants, brief them and monitor compliance daily.
Clean data, applying compliance and response time rules.
Analyse with multilevel models to separate within-person and between-person effects.
outputs: Repeated momentary reports, within-person patterns across contexts and time, compliance statistics and multilevel model estimates.
useWhen: For emotional and mood-related UX, mental health and wellbeing apps, momentary context of use and experiences that fluctuate through the day.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the phenomenon is rare or not tied to moments; use event-based diaries or critical incident interviews. Avoid when burden would be unacceptable for participants.
whyLost: It survived because remote tools made it cheap and it fills a clear gap between interviews and analytics; the risk is weak design, with long entry forms, no trigger logic and poor compliance.
whereToUse: Emotional UX; mental health apps; in-situ product experience capture.
example: A mindfulness app runs a 10-day EMA with 40 users, prompting six times daily about stress and app use. Multilevel models show stress drops after use only when sessions occur before 6 pm, informing reminder timing.
sources: Validity and Reliability of the Experience-Sampling Method (Csikszentmihalyi & Larson)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Csikszentmihalyi M & Larson R (1987) Validity and reliability of the experience-sampling method. J Nervous Mental Disease 175:526-536
Hektner JM, Schmidt JA & Csikszentmihalyi M (2007) Experience Sampling Method
Shiffman S, Stone AA & Hufford MR (2008) Ecological momentary assessment. Annu Rev Clin Psychol
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection
The Inquiry Series, Ch 33 — Participatory & Arts-Based Methods
Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
A Practical Guide to Experience-Sampling Procedures (Conner Christensen et al., 2003)

The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)

name: Experience-Based Co-Design
origin: Paul Bate and Glenn Robert, 2007 (NHS Institute for Innovation and Improvement)
summary: Service users and staff share stories of a service in joint workshops, identify the emotional highs and lows of the journey, and co-design improvements with designers.
description: Experience-based co-design treats stories of a service as the raw material for improvement. Patients (or other service users) and staff are first asked for stories of their experiences; instead of passing these to a design team, users and staff are brought together in workshops to share them. The shared journey, with its emotional highs and lows, becomes common ground, and users, staff and designers then work together on improvements. Telling stories is not just data collection: it lets people make sense of and rehearse their experiences, and the joint setting produces new understanding rather than recycled assumptions. In its established health-service form the method typically gathers user stories by narrative interview, often edited into a short film shown at the joint event, and runs small co-design groups over several weeks.
steps: Gather stories of the service separately from staff and from users, often through narrative interviews; a short edited film of user stories is common.
Identify the emotional high and low points of the journey in each group.
Hold a joint event where users and staff share stories (or watch the film) and agree priority moments to improve.
Form small co-design groups of users, staff and designers for each priority, meeting over several weeks.
Develop and trial improvements, checking them against the emotional highs and lows identified.
Hold a review event to share changes and plan follow-up.
outputs: A shared journey with emotional highs and lows, agreed priorities and co-designed service improvements.
useWhen: Improving a service where staff and user perspectives diverge and emotional experience matters, especially health and care.
avoidWhen: When power imbalances make honest sharing unsafe: users may hedge criticism with staff present and experiences may be questioned rather than validated. Deep involvement can also confine ideas to participants' lived experience. Consider separate interviews plus Journey Mapping, or skilled facilitation.
whyLost: It is well established in UK and Australian healthcare but is rarely named in mainstream UX, where co-design is usually framed as generative making sessions.
whereToUse: Health and care services, public services, internal service design, digital front doors to complex services.
example: A hospital outpatient clinic redesigning its booking app gathers patient and nurse stories, discovers that the lowest emotional point is the wait after a scan, and a mixed co-design group creates in-app result timelines and a nurse callback.
reference: Bate, P. and Robert, G. (2007). Bringing User Experience to Healthcare Improvement: The Concepts, Methods and Practices of Experience-Based Design. Oxford: Radcliffe.

name: Experiential Ethnography
origin: Term associated with Sands (2002), who studied sprinters and American football players by competing alongside them; summarised by Gratton and Jones (2010).
summary: An ethnography in which the researcher becomes a full, practising member of the group, using their own bodily and emotional experience of the activity as data.
description: In experiential ethnography the researcher does not just watch or talk to participants but takes part fully in their activity, so that their own sensations and feelings become data alongside observation and conversation. Sands (2002) frames this as moving through stages of membership: learning about the group (anticipatory socialisation), becoming a member (recruitment), learning its norms, values and behaviours (socialisation) and finally acceptance as one of the group, with each stage itself revealing something about the group. Its strength is access to otherwise hidden data, such as the pain, adrenaline and emotional swings of competition that a non-participant could not observe. Gratton and Jones warn of two weaknesses: the account can slide into autobiography with no analytical framework, and the researcher may 'go native' and select evidence that suits the group's self-image. The researcher therefore needs to stay 'objectively subjective', holding the participant and researcher roles in tension. It differs from autoethnography, where the researcher's own life is the main subject. For UX, it suggests a disciplined form of extended immersion: researchers who learn and practise a demanding user activity themselves (a trade, a sport, a caring role) over weeks, documenting how competence, community and the tools feel from inside.
steps: Choose a group and activity where the felt experience of doing it matters to the design question, and justify why immersion is needed.
Prepare by learning about the group's practices and norms (anticipatory socialisation) and plan how to gain entry and what to disclose.
Join and take part fully over an extended period, keeping detailed field notes of your own sensations, emotions and difficulties as well as others' behaviour.
Note each membership stage (recruitment, socialisation, acceptance) and what it reveals about the group and its tools.
Check your interpretations through conversations with other members and keep a reflexive record of how you may be going native.
Analyse the material against a theoretical or design framework rather than writing a personal story, and report your role openly.
outputs: Rich first-person and observational accounts of the activity, membership stages and tacit knowledge, interpreted against an explicit framework.
useWhen: The design problem depends on embodied, emotional or tacit aspects of a practice that users struggle to put into words, and the team has time for sustained participation.
avoidWhen: Time is short, participation would be unsafe or unethical, or the question can be answered by observing or interviewing users.
whyLost: Commercial UX timelines rarely allow weeks of participation, and first-person data is seen as unrepresentative; lighter forms such as 'eating your own dog food' and short immersion days are used instead without the method's discipline.
whereToUse: Fitness and sports products, wearables, trade and field-work tools, gig and delivery platforms, caring and health-management apps.
example: A researcher on a delivery-courier app works as a courier for six weeks, keeping nightly field notes on fatigue, weather, app interruptions and banter at pick-up points. Her account of how couriers learn to game batch offers, and how stressful mid-ride notifications feel, reshapes the notification design.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Experiential Gestalt Analysis Along Six Dimensions
origin: Adapted for UX from George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, Metaphors We Live By (1980)
summary: Describe an activity along participants, parts, stages, linear sequence, causation and purpose, then map what a metaphor adds onto the same dimensions to see what it structures.
description: Lakoff and Johnson treat a coherent experience as an experiential gestalt with natural dimensions: participants, parts, stages, linear sequence, causation and purpose. A polite conversation has speakers as participants, turns as parts, stages from opening to close, alternating turns, each turn prompting the next, and cooperative purpose. When it becomes an argument, the added elements (positions, adversary, attack, defence, retreat, truce) can be described on the same dimensions and correspond to the structure of war. Comparing the two tables shows exactly which parts of the experience come from the source concept and which from the base activity. Adapted for UX, the procedure analyses how an interface or service metaphor (a cart, a wallet, a conversation with an assistant) restructures an activity, and which expectations it imports.
steps: Describe the base activity on the six dimensions: participants, parts, stages, linear sequence, causation and purpose.
List what users perceive over and above the base activity when it is framed by the metaphor or when it changes character.
Re-describe the added elements on the same six dimensions.
Identify the source concept whose structure they match.
State which parts of the experience come from the source and which from the base activity, and note expectations the source imports that the product does not meet.
outputs: Two six-dimension tables (base activity and metaphorical overlay) and a list of imported expectations.
useWhen: Choosing or auditing an interface or brand metaphor, analysing how users frame an activity in interviews, and designing conversational products whose framing shapes turn-taking.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to identify metaphors in a large corpus (use the Metaphor Identification Procedure) or to test whether inferences carry over (use the metaphor inference-preservation check). The dimensions give outlines only.
whyLost: Conceptual metaphor theory is widely cited in HCI, but this specific six-dimension analysis has not been turned into a working procedure.
whereToUse: AI assistant personas, financial 'pots' and 'wallets', gamified learning, healthcare 'journeys', negotiation and dispute tools.
example: A team maps support chat as a conversation and then as a 'ticket queue'. The queue framing adds stages, waiting and an agent who processes rather than converses, which explains why customers report feeling processed, and the team reframes the opening turn.
reference: Lakoff, G. and Johnson, M. (2003). Metaphors We Live By (with a new afterword). Chicago: University of Chicago Press, pp. 77-86. (Original work published 1980.)

name: Experiment review meeting and design checklist
origin: Google, Microsoft and LinkedIn practice (Kohavi, Tang and Xu, 2020); King, Churchill and Tan (2017)
summary: A required pre-launch design checklist plus a standing cross-team meeting that vets upcoming experiments and reviews results first for trust, then for decisions.
description: Experimentation quality depends on governance as much as statistics. Before launch, each experiment completes a short checklist (hypothesis, key metric, practically meaningful change, power calculation) reviewed by an expert; Google required this until teams matured. A standing review meeting, separate from design critique and mixing product managers and designers who do not usually work together, covers two kinds of work. For upcoming experiments it questions the hypothesis and its supporting data, the methodology and its alternatives, how well the design expresses the hypothesis, and whether success metrics really test it. For launched experiments it first checks trustworthiness (sample ratio mismatch, guardrails, instrumentation), then results, transferable learning, anomalies and confounds, and records trade-offs in the overall evaluation criterion and institutional memory for meta-analysis.
steps: Require each experiment to complete a short checklist before start: hypothesis, key metric, minimum meaningful change, and power calculation.
Have an experienced reviewer sign off the checklist before launch.
Hold a standing review meeting, separate from design critique, inviting product managers, designers and data specialists from different teams.
For upcoming work, question the hypothesis, the data behind it, the method and its alternatives, the design and the success metrics.
For launched work, review trustworthiness first (sample ratio mismatch, guardrail metrics, instrumentation), then results and launch recommendation.
Discuss anomalies, possible confounds and what else could have been tested, and codify metric trade-offs into the overall evaluation criterion.
Record decisions and learning in a searchable archive for institutional memory and meta-analysis; relax the checklist as maturity grows.
outputs: Reviewed experiment designs, a record of decisions and trade-offs, and shared knowledge of what works across teams.
useWhen: Organisations scaling from a few to many experiments, or where tests are frequently underpowered, misinstrumented or misread.
avoidWhen: Very small teams running occasional tests where the meeting overhead exceeds its value, or mature cultures where the checklist has become bureaucratic.
whyLost: It survives under names like experiment council or metrics review in large tech firms, but its structured question set is rarely written down or adopted by UX teams.
whereToUse: Growth, product analytics and UX research teams in SaaS, e-commerce and marketplaces building an experimentation programme.
example: A marketplace sets up a fortnightly experiment review. A planned checkout test is sent back because its 2-week run cannot detect the 1% change the team cares about, and a launched search test is held because the review spots a sample ratio mismatch.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Cambridge University Press.

name: Experiment test-cell design strategy
aka: Test-cell portfolio design with a learning plan
origin: King, Churchill and Tan (2017), drawing on Netflix, Spotify, Etsy and Skyscanner practice
summary: Treat the set of hypotheses and test cells as a design task: write structured hypotheses, choose cells that each teach something distinct, test extremes first, and plan follow-ups.
description: Most A/B tests compare one shippable variant with control, which teaches little when it fails. This strategy designs experiments to learn. Hypotheses follow a template ('For [user group], if [change] then [effect] because [rationale], which will impact [measure]') with a learning statement for success and failure, are generated broadly by varying their parts, and are pruned with estimates, past data, cheap research and feasibility checks (minimum detectable effect, sample, business cycle). Cells are chosen to span the dimensions of interest and tabulated against them; redundant cells are dropped. In exploration, a deliberately extreme, unshippable variant shows whether an idea can move the metric at all (Skyscanner dropped sharing when even a pop-up did nothing). For large redesigns, a global phase tests divergent concepts on a small traffic share until one nears control, then a local phase optimises it (Etsy gained about 5% conversion).
steps: Write each hypothesis as 'for [user group], if [change] then [effect] because [rationale], which will impact [measure]', and add a learning statement for both success and failure.

Generate broadly by holding some parts fixed and varying others (behaviours, changes, user groups), then prune with ballpark value estimates, past tests, disconfirming evidence and cheap research such as pilots or usability tests.
Check feasibility for each survivor: minimum detectable effect, sample, allocation, behaviour lag and business cycle.
Choose cells so they span the dimensions you want to learn about, tabulate each cell against those dimensions, and drop cells that teach nothing another cell does not.
In exploration, include a realistic and a deliberately exaggerated variant; if even the extreme variant has no effect, drop the idea; for continuous variables test the extremes before finer steps.

For large redesigns, run divergent concepts on a small share of traffic (Etsy used 5%) in two-week iterations with qualitative research until one comes close to control, then optimise it with smaller A/B tests until it wins.
For each likely outcome, decide which experiment comes next and start designing follow-ups while results come in; keep unpursued and failed hypotheses on record.
outputs: A prioritised hypothesis set with learning statements, a cell-by-dimension table, a branching plan of next experiments and, for redesigns, a variant validated against the incumbent.
useWhen: Exploring a new product area, testing whether an idea can matter at all, or redesigning a complex page that cannot be reached by small iterative steps.
avoidWhen: Pure optimisation of a known-good design where one variant against control suffices, or when traffic is too low to support several cells; use qualitative research or sequential single tests.
whyLost: Experimentation tooling and training focus on analysing a single variant, so treating the cell set as a learning design is rarely taught outside a few mature product organisations.
whereToUse: Navigation and redesign programmes, new feature exploration, recommendation and pricing exploration in consumer apps, marketplaces and SaaS.
example: A travel app wonders whether social sharing matters. It tests a subtle share button it would ship and an intrusive pop-up it never would; neither moves bookings or shares, so the team abandons the idea instead of iterating button styles for months.
reference: King, R., Churchill, E. F. and Tan, C. (2017). Designing with Data: Improving the User Experience with A/B Testing. O'Reilly Media.

name: Expert and Key Informant Interviewing
donor: Anthropology, political science and knowledge elicitation
origin: Key informant tradition in anthropology; elite interviewing (Dexter, 1970); expert knowledge elicitation in cognitive task analysis
summary: Specialised interviewing of domain experts and organisational insiders that bypasses automated knowledge through incidents, exceptions and demonstration.
description: Experts have automated much of their skill, so asking 'how do you do X' produces textbook rationalisations rather than real process. Professional identity also discourages admitting uncertainty or workarounds. Key informant interviewing addresses this with tactics drawn from anthropology, elite interviewing and knowledge elicitation. The researcher prepares thoroughly to converse as a peer, uses critical incidents to anchor accounts in real difficult cases, asks about exceptions rather than rules, and where possible has the expert perform and narrate a task. Key informants, insiders with privileged views of an organisation or community, are also used to map structure, politics and context quickly, with their partiality acknowledged and triangulated.
steps: Demonstrate competence first: Read relevant material before the interview. Show the expert you know enough to have a conversation rather than a tutorial. This changes the dynamic from teacher→student to peer→peer.
Use critical incident technique: "Tell me about a time when [the task/problem] was particularly difficult." Specific incidents bypass automatisation and surface actual process.

Ask about exceptions, not rules: "When does the standard approach not work?" "What do you do differently in unusual cases?" Exceptions reveal the underlying structure that the rules describe imperfectly.

Use the think-aloud while doing approach: Ask the expert to perform a task while narrating their thinking. Concurrent verbalization (during the task) is more accurate than retrospective account (after the task).
outputs: Expert process descriptions grounded in incidents, catalogues of exceptions and cues, organisational context maps, and leads for further sampling.
useWhen: Specialist domains (clinical, legal, trading, engineering), early orientation in an unfamiliar organisation, or when designing tools for experts.
avoidWhen: When you need end-user experience or representative views; key informants are deliberately partial. Use end-user interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Widely practised as stakeholder or SME interviews, though the elicitation tactics for automated knowledge are often missing.
whereToUse: Enterprise and B2B tools, medical and legal technology, AI tooling for professionals, and stakeholder discovery.
example: Designing a tool for insurance underwriters, the researcher asks a senior underwriter about the last policy she declined against the guidelines. The exceptions reveal three unwritten risk cues that become explicit fields.
sources: The Science and Art of Interviewing (Blee)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Qualitative Methods in Information Retrieval Research (Fidel, 1993)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
From Hype to Practice (Jylkäs et al., 2019)
reference: Crandall, B., Klein, G. & Hoffman, R. R. (2006). Working Minds: A Practitioner's Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis. MIT Press.

extra.Why Experts Require Different Technique: Experts have automatised their expertise — they can no longer easily articulate what they do because it no longer requires conscious processing. Standard interview technique ("tell me how you do X") produces post-hoc rationalisation, not actual process description. Additionally, experts have professional identities that make them reluctant to reveal uncertainty or workarounds. The master/apprentice framing of contextual inquiry works better with experts than formal interviews.

name: Expert Skill Training Design (Deliberate Practice and Perceptual Exposure)
aka: Deliberate Practice Exercise Design (95 percent in three sessions)
Can't do / With effort / Mastered boards
donor: Expertise science, instructional design and perceptual learning
origin: Kathy Sierra (2015), simplifying deliberate practice research and drawing on Kellman and Kaiser (1994) on perceptual learning in flight training
summary: Design exercises that make users expert: sub-skill drills reaching 95 percent reliability within three sessions, and high-volume exposure to varied expert examples with fast feedback.
description: Sierra argues that products succeed when users become good at what the product helps them do, and that expertise comes from two designable things. Deliberate practice: list skills on three boards (Can't do, Can do with effort, Mastered), give beginners a minimum viable starter set, then drill one fine-grained sub-skill at a time with a pass/fail exercise that should reach 95 percent reliability within one to three 45-90 minute sessions. If it does not, the exercise is redesigned by splitting the sub-skill finer or lowering the criteria. Perceptual exposure: present many short, high-quality expert examples that differ on the surface but share an invariant, ask learners to classify or choose, and give prompt feedback, letting the pattern be learned implicitly. Kellman and Kaiser's non-pilots outperformed pilots on instrument reading after 432 such trials. Both are tested by comparing performance before and after, not by satisfaction.
steps: List the skills the product's users need as cards on three boards: Can't do, With effort, Mastered; mark a minimum viable starter set for beginners.
Pick one fine-grained sub-skill users cannot yet do reliably and write a pass/fail exercise with explicit criteria.
Run one to three sessions of 45-90 minutes, close together; the target is 95 percent reliability.
If the target is missed, split the sub-skill finer (fewer steps, one hand, one case) or lower the criteria (half speed) and retry.
For perceptual judgements, collect dozens to hundreds of short expert examples that vary on the surface but share the target pattern; avoid showing bad examples early.
Present them in a compressed period with a classify-or-choose task and feedback per trial or per block (for example blocks of 24).
Evaluate by comparing learners' outputs before and after; if gains are small, add more and more varied examples or shorten the feedback gap.
Keep few skills on the With-effort board and schedule de-automation drills for plateaued skills.
outputs: Ladders of sub-skill exercises with reliability criteria, exposure sets with classification drills, and before/after performance comparisons.
useWhen: Use when a product's value depends on users becoming skilled (creative tools, analytics, music, sport, clinical or safety tasks) and onboarding currently teaches features rather than competence.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple, infrequent tasks where the interface should remove the need for skill. Do not use it to judge whether users can use the interface: run Usability Testing, or an Experience Curve and Learning Study to measure learning. Deliberate practice is not intrinsically rewarding, so plan motivational support.
whyLost: It sits in instructional design and expertise science; product teams treat learning as onboarding copy and rarely design graded practice or exposure sets.
whereToUse: Creative and pro tools, language and music learning apps, data tools, training simulators, health self-management skills.
example: A video-editing app adds a drill that asks users to make an L-cut on short clips until they succeed 19 times in 20, then a gallery of 40 two-minute expert edits with a 'which cut works better' quiz and instant feedback. Edit quality on a standard task improves measurably after a week.
reference: Sierra, K. (2015). Badass: Making Users Awesome. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 98-153. Kellman, P. J. and Kaiser, M. K. (1994). Perceptual learning modules in flight training. Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society 38th Annual Meeting.

name: Expert vs. novice chunk size calibration
origin: Chase and Simon, 1973; Ericsson and Kintsch's long-term working memory, 1995
summary: Measures how large and how many meaningful chunks experts and novices perceive in the same display, so layouts and procedures can be tuned to each group's real capacity.
description: Experts perceive domain information in larger meaningful chunks: chess masters recall realistic positions far better than novices, but not random ones. Ericsson and Kintsch showed experts also use long-term working memory structures that expand effective capacity. For interfaces, this means the same screen loads experts and novices very differently. Calibration measures chunk size with recall reconstruction tasks (show a realistic display briefly, then ask participants to reconstruct it) and pause analysis, where pauses of more than about 2 seconds during reconstruction mark chunk boundaries. Comparing expert and novice results shows what groupings experts rely on, which can guide progressive disclosure, default layouts and training. Rigour comes from realistic versus scrambled control displays and from objective boundary measures.
steps: Recruit matched expert and novice groups, at least 8-12 each, with expertise defined by objective criteria (for example cases performed).
Prepare realistic displays and scrambled control versions with the same elements.
Show each display for a fixed short time (for example 5 seconds), then ask participants to reconstruct it from memory, recording the sequence and timing of placements.
Identify chunk boundaries from inter-placement pauses (above about 2 seconds) and co-placed elements; compute chunk count and size per group.
Compare realistic versus scrambled recall to confirm expert advantage derives from meaningful structure.
Use expert chunk structures to design layouts, groupings and training material, and set novice defaults to smaller chunks.
outputs: Chunk size and count for experts and novices, the specific chunk structures experts use, and layout or training recommendations.
useWhen: When a product serves both novices and experts, when designing training or adaptive interfaces, or when experts resist a simplified redesign.
avoidWhen: When users are homogeneous in expertise; a working memory load audit is sufficient.
whyLost: Expertise research is rich in psychology but UX treats expertise as a persona attribute rather than a measurable cognitive difference.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, air traffic control, trading platforms, developer tools, and radiology viewers.
example: Expert robotic surgeons reconstruct a console status screen in 3 chunks (instruments, camera, energy) while novices use 9 small ones. The redesign groups status by those three expert chunks and adds a guided novice mode.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 10 — Memory — The Architecture of Knowledge
reference: Ericsson, K. A. & Kintsch, W. (1995). Long-term working memory. Psychological Review, 102(2), 211-245.

name: Exploratory Data Analysis for Behavioural UX Data
origin: John Tukey, 1977
summary: Systematically examines behavioural datasets through distributions, plots and summaries before modelling, to find structure, anomalies and questions worth testing.
description: Exploratory data analysis, formalised by John Tukey, is the disciplined practice of looking at data before deciding what it means. For behavioural UX data, analysts inspect distributions of key metrics, check missing and duplicated values, examine relationships with scatterplots and cross-tabulations, compare segments and time periods, and look for anomalies that indicate tracking errors or unexpected user strategies. EDA deliberately generates hypotheses rather than testing them, so its outputs are questions and candidate explanations. Rigour comes from following a checklist (univariate, bivariate, temporal, segment views), documenting data quality issues, using robust summaries such as medians and quantiles, and clearly separating exploratory findings from confirmatory evidence to avoid the garden of forking paths.
steps: EDA protocol for behavioral data:
Distribution plots for all continuous variables (histogram + density): look for bimodality, extreme skew, or unexpected modes.
(2) Pairplots for all variable pairs: look for non-linear relationships, clustered patterns.
(3) Outlier analysis: flag any observation > 3 IQRs from Q3.
(4) Missing data pattern: visualize missingness across variables.
(5) Time trends: if longitudinal data, plot each variable over time before assuming stationarity.
outputs: Distribution plots, summary statistics, data quality notes, anomaly and outlier lists, candidate hypotheses and segmentation ideas.
useWhen: First contact with any analytics, telemetry or survey dataset; before building dashboards or models; when metrics behave unexpectedly.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting EDA findings as confirmed effects; follow with confirmatory analysis or experiments. Not needed when a pre-registered analysis is the explicit goal.
whyLost: Dashboards and pre-built analytics tools let teams skip the open-ended look at raw distributions, so averages and funnels are trusted without inspection.
whereToUse: Any UX analytics project before modeling. Prevents the most common data quality errors from contaminating findings.
example: Before reporting a drop in weekly active users, an analyst plots session distributions by platform and discovers an Android logging bug double-counting sessions in the baseline period.
sources: Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)

name: Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)
origin: Charles Spearman, 1904; Louis Thurstone, 1930s
summary: Reveals the latent constructs underlying a set of survey items by grouping items that co-vary, with reliability checked per factor.
description: EFA models observed item responses as driven by a smaller number of latent factors and estimates which items load on which factor. In Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook, a 30-item Likert survey aligned to Morville's Honeycomb (n = 300) yields three factors: Trust (Credible + Valuable, α = 0.84), Ease (Usable + Accessible, α = 0.81) and Engagement (Useful + Desirable + Findable, α = 0.86). The interpretive move is diagnostic: Engagement weakening while Ease stays strong is the classic drift signature. EFA findings are paired with interviews so that, for example, a drop in the Engagement factor and interview mentions of repetitiveness constitute a mixed-method signal. The Nash protocol also lists factor analysis for confirming ΔU components. Rigour depends on adequate sample size, defensible extraction and rotation choices and reliability per factor.
steps: Write items aligned to a theoretical framework (e.g. 30 Honeycomb items).
Field the survey to an adequate sample (the example uses n = 300).
Check factorability, choose extraction and rotation, and decide the number of factors.
Interpret and name factors from their loading patterns.
Compute Cronbach's α per factor (≥ 0.70).
Track factor scores over time and pair shifts with interview themes.
outputs: A factor structure with loadings, named constructs, reliabilities and factor scores.
useWhen: When developing or exploring the structure of a multi-item instrument, or reducing many attitudes to a few constructs.
avoidWhen: When the structure is already theorised and must be tested; use CFA or SEM instead.
whyLost: Taught widely but often replaced in UX by unvalidated single-item scores, or run with default settings and little judgement.
whereToUse: UX perception surveys, trust scales, segmentation inputs, drift monitoring surveys.
example: An e-commerce Honeycomb survey reduces 30 items to Trust, Ease and Engagement; Engagement drops while Ease holds, flagging drift rather than a usability break.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Quantitative User Experience Research (Chris Chapman & Kerry Rodden)

Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)

name: Exploratory factor analysis with parallel analysis
origin: Charles Spearman, 1904 (factor analysis); John Horn, 1965 (parallel analysis)
summary: Discovering the latent dimensions underlying a set of survey items, using parallel analysis to decide objectively how many factors to retain.
description: Exploratory factor analysis models item correlations as arising from a smaller number of latent factors. The critical decision is how many factors to retain. The widely used Kaiser rule (eigenvalues above 1) systematically over-extracts. Horn's parallel analysis compares observed eigenvalues with those from random data of the same size, retaining only factors whose eigenvalues exceed the 95th percentile of the random ones. A rigorous EFA checks factorability (KMO, Bartlett's test), uses common-factor extraction (principal axis or minimum residual, not principal components), applies an oblique rotation when factors are expected to correlate, and removes items with weak or cross-loadings iteratively. In UX it is mostly confined to academic scale development.
steps: Ensure a sample of at least about 200, or 5-10 respondents per item, and clean the data first.
Check factorability: KMO of 0.60 or above (0.80 or above preferred) and a significant Bartlett's test.
Run parallel analysis with 1,000 random datasets and retain factors whose eigenvalues exceed the 95th percentile of random eigenvalues.
Extract with principal axis or minimum residual factoring (factor_analyzer) and apply an oblique rotation such as oblimin or promax.
Remove items with primary loadings below about 0.40 or cross-loadings above about 0.30, one at a time, re-running after each removal.
Name factors from their highest-loading items and confirm the structure in a separate sample with CFA.
outputs: A retained factor count with parallel analysis plot, a rotated loading matrix, factor correlations and a refined item set.
useWhen: Developing new UX instruments (trust, perceived AI competence, financial confidence), checking whether a borrowed scale behaves as expected, or exploring the structure of a large attitude survey.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the structure is already theorised and should be tested (use CFA), when samples are under about 100, or for binary items without polychoric correlations.
whyLost: Factor analysis is taught in psychology and marketing but UX teams typically adopt off-the-shelf scales or write ad hoc surveys without structural checks.
whereToUse: New scale development for AI products, fintech trust, accessibility attitudes and B2B satisfaction surveys.
example: A team building an 'AI assistant trust' questionnaire collects 24 items from 420 users. The Kaiser rule suggests six factors, but parallel analysis retains three (competence, integrity, predictability), and 7 weak items are dropped.
sources: Horn, J. L. (1965) A rationale and test for the number of factors in factor analysis. Psychometrika
Fabrigar, L. R. & Wegener, D. T. (2012) Exploratory Factor Analysis
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Horn, J. L. (1965) A rationale and test for the number of factors in factor analysis. Psychometrika 30(2)

name: External and Multi-Instrument Validation of Analytics Metrics
aka: External data validation of internal metrics
donor: Measurement science; online experimentation; information science
origin: Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020); Jansen, Salminen, Jung and colleagues (2022-2024)
summary: Treats analytics figures as estimates and bounds their error by comparing independent instruments, such as two analytics installs or panel data, before relying on them.
description: Most numbers about people at scale are measurements, not counts: they come from a black-box chain of collection, filtering, sampling and modification, yet dashboards show them as crisp figures that anchor decisions. Jansen and colleagues show that two independently configured analytics installations report different numbers for the same site, panel-based and site-centric tools disagree, and sentiment tools disagree on the same texts. The method compares two or more independent instruments on the same phenomenon to establish a discrepancy range from which error can be estimated, and reports figures as estimates with that range. Kohavi et al. add comparison with external sources such as panels, surveys and published data, judged by agreement in trend and seasonality rather than absolute level. Agreement does not prove accuracy, but disagreement reveals fragile metrics.
steps: List the key numbers a decision rests on.
Identify at least two independent instruments for each, for example site-centric and panel-based analytics, two analytics installs, two sentiment tools or two human labellers.
Align definitions, scope and time periods so the instruments measure the same thing.
Collect the metric from each instrument and compute the discrepancy range.
Compare time series for agreement in trend and seasonality rather than absolute levels.
Report figures as estimates with their discrepancy range, and investigate large disagreements rather than settling by majority.
outputs: An error or discrepancy range per metric, documented definitional differences, and figures reported as estimates.
useWhen: Before high-stakes decisions on analytics numbers, when switching analytics vendors, or when audience or sentiment figures drive strategy.
avoidWhen: When configurations cannot be made comparable, or external sources are too opaque to interpret; absolute numbers rarely match. For checking within-experiment data integrity use sample ratio checks under A/B Testing.
whyLost: Dashboards present single figures, and teams rarely budget for a second instrument, so measurement error stays invisible.
whereToUse: Media and publishing analytics, marketing attribution, AI-labelled sentiment pipelines, executive dashboards.
example: A news site runs Google Analytics and Matomo side by side for a month and finds a 14% gap in unique visitors; the team reports audience as a range and fixes a consent-banner tagging gap.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press; Jansen, B. J., Aldous, K. K., Salminen, J., Almerekhi, H. and Jung, S. (2024). Understanding Audiences, Customers, and Users via Analytics. Springer.

name: Extreme and Deviant Case Sampling
donor: Qualitative methodology and public health (positive deviance)
origin: Patton, 1990 (purposeful sampling strategies); positive deviance approach from Marian Zeitlin and Jerry Sternin, 1990s
summary: Deliberately recruiting outliers, the most frustrated, most expert or unexpectedly successful users, to expose mechanisms and boundary conditions typical cases hide.
description: Typical cases show average experience; extreme cases show where systems break hardest or work unexpectedly well. Extreme case sampling selects participants at the tails of a relevant distribution, often identified from analytics, support data or survey scores. Deviant case sampling targets those who do not fit the emerging explanation, which makes them the strongest test of a theory. Positive deviance, from public health, studies people who succeed despite the same constraints as others, revealing workable strategies. Pairing extremes with typical cases sharpens comparison. Rigour lies in defining 'extreme' from the research question, using data to locate cases, and treating outliers as scope conditions rather than noise.
steps: Identify what counts as extreme for your research question: most experienced, most frustrated, fastest adopter, most resistant.
Analytic pair sampling: Pair extreme case sampling with typical case sampling. The comparison generates the most insight.
Use quantitative data (usage analytics, NPS scores) to identify participants at the extremes of distributions. Recruit from those extremes purposively.
Do not treat extreme cases as errors. Treat them as boundary conditions revealing scope conditions of your emerging theory.
outputs: A recruited set of extreme, deviant and typical comparison cases, contrast analyses, and identified boundary conditions or positive deviant strategies.
useWhen: Explaining what drives success or failure, testing an emerging theory, or finding strategies successful users have invented.
avoidWhen: When you need to describe typical experience or prevalence; extremes are by design unrepresentative. Use maximum variation or probability sampling.
whyLost: Recruiting tends to filter out 'unusual' users as noise, and few teams link analytics to recruitment to find the tails.
whereToUse: Power user research, churn analysis, savings and health behaviour change, and AI product misuse or over-reliance studies.
example: A savings app finds low-income users who save consistently despite the same pay volatility as others. Interviews reveal they split pay into labelled pots on payday, which becomes a default feature.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Power of Positive Deviance (Pascale, Sternin & Sternin)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2015). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Eye Tracking
origin: Reading research from the 1900s; HCI use from the 1980s; Just & Carpenter's eye-mind hypothesis, 1980
summary: Records where and how long people look using fixations, saccades and pupil size, revealing visual attention, search behaviour and processing load.
description: Eye tracking measures eye movements, typically with infrared corneal-reflection cameras, to record fixations (pauses where information is taken in), saccades (rapid jumps between fixations) and pupil diameter. In UX it shows what users notice, the order in which they scan, what they miss and where they search hesitantly. Pupil dilation can indicate cognitive load or arousal under controlled lighting. Outputs include heatmaps, gaze plots and metrics such as time to first fixation and dwell time on areas of interest. Rigour comes from calibration accuracy checks, defined areas of interest before analysis, adequate samples for quantitative heatmaps (around 30 or more), controlled stimuli, and remembering that looking is not the same as understanding, so gaze data should be paired with think-aloud or task outcomes.
steps: Define research questions and areas of interest on the stimuli.
Choose equipment (screen-based, glasses or webcam-based) appropriate to accuracy needs.
Recruit participants, excluding those whose eyewear prevents good calibration, with around 30 or more for heatmaps or 6 to 10 for qualitative gaze replays.
Calibrate each participant and check accuracy, typically within 0.5 to 1 degree of visual angle.
Run tasks, avoiding concurrent think-aloud if measuring gaze timing, and use retrospective think-aloud with gaze replay.
Analyse fixation, dwell and time-to-first-fixation metrics per area of interest, plus pupil data under controlled lighting.
Interpret alongside task success and verbal data.
outputs: Heatmaps, gaze plots, area-of-interest metrics (time to first fixation, dwell time, fixation counts) and pupillometry indicators.
useWhen: For visual hierarchy, scanning and search behaviour, ad and package visibility, reading flow and identifying what users fail to notice.
avoidWhen: Avoid for questions about comprehension or motivation alone, or when budget and expertise are limited; use usability testing, five-second tests or first-click testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Objective attention data; increasingly accessible via webcam-based tools; used in web, packaging, and ad research.
whereToUse: Visual hierarchy evaluation; advertising; reading flow; accessibility.
example: A lender tests its loan-approval screen and finds 70 percent of participants never fixate on the repayment schedule before accepting. Moving it beside the accept button raises fixation and comprehension scores.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 38 — FACS, Micro-Expression Analysis & Psychophysiology
Pupil diameter and load on memory (Kahneman & Beatty)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)

name: Eye-Movement Scanpath Analysis
origin: David Noton and Lawrence Stark, 1971 (scanpath theory); string-edit methods by Privitera and Stark (2000); ScanMatch (Cristino et al., 2010); MultiMatch (Jarodzka et al., 2010)
summary: Compares the sequences of fixations across users and designs with string-edit or vector methods, revealing reading strategies that heatmaps conceal.
description: Heatmaps aggregate where people look but discard order and timing. Scanpath analysis treats fixation sequences as strings over areas of interest (AOIs) or as vectors, then computes similarity: Levenshtein edit distance, ScanMatch's Needleman-Wunsch alignment with substitution matrices and duration, or MultiMatch's five dimensions (shape, direction, length, position, duration). Clustering similar scanpaths reveals distinct strategies (e.g. F-pattern versus layer-cake reading). Transition matrices and entropy measures show how structured the viewing is. This answers questions like 'do users read the warning before the button?' and 'does the redesign create one consistent strategy?'.
steps: Define AOIs on stimuli, and ensure eye-tracking data quality (accuracy below about 1 degree, low data loss).
Extract fixation sequences per participant and task, collapsing consecutive fixations within an AOI if appropriate.
Compute pairwise similarity using ScanMatch or MultiMatch, and transition matrices with stationary and transition entropy.
Cluster scanpaths to identify strategies; compare within-design and between-design similarity with permutation tests.
Check whether critical sequences occur (e.g. warning AOI fixated before action AOI) and their frequency.
Link strategies to task outcomes such as errors or time.
outputs: Similarity matrices, strategy clusters, AOI transition matrices, entropy measures and critical sequence rates.
useWhen: Order of attention matters: warnings, comparison tables, forms, dashboards, reading of AI explanations.
avoidWhen: When only overall attention distribution matters, or eye-tracking quality is poor (e.g. low-end webcams).
whyLost: Commercial eye-tracking tools promoted heatmaps and gaze plots; sequence analysis requires custom scripting.
whereToUse: Checkout reviews, consent screens, financial statements, clinical dashboards, search results.
example: In a medication ordering screen, only 38% of scanpaths fixate the allergy banner before the confirm button. After moving the banner into the confirmation area, the figure rises to 87%.
sources: Noton & Stark, Scanpaths in eye movements during pattern perception (1971), Science
Cristino et al., ScanMatch: A novel method for comparing fixation sequences (2010), Behavior Research Methods
Holmqvist et al., Eye Tracking: A Comprehensive Guide to Methods and Measures (2011)
reference: Holmqvist, K., et al. (2011). Eye Tracking: A Comprehensive Guide to Methods and Measures. Oxford University Press.

name: Eyes-free control inventory
origin: Gill, in Dix et al. (2022)
summary: Count every control available in a critical context, classify each as operable by touch or dependent on vision, and compute the share usable without looking.
description: In contexts such as driving, operating machinery or using a device in the dark, controls that need visual attention are costly or dangerous. The inventory lists every control available in the critical context, classifies each as mostly physicality-oriented (findable and operable by touch, shape, position and detents) or mostly visually oriented (touchscreen items, menus, unlabelled flat buttons), totals each group and computes the percentage operable without much visual input. Looking for patterns, such as recent computer-mediated controls losing physicality, shows where design has drifted. The authors present it as a rough, illustrative audit; its value is in making an otherwise invisible trend measurable and comparable across products or model years.
steps: Define the critical context in which eyes-free use matters.
List every control available to the user in that context.
Classify each as physicality-oriented or visually oriented, using agreed criteria and two raters where possible.
Total each group and compute the share operable without visual input.
Look for patterns, such as which functions or recent controls lack physicality, and compare with competitors or earlier versions.
outputs: Counts and a percentage of eyes-free controls, with patterns and design implications.
useWhen: Evaluating cars, machinery, medical equipment or wearables where users must operate controls while attending elsewhere.
avoidWhen: Avoid when visual attention is freely available; it is rough and judgement-based, so for safety claims add task-based measures such as glance studies.
whyLost: It was proposed as an illustrative audit in a single book and has no standard classification rules.
whereToUse: Automotive interiors, cockpit and control room design, fitness wearables, kitchen appliances and accessibility reviews for blind users.
example: An e-bike display team audits 24 controls and finds only six can be operated by feel, all of them legacy buttons. They add tactile detents to the two most-used ride-mode functions and remeasure.
reference: Dix, A., Gill, S., Ramduny-Ellis, D. & Hare, J. (2022). TouchIT: Understanding Design in a Physical-Digital World. Oxford University Press, pp. 448-453.

name: Faceted Classification Analysis (Ranganathan)
origin: S. R. Ranganathan, 1933 (Colon Classification); Classification Research Group, UK, 1950s
summary: Decomposes a domain into mutually exclusive facets with ordered foci, using rigorous principles of division to build scalable classification and filtering schemes.
description: Ranganathan replaced single hierarchical trees with facets, independent dimensions combined at need. His fundamental categories PMEST (Personality, Matter, Energy, Space, Time) guide facet discovery, and his canons govern sound division: each facet must use one characteristic of division, foci must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and citation order must be consistent. The UK Classification Research Group extended facet analysis methodology. E-commerce filters are faceted classification renamed, usually built without these principles, producing overlapping filters, mixed characteristics and missing values. Facet analysis offers testable quality criteria for any filter or tagging system.
steps: Collect a representative sample of items and user queries from the domain.
Identify candidate characteristics of division and group terms into facets, using PMEST as a prompt.
Check each facet uses a single characteristic and that foci are mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive.
Define the citation order and the controlled terms for each focus, with scope notes.
Classify a sample of items independently with two indexers and measure agreement (e.g. kappa per facet).
Validate with users: facet usage logs, filter tasks, and zero-result rates.
outputs: A facet schema with defined foci, citation order, scope notes, inter-indexer agreement and validation results.
useWhen: Designing filters, metadata schemas, tagging systems or navigation for large heterogeneous collections.
avoidWhen: Small collections where a simple list or hierarchy suffices.
whyLost: Web IA adopted 'faceted navigation' as a UI pattern, leaving the library science principles behind.
whereToUse: E-commerce filters, content libraries, design system documentation, research repositories, data catalogues.
example: A furniture retailer's 'Style' filter mixes material ('oak'), era ('mid-century') and room ('bedroom'). Facet analysis splits these into three facets, and filter-use success rises while zero-result filter combinations fall.
sources: Ranganathan, Prolegomena to Library Classification (3rd ed., 1967)
Broughton, Faceted classification as a basis for knowledge organization in a digital environment (2006), New Review of Hypermedia and Multimedia
Hearst, Design recommendations for hierarchical faceted search interfaces (2006), SIGIR Workshop
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert, 2014)
reference: Ranganathan, S. R. (1967). Prolegomena to Library Classification. Asia Publishing House.

name: Facial Action Coding
origin: Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen, 1978 (building on Carl-Herman Hjortsjö, 1969)
summary: Codes visible facial muscle movements into anatomically defined action units, manually or automatically, to analyse expressive responses during interaction.
description: FACS describes facial movements as action units (AUs), each linked to specific muscles, such as AU4 (brow lowerer) or AU12 (lip corner puller). Certified coders score the onset, apex, offset and intensity of AUs frame by frame, producing an objective description of expression independent of emotional interpretation. Combinations can be mapped to emotion categories, though research by Barrett and others shows facial configurations do not reliably map to internal emotions across contexts and cultures. In UX, the descriptive layer is the robust part: AU4 and AU7, for example, often accompany concentration or confusion. Automated tools now detect AUs from video. Rigour comes from coding AUs rather than emotions, using certified coders or validated software with reliability checks, time-locking to events and triangulating with other data.
steps: Obtain consent and record face video with good frontal lighting at 25-30 fps or higher.
Time-stamp interaction events so expressions can be aligned with them.
Code action units manually with certified coders, or automatically with validated software, checking reliability on a sample.
Focus analysis on AUs relevant to the question (e.g. AU4 brow lowering for confusion) rather than inferred emotion labels.
Align AU occurrences with events and compare across conditions or participants.
Triangulate interpretations with think-aloud, self-report or other physiological measures.
outputs: Action unit timelines, event-aligned expression counts and intensities, triangulated interpretations.
useWhen: Studies of moment-to-moment reactions where self-report is unreliable, conversational agent design and media or advertising evaluation.
avoidWhen: Claims about specific internal emotions from faces alone, or settings where camera recording raises privacy concerns; use self-report and observation.
whyLost: Manual FACS coding requires certification and many hours per minute of video; automated tools promised a shortcut but raised validity and bias concerns.
whereToUse: Emotional UX research; affective computing; conversational agent design.
example: A lending app studied loan decision screens. AU coding showed brow lowering at the APR disclosure and AU12 smiles of relief at approval; confusion at APR was confirmed in interviews and the disclosure was rewritten.
sources: Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1978). Facial Action Coding System. Consulting Psychologists Press.

name: Facial Electromyography (fEMG)
origin: Psychophysiological emotion research; applied to games by Ravaja, Mandryk, Nacke and others; described by Lennart E. Nacke in chapter 16
summary: Surface electrodes over facial muscles record tiny activations that indicate positive or negative emotional valence during play or use.
description: Electromyography measures the electrical activity of muscles. In facial EMG, small silver-silver chloride electrodes are placed on the skin above specific muscles: the brow muscle (corrugator supercilii) is associated with negative emotion, the cheek muscle (zygomaticus major) with positive emotion, and the eye muscle (orbicularis oculi) helps register high-arousal pleasant emotion over longer stretches. Because electrodes pick up activation too slight to see, fEMG can reveal valence that players do not express or report, which complements electrodermal activity, a measure of arousal only. Nacke notes that fEMG has been used to index fun and flow in games. Its drawbacks are practical: large movements such as talking, laughing or chewing create artefacts, so think-aloud cannot be combined with it, and the signal needs careful processing (for example log normalisation or a low-pass filter) before interpretation. For UX researchers, fEMG is one of the few continuous measures of whether a moment felt pleasant or unpleasant, useful for content, media and emotionally loaded interactions.
steps: Define the events or segments whose emotional valence matters and plan event markers.
Clean the skin and place electrodes over the corrugator, zygomaticus and, if needed, orbicularis oculi muscles.
Record a resting baseline before the task.
Run the session without talking, chewing or think-aloud, logging event times.
Filter and normalise the signal and remove movement artefacts.
Compare muscle activity in event windows against baseline and between conditions, and interpret alongside self-report and arousal measures.
outputs: Time series of facial muscle activity and event-locked valence indicators per participant and condition.
useWhen: You need a continuous, non-verbal indicator of positive versus negative emotion during an experience.
avoidWhen: Participants must talk, the setting is uncontrolled, or you lack signal-processing skills.
whyLost: Requires lab equipment, skin preparation and signal processing, and camera-based facial coding is easier to deploy, so product teams rarely use it.
whereToUse: Games, media and advertising testing, VR, emotionally loaded health or finance interactions.
example: During a horror game level, corrugator activity rises at an intended jump scare but also during a confusing map screen, flagging an unintended negative moment.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 16 (Nacke).

name: FACS-Lite UX Protocol
origin: Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen, 1978 (Facial Action Coding System); simplified UX adaptation later
summary: Codes a small set of facial action units, such as brow-lowering and lip-corner pull, during usability sessions to locate moments of confusion, frustration and enjoyment.
description: The Facial Action Coding System decomposes any facial expression into anatomically defined action units (AUs). A full FACS certification takes around 100 hours, so the UX adaptation restricts coding to a handful of diagnostically useful units: AU4 (brow lowerer) for concentration or confusion, AU12 (lip-corner puller) for enjoyment, AU17 (chin raiser) and AU14 (dimpler) for doubt or frustration. Coders review video frame by frame around pre-identified task moments and align codes with screen-recording timestamps. Rigour comes from coding behaviour rather than inferring emotion, from two independent coders with kappa above 0.70, and from treating automated tools such as OpenFace or FaceReader as a first pass that must be validated against human coding rather than a ground truth.
steps: Core action units for UX: AU4+AU5 = confusion/concentration. AU12 = enjoyment. AU17+AU23 = frustration. AU1+2 = surprise.
Coding protocol: Frame-by-frame review at task difficulty moments. Code AU presence/absence. Intensity A (trace) through E (maximum).
IRR: Two independent FACS coders. Calculate κ. Minimum κ > 0.70 before proceeding.
Map to interface events: Align FACS codes with screen recording timestamps. Interface events preceding frustration expressions = usability problem indicators.
Automated fallback: OpenFace or FaceReader as first-pass tool. Validate automatically on 20% sample.
outputs: Time-stamped AU codes per participant, inter-rater agreement statistics, event-locked expression timelines, and a list of interface moments with high confusion or frustration signatures.
useWhen: You need behavioural evidence of affect that does not rely on self-report, particularly when participants are polite, culturally reticent or unaware of their reactions, and you already record face video.
avoidWhen: Video quality is poor, participants are masked or off-camera, or you plan to infer discrete emotions from single AUs. For cheaper affective evidence use Think-Aloud with Emotional Annotation or post-task self-report.
whyLost: Full FACS is costly to learn, automated emotion recognition was oversold and then criticised for weak validity, and many teams abandoned facial coding altogether rather than adopting a disciplined subset.
whereToUse: Moderated and remote usability tests with webcams, evaluating error messages and decision points, game playtesting, and checking whether 'delight' moments actually produce enjoyment signals.
example: During remote tests of a lending app, two coders code AU4 and AU12 in the 20 seconds around loan approval. AU4 dominates at the repayment schedule while AU12 appears only after a reassuring confirmation, so the team moves the reassurance earlier.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 38 — FACS, Micro-Expression Analysis & Psychophysiology
reference: Ekman, P. & Friesen, W. V. (1978). Facial Action Coding System. Consulting Psychologists Press.

name: Factor rotation (Varimax vs. Oblimin)
origin: Henry Kaiser, 1958 (Varimax); Jennrich and Sampson, 1966 and Carroll, 1953 (direct oblimin family)
summary: Choosing between orthogonal (Varimax) and oblique (Oblimin, Promax) rotation so that the factor structure of UX constructs reflects whether they are correlated.
description: Rotation redistributes variance among retained factors to approach simple structure, where each item loads strongly on one factor. Varimax keeps factors uncorrelated; Oblimin and Promax allow them to correlate. Most UX constructs (usefulness, ease, trust, satisfaction) are correlated, so forcing orthogonality distorts loadings and inflates cross-loadings. Methodologists recommend starting with an oblique rotation: if factor correlations are all below about 0.32 (roughly 10% shared variance; Tabachnick and Fidell), an orthogonal solution is defensible. With oblique rotation, the pattern matrix (unique contributions) is interpreted for item assignment and the structure matrix (correlations) as a check. Rigour comes from justifying the choice and reporting the factor correlation matrix.
steps: Fit the EFA with an oblique rotation (Oblimin with delta 0, or Promax with kappa 4) as the default.
Inspect the factor correlation matrix.
If all factor correlations are below about 0.32, consider re-running with Varimax for simplicity and compare.
With oblique solutions, assign items using the pattern matrix and check the structure matrix for consistency.
Report the rotation method, its parameters and the factor correlation matrix.
outputs: A rotated loading matrix (pattern and structure where oblique), a factor correlation matrix and justification for the rotation.
useWhen: Every EFA of UX attitude or experience items, especially where constructs are theoretically related.
avoidWhen: Rotation is irrelevant with a single factor; for testing hypothesised structures use CFA, where correlations are estimated directly.
whyLost: Varimax is the SPSS default and is widely taught, so oblique rotation remains the specialist's choice.
whereToUse: Scale development in UX, trust and AI acceptance research and customer experience measurement.
example: Varimax on a 15-item SaaS experience survey gives messy cross-loadings. Oblimin reveals three factors correlated at 0.45-0.60 with clean pattern loadings, confirming the constructs are distinct but related.
sources: RELIABILITY procedures; syntax automation; parallel analysis via Python plugin
Kaiser, H. F. (1958) The varimax criterion for analytic rotation in factor analysis. Psychometrika
Tabachnick, B. G. & Fidell, L. S. (2019) Using Multivariate Statistics, 7th ed.
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C7 — SPSS for Survey Analysis — EFA, Reliability & Scale Validation
Quantitative User Experience Research (Chris Chapman & Kerry Rodden)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 50 — Factor Analysis — Discovering the Latent Structure of Experience
reference: Kaiser, H. F. (1958) The varimax criterion for analytic rotation in factor analysis. Psychometrika 23(3)

name: Factor Score Estimation, Indeterminacy and Extension Analysis
origin: L. L. Thurstone (regression method); indeterminacy debated by McDonald and Mulaik, 1979; texts by Harman (1976) and Gorsuch (1983)
summary: Estimates each respondent's score on factors from a factor solution, checks how determinate those scores are, and extends the solution to new variables without refactoring.
description: Factor scores cannot be computed exactly, only estimated. The robust simple option is to sum the variables that load highly on a factor with equal weights. The most common method, Thurstone's regression approach, treats each factor as a criterion to predict: the weights are the inverse of the item correlation matrix times the factor structure matrix, applied to standardised item scores. Estimated scores correlate more strongly with each other than the factors do (for example .67 against .50), which matters if they feed later analyses. The deeper issue is indeterminacy: a given solution is consistent with a range of possible factors, nearly identical when communalities are high but potentially even uncorrelated when they are low. Extension analysis correlates estimated factor scores (or uses a shortcut with the weights) with variables that were not in the analysis, giving their loadings on the existing factors without disturbing the original solution.
steps: Obtain a factor solution with pattern matrix, structure matrix and factor correlations from EFA or CFA.
Compute regression weights as the inverse item correlation matrix times the structure matrix (or choose unit weights on salient items, or Bartlett scores if unbiasedness matters).
Apply the weights to standardised item responses to obtain each respondent's estimated factor scores.

Check determinacy: compare intercorrelations of the estimated scores with the factor correlations, and inspect communalities or determinacy coefficients; treat scores from low-communality factors with caution.
For extension, multiply the correlations of new variables with the original items by the rescaled weights to get their structure loadings, then convert to pattern loadings.
Use the scores in segmentation or regression only with their estimation error acknowledged, or move to SEM to keep the factors latent.
outputs: Estimated factor scores per respondent, factor score weights, determinacy evidence, and loadings of new variables on existing factors.
useWhen: You need per-person scores from a factor analysis of a UX questionnaire to segment users, track individuals, or feed regression, or you want to place new items or metrics on an established factor structure.
avoidWhen: Unit-weighted scale scores are good enough (use scale scoring); the analysis can stay inside SEM, which avoids indeterminacy; communalities are low, so the scores are ambiguous. Do not treat estimated scores as error-free measurements.
whyLost: Analysts click 'save factor scores' in statistics software without knowing the method used or the indeterminacy problem, and textbooks for UX rarely discuss it.
whereToUse: Attitudinal segmentation from survey factor analyses; per-user construct scores joined to behavioural data; adding new questions or log metrics to an established questionnaire structure.
example: A streaming service factor-analyses a 24-item satisfaction survey into content, reliability and value factors and saves regression scores for clustering. The value factor has low communalities and its scores correlate .81 with reliability scores against a factor correlation of .55, so the team uses unit-weighted scores for value instead.
sources: Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
reference: Loehlin, J. C., & Beaujean, A. A. (2017). Latent Variable Models: An Introduction to Factor, Path, and Structural Equation Analysis (5th ed.). New York: Routledge.

name: Factor-analytic and correspondence-analytic persona development
aka: Factor-analytic persona development from information-need ratings
Factor-analytic persona development from service rating surveys
Multiple correspondence analysis for persona segmentation
donor: Individual-differences psychology, psychometrics and multivariate statistics
origin: Rashmi Sinha (CHI 2003); extended by Kim and Wiggins (2016) and, with multiple correspondence analysis, Laporte, Slegers and De Grooff (2012)
summary: Builds personas from dimension reduction of user survey data, using component loadings or correspondence-analysis clusters as the statistical core of each archetype.
description: Sinha argued that persona practice favours precision (rich detail) over accuracy (representative users). Her remedy surveys users on the importance of many dimensions of a domain, runs principal components analysis, and gives designers the rotated loadings as the motivational core of each persona; demographics flesh them out and targeted interviews verify them. Kim and Wiggins applied the same logic to service importance ratings, assigning each respondent to a factor by factor score and cross-tabulating with demographics. Where data are categorical or coded from open answers, multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) replaces PCA: cases, variables and categories are plotted in one space, discrimination measures show which variables drive each dimension, and visible clusters of cases become segment hypotheses, with demographics projected as supplementary variables. In every variant the statistics propose segments; designers and further qualitative research turn them into personas.
steps: List the dimensions of the domain (Sinha used 32 for a restaurant finder) from competitor review and a few exploratory interviews, and add demographic and behaviour items.
Field the questionnaire with importance or satisfaction ratings on a 5-point scale, aiming for about ten responses per variable (Sinha had 63 respondents, Kim and Wiggins 435).
Check factorability with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure and Bartlett's test of sphericity; for nominal or coded data, build a cases-by-categories matrix for MCA instead.

Extract components and compare four- to seven-component solutions with varimax or equamax rotation, keeping the most interpretable (Sinha kept five explaining 53% of variance); for MCA choose dimensions from inertia and Cronbach's alpha.
Save component scores or MCA object scores, assign each respondent to their highest-scoring component or visible cluster, and cross-tabulate with demographics.
Give designers the loadings or discrimination measures with a short explanation; they build each persona around primary and secondary motivations, merging components that are not distinct.
Test stability by removing outlier clusters or re-running with different variable sets, and watch for implausible clusters that signal coding errors or social-desirability bias.
Recruit high scorers on each component for interviews and observation to verify and enrich the personas.
outputs: Rotated components or MCA dimensions with loadings, per-respondent scores and segment membership, and a cast of personas grounded in those statistics.
useWhen: Information-rich or service-rich domains where personas should reflect different patterns of need, and a survey of a few hundred users is feasible; when stakeholders challenge persona representativeness.
avoidWhen: Small samples (below about ten per variable), data without factorable structure, or when behaviour logs are available (use clustering or latent class analysis on behaviour). It complements interviews and observation; it does not replace them. If types may not exist at all, run a taxometric check first.
whyLost: Persona practice moved towards qualitative synthesis and later towards behavioural clustering, and few design teams have the factor-analytic skills; the CHI 2003 short paper was cited more than it was applied.
whereToUse: Library and public-service portals, content-heavy products, marketplaces, B2B tools with many feature areas, children's or accessibility research where data are categorical.
example: A travel-booking site surveys 400 users on the importance of 30 trip attributes. PCA gives five components, such as 'flexibility and cancellation' and 'loyalty points'. Designers merge two weak components and write four personas, then interview the top scorers on each component to add context.
sources: A Factor Analysis Approach to Persona Development using Survey Data (Kim & Wiggins, 2016)
Using Correspondence Analysis to Monitor the Persona Segmentation Process (Laporte et al., 2012)
reference: Sinha, R. (2003). Persona development for information-rich domains. In CHI '03 Extended Abstracts on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 830-831). ACM.

name: Fake door, painted door and smoke tests
origin: Lean startup practice (Ries, Blank); described by Klein (2013), Croll and Yoskovitz (2013), Sharon (2016), Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020)
summary: Present an entry point, offer or landing page for something not yet built, count how many exposed people act on it, and compare with a preset threshold.
description: These tests estimate demand from behaviour rather than prediction. Forms vary by where the door sits: a landing page or crowdfunding page with a buy, pre-order or sign-up action reached by targeted ads (smoke test); an in-product button, menu item or field that leads to a 'coming soon' note (painted door or feature stub); or a static upgrade page with price and benefits, A/B tested across prices or messages. The metric is actions over exposures, judged against a threshold set before launch. Randomising exposure turns it into a controlled experiment that can also reveal harm: an inert coupon field at checkout reduced revenue by sending users off to hunt for codes. A click is intent, not purchase; asking for real commitment (pre-order, payment) is stronger. Ethics matter: keep exposure small, be honest with clickers and avoid harmful versions.
