steps: State the demand hypothesis and, before launch, the ratio of actions to exposures that will trigger building (or pivoting).
Choose the door: a landing or pre-order page reached by targeted ads, an in-product button or menu item, or a static price page.
Build the smallest credible entry point where users would expect it, plus an honest 'not available yet' message; for landing pages make the design credible.
Expose a known, small number of target users, ideally randomised against a control that does not see the door so the overall evaluation criterion can be compared.
Log exposures, clicks and flow progress; optionally ask a few questions at the start of the flow or A/B test prices and benefit wording.
Thank, apologise to and if possible compensate people who clicked; call sign-ups to learn what they thought was promised.
Compare the rate with the threshold and decide to build, pivot or drop, remembering that a click measures intent, not use or payment.
outputs: Interest ratio (actions over exposures) per offer, message or price, any effect of the door on the key metric, and a list of interested people to interview.
useWhen: Deciding whether to build a feature or product, which version or price to build first, or whether the mere presence of a feature changes behaviour.
avoidWhen: When traffic is not from the target market, when building would be nearly as quick as faking, or when a dead end could cause harm or serious frustration; use interviews, concierge MVPs or prototypes instead.
whyLost: It survives and is widely practised because it is cheap, behavioural and fits product analytics tooling.
whereToUse: Feature prioritisation in SaaS, new product lines in e-commerce, pricing tiers, premium upgrades and new app launches.
example: A grocery website adds a 'Download our shopping app' button for 5% of visitors with a coming-soon message. Clicks reach 3% of exposed users against a preset 2% threshold, so the team commissions the app and emails clickers a discount at launch.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Klein, L. (2013). UX for Lean Startups. O'Reilly Media; Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press.

name: Fast-Mapping Test of Incidental Label Learning
origin: Carey and Bartlett (1978); Markson and Bloom (1997)
summary: Introduce a new term incidentally during a task, without teaching it, then test after a delay what people retained about its form and meaning.
description: Fast mapping is the ability to form a partial meaning for a new word from minimal, incidental exposure. Carey and Bartlett introduced an unfamiliar colour word to children only by contrast with a known one ('the chromium tray, not the blue one'); a week later most remembered something about it, such as that it named a colour, and later work found retention for at least a month. Research varies number of exposures, spacing, context, word class and incidental versus direct teaching; distributed exposures across days beat the same number massed in one day, and learners use social, environmental and grammatical cues. For UX, the paradigm tests feature-name and icon-label learnability: whether users who meet a new product term in passing during normal use retain what it means, which is how most product vocabulary is actually learned.
steps: Choose the unfamiliar target terms, for example new feature names.
Embed each in an ordinary task, contrasting it with a known term where possible, without defining it.
Vary exposure count, spacing or context across conditions if those are the question.
After a delay of a week or more, test recognition of the term and what it means, scoring partial knowledge.
Compare retention across terms and conditions and choose or support the terms that stick.
outputs: Partial-knowledge retention scores by term, delay and exposure condition.
useWhen: Choosing or supporting new product vocabulary that users will meet in passing rather than through training, and comparing how well candidate names are retained.
avoidWhen: Avoid when users will be taught terms directly; test with a learning test instead. For choosing among names use Terminology Voting, and for immediate label comprehension use Labelling system analysis or first-click tests.
whyLost: It is a developmental psychology paradigm; UX tests label comprehension once, not incidental retention over time.
whereToUse: Feature naming in SaaS and consumer apps, financial and health terminology, onboarding without tutorials, AI capability names.
example: A fitness app introduces 'Strain' and 'Readiness' in passing on the dashboard. After one week, 70 per cent of testers can say what Readiness means but only 30 per cent know Strain, so Strain gets an inline explanation on first appearance.
reference: Carey, S. and Bartlett, E. (1978). Acquiring a single new word. Papers and Reports on Child Language Development, 15, 17-29.

name: Fault Tree Analysis
origin: H. A. Watson, Bell Laboratories, 1961-62 (Minuteman missile); NUREG-0492 Fault Tree Handbook, 1981
summary: A top-down Boolean logic diagram that decomposes an undesired outcome into combinations of basic events, revealing minimal cut sets and single points of failure.
description: Fault tree analysis starts from a precisely defined top event, such as 'user sends payment to wrong account', and asks what immediate events, combined through AND or OR gates, could cause it. Each branch is decomposed until reaching basic events: user errors, software faults, missing data, environmental conditions. Boolean reduction gives minimal cut sets, the smallest combinations of events sufficient to cause the top event; a cut set of size one is a single point of failure. With probabilities attached, the tree yields a quantitative top-event probability and importance measures. For UX it disciplines causal thinking: it distinguishes conditions that must co-occur from alternatives, and shows exactly where an interface safeguard breaks a chain.
steps: Define the top event precisely, including scope and system boundary.
Identify immediate causes and connect them with AND or OR gates, distinguishing user actions, system states and external conditions.
Decompose recursively until reaching basic events that can be observed or estimated.
Compute minimal cut sets by Boolean reduction, by hand or with FTA software.
Optionally assign probabilities from logs or HRA methods and compute top-event probability and Fussell-Vesely importance.
Target design changes at single-event cut sets first and verify that each change adds an AND condition the user must satisfy.
outputs: Fault tree diagram, list of minimal cut sets, single points of failure, optional top-event probability and importance ranking.
useWhen: Investigating or preventing a specific severe outcome with multiple contributing causes, including incidents reported by users.
avoidWhen: Exploring unknown problems with no defined top event; use contextual inquiry or HAZOP to find hazards first.
whyLost: FTA is taught in reliability engineering and rarely in design. UX root-cause discussions tend to be narrative rather than Boolean.
whereToUse: Payment errors, data loss incidents, privacy leaks, AI agent misactions, medication errors.
example: A healthcare messaging app investigates messages sent to the wrong patient. The fault tree reveals a cut set of two: autocomplete selecting a similarly named patient AND no patient photo shown on send. Adding the photo converts a two-event cut set into three.
sources: Vesely et al., Fault Tree Handbook (NUREG-0492, 1981)
Ericson, Hazard Analysis Techniques for System Safety (2005)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Vesely, W. E., et al. (1981). Fault Tree Handbook, NUREG-0492. US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

name: Feature Prioritisation Exercises with Users
origin: Described by Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed (2012); Value Mapping credited to Sarah Rink in Gray, Brown and Macanufo (2010)
summary: Users sort, choose or 'buy' from a set of feature cards under constraint, and choice counts or coded scores rank features by value and expected use.
description: These exercises turn feature preference into a constrained choice. In the card sort form, participants sort feature cards into four piles from most valuable to not valuable, then re-sort the most valuable pile by expected frequency of use; each card is coded 0-5 (0 not valuable, 1 least, 2 somewhat, 3 most valuable rarely used, 4 sometimes used, 5 used often), the median across participants gives rank and the standard deviation breaks ties, lower meaning more agreement. This separates immediate interest from likely usefulness. In Value Mapping, features are grouped in a table and each participant chooses about a third of them, or spends an imaginary budget such as 100 pounds; the table is coloured by how often each card was chosen, producing a heat map of interest. Both force trade-offs that rating scales do not.
steps: Write current and potential features on cards, grouped in a way that makes sense to participants.
Card sort form: ask participants to sort cards into four piles from most valuable to not valuable, then re-sort the most valuable pile by expected frequency of use.
Code each card 0-5, compute each card's median across participants and use the standard deviation to break ties.
Value Mapping form: ask each participant to choose about one card in three, or to spend a fixed imaginary budget across features.
Record each participant's choices and colour the feature table by how often each card was chosen, leaving never-chosen cards blank.
Rank features by preference and agreement, and discuss surprises with participants or stakeholders before using the order for planning.
outputs: A ranked feature list with agreement measures, or a colour-graded matrix of feature interest across groups.
useWhen: Roadmap and scope discussions where you need users' (or stakeholders') relative valuation of a set of features, and to settle internal disputes with evidence.
avoidWhen: When samples are small and you treat results as precise (medians are fragile; treat as directional), or when users cannot judge unfamiliar features. For statistically robust trade-offs use MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) or Conjoint Analysis; for problem rather than feature priority use Customer Problem Stack Ranking (CPSR).
whyLost: Constrained-choice exercises such as buy-a-feature remain common in workshops, which is why they survive, though coding and agreement analysis are often skipped.
whereToUse: SaaS roadmaps, internal tools, public service redesigns, stakeholder alignment workshops.
example: A banking app team gives 15 customers 30 feature cards and asks each to pick ten; the heat map shows almost no interest in social features but strong, consistent demand for bill splitting, which moves up the roadmap.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. and Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, p. 206; Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010). Gamestorming. O'Reilly Media.

name: Feature subset and stepwise selection
aka: Forward stepwise regression with a Bonferroni p-to-enter
origin: Classical regression practice (Mallows' Cp, Akaike's AIC, Schwarz's BIC); Liu and Motoda filter and wrapper methods
summary: Choose a smaller set of predictors by exhaustive, stepwise or filter search, judging subsets on held-out error or information criteria rather than training fit.
description: Subset selection reduces many candidate predictors to a smaller set for accuracy and interpretability. Best subset selection fits every model of each size and keeps the best by RSS or deviance, then chooses among sizes by cross-validation, Cp/AIC, BIC or adjusted R squared, never training RSS, which always falls as predictors are added. It is infeasible above about 40 predictors (over a million models at p = 20). Forward stepwise adds the most useful predictor each step (211 fits at p = 20) and works when n < p; backward needs n > p. Stepwise is greedy and may miss the best model. Machine-learning variants separate filters (distance, information, dependency, consistency measures, as in the Las Vegas filter) from wrappers (learner accuracy). Foster and Stine recommend a Bonferroni p-to-enter of 0.05/m. P-values from the selected model carry selection bias.
steps: Define the outcome and candidate predictors, discretising continuous inputs if using consistency filters.
Choose a search: best subset (up to about 40 predictors), forward, backward or random.
Choose an evaluation: a filter measure, or wrapper accuracy; for stepwise regression set p-to-enter at 0.05 divided by the number of candidates.
For each model size, keep the best model by training fit.
Estimate test error for each size by k-fold cross-validation, Cp/AIC, BIC or adjusted R squared.
Pick the size with the lowest estimate, or the smallest within one standard error of it, and refit.
Validate the chosen subset on held-out data and review it with domain experts; do not report naive p-values.
outputs: A sequence of best models by size, an error-versus-size curve, a selected predictor set, and its validated performance.
useWhen: You must reduce many behavioural, survey or product variables to an interpretable driver set, for example for key driver analysis or churn prediction.
avoidWhen: Predictors are many and correlated; prefer lasso or other shrinkage. Do not use for causal claims or report post-selection p-values. Information criteria fail when predictors outnumber cases.
whyLost: Stepwise regression survives in survey and driver analysis tools but usually without cross-validation or correction, so its rigour has been hollowed out.
whereToUse: Key driver analysis of satisfaction, churn and conversion models, survey item reduction, feature prioritisation analytics.
example: A subscription service has 60 candidate behavioural predictors of churn. Forward selection with 10-fold cross-validation and the one-standard-error rule keeps seven, which are reviewed with product managers before the model drives retention research.
sources: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
Regression and Key Driver Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, 2021)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Taylor, J. (2023). An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python, section 6.1. Springer; Liu, H., Yu, L., & Motoda, H. (2003). Feature extraction, selection, and construction. In The Handbook of Data Mining.

name: Feature-removal and latency-injection tests
donor: Online experimentation; human factors and performance engineering
origin: HCI response-time research (Miller, 1968; Galletta et al., 2006); Schurman and Brutlag (2009); Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020)
summary: Before optimising something, deliberately remove a feature or degrade a variable such as speed in a controlled test to learn how much it matters.
description: Improving a feature or making a system faster is costly; removing or slowing it is cheap. 'Experiment 0' asks what experiment should come before the planned one. Removing an existing feature shows whether it has value (Skyscanner deleted a flight ticker that moved no metric; Static Pixels removed a pre-authorisation step and transactions doubled). Latency injection adds a constant delay to treatment to estimate what a speed-up would be worth: assume local linearity and verify it with at least two delays (Bing used 100 and 250 ms; the larger gave about 2.5 times the effect), insert the delay where it mimics server slowness, and delay specific regions to learn where speed matters. The HCI tradition varies system response time in the lab, measuring task time, errors, strategy shifts, stress and satisfaction to find an appropriate pace for a task and user group.
steps: Before the first planned optimisation experiment, ask which experiment should precede it: removal, painted door or degradation.
For removal, instrument the feature, remove it for a randomised group and keep measuring engagement and the key metric; interpret protests from existing users and requests from new cohorts.
For latency, choose delay points that mimic real server slowness and run at least two delay levels (for example 100 and 250 ms) to check linearity.
Measure the overall evaluation criterion plus perceived-performance metrics (time to first result, above-the-fold time, Speed Index, time to successful click).
In lab studies, define response time and think time, randomise or counterbalance delay conditions, and measure task time, errors, strategy change and satisfaction for representative tasks.
Estimate value per millisecond or per feature, extrapolate cautiously to plausible speed-ups, and decide whether to invest, delete or deprioritise.
outputs: A go or no-go on investing in an area, features safe to delete, value of performance per unit time, and curves of performance and satisfaction against delay.
useWhen: Prioritising performance engineering, deciding whether to keep or optimise an existing feature, or setting response-time targets for a task.
avoidWhen: When degradation would seriously harm users or revenue beyond brief exposure, or when tests are underpowered (a null is not evidence that speed is irrelevant); use observational correlations with caution or lab studies instead.
whyLost: Teams are reluctant to make products deliberately worse, and the HCI response-time literature lost visibility as hardware got faster.
whereToUse: Web and app performance budgets, feature pruning in mature SaaS products, AI products where model latency trades against quality.
example: An AI search product debates investing in a faster model. Injecting 250 ms and 500 ms delays for 2% of users shows query success falls linearly at about 0.3% per 100 ms, which justifies the engineering work.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press; Galletta, D. F., Henry, R., McCoy, S. and Polak, P. (2006). When the wait isn't so bad. Information Systems Research, 17(1), 20-37.

name: Feminist Research Methods
origin: Feminist methodology from the 1970s to 1980s (Ann Oakley, 1981; Sandra Harding, 1987; Dorothy Smith)
summary: A set of epistemological commitments, including standpoint, relational ethics, attention to power and accountability, that reshape how research is designed, conducted and reported.
description: Feminist research methodology is not a single method but a set of epistemological commitments that reshape how research is designed, conducted, and reported: (1) the personal is political — research questions, findings, and who benefits from them are inherently political; (2) the researcher's positionality is always relevant and must be explicitly accounted for; (3) the research relationship involves a power differential that must be acknowledged and actively managed; (4) research should produce knowledge that is useful to those studied, not merely about them. These commitments transform every aspect of research design, from question formulation to participant consent to findings presentation.
steps: Standpoint epistemology: Acknowledge that knowledge is always produced from a standpoint. Your standpoint as a researcher shapes what questions you ask, what you notice, and what you report. Make this explicit.

Relational ethics: The researcher-participant relationship is a human relationship with ethical obligations. Reciprocity, respect, and accountability to participants are not optional extras — they are methodological requirements.

Avoiding epistemic violence: Epistemic violence occurs when a researcher's framework overrides and invalidates participants' own ways of knowing. Actively guard against imposing your categories on participants who use different ones.

Research for vs. research on: Feminist methodology asks: who benefits from this research? Design studies so that participants are not merely data sources but contributors who gain something from participation.

Accountability in reporting: Present findings in a way that is accountable to participants. Before publishing, consider: could this account harm the people whose experience generated it? Have you represented their perspective fairly?
outputs: A positionality statement, research design choices that address power, relational and accountability practices, findings reported with participants' perspectives centred, and impact commitments.
useWhen: Research involves marginalised groups, gendered or power-laden experiences (safety, health, money, care work), or products whose harms fall unevenly across users.
avoidWhen: It is a stance rather than a technique, so pair it with concrete methods. Do not adopt it as a label without changing practice; for participation-focused work, see Participatory Design.
whyLost: Commercial UX frames research as neutral and business-led, and explicit discussion of power and standpoint is often seen as political, so it remained in academia.
whereToUse: Femtech and reproductive health, online safety and harassment, domestic abuse-aware design, caregiving and gig-work platforms, and inclusive AI.
example: Designing location-sharing features, a team interviews survivors of domestic abuse with support-service partners, lets participants shape questions, and reports findings back to them first, revealing abuse vectors the original spec missed.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Harding, S. (ed.) (1987). Feminism and Methodology. Indiana University Press.

name: Fermi Estimation
origin: Enrico Fermi's teaching practice (1940s); popularised in Weinstein and Adam's Guesstimation (2008)
summary: Decomposes an unknown quantity into estimable factors, bounding each, to reach an order-of-magnitude answer and identify which assumptions matter most.
description: Fermi famously estimated the yield of the Trinity test by dropping paper scraps. Fermi estimation breaks a question ('how many users will hit this error each month?') into factors (users per month x proportion using feature x error probability per use x uses per user) and estimates each with plausible ranges. Errors in independent factors tend to partially cancel, giving surprisingly good order-of-magnitude answers. Extending with ranges and Monte Carlo simulation produces distributions and shows which factor dominates uncertainty, guiding research priorities. It disciplines UX sizing claims and opportunity estimates.
steps: State the quantity precisely, with units and time frame.
Decompose it into multiplicative or additive factors that are easier to estimate.
Estimate each factor as a range (e.g. 90% interval) from data, research or reasoning.
Combine point estimates for a quick answer, then simulate ranges with Monte Carlo for a distribution.
Identify the factors contributing most to uncertainty (sensitivity analysis).
Measure or research the dominant factors if the decision depends on them.
outputs: An order-of-magnitude estimate with a distribution, explicit assumptions and key uncertainty drivers.
useWhen: Sizing problems or opportunities quickly, sanity-checking claims, or prioritising what to measure.
avoidWhen: When precise measurement is cheap and available.
whyLost: UX research favours qualitative storytelling and rarely sizes problems numerically.
whereToUse: Opportunity sizing, problem prevalence estimates, research prioritisation, accessibility impact estimates.
example: Asked whether a rare error matters, a researcher estimates 2M monthly users x 15% using export x 3 exports each x 0.4% error rate, about 3,600 failures a month, enough to justify a fix.
sources: Weinstein & Adam, Guesstimation: Solving the World's Problems on the Back of a Cocktail Napkin (2008)
Hubbard, How to Measure Anything (3rd ed., 2014)
reference: Weinstein, L., & Adam, J. A. (2008). Guesstimation. Princeton University Press.

name: Fictional Inquiry
origin: Christian Dindler and Ole Sejer Iversen, 2007; rationale from Ricoeur
summary: Draws participants into a partly fictional narrative so they can imagine possibilities beyond their experience and answer questions that would feel odd in a normal interview.
description: Fictional inquiry builds a shared narrative space that temporarily suspends the conventions and structures of everyday life. Participants are drawn into a partly fictional frame, supported by props, in which characters can ask naive or strange questions and participants can play with possibilities that breach convention. In the original example schoolchildren were told that Martians were researching life on Earth, shown pretend messages and spacecraft images, and talked to the Martians over an audio link about their schoolbags. The fiction made it natural to explain the obvious and to imagine alternatives. Designers then extract themes with lightweight thematic analysis and use them as points of further inquiry. Its strength is reaching beyond participants' experiential horizon while staying anchored in their real practices.
steps: Choose the practice to be explored and design a fictional frame in which outsiders need it explained (for example visiting aliens or a future archive).
Make supporting props such as messages, images, costumes or an audio channel to make the fiction believable.
Draw participants into the fiction and let characters ask questions about their current practice and wishes.
Invite participants to propose changes within the fiction, where conventional constraints do not apply.
Record sessions and extract themes with lightweight thematic analysis.
Use the themes as starting points for further inquiry and concept development with the same participants.
outputs: Themes and design directions that extend beyond participants' habitual horizons.
useWhen: When participants (especially children) cannot easily articulate tacit practices or imagine alternatives in a conventional interview.
avoidWhen: When you need participants deeply involved in later design decisions; the technique stops short of that. Pair with Co-design Workshops or PICTIVE Participatory Prototyping for deeper involvement.
whyLost: It is known in the Scandinavian participatory design community but needs props and staging that few product teams invest in.
whereToUse: Children's products, education technology, workplace tools where practices are taken for granted, future concepts.
example: An edtech team frames sessions as a 'museum of 2080' curator who has never seen homework, and pupils explain and redesign their homework routines, revealing that parents act as hidden schedulers.
reference: Dindler, C. and Iversen, O. S. (2007). Fictional Inquiry: design collaboration in a shared narrative space. CoDesign, 3(4), 213-234.

name: Field Studies
origin: Field observation tradition in social science; applied to HCI from the 1980s
summary: Systematic observation and data collection in users' natural environments, including shadowing, site visits and work observation, to understand use in real context.
description: Field studies cover the family of methods conducted where people actually live and work, rather than in a lab. They include ethnographic observation, contextual inquiry, shadowing, site visits, fly-on-the-wall observation and in-situ interviews. Their value lies in revealing environmental constraints, interruptions, collaboration, physical artefacts and workarounds that shape use and are invisible in remote sessions. Rigour comes from a clear observation focus, structured note-taking that separates observation from interpretation, sampling across sites, roles and times of day, ethical consent for bystanders, prompt write-up, and triangulation of observation with interviews and artefacts. Observer effects must be acknowledged and reduced through longer or repeated visits.
steps: Define research questions and the settings, roles and times to sample.
Negotiate site access and consent, including for bystanders where relevant.
Prepare an observation guide and note-taking template that separates observation from interpretation.
Conduct visits of a half day or more, shadowing participants and asking questions at natural breaks.
Photograph environments and artefacts where permitted.
Write up notes within 24 hours and hold team debriefs.
Synthesise across sites, for example through affinity diagramming or work models.
outputs: Field notes, photographs, artefact collections, environment and workflow descriptions, and synthesised insights.
useWhen: For products embedded in physical or complex work environments, such as healthcare, industrial, retail or logistics settings.
avoidWhen: Avoid when environments are inaccessible or questions are narrow interface issues; use remote interviews, diaries or usability testing.
whyLost: It survives in service design and enterprise research, though often shortened to a couple of hours and without systematic time logging.
whereToUse: Healthcare; industrial design; enterprise workflows; any embedded-use product.
example: A field-service app team shadows technicians for two days each across five depots. They see technicians working with gloves in poor signal areas, leading to offline mode and larger touch targets.
sources: Shadowing and Other Techniques for Doing Fieldwork in Modern Societies (Czarniawska)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The Power of Data Triangulation (Chang & Classen, 2024)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. & Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Field Usability Testing
origin: Usability practice; described by Rosenbaum and Kantner, 2007, and reviewed by Morten Hertzum, 2020
summary: Users perform test tasks with a prototype or product in their own setting, trading lab control for validity and coverage of context-of-use problems.
description: In field tests users still solve tasks, but in their workplace, home or public setting among other people going about normal activities. This exposes far more aspects of mobile use and of cultural and organisational usability, improving coverage and validity, at the cost of control, robustness and logistics. In one study only 31% of 77 problems found concerned the product itself; the rest concerned context such as interfaced systems, environment, documentation and training. Preparation includes learning the site, planning observation and sometimes migrating the prototype to users' equipment. Think-aloud is often impossible in social settings, so evaluators interject occasional questions, rely on observation and post-task questions, or run retrospective think-aloud cued by screen recordings. Bystanders may make video consent impossible, and problem frequency is a weaker severity indicator than in the lab.
steps: Visit and learn the site, and plan how observation and recording will work.
Migrate the prototype to users' equipment if needed and check it works in place.
Give tasks, often open-ended, in the live setting.
Observe, interjecting occasional questions instead of continuous think-aloud.
Record the screen and avoid video of bystanders who have not consented.
Optionally hold a retrospective think-aloud cued by the screen recording.
Analyse product and context problems separately, treating frequency-based severity with care.
outputs: Product problems plus context-of-use problems (environment, interfaced systems, training, documentation).
useWhen: Mobile products, workplace systems embedded in other tools, and cultural or organisational settings that a lab cannot reproduce; exploring use of new features.
avoidWhen: When precise comparison or timing is needed (use lab Usability Testing) or when privacy and consent in the setting cannot be managed.
whyLost: It survived because mobile and enterprise products made context impossible to ignore, and remote tools lowered its cost.
whereToUse: Clinical systems on wards, retail point of sale, field service apps, logistics and mobile banking.
example: A field test of a warehouse picking app finds that gloves and scanner glare, not the interface, cause most errors. The team adds larger targets and a high-contrast mode.
reference: Hertzum, M. (2020) Usability Testing: A Practitioner's Guide to Evaluating the User Experience. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool.

name: Figure-Ground Audit
donor: Gestalt psychology, Escher and mathematical logic
origin: Adapted for UX from chapter III (Figure and Ground) of Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), which uses Escher's tilings to argue that the ground of a figure can carry as much information as the figure itself
summary: Study what an interface, a dataset or a research plan leaves out as deliberately as what it shows, because the absences have a shape of their own.
description: Hofstadter uses Escher's tessellations, where birds and fish define each other's outlines, to make a logical point: sometimes the set of things a system does not produce is as structured and informative as the set it does. In UX the 'figure' is what gets attention: the features on screen, the events in the analytics, the users who answered the survey. The 'ground' is everything else: options that were removed, actions that are not tracked, people who never signed up or churned before being asked. A figure-ground audit lists that ground explicitly and asks what shape it has. Missing states in an interface, untracked events in an analytics plan and missing groups in a sample are not random; they follow the assumptions of whoever drew the figure, and they often explain blind spots in findings.
steps: Choose the figure to audit: a screen or flow, an analytics tracking plan, a survey sample or a set of research findings.
List what the figure contains in one column.
In a second column list what could reasonably be there and is not: states, options, events, people, questions. Use competitors, earlier versions, support logs and domain experts to fill it.
Group the absences and look for a pattern in who or what is consistently left out.
For each group, decide whether the absence is deliberate and justified, or a blind spot.
Turn blind spots into design changes, extra tracking, recruitment targets or research questions.
outputs: A two-column figure and ground inventory, the patterns in what is missing, and a list of blind spots with actions.
useWhen: Reviewing a research plan or sample before fieldwork, auditing analytics coverage, or questioning why findings keep confirming what the team already believed.
avoidWhen: Early exploratory work where the figure itself is not yet defined, or as a substitute for actually collecting data from the missing groups.
whyLost: Survivorship bias and non-response bias are known in statistics, and figure-ground is known in visual design, but UX has no routine practice that treats absences as a dataset to analyse across screens, data and samples alike.
whereToUse: Research operations, analytics instrumentation reviews, inclusive design reviews, synthesis sessions before reporting.
example: An audit of a churn study shows every interviewee was still a paying customer; the ground is everyone who left in the first week. Recruiting five of them changed the top finding from pricing to onboarding.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Chapter III (Figure and Ground).

name: Findings Presentation Design
origin: Nancy Duarte's 'big idea' (Resonate, 2010); Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, Storytelling with Data (2015, 2020); Susan Weinschenk after Timothy Koegel (2007)
summary: Plan a research readout by writing one-sentence key message, storyboarding content on notes along a narrative arc, and building charts progressively live with an annotated leave-behind.
description: This procedure plans a findings communication before any slides are made. First the Big Idea: one complete sentence stating the researcher's point of view and what is at stake for the audience, tested aloud with a partner who keeps asking 'why?' and shortened into a repeatable phrase. Next, a ten-minute sticky-note brainstorm of every possible content item, edited against the Big Idea with a discard pile and appendix. The notes are then arranged around the audience's tension and its resolution, as plot, rising action, climax, falling action and call to action, or Weinschenk's current state, consequences, solution and call to action with a 30-60 second opening preview. For live delivery charts are built in stages (empty axes, reference line, each series); for reading alone, one or two fully annotated slides carry the narrative.
steps: After analysis, write the Big Idea as one sentence combining your point of view and what is at stake for this audience.
Read it aloud to a partner unfamiliar with the work for about ten minutes; let them question you, ask them to restate it, and revise.
Set a ten-minute timer and write every possible content item on separate sticky notes, aiming for twenty or more.
Group the notes, discard or move to an appendix anything that does not support the Big Idea, and decide whether to lead with the action.
Name the audience's tension and the action that resolves it, then arrange notes as plot, rising action, climax, falling action and ending (or current state, consequences, solution, call to action).
For a live readout, build each chart in stages with speaker notes; for stand-alone reading, make one or two annotated slides with takeaway titles.
Rehearse aloud, prepare for objections, and check the plan with a stakeholder before building slides.
outputs: A one-sentence key message and short phrase, an ordered storyboard with a discard pile, build slides with speaker notes, and an annotated stand-alone version.
useWhen: Preparing research readouts, executive summaries and recommendations for decision makers, especially when findings must lead to a decision or budget.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing exploratory or genuinely mixed findings into one persuasive sentence or manufactured tension; state uncertainty explicitly. A single 'slideument' meant for both live and reading use serves neither.
whyLost: It survives because storytelling with data is widely taught; the disciplined steps (partner testing, discard pile, separate live and read versions) are often skipped.
whereToUse: Research readouts, quarterly insight reviews, design reviews, executive briefings and survey or analytics presentations.
example: After a churn study, a researcher's Big Idea is that onboarding hides the savings feature and costs roughly a fifth of first-month retention. The live deck builds the retention chart month by month, and a single annotated slide goes to executives who missed the meeting.
sources: 100 Things Every Presenter Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2012)
Storytelling to Spur Action with Stakeholders (Reimer & Howley, 2023)
Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Knaflic, C. N. (2020). Storytelling with Data: Let's Practice! Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Firehouse (quick-response) research
origin: Paul Deutschmann and Wayne Danielson (1960)
summary: Prepares a survey and interviewers in advance so that interviewing starts within about a day of a major event, capturing how news or an incident spread before recall fades.
description: News diffuses within hours, so normal survey lead times would lose accurate recall of when and how people first heard. Deutschmann and Danielson prepared questionnaires and trained telephone interviewers before any event, then interviewed several hundred people in each of three cities about a day after major news stories. Standard measures are when and how the person first heard, the first channel, whom they told, what further information they sought, and what they did. Over 60 such studies exist. Rogers and Siedel surveyed 127 Albuquerque adults about the September 11 attacks: 92% knew by 10 a.m., those who heard first from media learned earlier than those who heard from other people, and 69% told others. Recall of highly salient news stays accurate for weeks, but less salient events need speed. The design principle, standing readiness to field research the moment an unpredictable event occurs, transfers to outages, incidents and viral moments.
steps: Prepare the questionnaire, sampling frame and recruitment channel before any event, and pilot them.
Define trigger criteria and who decides to activate the study.
Start interviewing or surveying within about 24 hours of the event.
Ask when and how respondents first heard, the first channel, whom they told, what information they sought and what they did.
Plot the cumulative percentage of people aware by hour and compare channels and early versus late knowers.
Archive the instrument and results so the next activation can compare events.
outputs: Diffusion curves of awareness by hour, channel mix, interpersonal relay rates and actions taken.
useWhen: Unpredictable events whose effects on users fade quickly: service outages, security incidents, major announcements, viral social posts, crises affecting a user base.
avoidWhen: Predictable events (schedule a normal study) or events of low salience where sampling a day later still captures too few aware people. Situation (home or work) shapes spread and must be recorded.
whyLost: It is a classic of news-diffusion research; product teams rarely keep a standing research instrument ready, relying on logs and social listening after incidents.
whereToUse: Incident and outage communication, trust and safety events, product launches with uncertain reach, public-sector emergency messaging, crisis communication for fintech or health services.
example: A payments company keeps a ready-to-send survey and an intercept panel. Within 12 hours of an outage it learns that 60% of affected merchants heard first from customers rather than from status emails, prompting proactive SMS alerts.
reference: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). New York: Free Press, ch. 2-3.

name: First-click testing
origin: Bailey and Wolfson (2013) analysis of US government website studies; tools such as Chalkmark (Optimal Workshop)
summary: Show participants a page and a task, record where and how fast they click first, and use the share of correct first clicks to judge whether the design guides people.
description: A correct first click strongly predicts success: across 12 government website studies, task success was 87 per cent when the first click was correct and 46 per cent otherwise, and a tree-testing analysis found 70 versus 24 per cent. Participants see an image, wireframe, prototype or live page with a realistic task and click where they would start. Location and time to first click are recorded and shown as click maps; concentrated clicks signal clarity, dispersed clicks confusion. Metrics are the percentage of correct first clicks, the share going to each distractor (any distractor drawing more than 5 to 10 per cent deserves attention) and time to first click, ideally compared between successful and unsuccessful clicks. Defining correct and acceptable targets before seeing results keeps analysis honest.
steps: Write a short plan and prepare page images, prototypes or live pages with realistic tasks that do not reveal it is a first-click test.
Define the correct and acceptable target areas before collecting data.
Recruit; for comparing two designs aim for about 100 participants per design in an unmoderated tool.
Show each task, then the page, and record first-click location and time.
After each task, ask confidence and difficulty ratings and why for low ratings.
Report percentage of correct first clicks, distractor shares and time to first click by success.
Revise labels, layout or navigation where distractors draw more than 5 to 10 per cent of clicks, and retest.
outputs: Click maps, percentage of correct first clicks, distractor shares, times to first click, and confidence and difficulty ratings.
useWhen: Checking navigation labels, page layouts or calls to action at any fidelity, especially when comparing alternative designs quickly and at scale.
avoidWhen: Avoid when tasks need scrolling, multi-step flows or recovery behaviour; use full usability testing or tree testing for hierarchy alone. Time to first click means little on its own.
whyLost: It survives because it is cheap, fast, tool-supported and backed by a clear predictive link to task success.
whereToUse: Homepages and landing pages, e-commerce category navigation, SaaS dashboards, government services and intranets.
example: An airline compares two home page designs with 100 participants each on the task of changing a booking. Design A gets 72 per cent correct first clicks and faster clicks; design B loses 30 per cent of clicks to a promotional banner.
reference: Bailey, B. & Wolfson, C. (2013), as cited in Albert, W. & Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience (3rd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 265-267.

name: First-difference and sibling fixed-effects models
origin: Standard econometric panel methods (Wooldridge, 2010); DAG interpretation by Imai and Kim (2017)
summary: Use repeated observations of the same units to remove all time-invariant unobserved differences between them, by demeaning within units or adding unit dummies.
description: With panel data, any confounder that differs between units but is constant over time can be eliminated. Pooled regression ignores this and is biased when unit traits correlate with treatment, with standard errors too small because of serial correlation. The within estimator demeans outcome and treatment by each unit's mean (equivalently, includes a dummy per unit); adding period dummies gives two-way fixed effects. Identification needs strict exogeneity conditional on the unit effect and within-unit variation in treatment, and time-invariant covariates drop out. Standard errors are clustered by unit, ideally with at least about thirty clusters. Comparing pooled and fixed-effects estimates shows how much unit-level confounding was removed: a marriage wage premium of 8.3% fell about 60% under fixed effects. It cannot fix reverse causality, feedback from past outcomes or time-varying confounders.
steps: Draw a DAG and judge whether confounding is plausibly time-invariant, with no feedback from past outcomes to treatment.
Structure the data as a panel of units (users, accounts, stores) by period.
Estimate pooled regression as a baseline.
Estimate the within estimator by demeaning or unit dummies; add period dummies for two-way fixed effects.
Cluster standard errors by unit (at least about thirty clusters).
Compare pooled and fixed-effects estimates and interpret the change as removed unit-level confounding; note remaining threats.
outputs: Within-unit effect estimates with clustered standard errors, and a comparison with pooled estimates.
useWhen: Repeated measures of the same users, accounts or sites where treatment varies over time and stable unobserved traits confound comparisons.
avoidWhen: When treatment is staggered with heterogeneous effects (two-way fixed effects can be biased; use modern staggered DiD), when reverse causality is likely, or when treatment barely varies within units.
whyLost: It is a workhorse in economics but UX analytics seldom builds panel datasets or reasons about unit-level confounding.
whereToUse: Account-level SaaS analytics, store or region rollouts, longitudinal survey panels, seat-level productivity tools.
example: An analytics team estimates whether enabling AI suggestions raises weekly tickets resolved per support agent. With agent and week fixed effects, stable skill differences drop out and the effect falls from 12% (pooled) to 5%.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Wooldridge, J. M. (2010). Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (2nd ed.). MIT Press.

name: Firsthand, Secondhand and Thirdhand Evidence Distinction
donor: Historical method and qualitative field research
origin: Expanded from the historians' primary and secondary source distinction by Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016)
summary: Tagging each piece of evidence by how many filters stand between the researcher and the event, so that reported and hearsay accounts are corroborated before they carry weight.
description: Yin lists this as one of five practices that apply to every mode of qualitative data collection. Firsthand evidence is what the researcher sees or hears directly. Secondhand evidence passes through one filter: a participant tells you what happened (though the fact that they said it is firsthand evidence of their account). Thirdhand evidence passes through two filters: someone tells you what another person said, or a news article quotes someone about an event. Yin does not ask researchers to discard second- and thirdhand material, since no study can observe everything, but to avoid relying on it alone and to seek corroboration from another source, which leads into triangulation. He pairs it with checks such as confirming that an interviewee was actually present at events they describe. In UX research much evidence is filtered: support agents relaying customer complaints, managers describing what their teams do, sales notes about why deals were lost. Marking each claim's remoteness during note-taking and synthesis makes it visible which findings rest on observed behaviour and which on reports of reports, and directs follow-up work to corroborate the latter.
steps: Define the three levels for the team with examples from the study domain
While taking notes, tag each claim as firsthand (observed), secondhand (reported by a participant) or thirdhand (reported about someone else's report)
For secondhand claims, check whether the participant was present at the event they describe
During synthesis, list which key findings rest only on second- or thirdhand evidence
Seek corroborating sources, such as direct observation, logs or documents, for those findings
In the report, state the evidence level behind each key finding
outputs: Notes and findings tagged by evidence remoteness, and a list of findings needing corroboration.
useWhen: Studies that rely on proxies, stakeholders, support or sales staff, or participants describing other people's behaviour.
avoidWhen: All data come from direct observation of the behaviour in question, such as a moderated usability test.
whyLost: UX synthesis usually treats all quotes and sticky notes as equal evidence; source-criticism traditions from history and journalism were never brought into practitioner synthesis methods.
whereToUse: Stakeholder and proxy interviews, internal discovery, B2B research via account teams, support-ticket and sales-note analysis.
example: In research on an expenses tool, a finance manager says staff 'always' photograph receipts at the end of the month. The researcher tags this as secondhand, since the manager did not watch it happen, and confirms it against upload timestamps before it goes into the report.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Fit indices (CFI/RMSEA/SRMR)
origin: Bentler, 1990 (CFI); Steiger & Lind, 1980 (RMSEA); cut-offs by Hu & Bentler, 1999; their use as fixed thresholds is critiqued by Kline (2023)
summary: Testing whether a hypothesised factor structure fits survey data using indices such as CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR before trusting scale scores or SEM paths.
description: Confirmatory factor analysis specifies in advance which items load on which factors and tests how well that model reproduces observed covariances. Because the chi-square test rejects almost any model at large N, approximate fit indices are used: the Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) compare the model with a null model; RMSEA estimates misfit per degree of freedom with a confidence interval; SRMR summarises residual correlations. Common guidelines (Hu and Bentler, 1999) are CFI and TLI of 0.95 or above, RMSEA of 0.06 or below and SRMR of 0.08 or below, but these are heuristics, not laws. Rigour comes from reporting all indices with the estimator used, inspecting local misfit through modification indices and residuals, and resisting atheoretical re-specification.
steps: Choose the estimator in advance (ML, or a robust variant such as MLM, MLR or MLMV for non-normal data) rather than trying several and keeping the best-fitting.
Report the model chi-square with degrees of freedom and p-value; treat a significant result as misfit to be explained, not dismissed because the sample is large.
Report RMSEA with its 90% CI, CFI and SRMR (TLI adds little beyond CFI); do not rely on the normed chi-square, GFI or AGFI.

Inspect the residual matrix (standardised and correlation residuals, investigating absolute correlation residuals above 0.10) to locate local misfit; only residuals can show whether misfit is trivial.
Treat fixed cut-offs such as Hu and Bentler's as rough guides only; dynamic, model-specific thresholds are better but still not decisive, and models with few degrees of freedom pass easily.
Respecify only where theory justifies it (ideally preregistered), consider equivalent models, and cross-validate any modification on a holdout sample.
Compare non-nested alternatives with AIC or BIC, and accept that retaining no model is a legitimate result.
outputs: A fit table, standardised loadings, factor correlations, invariance results and a judgement on whether the measurement model is acceptable.
useWhen: Validating a scale structure from an EFA in a new sample, checking that a standard instrument works in a new population, or as the measurement step before SEM.
avoidWhen: Avoid with samples below about 200, with poorly theorised structures (use EFA), or when the goal is simply a total score from a long-validated instrument.
whyLost: CFA requires SEM software and training typical of psychology or marketing doctoral programmes, so it stayed in academic and market research.
whereToUse: Cross-market UX measurement, scale validation for AI and trust instruments, and measurement models preceding SEM in strategic research.
example: A fintech team validates a three-factor trust scale in a holdout sample of 510. The model gives CFI 0.96, RMSEA 0.052 (90% CI 0.044-0.061) and SRMR 0.041, and scalar invariance holds across novice and expert investors, so segment means can be compared.
sources: Kline, R. B. (2023) Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling, 5th ed.
Hu, L. & Bentler, P. M. (1999) Cutoff criteria for fit indexes in covariance structure analysis. Structural Equation Modeling
Brown, T. A. (2015) Confirmatory Factor Analysis for Applied Research, 2nd ed.
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (Rex Kline)
A Primer on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (Joseph Hair et al.)
Hu & Bentler (1999) Cutoff criteria for fit indexes in covariance structure analysis
The Inquiry Series, Ch 49 — Structural Equation Modeling — From Quotes to Coefficients
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Hu, L. & Bentler, P. M. (1999) Cutoff criteria for fit indexes in covariance structure analysis. Structural Equation Modeling 6(1)

name: Fitts' Law Modelling
origin: Paul Fitts, 1954; Shannon formulation by MacKenzie, 1992
summary: Predicts and measures the time to acquire a target from its distance and size, calibrating target sizes and placements for pointing and touch interfaces.
description: Fitts' law states that movement time to a target grows linearly with the index of difficulty, ID = log2(D/W + 1), where D is distance and W is target width: MT = a + b·ID. The constants a and b depend on device, limb and context, so the rigorous use of the law is calibration, not quotation. Researchers run a multidirectional tapping task (ISO 9241-411) across a range of distances and widths, fit the regression and compute throughput in bits per second, then use the fitted model to predict times for proposed layouts. For touch, effective width and error rates matter as much as speed, and context such as gloves, vibration or one-handed use changes the parameters. A well-fitted model (R² above about 0.9) lets teams compare layouts quantitatively before building them.
steps: Define the device, input method and context of use (e.g. gloved touch, one-handed mobile, mouse).
Set up an ISO 9241-411 style multidirectional tapping task covering at least 3 distances and 3 widths.
Collect data from 12-20 participants with enough trials per condition (around 15-25) and record movement time and errors.
Compute effective width from endpoint spread and fit MT = a + b·log2(D/We + 1); check R² is above about 0.9.
Calculate throughput and use the fitted model to predict acquisition times for proposed layouts.
Set minimum target sizes and spacing that keep both predicted time and error rate within thresholds (e.g. errors below 4%).
outputs: Fitted Fitts' model parameters, throughput, predicted acquisition times per layout, calibrated minimum target sizes.
useWhen: Sizing and placing touch targets, designing for constrained contexts (gloves, motion, accessibility), comparing input devices or menu layouts.
avoidWhen: When performance is dominated by visual search or decision time rather than motor movement; use Hick's law or eye tracking.
whyLost: Still in use: Empirically robust; directly informs touchscreen and pointer interaction design guidelines.
whereToUse: Button/target sizing; menu design; touch interface; pointer-based interfaces.
example: A surgical touchscreen had to work with sterile gloves. Calibration with 16 clinicians showed gloved error rates exceeded 10% below 12 mm targets, so the team set a 15 mm minimum and moved critical controls nearer the resting hand position.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 3 — The Ballistics of the Human Body — Fitts' Law & Motor Control
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
The GOMS Family of User Interface Analysis Techniques (John & Kieras, 1996)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)

name: Five Rings of Buying Insight
origin: Adele Revella, Buyer Persona Institute (Buyer Personas, 2015)
summary: A decision-focused interview framework covering priority initiative, success factors, perceived barriers, buyer's journey and decision criteria, without asking about features.
description: Revella's framework interviews people who recently made a buying decision, asking them to narrate it from the first trigger. Five rings structure the analysis: the priority initiative (what changed that made them look), success factors (outcomes they expected, not features), perceived barriers (doubts and fears that nearly stopped them), the buyer's journey (who was involved, what sources they trusted, how alternatives were compared) and decision criteria (what actually differentiated the winner). Because barriers and true criteria are rarely volunteered, the method relies on open narrative prompts and probing of specific moments. It yields buyer personas grounded in decision behaviour, linking marketing, sales and product.
steps: Recruit 8 to 12 people who made the relevant purchase or adoption decision within the last few months, including some who chose a competitor.
Open by asking them to go back to when they first started thinking about the problem and what had changed.
Let them narrate the decision chronologically, probing each step for who was involved and what sources they trusted.
Probe for outcomes they expected, the doubts that gave them pause, and what would have made them walk away.
Ask what they would tell someone else making this decision to look for, to elicit real decision criteria.
Code transcripts into the five rings and synthesise a buyer persona with supporting quotes for each ring.
outputs: A buyer persona organised by the five rings, decision journey maps, barrier lists and real decision criteria with quotes.
useWhen: B2B and considered-purchase products where adoption depends on a decision process, for positioning, pricing, onboarding and win/loss analysis.
avoidWhen: Habitual low-consideration consumer behaviour or in-product usability questions; use analytics, diaries or usability testing.
whyLost: It lives in product marketing rather than UX research, so UX teams rarely use it despite overlap with jobs-to-be-done interviews.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS purchasing, fintech account opening, healthcare procurement, and onboarding design for trial-to-paid conversion.
example: A cybersecurity startup interviews ten recent buyers and three who chose a rival. The perceived barriers ring shows fear of a failed audit, not price, as the main hesitation, so onboarding now leads with compliance evidence.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 32 — Advanced Elicitation — The Archaeology of the Interview
reference: Revella, A. (2015). Buyer Personas. Wiley.

extra.The Five Rings: Priority Initiative: What triggers this decision? What circumstances in the buyer's personal or professional life caused them to seek a solution? Probe: "Take me back to when you first started thinking about this — what had changed?" Success Factors: What outcomes does the buyer expect? Not features — outcomes. What does success look like for them personally and professionally? Probe: "Once this is working, what will be different about your [work/life/situation]?" Perceived Barriers: What concerns, doubts, or fears prevent the buyer from committing? This is where most interview methods fail — participants do not volunteer barriers spontaneously. Probe: "What gave you pause? What would have made you walk away from this entirely?" Buyer's Journey: How did they gather information, evaluate alternatives, and reach a decision? Who else was involved? What sources did they trust? Probe: "Walk me through exactly what you did from the moment you decided to look for a solution to the moment you made your final decision." Decision Criteria: What specific attributes differentiated the solution they chose from the alternatives? These are their actual decision criteria — often different from stated criteria. Probe: "If you were advising someone else making this decision, what would you tell them to look for?"

name: Five-Layer Model of Game Evaluation
origin: Player Research (Brighton, UK); presented by Graham McAllister and Sebastian Long in chapter 8
summary: A layered lens that links appeal, understanding, usability, player experience and monetisation, used to choose research methods and explain how low-level problems surface as revenue problems.
description: The five-layer model was derived from Player Research's work on free-to-play games, where developers blamed poor revenue on economy balancing when the real cause was often in the game itself. From the bottom up the layers are appeal (does the game attract players to download it), understanding (do players know the rules and what is available), usability (can they do what the designer intends), player experience (do they enjoy it) and monetisation (do they pay). Each layer depends on those beneath it, so a problem seen at the top may originate far lower down. Premium games without in-app purchases use a four-layer version without monetisation. The studio maps each research method onto the layers it 'polishes' (high, medium or low), from concept tests and competitor analysis through usability and large-scale playtests to engagement diaries and analytics-driven playtests, producing a matrix that shows which methods are needed at which stage. For UX teams the model is a communication and planning tool: it helps stakeholders see that a conversion or retention problem may be an understanding problem and that no single method covers every layer.
steps: List the layers that apply to the product (drop monetisation for paid products).
For each planned or possible research method, rate how strongly it informs each layer.
Map methods onto development phases to build a layer-by-phase coverage matrix.
When a top-layer metric is poor, trace candidate causes down through the layers.
Choose the methods that cover the layers where causes are most likely.
Use the matrix in conversations with the team to show gaps in research coverage.
outputs: A coverage matrix of methods by layer and phase, and a causal explanation linking surface metrics to underlying issues.
useWhen: Planning a research programme for a game or app, or explaining to stakeholders why a revenue or retention problem needs usability or comprehension research.
avoidWhen: You need a validated measurement model; the layers are a practitioner heuristic rather than a tested construct.
whyLost: Published as a consultancy framework in a games book and not taken up as a general UX planning model.
whereToUse: Free-to-play and premium games, freemium apps, subscription products.
example: A mobile puzzle game has weak in-app purchase conversion; tracing down the layers, the team runs a usability playtest and finds players do not understand boosters, an understanding-layer problem.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 8 (McAllister and Long).

name: Five-Model Work Modelling (Contextual Design)
aka: Flow, sequence, artefact, cultural and physical models
origin: Hugh Beyer & Karen Holtzblatt, 1998
summary: Five complementary models of work practice, flow, sequence, artefact, cultural and physical, built from contextual inquiry to capture the whole context of work.
description: Contextual Design's five work models represent work practice from complementary perspectives. The flow model shows roles, responsibilities and communication between people. The sequence model shows the ordered steps, triggers, intents and breakdowns of a task. The artefact model shows the things people create and use and how they are structured. The cultural model shows the influences, values and constraints that shape behaviour. The physical model shows the environment and how its layout supports or hinders work. Models are built for each contextual inquiry participant, then consolidated across participants to reveal common structure and variation. Rigour comes from grounding every element in observed data, marking breakdowns explicitly and consolidating systematically rather than drawing idealised processes.
steps: Conduct contextual inquiries with 6 to 12 participants across relevant roles.
In interpretation sessions, build each relevant model for each participant from observed data.
Mark breakdowns (problems and workarounds) on the models with lightning bolts or equivalent markers.
Consolidate each model type across participants, identifying common patterns and variants.
Walk the consolidated models with stakeholders to identify design opportunities.
Use the models to drive visioning and storyboarding of new work practice.
outputs: Individual and consolidated flow, sequence, artefact, cultural and physical models, with breakdowns and design opportunities.
useWhen: For enterprise software, healthcare IT and complex workplace tools where work involves multiple roles, artefacts and environments.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple consumer flows or when no contextual inquiry data exists; use journey mapping or task analysis. The full set takes considerable time.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives primarily in Contextual Design practice; rarely applied in full outside specialized teams.
whereToUse: Enterprise software; healthcare IT; any complex workplace tool design.
example: A logistics firm's flow model shows dispatchers acting as an informal hub between drivers and customers, and the cultural model shows drivers distrusting central planning. The new routing tool adds driver-proposed changes.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Beyer H & Holtzblatt K (1998) Contextual Design
Holtzblatt K, Wendell JB & Wood S (2005) Rapid Contextual Design
reference: Beyer, H. & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Flow State Scale
origin: Jackson and Marsh (1996), building on Csikszentmihalyi's flow model (1975); revised as FSS-2 and DFS-2 by Jackson and Eklund; Rasch analysis by Tenenbaum, Fogarty and Jackson (1999), as reviewed in the Handbook
summary: A multi-item questionnaire that measures how strongly a person experienced flow during a specific activity, across the nine dimensions of Csikszentmihalyi's model.
description: The Flow State Scale turns Csikszentmihalyi's flow model into a questionnaire. The original version has 36 items, four per dimension, rated on a 5-point scale. The nine dimensions are challenge-skill balance, merging of action and awareness, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, concentration on the task at hand, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, transformation of time and autotelic (intrinsically rewarding) experience. The state version is completed straight after a specific episode; a dispositional version asks how often the person usually experiences each feature in that activity. The Handbook notes that flow arises when task demands call for intense concentration and match the person's skill, that boredom, anxiety and apathy result from other mismatches, and that Rasch analysis of the scale with 790 athletes flagged several misfitting items, so item-level checking matters. For UX the scale gives a structured way to measure absorption in creative tools, games, learning products and other tasks where deep engagement rather than mere ease is the goal. Its dimension profile shows which preconditions are missing: unclear goals, weak feedback or a poor challenge-skill match each point to different design fixes.
steps: Decide whether you need the state version (one session) or the dispositional version (typical experience with the product).
Choose a task long and demanding enough for absorption to occur, such as a full editing session, a game level or a coding exercise.
Administer the scale immediately after the episode, before any debrief that might colour recall.
Score the nine dimension subscales as well as a total, and check internal consistency and item fit in your sample.
Compare dimension profiles across designs, user segments or skill levels to see which flow preconditions are failing.
Follow up low-scoring dimensions with interviews or session replay to find the design causes.
outputs: Nine dimension scores and an overall flow score per participant and session, which can be compared across designs or user groups.
useWhen: The product's value depends on sustained absorption: creative tools, games, music software, learning apps, developer tools or fitness products.
avoidWhen: Tasks are short transactional flows where absorption is neither expected nor desirable, or when only a single quick item can be afforded.
whyLost: Flow is often cited in UX writing but rarely measured; the scale is long, licensed through sport-psychology publishers and little known outside sport and leisure research.
whereToUse: Games, creative and design software, IDEs, music production tools, language-learning and fitness apps.
example: A team redesigning a video editor's timeline runs two 40-minute editing sessions per participant, one on each design, and gives the Flow State Scale after each. The new design raises clear-goals and feedback scores but lowers sense of control, prompting a fix to the undo model.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Berger, B. G. and Tobar, D. A. (2007) 'Physical activity and quality of life: key considerations', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 27. Also Chapter 33 (Strauss, Büsch and Tenenbaum) on Rasch analysis of the scale.

name: fMRI for UX Research
origin: Seiji Ogawa, 1990 (BOLD contrast); neuromarketing applications from the early 2000s
summary: Measures blood-oxygen-level changes in the brain while people view or evaluate stimuli, to localise neural responses linked to reward, trust or preference.
description: Functional magnetic resonance imaging detects changes in blood oxygenation (the BOLD signal) that follow neural activity, giving spatial resolution of a few millimetres but slow temporal resolution of seconds. In the 2000s neuromarketing studies used fMRI to examine brand preference, such as McClure and colleagues' cola study, and a few HCI studies looked at trust, reward and website evaluation. Participants must lie still in a scanner, so interaction is limited to viewing stimuli and pressing buttons. Rigour requires block or event-related designs with many repetitions, careful statistical correction for multiple comparisons, pre-specified regions of interest and caution about reverse inference, inferring a mental state from activity in a region that serves many functions. Cost, artificiality and inferential limits explain why it has largely disappeared from applied UX.
steps: Specify a narrowly defined question and pre-register hypotheses about regions of interest.
Design block or event-related stimulus presentations compatible with lying in a scanner.
Recruit 20-30 participants and screen them for MRI safety.
Acquire data with appropriate controls and repeated trials per condition.
Pre-process and analyse with corrections for multiple comparisons, avoiding reverse inference.
Interpret findings alongside behavioural data and acknowledge limits of ecological validity.
outputs: Activation maps and region-of-interest contrasts between stimuli or conditions, linked to behavioural measures.
useWhen: Academic research on neural correlates of trust, reward or perception where findings will inform theory rather than a specific product.
avoidWhen: Almost all applied UX questions; use behavioural experiments, surveys, eye tracking or EEG instead. Avoid reverse inference, reading a mental state such as liking or trust from activation in one region, because regions serve many functions. Test-retest reliability is modest, whole-brain voxel searches produce chance hits unless corrected and replicated in pre-specified regions, and non-independent region selection inflates reported correlations (Vul et al., 2009).
whyLost: Extinct in applied UX: Cost, immobility, and artificial conditions make it impractical.
whereToUse: Academic research only; brand neuroscience; specialized perception studies.
example: A university lab partnered with a bank to study responses to security warning designs. fMRI showed reduced visual processing with repeated exposure, supporting polymorphic warnings, but the bank used behavioural tests for production decisions.
sources: Neural correlates of behavioral preference for culturally familiar drinks (McClure et al.)
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience, 4th ed. (2015)
Vul E, Harris C, Winkielman P & Pashler H (2009) Puzzlingly high correlations in fMRI studies of emotion, personality, and social cognition. Perspectives on Psychological Science 4(3)

Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
