whyLost: Recent and published in games literature; monetisation reviews outside games tend to focus on conversion rather than fairness.
whereToUse: Free-to-play mobile and online games, freemium apps, digital marketplaces with virtual currencies.
example: An inspection finds a mobile racer gates the final league behind a purchase-only car, violating FP1 and FP6, and the team adds an earnable route.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 15 (Paavilainen, Korhonen, Koskinen and Alha).

name: FREQUENCIES and DESCRIPTIVES (descriptive screening)
origin: SPSS FREQUENCIES and DESCRIPTIVES procedures; exploratory screening tradition following Tukey (1977)
summary: Systematically producing frequency tables and descriptive statistics for every variable before analysis, to catch coding errors, impossible values and distribution problems.
description: FREQUENCIES produces counts, percentages, valid and missing counts and optional percentiles and charts for each variable; DESCRIPTIVES gives means, standard deviations, ranges, skewness and kurtosis for scale variables and can save z-scores. Used as a deliberate screening pass, they reveal out-of-range codes, unexpected missingness, ceiling and floor effects, and highly skewed variables before they contaminate models. Rigour lies in running them on every variable, comparing results against the questionnaire's response options and expected sample sizes, and recording the problems found. In UX the step is usually skipped in favour of jumping to charts of headline means.
steps: Run FREQUENCIES on every categorical and rating variable and DESCRIPTIVES on every continuous variable, from syntax.
Compare observed values with permitted response options and flag any out-of-range or unlabelled codes.
Check valid N against expected N and investigate variables with more than about 5% missing.
Inspect skewness and kurtosis (values beyond about plus or minus 2 warrant attention) and look for ceiling or floor effects (more than about 15% at the extreme).
Save z-scores and flag absolute values above 3.29 as potential univariate outliers.
Record issues and fixes in the cleaning log before running inferential analyses.
outputs: Frequency tables, descriptive statistics, a list of anomalies and a cleaning log.
useWhen: The first analytic step for every survey or quantitative UX dataset, and after each new data wave.
avoidWhen: Not a substitute for multivariate screening (Mahalanobis distance) or for distributional checks with EXAMINE when assumptions matter.
whyLost: Dashboards and survey tools show headline charts instantly, so systematic univariate screening seems redundant to many UX teams.
whereToUse: Survey programmes, benchmarking studies and any SPSS-based analysis.
example: An e-commerce satisfaction survey's FREQUENCIES output shows a value of 11 on a 0-10 NPS item for 37 respondents. The cause is a platform export bug, fixed before the quarterly NPS is reported.
sources: Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
Tukey, J. W. (1977) Exploratory Data Analysis
Tabachnick, B. G. & Fidell, L. S. (2019) Using Multivariate Statistics, 7th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Tabachnick, B. G. & Fidell, L. S. (2019) Using Multivariate Statistics, 7th ed.

name: Front-Door Adjustment
origin: Judea Pearl (1995), Causal diagrams for empirical research
summary: Estimate the effect of a feature on an outcome when unmeasured factors confound both, by going through a measured step that the feature works through.
description: Backdoor adjustment needs every confounder to be measured. Often in product data it cannot be: the same unmeasured motivation makes people adopt a feature and also makes them retain. The front-door criterion offers another route when the feature affects the outcome only through a measurable intermediate step (a mediator) and that step is not itself driven by the hidden confounder except through the feature. You estimate two links that are each unconfounded, feature to mediator and mediator to outcome (adjusting for the feature), and combine them to recover the full causal effect. It is the diagram in which D causes M, M causes Y, and an unmeasured U affects both D and Y. The assumptions are strong and must be argued from how the product works, which is exactly why drawing the DAG with the team is part of the method.
steps: Draw a DAG of the feature (D), the outcome (Y), plausible unmeasured confounders (U) and the mechanism the feature works through (M).
Check the front-door conditions: D affects Y only through M; no unblocked backdoor path from D to M; every backdoor path from M to Y is blocked by D.
Make sure the mediator is logged reliably for every user (for example, the number of saved searches after adopting alerts).
Estimate the effect of D on M, then the effect of M on Y while adjusting for D.
Combine the two with the front-door formula, using bootstrap for intervals.
Stress-test the result: argue each assumption with product and engineering colleagues and compare with any experiment you can run.
outputs: A causal effect estimate for a feature that could not be randomised, with an explicit diagram of the assumptions it rests on.
useWhen: Observational product data where self-selection into a feature is driven by things you cannot measure, but the feature clearly acts through a logged mechanism.
avoidWhen: When an A/B test is possible, when the feature has effects that bypass the mediator, or when the mediator is affected by the same hidden motivation.
whyLost: Product analytics adopted regression adjustment and propensity scores, which only handle measured confounders. The front-door route is taught in causal inference courses but rarely appears in UX or analytics practice.
whereToUse: Feature adoption studies, onboarding analysis, retention attribution, health and education apps.
example: Users who turn on price alerts retain better, but so do more motivated shoppers. Alerts work only by bringing people back to saved items, which is logged, so the team estimates alerts to return visits and return visits to retention, and finds about a third of the raw difference is causal.
sources: Cinelli, C., Forney, A. & Pearl, J., A Crash Course in Good and Bad Controls (2022)
Pearl, J., Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference (2009)
reference: Pearl, J. (1995). Causal diagrams for empirical research. Biometrika, 82(4), 669-688. Cinelli, C., Forney, A., & Pearl, J. (2022). A crash course in good and bad controls. Sociological Methods & Research.

name: Front-end Instrumentation Decision (Tight versus Loose Design)
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1994
summary: A decision aid for how far to prestructure qualitative instruments before fieldwork, weighing study purpose, number of cases and familiarity with the setting.
description: Qualitative researchers disagree about how much to prepare instruments in advance. Miles and Huberman set out the arguments for little prior instrumentation, for a lot, and for 'it depends', and turn them into explicit factors. Loose designs suit studies needing rich context, locally grounded concepts, exploration, single complex cases and minimal researcher influence. Tight designs suit predefined concepts, confirmatory or evaluative aims, multiple cases where comparability matters, generalisation and links to surveys. The two stances favour different kinds of validity, so the choice is a design decision, not a matter of taste; the authors place themselves off centre, toward the structured end. The decision can differ by phase: an exploratory first wave can precede a tighter confirmatory one. Multi-case work typically uses a common semi-structured guide whose wording and order fieldworkers may adapt, revised between visits.
steps: Characterise the study: exploratory or confirmatory, single or multiple case, basic or applied, and how familiar the team is with the setting.
Mark which phases of the study are exploratory and which confirmatory.
Score the loose-versus-tight factors (need for local meaning, comparability across cases, predefined concepts, generalisation, links to quantitative data) and choose a position for each phase.
Build only the instruments needed at the outset; defer others until early data show what matters.
For multiple cases, write a common semi-structured guide whose wording and order fieldworkers may adapt.
Record the chosen stance and its rationale in the plan, and revise instruments between visits.
outputs: A stated instrumentation stance per phase, with rationale, and the starting set of instruments.
useWhen: Planning qualitative or multi-site studies where you must decide between an open conversation guide and a structured protocol, especially when several researchers or markets must produce comparable data.
avoidWhen: Studies whose structure is already fixed by a standard instrument or regulatory protocol. Over-structuring misses local meanings; under-structuring makes cross-case comparison and analysis unmanageable.
whyLost: UX teams tend to default to one house style of discussion guide rather than treating structure as a design variable chosen per study and phase. The explicit decision factors stayed in qualitative methodology texts.
whereToUse: Multi-country discovery studies, programmes mixing exploratory interviews with later evaluative rounds, and research ops templates for discussion guides.
example: A health-tech team planning interviews in five clinics needs comparable findings for a procurement decision, so it scores toward tight: a common guide with fixed topics and adaptable wording. A sixth, unfamiliar setting (home care) gets a loose first visit before the guide is extended to it.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Full Four-Level Affinity Diagram
donor: Contextual Design (HCI), drawing on Japanese KJ method
origin: Jiro Kawakita's KJ method, 1960s; adapted by Karen Holtzblatt & Hugh Beyer in Contextual Design, 1998
summary: Building a complete bottom-up affinity hierarchy from hundreds of contextual inquiry notes, labelled at four levels and walked top-down to drive design.
description: The Contextual Design affinity diagram organises hundreds of interpretation notes from contextual inquiry into a four-level hierarchy built bottom-up. Individual notes, each one observation or interpretation from one participant, are grouped in small clusters; each cluster is labelled with a first-person statement of the shared need or practice; these are grouped under broader work themes, and finally under three to five global concerns. Labels are written in the user's voice and must say something new, not just name a topic. The team then walks the wall from top to bottom, generating design ideas at each level. Rigour comes from volume (often 100 or more notes per participant group), grounding in interpretation sessions, and bottom-up grouping without predefined categories.
steps: Data collection: Each researcher: 8–15 contextual inquiry sessions, 100–150 data notes per researcher. One observation, quote, or interpretation per note.
Level 1 — Individual findings (yellow): Each note = one finding from one participant. Clusters of 3–8 related notes.
Level 2 — Work groups (pink labels): Name each cluster with the shared work practice or user need.
Level 3 — Work themes (blue labels): Broader work themes or design concerns grouping yellow clusters.
Level 4 — Global concerns (green labels): 3–5 global themes pervading the entire affinity.
Walking the wall: Read level 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. Design decisions emerge from this inversion.
outputs: A four-level affinity wall with user-voice labels, global concerns, and design ideas generated during the wall walk.
useWhen: Synthesising substantial contextual or field data (eight or more sessions) with a team, to build shared understanding and design direction.
avoidWhen: Small evaluative studies (use an issue log) or when categories are predefined by the question (use framework analysis).
whyLost: It was compressed into quick sticky-note clustering with topic labels, losing the bottom-up rule, user-voice labels and wall walk.
whereToUse: Enterprise and workplace software discovery, service design programmes, cross-functional team synthesis, and remote whiteboard workshops.
example: After 12 contextual inquiries with warehouse supervisors, a team builds a 600-note affinity. A global concern, 'I am always firefighting yesterday's exceptions', reorients the dashboard design toward exception queues.
reference: Holtzblatt, K. & Beyer, H. (2016). Contextual Design: Design for Life (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Full-control mental model analysis
origin: Combefis and Pecheur (2009, 2011); Maudoux, Pecheur and Combefis (2017); related to Rushby (2002) and Heymann and Degani (2007)
summary: Model a system's commands and observations, generate the minimal mental model that lets an operator control it without surprises, check real mental models against it and derive safe training units.
description: The system and the user's mental model are both described as labelled transition systems with commands (user-initiated) and observations (system-initiated). A mental model controls the system if, after any shared sequence, the commands it expects are available and every possible observation is expected; full control adds knowledge of all available commands. A minimisation algorithm generates the smallest full-control model, which defines what training and documentation must teach; if none exists, the design cannot be controlled without surprise. Checking a user's or manual's model against the system exposes automation surprises and mode confusion. The full-control model can also be decomposed into basic units, each safe on its own, giving a learning sequence and a learning-complexity metric.
steps: Model the system interface as a transition system distinguishing commands from observations.
Generate a minimal full-control mental model by minimisation; if none exists, flag the design as uncontrollable without surprise.
Model existing mental models, for example from manuals or training material, and check them for control and full control; failures are potential automation surprises.
Decompose the full-control model into basic sub-models such as sequences and loops.
Complete each unit with all observations the system can produce, so each unit is safe to use alone.
Order units for incremental training and report learning complexity as the minimal number of units.
outputs: A minimal normative mental model, control verdicts with problematic sequences, ordered learning units and a learning-complexity score.
useWhen: Designing or documenting automated, modal systems where operators must predict system behaviour, such as autopilots or medical machines.
avoidWhen: Avoid for open-ended consumer software; use mental model elicitation or teach-back with users. It assumes users act exactly on their model and handles only finite deterministic systems.
whyLost: It is recent formal-methods research with no practitioner tooling, so it remains in academic and safety-critical circles.
whereToUse: Aviation automation, medical devices, industrial control, driver-assistance systems and the training material for them.
example: An adaptive cruise control team models commands and alerts and finds no full-control model exists because one resume behaviour depends on hidden state. They add a visible mode indicator, regenerate the model and structure driver onboarding as five safe units.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Maudoux, G., Pecheur, C. & Combefis, S. (2017). Learning safe interactions and full-control. In Weyers, B. et al. (eds) The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction. Springer, pp. 297-318; Combefis, S. & Pecheur, C. (2009). A bisimulation-based approach to the analysis of human-computer interaction. EICS 2009.

name: Fun Toolkit
origin: Janet Read and Stuart MacFarlane (2006), refined by Read (2008); applied by Sim, Read and Horton in Chapter 1
summary: A set of three pictorial, writing-free survey tools (Smileyometer, Again Again table and Fun Sorter) for getting children to rate how much fun a product is.
description: The Fun Toolkit is a survey kit designed for children who cannot yet handle conventional questionnaires. The Smileyometer is a visual analogue scale of five faces from 'Awful' to 'Brilliant', coded 1 to 5. It is given before use, showing only a first screen, to capture expectations, and again after use to capture experienced fun; the difference between the two is itself informative. The Again Again table asks the child to tick yes, maybe or no to 'Would you like to do this again?' for each activity, which is coded 2, 1 and 0 and works as a behavioural-intention proxy for enjoyment. The Fun Sorter asks children to rank several products against criteria, so it is only meaningful in comparative studies. Because none of the tools need writing, they are quick to complete in a classroom. The chapter shows their main weakness: children tend to rate highly to please the adult (satisficing), so scores cluster near the top and are best read as relative rather than absolute. Pairing the toolkit with observation and retrospective problem reporting gives a fuller picture of usability and experience for children's products.
steps: Decide which tools fit: Smileyometer and Again Again table for a single product, add the Fun Sorter only when comparing products.
Show the child the opening screen and collect a 'before' Smileyometer rating of expectations.
Let the child use or play the product for a set but flexible period, observing as they go.
Collect the 'after' Smileyometer and the Again Again table (yes, maybe, no).
Code Smileyometer responses 1 to 5 and Again Again responses 2, 1, 0; compute averages and before-after differences.
Interpret scores alongside observation, watching for ceiling effects and satisficing, and note session factors such as time of day.
outputs: Before and after fun ratings, change scores, a would-play-again score and, in comparative studies, rankings of products.
useWhen: Evaluating games, apps or learning tools with children of roughly primary-school age, especially in schools or labs where writing or long questionnaires are impractical.
avoidWhen: Participants are teenagers or adults who can complete standard scales, or when you need fine-grained diagnostic data rather than overall appeal.
whyLost: It is well established in child-computer interaction research but rarely used outside it, since most commercial UX work involves adult users.
whereToUse: Children's games, educational software, toys with digital components, kids' apps.
example: A team testing a language-learning platform game with 7 to 8 year olds collects a Smileyometer rating from the start screen, lets each child play for about ten minutes, then collects a second Smileyometer and an Again Again response; most children say they would play again, but a third rate it lower after play than before, pointing to an experience that missed expectations.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Sim, G., Read, J. C. and Horton, M. (2016). Practical and ethical concerns in usability testing with children. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 1. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Function Allocation (Fitts List / MABA-MABA)
aka: Men are better at, machines are better at
origin: Paul Fitts et al., 1951 (Human engineering for an effective air-navigation and traffic-control system)
summary: Systematically decides which functions should be performed by people and which by machines, based on comparative strengths and the needs of the joint system.
description: The original Fitts list compared human and machine capabilities (humans better at improvisation and judgement; machines at speed, precision and repetition) to allocate functions. Later work criticised static allocation and proposed dynamic or adaptive allocation and the joint cognitive system perspective, in which the question is how people and automation coordinate rather than who does what. A rigorous allocation analysis lists system functions, evaluates candidate allocations against criteria (performance, workload, situation awareness, skill retention, accountability), and checks for leftover-task problems where people are given only what automation cannot do. With AI assistants this extinct method is suddenly central: every agentic feature is an allocation decision usually made by engineering convenience.
steps: List the system's functions independently of who or what performs them, from a goal-means or task analysis.
For each function, identify candidate allocations: human, machine, shared, or adaptive.
Evaluate candidates against explicit criteria: accuracy, speed, workload, situation awareness, skill decay, accountability, user values.
Check the residual human role for coherence, avoiding 'leftover' allocations that leave people monitoring without context.
Define handover and takeover protocols, including how humans are brought back into the loop.
Test the allocation with simulation or Wizard of Oz under normal and degraded automation conditions.
outputs: A function allocation matrix with rationale, handover protocols, and evaluation results for candidate allocations.
useWhen: Designing AI copilots, agents, automation features or any product that changes who does what.
avoidWhen: Purely manual tools with no automation decisions.
whyLost: The static Fitts list was rightly criticised and the topic faded from HCI as consumer software rarely automated whole functions. Generative AI has made it relevant again without the method being remembered.
whereToUse: AI writing and coding assistants, autonomous agents, smart home automation, clinical decision support.
example: A legal AI tool allocates clause extraction to the machine but leaves lawyers verifying hundreds of extractions with no context. Reallocation makes the AI flag only low-confidence clauses with reasoning, preserving lawyer situation awareness.
sources: Fitts (ed.), Human Engineering for an Effective Air-Navigation and Traffic-Control System (1951)
Dekker & Woods, MABA-MABA or Abracadabra? Progress on human-automation co-ordination (2002), Cognition, Technology & Work
reference: Fitts, P. M. (Ed.) (1951). Human Engineering for an Effective Air-Navigation and Traffic-Control System. National Research Council.

name: Functional Data Analysis
origin: James Ramsay and C. J. Dalzell, 1991; James Ramsay and Bernard Silverman, 1997 and 2005
summary: Treats each densely sampled record, such as a cursor path or continuous rating, as a smooth curve and analyses curves and their derivatives with functional means, registration, PCA and regression.
description: Many UX measurements are curves: cursor and stylus trajectories, continuous real-time ratings, pupil and other physiological traces, daily usage over a trial. Functional data analysis represents each record as a smooth function built from basis functions (B-splines are the flexible default) with a roughness penalty, rather than as many separate points. Smoothness makes derivatives estimable, and using velocity or acceleration is what sets the approach apart: differencing raw data would magnify noise. Data resolution limits which derivatives can be trusted. Curves vary in amplitude and in phase (the timing of features), so registration aligns landmarks by smooth time-warping before averaging; otherwise the mean curve blurs features nobody actually showed. Further tools include functional principal components to find the main modes of variation, functional correlation and regression relating curves to each other or to scalar outcomes, and differential-equation models of the dynamics.
steps: Check resolution: enough samples per curve feature and adequate signal-to-noise for the derivatives you plan to use (often only the first).
Choose a basis (for example B-splines) and a roughness penalty, selecting smoothing by generalised cross-validation, and convert each record into a function.
Register the curves to remove phase variation by aligning landmarks or by continuous time-warping.
Compute functional means and variance, and derivatives such as velocity and acceleration.
Apply functional PCA to find the main modes of variation, and functional regression to relate curves to design condition or to scalar outcomes.
Report curve-level results with pointwise or simultaneous confidence bands, and check that conclusions survive alternative smoothing and registration choices.
outputs: Smoothed curves and derivatives, registered mean curves, functional principal components, and functional regression coefficients with confidence bands.
useWhen: Outcomes are time-continuous or trajectory data and the shape, timing or dynamics of the curve matter: hesitation in cursor paths, moment-to-moment ratings of a video or game, physiological arousal over a task, usage curves over a trial.
avoidWhen: Records are sparse or irregular with few points per person (use growth curve or mixed models); a single summary such as total time answers the question; you need trajectory similarity for clustering rather than modelling (consider dynamic time warping). Registration and smoothing choices affect results.
whyLost: It is a specialist area of statistics with its own software; UX teams summarise curves into a few scalar metrics and lose the shape information.
whereToUse: Pointer and touch trajectory studies, continuous-response dial testing of media, physiological UX measurement, game telemetry, trial-period engagement curves.
example: A design team records cursor trajectories from 60 participants choosing between two pricing-page layouts. After registering paths, functional PCA shows the main mode of variation is a mid-path slowdown near the comparison table, which is stronger in layout A and predicts lower confidence ratings.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: Ramsay, J. O., & Silverman, B. W. (2005). Functional Data Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Springer.

name: Functional fixedness and mental set problems
aka: Mental set (Luchins water jars), fixation and negative transfer
origin: Maier, 1931; Luchins, 1942; Duncker, 1945
summary: Classic problems in which a familiar function or a practised procedure blocks a simpler solution, measuring how prior use and experience constrain problem solving.
description: In Duncker's candle problem, people must fix a candle to a corkboard with candles, matches and a box of tacks; when the box holds the tacks, solution rates are about half those when it is empty, because the box is seen as a container rather than a support. In Maier's two-string problem, 37 of 60 failed to use pliers as a pendulum weight within 10 minutes, but 23 of those solved it within a minute after a string was 'accidentally' set swinging. In Luchins's water jars, after practice items all solvable by one formula, only 23 percent used a simpler method on later items, while a control group used it consistently. The paradigm separates fixation produced by object presentation (functional fixedness) from fixation produced by practice (mental set).
steps: Choose or adapt a problem with an obvious but blocked solution and a less obvious workable one.
Create a fixation condition (object shown in its usual role, or a practice series that builds one procedure) and a control without it.
Randomly assign participants and set a time limit (for example 10 minutes).
Optionally add a hint condition (such as a subtle cue) for those who fail.
Record solution rates, time to solve and solution method.
Compare conditions, controlling the exact practice sequence.
outputs: Solution rates, times and methods by condition, and the effect of hints.
useWhen: Studying why expert or long-tenured users miss new, simpler workflows, or why a familiar control is not seen as usable for a new purpose.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating puzzle results as direct evidence about real tasks; for real workflow habits observe users in context.
whyLost: These are teaching classics in problem-solving research with no packaged UX use.
whereToUse: Feature migration and redesign, power-user tools, keyboard shortcut adoption, physical product and control design.
example: Long-time spreadsheet users are shown a new pivot feature after practising a manual formula method; only a quarter switch to the feature, while new users adopt it immediately, so release notes show it on users' own data.
sources: Duncker, K. (1945). On problem-solving. Psychological Monographs, 58
Luchins, A. S. (1942). Mechanization in problem solving: The effect of Einstellung. Psychological Monographs, 54
reference: Duncker, K. (1945). On problem-solving. Psychological Monographs, 58(5), whole no. 270.

name: Functional Localiser with Independent Split-Half ROI Analysis
aka: Functional localiser with independent split-half region-of-interest analysis
Independent localiser to avoid circular analysis
origin: Adapted for UX from cognitive neuroscience: Nancy Kanwisher with Josh McDermott and Marvin Chun, fMRI work begun in 1995 at Massachusetts General Hospital (published 1997)
summary: Define a functional brain region in each participant with a localiser contrast on half the data, then measure its response to the conditions of interest on the other half.
description: Brain regions with a given function sit in slightly different places in each person, so averaging over anatomy blurs them, and choosing a region from the same data used to measure it inflates effects (circular analysis). The functional localiser solves both. Each participant is scanned on a localiser contrast that isolates the function, such as faces versus objects, together with the experimental conditions. The data are split into independent halves: one half defines the participant's own region of interest, the other measures its response. Kanwisher's team used this to identify the fusiform face area, on the lateral fusiform gyrus and mostly right-lateralised, in almost every participant, and then tested its selectivity against many alternative explanations, later confirmed by single-cell recording and TMS. The same approach found place-, body- and mentalising-selective regions. For neuro-UX, it is the minimum standard for any claim that a design engages a specific functional region.
steps: Choose a localiser contrast that isolates the function of interest (for example faces versus objects, or scenes versus objects).
Scan each participant on both the localiser and the experimental conditions.
Split each participant's data into two independent halves (for example odd and even runs).
Use one half to define the participant's own region of interest from the localiser contrast.
Use the other half to measure the region's response to the conditions of interest.
Test the selectivity claim against alternative explanations with further contrasts and converging methods.
outputs: Individually defined functional regions and unbiased estimates of their response to each condition.
useWhen: Neuro-UX or consumer neuroscience studies that make claims about a specific functional region, such as face, scene or reward responses to interfaces, avatars or adverts.
avoidWhen: Whole-brain exploratory analyses, or when the research question can be answered behaviourally at far lower cost. A higher response to one category does not by itself show selectivity.
whyLost: fMRI is rare in UX, and neuromarketing studies often report regions chosen from the same data, without independent localisers.
whereToUse: Academic neuro-HCI, avatar and virtual human research, consumer neuroscience audits, evaluation of claims made by neuromarketing vendors.
example: A study claims a brand mascot 'activates the face area'. Re-analysing with a face localiser on odd runs and measurement on even runs shows the mascot's response falls between objects and faces, much weaker than the circular analysis suggested.
sources: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain (Bear et al., 2016)
reference: Kanwisher, N., McDermott, J. and Chun, M. M. (1997). The fusiform face area: a module in human extrastriate cortex specialized for face perception. Journal of Neuroscience, 17(11), 4302-4311.

name: Functional measurement (information integration)
aka: Functional measurement diagnosis of decision rules
Functional measurement of children's intuitive physics with judgement versus action responses
donor: Mathematical psychology; judgement and decision making
origin: Norman H. Anderson, 1970s-1980s; applied to consumer decisions by Jordan Louviere from 1974
summary: Replicated factorial rating experiments whose interaction patterns reveal whether people combine attributes additively, multiplicatively or otherwise, then yield interval-scale part-worths.
description: Information integration theory treats a rating as a linear function of an underlying overall value. Additive, multiplicative, distributive and other combination rules each predict a specific pattern of interactions in a factorial design, so ANOVA or regression on replicated ratings can falsify a model rather than merely fit one. If the right model holds, marginal means are interval-scale estimates of part-worths. Graphs of rating curves are read first: parallel lines indicate addition, diverging fans multiplication or complements, convergence substitutes. A developmental variant compares judgement with action responses on the same factorial task and finds dissociations, for instance children whose produced speeds follow physics while their judgements do not. The method is demanding but unusually diagnostic about decision rules, which ordinary conjoint analysis assumes rather than tests.
steps: Choose two or three attributes with at least three levels each (two levels only allow additivity to be rejected).
Build the complete factorial of profiles.
Have each respondent rate every profile at least twice on a graphic or line scale.
Plot rating curves for one attribute across levels of another and inspect for parallelism, fanning or convergence.
Run repeated-measures ANOVA or per-replication regressions, testing each effect against its replication-by-effect error.
Read the pattern: no interactions means additive; all interactions significant and positive means multiplicative; negative signs indicate substitutes.
Estimate part-worths from marginal means, predict ratings under the chosen model and test residuals.
Optionally collect action responses on the same task and compare their integration pattern with the judgements.
outputs: Diagnosed integration rule per respondent or group, interval-scale part-worths, value functions per attribute, and judgement-action comparisons.
useWhen: Feature, pricing and service trade-off research where it matters whether attributes compensate for each other or interact, with small attribute sets and willing participants.
avoidWhen: Avoid with more than three attributes or in quick field work, since replications are required; use choice-based conjoint or discrete choice modelling for large attribute sets.
whyLost: Choice-based conjoint and hierarchical Bayes estimation displaced metric rating designs in market research, and the replication burden made functional measurement unattractive.
whereToUse: Subscription bundles, delivery speed versus price, transport and mobility services, trust cues combined with price, educational tools.
example: A delivery app crosses fee, delivery window and courier rating in a 3 x 3 x 3 design rated twice by 40 users. Fanning curves show fee and speed interact multiplicatively, so discounts matter most for fast slots.
sources: Analyzing Decision Making: Metric Conjoint Analysis (Louviere, 1988)
Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
Anderson, N. H. (1981). Foundations of Information Integration Theory. Academic Press
reference: Anderson, N. H. (1981). Foundations of Information Integration Theory. New York: Academic Press.

name: Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS)
origin: Optical brain imaging from the 1990s; HCI use by Izzetoglu et al. (2004) and Hirshfield et al. (2007)
summary: A headband or cap of near-infrared emitters and detectors measures blood oxygenation in the outer cortex as a portable index of mental workload.
description: Near-infrared light passes a few centimetres through the scalp and skull; the wavelengths absorbed by oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin indicate local brain activity in the outer cortex. Compared with fMRI it measures only the surface and in less detail (about 1 cm resolution), but it is cheap, comfortable, portable and tolerant of movement, so it can be used during real tasks such as driving, and with awake infants, where it gives better spatial resolution than EEG. HCI studies have used it to distinguish task difficulty levels better than chance, predict workload in command and control, show that think-aloud and web-form layout add measurable workload, evaluate visualisations, and as an input channel. Signals are noisy and interpretation is hard, so studies need baselines, careful processing and collaboration with specialists.
steps: Define the conditions to compare (for example two interface designs or difficulty levels) and include rest baselines between blocks.
Fit the headband or cap with sources and detectors over the region of interest, usually prefrontal cortex for workload.
Record during repeated task blocks for each condition, logging task events.
Convert raw light signals to oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin and filter out motion and physiological noise.
Compare or classify conditions using block averages or machine-learning classifiers.
Triangulate with performance and subjective workload ratings, working with a neuroimaging specialist.
outputs: Haemodynamic responses per channel and condition, workload or mental-effort indices, and classification accuracy between conditions.
useWhen: You need a continuous, objective workload measure during realistic or mobile tasks where fMRI is impossible, such as driving, control rooms or comparing cognitively demanding designs.
avoidWhen: You lack specialist support, need deep brain measures, or a cheaper measure would answer the question; use NASA-TLX, pupillometry or task performance instead.
whyLost: It is established in neuroscience and neuroergonomics but requires equipment, signal processing and expertise that few UX teams have.
whereToUse: Automotive and aviation interfaces, control rooms, data visualisation, adaptive interfaces and learning technology.
example: A car maker compares two infotainment layouts in a driving simulator with 24 drivers wearing fNIRS headbands. Prefrontal oxygenation is higher with the nested menu, matching slower lane-keeping, so the flatter layout is chosen.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Ferrari, M., & Quaresima, V. (2012). A brief review on the history of human functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) development and fields of application. NeuroImage, 63(2), 921-935.

name: Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM)
origin: Erik Hollnagel, 2004-2012
summary: Models everyday work as coupled functions whose normal performance variability can resonate into unexpected outcomes, rather than as failure chains.
description: Listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix for systems engineering, FRAM describes a system as functions, each characterised by six aspects: input, output, precondition, resource, control and time. Analysts describe how functions are coupled and how the variability of each function's output (timing, precision) can combine and resonate to produce unexpected outcomes, good or bad. It is grounded in Safety-II: success and failure have the same sources, so understanding everyday performance matters more than counting errors. For UX, FRAM models service journeys or workflows across people, interfaces and automation to find where small, normal variations (a late update, an imprecise entry) amplify, guiding where to dampen variability or add monitoring.
steps: Define the purpose and scope of analysis (an event or typical work).
Identify functions and describe their six aspects from work-as-done data.
Characterise potential output variability for each function.
Map couplings and identify where variability can aggregate (functional resonance).
Propose ways to monitor and dampen unwanted variability or amplify useful variability.
Validate the model with practitioners.
outputs: FRAM model of coupled functions, variability analysis, resonance points, design and monitoring proposals.
useWhen: Complex sociotechnical services where outcomes emerge from normal variability rather than discrete failures.
avoidWhen: Simple linear tasks; HTA or UFMEA are more efficient.
whyLost: FRAM lives in resilience engineering and patient-safety circles, and its abstract hexagon diagrams are unfamiliar to designers. UX tends to study individual tasks rather than coupled organisational functions.
whereToUse: Hospital discharge, airline disruption handling, delivery networks, human-AI workflows.
example: A FRAM model of hospital discharge shows that slight delays in pharmacy sign-off couple with transport booking to cause evening discharges; the discharge app adds a predicted sign-off time.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Hollnagel E (2012) FRAM: The Functional Resonance Analysis Method
Hollnagel E (2004) Barriers and Accident Prevention
Hollnagel, FRAM: The Functional Resonance Analysis Method (2012)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Hollnagel E (2012) FRAM: The Functional Resonance Analysis Method: Modelling Complex Socio-technical Systems. Ashgate.

name: Functional-operation response-time accounting
origin: Allen Newell with Paul Rosenbloom and Bonnie John (John, Rosenbloom and Newell, 1985; John and Newell, 1987)
summary: Predict the time of a speeded response by chaining fixed functional operations (perceive, encode, attend, comprehend, task set-up, intend, decode, move) and summing stipulated operator times.
description: For speeded, practised, low-error tasks, Newell describes an abstract analysis at a finer grain than GOMS. The analyst does not write a running model but decomposes the response into a fixed order of functions: Perceive, Encode, Attend, Comprehend, Task set-up, Intend, Decode, Move. For each, they decide whether it is needed and how many operators or productions it takes, apply stipulated constants (production about 20 ms, minimal operator about 60 ms, perception about 40 ms, simple motor act about 60 ms) and sum. This gives about 220 ms for simple reaction and about 380 ms for two-choice reaction. For stimulus-response compatibility, the mapping is written as an algorithm of operators from stimulus to response: John's model fitted 27 compatibility situations with about 12% average error and predicted recall of command abbreviations, such as typing 'dlt' for 'delete' (about 2,573 ms predicted against 2,400 ms observed).
steps: Check the task fits the immediate-response paradigm: speeded, prepared person, controlled setting, simple practised stimulus-response rule.
Lay out the functions in fixed order (Perceive, Encode, Attend, Comprehend, Task set-up, Intend, Decode, Move) and mark which are needed.
For mapping tasks such as abbreviations or key assignments, write the mapping algorithm as a chain of operators from stimulus to response.
Assign stipulated constants (for example production 20 ms, minimal operator 60 ms, perception 40 ms, motor act 60 ms) to each operator.
Sum to predict response time for each design alternative or mapping rule.
Compare predictions with observed mean times from a small test and refine the algorithm if errors exceed about 15%.
outputs: Predicted response times per condition or mapping rule, and a predicted-versus-observed comparison.
useWhen: When choosing between mapping rules for codes, abbreviations, shortcuts, controls or alert-response assignments where milliseconds and compatibility matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid for tasks with errors, problem solving or long sequences (use Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) or GOMS / KLM). Many alternative algorithms are possible, constants are approximate, and errors are out of scope.
whyLost: It was a research demonstration of unified cognitive theory; KLM and GOMS offered coarser but easier predictions, and later cognitive architectures absorbed the idea.
whereToUse: Keyboard shortcut and abbreviation schemes, control-room and cockpit response mappings, game controls, voice command naming.
example: A trading platform compares two shortcut schemes. The functional analysis predicts the vowel-deletion scheme is about 300 ms slower per command than first-letter mnemonics, which a 12-person timing test confirms.
reference: John, B. E., Rosenbloom, P. S., & Newell, A. (1985). A theory of stimulus-response compatibility applied to human-computer interaction. Proceedings of CHI '85, 213-219; Newell, A. (1990). Unified Theories of Cognition. Harvard University Press.

name: Functionalism and Multiple Realisability in UI Design
origin: Hilary Putnam (1967); Jerry Fodor; collected in Haugeland (ed.), Mind Design II (1997)
summary: Defines interface elements by their functional role, the inputs, outputs and relations they support, so equivalent functions can be realised differently across platforms and modalities.
description: Functionalist philosophy of mind: mental states are defined by their functional role (causal relations to inputs, outputs, and other mental states), not by their physical substrate. Multiple realizability: the same functional state can be realized by different physical implementations. Applied to UX: the same user cognitive state (confusion, engagement, flow) can be produced by many different interface implementations — and any interface producing the right functional role produces the right experience.
steps: Identify the target cognitive/emotional state (e.g., flow, trust, engagement). Apply functional role analysis: what must be true of a design to produce this state?
(1) What inputs (interface properties) must be present?
(2) What other states must it connect to (preconditions, consequences)?
(3) What outputs (user behaviors) should it produce? Any design satisfying all three criteria should work — test multiple realizations.
outputs: Functional role specifications for key components, platform-specific realisations that preserve role, and equivalence tests across devices and modalities.
useWhen: Multi-platform and multimodal products, design systems spanning web, mobile, voice and wearables, and accessibility alternatives that must be functionally equivalent.
avoidWhen: For single-platform visual design questions, or when the team needs empirical user data rather than conceptual specification.
whyLost: It remained a philosophical thesis; design systems grew around visual components rather than functional roles, so the framing never migrated into practice.
whereToUse: Design principle formulation, cross-platform design consistency, AI system behavior design, emotional design research.
example: A bank's design system defines a 'confirm irreversible transfer' role by its required inputs, feedback and reversibility. The web modal, the watch double-tap and the voice assistant's spoken confirmation are tested to ensure all three realise the same role.
sources: Mind Design II — MIT Press (Haugeland, ed.)
reference: Haugeland J (Ed.) (1997) Mind Design II: Philosophy, Psychology, Artificial Intelligence. MIT Press

name: Funnel Analysis
origin: AIDA sales funnel (E. St. Elmo Lewis, 1898); digital conversion funnels from web analytics, late 1990s
summary: Measures the proportion of users completing each step of a defined sequence to locate where and for whom drop-off occurs.
description: Funnel analysis defines an ordered sequence of events, such as landing, sign-up, verification and first action, and calculates the share of users progressing from each step to the next within a time window. The biggest relative drops point to where to look. Rigour depends on careful event definitions, choosing whether steps must occur in strict order, setting a sensible conversion window, and segmenting by acquisition channel, device and user type, since aggregate funnels hide very different behaviours. Comparing funnels before and after changes requires controlling for seasonality and traffic mix, ideally through experiments. Funnels show where users leave but not why, so the method is strongest when paired with session replay, usability tests or intercept surveys at the leaking step.
steps: Define the target sequence and the exact events representing each step, verifying instrumentation.
Choose ordering rules and a conversion window appropriate to the flow (e.g. same session or 7 days).
Compute step-to-step and overall conversion rates over a stable period.
Segment by channel, device, platform, new versus returning and other relevant attributes.
Identify the largest relative drops and investigate them with qualitative methods.
Test fixes with A/B experiments and monitor funnel metrics post-launch.
outputs: Funnel chart, step conversion rates, segment comparisons, prioritised drop-off points.
useWhen: Onboarding, checkout, sign-up, multi-step forms and any conversion-critical flow with event tracking.
avoidWhen: Non-linear exploratory products where users do not follow fixed sequences; use path analysis instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Core product analytics technique; supported by all major analytics platforms.
whereToUse: Onboarding; checkout; multi-step forms; any conversion-critical flow.
example: A fintech onboarding funnel showed 71% of users dropping at ID verification on Android only. Session replays showed the camera permission prompt failing on certain devices, and a fix lifted completion by 18 points on Android.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Beasley, M. (2013). Practical Web Analytics for User Experience. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Funnel Matrix
origin: Jaime Levy (2015), extending the funnel matrix in Cooper and Vlaskovits, The Entrepreneur's Guide to Customer Development (2010), with stages informed by Croll and Yoskovitz, Lean Analytics (2013)
summary: A shared planning spreadsheet mapping each engagement stage, from suspect to reference user, to desired actions, business tasks, one metric, required features and learning questions.
description: The Funnel Matrix is a cross-functional planning grid that ties an early product to its business model. Rows are engagement stages: Suspect, Lead, Prospect, Customer, Repeat User and Reference User. Columns record the user's process (touchpoints, channels, activities), the desired action, the business task that drives it, one key metric per stage, the functionality required to support it and the validated-learning questions to answer. Filling it forces the team to decide what the minimum viable feature set really is, because every feature must earn its place against a stage and a metric. Levy uses it as the central metrics repository for a time-boxed experiment, and adapts it to maturity: optimising an existing MVP, speculating before one, or testing only the Suspect row with landing pages at concept stage. She prefers it to journey maps because it is benchmarked against real data.
steps: Define the stage rows from the business model, starting with the generic labels Suspect, Lead, Prospect, Customer, Repeat User and Reference User.
Fill the first row across every column before moving down: user's process, desired action, business task, metric, required functionality and validated-learning questions.
Choose one key metric per stage and reject vanity metrics.
Write learning questions that are measurable, and have a teammate cross-check each one.
Run the session as a cross-functional team in two to four hours and set a time limit for the experiment (Levy's TradeYa case used 60 days).
Instrument analytics to capture each stage's metric.
Update cells as data arrive and iterate the build-measure-learn cycle.
outputs: A completed matrix with a stage-by-stage metric plan, an MVP feature list and a set of measurable learning questions.
useWhen: Use it when a start-up or new product team must agree what to build first and how each stage of acquisition and engagement will be measured.
avoidWhen: Do not use it to understand why users drop out; use Funnel Analysis on real data and Customer problem interviews for that. Questions such as 'how intrigued were users' are not measurable and do not belong in it.
whyLost: It lives in the lean start-up and UX strategy niche around Levy's book; mainstream teams use AARRR dashboards and journey maps instead.
whereToUse: Marketplace and consumer start-ups, new product lines inside SaaS companies, and growth teams planning an MVP experiment.
example: A peer-to-peer trading app defines a Lead as someone who signs up with a social login and a Customer as someone who completes a trade. The matrix shows bidding, posting and a poll are needed for launch, while profiles and payments can wait.
reference: Levy, J. (2015). UX Strategy: How to Devise Innovative Digital Products that People Want. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. Chapter 9, pp. 205-225.

name: Future Workshop
origin: Robert Jungk and Norbert Müllert, 1970s-1987; adopted in Scandinavian PD (Kensing and Madsen, 1991)
summary: A three-phase workshop of critique, fantasy and implementation that lets affected people articulate problems and envision alternatives on their own terms.
description: The future workshop, named in the treatise among the Scandinavian participatory methods, structures participation in three phases. In the critique phase, participants list problems with the current situation without solution-talk. In the fantasy phase, they invert critiques into utopian visions, suspending constraints. In the implementation phase, they assess what can be realised and plan actions. The structure protects participants' framing of problems, separates divergent and convergent thinking, and is designed for people without design training. Kensing and Madsen paired it with metaphorical design to generate system visions with workers.
steps: Prepare: recruit affected participants, a facilitator and a neutral venue; agree the theme.
Critique phase: brainstorm and cluster problems with the current situation, using short statements.
Fantasy phase: invert the key critiques into ideal futures, banning feasibility objections.
Implementation phase: evaluate fantasies against constraints and identify realisable steps.
Agree action plans with owners and follow-up dates.
Feed outputs into design and report back to participants.
outputs: Critique clusters, utopian visions, prioritised implementation plans.
useWhen: Early-stage visioning with stakeholders, especially where power or trust issues exist.
avoidWhen: Detailed design or evaluation questions; use prototyping or testing instead.
whyLost: Overtaken by design-thinking ideation formats that drop the critique phase and the activist framing.
whereToUse: Civic services, union or worker-facing tools, NHS service redesign, community technology.
example: Library staff run a future workshop on a new self-service system; the critique phase surfaces fear of losing patron contact, and the fantasy phase produces a 'roaming librarian' concept that becomes the service model.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Jungk R & Müllert N (1987) Future Workshops: How to Create Desirable Futures
Kensing F & Madsen KH (1991) Generating visions: future workshops and metaphorical design. In Design at Work
Jungk & Müllert, Future Workshops: How to Create Desirable Futures (1987)
Kensing & Madsen, Generating visions: Future workshops and metaphorical design (1991), in Greenbaum & Kyng (eds.), Design at Work
reference: Kensing F & Madsen KH (1991) Generating visions: future workshops and metaphorical design. In Greenbaum & Kyng (Eds) Design at Work. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Future-Oriented Diary and Pre-Mortem Protocol
origin: Pre-mortem from Gary Klein, 2007; expectation-experience comparison from expectancy research
summary: Participants predict an experience before it happens and record the reality afterwards; the gap measures mental model accuracy, with a pre-mortem variant for risks.
description: This protocol pairs a prediction entry before a task with an experience entry immediately after. Participants say what they expect will happen, what will be easy or hard, and how long it will take; afterwards they report what actually happened. The gap between prediction and experience is the data: it locates inaccurate mental models, system behaviour users find systematically surprising, and miscalibrated confidence. The pre-mortem variant, adapted from Gary Klein's project risk technique, asks experienced users to imagine that a new feature has failed after six months and explain why, generating a risk inventory before launch. Both make expectations explicit rather than inferred after the fact.
steps: Prediction diary entry (before use): Before the participant begins a task or interaction, ask them to predict: "What do you think will happen? What will be easy? What will be difficult? How long do you think it will take?"
Experience diary entry (after use): Immediately after: "What actually happened? What was easier or harder than expected? How long did it actually take?"

Gap analysis: The gap between prediction and experience is your data. A prediction gap reveals: (a) where mental models are inaccurate, (b) where the system's behaviour is systematically unexpected, (c) where user confidence is miscalibrated.

Pre-mortem variant: Before a new feature or redesign launches, ask experienced users to imagine that the feature has failed completely after 6 months of use. "What went wrong? Why did users stop using it?" The resulting list is your risk inventory for user research.
outputs: Prediction-experience gap tables, mental model inaccuracies, calibration measures, and a user-generated risk inventory.
useWhen: Testing mental models of new or complex features, onboarding expectation-setting, or anticipating failure modes before a launch.
avoidWhen: When participants have no basis to predict (wholly novel concepts), or for routine tasks where predictions add nothing; use concept testing or usability tests.
whyLost: Pre-mortems are known as team rituals, but structured prediction-versus-experience recording with users is rarely run.
whereToUse: Onboarding, AI features where expectations are often wrong, financial products with delays (transfers, claims, loans), and feature launches.
example: Before a first international transfer, users predict arrival time and fees; afterwards they record reality. A consistent one-day overestimate of speed leads to clearer arrival estimates on the confirmation screen.
reference: Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review, 85(9), 18-19.

name: Futures Wheel
origin: Jerome Glenn, 1971
summary: Places a change at the centre and maps its direct, second-order and third-order consequences in rings, revealing knock-on effects and risks.
description: The futures wheel is a structured brainstorming method for exploring consequences. A trend or decision sits in the centre; first-order consequences are drawn around it; each generates second-order consequences, and so on. Participants label consequences as positive or negative, likely or speculative, and link interactions. Done rigorously, it uses diverse participants, evidence for first-order effects, and follow-up assessment of likelihood and impact, turning results into risk registers or research questions. For UX, it is a quick way to examine second-order effects of features, such as how a 'read receipts' feature changes social obligations, before launch.
steps: Write the change (feature, policy, trend) precisely in the centre.
With a diverse group, generate first-order consequences for different stakeholders.
For each, generate second- and third-order consequences, drawing links between rings.
Mark consequences as desirable or undesirable and estimate likelihood and impact.
Identify consequences needing evidence and convert them into research questions or metrics.
Feed high-impact negative consequences into design mitigations and monitoring.
outputs: A futures wheel diagram, prioritised second-order effects, research questions and mitigations.
useWhen: Assessing the downstream effects of a feature, policy or technology trend before committing.
avoidWhen: Well-understood changes with established evidence of effects.
whyLost: Futures tools are seen as speculative; UX evaluates features at first order through testing.
whereToUse: Social features, AI automation, policy changes, pricing changes, platform rules.
example: A futures wheel for 'AI auto-replies in messaging' surfaces third-order effects: recipients start distrusting quick replies, prompting a disclosure indicator and further research on norms.
sources: Glenn, The futures wheel (2009), in Glenn & Gordon (eds.), Futures Research Methodology Version 3.0, Millennium Project
Glenn, Futurizing teaching vs futures course (1972), Social Science Record
reference: Glenn, J. C. (2009). The Futures Wheel. In Futures Research Methodology 3.0. The Millennium Project.

name: Fuzzy DEMATEL
origin: DEMATEL: Battelle Memorial Institute, Geneva (Gabus and Fontela, 1970s); fuzzy extension with triangular fuzzy numbers and CFCS defuzzification; UX application by Zhou et al. (2022)
summary: Experts rate how strongly each factor influences every other; fuzzy matrix algebra then ranks factors by importance and separates causes from effects.
description: DEMATEL uses graph theory and matrix algebra to screen influencing factors in a complex system. Experts rate the direct influence of each factor on each other on a 0 to 4 scale. Because such judgements are vague, the fuzzy version converts ratings to triangular fuzzy numbers, defuzzifies each expert's matrix with the CFCS method and averages them into a direct relation matrix. This is normalised and the total relation matrix computed as T = D(I - D) inverse, capturing indirect influence. Row sums R and column sums C give centrality R + C (importance) and cause degree R - C (positive means cause, negative means effect). A causal diagram plots both. In UX it turns a long list of experience factors into a small set of causal levers.
steps: Build the factor list from literature and prior research, then trim it with a short questionnaire.
Have each expert rate the influence of every factor on every other: 0 none, 1 weak, 2 moderate, 3 strong, 4 very strong.
Convert ratings to triangular fuzzy numbers (for example none = 0, 0, 0.25; weak = 0, 0.25, 0.5).
Defuzzify each expert's matrix with CFCS and average across experts to obtain the direct relation matrix Z.
Normalise Z by the largest row or column sum to obtain D, then compute the total relation matrix T = D(I - D)^-1.
Compute row sums R and column sums C, centrality R + C and cause degree R - C.
Plot the cause-effect diagram and select key factors by centrality, prioritising high-centrality cause factors as design levers.
outputs: A ranked factor list, sets of cause and effect factors, and a cause-effect diagram.
useWhen: You have many interrelated experience factors and need to know which ones drive others, with only expert judgement available.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you can measure factors and outcomes from users directly; use key driver analysis or structural equation modelling. Results depend heavily on a small expert panel and on the starting factor list.
whyLost: It thrives in operations research and supply-chain studies and appears in HCI conference papers, but practitioners rarely need or trust expert-only causal maps.
whereToUse: Prioritising experience factors for complex products, service quality programmes, design system governance, and early strategy where user data is thin.
example: A music streaming team lists 19 experience factors and asks ten heavy users and critics to rate pairwise influence. Fuzzy DEMATEL shows catalogue richness and personalisation as high-centrality cause factors, while satisfaction with the player interface is mostly an effect.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Zhou, M. et al. (2022). Identifying Key Factors Influencing Mobile Music App User Experience in China Using a Fuzzy DEMATEL Method. DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, Springer, pp. 339-350.

name: Gabor-Granger Pricing
origin: André Gabor and Clive Granger, 1960s (Price as an indicator of quality, 1966)
summary: Asks purchase intention at a sequence of prices to build a demand curve and identify the revenue-maximising price.
description: Respondents are shown a product and asked if they would buy at a given price; depending on the answer, the price moves up or down a ladder, typically 5-7 price points. Aggregating gives the proportion willing to buy at each price, a demand curve, and multiplying by price gives a revenue curve with a maximum. The method is simple and suits single products with known value. Its weaknesses are hypothetical bias and anchoring from the starting price, so rigour comes from randomising start points, calibrating stated intent (e.g. 'definitely' responses weighted) and validating against behavioural tests.
steps: Define the product, context and 5-7 realistic price points.
Randomise the starting price across respondents to manage anchoring.
Ask purchase likelihood at each price, moving up after yes and down after no.
Calibrate stated likelihood (e.g. count only top-box, or apply calibration factors from past launches).
Construct demand and revenue curves with confidence intervals and identify revenue-maximising price by segment.
Validate with a live price test or fake-door experiment where possible.
outputs: Demand curve, revenue curve, price elasticity estimates and segment differences.
useWhen: Pricing a single, well-understood product or plan with a plausible price range.
avoidWhen: Products where features vary with price (use conjoint) or new categories with no reference (start with Van Westendorp).
whyLost: Pricing research sits outside UX, and the method's simplicity hides its biases.
whereToUse: Subscription plans, in-app purchases, B2B seat pricing, add-ons.
example: A meditation app's Gabor-Granger study with 1,200 users finds revenue peaks at $59 per year, but a live A/B price test shows actual conversion 40% lower than stated, so stated figures are recalibrated for future studies.
sources: Gabor & Granger, Price as an indicator of quality: report on an enquiry (1966), Economica
Nagle & Müller, The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing (6th ed., 2018)
reference: Gabor, A., & Granger, C. W. J. (1966). Price as an indicator of quality. Economica, 33(129), 43-70.

name: Galvanic Skin Response
origin: Charles Féré, 1888; Ivan Tarchanoff, 1890
summary: Measures changes in skin conductance driven by sweat gland activity as an index of physiological arousal, detecting stress or frustration moments during interaction.
description: Electrodermal activity reflects sympathetic nervous system activation: as arousal rises, eccrine sweat glands, particularly on palms and fingers, increase skin conductance. The signal has a slow tonic level and phasic responses (skin conductance responses) occurring one to three seconds after a stimulus. It indicates arousal intensity, not valence, so it cannot distinguish excitement from frustration without other data. In UX it is used to identify moments of stress, surprise or frustration in tasks, games and immersive experiences. Rigour comes from controlling temperature and movement, recording baselines, separating tonic and phasic components, time-locking responses to events, using within-subject comparisons because individual differences are large, and combining EDA with video, self-report or facial coding to interpret valence.
steps: Define events or segments of interest and how arousal relates to the research question.
Attach sensors to fingers or palm (or validated wrist devices) and control room temperature.
Record a resting baseline of several minutes before tasks.
Run tasks with precisely time-stamped events and record video for context, with 15-30 participants.
Decompose the signal into tonic and phasic components and count or measure responses in windows 1-4 seconds after events.
Interpret peaks alongside video, self-report or facial coding to determine valence.
outputs: Arousal timelines, event-locked response counts and amplitudes, annotated stress or frustration moments.
useWhen: Detecting frustration or stress in usability studies, games, VR, automotive and high-stakes tasks where self-report may be unreliable.
avoidWhen: When valence matters more than arousal, when participants move a lot, or when observation and think-aloud already reveal the issues. Arousal is not specific to one mental state: the polygraph is not accepted as a lie detector because sweating and heart-rate changes are not reliably linked to deception, so do not read stress, trust or deceit from this signal alone.
whyLost: It persists in psychophysiology, neuromarketing and games research but UX rarely invests in lab equipment and signal-processing expertise, and earlier wrist wearables produced unreliable data.
whereToUse: Emotional response research; frustration detection; high-stakes usability testing.
example: A telehealth app recorded EDA from 20 older adults during first video consultations. Phasic peaks clustered at the camera permission prompt, consistent with think-aloud remarks of anxiety, leading to a pre-call camera check.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 38 — FACS, Micro-Expression Analysis & Psychophysiology
Society for Neuroscience, Brain Facts: A Primer on the Brain and Nervous System, 8th ed. (2018)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Boucsein, W. (2012). Electrodermal Activity (2nd ed.). Springer.

name: Game Approachability Principles (GAP)
donor: Games user research and learning science
origin: Heather Desurvire and Charlotte Wiberg (2008 onward); presented in chapter 14 by Desurvire and Wixon
summary: Twenty-seven heuristics for checking how well a game teaches new and casual players to play, covering demonstration, practice, feedback, self-efficacy and knowledge transfer.
description: GAP complements the PLAY heuristics by focusing on approachability: how a game helps people who lack gaming conventions, or have little time, to get into it. The authors argue that as games grew more complex and audiences broadened, casual players became more likely to quit when a game felt hard and less likely to seek help from guides or forums, so learning support became critical. The 27 heuristics are grouped into categories such as demonstration and practice, demonstration of actions with feedback, self-efficacy and knowledge transfer. Examples include 'the game allows the player to practise', 'the player knows what actions they are able to perform', 'after the initial training period the player feels they have learned enough to play' and 'the game is similar to other games of a genre'. GAP is applied in the same inductive or deductive ways as PLAY, recording adherences, violations and enhancements. For UX teams outside games, GAP is a ready-made checklist for onboarding and learnability, grounded in ideas about modelling, practice and self-efficacy.
steps: Define the target novice or casual player and the skills the first session must teach.
Play through the first-time experience as that player would.
Check each GAP heuristic and record adherences, violations and enhancement ideas.
Pay particular attention to whether actions are demonstrated, practised with feedback and reinforced.
Compare findings across evaluators and prioritise violations that block early progress.
Validate key issues with a small first-time playtest.
outputs: A list of approachability problems and strengths in the first-time experience, organised by GAP category.
useWhen: Reviewing tutorials, onboarding or the first session of a game or complex app.
avoidWhen: The audience is expert and onboarding is not a concern, or you need behavioural evidence of learning.
whyLost: Specific to game design literature; general UX onboarding practice rarely draws on it.
whereToUse: Game tutorials, first-time user experience in apps, complex creative or professional software.
example: A GAP review of a mobile card game finds that combo moves are shown once but never practised with feedback, and the tutorial is redesigned.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 14 (Desurvire and Wixon).

name: Game Experience Questionnaire (GEQ)
origin: IJsselsteijn, de Kort and Poels, Game Experience Lab, Eindhoven (2008); used in Chapters 6 and 11
summary: A modular self-report questionnaire measuring player experience during and after play, including competence, immersion, flow, challenge, affect and tiredness.
description: The GEQ has four modules: a core module for the experience of play, an in-game module for brief measurement during play, a social presence module for play with others, and a post-game module for how players feel afterwards. Items are rated on a scale from 0 (not agree) to 4 (completely agree) and averaged into components. In the core module these are competence, sensory and imaginative immersion, flow, tension, challenge, negative affect and positive affect; the post-game module covers positive experience, negative experience and tiredness. Researchers choose modules to suit the study; Chapter 6 dropped the social presence and in-game modules because the game had no other players and short play time. The chapter also shows good practice: recode reversed items, check each component's Cronbach's alpha, drop items with low item-scale correlation and discard unreliable components before comparing conditions. In that study a tangible interface produced higher competence, immersion and positive affect than an equivalent tablet interface. Chapter 11 uses a home-made questionnaire under the same name, so check which instrument a report means.
steps: Choose the modules relevant to the study (core, in-game, social presence, post-game).
Administer the core and post-game modules immediately after a defined play session; use in-game items at breaks if needed.
Recode reversed items and compute component scores as item means.
Check reliability per component, removing weak items and setting aside unreliable components.
Compare components between conditions or versions with suitable tests.
Interpret results with interviews or observation to explain differences.
outputs: Component scores for player experience (competence, immersion, flow, challenge, affect, tiredness and so on) for each condition.
useWhen: Comparing game versions, controllers or interfaces on player experience, or tracking experience across iterations.
avoidWhen: Products are not games, or you need a short instrument with strong published validation; some GEQ components have shown weak reliability.
whyLost: Widely used in games research, but general UX teams tend to use broader instruments such as UEQ or AttrakDiff.
whereToUse: Video games, tangible and mixed-reality games, serious games, gamified interfaces.
example: A study compares a tangible block controller with a tablet version of the same puzzle game using the GEQ core and post-game modules; the tangible group scores higher on competence and positive affect, while flow and challenge do not differ.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Menestrina, Z., Conci, A., Siesser, A., Masu, R., Bianchi, M. and De Angeli, A. (2016). Tangible and graphical game interfaces: an experimental comparison. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 6. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Game Thinking Progression Design
origin: Amy Jo Kim, 2018
summary: Applies game design's player journey (onboarding, habit building, mastery) to product design, co-developed with early superfans through rapid prototyping.
description: Game thinking, as articulated by Amy Jo Kim, transfers how successful games structure experience to non-game products. It defines a player journey in three stages: onboarding (learning the ropes), habit building (a compelling core loop that brings people back) and mastery (deeper challenges and status for experienced users). Rather than designing for everyone, the team identifies early superfans, people who already have the problem intensely, and co-creates with them through fast, cheap prototypes and short test cycles. Progression milestones and the core learning loop are designed explicitly and validated against behaviour. Rigour comes from grounding loops in real user motivation, measuring retention at each journey stage, and iterating rather than adding mechanics.
steps: Map the mastery journey in four stages: discovery, onboarding, habit-building and mastery.
Discovery: what does a first-time visitor need to understand to decide to try the product?
Onboarding: what is the 'beginner's mind' moment for newcomers?
Habit-building: what core learning loop (trigger, activity, feedback, progress) keeps regulars returning?
Mastery: what does expert use look like and feel like, and what roles can enthusiasts take on?
For each stage, identify the intrinsic reward and write it as a job story.
