Select mechanics that amplify each stage's intrinsic reward (for example levelling for mastery, streaks for habit) and drop mechanics that do not map to a stage.
outputs: A player journey map, a core learning loop, superfan research insights, progression milestones and prototype test findings.
useWhen: New products seeking product-market fit, engagement-driven products, learning and community platforms where progression and mastery sustain use.
avoidWhen: Avoid for utilitarian tools where users want to finish and leave; avoid when engagement is not in users' interest.
whyLost: Gamification hype focused on surface mechanics; Kim's systems-level game thinking stayed within the startup coaching world.
whereToUse: Community platform design, enterprise software engagement, health behavior apps, learning products.
example: A language-learning startup identifies twelve superfans, maps their journey from first lesson to daily habit to conversational mastery, and prototypes a weekly challenge loop tested with them before scaling.
reference: Kim AJ (2018) Game Thinking: Innovate Smarter and Drive Deep Engagement with Design Techniques from Hit Games. Gamethinking.io

name: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-User Systems
origin: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, 1944; John Nash, 1950
summary: Models how users' choices interact strategically in multi-user products, predicting equilibria such as free-riding or gaming and testing design changes to incentives.
description: Game theory models situations where each actor's best choice depends on what others do. In multi-user products, such as marketplaces, reviews, referrals, social feeds and collaborative tools, individual behaviour that is sensible for one user can produce collective outcomes no one wants: review inflation, free-riding on shared content, race-to-the-bottom pricing. The method formalises the actors, their available strategies and payoffs, then identifies Nash equilibria and checks whether they match observed behaviour. Rigour comes from making payoffs explicit and grounding them in data, testing robustness to assumptions, and validating predictions with behavioural logs or controlled experiments. It moves teams beyond individual-level UX thinking to see how design rules create incentives across the whole population.
steps: Identify the actors (e.g. buyers, sellers, creators, moderators) and the strategic decisions each makes.
Specify strategies and estimate payoffs for each actor, using data where possible.
Build a payoff matrix or extensive-form model and identify equilibria.
Compare predicted equilibria with observed behaviour from logs or research.
Model proposed design changes as altered payoffs and predict the new equilibrium.
Validate with experiments or staged rollouts and monitor for unintended strategic responses.
outputs: Strategic model of actors and payoffs, equilibrium predictions, design changes ranked by predicted incentive effect.
useWhen: Marketplaces, social platforms, ratings and review systems, referral schemes and any feature where users' outcomes depend on each other.
avoidWhen: Single-user tools without strategic interdependence; standard usability and behavioural research suffice.
whyLost: Latent: Academically interesting; rarely applied in UX practice outside platform/marketplace design.
whereToUse: Social platforms; marketplace design; multiplayer features; incentive system design.
example: A freelance marketplace saw average ratings drift to 4.9. Modelling revealed mutual reciprocity as the equilibrium of a simultaneous reveal-later system; switching to blind double reviews was predicted and then shown to widen rating variance.
sources: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (von Neumann & Morgenstern)
reference: Osborne, M. J. (2004). An Introduction to Game Theory. Oxford University Press.

name: GameFlow Evaluation
donor: Games research, building on flow theory
origin: Sweetser and Wyeth (2005), based on Csikszentmihalyi's flow elements; applied by Hernandez Luna and Golightly in Chapter 8
summary: Evaluating enjoyment by checking a game against eight flow-based elements: concentration, challenge, player skills, control, clear goals, feedback, immersion and social interaction.
description: GameFlow translates Csikszentmihalyi's elements of flow into eight criteria for enjoyable games. Concentration: the game provides stimuli worth attending to. Challenge: difficulty matches skill and offers levels. Player skills: players can start without a manual and learning is part of the fun. Control: players feel in control of characters and of the interface and devices. Clear goals: overriding and intermediate goals are clear at the right time. Feedback: progress and actions get timely feedback. Immersion: players become less aware of their surroundings. Social interaction: the game supports competition, cooperation and chat. Each element comes with detailed criteria, so the model can be used as an expert review checklist or turned into statements for a post-play questionnaire. Chapter 8 does both: the authors and an industry expert analysed how freemium and advertising business models interrupt each element, then converted the criteria into a questionnaire that 15 players completed after short sessions with three mobile games, framed by semi-structured interviews. For UX, the model offers a structured vocabulary for enjoyment and for diagnosing what breaks it, such as ads or paywalls.
steps: Select the GameFlow elements and criteria relevant to the product and context of use.
For an expert review, play the product and judge each criterion, noting where and why it is met or broken.
For player evaluation, convert criteria into short agreement statements for a post-play questionnaire.
Have participants play for a fixed period, then complete the questionnaire.
Use semi-structured interviews before and after play to explain the ratings.
Summarise results by element and link breakdowns to specific design features.
outputs: Element-by-element ratings or judgements of enjoyment, with explanations of which design features support or break flow.
useWhen: You need to understand why a game or game-like experience is or is not enjoyable, or how a design decision such as monetisation affects enjoyment.
avoidWhen: The product is not intended to be engaging in a play sense, or you need a validated psychometric scale with norms.
whyLost: Known widely in games research but less used in general UX, where engagement is usually measured through analytics or generic satisfaction scales.
whereToUse: Mobile and console games, gamified apps, learning games, evaluating ads and in-app purchases.
example: A team compares three free mobile games and finds that banner ads around the play area hardly affect concentration, while full-screen video ads and waiting timers break concentration and immersion, leading some players to abandon play.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Hernandez Luna, C. L. and Golightly, D. (2016). Business models within mobile gaming experience. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 8. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Gameplay Metrics Analysis
origin: Game analytics practice at studios and in research by Anders Drachen and colleagues; described by Drachen and Shawn Connor (chapter 19) and Lysiane Charest (chapter 20)
summary: Designs in-game events, turns the resulting telemetry into gameplay metrics such as deaths, completion times and paths by level or map location, and analyses them to find where and how player behaviour departs from the design.
description: Every action in a game runs code that can be logged. Gameplay metrics analysis starts by designing events, such as a player firing a weapon, with related data (weapon, position, match time, outcome) and shared identifiers so that sequences can be reconstructed. Raw telemetry is summarised into gameplay metrics, for example average completion time per level, causes of death per level shown as a progress-frequency chart, or player positions over time plotted on the map. Drachen and Connor distinguish explorative analysis, such as drill-down through finer data and filters until an insight appears, from hypothesis-driven analysis, such as testing whether zombies on Level 10 are over-represented among causes of death; in practice the two alternate. Statistical models and machine learning extend the toolbox, from classification for churn or purchase prediction to clustering of play styles. For user researchers, metrics give precise behavioural records, reach far beyond lab samples, allow live hypothesis testing and connect to business metrics, while lab methods explain why. Charest shows how small studios can start with a few well-documented events around first-time experience, progression, level design and monetisation. The approach suits any product where behaviour unfolds in a space or sequence.
steps: Agree the design and research questions the data should answer.
Design and document events with context attributes and identifiers that link related events.
Validate the instrumentation in test builds before release.
Aggregate telemetry into gameplay metrics by level, map area, encounter or session.
Explore with drill-downs and visualisations (progress-frequency charts, map overlays) and test specific hypotheses.
Where needed, apply models such as clustering or churn prediction.
Triangulate findings with playtests or interviews and feed changes back for re-measurement.
outputs: Gameplay metrics, charts and map overlays showing where and how players progress, fail or deviate, plus tested hypotheses.
useWhen: A game or app is instrumented (or can be) and the team needs behavioural evidence at scale about progression, difficulty or feature use.
avoidWhen: Instrumentation is not possible, sample sizes are tiny, or the question is about feelings and reasons.
whyLost: Mainstream in games and product analytics teams, but in UX research it is often left to separate analytics teams, so researchers rarely design events themselves.
whereToUse: Games of all sizes, mobile apps, spatial and map-based products, learning platforms with levels or modules.
example: Telemetry shows 40 per cent of deaths in level 4 of a platform game come from falling in one room; a map overlay shows players miss a ledge, and a lighting change halves the deaths.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapters 19 (Drachen and Connor) and 20 (Charest).

name: Gamer Motivation Profile
origin: Nick Yee and Nicolas Ducheneaut at Quantic Foundry (Yee, 2015); chapter 28
summary: A factor-analytically derived survey inventory of gaming motivations, normed on hundreds of thousands of gamers, used to profile audiences, prioritise features, map competing games and segment players.
description: Quantic Foundry built the Gamer Motivation Profile by reviewing academic and industry motivation taxonomies, then iteratively collecting data through a five-minute online survey that gives gamers a personalised report, testing new items and re-running factor analysis. The model described, based on over 250,000 gamers, groups twelve motivations into six clusters: action (destruction, excitement), social (competition, community), mastery (challenge, strategy), achievement (completion, power), immersion (fantasy, story) and creativity. Respondents also list favourite and recent games, which lets analysts move between demographics, motivations and titles. Applications include generating an aggregate motivation profile for the audience of a game or genre to prioritise features; game space mapping, which ranks related titles by odds ratios within an audience and factor-analyses their motivations to plot two axes showing crowded and underserved spaces; and player segment analysis, which clusters gamers on motivations and demographics. The authors argue motivation frameworks give designers, marketers and researchers a shared vocabulary and cover a blind spot of telemetry: a game cannot track preferences it does not cater for. The same approach, a validated motivation inventory linked to behaviour, can be built for other product categories.
steps: Administer the motivation inventory to a sample of the target audience or draw on an existing normed data set.
Score each motivation and compare the audience profile against population norms.
Identify the most and least important motivations to prioritise features.
For competitive mapping, find titles over-represented in the audience by odds ratio and factor-analyse their players' motivations to build a two-axis map.
Cluster respondents on motivations and demographics to define player segments.
Link segments to telemetry, retention cohorts or purchasing behaviour where possible.
outputs: Audience motivation profiles, a game space map, and motivation-based player segments.
useWhen: Defining or understanding a game's audience, positioning against competitors, or explaining why particular players leave.
avoidWhen: You need a fully public, freely documented instrument, or your product is not a game and no equivalent inventory exists.
whyLost: A commercial instrument known in the games industry but not in general UX, where motivation segmentation is usually built ad hoc.
whereToUse: Game concept and positioning, live-service audience analysis, marketing segmentation.
example: Before a sequel, a studio profiles fans of the franchise and finds strategy and completion far above norms, so it invests in planning tools and collectibles rather than more action set-pieces.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 28 (Yee and Ducheneaut).

name: Gamestorming Workshop Games (Dot Voting, Speedboat, Staple Yourself)
donor: Facilitation, agile product management and process improvement
origin: Gray, Brown and Macanufo, 2010 (collection); Speedboat after Luke Hohmann's Innovation Games; Staple Yourself version credited to James Macanufo
summary: Short, structured workshop games that help a group converge (dot voting), surface obstacles (speedboat) or narrate a process by following one object through it (staple yourself).
description: Gamestorming packages facilitation moves as games with a defined opening, exploring and closing structure. Three are especially common in product teams. Dot voting gives each person a fixed budget of votes (about five) to place at the same time on a wall of options; the budget forces choices and the tally becomes the agenda for discussion, not the decision itself. Speedboat draws the product or goal as a boat held back by anchors; participants write dislikes or obstacles, optionally estimating how much faster the boat would go without each, and the group looks for recurring themes. Staple Yourself to Something follows a single object (an order, a ticket, an idea) from agreed start to end points through about seven big steps, capturing who does what and how long it takes, drawn live as a visual story. Post the Path is a variant in which people write the steps separately and compare versions to expose gaps and clashing terms.
steps: Choose the game for the job: dot voting to converge on a long list, speedboat to surface obstacles, staple yourself to make a process visible.
Dot voting: put the options on a wall, give each participant about five dots, have everyone vote at once (stacking allowed), tally and re-list by rank.
Dot voting: discuss the ranked list before deciding and check items that received no votes so nothing is dropped without cause.
Speedboat: draw a boat named after the product or goal with anchors, write the question beside it and give 5-10 minutes for people to post obstacles or dislikes as anchors.
Speedboat: discuss each note, keeping the group describing rather than solving, and cluster recurring themes.
Staple yourself: agree the object, start and end points, brainstorm and cut to about seven big steps, and agree what to capture per step (people, actions, time).
Staple yourself: narrate the object's journey step by step while the facilitator draws it, asking 'Who does what here?' and 'What's next?', and tying off branches and loops.
Photograph the outputs and record which items or themes go forward and why.
outputs: A ranked list of options with visible weighting; clustered obstacles with rough impact estimates; a visual narrative map of a process from the object's point of view.
useWhen: A team needs to narrow a long list quickly, air what is holding a product back, or build a shared picture of an undocumented process before improving it.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating dot votes as evidence of user need: open simultaneous voting invites bandwagon and status effects, so use Kano Analysis, MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) or a survey for user priorities. Speedboat with staff is not a substitute for Interviews or Contextual Inquiry with customers, and a staple-yourself map of today's process should be checked against Process Mining or field observation. Tallying slows in large groups.
whyLost: Survived and spread because the games are cheap, need no training and fit agile ceremonies; dot voting and speedboat (as 'sailboat') are now standard retrospective and workshop moves.
whereToUse: Sprint retrospectives, roadmap and backlog workshops, stakeholder alignment sessions, service and operations process reviews.
example: A fintech onboarding team runs a staple-yourself session following a single loan application from submission to payout, then a speedboat with support staff on the anchors slowing it; dot voting picks three anchors to investigate with customer interviews.
reference: Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010) Gamestorming: A Playbook for Innovators, Rulebreakers, and Changemakers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Gamification Research
origin: Deterding et al., 2011 (definition); grounded in self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan)
summary: Designs and evaluates game elements such as points, badges, streaks and challenges in non-game products, measuring effects on motivation and sustained behaviour.
description: Gamification is the use of game design elements in non-game contexts. Research on it asks two questions: which elements, for whom, change behaviour, and do the effects last? A rigorous approach grounds element choice in motivational theory, usually self-determination theory's needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness, and player-type models, then tests elements individually rather than as bundles. Measures combine behaviour (engagement, completion, retention) with motivation scales such as the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory to detect crowding out, where extrinsic rewards undermine intrinsic interest. Because novelty effects inflate early results, studies need follow-up of several weeks or more. Meta-analyses find positive but heterogeneous effects, which is why segmented analysis and long horizons separate durable designs from short-term spikes.
steps: Define the target behaviour and the motivational need it should serve (competence, autonomy, relatedness).
Select candidate game elements and map each to a motivational mechanism.
Prototype elements individually so their effects can be separated.
Run a randomised test with a control group, tracking behaviour for at least 4-8 weeks to get past novelty effects.
Measure intrinsic motivation before and after (e.g. Intrinsic Motivation Inventory) to detect crowding out.
Analyse effects by user segment and retain only elements with durable, positive effects.
outputs: Element-mechanism map, effect sizes per element over time, motivation change scores, segment-level findings.
useWhen: Fitness, learning, habit-forming and enterprise adoption products where sustained engagement is the goal.
avoidWhen: When the behaviour is intrinsically motivated or high-stakes and serious; points may trivialise it. Use behavioural diagnosis instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Broad industry adoption; though evidence for long-term effectiveness is mixed.
whereToUse: Fitness; education; enterprise tools; loyalty programs.
example: A language app tested streaks, leaderboards and badges separately. Streaks raised 30-day retention by 6 points, but leaderboards reduced motivation scores for bottom-quartile learners and were limited to opt-in leagues.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Deterding, S., Dixon, D., Khaled, R., & Nacke, L. (2011). From game design elements to gamefulness: Defining gamification. Proceedings of MindTrek '11, 9-15.

name: Gaussian Mixture Models for User Segmentation
origin: Finite mixture models (Pearson, 1894); EM estimation by Dempster, Laird and Rubin (1977); McLachlan and Peel (2000)
summary: Segments users with probabilistic mixture models that give each user a membership probability per segment, selecting the number of segments with information criteria.
description: Gaussian mixture models represent a population as a weighted mixture of K multivariate normal distributions, each a segment with its own mean and covariance. Unlike k-means, which assigns each user to one cluster and assumes spherical, equal-size clusters, GMMs give soft memberships and allow elongated, correlated and unequal clusters, which better reflects behavioural data where users blend patterns. Parameters are estimated with expectation-maximisation; the number of segments and covariance structure are chosen with BIC, and stability is checked by refitting on bootstrap samples. In psychology the equivalent is latent profile analysis. Rigour includes transforming skewed behavioural features, standardising, inspecting entropy (how cleanly users are classified), validating segments against held-out outcomes, and interpreting them with qualitative research.
steps: Fit GMM to behavioral feature matrix (sessions × features).
Select K using BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) — minimize BIC across K=2..10.
Each user gets a probability vector over K clusters.
Interpret cluster means as behavioral archetypes.
Uncertainty: high-entropy probability vectors (spread across clusters) = users who don't fit any archetype — design for them separately.
outputs: Segment profiles with means and covariances, membership probabilities per user, BIC comparison of solutions, classification entropy and validated segment descriptions.
useWhen: Behavioural segmentation from product analytics or survey data, identifying hybrid users, targeting research recruitment, and personalisation.
avoidWhen: With small samples (under a few hundred) or highly non-normal, categorical data (use latent class analysis); when you need explanations of motives, add qualitative research. Overly restrictive error structures (for example local independence or diagonal covariances imposed without checking) can overestimate the number of classes; adding direct effects for locally dependent indicators often reduces it, but can also hide real classes, so compare both by BIC.
whyLost: Segmentation in UX is mostly qualitative personas or k-means in analytics tools; probabilistic mixture modelling stays in statistics and data science teams.
whereToUse: User segmentation from behavioral data, persona validation from logs, adaptive interface design, feature adoption pattern analysis.
example: A music app fits GMMs to 40,000 users' listening features; BIC favours five segments. 18% of users have split membership between 'focus listening' and 'discovery', a group the team recruits for interviews about mixed-mode playlists.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning — Springer (Bishop)
Finite Mixture Models (Geoffrey McLachlan & David Peel)
Vermunt JK & Magidson J (2002) Latent class cluster analysis. In Hagenaars JA & McCutcheon AL (Eds) Applied Latent Class Analysis. Cambridge University Press
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
7 Clustering Methods for UX Researchers (carousel, n.d.)
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
8 Clustering Algorithms in Machine Learning that All Data Scientists Should Know (McGregor, 2020)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bishop CM (2006) Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer

name: Gaze-Contingent Moving-Window and Boundary Paradigms
aka: Gaze-contingent moving-window and boundary paradigms (In the Lab of Keith Rayner)
origin: George McConkie and Keith Rayner (1975) moving window; Rayner (1975) boundary paradigm
summary: Change on-screen text according to where the reader is looking, to measure how much is taken in per fixation and what is gained from previewing the next word.
description: Eye-tracking display-change techniques alter text depending on the current fixation. In the moving window, text outside a window of a set number of characters around fixation is masked and the window moves with the eyes; varying its size until reading is normal gives the perceptual span, about 3-4 letters left and 14-15 right of fixation for readers of English. In the boundary paradigm, a preview string sits in a target word's position and is replaced by the target when the eyes cross an invisible boundary during the saccade; comparing valid and invalid previews gives the preview benefit. In the disappearing-text variant the fixated word is masked early; reading stays normal if the word is visible for 50-60 ms. The findings underpin the E-Z Reader model of eye-movement control. The method needs a fast eye tracker and display changes completed within saccades.
steps: Set up a high-speed eye tracker and a display able to change content within a saccade (a few milliseconds).
For the moving window, mask text outside a window around fixation that moves with the eyes, and vary the window size across trials.
For the boundary paradigm, place a preview string at the target location and swap it for the target when the eyes cross an invisible boundary; compare valid and invalid previews.
For disappearing text, mask the fixated word after a set delay such as 50-60 ms.
Record fixation durations, gaze durations, skips and reading rate.
Find the window size at which reading becomes normal, or the size of the preview benefit, and compare across layouts, fonts or reader groups.
outputs: Perceptual span estimates, preview benefit, and fixation and reading-rate measures per condition.
useWhen: You need precise evidence on how much text people take in per glance, for example when designing narrow displays, scrolling text, subtitles or reading aids.
avoidWhen: You need ordinary usability or comprehension evidence; standard eye tracking or readability testing is far cheaper. Discourse-level inferences from these paradigms are tenuous.
whyLost: It needs specialist eye trackers and gaze-contingent software, and answers perceptual questions that UX usually settles with guidelines.
whereToUse: Smartwatch and heads-up displays, rapid serial or scrolling text, subtitles and captions, dyslexia and low-vision reading aids, and font design.
example: A smartwatch team uses a moving window to test how many characters users need around fixation to read notifications at normal speed. Reading degrades below a 12-character right-hand window, setting the minimum line length.
reference: McConkie, G. W., & Rayner, K. (1975). The span of the effective stimulus during a fixation in reading. Perception & Psychophysics, 17(6), 578-586; Rayner, K. (1975). The perceptual span and peripheral cues in reading. Cognitive Psychology, 7(1), 65-81.

name: General Morphological Analysis
origin: Fritz Zwicky, Caltech, 1940s-1969 (Discovery, Invention, Research through the Morphological Approach); computer-aided GMA by Tom Ritchey (1998 onward)
summary: Breaks a problem into dimensions with discrete options, then uses cross-consistency assessment to reduce the full configuration space to viable solutions.
description: Zwicky, an astrophysicist, used morphological analysis to explore all possible configurations of jet engines and astronomical objects. The problem is decomposed into parameters, each with a range of values, forming a morphological field whose cells represent all combinations, often millions. Ritchey's cross-consistency assessment (CCA) asks pairwise whether value combinations are compatible, eliminating inconsistent configurations and leaving a manageable solution space. This prevents premature fixation on familiar concepts, ensures systematic coverage of alternatives, and is valuable in design ideation, service concepts and policy scenarios.
steps: Define the problem and identify 4-8 key parameters (dimensions) of possible solutions.
For each parameter, list mutually exclusive values (typically 3-7).
Conduct cross-consistency assessment for every pair of values across parameters (consistent, inconsistent, conditionally consistent).
Use software or scripts to generate the reduced set of internally consistent configurations.
Explore the solution space: cluster configurations, identify novel combinations and evaluate them.
Select configurations for prototyping or scenario development.
outputs: A morphological field, cross-consistency matrix and a reduced set of viable configurations.
useWhen: Generating and structuring alternatives for complex design, service or strategy problems.
avoidWhen: Simple problems with few dimensions, or where intuitive ideation suffices.
whyLost: It originated in physics and defence analysis and needs facilitation and tooling; design adopted brainstorming instead.
whereToUse: Service concept generation, onboarding strategy, pricing and packaging options, AI feature concepts, policy design.
example: Designing a mobility subscription, a team defines six parameters (vehicle types, pricing model, booking horizon, etc.) giving 4,320 combinations; CCA reduces them to 64 consistent concepts, among them a novel weekend-only family bundle.
sources: Zwicky, Discovery, Invention, Research through the Morphological Approach (1969)
Ritchey, Wicked Problems, Social Messes: Decision Support Modelling with Morphological Analysis (2011)
Ritchey, Problem structuring using computer-aided morphological analysis (2006), Journal of the Operational Research Society
Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Ritchey, T. (2006). Journal of the Operational Research Society, 57(7), 792-801.

name: Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE)
origin: Kung-Yee Liang and Scott Zeger, 1986; Zeger, Liang and Albert, 1988
summary: A regression method for clustered or repeated outcomes that estimates population-average effects with a working correlation and robust sandwich standard errors.
description: When the same user, account or team contributes many observations, ordinary regression understates uncertainty. GEE fits a marginal model for the mean (any generalised linear model) and solves estimating equations that include a working correlation matrix, usually exchangeable or AR(1). Standard errors come from the sandwich estimator, which stays consistent even if the working correlation is wrong. The key decision is the target of inference. GEE coefficients describe the average effect across the population; a random-effects (mixed) model describes the effect for a given individual. For linear and Poisson models the two coincide, but for logistic and probit models population-average slopes are attenuated towards zero, more so as within-cluster correlation grows. For binary data the admissible correlation is bounded by the probabilities, so an exchangeable structure can be impossible with large clusters.
steps: Identify the clusters, the covariates that vary within clusters and those that are constant within them.
Decide whether the question is about population averages (GEE) or within-individual change (mixed model).
Choose a working correlation that reflects the design: exchangeable for members of a group, AR(1) for repeated measures over time.
Fit the model by iteratively reweighted least squares and use the sandwich variance for Wald tests and confidence intervals.
For binary outcomes check that the estimated correlation lies within admissible bounds and expect slopes smaller than a random-intercept logit would give.
Build the model with the usual selection, scale and interaction checks, and compare with a random-effects fit if subject-specific interpretation is also needed.
outputs: Population-average coefficients (odds ratios, rate ratios or mean differences) with robust standard errors, and the estimated working correlation.
useWhen: Estimating the average effect of a feature, policy or segment on repeated binary or count outcomes, such as conversion across sessions or weekly active status, when the decision concerns the whole user base.
avoidWhen: When individual trajectories or user-level effects are the question, or with continuous outcomes where a linear mixed model is simpler (use Multilevel Modelling (HLM / Mixed-Effects Models)); with very few clusters (below about 40) where sandwich errors are unreliable; or when only a variance correction is needed (Cluster-Robust Standard Errors).
whyLost: Widely used in epidemiology and clinical trials, but UX analysts typically choose either naive regression or mixed models and rarely meet the marginal-versus-conditional distinction.
whereToUse: Longitudinal product analytics, repeated-measures A/B analyses with binary outcomes, diary and ESM data with yes/no responses, multi-session usability benchmarks.
example: An e-commerce team estimates whether a new checkout raises purchase across each user's sessions. GEE with exchangeable correlation gives an average odds ratio of 1.12 for the whole base, the figure finance needs, while a random-intercept logit gives a larger per-user effect.
sources: Beyond t Test and ANOVA (Yu et al., 2022)
reference: Liang, K.-Y., & Zeger, S. L. (1986). Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika, 73(1), 13-22.

name: Generalizability Theory
origin: Lee Cronbach, Goldine Gleser, Harinder Nanda and Nageswari Rajaratnam, 1972
summary: Decomposes measurement variance into multiple sources (participants, tasks, raters, occasions) and designs studies that reach target reliability efficiently.
description: Classical reliability treats error as one undifferentiated term. G-theory uses ANOVA-style variance components to estimate how much score variation comes from the object of measurement (e.g. designs) versus facets such as tasks, raters, participants and occasions, and their interactions. A G-study estimates these components; a D-study then asks how reliability (generalizability coefficient) would change with different numbers of tasks, raters or participants. For UX benchmarks and heuristic evaluations, this tells you whether to add evaluators, tasks or participants to get dependable comparisons, and reveals when results mostly reflect which tasks were chosen.
steps: Define the object of measurement (e.g. product versions) and facets (tasks, participants, raters, occasions).
Collect data in a crossed design where possible (every rater rates every design on every task).
Estimate variance components with ANOVA or mixed models (e.g. gtheory or lme4).
Compute generalizability (relative) and dependability (absolute) coefficients.
Run D-studies varying the number of conditions per facet to find efficient designs reaching e.g. 0.8.
Report variance components so others can see which facets drive error.
outputs: Variance component estimates, G and Phi coefficients, D-study tables for optimal design.
useWhen: Designing benchmarks, expert reviews or rating studies with multiple sources of error.
avoidWhen: Single-facet measures where Cronbach's alpha or ICC suffices.
whyLost: It is a specialist educational measurement method; UX reliability discussion rarely goes beyond alpha and kappa.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks, heuristic evaluation panels, AI output quality rating, design critiques, accessibility audits.
example: A G-study of a competitive benchmark shows task-by-product interaction accounts for 35% of variance; the D-study recommends 12 tasks with 15 participants rather than 6 tasks with 30.
sources: Cronbach et al., The Dependability of Behavioral Measurements (1972)
Shavelson & Webb, Generalizability Theory: A Primer (1991)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability Theory. Springer.

name: Generative Design Loop
aka: Generative design loop: ideation, sketching and critiquing with go and stop modes
origin: Hartson and Pyla, 2012 and 2019; go and stop modes from Mason, 1968; sketching after Buxton, 2007
summary: A tight cycle of group ideation, sketching and critiquing grounded in research models, with idea generation (go mode) kept strictly apart from judgement (stop mode).
description: Generative design treats ideation, sketching, critiquing and refining as one fast loop rather than separate phases. The team first immerses itself in posted research models, personas and requirements, then holds ideation sessions each focused on one model. Ideas are pushed with named techniques: reframing, abstraction, the magic wand (assume any technology is possible, then work back), incubation, borrowing patterns from other domains and systematically traversing the dimensions of the problem space (for example mass, volume and visibility). Everything is talked through as user scenarios and sketched or mocked up physically. Mason's distinction between go-mode and stop-mode thinking is the discipline: critique begins only when ideas run dry, and then checks goals, fit with the work ecology, usability, emotional impact and meaningfulness, ideally with a broad cross-section of people including users. The loop is repeated many times.
steps: Post the research models, personas and requirements on the walls and walk the team through them.
Run ideation sessions of one model each, in go mode only: no evaluation, every idea sketched or noted.
Apply stimulus techniques deliberately: reframe, abstract, use the magic wand, borrow cross-domain patterns, and traverse each dimension of the problem space.
Talk in user scenarios and sketch everything; build rough physical mock-ups where form matters.
Switch to stop mode only when ideas run dry, critiquing sketches for goals, ecology fit, usability, emotional impact and meaningfulness.
Invite a wide cross-section of people, including users, to argue over the sketches while the designers listen.
Refine the surviving ideas and loop again, many times, before committing to a prototype.
outputs: Large sets of sketches and physical mock-ups, candidate design concepts and recorded critiques.
useWhen: A team has research models in hand and needs to generate and shape many concept alternatives quickly before committing to one.
avoidWhen: Critique here is informal and team-based; it does not tell you whether users can use or want the design, so follow with Prototype Testing, Usability Testing or Cognitive Walkthrough. Without prior research the loop just recycles team assumptions; run Contextual Inquiry or Interviews first.
whyLost: Survived because sketch-and-critique is the core of studio design education and maps directly onto design sprints; the explicit go/stop discipline is often dropped.
whereToUse: Concept development in product discovery, design sprints, studio critique cultures, hardware and service concepting.
example: A SaaS team designing alerting for warehouse managers runs three go-mode sessions on the flow model, using the magic wand to imagine alerts that predict stock-outs, then a stop-mode critique with two shift leads that kills half the sketches for ecology fit.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019) The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience. 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 14; Mason, J.G. (1968) How to be of two minds. Nation's Business, October, 94-97.

name: Generative Design Sessions (Co-Design Workshops)
origin: Elizabeth Sanders, 1990s-2000s; Sanders & Stappers, Convivial Toolkit, 2012; roots in Scandinavian participatory design
summary: Sensitised participants use open-ended making toolkits to express latent needs and ideal experiences, then narrate what they made.
description: Generative design rests on the idea that people know more than they can say, and that making can access latent needs that interviews and observation miss. Sanders' framework describes three levels: what people say, what they do and what they make. Participants are first sensitised over one to two weeks with reflective activities, then use generative toolkits (images, words, shapes, craft materials) to create artefacts such as ideal journeys or devices. The making process is observed, and participants narrate their creations; analysis covers artefacts, process and narration, and the gaps between them. The sensitisation, toolkit design and analysis distinguish it from ideation workshops.
steps: Sensitisation: 1–2 weeks before the session, send participants a "sensitisation package" — activities that prime them to reflect on the research topic (e.g., keeping a photo diary, completing a values card sort, drawing their current experience).

Toolkit design: Provide materials for making: foam, paper, pipe cleaners, printed images, stickers, markers. The toolkit should be generative (enabling creation of anything) not constrained (limiting to pre-defined options).

Making phase: Give participants a making prompt: "Create something that represents your ideal experience of [phenomenon]." Observe the making process — it reveals tacit knowledge that the finished artifact does not.
Narration phase: Ask participants to narrate their creation: "Tell me about what you made and why." The narrative adds the verbal layer to the pre-verbal making layer.

Analysis: Analyse both the artifacts (what was created) and the narrations (how participants explained their creation). The gap between making and narration is analytically important — it reveals tacit knowledge that participants could create but not explain.
outputs: Participant artefacts, sensitisation booklets, narration transcripts, and analysed themes about latent needs and aspirations.
useWhen: Early, fuzzy front-end research on future experiences, latent needs and aspirations, especially for new categories.
avoidWhen: Evaluating a defined design or measuring behaviour; use usability testing or analytics. Avoid with tight timelines that preclude sensitisation.
whyLost: 'Co-design' now usually means a brainstorming workshop with users; sensitisation, toolkit design and systematic analysis are commonly dropped.
whereToUse: Future-of-home and mobility concepts, health service redesign, children's products, and new category strategy.
example: Before designing a hospital discharge app, patients complete a week-long sensitisation booklet, then build their ideal 'first week home' timeline from cards. The timelines centre on a single person to call, not app features.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Sanders, E. B.-N. & Stappers, P. J. (2012). Convivial Toolkit: Generative Research for the Front End of Design. BIS Publishers.

name: Generic Error Modelling System (GEMS)
origin: James Reason, 1987-1990 (Human Error, 1990)
summary: Classifies errors by the cognitive level at which they occur, separating skill-based slips and lapses from rule-based and knowledge-based mistakes, each with distinct remedies.
description: GEMS integrates Rasmussen's skill-rule-knowledge framework with Reason's slips, lapses and mistakes. At the skill-based level, errors come from attentional failures (slips, such as capture errors) and memory failures (lapses). When a problem is detected, people move to the rule-based level, where they misapply good rules or apply bad ones. When no rule fits, they enter knowledge-based reasoning, prone to bounded rationality, confirmation bias and incomplete mental models. GEMS gives an explicit diagnostic flow: was the user monitoring, problem-solving or reasoning from first principles when the error occurred? The rigour comes from assigning each observed error to a mechanism, which then dictates the fix: forcing functions for slips, better feedback for lapses, clearer rules and signs for rule-based mistakes, and better representations for knowledge-based ones.
steps: Collect error incidents from usability sessions, support tickets, logs or critical incident interviews, with enough context to reconstruct intention.
For each incident, establish whether the intention was correct (execution failure) or incorrect (planning failure).
Classify execution failures as slips (attention: capture, description, mode errors) or lapses (memory: omissions, place-losing).
Classify planning failures as rule-based (misapplied good rule, applied bad rule, strong-but-wrong rule) or knowledge-based (incomplete model, confirmation bias, overconfidence).
Check classification reliability with a second coder and compute Cohen's kappa, targeting at least 0.6.
Map each error class to its remedy family and prioritise redesigns by frequency times severity.
outputs: An error inventory classified by GEMS level and mechanism, with reliability statistics and a remedy map.
useWhen: You have many observed errors and need to know why they happen in cognitive terms, so that fixes target mechanisms rather than symptoms.
avoidWhen: You have no error data yet; run usability testing or SHERPA first. For organisational accident causes, use the Swiss cheese model or STAMP.
whyLost: UX adopted Norman's slip-mistake distinction as a slogan but not Reason's detailed diagnostic machinery or coding reliability. Error classification is rarely done systematically in product teams.
whereToUse: Clinical software, trading platforms, enterprise admin tools, voice and AI assistants where users misunderstand mode or capability.
example: A pharmacy system shows recurring wrong-patient selections. GEMS coding shows most are description slips from identical-looking rows rather than knowledge failures, so the team redesigns row distinctiveness rather than adding training.
sources: Rasmussen, Information Processing and Human-Machine Interaction (1986)
reference: Reason, J. (1990). Human Error. Cambridge University Press.

name: Geometric mean reporting
origin: Classical statistics; recommended for small-sample task times by Cordes (1993) and Sauro and Lewis (2010)
summary: Reports the geometric mean of skewed measures such as task times as the best estimate of the typical value, with confidence intervals derived on the log scale.
description: For positively skewed data, the arithmetic mean overstates typical performance and the sample median is noisy and biased for small samples. Sauro and Lewis compared estimators on large usability datasets and found the geometric mean (the exponential of the mean of log values) had less error and bias in estimating the population median for sample sizes under about 25, while the sample median performed better above that. The geometric mean also makes multiplicative comparisons natural, for example one design taking 0.8 times as long. Rigour comes from computing confidence intervals on the log scale and back-transforming them, explaining clearly that the result estimates the median, and using it consistently across benchmark rounds.
steps: Confirm the measure is strictly positive and positively skewed, for example task times, page load times or ratios.
Compute the natural log of each value and calculate the mean and standard deviation of the logs.
Exponentiate the log mean to obtain the geometric mean.
Compute a 95% confidence interval on the log scale (log mean ± t × SD/√n) and exponentiate the limits to obtain an asymmetric interval.
For samples of about 25 or more, also report the sample median, and choose a consistent primary estimate for benchmarking.
Report results with wording such as 'typical completion time' and include the arithmetic mean only if total time or cost is the decision-relevant quantity.
outputs: Geometric means with asymmetric confidence intervals, consistently reported across studies, and multiplicative comparisons between designs.
useWhen: Reporting typical task times or other skewed positive measures in small-sample usability studies and benchmarks.
avoidWhen: Total time or cost is what matters (use the arithmetic mean, since totals scale with it), values include zeros, or data are bimodal.
whyLost: Spreadsheets and analytics tools default to the arithmetic mean, and the evidence for the geometric mean sits in specialist UX statistics books rather than in common practice.
whereToUse: Usability benchmark reports, competitive evaluations, design system performance metrics, internal tool efficiency studies.
example: In a 12-participant benchmark, the arithmetic mean for a transfer task was 71 seconds but the geometric mean was 48 seconds (95% CI 37 to 62). The team reported 48 seconds as typical and tracked it across quarterly rounds.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 39 — The Distribution of Human Performance — Why Averages Lie
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J., & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience: Practical Statistics for User Research (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann. Sauro, J., & Lewis, J. R. (2010). Average task times in usability tests: What to report? Proceedings of CHI 2010, 2347–2350.

name: Gestalt Experimental Phenomenology for Interface Perception
origin: Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka, 1912-1935
summary: Studies how users perceptually group, segregate and complete interface elements through controlled stimulus variation, diagnosing layout failures at the level of perception.
description: The Gestalt principles (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, figure-ground) are taught in every design course, but the treatise notes that what was lost is the research methodology behind them: careful experimental phenomenology, systematic variation of stimuli, and analysis of perceptual errors and illusions. In its recovered form, a researcher builds controlled variants of a layout that manipulate one grouping cue at a time, then asks participants to describe or act on what they see (which items belong together, what is foreground, what is clickable). Errors are treated as data revealing which cue dominates. This turns 'the layout feels cluttered' into a falsifiable claim about competing grouping cues, and provides diagnostic power for perceptual failures that remain among the most common sources of interface problems.
steps: Identify a perceptual failure hypothesis, such as users grouping a label with the wrong field.
Create 3-6 stimulus variants that manipulate one Gestalt cue at a time (spacing, colour, alignment, enclosure).
Show each variant briefly (for example 500 ms to 5 s) and ask participants to report groupings or select related items.
Record grouping judgements and errors; use 15-30 participants for within-subject comparisons.
Analyse which cue predicts grouping and where cues conflict, and identify the dominant cue.
Translate findings into layout rules for the design system.
outputs: Grouping-judgement data per variant, cue dominance ranking, perceptual layout rules.
useWhen: Dense forms, dashboards, pricing tables and design-system spacing decisions where mis-grouping causes errors.
avoidWhen: Problems driven by content, motivation or task flow rather than perception; use usability testing or cognitive walkthrough instead.
whyLost: The principles survived as slogans in design education while the experimental methodology was dropped. UX research rarely studies perception with experimental care.
whereToUse: Design systems, data-dense dashboards, checkout and pricing pages, AR overlays, accessibility for low vision.
example: On a mortgage calculator, users attach the 'per month' caption to the wrong figure. Four variants manipulating proximity and enclosure show enclosure overrides proximity, so the team adds subtle card boundaries.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Wertheimer M (1923) Laws of organization in perceptual forms
Koffka K (1935) Principles of Gestalt Psychology
Wagemans J et al. (2012) A century of Gestalt psychology in visual perception. Psychological Bulletin
reference: Wagemans J et al. (2012) A century of Gestalt psychology in visual perception I. Psychological Bulletin 138(6):1172-1217.

name: Gestalt Principles Audit
origin: Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka, 1910s-1920s
summary: Systematically checks a layout against perceptual grouping laws (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common region, figure-ground) to find where visual structure contradicts intended meaning.
description: The Gestalt principles describe how the visual system automatically organises elements into groups and wholes before conscious interpretation. Proximity, similarity, common region, continuity, closure, common fate and figure-ground determine which items users perceive as belonging together. A Gestalt audit treats these as testable predictions: for each screen, the auditor maps the intended information groups and compares them with the groups the principles predict users will perceive. Conflicts, such as a label closer to the wrong field or a colour shared by unrelated controls, are logged as defects. Rigour comes from making the predicted groupings explicit and then validating them quickly with users, for example with 50-millisecond or five-second exposure tests, first-click tests or grouping tasks. The audit is cheap, fast and especially valuable for dense dashboards, forms and safety-critical consoles.
steps: List the intended information groups and hierarchy for each screen under review.
Annotate each screen with the groups predicted by proximity, similarity, common region, continuity, closure and figure-ground.
Log every conflict between predicted perceptual groups and intended semantic groups, rating severity by task impact.
Validate the most severe conflicts with 5-10 users using brief exposure (50-500 ms or five-second) tests or grouping tasks.
Propose fixes such as spacing ratios (e.g. within-group gaps at most half of between-group gaps), shared containers or differentiated styling.
Re-test changed screens to confirm perceived grouping now matches intended structure.
outputs: Annotated screens, conflict log with severity ratings, spacing and styling recommendations, validation results.
useWhen: Reviewing dense layouts, forms, dashboards and control panels where misgrouping causes errors or slows scanning.
avoidWhen: When problems are about content, terminology or workflow rather than visual structure; use heuristic evaluation or usability testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Bedrock of visual design; directly applicable to layout and visual hierarchy.
whereToUse: Visual design; data visualization; icon design; layout.
example: A surgical device console grouped the 'stop infusion' button with navigation controls by shared colour. A Gestalt audit flagged the conflict; adding a common region around infusion controls cut first-click errors in a 5-second test from 30% to 5%.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Wagemans, J. et al. (2012). A century of Gestalt psychology in visual perception. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1172-1217.

name: Gesture Design and Fat Finger Error Taxonomy
origin: Josh Clark (2010, 2015); touch error research by Holz and Baudisch (2010) and Parhi et al. (2006)
summary: Classifies touch errors as proximity, acquisition, pressure or temporal errors from logs and observation, linking each type to a specific design intervention.
description: Generic 'mis-tap' counts do not tell designers what to change. A fat finger error taxonomy classifies touch failures by mechanism: proximity errors (hitting an adjacent target), acquisition errors (missing all targets), pressure or contact errors (touch not registered, or accidental long-press), and temporal errors (gestures misrecognised because of speed or timing, such as a slow swipe read as a drag). Each type implies a different remedy: spacing and larger hit areas for proximity, bigger targets or snapping for acquisition, feedback and touch-sensitivity tuning for pressure, and gesture thresholds or alternatives for temporal errors. Data come from touch logs (tap coordinates, nearest targets, undo or back events) and observation sessions. Holz and Baudisch's work on perceived input point explains systematic offsets that cause some errors.
steps: During mobile usability testing, code every touch error by type:
proximity (correct finger placement but wrong target activated),
acquisition (finger placement was far from intended target),
pressure (touch not registered or registered incorrectly),

temporal (gesture timing not matched). Compute error rate per type per screen. Proximity errors → increase target spacing. Acquisition errors → increase target size. Pressure errors → reduce pressure threshold or add haptic feedback.
outputs: Classified touch-error log with rates by type and screen, heatmaps of tap offsets, and targeted design fixes per error type.
useWhen: Mobile and tablet apps, kiosks, wearables, gesture-heavy interfaces and contexts with motion or gloves.
avoidWhen: For desktop pointer interfaces or when errors are conceptual (wrong intention) rather than motor; use usability testing focused on mental models.
whyLost: Mobile UX adopted platform tap-size guidelines and rarely analyses touch errors by type, and touch logging is often not instrumented.
whereToUse: Mobile usability testing, touch accessibility research, wearable device UX, any touch interface where error analysis is needed.
example: A grocery delivery app logs undo taps on quantity steppers; classification shows 70% are proximity errors between '+' and 'delete'. Moving delete behind a swipe and spacing the stepper cuts erroneous removals by half.
sources: Holz & Baudisch, The generalized perceived input point model and how to double touch accuracy by extracting fingerprints (CHI 2010)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 3 — The Ballistics of the Human Body — Fitts' Law & Motor Control
reference: Clark J (2015) Designing for Touch. A Book Apart

name: Gesture Elicitation Study
aka: Using people to determine the appropriate gesture
origin: Described by Dan Saffer (2008); formalised with agreement scores by Jacob Wobbrock and colleagues (2005, 2009)
summary: Shows participants the effect of each command and asks which gesture they would use, then finds consistent pairings across people to build a user-defined gesture set.
description: Rather than designers choosing gestures alone, elicitation draws on the intuitions of intended users. In the feature-to-gesture form, participants see a command's effect (the 'referent') and propose a gesture to trigger it; in the reverse form, a gesture is demonstrated and participants say what it should do. Proposals are grouped into identical gestures and patterns across participants show which pairings are intuitive. In the formalised academic version, agreement per referent is quantified with an agreement score, so that high-agreement gestures become the default set and conflicts are resolved explicitly. Saffer then filters candidates against practical criteria: sensor capability, task steps, limits of the body, and matching gesture complexity to task complexity.
steps: List the commands or features (referents) the gestural system must support, typically 10 to 30.
Show each referent's effect to participants (often 12 to 20) in randomised order and ask them to perform the gesture they would use, ideally thinking aloud.
Optionally run the reverse task: demonstrate candidate gestures and ask what each should trigger.
Group identical proposals per referent and calculate an agreement score per referent.
Assign the highest-agreement gesture to each referent, resolving conflicts where one gesture is proposed for several commands.
Filter the set against sensor capability, task steps, body limits and complexity matching, then validate it in a usability test.
outputs: A user-defined gesture set with agreement scores per command and a list of conflicts and low-agreement commands.
useWhen: Designing touch, mid-air, wearable, automotive or VR gesture vocabularies before engineering commits to a set.
avoidWhen: When participants have strong legacy bias from current platforms that you want to break, or when sensors cannot recognise proposed gestures. Saffer gives no sample size or agreement measure, so use the formalised protocol. For evaluating an existing set use Usability Testing.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, quick and gives defensible, quantifiable vocabularies for new input modalities.
whereToUse: XR and spatial computing, smart TVs, in-car controls, wearables, accessibility alternatives to touch.
example: A smart-glasses team shows 20 participants 18 commands such as 'dismiss notification' and 'take photo'; 'dismiss' reaches high agreement on a flick, while 'take photo' splits, so the team adds a voice alternative.
reference: Saffer, D. (2008). Designing Gestural Interfaces: Touchscreens and Interactive Devices. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, ch. 1; Wobbrock, J. O., Morris, M. R. and Wilson, A. D. (2009). User-defined gestures for surface computing. Proc. CHI 2009, 1083-1092.

name: Gesture-speech mismatch coding
aka: Gesture-speech mismatch coding as an index of readiness to learn
origin: Church and Goldin-Meadow, 1986; Perry, Church and Goldin-Meadow, 1988
summary: Code whether hand gestures accompanying an explanation convey information absent from the words; frequent mismatches mark someone in transition and ready to learn.
description: When people explain how they solved a problem, their gestures sometimes match their words and sometimes convey different but compatible information, such as saying the water is 'lower' while showing the glass's width. Goldin-Meadow's work found that children producing many such mismatches benefit most from instruction, and the finding holds across ages and tasks, from conservation and maths to gears and organic chemistry in adults. Mismatches can occur in over half of a learner's explanations at transitional points. The method requires video, separate coding of gesture with sound off and of speech, and classification of each explanation as matching, mismatching or contradictory. It reveals implicit knowledge that people cannot yet put into words.
steps: Ask participants to solve a task and explain their solution, recorded on video.
Transcribe speech and separately code gestures with the sound off, blind to speech.
For each explanation, classify gesture as matching speech, mismatching (different but compatible information) or contradicting.
Count mismatches per participant and classify them as transitional or stable.
Use the classification to predict who benefits from instruction, or relate it to later performance.
Check inter-coder reliability on a subset.
outputs: Proportion of mismatching explanations per participant, transitional versus stable classification, and links to learning outcomes.
useWhen: Studying emerging mental models during learning or onboarding, or finding implicit understanding that interviews miss, especially for spatial or procedural knowledge.
avoidWhen: Avoid without trained coders and video; for verbal mental model elicitation use teach-back or think-aloud methods.
whyLost: It requires labour-intensive video coding and is housed in developmental psychology.
whereToUse: Edtech, complex professional tools, spatial and 3D interfaces, data visualisation literacy, gestural interfaces.
example: Analysts explain a new dashboard's chart; those whose hands trace the correct trend while their words describe it wrongly learn fastest from a short tutorial, suggesting where to aim onboarding.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Church, R. B., & Goldin-Meadow, S. (1986). The mismatch between gesture and speech as an index of transitional knowledge. Cognition, 23
reference: Church, R. B., & Goldin-Meadow, S. (1986). The mismatch between gesture and speech as an index of transitional knowledge. Cognition, 23, 43-71.

name: Gibson's ecological approach
origin: James J. Gibson, The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception, 1979
summary: Analyses an interface as an environment offering directly perceivable information and action possibilities, focusing on invariants and information in the optic array rather than mental representations.
description: Gibson argued that perception is direct: the environment contains structured information (invariants in the optic array, such as texture gradients and optic flow) that specifies what it affords, without needing elaborate inference. Perception and action form a loop, and the unit of analysis is the animal-environment system. Applied to UX, the ecological approach asks what information the interface makes available for perceiving possibilities for action, how that information changes with movement and interaction (for example parallax, scroll, physical controls), and whether it specifies affordances unambiguously. Ecological interface design (Vicente and Rasmussen) is its most rigorous descendant. In mainstream UX, Gibson survives only through Norman's adaptation of 'affordance', with the original framework forgotten.
steps: Define the actor-environment system: who acts, with what body and tools, in what physical and digital environment.
Describe the information available to the actor, including invariants that persist and change during movement and interaction.
For each action the user must take, identify whether the information specifies it directly or requires inference, memory or convention.
Observe users in context (5-8 sessions) focusing on exploratory actions and perception-action loops rather than verbal reports.
Redesign to make action possibilities and system constraints directly perceivable, for example by mapping physical relationships and continuous feedback.
Evaluate with tasks under realistic conditions, including movement and divided attention.
outputs: An ecological analysis of information and action possibilities, observed perception-action breakdowns, and design changes that make actions directly specified.
useWhen: For physical, spatial, AR/VR, robotic and embodied interfaces; when designing controls for skilled operators in dynamic environments.
avoidWhen: For abstract information tasks dominated by language and convention; use cognitive walkthroughs or IA methods.
whyLost: Norman borrowed 'affordance' and redefined it as perceived affordance, and the rest of the framework was left in ecological psychology and specialist human factors.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, AR/VR, automotive controls, industrial teleoperation, and haptic interfaces.
example: An ecological analysis of a surgical robot shows instrument depth is not specified by any visual invariant in the 2D monitor view, forcing inference. Adding stereoscopic display and tool-tip shadow cues reduces depth errors in simulation.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Sensation and Perception
Gibson, J. J., The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979)
Whalen, J., Design for How People Think (2019)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (Gibson, 2015)
reference: Gibson, J. J. (1979). The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception. Houghton Mifflin.

name: Gigamapping
origin: Birger Sevaldson, Oslo School of Architecture and Design, 2000s; case by Peter Jones and OCAD University sLab, 2014-2015
summary: A very large visual model of the relationships in a complex system, built iteratively in studio from domain research and stakeholder workshops to support long-term vision building.
description: A gigamap can look like an infographic, but it is a team construct that evolves an underlying theory of a system. It draws on a deep dive of domain research, sessions with stakeholders and experts to elicit drivers, narratives and influence maps, and repeated studio critique that integrates these into subsystems and then a single wall-sized map. In the Canadian governance case reported by Kalbach, a national workshop with expert lightning talks, small-group sessions with 35 civic innovators, a symposium and a follow-up workshop fed a graduate team who built a map in three zones: forces of change over two decades (following the Three Horizons model), a spatial metaphor of today's ecosystem and a transformed future, and inset diagrams of citizen experiences. An early interactive template let participants engage with the draft. The rigour lies in iteration and critique, not in the drawing.
steps: Research the domain in depth through literature, data and expert sources.
Run stakeholder and expert sessions to elicit drivers, narratives and influence maps.
In studio sessions, integrate the inputs into subsystems and a first draft map.
Critique and revise the map repeatedly as a team, testing the implied theory of the system.
Share a template or interactive draft with participants and fold in their corrections.
Organise the final map in zones (for example forces of change, current and future system, lived experiences) and use it in vision-building sessions.
outputs: A wall-sized gigamap of the system with zones for change forces, current and future states and lived experiences, plus intermediate subsystem maps.
useWhen: A team faces a wicked, multi-actor problem (public services, healthcare, platforms) and needs a shared model of the whole system to frame where design can intervene.
avoidWhen: Too slow and skill-intensive for bounded product problems; use Journey Mapping or Stakeholder Mapping instead. The map encodes the team's theory, so where causal claims matter test them with Causal Loop Diagrams (System Dynamics) or field research rather than relying on the map.
whyLost: Stays in systemic design schools and public-sector innovation labs because it is time-intensive, needs trained facilitators and many iterations, and does not fit sprint cadences.
whereToUse: Government digital services, health systems, platform ecosystems, sustainability and policy design.
example: A national digital health service builds a gigamap from clinician workshops and patient research, showing how referral rules, funding cycles and app adoption interact, and uses it to pick three intervention points for product work.
reference: Kalbach, J. (2016) Mapping Experiences: A Complete Guide to Creating Value through Journeys, Blueprints, and Diagrams. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 336-339.

name: Gioia data structure coding (first-order to aggregate dimensions)
origin: Dennis Gioia and colleagues (from Gioia and Chittipeddi, 1991); codified in Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013)
summary: A two-level coding approach moving from informant-centric first-order concepts to researcher-centric second-order themes and then aggregate theoretical dimensions.
description: The Gioia approach gives qualitative analysis a visible, defensible structure. First-order concepts stay close to informants' own terms and can number 50 to 100 early on. The researcher then asks what is going on theoretically and groups first-order concepts into second-order themes that use researcher language and connect to concepts in the literature. Themes are distilled into a small number of aggregate dimensions. The method assumes informants are knowledgeable agents who can explain their own actions, while the researcher's job is to see patterns informants cannot. Rigour comes from preserving the informant voice at the first level, the explicit traceability from quotes to dimensions, and the iterative movement between data and literature.
steps: Open code transcripts using informants' terms as much as possible, producing first-order concepts; expect 50 to 100 initially and consolidate duplicates to roughly 20 to 40.
Look for similarities and differences among first-order concepts and group them into second-order themes, labelled in researcher language and linked to existing constructs where relevant.
Ask of each theme whether it suggests a concept that explains the phenomenon, and consult the literature to see whether it is known or novel.
Distil second-order themes into 2 to 5 aggregate theoretical dimensions.
Assemble the data structure diagram, and build a supporting table with 2 to 4 representative quotes per first-order concept.
Check coding with a second researcher acting as devil's advocate on 20% to 30% of data, and revise until disagreements are resolved.
outputs: A list of first-order concepts, second-order themes and aggregate dimensions, a data structure diagram, and a supporting quotes table.
useWhen: You need a transparent, theory-generating qualitative analysis that sceptical audiences can trace from quotes to concepts; studying identity, meaning-making or sensemaking.
avoidWhen: Quick tactical findings or usability problems; use thematic or framework analysis. Avoid when there is no time for literature engagement, which the second-order step requires.
whyLost: It is dominant in management and organisation research journals, but UX synthesis evolved through affinity diagramming and rarely encounters organisation-studies methods.
whereToUse: Identity and trust studies in fintech, enterprise adoption and sensemaking, platform worker research, AI tool use in professions.
example: From 24 interviews on informal lending, first-order concepts like 'lending to cousin is not a loan' and 'keeping it off paper' were grouped into themes such as 'relational obligation' and 'invisible ledger', which formed an aggregate dimension of 'informal lending identity', explaining resistance to logging peer loans in a fintech app.
sources: Gioia (Administrative Science Quarterly) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 28 — The Gioia Methodology — Identity-First Systematic Analysis
reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31.

name: Gioia Methodology
aka: Gioia methodology (grounded theory rigour with interpretive flexibility)
origin: Dennis Gioia, Kevin Corley and Aimee Hamilton, 2013 (Organizational Research Methods), building on Gioia's work from the 1990s
summary: Builds inductive theory by moving from informant-centric first-order concepts to researcher-centric second-order themes and aggregate dimensions, displayed in a transparent data structure.
description: The Gioia methodology offers a systematic route from interview data to new concepts while preserving informants' voices. Analysts first code first-order concepts in participants' own terms, often producing dozens of codes. They then look for similarities and differences, grouping these into second-order themes framed in theoretical language, and finally distil the themes into a small number of aggregate dimensions. The resulting data structure diagram shows every step from quotes to dimensions, making the inductive leap inspectable. A dynamic grounded model then shows how dimensions relate. Rigour comes from the explicit two-level coding, the visible data structure, and the assumption that informants are knowledgeable agents whose interpretations deserve to be represented before the researcher's.
steps: Conduct semi-structured interviews and code first-order concepts in informants' own language, staying close to their terms and accepting a large initial set of codes.
Compare first-order concepts to find similarities and differences, reducing them to a manageable set of about 20 to 40 concepts with descriptive labels.
Group first-order concepts into second-order themes that ask what is going on theoretically, moving to researcher-centric language.
Distil second-order themes into 2 to 5 aggregate dimensions that capture the overarching constructs.
Draw the data structure diagram linking first-order concepts, second-order themes and aggregate dimensions, with representative quotes for each concept in a supporting table.
Build a dynamic grounded model showing relationships and processes between the dimensions, and check it against the data and with a peer debriefer.
outputs: First-order concept list, second-order themes, aggregate dimensions, a data structure diagram, a quote table, and a dynamic grounded model.
useWhen: You want to derive new concepts or frameworks from interviews in a way stakeholders can audit, for example a model of how teams adopt a platform or why users trust automation.
avoidWhen: The aim is descriptive themes rather than conceptual models (use Reflexive Thematic Analysis), or the dataset is small and tactical.
whyLost: It lives in management journals and doctoral training, and almost never appears in UX books or courses, so practitioners rarely encounter it.
whereToUse: B2B adoption and organisational change, platform strategy, emerging AI work practices, and research frameworks presented to leadership.
example: From 25 interviews with engineering managers, first-order codes such as 'rerunning the AI's tests' and 'asking a senior to check' form the theme 'borrowed verification', within the aggregate dimension 'calibrating trust', guiding verification features in an AI coding tool.
sources: Gioia, Corley & Hamilton (2013) Organizational Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 28
Gioia (Administrative Science Quarterly) via Sage Handbook
Seeking Qualitative Rigor in Inductive Research (Gioia, Corley & Hamilton)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 28 — The Gioia Methodology — Identity-First Systematic Analysis
reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G. & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15-31.

extra.The Data Structure Diagram: The Gioia methodology's signature output is a data structure diagram — a visual hierarchy showing: first-order codes (left column) → second-order themes (middle column) → aggregate dimensions (right column). Arrows show the movement from specific to abstract. This diagram IS the findings. It makes your analytical choices visible and auditable. Every first-order code must trace to a second-order theme; every second-order theme must trace to an aggregate dimension. No orphan codes.

name: Give-and-Take Matrix
origin: Gray, Brown and Macanufo, 2010, inspired by matrix techniques in engineering, chemistry and design
summary: A square actor-by-actor matrix with each actor's motivation on the diagonal and, in every other cell, the value one actor can give another, exposing gaps and conflicts.
description: The give-and-take matrix maps how value flows among the actors in a system, from people on a task to organisations in a partnership. Actors are listed on both axes; rows are 'from' and columns 'to', so each cell holds one direction of flow.
