The diagonal holds each actor's primary motivation, a short phrase on what they want from the system. Working one actor at a time, the group asks 'What can I offer you?' for each cell. Some cells fill easily; empty or contested cells reveal unconnected actors or conflicting interests. The book is explicit that first entries are assumptions and that surveys or interviews before and after the mapping are needed to validate motivations and flows. It pairs naturally with stakeholder analysis and boundary mapping.
steps: List all actors in the system, people or organisations.
Draw a matrix with the actors on both axes, rows as 'from' and columns as 'to'.
Write each actor's primary motivation on the diagonal as a brief phrase.
Take one actor at a time and, for each cell in its row, ask 'What can I offer you?' and record the value that flows in that direction only.
Mark cells that are empty, unclear or conflicting.
Turn uncertain motivations and flows into questions and check them with interviews or surveys, then revise the matrix.
outputs: A completed actor-by-actor value matrix showing motivations, directional value flows, gaps and conflicts.
useWhen: Designing multi-sided products, partnerships or services where the team needs to see whether every actor gets something from every relationship.
avoidWhen: Entries are assumptions until checked; do not use it as evidence of motivations. Validate with Stakeholder Interview Protocol (Organisational Research) or Interviews, and for strategic interaction among actors consider Game-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-User Systems. With more than about ten actors the matrix becomes unwieldy; use Stakeholder Mapping.
whyLost: Known through Gamestorming but rarely run because value-network and ecosystem maps cover similar ground visually and the cell-by-cell discipline feels slow.
whereToUse: Marketplaces and platforms, B2B2C services, health and care ecosystems, partnership and integration strategy.
example: A food-delivery marketplace maps customers, couriers, restaurants and the platform; the courier-to-restaurant cell is empty, prompting interviews that reveal couriers could offer pickup-time feedback restaurants would value.
reference: Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010) Gamestorming: A Playbook for Innovators, Rulebreakers, and Changemakers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 177-178.

name: Glanceability Measurement
origin: Andrew Schall, contributed section in Albert and Tullis, 2022
summary: Assess whether information on a small screen can be seen and understood in a brief glance, using fixation counts, fixation durations and saccade lengths paired with comprehension.
description: Glanceability is the ability to view and understand information quickly. Wearable and mobile experiences often depend on users catching a cue during a short glance, such as a smartwatch notification or a two-factor authentication code. Eye-tracking indicators of good glanceability are relatively few fixations, short fixation durations and short saccades on the relevant area. Because short fixations could also mean users skipped content, eye metrics must be paired with measures of whether the information was correctly understood and how quickly. Designs are compared on both: better glanceability shows fewer, shorter fixations with equal or better comprehension. Related approaches in automotive human factors limit and measure glance time against set criteria.
steps: Define the glanceable information and the decision the user must make from it.
Present it in a realistic context, ideally with mobile or wearable eye tracking.
Record fixation count, fixation duration and saccade length on the relevant area.
Measure whether the user understood the information correctly, and how quickly.
Compare designs on eye metrics and comprehension together.
outputs: Eye-movement indicators and comprehension accuracy and speed per design.
useWhen: Designing notifications, watch faces, dashboards, in-car displays and any information meant to be read at a glance.
avoidWhen: Content meant for sustained reading, or when eye tracking is unavailable (use timed exposure tests such as the 5-Second Test with comprehension questions).
whyLost: Measurement of glances is established in automotive and wearables research, but mainstream UX teams rarely run eye-tracking studies on small screens.
whereToUse: Smartwatches, fitness trackers, lock-screen notifications, boarding passes, car dashboards and AR overlays.
example: Two smartwatch layouts for a 2FA code are compared with mobile eye tracking. Layout B needs one fixation instead of three with equal accuracy, so it ships.
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022) Measuring the User Experience: Collecting, Analyzing, and Presenting UX Metrics, 3rd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 181-182.

name: Global-local hierarchical letter task (Navon figures)
origin: David Navon, 1977
summary: Time identification of large letters made of small letters to measure whether people process overall shape before parts, and how each level interferes with the other.
description: Compound stimuli are built in which a large (global) letter is made of small (local) letters: consistent stimuli match (an H of Hs), inconsistent ones differ (an H of Ss). On each trial participants identify the letter at the global or local level, and response time and accuracy are recorded. With small, closely spaced local letters, global identification is faster and unaffected by local consistency, whereas local identification slows when the global letter conflicts: the global precedence effect. Spacing, size and density of the local elements change the advantage, so they are critical parameters. The paradigm gives two indices, a global advantage and a global-to-local interference score, and has been used with infants and clinical groups.
steps: Build compound stimuli, consistent and inconsistent, at controlled sizes and local-element spacing.
On each trial, cue the level to report (global or local) or block by level.
Record response time and accuracy over enough trials per cell (for example 40 or more).
Compute global advantage (local RT minus global RT) and interference from the unattended level.
Vary local element size and spacing to map where the advantage reverses.
Adapt the stimuli to interface elements (for example a layout shape made of icons) for applied questions.
outputs: Mean RT and accuracy by level and consistency, global advantage score and global-to-local interference score.
useWhen: Studying whether users see the overall structure of a dense display (dashboard, map, grid) before details, and how much element density supports or blocks that.
avoidWhen: Avoid generalising across sizes and densities, since the effect depends on them; for overall visual grouping use a Gestalt principles audit.
whyLost: It is a perception research paradigm with no packaged design application.
whereToUse: Dashboards and data visualisation, maps, icon grids, logos and composite marks, accessibility research with neurodivergent users.
example: A monitoring dashboard is tested with tiles at two densities; at high density, operators identify the overall alert pattern faster than individual tile states, and conflicting tile colours slow detail reading.
sources: Navon, D. (1977). Forest before trees: The precedence of global features in visual perception. Cognitive Psychology, 9
reference: Navon, D. (1977). Forest before trees: The precedence of global features in visual perception. Cognitive Psychology, 9, 353-383.

name: GMM Behavioural Clustering
origin: Mixture models from Karl Pearson, 1894; EM estimation by Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977; BIC by Schwarz, 1978
summary: Fits Gaussian mixture models to behavioural log features to find probabilistic user segments, choosing the number of segments by BIC and giving each user membership probabilities.
description: Gaussian mixture models assume the data are generated by a mixture of several multivariate normal distributions, each representing a latent segment. Fitted by expectation-maximisation, a GMM gives each user a probability of belonging to each segment rather than a hard label, and allows segments of different shapes and sizes, unlike k-means. The number of components is chosen with the Bayesian Information Criterion, balancing fit and complexity. Applied to behavioural features derived from logs, such as frequency, feature breadth, session length and recency, GMMs produce data-driven behavioural segments that can anchor or test personas. Rigour comes from careful feature engineering and scaling, BIC-based model selection, stability checks across samples, and qualitative validation of segments.
steps: Define the behavioural question and engineer features from logs over a fixed window, such as activity frequency, feature usage breadth, session depth and recency.
Transform and standardise features (for example log-transform skewed counts) and reduce dimensionality if needed with PCA.
Fit GMMs across a range of component numbers (for example 2 to 10) and covariance types, selecting the model with the lowest BIC.
Check stability by refitting on bootstrap samples or different time windows, and inspect membership probabilities for ambiguous users.
Profile each segment by feature means and outcomes such as retention or revenue, and name segments descriptively.
Validate segments qualitatively by interviewing users with high membership probabilities in each segment before turning them into personas.
outputs: A selected mixture model, BIC comparison, segment profiles, user-level membership probabilities, stability diagnostics, and behaviour-based persona foundations.
useWhen: You have rich behavioural logs and want data-driven segments for personas, targeting or product strategy, especially where users blend behaviours rather than fitting crisp groups.
avoidWhen: You lack sufficient behavioural data, features are mostly categorical (use latent class analysis), or you need to understand motivations without logs; use interviews or Q Methodology. Overly restrictive error structures (for example local independence or diagonal covariances imposed without checking) can overestimate the number of classes; adding direct effects for locally dependent indicators often reduces it, but can also hide real classes, so compare both by BIC.
whyLost: Personas are still built from demographics and interviews alone, and behavioural clustering sits with data science teams rarely involved in UX segmentation.
whereToUse: SaaS feature adoption segmentation, consumer app engagement personas, fintech behaviour segments, learning platforms, and targeting research recruitment.
example: A project-management SaaS fits GMMs to 40,000 accounts. BIC selects 5 segments, including 'solo planners' and 'meeting-driven teams'. Interviews with high-probability members confirm distinct needs, replacing three demographic personas.
sources: Schwarz (1978) Estimating the dimension of a model, Annals of Statistics
The Inquiry Series, Vol III, Ch 51
The Inquiry Series, C4 — Behavioural Log Analysis — From Clickstreams to Personas
Vermunt JK & Magidson J (2002) Latent class cluster analysis. In Hagenaars JA & McCutcheon AL (Eds) Applied Latent Class Analysis. Cambridge University Press
reference: Dempster, A. P., Laird, N. M. & Rubin, D. B. (1977). Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 39(1), 1-38.

name: GMM cluster interpretation
origin: Gaussian mixture modelling (Pearson, 1894; EM by Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977); profiling practice from market segmentation
summary: Turns fitted Gaussian mixture components into meaningful behavioural archetypes by profiling means, covariances and membership uncertainty against qualitative evidence.
description: A GMM outputs, for each component, a mixing weight, a mean vector and a covariance matrix, plus each user's posterior membership probabilities. Interpretation translates these into archetypes: which features deviate most from the population mean (standardised differences), how variables co-vary within a component, how large and how certain each group is, and how components differ on outcomes not used in clustering. Careful interpretation keeps the probabilistic nature visible, reporting uncertain users and overlap rather than turning components into crisp personas. It avoids naming clusters from a single feature and validates names with qualitative review of exemplar users.
steps: For each component, compute standardised mean differences from the overall mean for every feature and rank the largest.
Inspect within-component covariance to see characteristic co-variation (e.g. high trade frequency with small order size).
Report mixing weights and the distribution of posterior probabilities, identifying users with maximum membership below 0.7.
Profile components on external variables not used in clustering, such as retention, revenue and survey attitudes.
Pull 5-10 high-probability exemplar users per component for session replay or interviews and write a draft archetype description.
Name archetypes by behaviour, not demographics, and record the evidence for each name.
outputs: Archetype profiles with defining features, sizes, certainty, external outcome differences and exemplar evidence.
useWhen: After fitting a GMM to behavioural data, when segments will inform personas, targeting or design priorities.
avoidWhen: Avoid over-interpreting components from unstable fits or poorly chosen features; revisit feature construction and validation first.
whyLost: Data scientists fit mixtures but rarely do the interpretive work; UX researchers who could interpret them rarely see the model outputs.
whereToUse: Replacing demographic personas with behavioural archetypes in fintech, SaaS and media; tailoring onboarding to usage modes.
example: A GMM on investor logs yields a component with high weekday-morning activity, small frequent trades and tight covariance between news views and trades. Interviews with exemplar users confirm a 'news reactor' archetype, guiding a calmer news-to-trade flow.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 51 — Behavioral Clustering & Probabilistic Segmentation
reference: McLachlan, G. & Peel, D. (2000) Finite Mixture Models. Wiley.

name: Go-to-Market (Launch) Plan
origin: Product marketing and product management practice
summary: A coordinated plan for bringing a product or major release to its market: awareness, discovery, narrative, partners, materials, pricing, resourcing, and only dates the team can truly commit to.
description: A product that fits a market need still has to reach its customers. The go-to-market plan coordinates that effort across marketing, business development, sales, customer success and support. It covers how the target market will hear of the product, how people will discover what it offers, a narrative in which the customer is the hero and the product supports their journey, partners and business development, marketing and advertising materials, the pricing model, and the people and budget needed. Crumlish insists it is distinct from a roadmap: stakeholders who ask for the roadmap often want feature dates, so they should get a separate release plan containing only firm commitments. For UX teams the plan matters because launch messaging, onboarding and pricing pages are experiences too, and because launch success can overload the product on day one.
steps: Confirm the target market and the need the product meets, using existing market sizing and product-market fit evidence.
Plan awareness: the channels by which the target market will hear of the product.
Plan discovery: how people will learn what it offers (site, demos, trials, onboarding).
Write the narrative with the customer as hero and the product as support on their journey.
Line up partners and business-development stakeholders, and produce marketing and advertising materials.
Set the pricing model and check that pricing pages and plans are understandable to users.
Budget people and money and agree dates and roles with marketing, sales, business development, customer success and support.
Keep the launch plan separate from the roadmap and include only items and dates that can genuinely be committed; plan capacity for launch-day load.
outputs: A go-to-market plan and, where needed, a dated release plan (for example a Gantt-style template).
useWhen: Use when a new product or major release is approaching launch and several functions must act in concert.
avoidWhen: Avoid using it to set product direction; use a Now/Next/Later Outcome Roadmap. Test messaging and pricing with users before committing, for example with Fake door, painted door and smoke tests or Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter.
whyLost: It is routine in product marketing but sits outside most UX teams, who often meet launch decisions late.
whereToUse: New product launches, major releases, market expansions, B2B product introductions.
example: A productivity app emails the tens of thousands of people on its smoke-test sign-up list on launch day, reaching the top of its app-store category. The plan had included server capacity limits, so downloads were throttled rather than the service failing.
reference: Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People: From Designing to Thriving in a Product World. Rosenfeld Media, pp. 77-79, 165-166.

name: Go/No-Go Checkpoint and Project Risk Portfolio
aka: Planned go/no-go checkpoint and project risk portfolio
Early stopping point for data projects
origin: Jacqueline Nolis and Emily Robinson (2020), Build a Career in Data Science
summary: Build an agreed feasibility checkpoint and stopping rule into risky projects, and balance risky work with safer work across the team's portfolio.
description: Data projects fail because the data is not what was expected, contains no signal, or the customer did not want the result. Nolis and Robinson manage this risk up front. Get data samples before committing; where that is impossible, place an early go/no-go review in the timeline at which stakeholders reassess feasibility, and scope risky projects with an explicit cut-off, such as stopping if good data is not found within a month. Present the possibility of stopping at the outset so that stopping is not seen as failure. Run several projects at once so a risky model is backed by safer reports, show an MVP to customers early, and do not remove risk entirely, or the team stagnates. The practice transfers directly to ambitious research, AI features and analytics work in UX.
steps: Request samples of the data or materials before the project starts.
If that is impossible, schedule an early go/no-go review with stakeholders in the project timeline.
Define a cut-off condition and date for risky projects (for example, stop if usable data is not found within one month).
Present the possibility of stopping to stakeholders at the outset.
Hold a mix of risky and safe projects so the portfolio still delivers if one is stopped.
Show an MVP early and talk to customers.
If data is lacking, try substitutes with caution or start a separate instrumentation project.
outputs: A project timeline with a feasibility gate and explicit stopping rule, and a balanced project portfolio.
useWhen: Use it for analytics, machine-learning features or research programmes whose feasibility depends on data or access that cannot be confirmed in advance.
avoidWhen: It governs whether to continue, not what users need; pair it with Key Assumptions Check or Expected Value of Information Analysis for deciding which uncertainties matter. Substitute data often differs enough to cause real problems.
whyLost: Stage gates are standard in product development and data science, but UX research and design projects rarely set explicit kill criteria.
whereToUse: AI and ML features, behavioural analytics projects, research using logs or partner data, and innovation portfolios.
example: A loyalty team plans to analyse spend by past tier, but samples show only current tier is stored. The agreed two-week gate stops the analysis and starts an instrumentation project instead.
sources: Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Nolis, J. and Robinson, E. (2020). Build a Career in Data Science. Shelter Island, NY: Manning Publications, pp. 216-222.

name: Goal-Directed Persona Construction (Cooper's Method)
origin: Alan Cooper, The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1999), describing personas in use at his firm since 1992; method detailed in About Face by Cooper, Reimann and Cronin
summary: Builds personas from behavioural variables identified in interview data, defined by end goals, experience goals and life goals rather than demographics.
description: Cooper's original persona method is a synthesis procedure, not a creative writing exercise. Researchers interview users, identify 10-20 behavioural variables (activities, attitudes, aptitudes, motivations, skills), and place each interviewee on each variable's spectrum. Clusters of people who sit together across several variables reveal significant behaviour patterns, each of which becomes a persona. Personas are defined by goals: end goals (what they want to accomplish), experience goals (how they want to feel) and life goals (who they want to be), and a primary persona is chosen as the design target. In current practice personas have become demographic marketing sketches or invented composites, losing the variable mapping step that makes them traceable to evidence. The rigorous version allows anyone to audit why a persona exists.
steps: Conduct 6-8 behavioural interviews per target user type.

For each participant, identify end goals (task-level objectives), experience goals (emotional states sought) and life goals (identity-level aspirations); Cooper's earlier taxonomy also separates personal, corporate and practical goals from false goals, which are means mistaken for ends.
Cluster participants by goal pattern rather than demographics, and build one specific, named persona per major behavioural pattern ('precision, not accuracy').

Assemble the cast of characters on a single sheet with names, pictures, goals and a telltale quote (typically 3 to 12 personas, winnowed to about 3 to 7), including a negative persona showing whom the product is not designed for.
Choose the primary persona: one who must be satisfied and cannot be satisfied by an interface designed for any other persona; more than three primaries signals too broad a problem.
State each persona's goals explicitly as design requirements.
outputs: Behavioural variable map with interviewee positions, persona set with goals and behaviours, primary and secondary persona designation, and traceability to interview evidence.
useWhen: Synthesising generative interview research into design targets for a product with distinct user behaviour patterns, and resolving debates about who the product is for.
avoidWhen: When you lack behavioural interview data (do the research first), or when quantitative segmentation is needed for sizing; use cluster analysis or mixture models instead.
whyLost: Personas were absorbed into marketing as demographic profiles and 'proto-personas', and the behavioural-variable mapping step was cut as too slow.
whereToUse: Product vision research, design principle development, any product where emotional and identity goals matter alongside functional goals. More rigorous than demographic personas.
example: A field-service SaaS maps 18 technician interviews onto 12 behavioural variables. Two clusters emerge, 'route optimisers' and 'fix-first craftspeople', and choosing the latter as primary persona reorients the mobile app around diagnostics.
sources: Inmates Are Running the Asylum — Alan Cooper
About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design (Alan Cooper et al.)
reference: Cooper A, Reimann R, Cronin D & Noessel C (2014) About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design. 4th ed. Wiley

name: Goal-Directed Task Analysis (GDTA)
aka: Goal-Directed Task Analysis (GDTA) for situation awareness requirements
donor: Aviation human factors and cognitive engineering
origin: Mica Endsley (1993); Endsley and Rodgers (1994); Endsley and Jones (2012)
summary: Decompose a role into goals, subgoals and decisions, then list the information each decision needs to perceive, comprehend and project the situation, for display design and SA measurement.
description: GDTA is a cognitive task analysis that determines what situation awareness a role needs. Major goals of the role are identified, then subgoals, then the decisions each subgoal requires, and finally the SA requirements for each decision at three levels: level 1 data to perceive, level 2 comprehension of what the data mean together, and level 3 projection of what will happen next. It is organised by goals rather than physical tasks, done separately per role, covers normal and rare conditions, imposes no sequence or priority, and is kept independent of current technology. Data come from expert interviews, observation, verbal protocols and documents, with several experts analysed individually, pooled and validated by a wider group. The output drives SA-oriented design principles and supplies the queries used in SAGAT.
steps: Pick the role to analyse (for example on-call engineer versus incident commander).
Identify the role's major goals through expert interviews, observation, verbal protocols and documents.
Break each goal into subgoals.
For each subgoal list the key decisions, phrased as questions the person must answer.
Under each decision list the SA requirements: projections, comprehension and the data to perceive, without naming the technology that provides them.
Analyse several experts separately, pool the results and validate with a wider expert group.
Use the requirements to design displays and to write SAGAT queries for evaluation.
outputs: A goal-subgoal-decision hierarchy per role with SA requirements at three levels.
useWhen: Designing dashboards, monitoring tools or AI assistants for roles that must stay aware of a changing situation, and preparing SA-based evaluation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when work is procedural and stable; Hierarchical Task Analysis is enough. It does not show goal priority, which shifts over time, so pair it with observation of real episodes.
whyLost: It is standard in aviation, military and healthcare human factors but little known in UX, which designs dashboards from feature requests rather than SA requirements.
whereToUse: Operations and observability dashboards, fleet and logistics control, clinical monitoring, trading and risk desks, human oversight of AI agents.
example: For a fraud analyst role, the goal 'stop fraudulent payouts' yields the decision 'will this account cash out before review?', with level 3 needing projected time to withdrawal and level 1 needing account age and transfer velocity. The case view is rebuilt to show those first.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Endsley, M. R. and Jones, D. G. (2012). Designing for Situation Awareness: An Approach to User-Centered Design (2nd ed.). Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press.

name: Goal-Free Evaluation
origin: Michael Scriven (1972)
summary: Evaluate what a product or programme actually does for people, judged against their needs, while the evaluator is deliberately kept ignorant of its stated goals.
description: In goal-free evaluation the evaluator does not read proposals, objectives or success metrics. Only observable outcomes and documentable effects are studied, and they are judged against assessed participant needs. Scriven's reasons: studying stated objectives narrows attention and misses unanticipated outcomes, the label 'side effects' downgrades important consequences, and knowing the goals biases perception. Qualitative methods suit it because they are open to whatever effects occur. A strong variant runs a goals-based team and a goal-free team in parallel and compares their findings, a form of analyst triangulation. In UX it counters the tendency to evaluate features only against the KPI they were built to move.
steps: Arrange for the evaluator to be screened from goals, proposals, OKRs and success metrics; a gatekeeper filters materials.
Assess the needs of the people affected, independently of the product's intentions.
Observe use and interview users and bystanders to document actual effects, intended or not.
Compare documented effects with assessed needs, rating benefits and harms.
Optionally run a parallel goals-based evaluation and compare the two teams' findings.
outputs: A needs-referenced account of effects, including unanticipated benefits and harms.
useWhen: You suspect a product has effects beyond its stated aims, for example social, wellbeing or second-order effects, or when goal-based evaluation keeps confirming what the team hoped.
avoidWhen: You must report against agreed targets, or the evaluator cannot realistically stay ignorant of the goals. Funders and product owners may resist; use goal-based outcome evaluation with an explicit unintended-effects probe instead.
whyLost: It stayed within evaluation theory; product teams are organised around goals and metrics, so goal-blind evaluation feels counter-cultural.
whereToUse: Engagement-driven consumer apps, AI features, civic and health services, post-launch reviews of features with possible side effects.
example: An external researcher evaluates a teen social app without seeing its engagement targets. Interviews reveal sleep disruption and peer comparison effects the goal-based review had treated as out of scope.
reference: Scriven, M. (1972). Pros and cons about goal-free evaluation. Evaluation Comment, 3(4), 1-7.

name: GOMS / KLM
aka: Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules
origin: Stuart Card, Thomas Moran & Allen Newell, 1980 to 1983
summary: Predicts expert task execution time from first principles by decomposing tasks into goals, operators, methods and selection rules, or keystroke-level operators.
description: GOMS models describe skilled performance in terms of Goals, Operators (elementary actions), Methods (sequences of operators that achieve goals) and Selection rules (which method to choose). The Keystroke-Level Model is the simplest variant: a task is broken down into physical and mental operators, such as keystrokes (K about 0.2 s), pointing (P about 1.1 s), homing (H about 0.4 s) and mental preparation (M about 1.35 s), whose standard times are summed to predict expert execution time. The approach lets designers compare designs quantitatively before building or testing, and was validated against real performance within roughly 20 percent. Rigour comes from careful task decomposition, consistent application of the heuristics for placing mental operators, and recognising that models predict error-free expert performance, not learnability.
steps: Select benchmark tasks that experts perform frequently.
Write the method for each task in each design as a sequence of physical operators.
Insert mental operators using Card, Moran and Newell's placement heuristics.
Assign standard operator times, or calibrate them with local measurements.
Sum operator times to predict execution time per task and design.
Compare designs and, where stakes are high, validate predictions with timed expert users.
outputs: Predicted execution times per task and design, operator breakdowns showing where time goes, and quantitative design comparisons.
useWhen: For high-frequency expert tasks where seconds matter, such as call centres, data entry, trading or operator consoles, and for comparing designs before building.
avoidWhen: Avoid for novice learnability, error-prone or highly variable creative tasks; use cognitive walkthrough or usability testing.
whyLost: GOMS was a flagship HCI method in the 1980s-90s, but agile practice, the cost of modelling and focus on novice consumers made it essentially disappear from industry.
whereToUse: Expert task analysis; safety-critical system design; time-prediction for operator tasks.
example: A contact centre compares two address-entry designs with KLM. The redesigned postcode lookup saves 4.2 seconds per call, which at two million calls a year justifies the change before any build.
sources: The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (Card, Moran & Newell)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 16 — Cognitive Task Modeling — GOMS, KLM & CPM-GOMS
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Card SK, Moran TP & Newell A (1983) The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction
The GOMS Family of User Interface Analysis Techniques (John & Kieras, 1996)
GOMS Models: Simplified Cognitive Architectures (Kieras, n.d.)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Card, S. K., Moran, T. P. & Newell, A. (1983). The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: GOMS and KLM with Expert User Timing Studies
origin: Stuart Card, Thomas Moran and Allen Newell (1980, 1983)
summary: Predicts expert task times by decomposing tasks into GOMS methods and keystroke-level operators, calibrated with timing studies of real expert users and devices.
description: GOMS (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection rules) models skilled, error-free performance; its simplest variant, the Keystroke-Level Model, predicts execution time by summing standard operator times: keystroke (about 0.2 s for a skilled typist), pointing (about 1.1 s), homing hands between devices (0.4 s) and mental preparation (1.35 s), using placement rules for M operators. Predictions typically fall within about 20% of observed expert times. Its rigour, and its decline, lie in calibration: standard operator times are population averages from 1980s hardware. Running short timing studies with actual expert users on current devices to re-estimate operator times, especially for touch, and validating model predictions against observed times, makes KLM a cheap way to compare designs for high-frequency tasks without large experiments.
steps: Empirically derive KLM parameters for your specific user group and device: time 20+ participants performing each operator type in isolation.
Compute trimmed means.
For touch interfaces: separate tapping (0.3–0.5s) from swipe (0.2–0.4s).
For elderly users: K≈0.35s, P≈1.5s.
For expert keyboard users: K≈0.12s.
Apply updated parameters to KLM predictions for the target interface.
outputs: Task method decompositions, calibrated operator times for the target population and device, predicted versus observed task times, and design comparisons in seconds saved per task.
useWhen: High-frequency expert workflows such as call centres, data entry, trading, clinical documentation, and choosing between design alternatives before building.
avoidWhen: For novice use, learning, error-prone tasks or open-ended creative work, which GOMS does not model; use usability testing or cognitive walkthrough.
whyLost: GOMS was associated with desktop-era research and seen as laborious, and teams stopped calibrating operator times, so predictions on modern touch devices drifted and lost credibility.
whereToUse: Mobile UX performance prediction, accessibility-aware time estimates, expert vs. novice interface benchmarking, call-center UI optimization.
example: A contact-centre CRM compares two layouts for logging a call outcome. Calibrated KLM predicts 4.1 s saved per call, which at 60,000 calls a day justifies the redesign; a timing study with 8 agents confirms a 3.7 s saving.
sources: The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (Card, Moran & Newell)
reference: Card SK, Moran TP & Newell A (1983) The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction. Lawrence Erlbaum

name: Gower's Distance for Mixed-Data Clustering
origin: J. C. Gower (1971), Biometrics
summary: Measures similarity between users described by a mix of numbers and categories, so they can be clustered properly.
description: Persona and segment data mixes types: age and session counts are numeric, role and plan are categorical, some answers are yes or no. Standard k-means needs numeric data, and one-hot encoding distorts distances. Gower's distance scales each variable to 0 to 1 by its own type (range-normalised difference for numbers, match or mismatch for categories) and averages them. It pairs with hierarchical clustering or PAM (k-medoids). Bruce and Bruce also warn about dominant variables and scaling issues that silently shape clusters.
steps: Assemble mixed variables per user and decide which to include.
Compute the Gower distance matrix, optionally weighting variables.
Cluster with hierarchical clustering or PAM.
Choose the number of clusters with silhouette widths and interpretability.
Profile and name clusters, then validate with qualitative follow-up.
outputs: Segments based on all the data types you collected.
useWhen: Clustering survey or CRM data with categorical and numeric variables.
avoidWhen: Very large datasets (the distance matrix grows quadratically) or purely numeric data.
whyLost: UX segmentation commonly runs k-means on whatever is numeric and drops the rest.
whereToUse: Data-driven personas, B2B account segmentation, research panel stratification.
example: Clustering 900 B2B users on role, company size, plan and usage with Gower distance gives five segments; k-means on usage alone had missed the admin segment.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Gower, J. C. (1971). A general coefficient of similarity and some of its properties. Biometrics 27; Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 7.

name: GRADE Evidence Grading
donor: Evidence-based medicine and clinical guideline development
origin: GRADE Working Group, Gordon Guyatt and colleagues, 2000-2008
summary: Rates the certainty of a body of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low by assessing risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.
description: GRADE separates the quality of evidence from the strength of a recommendation. Evidence from randomised trials starts high and observational evidence low; ratings are downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency across studies, indirectness (different population or outcome), imprecision (wide intervals) and publication bias, and upgraded for large effects, dose-response or when confounding would reduce the effect. The Evidence-to-Decision framework then weighs benefits, harms, values, resources and feasibility. Research repositories in UX store 'insights' without any certainty grading, so a single five-person study and a replicated experiment look equally authoritative. GRADE offers a rigorous, transparent grading scheme.
steps: Define the question and the critical outcomes for the decision.
Gather the body of evidence for each outcome (studies, experiments, analytics).
Assign a starting certainty by design (experiments high, observational and qualitative lower).
Assess and document downgrades for bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias, and possible upgrades.
Assign a final certainty rating per outcome and present a summary-of-findings table.
Use an Evidence-to-Decision table to make and explain recommendations, stating strength (strong or conditional).
outputs: Certainty ratings per outcome, summary-of-findings tables and transparent recommendations.
useWhen: Building research repositories, writing design guidelines, or making recommendations from mixed-quality evidence.
avoidWhen: Single exploratory studies where grading adds little; or for qualitative evidence alone, consider GRADE-CERQual.
whyLost: Medical evidence frameworks were not part of UX's culture, which favours storytelling over graded certainty.
whereToUse: Insight repositories, design system guidelines, accessibility standards, AI product policy decisions.
example: A research repository tags each insight with GRADE certainty. A popular insight that 'users want dark mode' is rated low (indirect, self-report), while 'inline validation reduces errors' is rated high from replicated experiments.
sources: Guyatt et al., GRADE: an emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations (2008), BMJ
Lewin et al., Applying GRADE-CERQual to qualitative evidence synthesis findings (2018), Implementation Science
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)

name: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) for UX Outcomes
origin: Friedman (2001) gradient boosting; Chen & Guestrin (2016) XGBoost
summary: A high-accuracy model that builds many small trees in sequence, each correcting the last, for predicting churn, satisfaction or conversion.
description: Boosting fits a series of shallow trees where each new tree focuses on the errors of the ensemble so far. XGBoost adds regularisation and efficient computation, and it wins many prediction competitions on tabular data. Bruce and Bruce explain the key hyperparameters (learning rate, depth, subsampling, regularisation) and how to tune them with cross-validation to avoid overfitting. Paired with SHAP values, boosting becomes an explainable driver model for large behavioural datasets.
steps: Prepare a tabular dataset of user features and an outcome.
Split into training and test sets (or use cross-validation).
Tune learning rate, tree depth, subsampling and regularisation.
Evaluate on held-out data with AUC, precision and recall.
Explain predictions with SHAP values and validate surprising drivers qualitatively.
outputs: An accurate predictive model with explainable drivers.
useWhen: Large behavioural or survey datasets where prediction accuracy matters.
avoidWhen: Small samples or when a simple, transparent model is enough.
whyLost: Considered a data science tool; UX rarely builds predictive models.
whereToUse: Churn prediction, satisfaction prediction from telemetry, support contact prediction.
example: A model predicting which new customers will contact support within 30 days reaches AUC 0.84, and SHAP shows address validation errors are the top driver.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 6.

name: Graduated Assistance Levels
aka: Graduated assistance levels and assist recording
origin: Joseph Dumas and Beth Loring, 2008
summary: A four-step ladder of moderator help, from breaking a loop to telling the next step, with rules on when to assist and how to score assisted tasks.
description: An assist is any intervention that moves a participant towards completion and would not happen without a moderator. Assists let a test continue past an early blocker so later problems can still be observed, but too much help masks them. Dumas and Loring give criteria for assisting: the participant repeats unproductive behaviour, has tried alternatives and asks for help, is heading for a crash, nears the time limit, or wrongly believes the task is done. Think-aloud prompts, encouragement, task clarification and bug recovery are not assists. The ladder has four levels: 1 break the repeating sequence ('what do you think is going on here?'); 2 general hint; 3 specific hint naming the location; 4 tell the next step only. Levels can be skipped. Each task is recorded as completed, completed with assistance (type and count) or not completed, and summative tests restrict assists to level 4.
steps: Before testing, decide whether assists are allowed, at which levels, and whether assisted completion counts as success.
Wait until it is clear the participant is stuck and why; first ask them to keep trying if options are not exhausted.
Level 1: break the loop with a refocusing question or ask them to reread the task.
Level 2: give a general hint; Level 3: give a specific hint naming the location.
Level 4: tell the next step only; in summative tests use only this level.
Record each task outcome and every assist's level on the data sheet, keeping multiple moderators consistent.
Treat assists as problem evidence and account for them in success rates and ratings.
outputs: Task outcome codes with assist counts and levels, and continued observation of later task steps.
useWhen: Moderated usability tests where early blockers would otherwise hide later problems, and studies with several moderators needing consistent intervention.
avoidWhen: Comparative or benchmark tests where assists would distort results; unmoderated tests where no assist is possible (use Unmoderated Remote Testing with stopping rules).
whyLost: Moderators still help stuck participants, but usually ad hoc, without levels, criteria or recording, so assisted success is often reported as success.
whereToUse: Formative testing of complex software, onboarding flows and expert tools.
example: A participant cannot find the export menu in a reporting tool. The moderator gives a level 3 hint naming the menu, so the team still observes the confusing export dialog, and the task is coded as completed with one level-3 assist.
reference: Dumas, J.S. and Loring, B.A. (2008) Moderating Usability Tests: Principles and Practices for Interacting. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Graffiti walls
origin: Design research practice (documented in Martin and Hanington's Universal Methods of Design)
summary: Fix large paper with markers and an optional prompt in the place being studied so passers-by can write or draw anonymous comments, then photograph and analyse the walls across sites.
description: Graffiti walls collect candid, anonymous input in situ, without a researcher present. Large sheets of paper are fixed to a wall in the setting being studied, with markers attached on strings and optionally a guiding question. Passers-by write or draw whatever they like, often responding to each other. The walls are photographed daily (since content can be removed or overwritten) and finally taken down and analysed, comparing walls from different sites. The method suits sensitive or intrusive settings, such as public toilets, hospital corridors or staff rooms, where interviews or observation would be inappropriate, and it captures the vocabulary and tone people use among themselves. It offers no control over who contributes or how representative they are, and walls can be removed as vandalism.
steps: Choose sites and, optionally, a guiding question or prompt.
Get permission from site owners and post large paper with markers attached on strings.
Photograph each wall daily to preserve content that may be changed or removed.
After the set period (often one to two weeks), remove and collect the walls.
Code comments and drawings, compare across sites and note conversational threads between contributors.
outputs: Anonymous comments and drawings, a dated photo record, and coded themes compared across sites.
useWhen: Gathering candid, low-effort feedback in a physical place, especially sensitive settings where interviews or observation would intrude.
avoidWhen: When you need to know who said what, representative samples or depth; use intercept surveys or interviews. Unmoderated walls may attract offensive content.
whyLost: It survives mainly in design research, architecture and participatory community projects, rarely in digital product UX.
whereToUse: Physical service environments (hospitals, campuses, workplaces, transport hubs), retail, and the physical touchpoints of digital services.
example: A university trials graffiti walls in library study spaces asking 'What would make this space work better for you?'. Comments cluster on charging points and noise, which feeds both a space redesign and a room-booking app feature.
reference: Martin, B. and Hanington, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design (expanded and revised). Rockport Publishers, method 59.

name: Granger Causality Testing
origin: Clive Granger, 1969
summary: Tests whether past values of one time series improve prediction of another beyond its own past, a disciplined but limited form of temporal causal evidence.
description: X Granger-causes Y if lagged values of X significantly improve a model predicting Y from its own lags. Estimated within vector autoregression (VAR) models with stationarity checks and lag selection by information criteria, the test provides evidence about temporal precedence and predictive information. It is not proof of causation: common causes and unmeasured variables can produce Granger causality, and instantaneous effects are missed. Used carefully, it helps untangle feedback between metrics, such as whether support contacts predict churn or churn predicts support contacts, and whether engagement drives content creation or vice versa. The directed transfer function (Kaminski and Blinowska, 1991) is a multichannel, frequency-domain form of the same idea.
steps: Choose the time series pairs or sets and an appropriate aggregation interval.
Test for stationarity (ADF, KPSS) and difference or detrend as needed.
Fit a VAR model selecting lag length by AIC or BIC.
Run Granger tests in both directions and check residual diagnostics.
Report results as predictive precedence, and check robustness to lag choices and added control series.
Corroborate with experiments or other causal designs before acting.
outputs: VAR models, directional Granger test results and impulse response functions.
useWhen: Exploring temporal relationships and feedback between aggregated metrics with long series.
avoidWhen: Making strong causal claims, or with short series; use experiments or quasi-experiments. Lead-lag conclusions can be wrong when only part of an interacting system is recorded, because unmeasured parts can create or reverse apparent influence.
whyLost: It is standard in econometrics but rarely considered in product metric analysis, where correlation charts dominate.
whereToUse: Marketplace supply and demand dynamics, content creation and consumption, support load and churn.
example: A marketplace tests whether seller listings Granger-cause buyer visits or vice versa. Buyer visits predict new listings two weeks later but not the reverse, shifting growth investment to demand.
sources: Granger, Investigating causal relations by econometric models and cross-spectral methods (1969), Econometrica
Lütkepohl, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis (2005)
reference: Granger, C. W. J. (1969). Econometrica, 37(3), 424-438.

name: Graph-Theoretic Navigation Analysis
origin: Leonhard Euler, 1736; hypertext metrics by Botafogo, Rivlin and Shneiderman, 1992
summary: Models a site or app as a directed graph and computes path length, centrality and connectivity to find unreachable, overburdened or poorly linked content.
description: Any navigation structure can be represented as a directed graph: screens or pages are nodes, links are edges. Graph theory then provides precise metrics. Shortest path lengths show how many steps separate users from key content; centrality measures show which pages carry most navigational load; compactness and stratum metrics, proposed by Botafogo and colleagues for hypertext, characterise how interconnected and how linear a structure is. Strongly connected components reveal sections users cannot leave without the back button. The method is rigorous when the graph is extracted automatically from a crawl or app state model, metrics are weighted by actual traffic or task importance, and changes are simulated before implementation. It complements tree testing by covering the full link structure, not just the hierarchy.
steps: Crawl the site or export the app's screen map to build a directed graph of nodes and links.
Compute shortest path lengths from entry points to key task destinations.
Calculate centrality (degree, betweenness, PageRank) and identify overloaded hubs and orphaned nodes.
Weight metrics by traffic or task priority using analytics data.
Simulate structural changes (new links, merged sections) and recompute metrics.
Validate the preferred structure with tree testing or first-click testing before implementation.
outputs: Navigation graph, path length and centrality tables, orphan and bottleneck lists, simulated metric changes for redesign options.
useWhen: Large websites, intranets, documentation and multi-screen apps undergoing IA redesign.
avoidWhen: Small sites where a sitemap review is enough, or when the problem is labelling rather than structure; use card sorting or tree testing.
whyLost: Latent: Used in IA research; rarely applied in standard practice outside web analytics.
whereToUse: IA optimization; site redesign; search architecture.
example: A university website crawl of 9,000 pages found admissions deadlines were six clicks from the home page and that 1,200 pages were orphaned. Adding three cross-links cut the median path to key admissions pages from 5.2 to 2.8 clicks.
sources: Structural analysis of hypertexts (Botafogo, Rivlin & Shneiderman)
reference: Botafogo, R. A., Rivlin, E., & Shneiderman, B. (1992). Structural analysis of hypertexts: Identifying hierarchies and useful metrics. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 10(2), 142-180.

name: Graphic Conceptual Framework (Bins and Arrows)
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1984; expanded 1994
summary: A one-page diagram of the constructs a study will examine and the relationships the team is willing to bet on, drawn before fieldwork to bound data collection.
description: A conceptual framework names the main things to be studied and the presumed relationships among them. Bins are labels that hold many discrete events or behaviours (role conflict, onboarding friction, team climate); arrows are the influences the researcher expects. Frameworks range from descriptive catalogues of roles, settings and processes to directional, hypothesis-bearing models, and some emerge only from early fieldwork. The rigour lies in commitment: drawing only the arrows you would bet on exposes assumptions that otherwise steer sampling and questioning unseen. Miles and Huberman warn against the 'no-risk framework' with two-way arrows everywhere. In a team, each researcher draws a version independently and the versions are compared to surface disagreement before it fragments the data. The framework is revised after each round of data collection, so successive versions document how understanding changed. A first cut takes 30 to 60 minutes.
steps: Put the whole framework on one page as a diagram, no larger.
Name the bins: the events, settings, processes and constructs the study will attend to.
Draw only the arrows you would bet on, and avoid two-way arrows linking everything to everything.
In a team, have each researcher draw a version independently in 30 to 60 minutes, then compare and discuss the differences.
Map variables from prior research or internal knowledge onto your frame to find overlaps and contradictions.
Use the framework to decide who and what to sample and which questions the instruments must cover.
Revise and re-date the framework after each round of data collection, keeping earlier versions.
outputs: A one-page diagram bounding who and what will be studied, plus dated successive versions showing how the team's model evolved.
useWhen: Planning a qualitative or mixed-methods study with several researchers, or any discovery work where unstated assumptions about causes could narrow what gets collected.
avoidWhen: Purely open, grounded exploration where no constructs are yet defensible; there a sensitising list of topics is enough. A rigid framework forecloses what the field shows, and a global one commits to nothing.
whyLost: UX research plans usually start from research questions and discussion guides rather than a diagram of constructs, so the step of committing to relationships before fieldwork is skipped. It survives in qualitative evaluation and education research.
whereToUse: Multi-researcher discovery programmes, service and B2B studies with many actors, and longitudinal research where the team's model should be tracked over time.
example: Before a study of why small businesses abandon an invoicing product, three researchers each draw bins (cash-flow pressure, accountant influence, setup effort, perceived trust) and arrows. One draws no link from accountant influence to abandonment, which prompts adding accountants to the sample.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
A Step-by-Step Process of Thematic Analysis to Develop a Conceptual Model in Qualitative Research (Naeem et al., 2023)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Graphical Correspondence Analysis of Visual Representations
aka: Graphical correspondence analysis of a visual representation
donor: Graphic design, cartography, semiotics and diagram research
origin: Alan Blackwell and Yuri Engelhardt (2002), drawing on Bertin (1967) and MacEachren
summary: Analyse or design a display by listing which graphic resources (marks, symbols, regions, surfaces) carry meaning and by what kind of correspondence each does so.
description: Every visual representation is treated as marks on a surface meant to correspond to things the reader understands. The framework crosses four graphic resources with types of correspondence. Marks vary shape, size, orientation, texture, saturation and colour, and correspond literally, by mapping or by convention. Symbols range from geometric and depictive to figurative and acquired (letters, icons, logos). Regions use grids, borders, fills, white space and layering to express containment, separation and grouping. Surfaces may be literal maps, metric axes, ordered layouts or image-schematic spaces. Applying it yields an explicit inventory of what each part of a display means and why, including unused resources. Run backwards, it becomes a design method. Commentators add that correspondence knowledge is necessary but not sufficient: displays should also fit users' tasks and the domain's conceptual structure.
steps: Describe the surface and its viewing situation: medium, size, mounting and viewing distance.
Identify how the plane is partitioned into regions and the order in which they are read (white space, grids, borders).
For each region, state what each spatial dimension corresponds to (time, quantity, category, physical space) and whether the correspondence is literal, metrical or ordered.
List the marks and symbols used, the visual variables they vary and the convention by which each carries meaning.
Note unused resources such as colour or texture, and the labels and annotations that elaborate elements.
Check the correspondences against users' tasks (classification favours separation; magnitude favours scale mapping) and the domain's concepts, then list mismatches for critique or redesign.
outputs: An annotated inventory of correspondence conventions for each part of a display, with mismatches and unused resources for redesign.
useWhen: You are critiquing or designing a dense visual representation (dashboard, data visualisation, diagram, map, notation) and need to make its encoding explicit.
avoidWhen: You need evidence of how users actually read the display; follow with usability tests, eye tracking or comprehension tasks. It does not replace visual design skill and iteration.
whyLost: It lives in diagram research and an online HCI encyclopedia chapter; UX teams use ad hoc visual design critique or data-visualisation checklists instead.
whereToUse: Analytics dashboards, scientific and medical visualisations, timeline and scheduling interfaces, maps and notation-heavy professional tools.
example: A clinical dashboard team inventories its screen and finds colour encodes both ward and severity while the vertical axis means rank in one panel and time in another. Separating the encodings reduces misreadings in testing.
reference: Blackwell, A. F. Visual representation. In M. Soegaard & R. F. Dam (Eds.), The Encyclopedia of Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.), ch. 5. Interaction Design Foundation; Bertin, J. (1967). Sémiologie graphique. Paris: Gauthier-Villars.

name: Graphical Vector Autoregression for Experience Sampling Data
origin: Part of the network psychometrics toolkit described in Isvoranu et al. (2022), with R packages graphicalVAR, mlVAR, psychonetrics and mgm; discussed in the book with reference to Epskamp et al. (2018).
summary: Fitting a vector autoregressive model to repeated self-reports or behaviour logs to obtain a directed temporal network (what predicts what at the next moment) and an undirected contemporaneous network (what co-occurs within the same moment).
description: When people answer the same short questionnaire many times a day, or when behaviour is logged at regular intervals, the data can show how states influence each other over time. Graphical vector autoregression regresses each variable at one time point on all variables at the previous time point, with regularisation, and models the remaining same-moment associations as a partial correlation network. The result is a temporal network with arrows, read as predictive (Granger-type) relations, and a contemporaneous network. Versions exist for a single person, for many people with multilevel estimation, and for panel data. The book lists practical threats: these models need many reliable, stationary measurements; the sampling rate must be fast enough for the process studied; equal spacing between measurements is assumed unless continuous-time models are used; and predictive arrows are not proof of causation, which ultimately requires intervention. For UX, the method can show whether frustration tends to precede abandonment, whether stress predicts later use of a wellbeing feature, or how motivation, effort and use feed each other during habit formation.
steps: Choose a small set of states or behaviours to track and an interval that matches how fast they change.
Collect intensive repeated measures (experience sampling prompts or regular log aggregates) over days or weeks.
Check and handle trends, missing prompts and unequal spacing; detrend or model time as needed.
Fit a single-person graphical VAR or a multilevel VAR across participants.
Inspect the temporal, contemporaneous and, for multilevel models, between-person networks.
Interpret arrows as predictive relations, then test promising links with an intervention study.
outputs: Temporal (directed), contemporaneous and between-person networks of the tracked variables, per person or across the sample.
useWhen: You run diary or experience sampling studies, or have regular behavioural logs, and want to understand sequences and feedback among states rather than averages.
avoidWhen: There are fewer than several dozen measurements per person, measurement intervals are irregular and long, or stakeholders will read arrows as proven causes.
whyLost: UX diary studies are usually analysed qualitatively or with averages; intensive longitudinal modelling sits in clinical and personality psychology and needs statistical expertise.
whereToUse: Habit-formation studies, wellbeing and health apps, workplace tools where stress and productivity interact, learning products tracking motivation and practice.
example: Sixty users of a language-learning app answer five questions about motivation, boredom, perceived progress and stress four times a day for three weeks, alongside logged practice. A multilevel VAR shows that perceived progress predicts motivation at the next prompt and boredom predicts skipped practice, while stress links to boredom only within the same moment.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Greimas Actantial Model Analysis
origin: Algirdas Julien Greimas, 1966 (Sémantique structurale)
summary: Maps any narrative onto six roles (subject, object, sender, receiver, helper, opponent) to reveal how users and brands cast the product in their stories.
description: Greimas generalised Propp's folktale functions into six actants on three axes: desire (subject seeks object), communication (sender initiates the quest for a receiver) and power (helpers and opponents). Any story, including a user's account of adopting a product or a company's marketing narrative, can be mapped this way. The analysis reveals whether users cast the product as helper, opponent, object or sender, who the real subject is, and what the object of desire truly is. Comparing user narratives with the company's intended narrative exposes mismatches; mapping complaints shows when the product becomes an opponent. The semiotic square can extend analysis of underlying value oppositions.
steps: Collect narratives: interview stories, reviews, social posts, and the company's own marketing narrative.
For each narrative, identify the subject and object of desire.
Identify sender (what motivates the quest) and receiver (who benefits).
Identify helpers and opponents, noting where the product, competitors, institutions or people appear.
Compare actantial structures across user segments and against the intended brand narrative.
Derive implications for positioning, onboarding narrative and features that shift the product into the helper role.
outputs: Actantial maps per narrative, segment comparisons and narrative mismatch analysis.
useWhen: Understanding the role a product plays in users' lives and stories, and aligning brand narrative with lived experience.
avoidWhen: Task-level usability questions.
whyLost: Structural semiotics is taught in literature and some marketing schools, but rarely applied in UX research.
whereToUse: Brand and positioning research, health and fitness apps, financial planning tools, AI assistants' perceived role.
example: Analysing 60 reviews of a budgeting app, researchers find users cast the app as an opponent (a nagging parent) to the subject's desire for freedom. Repositioning it as a helper toward 'freedom from money worry' improves retention messaging.
sources: Greimas, Structural Semantics: An Attempt at a Method (1983 English translation of 1966)
reference: Greimas, A. J. (1983). Structural Semantics. University of Nebraska Press.

name: Greimasian Actantial Model for Task Narratives
origin: Algirdas Julien Greimas, 1966
summary: Maps a user task as a narrative of six actants (subject, object, sender, receiver, helper, opponent) to locate where motivation, goal or support breaks down.
description: Greimas reduced narrative structure to six actants present in any goal-directed action: Subject (who pursues), Object (the goal), Sender (the motivation or commissioning force), Receiver (the beneficiary), Helper (forces aiding) and Opponent (forces obstructing). The treatise proposes mapping any user task this way: the user seeks a goal, sent by their motivation, received by a beneficiary, aided by interface affordances that work and blocked by friction, confusion or error. The framework identifies where the narrative breaks: no clear Object, a Sender misaligned with what the design assumes, or Opponents invisible to the designer. It is especially useful when the beneficiary differs from the user (for example a carer acting for a parent).
steps: Select a task or journey and gather research data about it.
Identify the Subject and Object of the task from the user's perspective.
Identify the Sender (motivation) and Receiver (beneficiary), noting when they are third parties.
List Helpers and Opponents, including non-interface forces (family, policy, time).
Locate narrative breakdowns: unclear Object, misaligned Sender, unrecognised Opponents.
Redesign to clarify the Object, align with the true Sender and neutralise Opponents.
outputs: Actantial maps per task, breakdown diagnosis, design implications.
useWhen: Motivation and friction analysis, onboarding narratives, user story structuring, proxy-use scenarios.
avoidWhen: Low-level interaction problems; use usability testing or KLM.
whyLost: Almost unknown outside literary semiotics; never introduced into UX.
whereToUse: Onboarding, caregiver and proxy access flows, behaviour change apps, B2B buying journeys.
example: Mapping a pension consolidation task shows the Sender is a partner's insistence, not the user's goal; the Receiver is the household, so the redesign adds shared progress for partners.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Greimas AJ (1966) Sémantique structurale (Structural Semantics: An Attempt at a Method)
Barthes R (1977) Introduction to the structural analysis of narratives
reference: Greimas AJ (1983) Structural Semantics: An Attempt at a Method. University of Nebraska Press (orig. 1966).

name: Gricean maxim audit (Quantity/Quality/Relation/Manner)
origin: H. P. Grice, 'Logic and Conversation', 1975
summary: Evaluates interface and conversational messages against Grice's four maxims to find where text says too much or too little, misleads, is irrelevant or is unclear.
description: Grice's cooperative principle holds that conversational partners expect contributions to be as informative as required and no more (Quantity), truthful and evidenced (Quality), relevant (Relation), and clear, brief and orderly (Manner). Users read interface text as cooperative communication, so violations produce misunderstanding or unintended inferences. A Gricean maxim audit reviews each message, especially errors, confirmations, warnings and chatbot responses, against each maxim, records violations, and rates severity by consequence. It is particularly valuable for conversational interfaces and AI outputs, which can be fluent yet violate Quality (unsupported claims) or Quantity (padding). Rigour comes from using two independent reviewers, explicit criteria per maxim and validation with users on high-severity items.
steps: Collect all messages in scope: errors, warnings, confirmations, empty states, tooltips and conversational responses.
Define operational criteria for each maxim (for example Quantity: includes cause and next step, no unrequested detail).
Have two reviewers independently rate each message on each maxim as met, minor violation or major violation; reconcile disagreements.
Rate severity by consequence of misunderstanding (for example 1-4 scale) and prioritise major violations with high severity.
Rewrite flagged messages and test with 5-10 users using interpretation questions.
Encode maxim criteria into content guidelines and review checklists.
outputs: A message-by-maxim violation matrix with severity, rewritten messages, user interpretation results, and guideline updates.
useWhen: For error messages, warnings, chatbots, AI assistants, and any product where text drives decisions.
avoidWhen: When the issue is visual or interaction design rather than language; use heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Grice is foundational in linguistics and taught in conversation design, but rarely applied as a systematic audit in UX writing.
whereToUse: Conversational AI, clinical alerts, financial messages, legal and consent text, and developer error messages.
example: A surgical console error says 'Instrument fault. Contact support.' The audit flags Quantity (no cause or safe action) and Relation (support is irrelevant mid-procedure). The rewrite names the faulty arm and the immediate safe action.
sources: Gleason, J. B., The Development of Language
The Inquiry Series, Ch 18 — Pragmatics — What Language Actually Does
reference: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts. Academic Press.

name: Gricean Pragmatics Analysis
origin: H. Paul Grice, 1975
summary: Audits system messages and conversational turns against Grice's maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner to find where the system breaks conversational expectations.
description: Grice proposed that conversation rests on a cooperative principle, expressed as four maxims: say as much as needed and no more (quantity), say what you believe true and have evidence for (quality), be relevant (relation), and be clear, brief and orderly (manner). Listeners infer meaning, called implicature, when a speaker appears to flout a maxim. Users apply the same expectations to interfaces and especially to chatbots and AI assistants. A pragmatics audit codes each system utterance against the maxims and also looks for unintended implicatures, such as a vague error implying user fault. Rigour comes from coding transcripts with two coders, rating severity, and validating with users by asking what they inferred from messages. It is particularly useful for diagnosing why technically correct responses feel unhelpful or evasive.
steps: Collect system utterances: error messages, microcopy and samples of chatbot or assistant transcripts (e.g. 100-300 turns).
Code each utterance for violations of quantity, quality, relation and manner, noting the likely implicature.
Have a second coder code at least 20% and reconcile disagreements.
Test a sample of flagged utterances with 6-10 users, asking what they understood and inferred.
Rewrite violating utterances and prompt or response policies to satisfy the maxims.
Re-evaluate with users or by measuring downstream outcomes such as resolution rates and repeat queries.
outputs: Maxim violation log with implicatures, severity ratings, rewritten messages and conversational guidelines.
useWhen: Chatbots, AI assistants, voice interfaces, error messages and microcopy where tone and helpfulness matter.
avoidWhen: Visual or navigation problems; use usability testing or heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Siloed: Linguistics literature; content designers occasionally apply it implicitly.
whereToUse: Conversational design; microcopy; error messages; chatbot dialogue.
example: A bank's chatbot answered 'I can help with many things!' to specific dispute questions. The audit flagged relation and quantity violations in 38% of turns; rewritten responses with direct answers and next steps cut repeat queries by a quarter.
reference: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts (pp. 41-58). Academic Press.

name: Ground-truth labelling from qualitative review
donor: Content analysis / machine learning annotation practice
origin: Content analysis reliability (Krippendorff, 1980; Cohen's kappa, 1960) applied to ML annotation
summary: Researchers code a sample of sessions, tickets or transcripts against an explicit codebook to create reliable labels for training and validating classifiers.
description: Classifiers inherit the quality of their labels. This method treats labelling as qualitative research: build a codebook with operational definitions and examples of each state (e.g. frustrated, confused, exploring), train coders, double-code a substantial sample, measure inter-rater reliability and resolve disagreements before labels are used. Labelling from session replays or think-aloud data captures meaning that event logs miss, and the disagreements themselves often reveal ambiguous states worth studying. Rigour comes from a stratified sample covering edge cases, blind double coding, reliability thresholds, documented adjudication and auditing label drift over time.
steps: Draft a codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules, and anchor examples for each label.
Draw a stratified sample of sessions, oversampling suspected rare states, typically 200-500 for initial modelling.
Train 2-3 coders on 20-30 practice sessions and refine the codebook.
Double-code at least 20% of the sample blind and compute Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha, targeting 0.70 or above (0.80 for high-stakes uses).
Adjudicate disagreements, update the codebook, and record label confidence for ambiguous cases.
Re-audit a fresh sample periodically to detect drift in user behaviour or coder interpretation.
outputs: A labelled dataset with codebook, reliability statistics, adjudication log and confidence ratings, ready for model training and evaluation.
useWhen: Before training or validating any classifier of user states, intents or feedback categories, or evaluating LLM-based coding.
avoidWhen: Avoid when labels can be derived objectively from outcomes (e.g. purchase), or when states are too ambiguous for agreement; explore them qualitatively first.
whyLost: Labelling is often outsourced as low-skill work, separating it from the qualitative expertise that makes labels meaningful.
whereToUse: Frustration detection, support ticket classification, AI conversation quality evaluation, content moderation research.
example: Three researchers code 300 trading session replays for frustration with a codebook, reaching Krippendorff's alpha of 0.78. Disagreements cluster around 'deliberate hesitation' during large orders, which becomes a separate label.
sources: Pattern Classification (Richard Duda, Peter Hart & David Stork)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Peter Bruce, Andrew Bruce & Peter Gedeck)
Krippendorff, Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology
The Inquiry Series, Ch 54 — Linear Discriminant Analysis & Behavioral Classification
reference: Krippendorff, K. (2018) Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology, 4th ed. Sage.

name: Grounded Text Mining Approach (GTxA)
origin: Inaba and Kakai
summary: Combine grounded theory coding with dictionary-based text mining: write auto-coding rules from in vivo codes and revise them until machine and manual coding agree.
description: A qualitatively dominant hybrid for crossover analysis of text. It begins with a computational overview of the corpus (word frequencies, co-occurrence networks, correspondence analysis, keyword-in-context reading), then proceeds with constructivist grounded theory coding: initial line-by-line codes, focused codes and a hierarchy. Researchers then write explicit auto-coding rules from in vivo words and focused codes, apply them to the whole corpus, and quantify codes by group with cross-tabulations, chi-square tests and residuals. The machine coding is compared with manual coding and the rules are revised until they agree, which is the method's main check. Meta-inferences are drawn from the combined display and theoretical sampling continues to saturation. Tools such as KH Coder and MAXQDA support it. Its value is transparent, reproducible rules rather than opaque models; its weakness is that word-level rules lose context.
steps: Overview the corpus with word frequencies, co-occurrence networks, correspondence analysis and keyword-in-context reading.
Code a substantial sample with grounded theory: initial line-by-line codes, then focused codes grouped hierarchically.
Write auto-coding rules from in vivo words and focused codes and apply them to the full corpus.
Quantify codes by group and cross-tabulate, testing differences with chi-square and adjusted residuals.
Compare machine coding with manual coding on the same segments and revise rules until they agree.
Draw meta-inferences from the combined display and continue theoretical sampling to saturation.
outputs: A rule-coded corpus, group comparisons with statistics, and an integrated qualitative and quantitative display.
