useWhen: You have hundreds to thousands of open-text responses, support tickets or transcripts and need transparent, auditable coding that scales beyond manual reading while staying grounded in participants' words.
avoidWhen: Small corpora that can be read in full, or when semantic nuance matters more than coverage; for exploratory clustering at scale use topic modelling instead.
whyLost: It was published in nursing and education methodology, and UX moved from manual coding straight to topic models and LLM coding without the rule-validation step.
whereToUse: Open-ended survey responses, app reviews, support tickets, and checking LLM-assisted coding against grounded manual codes.
example: A health app codes 300 of 4,000 open survey answers by hand, writes dictionary rules from phrases such as 'forgot to log' and 'too many reminders', checks agreement with the manual codes, then compares code frequencies between new and long-term users.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Grounded Theory
origin: Barney Glaser & Anselm Strauss, 1967; later Strauss & Corbin (1990) and Charmaz (2006)
summary: A methodology for generating explanatory theory from data through iterative coding, constant comparison and theoretical sampling until categories are saturated.
description: Grounded theory builds theory inductively from data rather than testing prior hypotheses. Data collection and analysis proceed together: early interviews or observations are coded line by line (open coding), codes are related to one another around core categories (axial coding) and integrated into a central explanatory model (selective or theoretical coding). Constant comparison checks each new incident against existing codes and categories, while theoretical sampling chooses the next participants specifically to develop or challenge emerging categories. Memo writing captures analytic thinking throughout. Collection stops at theoretical saturation, when new data no longer adds properties to categories. The output is a theory of a process, not a list of themes, which is what distinguishes it from basic thematic analysis.
steps: Start with a broad research question and an initial sample of participants likely to experience the phenomenon.
Collect and transcribe data from the first few interviews, then code line by line using gerunds to capture actions and processes.
Write memos continuously, comparing incidents with codes and codes with categories.
Use theoretical sampling to select further participants who can develop or challenge emerging categories.
Relate categories through axial coding and identify a core category.
Continue until theoretical saturation, typically after 20 to 30 interviews, then integrate categories into an explanatory model.
Write up the theory with its categories, properties and conditions, supported by data excerpts.
outputs: An explanatory theory of the process under study, with core category, related categories and properties, memos and a coded dataset.
useWhen: When studying a poorly understood process or phenomenon where existing theory is inadequate, such as how trust in an AI tool develops over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you only need a descriptive summary of themes or have a fixed timeline of a few days; use thematic analysis or affinity diagramming.
whyLost: Vestigial: the name is widely invoked but practice is usually reduced to one round of coding into themes, losing theoretical sampling, constant comparison and theory building. It is often confused with thematic analysis and dismissed as too academic for product timelines.
whereToUse: Long-term research programs; generating theory from novel phenomena; design research publishing.
example: A health-tech researcher interviews 24 clinicians about adopting an AI triage assistant, sampling sceptics once an early 'earned trust' category emerges. The resulting theory shows trust is built through visible failure handling, informing the product's explanation design.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish
The Discovery of Grounded Theory (Glaser & Strauss)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 26
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Glaser BG & Strauss AL (1967) The Discovery of Grounded Theory
Strauss A & Corbin J (1990) Basics of Qualitative Research
Charmaz K (2014) Constructing Grounded Theory. 2nd ed
Orlikowski WJ (1993) CASE tools as organizational change. MIS Quarterly
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Full article: The Pursuit of Quality in Grounded Theory (tandfonline)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Secondary Analysis of Qualitative Data (Long-Sutehall et al., 2011)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Glaser, B. G. & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The Discovery of Grounded Theory. Aldine; Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing Grounded Theory (2nd ed.). Sage.

name: Grounded Visual Analysis
origin: Applications of grounded theory to visual data, 2000s (e.g. Konecki, 2011)
summary: Applies grounded theory's open coding, constant comparison and theoretical sampling to visual data such as photos, videos, screenshots and user-generated images.
description: Grounded Visual Analysis applies the constant comparative method and theoretical sampling principles of Grounded Theory to visual data — photographs, video clips, screenshots, diagrams, or any visual material. Just as textual Grounded Theory generates conceptual codes from textual data, Grounded Visual Analysis generates conceptual codes from visual elements and their patterns. It treats visual data not as illustration of findings but as the primary evidential material from which theory is generated.
steps: Open visual coding: View/examine visual data without pre-defined categories. For each image or clip, ask: what is happening here? What visual elements are most salient? What patterns or tensions are present? Apply codes to visual properties (composition, colour, focus, scale, relationship between elements) as well as content.
Constant comparison across visual data: Compare each new image to all previously coded images. What is the same? What is different? Does this image challenge existing codes or confirm them?

Theoretical sampling of visual data: After initial coding, collect additional visual data based on what the emerging theory requires — images from different contexts, different users, different time points.
Axial visual coding: Build categories around central visual themes. What causal conditions, contexts, and consequences surround each major visual pattern?

Triangulate with verbal data: Compare visual analysis findings to verbal data from the same participants or context. Convergence confirms; divergence reveals aspects of experience that one mode expresses but the other does not.
outputs: Open and axial visual codes, comparison memos, theoretically sampled image sets, visual categories, and triangulated findings with verbal data.
useWhen: Visual material is central, such as participant photos, screenshots of user set-ups, social media imagery, or interface screenshot collections, and you want inductive categories.
avoidWhen: Images are only illustrative of verbal findings, or you have predefined categories; use Qualitative Content Analysis. For meaning-making in designed visuals, use Multimodal Discourse Analysis.
whyLost: Visual data in UX is usually treated as illustration for decks rather than coded systematically, and visual grounded theory sits at a niche intersection of methods.
whereToUse: Photo diary studies, home-screen and workspace screenshot studies, social media imagery around products, and competitor interface audits.
example: Researchers collect 300 home-screen screenshots from banking app users. Open coding and comparison reveal a category of 'financial hiding', apps deliberately buried in folders, which interviews connect to money anxiety.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
reference: Konecki, K. T. (2011). Visual grounded theory: A methodological outline and examples from empirical work. Revija za sociologiju, 41(2), 131-160.

name: Group Task Analysis
donor: Human factors task analysis; participatory design
origin: Courage and Baxter, 2005, adapted from the Bridge method of Dayton, McFarland and Kramer, 1998
summary: Four to six users of one profile build one agreed task flow from trigger to end point in two hours, annotating steps with dislikes, exceptions, information needs and actors.
description: Group Task Analysis is a discount alternative to field observation when access, time or confidentiality block site visits. The team seeds 10-25 draft steps and decision points, including disputed ones, as a guess for participants to discard, add to or reword. After a warm-up flow ('making toast') to teach triggers, end points, assumptions and decisions, participants build the 'bridge' of steps on a wall canvas and annotate it with four colours of notes: information needed, disliked steps, exceptions and other actors. The moderator stands and probes but never writes, because a moderator who writes takes ownership of the flow and invalidates the data. After a break the quietest participant walks the flow on video and disagreements are resolved. Flows are redrawn within 24 hours, merged across at least two groups and analysed with an eight-question checklist. Group discussion surfaces steps individuals forget, but context and automatic steps are lost. It is not the same as Groupware Task Analysis (van Welie and van der Veer), which shares the acronym GTA but models the agents, work and situation of groups and organisations.
steps: Scope a task that fits two hours and draft 10-25 seed steps (rectangles) and decision points (diamonds), including disputed ones.
Recruit four to six participants of a single user profile per session, and plan at least two sessions.
Prepare a canvas, blank shapes, four sticky-note colours (information, dislikes, exceptions, actors) and pens for each participant.
Warm up, then train with a quick moderator-led 'making toast' flow covering trigger, end point, assumptions and decisions.
Present the seed steps as a guess; participants write the trigger and end point and build the flow while the moderator probes for notes and exceptions without writing.
After a break, have the quietest participant walk the flow on video and resolve disagreements before fixing it in place.
Redraw within 24 hours, merge flows across groups, analyse with a checklist and write specific recommendations with mock-ups.
outputs: A consensus task flow with triggers, end points, decision points, annotated dislikes, exceptions, information needs and actors, plus design recommendations.
useWhen: When you need a task model quickly and cannot observe users at work, for example for confidential, regulated or geographically dispersed work.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for observation where context matters or tasks are largely automatic; say-do gaps are likely. Use Contextual Inquiry or Hierarchical Task Analysis from observation where possible. No published reliability evidence.
whyLost: It appeared in the first edition of a practitioner handbook but was dropped as journey mapping and remote interviews took over; the underlying Bridge method also faded.
whereToUse: Enterprise and back-office workflows, healthcare administration, B2B onboarding, remote-first research where site visits are impossible.
example: An insurer cannot let researchers into claims offices. Two GTA sessions with five handlers each produce a merged claims flow with 14 'dislike' notes clustering on duplicate data entry, which drives the redesign brief.
reference: Courage, C., & Baxter, K. (2005). Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Requirements. San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 11; Dayton, T., McFarland, A., & Kramer, J. (1998). Bridging user needs to object oriented GUI prototype via task object design. In L. Wood (Ed.), User Interface Design. CRC Press.

name: Groupware Task Analysis (GTA, van der Veer)
origin: Gerrit van der Veer, Bert Lenting and Bas Bergevoet (1996); Martijn van Welie and Gerrit van der Veer, chapter 19 of Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
summary: Model a group's task world from agents, work and situation viewpoints, analyse the current model for problems, then envision a future task model to drive design.
description: Groupware Task Analysis models cooperative work in organisations. It is distinct from the atlas's Group Task Analysis, a Bridge-method workshop technique that shares the acronym. GTA rests on an ontology of tasks, goals, roles, agents, objects and events, viewed from three angles: agents (who does what, in which roles), work (task decomposition and flow) and situation (objects and environment). The current task model (task model 1) is built from field data and represented with task trees, object models and workflow diagrams, often in the EUTERPE tool. It is analysed heuristically and, where formalised, with verification constraints that flag problems such as roles without responsibility. An envisioned task model (task model 2) then describes how work should be done with the new system and, with scenarios, drives design and evaluation.
steps: Collect field data on the group's work through observation, interviews and documents.
Build the current task model across the agent, work and situation viewpoints, defining tasks, goals, roles, agents, objects and events.
Represent it with task trees, object models and workflow diagrams, using a tool such as EUTERPE.
Analyse the model heuristically and with verification constraints to list problems such as overloaded roles or unowned objects.
Envision the future task model that removes the problems with the new system.
Use the envisioned model with scenarios to specify the user virtual machine and to drive design and evaluation.
outputs: Current and envisioned task models (task trees, object models, workflow diagrams) and a problem list.
useWhen: Designing collaborative or workflow systems where several roles share objects and responsibilities, such as case management, security administration or clinical teams.
avoidWhen: Avoid for single-user tasks (use Hierarchical Task Analysis) or quick participatory flow mapping (use the Bridge-style Group Task Analysis workshop). Models grow large, and formal specification only pays off if checks are run.
whyLost: Its tool support and formal ontology belonged to 1990s-2000s European HCI research, and contextual design, journey maps and service blueprints displaced it in practice.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflow tools, access-control and security administration, hospital team coordination systems, collaborative AI agents in shared workspaces.
example: Analysing a bank's access-request process, the team models requesters, approvers and administrators and finds that the 'access right' object has no role responsible for revoking it. The envisioned model adds an owner role with periodic recertification tasks.
reference: van der Veer, G. C., Lenting, B. F. and Bergevoet, B. A. J. (1996). GTA: Groupware task analysis, modeling complexity. Acta Psychologica, 91, 297-322; van Welie, M. and van der Veer, G. C. (2003). In E. Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (pp. 447-476). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Groupware Walkthrough with Mechanics of Collaboration
aka: Group task model with mechanics of collaboration
donor: Computer-supported cooperative work; cognitive systems engineering
origin: David Pinelle and Carl Gutwin (early 2000s); presented by Luczak, Muehlfelder and Schmidt in Hollnagel (2003)
summary: Inspect a shared-workspace prototype by walking evaluators through realistic group scenarios whose collaborative subtasks are specified with seven mechanics of collaboration.
description: A discount inspection method for groupware, adapting the cognitive walkthrough to teamwork. Scenarios are written from observed group work, naming the activity, group goal, users and circumstances. Tasks list what is done, not how, and are split into individual and collaborative subtasks. Collaborative subtasks are specified by the mechanics of collaboration: explicit communication, implicit communication, coordination, planning, monitoring, assistance and protection. The task model deliberately avoids strict hierarchy or order because the tightness of coupling between collaborators varies. Evaluators then step through tasks, subtasks and alternative actions in the prototype at both loose and tight coupling, recording where the workspace fails to support awareness, hand-offs or protection of others' work. Unlike Group Task Analysis, which maps a group's task flow in a participatory session, this is an expert inspection of a specific collaborative interface.
steps: Observe real group work and write scenarios stating the activity, the group goal, the users and their circumstances.
List the tasks in each scenario as what must be achieved, not how.

Split tasks into individual and collaborative subtasks and specify each collaborative subtask by the mechanics it involves (explicit and implicit communication, coordination, planning, monitoring, assistance, protection).
List alternative actions a group could take for each collaborative subtask.
Walk two or more evaluators through the tasks, subtasks and actions in the prototype, once under loose and once under tight coupling.
Record each breakdown against the mechanic it violates and consolidate a groupware usability problem list.
outputs: A group task model of scenarios, tasks and collaborative subtasks; a list of groupware usability problems tagged by mechanic of collaboration.
useWhen: Early evaluation of real-time or asynchronous collaborative tools (shared whiteboards, co-editing, planning boards) before multi-user testing is practical.
avoidWhen: It is an inspection, not user testing, and depends on scenario realism; for observed team behaviour use Distributed Cognition Analysis or field testing, and for mapping a group's work in a workshop use Group Task Analysis.
whyLost: It belonged to the CSCW discount-evaluation wave of the early 2000s; collaborative products are now evaluated with ordinary usability tests and analytics, and the mechanics framework is rarely taught.
whereToUse: Multiplayer design and whiteboard tools, co-authoring and comment features, shared dashboards, AI agents acting inside shared workspaces.
example: Before beta, a project-planning tool is walked through for a scenario where two planners reschedule a milestone simultaneously. Under tight coupling evaluators find no implicit signal that the other person is dragging the same task, a monitoring and protection failure.
reference: Pinelle, D., Gutwin, C. and Greenberg, S. (2003). Task analysis for groupware usability evaluation. ACM TOCHI 10(4); Hollnagel, E. (Ed.) (2003). Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum, ch. 6, pp. 99-127.

name: Growth curve modelling
origin: Laird and Ware tradition; McArdle and Epstein (1987); Meredith and Tisak (1990); Raudenbush and Bryk (2002); nonlinear forms Browne and du Toit (1991), Grimm and Ram (2009)
summary: Models each person's repeated measures as an individual trajectory around an average curve, estimating mean change, individual differences in change and their predictors.
description: Growth curve models treat each person's scores over time as a weighted sum of time functions with person-specific coefficients. Fixed effects give the average starting level and rate; random effects give individual differences; their covariance shows whether starting level predicts change. The same model can be fitted as a multilevel (random-coefficient) model or as a structural equation model in which repeated measures load on intercept and slope factors. Forms include no growth, linear (loadings 0, 1, 2, 3), quadratic, latent basis (free loadings capturing any shape), exponential, logistic, sinusoidal and splines; unequal intervals change the loadings (for example 0, 1, 3, 7). Time-invariant covariates predict growth factors; time-varying covariates predict each wave. The approach uses all available data under a missing-at-random assumption and allows unequal timing, but needs at least two more occasions than the order of the highest random trend.
steps: Plan occasions to match the expected shape: at least three for a linear random slope, more for curves, placed where change is expected to bend.
Screen the data, plot individual trajectories, and code time meaningfully (for example months since sign-up, with zero at a substantive point).
Fit a random-intercept model, then add a random slope, and compare nested models by likelihood-ratio or chi-square difference tests.
Try latent basis or nonlinear forms where theory suggests a plateau or learning curve, and alternative residual covariance structures.
Handle missing waves with full-information maximum likelihood or multiple imputation; do not bin unequal measurement times as if they were equal.
Add person-level predictors of intercept and slope (segment, plan, prior experience) to form the conditional model.
Plot model-predicted individual curves against observed ones to check the model represents individuals, and report how growth factors were scaled.
outputs: Average trajectory, variances and covariance of growth parameters, effects of predictors on starting level and rate, and model-implied individual curves.
useWhen: Tracking satisfaction, trust, skill or usage across three or more waves of a panel or diary study, and asking who changes faster and why.
avoidWhen: Two waves only (use change scores or ANCOVA), very small samples, or when the theory concerns the change rule itself (use latent change score models). Aggregate curves can misrepresent every individual when people are heterogeneous; check with person-specific models.
whyLost: The methods live in developmental psychology and education statistics; UX longitudinal studies are usually analysed wave by wave with descriptive comparisons.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX benchmarks, onboarding and learnability studies, trust in AI assistants over months, habit formation in health apps, SaaS adoption panels.
example: A fitness app surveys 600 new users on perceived usefulness at weeks 1, 2, 4 and 8. A latent basis model shows most change happens by week 2, and users who set goals in onboarding start higher and decline more slowly.
sources: Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Mixed Models: A Flexible Approach to Correlated Data (Seltman, n.d.)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Ram, N. and Grimm, K. J. (2015). Growth curve modeling and longitudinal factor analysis. In R. M. Lerner, W. F. Overton and P. C. M. Molenaar (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 1 (pp. 758-788). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Guardrail metric monitoring
donor: Online experimentation / clinical trial safety monitoring
origin: Online experimentation practice (Kohavi et al.); data safety monitoring boards in clinical trials
summary: Tracks metrics that must not deteriorate while a primary metric is optimised, with thresholds that trigger investigation or rollback.
description: Guardrail metrics protect against shipping changes that win on the target metric but harm something important: latency, error rates, support contacts, unsubscribes, accessibility, user wellbeing or revenue. In experimentation, they are pre-specified with non-inferiority margins; after launch, they are monitored continuously with alerting thresholds. They echo safety monitoring in clinical trials, where efficacy is never judged without harm data. Rigour requires choosing guardrails that capture plausible harms identified through research, setting margins before data arrives, powering tests to detect meaningful degradation, and making escalation paths explicit. UX research contributes by identifying user-experience harms that standard engineering guardrails miss.
steps: Identify plausible harms of the change from research, risk review and past incidents.
Select 3-6 guardrail metrics covering system health, user experience and trust or wellbeing.
Set non-inferiority margins or alert thresholds before launch (e.g. support contacts may not rise by more than 5% relative).
Power experiments so a breach of the margin can be detected, using one-sided tests for degradation.
Monitor guardrails in dashboards with automated alerts and a named owner.
On a breach, pause or roll back and investigate with qualitative follow-up before resuming.
outputs: A guardrail set with thresholds, monitoring dashboards and alerts, and documented breach responses.
useWhen: Any experiment or launch optimising a primary metric, especially where gains could come at users' expense.
avoidWhen: Avoid using too many guardrails (false alarms multiply) or guardrails without pre-set thresholds.
whyLost: Guardrails are well established in mature experimentation cultures and spreading, though UX-specific harms are often missing from them.
whereToUse: A/B testing programmes, AI feature launches, fintech and health products, growth experiments.
example: A trading app's new one-tap order raises trade volume but its guardrail on order cancellations within 60 seconds rises 30% above threshold. Investigation shows accidental orders, and the team adds a confirmation for large trades.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020) Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, ch. 7. Cambridge University Press.

name: Guerrilla Research (Intercept and Rapid Testing)
origin: Popularised 2000s (Nielsen's discount argument; Krug 2000; lean UX)
summary: Rapid, low-cost intercept interviews, five-participant tests and remote sessions run inside agile cycles; useful for quick checks, weak for complex work systems.
description: The treatise describes the 'guerrilla substitution': brief intercept interviews, five-participant usability tests and remote moderated sessions became the standard toolkit as contextual inquiry declined. Practised well, guerrilla research catches obvious usability problems fast and keeps teams in contact with users. The treatise's critique is that it is often used beyond its range. It cannot surface deep understanding of work systems, organisational culture, artefact ecologies, informal workarounds or the social dimensions of tool use, and organisations that rely on it have degraded their capacity to understand complex systems. Recruiting convenience samples, no severity rating and no analysis protocol amplify its weaknesses. This entry captures the method with that perspective: legitimate as a quick evaluative check, risky as a substitute for field research.
steps: State a narrow evaluative question that a 10-20 minute session can answer.
Recruit participants who match the target user, not just whoever is nearby; screen with 2-3 questions.
Run 5-8 short sessions with a fixed task script and consistent prompts.
Log observed problems against tasks and rate severity.
Synthesise within 24 hours and state explicitly what the method cannot tell you.
Escalate to field research when findings point to workflow or context issues.
outputs: Quick problem list with severities, quotes, go/no-go signal for a design iteration.
useWhen: Early checks of comprehension, labels and flows on consumer-facing designs within a sprint.
avoidWhen: Complex professional work, organisational dynamics or high-stakes decisions; use contextual inquiry or ethnography.
whyLost: Survived and dominated because it is fast, cheap and legible to stakeholders: competitive displacement by faster methods.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, marketing pages, retail, early prototype comprehension checks.
example: A coffee chain's app team runs six intercept tests in-store on a new pre-order button and finds two label problems in an afternoon, but defers a staff workflow question to field observation.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J (1994) Guerrilla HCI: using discount usability engineering to penetrate the intimidation barrier
Krug S (2010) Rocket Surgery Made Easy
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Nielsen J (1994) Guerrilla HCI: Using discount usability engineering to penetrate the intimidation barrier. In Bias & Mayhew (Eds) Cost-Justifying Usability. Academic Press.

name: Guided home and technology tours (touchstone tours, technology biographies)
donor: Design ethnography; HCI home technology research
origin: Blythe, Monk and Park (2002), technology biographies; design research practice for touchstone tours
summary: Participants lead a tour of their home, workspace, bag or devices, demonstrating what they use, recalling their history with it and imagining better designs.
description: Letting the participant lead a tour of their own territory surfaces objects, places and practices a researcher would not know to ask about. In a touchstone tour, participants guide the researcher around a home, workspace, bag or computer desktop, talking about what matters, with light prompts and documentation by video, photos or sketches. Blythe, Monk and Park's technology biographies add structure across time: technology tours (demonstrating devices and software in use), personal histories (early memories of and reactions to devices), and guided speculation (imagining improved designs). Spanning past, present and future shows how a person's relationship with technology has changed. Analysis can be tabulated per task: goal, limitation, explanation, workaround, usability of the workaround and wish, then compared across tasks for cross-cutting design criteria. Participants may show tidied versions of their spaces, and privacy needs care.
steps: Agree the territory to tour (home, workspace, bag, desktop or phone) and obtain consent for photos and recording.
Let the participant lead, demonstrating the devices, objects and software they use (technology tour) and pointing out highlights, with light prompts.
Ask about early memories of and reactions to these objects (personal history).
Ask the participant to imagine improved designs or ideal versions (guided speculation).
Document with video, photos or sketches plus notes; debrief and transcribe soon after; share early insights with the participant for validation.
Tabulate each task (goal, limitation, explanation, workaround, usability of workaround, wish) and compare across tasks and participants for themes and design criteria.
outputs: Tour records (photos, video, sketches), a task-by-task matrix of workarounds and wishes, and cross-cutting design criteria.
useWhen: Early exploratory research into home, workplace or personal technology ecosystems, accessibility needs, and how people organise physical or digital belongings.
avoidWhen: When you need generalisable prevalence claims or the space is too private; use surveys or remote diary studies instead.
whyLost: It survives widely as part of in-home and contextual research, though the structured past-present-future biography and task matrix are less often used.
whereToUse: Smart home and IoT, assistive technology, personal finance and household admin, file and photo management, workplace tools.
example: Researchers for a smart home hub ask participants to tour every connected device in their homes, recount how each arrived and imagine a better setup. Most hubs sit unused in drawers because setup was done once by a relative, which shifts the design brief to re-onboarding.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Blythe, M., Monk, A. and Park, J. (2002). Technology biographies: field study techniques for home use product development. CHI '02 Extended Abstracts, 658-659.

name: Guidelines Review and Consistency Inspection
origin: Usability inspection literature (Nielsen and Mack, 1994); Shneiderman's expert-review taxonomy
summary: Experts check an interface against a written guideline set or style guide and across a product family for consistent terms, fonts, colours, layout and formats.
description: Two expert reviews work from documents rather than short heuristic lists. In a guidelines review, experts check every screen for conformance with a published set: WCAG and other W3C accessibility guidelines, platform guidelines from Apple, Google or Microsoft, government research-based guidelines, or an organisation's own style guide. Sets range from about 10 to over 1,000 items, so reviewers need time to absorb them and large interfaces can take days or weeks; shorter checkpoints can serve as heuristics. In a consistency inspection, experts check terminology, fonts, colour, layout and input and output formats within one interface and across a family of products and their help material, which matters most when several teams build parts of one system. Software aids include term concordances and string searches. A bird's-eye pass, printing or tiling every screen together, reveals inconsistencies at once. Reviewers should not have built the interface, and reviews should precede user testing.
steps: Choose the guideline set or style guide suited to platform, domain or legal requirement and decide which sections apply.
Give reviewers who did not build the interface time to learn the guidelines and task domain.
Inventory all screens, pages and supporting materials across the product family.
Check each item for conformance, recording violations with location and guideline reference.
Run automated aids: term concordances, string searches and accessibility validators.
Do a bird's-eye pass by printing or tiling all screens and scanning for inconsistent fonts, colours, terms and layout.
Report violations organised by guideline, ranked by importance and effort, and fix before user testing.
outputs: A conformance and consistency report organised by guideline, a term concordance and a prioritised fix list.
useWhen: Accessibility compliance, platform submission, design-system adoption audits, and large systems built by several teams.
avoidWhen: As proof of usability; conformance does not guarantee it and no users are involved. Pair with Usability Testing; for quick broad review use Heuristic Evaluation.
whyLost: It survived because accessibility law and design systems require conformance audits, though the bird's-eye consistency pass is less often done.
whereToUse: Public-sector services, design-system governance, multi-team enterprise suites and app store submissions.
example: A bank merging three product teams' apps tiles 240 screens on a wall. The review finds four names for the same 'payee' concept and three date formats, which are fixed in the design system.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
reference: Nielsen, J. and Mack, R.L. (eds) (1994) Usability Inspection Methods. New York: Wiley.

name: Guiding Principles and Antiprinciples
origin: Baxter, Courage and Caine, 2015; seeded with Microsoft product reaction cards (Benedek and Miner, 2002)
summary: A team lists the words it wants and never wants used about its product, defines each with a measure and method, and re-evaluates the product against both lists every release.
description: Specifications state goals yet teams still diverge. With personas in hand, the team brainstorms on sticky notes the words it would like users, marketing or reviewers to use about the product, using product reaction cards as a prompt, groups them and keeps no more than about ten guiding principles. Each is defined so it can be measured and given a method: 'easy to use' as 100% booking success without help in usability studies, 'fast' as results under 30 seconds in log analysis. The same is done for antiprinciples, things the team never wants said, such as 'ad-filled' (ads over 10% of the screen) or 'untrustworthy'. Antiprinciples are a strong check on feature creep. The rigour is the measurement: evaluation checkpoints are scheduled before and after launch and the lists are revisited each version.
steps: With personas visible, brainstorm desired descriptors on sticky notes, using reaction cards to start, and group them.
Keep up to about ten guiding principles.
Write a measurable definition and name the measuring method for each (for example task success in usability testing, response time in logs).
Repeat the process for antiprinciples, again with definitions and measures.
Schedule evaluations against both lists before and after launch.
Revisit and revise both lists at each version or market change.
outputs: A table of principles and antiprinciples, each with a definition, threshold and measurement method, plus an evaluation schedule.
useWhen: A team needs a shared yardstick for design decisions and critique, and a defence against feature creep, at the start of a product or major release.
avoidWhen: Unmeasured principles become slogans; if you cannot name a method, do not adopt the principle. The lists say what the team wants, not what users perceive, so check perception with Semantic Differential, AttrakDiff or Usability Testing.
whyLost: Design principles are everywhere, but the measurable definitions, antiprinciples and scheduled evaluations are usually skipped, leaving inspirational posters.
whereToUse: Design systems, product vision work, AI assistants (tone and trust principles), regulated products needing auditable quality goals.
example: A travel-booking team sets 'trustworthy' as no hidden fees found in checkout testing and antiprinciple 'pushy' as no more than one upsell per flow, then audits each release against both.
reference: Baxter, K., Courage, C. and Caine, K. (2015) Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Research Methods. 2nd edn. Waltham, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 2, pp. 44-46.

name: Guttman Scaling
origin: Louis Guttman, 1944; probabilistic extension by Robert Mokken (1971)
summary: Tests whether items form a cumulative hierarchy, so that endorsing a harder item implies endorsing all easier ones, revealing ordered stages of adoption or capability.
description: A Guttman scale is cumulative: if a respondent agrees with item 4, they also agree with items 1-3. The coefficient of reproducibility (target above 0.9) measures how well responses fit this pattern. Mokken scale analysis provides a probabilistic, nonparametric version with Loevinger's H coefficients (H above 0.3 weak, above 0.5 strong scale). Cumulative scales are natural for capability or adoption ladders: digital skills, feature maturity, privacy protective behaviours, automation trust. They reveal the order in which people acquire behaviours, which directly informs progressive onboarding.
steps: Draft items expected to form a cumulative hierarchy (e.g. increasingly advanced feature uses).
Collect binary or polytomous responses from a sample of users.
Order items by popularity and respondents by total score; inspect the response matrix for errors.
Compute the coefficient of reproducibility, or run Mokken scale analysis (H and Hi coefficients, monotonicity checks).
Remove or revise items that break the hierarchy, and test invariant item ordering across groups.
Use the scale to place users on stages and design progression accordingly.
outputs: A validated cumulative scale, item ordering and user stage distribution.
useWhen: Measuring progressive capability, adoption or maturity, where items naturally build on one another.
avoidWhen: Constructs without a natural order, or multidimensional behaviours.
whyLost: Classical test theory and factor analysis became the default for scale building, and deterministic Guttman scales rarely fit perfectly.
whereToUse: Feature maturity models, digital literacy, security hygiene, B2B platform adoption, onboarding progression.
example: A Mokken analysis of 10 spreadsheet features shows a strong scale (H = 0.56) from formatting through formulas, pivot tables and scripts, guiding the order of in-product tips.
sources: Guttman, A basis for scaling qualitative data (1944), American Sociological Review
Mokken, A Theory and Procedure of Scale Analysis (1971)
van der Ark, Mokken scale analysis in R (2007), Journal of Statistical Software
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces (Nielsen & Molich, 1990)
reference: Guttman, L. (1944). American Sociological Review, 9(2), 139-150.

name: Habit loop analysis
origin: Habit research by Wendy Wood and colleagues (2002 onwards), Graybiel's basal ganglia work, popularised as the cue-routine-reward loop by Charles Duhigg (2012); automaticity measures by Verplanken and Orbell (2003) and Gardner et al. (2012)
summary: Maps the cues, routines and rewards sustaining existing behaviours and measures their automaticity, explaining why old practices persist and how new ones could become habitual.
description: Habits are context-response associations learned through repetition and maintained with little intention; Wood and colleagues found around 43% of daily actions are performed habitually in the same context. A habit loop analysis identifies the stable context cues (time, place, preceding action, people) that trigger a routine, the routine itself, and the reward that reinforced it, for both the old behaviour you are replacing and the new behaviour you want. Rigour requires measuring automaticity with a validated scale, such as the 4-item Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index (SRBAI), and measuring context stability, rather than inferring habits from frequency. Lally and colleagues (2010) found habit formation took a median of 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254, which sets realistic expectations.
steps: Choose the old behaviour to displace and the new behaviour to establish, and define the performance context for each.
Through 8 to 15 contextual interviews or a 1 to 2 week diary study, record for each occurrence the time, place, preceding action, people present and immediate outcome.
Identify stable cues (present in at least about 70% of occurrences), the routine sequence and the immediate rewards, including social and emotional rewards.
Measure automaticity with the 4-item SRBAI (1 to 7 scale) for old and new behaviours; scores above about 5 indicate strong habits that will resist intention-based interventions.
Design the new behaviour to attach to existing stable cues, reduce friction in the routine and deliver an immediate reward, or disrupt the old behaviour's cues where possible.
Track repetition in a stable context and re-measure automaticity at about 4, 8 and 12 weeks, expecting formation over roughly 2 to 3 months.
outputs: Cue-routine-reward maps for old and new behaviours, automaticity scores, context stability evidence, and a habit-formation design with a measurement plan.
useWhen: A legacy behaviour persists despite a better alternative; designing for daily or repeated use; adoption decays after initial launch novelty.
avoidWhen: The behaviour is infrequent or highly deliberative (annual tax filing, major purchases), where habit is not the mechanism; use decision-focused methods instead. Avoid designing compulsive loops that harm users.
whyLost: Popularised habit models such as Duhigg's loop and Eyal's Hooked became workshop canvases, while validated automaticity measurement and context-stability analysis from habit science were dropped.
whereToUse: Health worker data entry, medication adherence, financial routines, learning apps, enterprise system adoption replacing paper or spreadsheets.
example: Health workers filled a paper register after digital entry because the end-of-day register ritual at the clinic desk was a strong habit (SRBAI 6.1). Attaching a 'close the day' digital tally to the same desk moment, and removing the blank register from the desk, lowered paper duplication over 10 weeks.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 24 — Behavior Models, Habits & the Anatomy of Non-Adoption
reference: Wood, W., & Rünger, D. (2016). Psychology of habit. Annual Review of Psychology, 67, 289–314; Gardner, B., Abraham, C., Lally, P., & de Bruijn, G.-J. (2012). Towards parsimony in habit measurement. IJBNPA, 9, 102.

name: Half-Normal Plot and Lenth's Method for Unreplicated Factorials
aka: Normal quantile plot of factor effects
origin: Cuthbert Daniel, 1959; Zahn (1975) guardrails; Russell Lenth, 1989
summary: Judge which effects in an unreplicated factorial are real by comparing them with the spread expected if most effects are noise, graphically (Daniel) or numerically (Lenth).
description: A factorial or fractional factorial run once has no degrees of freedom for error, so significance must rest on effect sparsity: most estimated effects are noise. Daniel's half-normal plot orders the absolute effects against half-normal quantiles; noise effects fall on a line through the origin, the 68 percent point gives an approximate standard error, and effects beyond guardrails are declared active, after which they are removed and the plot redrawn. A full normal plot of signed effects, with quantiles at (i - 3/8)/(k + 1/4), works the same way. Lenth's method gives a numeric version: s0 = 1.5 x median absolute effect, the pseudo standard error PSE = 1.5 x median of absolute effects below 2.5 s0, a margin of error ME = t(0.975, m/3 df) x PSE, and a simultaneous margin SME. Effects are drawn as bars with both lines.
steps: Estimate all m effects from the unreplicated two-level design.
Sort the absolute effects and plot them against half-normal quantiles at probabilities (i - 1/2)/m.
Read an approximate standard error at the 68 percent point and flag effects that lie well off the line through the origin.
Remove clearly active and borderline effects and replot to re-estimate the standard error.
For Lenth's method, compute s0, PSE, ME and SME and draw effects as bars with ME and SME lines.
Treat effects beyond SME as active, those between ME and SME as possibly active, and confirm them in a follow-up run.
outputs: A list of active effects with an approximate standard error, shown as a half-normal plot or a Lenth bar chart.
useWhen: Screening many factors (copy, layout, defaults, timing) in a single-replicate factorial or fractional factorial, such as a multivariate test with one observation per cell or an expert-rated design sweep.
avoidWhen: When many effects are expected to be real, which inflates the error estimate; replicated designs, where a proper error term exists (ANOVA for Multi-Design Comparisons (One-Way and Two-Way)); or heavily aliased designs where interactions cannot be assumed negligible.
whyLost: Standard in engineering DoE and Six Sigma screening, but UX multivariate tests are usually analysed one variant at a time and unreplicated factorials are rare.
whereToUse: Screening experiments on landing pages and onboarding, simulation and model-based sweeps, configuration testing for performance, offline evaluation of AI prompt variants.
example: An AI product team scores a 2^(6-2) fractional factorial of prompt settings once each on a quality rubric. Lenth's PSE puts the SME at 0.42; only temperature and example count exceed it, so later tests focus on those two.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 2 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2005)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Daniel, C. (1959). Use of half-normal plots in interpreting factorial two-level experiments. Technometrics, 1(4), 311-341; Lenth, R. V. (1989). Quick and easy analysis of unreplicated factorials. Technometrics, 31(4), 469-473.

name: Hallway Usability Testing (Krug Method)
aka: Discount Usability Testing Protocol (Nielsen's Original Method)
origin: Jakob Nielsen, 1989 (discount usability); Steve Krug, 2010
summary: Low-cost monthly usability tests with three participants, observed live by the team and followed by a debrief that commits to fixing the worst problems.
description: Steve Krug's method makes usability testing a lightweight organisational habit. Once a month, the team tests with three participants in a morning, using think-aloud on realistic tasks. Stakeholders observe live from another room, each noting the three most serious problems they saw. Over lunch, a debrief combines the lists, agrees the top problems and commits to the smallest fixes that will solve them, since 'tweaking' beats redesigning. The rigour lies not in sample size but in discipline: a fixed cadence, recruiting people who are reasonably representative, a written script, mandatory observation by decision-makers, and a deliberate focus on fixing the worst problems first rather than producing long reports. An earlier, different form is the hallway and storefront method of Gould and colleagues, who placed a mock-up kiosk of the 1984 Olympic Message System in a public hallway so that passers-by could try it and comment.
steps: Set a monthly rhythm: one morning of testing each month.
Recruit three participants who are reasonably representative of the users.
Test with three or four realistic scenarios of 15 to 20 minutes each, using think-aloud and a written script.
Have stakeholders watch live from another room, each noting the three most serious problems they saw.
Debrief the same day: combine the lists, agree the top problems and choose the smallest fixes that will solve them.
Fix the top problems before the next session and repeat; the iterative rhythm, not the single session, is the method.
outputs: A short list of the most serious usability problems, team-agreed fixes, and a regular testing rhythm that builds shared understanding.
useWhen: Teams without dedicated researchers, early and iterative design stages, and organisations needing to build a habit of watching users.
avoidWhen: Avoid for measurement, benchmarking, specialist or vulnerable user groups, or when the problem is not usability; use summative testing or properly recruited studies.
whyLost: 'Hallway testing' survived as a phrase, but the rigour of Krug's method (a monthly cadence, whole-team observation, a debrief limited to the top problems) was dropped in favour of ad hoc tests with colleagues.
whereToUse: Any product team without a dedicated UX researcher. The most actionable usability testing protocol for resource-constrained teams.
example: A small charity web team tests its donation flow with three supporters on the first Friday of every month; observers each list their top three problems, and the team fixes the shared top one before the next session.
sources: Don't Make Me Think / Rocket Surgery Made Easy — Steve Krug
Nielsen & Landauer, A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems (INTERCHI 1993)
Nielsen, Usability engineering at a discount (1989)

Gould, J. D., Boies, S. J., Levy, S., Richards, J. T. & Schoonard, J. (1987) The 1984 Olympic Message System: a test of behavioral principles of system design. Communications of the ACM 30(9), 758-769
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Krug S (2010) Rocket Surgery Made Easy: The Do-It-Yourself Guide to Finding and Fixing Usability Problems. New Riders

name: Harmonisation of Survey Questions and Background Variables
origin: Comparative survey programmes (ESS, ISSP, CSES); Ehling (2003); Granda et al. (2010)
summary: Making background and substantive measures comparable across countries or waves by designing a common input, mapping local items to agreed target variables, or recoding existing data.
description: Harmonisation is the deliberate work of making measures comparable when they are collected in different countries, languages, systems or waves. Input harmonisation fixes a common master questionnaire, developed sequentially, in parallel or simultaneously, and translates it. Output harmonisation lets each context ask locally appropriate items and maps them to an agreed target variable, such as ISCED for education or ISCO for occupation; this is ex-ante when the target and mapping tables are fixed before collection, ex-post when existing datasets are recoded afterwards. Rigour comes from documenting every deviation and mapping rule, and from assessing quality: is the concept relevant in each context, is the documentation complete, does the coding scheme fit, can each harmonised value be traced to its source, and are harmonised measures reliable. Collapsing to common categories always loses detail, and ex-post work is limited by what was originally asked.
steps: Decide between input harmonisation (one master questionnaire) and output harmonisation (local items mapped to target variables).
For ex-ante output harmonisation, define the target classification and require a mapping table from each country or product version before fieldwork.
For ex-post harmonisation, document the source variables and write explicit recoding rules for existing data.
Record every deviation from the master or target, with its rationale.
Assess quality: concept relevance per context, completeness of documentation, fit of the coding scheme, traceability from local to harmonised values, and reliability of the harmonised measures.
Publish the harmonised variables with their mapping documentation.
outputs: Harmonised variables, mapping tables and recoding rules, and a quality assessment of comparability.
useWhen: Comparing user segments across markets, merging survey data from different product lines or acquired companies, or keeping a tracker comparable after its questions change.
avoidWhen: Testing whether attitude scales mean the same thing across groups; use measurement invariance testing. Single-market studies need none of this.
whyLost: UX teams localise surveys by translation alone and rarely define target variables, so cross-market comparisons of role, education or company size silently mix definitions.
whereToUse: Global products comparing markets, post-acquisition research repositories, longitudinal trackers whose demographic and firmographic questions have changed.
example: A payments company compares merchant satisfaction in Brazil, India and Germany, where 'business size' was asked in local revenue bands. The team defines a target variable on employee count, maps each local item to it, documents losses of detail and reports results on the harmonised variable only.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Wolf, C., Schneider, S. L., Behr, D. and Joye, D. (2016). Harmonizing survey questions between cultures and over time. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 502-524). London: SAGE.

name: Hawkes Point Processes
origin: Alan G. Hawkes, 1971
summary: Models behavioural events as a point process where each event temporarily raises (or suppresses) the chance of further events, capturing bursts and cascades in interaction data.
description: A Hawkes process has a conditional intensity equal to a baseline rate plus decaying contributions from past events, so events cluster in self-exciting bursts, as in earthquake aftershocks or trading activity. The Behavioral Spectral Framework proposes representing behavioural events as point processes such as Hawkes models to capture self-excitation and suppression, as part of handling irregular sampling intelligently, alongside Lomb-Scargle periodograms and survival models of inactivity. The appeal for UX is that clicks, retries and messages are event-driven: a failed attempt may trigger a rapid cascade of retries (excitation), while a confusing screen may suppress further action. The playbook mentions the technique as a direction rather than a worked protocol, so the steps below follow standard practice.
steps: Collect event timestamps per user, with event types if relevant.
Specify a baseline rate and an excitation kernel (e.g. exponential decay).
Fit the model by maximum likelihood.
Interpret the branching ratio (how many follow-on events each event triggers) and decay time.
Compare parameters across cohorts or design variants.
Validate with goodness-of-fit checks and qualitative review of bursts.
outputs: Estimated baseline rates, excitation strengths and decay times per cohort.
useWhen: When interaction events cluster in bursts and you want to model contagion or retry cascades.
avoidWhen: When events are regular or few, or a simple rate comparison answers the question.
whyLost: Established in seismology, finance and social media research, but not in UX methods.
whereToUse: Retry storms in payments, notification cascades, social feed engagement, support contact bursts.
example: Modelling OTP retries as a Hawkes process shows each failure triggers about 0.6 further attempts within seconds, quantifying retry cascades before a UI change.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Hawkes, A. G. (1971). Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes. Biometrika, 58(1), 83–90.

name: HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study)
origin: ICI, UK, mid-1960s; codified by Trevor Kletz; IEC 61882
summary: A facilitated team review that applies guidewords such as NO, MORE, LESS, REVERSE and OTHER THAN to each design parameter to find deviations, causes and consequences.
description: HAZOP breaks a system into nodes and, for each parameter at each node, applies standard guidewords to generate deviations: NO flow, MORE pressure, LATE action, REVERSE sequence. A multidisciplinary team, led by an independent chair and a scribe, discusses each deviation's credible causes, consequences and existing safeguards, and records actions. Its power is that guidewords force systematic imagination: the team cannot skip combinations, and the independent chair prevents groupthink. Applied to UX, nodes become screens or system states, parameters become data, timing, user intent and notifications, and guidewords surface edge cases such as duplicate submissions, stale data and out-of-order events that ordinary design reviews miss.
steps: Define scope and split the user journey or system into nodes (screens, services, states).
For each node, list parameters: data values, timing, sequence, user intent, permissions, notifications.
Assemble a team of 4-8 (design, engineering, support, domain expert) with an independent chair and a scribe.
Systematically apply guidewords (NO, MORE, LESS, AS WELL AS, PART OF, REVERSE, OTHER THAN, EARLY, LATE, BEFORE, AFTER) to every parameter.
For each meaningful deviation, record causes, consequences, existing safeguards and recommended actions with owners.
Track actions to closure and repeat the HAZOP when the design changes materially.
outputs: HAZOP log of deviations, causes, consequences, safeguards and actions; a prioritised edge-case backlog.
useWhen: Designs with many states, integrations and concurrent events (payments, bookings, IoT, sync), particularly before build.
avoidWhen: Early concept work where parameters are undefined; use pre-mortem or scenario analysis instead.
whyLost: It is seen as an engineering safety ritual tied to process plants, and its sessions are long and disciplined. Design reviews in UX favour taste-based critique over systematic deviation analysis.
whereToUse: Payments and refunds, booking systems, connected devices, offline sync, AI agents executing multi-step actions.
example: A ride-hailing team HAZOPs the 'driver arrived' node. 'EARLY' plus 'location' reveals arrivals flagged at the wrong entrance of large venues; the team adds pickup-point confirmation and a grace period.
sources: IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies): Application guide
reference: IEC 61882:2016. Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) - Application guide.

name: HCI archaeology (stored application data analysis)
origin: Personal information management studies of files and email (for example Whittaker and Sidner, 1996; Whittaker et al., 2011)
summary: Study the organisational traces left in everyday tools (folder structures, email filing, bookmarks, contacts) to understand long-term information management without observing sessions.
description: Files, desktops, email clients, bookmarks and social networks store the residue of years of organising: how many folders, how deep, whether work and home are separated, whether the inbox doubles as a to-do list. Analysing these stored structures reveals long-term practices that observation sessions miss, without interfering with work or needing training. Studies of email filing and re-finding are classic examples. The method only sees what the tool stores, missing transient actions and intermediate states, so it suits long-term patterns rather than interface evaluation. Extraction may require custom software or reverse-engineering file formats. Privacy is the central concern: participants must be informed of risks, only strictly necessary data taken (headers, not message bodies), and data anonymised to the level of structure or who-corresponded-with-whom.
steps: Define the organisational question and identify which tools' stored data can answer it.
Obtain informed consent that explains the privacy risks and exactly what will be collected.
Limit collection to strictly necessary data (for example folder names and sizes, email headers rather than bodies).
Write or adapt extraction software to convert native formats into analysable structures, anonymising as you extract.
Analyse structures, categories, depths, sizes and change over time, comparing participants.
Pair with brief interviews where interpretation of structures is ambiguous.
outputs: Descriptions and metrics of how participants structure files, mail, bookmarks or contacts, and typologies of organising strategies.
useWhen: Designing file management, email, note-taking, bookmarking or knowledge tools where long-term organising habits matter.
avoidWhen: When you need to see in-the-moment behaviour, errors or intermediate states (use observation or logging), or when privacy risks cannot be managed.
whyLost: It belongs to a small personal information management research community; product teams rely on telemetry instead and rarely ask to inspect users' stored structures.
whereToUse: Cloud storage, email and productivity suites, note-taking and knowledge management, photo libraries, enterprise document management.
example: A cloud storage company, with consent, extracts anonymised folder trees from 40 users' drives. Most have shallow structures with huge 'Misc' folders and rely on search, so the team prioritises search and recency views over new folder features.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. and Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 338-339.

name: HEART Framework
origin: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu, Google, 2010
summary: Structures UX metric selection across Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success, using a Goals-Signals-Metrics process to link user goals to measurable data.
description: HEART was developed at Google to give large-scale web products user-centred metrics beyond page views. The five categories are Happiness (attitudes, often via surveys), Engagement (depth and frequency of use), Adoption (new users of a product or feature), Retention (users returning) and Task success (efficiency, effectiveness, error rate). The companion Goals-Signals-Metrics process is the method's core: for each relevant category, the team states the goal, identifies behavioural or attitudinal signals that indicate progress, and defines specific metrics, usually as rates or averages that can be compared over time or between experiment arms. Rigour comes from selecting only categories relevant to the product's goals, ensuring signals are actually instrumented and sensitive to change, and reviewing metrics with qualitative research so they do not drift from user value.
steps: Agree the product or feature goals with stakeholders.
Select the HEART categories relevant to those goals; not all five need to be used.
For each category, write goals, then candidate signals (behavioural or attitudinal) that would indicate progress.
Turn signals into specific metrics with definitions, data sources and time windows.
Check instrumentation, baselines and sensitivity, and set targets.
Review metrics regularly and in experiments, revisiting them as the product evolves.
outputs: Goals-Signals-Metrics table, metric definitions and baselines, UX dashboard and targets.
useWhen: Defining UX success metrics for a product or feature, aligning with OKRs, and instrumenting new launches.
avoidWhen: Small products without analytics infrastructure or when the question is exploratory; start with qualitative research. Do not let business and technical health metrics (the PULSE set: page views, uptime, latency, seven-day active users, earnings) stand in for HEART signals; they are indirect and ambiguous for UX, as more page views can mean popularity or users getting lost.
whyLost: Quantitative HRA belongs to nuclear and rail safety cases. UX lacks the habit of estimating error probabilities and the name collision with Google HEART obscures it further.
whereToUse: Metric framework design; OKR alignment; product analytics instrumentation.
example: A health booking app used GSM to define task success as the percentage of booking attempts completed within three minutes and retention as patients rebooking within 90 days, replacing a vague 'engagement' target.
sources: Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale (Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu)
Chapman, C. & Rodden, K., Quantitative User Experience Research (Apress, 2023)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale (Rodden et al., 2010)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Rodden, K., Hutchinson, H., & Fu, X. (2010). Measuring the user experience on a large scale: User-centered metrics for web applications. Proceedings of CHI 2010, 2395-2398.

name: HEART Human Reliability Assessment (with NARA and CARA)
aka: Human Error Assessment and Reduction Technique
origin: Jeremy Williams (1988); NARA by Gibson et al. (2008) for UK nuclear; CARA by Gibson and Kirwan (2008) for air traffic management
summary: Estimate a task's human error probability by classifying it as a generic task type and multiplying the nominal error rate by weighted error-producing conditions.
description: HEART is a first-generation human reliability assessment that rates whole tasks rather than decomposing them as THERP does, on the premise that reliability depends on the generic nature of the task. The analyst classifies the task into one of nine generic task types, from 'totally unfamiliar, performed at speed' to 'completely familiar, well designed, highly practised', each with a nominal human error probability and 5th and 95th percentile bounds. Relevant error-producing conditions are chosen from a list of 38, each with a maximum multiplier (unfamiliarity with an important but rare situation can multiply error by 17). For each, the analyst judges the assessed proportion of affect from 0.1 to 1, computes a weighting factor and multiplies it into the nominal value. NARA replaces the generic tasks with 18 nuclear tasks and CORE-DATA values; CARA adapts it to air traffic control. Not to be confused with Google's HEART metrics framework.
steps: Describe the task and the human failure event of concern, drawing on prior task and error analysis.
Classify the task into one of the nine generic task types (or a NARA or CARA task) and take its nominal human error probability.
Select the applicable error-producing conditions from the list of 38, using earlier qualitative analysis.
Judge the assessed proportion of affect (0.1 to 1) for each selected condition.
Compute each condition's weighting factor as ((maximum effect - 1) x proportion of affect) + 1 and multiply the nominal probability by all factors to obtain the assessed probability.
Target error reduction at the conditions with the largest weighting factors and re-assess the redesigned task.
outputs: An assessed human error probability per task with the main contributing error-producing conditions ranked by effect.
useWhen: Safety-critical interfaces (medical devices, control rooms, aviation, rail) where a quick, documented numerical error estimate is needed for a risk case or to compare design options.
avoidWhen: When detailed step-level analysis is needed (use THERP or SHERPA) or contextual, cognitive modelling of control modes (use CREAM). Generic task choice and proportion of affect are highly judgemental, and condition interactions and positive factors are not modelled.
whyLost: Human reliability assessment stayed in nuclear, rail and aviation safety cases; UX teams rarely produce probabilistic risk estimates, and the name now collides with Google's HEART framework.
whereToUse: Medical device use-error risk files (IEC 62366), infusion pumps, clinical decision support, financial trading confirmations, autonomous vehicle takeover requests.
example: For a home dialysis machine, the step 'reconnect line after alarm' is classed as a fairly simple task performed rapidly. Time shortage and poor feedback conditions raise its assessed error probability roughly tenfold, so the team adds a guided reconnection screen and re-assesses.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Williams, J. C. (1988). A data-based method for assessing and reducing human error to improve operational performance. Proceedings of the IEEE Fourth Conference on Human Factors and Power Plants.

name: Heart Rate and Heart Rate Variability Measurement
origin: Cardiovascular psychophysiology; its use in games user research is described by Lennart E. Nacke in chapter 16
summary: Records heart rate and the variation between beats during use, as indicators of emotional response and of mental effort or workload.
description: Cardiovascular measures are among the easiest physiological signals to collect. Heart rate can be taken with electrocardiography electrodes on the skin or, for many purposes, with a standard exercise heart-rate monitor. Nacke notes that heart rate responds to competition with human rather than computer opponents, has been used to model emotional responses to games, and with finger temperature can help separate emotions such as anger and fear. With good sensors, the interval between consecutive beats gives heart rate variability (HRV). Because a person's normally irregular rhythm becomes more regular under mental effort and cognitive workload, falling HRV is a useful workload indicator, already established in HCI and, he argues, under-used in games research. Heart rate is affected by age, posture, fitness, breathing and time of day, so within-person baselines and controlled posture matter, and active or motion-based play complicates interpretation. For UX research, HR and HRV offer a low-cost, continuous signal of arousal and effort to set beside task data and self-report.
steps: Choose the sensor (ECG electrodes for HRV quality, chest strap or optical monitor for heart rate only).
Control posture and physical activity, and record a resting baseline.
Run the session with event markers synchronised to the physiological recording.
Clean the signal, detect beats and compute heart rate and HRV measures for each segment.
Express values relative to each participant's baseline.
Compare segments or conditions and triangulate with self-report, performance and observation.
outputs: Baseline-corrected heart rate and HRV per segment, linked to events in the session.
useWhen: You want a cheap continuous indicator of arousal or mental workload across a task or play session.
avoidWhen: The activity involves significant physical movement, or you need to know whether an experience was pleasant or unpleasant. Arousal is not specific to one mental state: the polygraph is not accepted as a lie detector because sweating and heart-rate changes are not reliably linked to deception, so do not read stress, trust or deceit from this signal alone.
whyLost: Interpretation is ambiguous without other measures and the signal is easily confounded, so UX teams rarely invest in it outside specialist labs.
whereToUse: Games including multiplayer modes, driving and control interfaces, high-workload professional tools, VR.
example: HRV drops sharply while players manage a new crafting menu during combat, supporting the team's suspicion that the menu overloads players at that moment.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Society for Neuroscience, Brain Facts: A Primer on the Brain and Nervous System, 8th ed. (2018)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 16 (Nacke).

name: Heatmap and Scrollmap Interpretation Protocol
origin: Click and scroll heatmap tools from the mid-2000s (Crazy Egg 2005, later Hotjar); interpretation protocol by Dushyant Kanungo (2016)
summary: A structured protocol for reading click, move, attention and scroll maps, segmenting data and setting thresholds, so heatmaps produce defensible findings rather than impressions.
description: Heatmaps are popular because they look self-explanatory, which is exactly why they are misread. A rigorous interpretation protocol distinguishes map types: click maps show where people acted, move maps loosely approximate attention, attention or eye-tracking maps show fixations, and scroll maps show the proportion of visitors reaching each depth. It requires sufficient sample sizes (often a few thousand page views per segment), segmentation by device, traffic source and new versus returning users, since aggregate maps blend different behaviours, and comparison with a baseline or variant. Analysts look for specific signals: clicks on non-interactive elements, rage or dead clicks, steep scroll drop-offs above key content, and false floors. Findings are stated as hypotheses and confirmed with session recordings, usability tests or experiments.
steps: Heatmap interpretation protocol:

Compare attention heatmap to click heatmap — elements with high attention but low clicks = visible but not compelling; elements with low attention but high clicks = users are clicking without reading.
(2) Overlay scroll map to identify scroll depth at which each CTA becomes visible — first ensure users reach the element before worrying about its design.
(3) Code rage clicks as a frustration signal requiring qualitative investigation.
outputs: Segmented heatmap and scrollmap readings, list of signals (dead clicks, false floors, ignored calls to action) with sample sizes, and hypotheses for testing.
useWhen: Landing pages, long-form content, product pages and onboarding screens with enough traffic, and as triage before usability testing or A/B tests.
avoidWhen: With low traffic, highly dynamic or personalised pages where maps cannot align elements, or when you need to know why users behave as they do; use usability testing.
whyLost: Heatmap tools made the outputs easy to produce, so interpretation became impressionistic, and segmentation and sample-size discipline were rarely practised.
whereToUse: Landing page optimization, onboarding funnel analysis, e-commerce UX, content page design.
example: An e-commerce product page scroll map shows a sharp drop at 40% depth on mobile only, just above shipping information. Segmenting reveals a full-width image creating a false floor; replacing it raises views of shipping details from 38% to 61%.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Kanungo D (2016) UX Decoded: A Practical Guide to User Experience. BPB Publications

name: Hedonic Quality (HQ) Questionnaire
origin: Hassenzahl, Platz, Burmester & Lehner (2000); later expanded into AttrakDiff
summary: Seven bipolar items measuring a product's non-task appeal (interesting, exciting, original, innovative), separate from its ergonomic usability.
description: Hassenzahl's HQ questionnaire was one of the first instruments to measure user experience beyond usability. Its seven 7-point bipolar items are interesting–boring, costly–cheap, exciting–dull, exclusive–standard, impressive–nondescript, original–ordinary and innovative–conservative. In studies with industrial software prototypes and display types, factor analysis separated hedonic quality from ergonomic quality (simple, clear), and both contributed about equally to overall appeal. Hedonic quality did not correlate with mental effort while ergonomic quality did, evidence the two are distinct. The work grew into AttrakDiff with pragmatic quality and the stimulation, identification and evocation facets of hedonic quality.
steps: Administer the seven HQ items, alongside ergonomic or pragmatic quality items.
Average items for hedonic and ergonomic scores.
Plot the two dimensions to see whether a design is usable but dull, or exciting but awkward.
Relate both to overall appeal or preference with regression.
outputs: Separate hedonic and ergonomic quality scores and their contribution to appeal.
useWhen: Designs where delight, novelty or brand expression matter alongside usability.
avoidWhen: Purely functional tools where appeal is irrelevant.
whyLost: Superseded under a new name by AttrakDiff and later the UEQ.
whereToUse: Consumer products, automotive interiors, games, branded experiences.
example: Two music app concepts score equally on ergonomic quality, but one scores far higher on hedonic quality and wins on appeal.
reference: Hassenzahl, M., Platz, A., Burmester, M. & Lehner, K. (2000). Hedonic and ergonomic quality aspects determine a software's appeal. CHI 2000.

name: Heider-Simmel animation narration
origin: Fritz Heider and Marianne Simmel, 1944
summary: Viewers describe a short animation of moving geometric shapes; coding their narratives shows how readily motion alone leads them to attribute goals, emotions and relationships.
