description: Heider and Simmel showed a short silent animation of a small circle, a small triangle and a large triangle moving in and around a box with a door. Almost all viewers described a drama: a couple seeking peace and a bully who throws a tantrum when shut out. The shapes have no faces, so attributions of intention, emotion and relationship arise from motion and timing alone. Later imaging studies found such displays engage social-cognition brain regions. As a method, the narratives are coded for physical-motion versus mental-state and social terms, and motion parameters can be varied to see which produce agency. The book offers no coding scheme, so an established one must be used for scoring.
steps: Prepare a short silent animation of simple shapes moving and interacting, or motion variants of an interface element, robot or agent.
Show it to viewers individually without suggesting an interpretation.
Ask them to describe what happened in their own words.
Code narratives for physical-motion terms versus intentional, emotional and social attributions, with two coders.
Vary motion parameters (speed changes, contingency, approach and avoidance) between groups.
Compare attribution rates across variants.
outputs: Free narratives coded for intentional, emotional and social attributions, with attribution rates per motion variant.
useWhen: Testing how motion of an assistant, robot, vehicle, avatar or interface animation is read: as intentional, friendly, aggressive or mechanical.
avoidWhen: Avoid without a coding scheme from the literature; for emotional response to animations use self-report or physiological affect measures.
whyLost: It is a classic social perception demonstration and was never adapted as a motion-design evaluation method.
whereToUse: Social robots, autonomous vehicles' external signals, AI assistant avatars, motion design systems, game characters.
example: Delivery-robot movement variants are shown as abstract animations. When the robot pauses and turns towards pedestrians, viewers describe it as 'polite'; abrupt stops are read as 'nervous', guiding motion tuning.
sources: Heider, F., & Simmel, M. (1944). An experimental study of apparent behavior. American Journal of Psychology, 57
reference: Heider, F., & Simmel, M. (1944). An experimental study of apparent behavior. American Journal of Psychology, 57, 243-259.

name: Hermeneutic Circle
origin: Friedrich Schleiermacher and Wilhelm Dilthey, 19th century; Martin Heidegger and Hans-Georg Gadamer, 20th century
summary: An iterative interpretive method moving between parts and the whole of a text or dataset, revising each in light of the other until a coherent, deep interpretation emerges.
description: The hermeneutic circle is the methodological principle that understanding proceeds through an iterative movement between the parts of a text (or interaction, or cultural product) and the whole — understanding the parts in light of the whole, and revising understanding of the whole in light of the parts. No final 'correct' interpretation is reached — understanding deepens with each turn of the circle. Applied to UX qualitative data: the hermeneutic circle formalises the iterative nature of good qualitative analysis and guards against both premature closure (settling on an interpretation too quickly) and infinite regress (perpetual revision without ever reaching understanding).
steps: Initial reading — the whole: Read the full dataset (or a complete interview, observation, or case) to develop a preliminary understanding of the whole.
Attention to parts: Re-read specific segments that seem significant, puzzling, or contradictory. How do they relate to your preliminary understanding of the whole?
Revision of the whole: How does closer attention to these parts change your understanding of the whole? Revise your interpretation accordingly.
Iteration: Return to the parts, now read in light of the revised understanding of the whole. Each iteration deepens rather than replaces the previous understanding.

Productive friction: The hermeneutic circle is most productive when parts and whole are in tension — when a specific segment resists your understanding of the whole, or when your understanding of the whole cannot account for a specific segment. These points of resistance are where understanding is most deepened.
outputs: Iterative interpretive memos, revised whole-case interpretations, documentation of how puzzling parts changed the reading, and a coherent interpretive account.
useWhen: You need deep understanding of a small number of rich cases, transcripts or artefacts, especially where meaning is ambiguous or contradictions appear.
avoidWhen: You need fast, broad coverage or reproducible coding; use Qualitative Content Analysis or Template Analysis.
whyLost: It is a philosophical principle rather than a packaged procedure, so UX analysts rarely make it explicit, even though skilled synthesis implicitly relies on it.
whereToUse: In-depth interview synthesis, analysing contradictory feedback, persona refinement, IPA-style studies, and interpreting long-form user writing.
example: A researcher puzzled by a participant who praises a budgeting app yet stopped using it rereads the transcript as a whole, then the praise, then the whole again, recognising the praise as about who she wanted to be, not how she lived.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Gadamer, H.-G. (1975). Truth and Method. Sheed & Ward.

name: Hero Flows
origin: Jon Kolko, 2014
summary: Sketch only the ideal main paths through a product, derived from verb-noun activity lists, as success-only stories drawn one step per sheet.
description: Hero flows bridge product vision and detailed definition. The team lists verb-noun activity pairs across the whole product life cycle, from purchase to discard, then marks the most common, idealised and relevant ones and names the flows they form, such as first-time use and everyday use. For each flow a short story is written of a user completing it with nothing going wrong and technology that is ambitious but feasible. Each step is then drawn on its own sheet with a marker in simple shapes and words. Edge cases and errors are deliberately excluded so the team can see the core value clearly; together with a concept map, hero flows show both the forest and the trees. They are thinking artefacts, not specifications.
steps: List verb-noun activity pairs across the product life cycle, from purchase to discard.
Mark the most common, idealised and relevant pairs and group them into named hero flows.
Write a success-only story for each flow, ignoring edge cases and failures.
Keep technology pragmatic but aspirational in the stories.
Sketch each step on a separate sheet using simple shapes and words.
Review the flows together and iterate them as thinking artefacts before detailing edge cases.
outputs: Named hero flows, narrative stories and one-sheet-per-step paper sketches.
useWhen: A team needs to agree the core value path of a new product or feature before investing in detailed interaction design.
avoidWhen: Hero flows exclude errors and edge cases by design; do not ship them as specifications. Check that the ideal path matches how people actually work with Contextual Inquiry, and test it with Prototype Testing or Cognitive Walkthrough.
whyLost: Survives widely as 'happy path' user flows because it is fast, communicable and fits product kick-offs; Kolko's name and the verb-noun derivation are less known.
whereToUse: New product definition, consumer apps, health and wellbeing products, connected devices.
example: A mood-tracking app team writes a hero flow in which a user installs the app, sets a check-in frequency and replies to a text with a number, then later sees a graph linking Tuesday dips to a recurring meeting.
reference: Kolko, J. (2014) Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press, pp. 152-156.

name: Heuristic Evaluation
origin: Jakob Nielsen & Rolf Molich, 1990
summary: Several evaluators independently inspect an interface against recognised usability principles, producing a severity-rated list of problems without involving users.
description: Heuristic evaluation is an inspection method in which a small group of evaluators independently examine an interface and judge its compliance with a set of usability principles, most commonly Nielsen's ten heuristics. Each evaluator works alone, typically making two passes: one to understand the flow and another to inspect elements in detail. Findings are then aggregated, de-duplicated and rated for severity. The method rests on the observation that individual evaluators find only a fraction of problems, while three to five independent evaluators together find most of them. Rigour comes from independence before aggregation, citing the specific heuristic and location for each problem, using a shared severity scale and recognising that heuristics predict, but do not prove, user difficulty. The original 1990 paper proposed nine heuristics: simple and natural dialogue, speak the user's language, minimise user memory load, be consistent, provide feedback, provide clearly marked exits, provide shortcuts, good error messages and prevent errors. Nielsen's later ten (1994) revised and extended the list, adding help and documentation.
steps: Choose the heuristic set (for example Nielsen's ten, or domain-specific heuristics) and define scope and key tasks.
Brief 3 to 5 evaluators, ideally with usability and domain knowledge.
Have each evaluator inspect the interface independently in at least two passes, recording each problem, its location and the heuristic violated.

Optionally let evaluators speak their findings to an observer who records them; the observer may answer domain questions, and may give a hint only once an evaluator is clearly stuck and has noted the problem.
Merge findings into a single list and remove duplicates.
Have evaluators independently rate severity on a 0 to 4 scale and average the ratings.
Optionally hold a brainstorming debriefing with the designers to suggest fixes and note what works well.
Report prioritised problems with recommendations and validate the most severe with users where possible.
outputs: A consolidated, severity-rated list of usability problems mapped to heuristics and screens, with recommendations.
useWhen: Early in design or when time and budget prevent user testing; as a quick audit before testing to remove obvious problems.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the only evidence for high-stakes decisions or for novel interaction paradigms the heuristics do not cover; use usability testing with representative users. Evidence summarised in the HHS guidelines (2006) suggests that inspections produce roughly 1.3 false positives and 0.5 misses for every real problem found, so treat findings as candidates to confirm in testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Efficient expert method; widely taught and understood; useful when budget or time precludes user testing.
whereToUse: Any UI at any stage; particularly useful early in design before investing in user testing.
example: A SaaS analytics vendor runs a heuristic evaluation with four evaluators before a beta. They find no undo for deleting dashboards and inconsistent filter terminology, both fixed before user sessions begin.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J & Molich R (1990) Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. CHI
Nielsen J (1994) Heuristic evaluation. In Nielsen & Mack (Eds) Usability Inspection Methods
Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2006)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)

Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces: Exploration and Evaluation (Ó Broin, 2011)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld & Morville, 2006)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)

name: Heuristic Evaluation with Inter-Evaluator Reliability
origin: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich, 1990
summary: Heuristic evaluation as originally specified: several independent evaluators, aggregation of all unique problems, and measured overlap between evaluators to judge coverage and reliability.
description: Heuristic evaluation has evaluators inspect an interface against a set of usability heuristics. Nielsen and Molich found that single evaluators detect only about 20-50% of problems, so the method's validity depends on several evaluators (typically three to five) working independently and on aggregating every unique problem found by anyone, not averaging or voting. Evaluator independence must be preserved until individual reports are complete. Reliability is assessed by computing the overlap between evaluators (for example, any-two agreement) and how many problems were found by only one person, which indicates how far from saturation the evaluation is. Severity is rated afterwards, ideally independently. In current practice heuristic evaluation is often a single designer's review, which keeps the name but loses the statistical basis of the method.
steps: 3–5 evaluators: each independently evaluates the interface against all 10 heuristics.
No discussion during individual phases.
After all have finished: aggregate lists.
Count unique problems.
Measure evaluator reliability: Fleiss' κ on binary problem detection (did evaluator i find problem j?).
Low κ (< 0.40) means evaluators are finding different problems — discuss and align on heuristic interpretation before proceeding.
outputs: Individual evaluator reports, an aggregated list of unique problems with heuristics violated, evaluator overlap and any-two agreement statistics, and independent severity ratings.
useWhen: Early and cheap inspection of prototypes or live products, before user testing, and in audits where evaluator coverage must be justified.
avoidWhen: As a replacement for testing with users, for domain-specific tools where evaluators lack domain knowledge (use double experts or user testing), or with a single evaluator.
whyLost: Time pressure reduced it to one person's expert review, and the multi-evaluator aggregation and reliability analysis that underpin its effectiveness were forgotten.
whereToUse: Expert evaluation, design system auditing, pre-testing validation. The inter-evaluator reliability component is the most commonly skipped step.
example: Four evaluators independently review an insurance claims portal and find 47 unique problems, but only 9 are found by more than one evaluator. The low overlap prompts adding a fifth evaluator with claims expertise, who finds 8 more.
sources: Hertzum & Jacobsen, The evaluator effect (International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, 2001)
Nielsen J & Molich R (1990) Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. Proceedings of CHI '90, 249-256
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces (Nielsen & Molich, 1990)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces: Exploration and Evaluation (Ó Broin, 2011)
reference: Nielsen J & Molich R (1990) Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. Proceedings of CHI 1990:249-256

name: Heuristic Inquiry (Moustakas)
origin: Clark Moustakas (1990); Douglass and Moustakas (1985); draws on Michael Polanyi's tacit knowing
summary: A phenomenological inquiry in which the researcher's own intense experience of a phenomenon is central, worked through phases from immersion to creative synthesis.
description: Heuristic inquiry is a variant of phenomenology that puts the researcher's personal experience in the foreground. The researcher must have had an intense personal experience of the phenomenon, and so must the coresearchers studied. Drawing on Polanyi's tacit knowing and indwelling, it differs from descriptive phenomenology in seeking connectedness rather than detachment, depictions of personal significance rather than definitive structures, a creative synthesis that admits intuition, and participants who remain visible as whole persons. Analysis moves through immersion, incubation, illumination, explication and creative synthesis. Outputs include individual depictions, a composite depiction, exemplary portraits and a creative synthesis, often narrative or artistic. Its credibility rests on the researcher's self-knowledge and on returning depictions to coresearchers for recognition.
steps: Confirm that the researcher has had a personal, intense experience of the phenomenon and frame a question that matters to them.
Recruit coresearchers who have also experienced it intensely and gather their accounts in depth.
Immersion: live with the question, saturating yourself in the experience and the data.
Incubation: withdraw from intense focus so tacit understanding can form.
Illumination and explication: let themes and qualities emerge, then examine them in detail, including your own awareness.
Write individual depictions, check them with each coresearcher, then build a composite depiction and exemplary portraits.
Express the whole as a creative synthesis, often narrative or poetic, keeping participants visible as persons.
outputs: Individual and composite depictions, exemplary portraits and a creative synthesis of the lived experience.
useWhen: Deep exploratory work on emotionally significant experiences (loss, illness, caregiving, burnout) where a researcher with lived experience can access what others cannot.
avoidWhen: Avoid when findings must be auditable, generalisable or delivered quickly, or when the researcher lacks lived experience. Use descriptive phenomenology or interpretative approaches instead.
whyLost: It is personal, slow and hard to audit, so it has stayed in counselling, education and humanistic psychology.
whereToUse: Grief and end-of-life services, mental health products, caregiver tools, and designer-researchers working on experiences they share with users.
example: A researcher who has cared for a parent with dementia studies six other carers' experience of night-time vigilance. The creative synthesis shapes the tone and timing of a carer-support app's overnight features.
reference: Moustakas, C. (1990). Heuristic Research: Design, Methodology, and Applications. Newbury Park, CA: Sage.

name: Hick's Law Analysis
origin: William Hick, 1952; Ray Hyman, 1953
summary: Models decision time as a logarithmic function of the number and probability of choices, to estimate how option sets affect selection speed.
description: The Hick-Hyman law states that choice reaction time increases with the information content of the choice: RT = a + b·log2(n + 1) for n equally likely options, or more generally with the entropy of the choice set when probabilities differ. It applies to decisions where users already know the options and must select one, not to visual search through unfamiliar lists, where time grows roughly linearly. Its rigorous use in UX means checking whether that precondition holds, estimating choice probabilities from usage data, and fitting parameters for the specific context. This avoids the common misapplication of citing Hick's law to justify removing options. Properly applied, it shows that ordering by frequency, grouping and reducing entropy can speed selection, and that splitting choices across many levels can cost more than it saves.
steps: Confirm the task is a choice among known options rather than search through unfamiliar items.
Estimate option probabilities from usage logs and compute the entropy of the choice set.
Run a timed selection task with 10-20 participants across set sizes or layouts.
Fit RT against log2(n + 1) or entropy and check the fit.
Use the model to compare flat, grouped and frequency-ordered designs, including the added cost of extra navigation levels.
Choose the structure minimising total predicted time, then validate with usability testing.
outputs: Choice entropy estimates, fitted reaction-time model, predicted decision times for alternative option structures.
useWhen: Menu design, quick actions, keyboard shortcuts, settings and options panels used repeatedly by experienced users.
avoidWhen: Novice users scanning unfamiliar lists, where search time dominates; use eye tracking or tree testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Simple, memorable, and defensible with stakeholders; though often over-applied.
whereToUse: Navigation design; option set design; cognitive load reduction.
example: A point-of-sale app had 24 equally weighted product buttons. Usage logs showed 6 items accounted for 70% of sales; entropy-based modelling supported a frequency-weighted layout that cut median selection time by 0.4 seconds.
sources: Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 4(1), 11-26.

name: Hidden Markov Models of User Behaviour
aka: Hidden Markov Models for Navigation Analysis
origin: Leonard Baum et al. (1966); Lawrence Rabiner (1989)
summary: Infers latent user states (exploring, task-focused, confused, recovering) from clickstream sequences and estimates transitions between them.
description: An HMM models observed sequences as emissions from hidden states with transition probabilities. Given clicks, page visits or actions, inference recovers the most likely state sequence (Viterbi) and transition matrix. The treatise poses a classic question: is a long session engagement or confusion? An HMM trained on labelled sessions can separate these as different hidden states with different observable signatures, then label new sessions. This turns ambiguous metrics such as session length into state-based measures (time in 'confused' state). Model selection uses information criteria and interpretability, and states should be validated against qualitative evidence such as recordings or think-aloud.
steps: Define the observation alphabet (event types, page categories, dwell bins).
Optionally label a sample of sessions with states via observation or recordings.
Fit HMMs with different numbers of states using Baum-Welch or supervised estimation.
Select the model by BIC, held-out likelihood and interpretability.
Decode sessions with Viterbi and compute time-in-state metrics.
Validate states qualitatively and track state metrics across releases.
outputs: State definitions, transition matrix, per-session state sequences, state-based metrics.
useWhen: Interpreting long or ambiguous sessions, detecting confusion at scale, onboarding state inference.
avoidWhen: Short sessions with few events, or when simple funnels answer the question.
whyLost: Requires ML skills rarely present in UX teams; analytics tools offer funnels instead.
whereToUse: Onboarding flows, search behaviour, e-learning, complex SaaS configuration, support portals.
example: An HMM on tax software logs finds a 'looping' state where users alternate between two forms; 12% of sessions spend over five minutes there, pinpointing a confusing deduction section.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rabiner LR (1989) A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. Proc IEEE 77(2):257-286
Baum LE & Petrie T (1966) Statistical inference for probabilistic functions of finite state Markov chains. Ann Math Stat 37
Rabiner, A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition (1989), Proceedings of the IEEE
Zucchini, MacDonald & Langrock, Hidden Markov Models for Time Series (2nd ed., 2016)
Predicting UX Behavior with Hidden Markov Models (carousel, n.d.)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Rabiner LR (1989) A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. Proceedings of the IEEE 77(2):257-286.

name: Hierarchical (second-order) versus bifactor CFA
origin: Holzinger and Swineford (bifactor model); Schmid and Leiman (1957)
summary: Tests whether a general factor plus specific factors explains a multidimensional scale, and whether a total score, subscale scores or both are defensible.
description: Many UX questionnaires report both a total and subscales without testing whether either is justified. In a second-order model, first-order factors (subscales) load on a general factor. In a bifactor model each item loads directly on a general factor and on one specific factor, with all factors orthogonal. The second-order model is nested within the bifactor model, so they can be compared with a chi-square difference test, and the Schmid-Leiman transformation converts one to the other. Omega-hierarchical estimates how much total-score variance the general factor explains, indicating whether a total score is meaningful; subscale omegas show whether specific factors add reliable variance beyond it. Bifactor models tend to fit well for purely statistical reasons, so the choice should be stated a priori and judged on residuals and omega values, not on fit alone.
steps: State a priori whether a general factor is expected and how the specific factors relate to it.
Fit the first-order correlated-factors CFA as a baseline.
Fit the second-order and bifactor models.
Compare nested models with chi-square difference tests and inspect residual correlations.
Compute omega-hierarchical for the total score and omega-hierarchical-subscale values for each specific factor.
Decide whether to report a total, subscales or both, and document the reasoning.
outputs: Model comparison results and omega estimates supporting a decision on total versus subscale scoring.
useWhen: Validating or adapting a multidimensional UX questionnaire, or deciding whether to report a total score alongside subscales (for example usability and learnability).
avoidWhen: Small samples (CFA generally needs a few hundred respondents) or unidimensional scales. Do not choose the bifactor model on fit alone.
whyLost: It is routine in psychometric scale development but UX questionnaire use rarely goes beyond Cronbach's alpha and a single CFA.
whereToUse: Development or translation of UX, trust, AI-acceptance and wellbeing scales; deciding scoring for SUS-like instruments with proposed subscales.
example: A team adapting a trust-in-AI scale with competence, integrity and predictability subscales fits second-order and bifactor models on 600 responses. Omega-hierarchical is 0.82 but subscale omegas are below 0.2, so the team reports a single trust score.
sources: A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (5th ed.). New York: Guilford Press, pp. 258-260.

name: Hierarchical Log-Linear Analysis
aka: Hierarchical log-linear analysis of multi-way contingency tables
origin: Adapted for UX from categorical data analysis as presented in Mazzocchi (2008), citing Knoke and Burke (1980)
summary: Model the cell counts of a three-or-more-way cross-tabulation as main effects plus interactions on a log scale, and prune interactions to find which categorical variables are genuinely associated.
description: Two-way chi-square tests cannot say whether an association between two survey variables holds across a third or arises from it. Log-linear analysis writes the log of each cell frequency in a multi-way table as a constant plus main effects and all interactions, with no dependent variable, mirroring the general linear model. The saturated model reproduces the table exactly, so the analyst seeks the most parsimonious model whose expected frequencies still match the observed ones. Hierarchical selection by backward elimination starts at the highest-order interaction, using k-way and partial-association chi-square tests, and keeps the lower-order terms of any retained interaction. The chosen model is refitted, checked with likelihood-ratio and Pearson goodness-of-fit tests (a high p-value means it reproduces the table), and interpreted through parameter estimates against reference categories, exponentiated as odds. It shows association structure, not dependence of one variable on others.
steps: Cross-tabulate three or more categorical variables, recoding sparse categories so few cells hold frequencies of 1 or less.
Run hierarchical model selection by backward elimination from the saturated model.
Read the k-way tests (can all effects of order k and above be dropped?) and partial-association tests for each effect.
At each step remove the term whose deletion changes the likelihood-ratio chi-square least without significant loss of fit, keeping lower-order terms of retained interactions.
Refit the chosen model in a general log-linear procedure, adding 0.5 to cells to avoid zeros, and check likelihood-ratio and Pearson goodness of fit.
Try removing further terms and compare fit, then interpret parameter estimates against reference categories as odds and rank effects by their Z ratios.
outputs: A parsimonious set of main effects and interactions with fit statistics and parameter estimates.
useWhen: Survey or log data with three or more categorical variables (segment, platform, country, outcome) where you need to know which associations survive once the others are accounted for.
avoidWhen: When one variable is clearly the outcome (use logistic or multinomial regression); with sparse tables; for two variables only (use Chi-Square and Fisher's Exact Tests or Cross-Tabulation of UX Metrics).
whyLost: Logistic regression and dashboards of cross-tabs displaced it; it appears in social science and marketing texts but not in UX analytics practice.
whereToUse: Multi-country surveys, churn reasons by plan and tenure, feature adoption by platform and segment, trust and consent research.
example: A consent survey cross-tabulates trust in data use by gender by country. The three-way term and the gender-by-trust term drop out, leaving trust-by-country and gender-by-country, so country rather than gender explains trust differences.
sources: Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Mazzocchi, M. (2008). Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research. London: SAGE, Section 9.2; Knoke, D. and Burke, P. J. (1980). Log-Linear Models. Beverly Hills: SAGE.

name: Hierarchical structure analysis
donor: Information architecture and cognitive psychology of menus
origin: Menu depth/breadth research by Miller (1981), Kiger (1984) and Larson and Czerwinski (1998); Simon's 'Architecture of Complexity', 1962
summary: Analyses the depth, breadth, balance and consistency of an interface hierarchy, checking it against evidence on navigation performance and against how users group content.
description: Hierarchies trade depth against breadth. Research from the 1980s and 1990s found broad, shallow menus (for example 8x8 rather than 2x2x2x2x2x2) generally faster and less error-prone, provided items are well grouped and labelled, because each extra level adds a decision and a chance to go astray. Hierarchical structure analysis measures depth to each leaf, breadth at each node, balance (variation of depth), and consistency of classification principle at each level, then compares against user mental models from card sorting or tree testing. Simon's insight that near-decomposable hierarchies are easier to understand provides the theoretical basis. Today the term survives but usually means drawing a sitemap rather than analysing it.
steps: Export the full hierarchy (sitemap, menu tree, settings tree) with every node and leaf.
Compute depth to each leaf, breadth per node, mean and maximum depth, and depth variance; flag leaves deeper than 4 levels and nodes with fewer than 3 or more than about 12 unclustered children.
Check each level for a single, consistent classification principle (by task, object, audience or time).
Run a tree test with 50+ participants on 8-10 key tasks to measure success and directness.
Correlate failures with depth, breadth and classification inconsistencies.
Propose a restructured hierarchy and re-test with a new tree test.
outputs: Depth and breadth metrics, a structure diagnostics report, tree test results correlated with structural features, and a revised hierarchy.
useWhen: When menus, settings or sites have grown organically; when users cannot find features; before migrations or redesigns of navigation.
avoidWhen: When users mainly search or follow links rather than browse; analyse search logs and IA graph centrality instead.
whyLost: Menu depth-breadth research faded from practice after the 1990s; IA kept the vocabulary but dropped quantitative structure analysis.
whereToUse: Enterprise settings, e-commerce category trees, government sites, intranets, and device menus.
example: A surgical robot's settings tree reaches 7 levels with one branch holding 31 items. Restructuring to a maximum depth of 3 with consistent task-based grouping raises tree test success from 58% to 84%.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 6 — Strange Loops, Recursive Failures & Navigation Traps
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Larson, K. & Czerwinski, M. (1998). Web page design: implications of memory, structure and scent for information retrieval. Proceedings of CHI '98.

name: Hierarchical Task Analysis
origin: John Annett and Keith Duncan, 1967
summary: Decomposes a goal into sub-goals, operations and plans, using a P x C stopping rule to locate the steps where interface support matters most.
description: Hierarchical Task Analysis (Annett and Duncan) represents work as a hierarchy of goals and sub-goals, down to operations, with a plan at each level specifying the order and conditions under which sub-goals are carried out. Its distinctive rigour lies in the stopping rule: decomposition continues only while the product of the probability of inadequate performance (P) and the cost of that failure (C) is unacceptable. This focuses analytical effort on steps that are both error-prone and consequential, rather than exhaustively documenting everything. Data comes from observation, interviews, documents and walkthroughs with experienced performers. HTA is the foundation for many human-factors techniques, including SHERLOCK-style error prediction, workload analysis and training design.
steps: Define the top-level goal: What does the user ultimately want to achieve? State as an active goal.
Decompose to sub-goals: Continue decomposing until you reach operations — individual actions that cannot be further decomposed.
Specify plans: For each goal with multiple sub-goals: what plan governs how they are ordered? Sequential (1,2,3), conditional (if X then 1, else 2), or cyclic (repeat until condition).
Apply stopping rule: Stop decomposing when the cost of inadequate performance exceeds the cost of further analysis.
Apply P × C criterion: For each sub-goal: P = probability of failure without support; C = cost of failure. High P × C = design priority.
outputs: A hierarchical task diagram and tabular HTA with plans, P x C ratings for sub-goals, and a list of high-priority steps requiring interface, training or automation support.
useWhen: Designing or redesigning complex, procedural or safety-relevant work, such as clinical workflows, financial operations, industrial control or enterprise configuration, and you need to know where support matters.
avoidWhen: Tasks are exploratory, creative or poorly structured, where hierarchical goals do not exist in advance; use contextual inquiry or Cognitive Task Analysis instead.
whyLost: UX replaced it with user flows and journey maps that show sequence but not plans, conditions or P x C prioritisation, so the name survives without its analytic engine.
whereToUse: Clinical systems, payments operations, aviation and automotive interfaces, enterprise admin tools, and automation decisions for AI agents taking over task steps.
example: Analysing payroll correction in an HR platform, a team builds an HTA of 34 operations. P x C ratings flag 'confirm tax period' as rare but costly when wrong, so the interface adds a forced confirmation only at that step.
sources: Stanton, N. A. (2006) Hierarchical task analysis: developments, applications and extensions, Applied Ergonomics
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Annett J & Duncan KD (1967) Task analysis and training design
Stanton NA (2006) Hierarchical task analysis: developments, applications and extensions. Applied Ergonomics
Kirwan B & Ainsworth LK (1992) A Guide to Task Analysis
A Guide to Task Analysis (Kirwan & Ainsworth)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 16 — Cognitive Task Modeling — GOMS, KLM & CPM-GOMS
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
SHERPA: A Systematic Human Error Reduction and Prediction Approach (Embrey, 1986)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Annett, J. & Duncan, K. D. (1967). Task analysis and training design. Occupational Psychology, 41, 211-221.

name: Hierarchical topic modelling
origin: hLDA (nested Chinese restaurant process), Blei, Griffiths and Jordan, 2004/2010; hierarchical reduction in BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022)
summary: Organising topics into a tree of broad themes and narrower sub-topics, so large text corpora can be explored at the right level of detail for each decision.
description: Flat topic models force a single granularity. Hierarchical approaches produce a tree: either generatively (hLDA) or, more commonly today, by agglomerating fine-grained BERTopic clusters using the similarity of their c-TF-IDF or embedding representations. Executives can see a handful of broad themes while product teams drill into specific sub-topics. Rigour comes from choosing a linkage method, validating that merges are semantically sensible by reading documents, keeping the tree shallow enough to interpret (typically 2-3 levels), and labelling each level with consistent conventions. The hierarchy is an analytic aid, analogous to arranging codes into categories in qualitative analysis.
steps: Fit a fine-grained topic model (e.g. BERTopic with a small min_cluster_size giving 50-200 topics).
Compute the topic hierarchy (BERTopic hierarchical_topics with a chosen linkage, e.g. Ward or average).
Visualise the dendrogram and choose 2-3 cut levels that give interpretable groupings.
Read representative documents at each merge to confirm semantic coherence, and override merges that are wrong.
Label parent and child topics consistently and record definitions.
Report prevalence at each level and map leaf topics to owning teams or journeys.
outputs: A labelled topic tree, dendrogram, prevalence by level and a mapping of sub-topics to owners.
useWhen: Very large or diverse corpora where stakeholders need different levels of granularity, such as company-wide feedback or support data.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small or homogeneous corpora where a flat model with 10-20 topics suffices.
whyLost: Hierarchical topic models were academic for years; embedding-based tools made them practical only recently.
whereToUse: Enterprise voice-of-customer programmes, support taxonomy design, app store review analysis and research repository navigation.
example: A SaaS company's 200,000 support tickets yield 140 fine topics, merged into 12 parent themes such as 'billing' and 'integrations'. Product teams drill into child topics like 'Salesforce sync duplicates'.
sources: Blei, D. M., Griffiths, T. L. & Jordan, M. I. (2010) The nested Chinese restaurant process and Bayesian nonparametric inference of topic hierarchies. JACM
Grootendorst, M. (2022) BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure. arXiv:2203.05794
The Inquiry Series, C11 — Topic Modelling at Scale — LDA, BERTopic & Semantic Clustering
reference: Blei, D. M., Griffiths, T. L. & Jordan, M. I. (2010) The nested Chinese restaurant process and Bayesian nonparametric inference of topic hierarchies. Journal of the ACM 57(2)

name: High-Level GOMS Model for Choosing Functionality
origin: David E. Kieras, University of Michigan (GOMS tutorials building on Card, Moran and Newell, 1983)
summary: Write interface-independent GOMS methods for users' top-level goals, choose the system functions that keep those methods simple, then elaborate to keystroke level to predict performance.
description: Kieras argued that functionality is usually chosen haphazardly before interface design, although no interface can make up for a missing or badly chosen function, and that task analysis such as HTA rarely connects to performance prediction. A high-level GOMS model bridges the two. Goals refer only to the task, not the interface; operators are mental (think of, decide) or invocations of system functions treated as unanalysed units (update the database, not click UPDATE); methods show the order of these steps, the information users need and how they detect and correct errors. The team then picks functions that make these methods short and simple. Because the high-level methods become the top of a full GOMS model, lower levels can later be added down to keystrokes to predict learning and execution time, giving a usability-oriented form of requirements analysis.
steps: List the users' top-level goals and write high-level methods for each using only task terms, mental operators and system functions treated as black boxes.
Record in each method what information the user needs and how errors are detected and corrected.
Compare alternative function sets and choose the one that gives the shortest, simplest high-level methods.
Elaborate lower-level methods down to keystroke level, introducing interface specifics.
Use the full model to identify problems and to predict learning time (method length) and execution time (operators executed).
Revise functions, methods and interface choices and re-run the predictions.
outputs: Interface-independent task methods, a justified set of system functions and a full GOMS model with learning and execution time predictions.
useWhen: Defining the feature set of a complex expert tool (engineering, clinical, financial) before interface design, where task procedures are well understood and efficiency matters.
avoidWhen: Exploratory or discretionary products whose tasks are not yet known (use contextual inquiry or field studies first); when only interface details are in question (use the Keystroke-Level Model or NGOMSL directly).
whyLost: GOMS became associated with keystroke timing of finished designs, and feature decisions moved to product management and prioritisation frameworks, so the use of GOMS above the interface level was largely forgotten.
whereToUse: Requirements work for professional software, design tools, operator consoles and enterprise workflows where function choice drives efficiency.
example: For a circuit-design tool, the team writes methods for verifying a circuit: think of the circuit, enter it, simulate, decide and modify. Comparing function sets shows that a combined simulate-and-highlight function removes two decide steps, so it is specified before any screen is drawn.
sources: GOMS Models: Simplified Cognitive Architectures (Kieras, n.d.)
reference: Kieras, D. E. GOMS models: Simplified cognitive architectures [Tutorial slides, session 2a]. University of Michigan, n.d.

name: Highlighter test
origin: Gale (2014), GDS user research blog, 'A simple technique for evaluating content'
summary: Participants highlight text that raises their confidence in one colour and text that lowers it in another; marks are aggregated into a heat map showing what to keep or rewrite.
description: A low-fidelity content test. Each participant receives a printed or digital copy of the content and two highlighters: green for words or passages that make them feel more confident, red (or yellow) for those that make them less confident or confused. After each session the researcher transfers marks onto a master copy in matching colours, so darker areas show consistent effects across participants; digital tools can tally automatically. Other reaction pairs work too, such as helpful versus unhelpful, and large samples can be split so each group marks one reaction. A variant asks participants to sort words, phrases and questions by trust or confidence. It is quick, makes the effect of wording visible to the team immediately, and pairs well with a short interview about the marks.
steps: Choose the content and the reactions to capture, such as more versus less confident, or helpful versus unhelpful.
Give each participant a copy with one colour per reaction, or split a large sample so each group marks one reaction.
Ask participants to read and highlight, then briefly explain their main marks.
Transfer each participant's highlights onto a master copy, or tally words and phrases by reaction and participant count in a spreadsheet.
Read the density of colours to find passages that consistently build or erode confidence.
Rewrite negatively marked passages and retest with the intended audience.
outputs: An aggregated colour-coded copy of the content and word- or phrase-level counts of reactions.
useWhen: Evaluating guidance, forms, emails, policies, onboarding or error messages where confidence and clarity of wording matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a test of comprehension or task success; it measures felt confidence. Use cloze or comprehension tests and usability testing for those. Collation is manual and scoring rules beyond counting are informal.
whyLost: It survives through government content design communities and survey tools that offer highlighting as a feature.
whereToUse: Public sector services, healthcare information, fintech terms and emails, insurance policies, onboarding copy and AI explanation text.
example: A bank tests two versions of an overdraft email with 350 recipients each. Readers mark 'Contact an associate' as unhelpful far more than 'Talk to someone', supporting a switch to plain-language standards across notifications.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Gale, P. (2014). A simple technique for evaluating content. GOV.UK User Research Blog, 2 September 2014.

name: Hilbert Transform Instantaneous Amplitude and Phase
origin: David Hilbert's transform (early twentieth century); analytic signal formalised by Dennis Gabor (1946); presented by van Drongelen (2018) for neuroscience
summary: Form the analytic signal of a band-limited recording to read its moment-by-moment amplitude envelope, phase and frequency, and compare phases between channels.
description: The Hilbert transform supplies the imaginary part of the analytic signal. Its magnitude is the instantaneous amplitude (envelope), its angle is the instantaneous phase, and the derivative of phase gives instantaneous frequency. Applied to a band-limited signal dominated by one rhythm, it shows how strongly and at what phase the rhythm is present from moment to moment, which is the basis of envelope analysis, phase synchrony and phase-amplitude coupling. Van Drongelen introduces it to judge which of two simultaneously recorded signals leads: with a small phase difference, the signal with the earlier phase leads. The result is only meaningful when the signal is narrow-band, and a phase lead is a heuristic for sequence, not proof of causation, because a common source or relay chains can produce the same pattern.
steps: Band-pass filter the signal so a single rhythm dominates, for example alpha (8-12 Hz) EEG or a respiration band.
Compute the analytic signal (for example MATLAB or SciPy hilbert, which returns the signal plus j times its Hilbert transform).
Take the magnitude as instantaneous amplitude (envelope).
Take atan2 of the imaginary and real parts as instantaneous phase between minus pi and pi.
Differentiate the unwrapped phase and divide by 2 pi times the sample interval for instantaneous frequency.
Compare phases of two channels to estimate lead and lag or phase synchrony, discarding segments with very low amplitude.
outputs: Envelope, phase and instantaneous frequency time series, and phase differences or synchrony indices between channels.
useWhen: Analysing physiological recordings in UX studies, such as EEG band power over time, heart-respiration coupling or synchrony between participants, where moment-to-moment amplitude or phase matters.
avoidWhen: Avoid on broadband signals without filtering, and avoid treating phase lead as causation; use Granger-style methods with caution. For time-frequency maps across many bands use a continuous wavelet transform.
whyLost: It is a core tool in neuroscience and signal processing, but UX biometrics rarely goes beyond averaged band power or summary statistics.
whereToUse: Neuro-UX and EEG studies, hyperscanning of collaborating users, physiological stress monitoring, game and VR arousal research.
example: In a study of two people co-editing a document, the team filters both participants' EEG to the alpha band and computes Hilbert phase. Phase synchrony rises during smooth turn-taking and drops during edit conflicts, supporting the design of conflict indicators.
reference: Gabor, D. (1946). Theory of communication. Journal of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, 93(26), 429-457; van Drongelen, W. (2018). Signal Processing for Neuroscientists (2nd ed.). London: Academic Press, pp. 273-288.

name: Historical Research with External and Internal Source Criticism
origin: Homer Hockett, 1955; Robert Travers, 1969; as taught in behavioural research methods texts
summary: Reconstruct past events from primary and secondary sources, first testing each source's authenticity (external criticism) and then the credibility of its content (internal criticism).
description: Because the past cannot be observed, historical research tests the truthfulness of others' reports. Primary sources are either consciously transmitted (testimony, oral histories, letters, diaries, minutes, records, photographs, recordings) or unconsciously transmitted relics; secondary sources are accounts by non-witnesses and serve as supplementary witnesses. External criticism establishes genuineness: higher criticism tests authorship and date through anachronism checks, comparison with other evidence and physical analysis; lower or textual criticism reconstructs an original text from copies. Internal criticism then judges reliability using Travers's ten questions on the observer's competence, relation to events, pressure to distort, intent, expertise, habits, bias, delay before recording, memory and agreement with independent witnesses. Positive criticism seeks the real meaning; negative criticism seeks reasons to disbelieve. Records are incomplete and biased, and findings cannot be checked by experiment.
steps: Identify and specify the historical question and any working hypotheses.
Review existing accounts and collect primary and secondary sources (documents, tickets, specs, emails, recordings, oral histories).
Apply external criticism: check authorship and date, look for anachronisms, compare with other evidence and examine version histories or metadata.
Apply internal criticism using Travers's ten questions on each author's competence, position, pressures, intent, bias, delay, memory and corroboration.
Apply both positive criticism (establish the intended meaning) and negative criticism (seek reasons to disbelieve).
Drop sources that are inauthentic or irrelevant and weight the rest by credibility.
Write the account, citing the source and its assessed credibility for each key claim.
outputs: An evaluated body of evidence with credibility judgements and a sourced historical account.
useWhen: Reconstructing how a product, design system, policy or organisational decision came about, or reviewing an incident from records and recollections.
avoidWhen: Questions answerable by observing current behaviour; use field research. Where sources are sparse, state the limits rather than overreaching.
whyLost: UX treats documents as background desk research and rarely applies formal source criticism to the organisation's own records.
whereToUse: Design system archaeology, product decision histories, incident post-mortems, legacy enterprise replatforming and research repository audits.
example: Before redesigning a bank's loan approval flow, a researcher reconstructs why a manual review step exists. A compliance memo cited by staff turns out to post-date the step (an anachronism), while minutes from an earlier fraud incident corroborate the real origin.
sources: Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
reference: Mangal, S. K., & Mangal, S. (2013). Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences. New Delhi: PHI Learning.

name: Honeycomb × SNR × PBUH Scorecard
donor: UX evaluation; information theory; behavioural science
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Studio Aghora (uxguy.in)
summary: A weighted composite scorecard combining Morville's UX Honeycomb, SNR interface scores and PBUH adoption stages into one instrument for holistic product audits.
description: The Honeycomb × SNR × PBUH Scorecard fuses three lenses into a single audit instrument. Morville's UX Honeycomb contributes seven quality facets: useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible and valuable. The SNR Interface Evaluation Framework contributes a measure of information clarity on key screens. The PBUH model contributes a view of where users stall between perception, behaviour, utility and habit. Each lens is scored with explicit rubrics, then combined using weights agreed with stakeholders in advance, giving a product health score with traceable components. Its rigour comes from rubric definitions, multiple raters, fixed weights set before scoring and the ability to decompose the composite back into its parts, which prevents the single number from hiding where problems are.
steps: Agree the product scope, key tasks and weighting of the three lenses with stakeholders before scoring.
Score each Honeycomb facet on a defined 1 to 5 rubric using expert review and available research evidence.
Compute SNR scores for the screens supporting key tasks.
Rate each PBUH stage using analytics and research evidence.
Have at least two raters score independently and reconcile differences above one rubric point.
Combine scores using the agreed weights and present both the composite and the component breakdown.
Repeat on the same rubric for competitors or future releases to benchmark.
outputs: A composite product health score, component scores per lens, a heat map of weak facets and prioritised recommendations.
useWhen: For UX audits, product health reviews and competitive benchmarking where a multi-dimensional but comparable assessment is needed.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need causal evidence or user-reported attitudes; use experiments or standardised questionnaires such as SUS instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Vivek synthesis framework; enables multi-dimensional UX audit in one instrument.
whereToUse: UX audits; competitive benchmarking; product health reviews.
example: An e-commerce marketplace audits itself and two competitors. The scorecard shows strong desirability but low findability and poor SNR on search results, and the PBUH lens shows weak habit formation, focusing the next roadmap on search.
reference: Gopinath, V. Honeycomb × SNR × PBUH Scorecard (uxguy.in); Morville, P. (2004). User Experience Design (UX Honeycomb).

name: Horizon Scanning
origin: Futures studies and government foresight practice (for example OECD); sentiment variant by Pamela Pavliscak (2018)
summary: Systematically searches broad and peripheral sources for weak signals of change, organises them by lenses such as STEEP, and assesses what each could mean.
description: Horizon scanning is the foresight practice of collecting early signals of change, usually ten or more years out, from the periphery as well as the mainstream. Signals are gathered by scanners who sift reports and spotters who observe in person, from sources such as news, conferences, patents, crowdfunding, policy papers, datasets, fiction and everyday 'thoughtless acts'. They are organised under lenses such as STEEP (social, technological, economic, environmental, political) with tags, quotes and cross-references, and then judged for maturity and potential impact. Diverse teams and sources reduce blind spots. Pavliscak's variant adds an emotional layer: after an automated sentiment first pass, signals are rated with the Geneva emotion wheel to find those provoking the strongest feelings, which then feed future storytelling and props.
steps: Set the topic, scope and time horizon (often ten years or more) and the decisions the scan should inform.
Assemble a diverse team and a deliberately broad source list including peripheral sources such as patents, crowdfunding, fiction and policy papers.
Collect signals continuously, recording each with source, date, tags and a short description under STEEP lenses.
Cluster signals into themes and judge each for maturity and potential impact.
Optionally rate emotional resonance: run sentiment analysis as a first pass, then rate signals on an emotion wheel and graph which provoke the strongest feelings.
Discuss implications and possible responses, write short implication briefs, and carry key signals into scenario or speculative design work.
outputs: A tagged signal library or database, theme clusters, impact and emotion ratings, and implication briefs.
useWhen: Early strategy and discovery work on long-horizon products, or when a team needs to notice emerging behaviours and technologies before competitors.
avoidWhen: When you need evidence about current users: signals are noisy and impact is speculative, and they are easy to collect but hard to interpret. Automated sentiment is only a first pass. Use field research for present needs and Scenario-Based Design or Three Horizons Framework to turn signals into futures.
whyLost: It is routine in government and corporate foresight units but rarely sits inside UX teams, which focus on near-term releases.
whereToUse: Mobility, health, fintech and AI product strategy; innovation labs; long-range roadmapping.
example: A health-app team logs signals on brain-hacking supplements, ketogenic diet apps and home testing kits, rates their emotional charge, and picks the most polarising to prototype provocations for future-of-self-care workshops.
reference: Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Rockport Publishers, Method 62 (Horizon Scanning, by Stuart Candy).

name: Hosmer-Lemeshow Goodness-of-Fit Test
origin: Hosmer and Lemeshow (1980); Lemeshow and Hosmer (1982); companion tests by Stukel (1988) and Osius and Rojek (1992)
summary: A calibration test for binary regression that groups cases into deciles of predicted risk and compares observed with expected event counts in each group.
description: With continuous covariates almost every case has its own covariate pattern, so the Pearson and deviance statistics cannot be referred to chi-square. Hosmer and Lemeshow restore large expected counts by sorting cases on fitted probability and cutting them into about ten deciles of risk. Observed and expected events and non-events in each group form a g x 2 table whose Pearson statistic C is referred to chi-square on g-2 degrees of freedom (g in an external validation sample). The table itself shows where the model over- or under-predicts. The authors recommend pairing C with the Osius-Rojek normal approximation and Stukel's two-df test of the logistic tails, and stress that calibration and discrimination (ROC area) are separate properties to be reported together. Power is low below about 400 cases, and software tie-handling can change C.
steps: Fit the binary model and save each case's fitted probability.
Sort cases by fitted probability and split them into g = 10 groups at the percentiles (deciles of risk) rather than at fixed cut-points.
In each group sum observed events and fitted probabilities (expected events), and do the same for non-events.
Compute the Pearson chi-square C over the g x 2 table and refer it to chi-square on g-2 df, or on g df when testing in an external sample.
Inspect observed versus expected counts per decile, merging adjacent groups where expected counts are very small; treat fewer than 6 groups as uninformative.
Supplement C with the Osius-Rojek statistic and Stukel's score test, then examine case-level diagnostics.
outputs: The C statistic and p-value, a 10 x 2 table of observed and expected counts by risk decile, and companion fit tests.
useWhen: Checking that a churn, conversion or risk model's predicted probabilities can be read at face value, for example before using them to size an intervention or set an alert threshold.
avoidWhen: Choosing among several models that all fit (use likelihood or information criteria), samples below about 400 where no overall fit test has power, or when the question is ranking rather than calibration (use ROC analysis, or Brier Score and Calibration Analysis for a fuller picture).
whyLost: Product data science judges classifiers mainly by discrimination metrics and calibration plots, so this formal test from clinical epidemiology rarely appears in UX analytics.
whereToUse: Propensity and churn models used to target interventions; risk scores in health and fintech products; any model whose probabilities are shown to users or stakeholders.
example: A health app predicts which users will lapse within 30 days. The model's ROC area is good, but the deciles-of-risk table shows it predicts 40 percent lapse in the top decile where 62 percent lapse, so the outreach budget based on predicted counts is revised.
reference: Hosmer, D. W., & Lemeshow, S. (1980). Goodness of fit tests for the multiple logistic regression model. Communications in Statistics: Theory and Methods, 9(10), 1043-1069; and Hosmer, D. W., & Lemeshow, S. (2000). Applied Logistic Regression (2nd ed.), pp. 143-156, 186-188.

name: Hot sauce aggression paradigm
origin: Lieberman, Solomon, Greenberg and McGregor (1999)
summary: After exposure to content, participants portion hot sauce for a stranger said to dislike spicy food; the amount allocated serves as a behavioural measure of aggression.
description: Self-reported hostility is easily faked, so social psychologists developed small, ethical behavioural harm measures. In the hot sauce paradigm, participants are randomly assigned to content conditions (for example violent or non-violent song lyrics, games or media), then, under a cover story, prepare a sample of hot sauce for another participant who supposedly dislikes spicy food. The weight allocated is the aggression measure. The design yields a continuous behavioural outcome from a randomised manipulation, but it requires deception and full debriefing, and small symbolic harm may not generalise to real behaviour. Fans and non-fans of the content can respond differently, and correlational longitudinal studies sometimes disagree with lab findings.
steps: Randomly assign participants to content conditions (for example aggressive versus neutral content).
Expose them to the content under a plausible cover story.
Introduce a cover task in which they prepare hot sauce for another, fictitious participant who is said to dislike spicy food.
Weigh the sauce allocated and compare grams between conditions, accounting for moderators such as prior content preference.
Debrief fully about the deception and confirm no one was harmed.
outputs: Grams of sauce allocated by condition as a behavioural aggression index.
useWhen: Testing whether exposure to particular content or interaction design (hostile comment threads, aggressive game mechanics) causally changes how people treat others, in a lab with ethics approval.
avoidWhen: Product research without ethics oversight, or where symbolic harm is unlikely to reflect real behaviour; use observational toxicity metrics or validated self-report instead.
whyLost: It belongs to media-violence research in social psychology; UX rarely runs deception-based lab paradigms, and debate over external validity limits its appeal.
whereToUse: Trust and safety research on games, social platforms and comment systems, and studies of how design affects interpersonal hostility.
example: A games researcher tests whether a taunting post-match screen increases hostility. Players exposed to it allocate more hot sauce to a supposed next opponent than those who see a neutral screen, informing a redesign of the victory animation.
sources: The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Lieberman, J. D., Solomon, S., Greenberg, J. and McGregor, H. A. (1999). A hot new way to measure aggression: hot sauce allocation. Aggressive Behavior, 25(5), 331-348.

name: How Might We Questions
origin: Min Basadur at Procter and Gamble, 1970s; popularised by IDEO
summary: Turn a brief, problem statement or research insight into agreed 'How might we...' questions scoped neither too narrow nor too broad, then brainstorm and prioritise against them.
description: How Might We questions convert insights into openings for ideation. Each word does work: 'how' assumes solutions exist, 'might' permits failure and 'we' stresses collaboration. The team selects an insight or problem, drafts several HMW questions, and iterates the wording until it agrees one is neither so narrow that it embeds a solution nor so broad that it gives no grip. The agreed question frames a brainstorm, and the resulting ideas are prioritised. Good HMWs reframe the problem: 'How might we make waiting at the clinic feel useful?' opens more options than 'add a TV to the waiting room'.
steps: Select an insight, problem statement or brief from research.
Draft several HMW questions individually, varying scope and angle.
Compare them as a group and refine the wording to one agreed question, removing embedded solutions.
Check scope: if it suggests a single answer it is too narrow; if anything could answer it, it is too broad.
Brainstorm responses against the agreed question.
Prioritise the ideas, for example by dot voting or an effort and impact grid.
outputs: Agreed HMW questions and sets of ideas generated against them.
useWhen: Moving from synthesised research insights to ideation, or reframing a solution-led brief into an open problem.
avoidWhen: HMWs are only as good as the insight behind them; without research they reframe assumptions. Badly scoped questions stall ideation. If the problem itself is unclear, do Interviews or Jobs-to-be-Done Research first.
whyLost: Survived as a staple of design thinking because it is simple, teachable and links research to ideation.
whereToUse: Design sprints, service design, healthcare and public-sector workshops, product discovery.
example: After interviews show patients feel idle in waiting rooms, a clinic team rejects 'add a TV' and agrees 'How might we make waiting at the clinic feel useful?', generating ideas such as pre-visit symptom check-ins.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019) Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Beverly, MA: Rockport Publishers, method 63.

name: Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS)
origin: Shappell and Wiegmann (2000), from Reason's (1990) Swiss cheese model; external-factors level added by Reinach and Viale (2006)
summary: Code the human contributions to incidents at four nested levels, from unsafe acts up to organisational influences, then aggregate codes across incidents to find systemic patterns.
description: HFACS operationalises Reason's Swiss cheese model as a coding scheme. Each incident is coded at four levels: unsafe acts (errors and violations); preconditions for unsafe acts (substandard conditions and practices of operators); unsafe supervision (inadequate supervision, planned inappropriate operations, failure to correct known problems, supervisory violations); and organisational influences (resource management, organisational climate, operational process). A later variant adds external factors such as economic, policy and regulatory pressures. Because every incident is coded with the same categories, frequencies can be compared across many incidents, shifting attention from individual blame to the latent conditions that recur. It has been adapted to rail, mining, maritime and process industries, and categories normally need tailoring to the domain, with coder agreement checked.
steps: Gather the incident record: reports, interviews, logs and timelines.
Identify each unsafe act and classify it as an error (skill, decision or perceptual) or a violation.
For each unsafe act, identify the preconditions (operator state, environment, team practices) that enabled it.
Trace supervisory factors that allowed those preconditions to persist.
Trace organisational influences (resources, climate, processes) and, in the extended form, external factors.
Have two coders code independently on a sample and resolve disagreements to stabilise the categories.
Aggregate codes across incidents and target interventions at the most frequent supervisory and organisational causes.
outputs: A coded causal chain per incident across levels and frequency profiles of causal categories across incidents.
useWhen: When an organisation has a body of incident or post-mortem reports and wants to see systemic patterns behind user or operator errors, such as in operations, support or clinical settings.
avoidWhen: Avoid for a single incident needing deep causal reconstruction; use Root Cause Analysis and the 5 Whys or STAMP / STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis). Avoid applying aviation categories unmodified to software or service contexts.
whyLost: Embedded in aviation and safety regulation; UX rarely codes incident corpora, and blameless post-mortems in software use informal narrative instead.
whereToUse: Site reliability and incident post-mortems, clinical software adverse-event reports, fintech operations errors, content moderation mistakes.
example: A payments company codes 60 post-mortems of operator errors in its admin console. Few trace to individual slips alone; most share an organisational influence (no staging environment for refunds) and a precondition (alert fatigue), which redirect investment from training to tooling.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Shappell, S. A. and Wiegmann, D. A. (2000). The Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS). DOT/FAA/AM-00/7. Washington, DC: Federal Aviation Administration.

name: Human Factors and Ergonomics Audit Programme Design
origin: Colin Drury (1990, 1992, 2009) and colleagues, modelled on financial auditing; Drury and Dempsey in Salvendy and Karwowski (2021)
summary: Design an organisation-wide audit that samples task-operator-machine-environment units, measures them with a validated checklist against standards, and shows where human factors effort is most needed.
description: Drury and Dempsey treat inspection, checking and auditing as related functions and model the ergonomics audit on the accountant's audit. An audit evaluates the human factors function across divisions, plants or product lines, retrospectively or prospectively. The design questions are how to sample (unit, frame, technique; the natural unit is a task-operator-machine-environment combination), what to sample (from biomechanics to organisational factors), how to evaluate (standards, good practice, principles) and how to communicate. Breadth, depth and application time trade off, so several instruments are combined. An audit system is a methodology, not just a checklist: instruments must show validity, reliability, sensitivity and usability before use. Element-level scores predict outcomes better than overall scores, and most checklists in use are home-made and unvalidated. Reference instruments include the IEA checklist and the PAQ.
steps: Decide the audit's purpose: evaluating the human factors programme, setting priorities or anticipating needs.
Define the sampling unit (task-operator-machine-environment), the sampling frame and the sampling technique across sites, teams or product lines.
Choose or build instruments, combining broad and deep ones, with each item tied to a standard or principle.
Test the instruments for validity, reliability, sensitivity and usability before roll-out.
Collect data, analyse by element as well as overall, and report where resources should go.
Repeat at intervals to track the function over time.
outputs: Element-level quality scores by unit and site, a prioritised list of intervention areas and an audit report.
useWhen: Running a repeatable, sampled quality audit across many products, teams or sites, such as a UX quality or design-system compliance programme, rather than a one-off review.
avoidWhen: Overall audit scores rarely predict incidents and home-made checklists usually lack reliability evidence; for a single product use Heuristic Evaluation or Guidelines Review and Consistency Inspection.
whyLost: The audit literature lives in industrial and aviation ergonomics; UX 'audits' are usually one-off expert reviews with no sampling design or instrument validation.
whereToUse: Portfolio-wide UX or accessibility quality programmes, design-system adoption audits, service quality reviews across branches or regions.
example: A bank audits 60 sampled customer journeys across five product lines with a 40-item checklist, first checking inter-rater agreement on ten journeys. Element-level results show error-message items failing in lending only, so remediation is targeted there.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Drury, C. G. and Dempsey, P. G. (2021). Human factors and ergonomics audits. In Salvendy, G. and Karwowski, W. (Eds.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.). Wiley, ch. 33, pp. 853-879.

name: Human Factors Forensic Investigation
origin: Presented by David Meister, 2004, as a distinct application of human factors methods in litigation
summary: Determines, for a specific injury or incident, whether the conditions a person faced exceeded normal human capability, by recreating the situation and comparing measurements with human factors data and standards.
description: Forensic human factors applies a basket of methods (observation, interview, reference data, problem solving and sometimes small experiments) to a legal question of fault: were the environmental and technological conditions within the injured person's threshold capabilities? Meister treats it as the sharpest real-world test of whether human factors data and methods hold up outside research, because the expert must make claims about a specific person in a specific situation rather than average performance. In his example of a fall on restaurant stairs, the investigator interviews the plaintiff and patrons, measures lighting levels, stair angle and carpet friction, compares them with standards, and tests whether people with normal vision can descend safely under the lighting conditions. The method's outputs must withstand cross-examination, so documentation of data, methods and assumptions is part of the procedure. In digital products, similar questions arise in disputes over dark patterns, consent flows and medical device use errors.
steps: Analyse the questions posed by the legal or incident situation to define the specific human factors questions.
Recreate the performance situation, symbolically or physically, including the interface, environment and task as they were at the time.
Determine the human factors data needed (for example visibility and lighting standards, reading time, response time, interface guidelines).
Select methods to gather empirical data: measurement, observation, interviews, document review or a small experiment.
Collect and analyse the data and judge whether the conditions exceeded normal human capability or departed from accepted standards.
Document data, methods, assumptions and conclusions; brief counsel and testify if required.
outputs: A documented expert opinion on whether design or environmental conditions exceeded human capability and contributed to the incident.
useWhen: Litigation, regulatory investigations or serious incident reviews where the question is whether a product, interface or environment set people up to fail.
avoidWhen: The aim is design improvement rather than fault-finding (use incident analysis such as the Swiss cheese model or a blameless post-mortem); no reliable human factors data exist for the specific population or task. Average data may not describe an individual's performance.
whyLost: It belongs to a small community of expert witnesses and is rarely taught in UX, although regulation of dark patterns and digital consent is bringing similar questions to digital products.
whereToUse: Medical device use-error claims, dark-pattern and consent-flow disputes, accessibility litigation, vehicle and in-car interface incidents, workplace accidents involving software.
example: In a dispute over an unwanted subscription renewal, an expert recreates the cancellation flow as it was, measures reading load, contrast and number of steps, and runs a small test in which 40 people attempt to cancel. Only 35% succeed within five minutes, evidence that the flow exceeded what ordinary users could reasonably do.
sources: Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
reference: Meister, D. (2004). Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Human Performance Data Store Compilation from Published Research
aka: Human error-rate database from the literature
Archival HF data combination for prediction
origin: Sidney Munger, Robert Smith and Don Payne, American Institutes for Research, 1962; described further by David Meister, 1999 and 2004
summary: Extracts performance data from many published studies, classifies them with task and equipment taxonomies, and converts them to error probabilities and times for predicting performance in new designs.
description: Meister treats the published human factors literature as the discipline's formal knowledge, yet notes that it is rarely combined into anything predictive. The American Institutes for Research Data Store did exactly that: the team screened over 2,000 journal articles, accepted 163 that met strict criteria, and reformatted their data into probabilities and times for reading displays and operating controls, indexed by a taxonomy of control and display types. The common metric is human error probability (operations with one or more errors divided by total operations).
