Combined values feed combinatorial models such as THERP to predict function- or mission-level performance. Meister links this to use validation: research is validated when its assembled data predict real performance. Unlike meta-analysis, which estimates an average effect for one question, the Data Store builds a reusable, taxonomy-indexed reference table for prediction.
steps: Develop taxonomies of human function, equipment function and human-equipment interaction (for example starting from Fleishman and Quaintance's task taxonomy).
Define a review window (for example ten years) and search all research reports in it.

Apply acceptance criteria: adequate description of the measurement situation, no confounds, current technology, similarity to the target operational situation, and data convertible to a common metric.
Extract and classify performance data with the taxonomies, converting to human error probability and performance times.
Combine values in a combinatorial model (for example THERP) to predict performance of new designs.
Keep updating the store as studies appear, and check its predictions against measured system performance.
outputs: Tables of error probabilities and performance times by task and interface category, usable as inputs to predictive models and design guidelines.
useWhen: You need quantitative predictions of error or time for common interaction elements across many future designs, and a body of comparable studies exists, for example in safety-critical control interfaces.
avoidWhen: Studies are too heterogeneous or poorly reported (only 163 of 2,000+ were usable); you need an answer for a single question (use meta-analysis); the technology changes faster than the store can be updated. Lab experiments provoke errors, so rates may need correcting before prediction.
whyLost: It needed a sustained, funded effort; the store dated with its 1960s controls and displays, and few later HF or UX groups resourced its maintenance.
whereToUse: Organisational design-system research repositories that pool task times and error rates; safety-critical domains (medical devices, aviation, energy) needing error-rate inputs for risk models.
example: A medical device maker builds a store from 15 years of internal and published infusion-pump studies, indexed by input method and display type. The pooled probability of a keypad decimal error feeds a THERP-style model that compares a redesigned dose-entry screen with the current one before any summative test.
sources: Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
reference: Munger, S. J., Smith, R. W., & Payne, D. (1962). An Index of Electronic Equipment Operability: Data Store (Rep. No. AIR-C43-1/62-RP[1]). Pittsburgh, PA: American Institutes for Research.

name: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints
donor: Human-computer interaction; machine learning; qualitative methods
origin: Interactive machine learning (Fails and Olsen, 2003); human oversight principles in AI governance (e.g. EU AI Act, 2024)
summary: Scheduling deliberate points where researchers review, correct and approve AI outputs, so interpretive decisions stay with humans and errors are caught early.
description: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints place researcher judgement where it matters most: approving the codebook, reviewing code merges, validating second-order categories and signing off synthesis claims, plus reviewing flagged low-confidence items. They are distinct from quality gates: gates are automated thresholds, checkpoints are human decisions. Rigour comes from specifying what is reviewed, by whom, how much (e.g. 100% of theme statements, a sample of codes), recording decisions and corrections, and feeding corrections back into prompts or codebooks. Guarding against automation bias, where reviewers rubber-stamp plausible AI output, requires reviewers to examine evidence, not just summaries, and periodic blind checks.
steps: Identify decisions that must remain human: research questions, codebook approval, abstraction to themes, claims in reports.
Define each checkpoint's scope, reviewer, sample size and acceptance criteria.
Present evidence (quotes in context) alongside AI suggestions, not summaries alone.
Record every accept, edit or reject decision with a reason.
Feed corrections back into codebooks or prompts and re-run affected items.
Run periodic blind checks where reviewers code items without seeing AI suggestions, to monitor automation bias.
outputs: Checkpoint plan, decision logs, corrected outputs and measures of AI-human disagreement over time.
useWhen: Any AI-assisted research where findings will inform decisions, and particularly in sensitive or regulated domains.
avoidWhen: Do not use checkpoints as a fig leaf for large-scale unread automation; if reviewers cannot meaningfully examine evidence, reduce scale or automation.
whyLost: Popular AI analysis tools emphasise speed and automation, so deliberate human checkpoints are rarely designed.
whereToUse: AI-assisted research operations, health and finance research and policy-relevant UX studies.
example: In a 300-interview programme, researchers review every proposed theme with linked quotes. They reject 4 of 22 AI-proposed themes as artefacts of interview guide wording, and edits are fed into the next run.
sources: Fails, J. A. & Olsen, D. R. (2003) Interactive machine learning. IUI
Amershi, S. et al. (2014) Power to the people: The role of humans in interactive machine learning. AI Magazine
The Inquiry Series, C13 — The Full Agentic Research Pipeline — Whisper → spaCy → AI Coder → Synthesis
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Amershi, S., Cakmak, M., Knox, W. B. & Kulesza, T. (2014) Power to the people: The role of humans in interactive machine learning. AI Magazine 35(4)

name: Hyperscanning
origin: Montague et al. (2002) fMRI hyperscanning; Hari and Kujala (2009) two-person neuroscience; Cui, Bryant and Reiss (2012) fNIRS hyperscanning
summary: Record brain activity from two or more people simultaneously while they interact, and analyse their coupling as a unit.
description: Hyperscanning links recordings from interacting people so their brain activity can be analysed together. The first studies linked two fMRI scanners so a pair could play an interactive game while both were scanned; analysis looked at each brain's response before and after the partner's actions and at inter-brain correlation. EEG and especially fNIRS, which tolerates movement better, allow face-to-face interaction outside the scanner. Measures of inter-brain synchrony are then related to behavioural coordination such as cooperation, turn-taking or joint attention. The hurdles are motion (doubled with two participants), calibration and synchronisation between devices, and analysis methods for time-varying coupling. For UX, hyperscanning offers a way to study collaboration and co-presence as a property of the pair, for example in co-located gaming, shared screens or remote collaboration tools.
steps: Choose a modality that allows the interaction: fNIRS or EEG for face-to-face tasks, fMRI for screen-mediated games.
Design an interactive task (cooperation, competition, joint attention or conversation) with clear event markers.
Synchronise recordings and behaviour logs across both participants to a common clock.
Record pairs under the conditions of interest, such as co-located versus remote collaboration.
Analyse each brain's response to the partner's actions and between-brain coupling over time.
Relate coupling to behavioural coordination and outcomes, with specialist support for analysis.
outputs: Inter-brain synchrony measures linked to interaction events and conditions.
useWhen: Your research question concerns the quality of interaction between people, such as collaboration, co-play or teaching, and you have neuroimaging partners.
avoidWhen: Behavioural coordination measures, conversation analysis or interviews would answer the question; hyperscanning is technically demanding and costly.
whyLost: It is a frontier social neuroscience technique, too demanding and costly to cross into product research.
whereToUse: Remote collaboration and video-conferencing tools, multiplayer games, education technology and social VR.
example: A video-conferencing research group records fNIRS from pairs solving a puzzle in person and over video. Inter-brain synchrony drops with a half-second audio lag, supporting latency targets for the product.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Montague, P. R., et al. (2002). Hyperscanning: Simultaneous fMRI during linked social interactions. NeuroImage, 16(4), 1159-1164.

name: HyPersona semi-automated clustering algorithm selection
aka: Semi-automated clustering algorithm selection for personas
origin: Ditton, Swinbourne and Myers, 2022
summary: Run every combination of clustering algorithms and parameters, screen them on internal metrics and feature significance, then have an expert pick the set that yields distinct, theory-consistent personas.
description: HyPersona systematises the choice of clustering algorithm for quantitative personas. Clean numeric data, a dictionary of algorithms and parameter values, and optional domain features are input. Every combination is run and scored on silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin and a new Average Feature Significance metric (the share of features differing significantly at p < .05 across clusters and cluster pairs), plus cluster sizes. Combinations failing lenient preset thresholds are dropped with reasons recorded. For survivors, centroids are plotted as z-profiles and early-stage personas are written automatically. A domain expert merges functionally identical solutions, reviews the rest in metric order with AFS as the main guide, and judges fit to a behavioural theory and distinctness. In the published case, 12 combinations of hierarchical clustering, k-means and NMF on 519 residents yielded three personas judged against the Protective Action Decision Model.
steps: Prepare data: map ordinal answers to numbers, one-hot encode nominal ones, and impute missing values.
Define key and aggregate features from domain theory, and fix the number of clusters from theory.
Pilot to set lenient thresholds, for example silhouette below 0, Calinski-Harabasz below 10, Davies-Bouldin above 5, AFS below half the key features, or any cluster under 5 per cent.
Expand the algorithm-parameter dictionary into all combinations and run each, logging metrics and cluster sizes.
Drop combinations failing thresholds, recording why.
Plot centroid z-profiles and generate early-stage personas for survivors; merge functionally identical solutions.
Have a domain expert review survivors in metric order against theory and distinctness, then build full personas from the chosen set.
outputs: A metrics log, centroid profile graphs, early-stage persona texts, the selected algorithm, and final personas.
useWhen: You build personas from survey or behavioural data and want a transparent, reproducible choice of clustering algorithm rather than defaulting to k-means.
avoidWhen: There is no domain theory to judge solutions, or the number of segments is unknown; internal metrics favour convex clusters and thresholds are data-specific. For small qualitative samples use qualitative persona methods.
whyLost: It is a recent academic framework with one published case; practitioners rarely compare clustering algorithms systematically.
whereToUse: Survey-based segmentation, public-sector and health behaviour personas, disaster preparedness communications, any quantitative persona project.
example: A utilities company surveys 800 customers on energy behaviour and runs 20 algorithm-parameter combinations. Half are screened out as degenerate; an analyst picks a k-means solution whose four personas map cleanly onto a behaviour change model.
sources: Selecting a Clustering Algorithm (HyPersona) (Ditton et al., 2022)
reference: Ditton, E., Swinbourne, A., & Myers, T. (2022). Selecting a clustering algorithm: A semi-automated hyperparameter tuning framework for effective persona development. Array, 14, 100186. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.array.2022.100186

name: Hysteresis Testing with Ascending and Descending Sweeps
origin: Used in the van der Maas lab for proportional reasoning (Jansen and van der Maas 2001), the speed-accuracy trade-off (Dutilh et al. 2011) and apparent motion perception (Ploeger, van der Maas and Hartelman 2002), where the method of modified limits was applied.
summary: An experimental design that slowly increases and then decreases a control variable and checks whether the switch between two behaviours happens at different points on the way up and the way down.
description: Hysteresis means a system's state depends on its history: when a control variable is raised, the switch to a new state happens late, and when it is lowered again the switch back happens even later. It is one of the strongest signs of two co-existing stable states. The book describes demonstrating it by gradually varying a stimulus dimension (for example the aspect ratio of a motion display) in both directions and recording where percepts switch. Because a lagging switch could simply reflect slow responding, the method of modified limits is used: participants respond only after a whole trial, and trials of different lengths reveal at which parameter value the switch was perceived. A related test, inaccessibility, asks participants to hold an intermediate state (for example 75 percent accuracy) and checks whether they instead alternate between the two modes. In UX, hysteresis explains why restoring a feature, a price or a performance level may not win back users lost when it degraded, and why defaults that crossed a threshold stay sticky. Testing it directly gives evidence for designing asymmetric interventions.
steps: Choose a manipulable control variable that you think pushes behaviour between two states (for example latency, price, notification frequency, cognitive load).
Define an objective record of which state the participant is in at each level.
Present the variable in a slow ascending series and a slow descending series, counterbalancing order across participants.
Guard against response lag, for example by asking for a judgement only at the end of trials of varying length (method of modified limits).
Estimate the switch point in each direction and test whether the two differ; optionally test inaccessibility by asking participants to maintain an intermediate state.
Report the width of the hysteresis loop and its implications for recovery strategies.
outputs: Switch points for the upward and downward direction, the size of the hysteresis gap, and evidence on whether an intermediate state is stable.
useWhen: You need to know whether undoing a change will reverse its effect, or whether a behaviour switch reflects two stable states.
avoidWhen: You cannot vary the control variable gradually in both directions, or carry-over effects such as learning or fatigue would swamp any hysteresis.
whyLost: UX experiments usually compare fixed conditions between groups; within-person sweeps in both directions come from psychophysics and are rarely taught to product researchers.
whereToUse: Performance and latency tolerance, pricing and paywall thresholds, notification load, automation trust, game difficulty tuning.
example: In a lab study, response latency of a search box is raised from 100 ms to 2 s in small steps and then lowered again. Participants switch from typing full queries to waiting for suggestions at 900 ms on the way up but only switch back at 300 ms on the way down, showing that recovering speed alone will not restore the earlier behaviour quickly.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: i* goal and dependency modelling
aka: i* strategic dependency and goal modelling
Strategic dependency and strategic rationale models
origin: Eric Yu, 1993-1997; Mylopoulos, Chung and Yu, 1999; Chung on non-functional requirements
summary: Diagram actors, hard goals, soft goals, tasks and resources with dependency and means-end links to reason about who depends on whom and how options affect quality goals.
description: The i* framework models organisations and systems as actors who depend on each other to achieve goals, perform tasks and supply resources. Hard goals become functional requirements; soft goals (usability, safety, cost, accuracy) become quality requirements judged by degree of satisfaction. A strategic dependency model maps actors and the dependencies between them; a strategic rationale model opens up each actor to show how tasks, sub-goals and resources serve its goals, and lets candidate system solutions be compared with arguments for and against, including their effects on soft goals. Goal hierarchies resemble hierarchical task models minus sequence, but i* also represents relationships between agents and organisational structures that task models lack. Sutcliffe notes that it offers little process guidance for agreeing requirements and that industrial effectiveness of formal requirements models is not demonstrated.
steps: Identify actors: stakeholders, roles and systems, including automated agents.
Record each actor's hard goals, soft goals, tasks and resources.
Draw dependencies between actors for goals, tasks, resources and soft goals to form the strategic dependency model.
Open each key actor into a strategic rationale model with means-end and decomposition links showing how tasks and resources achieve goals.
Add candidate system solutions and mark their contributions (helps, hurts) to soft goals.
Use the diagrams with stakeholders to discuss vulnerabilities, negotiate requirements and choose among alternatives.
outputs: Strategic dependency and strategic rationale diagrams, with soft-goal contribution analysis of design alternatives.
useWhen: When requirements span several organisations, roles or automated agents, and you need to see dependencies, vulnerabilities and quality trade-offs before design.
avoidWhen: Avoid for single-user task design (use Hierarchical Task Analysis) or when stakeholders will not engage with formal notation. It gives little guidance on reaching agreement; pair with workshops.
whyLost: It is a staple of academic requirements engineering but rarely used in industry; UX models people through journeys and personas rather than actor dependencies.
whereToUse: Multi-party services (health, government, marketplaces), AI agent workflows with delegation, B2B platforms, socio-technical system redesign.
example: A telehealth service maps patient, GP, pharmacist and booking bot in i*. The dependency model reveals that the patient's 'prescription renewed quickly' soft goal depends on a pharmacist step no one owns, which becomes a requirement.
reference: Yu, E. S. K. (1997). Towards modelling and reasoning support for early-phase requirements engineering. Proceedings of the 3rd IEEE International Symposium on Requirements Engineering (RE'97), 226-235.

name: IA graph analysis
origin: Hypertext structural metrics by Botafogo, Rivlin and Shneiderman, 1992; network science metrics (Freeman, 1978)
summary: Treats an information architecture as a network of nodes and links and computes structural metrics that predict findability, bottlenecks and isolation.
description: Any site, app or knowledge base can be represented as a directed graph: nodes are pages, screens or content objects; edges are navigational links, relations or transitions. Graph analysis computes properties that matter for findability: path lengths between nodes, diameter, connectivity, centrality, clustering, and structural metrics such as Botafogo's compactness and stratum. These reveal whether important content is many hops from entry points, whether parts of the structure are poorly connected, and which nodes are bottlenecks. Weighting edges with real transition frequencies turns the structural graph into a behavioural one. Rigour comes from complete graph extraction, consistent node definitions, and validating structural predictions with tree tests or log-based task success.
steps: Extract the graph: crawl the site or export app routes and links, defining nodes and edges consistently (for example one node per template instance).
Load into a graph tool (NetworkX, Gephi) and compute node count, edge count, diameter, average shortest path, connected components and compactness.
Compute shortest path length from main entry points to each key task destination and flag destinations more than 3 clicks from entry in time-critical contexts.
Compute centrality measures to find hubs and bottlenecks, and community detection to compare clusters with the intended taxonomy.
Overlay behavioural transition weights from analytics to compare designed versus used structure.
Propose structural changes and simulate their effect on path lengths before validating with a tree test.
outputs: A network model of the IA, structural metrics, path-length maps to key tasks, centrality rankings, and recommended link changes.
useWhen: For large or legacy sites and apps, knowledge bases and settings structures; when planning IA changes; when findability problems are diffuse.
avoidWhen: For small sites where structure is obvious; use a card sort or tree test directly.
whyLost: 1990s hypertext research produced these metrics, but web IA moved to card sorting and sitemaps, leaving network analysis to SEO tools.
whereToUse: Enterprise intranets, documentation sites, government services, e-commerce, and surgical or industrial device menus.
example: Graph analysis of a surgical robot's 210-screen IA shows the instrument calibration screen is 6 hops from the home state and reachable only through settings. Adding a contextual link from the instrument status bar cuts it to 2 hops.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 7 — Graph Theory & the Architecture of Information
reference: Botafogo, R. A., Rivlin, E. & Shneiderman, B. (1992). Structural analysis of hypertexts: identifying hierarchies and useful metrics. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 10(2), 142-180.

name: Iatrogenic UX Harm Analysis
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Examines harm caused by interventions meant to protect users (regulations, safeguards, policies), as with cookie consent banners producing near-universal uninformed consent.
description: In medicine, iatrogenic harm is caused by treatment. The treatise defines iatrogenic UX harm as design harm caused by an intervention (regulatory, organisational or technical) intended to protect users. Its canonical case is the cookie consent epidemic: GDPR's informed-consent requirement was implemented almost universally through banners that undermined informed consent via choice overload, asymmetric defaults and dark-pattern accept buttons. The regulation acted as a vector transmitting a new pathogen across the European-facing web at once, which then spread globally. Research finds 80-95% click 'Accept All' without reading; virtually no one makes a genuinely informed decision. Iatrogenic analysis evaluates protective interventions for their actual user outcomes, including second-order harms such as habituation and consent fatigue.
steps: Identify the protective intervention and its intended user outcome.
Define measures of the intended outcome (for example informed consent) and possible harms (time, fatigue, habituation).
Measure real-world implementation and behaviour across products.
Compare outcomes with the intervention's goals and with alternatives.
Identify design features driving harm (defaults, asymmetry, frequency).
Recommend redesigned implementations or policy changes and evaluate them.
outputs: Evaluation of intended versus actual outcomes, iatrogenic harm estimates, redesign and policy recommendations.
useWhen: Evaluating consent flows, warnings, security friction, compliance-driven UI and safety features.
avoidWhen: When no protective intent is involved; use standard harm analysis.
whyLost: Original framing of the treatise; compliance UI is rarely evaluated for its effect on users.
whereToUse: Privacy and consent, security warnings, age verification, AI safety disclaimers, accessibility overlays.
example: An analysis of AI disclaimers shows users stop reading them after the third exposure while over-trusting outputs; replacing static disclaimers with contextual uncertainty cues improves verification.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Utz C et al. (2019) (Un)informed consent: studying GDPR consent notices in the field. CCS
Nouwens M et al. (2020) Dark patterns after the GDPR. CHI
Illich I (1976) Limits to Medicine: Medical Nemesis
reference: Nouwens M et al. (2020) Dark patterns after the GDPR: scraping consent pop-ups and demonstrating their influence. Proceedings of CHI 2020.

name: Icon and Screen Annotation
origin: Pamela Pavliscak's research practice, described 2018
summary: Participants capture their own home screen or desktop and annotate each icon with the meaning, emotion or value it holds, exposing how apps sit in their lives.
description: Icons on a personal device come to stand for feelings, people, values, actions or stories. In this elicitation the participant sketches or screenshots their home screen or desktop and annotates every icon with what it means to them and the role it plays, prompted explicitly for emotions or values (people rarely separate the two). The annotated screen then anchors a discussion about the target product, an analogous app, or how a product sits among its neighbours on the device. Because the artefact is the participant's own device rather than a researcher's stimulus, it surfaces relational meaning (guilt, comfort, obligation, habit) that direct questions about a single app tend to miss. Repeating the exercise later shows how meanings shift over time. Rigour comes from consistent prompts across participants and from interpreting annotations only with the participant's spoken explanations.
steps: Ask each participant to sketch or screenshot their current home screen or desktop before or at the start of the session.
Have them annotate every icon, not just the target app, with what it means to them or the role it plays.
Prompt explicitly for emotions and values attached to each app, accepting that participants will blend the two.
Discuss the annotations, focusing on the target app, analogous apps and the apps placed near it.
Ask about placement, folders and deleted or hidden apps as evidence of relationship.
Optionally repeat the exercise weeks later and compare annotations to see how meanings have shifted.
outputs: Annotated screens linking apps to emotions, values and roles; themes about the target product's place in the participant's device ecosystem.
useWhen: You want to understand the emotional and symbolic role of an app or category in people's lives, or where your product sits relative to competitors on a real device.
avoidWhen: Participants are uncomfortable sharing personal devices, or you need task-level usability evidence; use diary studies or usability testing instead. Personal screens are private and people may self-censor.
whyLost: It is a recent practitioner technique documented in one book, so it has not spread beyond emotion-focused design research.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, wellbeing and habit products, messaging and social apps, and competitive positioning studies on mobile.
example: A meditation app team asks 12 users to screenshot and annotate their home screens. Several place the app next to fitness trackers and label both 'guilt', which reframes the reminder strategy around self-compassion rather than streaks.
reference: Pavliscak, P. (2018). Emotionally Intelligent Design: Rethinking How We Create Products. O'Reilly Media.

name: Icon simulation test
donor: Safety ergonomics and standards for public information symbols
origin: Graphical symbol comprehension testing developed through ISO 9186 (first edition 1989) and ANSI Z535.3 (1991) for public and safety signage
summary: Measures whether users correctly interpret icons by showing them in a simulated context and scoring open-ended interpretations against standardised comprehension thresholds.
description: Standards bodies test public and safety symbols rigorously before adoption: participants see a symbol in a realistic context, describe its meaning in their own words, and judges score the answers against the intended referent. ISO 9186 sets an acceptance criterion of 66.7% correct comprehension for public information symbols, while ANSI Z535.3 requires 85% correct with no more than 5% critical confusions for safety symbols. An icon simulation test brings this protocol to UI: the icon is placed in a mocked-up context screen that simulates the real moment of use, and responses are categorised as correct, partly correct, wrong, opposite or critical confusion. Rigour comes from open-ended rather than multiple-choice responses, independent judging and pre-set thresholds.
steps: Define the referent for each icon in one sentence and decide the acceptance threshold: 66.7% correct for general function icons, 85% correct with at most 5% critical confusions for destructive, financial or safety actions.
Build a context screen for each icon that simulates the moment of use without textual labels that give away the meaning.
Recruit at least 50 participants for a standards-grade test, or 20 to 30 per segment for a diagnostic test, representative of the target users' language, age and digital experience.
Show each icon in context in randomised order and ask 'What does this symbol mean?' and 'What would you expect to happen if you selected it?', recording verbatim responses.
Have at least two judges independently categorise each response as correct, partly correct, wrong, opposite or critical confusion, resolving disagreements by discussion and reporting agreement.
Compute per-icon comprehension rates with 95% confidence intervals (adjusted Wald) and compare the lower bound against the threshold for high-stakes icons.
Redesign icons that fail, consider adding text labels, and retest with new participants.
outputs: Per-icon comprehension percentages with confidence intervals, critical confusion rates, categorised verbatims, and a pass or fail decision per icon against the threshold.
useWhen: Icons appear without labels, carry safety or financial consequences, or serve users across languages and literacy levels.
avoidWhen: Icons always have visible text labels, or you need to test navigation success rather than sign meaning; use first-click or task-based usability testing instead.
whyLost: The protocol stayed in standards and safety ergonomics, while UX teams adopted quick preference polls or multiple-choice recognition tests that inflate comprehension.
whereToUse: Medical devices, automotive HMIs, kiosks and ATMs, low-literacy fintech, global consumer apps, AI status icons.
example: A ride-hailing app tested an unlabelled shield icon intended as 'safety tools'. Only 38% interpreted it correctly and 12% read it as 'insurance purchase', a critical confusion; the team added a label and a distinct help symbol.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: ISO 9186-1:2014 Graphical symbols: Test methods, Part 1: Method for testing comprehensibility; ANSI Z535.3 Criteria for Safety Symbols.

name: Icon-based mental model drawing survey
aka: Icon-based mental model drawing survey with cluster classification
donor: Cognitive psychology and network quality of experience
origin: Yoshida, Tsukatsune and Niida (2020), from a survey conducted in 2009
summary: Survey respondents draw how a system works using a fixed icon set; drawings are coded by which icons appear and clustered into mental model classes linked to behaviour.
description: Drawing tasks reveal mental models but are hard to analyse at scale. This method constrains the drawing with a fixed palette of icons for the system's components, so a web survey can collect hundreds of drawings. In the source study, 772 respondents drew a communication connection in working and failed states using 48 icons. Non-serious drawings were excluded, each drawing was coded by which icon types it contained rather than how many, rarely used icons were dropped, and a two-step cluster analysis gave four mental model classes. These were related to ICT literacy (scored by multiple correspondence analysis), satisfaction with waiting times, chosen behaviour during failures and assumed causes (latent profile analysis). Mental model class varied with literacy and predicted different behaviour when the network failed. The icon set limits what can be expressed, and presence coding ignores structure such as arrows and arrangement.
steps: Design a fixed icon palette covering the system's components as users might imagine them, plus generic elements.
Ask respondents to draw the system in a normal state and in a failure state using the palette.
Exclude non-serious or empty drawings.
Code each drawing by which icon types it contains, and drop icons that almost nobody used.
Cluster drawings (for example two-step or latent class clustering) into mental model classes.
Relate classes to literacy, satisfaction, troubleshooting behaviour and assumed causes, and illustrate each class with typical drawings.
outputs: Mental model classes with typical drawings, and their links to user characteristics and behaviours.
useWhen: Understanding how large, varied user populations conceive of an invisible system (networks, cloud sync, AI models, payments) and how that shapes troubleshooting or trust.
avoidWhen: Small qualitative studies where free drawing and interviews give richer insight, or when the structure of relationships matters more than which components appear; then code arrows and layout as well.
whyLost: Mental model drawing is used qualitatively in UX, but the scaled, icon-constrained and clustered version has stayed in a few HCI papers.
whereToUse: Connectivity and smart-home troubleshooting, cloud storage and sync, data privacy and AI explanations, payment systems, security warnings.
example: A cloud storage provider asks 800 users to draw how a file gets from laptop to phone using 30 icons. Clusters separate users who imagine direct device-to-device transfer from those who include a server; the former blame their phone when sync fails, so error messages are rewritten to name the server step.
sources: Human Interface and the Management of Information (Yamamoto & Mori, 2020)
reference: Yoshida, H., Tsukatsune, K. and Niida, S. (2020). Analysis of mental model of users with network malfunction. In S. Yamamoto and H. Mori (Eds.), Human Interface and the Management of Information: HIMI 2020, Part I (LNCS 12184, pp. 312-328). Cham: Springer.

name: Iconographic-Iconological Analysis (Panofsky) and Iconological Context Analysis
origin: Aby Warburg; Erwin Panofsky (three steps, 1939); Karl Mannheim (documentary meaning); extended by Marion G. Müller (Iconological Context Analysis, 2003)
summary: Interpret images in three steps, from neutral description to conventional meanings to what they reveal about their culture, accounting for production and reception contexts.
description: Panofsky's method interprets images at three levels, each with its own object, required knowledge and corrective principle: pre-iconographical description of what is shown, iconographical analysis of conventional themes and motifs, and iconological interpretation of what the images reveal about the attitudes of their time and culture. Müller treats it as a qualitative, comparative and forensic method in which images are evidence for hypotheses about meaning in context. Her Iconological Context Analysis adds attention to visual form, six ideal-type production contexts (artistic, commercial, journalistic, scientific, political, private) and reception contexts, since an image made privately can take on new meaning when published. The method is inductive and holistic, needs cultural and historical knowledge, and is rooted in Western traditions, so interpretations must be referenced carefully to visual and textual sources.
steps: Collect the visual material and pose a problem-oriented research question, refining it as you go.
Classify visuals into your own types and tag every visual and textual source.
Describe prototype images neutrally (pre-iconographical), attending to details and differences in form and style; compare descriptions.
Iconographic analysis: bring visual and verbal sources together to attribute conventional meanings and form hypotheses.
Analyse the production context (artistic, commercial, journalistic, scientific, political, private) and how it shapes form and intended meaning.
Analyse reception contexts and what the images meant to their audiences.
Iconological interpretation: state what the images convey about the social, political and cultural context.
outputs: A referenced interpretation of an image set's meanings and what it says about its time, culture and makers.
useWhen: Analysing visual culture around a product category, brand imagery, competitors' visual language, or user-generated images, where meaning depends on cultural context.
avoidWhen: Quick interface critique or aesthetics scoring; use Semiotic Analysis of Interfaces or visual aesthetics questionnaires. Be cautious with non-Western material without relevant expertise.
whyLost: It belongs to art history and communication studies; UX visual analysis adopted semiotics and content analysis instead.
whereToUse: Brand and marketing imagery, AI-generated imagery audits, icon and illustration systems, social media and user-generated visual content.
example: A health brand team analyses 200 stock and competitor images of 'wellness', moving from description to conventions (white, young, outdoors) to what they say about who is imagined as healthy, and redesigns its illustration brief.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Müller, M. G. 'Iconography and iconology as a visual method and approach', in Margolis, E. and Pauwels, L. (eds.) (2011) The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods. London: SAGE.

name: Idea Contests
origin: Walcher, 2007; design elements after Bullinger and Möslein; participant motives after Füller
summary: An organisation invites the public or a target group to submit ideas on a theme, usually online, and experts, peers or participants rate them for rewards.
description: Idea contests use competition to stimulate creative contributions from outside the company. Gaubinger and colleagues describe ten design elements: media, organiser, task specificity, required elaboration (from idea to worked solution), target group, individual or team participation, contest period, reward, community functions and evaluation method. Online contests run in three phases: preparation (platform adapted, goal and legal terms written, idea call designed, community manager trained), campaign (members invited, ideas submitted and discussed in a shared pool, moderated and acknowledged) and evaluation (jury, peer review, self-assessment or a mix). Füller's ten participant motives, from playfulness and curiosity to recognition and money, and four participant types should shape the platform. Besides ideas, contests identify innovative users worth involving further.
steps: Set the ten design elements: media, organiser, task specificity, elaboration, target group, participation unit, period, reward, community functions and evaluation.
Prepare: adapt the platform, write the goal and intellectual property terms, design the idea call with topic visuals and train a community manager.
Launch the campaign, inviting the target group with clear goals and benefits.
Run the campaign: let members submit and discuss ideas in a shared pool, report new ideas, acknowledge contributors and moderate.
Evaluate submissions by jury, peer review, self-assessment or a combination.
Award rewards, feed back to participants and flag highly innovative contributors for further co-creation.
outputs: A pool of rated ideas, an engaged contributor community and a list of innovative users.
useWhen: An organisation wants a wide range of ideas from customers or experts beyond its own team, or wants to find lead users.
avoidWhen: Contests yield ideas, not evidence of need; popularity among contributors is not demand. Validate with Interviews, Kano Analysis or concept tests via Prototype Testing. Avoid where intellectual property cannot be cleanly assigned or where only a handful of knowledgeable participants exist; use Co-design Workshops instead.
whyLost: Lives in open-innovation and marketing departments; UX teams rarely own the platforms, legal terms and community management it needs.
whereToUse: Consumer goods, agricultural and industrial equipment, civic and public-sector innovation, developer ecosystems.
example: An agricultural machinery maker runs an online contest for farmers on reducing soil compaction; peer ratings and an expert jury shortlist ten ideas, and three top contributors join a co-design panel.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Gaubinger, K., Rabl, M., Swan, S. and Werani, T. (2015) Innovation and Product Management. Berlin: Springer, pp. 95-102.

name: Idealised Cognitive Model (ICM) Analysis
origin: Adapted for UX from George Lakoff, Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987), drawing on Fillmore (1982) and Sweetser (1987)
summary: Explain why some cases are poor examples of a concept by stating the idealised model it presupposes, checking its fit, and splitting the concept into converging submodels and metonymic stand-ins.
description: Lakoff argues that words are defined against idealised cognitive models whose background assumptions do not fit the world perfectly. 'Bachelor' presupposes a society where men marry at a typical age, so the pope is a poor bachelor because the model does not apply, not because he partly belongs. 'Mother' is a cluster of birth, genetic, nurturance, marital and genealogical models; 'real mother' sentences, compounds such as stepmother and extended senses each pick out submodels. Metonymic models (stereotypes, typical examples, ideals, paragons, salient examples) let a subcategory stand for the whole and create further prototype effects, detectable with 'X, but Y' frames and inference asymmetries. Adapted for UX, the analysis explains why users mis-sort items, why a category label fails for edge cases, and which stereotype users reason from.
steps: State the idealised model the term or category presupposes, including its background assumptions.
Test candidate cases for how well that background fits, separating poor fit from partial membership.
Where people's weightings conflict with their definitions, model the surrounding ICMs whose logic explains the weights.
If no single model covers all uses, list the converging submodels.
Probe submodels with 'real X' sentences, compound modifiers and extended senses in interviews or corpora.
Identify metonymic stand-ins (stereotype, typical case, ideal, paragon, salient example) and test them with 'X, but Y' contrast frames and inference asymmetries.
Summarise the composite prototype and the deviations it explains, and relate them to labels and categories in the product.
outputs: A model of the concept: background ICM, submodels, metonymic stand-ins, composite prototype and explained poor examples.
useWhen: Diagnosing category and label problems in navigation, taxonomies and forms, especially for socially loaded categories (family, employment, gender, account holder) where edge cases fail.
avoidWhen: Avoid when a quick quantitative check of typicality is enough (use category structure paradigms or tree testing); the analysis is interpretive and needs linguistic skill.
whyLost: Prototype theory reached UX as typicality ratings, while Lakoff's account of where prototype effects come from stayed in cognitive linguistics.
whereToUse: Government and insurance forms (household, dependant, partner), e-commerce taxonomies, HR systems, AI classification labels and content moderation categories.
example: A benefits form's 'head of household' question confuses multigenerational families. ICM analysis shows the label assumes a single-earner nuclear-family model; splitting it into who pays rent and who is the main contact removes the misfit.
reference: Lakoff, G. (1987). Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things: What Categories Reveal about the Mind. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, pp. 68-90.

name: IDEAS Participatory Design
aka: Interface Design Experience for the Autistic Spectrum
IDEAS participatory design sessions with autistic participants
origin: Laura Benton, Hilary Johnson and colleagues, 2011-2012; applied by Gillespie et al. 2017
summary: Structured participatory design sessions adapted for autistic participants using visual timelines, demonstrations, idea templates and multimodal expression of ideas.
description: IDEAS merges participatory design methods for children with TEACCH principles of structured teaching, to make design sessions predictable and accessible for autistic participants. Every session follows the same four parts: a visual timeline of the session with a recap of earlier sessions; demonstration and discussion of relevant existing software; idea generation supported by examples of good and bad technologies and by templates; and expression of the agreed idea, through drawing in the original and, in Gillespie et al.'s version, also speaking, writing or demonstrating. The structure lowers anxiety and lets participants contribute strengths rather than struggle with open-ended brainstorming. Gillespie et al. also paid autistic college students for feedback and evaluated the resulting game by filming play and coding behaviours with reliability checks.
steps: Plan a series of sessions with a constant structure and prepare a visual timeline for each.
Open each session with the visual timeline and a recap of what was done previously.
Demonstrate and discuss existing software relevant to the design problem.
Generate ideas using examples of good and bad technologies and structured templates.
Let participants express the agreed idea in their preferred mode: drawing, speaking, writing or demonstrating.
Compensate participants, offer deeper roles to those who want them, and build customisation into the resulting design.
outputs: Design ideas, sketches and feedback from autistic participants, and session records.
useWhen: Designing products with or for autistic users, or any participant group that benefits from predictable, structured sessions.
avoidWhen: When the structure would over-constrain participants who prefer open exploration. Designs may end up appealing mainly to those who designed them, so build in customisation; prompting during evaluation sessions can confound behaviour coding.
whyLost: It is known in autism and child-computer interaction research but rarely adopted in commercial neuro-inclusive design.
whereToUse: Neuro-inclusive apps, education and social skills tools, games, workplace software accessibility.
example: A study-planner app team runs four IDEAS sessions with autistic university students, each starting with a visual timeline; students draw or demonstrate features, producing a calendar with sensory-load warnings.
reference: Benton, L., Johnson, H., Ashwin, E., Brosnan, M. and Grawemeyer, B. (2012). Developing IDEAS: supporting children with autism within a participatory design session. Proc. CHI 2012; Gillespie, K. et al. (2017). Connecting through Kinect. In Marcus, A. and Wang, W. (eds) DUXU 2017, LNCS 10289, Springer, pp. 398-413.

name: Idiographic filter (iFACE)
origin: Nesselroade, Gerstorf, Hardy and Ram, 2007; iFACE by Molenaar, Smit, Boomsma and Nesselroade, 2012
summary: A person-specific factor model that lets each individual's indicators load differently while holding the latent dynamics equal across people, so the same process is compared fairly.
description: The idiographic filter starts from the observation that one construct can surface through different indicators in different people: stress as stomach trouble in one child, tremor in another. Instead of demanding identical loadings (classic factorial invariance), it splits the data box into one intensive time series (P-technique dataset) per person and fits a joint state-space model in which loadings are free per person but latent auto-regressions, cross-regressions and factor correlations are constrained equal. Good fit means the same latent process is being measured even though it shows itself differently; if loadings turn out identical, the model collapses to ordinary invariance. Measurement equivalence is thereby redefined dynamically: same process, not same trait expression. iFACE extends the approach to twin pairs to estimate person-specific heritability. Its rigour lies in an explicit, testable equality constraint at the latent level.
steps: Collect multivariate time series on the same variables for each of several people, with enough occasions per person for P-technique factor analysis (typically 50 or more).
Specify a state-space model with person-specific factor loadings and a latent process model (auto- and cross-regressions, factor correlations) constrained equal across persons.
Fit the joint model and test it against a model with loadings also constrained equal; if loadings do not differ, conclude ordinary factorial invariance.
If the idiographic model fits well, interpret each person's loading pattern alongside the shared latent dynamics.
Derive second-order factors where needed and express them on the observed variables by Schmid-Leiman or Cattell-White transformation.
Report which indicators carry the construct for whom, and use the shared latent scores for between-person comparison.
outputs: Per-person loading patterns, invariant latent dynamics (auto- and cross-regressions), second-order factors and a verdict on dynamic measurement equivalence.
useWhen: When an experience construct (frustration, engagement, stress) is tracked intensively per person through diaries, experience sampling or telemetry, and you suspect it shows through different signals in different users.
avoidWhen: Avoid with cross-sectional data or few occasions per person; use multigroup CFA invariance testing or Cross-Cultural Survey Equivalence Testing instead. The book describes it only in outline, so specialist modelling support is needed.
whyLost: It lives in developmental and lifespan methodology, where intensive longitudinal data are common; UX rarely collects enough occasions per person and has little state-space modelling expertise.
whereToUse: Longitudinal diary or experience-sampling programmes, wearable and health apps, adaptive products where per-user signals of stress or overload differ.
example: A mental-health app samples mood, sleep, app-opening bursts and typing speed daily for 90 days. An idiographic filter lets distress load on sleep for one user and typing speed for another, while testing that the distress dynamics are shared.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Nesselroade, J. R., Gerstorf, D., Hardy, S. A., & Ram, N. (2007). Idiographic filters for psychological constructs. Measurement, 5, 217-235; Molenaar, P. C. M., & Nesselroade, J. R. (2015). Systems methods for developmental research. In Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 1.

name: IHCLab Usability Test for Serious Games
aka: Group usability test for serious games
origin: Santana-Mancilla, Gaytan-Lugo and Rodriguez-Ortiz, IHCLab, University of Colima (Chapter 11)
summary: A summative lab method for serious games in which a group of 5 to 20 learners is introduced, shown a live demo, given a task list and then answers selectable questionnaires on heuristics, game experience and use for learning.
description: The IHCLab method evaluates finished serious games with all participants at once in a lab configured with a computer per user, cameras on faces, observers and a moderator with a projector. Sessions last an hour to an hour and a half in four phases. First, a ten-minute introduction and a short profile questionnaire. Second, a projected live demo that puts the game's controls in context. Third, participants work through a task list in the game while observers watch. Fourth, the team chooses one or more of three questionnaires: a game heuristics questionnaire of ten player-answered questions generalised from Desurvire's playability heuristics (consistency, customisation, predictable controls, skippable non-playable content, status information, help and training); a game experience questionnaire with four 1 to 10 ratings (fun, difficulty adapting to controls, excitement, ease of meeting the objective) and seven 5-point indicators such as efficiency, immersion and learning curve; and a two-question use for learning survey on comfort and motivation to use such a game for education. The method is practical for schools and universities, though its questionnaires are home-grown rather than validated.
steps: Set up a lab with one machine per participant, face cameras, observer positions and a projector.
Recruit 5 to 20 representative learners and open with an introduction and profile questionnaire.
Give a live projected demo of the game and its controls.
Hand out a task list and let participants complete it while observers note difficulties.
Administer the chosen questionnaires: heuristics, game experience, use for learning, or a combination.
Chart results per item and highlight heuristics or indicators with poor ratings for redesign.
outputs: Observer notes and per-item questionnaire results on usability heuristics, experience and perceived educational value.
useWhen: Evaluating finished educational or serious games with classes of learners when time and lab slots are limited.
avoidWhen: You need validated, comparable measures or detailed individual problem discovery.
whyLost: It is a lab-specific methodology published in one book chapter and not widely adopted.
whereToUse: Serious games, edtech, training simulations, university and school settings.
example: Twenty third-graders test a reading comprehension game together; the heuristics questionnaire shows poor results for customisation and for skipping text, the latter being intentional because reading is the learning goal.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Santana-Mancilla, P. C., Gaytan-Lugo, L. S. and Rodriguez-Ortiz, M. A. (2016). Usability testing of serious games: the experience of the IHCLab. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 11. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Illusory truth repetition test
origin: Hasher, Goldstein and Toppino, 1977; Fazio and colleagues, 2015
summary: People rate statements on a neutral dimension, then later judge the truth of those statements mixed with new ones, measuring how repetition alone raises belief.
description: In the exposure phase participants rate true and false statements on a dimension other than truth, such as how interesting they are. Later they judge the truth of those statements mixed with new ones. Repeated statements are judged true more often: in one study, 62 percent of repeated true statements versus 56 percent of new ones, and repetition raised belief in false statements even when people knew the correct answer. The usual explanation is processing fluency. Related effects include non-famous names becoming 'famous overnight' after one exposure. The design is rigorous when the first task is not a truth judgement, new-item controls are included, and true and false statements are analysed separately.
steps: Assemble true and false statements of the type in question, pretested for baseline belief.
Exposure phase: have participants rate a subset on a non-truth dimension (interest, clarity).
Insert a delay (minutes to days).
Test phase: present repeated and new statements and ask for truth judgements or ratings.
Counterbalance which statements are repeated across participants.
Compare truth judgements for repeated versus new items, separately for true and false statements.
outputs: Proportion judged true for repeated versus new items, separately for true and false statements.
useWhen: Evaluating how repeated claims in feeds, notifications, AI answers or marketing affect belief, or testing whether labels and corrections counter repetition.
avoidWhen: Avoid using a truth judgement in the exposure phase, which removes the effect; for broader misinformation interventions use field experiments on real platforms.
whyLost: It belongs to memory and misinformation research; product teams rarely measure belief change from repeated exposure.
whereToUse: Social media and news feeds, content moderation and fact-check labels, AI chat answers, health communication, advertising claims.
example: A news app tests whether a false claim shown twice in a feed is later rated more true than one shown once, and whether a 'disputed' label on first exposure removes the boost.
sources: Hasher, L., Goldstein, D., & Toppino, T. (1977). Frequency and the conference of referential validity. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 16
reference: Fazio, L. K., Brashier, N. M., Payne, B. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2015). Knowledge does not protect against illusory truth. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144, 993-1002.

name: Imagining Losing
origin: Jon Kolko, 2014
summary: Imagine a rival launches a product that beats yours, write the story and artefacts of that loss, and identify the strategic weakness it exposes.
description: Rather than reacting to competitors' existing products, the team presumes a competitor launches something new and its own product loses badly. Team members picture both products side by side, imagine two target shoppers comparing them aloud and buying the rival, and write what they say and why they chose it: messaging, features, price, brand or packaging. They then make the rival concrete by sketching its differentiator (pricing, wireframes of key features, even an org chart), writing its launch press release and a mock magazine article on their own product's defeat. The final step names the weakness in the current strategy that allowed the loss. It works like a pre-mortem applied to competition.
steps: Assume a competitor launches a new product and yours loses decisively.
Imagine two target shoppers comparing the products aloud and write their conversation.
Assume they buy the rival and list the reasons.
Sketch the rival's differentiator: pricing, wireframes of features, organisation behind it.
Write the rival's launch press release and a mock article about your product being overwhelmed.
Identify the strategic weakness that let the rival win and turn it into defensive product priorities.
outputs: A loss narrative, mock rival artefacts and a list of strategic weaknesses to address.
useWhen: Testing a product strategy or roadmap for blind spots, especially in crowded markets.
avoidWhen: It reflects the team's imagination of customers; ground the shopper dialogue in Interviews or Jobs-to-be-Done Switch Interviews, and benchmark real competitors with Competitive UX Benchmarking. For adversarial thinking about misuse rather than competition use Red Teaming.
whyLost: Known through Kolko's book but rarely operationalised; teams default to feature-comparison grids and generic pre-mortems.
whereToUse: Product strategy reviews, annual planning, consumer and SaaS markets with fast followers.
example: A budgeting-app team imagines a bank launching free automatic savings rules; the mock article blames their manual categorisation, prompting a roadmap shift to automation.
reference: Kolko, J. (2014) Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press, pp. 58-59.

name: Imbalanced Data Strategies (Undersampling, Oversampling, SMOTE)
origin: Chawla et al. (2002) SMOTE; cost-sensitive learning literature
summary: Techniques for modelling rare but important events, such as errors, cancellations or accessibility failures, without the model ignoring them.
description: When only 2% of sessions end in a critical error, a model that predicts "no error" is 98% accurate and useless. Imbalanced data strategies rebalance the training data by undersampling the common class, oversampling or up-weighting the rare class, or generating synthetic rare cases (SMOTE). Cost-based classification sets thresholds by the real cost of each mistake. Bruce and Bruce stress evaluating with precision, recall and lift rather than accuracy.
steps: Quantify the class imbalance and the cost of missing a rare case.
Try undersampling, oversampling, weighting or SMOTE on the training set only.
Fit the model and evaluate on an untouched test set with recall, precision and AUC.
Set the decision threshold using the cost of errors.
Review predicted rare cases qualitatively.
outputs: Models that actually detect rare but important user events.
useWhen: Predicting rare outcomes: critical errors, fraud, cancellations, complaints.
avoidWhen: Classes are balanced, or rare events are too few to learn from (under a few dozen).
whyLost: A modelling concern that UX analytics rarely encounters because it seldom models at all.
whereToUse: Error monitoring, support escalation prediction, safety-critical telemetry.
example: Oversampling failed-payment sessions lifts recall from 12% to 68%, surfacing a pattern of address-format errors in one region.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 5.

name: Immersion Tools
origin: Term from John Payne, 'From Experience Models to Immersion Tools', EPIC, 2014
summary: Games, simulations and wearable props that make a team enact research findings so the logic of users' decisions and constraints is understood and remembered.
description: Immersion tools turn research findings into activities a team does rather than reads. Simulation exercises evoke parts of the target audience's experience; games encode the rules and trade-offs that shape users' decisions so players feel them; costumes and props induce physical or cognitive states, as with the weighted suit Ford engineers wore to simulate driving while pregnant. The shared experience then grounds brainstorming and value propositions, helping teams carry intangibles such as fears and aspirations into design. Rowland and colleagues treat empathy as an aim, not a guaranteed result: an hour in a wheelchair does not convey life as a wheelchair user, so the claim should be concreteness, not understanding.
steps: Select research findings, decisions or constraints the team struggles to grasp from reports.
Design an activity that makes members enact them: a rule-based game, a situational simulation or a wearable prop.
Pilot the activity with one or two researchers to check it conveys the intended logic.
Run it with the team and debrief on what felt surprising or hard.
Use the shared experience to frame brainstorming and value propositions, linking ideas back to the underlying findings.
outputs: A shared, memorable understanding of users' decisions and constraints, and brainstorm material grounded in research.
useWhen: Research findings exist but stakeholders have not absorbed them, especially decision trade-offs or physical constraints.
avoidWhen: Do not use as a substitute for research with the people concerned; disability simulations in particular can mislead and offend. Use Inclusive Design Research or Assistive Technology Testing with real users, and Contextual Inquiry to observe constraints first-hand.
whyLost: Stays in design-anthropology consultancies and EPIC circles because it needs bespoke design per study and attracts criticism of simulated empathy.
whereToUse: Healthcare, financial hardship, connected products, enterprise workflows with complex trade-offs.
example: A utility company team plays a card game built from household research in which each turn forces a choice between heating and other bills, then brainstorms tariff features with that tension fresh.
reference: Rowland, C., Goodman, E., Charlier, M., Light, A. and Lui, A. (2015) Designing Connected Products: UX for the Consumer Internet of Things. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 191-193.

name: Immersive and Artefact-Based Research Reporting
origin: Tomer Sharon's research expo at Google (Webb and Sharon, 2010); Ziba project rooms; Kim Erwin's consumer insight maps (2011); Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015)
summary: Replace or supplement the written report with rooms, notebooks, posters and dense insight maps of field material that stakeholders walk through, browse and work with.
description: Immersive reporting recreates the field for people who were not there. In a research expo the team takes over a room for a day with a self-guided exhibit of posters, photographs, artefacts and video, and researchers are present to talk. A project room keeps culled field photos and bought local products on boards, constantly re-sorted into themes as understanding develops. Lighter forms include an artefact notebook, preferably electronic, where each collected item is labelled with what it is and its design implication; day-in-the-life storyboards merged across participants; office posters of top issues, quotes and personas; and consumer insight maps that place mindsets, activities and anxieties in fixed zones with overlays of current offerings. The aim is shared empathy and persistent visibility, not archiving.
steps: During fieldwork collect plenty of photos, video, quotes and physical or digital artefacts, with consent covering internal display.
Cull the material to the most telling items and label each with context and design implication.
Group the material into themes and choose formats: expo room, project room, notebook, posters, storyboards or an insight map.
For an expo, set up a walk-through exhibit and hold a full-day event with researchers present to answer questions.
Run an active exercise, for example showing photos with a 30-second commentary while attendees write observations, then turning them into design inputs.
Leave material up for days or keep it as a project room, re-sorting it as analysis continues and sharing early insights in team channels.
Pair vivid material with counts or the wider data so single cases are not over-weighted.
outputs: An exhibit or project room, labelled artefact notebook, storyboards, posters or an insight map, and team-generated design inputs.
useWhen: Global or ethnographic studies, large cross-functional teams, and situations where a written report would not convey context or emotion.
avoidWhen: Avoid when stakeholders need a precise decision record, when material cannot be displayed for privacy reasons, or when frequencies matter more than texture. Use a written report or decision memo instead.
whyLost: It survives in design-led organisations, though remote work has shifted rooms into digital whiteboards and video is rarely edited because it is time-consuming.
whereToUse: Cross-cultural research, service design programmes, new-product discovery and onboarding new team members to past research.
example: After fieldwork in three countries, a mobile-payments team runs a one-day expo with market-stall photos, receipts and short clips. Product managers who did not travel leave with fifteen written design inputs.
reference: Webb, J. and Sharon, T. (2010). Engaging teams with rich reporting: Recipe for a research findings expo. User Experience (UPA), 2010(3); Quesenbery, W. and Szuc, D. (2011). Global UX. Waltham, MA: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Immersive Experience Questionnaire (IEQ)
origin: Jennett, Cox, Cairns and colleagues (2008) at UCL; summarised in chapter 9
summary: A questionnaire that measures how immersed players were, covering cognitive involvement, real-world dissociation and emotional involvement, plus the game factors challenge and control.
description: The IEQ was developed to measure immersion as a graded experience of being absorbed in a game. It distinguishes player-related factors (cognitive involvement, real-world dissociation and emotional involvement) from game-related factors (challenge and control). Players complete it after a session, and a total immersion score can be supplemented by factor scores. Jennett and colleagues also showed that immersion relates to measurable behaviour, such as slower return to a real-world task after play, which gives the questionnaire some behavioural grounding. In UX research the IEQ is useful whenever 'engagement' is a goal but needs to be defined more precisely than time on task: it separates being mentally occupied from feeling cut off from surroundings and from caring about outcomes. It can be used to compare levels, versions or display technologies such as VR against flat screens. As with other player experience questionnaires, it reports perception after the fact and should be combined with observation to explain what caused high or low immersion.
steps: Choose the IEQ when immersion or absorption is the outcome of interest.
Standardise play duration and environment, since interruptions affect immersion.
Administer the questionnaire immediately after play.
Compute the total score and the five factor scores.
Compare between conditions and check reliability in your sample.
Relate low-scoring factors to specific moments using observation notes or recordings.
outputs: Total immersion score and factor scores for cognitive involvement, real-world dissociation, emotional involvement, challenge and control.
useWhen: Comparing designs or technologies whose aim is to absorb users, such as games, VR or narrative experiences.
avoidWhen: Sessions are too short or fragmented for immersion to develop, or the product's aim is efficiency rather than absorption.
whyLost: Developed in academic games research and seldom used where immersion is not a stated product goal.
whereToUse: Games, VR and AR, interactive storytelling, museum and media installations.
example: A VR studio compares a seated and a room-scale version of a level; the room-scale version scores higher on real-world dissociation but lower on control.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 9. Jennett, C., Cox, A. L., Cairns, P., et al. (2008). Measuring and defining the experience of immersion in games. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 66(9), 641-661.

name: Impedance Matching Analysis
origin: Maximum power transfer theorem (Moritz von Jacobi, c. 1840); impedance matching in transmission line and acoustic engineering
summary: Treats an interface as a coupling between a source (system) and load (user) and asks where mismatches in rate, granularity or format reflect energy back as friction.
description: In electrical systems, maximum power transfers when source and load impedances match; mismatches reflect energy, causing loss and distortion. Acoustic and mechanical engineering use matching layers and transformers to couple dissimilar media. As an analytical lens for UX, impedance matching asks whether the information rate, chunk size, vocabulary and pacing of a system match the user's capacity and goals at each interface. Mismatches produce 'reflections': repeated questions, backtracking, ignored outputs. The rigorous version quantifies both sides (system output rate and granularity versus measured user processing rate and needs) and designs 'transformers' (summaries, progressive disclosure, adaptive pacing). It remains an analogy-driven framework, so it should be paired with empirical measures.
steps: Identify the interfaces where information or control passes between system and user (or between teams).
Characterise the source: output rate, granularity, format, vocabulary, timing.
Characterise the load: user processing rate (e.g. reading speed, decision time), needed granularity, vocabulary.
Measure reflections: re-reads, follow-up questions, undo, abandonment at each interface.
Design matching elements (summaries, chunking, adjustable verbosity, pacing controls) to reduce mismatch.
Re-measure reflections and throughput after changes.
outputs: An interface mismatch map, reflection metrics and designed matching components.
useWhen: Systems that emit large or fast outputs to people (AI assistants, alerts, dashboards, reports), or handoffs between experts and novices.
avoidWhen: When the analogy adds nothing beyond standard usability analysis; prefer direct empirical methods.
whyLost: Physical analogies were never systematically translated into HCI, apart from loose references to 'bandwidth'.
whereToUse: LLM response length and structure, notification streams, executive dashboards, clinician-patient information handoffs.
example: An AI coding assistant emits 60-line answers; logs show users re-prompt for summaries 40% of the time. Adding an adjustable verbosity 'transformer' with a summary first matches load and halves re-prompts.
sources: Card, Moran & Newell, The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983)

name: Implicit Association Test (IAT)
origin: Anthony Greenwald, Debbie McGhee and Jordan Schwartz, 1998
summary: Measures the relative strength of automatic associations between concepts (e.g. a brand and 'trustworthy') from response-time differences in a categorisation task.
description: In the IAT, participants rapidly sort words or images into categories using two keys. When concepts that are strongly associated share a key, responses are faster. The D-score, computed from latency differences between compatible and incompatible blocks, indexes relative association strength. Brief IAT and single-category IAT variants shorten the procedure. The IAT has real limitations: test-retest reliability around 0.5 and modest prediction of individual behaviour, so it is best used for group-level comparisons. For UX and brand research it offers a measure less susceptible to self-presentation than stated attitudes, useful where users may not admit or know their associations.
steps: Define two target concepts (e.g. our app vs competitor) and two attribute categories (e.g. safe vs risky), with 4-6 stimuli each.
Implement the standard 7-block procedure or a Brief IAT using validated software.
Counterbalance block order across participants.
Compute D-scores using the Greenwald, Nosek and Banaji (2003) improved algorithm, excluding trials over 10 s and participants with excessive fast responses.
Compare group-level D-scores across conditions or segments, and correlate with explicit measures.
Interpret cautiously: report reliability and avoid individual-level claims.
outputs: Group D-scores, explicit-implicit comparison and reliability estimates.
useWhen: Measuring brand or feature associations where social desirability distorts self-report, at group level.
avoidWhen: Diagnosing individuals or predicting individual behaviour; use behavioural data. Avoid ethically sensitive labelling of participants.
whyLost: Contested validity debates and lab requirements kept it in social psychology and market research niches.
whereToUse: Brand perception of AI products, privacy trust, health app stigma, rebrand evaluation.
example: A mental health app tests whether its new name is implicitly associated with 'clinical' versus 'everyday'. The IAT shows a strong clinical association despite neutral explicit ratings, prompting a naming rethink.
sources: Greenwald, McGhee & Schwartz, Measuring individual differences in implicit cognition: The implicit association test (1998), JPSP
Greenwald, Nosek & Banaji, Understanding and using the IAT: I. An improved scoring algorithm (2003), JPSP
reference: Greenwald, A. G., McGhee, D. E., & Schwartz, J. L. K. (1998). JPSP, 74(6), 1464-1480.

name: Implicit learning paradigms: serial reaction time and artificial grammar
aka: Serial reaction time (SRT) task for implicit sequence learning
donor: Cognitive psychology; cognitive neuroscience of memory
origin: Arthur Reber, 1967; Nissen and Bullemer, 1987
summary: People respond to or memorise material built on hidden regularities; faster responses or above-chance classification without stateable rules show learning of structure without awareness.
description: In the serial reaction time task, a cue appears at one of four locations and the participant presses the matching key. Cues follow a repeating sequence (often 10 items) or a random order; greater speed-up in repeating blocks than random ones indexes sequence learning, which amnesic patients show normally even without recollection. In artificial grammar learning, people memorise letter strings of 6 to 8 letters generated by hidden rules; told afterwards that rules existed, they classify new strings as grammatical at about 70 percent accuracy while unable to state the rules. Both paradigms dissociate performance from verbalisable knowledge. Rigour depends on random or ungrammatical control material and on awareness checks, such as asking people to generate or describe the structure.
steps: Define the hidden structure: a repeating response sequence or a finite-state grammar over a small symbol set.
Serial reaction time: map four locations to four keys and run blocks of a repeating sequence (about 10 items) and random blocks.
Artificial grammar: have participants memorise grammatical strings, then tell them rules existed and ask them to classify new grammatical and ungrammatical strings.
Track reaction time over trials or classification accuracy against chance.
Probe awareness with verbal reports or a generation task.
Compare repeating-minus-random differences or accuracy with awareness measures.
outputs: Reaction-time learning curves and repeating-minus-random differences, grammaticality classification accuracy, and awareness measures.
useWhen: Testing whether users implicitly learn the regularities of a design system, navigation structure, keyboard workflow or naming scheme, and can judge new screens as fitting.
avoidWhen: Avoid without awareness checks, since some learning may be explicit; for explicit mental models use teach-back or think-aloud.
whyLost: Implicit learning is a laboratory topic and has not been linked to evaluating design consistency.
whereToUse: Design systems and consistency, keyboard-driven professional tools, games, onboarding to complex workflows.
example: Users work through screens from a design system, then classify new screens as 'from this product' or not. They classify at 72 percent accuracy without explaining why, while screens breaking a spacing rule are rejected.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Reber, A. S. (1967). Implicit learning of artificial grammars. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 6
