Nissen, M. J., & Bullemer, P. (1987). Attentional requirements of learning: Evidence from performance measures. Cognitive Psychology, 19
reference: Reber, A. S. (1967). Implicit learning of artificial grammars. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 6, 855-863.

name: Implicit Processing Assessment in UX Evaluation
origin: Greenwald et al., 1998 (IAT); Goldstein, 2015 (synthesis)
summary: Measures responses users cannot or will not report, using implicit techniques such as reaction-time association tests, priming and behavioural traces alongside self-report.
description: Much of what shapes user experience happens outside awareness: rapid evaluative judgments, primed associations and attentional capture that users cannot accurately report. Implicit processing assessment combines self-report with measures designed to tap these processes, such as reaction-time association tasks, affective priming, first-impression tests with very short exposures, and behavioural traces. The value lies in the dissociation: where implicit and explicit measures disagree, self-report is likely shaped by social desirability, rationalisation or limited introspective access. Rigour requires adequate trials and samples to overcome reaction-time noise, established paradigms rather than ad hoc tasks, and caution in interpretation given ongoing debates about the reliability and predictive validity of implicit measures.
steps: Research design implication: never rely solely on self-report for any UX variable that may be processed unconsciously.
For each research question, identify: is the phenomenon likely conscious (reportable) or unconscious (implicit)?
Conscious → survey, interview, think-aloud.
Unconscious → reaction time, eye-tracking, physiological measures, implicit association test, behavioral observation.
Mismatch between explicit attitude and implicit measure = valuable research finding.
outputs: Implicit association scores, priming effects, dissociations between implicit and explicit measures, and interpretation of where self-report misleads.
useWhen: Brand perception, trust, stigma-related products, and any case where social desirability or limited introspective access makes self-report unreliable.
avoidWhen: Avoid when explicit attitudes are what matter for the decision, when sample sizes are too small for reaction-time noise, or when the team cannot interpret implicit measures cautiously; use standard surveys and interviews.
whyLost: Implicit methods remain contested in psychology and require experimental software and statistical skill; UX practice centres on self-report and observed behaviour.
whereToUse: Trust research (explicit trust ratings often diverge from behavioral trust), aesthetic evaluation, emotional response measurement.
example: A telehealth service runs an online implicit association task with 200 users and finds that 'video consultation' is implicitly associated with 'less thorough' even among users who rate it highly, prompting design cues that signal clinical rigour.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Handbook of the Philosophy of Science (Thagard, 2007)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain (Bear et al., 2016)
reference: Greenwald AG, McGhee DE & Schwartz JLK (1998) Measuring individual differences in implicit cognition: The Implicit Association Test. JPSP 74(6)

name: Implicit vs. explicit measure mismatch analysis
origin: Dual-attitude and implicit measurement research (Greenwald and Banaji, 1995; Wilson, Lindsey and Schooler, 2000); multi-channel affect sensing (Picard, 1997)
summary: Treats systematic disagreement between what users report and what implicit, physiological or behavioural measures show as a finding to explain, not as noise to discard.
description: Explicit self-reports and implicit measures often diverge: a participant reports feeling calm while electrodermal activity and hesitation spike, or rates a flow 'easy' after visibly struggling. The usual response is to pick the measure judged more valid. The mismatch approach instead treats divergence as information. Social desirability, politeness to the researcher, lack of interoceptive awareness, reconstructive memory and dual attitudes each predict different mismatch patterns. Analysing where, when and for whom measures diverge reveals hidden anxiety, face-saving or adaptation. Rigour requires time-aligned data across channels, pre-defined thresholds for what counts as divergence relative to each person's baseline, and follow-up probes such as cued retrospective interviews to interpret mismatches rather than speculating.
steps: Choose paired measures for the constructs of interest, for example self-reported anxiety (a 1 to 7 rating) with electrodermal responses, or perceived ease (Single Ease Question) with task time and errors.
Record baselines for each participant (for example 2 to 5 minutes of rest for physiology) and time-align all channels to task events.
Standardise each measure within participant (z-scores against baseline) and define divergence, for example a self-report at or below the participant's median while the implicit measure exceeds +1 SD.
Map mismatches by task moment and participant, and classify patterns: under-reporting, over-reporting, delayed response or segment-specific divergence.
Run cued retrospective interviews, replaying the moments of mismatch to participants and asking what they were experiencing and why they rated as they did.
Interpret patterns against candidate mechanisms (social desirability, low awareness, adaptation) and report mismatches as findings with design implications.
outputs: Time-aligned multi-channel data, a mismatch map by moment and participant, mechanism interpretations from cued retrospection, and design implications.
useWhen: Stakes or social pressure may bias self-report (finance, health, employer-provided tools); satisfaction scores conflict with behaviour; studying anxiety or trust.
avoidWhen: Sample sizes are too small for within-person baselines, or you lack the equipment and expertise to collect reliable physiological data; use behavioural versus self-report comparison only.
whyLost: UX tends to report self-report and behavioural or biometric data side by side, choosing one when they conflict, so the mismatch itself is rarely analysed.
whereToUse: Loan and credit applications, medical decision interfaces, workplace tools, AI trust research, accessibility and older-adult research.
example: During a loan application, participants rated anxiety low (2 of 7) while heart rate variability dropped sharply at the income disclosure screen. Cued retrospection revealed fear of rejection hidden out of politeness, leading the team to explain how income data is used.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 37 — Picard's Affective Framework — Multi-Channel Emotion Measurement
reference: Picard, R. W. (1997). Affective Computing. MIT Press; Wilson, T. D., Lindsey, S., & Schooler, T. Y. (2000). A model of dual attitudes. Psychological Review, 107(1), 101–126.

name: Importance-Performance Analysis
origin: Martilla and James (1977) in the Journal of Marketing; cited by Veal and Darcy as a standard evaluation and service-quality technique in sport and leisure management
summary: Asks customers to rate how important each attribute of a service is and how well it performs, then plots the two scores on a grid to show where effort should go.
description: Importance-performance analysis is a survey-based evaluation technique. A list of service attributes is drawn up, and each respondent rates every attribute twice: once for how important it is to them and once for how well the provider currently performs on it. Mean scores are plotted on a two-dimensional grid with importance on one axis and performance on the other, and the grid is divided into four quadrants, usually at the overall means. Attributes that are important but performing poorly are the priority for action; important and well-performing ones should be maintained; unimportant but well-performing ones may be absorbing effort that could go elsewhere; and unimportant, poorly performing ones are low priority. Veal and Darcy list it alongside cost-benefit analysis and conjoint analysis as a formal technique for evaluating options, and note its closeness to the SERVQUAL approach, which compares expectations with performance. For UX teams it is a quick way to turn a satisfaction survey into a prioritised list of product attributes. Unlike regression-based key driver analysis, it uses stated importance rather than derived importance, so it is simple to explain but prone to everything being rated important.
steps: Identify the attributes of the product or service to assess, from earlier interviews, focus groups, support data or the literature.
Write paired items for each attribute: an importance rating and a performance (satisfaction) rating on the same scale.
Survey a representative sample of current users and compute the mean importance and mean performance for each attribute.
Plot each attribute on a grid with importance on one axis and performance on the other, and draw cross-hairs at the grand means or the scale midpoints.
Read off the four quadrants: concentrate here, keep up the good work, low priority and possible overkill.
Check the stability of the result by segment and, where possible, compare stated importance with importance derived from regression.
Turn the 'concentrate here' quadrant into a ranked backlog and repeat the survey after changes to track movement.
outputs: An importance-performance grid, a table of mean scores and gaps per attribute, and a short prioritised list of attributes needing attention.
useWhen: You need a simple, explainable way to prioritise many service or product attributes from user ratings, for example after a release or for an annual satisfaction programme.
avoidWhen: Respondents cannot judge importance meaningfully, the attribute list is unfinished, or you need causal evidence of what drives satisfaction or retention.
whyLost: UX adopted regression-based key driver analysis and NPS-style dashboards, and stated-importance ratings are criticised for ceiling effects, so the simpler grid stayed mainly in tourism, leisure and service marketing.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction surveys, service design programmes, SaaS feature satisfaction tracking, venue and event apps, public service digital channels.
example: A sports club booking app surveys 600 members on twelve attributes such as finding a free court, paying, cancelling and notifications. The grid shows cancelling a booking as highly important but rated poorly, while social sharing performs well but matters little, so the team moves effort from sharing features to a clearer cancellation flow.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Regression and Key Driver Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, 2021)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Martilla, J. A. and James, J. C. (1977) Importance-performance analysis. Journal of Marketing, 41(1), 77-79.

name: In Vivo Coding
origin: Grounded theory tradition (Glaser and Strauss, 1967; Strauss, 1987), as presented by Charmaz (2006)
summary: Code data with participants' own telling terms, then unpack and test each term rather than taking it at face value.
description: In vivo codes use the participants' own words as code labels, preserving their meanings in the coding itself. Charmaz identifies three useful kinds: general terms that everyone 'knows' but that condense significant meaning; a participant's innovative term that captures an experience; and insider shorthand of a particular group. The rigour lies in treating each term as problematic: asking what category it suggests, what implicit meanings it carries, and how people act on it, and comparing usage across participants. In vivo codes do not stand alone; they must be integrated into analytic categories. They also act as a check on the researcher's labels, showing whether the analyst has grasped what matters to participants. Classic examples include replacing researcher labels with the group's own terms after asking what members called themselves.
steps: While coding, attend to participants' language and mark terms that seem telling.
Record each term verbatim as a code, with its speaker and context.
In later sessions, ask participants what the term means and how they use it.
Compare instances of the term across participants and situations.
Ask what analytic category the term points to and what actions it is linked with.
Integrate the term into developing categories and use it to check your own code labels.
outputs: Codes anchored in participants' language, analysed meanings of key terms, and a check on researcher-imposed labels.
useWhen: Interview and field studies in communities with their own vocabulary (professionals, enthusiasts, subcultures), and when product language should match users' terms.
avoidWhen: Avoid stopping at catchy quotes: reproducing usage is not analysis. For large-scale vocabulary questions use content analysis or search-log analysis.
whyLost: UX teams quote participants freely but rarely code with their terms and interrogate them systematically.
whereToUse: Terminology and labelling decisions, content design, professional tools (clinical, legal, trading), community products.
example: Traders describe certain alerts as 'noise'. Interrogating the term across interviews shows it means alerts that arrive when no action is possible, which reframes the notification redesign around actionability.
reference: Charmaz, K. (2006). Constructing Grounded Theory: A Practical Guide through Qualitative Analysis. London: Sage, pp. 55-57.

name: In vivo problem-solving research
donor: Cognitive psychology of problem solving and creativity
origin: Kevin Dunbar (1995, 1999); Christensen and Schunn (2007)
summary: Record real working sessions of experts and code the transcripts for a specific cognitive process, measuring how often and with what consequence it occurs in natural work.
description: Lab studies of thinking often show processes are rare, while real work may show the opposite. Dunbar's in vivo method recorded real laboratory meetings of molecular biologists and immunologists and coded transcripts for a targeted cognitive process, here the use of analogy to solve problems. Scientists used 3 to 15 analogies per hour-long meeting, and Christensen and Schunn found design engineers developing medical plastic products proposed one about every 5 minutes, with an 'envelope' analogy leading to a paper-based design. This resolved the 'analogical paradox': analogy is rare in lab experiments but common in real work. The method combines naturalistic recording with a precise coding scheme, yielding frequencies, types and consequences of the process, and can be paired with in vitro lab studies to test mechanisms. It is time-consuming and cannot isolate variables.
steps: Choose the cognitive process of interest (for example analogy, hypothesis testing, error detection) and define it operationally.
Gain access to real working sessions (design reviews, lab meetings, incident calls) and record them with consent.
Transcribe and code each instance of the process with a defined scheme, including its type and source.
Trace the consequence of each instance (did it change the design, solve the problem, get discarded?).
Compute frequencies per hour and by type, and compare across teams or session types.
Where useful, follow up with controlled in vitro studies to test mechanisms suggested by the field data.
outputs: Frequency, type and consequences of the coded cognitive process in natural work settings.
useWhen: Designing tools for expert collaborative work (design, engineering, science, incident response) and you need to know how reasoning actually happens in meetings.
avoidWhen: When you need causal evidence or quick turnaround; use lab experiments or interviews. Access to real sessions may be impossible for confidential work.
whyLost: It sits in cognitive science of science and design studies; UX studies collaborative work with interviews or contextual inquiry but rarely codes cognitive processes in recorded sessions.
whereToUse: Collaborative design and whiteboarding tools, research and engineering platforms, AI assistants for brainstorming, incident management tools.
example: A team building an AI brainstorming assistant records 12 real product design meetings and codes analogies. Analogies from distant domains appear about every 8 minutes and most often come from one senior member, so the assistant is designed to suggest cross-domain analogies to everyone.
reference: Dunbar, K. (1995). How scientists really reason: scientific reasoning in real-world laboratories. In R. J. Sternberg and J. E. Davidson (eds), The Nature of Insight. MIT Press, pp. 365-395.

name: In-Context Gesture Teaching Plan
aka: In-context gesture teaching plan (coaching, levelling up, power-ups)
origin: Josh Clark (2015), adapting video-game tutorial design
summary: Plan how each gesture is taught at the moment of need: cues that match behaviour, in-context coaching, responses to mistakes and idleness, levels, and shortcuts unlocked as power-ups.
description: Gestures are invisible, and up-front tutorials, overlays and manuals fail because people dive in and skip them. Clark borrows from games. First, check that every element acts as it looks and that nothing acts in ways nothing signals; flat designs need motion or partial cues, such as a clipped tile hinting at a scroll. Coaching teaches by demonstration and practice in the live interface at the moment a gesture is first needed, ideally requiring the gesture to continue, and stops once the user has performed it. Responses to mistakes (a card that bounces back the right way) and idleness (a ghost hand after a pause) form a smart teaching layer. Levelling up teaches basics first and advanced moves only when needed. Power-ups reveal shortcuts as rewards after the slow route has been used repeatedly. The plan records, per gesture, its trigger, demonstration, practice, stop rule and error and idle responses.
steps: List the product's gestures and classify each as obvious (physical or digital precedent) or abstract (needs explicit help).
Check every element: does it look like something it does not act like, or act in ways nothing signals? Fix with behaviour or cues such as clipped tiles or animation.
For each gesture define the moment it is first needed and a demonstration plus practice step, preferably in the live interface.
Define a stop rule: stop hinting once the user performs the gesture.
Define responses to wrong gestures (redirect) and to idleness (an animated hint after a few seconds).
Sequence skills into levels, pausing to require a gesture only when it is critical.
For shortcuts, count uses of the slow route and after a threshold (the book's mock-up uses ten) reveal the gesture with an animation and ask the user to copy it.
outputs: A teaching map per gesture: trigger, demonstration, practice, stop rule, and error and idle responses.
useWhen: Use when designing touch, trackpad or spatial interfaces that rely on gestures, or when analytics show users never discover key shortcuts.
avoidWhen: Avoid front-loading instruction, which makes an app look complicated. The plan is a design hypothesis: check discoverability with Usability Testing or a Gesture Elicitation Study, and with first-use analytics after launch.
whyLost: It survived because coach marks, contextual hints and progressive onboarding are standard in mobile and game design, though the full plan with stop rules is less often written down.
whereToUse: Mobile apps, tablet reading and media apps, AR/VR interfaces, trackpad and pen tools, games.
example: A news app animates its dial until the reader moves it, then never shows the hint again. After a reader has used the menu ten times to reach saved articles, a short animation shows the two-finger swipe shortcut and asks them to try it.
reference: Clark, J. (2015). Designing for Touch. New York: A Book Apart, ch. 5.

name: In-product satisfaction tracking surveys (HaTS, CSat, NSAT)
donor: Survey methodology; marketing research; product analytics
origin: Google HaTS from 2006 (Müller, Sedley and Ferrall-Nunge); Microsoft NSAT; CSat programme practice at Google, Microsoft and Amazon
summary: A short, fixed satisfaction survey (one labelled rating plus open 'why?' questions) shown continuously to random samples of users and tracked over time within each population.
description: Continuous satisfaction tracking listens to customers over time rather than proving the effect of a release. Google's Happiness Tracking Survey samples users, not page views, into weekly random buckets and shows a small non-blocking invitation; anyone invited is excluded for at least twelve weeks. Page one asks overall satisfaction on a fully labelled 7-point bipolar scale, then open questions on frustrations, wished-for capabilities and what people like best. Chapman and Rodden generalise this into a CSat programme: a defined population, one ordinal rating (5 or 7 points, labelled, with midpoint), one open 'why?', minimal demographics, a baseline period after which wording and sources are frozen, and reporting of proportions with confidence intervals and top-2-box. Microsoft's NSAT is a scoring variant: a 4-point scale scored as % Very Satisfied minus % dissatisfied, plus 100. Rigour comes from random sampling, frozen instruments and within-population comparison only.
steps: Define the active-user population, the channel (in-product, email to known customers, or panel with validated screener) and the target number of completes per period.
Randomly assign users (not page views) to weekly buckets, show one bucket a non-blocking invitation, and exclude invitees from re-sampling for at least twelve weeks.
Ask the overall satisfaction question first on a fully labelled 5- or 7-point scale, then one or two open questions ('why did you give that rating?', frustrations, best-liked aspects).
Pre-test wording, run a baseline period to settle sources and scale, then freeze everything; if using NSAT, score % Very Satisfied minus (% Somewhat + % Very Dissatisfied) plus 100 (range 0-200).
Analyse rating proportions and top-2-box with confidence intervals over time within each population, marking launches on the time series.
Read or code all open answers split by positive and negative raters and frequency-sort themes to prioritise.
Report sample characteristics, trends with CIs, cautious group differences, comment themes and recommendations; keep closed-loop customer follow-up separate.
outputs: A satisfaction time series with launch markers and confidence intervals, top-2-box trends or NSAT scores, ranked frustrations and likes, and recommendations.
useWhen: When you need a steady listening channel on how satisfaction moves across releases, to detect and size change aversion after redesigns, and to surface recurring frustrations at scale.
avoidWhen: Avoid for attributing effects to a specific feature (ratings rarely move after launches; use an A/B test), for comparing countries or products (cultural response styles differ), or when you cannot commit to maintaining it. Driver analysis is defeated by collinearity; tying pay to CSat biases reporting.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, continuous and gives executives a trend line; HaTS published a disciplined template that many teams copy, though often without the random sampling and frozen wording.
whereToUse: SaaS and consumer apps with large active bases, post-redesign change-aversion monitoring, multi-product portfolios needing a common listening format.
example: After a navigation redesign in a banking app, weekly HaTS-style satisfaction dips for three weeks and recovers by week six; coded open answers show the dip is driven by a moved transfer button, which is then restored.
reference: Müller, H., Sedley, A., & Ferrall-Nunge, E. (2014). Survey research in HCI. In Ways of Knowing in HCI. Springer; Chapman, C., & Rodden, K. (2023). Quantitative User Experience Research. Apress, pp. 127-140.

name: Inattentional blindness detection
origin: Mack and Rock, 1998; Simons and Chabris's 'gorillas in our midst' study, 1999
summary: Tests whether users engaged in a demanding primary task fail to notice salient but unexpected events, such as alerts, that they would easily see if looking for them.
description: Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice a fully visible but unexpected object when attention is engaged elsewhere. Simons and Chabris showed around half of viewers counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit. Detection depends on the load of the primary task and the similarity of the unexpected item to attended items, not just on its salience. Testing it requires surprise: participants must not expect the event, so each participant can usually contribute only one 'critical trial', which drives sample size. The method complements salience audits, showing whether prominent design actually captures attention under realistic workload. Rigour comes from realistic task load, single critical trials, and careful post-trial questioning that avoids leading questions. An early informal example: in a test reported by Cooper (1999), a status bar announced every five minutes that a $50 note was taped under the participant's chair, and over a full day with more than a dozen participants nobody claimed it.
steps: Define the primary task at realistic load and the unexpected event (for example a new alert appearing mid-task).
Recruit enough participants for proportion estimates; since each gives one critical trial, aim for at least 20-30 per condition.
Run the task, introduce the event once without warning, and afterwards ask open then progressively specific questions ('Did you notice anything unusual?').
Compute detection rates per condition with confidence intervals and compare designs with a chi-square or Fisher's exact test.
Optionally include eye tracking to distinguish 'looked but did not see' from never fixated.
Redesign events to resemble attended features or interrupt the primary task channel, and re-test with new participants.
outputs: Detection rates per design and load condition, eye-tracking evidence where used, and design changes that improve capture of unexpected events.
useWhen: When critical alerts or changes must be noticed during demanding work, such as surgery, driving, monitoring or trading.
avoidWhen: When events are expected or users actively search for them; use visual search or d' testing instead.
whyLost: Widely known as a psychology curiosity, but rarely operationalised in UX because the one-trial design needs many participants.
whereToUse: Surgical and clinical displays, driver assistance HMIs, cockpit and control room design, and security monitoring.
example: In a simulation, 11 of 24 surgeons focused on suturing fail to notice a prominent yellow pressure warning. Moving the warning into the endoscopic field and pairing it with a tone raises detection to 22 of 24.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
Cooper, A., The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (Sams, 1999; 2004 reissue)
reference: Simons, D. J. & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.

name: Inclusive Design Research
origin: Roger Coleman (inclusive design, UK, 1994); popularised by Kat Holmes and Microsoft's Inclusive Design toolkit (2016)
summary: Research with people across disability, age, culture and cognition, recruiting from the margins to reveal exclusions that average-user research hides.
description: Inclusive design research treats exclusion as a mismatch between a person and a designed environment rather than a property of the person. Instead of recruiting a representative middle, the researcher deliberately recruits people at the edges: blind and low-vision users, people with motor, cognitive or hearing impairments, older adults, people with low literacy or limited bandwidth, and people experiencing temporary or situational limitations. Their workarounds expose design constraints that also affect everyone else. Rigour comes from a documented recruitment frame across a persona spectrum (permanent, temporary, situational), accessible study logistics (formats, consent, assistive technology, paid access support), and analysis that traces each finding to a specific exclusion mechanism rather than a generic 'accessibility issue'. It goes beyond WCAG compliance, which checks conformance, by asking whether people can actually accomplish meaningful goals.
steps: Define the exclusion spectrum for the product: list permanent, temporary and situational limitations across vision, hearing, motor, cognition, speech, language and context.
Recruit at least 5-8 participants from the edges of that spectrum, through disability organisations or specialist panels, budgeting for access support and fair compensation.
Adapt study logistics in advance: accessible consent forms, the participant's own devices and assistive technology, flexible session lengths and breaks.
Run sessions on real goals in the participant's own setup, observing workarounds, abandonment points and the effort each step costs.
Code every barrier against the mismatch it reveals (sensory, motor, cognitive, linguistic, situational) and note who else the same barrier affects.
Co-create or test solutions with the same participants and verify the fix extends to mainstream users.
Report findings as exclusion mechanisms with severity and reach, alongside any WCAG success criteria they map to.
outputs: Exclusion map across the persona spectrum, prioritised barrier list with affected populations, workaround catalogue, and design principles for inclusion.
useWhen: When a product serves the general public, regulated sectors, or ageing and diverse populations; when you need to know whether people can actually complete goals rather than whether the code conforms.
avoidWhen: When you only need a conformance check (use an accessibility audit against WCAG) or when you cannot fund access support and fair compensation, in which case partner with a disability organisation first.
whyLost: Still in use: Growing legal, ethical, and business case; Microsoft, BBC, and Apple frameworks widely adopted.
whereToUse: All digital products; especially public services, health, and education.
example: A UK bank tests its mobile cheque-deposit flow with a screen-reader user, a person with tremor and a user with dyslexia. The camera auto-capture timeout fails all three, and extending it plus adding a manual capture button also cuts abandonment among sighted users in low light.
sources: Mismatch: How Inclusion Shapes Design (Kat Holmes)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Holmes K (2018) Mismatch: How Inclusion Shapes Design. MIT Press

name: Incomplete Block Designs (BIBD, PBIB, Alpha and Test-versus-Control Designs)
origin: Frank Yates, 1936 (BIBD and recovery of interblock information); Bose and Nair, 1939 (PBIB); Cox, 1958 (reinforced designs); Patterson and Williams, 1976 (alpha designs); Bechhofer and Tamhane, 1981 (BTIB)
summary: Designs for when each block (often one participant) can take only some of the treatments, allocating subsets so comparisons stay balanced or nearly so, with block-adjusted analysis.
description: When a block holds fewer units than there are treatments, as when a participant can evaluate only three of nine prototypes, each block receives a subset. In a balanced incomplete block design every pair of treatments appears together in the same number of blocks, lambda, so all comparisons are equally precise; parameters must satisfy rt = bk and lambda(t - 1) = r(k - 1), and designs exist only for some combinations (for example t = 6, b = 10, k = 3, r = 5, lambda = 2). Partially balanced designs relax this into a few association classes when no practical BIBD exists; alpha designs give resolvable layouts for any block size; reinforced and BTIB designs maximise precision of test-versus-control comparisons. Intrablock analysis estimates treatment effects within blocks; treating blocks as random lets interblock information be recovered with REML. The design must be connected so every difference is estimable.
steps: Fix the number of treatments t and the block size k that a participant, session or unit can tolerate.

Choose a BIBD from published tables or software; if none of practical size exists, use a PBIB or alpha design with high efficiency factor, or a BTIB or reinforced design if comparisons with a control matter most.
Check the design is connected so every treatment difference is estimable.
Randomise the block labels, the allocation of treatment sets to blocks and the order of positions within each block.
Analyse with a block-plus-treatment model, reporting block-adjusted treatment means and contrasts.
Where blocks can be treated as random and there are enough treatments, estimate block and error variances by REML and use the combined intra- and interblock estimator.
outputs: Block-adjusted treatment means and contrasts with standard errors, an incomplete-block ANOVA, and the chosen design's efficiency.
useWhen: Within-subject comparisons of many variants (icons, copy options, voices, prototypes) where fatigue limits each participant to a few, or sessions, devices or days that cannot host every condition.
avoidWhen: When each block can take every treatment (use Randomised Complete Block Design (RCBD)); when only rank order of many items matters and a ready method exists (MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) already uses balanced incomplete designs); or with carryover effects not addressed by counterbalancing.
whyLost: Common in agriculture and sensory panels, and hidden inside MaxDiff and conjoint software, but rarely set up deliberately by UX researchers, who either show every variant or randomise subsets ad hoc.
whereToUse: Rating many design alternatives, voice or sound evaluation, icon and illustration testing, multi-variant concept tests, fatigue-limited participants such as clinicians.
example: Nine candidate app icons are rated by 36 participants, each seeing three. A BIBD with every pair of icons together in the same number of participants, randomised in order, gives block-adjusted means with equal precision for all 36 pairwise comparisons.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 2 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2005)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Yates, F. (1936). Incomplete randomized blocks. Annals of Eugenics, 7, 121-140; Hinkelmann, K., & Kempthorne, O. (2005). Design and Analysis of Experiments, Volume 2: Advanced Experimental Design. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 1-212.

name: Independent component analysis
aka: Blind source separation of variation patterns
origin: Cardoso and Souloumiac (1993) JADE algorithm; applied to manufacturing variation by Apley and Lee (2003)
summary: Separates several independent sources of variation mixed in correlated measurements by finding the rotation that makes estimated sources statistically independent, not merely uncorrelated.
description: Multivariate measurements are modelled as a linear mixture of a few underlying sources plus noise. Principal components analysis can count the sources from dominant eigenvalues, but its axes are distorted whenever the source patterns are not orthogonal, so each component may blend causes. Varimax-type rotation assumes each source touches a separate subset of variables. Blind source separation instead whitens the data and searches for the orthogonal rotation that minimises fourth-order cross-cumulants (the JADE criterion). This identifies the sources uniquely provided at most one is Gaussian. The result is a mixing matrix showing how each source shows up across variables and a score for each source per case. ICA can be read as another form of factor rotation; which rotation is more accurate depends on which assumptions hold, so the non-Gaussianity assumption should be checked.
steps: Run PCA and count dominant eigenvalues to set the number of sources p; estimate noise variance from the remaining small eigenvalues.
Whiten the data using the first p principal components.
Estimate the rotation that minimises fourth-order cross-cumulants (JADE) or use another ICA algorithm such as FastICA.
Compute the mixing matrix and recover each source's score per case by regression.
Plot histograms of the estimated sources and confirm that no more than one looks Gaussian.
Display each source pattern on a diagram of the product or journey so domain experts can name its cause, and compare with a varimax solution.
outputs: Estimated source patterns (mixing matrix) and per-case source scores, with a check of the non-Gaussianity assumption.
useWhen: Many correlated measurements are thought to be driven by a few independent causes, such as interaction telemetry, physiological signals or performance metrics, and PCA components look like blends.
avoidWhen: More than one source is likely Gaussian, or the goal is simply data reduction (use PCA) or latent constructs from questionnaire items (use factor analysis).
whyLost: ICA is established in signal processing, neuroimaging and quality engineering but has never been presented as a UX analysis technique.
whereToUse: Separating causes in web-performance metrics, multi-channel biometric or EEG data, sensor telemetry from devices, and mixed behavioural signals in product analytics.
example: An e-commerce team tracks ten page-timing metrics across 50,000 sessions. PCA shows two dominant components but each mixes network and rendering effects. ICA separates a source loading on time-to-first-byte and DNS (network) from one loading on script and layout timings (front-end), so each team gets its own signal.
sources: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: Apley, D. W. (2003). Principal components and factor analysis. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 193-214). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Indicators and Signposts Monitoring
origin: Military indications and warning (I&W) practice from the Cold War; structured technique in Heuer and Pherson (2010)
summary: Defines in advance observable indicators that would signal which of several scenarios or hypotheses is unfolding, and monitors them systematically.
description: Rather than waiting for certainty, analysts define for each scenario or hypothesis a set of indicators: observable events or trends that would be more likely if it were true. Good indicators are observable, valid (diagnostic between scenarios), reliable, stable and unique. A monitoring matrix tracks indicator status over time (e.g. green, amber, red), and changes trigger reassessment. For UX and product strategy, this turns research conclusions and scenario plans into living monitoring systems: which signals would tell us our assumptions about AI adoption, competitor behaviour or user needs are wrong?
steps: List the scenarios or hypotheses to discriminate between.
For each, brainstorm indicators that would be observable if it were unfolding.
Screen indicators for observability, diagnosticity, reliability and timeliness.
Define thresholds and data sources (analytics, research, market data) for each indicator.
Monitor on a fixed cadence and record status in an indicator matrix.
Trigger reassessment and decision reviews when indicators cross thresholds.
outputs: Indicator lists per scenario, a monitoring matrix and trigger-based decision reviews.
useWhen: Strategic uncertainty with competing futures or hypotheses, and when research conclusions need ongoing validation.
avoidWhen: Stable, well-understood domains where standard KPI monitoring suffices.
whyLost: It is an intelligence and military practice; product teams track KPIs but rarely define diagnostic indicators for hypotheses.
whereToUse: AI product strategy, market entry, regulatory change, platform shifts, long-term research programmes.
example: A fintech defines indicators distinguishing 'users want AI financial advice' from 'users want only automation'. Rising rates of follow-up questions on AI summaries trigger an earlier investment in advisory features.
sources: Heuer & Pherson, Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis (2nd ed., 2014)
Grabo, Anticipating Surprise: Analysis for Strategic Warning (2002)
reference: Grabo, C. M. (2002). Anticipating Surprise: Analysis for Strategic Warning. Joint Military Intelligence College.

name: Individualised Emotion Profiling (IZOF)
origin: Yuri Hanin, from 1978 (zones of optimal functioning for anxiety), extended to multiple emotions in the 1990s with Syrjä; described by Hanin in Chapter 2 of the Handbook
summary: Has each person recall their best and worst performances, describe the emotions that went with them in their own words, and establish personal intensity zones in which each emotion helps or hurts.
description: IZOF rejects the idea that one level of arousal or anxiety suits everyone; Hanin reports that roughly a third of athletes perform best at high, a third at moderate and a third at low anxiety. Profiling works within each person. They recall their best and worst performances and, helped by a stimulus list, choose their own emotion words. Each word is placed in one of four categories: pleasant and helpful (P+), unpleasant and helpful (N+), pleasant and harmful (P-) and unpleasant and harmful (N-). They then rate the intensity of each emotion for each performance, which gives a personal optimal or dysfunctional zone, traditionally a mean plus or minus half a standard deviation, or an interquartile range when repeated readings exist. Current states can be compared with these zones to predict and adjust performance. The approach shows that unpleasant emotions such as tension can help and pleasant ones such as complacency can hurt. In UX it suits high-stakes, performance-oriented use: live presenting, streaming, competitive gaming, trading, clinical or dispatch software. It reveals which feelings users see as useful, so designs need not try to remove all stress.
steps: Recruit users whose product use has clear performance outcomes, and ask each to recall a best and a worst recent session.
Have them generate their own emotion words for each, using a stimulus list as a prompt rather than a fixed scale.
Ask them to place each word in P+, N+, P- or N-, according to whether it felt pleasant and whether it helped.
Collect intensity ratings for each word for the best and worst sessions, and where possible for further sessions over time.
Derive individual optimal and dysfunctional zones and build a personal profile for each user.
Aggregate across users to find common helpful and harmful states, then relate them to product moments that trigger them.
outputs: Personal emotion profiles with idiosyncratic labels, helpful or harmful category, and intensity zones, plus a cross-user summary of the most common helpful and harmful states.
useWhen: Users perform under pressure with the product and you suspect that 'reduce stress' is too crude a design goal.
avoidWhen: Use is casual and low-stakes, participants cannot recall distinct good and bad sessions, or you need a quick standardised measure.
whyLost: Affect research in UX relies on standard scales such as PANAS or SAM, which cover the whole group; idiographic profiling is time-consuming and known mainly in applied sport psychology.
whereToUse: Presentation and live-streaming software, esports and competitive games, trading platforms, emergency dispatch and clinical systems, exam and assessment platforms.
example: A live-streaming tool team profiles 15 streamers. Many name 'buzzing' and 'on edge' as helpful (N+) during their best streams but 'flustered' as harmful when chat moderation tools fail. The team keeps the live-audience counter but simplifies moderation actions.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Hanin, Y. L. (2007) 'Emotions in sport: current issues and perspectives', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 2.

name: Individualised mixture profiles
aka: Individualised mixture profiles with bits-per-item scoring
origin: Cadez, Smyth and colleagues, c. 2001; presented by Ip, Cadez and Smyth, 2003
summary: Describe each user as their own weighting of shared behaviour components, shrunk towards the population mix, and score models by out-of-sample predictive bits per item.
description: The method applies latent-variable thinking to transaction or usage data. A global set of K mixture components describes typical baskets or sessions, fitted with EM on all transactions. Each individual then gets weights over those components estimated from their own history, with a Dirichlet prior that pulls people with little data towards the population weights. Each person's history is split by time, 70 per cent for training and 30 per cent for testing, and models are scored as predictive entropy in bits per item; a random guess scores log2 of the number of items. Components are described by items with lift above 1. On drugstore data, individualised models beat the global model across 1-200 components. The same chapter fits a two-type mixture of shopping rhythms (random versus regular inter-purchase gaps). Unlike hard segmentation, users are not forced into one segment.
steps: Choose the number of components K, trying a range.
Fit global components with EM on all transactions or sessions.
Estimate each person's component weights with Dirichlet shrinkage towards the population mix.
Split each person's history by time, 70 per cent train and 30 per cent test.
Score out-of-sample bits per item against the random baseline and the global model, and select K.
Describe each component by its high-lift items and interpret individual profiles as mixtures.
outputs: Per-person behaviour profiles, component descriptions, and predictive scores in bits per item.
useWhen: Users show repeated behaviour (purchases, feature use, content) and mix several modes, so soft per-user profiles are more truthful than hard segments.
avoidWhen: Most users have few events; component labels are interpretations. For one-off survey segmentation use latent class or cluster analysis.
whyLost: It came from early-2000s data mining research; product analytics moved to embeddings and hard segments, and the shrinkage and predictive-scoring discipline was not carried into UX.
whereToUse: Retail and grocery apps, streaming and content platforms, SaaS feature usage, personalisation research.
example: A grocery app models each shopper as a mix of components such as weekly family shop, quick snack run and baby care. A new parent's profile shifts towards baby care within weeks, informing research on life-event triggers.
reference: Ip, E., Cadez, I., & Smyth, P. (2003). Psychometric methods of latent variable modeling. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 215-246). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Information Architecture
donor: Library and information science; cognitive psychology
origin: Richard Saul Wurman, 1976 (term); Louis Rosenfeld & Peter Morville, 1998 (Information Architecture for the World Wide Web)
summary: The practice of designing organisation, labelling, navigation and search systems so people can find, understand and manage information, informed by research on users, content and context.
description: Information architecture is the structural design of shared information environments. Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango describe four interlocking systems: organisation (how content is grouped), labelling (how it is named), navigation (how people move through it) and search (how people query it). IA practice balances users (their tasks and mental models), content (its volume, types and metadata) and context (business goals, constraints and culture). As a research-driven practice it draws on card sorting, tree testing, content inventories, search log analysis and usability testing. Rigour comes from basing structures on evidence of user mental models and tasks rather than organisational charts, designing controlled vocabularies and metadata, testing structures before visual design, and measuring findability after launch.
steps: Audit existing content with a content inventory, noting types, volume, owners and metadata.
Research users' tasks and mental models with interviews, search log analysis and card sorting.
Define organisation schemes, controlled vocabularies and metadata.
Draft the hierarchy, labels and navigation and test them with tree testing.
Design search, including synonyms and facets, using search log evidence.
Validate the integrated design with usability testing and measure findability after launch.
outputs: Content inventory, site maps and hierarchies, labelling systems, controlled vocabularies, metadata schema and findability metrics.
useWhen: For information-dense products such as websites, intranets, documentation, e-commerce catalogues and enterprise tools, and for redesigns of navigation and search.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating IA as just a site map exercise without research; run card sorting, tree testing and search analysis. For simple single-task apps, a lighter flow design suffices.
whyLost: Still in use: Foundational practice; increasingly integrated with content strategy and SEO.
whereToUse: Any information-dense product; websites; enterprise tools; documentation systems.
example: A medical knowledge base reorganises 4,000 articles. Search logs show clinicians search by symptom while content is organised by specialty, so a faceted symptom-and-specialty structure is designed and tree tested, raising findability from 52 to 81 percent.
sources: Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld, Morville & Arango)
reference: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J. (2015). Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (4th ed.). O'Reilly.

name: Information Foraging Analysis
origin: Peter Pirolli and Stuart Card, Xerox PARC, 1995-1999
summary: Models information seeking as foraging that maximises information gain per unit cost, quantifying information scent, patch residence and diet choice.
description: Borrowing from optimal foraging theory in ecology, Pirolli and Card modelled users as foragers who move between information patches (pages, search results, documents) and decide when to leave a patch using Charnov's marginal value theorem: leave when the rate of gain in the current patch drops below the average rate in the environment. Information scent, the perceived value of a link from its proximal cues, determines navigation, and was computationally modelled with spreading activation (SNIF-ACT). Rigorous application measures scent quantitatively, predicts navigation choices and patch-leaving, and compares predicted and observed paths. UX retains 'information scent' as a slogan while dropping the models and measurements.
steps: Define the user's information goal precisely and the information environment (patches, links, cues).
Measure information scent: have participants or a semantic model rate how likely each link leads to the goal.
Predict navigation by choosing the highest-scent link at each step, and predict patch-leaving via the marginal value theorem.
Collect navigation and dwell data with logs or a tree-test-like task.
Compare predicted and observed paths and patch residence times; identify scent misleads and dead patches.
Rewrite labels and summaries to strengthen accurate scent and re-measure.
outputs: Scent ratings per link, predicted versus observed path match, patch residence analysis and label improvements.
useWhen: Diagnosing navigation, search results, documentation sites and content-heavy products where users hunt for information.
avoidWhen: Transactional flows with no information seeking.
whyLost: The slogan 'follow the scent' entered practitioner vocabulary without the quantitative modelling, which requires cognitive modelling skills.
whereToUse: Documentation portals, intranets, e-commerce category pages, search results and AI answer citations.
example: A developer docs site measures scent ratings for 40 nav labels against 12 tasks. Labels like 'Concepts' have low scent; renaming to task-oriented labels raises first-click success from 48% to 71%.
sources: Pirolli & Card, Information foraging (1999), Psychological Review
Pirolli, Information Foraging Theory: Adaptive Interaction with Information (2007)
reference: Pirolli, P., & Card, S. (1999). Information foraging. Psychological Review, 106(4), 643-675.

name: Information Service Evaluation (ISE) Model
origin: Larissa Schumann and Wolfgang Stock, 2014; applied by Ilhan, Fietkiewicz and Stock, 2017
summary: Evaluate a digital service on three linked dimensions, perceived quality, acceptance, and user need and satisfaction, combining fieldwork with a survey and cross-dimension correlations.
description: The ISE model frames evaluation of an information service around three dimensions. D1 perceived service quality covers ease of use, usefulness and trust. D2 acceptance covers adoption versus continued use, impact on behaviour and diffusion through recommendation. D3 covers user needs and satisfaction. Research questions are framed for each dimension and for relations between them. In the published application to a city parking-payment app, the team combined a case study, rapid ethnographic fieldwork and interviews with city authorities with a seven-point Likert online survey, reporting awareness and use rates, reasons for non-use, medians, Cronbach's alpha for each dimension and Spearman correlations between indicators. The result showed whether quality, acceptance and need actually align, for example that usefulness rather than ease of use related to use.
steps: Frame research questions for each ISE dimension and for relations between them.
Run case-study fieldwork and interviews with service owners and operators.
Build an online Likert survey covering the three dimensions plus awareness and reasons for non-use.
Report awareness, adoption and frequency of use.
Check internal consistency of each dimension (Cronbach's alpha).
Correlate indicators across dimensions with rank correlations, interpreting with care when the user subsample is small.
outputs: An awareness and usage profile, reasons for non-use, dimension reliability and cross-dimension correlations.
useWhen: Evaluating public or smart-city digital services, library and information services, or any service where adoption and need are in doubt as well as usability.
avoidWhen: Diagnosing interface problems (use Usability Testing) or when the user subsample will be too small for correlations.
whyLost: It remained within information science and smart-city research, while UX uses TAM or SUS-style questionnaires instead.
whereToUse: Smart-city apps, e-government, library services, transport and parking apps.
example: A city surveys 131 drivers about its parking app: 62% had never heard of it and 8% used it. Usefulness, not ease of use, tracked use and satisfaction, so the city invests in awareness and features, not UI polish.
reference: Ilhan, A., Fietkiewicz, K.J. and Stock, W.G. (2017) Do car drivers really need mobile parking payment? A critical evaluation of the smart service apparkB in Barcelona. In Marcus, A. and Wang, W. (eds) DUXU 2017, LNCS 10289. Cham: Springer, pp. 241-254.

name: Information-access-cost manipulation
origin: Ballard, Hayhoe, Pook and Rao, 1997 (block-copying); Gray and Fu, 2004, and Gray et al., 2006 (soft constraints)
summary: Experimentally vary how costly it is to reach task information in the interface and measure how people trade off remembering, looking and acting.
description: Two paradigms show that people choose between memory and the world by milliseconds of cost. In Ballard's block-copying task, participants copy a pattern of coloured blocks while eye-tracked; they glance back at the model before and after each pick-up, storing only colour or position per glance, and miss changes made to the model while looking elsewhere. In Gray and Fu's task, people program a simulated VCR from show information that is either always visible or hidden under grey boxes needing a click. When access costs even a little, people switch to memory, preferring imperfect memory over perfect information in the world, which raises errors. The soft-constraints view treats these as cost-benefit trade-offs at the scale of a few hundred milliseconds. Clark frames the dispute with the minimal-memory view as evidence of a testable science of how cognition spreads across mind and interface.
steps: Define a task that needs reference information (copying data between screens, entering details, comparing options).
Make the information available at different access costs, for example always visible versus covered and click-to-reveal versus on another tab, with a group that memorised it beforehand.
Record fixations, clicks, timing and errors; optionally change the reference covertly while the participant looks away to test what was retained.
Compare strategy mix (look up versus recall), re-inspection counts, time and error rates across cost conditions.
Interpret which resource people rely on at each phase and at what cost threshold they switch.
Translate into design: keep needed information visible where errors are costly, or deliberately raise access cost only where memorisation is desired.
outputs: Re-inspection counts, retrieval time costs, error rates and strategy descriptions per access-cost condition.
useWhen: When designing interfaces where users must carry information between places (forms, multi-tab workflows, comparisons, data entry) and memory errors are costly.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on self-report: participants describe neater strategies than they use. Time may not be the only cost that matters. For general memory load audits use Working memory load audit; for gaze alone use Eye Tracking.
whyLost: It lives in cognitive science and cognitive engineering labs; practitioners know 'recognition over recall' as a heuristic but rarely manipulate access cost experimentally.
whereToUse: Clinical data entry, financial transfers (copying account numbers), comparison shopping, multi-window enterprise tools, AI copilots that move information between contexts.
example: In a banking prototype, the payee's account number is either visible beside the entry field or on a previous screen. With one extra step, 60% of participants type from memory and error rates triple, so the number stays visible.
reference: Gray, W. D., & Fu, W.-T. (2004). Soft constraints in interactive behavior: The case of ignoring perfect knowledge in-the-world for imperfect knowledge in-the-head. Cognitive Science, 28(3), 359-382; Ballard, D. H., Hayhoe, M. M., Pook, P. K., & Rao, R. P. N. (1997). Deictic codes for the embodiment of cognition. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 20(4), 723-767.

name: Information-Seeking Mode Analysis
aka: Known-item, exploratory, re-finding and don't-know-what-you-need-to-know seeking
What must users already know? check
origin: Donna Spencer, 'Four modes of seeking information and how to design for them' (Boxes and Arrows); applied by Laura Martin (2019)
summary: Classify the seeking situations users bring to a site into four modes and check whether navigation, categories and search serve each, exposing structures that only support known-item lookup.
description: Spencer distinguishes four ways people look for information: known-item (they know what, not where), exploratory (no fixed target), re-finding (they have been there before) and don't-know-what-you-need-to-know (they are not yet sure of the question). Martin arranges the modes on two axes, certainty about what is sought and certainty about where it is, and turns them into a test question for any structure: what must a user already know to find this? A structure built from expert classification, such as tea organised by blend and region, works for known-item seekers and fails everyone else. The analysis walks each key seeking situation through the navigation and records the knowledge each step presumes, then adds browsing support where only lookup works. Its value is diagnostic rather than statistical: it makes the hidden knowledge requirements of a taxonomy explicit.
steps: From existing research, list the main seeking situations and assign each to one of the four modes.
For each situation, walk the navigation path and note at every step the knowledge the user must already hold, such as jargon or a classification scheme.
Mark paths where only known-item seeking succeeds and exploratory or uncertain seekers stall.
Add browsing support where gaps appear: definitions, alternative groupings by need or use, related links and entry points phrased in users' terms.
Check that search serves known-item and re-finding needs, for example through history, saved items and tolerant matching.
Re-walk the revised structure for each mode and record remaining gaps.
outputs: A mode-by-path gap list showing which seeking modes each part of the structure supports, with the knowledge each path presumes and proposed browsing aids.
useWhen: Auditing or designing navigation for catalogues, help centres and content sites where users range from experts who know the item name to novices who cannot yet frame the question.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the modes as measured categories: they blur in practice and Martin calls her two-axis chart unscientific. For behavioural evidence of how people actually seek, use Site search analytics, Tree Testing or Information Foraging Analysis.
whyLost: Spencer's modes are widely cited in IA writing but rarely run as an explicit audit; teams lean on search logs and tree tests, which measure findability for known targets and miss exploratory and uncertain seeking.
whereToUse: E-commerce category design, documentation and help centres, intranets, public-service sites, and deciding whether a chatbot is masking a structure that requires prior knowledge.
example: A specialist tea retailer's navigation uses blends, regions and flavoured teas. Walking the 'I like strong black tea' situation shows each step assumes classification knowledge, so the team adds a 'by taste and strength' grouping and short category definitions.
reference: Martin, L. M. (2019). Everyday Information Architecture. New York: A Book Apart, pp. 89-94; Spencer, D. 'Four modes of seeking information and how to design for them', Boxes and Arrows.

name: Informed Consent Procedure
origin: US Common Rule (revised 2018); research ethics practice; comprehension and process-consent work by Festinger et al. and Adams, Holman Jones and Ellis
summary: Give prospective participants key information first, in accessible plain language, check they understood it, record consent, and revisit it during longer studies.
description: Consent is a process, not a signature. The revised Common Rule asks for legally effective consent before participation, time to decide without coercion, understandable language, the information a reasonable person would want, a concise key-information section first and no waiver of rights. Basic elements include purpose, procedures and duration, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, compensation, contacts, voluntariness and possible data reuse. Children assent while guardians give permission. Electronic consent follows the same rules, with question channels, stored e-signatures and identity checks. The strongest evidence-backed aid is a comprehension quiz with corrected feedback using open recall questions. Accessible variants offer audio or video consent, screen-reader-friendly forms, reading aloud and tactile signature guides. In long studies, process consent revisits voluntariness at planned check-ins.
steps: Send a short invitation stating who you are, why the person was approached, what participation involves, how long it takes and how to reply.

Draft the consent form with a key-information summary first, then the required elements (purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality, compensation, contacts, voluntariness and withdrawal, data reuse) in plain language.

Provide accessible formats: electronic forms that work with screen readers, audio or video consent where the ethics board allows, reading aloud with a signature guide; obtain proxy or guardian permission and child assent where required.
After review, ask open-ended recall questions on key points (for example what happens if they want to stop) and correct every wrong answer until understood.
Record consent on paper or electronically, verifying identity for eConsent, and give the participant a copy.
For multi-session or longitudinal studies, schedule check-ins that restate voluntariness and ask about burden, discomfort and benefits, adjusting the study if needed.
outputs: Invitation letter, consent form or eConsent flow, signed or recorded consent, comprehension record and process-consent log.
useWhen: Every study involving people, especially recordings, sensitive topics, minors, vulnerable or disabled participants, remote and unmoderated research, or longitudinal studies.
avoidWhen: Never skip it; for minimal-risk, anonymous analytics or intercepts seek a documented waiver rather than improvising. Recognition-style quizzes (true or false) overstate understanding, so use recall questions.
whyLost: It survived because ethics boards, law and data-protection rules require it, though in UX it is often reduced to a click-through form without comprehension checks or process consent.
whereToUse: Diary and longitudinal studies, health and financial research, research with children or disabled people, AI data-collection studies that may reuse data.
example: A fintech diary study uses an eConsent flow with a three-question recall check about data reuse and withdrawal. At week two and week four the researcher checks in on burden and reminds participants they can stop without losing payment.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
reference: Festinger, D. S., Dugosh, K. L., Callahan, H. R., & Hough, R. A. (2023). Informed consent to research. In A. L. Nichols & J. E. Edlund (Eds.), The Cambridge handbook of research methods and statistics for the social and behavioral sciences, Vol. 1 (pp. 202-223). Cambridge University Press.

name: Innovation Diffusion Analysis
origin: Everett Rogers, Diffusion of Innovations (1962); Frank Bass diffusion model (1969)
summary: Analysis of how a product or feature spreads through a population using Rogers' adopter categories and innovation attributes, optionally modelled with Bass or S-curve forecasts.
description: Innovation diffusion analysis explains and forecasts adoption over time. Rogers identified five attributes that predict adoption rate (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability) and adopter categories along a normal distribution: innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%), early majority (34%), late majority (34%) and laggards (16%). Bass's model formalises the cumulative S-curve with coefficients for innovation (external influence) and imitation (word of mouth). In UX and product work, the method combines attribute assessment through interviews or surveys with fitting adoption curves to feature-usage logs, and can simulate adoption under different design scenarios with Monte Carlo methods. Its rigour lies in separating attribute-driven barriers from network effects and in forecasting with explicit uncertainty rather than assuming adoption will follow launch.
steps: Define the innovation (product, feature or behaviour) and the population that could adopt it.
Assess the five innovation attributes through interviews or a survey, identifying which attribute most limits adoption.
Extract adoption timestamps from logs and plot cumulative adoption, classifying adopters into Rogers' categories by time of adoption.
Fit a Bass diffusion model to estimate innovation (p) and imitation (q) coefficients, with confidence intervals.
Simulate adoption under alternative design or launch scenarios (for example improved trialability), using Monte Carlo runs to express uncertainty.
Interview representatives of the late majority and non-adopters to explain barriers, and recommend interventions targeted to each category.
outputs: Attribute assessment, adopter segmentation, fitted S-curve and Bass coefficients, scenario forecasts and targeted adoption interventions.
useWhen: Planning launches and rollouts, diagnosing stalled feature adoption, forecasting uptake of new behaviours, and choosing between trialability, observability or simplicity interventions.
avoidWhen: When adoption data is too sparse to fit curves or the product is not a discretionary choice (mandated enterprise tools follow organisational decisions, not diffusion dynamics); use change-management or task analysis instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Framework for adoption strategy; technology adoption lifecycle widely referenced.
whereToUse: New product launch; feature adoption strategy; cross-chasm product design.
example: A banking app's new budgeting feature plateaus at 11% adoption. A Bass fit shows a low imitation coefficient, and interviews reveal the feature is invisible to others, so the team adds shareable monthly summaries and simulates a lift in q before rollout.
sources: Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella)
Bass, A new product growth for model consumer durables (Management Science, 1969)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 56 — Monte Carlo Simulation & Predictive Forecasting
reference: Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed. Free Press

name: Innovation Tracer Study
origin: Project Hindsight (Isenson, 1969); TRACES (1968, 1973); Comroe (1977)
summary: Reconstruct, from interviews and records, the sequence of key events and decisions that produced an innovation, from the original need through research to launch.
description: A tracer study works backwards from a successful innovation to the events that produced it, using interviews with key participants, publications and archival records such as grants, patents and agency files. Project Hindsight traced 20 weapons systems; TRACES, Project Sappho and the Minnesota Innovation Project followed. Comroe traced about 500 key articles behind ten cardiopulmonary technologies and found 41 per cent were unrelated to the disease when published. Recurring findings: innovations need clusters of prior advances, often take around 19 years, and involve serendipity. Known weaknesses are that it is retrospective, studies only important successes, leans on publications so misses diffusion and consequences, and makes R&D look more rational than it was. In product organisations it can show how breakthrough features really emerged.
steps: Choose the innovation and define its start and end points.
Interview the key investigators, designers and decision-makers involved.
Collect publications, design documents, grants, patents, tickets and other records.
Order key events into a dated sequence, linking each to its evidence.
Identify decisions, clusters of enabling advances and chance events, and note what the record cannot show (failures, abandoned paths).
outputs: A dated, evidenced chain of key events and decisions behind the innovation.
useWhen: An organisation wants to learn how its successful products or features actually came about, for example to justify research investment or design R&D processes.
avoidWhen: You want to predict future innovation or learn from failures; tracers are retrospective and success-biased. Use a pre-mortem, case comparison including failures, or an after-action review for recent projects.
whyLost: It sits in science policy and innovation studies; product teams rarely run structured retrospective histories beyond short retros.
whereToUse: Research-impact cases for UX teams, R&D strategy, design-history work in large product companies.
example: A SaaS firm traces how its most adopted feature emerged, finding that three earlier research studies, a support-team spreadsheet hack and an accidental customer demo all fed in over four years.
reference: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). Free Press.

name: Inquiry Cycle Scenario Obstacle Analysis
origin: Potts, Takahashi and Antón, 1994; Potts, 1999 (ScenIC); formalised by van Lamsweerde and Letier, 2000 (KAOS)
summary: Walk scenarios of stakeholders, tasks and external events against system goals and specified outputs to discover obstacles, then add goals to maintain, avoid or repair those situations.
description: In the Inquiry Cycle, scenarios act as specific contexts for questioning a requirements specification. For each scenario of stakeholders, their tasks, external agents and events, analysts ask whether system output is relevant and acceptable to each stakeholder. Mismatches reveal obstacles: conditions, often caused by external agents or the environment, that could prevent a goal being achieved. Each obstacle prompts new or refined goals to maintain, avoid or repair the situation, and the specification is revised. Scenarios also supply input events for testing validation routines, and the cycle repeats. Van Lamsweerde and Letier formalised obstacle analysis in the KAOS goal-oriented method, checking goal achievability against environmental states drawn from scenarios. Sutcliffe recommends obstacle analysis as a requirements technique HCI could adopt; formal variants need detailed knowledge of the specification and environment.
steps: Write the system goals and the current specification of outputs.
Write scenarios covering stakeholders, their tasks, external agents and events, including unusual but plausible conditions.
Walk each scenario against goals and specified outputs, asking whether each output is relevant and acceptable to each stakeholder.
Record obstacles that could prevent goals, noting their cause (user, external agent, environment).
Derive goals to maintain, avoid or repair each obstacle situation and revise the specification.
Derive input events from scenarios as test data, and iterate the cycle until no new obstacles emerge.
outputs: An obstacle list, new or refined goals, a revised specification and scenario-derived test events.
useWhen: When specifying systems where external agents or environmental conditions can defeat user goals, such as safety, finance, logistics or automated decision systems.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for user research; it questions a specification, not users. Formal variants are heavy; for lightweight risk discovery use a Use Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (UFMEA) or pre-mortem.
whyLost: It stayed within requirements engineering; HCI uses scenarios for design inspiration rather than systematic obstacle discovery.
whereToUse: Automated and AI-driven services, safety-critical workflows, payments and identity verification, logistics and booking systems with external dependencies.
example: For a ride-hailing app's 'arrive safely' goal, walking scenarios surfaces obstacles such as a driver's phone dying mid-trip. New goals (trip continues on the passenger device, automatic safety check-in) enter the specification.
reference: Potts, C., Takahashi, K., & Antón, A. I. (1994). Inquiry-based requirements analysis. IEEE Software, 11(2), 21-32; van Lamsweerde, A., & Letier, E. (2000). Handling obstacles in goal-oriented requirements engineering. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, 26(10), 978-1005.

name: Inside-Out and Backwards Composing
origin: Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016), Chapter 11
summary: A drafting sequence for research reports that starts with the evidence displays (the inside) and the back-end material such as the methods appendix, and writes the surrounding narrative last.
description: Yin offers two ways to start composing a qualitative report without stalling. Composing inside out means drafting the 'inside' first: the quotations, word tables, vignettes, data arrays, pictures and numeric tables that will carry the evidence. Doing this forces a decision about exactly which evidence will be used, exposes gaps in the analysis that send the researcher back to the data, and lets the researcher test different sequences of the pieces; trying these sequences tends to reveal the beginning, middle and end of the 'outside' narrative. Yin argues this suits the inductive character of qualitative work, since insights come from concrete field events. Composing backwards means writing back-end material first, especially an extended methods statement covering the research lens, along with appendices such as an illustrative case and the reference list, so that a real part of the report exists before the main text. For UX researchers, who often get stuck on the executive summary, the approach yields an evidence-led deck or report in which every claim has its display already built, and keeps the narrative from drifting away from the data.
steps: List the candidate evidence pieces: quotes, word tables, vignettes, matrices, images and numeric tables
Edit and finalise each piece for presentation, starting anywhere, even with the easiest
Return to the data where a piece reveals an incomplete analysis
Arrange the pieces in alternative sequences and test which order tells the clearest story
Draft back-end material: methods and research-lens statement, appendices and references
Write the surrounding narrative, introduction and conclusions around the chosen sequence
outputs: A set of finished evidence displays in a tested sequence, a methods appendix, and a report narrative built around them.
useWhen: Writing up qualitative or mixed findings, especially when the author is stuck or the material is large.
avoidWhen: The output is a short decision memo whose conclusion is fixed in advance and needs only one or two supporting points.
whyLost: UX reporting habits come from consulting and product writing, which start from the headline recommendation; writing advice from qualitative methodology texts rarely reaches practitioners.
whereToUse: Research reports, readout decks, case studies and research repository entries.
example: After a diary study, a researcher builds twelve slides of quotes, a journey matrix and three participant vignettes before writing any headline. Shuffling them shows the strongest story starts with the vignettes, and the methods slide is written while the narrative is still unclear.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Insight sentence pattern
