origin: Design research and IDEO-style insight practice; structured insight formats in research communication
summary: A structured sentence format that states who, what they do or feel, why, and the implication, turning a finding into an actionable, evidence-bound insight.
description: Many reports present observations ('users find the dashboard confusing') rather than insights. The insight sentence pattern enforces a structure such as: [user group] [behaviour or belief] because [underlying reason or mechanism], which means [implication for the product], supported by [evidence and strength]. This forces researchers to name the mechanism, scope the claim to a population, and link it to a decision. Its rigour lies in the evidence clause: each insight cites the number and type of sources, notes counter-evidence and states confidence, preventing the format from becoming a slogan generator. Well-formed insights travel better across organisations and support traceability to design decisions.
steps: Draft the insight in the pattern: who, does or believes what, because why, so what, with evidence.
Check that the 'because' clause names a mechanism supported by data, not a restatement of the behaviour.
Scope the population precisely and avoid universal claims unsupported by the sample.
Attach evidence: number of participants or data sources, key quotes or metrics, and counter-evidence.
Assign a confidence level and test the sentence with a stakeholder for clarity and actionability.
Link each insight to decisions or prescriptions it informs.
outputs: A set of structured, evidence-tagged insight statements linked to decisions.
useWhen: Synthesising research into communicable findings for cross-functional teams and leadership.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing early exploratory observations into insight form before mechanisms are understood; keep them as open questions.
whyLost: Insight formats are widely used but often reduced to catchy statements with no evidence clause or mechanism, leaving the form without the rigour.
whereToUse: Research readouts, research repositories, strategy decks, design briefs.
example: Instead of 'users don't trust Tap to Pay', the insight reads: 'Experienced card users double-check every Tap to Pay transaction because the interface gives no settlement confirmation, so adoption stalls after first use (14 of 18 interviews; 62% double-check rate in logs).'
sources: Insight-driven research communication guidance (e.g. Sharon, It's Our Research)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Sharon, T. (2012) It's Our Research: Getting Stakeholder Buy-in for User Experience Research Projects. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Insight warmth ratings
aka: Insight measurement: warmth ratings and self-reported insight
Feeling-of-warmth ratings for insight versus routine problems
origin: Metcalfe and Wiebe, 1987; Bowden and Jung-Beeman; Kounios and colleagues, 2006
summary: While solving problems, people rate how close they feel to the answer at fixed intervals; sudden jumps mark insight, while steady climbs mark analytic progress.
description: Participants work on insight problems (such as rearranging dots or chain links) and analytic problems (such as algebra) and rate how close they feel to the solution every 15 seconds on a 7-point scale from cold to hot. For analytic problems, ratings climb steadily; for insight problems they stay around 2 to 3 and jump to 7 only at the end. A related procedure uses compound remote associates (pine, crab, sauce: 'apple') with a 30-second limit and asks after each solution whether it came by insight or analysis; in one study 56 percent were reported as insight. Later work shows insight solutions can still involve analytic steps. The method gives a time course of subjective progress rather than a single outcome.
steps: Select insight and analytic problems, or tasks in the product domain, pretested for difficulty.
Set a rating interval (15 seconds in the classic study) and a 7-point warmth scale from cold to hot.
Prompt ratings at each interval while participants work, and record solution time.
After each solution, ask whether it arrived suddenly (insight) or step by step.
Plot warmth trajectories per problem type and compute the proportion of insight solutions.
Compare trajectories between conditions, such as with and without a hint or tool.
outputs: Warmth trajectories, proportion of insight solutions, and time to solve.
useWhen: Studying how users experience progress on diagnostic, debugging or analytic tasks, or whether a tool makes progress feel gradual and visible.
avoidWhen: Avoid when interruptions for ratings would disrupt the task; puzzle tasks may not reflect real work. For workload use NASA-TLX or similar.
whyLost: It remains a problem-solving research technique without an applied home.
whereToUse: Data analysis and BI tools, debugging and developer tools, learning platforms, puzzle and game design.
example: Developers rate warmth every 30 seconds while fixing a seeded bug with and without an AI assistant; with the assistant, ratings climb steadily rather than jumping, matching reports that it makes progress feel predictable.
sources: Metcalfe, J., & Wiebe, D. (1987). Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving. Memory & Cognition, 15
reference: Metcalfe, J., & Wiebe, D. (1987). Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving. Memory & Cognition, 15, 238-246.

name: Insight-Based Evaluation
origin: Purvi Saraiya, Chris North and Karen Duca, 2005
summary: Instead of timing set tasks, let domain experts explore real data freely and count, time and rate the insights they report.
description: Task-time studies fit visualisation tools poorly: analysis is long and high level, users view data from many angles, questions emerge during exploration, and important discoveries are rare. Insight-based evaluation measures what visualisation is for. Domain experts receive realistic data from their own field and a tool, list their initial questions, then explore freely while thinking aloud for a fixed period. Every reported insight is recorded and timestamped, then coded for category, correctness, depth (breadth versus deep or hypothesis-generating) and domain value, ideally by independent experts. Tools or versions are compared on number of insights, their value and time to first insight. Shneiderman and colleagues present it as a first step beyond controlled tasks, complementing long-term case studies of real analysts.
steps: Recruit domain experts and prepare realistic data from their field.
Ask each participant to list initial questions of interest.
Let them explore freely with the tool while thinking aloud for a fixed period.
Record each insight with a timestamp.
Code insights for correctness, depth, category and domain value, ideally rated by independent experts.
Compare tools or versions on insight count, value and time to first insight.
outputs: Insight counts and value scores per participant and tool, and time to first insight.
useWhen: Evaluating visual analytics, dashboards, BI tools and exploratory data tools where discovery, not speed, is the goal.
avoidWhen: Routine operational dashboards with defined tasks (use task-based Usability Testing). Coding is subjective and sessions are short relative to real analysis; for long-term use, run diary or case studies.
whyLost: It is established in visualisation research but rarely used in product UX, which prefers task success metrics.
whereToUse: Bioinformatics and science tools, BI platforms, security analytics, AI-assisted data exploration.
example: A BI vendor compares its new AI-suggested charts with the current tool among 12 analysts exploring their own sales data. The new version yields more insights sooner, but independent raters judge fewer of them deep.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Saraiya, P., North, C. and Duca, K. (2005) An insight-based methodology for evaluating bioinformatics visualizations. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics 11(4).

name: Instant Data Analysis
origin: Jesper Kjeldskov, Mikael Skov and Jan Stage, 2004
summary: Run all test sessions in one day and identify problems in a team meeting straight after, from a note-taker's notes rather than video.
description: Video-based analysis of usability tests can take days per session. Instant Data Analysis compresses it: all sessions (typically four to six) run on one day, with a moderator who also analyses and a dedicated note-taker; no screen or video recordings are analysed. Immediately after the last session the team meets, walks through the notes to jog fresh memory, discusses what users experienced and agrees which problems to report, documenting them the same day. In the original comparison it found 85% of the critical problems a full video analysis found, in a fraction of the time, but missed many low-severity problems. Rigour rests on good notes, the shortest possible gap between sessions and analysis, and a structured walkthrough of each session in the meeting.
steps: Schedule all sessions on one day, typically four to six participants.
Assign a moderator who will also analyse and a dedicated note-taker.
Run the sessions with detailed time-stamped notes.
Meet immediately after the last session, usually for one to two hours.
Walk through the notes session by session, discuss and agree the problem list with severity.
Document the problems the same day.
outputs: A same-day, severity-rated problem list.
useWhen: Iterative development where findings are needed the next morning, and small teams without time for video analysis.
avoidWhen: When completeness or low-severity problems matter, or for summative and safety-critical testing; use full video-based analysis or Verbal Protocol Analysis.
whyLost: Its idea lives on in same-day debriefs and rapid testing cadences, usually without the name or its documented trade-off.
whereToUse: Agile sprints, startups, design sprints and RITE-style iterative testing.
example: A health-booking startup tests five users on Thursday and meets at 4 p.m. to walk through the notes. By 6 p.m. it has a list of eight problems, three critical, ready for Friday's sprint planning.
reference: Kjeldskov, J., Skov, M.B. and Stage, J. (2004) Instant data analysis: conducting usability evaluations in a day. Proceedings of NordiCHI 2004.

name: Institutional Ethnography
origin: Dorothy Smith (1978 onwards); M. L. Campbell (1998)
summary: Start from people's everyday experience of how things work and trace outward to the institutional practices, texts and discourses that coordinate it.
description: Institutional ethnography links the micro level of personal experience with the macro level of institutions. It begins with people in a subordinated or front-line position, treating them as experts on the actual work of their lives, and uses their accounts to locate a problematic: a point where their experience is shaped by something beyond the local setting. The researcher then follows that thread outward, interviewing professionals, administrators and staff and examining the texts (forms, records, policies, software fields) that coordinate work across sites, to show how ruling relations organise what happens locally. As in ethnomethodology, the people are not themselves the object of study; the institution is. Its rigour lies in keeping the standpoint of the starting group and in tracing actual textual and work connections rather than invoking abstract structure. Fuller procedure is in Smith's own writing.
steps: Begin with interviews and observation with people in the subordinated or front-line position about the everyday work of their lives and how things actually get done.
Identify a problematic: where their accounts point to practices, texts or decisions originating elsewhere.
Extend interviews to others in the institution, such as professionals, administrators and staff, who handle the same work from other positions.
Collect and trace the texts that coordinate the work (forms, records, policies, system fields) and how they travel.
Map how institutional practices and texts shape the starting experiences, keeping the standpoint of the starting group.
Write an account that shows the ruling relations from that standpoint.
outputs: An account of the institutional relations, texts and discourses that organise people's experience, mapped from their standpoint.
useWhen: Users' problems seem to originate in forms, records, policies or systems beyond the interface, for example in health, welfare, education or enterprise workflows.
avoidWhen: Consumer products without institutional mediation, or when you need quick interface findings; use Contextual Inquiry or Organisational Ethnography and Workplace Studies for workplace practice alone.
whyLost: It is rooted in feminist sociology and is described mainly in its own literature; service design reaches similar ground with blueprints but without the standpoint and textual tracing.
whereToUse: Health records and clinical software, benefits and immigration services, school systems, HR and compliance platforms, B2B workflow tools.
example: Starting from home-care workers' accounts of rushed visits, researchers trace the scheduling software's 15-minute visit codes back through commissioning contracts, showing that the app's time fields encode a funding rule, not a design choice.
reference: Smith, D. E. (2005). Institutional Ethnography: A Sociology for People. Lanham, MD: AltaMira Press.

name: Instrument Specification Frameworks for Mixed Methods
aka: Instrument specification frameworks for mixed methods instrument development
origin: Scherman and Zimmerman
summary: Plan a questionnaire and its qualitative instruments with matched specification tables that fix constructs, items, analyses and cross-strand alignment before any item is written.
description: A planning discipline borrowed from test construction. The questionnaire specification table maps each section to its construct, definition, number and type of items, coding and planned analysis, with an extra column stating how it aligns with qualitative data. A matching qualitative table maps each area of interest to its definition, sources (interviews, focus groups, documents, observations), analysis strategy and alignment with the quantitative strand. Writing these tables first exposes constructs with no items, items with no analysis, and qualitative areas that can never be compared with the survey. Inferences are later legitimated through quantitative validation (for example Rasch or IRT), qualitative credibility checks and crossover analyses that test whether the two strands measure the same thing. The cost is effort before any data collection.
steps: Define each construct or area of interest and link it to a research question.
Fill the questionnaire specification table: construct, definition, number and type of items, coding, planned analysis and alignment with qualitative data.
Fill the matching qualitative specification table: area, definition, sources, analysis strategy and alignment with the quantitative strand.
Check both tables for gaps: constructs without items, items without analysis, areas without a counterpart.
Write, pilot and revise the instruments against the tables.
Validate with quantitative, qualitative and crossover analyses and report which legitimation types were achieved.
outputs: Paired specification tables and aligned questionnaire and interview or observation instruments.
useWhen: Building a new survey alongside interviews or diary work, especially when qualitative findings are to be turned into items, or when the two strands must be compared later.
avoidWhen: Quick one-off pulse surveys, or when a validated instrument already exists; use Scale construction and validation for a pure psychometric build.
whyLost: Test blueprints are standard in educational measurement, but UX surveys are usually drafted item by item without a written specification.
whereToUse: Annual UX or relationship surveys, research programmes combining interviews and surveys, item generation from qualitative themes.
example: Before a developer-experience survey, a team specifies six constructs with item counts and analyses, and a parallel interview guide covering the same constructs; the alignment column later lets them check whether survey friction scores match the friction described in interviews.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Instrumental Variables (IV)
origin: Philip Wright (1928); Angrist, Imbens and Rubin (1996)
summary: Uses a variable that shifts exposure but affects outcomes only through exposure to estimate causal effects when users self-select into treatment.
description: An instrument must be relevant (it strongly predicts treatment) and valid (it affects the outcome only through treatment, the exclusion restriction). Two-stage least squares estimates the effect for compliers, the local average treatment effect. The treatise's transfer: when you cannot randomise who uses a new UI, find a plausible instrument, such as a server-side flag randomly assigned for technical reasons, a geographic boundary creating differential access, or a temporal event creating quasi-random exposure. Encouragement designs, where users are randomly nudged toward a feature, are the most practical UX instrument. Weak instruments (first-stage F below about 10) give biased estimates, and exclusion must be argued, not tested.
steps: Define the treatment (actual exposure) and the outcome; identify a candidate instrument.
Argue relevance and exclusion explicitly, ideally with a DAG.
Estimate the first stage and check instrument strength (F above 10).
Estimate the effect with 2SLS and robust standard errors.
Characterise compliers and state that the estimate is a LATE.
Test sensitivity to plausible exclusion violations.
outputs: LATE estimate, first-stage diagnostics, complier description, assumption statement.
useWhen: Opt-in features with self-selection, encouragement designs, natural experiments from technical randomness.
avoidWhen: When no credible instrument exists; a weak or invalid instrument is worse than an honest observational estimate.
whyLost: Rarely taught outside economics; exclusion arguments are unfamiliar to UX and analytics teams.
whereToUse: Feature adoption effects on retention, AI assistant usage effects, opt-in privacy controls, education nudges.
example: A random 50% of users receive an email encouraging use of a new budgeting feature; IV estimates that actually using it lowers overdraft incidents by 12% among compliers, while naive comparison suggested 35%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Angrist JD, Imbens GW & Rubin DB (1996) Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables. JASA 91:444-455
Angrist JD & Pischke J-S (2008) Mostly Harmless Econometrics
Angrist, Imbens & Rubin, Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables (1996), JASA
Cinelli, C., Forney, A. & Pearl, J., A Crash Course in Good and Bad Controls (2022)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Angrist JD, Imbens GW & Rubin DB (1996) Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association 91(434):444-455.

name: Intent Adjective Lists
aka: Words we are and are not
origin: Abby Covert, 2014
summary: List adjectives you want users to use about your work and a neutral, non-opposite list you accept it will not be, then use both as a decision filter.
description: Covert treats intent as the effect we want to have, expressed in language: every word chosen for where we are going implies another we walk away from. The exercise makes that explicit. The team writes a set of adjectives it wants users to use about what it makes, and a set it is content not to be described by. The two lists must neither repeat nor contradict each other, the second must not be a list of opposites, and every word should be neutral, so an outsider could not tell which list is the 'good' one. That constraint forces real trade-offs: Covert's own intent was accessible, beginner-friendly and broadly useful, accepting not being academic, expert-friendly or specialised. The lists then filter later decisions and settle disputes about tone and scope.
steps: Choose adjectives you want users to use to describe what you are making.
Choose adjectives you are content not to have used about it.
Check the lists neither repeat nor contradict each other and that the second is not simply antonyms of the first.
Replace any negative words so every adjective is neutral and the lists cannot be told apart by tone.
Share the lists with stakeholders and use them to test proposals and settle language and scope decisions.
outputs: Two short adjective lists that state intent and act as a filter for decisions.
useWhen: Starting a product, redesign or content project where stakeholders hold different unstated ideas of 'good'.
avoidWhen: The lists record intent, not user perception; check whether users actually perceive the product that way with Semantic Differential or AttrakDiff. Antonym lists or negative words defeat the exercise.
whyLost: Survives widely as 'this, not that' brand and tone lists because it is quick and clarifying, though Covert's neutral, non-opposite rule is often lost.
whereToUse: Brand and tone-of-voice work, content strategy, AI assistant personality, product redesign kick-offs.
example: A product manager's team, told by the CEO to be 'sleek', agrees 'calm, plain, reassuring' and accepts not being 'cutting-edge, minimal, exclusive', after research suggests sleek will feel cold to older users.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert, 2014)
reference: Covert, A. (2014) How to Make Sense of Any Mess: Information Architecture for Everybody. CreateSpace, ch. 2.

name: Intent Taxonomy Development for Conversational AI
origin: Dialogue act research (Austin, Searle; Traum & Larsson, 2003)
summary: Builds a hierarchical, mutually exclusive taxonomy of what users want from a conversational system, grounded in real utterances and validated for coder agreement.
description: Intent taxonomy development treats the set of user goals a conversational system must handle as a qualitative coding problem. Researchers sample real utterances from transcripts, search logs or support tickets, code them inductively, and organise codes into a hierarchy of intent families and specific intents with written definitions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and example utterances. The taxonomy is tested by independent coders for agreement (e.g. Cohen's kappa above 0.7), with confusable pairs refined or merged. Frequency counts show coverage and the long tail, guiding which intents to support. Grounding in dialogue act theory helps distinguish what users want from how they phrase it. Rigour comes from real data, reliability testing and periodic re-coding as usage evolves.
steps: Step 1: Collect 500+ real user utterances from existing channels (support transcripts, search logs, app store reviews).
Step 2: Open card sort of utterances — what does this user want to do?
Step 3: Cluster into intent categories.
Step 4: Test taxonomy completeness: for a new set of 100 utterances, can every one be classified into an existing intent?
Coverage < 80% = taxonomy is incomplete.
Step 5: Validate with users: show them the intent labels — do they recognize them as their goals?
outputs: An intent hierarchy with definitions and example utterances, coverage statistics, inter-rater agreement, confusion pairs and gaps for design.
useWhen: Designing or auditing chatbots, voice assistants and LLM agents; analysing support transcripts; prioritising which intents to support or route.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on a fixed taxonomy for open-ended LLM interactions without regular re-coding; avoid building from invented utterances rather than real data.
whyLost: Intent design is done by NLU engineers as a training-data task; the qualitative coding rigour that would make it a research method is absent.
whereToUse: Chatbot design, voice assistant development, LLM intent routing, search UX, customer service automation.
example: An insurer codes 3,000 chat logs, producing 42 intents in 8 families with kappa 0.81; 'is my claim stuck?' accounts for 19% of traffic but had no dedicated intent, so a status flow is built first.
reference: Traum DR & Larsson S (2003) The information state approach to dialogue management. In van Kuppevelt & Smith (Eds.) Current and New Directions in Discourse and Dialogue. Kluwer

name: Intention-to-Treat Analysis
origin: Austin Bradford Hill (1961) and Richard Peto et al. (1976); codified in CONSORT (1996 onward)
summary: Analyses all users in the arm they were randomised to, regardless of whether they actually experienced the treatment, preserving the benefits of randomisation.
description: In product experiments, not everyone assigned to a feature sees it: they never reach the page, the client fails to load, or they opt out. Analysing only those exposed (per-protocol or triggered analysis without care) breaks randomisation if exposure depends on user characteristics affected by treatment. ITT compares groups as randomised, estimating the effect of offering the treatment, which is unbiased though diluted. Triggered analysis is valid only when the trigger condition is identical and computed counterfactually in both arms. Complier average causal effects can then be recovered with IV methods. CONSORT-style flow diagrams make attrition visible.
steps: Record assignment for every randomised user and the point of assignment.
Define exposure precisely and log counterfactual triggers in control (would have seen the feature).
Analyse the primary outcome by assigned arm for all randomised users (ITT).
Run a triggered analysis only on counterfactually defined triggered users in both arms.
Estimate complier effects with IV (assignment as instrument) if needed.
Report a CONSORT-style flow diagram of assignment, exposure and attrition per arm.
outputs: ITT effect estimates, valid triggered or complier estimates, and a participant flow diagram.
useWhen: Any experiment where exposure or compliance is incomplete, including opt-in features and multi-step flows.
avoidWhen: Never wholly; but report triggered effects for interpretability when correctly constructed.
whyLost: Experimentation dashboards often filter to exposed users silently, and UX teams are unaware of the bias this introduces.
whereToUse: Feature experiments below the fold, onboarding variants, email-driven experiments, clinical and wellness apps.
example: A meditation app tests a new session player. Analysing only users who opened a session shows +12% completion, but ITT shows +2%, since the new player caused fewer weakly engaged users to open sessions at all.
sources: Hollis & Campbell, What is meant by intention to treat analysis? (1999), BMJ
Schulz, Altman & Moher, CONSORT 2010 Statement (2010), BMJ
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)

name: Intentional analysis
origin: Franz Brentano (1874) and Edmund Husserl's noesis and noema (Ideas, 1913); used in phenomenological psychology by Giorgi and others
summary: Analyses experiences as directed acts of consciousness, distinguishing how something is experienced (noesis) from what is experienced as meaningful (noema).
description: Phenomenology holds that consciousness is always consciousness of something: experiences are intentional, directed at objects. Husserl distinguished the noesis, the act of experiencing (perceiving, remembering, doubting, hoping), from the noema, the object as it is meant or experienced. Intentional analysis applies this to participants' accounts: for each experienced object, such as a claim form, a status screen or an approval message, it asks how the participant was relating to it (anticipating, fearing, checking, trusting) and what the object meant to them in that act. Two people looking at the same 'pending' screen may experience different noemata: a promise or a threat. For UX this exposes why identical interfaces produce different experiences. Rigour comes from systematically pairing acts and objects across meaning units and checking them against participants' language.
steps: Collect detailed first-person descriptions of a specific episode of use, using prompts that elicit what the participant was attending to and how, from 6 to 15 participants.
Divide each description into meaning units at shifts in meaning, and for each identify the object of attention.

For each object, characterise the noetic act (seeing, anticipating, doubting, remembering, evaluating) and the noematic sense (what the object meant as experienced, for example 'a verdict', 'a receipt').
Compare noetic-noematic pairs across participants for the same interface objects, noting where the same object is experienced in different modes.
Relate patterns to participants' situations and histories that shape their intentional stance.
Derive design implications for how objects should present themselves to support the intended mode of experience, and test with comprehension probes.
outputs: A table of meaning units with objects, noetic acts and noematic senses, cross-participant comparisons, and design implications for how interface objects are experienced.
useWhen: Identical designs produce divergent emotional responses; designing status, waiting and decision communications in high-stakes services.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural metrics or usability defects; use task-based testing. Not suitable without rich descriptive accounts.
whyLost: Its technical philosophical vocabulary keeps it in phenomenological psychology and nursing research, and UX has no equivalent vocabulary for the mode in which an interface object is experienced.
whereToUse: Insurance and benefits claims, medical results portals, loan decisions, job application tracking, AI explanations of decisions.
example: Participants experienced the 'Claim under review' status in two modes: some anticipated it as a receipt confirming progress, others doubted it as a verdict deferred. Adding an expected decision date and a list of checks completed shifted most accounts toward the receipt mode.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
reference: Husserl, E. (1913/1983). Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology and to a Phenomenological Philosophy, First Book. Nijhoff; Giorgi, A. (2009). The Descriptive Phenomenological Method in Psychology. Duquesne University Press.

name: Interaction Cycle (User Action Framework) Classification
aka: Interaction Cycle categorisation of UX issues
Sensitising questions for observing test users
origin: Andre, Hartson, Belz and McCreary, User Action Framework, 2001; adapted from Norman, 1986
summary: Classify observed UX problems and guidelines by where they arise in the user's cycle: planning, translation, physical action, outcome or assessment.
description: The Interaction Cycle adapts Norman's stages of action: the execution side is split into planning (what to do) and translation (how to do it), followed by physical actions; outcomes are the often invisible system effects; assessment covers perceiving and judging feedback. Each part heads a hierarchy of design issue categories (for example translation, then presentation of cognitive affordance, then legibility, then font colour contrast), which the User Action Framework uses to classify problems consistently and link them to guidelines and fixes. Translation accounts for most observed problems. Hertzum turns the stages into sensitising questions evaluators ask themselves while observing (can the user determine what the task requires, pick the right sub-goal, find the action, perform it, notice and understand feedback, judge progress), adding experiential questions on senses, emotion, thinking, doing, values and relationships.
steps: Before sessions, review the stage-based and experiential sensitising questions against the test objective and know the solution path for each task.
During sessions, use the questions to notice where users struggle: planning, translation, physical action, outcome or assessment.
For each recorded problem, decide which cycle part it affects.
Descend the category hierarchy to the specific issue, such as legibility of a cognitive affordance.
Use the category to find applicable guidelines and fixes.
In design, trace each task around the cycle, including system-initiated, multi-user and interrupted secondary tasks.
outputs: Problems classified by cycle stage and issue category, linked guidelines, and richer observation notes.
useWhen: Building consistent problem databases across studies, training evaluators to observe, and diagnosing where in the interaction a problem originates.
avoidWhen: Quick tests where a full classification adds little; interaction is not strictly cyclic, so do not force stages. For a lighter lens use Stages-of-Action Gulf Analysis.
whyLost: The full UAF classification needed tool support and training; the cycle survives only as a textbook organising scheme.
whereToUse: Usability problem repositories, evaluator training, and meta-analysis of test findings across products.
example: A research team classifies 300 problems from a year of tests. Most fall under translation, specifically unclear labels, which justifies a terminology programme over visual redesign.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019) The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience, 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, chapter 31. Norman, D.A. (1986) Cognitive engineering. In Norman, D.A. and Draper, S.W. (eds) User Centered System Design. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Interaction Entropy (Shannon)
origin: Claude Shannon, 1948
summary: Shannon entropy of each user's distribution of actions or categories, used as a measure of behavioural variety whose decline signals drift even when visit frequency holds steady.
description: Shannon entropy H = −Σ p log p measures the spread of a distribution; for a user's actions it is high when they use many features evenly and low when they repeat a few. Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook uses interaction entropy over the action distribution per user as the lead drift indicator, alongside category diversity per session, recommendation CTR and attention decay, because drift reduces variety even when frequency is constant. Illustrative values: entropy falling from 2.4 to 1.1 (generic) or 2.6 to 1.2 (e-commerce, 10,000 users over 3 months). Thresholds feed Bayesian updating (entropy < 1.5 for three sessions) and decision bars (entropy > 2.0 for 70% of active users within 4 weeks). The forward-thinking playbook also uses action entropy rising from 1.1 to 1.9 as a long-term validation signal.
steps: Define the action or category vocabulary from telemetry (user_id, session_id, ts, action, category).
Compute each user's action distribution per period.
Calculate H = −Σ p log p per user per period, normalising if comparing vocabularies of different size.
Track entropy longitudinally alongside frequency to separate narrowing from disengagement.
Set thresholds for intervention and decision bars (e.g. entropy < 1.5 triggers nudges; target > 2.0).
Pair low-entropy users with interviews or diaries to understand why.
outputs: Per-user entropy trajectories, drift thresholds and cohort comparisons.
useWhen: When frequency metrics look healthy but you suspect users are narrowing to shallow routines.
avoidWhen: When products are intentionally single-purpose; low entropy may mean efficient use rather than drift.
whyLost: Information-theoretic measures are rare in product analytics, which favour counts and rates.
whereToUse: E-commerce, OTT, super-apps, SaaS feature adoption, post-launch validation.
example: An e-commerce team sees entropy fall from 2.6 to 1.2 while logins hold; after re-onboarding with cross-category bundles, entropy rises from 1.2 to 2.4.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. Bell System Technical Journal, 27(3), 379–423.

name: Interaction Frogger
origin: Wensveen, Djajadiningrat and Overbeeke, 2004; extended by Stienstra, Bruns, Wensveen and Kuenen, 2012
summary: A framework for systematically designing how a user's action is coupled to feedback and feedforward, so that physical interactions feel natural and can shift behaviour.
description: Interaction Frogger lays out all the potential couplings between what a user does and what they perceive: feedforward (what the product communicates before the action about what will happen) and feedback (what it returns during and after). Couplings can be unified or broken along aspects such as time, location, direction, dynamics, modality and expression, and the designer decides which to unite. In the later behaviour-transformation use, designers iterate three steps: analyse current behaviour with attention to dynamics and expression; synthesise the mapping within the action-perception loop, using timing and scale to amplify or dampen feedback; and detail for subtlety at the limits of perceptual-motor sensitivity and users' skills. It gives tangible and product designers a vocabulary for making interactions self-explanatory without labels.
steps: Observe and describe the current action-perception loop, focusing on the dynamics and expression of the user's action.
List the feedforward and feedback the product gives at each moment of the action.
For each coupling aspect (time, location, direction, dynamics, modality, expression) decide whether action and feedback should be unified and how.
Synthesise a new mapping, using timing and scale to amplify or reduce feedback where behaviour should change.
Detail the couplings for subtlety, testing the limits of perceptual-motor sensitivity and users' skills with physical prototypes.
Iterate analysis, synthesis and detailing until the interaction is ready-to-hand.
outputs: Explicit, documented couplings between user actions and feedback and feedforward, embodied in prototypes.
useWhen: Designing tangible, physical or gestural interactions where meaning should come from the coupling of action and response rather than labels.
avoidWhen: The framework guides design, not evaluation; test whether couplings are understood with Prototype Testing or Think-Aloud Usability Testing (Contemporary Practice). The chapter account is brief, so consult Wensveen et al. (2004) for the coupling aspects before use. For screen-based affordance problems Affordance Analysis is lighter.
whyLost: Remains in Dutch industrial design schools and tangible-interaction research because it is abstract and needs physical prototyping skills most UX teams lack.
whereToUse: Connected devices, wearables, automotive controls, haptics, smart-home products.
example: A smart thermostat team realises turning the dial gives feedback only on a separate screen; they unify location and direction so the ring itself glows and resists as temperature changes.
reference: Wensveen, S.A.G., Djajadiningrat, J.P. and Overbeeke, C.J. (2004) Interaction frogger: a design framework to couple action and function through feedback and feedforward. Proceedings of DIS 2004, 177-184.

name: Interaction Logging and Instrumentation Planning
donor: Software engineering; web engineering; web analytics
origin: HCI field research on proxies and loggers (Hong et al. 2001 WebQuilt; Atterer et al. 2006 UsaProxy; Iqbal and Horvitz 2007 DART); Microsoft instrumentation programmes (Harris 2005-2006); tracking plans per Beasley (2013)
summary: Plans and builds the capture of user interaction data, through event tracking plans, in-app telemetry, proxies or desktop loggers, driven by research questions and privacy limits.
description: Log analysis is only as good as what was logged, and data cannot be collected retroactively. Instrumentation planning starts from research questions: what you want to measure and why decides which events, at what granularity, to capture. For a web product, the team walks the site, lists every meaningful user action, checks what is already tracked, and defines a category/action/label/value scheme robust enough for future events. Other routes suit other questions: instrumenting application code to log commands (Microsoft's opt-in programme logged billions of Office sessions and guided the ribbon redesign); proxies that log or rewrite traffic across many sites, or inject scripts to record mouse movements; and desktop activity loggers that record keyboard, mouse and window events across applications to study multitasking and interruption. Each needs consent, opt-out and limits on captured text.
steps: Derive the needed events and granularity from explicit research questions, stating for each what is captured and why.
Choose the capture route: analytics event tracking, in-app instrumentation, a logging proxy or script injection, or a desktop activity logger.
For web and app products, walk the interface, list every meaningful user action, and audit which are already tracked.
Define a naming taxonomy (for example category, action, label, value) and tag events by category and granularity so analyses can filter.
Build in consent, opt-out and privacy limits: capture that keys were pressed rather than which, truncate titles, exclude file names and addresses.
Have developers implement, then verify data on test sessions, including crash recovery and dropped events.
Parse, aggregate and visualise logs as counts, rates, sequences and paths, and revisit the plan as questions change.
outputs: A tracking plan and event taxonomy, instrumented builds or loggers, and validated event streams ready for analysis.
useWhen: Before launching or studying a product where behavioural data will answer research questions, or when existing analytics miss key actions.
avoidWhen: When you cannot secure consent or protect privacy; loggers are associated with spyware and users may forget they are logged. Collecting everything produces data junk, and low-level events do not reveal tasks; pair with interviews or Diary Studies to interpret.
whyLost: The research techniques were absorbed into commercial analytics SDKs and 'tracking plans', and UX researchers rarely take part in deciding what is captured.
whereToUse: SaaS and mobile apps, desktop productivity software, multi-site research studies, AI assistant usage analysis.
example: A transit app's UX team audits tracking and finds route searches are logged but zero-result searches are not; they add a search event with result count, revealing that 12% of rural searches return nothing.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. and Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 339-361; Beasley, M. (2013). Practical Web Analytics for User Experience. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Interaction Ritual Theory Design Lens
aka: IR theory lens for social games
origin: Collins (2004); turned into design guidelines for colocated games by Xu and MacIntyre in Chapter 9
summary: Analysing existing social experiences through the ingredients of successful face-to-face interaction to derive design guidelines for colocated, social products.
description: Collins' interaction ritual theory holds that successful social interactions share four ingredients: bodily copresence, a barrier to outsiders (a sense of who is taking part), a mutual focus of attention, and a shared mood. When these are present, emotions are observed and amplified in a feedback loop, producing group solidarity and 'emotional energy' that makes people want to repeat the interaction. Chapter 9 uses the theory as a lens to analyse many genres of social games, from card and board games to rhythm and motion games, and derives guidelines for each ingredient. Examples include natural mapping of body movement to game state, rewarding players for reading each other's expressions, signalling who is in the circle of play, common objects that every player attends to, turn structures that make players the focus of attention, and game-generated moments everyone can laugh at together. A subset of the guidelines is then built into a prototype and tested with groups. The lens helps teams avoid the pitfall of assuming colocation makes an experience social, when people may simply play 'alone together'.
steps: Identify the social experience you want to support and gather examples of existing products and activities in that space.
Analyse each example against the four ingredients: copresence, boundary, mutual focus and shared mood.
Derive design guidelines for each ingredient from what works in the examples.
Select the guidelines most relevant to your context and turn them into concrete design choices.
Build a prototype and observe groups using it, coding behaviours against the ingredients.
Refine the guidelines based on which behaviours appeared.
outputs: A set of theory-grounded design guidelines and evidence on which ones produced the intended social behaviours.
useWhen: Designing products for groups who share a physical space, such as party games, tabletop and AR experiences, museum or classroom technology.
avoidWhen: Interaction is solitary or purely remote, or the team needs immediate evaluative data rather than design direction.
whyLost: Sociological theories are rarely taught in UX, and turning them into actionable guidelines takes time.
whereToUse: Colocated multiplayer games, AR and tabletop systems, shared displays, social features in physical venues.
example: Designing a phone-based AR party game, a team adds a shared virtual object in the middle of the table that everyone must watch, and audio cues that make all players react at the same moment, and then observes more cross-player talk and laughter.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Xu, Y. and MacIntyre, B. (2016). NerdHerder: designing colocated physical-digital games with sociological theories. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 9. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Interaction-type versus situational-factor reasoning
origin: Judy Bowen and Annika Hinze, University of Waikato (Bowen and Hinze 2012; Bowen et al. 2014)
summary: List each device's input and output interaction types, relate situational factors to the interactions they impair, and subtract impaired channels to see which devices still serve a use case.
description: Devices are described by the interaction types of their widgets, such as touch, visual, audible, motion and location, split into inputs and outputs and optionally by information type (text, icons, maps, voice, alarm). A fixed relation links known situational factors, with value ranges where relevant, to the interactions they hinder: loud noise removes audio output, darkness or distance removes small text, vibration removes fine touch. When a situation occurs, the factors present at each device's location restrict the relation, the affected interactions are subtracted, and devices are classified as unusable, restricted or available and matched to the use case's needs. Originally used for medical devices taken into helicopters, it has been applied to repurposing public displays in emergencies. It can be implemented with ontologies and rules, though simple sets suffice.
steps: Model each device's widgets by interaction type, split into inputs and outputs, and optionally by information type.
Build the effects relation from all known situational factors, with value ranges, to the interaction types they impair.
For a given situation, record the factors actually present at each device's location.
Restrict the relation to those factors and subtract the affected interactions from each device.
Classify devices as unusable, restricted or available and match remaining capabilities to the use case's information and input needs.
Choose devices on a best-fit basis, or warn users how to adapt their use.
outputs: Per-device lists of available and affected interactions, recommended devices for a use case, and user warnings.
useWhen: Products must work across harsh or changing environments, or several devices could deliver the same information and you must pick which.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the environment is stable and known; ordinary context-of-use analysis suffices. It cannot capture unknown effects or individual differences, and ontologies are time-consuming.
whyLost: It exists in a handful of academic papers and its formal tooling deters practitioners, though the reasoning itself is simple.
whereToUse: Emergency alerting, medical devices in transport, industrial and field-service apps, automotive and multi-device ecosystems.
example: A field-service app team lists factors on oil rigs (noise above 100 dB, gloves, rain). Subtracting impaired channels leaves only large visual output and coarse touch on the tablet, so alarms move to a vibrating wrist device.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Bowen, J. & Hinze, A. (2017). Reasoning about interactive systems in dynamic situations of use. In Weyers, B. et al. (eds) The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction. Springer, pp. 319-342.

name: Intercept Survey
donor: Recreation, tourism and facility management research
origin: Long-standing visitor and user survey practice; Veal and Darcy describe it as the most common type of survey used by sport managers and set out sampling rules for it
summary: Questionnaire survey of people while they are using a site or service, with strict selection rules so the sample represents users rather than whoever is easiest to approach.
description: A site, user or visitor survey questions people at the place where they use a facility or service; when respondents are stopped as they enter or leave, or on their way, it is often called an intercept survey, and a cordon survey if all approaches are covered. Veal and Darcy describe it as managers' most common survey and give four uses: defining the catchment area, profiling users, collecting opinions, and, by comparing the user profile with census data, estimating who the non-users are. Interviewer completion is preferred to handing out forms, which gives low and self-selected response. Sampling must follow strict rules: when the interviewer is stationary and users move (ISUM), stop the next person through the gate as soon as the previous interview is finished; when users are stationary and the interviewer moves (USIM), follow a set route and approach every nth group. Because interview rates vary between quiet and busy periods, observed counts are used to weight the results. In UX the same discipline applies to in-product intercept surveys and in-store or event intercepts, where 'whoever answered' is not a sample of users.
steps: Define the population (all users of the site or service in a period) and what you need to learn about them.
Write a short questionnaire, about five minutes, covering origin, visit details, user profile and opinions.
Choose the selection mode: ISUM (stationary interviewer at entrances or exits, next person after each interview) or USIM (mobile interviewer on a fixed route, every nth group).
Schedule interviewing across days and times, and run parallel counts of users per period.
Train and supervise interviewers so they never choose respondents on any other basis.
Weight the results by the counts so busy and quiet periods are represented in proportion.
Analyse catchment, profile and opinion data, and compare the profile with population data to describe non-users.
outputs: A weighted user profile, catchment information, satisfaction and opinion data, and an estimate of under-represented groups.
useWhen: You need representative data about the people actually using a place, event or service, at the point of use.
avoidWhen: You need to reach non-users or lapsed users, or the interruption would harm the experience or safety at the site.
whyLost: It survives in UX as in-app and website intercept surveys, but the sampling rules and count-based weighting that make it representative are rarely applied.
whereToUse: Venues, events, stores, transport, museums and attractions, and in-product or website intercepts triggered during use.
example: At a marathon expo, interviewers at the two exits stop the next visitor after each completed interview, collecting 300 short interviews about the event app. Hourly gate counts show that the afternoon crowd was under-sampled, so afternoon responses are weighted up before satisfaction is reported.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: Intercultural Interaction Analysis (IIA) Tool
origin: Rudiger Heimgartner, Siemens VDO, 2005-2007
summary: Logs how users from different cultures interact with identical localised test tasks, pairs logs with a values questionnaire, and identifies significant cultural interaction indicators.
description: The IIA tool tests whether interaction parameters, not just content, should differ by culture. Starting from 118 candidate culture-sensitive parameters drawn from literature, such as information density, information speed and interaction speed, it presents semantically identical, localised test tasks that let users set those parameters: for example the number of points of interest on a map or the timing and frequency of navigation advice. A session has five parts: demographics, test tasks, Hofstede's VSM94 values questionnaire, the user's check of whether the computed values fit them, and a debrief. Mouse moves, clicks, pauses and settings are logged throughout. Group differences are tested with ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis and Tukey post hoc tests, and discriminant analysis checks whether interaction alone classifies culture. In two studies (102 and 916 valid datasets) Chinese users chose about twice the POI density of German or English users.
steps: Derive candidate culture-sensitive interaction parameters from theory and literature.
Build localised but semantically identical test tasks that let users set those parameters.
Add demographics, a cultural values questionnaire (VSM94) with a self-check of the computed values, and a debrief.
Log all interaction events during the session.
Run the tool online with users from each target culture, planning for high abort rates.
Test group differences with ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis and post hoc tests, and check classification with discriminant analysis.
Plot significant indicators as cultural fingerprints and map them to default settings or adaptive behaviour.
outputs: A list of statistically significant cultural interaction indicators and per-culture fingerprints that inform defaults or adaptive interfaces.
useWhen: Setting default density, pacing or notification parameters for products shipped across cultures, especially information-dense or in-car systems.
avoidWhen: When language groups are a poor proxy for culture or samples are from a single company; indicators are specific to the use cases tested. For broader cultural insight use Cross-Cultural UX Research; for attitude scales use Cross-Cultural Survey Equivalence Testing.
whyLost: It was a single-company research tool tied to in-car navigation; later cross-cultural work relied on A/B tests per market and dimension models.
whereToUse: Automotive and navigation interfaces, dashboards, global SaaS defaults, notification design across markets.
example: A global trading app builds identical tasks letting users set chart density and alert frequency; Japanese and Brazilian users differ significantly on alert frequency, so regional defaults are introduced.
reference: Heimgartner, R. (2007). A tool for cross-cultural human computer interaction analysis. In Aykin, N. (ed.) Usability and Internationalization: HCI and Culture, LNCS 4559. Springer, pp. 89-98.

name: Interesting Moments Grid
origin: Bill Scott (interaction events); term 'interesting moments' coined by Eric Miraglia at Yahoo!, mid-2000s
summary: A matrix of interaction events against on-screen actors in which the designer specifies the feedback for every cell, used as a specification and checklist for complex interactions.
description: Scott and Neil introduced the grid for drag and drop, whose apparent simplicity hides many micro-states. They list at least 15 events at which the user can be cued, from page load and hover through drag start, entering and leaving valid and invalid targets, to drop accepted or rejected, and six actors whose appearance can change: page, cursor, tool tip, drag object, its parent container and drop target. That gives 90 possible moments, each needing style and timing decisions. Actors go down the left, moments across the top, and the desired behaviour goes in each cell. The grid captures a whole interaction on one page and exposes holes; the authors say it suits any complex interaction. It survives today as component state matrices in design systems.
steps: List the events (moments) of the interaction across the top, from initial state to completion and failure.
List the actors whose appearance can change down the left (for example page, cursor, tool tip, object, container, target).
For each cell decide and record the visual, textual or motion feedback, or explicitly none.
Review the grid for empty or inconsistent cells and resolve them.
Hand the grid to engineering as the interaction specification.
Use it as a checklist when reviewing the build and in QA.
outputs: A one-page feedback specification for the interaction and a list of unhandled moments.
useWhen: Specifying rich, stateful interactions such as drag and drop, inline editing, uploads or AI streaming responses where small states are easily missed.
avoidWhen: Cell counts grow fast and the grid gives no way to prioritise or validate choices; check that feedback is noticed and understood with Usability Testing or Think-Aloud Usability Testing (Contemporary Practice). For whole-system state logic use State transition diagrams.
whyLost: The term faded with Yahoo!'s pattern library, but the practice lives on as component state matrices and interaction specs in design systems.
whereToUse: Design systems, rich web apps, file and media tools, AI chat interfaces with loading, streaming and error states.
example: A design-system team specifying a file-upload component grids eight moments (idle, hover, drag-over valid, drag-over invalid, uploading, paused, success, error) against five actors and finds no defined feedback for an invalid file dropped mid-upload.
reference: Scott, B. and Neil, T. (2009) Designing Web Interfaces: Principles and Patterns for Rich Interactions. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 26-29.

name: Interface Complexity Metrics
origin: Thomas McCabe, 1976 (cyclomatic complexity); adapted in HCI research from the 1990s
summary: Quantifies interface complexity with formal metrics, such as cyclomatic complexity of navigation, feature interaction counts and entropy, to compare and track complexity over time.
description: Software engineering measures code complexity with metrics such as McCabe's cyclomatic complexity, the number of independent paths through a program. Analogous metrics for interfaces count independent paths through a task flow, decision points per screen, states per component, feature interactions or information entropy. Visual complexity measures based on element counts, alignment and grouping have also been validated against perceived complexity. The method selects metrics appropriate to the question, computes them consistently across designs or releases, and validates them against user outcomes. Rigour comes from clear operational definitions, automated computation where possible so measurements are reproducible, and checking that metrics correlate with task time, errors or perceived complexity in your context, since complexity metrics without behavioural validation can mislead.
steps: Choose metrics suited to the question: path complexity of flows, decision points, component states, visual complexity or entropy.
Write operational definitions and, where possible, automate computation from design files, code or state models.
Compute metrics for the current design and for alternatives or past releases.
Validate selected metrics against user outcomes such as task time, errors or perceived complexity ratings.
Set thresholds or budgets for metrics that correlate with outcomes.
Track metrics over releases and flag increases for review.
outputs: Complexity metric definitions, scores per design and release, validation correlations, complexity budgets.
useWhen: Governing complexity in growing enterprise products and design systems, reviewing architecture, and evaluating AI-generated interfaces.
avoidWhen: One-off evaluations where usability testing will reveal problems more directly, or when metrics cannot be validated.
whyLost: Latent: Research-stage metrics; no standard tools or benchmarks in UX.
whereToUse: Design system complexity management; architecture review; AI-generated UI evaluation.
example: An ERP vendor computed decision points and independent paths for 120 workflows. Workflows above 15 independent paths had twice the error rate in support data, so the team set a path budget for new features.
sources: Handbook of the Philosophy of Science
reference: McCabe, T. J. (1976). A complexity measure. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, SE-2(4), 308-320.

name: Interface language predictability testing
origin: Draws on embodied simulation research (Bergen, 2012) and label testing practice in usability engineering
summary: Measures whether users can correctly predict what will happen when they act on a label or read a message, as a direct quantitative test of interface language.
description: Bergen's embodied simulation account suggests understanding language involves mentally simulating what it describes. If interface language is clear, users' simulations of an action's outcome should match what the system does. Predictability testing measures this directly: participants see a label, button or message in context and predict the outcome before acting, choosing from options or describing it freely. Prediction accuracy and confidence quantify clarity, and calibration (confidence versus accuracy) reveals dangerous confident errors. Unlike preference tests or comprehension questions, this targets the action-outcome link that matters for safety. Rigour comes from realistic context, randomised presentation, enough participants per label, and analysing errors by type.
steps: Select labels and messages linked to consequential or ambiguous outcomes.
Present each in realistic context to 15-30 participants (remote unmoderated is suitable) and ask for a predicted outcome and confidence (0-100%).
Code predictions as correct, partially correct or wrong, ideally with two coders.
Compute accuracy per label (target at least 80% for routine and 95% for irreversible actions) and identify confident errors (wrong with confidence above 70%).
Revise low-scoring labels and test alternatives side by side.
Add the test to content governance for new labels.
outputs: Prediction accuracy and confidence per label, a list of confident errors, and tested label alternatives.
useWhen: When naming actions with consequences, writing error and confirmation messages, or comparing label options.
avoidWhen: For exploratory vocabulary discovery; use interviews or card sorting first.
whyLost: Label testing exists in content design, but most teams test preference or comprehension rather than outcome prediction and calibration.
whereToUse: Fintech confirmations, healthcare actions, privacy settings, AI agent actions, and destructive operations.
example: For a surgical console's 'Release' button, only 46% of nurses correctly predict it disengages instruments; 30% confidently expect it to unlock the arm. Renaming to 'Disengage instruments' raises accuracy to 94%.
sources: Fodor, J., The Language of Thought (1975)
Lakoff, G., Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 17 — Mentalese, Compositionality & the Language of Thought
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Bergen, B. K. (2012). Louder Than Words: The New Science of How the Mind Makes Meaning. Basic Books.

name: Interface Tour and First-Impression Narration
origin: Steve Krug (2010) home page tour; Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed (2012) hybrid interview
summary: A short moderated segment in which participants narrate what a page or element is and predict what it does before clicking, exposing mismatches with their mental models.
description: At the start of a moderated session the participant looks at the home page or a comp without clicking and narrates whose site it is, what it is for and what they could do there. Krug fixes this at about three minutes and treats it as a realistic task, since every visitor must work out what a site is, and wrong first assumptions persist. Goodman and colleagues extend it into a guided tour: element by element and screen by screen the participant says what each control does, what a label means and what page would appear, all before acting. The rigour lies in capturing expectations before any action, because performing an action permanently alters the perception of its effect. Comparing predictions with the real behaviour yields a map of label and mental-model mismatches, plus a reading of the participant's domain knowledge for interpreting later task results.
steps: After the warm-up questions, open the home page or key screen from a bookmark and ask the participant what strikes them, whose it is, what they could do there and what it is for.
Allow scrolling but no clicking; if they click, ask them to return, and stop after about three minutes (four at most).
Optionally give one quick general task of about five minutes to see unprimed behaviour.

Tour the main screens element by element for about ten minutes, asking what each item does in a couple of words, what labels mean and, without clicking, what page would appear and what it would contain.
For each screen ask what matters most, what is missing, what they would do next and how they would get back to home or another major section.
When an action is finally taken, ask whether the result was what they expected, then run the remaining tasks.
Log every mismatch between prediction and actual behaviour, and the participant's apparent domain knowledge, for the debrief.
outputs: A list of mismatches between interface elements and users' expectations, evidence on whether the page communicates identity and purpose, and participant background for interpreting later problems.
useWhen: Early and every-round moderated tests of home pages, landing screens, comps and new navigation, when you need to know whether purpose and labels are understood before task performance contaminates perception.
avoidWhen: Avoid letting it drift into an opinion or aesthetics session; for timed first-impression data at scale use the 5-Second Test, and for label comprehension across many people use unmoderated first-click or tree tests.
whyLost: It survives as the routine 'first impressions' question at the start of moderated tests, though the systematic per-element expectation probing is often skipped.
whereToUse: Landing pages, onboarding screens, dashboards of new SaaS products, AI product entry points where users must infer what the system can do.
example: Before testing tasks on a new budgeting app, each participant narrates the home screen and predicts what 'Pots' and 'Insights' contain. Four of six expect 'Pots' to be savings accounts, which explains later failures in the transfer task.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Krug, S. (2010). Rocket Surgery Made Easy. New Riders, pp. 74-75, 123-124, 150-151; Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. and Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience, 2nd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 292-295.

name: Interim Case Summary
aka: Interim case summary with data accounting sheet
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 4, section F, with the Data Accounting Sheet box (Corbett and Wilson 1991 illustration) and the case study interview of Stiegelbauer et al. (1982).
summary: A provisional mid-study synthesis of what is known about a case, how good the supporting data are and what still has to be collected, paired with a grid showing which questions have data from which informants.
description: Partway through fieldwork the researcher writes a provisional account of the case, typically 10 to 25 pages, built on a common outline so cases stay comparable: the setting, a brief chronology, the current status of each research question (with what is unknown, puzzling or uncertain listed explicitly), a preliminary causal network, and methodological notes on confidence and problems. It reviews findings, looks hard at the quality of the data behind them and sets the agenda for the next wave of collection. A companion data accounting sheet arrays research questions against informants or informant groups and data sources, with each cell marked complete, incomplete, missing or not applicable, so gaps become visible. A lighter variant, the case study interview, has one researcher interview another for an hour with standard questions. The book suggests writing the summary about a third of the way into fieldwork and budgeting two or three days. In UX this is a mid-study readout that is honest about evidence gaps, and the accounting grid shows at a glance that, say, no admin user has been asked about permissions.
steps: Agree a common outline for all cases (context, chronology, status of each research question, emerging explanations, method notes).
About a third of the way through fieldwork, scan coded notes for each research question and draft the summary quickly.
For each question, state what is known, the confidence in it, and what remains puzzling or unanswered.
Build a data accounting sheet: research questions as rows, informant groups and data sources as columns, cells marked complete, partial, missing or not applicable.
Exchange summaries with colleagues and discuss blind spots and emerging cross-case themes.
Turn the gaps into the plan for the next round of sessions and recruitment.
outputs: A short provisional case report, a gap list, and a questions-by-informants coverage grid.
useWhen: Studies run over weeks or months, several researchers handle different cases, or there is still time to fix gaps in the data.
avoidWhen: Fieldwork is nearly finished and no further collection is possible, or the study is so small that a single synthesis suffices.
whyLost: UX timelines rarely include a formal mid-point; teams jump from fieldwork to final synthesis, so coverage gaps surface only when it is too late to recruit.
whereToUse: Longitudinal studies, multi-segment discovery, enterprise research with many roles per account.
example: Midway through research on a procurement tool across six client companies, each researcher writes a 12-page interim summary. The data accounting sheet shows that the question on approval bottlenecks has data from requesters and buyers but none from finance approvers at four of six companies, so the next fortnight's recruiting targets finance staff.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Interleaved experiments
origin: Joachims (2002); Chapelle et al. (2012); Radlinski and Craswell (2013)
summary: Merge two rankers' result lists into one alternating list shown to each user and credit clicks to the source algorithm, giving a highly sensitive paired comparison.
description: Comparing ranking algorithms with ordinary A/B tests needs large samples because between-user variance swamps small differences. Interleaving shows each user a single list built from both rankers: items alternate between the two lists, duplicates are removed, and which algorithm picks first is balanced (team-draft interleaving). Each click is credited to the algorithm that supplied the item, and preferences are aggregated across queries. Because every user sees both algorithms, the comparison is paired and can be one to two orders of magnitude more sensitive than an A/B test, making it a fast screening step before a full A/B test on business metrics. It is valid only when result slots are homogeneous and the change affects nothing outside the list.
steps: Generate both ranked lists for each query or request.
Interleave them alternately, removing duplicates and randomising or balancing which algorithm contributes first (team-draft).
Log which algorithm supplied each displayed item.
Credit clicks (or other engagement) to the supplying algorithm per query.
Aggregate wins across queries and test whether the preference differs from 50%.
Confirm promising rankers with a standard A/B test on the overall evaluation criterion.
outputs: A preference score between two rankers with a significance test.
useWhen: Screening many ranking or recommendation variants quickly with limited traffic.
avoidWhen: When result slots differ in size or presentation, the change affects other page areas, or business metrics (revenue, retention) are needed; use a standard A/B test.
whyLost: It is routine in search and information retrieval teams but little known in UX, where ranking quality is usually judged by A/B tests or relevance ratings.
whereToUse: Search engines, e-commerce search, content feeds, recommendation carousels and retrieval for AI assistants.
example: An e-commerce search team has six candidate ranking models. Interleaving pairs of models over two days of traffic identifies the two strongest, which then go into a full A/B test on revenue per search.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Chapelle, O., Joachims, T., Radlinski, F. and Yue, Y. (2012). Large-scale validation and analysis of interleaved search evaluation. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 30(1), 6.

name: Interpretation Session (Contextual Design)
origin: Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt, Contextual Design (1997); evolved version Holtzblatt and Beyer (2014)
summary: Within 48 hours of a field interview, the interviewer retells it to a small team who capture self-contained notes and work models together.
description: The interpretation session is the Contextual Design step that turns each contextual interview into shared team data. The interviewer and two to five colleagues from different functions meet within 48 hours. The interviewer tells the story from handwritten notes and memory while others ask questions to draw out overlooked detail. One recorder types numbered, self-contained notes on screen, each capturing one point: practice issues, identity and cultural observations, breakdowns, task patterns, use of time, place and devices, and design ideas. Other participants draw individual work models as detail emerges, such as Day in the Life, Relationship, Collaboration, Identity and Sequence models. Because everyone has a role, the team comes to own the data, and the notes feed directly into the affinity diagram. Most teams now hold a loose debrief instead.
steps: Hold the session within 48 hours of the interview, booking about two hours.
Gather the interviewer plus 2-5 cross-functional team members; remote participants can join.
The interviewer retells the interview in sequence from notes and memory.
Team members ask questions to draw out detail and say what should be captured, including design, marketing and business implications.
One recorder types numbered, self-contained notes in a shared document, one point per note.
Other participants draw the relevant work models for this user (Day in the Life, Relationship, Collaboration, Identity, Sequence, and Decision Point or Physical when relevant).
Store the notes for printing onto sticky notes for the affinity diagram and the models for consolidation.
outputs: Numbered interpretation notes and individual work models for each interviewed user, plus a shared team understanding.
useWhen: Contextual inquiry programmes with cross-functional teams who need to own the data and build an affinity diagram and consolidated models.
avoidWhen: Avoid when interviews are not contextual or when the team cannot meet promptly; a researcher's own debrief notes are then more realistic. For very large studies, consider rapid team debriefs with a structured template.
whyLost: The name survives as an informal debrief; the strict 48-hour timing, roles, self-contained notes and model drawing are usually dropped.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflow tools, clinical systems, field service apps and any team adopting contextual inquiry.
example: After each visit to a warehouse, the interviewer, a developer, a PM and a designer meet the next morning. In 90 minutes they record 70 notes and a sequence model of the picking task, which later reveal three handoff breakdowns.
sources: Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems (Beyer & Holtzblatt, 1997)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Holtzblatt, K. and Beyer, H. (2014). Contextual Design: Evolved. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool, pp. 18-20; Beyer, H. and Holtzblatt, K. (1997). Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems. San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Interpretive Description
origin: Sally Thorne, 1997 (with Kirkham and MacDonald-Emes); book 2008
summary: An applied qualitative approach that combines methodological flexibility with interpretive rigour, judging quality by whether findings are credible and useful for practice.
description: Interpretive Description (Sally Thorne) is a qualitative approach developed specifically for applied practice disciplines where research must be both epistemologically sound and practically useful. It occupies a middle ground: more structured than phenomenology, less theory-generating than Grounded Theory, less policy-oriented than Framework Analysis. It is appropriate when you want systematic interpretation of qualitative data in service of understanding that can be directly applied to practice — which describes most applied UX research.
steps: Establish the applied logic: Interpretive description begins with the recognition that the researcher has a substantive purpose. What will this research be used for? Who needs to understand what? Let this purpose guide analytic choices.
