Data collection: Multiple data collection approaches are encouraged — different methods access different aspects of the phenomenon. Do not rely on a single method.

Analytic strategy: Read for patterns, themes, and exceptions. Build interpretations that are responsive to the data and useful to practitioners. Seek logic beyond frequency — what matters is not what most people said but what understanding is revealed.

Thematic development as applied insight: Each theme should represent a genuine insight — something that practitioners would not have known without the research, and that can change how they understand and act.

Credibility through pragmatic utility: The quality criterion for interpretive description is not theoretical elegance but practical usefulness. Does the interpretation help practitioners understand something they need to understand?
outputs: Interpretive themes framed as applied insights, explicit links to practice implications, an audit trail, and credibility evidence including practitioner review.
useWhen: Research must be practically actionable for a practice discipline such as clinicians, designers or product teams, and you want rigour without committing to a single philosophical tradition.
avoidWhen: You aim to build formal theory (use grounded theory) or describe the essence of experience (use phenomenology). For simple descriptive summaries, a lighter thematic approach suffices.
whyLost: It is well established in nursing but unknown in UX, even though its pragmatic, practice-oriented logic closely matches what applied UX research needs.
whereToUse: Health and care products, clinical decision support, applied product discovery, service design, and any research done for a practitioner audience.
example: Studying how community nurses use a scheduling tool, researchers combine interviews and shadowing, build themes around practical dilemmas such as 'protecting visit time', and check credibility with nurse managers before translating them into design guidance.
sources: Developing Qualitative Methods — or Same Old Wine (PMC)
reference: Thorne, S. (2016). Interpretive Description: Qualitative Research for Applied Practice (2nd ed.). Routledge.

name: Interpretive Repertoires and Ideological Dilemmas
origin: Margaret Wetherell and Jonathan Potter, 1987 to 1992; Michael Billig et al., 1988
summary: Identifies the culturally shared repertoires of terms and metaphors people draw on, and the contradictions (ideological dilemmas) they navigate when talking about a topic.
description: Interpretive repertoires (Wetherell & Potter) are culturally shared building blocks of conversation — recurrently used systems of terms, metaphors, and figures of speech that construct a particular version of an object, person, or action. Ideological dilemmas (Billig) are the contradictions within common-sense ideology that force people to navigate between competing cultural commitments. Together, these concepts reveal how people draw on available cultural resources (repertoires) to manage social life, and how they navigate the contradictions between them. Applied to UX: they reveal the competing cultural frameworks available to users for making sense of technology — and the tensions between them.
steps: Identify interpretive repertoires: In your data, what recurrent systems of terms, metaphors, and phrases are used to construct versions of the phenomenon? Each repertoire is a coherent way of talking about something — and different repertoires construct it differently.
Map repertoire distribution: Who uses which repertoires? In what contexts? Repertoire use is not random — it is strategically deployed to accomplish interactional purposes.

Identify ideological dilemmas: Where do participants show inconsistency or tension between competing cultural commitments? ('I believe in privacy but I want personalisation.' 'I want simplicity but I need features.') These are ideological dilemmas.

Dilemma navigation analysis: How do participants navigate the tension? What rhetorical moves do they use to manage the contradiction? What does the navigation reveal about their priorities and values?

Application to design: Understanding the repertoires available to users for making sense of your product reveals what framings are available and which are absent — and which repertoire framings your product currently invokes.
outputs: A catalogue of interpretive repertoires, their distribution across speakers and contexts, documented ideological dilemmas, and design implications for framing and messaging.
useWhen: Users talk about a topic in contradictory ways, such as privacy versus convenience, AI as helper versus threat, or saving versus enjoying life, and you need to understand the cultural resources behind their talk.
avoidWhen: You need quick attitude measurement or task insight; use surveys or usability testing. For structured viewpoint segmentation, consider Q Methodology.
whyLost: It belongs to discursive psychology, which UX rarely meets, and its findings concern cultural framings rather than features.
whereToUse: Privacy and data products, AI adoption, sustainability and ethical consumption, personal finance messaging, and brand positioning.
example: Interviews on data sharing show users switch between a 'nothing to hide' repertoire and a 'they sell everything' repertoire. Consent copy that acknowledges both, offering benefit and control together, outperforms purely reassuring copy.
sources: Mapping the Language of Racism (Wetherell & Potter)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Billig, M., Condor, S., Edwards, D., Gane, M., Middleton, D. & Radley, A. (1988). Ideological Dilemmas. Sage.

name: Interrupted Time Series (ITS)
origin: Campbell and Stanley (1963); Wagner et al. (2002) segmented regression
summary: Models a long series of measurements before and after a change to estimate immediate level shifts and slope changes beyond the pre-existing trend.
description: Named in the treatise's borrowing matrix among epidemiology's key methods, ITS uses many time points before and after an intervention to estimate whether it changed the level and trend of an outcome, controlling for the pre-existing trend, seasonality and autocorrelation. It is one of the strongest quasi-experimental designs when no control group exists, and adding a comparison series makes it stronger. For UX, it evaluates releases, policy changes and outages with daily or weekly metrics such as support contacts, error rates or task completion. Typical requirements are at least 8-12 points per segment and attention to concurrent events that could explain changes.
steps: Define the intervention date and outcome series at consistent intervals.
Collect sufficient pre- and post-intervention points (ideally 12 or more each).
Fit segmented regression with terms for baseline trend, level change and slope change.
Model seasonality and autocorrelation (for example ARIMA errors).
Add a control series or outcome if available and check for co-interventions.
Report level and slope changes with CIs and visualise the counterfactual trend.
outputs: Level and slope change estimates, counterfactual plot, diagnostics.
useWhen: Evaluating whole-population changes (releases, regulations, pricing) with routinely collected metrics.
avoidWhen: Few data points or many simultaneous changes; consider DiD with a control group.
whyLost: Product analytics relies on simple before-after charts; time-series modelling sits with data science.
whereToUse: Support contact volumes, error rates, accessibility complaint trends, regulatory impact (consent, cancellation rules).
example: After a simplified cancellation flow, ITS on weekly complaints shows an immediate 30% level drop with no change in pre-existing slope, isolating the effect from a long-term decline.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Wagner AK et al. (2002) Segmented regression analysis of interrupted time series studies. J Clin Pharm Ther 27
Bernal JL, Cummins S & Gasparrini A (2017) Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions. Int J Epidemiol
Wagner et al., Segmented regression analysis of interrupted time series studies in medication use research (2002), Journal of Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics
Bernal, Cummins & Gasparrini, Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial (2017), International Journal of Epidemiology
Shadish, Cook & Campbell, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs (2002)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Bernal JL, Cummins S & Gasparrini A (2017) Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. International Journal of Epidemiology 46(1):348-355.

name: Interrupted-task recall test (Zeigarnik)
origin: Bluma Zeigarnik, Berlin, 1927, following Kurt Lewin's observation of waiters
summary: People attempt a series of short tasks, about half interrupted, then recall them; comparing recall of interrupted and completed tasks tests whether unfinished tasks stay active in memory.
description: Lewin noticed that waiters remembered unpaid orders better than settled ones. Zeigarnik gave participants a run of simple puzzles and tasks, interrupting roughly half before completion. Asked later what they remembered, participants were about twice as likely to recall interrupted tasks. She explained this as lack of closure keeping a task active. The effect is widely invoked in design (progress bars, cliffhangers, incomplete profiles), usually without running the test, and later replications are mixed, with effects depending on motivation and whether people expect to resume. The controlled version randomises which tasks are interrupted and compares recall ratios after a filler task. It is also a caution for interviews: people may over-report unfinished tasks.
steps: Prepare a set of short, comparable tasks (puzzles or product tasks).
Have each participant attempt all tasks, interrupting a random half before completion, with interruption counterbalanced across participants.
After a delay and filler activity, ask for free recall of all tasks attempted.
Optionally measure whether participants return to unfinished tasks when given free time.
Compute the ratio of interrupted to completed tasks recalled.
Check whether expectation of resuming or motivation moderates the effect.
outputs: Recall ratio of interrupted to completed tasks, and resumption rates if measured.
useWhen: Testing whether incomplete states (an unfinished profile, a paused course, a saved draft) are remembered and resumed more than completed ones.
avoidWhen: Avoid citing the effect as settled; replications are mixed. Interruption annoys people and can colour later ratings. For real resumption behaviour use cohort analytics.
whyLost: The name survives as a design rule of thumb, but the controlled recall test is almost never run, so the evidence behind design claims is rarely checked.
whereToUse: Onboarding checklists, course and content platforms, profile completion, saved carts, streaming cliffhangers.
example: A learning app interrupts half of short lessons at random with a 'continue later' screen; next-day recall and voluntary resumption are compared with completed lessons, showing a smaller effect than the team assumed.
sources: Zeigarnik, B. (1927). Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 9
reference: Zeigarnik, B. (1927). Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 9, 1-85.

name: Interviews
origin: Qualitative research interviewing tradition, early 20th century onward
summary: One-to-one conversations that explore people's experiences, needs, behaviours and reasoning in depth, the core qualitative data collection method in UX.
description: Research interviews are guided conversations in which a researcher explores a participant's experiences, practices, needs, motivations and mental models. They can be structured, semi-structured or unstructured, with semi-structured interviews most common in UX: a guide sets topics while allowing the researcher to follow interesting threads. Interviews are most reliable when they ask about specific past behaviour rather than hypothetical futures or general opinions. Rigour comes from clear research questions, a guide built around concrete recent episodes, open and non-leading questions, active listening and follow-up probes, careful recruitment for variation, recording and transcription, and systematic analysis such as thematic analysis rather than memory-based summaries.
steps: Define research questions and the decisions the interviews will inform.
Recruit 6 to 15 participants per segment, aiming for variation in relevant characteristics.
Write a semi-structured guide focused on specific past episodes ('tell me about the last time...').
Pilot the guide and refine questions that lead or confuse.
Conduct 45 to 60 minute sessions, using open questions and probes such as 'what happened next?'.
Record and transcribe with consent, and write a summary note after each session.
Analyse systematically, for example with thematic analysis, and report themes with evidence.
outputs: Transcripts, session notes, themes with supporting quotes, and insights about needs, behaviours and motivations.
useWhen: For discovery and need-finding, understanding motivations and context, eliciting mental models, and follow-up after quantitative findings.
avoidWhen: Avoid for measuring prevalence or predicting behaviour from stated intentions; use surveys or analytics. For observing actual use, use contextual inquiry or usability testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Versatile and accessible; central to virtually every discovery phase.
whereToUse: Discovery research; need-finding; mental model elicitation; post-task debrief.
example: A neobank interviews 12 freelancers about the last time they set aside money for tax. Most use a separate account with ad hoc transfers, leading to an automated tax pot feature.
sources: The Science and Art of Interviewing

name: Intraclass correlation (ICC)
aka: Intraclass correlation for rater or item reliability
origin: Shrout and Fleiss, 1979
summary: A reliability coefficient for continuous ratings that tells you how consistently targets are scored across judges or items, in agreement or consistency forms.
description: The intraclass correlation treats judges (or items) as a within-subjects factor and expresses reliability as the share of rating variance due to real differences between targets. Shrout and Fleiss distinguish cases: ICC(2,1) treats judges as a random sample and counts their mean differences against reliability (absolute agreement); ICC(3,1) treats judges as fixed and ignores mean shifts (consistency). Average-measure forms, ICC(2,k) and ICC(3,k), apply when the mean of k judges is the score you will use. The choice changes the answer markedly: in Maxwell et al.'s example the same data give ICC(2,1) = .29 and ICC(3,1) = .71. The same coefficient also appears in mixed models as the proportion of variance due to a random factor such as participant or team. Rigour lies in choosing the form by the question, not by which number is larger.
steps: Arrange the data as targets (rows) by judges or items (columns), with every judge rating every target where possible.
Decide whether systematic differences in judge leniency should count against reliability (agreement) or not (consistency).
Choose Case 2 (random judges, agreement) if judges stand for a wider pool, or Case 3 (fixed judges, consistency) if these judges are the only ones that matter.
Choose the single-measure form if one judge's score will be used, or the average-measure form if the mean of k judges will be used.
Compute from the two-way ANOVA mean squares (or a mixed model) and report the form, point estimate and 95% confidence interval.
Interpret against conventional bands (roughly below .50 poor, .50-.75 moderate, .75-.90 good, above .90 excellent) and improve rater training or anchors if low.
outputs: An ICC of a stated form with a confidence interval, and a judgement on whether rating data are reliable enough to use.
useWhen: When several researchers rate severity, task success quality, design quality or video-coded behaviour on continuous or many-point scales, or when you need the share of variance due to participants or teams.
avoidWhen: Avoid for nominal codes (use Cohen's Kappa and Krippendorff's Alpha (Inter-Rater Reliability)) and when you need to separate several error facets at once (use Generalizability Theory). It is sensitive to between-target range: homogeneous samples give low ICCs.
whyLost: It is standard in medicine, psychology and measurement science, but UX teams default to kappa or percentage agreement and seldom distinguish agreement from consistency forms.
whereToUse: Severity rating calibration across evaluators, expert design reviews, AI-output quality rating, coding of recorded sessions, mixed-model analysis of repeated measures.
example: Four researchers rate the severity of 30 usability problems on a 1-10 scale. ICC(2,1) of .45 against ICC(3,1) of .78 shows they rank problems similarly but one is systematically harsher, prompting a calibration session.
sources: Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420-428.

name: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI)
origin: Ryan (1982) and later self-determination theory researchers; its use as an enjoyment measure in games research is noted in chapter 9 (citing Mekler et al., 2014)
summary: A multi-dimensional questionnaire on the subjective experience of an activity, whose interest/enjoyment subscale is widely used as a measure of enjoyment in games user research.
description: The Intrinsic Motivation Inventory was built to assess people's experience of an activity in laboratory studies of motivation. It has several subscales, including interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, effort/importance, pressure/tension, perceived choice and value/usefulness, and researchers usually select the subscales that fit their question. The interest/enjoyment subscale was originally intended as the self-report measure of intrinsic motivation, but games researchers often use it on its own as a short, reasonably well-established measure of how much players enjoyed a game or a feature. Items are rated on a 7-point scale after the activity. For UX researchers, the IMI is a flexible option when they need an enjoyment or perceived-competence score that is grounded in motivational theory, for example to test whether gamification elements such as points or badges change enjoyment or only change behaviour. Because subscales can be mixed and adapted, comparability between studies depends on reporting exactly which items were used.
steps: Select the IMI subscales relevant to the question (often interest/enjoyment, competence and pressure/tension).
Adapt item wording to the activity while keeping the meaning.
Have participants complete the activity under the conditions being compared.
Administer the selected items immediately after the activity.
Score each subscale and check reliability.
Compare conditions and report exactly which items and wording were used.
outputs: Subscale scores such as interest/enjoyment, perceived competence and pressure/tension.
useWhen: You need a short, theory-based measure of enjoyment or perceived competence for an activity, including tests of game elements.
avoidWhen: You need a broad player experience profile or a measure tied to a specific domain such as usability.
whyLost: Known in psychology and gamification research but rarely in product UX, which defaults to satisfaction and NPS measures.
whereToUse: Games, gamified apps, learning and training products, behaviour change tools.
example: A language app tests streak badges; IMI enjoyment scores do not differ between conditions even though session counts rise, suggesting the badges drive habit, not enjoyment.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 9. Ryan, R. M. (1982). Control and information in the intrapersonal sphere: an extension of cognitive evaluation theory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43, 450-461.

name: Ishikawa (Fishbone) Diagram
origin: Kaoru Ishikawa, 1940s-1968 (Guide to Quality Control)
summary: Structures candidate causes of an effect under fixed category spines, ensuring a team considers people, process, tools, materials, environment and measurement.
description: The fishbone places the effect at the head and draws major cause categories as bones, traditionally the 6Ms: Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Mother Nature (environment). Teams brainstorm causes under each category, then sub-causes. The value is breadth: the fixed categories counter the tendency to blame the most salient cause, typically the user. In proper quality practice the diagram is only a hypothesis generator, followed by data collection (check sheets, Pareto analysis) to confirm which causes actually matter. UX versions often stop at the brainstorm. Adapted categories for digital products might be Users, Interface, Content, Data, Platform, Policy and Context.
steps: Write a specific, measurable effect statement at the head of the fish.
Choose 5-7 category bones suited to the product (e.g. users, interface, content, data, platform, policy, environment).
Brainstorm causes under each category with a cross-functional group, then add sub-causes by asking why.
Mark the causes for which evidence already exists and those that are hypotheses.
Collect data to test the top hypotheses using check sheets, log queries or targeted sessions, and draw a Pareto chart of confirmed causes.
Act on the vital few causes that account for most occurrences.
outputs: A categorised cause map, a hypothesis list, and a Pareto chart of verified causes.
useWhen: A team needs to broaden its thinking about causes of a known problem before investigating.
avoidWhen: When the causal structure involves interactions and feedback; use causal loop diagrams or fault trees. Never as a substitute for verification.
whyLost: Adopted as a whiteboard template without the Pareto and data-verification steps that made it a quality tool.
whereToUse: Churn spikes, support volume increases, quality defects in content or data, accessibility regressions.
example: An e-commerce team uses a fishbone for rising returns of apparel. Check sheets on 400 returns show that two causes under 'Content' (inconsistent size charts, misleading colour photography) explain 62% of returns.
sources: Ishikawa, Guide to Quality Control (1968; English 1976)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Ishikawa, K. (1976). Guide to Quality Control. Asian Productivity Organization.

name: Ising Attitude Network Model
origin: Causal attitude network model by Dalege et al. (2016), formalised as a random field Ising model with attention as inverse temperature (Dalege et al. 2018); fitted with IsingFit (Dalege et al. 2017).
summary: A model and analysis that treats an attitude as a network of binary feelings, beliefs and behaviours whose alignment depends on attention to the topic, fitted to survey data to reveal attitude structure and estimate its consistency.
description: In this model each node is an evaluative reaction toward an object (a belief such as 'is honest', a feeling such as 'angry', a behaviour such as 'eats meat'). Nodes influence each other through weighted links and have their own thresholds, and an external field such as a campaign can push all nodes. Attention or involvement works like inverse temperature: when people attend to the object, the network 'freezes' into a consistent positive or negative configuration and becomes hard to move (hysteresis); when attention is low, reactions are loosely connected and responsive to outside pressure but do not stick. Empirically, binary or dichotomised items are fitted with IsingFit, communities of items are detected (for example warmth and competence beliefs), and Gibbs entropy can quantify how consistent an attitude network is. A learning variant shows how repeated high attention strengthens links so that later consistency needs less attention. For UX and product research, the model gives a structured way to analyse attitudes to brands, features or technologies, to judge how settled they are, and to reason about why persuasion fails with highly involved users while low-involvement users are easily swayed but quickly revert.
steps: Write items for distinct beliefs, feelings and behaviours toward one attitude object, scored as binary or dichotomised.
Collect a large sample, ideally with a measure of involvement or attention to the topic.
Fit an Ising network with IsingFit and plot it, adding community detection to group related reactions.
Compare networks or connectivity between high- and low-involvement groups.
Estimate attitude consistency, for example with Gibbs entropy on small networks.
Use simulation of the model to reason about how involvement and messaging would change the attitude, and test those predictions.
outputs: An estimated attitude network with thresholds and item communities, connectivity and entropy comparisons between groups, and simulation-based predictions about persuadability.
useWhen: You are studying attitudes toward a product, brand or technology and need to understand their structure and stability, not only their average valence.
avoidWhen: Items are few or redundant, the sample is small, or the attitude object is not something people hold several distinct reactions toward.
whyLost: It comes from recent social psychology and statistical physics and has not been translated into product research practice, which relies on single attitude scores.
whereToUse: Attitudes to AI features, privacy and data sharing, sustainability behaviours, brand perception, health-behaviour apps.
example: Researchers survey 4,000 people about an electric-vehicle charging app using binary items on reliability, cost, environmental feelings and frustration. The network of highly involved drivers is dense and polarised while that of casual drivers is sparse, so the team targets casual drivers with simple reliability messaging and expects little movement among committed critics.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: ISO 9241-9 Device Assessment Questionnaire
origin: ISO (2000); used with Fitts' throughput testing by Young, Kehoe and Murphy in Chapter 7
summary: A standard post-task rating questionnaire for pointing and input devices, covering items such as smoothness, force, mental effort, accuracy, speed and overall evaluation.
description: ISO 9241-9 sets out how to evaluate non-keyboard input devices. Alongside performance testing with Fitts' throughput, it includes a comfort and usability questionnaire answered after each device is used. Items cover aspects such as the force required, smoothness of operation, mental effort, accuracy, speed of cursor movement and an overall evaluation, each on a bipolar rating scale. In Chapter 7 the questionnaire was given after a standard pointing task and again after 15 minutes of in-game play for each of four controllers (mouse, touchpad, Steam controller and DualShock 4), presented in counterbalanced order. Responses were treated as ordinal, compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests and shown as diverging stacked bar charts, and open-ended questions were added because earlier work suggested the standard items alone were not enough. The authors frame the battery as covering three linked concerns, functionality, usability and user experience (McNamara and Kirakowski), so that objective performance, ratings and comments are read together. The questionnaire is a ready-made, comparable way to capture how hardware feels to use.
steps: Select devices to compare and a counterbalanced order of use.
Have participants complete a standard task (for example multidirectional pointing) and, separately, a realistic in-context task with each device.
Administer the device assessment items after each device.
Add open-ended questions about what was good or bad about each device.
Analyse ratings as ordinal data with non-parametric tests and diverging stacked bar charts.
Read ratings alongside throughput, error data and comments to explain differences.
outputs: Per-device ratings of effort, smoothness, accuracy, speed, comfort and overall quality, with statistical comparisons and qualitative comments.
useWhen: Comparing controllers, mice, touchpads, styluses or other input hardware, or new input mappings in software.
avoidWhen: The interface does not involve a physical input device, or only overall satisfaction matters.
whyLost: Mostly used in input-device research; UX teams rarely evaluate hardware and often skip standardised device questionnaires.
whereToUse: Game controllers, peripherals, VR and AR controllers, automotive and medical input devices.
example: A group of players use four controllers in a shooter game; ratings show the Steam controller needs too little force for moving and aiming, while the mouse is rated smoothest and most accurate.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Young, G. W., Kehoe, A. and Murphy, D. (2016). Usability testing of video game controllers: a case study. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 7. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Isomorphism Check
aka: Mental model to system isomorphism mapping
origin: Adapted for UX from Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), chapters II and IV, where meaning arises when one structure maps onto another
summary: Lay the user's mental model and the system's real structure side by side and find exactly where the mapping between them breaks.
description: Hofstadter argues that symbols carry meaning only when there is an isomorphism, a part-for-part and rule-for-rule correspondence, between a formal system and something in the world. An interface works the same way: people act on a model of the system they carry in their heads, and things go wrong where that model and the real structure stop corresponding. An isomorphism check makes both structures explicit. You elicit the user's model (entities, relationships, the rules they believe apply) and draw the system's actual model (objects, states, rules) in the same notation, then pair the parts one by one. Elements with no partner, partners with the wrong relationship and rules that hold on one side but not the other are the places where users will form false beliefs, and they explain errors that look random in testing.
steps: Draw the system's model: the objects users deal with, how they relate, and the rules that change them, in plain words.
Elicit users' models through think-aloud, teach-back (ask them to explain the product to a new colleague) or a drawing task, with 5 to 8 people.
Redraw each user's model in the same notation as the system model.
Pair elements across the two models and mark each pair as matched, missing on one side, or mismatched in relationship or rule.
Check whether each mismatch predicts an error or confusion you have seen in testing, support tickets or analytics.
Decide per mismatch whether to change the system to fit the model, or change what the interface shows so the model can be corrected.
outputs: A side-by-side map of the user and system models with every broken correspondence marked and linked to the errors it causes.
useWhen: Users make errors that seem irrational, a product's underlying model is unusual (permissions, sync, versioning, billing), or before redesigning navigation built around internal structures.
avoidWhen: Simple linear flows with little hidden state, or when you only need to know whether a task succeeds rather than why.
whyLost: Mental model work in UX usually stops at describing what users believe. The stricter idea, that understanding depends on a structural correspondence you can check part by part, stayed in logic and cognitive science and was never turned into a routine audit.
whereToUse: Sharing and permissions models, sync and offline states, file and version systems, financial products with hidden rules.
example: Users believe a shared folder is a copy that belongs to them; the system treats it as a link to the owner's folder. The check shows 'delete' has no matching rule in the users' model, which explains why people delete shared work believing only their copy goes.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Chapters II (Meaning and Form in Mathematics) and IV (Consistency, Completeness, and Geometry).

name: Item Response Theory (IRT) / Rasch Model
origin: Georg Rasch, 1960; Frederic Lord, 1950s to 1980
summary: Models the probability of item responses as a function of a latent trait and item properties, enabling precise scale calibration, item selection and adaptive questionnaires.
description: Item response theory models how a person's level on a latent trait, such as perceived usability, digital literacy or trust, and the properties of each item jointly determine response probabilities. Item parameters include difficulty (location) and discrimination, and polytomous models such as the graded response model handle Likert items. Unlike classical test theory, IRT gives item-level information, shows where on the trait each item measures precisely, supports equating across versions, and makes computerised adaptive testing possible. For UX scales, IRT can identify redundant items, create short forms that preserve precision and check that items function equally across groups through differential item functioning analysis. Rigour comes from adequate samples (often 300 or more), checking unidimensionality and local independence, model fit assessment and DIF testing.
steps: Define the latent trait and assemble a pool of candidate items.
Collect responses from a large, diverse sample, typically 300 or more.
Check unidimensionality (for example with factor analysis) and local independence.
Fit an appropriate model, such as Rasch, 2PL or graded response, and assess item and model fit.
Inspect item parameters and information curves to find redundant or poorly discriminating items.
Test for differential item functioning across key groups such as language or age.
Build short forms or adaptive versions and validate them against the full scale.
outputs: Item difficulty and discrimination parameters, test and item information curves, DIF results, short forms and adaptive questionnaires.
useWhen: For developing and refining UX questionnaires, short-form creation, cross-cultural or cross-group fairness checks and adaptive surveys.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small samples or when using established scales unchanged; classical reliability checks may suffice. Not needed for one-off descriptive surveys.
whyLost: Latent: Used in assessment; rarely applied in UX scale design despite offering advantages over classical test theory.
whereToUse: UX scale development; adaptive survey design; usability scale validation.
example: A government digital service develops a digital confidence scale for 2,000 citizens. IRT shows four items cluster at low difficulty and one item functions differently for older adults, producing a fair 8-item adaptive version.
sources: Item Response Theory for Psychologists (Embretson & Reise)

name: Jobs-to-be-Done Research
origin: Clayton Christensen (Innovator's Solution, 2003); switch interview technique by Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek
summary: Research that frames demand as the progress a person is trying to make in a circumstance, using switch interviews to uncover the forces behind real purchase decisions.
description: Jobs-to-be-done reframes the unit of analysis from the customer to the job: the progress someone seeks in a particular circumstance, with functional, emotional and social dimensions. The most rigorous qualitative form is the switch interview, which reconstructs a recent, real decision to start or stop using a product as a timeline from first thought to purchase and use. Interviewers probe the four forces of progress: push of the current situation, pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new, and habit of the present. Rigour comes from interviewing people who actually switched recently (within roughly 90 days), anchoring on concrete events rather than opinions, and synthesising jobs as solution-agnostic statements. Findings explain competition beyond category boundaries and guide positioning and roadmaps.
steps: Define the decision to study (for example switching to or from your product) and recruit 10-15 people who made it within the last 90 days.
Conduct switch interviews reconstructing the timeline: first thought, passive looking, active looking, deciding, first use, ongoing use.
Probe for the four forces at each stage: push, pull, anxiety and habit, using concrete details such as dates, places and people involved.
Code interviews for circumstances, desired progress, alternatives considered (including non-consumption) and hiring or firing criteria.
Cluster cases into distinct jobs and write solution-agnostic job statements with their functional, emotional and social dimensions.
Translate jobs into positioning, onboarding and roadmap decisions, and test the riskiest assumptions.
outputs: Job statements, forces-of-progress diagrams, switch timelines, competing alternatives map and job-based segments.
useWhen: Understanding why people adopt, switch or churn; repositioning a product; finding non-obvious competitors; framing discovery research.
avoidWhen: When you need to measure the size or priority of needs across a population (use outcome-driven innovation or surveys), or for detailed interface usability questions.
whyLost: Still in use: Strong product strategy alignment; used in outcome-driven innovation methodology.
whereToUse: New product development; feature prioritization; positioning research.
example: A meal-kit company interviews 12 recent cancellers and finds the job is 'make weeknights feel under control', not 'cook new recipes'. The real competitor is a supermarket ready meal, leading to a 15-minute meal tier that reduces churn.
sources: Competing Against Luck (Clayton Christensen et al.)
When Coffee and Kale Compete (Alan Klement)
reference: Christensen CM, Hall T, Dillon K & Duncan DS (2016) Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice. Harper Business

name: Jobs-to-be-Done Switch Interviews
origin: Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek (The Re-Wired Group), 2000s; Clayton Christensen et al. (Competing Against Luck, 2016); Moesta (Demand-Side Sales 101, 2020)
summary: Reconstructs, in documentary detail, the timeline of a real switch to or from a product, identifying the forces (push, pull, anxiety, habit) that drove the decision.
description: Switch interviews focus on a specific recent purchase or switch, ideally within the last 60-90 days. The interviewer reconstructs the timeline like a documentary: first thought, passive looking, active looking, deciding, consuming, satisfaction. Specific memories (where were you, what did you do next, who else was involved) anchor recall. Analysis maps the four forces of progress: the push of the current situation, the pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new and habit of the present. Patterns across 10-20 interviews reveal the jobs and struggling moments. Many 'JTBD interviews' today are generic needs interviews with job statements, losing the timeline and forces analysis.
steps: Recruit people who recently switched (bought, cancelled or changed providers) within roughly 90 days.
Start at the moment of purchase and work backwards to the first thought, then forward to use.
Probe for concrete details (time, place, people, alternatives considered, what was happening in life) to cue memory.
Capture energy and emotion at key moments and listen for struggling moments.
Code each interview into a timeline and the four forces; cluster interviews to identify jobs.
Translate jobs and forces into design, messaging and onboarding (reduce anxiety, overcome habit).
outputs: Switch timelines, forces diagrams, job clusters and implications for product, marketing and onboarding.
useWhen: Understanding why people adopt, switch or abandon products, and what progress they seek.
avoidWhen: Usability evaluations or when no recent switching events exist to study.
whyLost: JTBD became a popular label and job-statement template, and the forensic timeline interview was simplified away.
whereToUse: SaaS acquisition and churn, consumer subscriptions, financial products, B2B purchasing.
example: Interviewing 15 people who switched from spreadsheets to a CRM, researchers find the push was a lost deal after a forgotten follow-up, and anxiety was data migration; onboarding is redesigned around a one-click import and first follow-up reminder.
sources: Christensen, Hall, Dillon & Duncan, Competing Against Luck (2016)
Klement, When Coffee and Kale Compete (2016)
reference: Christensen, C. M., Hall, T., Dillon, K., & Duncan, D. S. (2016). Competing Against Luck. HarperBusiness.

name: Joint Display
origin: Michael D. Fetters, Leslie A. Curry & John W. Creswell, 2013
summary: A table that integrates quantitative signals, qualitative mechanisms and prescribed changes row by row, making the path from evidence to decision traceable.
description: Joint displays are the integration device of mixed-methods research: a single table or figure that brings quantitative and qualitative results together so that meta-inferences can be drawn. Vivek Gopinath uses them as the mandatory end point of every stage: columns for area, quant signal, qual mechanism (quote or taxonomy code) and prescribed fix, often with effort and impact ratings and decision bars. In the payments case the columns are qual mechanism (quotes), quant evidence (SEM paths) and prescribed change; in the trading case, tree-test and SNR numbers sit beside quotes and fixes. The format is 'numbers explain where and how much; quotes explain why; the last column is the fix'. It is legible to research and design audiences and makes the logic of interventions auditable.
steps: List the problem areas or constructs where both quant and qual evidence exist.
Enter the quantitative signal for each (e.g. direct 59% → 89%, FR → TR −0.45).
Enter the qualitative mechanism with a verbatim quote or code (e.g. Mistake: 'Alerts should be in Markets').
Write a concrete prescribed fix per row.
Add effort and impact ratings and a decision bar per row.
Review with design and product partners and keep the table as the one-page deliverable.
outputs: A one-page integrated table linking metrics, mechanisms, fixes and thresholds.
useWhen: At the synthesis point of any mixed-methods study, or whenever stakeholders need traceable recommendations.
avoidWhen: When only one strand of data exists; a joint display without both strands adds nothing.
whyLost: Well established in health services and mixed-methods methodology, but UX reports usually keep qual and quant in separate sections.
whereToUse: Research readouts, design reviews, roadmap prioritisation, experiment debriefs.
example: A payments team's joint display pairs 'I re-enter card to be safe' with TR → DC −0.50 and prescribes one-tap verification and reassurance before 2FA.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Achieving Integration in Mixed Methods Designs (Fetters, Curry & Creswell)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 57 — Mixed-Methods Integration — The Technical Architecture of Triangulation
The Inquiry Series, Ch 49 — Structural Equation Modeling — From Quotes to Coefficients
The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Fetters, M. D., Curry, L. A., & Creswell, J. W. (2013). Achieving integration in mixed methods designs: Principles and practices. Health Services Research, 48(6pt2), 2134–2156.

name: Joint versus separate evaluation check
origin: Hsee (1996, 1998); Fox and Tversky (1995)
summary: Run side-by-side and one-at-a-time evaluation conditions, because hard-to-evaluate attributes gain weight only in comparison and preferences can reverse between modes.
description: Whether options are judged together or alone changes what matters. Under the evaluability principle, attributes whose values are hard to judge in isolation (number of dictionary entries) count only in comparison, while easy-to-judge attributes (a torn cover) dominate in separate evaluation; Hsee's used dictionaries reversed in willingness to pay between modes. Fox and Tversky's comparative ignorance work found that ambiguity aversion appears mainly in joint evaluation: pedestrians pricing bets on San Francisco and Istanbul temperatures showed a gap of about $16 jointly and $1.50 separately. The check runs a joint (within-subject, order counterbalanced) and a separate (between-subject) condition, tests the condition by option interaction, adds a same-source control, and reports the mode that matches how users meet the options in the product.
steps: Decide whether the real product decision is made side by side or one option at a time.
If unsure, run a joint condition (each person evaluates both, order counterbalanced) and a separate condition (one option per group).
Collect valuations, willingness to pay or preferences in both conditions.
Test the condition by option interaction; flag reversals as evaluability or comparative-ignorance effects.
Add a control pair from the same source to check the interaction is specific to the hard-to-evaluate or vague option.
Report results from the design that matches how users actually encounter the options.
outputs: Preference or willingness to pay under each mode, reversal flags, and the gap specific to the vague or hard-to-evaluate option.
useWhen: Testing pricing pages, plan comparisons, product listings or concept tests where research shows options side by side but users may see one at a time (or vice versa).
avoidWhen: When the real decision context is unambiguous and you can test in that mode directly. Neither mode gives the 'true' value, so do not average them.
whyLost: Concept and preference tests default to side-by-side comparison for efficiency, and the evaluability literature has not crossed into standard UX research training.
whereToUse: Pricing and plan pages in SaaS and telecoms, e-commerce product listings, insurance and investment product choice, concept testing.
example: An energy supplier tests a fixed-price and a usage-based tariff. Shown together, participants strongly reject the usage tariff; shown alone, it is valued about the same, so the team stops presenting it next to the fixed plan on the landing page.
reference: Hsee, C. K. (1996). The evaluability hypothesis. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 67(3), 247-257; Fox, C. R. and Tversky, A. (1995). Ambiguity aversion and comparative ignorance. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 110(3), 585-603.

name: Jootsing Workshop
donor: Mathematical logic and philosophy of mind
origin: Adapted for UX from Hofstadter's 'jumping out of the system', Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), chapter I; the word 'jootsing' was coined by Daniel Dennett in Intuition Pumps (2013)
summary: A reframing session where the team writes down the rules they take for granted about a product or problem, then breaks each one on purpose to see what becomes possible.
description: Hofstadter points out that some problems cannot be solved by working harder inside a system; you have to step outside it and look at its rules. Teams get stuck the same way. Their ideas stay within assumptions nobody has said out loud: that the user must sign up first, that the product is a screen, that the task happens in one sitting. A jootsing workshop makes those assumptions visible and then treats each one as a rule that can be broken. It differs from open brainstorming because it starts from a written list of the system's rules, so the new ideas are tied to a specific assumption and can be tested against it. Dennett, who named the move, adds a warning that applies here too: you can only jump out of a system you understand well, so the session works best after research has mapped the current one.
steps: Choose the system to question: a flow, a product, a business model or a research question.
List its rules with the team, framed as 'It must...', 'Users always...', 'We never...'. Aim for 20 or more, including the ones that feel too obvious to say.
Mark which rules come from evidence, which from habit or technology, and which nobody can explain.
For each habit or unexplained rule, write what the product would be if the rule were reversed or removed.
Pick the three most promising reversals and state what would have to be true for each to work.
Turn those conditions into research questions or quick prototypes.
outputs: A written list of the system's assumed rules, the evidence behind each, and a short list of rule-breaking concepts with the research needed to test them.
useWhen: A team keeps producing variations of the same idea, a mature product needs a step change, or research shows needs the current model cannot meet.
avoidWhen: The team does not yet understand the current system, or the constraints are real regulation or safety rules rather than habits.
whyLost: UX borrowed brainstorming and 'how might we' from design thinking but not the logician's move of first stating the system's rules exactly. Dennett named the move in 2013, long after design ideation methods had settled.
whereToUse: Strategy and discovery work, service redesign, research question framing, AI products where old interaction assumptions no longer hold.
example: A bank's team lists 'customers must log in to see their balance' as a rule from habit. Breaking it leads to a tested lock-screen balance widget that cut log-ins for balance checks by a third.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Dennett, D., Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Chapter I. Dennett, D. C. (2013). Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking. W. W. Norton.

name: Journey Mapping
origin: Service blueprinting (Shostack, 1984); popularised as customer journey mapping in the 2000s
summary: A visualisation of a user's experience across touchpoints and time, combining actions, thoughts, emotions and pain points to reveal opportunities across the end-to-end journey.
description: Journey mapping represents how a specific user or persona experiences a process across stages, channels and touchpoints, typically showing what they do, think and feel at each stage, along with pain points and opportunities. Related forms include service blueprints, which add backstage processes, and experience maps, which cover broader activities beyond one product. The value lies in seeing the experience end to end, revealing problems that arise between departments and channels. Rigour comes from basing the map on research rather than workshop assumptions, scoping it to a specific persona and scenario, marking evidence strength for each element, and quantifying key moments with data such as drop-off rates or satisfaction where available.
steps: Define the persona, scenario and journey boundaries (start and end points).
Gather evidence from interviews, diaries, analytics and support data covering the whole journey.

For current practice, optionally build a 'now' map with people who do the work: ask each to recall the last time they did it and write every step, then organise the steps together and add pains, joys, questions and ideas (Patton, 2014).
Identify the stages and the touchpoints and channels within each.
Map actions, thoughts, emotions and pain points at each stage, citing evidence.
Overlay quantitative data such as drop-off, time or satisfaction scores where available.
Run a workshop with cross-functional stakeholders to validate the map and identify opportunities.
Overlay opportunities in a different colour to find hot spots where ideas and pain cluster, prioritising high-frequency activities of critical users.
Prioritise opportunities and assign owners.
outputs: An evidence-based journey map, prioritised pain points and opportunities, and a shared cross-functional view of the experience.
useWhen: For cross-channel or multi-step experiences, service design, aligning departments, and identifying where to intervene in an end-to-end experience.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for research when made purely from assumptions; run interviews or diary studies first. For detailed interface problems, use usability testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Powerful stakeholder communication tool; bridges research and strategy; increasingly used in service design.
whereToUse: Service design; cross-channel experience; identifying intervention opportunities.
example: A telecom maps the journey of moving house, from notifying the provider to first bill. The map shows customers repeat their details to three departments, which leads to a single moving workflow.
sources: This is Service Design Doing (Stickdorn et al.)
Patton, J., User Story Mapping: Discover the Whole Story, Build the Right Product (O'Reilly, 2014)
The Power of Data Triangulation (Chang & Classen, 2024)

name: Judgement versus matched-chance choice test
aka: Judgement versus matched-chance choice test (competence, ambiguity and source preference)
origin: Heath and Tversky, 1991; Tversky and Fox, 1995; Fox and Tversky, 1995
summary: People choose between betting on their own judgement and a chance option of matched probability, revealing preference for sources of uncertainty they feel competent in.
description: Participants answer items and state calibrated confidence, then choose, item by item, between betting on their own answer and a lottery with the same probability of paying. Heath and Tversky found people preferred their own judgement in domains where they felt knowledgeable and the lottery where they did not, even at equal probability and even when their own bets paid less. Variants use complementary bets, lotteries set slightly above or below confidence, and pricing or certainty-equivalent versions that yield a per-person source-preference index. The effect is strongest when a clear and a vague option are seen side by side. The design is rigorous because probability is held constant, so remaining choice differences reflect preference for the source itself.
steps: Choose items from domains that differ in users' felt knowledge.
Collect answers and calibrated confidence with an incentive-compatible scoring rule.
For each item, offer a choice between betting on the own answer and a chance or system option with matched probability.
Collect self-rated knowledge per domain and, optionally, certainty equivalents to compute a source-preference index.
Analyse the share choosing their own judgement against confidence and knowledge, per person and overall.
Check that any ambiguity manipulation has not shifted perceived probability, and compare joint with separate evaluation.
outputs: Competence or source-preference curves, a per-person preference index, and the knowledge effect at equal probability.
useWhen: Studying when users will defer to an algorithm, recommendation or expert versus trusting their own judgement, at stated equal accuracy.
avoidWhen: Avoid reading choices as beliefs about accuracy; the effect appears mainly in joint evaluation. For calibration alone use Brier score analysis.
whyLost: Ambiguity and source preference are studied in decision science, but UX research on trust in automation relies on questionnaires rather than incentive-matched choices.
whereToUse: AI suggestions and autopilot features, robo-advice, recommender systems, medical decision aids, forecasting tools.
example: Users choose between their own pick and an AI suggestion stated to be equally accurate. They keep their own pick for music but defer to the system for tax categories, mapping where automation will be accepted.
sources: Heath, C., & Tversky, A. (1991). Preference and belief: Ambiguity and competence in choice under uncertainty. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 4
reference: Heath, C., & Tversky, A. (1991). Preference and belief: Ambiguity and competence in choice under uncertainty. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 4, 5-28.

name: Jupyter notebooks vs. scripts (analysis medium choice)
origin: Knuth's literate programming (1984); IPython Notebook, Fernando Pérez and Brian Granger (2011); Jupyter (2014)
summary: A deliberate decision about when analysis lives in exploratory notebooks and when it is promoted to tested, importable scripts, so UX analyses stay both explorable and reproducible.
description: Notebooks interleave code, output and narrative, which suits exploration and communicating analysis to stakeholders. Their weaknesses are hidden state (cells run out of order), poor diffing in version control and code duplicated across notebooks. Scripts and modules are linear, testable and diffable but less explorable. The rigorous practice is a two-tier workflow: notebooks for exploration and reporting, numbered and dated, and reusable logic (cleaning, scoring, modelling functions) promoted into a package that notebooks import. Before any result is reported, the notebook is restarted and run top to bottom, or executed headlessly, to prove it reproduces. Studies of public notebooks (Pimentel et al., 2019) found only a small minority reproduced the original results, which is the empirical case for these rules.
steps: Use notebooks for exploration and name them with a sequence number, date and initials (e.g. 01-2026-03-04-vg-sus-explore.ipynb).
Move any function used in more than one notebook, or longer than about 20 lines, into a src/ package with tests.
Clear outputs or use a tool such as jupytext or nbstripout before committing so diffs stay readable.
Restart the kernel and run all cells before sharing any figure or number; treat a failure as a bug.
Execute report notebooks headlessly (e.g. with papermill or nbconvert) in the pipeline so results are regenerated, not hand-edited.
Use scripts or pipeline tasks for production jobs such as nightly log aggregation or batch transcription.
outputs: A notebook convention, a src/ package of reusable analysis functions, headless-executable report notebooks and a reproducibility check before sharing.
useWhen: Any computational UX analysis that will be revisited, audited or extended, especially survey, log and causal analyses shared with stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Not needed for a one-off chart from a spreadsheet; a documented spreadsheet may suffice. For heavy production pipelines, use orchestrated scripts rather than notebooks.
whyLost: UX research rarely adopted software engineering norms because most quantitative work happened in spreadsheets or vendor dashboards; the notebook-versus-script debate stayed inside data science.
whereToUse: Research operations, quantitative UX teams, mixed-methods programmes with Python pipelines, and any regulated domain where analyses must be audited.
example: A SaaS research team explores churn drivers in a notebook, then promotes the session-feature functions to a package. The quarterly churn report notebook is run headlessly from raw logs each quarter, so the numbers in the deck always reproduce.
sources: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
Pimentel, J. F. et al. (2019) A large-scale study about quality and reproducibility of Jupyter notebooks. MSR 2019
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology 13(6)

name: Just Noticeable Difference and Weber Fraction Testing
origin: Ernst Weber (1834) and Gustav Fechner (1860); adaptive staircases by Levitt (1971)
summary: Measures the smallest perceivable change in a stimulus (size, colour, delay, price, sound) and the Weber fraction that predicts how it scales.
description: Weber observed that the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus magnitude (delta I / I = k). Psychophysics offers rigorous procedures to measure difference thresholds: the method of constant stimuli, method of limits and adaptive staircases such as the 2-down-1-up rule that converges on about 70.7% correct. Forced-choice designs (2AFC) control for response bias. UX makes constant decisions about perceptible differences, such as latency improvements, animation durations, colour states, haptic intensities and price changes, without measuring thresholds. JND testing answers questions like 'will users notice this 80 ms speedup?' with defensible data.
steps: Define the stimulus dimension, the reference level and the task (e.g. 'which of two versions felt faster?').
Choose a procedure: two-alternative forced choice with an adaptive staircase (e.g. 2-down-1-up) for efficiency.
Randomise presentation order and interval, and include catch trials.
Run each participant until the staircase has 8-12 reversals; estimate the threshold from the mean of the last reversals.
Fit a psychometric function across participants and compute the Weber fraction at several reference levels.
Translate thresholds into design specs (e.g. improvements below the JND are not worth shipping as perceptible features).
outputs: Difference thresholds, psychometric functions and Weber fractions per dimension, translated into design tolerances.
useWhen: Deciding whether a change in latency, animation, colour, sound, haptics or quantity will be perceived.
avoidWhen: Attitudinal or semantic questions; thresholds tell you about perception, not preference or meaning.
whyLost: Psychophysics is taught in perception courses and audio/display engineering, not UX. Teams rely on intuition or A/B metrics.
whereToUse: App performance budgets, dark mode and state colours, haptic design, audio cues, pricing displays.
example: A video app tests start-up delay at a 1-second reference. The JND is about 180 ms (Weber fraction ~0.18), so a planned 100 ms optimisation is deprioritised in favour of a larger one.
sources: Levitt, Transformed up-down methods in psychoacoustics (1971), JASA
reference: Gescheider, G. A. (1997). Psychophysics: The Fundamentals. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: K-means vs. GMM comparison
origin: K-means by Stuart Lloyd, 1957 (published 1982) and James MacQueen, 1967; Gaussian mixture EM by Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977
summary: Compares hard k-means clustering with probabilistic Gaussian mixture models on the same behavioural data to choose a segmentation that reflects real structure and uncertainty.
description: K-means assigns each user to the nearest centroid, assuming spherical clusters of similar size, and gives no measure of uncertainty. Gaussian mixture models assume users are drawn from a mixture of multivariate normal distributions with their own means and covariances, yielding soft membership probabilities and support for elongated, overlapping or unequal clusters. Comparing them exposes whether segments are crisp or blended: if GMM posteriors are mostly above 0.9, segments are distinct; if many users sit near 0.5, hard personas will mislead. Rigour comes from standardising features, running multiple initialisations, comparing solutions with stability and validation indices, and checking that the chosen model's assumptions fit the data.
steps: Build a standardised behavioural feature matrix and, if needed, reduce dimensions with PCA.
Run k-means for K = 2-10 with at least 20 random initialisations per K.
Fit GMMs for the same K range with full, diagonal and tied covariance options, selecting by BIC.
Compare solutions with adjusted Rand index between methods and bootstrap stability (Jaccard above 0.75 indicates stable clusters).
Inspect GMM posterior membership: report the share of users with maximum probability below 0.7 as ambiguous.
Choose the method whose assumptions and stability fit, and document why.
outputs: Two candidate segmentations with comparison metrics, membership uncertainty profiles and a justified choice.
useWhen: Behavioural segmentation from logs where you need to decide how crisp and how shaped segments are before building personas or targeting.
avoidWhen: Avoid with categorical or highly non-Gaussian features (use latent class analysis or k-prototypes), or with very small samples.
whyLost: Most UX segmentation uses k-means by default, or no clustering at all; probabilistic clustering is common in data science but rarely framed as a UX method.
whereToUse: Behavioural personas for fintech and SaaS, marketplace user types, health app engagement patterns.
example: For 80,000 investors, k-means gives four tidy segments, but a GMM shows 30% of users have no segment probability above 0.7. The team reports four archetypes with a 'hybrid' band rather than forcing users into personas.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 51 — Behavioral Clustering & Probabilistic Segmentation
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
reference: Bishop, C. M. (2006) Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, ch. 9. Springer.

name: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)
origin: Fix & Hodges (1951); Cover & Hart (1967)
summary: Classifies or predicts a case from the most similar past cases, a simple way to find "users like this one".
description: KNN stores the training data and, for a new case, finds the k most similar records using a distance metric on standardised variables, then predicts by majority vote or average. It makes no assumptions about the shape of relationships. Bruce and Bruce show it also works as a feature engine, adding a "neighbour score" to other models. For UX, the same similarity logic powers lookalike recruiting, matching a new user to behavioural archetypes, and finding comparable sessions to review.
steps: Choose and standardise predictor variables (z-scores) so none dominates distance.
Encode categories with one-hot variables or use Gower distance for mixed data.
Choose k by cross-validation.
Classify or predict new cases from their neighbours.
Inspect the nearest neighbours to explain individual predictions.
outputs: Predictions and lists of most-similar users or sessions.
useWhen: Lookalike finding, simple prediction with few variables, or explaining a prediction by example.
avoidWhen: Many irrelevant variables or very large datasets without indexing.
whyLost: A data science staple that UX analytics rarely uses directly.
whereToUse: Participant recruiting from analytics, behavioural archetype matching, recommendation audits.
example: To recruit people like churned users, a KNN on usage features finds 200 active users nearest to the churned profile for interviews.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 6.

name: Kano Analysis
origin: Noriaki Kano and colleagues, 1984
summary: A paired functional and dysfunctional survey that classifies features as must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent or reverse, showing which features satisfy and which merely prevent dissatisfaction.
description: Kano analysis rests on the observation that satisfaction is asymmetric: some attributes cause dissatisfaction when absent but no delight when present (must-be), some scale linearly (performance), and some delight when present but are not missed when absent (attractive). Each feature is asked as a pair: how do you feel if the product has it (functional) and if it does not (dysfunctional), with five answer options. The evaluation table classifies each response, and the modal category or continuous satisfaction and dissatisfaction coefficients (Better and Worse) characterise the feature. Rigour requires clear, concrete feature descriptions (ideally with visuals), sample sizes of at least 30-50 per segment, segment-level analysis because categories differ between user groups, and an optional self-stated importance question. Categories also drift over time as attractive features become expected.
steps: Select 10-25 candidate features and write each as a concrete, user-facing description, adding images or short demos where possible.
For each feature, ask the functional question (if present) and the dysfunctional question (if absent) with the standard five options: like, expect, neutral, tolerate, dislike.
Optionally add a self-stated importance rating per feature to break ties.
Field the survey to at least 30-50 respondents per segment of interest.
Classify each response pair with the Kano evaluation table and compute category frequencies plus Better and Worse coefficients.
Plot features on a Better-versus-Worse chart by segment and prioritise must-be gaps first, then performance, then selected attractive features.
outputs: Feature categorisation (must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent, reverse, questionable), Better and Worse coefficients and a prioritisation chart by segment.
useWhen: Prioritising features for a roadmap or release, deciding what is table stakes versus differentiating, and comparing how segments value features.
avoidWhen: When features are hard to describe without experiencing them (prototype first), when you need causal evidence of impact on behaviour (use experiments), or with very small samples. Treat attractive (delighter) classifications with caution: respondents have little frame of reference for genuinely novel features, and Chapman and Rodden (2023) list Kano among methods that promise more than they deliver; confirm priorities with behavioural evidence.
whyLost: Still in use: Strong feature prioritization tool; enables strategic differentiation decisions.
whereToUse: Feature roadmap prioritization; product strategy; competitive differentiation.
example: A project-management SaaS runs Kano with 220 users. Offline mode is attractive for field teams but indifferent for office teams, while SSO is must-be for enterprise admins, so the team bundles them into different plans.
sources: Kano et al., Attractive quality and must-be quality (Journal of the Japanese Society for Quality Control, 1984)
Chapman, C. & Rodden, K., Quantitative User Experience Research (Apress, 2023)
Lidwell, W., Holden, K. & Butler, J., Universal Principles of Design, 3rd ed. (2023)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Kano N, Seraku N, Takahashi F & Tsuji S (1984) Attractive quality and must-be quality. Journal of the Japanese Society for Quality Control 14(2):39-48

name: Kansei engineering
aka: Kansei engineering / perceptual image mapping with brand identity
origin: Hiroshima University from 1970; Mitsuo Nagamachi; lightweight adaptation by Pamela Pavliscak (2018)
summary: Maps users' feelings about products, captured as image words on semantic differentials, onto coded design elements (shape, colour, material) so design choices can target an intended emotional image.
description: Kansei engineering translates feelings into product properties. Its formal version has five parts: collect representative product samples, decompose them into design elements, gather the semantic space of image words, have users rate samples on those words, and map ratings to elements, often with statistical models. Zhu et al. extend it with brand-culture elements and 'mainstream' elements counted across a competitor library, then verify the final design with the same semantic differentials. A lightweight qualitative variant (Pavliscak) harvests emotion words from transcripts, diaries, reviews and social posts, clusters them, and takes the clusters back to participants in follow-up interviews or participatory sessions, because words like 'love' or 'distracted' mean little without context. Rigour comes from agreeing target words with experts, managers and users, using a balanced rating sample, and verifying the outcome on the same scales.
steps: Collect domain texts and stakeholder input (brand materials, manager interviews, reviews, transcripts) and extract candidate image or emotion words.
Screen to a short set of target image words agreed by experts, managers and users; for the lightweight form, cluster emotion words into themes instead.
Gather competitor or candidate products (for example 87 reduced to 60 after removing near-duplicates), decompose into shape, colour and material codes and count element frequencies.
Select about 10 highly varied representative samples and have a balanced user sample rate each on 7-point semantic differentials (-3 to +3) for every target word.
Average scores; treat means above 0 as matching the image, and map samples' coded elements to the words to find elements that satisfy all targets.
In the qualitative variant, take the word clusters into follow-up interviews or a participatory session to recover context and relate clusters to product properties.
Design by combining brand, mainstream and perceptual elements, then verify the final design with the same semantic differential on a fresh sample.
outputs: A table mapping design-element codes to image words, a design scheme, verification scores; or context-rich emotion-word clusters.
useWhen: When the brief is affective (make it feel 'professional and elegant') and you need traceable links between feelings and concrete visual or physical properties, especially for hardware, packaging or visual identity.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the decision is about function or task flow; use usability testing. Competitor element counts show popularity, not preference, and word lists without context mislead; for quick affect checks use Product Reaction Cards (Microsoft Desirability Toolkit) or the Semantic Differential.
whyLost: It remains strong in Japanese, Korean and Chinese industrial design research but is seen in Western UX as heavy and statistical; its pieces survive as semantic differentials and moodboards without the mapping step.
whereToUse: Consumer hardware, smart-home devices, automotive interiors, visual identity for apps, onboarding look and feel, AI assistant personality design.
example: A smart-home gateway brand targets 'technical, elegant, minimalist, professional'. Sixty-seven users rate ten competitor devices; elements scoring above zero on all four words are combined with brand motifs, and 71 users verify that the final design scores positive on every word.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Nagamachi, M. (1995). Kansei Engineering: A new ergonomic consumer-oriented technology for product development. International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics, 15(1), 3-11; Zhu, Z., Zhang, Z., Qin, Y., & Li, S. (2022). DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, pp. 142-154.

name: KAP survey and KAP-gap analysis
origin: Family-planning programmes in developing nations, 1960s; discussed by Everett Rogers
summary: A survey that measures knowledge of, attitude to and actual practice of an innovation separately, to locate the stage where adoption stalls (the KAP-gap).
description: KAP surveys measure three dependent variables about one innovation: whether people know about it, how they feel about it, and whether they practise it. Hundreds were run in Latin America, Africa and Asia from the 1960s to evaluate family-planning and other health programmes. Their characteristic finding is the KAP-gap: people know about and favour an innovation yet do not use it, typical of preventive innovations whose benefits are invisible or delayed. Rogers judges KAP surveys weak as science but valuable for policy, because they demonstrated latent demand and later served as before-and-after programme evaluations. He links the knowledge-attitude-practice order to the hierarchy-of-effects model. The diagnostic value lies in separating awareness, evaluation and behaviour so that an intervention targets the actual bottleneck rather than repeating awareness campaigns.
steps: Define the innovation or behaviour precisely and sample the target population.
Ask what respondents know about it (awareness and factual knowledge items).
Ask their attitude towards it (favourability, perceived benefit, intention).
Ask whether they practise it, preferably verified against behavioural data where available.
Compare the proportions at each level to locate and size the gap, by segment.
Repeat after an intervention to evaluate which level moved.
outputs: Proportions knowing, favouring and practising, by segment; the size and location of the KAP-gap; before-and-after change.
useWhen: When a feature, safety behaviour or preventive practice (two-factor authentication, backups, savings) has low adoption and you need to know whether the problem is awareness, attitude or action.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the sole evidence of practice where self-report is inflated; link to logs (see Survey linked to consented account (log) data). For deep reasons behind the gap use interviews or COM-B and Behaviour Change Wheel Analysis.
whyLost: It stayed in public health and development evaluation; UX tends to jump straight to funnels or attitude scales and rarely separates the three levels in one instrument.
whereToUse: Security and privacy features, health and wellbeing apps, financial wellbeing products, accessibility settings, any preventive or 'should do' behaviour.
example: A password manager's survey finds 85% know about two-factor authentication and 70% think it worthwhile, but only 22% have enabled it. The team stops awareness campaigns and redesigns the enrolment flow.
reference: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). New York: Free Press, ch. 2.

name: Kaplan-Meier curves for time-to-adoption
origin: Edward Kaplan & Paul Meier, 1958
summary: A non-parametric estimate of the proportion of users who have not yet adopted (or churned) over time, correctly accounting for users still under observation.
