description: The Kaplan-Meier estimator computes, at each event time, the conditional probability of surviving past it given survival so far, multiplying these to give a step curve. Plotted as one minus survival it becomes a cumulative adoption curve. Unlike naive cohort percentages, it uses censored users (those who joined recently or left the observation window) correctly, so adoption is not underestimated for recent cohorts. Curves for different groups can be compared with the log-rank test, and median time-to-adoption read directly from the curve. Rigour depends on a sensible time zero, non-informative censoring and showing numbers at risk under the plot.
steps: Define time zero and the adoption event for every user and record follow-up time plus an event or censoring indicator.
Compute the Kaplan-Meier estimate overall and for each comparison group (e.g. exposed versus not exposed to a new entry point).
Plot cumulative adoption (1 minus survival) with 95% confidence bands and a numbers-at-risk table at regular intervals.
Read median time-to-adoption and adoption proportion at fixed horizons such as 7, 30 and 90 days.
Compare groups with the log-rank test and, if covariate adjustment is needed, move on to a Cox model.
Check that censoring is not informative, for example that users are not censored because they uninstalled.
outputs: Cumulative adoption or retention curves with confidence bands, median times, fixed-horizon proportions and log-rank comparisons.
useWhen: Describing how quickly users adopt a feature, reach activation or churn, especially with staggered sign-ups and incomplete follow-up.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to adjust for several confounders (use Cox) or when competing events exist, e.g. account closure precludes adoption (use cumulative incidence functions).
whyLost: Product analytics tools show cohort retention tables that ignore censoring, and the clinical vocabulary never transferred. Analysts with biostatistics backgrounds use it but it is not part of standard UX practice.
whereToUse: Feature launches, onboarding activation timing, subscription retention, health-app adherence and time-to-value tracking.
example: After launching Quick Reorder, the team plots Kaplan-Meier adoption curves for users who joined before and after the redesign. Median time to first use falls from 41 to 16 days, and the log-rank test confirms the difference.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
Kaplan & Meier (1958) Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations
The Inquiry Series, Ch 44 — Survival Analysis, Longitudinal Design & Behavioral Drift
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
reference: Kaplan, E. L. & Meier, P. (1958) Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 53(282), 457-481.

name: Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance (W)
aka: Kendall's coefficient of concordance (W) for agreement among several judges
origin: Maurice Kendall and Bernard Babington Smith, 1939
summary: Measures, from 0 to 1, how far several judges agree when each ranks the same set of objects, and tests whether their consensus ordering can be trusted.
description: Kendall's W summarises agreement among m judges who each rank the same n objects. It runs from 0 (no agreement) to 1 (identical rankings) and cannot be negative. A tie-corrected version handles judges who give two objects the same rank and equals the uncorrected value when there are no ties. Its classic use is as a gate: only if independent judges agree significantly can their mean ranks serve as a scale or consensus ordering, for example ranking photographs for attractiveness rather than relying on the researcher's own judgement. Significance comes from exact probabilities, tables for 3-7 objects, or a chi-square approximation for more than 7. Unlike kappa, Krippendorff's alpha or the ICC, it addresses ordinal ranking by several raters directly. A significant W shows agreement beyond chance, not that agreement is high enough for every purpose.
steps: Have each of m judges independently rank the same n objects (designs, usability issues, features), allowing ties where unavoidable.
Compute W, using the tie-corrected formula if any judge has tied ranks.
Test significance with the exact probability, with tables when n is 3-7, or with the chi-square approximation when n is above 7.
If agreement is significant, use the mean ranks as the consensus ordering and report W alongside it.
If agreement is weak, treat the ranking as unreliable: examine which judges or objects diverge and clarify criteria before re-ranking.
outputs: W between 0 and 1, its p value, and a consensus rank order of the objects.
useWhen: Experts, stakeholders or participants rank the same set of items (severity of issues, design concepts, feature priorities) and you need to know whether a shared ordering exists before acting on the average.
avoidWhen: Judges assign categories (use Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha) or continuous ratings (use the ICC); only two judges (use Spearman's or Kendall's tau). Do not read a significant W as proof of strong agreement: with many objects small W values become significant.
whyLost: UX agreement checks focus on coding reliability for qualitative data, so rank agreement among experts is rarely tested; prioritisation workshops average ranks without asking whether they agree.
whereToUse: Severity ranking of usability findings by several evaluators; stakeholder prioritisation of roadmap items; expert ranking of design concepts; checking agreement in card-ranking or preference tasks.
example: Five researchers independently rank twelve usability issues from a banking app by severity. W = 0.71 (p < .001) shows strong concordance, so the mean ranks are used to order the fix list; a second round on a different feature set gives W = 0.22, prompting a calibration session on the severity criteria.
reference: Kendall, M. G., & Babington Smith, B. (1939). The problem of m rankings. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 10, 275-287.

name: Kernel Density Estimation
aka: Kernel density estimation (Parzen windows) with window-width choice
origin: Rosenblatt (1956) and Parzen (1962)
summary: Estimate the shape of a distribution by averaging a small kernel centred on each observation, choosing the bandwidth so the estimate neither hides structure nor shows noise.
description: Kernel density estimation places a window function, usually Gaussian, on every observation and averages them, so each point contributes to the estimated density according to its distance. The window must itself be a density so the estimate integrates to one. The bandwidth h controls everything: too wide and the estimate is smooth but loses structure such as bimodality; too narrow and it becomes a series of spikes at the data points. Duda, Hart and Stork show widths shrinking with the square root of n and point to cross-validation for choosing h; Bishop derives the histogram, kernel and k-nearest-neighbour estimators from the same idea. The k-nearest-neighbour estimate lets the region grow until it holds k points, adapting resolution to local density. Per-group densities can also be compared or turned into a classifier.
steps: Collect the observations for one or more variables.
Choose a kernel that is itself a density, typically Gaussian.
Choose a bandwidth by a rule of thumb or by cross-validation, and try at least one wider and one narrower value.
Evaluate the estimate on a grid by averaging the kernels centred on every observation.
Inspect for over-smoothing (lost modes) or under-smoothing (spiky noise) and settle the bandwidth.
Optionally estimate densities per group and compare them, or use a k-nearest-neighbour estimate where data density varies widely.
outputs: A smooth density curve or surface, per-group densities for comparison and, optionally, a nonparametric classifier.
useWhen: When the shape of a distribution matters, for example whether task times or satisfaction scores are bimodal, revealing two user groups that a mean would hide.
avoidWhen: Avoid on small samples or many dimensions, where estimates are unreliable; use histograms or parametric fits instead. For segmentation with explicit components use Gaussian Mixture Models for User Segmentation.
whyLost: It is common in data science plotting (density and violin plots) but rarely chosen deliberately, so bandwidth choices go unexamined.
whereToUse: Task-time and latency analysis, session-length and engagement distributions, click or gaze position maps, score distributions across segments.
example: A density plot of time-to-first-value for new SaaS accounts shows two peaks, at about 10 minutes and 3 days. Following the slow peak leads to accounts waiting for an admin invite, which becomes the onboarding fix.
reference: Parzen, E. (1962). On estimation of a probability density function and mode. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 33(3), 1065-1076; Duda, R. O., Hart, P. E. and Stork, D. G. (2001). Pattern Classification (2nd ed.). New York: Wiley, ch. 4.

name: Key Assumptions Check
origin: US intelligence community tradecraft; documented by Richards Heuer and Randolph Pherson (2010)
summary: Systematically lists the assumptions underpinning a judgement, rates each as solid, caveated or unsupported, and identifies what would invalidate them.
description: Every analysis rests on assumptions that are rarely stated. The key assumptions check, done at the start and end of a project, asks the team to list working assumptions, then for each ask: why do we believe this? what could make it untrue? has it been true in the past? if wrong, would it change our conclusion? Assumptions are rated as solid, correct with caveats, or unsupported, and unsupported key assumptions become research questions or monitoring indicators. In product research, this exposes taken-for-granted beliefs about users, markets and technology before they shape study design and conclusions.
steps: Gather the team and state the current judgement or plan (e.g. product strategy, study conclusions).
List all assumptions, stated and unstated, using prompts ('what must be true for this to work?').
For each, ask why it is believed, under what conditions it fails, and whether it has held historically.
Rate each as solid, caveated or unsupported, and as key or non-key for the conclusion.
Convert key unsupported assumptions into research questions, tests or monitoring indicators.
Repeat the check at the end of the analysis and when new evidence arrives.
outputs: An assumptions register with ratings, failure conditions and linked research or monitoring actions.
useWhen: At the start of research programmes, before strategic decisions, and when reviewing conclusions.
avoidWhen: Very small, routine studies with no strategic consequences.
whyLost: Assumption mapping exists in lean startup practice, but without the intelligence tradecraft discipline of rating and revisiting.
whereToUse: Product strategy, new market entry, AI feature bets, research plans.
example: A team planning an AI scheduling assistant lists 'users trust calendar access' as solid. The check shows it is unsupported for enterprise customers, so a security review study is added before build.
sources: Heuer & Pherson, Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis (2nd ed., 2014)
US Government, A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques for Improving Intelligence Analysis (2009)
reference: Heuer, R. J., & Pherson, R. H. (2014). Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis. CQ Press.

name: Key Driver Analysis (Regression-Based)
origin: Customer satisfaction driver modelling (1980s-90s); MeasuringU practice
summary: Finds which aspects of an experience most strongly predict an overall outcome such as satisfaction, NPS or SUS.
description: Ask users to rate an overall outcome and a set of specific attributes (ease of finding documents, speed, price for value). Regress the outcome on the attributes; standardised coefficients estimate how much each attribute drives the outcome. Plotting importance (coefficient) against performance (mean rating) produces a quadrant chart that shows where to invest: important attributes rated poorly. Sauro and Lewis's training highlights that correlated attributes make coefficients unstable, so factor analysis to group attributes, relative weights or Shapley-style decomposition give more trustworthy importance estimates.
steps: Survey users on an overall outcome and 8 to 20 specific attributes.
Check correlations among attributes; consider grouping them with factor analysis.
Run multiple regression of the outcome on the attributes (or factor scores).
Use standardised coefficients or relative-weight analysis to rank drivers.
Plot importance against performance and target high-importance, low-performance areas.
outputs: A ranked list of experience drivers and an importance-performance map.
useWhen: Prioritising improvement areas from survey data with many attribute ratings.
avoidWhen: Attributes are highly collinear and samples are small, unless using relative weights or random-forest importance.
whyLost: Widely used in market research, but UX teams usually prioritise from qualitative findings or stakeholder opinion instead.
whereToUse: Customer experience surveys, retrospective benchmarks, product satisfaction trackers.
example: For an insurer, "easy to file a claim online" has the largest coefficient on NPS but the lowest rating, so it heads the roadmap.
sources: Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Regression and Key Driver Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, 2021)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Sauro & Lewis, Factor and Discriminant Analysis training (2021); Sauro & Lewis (2016), chapter 10.

name: Key Experience Definition
origin: Jaime Levy (2015), taking the term from a Lane Halley Lean UX slide; Dan Saffer's single-interaction example
summary: Identify the one or two feature sets or interactions that make a product uniquely valuable, using persona and competitive prompts, rather than listing features.
description: The key experience is the feature set that defines a product's value innovation and competitive advantage; it may be a single interaction, as with Twitter's original 140-character post. Levy uses it to narrow an MVP to what must be validated. A first pass asks what would make the provisional persona love the product, which moment of the journey is unique, which scenario resolves a shortfall found in competitive analysis, and what workarounds people use now. If the answer looks like a feature list, a second pass asks sharper questions: what customers can do here that they cannot do with competitors, which pain is unsolved, how the solution would appear on screen, and what customers would do next and whether they would see the value. Benefits are expressed as user-visible scenarios.
steps: Gather the provisional persona, journey and competitive analysis.
Answer the four first-pass prompts: what would make the persona love it, which journey moment is unique, which scenario resolves a competitive shortfall, and what workarounds people use now.
Check whether the result is a feature list; if it is, answer the four sharper prompts about unique capability, unsolved pain, on-screen form and next action.
Reduce the answer to one or two key experiences, each written as a user-visible scenario.
Feed the key experiences into feature comparison, storyboarding and MVP experiments.
outputs: One or two key experience statements expressed as scenarios.
useWhen: Use it when an MVP or new product has a sprawling feature list and the team must agree what defines its value.
avoidWhen: It rests on provisional assumptions; validate the key experience with Customer problem interviews, a Concierge MVP or Fake door, painted door and smoke tests. 'Key' means few; a full feature list belongs to a later release.
whyLost: The idea lives on as the core value proposition, 'aha moment' or core loop, so Levy's term and prompts are rarely cited.
whereToUse: Start-ups, new product lines, marketplace and platform products, and MVP scoping in larger companies.
example: A wedding-venue marketplace starts with a feature list, but discovery shows vendor coordination is the major pain. The key experience becomes booking a venue packaged with its vendors, which the MVP tests first.
reference: Levy, J. (2015). UX Strategy: How to Devise Innovative Digital Products that People Want. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 124-128.

name: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM)
origin: Stuart Card, Thomas Moran and Allen Newell, 1980
summary: Predicts expert task time by summing standard operator times for keystrokes, pointing, homing, mental preparation and system response.
description: KLM is the simplest member of the GOMS family. A task is written as a sequence of operators: K (keystroke, about 0.2-0.28 s), P (point with mouse, about 1.1 s), H (home hands between devices, about 0.4 s), M (mental preparation, about 1.35 s), B (button press) and R (system response). Heuristic rules specify where M operators are placed. Summing the sequence gives a prediction for an expert, error-free performer. The treatise's worked example, copying a paragraph between documents ([H mouse][P paragraph][K Ctrl][K C][P destination][K Ctrl][K V]), yields roughly 3.8 s with 1983 parameters. With modern validation, predictions usually fall within 20-30% of measured times, an accuracy few contemporary UX methods approach, and the model needs no user testing to produce a falsifiable prediction.
steps: Define the task and the design alternative precisely, including the starting state.
Write the physical operator sequence (K, P, H, B) for the expert method.
Insert M operators using the Card-Moran-Newell placement heuristics.
Add R for system response times where the user must wait.
Sum operator times, using updated parameters for touch or mobile where relevant (for example Fitts-based P).
Compare alternatives and, where stakes are high, validate against timed expert trials.
outputs: Predicted execution time per task and design, operator breakdown, identified bottlenecks.
useWhen: Quickly comparing designs for routine expert tasks, shortcut and command design, form layout for power users.
avoidWhen: Learnability questions, novice users or tasks dominated by problem solving; use cognitive walkthrough instead.
whyLost: Seen as limited to desktop expert use and lost when HCI curricula moved away from cognitive modelling; few practitioners know the operator values.
whereToUse: Keyboard-heavy enterprise tools, POS systems, mobile form factors (with touch KLM extensions), voice command flows.
example: A banking back-office team uses KLM to compare a dropdown versus a typed code for transaction category; KLM predicts 2.9 s versus 1.6 s per entry, worth around 90 staff hours per month.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Card SK, Moran TP & Newell A (1980) The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems. CACM 23(7)
Kieras D (2001) Using the Keystroke-Level Model to Estimate Execution Times
The GOMS Family of User Interface Analysis Techniques (John & Kieras, 1996)
GOMS Models: Simplified Cognitive Architectures (Kieras, n.d.)
reference: Card SK, Moran TP & Newell A (1980) The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems. Communications of the ACM 23(7):396-410.

name: Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation
origin: Donald Kirkpatrick (1959; 1976); multilevel extension by Sitzmann and Weinhardt (2019)
summary: Evaluate a training or learning intervention at four levels: trainee reactions, learning acquired, behaviour change in real use, and organisational results.
description: The Kirkpatrick model is the most widely used frame for evaluating training. Level 1, reactions, asks whether trainees liked the training and found it useful. Level 2, learning, tests whether targeted knowledge and skills were acquired against the objectives. Level 3, behaviour, observes whether performance changed on the job, after time for transfer. Level 4, results, tracks organisational outcomes such as costs, efficiency, quality, turnover and return on investment. Evaluation is planned during needs analysis so each level has criteria, and it should explain why training worked, not just whether. Critics note the levels lack theory and are not necessarily causally linked: high satisfaction does not imply learning, nor learning transfer, so a multilevel view is recommended.
steps: Before training, define learning objectives from organisational, task and person needs analysis so each level has explicit criteria.
Level 1: collect reactions (liking, perceived usefulness, ratings of materials) at the end of training.
Level 2: test acquisition of the targeted knowledge and skills against the objectives, ideally with a pre-test.
Level 3: observe or measure behaviour in real use after allowing time for transfer, for example 4-12 weeks later.
Level 4: track organisational outcomes such as support costs, efficiency, quality, turnover and ROI.
Compare levels to find where the chain breaks, then redesign the training, job aids or post-training climate.
outputs: Evidence of effectiveness at four levels, a diagnosis of where the chain from reaction to results breaks, and an ROI estimate.
useWhen: Evaluating onboarding programmes, in-product tutorials, customer academies, internal tool training and UX or research training for teams.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating Level 1 satisfaction as evidence of success or assuming levels cause each other; when you need causal claims use a controlled experiment, and for programme logic use a logic model.
whyLost: It is standard in corporate learning and HR, but UX teams evaluating onboarding usually stop at completion rates and satisfaction and do not borrow the four-level structure.
whereToUse: Enterprise software onboarding, customer education, clinical system go-live training, AI tool adoption programmes.
example: A hospital evaluates EHR training: Level 1 ratings are high and Level 2 quiz scores pass, but Level 3 observation shows nurses still use paper workarounds for medication reconciliation. The break is at transfer, so the team adds at-the-elbow support and a job aid.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Kirkpatrick, D. L. (1976). Evaluation of training. In R. L. Craig (Ed.), Training and Development Handbook. New York: McGraw-Hill; Bisbey, Grossman, Panton, Coultas and Salas in Salvendy, G. and Karwowski, W. (Eds.) (2021). Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.). Wiley, ch. 16, pp. 424-425.

name: KLM timing with expert user calibration
origin: Card, Moran and Newell, 1980; recalibration for touch and mobile by Holleis et al., 2007
summary: Predicts expert task times with the Keystroke-Level Model using operator times measured on the actual users and devices, rather than generic 1980s desktop values.
description: KLM operator values were derived for desktop keyboards and mice in the late 1970s. On touchscreens, specialised consoles, gloves or voice, they can be badly wrong. Expert user calibration measures operator times directly: keystroke or tap time, pointing time (or Fitts parameters), homing, mental preparation and system response, using short benchmark tasks with skilled users. Holleis and colleagues produced mobile operator values in this way. The calibrated model is then used to predict and compare designs. Calibration is the difference between a teaching exercise and a defensible prediction. Rigour comes from calibrating on experts at asymptotic performance, using enough repetitions, and validating predictions on separate tasks.
steps: Recruit 5-10 skilled users of the target device or a comparable one.
Design micro-tasks isolating each operator (repeated taps, pointing to targets of varied distance and size, gestures, mental decisions).
Collect at least 20-30 repetitions per operator per user after practice, discarding initial trials.
Compute median operator times and Fitts parameters, and estimate the M operator from tasks with and without decisions.
Build KLM sequences for candidate designs using calibrated values.
Validate on 2-3 full tasks; accept the model if predictions fall within about 20% of observed expert times.
outputs: A calibrated operator table for the device and population, predicted task times per design, and validation results.
useWhen: When predicting expert times on non-standard devices or input methods, or when decisions rest on seconds saved.
avoidWhen: When users are not skilled or tasks are not routine; use usability testing.
whyLost: KLM is taught but rarely used, and those who use it usually apply textbook values; calibration requires a study few teams prioritise.
whereToUse: Surgical consoles, automotive touchscreens, point-of-sale, warehouse scanners, and gesture shortcuts.
example: Calibrating on 8 surgeons shows gloved taps take 0.42 s, not 0.2 s. The calibrated model predicts a new shortcut gesture saves 1.6 s per instrument change rather than the 2.4 s claimed with textbook values.
sources: Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 16 — Cognitive Task Modeling — GOMS, KLM & CPM-GOMS
reference: Holleis, P., Otto, F., Hussmann, H. & Schmidt, A. (2007). Keystroke-level model for advanced mobile phone interaction. Proceedings of CHI 2007.

name: KLM timing with log-normal correction
origin: Card, Moran and Newell, 1980; distributional extensions in later stochastic GOMS work
summary: Extends Keystroke-Level Model predictions from single point estimates to log-normal time distributions, giving predicted percentiles rather than only expert mean times.
description: The KLM predicts expert, error-free task time by summing operator times: K (keystroke, about 0.2-0.28 s), P (point, about 1.1 s or via Fitts), H (home hands, 0.4 s), M (mental preparation, 1.35 s) and R (system response). It yields a mean, but real operator times are right-skewed, and the summed task time is better described by a log-normal distribution. The correction assigns each operator a log-normal distribution with its KLM value as the median and an empirically set dispersion, then sums them by Monte Carlo simulation to produce predicted percentiles. This shows how often a task will exceed a time limit, which matters for time-critical work. Rigour requires calibrating dispersion from observed data and documenting M placement rules.
steps: Write the KLM operator sequence for each task variant using Card, Moran and Newell's M placement heuristics.
Assign median times to operators (published values or local calibration) and a log-scale dispersion, typically sigma 0.3-0.5, from pilot data with 5-8 users.
Simulate at least 10,000 task executions by sampling operator times and summing them.
Report the median, 90th and 95th percentile task times and the probability of exceeding any time limit.
Compare variants on both median and tail, and validate against observed task times; aim for prediction within about 20% of observed medians.
Use the tail estimates to set design targets for time-critical tasks.
outputs: Operator sequences, predicted task time distributions with percentiles, probability of exceeding time limits, and validation against observed data.
useWhen: When comparing designs for time-critical or high-frequency expert tasks before building them, and when the tail of task time matters.
avoidWhen: When users are novices, tasks are exploratory, or errors dominate; use usability testing or cognitive walkthrough instead.
whyLost: KLM itself is a lost classic in mainstream UX; the distributional correction is mostly confined to research, so practitioners rarely know it exists.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial control, call centre software, point-of-sale, data entry tools, and keyboard shortcut design.
example: A KLM for an emergency instrument swap predicts 4.2 s median, but simulation shows a 12% chance of exceeding 6 s, the surgical tolerance. Removing one M by colocating controls drops the exceedance probability to 3%.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
Card, S., Moran, T. & Newell, A., The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983) and GOMS/KLM literature
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 4 — Time, Rhythm & the Three Timescales of Experience
reference: Card, S. K., Moran, T. P. & Newell, A. (1980). The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems. Communications of the ACM, 23(7), 396-410.

name: Knowledge Auditing
donor: Knowledge management and cognitive task analysis
origin: Knowledge management literature, 1990s (Nonaka and Takeuchi, 1995); knowledge audit interviews in CTA (Klein and colleagues)
summary: Systematically inventories the declarative, procedural and tacit knowledge an organisation depends on, where it resides, how it flows, and where single points of failure exist.
description: Much of what makes work succeed is not written down: it lives in experienced people, informal routines and artefacts like annotated spreadsheets. A knowledge audit makes this visible. It first defines the types of knowledge required for a process (declarative know-what, procedural know-how, conditional know-when and tacit judgement), then locates each in people, documents, tools or practices. Tacit knowledge is elicited with cognitive task analysis techniques such as critical decision method interviews and stimulated recall. Gap analysis identifies knowledge that is required but undocumented, held by a single person, or lost at hand-offs. Rigour comes from structured elicitation per source and from mapping flows, not just stock, of knowledge.
steps: Knowledge inventory: Map types of knowledge required: declarative (know-what), procedural (know-how), contextual (know-when), relational (know-who).
Source identification: For each knowledge type: where does it reside? In people's heads, documents, artefacts, procedures? Identify critical single-points-of-failure.
Elicitation per source: For tacit individual knowledge: stimulated recall + critical incident + contextual inquiry. For document-embedded knowledge: document analysis and provenance tracing.
Gap analysis: What knowledge is required but undocumented or held by only one person? These gaps are organisational risks and design opportunities.
Knowledge map output: What is known, where it lives, how it flows, where the critical gaps are.
outputs: A knowledge inventory, a knowledge map showing sources and flows, critical gaps and single points of failure, and requirements for tools, documentation or AI support.
useWhen: Designing internal tools, knowledge bases, onboarding or AI assistants intended to capture expertise, or when expert attrition, automation or reorganisation threatens how work gets done.
avoidWhen: The domain is simple and well documented, or you only need end-user usability findings; use usability testing or a standard contextual inquiry.
whyLost: It sits in knowledge management and enterprise consulting, which UX rarely engages with, and product teams tend to assume documentation already describes the work.
whereToUse: Enterprise and internal tools, customer support platforms, AI copilots and retrieval systems, clinical operations, and legacy system replacement.
example: Before building an AI assistant for claims handlers, a team audits knowledge and discovers fraud-detection heuristics live with three senior staff and an unofficial spreadsheet. These are elicited and become explicit features and training data.
reference: Nonaka, I. & Takeuchi, H. (1995). The Knowledge-Creating Company. Oxford University Press.

name: Kolmogorov Complexity Estimation
origin: Andrey Kolmogorov, 1965; Ray Solomonoff, 1964; Gregory Chaitin, 1966
summary: Estimates the irreducible complexity of an interface or interaction by its shortest description, using compression or rule-length proxies to separate essential from accidental complexity.
description: Kolmogorov complexity is the length of the shortest program that produces a given object. It is uncomputable in general, but practical estimates use compression ratios or the minimum description length of a structure. In UX the idea is to ask how short a complete description of an interface's behaviour or layout can be. A screen governed by a few consistent rules compresses well; one full of exceptions does not. The method estimates complexity from serialised layouts, design-system rule sets or interaction state models, for example by compressing a structured description or counting rules and exceptions needed to specify behaviour. Rigour comes from using a consistent representation across compared designs and correlating estimates with user performance, since compressibility is a proxy for learnability rather than a direct user measure.
steps: Choose a consistent representation: serialised layout trees, a state machine of interactions, or a rule-and-exception specification.
Encode each design variant in that representation at the same level of detail.
Estimate complexity via compressed size (e.g. gzip or LZMA) or by counting rules plus exceptions needed for a full description.
Separate essential complexity (required by the domain) from accidental complexity (inconsistencies and exceptions).
Compare variants and correlate estimates with learnability or error data from users where available.
Target the exceptions that contribute most to description length for simplification.
outputs: Complexity estimates per design, list of exceptions and inconsistencies inflating description length, simplification targets.
useWhen: Comparing design-system consistency, evaluating AI-generated interfaces, auditing legacy enterprise interfaces with accumulated exceptions.
avoidWhen: When you need direct evidence of user difficulty; usability testing or task analysis are more direct. Not suitable for teams without technical modelling skills.
whyLost: Latent: Theoretical; no direct UX application tools exist; intellectually powerful for complexity reasoning.
whereToUse: Interface complexity theory; AI-generated UI; adaptive interface research.
example: A surgical console had 38 screens built by different teams. Encoding interaction rules showed 112 exceptions to 9 base patterns; consolidating the most frequent exceptions halved the description length and cut new-user errors in training.
sources: Information Theory Inference and Learning Algorithms
An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications (Li & Vitányi)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 1 — Entropy, Complexity & the Information Architecture of Interaction
Things That Keep Us Busy (Janlert & Stolterman, 2017)
Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: Li, M., & Vitányi, P. (2008). An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications (3rd ed.). Springer.

name: Kolmogorov Complexity for Interface Consistency Measurement
aka: Minimum description length of interaction grammars
origin: Andrey Kolmogorov (1965); minimum description length by Jorma Rissanen (1978); MacKay (2003)
summary: Estimates interface consistency as the length of the shortest rule set or compressed description that generates its interactions; shorter descriptions mean a more learnable, consistent grammar.
description: Kolmogorov complexity is the length of the shortest program that produces a given output. It is uncomputable in general, but it can be approximated by compression or by the minimum description length principle. Applied to interfaces, consistency can be framed as compressibility: if a single rule (for example 'swipe left always deletes, with undo') covers many cases, the interaction grammar is short; if each screen has its own exceptions, the shortest description is long. The method encodes interactions as a formal grammar or action-response table, counts rules and exceptions, or compresses the encoded table, and compares versions. Lower description length predicts faster learning and fewer errors, echoing task-action grammar from early HCI. It provides a quantitative consistency metric for design systems and audits.
steps: Enumerate all interaction rules users must internalize to use the product correctly.
Each rule is: 'when condition X, action Y produces result Z'.
Count the rules and their exceptions.
Each exception adds complexity.
Compute a proxy KC: total rules + 2× (number of exceptions).
Compare: if redesign reduces rule count by > 20%, predict measurable improvement in learnability.
Target: < 15 rules for consumer products, < 30 for professional tools.
outputs: Formal encoding of interaction rules, rule and exception counts, compression-based complexity estimates, and comparisons across versions or products.
useWhen: Design system audits, comparing product versions for consistency, enterprise suites with many modules, and predicting learnability of command sets or gestures.
avoidWhen: For small interfaces where inconsistencies are obvious by inspection, or when teams lack capacity to encode interactions formally; use heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Algorithmic information theory has no tradition in UX, and the early HCI grammar models it resembles (such as task-action grammar) were abandoned in the 1990s.
whereToUse: Design system consistency auditing, learnability measurement, expert vs. novice cognitive load analysis.
example: An ERP suite encodes how 'delete' works across 14 modules and needs 11 rules plus 9 exceptions. After harmonisation the description drops to 3 rules and 1 exception, and new-user error rates on deletion tasks fall in testing.
sources: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms — David J.C. MacKay
Rissanen, Modeling by shortest data description (Automatica, 1978)
reference: MacKay DJC (2003) Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms. Cambridge University Press

name: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Tests
origin: Andrey Kolmogorov (1933) and Nikolai Smirnov (1939)
summary: Compare a sample's empirical cumulative distribution with a hypothesised one, or two samples' distributions with each other, using the largest vertical gap as the test statistic.
description: The test avoids the arbitrary binning of a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. The empirical distribution function gives the proportion of observations at or below each value and converges uniformly to the true distribution. In the one-sample test, the statistic is the largest absolute difference between the empirical and a fully specified continuous distribution; multiplied by the square root of n, it is compared with the Kolmogorov limiting distribution, rejecting at 5 percent above about 1.36. The two-sample test uses the largest difference between two empirical distributions, scaled by the square root of mn/(m+n), to test whether two independent samples share one continuous distribution. Because it responds to any difference in shape, location or spread, it can show that two designs' task-time distributions differ even when their medians do not. The statistic also yields a confidence band for an unknown distribution.
steps: State the null: the sample follows a specified continuous distribution (one-sample) or two samples share one distribution (two-sample).
Sort the data and compute the empirical cumulative distribution function(s).
Find the largest absolute vertical difference between the empirical and hypothesised functions, or between the two empirical functions.
Scale it: by the square root of n (one-sample) or of mn/(m+n) (two-sample).
Compare with the Kolmogorov critical value (about 1.36 at 5 percent) or report the p-value.
Plot the empirical distributions together to show where they diverge, and judge whether the difference matters in practice.
outputs: A test statistic, p-value and an empirical distribution plot showing where distributions diverge.
useWhen: Comparing whole distributions of task times, ratings or session lengths between two designs or periods, or checking whether data fit an assumed distribution before modelling.
avoidWhen: Estimating the hypothesised distribution's parameters from the same data invalidates the simple one-sample test (use a Lilliefors-type correction); the asymptotic critical values are approximate for small samples; with very large n trivial differences become significant. For location shifts alone the Mann-Whitney U test is more powerful.
whyLost: UX statistics teaching centres on comparing means and medians, so tests of whole distributions are seldom introduced.
whereToUse: Performance and latency studies, A/B tests where effects sit in the tail, distribution drift checks for telemetry, checking normality assumptions.
example: Two onboarding flows have similar median completion time, but the two-sample test on 800 sessions each is significant; the plot shows the new flow removes the slow tail above five minutes.
reference: DeGroot, M. H. and Schervish, M. J. (2012). Probability and Statistics (4th ed.). Boston: Pearson, section 10.6, pp. 657-666.

name: KOMPASS Complementary System Design
donor: Cognitive systems engineering and work psychology
origin: Toni Wäfler, Gudela Grote, Anna Windischer and Cornelia Ryser, ETH Zurich; chapter 20 of Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
summary: Rate a work system against complementarity criteria at three levels, then run a facilitated participatory process to agree a design philosophy and derive human-automation requirements.
description: KOMPASS rejects allocating functions by comparing what humans and machines do best. Instead it asks whether people and automation complement each other so that humans keep control and meaningful work. Criteria sit at three levels: human-machine function allocation (process transparency, dynamic coupling, decision authority), the individual work task (task completeness, planning requirements, communication requirements, polyvalence) and the work system (collective autonomy). Trained analysts first rate existing systems against the criteria. A facilitated design team then agrees a shared design philosophy and evaluation concept, derives concrete requirements, and checks those requirements against the same criteria. The combination of explicit criteria and a participatory process is what distinguishes it from Fitts-list and levels-of-automation approaches.
steps: Assemble trained analysts and a cross-functional design team including operators.
Rate the existing work system on each criterion at the three levels: human-machine allocation, individual task and work system.
Feed the ratings back to the design team and facilitate agreement on a design philosophy for how people and automation should share work.
Agree an evaluation concept stating how designs will be judged against the criteria.
Derive concrete requirements for the automation and the tasks from the philosophy.
Check each requirement against the criteria and revise until it supports transparency, decision authority and task completeness.
outputs: Criterion ratings of the current system, an agreed design philosophy, and a set of requirements checked for complementarity.
useWhen: Introducing or redesigning automation in operational settings where operators must stay in control: production, logistics, control rooms and AI-assisted professional work.
avoidWhen: Avoid for consumer interfaces without a work system, or when no trained analysts are available; for a quick allocation sketch use Function Allocation (Fitts List / MABA-MABA) or Levels of Automation Analysis.
whyLost: It was published in European work-psychology and industrial-automation circles and needs trained analysts, so it never crossed into product UX.
whereToUse: AI copilots for operations staff, warehouse automation, clinical decision support, automated monitoring dashboards.
example: A logistics firm adding automatic route assignment rates the current system low on process transparency and decision authority. The design team agrees that dispatchers must be able to see and override every assignment, which becomes a requirement for explanation panels and override controls.
reference: Wäfler, T., Grote, G., Windischer, A. and Ryser, C. (2003). KOMPASS: A method for complementary system design. In E. Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (pp. 477-502). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Laban Effort Workshop
aka: Laban Effort Workshop for Embodied Design
origin: Framework: Rudolf Laban, early 20th century; workshop: Scott Sullivan and Erik Dahl, from 2012, later at Adaptive Path
summary: A movement workshop in which participants embody Laban's weight, space and time qualities and eight efforts, then apply them to scenarios involving people and devices.
description: Laban's Effort framework describes movement along three binary qualities: weight (light or strong), space (direct or indirect) and time (sudden or sustained), whose combinations give eight efforts such as gliding and pressing. In the workshop participants first notice how they normally walk, then embody each pole on its own, then combine qualities into efforts and switch one quality at a time to cycle through all eight, reflecting on how each changes feeling and thought. Efforts are tried exaggerated, toned down for a public setting and isolated to one body part. The second half places efforts in scenarios: assigned efforts in a shared, shrinking space, joint tasks between people starting from different efforts, and observing someone's physical use of a device before altering the device or setting. The result is bodily awareness and a shared vocabulary for physical interaction.
steps: Have participants walk normally and notice feet, arms and pace.
Embody each pole on its own: light, strong, direct, indirect, sudden, sustained.
Combine qualities into an effort (for example light, direct and sustained gives gliding) and switch one quality at a time through all eight efforts, reflecting after each.
Explore each effort exaggerated, toned down for a public setting and isolated to one body part.
Assign efforts and have people interact in a shared space, shrinking the space to force contact.
Run realistic scenarios, such as two people completing a joint spatial task from different efforts.
Observe a person using a device or setting, change the device or environment, and observe how the movement quality changes.
Debrief to capture the vocabulary and design ideas that emerged.
outputs: Participant reflections, a shared vocabulary for describing movement qualities, and ideas for changing devices or environments.
useWhen: Designing wearables, gesture, automotive or IoT interactions where the quality of bodily movement matters and the team lacks words for it.
avoidWhen: Produces vocabulary and ideas, not evidence; there are no measures. To learn how people actually move with a product use Embodied Experience Research, Sensory Ethnography or video-based field observation, and evaluate gesture designs with Prototype Testing.
whyLost: Confined to a few design studios and wearables practitioners because it needs a skilled movement facilitator and teams are uneasy with physical exercises.
whereToUse: Wearables, gesture and motion interfaces, VR and AR, automotive interiors, smart-home devices.
example: A smartwatch team uses the workshop to contrast 'flicking' and 'pressing' efforts, then redesigns a dismiss gesture so it feels light and sudden rather than strong and sustained.
reference: Sullivan, S. (2017) Designing for Wearables: Effective UX for Current and Future Devices. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 125-130.

name: Labelling system analysis
origin: Rosenfeld and Morville, Information Architecture (1998 onwards)
summary: Inventory every label in a system in one table, benchmark against competitors' labels, and tune the raw list into a consistent, scoped labelling system with room to grow.
description: Labels form a system, so they should be examined together. A labelling table lists every label per navigation system with the heading and title of its destination, exposing variant names, the same page labelled differently in different places, missing headings and inconsistent style and capitalisation; it extends a content inventory. Competitive and comparable analysis records the labels other environments use for equivalent content, revealing de facto conventions (for example eight financial sites converging on 'personal finance'). Tuning turns any raw candidate list into a system: sort and de-duplicate, set conventions for usage, punctuation, case and style, check gaps by adding phantom labels for anticipated topics, avoid cop-out categories such as 'Miscellaneous', and bound the scope. Search logs and usability tests then keep tuning it after launch.
steps: Walk the whole system, manually or with a crawler, and record each label with its destination's heading and title, grouped by navigation system.
Scan the table for inconsistent names, multiple labels for the same destination, missing headings, and style or case problems.
Visit competitors' or best-in-class environments and record their labels for equivalent content and functions.
Identify recurring patterns and de facto conventions across environments.
Combine candidates into a raw list, sort alphabetically and remove duplicates.
Set conventions for usage, punctuation, case and style; add phantom labels for anticipated content to test that conventions hold.
Bound the scope to current and anticipated content and audiences, then keep tuning after launch with search log analysis and usability tests.
outputs: A complete labelling table, a list of inconsistencies, evidence of industry conventions, and a consistent labelling system with style rules.
useWhen: Redesigning navigation, merging sites or products, or building a design system's content conventions.
avoidWhen: Avoid building full tables for large indexing vocabularies unless restricted to segments. Borrowing competitors' labels can copy bad ideas, so validate with card sorting or tree testing.
whyLost: Navigation labels are still discussed, but the systematic table, benchmark and tuning procedure is often reduced to ad hoc copy edits.
whereToUse: Website and intranet redesigns, e-commerce taxonomies, SaaS navigation, mergers of product lines and content design systems.
example: A car hire site's labelling table shows three variants of the company name and a contact page labelled both 'Contact Us' and 'Customer Care'. The team sets one convention per concept and checks it with a tree test.
reference: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J. (2015). Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (4th ed.). O'Reilly Media.

name: Labov Narrative Analysis
origin: William Labov and Joshua Waletzky, 1967; Labov (1972, Language in the Inner City)
summary: Segments personal stories into abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution and coda, revealing what tellers consider reportable and why it matters.
description: Labov showed that oral narratives of personal experience share a structure: an abstract (what the story is about), orientation (who, when, where), complicating action (temporally ordered clauses: then what happened), evaluation (why it is worth telling, the teller's stance), resolution and coda (return to the present). Evaluation is the key analytic target, showing what mattered emotionally and morally. Applying this to interview stories about product experiences distinguishes events from their significance, compares how different users evaluate similar events, and identifies the 'most reportable event' that motivates a story, valuable for understanding complaints, switching and advocacy.
steps: Elicit stories of specific experiences (e.g. 'tell me about the time your payment failed').
Transcribe carefully and segment into clauses.
Code clauses as abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution or coda.
Analyse evaluation devices (intensifiers, comparators, explicatives, direct speech) to identify stance and significance.
Identify the most reportable event in each story and compare across participants.
Relate patterns of evaluation to design and service implications.
outputs: Structurally coded narratives, analyses of evaluation and reportability, and cross-story comparisons.
useWhen: Interview research rich in stories about incidents, complaints, switching or memorable experiences.
avoidWhen: Data without narratives (e.g. survey ratings) or when broad thematic coverage is the goal.
whyLost: Sociolinguistic methods are rarely taught in UX, which codes interview content thematically without attention to narrative structure.
whereToUse: Customer complaint research, critical incident interviews, switching interviews, healthcare patient experience.
example: In 25 stories about fraud alerts, evaluation clauses cluster not on the money at risk but on feeling accused ('like I was a criminal'), redirecting the redesign toward respectful alert language.
sources: Labov & Waletzky, Narrative analysis: Oral versions of personal experience (1967), in Helm (ed.), Essays on the Verbal and Visual Arts
Labov, Language in the Inner City (1972)
Riessman, Narrative Methods for the Human Sciences (2008)
reference: Labov, W., & Waletzky, J. (1967). Narrative analysis. In J. Helm (Ed.), Essays on the Verbal and Visual Arts. University of Washington Press.

name: Ladder of causation (association/intervention/counterfactual)
origin: Judea Pearl, 2000; popularised in The Book of Why, 2018
summary: A three-level framework classifying questions and evidence as association (seeing), intervention (doing) or counterfactual (imagining), clarifying what each study can prove.
description: Pearl's ladder sorts causal claims by the information needed to support them. Rung one, association, answers what users who did X also did; correlations, funnels and segment comparisons live here. Rung two, intervention, answers what happens if we make users do X; randomised experiments and adjusted observational analyses reach it. Rung three, counterfactual, answers what would have happened to this specific user had we acted differently; it requires structural models and stronger assumptions. Data from a lower rung cannot answer a higher-rung question without assumptions. For UX, the ladder is a classification tool for research questions and claims, exposing reports that reach rung-three language on rung-one evidence.
steps: List each research question and each claim in a plan or report.
Classify each by rung: association, intervention or counterfactual, based on the wording of the claim.
Classify the evidence supporting each claim by the rung it can reach (e.g. survey correlation is rung one; an A/B test is rung two).
Flag mismatches where the claim sits higher than the evidence, and either reword the claim or plan a design to climb the ladder.
For rung-two needs, choose an experiment or quasi-experiment; for rung-three, specify the structural model and assumptions required.
outputs: A rung classification of questions and claims, a mismatch list and a plan for evidence that matches the decision's causal demands.
useWhen: Planning research for decisions that hinge on cause and effect, and reviewing reports or dashboards before leadership acts on them.
avoidWhen: Avoid as an end in itself for purely descriptive or exploratory work where no causal decision is at stake.
whyLost: The framework is recent and appears mostly in popular science and CS courses, so UX teams rarely use it as an explicit checklist despite constant causal claims.
whereToUse: Research planning, insight review boards, growth analytics, AI personalisation claims and executive briefings.
example: A report claims a community feature caused 12% higher retention based on comparing users who joined communities with those who did not. The ladder review marks the claim as rung two on rung-one evidence, and the team plans a staggered rollout instead.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Book of Why (Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 45 — The Causal Revolution — Pearl's Ladder & the Fundamental Problem
reference: Pearl, J. & Mackenzie, D. (2018) The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect. Basic Books.

name: Laddering (Means-End Chain Analysis)
donor: Consumer and marketing research, from personal construct psychology
origin: Jonathan Gutman, 1982; formalised by Thomas Reynolds and Gutman, 1988
summary: A structured 'why is that important?' probing sequence linking product attributes to functional consequences, psychosocial consequences and personal values, aggregated into a Hierarchical Value Map.
description: Means-end chain theory holds that people value product attributes because of the consequences they produce and value those consequences because they serve personal values. Laddering elicits these chains in one-to-one interviews: the participant names distinguishing attributes, and the interviewer repeatedly asks why each matters until the participant reaches a value. Interviewers use specific techniques when participants stall, such as imagining the absence of an attribute or redirecting to a third person. Ladders are content-coded, summarised in an implication matrix counting direct and indirect links, and drawn as a Hierarchical Value Map showing dominant pathways above a cut-off. The rigour lies in the coding and aggregation, which turns idiosyncratic interviews into a structured map of motivation.
steps: Opening elicitation: Ask participant to identify important attributes of the product. Generate 4–8 attributes.
Ladder probing — upward: For each attribute, ask 'Why is [attribute] important to you?' Follow the chain upward with repeated 'why' probing until reaching a terminal value.
Handling abstraction resistance: 'Imagine you didn't have [consequence] — what would be different?' or 'What would that mean for you in your daily life?'
Hierarchical Value Map (HVM): Aggregate ladders across participants showing how attributes connect to consequences and values, with link frequency indicating prevalence.
Application: The HVM reveals which product attributes connect to which personal values for which user segments — directly informing positioning and design priority.
outputs: Individual ladders, a coded attribute-consequence-value set, an implication matrix, and a Hierarchical Value Map of dominant motivational pathways.
useWhen: You need to understand why features matter, connect product attributes to deeper motivations for positioning or prioritisation, or explain preferences that surveys show but cannot explain.
avoidWhen: Participants have little experience with the category, or you need to discover unknown problems rather than explain preferences; use contextual inquiry. Avoid on topics where repeated why questions feel intrusive without careful rapport.
whyLost: UX adopted the 'five whys' as an informal probe but not the coding, implication matrix and value map, while the full method stayed in advertising and consumer research.
whereToUse: Value proposition and pricing research, feature prioritisation, persona motivation layers, B2B purchase drivers, and sustainability or health behaviour products.
example: Laddering 20 users of a budgeting app shows 'auto-categorisation' links to 'less time on admin', then 'feeling in control', then 'security for my family'. The value map reframes marketing around control and family security rather than automation.
sources: Reynolds & Gutman (1988) Journal of Advertising Research
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Reynolds, T. J. & Gutman, J. (1988). Laddering theory, method, analysis, and interpretation. Journal of Advertising Research, 28(1), 11-31.

name: Lag Sequential Analysis
origin: Gene Sackett, 1979; applied to HCI by Sanderson and Fisher, 1994
summary: Tests which behaviours follow which others at lags 1, 2 and beyond more often than chance, given base rates, turning interaction sequences into statistically supported patterns.
description: Lag sequential analysis computes transitional probabilities between coded behaviours at defined lags and compares them with the probabilities expected from base rates, using adjusted residuals (z-scores) to identify significant contingencies. Sanderson and Fisher brought it to HCI as part of exploratory sequential data analysis. The treatise notes it is almost unknown in UX, which relies on session recordings and heatmaps that make patterns visually salient but provide no statistical basis for distinguishing real patterns from coincidental clustering. Consequently analysts see patterns that are not significant and miss ones that are. Recovered, LSA tests claims such as 'error messages are followed by help access' or 'search refinements follow zero-result pages' with proper chance correction. Rated HIGH recovery priority. Not to be confused with latent semantic analysis, also abbreviated LSA, a text-analysis technique sometimes used to build personas.
steps: Define a mutually exclusive, exhaustive coding scheme for events or states.
Code sequences from logs or video, ensuring sufficient events (several hundred transitions at least).
Build lag-1 (and higher-lag) transition frequency matrices.
Compute expected frequencies from base rates and adjusted residuals for each transition.
Flag transitions with |z| greater than 1.96 (correcting for multiple comparisons) as significant.
Interpret significant contingencies and validate on a holdout sample.
outputs: Transition matrices, significant contingency map, statistically supported sequence patterns.
useWhen: Analysing clickstreams, video-coded sessions or conversational turns where claims about sequence are made.
avoidWhen: Very sparse data or uncoded raw logs with thousands of event types; aggregate first or use HMMs.
whyLost: Never part of UX training; displaced by visual tools (recordings, heatmaps, funnels) that require no statistics.
whereToUse: Product analytics, chatbot conversation logs, error recovery analysis, onboarding sequences.
example: In 40,000 sessions of a SaaS app, LSA shows 'validation error' to 'abandon' at lag 1 has z = 9.4, while the much-discussed 'help click' to 'abandon' is not above chance.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Sackett GP (1979) The lag sequential analysis of contingency and cyclicity in behavioral interaction research
Sanderson PM & Fisher C (1994) Exploratory sequential data analysis: foundations. Human-Computer Interaction 9(3)
Bakeman R & Quera V (2011) Sequential Analysis and Observational Methods
Sackett, The lag sequential analysis of contingency and cyclicity in behavioral interaction research (1979), in Osofsky (ed.), Handbook of Infant Development
Bakeman & Gottman, Observing Interaction: An Introduction to Sequential Analysis (2nd ed., 1997)
Bakeman & Quera, Sequential Analysis and Observational Methods for the Behavioral Sciences (2011)

name: Lagged Multilevel Models with Autocorrelation and Time-Trend Control
aka: Autocorrelated errors for missing occasions and unequal intervals
origin: Wolfgang Viechtbauer, 2022; Bolger and Laurenceau, 2013
summary: Test whether a predictor at one prompt foretells the outcome at the next, controlling for the outcome's carry-over and time trends, with person-varying effects and uneven intervals handled.
description: Concurrent associations in repeated data cannot show direction. Using the previous prompt's predictor puts the presumed cause first. Adding the lagged outcome with a random slope controls autocorrelation (emotional inertia), so the lagged predictor shows its unique effect; adding time of day and day, with random effects, guards against confounding by daily rhythms, without which autocorrelation is biased. Effective lags can be long (about 135 minutes when prompts are 90 minutes apart and events are recalled since the last beep), and intervals vary, so analysts interact the lag with interval length or use continuous-time models. Bolger and Laurenceau show a spatial-power AR(1) error structure that uses exact time gaps, and that maximum-likelihood estimates stay valid when days are missing at random (rerunning with 20% of days deleted gave the same conclusions). Overnight lags are set to missing; in the handbook example about 23% of rows were lost to lagging and missingness.
steps: Build lagged predictor and outcome variables within day and person, setting overnight lags to missing.
Fit the outcome on the lagged predictor with a random intercept and random slope.
Add the lagged outcome with a random slope to control autocorrelation.
Add time of day and day with random effects, plus any group interactions.
Where spacing varies, interact the lag with interval length or use a spatial-power (continuous-time AR(1)) error structure.
Fit by maximum likelihood so missing occasions are handled under missing-at-random assumptions.
Report the number of observations used and the share lost to lagging.
outputs: Lagged effects net of autocorrelation and trends, with average and person-specific inertia estimates.
useWhen: Diary, ESM or dense logged data where you want evidence on temporal order, such as whether an experience predicts later mood or behaviour.
avoidWhen: Sparse or very irregular data, or when causal claims are needed; use an experiment or micro-randomised trial. Lagged effects remain correlational.
whyLost: UX longitudinal data are rarely dense enough or analysed with multilevel time-series models; the techniques sit in psychology methods texts.
whereToUse: Wellbeing and habit apps, productivity tools, AI assistant longitudinal studies, and telemetry joined to repeated self-reports.
example: In a 14-day study of a coding assistant, a frustrating interaction at one prompt predicts lower willingness to use the assistant at the next prompt, net of prior willingness and time of day; the effect varies widely across developers.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Language auto-detection
origin: Spoken language identification research (NIST LRE evaluations from 1996); built into Whisper (Radford et al., 2022)
summary: Automatically identifying the language spoken in each recording or segment so multilingual research audio is routed to the right transcription settings and analysts.
description: Whisper predicts the language of the first 30 seconds of audio from 99 languages and returns probabilities. In multilingual research, including code-switching participants, this lets a pipeline route files to language-specific models, translators and analysts, and flag recordings that need human review. Rigour comes from not trusting detection on short or noisy clips, checking detection confidence, detecting language per segment for code-switching speakers rather than per file, and fixing the language explicitly once known, because a wrong detection makes Whisper transcribe or even translate into the wrong language.
steps: Run detection on a clean speech segment (skip initial silence or moderator introductions) of at least 30 seconds.
Record the top language and its probability; flag files with top probability below about 0.80 for human review.
For known code-switching populations, run detection per segment (e.g. per diarised turn) and store a language tag per segment.
Once a file's language is confirmed, transcribe with the language parameter set explicitly rather than auto-detect.
Report language composition of the corpus and route segments to analysts fluent in each language.
outputs: Per-file and per-segment language tags with probabilities, a review list and a language composition summary.
useWhen: Multinational or multilingual UX research programmes, migrant and diaspora user studies, and global product feedback audio.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary when all participants are recruited in one language; set the language explicitly then. Avoid relying on it for closely related languages or dialects without review.
whyLost: An emergent capability bundled with modern speech models, used widely but rarely validated.
whereToUse: Global SaaS research, emerging markets fintech, public services in multilingual regions and international diary studies.
example: An emerging-markets payments app collects 200 voice-note diaries in Hindi, English and Hinglish. Per-segment detection flags 31% of notes as code-switched, which are routed to bilingual analysts rather than auto-translated.
sources: Radford, A. et al. (2023) Robust speech recognition via large-scale weak supervision. ICML
The Inquiry Series, C9 — Whisper — Batch Transcription at Scale
reference: Radford, A. et al. (2023) Robust speech recognition via large-scale weak supervision. ICML 2023

name: Language Sample Analysis (CHAT Transcription and Mean Length of Utterance)
origin: Roger Brown (1973), A First Language; CHILDES launched in 1984 by Brian MacWhinney and Catherine Snow
summary: Transcribe natural speech in a standard format, segment it into utterances and morphemes, and compute measures such as mean length of utterance to compare over time or against norms.
description: Brown's team recorded children monthly at home, transcribed the tapes and analysed them in a weekly seminar. Mean length of utterance is the average number of morphemes per utterance in a spontaneous sample, an index of grammatical development up to about 4.0, with Brown's five stages in steps of 0.5. About half an hour of conversation yields roughly 100 eligible utterances. Utterances are segmented by a two-of-three rule (bounded by silence, terminal intonation, a natural grammatical unit); unintelligible utterances and repetitions are excluded; Brown's rules define what counts as a morpheme. CHAT is the standard transcription format, and CLAN programs compute MLU, vocabulary lists and grammatical profiles automatically, while the shared CHILDES database allows pooled, standardised comparison. The disciplined segmentation is what transfers: it makes length and complexity of spoken input comparable across people and sessions.
steps: Record about 30 minutes of natural conversation.
Transcribe it exactly in a standard format such as CHAT.
Segment utterances using the two-of-three criteria and exclude unintelligible utterances and repetitions.
Divide utterances into morphemes using explicit rules (or count words for highly inflected languages).
Compute MLU and other measures with software such as CLAN.
Compare with normative data or across sessions and groups.
outputs: Mean length of utterance, developmental stage, vocabulary lists and grammatical profiles.
useWhen: Characterising how people actually phrase spoken or typed input, for example the length and complexity of utterances to a voice assistant, across user groups or over time.
avoidWhen: MLU is invalid beyond about 4.0 and inflates in inflected languages; spontaneous speech underestimates knowledge and depends on chance. For interactional structure use Conversation Analysis; for vocabulary contrasts use Corpus Keyness Analysis.
whyLost: It is a clinical and developmental standard with no counterpart in UX, which analyses conversational logs with ad hoc counts.
whereToUse: Voice and chat interfaces, children's products, accessibility research with speech or language impairments.
example: A children's reading app segments recordings of 40 children talking to its voice tutor with CHAT conventions. Children aged five average an MLU of 3.1, so the tutor's prompts are shortened to match.
reference: Brown, R. (1973). A First Language: The Early Stages. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press; Berko Gleason, J. and Bernstein Ratner, N. (Eds.) (2022). The Development of Language (10th ed.). Plural Publishing.

name: Large Language Model Evaluation
donor: Natural language processing and machine learning evaluation
origin: Human evaluation traditions from machine translation (BLEU-era human judgement, 2000s); LLM-as-judge and rubric evals from 2022 onwards
summary: Structured evaluation of LLM-powered experiences combining rubric-based human ratings, automated metrics and task-level user outcomes such as success, hallucination and trust.
description: LLM evaluation assesses generative AI features at three levels: output quality (accuracy, groundedness, hallucination, safety, tone), task outcome (did the user accomplish the goal, with how many turns and corrections), and experience (trust calibration, perceived usefulness, reliance). Because outputs are open-ended and stochastic, rigour requires a curated evaluation set representing real user intents, written rubrics with anchored scale points, multiple raters with measured agreement (for example Krippendorff's alpha of 0.67 or above), repeated sampling per prompt, and separate reporting of rare but severe failures. Automated LLM-as-judge scoring can scale evaluation but must be calibrated against human ratings. UX researchers contribute the intent taxonomy, the rubric, and links between output quality and behaviour in logs.
steps: Build an evaluation set of 100-500 real or realistic prompts stratified by user intent, difficulty and risk, drawn from logs or research.
Write a rubric with anchored levels for each dimension (for example correctness, groundedness, completeness, tone, safety).
Have at least two trained raters score a calibration subset, compute inter-rater agreement and refine the rubric until agreement is acceptable.
Generate multiple outputs per prompt to capture variability, and score all of them, optionally with an LLM judge calibrated against human scores.
Run task-based sessions or log analysis linking output quality to user outcomes: task success, retries, edits, abandonment and expressed trust.
Report scores by intent segment, track severe failure rates separately, and re-run the set on every model or prompt change as a regression suite.
outputs: Evaluation dataset, scoring rubric, inter-rater agreement, quality and hallucination rates by intent, severe-failure log and a regression benchmark.
useWhen: Shipping or changing any LLM-based feature, choosing between models or prompts, and monitoring quality drift after launch.
avoidWhen: When the question is whether users need an AI feature at all (start with discovery research), or when you lack representative prompts, since evaluating on synthetic prompts alone misleads.
whyLost: Still in use: Rapidly evolving; essential for AI product teams; no standardized methodology yet.
whereToUse: Any AI-powered product feature; chatbot; copilot; AI search.
example: A legal-tech SaaS compares two models for contract summarisation using 300 real clauses and a five-dimension rubric. The cheaper model scores similarly on average but omits indemnity caps in 7% of cases, so the team keeps the stronger model for that clause type.
sources: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (Liang et al., 2022)
Krippendorff, Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Liang P et al. (2022) Holistic Evaluation of Language Models. arXiv:2211.09110

name: Large-Scale Playtest
donor: Games user research (console and PC publishers)
origin: Industry practice at game publishers such as Microsoft Game Studios; described in the book by Michael C. Medlock (chapter 7) and by Graham McAllister and Sebastian Long of Player Research (chapter 8)
summary: Many players play a build at the same time and then answer a structured questionnaire, so the team gets quantified attitudes about whether the designed experience is enjoyed.
description: A large-scale playtest answers the question 'are players enjoying the experience we designed?' rather than 'can they use it?'. Groups of target players play a near-complete build in a room with several seats, then complete a carefully designed questionnaire about appeal, enjoyment, difficulty, art style, features and core mechanics; a few may join a short group interview. Player Research describe a minimum of 36 players run as three groups of 12 in one day, with about an hour of play and 25 minutes of questions, followed by several days of analysis. Medlock's overview names variants by scope: the initial experience playtest covers roughly the first two hours of play, the extended playtest runs over days (for example two days and 16 hours) to show how ratings change across levels, and the benchmark playtest uses a standardised questionnaire and larger sample so that results can be compared with other titles tested in exactly the same way. Because attitudes only mean something against a reference, the method depends on consistent questions and enough participants for statistical comparison. It complements small-sample usability playtests, which find problems but cannot quantify liking. For UX teams outside games, the same pattern suits any experiential product where enjoyment, not task success, is the main outcome.
steps: Agree the questions the team needs answered and which of them must be quantified.
Write or reuse a standardised questionnaire with rating items per game area plus a small number of open questions.
Recruit a target-audience sample large enough for comparison (the book suggests at least 25 to 36 players).
Run groups of players simultaneously on the same build, with a fixed play period and minimal moderator intervention.
Administer the questionnaire straight after play and, optionally, hold a short group interview.
Analyse ratings by game area and segment, code open responses, and compare against earlier builds or benchmark titles.
Report results structured by the team's questions and track them across builds.
outputs: Rating distributions and comparisons by game area, coded open comments, and a benchmark for later builds or titles.
useWhen: A build is feature-rich enough to judge the experience and you need to know how much players like it, or how it compares with a previous build or competitor.
avoidWhen: Basic usability problems are still present, or you need to know why players feel as they do; self-report alone will not explain causes.
whyLost: Standard practice at large game publishers but rarely used outside games, where enjoyment is seldom treated as the primary outcome and labs are built for one-to-one sessions.
whereToUse: Games, entertainment and media apps, learning products, fitness and other experience-led products.
example: A studio runs 36 players through the first two hours of a racing game in three sessions of 12, then compares fun and difficulty ratings for each track with the previous milestone build.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapters 7 (Medlock) and 8 (McAllister and Long).

name: Latent change score models
aka: Latent change score and differential-equation models of change
origin: McArdle and Hamagami (2001); Boker (2001); Ram and Grimm
