summary: Writes the theory of change as a rule for each occasion-to-occasion change, solves it, and fits it to repeated measures to test competing change processes.
description: A latent change score model expresses each score as an initial level plus the sum of latent changes between occasions. It is equivalent to a standard growth model but makes the change process explicit, so each change can depend on the current level, on other variables or on external inputs. Ram and Grimm recommend starting from a differential equation that states the theory: constant change gives linear growth, change proportional to level gives exponential growth, change towards a carrying capacity gives a negative exponential (a learning curve with a ceiling), and time-varying rate or capacity can represent an intervention. The solved function is fitted with person-level random coefficients in SEM or multilevel software, and parameters are read as named process quantities such as rate, capacity and initial condition. Competing change rules are compared formally.
steps: State the hypothesised change rule as a differential equation (dy/dt) or difference equation, for example change proportional to the distance from a ceiling.
Solve it over the observation window to obtain the expected trajectory function.
Specify the model in SEM as latent changes between occasions, or as a nonlinear mixed model, adding person-level random coefficients.
Fit competing change rules (constant, proportional, ceiling-seeking, coupled with another variable) and compare them with information criteria or likelihood-ratio tests.
Interpret the winning model's parameters as process quantities and test whether an intervention changes rate or capacity.
outputs: Estimates of change-process parameters (rate, capacity, coupling) and formal tests between alternative theories of change.
useWhen: There is a theory about how change works, such as learning towards a skill ceiling or trust that grows with use and falls after errors, and several waves of data to test it.
avoidWhen: The aim is only to describe average trajectories (use growth curve modelling), there are too few occasions, or nobody on the team can formulate the mathematics.
whyLost: It needs mathematical formulation that UX teams rarely attempt, and it remains a specialist tool in developmental and ageing research.
whereToUse: Learnability and skill acquisition studies, trust calibration in AI products, coupled dynamics such as engagement and satisfaction across a subscription lifecycle.
example: A language-learning app models weekly test scores as change towards a personal ceiling. Comparing a constant-rate model with a ceiling-seeking model shows the latter fits better, and users who enable spaced review have a higher ceiling but the same rate.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Ram, N. and Grimm, K. J. (2015). Growth curve modeling and longitudinal factor analysis. In R. M. Lerner, W. F. Overton and P. C. M. Molenaar (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 1 (pp. 758-788). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Latent Class Analysis for Personas
origin: Lazarsfeld (1950); modern estimation by Goodman (1974)
summary: Finds hidden user types from patterns of categorical survey answers, giving probabilistic, statistically tested segments.
description: Cluster analysis on survey data is popular for personas but has no statistical test for the number of groups and handles categorical answers poorly. Latent class analysis assumes an unobserved categorical variable (the user type) explains patterns in responses, and estimates both how many classes exist and each person's probability of belonging to each. Model fit statistics (BIC, entropy) guide the number of classes, and class profiles describe how each type answers. Sauro and Lewis position it as the advanced route to persona development, above k-means clustering in rigour.
steps: Survey a large sample (several hundred) on categorical behaviours, needs and attitudes.
Fit LCA models with 1 to k classes from many random starts.
Choose the number of classes using BIC, bootstrap likelihood tests, K-fold cross-validation and interpretability.

Check local fit with bivariate residuals; for flagged indicator pairs, add direct effects or set the offending covariate inactive (one documented rule drops the variable with the highest residual until all are below about 4), then refit.
Where personas must hold within subgroups such as age bands, rerun the model separately for each group and reconcile classes across groups.
Add further descriptive variables as inactive covariates to enrich profiles without changing the classes.
Profile each class by its response probabilities and name it.
Validate classes against behaviour data and build a classification tool (for example a scoring equation or discriminant analysis) to type new users.
outputs: Statistically supported user segments with membership probabilities.
useWhen: Data-driven persona projects with categorical or mixed survey data.
avoidWhen: Samples under about 300, or when segments must be defined by business rules. Overly restrictive error structures (for example local independence or diagonal covariances imposed without checking) can overestimate the number of classes; adding direct effects for locally dependent indicators often reduces it, but can also hide real classes, so compare both by BIC.
whyLost: Requires specialist software (Mplus, Latent GOLD, poLCA) and its home is sociology and psychometrics, not design.
whereToUse: Persona development, market segmentation, onboarding personalisation.
example: A fitness app survey of 1,200 users yields four classes; one "data-anxious beginners" class (18%) was invisible in earlier qualitative personas.
sources: Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Vermunt JK & Magidson J (2002) Latent class cluster analysis. In Hagenaars JA & McCutcheon AL (Eds) Applied Latent Class Analysis. Cambridge University Press
Rasca SI, Markvica K & Biesinger B (2023) Persona design methodology for work-commute travel behaviour using latent class cluster analysis. Multimodal Transportation 2
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Persona Design Methodology for Work-Commute Travel Behaviour Using Latent Class Cluster Analysis (Rasca et al., 2023)
Introduction to Latent Class Modeling using Latent GOLD (Statistical Innovations, 2015)
reference: Sauro & Lewis, Factor and Discriminant Analysis training (2021); Collins & Lanza (2010), Latent Class and Latent Transition Analysis.

name: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for Qualitative Scale-Up
aka: Latent Dirichlet Allocation for large corpora
origin: David Blei, Andrew Ng and Michael Jordan, 2003; Roberts et al. STM (2014)
summary: Discovers latent topics in large text corpora such as reviews, tickets and survey comments without predefined categories, enabling qualitative synthesis at scale.
description: LDA models each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as a probability distribution over words, fitted to explain word co-occurrence. The treatise's transfer: apply to app reviews, support transcripts, open-ended survey responses and NPS comments, where thousands to millions of items exceed manual coding. LDA discovers latent problem themes without pre-specifying categories; outputs need interpretive labelling but the structure is data-driven. Structural topic models add covariates (rating, platform, date) so topic prevalence can be compared across segments and time. Rigour requires preprocessing decisions, choosing K via coherence and held-out likelihood, and validating topics by reading representative documents. Embedding-based topic models are modern alternatives.
steps: Assemble and clean the corpus (deduplicate, remove boilerplate, handle languages).
Tokenise, remove stop words and build a vocabulary.
Fit models across a range of K and assess coherence and exclusivity.
Label topics by reading top words and the most representative documents.
Model topic prevalence against covariates (rating, version, segment) with STM if needed.
Validate a sample manually and feed topics into deeper qualitative follow-up.
outputs: Labelled topics, topic prevalence by segment and time, representative quotes.
useWhen: Large volumes of unstructured feedback where manual coding is infeasible.
avoidWhen: Small corpora (hundreds of items) where human coding is more accurate; short texts where embeddings work better.
whyLost: LDA is standard in computational social science but UX teams rarely handle corpora large enough or have the skills, and it is now being displaced by embedding-based methods.
whereToUse: App store reviews, support tickets, NPS verbatims, community forums, AI chat logs.
example: STM on 180,000 reviews of a ride-hailing app reveals a 'pickup pin' topic whose prevalence doubled after a map update, unnoticed in star ratings.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Blei DM, Ng AY & Jordan MI (2003) Latent Dirichlet allocation. JMLR 3:993-1022
Roberts ME, Stewart BM & Tingley D (2014) Structural topic models for open-ended survey responses. AJPS
Blei, D. M., Ng, A. Y. & Jordan, M. I. (2003) Latent Dirichlet Allocation. Journal of Machine Learning Research
Röder, M., Both, A. & Hinneburg, A. (2015) Exploring the space of topic coherence measures. WSDM
The Inquiry Series, C11 — Topic Modelling at Scale — LDA, BERTopic & Semantic Clustering
A Practical Guide to Sentiment Analysis (Erik Cambria et al.)
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Blei, Ng & Jordan (2003) Latent Dirichlet Allocation
The Inquiry Series, Ch 55 — Natural Language at Scale — Computational Qualitative Analysis
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Blei DM, Ng AY & Jordan MI (2003) Latent Dirichlet allocation. Journal of Machine Learning Research 3:993-1022.

name: Latent semantic analysis persona clustering
aka: Semantic similarity clustering of interview text
origin: Miaskiewicz, Sumner and Kozar, 2008; LSA from Landauer, Foltz and Laham, 1998
summary: Cluster participants into personas by the semantic similarity of their free-text answers, computed with latent semantic analysis, then check agreement with expert groupings.
description: Participants answer semi-structured questions about goals, needs and frustrations. Their texts are compared pairwise with latent semantic analysis, giving a cosine similarity matrix between participants, which is clustered with hierarchical agglomerative clustering; clusters become personas. Miaskiewicz et al. reported agreement with experts above kappa 0.60, but Brickey, Walczak and Burgess found only fair agreement (kappa 0.31) and lopsided clusters (12, 5 and 1) with 18 participants. Results depend on the reference corpus behind the semantic space, and the method needs specialist tools. LSA has since been superseded by word and sentence embeddings, so the approach survives mainly as a precursor to embedding-based clustering of qualitative text.
steps: Collect free-text answers to the same semi-structured questions about goals, needs and frustrations.

Choose or build a semantic space, preferably from a domain corpus: weight the term counts (for example by tf-idf, so that shared rare words count more) and reduce them by singular value decomposition.
Compute LSA cosine similarities between every pair of participants' texts.
Run hierarchical agglomerative clustering on the similarity matrix and choose the number of clusters.
Check agreement with an expert clustering using Cohen's kappa, aiming for at least 0.6.
Turn acceptable clusters into personas, reviewing unbalanced or singleton clusters by hand.
outputs: A participant similarity matrix, persona clusters, and agreement statistics against expert grouping.
useWhen: You want a reproducible text-based grouping of interview participants to compare with analyst judgement, and modern embeddings are not available.
avoidWhen: Samples are small or you have access to modern sentence embeddings; LSA depends heavily on its corpus and can produce very unbalanced clusters. Use expert affinity work or embedding-based clustering instead.
whyLost: LSA was overtaken by neural embeddings and LLM-assisted coding, and published agreement with experts was inconsistent.
whereToUse: Historical comparison for text-based persona methods; small archives of interview text where reproducibility matters.
example: A research team clusters 40 open-ended survey answers about remote work using semantic similarity, then compares the clusters with researchers' affinity groups. Low kappa leads them to treat the automated grouping only as a check.
sources: A Comparative Analysis of Persona Clustering Methods (Brickey et al., 2010)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Miaskiewicz, T., Sumner, T., & Kozar, K. A. (2008). A latent semantic analysis methodology for the identification and creation of personas. Proceedings of CHI 2008, 1501-1510.

name: Latent Variable Interaction Modelling in SEM
aka: Interaction effects in structural equation models
Nonlinear and interaction effects among latent variables (Kenny-Judd)
origin: David Kenny and Charles Judd, 1984; Robert Ping, 1993-1996; Kenneth Bollen, 1995-1996 (two-stage least squares); Karl Joreskog, 2000 (latent variable scores)
summary: Tests whether the effect of one latent construct depends on another, or is curved, while keeping measurement error in the model rather than multiplying error-laden scale scores.
description: Multiplying two scale means to test moderation carries both scales' measurement error into the product and weakens the test. SEM approaches keep the constructs latent. In the Kenny-Judd product-indicator approach, products of the indicators of two latent variables become indicators of an interaction factor, with loadings and error variances fixed as functions of the original measurement parameters; Ping's two-step variant takes these values from a prior measurement model. Squares of indicators carry quadratic effects in the same way. Alternatives are a multiple-group model comparing slopes across moderator levels (simple, but it loses power and can create small groups), the product of latent variable scores with bootstrapped standard errors (recommended by Schumacker and Lomax), Bollen's two-stage least squares with instrumental variables, and full maximum likelihood or Bayesian MCMC estimators for nonlinear SEM (latent moderated structural equations), which avoid product indicators but need larger samples.
steps: Make each latent variable unidimensional, centre all indicators at zero, and fit a measurement model recording loadings and error variances.

Choose an approach: product indicators (Kenny-Judd or Ping two-step), latent variable scores, multiple-group comparison of slopes, two-stage least squares, or a full ML or Bayesian nonlinear SEM estimator.
For product indicators, form products of selected indicator pairs (not every pair is needed) and compute their loadings and error variances from the measurement estimates.
Fix these values in a structural model containing the interaction (or quadratic) latent term and estimate it; re-run to check measurement parameters have not shifted.
Compare the main-effects and interaction models with a chi-square difference test and the change in R-squared; use robust or bootstrap standard errors because product terms are non-normal.
Probe a significant interaction by plotting the simple slope of the predictor at low, mean and high values of the moderator.
outputs: Interaction (or quadratic) path coefficient with robust or bootstrapped standard error; fit and R-squared change between main-effects and interaction models; simple-slope plots.
useWhen: A survey model hypothesises that one construct strengthens or weakens another's effect (for example ease of use matters more when perceived risk is high), and both are measured with multi-item scales.
avoidWhen: Constructs are single observed variables (use ordinary moderation analysis); samples are small (under a few hundred), where full-information methods are unstable; the moderator is a genuine grouping variable (use multiple-group SEM directly). ML standard errors and chi-square are unreliable with product indicators.
whyLost: Most UX moderation analysis uses PROCESS-style regression on averaged scales, and latent interaction methods are fiddly to specify and need large samples.
whereToUse: Technology acceptance and trust models for AI features; testing whether perceived risk moderates usefulness in fintech or health adoption; curved relationships such as satisfaction plateauing with feature richness.
example: An AI assistant survey (n = 900) tests whether perceived accuracy matters more to intention to use when perceived stakes are high. A latent moderated SEM finds a positive interaction; simple slopes show accuracy has twice the effect for high-stakes users, which shifts design effort towards visible confidence cues in high-stakes flows.
sources: A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
reference: Kenny, D. A., & Judd, C. M. (1984). Estimating the nonlinear and interactive effects of latent variables. Psychological Bulletin, 96, 201-210.

name: Latin Square and Williams Counterbalancing
origin: Ronald Fisher (1925-1935); Evan Williams (1949) for carryover-balanced designs
summary: Orders conditions in within-subjects studies so each appears equally often in each position, and with Williams designs, follows each other equally often.
description: In within-subject usability studies, order and carryover effects (practice, fatigue, learning) confound condition comparisons. A Latin square assigns condition orders so each condition appears once in each position across a set of participants. A Williams (balanced Latin square) design additionally ensures each condition immediately follows every other equally often, balancing first-order carryover; for an odd number of conditions, two squares are needed. Analysis should include order and participant as factors. Many UX studies 'randomise' with a handful of participants, which leaves imbalance; or they simply fix order. Proper counterbalancing is cheap rigour.
steps: List the conditions (designs, tasks) to be compared within subjects.
Generate a Williams design for the number of conditions (one square for even n, two for odd n).
Recruit participants in multiples of the number of sequences so the design is complete.
Assign participants to sequences at random.
Analyse with mixed models including condition, period and (optionally) carryover terms, with participant as random effect.
Report order effects and check whether any condition shows asymmetric transfer.
outputs: A balanced condition order plan, estimates free of first-order order effects, and period/carryover diagnostics.
useWhen: Within-subjects comparisons of designs or tasks in lab or remote studies.
avoidWhen: Strong asymmetric transfer (e.g. learning a concept that cannot be unlearned); use between-subjects designs.
whyLost: Small UX studies often fix order or use loose randomisation, and the statistical rationale was dropped from practitioner training.
whereToUse: Prototype comparisons, benchmark studies, accessibility comparisons, voice versus touch studies.
example: A study compares four checkout prototypes with 16 participants. Using a Williams design, analysis reveals a strong period effect (later checkouts faster) that would otherwise have favoured the last-presented design.
sources: Williams, Experimental designs balanced for the estimation of residual effects of treatments (1949), Australian Journal of Scientific Research
MacKenzie, Human-Computer Interaction: An Empirical Research Perspective (2013)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 2 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2005)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
reference: Williams, E. J. (1949). Australian Journal of Scientific Research, 2(3), 149-168.

name: Lattice of Value
origin: Alan Dix, c. 2007-2008, building on Jonathan Grudin's critical mass argument
summary: Maps the adoption states of two or more user groups and checks that each adoption step gives the adopting group more perceived value than cost.
description: Many products only work when several kinds of people adopt them: web developers and web users, teachers, parents and children, buyers and sellers. Dix draws a lattice of states, from no group having the product, through one or other group having it, to all having it. The analysis asks, for each transition, whether the adopting group gets perceived present value that exceeds its costs (money, download time, learning effort), with future value discounted. Each group needs value on its own in the early states, the zero-point value, or there is no initial use; the combined state must add value for everyone to drive growth through feedback loops. Where a step fails, guidelines follow: think about the path, increase zero-point value, identify cliques, understand relationships, create community value and leverage existing products.
steps: Identify the groups whose adoption the product depends on.
Lay out the lattice of states from no group having the product to all groups having it.
For each transition, judge whether the adopting group gets perceived present value exceeding its costs, discounting future value.
Where a step fails, raise zero-point value, lower initial cost, target cliques that adopt together, or leverage existing products.
Check that the combined state gives extra value to every group, creating feedback loops for growth.
Validate the value judgements with research on each group before committing to a launch path.
outputs: A lattice diagram of adoption states with value and cost judgements per transition and a preferred adoption path.
useWhen: Launch strategy for multi-sided platforms, collaborative tools and network-effect products where one group's value depends on another's adoption.
avoidWhen: For single-user products with no network dependency. The source is a slide outline, so check Dix's fuller papers; value judgements are assumptions until researched. For quantitative spread modelling use Epidemic Models (SIR/SEIR) for Adoption and Virality.
whyLost: It circulated as talks and short papers and was overshadowed by growth-hacking and two-sided marketplace frameworks from business literature.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, education platforms linking teachers and parents, developer ecosystems, collaboration and messaging tools.
example: A school messaging app maps teacher, parent and pupil adoption; teachers get no value until parents join, so the team adds a standalone class planner (zero-point value) and a parent view that works by SMS without an install.
sources: Designing to be Used: Adoption and Appropriation (Dix, 2008)
reference: Dix, A. (2008). Designing to be used: adoption and appropriation. Invited talk, Berlin, 12 February 2008, Lancaster University.

name: Layered Elaboration
origin: Walsh and colleagues (2010); adapted by Moffatt et al. for TableTalk Poker in Chapter 10
summary: A paper prototyping technique in which participants build and change an interface on stacked transparencies, each layer holding one element, so ideas can be added without destroying earlier ones.
description: Layered elaboration uses sheets of transparency laid over each other so that designs can be built and revised in layers. In the TableTalk Poker project, each layer held one salient interface element: the table, players, cards, prompts or chat. Water-soluble markers and sticky notes let participants move, add and remove buttons, text and screens on the fly. The team made three rough variants, briefed participants on the basics of the game, and then simulated play with sticky notes while participants carried out tasks such as joining a game, raising a bet, checking, calling, folding and chatting, thinking aloud as they went. Researchers watched for gaps in the interaction and noted desired layout changes. Because paper reduced attachment to any one design, participants mixed and matched elements across variants and reached a consensus design heavily shaped by their ideas. The team used younger adults without online gaming experience as proxies, because prototyping with older adults had proved difficult in earlier work, and then moved to iterative usability testing with older adults.
steps: Prepare a few rough design variants split into layers, one element per transparency.
Brief participants on the domain so they understand the tasks.
Ask participants to perform tasks on the layered prototype, simulating system responses with sticky notes, while thinking aloud.
Invite participants to move, redraw, add or remove elements on any layer.
Repeat across variants and discuss as a group to converge on a preferred design.
Photograph each state and carry the consensus design into higher-fidelity prototyping and testing.
outputs: A participant-shaped consensus design, photographed intermediate versions and notes on interaction gaps.
useWhen: Early co-design of screen layouts with non-designers, especially when you want them to build on each other's ideas.
avoidWhen: The design depends on motion, timing or rich interaction that paper cannot represent.
whyLost: Digital prototyping tools have displaced physical paper and transparency methods in most teams.
whereToUse: Game interfaces, apps for novice or older users, children's products, early concept work.
example: Three women new to online gaming rework a poker table interface on transparencies, moving the chat layer and simplifying prompts, and agree a design that combines the table layout of one variant with the prompts of another.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Moffatt, K., Shim, N., Birnholtz, J. and Baecker, R. M. (2016). Testing the usability, usefulness, and user experience of TableTalk Poker, a social game for seniors. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 10. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Layering and Separation
origin: Edward Tufte, 1990
summary: Organises dense information into visually distinct layers through colour, weight and value, so primary content stands forward and supporting context recedes.
description: Layering and separation is Tufte's principle that complex information becomes readable when it is organised into visually distinct strata. Using differences in colour, value, weight and saturation, primary data is placed on the top visual layer while grids, labels and contextual data recede into lighter, quieter layers. Tufte also warns of the '1+1=3' effect: two adjacent strong elements create a third, unintended visual element (the space between them) that adds noise. As a method, the analyst inventories what information a display contains, ranks it by task importance, assigns layers, and checks whether visual weight matches importance. Rigour comes from basing the ranking on task analysis and verifying the result with search or comprehension tasks.
steps: For any complex UX research visualization or interface design: identify information layers (primary data, secondary context, annotation, background structure).
Assign distinct visual properties to each layer: primary data = darkest/most saturated, secondary = lighter, annotation = smallest/most restrained, background = barely visible.
Test: can a viewer correctly identify the layer of any element in < 1 second?
outputs: A layered visual hierarchy specification, reduced visual noise, interface or chart redesigns with distinct primary, secondary and background layers.
useWhen: Dense interfaces and displays: dashboards, maps, clinical and trading screens, data-heavy reports, where everything currently competes for attention.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a purely aesthetic exercise without checking with users which information is primary; for task priority questions, do task analysis first.
whyLost: Visual hierarchy is taught as a design rule of thumb; Tufte's analytic method of designing and evaluating layers, including '1+1=3' effects, is rarely applied.
whereToUse: Dashboard design, complex data visualization, research report design, information architecture visual hierarchy.
example: A trading platform redesigns its order book by pushing gridlines and historical data into light grey and keeping live bids in high-contrast type; traders locate the best bid 30% faster in testing.
reference: Tufte ER (1990) Envisioning Information. Graphics Press

name: Lead User Method
origin: Eric von Hippel, 1986; Urban and von Hippel (1988); Lilien et al. (2002)
summary: Finds users ahead of an important trend who expect high benefit from a solution, and develops the solutions they have already built into concepts and products.
description: Lead users face needs that will become general in a market months or years before most users, and expect high benefit from solving them, so many have already built their own solutions. Von Hippel argues producers should systematically search for and develop lead users' innovations instead of dismissing them as outliers. The standard process has five steps: start the project with an interdisciplinary team, search field and goals; identify needs and trends from reports and experts; identify lead users by screening a sample or by pyramiding (asking experts for referrals to people further ahead, including in analogous markets), or through netnography, contests and toolkits; run a joint concept design workshop with lead users, R&D and marketing; and test concepts with ordinary users. At 3M, lead user projects were forecast to sell over eight times as much as traditional projects.
steps: Form an interdisciplinary team and define the search field, goals and constraints.
Identify important market and technology trends from reports, literature and expert interviews.
Find lead users by screening a sample for lead-user characteristics, or by pyramiding referrals, including people in analogous fields; netnography, contests and toolkits are alternatives.
Collect the solutions and prototypes lead users have already developed.
Run a two- to three-day concept design workshop with lead users, R&D and marketing, agreeing remuneration and IP terms up front.
Test resulting concepts with average users, optionally with conjoint, and evaluate commercial attractiveness.
outputs: Breakthrough product concepts and user-built prototypes with commercial potential, plus a network of lead users.
useWhen: Seeking breakthrough rather than incremental innovation, especially in fast-moving or technical fields where some users already improvise solutions.
avoidWhen: When you need to understand mainstream users' current needs; lead users are atypical by design. Screening is inefficient and relies on self-assessment. For mainstream needs use Contextual Inquiry or Jobs-to-be-Done Research.
whyLost: It is standard in innovation management but UX research focuses on representative or average users and often treats extreme users only as inspiration.
whereToUse: Developer tools, medical devices, maker and creator tools, B2B platforms, AI tooling where power users build workarounds.
example: An AI writing-tool company pyramids from prompt-engineering experts to legal clerks who have scripted their own citation checkers, runs a concept workshop with them, and tests the resulting citation feature with ordinary users.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: von Hippel, E. (1986). Lead users: a source of novel product concepts. Management Science, 32(7), 791-805; Lilien, G. L., Morrison, P. D., Searls, K., Sonnack, M. and von Hippel, E. (2002). Performance assessment of the lead user idea-generation process. Management Science, 48(8), 1042-1059.

name: Lean validated-learning experiments (MVP tests and hypothesis briefs)
aka: Proxy test on an adjacent system
Hypothesis statements and lean market experiments
origin: Eric Ries, The Lean Startup (2011); Steve Blank (2005); term MVP from Frank Robinson (2001)
summary: Write each idea as a falsifiable hypothesis with a metric, list the riskiest assumptions, and test them with the smallest artefact or market experiment before building more.
description: Validated learning treats product ideas as hypotheses. A brief states what the team wants to learn, the hypothesis ('We believe that [solution] for [user] will result in [outcome]; we will know when we see [measurable result]'), how to run it safely, and which measures would invalidate it or stop it. The riskiest assumptions about users, solution and feasibility are listed and the biggest tested with the smallest artefact, which is often not a prototype: an explainer video, landing page, contract MVP (non-binding letters of intent with a preset signature threshold, such as 500), a proxy test on an existing platform, a concierge service, a design comic in interviews, or a deliberately less-than-minimal release to development partners measured by usage. MVPs test business viability, not functional viability. In practice the label 'MVP' often survives without pre-stated thresholds, which removes the rigour.
steps: Frame the opportunity and write each concept as a falsifiable hypothesis with a measurable result; without a metric there is no testable hypothesis.
List the assumptions that would force a rethink if false (users and problems, solution and behaviour, technical risk) and pick the few biggest.
Write a brief: what to learn and why, how to run it, whether it is safe, the threshold that justifies further work, and measures that invalidate it or stop it.
Choose the smallest test: explainer video, landing page, contract MVP with a preset signature count, proxy test on an adjacent system, concierge service, design comic or a limited release.
Run it with real target users (interviews, intercepts, feature toggles to growing groups, or in-product metrics) for days to weeks.
Weigh behaviour over stated opinion; interview selected respondents to understand motivations.
Compare results with the preset threshold and decide to persevere, pivot or drop; roll facts back into the assumption list and design the next test.
outputs: An assumption list, experiment briefs, evidence per hypothesis against preset thresholds, and a persevere, pivot or drop decision.
useWhen: Early product strategy and discovery when market demand and user behaviour are the main risks and building fully would be costly.
avoidWhen: When the risk is technical or regulatory feasibility, or when a low-quality MVP would give a false negative; use technical spikes or prototypes. Fake launches involve mild deception and need ethical care.
whyLost: The vocabulary is ubiquitous, but 'MVP' often means a first release rather than an experiment with a preset invalidation threshold, so the learning discipline is gutted.
whereToUse: Startups, new product lines in established firms, B2B SaaS discovery with design partners, AI product bets.
example: A B2B team believes HR managers will pay for an AI policy assistant. They pitch it openly as not yet built and set a threshold of 20 signed letters of intent from 100 pitches; 9 sign, so they pivot to a narrower compliance use case before writing code.
sources: Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business.

name: Learning Gap Analysis
origin: Julie Dirksen, Design for How People Learn, 2012; Bloom's revised taxonomy; Gery's proficiency levels; chapter by Stacie Rohrbach in Hanington and Martin
summary: Describe the current and preferred states of a task, then classify each gap as knowledge, skill, motivation, environment or communication so the right kind of design response follows.
description: Gap analysis asks why people are not doing what a design expects, and refuses to assume the answer is more instruction. The team frames the current state with questions such as what goes wrong when people cannot do the task and how you would know. It defines the preferred state using Bloom's revised taxonomy for the level of mastery and a proficiency scale for how well people must perform. Each gap between the two is then classified by Dirksen's types: knowledge, skill, motivation, environment or communication. The type points to the response: an environment gap calls for changing the setting, not training; a skill gap needs practice, not information. The classified gaps then brief ideation.
steps: Choose the task or behaviour and ask the current-state questions: what goes wrong, for whom, and how would you know.
Define the preferred state, specifying the Bloom's level and proficiency people need to reach.
List each gap between current and preferred states.
Classify each gap as knowledge, skill, motivation, environment or communication.
Match design responses to gap types (information, practice, incentive, environmental change, clearer messaging).
Use the classified gaps as the brief for ideation.
outputs: A list of gaps by type and an ideation brief matching response types to them.
useWhen: Designing onboarding, training, self-service or behaviour-change features where people are not doing what the product expects.
avoidWhen: It assumes the target task is the right goal and treats gaps as separate when they interact. Diagnose gaps with evidence from Contextual Inquiry, Usability Testing or COM-B and Behaviour Change Wheel Analysis rather than team opinion.
whyLost: Stays in instructional and learning design; UX teams tend to jump to tooltips and tutorials without classifying the gap.
whereToUse: Onboarding, enterprise software adoption, self-service kiosks, health behaviour change, e-learning.
example: A supermarket's self-checkout problem is classified as an environment gap (poor signage and bagging area layout), not a skill gap, so the team redesigns the space rather than adding on-screen tutorials.
reference: Dirksen, J. (2012) Design for How People Learn. Berkeley, CA: New Riders; Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019) Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Beverly, MA: Rockport Publishers, method 57.

name: Least Competent User Recruitment and Best-Case Ringer Check
aka: Least competent users and competence bracketing
origin: Jeffrey Rubin and Dana Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing (2008)
summary: Bracket a small usability-test sample by competence: always include the least skilled plausible users, use an expert insider only as an early go/no-go check.
description: A sampling discipline for small qualitative usability tests. The least competent user (LCU) is the least skilled person who could plausibly use the product, defined on the profile's own scales. Including one or more LCUs in every round, even for expert markets, gives a reading of ease of learning: if they muddle through, most others will; if they fail, the failure points to fundamental problems of intuitiveness, orientation or organisation rather than automatically demanding redesign. Early on, LCUs show mental models not yet shaped by competing products. At the other bracket, a best-case test with an experienced insider (a ringer) acts as a go/no-go gate: if even they struggle, testing stops and design resumes. The rigour lies in controlling who arrives, because recruiters, account managers and sales staff tend to send top performers who work around flaws and make the product test out better than it is.
steps: When writing the user profile and screener, define the least competent user on the profile's own scales (domain, computer and product experience, education).
Recruit at least one LCU into every test round, even when most target users are expert.

Optionally run an early best-case session with an experienced internal ringer; if they fail core tasks, return to design before testing further, and if they pass, follow quickly with less experienced users.
In early exploratory rounds, use LCUs to observe mental models before prior products have shaped them.
Control the recruiting channel so customers, recruiters or sales staff cannot fill the sample with high achievers; cap such 'best' participants at one or two per round and document the trade-off.

Interpret asymmetrically: LCU success suggests most groups will cope, while LCU failure flags fundamental intuitiveness, orientation or instruction problems to investigate rather than an automatic redesign.
outputs: A sample with a known spread of competence, a reading of ease of learning, and an early go/no-go signal from the ringer check.
useWhen: Small formative usability tests where the team needs confidence that novices and marginal users can cope, or an early check that a design is worth testing with real users at all.
avoidWhen: Summative benchmarking that needs a representative sample, where deliberately skewing competence would bias metrics; use stratified recruitment to the real population mix instead. Do not read a single LCU failure as proof that redesign is needed.
whyLost: Recruiting practice drifted towards matching personas and quotas, and convenience panels rarely let teams pick competence deliberately. The ringer idea survives informally as 'dogfooding', without the explicit stop rule.
whereToUse: Enterprise and professional tools sold as 'for experts', B2B pilots where customers choose the participants, government and health services that must work for low-literacy or low-confidence users.
example: A B2B analytics vendor's customer offers its five best analysts for a dashboard test. The researcher accepts two, recruits two LCUs who have only consumed reports, and first runs an internal ringer; the ringer stalls on filter setup, so the round is postponed until the filter model is reworked.
reference: Rubin, J. and Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of Usability Testing (2nd ed.). Indianapolis: Wiley.

name: Leave-one-out cross-validation
origin: Peter Lachenbruch & M. Ray Mickey, 1968; Mervyn Stone, 1974
summary: Estimates how well a model generalises by training on all but one case and testing on the excluded case, repeated for every case.
description: Evaluating a classifier or model on the data used to fit it overstates performance. LOO-CV fits the model n times, each time leaving one observation out and predicting it, then aggregates prediction errors. It uses nearly all data for training each time, which suits small UX datasets such as 50-300 labelled sessions or participants. Its estimates have low bias but can have high variance, and for large datasets 5- or 10-fold cross-validation is more efficient. Rigour requires that all preprocessing and feature selection occur inside each fold to avoid leakage, and that when participants contribute multiple observations, all of a participant's data are left out together (leave-one-subject-out).
steps: Define the performance metric (accuracy, AUC, RMSE) and decide the unit to leave out (observation or participant).
For each unit, fit the full pipeline (scaling, feature selection, model) on the remaining data.
Predict the held-out unit and record the prediction.
Aggregate predictions to compute performance metrics and a confusion matrix.
Compare against a baseline (e.g. majority class or mean prediction) and against k-fold results for stability.
outputs: An approximately unbiased estimate of out-of-sample performance with per-case predictions for error analysis.
useWhen: Small samples where holding out a separate test set would waste data, such as classifier validation on a few hundred labelled sessions.
avoidWhen: Avoid for large datasets (use k-fold), for time-ordered data (use forward-chaining validation) or when observations from the same user would leak across folds.
whyLost: It is standard in statistics and ML but rarely used in UX, where models are seldom built or validated by researchers.
whereToUse: Validating small-sample classifiers of user states, predictive models from usability studies, and PLS or LDA models.
example: With 240 labelled sessions from 60 participants, the team uses leave-one-subject-out validation, which reveals that accuracy falls from 91% (observation-level LOO) to 84% once participant-level leakage is removed.
sources: Pattern Classification (Richard Duda, Peter Hart & David Stork)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Peter Bruce, Andrew Bruce & Peter Gedeck)
Stone (1974) Cross-validatory choice and assessment of statistical predictions
The Inquiry Series, Ch 54 — Linear Discriminant Analysis & Behavioral Classification
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
reference: Stone, M. (1974) Cross-validatory choice and assessment of statistical predictions. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 36(2), 111-147.

name: Legitimacy analysis and access-rights audit
aka: Legitimacy analysis and rights-based socio-technical specification
donor: Political philosophy and law; computer security (access control)
origin: Brian Whitworth with Aldo de Moor (2002-2003) and Adnan Ahmad (2011-2014)
summary: Test each social rule a system enforces in code for fairness to the parties and benefit to the community, by modelling permissions as actor-entity-operation rights against explicit legitimacy principles.
description: Whitworth argues that online, code acts as law, and physical laws do not transfer, keep pace or have jurisdiction, so designers must re-derive what is legitimate for each application, as a jury applies the spirit of a law. Legitimacy is fairness (consequences match contributions) plus public good. The analysis models a social system as entities (personas, groups, agents, items, spaces, rights) and operations (null such as view, use, communication, social), allocates every non-null right to an accountable actor, and works through creation, display, delegation and re-allocation to decide whose consent each act needs. The result is a set of 18 proposed axioms, such as self-ownership of personas, prior mutual consent for communication, creator ownership, transparency of creation conditions and mutual consent for display. The audit form applies them hands-on to live systems: unfriending, banning, deleting posts, withdrawing uploads.
steps: List the social acts the system supports (post, delete, copy, join, ban, view, message, display).
Inventory entities (personas, items, spaces, groups) and, for each role (owner, parent, ancestors, offspring, local public), write rights as actor-entity-operation triplets.
Exercise the live system: create, use, edit and delete a persona and items, and record what can and cannot be changed and what remains.
Test notification and consent: are unfriended, banned or removed people told; are creation conditions visible before creating?
For each act ask whether the coded rule is fair to every party (consequences match contributions) and serves the community.
Check findings against the 18 legitimacy principles and record violations.
Propose rule changes as design requirements and check them for mutual consistency.
outputs: A rights table by role, a list of rules judged legitimate or illegitimate, principle violations, and proposed permission and consent requirements.
useWhen: When designing or reviewing permissions, moderation, sharing and ownership rules in social, collaborative or multi-tenant software.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the 18 axioms as an agreed standard; they are the authors' proposal and opinionated. For legal compliance use privacy and regulatory review; for stakeholder values more broadly use Value-Sensitive Design.
whyLost: It comes from a single research programme and course text; HCI took up privacy and values work but not formal legitimacy analysis of access rights.
whereToUse: Social networks and communities, collaborative documents, moderation tools, shared family accounts, marketplaces, AI agents acting on users' behalf.
example: A team-workspace product audits who can delete a departed member's documents. The analysis shows admins can silently erase contributions; the rule is changed so content is transferred, with notification to collaborators.
reference: Whitworth, B., & de Moor, A. (2002). Legitimate by design: Towards trusted virtual community environments. HICSS 2002; Whitworth, B., & Ahmad, A. (2014). The Social Design of Technical Systems (2nd ed.). Interaction Design Foundation.

name: Levels of Automation Analysis
origin: Thomas Sheridan and William Verplank, 1978; Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens, 2000
summary: Rates automation at each information-processing stage (acquisition, analysis, decision, action) on a 10-point scale to evaluate workload, trust and out-of-the-loop risk.
description: Sheridan and Verplank's ten-level scale runs from the computer offering no assistance to the computer acting entirely autonomously and ignoring the human. Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens added four stages: information acquisition, information analysis, decision selection and action implementation, each of which can be automated to a different level. The analysis profiles a system as a vector of levels and evaluates primary consequences (workload, situation awareness, complacency, skill degradation) and secondary ones (reliability, cost of errors). It gives designers a precise vocabulary instead of 'AI-powered', and predicts known pathologies: high automation at decision stages with imperfect reliability produces automation bias.
steps: Decompose the feature into the four stages: acquisition, analysis, decision, action.
Assign the current and proposed level of automation (1-10) for each stage.
Estimate automation reliability at each stage from model evaluations or logs.
Evaluate human performance consequences: workload, situation awareness, complacency and skill loss; flag high decision automation with reliability below roughly 0.9.
Prototype alternative profiles and test with users using detection of automation errors as a key measure.
Choose the profile that balances efficiency with error detection, and document override and transparency mechanisms.
outputs: An automation profile per feature, predicted risks, and empirical comparison of profiles.
useWhen: Deciding how much an AI feature should suggest, decide or act, and how to expose it.
avoidWhen: Features without automated decision or action components.
whyLost: Known from human factors textbooks, but product teams discuss automation as a binary capability. It is rarely operationalised in AI product reviews.
whereToUse: AI agents, autocomplete and autocorrect, fraud decisions, clinical alerts, autonomous driving interfaces.
example: An expense tool's AI categoriser is set at level 7 for action (executes then informs). Testing shows users catch only 30% of miscategorisations, so it moves to level 5 (executes if the user approves) for amounts above a threshold.
sources: Sheridan & Verplank, Human and computer control of undersea teleoperators (1978), MIT
Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens, A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation (2000), IEEE Transactions on SMC-A
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
User Experience (UX) meets Artificial Intelligence (AI) (Wiberg & Stolterman Bergqvist, 2022)
reference: Parasuraman, R., Sheridan, T. B., & Wickens, C. D. (2000). A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation. IEEE Trans. SMC Part A, 30(3), 286-297.

name: Levels-of-Description Analysis
origin: Adapted for UX from Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), the 'Ant Fugue' dialogue and chapter X (Levels of Description, and Computer Systems)
summary: Describe the same behaviour at several levels, from clicks to tasks to goals to the organisation, and look for patterns that only appear at one level.
description: In the Ant Fugue, Aunt Hillary is an ant colony that holds conversations although no single ant knows anything; the meaning exists only at the level of the whole colony. Hofstadter's point is that a system can be described at several levels, each with its own regularities, and that explanations often fail because they look at the wrong level. UX data is usually analysed at one level: click paths, or tasks, or goals. This method writes up the same set of observations at four or five levels in parallel and compares them. Problems that look like noise at the click level can be obvious at the goal level, such as people repeating a task because their real goal spans several sessions, and organisational patterns can explain individual behaviour that interviews treat as personal preference.
steps: Pick a behaviour to explain and gather the data you have on it: logs, observation, interviews.
Define the levels you will use, for example action (clicks and keystrokes), task, goal, role or team, and organisation or market.
Describe the behaviour at each level separately, using only evidence that belongs to that level.
Note the regularities that appear at each level and check whether they are visible from the levels above and below.
Mark patterns that appear at one level only; these are usually where explanations have been going wrong.
Write the explanation at the level where the pattern lives, and design the intervention for that level.
outputs: A level-by-level description of one behaviour, with the patterns each level reveals and a statement of which level an intervention should target.
useWhen: Quantitative and qualitative findings seem to contradict each other, fixes at the interface level have not changed outcomes, or behaviour emerges from groups rather than individuals.
avoidWhen: Simple usability defects with an obvious local cause, or when you have data at only one level.
whyLost: Levels of description are standard in cognitive science and systems thinking but UX teams split work by data type instead: analysts own clicks, researchers own goals. Nobody owns the comparison across levels.
whereToUse: Collaboration tools, enterprise software, marketplaces, any product where team or market behaviour shapes individual use.
example: Click data shows people abandoning an expense form; at the goal level they are collecting receipts across a week; at the team level, managers approve on Fridays. The fix is a saved-draft weekly report, not a shorter form.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Dialogue ...Ant Fugue, and Chapter X (Levels of Description, and Computer Systems).

name: Leverage Points Analysis (Meadows)
aka: Places to intervene in a system
origin: Donella Meadows, 1997-1999 (Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System)
summary: Ranks possible interventions in a system from weak (parameters, numbers) to strong (feedback structure, rules, goals, paradigms) to find where change is most effective.
description: Meadows listed twelve places to intervene, in increasing order of effectiveness: constants and parameters; buffer sizes; stock-and-flow structure; delays; balancing feedback loops; reinforcing feedback loops; information flows; rules; power to self-organise; goals; paradigms; and the power to transcend paradigms. Most organisational effort goes to the weakest points (tweaking numbers), while the strongest are hardest and most resisted. Applied after mapping a system (e.g. with causal loop diagrams), the list classifies candidate interventions and challenges teams to consider structural ones such as changing information flows (who sees what) or goals (what metric the product optimises).
steps: Map the system with causal loops or stocks and flows, based on research.
List candidate interventions from the team and stakeholders.
Classify each intervention by Meadows' leverage level.
Generate additional interventions at higher leverage levels (information flows, rules, goals).
Assess feasibility, risks and resistance for each.
Prioritise a portfolio including at least one higher-leverage intervention, with monitoring.
outputs: A leverage-classified intervention list, new structural options and a prioritised portfolio.
useWhen: Systemic problems (wellbeing, misinformation, marketplace fairness) where parameter tweaks have failed.
avoidWhen: Contained usability problems with clear local fixes.
whyLost: It is cited in sustainability and systems thinking circles; UX treats it as an inspirational essay rather than an analytic step.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing, platform governance, sustainability features, healthcare services, AI alignment of product goals.
example: A social app tried to reduce compulsive use with time limits (a parameter). Leverage analysis leads to changing information flows (showing users their weekly regret ratings) and the goal metric (from time spent to satisfied sessions).
sources: Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999), Sustainability Institute
Meadows, Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)
Abson et al., Leverage points for sustainability transformation (2017), Ambio
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Meadows, D. H. (1999). Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System. The Sustainability Institute.

name: Lexical decision with semantic priming
aka: Lexical decision task with semantic priming
origin: Meyer and Schvaneveldt, 1971
summary: People decide as fast as possible whether letter strings are words; faster decisions after related words reveal which concepts a preceding cue activates.
description: Letter strings are shown and participants decide as quickly as possible whether each is a word. In the paired version both strings must be words for a 'yes'. Associated pairs (bread-wheat) are accepted faster than unrelated pairs (chair-money), a result explained by spreading activation in semantic memory. The priming effect, the difference in reaction time, is a fine-grained, implicit measure of associative strength that does not depend on people reporting their associations. The task needs non-word foils and speed instructions, and is typically run with dozens of items per condition. Applied versions use a brand, screen or heading as the prime and test which labels or concepts it speeds.
steps: Choose primes (words, brand cues, headings, images) and targets that are related or unrelated, plus pronounceable non-word foils.
Balance targets for length and frequency across conditions.
Present the prime briefly, then the target, and ask for a word or non-word decision as fast as possible.
Run enough trials (for example 30 or more per condition) with randomised order.
Exclude errors and outliers, then compare reaction times for related versus unrelated targets.
Report the priming effect per prime and per participant group.
outputs: Lexical decision reaction times for related versus unrelated targets and a priming effect per cue.
useWhen: Testing whether a brand, context, category heading or prior screen activates intended concepts, or whether labels are semantically linked to their section in users' minds.
avoidWhen: Avoid when explicit association data would suffice; for overall implicit attitudes use the Implicit Association Test.
whyLost: It is a core psycholinguistics tool, but UX relies on explicit labelling studies such as card sorting and tree testing.
whereToUse: Brand and naming research, navigation labelling, content strategy, voice and conversational interfaces.
example: A bank tests whether its new brand cue primes 'secure' and 'modern'. After the logo, 'secure' is recognised 25 ms faster than after a control logo, but 'modern' shows no priming.
sources: Meyer, D. E., & Schvaneveldt, R. W. (1971). Facilitation in recognizing pairs of words. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 90
reference: Meyer, D. E., & Schvaneveldt, R. W. (1971). Facilitation in recognizing pairs of words: Evidence of a dependence between retrieval operations. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 90, 227-234.

name: LICUR and ISOA person-oriented pattern classification
aka: Linking of Clusters after Removal of a Residue
LICUR and ISOA: person-oriented classification of patterns over time
origin: LICUR: Lars Bergman (1988), Bergman, Magnusson and El-Khouri (2003); ISOA: Bergman, Nurmi and von Eye (2012)
summary: Clusters people's multivariate profiles at successive times and tests which movements between profile types occur more or less often than chance.
description: The person-oriented approach treats a person's pattern of scores, not single variables, as the unit of analysis. LICUR first removes a small residue of unclassifiable outliers, clusters profiles separately at each time point, and cross-tabulates cluster membership between adjacent times. Configural frequency analysis then identifies transitions that occur more often than chance (types) and less often (antitypes); the same linking can join profiles from different domains. ISOA instead pools every person-at-a-time profile, classifies them all together into one time-invariant set of typical states, checks that the classification holds at every time, and then studies changes in state frequencies and individual movement between states, displayed as stream charts. Both methods show stable and changing individuals and sequences that never occur, which variable-oriented averages hide.
steps: Choose the profile variables (for example usage, satisfaction and confidence scores) and the time points.
LICUR: remove a residue of cases that fit no cluster (typically a few per cent), then cluster profiles separately at each time point.
LICUR: cross-tabulate cluster membership between adjacent times and test each cell against chance with configural frequency analysis to find types and antitypes.
ISOA: pool all person-occasion profiles, classify them into a single set of typical states, and check that the states are equally well represented at each time.
ISOA: track state frequencies over time and individual transitions, and draw stream (Sankey-style) charts.
Interpret stable individuals, common pathways and sequences that never occur, and relate them to background variables.
outputs: Cluster solutions per time point or a shared state classification, transition tables with types and antitypes, and stream charts of movement.
useWhen: Panel or diary data where the question is how users move between recognisable patterns over time, such as engagement or attitude profiles, rather than how averages change.
avoidWhen: Single-wave data, or when the interest is in average change (use growth curve modelling). LICUR assumes clusters are comparable over short periods; ISOA assumes one classification fits all times, which must be checked. For model-based transitions with uncertainty, use latent transition or hidden Markov models.
whyLost: The person-oriented school is centred in Scandinavian developmental research; UX segmentation has stayed static and variable-oriented.
whereToUse: Customer lifecycle panels, longitudinal UX benchmarks, health-app engagement over months, cohort analyses of feature adoption profiles.
example: A SaaS company clusters 3,000 accounts each quarter on seat use, feature breadth and support contacts. LICUR shows that moving from 'narrow heavy use' to 'broad use' happens far more than chance, while moving from 'light use' directly to 'broad use' is an antitype, so onboarding targets the intermediate step.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: von Eye, A., Bergman, L. R. and Hsieh, C.-A. (2015). Person-oriented methodological approaches. In R. M. Lerner, W. F. Overton and P. C. M. Molenaar (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 1 (pp. 789-842). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Life-History Interviewing
origin: Chicago School, 1920s; Schütze, 1977; Blee & Taylor, 2002
summary: Invites participants to narrate their life or a long-term domain history in their own order, revealing how past experiences shape current behaviour and meaning.
description: Life-history or biographical narrative interviewing asks participants to tell the story of their life, or of their relationship with a domain such as money, illness, or work tools, in their own order and words. The interviewer begins with a single open narrative prompt and avoids interrupting, then follows up on the narrative's own themes and turning points before asking any external questions. Because people organise experience as narrative, this reveals how past events, identities and relationships explain present choices and resistance, which topic-driven interviews miss. Analysis reconstructs timelines, turning points and biographical patterns across participants. Rigour comes from minimal steering during the main narrative, careful transcription and ethical attention to sensitive disclosures.
steps: Life-history interview protocol for technology use:
Start: 'Tell me about the first time you remember using [product or product category].'
Follow the timeline: 'And then what happened with your use of it?'
Probe critical moments: 'When did your relationship with it change significantly?'
Present: 'How does your past experience affect how you use it now?'
Analyze: map critical moments on a timeline; identify what events shifted the relationship; connect to current behavior patterns.
outputs: Narrative transcripts, timelines of turning points, identified biographical patterns and their links to current product use and needs.
useWhen: Understanding long-term relationships with money, health, work or technology, and why people persist with or resist certain tools.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need specific feedback on a design or when time is short; avoid for topics participants find traumatic without proper safeguards.
whyLost: Life-history work lives in sociology and oral history; UX interviews are short and topic-driven, leaving no room for biographical narrative.
whereToUse: Longitudinal product research, migration UX research, professional tool adoption research, any product with a history.
example: A health worker refuses to abandon a paper form; a life-history interview reveals it was a lifeline during a past system outage, explaining her distrust and leading to an offline-first design.
sources: The Science and Art of Interviewing — Kathleen Blee
The Science and Art of Interviewing (Blee)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 32 — Advanced Elicitation — The Archaeology of the Interview
The Science and Art of Interviewing (Kathleen Blee)
The Polish Peasant in Europe and America (Thomas & Znaniecki)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Blee KM & Taylor V (2002) Semi-structured interviewing in social movement research. In Klandermans B & Staggenborg S (Eds.) Methods of Social Movement Research. University of Minnesota Press

name: Likelihood Ratio Tests
origin: Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson (1933); generalised test with Wilks' chi-square approximation (Wilks, 1938)
summary: Compare how well data are explained under a null and an alternative by the ratio of their maximised likelihoods, rejecting the null when the ratio is small.
description: A likelihood ratio test compares the likelihood of the data at parameter values allowed by each hypothesis. For two simple hypotheses the statistic is the likelihood under the null divided by that under the alternative, and the null is rejected below a critical value chosen for the desired Type I error; the Neyman-Pearson lemma shows this is the most powerful test at that level. The critical region is usually rewritten in terms of a simpler statistic with a known distribution; with discrete data exact levels such as 0.05 may be unattainable. For composite hypotheses the generalised test uses the maximum likelihood under the null restriction over the unrestricted maximum, and in large samples minus twice the log ratio is approximately chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restricted parameters. This is the machinery behind comparing nested models, for instance a logistic regression with and without a design factor.
steps: Write the likelihood for the model of the data.
Maximise it under the null restriction and without restriction (or evaluate it at the two simple hypotheses).
Form the ratio of the two maximised likelihoods.

Find the critical value from the exact distribution of an equivalent statistic, or compare minus twice the log ratio with a chi-square distribution whose degrees of freedom equal the number of restricted parameters.
Reject the null when the ratio is small (minus twice the log ratio large) and report the p-value with the effect estimates.
outputs: A test statistic, critical region and p-value; for simple hypotheses, the most powerful test at the chosen level.
useWhen: Testing whether adding a factor (design variant, segment, interaction) improves a nested model such as logistic, Poisson or mixed-effects regression of UX outcomes.
avoidWhen: The chi-square approximation needs reasonably large samples and nested models; for small samples use exact or Permutation Test (Resampling Significance Test) approaches, and for non-nested models use information criteria such as BIC model selection (K=2..10).
whyLost: UX analysts meet it only implicitly inside regression software output, so the logic of comparing nested models is rarely made explicit or reported.
whereToUse: Analysing completion or conversion with logistic regression, testing interaction terms in experiment analysis, choosing among nested survey models.
example: A team models checkout completion by device and new versus old flow. The likelihood ratio test of the model with a device-by-flow interaction against the one without gives chi-square 9.8 on 2 degrees of freedom, so the flow effect differs by device.
sources: Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Neyman, J. and Pearson, E. S. (1933). On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses. Phil. Trans. Royal Society A, 231; Chihara, L. M. and Hesterberg, T. C. (2011). Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R. Wiley, section 8.4.

name: Likert Scale Design
origin: Rensis Likert, 1932
summary: Constructs multi-item summated attitude scales from agreement statements, with item analysis and reliability checks, to measure an attitude more validly than single questions.
description: Likert's original method was not a single agree-disagree question but a procedure for building a scale: write many statements about an attitude object, administer them, keep items that correlate well with the total, and sum responses into a score. Most UX surveys keep the response format and discard the procedure, using single Likert-type items and treating them as interval data. The rigorous approach defines the construct, writes balanced items, pilots them, runs item analysis (item-total correlations, Cronbach's alpha above about 0.7, ideally factor analysis), and analyses summed scales rather than individual items. Response format decisions, such as 5 versus 7 points, labelled anchors and a midpoint, should be deliberate. Single items should be analysed as ordinal, using medians and non-parametric tests or top-box proportions.
steps: Define the construct to measure and write 10-20 candidate statements covering it, mixing positive and negative wording carefully.
Choose a response format (typically 5 or 7 points with fully labelled anchors).
Pilot with 50-100 respondents representative of the target population.
Run item analysis: drop items with item-total correlations below about 0.3 and check Cronbach's alpha of 0.7 or above.
Check dimensionality with exploratory factor analysis if the construct may have facets.
Field the final scale and analyse summed scores; analyse single items as ordinal data.
outputs: Validated multi-item attitude scale, reliability statistics, scoring instructions, scale scores for respondents.
useWhen: Measuring attitudes and perceptions such as trust, satisfaction or perceived value where no validated scale exists.
avoidWhen: When a validated instrument already exists (SUS, UEQ, UMUX-Lite), or when you need behaviour rather than attitudes; use analytics or observation.
whyLost: The response format survived and became ubiquitous, but the scale-construction procedure (item analysis, summation, reliability) was largely dropped, leaving single items analysed as if they were interval measures.
whereToUse: Any attitudinal survey; satisfaction measurement; scale construction.
example: An AI writing assistant team needed to measure trust. They drafted 16 items, piloted with 120 users, removed 6 weak items and achieved alpha of 0.88 on a two-factor scale that then tracked trust across model releases.
sources: A technique for the measurement of attitudes (Rensis Likert)
Scale Development: Theory and Applications (Robert DeVellis)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: Likert, R. (1932). A technique for the measurement of attitudes. Archives of Psychology, 22(140), 1-55.

name: LIME for local explanation
origin: Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh & Carlos Guestrin, 2016
summary: Explains an individual AI prediction by fitting a simple interpretable model to the black-box model's behaviour around that specific case.
description: LIME perturbs the input around a case of interest, records how the model's predictions change, and fits a sparse linear model weighted by proximity, yielding the features that most influenced that prediction locally. It is model-agnostic and works for tabular data, text (which words drove a classification) and images. For UX research, LIME helps audit specific decisions users complain about and prototype explanation content. Its limits are well documented: explanations can be unstable across runs, depend on perturbation and kernel width choices, and can be manipulated. Rigour requires repeated runs to check stability, comparison with SHAP, and validation that explanations help real users.
steps: Select cases to explain, prioritising complaints, edge cases and high-stakes decisions.
Configure LIME with an appropriate perturbation strategy and kernel width for the data type.
Generate explanations limited to 5-10 features for readability.
Rerun each explanation 10 or more times with different seeds and check that the top features are stable.
Compare with SHAP attributions and flag disagreements.
Use stable explanations to audit decisions and draft user-facing explanation prototypes for testing.
outputs: Local explanations for selected predictions, stability assessments and candidate explanation content for users.
useWhen: Investigating specific AI decisions, especially for text classifiers or opaque models, and prototyping case-level explanations.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on single LIME runs, using it for global model understanding (use SHAP or global surrogates), or presenting it as ground truth to regulators.
whyLost: LIME is well known in ML research and responsible AI, but stays with data scientists rather than UX researchers.
whereToUse: Content moderation decisions, loan or investment recommendations, support ticket routing, AI-driven health triage.
example: Users complain that an investment app labelled their portfolio 'aggressive'. LIME on 20 such cases repeatedly highlights a single crypto holding as the driver, prompting both a model review and clearer explanation copy.
sources: Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin (2016) Why should I trust you? Explaining the predictions of any classifier
The Inquiry Series, Ch 58 — AI Explainability & Value Alignment Audit
reference: Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S. & Guestrin, C. (2016) 'Why should I trust you?': Explaining the predictions of any classifier. KDD '16, 1135-1144.

name: Lincoln and Guba Trustworthiness Criteria
origin: Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba, 1985 (Naturalistic Inquiry)
summary: Replaces positivist validity and reliability with credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability, each secured by specific techniques such as member checking and audit trails.
description: Lincoln and Guba argued that qualitative research should not be judged by quantitative criteria but has its own parallel standards. Credibility (parallel to internal validity) is supported by prolonged engagement, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative case analysis and member checking. Transferability (external validity) is supported by thick description that lets readers judge applicability to their context. Dependability (reliability) and confirmability (objectivity) are supported by an audit trail documenting raw data, analytic decisions and reflexive notes, which an external auditor could follow. The framework turns 'qualitative is subjective' into a set of checkable practices. Its rigour comes from planning these techniques into the design rather than asserting trustworthiness afterwards.
steps: Plan trustworthiness techniques at the design stage, mapping each of the four criteria to at least one concrete technique and recording the plan in the research protocol.
Secure credibility through triangulation of sources or methods, peer debriefing with a researcher outside the project, and member checking of key interpretations with a subset of participants.
Search actively for negative cases and revise interpretations until they account for disconfirming evidence or the exceptions are explicitly explained.
Write thick description of participants, setting and context so readers can judge transferability to their own product or population.
Maintain an audit trail of raw data, codebooks, memos, decision logs and reflexive notes throughout the study, not reconstructed afterwards.
Report which techniques were used for each criterion, what they changed, and remaining limitations, in a dedicated methods or trustworthiness section.
outputs: A trustworthiness plan, triangulation and member-checking records, negative case notes, thick description, an audit trail, and a trustworthiness section in the report.
