Data come from video of viewers in the lab or fixed cameras at home, coded frame by frame. Visual orientation is not comprehension, and home studies predate multi-screen use, so modern applications must code phones and second screens too.
steps: Record viewers with a camera facing them, in the lab or, with consent, a fixed camera at home.
Code the frame at which each look at the screen starts and ends, with a second coder on a sample for reliability.
Compute the look-length distribution and the hazard function: the probability a look ends in each interval given it has lasted so far.
Optionally present timed distractors or a secondary reaction-time probe at different look durations.
Relate look positions to content events such as cuts, segment boundaries or ads.
Test later recognition of content snippets to link look depth to retention.
outputs: Look counts, look-length distributions, hazard functions, distractor effectiveness by look duration, and links between look depth and recall.
useWhen: You need to understand how engagement builds and breaks over time with screen content, especially in multi-tasking or living-room settings, or with children who cannot self-report.
avoidWhen: You need to know where on screen people look or whether they understood; use eye tracking or comprehension tests instead.
whyLost: It comes from television research in developmental psychology; digital products measure engagement through logs and dwell time without hazard modelling.
whereToUse: Streaming and TV interfaces, autoplay and ad breaks, children's media, second-screen experiences and in-car displays.
example: A streaming service records families watching at home and codes looks at the TV versus phones. Hazard analysis shows looks under three seconds rarely survive the autoplay countdown, so the countdown is lengthened for kids' profiles.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Anderson, D. R., & Kirkorian, H. L. (2015). Media and cognitive development. In L. S. Liben & U. Müller (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 2, pp. 949-994. Wiley.

name: Looking-time paradigms (preferential looking, habituation, violation of expectation)
aka: Looking-time paradigms: preferential looking and habituation with novelty-preference test
origin: Robert Fantz, 1956-1961; infant-controlled habituation, Cohen, 1976; violation of expectation, Baillargeon and Spelke, 1980s
summary: Infer discrimination, memory and expectation in people who cannot report by measuring how long they look, as looking falls to familiar displays and rises to new or surprising ones.
description: In Fantz's preferential-looking method, two displays are shown side by side and an observer records which is looked at more. In habituation, one display repeats until looking falls below a criterion, then a novel and the familiar display are shown; longer looking at the novel item shows discrimination, and varying the delay measures memory. Violation-of-expectation designs pair an expected and an unexpected event; longer looking at the unexpected one suggests an expectation was broken. Feature occlusion and hybrid stimuli reveal which features drive recognition, and eye tracking shows which parts were scanned. Interpretation is contested (familiarity versus novelty preference), so rigorous studies use blind coding, counterbalancing, test-trials-only checks and converging action measures.
steps: Choose stimuli that differ only in the property of interest.
Familiarisation: present one stimulus repeatedly and record looking per trial, by blind observer or eye tracker.
Stop when looking falls below a set fraction of the first trials (infant-controlled criterion) or after a fixed time.
Test: present novel and familiar stimuli, or expected and unexpected events, counterbalancing side and order.
Compare looking times; vary the familiarisation-test delay to measure memory, or occlude features to find which drives the effect.
Add converging checks: a test-trials-only group or an action measure such as anticipatory looking.
outputs: Novelty-preference scores, habituation rates and looking-time differences by condition, with gaze maps if recorded.
useWhen: Studying perception and expectation in users who cannot give verbal reports (infants, young children, some disabled users) or measuring implicit surprise at interface behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid strong conclusions from looking time alone, since its meaning is debated; with verbal adults use direct report or eye tracking with tasks.
whyLost: It is the workhorse of infant research but has had little uptake in UX, which rarely designs for pre-verbal users and uses eye tracking with tasks instead.
whereToUse: Products for babies and toddlers, children's media and toys, accessibility research, character and icon recognition.
example: A children's app tests which part of a character drives recognition by occluding the head or body after familiarisation; toddlers look longer at a new character only when heads differ, so the design keeps head shapes distinct.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
Fantz, R. L. (1961). The origin of form perception. Scientific American, 204
Baillargeon, R., Spelke, E. S., & Wasserman, S. (1985). Object permanence in five-month-old infants. Cognition, 20
reference: Fantz, R. L. (1961). The origin of form perception. Scientific American, 204(5), 66-72.

name: Lorenz Curve and Gini Coefficient for Engagement Concentration
origin: Max Lorenz (1905); Corrado Gini (1912); Herfindahl-Hirschman index (1945/1950)
summary: Plots and quantifies how unequally activity, value or exposure is distributed across users, creators or items.
description: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of a quantity (sessions, revenue, views) against the cumulative share of units ranked from smallest to largest; the Gini coefficient is twice the area between the curve and the line of equality, from 0 (perfect equality) to 1. Concentration measures such as the Herfindahl index complement it. For products, these measures reveal dependence on a few power users, inequality of exposure among creators or sellers, and fairness of recommendation systems. Tracking Gini over time shows whether changes broaden or concentrate engagement, which raw averages hide.
steps: Choose the quantity and units (e.g. views per creator, sessions per user, revenue per account).
Sort units by the quantity and compute cumulative shares.
Plot the Lorenz curve and compute the Gini coefficient with bootstrap confidence intervals.
Compute complementary measures (top 1% share, Herfindahl index, Palma ratio).
Compare across segments, time or experiment arms.
Interpret implications for risk (dependence on few users), fairness and design.
outputs: Lorenz curves, Gini coefficients and concentration metrics with trends and comparisons.
useWhen: Assessing concentration of engagement, revenue or exposure, and the fairness effects of algorithms or features.
avoidWhen: When the distribution shape is irrelevant to the decision.
whyLost: Product dashboards focus on totals and averages; inequality measures are seen as economics, not UX.
whereToUse: Creator platforms, marketplaces, recommendation systems, community participation, B2B account usage.
example: A marketplace's new ranking algorithm raises total sales 3% but increases the Gini of seller sales from 0.71 to 0.79, prompting a fairness review and an exposure floor for new sellers.
sources: Lorenz, Methods of measuring the concentration of wealth (1905), Publications of the American Statistical Association
reference: Cowell, F. A. (2011). Measuring Inequality (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.

name: LOSA and Threat and Error Management (TEM)
origin: Robert Helmreich and the University of Texas Human Factors Research Project with Continental Airlines, 1990s; ICAO Doc 9803 (2002)
summary: Trained observers record threats, errors and undesired states during normal operations under strict non-jeopardy conditions, then analyse how they were managed.
description: LOSA observes routine work, not incidents. Peer observers ride along on normal flights and code, with a standard form, the threats (external complications such as weather or ATC), errors made by the crew, whether each was detected and managed, and any undesired aircraft states that followed. Data are confidential and de-identified, which is what makes honest observation possible. The TEM framework then reveals which threats are most frequent, which errors go unmanaged and which countermeasures work. For UX this is an exceptional model for observing expert users of complex tools in their real work: it counts errors that never become incidents, measures recovery, and reveals the gap between procedures and practice.
steps: Agree with the organisation the ten LOSA operating characteristics, especially anonymity, voluntary participation and non-jeopardy.
Train observers who know the domain to use a TEM coding form for threats, errors, undesired states and their management.
Observe a representative sample of normal work sessions (aviation LOSAs typically use 50-100+ observations).
Code each threat and error with type, who detected it, response (managed, mismanaged, unmanaged) and outcome.
Aggregate to find prevalence and mismanagement rates, and identify the threats and interface features most associated with unmanaged errors.
Feed back findings to frontline users and designers, and repeat the audit after changes to measure improvement.
outputs: TEM database, prevalence and management rates for threats and errors, priority targets for design and training.
useWhen: Expert professional users operate complex software in high-stakes settings and you need to see everyday errors and recoveries, not just incidents.
avoidWhen: Consumer products with short sessions, or settings where anonymity cannot be guaranteed; use session replay analysis or diary studies.
whyLost: It requires organisational trust and trained domain observers, and its output is safety data rather than product features. UX field research rarely codes errors systematically.
whereToUse: Air traffic tools, clinical teams using EHRs, security operations centres, financial trading desks, network operations.
example: A security operations team allows 60 anonymised shift observations of analysts using a SIEM. TEM coding shows alert-triage errors are usually caught but alert-suppression errors go unmanaged 40% of the time, prompting a redesign of suppression rules UI.
sources: ICAO, Line Operations Safety Audit (LOSA), Doc 9803 (2002)
Helmreich, Klinect & Wilhelm, Models of threat, error and CRM in flight operations (1999)
reference: ICAO (2002). Line Operations Safety Audit (LOSA), Doc 9803.

name: Loss aversion measurement
origin: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) and cumulative prospect theory (Tversky and Kahneman, 1992), which estimated a median loss aversion coefficient of about 2.25
summary: Estimates how much more heavily users weigh losses than equivalent gains in a product context, yielding a loss aversion coefficient to guide framing and change design.
description: Prospect theory proposes that outcomes are evaluated as gains or losses from a reference point, with losses weighted more heavily; Tversky and Kahneman estimated the coefficient lambda at about 2.25. Later work shows lambda varies by domain, stakes and person, and some studies find much smaller effects for routine amounts. Loss aversion measurement estimates lambda for your users and domain, typically through mixed gambles (accept or reject a 50/50 chance to win X or lose Y) or through paired gain and loss framings of product changes (losing a feature versus gaining it). The coefficient tells you how much benefit a change must deliver to offset what users lose, which is central to migrations, price changes and feature removals. Rigour requires incentive-compatible or realistic stakes and enough trials per person for stable estimates.
steps: Choose the domain of interest (money, time, features, status) and define the reference point users hold, for example their current plan or their current workflow.

Build a mixed-gamble task with 20 to 50 trials varying gain and loss amounts (for example gains of 10 to 40 against losses of 5 to 20 units), or a set of paired product scenarios framed as equivalent gains and losses.
Run the task with at least 50 to 100 participants from the target population, using real or realistic stakes where ethically feasible.
Estimate lambda per participant by fitting the acceptance threshold (the gain-to-loss ratio at which acceptance reaches 50%) or with a logistic choice model, and summarise the median and spread.
Translate lambda into design thresholds: a change that removes value worth L must provide perceived gains of roughly lambda times L to be accepted.
Validate predictions against real behaviour, such as uptake of a migration or churn after a feature change, and update estimates.
outputs: Distribution of loss aversion coefficients for your users and domain, segment differences, and quantitative thresholds for framing and compensating changes.
useWhen: Planning migrations, feature removals, price or plan changes, or framing decisions where users must give something up to gain something.
avoidWhen: You only need to choose between two framings of a message; an A/B test of the framings is quicker. Avoid when stakes cannot be made realistic, since hypothetical gambles may overstate or understate lambda.
whyLost: Loss aversion is cited constantly in UX but almost never measured: designers apply the textbook 2 to 1 ratio as a slogan rather than estimating it for their users and stakes.
whereToUse: Product migrations and redesigns, subscription pricing changes, savings and investment framing, health insurance plan changes, deprecating legacy features.
example: Before retiring a paper-like batch entry mode, a team measured lambda for time saved versus time lost among clinic staff and found a median of 2.8. The new mode saved 40 seconds per record but cost 20 seconds in a rare case, so they removed that loss rather than relying on net benefit.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1992). Advances in prospect theory: Cumulative representation of uncertainty. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 5(4), 297–323; Gächter, S., Johnson, E. J., & Herrmann, A. (2022). Individual-level loss aversion in riskless and risky choices. Theory and Decision, 92, 599–624.

name: Lostness metric
origin: Smith (1996), Interacting with Computers
summary: A navigation score from 0 upwards combining revisits and unnecessary pages, computed from distinct pages visited, total visits and the minimum pages needed for a task.
description: For each participant and task, count N, the number of different pages visited; S, the total pages visited including revisits; and R, the minimum number of pages needed. Lostness L = sqrt[(N/S - 1)^2 + (R/N - 1)^2]. The first term grows with revisits, the second with visits to pages that were not needed; a perfect path scores 0. Smith observed that participants scoring under 0.4 showed no signs of being lost, while those above 0.5 clearly appeared lost. The metric is useful in navigation and information architecture studies alongside task success, because it captures how efficiently people found their way and not just whether they arrived. It needs a known optimal path and logged page sequences from task-based sessions.
steps: Define each task's optimal path and set R, the minimum number of pages needed.
Run task-based sessions and log every page visit per participant per task, using a tool, logger or video.
Count N (distinct pages) and S (total visits including revisits).
Compute L = sqrt[(N/S - 1)^2 + (R/N - 1)^2] for each participant and task.
Classify scores below 0.4 as not lost and above 0.5 as lost; report mean L and the share lost per task or design.
Compare designs or re-measure after changes, alongside task success and time.
outputs: A lostness score per participant and task, task averages, and the share of participants classed as lost.
useWhen: Evaluating navigation or information architecture in task-based tests where the optimal path is known and you need an efficiency measure beyond success.
avoidWhen: Avoid computing it from analytics logs where intent and optimal path are unknown; it becomes meaningless. Pair it with task success because it ignores time and outcome; thresholds come from one original study.
whyLost: It appears in UX metrics books but is rarely used, because analytics teams lack task intent and usability teams seldom log full page paths.
whereToUse: Website and intranet navigation tests, help centres, documentation sites, e-commerce category structures and multi-screen app flows.
example: In a help-centre test, a participant visits 8 pages, 6 of them distinct, on a task needing 3, giving L = 0.56. Half the participants exceed 0.5 on the billing task, pointing to a misleading category label.
reference: Smith, P. A. (1996). Towards a practical measure of hypertext usability. Interacting with Computers 8(4), 365-381.

name: Love and Breakup Letters
origin: Smart Design, devised 2009; breakup letters piloted with conference attendees in 2010
summary: Participants write a short personal letter to a product or brand, declaring love or ending the relationship, then read it aloud, revealing drivers of loyalty and abandonment.
description: A projective writing exercise in which the product is personified as a partner. Asking people directly what they love or hate tends to return surface answers shaped by what they think the researcher wants; addressing a letter to the product brings back salient emotional moments. Love letters reveal what creates delight and loyalty so strengths can be extended; breakup letters reveal when and why the relationship soured and what replaced the product. Each participant writes only one kind of letter so they can immerse in one emotion. Sessions of five to ten people run like a focus group: about ten minutes of silent writing, reading aloud, then discussion, which lets the researcher note tone and body language. It works best aimed at a whole product, brand or broad experience rather than a single feature, and also serves as a workshop icebreaker.
steps: Decide the subject (a whole product, brand or experience) and the letter type: all love, all breakup, half and half, or participant's choice, never both from one person.
Recruit five to ten participants per session, in person with paper or laptops, or remotely with a private shared document each.
Give instructions and an example letter about an unrelated product so the tone is clear without seeding content.
Allow about ten minutes of silent writing.
Ask each participant to read their letter aloud, recording it on video and noting emotion, tone and body language.
Let participants discuss each other's letters, noting agreement and argument, and ask follow-up questions.
Collect all letters and thematically analyse letters and notes for two or three common themes, feeding problem trees or problem statements.
outputs: Handwritten or typed letters, video of readings, notes on delivery and discussion, and themes of attachment and abandonment.
useWhen: You need to understand why people stay loyal to or leave a product or brand, or want an emotionally rich opener for a workshop or group interview.
avoidWhen: You need feature-level diagnosis or behavioural evidence; use usability testing, churn analysis or switch interviews instead. Readings can become performative in groups, and personal disclosure needs care.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, memorable and well documented in popular methods books, and it produces quotable artefacts for stakeholders.
whereToUse: Churn and retention research, brand perception, subscription products, internal tools being replaced, and workshop warm-ups.
example: A fitness app team runs three sessions of breakup letters with lapsed subscribers. Several letters blame guilt-inducing reminders, which leads to a redesign of notification tone and frequency.
sources: UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
reference: Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Rockport Publishers, Method 72.

name: Low-Fidelity Motion Prototyping
origin: Sarah Drasner (2017), crediting Yaroslav Zubko for GIF prototypes of basic UI shapes; Kathryn McElroy (2016)
summary: Build a quick moving version of a proposed animation, using simple shapes or a static screenshot with only moving parts animated, to iterate timing and win buy-in.
description: Motion is hard to judge from static mock-ups, and building a whole interface to try an animation is wasteful. Drasner describes two quick routes. In the first, simple shapes stand in for interface elements and are animated until the motion feels right. In the second, a screenshot or flattened mock-up is set as a background and only the elements that move are positioned on top, which is fast yet looks close to final and suits stakeholder meetings. McElroy adds animation storyboards and presentation-tool transitions such as Keynote Magic Move. Tools include Principle, Framer, After Effects, Keynote or plain code; Drasner prefers code because an approved prototype can be cleaned up and reused. Timing and easing will be redone many times, so the team must be willing to discard favourites and choose tools that make re-timing cheap.
steps: Storyboard the key states and transitions of the proposed animation.
Choose a route: abstract shapes standing in for UI elements, or a flattened screenshot with only moving elements positioned on top.
Build the motion in a prototyping tool, presentation software or code.
Iterate timing and easing many times, discarding versions that do not work.
Show the prototype to the team or stakeholders and gather reactions.
If approved, clean up and reuse the code or hand over timing values to engineering.
outputs: A moving prototype (GIF, tool file or code) with agreed timing and easing values.
useWhen: Use it when a transition, micro-interaction or animated explanation must be judged and agreed before engineering builds it.
avoidWhen: It shows how motion looks, not whether it helps users; test comprehension and distraction with Usability Testing or the 5-Second Test. Prototyping tools take time to learn, and CSS makes re-timing painful once several animations share an element.
whyLost: It survives because motion design became a standard part of interface work and modern tools make quick animated prototypes cheap.
whereToUse: Onboarding animations, loading and state transitions, data visualisation transitions, marketing sites and mobile micro-interactions.
example: A travel app overlays an animated card on a screenshot of its search results to test how a fare alert slides in. Three timing variants are shown to the team, and the chosen easing curve is handed to engineers as values.
reference: Drasner, S. (2017). SVG Animations: From Common UX Implementations to Complex Responsive Animation. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 208-210. McElroy, K. (2016). Prototyping for Designers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 114-118, 264-265.

name: M-Mode / I-Mode Observation
origin: Adapted for UX from the MU-puzzle in Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), chapter I
summary: Code each moment of a session by whether the person is applying rules mechanically or stepping back to reason about the system, and study what makes them switch.
description: In the MU-puzzle Hofstadter separates working inside a system, applying its rules step by step (the Mechanical mode), from thinking about the system, noticing patterns and asking whether the goal is reachable at all (the Intelligent mode). People using software move between the same two modes. Most of the time they follow learned steps without thought; when something unexpected happens they shift to reasoning about how the product works. Those shifts are expensive and revealing: they mark where the interface stopped carrying people and where their understanding gets tested. This method adds a mode code to ordinary usability or field observation. Every segment is coded M (following steps, little hesitation, no talk about the system) or I (pausing, theorising aloud, trying something to see what happens), and the analysis focuses on the triggers for each switch into I-mode and on whether people come back to M-mode with a correct theory or a wrong one.
steps: Run normal think-aloud sessions or field observation, recorded so moments can be timestamped.
Agree on markers for each mode before coding, such as hesitation over 3 seconds, statements about how the system works, or exploratory clicks for I-mode.
Code the timeline of each session into M and I segments; have two people code a sample and resolve differences.
List every switch from M to I with what happened just before it.
Group the triggers (unexpected state, missing feedback, broken pattern, error message) and note the theory each person formed.
Prioritise triggers that are frequent, long-lasting or lead to wrong theories.
outputs: A timeline of mechanical and reasoning modes per participant, a ranked list of triggers that knock people out of routine use, and the theories they form at each.
useWhen: Studying routine or expert use where people rarely voice problems, comparing learnability between versions, or finding where automation surprises users.
avoidWhen: First-time exploratory use, where nearly everything is reasoning, or very short tasks with too few segments to code.
whyLost: Usability coding counts errors and task time but rarely codes the kind of thinking people are doing. Hofstadter's distinction was framed as a lesson about formal systems, so it never reached evaluation practice.
whereToUse: Expert tools, operations consoles, form-heavy workflows, automation and AI features that sometimes act on their own.
example: In an invoicing tool, accountants stay in M-mode until the tax total changes after they edit a date. Every participant switches to I-mode there, and half leave with the wrong theory that the date sets the tax rate, which explains a run of support tickets.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Chapter I (The MU-puzzle).

name: Magic Thing Role-Play
origin: Giulio Iacucci, Carlo Iacucci and Kari Kuutti, 2002
summary: A designer shadows participants through daily life carrying an open-ended mock-up, the 'magic thing', and together they invent and act out future use scenarios in situ.
description: The magic thing is a deliberately simple, unrestricted mock-up of a future device, for example a block of wood or foam. Because it does nothing in particular, participants are free to imagine it doing anything. A designer follows participants as they go about their ordinary activities; when an interesting situation arises, designer and participant improvise what the magic thing could do there and act it out. The method combines shadowing with performance, so ideas are generated in the real context, with its interruptions, objects and social constraints, rather than in a meeting room. It is a close relative of bodystorming and experience prototyping but places the participant, not the designer, at the centre of the enactment.
steps: Make a simple, open-ended mock-up with no fixed functions (the magic thing).
Brief participants that the object can do whatever they need it to do.
Shadow each participant through a normal day or work shift in their own setting.
When an interesting situation arises, pause and invite the participant to show what the magic thing would do; act out the scenario together.
Record enactments with photos, video or notes, including the situation that triggered them.
Collate enacted scenarios into candidate services and product features for later prototyping.
outputs: Enacted, context-anchored future use scenarios and envisioned services and features.
useWhen: Early concept generation for mobile or ubiquitous technology where context of use shapes what is useful.
avoidWhen: When participants are uncomfortable performing, when shadowing is intrusive or unsafe, or when you need evaluation of a defined concept (use Experience Prototyping or Prototype Testing).
whyLost: It was a research technique of the early 2000s mobile era; ideas from it were absorbed into bodystorming and experience prototyping, and the name faded.
whereToUse: Wearables, field-worker tools, smart home and AR concepts, healthcare at point of care.
example: A designer follows a home-care nurse with a foam block; at a locked medicine cabinet the nurse acts out the block 'showing' the patient's latest dosage change, which becomes a concept for a proximity-triggered care note.
reference: Iacucci, G., Iacucci, C. and Kuutti, K. (2002). Imagining and experiencing in design, the role of performances. Proc. NordiCHI '02, 167-176.

name: Magnitude Estimation and Stevens' Power Law
origin: S. S. Stevens, 1950s (On the psychophysical law, 1957; Psychophysics, 1975)
summary: Participants assign numbers proportional to perceived magnitude, yielding ratio-scale data and power-law exponents that describe how perception scales with the stimulus.
description: In magnitude estimation, participants see a reference stimulus (modulus) and assign numbers to others in proportion: twice as intense gets twice the number. Geometric means across participants, plotted against stimulus intensity on log-log axes, typically give a straight line whose slope is the power-law exponent (psi = k x phi^n). Exponents differ by dimension: perceived brightness is compressive (about 0.33), electric shock expansive (about 3.5). Magnitude estimation was used in early HCI and usability research (McGee, 2003, applied it to usability judgements), offering ratio-level measurement of subjective experience that Likert scales cannot provide.
steps: Select stimuli spanning the range of interest (e.g. 6-10 levels of load time or visual clutter).
Present a modulus stimulus with an assigned or free number, then present test stimuli in random order with repeats.
Instruct participants to assign numbers proportional to perceived magnitude, allowing any positive number.
Normalise each participant's responses and compute geometric means per stimulus.
Fit a power function by linear regression on log-log values and report the exponent with confidence intervals.
Use the exponent to predict perceived improvement from physical changes, or compare designs on ratio-scale judgements.
outputs: Ratio-scale perception data and power-law exponents per dimension or design.
useWhen: You need ratio-level comparisons of perceived quantities, such as 'how much slower does it feel?' or 'how much more cluttered?'.
avoidWhen: Participants who struggle with numerical judgement, or when only rank order matters; use paired comparisons.
whyLost: Likert scales became the default, and ratio scaling was seen as cumbersome. McGee's usability magnitude estimation never caught on.
whereToUse: Perceived performance budgets, visual density, sound loudness in notifications, perceived price fairness.
example: A web team measures perceived slowness for load times from 0.5 to 8 seconds. The exponent of 0.6 shows halving a 4-second load feels like a 34% improvement, not 50%, setting realistic expectations.
sources: Stevens, Psychophysics: Introduction to Its Perceptual, Neural, and Social Prospects (1975)
Stevens, On the psychophysical law (1957), Psychological Review
McGee, Usability magnitude estimation (2003), Proceedings of HFES
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
reference: Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153-181.

name: Making and Testing Predictions (Two-Envelope Informant Feedback)
aka: Prediction testing of a case analysis
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1984; expanded 1994
summary: Validate a qualitative case analysis by writing explicit predictions with supporting and spoiling factors, then months later asking informants what happened before showing them the prediction.
description: A prospective test of a qualitative explanation. From the causal network and matrices, the analyst writes one precise prediction per main outcome (usually four or five) with up to five weighted supporting factors and five possible spoilers. After 6 to 12 months the prediction is sent to at least two informants in different roles in two envelopes. Envelope one asks them to describe the current situation and rank its causes without seeing the prediction; envelope two then shows the prediction and asks them to rate each factor's pertinence. Comparing predicted and actual outcomes, and the overlap of reasons, tests the analysis while keeping informants blind to the analyst's reasoning. Having a second analyst generate predictions from the case report also tests how explicit it is. In the original school study 58% of assigned causes fully agreed with informants. Allow one to two days per complex case.
steps: For each main outcome, write one precise prediction derived from the causal streams and related matrices.
List and weight up to about five supporting factors and five possible spoilers.
Review any possible harm to informants from the predictions.
After 6-12 months send envelope one to at least two informants in different roles: describe the current situation and rank the contributing factors.
Then send envelope two: the prediction with a pertinence rating table for each factor.
Compare predicted and actual outcomes and the overlap of reasons, and follow up discrepancies by phone.
Optionally have a second analyst make predictions from the case report to test its explicitness.
outputs: Prediction accuracy ratings per outcome and agreement figures on causes, plus documented reasons for misses.
useWhen: Longitudinal qualitative or case-study work where a causal explanation will inform decisions and you can return to the same informants months later.
avoidWhen: One-off studies without access to informants later, or settings where unforeseeable events dominate outcomes. It relies on self-report unless you revisit; pay informants for their reading time.
whyLost: UX research rarely revisits explanations after delivery, and most validation stops at member checking of findings rather than prospective prediction.
whereToUse: Enterprise adoption studies, service redesign pilots, and any case where a team has claimed why a rollout will succeed or fail.
example: After studying a CRM rollout at three sales offices, a researcher predicts that office B will abandon the mobile app within nine months, citing manager indifference and weighing a possible spoiler. Nine months later two informants independently describe partial abandonment and rank manager indifference first.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Manifold learning
origin: Isomap by Tenenbaum, de Silva & Langford, 2000; LLE by Roweis & Saul, 2000
summary: A family of methods that assume high-dimensional user data lies on a lower-dimensional curved surface and recover its intrinsic coordinates.
description: Manifold learning starts from the idea that although users are described by hundreds of variables, real behaviour varies along a few underlying degrees of freedom, such as engagement and sophistication, arranged on a curved manifold. Methods such as Isomap (geodesic distances), locally linear embedding, Laplacian eigenmaps, diffusion maps, t-SNE and UMAP attempt to unfold it. For UX, the payoff is identifying the intrinsic dimensionality of behaviour and continuous trajectories, such as how users progress from novice to expert, rather than forcing discrete segments. Rigour involves estimating intrinsic dimension, comparing methods, checking neighbourhood preservation (trustworthiness and continuity scores) and validating interpretations with external data.
steps: Construct and standardise the behavioural feature matrix, removing noise with PCA if dimensions are very high.
Estimate intrinsic dimensionality (e.g. maximum likelihood estimator or PCA residual variance) to decide target dimensions.
Apply two or more manifold methods (e.g. Isomap, diffusion maps, UMAP) with a range of neighbourhood sizes.
Evaluate embeddings with trustworthiness and continuity metrics (values above 0.9 indicate good neighbourhood preservation).
Interpret embedding coordinates by correlating them with original features and outcomes.
Track user trajectories over time in the embedding to study progression or drift.
outputs: Low-dimensional coordinates of the user space, intrinsic dimension estimates, quality metrics and interpretations of behavioural continua and trajectories.
useWhen: When behaviour appears to vary continuously and you want to understand progression, continua or the true number of behavioural dimensions.
avoidWhen: Avoid when linear PCA suffices, with small samples (manifold estimates are unstable), or when stakeholders need simple explainable segments.
whyLost: It is an academic ML topic; UX has absorbed only its most popular tools (t-SNE, UMAP) without the underlying framing.
whereToUse: Expertise progression in complex tools, behavioural drift analysis, learning curves in education technology and investment platforms.
example: Diffusion maps on 18 months of trading behaviour reveal a one-dimensional progression from cautious single-asset holders to diversified active traders. Plotting user trajectories shows most stall at a specific point linked to options education.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
Tenenbaum, de Silva & Langford (2000) A global geometric framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: Tenenbaum, J. B., de Silva, V. & Langford, J. C. (2000) A global geometric framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Science, 290(5500), 2319-2323.

name: Manipulation check
aka: Construct validity check of a manipulation
origin: Long-standing experimental practice; recent critiques by Hauser, Ellsworth and Gonzalez (2018) and Ejelöv and Luke (2020)
summary: Measure whether an experimental manipulation actually moved the intended construct, and not merely related ones, ideally in pilots or with its position counterbalanced.
description: An experiment that varies 'trust cues' or 'urgency' assumes the manipulation changed users' perceived trust or urgency. A manipulation check tests that assumption, supporting internal and construct validity. Only about a third of published studies report one, usually a single self-report item. Good practice measures the target construct plus related and unrelated constructs for convergent and divergent evidence, uses more than one kind of measure (self-report, open text, behaviour), and sets failure criteria in advance. A failed check may reflect a poor measure, an insensitive check or a failed manipulation. Because the check is itself an event that can sharpen or dampen the state it measures and change later behaviour, it is best placed in pilots, or its position counterbalanced in the main study with order effects tested. Results should be analysed as strength, not just pass or fail.
steps: Define the construct the manipulation should change, plus related constructs it should not change and unrelated ones as controls.
Choose measures: self-report items, open-text responses or behavioural indicators.
Set failure criteria in advance, including what you will do if the check fails.
Run the check in a pilot study, or counterbalance its position (before or after the outcome) in the main study and test for order effects.
Analyse the strength of the effect on the target construct and the absence of effects on divergent constructs, not just pass or fail.
Report the check fully, including failures.
outputs: Evidence that the manipulation moved the intended construct, with convergent and divergent validity information.
useWhen: Any experiment, survey vignette or A/B test that manipulates a psychological state or perception (trust, urgency, social presence, perceived price) rather than a purely physical change.
avoidWhen: When the manipulation is the product change itself and the outcome is behaviour you care about regardless of mechanism; then a check adds burden without informing the decision.
whyLost: UX experiments rarely theorise the psychological construct a change is meant to move, so the check is skipped or reduced to one item.
whereToUse: Persuasive design, trust and safety, AI explanation studies, pricing perception tests and concept tests in fintech and health.
example: A bank tests security badges meant to raise perceived trust at sign-up. A pilot shows the badges raise perceived security but not perceived trustworthiness of the company, so the team reframes the hypothesis before the full A/B test.
sources: Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Hauser, D. J., Ellsworth, P. C. and Gonzalez, R. (2018). Are manipulation checks necessary? Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 998.

name: Mann-Whitney U test
origin: Frank Wilcoxon, 1945; Henry Mann and Donald Whitney, 1947
summary: A non-parametric test comparing two independent groups on ordinal or skewed outcomes, such as task times or rating scores, without assuming normality.
description: The Mann-Whitney U test ranks all observations from both groups together and tests whether values from one group tend to be larger than those from the other. It is the default alternative to the independent t-test when outcomes are ordinal (single Likert items, SEQ scores) or heavily skewed (task times, error counts) and samples are small. Its null hypothesis is stochastic equality, P(X greater than Y) = 0.5; it only tests medians if both distributions have the same shape. Rigour comes from reporting the U statistic, exact or normal-approximation p-value, tie handling and an effect size such as the rank-biserial correlation or common-language effect size, rather than a p-value alone. For paired designs the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is used instead.
steps: Confirm the design has two independent groups and the outcome is ordinal or a skewed continuous measure.
Plot both distributions (histograms or box plots) and check whether shapes are similar before interpreting the result as a median difference.
Run the test (scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu or pingouin.mwu) with a two-sided alternative unless a direction was pre-registered.
Use the exact test for small samples (roughly n below 20 per group without ties) and the normal approximation with tie correction otherwise.
Report U, p, group medians with interquartile ranges, and the rank-biserial correlation (about 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large).
For task times, consider also comparing geometric means on log-transformed data as Sauro and Lewis recommend.
outputs: U statistic, p-value, group medians and IQRs, and a rank-based effect size with confidence interval.
useWhen: Comparing two designs or user groups on single-item ratings, task times, error counts or other skewed outcomes, particularly with small to moderate samples.
avoidWhen: Avoid for paired or repeated-measures data (use Wilcoxon signed-rank), for more than two groups (use Kruskal-Wallis), or for multi-item scale scores that are approximately normal (a Welch t-test is more powerful). For ordinal outcomes with covariates use ordinal regression.
whyLost: It survived because it is taught in every introductory statistics course and is robust for the small, skewed samples typical of usability testing.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarking, comparative evaluation of prototypes, accessibility studies with small samples and satisfaction comparisons between segments.
example: An e-commerce team compares checkout task times for two designs with 14 and 15 participants. Times are right-skewed, so a Mann-Whitney test shows design B faster (rank-biserial r = 0.42), reported with medians of 74 s and 112 s.
sources: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016) Quantifying the User Experience, 2nd ed.
Mann, H. B. & Whitney, D. R. (1947) On a test of whether one of two random variables is stochastically larger than the other. Annals of Mathematical Statistics
The Inquiry Series, C2 — Quantitative UX Analysis in Python — Descriptive to Inferential
The Inquiry Series, Ch 42 — Ordinal Logic — Treating Likert & Survey Data Correctly
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
reference: Mann, H. B. & Whitney, D. R. (1947) On a test of whether one of two random variables is stochastically larger than the other. Annals of Mathematical Statistics 18(1)

name: MANOVA and MANCOVA (Multivariate Analysis of Variance and Covariance)
aka: Multivariate analysis of variance and covariance (MANOVA and MANCOVA)
origin: Multivariate extension of Fisher's ANOVA; Harold Hotelling, 1931; Samuel Wilks, 1932
summary: Tests whether groups differ on several correlated outcome measures at once, optionally adjusting for covariates, before any single outcome is examined.
description: MANOVA extends ANOVA to two or more metric outcomes analysed together with one or more categorical factors. Instead of comparing single means it compares group mean vectors, taking the covariance among the outcomes into account, which controls the inflated Type I error of running a separate ANOVA per measure and can detect differences that only appear in a combination of measures. The overall test is reported with Wilks' lambda, Pillai's trace or Hotelling's T-squared (Pillai is the most robust when assumptions wobble). Designs may be one-way, factorial, between-subjects, within-subjects or mixed; the within-subjects multivariate approach is a separate use. MANCOVA adds interval covariates, so groups are compared on the outcomes after adjusting for, say, prior experience. A significant omnibus result is followed by comparisons of group centroids or univariate tests, ideally with discriminant function analysis to see which combination of outcomes separates the groups.
steps: Choose two or more conceptually related metric outcomes (for example time, effort rating and satisfaction) and the categorical factor(s); add interval covariates for MANCOVA.
Check assumptions: approximate multivariate normality, linear relations among outcomes, homogeneity of covariance matrices (Box's M) and at least 15-20 observations per cell.
Run the omnibus multivariate test and report Wilks' lambda, Pillai's trace or Hotelling's T-squared with its F approximation and an effect size.
If significant, locate the differences with univariate follow-ups (with alpha adjustment), centroid comparisons or discriminant function analysis.
For MANCOVA, check that covariate slopes are homogeneous across groups and interpret group differences on the adjusted outcomes.
Report adjusted or unadjusted means per outcome and group together with the multivariate result.
outputs: Multivariate test table (Wilks, Pillai, Hotelling), homogeneity tests, adjusted means per outcome and group, follow-up comparisons.
useWhen: Comparing designs, versions or user groups on a set of correlated outcomes that together represent one concept (efficiency, satisfaction, effort) when you want a single protected test before looking at individual measures.
avoidWhen: Outcomes are unrelated or chosen without theory (analyse them separately with alpha correction); cells are small or covariance matrices very unequal; outcomes are binary or ordinal. With very large samples trivial differences become significant, so report effect sizes. For nested or repeated data use multilevel models.
whyLost: UX teams tend to analyse each metric separately with t-tests or ANOVA, and multivariate output is harder to explain to stakeholders, so MANOVA stays in academic HCI and psychology.
whereToUse: Summative comparisons of design variants on SUS, task time and error together; comparing user segments on several attitude scales; evaluating training or onboarding programmes on multiple outcomes while adjusting for prior experience.
example: A SaaS team compares three onboarding flows on time to first project, perceived effort (SEQ) and confidence. A one-way MANCOVA adjusting for prior tool experience gives Pillai's trace = 0.14, p = .002; follow-ups show the guided flow lowers effort and raises confidence without changing time.
sources: A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: Singh, K. (2007). Quantitative Social Research Methods. New Delhi: Sage Publications.

name: Manual Materials Handling Assessment (NIOSH Lifting Equation, ACGIH TLVs, Snook Tables)
aka: Recommended Weight Limit and Lifting Index
origin: NIOSH Work Practices Guide (1981); revised equation by Waters, Putz-Anderson, Garg and Fine (1993); ACGIH lifting TLVs; psychophysical tables by Snook and Ciriello (1991)
summary: Score a lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling or carrying task against biomechanical and psychophysical limits to judge low-back injury risk and justify redesign of the task or product.
description: Three complementary tools for physical load. The 1981 NIOSH guide set an action limit tied to roughly 3,400 N of spinal compression and a maximum permissible limit about three times higher; the 1993 revised equation computes a Recommended Weight Limit by discounting a 23 kg load constant through horizontal, vertical, distance, asymmetry, frequency and coupling multipliers, and a Lifting Index (load divided by RWL) above 1.0 signals increased risk. ACGIH threshold limit values give weight limits for twelve lift-origin zones by frequency and duration. The psychophysical approach has workers adjust a load until it feels acceptable for an 8-hour shift; Snook and Ciriello's tables give, by sex, the percentage of the population that finds a given lift, push, pull or carry acceptable, and are the usual tool for pushing and pulling. Scoring before and after redesign turns ergonomics into a quantified business case. Validation studies find the revised equation conservative.
steps: Identify problem jobs from injury records or discomfort surveys and ask the people doing them which tasks cause trouble.

For each lift or lower, measure at origin and destination: horizontal distance from mid-ankles to the load centre, vertical height, asymmetry angle, frequency, hand-object coupling quality and vertical travel distance.
Compute RWL = 23 kg x HM x VM x DM x AM x FM x CM and the Lifting Index = load / RWL; flag any LI above 1.0.
Cross-check against the ACGIH TLV for the lift-origin zone and frequency.
For pushing, pulling and carrying, and as a check on lifts, look up the Snook (Liberty Mutual) table for the task parameters to get the percentage of male and female workers who find it acceptable.
Redesign (shorten horizontal reach, raise origin height, add handles, reduce frequency, add lifting aids) and re-score to show the before-and-after improvement.
outputs: Recommended weight limit, lifting index, TLV comparison and percentage of the population accommodated, with before-and-after scores for the redesign case.
useWhen: Designing physical products, packaging, retail and warehouse workflows, field-service kits or devices that people lift, carry, push or pull repeatedly, where injury risk must be quantified.
avoidWhen: Highly dynamic, one-handed or team lifts outside the equations' assumptions; purely digital products. For whole-body postures use Anthropometric Analysis or posture tools; for perceived effort alone use the Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale.
whyLost: It belongs to occupational safety and industrial engineering; UX moved into screen-based products and rarely owns physical work design, even where service design reshapes physical tasks.
whereToUse: Service design for warehouses, delivery and retail staff, medical equipment carts, hardware and packaging design, exoskeleton and assistive-device evaluation.
example: A grocery delivery service redesigns its tote crates. Scoring the van-to-doorstep lift gives an LI of 1.4; adding side handles and halving the crate depth brings it to 0.9, and the Snook carry table shows acceptability rising from 60 to 85 percent of female drivers.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Waters, T. R., Putz-Anderson, V., Garg, A. and Fine, L. J. (1993). Revised NIOSH equation for the design and evaluation of manual lifting tasks. Ergonomics, 36(7), 749-776; Snook, S. H. and Ciriello, V. M. (1991). Ergonomics, 34(9), 1197-1213.

name: Many-Facet Rasch Measurement
origin: John Michael Linacre (1989), implemented in the FACETS program; applications in sport and rehabilitation reviewed by Strauss, Büsch and Tenenbaum in Chapter 33 of the Handbook
summary: Extends the Rasch model beyond persons and items to further facets such as raters, tasks or occasions, so each can be placed on one scale and rater severity can be measured and corrected.
description: Standard Rasch models treat data as a two-way matrix of persons by items. The many-facet Rasch model adds further facets, such as the raters who judge responses, the tasks, the occasion or person characteristics, giving a structure of persons by items by raters and so on. Each element is estimated on a common logit scale: person ability, item difficulty, rater severity and task difficulty. Fit statistics show which raters are inconsistent, and interaction terms show bias, for example a rater who is harsh only on one group. The Handbook describes uses in sport and rehabilitation. These include recalibrating a gross motor test with eight facets, analysing judged sports, where the model has exposed unfair ice-skating judges, and a two-facet analysis of the Borg scale showing it reflects cumulative exertion. For UX the model fits any design where several judges rate several things: expert reviews and severity ratings of usability problems, human evaluation of AI or search output, design-critique scoring, accessibility audits and graded usability tasks. It gives fair scores that are corrected for which rater happened to judge which item, and shows which raters need recalibration.
steps: Define the facets in your rating design, for example participants or outputs, criteria, raters and tasks.
Make sure the design links facets (raters overlap on some items), because disconnected subsets cannot be placed on one scale.
Collect ratings on a consistent ordinal scale.
Fit the model with Rasch software that supports facets, and check category functioning.
Inspect rater severity and fit, and bias interactions between raters and other facets.
Report fair, severity-adjusted scores and give feedback to misfitting raters.
outputs: Logit measures for every element of every facet (such as output quality, criterion difficulty and rater severity), fit statistics and fair adjusted scores.
useWhen: Several raters score many items or outputs and not every rater sees every item, so raw averages are confounded with rater harshness.
avoidWhen: A single rater scores everything, data are too sparse to link facets, or a simple agreement statistic is enough.
whyLost: UX teams use kappa or simple averages for rater data; Rasch tools are specialised and known mainly in language testing and educational assessment.
whereToUse: Human evaluation of LLM and search output, heuristic evaluation programmes, design critiques, accessibility audits, scored usability benchmarks.
example: A team running human evaluation of chatbot answers has 20 raters each scoring a different subset of 2,000 responses on helpfulness. A many-facet Rasch analysis shows two raters far more lenient than the rest and one inconsistent; fair scores change the ranking of two model versions.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Strauss, B., Büsch, D. and Tenenbaum, G. (2007) 'New perspectives on measurement and testing in sport psychology', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 33.

name: Market Share Attraction Model
origin: Lee Cooper and Masao Nakanishi, 1988
summary: Models each alternative's share of a category as its attraction divided by the total attraction of all alternatives, with attraction a multiplicative function of its own attributes.
description: Shares lie between 0 and 1 and sum to 1 across competitors, so they cannot be modelled one at a time with ordinary regression. The attraction model gives each alternative an attraction equal to a constant times its explanatory variables (price, distribution, advertising, features) raised to alternative-specific powers, with dummy variables entering as exponentials, and sets its share equal to its attraction over the summed attraction of all alternatives. This guarantees logically consistent shares and lets a change in one competitor's mix redistribute share across all. Estimation picks a benchmark alternative, divides each share by the benchmark's share and takes logs, giving J - 1 linear equations estimated jointly with correlated errors; only differences from the benchmark's parameters are identified. Unlike discrete choice models, which work on individual choices, the attraction model works on aggregate share time series.
steps: Assemble time series of shares and of positive-valued explanatory variables for every alternative (exponentiate dummies; avoid rates of change that can be negative).
Choose a benchmark alternative.
Form the log ratio of each alternative's share to the benchmark's share and the corresponding log ratios of explanatory variables.
Estimate the J - 1 linear equations jointly, allowing correlated errors across equations.
Interpret the identified parameters as differences from the benchmark, and simulate shares under changed prices, features or promotion for one or more alternatives.
outputs: Share response of each alternative to its own and competitors' marketing or product variables, and simulated share scenarios.
useWhen: You have aggregate share data over time for competing apps, plans, products or channels (for example app-store or retail panel data) and want to understand and simulate competitive response.
avoidWhen: You have individual choice data (use discrete choice models or a conjoint simulator); explanatory variables can be zero or negative; very few periods are available. Only relative parameters are identified.
whyLost: It is a marketing-science model for brand managers; UX and product teams rarely work with aggregate competitive share series.
whereToUse: Competitive strategy for apps and subscription services, plan mix within a product line, channel share between self-service and assisted support, marketplace share among sellers.
example: A streaming service models weekly category share against three competitors using price, catalogue size and promotion. Simulations suggest a 10% catalogue increase gains about two share points, mostly from the smallest competitor, which informs content investment more than a price cut would.
sources: Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
reference: Cooper, L. G., & Nakanishi, M. (1988). Market Share Analysis: Evaluating Competitive Marketing Effectiveness. Boston: Kluwer Academic Publishers.

name: Markov Chain Funnel Modelling
origin: Andrey Markov (1906); absorbing chain theory by John Kemeny and J. Laurie Snell (Finite Markov Chains, 1960); attribution use by Anderl et al. (2016)
summary: Models user journeys as states with transition probabilities, including absorbing states like conversion and exit, to compute completion probabilities and step importance.
description: Linear funnels assume users move forward step by step, but real journeys loop, skip and backtrack. A Markov chain estimates the probability of moving from each state (page, screen, step) to every other. With absorbing states for success and abandonment, the fundamental matrix N = (I - Q)^-1 gives expected visits to each state and absorption probabilities from any starting point. Removal effects, setting a state's transitions to exit, quantify each state's contribution to conversion. Higher-order chains capture memory. This gives a principled, whole-journey model for diagnosing where loops waste effort and which steps matter most.
steps: Define states at an appropriate granularity and absorbing states (conversion, exit, timeout).
Estimate the transition matrix from session logs, checking sample size per row.
Compute the fundamental matrix, expected steps to absorption and absorption probabilities.
Calculate removal effects for each state to gauge its contribution to success.
Test whether a first-order model is adequate versus higher-order (e.g. likelihood ratio or BIC).
Simulate design changes by modifying transition probabilities and predict their effect on conversion.
outputs: Transition matrices, absorption probabilities, expected path lengths, state removal effects and what-if simulations.
useWhen: Non-linear journeys with loops and multiple entry points, or for attribution across touchpoints.
avoidWhen: Simple linear flows where a standard funnel suffices, or sparse data with many states.
whyLost: Funnel visualisations in analytics tools assume linear steps; Markov modelling requires matrix algebra few UX teams practise.
whereToUse: E-commerce browsing, SaaS onboarding, help centre navigation, multi-channel marketing journeys.
example: A travel site models 18 states. Removal effects show the 'compare' page contributes 22% of bookings despite low traffic, while a 'deals' page creates loops that add 1.8 expected steps without raising conversion.
sources: Anderl, Becker, von Wangenheim & Schumann, Mapping the customer journey: Lessons learned from graph-based online attribution modeling (2016), International Journal of Research in Marketing
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Kemeny, J. G., & Snell, J. L. (1960). Finite Markov Chains. Van Nostrand.

name: Markov Decision Process Models of Interaction
donor: Operations research; reinforcement learning; computational cognitive science
origin: Bellman (1957) for MDPs; computational rationality in HCI by Howes, Lewis, Oulasvirta and colleagues, 2009-2018
summary: Models users as agents choosing actions to maximise expected reward under cognitive and perceptual bounds, and derives predicted optimal behaviour for a given interface.
description: An MDP specifies states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards; a POMDP adds partial observability, which suits users who cannot see everything. Computational rationality assumes users adapt their strategies optimally to the interface, given bounds such as limited visual acuity and memory. Solving the model (often by reinforcement learning) yields predicted behaviour: where users look, when they give up, which menu strategies they adopt. Comparing interfaces then means comparing the optimal policies and their expected costs. This gives UX a principled theory of why users behave as they do, and a way to explore design spaces in simulation before testing.
steps: Define the task as states, actions, observations and rewards, including time costs and task success value.
Specify bounded cognitive and perceptual constraints (foveal vision, memory decay, motor noise) based on literature.
Solve for the optimal or near-optimal policy using dynamic programming or reinforcement learning.
Generate predicted behaviour (fixations, clicks, abandonment, strategy choice) for each design variant.
Validate against empirical data from a small study or logs, checking qualitative patterns and quantitative fit.
Use the model to explore further design variants and to explain observed behaviour.
outputs: A formal user model, predicted policies and behaviours for designs, and validation statistics.
useWhen: You need to explain adaptive strategies or optimise layouts and menus in a large design space.
avoidWhen: Exploratory problems with unclear goals or rewards; qualitative research is needed first.
whyLost: It requires machine learning and cognitive modelling expertise uncommon in UX teams, and is published in CHI and cognitive science rather than practitioner venues.
whereToUse: Menu and layout optimisation, notification timing, adaptive interfaces, recommender interaction design.
example: A POMDP model of visual search through a product grid predicts that users adopt a left-column strategy when thumbnail quality is low. Testing confirms it, and the design team improves thumbnails rather than reordering items.
sources: Oulasvirta, Kristensson, Bi & Howes (eds.), Computational Interaction (2018)
Lewis, Howes & Singh, Computational rationality: Linking mechanism and behavior through bounded utility maximization (2014), Topics in Cognitive Science
Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2018)
reference: Lewis, R. L., Howes, A., & Singh, S. (2014). Computational rationality. Topics in Cognitive Science, 6(2), 279-311.

name: Marr's Three Levels Applied to a Socio-Technical Task
aka: Computational account of a work task
origin: Adapted for UX from David Marr's (1982) levels of analysis, via Edwin Hutchins's (1995) application to ship navigation
summary: Describe what a work system computes independent of representation, then the representations and algorithms one tradition uses, then their physical implementation, contrasting traditions to expose hidden assumptions.
description: Marr argued that an information-processing system must be understood at three levels: the computational theory of what is computed and why, the representation and algorithm that carry it out, and the physical implementation. Hutchins applies this to a ship's navigation team. The computational level states the mapping between kinds of information and the constraints it satisfies, free of any tradition's representational assumptions. He contrasts Western chart-based fixing, where lines of position intersect on a chart, with Micronesian etak navigation, where the canoe is held fixed and a reference island moves under the star bearings, to show the same computation resting on radically different representations. Levels nest: what is implementation for the whole system becomes the computational task for the practitioners, so tools set the constraints of people's work. For UX this separates the job from today's tools before redesigning them.
steps: State the computational problem the work system solves and its constraints, without representational assumptions.
Keep illustrations sparse and label which level each example belongs to.
Find at least two traditions, tools or cultures that solve the same problem with different representations.
Describe the representation and algorithm used by the tradition under study.
Describe its implementation in tools, media and people.
Note where the system's implementation becomes the practitioners' computational task, and identify which constraints a redesign could remove.
outputs: A layered account separating what is computed, how it is represented and how it is physically done, with design options that change representation without changing the computation.
useWhen: Reframing a work domain before redesign or automation, especially when current tools so shape the work that teams cannot separate the goal from the procedure.
avoidWhen: Examples inevitably carry a culture's assumptions; the analysis is interpretive and slow. For a practical decomposition of current tasks use Hierarchical Task Analysis; for constraint-based domain modelling use Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA).
whyLost: Marr's levels are standard in cognitive science teaching, but Hutchins's application to work systems was read as theory and never turned into a practitioner method.
whereToUse: Replacing legacy professional tools, designing AI assistance for expert work, comparing manual, spreadsheet and automated versions of the same job.
example: Redesigning expense approval, a team first states the computation (match each claim against policy and budget constraints), then contrasts the paper form, the spreadsheet and a chat-based assistant as representations, revealing that the 'monthly batch' step is an artefact of the spreadsheet implementation.
reference: Marr, D. (1982). Vision. San Francisco: W. H. Freeman; Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, pp. 49-58.

name: Mathematical Metaphor Analysis for Data Visualisation
origin: Adapted for data visualisation from Lakoff and Núñez's mathematical idea analysis (Where Mathematics Comes From, 2000) and conceptual metaphor theory (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980); the chart-specific metaphors and audit steps are the atlas's own extension, as the book discusses only Venn diagrams and graphs of functions.
summary: Audits visualisations for the conceptual metaphors they rely on, such as more is up or time is a path, predicting misreadings when encodings violate those metaphors.
description: Lakoff and Núñez argue that mathematical understanding rests on conceptual metaphors grounded in bodily experience: numbers as collections, arithmetic as object manipulation, functions as motion along a path, and more as up. Visualisations inherit these metaphors. Viewers expect higher to mean more, left-to-right to mean later in time, bigger area to mean larger quantity, and closeness to mean similarity. When an encoding violates the metaphor, for example an inverted y-axis, a ranking where 1 is at the bottom, or a radial chart where time runs counter-clockwise, readers make predictable errors even when legends are correct. The method lists the metaphors each chart relies on, flags violations and conflicts between metaphors, and tests comprehension of flagged charts with quick judgement tasks.
steps: For any data visualisation, identify the conceptual metaphors it employs.
For example, a bar chart uses MORE IS UP (quantity mapped to vertical height) and CATEGORIES ARE CONTAINERS (bars as separate spatial regions).
Test whether users' intuitions align with the mathematical properties of each metaphor.
For each metaphor, find the breaking point where the intuitive metaphor diverges from the mathematical reality.
Design to minimise metaphor violations.
outputs: Metaphor inventory per visualisation, flagged violations and conflicts, comprehension test results, and recommended encodings.
useWhen: Dashboards, financial and health data displays, data journalism, analytics products and any chart where misreading has consequences.
avoidWhen: When the problem is data quality or statistical literacy rather than encoding; use comprehension testing or data literacy research.
whyLost: Conceptual metaphor theory stayed in cognitive linguistics, while visualisation research adopted perceptual effectiveness rankings (Cleveland and McGill) instead.
whereToUse: Data visualization design, dashboard design, financial data UX, scientific data communication, AI output visualization.
example: A cloud cost dashboard shows savings as downward bars. Metaphor analysis flags a 'more is up' conflict, and a comprehension test shows 30% of finance users read the largest saving as the smallest; the chart is redrawn with upward bars.
sources: Where Mathematics Comes From — George Lakoff
Lakoff & Johnson, Metaphors We Live By (1980)
reference: Lakoff G & Núñez RE (2000) Where Mathematics Comes From: How the Embodied Mind Brings Mathematics into Being. Basic Books

name: Matrix Analysis (Miles & Huberman)
origin: Jane Ritchie and Liz Spencer, National Centre for Social Research, late 1980s (Framework); Miles and Huberman matrix displays
summary: Summarises qualitative data into purpose-built case-by-dimension matrices, reading across rows for cases and down columns for patterns, to answer several research questions systematically.
description: Matrix analysis (Spencer et al.) involves constructing bespoke matrices in which the rows represent cases (participants) or time points, and the columns represent dimensions defined by the research questions. Unlike Framework Analysis (which uses a pre-existing thematic framework), matrix analysis builds matrices specifically tailored to the current research question. It is particularly useful in evaluation research and applied policy research where multiple specific questions must be answered from the same dataset.
steps: Define the matrix dimensions: Each column of the matrix should correspond directly to a research question or a key dimension of the analysis.
Unit of analysis: Each row should represent a coherent unit — a participant, a site, a time point, a case.
Population of cells: For each cell, summarise the relevant data in 2–4 sentences. The summary is interpretive, not descriptive — it makes the analytical meaning of the data visible.
Read across rows: What is the full picture for this participant/case? What pattern of responses does this person show?
Read down columns: What is the pattern across all participants on this dimension? Where is there convergence? Where is there divergence?
Cross-matrix synthesis: Build a higher-order analysis that integrates patterns from multiple columns. What do the patterns across dimensions tell you that no single dimension reveals alone?
outputs: Populated analysis matrices with cell summaries and source references, within-case and cross-case patterns, typologies, and an audit trail linking claims to data.
useWhen: You have multiple defined research questions, a moderate dataset (about 10 to 50 cases), several analysts, and need transparent comparison across participants or segments.
avoidWhen: The analysis is highly exploratory with no defined dimensions; start with Reflexive Thematic Analysis or grounded theory. For very small studies, matrices may add overhead.
whyLost: Spreadsheets of notes are common in UX, but the disciplined framework procedure, with defined dimensions, summarised cells, source references and two-direction reading, stayed in health and policy research.
whereToUse: Multi-segment interview studies, evaluation research, longitudinal studies across time points, team synthesis, and research repositories.
example: A fintech team interviews 24 small-business owners across three segments. A matrix with columns for each research question shows retailers depend on cash-flow forecasts while service firms care about invoicing, guiding segment-specific roadmaps.
sources: Framework Analysis and Matrix Methods (Ritchie & Spencer)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Miles MB & Huberman AM (1994) Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook. 2nd ed
Miles MB, Huberman AM & Saldaña J (2014) Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook. 3rd ed
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Gale, N. K. et al. (2013). Using the framework method for the analysis of qualitative data in multi-disciplinary health research. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 13, 117.

name: Matrix completion (Hard-Impute)
aka: Matrix completion by iterative principal components
origin: Mazumder, Hastie and Tibshirani (2010), Spectral regularization algorithms for learning large incomplete matrices, JMLR
summary: Fills missing entries of a data matrix by repeatedly fitting a low-rank principal-components approximation and replacing gaps with its predictions until the fit stops improving.
description: Hard-Impute treats a data matrix with gaps as approximately low rank. Each column is standardised and missing entries start at their column means; the first M principal components of the completed matrix are computed, missing entries are replaced by their rank-M approximation, and the squared error on observed entries is recalculated. The loop repeats until that error stops falling. The same machinery serves two purposes: imputing scattered missing values before analysis, and recommendation, where most entries are missing by design (the Netflix matrix was about 99% empty) and user scores and item loadings read as memberships in 'cliques' and 'genres'. The number of components is chosen by hiding some observed entries and checking how well they are recovered. The method assumes values are missing at random and finds a local, not global, optimum.
steps: Standardise each column and fill every missing value with its column mean of observed values.
Compute the first M principal components of the completed matrix (its rank-M approximation).
Replace each originally missing entry with its rank-M approximation.
Recompute squared error on observed entries only and repeat the previous two steps until it stops decreasing.
Choose M by masking a further 5-10% of observed entries, re-running, and picking the rank that recovers them best.
Return the imputed matrix with approximate component scores and loadings, and check that missingness is plausibly random before using them.
outputs: A completed matrix, imputed values, and approximate component scores (user groupings) and loadings (item groupings).
useWhen: Wide numeric matrices with scattered gaps (survey grids, feature-by-user ratings) or sparse preference data where a low-rank structure is plausible.
avoidWhen: Missingness is informative, such as users skipping items they dislike; then model the missingness (see the missing-value check model) or use MICE with appropriate predictors. Not suited to small matrices or mixed categorical data.
whyLost: It is a core recommender-system and machine-learning technique that UX researchers meet only inside products, not as a research analysis tool.
whereToUse: Large rating grids in surveys, feature-importance matrices with partial coverage, content preference studies, prototyping recommendation logic from research data.
example: A streaming service's research team has ratings of 200 shows from 5,000 panel members, each rating about 20. Hard-Impute with five components recovers held-out ratings well and reveals a 'documentary and true crime' cluster that informs a new browse row.
sources: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: Mazumder, R., Hastie, T. and Tibshirani, R. (2010). Spectral regularization algorithms for learning large incomplete matrices. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11, 2287-2322.

name: MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling)
