origin: Jordan Louviere and George Woodworth (1987-1990); Finn and Louviere (1992); Louviere, Flynn and Marley (2015)
summary: Respondents repeatedly choose the most and least important items from small subsets, producing ratio-quality importance scores without scale-use bias.
description: Rating scales suffer from everyone rating everything as important, and from cultural differences in scale use. MaxDiff shows respondents subsets of items (typically 4-5 per screen) from a list of 10-30, asking for the best and worst. Balanced incomplete block designs ensure each item appears equally and with each other item. Hierarchical Bayes multinomial logit estimates individual-level utilities, which can be rescaled to probability shares. The method discriminates strongly and works across cultures. Vestigial use runs MaxDiff in survey tools with poor designs and only counts-based scores, and uses it for things that are not comparable, such as features with very different scopes.
steps: Define a list of comparable items (features, needs, messages), worded at similar levels of specificity.
Generate a balanced design: each respondent sees each item about 3 times, 4-5 items per set.
Field to an adequate sample (e.g. 200+ per segment of interest).
Estimate utilities with hierarchical Bayes MNL; check fit (RLH) and remove speeders.
Rescale to probability shares and compare segments with credible intervals.
Optionally add an anchored question to identify absolute importance thresholds.
outputs: Individual and aggregate importance scores, segment comparisons and anchored thresholds.
useWhen: Prioritising features, needs, value propositions or messages across many items.
avoidWhen: Items of very different scope, or when you need absolute willingness to pay (use conjoint or BDM).
whyLost: Survey platforms made it a menu option, removing design and estimation rigour; results are often treated as precise rankings without uncertainty.
whereToUse: Roadmap prioritisation, onboarding message testing, needs research for JTBD, international product research.
example: A project management tool tests 20 candidate features with 600 users via MaxDiff. Three features take 40% of preference share among team leads but barely register among individual contributors, shaping a tiered roadmap.
sources: Louviere, Flynn & Marley, Best-Worst Scaling: Theory, Methods and Applications (2015)
Finn & Louviere, Determining the appropriate response to evidence of public concern (1992), Journal of Public Policy & Marketing
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Louviere, J. J., Flynn, T. N., & Marley, A. A. J. (2015). Best-Worst Scaling. Cambridge University Press.

name: Maximization and Regret Scales (Schwartz)
origin: Schwartz, Ward, Monterosso, Lyubomirsky, White and Lehman, 2002; satisficing concept from Herbert Simon
summary: Two companion self-report scales: a 13-item measure of seeking the best option rather than a good-enough one, and a 5-item measure of susceptibility to regret.
description: The Maximization Scale has 13 agreement items rated 1-7 and summed (13-91): imagining all alternatives, channel surfing, difficulty choosing gifts, never settling for second best. Scores of 65 or more are clearly maximizing and 40 or less clearly satisficing; in several thousand respondents the mean was about 50 with no sex difference. High scorers compare more, take longer to decide, regret more, feel worse about purchases and report lower happiness and life satisfaction. The Regret Scale has five 1-7 items; item 1 is reverse-scored (8 minus the rating) and the items summed. Almost everyone high on maximizing scores high on regret. Together they characterise a decision style that moderates how people react to choice sets and comparison tools. Later literature questions the maximization factor structure and the dated item wording, so use revised short forms where possible.
steps: Decide whether decision style is a moderator or segmenting variable in your study and choose the full or a validated short form.
Administer the 13 Maximization items and 5 Regret items on 1-7 agreement scales, ideally before the main task to avoid contamination.
Sum the Maximization items (13-91) and the Regret items after reversing item 1 (8 minus rating).
Use scores continuously, or flag 65+ as maximizers and 40 or less as satisficers for descriptive segmentation.
Relate scores to behaviour (number of comparisons, decision time, returns) and to satisfaction or regret after choice.
outputs: A maximizing score and a regret-proneness score per participant, and their relation to choice behaviour and satisfaction.
useWhen: When studying choice-heavy experiences (comparison shopping, plan selection, recommendation lists) and you suspect people with different decision styles need different numbers of options or reassurance.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a stand-alone persona generator or for momentary regret about a specific choice (use a state measure). Evidence is correlational and maximizing is domain-specific; consider a domain-adapted measure.
whyLost: They are well known in consumer psychology and behavioural economics but rarely administered in UX studies, which treat choice overload as uniform.
whereToUse: E-commerce filtering and comparison, insurance and telecom plan pickers, dating apps, streaming recommendation, return and post-purchase flows.
example: An energy-tariff comparison site gives the scales to 400 users before a test. Maximizers open twice as many tariffs and report more regret; the team adds a 'best for you' default with an easy 'see all' route.
reference: Schwartz, B., Ward, A., Monterosso, J., Lyubomirsky, S., White, K., & Lehman, D. R. (2002). Maximizing versus satisficing: Happiness is a matter of choice. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1178-1197.

name: Maximum Likelihood and Method-of-Moments Estimation
aka: Point estimation by maximum likelihood and method of moments
Maximum likelihood estimation and estimator properties
origin: Method of moments: Karl Pearson (1894); maximum likelihood: R. A. Fisher (1912, 1922)
summary: Estimate the parameters of a distribution by matching sample moments or by maximising the likelihood of the observed data, and judge estimators by bias, efficiency, mean square error and consistency.
description: Point estimation gives a single best value for a model parameter. The method of moments sets sample moments (mean, variance) equal to their theoretical expressions and solves for the parameters; it is simple and gives starting values. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter values under which the observed data are most probable, usually by maximising the log-likelihood numerically; MLEs are consistent, asymptotically efficient and invariant to transformation, so the MLE of a function of a parameter is that function of the MLE. Estimators are compared by bias, variance, mean square error and consistency. In UX the point is choosing an appropriate distribution for skewed quantities such as task times, session lengths or time-to-churn (for example lognormal or Weibull) and fitting it properly, rather than summarising them with a mean and standard deviation.
steps: Choose a candidate distribution that fits the data-generating process (for example lognormal for task times, Weibull for time to event, Poisson for counts).
Compute method-of-moments estimates as a quick check and starting values.
Write the log-likelihood and maximise it numerically to obtain the MLEs.
Obtain standard errors or confidence intervals from the observed information or by bootstrap.
Check fit with a probability plot or by comparing observed and fitted frequencies, and compare candidate distributions with AIC or BIC.
Report the fitted parameters and derived quantities (for example median or 90th percentile) using the invariance property.
outputs: Parameter estimates with standard errors, fitted distributions, goodness-of-fit checks and derived quantities.
useWhen: When you need a fitted distribution for skewed UX measures, for simulation or forecasting, or when reading and building models (logistic, survival, mixture) whose estimation rests on likelihood.
avoidWhen: Avoid fitting a parametric distribution blindly to small or heavily mixed samples; use Bootstrap methods for confidence intervals or nonparametric summaries. With strong prior information and small samples, Bayesian Estimation for Small-Sample UX Studies is better.
whyLost: It is foundational in statistics but hidden inside software, so UX practitioners use its outputs without choosing distributions or checking fit.
whereToUse: Task-time and latency modelling, survival of subscriptions, event-rate modelling, inputs to Monte Carlo forecasts.
example: A team models checkout times, which are right-skewed. A lognormal fitted by maximum likelihood gives a median of 74 seconds and a 90th percentile of 190 seconds, which becomes the benchmark rather than a misleading mean of 102 seconds.
sources: Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
reference: Casella, G. and Berger, R. L. (2001). Statistical Inference (2nd ed.). Pacific Grove, CA: Duxbury, pp. 312-324; Fisher, R. A. (1922). On the mathematical foundations of theoretical statistics. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 222, 309-368.

name: MCMC convergence diagnostics
aka: Checking MCMC output before trusting a Bayesian fit
Rhat and effective sample size checks
origin: Heidelberger and Welch (1983); Gelman and Rubin (1992); Geweke (1992); Stan developers
summary: Checks that Markov chain Monte Carlo samples have explored the posterior properly and are precise enough before any Bayesian estimate is reported.
description: A Bayesian model fitted by MCMC produces samples that are only usable if the chains have reached the stationary distribution, mixed well and yielded enough effectively independent draws. The routine runs several chains from dispersed starting points and checks them by plots and statistics: trace plots for stationarity and rapid mixing, rank (trank) plots in which all chains should overlap evenly, autocorrelation and cumulative-mean plots, the Gelman-Rubin statistic (Rhat) near 1.00, effective sample size adequate for the quantity wanted, and stationarity tests such as Geweke and Heidelberger-Welch. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo adds diagnostic warnings (divergent transitions, maximum treedepth) that usually point to a problem in the model, not the software. No diagnostic proves convergence and regions a chain never visited cannot be seen, so warnings are treated as diagnoses to fix rather than noise.
steps: Prepare a trimmed data list with only the variables used and transformations computed in advance.
Debug with one short chain, then run about four chains from dispersed starting points; discard warmup samples.
Read Rhat (should be 1.00; values above about 1.01 signal non-convergence) and effective sample size (a few hundred for means, many more for tail quantiles).
Inspect trace, rank (trank), autocorrelation and cumulative-mean plots; one chain sitting apart for long stretches means poor exploration.
Where needed, apply stationarity tests (Geweke, Heidelberger-Welch, Kolmogorov-Smirnov on chain halves) and batch means to decide whether precision is adequate.
Treat divergent transitions, treedepth warnings and slow sampling as model problems: use weakly informative priors, reparameterise multilevel models, or remove redundant parameters.
Refit until all checks pass and record the diagnostics table and warnings resolved alongside the results.
outputs: A diagnostics table (Rhat, effective sample size), trace and rank plots, and a record of warnings and the fixes applied.
useWhen: Any Bayesian analysis fitted by sampling (Stan, brms, PyMC, JAGS), including multilevel models of task times, ratings or conversion, before results reach a report.
avoidWhen: Conjugate or analytic models (such as a beta-binomial) need no sampler checks. Diagnostics cannot prove correctness, so pair them with prior and posterior predictive checks.
whyLost: UX teams adopting Bayesian tools often use defaults through friendly front ends and treat sampler warnings as noise; the checking routine stays inside statistics training.
whereToUse: Bayesian A/B testing, small-sample usability benchmarks, multilevel survey models, any research report built on brms or PyMC output.
example: A team fits a multilevel model of task times across 40 participants and 12 tasks in brms. Rhat is 1.03 and there are 80 divergent transitions; switching to a non-centred parameterisation and tighter priors on group-level standard deviations removes the divergences before the estimates are shared.
sources: Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella, 2010)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: Gelman, A. and Rubin, D. B. (1992). Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science, 7(4), 457-472.

name: McNemar Exact Test for Paired Proportions
origin: Quinn McNemar (1947)
summary: Compares success rates when the same participants tried both designs.
description: In within-subjects studies each person attempts the task on both designs, so the two completion rates are not independent and the two-proportion test is wrong. McNemar's test looks only at the discordant pairs: people who succeeded on A but failed on B, and the reverse. If the designs were equally good these should be roughly equal. The exact version uses a binomial test on the discordant counts and works with small samples. Sauro and Lewis pair it with an adjusted-Wald interval for the difference in matched proportions, so the size of the improvement can be reported too.
steps: Build the 2×2 table of outcomes per participant: both succeed, A only, B only, both fail.
Take the discordant counts b (A only) and c (B only).
Run an exact binomial test of b against b + c with p = 0.5 (or the mid-p variant for less conservatism).
Compute an adjusted interval for the difference in matched proportions.
Report the discordant counts, p-value and interval.
outputs: A test of whether one design succeeds more often for the same people.
useWhen: Within-subjects comparisons of binary outcomes: success, preference, error presence.
avoidWhen: Different people saw each design (use the N-1 two-proportion test).
whyLost: Within-subjects designs are common in UX but analysts reach for the independent-groups tests they know.
whereToUse: Counterbalanced prototype comparisons, before/after studies with the same panel, competitive head-to-heads.
example: Fifteen people try both search layouts. Six succeed only on the new one, one only on the old. The exact McNemar p is 0.125, so a larger sample is needed before claiming the win.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: McNemar, Q. (1947). Note on the sampling error of the difference between correlated proportions. Psychometrika 12.

name: Measurable UX Honeycomb
aka: Morville's UX Honeycomb with behavioural proxies
origin: Peter Morville, 2004; behavioural proxies by Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Morville's seven UX qualities turned into measurable behavioural proxies and survey constructs, used as the anchor dimensions for detecting where engagement erodes.
description: Peter Morville's 2004 honeycomb lists seven qualities of good UX: useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible and valuable. It is widely reproduced as a poster but rarely measured. Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook operationalises each facet as a behavioural proxy: Useful → unprompted return to feature; Desirable → exploration beyond minimal path; Findable → short path to target content across sessions; Accessible → completion parity across devices or modalities; Usable → error rate, success rate, time-on-task stability; Credible → adoption of recommendations without double-checking; Valuable → long-term retention, upgrade, advocacy. A 30-item Likert survey aligned to the facets is factor-analysed; in the worked example the seven collapse into Trust (credible + valuable), Ease (usable + accessible) and Engagement (useful + desirable + findable). The playbook justifies Honeycomb over HTA (bounded tasks) and Information Foraging Theory (drift is absence of foraging).
steps: List the seven Honeycomb facets and decide which are plausible drift dimensions for the product.
Map each facet to a behavioural proxy available in telemetry (e.g. Credible → recommendation adoption without double-checking).
Write a 30-item Likert survey aligned to the facets.
Run EFA on the survey (example n = 300) and report Cronbach's α per factor (Trust 0.84, Ease 0.81, Engagement 0.86).
Read the signature: Engagement weakening while Ease stays strong indicates drift rather than a usability break.
Track proxies longitudinally and tie qualitative quotes to facets (e.g. 'Recommendations feel off' → Credible erosion).
outputs: A facet-to-proxy measurement map, factor structure with reliabilities, and a diagnosis of which facets are eroding.
useWhen: When you need a simple, teachable framework to locate perception-level erosion across a whole product.
avoidWhen: For bounded task diagnostics such as checkout (use HTA or usability testing); the honeycomb is too coarse for step-level errors.
whyLost: The honeycomb survived as a slide but not as a measurement model; rigour was lost when it became a checklist.
whereToUse: E-commerce, content and OTT, SaaS health scoring, drift and retention research.
example: An e-commerce app's survey shows Ease strong but Engagement weak, and interviews cite 'I only open for daily deals now', pointing to Desirable and Credible erosion rather than a usability defect.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
reference: Morville, P. (2004). User Experience Design (the UX Honeycomb), Semantic Studios.
keywords: useful usable desirable findable accessible credible valuable

name: Measurement-Burst Design
origin: Named after Stawski et al. (2015); worked example Dejonckheere et al. (2018)
summary: Repeat short bursts of intensive experience sampling at long intervals to study both moment-to-moment dynamics and how those dynamics change over months.
description: A measurement-burst design nests intensive repeated measurement inside a longitudinal study. Each burst is a few days of experience sampling with several prompts a day, capturing within-person dynamics such as emotional variability or the link between context and behaviour. Bursts are then repeated at intervals of months, so the analyst can estimate both short-term processes and long-term change, and individual differences in each. In the worked example, 202 participants completed three seven-day bursts at baseline, 4 and 10 months, each opened by a lab session, with ten semi-random prompts a day; a within-person index was computed per burst and related to later change in symptoms. Compliance stayed around 87-88% per wave with per-wave payment and a completion bonus. Identical schedules and items across bursts are essential, and attrition grows as the gap between bursts lengthens.
steps: Define the slow outcome (for example retention, wellbeing, skill) and the fast within-person process expected to drive it.
Schedule several bursts of a few days of intensive sampling separated by months (for example 7-day bursts at 0, 4 and 10 months).
Open each burst with a baseline session, questionnaires and device or app set-up.
Run the same semi-random schedule and items in every burst (for example 10 prompts a day).
Compute the within-person process per participant and burst, then relate it to between-person differences and later change, typically with multilevel models.
Pay per burst plus a completion bonus and over-recruit to cover attrition between bursts.
outputs: Within-burst dynamics per participant and wave, and their links to longer-term change.
useWhen: You need to know how daily experience with a product evolves as users move from novice to habitual use, or whether in-the-moment patterns predict later outcomes.
avoidWhen: Questions answerable with a single ESM period or with logs alone; use Experience Sampling Method or a Longitudinal Panel Study. Avoid if you cannot sustain participant contact for months.
whyLost: It is established in developmental and clinical psychology, but UX longitudinal research rarely combines intensive sampling with long follow-up.
whereToUse: Habit-forming and wellbeing apps, learning products, wearables, workplace tools during adoption, AI assistants as reliance develops.
example: A language-learning app runs three 7-day bursts at signup, 3 and 9 months, prompting learners five times a day about motivation and context; burst-level drops in motivational variability predict who stops studying by month nine.
sources: Designing an Experience Sampling Study (Dejonckheere & Erbas, 2021)
The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Dejonckheere, E., & Erbas, Y. (2021). Designing an experience sampling study. In I. Myin-Germeys & P. Kuppens (Eds.), The open handbook of experience sampling methodology (pp. 33-70). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven.

name: Measurement-error modelling
aka: Modelling measurement error in outcomes and predictors
origin: Spearman's disattenuation; SEM single-indicator form described by Hayduk and Bollen; Savalei (2018); Bayesian errors-in-variables treatment by McElreath (2020)
summary: Treats observed scores as noisy measures of true values, using known standard errors or reliabilities, so regression and path estimates are not distorted by measurement error.
description: Many UX variables are measured with known uncertainty: a success rate from a handful of participants, a rating averaged over few raters, a scale score with reliability below 1. Plugging such values into a regression as if exact biases coefficients, and not always towards zero. In the Bayesian errors-in-variables form, each true value is a parameter and the observed value is a draw around it with its known standard error, so imprecise points are shrunk and precise points carry more weight. In structural equation modelling, a single scale score becomes the sole indicator of a latent variable with loading 1 and error variance fixed at (1 - reliability) times its variance; this removes error from structural paths without changing fit. Because reliability is uncertain, estimates are rerun over a range of plausible values. Correlated errors must be modelled or the correction overshoots.
steps: Draw the causal diagram including the measurement step (true value, error, observed score) and note anything that affects error size, such as sample size per unit.
Obtain error information: standard errors per data point, or a reliability estimate for each scale from the sample, the manual or prior studies.
Bayesian route: declare true values as parameters with observed ~ Normal(true, se), and give error-prone predictors a prior that reflects their own causes.

SEM route: make each single scale score the indicator of a latent variable with loading 1 and error variance fixed to (1 - reliability) x observed variance; give covariates a small error (about 5%) rather than none.
Fit the model, check the sampler or estimation, and compare coefficients with and without the error model; plot observed against estimated true values to see shrinkage.
Run a sensitivity analysis across plausible reliabilities or error sizes and report the source of each reliability value.
outputs: Corrected coefficients or path estimates, posterior estimates of true values, shrinkage plots, and a sensitivity range across error assumptions.
useWhen: Regressing outcomes on aggregates estimated from very different sample sizes, or using single questionnaire totals such as SUS in path models where unreliability could bias conclusions.
avoidWhen: No defensible error model exists (no standard errors or reliability information), or measures are near-perfectly reliable. With several indicators per construct, a full latent-variable model is better than a single-indicator fix.
whyLost: UX analysis routinely averages data and discards uncertainty before modelling; errors-in-variables methods stay in psychometrics and Bayesian statistics texts.
whereToUse: Key driver analyses on survey scales, cross-feature analyses of success rates from uneven samples, SEM of UX constructs, meta-analysis of benchmark studies.
example: A team regresses overall satisfaction on per-feature task success rates, but rates come from 3 to 40 participants each. Adding each rate's standard error as a measurement model halves the apparent effect of two features whose extreme rates came from tiny samples.
sources: A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan (2nd ed.). CRC Press, pp. 490-499; Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (5th ed.). Guilford Press, pp. 276-282.

name: Measures of Effectiveness Hierarchy Across System Levels
aka: Tracing human performance to system success
origin: David Meister, 2004, drawing on operations research MOE handbooks (Rau, 1974) and Meister (1985)
summary: Decomposes a system into levels from workstation to command, sets suitable measures at each, and traces how operator performance and errors propagate to overall mission success.
description: Because human performance matters only through system output, Meister argues measurement must cover every relevant subsystem level and mission phase. Each level has its own measures: lower levels use performance measures (detection range, response time, errors), higher levels use effectiveness measures (mission success), and operator measures must be transformed as they move up (an operator's detection becomes an estimated target range for the commander). Time and error suit every level except the terminal one. The dependency of each level on the others has to be established, and measures that vary over time and across levels are the most informative. Where a direct causal trace is impossible, researchers should at least show parallel variation between human performance and system success. In product terms the levels might be screen, task, journey, account and business outcome, making this the human factors ancestor of metric trees that link UX metrics to business results.
steps: Map the system levels and subsystems from individual workstation or screen through team and journey up to the executive or business level, noting parallel subsystems.
Rank functions by importance to the system goal and select which ones to measure.
Choose measures suited to each level (performance measures low, effectiveness measures high) and define how lower-level values transform into higher-level ones.
Determine how each level depends on the others.
Collect data on the inputs people receive, what they do with them, and how deviations such as errors and delays affect other elements.
Trace, graphically if possible, the flow of effects up and down the levels to terminal output; where tracing fails, correlate variation in human performance with variation in system success.
outputs: A level-by-level measure set and an evidence-based account of how human performance contributes to system effectiveness.
useWhen: Justifying or prioritising human factors and UX work by showing how task-level errors and delays affect operational or business outcomes, in multi-person or multi-step systems.
avoidWhen: Simple single-user products where a metrics framework such as HEART suffices; the system cannot be observed across levels (use modelling such as task network simulation instead). Physical effectiveness measures can hide the human contribution.
whyLost: It was framed in military operations research; product teams rebuilt the idea as metric trees and UX-to-revenue chains without the cross-level dependency analysis.
whereToUse: Enterprise and operational software (contact centres, logistics, clinical systems), marketplaces with multiple user roles, and metric-tree design linking UX metrics to business KPIs.
example: A logistics company maps measures from scanner-screen errors to depot dispatch time to on-time delivery rate. Tracing shows a 3% mis-scan rate at loading adds an average 12 minutes per route and explains most of the variation in late deliveries between depots, which justifies redesigning the scanner confirmation screen.
sources: Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
reference: Meister, D. (2004). Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Mechanism Decomposition for Generalising Results
aka: Mechanism decomposition for generalising experimental results
origin: Alan Dix (2020)
summary: Break an experimental task into steps, reason about how each responds to the manipulated factor, and time the steps so a predictive formula replaces a single 'optimum'.
description: A study that finds one best setting rarely transfers. Dix revisits an early mobile study that declared one font size best for searching paginated menus. Decomposed, the task is visual search of a screen, paging to the next screen and selecting the item. Larger fonts help search and selection but increase paging, so the optimum is a trade-off set by menu length and screen resolution. With step times taken separately from logs, an exact page count and an empirical page-down time, one could write a formula that gives the best font size for any menu length and predicts other tasks with similar steps. Thinking in mechanisms also separates interpolation from extrapolation and makes replication meaningful.
steps: Write the experimental task as a sequence of user steps.
For each step, predict how the manipulated factor will affect it and in which direction.
Identify trade-offs between steps that make any single optimum specific to the task and device.
Instrument logs to time steps separately, and compute deterministic quantities (such as page counts) exactly.
Combine the step models into a formula or algorithm that predicts performance for new task parameters.
Use the model to make predictions before the study and to analyse and bound generalisation afterwards.
outputs: A predictive step model in place of a single best value, with explicit limits of generalisation.
useWhen: Comparing design parameters (sizes, densities, page lengths) where results must transfer to other screens, content volumes or tasks.
avoidWhen: You cannot log step-level timings, or you only need a one-off decision for a fixed context; a simple A/B comparison may suffice. Device details such as points versus pixels can dominate.
whyLost: UX experiments are usually reported as winner-takes-all comparisons; modelling mechanisms requires cognitive-modelling skills few teams have.
whereToUse: Mobile and wearable layout parameters, list and pagination design, search result density, automotive and kiosk interfaces.
example: An e-commerce team testing product-grid density decomposes browsing into scanning, scrolling and tapping, times each from logs, and builds a model predicting the best density for each category size rather than shipping one global winner.
reference: Dix, A. (2020). Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data. Morgan & Claypool. doi:10.2200/S00974ED1V01Y201912HCI044

name: Mechanism Design
origin: Leonid Hurwicz, 1960s-1970s; Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson (Nobel 2007)
summary: Works backwards from a desired outcome to design the rules, information and incentives of a system so that self-interested users produce that outcome.
description: Mechanism design inverts game theory: instead of predicting behaviour from fixed rules, it asks which rules will make strategic participants produce a desired outcome. Key properties are incentive compatibility (truthful behaviour is each participant's best strategy), individual rationality (participation is worthwhile) and efficiency or fairness of the outcome. In product terms, the 'mechanism' includes matching rules, pricing, reputation systems, what information is revealed when, and how rewards are allocated. A rigorous application specifies the objective formally, enumerates the information each party holds privately, proposes rules, proves or simulates their incentive properties, and then tests them with real users, since bounded rationality means people do not always follow the theoretically optimal strategy. Market designers such as Roth applied it successfully to kidney exchange and school choice.
steps: State the platform's objective formally (e.g. maximise successful matches subject to fairness constraints).
Identify participants, their private information and their likely strategic incentives.
Propose candidate rules: matching algorithm, pricing, information disclosure and reputation rules.
Analyse or simulate incentive compatibility and individual rationality under each candidate.
Pilot the preferred mechanism with real users and check for deviations from predicted behaviour.
Refine the interface so the incentive-compatible strategy is also easy to understand and act on.
outputs: Formal objective, mechanism specification, incentive analysis or simulations, pilot behavioural results.
useWhen: Designing marketplaces, allocation systems, bidding, reputation and reward schemes where participants can game the rules.
avoidWhen: Products without strategic participants or scarce resources; and where you lack data to estimate preferences.
whyLost: Rigorous in economics and computer science, it requires formal modelling skills UX teams rarely have, so platform rules are usually set by product and growth teams without explicit incentive analysis.
whereToUse: Marketplace platforms; auction UI; incentive and reward system design.
example: A volunteer shift app let volunteers grab shifts first-come-first-served, leaving unpopular slots empty. A redesigned mechanism using ranked preferences and a deferred-acceptance match filled 96% of shifts and reduced last-minute dropouts.
sources: Who Gets What and Why (Alvin Roth)
reference: Hurwicz, L., & Reiter, S. (2006). Designing Economic Mechanisms. Cambridge University Press.

name: Media Use and Exposure Measurement
origin: Anderson et al. (1985); Huston et al. (1990); Roberts, Foehr and Rideout (2005); Anderson and Hanson (2009); Vandewater and Lee (2009)
summary: Defines what counts as media exposure, chosen or ambient, quantity or content, single or simultaneous, then picks among seven measurement modes by accuracy, cost, reactivity and privacy.
description: Communication research learned that 'screen time' is not one thing. Foreground exposure is chosen; background exposure is incidental, and a set being on is barely related to looking. Eyes on screen is the best foreground measure, though looking is not attending. A media diet has both quantity and content. Total use counts clock time with any medium; total exposure sums simultaneous media, so 7 h 38 min of use became 10 h 45 min of exposure for 8- to 18-year-olds. Seven modes trade accuracy against cost: global estimates (cheap, used in national surveys, less accurate), time-use diaries, programme-level media diaries in 15-minute slots (among the most accurate), video observation (costly), experience sampling (disruptive), people meters (invasive) and tracking software (accurate, but privacy-heavy). Category definitions matter: excluding texting removed about two hours a day.
steps: Decide whether foreground, background or both is the target and define attention operationally, for example eyes on screen.
Separate quantity from content type to describe the media diet.
Decide whether to report use (clock time) or exposure (summing simultaneous media).

Choose a mode, global estimate, time diary, media diary at fixed intervals such as 15 minutes, video observation, experience sampling, meter or tracking software, weighing accuracy, cost, reactivity and privacy.
Fix and report category definitions (which devices and activities count) and keep them stable for trend comparisons.
Where possible, calibrate cheap global estimates against a more accurate mode in a subsample.
outputs: Time-in-media and exposure estimates by medium, content type and context, with a known bias profile.
useWhen: Studying screen time, attention, digital wellbeing or media diets, especially for children and families, or when a product claims to change usage time.
avoidWhen: When you only need in-product usage from your own logs (use Log File Analysis). Global estimates are inaccurate, observation costly, experience sampling disruptive, and meters or tracking invasive; choose consciously.
whyLost: UX relies on in-app analytics for time spent and rarely confronts background exposure, multitasking or definitional choices that media research formalised.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing features, children's apps and parental controls, streaming and smart TV, attention-economy ethics reviews.
example: A children's video app claiming to reduce screen time asks parents to keep 15-minute media diaries for a week and compares them with device tracking in a subsample, revealing substantial background TV the app's logs never saw.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Calvert, S. L. (2015). Children and digital media. In Lerner, R. M., Bornstein, M. H. and Leventhal, T. (eds) Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 4. Wiley, pp. 375-415.

name: Median Polish of Two-Way Tables
aka: Median polish of two-way tables, with two-way plots, coded residuals and diagnostic plot for re-expression
One degree of freedom for non-additivity
origin: John W. Tukey (1977)
summary: Fit common, row and column effects to a two-way table by repeatedly removing medians, then inspect residuals and a diagnostic plot suggesting re-expression.
description: Median polish is a resistant alternative to two-way analysis of variance for exploring a table such as task by design or segment by month. Row medians are subtracted, then column medians of the remainder, and the cycle repeats until changes are negligible, leaving a common term, row effects, column effects and residuals. Because medians are used, a few extreme cells do not distort the effects; instead they stand out as large residuals. Tukey then draws a two-way plot of the fit, codes the residuals and computes comparison values (row effect times column effect divided by the common term). Plotting residuals against comparison values gives a diagnostic: a slope near 1 suggests a multiplicative structure, so logs should be taken; other slopes give a PLUS-one fit. The method extends to three-way tables.
steps: Arrange the response (for example median task time) in a rows-by-columns table.
Subtract each row's median, then each column's median of what remains.
Repeat until the changes are negligible, typically two to four cycles.
Record the common value, row effects, column effects and residuals.
Draw a two-way plot of the fit and a coded display that highlights large residuals.
Compute comparison values and plot residuals against them; fit a slope.
If the slope is near 1, take logs and refit; otherwise consider a PLUS-one fit, and investigate cells with large residuals.
outputs: Resistant row and column effects, a residual table highlighting unusual cells, two-way and diagnostic plots, and a suggested re-expression.
useWhen: Exploring benchmark or analytics tables (task by product version, segment by month, page by device) where a few extreme cells would distort means and you want to see the structure and the anomalies.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need inferential tests or have many factors and covariates; use Multilevel Modelling (HLM / Mixed-Effects Models) or ANOVA-based approaches. The diagnostic plot needs judgement and rarely gives a clear answer from small tables.
whyLost: Tukey's exploratory tools were overshadowed by model-based statistics and spreadsheet pivot tables, and are seldom taught outside statistics.
whereToUse: Competitive benchmarks, conversion tables by channel and segment, longitudinal metric tables, cross-site usability comparisons.
example: A benchmark table of median task times for eight tasks across five competitor apps is median-polished. Row and column effects show one app slower overall, while a single large residual flags one task on one app as a specific failure worth investigating.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
reference: Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory Data Analysis. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, chapters 10-13.

name: Mediation analysis
origin: Baron & Kenny, 1986; bootstrap indirect effects by Preacher & Hayes, 2004/2008; causal mediation by Robins, Greenland and Pearl, 1992-2001
summary: Decomposes the effect of a cause on an outcome into a direct path and an indirect path through a mechanism, quantifying how a design change works.
description: Mediation analysis estimates whether X affects Y through an intermediate variable M, for example a redesign increases adoption because it raises perceived trust. The indirect effect (the product of the X-to-M and M-to-Y paths) is tested with bootstrap confidence intervals rather than the outdated Baron and Kenny causal-steps logic. Modern causal mediation makes the assumptions explicit: no unmeasured confounding of X-M, M-Y and X-Y, and no M-Y confounder affected by X. Rigour requires temporal ordering (M measured after X and before Y), ideally a randomised X, and sensitivity analysis for unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding. It is the quantitative bridge between a qualitative mechanism story and a measurable causal claim.
steps: Specify the mechanism from qualitative evidence and draw it as a causal diagram including likely confounders of M and Y.
Design measurement so X precedes M and M precedes Y; randomise X where possible.
Fit the mediator model (M on X plus covariates) and the outcome model (Y on X and M plus covariates).
Estimate the indirect effect with 5,000 or more bootstrap resamples and report the 95% percentile or bias-corrected interval.
Report the proportion mediated with caution and run a sensitivity analysis (e.g. the rho parameter of Imai et al.) for unmeasured M-Y confounding.
Interpret the mechanism in design terms and state the assumptions that would overturn it.
outputs: Direct, indirect and total effect estimates with bootstrap intervals, proportion mediated, a sensitivity analysis and a defensible mechanism statement.
useWhen: When you know or have tested that a change works and need to show why, or when choosing which intermediate experience metric to optimise.
avoidWhen: Avoid with cross-sectional single-survey data where ordering is unknown, when X is not randomised and confounders are unmeasured, or with tiny samples; use qualitative process tracing or a randomised mediator manipulation instead.
whyLost: Baron and Kenny's steps were widely misused and discredited, and the modern causal version needs assumptions most UX teams never articulate. It stayed in psychology and epidemiology.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption research in fintech, AI product explainability effects, onboarding mechanism studies, and justifying north-star intermediate metrics.
example: An experiment shows a new portfolio summary raises weekly retention. Mediation analysis finds 60% of the effect runs through reduced anxiety scores measured on day 3, so the team prioritises anxiety-reducing features over more data density.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis (Andrew Hayes)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers
Transforming UX Research with Structural Equation Modeling (Jozranjbar, n.d.)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed. Guilford Press.

name: Mediation analysis across activity hierarchy
origin: Aleksei Leont'ev's activity-action-operation hierarchy, 1978; applied to HCI by Kuutti (1996) and Kaptelinin and Nardi (2006)
summary: Analyses how tools mediate work at three levels, activity (motive), action (goal) and operation (conditions), and how use shifts between levels as skills automate or break down.
description: Leont'ev described human activity as a hierarchy: activities driven by motives, actions directed at conscious goals, and operations performed automatically under conditions. Tools mediate each level differently. As skill develops, actions become operations (automated); when breakdowns occur, operations become conscious actions again. Mediation analysis maps how a tool supports each level and examines transitions. A well-designed tool supports the motive, makes goals achievable and lets operations automate; poor tools force operations back into conscious attention. In UX this connects interface details to deeper motives, and explains why small interaction friction disrupts expert work. Rigour comes from observing breakdowns where levels shift, and from interviews that connect actions to motives.
steps: Identify the activity and its motive through interviews (for example 'restoring patient health safely').
Decompose into actions with goals and operations with conditions, through observation and task analysis.
For each level, describe how the tool mediates it: what it supports, constrains or ignores.
Observe breakdowns where operations become conscious actions and record the trigger (at least 3-5 work sessions).
Identify misalignments, such as tools optimised for actions that do not serve the motive.
Propose design changes that support automation of operations and alignment with motives.
outputs: A three-level activity hierarchy model, mediation analysis per level, breakdown records, and design recommendations.
useWhen: When studying tools in professional practice, explaining why technically usable tools disrupt work, or connecting UI decisions to motives.
avoidWhen: When you need quick usability findings on discrete tasks; use usability testing or HTA.
whyLost: Activity theory's hierarchy was influential in 1990s HCI but was displaced by simpler task analysis and jobs-to-be-done framing.
whereToUse: Clinical tools, professional creative software, enterprise workflows, and AI assistants for experts.
example: Surgeons' instrument swaps are automated operations on their old system, but on the new robot a confirmation dialog forces them into conscious action mid-procedure. Analysis shows this undermines the motive of uninterrupted focus, and the dialog is replaced by a reversible action.
sources: Newell, A., Unified Theories of Cognition (1990)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
reference: Kaptelinin, V. & Nardi, B. A. (2006). Acting with Technology: Activity Theory and Interaction Design. MIT Press.

name: Member Checking
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985
summary: Sharing specific interpretations with a diverse subsample of participants to check resonance, treating disagreement as data rather than as correction.
description: Member checking is the process of sharing your analytical interpretations with participants to check whether they recognise their experience in your analysis. It is NOT: showing participants a draft report, asking if they agree with your conclusions, or using participant approval as proof of validity. Participants are not co-authors of the analysis — they are informants about whether the interpretation resonates with their experience.
steps: What to share: Share your interpretation of specific themes — not the full report. "I noticed that several participants described a moment where they stopped trusting the system. I'm interpreting this as a trust collapse triggered by perceived unpredictability. Does this match your experience?"
How to ask: Open-ended, not leading. "Does this capture your experience?" not "Is this correct?" The former invites elaboration and correction; the latter invites agreement.
Who to check with: A purposive subsample of participants — those who represent diversity in your sample (not just the most articulate or most agreeable).

What to do with disagreement: Participant disagreement is data, not error correction. If a participant disagrees with your interpretation, ask: why do they see it differently? Is this a data-based correction or a politically motivated one? Document the disagreement and your reasoning.
outputs: Participant responses to specific interpretations, a record of agreements, elaborations and disagreements, and revised or qualified interpretations.
useWhen: When interpretations concern participants' own experience and meaning, especially across cultures, with marginalised groups, or where misinterpretation carries ethical risk.
avoidWhen: When findings concern behaviour participants cannot introspect on (use observation or analytics), or when sharing interpretations could cause harm or bias later waves of a longitudinal study.
whyLost: It decayed into sending participants a summary or asking 'did we get it right', which yields polite agreement and little validation.
whereToUse: Health and social care research, participatory design, global and cross-cultural studies, and co-design programmes with ongoing participant panels.
example: After interviews with gig workers about algorithmic pay, the team shares its interpretation of 'pay as gamble' with six varied participants. Two reject the gambling frame and describe it as 'being managed', refining the model.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Qualitative Methods in Information Retrieval Research (Fidel, 1993)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Analysing and Presenting Qualitative Data (Burnard et al., 2008)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Membership Categorisation Analysis
origin: Harvey Sacks, 1972; developed by Stephen Hester and Peter Eglin, 1997
summary: Analyses how people invoke social categories, such as novice, admin or patient, and their bound activities to accomplish actions in talk and text, including interface language.
description: Membership Categorisation Analysis, founded by Harvey Sacks, examines how people use categories in practice. Categories belong to collections (membership categorisation devices, such as 'family' or 'stage of life') and carry category-bound activities and predicates: we expect certain things of a 'beginner' or an 'admin'. By invoking a category, speakers justify, excuse or account for actions ('I'm not a tech person, so...'). MCA collects these invocations from transcripts and user-generated text and analyses what they accomplish, what inferences they license and what they exclude. Applied to interfaces, it audits the categories a product imposes on users and checks them against those users apply to themselves. Rigour comes from grounding claims in actual category use rather than analyst-imposed labels.
steps: Identify category invocations: In interview transcripts or user-generated content, mark every moment where a category is explicitly or implicitly invoked: 'as a user,' 'for someone like me,' 'unlike professionals,' 'that's for tech people.'

Category-bound activities analysis: What activities does the invoked category make relevant? Categories come pre-loaded with expected activities — invoking 'novice' makes asking for help relevant; invoking 'expert' makes independent action relevant.
Category-based inference analysis: What do users assume follows from a category? 'This is a children's product' triggers a set of assumptions about safety, simplicity, and appropriate content.

Interface category audit: What categories does the interface's language and design invoke? 'Advanced Settings' invokes a category of user who is not the default — what does that categorisation do to users who find themselves on that page?
outputs: A catalogue of category invocations, category-bound activities and predicates, inference patterns, and an interface category audit comparing system labels with users' self-categorisations.
useWhen: Personas, roles, permissions or labelling are contested, users describe themselves in ways the product does not anticipate, or self-categorisation ('not a numbers person') affects engagement.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural measures or task performance; categories in talk are not demographics. For broader discourse and power questions, use Critical Discourse Analysis.
whyLost: It is a specialist offshoot of conversation analysis taught almost exclusively in sociology departments, and UX treats categories as segmentation variables rather than as things people do in talk.
whereToUse: Role and permission design, persona critique, onboarding self-selection ('I am a...'), community and marketplace labels, and health or finance products where identity affects engagement.
example: In interviews about an investing app, users repeatedly say 'I'm not an investor, I'm just saving'. MCA shows 'investor' is bound to risk-taking and expertise, so onboarding language is reframed around 'growing savings', lifting completion.
reference: Hester, S. & Eglin, P. (eds.) (1997). Culture in Action: Studies in Membership Categorization Analysis. University Press of America.

name: Memorability Testing
origin: Jakob Nielsen, Usability Engineering (1993), as one of five usability attributes; caution from Mayes, Draper, McGregor and Oatley (1988)
summary: Measure how easily casual users return to a system after time away, by timing returning users on typical tasks or testing recall of commands and icons after a session.
description: Memorability is one of Nielsen's five usability attributes and matters for casual users of utilities, occasional applications and quarterly tasks, and for people returning from holidays. It is rarely tested thoroughly. Nielsen gives two versions. The performance version recruits users who have used the system before and been away for a specified interval, and times them on typical tasks. The memory version asks users after a session to explain what commands do, name the command for an action or draw the icon for a function, and scores correct answers. The performance version is more representative. The memory version is cheaper but misleads for recognition-based interfaces: Mayes and colleagues found users could not recall menu contents away from the system yet used the menus without difficulty.
steps: Decide which version fits: returning casual users (performance) or post-session recall (memory).
For the performance version, recruit users who used the system before and have been away for a specified interval, such as a month or a quarter.
Time them on typical tasks and count errors, comparing with their earlier performance or with frequent users.
For the memory version, at the end of a session ask users to explain given commands, name the command for given actions, or draw icons for given functions.
Score task times or the number of correct answers as the memorability measure.
Interpret recall scores cautiously for interfaces that rely on visible options and recognition.
outputs: Task times and error counts for returning users, or a memorability score from recall items.
useWhen: Products used intermittently: tax and benefits services, expense tools, annual enrolment, admin consoles, devices configured rarely.
avoidWhen: Avoid recall tests for graphical, recognition-based interfaces, where they understate memorability; for first-use learning use a learnability or experience-curve study instead.
whyLost: Learnability and first-use success dominate testing agendas, and returning-user studies need recruitment across a delay, so memorability is cited as an attribute but seldom measured.
whereToUse: Government services, insurance renewals, quarterly reporting tools, smart-home device settings, infrequently used features of SaaS products.
example: A payroll product invites customers who last ran year-end processing eleven months earlier to repeat it on the current release. Median time is double that of the previous year's final run, concentrated on finding the submission step, so the team adds a resumable checklist.
reference: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering. Boston: AP Professional, pp. 31-32, 194.

name: Memory Work
donor: Feminist sociology and qualitative sport and leisure research
origin: Collective memory-work, usually traced to Frigga Haug's group in Germany; cited by Veal and Darcy via Onyx and Small (2001) and Markula and Friend (2005)
summary: Participants each write a short account of a remembered experience on the topic, then read the accounts aloud and analyse them together as a group.
description: Memory work is a structured way of eliciting people's memories of events, which Veal and Darcy describe as a focus group aided by individual writing. Each participant writes a short account of a specific experience related to the research topic, for example power relationships in a sport organisation. The written accounts are read aloud in a group session and discussed, and the discussion may be followed by further writing or interviews. Writing first gives each person time to recall an episode in detail and in their own words before group dynamics take hold, while the group discussion brings out common patterns, differences and the taken-for-granted assumptions inside each story. In its original collective form participants act as co-researchers, analysing their own stories rather than handing them to a researcher. For UX it offers a route into experiences that are emotional, social or embarrassing, such as first encounters with a technology, moments of exclusion, or breakdowns of trust, and it fits co-design work where participants should own the interpretation. It needs a group with enough trust to share personal writing.
steps: Choose a focused trigger, such as 'a time when an app made you feel left out', and recruit a small group with shared relevant experience.
Ask each person to write a short, concrete account of one specific episode, in the third person if that eases disclosure.
Bring the group together and have each account read aloud.
Discuss each account: what happened, what was assumed, what is missing, and how it compares with the others.
Identify common themes and contradictions across the accounts with the participants.
Optionally ask for rewritten or further accounts, or follow up with individual interviews.
Combine the texts and discussion notes into an analysis that participants can check.
outputs: A set of written memory accounts, recorded group discussion, and jointly identified themes about the experience.
useWhen: You want rich, reflective accounts of sensitive or formative experiences and want participants to take part in interpretation.
avoidWhen: Participants lack trust or time, writing would exclude some people, or you need behavioural detail best gathered by observation.
whyLost: It is little known outside feminist and educational research, and UX interviews and focus groups rarely include a structured individual writing stage.
whereToUse: Inclusive design research, onboarding and first-use experiences, trust and safety, workplace tools, community and co-design programmes.
example: To understand why older members stop using a club's app, six members each write about a time they felt shut out by club technology, read the stories aloud and find a shared theme of being told 'it is all on the app' at the moment they needed a person.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Onyx, J. and Small, J. (2001) Memory-work: the method. Qualitative Inquiry, 7(6), 773-786.

name: Mental Chronometry
origin: F. C. Donders (1868); Saul Sternberg (1969)
summary: Infers the duration and structure of mental processing stages from response times under systematically manipulated conditions.
description: Named in the treatise's borrowing matrix for cognitive science, mental chronometry measures response times to infer cognitive processes. Donders' subtraction method compares tasks differing by one stage; Sternberg's additive factors method shows that factors affecting the same stage interact while those affecting different stages add. Related laws (Hick-Hyman for choice, Fitts for pointing) give predictive models. In UX it lets researchers attribute slowness to specific stages, such as visual search, decision or response selection, and test whether a design change shortens the stage it targets. Rigour requires many trials, control of speed-accuracy trade-offs and appropriate RT distributions (often log-transformed or ex-Gaussian).
steps: Hypothesise processing stages involved in the interaction.
Design conditions that selectively manipulate each stage (for example number of options, visual clutter).
Collect many trials per participant and condition, recording RT and accuracy.
Clean and transform RTs; analyse with mixed models.
Test additivity or interactions to locate stage effects.
Translate findings into design choices that target the slow stage.
outputs: RT estimates per condition, stage attribution, design implications.
useWhen: Optimising high-frequency micro-interactions, menus, icons, alerts and decision screens.
avoidWhen: Long, multi-step tasks where RT is confounded by many stages; use KLM or task analysis.
whyLost: Considered lab psychology; UX measures overall task time instead of stage-level processing.
whereToUse: Icon recognition, menu design, notification triage, AR overlays, gaming UI.
example: Menu RT grows with item count far less with alphabetic ordering than with categorical ordering for known-item search, an interaction revealing the search stage dominates.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Donders FC (1868/1969) On the speed of mental processes. Acta Psychologica 30
Sternberg S (1969) The discovery of processing stages. Acta Psychologica 30
Posner MI (1978) Chronometric Explorations of Mind
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
reference: Sternberg S (1969) The discovery of processing stages: extensions of Donders' method. Acta Psychologica 30:276-315.

name: Mental imagery paradigms: rotation, scanning and scaling
origin: Shepard and Metzler, 1971 (rotation); Kosslyn, Ball and Reiser, 1978 (scanning)
summary: Reaction-time paradigms that infer how people transform mental images, by measuring how response time grows with rotation angle, scanned distance or imagined size.
description: A family of chronometric tasks used to study visual imagery. In mental rotation, participants judge whether two drawings of 3-D block objects are the same object rotated or mirror images; reaction time for 'same' pairs rises linearly with angular disparity (roughly 2 s at 40 degrees, 4 s at 140 degrees), and the slope estimates rotation rate. In image scanning, people memorise a map with marked locations, then mentally move a speck between named points; RT rises linearly with map distance. Image-size and mental-walk variants show that small imagined details take longer to verify. Chambers and Reisberg's ambiguous-figure test checks whether images can be reinterpreted from memory. The rigour lies in parametric manipulation of a single variable and the linear-fit test, though the inference to analogue images has been disputed by propositional accounts (Pylyshyn).
steps: Choose the parameter to vary (angular disparity, map distance or imagined size) and define 5-7 evenly spaced levels.
For rotation, build same and mirror pairs at each angle; for scanning, have participants memorise a map until they can redraw it accurately.
Present trials in randomised order and record reaction time and accuracy for each response.
For scanning, cover every pair of locations (for example 21 trips among 7 points) so distance is not confounded with particular landmarks.
Discard error trials, then fit a linear regression of RT on the manipulated parameter for each participant.
Report the slope (for example degrees per second) and intercept, and compare slopes between display conditions.
outputs: Reaction-time functions against angle, distance or size; slopes as rotation or scanning rates; error rates by condition.
useWhen: You need to quantify the cognitive cost of rotated, mirrored or rescaled views, for example map orientation, AR overlays, CAD viewpoints or instructional diagrams.
avoidWhen: You want to know what people think or prefer rather than processing cost; data support more than one theoretical explanation, so do not claim an 'image' mechanism. For general navigation questions use wayfinding or tree testing instead.
whyLost: It stayed inside cognitive psychology's imagery debate and is framed as a test of theories rather than of designs. UX teams rarely run parametric RT studies.
whereToUse: Heading-up versus north-up maps, AR and VR navigation aids, 3-D product configurators, assembly instructions, medical imaging viewers.
example: A navigation app team shows drivers map snippets at 0-180 degrees offset from their heading and asks whether a turn is left or right. RT rises steeply beyond 90 degrees, supporting a heading-up default for turn-by-turn mode.
reference: Shepard, R. N., & Metzler, J. (1971). Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects. Science, 171, 701-703.

name: Mental Model Diagram
origin: Indi Young, 2008
summary: Builds a large diagram of users' tasks, thoughts and motivations grouped into towers and mental spaces, aligned beneath with the features that support them.
description: Indi Young's mental model diagram represents what people think, feel and do while pursuing a purpose, independent of any product. Non-directed interviews are transcribed and decomposed into atomic task-like behaviours, which are grouped bottom-up into towers and then into mental spaces arranged left to right across the diagram. Beneath a horizontal line, the team maps the features, services and content that currently support each tower. Gaps and weak support become opportunity areas, while the upper half remains stable over years because it describes people rather than technology. Rigour comes from deep, non-directed interviewing, faithful extraction of participants' own reasoning, and disciplined bottom-up grouping that resists imposing product categories.
steps: Step 1: Conduct 8–15 behavioral interviews.
Step 2: Extract behaviors and motivations as individual 'task' statements.
Step 3: Group related tasks into 'mental space' towers.
Step 4: Align existing product features to towers.
Step 5: Identify alignment gaps.
Build: a visual diagram with user behaviors above a horizontal line and product features below.
Width of alignment = product-market fit visualization.
outputs: A mental model diagram with towers and mental spaces, a support layer of current features, gap analysis and opportunity areas.
useWhen: Strategy and discovery work on broad problem spaces where you need a durable map of user reasoning independent of the current product, to find gaps and align teams.
avoidWhen: Avoid for narrow usability questions or when time is short; the full method needs many non-directed interviews and substantial synthesis. Use journey mapping or a jobs-to-be-done analysis for lighter needs.
whyLost: The full method is labour-intensive; 'mental model' became a loose phrase in UX, and the diagram was replaced by quicker journey maps.
whereToUse: Product gap analysis, roadmap prioritization, feature discovery research, product strategy validation.
example: A bank interviews 24 people about managing household money and builds a diagram with towers like 'decide whether we can afford it'; the support layer shows no feature addresses joint decision-making between partners.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
reference: Young I (2008) Mental Models: Aligning Design Strategy with Human Behavior. Rosenfeld Media

name: Mental Model Elicitation (Expected IA)
origin: Kenneth Craik, 1943 (mental models); expected-IA protocol in Gopinath, 2025
summary: Short contextual interviews asking where users expect to find a function and why, sketched as an 'expected IA' and compared with the real IA to predict misroutes.
description: Mental models are users' internal guesses of where something should be; when they do not match the information architecture, users wander, backtrack or give up. In the forward-thinking playbook the method is deliberately light: 4–8 quick contextual interviews with a prompt such as 'If you wanted to set a price alert, where would you look first? Why?', simple diagrams of each participant's expected IA, and a comparison with the actual IA. In the worked example 5 of 8 participants said alerts should be under Markets while the app placed them under Notifications, a mismatch that predicts confusion before any tree test. Verbatims and sketches are compiled in one worksheet and coded with short low-granularity labels such as 'Alerts under Markets' or 'Notifications = OS updates'. Combined with CPM-GOMS, it yields a falsifiable hypothesis about why and where time will spike.
steps: Choose the target functions whose location is in question.
Run 4–8 quick contextual interviews asking where participants would look first and why.
Sketch each participant's expected IA as a simple diagram.
Compile verbatims and sketches into one worksheet (participant, exact quote, expected IA, initial hunch).
Code utterances with short labels and count agreement (e.g. 5/8 expect Alerts under Markets).
Compare expected and actual IA and write a falsifiable misroute hypothesis for tree testing.
outputs: Expected-IA sketches, label codes, agreement counts and a misroute hypothesis.
useWhen: Early in IA work or before a tree test, to predict where and why users will misroute.
avoidWhen: When you need quantitative findability evidence; follow up with a tree test or first-click test.
whyLost: Mental-model research survives in UX, though often as an unstructured conversation rather than a coded comparison with the actual IA.
whereToUse: Navigation redesigns, fintech feature placement, enterprise settings, IA migrations.
example: Five of eight trading-app users say price alerts belong under Markets while the app buries them in Notifications, predicting misroutes later confirmed at 31% in a tree test.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Mental Models: Aligning Design Strategy with Human Behavior (Indi Young)
The Design of Everyday Things (Don Norman)
reference: Young, I. (2008). Mental Models: Aligning Design Strategy with Human Behavior. Rosenfeld Media.

name: Mentalese consistency check
donor: Philosophy of mind and cognitive science
origin: Jerry Fodor's language of thought hypothesis, 1975
summary: Tests whether users across roles hold the same underlying concepts for interface terms, by eliciting their conceptual representations rather than their vocabulary.
description: Fodor's language of thought hypothesis proposes that thinking occurs in an internal representational system, 'Mentalese', distinct from natural language. Whatever its status as a theory, it suggests a useful distinction for UX: users can share a word but not a concept, or share a concept expressed with different words. A Mentalese consistency check elicits the concepts users attach to key terms using non-verbal or structured methods, such as sorting scenarios, predicting outcomes, or drawing what the term refers to, and compares these across roles and with the system's model. Where concepts diverge under the same word, the interface is ambiguous even if every label passes a copy review. Rigour comes from scenario-based elicitation and systematic comparison across groups.
steps: Select critical terms used across roles (for example 'case', 'save', 'complete', 'session').
Write 8-12 scenarios illustrating different possible referents or effects of each term.
Ask participants from each role (5-8 per role) to judge which scenarios the term applies to and predict system effects.
Compare judgement patterns across roles and with the system's actual model; compute agreement (for example Fleiss' kappa within and between roles).
Flag terms with between-role agreement below about 0.6 or mismatches with system behaviour.
Resolve by splitting terms, adding qualifiers, or adjusting system behaviour, then re-check.
outputs: Concept maps per term and role, agreement statistics, divergences from the system model, and terminology changes.
useWhen: For multi-role systems, cross-disciplinary products, and terms carried across organisations or languages.
avoidWhen: When users are homogeneous and terminology is standard; a simple vocabulary review is enough.
whyLost: The language of thought is a philosophical hypothesis with no tradition of applied use; the practical idea of eliciting concepts rather than words has not been named in UX.
whereToUse: Healthcare systems shared by clinicians and administrators, legal tech, enterprise platforms, and AI assistants interpreting user intent.
example: Surgeons, nurses and administrators all endorse 'Complete' as a clear label, but scenario judgements show surgeons mean 'procedure finished', nurses 'counts reconciled' and admins 'billed'. Agreement between roles is 0.31, so the state is split into three explicit statuses.
sources: Fodor, J., The Language of Thought (1975)
Lakoff, G., Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 17 — Mentalese, Compositionality & the Language of Thought
reference: Fodor, J. A. (1975). The Language of Thought. Harvard University Press.

name: Mere exposure and incidental exposure preference test
origin: Robert Zajonc, 1968; Perfect and Askew, 1994
summary: Expose people to stimuli at controlled frequencies, or incidentally beside another task, then measure liking, showing how much preference comes from familiarity alone.
description: In the mere exposure paradigm, unfamiliar stimuli (shapes, characters, faces, logos) are shown at systematically different frequencies, often too briefly to notice repetition; later ratings show that liking rises with exposure, even without recognition. The incidental variant has people read articles each faced by an advertisement they are not told to attend to; later the seen adverts are rated more appealing although people recognise only a few of them. Very high exposure can tip into boredom, and familiar brands can produce ambivalence. For UX the paradigm is both a method and a caution: existing users have had heavy exposure to the current design, so part of any preference for it is familiarity rather than merit. Rigour depends on counterbalancing which stimulus gets which frequency, unexposed control items and a separate recognition check.
steps: Choose stimuli new to all participants (logos, icons, layouts, adverts) and include unexposed control items.
Assign exposure frequencies (for example 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 25 showings) and counterbalance stimulus-to-frequency assignment across participants.
Present stimuli briefly in a mixed sequence under a cover task, or beside content people are reading.
After a delay, collect liking or preference ratings for all stimuli, including unshown ones.
Run a separate recognition test to see whether the effect holds without awareness.
Plot liking against exposure frequency and estimate the familiarity share of any preference.
outputs: A liking-by-exposure curve, rating differences between exposed and unexposed items, and recognition rates.
useWhen: Interpreting redesign tests where current users prefer the old design, testing brand and icon familiarity, or estimating the implicit effect of banner and in-feed ads.
avoidWhen: Avoid when stimuli cannot be counterbalanced, since quality is confounded with frequency; for explicit attitude measurement use a semantic differential.
whyLost: The effect is widely cited but almost never run as a controlled test; teams discuss change aversion without measuring how much is familiarity.
whereToUse: Rebrands, icon and logo redesigns, advertising and sponsored content, misinformation exposure, A/B tests with long-tenured users.
example: Before a logo change, new and old marks are shown at counterbalanced frequencies to fresh participants; the old mark's advantage disappears at equal exposure, so the existing preference is judged to be familiarity.
sources: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology Monograph Supplement, 9
reference: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2, Pt. 2), 1-27.

name: Messaging Strategy Meeting
aka: Messaging strategy meeting (buyer expectations versus capabilities, ranked for competitiveness and buyer value)
Competitive ranking and relative value ranking
origin: Adele Revella (2015), Buyer Personas
summary: A two-session workshop that matches the team's capabilities to research-based buyer expectations, then ranks each statement for competitive uniqueness and value to the buyer.
description: Revella's messaging meeting turns buyer persona research into ranked, evidence-backed claims. Four to six people (a solution expert, a competitive expert and the eventual writer) work with a moderator who speaks for the persona, in about three hours on each of two days, and no copywriting happens in the room. Participants privately list up to ten capabilities, which the moderator merges; 16 to 20 insight headlines from the persona become a Buyer's Expectations list. Day 1 reads each expectation aloud with its buyer quotes and matches it to specific capability proof, dropping expectations the company cannot meet and noting orphan capabilities. Day 2 ranks each statement 1 to 3 for competitive uniqueness and A to C for buyer value. Sorting yields the short-message bullets and a positioning statement.
steps: Before the meeting, collect each participant's private list of up to ten capabilities and merge them into a Capabilities List.
