Copy 16 to 20 insight headlines from the buyer persona research into a Buyer's Expectations list.
Day 1: read each expectation aloud with its buyer quotes; remove expectations you cannot meet and match each remaining one to specific capability proof, with the moderator challenging generic claims.
Day 2: rank each statement 1 (competitors cannot claim it), 2 (they can, but you can prove superiority) or 3 (easily matched).
Rank each statement A, B or C for value to the buyer, judged from the urgency in quotes or from a survey.
Sort, pick the top statements for about five short-message bullets and a positioning statement, and hand the spreadsheet and persona to copywriters.
outputs: A ranked spreadsheet of capability statements, about five short-message bullets and a positioning statement.
useWhen: Use it when product marketing, product and UX need to agree which value claims to lead with on landing pages, onboarding or sales material.
avoidWhen: Value rankings are judgements unless tested; validate them with a Preference Test, MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) or message testing. It needs real buyer interviews behind the persona; without them use Customer problem interviews first.
whyLost: It belongs to B2B product marketing, where it is still used, but UX teams rarely join messaging work despite owning much of the copy users see.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS positioning, landing and pricing pages, onboarding copy, sales enablement and product launches.
example: A network-services supplier finds its buyers care most about fallout from a flawed release rather than new features. Most high-value statements rank 2 competitively, so messaging leads with proven reliability evidence.
reference: Revella, A. (2015). Buyer Personas: How to Gain Insight into Your Customer's Expectations, Align Your Marketing Strategies, and Win More Business. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, ch. 8.

name: Meta-Analysis of UX Studies
origin: Gene Glass (1976) coined the term; DerSimonian and Laird (1986) random-effects model; Cochrane Collaboration (1993)
summary: Statistically combines effect sizes from multiple studies or experiments, estimating an overall effect, its heterogeneity and moderators.
description: Organisations run hundreds of studies and experiments but rarely combine them. Meta-analysis converts each study's result into a common effect size with its variance, pools them (fixed or random effects, the latter allowing true effects to vary), and quantifies heterogeneity (tau squared, I squared, prediction intervals). Meta-regression explores moderators like platform or market. Publication bias checks (funnel plots, Egger's test) are directly relevant to internal research too, as unreported null tests bias institutional memory. Within a company, meta-analysis of past A/B tests yields realistic priors and shows whether design patterns generalise.
steps: Define the question and inclusion criteria for studies or experiments.
Extract effect sizes and their standard errors consistently (e.g. log odds ratios, standardised mean differences).
Fit a random-effects model and report the pooled effect, confidence interval and prediction interval.
Quantify heterogeneity (I squared, tau) and run meta-regression on planned moderators.
Assess small-study or publication bias with funnel plots and sensitivity analyses.
Summarise implications, including when the pattern should not be expected to replicate.
outputs: Pooled effect sizes, heterogeneity estimates, moderator analyses, forest plots and bias assessment.
useWhen: Synthesising multiple experiments or studies on a recurring design question, or building priors.
avoidWhen: Studies too heterogeneous in question or measures to combine meaningfully; use narrative or qualitative synthesis.
whyLost: UX research operations focus on new studies and repositories of insights, not quantitative synthesis.
whereToUse: A/B test programmes, design pattern libraries, benchmark programmes, academic HCI syntheses.
example: A retailer meta-analyses 47 past tests of urgency messages. The pooled effect on conversion is small (+0.8%) with wide prediction interval and evidence of small-study effects, so urgency is no longer a default recommendation.
sources: Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins & Rothstein, Introduction to Meta-Analysis (2009)
DerSimonian & Laird, Meta-analysis in clinical trials (1986), Controlled Clinical Trials
Higgins et al. (eds.), Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (2019)
The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
reference: Borenstein, M., et al. (2009). Introduction to Meta-Analysis. Wiley.

name: Metaphor Exploration
aka: Organisational, functional and visual metaphor brainstorming
origin: Rosenfeld and Morville, Information Architecture, 1998 onwards
summary: Brainstorm organisational, functional and visual metaphors for an information environment, then test each against real content and user scenarios before adopting any.
description: Metaphors explain, excite and persuade, so they are useful idea generators for information environments. Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango distinguish three kinds: organisational metaphors borrow a familiar system's structure (a car dealership's departments), functional metaphors borrow its tasks (a library's browsing shelves, searching the catalogue, asking the librarian) and visual metaphors borrow its graphics. The team brainstorms freely with clients or colleagues, then reviews critically: it populates a rough metaphor-based architecture with random items of expected content to see whether they fit, and runs one or two user scenarios through it. The check matters because people fall in love with metaphors, and strong metaphors limit growth, as the mid-1990s Internet Public Library and 'virtual town' communities showed.
steps: Tell participants up front that this is an exercise, not a commitment.
With clients or colleagues, brainstorm candidate metaphors for the environment.
For each candidate, work out its organisational, functional and visual applications.
Build a rough architecture for the strongest metaphors and populate it with random items from the expected content.
Run one or two user scenarios through each to see where the metaphor breaks.
Decide what, if anything, to carry forward, often a partial or functional metaphor only.
outputs: Candidate organising ideas and a judgement of which metaphors survive content and scenario checks.
useWhen: Early IA or concept work for a new information space where the team needs fresh organising ideas.
avoidWhen: Metaphors limit growth and can confuse users who do not share them; test understanding with Tree Testing, Card Sorting or Mental Model Elicitation (Expected IA). For analysing the metaphors users themselves use, use Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) or Metaphor Identification Procedure (MIP/MIPVU).
whyLost: Interface metaphors are still adopted, but the critical content-and-scenario check is usually skipped, and literal metaphors fell out of favour after skeuomorphism.
whereToUse: Intranets, digital libraries, learning platforms, AI assistants (the 'assistant' or 'copilot' metaphor), spatial and VR interfaces.
example: A research-repository team brainstorms 'library', 'newsroom' and 'lab notebook' metaphors; populating each with real study artefacts shows only the newsroom's functional tasks (file, tag, publish) scale, so they adopt those verbs without the visuals.
reference: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. and Arango, J. (2015) Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond. 4th edn. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Metaphor Identification Procedure (MIP/MIPVU)
origin: George Lakoff and Mark Johnson (Metaphors We Live By, 1980); Pragglejaz Group (2007); Gerard Steen et al. (MIPVU, 2010)
summary: Reliably identifies metaphorically used words in user language and groups them into conceptual metaphors that reveal how users think about a product or domain.
description: Conceptual metaphor theory holds that we understand abstract domains through concrete ones (ARGUMENT IS WAR; TIME IS MONEY). Identifying metaphors in discourse used to be intuitive and unreliable. The Pragglejaz Group's MIP gives a step-by-step procedure: read the text, determine lexical units, establish each unit's contextual meaning, check whether it has a more basic meaning in other contexts, and mark it metaphorical if the contextual meaning contrasts with but can be understood by comparison with the basic one. MIPVU refines this and reports high inter-coder reliability. Applied to interviews and reviews, it reveals users' conceptual models (the cloud as a place, AI as a person, money as water) that shape expectations and errors.
steps: Select texts: interview transcripts, reviews, support chats about the domain.
Apply MIP/MIPVU word by word: determine lexical units, contextual and basic meanings, and mark metaphor-related words, using a dictionary such as Macmillan for basic senses.
Check reliability with two coders on a sample (kappa typically above 0.8 is attainable).
Group metaphor-related words into source-target mappings (e.g. DATA IS A LIQUID: leaks, flows, streams).
Compare dominant metaphors across segments and contexts, and relate them to expectations and errors.
Use productive metaphors in interface language and avoid misleading ones.
outputs: Reliably coded metaphors, conceptual metaphor inventory, segment comparisons and language recommendations.
useWhen: Understanding how users conceptualise abstract products (cloud, AI, privacy, money) and designing interface metaphors and copy.
avoidWhen: Concrete, task-focused language where metaphor is minimal.
whyLost: Cognitive linguistics methods stayed in linguistics; UX discusses interface metaphors without analysing users' metaphors systematically.
whereToUse: AI assistants, privacy settings, cloud storage, personal finance, health conditions.
example: MIPVU analysis of 40 interviews about an AI assistant finds users predominantly use AI IS AN EMPLOYEE metaphors, expecting accountability; the product adds visible 'work history' and correction features.
sources: Pragglejaz Group, MIP: A method for identifying metaphorically used words in discourse (2007), Metaphor and Symbol
Steen et al., A Method for Linguistic Metaphor Identification: From MIP to MIPVU (2010)
Lakoff & Johnson, Metaphors We Live By (1980)
reference: Pragglejaz Group (2007). Metaphor and Symbol, 22(1), 1-39.

name: Metaphor Inference-Preservation Check
aka: Metaphor inference-preservation check (model-building constraints for a proposed metaphor)
origin: George Lakoff and Rafael Núñez (2000), building on Chiu (1996)
summary: Test a proposed metaphor by carrying every source-domain inference through the mapping and checking that each target property is produced and none wrongly.
description: Lakoff and Núñez treated all properties and inferences of a target domain (arithmetic) as data a metaphor analysis must account for, and imposed five constraints: the metaphor arises from everyday co-occurrence of source and target; every target property and inference follows from source plus mapping; the analysis fits and extends what is known; it is maximally general; and it fits what is known about embodied cognition. Starting from earlier proposals, they revised mappings until the constraints held. Most candidate sources failed, and even the four good grounding metaphors (object collection, object construction, measuring stick, motion along a path) did not all supply zero or negatives, which needed an extra metaphor. For interface design, the same discipline checks a proposed interaction metaphor (folders, carts, wallets, timelines) for inferences users will draw that the system does not honour, and for system behaviours the metaphor cannot explain.
steps: List all properties, behaviours and inferences of the target system that the metaphor must account for.
Propose a source domain that users actually experience together with the target in everyday life.
Write the mapping table of source-to-target correspondences.
Carry each source inference through the mapping and check whether the target honours it, marking false inferences.
Check that every target property is produced by some mapping, and record gaps (behaviours the metaphor cannot explain).
Revise the mapping, add a supplementary metaphor or change the design, and iterate until coverage is complete and consistent.
outputs: A validated mapping table, a list of false inferences and uncovered behaviours, and design or copy changes to close them.
useWhen: You are choosing or auditing an interaction or explanatory metaphor (for a file system, wallet, AI memory, data pipeline) and want to predict where it will mislead users.
avoidWhen: You need to know which metaphors users spontaneously hold; elicit them with interviews, ZMET or metaphor identification first, then apply this check. The evidence base outside clearly distinct domains is thin.
whyLost: It is presented as internal methodology in a cognitive science book about mathematics, so designers adopted the idea of metaphor without its validation discipline.
whereToUse: Interface and product metaphors, AI system explanations, onboarding copy, financial and data products, and educational technology.
example: A team describing an AI assistant's memory as a 'notebook' maps notebook inferences and finds users would expect to see, edit and tear out pages, none of which the system supports, so it adds a visible memory list with delete controls.
reference: Lakoff, G., & Núñez, R. E. (2000). Where Mathematics Comes From: How the Embodied Mind Brings Mathematics into Being. Basic Books.

name: Metaphor-based icon simulation test
donor: Cognitive linguistics (conceptual metaphor theory) and icon comprehension testing
origin: Combines Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual metaphor theory (1980) with icon comprehension testing traditions (ISO 9186) and embodied simulation accounts of meaning (Barsalou, 1999)
summary: Tests whether users possess the source-domain experience a metaphorical icon depends on, by asking them to simulate and predict what tapping it will do.
description: Most interface icons are metaphors: a trash can for deletion, a floppy disk for saving, a wallet for stored value. Embodied cognition holds that understanding a metaphor involves mentally simulating the source experience. If a user has never handled the source object, or handles it differently, the simulation fails or produces the wrong prediction. This test separates two layers that ordinary icon tests conflate: recognising the depicted object, and simulating the right action from it. Participants first name the object, then describe what they would expect to happen if they used it, and finally predict the system consequence. Rigour comes from scoring each layer separately, sampling users with different source-domain experience, and using pre-set pass thresholds rather than impressionistic judgement.
steps: Select the metaphorical icons that carry critical or irreversible actions, and for each write down the intended source object, the intended simulated action and the intended system consequence.

Recruit at least 15 to 20 participants per segment, deliberately including users whose material environment differs from the designers' (for example no desktop computers, no paper filing, cash-only economies).
Present each icon in isolation, then in context, and ask in sequence: 'What object is this?', 'What would you do with this object in daily life?', 'If you tap it here, what will happen?'
Score each response on three layers (object recognised, source action correct, system consequence correct) using a pre-agreed rubric, with a second scorer on at least 25% of responses.

Apply a pass criterion per icon, for example at least 85% correct system-consequence predictions and no more than 5% critical confusions for destructive actions, following ANSI Z535.3 practice for safety symbols, or 66.7% under ISO 9186 for general symbols.
Diagnose failures by layer: object not recognised means a depiction problem; object recognised but wrong action means a metaphor transfer failure requiring a different source domain or a text label.
Redesign and retest failing icons with fresh participants until they meet the threshold.
outputs: Per-icon, per-segment scores on recognition, source-action simulation and consequence prediction, a list of critical confusions, and design recommendations by failure layer.
useWhen: Shipping icon-heavy interfaces to users with different material cultures, literacy levels or ages; icons trigger irreversible or financial actions.
avoidWhen: Icons are always paired with clear text labels and users read them, or the icon set is a mature platform convention for an expert audience; use a standard first-click test.
whyLost: UX icon testing collapsed into simple recognition or preference tests, and the embodied simulation layer from cognitive science was never operationalised, so failures caused by missing source experience go undiagnosed.
whereToUse: Low-literacy and first-time smartphone users, healthcare devices, kiosks, cross-cultural apps, children's products.
example: In a clinic tablet app, rural health workers recognised the trash-can icon as a bin but simulated 'storing for later', because at their clinic waste paper was kept and reused. Destructive-action predictions were only 40% correct; adding the label 'Delete forever' and a confirmation raised correct predictions above 90%.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 19 — Neural Framing & the Architecture of Meaning
reference: Lakoff, G., & Johnson, M. (1980). Metaphors We Live By. University of Chicago Press; ISO 9186-1:2014 Graphical symbols: Test methods, Part 1: Method for testing comprehensibility.

name: Method Lifecycle Analysis
donor: Diffusion of innovations / history of science
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Places a method on a lifecycle of lab development, early adoption, mainstream simplification, decline and obsolescence, to anticipate degradation.
description: The treatise argues methods have lifecycles. A method begins in an academic or research lab, refined against theory and validated in controlled studies. Early adoption follows among practitioners close to the research context through training, associations or conferences. If it reaches critical mass it enters mainstream practice, typically becoming simplified, standardised and stripped of theoretical nuance. Decline then follows from some combination of the seven causes. Lifecycle analysis shows that the mainstream phase itself is where vestigialisation happens, so organisations can protect a method's rigour while scaling it, for example by maintaining a canonical protocol, training and quality checks.
steps: Gather the method's publication history, adoption evidence and current practice descriptions.
Date its phases: development, early adoption, mainstream, decline.
Compare current practice with the original protocol to measure simplification.
Identify at-risk elements (theory, analysis steps, quality checks).
Plan protections: canonical protocols, training, quality review.
Revisit periodically.
outputs: Lifecycle timeline, fidelity gap analysis, protection plan.
useWhen: Scaling a method across a large team, or auditing whether a popular method has degraded.
avoidWhen: Brand-new methods with no adoption history.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: ResearchOps, method playbooks, UX education.
example: A team scaling 'jobs-to-be-done' interviews to 30 PMs documents the original protocol and adds review checklists to avoid it becoming a vestigial survey.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 19/31 (Lifecycle of a UX Method).

name: Method Recovery Priority Index
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Rates lost and cross-domain methods on evidence base, recovery feasibility and expected impact (1-5 stars) to assign HIGH or MEDIUM revival priority.
description: The treatise's appendix rates candidate methods on three dimensions: Current Evidence Base (how much validated research supports the method), Recovery Feasibility (how practical it is to revive in contemporary contexts) and Expected Impact (the improvement in UX outcomes widespread recovery would bring), each scored one to five stars, with an overall priority of HIGH or MEDIUM. For example, Wizard of Oz scores 4/5/5 (HIGH), Braun and Clarke thematic analysis 5/5/5 (HIGH), and CWA and STAMP/STPA 5/2/5 (MEDIUM because feasibility is low). The index makes recovery investment explicit and comparable, and can be applied by any team to its own candidate methods with local feasibility judgements.
steps: List candidate methods for recovery or adoption.
Rate evidence base from the literature (1-5).
Rate recovery feasibility given skills, tools, time and organisational context (1-5).
Rate expected impact on decisions and user outcomes (1-5).
Assign priority (for example HIGH when impact and evidence are high and feasibility is at least 3).
Plan recovery for HIGH methods and revisit ratings annually.
outputs: Scored priority table, recovery roadmap.
useWhen: Planning training, method adoption and ResearchOps investment.
avoidWhen: Single-study method choice.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research leadership planning, curricula, professional association agendas.
example: A research org scores 15 methods; DiD and multilevel modelling score HIGH with feasibility 4 given its data team, so both become quarterly training priorities.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Drummond MF et al. (2015) Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes (priority-setting analogue)
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Appendix B (Method Recovery Priority Index).

name: Methodological Diversity as Risk Management
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Treats a research organisation's method range as a portfolio, maintaining dormant competence in diverse methods as insurance against changing conditions.
description: The treatise draws on agricultural monoculture: identical crops are maximally efficient in good conditions and maximally vulnerable to pathogens and stress. A research organisation relying on one methodological approach is efficient when it fits and maximally vulnerable when conditions change (new technologies, new questions, regulation). Methodological diversity is therefore organisational risk management, and maintaining dormant capacity is like insurance: costly when unused, valuable when needed. The practice audits the method portfolio against anticipated questions, identifies concentration risk (for example only interviews and A/B tests) and invests in training, partnerships and protocols to keep a broader range available.
steps: Inventory methods the team can execute competently today.
Map them against the question types the organisation faces or may face.
Identify concentration risk and uncovered question types.
Decide which dormant capacities to maintain (training, partners, templates).
Exercise dormant methods periodically through small projects.
Review the portfolio annually alongside strategy changes.
outputs: Method portfolio map, coverage gaps, capacity maintenance plan.
useWhen: Research org planning, after strategy shifts (for example AI products, regulation).
avoidWhen: Very small teams where focus is necessary; partner externally instead.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research leadership, ResearchOps, agencies, in-house labs.
example: A fintech research team relying on interviews and A/B tests adds causal inference and UFMEA capacity before entering regulated lending, which pays off in the regulator's first review.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Markowitz H (1952) Portfolio selection. J Finance (portfolio analogy)
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 34 (Methodological Diversity as Risk Management).

name: Metric Quality Audit
aka: Signs of success and signs of trouble checklist
origin: Croll and Yoskovitz (2013), after Avinash Kaushik; Bob Frost (2007)
summary: Checks each tracked metric against explicit quality criteria and known failure signs, dropping vanity metrics that change no decision and fixing those that invite gaming.
description: The audit combines two checklists. Croll and Yoskovitz define a good metric as comparative, understandable, a ratio or rate, and behaviour-changing; the test for vanity is to ask what you will do differently because of the number. Totals such as sign-ups, hits, page views, followers and downloads are vanity; percentage of users active is actionable. They also classify metrics as qualitative or quantitative, exploratory or reporting, leading or lagging, correlated or causal. Frost adds seven signs of success (pedigree back to a critical success factor, line of sight to action, proper comparatives, encourages right actions, valid and reliable, graphic reporting, cost effective) and eight signs of trouble, including one-number indices that mask offsetting changes, starting from available data (the lamp-post problem), ratios that invite denominator management, unquestioned vendor metrics, complex formulas and drowning in metrics.
steps: List the metrics the team checks regularly, starting with the three to five looked at daily.
For each, check whether it is comparative, understandable, a rate or ratio, and traceable to a goal or critical success factor.
Ask what you would do differently based on it; mark those without an answer as vanity.
Check for signs of trouble: composite indices, metrics chosen because data existed, ratios whose denominator can be gamed, vendor defaults, formulas outsiders cannot explain, and too many metrics.
Test comprehension by asking people outside the team to explain each metric.
Drop or replace failing metrics and pair related ones (for example conversion rate with time to purchase) to expose trade-offs.
outputs: A pruned, actionable metric set with documented rationale and a list of metrics at risk of gaming.
useWhen: When dashboards have grown unwieldy, before adopting a new metric framework, or when metrics seem to drive odd behaviour.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for validating what metrics measure; pair with External and Multi-Instrument Validation of Analytics Metrics. Beware false metrics that people game, such as sales pay tied to pipeline size.
whyLost: 'Vanity metrics' survives as a slogan, but the systematic checklist audit is seldom carried out.
whereToUse: Product dashboards, OKR reviews, UX measurement programmes, AI product evaluation metrics.
example: A learning platform's dashboard tracks total registered learners; the audit replaces it with the percentage completing a lesson within seven days of sign-up and pairs it with lesson satisfaction.
reference: Croll, A. and Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics. O'Reilly Media; Frost, B. (2007). Designing Metrics: Crafting Balanced Measures for Managing Performance. Dallas, TX: Measurement International.

name: Metric-wellbeing gap measurement
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Methods Atlas; informed by subjective wellbeing measurement (Diener, 1984) and digital wellbeing research
summary: Quantifies the divergence between the metric a product optimises and users' measured wellbeing or long-term outcomes, showing when success on the metric masks harm.
description: Products often succeed on engagement metrics while users feel worse or make poorer decisions. This method pairs behavioural metrics with validated wellbeing or outcome measures for the same users (such as anxiety, decision confidence, financial health or regret) collected through surveys or experience sampling, and models the relationship. A gap exists when high metric values coincide with flat or worse wellbeing, or when increments in the metric yield diminishing or negative wellbeing returns. Rigour requires validated wellbeing instruments, linking at the user level with consent, longitudinal measurement to separate cause from selection, and segment-level analysis because harms often concentrate in vulnerable groups.
steps: Select the optimised metric (e.g. weekly sessions) and validated wellbeing or outcome measures relevant to the domain (e.g. a financial anxiety scale).
Recruit a consented panel of at least 300-500 users and link survey responses to behavioural data.
Measure wellbeing at baseline and again after 4-12 weeks, or use experience sampling around product use.
Model wellbeing as a function of the metric, plotting the relationship and testing for non-linearity.
Compute a gap index, such as the proportion of high-metric users in the bottom wellbeing quartile, by segment.
Report the gap with guardrail recommendations and, where possible, test alternative designs experimentally.
outputs: A quantified metric-wellbeing relationship, gap indices by segment and recommendations for guardrails or objective changes.
useWhen: When engagement or conversion is optimised in domains where user wellbeing or outcomes matter, such as finance, health, social and gaming.
avoidWhen: Avoid when no validated wellbeing measure fits the domain, without user consent for linking data, or for low-stakes utilities.
whyLost: Product teams track what is easy to log; wellbeing measurement requires surveys, consent and longitudinal design that rarely fit sprint cycles.
whereToUse: Investment and trading apps, social media, mobile games, health and fitness apps, AI companions.
example: An investment platform links engagement data with a financial anxiety scale for 800 users. The top engagement decile has anxiety scores 0.6 SD higher than median users, prompting a calmer notification strategy and an anxiety guardrail.
sources: Peters, Calvo & Ryan (2018) Designing for motivation, engagement and wellbeing in digital experience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 58 — AI Explainability & Value Alignment Audit
reference: Peters, D., Calvo, R. A. & Ryan, R. M. (2018) Designing for motivation, engagement and wellbeing in digital experience. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 797.

name: Micro-Phenomenological Interviewing
origin: Pierre Vermersch, 1994 (explicitation interview); Claire Petitmengin, 2006 (micro-phenomenology)
summary: A guided interview that helps participants re-evoke a specific singular moment and describe its fine-grained, pre-reflective experiential structure, which ordinary recall misses.
description: Micro-phenomenology (Claire Petitmengin) and the Explicitation Interview (Pierre Vermersch) are techniques for accessing the detailed lived experience of specific moments — including the pre-reflective, bodily, and implicitly enacted aspects of experience that ordinary retrospective description cannot reach. Where standard phenomenological interviews produce generalised accounts ('usually when I do X...'), micro-phenomenology aims at one specific singular moment: 'right at that moment, what was happening in your experience?' Applied to UX: it accesses the moment-by-moment phenomenological texture of a specific interaction — the exact sequence of awarenesses, doubts, decisions, and embodied responses that constitute the interaction as it is lived.
steps: Select a specific singular moment: 'I'd like to understand what happened for you at one very specific moment — the moment when you realised something wasn't working as expected. Can you go back to that particular moment?'

Evocation posture: Help the participant return experientially to the moment — not report about it. Use: 'As you return to that moment — what do you notice first?' 'As you are there, what is happening in your body?' The present-tense phrasing is deliberate.

Sequential micro-structure: Once the participant is in evocation, explore the temporal micro-structure: 'Just before that, what happened?' 'At that precise moment, what was the first thing you were aware of?' 'And then?'

Pre-reflective access: Guide the participant toward what was happening before they started thinking about it: 'Before you had time to think — what was already happening?' 'Was there a bodily sense of anything?'
Analysis: Build a detailed temporal map of the experiential sequence for this singular moment. Compare across participants to identify shared experiential structures.
outputs: Detailed descriptions of singular moments, temporal and diachronic maps of experience, synchronic structure of each phase, and generic structures across participants.
useWhen: You need to understand fast, implicit moments such as the instant of distrust, a decision to abandon, an insight or an error, where users give generalised or rationalised accounts.
avoidWhen: You need breadth across many users or general opinions; use semi-structured interviews or surveys. Avoid if interviewers are untrained, as leading questions destroy the method.
whyLost: It is rooted in French phenomenology and requires extensive training in non-inductive questioning, so it has stayed in cognitive science and education research.
whereToUse: Trust and security decisions, error and recovery moments, expert decision-making, meditation and wellbeing products, and responses to AI outputs.
example: Investigating why users ignore a phishing warning, a researcher asks each participant to re-evoke one specific instance. Descriptions reveal a felt sense of 'this is routine' forming before the warning was read, informing warning timing.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Petitmengin C (2006) Describing one's subjective experience in the second person. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 5:229-269
Petitmengin C et al. (2019) Discovering the structures of lived experience. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences
reference: Petitmengin, C. (2006). Describing one's subjective experience in the second person. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 5, 229-269.

name: Microgenetic Method with Dense Sampling
origin: Werner (1956); Vygotsky; Siegler and Crowley (1991); Kuhn; Granott and Parziale (2002); Adolph and Robinson
summary: Observe the same people very densely while change is happening, coding strategy and support trial by trial, to see how skills actually emerge.
description: Microgenetic research spans the period of change, samples observations densely relative to the rate of change, and analyses them trial by trial. Siegler's overlapping-waves model shows several strategies coexisting and shifting in frequency rather than jumping stage to stage. A task analysis splits the target skill into components; sessions are segmented into episodes coded for components passed and failed and for the helper's scaffolding level. Adolph and Robinson add a design check: daily records of infant motor skills showed skills appearing, vanishing and returning, but when the same records were subsampled weekly about half looked like sudden jumps, and nearly all did monthly. Sampling density therefore determines the shape of change you see. Short-term change in a session need not mirror lasting learning.
steps: Task-analyse the target skill into components and the coordination between them.
Run a short dense phase: record the behaviour every session or every day for each participant across the period of change.
Code each trial or episode for the strategy used (allowing several coexisting strategies), components passed or failed, and the support or scaffolding given.
Plot individual trajectories of strategy mix, performance and support, identifying phases, regressions and transitions.
Resample the dense record at wider intervals (every 2, 4, 7, 14 and 30 days) and classify the apparent trajectories as gradual or abrupt.
Choose the field sampling frequency that preserves the variability that matters, and report time as exposure or practice as well as calendar time.
outputs: Trial-by-trial strategy and support records, individual trajectories, the proportion of trajectories that look abrupt at each simulated interval, and a recommended sampling cadence.
useWhen: Studying how users learn a complex tool, adopt an AI assistant, or switch strategies over days or weeks, and when choosing a diary or telemetry cadence.
avoidWhen: You need population estimates or have little access to participants; dense sampling is costly, labour-intensive and can cause practice effects. Use a longitudinal panel or cohort analytics for broad trends.
whyLost: It is labour-intensive and developed for child development; UX longitudinal work uses sparse diary check-ins and rarely tests what its sampling interval hides.
whereToUse: Onboarding to professional software, AI copilot adoption, learning apps, accessibility tool learning, game skill progression.
example: Before fixing a weekly diary cadence for a new code assistant, a team logs daily usage and strategies for 12 developers over three weeks. Subsampling shows weekly check-ins would miss repeated abandon-and-return cycles, so the study uses short daily prompts instead.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Siegler, R. S., & Crowley, K. (1991). The microgenetic method: A direct means for studying cognitive development. American Psychologist, 46(6), 606-620.

name: Microinteraction Testing Protocol
origin: Dan Saffer (2013), building on Lean UX
summary: A five-step test of one small interaction: elicit expectations first, observe unaided use, step through with think-aloud, ask what it should remember, then ask for the one fix.
description: Saffer adapts user testing to single microinteractions, where trigger, rules, feedback and loops are tightly coupled, so the prototype must be as high-fidelity as possible. Because the need for the feature is usually assumed, the test targets four things: the true goal (not a process step), which data matter, whether microcopy is needed and understood, and timing and flow. Goals and data come mainly from conversation, copy issues from observation. Expectations, prior experience and the one desired outcome are elicited before exposure, then unaided use is measured, then a think-aloud walk-through asks the participant to explain the rules, which exposes gaps between the designed and perceived model. The procedure is run in two rounds with revision between. Saffer warns that small behavioural differences need large samples: at least 20 users, ideally hundreds or thousands, for quantitative claims.
steps: Before showing the prototype, ask how participants expect it to work, whether they have used anything similar, the one thing they want to accomplish and whether any single piece of information would make it unnecessary.
Have them use the microinteraction unaided and capture quantitative data (success, time, errors) during or immediately after.
Step through it with them thinking aloud and ask them to explain its rules; note discrepancies with the designed rules.
Ask what they would want it to remember about them if they came back tomorrow.
Ask for the one thing that should be fixed.
Revise the design and repeat with a second set of participants.
Treat quantitative differences as indicative unless you have at least 20, and preferably far more, users; avoid pausing mid-flow in ways that make people miss feedback.
outputs: Validated goal and data needs, microcopy and timing issues, discrepancies between perceived and designed rules, and baseline metrics.
useWhen: Refining a single trigger-rules-feedback unit such as a toggle, autosave, password field, swipe action or notification, where flow and rule comprehension decide success.
avoidWhen: Avoid for whole-journey evaluation (use Moderated Usability Testing) or when only low-fidelity prototypes exist; for small effect sizes use A/B Testing on live traffic.
whyLost: Microinteractions are usually tested incidentally inside broader usability sessions, so the dedicated expectation-first protocol is rarely run.
whereToUse: Design systems components, mobile gestures, AI assistant suggestion chips, fintech confirmation flows.
example: A banking app tests a new 'round-up savings' toggle. Participants first describe what they expect it to do; most assume it rounds up every purchase including transfers, revealing a rule the microcopy must state.
reference: Saffer, D. (2013). Microinteractions: Designing with Details. O'Reilly Media, Appendix A.

name: Miles and Huberman Analytic Displays
aka: Miles and Huberman Data Display Analysis
origin: Matthew Miles & A. Michael Huberman, 1984 (Qualitative Data Analysis); 3rd ed. with Johnny Saldaña, 2014
summary: A three-part analytic system of data reduction, structured data displays (matrices, networks) and explicit conclusion verification for systematic applied qualitative analysis.
description: Miles and Huberman argued that qualitative analysis fails mostly because researchers keep data as unbroken text that cannot be overviewed. Their framework has three concurrent components: data reduction (memoing, coding, pattern noting), data display (case-ordered meta-matrices, conceptually ordered displays, time-ordered matrices, causal networks) and conclusion drawing with verification (negative cases, rival explanations, member checks, comparing cases where a finding should and should not appear). Displays are the analytic engine: rows of cases against columns of themes reveal within-case and cross-case patterns simultaneously. Their sourcebook catalogues dozens of display types with tactics for generating and testing meaning, making qualitative inference explicit, replicable and auditable.
steps: Write analytic memos and develop a start list of codes from your research questions, then code the data and note emerging patterns.
Choose a display suited to the question: a case-ordered meta-matrix for cross-participant comparison, a time-ordered matrix for change, or a causal network for explanation.
Populate cells with condensed summaries and short quotes, keeping a decision rule for what goes into each cell so displays are reproducible.
Read across rows and down columns to note patterns, contrasts, clusters and outliers; record each tentative conclusion as a memo.
Verify each conclusion using negative cases, rival explanations, checks with participants and comparison of cases where the finding should and should not hold.
Report the displays alongside conclusions so readers can see the evidence behind every claim.
outputs: Case-by-theme meta-matrices, time-ordered and conceptually ordered displays, causal network diagrams, and a list of verified conclusions with evidence.
useWhen: Multi-site or multi-segment studies, evaluation research, or any study with more than about ten cases where cross-case patterns and explanations must be defended.
avoidWhen: For a handful of usability sessions or purely exploratory immersion where premature structure would constrain discovery; use rapid debriefs or open coding instead.
whyLost: Spreadsheets of quotes and sticky-note walls replaced deliberate display design, and the sourcebook's density kept it within academic evaluation research.
whereToUse: Multi-market studies, enterprise rollouts across sites, service evaluations in health and public sector, and longitudinal programmes needing traceable synthesis.
example: A payments company studies merchant onboarding across five countries. A case-ordered meta-matrix (merchants by onboarding barriers) shows that document verification delays explain churn only where local IDs are not machine-readable, a pattern invisible in the per-market reports.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (Miles & Huberman)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 29
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M. & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). Sage.

extra.The Three Components: Data Reduction: Selecting, focusing, simplifying, abstracting, and transforming raw data. This includes: writing memos (analytic notes on what you are finding), coding (applying conceptual labels), and pattern noting (identifying recurring patterns before formal coding). Data reduction is not about removing data — it is about making it manageable and conceptually ordered. Data Display: Organised assemblies of information that allow conclusion drawing. Displays include: matrices (cases × themes), networks (showing relationships between concepts), causal flow charts, and taxonomies. The critical insight from Miles & Huberman: you cannot analyse what you cannot see. Most qual analysis fails because researchers keep their data as text, which is impossible to overview. Display tools make patterns visible. Conclusion Drawing & Verification: From the beginning of data collection, the researcher is noting regularities, patterns, explanations, causal flows, and propositions. These tentative conclusions are then verified against the data. Verification strategies: looking for negative cases, checking rival explanations, getting feedback from participants (member checking), comparing cases where the finding should be present and where it should be absent.
extra.Key Display Tools: Case-ordered descriptive meta-matrix: Rows = participants, columns = themes. Cells contain summary data for each participant on each theme. Shows both within-case patterns and cross-case comparisons simultaneously. Conceptually ordered display: Organises data around a conceptual framework (theoretical, causal, or experiential). Not organised by participant or time — organised by concept. Best for building toward theoretical explanation. Causal network: A network diagram showing the causal relationships between variables as found in the data. Not imposed before analysis — built from the data. Arrows indicate direction of causal influence; node sizes indicate centrality. Event-listing matrix: Chronicles events chronologically for each case. Used for process-oriented research where temporal sequence matters.

name: Mindfulness-based first-person inquiry
aka: Shamatha-vipashyana as a method of examining experience
donor: Contemplative traditions, phenomenology and cognitive science
origin: Buddhist mindfulness/awareness practice, proposed as a scientific method by Varela, Thompson and Rosch, 1991
summary: A disciplined first-person method in which a trained observer notices, labels and slows down experience to describe feeling tone, intention and attention shifts without judgement.
description: Varela, Thompson and Rosch argued that cognitive science lacked a disciplined way of examining experience, and proposed mindfulness/awareness practice as one. The observer anchors attention (on the breath or a routine action), notices each departure without judgement and returns, labels mental events by type ('thinking', 'planning') rather than following their content, and slows actions to catch the intention before movement. Category lists such as feeling tone (pleasant, unpleasant, neutral) serve as prompts, not a coding scheme. The authors contrasted this with Wundt-style introspection, which imposed theory-given elements. The revised edition qualifies the method: observation alters experience, and the original framing is now described as naive. For UX the transferable elements are researcher self-training in non-judgemental noticing, typed labelling of experience, and slowed action to reveal micro-intentions, with findings treated as provisional.
steps: Choose a simple anchor for attention, such as the breath or a routine product action.
Attend to it; each time attention wanders, notice this without judgement and return.
When a mental event arises, label its type briefly ('thinking', 'feeling', 'planning') instead of following its content.
For a chosen moment, ask how it arose, under what conditions, what the reaction was and where the sense of 'I' occurred.
Slow a routine action right down to notice the intention and feeling tone before each movement.
Use a category list (feeling tone, impulse towards or away, intention, attention) as prompts, not as a fixed coding scheme.
Record observations soon afterwards and compare them with others' reports or with third-person data.
outputs: First-person descriptions of feeling tone, impulse, intention and attention shifts, and how these change with practice.
useWhen: Researchers want to sharpen their own perception of micro-moments of experience, or to generate hypotheses about intention and friction in routine interactions.
avoidWhen: You need findings generalisable to users, or a quick method. Observation changes what is observed, category lists import theory, and trained and untrained observers report differently; the practice carries religious and cultural context participants may not share. Use micro-phenomenological interviewing for eliciting others' experience.
whyLost: It remained in contemplative science and neurophenomenology, required long training under a teacher, and its own authors later questioned its framing as inner observation.
whereToUse: Researcher training, autoethnographic pilots of habitual interactions, wellbeing and meditation apps, notification and attention design.
example: Before a study on compulsive feed checking, researchers spend a week slowing down their own unlocks and noting the feeling tone and intention preceding each. Their notes produce probe questions about boredom and anticipation for later micro-phenomenological interviews.
reference: Varela, F. J., Thompson, E., & Rosch, E. (1991/2016). The Embodied Mind: Cognitive Science and Human Experience. MIT Press.

name: Mini Creative Brief
origin: Jared Spool, User Interface Engineering, from one of his clients; described by Connor and Irizarry, 2015
summary: A one-page summary of purpose, personas, scenarios, business goals and design principles, read aloud at the start of every design meeting and used as the yardstick in critique.
description: Long creative briefs are quickly ignored, so the mini creative brief condenses a project's foundation onto a page or less: problem statement or purpose, key personas, main scenarios, business goals and design principles. It is read at the start of design meetings and critiques, at UIE by a different person each time, so the team keeps its objectives in mind. Connor and Irizarry give guidance on each element: half-page personas without stereotyped demographics, scenarios based on real observations including thoughts and emotions, goals tied to measurable behaviour change rather than outputs (raise authenticated visits by 15 per cent rather than add a 'remember me' feature), and principles specific enough to eliminate more ideas than they keep. Critique comments are then referred back to the brief.
steps: Draft the problem statement or product purpose in a sentence or two.
Summarise key personas, main scenarios, measurable business goals and design principles.
Cut to one page or less and post it where the team can see it.
Read it aloud at the start of each design meeting or critique, rotating the reader.
Tie critique comments back to specific goals, scenarios or principles in the brief.
Refine goals or principles that prove too vague to settle a disagreement.
outputs: A visible one-page statement of objectives used as the reference for design critique.
useWhen: A design team needs a shared, short reference to keep critique focused on objectives rather than taste.
avoidWhen: The brief is only as good as the research behind its personas and scenarios; if they are invented, build them from Interviews or Contextual Inquiry first. Vague principles like 'fun' make it useless.
whyLost: Survives as the one-pager and product brief common in product teams; the read-aloud ritual is less common.
whereToUse: Design critique, agile product teams, agency projects, cross-functional squads.
example: A SaaS squad reads its brief before each critique; when a stakeholder asks for a dashboard redesign, the team points to the goal of cutting support tickets for exports by 20 per cent and refocuses.
reference: Connor, A. and Irizarry, A. (2015) Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 58-65.

name: Minimal Fix Cycle
aka: Minimal fix cycle (the least you can do: tweak, don't redesign)
origin: Steve Krug, 2010
summary: Fix each observed usability problem with the smallest change likely to stop it, escalating to stronger or different tweaks before any redesign, and prefer removing things.
description: Krug's maxim is to do the least you can do. After testing, teams are tempted to restate each problem as a need for redesign, which delays fixes and introduces new problems. Instead, each observed problem gets the smallest, simplest change likely to fix it for most people, usually a change of size, position, appearance or wording. If it fails, the tweak is made stronger ('louder') or a different tweak is tried; only when tweaks are exhausted is redesign considered. A second principle is to take something away, because noise is often the real problem and adding instructions or emphasis makes it worse. Each fix is checked for side effects and verified by inspection, a few hallway tests on the relevant scenario, an unmoderated remote test or an A/B test.
steps: Start from a problem actually observed in testing, not a restated need for redesign.
Ask what the smallest, simplest change is that might fix it for most people, and consider removing distracting material first.
Make the change.
If it does not work, try the same tweak more strongly, or a different tweak.
When the problem is fixed, check that nothing else has broken.
Verify by inspection, a few hallway tests of the scenario, an unmoderated remote test or an A/B test before the next round.
outputs: Quick, low-risk fixes in place before the next test round, with a record of what was tried.
useWhen: After a round of usability testing, when a small team must fix the worst problems quickly with limited resources.
avoidWhen: Tweaks cannot fix a wrong concept or missing capability; if testing shows users do not understand what the product is for, return to Interviews or Prototype Testing of alternatives. Watch for side effects, and be wary of deferring serious problems to a future redesign that never comes.
whyLost: Survives because it suits iterative, lean teams and Krug's books remain widely read.
whereToUse: Small product teams, e-commerce checkout and sign-up flows, content sites, internal tools.
example: Users miss a promo-code field in an e-commerce checkout; the team first enlarges and relabels it, then removes an adjacent banner, and five hallway tests show the problem gone.
reference: Krug, S. (2010) Rocket Surgery Made Easy: The Do-It-Yourself Guide to Finding and Fixing Usability Problems. Berkeley, CA: New Riders, pp. 110-119.

name: Minimal Manual and Guided Exploration Cards
origin: John M. Carroll and colleagues (1987-88); Carroll (1990), The Nurnberg Funnel
summary: Replace bulky documentation with short task cards or a minimal manual that get users doing real work quickly and help them check success and recover from errors.
description: Minimalism reacts against the profusion of documentation: give users only what they need to start common real tasks, because people do not read large manuals but do benefit from minimal ones. A guided exploration card has a short task heading, a few concrete steps, a check that confirms success and a recovery section for the commonest error (for example forgetting the equals sign when entering a spreadsheet formula). Nielsen frames it within wider documentation advice: procedures in task order, ways for users to check success, three levels of documentation (reference cards, tutorials and reference manuals), and self-contained volumes. The rigour comes from building the cards around observed real tasks and errors and testing them with new users.
steps: Identify the common real tasks new users must be able to start with, ideally from observation or support data.
Write one short card or section per task with a clear heading and a few concrete steps in task order.
Add a check that lets users confirm they succeeded.
Add a recovery section for the commonest error on that task.
Keep detail out; point experts to reference material instead.
Test the cards with new users and revise where they stall or err.
outputs: A set of task cards or a minimal manual, with success checks and error-recovery advice.
useWhen: Use it when designing onboarding, quick-start guides, help articles or in-product guidance for new users of complex tools.
avoidWhen: It cannot contain everything; experts still need reference material. To find which tasks and errors matter use Usability Testing and Documentation Usability Testing rather than guessing.
whyLost: It remains a cornerstone of technical communication, and its ideas live on in task-based help and onboarding tips, but UX teams rarely cite or apply it as a method.
whereToUse: Quick-start guides, in-app onboarding, developer getting-started docs, medical device instructions and enterprise rollouts.
example: A spreadsheet-based budgeting SaaS replaces a 30-page guide with eight cards. The 'add a formula' card ends with a check that the total updates and a recovery note for missing equals signs, cutting related support tickets.
reference: Carroll, J. M. (1990). The Nurnberg Funnel: Designing Minimalist Instruction for Practical Computer Skill. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering, pp. 153-155.

name: Minimum description length estimation
origin: Jorma Rissanen, 1978, building on Kolmogorov (1965) and Solomonoff (1964)
summary: Estimates interface complexity as the length of the shortest description needed to specify it, approximated by compression, to compare designs' structural regularity objectively.
description: Kolmogorov complexity defines the complexity of an object as the length of the shortest program that produces it; it is uncomputable, but the minimum description length principle approximates it by the shortest two-part code (model plus data given model). In UX the object is a layout, a navigation structure or an interaction grammar. A design built from a few consistent rules has a short description; a design full of exceptions has a long one. Practically, analysts encode screens or task flows in a structured representation and use a general compressor (gzip, LZMA) or a hand-built grammar to estimate description length, then compare variants. The rigour lies in fixing the encoding scheme before comparing, using normalised compression distance for pairs, and treating results as relative rankings, not absolute truths.
steps: Choose the object to measure (screen layouts, navigation graph, command grammar) and define a fixed, documented serialisation format for it.
Serialise each design variant identically, removing incidental noise such as IDs and timestamps.
Compress each serialisation with at least two compressors (for example gzip and LZMA) and record compressed size; use the ratio compressed/raw as the description-length estimate.
For pairs of designs or screens, compute normalised compression distance NCD = (C(xy) - min(C(x),C(y))) / max(C(x),C(y)) to quantify consistency across screens.
Alternatively write a two-part MDL code: count the rules needed to generate the design plus the exceptions not covered by rules.
Rank variants by estimated description length and test whether the ranking predicts learnability, for example via trials-to-criterion with 8-12 novice participants.
outputs: Description-length estimates per variant, a consistency (NCD) matrix across screens, a list of exceptions inflating complexity, and optionally validation against learnability data.
useWhen: When comparing design systems or interaction grammars for internal consistency; when arguing that a redesign is structurally simpler; when auditing sprawl in large enterprise products.
avoidWhen: When perceived visual complexity or aesthetics is the question (use rated complexity scales or eye tracking), or when designs cannot be serialised comparably. It is a structural proxy, not a usability measure.
whyLost: Kolmogorov complexity and MDL live in theoretical computer science and statistics; their uncomputability and abstract framing meant they never crossed into UX despite obvious relevance to consistency and learnability.
whereToUse: Design system governance, enterprise suites with many modules, command-line and gesture grammars, and AI agent tool schemas.
example: A SaaS team compares two settings architectures. Serialised as JSON and compressed, variant B is 31% shorter because its sections follow one pattern; a learnability study with 10 new admins confirms B reaches criterion in fewer trials.
sources: MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
Shannon, C. E., A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 1 — Entropy, Complexity & the Information Architecture of Interaction
reference: Rissanen, J. (1978). Modeling by shortest data description. Automatica, 14(5), 465-471.

name: Minimum Viable Conversation Worksheet
origin: Erika Hall (2018), Conversational Design
summary: Before sketching screens, a team writes the concept, scripts the exchange and fills a two-column customer and system worksheet across nine moments from context to closure.
description: Hall proposes working in the order Concept, Script, Sketch: first a device-independent concept and reason to exist, then the exchange of information over time scripted collaboratively on a whiteboard, in a text editor or in Twine, and only then the interface. The Minimum Meaningful Conversation is the thought experiment that precedes an MVP: start from the customer's intent and ask how they express the need, what is exchanged, what they must give, which choices are offered, how to close by showing value and how to leave the door open. The worksheet pairs Customer and System columns across nine rows: Context, Event, Intention, Introduction, Orientation, Action, Guidance, Error and Closure. Working it through together exposes where the system makes demands without offering value, before any screen exists.
steps: Define the concept: the big idea and its reason to exist, independent of device or channel.
Script the exchange of information collaboratively on a whiteboard, in a text editor or in Twine.
Answer the key questions: how the customer expresses the need, what is exchanged, what they must give, what choices are offered, how to close showing value and how to keep the door open.
Fill the worksheet's Customer and System columns for each row: Context, Event, Intention, Introduction, Orientation, Action, Guidance, Error and Closure.
Read the completed worksheet aloud to find rows where the system asks without giving or gives no guidance on errors.
Only then sketch the interface that supports the exchange, showing how it fits the person's wider life across channels.
outputs: A concept statement, a scripted exchange and a completed customer and system worksheet.
useWhen: Use it at the start of a new service, flow or chatbot when the team is tempted to jump straight to screens.
avoidWhen: It is a thought experiment; check the script against real language and needs with Interviews or a Sample Dialog Table Read, and test the resulting design with Wizard of Oz Prototyping or Usability Testing.
whyLost: It appears in one short book; teams adopted conversational design for chatbots but rarely this structured worksheet for screen-based products.
whereToUse: Chatbots and voice assistants, sign-up and onboarding flows, customer service journeys and transactional services in banking or insurance.
example: An insurer designing a claims flow fills the Error row and realises the system has no response when a customer lacks a policy number. The script adds lookup by date of birth before any screen is drawn.
reference: Hall, E. (2018). Conversational Design. New York: A Book Apart, pp. 114-117.

name: Misinformation and leading-question paradigm
origin: Loftus and Palmer, 1974; Loftus, Miller and Burns, 1978
summary: An experiment showing an event, then feeding one group misleading information or loaded question wording, to measure how post-event suggestion distorts later memory reports.
description: Participants view an event, then answer questions in which one group receives misleading information, often embedded naturally in a question. Later memory is compared with a control group. Loftus, Miller and Burns (1978) showed a car at a stop sign; a question mentioning a yield sign raised false recognition of a yield-sign slide. Loftus and Palmer (1974) found that the verb 'smashed' versus 'hit' produced speed estimates of 41 versus 34 mph and, a week later, 32 versus 14 per cent false reports of broken glass. Lindsay (1990) showed the effect is a source-monitoring error: it was larger when misinformation came from the same narrator straight after the event than two days later in a different voice. The effect survives explicit warnings. For UX it is a direct test of how interview and survey wording contaminates users' recall of their experiences.
steps: Show all participants the same event, such as a recorded session, video or product walkthrough.
Randomly assign participants to a misleading-information group and a control group.
Embed the manipulation naturally, for example one leading question among 20, or a loaded verb in a single question.
After a delay (minutes to a week), test memory with forced-choice recognition or open questions that include the critical detail.
Vary source similarity if relevant, for example same versus different voice or medium, to test source confusion.
Compare the proportion of misled reports or false recognitions between groups with a test of proportions.
outputs: Proportion of misled reports or false recognitions per condition, estimate shifts caused by wording, and size of the source-confusion effect.
useWhen: You need evidence on how your research instruments or in-product messaging alter what users remember, for example post-incident interviews, satisfaction surveys, or support scripts.
avoidWhen: Do not use deception that could harm participants; for routine wording checks a cognitive pretest of the questionnaire is cheaper. Warnings do not remove the effect, so do not treat a disclaimer as a fix.
whyLost: It is framed around eyewitness testimony and law, so UX practitioners absorbed the lesson 'avoid leading questions' as a rule of thumb without running the experiment.
whereToUse: Interview guide validation, post-incident and complaint investigations, retrospective satisfaction surveys, AI assistants that summarise past sessions back to users.
example: A fintech team tests whether asking 'How frustrating was the failed transfer?' versus 'How did the transfer go?' changes later recall. A week on, the loaded group reports more errors than logs show, so the team rewrites its post-support survey.
reference: Loftus, E. F., & Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13, 585-589; Loftus, E. F., Miller, D. G., & Burns, H. J. (1978). Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4, 19-31.

name: Misinformation correction test
donor: Judgement and decision making; political psychology
origin: Nyhan and Reifler, 2010
summary: A between-groups experiment comparing belief ratings after misleading content with and without a correction, split by prior attitude, to test whether corrections work or backfire.
description: Participants read content containing a false implication; one group also reads a correction. All then rate agreement with the false claim. Nyhan and Reifler (2010) used a mock news story implying Iraq had weapons of mass destruction; the correction reduced belief among very liberal participants, had no effect among centrists and increased belief among conservatives, the so-called backfire effect. Because the outcome depends on prior attitudes, samples must be profiled and results analysed by subgroup. Later replications suggest backfire is rarer than first reported, so the test is better seen as measuring correction effectiveness across segments. In UX it suits fact-check labels, AI output corrections, and product messaging that retracts earlier claims.
steps: Write a stimulus containing the misleading claim, in the format users will actually meet it.
Write a correction in the candidate design (label, banner, inline note) and, if useful, several correction variants.
Measure prior attitudes or relevant identity before exposure so results can be split.
Randomly assign participants to no-correction and correction conditions, aiming for at least 50 per cell per subgroup.
Collect agreement ratings with the false claim and with a control claim on the same scale.
Compare belief by condition within each prior-attitude subgroup, testing the condition-by-attitude interaction.
outputs: Belief ratings with and without correction by subgroup; correction effect sizes; evidence of null or reverse effects.
useWhen: You must decide how to correct false or outdated information: AI hallucination notices, content moderation labels, health misinformation, product recall messages.
avoidWhen: The audience has no prior stake in the claim and a simple comprehension test would do. Do not generalise backfire from one study; later work questions how often it occurs. Avoid with small or unprofiled samples.
whyLost: It belongs to political psychology and communication research; UX teams test labels with preference or click metrics rather than belief change.
whereToUse: Generative AI correction UI, community notes and fact-check labels, health apps, financial disclosures, retractions of product claims.
example: An AI assistant team tests three correction designs for a wrong answer it gave earlier. Belief in the wrong figure falls with an inline strike-through plus source, but not with a footnote, and sceptical users are unaffected by either.
reference: Nyhan, B., & Reifler, J. (2010). When corrections fail: The persistence of political misperceptions. Political Behavior, 32, 303-330.

name: Missing data handling with MICE imputation
origin: Donald Rubin, 1987 (multiple imputation); van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011 (MICE)
summary: Replacing missing survey or behavioural values with multiple plausible imputations, then pooling results, so estimates are not biased by who skipped questions.
description: Missing data are rarely random: busy, dissatisfied or less literate users skip more items. Listwise deletion discards cases and biases estimates unless data are missing completely at random (MCAR); single mean imputation shrinks variance. Multiple imputation by chained equations models each incomplete variable from the others in turn, generates m complete datasets with appropriate random variation, analyses each, and pools estimates with Rubin's rules so uncertainty from missingness is reflected in standard errors. It is valid under missing at random (MAR) assumptions given the variables included. Rigour comes from diagnosing the missingness pattern, including auxiliary variables that predict missingness, imputing enough datasets, checking imputed distributions and running sensitivity analyses for missing-not-at-random scenarios.
steps: Describe the missingness pattern: percentage missing per variable and per respondent, and which variables predict missingness.
Decide the assumption (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) and include auxiliary variables related to missingness in the imputation model.
Impute with MICE (e.g. scikit-learn IterativeImputer with sample_posterior=True, or statsmodels MICE), using m of at least 20 or roughly the percentage of incomplete cases.
Check convergence across iterations and compare imputed with observed distributions.
Fit the analysis model on each imputed dataset and pool estimates and standard errors with Rubin's rules.
Compare against complete-case results and a delta-adjusted MNAR sensitivity scenario, and report all three.
outputs: Pooled estimates with correct standard errors, missingness diagnostics and a sensitivity comparison.
useWhen: Surveys with more than about 5% missing on key variables, longitudinal or diary studies with drop-out, and SEM or regression on incomplete data.
avoidWhen: Avoid for trivial missingness (under about 5% and plausibly MCAR), for data structurally not applicable (skip logic), or where full-information maximum likelihood in SEM handles missingness directly.
whyLost: Multiple imputation is standard in epidemiology and clinical trials but UX tools default to deleting incomplete responses, and the statistical machinery was never taught in UX curricula.
whereToUse: Satisfaction tracking, diary and longitudinal studies, health app outcome research and survey-to-SEM pipelines.
example: A diary study of a budgeting app loses 30% of entries by week three, mostly among users who stopped budgeting. MICE with engagement data as auxiliaries shows that the complete-case analysis overstated satisfaction by 0.6 points on a 7-point scale.
sources: Rubin, D. B. (1987) Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys
van Buuren, S. (2018) Flexible Imputation of Missing Data, 2nd ed.
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: van Buuren, S. & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, K. (2011) mice: Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations in R. Journal of Statistical Software 45(3)

name: Missing-value pattern check model
origin: Dorian Pyle (2003), in Ye's Handbook of Data Mining
summary: Recodes every input as present or missing and models the outcome from that pattern alone, to test whether missingness itself carries information before imputing.
description: Pyle argues that values are almost never missing at random. Before any imputation, copy the data set, replace each input with 1 if present and 0 if missing, keep the outcome, and fit a tree model (he uses a CHAID-style tree) of the outcome on these flags alone. If the tree predicts the outcome, the pattern of missingness is informative: it should be kept as features, and any replacement method must not destroy it. Pyle prefers replacement that preserves each variable's distribution and its relationships with others rather than mean substitution, which shrinks variance. The check is quick, model-agnostic and makes a hidden assumption visible. It shows that missingness matters, not why it occurs, so the reasons still need investigation.
steps: Copy the data set so the original values are untouched.
Recode each input variable as 1 (present) or 0 (missing), keeping the outcome variable as it is.
Fit a decision tree of the outcome on the missingness flags, with cross-validation to avoid overfitting.
Inspect which flags split the tree and how much predictive accuracy they give compared with a null model.
Keep informative flags as features in later models, and choose an imputation method that preserves distributions and relationships.
Investigate why the predictive fields are missing (skip logic, tracking gaps, user choice) with the data owners or users.
outputs: A tree showing which missingness patterns predict the outcome and how strongly, and a decision on flags and imputation method.
useWhen: Before imputing or dropping incomplete records in survey, CRM or analytics data, especially when missing fields could reflect user behaviour such as skipping optional steps.
avoidWhen: Data that are complete or missing by design (planned missingness). The check does not explain causes; follow it with investigation, and use formal missing-data models (MICE, selection models) for inference.
whyLost: Missing data in UX are usually treated as a cleaning chore; the idea that missingness is itself a signal lives in data-mining practice and is rarely made explicit.
whereToUse: Profile-completion and onboarding data, survey item non-response, CRM records, telemetry with tracking gaps, churn and conversion models.
example: Before modelling trial-to-paid conversion, a SaaS team flags missing profile fields. A tree on the flags alone predicts conversion well: users who skipped 'company size' rarely convert. The flag is kept as a feature and onboarding research explores why that field is skipped.
reference: Pyle, D. (2003). Data collection, preparation, quality, and visualization. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 365-392). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Mixed Methods Case Study Designs (CS-MMR and MM-CSR)
origin: Guetterman and Fetters (2018); Cook and Kamalodeen (2020); Creswell and Creswell (2018)
summary: Either embed a mixed methods design inside a bounded case study (CS-MMR) or use a mixed study, usually a survey, to select cases for depth (MM-CSR).
description: Two related designs are named by whichever approach starts the study. In case study mixed methods research (CS-MMR) the case is bounded first and a core mixed design is embedded inside it, for example pre-post measures combined with observation and interviews within one organisation. In mixed methods case study research (MM-CSR) a mixed or quantitative study comes first and its results are used to choose cases for in-depth qualitative study, such as extreme, typical or contrasting respondents. Creswell adds a deductive variant, in which cases are fixed in advance, and an inductive variant, in which case profiles are generated from merged results. Rigour comes from stating which approach leads, bounding cases explicitly, analysing within each case before integrating across them, and combining skill sets in the team so that one data type does not dominate by default.
steps: Decide which approach leads: the case (CS-MMR) or the mixed study (MM-CSR), and whether cases are fixed in advance or derived from results.
For CS-MMR, bound the case in time, place and unit, then embed a core design such as pre-post measures plus observation and interviews.
For MM-CSR, run the survey or quantitative study first and choose cases from its results using explicit criteria (typical, extreme, contrasting).
Analyse each case separately with both data types, then compare and integrate across cases.
Staff the team to cover both qualitative and quantitative skills and monitor bias towards either data type.
outputs: Case descriptions informed by mixed data, case profiles derived from merged results, and cross-case comparisons.
useWhen: You are studying a few customer organisations, teams or sites in depth and need both measured outcomes and an account of how and why they differ.
