avoidWhen: A single-method case study is enough (use Case Study Method), or you need population estimates rather than case understanding (use a survey).
whyLost: UX case studies of accounts or deployments are common but rarely designed as mixed methods with explicit case selection logic; the formal designs remain in education and health research.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise account research, rollout studies across sites, selecting interviewees from survey segments.
example: A SaaS team surveys 400 customer admins, selects six accounts with high licence counts but low activation as cases, and within each combines usage logs, admin interviews and workflow observation to explain the gap.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Mixed Methods Evaluation and Scaffolded Intervention Design
donor: Public health trials and programme evaluation
origin: Fetters (2020) scaffolded design; MRC complex intervention framework; Chu, Yin and Liu; Creswell and Creswell (2018)
summary: Develop, implement and evaluate a complex intervention in phases, using mixed methods at each phase and a convergent process evaluation alongside the outcome trial.
description: A phased programme design rather than a single study. Creswell's mixed methods evaluation design places core designs along the evaluation sequence, from needs assessment through programme development and process evaluation to outcome evaluation. Fetters' scaffolded design, combined with the MRC framework for complex interventions, makes this concrete. Development collects site context and feasibility data and builds the intervention on an explicit theory, refined in iterative pilots. Implementation uses train-the-trainer cascades, structured communication between central and local teams, monitoring against standard procedures and an implementation matrix recording how sites vary. Evaluation runs an outcome trial and, alongside it, a convergent process evaluation of fidelity, delivery, reach, receipt and context, merged in joint displays. Its rigour lies in linking each phase's findings to the next and in separating failure of the idea from failure of delivery.
steps: Needs assessment and development: collect site context with information sheets, interviews and feasibility questionnaires.
Build the intervention on a stated programme theory and refine it through iterative pilots.
Implementation: set up train-the-trainer cascades, structured central-local communication and monitoring against standard procedures.
Record site variation in an implementation matrix (what was adapted, where and why).
Evaluation: run the outcome trial with pre-specified outcomes.
Run a convergent process evaluation of fidelity, delivery, reach, receipt and context, and merge it with outcomes in joint displays.
outputs: A theory-based intervention, implementation records and site matrix, and integrated outcome and process findings.
useWhen: Rolling out a complex service, programme or multi-site change where you must learn whether it works and, if not, whether the idea or its delivery failed.
avoidWhen: Single feature changes that can be A/B tested in days; use A/B Testing. If only delivery quality matters, use Process and Implementation Evaluation alone.
whyLost: It belongs to public health and programme evaluation, where multi-year complex interventions are normal; product teams rarely frame launches as phased interventions.
whereToUse: Enterprise rollouts across regions, digital health programmes, onboarding or training programmes, service redesigns across branches.
example: A bank rolling out a new advisor tablet tool across 40 branches pilots it in three, records local adaptations in a matrix, then runs a stepped rollout with outcome metrics plus interviews and observation on fidelity and reach, explaining why two regions saw no gain.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Mixed Methods Experimental (Embedded) Design
aka: Qualitative data embedded in a trial
donor: Health sciences intervention trials; evaluation research
origin: Creswell et al. (2003); Creswell and Plano Clark (2018); Sandelowski (1996); multilevel variant Tashakkori and Teddlie (1998)
summary: Add a secondary qualitative strand before, during or after an experiment so participants' experiences shape its design, explain its process or interpret its outcomes.
description: A complex design in which a core mixed methods design is embedded as a supportive strand inside a primary experiment or trial, written QUAN(qual). Qualitative data can enter before the experiment (an embedded exploratory sequential design, to shape recruitment, procedures or the intervention), during it (an embedded convergent design, capturing participants' experience alongside pre and post measures), or after it (an embedded explanatory sequential design, to explain outcomes). The connection points are the integration points and should be drawn on a procedural diagram. Creswell's earlier concurrent embedded strategy, from which this grew, also covers the multilevel variant, in which different methods are used at different organisational levels. Rigour requires a sound experiment first, an explicit reason for each qualitative component, and integration at stated points rather than an afterthought. Weaknesses include unequal evidence between strands and discrepancies that need resolving.
steps: Design a rigorous experiment or trial as the primary study, with outcomes and analysis fixed in advance.
State explicitly why qualitative data are being added (shape the intervention, understand process, explain results).
Choose the entry points: before (exploratory), during (convergent) and/or after (explanatory) the experiment.
Collect qualitative data at one or several time points as resources allow, without contaminating the experimental conditions.
Analyse each strand separately, then integrate at the stated points: adjust procedures, compare in-trial experience with measured outcomes, or explain results.
Draw a procedural diagram showing the experiment, qualitative boxes and integration points in QUAN(qual) notation.
outputs: Experimental results accompanied by qualitative evidence on participants' experience, process and reasons for effects, plus a procedural diagram.
useWhen: An A/B test or trial needs an explanation of why the effect occurred, a check on how participants experienced each arm, or formative input before launch.
avoidWhen: When the experiment cannot be run rigorously, or when the qualitative work would change participants' behaviour in one arm only. For post-hoc explanation of surveys use Sequential Explanatory Design.
whyLost: UX teams often pair experiments with interviews informally, but the explicit design, timing logic and integration points remain in health sciences methodology.
whereToUse: A/B tests of onboarding, pricing or AI features; clinical-grade product trials; experiments with surprising or null results.
example: A subscription app runs a pricing-page A/B test and, during it, interviews ten users from each arm about how they read the plans; after the test, the qualitative strand explains why the higher-converting variant also raised refund requests.
reference: Creswell, J. W., & Creswell, J. D. (2018). Research design: Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods approaches (5th ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE. Chapter 10.

name: Mixed Methods Grounded Theory (MM-GT)
origin: Johnson, McGowan and Turner (2010); Creamer (2018); Johnson and Walsh (2019)
summary: Build or test a context-specific theory by running grounded theory's constant comparison and theoretical sampling across both qualitative and quantitative data.
description: Mixed methods grounded theory treats grounded theory and quantitative analysis as one integrated methodology rather than two studies stapled together. Planning uses a mixing template: for each level (paradigm, framework, assumptions, design, data, analysis, reporting) the researcher records what each method contributes and where they reinforce each other, for example abductive theoretical sampling. Two designs are common. In the linked-strands design the qualitative and quantitative strands stay separate, and an abductive loop is triggered whenever their results conflict. In the embedded design, constant comparison is applied to qualitative and quantitative material as a single dataset. Rigour comes from naming the grounded theory variant and the mixed design explicitly, showing theoretical sampling, saturation and memoing, and producing an actual theory model rather than a list of themes. Reviews find many published MM-GT studies generate little theory; building theory qualitatively and then testing it quantitatively is recommended but under-used.
steps: State the purpose and fill the mixing template at planning, recording each method's contribution at the levels of paradigm, design, data, analysis and reporting.
Choose between separate linked strands and an embedded design in which constant comparison runs over both data types.
Code the qualitative data (initial, focused, theoretical codes) and analyse the quantitative data, sampling theoretically between exploring and checking.
Where the strands disagree, generate new explanations abductively and return to both datasets to test them.
Build an integrated visual model of the emerging theory, showing which evidence supports each relation.
Report against grounded theory criteria (theoretical sampling, saturation, memoing, theory produced) and mixed methods criteria (named design, integration, procedural diagram, legitimation).
outputs: A grounded theory model supported by both qualitative and quantitative evidence, with a procedural diagram and a record of how conflicts were resolved.
useWhen: You need an explanatory model of a behaviour or adoption process in a specific context and have, or can collect, both interview data and usage or survey data to sample and test against.
avoidWhen: You only need descriptive themes (use Thematic Analysis) or a straightforward follow-up explanation of survey results (use Sequential Explanatory Design). Avoid it if no one on the team can run grounded theory properly; the reviews show the hybrid often collapses into neither.
whyLost: It lives in education and health methodology handbooks and requires fluency in two demanding traditions. UX teams usually run interviews and analytics in parallel without a shared theory-building logic.
whereToUse: Theory of adoption or churn for a product category; explaining segments found in behavioural data; long-running discovery programmes where qualitative findings must be checked at scale.
example: A fintech team builds a grounded theory of why small businesses abandon automated bookkeeping from 20 interviews, then theoretically samples account logs to check whether the proposed trigger (first tax-period mismatch) precedes churn, revising the model where logs disagree.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Mixed Methods Phenomenological Research (MMPR)
origin: Mayoh and Onwuegbuzie (2015)
summary: Pair a phenomenological study of lived experience with a quantitative phase in one of five sequences, to orient, explain, extend or cross-validate findings.
description: MMPR keeps a genuine phenomenological strand, with bracketing, in-depth experiential interviews and member checking, and combines it with a quantitative phase according to purpose and dominance. Five models are named: phen then QUAN (lived experience shapes a dominant quantitative study); quan then PHEN (a preliminary measure orients a dominant phenomenological study); QUAN then phen (phenomenology explores unexpected quantitative findings); PHEN then quan (a quantitative phase extends phenomenological findings to a wider group); and quan + phen concurrently, to cross-validate. Integration is done in a joint display, and discordance between strands is treated as a finding rather than error. The rigour lies in choosing the model deliberately and in stating meta-inferences that neither strand could support alone; designs can shift during a study, and such changes must be reported.
steps: Choose one of the five sequences by purpose (orient, explain, extend, cross-validate) and by which strand is dominant.
Run phenomenological interviews with bracketing, descriptive analysis and member checking.
Run the quantitative phase with records or standardised measures of the same phenomenon.
Integrate both strands in a joint display aligned by participant or theme.
Treat discordance as a finding, explain it, and state the meta-inferences; report any change of design during the study.
outputs: Phenomenological themes, statistics and meta-inferences presented in one joint display.
useWhen: A standard measure seems to miss what people experience, or experiential findings need to be checked or extended across a larger population.
avoidWhen: When you only need usability findings or attitude scores; use Phenomenological Research alone for depth or a validated questionnaire alone for scale.
whyLost: Phenomenology itself is rare in UX, and its combination with quantitative strands is mostly published in health and sport psychology.
whereToUse: Checking whether a wellbeing, fatigue, trust or workload questionnaire captures users' lived experience; health and wellbeing apps; AI companions.
example: A meditation app's interviews describe sustained low-level anxiety that its in-app mood score does not register; a concurrent quan + phen design shows the score misses it, prompting a new item set.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Mixed Methods Research
origin: Formalised by John Creswell, Abbas Tashakkori and Charles Teddlie, 1990s-2000s
summary: Deliberately integrates qualitative and quantitative methods in one study design so each compensates for the other's limits, with explicit points of integration.
description: Mixed methods research combines qualitative and quantitative data within a single study or programme, with a planned rationale for doing so. Creswell's core designs are convergent (collect both in parallel and compare), explanatory sequential (quantitative then qualitative to explain results) and exploratory sequential (qualitative then quantitative to test or measure what was found). What distinguishes mixed methods from simply running two studies is integration: deciding in advance where and how the strands connect, through sampling, instrument design, joint displays or meta-inferences. Rigour comes from stating the purpose of mixing (triangulation, complementarity, development, expansion), choosing a design accordingly, maintaining quality standards for each strand, and explicitly handling convergence and divergence between results rather than presenting them side by side.
steps: State the research questions and the purpose of mixing (e.g. explanation, development, triangulation).
Choose a design: convergent, explanatory sequential or exploratory sequential, and plan the timing and priority of strands.
Plan integration points: how sampling, instruments or analysis will connect the strands.
Collect and analyse each strand to its own quality standards.
Integrate results using joint displays that place quantitative and qualitative findings side by side by theme.
Draw meta-inferences, explicitly addressing convergence, complementarity and contradiction.
outputs: Mixed methods design diagram, strand findings, joint displays, integrated meta-inferences.
useWhen: Substantial research programmes, complex questions needing both breadth and depth, and decisions requiring both scale and explanation.
avoidWhen: Narrow questions answerable by one method, or when time does not allow both strands to meet quality standards.
whyLost: Still in use: Recognized as gold standard for complex UX questions combining breadth and depth.
whereToUse: Any substantial UX research program; product-market fit assessment; feature evaluation.
example: A telehealth provider ran an exploratory sequential study: 14 interviews identified five barriers to video consultations, which became survey items fielded to 2,000 patients, sizing each barrier by age group.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Multimethod Research
Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (Creswell & Plano Clark)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Creswell, J. W., & Plano Clark, V. L. (2017). Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Mixed Qualitative-Quantitative Group Interview (QQGI)
origin: Christopher N. Chapman and Edwin Love, Microsoft Hardware, c. 2007-2008
summary: A group session that demonstrates concepts, has each person complete a MaxDiff or conjoint survey individually, analyses it on the spot, then discusses the results with the same respondents.
description: A hybrid that fields a choice-based preference survey inside an in-person group. Concepts are demonstrated in depth, often under NDA, so confidential products never enter leak-prone online panels. Each respondent completes a MaxDiff or choice-based conjoint (typically 15-20 minutes) individually before any discussion, to avoid mutual influence. During a break an analyst estimates the results and hands top-level findings to the moderator, who then probes why people chose as they did and who liked or disliked the top and bottom items. Advantages: people can see and touch the product, attention is observed so data quality is high, the respondent mix is known, and the qualitative explanation comes from the same people the same day. Samples are small, so balanced randomisation matters and confidence intervals are wide; Chapman reports small-group shares broadly matching much larger online samples.
steps: Recruit representative target-market respondents into groups of about ten, typically eight to ten groups, avoiding convenience samples near the company.
Secure confidentiality with NDAs and control of visuals; introduce the category and let respondents discuss how they use it.
Demonstrate each concept in depth, allowing clarifying questions but no opinions yet.
Administer the MaxDiff or conjoint survey individually on devices or paper before any discussion, using a balanced randomised design.
During a break, have an associate estimate utilities or shares and give the moderator the headline results.
Ask respondents how they made their choices, then share high-level results and probe who liked the top and bottom items and why.
Combine results across groups, and switch to a larger online sample when tighter estimates are needed for forecasting.
outputs: Item or concept preference estimates with intervals, plus qualitative explanations from the same respondents, available the same day.
useWhen: You need early, rigorous preference data on confidential concepts, with the reasons behind choices, and can afford a team with both qualitative and quantitative skills.
avoidWhen: You need precise market-share forecasts or segment-level estimates; run a full online conjoint or MaxDiff with a large sample instead. It is expensive and preparation-heavy.
whyLost: It needs mixed qualitative and quantitative skills in one team and in-person logistics, so it stayed in market research and a few hardware groups.
whereToUse: Hardware and device concepts, confidential feature prioritisation, pricing and packaging exploration in B2B and consumer products.
example: A videoconferencing team shows six unreleased features to groups of ten IT buyers, runs a MaxDiff on tablets, and after a 15-minute break discusses why noise cancellation ranked top and transcription bottom.
reference: Chapman, C., & Rodden, K. (2023). Quantitative User Experience Research. Apress, pp. 204-205; Orme, B. K. (2010). Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (2nd ed.), ch. 13.

name: Mixed-Fidelity and Audience-Centric Prototype Planning
aka: Mixed-fidelity prototype specification (five dimensions of fidelity)
origin: McCurdy, Connors, Pyrzak, Kanefsky and Vera (2006), CHI; applied by Kathryn McElroy (2016)
summary: Plan each prototype by setting fidelity separately on five dimensions to suit the assumption tested or the audience addressed, instead of choosing one overall low, mid or high level.
description: McElroy warns that too high a fidelity makes people comment on polish while too low leaves them without context. Following McCurdy and colleagues, she splits fidelity into five independent dimensions: visual refinement, breadth of functionality, depth of functionality, interactivity and data model. Each prototype goal is run through the dimensions to give a mixed-fidelity specification, for example low visual refinement with high depth to test one task in detail, with realistic data so that extremes such as very long titles appear. For communication rather than testing, she plans around one named audience and one decision: rough artefacts for designers, mid or mixed fidelity for stakeholders, specifications for developers, and polished non-functional pieces with rougher working ones for investors, presented as a user scenario with an explicit ask.
steps: State the prototype's goal: the assumption to test, or the one audience and the decision or reaction you want from them.
Decide what content and interactions are needed for that goal.

For each of the five dimensions (visual refinement, breadth, depth, interactivity, data model), decide whether it must be low, medium or high, keeping every dimension that does not serve the goal as low as possible.
Use real or realistic data wherever the data model matters, including extreme cases.
Build to that specification; when presenting, frame it as a scenario of a named user and say up front what feedback is wanted.
Check during testing or review whether low dimensions distracted people, and record feedback.
Raise fidelity on further dimensions in later iterations as assumptions are settled.
outputs: A per-dimension fidelity specification for each prototype, the prototype itself, and recorded feedback or decisions.
useWhen: Use it when deciding what to build next to test an assumption cheaply, or when preparing a prototype for stakeholders, developers or investors.
avoidWhen: The plan is not the test; evaluate the result with Prototype Testing or Usability Testing. A polished prototype shown to stakeholders can overpromise what development can deliver; for evidence on how fidelity affects findings see the Prototype Fidelity Validation Study.
whyLost: Most teams still speak of low, mid and high fidelity; the five-dimension specification is cited in HCI but rarely applied as a planning step.
whereToUse: Product discovery, hardware and wearable projects, design reviews, investor pitches and handoffs to engineering.
example: A meditation app needs to know whether users find new sessions in a menu, so the prototype has full menu breadth, realistic session titles and greyscale visuals. For the board, the same flow is shown polished inside a short user scenario.
reference: McCurdy, M., Connors, C., Pyrzak, G., Kanefsky, B. and Vera, A. (2006). Breaking the fidelity barrier: an examination of our current characterization of prototypes and an example of a mixed-fidelity success. Proc. CHI 2006. McElroy, K. (2016). Prototyping for Designers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 26-28, 39-59, 77-86.

name: Mixed-Method Counterfactual Framework for Complex Interventions
aka: Defining the counterfactual for complex interventions
origin: Michael Bamberger (2012), adapted from Bamberger, Rugh and Mabry, RealWorld Evaluation (2012)
summary: A two-step way to estimate what would have happened without a complex, multi-actor intervention: choose attribution, contribution or substitution analysis, then combine several counterfactual approaches.
description: Complex interventions have many components and funders, change in nonlinear ways and shift their outcomes, so experimental rigour is rarely possible. Bamberger's framework first sets the level of claim the evidence can support. Attribution analysis needs a matched comparison group and credits differences to the intervention. Contribution analysis asks what one actor added to a change produced jointly with others. Substitution analysis estimates the net extra resources an input created after diversion or multiplier effects. The second step defines the counterfactual by combining approaches: statistical comparison, theory-based comparison of predicted and observed processes with rival hypotheses tested, participatory judgement such as Most Significant Change, and expert or stakeholder rating scales. The design is strengthened by splitting the programme into evaluable parts, portfolio analysis, reconstructed baselines and secondary data, and estimates are triangulated.
steps: Assess what comparison group, if any, is available.
Choose attribution analysis (matched comparison exists), contribution analysis (several actors produce the outcome jointly) or substitution analysis (the question is net added resources).

Select one or more counterfactual approaches: statistical, theory-based (theory of change versus observed, testing rival explanations), participatory (for example Most Significant Change) and rating scales.
Strengthen the design by breaking the intervention into evaluable components, analysing the portfolio, reconstructing baselines and drawing on secondary data and other studies.
Triangulate the estimates and report the effect at the chosen level with the evidence behind it.
outputs: An effect estimate at an explicitly stated level (attribution, contribution or substitution) with the triangulated evidence supporting it.
useWhen: Judging the impact of a programme of overlapping launches, a cross-team initiative or a partnership where no holdout exists and many actors influence the outcome.
avoidWhen: When a randomised experiment or clean quasi-experiment is feasible (use A/B testing, difference-in-differences or synthetic control); agreement with a theory of change is not proof unless rival explanations are tested.
whyLost: It grew up in development evaluation for donors and NGOs, while UX and product teams frame impact through experiments and rarely meet the language of contribution or substitution.
whereToUse: Evaluating accessibility or digital-inclusion programmes, platform-wide initiatives, public-sector services and partner-delivered features.
example: A health service rolls out a booking app alongside a national campaign and new clinic hours. With no holdout, the team claims contribution rather than attribution, combines a theory-of-change comparison, staff ratings and a Most Significant Change exercise, and triangulates them into a bounded estimate of the app's share.
sources: Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
reference: Bamberger, M. (2012). Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation. Impact Evaluation Notes No. 3. Washington, DC: InterAction.

name: Mixed-Methods Behavioral Drift Detection Framework
donor: UX research, telemetry analytics and Bayesian modelling
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A five-step mixed-methods pipeline detecting when users stay active but engagement erodes qualitatively, from Honeycomb anchoring through surveys, telemetry, DriftScore modelling and bandit-optimised interventions.
description: Behavioral drift is defined as users remaining active while their engagement changes qualitatively: repeating shallow actions, ignoring micro-feedback such as toasts and nudges, and reducing variety even when frequency is constant. Drift is not churn; it is the erosion of desirability and trust while activity persists, and is detectable earlier. The pipeline: (1) anchor in Morville's UX Honeycomb with behavioural proxies; (2) a 30-item Honeycomb Likert survey with EFA plus semi-structured interviews and affinity mapping; (3) longitudinal telemetry tracking interaction entropy, category diversity, recommendation CTR and attention decay, with diary and interview signals; (4) Bayesian updating of drift risk and a 0–1 DriftScore; (5) adaptive interventions (re-onboarding, dynamic UI scaling, context-aware nudging) optimised with Thompson Sampling and validated by A/B and longitudinal interviews. Honeycomb is chosen over HTA (bounded tasks) and IFT (drift is the absence of foraging).
steps: Anchor drift dimensions in Morville's Honeycomb and map each to a behavioural proxy (e.g. Desirable → exploration beyond minimal path; Credible → adopting recommendations without double-checking).
Field a 30-item Likert survey aligned to the Honeycomb (worked example n = 300) and run EFA; the example yields Trust, Ease and Engagement factors (α = 0.84, 0.81, 0.86).

Run semi-structured interviews ('Tell me about the last time you discovered something new here') and affinity-map themes such as repetitive content, off-target recommendations and notification fatigue; double-code 30–40% with κ ≥ 0.70.
Track telemetry longitudinally: Shannon interaction entropy, categories per session, promo/recommendation CTR, scroll depth and dwell, and frequency versus variety.
Update drift probability with Bayes (prior 20%; after three sessions with entropy < 1.5 and CTR < 25%, posterior ≈ 65%) and compute a weighted 0–1 DriftScore.
Deploy adaptive interventions (personalised re-onboarding, dynamic UI scaling, context-aware nudging) and allocate them per user with Thompson Sampling.
Validate with A/B tests on DriftScore reduction and entropy lift plus longitudinal interviews, against a decision bar (e.g. entropy > 2.0 for 70% of active users within 4 weeks).
outputs: Honeycomb proxy map, factor structure with reliabilities, longitudinal drift indicators, per-user DriftScores and posterior drift risk, intervention policy and validation results.
useWhen: When a product works and is bug-free but engagement depth fades: users log in yet stop exploring or ignore nudges.
avoidWhen: For bounded task failures such as checkout errors (use HTA or usability testing) or when telemetry is unavailable.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; engagement metrics usually track frequency, which hides qualitative erosion until churn.
whereToUse: E-commerce, OTT and content apps, calendars and productivity tools, fintech dashboards, recommendation-driven products.
example: In an e-commerce app with 10,000 users over 3 months, entropy fell from 2.6 to 1.2 and promo CTR from 47% to 19% while cart completion dipped only 62% to 58%; re-onboarding and adaptive nudges lifted entropy from 1.2 to 2.4 and promo CTR by 23 points.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
The Inquiry Series, Ch 24 — Behavior Models, Habits & the Anatomy of Non-Adoption
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study.

name: Mixed-Methods Integration Typology
aka: Six mixed methods strategies (Creswell et al., 2003)
origin: Creswell & Plano Clark, 2007/2017
summary: Specifies how qualitative and quantitative strands connect (explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, convergent, embedded) and integrates them deliberately, for example through joint displays.
description: Mixed-methods integration typology, formalised by Creswell and Plano Clark, distinguishes core designs by how qualitative and quantitative strands relate. In an explanatory sequential design, quantitative results are explained by subsequent qualitative work; in an exploratory sequential design, qualitative findings build an instrument or hypotheses tested quantitatively; in a convergent design, both strands are collected in parallel and compared; in embedded designs, one strand supports the other within a larger study. The defining requirement is integration: connecting samples, building instruments, merging results in joint displays, and drawing meta-inferences. Rigour comes from choosing the design for the question, specifying the point of integration in advance, and reporting where strands converge, complement or conflict.
steps: Declare your integration type before data collection. It determines sequence, priority, and purpose of each strand.
At the integration point: build a joint display showing both strands simultaneously.
For convergent designs: compare findings from each strand explicitly. Document both convergence and divergence. Divergence requires explanation.
outputs: A chosen integration design, an integration plan, joint displays linking qual and quant findings, and meta-inferences with explicit agreement or discordance.
useWhen: Studies combining analytics or surveys with interviews or observation, explaining quantitative patterns, building instruments from qualitative work, or triangulating findings.
avoidWhen: Avoid labelling a study 'mixed methods' when strands are merely run side by side; if integration is not planned, report them as separate studies.
whyLost: UX does mixed methods constantly but informally; formal designs and integration techniques from methodology literature are rarely used, so strands are not truly integrated.
whereToUse: Research program design, product development research, any study where multiple data types are needed.
example: Clustering of investment app users finds five archetypes; an explanatory sequential follow-up interviews six users per cluster, and a joint display links each cluster to the motives explaining its behaviour.
sources: Mixed Methods — short guide to applied mixed methods research
Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
The Inquiry Series, Ch 57 — Mixed-Methods Integration — The Technical Architecture of Triangulation
The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Creswell JW & Plano Clark VL (2017) Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research. 3rd ed. Sage

name: Mixture Experiments (Simplex-Lattice and Simplex-Centroid Designs)
donor: Statistics (design of experiments; chemical and food formulation)
origin: Henry Scheffe, 1958; John Cornell's Experiments with Mixtures (2002) as the standard account
summary: Designs and models for factors that are shares of a fixed whole summing to 100 percent, so the response depends on the blend rather than absolute amounts.
description: In a mixture experiment the factors are proportions that must sum to one, so changing one forces another to change and ordinary factorial designs cannot be used. The design space is a simplex. Simplex-lattice designs place points at equally spaced proportions; simplex-centroid designs use the pure components, every equal blend of subsets and the overall centroid (2^k - 1 points); axial designs add points along component axes so all components are present. Responses are modelled with Scheffe canonical polynomials, which have no intercept, and results are shown as contours on triangular coordinates. Lower and upper bounds on components, and process variables, can be added. Coefficients describe blending behaviour rather than separate component effects, which is the main interpretive trap.
steps: Define the k components and confirm their proportions must sum to 1, adding any lower or upper bounds.
Choose a simplex-lattice, simplex-centroid or axial design with at least as many distinct blends as model parameters, plus replicates of some points for an error estimate.
Randomise the run order.
Fit a linear or quadratic Scheffe canonical polynomial without intercept.
Plot the fitted response on simplex coordinates and identify the best blend, then confirm it with a follow-up run.
Add process variables or constrained-region designs if the blend interacts with other settings.
outputs: A fitted canonical polynomial, response contours on the simplex, and a recommended blend.
useWhen: Optimising how a fixed budget is divided: screen area among content types, notification mix across channels, feed composition across sources, or session time across activities.
avoidWhen: Factors that can vary independently (use Fractional Factorial Experiments or Response Surface Methodology); live adaptive allocation questions (Multi-Armed Bandit Testing for Adaptive UX); or when only a few discrete layouts are possible.
whyLost: Mixture designs belong to formulation chemistry, food science and pharmaceutics; UX teams facing composition questions run a handful of ad hoc A/B variants instead.
whereToUse: Feed and recommendation mix, home-screen composition, notification portfolios, marketing channel mix in product-led growth.
example: A news app tests how splitting the home feed among breaking news, personalised stories and video affects session length. A simplex-centroid design with seven blends shows the quadratic model peaks near 50/35/15, a blend no one had tested.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
reference: Scheffe, H. (1958). Experiments with mixtures. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 20(2), 344-360; Hinkelmann, K., & Kempthorne, O. (2008). Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (2nd ed.), pp. 519-523.

name: Mixture of Regressions (Latent-Class Regression, Mixtures of Experts)
aka: Mixture of linear and logistic regressions
origin: Adapted for UX from Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006); mixture of experts from Jacobs et al. (1991) and hierarchical mixture of experts from Jordan and Jacobs (1994)
summary: Fit several regression or logistic models at once, one per hidden subgroup, with EM estimating each case's membership, to reveal segments that respond to drivers differently.
description: A single regression assumes everyone responds to predictors the same way. A mixture of K regressions gives each latent component its own coefficients, with shared or separate noise and mixing proportions, fitted by expectation-maximisation. In the E step each component's responsibility for each case is computed from the current fits; in the M step mixing proportions become average responsibilities and each component is refitted by weighted least squares (or weighted logistic regression) with responsibilities as case weights. When mixing proportions depend on inputs through a gating function the model becomes a mixture of experts, in which components specialise in regions of input space; nesting gates gives a soft, probabilistic decision tree. Such mixtures can represent multimodal outcomes a single regression cannot. For UX, the components are candidate segments defined by how satisfaction or conversion responds to drivers, not by who users are; this application is an adaptation rather than part of the source text.
steps: Choose the component model (linear for a continuous outcome such as satisfaction, logistic for a binary one such as conversion) and a range of candidate K.
Initialise component coefficients, mixing proportions and noise variance, using several random starts.
E step: compute each component's responsibility for each case from the current fits.
M step: set mixing proportions to mean responsibilities, refit each component by weighted least squares or weighted logistic regression, and update the noise variance.
Iterate until the log-likelihood converges, keep the best of the starts, and choose K with an information criterion and interpretability.
Optionally model membership from case attributes (mixture of experts) so new users can be assigned to segments.
Inspect each component's coefficients and the cases it claims, and validate segments on held-out data.
outputs: A set of component regressions, the share of cases each explains, per-case membership probabilities and a predictive distribution that can be multimodal.
useWhen: Key driver analysis where different users plausibly weigh the same drivers differently, or when residuals from a single model look bimodal.
avoidWhen: Small samples (components become unstable), or when segments are better defined by attributes than by response patterns (use Latent Class Analysis for Personas or Gaussian Mixture Models for User Segmentation). Local maxima and the choice of K need care.
whyLost: It sits in machine learning and marketing-science texts; UX driver analysis uses one regression per pre-defined segment instead.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and NPS driver studies, pricing response, conversion models across mixed audiences, feature adoption models.
example: A SaaS satisfaction survey fitted with one regression shows weak drivers. A three-component mixture finds one group driven by reliability, one by price and one by integrations, with membership predicted by company size, so the roadmap is split accordingly.
sources: Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
reference: Bishop, C. M. (2006). Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. New York: Springer, Section 14.5; Jacobs, R. A., Jordan, M. I., Nowlan, S. J. and Hinton, G. E. (1991). Adaptive mixtures of local experts. Neural Computation, 3(1), 79-87.

name: ML Process Canvas
aka: ML-Process Canvas and ML Lifecycle Canvas
origin: Zhou, Gong, Qi and Sun, CHI Extended Abstracts 2019; ML Lifecycle Canvas by Zhou, Sun, Zhang, Liu and Gong, 2020
summary: A concept-stage paper canvas that links the UX challenges an ML component creates to the user, scenario and ML-system factors behind them, to surface design opportunities.
description: The ML-Process Canvas helps designers think about machine learning during conceptual design without abandoning their usual activities. It first prompts the designer to name the UX challenges that ML introduces, such as uncertain or wrong outputs, then to describe the user, the scenario and the elements of the ML system (data, model, feedback) that could affect each challenge. Findings are organised on the canvas linked to those elements, and the designer reads across for design opportunities; in the published example, system responses were kept low-key because the model could not guarantee correct outputs. The later ML Lifecycle Canvas folds the ML development process into conceptual design, treating ML, users and situation as one whole and giving designers and data scientists a shared artefact.
steps: Use the canvas during conceptual design alongside normal research synthesis.
Identify the specific UX challenges the ML component creates (for example error, uncertainty, cold start, opacity).
Describe the user, the scenario and the ML system elements (data, model, learning loop) that could affect each challenge.
Organise findings on the canvas linked to those elements, ideally with a data scientist present.
Read across the canvas for design opportunities and record candidate responses, such as softening outputs where confidence is low.
outputs: A completed canvas linking ML-induced UX challenges to user, scenario and system factors, with candidate design responses.
useWhen: Concepting an AI or ML feature where designers and data scientists need a shared view of how model behaviour will affect users.
avoidWhen: Concept stage only, not for prototyping; its fixed questions cannot cover every case and may narrow creative work, and it was not co-developed with practitioners. Consult the primary papers for the fields. To evaluate real model behaviour with users use Prototype / Wizard-of-Oz A/B Test, Wizard of Oz Prototyping or AI Explainability Auditing for UX.
whyLost: Published in HCI venues but rarely adopted; practitioners use broader AI design guidelines and team-specific canvases instead.
whereToUse: AI features in SaaS, recommendation systems, health triage tools, generative AI assistants.
example: A health-app team concepting symptom triage maps the challenge 'model may misclassify rare conditions' to sparse training data and anxious users, and decides outputs should suggest next steps rather than name diagnoses.
sources: User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
reference: Zhou, Z., Gong, Q., Qi, Z. and Sun, L. (2019) ML-Process Canvas: a design tool to support the UX design of machine learning-empowered products. CHI EA 2019; Abbas, A.M.H., Ghauth, K.I. and Ting, C.-Y. (2022) User experience design using machine learning: a systematic review. IEEE Access, 10, 51501-51514.

name: Mobile Adaptation by Use-Context Reduction
origin: Jenifer Tidwell (2010), drawing on Brian Fling, Mobile Design and Development (2009)
summary: Derive a mobile product from what users need in mobile contexts, strip it to those tasks, exploit device hardware, linearise content and streamline the commonest sequences.
description: Rather than porting a desktop product, this practice starts from mobile use contexts: needing a fact right now, filling a few spare minutes, social connection, being told something urgent, and relevance to the current place. The team selects the few tasks those contexts call for and strips the mobile version to them, removing sidebars, extra content and stacked headers, while keeping a clear link to the full product, because many people only have phones. Navigation may become narrower and deeper. Device capabilities such as location, camera, voice, gestures and haptics are added where they serve the chosen tasks. Content is ordered into a single readable column, which also helps screen readers, and the commonest sequences are optimised: minimal typing, few page loads, no sideways scrolling, few taps and targets of at least 1 cm. Mobile-first and responsive design absorbed most of this.
steps: List the mobile use contexts that apply: fact now, spare minutes, social, alerts, location.
Choose the few tasks mobile users need in those contexts and remove everything else from the mobile version.
Provide an obvious route to the full product, or build a complete mobile version, so nothing becomes unreachable.
Narrow and deepen the navigation if the top level is too broad for a small screen.
Add device capabilities (location, camera, voice, haptics, background running) that serve the chosen tasks.
Order content linearly so it reads well in one column.
Streamline the commonest sequences: minimal typing, fewer page loads and bytes, no sideways scrolling, fewer taps, targets of at least 1 cm.
outputs: A reduced mobile information architecture, prioritised task flows and a list of device-capability features.
useWhen: Use when creating or overhauling a mobile app or site from an existing desktop product, or when mobile analytics show users only ever do a few things.
avoidWhen: Avoid guessing contexts: establish real mobile use with Mobile ethnography or Diary Studies first, and check the result with Mobile Device Usability Testing. Do not strip content that phone-only users need.
whyLost: It was absorbed into mobile-first and responsive design practice, so the use-context reduction step is often skipped in favour of simply reflowing the desktop layout.
whereToUse: Travel, retail, banking and public-service apps; field-worker tools; content sites with heavy phone traffic.
example: An airline's mobile redesign starts from at-the-airport contexts and keeps flight status, check-in, boarding pass and disruption alerts on the first screen, with fare search one tap away. Gate-change alerts use push and location.
reference: Tidwell, J. (2010). Designing Interfaces: Patterns for Effective Interaction Design (2nd ed.). Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 441-447.

name: Mobile Device Usability Testing
origin: Practice described by Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed (2012); sled example by Patrick Kennedy
summary: Usability testing adapted to phones and tablets, recording screen, fingers and face with a sled or document camera, or testing in real mobile contexts.
description: Mobile interaction involves small keyboards, gestures, side buttons, movement and interruption, so desktop screen recording misses much of what matters. The adaptation records three channels: screen activity, finger movements and optionally the face. Set-ups range from a sled (a rig holding small cameras over the device, with feeds combined into picture-in-picture), to a desk-mounted document camera with better image but restricted movement, to commercial sleds, to field tests in streets, cars and public transport with at least two researchers, one filming and one interviewing. The session protocol otherwise follows an in-person usability test. The guiding principle is location: the lab teaches a lot, but context-dependent behaviour such as one-handed use, glare or interruptions needs testing where the device is actually used. Modern remote tools now capture screen and touches on participants' own devices.
steps: Decide what must be seen: screen, finger movements, face, surroundings.
Choose a set-up: camera sled over the device, desk-mounted document camera, mirrored screen with touch indicators, or field recording on the participant's own phone.
Pilot the rig so it does not change grip or posture more than necessary.
Run the session as a standard moderated test with realistic tasks, including gestures and interruptions.
For field tests, send at least two researchers, one filming and one interviewing, and choose realistic contexts such as transit or walking.
Combine feeds into picture-in-picture recordings and analyse touches, errors and context effects alongside verbal data.
outputs: Picture-in-picture recordings, usability problems linked to touch and gesture behaviour, and context-specific findings.
useWhen: Evaluating native apps, mobile web and tablet interfaces, especially gesture-heavy or on-the-go tasks.
avoidWhen: Avoid elaborate rigs when unmoderated remote tools with touch capture suffice; use field methods such as Diary Studies when long-term context matters more than task performance.
whyLost: It survived and became standard as mobile became the primary platform, with hardware rigs largely replaced by software capture.
whereToUse: Mobile banking, delivery and travel apps, health trackers, any product used while moving.
example: A ride-hailing team records participants booking a car on their own phones at a busy station, revealing that the confirm button sits under the thumb's resting position and causes accidental bookings.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. and Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience, 2nd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 300-302.

name: Mobile ethnography
origin: Practitioner sources: Korostoff (2014), Bailey (2014), Cribbett (2015), Hudson (2016); Ethnobot by Tallyn et al. (2018)
summary: Participants capture their own in-context experiences with phones, wearable cameras or a prompting chatbot, extending observation to times the researcher is absent, then review records in interview.
description: Mobile ethnography combines ethnographic observation with diary study: the participant, not the researcher, records what happens. Capture can be passive (a clip camera photographing every 30 seconds, with no conscious action), active (guided journal entries, video, prompted answers and sound bites recorded in the moment) or mixed. Passive capture shows natural behaviour but misses meaning; active capture gives detail but interrupts flow and depends on what people choose to record. Tools range from dedicated apps that log per-touchpoint ratings, photos and locations on a timeline to chatbots that ask preset questions and request photos as people move through a setting. Rigour comes from pairing the captured record with a follow-up interview in which the participant explains the moments, and from deciding the capture mode deliberately rather than by tool default.
steps: Define the ethnographic objectives and the moments or touchpoints you want captured.
Choose passive capture (for example a wearable camera taking a photo every 30 seconds), active capture (journal entries, video, prompted responses) or a mix, and choose the tool.
Brief participants on what and when to capture; for active capture, schedule or trigger prompts that ask about time, environment, social pressure, motivation and prior experience.
If using a chatbot, programme preset questions with response buttons plus open prompts for comments and photos, and pilot it to check the options are not too restrictive.
Collect timelines of photos, ratings and notes over the study period, monitoring compliance without steering content.
Review each participant's timeline with them in an in-depth interview, using captured moments as cues.
Count structured responses, code interviews and comments (two coders where possible), and optionally build an experience map of peaks and pain points.
outputs: Participant-generated multimedia timelines, touchpoint ratings, coded interview themes and optional experience maps of peaks, opportunities and pain points.
useWhen: Behaviour happens across places and times a researcher cannot attend, such as commutes, shopping trips, events or home routines, and you need in-the-moment records rather than recall.
avoidWhen: Avoid for private or sensitive settings where cameras are inappropriate, or where you need to see detail the participant will not notice; use contextual inquiry or shadowing. Passive capture alone gives no meaning and active capture disrupts the behaviour; analysis is labour-intensive. Preset chatbot options can feel restrictive.
whyLost: Survives because smartphones made it cheap and remote research platforms package it; it is widely used in market research and UX discovery.
whereToUse: Retail and omnichannel journeys, travel and events, food and household routines, health self-management, and remote discovery where travel budgets are limited.
example: A grocery app team asks 15 shoppers to log each shopping trip for two weeks with photos and a one-tap rating at each stage. Debrief interviews built on the timelines show that list-making happens on paper at the fridge, not in the app.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Marsh, S. (2018). User Research. Kogan Page, pp. 162-164; Tallyn, E. et al. (2018), Ethnobot, as described in Preece, Sharp & Rogers (2019).

name: Mobile Phone Usability Questionnaire (MPUQ)
origin: Ryu, 2009, from Ryu and Smith-Jackson's doctoral work
summary: A 72-item questionnaire for mobile phones that scores six usability factors, from ease of learning and use to typical phone tasks and affective aspects.
description: The MPUQ is a specialised questionnaire assembled from proven general instruments and tailored to mobile handsets. Its 72 items load on six factors: ease of learning and use; helpfulness and problem-solving capabilities; affective aspects and multimedia properties; commands and minimal memory load; control and efficiency; and typical tasks for mobile phones. Sample items ask whether it is easy to change the ringer signal, whether the user can personalise it, whether they feel excited using it, and whether the phone book is easy to use. Shneiderman et al. present it as an example of device-specific measurement and stress that no single score should stand alone: triangulate with observation, interviews and logs. The item set reflects feature phones, so any reuse needs adaptation for smartphones and re-checking of reliability and factor structure.
steps: Decide whether device-specific diagnosis is needed or a general scale (SUS, UMUX-Lite) will suffice.
Have participants use the device for representative tasks before administering the questionnaire.
Administer the 72 items, adapting dated items carefully if necessary.
Score each of the six factors and compare across devices or versions.
If items were altered, check reliability (for example Cronbach's alpha of 0.70 or more per factor) and factor structure.
Triangulate factor scores with observed task performance and usage logs.
outputs: Six factor scores describing the usability of a mobile device, comparable across products or versions.
useWhen: When comparing handsets or device-level experiences where factor-level diagnosis (memory load, control, affect) matters more than a single summary score.
avoidWhen: Avoid for modern app evaluation without revalidation; it is long and dated. For short, general measurement use System Usability Scale (SUS) or UMUX-Lite.
whyLost: It was built for the feature-phone era; smartphones changed the tasks, and short general scales such as SUS proved adequate for phones.
whereToUse: Historical benchmark for device-specific scale construction; possible template for new device classes such as wearables or in-car systems.
example: A wearables team adapts MPUQ's six-factor structure to build a smartwatch questionnaire, rewording ringer and phone-book items for notifications and contacts, then revalidates it with 250 users.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Shneiderman, B., Plaisant, C., Cohen, M., Jacobs, S., Elmqvist, N., & Diakopoulos, N. (2018). Designing the User Interface (6th ed., Global Edition). Harlow: Pearson, pp. 190-191, Table 5.5 (MPUQ after Ryu, 2009).

name: Mobile Touch Layout Audit (Grip and Thumb Zones, Target Size and Spacing)
aka: Touch target size and spacing audit
origin: Josh Clark, Designing for Touch (2015), synthesising Steven Hoober's 2013 observation of 1,300+ phone users, Hoober and Shank's tablet studies and Microsoft touch-accuracy research
summary: Inspect a mobile or tablet layout against grip-based thumb zones, hand occlusion and physical touch-target thresholds to flag misplaced, undersized or crowded controls.
description: This checklist inspection treats touch layout partly as industrial design. Phones are held one-handed (about 49%), cradled (36%) or two-handed (15%), and thumbs make about 75% of taps, so a comfortable arc sits at the bottom of the screen opposite the thumb; phablets, tablets and hybrids shift the zone to sides and corners. Frequent controls belong in the zone, destructive ones just outside, content above controls because the hand hides what is below, and feedback above the finger. Target size is checked in physical units: Microsoft data show miss rates of about 1 in 30 at 5 mm, 1 in 100 at 7 mm and 1 in 200 at 9 mm. Clark sets 7 mm (44 px, pt or dp) as the minimum, 9-11 mm for risky or out-of-zone targets, 10-15 mm for users with limited motor control, and 2 mm spacing between 7 mm targets.
steps: List the device classes in scope and the grips used on each, from observation or published grip studies; design for the most constrained grip.
Draw easy, stretch and hard thumb zones per grip and overlay them where devices or hands overlap.
Check that frequent and primary controls sit in the shared easy zone and destructive or data-changing controls just outside it.
Check hand occlusion: content and labels above controls, touch feedback above the finger, and no clashes with OS or browser toolbars.
With the viewport set to device-width, list every target's size and spacing; flag targets under 44 x 44 px (7 mm), allowing 44 x 30 only where space forces it.
Flag destructive or edge and corner targets under 57-69 px (9-11 mm), and 7 mm targets closer than 2 mm (13 px) apart.
Raise sizes to 10-15 mm for audiences with limited motor control and report violations with recommended changes.
outputs: Thumb-zone diagrams per form factor, a control-placement plan, and a list of undersized, crowded or misplaced targets with recommended sizes.
useWhen: Design reviews and expert inspections of mobile apps, responsive sites and tablet or hybrid interfaces before or alongside user testing.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating grip shares and thresholds as fixed laws: grips change with context and platform conventions force compromises. When you need sizes for a new device or population, run an empirical touch-target study instead.
whyLost: Platform minimums such as 44 pt survive as rules of thumb, but the grip-based zone analysis and the risk-scaled size thresholds are rarely applied systematically.
whereToUse: Mobile banking and payments, e-commerce checkout, health apps for older adults, tablet point-of-sale, foldable and large-screen phones.
example: An audit of a payments app finds the 'Send' button bottom-centre in the easy zone but 'Cancel transfer' flush beside it at 36 px. The team moves cancellation to the top bar and enlarges it to 57 px, removing the main source of accidental cancellations.
reference: Clark, J. (2015). Designing for Touch. New York: A Book Apart, ch. 1-2; Hoober, S. (2013). How do users really hold mobile devices? UXmatters.

name: Mock-up and Trial Sessions (Cooperative Prototyping)
origin: UTOPIA project (Ehn, Kyng, Bødker et al.), 1981-1985; Bødker and Grønbæk (1991)
summary: Users try out tangible mock-ups and early prototypes in simulated work situations, modifying them with designers on the spot.
description: In the UTOPIA project with Nordic graphic workers, designers built mock-ups of page-layout systems from cardboard, paper and slides so typographers could experience and evaluate future technology in realistic work situations. The treatise lists mock-up and trial sessions among the core Scandinavian methods. Cooperative prototyping (Bødker and Grønbæk) extended this with computer prototypes modified during sessions. The rigour lies in grounding evaluation in simulated real work, letting users' tacit skills surface through use rather than description, and treating the mock-up as a shared language rather than a test object. Unlike usability testing, users co-author changes.
steps: Build a mock-up or modifiable prototype representing the future system in its work setting.
Prepare realistic work scenarios drawn from current practice.
Have users enact the scenarios with the mock-up, thinking aloud and improvising.
Pause to discuss breakdowns and modify the mock-up together on the spot.
Record changes and the reasons users gave for them.
Iterate across sessions, gradually increasing fidelity.
outputs: Evolved mock-ups, documented breakdowns and user-authored changes, requirements grounded in tacit skill.
useWhen: Designing tools for skilled work where tacit knowledge matters and users should co-author design.
avoidWhen: When summative performance data is needed; use controlled usability testing.
whyLost: Collapsed into prototype testing where users evaluate but do not co-author; the political framing was lost.
whereToUse: Professional creative tools, clinical devices, factory HMIs, assistive technology.
example: Radiographers enact a scan-booking scenario with a foam-board console mock-up and rearrange controls to match their two-handed positioning routine; the arrangement is carried into the hardware design.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Ehn P & Kyng M (1991) Cardboard computers: mocking-it-up or hands-on the future. In Design at Work
Bødker S & Grønbæk K (1991) Cooperative prototyping. IJMMS 34(3)
reference: Ehn P & Kyng M (1991) Cardboard computers: mocking-it-up or hands-on the future. In Greenbaum & Kyng (Eds) Design at Work. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Mode Effects Analysis in Survey Administration
origin: de Leeuw, 2005; Dillman et al., 2014
summary: Checks and designs for how administering a survey by web, app, phone, in person or SMS changes who responds and how they answer.
description: Mode effects are differences in survey results caused by how a survey is administered. Modes differ in who they reach (selection effects) and in how respondents answer (measurement effects): interviewer-administered modes increase social desirability and acquiescence, aural modes produce recency effects while visual modes produce primacy effects, and small screens increase satisficing and item nonresponse. Mode effects analysis plans for these differences through unified mode design (constructing questions that function equivalently across modes), randomised split-mode experiments to estimate measurement effects, and statistical adjustment when modes are mixed. In UX it is essential when moving surveys between channels, combining in-app and email samples, or reaching low-literacy or offline users by phone, so that trend breaks are not misinterpreted.
steps: When a UX survey must be administered in multiple modes (e.g., mobile and desktop): test for mode effects before reporting aggregate results.
Run the same survey on a random split of participants across modes.
For each item, test: Mann-Whitney U test for significant differences between modes.
If significant: report mode-specific results, not aggregates.
Key rule: never compare results collected in different modes without testing for mode effects.
outputs: Mode comparison estimates, a mode-appropriate unified questionnaire, adjusted results, and guidance on which modes can be pooled.
useWhen: Surveys administered across channels (in-app plus email, phone for low-literacy users), trend comparisons where the mode changed, and sensitive topics.
avoidWhen: Avoid when a single mode is used consistently and comparisons over time keep that mode; then focus on other error sources.
whyLost: UX surveys switch channels for convenience (in-app, email, intercepts) without recognising that mode alters responses, so trend breaks are misread as experience changes.
whereToUse: Multi-channel UX research programs, CSAT surveys administered across devices, international UX research where mode varies by region.
example: A telecom moves its satisfaction survey from phone to SMS and scores drop by 8 points; a split-sample test shows most of the drop is a mode effect (less social desirability), not worse service.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
reference: de Leeuw ED (2005) To mix or not to mix data collection modes in surveys. Journal of Official Statistics 21(2):233-255

name: Model Cards
origin: Margaret Mitchell et al. (2018), 'Model Cards for Model Reporting'
summary: Publish a short structured document with each model stating how it was built and evaluated, its intended uses and users, performance across groups, and its limitations.
description: A model card accompanies a trained model and discloses what stakeholders need to judge whether it fits their purpose, covering ethical and fairness considerations as well as metrics. Standard sections are model details; intended use, including primary uses, users and out-of-scope uses; factors (demographic, environmental, technical); metrics, decision thresholds and variation; evaluation data; training data; quantitative analyses, both unitary and intersectional; ethical considerations; and caveats and recommendations. Cards sit within a wider responsible-AI process: finding sources of bias at each stage, understanding data limits with domain experts and affected people, and weighing trade-offs between privacy, compression and fairness. Because cards must be updated with every model version, generation should be automated. For UX, the intended-use, factors and caveats sections are where user research about contexts and affected groups becomes a durable, checkable commitment.
steps: Review sources of bias across training data, labelling, features, objective and evaluation.
Run fine-grained evaluation sliced by relevant groups and their intersections.
Fill each section: model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses, ethical considerations, caveats and recommendations.
Involve domain experts and affected users in drafting intended and out-of-scope uses.
Publish the card with the model and link it from product documentation where users or customers can see it.
Regenerate the card on every model update, ideally automatically from the evaluation pipeline.
outputs: A model card per model version, with sliced evaluation results and documented intended uses and limits.
useWhen: Shipping or procuring ML models, especially where decisions affect people (credit, hiring, health, moderation), or where downstream teams must decide whether a model fits their context.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for asking whether the product should be built; manual cards become stale for frequently updated models unless automated. For testing behaviour use Behavioural Testing of ML Models.
whyLost: Model cards are established in responsible-AI practice and on model hubs, but they are written by ML teams, and UX research rarely feeds their intended-use and factors sections.
whereToUse: AI features in regulated domains, internal model catalogues, B2B AI products whose customers need transparency, public-sector algorithms.
example: A bank's card for a credit-limit model lists applicants with thin credit files as an out-of-scope use after sliced evaluation shows much higher error for them. The research team's interviews with such applicants shape the caveats, and the product routes them to manual review.
reference: Mitchell, M., Wu, S., Zaldivar, A., Barnes, P., Vasserman, L., Hutchinson, B., Spitzer, E., Raji, I. D. and Gebru, T. (2019). Model cards for model reporting. Proceedings of the Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT* 2019).

name: Model checking usability properties
donor: Software engineering (formal methods, model checking, theorem proving)
origin: Dix's PIE model (1987-1991); Abowd and colleagues (1994-1995); Campos and Harrison (IVY, 2008 templates); Loer and Harrison; Paterno; Palanque and Bastide
summary: Model the interface formally, state generic usability properties such as reversibility, feedback and consistency as logical formulae, and let a model checker or prover test every reachable state.
description: A formal model of an interface can be analysed exhaustively. Model checking represents it as a finite-state machine and examines every reachable state, returning a counterexample when a property fails; theorem proving handles infinite states with analyst guidance. Generic usability properties have been catalogued: reversibility, undo within N steps, deadlock freedom, task completeness, predictability, reachability, honesty, feedback, behavioural consistency, visibility and more. Campos and Harrison's templates turn these into parameterised formulae over actions, states and modes, instantiated by choosing a guard, filters linking hidden state to its perceivable counterpart, and modes. Industrial results include 98 design errors found in a cockpit window manager from 563 properties. Adding assumptions about what information prompts each user step restricts checks to plausible behaviour.
steps: Choose the scope: interface only, functional core, and possibly user tasks.
Model the system in a tool-supported notation such as statecharts, interactors or Petri nets, separating perceivable attributes, actions and modes.
Select usability properties from the catalogue and instantiate templates with concrete guards, filters and modes (for example that a pump status colour always matches pump flow).
Run the model checker over the full state space, or prove the theorem by induction over reachable states.
Interpret counterexamples or failed proofs as candidate design problems, using a trace visualiser.
Optionally add assumptions about the information that prompts each user step and re-check under them.
Amend the model or design and re-check until results match expectations.
outputs: A list of properties that hold or fail, counterexample traces, identified design problems, and sometimes generated test cases.
useWhen: Verifying safety-critical or highly modal interfaces where a missed inconsistency could cause harm and exhaustive coverage matters.
avoidWhen: Avoid for everyday products where usability testing finds problems more cheaply; state explosion, hard notations and the effort of phrasing properties are major costs. Use heuristic evaluation or cognitive walkthrough instead.
whyLost: Formal methods require specialist skills and fit regulated engineering; UX practice moved to empirical testing and rarely writes formal models.
whereToUse: Medical devices, avionics, nuclear and industrial control rooms, automotive HMI, and design systems with complex mode logic.
example: An infusion pump team models its number-entry interface and checks predictability and reversibility. The checker finds a mode where a key press silently changes units, which the team removes before summative testing.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Oliveira, R., Palanque, P., Weyers, B., Bowen, J. & Dix, A. (2017). State of the art on formal methods for interactive systems; Harrison, M. D. et al. (2017). The specification and analysis of use properties of a nuclear control system. Both in Weyers, B. et al. (eds) The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction. Springer.

name: Model Human Processor calculation
origin: Card, Moran and Newell, 1983, Xerox PARC
summary: Predict interaction times before a system exists by describing behaviour as cycles of perceptual, cognitive and motor processors with standard parameter values and principles.
description: The Model Human Processor is an engineering-style model of the user for designers, built for approximate, zero-parameter predictions made at design time. It has long-term memory, working memory, and visual and auditory image stores, each with code, capacity and decay, and three processors: perceptual (cycle about 100 ms, range 50-200), cognitive (about 70 ms, range 25-170) and motor (about 70 ms, range 30-100). Principles P0-P9 cover the recognise-act cycle, variable processor rates, encoding specificity, discrimination, Fitts' law, the power law of practice, Hick's law, rationality and problem spaces. Card, Moran and Newell wrote their chapter as small calculable problems, such as how long an editing step takes. Newell later called Soar a second iteration of the MHP. Parameter ranges are wide, so predictions suit comparing designs rather than exact times. KLM and GOMS grew out of it.
steps: Describe the user's activity at the interface as a sequence of perceptual, cognitive and motor processor cycles and memory stores used.
Identify which operating principles apply (for example Fitts' law for pointing, Hick's law for choice, power law of practice for learning).
Insert the standard parameter values (perceptual about 100 ms, cognitive about 70 ms, motor about 70 ms, with their ranges) without fitting them to the situation.
Compute predicted times for each design alternative, using the ranges to give fast, typical and slow estimates.
Compare alternatives and decide whether differences are large enough to matter, then check key predictions with a small timing test.
outputs: Approximate a priori time predictions, with fast-to-slow ranges, for interface tasks and design alternatives.
useWhen: When you need quick, defensible estimates of whether one design will be faster than another before building it, especially for short, expert, repetitive interactions.
avoidWhen: Avoid for novice behaviour, errors, problem solving or long tasks; use Keystroke-Level Model (KLM), GOMS / KLM or ACT-R Cognitive Modelling. Wide parameter ranges make absolute times unreliable.
whyLost: Its parameters are still taught, but practitioners skipped the calculation in favour of KLM operators or testing, and the full model is seldom applied.
whereToUse: Expert and high-frequency interfaces (call centres, trading, point of sale, games), in-car and wearable glanceable interactions, teaching cognitive engineering.
example: A point-of-sale team compares a two-level menu with a single grid of 24 buttons. MHP calculation with Hick's and Fitts' laws predicts about 400 ms saved per item for the grid, enough over 300 daily transactions to justify it.
reference: Card, S. K., Moran, T. P., & Newell, A. (1983). The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Model-Based (Linked) Meta-Analysis
origin: Betsy Jane Becker, 1992; Becker and Schram, 1994
summary: Pool the correlation matrices among a model's variables across studies and fit regression or path models to the pooled matrix to estimate direct, partial and indirect effects.
description: Instead of pooling one bivariate effect, model-based meta-analysis starts from a theoretical model drawn as a path diagram and collects all correlations among its variables from each study. Unreported cells are marked missing, and the covariances among each study's correlations are estimated. Homogeneity is tested, between-study variance estimated, and a fixed or random-effects mean correlation matrix is computed by generalised least squares. Standardised regression or path models are then fitted to the pooled matrix, giving partial and indirect effects, model comparisons and moderator analyses by subgroup. A useful by-product is a map of links that no study has examined. Limitations are missing correlations and fractionated evidence: different cells of the matrix may rest on different samples, so random-effects models are preferred.
steps: Specify the model as a path diagram, and use its constructs and instruments as search terms and inclusion rules.
Code each study's correlation vector, marking unreported cells as missing.
Estimate the covariances among each study's correlations.
Test homogeneity, estimate between-study variance and compute a mean correlation matrix by GLS.
Fit the regression or path model to the pooled matrix, reporting slopes, standard errors and tests.
Run moderator analyses by subgroup and map which links lack evidence.
outputs: A pooled correlation matrix, path coefficients with tests, and a gap map of unstudied relationships.
useWhen: Testing a multi-variable model of UX constructs (for example technology acceptance: ease of use, usefulness, intention, use) across many published or internal studies.
avoidWhen: Few studies report the full set of correlations, or the question is a single bivariate effect; use a standard meta-analysis.
whyLost: UX lacks a culture of pooling correlational studies, and MASEM requires specialist statistical skills.
whereToUse: Synthesis of TAM and UTAUT research, trust-in-AI models, and internal survey programmes measuring the same constructs across products.
example: A team pools 45 studies measuring perceived ease of use, usefulness, trust and intention to use AI assistants. The fitted path model shows trust's effect on intention runs largely through usefulness, and the gap map shows no study linked trust with actual logged use.
sources: The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
