reference: Becker, B. J. Ch. 20. In Cooper, H., Hedges, L. V., & Valentine, J. C. (Eds.) (2009). The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Russell Sage Foundation.

name: Model-Free Predictor Importance Screening
origin: Adapted for UX from Kuhn and Johnson, Applied Predictive Modeling (2013); Relief by Kira and Rendell (1992), ReliefF by Kononenko (1994), MIC by Reshef et al. (2011), LOESS by Cleveland and Devlin (1988)
summary: Score each candidate predictor's relationship with an outcome using a statistic matched to the data types, plot effect against significance, and check scores against a permutation baseline before shortlisting.
description: Before or instead of fitting a model, each predictor can be scored on its own as a triage step for large predictor sets. The statistic depends on data types: correlation, a LOESS pseudo R squared for curved relationships, or the maximal information coefficient for arbitrary shapes when both are numeric; a t-test on the difference in means for a binary predictor, displayed as a volcano plot of -log10(p) against effect so large-but-noisy and small-but-precise effects are distinguished; the area under the ROC curve treating the predictor itself as the score for a categorical outcome; and odds ratios with Fisher's exact test for two binary variables. ReliefF works for any type and can reflect interactions by comparing nearest same-class and different-class neighbours. Because its scores lack a natural threshold, the outcome labels are shuffled many times to build a null distribution, and observed scores are expressed in standard deviations above chance.
steps: Match the score to the outcome and predictor types: correlation, LOESS pseudo R squared or MIC; t-test with volcano plot; per-predictor ROC AUC; odds ratio with Fisher's exact test; gain ratio; or ReliefF.
Compute the score for every candidate predictor on the training data only.
Plot effect size against significance (volcano plot) or compare several scores in a scatter-plot matrix.
For scores without a natural threshold, permute the outcome labels many times (for example 500) and recompute to build a null distribution.
Shortlist predictors that stand well above the null, applying multiplicity control, then examine them with plots and domain knowledge.
Remove redundant, highly correlated survivors, look for interactions the univariate scores miss, and repeat any filtering inside resampling if it feeds a model.
outputs: A ranked list of predictors with scores, volcano plots and permutation-based standard scores.
useWhen: Exploring which of hundreds of logged behaviours, survey items or attributes relate to churn, conversion or satisfaction before modelling, or explaining drivers without committing to one model.
avoidWhen: When a well-validated model is available, whose importances (for example SHAP Driver Analysis or Random Forest Key Driver Analysis) are usually more reliable. Univariate scores pick redundant predictors, miss joint effects and say nothing about direction or form.
whyLost: It belongs to predictive-modelling practice; UX analysts tend to jump to a single regression or random forest and read its importances.
whereToUse: Churn and retention analytics, feature adoption studies, large survey batteries, instrumentation audits deciding which events matter.
example: A subscription app screens 240 logged events against 90-day churn. A volcano plot flags 'exported data' as a large, precise effect, while ReliefF scores 9 SD above the permutation null for an interaction between plan type and reminder settings that correlations missed.
reference: Kuhn, M. and Johnson, K. (2013). Applied Predictive Modeling. New York: Springer, pp. 463-486.

name: Moderated Usability Testing
origin: Usability labs, 1980s (e.g. IBM, Digital Equipment Corporation)
summary: A usability test in which a facilitator guides each session live, probing behaviour and adapting follow-up questions to understand problems in depth.
description: In moderated usability testing a researcher conducts each session in real time, in person or remotely, introducing tasks, observing behaviour and asking follow-up questions. The facilitator can clarify task misunderstandings, probe unexpected behaviour and explore the reasoning behind actions, which makes it well suited to complex flows, early concepts and specialist users. The trade-off is that the facilitator can also bias participants. Rigour comes from a written discussion guide with consistent task wording, neutral probes, deliberate decisions about when to intervene, separating observation from interpretation through note-takers or observers, and debriefing with observers after each session. Small samples of five to eight participants per segment are typical for formative work.
steps: Write a discussion guide with introduction, warm-up questions, task scenarios and debrief questions.
Recruit 5 to 8 participants per segment and schedule 45 to 60 minute sessions.
Pilot the guide and adjust timing and wording.
Facilitate sessions using neutral language, asking open follow-ups such as 'what did you expect to happen?' after tasks.
Have a separate note-taker log observations and quotes with timestamps.
Debrief with observers after each session and capture emerging issues.
Analyse across sessions, rate severity and report recommendations.
outputs: Detailed observations and quotes, explanations of why problems occur, severity-rated findings and recommendations.
useWhen: For complex task flows, early concepts and prototypes that need explanation, specialist or vulnerable users, and when qualitative depth matters.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need large samples or rapid turnaround across many variants; use unmoderated remote testing. Avoid probing during timed tasks used for benchmarks.
whyLost: Still in use: Richer than unmoderated; enables real-time hypothesis adjustment; essential for nuanced insight.
whereToUse: Complex task flows; early-stage concepts; when qualitative depth is needed.
example: A clinical trial platform runs moderated remote sessions with six research coordinators. Probing reveals that they export data to spreadsheets because they distrust the in-app audit trail, an insight unmoderated tests would have missed.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Dumas, J. S. & Loring, B. A. (2008). Moderating Usability Tests: Principles and Practices for Interacting. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Moderation (interaction effects)
origin: Reuben Baron & David Kenny, 1986; probing methods by Leona Aiken & Stephen West, 1991
summary: Tests whether the effect of one variable on an outcome depends on the level of a third variable, revealing for whom and when a design works.
description: Moderation asks whether a relationship changes across conditions: does a redesign reduce errors for novices but not experts, or does a trust badge raise conversion only on mobile? It is modelled by adding a product term (X times W) to a regression; a reliable interaction coefficient means the slope of X differs by W. Rigour lies in centring continuous predictors, powering the study for the interaction (which typically needs around four times the sample of a main effect of similar size), probing with simple slopes at meaningful values and Johnson-Neyman regions, and pre-registering moderators rather than hunting through segments. Epidemiology calls the same idea effect modification, and it underpins heterogeneous treatment effect analysis in experimentation.
steps: Pre-specify the focal predictor, the moderator and the theoretical reason the effect should differ.
Power the study for the interaction specifically; plan roughly four times the sample needed to detect the main effect.
Mean-centre continuous predictors and fit the model with both main effects and the product term.
Probe a significant interaction with simple slopes at the moderator's mean and plus or minus one SD, or at real segment values.
Compute the Johnson-Neyman interval to show the moderator range where the effect is non-zero.
Plot predicted outcomes by moderator level and report the interaction effect size with a confidence interval.
outputs: Interaction coefficients, simple-slope estimates, Johnson-Neyman regions and interaction plots showing which users or contexts the effect holds for.
useWhen: When you suspect a design effect varies by expertise, device, segment, market or context, and need to state for whom a change works.
avoidWhen: Avoid post-hoc segment fishing across dozens of moderators, underpowered samples, or when you need the mechanism rather than the condition (use mediation analysis).
whyLost: UX teams usually split results by segment informally instead of testing interactions, so differences in subgroup p-values get misread as moderation. The formal method stayed in psychology and epidemiology.
whereToUse: Personalisation decisions, accessibility and expertise effects, mobile versus desktop A/B results, heterogeneous treatment effects in experiments, and market-specific launches.
example: A fintech A/B test shows a simplified onboarding has no average effect on completion. An interaction with prior investing experience reveals a 9-point gain for first-time investors and a 4-point loss for experienced ones, leading to an adaptive flow.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis (Andrew Hayes)
Multiple Regression: Testing and Interpreting Interactions (Leona Aiken & Stephen West)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Aiken, L. S. & West, S. G. (1991) Multiple Regression: Testing and Interpreting Interactions. Sage.

name: Modular Grid, Type Scale and Page Proportioning
aka: Modular scale for type sizes and page subdivision
Page and textblock proportioning with a margin canon
Modular page grid with a baseline grid
origin: Traditional size series and Renaissance page canons (Villard de Honnecourt as reconstructed by Jan Tschichold); Le Corbusier's Modulor; codified by Bringhurst (2004) and Spiekermann (2022)
summary: Derive type sizes, spatial units, grid modules and margins from a small set of related proportions so every dimension in a layout belongs to one system.
description: This practice replaces ad hoc sizes with a proportional system. A type scale restricts sizes to a prearranged series: the traditional 6-72 point series, or one generated from a ratio such as the golden section, where two interlocking strands (for example 6 8 10 13 16 21 26 34) give flexibility. A modular scale converted to layout units acts like a measuring stick for subdividing the page. Page and textblock proportions are chosen from harmonious ratios (2:3, 3:4, 1:√2 and others) suited to content, with the textblock placed high and toward the spine and margins defined as fractions of page width and height, as in the Villard-Tschichold canon where margins of one ninth make textblock depth equal page width. A modular grid divides the page into equal modules sharing its proportion, with columns as module multiples minus gutters, and all type sitting on a fine baseline grid, which gives the coherence of bricks in a building.
steps: Establish practical limits: screen breakpoints or sheet sizes, binding or device constraints.
Choose one or two base ratios (traditional series, golden section, 1:2, a musical interval or a project-specific proportion).
Generate the type scale and select a small subset of sizes for the job, starting from body text size.
Choose page or viewport proportions and a textblock proportion that contrasts purposefully with them.
Define a modular grid: module size in the page's proportion, columns as module multiples minus gutters, and a baseline unit (for example 4 px or 1.5 mm) on which all type sits.
Set margins as fractions of width and height (for example s = w/9, t = h/9, e = 2s, f = 2t) or as multiples of the base unit.
Encode the scale, grid and spacing as design tokens or a style sheet, test on real content, and adjust in typographic increments.
outputs: A named type scale, spacing units, grid specification (modules, columns, gutters, baseline) and margin proportions, often as design tokens.
useWhen: Use when establishing a design system, editorial template or document format, or when layouts feel inconsistent because sizes and spaces were chosen one at a time.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating proportional harmony as evidence of usability; check hierarchy and scanning with First-click testing or Eye Tracking. Too many sizes or a rigid single-ratio scale defeats the purpose.
whyLost: It survived because grids, type scales and spacing tokens became the backbone of design systems and CSS layout.
whereToUse: Design systems, editorial and publishing products, dashboards, report and document templates, marketing sites.
example: A fintech design system adopts a 1.25 ratio type scale with seven sizes, a 4 px baseline and a 12-column grid with 24 px gutters. Engineers implement them as tokens, and inconsistent one-off sizes in the codebase fall from 41 to 7.
reference: Bringhurst, R. (2004). The Elements of Typographic Style (version 3.0). Point Roberts, WA: Hartley & Marks, pp. 45, 143-178. Tschichold, J. (1991). The Form of the Book. Vancouver: Hartley & Marks.

name: Modular Interface Evaluation (Fodor's Criteria)
origin: Adapted for UX from Jerry Fodor's criteria for modular input systems (The Modularity of Mind, 1983); the book characterises perceptual and language input systems and offers no interface evaluation procedure.
summary: Evaluates which interface responses rely on fast, automatic, encapsulated perceptual processes versus slow central reasoning, designing critical signals for the former.
description: Fodor argued that input systems such as vision and language parsing are modular: domain-specific, mandatory, fast, informationally encapsulated (unaffected by beliefs) and shallow in output, in contrast to slow, flexible central reasoning. Modular interface evaluation applies these criteria to interface signals, asking which information users must process quickly and reliably and whether it is presented in forms that engage modular perception (distinct colour, motion, sound, spatial position) or forms that require central interpretation (codes, text, calculation). Signals critical under time pressure should exploit modular processing; information requiring judgement can rely on central processes. Rigour comes from a systematic signal inventory, grounding in perception research, and confirming classifications with reaction-time or detection measures.
steps: Module quality audit for design systems: for each interface component, evaluate:
Domain-specificity (does it do exactly one thing?),
Mandatory operation (does it always behave consistently?),
Informational encapsulation (does it work without depending on external state?),
Graceful failure modes (when it fails, does it fail predictably?). Score each criterion 0–2. Components scoring < 6/8 are architectural debt.
outputs: A classification of interface signals by processing type, identified signals that wrongly rely on central reasoning, and redesigns using perceptually modular cues.
useWhen: Safety-critical warnings, time-pressured interfaces, automotive and medical displays where responses must be fast and resistant to distraction.
avoidWhen: Avoid when tasks are deliberative by nature; the modularity framework is contested, so prefer empirical reaction-time testing for final decisions.
whyLost: Fodor's modularity thesis shaped 1980s cognitive science; HCI absorbed preattentive processing findings but dropped the framework itself.
whereToUse: Design system architecture, component library design, microfrontend UX architecture, API design.
example: An infusion pump's critical alarm relies on reading a text code; reclassifying it to use a distinct sound and colour, processed automatically, cuts response times in simulation.
sources: The Modularity of Mind — Jerry Fodor
reference: Fodor JA (1983) The Modularity of Mind. MIT Press

name: Momentary Item Writing and ESM Questionnaire Construction
origin: Eisele, Kasanova and Houben, 2022; Palmier-Claus et al., 2011; Silvia et al., 2014
summary: Write short, state-focused items with explicit time references and assemble them into a brief repeated questionnaire whose order, branching and length limit bias and burden.
description: Momentary items must capture states, not traits: adding 'right now' to a trait question does not make it momentary. 'Right now' suits states; 'since the last beep' suits rare, ongoing or hard-to-report events. Mixing references changes meaning, turning a concurrent association into a prospective one. The item checklist: short; no extreme wording; consider implicit rather than explicit assessment; avoid negatives and jargon; no reflective questions; relevant in every context the participant may be in. For assembly, put transient states first and context last, consider randomising within groups, group items by time frame and scale, and aim for under three minutes. Branches should be equally long so participants cannot shorten the survey by answering strategically; alternatives are adaptive follow-ups or planned missing designs. Control items (pain, whether a question bothered the participant) help detect reactivity. Ask about states and contexts separately and model their association rather than asking compound questions.
steps: Define each construct as a state with its time scale.
Choose 'right now' or an interval reference ('since the last beep') per item, and align references for items you will relate concurrently.
Word items against the checklist (short, no extremes, no negatives or jargon, no reflection, relevant in all contexts) and test wording with the target population.
Choose response scales and use them consistently across items.
Order items from transient states to context, and decide on randomisation within groups.
Keep completion under about three minutes using equal-length branching, adaptive follow-ups or a planned missing item subset.
Add control and reactivity items, pilot, and check that items show within-person variance.
outputs: A short momentary questionnaire with documented item rationale, time references and branching logic.
useWhen: Designing in-the-moment surveys for ESM, in-app micro-surveys or diary prompts that will be answered many times by the same people.
avoidWhen: One-off retrospective surveys, where standard question-writing principles apply; avoid compound items such as 'how frustrated are you when X'.
whyLost: UX in-product surveys borrow one-off survey wording; the specific craft of repeated momentary items stayed in clinical ESM research.
whereToUse: In-app intercepts repeated over time, diary studies, wearable-linked prompts and longitudinal AI assistant evaluations.
example: Instead of asking 'How annoyed are you when the assistant misunderstands you?', a team asks 'How annoyed do you feel right now?' and, separately, 'Since the last prompt, did the assistant misunderstand you?' and models the link.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Monte Carlo Evaluator-Aggregation Curve
aka: Monte Carlo aggregation of evaluator detections
Random aggregate resampling of evaluator-by-problem matrix
origin: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich, CHI 1990
summary: Estimate how many evaluators you need by resampling random groups from an evaluator-by-problem matrix and plotting the share of known problems each group size finds.
description: Nielsen and Molich collected independent heuristic-evaluation reports from 34 to 77 evaluators on four interfaces, scored them against a master list of known problems and recorded a binary evaluator-by-problem matrix. For every group size they drew between five and nine thousand random sets of evaluators, took the union of their problems and averaged the proportion found. The four curves had a common shape: a steep rise to about five evaluators, flattening to ten. Random rather than best evaluators were used because organisations must use available staff. Sorting the matrix by evaluator success and problem ease shows that detection is not cumulative, which is why aggregation pays. Later critiques note the curve is relative to known problems only, assumes perfect merging and consensus on false positives, and depends heavily on evaluator expertise.
steps: Have a pool of evaluators (ideally 20 or more) independently evaluate the same interface.
Build a master list of known problems and revise it after a first pass, since evaluators find problems the researchers missed.
Score each report against the list and record a binary evaluator-by-problem matrix; plot it sorted by evaluator success and problem ease.
For each group size from 1 to the pool size, draw thousands of random groups (Nielsen and Molich used 5,000 to 9,000) with replacement.
Take the union of each group's problems and compute the proportion of known problems found.
Average across draws, plot mean proportion against group size and tabulate selected sizes.
Choose the evaluator count where marginal gain flattens (often 3 to 5) and report that the curve is relative to known problems only.
outputs: A discovery curve and table of proportion of known problems found by number of evaluators, per interface.
useWhen: Deciding how many evaluators or test participants to use when you already have, or can collect, a full detection matrix; comparing evaluator pools or methods.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the known-problem list is small or unvalidated; for planning from a single small study use the Problem Discovery Sample Size Model or Capture-Recapture Estimation of Usability Problems.
whyLost: Practitioners adopted the conclusion ('three to five evaluators') but not the resampling procedure, which needs large evaluator pools few teams have.
whereToUse: Research operations calibrating expert-review panels, accessibility audit teams, or AI-assisted evaluators against humans.
example: A design-system team has 15 designers independently review a new checkout. Resampling shows four reviewers find 70% of known issues and eight find 85%, so they standardise on panels of four.
sources: Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces: Exploration and Evaluation (Ó Broin, 2011)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces (Nielsen & Molich, 1990)
reference: Nielsen, J. and Molich, R. (1990). Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. Proceedings of CHI '90, ACM, 249-256.

name: Monte Carlo Journey Simulation
origin: Stanisław Ulam & Nicholas Metropolis, 1940s; funnel application in Gopinath, 2025
summary: Simulates thousands of synthetic user journeys from observed step success probabilities to forecast end-to-end completion as a distribution with intervals and to test what-if improvements.
description: Monte Carlo simulation estimates outcomes by repeated random sampling. Applied to UX funnels, each virtual user passes or fails each step according to empirical step probabilities, and the share completing across many runs gives a completion distribution rather than a single number. In Vivek Gopinath's playbook, step probabilities of 81%, 75%, 85% and 95% across 10,000 virtual users give a mean completion of 49% [46%, 52%]; improving OTP to 92% gives 54% [51%, 57%], showing small step tweaks compound into larger overall lifts. Assumptions are stated explicitly: stationarity, approximate independence of steps, like-for-like traffic and no leakage. Sensitivity checks vary the improved step by ±10–20%, split by segment, and scale by expected weekly starts. CIs can be converted to SD with SD ≈ (upper − lower)/(2 × 1.96). The same technique forecasts ΔU under redesign scenarios in the Nash protocol.
steps: Collect empirical step-level success probabilities from experiments or analytics.
For each of 10,000 virtual users, sample success or failure at each step using those probabilities.
Aggregate the share of virtual users finishing and repeat to obtain a completion distribution.
Report the mean and 95% interval.
Run what-if scenarios by changing the probability of a target step.
Run sensitivity checks (best/mid/worst ±10–20%, segment splits, volume scaling) and state assumptions.
Compare the forecast with the observed lift after launch.
outputs: Completion distributions per scenario with intervals, what-if lifts and stated assumptions.
useWhen: When stakeholders ask what impact to expect at rollout and which step improvement matters most.
avoidWhen: When step outcomes are strongly correlated or traffic mix will change; model dependencies explicitly or use observed cohort data.
whyLost: Common in finance and engineering, but UX researchers rarely forecast impact with uncertainty.
whereToUse: Onboarding and KYC funnels, checkout, roadmap business cases, design adoption scenarios.
example: A trading app forecasts that raising OTP success to 92% lifts end-to-end completion from about 49% to 54%, and later observes a larger lift than predicted.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Metropolis, N., & Ulam, S. (1949). The Monte Carlo method. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 44(247), 335–341.

name: Monte Carlo simulation for completion rate forecasting
origin: Stanislaw Ulam & John von Neumann, 1946-1949 (Los Alamos)
summary: Forecasts the range of likely completion or adoption rates for a flow by repeatedly simulating users through uncertain step-level probabilities.
description: Instead of a single forecast, Monte Carlo simulation represents each uncertain input (step pass-through rates, traffic, effect of a redesign) as a probability distribution, typically drawn from study data, and simulates thousands of possible outcomes. The result is a distribution of completion rates from which you can read medians, intervals and the probability of hitting a target. For a five-step onboarding with each step's pass rate estimated from a usability study or analytics, simulation propagates uncertainty that point estimates hide. Rigour lies in grounding input distributions in data (e.g. Beta distributions from observed successes and failures), modelling correlations between steps, running enough iterations (10,000 or more) and checking sensitivity to assumptions.
steps: Map the flow into steps and identify uncertain inputs: per-step completion probabilities, traffic, expected redesign effects.
Specify a distribution for each input from data, e.g. Beta(successes + 1, failures + 1) for step pass rates from a study.
Model dependencies between steps where evidence suggests correlation (e.g. users who struggle early also struggle later).
Simulate at least 10,000 iterations, computing end-to-end completion for each.
Summarise the outcome distribution with median, 80% and 95% intervals and the probability of exceeding targets.
Run sensitivity analysis (e.g. tornado chart) to show which steps most influence the forecast.
outputs: A probabilistic forecast of completion or adoption, probabilities of meeting targets and a sensitivity ranking of steps.
useWhen: Forecasting the impact of redesigns before launch, setting realistic targets, or communicating uncertainty from small-sample usability data.
avoidWhen: Avoid when inputs are pure guesses with no data or expert calibration, or when a simple analytic calculation conveys the uncertainty adequately.
whyLost: Monte Carlo is standard in finance, engineering and operations research, but UX forecasts are usually single numbers or not made at all.
whereToUse: Onboarding and checkout redesigns, KYC flows in fintech, feature adoption forecasts, research-backed business cases.
example: Usability testing of a new KYC flow gives per-step success counts from 12 participants. Simulation with Beta distributions forecasts a median completion of 71% (80% interval 58-81%), with only a 22% chance of reaching the 80% target, prompting a fix to the ID upload step.
sources: Monte Carlo Methods with R (Christian Robert & George Casella)
Metropolis & Ulam (1949) The Monte Carlo method
Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 56 — Monte Carlo Simulation & Predictive Forecasting
Four Ways to do Project Analysis (Crawford, n.d.)
Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella, 2010)
Scenario Analysis, Decision Trees and Simulation for Cost Benefit Analysis of Cargo Screening Processes (Sherman et al., 2010)
reference: Robert, C. P. & Casella, G. (2010) Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R. Springer.

name: Mood and transient-context check for global self-reports
donor: Judgement and decision making; social psychology
origin: Schwarz and Clore, 1983
summary: A design and analysis check that treats global ratings (satisfaction, life quality) as sensitive to transient mood and records or neutralises the conditions that shift it.
description: When people answer global evaluative questions they consult how they feel and can mistake pre-existing mood for a reaction to the target. In Schwarz and Clore's telephone interviews, life satisfaction was higher on sunny days, but asking about the weather as an aside removed the difference while current mood reports were unchanged: once a transient cause is salient, people discount it. Happy moods also favour heuristic processing and sad moods detailed processing. For surveys this means global ratings collected after an emotionally loaded task, during an outage, or under notable external conditions carry mood that is not about the product. The check is to record those conditions, randomise the timing of global items, compare across conditions and, where appropriate, make the transient cause salient. Feelings genuinely caused by the product are valid data, so the aim is attribution, not removal.
steps: Identify global ratings collected after emotionally loaded tasks, failures, or under notable conditions (outages, weather, news events, time pressure).
Record those conditions alongside each response, or randomise whether global questions come before or after the loaded task.
Compare global ratings across conditions to estimate mood carry-over.
Where appropriate, make the transient cause salient (for example a brief aside about a known outage) so respondents can discount it.
Interpret and report global ratings with the mood context stated, separating product-caused from incidental affect.
outputs: Context-aware global ratings and an estimate of how much incidental mood shifted them.
useWhen: When interpreting satisfaction, NPS or wellbeing ratings that fluctuate with events outside the product, or when a test session includes a frustrating task before the final questionnaire.
avoidWhen: Avoid over-correcting when the feeling is caused by the product itself. Misattribution manipulations change interpretation and need care; for systematic context effects of question order use Mode Effects Analysis in Survey Administration and order randomisation.
whyLost: Known in survey methodology and social psychology, but UX teams rarely log contextual conditions or randomise global item placement.
whereToUse: Post-session questionnaires, in-product satisfaction tracking during incidents, wellbeing and health apps, seasonal products.
example: A travel app's satisfaction drops sharply during a week of airline strikes. Logging strike exposure shows the dip is confined to affected users, so the team does not roll back a coincident release.
reference: Schwarz, N., & Clore, G. L. (1983). Mood, misattribution, and judgments of well-being. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 45(3), 513-523.

name: Mood Boards
origin: Long-standing design practice; UX accounts by Kolko, 2014, Hartson and Pyla, 2019, and Hanington and Martin, 2019
summary: Collages of images, colours, textures, type and other material that define a candidate emotional theme, aesthetic, audience or setting, used to choose and then elaborate a visual direction.
description: Mood boards externalise aesthetic conversations that are otherwise vague. The more rigorous versions start from words, not pictures. Kolko's route begins with emotional requirements: for each, the team lists the situations, places, objects and people it evokes and their opposites, abstracts these into colours, shapes, textures, materials and patterns, then gathers matching images and assembles boards. Hartson and Pyla make one board per candidate theme or metaphor from ideation, compare them, adopt one, and elaborate it per channel (visual, motion, tone, audio) with more detailed boards. Hanington and Martin also use image boards for target audiences and use environments, as reminders for the designer, consensus artefacts for the team and a way to show clients the intended direction. Building boards together gives the team ownership of the visual definition.
steps: Agree the focus: an emotional requirement, candidate theme, target audience or use environment.
For emotional themes, list evocative situations, objects and people and their opposites, then abstract them into colours, shapes, textures, materials and patterns.
Collect candidate images and samples from photography, magazines, the web and physical materials.
Edit to the most representative items and compose one board per theme, homogenising the elements.
Compare boards with the team or client and adopt one direction.
Elaborate the adopted theme per channel (visual, motion, sound, tactile) with detailed boards, and hand them to visual designers as the start of a visual language.
outputs: Mood or image boards, metaphor and abstraction tables, and an adopted emotional or aesthetic theme.
useWhen: Setting the visual and emotional direction of a product or brand, or aligning stakeholders on aesthetics before visual design.
avoidWhen: Boards reflect designer taste, not user data, and drift towards cliché. Check that the intended feeling lands with users using Semantic Differential, AttrakDiff or Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM), and research the audience with Interviews rather than stock imagery.
whyLost: Survives as a core visual design practice because it is cheap, persuasive and well suited to client and stakeholder alignment.
whereToUse: Brand and visual design, consumer apps, hospitality and retail, physical products, game art direction.
example: A national parks website team turns the requirement 'vibrant nature' into green and ochre palettes, rough textures and candid outdoor photography, compares three boards with rangers, and adopts one for the design system.
reference: Kolko, J. (2014) Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press, pp. 157-160.

name: Moral Dilemma Interview
origin: Lawrence Kohlberg, 1956 onwards, extending Piaget's work on moral reasoning
summary: Present a dilemma in which every option has a cost, ask what should be done and why, and classify the reasoning rather than the choice.
description: Kohlberg presented 72 boys aged 10 to 16 with dilemmas forcing a choice between two imperfect alternatives, the best known asking whether a man should steal a drug his sick wife needs, and followed many of them every three years for 20 years. From the reasons given, not the choices, he described six stages in three levels: preconventional, conventional and postconventional. The stage scheme has been criticised for gender and cultural bias, notably by Gilligan. For UX the durable core is the elicitation form: a scenario with a real trade-off (privacy against convenience, safety against autonomy) followed by probes on the reasons. This reveals how people weigh competing values better than asking them to rate each value in isolation. Rigour comes from carefully balanced scenarios, consistent probes, and a coding scheme applied by more than one coder.
steps: Write three to five short scenarios in which every option carries a real cost to someone.
Present each scenario and ask what the protagonist should do.
Probe for reasons: why, what if circumstances changed, who is affected and what would make the other choice acceptable.
Record answers verbatim.
Code the reasoning into categories, using Kohlberg's stages or a scheme suited to the topic, with two coders and an agreement check.
Repeat with the same participants over time if you are studying change in reasoning.
outputs: Choices plus coded reasoning per participant and scenario; for longitudinal designs, change in reasoning over time.
useWhen: You are researching ethics, trust or value trade-offs (privacy, safety, fairness) and need to know how people reason under conflict, not just what they say they value.
avoidWhen: You need to predict actual behaviour; hypothetical dilemmas often diverge from real choices, so pair with behavioural data or field observation. Avoid using Kohlberg's stages uncritically as a ranking of people.
whyLost: It is a developmental psychology instrument tied to a contested stage theory, so UX borrowed value elicitation methods without its dilemma-and-reasoning structure.
whereToUse: Value-sensitive design, AI ethics and fairness research, health data sharing, content moderation and safety features.
example: A health app team presents 15 users with a dilemma about sharing location data with family during a medical emergency. Coding the reasons shows most weigh autonomy over safety unless a clinician is involved, shaping consent defaults.
reference: Kohlberg, L. (1958). The development of modes of moral thinking and choice in the years 10 to 16. Doctoral dissertation, University of Chicago.

name: Morville's User Experience Honeycomb
origin: Peter Morville, Semantic Studios, 2004
summary: A seven-facet framework (useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible, valuable) used to diagnose and prioritise where an experience falls short.
description: Morville drew the honeycomb to move IA and UX beyond usability alone. Its facets are useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible and valuable (the centre). The intended use is diagnostic and strategic: teams choose which facets matter most for a product and context, assess each with appropriate evidence, and re-weight priorities. Many teams now treat it as a poster. Made rigorous, each facet is operationalised with a measure (e.g. findability with tree testing success, credibility with Stanford web credibility guidelines or a validated scale, accessibility with WCAG audit), scored, and tracked, turning a diagram into a balanced scorecard.
steps: With stakeholders, rank the seven facets by importance for this product, user segment and context, and record the rationale.
Operationalise each facet with a measure: e.g. task success (usable), tree testing (findable), WCAG audit (accessible), credibility scale (credible), willingness to pay or retention (valuable).
Collect data for each facet using the appropriate method and sample.
Score facets on a common normalised scale and plot against importance to reveal gaps.
Prioritise improvements where important facets score lowest.
Re-measure each release to track the profile over time.
outputs: A weighted facet profile with evidence-based scores, gap analysis and prioritised improvements.
useWhen: Product strategy reviews, setting a balanced UX scorecard, or diagnosing why a usable product still fails.
avoidWhen: When you need causal explanations of a specific problem; use targeted research methods.
whyLost: The honeycomb became a slide illustration and lost its role as a diagnostic, prioritisation tool with measures.
whereToUse: Content-rich sites, health information, government services, marketplaces, AI products where credibility matters.
example: A health information site scores well on usable and findable but poorly on credible. Credibility interviews and a validated scale lead to visible author credentials and review dates, raising trust and return visits.
sources: Morville, User Experience Design (2004), Semantic Studios
Morville & Rosenfeld, Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (3rd ed., 2006)
reference: Morville, P. (2004). User Experience Design. semanticstudios.com.

name: Most Significant Change
origin: Rick Davies, 1996; Jess Dart and colleagues, 2000
summary: Participatory monitoring in which stakeholders collect stories of change and review panels select, and justify, the most significant ones at each level.
description: Most significant change replaces predefined indicators with stories. Stakeholders agree broad domains of change to monitor; stories of change are collected regularly from participants and front-line staff on a standard form that records what happened, who was involved and why the storyteller thinks it matters. Panels at successive levels of the organisation read the stories and select the most significant in each domain against agreed criteria, recording their reasons, and the selections and reasons are fed back. A yearly document of selected stories goes to funders and decision-makers. The rigour lies in transparent, repeated selection: the method surfaces what different groups value and makes those values debatable, and it captures unexpected outcomes that indicator systems miss.
steps: Agree two to five broad domains of change with stakeholders (for example changes in practice, in wellbeing, in relationships).
Collect stories of change regularly, such as monthly, using a standard form: title, recorder, date, who was involved, what happened, and why it matters to the storyteller.
At each organisational level, convene a review panel that reads the stories in each domain and selects the most significant, recording its reasons.
Feed the selected stories and the reasons back to storytellers and lower levels.
Optionally verify selected stories with the people involved.
Compile an annual document of selected stories and selection rationales for funders and decision-makers, and use it to discuss values and direction.
outputs: A filtered collection of significant change stories, documented selection rationales, and dialogue about what stakeholders value.
useWhen: Monitoring outcomes of a long-running programme or product where impacts are diverse, hard to predict or poorly captured by metrics.
avoidWhen: When you need prevalence or average effect sizes; selection favours positive, vivid stories. Pair with outcome metrics or a survey.
whyLost: It is standard in development evaluation but UX outcome measurement has defaulted to analytics and satisfaction scores.
whereToUse: Civic tech, health and education programmes, enterprise rollouts, long-term product impact reviews.
example: A financial-wellbeing app collects monthly stories of change from users and coaches; a regional panel and then the leadership team select stories, revealing that users value reduced arguments about money more than savings totals.
reference: Davies, R. and Dart, J. (2005). The 'Most Significant Change' (MSC) Technique: A Guide to Its Use; Patton, M. Q. (2002). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (3rd ed.). Sage, pp. 196-197.

name: Motion and Position Tracking of Participants
origin: HCI practice surveyed by Lazar et al.; worked example Ball, North and Bowman (2007)
summary: Measure where and how participants move, using markers, wearables or depth cameras, to study physical behaviour during interaction.
description: Motion tracking records participants' position, orientation and movement while they use a system. Commodity devices such as phone accelerometers, fitness bands, smartwatches, game controllers and depth cameras give ready-made sensing; custom sensors in clothing, chairs or wheelchairs extend it; camera-and-marker systems track people across large spaces. In a classic study, participants wore a marker hat while searching data on a 24-monitor wall; wider displays led to more physical and less virtual navigation, which participants preferred. VR studies place sensors on head and limbs. Rigour depends on choosing measures that answer the question, calibrating sensors, synchronising streams with task events, and processing that separates people, gestures and surroundings. Consumer sensors have accuracy limits and natural settings produce complex data, so engineering support is often needed.
steps: Decide which movements or positions answer the research question, such as walking distance, head orientation or gesture frequency.
Choose commodity sensors (wearables, phones, depth cameras) or custom or marker-based systems.
Attach and calibrate markers or sensors, checking accuracy in the actual space.
Record movement synchronised with task events and conditions.
Process streams to extract people, gestures, positions and derived measures.
Relate movement measures to conditions, performance and preferences with appropriate statistics.
outputs: Position, orientation and movement records per participant and condition, with derived measures such as physical versus virtual navigation.
useWhen: Physical movement is part of the interaction: large displays, VR and AR, gesture interfaces, retail or hospital spaces, exergames and accessibility for mobility impairments.
avoidWhen: Interaction is purely on a small screen, or observation and video coding would do; use behavioural mapping or usability testing instead.
whyLost: It thrives in VR, ergonomics and ubiquitous computing labs but needs engineering support that most UX teams lack.
whereToUse: VR and AR products, large and wall displays, smart spaces, fitness and rehabilitation technology, and automotive cabins.
example: A VR training vendor tracks head and hand movement of 20 trainees. Novices turn their heads twice as often as experts to find controls, so key controls are moved into the forward field of view.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Ball, R., North, C., & Bowman, D. A. (2007). Move to improve: Promoting physical navigation to increase user performance with large displays. Proceedings of CHI 2007, ACM.

name: Motion Design Language and Animation Tokens
aka: Motion design language and animation tokens in a component library
origin: Sarah Drasner (2017), citing Google Material Design as the first major brand motion guideline
summary: Take a documented, brand-led stance on motion and encode it as named easings, timing units and a small set of reusable animations in the component library.
description: Animation is usually bolted on at the end, so it lacks cohesion and grows uncontrolled. A motion design language starts from an opinion about how the brand moves (formal brands more linear, friendly brands livelier) rather than borrowing another company's, and documents rules such as 'glide, never flip' so teams stop re-debating them. Motion is designed with mock-ups, palettes and storyboards and kept in a living style guide. In code, the language becomes tokens: named easings for entrance, exit and their emphasis variants; timing units t1 to t5, like heading levels, with a default near 0.25 seconds; a shared fill-mode class; a starting set of five or six keyframe animations; and reusable animated components for frequent patterns such as loader-to-success, exposing timing and easing as parameters. Like an oversized colour palette, too many animations bloat code and erode cohesion.
steps: Audit existing animation across the product and list each pattern, duration and easing in use.
Decide a motion stance consistent with the brand and write down a few explicit rules.
Define named easings for entrance, exit, entrance emphasis and exit emphasis.
Define timing units t1 to t5 with a default (around 0.25 s) and map each to typical uses.
Create a small set of keyframe animations (five or six) and add more only when needed.
Build reusable animated components for frequent patterns and expose timing and easing as parameters.
Document everything in the living style guide with demos, and review new motion against it.
outputs: Documented motion principles, easing and timing tokens, and reusable animated components.
useWhen: Use when a product or design system has inconsistent, ad hoc animation, or when brand expression through motion matters.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the language as validated: check comprehension and comfort with Microinteraction Testing Protocol or Usability Testing, and respect reduced-motion settings (see Accessibility Evaluation).
whyLost: It survived because design systems now routinely include motion tokens, following Material Design and similar public guidelines.
whereToUse: Design systems, consumer apps with strong brands, onboarding flows, data visualisation transitions.
example: A banking app defines three easings and five timing units, replaces 37 bespoke transitions with six shared animations, and adds a reduced-motion variant for each. Reviews no longer debate durations.
reference: Drasner, S. (2017). SVG Animations: From Common UX Implementations to Complex Responsive Animation. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, ch. 17.

name: Motivational Interviewing Applied to UX
aka: Motivational Interviewing for Behaviour Change Research
origin: Miller & Rollnick, 1991
summary: Adapts motivational interviewing techniques (open questions, reflections, eliciting ambivalence and change talk) to research how users think about changing behaviour.
description: Motivational interviewing, developed by Miller and Rollnick, is a collaborative conversational style for exploring a person's own reasons for change. Its core skills, known as OARS (open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries), together with the elicitation of 'change talk' and 'sustain talk', make it well suited to research about behaviours users are ambivalent about: saving, exercising, medication adherence, reducing screen time. Adapted for research, the interviewer does not steer towards change but maps the participant's ambivalence, values and perceived barriers, which are typically hidden behind socially desirable answers. Rigour comes from training in reflective listening, separating research from intervention through ethics review, and coding transcripts for change and sustain talk.
steps: MI techniques for UX research:
Open questions: 'What's your relationship with [behavior]?' rather than 'Why don't you use this feature?'
Reflective listening: reflect back what users say without evaluation.
(3) Elicit change talk: 'If you did start [behavior], what would be different?'
Explore ambivalence: 'What makes it hard? What would make it easier?' MI surfaces the real barriers that users are reluctant to articulate to a researcher associated with the product.
outputs: Maps of ambivalence (reasons for and against change), change and sustain talk excerpts, readiness profiles and design implications for behaviour change products.
useWhen: Research for health, finance, sustainability and habit products, where users are ambivalent about a change and direct questions produce socially desirable answers.
avoidWhen: Avoid using it to persuade research participants; the aim is understanding. Avoid when topics are not about behaviour change, and do not substitute for clinical care.
whyLost: MI is a clinical intervention with certification and fidelity coding; UX has not adapted it as a research protocol, and the line between research and intervention needs care.
whereToUse: Health behavior change app research, sustainability UX research, financial behavior research, any product addressing behavior change.
example: A smoking-cessation app team uses MI-style reflections in interviews and uncovers that users value cigarettes as their only private break, so the product adds 'replacement break' features rather than more warnings.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 32 — Advanced Elicitation — The Archaeology of the Interview
Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change (Miller & Rollnick)
reference: Miller WR & Rollnick S (2012) Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change. 3rd ed. Guilford Press

extra.Four Core MI Techniques: Open questions: Questions that cannot be answered yes/no. "What would need to be different for you to use it more?" "What concerns do you have about making that change?" Affirmations: Genuine recognition of the participant's efforts and strengths — not compliments. "It sounds like you've put real thought into how to make this work for you." This builds the relationship that makes honest disclosure possible. Reflective listening: Reflecting the participant's meaning back to them, slightly amplified. If the participant says "It's just a bit slow," you might reflect: "So the slowness is affecting your willingness to use it at all." This surfaces implicit meaning. Eliciting change talk: Ask about both sides of the ambivalence directly. "What do you like about it?" then "What are the downsides for you?" then "If things stayed exactly as they are, what would happen?" The gap between the ideal and the actual is where the real research data lives.

name: Motivational-Interviewing Dialogue Scripting for Behaviour-Change Chatbots
aka: MI versus confrontational counselling chatbot scripts
origin: William Miller and Stephen Rollnick's motivational interviewing (1991 onwards), operationalised as chatbot scripts by Lean Leeuwis and Linwei He (2023)
summary: Write a behaviour-change chatbot's dialogue with motivational-interviewing moves (user as expert, shared agenda, open questions, reflections, affirmations, optional plan) instead of confrontation.
description: Motivational interviewing aims at self-persuasion: the person voices their own reasons for change rather than being told. Leeuwis and He translated it into a chatbot script with two components. The relational component, the MI spirit of acceptance, collaboration, evocation and compassion, is carried by natural, person-like language and emoticons. The technical component is a sequence of moves: position the user as the expert on their situation, agree the conversation's goal together, invite thoughts and feelings about change with open questions, reflect and affirm, help name goals and barriers, and offer a plan only if the user wants one. Their contrasting confrontational script judged behaviour, gave unsolicited advice and urged readiness. With matched length and content and a style manipulation check, neither style won overall, but MI raised satisfaction for users with higher self-efficacy, and both raised intention to change. The paired scripts are a ready manipulation for tone testing.
steps: Define the target behaviour and the conversation's scope with clinical or domain experts.
Draft the opening so it positions the user as the expert on their own situation and proposes agreeing a goal for the chat together.
Write open questions about the user's thoughts and feelings on change, with reflection and affirmation templates for likely answers.
Add a section that helps the user name goals and barriers, and offer to build a plan only if the user opts in.
Carry the MI spirit through person-like wording and sparing emoticons, and review every line against MI principles (no judgement, no unsolicited advice).
If testing tone, write a confrontational or neutral counterpart matched in length and content and verify the style difference with a manipulation check such as the CEMI scale.
Pilot with target users and revise turns where users disengage or feel judged.
outputs: An MI-consistent chatbot script with example utterances and response templates, optionally paired with a matched contrasting script for experiments.
useWhen: Designing health, coaching, financial wellbeing or onboarding bots that aim to strengthen users' own motivation rather than instruct them.
avoidWhen: When the team needs to learn what motivates users before scripting (use Motivational Interviewing Applied to UX as a research interview); for purely transactional bots; or as a substitute for clinical care where risk is high. To judge whether the script works, run an experiment rather than relying on expert review.
whyLost: It is established in digital-health research, but product conversation design rarely draws on counselling frameworks and tends towards directive tips and nudges.
whereToUse: Smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, physical activity, medication adherence, debt management and habit-forming coaching products.
example: A smoking-cessation bot opens with 'You know your situation best; what would you like to get out of today's chat?' and reflects the user's mixed feelings before offering a quit plan. In an eight-minute session study it matched a confrontational version overall but scored higher satisfaction among confident users.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Leeuwis, L., & He, L. (2023). In Følstad et al. (Eds.), Chatbot Research and Design (LNCS 13815). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-25581-6_1

name: Mouse-Tracking of Decision Conflict
origin: Michael Spivey, Marc Grosjean and Günther Knoblich, 2005; Jonathan Freeman and Nalini Ambady, MouseTracker (2010)
summary: Analyses the curvature and timing of cursor movements toward choices to reveal hidden attraction to the unchosen option during a decision.
description: In mouse-tracking studies, participants start at the bottom centre and move to one of two response options at the top corners. Because the hand moves continuously while the decision unfolds, trajectories curve toward the competing option when it exerts pull. Measures include maximum deviation, area under the curve, x-flips (direction changes) and initiation time. These indices reveal conflict, ambivalence and the time course of competing considerations, which final choices hide. Unlike session replay heatmaps, mouse-tracking uses controlled, normalised trajectories and statistical comparison. In UX it measures hesitation at consent dialogues, pricing choices and trust decisions.
steps: Design a two-option choice screen with a start button at bottom centre and options in the top corners.
Require movement to begin within a time limit (e.g. 400 ms) to ensure online decision tracking.
Record cursor coordinates at high sampling rate; time-normalise trajectories into 101 steps.
Compute maximum deviation, area under the curve, x-flips and initiation time.
Compare conditions with mixed-effects models, and inspect bimodality to distinguish graded pull from discrete changes of mind.
Relate conflict measures to later behaviour (e.g. regret, cancellations).
outputs: Trajectory plots and conflict indices per condition, with statistical comparisons.
useWhen: Measuring ambivalence or temptation in binary choices: consent, upsell, risky actions, AI suggestions.
avoidWhen: Touch-only interfaces (use touch trajectory analogues carefully) or complex multi-step tasks.
whyLost: It is a cognitive science paradigm; UX uses session replays without controlled designs.
whereToUse: Cookie consent, subscription upsells, privacy permissions, misinformation labelling, recommendation acceptance.
example: An insurer tests add-on cover offers. Mouse trajectories show strong pull toward 'decline' even when users accept, indicating pressured acceptance; the team reframes the offer and cancellations fall.
sources: Spivey, Grosjean & Knoblich, Continuous attraction toward phonological competitors (2005), PNAS
Freeman & Ambady, MouseTracker (2010), Behavior Research Methods
Kieslich et al., Mouse-tracking: A practical guide (2019), in Schulte-Mecklenbeck et al. (eds.), A Handbook of Process Tracing Methods
reference: Freeman, J. B., & Ambady, N. (2010). MouseTracker. Behavior Research Methods, 42(1), 226-241.

name: Movement notation for gesture analysis
aka: Movement Notation for Gesture Documentation and Analysis
origin: Labanotation: Rudolf Laban (1920s); Benesh notation: Rudolf and Joan Benesh (1956); EWMN: Noa Eshkol and Avraham Wachman (1958); brought to interaction design by Saffer (2008)
summary: Borrow dance notation systems, or their core questions, to record precisely which body parts move, how, for how long and in what stages, for gesture design and analysis.
description: Dance notations put three-dimensional movement on paper. Labanotation uses a vertical staff read upwards, with columns for body parts and sides and symbols for direction, level and duration. Benesh notation maps a five-line staff from head to floor and reads left to right. Eshkol Wachman notation treats the body as jointed limbs and plots their positions on a sphere in 45-degree steps; it has been used in physical therapy, animal behaviour research and early autism diagnosis. Laban's effort qualities (space, weight, time, flow) help judge whether a gesture's character suits the function it triggers. Full notation takes hours for simple movements and is hard to read, so designers usually borrow a subset, but every gesture record should state body parts and positions, duration, stages with start and end points, and the system's response.
steps: Choose a notation (Labanotation, Benesh or EWMN) or agree a lightweight subset for the team.
Record which body parts are involved and their starting positions.
Record the duration and timing of the movement.
Break the movement into stages, each with a start and end point.
Add the system's response to each stage.
Optionally rate the gesture's effort qualities (space, weight, time, flow) against the character of the triggered feature.
Embed notation elements in keyframes, storyboards or specifications, and use the same scheme to code observed user gestures.
outputs: A precise, reproducible record of designed or observed gestures, suitable for specification, comparison and coding.
useWhen: Specifying or analysing body-based interaction, such as touchless gestures, VR and AR input, motion games or rehabilitation tools, where verbal descriptions are ambiguous.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple taps and swipes where standard gesture vocabularies suffice; full notation is slow and hard to read, so use video plus a lightweight template.
whyLost: Notation is a specialist skill from dance, and design teams default to video and prose; Saffer's adaptation was seldom taken up.
whereToUse: VR and AR interaction design, gesture-controlled automotive and smart TV interfaces, fitness and physiotherapy apps, and motion-capture games.
example: A VR fitness team specifies a punch gesture as shoulder, elbow and wrist positions across three stages with timings and the haptic response at contact. The same scheme codes playtest videos, revealing that tired users drop the elbow stage, which the detector then tolerates.
reference: Saffer, D. (2008). Designing Gestural Interfaces: Touchscreens and Interactive Devices. O'Reilly Media, ch. 5.

name: Multi-Armed Bandit Testing for Adaptive UX
donor: Statistics, operations research and reinforcement learning
origin: William Thompson (1933); Robbins (1952); upper confidence bound algorithms by Auer et al. (2002)
summary: Adaptive experiments that shift traffic toward better-performing variants during the test, using Thompson sampling or UCB to balance learning against serving users the best option.
description: A fixed A/B test splits traffic evenly until the end, accepting the cost of showing an inferior variant to half of users. Multi-armed bandits treat each variant as an arm with unknown reward and allocate traffic adaptively: Thompson sampling draws from each arm's posterior distribution (for example a Beta distribution for conversion) and serves the arm with the highest draw, while UCB serves the arm with the highest optimistic estimate. Over time traffic concentrates on the best arm, reducing regret. Bandits suit short-lived decisions (headlines, promotions), many variants and personalisation via contextual bandits. The trade-offs are real: adaptive allocation complicates unbiased effect estimation, is vulnerable to time-varying effects and delayed rewards, and is poor for learning why something works. Rigour means choosing bandits for optimisation, not inference, and logging allocation probabilities.
steps: Implement Thompson sampling or UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) algorithm.
Initialize: equal traffic to all variants.
After each observation: update posterior (Thompson) or confidence bound (UCB).
Shift traffic toward higher-performing variant.
Stop when posterior probability that the best variant is best exceeds 0.95.
Compare total cost (regret) to equivalent fixed A/B test.
outputs: Allocation trajectories, posterior estimates per variant, cumulative regret, chosen winning variant, and logged propensities for later analysis.
useWhen: Optimising many variants quickly, time-limited content such as campaigns or headlines, personalisation with contextual bandits, and cases where serving losing variants is costly.
avoidWhen: When you need an unbiased effect estimate or a causal explanation, when rewards are delayed (retention), or when guardrails must be assessed; use a fixed A/B test.
whyLost: Bandits matured in machine learning and ad tech; UX research culture is built on hypothesis testing and explanation, so adaptive allocation is seen as an engineering optimisation rather than a research method.
whereToUse: Feature rollouts where delayed testing is costly, personalization testing, any experiment where learning speed matters.
example: An e-commerce site tests six hero banners for a 10-day sale using Thompson sampling. By day three, 70% of traffic goes to two banners, recovering most of the conversion that an even split would have lost.
sources: Russo et al., A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling (Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 2018)
Bandit Algorithms for Website Optimization (John Myles White)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 47 — Experimental Design — From A/B to Quasi-Experiments
The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design
Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Russo DJ, Van Roy B, Kazerouni A, Osband I & Wen Z (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling. Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 11(1):1-96

name: Multi-Attribute Utility Analysis (MAUT/SMART)
origin: Ralph Keeney and Howard Raiffa (1976); Ward Edwards' SMART (1977) and Edwards and Barron's SMARTER (1994)
summary: Evaluates alternatives on multiple attributes with explicit single-attribute utility functions and trade-off weights derived by swing weighting.
description: MAUT formalises trade-offs: each attribute gets a value or utility function mapping its range to 0-1, and weights reflect how much the decision-maker values swinging each attribute from worst to best. Swing weighting avoids the common error of weighting by abstract importance without regard to ranges. SMART and SMARTER simplify elicitation (rank-order centroid weights). The additive model ranks alternatives, and sensitivity analysis shows how robust the choice is. For UX, MAUT supports decisions where user outcomes compete with cost, risk and accessibility, and can model users' own multi-attribute choices.
steps: Define objectives and measurable attributes with ranges for each alternative.
Elicit single-attribute value functions (linear or curved) with stakeholders or users.
Elicit weights with swing weighting: rank swings from worst to best, then assign relative points.
Score alternatives and compute weighted totals.
Run sensitivity analysis on weights and value functions; identify dominated alternatives.
Document trade-offs and the rationale for the final decision.
outputs: Value functions, swing weights, alternative scores, sensitivity analysis and decision rationale.
useWhen: Complex design or product decisions with several measurable, competing objectives.
avoidWhen: Decisions with few attributes or where one constraint dominates.
whyLost: Decision analysis lives in operations research and policy; product teams use informal scoring.
whereToUse: Platform choices, design system adoption, accessibility trade-offs, AI model selection balancing quality, latency and cost.
example: Choosing among three LLMs for a support bot, swing weighting shows the team values a jump in resolution rate more than a 50% cost cut; the mid-cost model wins and the result is robust to weight changes of plus or minus 20%.
sources: Keeney & Raiffa, Decisions with Multiple Objectives (1976)
Edwards & Barron, SMARTS and SMARTER (1994), Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
Goodwin & Wright, Decision Analysis for Management Judgment (5th ed., 2014)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Keeney, R. L., & Raiffa, H. (1976). Decisions with Multiple Objectives. Wiley.

name: Multi-Channel Affective Measurement
origin: Rosalind Picard, MIT Media Lab, 1997 (Affective Computing)
summary: Measures emotional response by triangulating self-report, physiological signals and behaviour in the same session, exposing mismatches between what users say and what they feel.
description: Emotion is not a single signal. Self-report captures what people are willing and able to articulate; physiology (electrodermal activity, heart rate variability, pupil dilation) captures arousal without valence; behaviour (facial expression, hesitation, posture, interaction patterns) captures expression shaped by social context. Picard's affective computing framework treats each channel as a partial, noisy measurement of an underlying affective state. The rigour comes from declaring channels and hypotheses before collection, synchronising all channels to interface events, and treating disagreement between channels as data rather than error: a participant who says a flow was 'fine' while skin conductance spikes at a fee disclosure is telling you something no single channel could. Post-hoc selection of whichever channel supports a story is the characteristic failure the protocol is designed to prevent.
steps: Declare all channels before data collection. Post-hoc triangulation is selection bias.
Collect all channels simultaneously or within the same session.
Implicit vs. explicit mismatch analysis: Participant says 'it was fine' but shows elevated GSR and long hesitation times. The mismatch IS the finding — report it, do not average it away.
outputs: A time-synchronised affective record per participant, event-locked arousal and expression profiles, a list of self-report versus physiology mismatches, and emotion hotspots mapped to specific interface moments.
useWhen: Emotion is central to the outcome (trust, anxiety, delight) in high-stakes flows such as loan applications, medical results or payments, and you suspect users under-report or cannot articulate their reactions.
avoidWhen: You need only task success or attitudes; the cost of sensors and analysis is not justified. Avoid treating physiology as valence. For lighter evidence use Think-Aloud with Emotional Annotation or a validated self-report scale such as SAM or PANAS.
whyLost: It requires sensors, signal-processing skills and synchronisation tooling that few UX teams have, and commercial biometrics vendors sold single-channel dashboards that blurred the triangulation logic.
whereToUse: Fintech onboarding and credit decisions, health result delivery, automotive and in-car interfaces, games, and evaluating AI agents whose behaviour may provoke unease users will not voice.
example: A bank tests its loan-application flow with 16 participants wearing EDA wristbands and webcam expression capture. Most rate the flow as easy, yet arousal peaks and brow-lowering cluster at the credit-check consent screen; reframing that screen reduces both the peak and drop-off.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 37 — Picard's Affective Framework — Multi-Channel Emotion Measurement
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
reference: Picard, R. W. (1997). Affective Computing. MIT Press.

name: Multi-dimensional In-depth Long-term Case studies (MILC)
aka: Multi-dimensional long-term case studies of expert tools
Long-term case studies of tool use
origin: Shneiderman and Plaisant (2006), BELIV workshop
summary: Follow a few expert users solving their own problems with a complex tool over weeks or months, combining interviews, diaries, logs and outcomes to judge real benefit.
description: For complex tools such as visual analytics or creativity software, changes in strategy and real benefits appear only after weeks of use, so short lab tasks miss them. MILC studies a small number of experts in their own workplaces, with their own data and goals. A study opens with an interview confirming a real problem, available data and a schedule; then training, two to four weeks of novice use, two to four weeks of mature use, and a semi-structured exit interview. Throughout, diaries, usage logs, questionnaires, observation and outcomes such as decisions or publications give several views. The researcher may help participants and feed tool improvements back during the study, reducing the usual distance to gain depth. Success is judged by whether users reach their own goals, not imposed tasks.
steps: Recruit a few expert users (often three to six) with real, ongoing problems and data suited to the tool.
Hold an initial interview confirming the problem, the data available, goals and a study schedule.
Run an introductory training session.
Follow two to four weeks of novice use, then two to four weeks of mature use, collecting usage logs, participant diaries, periodic observation and short questionnaires.
Fix or improve the tool as problems surface and record each change and its date.
Close with a semi-structured exit interview on discoveries, benefits, collaboration and frustrations.
Write a case report per user and compare across cases for recurring patterns.
outputs: Rich per-user case reports of real use, discoveries, benefits and frustrations, plus a history of tool improvements.
useWhen: You are evaluating an expert or exploratory tool whose value depends on insight, strategy change or discovery over time rather than task speed.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need generalisable or comparative results, or the tool supports simple, well-defined tasks; use controlled usability tests or A/B tests. It is very time-consuming, samples are small and the researcher's involvement shapes findings.
whyLost: It is costly and slow and does not yield the comparative numbers academic reviewers and product teams prefer, so it stayed within visualisation research.
whereToUse: Analytics and BI products, developer and data-science tools, AI copilots for professional work, scientific software and design tools.
example: A team building an AI assistant for financial analysts deploys it to four analysts for six weeks on their live coverage. Logs and diaries show heavy early use for summarising, while exit interviews reveal it changed how two analysts screen companies, a benefit no lab task captured.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C. (2006). Strategies for evaluating information visualization tools: multi-dimensional in-depth long-term case studies. BELIV '06, ACM.

name: Multi-modal signal separation
donor: Signal processing and multisensory human factors
origin: Source separation from signal processing (blind source separation, 1980s-90s) applied to display modality allocation in human factors, building on Wickens (1984)
summary: Analyses whether concurrent signals in different sensory channels remain distinguishable, and reallocates them so critical messages are not masked by competing signals.
description: In signal processing, source separation recovers independent signals from a mixture. The UX analogue asks whether users can separate concurrent alerts, sounds, haptics and visuals that arrive together, or whether they blur into a single undifferentiated stream. The method inventories every signal source, maps its modality, frequency band, timing and spatial location, and identifies overlaps where two signals share a channel and are likely to mask each other (for example two tones within the same critical band, or two flashing elements in peripheral vision). It then reallocates signals across modalities or dimensions so that each critical message occupies a distinct channel. Rigour comes from measuring physical properties (frequency, loudness, onset timing) and testing identification accuracy under realistic concurrency.
steps: Inventory all signal sources in the environment, including other devices, with modality, frequency or colour, onset pattern, duration and location.
Plot signals on a channel map (modality by dimension by time) and mark overlaps occurring within 500 ms of each other or in the same auditory critical band.
Measure the ambient noise floor and check each auditory alert sits at least 10-15 dB above masked threshold, per common alarm standards.
Run an identification test where participants (8-15) must name which of several concurrent signals occurred; target at least 90% correct identification for critical alarms.
Reallocate confused signals to different modalities, rhythms or spatial locations, and prioritise or suppress lower-priority signals during critical events.
Re-test identification accuracy and response time under the worst-case concurrency scenario.
outputs: A channel allocation map, a list of masking conflicts, identification accuracy per signal, and a revised multimodal signal scheme.
useWhen: When many devices or features emit alerts in the same environment; when users report not knowing which alarm is sounding; when adding haptic or audio feedback to an existing product.
avoidWhen: When signals are rare and isolated; a simple notification review suffices. For attention allocation without concurrency problems, use a saliency or pre-attentive audit.
whyLost: The concept is mature in signal processing and auditory alarm research, but UX teams design per product, not per environment, so cross-device masking is rarely analysed.
whereToUse: Operating theatres and ICUs, vehicle cockpits, smart homes, wearables, and multi-app mobile notification ecosystems.
example: In an ICU, infusion pumps and ventilators use similar 960 Hz tones. A separation analysis shows nurses identify the source correctly only 54% of the time; giving the pump a distinct rhythmic pattern and a bedside light raises identification to 93%.
sources: Van Drongelen, W., Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
