The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent
reference: Wickens, C. D. (2002). Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 3(2), 159-177.

name: Multi-pass analysis pipeline
origin: Draws on multi-cycle coding (Saldaña) and grounded theory's open, axial and selective coding (Strauss and Corbin, 1990); implemented with LLM APIs from 2023
summary: Splitting AI-assisted qualitative analysis into separate, checkable passes, such as segmenting, first-order coding, consolidation, second-order categorisation and synthesis, rather than one prompt.
description: Asking a model to 'find themes' in a corpus in one step produces unverifiable, often generic output. A multi-pass pipeline mirrors established qualitative cycles: pass one segments and cleans; pass two applies first-order codes segment by segment with evidence; pass three consolidates near-duplicate codes into a codebook; pass four groups codes into second-order categories; pass five drafts synthesis with links to evidence. Each pass has a narrow task, a schema, logged outputs and a human review point. Rigour comes from the separation (errors are traceable to a pass), from never letting later passes see only summaries without evidence, and from human decisions at the abstraction steps.
steps: Define the passes and each pass's input, output schema and review owner.
Pass 1: segment transcripts by speaker turn and remove moderator text and personal data.
Pass 2: generate first-order codes per segment with verbatim evidence, validated against the schema.
Pass 3: cluster and merge similar codes into a draft codebook; a researcher reviews merges.
Pass 4: propose second-order categories with linked codes; researchers revise and approve.
Pass 5: draft synthesis statements, each linked to supporting codes and quotes, and check counts of participants per theme.
Log every pass's outputs and keep them so any theme can be traced back to segments.
outputs: Pass-by-pass outputs, a reviewed codebook, second-order categories and evidence-linked synthesis.
useWhen: Large-scale AI-assisted qualitative analysis where traceability from themes to quotes matters.
avoidWhen: Overkill for small studies; avoid single-prompt 'summarise the themes' approaches altogether for anything reported as research.
whyLost: The idea mirrors classic qualitative cycles, but popular AI tools offer one-click summarisation that hides the passes.
whereToUse: Research operations, continuous discovery programmes, large interview studies and multilingual synthesis.
example: A SaaS team analysing 180 churn interviews runs five passes. At pass 3 a researcher splits a merged code 'pricing' into 'price level' and 'pricing model confusion', which become distinct themes with different owners.
sources: Saldaña, J. (2021) The Coding Manual for Qualitative Researchers, 4th ed.
Strauss, A. & Corbin, J. (1990) Basics of Qualitative Research
Gao, J. et al. (2024) CollabCoder: A lower-barrier, rigorous workflow for inductive collaborative qualitative analysis with large language models. CHI
The Inquiry Series, C12 — AI Agents for Structured Qualitative Analysis at Scale
reference: Saldaña, J. (2021) The Coding Manual for Qualitative Researchers, 4th ed.

name: Multi-procedure elicitation consistency check
aka: Choice versus rating versus pricing comparison
origin: Tversky, Sattath and Slovic, 1988; Tversky, Slovic and Kahneman, 1990; Shafir, Simonson and Tversky, 1993
summary: Elicit the same preference with formally equivalent procedures (choice, matching, pricing, rating, choosing versus rejecting) and compare the orderings to see whether the response mode drives the answer.
description: Normative theory says preference should not depend on how it is asked. This check runs two or more equivalent procedures in separate groups with the same options. In choice versus matching, one group chooses and other groups each fill a blank so the options are equal; the more important attribute wins far more often in choice (68 versus 4 percent in one safety-versus-cost example). In preference reversals, people choose the safer bet but price the long shot higher; adding a sure amount between the two prices separates intransitivity from overpricing. In choose versus reject, an enriched option with strong positives and negatives can be both chosen and rejected by majorities. Discrepancies show that the instrument is shaping the answer, so no single procedure gives the true preference.
steps: Choose two or more procedures that should yield the same order (choice, matching, pricing, rating, choose versus reject).
Run them in separate groups with identical options, to avoid memory effects.
For matching, use four groups that each fill one blank cell, then derive the implied preference.
Translate every response into an implied preference ordering.
Compare shares between procedures (for example choice share against matching share) and test the difference.
For reversals, add a sure amount between the two prices to locate the source of the inconsistency.
Report which mode was used and the size and direction of discrepancies.
outputs: Implied preference shares per procedure, the size and direction of discrepancies, and a diagnosis of reversal sources.
useWhen: Before trusting a single preference instrument (a survey rating, a pricing question, a forced choice) to drive product or pricing decisions.
avoidWhen: Avoid within-person designs that add memory effects; when only one decision format exists in the product, test that format directly with discrete choice modelling.
whyLost: Procedure invariance violations are textbook decision science, but UX and market research rarely run two equivalent instruments side by side.
whereToUse: Plan and pricing research, feature prioritisation surveys, MaxDiff versus rating comparisons, consent and settings design.
example: Users choose a plan with better support over a cheaper one, but when asked what price would make them equal, their answers imply the cheaper plan; the team reports both and tests the real checkout format.
sources: Tversky, A., Sattath, S., & Slovic, P. (1988). Contingent weighting in judgment and choice. Psychological Review, 95
Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974 paper) (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
reference: Tversky, A., Sattath, S., & Slovic, P. (1988). Contingent weighting in judgment and choice. Psychological Review, 95, 371-384.

name: Multi-stream field capture (computational ethnography)
origin: Weibel et al. (2014); Zheng et al. (2015)
summary: A portable sensor kit records audio, gaze, body position, room and screen video and input events in a real setting, then aligns the streams for joint analysis.
description: Developed to study how physicians use electronic medical records during patient visits, the approach packs a microphone array, remote eye tracker, webcam, depth camera, room video and screen and input capture into a rolling case that can be set up in about ten minutes. Analysis synchronises all streams, segments body-tracking data into clinician, patient and objects, derives gaze and gestures, separates speakers by audio direction, analyses computer events, and displays everything on a shared timeline. The rigour lies in making observation of a real, unrepeatable encounter quantifiable and replayable: questions such as how long a clinician looks at the screen while the patient speaks can be answered exactly rather than estimated from field notes.
steps: Assemble the sensors (microphone array, eye tracker, cameras, depth sensor, screen and input logger) in a portable case.
Agree consent and privacy procedures with everyone who will be recorded, including bystanders.
Install the kit around the workstation in the real room; aim for a set-up of about ten minutes so routine work is not disrupted.
Record complete encounters rather than fragments.
Synchronise audio and video streams to a common clock.
Segment body-tracking data into people and objects, derive gaze and gestures, and separate speakers using directional audio.
Analyse computer events and screen capture, then review all streams together in a timeline tool to code episodes.
outputs: A time-aligned multimodal record of real encounters and quantitative measures such as gaze share, turn-taking and screen time.
useWhen: Interaction in a real setting is multi-party and multimodal, and you need precise, replayable measurement rather than observer notes.
avoidWhen: Avoid where recording is ethically or legally impossible, or where a single observer with field notes would answer the question; equipment, processing and privacy burdens are high.
whyLost: It needs specialist hardware and signal-processing skills and suits funded research settings, so it remained in medical informatics and HCI labs.
whereToUse: Clinical systems, bank branch or retail counter tools, control rooms, classroom technology and any screen used during face-to-face service.
example: A bank piloting a tablet for in-branch mortgage advice records ten advisory sessions. Aligned gaze and speech data show advisers look at the tablet for 60 per cent of the time customers are speaking, prompting a redesign that moves form entry to after the conversation.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Weibel, N. et al. (2014) and Zheng, K. et al. (2015), as described in Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. & Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 391-394.

name: Multidimensional scaling and perceptual mapping
aka: Multidimensional scaling of timbre dissimilarity ratings
origin: Psychological scaling of judged similarity of letters and Morse code signals; timbre spaces from Grey (1977); positioning maps in the marketing literature (Kotler and Keller and others)
summary: Places items in a low-dimensional map so that distances match judged dissimilarities, revealing the perceptual dimensions people use and where products or designs sit on them.
description: Multidimensional scaling takes a matrix of pairwise dissimilarities, from direct ratings, card-sort co-occurrence or confusions, and positions items in two or three dimensions to minimise stress, the mismatch between map distances and the data. Dimensions are then named from the properties of items at their extremes; timbre studies, for example, consistently recover attack time and brightness. Marketing positioning adds an ideal product point and reads real-to-ideal distances, on the assumption that shorter distance means stronger preference, to find open positions. MDS needs no predefined attributes, unlike factor analysis of feature ratings, so it can surface dimensions the team did not anticipate. The rigour lies in collecting the full pairwise matrix from users, reporting stress, choosing dimensionality on evidence, and checking whether the data are better represented by a tree. In UX the 'perceptual map' often survives only as an opinion-based 2x2.
steps: Choose 8-25 items (products, sounds, icons, features) equated on irrelevant properties such as loudness or size.
Collect dissimilarities: rate every pair on a scale (for example 1-10), or derive them from card-sort co-occurrence or confusion counts.
Average across participants into a dissimilarity matrix, or keep individual matrices for an individual-differences (INDSCAL) solution.
Run MDS for one to four dimensions and choose the solution from the stress elbow and interpretability.
Name each dimension from the measurable properties of items at its ends, ideally by regressing item properties onto the coordinates.
For positioning, elicit the segment's ideal product and place it on the map, then read gaps and real-to-ideal distances.
Before trusting the map, check nearest-neighbour centrality and reciprocity, and use a tree representation if hubs dominate.
outputs: A low-dimensional perceptual map with stress values, named dimensions, and, for positioning, ideal points and open regions.
useWhen: Discovering how users perceive a set of competing products, brands, sounds or visual styles without imposing attributes; checking whether a brand's intended position matches perception.
avoidWhen: Items form clear hierarchies or categories (use cluster analysis or trees), the item set includes category labels or prototypes that create hubs, or there are too many items for full pairwise comparison (use card sorting with co-occurrence).
whyLost: Full pairwise judgements are tedious and dimension naming is interpretive; UX teams kept the visual form of the perceptual map but replaced data with stakeholder placement.
whereToUse: Competitive positioning, sonic branding and notification sound design, visual style and icon families, tone of voice, card-sort analysis.
example: A smart-home company has 30 users rate the dissimilarity of every pair of 12 alert sounds. A two-dimensional MDS solution separates urgency (attack time) from pleasantness (brightness), showing two alerts that users cannot tell apart and a gap for a calm but urgent tone.
sources: The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)

name: Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network Prediction
origin: Back-propagation (the generalised delta rule) from Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986); presented as a practical prediction method with a tuning experiment by Glenn Myatt (2007)
summary: Trains a layered network of weighted nodes on example records to predict a numeric or categorical outcome, tuning layers, cycles and learning rate against cross-validated accuracy.
description: A multilayer perceptron has an input layer with one node per normalised descriptor variable, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer with one node per response. Every connection carries a weight, initially random, and each node combines its weighted inputs through an activation function. During learning, training examples are presented one at a time and backpropagation adjusts the weights to reduce the error between predicted and actual outputs; one presentation is a cycle (epoch). The analyst sets the number of hidden layers and nodes, the number of cycles and the learning rate. Myatt treats model building as a designed experiment: try combinations of inputs, hidden layers and cycle counts, score each with cross-validated r squared or error, watch for the point where accuracy stops rising or falls (overtraining), and pick the simplest model that performs well. Networks capture non-linear relationships and tolerate noise, but they are a black box, so for UX work they suit prediction tasks where accuracy matters more than explanation, and should be paired with an explanation method or a simpler comparison model.
steps: Define the outcome to predict (for example 30-day retention or task time) and the accuracy the decision needs.
Prepare and normalise descriptor variables; dummy-code categories.
Hold out a test set or set up k-fold cross-validation.
Design a tuning grid over input sets, number of hidden layers and nodes, number of cycles and learning rate.
Train each configuration and record cross-validated accuracy, plotting accuracy against cycles to spot overtraining.
Choose the simplest configuration with near-best accuracy and compare it with a transparent model such as a regression or decision tree.
Inspect mispredicted cases and translate outputs back to original units before reporting.
outputs: A trained prediction model, a table of tuning results and cross-validated accuracy figures.
useWhen: You have hundreds or more labelled records, relationships are likely non-linear, and prediction accuracy matters more than an explanation.
avoidWhen: Samples are small, stakeholders need to understand why a prediction was made, or a regression or tree performs as well.
whyLost: Within UX, simpler interpretable models and, more recently, gradient boosting dominate tabular prediction; neural networks are left to data science teams.
whereToUse: Churn and retention scoring, predicting task time or satisfaction from telemetry, lead and upgrade propensity, personalisation.
example: A team predicts which trial users will convert from 12 behavioural features. A one-hidden-layer network at 10,000 cycles reaches a cross-validated accuracy similar to a two-layer version, so the simpler model is kept and benchmarked against logistic regression before being used to time an upgrade prompt.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)

name: Multilevel Model for Dyadic Diary Data (Distinguishable Dyads)
donor: Social and personality psychology (close relationships research)
origin: Raudenbush, Brennan and Barnett, 1995; Kenny, Kashy and Cook, 2006; Bolger and Shrout, 2007
summary: Analyse diary data from both members of a pair in one model, estimating each partner's process separately and how the partners' daily residuals and person-level effects correlate.
description: When both members of a pair keep a diary on the same days, their data are not independent: the pair is the sampled unit. Analysing each partner separately avoids the problem but discards the most interesting questions. The model treats occasions as nested within pairs and writes two parallel equations, one per distinguishable member (partner A and B, patient and carer, buyer and seller), using role dummies with no common intercept so each member has their own intercept and slopes. At level 1 the partners' same-day residuals may correlate and each series may be autocorrelated. At level 2 their random intercepts and slopes may correlate, so you can ask whether a strongly reactive member tends to have a strongly reactive partner. Predictors are split into person means and deviations for each member. A three-level model is not identifiable for distinguishable pairs, and complex error structures may not converge in all software.
steps: Confirm members are distinguishable by a meaningful role; otherwise use an indistinguishable-dyad approach.
Stack the data so each pair has one block of rows per member, with pair id, person id, day, one role dummy per member and the outcome.
Grand-mean centre each predictor, then split it into person means and person-mean deviations separately for each member; centre and rescale time.
Plot each pair's two series in panels to inspect co-movement and trends.
Fit a model with no global intercept: each role dummy and its interactions with within-person and between-person predictors and time.
Add random intercepts and within-person slopes for each member, with their covariances, at the pair level.
Specify level-1 errors that allow same-day correlation between partners and autocorrelation over days.
Report fixed effects per member, slope variances and cross-partner covariances, with a spaghetti plot of fitted lines and ellipses of random effects.
outputs: Within-person effects per member, between-pair heterogeneity, same-day partner residual correlation, and correlation of partners' intercepts and slopes.
useWhen: Diary or repeated-measures studies where two linked people both report on the same occasions, such as couples sharing a product, carer and patient, or buyer and seller.
avoidWhen: Only one member reports, or reporting occasions do not coincide; for interview data from pairs use qualitative dyadic analysis.
whyLost: UX research rarely collects synchronised data from both sides of a relationship, and the models live in close-relationships methodology.
whereToUse: Shared household finance and smart home products, care-coordination apps, marketplace buyer-seller research, and collaborative workplace tools.
example: In a 21-day diary with 60 carer-patient pairs using a medication app, missed-dose alerts raise the carer's evening stress more than the patient's, and pairs where the carer is highly reactive tend to have a highly reactive patient.
reference: Bolger, N. and Laurenceau, J.-P. (2013). Intensive Longitudinal Methods: An Introduction to Diary and Experience Sampling Research. New York: Guilford Press.

name: Multilevel Modelling (HLM / Mixed-Effects Models)
origin: Harvey Goldstein (1986); Stephen Raudenbush and Anthony Bryk (1992, 2002)
summary: Models nested data (events within sessions within users within products) to partition variance and produce correct standard errors for repeated measures.
description: Multilevel models include random effects for each level of a hierarchy, partitioning variance and accounting for non-independence of observations within units. Without them, repeated observations from one user are treated as independent, inflating effective sample size and producing anti-conservative inference. The treatise calls this essential for any UX study with repeated measures, multiple sessions per user or multi-site data, and notes most UX statistical analysis ignores clustering entirely, treating 100 clicks from one user as 100 observations, which systematically produces false confidence. Mixed models also handle unbalanced designs, crossed random effects (participants and tasks) and growth curves for longitudinal data. Rated HIGH priority.
steps: Identify the nesting or crossing structure (events, sessions, users, tasks, sites).
Specify fixed effects for predictors of interest and random intercepts (and slopes) for grouping levels.
Fit with appropriate likelihood (for example glmer for binary outcomes) and check convergence.
Compute intraclass correlations to see variance at each level.
Compare models with likelihood ratio tests or information criteria.
Report fixed effects with correct CIs and variance components.
outputs: Effect estimates with valid uncertainty, variance components, ICCs, growth curves.
useWhen: Repeated-measures usability studies, diary and ESM data, clickstreams, multi-product benchmarks.
avoidWhen: Truly independent single observations per participant; ordinary regression suffices.
whyLost: UX statistics training stops at t-tests and chi-square; analytics tools aggregate away the nesting.
whereToUse: Benchmark programmes, longitudinal studies, A/B tests with repeated sessions, multi-site research.
example: A within-subjects test of two dashboards with 12 users and 10 tasks each shows p = 0.01 with a naive t-test on 120 trials, but p = 0.21 with crossed random effects for users and tasks.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Multimodal Discourse Analysis
aka: Kress and van Leeuwen visual grammar
origin: Gunther Kress and Theo van Leeuwen, 1996 (Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design)
summary: Analyses how text, image, layout, colour, sound and motion combine or conflict to make meaning in interfaces, using representational, interactional and compositional metafunctions.
description: Multimodal discourse analysis treats every semiotic mode in an interface as meaningful and analyses how they work together. Following Kress and van Leeuwen, each mode is examined for three functions: representational (what it depicts and which actions or participants it shows), interactional (the relationship it constructs with the viewer, through gaze, distance, angle and modality), and compositional (how elements are arranged, with given-new and ideal-real positioning, salience and framing). The analysis then asks whether modes reinforce one another or contradict, since contradictions such as cheerful illustration on a serious financial warning create confusion and mistrust. Rigour comes from applying the framework consistently across a defined set of screens rather than offering aesthetic critique.
steps: Mode inventory: For each key screen, list all active semiotic modes: linguistic (text), visual (images, icons), spatial (layout), aural (sound), gestural (animation).
Representational analysis: What does each mode represent? What processes, participants, and circumstances does it show?
Interactional analysis: What relationships between interface and user does each mode enact? (Demand vs. offer; close vs. distant; high vs. low modality.)
Compositional analysis: How are modes combined? What is given vs. new? What is ideal vs. real? What has visual salience?
Coherence vs. conflict: Do modes reinforce each other or contradict? Conflicts are the source of users reporting something 'feels wrong' without knowing why.
outputs: A mode inventory per screen, a metafunction analysis, a list of cross-modal conflicts with severity, and design recommendations for coherence.
useWhen: Visual and verbal elements carry the message: marketing and onboarding screens, illustration systems, data visualisation, warnings, video and motion-heavy products, or brand redesigns.
avoidWhen: The interface is mostly functional forms with little visual rhetoric, or you need behavioural outcome data; pair with usability or comprehension testing instead.
whyLost: Its academic vocabulary is dense, design teams rely on visual intuition and brand guidelines, and the method was taught in linguistics and media studies rather than design or HCI programmes.
whereToUse: Design-system illustration guidelines, health and finance warning screens, onboarding carousels, dashboards, AI-generated imagery in products, and accessibility reviews of meaning carried only visually.
example: A mental-health app pairs crisis-line information with bright, playful illustrations. Analysis shows the interactional meaning (casual, distant) contradicts the linguistic urgency; a calmer visual treatment and direct-gaze photography test better for trust.
sources: Reading Images: Grammar of Visual Design (Kress & van Leeuwen)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Kress, G. & van Leeuwen, T. (2006). Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design (2nd ed.). Routledge.

name: Multimodal Opportunity Assessment
origin: Park and Alderman, 2018
summary: A question-led assessment of user needs, context and existing product modes to decide which senses and modalities a product should use and how the change will affect users.
description: Park and Alderman present this as the starting workflow for any multimodal product, beginning from people rather than technology and extending empathy work to the senses. Designers answer a set of questions about needs: interference and situational or permanent disability, the value of optional modes, whether another sense would feel more natural, whether users must keep focus elsewhere, whether an added modality strengthens perception or memory, human limits technology could cover, personal preferences and whether novelty is appropriate. Context is assessed with contextual inquiry, context-of-use analysis and scenarios extended with multimodal considerations, including non-users who share the environment. The intended change is then classified as adding, augmenting or replacing a mode, or creating a new multimodal product, each with its own cost: augmentation adds cognitive load, replacement demands relearning.
steps: Work through the needs questions: interference and disability, optional modes, more natural senses, focus elsewhere, strengthened perception, human limits, preferences and novelty.
Assess the context of use: what people perceive and do at the moment of use and what object or activity the product replaces, using contextual inquiry and scenarios.
Include non-users who share the environment and could be affected (bystanders, pedestrians, family members).
Classify the change as adding, augmenting or replacing a mode, or a new multimodal product.
Weigh each change's cost to users, such as added decision load or relearning effort.
Form hypotheses about modalities and explore them with physical prototypes and open-ended trial and error.
outputs: Hypotheses about which modalities to support, a classified mode change, and interference, substitution and focus requirements.
useWhen: Deciding whether and how a product should use sound, voice, haptics, light or gesture alongside or instead of a screen.
avoidWhen: The question list is not exhaustive and produces hypotheses only; observe real contexts with Contextual Inquiry or Sensory Ethnography and test prototypes with users. For workload trade-offs between channels use Multiple Resource Theory for Multimodal UX Design.
whyLost: A recent book-based workflow with little uptake; multimodal decisions are usually driven by hardware roadmaps rather than structured assessment.
whereToUse: Smart-home devices, voice assistants, automotive, wearables, accessibility features, safety alarms.
example: A smoke-alarm team replaces a low-battery chirp with a coloured light and a blaring alarm with a spoken alert naming the room, after the assessment flags interference with sleep and a need to locate the source.
reference: Park, C.W. and Alderman, J. (2018) Designing Across Senses: A Multimodal Approach to Product Design. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, ch. 7.

name: Multimodal Website Analysis Framework (Pauwels)
aka: Multimodal framework for analysing web phenomena
origin: Luc Pauwels (2005; revised 2011)
summary: Analyse a website in six phases, from first impressions and feature inventories to multimodal, audience, structure and context analysis, to read what it says about its makers.
description: Pauwels treats websites as cultural expressions to be decoded, not only interfaces to be evaluated. His model moves from easily counted features to interpretation of metaphorical and symbolic meanings. It begins with recorded first impressions and the analyst's affective reactions, then inventories features and topics, including a negative analysis of meaningfully absent elements, using coding sheets and several coders. It continues with intra-modal analysis of text, typography, images, sound and layout and their cross-modal interplay, then embedded points of view, constructed personae and implied audiences, then information organisation, navigation, gate-keeping and links, and finally the context of senders, platforms and cultural hybridity. Analysis is seen as a meeting of producer, audience and researcher cultures. It must be tailored to the research question; not every phase pays off, and sampling a changing web is hard.
steps: Phase 1: record first impressions of look and feel, likely genre and purpose, and your own affective reactions.
Phase 2: inventory features and content topics, categorise and count them, and note meaningful absences, using a standard coding sheet and at least two coders.
Phase 3: analyse each mode (written text, typography, images, sound, layout), then cross-modal interplay, then an in-depth negative analysis.
Phase 4: analyse embedded points of view, constructed personae, implied primary and secondary audiences and goals.
Phase 5: analyse information organisation, navigation options and constraints, priming and gate-keeping devices, interactive features and external links.
Phase 6: analyse the context of senders, sources, platform constraints and cultural hybridity, and draw inferences.
outputs: Coded feature and topic counts plus an interpretation of the site's values, voice, implied audiences and cultural position.
useWhen: Competitive or cultural analysis of websites and apps, auditing what a product implicitly says about who it is for, or studying user-made sites and profiles.
avoidWhen: Finding usability problems; use Heuristic Evaluation or usability testing. Avoid when you cannot sample a stable version of the site.
whyLost: It comes from visual sociology and media studies; UX site audits focus on usability and conversion rather than cultural meaning.
whereToUse: Competitor and market analysis, brand audits, inclusion and representation audits, localisation reviews, creator and portfolio platforms.
example: A neobank compares its site with five competitors using the six phases and finds that, despite neutral copy, its imagery, personae and gate-keeping steps all imply a young salaried urban user, excluding the freelancers it wants to attract.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Pauwels, L. 'Researching websites as social and cultural expressions: methodological predicaments and a multimodal model for analysis', in Margolis, E. and Pauwels, L. (eds.) (2011) The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods. London: SAGE.

name: Multiple comparisons correction
origin: Bonferroni inequality (Carlo Bonferroni, 1936; applied by Dunn, 1961); Holm's step-down procedure (1979); Benjamini and Hochberg's false discovery rate (1995)
summary: Controls the inflated chance of false positives when many metrics, segments or variants are tested, using family-wise or false discovery rate procedures.
description: With an alpha of 0.05, testing 20 independent null comparisons gives about a 64% chance of at least one false positive. UX analyses routinely test many metrics, segments, variants and survey items, then report the significant ones. Corrections control this inflation. Family-wise error rate (FWER) methods, Bonferroni (alpha divided by number of tests) and the more powerful Holm step-down procedure, limit the probability of any false positive and suit confirmatory decisions. False discovery rate (FDR) methods, notably Benjamini-Hochberg, limit the expected proportion of false positives among discoveries and suit exploratory screening of many metrics. Rigour also includes reducing the number of tests through a pre-registered primary metric and treating secondary findings as exploratory.
steps: List all planned comparisons: metrics, segments, variants and time windows; designate one or a few primary outcomes in advance.
Decide the error rate to control: FWER for confirmatory decisions (use Holm), or FDR for exploratory screening (use Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05 or 0.10).
For Holm, sort p-values ascending and compare the k-th smallest with alpha/(m − k + 1), stopping at the first non-significant result.
For Benjamini-Hochberg, sort p-values and find the largest k where p(k) ≤ (k/m)q; reject hypotheses 1 to k.
Report both raw and adjusted p-values, along with effect sizes and intervals.
Label unplanned or segment-level findings as exploratory and confirm important ones in a follow-up test.
outputs: Adjusted p-values or decisions under FWER or FDR, a clear separation of confirmatory and exploratory findings, and follow-up test recommendations.
useWhen: Testing multiple metrics, segments, variants or survey items; reviewing dashboards with many significance flags; post-hoc comparisons after ANOVA.
avoidWhen: Only one pre-registered primary comparison is being tested; or Bayesian hierarchical models are used, which handle multiplicity through partial pooling.
whyLost: Corrections are taught in statistics courses but experimentation dashboards often flag dozens of metrics as significant without adjustment, and segment fishing is common.
whereToUse: A/B tests with many metrics, survey crosstabs, multi-variant tests, analytics segment exploration.
example: A Trust Badge test reported significant gains in 3 of 24 metric-segment combinations. After Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05, none remained significant, and the team ran a follow-up test focused on the one pre-registered metric.

name: Multiple regression
origin: Francis Galton and Karl Pearson (1880s-1900s); least squares from Legendre and Gauss (1805-1809)
summary: Models a continuous outcome as a weighted sum of several predictors, estimating each predictor's unique contribution while holding the others constant.
description: Multiple regression fits an outcome such as task time, error count or a SUS score as a linear combination of predictors, for example interface complexity, user expertise and device type. Each coefficient estimates the expected change in the outcome per unit change in that predictor, conditional on the others, which is what separates it from a pile of bivariate correlations. Rigour comes from pre-specifying the model, checking assumptions (linearity, independent errors, homoscedasticity, normal residuals, low collinearity), reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than p-values alone, and validating predictive accuracy on held-out data. In UX it is the workhorse behind driver analysis, benchmarking and predicting error rates from design attributes, but it is descriptive unless the causal structure justifies the covariates chosen.
steps: Write the outcome, the candidate predictors and the reason each is included before looking at the data, ideally with a causal diagram.
Plan sample size: a common rule is at least 10-20 observations per predictor, or run a power analysis (e.g. G*Power, f2 = 0.15 for a medium effect).
Clean and code predictors: centre continuous variables, dummy-code categories with a clear reference level, and inspect distributions.
Fit the model and inspect diagnostics: residual plots, Q-Q plot, VIF (investigate above 5, act above 10) and Cook's distance (flag above 4/n).
Report standardised and unstandardised coefficients with 95% confidence intervals, plus R-squared and adjusted R-squared.
Validate with k-fold cross-validation (k = 5 or 10) and report out-of-sample RMSE or R-squared, not only in-sample fit.
Translate coefficients into design language, e.g. each additional form field adds 4.2 s (95% CI 3.1-5.3) to completion time.
outputs: A fitted model with coefficients, confidence intervals, explained variance, diagnostic plots, cross-validated prediction error and a plain-language driver ranking.
useWhen: Predicting a continuous UX outcome from several design or user attributes; key-driver analysis of satisfaction; estimating how much of a metric each factor explains while controlling for the others.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the outcome is binary or a count (use logistic or Poisson regression), when predictors vastly outnumber cases (use PLS or regularised regression), or when you need causal claims without a defensible adjustment set (use an experiment or DAG-guided analysis).
whyLost: It survives in survey driver analysis but is often run as a click-through in a tool, with no diagnostics, no validation and coefficients read causally. The rigour lives in quantitative UX teams rather than general practice.
whereToUse: Satisfaction driver analysis, benchmarking studies, predicting task time or error rate from interface metrics, pricing and plan research, and model-based design trade-offs in SaaS and fintech.
example: A trading app team regresses order-entry error rate on screen complexity score, user tenure and device. Complexity carries a coefficient of 0.8 errors per 100 orders per point after adjusting for tenure, which justifies simplifying the order ticket before onboarding work.

name: Multiple Resource Theory for Multimodal UX Design
donor: Engineering psychology and aviation human factors
origin: Christopher Wickens (1980, 1984, 2002)
summary: Predicts interference between concurrent tasks from their demands on separate resources (modality, code, stage and visual channel) and assigns interface information to reduce conflict.
description: Wickens' multiple resource theory proposes that attention draws on partly separate pools defined by four dimensions: processing stage (perception and cognition versus response), perceptual modality (visual versus auditory), processing code (spatial versus verbal), and visual channel (focal versus ambient). Tasks that share resources interfere more than tasks using different ones; for example, reading a text notification while navigating a map competes visually and verbally, whereas a spoken direction while watching the road shares less. The computational model sums demand scores and resource-conflict penalties to predict interference. In UX this supports designing in-car, wearable, AR, cockpit-like and multitasking interfaces: allocate information to modalities and codes that do not conflict with the primary task, then validate with dual-task performance and workload measures such as NASA-TLX.
steps: Map each interface element to its primary resource pool: text/labels (visual-verbal), icons (visual-spatial), audio feedback (auditory-verbal), spatial navigation (visual-spatial).
For complex tasks with dual demands: route elements to different pools.
Example: visual task with audio secondary feedback = minimal interference.
Visual task with text instructions = high interference (same pool).
Measure dual-task interference: performance on primary task with vs. without secondary task.
outputs: Task demand profiles across the four dimensions, predicted interference scores, modality assignments for interface information, and dual-task validation results.
useWhen: Driving, aviation, medical monitoring, AR and wearables, voice-plus-screen experiences, and any product used while doing something else.
avoidWhen: For single-task desktop interfaces with no concurrent activity; standard usability testing is enough.
whyLost: It is foundational in aviation and automotive human factors but rarely taught in UX, where multimodal design is decided by intuition.
whereToUse: Multi-modal interface design, dashboard design for demanding contexts, vehicle HMI, surgical robot interface, industrial IoT.
example: An in-car navigation team plans to show text messages on the central screen. Multiple resource analysis predicts high visual-verbal conflict with driving, and a simulator dual-task study confirms lane deviation increases, so messages are read aloud with a steering-wheel reply.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition — Benjamin Martin Bly
Wickens, Multiple resources and performance prediction (Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 2002)
Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (Wickens et al.)

name: Multitrait-multimethod CFA and informant discrepancy models
aka: Multitrait-multimethod CFA and common-method variance models
Informant discrepancy and multitrait-multimethod modelling of observers, parents and self-report
origin: Campbell and Fiske, 1959; CTC(M-1) by Eid, 2000; Kenny and Kashy on correlated uniqueness; De Los Reyes and Kazdin, 2005
summary: Confirmatory factor models that measure several traits by several methods or informants and separate construct variance from method variance, instead of averaging disagreeing sources.
description: Campbell and Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix measures several traits with several methods to assess convergent and discriminant validity. CFA versions model it directly. The correlated trait-correlated method model often fails (about 75% improper solutions in one review); correlated uniqueness models treat method effects as error covariances; CTC(M-1) takes one method as reference and models others as deviations from it; multilevel models handle interchangeable raters such as several customers rating one product; trifactor models handle multiple informants. Developmental research adds that disagreement between informants (parents, teachers, observers, self) is systematic and predictable from age, context and construct, and that each source adds unique predictive information. A general common-method factor is defensible only with marker variables such as a social-desirability scale. Plan multiple methods at the design stage.
steps: Measure each trait with at least two structurally different methods or informants (for example self-report, observer rating, telemetry).
Choose the model: CTCM, correlated uniqueness or CTC(M-1) for structurally different methods; multilevel or trifactor models for interchangeable raters or multiple informants.
If testing common-method bias with a general factor, include marker variables such as a social-desirability scale.
Fit the model and evaluate global fit (CFI, RMSEA) and local fit, watching for inadmissible estimates.
Interpret trait (convergent) and method variance components and discriminant validity across traits.
Model predictors of informant discrepancy (context, user group, construct) rather than averaging sources.
outputs: Trait and method variance estimates, convergent and discriminant validity evidence across methods, and predictors of informant disagreement.
useWhen: When the same construct (engagement, workload, trust, satisfaction) is measured by self-report, observers and behavioural data, and you need to know how much each reflects the construct versus its method.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small samples (CFA typically needs 200 or more) or a single method; then use Convergent and Discriminant Validity (CR, AVE, Fornell-Larcker, HTMT) or simple Triangulation. CTCM models frequently fail to converge.
whyLost: It is core psychometrics, but UX seldom has multi-method data on the same construct in one sample, and lacks SEM skills; triangulation is done qualitatively.
whereToUse: Engagement and wellbeing metrics combining surveys and telemetry, workload measurement, multi-rater enterprise feedback, child and family products with parent and child reports.
example: A learning platform measures engagement by student self-report, teacher rating and log-derived activity. A CTC(M-1) model with self-report as reference shows teacher ratings carry a large method factor tied to grades, so the team weights logs and self-report for the engagement metric.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
reference: Campbell, D. T., & Fiske, D. W. (1959). Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix. Psychological Bulletin, 56(2), 81-105; Eid, M. (2000). A multitrait-multimethod model with minimal assumptions. Psychometrika, 65, 241-261.

name: Multivariate Statistical Process Control (PCA-Based T-Squared and Q Charts)
origin: Harold Hotelling (1931, 1947); Jackson and Morris (1957) for Q, with limits by Jackson and Mudholkar (1979); Hawkins (1974); set out by J. Edward Jackson (1991)
summary: Monitor many correlated metrics with one statistic for unusual levels (T-squared) and one for unusual patterns (Q), then use component scores to diagnose the cause.
description: Separate control charts on correlated metrics inflate false alarms (nine independent charts at 95 percent signal about a third of the time) and miss joint departures. Jackson sets four goals: one answer to whether the process is in control, a specified overall Type I error, account of the correlations, and a route to diagnosis. Hotelling's T-squared, the sum of squared standardised principal component scores, gives the single answer with an F-based limit; a point can sit inside every univariate band yet outside the T-squared ellipse. When fewer components than variables are kept, the residual sum of squares Q tests whether an observation fits the model at all; a large Q flags bad data, instrumentation faults or a changed correlation structure. Only after a signal are component scores or residuals examined to find which metric moved. Subgroup versions split T-squared into mean and dispersion parts.
steps: Collect a stable base period, then compute means and the covariance or correlation matrix of the metrics.
Run PCA and choose the number of components k with a stopping rule.
For each new observation compute component scores and T-squared and compare T-squared with its F-based limit.
Compute Q from the residuals of the k-component reconstruction and compare it with the Jackson-Mudholkar limit.
Examine T-squared and Q first; only when one signals, inspect component scores or residual contributions to diagnose which metrics moved.
Watch component charts for trends even when in control, and use Bonferroni limits if plotting several component charts.
Re-estimate the base period when the correlation structure has genuinely changed, since drift inflates Q.
outputs: T-squared and Q charts, component-score charts, contribution plots showing which metrics drive a signal, and a control ellipse for pairs of metrics.
useWhen: Monitoring a product health dashboard of correlated metrics (sessions, conversion, latency, error rate, support contacts) with one alarm and a controlled false-alarm rate.
avoidWhen: A single metric (use Statistical Process Control (Control Charts)); very short histories that cannot provide a stable base period; or metrics with strong seasonality that has not been modelled out first.
whyLost: MSPC is routine in chemical, semiconductor and pharmaceutical manufacturing, but product analytics relies on per-metric thresholds and anomaly detectors that ignore correlation.
whereToUse: Product health and guardrail monitoring, instrumentation quality checks, experiment platform sanity checks, service operations dashboards.
example: A marketplace tracks seven correlated funnel metrics daily. One day every metric is within its own band, but Q jumps; contributions point to add-to-cart rising while checkouts stay flat, which traces to a broken tracking event rather than a real behaviour change.
sources: A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: Jackson, J. E. (1991). A User's Guide to Principal Components. New York: Wiley. pp. 19-25, 34-41, 123-141; Jackson, J. E., & Mudholkar, G. S. (1979). Control procedures for residuals associated with principal component analysis. Technometrics, 21(3), 341-349.

name: Multiverse and Specification Curve Analysis
origin: Sara Steegen, Francis Tuerlinckx, Andrew Gelman and Wolf Vanpaemel (2016); Uri Simonsohn, Joseph Simmons and Leif Nelson (2020)
summary: Runs an analysis under every reasonable combination of analytic choices and reports the distribution of results, exposing how fragile a finding is.
description: Any analysis involves many defensible choices: exclusion rules, metric definitions, time windows, covariates, model types. Each path through this 'garden of forking paths' could give a different answer. Multiverse analysis enumerates the reasonable choices and runs all combinations; specification curve analysis plots the sorted estimates and indicates which choices drive variation, with a permutation-based joint test. If a finding holds across most specifications, it is robust; if it appears only under a few, it was probably a by-product of choice. Product analytics and UX metrics are especially vulnerable because metric definitions are flexible.
steps: List every analytic decision point and the reasonable options at each (e.g. 3 exclusion rules x 4 windows x 2 models).
Justify inclusion of options in advance, ideally pre-registered.
Run the analysis for every combination and store estimates and uncertainty.
Plot the specification curve: estimates sorted by size with indicators of which choices were used.
Conduct inference across specifications (e.g. permutation test of the share of significant same-sign results).
Report the full distribution and identify choices that change conclusions.
outputs: A specification curve plot, the distribution of estimates and identification of influential choices.
useWhen: Findings rest on analytic choices with no single correct option, especially high-stakes metric claims.
avoidWhen: Simple pre-registered analyses with clearly correct choices.
whyLost: It arose from the psychology replication crisis, which UX largely did not engage with.
whereToUse: Retention and engagement claims, survey index construction, A/B metrics with flexible definitions, research repository meta-claims.
example: A claim that dark mode increases session length holds in only 14 of 96 specifications, mostly those excluding sessions under 10 seconds. The team reports the effect as not robust.
sources: Steegen et al., Increasing transparency through a multiverse analysis (2016), Perspectives on Psychological Science
Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson, Specification curve analysis (2020), Nature Human Behaviour
reference: Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2020). Nature Human Behaviour, 4, 1208-1214.

name: Mumble Screens
origin: Jakob Nielsen (1993); Nygren et al. (1992) for the task analysis use
summary: Prototype screen layouts with every letter replaced by 'm' so grouping, alignment and hierarchy can be judged apart from content.
description: A mumble screen is a layout with its text replaced by strings of the letter m of the same lengths. Removing readable content forces reviewers to judge the screen's structure: whether related items group together, whether alignment and spacing make the hierarchy obvious, and whether the eye lands where it should. Nielsen recommended it under the principle of simple and natural dialogue; the screen can be abstracted further by replacing images and controls with blocks. A second use, from Nygren and colleagues, is as a task analysis probe: show users mumbled versions of forms they know and see whether they can still find or infer information from layout alone. If they can, the new design should preserve those layout cues. Today the idea survives as greyboxing, greeked wireframes and the blur test, usually without the task analysis use.
steps: Take a screen design and replace all text with 'm' strings of the same length, keeping font sizes and weights.
Optionally replace images and controls with plain blocks for a further level of abstraction.
Review grouping, alignment, white space and visual hierarchy, noting where the structure does not show which items belong together.
Revise the layout and repeat until the intended grouping is visible without content.
For task analysis, show users mumbled versions of familiar paper or legacy forms and ask them to point to specific information.
Carry any layout cues users rely on into the new design.
outputs: A layout critique and revised layout; evidence of which information users locate from layout alone.
useWhen: Use early in visual design, or when replacing a familiar legacy form, to check that layout alone conveys structure.
avoidWhen: Avoid for judging comprehension or content: real text changes line breaks and emphasis, so test with real content via Usability Testing or First-click testing. For overall first impressions use the 5-Second Test.
whyLost: The name faded; the idea lives on as greeked wireframes, greyboxing and the blur or squint test, while the task analysis use is largely forgotten.
whereToUse: Dashboard and form design, migrations from paper or legacy systems, design system layout templates.
example: An insurer replacing a paper claims form shows adjusters a mumbled version; they still point straight to the policy number box by its position. The digital form keeps that box top right.
reference: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering. Boston: AP Professional, p. 117. Nygren, E., Johnson, M., Lind, M. and Sandblad, B. (1992), cited therein.

name: MUSHRA Listening Test (ITU-R BS.1534)
aka: Multiple Stimuli with Hidden Reference and Anchor
origin: ITU-R Recommendation BS.1534, 2001 (revised 2015)
summary: A standardised listening test in which trained listeners rate several audio versions against a known reference, with a hidden reference and low-quality anchors to validate ratings.
description: MUSHRA asks listeners to rate multiple stimuli on a 0-100 continuous quality scale, simultaneously, with free switching between them and an open reference. Among the stimuli are a hidden copy of the reference and one or more anchors (e.g. a 3.5 kHz low-pass filtered version). Listeners who fail to rate the hidden reference near 100 are excluded under post-screening rules. The design yields sensitive, reliable comparisons for intermediate audio quality. For UX, it is a model of rigour for any perceptual comparison: voice assistant TTS, notification sounds, call quality, audio in video products. Its anchors and hidden reference make rater reliability measurable.
steps: Prepare stimuli: the reference, the systems under test, a hidden reference and the standard anchors, loudness-normalised.
Recruit and train listeners (typically 15-20 experienced listeners) with a familiarisation phase.
Run trials with all stimuli for an item presented together in random order, rated on 0-100.
Apply post-screening: exclude listeners rating the hidden reference below 90 for more than 15% of items.
Analyse with mixed models or ANOVA, reporting means and 95% confidence intervals per system.
Relate quality differences to perceptual attributes through follow-up descriptive analysis if needed.
outputs: Mean quality scores with confidence intervals per system, listener reliability data.
useWhen: Comparing voice synthesis, codecs, noise suppression, audio branding or alert sounds at intermediate quality differences.
avoidWhen: Very small impairments (use ITU-R BS.1116 ABX-style tests) or general preference questions in context.
whyLost: Audio quality testing lives in audio engineering, and UX teams rarely evaluate sound with standardised methods.
whereToUse: Voice assistants and TTS, video conferencing, hearing-aid apps, games, in-car audio cues.
example: A voice AI team compares four TTS voices in MUSHRA with 20 listeners; the hidden reference screens out three unreliable raters, and one voice is shown to be significantly more natural on long passages.
sources: ITU-R BS.1534-3 (2015) Method for the subjective assessment of intermediate quality level of audio systems
Bech & Zacharov, Perceptual Audio Evaluation: Theory, Method and Application (2006)
reference: ITU-R (2015). Recommendation BS.1534-3.

name: Music-to-Interaction Quality Matching
aka: Movies, maps, mechanisms, prototypes and matching test
origin: Hummels, Cruz Restrepo and Overbeeke, 2009, TU/e master's class 'Aesthetics of interaction'
summary: Translate the experiential quality of a piece of music into a product interaction via films, interaction maps, foam mechanisms and prototypes, then test with a music-to-prototype matching exercise.
description: Teams of three or four receive a piece of classical music and must design an interactive product whose interaction carries the same quality. Five methods alternate sensorial and analytical work. A one-minute film links the music to a quality of interaction; an interaction map abstracts the film into keywords and graphics; interaction mechanisms are built from neutral white foam-board squares so attention stays on movement rather than appearance; a prototype product is then built in cycles of doing and reflecting; finally, in a matching experiment, people listen to each piece of music and choose the prototype that matches it. The match rate gives a rough check on whether the intended expressive quality is recognisable.
steps: Assign each team a piece of music with a distinct character.
Make a one-minute film showing the link between the music and a quality of interaction.
Abstract the film into an interaction map of keywords and graphics.
Build interaction mechanisms in neutral white foam board, focusing on movement and response rather than looks.
Build a working prototype whose interaction has the same experiential quality, iterating between making and reflecting.
Run a matching test: participants hear each piece and choose the prototype that matches; tally matches.
outputs: Prototypes with an intended expressive quality and a match tally showing whether that quality is recognised.
useWhen: Exploring the aesthetic or expressive quality of an interaction (rhythm, flow, tension) in physical or motion design, or training designers' sensitivity to it.
avoidWhen: A teaching exercise with no reported results; the matching test is a rough check, not a validated measure. For measuring perceived qualities use Semantic Differential or AttrakDiff, and for usability use Prototype Testing.
whyLost: Confined to design education at TU Eindhoven and aesthetics-of-interaction research; commercial teams rarely invest in expressive quality this way.
whereToUse: Motion and animation systems, tangible products, automotive interiors, game feel, sonic branding.
example: A design-system team adapts it to motion: each designer animates a transition to one of three pieces of music, and colleagues match animations to music to check that 'calm' and 'urgent' motion are distinguishable.
reference: Hummels, C., Cruz Restrepo, M. and Overbeeke, K. (2009) Designing the melody of interaction through movies, maps, mechanisms, prototypes and presentations. CHI 2009 Extended Abstracts, 2647-2650.

name: Musical ability screening (Gold-MSI, PROMS, MBEA)
origin: Law and Zentner, 2012 (PROMS); Müllensiefen and colleagues, 2014 (Gold-MSI); Peretz and colleagues (MBEA)
summary: Standardised batteries that profile participants' musical perception and engagement, replacing a binary musician label and flagging congenital amusia, for studies that depend on hearing sound differences.
description: Studies of audio interfaces often split participants into 'musicians' and 'non-musicians' by training, which misclassifies trained but unmusical people and able but untrained ones. Music psychology offers better tools. PROMS (Profile of Music Perception Skills) and the Gold-MSI (Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index) combine perceptual subtests with self-report of engagement and give a profile across domains such as pitch, rhythm and timbre; subtests show domain-specific training effects. The MBEA (Montreal Battery of Evaluation of Amusia), normed on a large sample, identifies the roughly 2-4% of people who are congenitally amusic: they need pitch differences of two or three semitones to notice a change and lose tones held over 3-5 seconds. That matters for any product that codes information in pitch or melody, such as two ringtones distinguishing internal and external calls. The book gives no items or scoring, so use the original instruments.
steps: Identify which auditory abilities the product or study relies on (pitch discrimination, rhythm, timbre, melodic memory).
Choose the matching instrument: Gold-MSI for a quick sophistication index, PROMS for a perceptual profile, MBEA where amusia must be detected.
Administer it before the main study, using the original stimuli and scoring.
Score subtests and keep the profile rather than collapsing to musician versus non-musician.
Stratify or covary results by ability, and flag participants below amusia cut-offs.
Feed findings back into design, for example adding non-pitch cues where amusic users would miss a distinction.
outputs: An ability profile per participant, an amusia flag where relevant, and results stratified by auditory ability.
useWhen: When evaluating sound-based alerts, earcons, sonification or music features whose effectiveness depends on perceptual discrimination, or recruiting a sample that must span hearing ability.
avoidWhen: Avoid when sound is incidental to the study. It is not a hearing test: screen hearing thresholds separately (audiometry). For preference among sounds use Listening survey for product sounds.
whyLost: Music psychology instruments are unknown in UX; audio teams rely on self-declared musicianship or none at all.
whereToUse: Alerting in healthcare and industrial devices, ringtones and notification design, music and audio apps, accessibility of sonification.
example: A hospital pump maker tests two pitch-coded alarms. MBEA screening of 60 nurses finds two amusic participants who cannot tell the alarms apart, so the design adds a rhythm difference as a redundant cue.
sources: The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Müllensiefen, D., Gingras, B., Musil, J., & Stewart, L. (2014). The musicality of non-musicians: An index for assessing musical sophistication in the general population. PLoS ONE, 9(2), e89642.

name: Mutual Information Between Two Variables
origin: Claude Shannon (1948); as presented by David MacKay (2003)
summary: Measure how many bits of uncertainty about one variable are removed, on average, by knowing another, as I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y), to quantify dependence between categorical variables.
description: Mutual information extends entropy from one variable to a pair. MacKay defines the joint entropy H(X,Y), the conditional entropy H(X|y) for one value of y and H(X|Y) averaged over y, the chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X), and the mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y), which is symmetric and never negative. It is the average reduction in uncertainty about x from learning y. Conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) is computed within each value of z and averaged, which helps when a third variable may confound. Unlike correlation it captures any form of dependence among categorical values and is measured in bits. MacKay warns that learning one particular value of y can increase uncertainty about x even though the average decreases, and that Venn-diagram pictures of three-variable entropies mislead.
steps: Tabulate the joint distribution of two categorical variables from counts, for example entry page by task outcome.
Compute the marginal entropies H(X) and H(Y) in bits.
Compute the conditional entropy H(X|Y) by averaging H(X|y) over y weighted by P(y).
Compute I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y), equivalently H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y).
Where a third variable may confound, compute I(X;Y|Z) within levels of Z and average.
With small tables, correct for bias or compare with values from shuffled data before interpreting.
outputs: Mutual information in bits, with the marginal and conditional entropies, showing how informative one variable is about another.
useWhen: Ranking which user attributes, entry points or answers best predict an outcome; choosing screener or onboarding questions that carry the most information; quantifying redundancy between categorical measures.
avoidWhen: Estimates from small count tables are biased upwards; it gives no direction or causal reading. For a significance test of association use Chi-Square and Fisher's Exact Tests; for single-variable uncertainty use Shannon Entropy Audit.
whyLost: UX analysts use correlation and chi-square for association, and information-theoretic measures stayed in communication engineering and machine learning.
whereToUse: Onboarding question design, segmentation variable selection, navigation analytics, feature selection for personalisation.
example: An onboarding flow asks five questions. Mutual information with 30-day retention shows 'team size' carries 0.21 bits and 'industry' only 0.02, so industry is dropped and the flow shortened.
sources: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay, 2003)
reference: Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. Bell System Technical Journal, 27; MacKay, D. J. C. (2003). Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms. Cambridge University Press, ch. 8, pp. 138-145.

name: Mystery Shopping
origin: Long-standing market research practice; described by Veal and Darcy as a potentially fruitful but underexploited form of observation in sport facilities
summary: A trained researcher uses a service incognito, as an ordinary customer would, and reports against a checklist of quality features.
description: Mystery shopping is a form of observational research in which the researcher plays the role of a user, visitor or customer to find out what the experience of using a facility, product or service is really like. The mystery shopper uses the facilities or services on an incognito basis, carrying a checklist of features to observe, such as cleanliness, the availability and clarity of information, and staff performance, and writes a report after the visit. Veal and Darcy point out that it draws on the observer's expertise to judge service quality and to notice details, for example safety problems, that routine users might miss. They also warn that ethical and industrial relations issues can arise because of the deception involved, since the researcher is typically acting for management and staff are being assessed without knowing it. In UX and service design the method is useful for evaluating end-to-end journeys that cross digital and human touchpoints, such as sign-up, delivery, returns or support, where lab testing cannot reproduce the real service and staff behaviour.
steps: Define the journey or service episodes to be evaluated and the standards they should meet.
Build a checklist of observable features, with clear rating criteria, covering every touchpoint in the journey.
Agree the ethical position with management and, where appropriate, staff representatives, including how findings about individuals will be used.
Brief and train shoppers to behave like typical customers and to record observations soon after each episode.
Carry out the visits or online journeys across a planned spread of locations, channels, days and times.
Compile checklist scores and narrative reports, and look for patterns rather than blaming individual staff.
Feed the findings into journey maps and service blueprints and recheck after changes.
outputs: Completed checklists and narrative reports for each episode, aggregated scores by touchpoint, and a list of service and experience failures.
useWhen: You need an honest picture of a live, multi-channel service experience as customers actually receive it, including staff behaviour and offline steps.
avoidWhen: Covert assessment of staff would breach trust or agreements, the service cannot be used without real personal or financial commitments, or the issue is purely interface usability.
whyLost: UX grew around lab and remote testing of interfaces, while mystery shopping stayed in retail operations and quality assurance; its deception and staff-monitoring connotations also make researchers wary.
whereToUse: Omnichannel retail, banking and insurance onboarding, customer support, delivery and returns, hospitality and venue booking, public services.
example: A ticketing company asks researchers to buy, transfer and refund tickets as ordinary fans across the app, phone line and stadium box office. Checklists show that the refund promise in the app is not honoured at the box office, a failure no usability test of the app alone would have found.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: N-1 Two-Proportion Test
origin: Pearson; N-1 adjustment recommended by Campbell (2007) and adopted for UX by Sauro & Lewis
summary: Compares two independent success or conversion rates accurately, even when samples are small.
description: Comparing completion or conversion rates between two designs, tested on different people, is the most common quantitative UX comparison. The classic chi-square test is inaccurate when expected cell counts are small, and Fisher's exact test is overly conservative, so real differences get missed. Campbell's simulation work showed that multiplying the chi-square statistic by (N−1)/N gives accurate Type I error rates across almost all sample sizes, as long as every expected count is at least one. The equivalent z-test version also yields a confidence interval around the difference, which tells stakeholders how big the improvement might be, not only whether it is real.
steps: Record successes and totals for each independent group.
Check that every expected cell count is at least 1; if not, use Fisher's exact test.
Compute the pooled proportion and z = (p1 − p2) / sqrt(P(1−P)(1/n1 + 1/n2)), then multiply by sqrt((N−1)/N).
Convert to a two-tailed p-value.
Compute an adjusted-Wald interval around the difference and report both.
outputs: A p-value and an interval for the difference between two rates.
useWhen: Between-subjects comparisons of success, conversion, click-through or preference rates.
avoidWhen: The same people saw both designs (use McNemar), or there are more than two groups (use chi-square with follow-ups).
whyLost: Analytics tools default to large-sample z-tests, and most UX practitioners never meet the small-sample correction.
whereToUse: Small A/B tests, competitive benchmarks, prototype comparisons with 20 to 50 people per arm.
example: Design A: 11 of 20 complete; design B: 18 of 21. The N-1 test gives p = 0.02 and the 90% interval for the difference runs from about 12 to 50 points.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Campbell, I. (2007). Chi-squared and Fisher-Irwin tests of two-by-two tables with small sample recommendations. Statistics in Medicine 26.

name: Naive Bayes Classification
origin: Bayes' theorem with independence assumption; widely used in text classification since the 1990s
summary: A fast, simple classifier that predicts categories (such as ticket topic or churn risk) from features assumed independent.
description: Naive Bayes estimates, for each class, the probability of each feature value, then multiplies them to score a new case. The "naive" assumption that features are independent is usually wrong, but the ranking of classes is often still good. It trains in seconds, needs little data and is easy to explain. In UX research it is useful for auto-tagging open-ended survey responses or support tickets into known codes after a human has coded a training set, and as a quick baseline before more complex models.
steps: Code a training set by hand (for example 500 verbatims into themes).
Convert text or categorical predictors into features (words, answers).
Estimate class priors and conditional probabilities, with smoothing for unseen values.
Predict classes for new cases and evaluate with a confusion matrix on held-out data.
Review misclassified examples and refine codes or features.
outputs: A classifier that tags new records into known categories.
useWhen: Scaling up manual coding of text or categorical data with a simple, transparent model.
avoidWhen: Features are strongly dependent and calibrated probabilities matter.
whyLost: UX qualitative coding stayed manual while text classification grew up in data science.
whereToUse: Support ticket triage, open-ended survey coding, app review analysis.
example: After coding 600 app reviews, a Naive Bayes model tags 20,000 more into eight themes at 81% accuracy, enough to track theme trends weekly.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, chapter 5.

name: Named entity recognition for UX research domains
origin: NER defined at MUC-6, 1995; spaCy EntityRuler and trainable NER
summary: Training or configuring entity recognition to detect UX-relevant entities, such as product features, competitors, devices, workflows and emotions, in transcripts and feedback.
description: Generic NER detects people, organisations and places, which is useful mainly for anonymisation. UX research needs domain entities: feature names, screens, competitor products, job roles, workarounds, devices and emotions. spaCy supports rule-based patterns (EntityRuler) and trainable statistical NER on annotated examples. A hybrid approach typically works best: rules for known vocabulary, trained models for variants and new mentions. Rigour comes from a clear annotation guideline, double annotation with agreement measurement, held-out evaluation with precision, recall and F1, and error analysis. Generic NER is also used to detect personal names and places for anonymisation, with high recall prioritised.
steps: Define an entity schema of 5-12 types with written definitions and examples.
Build an EntityRuler with known terms (feature names from the product, competitor list).
Annotate 300-1,000 sentences with two annotators, measuring agreement (e.g. F1 between annotators of 0.80 or above) and refining guidelines.
Train or fine-tune the NER component on the annotated data, holding out 20% for evaluation.
Evaluate per entity type and inspect errors, especially missed variants and false positives.
Deploy with the rules first and model second, and re-evaluate when the product vocabulary changes.
outputs: An entity schema and guideline, an annotated corpus, a trained NER component with per-type scores, and entity mentions across the corpus.
useWhen: Large corpora of interviews, feedback or tickets where systematic counts of feature, competitor or emotion mentions are needed, and for anonymisation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the corpus is small or the questions are about meaning and context rather than mentions; manual coding is better there.
whyLost: Domain NER requires annotation effort and NLP skills that UX teams rarely have, so it stayed in text analytics and computational linguistics.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer analytics, competitive intelligence from interviews, feedback triage and transcript anonymisation.
example: A fintech research team trains NER for 'feature', 'competitor' and 'workaround' across 220 transcripts. It reveals 140 mentions of spreadsheet workarounds, concentrated among small-business users, which prompts a dedicated study.
sources: Grishman, R. & Sundheim, B. (1996) Message Understanding Conference-6: A brief history. COLING
Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft
The Inquiry Series, C10 — spaCy — Building NLP Pipelines for Qualitative Research
reference: Grishman, R. & Sundheim, B. (1996) Message Understanding Conference-6: A brief history. COLING 1996

name: Narrative Inquiry
origin: D. Jean Clandinin and F. Michael Connelly, 1990 to 2000 (Narrative Inquiry)
summary: Studies experience through the stories people live and tell, working within a three-dimensional space of temporality, sociality and place, and keeping stories whole rather than fragmenting them.
description: Narrative inquiry treats story as both the phenomenon and the method: people understand their lives narratively, so research should attend to stories in context. Clandinin and Connelly define a three-dimensional inquiry space: temporality (past, present and future), sociality (personal and social conditions, including the researcher's relationship to participants) and place. Researchers collect field texts such as conversations, journals, artefacts and field notes over extended relationships, write tentative interim texts shared with participants, and only then compose research texts. Unlike thematic coding, narrative inquiry resists breaking stories into fragments, keeping sequence and context intact. Its rigour lies in relational responsibility, sustained engagement and 'wakefulness' to simplification.
steps: Field texts (data collection): Collect field texts — stories told through interviews, journal entries, letters, photographs, documents, oral histories.
Maintain narrative stance: Resist the analytical impulse to fragment stories into codes before the full narrative is preserved.
Interim texts: Write early interpretations that are tentative and open to revision as more field texts are gathered.
Research texts (final accounts): Transform field texts into research texts that tell a story about the experience while honouring the narrative complexity of participants' own stories.
Wakefulness: Continuously guard against reducing rich life complexity to a simple analytical category.
outputs: Field texts, interim narrative accounts negotiated with participants, final narrative research texts, and cross-narrative resonances that inform design.
useWhen: Experience unfolds over time and context, such as illness, education, caregiving or career, and you need to understand the meaning of a journey rather than discrete tasks.
avoidWhen: You need structured, comparable data across many participants or answers to tactical questions; use semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis or a diary study.
