whyLost: It requires long relationships and produces narrative texts rather than actionable lists, which clashes with sprint-based research, so it stayed in education and health research.
whereToUse: Long-term health conditions, education and learning products, caregiving and family services, career platforms, and longitudinal research programmes.
example: A diabetes app team follows 6 newly diagnosed people over 4 months, co-writing their narratives. The stories show the app is experienced as a reminder of failure after setbacks, leading to a 'fresh start' mode after missed weeks.
sources: Narrative Methods for the Human Sciences (Riessman)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Clandinin, D. J. & Connelly, F. M. (2000). Narrative Inquiry: Experience and Story in Qualitative Research. Jossey-Bass.

name: Narrative Oriented Inquiry (NOI)
origin: Dave Hiles and Ivo Čermák; draws on Mishler (1986), Herman and Vervaeck (2001), Lieblich, Tuval-Mashiach and Zilber (1998), Emerson and Frosh (2004)
summary: Segment a narrative interview into a working transcript and read it through six perspectives: what is told versus how, four Lieblich readings, and critical narrative analysis.
description: NOI is a staged analytic model for narrative interviews. It holds that narrative data have a double signature (social constructionist and phenomenological) and a double context (the story and the occasion of telling). The interview is turned into a working transcript segmented into numbered episodes, events, moments, asides and emphases, keeping every utterance of both speakers. The first perspective separates fabula, what is told (bounded motifs), from sjuzet, how it is told (unbounded motifs such as evaluations and hesitations). Perspectives two to five apply Lieblich's holistic-content, holistic-form, categorical-content and categorical-form readings. The sixth is critical narrative analysis of breaches between person and social context. Transparency about each interpretive step is required, and perspectives are chosen to fit the question, text and sample size, since the working transcript is already an interpretation.
steps: Choose a biographical or topic-focused narrative interview format.
Make a working transcript: segment into numbered episodes, events, moments, asides and emphases, keeping all utterances of both speakers without tidying.
Perspective 1: separate fabula (what is told, bounded motifs) from sjuzet (how it is told, unbounded motifs), marking the latter.
Perspectives 2-5: apply Lieblich's holistic-content, holistic-form, categorical-content and categorical-form readings as fits the question.
Perspective 6: run a critical narrative analysis around breaches between the person and their social context.
Report transparently how each interpretive step was taken and what each perspective added.
outputs: A multi-perspective interpretation of a person's story and of how they tell it.
useWhen: Small numbers of long narrative interviews about significant experiences (diagnosis, migration, career change, financial crisis) where how people tell their story matters as much as what happened.
avoidWhen: Large samples or task-focused interviews; use Thematic Analysis. For a looser narrative stance use Narrative Inquiry; for clause-level structure use Labov Narrative Analysis.
whyLost: It is a specialist model in Czech and British narrative psychology; UX uses stories but rarely analyses narrative form systematically.
whereToUse: Health journeys, life-event products (bereavement, relocation, job loss), longitudinal customer stories, service failure accounts.
example: Analysing six long interviews about receiving a cancer diagnosis through a patient portal, researchers separate the sequence of events from the way patients tell them, finding that hesitation and self-blame cluster around the moment results appeared before a doctor's call.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Hiles, D. and Čermák, I. 'Narrative psychology', in Willig, C. and Stainton Rogers, W. (eds.) (2008) The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology. London: SAGE.

name: Narrative Usability Test
origin: Listed in Michael C. Medlock's overview of GUR methods (chapter 7)
summary: A one-to-one test in which players work through a prototype of a game's story before it is built, to find confusion, gaps in logic and mismatched expectations.
description: Narrative usability applies observational usability testing to story rather than interface. Before a narrative is implemented in the game, participants go through a prototype of it from beginning to end (for example scripts, storyboards, animatics or a simple text version) while the researcher observes and asks them to explain what is happening and why. The aim is to reveal areas of confusion, misaligned expectations, interactions with genre conventions and gaps in logic, so writers and designers can either correct the story or deliberately embrace the beliefs players form. Because it happens early, changes are cheap. Medlock notes its main limit: it shows whether the story is understood, not whether players will like it, and gives little data on feelings about the narrative. Outside games, the same approach suits any product that relies on a sequence of explanation, such as onboarding stories, explainer videos, or guided tutorials, where comprehension of the sequence is the question.
steps: Prepare a low-cost prototype of the narrative (script, storyboard, animatic or text) covering the full arc.
Define the key story beats, motivations and facts players must understand.
Run one-to-one sessions in which each participant goes through the prototype in order.
At planned points, ask participants to summarise what has happened, predict what comes next and explain characters' motives.
Note confusions, wrong inferences and genre-based expectations.
Report comprehension problems by beat and agree with writers which to fix and which to keep.
outputs: A list of story beats with comprehension problems, mistaken inferences and expectation mismatches.
useWhen: A story or sequenced explanation is being written and changes are still cheap.
avoidWhen: You need to know whether players will enjoy or care about the story.
whyLost: Narrative is usually judged by writers and directors rather than tested, and comprehension testing of stories is rare outside a few game studios.
whereToUse: Story-driven games, interactive fiction, onboarding narratives, explainer and training content.
example: Players read an animatic of a role-playing game's opening and three of six believe the mentor is the villain; the writers add a scene that clarifies her motive.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 7 (Medlock).

name: NASA-TLX
origin: Sandra Hart and Lowell Staveland, NASA Ames, 1988
summary: A six-dimension subjective workload measure (mental, physical and temporal demand, performance, effort, frustration) producing an overall workload score per task.
description: NASA-TLX was developed at NASA Ames to measure perceived workload in complex tasks such as piloting. Participants rate six subscales on 0-100 scales: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance (reverse-anchored from good to poor), effort and frustration. The original version weights subscales through 15 pairwise comparisons; the Raw TLX simply averages them and performs comparably in most studies. The method's strength is sensitivity to design differences and its diagnostic subscales, which show whether workload stems from time pressure, mental demand or frustration. Rigour comes from administering it immediately after each task, comparing within subjects where possible, reporting subscale profiles not just the total, and keeping interpretation relative, since absolute TLX values vary widely across task types.
steps: Define tasks to compare and administer TLX immediately after each one.
Explain each subscale definition to participants before the first rating, noting the reversed performance anchor.
Collect ratings on 0-100 scales in 5-point increments for all six subscales.
Optionally run the 15 pairwise comparisons for weighting, or use the Raw TLX average.
Analyse totals and subscale profiles, using within-subject comparisons with 12-24 participants.
Relate high subscales to design causes and pair with performance data.
outputs: Overall workload score per task and condition, subscale profiles, statistical comparisons between designs.
useWhen: Comparing interface alternatives for demanding tasks, safety-critical systems, clinical tools, automotive and enterprise workflows.
avoidWhen: Simple, low-demand consumer tasks where differences will be small; SUS or task metrics are more informative.
whyLost: Still in use: Validated; widely used in human factors and increasingly in UX.
whereToUse: Task workload assessment; comparing interface alternatives; safety-critical design.
example: An EHR vendor compared two medication reconciliation designs with 16 nurses. The new design reduced Raw TLX from 58 to 41, mainly through lower temporal demand and frustration, with no change in accuracy.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Hart, S. G., & Staveland, L. E. (1988). Development of NASA-TLX (Task Load Index): Results of empirical and theoretical research. Advances in Psychology, 52, 139-183.

name: Nash Equilibrium Analysis
origin: John F. Nash, 1950
summary: Identifies strategy profiles where no player can improve their payoff by deviating alone, explaining why inferior designs persist and what would have to change for a new form to win.
description: A strategy profile (s1*, ..., sn*) is a Nash equilibrium if, for every player i, playing si* yields at least as much as any alternative given all others play their equilibrium strategies. Three properties matter for design research: equilibrium is stable but not necessarily optimal (as in the Prisoner's Dilemma), systems can have multiple equilibria, and disruption requires a change in the environment rather than a better individual choice. Vivek Gopinath's paper uses it as a diagnostic and generative lens rather than a precise predictor, because design actors are partially rational with incomplete information. Players include makers, suppliers, retailers, users, critics, regulators and craft communities; payoffs include cultural legitimacy, perceived quality, adoption and recognition. Mixed-strategy equilibria explain hybrids such as Indian homes keeping both dining chairs and floor seating, each activated by context. The lens is operationalised through the Deviation Utility model.
steps: List the players in the design ecosystem.
List each player's available strategies.
Describe the payoffs each strategy combination yields, including cultural, social and material payoffs.
Check whether any single player gains by deviating unilaterally from the current form.
Distinguish stability, stagnation (collectively suboptimal equilibrium) and multiple or mixed-strategy equilibria.
Identify environmental changes (technology, regulation, cultural movement, new channels) that would shift payoffs for several players at once.
outputs: A player-strategy-payoff map, equilibrium diagnosis and candidate levers for change.
useWhen: When designs, standards or conventions persist despite better alternatives, or when adoption depends on several actors moving together.
avoidWhen: When a single user's choice is independent of others' choices; standard usability and preference research suffices.
whyLost: Central to economics, rarely translated into design research instruments.
whereToUse: Platform standards, payment methods, marketplaces, craft and cultural products, media formats.
example: Analysing three-act film structure, studios, distributors, audiences, critics and filmmakers all face penalties for deviating, explaining why a demonstrably engaging non-linear form fails in mainstream cinema but thrives on the festival circuit.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Nash, J. F. (1950). Equilibrium points in n-person games. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 36(1), 48–49.

name: Nash Equilibrium Design Research Protocol
donor: Game theory, behavioural economics and design theory
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A six-stage protocol (Predict, Diagnose, Prove, Forecast, Prescribe, Validate) that maps a design ecosystem's players and payoffs, measures ΔU and targets interventions at what keeps a form in equilibrium.
description: The protocol treats a stable design form as a Nash equilibrium: a state where no single actor (maker, user, retailer, critic, cultural norm) gains by deviating unilaterally, regardless of whether a superior alternative exists. It distinguishes design stability (the form still satisfies all players' payoffs) from design stagnation (a collectively suboptimal equilibrium), and introduces the design plateau: a form that no longer serves needs, whose stakeholders know better options exist, yet persists because individual switching costs exceed individually capturable gains. Plateaus dissolve through ecosystem change that shifts payoffs for several players at once, not through a better object alone. The six stages run from ecosystem mapping and baseline ΔU, through qualitative coding against ΔU components, statistical confirmation (surveys, factor analysis, SEM), Monte Carlo scenario forecasting and targeted prescriptions, to validation by trials and re-estimated ΔU. Cases include the Indian pressure cooker, Khurja ceramics, floor seating and the three-act film structure.
steps: Predict: map the ecosystem's players, their strategies and the payoff structures maintaining the current form, and compute a baseline ΔU for the proposed alternative.
Diagnose: gather think-alouds, in-depth interviews and contextual observation, and code evidence against ΔU components to find the drivers of Uh, E and P.
Classify the situation as stability, stagnation or plateau, and note mixed-strategy or multiple co-existing equilibria.
Prove: test with surveys, factor analysis and SEM whether the identified components statistically predict preference for the existing form.
Forecast: simulate adoption under redesign scenarios (e.g. SNR raised from 0.35 to 0.75 and E halved) with Monte Carlo to express uncertainty.

Prescribe: design interventions at the most negative components (raise SNR, reduce E, build T, restructure the ecosystem around P), including channel or institutional changes, not only object changes.
Validate: confirm with controlled trials, A/B tests where possible, longitudinal observation and qualitative follow-up; re-estimate ΔU against baseline and synthesise in a joint display.
Check ethics: work with communities on which components they wish to preserve, especially in craft contexts.
outputs: Ecosystem player-payoff map, ΔU baseline and component profile, equilibrium classification, scenario forecasts, targeted interventions and a validation comparison.
useWhen: When a design form persists despite better alternatives, when planning disruptive redesigns, or when working with craft, cultural or platform ecosystems with many interdependent actors.
avoidWhen: For single-user usability problems with no ecosystem dynamics; use usability testing. Avoid using the power analysis against the communities studied.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; game theory has rarely been operationalised as a design research instrument.
whereToUse: Platform and payment migrations, enterprise software replacement, craft and cultural product design, media formats, marketplace design.
example: Analysing why the whistle-valve pressure cooker persists, a researcher maps manufacturers, retailers, users, repair shops and sensory norms, finds high Uh, low T and high P, and recommends building repair-ecosystem trust before launching a silent digital model.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Equilibrium and the Design Object, Section 9.1.

name: Natural frequencies and transparent risk formats
aka: Fast-and-frugal trees and transparent risk formats
donor: Cognitive psychology of judgement; medical decision making
origin: Gerd Gigerenzer and Ulrich Hoffrage, 1995, and the ABC Research Group
summary: Express risks as counts in an imagined population and absolute rather than relative changes, then test whether people's probability judgements become accurate.
description: People given a test's accuracy and a disease's base rate as percentages routinely neglect the base rate: told a test is 95 percent accurate, many conclude a positive result means a 95 percent chance of disease. Recasting the same information as natural frequencies (of 100,000 people, 100 have the disease, 95 of them test positive, and about 4,995 of the healthy also test positive) makes the correct answer, under 2 percent, easy to read off. The same programme recommends absolute over relative risk (a pill scare reported as a '100 per cent' increase was 1 in 7,000 to 2 in 7,000) and fast-and-frugal decision trees as transparent decision aids. As a research method, formats are compared in experiments on judgement accuracy, and the natural-frequency table is a working tool for checking calculations.
steps: Identify the probability judgement users must make (for example the chance a positive alert is real).
Build a natural-frequency version: pick a reference population (for example 1,000 or 100,000), apply the base rate, then apply sensitivity and false-positive rate to each group.
Lay out a 2 x 2 table of outcome by test result and read the positive predictive value from the positive row.
Create matched presentation formats: conditional probabilities, natural frequencies, icon arrays, and absolute versus relative risk.
Randomly assign participants to formats and ask for the probability judgement and a decision.
Score accuracy against the correct value and compare formats; check comprehension with a teach-back question.
outputs: A natural-frequency table with the correct probability, accuracy and decision rates by format, and a recommended risk format.
useWhen: Any interface that communicates test results, alerts, fraud flags, model predictions or treatment risks, where users must combine base rates with accuracy.
avoidWhen: Avoid when base rates are unknown or vary widely by user, since a single frequency tree will mislead; for classifier evaluation use confusion-matrix metrics.
whyLost: It is standard in medical risk communication research but rarely tested in product interfaces, where percentages and relative risks dominate.
whereToUse: Health and screening apps, fraud and security alerts, AI confidence displays, insurance and financial risk disclosures.
example: A fraud-alert screen states '95 percent accurate'. A study compares this with 'of 1,000 flagged payments, about 20 are fraud' and finds users stop cancelling legitimate payments at the same rate as genuine fraud.
sources: Heuristics and Biases: The Science of Decision Making (Dale, 2015)
Gigerenzer, G., & Hoffrage, U. (1995). How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats. Psychological Review, 102
A Practical Guide to Designing with Data (Suda, 2010)
reference: Gigerenzer, G., & Hoffrage, U. (1995). How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats. Psychological Review, 102, 684-704.

name: Naturalistic Decision Making / Recognition-Primed Decision Model
origin: Gary Klein, 1989-1999
summary: Describes how experts recognise situations and mentally simulate a single workable option, implying interfaces should support recognition rather than option comparison.
description: Klein's research with firefighters, commanders and nurses found that experts in real conditions rarely compare options analytically. They recognise a situation as an instance of a known pattern, which brings cues, goals, expectancies and a typical action, then mentally simulate that action; if it works they act, otherwise they modify or try the next. Decision quality comes from the richness of the pattern library. The treatise's transfer: expert users of complex tools pattern-match and act, so UX for experts should support recognition through consistent visual language, strong affordances and predictable behaviour, reducing the need for deliberation. Methodologically, NDM uses cognitive task analysis such as the Critical Decision Method to elicit cues and expectancies. Rated HIGH priority.
steps: Identify critical, time-pressured decisions made by expert users.
Conduct Critical Decision Method interviews on specific challenging incidents, probing cues, expectancies and options considered.
Extract the cues experts use to recognise situation types and their typical actions.
Build decision requirements tables linking decisions, cues, difficulties and errors.
Design displays that make recognition cues salient and support mental simulation.
Evaluate with scenario-based simulations under time pressure.
outputs: Decision requirements tables, cue inventories, recognition-supporting design requirements.
useWhen: Expert, time-pressured, high-stakes tools: clinical, security, emergency, trading, operations.
avoidWhen: Novice consumer choices where deliberate comparison is appropriate (for example insurance plan comparison).
whyLost: Lives in defence and human factors; consumer UX focused on novices and choice architecture.
whereToUse: SOC analyst consoles, ICU dashboards, dispatch, incident response tooling, air traffic control.
example: Critical Decision Method interviews with SOC analysts show they triage alerts by three recognisable cue patterns; the console redesign surfaces those cues in alert cards and cuts triage time by 30%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Klein G (1998) Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions
Klein GA, Calderwood R & MacGregor D (1989) Critical decision method for eliciting knowledge. IEEE SMC
Lipshitz R et al. (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making. J Behav Decis Making 14(5)
Klein, Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions (1998)
Klein, A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making (1993), in Klein et al. (eds.), Decision Making in Action
reference: Klein G (1998) Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions. MIT Press.

name: Navigation Design Patterns
origin: Christopher Alexander's pattern language (1977) applied to interfaces; Jenifer Tidwell, Designing Interfaces (2005)
summary: A repertoire of proven navigation structures, such as mega-menus, faceted navigation, breadcrumbs and progressive disclosure, chosen and evaluated against content and task needs.
description: Navigation design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring navigation problems, documented in pattern libraries such as Tidwell's Designing Interfaces. They include global and local navigation, mega-menus, faceted navigation and filters, breadcrumbs, tabs, hub-and-spoke, progressive disclosure and bottom navigation on mobile. Following Alexander's pattern language, each pattern describes a context, a problem, forces in tension and a solution. Using patterns well is a research question as much as a design one: the right choice depends on content volume and structure, users' tasks and mental models, and device constraints. Rigour comes from matching patterns to evidence about tasks and structure, testing them with tree tests, first-click tests and usability sessions, and measuring navigation success after launch.
steps: Clarify the content structure, scale and primary user tasks from IA research.
Identify candidate patterns that fit the structure and device constraints.
Document the forces each pattern balances, such as discoverability versus screen space.
Prototype the most promising patterns with realistic content.
Test with first-click tests, tree tests or usability sessions on key tasks.
Select the pattern, document it in the design system, and monitor navigation metrics after launch.
outputs: Selected navigation patterns with rationale, prototypes, test results and design system documentation.
useWhen: For complex websites, e-commerce catalogues and enterprise applications choosing or revising navigation structures.
avoidWhen: Avoid copying patterns without evidence that they fit your content and tasks; start with card sorting and tree testing. Not a research method on its own.
whyLost: Still in use: Pattern libraries enable consistent application; documented in Designing Interfaces.
whereToUse: Complex websites; e-commerce; enterprise applications.
example: An electronics retailer compares a mega-menu with faceted category landing pages for 3,000 products. First-click tests with 100 users show faceted landing pages lead to 23 percent more correct first clicks for comparison tasks.
reference: Tidwell, J., Brewer, C. & Valencia, A. (2020). Designing Interfaces (3rd ed.). O'Reilly.

name: Nearest-neighbour centrality and reciprocity diagnostic
origin: Amos Tversky and J. Wesley Hutchinson (1986)
summary: Before trusting an MDS map of similarity or card-sort data, computes how concentrated and how mutual nearest-neighbour links are; values above geometric bounds show the map misleads.
description: For each item, find its nearest neighbour in the raw data (highest similarity, most co-occurrence or most confusions). Centrality (C) is the mean of the squared counts of how often each item is someone's nearest neighbour; reciprocity (R) is the mean rank of each item in its own neighbour's ordering. Geometry constrains both: in two dimensions no more than five items can share a nearest neighbour, and for points sampled from a continuous space both statistics stay below about 2. Across 100 published data sets, perceptual stimuli mostly stayed within bounds, but conceptual sets including a category name or prototypical member reached centrality of 15.7 while their 2D maps showed about 1.8. Trees tracked the statistics; 3D maps did not. So high C and R in the data indicate hub structure that spatial maps cannot represent, and a low C to R ratio points instead to outliers.
steps: For each item, identify its nearest neighbour in the data, with a stated rule for ties.
Compute centrality C as the mean of squared nearest-neighbour counts across items, and reciprocity R as the mean rank of each item in its neighbour's similarity order.
Compute the same statistics from the distances in the fitted MDS map.
If the data exceed about 2 and the map does not, prefer a tree, cluster or hybrid representation over the spatial map.
Name the hub items and check whether they are category labels, umbrella features or prototypical members.
outputs: C and R for data and model, a list of hub items, and a recommendation on whether to use a spatial map, a tree or a hybrid.
useWhen: Card-sort, similarity-rating or confusion data are about to be summarised as a 2D map, especially when items mix general and specific concepts.
avoidWhen: Very small item sets (bounds are rough) or when a tree or cluster representation has already been chosen. Including a category label among items inflates centrality by design, so remove it or interpret accordingly.
whyLost: It was published in mathematical psychology as a model-selection diagnostic and never entered card-sorting or IA toolkits.
whereToUse: Information architecture, card-sort analysis, feature similarity studies, brand and concept maps, navigation label research.
example: A similarity study of 20 product features shows 'Dashboard' as the nearest neighbour of 9 others (C about 5). The 2D map spreads it out as one point among many, so the team switches to a tree and treats 'Dashboard' as a hub concept in the navigation.
reference: Tversky, A. and Hutchinson, J. W. (1986). Nearest neighbor analysis of psychological spaces. Psychological Review, 93(1), 3-22.

name: Negative Case Analysis
origin: Analytic induction (Florian Znaniecki, 1934; Alfred Lindesmith, 1947); formalised as a credibility technique by Lincoln and Guba, 1985
summary: Actively searches for cases that contradict emerging patterns and revises interpretations until they account for them, guarding qualitative analysis against confirmation bias.
description: Once a pattern appears in qualitative data, analysts tend to stop looking for evidence against it. Negative case analysis reverses this: every emerging claim is treated as a hypothesis, and the analyst deliberately searches for participants, episodes or data points that do not fit. Each negative case is then examined. It may require revising the claim, narrowing its scope, adding a condition, or identifying a separate pattern. Rooted in analytic induction, the technique aims for interpretations that account for all cases or explain exceptions explicitly. It is a core credibility strategy in Lincoln and Guba's framework. Its rigour comes from documenting the search, the cases found and the revisions made, rather than mentioning exceptions in passing.
steps: State each emerging finding as an explicit, testable claim with its intended scope.
Systematically search the full dataset for disconfirming evidence, including participants who behaved differently, contradictory statements and unexpected outcomes.
If needed, recruit additional participants likely to contradict the claim, such as power users, churned users or a different segment.
Examine each negative case to determine whether it reflects data error, a different condition, or a genuine limit to the claim.
Revise the claim by narrowing scope, adding conditions or creating a separate finding, and recheck against all data.
Report negative cases and the resulting revisions alongside each finding.
outputs: Explicit claims, a log of negative cases found and examined, revised findings with conditions and scope, and reported exceptions.
useWhen: Any qualitative synthesis where findings will drive decisions, especially when a pattern emerged quickly, the team has a preferred hypothesis, or stakeholders will challenge the findings.
avoidWhen: It should rarely be skipped. For quantitative data, use outlier analysis and robustness checks instead.
whyLost: Confirmation bias; researchers stop when the pattern appears
whereToUse: Interview synthesis, usability findings, persona development, research repositories, and validating AI-generated summaries that tend to over-generalise.
example: A team concludes users abandon a savings app because of fees. A search finds 4 of 14 churned users never encountered fees; their accounts reveal goal completion as a second churn path, leading to a 'next goal' feature.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 27
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Analysing and Presenting Qualitative Data (Burnard et al., 2008)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Negative Case Analysis and Rival Explanations
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985 (Naturalistic Inquiry); rival explanations from Robert Yin's case study method
summary: Actively searching for data that contradict an emerging explanation and testing it against rival explanations, the main safeguard against confirmation bias in qualitative work.
description: Qualitative analysts naturally notice what fits their developing story. Negative case analysis reverses this: after each analytic pass the researcher states the working explanation, then searches for incidents that contradict it, and decides whether to refine the explanation with specified conditions, revise it fundamentally, or collect more data. Rival explanation testing generates at least two alternative accounts for each major finding and compares how well each accounts for all the data, including the anomalies. Both are reported openly; a study claiming no negative cases signals that the search was not conducted. The technique converts qualitative interpretation into something closer to falsification and is one of Lincoln and Guba's credibility techniques.
steps: After every axial coding session: List your current working theory. Now actively search your data for incidents that contradict it. These are negative cases — data points that do not fit your emerging explanation.

For each negative case: Ask — does this require me to (a) refine my theory to account for this as an exception with specifiable conditions, (b) revise my theory fundamentally, or (c) collect more data in this domain (theoretical sampling)?

Rival explanations: For each major finding, generate at least 2 alternative explanations that would also fit the data. Systematically compare your preferred explanation against each rival. Which one better accounts for all the data, including negative cases?
Document in findings: Report your negative cases and how you handled them. A study that reports zero negative cases is not rigorous — it means you stopped looking when you found confirmation.
outputs: A documented list of negative cases and how each was handled, a rival-explanations table per finding, and a refined explanation with scope conditions.
useWhen: Before presenting any qualitative finding that will drive a significant decision, when the team has a favoured hypothesis, or when findings look suspiciously clean.
avoidWhen: Purely descriptive inventories (feature request lists) where no explanatory claim is made; there, focus on coverage instead.
whyLost: Stakeholder pressure for confident, tidy narratives and the absence of review culture in industry mean disconfirming evidence is rarely sought or reported.
whereToUse: Strategy research, pricing and adoption studies, AI product evaluations where teams are invested in a hypothesis, and research review or critique sessions.
example: A team believes users abandon a meal-kit subscription because of price. Searching for negative cases reveals high-income churners who cite menu fatigue; testing rivals shows that variety, not price, explains most cancellations.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Negative Control Analysis
origin: Marc Lipsitch, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen and Ted Cohen (2010); placebo tests in econometrics
summary: Tests an analysis on an outcome or exposure that should show no effect; any 'effect' found reveals confounding or bias in the method.
description: A negative control outcome is one that cannot plausibly be affected by the treatment but shares the same confounders; a negative control exposure is one that cannot affect the outcome but shares confounding with the real exposure. If the analysis finds an effect on a negative control, the method is biased. Examples in UX: a new search feature should not change the rate of password resets; users exposed to a campaign last month should not show effects before it started. Negative controls are cheap, powerful falsification checks for observational analyses and also for A/B tests with suspected sample ratio mismatch or instrumentation issues.
steps: Identify the main causal analysis and its likely sources of bias (self-selection, seasonality, instrumentation).
Choose negative control outcomes affected by the same biases but not by the treatment.
Choose negative control exposures or placebo times (e.g. a fake launch date) where appropriate.
Run the identical analysis pipeline on the negative controls.
Interpret non-null results as evidence of bias and adjust or abandon the method.
Report negative control results alongside main estimates.
outputs: Negative control estimates that validate or challenge the causal analysis.
useWhen: Any observational or quasi-experimental claim, and as a check on experiment instrumentation.
avoidWhen: When no plausible negative control exists; use sensitivity analysis instead.
whyLost: It is standard practice in pharmacoepidemiology but almost unknown in product analytics.
whereToUse: Feature adoption studies, campaign evaluations, health app outcome claims, before-after analyses.
example: Users who enabled AI summaries appear to churn 30% less. A negative control outcome, churn in the month before enabling, shows a similar 'effect', revealing selection bias.
sources: Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen & Cohen, Negative controls: a tool for detecting confounding and bias in observational studies (2010), Epidemiology
Arnold et al., Negative control outcomes: a tool to detect bias (2016), International Journal of Epidemiology
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Lipsitch, M., Tchetgen Tchetgen, E., & Cohen, T. (2010). Epidemiology, 21(3), 383-388.

name: Nested and Multilevel Sampling
origin: Multilevel theory in organisational research (Klein & Kozlowski, 2000); nested sampling designs in mixed methods (Onwuegbuzie & Collins, 2007)
summary: Sampling individuals within teams, departments and organisations, and collecting data at each level, so organisational context is analysed rather than ignored.
description: In organisational settings, individuals' experiences are shaped by the team, department and company they belong to. Sampling only individuals, often one or two per company, confounds personal and contextual effects. Nested sampling maps the hierarchy (organisation, unit, team, individual), selects units at each level, and samples several individuals within each so that within-unit and between-unit variation can be compared. Organisation-level data such as policies, tools, size and structure are collected alongside interviews. Analysis treats cross-level relationships as findings: where organisational logics conflict with individual practice, or how team norms change the same tool's use. Quantitative variants support multilevel models.
steps: Map the levels: Organisation → department → team → individual. Each level is a potential unit of analysis and source of variation.
Sample at each level: Do not sample only individuals and ignore the organisational context. The team and organisation within which individuals are nested shape their experience.
Interlevel data collection: When selecting an individual, also collect organisational-level data providing context.
Interlevel analysis: Treat interlevel relationships as data. How does organisational context shape individual experience? Where do individual and organisational logics conflict?
outputs: A multilevel sampling frame, paired individual and unit-level data, cross-level analysis, and explanations separating individual from contextual effects.
useWhen: B2B and enterprise research where adoption and experience depend on team or organisational context, such as rollouts or admin-user dynamics.
avoidWhen: Consumer products with independent individual users; use purposive or maximum variation sampling.
whyLost: Recruiting several people per customer account is hard and slow, so B2B studies sample individuals across many accounts and lose context.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS adoption, healthcare systems across hospitals, education platforms across schools, and internal tool research.
example: Studying a CRM rollout, researchers sample three companies, two sales teams in each and four reps per team. Differences in use are explained by team-level quota policies rather than individual skill.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Multilevel Theory, Research, and Methods in Organizations (Klein & Kozlowski)
Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Klein, K. J. & Kozlowski, S. W. J. (Eds.) (2000). Multilevel Theory, Research, and Methods in Organizations. Jossey-Bass.

name: Net Promoter Score
origin: Fred Reichheld, Bain & Company and Satmetrix, 2003
summary: A single 0-10 likelihood-to-recommend question; promoters (9-10) minus detractors (0-6) gives a loyalty score from -100 to +100.
description: NPS asks 'How likely are you to recommend [product] to a friend or colleague?' on an 11-point scale. Respondents scoring 9-10 are promoters, 7-8 passives and 0-6 detractors; NPS equals the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors. Reichheld claimed it predicted growth better than other measures, a claim later research has disputed. Its strengths are simplicity, executive familiarity and benchmarking. Its weaknesses are statistical: collapsing an 11-point scale into three categories discards information and increases variance, so margins of error are wide unless samples are large. Rigour comes from consistent timing and sampling, reporting confidence intervals, always asking a follow-up open question for reasons, analysing the full distribution or mean, and not treating NPS as a measure of usability.
steps: Define the population and trigger (relationship survey at a fixed interval, or transactional after an event).
Ask the standard question with the 0-10 scale and an open follow-up asking for the main reason.
Sample randomly and collect enough responses; a margin of error of ±5 points typically needs several hundred responses.
Calculate NPS with confidence intervals and also report the mean and distribution.
Code open-ended reasons thematically or with text analytics, split by promoters and detractors.
Track over time and segment, and connect drivers to product changes.
outputs: NPS with confidence intervals, response distribution, coded reasons by group, trend and segment reports.
useWhen: Relationship loyalty tracking, executive reporting and benchmarking against industry figures.
avoidWhen: Measuring usability or task experience (use SUS, UMUX-Lite or task metrics), products users cannot recommend (e.g. internal tools), or small samples. Its cut-offs are arbitrary, 7 and 8 responses are discarded, the difference score amplifies noise, scale use varies across cultures and the evidence for its link to growth is contested; it correlates highly with plain satisfaction, which is often the better measure.
whyLost: Still in use: Executive-friendly simplicity; enables benchmarking; but over-relied upon as sole UX metric.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction tracking; executive reporting; loyalty measurement.
example: A B2B payroll provider tracked NPS quarterly with 900 responses. Coding detractor comments showed most cited payment run errors, not the interface, redirecting investment to reliability engineering.
sources: The One Number You Need to Grow (Fred Reichheld)
Chapman, C. & Rodden, K., Quantitative User Experience Research (Apress, 2023)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
reference: Reichheld, F. F. (2003). The one number you need to grow. Harvard Business Review, 81(12), 46-54.

name: Netnography
origin: Robert V. Kozinets, late 1990s; books 2010 and 2020
summary: Adapts ethnography to online communities, combining archived data, real-time observation and interaction to understand digital cultures, norms and identities.
description: Netnography (Robert Kozinets, 2010/2020) is an adaptation of ethnographic methods for studying online communities and digital culture. It treats online communities as real social communities deserving the same ethnographic attention as physical communities — with specific adaptations for the textual, asynchronous, and often pseudonymous nature of online interaction. In UX research, netnography is appropriate for understanding how user communities form around products, how users collectively develop workarounds, how opinions about product changes form and spread, and what social norms govern discussion in product communities.
steps: Site identification and access: Identify the online communities relevant to your research question. Determine access type: full member (active participant), lurker (observer only), or archival (using public historical data). Declare which you will use.
Cultural entrée: Observe the community before posting or engaging. Understand the community's norms, vocabulary, hierarchies, and conventions. What counts as appropriate behaviour here?
Data collection: Collect: archived posts and discussions, real-time observation notes, interviews with community members (with consent), your own participation reflections.

Ethical netnography: Public ≠ consented. Just because content is publicly accessible does not mean its creators expected or consented to it being used in research. Apply the Public Benefit / No Harm test rigorously. Pseudonymise all identifiers.
Analysis: Apply ethnographic analysis — cultural themes, social norms, identity performance, meaning-making — to the digital data.
outputs: A documented site and data set, immersion journal, cultural themes, community norms and identities, and implications for community-centred products.
useWhen: Users form communities online around your product or domain (gaming, crypto, health conditions, creators, open source) and you need cultural understanding rather than complaint counts.
avoidWhen: You need representative population data, or the community is private or vulnerable and consent is impractical; use interviews with consent. For simple review mining, use Social Media and Digital Trace Data Analysis.
whyLost: Marketing adopted 'social listening' dashboards, which reduce communities to sentiment counts and drop the ethnographic immersion and ethics that netnography requires.
whereToUse: Gaming and creator platforms, patient communities, crypto and fintech communities, open-source products, and community-led growth.
example: A team researching a fitness platform spends 8 weeks in its subreddit and Discord. Netnography reveals 'streak shame' rituals, users publicly confessing breaks, which inspires a forgiving streak feature and community celebrations of returns.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Kozinets, R. V. (2020). Netnography: The Essential Guide to Qualitative Social Media Research (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Network Analysis
origin: Jacob Moreno, 1934 (sociometry); formalised by Wasserman and Faust, 1994
summary: Maps and measures relationships among users, content or features as a network, revealing communities, influencers, bridges and structural dependencies.
description: Network analysis represents entities as nodes and relationships as edges, then computes structural properties. Social network analysis, from Moreno's sociograms onward, measures centrality (who is most connected or most between), clustering, communities and structural holes. In UX contexts networks can be built from user interactions (follows, messages, collaboration), content links or co-usage of features. The analysis shows how communities form, who brokers information, which features are used together, and how changes might ripple through. Rigour comes from defining nodes and edges precisely, choosing appropriate thresholds and time windows, using validated community detection algorithms, checking robustness to parameter choices, and combining structure with qualitative understanding of what relationships mean. Ethical handling of relational data is essential because it reveals information about people who did not consent individually.
steps: Define nodes and edges precisely (e.g. users as nodes, collaboration on a document as edges) and the time window.
Extract relational data from logs or surveys, applying privacy safeguards.
Compute network metrics: degree, betweenness, clustering and density.
Detect communities with a validated algorithm (e.g. Louvain) and test robustness to parameters.
Interpret structures with qualitative research into what relationships mean.
Use findings to design features (e.g. supporting bridges) and simulate effects of changes.
outputs: Network maps, centrality and community metrics, identified brokers and isolated groups, design implications.
useWhen: Social and collaborative products, community platforms, enterprise adoption analysis and feature co-usage studies.
avoidWhen: Products without meaningful relationships between users or items, or where relational data cannot be ethically obtained.
whyLost: Latent: Used in social media research; growing in UX for community and platform design.
whereToUse: Social feature design; content recommendation; community product research.
example: An enterprise collaboration tool mapped co-editing networks across a client's departments. Finance was isolated with one bridging user; designing cross-team templates and onboarding that bridge increased cross-department collaboration.
sources: Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications (Wasserman & Faust)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications. Cambridge University Press.

name: Network exposure threshold analysis
aka: Network exposure and individual threshold analysis
origin: Granovetter (1978) threshold models; Markus (1987) critical mass; Valente (1995) network thresholds
summary: Tracks, for each person, the share of their network that has already adopted, and takes its value at the moment they adopt as their personal threshold.
description: A threshold is the number or share of others who must adopt before an individual does; critical mass is its system-level counterpart. Valente's procedure needs network ties and adoption dates for every member of a bounded system. For each person and period, exposure is the percentage of network partners who have adopted; exposure at the person's own adoption is their threshold. People are classified by innovativeness relative to the whole system and relative to their own network, which separates low-threshold early adopters from people who adopt late simply because their contacts did. Threshold lag (exposed but not yet adopting) is distinguished from lack of exposure. The 'turbocharger' effect is the extra variance in adoption timing explained by adding network variables to individual ones. Few data sets have both full networks and dates, and innovations whose use is invisible to others weaken threshold effects.
steps: Define a bounded system (a team, organisation or workspace) and collect its ties and each member's adoption date.
For each person and period, compute exposure as the percentage of their network partners who have adopted.
Record exposure at the period of adoption as the person's threshold.
Classify each person's innovativeness relative to the system and relative to their own network.
Identify people with threshold lag (highly exposed non-adopters) and unexposed non-adopters as separate groups.
Test the distribution of thresholds and estimate how much variance in adoption timing network variables add beyond individual ones.
outputs: Individual thresholds, exposure curves over time, groups of lagging and unexposed non-adopters, and a turbocharger estimate.
useWhen: Collaboration or communication products where adoption spreads through visible use by colleagues, and the team can observe who works with whom and when each person started.
avoidWhen: Products whose use is invisible to others, systems without bounded networks, or when only aggregate adoption curves exist (use diffusion curve models).
whyLost: It is a diffusion-research method that requires complete network and timing data, which rarely existed outside a few classic studies; product analytics now holds such data but the method has not crossed over.
whereToUse: Workspace and collaboration SaaS, enterprise rollouts, multiplayer and social features, internal tool adoption, messaging products.
example: A collaboration tool computes, for each user in 300 company workspaces, the share of their frequent collaborators already using a new shared-board feature. Median threshold is 40%; a group with 80% exposure who have not adopted becomes the target for interviews about blockers.
reference: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). New York: Free Press, ch. 8; Valente, T. W. (1995). Network Models of the Diffusion of Innovations. Cresskill, NJ: Hampton Press.

name: Network Super-Spreader Analysis of Design Patterns
origin: Network epidemic modelling (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2001); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Models pattern spread over the network of platforms, design systems and publications to identify super-spreader nodes where intervention has outsized effect.
description: Network epidemiology recognises that transmission follows contact networks and that highly connected nodes, super-spreaders, drive epidemics disproportionately. The treatise identifies UX super-spreaders: large platforms, design system providers and influential design thought-leaders and publications. When a major design system adopts a flawed pattern, it transmits it to all products built on it simultaneously; when a widely read publication promotes a pattern as best practice, adoption accelerates. Network models identify these nodes and prioritise them as intervention targets: regulatory pressure on platforms, engagement with design system maintainers and attention to influential publications have greater population impact than equivalent effort on individual products.
steps: Construct the network of influence: products, design systems, platforms, publications and links (dependencies, citations, copying).
Compute centrality measures (degree, betweenness, eigenvector) and identify hubs.
Overlay pattern adoption timing to see spread paths.
Simulate spread and targeted interventions on high-centrality nodes.
Prioritise engagement with super-spreader nodes.
Monitor downstream adoption after intervention.
outputs: Influence network, super-spreader list, simulated intervention impact.
useWhen: Planning ecosystem-level interventions against harmful patterns or to spread good ones.
avoidWhen: When network data cannot be assembled credibly.
whyLost: Network epidemiology never applied to design ecosystems.
whereToUse: Regulators, design-system governance, standards bodies, accessibility advocacy.
example: Mapping npm dependencies shows three UI kits underlie 60% of a sector's checkout pages; fixing a pre-ticked consent component in those kits removes the pattern from most of the sector.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Pastor-Satorras R & Vespignani A (2001) Epidemic spreading in scale-free networks. Phys Rev Lett 86
reference: Pastor-Satorras R & Vespignani A (2001) Epidemic spreading in scale-free networks. Physical Review Letters 86(14):3200-3203.

name: Neural frame audit
donor: Cognitive linguistics (frame semantics, conceptual metaphor theory)
origin: Charles Fillmore (frame semantics, 1976–1982) and George Lakoff (Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things, 1987; Don't Think of an Elephant, 2004); operationalised as a UX protocol in Gopinath's Methods Atlas
summary: Elicits free associations to a product name or key term, codes them into the conceptual frames they activate, and checks whether those frames support or undermine the intended meaning.
description: Frame semantics holds that every word evokes a structured scene, with roles, expectations and values, and that people reason within the frame a word activates rather than from its dictionary definition. A neural frame audit applies this to product language. Participants give rapid free associations to a product name, feature label or category term; associations are coded into frames (for example 'wallet' evoking loss, theft, pickpocketing, cash or carrying) and the roles and inferences each frame licenses are made explicit. The audit compares the frame users actually activate with the frame the product team intended. Rigour comes from timed elicitation that limits deliberate rationalisation, structured coding with a second coder, and sampling across the segments whose frames are likely to differ, such as rural and urban or first-time and experienced users.
steps: List the 3 to 10 load-bearing terms to audit: product name, category noun, primary actions and key metaphors (for example 'wallet', 'top up', 'credit').

Recruit 12 to 30 participants per segment whose frames may differ, and run a timed free-association task: show each term and collect the first 3 to 5 words or images within about 20 seconds, in the participant's own language.
Follow with a short laddering probe on the first association: 'What happens in that situation? Who is involved? What could go wrong?' to surface the frame's roles and expected events.
Code associations into candidate frames using a codebook developed on the first 20% of data; have a second coder code at least 25% and aim for Cohen's kappa of 0.70 or above before proceeding.
For each term, tabulate frame frequencies by segment and record the inferences each dominant frame licenses (for example 'wallet' implies money can be stolen or lost).

Compare dominant frames against the intended frame and flag terms where the intended frame is activated by fewer than about half of participants in any priority segment, or where a threat frame dominates.
Generate alternative terms, re-run the elicitation on them with fresh participants, and select terms whose dominant frame matches intent.
outputs: A frame inventory per term and segment, frequency tables of activated frames, a list of licensed inferences and risks, and recommended term replacements with comparative evidence.
useWhen: Naming a product or feature, entering a new culture or literacy context, or when adoption data suggests a label is creating distrust or the wrong mental model.
avoidWhen: The question is whether users can find or operate a labelled control (use tree testing or first-click testing), or the vocabulary is technical and fixed by regulation.
whyLost: Frame analysis lived in cognitive linguistics and political communication (for example the FrameWorks Institute), where it is rigorous, but UX naming work drifted to preference polls and brand workshops that ask which name users like rather than what scene it evokes.
whereToUse: Naming in financial inclusion and health products, AI feature naming, public-sector service labels, market entry localisation.
example: A payments team tested 'Digital Wallet' with first-time rural users in India. Dominant associations were theft, loss and 'phone gets stolen, money gone', a threat frame; 'Bank on phone' activated a safety and institution frame and was adopted for onboarding copy.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 19 — Neural Framing & the Architecture of Meaning
reference: Lakoff, G. (1987). Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things: What Categories Reveal about the Mind. University of Chicago Press; Fillmore, C. J. (1982). Frame Semantics. In Linguistics in the Morning Calm.

name: Neurophenomenology
aka: Neurophenomenology: pairing trained first-person reports with neural or physiological data
First-person and third-person bridging with an expert practitioner
origin: Francisco Varela (1996); standard example Lutz, Lachaux, Martinerie and Varela (2002)
summary: Pair trained, detailed first-person descriptions of an experience with time-locked brain or body data, using each to constrain interpretation of the other.
description: Neurophenomenology rejects treating either brain data or self-report as ground truth. Participants are trained to describe a specific kind of experience precisely, often with micro-phenomenological interviewing. They perform repeated trials while physiological data are recorded, and give a structured report after each trial. Trials are then grouped by experiential category derived from the reports, and the neural data are analysed by those groups; surprising physiological patterns in turn prompt further first-person inquiry. In the standard example, trials sorted by participants' reported readiness revealed distinct brain synchrony patterns that averaged analysis had hidden. A variant alternates scanning an expert practitioner with debriefs, re-instructs, rescans, and tests the resulting distinction in novices. Cautions: an instruction is not the same as performing it, small samples of trained observers limit generality, and physiological signals in applied settings are noisy.
steps: Train participants to describe the target experience precisely, for example with micro-phenomenological interviews.
Run repeated trials of a task while recording time-locked physiological data (EEG, skin conductance, eye tracking).
After each trial, collect a structured first-person report.
Derive experiential categories from the reports and group trials by them.
Analyse the physiological data by those groups, and use unexpected physiological patterns to prompt further first-person inquiry.
With expert participants, alternate recording and debriefing, re-instruct and re-record, then test the resulting distinction in novices.
Report both sides and how each constrained the other.
outputs: Experience-based categories of trials with matching physiological signatures, and refined descriptions of the experience.
useWhen: You pair biometrics with qualitative inquiry and need to explain variation in signals that averaged analyses hide, such as different kinds of 'confusion' or 'flow'.
avoidWhen: You cannot train participants or run many trials, or biometric data are not needed; use micro-phenomenological interviews or think-aloud alone.
whyLost: It is a demanding research programme in consciousness science and contemplative neuroscience, and UX biometrics rarely invest in trained first-person reports.
whereToUse: Flow and immersion in games, meditation and wellbeing apps, attention and interruption research, and validating affect-sensing models.
example: A meditation app team records EEG during guided sessions and collects micro-phenomenological reports after each. Sessions reported as 'sleepy calm' and 'alert calm' show distinct EEG patterns, so the app's feedback stops treating both as success.
sources: Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Varela, F. J. (1996). Neurophenomenology: A methodological remedy for the hard problem. Journal of Consciousness Studies, 3(4), 330-349; Lutz, A., Lachaux, J.-P., Martinerie, J., & Varela, F. J. (2002). Guiding the study of brain dynamics by using first-person data. PNAS, 99(3), 1586-1591.

name: NGOMSL
origin: David Kieras, 1988-1997
summary: Structured natural-language GOMS notation that predicts both execution time and learning time from the number and complexity of methods.
description: NGOMSL, listed in the treatise's glossary as the natural-language member of the GOMS family, writes methods as program-like statements ('Method for goal: delete file. Step 1. Accomplish goal: select file...'). Because each statement corresponds to a production rule in cognitive complexity theory, counting statements yields estimates of learning time, and counting executed statements plus operators yields execution time. This makes NGOMSL distinctive: it predicts how much there is to learn and how much transfer exists between consistent methods, quantifying the benefit of consistency. Its rigour comes from explicit, inspectable method descriptions that any analyst can audit, and from its grounding in Kieras and Polson's cognitive complexity theory.
steps: List the user goals and top-level tasks to be modelled.
Write NGOMSL methods for each goal, step by step, down to primitive operators.
Identify shared submethods across tasks to quantify consistency and transfer.
Count new statements to estimate learning time (around 30 s per statement in classic estimates).
Estimate execution time from statement counts and operator times.
Compare alternative designs on learning and execution predictions.
outputs: Method listings, learning-time and execution-time predictions, consistency and transfer analysis.
useWhen: Evaluating consistency of a command set or design system, estimating training cost for enterprise software.
avoidWhen: Highly visual, exploratory or parallel tasks; use CPM-GOMS for parallelism or usability testing for exploration.
whyLost: GOMS family modelling faded as iterative testing became cheap and as interfaces became less procedural. NGOMSL's learning predictions were never taught widely.
whereToUse: Enterprise suites with training costs, design-system consistency audits, migration between product versions.
example: An ERP vendor writes NGOMSL methods for approving, rejecting and escalating purchase orders in two designs. The unified design shares 70% of statements and is predicted to cut training time by about a third.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kieras DE (1997) A guide to GOMS model usability evaluation using NGOMSL. In Handbook of HCI
Kieras, A Guide to GOMS Model Usability Evaluation using NGOMSL (1997), in Helander et al. (eds.), Handbook of Human-Computer Interaction
The GOMS Family of User Interface Analysis Techniques (John & Kieras, 1996)
GOMS Models: Simplified Cognitive Architectures (Kieras, n.d.)
reference: Kieras DE (1997) A guide to GOMS model usability evaluation using NGOMSL. In Helander M et al. (Eds) Handbook of Human-Computer Interaction. Elsevier.

name: Niche Construction and Work Artifact Analysis
donor: Evolutionary biology (niche construction) and cognitive anthropology
origin: Niche construction theory (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman, 2003); cognitive niche ideas from Andy Clark; artefact models from Contextual Design
summary: Cataloguing and analysing the notes, spreadsheets and physical workarounds users create to repair systems, as precise evidence of unmet needs.
description: Niche construction refers to the way organisms modify their environment to make it more habitable. In UX research, users engage in cognitive niche construction when they modify their digital or physical environment to compensate for interface failures — creating post-it notes, custom spreadsheets, printed cheat sheets, physical labels, workaround procedures. These artifacts are not noise — they are the most precise data you can collect about unmet needs. Every workaround specifies exactly what the system fails to do.
steps: During CI or observation: Actively look for artifacts. Scan the physical environment: post-it notes on screens, stickers on hardware, printed documents with annotations, personal notebooks, custom labels. Scan the digital environment: desktop files, browser bookmarks, copy-paste documents, personal databases.

Photograph and catalog every artifact: With participant permission, photograph all artifacts. Note: location (where is it?), proximity (is it always within reach?), frequency of use (evidence of wear and handling).

Analyse each artifact for three things: (1) What information does it contain that the system fails to surface? (Gap in information provision.) (2) What action does it support that the system fails to afford? (Gap in affordance.) (3) What mental model does its structure reveal? (Gap in conceptual alignment.)

Ask about each artifact: "Tell me about this — what is it for?" "When do you use it?" "How long have you had it?" "What would happen if you didn't have it?" These questions reveal the system failure the artifact compensates for.
outputs: A photographed artefact catalogue, analysis of information, affordance and mental model gaps per artefact, and derived requirements.
useWhen: Field studies of established workflows where users have adapted their environment, especially legacy systems and complex professional work.
avoidWhen: New-to-world products with no existing practice, or fully digital consumer flows with little room for user-created artefacts; use diaries or generative sessions.
whyLost: Artefact collection is mentioned in contextual inquiry, but systematic coding of artefacts is usually skipped in favour of interview quotes.
whereToUse: Healthcare, logistics, manufacturing, finance operations, small business tools and any legacy system replacement project.
example: Visiting hospital wards, researchers photograph handwritten bed-status boards beside the electronic system. Analysing the boards reveals that nurses track 'expected discharge time', a field the system lacks.
sources: Niche Construction: The Neglected Process in Evolution (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Odling-Smee, F. J., Laland, K. N. & Feldman, M. W. (2003). Niche Construction. Princeton University Press.

name: Nine-Tier Metric Statement (LAVA Metric Grammar)
origin: John Armitage, SAP Project LAVA, 2010-2014
summary: A template that builds a quantitative finding up from subject and value through time, change, goal assessment, cause, forecast and recommended action.
description: Armitage treats a metric as a grammatical statement whose elements stack in nine tiers, in the order quantitative systems are typically built. Entity names the subject (dimension and member); Value adds the measure and number, the entity-measure-value triad underlying all business intelligence; Time fixes the point; Change compares with another point; Period aggregates over a span with change from the comparison period; Assessment compares with plan or goal, as a flag or scaled gap; Interpretation adds a peer comparison or root cause; Prediction adds a forecast with explicit confidence; Action proposes a response with a link to carry it out. Higher tiers can be shown without lower ones, and the full chain can be read out as plain sentences for text or voice delivery. It makes explicit what a reader needs to act on a number.
steps: Name the entity: dimension and member, with hierarchy or extra dimensions if needed.
Attach the measure and its value, and fix the time point.
Add change against a reference point and express the value over a period with change from the comparison period.
Assess against plan or goal, as a binary flag or a scaled gap.
Add interpretation: comparison with peers or a known, evidenced cause.
Add a prediction with explicit confidence, then propose an action with a link to where it can be taken.
Render the chain as plain sentences for reports, alerts or voice, omitting tiers the audience does not need.
outputs: Metric statements, or their sentence renderings, that carry context, judgement, cause, forecast and recommendation.
useWhen: Designing dashboards, KPI reports, automated insight alerts or research readouts where readers must act on numbers.
avoidWhen: When causes and forecasts lack evidence, since the template makes speculation look authoritative. Recommendations can seem obvious or condescending in well-understood contexts, and long chains are cumbersome to read linearly.
whyLost: It came from an internal SAP design programme and a self-published book, so it never entered UX or analytics curricula.
whereToUse: Analytics products, executive dashboards, AI-generated insight summaries, UX research metric reporting.
example: A UX team rewrites a dashboard tile as: 'Checkout completion for mobile in May was 61%, up 3 points on April but 4 under goal; likely cause is the new address form; 70% chance June stays below goal; review form errors.'
reference: Armitage, J. (2015). Bringing Numbers to Life: LAVA and Design-Led Innovation in Visual Analytics. Self-published, pp. 225-232.

name: Nominal Group Technique
origin: Andre Delbecq and Andrew Van de Ven, 1968 to 1971
summary: A structured group process of silent generation, round-robin sharing, clarification and independent voting that prevents dominant voices from shaping collective judgement.
description: Unstructured group discussions are distorted by status, confidence and talkativeness. The Nominal Group Technique (Delbecq and Van de Ven) structures a meeting so that individuals generate ideas silently and independently first, typically for 10 to 15 minutes. Ideas are then shared one at a time in round-robin order and recorded verbatim without debate, discussed only to clarify meaning, and ranked or rated privately by each participant. Votes are aggregated mathematically, and an optional second discussion and re-vote addresses items with divergent scores. The group is 'nominal' because members work individually within a group setting. Its rigour lies in separating generation from evaluation and replacing negotiation with independent, aggregated judgement.
steps: Silent idea generation: Participants work individually in silence for 10–15 minutes, writing responses on paper. No discussion.
Round-robin recording: Each participant shares one idea in turn. All ideas recorded visibly. No evaluation during this phase. Continue until all ideas are recorded.
Clarification discussion: The group discusses each idea for clarification only — questions of understanding are answered; advocacy is not permitted.
Individual ranking/rating: Each participant independently ranks or rates each idea. Votes are tallied.
Discussion and re-vote (optional): Discuss ideas with significantly divergent vote patterns. Allow final re-vote after discussion.
outputs: A complete idea list, aggregated rankings or ratings, a prioritised shortlist, and a record of where opinion diverged.
useWhen: You need to generate and prioritise requirements, risks, problems or research questions with a team or stakeholder group of about 5 to 12 people, especially where hierarchy could bias the outcome.
avoidWhen: You want free-flowing exploration, relationship building or co-design; use a facilitated workshop. For dispersed experts or anonymous judgement over time, use the Delphi Method.
whyLost: Design-thinking workshops popularised dot-voting and brainstorming, which kept the sticky notes but lost NGT's silent generation, round-robin recording and private ranking.
whereToUse: Stakeholder prioritisation, research planning, clinical and service design with mixed-status teams, retrospectives, and patient or user advisory panels.
example: A hospital digital team runs NGT with nurses, doctors and administrators to prioritise pain points in shift handover software. Silent generation surfaces 41 issues; private ranking puts a nurse-raised medication-reconciliation issue first, which open discussion had previously overlooked.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
100 Things Every Presenter Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2012)
reference: Delbecq, A. L., Van de Ven, A. H. & Gustafson, D. H. (1975). Group Techniques for Program Planning. Scott, Foresman.

name: Non-Criterion Task Flagging and Source-of-Error Analysis
origin: Jeffrey Rubin and Dana Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing (1994; 2nd ed. 2008)
summary: Flag test tasks that fall below a preset success criterion, then attribute every observed error to the product component or components responsible, with primary and secondary causes.
description: Rubin and Chisnell describe this as the move from task orientation to product orientation in analysing a usability test. Each task has a success criterion and time benchmark set in advance: about 70 percent of participants for a typical early assessment test, rising towards 95 percent across iterations. Tasks below criterion are flagged. Errors are defined beforehand as divergences from expected behaviour, and then, for every error by every participant, the analyst identifies the responsible component or combination of components, separating primary from secondary culprits. Notes, logs, recordings, other observers and participant backgrounds are used for hard cases, ideally in a workshop with observers. Fixes are deliberately withheld until sources are known. The rigour lies in exhaustive, per-error attribution rather than a list of memorable problems, which explains why tasks fail and where differences between compared versions come from.
steps: Before testing, set a success criterion and a time benchmark for each task (about 70 percent completion for an early assessment test, higher for later iterations).
Define what counts as an error, using pilot sessions if needed; for summative tests fix the definitions before the study.
After summarising performance, flag every task whose completion falls below its criterion.
For each error by each participant on flagged tasks, identify the responsible component or combination, noting primary and secondary culprits.
Resolve hard cases by reviewing recordings, logs, observer notes and the participant's background.
Run the attribution as a workshop with observers where possible, and do not propose fixes until sources are identified.
Report a three-column table of task, source of error and recommendation, and feed it into criticality ranking.
outputs: Flagged task list; component-level problem list with primary and secondary causes; task / source of error / recommendation table; input to severity ranking.
useWhen: Analysing moderated usability tests, especially comparative or iterative ones, when you must explain why tasks failed and which components to change rather than just report completion rates.
avoidWhen: It is labour-intensive and multi-component problems are hard to attribute; for quick formative rounds a Usability Issue Log and Issue-Based Metrics or a Usability Test Debrief Meeting may be enough. Set the criterion to suit the test stage.
whyLost: Success thresholds and issue lists survive, but the exhaustive per-error attribution to components has mostly been replaced by quick affinity sorting of observed issues.
whereToUse: Regulated or high-stakes products (medical devices, banking), comparative tests of two designs, and benchmark programmes where traceable reasoning from failure to component matters.
