example: Booking a hotel with reward points fails for most participants. Attribution shows three sources: the site never says users must sign in first, the points widget sits unnoticed at the lower right, and 'Customer Service' is read as phone or chat rather than FAQs.
reference: Rubin, J. and Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of Usability Testing: How to Plan, Design, and Conduct Effective Tests (2nd ed.). Indianapolis, IN: Wiley, pp. 258-261, 281-282.

name: Non-Evaluative Listening and the Pause Rule
origin: Indi Young's non-evaluative listening stance (Practical Empathy, 2015); the timed pause rule and interruption count are the atlas's own operationalisation and do not appear in Young's book.
summary: An interviewing discipline of listening to understand rather than react, using deliberate silence and non-evaluative reflection to surface participants' deeper reasoning.
description: Indi Young distinguishes listening to react (preparing a response while the other person speaks) from listening to think (fully receiving what is said before forming any response). Most researchers, even experienced ones, listen to react and so take in only the part of an answer that fits their existing model. Young's non-evaluative stance asks the listener to notice their own emotional reactions, set aside judgement by imagining a situation in which the speaker's view makes sense, and return to curiosity. The atlas adds a practical pause rule: when the participant stops speaking, wait two to three seconds before responding, which gives the participant room to elaborate, correct themselves or reveal the thought behind the answer.
steps: Before the session, write your research questions on a card and keep it face down once the session begins: the questions mark the territory, not a script, so follow the participant into their own territory.
When the participant finishes speaking, wait about two seconds before responding and resist the impulse to fill the silence; participants often fill it themselves with what matters most.
Notice your own emotional reactions, assumptions and classifications as they arise; set them aside by imagining a situation in which the speaker's view makes sense, then return to curiosity.
Before asking the next question, reflect back what you heard ('It sounds like...') without evaluation or interpretation.
After the session, review the recording and mark every moment you spoke within one second of the participant finishing; aim for fewer than five such interruptions per hour.
outputs: Richer, less led transcripts; an interruption count per session as a quality metric; reflected summaries of participants' reasoning.
useWhen: Generative interviews about reasoning, motivation and inner thinking, and when coaching interviewers who talk too much or lead participants.
avoidWhen: Structured task-based sessions where tight time control matters (usability testing with fixed tasks); use a systematic probe schedule instead.
whyLost: Interview training in UX focuses on question lists and scripts, and the listening skill itself is rarely taught, practised or measured.
whereToUse: Generative discovery, mental model research, interviewer training programmes, and sensitive topics in health or personal finance.
example: An interviewer studying how freelancers set prices stops filling silences. After a three-second pause, a participant adds that she under-prices out of fear of losing her only client, which becomes the central insight.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 32 — Advanced Elicitation — The Archaeology of the Interview
reference: Young, I. (2015). Practical Empathy: For Collaboration and Creativity in Your Work. Rosenfeld Media.

name: Non-Inferiority and Equivalence Trials for Design Changes
origin: Clinical trial methodology from the 1980s-1990s; ICH E9 and E10 guidelines (1998, 2000); CONSORT extension (Piaggio et al., 2006/2012)
summary: Tests whether a new design is not worse than the current one by more than a pre-specified margin, the right question for simplifications, migrations and cost-saving changes.
description: Many design changes aim not to improve a metric but to avoid harming it: a cheaper infrastructure, a simpler UI, an accessibility fix, removing a feature. Failing to find a significant difference in a standard A/B test does not prove no harm. Non-inferiority trials define a margin (the largest acceptable loss) in advance and test whether the confidence interval's lower bound lies above minus the margin. The margin must be justified clinically, or here, by business and user impact. Sample sizes are planned for this hypothesis. This brings honest inference to the many 'no significant difference, ship it' decisions in product teams.
steps: Specify the primary metric and justify the non-inferiority margin (e.g. no more than 0.5 percentage point loss in conversion).
Compute sample size for the non-inferiority hypothesis at the desired power.
Run the randomised test, using intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.
Compute the one-sided confidence interval (e.g. 97.5%) for the difference.
Conclude non-inferiority only if the lower bound exceeds minus the margin in both analyses.
Report the margin rationale and the CI, not just a p-value.
outputs: A justified margin, CI-based non-inferiority conclusion and transparent reporting.
useWhen: Shipping simplifications, migrations, accessibility changes, cost reductions or removals where harm must be ruled out.
avoidWhen: When you expect and need improvement; use a superiority test.
whyLost: Product experimentation platforms default to superiority tests, and teams misread non-significance as equivalence.
whereToUse: Platform migrations, design system rollouts, feature deprecations, AI model swaps to cheaper models.
example: Moving to a cheaper LLM for support replies, the team pre-specifies a margin of 1 point on resolution rate. The lower bound of the CI is -0.6, so non-inferiority is concluded and the change ships.
sources: Piaggio et al., Reporting of noninferiority and equivalence randomized trials: extension of the CONSORT 2010 statement (2012), JAMA
FDA, Non-Inferiority Clinical Trials to Establish Effectiveness: Guidance for Industry (2016)

name: Non-Negative Matrix Factorisation for Behavioural Analysis
aka: Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF) for Usage Archetypes
origin: Daniel Lee and Sebastian Seung, 1999 (Paatero and Tapper 1994 as positive matrix factorisation)
summary: Decomposes a users-by-features usage matrix into additive, non-negative archetypes so each user is described as a weighted mix of interpretable usage styles.
description: NMF factorises a non-negative data matrix into two non-negative matrices, producing parts-based, additive representations. Unlike PCA, factors have no negative loadings, so each is interpretable as a coherent pattern that adds to others. The treatise's transfer: apply to clickstream matrices where rows are users or sessions and columns are features, actions or screens. NMF yields K archetypes, each a distinct usage style, and users are described as weighted combinations rather than forced into exclusive clusters, which matches reality where one person is part 'reporter', part 'collaborator'. Choosing K uses reconstruction error, stability across runs and interpretability. Archetypes ground personas in behavioural data. Rated MEDIUM priority.
steps: Build a users-by-events matrix of counts or durations over a defined window, restricted to key events covering the most fundamental interactions (Pipedrive used 40 of several hundred).
Normalise (for example TF-IDF style or per-user scaling) to reduce dominance of heavy users.
Fit NMF for a range of K (for example 3-12) with multiple initialisations.
Choose K using reconstruction error, stability and interpretability.

Assign each user to the archetype with the highest weight in their row of W, name each archetype from the top-ranked events in its row of H, and validate with qualitative interviews of high-weight users.
Track archetype weights over time and use them for segmentation and personas.
outputs: Archetype definitions, per-user archetype weights, archetype trends.
useWhen: Large behavioural logs where overlapping usage styles need discovery, persona grounding.
avoidWhen: Small samples, or when exclusive segments are operationally required.
whyLost: Lives in data science; UX segmentation relies on surveys or k-means clusters that force exclusive membership.
whereToUse: SaaS feature adoption, creative tools, streaming, banking app usage, developer platforms.
example: NMF on a project-management tool's logs finds five archetypes; 'planner' weight predicts seat expansion, so the onboarding emphasises planning features for new admins.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lee DD & Seung HS (1999) Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization. Nature 401:788-791
Paatero P & Tapper U (1994) Positive matrix factorization. Environmetrics
Lee & Seung, Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization (1999), Nature
Brunet et al., Metagenes and molecular pattern discovery using matrix factorization (2004), PNAS
Lenk, K. (2022) Identifying behavioral personas with cluster analysis. Pipedrive R&D Blog
Identifying Behavioral Personas with Cluster Analysis (Lenk, 2022)
Personas Changing Over Time (Jung et al., 2019)
Explaining Data-Driven Personas to End Users (Jung et al., 2020)
reference: Lee DD & Seung HS (1999) Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization. Nature 401:788-791.

name: Non-Probability Sample Adjustment (Sample Matching and Propensity Weighting)
origin: Rivers (2007) sample matching; Schonlau and colleagues on propensity adjustment with reference surveys
summary: Reducing and correcting selection bias in opt-in samples through recruitment design, sample matching and propensity weighting against a small probability reference survey.
description: Most UX surveys use opt-in samples: panels, intercepts, social recruitment. This method treats their selection bias as something to design against and adjust for. At recruitment, diverse channels and quotas reduce bias; sample matching draws a target sample from a frame and selects the closest panel member for each target case. After fieldwork, post-stratification, raking or calibration align known margins. The stronger correction runs a small probability reference survey in the same mode with shared questions, fits a logistic model of membership (opt-in versus reference) and weights opt-in cases by inverse propensity. Results are then validated against external benchmarks and reported as indications rather than population estimates. The key limitation is explicit: adjustment removes only the bias explained by the model variables, and weighting increases variance.
steps: Spread recruitment across several channels and set quotas on variables known to relate to the outcomes.
Optionally draw a target sample from a frame and match each target case to the closest panel member on shared covariates.
After fieldwork, weight to known margins by post-stratification, raking or calibration.
Run a small probability reference survey in the same mode, with the covariates and some outcome questions in common.
Fit a logistic model of membership (opt-in versus reference) and weight opt-in cases by inverse propensity, trimming extreme weights.
Validate adjusted estimates against external benchmarks and report them as indications with the basis of adjustment stated.
outputs: Adjusted estimates, the weighting model and a statement of the assumptions and residual bias risk.
useWhen: Using online panels or in-product opt-in surveys to estimate prevalence or sizes (how many users want X, share of a market) where decisions depend on the level, not just comparisons.
avoidWhen: Qualitative or purely comparative studies where population levels are not claimed. For causal comparison of groups use propensity score matching in its causal sense; for probability samples ordinary survey weighting suffices.
whyLost: UX reporting often quietly treats panel results as population figures; adjustment requires a reference survey and statistical skill that research teams seldom budget for.
whereToUse: Market sizing with panel data, opt-in feedback programmes, research panels recruited from engaged users, AI product adoption estimates from self-selected users.
example: A note-taking app estimates how many users would pay for an AI tier from an in-app opt-in survey dominated by power users. A 400-person probability sample drawn from the user database with the same covariates feeds a propensity model, and the adjusted willingness-to-pay share drops from 31% to 18%.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Vehovar, V., Toepoel, V. and Steinmetz, S. (2016). Non-probability sampling. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 329-345). London: SAGE.

name: Non-Response Bias Assessment
origin: Long-standing survey practice; described by Gratton and Jones (2010) as profiling the achieved sample, comparing it with population figures and comparing follow-up respondents with original respondents.
summary: Checking whether the people who answered a survey differ from those who did not, before generalising the results.
description: Almost no survey gets answers from everyone it samples. People lack time, motivation or the right knowledge, fill it in wrongly or cannot be reached, so the achieved sample can differ from the population in ways that skew results. Gratton and Jones describe three checks. First, profile the achieved sample on age, gender and other relevant variables, often graphically, to spot unusual patterns. Second, where population figures exist, compare the respondents against them; if one group is under-represented the sample is biased in that respect. Third, send a follow-up (letter or email with another copy of the questionnaire and a fresh cut-off date, worded as a reminder rather than a repeat of the original appeal, and without coercion) and compare those who respond late with the original respondents, treating late responders as a proxy for non-responders. In UX, product data makes this unusually powerful: the user database records plan, tenure, activity level and platform for every sampled person, so respondents can be compared with non-respondents directly, and survey results can be weighted or caveated when the heaviest users are over-represented.
steps: Before fielding, record the characteristics of everyone in the issued sample (from the sampling frame or product data).
After the main cut-off, compare respondents with the issued sample or population on those characteristics, using tables or charts.
Send a follow-up reminder to non-respondents with a new copy or link and a fresh deadline, framed as a reminder and without pressure.
Compare late (follow-up) respondents with early respondents on key answers and characteristics.
Decide whether differences matter for the conclusions; weight the data, restrict claims to the groups that responded, or caveat the findings.
Report response rate and the results of the bias checks alongside the survey findings.
outputs: Response-rate figures, a respondent versus non-respondent (or population) comparison table, early versus late comparisons, and a judgement on how far results can be generalised.
useWhen: Survey findings will inform decisions or be quoted as representing the user base, especially with low response rates or one-off email and in-app surveys.
avoidWhen: The study makes no claim of representativeness, such as a recruitment screener or an exploratory qualitative survey.
whyLost: UX surveys are often treated as directional, and response rates of a few per cent are accepted without asking who did not answer; the check belongs to survey methodology training that many UX researchers have not had.
whereToUse: In-app satisfaction surveys, relationship NPS, churn and cancellation surveys, annual user surveys, B2B customer studies.
example: An annual user survey shows 70% satisfaction. Joining responses to account data reveals that respondents log in four times as often as non-respondents. A reminder wave brings in lighter users, whose satisfaction is notably lower, so the team reports results by activity band rather than a single headline figure.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Non-Verbal Cue Analysis in Think-Aloud
aka: Non-verbal cue analysis in think-aloud tests
origin: Yammiyavar, Clemmensen and Kumar, CULTUSAB project, 2007
summary: Video-code gestures and facial expressions during think-aloud sessions and have multiple interpreters read them, recovering confusion and affect that users never verbalise.
description: Think-aloud data miss much of what users feel, especially when users fall silent or say something polite. Yammiyavar and colleagues filmed think-aloud sessions with cameras on face and hands as well as screen, replayed them to find recurring and strategically important gestures and expressions, counted their frequency, and extracted stills and clips. These were interpreted by independent reviewers, by acquaintances of the user, by strangers of the same age and culture, and by the user three days later. Gestures quantified, simplified or pointed at fuzzy thoughts; expressions revealed surprise, satisfaction, confusion, deep thought, frustration and boredom, often while the user was silent or saying something contradictory. Triangulating interpreters guards against single-coder bias, and merging agreed interpretations into the verbal protocol produces a richer record of where problems occur.
steps: Record think-aloud sessions with a camera on the participant's face and hands as well as screen capture.
Replay recordings to identify recurring and strategically placed gestures and facial expressions.
Count their frequencies per participant and task.
Extract stills and short clips around each cue.
Have at least two independent interpreters, ideally including acquaintances or same-culture strangers, and the participant at a later date, label each cue.
Keep interpretations where interpreters agree and merge them with the verbal protocol, marking where affect contradicts or replaces speech.
outputs: An enriched think-aloud protocol marking affect and intent where speech is absent or contradictory, with cue frequencies.
useWhen: Cross-cultural testing, or with participants who verbalise little, when you suspect politeness or silence is hiding confusion or frustration.
avoidWhen: Avoid when budgets are tight or samples tiny; for scalable affect measurement consider Automated facial expression analysis, and for systematic coding use Facial Action Coding.
whyLost: It is labour-intensive and culturally bound, so it stayed in cross-cultural HCI research while industry relied on verbal data or automated emotion tools.
whereToUse: International product launches, tests with high-power-distance cultures, children or older adults who verbalise little.
example: A travel site tests in India and Denmark. Indian participants rarely criticise aloud, but coded frowns and pauses cluster on the fare-rules page, which becomes the top redesign item.
reference: Yammiyavar, P., Clemmensen, T. and Kumar, J. (2007). Analyzing non-verbal cues in usability evaluation tests. In N. Aykin (Ed.), Usability and Internationalization, LNCS 4559. Springer, 462-471.

name: Nonignorable (MNAR) Missing-Data Modelling
origin: Little and Rubin (1987) taxonomy; Ibrahim, Chen and Lipsitz (2001); Lee and Tang (2006) for SEM
summary: Model the chance that each value is missing as depending on the value itself, fit it jointly with the substantive model, and compare it with a missing-at-random assumption.
description: Data are nonignorable missing when the probability of a value being missing depends on that value, as when dissatisfied users skip satisfaction items or struggling users drop out of a diary study. Multiple imputation and full-information ML assume missing at random and can be biased then. Lee's approach defines a missingness indicator for every item and models each by logistic regression on the item values and optionally the latent variables, assuming indicators are conditionally independent given the latent variables. Missing values, latent variables and parameters are sampled jointly by Gibbs and Metropolis-Hastings steps. Bayes factors compare a MAR model with several nonignorable mechanisms, then substantive models are compared under the chosen one. Because the mechanism's form can never be verified from the data, and complex mechanisms become unidentifiable, the method is best used as a sensitivity analysis showing how conclusions change under plausible departures from MAR.
steps: Define a missingness indicator for every item or wave.
Specify a simple logistic model for each indicator on the item values and, optionally, the latent variables, keeping it identified.
Augment the data with missing values and latent variables and sample all unknowns jointly.
Fit a MAR version and several nonignorable mechanisms and compare them by Bayes factor.
Compare substantive models under the selected mechanism.
Report how key estimates change between MAR and nonignorable assumptions, framing the result as sensitivity analysis rather than proof.
outputs: Substantive estimates under a nonignorable mechanism, the estimated missingness model, Bayes factors against MAR, and a sensitivity comparison.
useWhen: Surveys, panels or diary studies where the reason for non-response plausibly relates to the answer, such as satisfaction among churning users or symptom reports in health apps.
avoidWhen: When MAR is plausible given observed covariates (use Missing data handling with MICE imputation); when selection is into the sample rather than item non-response (Type-2 Tobit Sample Selection Model with Heckman Two-Step Estimation); or without the expertise to defend an untestable mechanism.
whyLost: UX teams rarely model missingness at all, and when they do they stop at MAR-based imputation; MNAR modelling stays in biostatistics and methodological research.
whereToUse: Longitudinal satisfaction tracking, health and wellbeing apps with dropout, post-churn surveys, NPS programmes with low response from detractors.
example: A mental-health app's weekly mood survey loses users whose mood worsens. A nonignorable model in which missingness depends on the unobserved score is favoured by Bayes factor, and the estimated improvement over eight weeks shrinks by a third compared with the MAR analysis.
sources: Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
reference: Lee, S.-Y. (2007). Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 375-389; Little, R. J. A., & Rubin, D. B. (1987). Statistical Analysis with Missing Data. New York: Wiley.

name: Norm Development and Standard-Score Transformation
origin: William McCall (T scale), 1922; Mehrens and Lehmann, 1991
summary: Standardise an instrument on a representative sample and convert raw scores to z, T, stanine or percentile scores so individual results can be interpreted against a norm group.
description: Raw scores cannot be compared across subtests, instruments or people without a reference. Norm development administers the final instrument to a large, representative standardisation sample, computes its mean and SD, and provides derived scores: z = (X - M)/SD; T = 10z + 50 (McCall's T scale); C scores and stanines (nine bands); and percentile, age or grade norm tables. Individual or product scores are then read against the norm group, for example as 'at the 70th percentile'. As Mehrens and Lehmann stress, norms describe actual performance, not standards of what is good, and they are only as meaningful as the norm group is relevant: a score's percentile changes with the reference population. Norms need periodic renewal as populations and products change.
steps: Define the population the norms should represent and draw a large representative standardisation sample.
Administer the final instrument under standard conditions.
Compute the mean and SD, and check the score distribution.
Convert raw scores to z and T scores (or stanines and C scores).
Build percentile tables, and age, segment or product-category norms where relevant.
Publish the norms with a description of the norm group, and interpret individual scores against them, refreshing norms periodically.
outputs: Conversion tables and norm tables (percentiles, standard scores) with documentation of the norm group.
useWhen: Giving meaning to scores from a questionnaire or benchmark used repeatedly across products, teams or releases, such as an in-house UX scale.
avoidWhen: Small or unrepresentative reference samples; norms from the wrong population mislead. Do not treat a norm as a target or quality standard.
whyLost: UX uses ready-made norms (for example SUS percentiles and SUPR-Q) but rarely builds its own for in-house instruments, and the derivation is unfamiliar.
whereToUse: In-house UX benchmark questionnaires, design-system adoption scores, competitive benchmarks and accessibility audit scores.
example: An enterprise software company has collected its own 8-item usability scale from 4,000 users across 20 products. It builds percentile and T-score tables by product category, so a new product scoring 62 is reported as the 35th percentile for admin tools.
sources: Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
reference: Mangal, S. K., & Mangal, S. (2013). Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences. New Delhi: PHI Learning.

name: Noun-Verb Requirements
origin: Abby Covert, 2014; noun-verb analysis has older roots in object-oriented software analysis
summary: List the nouns and the verbs that apply to them, join them into 'who can do what' sentences, prioritise them, and strip out implied interfaces, interactions and vague quality words.
description: Covert treats nouns as the objects, people and places in a mess and verbs as the actions that can be taken on them. Verbs do not exist without nouns, and nouns often arise from verbs: a post exists only after posting. Combining nouns with appropriate verbs yields requirement sentences that say who should be able to do what in the eventual state, such as 'an author can write a post'. Making them concrete and prioritising them clarifies what is being built: an interface that prioritises reading differs from one that prioritises writing even with identical requirements. Strong requirements describe results without saying how; weak ones smuggle in interaction ('one click'), interface ('button') or ambiguous quality ('easily'). Each term is checked for alternatives and associations before it enters the controlled vocabulary.
steps: List the nouns: objects, people and places in the domain.
List the verbs that can apply to each noun.
Consider alternative terms and their associations, and settle a controlled vocabulary.
Combine nouns and verbs into requirement sentences of the form 'actor can verb object'.
Make the sentences concrete and prioritise them.
Rewrite any requirement that implies an interaction, an interface element or an unmeasurable quality.
outputs: A prioritised list of actor-can-verb-object requirement statements and a controlled vocabulary.
useWhen: Defining scope and the conceptual model of a new product or feature before wireframing, especially where stakeholders talk in screens and buttons.
avoidWhen: The nouns and verbs should come from users' language, not only stakeholders'; elicit them with Interviews, Card Sorting or Free Listing and Cultural Salience Analysis. For formal vocabularies use Thesaurus and Controlled Vocabulary Construction (ISO 25964).
whyLost: Lives on under other names, chiefly object mapping in object-oriented UX and domain modelling, with its IA and software-analysis origins rarely credited.
whereToUse: SaaS and enterprise tools, content management, marketplaces, APIs and design-system modelling.
example: A client asks for a 'homepage made of buttons'; noun-verb work yields 'an editor can update a featured story' and 'any visitor can browse stories', revealing he wants changeable content, not buttons.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert, 2014)
reference: Covert, A. (2014) How to Make Sense of Any Mess: Information Architecture for Everybody. CreateSpace, ch. 4.

name: Novelty, primacy and long-term effect estimation
origin: Hohnhold, O'Brien and Tang (2015); Kohavi et al. (2012); Google search redesign practice (King, Churchill and Tan, 2017)
summary: Check whether an experiment's effect decays (novelty) or grows (learning, change aversion) over time, and use cohort, post-period or staggered designs to estimate the long-term effect.
description: Short A/B tests assume a constant treatment effect, but visible changes often provoke novelty clicks or change aversion that fade as users adapt. Per-day effect plots, using each day's own visitors rather than cumulative plots that create false trends, show decline (novelty) or growth (primacy, learning). Segmenting by usage frequency helps: in Google's 2010 search redesign, high-frequency users who met the change most looked better early, and others converged after a longer run; large visual changes may need about six weeks. New users are a check: if a change wins only for them, suspect novelty. For durable estimates, cohort analysis tracks stable signed-in users; post-period analysis switches the treatment off and measures the residual learned effect (Google found users learned to click fewer ads as ad load rose); time-staggered treatments start a second copy later and declare convergence when the two agree.
steps: Plot the treatment effect for each day using that day's visitors only, and plot the effect for the cohort first exposed on day one or two.
Segment by usage frequency and tenure: if high-frequency users already look better, exposure and learning are driving the early result.
Compare new users: a change that is flat or negative for them is not explained by habituation; one that wins only for them suggests novelty.
If a trend appears, extend the run until the effect stabilises (large visual changes may need about six weeks) and make longer durations the default for visual changes.

When the long-term effect matters, choose a design: stable signed-in cohort reweighted by pre-experiment strata, post-period analysis after switching the treatment off, or a time-staggered second treatment copy.
Test convergence, separate user-learned from system-learned effects, and model learned effects to forecast long-term impact from future short tests.
outputs: A judgement on whether a short-term effect is stable, a suitable test duration, a long-term effect estimate and short-term proxies for it.
useWhen: Visible redesigns, changes to habitual flows, ad load or notification frequency changes, and any test where early wins or losses may not persist.
avoidWhen: Invisible back-end changes with no learning component, or when traffic does not allow long runs; then rely on surrogate metrics and post-launch monitoring.
whyLost: Experiment platforms report cumulative lift over fixed short windows, and long-term designs need patience and infrastructure few teams have.
whereToUse: Search and feed redesigns, ad-supported products, notification strategy, navigation changes in mature SaaS and consumer apps.
example: A news app's redesigned home feed shows a 6% engagement lift in week one. Per-day plots show the lift decaying to zero by week three among existing users, so the team does not credit the redesign and investigates what caused the novelty spike.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Hohnhold, H., O'Brien, D. and Tang, D. (2015). Focusing on the long-term: it's good for users and business. Proceedings of KDD 2015, 1849-1858.

name: Now/Next/Later Outcome Roadmap
origin: Product management practice; Janna Bastow (ProdPad) is credited with championing the Now/Next/Later format (c. 2012)
summary: A roadmap that places outcomes, grouped into strategic themes tied to company objectives, in three receding horizons (Now, Next, Later) instead of committing features to dates.
description: The outcome roadmap separates direction from delivery dates. It has three columns: Now holds what the team is actively building; Next holds items being shaped with stakeholders so they are ready when capacity opens; Later holds important but speculative or dependent ideas, captured but not yet researched. Items are outcomes (double retention, re-engage lapsed users) rather than features, which are tentative solutions, and they are grouped by strategic themes such as growth or revenue rather than product areas, tied to company objectives or OKRs. Prioritisation decides which column an idea goes in. The roadmap is a proposal leadership must buy into, refreshed monthly against actual work and reviewed quarterly. When stakeholders demand dates, they get a separate release plan containing only genuine commitments, because any roadmap will otherwise be read as a promise.
steps: Gather inputs from the product vision, user feedback and research, data and the wider team.
Express candidate items as outcomes rather than features and group them under strategic themes that ladder up to company objectives or OKRs.
Prioritise candidates (for example with an effort-impact sort or RICE) and place each in Now, Next or Later.
Present the roadmap to leadership as a proposal and revise until it is endorsed.
Each month or sprint compare actual work with the roadmap and escalate drift.
Each quarter review with stakeholders what was done and what moves Later to Next and Next to Now; publish an update at least quarterly.
If dates are needed, map horizons to rough periods (for example Now = this quarter, Next = following six months, Later = up to 18 months) and give a separate release plan of firm commitments.
outputs: A thematic Now/Next/Later roadmap of outcomes, optional audience-specific views, and a separate release plan where needed.
useWhen: Use when a team needs shared direction without false precision, especially when discovery is ongoing and solutions are not yet known.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting it as a delivery schedule; use a Go-to-Market (Launch) Plan for dated commitments. It does not decide what users need: ground outcomes in Jobs-to-be-Done Research or an Opportunity Solution Tree.
whyLost: It survived because it lets teams commit to outcomes without promising feature dates, fitting agile delivery and continuous discovery.
whereToUse: SaaS product teams, platform teams, design system roadmaps, research roadmaps.
example: A mental-health subscription service places 'raise paid conversion' and 'reduce first-week churn' in Now, 'enterprise readiness for insurers' in Next, and 'group therapy' in Later. Leadership endorses it, and sales gets a separate release plan with only two dated items.
reference: Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People: From Designing to Thriving in a Product World. Brooklyn: Rosenfeld Media, ch. 10, pp. 163-187.

name: Nudge Design
origin: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, 2008
summary: Structures choice architecture (defaults, ordering, framing, social norms, timing) to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice, then tests the effect.
description: A nudge is any aspect of choice architecture that alters behaviour predictably without forbidding options or significantly changing economic incentives. Typical tools are defaults, option ordering, salience, social norms, feedback, reminders and simplification. In UX, nudge design means auditing an existing choice environment, identifying the choice architecture levers already in play (every interface has defaults, whether chosen deliberately or not), and redesigning them toward outcomes users would endorse on reflection. Rigour rests on three practices: tying each nudge to a mechanism, testing it experimentally against a control because effects are often smaller than headline studies suggest, and applying transparency and reversibility tests so nudges do not drift into sludge or dark patterns. Meta-analyses show defaults are typically the strongest lever.
steps: Identify the decision and the outcome users would endorse on reflection.
Audit current choice architecture: existing defaults, option order, framing, salience and timing.
Select candidate nudges, prioritising defaults and simplification, and state the expected mechanism.
Apply ethics checks: is it transparent, easy to opt out of, and aligned with user welfare?
Run a randomised experiment against the current design with pre-registered primary metrics.
Monitor longer-term outcomes and opt-out rates to detect backfire or reactance.
outputs: Choice architecture audit, nudge specification with mechanism and ethics rationale, experimental effect estimates.
useWhen: Onboarding settings, privacy and security choices, health and financial decisions where a better default or framing benefits users.
avoidWhen: When users need deliberate, informed choice (e.g. medical consent) or when the nudge benefits only the business; use transparent decision aids instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Widely adopted in product, public policy, and health design; though ethical concerns are growing.
whereToUse: Onboarding; default settings; health behavior; financial decision-making products.
example: A password manager changed the default for two-factor authentication from off to on during setup with a single-tap opt-out. In a four-week test, activation rose from 18% to 71% with an opt-out rate of 9%.
reference: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness. Yale University Press.

name: Number Needed to Treat and Harm
origin: Andreas Laupacis, David Sackett and Robin Roberts, 1988
summary: Expresses an intervention's effect as how many users must be exposed for one to benefit (NNT) or be harmed (NNH), making trade-offs concrete.
description: Relative effects (a 20% lift) are easily misunderstood. NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: if a design reduces abandonment from 10% to 8%, 50 users must see it to prevent one abandonment. NNH, similarly, is the reciprocal of absolute risk increase for an adverse outcome, such as accidental purchases or complaints. Reporting both side by side shows whether benefits outweigh harms, and confidence intervals around them highlight uncertainty. This brings ethical clarity to experiments with dark-pattern risks and helps stakeholders reason about impact in human terms.
steps: Identify the benefit outcome and any harm outcomes for an intervention.
Compute absolute risk differences between treatment and control for each, with confidence intervals.
Convert to NNT and NNH (1 / absolute difference) and their intervals, handling intervals that cross zero carefully.
Express results as 'for every X users exposed, one gains benefit; for every Y, one is harmed'.
Weigh benefits against harms, considering severity.
Include NNT/NNH in experiment reports and decision memos.
outputs: NNT and NNH with confidence intervals and a benefit-harm summary.
useWhen: Communicating experiment results, especially where interventions carry potential harms.
avoidWhen: Continuous outcomes without meaningful thresholds, unless dichotomised thoughtfully.
whyLost: Product teams report relative lifts that look impressive; harm outcomes are rarely tracked alongside.
whereToUse: Persuasive design experiments, upsells, notifications, health app nudges, AI safety features.
example: A pre-checked insurance add-on increases attach rate (NNT 12 for one extra sale) but also refund requests (NNH 30). Leadership sees that every 2.5 extra sales brings one dissatisfied customer and removes the default.
sources: Laupacis, Sackett & Roberts, An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment (1988), New England Journal of Medicine
Altman, Confidence intervals for the number needed to treat (1998), BMJ
reference: Laupacis, A., Sackett, D. L., & Roberts, R. S. (1988). NEJM, 318(26), 1728-1733.

name: Object Elicitation Interview
donor: Material culture studies and qualitative psychology
origin: Material culture and qualitative interviewing traditions; formalised in qualitative psychology (Willig, 2016)
summary: Participants bring meaningful objects to the interview, which anchor discussion and help bridge from concrete, sensory detail to broader experience and meaning.
description: Object elicitation (Willig, 2016; objects used in clinical and qualitative interviewing) involves participants bringing physical objects that are meaningful to their experience, which are then used as interview stimuli. Objects anchor abstract or emotionally complex experiences in the concrete, multi-sensory world — they allow participants to show rather than only tell, and they access sensory and tactile dimensions of experience that purely verbal methods miss.
steps: Brief participants in advance: 'Before our interview, I'd like you to choose one or two objects that feel meaningful to your experience of [phenomenon]. Bring them to the interview. They can be anything.'
Opening with the object: Begin the interview by asking about the object: 'Tell me about this object and why you brought it.' Let the object-story be the entry point.

Sensory engagement with the object: Encourage participants to handle the object during the interview. 'What does it feel like to hold this?' 'When you look at it, what comes to mind?' Sensory engagement with the object mediates richer recall.
Moving from object to experience: Use the object as a bridge: 'This object seems connected to [theme] — can you tell me more about that?'

Analysis: Analyse both the object chosen (what the participant chose to represent their experience) and the narrative around the object (how it is talked about). The choice of object is itself a form of data.
outputs: Photographs or records of chosen objects, interview narratives anchored in them, analysis of object choice and discussion, and insights into meaning and practice.
useWhen: Experience is tied to material things, such as money tools, medication, devices, workspaces or sentimental items, or abstract topics need a concrete starting point.
avoidWhen: Topics have no material dimension, or object choice could be burdensome or exposing; use Photo Elicitation or standard interviews.
whyLost: UX artefact analysis focuses on workplace documents and screens, while object-based interviewing stayed in material culture, psychology and museum studies.
whereToUse: Personal finance (wallets, notebooks), medication management, home technology, legacy and digital inheritance, and physical-digital product ecosystems.
example: Older adults are asked to bring 'something you use to keep track of your money'. Notebooks, envelopes and a printed bank statement anchor interviews revealing that physical records are trusted as proof, shaping a printable statement feature.
sources: When Words Fail Us — Elicitation Techniques (PMC 2024)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Willig, C. (2016). Reflections on the use of object elicitation. Qualitative Psychology, 4(3), 211-222.

name: Objective-Question-Method Chain
origin: Popularised for UX by David Travis (Think Like a UX Researcher, 2019); rooted in classic research-design teaching
summary: A planning discipline that derives research methods from decision-linked objectives and research questions, producing a documented chain stakeholders agree to before fieldwork.
description: The chain inverts the common habit of choosing a method first ('let's run a survey') and back-filling a rationale. It starts from the decision the team must make, states objectives as information needs, decomposes each into two to five answerable research questions, and only then selects the method that yields valid evidence for each question with the available population, time and budget. The full chain (objective, question, method, participants, analysis plan, intended use of findings) is written down and shared before fieldwork, acting as a contract with stakeholders. Its rigour lies in traceability: every session, item and analysis step can be justified by a question, and every question by a decision. Gaps and redundant methods become visible, and post-hoc reframing of results becomes harder.
steps: Define objectives: What does the team need to know to make a good decision? State objectives as information needs, not methods ("understand why users abandon the checkout flow" not "run a usability test").
Derive research questions: What specific questions, if answered, would satisfy each objective? Each objective typically generates 2–5 research questions. Write them as questions, not hypotheses.

Select methods: For each question: which method provides valid evidence for this specific question, with this population, in this timeframe? Map methods to questions. If multiple methods answer the same question, choose the lowest cost.
Document the chain: Objective → Research Question → Method → Participant → Analysis Plan → How findings will be used. Share this before fieldwork. This is your contract with stakeholders.
outputs: A one-page research plan table linking objectives, research questions, methods, sample, analysis plan and decision use; an explicit list of questions out of scope.
useWhen: At the start of any study or research roadmap, when stakeholders arrive with a method request, when several teams compete for research capacity, or when you need to defend why a method was chosen.
avoidWhen: For tiny tactical checks where the question and method are obvious (a five-user usability retest); for open-ended exploratory immersion where questions should emerge from fieldwork, use ethnographic or grounded approaches with a lighter charter.
whyLost: Agile cadences and tool-led research ops encourage method-first requests ('book five interviews'), so the written chain is skipped and its logic survives only as a slogan.
whereToUse: Research intake processes, quarterly research roadmaps, research ops templates, and stakeholder kick-offs for high-stakes decisions in fintech, health and enterprise SaaS.
example: A banking team asks for a survey on why customers abandon loan applications. Mapping the chain shows the objective is to locate where and why abandonment happens, which funnel analytics plus session-replay review and ten follow-up interviews answer better than a survey. The plan is signed off before recruitment begins.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher (David Travis)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Travis, D. & Hodgson, P. (2019). Think Like a UX Researcher. CRC Press.

name: Observation frameworks (AEIOU and checklists)
donor: Design ethnography; business anthropology; programme evaluation
origin: AEIOU: Doblin Group, Chicago, 1990s (described by Christina Wasson, 2000); Robson and McCartan (2016); Patton (2002); DECIPHER: Pavliscak (2018)
summary: Use a fixed set of categories, such as AEIOU or Robson's nine items, to structure what you notice in field observation and to seed the first coding scheme.
description: Observation frameworks give observers a checklist so attention is spread systematically. AEIOU covers Activities (goal-directed actions), Environments (the whole setting), Interactions (between people and things), Objects (including repurposed ones) and Users (roles and values). Robson and McCartan's nine items are space, actors, activities, objects, acts, events, time, goals and feelings; a lighter version is person, place, thing. Patton's sensitising framework adds the programme's native language, informal time, nonverbal cues, unobtrusive indicators, documents and what does not happen, and asks for descriptive rather than interpretive adjectives. DECIPHER (dreams, etiquette, contradictions, images, peaks, hacks, extremes, rituals) directs long-term research to emotional edges. All work as note-taking worksheets in the field and as starter codes afterwards, but they sensitise rather than dictate.
steps: Set a clear observation goal and choose a framework: AEIOU, person/place/thing, Robson's nine items, Patton's data sources or DECIPHER for emotional signals.
Brief all observers on the categories and print a worksheet per observer.
On entering a new site, spend about ten minutes listing everything you can see under each category, and turn the list into questions to ask.
Observe planned activities as bounded units with a start, participants, interactions and closure; stay alert in informal time between them.
Describe settings with descriptive, not interpretive, adjectives; record participants' own terms and note significant absences.
Split the team across people and areas, review notes daily separating observation from opinion, and check interpretations with informants.
Stop when patterns repeat and all main stakeholder groups have been observed; use the categories as starter codes and add subcategories as patterns appear.
outputs: Categorised field notes, an observation inventory with follow-up questions, activity mini-cases and a starter coding scheme.
useWhen: Starting observation in an unfamiliar setting, coordinating several observers, or training novices to notice more than the obvious.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the categories as a measurement scheme; for counts and rates use structured observation with defined codes. Preset categories can blinker observers, categories overlap, and the interactions between them often matter most.
whyLost: AEIOU survives because it is short, memorable and taught in design schools; the fuller sensitising checklists from evaluation and sociology are less known in UX.
whereToUse: Retail and hospitality spaces, workplaces, clinics, homes and event venues, and any discovery field visit or design-school style site observation.
example: A team studying home-security habits uses AEIOU sheets on each home visit. Under Objects they log an alarm code written on paper by the door and a propped-open side door, which become probes for later interviews about convenience versus security.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Wasson, C. (2000). Ethnography in the field of design. Human Organization 59(4); Robson, C. & McCartan, K. (2016). Real World Research (4th ed.). Wiley; Patton, M. Q. (2002). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Observer Judgement Study of Facial Expressions
aka: Observer judgement study of facial expressions (accuracy and agreement)
origin: Psychology of emotion, reviewed in Ekman, Friesen and Ellsworth (1972)
summary: Naive observers label photographs or video of faces; their agreement shows what faces convey, and comparison with an independently known state shows accuracy.
description: Instead of coding facial muscle movements, this design asks untrained observers what a face conveys. Agreement studies show faces in random order and collect forced-choice labels from a fixed word list, free labels or pleasant-unpleasant ratings, then compute agreement per face. Accuracy studies record faces under conditions whose emotional state is independently known (a stress versus a calm interview, a surgery film versus a travelogue) and test whether observers can tell them apart. Many early accuracy studies were inconclusive because the criterion emotion was poorly established. Known artefacts matter: happy and sad are default guesses for neutral faces, and omitting a neutral option changes results. For UX, the design validates whether recorded participant faces, avatars, robot faces or emoji-like feedback actually communicate the intended state to ordinary people, and supplies a human benchmark for automated emotion recognition.
steps: Record faces (or render avatars) under conditions whose emotional state is independently known or intended.
Prepare a response format: forced choice from a word list including a neutral option, free labels, or pleasant-unpleasant ratings.
Show the stimuli to naive observers in random order, typically 20 or more observers.
Collect labels or ratings for each face.
Compute agreement per face and, where a criterion exists, accuracy against the known condition, correcting for chance and default guesses.
Compare agreement and accuracy across expression sets, designs or automated classifiers.
outputs: Agreement percentages per face, accuracy against criterion conditions, and confusion patterns between emotions.
useWhen: You need to know whether faces (participants', avatars', robots' or characters') convey a specific state to ordinary viewers, or need a human benchmark for emotion AI.
avoidWhen: You need to know what the person actually felt; observer labels measure perceived emotion. Use self-report, physiology or FACS coding for that.
whyLost: UX adopted automated facial coding and FACS, skipping the simpler observer-judgement designs that test what faces communicate.
whereToUse: Avatar and character design, social robots, video-based emotion AI validation, telehealth and video interview tools.
example: A social robot team shows 40 observers clips of the robot's six expressions with a neutral option available. 'Concern' is labelled sad 60% of the time, so the eyebrow animation is redesigned before field trials.
reference: Ekman, P., Friesen, W. V., & Ellsworth, P. (1972). Emotion in the Human Face: Guidelines for Research and an Integration of Findings. Pergamon Press.

name: OKR Alignment (Objectives and Key Results)
origin: Developed at Intel by Andy Grove and popularised at Google by John Doerr; described for UX and product people by Crumlish (2022)
summary: State team objectives with measurable key results and align them so each team's objectives deliver the key results of the level above, linking roadmaps to strategy.
description: Objectives are goals or outcomes; key results are measurable statements that can confirm or falsify whether an objective was met, or measure how much of it was achieved. OKRs are aligned up and down an organisation: a team's objectives, if achieved, should deliver the key results of the team or leader it reports to. Crumlish treats them as the framing device that ties a product roadmap to company strategy, with the product leader negotiating what commitments product can make towards larger objectives, and outcomes on the roadmap laddering up to them. Progress is reviewed during the quarter and reset in quarterly planning against the annual plan. The discipline lies in writing key results that could fail and in checking the chain in both directions.
steps: Start from the organisation's objectives for the year and the quarter or half.
For each objective, write two to five key results that are measurable and could show the objective was not met, or measure partial achievement.
At each level down, write team objectives that would deliver the key results above, and check the chain upwards and downwards.
Use the objectives as the top level of the roadmap so that outcomes and themes ladder up to them.
Review progress against key results during the quarter as part of routine data analysis.
In quarterly planning, score the past quarter, review against the annual plan and set the next quarter's OKRs.
outputs: A nested set of objectives and measurable key results linking team roadmaps to company strategy, with quarterly progress reviews.
useWhen: Use it to connect UX and product work to company outcomes and to decide which design problems deserve roadmap space.
avoidWhen: A key result can move without the objective improving; validate UX key results with UX KPIs with Baselines and Pre-Set Success Thresholds or the HEART Framework, and audit them with a Metric Quality Audit. OKRs do not tell you what users need; use discovery research for that.
whyLost: It survived because it is simple, scales across large organisations and was adopted by influential technology companies.
whereToUse: Product and design team planning, research roadmaps, design system teams and cross-functional squads.
example: A health app's objective is to help members stay on treatment; one key result is raising 90-day medication adherence from 58% to 65%. The design team's objective, to make refill reminders actionable, ladders up to it.
reference: Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People: From Designing to Thriving in a Product World. Rosenfeld Media, pp. 28, 54, 169-170. Doerr, J. (2018). Measure What Matters. New York: Portfolio.

name: Old Brain / New Brain Design Audit
origin: Susan Weinschenk, 2009; drawing on MacLean's triune brain model
summary: Audits a design for how it engages fast, automatic responses (danger, faces, food, novelty) versus deliberative reasoning, ensuring key elements work at both levels.
description: Susan Weinschenk's 'old brain / new brain' framing, derived from the triune brain model, divides processing into fast, automatic responses to danger, faces, food, novelty and movement, emotional responses, and slow deliberative reasoning. Although the anatomical model is outdated, the practical idea maps onto well-supported dual-process accounts. The audit examines each key screen for what will capture automatic attention, what emotional tone it sets, and whether deliberative content supports the decision once attention is captured. Mismatches, such as decorative imagery outcompeting a critical warning, are flagged. Rigour comes from framing findings in contemporary attention and dual-process terms, avoiding manipulative uses, and validating predictions with eye tracking, first-click or five-second tests.
steps: Old-brain filter test for landing pages and critical interfaces:
Show the interface for 50ms (single frame).
(2) Ask: 'What caught your attention?'
Code responses: contrast elements, faces, movement indicators, large text.
(4) Compare to intended attention hierarchy.
(5) Elements that pass the 50ms filter = old-brain salient. Elements that don't = invisible to first-pass attention. Redesign: ensure the most critical element passes the old-brain filter first.
outputs: An audit of automatic attention triggers and deliberative content per screen, mismatches between what grabs attention and what matters, and redesign suggestions.
useWhen: Landing pages, alerts, onboarding, and persuasion-sensitive screens where first impressions and automatic attention shape outcomes.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting the triune brain as anatomy (it is outdated); avoid manipulative exploitation of automatic responses. Prefer dual-process framing and empirical testing.
whyLost: The underlying triune-brain neuroscience was discredited, so the method was dismissed with it, although its practical dual-process audit remains useful.
whereToUse: Landing page design, notification design, mobile first-screen design, critical alert design.
example: A surgical alert system relies on a small text banner; the audit shows nothing triggers automatic attention, so the redesign adds motion onset and a distinct sound for critical alerts only.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Weinschenk S (2009) Neuro Web Design: What Makes Them Click? New Riders

name: One-way sensitivity analysis
origin: Standard capital budgeting practice; worked example from Brealey and Myers, Principles of Corporate Finance
summary: Vary each input of a value model one at a time between pessimistic and optimistic estimates to see which assumptions drive the result and deserve further research.
description: A project's value, such as net present value, depends on assumptions about market size, share, price and costs. One-way sensitivity analysis builds a spreadsheet model, gives each input a pessimistic, expected and optimistic value, and sets each input to its extremes in turn while holding the others at expected. Tabulated ranges show which assumptions dominate. In the textbook scooter example, market share swung value from about minus 104 to plus 173 million while market size barely mattered. Its practical use is deciding where additional information is worth buying: research effort should go to the inputs with the widest swing. A tornado chart, sorting inputs by range, is the usual display. Interactions between variables are not captured.
steps: Build a spreadsheet model that computes the outcome (NPV, revenue, cost to serve) from explicit assumptions.
Give each input a pessimistic, expected and optimistic value, ideally from evidence or calibrated estimates.
Holding all other inputs at expected, set one input to its pessimistic then optimistic value and record the outcome.
Repeat for every input and tabulate the outcome ranges.
Sort inputs by range, optionally as a tornado chart.
Direct research or data collection to the inputs with the widest ranges, and revisit the analysis as estimates improve.
outputs: A table or tornado chart of outcome ranges per input, and a ranked list of assumptions that most need evidence.
useWhen: Building a business case for a feature or product and deciding which assumptions research should test first.
avoidWhen: Avoid when inputs interact strongly or you need a probability distribution of outcomes; use Monte Carlo simulation or scenario analysis. It changes one variable at a time only.
whyLost: It is routine in finance but UX researchers rarely see or own the value model, so they do not use it to target research.
whereToUse: Product strategy, pricing and business cases, research roadmap prioritisation, and justifying research spend.
example: A fintech team's business case for a savings feature rests on adoption rate, average balance and interest margin. Sensitivity analysis shows adoption rate swings value ten times more than the others, so the research plan focuses on a fake-door test of adoption before any balance modelling.
sources: Four Ways to do Project Analysis (Crawford, n.d.)
reference: Brealey, R. A. & Myers, S. C. (1996). Principles of Corporate Finance (5th ed.). McGraw-Hill, as used in Crawford, G. (n.d.). Four Ways to do Project Analysis.

name: Online and crowdsourced experiments with quality controls
aka: Crowdsourced HCI experiments with quality controls
Crowdsourced data collection with quality controls
origin: Kittur, Chi and Suh (2008); Heer and Bostock (2010); Paolacci, Chandler and Ipeirotis (2010)
summary: Run controlled experiments in the browser with large samples of online or paid crowd participants, using designed-in quality checks, fair pay and dropout analysis.
description: Browser-based platforms and crowd marketplaces (MTurk, Prolific, CloudResearch) let researchers run experiments with hundreds of participants in days. Results usually match the lab, even for perception and reaction-time tasks: Heer and Bostock replicated lab perception studies on MTurk with wider variance but the same conclusions at one-sixth of the cost. Quality must be designed in: questions with known answers, making accurate answers as easy as careless ones, screening for rushed or repeated responses, redundancy and agreement models, instruction checks, and logging tab-hidden focus loss. Instructions must stand alone and be pictorial where possible; sessions should be short, since dropout can reach 69%, and dropout must be analysed by condition. Pairing with a small lab study corroborates both: Meyer and Bederson's 221 online participants matched 18 in the lab. Fair pay and treatment of workers is an ethical requirement.
steps: Choose a platform, host and recruitment source (crowd marketplace or own panel), and decide whether a custom web app is needed for logging.
Write stand-alone, pictorial instructions with success criteria, and add an instruction or comprehension check.
Build in quality controls: known-answer questions, attention checks, timing and repetition screens, and logging of focus loss and response times.
Set fair pay based on realistic completion time and keep sessions short; pilot tasks and software with a small worker sample.
Run the study, monitor quality and engage worker communities to resolve problems fairly.
Analyse dropout by condition, report exclusions and which participants each analysis includes.
Where possible, run the same study with a small lab sample and compare result patterns; investigate discrepancies.
outputs: Large-sample, quality-screened experimental data with exclusion and dropout reports, and optionally corroborating lab results.
useWhen: Perception, comprehension, preference and visualisation experiments that need large or diverse samples quickly, or testing hypotheses from analytics on an independent sample.
avoidWhen: When the target users are specialists unlikely to be crowd workers, tasks need observation or physical setups, or timing precision below network latency matters; use lab studies or recruited panels of real users.
whyLost: It survives and has grown, because platforms like Prolific make large controlled samples cheap and fast.
whereToUse: Visualisation and dashboard design, copy and comprehension tests, AI output evaluation, icon recognition, pricing and choice experiments.
example: A health app team tests three risk-chart designs for comprehension with 600 Prolific participants, using known-answer items and excluding 8% who failed checks. A lab session with 12 patients confirms the same ranking.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)

name: Online and Remote Qualitative Research Adaptations
donor: Qualitative social research and internet research
origin: Online interviewing literature from the 2000s (Salmons; James and Busher); widespread adoption from 2020
summary: Adapts interviews, think-aloud and observation for video, chat and asynchronous channels, addressing rapport, environment, consent, data loss and the strengths of each digital mode.
description: Remote research is not simply in-person research over video. Each channel changes what data you get. Video calls lose body language below the shoulders, shared physical context and some rapport cues, but gain access to participants in their own environment and screen sharing for remote think-aloud. Asynchronous text interviews give participants time to reflect and suit sensitive topics, but lose spontaneity. Rigorous adaptation means planning rapport building explicitly, briefing participants on technology, recording and privacy, piloting the setup, choosing synchronous or asynchronous modes deliberately, and documenting observational limits in the report. Digital think-aloud needs careful handling of latency, screen-sharing fatigue and participants' unfamiliarity with tools. The rigour lies in treating mode as a methodological decision with known effects.
steps: Rapport in digital environments: Building the research relationship without physical co-presence requires: longer warm-up conversations, careful attention to what participants can see in the researcher's video frame, explicit discussion of how the technology will be used.

Managing the digital environment: Briefing participants on: screen sharing, recording consent, muting background noise. Technical problems are not interruptions to research — participants' responses to technical failure are data.

Asynchronous qualitative data: Text-based asynchronous interviews (via email, messaging apps, or online platforms) allow participants to respond in their own time, to choose their words carefully, and to share images and documents easily. The absence of real-time dynamics changes the data character.

Observational limitations: Video interviews lose: body language below the torso, spontaneous environmental observations, and the researcher's co-presence in the participant's physical context. Compensate with explicit questions about the environment.

Digital think-aloud: Screen-sharing enables remote think-aloud protocols. Participants can share their screen while narrating their interaction with a digital product in their natural environment — ecological validity advantage over lab-based think-aloud.
outputs: A remote study protocol with mode rationale, technology and consent briefing materials, recordings and transcripts, and documented observational limits.
useWhen: Participants are geographically dispersed, hard to reach, or more comfortable at home; budgets are tight; or the product is itself used remotely on personal devices.
avoidWhen: Physical context, environment or embodied interaction matter (use field methods such as Walking Interview or contextual inquiry), or participants lack reliable connectivity or devices.
whyLost: It is active and dominant since 2020, though many teams adopted remote tools without adapting rapport, consent and observational practices to the medium.
whereToUse: Global SaaS and consumer apps, remote usability testing, sensitive topics via asynchronous text, accessibility research with participants using their own assistive technology, and rapid discovery.
example: A mental-health startup offers participants a choice between video and asynchronous chat interviews. Chat participants disclose more about medication side-effects, so the team uses chat for sensitive topics and video for app walkthroughs.
sources: A Pilot Study Conducting Online Think Aloud Qualitative Method (PMC 2022)

Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)

name: Online Research Communities (MROCs)
origin: Market research practice from the 2000s; Ray Poynter, The Handbook of Online and Social Media Research (2010)
summary: Recruit people into a moderated open or closed online community and run discussions, diaries, polls and co-creation activities with them over weeks or months.
description: An online research community recruits a targeted group into a moderated, usually private, community where members give attitudes, opinions and ideas over an extended period. Unlike panel members, who answer surveys in isolation, community members interact with one another and a moderator, test hypotheses, develop ideas, evaluate products and comment on services. Short-term communities address one issue over a few weeks; long-term ones serve many projects. Closed communities, entered by invitation and a profile questionnaire, suit sensitive topics. Activities include discussions, online focus groups, polls, diaries and journals, idea sessions, collages, games and questionnaires. The rigour lies in community management: deliberate profiling and recruitment, over-recruitment for drop-out, codes of behaviour, and sustained trust and engagement. Members become experienced and self-selected, so findings drift from naive users over time.
steps: Decide the community type, open or closed, short or long term, and whether to build or rent a platform.
Set size, over-recruitment for drop-out and duration.
Recruit and profile members, considering their motivations and refreshing membership periodically.
Set a code of behaviour, privacy rules and data security.
Run a planned calendar of activities (discussions, polls, diaries, idea sessions, focus groups, questionnaires) and observe member interaction.
Maintain community health with regular moderator presence, feedback on how input was used, and incentives.
Analyse activity outputs per project and track member tenure to watch for professionalisation.
outputs: Longitudinal qualitative and quantitative feedback from engaged members, and a standing resource for rapid studies.
useWhen: Organisations needing frequent, fast access to a defined customer group for iterative feedback, co-creation and longitudinal tracking.
avoidWhen: Studies needing naive or representative users, or behavioural observation; recruit fresh participants instead. Avoid when sponsor marketing aims would compromise research independence.
whyLost: Strong in market research, but UX teams more often use standing recruitment panels and one-off studies, and community management is seen as a marketing job.
whereToUse: Consumer brands with loyal users, B2B customer advisory communities, healthcare patient communities, games.
example: A meal-kit company runs a closed 300-member community for six months. Weekly activities test recipe card layouts, a diary captures cooking nights, and a poll prioritises features; members are refreshed quarterly to limit expert bias.
reference: Poynter, R. (2010). The Handbook of Online and Social Media Research. Chichester: Wiley.

name: Ontology/taxonomy/choreography audit
origin: Dan Klyn's ontology/taxonomy/choreography model of information architecture, around 2010; ontology and taxonomy lessons in Abby Covert, How to Make Sense of Any Mess, 2014, which mentions choreography only in passing and gives no audit procedure. The three-layer audit procedure is the atlas's own synthesis.
summary: Maps an information space at three layers, ontology (what things are), taxonomy (how they are classified) and choreography (how people move through them), to diagnose where IA breaks.
description: Covert distinguishes three layers of information architecture. Ontology is the set of things that exist in the space and what is meant by each term; taxonomy is how those things are arranged and classified; choreography is the rules for interaction and movement through the structure. Many IA redesigns only reshuffle the taxonomy, while the real problem is ontological, for example teams and users meaning different things by 'account', 'project' or 'member', or choreographic, such as an order of steps that contradicts users' expectations. The method elicits terms and definitions from stakeholders and users (controlled vocabulary workshops, interviews, card sorts), identifies conflicts in meaning, maps classification schemes, and traces key journeys through the structure. Findings are recorded as a shared vocabulary and diagrams for each layer.
steps: Before any IA redesign:
Ontology audit — what are the fundamental entities in this domain? Are they correctly identified?
(2) Taxonomy audit — how are entities classified? Do the classification criteria match users' classification criteria?
(3) Choreography audit — what paths through the taxonomy do users take for each goal? Sequence the redesign: fix ontology first, taxonomy second, choreography third.
outputs: Controlled vocabulary with definitions, ontology conflicts, taxonomy diagrams, choreography maps of key journeys, and diagnosis of which layer drives each problem.
useWhen: IA redesigns, products with confusing terminology, mergers of systems or organisations, and SaaS products whose core objects are misunderstood.
avoidWhen: When the vocabulary is already shared and the problem is only labelling or navigation depth; use tree testing.
whyLost: Covert's book is popular, but the three-layer diagnosis is usually reduced to card sorting and sitemap work, leaving ontology unexamined.
whereToUse: IA redesign, search and navigation redesign, content strategy, any product where users can't find things.
example: A project-management SaaS finds 'workspace', 'team' and 'organisation' are used interchangeably by staff and users. Ontology mapping resolves definitions before navigation is redesigned, and support tickets about permissions drop.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess — Abby Covert

name: Open Coding (Constant Comparative Method)
origin: Barney Glaser & Anselm Strauss, 1967 (The Discovery of Grounded Theory); elaborated by Strauss & Corbin, 1990
summary: Line-by-line coding of raw qualitative data, constantly comparing each new incident and code with all existing ones to build grounded, saturated concepts.
description: Open coding is the first stage of Grounded Theory analysis. You break the data apart, line by line or sentence by sentence, and apply descriptive codes that stay as close to the data as possible. The constant comparative method means that every new code is immediately compared to all existing codes — if two codes represent the same phenomenon, they are merged into a single code. If a code covers two distinct phenomena, it is split. This process continues until you can no longer find incidents that require new codes (theoretical saturation).
steps: Read the entire transcript once without coding. Write a one-paragraph summary of what the session was about. This is your orienting memo.

Begin line-by-line coding from the top of the transcript. For each meaningful unit (clause, sentence, or short paragraph), ask: "What is happening here? What is this person doing, thinking, or feeling? What category does this belong to?"
Write codes in the margin. Keep codes short (3–5 words) and active (use gerunds: "avoiding the feature" not "avoidance").
After every 5–10 codes: compare each new code to all existing codes. Merge identical codes. Split codes that cover more than one phenomenon.
Write a memo for every code that surprises you or challenges your expectation. These memos are your analytic raw material.
After completing one transcript: compile a full code list. Repeat with the next transcript, constantly comparing new codes to existing ones.
Stop when new transcripts add no new codes. This is saturation — but only if you have used theoretical sampling (see Method 14) to ensure the absence of codes is meaningful, not accidental.
outputs: A code list with definitions, in-vivo and descriptive codes, code memos, and a record of merges, splits and saturation status.
useWhen: When you need concepts that genuinely emerge from data rather than from a prior framework, especially in new domains, novel behaviours, or when explaining a process no existing model covers.
avoidWhen: When the questions are tightly defined and a coding frame already exists (use framework analysis or Mayring content analysis), or when time permits only rapid synthesis (use a rapid affinity or debrief matrix).
whyLost: UX practice compressed it into sticky-note clustering without line-by-line coding, memoing or theoretical sampling, so the name survives while the comparative discipline does not.
whereToUse: Foundational discovery for new product categories, trust and adoption studies in health and fintech, AI product behaviour research, and any study meant to produce a reusable conceptual model.
example: Analysing 20 interviews with rural health workers about a digital records app, a researcher codes line by line and repeatedly compares incidents of 'double-entering on paper'. Merging and splitting codes surfaces a concept of 'insurance against system loss' that reframes the design problem.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick ed.)

Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
