extra.Two Types of Code: In-vivo codes: Codes taken directly from the participant's own words. They preserve the participant's framing and are often the most analytically powerful. Example: a participant says "I just stopped trusting it" → code: "stopped trusting it." Descriptive codes: Researcher-generated descriptions of what is happening in the data. Less tied to specific language but more comparable across participants. Example: "trust collapse following system error."

name: Open, axial and selective coding pipeline
origin: Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, The Discovery of Grounded Theory (1967); the three-stage pipeline formalised by Strauss and Corbin, Basics of Qualitative Research (1990)
summary: A staged coding procedure that fractures data into concepts, relates them around axes of conditions, actions and consequences, then integrates them into one core theory.
description: Grounded theory generates theory from data rather than testing prior hypotheses. Strauss and Corbin's pipeline has three stages. Open coding breaks data into line-by-line or incident-level concepts and groups them into categories with properties and dimensions. Axial coding reassembles categories by relating each to subcategories through a coding paradigm of conditions, actions and interactions, and consequences. Selective coding chooses a core category that explains most variation and integrates the others around it into a storyline. The process runs alongside constant comparison, memo writing and theoretical sampling, so later interviews target gaps in emerging categories. Rigour comes from this iteration, from extensive memoing, and from testing the theory against negative cases, not from coding volume. UX often borrows the label while doing a single round of theme clustering.
steps: Collect an initial set of 6 to 10 interviews or observations around a broad research question, transcribed verbatim.

Open code line by line or incident by incident, naming concepts with gerunds where possible (for example 'hedging against audit'), and write memos on each emerging category's properties and dimensions.
Use constant comparison: compare each new incident with prior incidents in the same category and refine category definitions in memos.
Axial code by relating categories using the paradigm of causal conditions, context, intervening conditions, action and interaction strategies, and consequences, diagramming the relations.
Theoretically sample: select the next participants or sites to fill gaps and test variation in the emerging categories, typically reaching 20 to 30 interviews.
Selective code by identifying the core category that relates to most others, writing the storyline, and validating it against all cases, including negative cases.
Stop when theoretical saturation is reached, when new data add no new properties to core categories, and document the theory as propositions with a diagram.
outputs: A codebook with category properties and dimensions, analytic memos, axial diagrams, a core category and storyline, and a substantive theory expressed as propositions.
useWhen: Explaining a process or phenomenon with no adequate existing theory, such as why users distrust a system, how adoption unfolds, or how teams negotiate tool use.
avoidWhen: You have a predefined question needing quick descriptive answers (use framework or thematic analysis), or no ability to sample iteratively; grounded theory without theoretical sampling becomes ordinary coding.
whyLost: UX adopted the vocabulary of 'coding' and 'grounded' but fixed samples, compressed timelines and sticky-note affinity work removed theoretical sampling, constant comparison and memoing, which are the method's core.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption studies, new-domain discovery, B2B workflow research, AI use in professional settings, health worker behaviour.
example: From 20 rural health worker interviews, open coding produced 140 codes; axial coding related 'audit exposure', 'paper as proof' and 'device dependency' around a core category, 'protecting the self from blame'. The resulting theory of digital distrust explained why workers kept paper duplicates even when the app worked.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 26 — Grounded Theory — Generating Theory from Data
reference: Strauss, A., & Corbin, J. (1990). Basics of Qualitative Research: Grounded Theory Procedures and Techniques. Sage; Glaser, B. G., & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The Discovery of Grounded Theory. Aldine.

name: Operationalization protocol
donor: Philosophy of science and social science methodology
origin: Percy Bridgman's operationalism, 1927; developed in social science methodology by Lazarsfeld (1958) and others
summary: Translates an abstract construct into specific, observable indicators and procedures, documenting how each indicator maps to the construct and what it leaves out.
description: Operationalisation is the bridge between a concept such as 'ease of use' and data. A rigorous protocol specifies the construct's dimensions, chooses indicators for each, defines the exact measurement procedure (instrument, wording, timing, scoring, units), and states the expected relationships between indicators. Lazarsfeld's sequence of imagery, specification of dimensions, selection of indicators, and formation of indices remains a sound template. Good protocols also record what each indicator misses (construct under-representation) and what irrelevant variance it may capture. In UX the step is commonly skipped: teams pick a familiar metric because it is available, leading to measures that do not represent what stakeholders mean.
steps: Write a one-paragraph conceptual definition of the construct, citing literature or stakeholder interviews.
Break it into dimensions (for example ease of use as efficiency, learnability, error tolerance and perceived effort).
Select at least two indicators per dimension, mixing behavioural and attitudinal where possible.
Specify the exact procedure for each indicator: instrument, wording, scale, timing, scoring rule and unit.
State expected correlations between indicators (convergent) and with unrelated measures (discriminant), and pilot with 5-10 participants.
Record known gaps and threats, and freeze the protocol before main data collection.
outputs: An operationalisation table (construct, dimensions, indicators, procedures, expected relations), pilot results and a frozen measurement plan.
useWhen: Before any metric programme, benchmark, survey, or experiment, especially when stakeholders use vague terms like engagement, trust or ease.
avoidWhen: For purely exploratory qualitative research aimed at discovering what constructs exist; do interviews or ethnography first.
whyLost: UX inherited ready-made metrics (SUS, NPS, conversion) and skipped the step of deciding what they should measure.
whereToUse: Product metrics frameworks, OKRs, AI trust measurement, regulated medical usability (IEC 62366), and benchmarking programmes.
example: A surgical robotics team asked for 'ease of use' data. The protocol splits it into setup efficiency (time to dock), error tolerance (recoverable errors per case), learnability (cases to proficiency) and perceived workload (NASA-TLX), each with a specified procedure.
sources: Dix, A., Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data (2020)
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Leavy, P., Research Design: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed Methods, Arts-Based, and Community-Based Participatory Research Approaches (2017)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 8 — Measurement Theory — Before You Measure Anything
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)

name: Opinion Dynamics Simulation
origin: Voter and majority models from statistical physics; bounded confidence models by Deffuant et al. (2000) and Hegselmann and Krause (2002); the Hierarchical Ising Opinion Model by van der Maas, Dalege and Waldorp (2020).
summary: Agent-based simulations in which people with opinions interact under simple rules (copying, averaging, ignoring those too different) to explore how consensus, clusters or polarisation emerge in a community.
description: Opinion dynamics models share three building blocks: a network of who talks to whom, an interaction rule, and a definition of opinion as discrete or continuous. In voter models an agent copies a neighbour; in majority models it adopts the local majority. In bounded confidence models, agents only move toward others whose opinions lie within a bound: wide bounds give consensus, narrow bounds give stable clusters and polarisation, and raising the bound after polarisation may not undo it. The book's own Hierarchical Ising Opinion Model gives each agent a cusp-shaped opinion driven by information and attention, with interactions that raise attention. It reproduces a persuasion paradox: highly attentive activists entering a low-attention community can raise opponents' attention and polarise them rather than convert them. The book is frank that empirical data rarely discriminate between such models, so their main value is qualitative and robust predictions, such as that zealots increase polarisation. For UX researchers, these simulations are a thinking tool for community products, review systems, social features and advocacy campaigns, letting teams explore how design levers like exposure range or prompting engagement could shift group-level outcomes.
steps: Define the research question at group level, for example whether a feed setting could reduce polarisation in a community.
Choose a network topology, an opinion definition (binary, continuous, or cusp with attention) and an interaction rule matching the question.
Implement the model in NetLogo or R, starting from published versions such as Deffuant, Hegselmann-Krause or HIOM.
Run parameter sweeps for the design-relevant levers, such as exposure bound, share of highly engaged users or noise.
Record group outcomes (consensus, number of clusters, polarisation) across many runs and check for hysteresis by reversing parameter changes.
Compare the qualitative patterns with whatever field data exist and present results as scenarios, not forecasts.
outputs: Maps of how group outcomes such as consensus, clustering and polarisation depend on interaction rules and parameters, plus scenario narratives for design decisions.
useWhen: A design decision affects who sees or interacts with whom in a community and you need to reason about emergent group outcomes that small user studies cannot show.
avoidWhen: Stakeholders expect quantitative forecasts, or the product has no meaningful peer interaction.
whyLost: These models live in physics and computational sociology journals, are hard to validate against data, and require simulation skills seldom found in UX teams.
whereToUse: Social platforms and feeds, community forums, review and rating systems, internal collaboration tools, behaviour-change campaigns that rely on peer influence.
example: A forum product considers showing users only posts close to their past stance. A bounded confidence simulation shows that narrowing exposure produces stable separate clusters and that widening it later does not restore a shared middle, prompting the team to test cross-cutting exposure with small cohorts before rollout.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Opinion leader identification
origin: Katz and Lazarsfeld (1955); Kelly et al. (1997); Valente et al. (2002); synthesised by Rogers (2003)
summary: Identify the people others turn to for advice using sociometric, key-informant, self-designation or observation methods, then recruit them to spread an innovation and measure the effect.
description: Diffusion research shows that adoption flows through informal advice networks, so finding the people others consult is a practical lever. Four measurement methods are roughly equally valid: sociometric (ask every member of a bounded system whom they seek advice from, with limited, unlimited or roster choices), key informants (a person nominated by two or more informants counts as a leader), self-designation (a scale suited to random samples) and observation (for example noting who is most often greeted and well liked). Hybrid ladders ask each nominee to name someone more influential until a person names themselves. Interventions then train leaders, give them prompts and tasks, retrain them over time and evaluate with before-after surveys against control units. Effects are reliable when enough leaders are recruited; failures in the literature recruited under about 15 per cent of the audience.
steps: Define the topic and the bounded system (team, organisation, community), since leadership is topic-specific.
Choose a method: sociometric census, key informants, self-designation scale or observation.
Identify leaders as the most nominated people, or anyone nominated by two or more informants.
Recruit enough leaders to reach about 15 per cent of the audience; where possible assign each person to the leader they nominated.
Train leaders, give them prompts and tasks, and retrain them periodically so they do not lapse.
Evaluate with before-after surveys or behavioural measures in intervention and control units.
outputs: A list of opinion leaders and their network position, and a measured effect of leader-led diffusion against controls.
useWhen: Adoption of a product, feature or behaviour depends on peer influence within a bounded group, such as enterprise rollouts or community health programmes.
avoidWhen: Avoid in open, unbounded consumer markets where no census is possible, or when adoption is driven by price or mandate; use segmentation or experiments instead. Sociometry needs a full census, and leaders lapse without retraining.
whyLost: It belongs to communication and public health intervention research; UX teams rarely own rollout or measure diffusion through networks.
whereToUse: Enterprise software rollouts and champions programmes, clinical tool adoption, developer communities, and behaviour-change services.
example: Before rolling out a new clinical records system across a hospital, the research team asks every nurse whom they ask for help with the current system. The 12 most-nominated nurses become trained champions on each ward, and adoption metrics are compared with two wards using standard training.
reference: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). Free Press; Kelly, J. A. et al. (1997), as cited there.

name: Opportunity Solution Tree
origin: Teresa Torres, 2016; published in Continuous Discovery Habits (2021)
summary: A living visual map linking a desired product outcome to research-derived opportunities, candidate solutions and assumption tests, kept current through weekly customer interviews.
description: The opportunity solution tree structures continuous discovery as a hierarchy: a single measurable desired outcome at the root, opportunities (unmet needs, pain points and desires drawn from customer interviews) beneath it, solutions under each opportunity, and assumption tests under each solution. Opportunities are broken into smaller sub-opportunities until they are tractable. The tree makes reasoning visible: teams compare and contrast sibling options rather than evaluating ideas in isolation, and every solution traces back to evidence and to the outcome. Rigour comes from deriving opportunities from story-based interviews (not feature requests), keeping the tree updated weekly, choosing a target opportunity explicitly, generating multiple solutions per opportunity, and testing the riskiest assumptions before building. It functions as both a synthesis artefact and a decision record.
steps: Desired outcome at the top: The business or product metric research is helping move. Keeps the tree anchored to consequential decisions.
Map opportunities from research: Each opportunity is an unmet user need, stated at the level of the user's goal. Not solutions.
Multiple solutions per opportunity: 2–5 candidate solutions per opportunity before any are tested. Prevents premature commitment.
Experiments per solution: Each solution has a testable assumption and an experiment. This is where research connects to product action.
Update after every research session: The OST is not a report — it is a living model updated in real time.
outputs: A maintained opportunity solution tree, interview snapshots, a chosen target opportunity, compared solution sets and an assumption test backlog.
useWhen: Product teams practising continuous discovery who need to connect ongoing research to outcome-based roadmaps and to explain why they are building what they are building.
avoidWhen: When there is no agreed measurable outcome, or for one-off evaluative studies; then define the outcome first or use a standard research plan.
whyLost: Still in use: Continuous discovery methodology integration; widely taught in product communities.
whereToUse: Continuous discovery programs; OKR-connected research; product strategy. Continuous discovery programs, product discovery, research-to-roadmap translation, cross-functional product teams.
example: A fintech team's outcome is increasing monthly savings deposits. Weekly interviews surface the opportunity 'I don't know how much I can safely save after bills', which they target with three solutions, testing a 'safe to save' estimate via a fake-door experiment before building.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
Opportunities for Generative AI in UX Modernization (Houde et al., 2022)
reference: Torres T (2021) Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products That Create Customer Value and Business Value. Product Talk

name: Optimal Design Criteria and Design Efficiency (A-, D-, E-Optimality)
origin: Abraham Wald (1943), Ehrenfeld (1953) and Jack Kiefer (1958, 1975); efficiency factor after Yates; Hedayat and Majumdar (1984) for control comparisons
summary: Compare candidate experimental layouts before running them by how precisely they estimate the comparisons that matter, using the efficiency factor and A-, D- or E-criteria.
description: Optimal design theory scores a design's information matrix before any data are collected. The efficiency factor of a block design is the average variance of pairwise treatment differences under an unblocked design with the same replication divided by that under the candidate; it has a known upper bound, so a design's closeness to the best possible can be judged. D-optimality maximises the determinant of the information matrix (smallest joint confidence region), A-optimality minimises the average variance of the contrasts, and E-optimality minimises the variance of the worst-estimated contrast. Balanced designs such as BIBDs, Latin squares and Youden squares are optimal on all three (Kiefer's universal optimality). For test-versus-control designs, A-optimality is applied to control comparisons only. Hinkelmann and Kempthorne warn that optimality is tied to one criterion while real experimenters have several, so a near-balanced design with checked efficiency is often the practical answer.
steps: State the comparisons of interest: all pairs, test versus control, or model parameters.
List candidate designs that respect practical constraints such as block size, number of participants or sessions.
Compute each candidate's information matrix from its incidence or model matrix.
Score candidates on the efficiency factor against its upper bound and on the A-, D- or E-criterion that matches the inferential goal.
Prefer a balanced design where one exists; otherwise choose a candidate with efficiency close to the bound (above about 0.8 is a common target), weighing other practical criteria.
Record the chosen design's efficiency in the study plan so loss from dropouts can be assessed later.
outputs: Efficiency factors and optimality scores for each candidate design, and a justified choice of layout.
useWhen: Planning conjoint, MaxDiff, multi-variant or incomplete-block studies where layout choices affect precision, or checking a vendor-generated design before fielding.
avoidWhen: Simple two-arm A/B tests where power analysis is all that is needed (Statistical power analysis); designs that must adapt to prior beliefs (Bayesian Design of Experiments for UX); exploratory or qualitative work where estimation precision is not the goal.
whyLost: D-efficiency survives inside conjoint and choice-modelling software, but UX researchers rarely compare designs themselves and the criteria remain the province of statisticians.
whereToUse: Conjoint and discrete choice studies, MaxDiff designs, multi-factor experiments with constrained sessions, incomplete-block rating studies.
example: A pricing team's software proposes a 12-task choice design with D-efficiency 0.71. Comparing three alternatives, they choose one at 0.93 with the same participant burden, cutting the sample needed for the same precision by roughly a quarter.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 2 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2005)
reference: Kiefer, J. (1958). On the nonrandomized optimality and randomized nonoptimality of symmetrical designs. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 29, 675-699; Hinkelmann, K., & Kempthorne, O. (2005). Design and Analysis of Experiments, Volume 2, pp. 43-52, 196-212.

name: Option set design for low-bandwidth environments
donor: Behavioural economics of scarcity and cognitive psychology
origin: Mullainathan and Shafir's Scarcity (2013) on cognitive bandwidth, combined with Hick-Hyman law (1952–1953) and choice architecture (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008)
summary: Designs and tests option sets for users with constrained cognitive, time or connectivity bandwidth, minimising options, sequencing choices and making safe defaults explicit.
description: Scarcity research shows that people under poverty, time pressure or high workload have reduced cognitive bandwidth, measurable as lower fluid intelligence and executive control scores; Mani and colleagues (2013) found effects comparable to losing a night's sleep. Users in under-resourced clinics, informal markets or on intermittent connections face both cognitive and technical bandwidth limits. This method redesigns option sets for these conditions: fewer simultaneous options, staged decisions, triage-first ordering, offline-safe defaults, and option labels that need no comparison work. Rigour comes from testing designs under realistic load (dual-task conditions, time pressure, interruption, low connectivity) rather than in quiet labs, and from measuring error rates on critical choices, not just speed.
steps: Characterise the bandwidth constraints in the field: decision time available, interruptions per hour, concurrent tasks, literacy, and network quality (latency, outages), through at least 2 to 3 days of observation.
Map each decision point and count simultaneous options, comparisons required and information needed per option.
Redesign so that critical decisions show no more than about 3 to 5 options at once, are sequenced from most to least consequential, and include an explicit safe default for the common case.
Make every option work offline or degrade gracefully, and avoid choices that require loading remote content before they can be compared.
Test original and redesigned sets with 8 to 15 representative users under realistic load, for example a secondary counting task, a 30-second time limit or scripted interruptions.
Compare critical-choice error rates, decision time and NASA-TLX workload scores, and iterate until critical error rate is at or near zero.
outputs: A bandwidth profile of the use context, redesigned option sets with sequencing and defaults, and comparative error, time and workload data under realistic load.
useWhen: Designing for frontline workers, low-income users, emergency or clinical triage, or regions with unreliable connectivity, where wrong choices carry real cost.
avoidWhen: Users are unhurried experts who need full option breadth and comparison, such as analysts configuring complex tools; use standard usability testing and progressive disclosure there.
whyLost: Scarcity research influenced development economics and policy design but rarely entered UX method toolkits, which assume unhurried, well-resourced, always-online users.
whereToUse: Community health and triage apps, agricultural and microfinance services, government benefit applications, field-service and logistics tools, emergency response interfaces.
example: A clinic triage screen offered 14 symptom categories at once. Redesigned as three danger-sign questions first, then 4 categories, with offline default 'refer if unsure', it cut triage misclassification under time pressure from 18% to 6% in simulated sessions with nurses.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Mullainathan, S., & Shafir, E. (2013). Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much. Times Books; Mani, A., Mullainathan, S., Shafir, E., & Zhao, J. (2013). Poverty impedes cognitive function. Science, 341(6149), 976–980.

name: Ordinal Regression
origin: Peter McCullagh, 1980 (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B)
summary: Models Likert and other ordered-category responses as ordinal, not interval, estimating how predictors shift the odds of higher response categories.
description: Likert items are ordered categories: the distance between 'agree' and 'strongly agree' is not known to equal that between 'neutral' and 'agree'. Treating them as interval numbers and comparing means can produce misleading effects, including spurious differences or even sign reversals, as shown by Liddell and Kruschke (2018). Ordinal regression, typically the proportional odds or cumulative link model, models the probability of responding at or below each category threshold as a function of predictors. Coefficients express how predictors shift the latent response, interpretable as odds ratios. Assumptions such as proportional odds are tested, and mixed-effects or Bayesian versions handle repeated measures. Its rigour lies in matching the model to the measurement level of the data.
steps: Confirm the outcome is an ordered categorical variable, such as a single Likert item or ordered rating, and inspect the response distribution.
Specify a cumulative link model (logit or probit) with relevant predictors such as design variant, segment or task.
Fit the model in a suitable tool (for example R ordinal, statsmodels OrderedModel, SPSS PLUM or brms) and add random effects for participants if responses are repeated.
Test the proportional odds assumption, for example with a Brant test or by comparing to a partial proportional odds model.
Report odds ratios with confidence or credible intervals and predicted probabilities for each category, rather than mean scores.
Visualise predicted category distributions by condition to communicate results to stakeholders.
outputs: Model coefficients and odds ratios, threshold estimates, assumption tests, predicted category probabilities and plots of response distributions by condition.
useWhen: Analysing single Likert items, satisfaction ratings, ease ratings (such as SEQ) or any ordered categorical outcome, especially when comparing groups or designs.
avoidWhen: The outcome is a validated multi-item scale score that approximates interval data (such as SUS totals), where linear models are often acceptable; or the categories are unordered (use multinomial models).
whyLost: Likert data is treated as interval in most UX studies because spreadsheet tools default to means and t-tests, and ordinal models are rarely taught to practitioners.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and CSAT surveys, post-task ratings, A/B tests with rating outcomes, survey programmes tracked over time, and benchmark studies.
example: Reanalysing 6 months of satisfaction surveys with ordinal regression, a team finds the redesign shifted responses mainly from 'neutral' to 'agree' for new users, while mean comparisons had suggested no change overall.
sources: LOGISTIC REGRESSION procedures; Hayes PROCESS macro v4
Liddell & Kruschke (2018) Analyzing ordinal data with metric models: What could possibly go wrong? Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
The Inquiry Series, Vol III, Ch 42
The Inquiry Series, Ch 42 — Ordinal Logic — Treating Likert & Survey Data Correctly
The Inquiry Series, C2 — Quantitative UX Analysis in Python — Descriptive to Inferential
The Inquiry Series, C8 — SPSS for Regression, Moderation & Mediation
Quantitative User Experience Research — Chris Chapman
Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: McCullagh, P. (1980). Regression models for ordinal data. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 42(2), 109-142.

name: Ordinal Trend Tests for Contingency Tables (Linear-by-Linear and Cochran-Armitage)
aka: Test for linear trend in proportions
origin: Cochran (1954) and Armitage (1955) for trend in proportions; linear-by-linear association model in the Goodman tradition; presented by Alan Agresti, 1996
summary: One-degree-of-freedom tests and a matching model for whether an ordered outcome rises or falls across ordered groups, far more powerful than a nominal chi-square.
description: A chi-square test of independence ignores category order and spreads its power across many degrees of freedom. When rows, columns or both are ordinal, scores are assigned to categories and the correlation r between row and column scores is tested: M squared = (n - 1) r squared, referred to chi-square on 1 df. With a binary column this becomes the Cochran-Armitage test for a linear trend in a proportion across ordered groups; with a binary row it compares mean scores, and midrank scores give rank tests such as Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney. The linear-by-linear association loglinear model gives the same test plus an estimated local odds ratio. Scores should reflect plausible distances, and because conclusions can shift with unbalanced data, a sensitivity check with two or three score sets is advised.
steps: Assign monotone scores to row and column categories (midpoints, equal spacing or midranks).
Compute the Pearson correlation r between row and column scores over all n observations.
Compute M squared = (n - 1) r squared and refer it to chi-square on 1 df, or M to the standard normal for a one-sided trend.
If one variable is binary, read the result as a trend in the proportion across ordered groups (Cochran-Armitage) or a difference in mean scores.
If one variable is nominal with more than two categories, use the row-means score statistic on I-1 df instead.
Optionally fit the linear-by-linear association model to estimate the local odds ratio and check fit with G squared.
Repeat with alternative sensible scores and report whether the conclusion holds.
outputs: M squared and p-value, the score correlation, and an estimated local odds ratio with fit statistics.
useWhen: Testing whether satisfaction bands, Likert responses or task outcomes shift with an ordered factor such as usage frequency, plan tier, age band or number of onboarding steps completed.
avoidWhen: Both variables nominal (use Chi-Square and Fisher's Exact Tests); a non-monotone pattern is expected, where the trend test loses its power advantage; or covariates must be adjusted, where Ordinal Regression is better.
whyLost: UX survey crosstabs are usually run with the default Pearson chi-square, and order-aware tests remain a categorical-data-analysis topic rarely taught outside statistics.
whereToUse: Survey crosstabs by ordered segments, dose-response questions in onboarding or engagement, tracking studies with banded metrics.
example: A survey team crosses five satisfaction levels with four bands of weekly use (n = 2,400). The nominal chi-square on 12 df is borderline, but M squared on 1 df gives p = 0.002, showing satisfaction rises steadily with use; equal and midpoint scores agree.
sources: An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Agresti, A. (1996). An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis. New York: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 34-39, 180-185.

name: Ordinal vs. interval distinction
origin: S. S. Stevens, 'On the theory of scales of measurement' (1946); debate on Likert analysis by Jamieson (2004), Norman (2010) and Liddell and Kruschke (2018)
summary: Determines whether rating data can be treated as interval (equal distances) or only ordinal (ranked), and chooses summaries and models that respect the scale's properties.
description: Stevens defined four levels of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio, each permitting different operations. A single Likert item, for example 1 to 5 agreement, is ordinal: the distance from 'agree' to 'strongly agree' is not guaranteed to equal that from 'neutral' to 'agree'. Means and t-tests assume interval properties. Norman (2010) argued parametric tests are robust in many cases, especially for multi-item scale totals, while Liddell and Kruschke (2018) showed that treating ordinal data as metric can produce wrong conclusions, including inverted effects, when distributions differ in shape. The practical rule is to treat single items as ordinal, consider summed multi-item scales as approximately interval if validated, and use ordinal models when distributions are skewed, have ceiling effects or differ in variance.
steps: Classify each measure: single rating item, multi-item validated scale (for example SUS or UMUX-Lite) or a behavioural count or time.
For single items, report the distribution (percentages per response option) and medians, and use top-box or top-two-box shares where interpretable.
Check distributions for ceiling or floor effects, skew and unequal variances between groups.

Analyse single items with ordinal models (cumulative logit or probit regression) or rank-based tests, and reserve means and t-tests for validated multi-item scales with approximately symmetric distributions.
Where both approaches are plausible, run both and report whether conclusions differ.
Communicate results in terms of response distributions or probabilities (for example 'the probability of rating 4 or 5 rose from 52% to 61%').
outputs: A measurement-level classification for each metric, distributions, appropriate ordinal or interval analyses, and a sensitivity comparison where relevant.
useWhen: Analysing satisfaction, Likert, NPS-style or single-item ratings, and reviewing dashboards that average rating scales.
avoidWhen: Measures are validated multi-item scales with well-behaved distributions, where interval treatment is generally acceptable; or the data are behavioural ratio measures.
whyLost: Measurement theory is taught in psychology but UX dashboards average everything, and the convenience of a single mean has overridden concerns about scale properties.
whereToUse: Satisfaction surveys, post-task ratings, CSAT dashboards, NPS analysis, in-product feedback widgets.
example: Six months of satisfaction ratings had been reported as a mean rising from 3.9 to 4.0. Reanalysis as ordinal showed more 5s but also more 1s after a release, a polarisation hidden by the mean, which an ordinal regression confirmed.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 42 — Ordinal Logic — Treating Likert & Survey Data Correctly
reference: Stevens, S. S. (1946). On the theory of scales of measurement. Science, 103(2684), 677–680; Liddell, T. M., & Kruschke, J. K. (2018). Analyzing ordinal data with metric models: What could possibly go wrong? Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 79, 328–348.

name: Organisational Ethnography and Workplace Studies
origin: Workplace studies at Xerox PARC and Lancaster in the 1980s to 1990s (Suchman; Heath and Luff; Hughes)
summary: Long-term immersive study of how work is actually accomplished, including coordination, workarounds and breakdowns, compared with how procedures say it should be done.
description: Organisational ethnography and workplace studies (originating in sociology and later developed in CSCW research) examine how work is practically accomplished within organisations. They reveal the gap between formal procedure and actual practice — the workarounds, informal knowledge systems, and social negotiations that enable work to happen. CSCW (Computer-Supported Cooperative Work) ethnography specifically examines how technology mediates collaborative work, making it directly applicable to enterprise UX research.
steps: Extended fieldwork (weeks to months): Cannot be done as a two-hour observation. Requires sufficient time to move past the 'front stage' performance of work to the 'backstage' practices.
Work practice documentation: Document not just what workers do but how they co-ordinate: how they alert each other, hand off work, resolve conflicts, repair failures, and adapt to unexpected events.
Breakdown analysis: Pay special attention to breakdowns — moments when the smooth flow of work is interrupted. Breakdowns reveal the tacit infrastructure that normally makes work possible.

Artefact archaeology: Analyse all the physical and digital artefacts produced by work: forms, logs, spreadsheets, whiteboards, post-it notes. Each artefact is evidence of a need the formal system failed to meet.

Participation in work: Where feasible and ethical, participate in the work alongside workers. The knowledge gained through doing work is qualitatively different from the knowledge gained through watching it.
outputs: Thick field notes, accounts of coordination and articulation work, a catalogue of workarounds and breakdowns, artefact analyses, and requirements grounded in actual practice.
useWhen: Designing or replacing systems for complex, collaborative work such as control rooms, hospitals, logistics, finance operations or support centres, where formal process differs from practice.
avoidWhen: You lack weeks of access or need quick tactical answers; use contextual inquiry or shadowing. For individual consumer behaviour, a diary study is more suitable.
whyLost: Commercial UX compressed ethnography into two-hour site visits, and the extended fieldwork that made CSCW workplace studies insightful became too slow and expensive for product cycles.
whereToUse: Enterprise and internal tools, healthcare IT, operations and logistics platforms, AI automation of knowledge work, and collaborative software.
example: Before automating dispatch, a logistics company embeds a researcher in a control room for 6 weeks. She documents how dispatchers glance at colleagues' screens to anticipate problems, informal coordination the planned automation would have destroyed.
sources: Qualitative Methods in Information Retrieval Research (Fidel, 1993)
reference: Heath, C. & Luff, P. (2000). Technology in Action. Cambridge University Press.

name: Out-of-Box Setup Testing
aka: Out-of-Box Setup Testing with a Complaint Threshold
origin: Practice reported from BRCK and Sifteo in Rowland et al. (2015)
summary: Observe people unboxing and setting up a physical product unaided, revise guides and packaging, and retest weekly until a simple time or complaint threshold is met.
description: Connected and consumer hardware products often fail at first contact: people skim quick-start guides, misread status lights and are unsure of cable orientation. Out-of-box testing hands participants the product exactly as shipped and watches unboxing, guide use, physical connection and registration without help. Its distinctive rigour is a simple stopping rule. BRCK set a 10 to 20 minute set-up target; Sifteo, unable to change a battery mechanism, tested ten arrow-sticker versions and each week had 10 to 15 people try set-up until fewer than 2 in 10 complained. Because problems are often found after hardware is frozen, fixes target the cheapest layers first: instructions, labels, packaging, videos and online help. Support contacts after launch continue the evaluation.
steps: Give participants the packaged product exactly as shipped, with no briefing beyond the scenario.
Observe unboxing, use of printed guides, physical connection, power-up and registration without help.
Record confusions and time to a working state.
Set a simple threshold, such as set-up within 10 to 20 minutes or fewer than 2 in 10 participants complaining.
Revise the cheapest layers first when hardware is frozen: instructions, labels, stickers, packaging, videos and online help, keeping print and on-screen diagrams identical to the shipped part.
Retest weekly with 10 to 15 fresh participants until the threshold is met.
After launch, keep monitoring set-up problems through support contacts.
outputs: Set-up times, complaint rates, a list of first-run failures, and revised guides, labels and packaging.
useWhen: Launching hardware, IoT devices, kits or any product whose first use requires physical assembly, pairing or account set-up.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the only test of ongoing use; for software-only onboarding use Moderated Usability Testing or funnel analytics.
whyLost: It lives in hardware companies and consumer electronics teams, while mainstream digital UX rarely handles physical packaging.
whereToUse: Smart home devices, wearables, medical devices for home use, routers, subscription boxes with app pairing.
example: A smart-thermostat start-up runs weekly unboxing sessions with 12 people. Pairing failures drop below 2 in 10 after a coloured wiring sticker and a QR code to a video are added.
reference: Rowland, C., Goodman, E., Charlier, M., Light, A. and Lui, A. (2015). Designing Connected Products: UX for the Consumer Internet of Things. O'Reilly Media.

name: Outcome-Driven Innovation
origin: Anthony Ulwick, Strategyn, early 1990s; published in What Customers Want (2005)
summary: Quantitative jobs method that rates standardised desired-outcome statements for importance and satisfaction, then uses the opportunity score to locate underserved needs.
description: Outcome-driven innovation operationalises jobs-to-be-done quantitatively. Researchers first map the core job into steps (define, locate, prepare, confirm, execute, monitor, modify, conclude) and capture 50-150 desired outcome statements in a fixed syntax: direction, metric, object and context, such as 'minimise the time it takes to reconcile a transaction'. A large survey then rates each outcome for importance and current satisfaction. The opportunity algorithm, importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0), identifies underserved outcomes (scores above roughly 10 on a 0-20 scale) and overserved ones. Segmenting respondents by their unmet outcomes reveals needs-based segments. Its rigour lies in the standardised statement syntax and sample sizes large enough for segment-level estimates; it is often discussed but rarely executed in full.
steps: Define the job executor and core functional job, and map it into job steps using the universal job map.
Conduct 12-20 qualitative interviews to capture desired outcome statements, written as direction, metric, object and clarifier.
Deduplicate and refine to 50-150 statements, then field a survey to 180-600 job executors rating importance and satisfaction on 5-point scales.
Compute top-two-box percentages and opportunity scores (importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0)) for each outcome.
Plot the opportunity landscape and flag underserved outcomes (score above about 10) and overserved ones.
Run cluster analysis on outcome ratings to find needs-based segments and prioritise features against the underserved outcomes.
outputs: Job map, desired outcome statements, opportunity scores and landscape plot, needs-based segments and prioritised innovation targets.
useWhen: Prioritising a roadmap in a mature market, finding underserved needs at scale, building needs-based segments and sizing opportunities.
avoidWhen: When the job is not yet understood (start with qualitative JTBD interviews), when you cannot reach a few hundred job executors, or for novel categories where people cannot rate outcomes meaningfully.
whyLost: Latent: Rigorous and powerful; complex process; used in specialized product strategy contexts.
whereToUse: Product portfolio decisions; market segmentation; competitive strategy.
example: An accounting SaaS surveys 400 bookkeepers on 92 outcomes. 'Minimise the time to identify the source of a reconciliation discrepancy' scores 15.2, well above others, redirecting a quarter's roadmap from reporting features to discrepancy tracing.
sources: Jobs to be Done: Theory to Practice (Anthony Ulwick)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Ulwick AW (2005) What Customers Want: Using Outcome-Driven Innovation to Create Breakthrough Products and Services. McGraw-Hill

name: Overconfidence Calibration for UX Researchers
donor: Judgement and decision-making psychology and forecasting
origin: Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein (1977); calibration training later applied in forecasting by Tetlock and in measurement by Hubbard
summary: Elicits researchers' and users' 90% confidence intervals or probability forecasts, scores how often they contain the truth, and trains teams toward well-calibrated predictions.
description: Calibration measures whether stated confidence matches accuracy: a well-calibrated person's 90% confidence intervals contain the true value about 90% of the time, and events they rate 70% likely occur about 70% of the time. Most people, including experts, are overconfident, with nominal 90% intervals capturing the truth only 40-60% of the time. For UX teams the method has two uses. First, researchers and stakeholders record predictions before studies (for example task success rate or conversion lift) and are scored afterwards with hit rates or Brier scores, revealing systematic overconfidence and making the value of research visible. Second, user confidence ratings during tasks can be compared with actual correctness to locate interfaces that make people confidently wrong. Calibration improves measurably with feedback and practice.
steps: Researchers provide 90% CI estimates for study outcomes.
After study, compute hit rate.
Calibration target: hit rate within ±10% of stated confidence level.
Run as Discovery Series exercise.
outputs: Hit rates for confidence intervals, Brier scores, calibration curves for researchers and users, and records of pre-study predictions against outcomes.
useWhen: Before studies and experiments to log predictions, when estimating metrics for business cases, and for interfaces where user confidence must match accuracy (finance, health, AI outputs).
avoidWhen: When there will be no ground truth to score predictions against, or for purely exploratory research without quantitative outcomes.
whyLost: Calibration lives in forecasting, intelligence analysis and decision science; UX teams rarely record predictions, so their overconfidence is never measured or corrected.
whereToUse: Research team debiasing, forecast-based planning, pre-registration.
example: Before an onboarding A/B test, eight product team members give 90% intervals for the activation lift; only two intervals contain the observed 1.8% lift. Repeating the exercise over six experiments narrows the team's estimates and tempers roadmap commitments.
sources: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974 paper) (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
reference: Fischhoff B, Slovic P & Lichtenstein S (1977) Knowing with certainty: The appropriateness of extreme confidence. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 3(4):552-564

name: OWAS posture analysis
origin: Ovako Oy steel company, Finland, 1973 (Karhu, Kansi and Kuorinka, 1977); applied to treadmills by Gao et al. (2022)
summary: Observe users on video, code each posture of back, arms and legs with the OWAS scheme and assign an action category from AC1 (no action) to AC4 (act immediately).
description: OWAS classifies whole-body working postures by combining codes for back, arms, legs and the load handled. Each combination maps to one of four action categories: AC1 normal, no action needed; AC2 slightly harmful, improve in the near future; AC3 distinctly harmful, improve as soon as possible; AC4 extremely harmful, improve immediately. Observers film users without interference, keeping the whole body in frame, sample postures over time, count how often each combination occurs per activity, and code poor postures. Because it rates the frequency and severity of postures rather than a single snapshot, it supports prioritising physical design changes. In product UX it extends evaluation of physical devices beyond task success to injury risk.
steps: Define the activities of use to observe.
Film users unobtrusively over sampled periods, keeping the whole body in frame.
Sample postures at regular intervals and count posture combinations per activity.
Code each posture for back, arms, legs and load with the OWAS chart.
Assign each combination an action category from AC1 to AC4 and compute the share of time in each.
Prioritise design changes for AC4 and AC3 postures, then AC2, and re-observe after redesign.
outputs: Posture codes and action categories per activity, time shares by category, and a prioritised list of ergonomic improvements.
useWhen: Evaluating physical products, kiosks, equipment or workstations where repeated or sustained postures could cause strain or injury.
avoidWhen: Avoid for purely screen-based tasks with seated users; for detailed upper-limb risk use RULA instead. Coarse codes miss fine hand and wrist strain, and small observation samples weaken conclusions.
whyLost: It is a standard occupational ergonomics tool that rarely crosses into UX teams, who seldom evaluate bodily strain.
whereToUse: Fitness and medical equipment, retail and warehouse devices, kiosks and point-of-sale stations, vehicle interiors and shared workstations.
example: A gym equipment maker films members using a treadmill console. Reaching to grip the heart-rate handles while running codes as AC3, so the redesign adds a chest-strap pairing prompt and moves the handles.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Karhu, O., Kansi, P. & Kuorinka, I. (1977). Correcting working postures in industry: a practical method for analysis. Applied Ergonomics 8(4), 199-201; Gao, M. et al. (2022). Usability Assessment and Improvement Plan for Treadmills in Campus Gym. DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, Springer, pp. 401-413.

name: P(error) logistic regression
origin: Logistic regression: Cox, 1958; applied to pointing error rates in HCI by Bi and Zhai (2016) among others
summary: Models the probability that an interaction fails from design and context variables, giving a curve that shows the size or time needed for an acceptable error rate.
description: Instead of reporting a single error rate, logistic regression models log(p/(1-p)) = b0 + b1x1 + ..., where p is the probability of error and the predictors are target size, distance, glove use, time pressure, user experience and so on. The fitted curve gives the predicted error probability at any design value, with confidence intervals, and identifies which factors matter once others are controlled. Mixed-effects logistic models add random intercepts for participants and items, which is essential because repeated trials from one user are not independent. The design team can then read off the target size required for, say, P(error) below 1%. Rigour comes from sufficient events (at least 10 errors per predictor), checking calibration, and avoiding extrapolation beyond tested ranges.
steps: Specify the binary outcome (error or not) and candidate predictors (size, distance, condition, user group, fatigue).
Collect trial-level data across a range of predictor values; ensure at least 10 error events per predictor parameter.
Fit a mixed-effects logistic regression with random intercepts for participant (and item if relevant).
Check model fit and calibration (for example Hosmer-Lemeshow or calibration plot) and report odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
Invert the curve to find the design value at which predicted P(error) meets the risk threshold (for example 1% for routine, 0.1% for critical actions).
Validate predictions on a held-out sample or follow-up study.
outputs: Fitted error-probability curves, odds ratios per factor, design thresholds for acceptable error rates, and model diagnostics.
useWhen: When you have trial-level interaction data and need to set design parameters to an error budget, or to know which factors drive errors.
avoidWhen: When errors are too rare to model (fewer than about 30 events) or when the question is qualitative error mechanisms; use error taxonomies or incident analysis.
whyLost: UX reports aggregate error percentages; regression modelling sits with statisticians, and few teams collect trial-level data needed for it.
whereToUse: Touch and pointing design, form validation, safety-critical inputs, voice recognition thresholds, and checkout error reduction.
example: Using 6,000 gloved taps, a model shows each extra millimetre of target width halves the odds of error (OR 0.52) while table vibration doubles them. Inverting the curve, the team specifies 15 mm buttons to keep predicted error below 1% even under vibration.
sources: Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 3 — The Ballistics of the Human Body — Fitts' Law & Motor Control
reference: Hosmer, D. W., Lemeshow, S. & Sturdivant, R. X. (2013). Applied Logistic Regression (3rd ed.). Wiley.

name: P-value correct interpretation
origin: Ronald Fisher (1925) and Neyman-Pearson hypothesis testing (1933); misinterpretations catalogued by Goodman (2008) and the ASA Statement on p-values (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016)
summary: Applies the correct meaning of a p-value, the probability of data at least this extreme if the null model were true, and avoids its common misreadings in UX decisions.
description: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis and all model assumptions are true, of observing data at least as extreme as those observed. It is not the probability that the null is true, not the probability that the result is due to chance, and not a measure of effect size or importance. The ASA's 2016 statement set out six principles, including that scientific conclusions should not rest only on whether p passes 0.05. In UX, misinterpretation leads to shipping trivial effects with large samples, dismissing important effects with small samples, and treating p = 0.06 and p = 0.04 as opposites. Correct interpretation pairs p-values with effect sizes and confidence intervals, pre-specified alpha and power, and attention to multiple testing and analytic flexibility.
steps: State the null and alternative hypotheses and the alpha level (commonly 0.05) before seeing data, along with the planned test.
Check the test's assumptions (independence, distribution, equal variances or appropriate corrections) and choose an alternative test if violated.
Report the exact p-value (for example p = 0.032, not p < 0.05) together with the effect size and its 95% confidence interval.
Interpret using correct wording: 'If there were no true difference, data this extreme would occur about 3% of the time', not 'there is a 97% chance the variant is better'.
Judge practical significance against a pre-defined smallest effect of interest, separately from statistical significance.
For non-significant results, report the interval and power, and do not claim 'no effect' unless an equivalence test supports it.
outputs: Correctly worded statistical results with exact p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals and explicit statements of practical significance.
useWhen: Reporting any frequentist test in UX research, A/B testing or survey analysis, and reviewing others' statistical claims.
avoidWhen: Questions are better answered with estimation (intervals and effect sizes alone) or Bayesian probabilities, such as 'how likely is B better than A'; use credible intervals then.
whyLost: P-values are used everywhere in UX and experimentation dashboards, but the interpretation has been reduced to a binary 'significant or not', and the original logic is widely misunderstood.
whereToUse: A/B test readouts, survey comparisons, usability benchmark comparisons, experimentation governance and research review.
example: A Trust Badge test returned p = 0.21 with 400 users per arm, and a stakeholder concluded the badge 'does nothing'. Re-reporting the 95% CI for the uplift (-1.2% to +5.4%) and the study's 35% power showed the test was inconclusive, not negative.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Wasserstein, R. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA statement on p-values: Context, process, and purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2), 129–133.

name: PACT Analysis
origin: David Benyon, Phil Turner and Susan Turner (2005); used in HCI texts including Dix et al.
summary: A structured framework for scoping interactive systems by analysing the People, Activities, Contexts and Technologies involved and how they constrain each other.
description: PACT analysis provides a compact checklist for understanding the design space before design begins. People covers physical, psychological and social differences, skills and knowledge; Activities covers temporal aspects (frequency, interruptions, time pressure), cooperation, complexity, safety-criticality and content; Contexts covers physical, social and organisational settings; Technologies covers input, output, communication and content capabilities. The insight is that these elements co-evolve: changing a technology changes activities and contexts. A rigorous PACT analysis is populated from research evidence rather than brainstorming, notes the variability within each element, and produces scenarios and requirements traceable to specific PACT combinations. It is taught widely in HCI courses but rarely used explicitly in industry, where it is replaced by ad hoc personas and journey maps.
steps: People: Who are the users? What range of: physical abilities, cognitive abilities, cultural backgrounds, prior knowledge, task experience, emotional states, and goals? Do not assume a single user type.

Activities: What tasks are performed? What is their temporal structure (frequency, duration, sequence)? What is their cognitive demand? What cooperation is involved? What are the consequences of errors?

Contexts: Physical context (environment, lighting, noise, space), social context (alone or with others, formal or informal setting), organisational context (rules, workflow, culture), technical context (other technologies in use).
Technologies: What technologies already exist in this context? What input/output devices? What interaction styles? What technical constraints (network speed, device capabilities)?
outputs: Completed PACT tables per user group, identified variability and constraints, scenarios for key PACT combinations, and derived requirements.
useWhen: Scoping new systems, especially in complex or safety-critical settings, briefing teams, and structuring research plans across contexts and technologies.
avoidWhen: For narrow interface optimisation where people, contexts and technology are fixed and known; use task analysis or usability testing instead.
whyLost: It remained an academic teaching framework; industry adopted personas and journey maps, which cover parts of PACT but rarely contexts and technologies systematically.
whereToUse: Pre-design requirements gathering, accessibility analysis, enterprise software scoping, safety-critical system design.
example: Designing an anaesthetic record system, a team builds PACT tables showing gloved hands, sterile constraints, time-critical activities and noisy theatres. The analysis rules out touchscreen-only input and leads to voice and foot-pedal options for some actions.
reference: Benyon D (2014) Designing Interactive Systems: A Comprehensive Guide to HCI, UX and Interaction Design. 3rd ed. Pearson

name: Paired Interviews
origin: Qualitative market research practice; UX guidelines from Barker (2005), adapted by Sophie Marsh
summary: Interview two people who already know each other together, so they prompt, clarify and build on each other's accounts and reveal contrasts.
description: A paired interview is not two interviews run at once but a designed conversation in which two participants interact, prompt each other, seek clarification and build on each other's stories. This can reduce discomfort, give more thinking space and produce fuller accounts, while similarities and differences between the two can be explored directly. It suits research into collaboration and shared workflows (people who work together), comparing practice across teams or offices (people doing the same task in different places), and sensitive topics or research with children and teenagers, where a friend present makes people more open. A variant, paired retrospective think aloud, interviews two people straight after an activity they did together so the activity is not interrupted. It is distinct from co-discovery usability testing, where pairs use a product together.
steps: Decide whether the topic suits pairs: collaboration, cross-team comparison, a sensitive topic, or young participants.
Recruit pairs who already know each other professionally or personally, considering gender pairing for teenagers.
Prepare the guide as for individual interviews, with warm-up, main questions and wrap-up.
Alternate which participant answers first and make sure both contribute.
Treat silence as not yet heard rather than agreement, and invite the quieter partner directly.
Watch for domination in hierarchical pairs (manager and report, parent and child) and redirect questions.
Explore similarities and differences between the two accounts, allowing well over 30 minutes per session.
outputs: Co-constructed accounts from each person, plus explicit contrasts and agreements between partners.
useWhen: You are studying shared workflows, joint decisions or households, comparing practice between sites, or interviewing teenagers or people on sensitive topics who will open up with a peer.
avoidWhen: The topic is private to one person, or one partner may dominate or censor the other (for example, abuse or workplace grievances); use individual interviews instead.
whyLost: It survives in market research and UX because it is cheap, doubles coverage per session and fits collaborative products.
whereToUse: B2B collaboration tools, household finance and energy products, family apps, education technology and youth research.
example: A banking team interviews couples together about joint accounts. Partners correct each other's accounts of who moves money and when, revealing an invisible 'household treasurer' role the app never supports.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
reference: Marsh, S. (2022). User Research (2nd ed.). Kogan Page; Barker, I. (2005). Fast-tracking research with paired interviews. Step Two Designs.

name: Paired Resampling Comparison of Predictive Models
aka: Paired resampling comparison of predictive models (performance-ceiling strategy)
Performance ceiling then simplest adequate model
origin: Kuhn and Johnson (2013); comparison methods from Hothorn et al. (2005) and Eugster et al. (2008)
summary: Fit several model types on identical resamples, find the best achievable performance, then use paired comparisons of resampled metrics to keep the simplest model that is not meaningfully worse.
description: No model type is best for every problem, so Kuhn and Johnson recommend a three-step strategy. First fit flexible, opaque models such as boosted trees or support vector machines to find the performance ceiling. Then fit simpler, more interpretable models on the same resamples. Finally adopt the simplest model that reasonably approaches the ceiling, weighing interpretability, prediction speed and deployment. Because every model is evaluated on identical resampled data sets, the metrics are paired, so a paired t-test or confidence intervals on per-resample differences, adjusted for multiplicity when many pairs are compared, tell whether a difference is real. Differences must also be judged for practical meaning: a credit model comparison found a 0.1 per cent accuracy difference with an interval spanning zero, so the logistic regression was kept.
steps: Create one set of resamples (for example five repeats of 10-fold cross-validation) and reuse it for every candidate model.
Tune and evaluate flexible, low-interpretability models to establish the performance ceiling.
Tune and evaluate simpler, more interpretable models on the same resamples.
Compute per-resample differences in the chosen metric between pairs of models.
Form confidence intervals or paired tests for the mean differences, adjusting for multiplicity.
Choose the simplest model whose performance is not meaningfully below the ceiling, considering interpretability and deployment, and confirm it on the held-out test set.
outputs: Box or parallel-coordinate plots of resampled metrics, confidence intervals for pairwise differences and a justified model choice.
useWhen: Choosing among candidate models for churn prediction, propensity, intent classification or ranking where interpretability and explainability to users or regulators matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating statistically detectable differences as decisive when they are practically trivial. For validating a single chosen model use Predictive Model Validation; for explaining it use SHAP Explanations for Behavioural Models.
whyLost: It is standard in applied predictive modelling but UX teams rarely own model selection, so the case for simpler, explainable models is seldom made with evidence.
whereToUse: Churn and propensity models, recommendation features, credit and risk scoring with explanation duties, AI feature triage.
example: A product analytics team compares gradient boosting with logistic regression for predicting trial conversion over 50 shared resamples. The AUC difference is 0.004 with an interval spanning zero, so the logistic model is chosen because its drivers can be shown to sales teams.
reference: Kuhn, M. and Johnson, K. (2013). Applied Predictive Modeling. New York: Springer, pp. 78-80, 221-224, 506-507; Hothorn, T., Leisch, F., Zeileis, A. and Hornik, K. (2005). The design and analysis of benchmark experiments. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 14(3), 675-699.

name: Paired-associate learning with imagery and generation manipulations
origin: Bower and Winzenz, 1970; Slamecka and Graf, 1978
summary: Participants learn cue-target pairs under different encoding instructions, then recall targets from cues, to measure which encoding strategy produces better retention.
description: Participants study word pairs (boat-tree) and are later shown the first word and asked for the second. The encoding instruction is the manipulated variable. Bower and Winzenz (1970) presented 15 pairs for 5 seconds each; those told to form an interacting mental image recalled more than twice as many as those told to repeat the pair silently. Slamecka and Graf (1978) compared reading full pairs (king-crown) with generating the second word from a stem (king-cr___) and found 28 per cent more pairs remembered after generation, the generation effect. The design isolates encoding effects because the test is identical across conditions. For UX it offers a controlled way to test whether onboarding, training or labelling designs that make users generate or visualise associations improve retention of shortcuts, codes or terminology.
steps: Build a list of cue-target pairs representative of the material (for example 15 command-shortcut or term-meaning pairs).
Assign participants randomly to encoding conditions (rote repetition, interactive imagery, generation from a stem).
Present each pair for a fixed time, such as 5 seconds, counterbalancing pairs across conditions.
Check instruction compliance with a brief strategy question after study.
After a delay, show each cue and ask for the target; score exact or lenient matches.
Compare proportion recalled across conditions and report effect sizes.
outputs: Proportion of targets recalled to the cue per encoding condition; generation and imagery effect sizes.
useWhen: You are choosing between onboarding or training designs meant to make users remember mappings: shortcuts, icons to functions, codes, vocabulary.
avoidWhen: Retention is not the goal, or the material is procedural skill rather than associations; use a learnability study with realistic tasks instead. Results depend on compliance with instructions.
whyLost: It is a classic laboratory memory paradigm that UX rarely borrows because retention is seldom measured directly in product research.
whereToUse: Onboarding for complex tools, keyboard-shortcut teaching, language and education apps, medical coding interfaces, icon-function learning.
example: A design tool tests teaching shortcuts by showing them (read) versus asking users to guess the key first (generate). After two days, the generate group recalls more shortcuts, so the tutorial adopts a guess-then-reveal pattern.
reference: Bower, G. H., & Winzenz, D. (1970). Comparison of associative learning strategies. Psychonomic Science, 20, 119-120; Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4, 592-604.

name: PANAS Affect Measurement
origin: David Watson, Lee Anna Clark and Auke Tellegen, 1988
summary: A validated 20-item self-report of positive and negative affect, usable momentarily or over periods to measure the emotional impact of experiences.
description: The PANAS, listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix under clinical research, measures two largely independent dimensions: positive affect (enthusiastic, alert, active) and negative affect (distressed, upset, nervous), each with 10 items rated 1-5. Time-frame instructions ('right now', 'today', 'past week') adapt it to momentary or period assessment, and short forms (I-PANAS-SF, 10 items) suit repeated measures. Its value for UX is a well-validated affect measure with norms, unlike ad hoc emoji ratings. It pairs naturally with experience sampling and with before-after designs to assess how an interaction changes affect, and the two-factor structure distinguishes reducing frustration from creating delight.
steps: Choose the version (full, short form) and time frame matching the research question.
Administer before and after an experience, or within ESM prompts.
Score PA and NA separately; do not combine into one index.
Analyse change with paired or multilevel models.
Compare against published norms where relevant.
Interpret PA and NA effects separately in design decisions.
outputs: PA and NA scores, change estimates, comparisons across designs or contexts.
useWhen: Measuring emotional impact of experiences, stressful flows, wellbeing products.
avoidWhen: When specific emotions (for example trust, shame) are of interest; use targeted measures.
whyLost: UX uses single-item satisfaction or bespoke emotion scales; clinical instruments rarely cross over.
whereToUse: Health diagnosis flows, debt collection UX, gaming, meditation apps, customer service interactions.
example: Comparing two loan-decline messages, the redesigned version leaves PA unchanged but cuts NA by 0.4 SD, informing the rollout.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Watson D, Clark LA & Tellegen A (1988) Development and validation of brief measures of positive and negative affect: the PANAS scales. JPSP 54(6)
Thompson ER (2007) Development and validation of an internationally reliable short-form of the PANAS. J Cross-Cultural Psych
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Watson D, Clark LA & Tellegen A (1988) Development and validation of brief measures of positive and negative affect: the PANAS scales. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 54(6):1063-1070.

name: Paradigm Mapping and Positioning
origin: Guba & Lincoln, 1994
summary: Locates a study within a research paradigm (positivist, post-positivist, interpretivist, critical) before data collection, so methods, validity criteria and claims are consistent.
description: Paradigm mapping requires you to make explicit where your research sits across two axes: ontology (what is the nature of reality?) and epistemology (what is the relationship between the researcher and the researched?). The four major paradigms — positivism, post-positivism, interpretivism, and critical theory — each demand different methods, different validity criteria, and different ways of reporting findings. Most UX researchers operate implicitly within interpretivism without naming it, which leads to inconsistent method choices and indefensible analytical decisions.
steps: Before designing your study: write one paragraph answering — what is the nature of the reality I am investigating? Is it fixed and knowable (positivist), or constructed in social interaction (interpretivist)?
Write a second paragraph: what is my relationship to this reality? Am I an objective observer or am I part of what I am studying?
Map your answers to the quadrant. Now check: does your chosen method fit your paradigm? Mismatches (e.g., conducting interviews but claiming objective truth) invalidate your findings.
Document your paradigmatic position in a methods section. This is required in academic qual research and increasingly expected in rigorous industry research.
outputs: A written paradigm statement, aligned method and validity criteria, a defensible analysis plan, and a clear statement of the kinds of claims findings can support.
useWhen: Planning studies, mixing methods, defending qualitative findings to quantitative stakeholders, and supervising or reviewing research.
avoidWhen: Avoid turning it into philosophical debate that stalls quick, low-risk work; for routine evaluative tests, a single line stating the stance suffices.
whyLost: UX imported methods without their philosophical foundations; paradigms are taught in academic research degrees but treated as irrelevant in industry.
whereToUse: Research planning and study briefs in any organisation mixing qualitative and quantitative work; research leadership and review processes; defending qualitative evidence in data-driven product organisations; training junior researchers to justify method choices.
example: A health insurance team asks for '80% of users want X' from 12 interviews; the researcher's paradigm statement clarifies that interpretivist findings show the range and reasons for needs, not prevalence, and adds a survey for prevalence.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 25 — The Philosophy of Seeing — Epistemological Foundations of Qualitative Inquiry
reference: Guba EG & Lincoln YS (1994) Competing paradigms in qualitative research. In Denzin NK & Lincoln YS (Eds.) Handbook of Qualitative Research. Sage

extra.The Four Paradigms: Positivism: Reality exists independently of the researcher. The researcher is objective and separate from the researched. Methods: controlled experiments, surveys with validated scales. Findings must be replicable and generalisable. Post-positivism: Reality exists but is only imperfectly knowable. The researcher must control for bias. Methods: quasi-experiments, structured observation. Findings are probabilistic and falsifiable. Interpretivism / Constructivism: Reality is socially constructed. Researcher and participant co-produce knowledge. Methods: grounded theory, phenomenology, ethnography. Findings are contextually situated and transferable, not generalisable. Critical Theory / Transformative: Reality is shaped by social, political, and historical forces. Research is inherently political and aimed at liberation. Methods: participatory action research, feminist research. Findings must challenge power structures.

name: Parallel analysis
origin: John Horn, 1965
summary: Determines how many factors or components to retain by comparing observed eigenvalues with those from random data of the same size, keeping only those that beat chance.
description: The number-of-factors decision is the most consequential step in factor analysis, and the popular Kaiser rule (eigenvalues above 1) consistently retains too many. Parallel analysis generates many random datasets with the same number of respondents and items, computes their eigenvalues, and retains factors whose observed eigenvalues exceed the 95th percentile of the random ones. Simulation studies show it is among the most accurate retention methods. It can be run on principal components or on the reduced correlation matrix for common factors, and with polychoric correlations for ordinal items. It is a few lines of code in R (psych::fa.parallel) or Python.
steps: Prepare the item response matrix and decide whether you are extracting components or common factors.
Generate at least 500-1,000 random or permuted datasets with identical dimensions.
Compute eigenvalues for each random dataset and take the 95th percentile for each position.
Retain factors whose observed eigenvalues exceed the corresponding 95th-percentile random eigenvalue.
Cross-check with the scree plot, the MAP test and interpretability, and report all in the analysis.
outputs: An evidence-based number of factors to retain, with a parallel analysis plot showing observed versus random eigenvalues.
useWhen: Every EFA or PCA where the number of dimensions is not fixed by theory.
avoidWhen: Not needed when a confirmatory structure is being tested, and less reliable with very small samples or highly skewed items.
whyLost: UX teams learn factor analysis from tool defaults that apply the Kaiser rule, and parallel analysis is rarely mentioned outside psychometrics texts.
whereToUse: Questionnaire development for trust, satisfaction and AI-reliance; persona attribute reduction; dimensionality checks before clustering.
example: A satisfaction survey with 30 items shows seven eigenvalues above 1, but parallel analysis supports only three factors, giving a cleaner and more stable instrument.
sources: Quantitative User Experience Research (Chris Chapman & Kerry Rodden)
Horn (1965) A rationale and test for the number of factors in factor analysis
The Inquiry Series, Ch 50 — Factor Analysis — Discovering the Latent Structure of Experience
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
reference: Horn, J. L. (1965) A rationale and test for the number of factors in factor analysis. Psychometrika, 30(2), 179-185.

name: Parallel Design
origin: Nielsen and Faber, 1996; HHS guideline 1:10, 2006; Dow et al., 2010 (parallel prototyping)
