summary: Several designers independently create different designs or low-fidelity prototypes, which are evaluated to learn what works before the best elements are merged into one design for iteration.
description: Individual designers tend to settle on an early, satisfactory but suboptimal solution, and group brainstorming does not reliably do better. Parallel design counters this by having several designers work independently on the same brief, aiming to saturate the design space before anything is chosen; the more varied and independent the proposals, the better the merged result. The HHS guidelines recommend starting a site with parallel design followed by iterative design and usability testing. Dow and colleagues' parallel prototyping adds evidence that building several distinct low-fidelity prototypes reduces fixation and 'hill climbing' and keeps critique on designs rather than designers. Each alternative is tested or inspected to learn how people respond to its elements, not to pick a winner, and the strongest elements are combined. In Nielsen's diversified parallel design each designer optimises for a different aspect, such as novice users, expert users or a non-verbal interface, and existing competitor products can stand in as further parallel designs.
steps: Write one brief and give it to three or more designers or pairs who work without seeing each other's work.
Have each produce a distinct design or low-fidelity prototype within the same short time box.
Push for variety: if proposals converge, ask for further alternatives until the design space feels saturated.
Test or inspect each alternative with a few users or experts, noting which elements work and why.
Merge the best elements into one design, checking the result is coherent rather than a patchwork.
Continue with iterative design and usability testing on the merged design.
outputs: Several independent designs with feedback on their elements, and a merged design ready for iteration.
useWhen: Early in design when the solution space is wide and the team risks fixating on its first idea.
avoidWhen: Needs more upfront effort and merging can produce incoherent hybrids. Running it as a group brainstorm loses the independence that makes it work. To decide between finished alternatives quantitatively use A/B Testing or Competitive UX Benchmarking; to evaluate the alternatives use Prototype Testing or Usability Testing.
whyLost: Teams still say they explore alternatives, but the independence, saturation and element-level testing are usually dropped in favour of one designer's options reviewed in a meeting.
whereToUse: New product concepts, dashboards, onboarding flows, navigation redesigns, design sprints.
example: Three designers independently prototype an analytics dashboard; five users try each, and the final design combines one prototype's navigation with another's chart layout.
reference: Dow, S.P., Glassco, A., Kass, J., Schwarz, M., Schwartz, D.L. and Klemmer, S.R. (2010) Parallel prototyping leads to better design results, more divergence, and increased self-efficacy. ACM TOCHI, 17(4), 18; Nielsen, J. and Faber, J.M. (1996) Improving system usability through parallel design. IEEE Computer, 29(2), 29-35.

name: Parallel processing with async
origin: Python asyncio (PEP 3156, 2012-2014)
summary: Running many independent analysis tasks concurrently, such as LLM coding requests per transcript segment, to cut processing time while respecting API rate limits.
description: Most AI-assisted coding time is spent waiting for API responses. Python's asyncio lets a pipeline send many requests concurrently, bounded by a semaphore so rate limits and costs are respected, and gather results as they complete. This turns days of sequential processing into hours. Rigour concerns are practical but real: concurrency limits, exponential backoff on rate-limit errors, idempotent writes so partial runs resume without duplication, deterministic ordering of results, and logging per request. Concurrency must not change the analysis: each segment should get identical prompts and settings regardless of order.
steps: Identify tasks that are independent (e.g. coding each segment) and suitable for concurrency.
Use an async client and an asyncio.Semaphore to cap concurrent requests within provider limits (e.g. 5-20).
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for rate-limit and transient errors.
Write each result keyed by segment ID so reruns skip completed segments.
Record per-request metadata (model, latency, tokens, errors) and monitor cost.
Verify after the run that every input has exactly one valid output.
outputs: A concurrent processing module, complete per-segment outputs, and logs of latency, tokens, cost and errors.
useWhen: AI-assisted coding or enrichment of large corpora where sequential calls would take too long.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary for small batches; avoid exceeding provider rate limits or data-processing terms. Consider provider batch APIs for non-urgent, cheaper processing.
whyLost: A software engineering concern that became relevant to researchers only with API-based AI analysis.
whereToUse: Large interview or feedback corpora, multilingual analysis and continuous research pipelines.
example: Coding 12,000 segments sequentially would take about 20 hours. With a semaphore of 10 concurrent requests and backoff, the run completes in about 2.5 hours, and a completeness check confirms 12,000 valid outputs.
sources: The Inquiry Series, C13 — The Full Agentic Research Pipeline — Whisper → spaCy → AI Coder → Synthesis
reference: van Rossum, G. (2012) PEP 3156: Asynchronous IO Support Rebooted

name: Pareto Analysis
origin: Principle after Vilfredo Pareto; applied to quality by Joseph Juran in the 1940s-1950s
summary: Ranks problem or error categories by frequency in a bar chart with a cumulative percentage line, to find the few causes behind most problems.
description: A Pareto diagram orders the frequencies of defect or error categories from most to least frequent, with a cumulative percentage line, to separate the vital few from the trivial many. Its rigour lies less in the chart than in the data behind it. In the worked example a health insurer aiming to halve claim-processing errors forms a cross-functional team, agrees a list of error categories from experience and a process review, audits a random sample of 1,000 claims end to end, and records every error by category, with agreed coding rules for ambiguous cases and for cases carrying several errors. Frequencies and cumulative percentages are tabulated and the leading categories become improvement targets. The chart also communicates priorities clearly to management and production teams.
steps: Form a team spanning the stages of the process or journey under study.
Agree a list of problem or error categories from experience and a process review.
Take a random sample of cases (for example 1,000 transactions or sessions) and audit each end to end.
Record every problem by category, agreeing rules for ambiguous and multiple codings and checking coder agreement.
Tabulate category frequencies and cumulative percentages, and draw bars in descending order with the cumulative line.
Focus improvement on the few categories that account for most problems, then repeat after changes to confirm the shift.
outputs: An ordered frequency table and Pareto chart identifying the vital few problem categories.
useWhen: Prioritising fixes among many usability issues, support contact reasons, form errors or defect types when frequency is a reasonable proxy for impact.
avoidWhen: When severity varies hugely between categories, since frequency alone can bury rare but critical problems; combine with Severity Rating with Impact x Frequency x Persistence. Category definitions drive the result.
whyLost: It is a staple of quality management, but UX teams prioritise by severity ratings or gut feel and rarely build audited frequency tables.
whereToUse: Form and checkout errors, support contact drivers, claims and onboarding operations, accessibility issue triage.
example: An insurer's digital claims team audits 1,000 abandoned online claims, codes reasons, and finds that three categories (missing policy number, photo upload failure, unclear incident date) account for 72% of abandonments.
sources: Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
reference: Newbold, P., Carlson, W. L. and Thorne, B. M. (2022). Statistics for Business and Economics (10th ed., Global Edition). Pearson, pp. 36-38.

name: Partially Ordered Meta-Matrix
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 7, section B.
summary: A master chart that stacks comparably formatted case-level displays into one large table, then progressively reduces, partitions and clusters it to compare cases.
description: Cross-case analysis multiplies the data by the number of cases. The meta-matrix first makes cases comparable through common codes, displays and reporting formats, then assembles them coherently and in one place. Each case gets the same small display; in the book's example, rows are users and columns are feelings and concerns, how the innovation looked, what the user was doing most, and problems. Cells hold telegraphic phrases drawn from coded data under explicit decision rules. The analyst then stacks all case-level displays on one very large sheet or wall chart, the 'monster-dog', whose principle is inclusion of all relevant condensed data. From there the data are further reduced into short quotes, phrases, ratings and symbols, partitioned in new ways and clustered so that contrasts between sets of cases stand out. Later, meta-matrices can be ordered conceptually, by cases from strong to weak on a variable, or by time. The book recommends starting cross-case work this way to see the general territory before imposing order. In UX it is the step between per-participant notes and themes: a single table showing every participant's answers to the same questions.
steps: Define a common case-level display (rows such as participants within each account, columns for key questions).
Fill one display per case from coded data using shared decision rules.
Stack all case displays into one large table or wall chart.
Reduce cell entries to short phrases, ratings or symbols.
Partition and cluster rows or cases to bring out contrasts, trying several groupings.
Choose an ordering (by a key variable, outcome or time) and move on to ordered meta-matrices.
outputs: A single cross-case master table, reduced and clustered versions of it, and first cross-case observations.
useWhen: You have several comparable cases (accounts, sites, segments) and need an overview before deciding how to order or explain.
avoidWhen: Cases were studied with different questions or formats, so cells would not be comparable.
whyLost: UX synthesis jumps from notes to affinity clusters, losing the case structure; spreadsheet 'research grids' come close but are seldom reduced and partitioned deliberately.
whereToUse: Multi-account B2B research, multi-country studies, comparing pilot sites, research repositories.
example: After studying eight companies piloting a contract-management tool, the team builds a meta-matrix with one block per company and rows for legal, sales and finance users; columns cover first reaction, main use, problems and workarounds. Reducing cells to short tags and clustering by company size reveals that small firms' problems are all about templates while large firms' are about approvals.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Participant Interview Chain
origin: Michael Quinn Patton, wilderness education programme evaluation
summary: Participants are trained briefly and paired to interview each other repeatedly over a programme, producing both shared reflection and longitudinal evaluation data.
description: In Patton's evaluation of a year-long wilderness education programme with 40 participants, people were paired after brief training in probing and note-taking and interviewed each other with a ten-question open-ended guide lasting about two hours. Each was responsible for documenting a partner's experience through the year, and participants reinterviewed each other, across groups, after each ten-day trip. The design served the programme's need for sharing and reflection and the evaluation's need for data at once. The trade-offs are minimal interviewer training, variable data quality and limited confidentiality, so the data are treated as participant-generated with explicit quality caveats. A related option is data collection by programme staff, which raises subjectivity concerns but increases commitment and rapport.
steps: Design a short open-ended interview guide of about ten questions.
Train participants briefly in asking follow-up probes and taking notes.
Pair participants to interview each other, with each responsible for documenting a partner's experience.
Repeat the interviews at programme milestones, varying the pairs.
Collect the notes centrally and treat them as evaluation data, recording the quality and confidentiality limits.
Complement with a sample of researcher-led interviews to check depth and consistency.
outputs: Repeated participant-generated interview records over time, plus reflection that benefits the participants themselves.
useWhen: You are evaluating a long programme, cohort or community (onboarding cohorts, training, beta communities) where peer reflection is itself valuable and researcher access is limited.
avoidWhen: Topics are sensitive or confidential, or you need consistently deep, comparable data; use researcher-led or longitudinal qualitative interviews instead.
whyLost: It is an evaluation technique from one programme example and trades data quality for participation, which UX rarely accepts.
whereToUse: Customer education cohorts, accelerator or community programmes, internal change programmes and long beta tests.
example: A developer platform runs a twelve-week beta cohort and pairs participants to interview each other after each sprint. The notes show where setup frustration peaks, while participants report the exchanges helped them learn.
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2002). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Participant Map-Making Elicitation
aka: Participant map-making elicitation (spatial, social and home-technology maps)
origin: Elicitation framing after Sanders and Stappers (2013); cognitive maps after Donna Lanclos (2014); social maps after Paul Adams (2010); felt board after Rode, Toye and Blackwell (2004)
summary: Participants draw or build a map of places, people or devices, and the map anchors an interview about routines, relationships and infrastructure.
description: A family of generative techniques in which the participant makes a map that then drives the interview. In spatial mapping they draw a known place such as their home and add detail in response to study prompts (router and sockets for setup context, 'where do you feel safest?' for needs), or draw a movement such as a commute. In cognitive mapping the prompt is an activity and the map shows the network of places, devices, websites and transport involved. In social mapping the participant places people on sticky notes nearer or farther by closeness, clusters and names groups, then marks the communication tools used with each with coloured stickers. A tangible variant uses a felt board divided into rooms on which people place appliance tokens and say which they set in advance. Maps do not speak for themselves: they must be interpreted with the participant's explanations.
steps: Choose the starting prompt: a place (spatial map), an activity (cognitive map), the people who matter (social map) or the devices in a home (felt board).
Provide materials: large paper, pens, sticky notes, four or five sticker colours, or a room board with tokens, and record audio or video.
Ask the participant to draw or place items, using a concrete prompt such as 'people you contact once a week or more' and letting them check phones to jog memory.
Have them arrange items by distance, frequency or intimacy, cluster and name groups, and rearrange as they remember more.
Layer prompts tied to the research questions: infrastructure, tools used with each person, devices set in advance, feelings of safety.
Probe concrete recent instances, such as the last contact with a person or the last time a device was configured, in about 45 minutes one-to-one.
Analyse maps only together with interview notes, and compare across participants for recurring patterns.
outputs: Participant-made maps of spaces, networks or household technology, with explanations and stories; cross-participant patterns of routines, channels and infrastructure.
useWhen: Your product is embedded in physical space, social relationships or a multi-device home, and you need participants' own view of that context.
avoidWhen: You need precise behavioural frequencies or the context is purely within one app; spatial maps handle websites and apps poorly. Use diary studies, analytics or contextual inquiry instead.
whyLost: It lives in design and HCI research as scattered variants under different names, so it is seldom taught as one technique with a clear protocol.
whereToUse: Smart home and IoT, messaging and social products, mobility and commuting, education spaces and household services.
example: A smart home security team asks 10 households to draw their home and mark where they feel safest and where devices sit. Maps reveal that cameras are placed where people feel least safe, not at entry points, informing installation guidance.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Rode, J., Toye, E., & Blackwell, A. (2004). The fuzzy felt ethnography: understanding the programming patterns of domestic appliances. Personal and Ubiquitous Computing, 8(3-4), 161-176.

name: Participant Recruiting and Screener Design
aka: Recruit loosely and grade on a curve
Participant tracking database and watch list
User-group prioritisation grid (gold, silver and bronze user groups)
Persona-matched recruiting screener with incidence estimation
origin: UX and market research practice (Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed; Baxter, Courage and Caine; Young; Krug; Marsh; Chandler)
summary: Define who you need in behavioural terms, write a brief and a short masked screener with quotas, find and schedule candidates, and protect against no-shows and professional participants.
description: Recruiting decides whether findings mean anything. Start with a behavioural profile, not demographics alone (Marsh's Prince Charles and Ozzy Osbourne share a demographic profile). Young derives segments from a task-by-performer matrix; Travis and Hodgson prioritise groups on a learning-versus-access grid. The brief states dates, length, numbers, incentive, quotas per characteristic and exclusions. The screener (10 to 20 questions, 5 to 10 minutes) asks logistics first and eliminating questions next, masks the qualifying answer with decoys, uses knowledge tests for claimed expertise, ends with an open question to judge articulacy, and excludes industry, competitor and UX workers. Combining criteria multiplies incidence: Microsoft's persona screener needed a household at about 0.8 per cent incidence. Chandler works backwards from analytic N to invitations. Tracking databases cap participation and flag fraud; about one in four or five recruits fails to attend.
steps: Write a behavioural target profile with stakeholders, list segments, exclusions and quotas (qualitative studies typically 3 to 5 per group), and estimate joint incidence by multiplying the proportions of each criterion.
Write the recruitment brief: dates, location, session length, number of participants, slots, incentive, quotas per characteristic and who you do not want.

Draft the screener: introduction, logistics and availability first, eliminating behavioural questions next, demographics last; mask qualifying answers with decoys, add knowledge-test questions and one open question for articulacy; keep it under about 20 questions.
Pilot the screener on known fits and misfits, check branching, and get stakeholder sign-off.

Recruit through customer lists, intercepts, social media, panels or agencies; for surveys compute invitations from the analytic N allowing about 12% exclusions and response rates of roughly 30% web to 60% in person.
Check candidates against a participant log (cap at about one study every three months, flag no-shows and dishonest participants) and verify identity on arrival.
Confirm in writing, remind the day before and on the day, schedule sessions mid-week, and over-recruit about one per four or five or keep a paid floater.
After the study, compare participants against the intended segments and monitor per-question qualification rates to relax over-restrictive criteria.
outputs: Target profile, recruitment brief, screener with qualifying answers, quota grid, participant schedule and tracking log.
useWhen: Any qualitative or quantitative study with recruited participants, setting up research operations, or recruiting against personas or behavioural segments.
avoidWhen: Early formative tests where almost anyone will hit the problems; there Krug's 'recruit loosely and grade on a curve' with three users per round is enough. Do not over-specify demographics, screen out quiet or hard-to-reach people, or rely on email-only screening for paid studies.
whyLost: It survives because every study needs participants, but the rigour (behavioural criteria, masked questions, incidence estimation, fraud controls) is unevenly practised.
whereToUse: All UX research, especially B2B specialist recruiting, unmoderated panels prone to fraud, persona-based programmes and accessibility research.
example: A rail-ticket app needs six 45-minute sessions balanced across travel frequency (2/2/2), digital confidence and booking channel. The screener asks availability first, masks the travel question among decoys, excludes transport and UX workers, and keeps one paid floater.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M., & Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience: A Practitioner's Guide to User Research (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 6.

name: Participate, Compete, Win (PCW) Framework
aka: Participate, Compete, Win (PCW) framework with feature importance scoring
origin: Constant Contact, 2018; procedure by Sandra Teare, Linda Borghesani and Stuart Martinez (case study in Albert and Tullis, 2022)
summary: Label each product initiative Participate, Compete or Win, with matching usability targets and sample sizes, prioritise features by card sort scores, and test the top features against one competitor.
description: The framework ties product ambition to explicit usability goals. Participate (a minimum viable product) needs at least 80% task success and average ratings of at least 3 out of 5 for usability, trust and learnability, with 10 participants. Compete needs parity with a chosen competitor, with 15-20 participants within-subjects or about 25 between-subjects. Win needs a meaningful, statistically significant 30% difference, with about 30 participants within-subjects or 64 between-subjects. A feature audit collects competitors' features from their sites, reviews and marketing; participants sort features into Must have, Nice to have and Not important, giving a feature importance score of 3 x Must + 2 x Nice - 1 x Not important. Summing scores for the features each product offers gives an availability score. Top features become tasks in a summative head-to-head test.
steps: Assign the initiative a Participate, Compete or Win tier with its success, rating and sample-size criteria.
Audit competitor features from products, reviews, comparison sites and marketing.
Run a feature prioritisation card sort with target users (Must have, Nice to have, Not important).
Compute feature importance scores (weights 3, 2, -1) and an availability score per product.
Choose one main competitor and write tasks around the top features.
Run the summative test, measuring task success and ease of use, and report average and end-to-end workflow success.
Compare results against the tier's criteria, iterate, and later validate prototype results on the live product.
outputs: Feature importance ranking, availability scores per product, and task success and ease ratings against tier goals.
useWhen: A product organisation wants usability goals set in advance in proportion to each initiative's competitive ambition, with a defensible feature priority.
avoidWhen: Prototype-versus-live comparisons carry artefact effects, participants must be equally familiar with both products, and workflow success is capped by the weakest step. Card-sort importance is stated preference; for sharper priorities use MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) or Kano Analysis, and for sample sizes use Sample Size Planning for Summative UX Studies.
whyLost: A single company's internal framework, published as a case study; most organisations set usability targets ad hoc, if at all.
whereToUse: SaaS product portfolios, competitive feature launches, MVP gating, roadmap reviews.
example: An email-marketing SaaS labels its new template editor 'Compete', tests 20 users on both its own and a rival's editor for the top five features, and finds parity on success but lower trust ratings.
reference: Teare, S., Borghesani, L. and Martinez, S. Case study 11.2 in Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022) Measuring the User Experience. 3rd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 285-291.

name: Participation-Rate Demand Estimation
origin: Leisure and sport facility planning; worked example in Veal and Darcy's chapter on analysing secondary data
summary: Estimates likely demand by applying segment-specific participation rates from a national survey to the local population in each segment, then compares it with existing capacity.
description: This secondary-data method gives a 'ball park' estimate of demand before investing in a facility or service. Veal and Darcy's worked example asks whether a town needs more basketball courts. Age-specific participation rates come from a national survey, and the town's population by age from the census. Multiplying rate by population for each age group and summing gives the expected number of participants, and with a visit rate, weekly visits; because the town is younger than average, local demand is higher than the national rate implies. Typical facility capacity is then estimated, existing capacity subtracted, and the shortfall converted into the number of new facilities needed. Inserting population forecasts gives a simple demand forecast, and household expenditure data can turn visits into spending. The authors stress that the result is not a precise prediction, since local supply, programming and tradition change actual use, but note that investors often skip even this simple check and rely on hunches. Asking people whether they would use a hypothetical facility is, they argue, much less reliable. For product teams it is a transparent market-sizing method built from known adoption rates and segment sizes.
steps: Identify the segments that most affect take-up (for example age, role, company size) and find benchmark participation or adoption rates for each.
Obtain the size of each segment in the target market from census, market or customer data.
Multiply rate by segment size and sum to estimate total users, then apply a frequency of use to estimate total visits or sessions.
Estimate the capacity of a typical unit of supply and of the existing supply in the market.
Subtract existing capacity from estimated demand to find unmet demand, and convert it into units needed.
Rerun with forecast segment sizes for future years and test sensitivity to the rates used.
Present the result as a ball-park range, together with its assumptions.
outputs: A segment-by-segment demand table, estimated unmet demand, and a simple forecast with stated assumptions.
useWhen: You must judge whether a market, location or segment can support a new product, feature or service before investing, and benchmark rates exist.
avoidWhen: No credible benchmark rates exist for comparable populations, or the product is so new that past participation says little about future use.
whyLost: UX researchers leave market sizing to product and strategy teams, who tend to use top-down TAM figures or stated-intention surveys rather than this bottom-up, segment-adjusted calculation.
whereToUse: Product strategy and market entry, local service planning, sports and fitness services, public digital services, localisation decisions.
example: Before launching a junior sports booking feature in a new city, a team applies national participation rates for each age band to the city's census population, finds expected demand is about a third higher than the national average because of a young population, and prioritises that city.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: Participatory Action Research (PAR)
donor: Social psychology, adult education and development studies
origin: Kurt Lewin's action research, 1946; Orlando Fals-Borda and Paulo Freire, 1970s
summary: Research conducted with a community as co-researchers through plan-act-observe-reflect cycles, aiming at real change rather than only knowledge.
description: Participatory action research joins Lewin's cyclical action research with the emancipatory traditions of Fals-Borda and Freire. Community members co-own the research: they shape the question, collect data in their own community, interpret findings and decide on action. Work proceeds in cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting, each generating new knowledge and change. Rigour comes from transparent power sharing, documented cycles and reflexivity, and validity is judged partly by whether actions improve the situation. In UX it moves design authority toward affected communities, which suits contexts where outsiders lack access or legitimacy, but it demands long time horizons and genuine willingness to cede control.
steps: Community partnership: Establish a research partnership with the community. The research question is co-developed — not imposed by the researcher. The community must have genuine authority over the research direction.

Co-research training: Train community members in data collection methods relevant to the research question. They collect data in their own community — often accessing information that outside researchers cannot.
Iterative cycles: PAR cycles through: Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Plan again. Each cycle produces new data and new actions. The research is not complete until the cycle produces change.
Co-analysis: Community members participate in data analysis — their interpretations are primary data, not validation of researcher interpretations.
outputs: A co-owned research agenda, community-collected data, cycle logs, co-analysed findings and implemented changes with documented effects.
useWhen: Long-term work with communities affected by a service or technology, especially marginalised groups, civic tech and public services.
avoidWhen: Short commercial projects where the organisation will not share decision authority; use co-design sessions or member checking instead.
whyLost: Its timescales and power-sharing conflict with product cycles, so it remains in community health, education and development research.
whereToUse: Civic and government services, community health programmes, financial inclusion, accessibility, and platform-worker tools.
example: A city council partners with residents of a public housing estate to redesign its repairs reporting service. Residents collect neighbours' stories, co-analyse them and pilot a text-message reporting channel over three cycles.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Reason, P. & Bradbury, H. (Eds.) (2008). The SAGE Handbook of Action Research (2nd ed.). Sage.

name: Participatory Design
donor: Scandinavian workplace democracy and trade union movement
origin: Kristen Nygaard and colleagues, 1970s (NJMF project); UTOPIA project (Ehn and colleagues), 1981 to 1986
summary: Involves users as active design partners with real influence over outcomes, using workshops, mock-ups and generative tools to design with people rather than for them.
description: Participatory design treats the people affected by a system as co-designers with legitimate authority over it. It originated in Scandinavian projects of the 1970s and 1980s, where trade unions and researchers worked together to ensure workers shaped the technologies that changed their work. Its techniques include future workshops, mock-ups, design games, low-fidelity prototyping and generative toolkits. The central commitments are mutual learning between designers and users, sharing power over decisions and designing for the participants' own interests. Rigour comes from involving participants across the process rather than in a single session, transparent decision rules, deliberate management of power imbalances, accessible tools that do not privilege professional designers, and documented evidence of how participant input changed outcomes.
steps: Identify the communities and stakeholders affected and agree the scope and decision power they will have.
Build relationships and mutual learning through early sessions and site visits.
Run a series of workshops using accessible tools such as mock-ups, design games and storyboards.
Facilitate to balance power, ensuring quieter and less powerful voices are heard.
Iterate prototypes with participants across several cycles.
Document decisions and how participant input shaped them, and report back to participants.
outputs: Co-created concepts and prototypes, shared requirements, documented decision rationale and stronger stakeholder ownership.
useWhen: For public services, health, community technology, accessibility and workplace systems where those affected must have a real voice.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there is no willingness to share decision power, which makes participation tokenistic; use interviews and usability testing and be honest about their role.
whyLost: Vestigial: Time-intensive; power dynamics require careful management; lives mainly in public sector and social impact design.
whereToUse: Public services; health; community tech; accessibility design.
example: A city council co-designs a social care booking app with care recipients, family carers and care workers over six workshops. Participants insist on carer delegation features that were missing from the original brief.
sources: Routledge International Handbook of Participatory Design (Simonsen & Robertson)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Ehn P (1988) Work-Oriented Design of Computer Artifacts
Greenbaum J & Kyng M (Eds) (1991) Design at Work: Cooperative Design of Computer Systems
Simonsen J & Robertson T (Eds) (2012) Routledge International Handbook of Participatory Design
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Simonsen, J. & Robertson, T. (Eds.) (2012). Routledge International Handbook of Participatory Design. Routledge.

name: Participatory Design with Co-creation Probes
donor: Scandinavian participatory design and design research
origin: Probe methods from Gaver et al. (1999); generative toolkits by Elizabeth Sanders (2000s); documented in Martin and Hanington (2012)
summary: Participants complete open-ended probe and making activities over time, then co-create concepts with researchers, so their own expression shapes design directions.
description: This approach combines the probe tradition, where participants complete ambiguous stimulus packages at home over days or weeks, with generative co-design sessions in which participants use toolkits of images, words and shapes to make artefacts expressing their experiences and ideal futures. The probe phase sensitises participants and surfaces latent experiences; the co-creation phase lets them externalise needs they cannot easily articulate in interviews. Unlike structured diaries, probes are deliberately open, and unlike conventional ideation, participants are treated as experts of their experience. Rigour comes from a clear sensitisation-to-session sequence, careful facilitation that asks participants to explain what they made, recording the 'say, do, make' triangulation, and analysing artefacts together with participants' explanations rather than interpreting them alone.
steps: Design probe package:
disposable camera with 10 prompts ('photograph something that represents your relationship with this software'),
a diary with open sentence completions ('Today I felt... when I tried to...'),
a map ('draw how information flows through your day'). Mail to 6–10 participants. 2-week completion period. Analyze: what did participants choose to document? Where did they struggle with the probes?
outputs: Completed probe materials, participant-made artefacts with explanations, co-created concepts, and themes linking past experience to desired futures.
useWhen: Early discovery on emotionally rich or tacit topics, service and health design, and projects where users should have a voice in shaping direction.
avoidWhen: When you need to evaluate specific designs or measure prevalence, or when participants cannot commit time across several weeks; use interviews or concept testing.
whyLost: Commercial UX compressed discovery into interviews and workshops run by designers; multi-week probe sequences followed by participant making sessions are seen as slow and hard to analyse.
whereToUse: Early design exploration, non-standard user populations, designing for values and life contexts. Probes reveal what participants cannot articulate in interview.
example: A diabetes care service sends 10 patients a two-week probe kit, then runs co-creation sessions where they build their 'ideal week' with collage tools. Several patients design a weekly check-in rather than daily logging, reshaping the app's engagement model.
sources: Universal Methods of Design — Bella Martin
Sanders & Stappers, Convivial Toolbox: Generative Research for the Front End of Design (2012)
Gaver, Dunne & Pacenti, Design: Cultural Probes (Interactions, 1999)
reference: Sanders EB-N & Stappers PJ (2012) Convivial Toolbox: Generative Research for the Front End of Design. BIS Publishers

name: Participatory GIS and Research Mapping
origin: PPGIS literature (Kwan 2002; Sieber 2006; Ghose 2007); Collins' Interactive Watershed project; McKinnon on cartographic practice
summary: Community members contribute local knowledge, media and stories that are linked to locations in a shared georeferenced map used for analysis, discussion and planning.
description: Participatory GIS brings community knowledge into spatial analysis and planning as data. McKinnon distinguishes maps used to collect, explore and display data from mere reference maps. In Collins' design, PGIS runs inside participatory action research cycles: participants complete a survey and interviews, create their own place-based material (photographs, rephotography, drawings, poems, measurements) and contribute it to a shared site, while the researcher builds a georeferenced database with type and sub-type attributes aligned to public GIS layers, linking each item to its location. Group meetings then use the map to discuss alternatives, and contributed material is coded for themes recurring across participants. The aim includes empowering marginal groups, but software cost, skills, the digital divide and local politics all shape outcomes, and the researcher can end up translating local knowledge rather than participants mapping it themselves.
steps: Frame the project within participatory action research cycles of planning, acting, observing, evaluating and reflecting.
Recruit participants and agree the time commitment (about 12 hours each in the source project).
Run an online survey (about 30 minutes) and an initial interview (1-2 hours).
Have each participant create place-based material and contribute it to a shared site (about 6 hours).
Build a georeferenced database in GIS software with type and sub-type attributes, aligned to public layers, linking every item to its location.
Hold follow-up interviews (1-2 hours) and group meetings before and after (3-4 hours) using the map.
Code contributed material for themes that recur across participants and places.
outputs: An interactive cultural map and knowledge base, themes about place, and input to planning decisions.
useWhen: The product or service is place-based and local knowledge about where things happen (safety, access, routes, services) should shape design or policy.
avoidWhen: When location is incidental to the question, or participants lack access to the tools; use Participant Map-Making Elicitation for quick hand-drawn maps.
whyLost: It belongs to geography and planning and needs GIS skills; UX location research tends to rely on analytics heatmaps rather than participatory mapping.
whereToUse: Mobility and transit, delivery and logistics, civic tech, real estate, tourism, public health and accessibility mapping.
example: A micromobility operator invites 25 riders and residents to pin photos and notes about unsafe junctions and parking conflicts to a shared map, then uses group sessions over the map to set no-parking zones.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: McKinnon, I. 'Expanding cartographic practices in the social sciences'; Collins, D. 'Participatory geographic information systems (PGIS) in visual research', in Margolis, E. and Pauwels, L. (eds.) (2011) The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods. London: SAGE.

name: Participatory Trial Design with Visual Participatory Analysis
origin: Mannell and Prost; EVE project in Samoa
summary: Embed participatory qualitative work inside a trial so communities shape randomisation, define meaningful outcomes and co-interpret results through artist-made images.
description: A design for running a randomised trial with the affected community rather than on it. Participation enters at three stages. Before the trial, trained community representatives collect local stories and run key informant interviews that inform recruitment and randomisation, sometimes through a public randomisation draw. Stakeholder focus groups then define what a meaningful change in the outcome would look like, so success criteria reflect local values rather than only the researchers' metrics. After the trial, Visual Participatory Analysis has a local artist and community members translate quantitative findings into drawings, shown in a public exhibition and co-analysis workshops that ask why the intervention did or did not work; those insights are treated as data for interpreting the effects. Its rigour lies in keeping the trial's statistical design intact while making outcome definition and interpretation accountable to participants.
steps: Train community representatives to gather local artefacts and stories and to run key informant interviews.
Use those findings to set recruitment and randomisation procedures, for example a public randomisation draw.
Run stakeholder focus groups to define what a meaningful change in each outcome would be.
Run the trial with its pre-specified outcomes and analysis plan unchanged.
Work with a local artist to turn the quantitative results into images.
Exhibit the images and run co-analysis workshops; record participants' explanations as data for interpreting the effects.
outputs: Locally meaningful outcome definitions, trial results, and documented community interpretations of why effects did or did not occur.
useWhen: An experiment affects a community whose sense of success may differ from the team's, and buy-in, legitimacy or interpretation of results matters as much as the effect size.
avoidWhen: Fast product experiments with short cycles; the formative work takes years in its home field. For quick alignment on metrics use stakeholder workshops; for routine tests use A/B Testing.
whyLost: It comes from global health trials and depends on long formative periods, ethics oversight and community structures that product teams rarely have.
whereToUse: Civic tech, health and education programmes, platform policy changes affecting creator or seller communities, and any experiment where participants should help define success metrics.
example: Before testing a new payout schedule for delivery couriers, a platform convenes courier groups to define what a meaningful earnings-stability improvement is, then after the trial shows illustrated results at courier hubs and records their explanations of the mixed effects.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Participatory Video
origin: Fogo Process, 1967; Pink, 2007
summary: Participants film their own lives, routines or concerns, then review and edit footage with researchers, producing both data and participant-authored narratives.
description: Participatory video puts cameras in participants' hands so that they document aspects of their lives and decide what is important to show. Researchers provide training and prompts, participants film over days or weeks, and then footage is reviewed together, with participants explaining, selecting and sometimes editing it into short narratives. The method shifts authorship and surfaces contexts, routines and priorities that outsiders would not think to ask about. Analysis covers both the footage and the participants' commentary. Rigour lies in clear prompts, informed consent for participants and anyone filmed, joint interpretation sessions, systematic coding of footage, and reflexivity about how the act of filming shapes what is shown.
steps: Provide participants with a simple video task: 'Over the next week, record any moment when you interact with [product] that feels notable — good, bad, or surprising'. Collect videos at the end of the week. Analysis:
What did participants choose to record (content)?
(2) How did they record it (point of view, framing)?
(3) What did they not record (absence analysis)? Supplement with a reflection interview: 'Walk me through what you recorded and why.'
outputs: Participant-made videos, participant commentary on footage, coded themes, and stakeholder-facing films that communicate experience directly.
useWhen: Understanding contexts researchers cannot easily enter (homes, rural communities, workplaces), giving voice to marginalised users, and building stakeholder empathy.
avoidWhen: Avoid when privacy risks for participants or bystanders are high, when participants lack time or equipment, or when quick answers are needed; use diary studies instead.
whyLost: It is rooted in development and visual anthropology; UX uses video mostly as researcher-captured evidence, not as participant-authored research.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX research, mobile product research, physical-digital hybrid product research, any product used in diverse real-world contexts.
example: Farmers in a crop-insurance pilot film a week of their work; reviewing footage together reveals that claims are delayed because photo evidence must be taken at specific times, which leads to an offline-capture feature.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection — Flick (ed.)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection
The Inquiry Series, Ch 33 — Participatory & Arts-Based Methods
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
reference: Pink S (2007) Doing Visual Ethnography. 2nd ed. Sage

name: Partnered Play Study
donor: Games user research and social learning theory
origin: Moffatt, Shim, Birnholtz and Baecker (Chapter 10), drawing on Bandura's social learning and Isbister's work on spectating
summary: Comparing people who use a system alone with people paired with a non-controlling partner, and analysing the partners' private conversation to understand social experience, learning and decision-making.
description: In the TableTalk Poker study, older adults were randomly assigned to solo play or partner play. In partner play, one person controlled the game while a nonplaying partner shared the same view and could only talk to their partner over a private voice channel and use the public chat. Partners were re-paired between the two four-hour sessions to mix personalities and skills. The recorded voice chats became the main data: they show, without asking anyone to think aloud, how people explain decisions, teach, negotiate and joke. Inductive analysis of these transcripts was triangulated with field notes from researchers rotating behind participants, short exit interviews, an engagement scale, a social attraction measure, a knowledge quiz before and after, and log data on betting behaviour. The design answers three questions at once: does pairing change the social experience, engagement and the quality of decisions. Formative work for the same project used a related set-up, pairing novice players with an advisor in a face-to-face game and observing the learning that resulted. For UX, the set-up is a natural way to elicit reasoning and to study shared or assisted use.
steps: Define research questions about social experience, engagement and task performance.
Randomly assign participants to solo use or partner use, and within pairs to the controlling and non-controlling roles.
Give partners a shared view and a private, recorded voice channel; give solo participants equivalent conditions without a partner.
Run extended sessions, re-pairing partners between sessions if appropriate.
Collect transcripts, observation notes, logs and short questionnaires on engagement and relationship.
Analyse transcripts inductively for themes and compare groups on logs and questionnaire measures.
outputs: Themes on how partners collaborate, teach and talk, plus comparisons of engagement and behaviour between solo and partnered use.
useWhen: Studying products used together or with help (co-play, caregiving, assisted shopping) or when you want natural verbal reasoning without think-aloud.
avoidWhen: Use is inherently solitary, or sample sizes are too small for comparison and you only need usability problems.
whyLost: It needs long sessions, careful set-up and heavy transcript analysis; UX teams usually test individuals one at a time.
whereToUse: Social and multiplayer games, products for older adults, family and shared-device products, assisted or guided services.
example: Older adults play online poker either alone or with a remote partner who can only advise; partner chats are full of teaching and joking, while solo players barely use the text chat, and partnered players report higher engagement.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Moffatt, K., Shim, N., Birnholtz, J. and Baecker, R. M. (2016). Testing the usability, usefulness, and user experience of TableTalk Poker, a social game for seniors. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 10. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Passive sensing combined with self-report
aka: Combining passive smartphone sensing with self-report
origin: Aipperspach, Rattenbury, Woodruff and Canny (2006); StudentLife, Dartmouth (Wang et al., 2014; Harari et al., 2017)
summary: Collect continuous behavioural data from home sensors or phones and relate it to interviews, experience sampling and validated surveys that supply context and ground truth.
description: Sensors record what people do without effort on their part: location and dwell time, sleep, conversation, movement, nearby devices and app use. On their own such logs lack meaning, so the design pairs them with self-report. In one study, in-home location sensors were modelled into places of activity and residents were interviewed about them; an odd place spanning kitchen table and couch turned out to reflect a birthday party. In StudentLife, phones sensed 48 students over a ten-week term alongside experience-sampled stress and mood, validated mental health surveys before and after, and grades as outcomes; the linked data revealed declines in sleep and activity towards term end. Rigour comes from defining ground truth in advance, anonymising carefully and explaining anomalies with participants rather than guessing.
steps: Define the behaviours to sense and the outcomes or self-reports that will serve as ground truth.
Deploy passive sensing (home sensors or a phone app) and agree data transfer, storage, anonymisation and consent arrangements before collection.
Collect for a defined period, typically weeks to a full term, adding brief experience-sampling prompts for mood, stress or context.
Administer validated surveys before and after, and gather outcome data.
Model raw events into meaningful units such as places, routines or sessions.
Interview participants about derived patterns and anomalies to validate and explain them.
Mine the linked dataset for correlations and trends against events such as deadlines.
outputs: A linked behavioural and self-report dataset, validated activity models, correlations with outcomes, and explanations of anomalies.
useWhen: You need objective, continuous behavioural data over time and also need to know what it means to the people producing it.
avoidWhen: Avoid when consent or privacy cannot be managed, or when a diary study would answer the question; logs without interviews miss context, and correlations are not causes.
whyLost: It requires engineering, data infrastructure and ethics approval for continuous sensing, so it lives in ubicomp and digital health research rather than routine UX work.
whereToUse: Digital health and wellbeing apps, wearables, smart-home products, workplace analytics and any product that already collects telemetry.
example: A sleep app links nightly phone-sensed sleep with a morning one-question mood prompt for 200 users over eight weeks. Interviews with users whose data diverged reveal that late-night phone use was often caring for infants, not doom-scrolling, changing the coaching content.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Aipperspach, R. et al. (2006), in Lazar, Feng & Hochheiser (2017), p. 441; Harari, G. et al. (2017), StudentLife, in Preece, Sharp & Rogers (2019).

name: Passive UX Surveillance
origin: Passive disease surveillance; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Instruments products to detect defined UX failure events (traps, navigation failures, error loops, design-caused abandonment) as a by-product of normal use.
description: Passive surveillance in public health mines records created for other purposes (hospital discharges, lab reports, death certificates). The treatise's equivalent is behavioural analytics, but redirected: current practice tracks aggregate metrics (conversion, retention, session length) with poor sensitivity to specific failures. UX surveillance instruments products to detect specific UX failure events, defined by behavioural signatures indicating cognitive traps, navigational failures, error-recovery sequences and abandonment likely to reflect design failure rather than changed intent. Like disease surveillance, it needs explicit case definitions, known sensitivity and specificity, routine reporting and thresholds that trigger investigation. Across products it would enable genuine population-level analysis.
steps: Write case definitions for failure events (for example three validation errors on one field within 60 s).
Instrument events and validate definitions against recordings or labelled sessions for sensitivity and specificity.
Compute incidence rates per user-period and segment.
Set baselines and alert thresholds (for example control charts).
Report routinely and trigger outbreak investigation when thresholds are crossed.
Review and update case definitions periodically.
outputs: Failure event definitions, incidence dashboards, alerts, validated surveillance data.
useWhen: Large products needing continuous detection of UX failures and early warning after releases.
avoidWhen: Low-traffic products where events are too rare; use active or sentinel surveillance.
whyLost: Analytics evolved for marketing and growth, not harm detection; no case-definition discipline.
whereToUse: Banking, e-commerce, public services, SaaS, AI assistants (failure turns).
example: A tax portal defines 'form loop' events and sees incidence jump from 0.4% to 3% after a release; the alert triggers an investigation within a day.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Thacker SB & Berkelman RL (1988) Public health surveillance in the United States. Epidemiologic Reviews 10
CDC (2001) Updated guidelines for evaluating public health surveillance systems. MMWR 50(RR-13)
reference: German RR et al. (2001) Updated guidelines for evaluating public health surveillance systems. MMWR Recommendations and Reports 50(RR-13):1-35.

name: Path Analysis
origin: Clickstream analysis, Catledge and Pitkow, 1995; sequential pattern mining, Agrawal and Srikant, 1995
summary: Examines the actual sequences of screens and events users follow, revealing common routes, loops, detours and unexpected exits relative to intended flows.
description: Path analysis reconstructs sequences of page views or events within sessions and summarises them, typically as Sankey diagrams, tree views or frequent sequence patterns. It answers questions funnels cannot: what users do before and after a key event, which detours they take, and where they loop back. Rigour comes from cleaning sessions (bots, reloads, duplicate events), choosing the right event granularity, anchoring on a meaningful start or end point, and using sequence mining to find statistically frequent patterns rather than reading the most visible lines in a diagram. Comparing paths of successful and unsuccessful users is particularly informative. Note that this is distinct from statistical path analysis in structural equation modelling, which shares the name.
steps: Define the scope: a start event (e.g. landing) or end event (e.g. purchase) and the event granularity.
Clean the data by removing bots, collapsing reloads and standardising event names.
Generate path visualisations forward from the start or backward from the end.
Mine frequent sequences and compare paths of successful and unsuccessful sessions.
Identify loops, back-and-forth navigation and unexpected detours.
Investigate key patterns with session replay or usability testing and test IA changes.
outputs: Path diagrams, frequent sequence lists, success versus failure path comparisons, navigation issues.
useWhen: Navigation optimisation, content discovery and understanding non-linear journeys in apps and websites.
avoidWhen: Low-traffic products or when you need reasons for behaviour; use usability testing or interviews.
whyLost: Still in use: Navigation insight; supported by analytics platforms.
whereToUse: Navigation optimization; content discovery analysis; user flow design.
example: An insurance site found 40% of claim starters visited the FAQ, returned to the claim form and then left. Path analysis pinpointed a question about excess fees; adding the answer inline reduced the loop and raised claim submissions.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience
Characterizing browsing strategies in the World-Wide Web (Catledge & Pitkow)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Catledge, L. D., & Pitkow, J. E. (1995). Characterizing browsing strategies in the World-Wide Web. Computer Networks and ISDN Systems, 27(6), 1065-1073.

name: Path-Coded Prototype Test
origin: Alec Scharff, Plaid research team, presented at Quant UX Con 2024
summary: Give every end screen of a branching prototype its own code word, which participants type back into the research platform, so each person's chosen path becomes countable data.
description: Clickable prototypes usually run outside the research platform, so the platform cannot see which route a participant took. The path-coded test closes that gap without analytics instrumentation. The prototype is built with explicit decision points, and every terminal screen displays a unique code word, so each code maps to exactly one click path. Participants work through the flow inside an unmoderated mission, explain their choices aloud on video when prompted, then return and enter the code. The researcher receives a structured path answer alongside the spoken rationale. Run with large samples per design (Plaid used more than 150), it turns a qualitative-style session into choice proportions that can carry confidence intervals and be compared across design variants, while the videos explain why people chose as they did.
steps: Build a branching prototype of the flow with explicit decision points and a distinct terminal screen for every possible path.
Assign a unique, unambiguous code word to each terminal screen and keep a key mapping each code to its click path.
Add prompts at each decision point asking participants to explain their choice aloud on video.
Launch the prototype from an unmoderated research platform and ask participants to type the end-screen code into a structured question.
Clean the codes (mistyped or missing entries) and tabulate path proportions per design variant.
Compute confidence intervals for each proportion and compare variants, then review videos for the reasons behind each path.
outputs: Proportion of participants taking each path for each design, with confidence intervals and linked verbal rationales.
useWhen: Comparing two or more designs of a decision-heavy flow (payment method, onboarding, plan choice) when you need both how many people choose each route and why, without instrumenting the prototype.
avoidWhen: When you need back-tracking, hesitation or time data (codes record only the end path; use moderated usability testing or a prototype tool with click analytics); for live products, where A/B testing gives real behaviour.
whyLost: It is a practitioner workaround shared at a conference rather than a documented method, and many prototyping tools now offer built-in path analytics, so the trick is rarely written up.
whereToUse: Fintech payment and account-linking flows, onboarding choices, pricing-plan selection and any unmoderated study run on platforms that cannot read prototype events.
example: A payments team tests two versions of a payment-setup flow with over 150 participants each. End-screen codes show the bank-payment option chosen by 39% with the initial design and 72% with the improved one, and the videos reveal that clearer security wording drove the shift.
sources: Empowering Qualitative Researchers with Quantitative Techniques (Scharff, 2024)
reference: Scharff, A. (2024). Empowering qualitative researchers with quantitative techniques [Conference slides]. Quant UX Con 2024.

name: Pattern detection across 300+ transcripts
origin: Cross-case analysis (Miles and Huberman, 1994); scaled with computational and LLM tools from the 2020s
summary: Systematically identifying patterns, such as co-occurring codes, segment differences and rare but important cases, across hundreds of coded transcripts, with evidence for each.
description: Once hundreds of transcripts are coded, cross-case analysis can move beyond a few memorable stories. Using a case-by-code matrix, researchers examine which codes co-occur, how codes vary by segment, sequences in narratives, and outliers. Miles and Huberman's matrix displays provide the qualitative foundation; computation provides scale. Rigour comes from participant-level rather than mention-level counts, matrix displays that link to evidence, explicit search for negative cases, caution about treating counts from purposive samples as prevalence, and validating notable patterns by reading the underlying transcripts.
steps: Build a case-by-code matrix (participants by codes) with participant attributes.
Compute participant-level code frequencies by segment and co-occurrence statistics (e.g. Jaccard or lift).
Identify candidate patterns: strong co-occurrences, segment differences and sequences.
For each candidate, read at least 5-10 supporting cases and actively look for disconfirming cases.
Identify rare but consequential cases (e.g. safety issues) that frequency-based methods would miss.
Report patterns with matrix displays, counts out of N, quotes and limitations of the sample.
outputs: Case-by-code matrices, co-occurrence and segment comparison displays, validated pattern statements and negative cases.
useWhen: Very large qualitative programmes (hundreds of interviews), research repositories and multi-study synthesis.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting counts from purposive samples as population estimates; follow up with a survey for prevalence. Not needed for small studies.
whyLost: Cross-case matrices are a classic but laborious technique; scale and tooling only recently made them practical for hundreds of transcripts.
whereToUse: Research repositories, continuous discovery programmes, global studies and meta-synthesis of past research.
example: Across 320 customer interviews, the matrix shows 'shared account' and 'permission confusion' co-occur in 71 of 88 family-plan participants. Reading cases confirms the pattern, and a negative case reveals a workaround worth productising.
sources: Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M. & Saldaña, J. (2019) Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook, 4th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C13 — The Full Agentic Research Pipeline — Whisper → spaCy → AI Coder → Synthesis
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994) Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed.

name: Pattern Language Analysis for Interaction Design
origin: Christopher Alexander (A Pattern Language, 1977); adapted to interaction design by Jenifer Tidwell (1999, 2005) and Jan Borchers (2001)
summary: Analyses recurring design problems as patterns with context, forces, solution and known uses, distinguishing universal problems from product-specific ones to guide design system decisions.
description: Alexander defined a pattern as a recurring problem in a context, the forces that make it hard, and a solution that resolves those forces, linked into a language of patterns at different scales. Tidwell and Borchers adapted this to interaction design. As a research method, pattern analysis studies many products or many screens of one product to identify recurring problems and their solutions, documents the forces (competing user needs and constraints) behind each, and records known uses and evidence of effectiveness. This distinguishes universal problems with established solutions from genuinely product-specific ones, and exposes where a pattern is used without its forces holding. Today 'patterns' usually means component libraries, losing the problem, context and forces that made Alexander's formulation analytical.
steps: For each usability problem, formulate it as a pattern with four parts.
Context: in what situations does the problem arise?
Problem: what competing forces create it?
Solution: what design arrangement resolves the forces?
Consequences: what does the solution compromise?

Compare implementations across many products or devices (for example a physical device collection plus observation of people using them) to separate durable practice from novelty, keeping common but harmful practices as antipatterns.
Check whether the problem-solution pair is already documented in an established catalogue such as Tidwell's; if so, use the established solution, and if not, document it as a new pattern.
outputs: Pattern catalogue entries with problem, context, forces, solution, known uses and evidence; links between patterns; and identification of misapplied patterns.
useWhen: Building or auditing design systems, competitive analysis of recurring interaction problems, and onboarding designers to a domain.
avoidWhen: When a problem is novel with no comparable solutions, or when evidence of pattern effectiveness is needed; supplement with testing.
whyLost: Pattern languages were reduced to UI component libraries and pattern galleries, dropping the forces and context that make a pattern a reasoned solution.
whereToUse: Design system development, usability problem taxonomy, cross-product research synthesis, design knowledge management.
example: Analysing 25 fintech apps, a team documents the 'confirm before irreversible transfer' pattern with its forces (speed versus error prevention). They find their app uses the confirmation dialog even for reversible actions, eroding attention to the dialogs that matter.
sources: A Pattern Approach to Interaction Design (Jan Borchers)
Hoober, S. & Berkman, E., Designing Mobile Interfaces (O'Reilly, 2011)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Tidwell J (2010) Designing Interfaces: Patterns for Effective Interaction Design. 2nd ed. O'Reilly Media

name: Pattern-Led First-Person Ideation
origin: Indi Young, 2015
summary: An idea session that opens by voicing research patterns aloud in the first person with participants' words, and extends real scenes rather than inventing scenarios.
description: Young designed this session to keep ideation tied to what was actually heard in listening sessions. The person who did the listening represents participants' voices: after a reminder of organisational goals, they describe a pattern and its summaries aloud using 'I', participants' quotes and summary verbs, so collaborators hear reasoning rather than a report. Ideas start from actual scenes, which collaborators extend in different directions, instead of invented scenarios. Any demographic statement ('older users...') is reframed as reasoning. Only notes with working titles are kept, and the group revisits them a day later before any sketching. A variant, the 'design-less design session', is a short pre-session that discusses only people and scenes, with no solutions allowed.
steps: Remind the group of the organisational goals the session serves.
Have the listener describe one pattern and its summaries aloud, speaking as 'I' with participants' quotes.
Pick real scenes from the research and let collaborators extend them in different directions.
Reframe any demographic statements into reasoning and motivations.
Keep notes only, giving each idea a working title; avoid formal idea documents.
Revisit the notes a day later before sketching anything.
Optionally hold a short design-less session first that discusses people and scenes only.
outputs: Notes of ideas tied to specific research patterns and organisational goals.
useWhen: A team has rich qualitative patterns, such as from listening sessions or mental model research, and wants ideation that stays faithful to them.
avoidWhen: It depends on deep prior research; without it, first-person voicing becomes fiction. Gather the patterns with Interviews or Mental Model Diagram work first. Do not claim ownership of solutions or set early ideas in stone.
whyLost: Known mainly through Young's book; most ideation sessions start from 'How might we' prompts or personas instead of voiced patterns.
whereToUse: Service design, healthcare and financial products, content strategy, any team with mental-model research.
example: A pension provider's researcher voices a pattern ('I put off checking because I'm scared of the number') and the team extends a real scene of someone opening a statement, generating gentler disclosure ideas.
reference: Young, I. (2015) Practical Empathy: For Collaboration and Creativity in Your Work. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media, pp. 119-124.

name: PBUH Framework (Perception–Bias–Utility–History)
donor: HCI theory drawing on cognitive psychology, behavioural economics, reinforcement learning and systems theory
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2026
summary: A stateful model treating behaviour at time t as a function of perception, cognitive bias, utility and prior history, so UX research models state transitions rather than static usability.
description: PBUH formalises user behaviour as Behavior_t = f(P_t, B_t, U_t, H_t-1), where P is perception, B cognitive bias, U utility (objective and perceived) and H the historical state. History accumulates (H_t = H_t-1 + Experience_t), bias is a function of prior history (B_t = f(H_t-1)), perception depends on the interface and history (P_t = f(Interface, H_t-1)), and perceived utility is constructed from objective utility filtered through perception and bias (U_perceived = f(U_objective, P_t, B_t)). The framework bridges Neisser and Gibson's constructive perception, dual-process theory, Prospect Theory's reference points, reinforcement learning's reward history and state-space models. Its rigour lies in making path dependence explicit: the same screen can produce different behaviour depending on accumulated experience, and small perceptual or bias distortions compound into behavioural drift. The paper positions it as a theoretical foundation; empirical validation and simulation are named as future work.
steps: Define the behaviour of interest at time t and the observation window, treating each session or exposure as a time step rather than an independent trial.

Instrument the four state variables: perception P_t (what users notice and how they read the interface), bias B_t (e.g. loss aversion, framing sensitivity), objective utility U_objective (time, money, steps saved) and history H_t-1 (prior experiences with the product).
Log each interaction as an Experience_t event so the historical state can be updated as H_t = H_t-1 + Experience_t.

Model bias as conditioned on prior history (B_t = f(H_t-1)) and perception as conditioned on interface and history (P_t = f(Interface, H_t-1)), for example by segmenting users by prior bad experiences.
Estimate perceived utility as U_perceived = f(U_objective, P_t, B_t) and quantify the gap between perceived and objective utility for each segment.
Track how small perceptual or bias distortions accumulate across time steps to detect behavioural drift before it shows up as churn.
Use the fitted state model for predictive UX (anticipate undesirable transitions) and adaptive interfaces that adjust to inferred user state to close the perceived-versus-objective utility gap.
outputs: A state-space specification of user behaviour, measured state variables per user over time, a perceived-versus-objective utility gap, and hypotheses about which state transitions drive drift.
useWhen: When behaviour is path-dependent (trust after a failed payment, habituation to nudges), when the same design performs differently for new and veteran users, or when building predictive or adaptive experiences.
avoidWhen: When you need a quick usability verdict on a bounded task; use usability testing or tree testing. Without longitudinal data the history term cannot be estimated.
whyLost: Original framework proposed by Vivek Gopinath; it addresses the gap that HCI models typically assume static interaction between affordances and cognition.
whereToUse: AI-mediated interaction, fintech trust recovery, subscription and habit products, adaptive onboarding, behavioural drift monitoring.
example: A trading app sees new users who suffered a failed order hesitate on every subsequent order. Modelling H_t-1 (prior failure) as raising B_t (loss aversion) explains why perceived utility stays low despite a fixed bug, and justifies an adaptive reassurance state for that cohort.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2026), Modeling Stateful User Behavior: A Perception–Bias–Utility–History (PBUH) Framework for Dynamic UX Systems
reference: Gopinath, V. (2026). Modeling Stateful User Behavior: A Perception–Bias–Utility–History (PBUH) Framework for Dynamic UX Systems.

name: PCA
origin: Karl Pearson, 1901; Harold Hotelling, 1933
summary: Summarises many correlated variables in a few orthogonal components that capture the most variance, revealing the main axes along which users differ.
description: PCA rotates a standardised data matrix into uncorrelated components ordered by variance explained. The first few components often capture most of the structure in behavioural or survey data, for instance an activity-intensity axis and an exploration-versus-routine axis. Unlike factor analysis, PCA models total variance and has no latent-variable claim. It is used for compression before clustering, visualising user spaces, removing collinearity and detecting dominant behavioural dimensions. Rigour requires standardising variables, choosing components by parallel analysis or cross-validated reconstruction rather than arbitrary cut-offs, interpreting loadings carefully, and recognising that PCA captures only linear structure and is sensitive to outliers and scaling.
steps: Construct the feature matrix and standardise each variable to mean 0 and SD 1; log-transform heavily skewed counts first.
Run PCA and inspect the scree plot and cumulative variance explained.
Choose the number of components with parallel analysis or a variance target (often 70-90%), justified for the purpose.
Interpret components using loadings above about 0.4 in absolute value and name them by their dominant features.
Plot users in component space, colour by known outcomes or segments, and check outlier influence.
Use component scores downstream (clustering, regression) and report variance retained.
outputs: Component loadings, variance explained, component scores per user and low-dimensional maps of the user space.
useWhen: Reducing dozens or hundreds of behavioural or survey variables before clustering, modelling or visualisation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when relationships are strongly non-linear (use UMAP or t-SNE for visualisation), when you need latent constructs (use factor analysis), or with mostly categorical data (use MCA).
whyLost: It survived because it is simple, built into every tool and widely taught in data science; UX researchers increasingly encounter it through analytics teams.
whereToUse: Behavioural mapping in fintech and SaaS, survey dimension summaries, feature reduction before segmentation.
