example: Reducing 200 investor behaviour variables with PCA, the team finds that three components explain 68% of variance: activity intensity, risk appetite and research depth, which become the axes of a user archetype map.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
Sinha R (2003) Persona development for information-rich domains. CHI 2003 Extended Abstracts
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
A Comparative Analysis of Persona Clustering Methods (Brickey et al., 2010)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Jolliffe, I. T. & Cadima, J. (2016) Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 374(2065), 20150202.

name: PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) Cycle
origin: Walter Shewhart (1939) and W. Edwards Deming (1950s); used as a research-to-implementation model by Chang and Classen at Legacy Health (2024)
summary: Run research-led service change as a loop: plan with business and user research, pilot the change, check outcomes against measures, then standardise and scale.
description: PDCA is the quality-management loop of planning a change, trying it on a small scale, checking the result and acting on what was learned. Chang and Classen use it as a frame for research-led service improvement in healthcare. Plan has two strands: a business assessment using market research, leakage analysis, surveys and operational data, and user research combining surveys, dashboards and benchmarking with interviews, focus groups, usability studies and contextual inquiry; a service blueprint workshop then turns triangulated pain points into solutions and an action plan. Do uses a prioritisation framework to choose a pilot group and runs the change there. Check analyses pilot outcomes and staff feedback against success measures. Act shares learning, standardises, spreads and hands over to operations, then restarts the loop. Dashboards and leadership reviews run through every phase.
steps: Plan: assess the business problem with quantitative data to set objectives and success measures.
Plan: run user research scoped to those objectives, triangulating customer and staff pain points across qualitative and quantitative sources.
Plan: hold a service blueprint workshop where stakeholders generate solutions, and write an action plan.
Do: choose a pilot group with a prioritisation framework and run the change there for a defined period.
Check: analyse pilot outcomes and staff feedback against the success measures set in Plan.
Act: share learning, standardise the change, spread and scale it, hand it to the operational owner, and restart the cycle on the next problem.
outputs: An action plan, pilot results against measures, a standardised and scaled process, and KPIs with owners for ongoing monitoring.
useWhen: Service and operational change in complex organisations (healthcare, government, retail operations) where research must lead to piloted, owned and scaled improvements.
avoidWhen: Pure software features where controlled experiments are possible (use A/B Testing or Lean validated-learning experiments); or when the problem is not yet understood, where open discovery research should come before any Plan phase.
whyLost: PDCA thrives in healthcare and manufacturing quality improvement; product teams use the same loop as build-measure-learn or pilot-and-scale, usually without its origin or its emphasis on standardising and handing over.
whereToUse: Healthcare access and scheduling, public services, contact centres, retail and logistics operations, internal tools rollouts.
example: A health system's research shows patients cannot book online for some clinics. A pilot of online scheduling in a selected clinic group, including an obstetrics clinic thought unsuitable, cuts phone volume; the change is then standardised and rolled out system-wide.
sources: The Power of Data Triangulation (Chang & Classen, 2024)
reference: Chang, Y.-S., & Classen, N. (2024). The Power of Data Triangulation: Influencing Key Stakeholders via Combining Quantitative and Qualitative Research Findings on a Customer Journey Map. Quant UX Con 2024, conference slides; Deming, W. E. (1986). Out of the Crisis. Cambridge, MA: MIT CAES.

name: Peak moment design
origin: Kahneman and colleagues' peak-end rule (Fredrickson and Kahneman, 1993; Kahneman et al., 1993; Redelmeier and Kahneman, 1996); popularised by Chip and Dan Heath, The Power of Moments (2017)
summary: Designs and tests the most intense and final moments of an experience, because remembered evaluations depend disproportionately on the peak and the end rather than duration.
description: Remembered experience differs from moment-to-moment experience. Kahneman and colleagues found that retrospective evaluations are well predicted by the average of the most intense moment and the final moment, with duration largely neglected. In the cold-water study, participants preferred repeating a longer trial that ended slightly less painfully. In UX, users' willingness to return and recommend rests on remembered experience, so the peak (best or worst) and end moments matter disproportionately. Peak moment design identifies these moments empirically, designs them deliberately, and measures both momentary and retrospective evaluations. Rigour requires measuring moment-level affect, testing whether peaks and ends actually predict the retrospective rating in your context, and avoiding manipulation that improves memory while worsening the experience itself.
steps: Map the journey and collect momentary ratings at key points (for example a 1 to 7 affect rating after each step) from 15 to 40 users in testing or via diary or in-product prompts.
Collect a retrospective overall evaluation and intention to return after completion, and again after 1 to 7 days to capture remembered experience.
Test the peak-end relationship by regressing retrospective ratings on peak, end and average momentary ratings to identify which moments drive memory.
Remove or soften the worst negative peaks first, then design a positive peak and a strong ending, such as a meaningful success moment, recognition or tangible proof.
Run a comparative test of the redesigned peak and end, measuring both momentary averages and retrospective ratings.
Check that improvements to remembered experience do not hide worse momentary experience or mislead users.
outputs: Moment-level affect profiles, a model of which moments predict remembered experience, redesigned peak and end moments, and comparative retrospective ratings.
useWhen: Services with distinct episodes (applications, claims, onboarding, deliveries, medical visits); success screens that feel flat; improving recommendation and return intent.
avoidWhen: Continuous-use tools where overall efficiency dominates and episodes are not memorable; focus on usability and performance instead.
whyLost: The peak-end rule is widely cited and 'delight moments' are common, but teams rarely measure moment-level affect or test whether peaks and ends drive memory in their product.
whereToUse: Loan approvals and fintech onboarding, health appointments and results, e-commerce delivery and returns, travel, government services, AI task completion.
example: A platform's digital form submission ended with a plain 'Saved' toast, whereas paper ended with a stamp and a signature ritual. Redesigning the end moment as a daily summary with a supervisor acknowledgement raised retrospective satisfaction from 4.1 to 5.6 on a 7-point scale without changing task time.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 36 — Emotional Design Hierarchies & the Aesthetic-Usability Effect
reference: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401–405.

name: Pearl's do-calculus
origin: Judea Pearl, 1995
summary: A set of three formal rules for deciding whether an interventional quantity P(Y | do(X)) can be computed from observational data given a causal graph.
description: Do-calculus distinguishes seeing from doing: P(Y | X) is what we observe among users who happened to use a feature, while P(Y | do(X)) is what would happen if we made everyone use it. Given a causal DAG, Pearl's three rules (insertion or deletion of observations, action/observation exchange, insertion or deletion of actions) transform interventional expressions into observational ones where possible. The calculus is complete: if an effect is identifiable from the graph, the rules will find the formula, and if not, no adjustment can rescue it. For UX, its value is less in hand derivation and more in using software that applies it to say whether log data can answer a causal question at all.
steps: Translate the product question into an interventional query, e.g. the effect on retention of do(enable auto-invest).
Draw the causal DAG including unmeasured variables as latent nodes, drawing on qualitative research and domain experts.
Use an identification tool (e.g. DAGitty, DoWhy or the R package causaleffect) to apply do-calculus and return an identifying formula or a non-identifiability result.
If identifiable, implement the estimand (backdoor, front-door or a more general formula) with appropriate estimators.
If not identifiable, state which additional measurement or experiment would make it so.
Document the graph and derivation so reviewers can challenge the assumptions rather than the arithmetic.
outputs: A formal statement of whether a causal question is answerable from available data, with the identifying formula or the experiment needed.
useWhen: When stakeholders want causal answers from observational logs and you need to know whether that is possible before investing in analysis.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you can simply run a randomised experiment, or when the team cannot agree on any causal graph; start with a DAG workshop first.
whyLost: It is mathematically heavy and taught in computer science and epidemiology, not UX programmes. Product teams default to correlational dashboards or A/B tests.
whereToUse: Causal questions in fintech, health and marketplaces where experiments are restricted, and analysis of AI-recommendation effects from logs.
example: A wealth platform wants the effect of its risk-score display on portfolio diversification, but cannot randomise for regulatory reasons. Do-calculus over the agreed DAG shows the effect is identifiable via the front-door path through rebalancing actions, which the team then estimates.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
The Book of Why (Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 45 — The Causal Revolution — Pearl's Ladder & the Fundamental Problem
reference: Pearl, J. (1995) Causal diagrams for empirical research. Biometrika, 82(4), 669-688.

name: Peer Tutoring Evaluation
origin: Höysniemi, Hämäläinen and Turkki (2003)
summary: One child learns a product and then tutors a second child through it; usability problems and mental models are distilled from their dialogue.
description: Young children struggle with concurrent think-aloud, but they readily explain things to each other. In peer tutoring one child first tries out the product, then becomes tutor to a second child and helps that child use it. The tutor's explanations expose how the product was understood, and the tutee's difficulties expose usability problems, both in natural speech. The method was developed to evaluate a physically interactive computer game. Its validity depends on the role relationship: the tutor must actually tutor and the tutee must accept being taught by a peer. When tutors forget the role the pair behaves like a co-discovery pair, and tutors may take over the task instead of explaining it, so facilitators should brief roles clearly and code dialogue with that in mind.
steps: Recruit pairs of children of similar age and brief the first child that they will later teach a friend.
Let the first child explore and learn the product alone or with light guidance.
Introduce the second child and ask the first to help them use the product, without taking over.
Video-record the session, capturing dialogue and screen or play space.
Code the dialogue for the tutor's explanations (understanding) and the tutee's difficulties (problems).
Note episodes where the tutor took over or the pair drifted into co-discovery, and weigh those data accordingly.
outputs: Recorded tutor-tutee dialogue revealing children's mental models and a list of usability problems.
useWhen: Evaluating games, educational or physical-interactive products with children roughly 7 to 12 who can explain but not think aloud fluently.
avoidWhen: Avoid with very young children or unequal pairs; use Problem Identification Picture Cards for pre-verbal reporting or adult Think-Aloud Protocol for older teens.
whyLost: It stays within child-computer interaction research; most industry child testing uses adapted moderated sessions instead.
whereToUse: Edtech apps, children's games, museum interactives, toys with companion apps.
example: A maths-game studio has one 9-year-old learn the game, then teach a classmate. The tutor explains coins as 'lives', revealing a misunderstanding the onboarding never addressed.
reference: Höysniemi, J., Hämäläinen, P. and Turkki, L. (2003). Using peer tutoring in evaluating the usability of a physically interactive computer game with children. Interacting with Computers 15(2), 203-225.

name: Perceived attributes of innovations measurement
origin: Holloway, 1977; Moore and Benbasat, 1991; Kearns, 1992
summary: A validated survey of how potential adopters perceive an innovation's relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability, used to explain or predict adoption.
description: Rogers's five perceived attributes of an innovation explain 49-87% of the variance in rate of adoption. Moore and Benbasat turned them into an instrument: they pooled 75 items, ran four rounds of sorting by expert judges, surveyed 540 employees in seven companies and factor-analysed the results, yielding 28 items (15 in a short form) for the five attributes plus voluntariness, image and result demonstrability, validated by comparing adopters and non-adopters. Kearns first elicited attributes with triads of innovation cards (how are two alike and different from the third), finding 25 attributes for eight computer innovations across 127 municipalities, then had respondents rank innovations on each. Attributes can be measured before adoption, through analogy, a description of a hypothetical innovation or acceptability testing, to predict uptake. Rogers advises writing items anew for each innovation and population, and studying failures as well as successes.
steps: Elicit the attributes that matter to the target population, for example with triads of innovation cards, or start from the five standard attributes.
Write items for this innovation and population, adapting Moore and Benbasat's 28-item (or 15-item) instrument.
Pretest and refine items, using expert sorting rounds to check that items fall under their intended attribute.
Survey potential and actual adopters (a few hundred respondents for factor analysis).
Factor-analyse and check validity by comparing adopters and non-adopters.
Use attribute scores to explain or predict adoption and to target the weakest attribute in design or communication.
outputs: An attribute profile for each innovation or feature, validity evidence and predictors of adoption rate.
useWhen: When forecasting or diagnosing uptake of a new product, feature or workflow, particularly in organisational or B2B settings where adoption is a deliberate decision.
avoidWhen: Avoid for continuous, low-stakes features where usage analytics are faster. Cross-sectional data catch only part of shifting perceptions; for usefulness and ease of use alone use Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) Questionnaires.
whyLost: It is well known in information systems and diffusion research, but UX adopted the narrower TAM and rarely measures trialability or observability.
whereToUse: Enterprise software rollouts, health technology adoption, AI tools at work, B2B onboarding, public-sector digital services.
example: Before launching an AI meeting summariser to 3,000 staff, an IT team surveys pilot users: high relative advantage but low observability. They add shareable summaries so benefits are visible to colleagues, and adoption rises.
reference: Moore, G. C., & Benbasat, I. (1991). Development of an instrument to measure the perceptions of adopting an information technology innovation. Information Systems Research, 2(3), 192-222.

name: Perceived duration audit
origin: Time perception research from Vierordt (1868) onwards; applied to waiting by Maister (1985) and to progress indicators by Harrison et al. (2007)
summary: Compares how long waits and interactions feel with how long they actually take, identifying where perceived duration, not clock time, drives frustration.
description: Perceived duration diverges systematically from clock time: unfilled, uncertain or anxious waits feel longer, and progress feedback, occupied time and predictable rhythm make them feel shorter. Vierordt's law shows short intervals tend to be overestimated and long ones underestimated. A perceived duration audit pairs objective timing with participants' retrospective or prospective estimates and their ratings of acceptability, then identifies waits where the perception gap is largest. Remedies differ from engineering speedups: progress indicators, skeleton screens, optimistic UI, and explaining waits. Rigour comes from collecting verbal estimates or reproduction tasks immediately after each wait, comparing against logged durations, and accounting for anchoring.
steps: Identify all waits and delays in the flow and log their actual durations.
Run sessions with 8-15 participants; immediately after selected waits, ask for a duration estimate in seconds or a reproduction (press and hold for as long as the wait felt).
Collect an acceptability rating per wait on a 7-point scale.
Compute the ratio of perceived to actual duration per wait; flag ratios above 1.3 and waits rated below the scale midpoint.
Classify flagged waits by cause (uncertainty, no feedback, anxiety, idle time) and select remedies such as determinate progress bars, staged messaging or pre-loading.
Re-test the redesigned waits and compare perception ratios and acceptability.
outputs: A table of actual versus perceived durations, perception ratios and acceptability per wait, with cause codes and remedies.
useWhen: When performance cannot be improved quickly; when users complain about slowness that metrics do not confirm; when designing loaders, uploads, payments or AI generation waits.
avoidWhen: When latency is already below perceptual thresholds or the problem is actual task time; use temporal cognition mapping or KLM.
whyLost: Time perception is a mature research area, but UX tends to treat speed as an engineering metric, measuring clock time only.
whereToUse: Payment processing, medical imaging loads, AI response streaming, onboarding verification, and file uploads.
example: A fintech identity check takes 9 s but users estimate 20 s and rate it poorly. Adding staged status messages leaves clock time unchanged but halves the estimated duration and raises acceptability from 3.1 to 5.4.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
Card, S., Moran, T. & Newell, A., The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983) and GOMS/KLM literature
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 4 — Time, Rhythm & the Three Timescales of Experience
reference: Harrison, C., Amento, B., Kuznetsov, S. & Bell, R. (2007). Rethinking the progress bar. Proceedings of UIST 2007.

name: Perceptual Colour-Difference Check in a Uniform Colour Space
origin: Colour-matching experiments and Grassmann's laws; David MacAdam (1942) ellipses; CIE u'v' (1976) and CIELAB (1976) spaces
summary: Judge whether two colours are perceptibly different by converting them to a perceptually uniform space such as CIELAB or u'v' and comparing their distance with a just-noticeable threshold.
description: Colour matching experiments show trichromacy and near-linear matching, which underpin linear spaces such as CIE XYZ. But just-noticeable differences, found by altering a colour until observers can only just tell it changed, form MacAdam ellipses whose size varies strongly across the CIE xy diagram, so raw xy distance is a poor guide. A uniform colour space is one where coordinate distance fairly reflects perceived difference, so distances below a threshold mean colours cannot be told apart. CIE u'v' improves chromaticity uniformity, and CIELAB, which includes lightness, is the most widely used. The check is calculable from colour values alone. Forsyth and Ponce warn that comparing small differences is useful but comparing large differences is usually dangerous, and perceived colour also depends on surround, illumination and adaptation.
steps: Express the colours to compare in device-independent coordinates (convert sRGB to CIE XYZ with the display white point).
Convert them to a uniform space: CIE u'v' for chromaticity only, or CIELAB to include lightness.
Compute the Euclidean distance (Delta E) between each pair.
Compare the distance with a just-noticeable threshold (a Delta E of about 2-3 is commonly treated as just noticeable) to judge whether users could tell them apart.
Use the check only for small differences; do not rank large differences against each other.
Confirm critical distinctions under realistic surrounds and displays, and test with colour-vision deficiency simulations.
outputs: A colour-difference value per pair and a judgement of distinguishable or not.
useWhen: Checking that status colours, chart series, map categories or brand variants are distinguishable, and that colour tokens in a design system are not near-duplicates.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for contrast-ratio accessibility checks for text, which use luminance contrast (WCAG), and avoid ranking large differences. For category legibility in real use, test with users.
whyLost: Colour scientists and print and display engineers use it routinely, but UX teams rely on contrast ratios and eyeballing, rarely computing perceptual distance.
whereToUse: Design systems and token audits, data visualisation palettes, dashboards with status colours, cross-device brand colour management.
example: A design system audit computes CIELAB distances between 48 colour tokens and finds three pairs below Delta E 2, including two 'warning' oranges. The team merges them, reducing the palette without any visible change.
sources: Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: MacAdam, D. L. (1942). Visual sensitivities to color differences in daylight. Journal of the Optical Society of America, 32(5), 247-274; Forsyth, D. A. and Ponce, J. (2011). Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (2nd ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall, pp. 68-72, 83-86.

name: Perceptual effectiveness review of charts
aka: Perceptual effectiveness review of a data graphic
origin: Stephen Few (2013), drawing on Ware and Gestalt psychology; rooted in Cleveland and McGill (1984)
summary: Judge a chart against perceptual criteria for its message, explain each failure with perception science, and redesign with encodings people read more accurately.
description: A visualisation succeeds to the degree that people can easily, efficiently, accurately and meaningfully perceive its story. Few's review asks five questions: does the display clearly show how values relate, represent quantities accurately, make comparison easy, make ranked order easy to see, and make obvious how to use the information? Each judgement is backed by a perceptual reason. A 3-D pie with a legend passes only the first: areas, angles and arc lengths are poorly perceived, legends force look-ups and perspective inflates front slices. A ranked, directly labelled bar chart passes all five because position and length on a common baseline are read accurately. Gestalt principles, preattentive attributes and working-memory limits supply the reasons, grounding critique in evidence rather than taste.
steps: Identify the message and the relationship in the data the chart must convey (ranking, part-to-whole, trend, comparison).
State the five criteria: relationship shown, quantities accurate, comparison easy, ranking visible, use obvious.
Judge the display against each criterion as yes, no or partly, giving the perceptual reason.

Check the chart's honesty: an anchored or clearly marked origin, a labelled scale, no area or volume icons that exaggerate differences, absolute values alongside percentages, stated margins of error and a statement of which average is shown.
Redesign using more accurately perceived encodings, such as position and length on a common scale, direct labels and sorted order.
Judge the redesign again, and where stakes are high confirm with a quick task test of reading accuracy.
outputs: A criterion-by-criterion verdict with perceptual reasons, and an improved chart design.
useWhen: Reviewing dashboards, reports and in-product charts before release, or settling disagreements about chart design.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it alone for high-stakes displays; it is an expert illustration, not a scored method, so add user tests of reading accuracy.
whyLost: It is standard in data-visualisation practice but sits outside most UX research toolkits, which test dashboards for usability rather than perceptual accuracy.
whereToUse: Analytics and BI dashboards, fintech portfolio views, health data displays, internal reporting and research readouts.
example: A SaaS usage dashboard shows plan mix as a 3-D pie. The review shows users cannot rank plans or compare slices, so it becomes a sorted, directly labelled bar chart, and a quick test shows reading errors fall sharply.
sources: A Practical Guide to Designing with Data (Suda, 2010)
reference: Few, S. (2013). Data Visualization for Human Perception. In Soegaard, M. & Dam, R. F. (eds) The Encyclopedia of Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Interaction Design Foundation; Cleveland, W. S. & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception. Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(387), 531-554.

name: Perceptual load distractor paradigm
aka: Perceptual load distractor paradigm (Lavie's load theory)
origin: Lavie, 1995; Forster and Lavie, 2008; Raveh and Lavie, 2015
summary: A reaction-time task crossing low and high perceptual load with an irrelevant distractor, measuring how much spare attention leaks to distractors at each load level.
description: Participants search for a target letter (X or N) and press the corresponding key. Load is manipulated through the display: low load places the target among identical small o's, high load among varied letters. On some trials a task-irrelevant distractor, such as a cartoon character, appears nearby. Forster and Lavie (2008) found the distractor slowed the easy task more than the hard one: low-load tasks leave spare capacity that spills to irrelevant stimuli. Raveh and Lavie (2015) extended this across senses, showing that hard visual search lowered detection of an occasional tone (inattentional deafness). The distractor's own power also matters; a siren breaks through regardless. In UX the paradigm predicts when users will notice or ignore peripheral elements such as ads, alerts and status cues depending on the demand of the primary task.
steps: Define a primary task and build low-load and high-load versions that differ only in perceptual demand.
Choose a task-irrelevant distractor (ad, badge, animation, sound) and present it on a fixed proportion of trials, for example 10-25 per cent.
Randomise load and distractor presence within participants across many trials.
Record reaction time and accuracy on the primary task, and optionally detection of the distractor.
Compute the distractor cost (RT with minus without distractor) at each load level.
Test the load-by-distractor interaction; a larger cost at low load indicates spare-capacity spillover.
outputs: Reaction time by load and distractor condition; distractor cost per load level; detection rates for peripheral or cross-modal signals.
useWhen: You must predict whether a peripheral alert, ad or cue will be noticed, or will distract, during tasks of differing demand: driving, monitoring, checkout, coding.
avoidWhen: You only need to know whether people notice something in a realistic flow; an inattentional blindness test or eye tracking may be more direct. Distractor salience confounds load effects if not controlled.
whyLost: Load theory is well known in attention research and human factors, but UX rarely runs controlled RT designs and tends to reason about distraction informally.
whereToUse: In-car and cockpit displays, alerting in clinical dashboards, ad placement, notification design, AR overlays.
example: An in-vehicle team tests whether a low-fuel icon is noticed during easy versus dense navigation screens. Detection drops sharply under high load, so the alert is paired with a tone timed for low-load moments.
reference: Lavie, N. (1995). Perceptual load as a necessary condition for selective attention. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 21, 451-468; Forster, S., & Lavie, N. (2008). Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 14, 73-83.

name: Percolation and Phase Transition Analysis
origin: Simon Broadbent and John Hammersley (1957); Mark Granovetter's threshold models (1978); Duncan Watts' global cascades model (2002)
summary: Identifies critical thresholds at which local connections suddenly produce system-wide effects, such as network-wide adoption, virality or collapse.
description: Percolation theory studies when randomly occupied sites or links form a connected cluster spanning the system; at a critical probability, the system undergoes a sharp phase transition. Network science extends this to cascades: Watts' model shows global adoption is possible only in a window of connectivity and thresholds. Granovetter's threshold model explains how small differences in individual thresholds produce very different collective outcomes. For UX in networked products, this explains why features adopted by groups (shared workspaces, messaging, marketplaces) show nonlinear adoption, and helps identify the density of active users or connections needed before network effects take off.
steps: Represent the relevant network (users, teams, buyers and sellers) and the spreading process (adoption, sharing, liquidity).
Estimate individual thresholds or adoption probabilities from data or experiments.
Simulate percolation or cascade models across densities and threshold distributions.
Identify critical points where giant components or global cascades emerge.
Compare current state with critical points by market, team size or segment.
Design interventions (seeding, lowering thresholds, increasing local density) and test them.
outputs: Critical threshold estimates, phase diagrams, seeding strategies and segment-level positioning relative to tipping points.
useWhen: Products with network effects or social contagion, especially when adoption is stalled or uneven.
avoidWhen: Single-player products where users' value does not depend on others.
whyLost: Statistical physics is far removed from UX training, and growth teams use simpler heuristics like 'activation thresholds'.
whereToUse: Collaboration tools, marketplaces by city, social apps, payment networks, developer ecosystems.
example: A team collaboration tool finds that workspaces cross a percolation threshold when about 35% of members are weekly active; below it, usage collapses. Onboarding is redesigned to activate small subgroups densely rather than many users thinly.
sources: Watts, A simple model of global cascades on random networks (2002), PNAS
Granovetter, Threshold models of collective behavior (1978), American Journal of Sociology
Stauffer & Aharony, Introduction to Percolation Theory (2nd ed., 1994)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)

name: Performance Budget
origin: Web performance practice; presented by Lara Hogan (2014) from Etsy practice
summary: Agree measurable maxima for load time, page weight and perceived speed at a project's start, and trade any design addition that exceeds them against savings elsewhere.
description: A performance budget makes the trade-off between aesthetics and speed explicit before design begins. The team chooses metrics such as total load time, page weight and Speed Index (today often Core Web Vitals), and sets a maximum for each from competitor benchmarks or industry expectations, for example two seconds. Each budget line names the measuring tool, the test conditions (for example a median of five runs on a throttled 3G profile) and its scope, such as all pages, the home page or a breakpoint. The budget is written into project documentation, explained to every designer and developer, shown on dashboards and measured routinely. When a richer image, font or script pushes a metric over, the team finds an equivalent saving elsewhere or negotiates a removal. The budget is tightened as the team improves. Its rigour comes from being measurable and checked continuously rather than at launch.
steps: Choose the metrics (load time, page weight, Speed Index or Core Web Vitals), per breakpoint for responsive sites.
Set a maximum for each from competitor benchmarks or industry expectations, staying well below rivals.
For each line specify the tool, test conditions (for example median of five runs on a throttled 3G profile) and scope.
Record the budget in project documentation and walk the whole team through it, including designers.
When a design addition would exceed the budget, find a compensating saving or negotiate what to remove.
Measure routinely in continuous integration and real-user monitoring, and show results on a dashboard.
Revise the budget as performance improves and standards change.
outputs: A budget table (metric, maximum, tool, conditions, scope) and ongoing compliance measurements.
useWhen: Use from the start of any web or app project where speed affects conversion, retention or access on slow networks, especially when design wants rich media.
avoidWhen: Avoid setting unmeasurable goals, and remember budgets blur at breakpoints such as device rotation. To learn how much speed matters to your users, run Feature-removal and latency-injection tests or A/B Testing rather than assuming.
whyLost: It survived because performance links directly to conversion and search ranking, and modern build tools can enforce budgets automatically.
whereToUse: E-commerce, media sites, emerging-market products, progressive web apps, design system components.
example: A retailer sets an 800 KB page weight and 2 s load budget. When a hero video is proposed, the team pays for it by switching to a system font and lazy-loading reviews, and the build fails any pull request that breaks the budget.
reference: Hogan, L. C. (2014). Designing for Performance: Weighing Aesthetics and Speed. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 102-103, 129-130.

name: Performance Ethnography
origin: Dwight Conquergood (1985 onwards); D. Soyini Madison; Judith Hamera
summary: Study the expressive, embodied and affective side of a culture, including the research act itself as performance, with explicit attention to the ethics of representation.
description: Performance ethnography treats performance both as what is studied (rituals, everyday displays, how events look, sound and change, which emotions are authorised or silenced) and as a way of studying it, often by doing what participants do. It offers a methodological infrastructure rather than a recipe: key concepts (performance, performativity, aesthetics), genealogies of the field, and Conquergood's moral map of stances to avoid: the custodian's rip-off, the enthusiast's infatuation, the curator's exhibitionism and the cynic's cop-out, with dialogical performance at the centre. The researcher keeps asking whose voice is represented and to what end. Outputs can be written accounts or staged performances. It differs from ethnodrama, which stages findings after the fact, because performance here is part of fieldwork and analysis. Its discipline lies in reflexivity about stance rather than in procedure.
steps: Ask how performance emerges at the site and whether participants themselves regard it as performance.
Locate the performance in time, place, history and institutions.
Name the scholarly conversations your use of 'performance' joins and the concepts you are using.
Co-perform with participants where possible and document embodied and sensory experience.
Treat your own research presence as a performance and reflect on it in field notes.
Check your stance against the moral map and decide where the work can make meaningful interventions.
outputs: Ethnographic accounts of embodied and expressive practice, reflexive notes on stance, and sometimes staged performances.
useWhen: Understanding communities whose practices are expressive or embodied (creators, gamers, performers, fitness communities) and where representing them fairly matters.
avoidWhen: You need task-level requirements or quick usability findings; use Contextual Inquiry. Avoid if the team cannot commit to sustained engagement and ethical reflection.
whyLost: It is grounded in performance studies and critical theory, and its outputs rarely look like product deliverables.
whereToUse: Creator economy and live-streaming products, music and dance apps, gaming communities, social platforms, cultural institutions.
example: Researching a live-streaming app, a researcher streams alongside creators for six weeks, documenting how they perform authenticity for audiences and reflecting on her own on-camera presence, before advising on features that reward rehearsed intimacy.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Denzin, N. K. and Lincoln, Y. S. (Eds.) (2017). The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (5th ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Performance Validity (Effort) Testing
origin: Hiscock and Hiscock's Forced Choice Digit Memory Test (1989); Green, Rohling, Lees-Haley and Allen (2001); Green (2007)
summary: Embed tasks so easy that anyone trying passes them, and treat scores below a cutoff, especially near chance, as evidence that a participant's whole session is invalid.
description: Clinical judgement is poor at detecting low effort; only specific validity tests work. These tests are free-standing or embedded in a battery and have a pass cutoff. In the Forced Choice Digit Memory Test a person sees a five-digit number and then picks it from a pair with a new number, over 32 trials; even severely amnesic patients score near perfectly unless distracted, so the cutoff is at least 90% correct, and scores near chance (50%) suggest deliberate failure. Green and colleagues found in 904 patients that low effort suppressed scores four and a half times more than moderate to severe brain injury, and that it affects the whole battery. Incentives drive failure. Person-fit statistics can additionally flag aberrant patterns such as inattention on easy items. Scores near the cutoff are ambiguous.
steps: Choose or embed an effort measure that genuine participants pass easily, such as a forced-choice recognition task or trivially easy items within the main task.
Set a cutoff (for example 90% correct) and note the chance level for the format.
Administer it within the session, especially where incentives could motivate rushing, under-performance or over-performance.
Score each participant; treat failures, and particularly near-chance scores, as invalidating that participant's other scores.
Interpret near-cutoff scores cautiously and report exclusion rules and counts before analysis.
Optionally compute person-fit statistics to flag aberrant response patterns.
outputs: A pass/fail validity flag per participant and documented exclusion rules.
useWhen: Unmoderated performance tests, crowdsourced cognitive or perception tasks, paid panels and incentivised studies where low effort can masquerade as poor usability.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating failure as proof of deliberate deception, and avoid it in moderated sessions where effort is observable. For questionnaires, use survey data cleaning and attention checks instead.
whyLost: It is standard in forensic and clinical neuropsychology, but UX teams screen surveys for careless responses without carrying embedded effort tests into performance tasks.
whereToUse: Remote unmoderated usability benchmarks, online perception and memory experiments, accessibility studies with paid panels, AI evaluation with crowd raters.
example: An unmoderated benchmark of a tax tool embeds three trivially easy tasks. Eleven of 200 panellists fail two or more and also show the slowest times and lowest success, so excluding them by the pre-registered rule removes an apparent usability problem.
reference: Green, P., Rohling, M. L., Lees-Haley, P. R. and Allen, L. M. (2001). Effort has a greater effect on test scores than severe brain injury in compensation claimants. Brain Injury, 15(12), 1045-1060; Kolb, B. and Whishaw, I. Q. (2021). Fundamentals of Human Neuropsychology (8th ed.). New York: Worth, ch. 28.

name: Permutation Test (Resampling Significance Test)
origin: R. A. Fisher (1935) and E. J. G. Pitman (1937); popularised by computing power and Julian Simon's resampling movement
summary: Tests whether two groups really differ by shuffling the group labels thousands of times to see how often chance alone gives a gap as large.
description: Instead of relying on formulas and distributional assumptions, a permutation test asks directly: if the design made no difference, how often would randomly reassigning participants to groups produce a difference as large as the one observed? Pool all observations, shuffle and split them into groups of the original sizes many times, and compute the difference each time. The proportion of shuffled differences at least as extreme as the real one is the p-value. Bruce and Bruce present it as the data scientist's default because it works for any statistic, including medians, ratios and session stickiness, and is easy to explain to stakeholders.
steps: Compute the observed statistic (difference in means, medians, rates, anything).
Pool the data from both groups.
Repeatedly shuffle and split the pool into groups of the original sizes, recomputing the statistic (1,000 to 10,000 times).
Calculate the proportion of permuted statistics as or more extreme than the observed one.
Report this p-value with a histogram of the permutation distribution.
outputs: An assumption-light p-value and a visual null distribution.
useWhen: Small or skewed samples, unusual statistics (medians, percentiles, ratios), or audiences who distrust formulas.
avoidWhen: Observations are not exchangeable under the null (for example clustered or paired data, unless permuted within pairs).
whyLost: UX statistics teaching is built on classical tests; resampling arrived with data science but never crossed into usability practice.
whereToUse: Small A/B tests, task time comparisons with outliers, custom engagement metrics.
example: Median session duration is 41 s longer on a new homepage. In 10,000 shuffles, only 2.3% produce a gap that large, giving p = 0.023.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce, P. & Bruce, A. (2017). Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, chapter 3.

name: Person-specific time-series modelling (P-technique, GIMME)
aka: Replicated P-technique and dynamic factor analysis
donor: Psychometrics, time-series analysis and neuroimaging connectivity
origin: Cattell (1952) P-technique; Molenaar (1985) dynamic factor analysis; Molenaar (2004) ergodicity argument; Gates and Molenaar (2012) GIMME
summary: Models each person's own intensive repeated measurements, with lagged effects, and generalises across people only where person-specific structures agree.
description: Molenaar showed through ergodic theory that results from between-person analyses apply to individuals only if the process is stationary and identical across people, conditions that learning and development violate. Analysis therefore starts within the person. P-technique factor-analyses one person's occasions-by-variables matrix; dynamic factor analysis adds lagged loadings or latent auto- and cross-regressions in state-space form to capture carry-over from one occasion to the next. GIMME builds on this: it fits a unified SEM of contemporaneous and lagged paths to each person's series, adds a path to the group structure only if it significantly improves fit for at least 75% of individuals, then searches person-specific paths. In a simulation, pooling three nearly identical families produced paths that existed in none of them. Typical data are P-data: few people, many occasions (often over 50).
steps: Decide whether the question concerns between-person differences or within-person processes, using Cattell's data box (persons x variables x occasions).
Collect intensive repeated measures of the same variables from each person at many, ideally equally spaced, occasions (50 or more via experience sampling, diaries or telemetry).
Fit a P-technique or dynamic factor (state-space) model per person, including lagged effects; allow time-varying parameters if the process is nonstationary.
For network questions run GIMME: free group-level paths one at a time, keeping each only if significant for at least 75% of people, and prune paths that fall below that majority.
Use the group structure as each person's starting model, add person-specific paths while they improve fit, prune non-significant ones, and fit a final confirmatory model per person.
Compare person-specific structures and aggregate only where homogeneity holds.
outputs: Person-specific factor loadings and dynamics (auto- and cross-lagged effects), a shared group network with individual weights, and person-specific extra paths.
useWhen: Experience sampling, diary or sensor studies with many occasions per person, where the question is how states or behaviours influence each other within individuals, such as stress, app use and mood.
avoidWhen: Few occasions per person (use growth curves or multilevel models), irregular sampling without continuous-time extensions, or questions purely about differences between people.
whyLost: These methods need intensive longitudinal data and specialist software; UX diary studies are usually analysed qualitatively or by pooled averages that assume everyone works the same way.
whereToUse: Digital health and wellbeing apps, experience sampling of notification load, wearable data, personalisation research, longitudinal AI-assistant use.
example: A mental-health app collects mood, sleep, app use and social contact twice daily from 40 users for 10 weeks. GIMME finds a group path from poor sleep to next-day low mood in most users, while app use lifts mood only for a subgroup, informing personalised nudges.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Designing an Experience Sampling Study (Dejonckheere & Erbas, 2021)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Molenaar, P. C. M. and Nesselroade, J. R. (2015). Systems methods for developmental research. In R. M. Lerner, W. F. Overton and P. C. M. Molenaar (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 1 (pp. 652-682). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Persona Bug Bash and QA Scripts
origin: Microsoft practice reported by Pruitt and Adlin; Mulder and Yaar (2007)
summary: QA staff and colleagues use the product in role as specific personas for a fixed session, logging bugs and UX issues per persona and prioritising them by persona impact.
description: Personas are usually used upstream in design, but they can also steer quality assurance. QA teams trained in the personas and their supporting data, including hardware and connection context, can judge which of an exploding number of test cases are plausible and frequent, and derive test cases from design scenarios. In the bug bash, staff split into one team per persona, read its profile and scenarios, then use the product as that persona for a fixed period such as four hours, logging code bugs, UX problems and fit-and-finish issues. Duplicates and non-reproducible issues are removed and results are reported per persona. Structured QA can carry separate scripts per persona, and the bug tracker can rank issues by impact on each persona. Evidence is limited to practitioner reports, and role-playing staff are not real users.
steps: Train QA and participating staff on the personas and their data, including devices, connection and context.
Use personas and design scenarios to prioritise and write test cases, with separate scripts per persona where QA is structured.
Form one bash team per persona and have each read its persona and scenarios.
For a fixed period, such as a four-hour session, use the product as that persona, logging code bugs, UX problems and fit-and-finish issues.
Remove duplicates and non-reproducible issues.
Report counts and issues per persona and tag each bug with the personas it affects, ranking by persona impact.
outputs: Bug and UX issue lists per persona, persona-prioritised test plans, and a persona-impact field in the bug tracker.
useWhen: Pre-release QA cycles where personas exist and you want test coverage and bug triage aligned with real user priorities.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating it as user evidence; staff role-play cannot replace Usability Testing with real users, and weak personas will mislead triage.
whyLost: Personas fell out of favour in many teams and QA became automated, so persona-driven manual testing rarely happens.
whereToUse: Enterprise software releases, accessibility-focused releases with assistive-technology personas, games with distinct player types.
example: A tax-software team runs a Friday bug bash with three persona teams. The 'first-time freelancer' team logs twice as many blocking issues as the 'accountant' team, shifting release priorities.
sources: The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Adlin, T. and Pruitt, J. (2010). The Essential Persona Lifecycle. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 156-157; Mulder, S. and Yaar, Z. (2007). The User Is Always Right. New Riders, pp. 274-275.

name: Persona Enactment and Empathic Role-Play
aka: Persona role-play with users in co-design
Persona enactment: co-design and role-play with personas
origin: Lene Nielsen, 2011-2019; stop-go improvisation from Brandt and Grunnet, 2000; rehearsal remapping by Erin Beierwaltes and Aaron White in Patton, 2014
summary: Users or team members act out scenarios in the role of data-based personas or stakeholders, with simple props, to generate ideas, build shared understanding or challenge journey assumptions.
description: Enactment puts personas into bodies. In Nielsen's co-design form, users and project staff receive persona descriptions and scenarios varying in situation and context, build a makeshift stage from paper and props, assign roles (one plays the persona, others play people or objects) and act the scenario through, explaining choices to a moderator; then they repeat it as a contrasting persona. In the Arla Foods canteen case a two-day workshop produced more than twenty ideas, four taken forward. Variants include hired actors filmed in short documentary-style persona films, masks, dollhouses or Lego figures, and stop-go improvisation in which the audience halts a scene and proposes alternatives. Hanington and Martin's empathic role-play has designers act users and stakeholders while an observer documents problems. Rehearsal remapping gives actors only persona goals, observes silently, then rebuilds the journey map from what actors actually did.
steps: Start from data-based personas and choose a small number that contrast in behaviour and context.
Write scenarios varying situation and context; for remapping, give only goals, not steps.
Build a simple stage and props, assign roles, and appoint a moderator and silent observers.
Act each scenario from start to end, with the persona player explaining choices aloud; allow the audience to stop and redirect scenes if using stop-go.
Repeat the scenario from another persona's perspective.
Document with planned photos, video and notes, since role-play is not self-documenting.
Debrief: collect ideas, pains and gains, divergences from the existing journey map and assumptions needing evidence.
outputs: Product and service ideas, enactment notes and video, rebuilt journey maps, and a list of assumptions to test.
useWhen: A team needs ideas that take a persona's perspective, wants users as co-designers, or wants to stress-test a journey map's assumptions.
avoidWhen: Team members are not users, so enactment tests assumptions rather than replacing Usability Testing or Contextual Inquiry. It appeals to emotion more than analysis, can be unrealistic or hurtful when caricaturing people, and persona films that look like real users raise validity and ethics questions. For participatory work with real users consider Co-design Workshops.
whyLost: Rooted in Scandinavian participatory design and drama-based design; many teams find acting uncomfortable and hard to document, so it stays niche.
whereToUse: Service design, public-sector digital services, food and retail innovation, agile teams validating story maps.
example: A public-services portal team gives two actors persona goals only (renew a disability benefit), watches silently, and rebuilds the journey map from their paths, finding a document-upload detour the original map missed.
reference: Nielsen, L. (2019) Personas: User Focused Design. 2nd edn. London: Springer, pp. 108-111.

name: Persona Prioritisation by Value and Influence
aka: Primary, secondary, unimportant and excluded personas
donor: Customer relationship management and decision analysis
origin: Steve Mulder and Ziv Yaar (2007); John Pruitt and Tamara Adlin (2006, 2010)
summary: Rank personas using linked CRM value data and stakeholders' private 100-point allocations, then label each primary, secondary, unimportant or excluded.
description: Personas are useful only if the team agrees whom to design for when needs conflict. Two complementary procedures do this. Mulder and Yaar link survey respondents to CRM records (spend, transactions, frequency) so each persona has a financial value, then weigh influence on others and reputation; in their brokerage case the feature-hungry segment had the lowest revenue per trade, so another persona was prioritised. Pruitt and Adlin have stakeholders rough-rank persona skeletons, add data on frequency, market size, revenue and strategic importance, and then privately allocate 100 points with no ties except zero. Posted scores expose misalignment, which is discussed until agreed weights emerge. Labels follow: primary (usually one, at most two, wins conflicts), secondary, unimportant and excluded. Priorities can differ by product area.
steps: Where possible, link persona survey respondents to CRM data and compute value per persona (for example revenue per transaction or share of spend).
Present persona skeletons with data on frequency of use, market size, revenue and strategic importance, and ask who must be made exceptionally happy.
Have each stakeholder privately allocate 100 points across personas, with no ties except zero.
Post scores in a persona-by-stakeholder grid and discuss discrepancies until agreed weights emerge; allow more than one meeting.
Ask who is missing and add assumption skeletons for any groups not yet represented.
Label each persona primary (one, at most two), secondary, unimportant or excluded, per product area if needed.
Record the weights for use in feature prioritisation matrices.
outputs: An agreed persona priority list with value figures and weights, including primary, secondary and excluded (anti-)personas.
useWhen: After creating personas, when teams disagree about whom to design for, or when feature decisions need weighting by user group.
avoidWhen: Avoid with more than about 8-10 skeletons, and do not treat current revenue as future potential. The neediest persona is not automatically the most important; if personas are not research-based, validate them first.
whyLost: Teams still say 'primary persona' but rarely ground the choice in value data or a structured stakeholder allocation.
whereToUse: Fintech and trading platforms, B2B SaaS with distinct buyer and user roles, marketplaces with several sides.
example: An investing app team allocates 100 points across five personas; finance gives most to active traders and design to first-time savers. CRM data on lifetime value settles the primary persona for the order screen while savers stay primary for onboarding.
sources: The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Mulder, S. with Yaar, Z. (2007). The User Is Always Right: A Practical Guide to Creating and Using Personas for the Web. Berkeley, CA: New Riders; Adlin, T. and Pruitt, J. (2010). The Essential Persona Lifecycle. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Persona Socialisation and Communication Campaigns
origin: Pruitt and Adlin, 2006 and 2010; Mulder and Yaar, 2007; talk-show enactment by Steve Portigal reported by Quesenbery and Szuc, 2011
summary: A planned campaign that introduces personas to each audience in small chunks, with named wranglers, artefacts and staged enactments, so personas are used in decisions rather than filed away.
description: Almost nobody reads persona foundation documents, so Adlin and Pruitt plan persona communication as a staged campaign. The team writes a strategy of widening circles of buy-in tied to milestones, analyses each audience's decisions and information needs, and appoints a wrangler per persona to answer questions and guard key traits. A kickoff explains the method, data and validation before the personas themselves. Detail is then disclosed progressively through planned artefacts: teasers, comparison aids such as rosters and trading cards, and enrichers such as one-pagers, quote posters, email aliases and a persona room or site. Mulder and Yaar add tailored presentations, quizzes, role-play in meetings and life-size cut-outs. Portigal's 'Segments Come Alive' stages researchers in character on a talk show, interviewed by a host and then the audience; questions they cannot answer reveal research gaps.
steps: Write a communication strategy: audiences, what each needs, when and how, tied to project milestones.
Appoint a wrangler for each persona and agree the traits that must not change.
Hold a kickoff that explains the method, data and validation before introducing the personas.
Disclose detail progressively through planned artefacts (teasers, rosters, one-pagers, quote posters, persona site).
Run interactive formats: quizzes on which persona fits a situation, role-play in meetings, or a talk-show enactment with audience questions.
Report later research findings by persona, with real user clips, to keep credibility.
Track usage, retire personas that prove wrong rather than patching them, and re-introduce personas to new staff.
outputs: A communication plan, persona artefacts, named wranglers, a persona site or room, and a list of knowledge gaps surfaced by enactments.
useWhen: Personas exist but are not used in decisions, or a large organisation needs them adopted across functions.
avoidWhen: Campaigning cannot rescue personas built without data; check them first with Persona Validation Against Behavioural Data or rebuild them with Goal-Directed Persona Construction (Cooper's Method). Cute artefacts can put off analytical cultures, and over-promising damages credibility.
whyLost: Persona posters survived, but the planned campaign, wranglers, maintenance and retirement rules are usually skipped, which is one reason personas gather dust.
whereToUse: Large product organisations, banks and insurers, agencies handing over research, research operations teams.
example: An insurer's research team runs a talk-show session in which researchers play three customer segments; engineers' questions about claims anxiety go unanswered, prompting a targeted interview study.
sources: The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Adlin, T. and Pruitt, J. (2010) The Essential Persona Lifecycle: Your Guide to Building and Using Personas. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Persona Story Crafting
aka: Persona story crafting with story element chart and retell test
origin: Whitney Quesenbery, 2006, building on Denning, Erickson and Decker
summary: Write short persona stories from research using a story element chart, edit them aloud, and test them by asking someone to retell the story and its point.
description: Quesenbery's procedure makes persona stories deliberate instead of decorative. The writer first chooses the story's purpose: to set context, illustrate a problem or present a proposal. A story element chart is then filled in: the story's goal, the persona and other characters, situation, the persona's goal, the trigger, the actions and the resolution. Real anecdotes and quotes from research supply the material. The draft is short and sequential, and is edited by reading aloud, cutting jargon, passive voice, judgements and click-by-click interface steps; first or third person is chosen by use. The test is a retell: someone else describes the character, retells the events and states the point. Stories stay under about 350 words, with more written as questions arise.
steps: Choose the story's purpose: context, problem or proposal.
Fill the story element chart: story goal, characters, situation, persona goal, trigger, actions, resolution.
Gather real anecdotes and quotes from research to populate it.
Draft a short sequential story of under about 350 words.
Edit aloud, cutting jargon, passive voice, judgements and click-by-click steps; choose first or third person.
Ask another person to describe the character, retell the events and state the point; revise where they cannot.
Check it rings true against the research and add new stories as questions arise.
outputs: Short, tested persona stories for context, problems and proposals.
useWhen: Personas exist and the team needs them to carry specific context, problems or design proposals to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Back-story drifts into irrelevance and caricature; stories that make no sense signal personas not grounded in data. Ground the material in Interviews or Narrative Inquiry, and for evaluating a proposed flow use Narrative Usability Test or Scenario-Based Design.
whyLost: Persona narratives are still written, but the element chart, aloud editing and retell test are rarely used, so stories become filler.
whereToUse: Persona packs, stakeholder presentations, design proposals, service design narratives.
example: A fintech team writes a 300-word proposal story in which a freelancer receives a late-payment alert and chases an invoice; a product manager retelling it misses the point, so the trigger is rewritten.
reference: Quesenbery, W. (2006) Storytelling and narrative. In Pruitt, J. and Adlin, T., The Persona Lifecycle: Keeping People in Mind Throughout Product Design. San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 521-554.

name: Persona User Story Workshop
aka: Persona user story workshop for agile teams
origin: Nielsen, Larusdottir, Jeppesen and Kjoller, 2018, in three Danish Scrum organisations; builds on Winter et al., 2012
summary: Cross-functional groups write user stories for the same epic from two contrasting personas, then derive test tasks, making user diversity tangible in the backlog.
description: Agile user stories often name a generic 'user', which hides who the product serves. In this workshop, groups mixing business, UX and ideally development staff each receive two personas chosen to be as different as possible. They write stories for one epic first from one persona's perspective, then from the other's, in the form 'As [persona, role], I want to... in order to...', and note test tasks for the stories. Plenary discussion compares the two sets. In the Danish experiments the diversity of users became tangible, managers' involvement built buy-in, proto-personas prompted participants to question the data, while detailed personas were trusted even where thin.
steps: Form cross-functional groups of business, UX and development staff.
Give each group two maximally contrasting personas and one epic.
Write user stories for the epic from the first persona's perspective.
Write stories for the same epic from the second persona's perspective.
Derive test tasks for the stories.
Compare the two story sets in group and plenary discussion and carry differences into the backlog.
outputs: User stories and test tasks per persona and shared awareness of user diversity.
useWhen: An agile team writes stories for a generic user and needs to bring persona differences into backlog and acceptance criteria.
avoidWhen: The first persona anchors the second, unfamiliar personas are hard to write for, the story format cannot hold the discussion, and a customer representative may compete with personas. Personas must be grounded; check them with Persona Validation Against Behavioural Data, and test the resulting stories with Usability Testing.
whyLost: Reported in research on Danish Scrum teams; most teams name personas in stories without running a structured contrastive workshop.
whereToUse: Agile product teams, public-sector digital services, enterprise SaaS backlogs.
example: A payroll SaaS team writes stories for a 'year-end reporting' epic as a small-business owner and as an accountant managing 40 clients; the second set adds bulk actions the first missed.
reference: Nielsen, L. (2019) Personas: User Focused Design. 2nd edn. London: Springer, pp. 117-120.

name: Persona Validation Against Behavioural Data
origin: Pruitt & Adlin, 2006; Sinha, 2003
summary: Tests whether qualitative personas correspond to real, distinguishable groups in behavioural and survey data, and measures how much of the user base each represents.
description: Persona validation treats personas as hypotheses about segments and tests them against data. Each persona is operationalised as a set of measurable attributes (survey items, behavioural signatures); users are then classified, using rules, discriminant analysis or cluster comparison, to estimate how many users each persona represents and how well personas separate. Personas that cover few users, overlap heavily or cannot be distinguished are merged, revised or retired, and missing segments that emerge from data are investigated qualitatively. The method preserves the empathic value of personas while preventing them from becoming fiction. Rigour depends on pre-specifying classification criteria, using cross-validation, and triangulating quantitative fit with fresh qualitative evidence.
steps: Step 1: Construct personas from qualitative research (behavioral interviews, contextual inquiry).
Step 2: Operationalize each persona as a set of measurable behavioral characteristics (e.g., 'uses feature X >3x/week, session duration <10min, mobile-first').
Step 3: In analytics data, identify users matching each persona's behavioral profile.
Step 4: Compute: what % of your user base matches each persona?
Step 5: If a persona has < 5% behavioral representation, reconsider its priority or validity.
outputs: Persona prevalence estimates, discriminating behaviours, classification accuracy, revised or merged personas, and a validity report.
useWhen: When personas drive strategy or roadmaps, when stakeholders doubt them, or when personas have aged and the user base has shifted.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there is too little data to segment, or when personas are used only as lightweight empathy aids; validate with interviews instead.
whyLost: Personas were adopted as communication artefacts and rarely revisited; the lifecycle stage of validating them against data was skipped.
whereToUse: Data-driven persona validation, product strategy prioritization, cross-functional alignment between UX and data teams.
example: A SaaS company classifies 20,000 accounts against its four personas using survey items and usage data; one persona covers under 3% of users and two others cannot be separated, so the set is rebuilt.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Pruitt J & Adlin T (2006) The Persona Lifecycle: Keeping People in Mind Throughout Product Design. Morgan Kaufmann

name: Persona validation with the Persona Perception Scale
aka: Persona validation by the represented users with a persona perception questionnaire
origin: Salminen and colleagues (Persona Perception Scale); applied by Castelo Branco et al., 2020
summary: Ask the people a persona set describes to rate each persona's credibility, similarity and empathy, and say which persona most resembles them, to check the personas ring true.
description: Personas are rarely checked against the people they claim to represent. The Persona Perception Scale, built by Salminen and colleagues from psychology, persona and HCI literature with content validation, measures perceptions such as credibility, consistency, completeness, clarity, likability, empathy, similarity and willingness to use. Castelo Branco et al. selected credibility, similarity and empathy items to fit their aims and added identification questions: which persona looks like you, thinks like you, shares your interests. They sent the questionnaire to the population the personas were derived from; 70 of 130 original respondents answered, nobody disagreed on credibility, and two of four personas drew most identification. The approach is descriptive but gives a cheap reality check. Low identification with a persona does not necessarily make it invalid, since it may represent a genuine minority segment.
steps: Select items from the Persona Perception Scale that fit the project's aims (for example credibility, similarity, empathy).
Build an online questionnaire presenting each persona with Likert agreement items, randomising persona order.
Add identification questions: which persona looks like you, thinks like you and shares your interests.
Send it to the population the personas were built from, explaining the purpose; aim for a response from at least half the source sample.
Tabulate agreement per item and identification votes per persona; compare identification shares with segment sizes from the source data.
Revise or merge personas that score low on credibility; keep low-vote personas that match genuine minority segments.
outputs: Agreement distributions per perception criterion and a ranking of self-identification per persona.
useWhen: When personas were generated from surveys, clustering or AI and stakeholders doubt whether they reflect real users, or before investing in persona-driven design.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the only validation: self-recognition is not behavioural accuracy, so pair with Persona Validation Against Behavioural Data. Positively worded items invite acquiescence.
whyLost: Persona practice values storytelling over measurement; validated persona perception instruments stayed within a small academic community.
whereToUse: Data-driven and AI-generated personas, B2B persona sets, education and public-service products with reachable user populations.
example: A university app team clusters survey data into four student personas, then asks 300 students to rate them. One persona scores low on credibility and almost nobody identifies with it, so it is merged into its neighbour.
sources: Does This Persona Represent Me? (Castelo Branco et al., 2020)
reference: Castelo Branco, K. da S., Oliveira, R. A., da Silva, F. L. Q., Rabelo, J. de H., & Marques, A. B. S. (2020). Does this persona represent me? IHC 2020. ACM. doi:10.1145/3424953.3426648

name: Persona-Weighted Feature Prioritisation Matrix
origin: Geoffrey Moore's target customer value matrix (1991); Pruitt and colleagues, Microsoft Windows team (2005); Mulder and Yaar (2007); Adlin and Pruitt (2010)
summary: Scores each candidate feature for each persona, typically from -1 to +2, weights scores by persona priority, and ranks features by the weighted sum.
description: The matrix makes the link from personas to roadmap explicit. Must-have features are set aside; the remaining candidates are rows and each persona is a column, weighted by agreed business importance (for example market size and revenue) with weights summing to 100. Each cell is scored 2 (needed, great value), 1 (useful), 0 (indifferent) or -1 (the persona is confused, annoyed or harmed). Scores ideally come from persona-matched users rating features or allocating a fixed sum of money; when a committee scores, guessed or disputed cells are flagged for later data. Weighted sums are computed and features sorted. Mulder and Yaar's variant starts with directed brainstorming per persona goal against business objectives, rates items 1-5 per persona with the primary persona weighted three times and secondary twice, and adds effort and phase columns. Microsoft's team found it pushed pet features down and made reasoning explicit.
steps: Set aside must-have features and list candidate features as rows; optionally brainstorm features per persona goal against business objectives first.
Add one column per persona with weights summing to 100, based on market size, revenue or strategic priority.
Score each cell 2, 1, 0 or -1, preferably from research with persona-matched users (ratings, surveys or a fixed-budget allocation).
If a committee scores, flag guessed or disputed cells and schedule research to resolve them.
Compute the weighted sum per feature, sort, and add effort and phase columns.
Investigate surprises rather than accepting them, allow argued exceptions for cost, timing or competition, and share the matrix with developers and QA to explain decisions.
outputs: A ranked feature list with weighted scores and persona rationale, effort and phasing.
useWhen: Release planning when a team has validated personas and must trade off features across several user types.
avoidWhen: When personas are not grounded in data or weights are political; committee scores are assumptions and carry personal bias. For direct user trade-offs use MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) or Conjoint Analysis; for effort-value triage use Effort × Impact Prioritisation Grid.
whyLost: Personas often became posters rather than decision tools, and the scoring discipline was dropped in favour of informal 'which persona is this for' debates.
whereToUse: SaaS and enterprise products with multiple roles, platform releases, accessibility and inclusive feature trade-offs.
example: A clinic-management SaaS weights personas Receptionist 50, Clinician 35 and Practice Owner 15; a feature scoring 0, 1 and 2 earns 0x50 + 1x35 + 2x15 = 65, while bulk SMS reminders score 160 and move to the next release.
sources: The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Pruitt, J., Miner, T., Lovejoy, T., Graf, R., Hoek, T. and Boettcher, S. (2005). Personas: a case study by Microsoft Corporation. In Courage, C. and Baxter, K. Understanding Your Users. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 84-86; Adlin, T. and Pruitt, J. (2010). The Essential Persona Lifecycle. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Personas
origin: Alan Cooper, 1983 (published in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum, 1999)
summary: Archetypal user representations, built from research data, that summarise goals, behaviours and contexts so teams design for specific people rather than themselves.
description: Personas are fictional but evidence-based characters that represent distinct groups of users, each with goals, behaviours, contexts, frustrations and needs. Alan Cooper introduced them in interaction design to counter self-referential and 'elastic user' thinking, giving teams a concrete person to design for. Persona quality depends entirely on their grounding: good personas are derived from patterns in qualitative research, often supported by quantitative segmentation, and are differentiated by behaviour and goals rather than demographics. Rigour comes from identifying behavioural variables, mapping participants on them to find clusters, validating segment sizes where possible, documenting the evidence behind each attribute, and retiring or updating personas when the user base changes. Proto-personas based on assumptions should be labelled as such.
steps: Conduct or gather qualitative research with 10 or more participants across expected segments.
Identify behavioural variables, such as goals, frequency of use and expertise, from the data.
Map each participant on each variable and look for clusters of participants who share patterns.
Synthesise each cluster into a persona with goals, behaviours, context and pain points, citing evidence.
Validate segments and their relative size with survey or analytics data where possible.
Prioritise primary and secondary personas and share them with scenarios.
Review personas at least annually and update them as evidence changes.
outputs: A small set of evidence-based persona profiles with goals, behaviours, contexts and pain points, plus segment sizes where validated.
useWhen: When aligning a team on who they are designing for, onboarding new staff, or prioritising features against distinct user goals.
avoidWhen: Avoid when no research exists to ground them, which yields stereotypes; run discovery research first. For quantitative targeting, use cluster analysis segments instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Communication tool with broad stakeholder appeal; though evidence for decision-making impact is mixed.
whereToUse: Product strategy alignment; design direction-setting; onboarding new team members.
example: A payroll SaaS builds three personas from 18 interviews and product analytics: the occasional small-business owner, the in-house payroll specialist and the accountant managing many clients. The roadmap prioritises bulk actions for the accountant persona.
sources: The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (Cooper)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
