Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
A Comparative Analysis of Persona Clustering Methods (Brickey et al., 2010)
UX Methodology Study by Data Analysis (Lee & Park, 2021)
reference: Cooper, A. (1999). The Inmates Are Running the Asylum. Sams; Pruitt, J. & Adlin, T. (2006). The Persona Lifecycle. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Persuasive technology analysis
aka: Persuasive technology analysis (functional triad and influence-strategy audit)
origin: B. J. Fogg, Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab, 1998-2003
summary: Code each element of a product, or every product in a category, by functional-triad role and influence strategy to map where persuasion comes from and where gaps lie.
description: Fogg's functional triad classifies how computing products persuade: as tools (making behaviour easier), as media (providing simulated experience) and as social actors (using social cues). The analysis inventories a product's elements and codes each by triad role and by specific strategy: reduction, tunnelling, tailoring, suggestion, self-monitoring, surveillance or conditioning for tools, simulation types for media, and social cues and influence principles for social actors. It distinguishes macrosuasion (persuasion is the product's purpose) from microsuasion (persuasive elements embedded in other products). Applied across a market, it counts strategies per product; a review of 72 mobile health apps found most relied on tracking, analysis or reference material and almost none used social or simulation strategies. Tactics, the implementation of each strategy, are recorded separately, and each element is screened for ethical red flags.
steps: Define the target attitude or behaviour and whether persuasion is the product's main purpose (macro) or embedded (micro).
Inventory user-experience elements: screens, messages, features, notifications, characters.
Code each element by triad role (tool, medium, social actor) and by strategy from the captology list, using a written codebook.
Record the tactic for each strategy (for example how tracking is captured, how often and with what metaphor).
For a category review, apply the same codes to every product with two coders and count strategy frequencies.
Compare strategies used with those suited to the goal and audience, flagging gaps and overused patterns.
Screen each element for ethical red flags: coercion, deception, covert conditioning or surveillance.
outputs: A strategy-by-element map for one product, or a strategy frequency table across a market, with gaps, opportunities and ethical flags.
useWhen: Competitive reviews of behaviour-change products, auditing the persuasive design of an existing product, or generating ideas from unused strategies.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the presence of a strategy as evidence it works; test effects separately. For diagnosing a single target behaviour use the Fogg Behavior Model diagnostic; for dark patterns use deceptive pattern analysis.
whyLost: Captology is still cited, but the systematic coding procedure gave way to informal 'persuasive design' pattern lists and newer frameworks such as persuasive systems design and COM-B.
whereToUse: Health, fitness and finance apps, sustainability products, edtech, ethical design reviews, market landscape analysis.
example: A savings start-up codes 30 competitor apps and finds nearly all use self-monitoring while none use simulation, so it prototypes a feature that shows a simulated future balance.
reference: Fogg, B. J. (2003). Persuasive Technology: Using Computers to Change What We Think and Do. San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Persuasive Technology Ethics Assessment
aka: Persuasive technology ethics assessment (intentions, methods, outcomes and stakeholder gain-loss analysis)
origin: B. J. Fogg (2003), after Freeman's (1984) stakeholder theory; outcome matrix from Berdichevsky and Neuenschwander (1999)
summary: Judge a persuasive product by its intentions, methods and foreseeable outcomes, check targeting of vulnerable groups, and tabulate each stakeholder's gains and losses against stated values.
description: Fogg notes that interactive persuasion has built-in advantages over users: novelty hides intent, computers borrow a reputation for fairness, they persist without tiring, control which interactions are possible, display emotion without responding to it, and cannot take responsibility. The assessment examines intent; methods, first asking whether the tactic would be ethical if a person used it (deception and coercion always fail; conditioning and surveillance must be overt and supportive); and outcomes, using an intended-by-predictable matrix to assign responsibility to designers, distributors and users. Targeting vulnerable groups is unethical. For hard cases a structured stakeholder analysis lists every party's gains (money, learning, power) and losses (autonomy, privacy, dignity) and weighs the inequities against values written down openly. Because verdicts depend on values, outsiders and affected people should take part.
steps: State the designers' intent and judge whether it is good, contested or unethical.
List each persuasive method; imagine a human doing the same and judge it, flagging deception, coercion, covert conditioning, punitive surveillance and exploitative emotional appeals.
List intended and reasonably foreseeable unintended outcomes (misuse, overuse, unintended users) and assign responsibility with the intent-by-predictability matrix.
Check whether any vulnerable group (children, older, bereaved or lonely people, employees) is targeted or likely to be reached.
List all stakeholders, including families and communities, and tabulate each one's gains and losses.
Identify who gains most and who loses most, judge the inequities against explicitly written values, and record mitigations.
Revisit after launch and mitigate harms once they become known.
outputs: A written ethics judgement with a stakeholder gain-loss table, flagged methods, foreseeable harms, stated values and mitigations.
useWhen: Designing or reviewing nudges, gamification, notifications, retention flows, behaviour-change apps or AI agents that persuade.
avoidWhen: You need a legal compliance check or an empirical measure of harm; use regulatory review or deceptive-pattern audits with user data. Applied once at design time it misses emergent harms, and analysts with a stake in the product bias the verdict.
whyLost: Fogg's captology became influential for growth design while its ethics chapter was largely ignored; product ethics reviews today are ad hoc.
whereToUse: Health behaviour change, fintech savings nudges, social and gaming engagement loops, workplace monitoring tools, persuasive AI assistants.
example: A fitness app's streak-loss notifications are reviewed: users gain motivation but lose autonomy and some feel shame, while the company gains retention. The team removes guilt copy and adds a pause option.
reference: Berdichevsky, D., & Neuenschwander, E. (1999). Toward an ethics of persuasive technology. Communications of the ACM, 42(5), 51-58.

name: Phenomenography (Marton)
origin: Ference Marton, 1975-1981; Marton and Booth (1997)
summary: Maps the limited set of qualitatively different ways people understand a phenomenon into a hierarchical outcome space of categories of description.
description: Phenomenography asks not what a phenomenon is but how people experience or understand it, and finds that understandings fall into a small number of qualitatively distinct categories. The outcome space orders these categories by complexity and inclusiveness; categories are not frequencies but the logical structure of variation. The treatise's transfer: how do users conceptually understand 'privacy settings'? Phenomenography maps the distinct ways of understanding and how they relate, yielding a structured taxonomy of mental models more useful for design than average responses. Each level suggests what content or scaffolding helps users move toward more complete understandings.
steps: Choose the phenomenon and recruit 15-30 participants with varied experience.
Conduct open interviews built around concrete problems or scenarios involving the phenomenon.
Transcribe and read the pool of meanings as a whole, across participants.
Iteratively form categories of description focused on variation in meaning.
Order categories into a hierarchical outcome space by inclusiveness.
Use the outcome space to design content and interactions that support each level.
outputs: Categories of description, hierarchical outcome space, design implications per level.
useWhen: Concepts users understand in qualitatively different ways (privacy, AI, investing, encryption).
avoidWhen: When prevalence is the question; quantify categories later with a survey.
whyLost: Rooted in education research and never introduced to UX training.
whereToUse: Privacy controls, AI capability explanations, investment education, security features, help content.
example: Interviews about 'end-to-end encryption' yield four categories, from 'a password' to 'only devices hold keys'; help content is layered to move users between levels.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Marton F (1981) Phenomenography: describing conceptions of the world around us. Instructional Science 10
Marton F & Booth S (1997) Learning and Awareness
reference: Marton F & Booth S (1997) Learning and Awareness. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Phenomenological Reduction (Epoché)
origin: Edmund Husserl, 1913; Giorgi, 2009 (descriptive phenomenological method)
summary: Brackets designers' and researchers' knowledge of how the product is supposed to work, so analysis starts from the user's lived experience as described.
description: The epoché is Husserl's method for phenomenological investigation: deliberately "bracketing" (setting aside) everything you believe you know about a phenomenon — its causes, its context, its theoretical explanations — in order to encounter the phenomenon itself as it appears in consciousness. In UX research this translates to: before analysing a user's experience, bracket your knowledge of what the interface is supposed to do, what the user was supposed to want, and what the design team intended. You start only from what the participant described experiencing.
steps: Pre-analysis bracketing: Before reading a transcript, write a bracketing memo: list everything you know about the product, the design decisions, the prior research, and your hypothesis. These are now bracketed — you consciously set them aside for the duration of analysis.
Read the transcript once without marking: Your only task is to describe what the participant experienced, in their terms. Do not explain it. Do not interpret it. Just describe.

Identify intentional objects: What was the participant's consciousness directed toward at each moment? What were they attending to, avoiding, confused by, or seeking? These are the phenomenological data.

Eidetic variation: For each theme you identify, ask — what would have to change for this experience to no longer be what it is? This reveals the essential (invariant) structure of the experience, as opposed to its accidental features.
outputs: A bracketing record of set-aside assumptions, experience descriptions in participants' terms, essential structures of the experience, and design implications.
useWhen: Studying lived experience of complex, emotional or high-stakes processes (claims, diagnoses, bereavement, financial hardship), and analysing data where team intentions colour interpretation.
avoidWhen: Avoid for task-level usability questions or when you need measurement; full phenomenological analysis is slow, so use thematic analysis when depth is less critical.
whyLost: Phenomenology is philosophically demanding; UX borrowed the words 'lived experience' without the method of bracketing that makes it rigorous.
whereToUse: Health, insurance, government and financial services where processes are emotionally charged; service design for life events; AI products where teams' technical knowledge obscures how users experience system behaviour; any synthesis where design intent biases interpretation.
example: A team studying digital health insurance claims brackets its knowledge of the claim workflow; analysing accounts as described reveals that claimants experience the process as 'being doubted', not as 'a form', which reshapes the tone of messages.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
reference: Giorgi A (2009) The Descriptive Phenomenological Method in Psychology: A Modified Husserlian Approach. Duquesne University Press

name: Phenomenological Research
origin: Edmund Husserl (philosophy), early 20th century; Amedeo Giorgi (descriptive method), 1970; Jonathan Smith (IPA), 1996
summary: Studies lived experience from the first-person perspective to describe the essential structure and meaning of an experience as it is lived.
description: Phenomenological research aims to describe what an experience is like for those who live it and to identify its essential structure. Descriptive phenomenology, following Husserl and Giorgi, asks researchers to bracket their assumptions and describe the invariant structure of an experience. Interpretative phenomenological analysis, developed by Jonathan Smith, accepts a double hermeneutic in which the researcher interprets the participant's sense-making, and focuses on a small, homogeneous sample analysed case by case. In UX it suits emotionally significant experiences such as anxiety, grief, disability or trust in automation. Rigour comes from in-depth interviews focused on concrete lived episodes, careful idiographic analysis of each case before cross-case comparison, explicit reflexivity and close grounding of interpretations in participants' words.
steps: Define the phenomenon precisely, for example 'the experience of receiving a frightening test result through an app'.
Recruit a small, homogeneous sample, typically 3 to 10 participants for IPA.
Conduct in-depth interviews that elicit detailed descriptions of specific lived moments rather than opinions.
Write a reflexive memo on your own assumptions before and during analysis.
Analyse each case in depth, noting experiential statements and developing personal experiential themes.
Compare across cases to identify shared group experiential themes.
Write an account that stays close to participants' words and draws design implications.
outputs: Rich descriptions of lived experience, case-level and group experiential themes, and implications for designing sensitive moments.
useWhen: For emotionally significant or sensitive experiences, accessibility and disability experiences, and understanding what an experience means to people.
avoidWhen: Avoid for behavioural or usability questions or when large, heterogeneous samples are needed; use usability testing or surveys.
whyLost: Siloed: Philosophical rigor required; applied mainly in healthcare and education UX research.
whereToUse: Emotional design; accessibility; products addressing sensitive life experiences.
example: A patient portal team interviews eight people who received cancer screening results online. IPA shows that the moment of seeing results alone at night is experienced as abandonment, leading to options to schedule results with a clinician call.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis: Theory, Method and Research (Smith, Flowers & Larkin)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 30
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Smith JA, Flowers P & Larkin M (2009; 2nd ed 2022) Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis: Theory, Method and Research
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Smith, J. A., Flowers, P. & Larkin, M. (2009). Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis: Theory, Method and Research. Sage.

name: Photovoice
origin: Caroline Wang & Mary Ann Burris, 1994-1997
summary: Participants photograph and caption moments that represent their experience, then discuss them, revealing what they define as notable and what goes unseen.
description: Photovoice was developed in community health research to put cameras in the hands of people whose perspectives are rarely heard, with the aim of informing policy and change. Participants photograph moments representing their experience of a topic, caption each image (what is happening, why it was photographed, what it means), and then discuss selected images individually or in groups, often using the SHOWeD question sequence. Analysis looks both at content and at choices: what participants considered worth photographing reveals their implicit theory of the phenomenon, while omissions point to tacit, unremarkable practice. It gives participants control over representation and produces vivid material for stakeholder communication.
steps: Brief participants: "Over the next [duration], photograph moments that represent your experience of [phenomenon]. You decide what is notable. There are no wrong photographs."
Caption requirement: For each photograph, participants write (or audio-record) a caption answering: What is happening here? Why did you photograph this? What does this mean to you?
Return and discuss: After the photography period, meet with participants (individually or in groups) to discuss their photographs. Ask them to select their most important image and explain why.

Analysis — what participants chose to photograph: The selection is as informative as the content. What participants considered notable, photographable, and worth documenting reveals their implicit theory of the phenomenon. What they did NOT photograph reveals what they considered unremarkable — which may be the tacit knowledge most invisible to verbal methods.
outputs: Captioned participant photographs, discussion transcripts, coded themes about content and selection, and exhibition-ready material.
useWhen: Exploring lived experience in context, with communities whose voice is underrepresented, or where visual environment matters (home, neighbourhood, workplace).
avoidWhen: When privacy or safety risks of photography are high, or when precise behavioural data are needed; use interviews or diaries with text entries.
whyLost: It is established in public health and community research, but UX diary tools rarely structure photo selection, captioning and discussion as the method requires.
whereToUse: Health and accessibility research, financial inclusion, community and civic tech, and home and family technology studies.
example: Older adults photograph moments when technology helped or hindered them over three weeks. Several photograph handwritten password books beside tablets, sparking a discussion that reshapes an account recovery design.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
Photovoice: Concept, Methodology, and Use for Participatory Needs Assessment (Wang & Burris)
Harper (2002) — Talking about Pictures: A Case for Photo Elicitation
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Wang, C. & Burris, M. A. (1997). Photovoice: Concept, methodology, and use for participatory needs assessment. Health Education & Behavior, 24(3), 369-387.

name: Physical-Metaphor Gesture Design
aka: Physical-metaphor gesture design (information as physical object)
origin: Josh Clark (2015), drawing on Don Norman's Living with Complexity; radial menu evidence from Kurtenbach and Buxton (1994)
summary: Replace buttons with direct manipulation by treating data objects as physical things, mapping the verbs they afford to actions, and checking gestures for conflicts and discoverability.
description: Clark calls buttons a hack: workarounds for when direct interaction is impossible, which add effort and complexity. The practice challenges every button and reimagines data as physical objects, such as a date range as a stretchable band or items as cards to flip, stack or throw aside, then matches verbs to nouns. Borrowing from the real world takes four forms: one-to-one interactions, established notation, physics, and honouring physical constraints; the rule is to import the action, not the object. Abstract and multi-finger gestures are expert shortcuts and always need a visible slow route. Gesture density must be managed: cede gestures to the operating system and browser, prefer edge gestures for system actions, and use radial menus for compact, stable tool sets, which Kurtenbach and Buxton showed users learn to operate by marking.
steps: Inventory buttons and controls and ask, for each, whether the content itself could be manipulated directly.
Name the interface's nouns, list the physical verbs each affords and assign each verb a data meaning.
Choose a borrowing route for each action: one-to-one interaction, symbols or notation, physics, or physical constraints, borrowing the action rather than the artefact.
Add abstract or multi-finger gestures only as shortcuts alongside visible controls, and check accessibility for people with limited hand mobility.
Check conflicts with operating system and browser gestures and between your own gestures; give gestures room and anticipate accidental edge swipes.
Use radial menus for stable sets of up to about eight items (three or four on phones) and never reorder them dynamically.
Prototype on the target device and test discoverability with users.
outputs: A gesture map linking objects, verbs and data actions, with conflicts resolved and visible fallbacks defined.
useWhen: Use it when designing touch, tablet, pen or spatial interfaces where direct manipulation could replace control clutter.
avoidWhen: Gestures are hard to discover; test them with Usability Testing on devices, and use a Gesture Elicitation Study when you need to learn which gestures users themselves propose. Avoid overriding browser or system gestures.
whyLost: Common gestures such as swipe-to-delete became platform conventions, but the derivation method lost favour as flat design and accessibility concerns brought visible controls back.
whereToUse: Tablet creative tools, to-do and email apps, maps and timelines, pen interfaces and AR or VR products.
example: A calendar app replaces start and end date pickers with a band users stretch with two fingers, keeping visible date fields as the fallback. A test shows the stretch is found by most users only after a one-time hint.
reference: Clark, J. (2015). Designing for Touch. New York: A Book Apart, ch. 4. Kurtenbach, G. and Buxton, W. (1994). User learning and performance with marking menus. Proc. CHI '94.

name: Physicality breakdown audit
aka: Physicality properties audit for breakdown and repair
origin: Dix, Gill, Ramduny-Ellis and Hare (2022), building on Heidegger's ready-to-hand and breakdown
summary: Check a hybrid physical-digital device against physical-world rules to judge how users will notice, understand and repair failures.
description: Physical things show their state, act where and when they are touched, and respond in proportion to effort; digital and hybrid devices often break all three. Usability tests concentrate on first use and success, but long-term usability depends on how breakdowns are detected and repaired, when the tool stops being ready-to-hand and becomes an object of attention. The audit checks each rule in turn, then asks for each break how a user would notice something has gone wrong, what extra visibility repair needs, whether actions can be undone through a natural inverse, and whether irreversible actions are protected. Findings lead to physical or digital put-backs such as indicator lights, displays, haptic kicks, recessed or shaped controls.
steps: Take the device and its task in the real context of use.
Check visibility of state, spatial and temporal locality of effect, and proportional response to effort.
For each rule that is broken, ask how a user would detect that something went wrong.
Ask what extra visibility a user needs to repair the problem.
Check reversibility through natural inverse actions, and protection of irreversible actions.
Propose physical or digital put-backs such as lights, displays, haptic feedback, shaping or recessing controls, and test them with breakdown scenarios.
outputs: A list of breakdown points and redesign ideas for detection, repair and protection.
useWhen: Designing appliances, medical devices, remote controls or smart products where accidental or silent failures matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for testing with users; it is an expert lens. For error prediction with probabilities use human error analysis methods such as SHERPA.
whyLost: It is a framework from one book with no packaged procedure and little practitioner exposure.
whereToUse: Smart home devices, medical equipment, automotive controls, kitchen appliances and IoT products.
example: A dishwasher's flush touch button starts a cycle when brushed by a passing hip, with no visible change until water runs. The audit recommends recessing the button and adding a light and a short delay before the cycle commits.
reference: Dix, A., Gill, S., Ramduny-Ellis, D. & Hare, J. (2022). TouchIT: Understanding Design in a Physical-Digital World. Oxford University Press, pp. 133-136, 189-191, 212-215.

name: Physigrams (Device-Unplugged Modelling)
aka: Physigram modelling of the device unplugged
donor: Formal methods in HCI; product design
origin: Alan Dix, Masitah Ghazali, Steve Gill and colleagues, 2007-2009
summary: State diagrams of what a device's physical controls do with the power off, mapped to the system's logical states to expose hidden state, missing feedback and poor inverses.
description: Physigrams separate the physical behaviour of a control from the digital state it drives. The analyst imagines the device unplugged (battery out, wires cut) and draws each control's physical states as an extended state transition network, with special transition types: user-driven moves, bounce-back to a stable state, transient tension states that last only while held (dashed outlines), give, detents and end stops, and autonomous transitions such as spring return. A separate network models the system's logical states, and the two are linked by state mappings or shared action labels. The rigour lies in checking named properties against the mapping: exposed versus hidden state, adequacy of logical feedback for bounce-back controls, natural inverse actions that allow correction after overshoot, give that reveals possible movement, and compliant interaction where user and system change state through the same control movement.
steps: List the device's physical controls and, imagining it unplugged, record every movement each control physically affords.
Draw a physigram per control: stable states, transient tension states (dashed), bounce-back and autonomous transitions, give, detents and end stops.
Model the system's logical states separately as a state transition network.
Link physical and logical models, either state to state or through named actions on transitions.
Classify each piece of state as exposed (visible in the control's position) or hidden, and check that bounce-back controls get adequate logical feedback.
Check for natural inverse pairs, give and compliant interaction, and relate failures to the feedback loops (physical, simulated device, semantic, environmental).
Compare alternative physical designs for the same function and propose redesigns or added feedback where properties fail.
outputs: Paired physical and logical state diagrams, a physical-to-logical mapping, and a list of property failures (hidden state, missing inverses, poor feedback) with design changes.
useWhen: Designing or comparing hardware controls, appliances, automotive or medical panels, wearables and tangible interfaces where physical feel and digital state can diverge; communicating control behaviour between industrial designers and software teams.
avoidWhen: Purely screen-based interfaces, or continuous inputs such as pressure and touch that the notation handles poorly. Live safety-critical panels may not be explorable, so behaviour must be guessed; pair with hands-on testing.
whyLost: It lives in formal-methods HCI literature and a few product design studios; UX teams rarely model hardware, and the notation has little tool support.
whereToUse: Smart-home devices, in-car controls, kitchen appliances, game controllers, medical device panels, and any product where a bounce-back button or rotary encoder hides system state.
example: A team designing a smart thermostat compares a detented dial with a free-spinning encoder. Physigrams show the encoder hides the setpoint and lacks a natural inverse, so the team adds a detent and an on-dial indicator.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Dix, A., Ghazali, M., Gill, S., Hare, J. and Ramduny-Ellis, S. (2009) Physigrams: modelling devices for natural interaction. Formal Aspects of Computing 21(6), 613-641.

name: Physiological Signal Acquisition and Digital Filtering
aka: Band-pass and notch filtering of biosignals
Filter type selection (Butterworth, Bessel, Chebyshev, elliptic)
origin: Adapted for UX from standard electrical engineering practice as presented by van Drongelen (2018), citing Marven and Ewers (1996) and Chirlian (1994)
summary: Choose a sample rate and antialiasing filter, then remove drift, mains hum and out-of-band noise from biosignals with digital filters chosen for the roll-off versus phase trade-off.
description: Every physiological measure in UX research (EEG, ECG and heart rate, EDA, EMG) passes through the same chain: transducer, amplifier, analogue filters, an antialiasing filter, then the analogue-to-digital converter. Frequencies above half the sample rate must be removed before digitising or they reappear as false aliases, and sampling at about five times the highest frequency of interest is common. After recording, digital filters remove DC offset and slow drift, isolate the band of interest, and strip mains interference at 50 or 60 Hz. Filters are characterised by pass, stop and transition bands, Bode plots and impulse responses, and implemented as IIR or FIR designs: Butterworth is the usual compromise, Bessel preserves waveform shape, and Chebyshev and elliptic give steeper roll-off at the cost of ripple. IIR filters shift phase, so forward-backward (zero-phase) filtering is used when timing matters. Poor choices here silently distort every downstream metric.
steps: Decide the highest frequency of interest and sample well above twice it, commonly about five times.
Apply an analogue antialiasing filter below the Nyquist frequency before digitisation.
Remove DC offset and slow drift by demeaning or high-pass filtering.
Apply a band-pass filter matched to the signal of interest (for example 15-45 Hz for QRS detection in ECG).
Remove mains interference with a band-stop (notch) filter around 50 or 60 Hz, without relying on it to rescue a poor recording.
Choose the filter type by the trade-off between roll-off and phase response, using forward-backward filtering when event timing matters.
Inspect the Bode plot and impulse response before applying a filter, and document all settings.
outputs: Clean, band-limited digital signals ready for averaging, spectral or event analysis, with documented acquisition and filter settings.
useWhen: Any UX study collecting EEG, ECG, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity or EMG, including consumer wearables, where raw signals need preprocessing before metrics are computed.
avoidWhen: When using validated vendor pipelines whose settings are documented and fit the question; filtering cannot fix a poorly recorded signal, and notch filters can create oscillatory artefacts at discontinuities.
whyLost: UX teams buy biometric platforms that hide preprocessing, so sampling and filtering decisions are rarely examined or reported.
whereToUse: Neuro-UX and biometric lab studies, wearable-based field studies, automotive driver monitoring, game and VR arousal research.
example: A VR study's heart-rate data show spikes that turn out to be mains hum and headset motion. Sampling at 500 Hz, a 0.5-40 Hz zero-phase band-pass and a 50 Hz notch give clean R-peaks for heart rate variability analysis.
reference: van Drongelen, W. (2018). Signal Processing for Neuroscientists (2nd ed.). London: Academic Press.

name: Piagetian Clinical Interview
aka: Animacy and property-attribution interview with children
origin: Jean Piaget, Geneva, from the 1920s; animacy interview revised by Carey, Gelman and colleagues
summary: Interview a child while they work on a concrete problem, letting each explanation shape the next question, to reveal how they reason rather than whether they are right.
description: Piaget held that children think differently from adults rather than knowing less. Borrowing from psychiatric interviewing, he replaced fixed question lists with flexible probing: the child works with a concrete task, explains each answer, and the next question follows from that explanation. Wrong answers are the most informative data because they expose the underlying model. A well-known application is the animacy interview, where children say which entities are alive and which can feel, think, grow or move by themselves. Later work showed Piaget overestimated animism because of reliance on verbal justifications, unfamiliar items and the ambiguous word 'alive' (often heard as 'animal'); with simple yes-no property questions and familiar items, preschoolers are broadly accurate. Today this makes the method a direct way to learn how children categorise robots, voice assistants and on-screen agents.
steps: Give the child a concrete task, object or set of familiar entities (animals, plants, artefacts and the target technologies).
Ask what they think will happen, or simple yes-no property questions such as 'can it feel sad?', 'can it think?', 'does it move by itself?'.
Ask the child to explain each answer in their own words, without relying on the justification alone.
Choose the next question from the explanation rather than a fixed list, and try a gentle counter-suggestion to test how firmly the idea is held.
Avoid ambiguous terms like 'alive', or check what the child takes them to mean.
Record answers and explanations verbatim, and code reasoning patterns or attribution profiles by entity and age group.
outputs: Accounts of children's reasoning and mental models, and attribution profiles per entity and age group.
useWhen: You are designing for children and need to understand how they reason about a system, especially agents, robots and AI that blur the line between alive and not.
avoidWhen: You need comparable, standardised data across many children; flexible questioning is hard to compare and easy to lead. Use structured tasks or observation instead, and always follow child consent and assent ethics.
whyLost: Child UX research uses observation and simplified usability testing; the clinical interview stayed in developmental psychology and education.
whereToUse: Children's apps and games, educational technology, voice assistants and social robots in the home, and AI literacy research.
example: A smart speaker team asks 5- to 8-year-olds whether the assistant can feel sad, think or be hurt, following each explanation. Younger children attribute feelings when it uses their name, which informs personality design.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
reference: Piaget, J. (1929). The Child's Conception of the World. London: Kegan Paul; Opfer, J. E., & Gelman, S. A. (2011). Development of the animate-inanimate distinction. In U. Goswami (Ed.), Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development, ch. 8.

name: PICTIVE Participatory Prototyping
aka: Plastic Interface for Collaborative Technology Initiatives through Video Exploration
origin: Michael Muller, Bellcore, 1991 (CHI)
summary: Users and developers jointly build low-fidelity interfaces from office supplies on a shared table, video-recorded, so users have equal power over the design.
description: PICTIVE deliberately uses low-tech materials (sticky notes, pens, coloured paper, plastic overlays) so that users, not just designers fluent in tools, can manipulate the design directly. Sessions bring users and developers together around a shared design surface, with a video camera recording the evolving design and rationale. The method has an explicit political aim of equalising power, and it produces both artefacts and recorded reasoning. Unlike paper prototyping for testing, PICTIVE is co-creation. It suits contexts where users' tacit work knowledge must shape the design and where developer-led prototyping would dominate.
steps: Prepare a kit of low-fidelity components representing interface elements and a large shared surface.
Invite users and developers in roughly equal numbers; agree that users lead the design.
Start from users' work scenarios and have them build or modify the interface collaboratively.
Video-record the surface and conversation continuously to capture design rationale.
Walk through scenarios with the co-built design, iterating together.
Analyse recordings for requirements and rationale, and return results to participants.
outputs: Co-created low-fidelity designs, video records of design rationale and requirements grounded in users' work.
useWhen: Designing tools for specialist work where users' expertise must drive design, and in power-imbalanced settings.
avoidWhen: Mass-market consumer products where participants cannot represent users, or for evaluation of finished designs.
whyLost: Digital design tools and designer-led workshops replaced it, and participatory design's political commitments faded in industry.
whereToUse: Clinical systems, union and workplace tools, public sector services, accessibility co-design.
example: Nurses and developers build a medication handover screen with PICTIVE materials; nurses insist on placing pending tasks on the left as on their paper sheets, a requirement developers had missed.
sources: Muller, PICTIVE: An exploration in participatory design (1991), Proceedings of CHI
Muller, Participatory design: The third space in HCI (2003), in Jacko & Sears (eds.), The Human-Computer Interaction Handbook
reference: Muller, M. J. (1991). PICTIVE: An exploration in participatory design. CHI '91, 225-231.

name: Picture Card Elicitation
origin: Design research practice informed by activity theory (Nardi)
summary: Participants sort and arrange a prepared deck of image cards of products, places and activities, then use chosen cards to tell true stories about their lives.
description: The researcher prepares a deck of up to about 100 cards, each with an image and caption of a product, service, place, person or activity relevant to the domain, plus blanks for anything missing. In the session participants first sort out the cards that apply to them, then pick cards to tell true stories, prompted on time, place, relationships and feelings. Cards can also be laid out as timelines or future scenarios. The cards lower the effort of recall and give participants something concrete to point at, which works well near the end of a field visit and with couples or families who prompt each other. Rigour depends on a piloted, balanced card set and on recording the stories rather than only the sorts, because the deck inevitably frames what is discussed.
steps: Design a deck of up to about 100 captioned image cards covering products, services, places and activities in the domain, plus blank cards.
Pilot the deck with two or three people and remove ambiguous or leading images.
Ask participants to sort out the cards that are part of their lives, writing missing items on blanks.
Ask them to pick cards and tell true recent stories, probing on when, where, with whom and how they felt.
Have them lay cards out as a timeline of a typical day or as a scenario of a desired future.
Photograph layouts, record the stories, and analyse stories and recurring card combinations across participants.
outputs: Stories anchored to cards, photographed card sorts and timelines, and recurring combinations of activities, places and products.
useWhen: You need participants to talk concretely about a broad activity space (travel planning, money, household routines), especially in field visits or with families.
avoidWhen: You cannot afford careful card design, or you need unframed discovery; the deck shapes what is discussed. Use open interviews or contextual inquiry instead.
whyLost: Card-based generative tools survive in design consultancies, but this specific story-elicitation protocol is rarely documented beyond methods compendia.
whereToUse: Travel, household finance, family products, retail journeys and service design discovery.
example: A travel booking team gives families 80 picture cards of booking sites, guidebooks, relatives and places. Laying cards out as a planning timeline shows grandparents are consulted before any site is opened, prompting shared trip-planning features.
reference: Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Rockport Publishers, Method 84.

name: Plain-Language Redrafting of Legal and Regulatory Documents
origin: Fair Work Commission (Australia) plain-language initiative from 2015, tested by Wallis Market and Social Research (2016 pilot, 2021)
summary: Rewrite legal or policy documents so readers can find and understand obligations without changing legal effect, using structural, linguistic and digital techniques tested with users.
description: Legal and regulatory documents are read by employers, employees and customers who need answers, not by lawyers alone. Plain-language redrafting keeps the legal effect but reorganises and rewrites the text: clauses are put in a logical order and grouped into consistently named parts, dense paragraphs become short sentences and point form, legal terms give way to familiar words, and rates appear in tables with pre-calculated values. Notes and examples are added only where they help. User testing of the Fair Work Commission awards gave practical rules: tables and point form are widely valued; notes help only when plain, clearly related and purposeful; long examples belong behind expanding text; cross-references depend on how far away and how long the target is; links must land on the exact passage; and digital aids such as hover text and expanding text need consistent use and a visible signal.
steps: Reorder clauses into a logical sequence and group them into parts with consistent, intuitive names.
Break dense paragraphs into short sentences and point form and replace legal terms with familiar words, checking with legal reviewers that meaning is unchanged.
Put rates and option sets into tables, including pre-calculated values such as hourly penalty rates.
Add notes only where they are plainly written, clearly related to the clause and add context, and add examples to complex clauses, hiding long ones behind expanding text.
Decide each cross-reference by proximity and length: restate brief distant content, link only to distant content, and make every link land on the specific passage.
Use hover text for definitions and expanding text for examples consistently, with a visible signal, and provide a glossary for print readers.
Test old and new versions with representative readers, probing for concrete benefits rather than stated preference.
outputs: Redrafted documents, a drafting style guide with tested rules, and user-testing findings.
useWhen: Terms and conditions, policies, benefit rules, regulatory guidance or contracts that users must act on and frequently misread.
avoidWhen: When you need to measure whether readers understand the text, use Readability Testing or Documentation Usability Testing rather than relying on the redraft; do not use it where wording changes would alter legal effect without legal sign-off.
whyLost: It survives because regulators and public bodies mandate plain language and content design teams have adopted it, though tested rules for notes, links and digital aids are rarely written down.
whereToUse: Government services, employment and pay rules, financial product disclosures, healthcare consent and platform terms of service.
example: A payroll platform rewrites its in-app guidance on overtime rules: rates move into a table with pre-computed hourly figures, definitions appear as hover text and examples sit behind expanding text. Side-by-side testing with small employers is followed by probing questions to check they can now explain entitlements to staff.
sources: Modern Awards User Experience Research Report (Wallis Market and Social Research, 2021)
reference: Wallis Market and Social Research (2021). Modern Awards User Experience Research: Report. Prepared for the Fair Work Commission, March 2021.

name: Planned contrasts
origin: Experimental design tradition; endorsed by Wilkinson and the APA Task Force (1999) and Rosnow, Rosenthal and Rubin (2000)
summary: Tests a small set of theory-driven comparisons among group means with contrast weights summing to zero, instead of an omnibus F followed by post hoc tests.
description: Each research question is written as a contrast: a weighted sum of group means whose coefficients sum to zero, with zero for groups not involved. 'New design versus the average of the two old ones' becomes weights of 1, -0.5 and -0.5. The contrast is tested with a t or F using the within-groups error, and reported with a confidence interval and standardised effect size. With k groups at most k - 1 linearly independent contrasts exist; with equal group sizes two contrasts are orthogonal when the cross-products of their coefficients sum to zero. Planned contrasts need no significant omnibus F and are more powerful than post hoc tests, which dilute power when ineffective groups are added. Contrasts are not robust to unequal variances even with equal n, so a separate-variance t is used when variances may differ, and the family of contrasts needs a decision about error-rate control.
steps: Before seeing data, write each question as contrast coefficients that sum to zero, with zero for groups not involved.
Check the set: at most k - 1 contrasts, and with equal n confirm orthogonality by checking that coefficient cross-products sum to zero.
Estimate each contrast value and its standard error from group means and the within-groups variance.
Test with t or F; use a separate-variance t if group variances may differ.
Report the confidence interval and a standardised effect size for each contrast.
Decide the family of contrasts and apply multiple-comparison control where several are tested.
outputs: Estimates, tests, confidence intervals and effect sizes for each planned comparison.
useWhen: Comparing three or more design variants where specific questions are known in advance, such as each new variant against control or the redesign against the average of current versions.
avoidWhen: Comparisons are chosen after looking at the data (use post hoc procedures with appropriate correction), or the design has only two groups (a t test suffices).
whyLost: UX statistics training teaches omnibus ANOVA followed by post hoc tests, and software defaults reinforce that route, so contrast coding is rarely taught or used.
whereToUse: Multi-arm usability benchmarks, A/B/n tests with structured hypotheses, concept tests with control conditions, preference studies comparing families of designs.
example: A checkout study compares current, redesign A, redesign B and A+B combined. Planned contrasts test redesigns against current (3, -1, -1, -1) and A against B (0, 1, -1, 0), giving more power than an omnibus ANOVA with Tukey tests across all six pairs.
sources: Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
reference: Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D. and Kelley, K. (2018). Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data: A Model Comparison Perspective (3rd ed.). New York: Routledge, pp. 170-215.

name: Planning-Fallacy Debiasing
aka: Planning-fallacy debiasing by recall-relevance and observer forecasts
donor: Judgement and decision making; social psychology
origin: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) planning fallacy; Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994)
summary: Reduce optimistic completion-time estimates by making people tie past completion times to the current task, or by asking uninvolved observers to forecast.
description: Planners take an inside view built on success scenarios and discount their own history of lateness. In Buehler, Griffin and Ross's studies even 99 per cent confidence estimates were too early, and students finished theses 22 days later than predicted and seven days later than their own worst case. Observers given the plan and past records predicted later and more accurately. Simply asking for aggregate frequencies or pessimistic scenarios did not help. The recall-relevance procedure, in which people state when they would finish if they finished as typically as on similar past tasks and write a scenario leading to that time, eliminated the optimistic bias in one study. It is a cheap debiasing protocol for research and design project estimates.
steps: Ask the estimator to recall how far before or after deadlines similar past tasks were actually finished.
Ask when this task would be finished if it went as those past tasks typically did.
Ask for a plausible scenario, grounded in that experience, leading to the typical finishing time.
Only then elicit the estimate.
Optionally obtain an independent observer's forecast from the plan and past record, and compare the two.
outputs: Less optimistic, history-anchored time estimates and an observer comparison.
useWhen: Estimating research timelines, recruitment lead times, design sprints or roadmap commitments, or studying how users predict their own task durations.
avoidWhen: Reliable reference-class data exist; then use reference-class forecasting directly. The procedure was tested on a single task, and incentives for speed push even observers towards the inside view.
whyLost: It stayed in judgement research; UX and product teams rely on estimation rituals rather than debiasing protocols.
whereToUse: Research operations planning, agency proposals, roadmap estimation, user-facing features that ask people to set goals or deadlines.
example: Before committing to a six-week diary study, the lead researcher recalls that the last three studies ran two to three weeks late because of recruitment. The plan is reset to nine weeks and a colleague's independent estimate agrees.
reference: Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the 'planning fallacy': Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366-381.

name: Playability Heuristic Evaluation
origin: Federoff (2002), Desurvire, Caplan and Toth (2004), Isbister and Schaffer (2008); taught in Chapter 2 and adapted in Chapter 11
summary: An expert inspection of a game against game-specific heuristics covering interface, mechanics, story and play, rather than Nielsen's productivity-software list.
description: Nielsen's heuristics were written mainly for productivity tools and miss what makes games work, such as pace, challenge, goals, heads-up displays and gameplay. Game-specific sets fill that gap. Federoff's 40 heuristics fall into interface, mechanics and play; HEP has 43 heuristics across play, story, mechanics and usability; Schaffer's 29 cover general, GUI and play. The evaluation follows the usual heuristic method: evaluators play the game individually, note violations, then merge findings with teammates. The book's teaching template records each finding as a row with the heuristic, a severity (for example 'Important'), a description of the problem and an actionable recommendation. Findings then feed research questions for later usability tests and playtests. Chapter 11 shows a variant in which ten generalised heuristics from Desurvire's work are turned into questions that players themselves answer after play, combining inspection with user opinion. The method is cheap and fast, but it reflects the evaluator's judgement, so it complements rather than replaces testing with players.
steps: Choose a game heuristic set (for example Federoff, HEP or Schaffer) suited to the genre and stage.
Have each evaluator play the game independently, focusing on interface, mechanics, story and play.
Record each violation with the heuristic broken, where it occurs and evidence.
Merge findings across evaluators and remove duplicates.
Rate severity and write an actionable recommendation for each issue in a summary table.
Turn the most important issues into research questions for usability tests and playtests.
outputs: A table of heuristic violations with severity ratings, descriptions and recommendations, plus research questions for later testing.
useWhen: Early or mid development of a game or gamified product, before or alongside player testing, or when access to players is limited.
avoidWhen: You need evidence of actual player behaviour or enjoyment, or evaluators do not know the genre.
whyLost: Survived as a standard games user research method because it is quick and cheap; it remains less common outside games.
whereToUse: Video games, serious games, gamified apps, game-like onboarding.
example: A student team reviewing a racing game flags a violation of 'provide clear goals, present the overriding goal early': the current goal is hard to find on a cluttered screen, rated Important, with the recommendation to show the goal clearly before each race starts.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Fabricatore C, Nussbaum M & Rosas R (2002) Playability in action videogames: A qualitative design model. Human-Computer Interaction 17(4)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces: Exploration and Evaluation (Ó Broin, 2011)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Putnam, C., Zagal, J. P. and Cheng, J. (2016). You are not the player: teaching games user research to undergraduate students. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 2. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Player Centered Design
aka: Player Centered Design (gamification process with mission definition)
Gamification game plan (economy, rules, engagement loop)
Gamification mission definition (current scenario, target outcome, S.M.A.R.T. mission)
origin: Janaki Mythily Kumar and Mario Herger (2013), Gamification at Work; engagement loop after Amy Jo Kim
summary: Design gamification by understanding the player, setting a S.M.A.R.T. mission, choosing motivational drivers and mechanics, and managing it as a monitored, ongoing programme.
description: Kumar and Herger extend user-centred design to gamified business software, adding engagement to efficiency, effectiveness and satisfaction. The five steps are: know the player (a player persona), identify the mission, understand human motivation, apply mechanics, and manage, monitor and measure. The mission step contrasts the current scenario with the behaviour the business wants, traces the gap to a root cause players can act on and writes a specific, measurable, actionable, realistic, time-bound mission that does not obstruct core work. Mechanics such as points, badges, leaderboards, challenges, journeys and narrative are combined in a game plan of economy, rules and a core engagement loop (motivate emotion, call to action, re-engage, feedback and reward). Gamification is treated as a programme: playtest, pilot, monitor fatigue, plan releases ahead and review legal and ethical limits.
steps: Observe and interview players to describe the current scenario, and build a player persona.
Interview stakeholders to define the target outcome as a behaviour change, and trace the gap to a root cause players can act on.
Write a S.M.A.R.T. mission (for example, raise training completion from 10% to 80% in three months) and check it will not obstruct critical business processes.
Select motivational drivers suited to this player and mission, then choose mechanics and decide which act as currencies in the game economy.
Write the game rules (points per action, partial credit, who judges quality) and design the core engagement loop.
Playtest at increasing fidelity, pilot, then roll out in phases with opt-in participation.
Monitor motivation through observation or interviews, counter fatigue by unlocking features over the player life cycle, and track a small set of metrics against the mission each release.
Review legal and ethical issues (works councils, privacy, virtual currency, data ownership) and design against cheating.
outputs: A player persona, mission statement, game plan (economy, rules, engagement loop), metrics plan and release roadmap.
useWhen: Use it when a business wants to motivate a specific behaviour in employees, community members or customers and is considering gamification.
avoidWhen: Gamification cannot fix a bad business model or a task nobody values; first check the underlying motivation with Interviews or Jobs-to-be-Done Research. Bolted-on points and badges fail, leaderboards can demotivate newcomers, and manipulative designs need a Persuasive Technology Ethics Assessment.
whyLost: It thrived briefly in the enterprise gamification wave of the early 2010s and survives in community and learning platforms, but gamification fell out of fashion in mainstream UX.
whereToUse: Enterprise software, developer and support communities, training platforms, call centres and loyalty programmes.
example: A software vendor's developer community sets a mission to cut median answer time on its forum to under four hours within six months. Points for accepted answers, badges and a weekly leaderboard are piloted with opt-in members and monitored for gaming.
reference: Kumar, J. M. and Herger, M. (2013). Gamification at Work: Designing Engaging Business Software. Aarhus: The Interaction Design Foundation, pp. 27-33, 49-57, 69-101.

name: Player Experience Inventory (PXI)
origin: Vanden Abeele, Nacke, Mekler and Johnson (2016); described in chapter 9 as still in development at the time
summary: A player experience questionnaire linked to the MDA framework that measures functional consequences of design, psychosocial consequences and overall enjoyment.
description: The PXI aims, like the GEQ, to measure player experience broadly, but it is built on a means-end view connected to the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) framework. It separates functional consequences, which correspond to dynamics (for example ease of control, clarity of goals, progress feedback, audiovisual appeal, challenge), from psychosocial consequences, which correspond to aesthetics (for example mastery, curiosity, immersion, autonomy, meaning), and adds a measure of overall enjoyment. This structure lets a researcher see whether a weak experience stems from a functional problem the design team can fix directly or from the emotional layer. The chapter notes that, at the time of writing, the measure was still being validated, and later published versions should be preferred. For UX research the PXI is a model of how to connect design-level attributes to experiential outcomes in one instrument, and can be applied to any interactive entertainment or playful product.
steps: Obtain the current validated item set.
Plan play sessions that exercise the features under study.
Administer the PXI after play.
Score functional and psychosocial subscales and enjoyment.
Check reliability and, with enough data, whether functional scores predict psychosocial ones and enjoyment.
Trace low psychosocial scores back to the functional subscales and design features that may cause them.
outputs: Subscale scores for functional and psychosocial consequences plus overall enjoyment.
useWhen: You want to link specific design qualities to experiential outcomes in a game or playful product.
avoidWhen: You need a very short measure or one validated in your exact domain.
whyLost: Recent and academic; not yet known outside games research.
whereToUse: Games, playful learning, VR experiences, gamified products.
example: A puzzle game scores low on mastery; the PXI shows weak progress feedback scores, and the team adds a clearer level-completion summary.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 9. Vanden Abeele, V., Nacke, L. E., Mekler, E. D. and Johnson, D. (2016). Design and preliminary validation of The Player Experience Inventory. CHI PLAY Companion.

name: Player Experience of Need Satisfaction (PENS)
origin: Ryan, Rigby and Przybylski (2006); summarised in chapter 9 by Brühlmann and Mekler
summary: A proprietary questionnaire, grounded in self-determination theory, that measures how far a game satisfies players' needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness.
description: PENS investigates the 'motivational pull' of video games. It is based on self-determination theory, which holds that people are drawn to activities that satisfy three basic psychological needs: autonomy (the volitional, self-chosen aspects of an activity), competence (a sense of control and mastery) and relatedness (connection to others). Players rate statements about each need after play; the original work also includes subscales on intuitive controls and presence. Scores have been linked to enjoyment and willingness to keep playing, which makes PENS attractive to studios interested in long-term engagement rather than momentary liking. Brühlmann and Mekler point out that it is proprietary, which limits free use and independent scrutiny. For UX research more broadly, PENS shows how a motivational theory can be turned into a diagnostic: low autonomy points to over-constrained flows, low competence to poor feedback or difficulty, and low relatedness to weak social features. Similar need-satisfaction measures are used for workplace and health apps.
steps: Confirm licensing and obtain the PENS items.
Define which needs matter most for the design question and which product areas players will experience.
Run play sessions long enough for autonomy, competence and social features to be experienced.
Administer PENS straight after play, alongside an overall enjoyment or intention-to-continue measure.
Score each need subscale and check reliability in your sample.
Interpret low subscales against specific design features and follow up with interviews.
outputs: Subscale scores for autonomy, competence and relatedness (and related subscales) per player and condition.
useWhen: You want to understand why a game or app does or does not motivate continued use, in terms of basic psychological needs.
avoidWhen: You cannot license the instrument, or the product has no meaningful choice, challenge or social element.
whyLost: Proprietary status and its games framing kept it out of general UX practice, although self-determination theory is well known in product design.
whereToUse: Games, fitness and learning apps, social platforms, workplace tools where motivation matters.
example: A studio finds high competence but low autonomy scores for a linear campaign and adds optional routes; autonomy scores rise in the next playtest.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 9. Ryan, R. M., Rigby, C. S. and Przybylski, A. (2006). The motivational pull of video games: a self-determination theory approach. Motivation and Emotion, 30, 344-360.

name: Playtesting
origin: Procedures developed at Microsoft game studios (Pagulayan et al. 2003); taught in Chapter 2
summary: Having a sizeable group of target players play to a time or in-game point and then answer survey questions about their attitudes and experience.
description: In games user research, playtesting is distinguished from usability testing. Usability asks whether players can do and understand things; playtests ask what players think and feel, for example how fun a level is, whether the pace is right or how they rate the graphics. Because the data are attitudes, playtests need larger samples than usability tests, ideally around 30 players per group if parametric comparisons are planned. Participants play for a set time or until a given in-game event, stop and answer a survey, then resume, repeating this two or three times. A key skill is translating research questions (what the team wants to know) into playtest questions (what players are asked): closed rating items such as satisfaction with the art style, and paired open questions asking what players liked most and least. Teams work out research questions by playing the game themselves and listing what target players may like, dislike, find easy or difficult. Analysis compares groups with t-tests, ANOVA or non-parametric equivalents. Many sessions can be run in parallel in a lab with several stations.
steps: Define research questions about player attitudes, informed by earlier heuristic and usability findings.
Write playtest questions for each research question: closed rating items plus 'liked most' and 'liked least' open items.
Recruit target players, enough for planned group comparisons.
Set play segments by time or in-game event, with survey breaks between segments.
Run sessions, often several players in parallel, collecting survey responses at each break.
Analyse ratings by segment and group with suitable tests and code open answers.
Report findings against research questions with recommendations.
outputs: Attitude ratings per segment and group, coded open-ended comments, and statistical comparisons.
useWhen: You need to know how target players feel about a game's fun, pace, difficulty or look, beyond whether they can use it.
avoidWhen: The question is about whether players can complete tasks (use usability testing), or you cannot recruit enough players.
whyLost: Survived as a core games user research method; it is less common outside games, where attitude surveys are run separately from usage.
whereToUse: Video games, game levels, gamified products, entertainment apps.
example: Ten players at a time play the first level of an Xbox game for 15 minutes, switch to a computer to answer questions on difficulty and satisfaction with the art, and repeat for the next two segments; ratings show difficulty spiking in the second segment.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Putnam, C., Zagal, J. P. and Cheng, J. (2016). You are not the player: teaching games user research to undergraduate students. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 2. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Pleasure-purpose activity mapping
aka: Pleasure machines, purpose engines and balanced folk typology
origin: Paul Dolan; White and Dolan, 2009 (German DRM study); Dolan and Kudrna's ATUS analyses
summary: Rate each activity or episode separately for pleasure and for purpose, plot one against the other, and classify activities and people by their balance.
description: Dolan defines happiness as experiences of pleasure and purpose over time and argues that purpose (fulfilment and meaning versus boredom and futility) is felt in the moment, not only judged about life overall. In his German Day Reconstruction Method study and the 2010 American Time Use Survey, episodes were rated 0-6 for pleasure (happy) and purpose (worthwhile, meaningful). Averages per activity are plotted with a diagonal of equality: TV, eating and commuting fall on the pleasure side; volunteering, work and time with children on the purpose side, and rankings by each differ. Subtracting purpose from pleasure for people who did two contrasting activities (work and TV) classifies them as balanced folk (about 60%), purpose engines (about 30%) or pleasure machines (about 10%). In a lab variant, 20 students' ratings of everyday activities predicted 80 binary choices, pleasure more strongly. Company changes both ratings.
steps: Choose the activities, tasks or episodes to rate, from a Day Reconstruction Method, time-use diary or a list of product activities.
For each, ask separately how much pleasure (happiness) and how much purpose (worthwhile, meaningful) was felt, on 0-6 in diaries or 0-10 when self-administered.
Record who the person was with and the context, since company shifts both ratings.
Average ratings per activity and plot pleasure against purpose with a line of equality; rank activities on each dimension separately.
For two contrasting activities, subtract each person's purpose rating from their pleasure rating and classify people as balanced, pleasure-dominant or purpose-dominant.
Optionally test whether the ratings predict later choices between pairs of activities.
outputs: A pleasure-by-purpose map of activities, separate rankings, a typology of respondents and the relative weight of each in predicting choice.
useWhen: When designing for wellbeing rather than time-on-task, judging whether product activities feel worthwhile as well as enjoyable, or segmenting users by what they seek from an activity.
avoidWhen: Avoid for causal claims: people choose activities and company by mood, so effects may reverse. Classification uses only people who did both contrasting activities that day (about 20% in the German sample). For wellbeing outcomes alone use Subjective well-being questionnaires (SWLS, SHS, ONS4).
whyLost: It belongs to wellbeing economics; UX measures pleasure (satisfaction, delight) but rarely measures felt purpose as a separate dimension.
whereToUse: Social media and attention-economy products, learning and fitness apps, workplace tools, games, digital wellbeing features.
example: A language-learning app asks users to rate each session type for pleasure and purpose. Games score high on pleasure and low on purpose, grammar drills the reverse; the team designs a session type that sits near the diagonal and tracks its uptake.
reference: Dolan, P. (2014). Happiness by Design: Change What You Do, Not How You Think. New York: Hudson Street Press; White, M. P., & Dolan, P. (2009). Accounting for the richness of daily activities. Psychological Science, 20(8), 1000-1008.

name: PLS regression for small samples
origin: Herman Wold, 1966-1975; developed in chemometrics by Svante Wold, 1980s
summary: Regresses an outcome on many correlated predictors by projecting them onto a few latent components that maximise covariance with the outcome, working when cases are few.
description: PLS regression handles the classic small-sample UX problem: dozens of correlated predictors (interface metrics, attitude items, behavioural counts) but only 20-60 participants. Ordinary least squares breaks down under collinearity or when predictors exceed cases; PLS extracts a small number of orthogonal components that capture predictor variance most relevant to the outcome, then regresses on those. Developed for chemometrics, where spectra have hundreds of collinear wavelengths and few samples, it is rigorous when the number of components is chosen by cross-validation and predictor importance is read through VIP scores rather than raw weights. It predicts well but its components are not causal constructs.
steps: Assemble a predictor matrix X (e.g. 30 interface metrics) and outcome y for each participant or screen; standardise all variables.
Fit PLS models with 1 to 10 components and choose the number minimising cross-validated prediction error (leave-one-out or 10-fold).
Report Q-squared (cross-validated R-squared); values above 0.5 are generally considered good predictive relevance.
Compute Variable Importance in Projection scores and treat VIP above 1.0 as influential, below 0.8 as candidates for removal.
Refit with the reduced predictor set and confirm predictive performance does not degrade.
Interpret the leading components by their loadings and validate any design implication with a targeted study.
outputs: A predictive model with chosen component count, Q-squared, VIP-ranked predictors and component loading plots.
useWhen: Small samples with many collinear predictors, such as predicting error rates from many interface complexity measures across 25 screens, or satisfaction from many correlated attitude items.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need unbiased causal coefficients, when predictors are few and uncorrelated (use ordinary regression), or when sample is large enough for regularised regression with clearer interpretation.
whyLost: It lived in chemometrics and later PLS-SEM marketing research, and UX researchers rarely encounter it in standard statistics training. Small-sample UX teams default to correlations instead.
whereToUse: Benchmarking small sets of screens or products, design-metric prediction in early-stage SaaS, B2B studies with few accounts, and enterprise tools with small specialist user bases.
example: A B2B analytics team has error rates for 22 dashboard screens and 35 complexity metrics. PLS with two components predicts errors with Q-squared of 0.62, and VIP scores single out visual density and number of filters as the levers to simplify.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Wold, Sjöström & Eriksson (2001) PLS-regression: a basic tool of chemometrics
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers
A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
reference: Wold, S., Sjöström, M. & Eriksson, L. (2001) PLS-regression: a basic tool of chemometrics. Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems, 58(2), 109-130.

name: PLS-SEM
aka: Partial least squares structural equation modelling
origin: Herman Wold, 1970s to 1982; popularised by Joseph Hair and colleagues (A Primer on PLS-SEM, 2014)
summary: Estimates relationships between latent constructs measured by survey items using a variance-based approach, suited to prediction-oriented models and modest sample sizes.
description: Structural equation modelling links latent constructs, such as trust, perceived usefulness or effort, measured by multiple survey items, in a path model. PLS-SEM estimates these models by iteratively maximising explained variance in the endogenous constructs, rather than reproducing the covariance matrix as CB-SEM does. This makes it robust with smaller samples, non-normal data and complex models, and suited to prediction-oriented research. Rigour comes from evaluating the measurement model (indicator loadings, composite reliability, average variance extracted, discriminant validity using HTMT) before the structural model (path coefficients with bootstrapped confidence intervals, R squared, effect sizes and out-of-sample predictive power with PLSpredict). Constructs should come from theory or qualitative work, and causal interpretation depends on design and stated assumptions.
steps: Specify the path model from theory or qualitative findings, ideally checked with a DAG, defining constructs and their indicators.
Collect survey data with at least 3 items per reflective construct, using a sample size justified by power analysis (often 100 to 300 respondents).
Assess the measurement model: loadings above 0.70, composite reliability between 0.70 and 0.95, AVE above 0.50 and HTMT below 0.85 to 0.90.
Estimate the structural model and bootstrap (for example 5,000 resamples) to obtain confidence intervals for path coefficients.
Evaluate explanatory and predictive power using R squared, f squared and PLSpredict, and test mediation or moderation if hypothesised.
Report the model, diagnostics, effects and limitations, linking constructs back to qualitative evidence.
outputs: A validated measurement model, path coefficients with bootstrap intervals, explained variance, predictive metrics, and a path diagram linking constructs to outcomes.
useWhen: You want to test how latent attitudes, such as trust, perceived risk and ease, drive intentions or adoption, with a moderate sample and a prediction-oriented aim.
avoidWhen: You need strict theory testing with global fit indices (use CB-SEM), have fewer than about 3 items per construct, or only need simple driver analysis (use regression). Avoid causal claims without a design to support them.
whyLost: Excel and t-tests remain the standard quantitative toolkit for many UX researchers, and SEM sits in marketing and information systems research.
whereToUse: Technology acceptance and trust studies, fintech and health adoption research, survey programmes on AI acceptance, and quantifying qualitative models.
example: A payments team surveys 240 merchants and fits a PLS-SEM where interface trust reduces double-checking behaviour, which in turn increases Tap to Pay adoption. The indirect effect is significant, focusing design on trust signals at payment completion.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Vol III, Ch 49
The Inquiry Series, Ch 49 — Structural Equation Modeling — From Quotes to Coefficients
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (Rex Kline)
A Primer on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (Joseph Hair et al.)
Structural Equations with Latent Variables (Kenneth Bollen)
A Primer on PLS-SEM — Hair et al.
Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Hair, J. F., Hult, G. T. M., Ringle, C. M. & Sarstedt, M. (2022). A Primer on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Pluralistic Walkthrough
origin: Randolph Bias (1994)
summary: Users, developers and usability specialists step together through scenario screens, each writing their next action before discussing, with users speaking first.
description: A group inspection in which everyone plays the role of a typical user. Task scenarios are presented as sequences of prototype screens; for each screen, every participant independently writes down the actions they would take to reach the next screen, without conferring. The group then discusses, with representative users answering first and developers and specialists commenting from the user's perspective rather than defending the design. Issues are logged per step.
