Independence before discussion is the method's rigour: it prevents designers' knowledge from anchoring users. It is strong on detailed task steps, builds shared understanding, and suits safety-critical systems and participatory settings. Its costs are scheduling everyone at once, moving at the pace of the slowest participant and covering few scenarios.
steps: Prepare task scenarios as sequences of paper or on-screen prototype screens.
Assemble representative users, developers, usability specialists and stakeholders, and brief them that users lead and designers do not defend.
For each screen, have every participant write down the action they would take, without conferring.
Reveal answers with users first, then discuss differences and problems from the user's perspective.
Log each usability issue against the step where it arose.
Repeat round by round until all scenarios are done, then prioritise the issue log.
outputs: A step-linked issue list, shared understanding between users and the team, and domain insight for developers.
useWhen: Early paper-prototype reviews where users and developers can meet, especially for procedural or safety-critical workflows.
avoidWhen: Avoid when stakeholders are likely to dominate, or many scenarios must be covered; use Cognitive Walkthrough for expert-only inspection or Moderated Usability Testing for realism.
whyLost: Remote iteration and cheap one-to-one testing made synchronised group walkthroughs look slow and costly, and the method faded after the 1990s.
whereToUse: Clinical and public-sector workflow systems, co-design workshops with frontline staff, regulated procedures.
example: Hospital ward clerks, developers and a UX lead step through a new admissions screen. Clerks write that they would re-enter the NHS number, exposing a double-entry step that developers had assumed was pre-filled.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Bias, R. G. (1994). The pluralistic usability walkthrough: coordinated empathies. In J. Nielsen and R. L. Mack (Eds.), Usability Inspection Methods. Wiley.

name: Points-of-View Skill Documentaries
aka: First-, second- and third-person perspective documentation
origin: TU/e master's class 'Designing for points of view' (Hummels, Overbeeke, Trotto, Cruz Restrepo, 2006-2011); Trotto, Hummels and Cruz Restrepo, 2011
summary: A skill owner and peers make first-, second- and third-person video documentaries of a skill, and build a prototype that lets someone else experience its essence.
description: Grounded in the phenomenological view that designers design from a first-person perspective while intermittently taking a third-person one, this five-day exercise makes the shifts explicit. A student documents his own skill on video (first person). He then shows and tells a peer in situ what the skill means to him, and the peer makes his own documentary (second person); the owner uses the peer's film as a mirror to refine his own. Next the owner builds a tool that lets a third person experience the salient element of the skill; that person learns it on video within an hour and makes a reflective documentary. Finally the owner presents all three films and the design and reflects. All perspectives turned out different, and students later took first- and second-person stances more often, for example in interviews.
steps: Day 1: the skill owner makes a short video documentary of their own skill from the first-person view.
Day 2: the owner shows and tells a peer in situ what the skill means; the peer makes their own short documentary.
The owner watches the peer's film as a mirror and refines their own film.
Days 3-4: the owner builds a tool or prototype that lets a third person experience the salient element of the skill.
Day 4: a third person learns the new skill on video within about an hour and turns the footage into a reflective documentary.
Day 5: the owner presents the three films and the design side by side and reflects on the differences between perspectives.
outputs: Three perspective videos, a skill-transfer prototype and written reflections on the differences between perspectives.
useWhen: Training designers or researchers to notice the difference between their own experience and others', or designing products that transfer an embodied skill.
avoidWhen: A teaching exercise; research use is an adaptation. To understand users' lived experience use Micro-Phenomenological Interviewing or Phenomenological Research, and for self-study as data use Autoethnography.
whyLost: Confined to design education at TU Eindhoven; five days and video production are hard to justify in product teams.
whereToUse: Design and research training, sports and craft products, rehabilitation and learning technologies.
example: A snowboarder's carving skill is distilled into 'moulding a soft material with a fixed extension of the body' and becomes glove-mounted utensils for carving sandwiches, which a novice learns on video.
reference: Trotto, A., Hummels, C. and Cruz Restrepo, M. (2011) Towards design-driven innovation: designing for points of view using intuition through skills. Proceedings of DPPI 2011, 3-10.

name: Poisson and Negative Binomial Regression for Counts and Rates
origin: Generalised linear model framework of Nelder and Wedderburn (1972); presented by Agresti (1996) and Demidenko (2004)
summary: Regression for event counts, or rates with an exposure offset, giving multiplicative effects, with a check for overdispersion and a negative binomial or random-effect model when it appears.
description: Poisson regression models the log of the expected count as a linear function of predictors, so exp(beta) is a rate or count ratio per unit change. For rates, the log of exposure (time, sessions, users) enters as an offset with its coefficient fixed at 1. Effects are tested by likelihood ratio, and fit is checked with Pearson and deviance statistics and adjusted residuals. Real counts are usually more variable than the Poisson allows because of unmeasured heterogeneity; slopes stay unbiased but standard errors are too small. Comparing variances with means within groups, or a score or F test, reveals this. Remedies include negative binomial regression (gamma-distributed heterogeneity), Poisson with normal random intercepts, GEE for counts, and conditional Poisson for many small clusters. For Poisson models, population-average and subject-specific slopes coincide.
steps: Plot mean counts against grouped predictor values to judge whether a log-linear form is reasonable.
Fit log(expected count) = alpha + beta x by maximum likelihood, including log(exposure) as an offset for rates.
Interpret exp(beta) as the rate or count ratio per unit change and test effects with likelihood ratio statistics.
Check fit on grouped data with X squared, G squared and adjusted residuals, treating residuals beyond about 2 as notable.
Compare variances with means within predictor groups and run an overdispersion score or F test.
If overdispersed, refit as negative binomial, random-intercept Poisson, or GEE for counts; with many small clusters consider conditional Poisson.
Report rate ratios with confidence intervals from the model that accounts for the extra variation.
outputs: Rate or count ratios with confidence intervals, fitted counts, and fit and overdispersion diagnostics.
useWhen: Modelling errors per task, support tickets per account, crashes per thousand sessions, or feature uses per week against design, segment or usage predictors.
avoidWhen: Counts with many structural zeros (use Zero-inflated count models); a single rate with no predictors (Poisson and Weibull Event-Rate Modelling); time-to-event questions (Cox Proportional Hazards Survival Analysis); or small expected counts where large-sample fit tests mislead.
whyLost: Product teams often average counts and run t-tests or treat rates as proportions; count regression is routine in epidemiology and econometrics but seldom taught in UX quantitative training.
whereToUse: Error and incident analysis, support and complaint volumes, engagement event counts, usability error counts across repeated tasks.
example: A banking app compares failed logins per 1,000 sessions across three authentication designs with a session-count offset. The Poisson fit shows strong overdispersion (variance six times the mean), so a negative binomial model is used; the new design's rate ratio is 0.71 with a wider, honest interval.
sources: An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Agresti, A. (1996). An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis. New York: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 80-93; Demidenko, E. (2004). Mixed Models: Theory and Applications. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Poisson and Weibull Event-Rate Modelling
origin: Poisson (1837); Weibull (1951)
summary: Models how often events happen (errors, support calls, crashes) and how the risk changes over time.
description: Counts of events per unit of time or exposure, such as errors per thousand sessions or support contacts per week, follow Poisson distributions, which give proper intervals and tests for rates. When the time until an event matters (time to first error, time to abandonment), the exponential distribution assumes a constant rate while the Weibull allows the rate to rise or fall over time, revealing whether problems cluster early (onboarding) or emerge later (wear-out). Bruce and Bruce introduce these as tools for estimating failure rates.
steps: Define the event and the exposure (sessions, users, days).
Estimate the rate and a Poisson confidence interval.
Compare rates across versions with a Poisson or negative binomial regression.
For time-to-event data, fit exponential and Weibull models and check the shape parameter.
Use the shape to tell whether risk is concentrated early or late.
outputs: Event rates with intervals and a picture of how risk changes over time.
useWhen: Monitoring errors, crashes, contacts or other countable events.
avoidWhen: Events are strongly clustered (use negative binomial) or depend heavily on covariates not modelled.
whyLost: Reliability engineering vocabulary never transferred to UX metrics programmes.
whereToUse: Error monitoring, support demand, onboarding drop-off timing.
example: A Weibull fit to time-to-first-error gives a shape below 1, meaning risk is highest in the first minutes, which focuses fixes on first-run screens.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Predicting User Behavior: The Must-Know Distributions for UX & HF Researchers (carousel, n.d.)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 2.

name: Poka-Yoke (Mistake-Proofing) Analysis
origin: Shigeo Shingo, Toyota, 1960s; Zero Quality Control (1986)
summary: Systematically classifies and applies control and warning devices that prevent errors or make them immediately evident at the point of occurrence.
description: Shingo distinguished between errors (human slips) and defects (their consequences) and argued defects can be eliminated by catching errors at source. Poka-yoke devices use contact, fixed-value or motion-step methods and act either as controls (stopping the process) or warnings (signalling). John Grout's work systematised the approach for services and design. In UX the idea survives as 'forcing functions' or 'constraints' from Norman, but the systematic process of analysing each error-prone step, choosing a detection method and preferring controls over warnings is rarely followed. Done properly, it pairs with an error analysis such as SHERPA and yields measurable defect reductions.
steps: List error-prone steps from error analyses, logs or tests, with their resulting defects.
For each, decide whether the error can be prevented (control) or only detected (warning), preferring prevention.
Choose a detection method: contact (checking a property), fixed-value (counting required items) or motion-step (checking sequence).
Design the device: input constraints, interlocks, checklists that block progress, validation at entry.
Estimate the cost of false blocking and design a safe override path for legitimate exceptions.
Measure defect rates before and after and monitor overrides for misuse.
outputs: A poka-yoke inventory mapping error-prone steps to prevention or detection mechanisms with measured impact.
useWhen: Recurring user errors with clear signatures, such as invalid data entry, skipped steps or wrong item selection.
avoidWhen: Errors rooted in misunderstanding goals or knowledge, where constraints frustrate users; use mental model research.
whyLost: The idea was absorbed into UX as 'constraints' and 'forcing functions' via Norman, while Shingo's classification and measurement were forgotten.
whereToUse: Form design, onboarding checklists, medication administration, warehouse picking, financial approvals.
example: A pharmacy app blocks dispensing until the barcode on the package matches the prescription (fixed-value control), reducing wrong-drug errors to near zero, with a pharmacist override that is logged and reviewed weekly.
sources: Shingo, Zero Quality Control: Source Inspection and the Poka-Yoke System (1986)
Grout, Mistake-Proofing the Design of Health Care Processes (AHRQ, 2007)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Shingo, S. (1986). Zero Quality Control. Productivity Press.

name: Polar Coordinate Analysis
origin: Sackett (1980); optimised by Anguera (1997)
summary: Map how one focal behaviour relates to every other coded behaviour as vectors whose quadrant shows activation or inhibition and whose length shows significance.
description: A technique from systematic observation that builds on lag sequential analysis. Starting from a reliable sequential record of coded behaviours, the analyst chooses a focal behaviour and computes adjusted residual Z-scores for each conditional behaviour across prospective lags (what follows the focal behaviour) and retrospective lags (what precedes it). These are reduced to two summary statistics per behaviour, which define a vector: its quadrant indicates whether the relation is mutual activation, mutual inhibition, or activation in one direction and inhibition in the other, and its length indicates statistical significance (vectors longer than about 1.96 are significant at p < .05). Repeating the analysis with each category as focal gives a map of the behavioural system. Software such as HOISAN computes the vectors. Its rigour depends on reliable coding (kappa) and on enough events per category.
steps: Build an observation instrument and code sessions sequentially, keeping the order of events.
Check inter-observer reliability (for example kappa above 0.80) and data quality.
Choose a focal behaviour, or run each category in turn as the focal one.
Compute adjusted residuals for each conditional behaviour across prospective and retrospective lags and combine them into vector components.
Plot vectors and read quadrant (type of relation), angle and length; treat lengths above 1.96 as significant.
Interpret which behaviours activate or inhibit the focal behaviour and check against the session context.
outputs: Vector maps showing which behaviours activate or inhibit a focal behaviour, with significance.
useWhen: You have coded sequences of interaction (moderator and participant, user and assistant, team members) and want to know which events prompt or suppress a target behaviour.
avoidWhen: Sparse or unreliable coding, or very many categories without a clear focal behaviour; for simple transition probabilities use Lag Sequential Analysis, for frequent paths in logs use Sequential Pattern Mining.
whyLost: It lives in Spanish and Latin American observational methodology and sport science, with specialised software and little English-language exposure in HCI.
whereToUse: Conversational AI and chatbot transcripts, moderated session analysis, collaborative and multiplayer interaction, support calls.
example: Coding 40 chatbot sessions, a team takes 'user rephrases request' as focal and finds that 'bot asks clarifying question' inhibits it while 'bot gives generic answer' strongly activates it.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: Polarising-Item Feedback Analysis with Entropy
origin: Eric Colson, Stitch Fix, as reported by King, Churchill and Tan (2017)
summary: Finds items customers tend either to love or hate by computing entropy over their feedback ratings, then uses responses to those items to learn individual preferences.
description: Some items split opinion: most people rate them very high or very low. Because a customer's reaction to such an item reveals a lot about their taste, these polarising items are valuable probes. The method computes an entropy-based measure over each item's rating distribution after the fact to flag polarising items, then deliberately includes them in recommendations to learn about each customer, accepting a short-term drop in purchase likelihood for better long-term fit. The authors liken it to a batter who makes a pitcher throw many pitches to learn what they have. It is not an A/B test but a learning procedure, justified only where the key metric rewards long-term relationship rather than single-order conversion. The source gives no formula or thresholds, so the entropy measure and cut-offs must be designed and validated locally.
steps: Collect explicit feedback ratings per item across customers.
Compute an entropy-based dispersion measure over each item's rating distribution, checking also for bimodality so that uniformly mixed ratings are not mistaken for polarisation.
Flag items above a locally chosen threshold as polarising and review them qualitatively.
Include polarising items deliberately for customers whose preferences are uncertain.
Feed the responses into preference profiles and recommendation models.
Monitor the short-term conversion cost against long-term retention or satisfaction to confirm the trade-off pays.
outputs: A list of polarising items and richer individual preference profiles.
useWhen: Personalised products with explicit feedback, such as styling, food boxes, media or learning, where learning a customer's taste early improves long-term fit.
avoidWhen: When the key metric is single-session conversion, or feedback volume per item is low. It lowers short-term purchase rate and has low confidence as a stand-alone method; for causal claims use A/B Testing or Multi-Armed Bandit Testing for Adaptive UX.
whyLost: It is a proprietary data-science practice described anecdotally, never written up as a general research method.
whereToUse: Subscription boxes, fashion and recipe recommenders, music and video discovery, onboarding taste quizzes.
example: A recipe-box service finds coriander-heavy dishes have high rating entropy and includes one in each new customer's second box; responses sharpen recommendations and improve 90-day retention despite a dip in week-two ratings.
reference: King, R., Churchill, E. F. and Tan, C. (2017). Designing with Data: Improving the User Experience with A/B Testing. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 160-162.

name: Polite Software Evaluation
origin: Brian Whitworth (2005)
summary: Inspect software against five politeness requirements (respect, visibility, helpfulness, remembering, responsiveness) to find selfish behaviour that drives users to uninstall.
description: Whitworth defines politeness as giving users more choice than the law requires, in ways that are desired, rightful and optional. Selfish software commits social errors: changing settings, running hidden processes, nagging, forgetting answers. The inspection checks five requirements. Respect: no pre-emptive acts on user-owned or shared resources. Visibility: declare who you are and what you are doing. Helpfulness: offer clear, understandable choices, not choices hidden behind other choices. Remembering: carry past choices forward. Responsiveness: accept correction and do not interrupt. Findings are classified into impolite types (blameware, pryware, nagware, strikeware, forgetware) with remedies such as meta-choices like 'Yes to all'. It is judgement-based with no severity scale, but its choice-dependency analysis of installers and settings is concrete and repeatable.
steps: Install the software and record every choice offered, including hidden or pre-selected ones (choice dependency analysis).
List background processes and startup items it adds and check whether each declares itself.
Check for pre-emptive changes to shared or user-owned resources such as home page, file associations and startup.
Check whether registration asks for data the task does not need.
Use the software over several sessions and note repeated questions and forgotten choices.
Classify findings by requirement and impolite type, and propose fixes such as meta-choices and remembered preferences.
outputs: A list of politeness violations by requirement and impolite type, with proposed remedies.
useWhen: Auditing installers, permission flows, notification strategies, consent prompts or any product suspected of nagging or overriding user choices.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a general usability review; it covers social conduct only. For manipulative design use a dark-pattern audit; for overall usability use Heuristic Evaluation.
whyLost: It came from academic social-computing work and was overshadowed by dark-pattern and privacy-by-design vocabularies that cover similar ground.
whereToUse: Browser extensions, mobile permission flows, AI assistants that act on user resources, notification-heavy consumer apps.
example: A desktop AI assistant is audited: it silently adds a startup item and re-asks for calendar access every launch. Both are flagged (visibility, forgetware) and fixed with a declared background service and a remembered choice.
reference: Whitworth, B. and Ahmad, A. (2014). The Social Design of Technical Systems, 2nd ed.

name: Politeness Theory Analysis (Brown and Levinson)
origin: Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson, 1978/1987 (Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage), building on Goffman's concept of face
summary: Analyses interface and conversational messages as potential threats to users' positive and negative face, and evaluates the politeness strategies used to mitigate them.
description: Brown and Levinson proposed that people have positive face (wanting to be approved of) and negative face (wanting freedom from imposition). Requests, corrections, refusals and warnings are face-threatening acts (FTAs). The weight of an FTA depends on social distance, power and imposition rank. Speakers choose strategies: bald on record, positive politeness, negative politeness, off record, or not doing the act. Interfaces and AI agents constantly perform FTAs: error messages, upsells, permission requests, refusals by AI, collections notices. Systematic analysis of strategies, and testing them with users from different cultures, improves acceptance and reduces offence.
steps: Inventory messages that perform FTAs: errors, refusals, requests, reminders, warnings, corrections.
Classify the face threatened (positive or negative, user or system) and estimate distance, power and imposition.
Code the politeness strategy used for each message.
Generate alternative versions using different strategies appropriate to the weight of the FTA.
Test versions with users (comprehension, perceived respect, compliance), including cross-cultural samples.
Create guidelines mapping FTA types to recommended strategies in the voice and tone system.
outputs: FTA inventory, strategy coding, tested alternatives and politeness guidelines.
useWhen: Designing errors, refusals, reminders, AI responses and any message that imposes on or corrects users.
avoidWhen: Neutral informational content with no face threat.
whyLost: Pragmatics is taught in linguistics; UX writing relies on tone guidelines without theoretical grounding.
whereToUse: AI assistant refusals, debt collection messages, healthcare reminders, password errors, content moderation notices.
example: An AI assistant's refusals tested as bald on record ('I can't help with that') are rated rude; negative politeness versions acknowledging the user's goal and offering alternatives raise perceived respect without increasing harmful completions.
sources: Brown & Levinson, Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage (1987)
reference: Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness. Cambridge University Press.

name: Polychoric Correlation for Rating-Scale Items
origin: Karl Pearson (tetrachoric, 1900); polychoric generalisation by Ritchie-Scott (1918) and Olsson (1979)
summary: Correlate two rating-scale items by treating each response as a cut of a continuous latent attitude, with thresholds showing how the scale points spread.
description: Short rating scales restrict the values Pearson's r can take, so r understates and blurs association between items. The polychoric correlation assumes each respondent holds a continuous, normally distributed value and picks the scale point whose interval contains it. It estimates the correlation between the two latent variables and the threshold (tau) cut points between adjacent scale points; for binary items it reduces to the tetrachoric correlation. It is read like r, and the thresholds show whether categories discriminate across the latent range or bunch together. A matrix of polychoric correlations is the appropriate input for factor analysis of Likert-type items. Chapman and Feit show the estimate exceeding Pearson's r for two five-point satisfaction items (0.62 against 0.59) and recommend a jittered scatterplot first because ordinal pairs overplot.
steps: Plot the two items against each other with jitter to see the joint distribution.
Keep respondents who answered both items.
Compute Pearson's r for reference.
Compute the polychoric correlation (for example psych::polychoric in R) for the pair or for a set of items.
Interpret the coefficient as you would r.
Inspect each item's thresholds to judge whether scale points spread evenly across the latent continuum, and watch for warnings from sparse cells.
outputs: A polychoric correlation coefficient or matrix and threshold estimates per item.
useWhen: When relating or factor-analysing rating-scale items with five or fewer points, or checking whether a scale's categories discriminate.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the latent-normal assumption is implausible or cells are very sparse; collapse categories or use Spearman correlation. For full item calibration use Item Response Theory (IRT) / Rasch Model.
whyLost: Survey tools report Pearson correlations by default and few UX researchers move into psychometric software.
whereToUse: Questionnaire development, factor analysis of satisfaction or UX scales, driver analysis on Likert data.
example: A team factor-analysing a 12-item onboarding questionnaire on five-point scales finds Pearson-based loadings blurred. Using a polychoric matrix, two clean factors emerge, and thresholds show the bottom two scale points are rarely distinguished.
sources: R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
reference: Olsson, U. (1979). Maximum likelihood estimation of the polychoric correlation coefficient. Psychometrika, 44(4), 443-460; Chapman, C. and Feit, E. M. (2019). R for Marketing Research and Analytics (2nd ed.). Cham: Springer, pp. 104-106.

name: Polynomial, Spline and Generalized Additive Models
origin: Hastie & Tibshirani (1986) generalized additive models
summary: Models curved relationships, such as satisfaction rising then falling with feature count, instead of forcing straight lines.
description: Many UX relationships are not linear: ease ratings may rise with experience then plateau, conversion may peak at a moderate number of options, page speed may matter only past a threshold. Polynomial terms add curvature, splines fit flexible curves joined at knots, and generalised additive models (GAMs) learn a smooth curve for each predictor automatically while staying interpretable. Bruce and Bruce show how partial residual plots reveal the need for these models.
steps: Plot each predictor against the outcome or partial residuals to spot curvature.
Try polynomial terms for simple curves, or splines with a few knots.
Fit a GAM to learn smooth functions per predictor.
Compare models with cross-validation to avoid overfitting.
Plot the fitted curves and describe thresholds or plateaus in plain language.
outputs: Curves showing where effects start, peak or level off.
useWhen: You suspect thresholds, plateaus or diminishing returns in UX data.
avoidWhen: Small samples where flexible curves will overfit.
whyLost: UX analyses default to linear models and averages, missing thresholds that drive design decisions.
whereToUse: Performance budgets, choice overload studies, learning curves, pricing pages.
example: A GAM of page load time against conversion shows a flat effect until 2.4 s, then a steep drop, setting a clear performance budget.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 4.

name: Pooling and testing preferences across data sources
aka: Combining revealed and stated preference choice data
Testing preference regularity across groups, conditions or methods
origin: Morikawa (1989); Bradley and Daly (1992); Swait and Louviere (1993)
summary: Tests whether choice data from different sources, groups or methods share the same trade-offs once differences in response noise are allowed for, then pools them if they do.
description: In logit-type choice models every coefficient is the product of a scale factor (inverse of noise) and the underlying part-worth. Two data sets can therefore show different coefficients purely because one is noisier, and naive comparisons confuse noise with taste. Preference regularity means the coefficient vectors are proportional. The procedure estimates separate models, plots one set of coefficients against the other (points should fall on a line through the origin), then fits a pooled model with common coefficients and a free relative scale, found by grid search or an artificial nested logit. A likelihood-ratio test compares pooled and separate fits; if pooling is rejected, differing parameters are freed and the test repeated. Applied to revealed (market) and stated (experimental) data, this 'data enrichment' combines realistic but collinear market choices with clean but hypothetical survey choices; forecasts use market constants with jointly estimated attribute weights.
steps: Collect the data sets to compare: market choices and a stated-choice task that mirrors them, or the same choice task in different segments, conditions or formats.
Estimate the same model separately for each, excluding alternative-specific constants from the comparison.
Plot coefficient pairs against each other and, for several groups, run PCA on the coefficient vectors to see whether they are proportional.
Fit a pooled model with common coefficients and a free relative scale per data set, found by grid search or nested logit.
Compute -2[LL(pooled) - sum of LL(separate)] and compare with chi-square on the difference in parameters; if rejected, free the differing parameters and retest.
Forecast with market-based constants and pooled attribute weights, and validate on holdout market data.
outputs: Relative scale estimates, a verdict on whether preferences are shared, and an enriched pooled choice model.
useWhen: Combining conjoint or choice-experiment results with behavioural data, comparing segment preferences, or comparing elicitation formats such as ratings and choices.
avoidWhen: Only one data source exists, or the models are not logit-type. Scale differences are not preference differences, and latent class models may over-segment by confusing them; if market coefficients have wrong signs, rely on stated weights.
whyLost: It is standard in transport and marketing choice modelling but requires econometric software and skills that UX research teams rarely have; conjoint results are usually reported in isolation.
whereToUse: Pricing and packaging research, plan-tier design, feature trade-off studies validated against product usage, cross-market preference comparisons.
example: A subscription service runs a choice experiment on plan features and also has observed plan switches. Separate models look different, but a scale-adjusted pooled model is retained: the survey data are about 30% noisier, not different in taste, so the two are combined to forecast uptake of a new tier.
reference: Louviere, J. J., Hensher, D. A. and Swait, J. D. (2000). Stated Choice Methods: Analysis and Applications. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, pp. 227-251 and 354-381.

name: Pooling the Polls: State-Space Tracking with House Effects
aka: Local-level dynamic linear model for survey series
origin: Simon Jackman, 2005; Nathaniel Beck, Jean-Paul Rosenthal and Simon Jackman, 2006
summary: Combines repeated surveys from several vendors or panels into one daily latent trend, treating each reading as noisy and possibly biased, and estimates every source's bias alongside the trend.
description: When several sources measure the same quantity at different times, such as competing pollsters or several survey vendors and panels, their readings disagree because of sampling error, timing and systematic house effects. This model treats each reading as the latent level on its field date plus a constant bias for its source plus sampling error with variance p(1 - p)/n. The latent level follows a daily random walk (or local linear trend) whose innovation variance is estimated. Because levels and house effects are not separately identified from the readings alone, the series is anchored with known benchmarks, such as actual election results at each end, or with a sum-to-zero constraint on biases, which identifies only relative biases. Fitting by Gibbs sampling with forward filtering and backward sampling gives a smoothed daily estimate with credible bands. In 239 Australian polls, one face-to-face pollster overstated Labor by about 2.7 points.
steps: Assemble every reading with its date (the midpoint of fieldwork), source and sample size; treat different modes from one source as separate sources.
Set each reading's sampling variance from its proportion and sample size, inflating for design effects where known.
Specify a daily latent level following a random walk (or local linear trend) and a constant bias term per source.
Anchor the scale with known benchmarks (for example billing data, census figures, election results) or impose a sum-to-zero constraint on source biases.
Place priors on biases and the innovation standard deviation at plausible magnitudes, fit by MCMC and check mixing, since biases correlate strongly with the level.
Report the daily level with credible bands and each source's bias with its interval.
outputs: A smoothed daily estimate of the latent level with uncertainty, an estimated bias for each source, and the innovation variance.
useWhen: You track one metric (satisfaction, awareness, NPS, intent) from several surveys, vendors, panels or modes over time and need a single trend plus an account of each source's systematic offset.
avoidWhen: One consistent source and method is available (simple smoothing suffices); no benchmark exists and absolute bias matters (only relative biases are identified); readings measure different constructs. Stated sample sizes ignore weighting and design effects, so uncertainty can be understated.
whyLost: Poll aggregation is a political-science and election-forecasting technique; UX trackers rarely combine multiple sources, and usually switch vendors with a break in the series.
whereToUse: Brand and satisfaction trackers fed by several vendors, combining in-product micro-surveys with email surveys and panels, multi-market tracking, monitoring AI product trust across sources.
example: A bank tracks satisfaction from an in-app survey, an email survey and a quarterly panel. A state-space model anchored to the panel shows the in-app survey reads 6 points higher on average, and the pooled daily trend reveals a dip after a login change that none of the sources showed clearly on its own.
sources: Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
reference: Jackman, S. (2005). Pooling the polls over an election campaign. Australian Journal of Political Science, 40, 499-517.

name: Population Attributable Harm Estimation
origin: Levin (1953) population attributable risk; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Estimates how much population-level UX harm is attributable to a specific pattern, combining exposure prevalence with relative risk to show what removing it would prevent.
description: The treatise asks 'how many users are exposed to this pattern across the ecosystem, and what is the attributable harm at population level?' Attributable fraction methods answer this: the population attributable fraction combines exposure prevalence with the relative risk of harm among exposed versus unexposed users, giving the share of harm that would disappear if exposure were removed. The treatise's arithmetic (1% unintended purchases across 50 million monthly users equals 500,000 harms a month) illustrates the scale logic. Rigour needs a credible relative risk estimate, ideally from experiments or well-controlled observational studies, and attention to confounding.
steps: Define harm outcome and exposure (pattern presence).
Estimate exposure prevalence in the population.
Estimate relative risk of harm given exposure from experiments or adjusted observational data.
Compute attributable fraction and attributable cases with uncertainty intervals.
Translate into preventable harm (money, hours, incidents) per period.
Use estimates to prioritise interventions across patterns.
outputs: Attributable fractions, preventable harm estimates, prioritisation ranking.
useWhen: Making the case for removing a pattern, comparing patterns, regulatory impact assessment.
avoidWhen: When no credible relative risk can be estimated.
whyLost: UX rarely estimates counterfactual population harm; business cases use revenue only.
whereToUse: Dark pattern removal decisions, regulators, consumer advocacy, ethics reviews.
example: Pre-ticked insurance add-ons have 18% exposure and a relative risk of 6 for unwanted purchases; the attributable fraction is 47% of all unwanted add-on purchases.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Levin ML (1953) The occurrence of lung cancer in man. Acta Unio Int Contra Cancrum 9
Rockhill B, Newman B & Weinberg C (1998) Use and misuse of population attributable fractions. AJPH 88(1)
Levin, The occurrence of lung cancer in man (1953), Acta Unio Internationalis Contra Cancrum
Rockhill, Newman & Weinberg, Use and misuse of population attributable fractions (1998), American Journal of Public Health
reference: Rockhill B, Newman B & Weinberg C (1998) Use and misuse of population attributable fractions. American Journal of Public Health 88(1):15-19.

name: Positionality audit (product framing)
donor: Feminist standpoint theory, critical discourse analysis and qualitative reflexivity
origin: Standpoint theory (Harding, 1986; Haraway, 1988) and critical discourse analysis (Fairclough, 1989), applied to product language alongside Lakoff's frame semantics
summary: Examines from whose social position a product's language, metaphors and defaults are written, exposing assumptions that exclude or alienate users in other positions.
description: Every product speaks from somewhere: it assumes an urban salaried user, a bank account, a desk, a private phone, a literate first language. A positionality audit makes that standpoint explicit by examining the frames, defaults, examples and implied reader of a product, then comparing them with the positions of the people it is meant to serve. It differs from a researcher positionality statement because the object of analysis is the artefact and the team that made it, not only the researcher. Rigour comes from a structured protocol: cataloguing implied-user cues across the product, profiling the design team's own positions, and validating suspected mismatches with users from the excluded positions rather than relying on the team's imagination of them.
steps: Assemble a corpus of the product's language and assets: onboarding copy, examples, placeholder names, illustrations, default settings, required fields and error messages.
Code each item for implied-user cues (assumed income, location, literacy, device ownership, gender, family structure, institutional access) using a codebook of 8 to 12 dimensions.
Profile the positions of the design and research team on the same dimensions, anonymously, to identify where team and implied user coincide.
Profile target user positions on the same dimensions from existing research or a short survey, and mark dimensions where the implied user diverges from at least 20% of the target population.
Validate each divergence with 5 to 8 users from the affected position through walk-through interviews asking 'Who do you think this was made for?' and 'Where does this not fit your life?'
Prioritise mismatches that block tasks or signal exclusion at moments of trust, and rewrite or redesign with participants from the affected position.
outputs: An implied-user profile of the product, a team positionality profile, a divergence map against target users, and validated, prioritised mismatches with redesign proposals.
useWhen: Building for users socially distant from the team; launching in new markets; reviewing products for inclusion, equity or regulatory fairness concerns.
avoidWhen: The team and users genuinely share positions (internal tools built by their users), or when the problem is purely functional; avoid using it as a box-ticking diversity exercise without user validation.
whyLost: Positionality is discussed in qualitative research as researcher reflexivity, but it has rarely been turned into an audit of artefacts in UX, where inclusion work tends to focus on accessibility checklists.
whereToUse: Financial inclusion, public services, global health, AI assistant persona and default design, localisation programmes.
example: An insurance claims app used examples like 'your employer' and 'your GP' and required a fixed address. The audit showed the implied user was a salaried urban homeowner; informal workers in the target segment read the product as 'not for people like me', and replacing examples and making address optional lifted claim starts.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 19 — Neural Framing & the Architecture of Meaning
reference: Haraway, D. (1988). Situated Knowledges: The Science Question in Feminism and the Privilege of Partial Perspective. Feminist Studies, 14(3), 575–599.

name: Positionality Audit and Reflexivity Journal
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Finlay, 2002
summary: Systematically documents how the researcher's identity, assumptions and reactions shape data collection and interpretation, through a pre-study audit and ongoing journal.
description: Positionality refers to the researcher's social identity, values, beliefs, and prior experiences that inevitably shape what they notice, how they interpret it, and what they choose to report. A reflexivity journal is an ongoing document — maintained throughout a study — in which the researcher records their reactions, interpretations, and evolving understanding. In interpretivist research, reflexivity is not optional: it is the primary quality assurance mechanism, because the researcher is the instrument.
steps: Before fieldwork — Positionality Statement: Write 400–600 words describing your relationship to the research topic. Include: professional background, cultural identity, prior experience with participants, and any personal stake in the findings. This goes into your methods documentation.

During fieldwork — Reflexivity Journal Entry after every session: Record: (a) What did you notice first? (b) What surprised you? (c) What confirmed your expectations? (d) What made you uncomfortable? (e) How might your presence have affected the participant's responses?

During analysis — Bracketing memo: Before coding each transcript, write a bracketing memo: "Before I read this, I expect to find X because…" After coding: "What I actually found was Y. The difference was Z." This surfaces the gap between expectation and data.

In reporting — Reflexive disclosure: Describe your positionality and its potential influence on findings. Do not present this as a limitation — present it as an honest account of how knowledge was produced.
outputs: A positionality statement, a dated reflexivity journal, a list of assumptions checked against data, and an audit trail supporting the credibility of findings.
useWhen: Interpretive qualitative research, research on topics close to the team's own experience or far from it, and any study where researcher influence could shape findings.
avoidWhen: Not a substitute for analytic rigour; avoid as performative self-disclosure in reports. For quick evaluative tests, a short bias checklist is enough.
whyLost: Reflexivity is foundational in qualitative social science, but UX treats researcher neutrality as given and has no ritual for recording influence.
whereToUse: Discovery and ethnographic research, particularly cross-cultural work, research with marginalised or vulnerable groups, sensitive domains (health, debt, identity), and teams researching their own users or industry, where familiarity or distance biases interpretation.
example: A researcher studying gig workers notes in her journal that she expected exploitation stories and kept probing for them; re-reading transcripts with that note reveals more pride and autonomy than her early synthesis showed.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 25 — The Philosophy of Seeing — Epistemological Foundations of Qualitative Inquiry
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (O'Brien et al., 2014)
A Step-by-Step Process of Thematic Analysis to Develop a Conceptual Model in Qualitative Research (Naeem et al., 2023)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Lincoln YS & Guba EG (1985) Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage

name: Positionality Audit for Global Products
origin: Inspired by Nicholas Dirks, 2001 (Castes of Mind), on how classification systems encode the classifier's worldview
summary: Auditing a product's categories, mandatory fields and flows to identify where they encode designers' cultural assumptions rather than users' realities.
description: Dirks showed how colonial census categories did not simply describe Indian society but reshaped it in the administrators' image. A positionality audit applies this insight to digital products: every classification system (user types, content categories, form fields, relationship options) originates in someone's social reality and can impose it on others. The audit asks who designed each category, which elements are mandatory, and what identities, relationships or practices cannot be expressed. Names and gender fields are typical flashpoints: single given and family name fields, fixed title lists and binary gender options fail many users. Findings are tested with users from non-dominant contexts, producing evidence-based changes to data models.
steps: Who designed the categories? For every classification system in your product (user types, content categories, task flows, form fields): what cultural context did it come from? Whose social reality does it represent?

What is mandatory vs. optional? Mandatory fields, categories, and flows impose the designer's framework on users who may not share it. Document every mandatory element and question its cultural assumptions.

What is missing? What social realities, identity categories, relationship types, or cultural practices cannot be expressed in the current category system? Conduct research with users from the non-dominant cultural context to identify category impositions.

Name vs. gender fields: The most culturally imposed fields in most global products. Research: how do target users name themselves? What gender categories exist and are meaningful in their cultural context? How do naming conventions, honorifics, and title systems differ?
outputs: An inventory of categories and mandatory fields with their cultural assumptions, a list of inexpressible realities, and data-model change recommendations.
useWhen: Before launching in new regions, when redesigning sign-up and profile data models, or when complaints suggest users cannot represent themselves.
avoidWhen: Products with no user-facing classification or personal data; or when used as a desk exercise without validating with affected users.
whyLost: It draws on postcolonial scholarship rarely read in design; mainstream practice reduces it to inclusive-language guidelines.
whereToUse: Identity and KYC flows, healthcare records, government services, social and dating platforms, and HR systems.
example: A global HR platform audits its employee profile and finds that 'emergency contact relationship' offers only nuclear family options. Interviews in Ghana and the Philippines lead to free-text and extended family options.
reference: Dirks, N. B. (2001). Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India. Princeton University Press.

name: Positive Design Contagion Strategy
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Deliberately increases the transmissibility and persistence of good design patterns through awards, open pattern libraries, business-value case studies and regulatory floors.
description: The treatise argues good design can spread like disease, and that understanding positive contagion matters as much as understanding pathogen transmission. Mechanisms include awards and recognition (reputational incentives diffusing as competitors match recognised excellence), open design systems and pattern libraries (making good patterns as easy to copy as bad ones), case studies demonstrating business value (economic incentives) and regulatory requirements for accessibility and transparency (raising the floor). Intervention programmes should increase the basic reproduction number of good design: more transmissible, more persistent when adopted and more resistant to displacement by inferior patterns under competitive pressure. The strategy pairs with vector analysis, using the same channels for good patterns.
steps: Select beneficial patterns with evidence of user benefit.
Package them for easy transmission: open components, documentation and code.
Seed adoption through super-spreader nodes (major design systems, platforms).
Publish business-value case studies and recognise adopters.
Advocate for standards or regulation that make the pattern the floor.
Measure adoption R and persistence over time.
outputs: Packaged good patterns, adoption metrics, contagion plan.
useWhen: Spreading accessible, honest or safety patterns across an organisation or industry.
avoidWhen: Patterns without clear evidence of benefit.
whyLost: Original framing of the treatise.
whereToUse: Design-system teams, government design standards, accessibility advocacy, industry consortia.
example: A government publishes an open 'clear cancellation' component and case study showing reduced complaints; adoption spreads to 40% of regulated firms within a year.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed
Centola D (2018) How Behavior Spreads: The Science of Complex Contagions
reference: Centola D (2018) How Behavior Spreads: The Science of Complex Contagions. Princeton University Press.

name: Post-Release Follow-Up Study of Installed Systems
origin: Jakob Nielsen (1993), usability engineering lifecycle stage 11; Grudin, Ehrlich and Shriner (1987) on impact on future releases
summary: A planned study of how a released product is actually used, combining field visits, logging, complaints and economic data, treating the release as the prototype of the next version.
description: After release, Nielsen argues, the main usability objective is data for the next version: the released product is a prototype of its successor. The study is planned as a lifecycle stage rather than left to chance. It combines several sources: routine marketing satisfaction data compared with lab predictions, field visits with interviews, questionnaires and observation of naturally occurring tasks, logging from instrumented versions, passive sources such as complaints, modification requests, help-line calls and defect tracking adapted for usability, course instructors' knowledge of learning problems, and economic data on the quality and cost of users' work compared with pre-introduction baselines. In Nielsen's survey of specialists such studies were rated 4.3 of 5 for impact yet used in only 46% of projects.
steps: Plan the follow-up study before release, with named questions for the next version and a budget.
Collect routine satisfaction and marketing data and compare them with predictions from lab testing.
Visit users to interview, survey and observe actual use on naturally occurring tasks.
Instrument the product to log feature use and errors, with consent and privacy safeguards.
Mine complaints, modification requests, help-line calls and defect reports for usability causes.
Ask trainers and instructors about common learning problems.
Compare economic and work-life data (time, quality, absenteeism) with pre-introduction baselines and feed findings into requirements for the next version.
outputs: An evidence base on real use, problems, changing needs and economic impact, translated into requirements for the next release.
useWhen: After launch of a major release or enterprise deployment, when the next version's priorities should rest on real use rather than lab predictions.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying only on complaints, which come mostly from dissatisfied and vocal users. If you only need to measure a release's effect on metrics, use a pre-post comparison with confound checks.
whyLost: Continuous delivery and analytics dashboards replaced planned follow-up studies; teams monitor metrics but rarely combine field visits, support data and economic outcomes into a deliberate study.
whereToUse: Enterprise and B2B deployments, public-sector systems, clinical software, hardware products with long release cycles.
example: Six months after rolling out a field-service app, a utility visits 12 technicians, analyses 3,000 help-desk tickets and compares job completion times with the old paper process. Offline sync failures dominate tickets, making them the first priority for version 2.
reference: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering. Boston: AP Professional, pp. 109-113; Grudin, J., Ehrlich, S. F. and Shriner, R. (1987). Positioning human factors in the user interface development chain. Proceedings of CHI+GI '87, 125-131.

name: Post-Task Confidence and Disaster Rate
origin: Term popularised by Gerry McGovern (2010); measurement procedure from Jeff Sauro's MeasuringU benchmarking practice (2018)
summary: After each task, rate confidence of success; failures given the top confidence rating count as disasters, reported per task as the rate of users who failed without knowing.
description: A post-task item asks participants how confident they are that they completed the task successfully, usually on a seven-point scale (not to be confused with a statistical confidence interval). Confidence alone is a task metric that can be compared across tasks and versions, and it can feed a summarised usability metric. Crossed with binary completion it gives the disaster rate: the share of participants who failed but chose the top confidence point. Sauro treats this as worse than ordinary failure, because people leave believing an order went through or carrying wrong information, so the problem never reaches support and is invisible in satisfaction data. The rigour depends on precise, predefined success criteria and on a consistent scale, since a five-point scale makes the top category looser.
steps: Define success criteria for every task before testing so each attempt can be coded as success or failure without debate.
After each task ask a seven-point confidence item (five, nine or eleven points are possible but change the meaning of the top point) about having completed the task successfully.
Report mean confidence per task with confidence intervals, alongside completion rate.
Count failed attempts that received the top scale point and divide by the number of participants attempting the task to get the disaster rate.
Flag tasks with high disaster rates and review the recordings or open answers to find what misled participants.
Track confidence and disaster rate across benchmark rounds and competitor products.
outputs: Per-task mean confidence with intervals, per-task disaster rate, and a short list of tasks where the interface misleads users about their success.
useWhen: Benchmarks and summative tests of tasks where silent failure is costly: checkout, bookings, financial transactions, form submissions, information lookup where a wrong answer looks plausible.
avoidWhen: Avoid when success cannot be coded reliably or tasks are open-ended exploration; in formative think-aloud sessions direct observation of misunderstanding is more informative. Do not read confidence as satisfaction; use SEQ or SUS for perceived ease.
whyLost: Confidence items are sometimes collected but rarely crossed with completion, so the disaster count is not reported; most teams rely on completion and ease ratings alone.
whereToUse: E-commerce and travel checkouts, banking transfers, health information tasks, AI assistants whose wrong answers sound authoritative.
example: In a benchmark of an insurance quote flow, 22% of participants who chose the wrong cover level rated themselves extremely confident. The team added a cover summary step and the disaster rate fell to 6% in the next round.
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience. Denver, CO: MeasuringU Press, pp. 99-101, 270-275.

name: Post-UX Thought Experiments
aka: Our users versus their users ad
origin: Kathy Sierra (2015)
summary: Short written team exercises that shift attention from the product experience to what users can do, show and say about themselves after using it.
description: Sierra calls the experience after the clicking stops the 'post-UX UX' and offers a set of thought experiments to design for it. In the ideal review, the team writes the review it hopes a user would post and checks whether it talks about the product or about the reviewer's results; the better review is about the user. In the post-UX documentary, the team imagines a camera crew following a user for minutes to weeks after leaving the product, repeated for novice to expert. The dinner-party exercise asks what the product gives users to talk about or show that is not about the product. In brand meetings 'our' is replaced with 'our users'. A competitive ad shows your users outperforming competitors' users in the wider task. Together they redirect goals from features to user capability.
steps: Write the ideal user review without regard to sales, then compare a product-focused and a user-focused version.
Write a post-UX documentary script describing what a camera would see and hear after use, for a chosen time frame and for several skill levels.
Write the dinner-party scenario: what can the user talk about or show that is not about the product?
Rewrite brand and marketing goals by replacing 'our' with 'our users'.
Sketch an imaginary advert in which your users beat competitors' users at the bigger goal.
Compare the narratives and turn recurring user outcomes into design and success criteria.
outputs: Narratives, reviews and rewritten goals that reorient product, support and marketing towards user results.
useWhen: Use it at kick-off or vision stage to move a team from feature thinking to the outcomes users care about.
avoidWhen: The narratives are imagined; to learn what users actually achieve and value use Jobs-to-be-Done Research, Diary Studies or Interviews. Do not let it become a marketing testimonial exercise.
whyLost: It is a set of informal prompts in one book; outcome framing survived instead through Jobs-to-be-Done and the press release exercise.
whereToUse: Learning products, creative tools, fitness and health apps, developer platforms and B2B tools where user mastery drives retention.
example: A language-learning app team writes the documentary of a user three weeks in: she orders confidently in a cafe abroad. The team reframes its success metric from streaks to conversations held.
reference: Sierra, K. (2015) Badass: Making Users Awesome. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 23-24, 55-61.

name: Posterior credible intervals
origin: Bayesian inference tradition (Laplace; Jeffreys, Theory of Probability, 1939); modern practice in Gelman et al. (Bayesian Data Analysis) and Kruschke (2015)
summary: Reports the range within which a parameter lies with a stated probability given the data and prior, providing intuitive uncertainty statements for UX metrics.
description: A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability given the model and data, which is how most stakeholders already misinterpret frequentist confidence intervals. Credible intervals can be equal-tailed (2.5th to 97.5th percentiles) or highest density intervals, the narrowest range containing 95% of the posterior. Kruschke recommends combining HDIs with a region of practical equivalence (ROPE) to decide whether an effect is meaningfully different from zero. Credible intervals work for any posterior quantity: rates, differences, ratios and predictions. Rigour comes from reporting the prior, checking model fit, using enough posterior samples for stable intervals, and stating the decision rule that links intervals to actions.
steps: Fit a Bayesian model appropriate to the metric, such as Beta-Binomial for rates, log-normal for times or ordinal regression for ratings, with a stated prior.
Draw sufficient posterior samples (for example at least 4,000 effective samples) and check convergence diagnostics such as R-hat below 1.01 where MCMC is used.
Compute the 95% (or 89%, following McElreath) equal-tailed or highest density interval for each quantity of interest.
Define a region of practical equivalence based on the smallest meaningful effect, for example ±1 percentage point in conversion.
Apply the decision rule: effect credible if the HDI lies outside the ROPE, practically equivalent if inside, undecided otherwise.
Report intervals with plain-language statements, such as 'there is a 95% probability the completion rate is between 72% and 89%'.
outputs: Credible intervals for key parameters, ROPE-based decisions, posterior plots and plain-language uncertainty statements.
useWhen: Communicating uncertainty to stakeholders, making decisions on small or sequential samples, or reporting any parameter estimated with a Bayesian model.
avoidWhen: The organisation's governance requires frequentist error-rate guarantees (for example regulated trials), or no defensible prior or model is available; report confidence intervals and explain them properly.
whyLost: UX statistics training and tooling is frequentist, and credible intervals require modelling skills and software that most teams have not adopted.
whereToUse: Small-sample usability benchmarks, low-traffic A/B tests, satisfaction metrics, fintech and health experiments.
example: A fintech A/B test reported a posterior uplift of 2.8% with a 95% HDI of 0.6% to 5.1% against a ROPE of ±0.5%, so the team concluded the effect was practically meaningful and could state a 97% probability that the uplift exceeded 0.5%.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
reference: Kruschke, J. K. (2015). Doing Bayesian Data Analysis (2nd ed.). Academic Press; McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking (2nd ed.). CRC Press.

name: Posterior Rank Probabilities for Latent Scores
aka: Posterior probability of being ranked first
Posterior rank probabilities for latent scores (order-statistic inference)
origin: Joshua Clinton, Simon Jackman and Douglas Rivers, 2004
summary: Ranks units within every posterior draw of their scores, then reports each unit's probability of holding each rank, so claims like 'best' or 'worst' carry honest uncertainty.
description: League tables of designs, features, teams or products present a single order, but if the underlying scores are uncertain, so is the ordering. Given posterior draws of each unit's score from any Bayesian model (a latent factor, an ideal point, a group mean, an item parameter), the units are sorted within each draw. Storing those ranks over many draws gives a probability distribution over each unit's rank, over which unit holds a given rank, or over complete orderings. The method tested a widely reported claim that one US senator was the most liberal: in the posterior no senator was unambiguously most liberal, the leader topping the list in about 30% of draws and the named senator in about 11%. Similarly, among US states on a social-indicators factor, the most likely worst-off state held that position with probability of only .30. When units are tightly bunched they share rank mass, which is the honest answer rather than a failure.
steps: Fit a Bayesian model that yields posterior draws of the scores to be ranked (for example satisfaction by product area, success rate by design, latent quality by vendor).
For each saved draw, rank the units' scores.
Tabulate, for each unit, the share of draws in which it holds each rank, and the probability it is first, last or in the top k.
Plot rank probability distributions for the units of interest.
Report probabilities for the specific claim (for example the probability that design C is best) instead of a single ordered list.
Use enough draws for stable small probabilities and check sensitivity of rank probabilities to the priors.
outputs: Rank probability distributions per unit and the probability that a unit is first, last or in the top k.
useWhen: Stakeholders want a ranking or a 'winner' among designs, features, markets, support teams or vendors whose scores are estimated with uncertainty.
avoidWhen: Units are measured exactly (simple ranking suffices); you only need pairwise comparisons; no model with posterior draws is available (a bootstrap of ranks is a frequentist substitute). Rank probabilities are fragile when the data barely separate units, which should then be reported plainly.
whyLost: It is a by-product of MCMC output known mainly in political methodology and health-provider league tables; UX dashboards present point rankings.
whereToUse: Multi-variant design tests, feature prioritisation surveys, benchmark comparisons of competitors, ranking help-centre articles or support agents, model leaderboards for AI features.
example: A team estimates success rates for six navigation variants from 30 participants each. The variant with the highest point estimate is ranked first in only 41% of posterior draws and two others in 25% and 22%, so the team reports 'no clear winner among three' and runs a larger test on those three.
sources: Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
reference: Clinton, J., Jackman, S., & Rivers, D. (2004). The statistical analysis of roll call data. American Political Science Review, 98, 355-370.

name: Power-Law Distribution Analysis
origin: Vilfredo Pareto (1896); George Zipf (1949); rigorous fitting by Aaron Clauset, Cosma Shalizi and Mark Newman (2009)
summary: Tests whether usage, content popularity or query frequency follows a power law, with proper estimation and comparison against alternative heavy-tailed distributions.
description: Many product phenomena are heavy-tailed: a few users generate most activity, a few queries dominate search, a few items get most views. Claims of 'power laws' are often made from straight-ish lines on log-log plots, which is unreliable. Clauset, Shalizi and Newman's method estimates the exponent by maximum likelihood, selects the lower cutoff x_min via Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, tests goodness of fit with bootstrapping, and compares the power law against log-normal, exponential and stretched exponential alternatives with likelihood ratio tests. Getting the distribution right matters: it determines whether averages are meaningful, how to sample users for research and how to design for the head versus the long tail.
steps: Collect the quantity (e.g. sessions per user, views per item, queries per term).
Plot the complementary cumulative distribution on log-log axes for exploration only.
Estimate x_min and the exponent alpha by maximum likelihood (e.g. powerlaw Python package).
Run bootstrap goodness-of-fit tests (p above 0.1 supports plausibility).
Compare against log-normal and other alternatives with likelihood ratio tests.
Interpret implications: concentration, sampling strategies, and design for head and tail.
outputs: Fitted distribution parameters, goodness-of-fit and model comparison results, and design implications.
useWhen: Analysing concentration of usage, content, queries, errors or revenue, and planning research sampling.
avoidWhen: Small datasets (under a few hundred observations in the tail) where distinctions are untestable.
whyLost: The 'long tail' entered product vocabulary as a slogan without the statistical methods to test it.
whereToUse: Search query analysis, content libraries, creator platforms, power user research, error frequency analysis.
example: A music app finds track plays fit a log-normal better than a power law; this implies the 'long tail' is thinner than assumed, and discovery features should target the mid-tail instead.
sources: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman, Power-law distributions in empirical data (2009), SIAM Review
Newman, Power laws, Pareto distributions and Zipf's law (2005), Contemporary Physics
Predicting User Behavior: The Must-Know Distributions for UX & HF Researchers (carousel, n.d.)
reference: Clauset, A., Shalizi, C. R., & Newman, M. E. J. (2009). SIAM Review, 51(4), 661-703.

name: Pragmatic (Budget and Feasibility) Sample Sizing
aka: Cost, feasibility and heuristic sample sizing
origin: Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015), drawing on expert ranges from Nielsen, Tullis and Wood, Krueger and Casey, Guest et al. and others
summary: When power analysis or saturation cannot be used, set and justify sample size openly from budget, fixed constraints or published norms, and explain the trade-off to stakeholders.
description: Power analysis and saturation are the ideals, but budgets, schedules and access usually decide. A cost analysis divides the incentive budget by cost per participant. A feasibility analysis allocates fixed sessions across user groups by importance and population size: with only four focus groups for a hospital discharge study, eight administrators fit in one group, a sample of the 30 clinicians in another, and the large patient population gets two. Heuristics come from local standards and published expert ranges, such as 12 to 20 qualitative interviews, 15 to 30 for card sorts, 6 to 8 per focus group with 3 to 4 groups per participant type, 5 per think-aloud iteration, and 15 to 30 for quantitative usability tests. The rigour lies in being explicit about the basis and what it means for reliability.
steps: Try power analysis for quantitative work or plan for saturation for qualitative work first.
If neither is feasible, list fixed constraints: budget, time, available sessions, population size, equipment and prototypes.
Compute N from budget (budget divided by cost per participant) or allocate fixed sessions across user groups by importance and population size.
Check the result against local standards and published expert ranges, reading the original sources rather than quoting ranges blindly.
Explain to stakeholders what the limit means for reliability and offer a narrower scope as an alternative.
outputs: A justified sample size and allocation across groups, with stated limitations.
useWhen: Budget or access caps the study, populations are tiny, or stakeholders need a defensible number quickly.
avoidWhen: You need to detect small effects or make precise estimates; small samples reveal only large or common effects. Use formal sample-size planning instead.
whyLost: It survives because it reflects how most UX studies are actually sized, though the justification step is often omitted.
whereToUse: Agency and in-house studies under fixed budgets, B2B and specialist audiences, multi-segment qualitative studies.
example: With budget for 12 interviews across three segments, a team allocates six to the core segment and three each to two smaller ones, and tells stakeholders that findings for the small segments are indicative only.
reference: Baxter, K., Courage, C., & Caine, K. (2015). Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Research Methods (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 5.

name: Pragmatic Competence Analysis for Interface Language
origin: H. P. Grice (1975) conversational maxims; developmental pragmatics in Gleason (ed.), The Development of Language
summary: Audits interface and conversational language against pragmatic expectations, Grice's maxims, implicature and politeness, and tests what users infer beyond the literal words.
description: Pragmatics studies how people infer meaning beyond literal content using context and shared conventions. Grice proposed that speakers follow a cooperative principle with maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner; when an utterance seems to violate one, listeners infer an implicature. Users apply the same expectations to interfaces, especially conversational ones: an error message that says less than needed implies there is nothing more to know, an overly polite refusal implies optional compliance, and an irrelevant suggestion implies the system misunderstood. Developmental research shows pragmatic competence varies with age, culture and neurodiversity, so implied meanings are not universal. The method audits strings and dialogue turns against the maxims, predicts likely implicatures, and tests users' inferences with comprehension probes.
steps: Apply Gricean maxim analysis to all interface text:
Quantity — does the message say exactly as much as needed?
(2) Quality — is the message truthful and not misleading?
(3) Relation — is the message relevant to the user's current context?
(4) Manner — is the message clear, brief, and orderly? For each text element, score violations on 1–4 and prioritize the highest-violation elements for rewrite.
outputs: Maxim-by-maxim audit of strings and dialogue flows, predicted implicatures, observed user inferences, and rewritten language for clarity across user groups.
useWhen: Chatbots and voice assistants, error messages, notifications, AI refusals and products for children, older adults or neurodivergent users.
avoidWhen: For purely visual or structural problems, or when standard comprehension testing already explains the issue.
whyLost: Pragmatics is well developed in linguistics and child-language research but UX writing adopted style guides rather than pragmatic theory.
whereToUse: Error message design, onboarding copy, chatbot dialogue design, microcopy auditing.
example: A banking chatbot replies 'I can help with many things!' when asked to dispute a charge. Users infer disputes are impossible (relation maxim) and leave; a reply naming the dispute path and handoff fixes completion.
sources: The Development of Language — Jean Berko Gleason
Grice, Logic and conversation (in Syntax and Semantics 3, 1975)
reference: Grice HP (1975) Logic and conversation. In Cole P & Morgan JL (Eds.) Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts. Academic Press

name: Pre-attentive feature audit
origin: Anne Treisman's feature integration theory, 1980; applied to visualisation by Healey and Enns (2012) and Ware
summary: Checks whether critical elements differ from their surroundings in a single pre-attentive feature strongly enough to pop out, rather than requiring serial search.
description: Some visual features, including colour hue, orientation, size, motion, flicker and enclosure, are processed in parallel across the visual field, so a unique target 'pops out' in under about 200-250 ms regardless of the number of distractors. Conjunctions of features (for example red and vertical among red horizontals and green verticals) usually require serial search, with time increasing per item. A pre-attentive feature audit lists each critical element, identifies the feature it relies on to stand out, and checks whether that feature is unique among distractors and differs strongly enough. Overuse of the same feature (everything red) destroys pop-out. Rigour comes from measuring search slopes in a quick visual search test, where flat slopes (below about 10 ms per item) indicate pre-attentive pop-out.
steps: List the elements that must be found immediately (alerts, status changes, primary actions).
For each, identify the distinguishing feature and list all other elements on screen sharing that feature.

Flag targets that rely on feature conjunctions, share their feature with 3 or more distractors, or use weak differences (for example small hue shifts, or colour alone for colour-vision-deficient users).
Run a visual search test: 10-15 participants, set sizes such as 8, 16 and 32 elements, measuring response time slopes per item.
Treat slopes under about 10 ms per item as pop-out and above about 20-30 ms per item as serial search; redesign serial-search targets.
Reserve pre-attentive features for critical signals in the design system and re-test.
outputs: A feature audit table, search slope results per target, and a reservation scheme for pre-attentive features.
useWhen: For dashboards, monitoring displays, alert design and data visualisation where critical items must be noticed instantly.
avoidWhen: When the problem is meaning or decision-making rather than detection; use comprehension testing.
whyLost: Visualisation researchers use it, but UX visual design relies on intuition and brand styling, often spending pre-attentive features on decoration.
whereToUse: Clinical monitors, control rooms, financial dashboards, maps, and status indicators in design systems.
example: On a surgical console red is used for alerts, the brand logo, three buttons and a progress bar. The audit shows alerts have a 38 ms-per-item search slope; reserving red and adding motion for alerts brings the slope to 4 ms.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
