Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Treisman, A. M. & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

name: Pre-attentive processing analysis
origin: Treisman's feature integration theory, 1980; scene gist research by Potter (1975) and Oliva (2005)
summary: Analyses what users perceive within the first fraction of a second of seeing a screen, before focused attention, to check whether its gist communicates the right state.
description: Within about 50-100 ms people extract the gist of a scene: its category, layout and dominant features. Lindgaard and colleagues found web page aesthetic judgements form within 50 ms. Pre-attentive processing analysis examines what a screen communicates at this level, as distinct from what users eventually find by searching. It combines expert analysis of global features (layout, colour distribution, contrast, grouping) with brief-exposure tests in which participants see the screen for 50-500 ms and report what state it is in or what they noticed. For safety displays, the question is whether a normal versus abnormal state is distinguishable at a glance. Rigour comes from controlled exposure times, masking to prevent afterimages, and comparing several screen states.
steps: Define the gist each screen state must communicate (for example normal, warning, critical; or ready versus not ready).
Analyse global features per state: overall colour distribution, contrast, layout changes, motion; flag states that differ only in small local details.
Run brief-exposure trials with 12-20 participants: present screenshots for 50, 100 and 250 ms followed by a mask, and ask them to classify the state.
Compute classification accuracy per exposure duration and state; target above 90% at 250 ms for safety-critical distinctions.
Redesign states that fail by changing global features rather than adding local detail.
Re-test with fresh participants.
outputs: Gist requirements per state, global feature analysis, classification accuracy by exposure time, and redesigned state encodings.
useWhen: For monitoring and status displays, landing pages, product first impressions, and any glanceable interface such as watches or car dashboards.
avoidWhen: For detailed reading or complex decision tasks; use comprehension tests or think-aloud.
whyLost: Gist research is well established in vision science but practitioners use only the commercial five-second test, which measures recall rather than glance-level perception.
whereToUse: Surgical console status, vehicle displays, smartwatch complications, operations dashboards and first-impression testing.
example: A surgical console's normal and fault states differ only in a small status icon; at 100 ms participants classify them at chance. Changing the header bar colour in fault states raises classification to 96% at 100 ms.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Sensation and Perception
Gibson, J. J., The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979)
Whalen, J., Design for How People Think (2019)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
reference: Oliva, A. (2005). Gist of the scene. In L. Itti, G. Rees & J. Tsotsos (Eds.), Neurobiology of Attention. Elsevier.

name: Pre-post release comparison with confound checklist
aka: Before-and-after release comparison with analytics rates
origin: Beasley (2013); Wendel (2014)
summary: Compare a behaviour rate in stable periods before and after a release with a two-proportion test, then reason through time, experience, data-quality and population confounds against a care threshold.
description: When an A/B test is impossible, teams still need a defensible read of a release. The target behaviour is reframed as a binary rate (conversion, exit, reached a page, event occurred). A long, stable before period without outages, holidays or other changes is compared with about two weeks or 5,000 visitors after, using a two-proportion (N-1 chi-square) test with a confidence interval and a chart of the rate over time with the release marked. A smallest-change-worth-caring-about threshold is set first. Then four non-product explanations are checked: time effects (season, weekday), growing user experience, data availability or quality changes (sharp and often hidden), and population composition, countered by following a fixed group. If confounds could push the effect below the threshold, stop; if not, treat it as an initial estimate and confirm with a model using those factors as controls.
steps: Name the behaviour the change should affect and reframe it as a rate (for example unique visitors reaching the target page divided by all unique visitors).
Set the smallest change you would care about before looking at the data.
Choose a before period as long and stable as possible, free of outages, holidays, campaigns and other releases.
Collect after data (start at about two weeks or 5,000 visitors), segmenting to target users if the change affects only some.
Compare rates with a two-proportion test, report the confidence interval and chart the rate over time with the release marked.
Check confounds: time effects, user experience effects, data availability or quality changes, and population composition (follow a fixed group).
Stop if confounds could push the effect below the threshold; otherwise confirm with a statistical model that uses those factors as controls.
outputs: Before and after rates, a test result with confidence interval, a release-marked chart and a list of candidate control variables.
useWhen: Small teams or sites without experimentation infrastructure, or changes that cannot be randomised, where a large effect is expected and nothing else changed.
avoidWhen: When other changes, campaigns or seasonal shifts coincide with the release, or effects are small; use A/B tests, interrupted time series or difference-in-differences.
whyLost: It survives in everyday analytics practice because it needs no experimentation platform, though the confound checklist is often skipped.
whereToUse: Content sites, small e-commerce, public-sector services, internal tools and apps without feature flags.
example: A retailer adds guest checkout and compares conversion over eight stable weeks before (1.43%) and three weeks after (1.46%). The difference is not significant and the team checks no campaign coincided; they keep the design since it is no worse.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Beasley, M. (2013). Practical Web Analytics for User Experience. Morgan Kaufmann; Wendel, S. (2014). Designing for Behavior Change. O'Reilly Media.

name: Pre-registration
origin: Clinical trial registration (ICMJE 2005); open-science pre-registration (Nosek et al. 2018)
summary: Records hypotheses, primary outcomes, sample size and analysis plan before data collection to prevent outcome switching and p-hacking.
description: The treatise repeatedly cites pre-registration: research protocol pre-registration as a DAG revival context, and pre-registration of hypotheses as missing from industry A/B testing. Pre-registration time-stamps a plan specifying hypotheses, primary and secondary outcomes, sample size with power justification, exclusion rules and analysis, separating confirmatory from exploratory findings. It counters the garden of forking paths, where flexible analysis turns noise into apparent effects. In product organisations it can be lightweight: an internal registry where experiment and study plans are frozen before launch and results are reported against them, including null results.
steps: Write hypotheses and designate one or a few primary outcomes.
Justify sample size with a power or precision analysis.
Specify exclusion rules, analysis models, multiplicity corrections and stopping rules.
Register the plan in an internal or public registry with a timestamp.
Run the study and analyse as planned; label deviations and exploratory analyses.
Report all registered outcomes, including nulls.
outputs: Time-stamped protocol, confirmatory results, transparent deviation log.
useWhen: Experiments and quantitative studies informing significant decisions; claims shared externally.
avoidWhen: Purely exploratory qualitative discovery, though a brief intent note still helps.
whyLost: Pre-registration is standard in clinical trials and growing in psychology, but product teams see it as bureaucratic, and experimentation platforms rarely enforce it.
whereToUse: Experimentation platforms, UX benchmarks, research claims in sales or regulatory contexts.
example: An e-commerce team registers 'checkout completion' as primary outcome; when a secondary metric moves but the primary does not, the result is reported as null rather than reframed as a win.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nosek BA et al. (2018) The preregistration revolution. PNAS 115(11)
Simmons JP, Nelson LD & Simonsohn U (2011) False-positive psychology. Psychological Science
The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
reference: Nosek BA et al. (2018) The preregistration revolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(11):2600-2606.

name: Precedent Search
aka: Search in and out of the box
origin: Sheena Iyengar, Think Bigger, 2023, adapting Lloyd Trotter's GE best-practice matrix (1990s)
summary: For each subproblem, collect proven precedents from the problem's own domain and, mostly, from other domains found by reformulating the question, verifying each tactic with evidence and experts.
description: Iyengar's precedent search fills the rows of a Choice Map, one per subproblem, with about five tactics each: two non-redundant in-domain best practices and at least three from other domains, so no row is wholly in-domain. Searches start domain-specific, then reformulate the question agnostically (domain removed), partially (one level wider) and in parallel (other domains that fit the agnostic version, each searched). Only past successes count, not failures or current projects, and only the part that drove success is copied. Each tactic needs evidence, a concrete example of it producing a result, and an explanation of why it works from an expert in the tactic's own domain. Teams search individually and pool per row. In her course data, maps with fifteen or more mostly out-of-domain tactics produced ideas peers rated more creative.
steps: Phrase each subproblem in domain terms and search for in-domain best practices; enter the two strongest.
Reformulate each subproblem agnostically, partially and in parallel, listing other domains that face the same agnostic problem, and search each.
Collect a long list of leads and keep only past successes with evidence of a result.
Verify each tactic's contribution with an expert from that tactic's domain and ask why it works.
Enter at least three out-of-domain tactics per row with short markers and micro-notes, citing sources and checking patents.
In teams, search individually, then pool and discuss per row before combining tactics into ideas.
outputs: A filled Choice Map (for example five subproblems by five tactics) with evidence notes per tactic.
useWhen: A team has a well-broken-down problem and wants solution ideas grounded in what has demonstrably worked elsewhere.
avoidWhen: Copy parts, not wholes; online best-practice claims are often opinion. Precedents show what worked in another context, not that it will work for your users; test with Prototype Testing or A/B Testing. For systematic competitor review use Competitive UX Benchmarking; for engineered inventive principles use TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving).
whyLost: UX keeps the loose habit of collecting inspiration and competitor screenshots, but the out-of-domain quota, evidence rule and expert verification are rarely applied.
whereToUse: Service innovation, healthcare logistics, public services, onboarding and waiting experiences, education products.
example: A transit app team tackling platform waiting searches Disney queues, serpentine retail lines and colour-coded checkout, verifies with a theme-park operations expert why visible progress reduces perceived wait, and prototypes a live 'trains away' display.
reference: Iyengar, S. (2023) Think Bigger: How to Innovate. New York: Columbia University Press, pp. 130-157.

name: Predicate logic for invariants
origin: Floyd (1967) and Hoare (1969) on program assertions; interaction properties formalised by Dix and Harrison (PIE model, 1980s)
summary: Writes the properties an interface must always satisfy as logical statements, so that designs and implementations can be checked against them systematically.
description: An invariant is a condition that must hold in every reachable state. Expressed in predicate logic, interface invariants make design intentions testable: 'for all states s, displayed_mode(s) = actual_mode(s)'; 'for all states s, if armed(s) then stop_enabled(s)'; 'for all actions a, if destructive(a) then reversible(a) or confirmed(a)'. Dix and Harrison's work defined classes of interaction properties such as predictability, observability and reachability in this way. Invariants can then be checked by model checkers, property-based tests or runtime assertions. Rigour comes from precise variable definitions, quantifiers that cover all states and actions, and linking each invariant to a hazard or usability principle.
steps: Identify hazards and usability principles that must never be violated (mode visibility, reversibility, stop availability, consent).
Define the state variables and predicates needed to express them unambiguously.
Write each invariant in predicate logic with explicit quantifiers, and a plain-language paraphrase for stakeholders.
Check invariants against a state model with a model checker (for example NuSMV, UPPAAL or TLA+) or encode them as property-based tests running thousands of generated action sequences.
Investigate every counter-example trace, deciding whether to change the design or refine the invariant.
Keep invariants as living requirements, re-checking at each release.
outputs: A catalogue of formal invariants with plain-language versions, verification results, counter-example traces, and regression tests.
useWhen: When certain design properties must hold universally, such as safety, privacy consent, reversibility or mode visibility, and you need evidence.
avoidWhen: When requirements are exploratory or still changing weekly; use heuristic evaluation and scenario walkthroughs until the design stabilises.
whyLost: The logic is standard in verification research but UX expresses principles as guidelines, not checkable statements, so invariants live in engineering if anywhere.
whereToUse: Medical devices, autonomous vehicles, financial controls, privacy and consent flows, and AI agent guardrails.
example: An AI agent platform formalises 'for all actions a, if a sends external email then user_confirmed(a)'. Property-based testing finds a retry path that resends without confirmation, which is fixed before launch.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Dix, A. J. (1991). Formal Methods for Interactive Systems. Academic Press.

name: Predict Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 1: Predict with CPM-GOMS and Mental Models
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 1 of the forward-thinking loop: pair CPM-GOMS time predictions with mental-model interviews to produce falsifiable hypotheses and decision bars before any testing.
description: Prediction front-loads insight: before recruiting participants, the researcher models task structure and estimates where bottlenecks will occur. The quant lens is CPM-GOMS with operator estimates (cognitive about 1.2s, perceptual about 0.4s, motor 0.2–0.3s) summed along the task to predict ideal completion time and the cost of misroutes. The qual lens is 4–8 quick contextual interviews asking where users would look first and why, sketched as an 'expected IA' and compared with the actual IA. Combined, they produce a hypothesis such as 'users will misroute to Notifications when creating Alerts, leading to 2–3× longer task time than predicted'. Rigour comes from setting a decision bar up front and logging qual with the first two Miles & Huberman steps (compiling, disassembling) plus a recursive evidence log of expected loop points. The stage is explicitly hypothesis generation, not proof.
steps: Decompose the target task into CPM-GOMS operators: cognitive ≈ 1.2s, perceptual ≈ 0.4s, motor ≈ 0.2–0.3s (e.g. 5 characters × 0.2s = 1s of typing).
Sum the operators to predict ideal completion time (≈ 5.5–6.0s for the price-alert example) and estimate added time per misroute (two wrong tabs add 6–10s).
Set a decision bar up front, e.g. predicted ideal 6s; an observed median above 15s is classified as a significant breakdown.
Run 4–8 contextual interviews asking 'If you wanted to set a price alert, where would you look first? Why?' and sketch each participant's expected IA.
Compile verbatims and sketches into one worksheet (participant, exact quote, expected-IA notes, initial hunch) and code each utterance with short low-granularity labels.
Keep a recursive evidence log: capture the described order (e.g. Settings → Back → Markets), mark expected loop points and flag them as risk loops.
Triangulate: compare CPM-GOMS time if the expected location is correct against added misroute time, and write a falsifiable hypothesis for Stage 2.
outputs: Predicted task time benchmark, expected-versus-actual IA comparison (e.g. 5/8 expect Alerts under Markets), risk-loop list, falsifiable hypothesis and decision bar.
useWhen: Before usability testing of routine, well-defined flows, to sharpen hypotheses and give benchmarks for observed data.
avoidWhen: For creative or ill-structured tasks where GOMS does not apply; avoid vague hypotheses such as 'users might struggle'.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; predictive modelling largely vanished from UX practice in favour of observe-first testing.
whereToUse: Fintech navigation, settings and alert flows, enterprise forms, any routine high-frequency task.
example: Before testing a trading app, the researcher predicts a 6s ideal for creating a price alert while 5 of 8 interviewees expect alerts under Markets rather than Notifications, yielding the hypothesis of a 2–3× longer task time.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Bonnie E. John & Wayne D. Gray (1995), CPM-GOMS: An Analysis Method for Tasks with Parallel Activities, CHI '95 Conference Companion
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 1.

name: Prediction markets
origin: Galton, 1907 ('Vox Populi'); corporate prediction markets from the 1990s; Surowiecki, 2004
summary: Participants trade shares in mutually exclusive outcomes, or estimate others' behaviour independently; aggregated prices or estimates are read as crowd probabilities for product questions.
description: Instead of asking 'would you buy this?', a prediction market asks people to bet on what others will do. In the market form described for product research, each participant receives a stake (for example $10) to buy shares in answer options whose prices sum to 1 and move with demand; the market closes when prices stabilise, around 150 participants, and payouts equal shares times final price, so participants are rewarded for accuracy rather than for expressing their own preference. A simpler form aggregates independent estimates of a quantity, such as how many people will buy in six months. Crowds outperform individuals on simple questions with definite answers when members are diverse and independent; authority and social influence spoil the aggregate. Cash incentives and trickle-in participation are what make the prices informative.
steps: Write a market question that is measurable, specific and concise, with mutually exclusive options.
Recruit a diverse panel that can enter over time, and fund a cash stake per participant.
Give each participant a fixed budget and require them to spend most of it (for example at least $7 of $10) within a time limit (for example 10 minutes).
Let prices update with demand, keeping option prices summing to 1, and keep participants independent of each other's reasoning.
Close when prices stabilise and pay out shares times final price.
Read final prices as probabilities and compare them with survey results and, later, with actual outcomes.
outputs: Option probabilities from final prices or an aggregate forecast, with a later accuracy check against outcomes.
useWhen: Forecasting demand, choosing between concepts or estimating launch outcomes where self-reported purchase intent is unreliable.
avoidWhen: Avoid for creative or open questions where averaging produces mediocrity, with thin markets or panels lacking relevant knowledge, or where social influence cannot be prevented; use a Delphi method for expert judgement.
whyLost: Markets need real money, platforms and sizeable panels, and corporate experiments faded after the 2000s, leaving the method to economics and forecasting communities.
whereToUse: Concept and feature selection, demand forecasting, internal launch-date and adoption forecasts, pricing tier choices.
example: Instead of asking 150 panellists whether they would buy each of four smart-home concepts, a team runs a market on which concept will sell most in six months; prices pick a different winner from the intent survey, and early sales later confirm the market.
sources: Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
Wolfers, J., & Zitzewitz, E. (2004). Prediction markets. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 18
reference: Parker, J. (2022). Betting markets: Utilizing gamification and incentives to conduct market research cheaper, faster and more accurately. In Proceedings of the 2022 Quantitative User Experience Conference, pp. 332-342.

name: Predictive Forecasting of Metric Side-Effects
origin: Bob Frost, 2007
summary: Before a draft metric set is deployed, a group reviews each metric to forecast the behaviours and consequences it will provoke, and revises the set accordingly.
description: Metrics change behaviour, often in ways nobody intended. Frost presents predictive forecasting as the last of five things to get right when starting a metrics design: once a set of metrics is drafted, a group of observers works through it one metric at a time, like organised brainstorming, asking what will change once it is deployed, what new behaviours people may show, which existing good and bad behaviours may change, and what further consequences may follow. He advises including fresh eyes and a cynical thinker or two, and reports that the exercise usually produces surprising insights and important revisions; teams that skip it meet the surprises in live use. It complements his 'unintended consequences' sign of trouble and a design, use, audit and improve cycle.
steps: Draft the metric set and its intended use (targets, incentives, dashboards).
Assemble observers including people outside the team and at least one sceptic.
For each metric, ask what will change once it is deployed and reported.
Ask what new behaviours may appear and which existing good or bad behaviours may change, including gaming of numerators or denominators.
Trace further consequences of those changes for users, staff and other metrics.
Revise metrics or add balancing and guardrail metrics before implementation, and schedule a post-launch audit.
outputs: A list of forecast behavioural effects per metric and revisions or balancing metrics added to the set.
useWhen: Before introducing KPIs, OKRs, success metrics for AI models, or incentive-linked targets for teams or users.
avoidWhen: As a replacement for post-launch monitoring; forecasts miss things, so pair with periodic audit and Guardrail metric monitoring.
whyLost: It sits in performance-management literature, while product teams adopt metrics from frameworks without a consequence review.
whereToUse: Product OKRs, support team targets, engagement metrics for consumer apps, reward models and evaluation metrics for AI products.
example: Before making 'tickets closed per hour' a support target, a review group forecasts premature closures and reopen loops, so the team pairs it with reopen rate and customer effort score.
reference: Frost, B. (2007). Designing Metrics: Crafting Balanced Measures for Managing Performance. Dallas, TX: Measurement International, p. 74.

name: Predictive Human Error Analysis (PHEA)
origin: David Embrey, Human Reliability Associates, early 1990s
summary: A taxonomy-driven walkthrough of a task analysis that predicts planning, action, checking, retrieval, communication and selection errors with their consequences and recovery.
description: PHEA is a close relative of SHERPA used heavily in chemical process safety. It uses a broader error taxonomy covering planning errors as well as execution, and emphasises performance-influencing factors such as time pressure, feedback quality and procedure clarity. Each task step is examined with the taxonomy, and analysts record error description, consequences, recovery points and error-reduction measures. Its strength is the explicit link between context (performance-influencing factors) and error likelihood, which helps teams see that the same interface can be safe in a calm setting and dangerous under interruption. In UX it can be run as a structured workshop with engineers and support staff, producing a shared error forecast.
steps: Produce or reuse an HTA and agree the scenario conditions (time pressure, interruptions, user expertise).
Walk each step with the PHEA taxonomy: planning, action, checking, retrieval, transmission and selection errors.
List performance-influencing factors present for each step, such as poor feedback, similar options or fatigue.
Record consequences and recovery opportunities, noting whether the interface makes recovery visible and easy.
Rate likelihood qualitatively and prioritise steps with high consequence and low recovery.
Specify error-reduction measures and assign owners; revisit after the next design iteration.
outputs: PHEA worksheet, a list of performance-influencing factors per step, prioritised error-reduction measures.
useWhen: Procedural tasks performed under variable context (shift work, interruptions, alarms) where the team wants a structured error forecast.
avoidWhen: Exploratory discovery phases or tasks with little procedure; use field observation instead.
whyLost: It sits in process-industry consulting and HSE literature, not HCI venues. UX rarely models context factors explicitly as error drivers.
whereToUse: Operations consoles, warehouse and logistics apps, clinical documentation, customer support tools.
example: A logistics firm runs PHEA on its handheld picking app and identifies that interruptions during scanning drive retrieval errors. A persistent 'where you were' banner reduces mis-picks in pilot by a measurable margin.
sources: Embrey, Quantitative and qualitative prediction of human error in safety assessments (1992)
Kirwan, A Guide to Practical Human Reliability Assessment (1994)
reference: Kirwan, B. (1994). A Guide to Practical Human Reliability Assessment. Taylor & Francis.

name: Predictive Model Validation
origin: Stone, 1974; Kuhn & Johnson, 2013
summary: Tests whether models predicting UX outcomes such as churn, conversion or satisfaction generalise to new data, using cross-validation, holdout sets and calibration checks.
description: Predictive model validation asks whether a model's performance will hold for data it has not seen. Following Kuhn and Johnson, the analyst splits data into training and test sets, or uses k-fold or time-based cross-validation, tunes models only within training folds, and evaluates on held-out data with metrics appropriate to the task: AUC, precision and recall for imbalanced outcomes, RMSE for continuous ones, and calibration for probability estimates. Performance is compared with simple baselines such as the base rate or a logistic model. Leakage checks ensure that predictors do not contain information from after the outcome. Rigour comes from pre-specifying the validation scheme, reporting uncertainty in performance estimates, and monitoring for drift after deployment.
steps: Validation protocol for UX predictive models:
Split data: 70% training, 30% held-out test.
(2) Within training: cross-validation (10-fold CV) for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
(3) Evaluate on held-out test set only once.
(4) Report: both training CV accuracy AND held-out test accuracy. Large gap (> 5pp) = overfitting.
(5) Temporal validation: for time-series data, use time-based split (train on months 1–9, test on months 10–12).
(6) Subgroup analysis: validate performance separately for key user segments.
outputs: Cross-validated performance metrics, calibration plots, comparison against baselines, overfitting diagnostics and a documented validation report.
useWhen: Whenever a model will inform decisions: churn prediction, propensity scores, satisfaction drivers, lead scoring or segmentation models used in production.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating validation as optional for explanatory models presented as predictive; for purely descriptive analysis, focus on effect sizes and uncertainty instead.
whyLost: UX analytics often fits models on all available data and reports in-sample fit; validation discipline sits with ML engineering, not research.
whereToUse: Churn prediction, feature adoption modeling, user segmentation validation, NPS driver analysis.
example: A subscription service's churn model reports 92% accuracy in-sample; five-fold time-split cross-validation drops it to 71%, barely above the 68% base rate, so a planned intervention is put on hold.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Dangerous Statistical Mistakes in UX & Human Factors Research (carousel, n.d.)
User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Introduction to Latent Class Modeling using Latent GOLD (Statistical Innovations, 2015)
Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Kuhn M & Johnson K (2013) Applied Predictive Modeling. Springer

name: Preference Test
origin: Long-standing design practice; graded-embellishment variant by John Armitage, Business Objects, 2005
summary: Participants view two or more design versions, choose the one they prefer and explain why, with presentation order randomised to control order bias.
description: A preference test asks which of two (or several) versions a participant prefers and why. It measures stated preference, not behaviour, so it complements rather than replaces task-based testing or live split tests. Versions should differ in only one or two elements so the reasons are interpretable. Order or labelling must be randomised per participant, and counts normalised for label swaps, because first-shown and A-labelled options attract choices. The open 'why' answers are thematically analysed and often reveal novelty or familiarity effects. Armitage's graded-embellishment variant shows one design in several versions with styling added cumulatively on identical layout and data (for example bars and sparklines, then frames and shading, then gradients or traffic-light backgrounds), locating the point where decoration stops helping. A near 50/50 split signals that neither option is clearly better.
steps: Prepare versions that differ in one or two elements, or a graded series adding treatments cumulatively on identical layout and content.
Choose delivery: in person, or an online survey with static images or prototype links and instructions on a separate intro page.
Randomise which version appears first or is labelled A for each participant.
Have participants use the target device, ideally their own, and ask one either/or (or 'most effective') question followed by an open 'why?'.
Count preferences after normalising for label swaps and test the split against chance; a near 50/50 split means return to an earlier design stage.
Thematically analyse the reasons, watching for novelty and familiarity effects.
Confirm important choices with behavioural data such as task testing or a live A/B test.
outputs: Preference counts or proportions per version and a thematic summary of reasons.
useWhen: Choosing between visual treatments, icons, copy variants or levels of embellishment when behavioural differences are small or hard to measure.
avoidWhen: Avoid when versions differ in many ways, or when the decision depends on performance; use A/B Testing or Moderated Usability Testing. Beware chooser-user gaps when participants are buyers rather than end users. Showing old and new versions side by side tends to draw a stated preference for the newer one (Wallis Market and Social Research, 2021), so probe for concrete benefits or add an objective comprehension task rather than relying on preference alone.
whyLost: It survives widely, though often confused with live A/B testing and frequently run without order randomisation.
whereToUse: Dashboard styling, icon sets, marketing pages, onboarding illustrations, AI response formats.
example: A BI vendor shows customers five versions of the same sales dashboard with increasing decoration. Most prefer the middle levels and reject traffic-light backgrounds as distracting.
sources: UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Modern Awards User Experience Research Report (Wallis Market and Social Research, 2021)
reference: Cirucci, A. M. and Pruchniewska, U. M. (2022). UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies. Routledge, pp. 157-163; Armitage, J. (2015). Bringing Numbers to Life, pp. 116-119.

name: Preinventive Forms Task
origin: Finke, 1990, 1995 (creative cognition)
summary: A timed generative exercise: combine three random parts into an object first, then interpret it within an assigned category, producing ideas and creativity measures.
description: From Finke's creative cognition programme. Three of 15 simple parts (sphere, cube, cone, wire, tube, hook, wheels, handle and others) are chosen at random. Within one minute participants combine them into an interesting object without aiming at anything familiar or useful; parts may change size, position, orientation and material but not shape. Only then is a category assigned (furniture, appliances, transport, toys, tools and so on), and participants have one minute to interpret the form as something in that category and explain how it works. A single half-sphere, wire and hook form became a lawn lounger, earrings and a sled. Separating generation from interpretation counters fixation, and people find more creative uses for forms they built themselves, paralleling the generation effect. Outputs are starting points needing long development, not finished designs.
steps: Prepare a set of about 15 simple parts and a list of 6-8 product categories.
Draw three parts at random for each participant or round.
Give one minute to combine them into an interesting form, allowing changes of size, position, orientation and material but not shape.
Only after the form is fixed, assign a category at random.
Give one minute to interpret the form as an object in that category and explain how it works.
Have independent judges rate interpretations for originality and practicality, then select promising ones for development.
outputs: Preinventive forms, interpretations, and creativity ratings; a pool of unconventional concepts.
useWhen: Ideation is stuck in familiar solutions, or you want to study fixation and creative performance under controlled conditions.
avoidWhen: You need user-grounded concepts or problem framing; forms are not linked to user needs. Use it as a warm-up or divergence tool, not as evidence.
whyLost: It stayed a laboratory creativity paradigm; design practice adopted looser brainstorming and morphological methods instead.
whereToUse: Design sprint divergence, physical and hardware product ideation, workshop warm-ups, research on design fixation.
example: A smart-home team runs ten rounds of preinventive forms with the category fixed to 'kitchen device'. Two interpretations, a hook-and-tube spice dispenser and a rolling timer, seed concepts that conventional brainstorming had not produced.
reference: Finke, R. A. (1990). Creative Imagery: Discoveries and Inventions in Visualization. Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.

name: PrEmo Non-Verbal Emotion Self-Report
origin: Pieter Desmet with Hekkert and Jacobs (2000); PrEmo2 by Laurans and Desmet (2012, 2017)
summary: Respondents rate how well each of 14 animated cartoon characters, expressing distinct emotions, matches their current feeling about a product, without relying on words.
description: PrEmo is a validated non-verbal self-report instrument. An animated character expresses 14 emotions through facial expression, body movement and sound, seven positive and seven negative, based on Ortony, Clore and Collins' theory, grouped into well-being (joy, hope, sadness, fear), expectation (satisfaction, dissatisfaction), social (pride, admiration, shame, contempt) and material (fascination, attraction, boredom, disgust) domains. Respondents click each character to play its one-second animation and rate on a 5-point scale how strongly it matches their current feeling. Because it does not rely on emotion words, it works across languages and with children, and it can measure emotions evoked by separate product aspects. It can also be applied at each stage of a journey to build an emotional profile across an experience. It is a licensed instrument, and characters may still be read differently across cultures.
steps: Define the moment of measurement and expose the participant to the product, feature or journey stage.
Present the 14 animated characters in the web tool.
Have the participant play each one-second animation and rate how well it matches their current feeling on a 5-point scale.
Repeat at each product aspect or journey stage, keeping timing consistent.
Summarise ratings per emotion and per domain, and compare products, features or stages.
Follow up high-rated emotions in interview to learn their causes.
outputs: Emotion profiles across 14 emotions per product, feature or journey stage, and comparisons between them.
useWhen: You need a quick, language-independent measure of the specific emotions a product or stage evokes, including with children or in multilingual studies.
avoidWhen: You need continuous or unconscious measures, or only overall valence and arousal; use physiology or the Self-Assessment Manikin instead. Licensing may be a barrier.
whyLost: It is well known in design-and-emotion research but licensed and narrower than the generic satisfaction scales UX teams default to.
whereToUse: Consumer products and packaging, automotive interiors, games, children's products and emotional journey mapping.
example: A car-sharing service asks 50 users to rate PrEmo characters at booking, unlocking and returning the car. Contempt and dissatisfaction peak at return, focusing redesign on the parking confirmation step.
reference: Laurans, G. F. G., & Desmet, P. M. A. (2017). Developing 14 animated characters for non-verbal self-report of categorical emotions. Journal of Design Research, 15(3/4), 214-233.

name: Prerequisite Training to Criterion Before Usability Testing
origin: Jeffrey Rubin and Dana Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing (2nd ed., 2008)
summary: Train participants to a predefined, tested proficiency before a usability test so the test can examine ease of use for experienced users or advanced features.
description: Most usability tests observe novices and so measure ease of learning. Prerequisite training deliberately moves participants along the learning curve to a pre-established criterion first. Rubin and Chisnell give three uses: guaranteeing domain skills the product assumes (photography skill for a retouching tool), simulating users with a week or a month of use when no such users exist yet, and reaching advanced features or skipping basics already validated. The rigour comes from the criterion test: a defined skill set, a measuring instrument with real examples, and training repeated on failed items until everyone meets the same level, which equalises proficiency across participants and makes their errors attributable to the design rather than to unfamiliarity. Observing the training itself also shows how people learn the product.
steps: Define the knowledge and skills of the target experience level, for example a user one week into using the product.
Build a criterion test or 'check yourself' quiz using realistic examples that measures that level.
Build a training package (self-paced, instructor-led or online); two to three hours can often reach a week-old level.
Give the criterion test, train only on the failed items and retest until each participant meets the criterion.
For very simple products, add a forgetting gap of a few days to a week between training and test.
Run the usability test with harder, more advanced tasks than you would give novices.
If others deliver the training, rely on the criterion test for consistency, and optionally observe the training informally to learn how people learn.
outputs: Performance and problem data from participants of known, equalised proficiency; evidence on ease of use for experienced users and on advanced features; notes on how people learn the product.
useWhen: Products that assume prior expertise, pre-launch tests that need experienced users who do not yet exist, and studies of advanced or power-user features.
avoidWhen: Avoid when first-use learnability is the question, or when time and budget cannot cover what can be a day per participant. If real experienced users can be recruited, test them instead; for learning over time use a learnability (experience curve) study.
whyLost: It adds cost and time per participant and raises a bias objection (the trainer shapes behaviour), so most teams test novices or recruit existing users instead.
whereToUse: Professional and enterprise tools, clinical systems, creative software, developer platforms and new versions of complex SaaS products before an installed base exists.
example: Before testing a new automation builder in a CRM, participants complete a 90-minute course on records and workflows and must score 90% on a criterion quiz. The test then concentrates on branching logic, where trained users still make the same error, showing a design fault rather than inexperience.
reference: Rubin, J. and Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of Usability Testing: How to Plan, Design, and Conduct Effective Tests (2nd ed.). Indianapolis, IN: Wiley, pp. 187-192.

name: Prescribe Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 5: Prescribe, from evidence to design action
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 5 of the forward-thinking loop: translate hazard ratios, SHAP drivers and quotes into mechanism-linked fixes placed on an effort × impact grid, each with a decision bar.
description: Prescribing turns statistical drivers and qualitative mechanisms into actionable fixes. The researcher reviews top quant drivers (SNR, mistake rate, retries), cross-checks them with qual evidence, drafts prescriptions in a 'because → therefore' structure, places each on an effort × impact grid and attaches decision bars. An evidence ⇒ prescription table records problem area, quant driver, qual mechanism, design prescription, effort and impact. QCA sufficiency results are used to bundle fixes: if Low SNR * High Mistakes is sufficient for failure, labelling and SNR uplift ship together. Mechanism memos and one quote per fix keep the mechanism salient in design review. Rigour comes from refusing insights without fixes, quantifying effort, and binding each fix to a threshold such as tree success ≥ 85%, OTP success ≥ 80% within 3 attempts, TLX frustration ≤ 40/100 and end-to-end completion ≥ 60%.
steps: Review the top quantitative drivers from Prove and Forecast (e.g. HR per mistake = 1.31, first-click 74% vs 49%, OTP 65% → 80% predicts +5 points).
Cross-check each driver with qualitative evidence to name its mechanism (e.g. 'I looked under Notifications, not Markets').
Draft prescriptions in 'because → therefore' form and record them in an evidence ⇒ prescription table with effort and impact ratings.
Place fixes on an effort × impact grid: low effort/high impact now, high effort/high impact on the roadmap, low/low opportunistic, high effort/low impact deferred.
Bundle fixes that QCA shows are jointly sufficient (do not ship labelling without SNR uplift if Low SNR * High Mistakes drives failure).
Attach a decision bar to each prescription, e.g. first-click ≥ 75%, tree direct ≥ 85%, HR ≤ 0.80, OTP success ≥ 80%, TLX frustration ≤ 40/100.
Attach one representative quote per fix for design review.
outputs: An evidence ⇒ prescription table, an effort × impact grid, mechanism memos and per-fix decision bars.
useWhen: After evidence exists and a team needs a prioritised, defensible set of changes.
avoidWhen: When evidence is thin or mechanisms are unknown; return to Diagnose rather than prescribing from opinion.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; most research reports stop at insights without bound fixes or thresholds.
whereToUse: Design reviews, roadmap planning, research readouts for product leadership.
example: The trading app team moves Alerts to top nav (low effort, high impact), renames to 'Price Alerts', adds a rule wizard with examples (medium effort, high impact) and extends the OTP window with reassurance copy (low effort, medium impact).
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 5.

name: Presentation models (PM/PIM/PMR)
aka: Contractual utility refinement of UI designs
origin: Judy Bowen and Steve Reeves, University of Waikato (2006 onwards)
summary: Describe each screen or mode as widget triples, link screens in a navigation state model, map behaviours to specified functions, and check for gaps, deadlocks and refinement violations.
description: Presentation models give informal design artefacts such as prototypes and storyboards a formal meaning without replacing them. Each window, dialogue or mode becomes a presentation model listing every widget as a triple of name, category and behaviours; sensors, speech and gestures count as widgets. Behaviours are split into interactive behaviours (navigation and presentation) and system behaviours (functionality). A presentation interaction model is a state machine with one state per window or mode, used to check reachability, deadlocks and navigation length. A presentation model relation maps system behaviours to operations in a formal specification, exposing interface functions the specification lacks and specified functions with no widget. Alternative designs are compared by refinement: system behaviours must be equal and interactive behaviours of the new design must include the old.
steps: Collect the design artefacts: prototypes, storyboards and scenarios.
Write one presentation model per window, dialogue or mode, with a triple per widget (name, category, behaviours).
Classify each behaviour as interactive (navigation, presentation) or system (functionality).
Build the presentation interaction model with one state per presentation model; check reachability, deadlocks and navigation sequence length.
Build the presentation model relation mapping each system behaviour to a specified operation; flag unmapped behaviours and specified operations with no widget.
Compare alternative or restricted designs for refinement: equal system behaviours, and a superset of interactive behaviours.
Optionally combine the models into one formal model and check safety properties with a model checker.
outputs: A widget and behaviour inventory per screen or mode, a navigation state model, a behaviour-to-function map, and lists of gaps, deadlocks and refinement violations.
useWhen: Checking that a UI design and a functional specification agree, or that a redesign preserves all functionality, in safety-critical or regulated software.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to know whether the design is usable; it does not model the user, so pair it with usability testing. Hand-built models can be incomplete.
whyLost: It needs formal specification skills and fits regulated engineering processes, so it stays in formal methods research.
whereToUse: Medical and industrial control software, regulated fintech systems, design system audits and large redesigns that must preserve functionality.
example: A plant control redesign turns pump sliders into read-only displays in abnormal mode. The behaviour-to-function map shows the new screen triggers automation the specification never defined, so the specification is extended before build.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Bowen, J. & Reeves, S. (2008). Formal models for user interface design artefacts. Innovations in Systems and Software Engineering 4(2), 125-141; Bowen, J. & Reeves, S. (2017). Combining models for interactive system modelling. In Weyers, B. et al. (eds) The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction. Springer, pp. 161-182.

name: Presentation-invariance (framing robustness) check
donor: Medical decision making; behavioural decision research
origin: McNeil, Pauker, Sox and Tversky (1982); Tversky and Kahneman (1986)
summary: Present the same decision information in several equivalent formats to random groups; a preference that holds across formats is firm, while a reversal shows the format is deciding.
description: Rational choice assumes description invariance: equivalent descriptions should yield the same choice. They often do not. McNeil and colleagues gave patients, radiologists and students identical lung-cancer outcomes framed as survival or mortality; radiation was chosen by 42% versus 25% across frames, and physicians were no less affected. Other equivalent formats also flip preferences: complementary percentages (10% versus 5% unemployment against 90% versus 95% employment), transparent versus coalesced layouts (a coalesced layout led 58% to a dominated option), and individual versus group perspective. The check systematically lists the equivalent formats for a decision screen, randomises participants to them and compares choice shares. Robust preferences can be reported as user preferences; format-dependent ones are design problems, since the interface, not the user, is determining the choice.
steps: List the equivalent formats for the decision: gain or loss frame, complementary percentages, aggregated or segregated layout, individual or group perspective, named or unnamed options.
Randomly assign participants to formats, counterbalancing order if several formats are given within person.
Measure choice shares for each format.
Test differences and flag decisions whose majority choice flips between formats.
Report preferences only where they are stable, and treat flips as a design problem (for example showing both frames).
outputs: Choice shares by format and a list of decisions that are robust or format-dependent.
useWhen: Designing consent, pricing, risk communication, plan comparison or AI recommendation screens where wording or layout could steer choices.
avoidWhen: When the goal is deliberately to persuade toward a known-good option and the frame choice is already ethically justified; then test outcomes directly with an A/B test.
whyLost: It lives in medical decision-making and behavioural economics; UX tests copy variants for conversion rather than for robustness of user preference.
whereToUse: Health risk communication, financial product disclosures, privacy consent, SLA and uptime displays, insurance and plan comparison pages.
example: A hosting company shows two plans' uptime as '99.5% available' or '0.5% downtime'. The cheaper plan wins only in the downtime frame, so the comparison page shows both figures to avoid the format deciding for users.
reference: McNeil, B. J., Pauker, S. G., Sox, H. C. and Tversky, A. (1982). On the elicitation of preferences for alternative therapies. New England Journal of Medicine, 306(21), 1259-1262.

name: Prestructured Case
donor: Qualitative evaluation and multi-site policy research
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 4, section H, from the Louis and Miles (1990) study of reform in six urban high schools.
summary: Writing the full outline of the final case report, including its data displays, before any data are collected, then filling it in over successive field visits.
description: When time is short, research questions are well specified and there is an explicit conceptual framework and sampling plan, the researcher can design the end product first. The prestructured case is a detailed outline of the case report, with planned matrices and other displays and the narrative sections that accompany them, built before fieldwork. It acts as a shell for the data to come, and in the book's words lets data collection be 'driven by the anticipated product'. The team also plans within-case sampling of key actors, events and processes, and sequences which research questions to focus on in each visit. After each visit raw notes are coded directly, without full write-ups, and entered straight into the displays, with analytic text drafted alongside; missing or unclear cells become targets for the next visit. The final case is ready shortly after the last visit. The approach trades openness for speed and cross-case comparability. In UX it suits rapid, repeated studies where the deliverable is known in advance, such as quarterly account health research or a multi-market localisation study.
steps: Fix the research questions, conceptual framework and sample of cases.
Draft the report outline section by section, including empty matrices and charts each section will need.
Plan which roles, events and processes must be sampled in each case to fill the displays.
Sequence the questions across visits or sessions.
After each round, code notes directly and enter data into the displays, drafting analytic text as you go.
Treat empty or ambiguous cells as the agenda for the next round; finalise soon after the last session.
outputs: A comparably structured case report for each case, delivered quickly after fieldwork.
useWhen: Questions and framework are clear, timelines are tight, and several cases must be comparable.
avoidWhen: The study is exploratory, the framework is uncertain, or you risk seeing only what the outline expects.
whyLost: UX favours either open-ended discovery or templated usability reports; designing the report shell first for qualitative case work is not commonly taught.
whereToUse: Repeated customer account reviews, multi-country studies, programme evaluations, research ops templates.
example: A team studying how eight enterprise customers roll out a new admin console writes a 15-page outline first: context, rollout chronology, a role-by-reaction matrix, a problems-and-coping table, results. Each two-day site visit fills specific cells; after the last visit each case report is finished within a week and directly comparable.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Price elasticity revenue-curve test
aka: Price elasticity from a log-log regression with the optimal markup
origin: Standard microeconomic pricing; presented for start-ups by Croll and Yoskovitz, 2013
summary: Expose buyers to several real prices, record purchases at each, and estimate elasticity and the revenue or profit peak, rather than asking hypothetical willingness-to-pay questions.
description: Survey pricing methods ask what people would pay; this method observes what they do. Price points are shown to cohorts, segments, stores or periods (for example via discount codes or randomised splits), buyers are counted, and revenue is charted against price to find its peak; one recommendation is to price about 10 percent below the peak to encourage growth. Where price has varied over time or across stores, a regression of log sales on log price gives elasticity directly: the slope is the percentage change in sales for a 1 percent price change. With constant elasticity below -1 and unit cost c, the profit-maximising price is c times elasticity divided by (1 + elasticity). Rigour comes from randomised exposure where possible, enough buyers per price, and caution about confounded observational price variation.
steps: Choose four to six price points spanning a plausible range.
Randomly assign cohorts, segments or periods to each price, ideally via randomised checkout splits or unique codes.
Record buyers and units per price over a fixed period long enough to cover weekly cycles.
Compute revenue (and margin, if unit cost is known) per price and chart the curve.
Optionally fit log sales on log price to estimate elasticity; with elasticity below -1, compute the optimal price as cost x elasticity / (1 + elasticity).
Predict sales and profit at current and candidate prices and judge whether the gain justifies a change.
Set the price, often slightly below the revenue peak, and monitor for leakage and perception effects.
outputs: A revenue or profit curve by price, an elasticity estimate, predicted sales at candidate prices, and a recommended price.
useWhen: Setting or changing price for a live product with enough traffic to observe purchases at several prices.
avoidWhen: Avoid when tests could leak and anger customers, when traffic is too low, or before launch; use Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger surveys for early ranges. Very low prices can signal low quality.
whyLost: Live price tests sit with growth, pricing and finance teams rather than UX research, and fairness concerns limit their use.
whereToUse: SaaS plans, e-commerce, marketplaces, in-app purchases, subscription renewals.
example: A design-tool start-up tests four monthly prices through randomised checkout splits; revenue peaks at $12, so it launches at $11 and monitors churn by cohort.
sources: Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
reference: Croll, A., & Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics: Use Data to Build a Better Startup Faster. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Prior and posterior predictive checks
origin: Box (1980); Rubin (1984); Gelman, Meng and Stern (1996); Gabry et al. (2019)
summary: Simulates data from a model's priors before fitting, and from its posterior after fitting, to see whether its assumptions imply plausible outcomes and where it misdescribes the data.
description: Prior predictive simulation draws parameter values from the priors alone and pushes them through the model to produce simulated outcomes, showing in the units of the outcome what harmless-looking priors imply. McElreath's example: an intercept prior of Normal(178, 100) gave 4% of simulated people negative height. Flat priors on logit scales pile probability at 0 and 1. Priors are then tightened using pre-data knowledge only. Posterior predictive checks run after fitting: for every posterior draw a data set of the same size is simulated, carrying full parameter uncertainty, and the simulations are compared with the real data. First compare on the summary the model uses, as a software check; then on features it does not use, chosen with domain knowledge, such as runs, zero counts or per-participant patterns. The aim is to find where the model fails and whether that matters, not to test truth.
steps: Write the full model with a prior for every parameter, using knowledge of ranges, signs and theory but never the sample itself.
Draw 100 to 10,000 values from the priors, simulate outcomes or regression lines, and plot them against known limits (no negative task times, conversion between 0 and 1).

Reshape priors that allow absurd outcomes (for example standardise variables and use Normal(0, 1) slopes, or log-normal priors for positive effects) and repeat; for link functions check implied probabilities.
Fit the model and, for each posterior draw, simulate a data set of the same size as the observed one.
Compare simulated and observed data on the statistic the model fits, then on features it does not use, such as longest run, share of zeros or per-participant spread.
Judge whether any misfit matters for the decision, revise the model where it does, and report the checks and prior sensitivity.
outputs: Plots of prior-implied and posterior-predicted outcomes against observed data, documented priors, and a list of data features the model misses.
useWhen: Any Bayesian model of UX data, particularly multilevel, logistic or count models and small samples where priors matter.
avoidWhen: Not a substitute for out-of-sample validation of predictive accuracy (use cross-validation). Choosing priors after looking at the data turns the prior check into a form of p-hacking.
whyLost: These checks are routine in modern Bayesian workflow but UX adoption of Bayesian methods has focused on headline posteriors, not model criticism.
whereToUse: Bayesian A/B tests, task-time and rating models, small-sample benchmarks, forecasting models of adoption or churn.
example: Before modelling conversion with a logistic regression, a team simulates from Normal(0, 10) priors and sees most implied conversion rates near 0% or 100%; switching to Normal(0, 1.5) gives plausible spread. After fitting, posterior predictions underpredict the share of zero-purchase users, prompting a zero-inflated model.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
reference: McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan (2nd ed.). CRC Press, pp. 62-68 and 82-97.

name: Prior elicitation from qualitative research
origin: Structured expert elicitation (O'Hagan et al., Uncertain Judgements, 2006; SHELF framework by Oakley and O'Hagan); applied to linking qualitative UX evidence to quantitative priors in The Inquiry Series
summary: Converts evidence and expert judgement from qualitative research into explicit probability distributions that serve as priors for subsequent quantitative tests.
description: Qualitative research often produces strong beliefs about effects, for example that a trust badge will matter for first-time users, but these beliefs are lost when the A/B test starts from zero. Structured prior elicitation captures them as explicit distributions. Following frameworks such as SHELF, experts who know the qualitative evidence give quantiles (for example median, 25th and 75th percentiles) for the quantity of interest, individually and then through facilitated discussion, avoiding anchoring and overconfidence. A distribution, such as a Beta for a rate or a Normal for a log-odds effect, is fitted to the agreed quantiles. Rigour comes from documenting the evidence base, training elicitors in calibration, using the roulette or quantile method, and running sensitivity analyses so that the prior informs but does not dominate.
steps: Define the quantity precisely, such as the conversion rate of the control or the relative uplift from the trust badge among first-time users.
Compile an evidence dossier from qualitative studies, past experiments and benchmarks, and share it with 3 to 6 elicitors.
Brief elicitors on biases (anchoring, overconfidence) with a short calibration exercise on known quantities.
Elicit individual judgements privately using quantiles (lower plausible, 25th, median, 75th, upper plausible) or the roulette method.
Hold a facilitated discussion to reach a consensus distribution, or pool individual distributions mathematically, and fit a parametric distribution to the result.
Translate into prior strength (for example a Beta prior equivalent to 50 observations), pre-register it, and plan a sensitivity analysis with a weaker prior.
outputs: An evidence dossier, individual and consensus elicited distributions, a fitted prior with stated effective sample size, and a sensitivity plan.
useWhen: Low-traffic experiments where prior knowledge is substantial; linking qualitative and quantitative research programmes; decisions requiring explicit expert judgement.
avoidWhen: Little relevant prior evidence exists, stakeholders would distrust informative priors, or the experiment has enough data that priors will not matter; use weakly informative priors instead.
whyLost: Structured elicitation is established in decision analysis, health economics and risk assessment, but UX treats qualitative and quantitative research as separate tracks and rarely formalises beliefs.
whereToUse: Fintech and health experiments with limited traffic, B2B products, feature bets in early markets, AI feature evaluations.
example: Before testing a trust badge on a fintech sign-up page, researchers who had run 20 interviews elicited a median uplift of 4% (50% interval 1% to 8%). Encoded as a prior, it allowed a decision after 3,000 sign-ups instead of 9,000, with a sensitivity check showing the conclusion held under a weak prior.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design
reference: O'Hagan, A., Buck, C. E., Daneshkhah, A., Eiser, J. R., Garthwaite, P. H., Jenkinson, D. J., Oakley, J. E., & Rakow, T. (2006). Uncertain Judgements: Eliciting Experts' Probabilities. Wiley.

name: Prior-Precision Sensitivity Sweep with Tipping-Point Prior Weight
aka: Equivalent prior sample size tipping point
origin: Presented by Simon Jackman, 2009, as a worked example combining a Florida 2000 poll with an election-history prior
summary: Keeps an informative prior's mean fixed while scaling its precision, plots how the posterior and decision change, and reports the prior weight in equivalent respondents needed to reverse the conclusion.
description: An informative prior built from past data (earlier releases, benchmarks, previous studies) can dominate a small new study. Rather than argue about whether to use it, this analysis sweeps its weight. A conjugate prior such as Beta(a, b) is rewritten as Beta(a/lambda, b/lambda): the prior mean is unchanged while its effective sample size, (a + b)/lambda, shrinks as lambda grows. Because the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data estimate, sweeping lambda from very small (prior dominates) to very large (data dominate) traces how inference moves between them. The decision quantity, for example the probability that a conversion rate exceeds a target, is plotted against lambda, and the point where it crosses the decision threshold is translated into an equivalent number of observations. In Jackman's example only a prior worth about 2,700 respondents would have reversed the poll's call, a concrete number decision-makers can judge.
steps: Build an informative prior from relevant past data and express it as a conjugate density with a clear effective sample size.
Introduce a precision multiplier that keeps the prior mean fixed while changing its effective sample size.
Combine the prior with the current data across a wide grid of multiplier values (for example on a log scale from 0.001 to 1000).
Plot the posterior mean, 95% interval and the posterior probability of the decision-relevant event against the multiplier.
Find where the decision probability crosses the decision threshold and convert that multiplier into an equivalent number of observations.
Judge whether that much prior weight is plausible given how exchangeable past and present data are, and report the sweep alongside the main result; vary the prior mean separately if it is contested.
outputs: A sensitivity plot of posterior summaries against prior weight and the tipping-point prior weight expressed as an equivalent sample size.
useWhen: A Bayesian analysis uses an informative prior from earlier releases, benchmarks or other markets, and stakeholders need to see how much the conclusion depends on it.
avoidWhen: The prior's location itself is disputed (the sweep tests precision, not mean; run alternative priors); non-conjugate models where reweighting is not straightforward (use power priors or full refits); the data alone are decisive.
whyLost: Bayesian UX work usually reports one prior or a weakly informative default; systematic prior sensitivity with a tipping point is described in textbooks but rarely operationalised.
whereToUse: Small-sample usability benchmarks using historical priors, A/B tests with priors from past experiments, rolling out a change to a new market using evidence from another, health and fintech decisions with regulatory scrutiny.
example: A team tests a redesigned sign-up flow with 80 users, using a prior from 12 earlier flow tests worth 400 users that puts completion around 70%. The sweep shows the data alone give a 91% probability the new flow beats the 75% target, and only a prior weight above 650 users would drop it below 80%, so the launch proceeds.
sources: Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
reference: Jackman, S. (2009). Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons.

name: Probability inflation ratio
donor: Judgement and decision-making research (calibration and overconfidence)
origin: Calibration research by Lichtenstein, Fischhoff and Phillips (1982) and the planning fallacy (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979); applied to feature adoption forecasts in The Inquiry Series
summary: Quantifies how much stakeholders or users overestimate the probability of a behaviour by dividing predicted probability by observed frequency.
description: Teams routinely overestimate how often users will adopt features, complete flows or use advanced functions, through availability, representativeness and optimism biases. The probability inflation ratio makes the bias measurable: collect explicit probability forecasts before data exists, then divide the forecast by the observed rate. A ratio of 1.0 is perfectly calibrated; 3.0 means the event was predicted three times as often as it happened. Tracked across forecasts and forecasters, it shows systematic bias by person, feature type or user segment, and can be used to discount future estimates. Rigour comes from recording forecasts in writing in advance, defining the behaviour and denominator precisely, and pairing the ratio with a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score.
steps: Define the behaviours to forecast with an exact numerator, denominator and time window, for example 'share of active health workers who use the referral feature at least once in 30 days'.
Before launch or before data is visible, collect written probability forecasts from each stakeholder or participant, ideally a central estimate plus an 80% interval.
After the window closes, compute the observed rate from logs and the inflation ratio as forecast divided by observed for each forecaster and behaviour.
Aggregate ratios using the geometric mean (ratios are multiplicative) and compute Brier scores to separate calibration from discrimination.
Break results down by forecaster role and behaviour type (basic versus advanced features, new versus habitual behaviours) to find systematic inflation patterns.
Feed back results to forecasters and apply the historical ratio as a correction factor in roadmap business cases, re-estimating every 2 to 4 forecasting cycles.
outputs: Inflation ratios and Brier scores per forecaster and behaviour type, a calibration chart, and a correction factor for future adoption forecasts.
useWhen: Roadmaps rely on adoption assumptions; stakeholders consistently expect higher use of advanced features; you want to show the gap between belief and behaviour with a single defensible number.
avoidWhen: Behaviours cannot be measured reliably in logs, or the number of forecasts is too small to distinguish bias from noise (fewer than about 10 forecast-outcome pairs); use a qualitative prediction gap discussion instead.
whyLost: Calibration scoring is routine in forecasting research and intelligence analysis but product teams rarely record forecasts in advance, so there is nothing to score.
whereToUse: Feature prioritisation, business cases, AI feature adoption planning, public-sector digital rollouts, health programme design.
example: District managers forecast that 60% of community health workers would use an advanced symptom checker monthly; observed use was 12%, an inflation ratio of 5.0. Across 14 features, advanced features averaged 3.8 and basic features 1.3, which led the programme to discount advanced-feature business cases.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 21 — Heuristics, Biases & the Architecture of Judgment
reference: Lichtenstein, S., Fischhoff, B., & Phillips, L. D. (1982). Calibration of probabilities: The state of the art to 1980. In Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky (Eds.), Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Cambridge University Press.

name: Probability Sampling
origin: Standard survey-sampling practice; presented by Gratton and Jones (2010) as the four main quantitative sampling techniques: random, stratified random, cluster and systematic.
summary: Choosing survey or study participants by a chance process from a defined population so that results can be generalised with a known margin of error.
description: Probability sampling gives every member of a defined population a known, non-zero chance of selection. Gratton and Jones set out four variants. Simple random sampling gives everyone an equal chance, using a draw, a random number table or software. Stratified random sampling divides the population into subgroups (for example by age or sex) and draws randomly within each, so that each subgroup is properly represented. Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups (such as teams or sites) and studies everyone in them. Systematic sampling takes every kth case from a list or a stream of people, which works only when the list order is not itself patterned. The book stresses that the first step is defining the population, that sample size, not the percentage of the population, drives precision, and that every subgroup to be compared needs enough cases. For UX researchers, most participant pools are convenience or panel samples, so claims such as '40% of users want X' are often stated with no basis for generalisation. Drawing an intercept or email sample at random from the real user base, stratified by plan or platform, is cheap with product data and makes survey percentages defensible.
steps: Define the population precisely (for example all accounts active in the last 90 days) and obtain a sampling frame such as a user list.
Decide which subgroups must be compared and whether to stratify on them (plan tier, platform, region).
Choose the variant: simple random, stratified random, cluster (random selection of teams, sites or organisations) or systematic every kth case.
Set the target achieved sample size from the precision you need overall and within each subgroup, allowing for expected non-response.

For stratified designs, choose proportional or optimal (Neyman) allocation across strata; when the sample is a sizeable fraction of a small population (roughly 5% or more), apply the finite-population correction to standard errors and sample-size calculations.
Draw the sample with software or a random number generator and log the seed and frame date.
Field the study, then compare the achieved sample against the frame to check representativeness before generalising.
outputs: A documented, randomly drawn sample list, stratum allocations and the margins of error that apply to the results.
useWhen: You want to report proportions or averages for a user population (attitudinal surveys, satisfaction tracking, feature-demand estimates) and you have a list or stream of users to draw from.
avoidWhen: The aim is qualitative depth rather than generalisation, or no sampling frame exists; purposive or theoretical selection then fits better.
whyLost: UX research leans on small qualitative samples, recruitment panels and in-product prompts shown to whoever passes by, so formal sampling design is rarely taught in UX courses and is left to market research or data science teams.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction and NPS surveys, feature-prioritisation surveys, B2B studies sampling organisations as clusters, intercept surveys on high-traffic pages.
example: A SaaS team wants to know how many admins would use a new audit-log feature. Rather than surveying the most engaged forum users, they export all 12,000 admin accounts, stratify by plan tier, randomly draw 400 per tier and email the survey, so the tier estimates come with known margins of error.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Newbold, P., Carlson, W. L. & Thorne, B. M., Statistics for Business and Economics, 10th ed. (2022)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Problem Discovery Sample Size Model (1 − (1 − p)^n)
origin: Virzi (1992), Nielsen & Landauer (1993); small-sample p adjustment by Lewis (2001)
summary: Plans how many users a formative test needs to find problems of a given frequency, and checks how many remain unseen.
description: The famous "five users find 85% of problems" claim is a special case of the cumulative binomial model: the chance of seeing a problem at least once in n users is 1 − (1 − p)^n, where p is how often that problem affects users.
