Five users find 85% of problems only if the average p is about 0.31. Lewis showed that p estimated from a small test is inflated and corrected it by averaging a Good-Turing adjustment with a normalisation step. Used properly, the model turns sample size into a deliberate choice: "we want a 90% chance of seeing any problem that affects at least 15% of users", which needs 15 people. It also estimates how many problems the study probably missed.
steps: Decide the smallest problem frequency p you care about and the discovery probability you want (for example p = 0.15 at 90%).
Solve n = ln(1 − goal) / ln(1 − p) and round up.
Run the test and record a participant-by-problem 0/1 matrix.
Estimate p from the matrix and apply Lewis's adjustment (average of Good-Turing and normalisation) to deflate it.
Compute the expected proportion of problems found and the likely number still undiscovered; decide whether to run more sessions.
outputs: A justified formative sample size and an estimate of undiscovered problems.
useWhen: Planning iterative formative tests and defending the number of sessions to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Summative measurement, where sample size depends on precision and power instead.
whyLost: The "five users" slogan survived while the model behind it, and its conditions, was forgotten. Teams either test five by habit or dismiss small tests altogether.
whereToUse: Agile research sprints, safety-critical formative evaluation, budgeting research.
example: A medical device team wants a 95% chance of seeing any use problem affecting at least 10% of users, which requires 29 participants rather than five.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces: Exploration and Evaluation (Ó Broin, 2011)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Lewis, J. R. (2001). Evaluation of procedures for adjusting problem-discovery rates estimated from small samples. IJHCI 13(4).

name: Problem Discovery, Selection and Solution Validation Cycle
aka: Problem discovery, problem selection and solution validation (iterative elimination tournament)
origin: Will Larson (2019), An Elegant Puzzle, from his blog Irrational Exuberance
summary: A three-phase planning round in which a team discovers candidate problems, selects a portfolio and validates its chosen solution cheaply before building.
description: Larson frames product planning, for an engineering lead covering for a missing product manager, as an iterative elimination tournament: each round has problem discovery, problem selection and solution validation, and doing all three well earns another round with more scope. Discovery populates the problem space from users' pain (broad surveys plus deep interviews across segments), users' purpose, benchmarks against similar and very different companies, cohorts hidden in top-level distributions, competitive advantages and moats, and compounding leverage. Selection narrows to a portfolio by asking what is needed to survive this round and the next, what would win, how the choice changes over six-month, two-year and five-year horizons, industry trends, rough return on investment and learning experiments. Validation de-risks the approach: write the customer launch letter, find prior art through trusted people, recruit reference users, run cheap experiments and test switching costs.
steps: Discovery: list candidate problems from users' pain (surveys plus interviews across segments), users' purpose, benchmarks, hidden cohorts, competitive advantages, moats and compounding leverage.

Selection: filter to a problem portfolio by survival this round and next, what would win a round, six-month, two-year and five-year horizons, industry trends, rough return on investment and experiments that ease future selection.
Validation: write the customer launch letter for the chosen solution.
Find prior art through people you trust rather than conference talks.
Recruit reference users willing to go first; if none can be found, doubt the project.
Run the cheapest experiment that could invalidate the approach, including whether users would pay the switching cost.
Repeat the round with the larger scope earned.
outputs: A selected problem portfolio and a validated solution approach with reference users.
useWhen: Use it when a team, especially a platform or infrastructure team without a product manager, must choose what to work on next and de-risk it.
avoidWhen: It is a planning frame, not a research method; the discovery phase needs real Surveys, Interviews and Customer problem interviews. For mapping problems to outcomes in detail, an Opportunity Solution Tree is more structured.
whyLost: It is well known in engineering management circles, while product teams use similar cycles under names such as continuous discovery and dual-track agile.
whereToUse: Platform and infrastructure teams, internal tools, developer products and engineering-led start-ups.
example: A developer-platform team surveys internal users and interviews eight teams, selects deployment speed as its problem, writes the launch letter, and recruits two reference teams to pilot a new pipeline before committing a quarter to it.
reference: Larson, W. (2019). An Elegant Puzzle: Systems of Engineering Management. San Francisco: Stripe Press, section 3.2.

name: Problem Framing and Idea-Working Games (Think Bigger)
origin: Sheena Iyengar, Think Bigger course, Columbia Business School, about 2012-2022; Innovation Marketplace with Carl Blaine Horton
summary: Linked exercises for choosing and structuring a problem: laddering it to a sweet spot, pitching it to test passion and support, and breaking it into five subproblems.
description: Iyengar argues that choosing the problem is the step people spend least time on and should spend most. Step Analysis rewrites a problem as an open 'how' question with no embedded solution, places it mid-chart and restates it two levels wider and two narrower to find where motivation and feasibility peak; in groups each person charts alone before pooling. The Passion Test has the person describe the problem to around 25 people and judge whether their excitement grows; the classroom Innovation Marketplace scales this to rotating trios, before-and-after passion ratings (1-7), revised statements and play-money investments in others' problems (she reports about 35 per cent revise their pitch). Subproblem breakdown lists every subproblem question, groups and cuts repeatedly to about five, checks with experts, users and outsiders, parks solutions in a 'sparking lot', and applies the Eighty Percent Test: would solving all of them solve at least 80 per cent of the problem?
steps: Write the problem in under three sentences, then as an open 'how' question without an embedded solution, moving numeric targets to implementation.

Step analysis: place it mid-chart, restate it two levels wider and two narrower, and choose the tier where motivation is highest and the problem still solvable; in groups chart individually, then pool.
Passion test: pitch the problem in under a minute to many people (rotating trios in a group), rating passion 1-7 before and after and recording revisions.
In a group marketplace, have each person invest three unequal play-money amounts in others' problems and tally support.
Subproblem breakdown: list every subproblem question, then group and cut repeatedly, from memory, until about five remain.
Check the breakdown with experts, users and outsiders, parking solution ideas in a sparking lot, and revise at least once.
Apply the Eighty Percent Test and carry the subproblems forward as rows of a Choice Map.
outputs: A scoped open problem question, passion ratings and peer investment tallies, and three to five subproblems with a sparking lot of parked ideas.
useWhen: Starting an innovation project or discovery phase where the team has not agreed what problem it is solving or how to break it down.
avoidWhen: Passion and peer investment measure the team's energy, not users' need; establish need with Interviews or Jobs-to-be-Done Research. The reported outcome figures are classroom tallies without published method. For causal problem diagnosis use Root Cause Analysis and the 5 Whys or Ishikawa (Fishbone) Diagram; for structuring opportunities against outcomes use Opportunity Solution Tree.
whyLost: Lives in Iyengar's business-school teaching; design teams use 'why-how laddering' and HMW framing but rarely the passion test, marketplace or 80 per cent check.
whereToUse: Innovation programmes, corporate retreats, early product discovery, social enterprise and public-sector challenges.
example: A travel startup steps 'help blind people plan holidays' down to five subproblems (navigation, accessible hotels and activities, safety, cost, location), checks them with blind travellers, and confirms solving them would cover most of the problem.
reference: Iyengar, S. (2023) Think Bigger: How to Innovate. New York: Columbia University Press, pp. 76-107.

name: Problem Identification Picture Cards (PIPC)
origin: Wolmet Barendregt; Barendregt, Bekker and Baauw (2008)
summary: Children drop emotion picture cards into a box whenever they feel that emotion while using a product, giving non-verbal, time-located reports of problems and fun.
description: Young children rarely sustain think-aloud. PIPC gives them a non-verbal channel: a set of picture cards, each showing an emotion that maps to a category of usability problem or fun issue, and a box. While playing, the child places a card in the box each time they experience the shown emotion. Card placements, aligned with the session recording, locate both problems and positive moments in time and classify them. In a study with children aged five and six, children explicitly expressed more problems with the cards than in think-aloud sessions. Bekker notes that each adaptation for children can add its own challenges, so the cards must be explained carefully and practised before tasks begin.
steps: Prepare picture cards whose emotions map to problem and fun categories, and a box.
Explain each card to the child and practise placing cards on a warm-up activity.
Video-record the session so card placements can be time-aligned.
While the child uses the product, they place a card in the box each time they feel the shown emotion.
Align each placement with the recording and identify the cause.
Classify by card category into problems and fun issues and compile a list.
outputs: Time-located positive and negative indications by category, and a problem and fun list.
useWhen: Evaluating games and products with children aged about five to seven who cannot think aloud reliably.
avoidWhen: Avoid with children who verbalise well (use Think-Aloud Protocol or Peer Tutoring Evaluation) or where handling cards interferes with the interaction.
whyLost: It stays in academic child-computer interaction; industry child testing relies on observation and parent-mediated sessions.
whereToUse: Preschool apps, educational games, toy-companion apps, museum interactives.
example: A studio tests a counting game with six-year-olds. Most 'confused' cards fall on a level-select screen children never mention aloud, prompting a simpler map.
reference: Barendregt, W., Bekker, M. M. and Baauw, E. (2008). Development and evaluation of the problem identification picture cards method. Cognition, Technology and Work 10(2), 95-105.

name: Problem isomorph comparison
origin: Kaplan and Simon, 1990; Tower of Hanoi isomorphs, Hayes and Simon, 1977
summary: Give groups the same problem in structurally identical but differently presented versions, then compare solution time and hints to isolate the effect of representation.
description: Isomorphs share the same underlying structure and solution but differ in presentation. Because the logic is constant, differences in performance can be attributed to representation alone. Kaplan and Simon (1990) presented the mutilated checkerboard problem (can 31 dominoes cover a board with two opposite corners removed?) blank, coloured, labelled 'black' and 'pink', or 'bread' and 'butter'. The bread-and-butter group, whose labels most stressed that neighbouring squares differ, solved it twice as fast and needed about 1 hint against 3.14 for the blank group. Think-aloud protocols revealed the moment the representation changed. Classic isomorph sets include Tower of Hanoi variants and river-crossing problems such as hobbits and orcs. In UX the method directly tests whether a visualisation, metaphor or label makes a task easier.
steps: Define the task and verify formally that all versions are true isomorphs with the same solution path.
Create versions that differ only in presentation (labels, colours, metaphor, visual layout).
Randomly assign participants to versions, typically 10-20 per version.
Give hints by a fixed rule, for example after set intervals without progress, and log each hint.
Collect think-aloud protocols to identify when and how the representation shifts.
Compare solution time, success rate and hints across versions, and relate differences to protocol evidence.
outputs: Solution time, success rate and hints per version; protocol evidence of the representation used and when it changed.
useWhen: You want to know whether a representation (chart type, metaphor, terminology, layout) changes how easily users solve the same problem, such as configuring rules or reading complex data.
avoidWhen: Versions cannot be made truly equivalent, or the task has no clear solution; use comparative usability testing instead. Hints must follow a fixed rule or they confound results.
whyLost: UX compares designs with A/B or usability tests but rarely enforces strict isomorphism, so the representational effect is confounded with content changes.
whereToUse: Data visualisation, rule builders, permissions and access configuration, scheduling and logistics tools, educational products.
example: A security product presents the same access-control problem as a matrix, a node graph and a sentence builder. Users solve it fastest with the sentence builder and protocols show the matrix hides inheritance, guiding the redesign.
reference: Kaplan, C. A., & Simon, H. A. (1990). In search of insight. Cognitive Psychology, 22, 374-419.

name: Problem-Behaviour Graph
aka: Search plot of a verbal protocol
origin: Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, Human Problem Solving (1972); Newell (1967)
summary: Plot a think-aloud protocol as a graph of knowledge states and operator applications to show search, backtracking and repetition during problem solving.
description: The problem-behaviour graph represents a verbal protocol as search through a problem space. Each node is a state of knowledge; each horizontal segment is the application of an operator that moves to a new state. When the person returns to an earlier state, a vertical line drops down and a new horizontal line starts from that state; reapplying an operator already used is marked with a double line. Read from top left, the graph shows depth of search, backtracking and repetition at a glance, and stretches can be annotated with the subgoal being pursued. Newell and Simon's classic example of one subject solving DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT has 238 nodes over about 30 minutes, about 7 seconds per state. The graph also served as the target for moment-by-moment cognitive simulations.
steps: Record and transcribe a person thinking aloud while solving a well-defined problem or task.
Segment the protocol into successive states of knowledge and identify the operator applied at each step.
Draw the initial state at top left and each operator application as a horizontal segment to a new state.
When the person returns to an earlier state, drop a vertical line and continue from that state on a new line.
Mark reapplied operators with double lines and annotate stretches with the current subgoal.
Count nodes, backtracks and repetitions and compute mean time per state to compare participants or designs.
outputs: A search graph showing depth, backtracking and repetition, with node counts and mean residence time per state.
useWhen: Analysing problem solving in well-structured tasks such as configuration, diagnosis, troubleshooting or puzzle-like interfaces, especially when comparing how designs change search behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid for ill-structured or highly social tasks, or where participants use different problem spaces. For routine usability findings, standard think-aloud analysis is enough.
whyLost: It required painstaking protocol encoding and belonged to cognitive simulation research; HCI moved to lighter think-aloud analysis and GOMS-style models.
whereToUse: Troubleshooting wizards, IT and network configuration tools, spreadsheet modelling, diagnostic decision support, developer tooling.
example: Engineers think aloud while configuring firewall rules in two designs. Graphs for the old design show repeated returns to the same state after failed rule tests, quantifying wasted search that the new preview feature removes.
reference: Newell, A. and Simon, H. A. (1972). Human Problem Solving. Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall.

name: Procedural Diagrams and Notation for Mixed Methods Designs
aka: Embedding core designs into complex designs
origin: Janice Morse (1991) notation; Ivankova, Creswell and Stick (2006) diagram conventions; Creswell and Plano Clark
summary: Draw the study's data collection, analysis, integration and interpretation steps over time in a one-page diagram, labelled with QUAN/qual notation, so reviewers see the design at a glance.
description: A procedural diagram is a figure of a study's design, now expected by the Journal of Mixed Methods Research and recommended in NIH best-practice guidance. Boxes show quantitative and qualitative collection and analysis steps, arrows show sequence over time, circles mark interpretation or decision points, and the point of integration is explicitly marked. Each phase carries its aim, a timeline runs alongside, colour or shading separates strands, and the title names the design and topic. Ivankova and colleagues use three columns: stages, procedures and products. Morse's notation labels priority and timing: capitals for the dominant strand (QUAN, QUAL), lower case for the supplementary one, '+' for concurrent, an arrow for sequential, and parentheses for an embedded strand. For complex designs, the steps of the larger framework (an evaluation, an intervention trial) are listed first and core designs embedded at the points where both data types are collected.
steps: List the steps of the overall study framework, such as an evaluation or product cycle.
Draw a box for each quantitative and qualitative collection and analysis step, with arrows showing sequence over time.
Mark where data are merged or connected, and add circles for interpretation and decision points.
Attach the aim of each phase, a timeline, and the products of each stage if using the three-column format.
Shade strands differently and label them with notation: QUAN or QUAL for priority, '+' for concurrent, an arrow for sequential, parentheses for embedded.
Title the diagram with the design name and topic, and check it remains linear and legible.
outputs: A one-page procedural diagram and a notation string summarising the design.
useWhen: Planning and communicating multi-method research programmes, research proposals, and studies where stakeholders need to see how strands connect.
avoidWhen: Single-method studies. For tracing how each conclusion builds into the meta-inference, a methods-inference map is more detailed.
whyLost: UX research plans are written as prose or slide timelines; the notation and diagram conventions are taught only in academic mixed methods courses.
whereToUse: Research roadmaps combining analytics, surveys and interviews; research operations templates; funding or governance proposals.
example: A research lead plans a quarter combining log analysis, a survey and follow-up interviews on checkout abandonment. The diagram, labelled quan -> QUAL with integration points marked, shows stakeholders that interview sampling depends on survey results, securing time between phases.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Ivankova, N. V., Creswell, J. W. and Stick, S. L. (2006). Using mixed-methods sequential explanatory design: from theory to practice. Field Methods, 18(1), 3-20.

name: Process Analysis with Process Map
origin: User and task analysis practice, Hackos and Redish, 1998
summary: A focused field study that follows a multi-step, multi-person process with fixed questions per step and draws the result as a validated process map.
description: Process analysis traces a process that may span days and several people, from its trigger to its end, by interviewing and observing the people at each step. Unlike contextual inquiry it starts from a prepared question set and does not need the apprenticeship stance. For every step the researcher asks what triggers it, who does it, what information goes in and comes out, who acts next, how completion is known, which errors occur and how often, and what slows things down. Links to other processes and conditions that reopen a step are noted. The sequence is then drawn as a process map and checked with participants. Its rigour comes from asking the same questions at every step, which makes gaps, re-entry of information and hand-off failures visible and comparable.
steps: Define the process to study, its start trigger and its end state.
Identify the people and roles involved at each step and arrange interviews and observation, planning several visits for long processes.
At each step ask the standard questions: trigger, actor, inputs, outputs, next person, completion signal, errors and their frequency, and roadblocks.
Observe the work as well as asking, to catch deviations from the official process.
Note links to other processes and the conditions under which steps are reopened.
Draw the process map and validate it with the people involved.
outputs: A validated process map plus a step-level table of triggers, inputs, outputs, errors and roadblocks.
useWhen: Redesigning tools that support a process involving several people or days (claims, onboarding, procurement, check-in), or locating hand-off failures and duplicated data entry.
avoidWhen: Single-user, single-session tasks (use Hierarchical Task Analysis) or open-ended discovery of needs and culture (use Contextual Inquiry). People describe the official process, so do not rely on interviews alone.
whyLost: Its question set was absorbed into service blueprinting and journey mapping, which often drop the per-step error and frequency questions and the validation step.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS workflows, healthcare admissions, insurance claims, government services, internal tooling and back-office operations.
example: A fintech team maps small-business loan approval across applicant, broker, underwriter and compliance. The map shows the applicant's income data being re-keyed three times and a reopen loop that adds four days on average.
reference: Hackos, J.T. and Redish, J.C. (1998) User and Task Analysis for Interface Design. New York: Wiley.

name: Process and Implementation Evaluation
origin: Programme evaluation practice; RAND Change Agent Study (McLaughlin, 1976); Patton (1997)
summary: Study how a programme or rollout actually operates and what people experience, to check what was really delivered before judging its outcomes.
description: Process evaluation describes how a programme produces results from the perspectives of participants, staff and outsiders. Implementation evaluation asks what was actually delivered as opposed to what was planned. Patton criticises pure pre-post outcome studies as an 'empty box' that cannot say what produced, or failed to produce, results. Core questions are what participants experience, what services are given, what staff do, what it is like to be in the programme and how it is organised. The RAND Change Agent Study found 'mutual adaptation' between innovations and settings, and in one outreach programme the door-to-door work differed from its design. Process findings make null outcomes interpretable and isolate the critical elements for replication. In UX it is the counterpart to measuring launch metrics.
steps: Describe the programme or rollout as designed from documents, logic models and staff accounts.
Observe activities and interview participants and staff about what actually happens.
Ask the implementation questions: what users experience, what is delivered, what staff do and how it is organised.
Compare observed practice with the design and record adaptations and their reasons.
Report processes so that outcome findings can be linked to what was actually delivered, and identify critical elements.
outputs: A description of processes and implementation variations, and the critical elements for replication or scaling.
useWhen: Rolling out a service, internal tool, design system or behaviour-change programme across sites or teams, or interpreting disappointing outcome metrics.
avoidWhen: The intervention is fully automated and identical for everyone, so implementation cannot vary; then focus on outcome measurement. Keep design and practice clearly separated in reporting.
whyLost: It belongs to programme evaluation; product teams measure outcomes from telemetry and rarely study how human-delivered parts were implemented.
whereToUse: Service design, enterprise software rollouts, digital health programmes, design-system adoption, customer onboarding programmes.
example: A clinic triage tool shows no improvement in waiting times. Process evaluation finds two of five sites bypass the tool at peak times, so the null result reflects implementation, not the design.
sources: User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2002). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Process Coding
origin: Anselm Strauss and Juliet Corbin (1990; 1998); exemplars Wiener (1983), Fujimura (1988)
summary: Trace how action and interaction change, or stay the same, over time in response to changing conditions, identifying phases, turning points and subprocesses.
description: Coding for process runs alongside axial coding in grounded theory. Instead of developing properties of categories, the analyst follows sequences of action and interaction over time and links their changes to changes in conditions. Attention goes to shifts, turning points, alignment and misalignment between actors, routines, responses to contingencies, and how the consequences of one sequence become the conditions for the next. A process may be expressed as stages or phases, but only where the data support it, and it can be broken into subprocesses of tactics, strategies and routines. Guiding questions include why something stays the same, how it changes, and what happens when contingencies interrupt. A process can become the core category of a theory, at micro or macro level.
steps: Name the action or interaction process being traced.
Read the data in sequence, noting shifts in action and the conditions that produced them.
Identify turning points, reinforcers and moments of alignment or misalignment between actors.
Break the process into phases or sequences only where the data support it, allowing variation in rate and order.
Break it into subprocesses of tactics, strategies and routines.
Show how consequences of one sequence become conditions for the next.
Compare with further cases to add steps and variation.
outputs: A named process with phases or sequences, subprocesses, turning points and the conditions driving change.
useWhen: Longitudinal or retrospective studies of adoption, onboarding, learning, recovery or switching, where change over time is the point.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing every experience into stages; for snapshot questions, thematic analysis is simpler. For quantitative event sequences, use process mining or sequence analysis.
whyLost: UX journey maps capture stages but rarely the conditional mechanics of change that process coding demands, so it stays in academic grounded theory.
whereToUse: Onboarding and habit formation, switching between providers, chronic condition self-management, enterprise tool adoption.
example: A diary study of small businesses moving to a new accounting tool is coded for process. The analysis finds a turning point when the first VAT return succeeds, after which workarounds stop, so the team designs onboarding around reaching that moment.
reference: Strauss, A. and Corbin, J. (1998). Basics of Qualitative Research: Techniques and Procedures for Developing Grounded Theory (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage, pp. 163-179.

name: PROCESS macro (Hayes) for moderation and mediation
origin: Andrew F. Hayes, 2012 (PROCESS); v4 released 2022; building on Baron and Kenny (1986) and Preacher and Hayes (2004, 2008)
summary: Using Hayes's PROCESS models to test whether a UX effect operates through a mechanism (mediation) or depends on user characteristics (moderation), with bootstrapped inference.
description: PROCESS is a regression-based macro for SPSS, SAS and R that implements over 90 numbered templates for mediation, moderation and their combinations (conditional process analysis). Model 4 tests simple mediation (X to M to Y), Model 1 simple moderation (X by W predicting Y), and Models 7 and 14 moderated mediation. It estimates indirect effects with percentile bootstrap confidence intervals, probes interactions with simple slopes and Johnson-Neyman regions, and reports an index of moderated mediation. Rigour comes from specifying the model from theory before analysis, mean-centring where appropriate, using at least 5,000 bootstrap samples, and recognising that cross-sectional mediation cannot establish temporal or causal ordering; the X to M to Y order must be justified by design.
steps: Specify the conceptual model (which variable is X, M, W, Y and covariates) and choose the matching PROCESS model number.
Install PROCESS v4 and run it from syntax, e.g. process y=sat/x=design/m=ease/model=4/boot=5000/seed=2026.
For moderation, request simple slopes at the 16th, 50th and 84th percentiles of W and the Johnson-Neyman region.
Interpret indirect effects as significant only if the 95% bootstrap CI excludes zero; for moderated mediation check the index of moderated mediation CI.
Check standard regression assumptions and use heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (hc3) where needed.
Report path coefficients, the indirect effect with CI and a diagram, and state the causal assumptions.
outputs: Path coefficients, indirect and conditional effects with bootstrap CIs, Johnson-Neyman regions and a model diagram.
useWhen: Testing mechanism hypotheses from qualitative work (e.g. a redesign improves satisfaction via perceived control) and whether effects differ by segment, especially in experiments where X is randomised.
avoidWhen: Avoid with latent variables and multiple indicators (use SEM), with clustered or longitudinal data (use multilevel or longitudinal models), and for causal mediation claims from purely cross-sectional observational data.
whyLost: PROCESS is ubiquitous in academic psychology and communication research but rarely used in UX practice, where mechanism testing is uncommon.
whereToUse: Experiments on fintech trust, health app adherence mechanisms, AI explanation effects and onboarding redesigns.
example: An AI product randomises users to explanations or no explanations. PROCESS Model 7 shows explanations increase reliance via perceived understanding, but only for novice users (index of moderated mediation CI excludes zero).
sources: LOGISTIC REGRESSION procedures; Hayes PROCESS macro v4
Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed.
Baron, R. M. & Kenny, D. A. (1986) The moderator-mediator variable distinction. JPSP
Preacher, K. J. & Hayes, A. F. (2008) Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects. Behavior Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, C8 — SPSS for Regression, Moderation & Mediation
reference: Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed.

name: Process Mining
donor: Business process management and computer science
origin: Wil van der Aalst, Eindhoven, late 1990s-2011 (Process Mining, 2011/2016)
summary: Discovers the actual process model from event logs, checks conformance to the intended flow, and shows bottlenecks and deviations.
description: Process mining requires event logs with a case identifier, activity name and timestamp. Discovery algorithms (alpha, heuristic miner, inductive miner) build process models such as Petri nets or BPMN from the logs. Conformance checking replays logs against an intended model to quantify fitness and locate deviations. Enhancement overlays performance: waiting times, rework loops, bottlenecks. For UX, this formalises the comparison between the designed flow and what users actually do, at scale, with quantitative fitness metrics. It is particularly suited to multi-step, multi-actor processes such as claims, onboarding with verification or B2B approval flows.
steps: Extract an event log with case ID, activity, timestamp and optional resource and attributes.
Clean and abstract activities to a meaningful level; filter infrequent noise variants.
Discover process models with the inductive miner (guaranteeing sound models) and inspect variants.
Run conformance checking against the intended design flow and compute fitness and precision.
Analyse performance: throughput times, waits, loops and handovers between actors.
Investigate deviations with qualitative research, then redesign and re-mine to measure change.
outputs: Discovered process models, variant frequencies, conformance metrics, bottleneck and rework analyses.
useWhen: Multi-step processes with good event logs where you need to see the real flow and its deviations.
avoidWhen: Unstructured exploratory behaviour without clear cases, or poor event logging.
whyLost: It belongs to BPM and enterprise analytics, rarely taught in UX; product analytics tools offer only path diagrams.
whereToUse: Insurance claims, KYC onboarding, procurement and approval tools, healthcare pathways, support ticket lifecycles.
example: A lender mines 80,000 loan applications and finds only 41% follow the designed path; 23% loop through document re-upload three or more times, adding a median 4 days. Redesigning document guidance halves the loops.
sources: van der Aalst, Process Mining: Data Science in Action (2nd ed., 2016)
IEEE Task Force on Process Mining, Process Mining Manifesto (2011)
reference: van der Aalst, W. M. P. (2016). Process Mining: Data Science in Action. Springer.

name: Process Tracing
donor: Political science and comparative historical analysis
origin: Alexander George (1979); Stephen Van Evera (1997); George and Bennett (2005); Beach and Pedersen (2013)
summary: Tests causal explanations within a single case by examining whether the predicted sequence of intermediate steps and evidence is present, using formal evidential tests.
description: Process tracing examines the causal chain linking a cause to an outcome within a case, asking what observable implications each step of a hypothesised mechanism would leave. Van Evera classified evidential tests by necessity and sufficiency: straw-in-the-wind (weak), hoop (necessary: failing eliminates the hypothesis), smoking gun (sufficient: passing strongly confirms) and doubly decisive. Bayesian process tracing formalises updating. In UX, single cases are common: one enterprise customer's failed rollout, one user's journey to churn, one incident. Process tracing turns case narratives into disciplined causal inference, with rival hypotheses tested against specific evidence. This is the political-science sense of the term. In cognitive engineering, process tracing (Woods) instead reconstructs how practitioners' behaviour and reasoning unfold over time in field or simulated work, which this entry does not cover.
steps: Define the outcome and candidate causal explanations, including rivals.
For each explanation, specify the mechanism as a sequence of steps and the evidence each step should leave.
Classify predicted evidence as hoop, smoking-gun, straw-in-the-wind or doubly decisive tests.
Collect evidence: logs, documents, emails, interviews, timelines, with attention to source reliability.
Evaluate each hypothesis against the tests, eliminating those that fail hoop tests.
Write a causal narrative with the evidence chain, and state remaining uncertainty.
outputs: Mechanism diagrams, evidence-test tables, eliminated and supported hypotheses and a defensible causal account.
useWhen: Explaining a single important case (an account churn, a failed launch, an adoption success) where comparison or experiments are unavailable.
avoidWhen: Questions about population-level effect sizes; use quantitative causal methods.
whyLost: Case-based causal inference is taught in political science; UX case studies are usually descriptive narratives.
whereToUse: Enterprise account reviews, incident investigations, launch retrospectives, policy change effects.
example: Why did a hospital abandon a scheduling tool? A hoop test (clinicians used it in the first month) passes for the 'workflow mismatch' hypothesis, while a smoking gun (emails showing a leadership change cancelled funding) confirms an organisational explanation instead.
sources: George & Bennett, Case Studies and Theory Development in the Social Sciences (2005)
Van Evera, Guide to Methods for Students of Political Science (1997)
Beach & Pedersen, Process-Tracing Methods: Foundations and Guidelines (2013)
Collier, Understanding process tracing (2011), PS: Political Science & Politics
reference: Collier, D. (2011). Understanding process tracing. PS: Political Science & Politics, 44(4), 823-830.

name: Procrustes Analysis
origin: Named by Hurley and Cattell (1962); least-squares orthogonal solution by Schonemann (1966); generalised Procrustes analysis by Gower (1975)
summary: Rotate one set of factor loadings or map coordinates to match a target as closely as possible, and use the remaining misfit to judge how similar two solutions are.
description: Factor, component and multidimensional scaling solutions are defined only up to rotation, so two solutions can look different while describing the same structure. Procrustes analysis finds the transformation T that brings matrix A as close as possible to target B in least squares. With T constrained to be orthonormal, Schonemann's solution uses the singular value decomposition of A'B; centring and scaling may be added. The residual sum of squares, and congruence coefficients per dimension, measure how similar the solutions are once arbitrary rotation is removed. Generalised Procrustes analysis fits several configurations to a common consensus at once, and oblique and maximum-congruence variants exist. Jackson uses it to check whether simplified rounded vectors capture a real solution; Krzanowski used it to choose variable subsets. The main caution is that flexible transformations can make unrelated matrices fit, and no standard significance test exists, so permutation baselines help.
steps: Obtain the two configurations to compare (loadings, component scores or MDS coordinates) with matched rows.
Choose the target: a hypothesised pattern, the original-language solution, or the full-variable solution.
Centre, and if wanted scale, both matrices, then compute the orthonormal rotation from the SVD of A'B.
Apply the rotation and compute the residual sum of squares and the congruence coefficient for each dimension.
Judge misfit against a baseline, for example by repeating the fit with randomly permuted rows.
Use generalised Procrustes for more than two configurations, or oblique versions when dimensions may correlate.
outputs: A rotation matrix, the rotated configuration, residual misfit and per-dimension congruence coefficients.
useWhen: Checking whether a translated questionnaire reproduces the original factor structure, whether two segments' perceptual maps agree, or whether a short form preserves a long form's components.
avoidWhen: Formal tests of measurement equivalence across groups (use Cross-Cultural Survey Equivalence Testing or multigroup CFA); interpreting a single solution (Factor rotation (Varimax vs. Oblimin)); or very small matrices where any rotation fits.
whyLost: Used in sensory science, morphometrics and psychometrics, but UX researchers comparing scale structures or maps across groups usually eyeball them side by side.
whereToUse: Localised survey instruments, multi-market perceptual mapping, comparing card-sort MDS solutions across user groups, sensory and brand panels.
example: A UX team translates a 20-item usability questionnaire into Japanese. After Procrustes rotation to the English loadings, congruence is 0.96 and 0.94 for two factors but 0.71 for the third, so its items go back for cognitive pretesting.
sources: A User's Guide to Principal Components (Jackson, 1991)
reference: Schonemann, P. H. (1966). A generalized solution of the orthogonal Procrustes problem. Psychometrika, 31(1), 1-10; Gower, J. C. (1975). Generalized Procrustes analysis. Psychometrika, 40(1), 33-51; Jackson, J. E. (1991). A User's Guide to Principal Components, pp. 167-172.

name: Product Accident Scenario Analysis (Hazard Patterns)
origin: Colin Drury and Maurice Brill (1983), Human factors in consumer product accident investigation
summary: Group past product accidents into a few hazard patterns covering victim, product, environment and task, then interview new cases about each stage of the task leading to injury.
description: Most accident classifications cover person, equipment and environment. Drury and Brill add the task, seeking the mismatch between task demands and the capacity of the body subsystem involved. Archival accident reports are sorted into hazard patterns (scenarios), each describing victim, product, environment and task; a pattern set is useful if no more than six patterns cover more than 90% of in-depth cases. The patterns then shape an interview questionnaire for new incidents, recording victim, environment and product details and task performance at four moments: the intended action, the point where it could not be completed as intended, any new or corrective action, and the injury. Demand is judged against capacity at each stage. It is more descriptive than a case-crossover design but better at revealing human factors causes.
steps: Collect in-depth archival accident or incident reports for the product class.
Classify them into hazard patterns describing victim, product, environment and task, aiming for six or fewer patterns covering over 90% of cases.
Build an interview questionnaire from the patterns.
For each new accident, record victim data (age, body part), environment (indoor or outdoor, lighting) and product data (type, shape, weight).
Reconstruct the task at four stages: intended action, failure to complete, corrective action, injury.
Judge task demands against human capacity at each stage and derive design countermeasures for each pattern.
outputs: A small set of hazard scenarios covering most accidents, and per-case descriptions of task-demand mismatches with countermeasures.
useWhen: Investigating injuries or serious use errors with physical or connected consumer products where incident reports exist.
avoidWhen: Avoid where there are too few cases to form patterns or where exposures are transient and countable; use a case-crossover design for transient risk factors, or Critical Incident Technique for non-injury problems.
whyLost: It belongs to consumer product safety research and regulation, which UX teams seldom touch, even for physical products.
whereToUse: Smart-home devices, kitchen appliances, e-scooters and e-bikes, fitness equipment, children's products, medical devices used at home.
example: An e-scooter company classifies 400 injury reports into five hazard patterns, one being riders braking on wet surfaces while signalling. Interviews about each stage show the brake lever cannot be reached while signalling, leading to a redesigned grip.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Drury, C. G. and Brill, M. (1983). Human factors in consumer product accident investigation. Human Factors, 25(3), 329-342.

name: Product Box
origin: Luke Hohmann's Innovation Games (2006); also credited to Jim Highsmith and Bill Shackelford
summary: Teams design and then pitch the retail box for an idea, forcing explicit choices about its name, audience, headline features and benefits.
description: Product Box asks a team to make the shrink-wrapped retail box that would sell an idea, whether or not the product will ever be physical. The box is a focusing device: its limited faces force decisions about name, tagline, intended buyer and the few features worth printing. The second half matters as much as the making. When teams sell their boxes to each other, features turn into benefits, audible in phrases such as 'so that' and 'because', which shows what people believe the value really is. Run divergently, each team produces its own box; run convergently, a second round merges the strongest elements into one shared box. Hohmann's original use was with customers as an elicitation game; Gamestorming describes it mainly with internal teams, for topics from a new application to 'the ideal hire'.
steps: Prepare blank boxes or card, markers, stickers, craft paper and some real packaging (cereal boxes work well) as reference.
Lay out candidate names, buyers and features, giving just enough information for teams to start.
Give teams at least 30 minutes to design the box as if found on a retail shelf: name, who it is for, tagline, three to five compelling features and benefits, and imagery.
Have each team sell its box to the room in a short, optionally timed pitch, with teams voting for prizes.
Listen and note where features are translated into benefits ('so that', 'because') and which ones every box repeats.
If alignment is the goal, compare boxes for similarities and differences and run a second round to build one shared box.
Photograph or keep the boxes on display and record pitches where this is not disruptive.
outputs: Physical boxes and recorded pitches showing the features, benefits, audience and positioning a team (or customers) chooses to foreground.
useWhen: Use it to align a team on what an idea is for and which few features carry its value, or as a light-touch way to open a vision or kick-off workshop.
avoidWhen: Do not treat internal boxes as evidence of customer demand; for that use Concept Testing with target users or Kano Analysis. When customers build the boxes it becomes a research activity and needs the interpretive care of Co-design Workshops.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, playful, physical and produces a memorable artefact, and it was popularised through both Innovation Games and Gamestorming.
whereToUse: Product kick-offs, roadmap themes, internal tools, start-up positioning, and customer advisory sessions in B2B SaaS.
example: A fintech team planning a savings feature runs three boxes in parallel; every box leads with 'round-ups' and none mentions fees. A second round produces one box whose tagline becomes the draft value proposition, later checked in concept interviews.
reference: Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010) Gamestorming: A Playbook for Innovators, Rulebreakers, and Changemakers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 161-163.

name: Product Concept Statement (with the Wheel lifecycle)
aka: Product concept statement and Wheel lifecycle
origin: Rex Hartson and Pardha Pyla, The UX Book (2012; 2nd edn 2019)
summary: A 100-150 word statement of who a product is for, how it is used, what it offers and the experience it aims for, used as the project's yardstick.
description: A product concept statement is a short vision paragraph for all stakeholders, iterated until every phrase is concrete. It answers five questions: the product's name, its users, how they will use it, the problems it solves or features that distinguish it, and the design vision and emotional impact goals. It is posted in the studio, used to judge scope, and revised as research reveals new concerns; large systems may need one per subsystem. In The UX Book it opens the Wheel lifecycle, a cycle of understanding needs, designing, prototyping and evaluating whose rigour is tuned to where a project sits in a space of interaction complexity against domain complexity. The funnel model adds scope: a large early funnel (sprint 0) for research and conceptual design, then small late-funnel design chunks, each a mini Wheel, delivered one sprint ahead of development.
steps: Answer the five prompts: product name; users; how they will use it; problems solved or distinguishing features; design vision and emotional impact goals.
Draft the statement in about 100-150 words.
Iterate, replacing every vague phrase with a specific one until each word earns its place.
Place the project in the complexity space (interaction against domain complexity) and note risk, familiarity and resources to choose how much rigour the lifecycle needs.
Use the statement in an early-funnel sprint 0 to scope research and conceptual design; post it where the team works.
In the late funnel, judge each feature chunk against the statement before running its mini Wheel ahead of the development sprint.
Revise the statement whenever research surfaces new users, content or concerns.
outputs: A short, specific concept statement; a tailored process plan with an early-funnel scope and per-sprint design chunks.
useWhen: Use it at project start to make a vague brief concrete enough to scope research and judge features, and to agree how much up-front design a project needs before chunked delivery.
avoidWhen: It records the team's intent, not user need; ground it with Contextual Inquiry or Interviews before treating it as settled, and check the resulting concept with Prototype Testing. Not suited to products that cannot be released in chunks without an early funnel.
whyLost: Vision statements survive because every team needs a shared yardstick for scope; Hartson and Pyla's version is widely taught in HCI courses, though the Wheel's complexity-based tailoring is less often applied.
whereToUse: New product initiatives, kiosks and multi-platform systems, agile teams negotiating sprint 0, and student or consultancy projects needing a project charter.
example: A transit agency's ticketing kiosk team drafts a 128-word statement, then sharpens 'easy to use' into 'buy a ticket in under a minute without an account'. A large early funnel defines the conceptual design before fare features ship sprint by sprint.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019) The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience. 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann. Chapters 2-4 and Section 5.6.

name: Product Reaction Cards (Microsoft Desirability Toolkit)
aka: Desirability testing with product reaction cards
origin: Joey Benedek and Trish Miner, Microsoft, 2002
summary: Participants pick, from 118 positive and negative adjectives, the words that describe a product, narrow to five and explain them, revealing its perceived character and emotional profile.
description: Benedek and Miner created 118 cards, each with an adjective, about 60% positive and 40% negative, to capture desirability, which standard usability measures miss. After using a product, participants choose every word that describes it, then narrow to the five that best describe it and explain why. Online, each word is shown with a check box. Baxter et al. describe a variant in which participants choose five to ten cards and present it as a summative check on emotional response, often added at the end of a usability session. Analysis counts word frequencies and the positive-to-negative balance across participants, often shown as a word cloud, and compares profiles across designs or against intended brand attributes. The explanations carry most of the value, because participants may pick polite words. The method is qualitative more than psychometric; use the same list and order when comparing products.
steps: Define the intended brand or experience attributes in advance so results can be compared against them.
After the participant has used the product, present all 118 words (cards on a table or check boxes online, in randomised order).
Ask the participant to select every word that describes the product.
Ask them to narrow to the five words that best describe it (some variants allow five to ten).
Probe, or ask in writing, why they chose each of the final words.
Count word frequencies and the positive versus negative balance across participants (typically 10 to 30).
Present a frequency table or word cloud, compare with the intended attributes and summarise the explanations.
outputs: Word frequencies, positive and negative balance, a word cloud, comparison with intended attributes and verbatim reasons for chosen words.
useWhen: When you need a quick, structured read of how a product or redesign feels, to compare designs on emotional tone, or to check alignment with brand values.
avoidWhen: Avoid for psychometrically robust comparison (use AttrakDiff or UEQ (User Experience Questionnaire)); small samples make frequency differences fragile and long word lists fatigue online respondents.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, free, easy to explain to stakeholders and fits the end of any usability session.
whereToUse: Brand-led redesigns, visual design evaluation, onboarding, AI assistant tone, competitive comparisons.
example: After testing a redesigned booking page, 20 participants most often choose 'clean' and 'fast' but also 'impersonal'; their explanations point to generic copy, prompting work on tone of voice.
reference: Benedek, J., & Miner, T. (2002). Measuring desirability: New methods for evaluating desirability in a usability lab setting. Usability Professionals' Association 2002 Conference, Orlando, FL.

name: Product Stance and Emotional Requirements
origin: Jon Kolko, Well-Designed (2014)
summary: Define a product's personality as four or five specific traits, then turn them into testable 'Our product will ...' requirements that arbitrate design decisions.
description: Product stance is the attitude a product takes towards its users, somewhere between brand and utility. Because people anthropomorphise products, use becomes a dialogue, and an inconsistent stance jars as much as an inconsistent friend. Kolko's procedure starts by imagining the product as a person in particular situations (anxious, under threat, in a meeting), then choosing four or five highly specific aspirational traits; 'luxury' or 'friendly' are too vague. The traits are justified in the idiom the organisation trusts: data for engineers, precedent for marketing, existing brand language in large firms. They are then rewritten as emotional requirements ('Our product will anticipate negative reactions') and entered into the same tracker as functional requirements, so they can be tested after build and used to settle disputes about features, content, pricing and aesthetics.
steps: Imagine the product as a person and describe how it would behave in several concrete situations.
Choose four or five specific, aspirational emotional traits and reject generic ones.
Justify each trait in a form the team culture accepts (data, precedent, brand language or strong design opinion).
Write each trait as one or more 'Our product will ...' emotional requirements.
Enter them in the requirements or defect tracker alongside functional requirements.
Use them to arbitrate decisions on features, content, interactions, pricing and aesthetics, and test the built product against them.
outputs: A trait list and a set of emotional requirements logged with functional requirements and checked after build.
useWhen: Use it when a product's tone and behaviour drift between teams, or when a team needs a principled way to decide between functionally equivalent options.
avoidWhen: Traits chosen in a room are assumptions; check how users actually perceive the product with Semantic Differential ratings or Desirability-style reaction studies, and use Interviews to learn which emotions matter. Not a substitute for a Voice and Tone Framework with Decision Matrix when only copy is at issue.
whyLost: Brand personality traits are now common, but the step that gave the method its rigour (writing traits as testable requirements in the tracker) is usually dropped, leaving adjective lists on a slide.
whereToUse: Consumer health and wellbeing apps, conversational AI assistants, fintech onboarding, and any product where trust and tone drive retention.
example: A mental health app picks 'supportive, lighthearted, dependable, casual'. Requirements such as 'Our product will always affirm before it corrects' become tickets, and a QA pass flags error messages that scold.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Kolko, J. (2014). Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press, pp. 119-126.

name: Product Test Designs (Blind/Branded, Monadic/Paired, Studio/Home-Use)
aka: Product test designs (full or partial, studio or home-use, blind or identified, monadic or comparison)
origin: Marketing research practice (German product-testing literature, via Gaubinger et al., 2015); sponsor-blind ethics from Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015)
summary: Design a product evaluation by choosing whole or partial product, studio or home use, blind or branded presentation, and single or compared products, each controlling a different bias.
description: Product tests measure subjectively perceived features to establish customer value, best component design or real-world usability. Four design choices define them. Full or partial: test the whole product or selected features. Studio or home-use: studio tests give control but transfer poorly; home-use tests are realistic but uncontrolled. Blind or identified: blind tests remove brand, shape and colour, while identified tests predict buying better; running both isolates the brand effect. Monadic or comparison: comparisons sharpen discrimination but make people hunt for trivial differences, whereas separate monadic groups compared by polarity profiles level shared biases. Sponsor-blind studies, which conceal that a competitor's product is the subject, are acceptable only if participants would not have refused had they known; recruiters list several possible sponsors at screening and the true sponsor is revealed at the end.
steps: Decide full test (whole product) or partial test (selected features, brand or operation).
Choose studio testing for control and spontaneous reactions or home-use or beta testing for realism; include lead users in industrial markets.
Choose blind, identified or partly neutralised presentation; run blind and identified versions in parallel to estimate the brand effect.
Choose monadic, sequential or side-by-side comparison, or several monadic groups compared on a semantic differential.
For sponsor-blind studies use a third-party recruiter, list several possible sponsors at screening, exclude candidates who object, and reveal the sponsor at debrief.
Collect perceptions and judgements, plus performance, error and failure data in field tests.
outputs: Acceptance and preference data per variant, brand-effect estimates, and error and failure statistics.
useWhen: Comparing your product with competitors, measuring brand halo on perceived usability or quality, or choosing between studio and in-home evaluation.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural causal evidence at scale; use A/B tests. Studio tests lack external validity, home-use tests cannot confirm instructions were followed, and blind tests by a market leader become de facto identified tests.
whyLost: It remains standard in consumer-goods marketing research, while UX usually tests one branded product without designing for brand or comparison bias.
whereToUse: Competitive benchmarking, hardware and consumer devices, rebrands, AI assistant comparisons, white-label products.
example: A bank compares its app with a rival's in a sponsor-blind study, running blind and branded cells. Branded scores rise 0.8 points for the rival, showing much of its perceived ease comes from brand.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Gaubinger, K., Rabl, M., Swan, S., & Werani, T. (2015). Innovation and Product Management. Springer, pp. 187-189.

name: Profile Analysis (Parallelism, Levels and Flatness)
origin: Greenhouse and Geisser (1959) on profile data; presented by Alvin Rencher (2002)
summary: Compare groups' mean profiles across several measures on the same scale by testing in order whether profiles are parallel, at the same level, and flat.
description: When variables are commensurate, sharing units and similar variances (a battery of rating attributes on the same scale, or repeated measurements), each group's mean profile is the line joining its variable means. Profile analysis asks three ordered questions using contrasts of successive differences. First, parallelism: are segment-by-segment changes equal across groups, meaning no group-by-variable interaction? This is a Hotelling T-squared test on the contrasts. Only if profiles are parallel do the next two make sense: equal levels, whether one group scores uniformly higher (a t-test on summed scores), and flatness, whether the combined profile is level across variables. If profiles are not parallel, the interaction is interpreted from the plot. One-sample profile analysis tests flatness of a single mean vector, and several groups are handled by MANOVA on contrasts.
steps: Confirm the variables are commensurate: same scale and broadly similar variances.
Form successive-difference contrasts across the variables.
Test parallelism with Hotelling T-squared (or MANOVA for more than two groups) on the contrasts.
If profiles are parallel, test equal levels with a t-test on each person's total.
If profiles are parallel, test flatness of the combined profile.
If profiles are not parallel, plot them and interpret where the group-by-variable interaction lies.
outputs: Results of the parallelism, levels and flatness tests, with profile plots for each group.
useWhen: Comparing segments (novices and experts, markets, personas) across a set of attribute ratings on one scale, or comparing groups' trajectories over repeated measurements.
avoidWhen: Variables on different scales, where profile shape is meaningless; when univariate repeated-measures ANOVA with sphericity corrections answers the question (Repeated-measures and mixed (split-plot) ANOVA); or when individual trajectories matter (Growth curve modelling).
whyLost: A standard multivariate textbook topic used in psychology and education, but UX segment comparisons usually run one test per attribute and inflate error.
whereToUse: Brand and product attribute ratings across segments, persona validation, competitive perception studies, pre/post attribute batteries.
example: Experts and novices rate a design tool on six attributes on a 7-point scale. Profiles are not parallel (T-squared p = 0.01): experts rate power and speed higher but learnability far lower, which a single overall score would hide.
reference: Rencher, A. C. (2002). Methods of Multivariate Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Wiley-Interscience. pp. 139-145, 199-203.

name: Programmatic Labelling with Weak Supervision
origin: Snorkel, Stanford AI Lab (Ratner et al., 2017); medical case from Dunnmon et al. (2020)
summary: Encode experts' labelling heuristics as functions, apply them to unlabelled data and combine their noisy, conflicting votes into training labels, checked against a small hand-labelled sample.
description: Weak supervision replaces most hand labelling with labelling functions that encode heuristics: keywords, regular expressions, database lookups or other models' outputs. Each function labels only what it recognises and may be wrong, and functions can conflict, so their outputs are combined, denoised and reweighted into most-likely labels by a label model. A small hand-labelled sample is recommended to estimate each function's accuracy and to inspire better functions. Advantages include cost, since expertise is captured once and can be versioned and reused; privacy, since only a cleared subsample needs human inspection; and adaptivity, since functions can be reapplied when data or requirements change. A model trained on the programmatic labels can generalise to cases no function covers. For research teams, it offers a way to scale qualitative coding schemes to large volumes of feedback with explicit, auditable rules.
steps: Hand-label a small sample to learn the patterns and to estimate heuristic accuracy.
Write labelling functions that encode expert heuristics (keywords, regular expressions, lookups, other models' outputs).
Apply all functions to the unlabelled data.
Combine, denoise and reweight the functions' conflicting outputs into most-likely labels with a label model.
Check label quality against the hand-labelled sample and revise weak functions.
Optionally train a model on the labels to generalise beyond function coverage, and reapply the functions when data or requirements change.
outputs: A programmatically labelled data set, a reusable and versioned set of labelling functions, and accuracy estimates per function.
useWhen: Labelling large volumes of feedback, tickets, reviews or sessions where expert rules exist but hand labelling everything is too slow, costly or privacy-sensitive.
avoidWhen: Labels can be too noisy when heuristics are weak or categories subtle; for small sets or nuanced interpretation use Content Analysis with Cohen's Kappa and Krippendorff's Alpha (Inter-Rater Reliability), and for a gold standard use Ground-truth labelling from qualitative review.
whyLost: It is an ML engineering technique; UX researchers who code data at scale tend to choose between manual coding and opaque classifiers, missing this rule-based middle path.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer pipelines, app review mining, support ticket triage, training data for AI product features.
example: A research team codes 300 support tickets by hand, then writes 15 labelling functions for its 'billing confusion' and 'login failure' codes. Applied to 80,000 tickets and checked against the hand sample, they reach usable accuracy and are rerun monthly.
reference: Ratner, A. et al. (2017). Snorkel: rapid training data creation with weak supervision. Proc. VLDB Endowment, 11(3); Huyen, C. (2022). Designing Machine Learning Systems. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly, pp. 94-98.

name: Progress communication audit
origin: Goal-gradient hypothesis (Hull, 1932; Kivetz, Urminsky and Zheng, 2006), endowed progress effect (Nunes and Drèze, 2006) and progress bar perception research (Myers, 1985; Harrison et al., 2007)
summary: Audits how a product communicates progress and completion against users' reference points, identifying where feedback creates felt loss, stalls motivation or undermines satisfaction.
description: Users judge progress relative to reference points: where they expected to be, what the previous system offered, and how far there is to go. The goal-gradient effect shows effort accelerates near a goal; the endowed progress effect shows a loyalty card with 2 of 10 stamps pre-filled was completed by 34% of customers versus 19% for a blank 8-stamp card. Progress bars with accelerating rather than decelerating motion are perceived as faster. A progress communication audit inspects every progress and completion signal (steps, bars, counters, confirmations, success screens) for these effects, and checks whether the completion moment delivers a felt gain relative to the previous practice. Rigour comes from mapping reference points empirically and testing alternatives with completion and satisfaction measures.
steps: Inventory all progress and completion signals across key flows: step indicators, bars, percentages, counters, waits, confirmations and success screens.
Elicit users' reference points for each flow through 6 to 10 interviews: how long they expect it to take, what 'done' looked like in their previous method, and what proof of completion they value.
Evaluate each signal against principles: show early endowed progress, avoid decelerating bars and late surprise steps, give accurate remaining effort, and provide tangible proof of completion.
Identify reference-point losses where the new system offers less than the previous practice, such as no stamp, receipt or visible artefact compared with a paper form.
Prototype improved signals and test them with 5 to 8 users for perceived duration and satisfaction, or A/B test in production on completion rate and post-task satisfaction.
Report changes with measured effects and add progress-signal standards to the design system.
outputs: An inventory of progress signals with issues against reference points, prototype alternatives, and measured effects on completion and satisfaction.
useWhen: Long or multi-step flows have mid-flow abandonment; digital processes replace tangible paper rituals; completion screens fail to generate satisfaction.
avoidWhen: Flows are short single-step actions; focus on response time and feedback latency instead.
whyLost: Progress bars are designed as visual components, and the behavioural research on reference points and perceived progress has not been turned into a standard audit in UX practice.
whereToUse: Onboarding and KYC flows, insurance claims, loan applications, learning products, health data entry, long AI generation tasks.
example: Health workers felt less satisfied submitting a digital form than a paper one, because paper ended with a stamped carbon copy. The audit found the success screen offered only a small tick; adding a reference number, a day's tally and a shareable receipt increased post-task satisfaction scores.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Nunes, J. C., & Drèze, X. (2006). The endowed progress effect: How artificial advancement increases effort. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(4), 504–512; Kivetz, R., Urminsky, O., & Zheng, Y. (2006). The goal-gradient hypothesis resurrected. Journal of Marketing Research, 43(1), 39–58.

name: Project structure for reproducible research
origin: Noble (2009) on organising computational biology projects; Cookiecutter Data Science template (DrivenData, 2016)
summary: A standard, templated folder layout that separates raw data, processed data, code, notebooks and outputs so any UX study can be rerun and audited.
description: A reproducible project structure encodes good practice in the file system. Raw data is immutable and read-only; every processed file is regenerated by code; notebooks, source code, figures and reports each have a fixed home; and a README states how to rebuild results end to end. Templating the layout (for example with cookiecutter) means every study in a research organisation looks the same, so colleagues can audit, reuse and hand over work. The rigour comes from the directional flow (raw to interim to processed to outputs), from relative paths via pathlib rather than hard-coded personal paths, and from a single entry point (a Makefile or pipeline script) that reproduces every figure.
steps: Generate each new study from a shared cookiecutter template rather than an empty folder.
Place original exports (survey files, transcripts, logs) in data/raw and make them read-only; never edit them by hand.
Write all transformations as code that reads from data/raw and writes to data/interim or data/processed.
Keep notebooks in notebooks/, reusable functions in src/, and generated figures and tables in reports/.
Use pathlib with paths relative to the project root, never absolute personal paths.
Provide one command (e.g. make all) that rebuilds every reported output from raw data, and test it before delivery.
Document data sources, consent constraints and the rebuild command in the README.
outputs: A consistent project skeleton, immutable raw data, a rebuild command and a README that lets anyone regenerate the findings.
useWhen: Any multi-week quantitative or computational qualitative study, research repositories shared across a team, and studies that will be reused or audited.
avoidWhen: Overkill for a single afternoon's ad hoc chart; a dated, documented notebook is enough there.
whyLost: UX research organisations invested in insight repositories for findings but not in reproducible structures for the analyses that produce them.
whereToUse: Research operations, tracking studies, survey programmes, log analysis and AI-assisted qualitative pipelines.
example: A fintech research team adopts a template for all studies. When an auditor asks how a reported 12-point SUS improvement was computed, the team reruns make all from the raw export and reproduces the figure exactly.
sources: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
Noble, W. S. (2009) A quick guide to organizing computational biology projects. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Noble, W. S. (2009) A quick guide to organizing computational biology projects. PLOS Computational Biology 5(7)

name: Projective Techniques
aka: Projective techniques (picture/animal boards, sentence completion, TAT, word association, brand personification)
Projective question types for focus groups
Sentence completion for emotions and values
donor: Clinical and personality psychology; market research
origin: Jung (word association); Murray and Morgan (TAT, 1930s); adapted for market research and focus groups (Krueger, 1998)
summary: Indirect prompts (animal boards, sentence stems, personification, picture stories, word association) let people project attitudes onto a frame, surfacing associations they would not state directly.
description: Projective techniques ask people to respond to an ambiguous or indirect frame instead of a direct question, on the premise that attitudes, motives and feelings are partly outside awareness or socially awkward to state. Formats include sentence completion ('using the app is...'), personification ('if this website were a person, who would it be?'), analogy and fantasy questions, picture storytelling (the TAT asks for a story about each ambiguous picture), word association, and boards of locally meaningful animals matched to products or institutions. Comparative variants test brand fit: participants personify the organisation and then the product, or build one collage for the brand and another after using the product, and mismatches point at the product parts responsible. Rigour depends on locally piloted stimuli, writing answers before discussion, a coding scheme with trained coders and inter-rater checks, and treating results as prompts for probing rather than diagnoses.
steps: Choose one or two formats that fit the question: sentence stems, personification, animal or picture board, picture stories or word association.
Prepare stimuli and pilot them locally, checking what images or animals mean in the participants' culture.
Write stems or prompts covering the domain and, indirectly, the product (for example 'when my routine is interrupted, I feel...', 'to me the app means...').
Have each person answer individually, ideally in writing, before any group discussion.
Probe the qualities, images and words that come up: why that animal, that person, that ending.
Code responses with a predefined scheme (emotions, values, motive imagery, tone) using two coders and an agreement check.
For brand fit, run the same projective question for the brand and the product and locate the causes of mismatches.
Look for associations repeated across participants or groups and validate them with other methods.
outputs: Associations, metaphors and emotional descriptors for products, brands or institutions; coded themes; lists of brand-product mismatches and candidate design changes.
useWhen: People are unlikely to state feelings directly (cross-cultural or hierarchical settings, trust, status, embarrassment), or you need the emotional or brand meaning of a product.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural evidence or precise measurement; answers are easily over-read and some participants find the formats silly. Use observation, usability testing or validated scales instead. Claims about the unconscious are contested.
whyLost: Projective prompts survive as focus-group icebreakers, but the scoring schemes, local piloting and coder checks that made them rigorous were dropped, and clinical projective tests fell out of favour.
whereToUse: Brand and concept research, financial services and trust in emerging markets, emotional design, and tone-of-voice work for AI assistants.
example: In rural Kenya a team shows a board of local animals and asks which fits each money service. The bank is an elephant, strong and safe, while mobile money is a cheetah, fast but liable to attack from behind, which opens a discussion of distrust that leads to new feature concepts.
sources: Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
reference: Krueger, R. A. (1998). Developing Questions for Focus Groups. Sage; Murray, H. A. (1943). Thematic Apperception Test. Harvard University Press.

name: Prompt UX Research
origin: Grew from conversational UI research (2016 onwards) and generative AI product practice from 2022
summary: Research on prompt-driven interfaces that tests how people discover capabilities, form mental models of the AI, phrase requests and recover from poor outputs.
description: Prompt UX research addresses the 'blank box' problem of generative and conversational interfaces: users must guess what the system can do and how to ask. It studies capability discoverability, the mental models people form about the model's knowledge and limits, prompt formulation strategies, iteration and repair after unsatisfactory outputs, and trust calibration. Typical designs combine task-based sessions with think-aloud, analysis of logged prompt sequences (reformulation rate, turns to success, abandonment), and mental-model elicitation before and after use. Rigour comes from realistic open tasks rather than scripted prompts, coding prompt logs against an intent and repair taxonomy, and distinguishing failures of the model from failures of the interface such as missing suggestions, poor affordances or unclear scope.
steps: Define the core user intents and the capability boundaries you want users to discover.
Elicit prior mental models: ask 6-12 participants what they expect the assistant can and cannot do before first use.
Run open-ended task sessions with think-aloud, letting participants phrase requests in their own words.
