Log every prompt, response and reformulation, and code them for intent, strategy, repair type and outcome.
Compute behavioural indicators from logs at scale: reformulation rate, turns to success, abandonment after first response, use of suggested prompts.
Re-elicit mental models after use, compare with actual capabilities, and identify interface changes such as starter prompts, scoping cues or examples.
outputs: Intent and repair taxonomy, prompt-log metrics, mental-model gaps, and interface recommendations for discoverability and recovery.
useWhen: Designing or improving chat assistants, copilots, AI search and any interface where the main input is free-form natural language.
avoidWhen: When the issue is output quality rather than interaction (use LLM evaluation), or when the feature is not yet built (use Wizard of Oz prototyping).
whyLost: Still in use: New discipline emerging rapidly with LLM adoption.
whereToUse: Chatbots; AI copilots; prompt-based tools; AI search interfaces.
example: A spreadsheet copilot's logs show 38% of first prompts are abandoned after one reply. Sessions reveal users think the assistant cannot see their data; adding a visible 'Using: Sheet1, rows 1-500' scope chip halves first-turn abandonment.
sources: Amershi et al., Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019)
reference: Amershi S et al. (2019) Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. CHI 2019

name: Propensity Score Matching
origin: Paul Rosenbaum and Donald Rubin, 1983
summary: Balances treated and untreated users on observed covariates via their estimated probability of treatment, approximating a randomised comparison from observational data.
description: Listed in the treatise's causal inference curriculum and its borrowing matrix, propensity score methods estimate each unit's probability of receiving treatment given observed covariates, then match, stratify or weight so that treated and comparison groups are balanced. Rosenbaum and Rubin showed that conditioning on the propensity score suffices to remove bias from observed confounders. Its limit is fundamental: it cannot correct for unobserved confounders, so sensitivity analysis (for example Rosenbaum bounds or E-values) is essential, and covariates must be chosen with a causal model, avoiding post-treatment variables. In UX it suits comparisons between users who did and did not adopt a feature when an experiment was not run.
steps: Define treatment, outcome and pre-treatment covariates using a DAG.
Estimate propensity scores with logistic regression or a flexible model.
Match, stratify or weight, and check covariate balance (standardised differences below 0.1).
Trim units outside common support.
Estimate the effect on the balanced sample.
Run sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding and report it.
outputs: Balance diagnostics, effect estimate, sensitivity analysis.
useWhen: Observational comparisons of adopters versus non-adopters with rich pre-treatment data.
avoidWhen: When key confounders (motivation, intent) are unmeasured and no sensitivity analysis is possible.
whyLost: Common in tech data science teams and health research, but rarely in UX research, which leaves causal claims to experimentation teams.
whereToUse: Feature adoption impact, accessibility settings outcomes, programme evaluations of onboarding calls.
example: Users who joined a webinar retained 25% better; after matching on prior activity and plan, the gap shrinks to 6%, with an E-value showing modest robustness.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rosenbaum PR & Rubin DB (1983) The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika 70(1):41-55
Austin PC (2011) An introduction to propensity score methods. Multivariate Behav Res
Rosenbaum, P. R. & Rubin, D. B. (1983) The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika
Hernán, M. A. & Robins, J. M. (2020) Causal Inference: What If
King, G. & Nielsen, R. (2019) Why propensity scores should not be used for matching. Political Analysis
The Inquiry Series, C5 — Causal Inference in Python — DAGs, Target Trial Emulation & Sensitivity Analysis
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
reference: Rosenbaum PR & Rubin DB (1983) The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika 70(1):41-55.

name: Prospect Theory Application
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1979
summary: Applies prospect theory's reference dependence, loss aversion and probability weighting to design and test how options, prices and risks are presented.
description: Prospect theory describes choice under risk with three core features: outcomes are evaluated as gains or losses relative to a reference point; losses weigh roughly twice as much as equivalent gains; and small probabilities are overweighted while moderate-to-high ones are underweighted. In UX it becomes a method for systematically analysing and testing the presentation of choices. Analysts identify the reference point users bring to a decision, the framing of each option as gain or loss, and how probabilities are communicated, then design alternative framings and test their effects on choice and comprehension. Rigour lies in predicting direction of effect from the theory before testing, using between-subjects designs to avoid contrast effects, and measuring both choice and understanding so that persuasive framings do not reduce informed decision-making.
steps: Identify the decision, the options and the reference point users are likely to hold.
Classify current presentation of each option as gain or loss framed, and note how probabilities are shown.
Write predictions from prospect theory for alternative framings (e.g. loss framing increases uptake of protective options).
Build between-subjects variants differing only in framing.
Test with an online sample or live A/B test large enough to detect a 5-point difference (typically several hundred per arm).
Measure choice and comprehension, and reject framings that raise uptake but lower understanding.
outputs: Framing analysis of current design, theory-derived predictions, experimental choice and comprehension results.
useWhen: Pricing pages, insurance and protection add-ons, subscription cancellation, health risk communication and financial products.
avoidWhen: Low-stakes choices without uncertainty or clear reference points; and where framing would be used to push choices against user interest.
whyLost: Latent: Theory widely cited; systematic UX application remains rare.
whereToUse: Pricing UI; risk communication; insurance/financial products; subscription cancellation design.
example: An insurer tested 'Protect your £600 phone' against 'Avoid losing £600 if your phone breaks'. The loss frame lifted add-on uptake by 4 points but comprehension of the excess fell, so the team combined loss framing with an explicit excess statement.
reference: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263-291.

name: Prospective memory audit
origin: Prospective memory research by Einstein and McDaniel, 1990; applied to aviation and medicine by Dismukes (2012)
summary: Identifies every point where users must remember to perform an action later and evaluates whether the design provides cues to prevent forgotten intentions.
description: Prospective memory is remembering to carry out an intended action in the future: event-based (when X happens, do Y) or time-based (at 3 pm, do Y). Failures are a major source of errors in aviation and medicine, often triggered by interruptions, task switching and the absence of salient cues at the moment of action. A prospective memory audit lists each deferred intention a workflow creates (for example 'resume the infusion after the scan', 'save before closing', 'complete the second signature'), classifies its type, measures the delay and interruptions between intention and action, and checks whether a cue is present at the right moment. Dismukes' work shows that distinctive, well-timed cues and forcing functions dramatically reduce these errors.
steps: Map workflows to identify every deferred intention, including those created by interruptions.
Classify each as event-based or time-based and estimate the delay and likelihood of interruptions in between.
Check for a cue at the moment of action: is there a reminder, a visible pending state, or a forcing function?
Mine incident reports, support logs or observation notes for forgotten actions and match them to intentions.
Rate risk using delay length, interruption likelihood, cue absence and consequence severity.
Design cues (pending-state indicators, reminders, checklists, forcing functions) and test with 6-10 users including an interruption manipulation.
outputs: An inventory of deferred intentions with risk ratings, incident linkage, and cue or forcing-function designs.
useWhen: In workflows with interruptions, handovers or deferred steps; in safety-critical or compliance-heavy processes.
avoidWhen: For single-session tasks completed without delay; use working memory audits or standard usability testing.
whyLost: Prospective memory is a well-developed research area in aviation and medicine but UX rarely thinks in these terms, framing such failures as user forgetfulness.
whereToUse: Clinical workflows, surgical robot setup, banking (scheduled transfers), project management tools, and AI agents that hand tasks back to users.
example: An audit of a robotic surgery workflow finds the intention 'recalibrate camera after port change' has no cue; it is missed in 1 in 9 cases. A pending-task badge on the camera view eliminates misses in simulation.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 10 — Memory — The Architecture of Knowledge
reference: Dismukes, R. K. (2012). Prospective memory in workplace and everyday situations. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 21(4), 215-220.

name: Protocol-Aided Document Evaluation (Schriver)
origin: Karen Schriver, 1991-1997 (Carnegie Mellon Document Design Center)
summary: Captures readers' real-time processing of a document through think-aloud protocols to locate comprehension failures and predict revisions that improve understanding.
description: Document design research studied how the visual organisation of text and graphics affects comprehension and usability, and by the 1980s had rigorous methods for testing comprehension, navigation and recall. The treatise singles out Karen Schriver's Dynamics in Document Design (1997) and its protocol-based evaluation methods, in which readers' processing of a document is captured in real time, as far more sophisticated than anything routinely used in content UX. In protocol-aided revision, representative readers think aloud while reading a draft; analysts code points of confusion, misreading and inference, then revise. Schriver showed that writers trained with reader protocols became markedly better at predicting readers' problems. The treatise notes content decisions today are driven by brand guidelines and intuition rather than empirical understanding of how audiences process content.
steps: Select representative readers, including low-literacy and non-native readers where relevant.
Have each read the document or content flow while thinking aloud, with comprehension questions after.
Transcribe and code protocols for misreadings, inference gaps, skipped sections and navigation problems.
Locate each problem in the text and categorise by cause (wording, structure, visual hierarchy, graphics).
Revise and re-test with new readers.
Measure comprehension and task accuracy before and after.
outputs: Coded reader protocols, located comprehension problems, revised content, comprehension metrics.
useWhen: Consent forms, instructions, policy content, financial disclosures, medical information, onboarding copy.
avoidWhen: Microcopy where A/B testing with behavioural outcomes is cheaper and sufficient.
whyLost: Document design was absorbed into technical communication and never integrated with UX content practice.
whereToUse: Terms and consent UX, insurance policy documents, medication leaflets, AI output explanations, regulatory disclosures.
example: Reader protocols on a pension transfer warning show readers interpret 'guaranteed benefits' as guaranteed growth; revision and retest raise correct comprehension from 41% to 83%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Schriver KA (1997) Dynamics in Document Design: Creating Texts for Readers
Schriver KA (1991) Plain language through protocol-aided revision. In Plain Language: Principles and Practice
De Jong M & Schellens PJ (1997) Reader-focused text evaluation. J Business and Technical Communication
Modern Awards User Experience Research Report (Wallis Market and Social Research, 2021)
reference: Schriver KA (1997) Dynamics in Document Design. Wiley.

name: Prototype / Wizard-of-Oz A/B Test
origin: Wizard-of-Oz technique: J. F. Kelley, 1984
summary: A randomised comparison of design variants using prototypes or human-simulated systems, measuring the same task and metrics as a live A/B test when shipping code is impossible.
description: The randomised A/B test is the gold standard for proving a design change caused improvement, but it needs shipped code and traffic. When shipping is impossible, Vivek Gopinath's playbook runs the comparison on low-fidelity prototypes or Wizard-of-Oz simulations with the same task and metrics. In the worked example, 600 participants are randomised to the old or new IA for 'Create a price alert for stock ABC', logging time to completion or abandonment, error type and clicks; completion rises from 62% to 81%, median completion time falls from 214s to 182s and median abandonment time rises from 46s to 71s. Decision bars and guardrails are set upfront and results feed a Cox survival model.
steps: Set decision bars and guardrails before the test (e.g. completion ≥ 80%, HR ≤ 0.80, no error increase elsewhere).
Build control and variant prototypes (or a Wizard-of-Oz simulation) that differ only in the change under test.
Randomise participants to arms with adequate sample size (the example uses N = 600).
Run the identical task and log completion or abandonment time, error types and clicks.
Compare completion, median completion time and median abandonment time, and fit a survival model.
Issue a verdict against the bars and plan a confirmatory live test.
outputs: Arm-level outcome comparison, survival inputs and a decision bar verdict.
useWhen: When a change must be tested causally before engineering investment, or live traffic is too low or risky.
avoidWhen: When prototype fidelity would distort behaviour (e.g. real money or real latency matters); confirm with a live test.
whyLost: A/B testing survives because it is the clearest causal tool; prototype variants are less used but well known.
whereToUse: IA changes, onboarding concepts, AI assistant concepts simulated by humans, fintech flows.
example: A trading app tests a new alerts IA on prototypes with 600 randomised participants and sees completion rise from 62% to 81% before writing any production code.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Kelley, J. F. (1984). An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 2(1), 26–41.

name: Prototype Fidelity Validation Study
aka: Prototype fidelity validation against a real product (Equinox study)
origin: Gill et al. (2008), Equinox study; Hare's Flickr Friend prototypes
summary: Build prototypes of an existing product at several fidelities, run identical trials on each and on the real product, and see which fidelity reproduces real-product results.
description: Prototype testing assumes the prototype behaves like the eventual product. This study tests that assumption by using an existing product as a datum. Gill and colleagues took the Equinox phone and built a high-fidelity prototype (real mouldings plus interactive electronics and a Flash interface), a low-fidelity foam 'sketch' prototype, and a touchscreen-only software prototype, then ran identical user trials on all and on the real phone. Tangible prototypes behaved like the real phone while the software-only one did not; a picture-on-block version failed because button edges could not be felt. The low-fidelity tangible prototype took about 80 per cent less build time yet matched the real phone better than software. The result is evidence-based guidance on which fidelity dimensions matter for a product class.
steps: Choose an existing product, similar to the one being designed, as the datum.
Build prototypes that vary physical and visual fidelity independently (for example foam with real buttons, screen-only, full mock-up).
Run identical tasks and measures with comparable participants on each prototype and the real product.
Compare each prototype's results (errors, times, ratings) with the real product's.
Derive fidelity guidance, such as medium visual with high physical fidelity, for future prototyping.
outputs: Evidence on which fidelity dimensions reproduce real-product behaviour, and fidelity guidance for the product class.
useWhen: A team prototypes physical, embedded or multimodal products and needs to know how far to trust cheap prototypes, or before a large programme of prototype testing.
avoidWhen: No comparable existing product exists to serve as a datum, or the product is purely screen-based and screen prototypes are already faithful.
whyLost: It was a one-off research study; practitioners choose prototype fidelity by convention rather than by validation.
whereToUse: Consumer electronics, medical devices, automotive controls, wearables, voice and multimodal devices.
example: A medical-device team compares a 3D-printed infusion pump shell with real buttons, a tablet simulation and the current pump. The printed shell reproduces button-press errors seen on the real pump; the tablet does not.
reference: Dix, A., Gill, S., Ramduny-Ellis, D., & Hare, J. (2022). TouchIT: Understanding Design in a Physical-Digital World. Oxford University Press, pp. 460-468.

name: Prototype Testing
origin: Paper prototyping in HCI, 1980s to 1990s; Snyder (2003)
summary: Evaluates low to high fidelity prototypes with users to test concepts, flows and interactions before committing to full implementation.
description: Prototype testing puts representations of a design, from paper sketches and clickable wireframes to high-fidelity interactive prototypes, in front of users to learn whether the concept and interaction work before building. The fidelity should match the question: low-fidelity prototypes invite feedback on concepts and structure, while high-fidelity prototypes test details such as visual hierarchy and microcopy. Its value lies in cheap, fast learning that reduces costly rework. Rigour comes from defining what the prototype must answer, making sure the critical paths work, using realistic content and data, framing sessions as tests of the design not the participant, and avoiding treating enthusiasm for a concept as evidence of future use.
steps: Define the questions the prototype must answer and choose a fidelity that fits them.
Build the prototype covering the critical paths with realistic content.
Write task scenarios and questions focused on those paths.
Test with 5 to 8 participants per round, moderated or unmoderated.
Record where the concept or interaction breaks down and why.
Iterate the prototype and test again, ideally in rapid cycles.
outputs: Evidence about concept comprehension and interaction problems, iterated designs and reduced implementation risk.
useWhen: Any design project, especially early before significant development investment, and when comparing alternative concepts.
avoidWhen: Avoid using prototype reactions to forecast adoption or demand; use experiments or market tests. Avoid when the experience depends on real data or performance the prototype cannot mimic.
whyLost: Still in use: Core design validation method; enables fast learning before expensive development.
whereToUse: Any design project; most valuable early in the process before costly commits.
example: An AI note-taking startup tests a clickable prototype of meeting summaries with seven managers. Most distrust summaries without links to transcript moments, so source links become a core feature before engineering begins.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Snyder C (2003) Paper Prototyping: The Fast and Easy Way to Design and Refine User Interfaces
Rettig M (1994) Prototyping for tiny fingers. CACM 37(4)
Snyder, Paper Prototyping: The Fast and Easy Way to Design and Refine User Interfaces (2003)
Rettig, Prototyping for tiny fingers (1994), Communications of the ACM
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish, 1999)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
reference: Snyder, C. (2003). Paper Prototyping: The Fast and Easy Way to Design and Refine User Interfaces. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Prototype-Scenario Reconstruction from Conventional Expressions
aka: Cognitive model of an emotion concept
origin: Adapted for UX from George Lakoff and Zoltán Kövecses's analysis of anger (in Lakoff, 1987), using Lakoff and Johnson's (1980) metaphor techniques
summary: Collect everyday expressions for a concept, find the metonymies and metaphors they share, and assemble them into a staged prototypical scenario whose minimal variants explain the concept's other forms.
description: Lakoff and Kövecses started from about three hundred thesaurus entries for anger. They noted the inferences speakers draw between idioms, stated the folk theory of anger's physiological effects (heat, pressure, agitation, impaired perception), grouped expressions as metonymies of those effects, and identified metaphors such as anger as hot fluid in a container with their entailments. These converge on a five-stage prototypical scenario: offending event, anger, attempt at control, loss of control, retribution. Non-prototypical kinds are then described as minimal differences from the prototype, each naming the stage that changes, with example sentences: redirected, frustrated, controlled, suppressed, immediate explosion and others. Adapted for UX, the same procedure can reconstruct a cultural folk model of concepts such as 'saving', 'privacy' or 'being in control' from how users talk, giving a staged script against which experiences and messaging can be designed.
steps: Collect conventional expressions for the concept from thesauri, corpora, reviews, support tickets or interviews.
Note the inferences that link expressions to one another.
State the folk theory of the concept's causes and effects and sort expressions as metonymies of those effects.
Identify the conceptual metaphors and their entailments.
Assemble metaphors and metonymies into a staged prototypical scenario and list the entities it requires.
Describe each non-prototypical case as a minimal variant, naming the stage that differs and giving example expressions.
outputs: A staged prototypical scenario for the concept and a catalogue of recognised variants, each tied to example expressions.
useWhen: Understanding the cultural model behind an emotionally loaded concept your product touches, such as debt, privacy, trust or frustration, before designing flows, messages or support scripts.
avoidWhen: It describes a folk model, not a scientific one, and several models may coexist across cultures; validate with users. For identifying metaphors in a text use Metaphor Identification Procedure (MIP/MIPVU); for eliciting personal metaphors use Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET).
whyLost: It is a cognitive linguistics case study rather than a packaged method, and UX metaphor work has focused on interface metaphors rather than users' folk models of concepts.
whereToUse: Personal finance, health and mental-wellbeing products, customer complaint handling, AI assistants that must respond to user emotion.
example: A debt-advice service collects 400 phrases customers use about debt ('drowning', 'getting on top of it', 'buried in bills'). The reconstructed scenario has stages from overwhelm to regaining control, and the onboarding is reworked to meet users at the 'drowning' stage before offering plans.
reference: Lakoff, G. (1987). Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things: What Categories Reveal about the Mind. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, Case study 1, pp. 380-415; Lakoff, G. and Johnson, M. (1980). Metaphors We Live By. University of Chicago Press.

name: Prove Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 3: Prove with Experiments and Causal Models
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 3 of the forward-thinking loop: show a design change caused improvement using A/B tests, Cox survival models, QCA and counterfactual probing, with fallbacks when randomisation is impossible.
description: Proving answers 'Did our change cause improvement, or was it coincidence?' by showing that changing X changes Y and ruling out chance, seasonality and user mix. The playbook gives a selection rule: randomised A/B as gold standard; prototype or Wizard-of-Oz A/B when shipping code is impossible; Cox proportional hazards when the question is when users abandon, not just whether; Rubin's potential outcomes with matched cohorts when randomisation is impossible; Bradford Hill criteria as a principled checklist for observational data. Small-N moderated data are analysed with crisp-set QCA for sufficient condition combinations, and counterfactual probing in interviews explains the mechanism behind the hazard ratio. Decision bars are set upfront (completion ≥ 80%, HR ≤ 0.80, no error increase elsewhere). Rigour includes testing the proportional hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residuals and always checking guardrails.
steps: Set decision bars before the test, e.g. completion ≥ 80% (up from 62%), hazard ratio of abandonment ≤ 0.80, and no increase in error rates elsewhere.
Randomise participants to control and variant (the worked example uses N = 600) on the same task, logging time to completion or abandonment, error type and clicks.
Compare completion, median completion time and median abandonment time between arms (62% vs 81%; 214s vs 182s; 46s vs 71s).
Fit a Cox model h(t|X) = h0(t)·exp(β1·Variant + β2·SNR + β3·Mistake rate), report HRs with 95% CIs, and test proportional hazards with Schoenfeld residuals.
For small moderated samples, run crisp-set QCA on calibrated conditions (e.g. Low SNR, High Mistakes, High TLX, Timed OTP) to find sufficient paths to abandonment.
Use counterfactual probing in interviews to explain the mechanism, and write mechanism memos linking the QCA path, quotes and HRs.
If randomisation is impossible, match cohorts under the Rubin model to estimate ATE and use Bradford Hill criteria (temporality, strength, consistency, plausibility) as a narrative check.
Deliver the A/B table, Cox table, mechanism quotes, guardrail checks and a decision bar verdict.
outputs: A/B results, Cox hazard ratio table with CIs, QCA solution, mechanism quotes and a pass/fail verdict against pre-set bars.
useWhen: When a fix must be shown to cause improvement before rollout, and when timing of abandonment matters.
avoidWhen: When traffic or prototypes are unavailable and no comparison cohort exists; then use Bradford Hill as a confidence checklist rather than claiming proof.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; causal and survival methods are standard in medicine but rarely joined to qual mechanism work in UX.
whereToUse: Onboarding, checkout and KYC funnels, alert creation, any flow where abandonment timing matters.
example: A new IA for price alerts lifts completion from 62% to 81%; the Cox model gives HR 0.68 [0.59, 0.77] for the variant, HR 0.92 per +0.10 SNR and HR 1.28 per extra mistake per minute, and QCA shows Low SNR * High Mistakes is sufficient for abandonment.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 3.

name: Provocative Scenarios and Extreme Characters
origin: Pastiche: Blythe and Wright (2006); caricature: Bødker, Nielsen and Petersen (2000); extreme characters: Djajadiningrat, Gaver and Frens (2000)
summary: Fictional or exaggerated scenarios and characters, such as Scrooge meeting a smart meter, used to provoke design teams into discussing social and cultural consequences of a concept.
description: These techniques treat scenarios as containers of ideas and tools for dialogue rather than distillations of fact. Pastiche scenarios place well-known fictional characters in front of a proposed technology; because readers already know how Scrooge or Bart Simpson thinks, they can imagine responses that a bland persona would never prompt. Caricature scenarios exaggerate a design's benefits and its problems so far that both enthusiasts and sceptics are pushed to question their positions, making key design points more salient. Extreme characters are invented users with exaggerated emotional attitudes (a drug dealer's phone, a pope's diary) that open aesthetic and cultural possibilities. All three deliberately depart from the factual scenarios of scenario-based design, and are best used for exploring the social, ethical and cultural issues an innovation raises.
steps: State the technology concept and the social or cultural questions you want to open up.
Choose two to four devices: familiar fictional characters (pastiche), exaggerated best and worst cases (caricature), or invented users with extreme emotional attitudes.
Write short scenarios in which each character meets and uses the concept, staying true to the character's known personality.
Write a paired optimistic and pessimistic caricature of the same use.
Read the scenarios aloud in a team or stakeholder session and discuss how each character responds and what issues surface.
Record the issues raised and turn them into design questions or requirements to investigate.
outputs: A set of provocative scenarios and a list of social, cultural and ethical issues and design possibilities they surfaced.
useWhen: Use them early, when a team's thinking about a concept is narrow or uncritically optimistic, especially for technologies with social consequences (surveillance, care, AI agents).
avoidWhen: They generate questions, not evidence about real users; follow up with Interviews, Ethnographic Research or Speculative and Design Fiction Research with participants. Avoid when stakeholders need factual scenarios for requirements, where Scenario-Based Design is the right tool.
whyLost: They stayed largely in academic interaction design and experience-centred design research; mainstream practice prefers persona-based scenarios that look evidential.
whereToUse: AI products, smart home and care technologies, civic tech, and ethics reviews of new features.
example: An AI email assistant team writes scenarios in which Sherlock Holmes, a paranoid caricature and an over-trusting caricature each use auto-reply. The discussion surfaces impersonation and consent issues the team then probes in interviews.
reference: Blythe, M. and Wright, P. (2006). Pastiche scenarios: Fiction as a resource for analysing user experience. Interacting with Computers, 18, 1139-1164; Djajadiningrat, J.P., Gaver, W.W. and Frens, J.W. (2000). Interaction relabelling and extreme characters. Proceedings of DIS 2000, pp. 66-71.

name: Proxemic Analysis
origin: Edward T. Hall, 1963-1966 (The Hidden Dimension); proxemic interaction in HCI by Saul Greenberg et al. (2011)
summary: Analyses how distance, orientation, movement and identity between people and devices shape interaction, using Hall's intimate, personal, social and public zones.
description: Hall described culturally variable distance zones: intimate (0-45 cm), personal (45-120 cm), social (1.2-3.6 m) and public (beyond 3.6 m), and how people use space to regulate interaction. Greenberg and colleagues extended proxemics to ubiquitous computing with five dimensions: distance, orientation, movement, identity and location. Rigorous proxemic analysis records spatial configurations through video, floor plans or tracking, codes them, and relates them to interaction behaviours such as privacy management, turn-taking and engagement. It is essential for shared screens, kiosks, voice assistants in homes, AR/VR social spaces, retail and in-car experiences.
steps: Define the setting and the interactions of interest (e.g. sharing a screen, approaching a kiosk).
Record spatial data with overhead video, floor plan notation or sensors, with consent.
Code distance zones, body orientation, movement and identity of actors over time.
Relate spatial configurations to interaction events (initiating use, privacy shielding, disengaging).
Compare across cultures or contexts where zones may differ.
Design proxemic-aware behaviours (e.g. content shifting as people approach) and test them in situ.
outputs: Coded spatial-interaction data, proxemic patterns and design requirements for spatially aware interfaces.
useWhen: Designing for shared, public, ambient or embodied interactions where physical arrangement matters.
avoidWhen: Private single-user screen interactions without spatial variation.
whyLost: Screen-based UX ignored bodies in space; proxemic interaction remained an academic ubicomp topic.
whereToUse: Retail kiosks, ATMs (shoulder surfing), smart displays, AR/VR social apps, hospital bedside devices, cars.
example: At pharmacy kiosks, proxemic coding shows users angle their bodies to shield screens when others enter personal distance; the kiosk adds privacy filters and hides medication names when a second person is detected nearby.
sources: Greenberg et al., Proxemic interactions: The new ubicomp? (2011), ACM Interactions
Marquardt & Greenberg, Proxemic Interactions: From Theory to Practice (2015)
reference: Greenberg, S., et al. (2011). Proxemic interactions: The new ubicomp? ACM Interactions, 18(1), 42-50.

name: Proxemics Applied to Interface Design
origin: Edward T. Hall, 1966; proxemic interaction (Greenberg et al. 2011)
summary: Uses Hall's intimate, personal, social and public zones as a principled model for how intrusive interface elements may be, given the user-system relationship.
description: Hall showed that human interaction is regulated by four spatial zones (intimate 0-45 cm, personal 45 cm-1.2 m, social 1.2-3.6 m, public 3.6 m+), with culturally varying norms, and that violations produce discomfort, distrust and withdrawal. The treatise maps these to interfaces: full-screen takeovers and modals violate the intimate zone and are appropriate only when trust is established; notifications and banners operate in the personal zone, where too many too soon feel like a stranger standing too close. The metaphor makes 'intrusive design' visceral and gives a basis for deciding when and how to intrude. In XR and ubiquitous computing, proxemics applies literally to distances between people, devices and virtual content.
steps: Inventory interface interruptions and content by their zone (modal, overlay, notification, ambient).
Characterise the relationship stage with the user (new, established, trusted) for each touchpoint.
Flag zone violations: intimate-zone intrusions early in the relationship or unrequested.
Research comfort through interviews or experiments varying intrusiveness and timing.
Define a proxemic policy for escalation from public to intimate zones.
In XR, measure physical distances and comfort directly.
outputs: Zone map of interruptions, violation list, proxemic interruption policy.
useWhen: Notification strategy, modal and overlay design, onboarding prompts, AR/VR spatial UI.
avoidWhen: When intrusion is safety-critical and must override comfort (alarms).
whyLost: Anthropological theory never formalised as a UX method; intrusiveness judged by intuition and metrics.
whereToUse: Push notification strategy, mobile density, AR/VR layouts, in-car displays, AI proactive suggestions.
example: A new banking user receives a full-screen upsell on second login; the proxemic policy restricts intimate-zone takeovers until after 30 days or a user-initiated action, reducing early uninstalls.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Greenberg S et al. (2011) Proxemic interactions: the new ubicomp? interactions 18(1)
Müller J et al. (2010) digital proxemics work presented at NordiCHI
reference: Hall ET (1966) The Hidden Dimension. Doubleday.

name: Proxy and Surrogate Participant Research
origin: Industry practice reported by Quesenbery and Szuc (2011) and Moreno de Oliveira et al. (2022)
summary: When real users are unreachable, research stand-in informants such as support staff, internal experts or diaspora communities, then correct for proxy bias and confirm with real users.
description: Proxy research uses people who know the target users well, or resemble them, as informants when direct contact is restricted by contracts, distance, time or budget. Organisational proxies include customer support staff, who talk to users more than anyone else, and product or field staff. Cultural proxies include recent arrivals from the target country, local diaspora communities, internal staff who have worked in the market, and artefacts such as parallel-language versions of sites. Proxy knowledge can feed interviews, questionnaires, proto-personas, journeys and prototype tests. The rigour lies in naming the gap explicitly: proxies do not share users' behaviours and needs, diaspora communities show a 'time capsule' effect of the migration period, and every proxy-derived requirement should be confirmed with real users. One practitioner estimates cultural proxies get you about 20 percent of the way.
steps: Document why direct user contact is not feasible and what decisions the proxy research must support.
Select proxies who interact with or resemble users often: support and product staff, internal market experts, recent migrants, local cultural groups.
Interview proxies (about one hour each), tracking certainties, suppositions and doubts in a matrix until certainties dominate.
Collect artefacts such as target-language sites and parallel-language editions to see how content and layout transform.
Build proto-personas, journeys or scenarios from proxy knowledge and validate priorities with a questionnaire to a wider proxy group.
Record how proxies differ from users (role, acculturation, generation, time since migration) beside each finding.
Confirm proxy-derived requirements with real users through at least one usability test or in-market study before committing.
outputs: Proxy-derived requirements, proto-personas and journeys with explicit bias notes, and confirmation results from real users.
useWhen: Users are contractually, geographically or practically unreachable (B2B customers behind account managers, overseas markets without travel budget) and some evidence beats none.
avoidWhen: Real users can be reached at reasonable cost, or the decision is high-stakes and proxy bias could mislead; do direct interviews or in-market research instead.
whyLost: Proxies are used constantly but informally, usually as a shortcut that replaces users rather than a structured method with bias correction and validation.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise software, admin tools, international and localisation research, healthcare where patients are hard to reach.
example: A B2B e-commerce team cannot reach store administrators, so it interviews support staff, builds a proto-persona and tests a configuration prototype with them, then confirms the requirements in a usability test with five real administrators.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Quesenbery, W., & Szuc, D. (2011). Global UX: Design and Research in a Connected World. Morgan Kaufmann; Moreno de Oliveira, G., et al. (2022). Reporting the application of user experience tools and proxy users in an industrial process based on Double Diamond. DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, Springer.

name: PSSUQ / CSUQ (Post-Study and Computer System Usability Questionnaires)
origin: James R. Lewis at IBM (1992, 1995; version 3 in 2002)
summary: A 16-item IBM questionnaire with subscales for system usefulness, information quality and interface quality.
description: Developed at IBM by Jim Lewis, the PSSUQ is administered after a lab study and the near-identical CSUQ is worded for field surveys. Sixteen seven-point items load on three factors: system usefulness, information quality (error messages, documentation, feedback) and interface quality. Unlike SUS, which gives one score, the PSSUQ's subscales point at where the problem lies, and it has published norms from IBM studies. Lower scores are better, a source of confusion. It has excellent reliability and was among the first usability questionnaires validated with factor analysis.
steps: Administer the 16 items at the end of the session (PSSUQ) or in a survey of users (CSUQ).
Allow N/A responses and average available items.
Compute the overall score and three subscale scores (items 1-6, 7-12, 13-15).
Compare with the published normative means and confidence intervals.
Use subscale differences to direct improvement work.
outputs: An overall usability score plus diagnostic subscales.
useWhen: Enterprise and business software where information quality (messages, help) matters as much as the interface.
avoidWhen: You need a very short instrument or modern web norms (use UMUX-Lite or SUPR-Q).
whyLost: SUS won on brevity and free use; the PSSUQ's IBM origins and reversed scoring made it feel dated.
whereToUse: B2B software, admin consoles, documentation-heavy products.
example: A CRM scores well on interface quality but poorly on information quality, which leads the team to rewrite error messages rather than redesign screens.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Lewis, J. R. (2002). Psychometric evaluation of the PSSUQ using data from five years of usability studies. IJHCI 14.

name: Psychoacoustic Principles in Audio UX Design
origin: Auditory scene analysis by Albert Bregman (1990); earcons by Blattner, Sumikawa and Greenberg (1989)
summary: Designs and evaluates interface sounds using psychoacoustic principles, auditory streaming, masking, urgency mapping and entrainment, testing identification, discrimination and annoyance.
description: Interface sounds are usually chosen by taste, yet psychoacoustics predicts how they will be perceived. Auditory streaming determines whether sounds group or separate based on frequency proximity and timing, which matters when alerts overlap. Masking means sounds in the same frequency band as background noise go unheard. Perceived urgency follows measurable parameters such as pitch, speed and repetition (Edworthy's work on alarm design). Entrainment to rhythm affects pacing and arousal. Earcons (abstract musical motifs) and auditory icons (everyday sounds) differ in learnability. The method specifies sound parameters from these principles, then tests them with listeners for detection in realistic noise, identification accuracy, discriminability within the sound set, urgency ranking and annoyance over repeated exposure. Medical alarm standards show how rigorous this can be.
steps: Apply psychoacoustic principles to audio interface design:
Notification sound design — use auditory streaming principles to ensure notification sounds are perceptually segregated from background audio.
(2) Feedback sound timing — design sounds to arrive within 100ms of the triggering action for psychoacoustic integration.
(3) Alert hierarchy — use increasing harmonic dissonance to signal increasing urgency levels. Measure: can users identify alert priority from sound alone with > 80% accuracy?
outputs: Sound specifications with acoustic parameters, detection and identification accuracy, confusion matrices, urgency rankings and annoyance ratings over exposure.
useWhen: Notification and alert design, voice and audio interfaces, medical devices, automotive, wearables, games and accessibility audio cues.
avoidWhen: When sound is purely decorative and carries no information; standard preference testing suffices.
whyLost: Psychoacoustics stayed in audio engineering, music psychology and alarm standards, while UX teams treated sound as branding handled by sound designers.
whereToUse: Voice assistant audio design, notification sound design, accessibility (visual impairment), spatial audio UX, AR audio design.
example: An infusion pump maker tests eight alarm sounds in recorded ward noise. Two high-priority sounds are confused 30% of the time, and a low-priority chime is rated more urgent than a high-priority alert, so the set is redesigned by urgency parameters.
sources: The Science and Psychology of Music — William Forde Thompson
Edworthy, Loxley & Dennis, Improving auditory warning design (Human Factors, 1991)
reference: Thompson WF (2009) Music, Thought, and Feeling: Understanding the Psychology of Music. Oxford University Press

name: Psychometric Meta-Analysis (Hunter-Schmidt Artifact Correction)
origin: John Hunter and Frank Schmidt, 1977 onwards; Hunter and Schmidt, 2004; Schmidt, Le and Oh, 2009
summary: Correct pooled correlations for measurement error, range restriction and other artifacts to estimate relations between constructs rather than between imperfect measures.
description: Observed correlations understate true relations because of study artifacts. Unsystematic artifacts such as sampling error and data errors average out; at least ten systematic artifacts, notably measurement unreliability and range restriction, attenuate correlations by a multiplier. Psychometric meta-analysis corrects each study individually when artifact values are available, or, when they are not, meta-analyses observed correlations and then corrects the mean and variance using distributions of artifact values. Variance due to sampling error and artifact variation is removed, leaving the residual SD of true correlations, which shows whether a relation generalises. The approach originated in validity generalisation for personnel tests. Without corrections, meta-analytic inputs to path models are biased. The correct type of reliability coefficient must be used: inappropriate coefficients undercorrect.
steps: Gather artifact values (reliabilities of both measures, range-restriction ratios) from the studies or other sources.
If values are available for nearly all studies, correct each correlation and its sampling variance and meta-analyse the corrected values.
Otherwise meta-analyse observed correlations and divide the mean by the mean compound attenuation multiplier.
Correct the variance by removing sampling-error variance and variance due to artifact variation.
Report the corrected mean correlation and the residual SD of true correlations with credibility intervals.
outputs: A corrected mean correlation, the true-score SD, and credibility intervals showing how far the relation generalises.
useWhen: Pooling correlations between UX constructs measured with imperfect scales, such as usability and satisfaction, or a metric and retention, across studies or products.
avoidWhen: Pooling experimental mean differences without reliability data, or when artifact values are unknowable; use standard random-effects meta-analysis and note attenuation.
whyLost: UX rarely pools correlational evidence across studies, and the correction methods stayed in personnel psychology.
whereToUse: Meta-analyses of questionnaire validity (SUS, UMUX, NPS), cross-product metric relationships and research repository synthesis.
example: Pooling 30 studies relating SUS to task success gives an observed mean r of .25. After correcting for SUS reliability and restricted ranges of task difficulty, the estimated construct-level correlation is about .40, with modest residual variation.
sources: The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
reference: Schmidt, F. L., Le, H. & Oh, I.-S. Ch. 17. In Cooper, H., Hedges, L. V., & Valentine, J. C. (Eds.) (2009). The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Russell Sage Foundation.

name: Psychometric Network Analysis
origin: Developed over the past fifteen years by the Psychosystems group in Amsterdam and others; summarised in Isvoranu et al. (2022), Network Psychometrics with R.
summary: Estimating a network in which questionnaire items are nodes and edges are partial correlations, to see how individual beliefs, feelings and behaviours reinforce each other instead of assuming they reflect one latent factor.
description: Survey analysis in UX usually assumes that items reflect a common latent cause, such as satisfaction or trust, and sums them. Network psychometrics treats the items themselves as interacting components. A Gaussian graphical model (or an Ising model for binary items, or a mixed graphical model for mixed data) estimates conditional associations between every pair of items after controlling for all others, usually with regularisation to remove spurious edges. The network is visualised, central items are identified with measures such as strength, betweenness or bridge centrality, communities of items are detected, and networks from different groups are compared with permutation tests or bootstrapping. The book stresses the limits: cross-sectional networks are descriptive, not causal; missing nodes distort results; self-report dominates; and replicability needs stability checks. For UX researchers the method shows which perceptions are hubs (for example whether 'feels in control' links usability and trust items), how attitude structures differ between segments, and which components might be worth targeting.
steps: Select items that each measure a distinct belief, feeling or behaviour and avoid near-duplicate wording that creates trivial edges.
Collect a large sample and choose the estimator matching the data type (Gaussian graphical model, Ising model or mixed graphical model).
Estimate a regularised network and visualise it.
Compute centrality and detect communities of items.
Check edge and centrality stability with bootstrapping before interpreting.
Compare networks across segments or time with a network comparison test and report the findings as associations, not causes.
outputs: A network diagram of survey items with edge weights, centrality indices, item communities, stability estimates and between-group comparisons.
useWhen: You have multi-item attitude, trust or experience survey data and want to understand how components relate, or suspect that a single summed score hides structure.
avoidWhen: The sample is small relative to the number of items, items are redundant, or the question requires causal claims from cross-sectional data.
whyLost: UX survey practice relies on summed scales and factor analysis; network methods spread mainly through clinical psychology and need R tooling and care to avoid over-interpreting unstable edges.
whereToUse: Trust and attitude surveys, technology acceptance studies, satisfaction and loyalty drivers, wellbeing and digital-stress questionnaires.
example: A banking app collects 18 items on security, convenience, control and anxiety from 2,500 users. The network shows 'I understand what the app does with my money' as a hub bridging the convenience and anxiety clusters, and the network for older users has much stronger anxiety links, which shapes the research agenda for explanatory messaging.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Psychophysical Threshold Methods (JND)
origin: Gustav Fechner (1860); Ernst Weber (1834); adaptive staircases (Levitt 1971)
summary: Measures detection and discrimination thresholds for interface parameters (contrast, size, latency, haptics) using controlled stimulus variation.
description: The treatise's quantitative curriculum includes psychophysics methods. Classical procedures (method of limits, adjustment, constant stimuli) and adaptive staircases estimate the absolute threshold for detecting a stimulus and the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli. Weber's law states the JND is roughly a constant proportion of the baseline. In UX these answer questions designers usually settle by opinion: how much latency users notice, how large a contrast difference is perceptible, what haptic intensity is felt, how much a progress bar must move to look like progress. Results give defensible parameter thresholds for design systems and performance budgets.
steps: Choose the parameter and a stimulus range spanning undetectable to clearly detectable.
Select a procedure: constant stimuli for precision, adaptive staircase for efficiency.
Run a forced-choice task (for example two-interval: which was faster?) with 15-30 participants.
Fit a psychometric function per participant and estimate threshold (for example 75% correct).
Aggregate thresholds and examine variation by device or population.
Set design or performance budgets below the detection threshold where invisibility is desired.
outputs: Psychometric functions, thresholds and JNDs, parameter guidance.
useWhen: Latency budgets, animation timing, contrast and colour, haptics, audio cues, compression quality.
avoidWhen: Questions about meaning or preference rather than perception.
whyLost: UX dropped experimental perception research in favour of guidelines and A/B tests.
whereToUse: Performance engineering, design tokens, XR rendering, wearables haptics, video streaming quality.
example: A staircase study finds users detect added input latency at about 70 ms on touch scrolling, setting the platform's performance budget.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Gescheider GA (1997) Psychophysics: The Fundamentals. 3rd ed
Levitt H (1971) Transformed up-down methods in psychoacoustics. JASA
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Gescheider GA (1997) Psychophysics: The Fundamentals. 3rd ed. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Public display interaction observation
origin: Ihara, Adachi and Watanabe (2017) adapting AIDA; Dix and colleagues on public interaction roles
summary: Observe passers-by at a public installation, count how many reach each stage from noticing to acting, and map the roles of performer, audience and bystander.
description: Public technologies fail first at noticing and approaching, not at use, so ordinary usability tests miss most of the loss. The AIDA approach treats uptake as a funnel: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action. Problems are anticipated per stage before deployment; then, in a real public space with unrecruited people, an observer counts those passing, stopping, trying and succeeding, supported by system logs, and stage-to-stage conversion locates the drop-off. The role analysis complements it: people around an interaction become performers (sometimes unwitting), audience, bystanders or passers-by. Designers decide which transitions to encourage (the honeypot effect) or prevent, classify interaction and information as public or private, and check whether the performer wants to be seen against whether others want to see, exposing privacy and intrusion risks.
steps: Before deployment, map anticipated problems to each AIDA stage and to each role around the installation.
Deploy in a real public space without recruiting or instructing people.
Have a seated observer count people passing, stopping, trying and succeeding over defined periods, and collect system logs in parallel.
Compute stage-to-stage conversion and note the behaviours behind each drop-off.
Map who acts as performer, audience, bystander and passer-by, and which role transitions occur.
Classify interactions and information as public or private and check the performer-wants versus others-want matrix for privacy and intrusion.
Assign a solution type per stage (for example signage for attention, demonstration for interest) and redesign.
outputs: Stage counts and conversion rates, stage-specific problems and fixes, a role map and privacy or intrusion requirements.
useWhen: Evaluating kiosks, digital signage, interactive installations, ticket machines or shared screens in real public settings.
avoidWhen: Avoid for private or individual devices; use usability testing. Counts are approximate, demographics are unknown and a single day of data is fragile; plan several sessions.
whyLost: It grew in academic public-display research and marketing, and few product teams ship public installations or study unrecruited passers-by.
whereToUse: Retail and museum installations, transport ticketing and wayfinding screens, self-service kiosks, smart-city displays and in-store QR or NFC experiences.
example: A museum trials a QR-to-phone audio guide sign. Of 353 passers-by, 57 stopped and 21 tried it; the instruction sheet beside the display went unnoticed, so the team moves instructions onto the screen itself.
reference: Ihara, M., Adachi, T. & Watanabe, H. (2017). Designing User Experiences of Novel Technologies. DUXU 2017, LNCS 10289, Springer, pp. 233-240; Dix, A. et al. (2022). TouchIT. Oxford University Press, pp. 308-314.

name: Publication Bias Diagnosis and Adjustment
aka: Begg and Mazumdar rank correlation test
Fail-safe N and funnel graph for the file-drawer problem
origin: Rosenthal, 1979; Hedges, 1984; Begg and Mazumdar, 1994; Egger et al., 1997; Duval and Tweedie, 2000
summary: Detect and gauge the impact of missing unfavourable studies in a synthesis using funnel plots, asymmetry tests, fail-safe N, trim and fill and selection models.
description: Publication bias arises when whether a study is published or reported depends on its results; related biases include selective outcome and subgroup reporting and time-lag bias, where null results appear later. Diagnosis uses a funnel plot of effect size against precision or sample size, whose asymmetry suggests small null studies are missing, tested with the Begg-Mazumdar rank correlation or Egger's regression. Impact is gauged with Rosenthal's fail-safe N (the number of unpublished null studies needed to remove significance; above 5k + 10, where k is the number of studies, is conventionally taken as robust), trim and fill, which imputes missing studies and an adjusted pooled effect, selection models with weight functions on p-values or effect sizes, or restriction to large studies. Because the selection mechanism is unknown, adjustments are sensitivity analyses. Asymmetry can also reflect genuine heterogeneity or small-study effects, and funnel plots are informative only with many studies.
steps: Draw a funnel plot of effect size against precision (or sample size).
Test asymmetry with the Begg-Mazumdar rank correlation or Egger's regression of the standard normal deviate on precision.
Compute fail-safe N and compare it with 5k + 10.
Apply trim and fill to estimate the number of missing studies and an adjusted pooled effect.
Fit selection models with p-value or effect-size weight functions.
Check for outcome-reporting and time-lag biases, and model plausible moderators that could explain asymmetry.
Report all adjustments as sensitivity analyses alongside the unadjusted estimate.
outputs: A diagnosis of likely publication bias and a range of adjusted pooled estimates.
useWhen: Any meta-analysis or evidence review, including syntheses of internal A/B test archives where losing or null tests are less often written up.
avoidWhen: Fewer than about ten studies, where funnel tests have little power; state the risk qualitatively. Adjustments rest on untestable assumptions.
whyLost: UX rarely performs formal syntheses, and teams seldom recognise that their own experiment and case-study archives are filtered toward wins.
whereToUse: Meta-analyses of HCI literature, internal experiment archives, vendor case-study claims and research repository reviews.
example: A growth team pools 60 documented pricing-page tests and finds strong funnel asymmetry: small tests with large lifts dominate. Trim and fill imputes 14 missing tests and halves the pooled lift, tempering the forecast for the next redesign.
sources: The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
reference: Sutton, A. J. Ch. 23. In Cooper, H., Hedges, L. V., & Valentine, J. C. (Eds.) (2009). The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Russell Sage Foundation.

name: Purposeful Selection of Covariates
origin: David Hosmer and Stanley Lemeshow, 1989 (2nd ed. 2000), drawing on Bendel and Afifi (1977) and Mickey and Greenland (1989) for the 0.25 screening level
summary: An analyst-led procedure for choosing regression covariates that combines univariable screening, confounder checks, add-back, scale checks and interaction tests instead of mechanical stepwise selection.
description: Purposeful selection treats model building as a judgement the analyst owns, with statistics as support rather than substitute. Every candidate is first examined on its own; anything with a univariable p below 0.25, plus anything known to matter, enters one multivariable model. Variables are then removed only when they neither contribute (Wald and likelihood ratio tests) nor act as confounders, judged by a marked change in other coefficients when they are dropped. Excluded candidates are added back one at a time, continuous covariates are checked for linearity in the logit with quartile design variables or fractional polynomials, and plausible interactions are tested singly. Hosmer and Lemeshow contrast this with stepwise and best-subsets routines, which admit noise variables, report p-values that are not true significance levels and miss confounding that only appears collectively. The result is a staged sequence of models, each defensible on both statistical and subject-matter grounds.
steps: Analyse each candidate alone: likelihood ratio chi-square and odds ratios for categorical variables, a univariable fit plus a lowess smooth on the logit scale for continuous ones, and a check for zero cells.
Enter every variable with univariable p below 0.25 and every variable of known substantive importance into one multivariable model.

Remove variables that are non-significant by Wald test, refit, confirm with a likelihood ratio test, and restore any variable whose removal shifts other coefficients markedly (a common rule of thumb is a change above about 20 percent).
Repeat delete-refit-verify, then add back each originally excluded variable one at a time to form the preliminary main effects model.
Check the scale of each continuous covariate with quartile design variables or fractional polynomials and adopt a transformation only if it is significant and makes substantive sense.
List plausible interactions, add each product term singly, and keep those significant by likelihood ratio test to form the preliminary final model.
Pass the model to goodness-of-fit and diagnostic checks before interpreting it.
outputs: A documented sequence of models (preliminary main effects, main effects with correct scales, preliminary final model with justified interactions) and the rationale for each inclusion.
useWhen: Building an explanatory logistic, ordinal or matched regression where the team needs to know why each variable is in the model, for example drivers of churn, task failure or support contact, and the number of events per parameter is adequate.
avoidWhen: Pure prediction with many candidate features, where penalised or cross-validated selection is better (see Feature subset and stepwise selection); causal questions with a known causal structure, where DAG-informed covariate selection is the right tool; and small samples with few events per parameter, where Wald statistics are unstable.
whyLost: UX analysts usually inherit either automatic stepwise routines or machine-learning feature selection, and the slower, documented judgement of clinical biostatistics never travelled with logistic regression into product analytics.
whereToUse: Explanatory models of retention, conversion or task success in SaaS and fintech; survey driver analysis; any model whose coefficients will be presented to stakeholders as reasons.
example: A fintech team models whether new users complete identity verification. Device type enters at univariable p = 0.18 and, though not significant later, is kept because dropping it shifts the document-type coefficient by 30 percent; a tested interaction of age by device type is then retained.
reference: Hosmer, D. W., & Lemeshow, S. (2000). Applied Logistic Regression (2nd ed.). New York: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 91-116.

name: Purposive Sampling (Maximum Variation and Criterion)
origin: Michael Quinn Patton, 1980/1990 (Qualitative Evaluation and Research Methods)
summary: Deliberately selecting information-rich participants by criteria derived from the research question, either spanning variation or meeting a defined threshold.
description: Purposive sampling selects participants because they can best inform the research question, not to estimate population parameters. Patton catalogued many strategies; two dominate applied work. Maximum variation sampling chooses participants spanning the widest range on three or four dimensions thought to matter, so that shared patterns are robust and differences are documented. Criterion sampling includes only cases meeting a defined threshold, such as users who abandoned onboarding within seven days. Rigour comes from deriving criteria from research questions, documenting them and borderline decisions, and reporting the rationale so readers can judge transferability. In practice UX screeners often default to demographics and convenience rather than information-rich criteria.
steps: Define characteristics that make a participant information-rich for your specific question. Criteria must flow from research questions, not convenience.
Maximum variation sampling: Identify 3–4 key variation dimensions. Deliberately recruit participants representing the full range on each.
Criterion sampling: All participants meet a specific threshold criterion. State explicitly. Document borderline cases and rationale.
Document your sampling rationale — why these participants and not others is a methodological decision requiring reporting.
outputs: A sampling frame with explicit criteria and variation dimensions, screeners derived from them, and a documented sampling rationale.
useWhen: Nearly all qualitative UX studies, especially when segments differ meaningfully or when a specific behaviour defines who can inform the question.
avoidWhen: When you need statistical generalisation or prevalence estimates; use probability sampling.
whyLost: Recruitment is outsourced to panels with demographic screeners, so criteria rarely flow from research questions and rationale is seldom documented.
whereToUse: Screener design, research ops recruitment, multi-segment discovery, and B2B studies with role and company-size variation.
example: Studying invoice approval software, the team samples for maximum variation on company size, approval chain length and ERP type, rather than on age and gender, uncovering three distinct approval patterns.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2015). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Pyramid Principle for Research Synthesis
origin: Barbara Minto, McKinsey, 1970s (The Pyramid Principle, 1987); applied to UX research readouts by Reimer and Howley (2023)
summary: Structure findings as a pyramid: one governing insight answering the business question, a few supporting findings each answering why, and the evidence beneath each.
description: The Pyramid Principle forces synthesis rather than summary. The top holds a single key message that answers the business objective. Beneath it sit a small number of supporting findings, each answering the question 'why should I believe that?', and beneath each the specific data points that evidence it. Minto's discipline is that each level summarises the ideas below it and ideas at one level are of the same kind and logically ordered. Reimer and Howley stress that knowing which data are not needed matters as much as finding the right data: anything that supports no finding is dropped. The finished pyramid then becomes the content plan for a story arc or deck. Its rigour lies in testing every link, so that a stakeholder who reads only the top line gets the answer and one who digs finds the evidence.
steps: Write down the business objective or question the research must answer.
Draft the single key message that answers it in one sentence.
Group the evidence into three to five supporting findings, each answering why the key message holds.
Place specific data points (quotes, percentages, observations) under each supporting finding.
Test each level: every finding must support the message, every data point a finding; drop or park anything that does not.
Use the pyramid as the outline for the readout, leading with the key message.
outputs: A hierarchical message map from headline insight to evidence, used as the outline for a report or presentation.
useWhen: Turning a large body of mixed-method findings into a readout for executives or decision-makers who need the answer first.
avoidWhen: Early exploratory synthesis where the answer is not yet known (use Affinity Diagramming or thematic analysis first); or when the audience needs a balanced descriptive account rather than an argued answer, as in a research archive.
whyLost: It survived because consulting alumni carried it into product organisations and because it matches how executives read; in UX it is often used without credit to Minto.
whereToUse: Executive readouts, strategy research, quantitative UX reports, research briefs for product reviews.
example: A pet-services startup's concept test yields 40 slides. The pyramid reduces it to one message (strong financial potential, but marketing and design work needed before launch) supported by pricing, awareness and feature findings, each with two or three data points.
sources: Storytelling to Spur Action with Stakeholders (Reimer & Howley, 2023)
reference: Minto, B. (1987). The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking. London: Minto International.

name: Q Methodology
origin: William Stephenson, 1935; developed for political science by Steven R. Brown, 1980
summary: Participants rank-sort 40 to 80 statements into a forced distribution; by-person factor analysis reveals a small number of shared viewpoints and what distinguishes them.
description: Q methodology, devised by William Stephenson in 1935, studies subjectivity systematically. A concourse of everything said about a topic is reduced to a balanced Q-set of 40 to 80 statements. Each participant sorts all statements into a forced, quasi-normal grid from most disagree to most agree, so every placement is relative to every other. Sorts are then correlated person by person and factor analysed, typically with centroid or principal components extraction and varimax or judgemental rotation; each factor is a shared viewpoint, expressed as an idealised sort. A post-sort interview explains placements at the extremes. Because the people, not the statements, are the variables, Q needs modest samples and reveals the structure of opinion rather than its distribution. Rigour comes from a well-balanced Q-set, the forced distribution and transparent factor decisions.
steps: Develop the Q-set (40–80 statements): Represent the full range of perspectives on the topic. Sources: interviews, literature, media. Include minority views, not just majority positions.
Design the sorting grid: Forced quasi-normal distribution (e.g., −5 to +5, fewer slots at extremes). Forces discriminating choices.
Sorting session: Participant sorts all statements into the grid. Then conduct a post-sort interview: 'Tell me about the statements you placed at the extremes — why?'
Factor analysis: Correlate Q-sorts across participants. Extract factors (clusters of similar Q-sorts). Rotate to simple structure.
Interpret factors: Each factor represents a shared viewpoint. The factor array (the ideal Q-sort for that factor) shows what someone holding this viewpoint values and rejects.
outputs: A Q-set, completed sorts, a factor solution with loadings, idealised factor arrays, distinguishing and consensus statements, and narrative descriptions of each viewpoint.
useWhen: You want to identify the distinct perspectives that exist on a contested or subjective topic, such as attitudes to data sharing, AI, money or health, with a modest sample of 20 to 60 participants.
avoidWhen: You need to know how prevalent each viewpoint is in a population; Q does not estimate prevalence. Follow up with a survey built on the factors, or use cluster or latent class analysis on survey data.
whyLost: It requires specialised software and factor-analytic judgement, and its inverted logic (correlating people rather than variables) is unfamiliar, so UX teams default to card sorts or attitudinal surveys.
whereToUse: Segmenting attitudes to privacy, AI and automation, financial behaviour, clinical decision-making, stakeholder alignment workshops, and value-based persona development.
example: A health-data platform runs 40 Q-sorts on statements about sharing records. Three viewpoints emerge: 'altruistic sharers', 'control-first pragmatists' and 'institutional sceptics'. Consent design is then tailored so each group sees the controls it cares about.
sources: Watts, S. & Stenner, P. (2012) Doing Q Methodological Research
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Stephenson W (1953) The Study of Behavior: Q-Technique and Its Methodology
Brown SR (1993) A primer on Q methodology. Operant Subjectivity 16:91-138
Watts S & Stenner P (2012) Doing Q Methodological Research
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Brown, S. R. (1980). Political Subjectivity: Applications of Q Methodology in Political Science. Yale University Press.

name: Qi2He Cross-Cultural Co-Design Framework
origin: Nick Bryan-Kinns, Wei Wang and Tingting Ji, 2022
summary: A co-design framework that structures cross-cultural co-design on the four stages of traditional Chinese literary composition, from skill sharing to joint production.
description: Qi2He takes its structure from Eastern epistemology rather than Western design-thinking stages. Its authors adapted traditional Chinese literature composition methods to organise co-design between people from different cultures. The four stages move from technical skill development and sharing, through cultural sharing, to co-design innovation and evaluation across cultures using in-situ making, and finally co-design refinement, production, presentation and evaluation. The framework treats culture as a source of inspiration and reflection rather than as a variable to control, and builds mutual learning of skills and cultural context before joint making begins. The book summary gives no materials, timings or evaluation criteria, so practitioners should work from the source paper before running it.
steps: Stage 1, skill sharing: participants from each culture teach and practise the technical skills the project needs, such as a craft or a prototyping tool.
Stage 2, cultural sharing: participants share cultural practices, meanings and references relevant to the design theme.
Stage 3, co-design innovation: mixed-culture groups generate and evaluate ideas through in-situ making, reflecting across cultures.
Stage 4, refinement and presentation: groups refine, produce and present artefacts and evaluate them with members of both cultures.
Document reflections at each stage on how cultural difference shaped ideas, consulting the source paper for materials and timings.
outputs: Co-designed artefacts evaluated across cultures and reflections on cultural exchange during design.
useWhen: Co-design projects that bring together participants from different cultural traditions, especially craft or cultural heritage work.
avoidWhen: When you need a lightweight or fast workshop format, or when cultural exchange is not central. The book offers no protocol detail; use Co-design Workshops or Cross-Cultural UX Research approaches if you cannot follow the source paper.
whyLost: It is recent (2022) and published in academic HCI, so it has not yet been taken up in practice.
whereToUse: Cross-cultural product teams, cultural heritage and craft technology, global design education, localisation co-design.
example: A UK-China team designing a music learning app runs Qi2He: each side teaches an instrument technique, shares musical traditions, makes hybrid prototypes together, then presents and evaluates them with learners in both countries.
reference: Bryan-Kinns, N., Wang, W. and Ji, T. (2022). Qi2He: A co-design framework inspired by eastern epistemology. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 160, 102773.

name: Qual-to-Quant Bridge (Theme-to-Construct Operationalisation)
origin: Exploratory sequential mixed-methods design (Creswell & Plano Clark); scale development practice (DeVellis)
summary: Converting qualitative themes into defined constructs and survey items in participants' language, then pretesting and validating them with factor analysis.
description: This bridge turns qualitative insight into something measurable at scale. For each major theme, the researcher defines the underlying construct and its observable indicators, drafts candidate items using participants' own language (which improves face validity), and pretests the items with cognitive interviews.
