The items are then fielded to a sample large enough for exploratory factor analysis (typically 200 or more), checked for expected structure and reliability, and confirmed on a fresh sample with confirmatory factor analysis. The result is a validated scale grounded in user experience rather than borrowed from another context. Reporting what the quantitative construct captures and what it misses keeps the link to the qualitative origin honest.
steps: From each major qualitative theme, derive: what is the underlying construct? What observable behaviours or self-report items would indicate its presence?
Write candidate items using participants' own language from the qualitative phase — in-vivo language produces more face-valid items.
Cognitive interview candidate items with 5–8 members of the target population.
Run Exploratory Factor Analysis to determine whether items group as expected.
Validate with CFA. Report both what the quantitative construct captures and what it misses.
outputs: Construct definitions, an item pool in user language, cognitive pretest results, EFA and CFA results, reliability statistics, and a validated scale.
useWhen: When qualitative research uncovers a concept (trust, anxiety, control) that needs measuring across a population or over time.
avoidWhen: When a validated scale for the construct already exists and fits your population; adopt it instead. Avoid without sample sizes for factor analysis.
whyLost: UX rarely has psychometric expertise in-house, so themes are turned into ad hoc survey questions without validation.
whereToUse: Trust in AI products, financial anxiety measures, clinical app experience scales, and custom UX metrics for product dashboards.
example: Interviews about an AI writing assistant reveal 'authorship anxiety'. Twelve items drafted from participants' words are pretested, fielded to 400 users, and reduced to a reliable six-item scale tracked quarterly.
sources: Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (Creswell & Plano Clark)
reference: DeVellis, R. F. (2017). Scale Development: Theory and Applications (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Qualitative Comparative Analysis
origin: Charles Ragin, 1987 (crisp-set); 2000 (fuzzy-set)
summary: A case-based method using Boolean logic and set theory to identify combinations of conditions that are necessary or sufficient for an outcome across small to medium numbers of cases.
description: Qualitative Comparative Analysis, developed by Charles Ragin, bridges case-oriented and variable-oriented research. Each case, such as a customer account, team or product deployment, is described by a set of conditions and an outcome, coded as crisp (0 or 1) or fuzzy (degrees of membership) sets. A truth table lists all observed combinations of conditions, and Boolean minimisation identifies which configurations are consistently linked to the outcome. QCA embraces conjunctural causation (conditions matter in combination), equifinality (different paths lead to the same outcome) and asymmetry. It suits 10 to 50 cases, where statistics are weak but cases are too many to compare by eye. Rigour comes from theory-based condition selection, transparent calibration, consistency and coverage thresholds, and returning to cases to interpret solutions.
steps: Define the outcome and select 10 to 50 cases with variation in the outcome.
Choose 3 to 6 conditions based on theory and case knowledge.
Calibrate conditions and outcome into crisp or fuzzy set membership with documented thresholds.
Build a truth table of configurations and assess consistency (typically 0.8 or higher).
Run Boolean minimisation to derive solution pathways and report consistency and coverage.
Test for necessary conditions separately.
Return to cases to interpret pathways and check robustness to calibration choices.
outputs: Truth tables, solution pathways (combinations of conditions sufficient for the outcome), consistency and coverage metrics, and case interpretations.
useWhen: When comparing a modest number of cases (for example enterprise deployments, sites or teams) to find which combinations of conditions lead to success or failure.
avoidWhen: Avoid with very few cases (under about 10) or large samples suited to regression; use case studies or regression. Not suitable when conditions cannot be meaningfully calibrated.
whyLost: Latent: Powerful for small-n comparative studies; largely unknown in UX; imported from political science.
whereToUse: Cross-cultural UX; comparative product studies; policy design research.
example: An enterprise SaaS vendor analyses 28 customer rollouts. QCA shows successful adoption follows either executive sponsorship with training or an internal champion with simple data migration, two distinct pathways that shape onboarding playbooks.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis
reference: Ragin, C. C. (1987). The Comparative Method. University of California Press; Ragin, C. C. (2008). Redesigning Social Inquiry: Fuzzy Sets and Beyond. University of Chicago Press.

name: Qualitative Cross-Case Scatterplot
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1994
summary: Plot each case as a point on two carefully scaled qualitative dimensions to reveal clusters, distances and outliers that a matrix's cut points hide, then return to the case data.
description: Matrices sort cases into cells and throw away how close or far apart they are. The scatterplot keeps that information: the analyst scales each case carefully on two dimensions thought to be related, plots them, and reads the pattern against a stated hypothesis. Where a value changed between periods, two points joined by an arrow show the movement; over-time variants place cases in panels for successive periods and circle case families. Families then prompt a search for an intervening variable. In the source example, pressure to adopt plotted against latitude to change refuted a 'bargain' hypothesis and showed latitude rising later. Scaling may need summed indices; when cases cannot be scaled finely, the analyst falls back to a contingency table. Conclusions must be confirmed in the case reports, with attention to reversed or third-variable causation. Plotting 12 already scaled cases takes 10 to 15 minutes.
steps: Pick two dimensions you believe are related and state the expected pattern.
Scale each case on both dimensions, building summed indices and returning to case reports where needed.
Plot the cases, drawing arrows where values changed between periods.
Read clusters, quadrants and outliers against the hypothesis.
Circle case families and look for an intervening variable that explains them.
Check outliers and conclusions in the case data, watching for reversed or third-variable causation.
Fall back to a contingency table if the scaling is too coarse.
outputs: A scatterplot of cases with families and change arrows, and a written interpretation checked against case data.
useWhen: Studies of 8 to 30 cases (accounts, teams, sites, participants) where you have rated each case on several dimensions and want to test an if-then idea visually.
avoidWhen: Cases rated only by impression; scores must be defensible. With large samples, use quantitative analysis instead.
whyLost: UX teams use 2x2 matrices for prioritisation but rarely plot rated cases from qualitative data to test a hypothesis and then return to the evidence.
whereToUse: B2B account studies, multi-team tool adoption research, and diary studies with per-participant ratings.
example: Twelve customer teams are scaled on admin support and depth of workflow automation. Most fall on a diagonal, but two high-support teams have low automation; returning to the notes shows both run on legacy SSO, which becomes a product finding.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Qualitative Meta-Synthesis
origin: George Noblit & Dwight Hare, 1988 (Meta-Ethnography); Sandelowski & Barroso, 2007
summary: Systematically synthesising findings from completed qualitative studies into higher-order interpretations that no single study could produce.
description: Meta-synthesis treats the findings of existing qualitative studies as data. Unlike meta-analysis, which pools effect sizes, it integrates concepts, themes and theoretical propositions. Noblit and Hare's meta-ethnography translates concepts from one study into another, identifies refutations, and builds a 'line of argument' synthesis. The process involves a defined question, systematic search and selection (often reported with PRISMA or ENTREQ), quality appraisal, and a three-order construct analysis: participants' views, original authors' interpretations, and the synthesist's new interpretation. Findings robust across studies are distinguished from context-specific ones. In organisations it can also synthesise an internal research archive, turning past studies into cumulative knowledge.
steps: Systematic search and selection: Define inclusion criteria. Use PRISMA reporting standards for the search process.
Quality appraisal: Apply a trustworthiness appraisal framework. Studies failing basic credibility or confirmability criteria are excluded.
Three-order construct analysis: First-order = what participants said. Second-order = what original researchers concluded. Third-order = what you conclude from comparing across studies.
Report: Distinguish between findings robust across studies and findings appearing in only one or two specific contexts.
outputs: A documented search and selection record, quality appraisal, translation tables of concepts across studies, and a synthesised line-of-argument model with robustness ratings.
useWhen: When many studies exist on a topic (internal or published) and you need cumulative, evidence-weighted understanding before commissioning new research.
avoidWhen: When few or poor-quality studies exist, or when a quick literature scan suffices; use a rapid review or new primary research.
whyLost: It is standard in health evidence synthesis, but UX rarely treats its own archives or published studies as data for formal synthesis.
whereToUse: Research repository synthesis, health product evidence reviews, accessibility research, and strategy work drawing on academic literature.
example: A digital health company synthesises 14 internal and 9 published studies on medication adherence apps. The line-of-argument model shows that 'feeling monitored' undermines adherence across contexts, guiding notification design.
sources: Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Handbook for Synthesizing Qualitative Research (Sandelowski & Barroso)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Noblit, G. W. & Hare, R. D. (1988). Meta-Ethnography: Synthesizing Qualitative Studies. Sage.

name: Qualitative Research Protocol as Mental Framework
donor: Case study and qualitative field research
origin: Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016), building on his case study protocol
summary: A set of topics and questions addressed to the researcher, each paired with likely sources of evidence, that is carried in the head to guide conversational fieldwork instead of a scripted interview guide.
description: Yin separates a protocol from an instrument. An instrument scripts the spoken questions or tasks a participant receives; a protocol states the topics and questions the researcher must answer through the whole line of inquiry. Protocol questions are written to the fieldworker (for example 'Ask about how long R has lived here, and why'), and each is accompanied by the sources of evidence that might answer it: interviews, documents, observation. In the field the researcher does not read from it. The protocol is internalised as a mental framework, like a doctor's clinical line of questioning or a detective's working hypotheses, and spoken questions are composed on the spot in natural conversation. Yin gives three benefits: it keeps the original questions in view, it points to chances to seek contrary as well as supporting evidence, and it helps evidence converge across sources. When something unexpected turns up, the protocol is paused and revised. In multi-site work the same protocol supports parallel data collection, with the fieldworker composing a written answer to each question per site. For UX, it is an alternative to the scripted discussion guide when studying workplaces, services or organisations through mixed sources.
steps: Group the study's research questions into topics covering the full line of inquiry
Write each protocol question in the voice of the researcher, not as words to be spoken to a participant
Next to each question, list the anticipated sources of evidence: who to talk to, which documents, what to observe
Add operational definitions for key terms and distinguish observed events from reported ones
Study the protocol until it can be carried in the head; do not read from it during fieldwork
In the field, compose spoken questions on the spot and seek contrary as well as supporting evidence
After each site or session, write an answer to each protocol question citing the evidence, and revise the protocol if discoveries require it
outputs: A topic-by-question protocol with evidence sources, and per-site or per-study written answers to each protocol question that support cross-site comparison.
useWhen: Field studies, customer site visits or service research that draw on interviews, documents and observation together, especially across several sites or fieldworkers.
avoidWhen: You need identical wording across participants for comparison, as in a survey, a standardised usability task script or a quantitative interview.
whyLost: UX practice standardised on the printed discussion guide, which blends researcher questions with participant wording; the idea of a private protocol answered from multiple evidence sources stayed within case study methodology.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise discovery, service design research, multi-site contextual studies, research ops templates.
example: Before visiting six hospital pharmacies, a team writes protocol questions such as 'How are urgent orders escalated, and who decides?' with sources listed as the pharmacist interview, the escalation log and observation of the morning rush. At each site they converse freely, then fill in an answer per question, making the six sites directly comparable.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Qualitative Trajectory Arrays (Sentiment Drift Forecasting)
donor: Qualitative data display (Miles & Huberman) applied to longitudinal diaries
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Convert diary or ESM entries into per-participant trajectories of clarity, trust and frustration, cluster them into patterns such as 'fragile success', and use them to qualify quantitative forecasts.
description: Monte Carlo and SHAP extrapolate numbers; diaries and experience sampling extrapolate feelings over time. The playbook argues that even if completion rises short-term, negative sentiment drift predicts future drop-off ('Even when I succeeded, I felt drained'; 'After three tries, I stopped trusting the feature'). Diary entries are arrayed with columns for session index, perceived clarity (−2..+2), trust (1..5), frustration (0..100), success (Y/N) and a key quote, then sorted by outcome and clustered into patterns such as 'fast trust gain', 'fragile success' and 'churn risk'. Clusters are triangulated with top SHAP drivers (e.g. high mistake rate clusters with fragile success) and turned into what-if notes. The deliverable is a panel of two or three curated trajectories shown beside forecast curves to argue for emotional sustainability.
steps: Run a diary or ESM study across multiple sessions with structured prompts for clarity, trust and frustration plus an open quote.
Array entries per participant: session index, clarity (−2..+2), trust (1..5), frustration (0..100), success (Y/N), key quote.
Sort trajectories by outcome and cluster them into patterns (e.g. fast trust gain, fragile success, churn risk).
Link clusters to the top quantitative drivers from SHAP or survival models.
Write what-if notes, e.g. 'If SNR uplift holds and the rules wizard ships, expect the fragile cluster to shrink.'
Present two or three curated trajectories alongside Monte Carlo curves and re-check them at 1, 3 and 6 months after launch.
outputs: Trajectory clusters, curated example trajectories and what-if statements qualifying forecasts.
useWhen: When forecasting adoption or retention and emotional sustainability may diverge from short-term completion.
avoidWhen: When only a single-session snapshot is possible; use post-task questionnaires instead.
whyLost: Original technique by Vivek Gopinath building on qualitative data display.
whereToUse: Onboarding, trading and investing apps, health behaviour apps, AI assistants.
example: Diaries from a trading app show a cluster of users who complete price alerts but report rising frustration and falling trust; the team flags them as 'fragile success' and prioritises the rule wizard.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Section 5.3 and 'Qualitative Trajectories to Complement Forecasts'.

name: Quality Criteria Sets for Qualitative and Grounded Theory Research
aka: Strauss and Corbin criteria for evaluating grounded theory research
Yardley's quality criteria for qualitative research
donor: Sociology, health psychology and qualitative methodology
origin: Strauss and Corbin (1990, 1998); Charmaz (2006); Yardley (2000); Whittemore, Chase and Mandle (2001); Patton (2002)
summary: Choose a named set of quality criteria that fits the study's paradigm, plan how each will be met, and use the same set to appraise the finished work.
description: Qualitative quality depends on which criteria an audience applies. Strauss and Corbin give seven research-process questions (sampling, categories, indicators, theoretical sampling, hypotheses, discrepancies, choice of core category) and eight grounding criteria for grounded theory. Charmaz judges credibility, originality, resonance and usefulness. Yardley's four characteristics are sensitivity to context, commitment and rigour, transparency and coherence, and impact and importance, with constructivist additions such as reflexivity and negative-case analysis. Whittemore adds explicitness, congruence and vividness. Patton contrasts five sets: traditional scientific, constructivist, artistic and evocative, critical change, and evaluation standards. The procedure is the same across all of them: name the set, design for it, report against it, and anticipate critiques from other sets. It extends the single Lincoln and Guba frame common in UX.
steps: Identify the study's purpose, paradigm and audiences, and which criteria set or sets they will apply.
Select a named set, such as Yardley, Charmaz, Strauss and Corbin, or Whittemore, and state it in the research plan.
For each criterion, write the strategy that will meet it (audit trail, negative cases, reflexive memo, member responses, thick description).
Apply the strategies during fieldwork and analysis, keeping memos as evidence.
Appraise the finished report against each criterion, noting and justifying departures.
Anticipate how audiences using other criteria sets will critique the work and address this in the report.
outputs: An explicit quality framework in the plan, a criterion-by-criterion appraisal of the report, and anticipated critiques.
useWhen: Planning or reviewing qualitative studies whose credibility will be challenged, auditing a research repository, or teaching junior researchers what good qualitative work looks like.
avoidWhen: You want a numeric score; none of these sets gives one, and they depend on honest reporting. For quantitative work use validity frameworks such as threats-to-validity audits.
whyLost: Academic qualitative research uses these sets routinely; UX practice, if it appraises qualitative work at all, cites only Lincoln and Guba or nothing.
whereToUse: Research review boards in large UX teams, research repositories, academic-industry partnerships, peer review of synthesis.
example: A research lead reviews a discovery study against Yardley's criteria and finds no audit trail and no negative cases, so asks for a short appendix of coding memos and disconfirming quotes before the findings go to leadership.
reference: Yardley, L. (2000). Dilemmas in qualitative health research. Psychology and Health, 15, 215-228.

name: Quality Function Deployment (House of Quality)
origin: Yoji Akao, 1966; Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Kobe shipyard, 1972; Hauser and Clausing (1988)
summary: A cross-functional team fills a cascade of matrices linking weighted customer requirements to measurable product, part, process and production characteristics.
description: QFD translates the voice of the customer into engineering decisions through a planning team drawn from all functions and a series of House of Quality matrices. Customer requirements (WHATs) are gathered from surveys, complaints, returns and trends, structured into levels, weighted and classified with the Kano model. The team rates its own and competing products from the customer's view, defines solution-neutral measurable features (HOWs) with targets and direction of improvement, and fills a relationship matrix (commonly 9/3/1) to compute technical importance. The 'roof' records positive and negative correlations between features, exposing conflicts; technical benchmarks and difficulty estimates complete the house. Critical HOWs become the WHATs of the next house in the four-phase cascade: product, part, process and production planning. Its rigour is traceability from every engineering target back to weighted customer needs.
steps: Gather customer requirements, structure them into primary, secondary and tertiary levels with importance weights, and classify them with Kano.
Rate your own and competing products on each requirement from the customer's view and add strategic positioning; revise weights if needed.
Define solution-neutral, measurable product features (HOWs) with target values and direction of improvement.
Fill the relationship matrix (for example 9 strong, 3 medium, 1 weak) and compute absolute and relative technical importance.
Fill the roof with positive and negative correlations between features to expose trade-offs.
Benchmark competitors technically, contrast with customer perceptions, and estimate the difficulty of changing each feature.
Select the critical features and carry them as WHATs into the next house (parts, process, production), keeping matrices small enough to stay readable.
outputs: Prioritised engineering characteristics with target values traceable to weighted customer requirements, competitive comparisons and a documented cross-functional plan.
useWhen: Complex products, especially hardware or hardware-software systems, where many teams must align specifications with customer needs and trade-offs must be explicit.
avoidWhen: When customer data are thin or unreliable (garbage in), or for fast-moving software where a full cascade is overkill. It grows confusing quickly, is often seen as subjective, meets organisational resistance and needs training. For lighter needs-to-requirements tracing use Requirements Traceability Matrix for UX.
whyLost: It is standard in automotive and manufacturing quality engineering, but UX and agile software teams rarely build structured needs-to-specification matrices.
whereToUse: Medical devices, automotive HMI, consumer electronics, connected hardware, regulated software requirements.
example: A smart-thermostat team links weighted needs such as 'easy to set a schedule' to measurable features like steps-to-schedule and display contrast; the roof shows a conflict between display brightness and battery life, resolved before industrial design is frozen.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Hauser, J. R. and Clausing, D. (1988). The house of quality. Harvard Business Review, 66(3), 63-73; Akao, Y. (1990). Quality Function Deployment: Integrating Customer Requirements into Product Design. Productivity Press.

name: Quality gates at each pipeline stage
donor: Software engineering; manufacturing quality control; data engineering
origin: Stage-gate and statistical quality control traditions (Shewhart, 1931); data validation in pipelines (e.g. Great Expectations, 2017)
summary: Defining measurable acceptance criteria between stages of a research pipeline so poor-quality transcripts, parses or codes are caught before they contaminate findings.
description: In a multi-stage pipeline errors compound: a hallucinated transcript passage becomes a coded segment, then a theme. Quality gates set explicit, measurable thresholds at each hand-off, for example transcription WER and confidence, diarisation sanity checks, NLP component F1, LLM schema validity and quote-verification rates, and human-AI coding agreement. Failing items are halted, flagged or routed to review rather than passed silently. Rigour comes from setting thresholds before running, automating checks, recording pass and fail rates in run reports, and periodically auditing items that passed to make sure gates are not too lenient.
steps: List each stage's outputs and the failure modes that matter for findings.
Set thresholds before running, e.g. sampled WER of 10% or below, at least 98% schema-valid outputs, 100% verbatim quote match, kappa of 0.70 or above against human coders.
Automate checks in the pipeline and halt or quarantine failing items.
Route quarantined items to human review with the reason for failure.
Audit a random sample of passed items each run (e.g. 5%) to estimate leakage.
Report gate statistics with every set of findings.
outputs: Gate definitions, automated checks, quarantine queues and a quality report per run.
useWhen: Any automated or AI-assisted research pipeline, especially at scale or where findings inform major decisions.
avoidWhen: Excessive for manual small studies, where the researcher's own reading serves as the check.
whyLost: Researchers rarely treat their analysis as a production process, so manufacturing-style quality control never migrated.
whereToUse: AI-assisted qualitative analysis, transcription programmes, feedback analytics and research repositories.
example: A pipeline's quote-verification gate quarantines 3% of coded segments whose quotes do not appear in transcripts. Investigation reveals a prompt change had caused paraphrasing, which is fixed before the report is produced.
sources: Shewhart, W. A. (1931) Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product
Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C13 — The Full Agentic Research Pipeline — Whisper → spaCy → AI Coder → Synthesis
reference: Shewhart, W. A. (1931) Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product

name: Quantitizing and Qualitizing
origin: Caracelli and Greene (1993); Tashakkori and Teddlie (1998); Sandelowski, Voils and Knafl (2009)
summary: Convert qualitative codes into variables for statistical analysis, or quantitative scores into categories for sorting qualitative data, to integrate mixed datasets.
description: Quantitizing turns qualitative codes into variables, usually present or absent per case, sometimes counts, which can be exported from qualitative software for statistical analysis. In a worked example, 55 interviews were coded for having a critical parent, peer or sibling and for an eating disorder; cross-tabulation showed 56.3% of those with a disorder had such a person against 12.8% without. Qualitizing works the other way: quantitative scores are turned into categories or a typology, and qualitative data are then used to flesh out each type. Rigour comes from planning the transformation at the design stage, using matching measures across instruments, defining coding rules for presence and absence, and interpreting results jointly with the original data rather than as stand-alone statistics.
steps: Plan the transformation at the design stage and decide which codes or scores will be converted.
Use matching measures across qualitative and quantitative instruments where possible.
Code the qualitative data with explicit rules for presence, absence or intensity.
Convert codes into binary or count variables per case, or quantitative scores into categories.
Analyse, for example by cross-tabulation or by comparing types.
Interpret the results together with the original excerpts or cases.
outputs: A case-by-variable matrix, cross-tabulations, and typologies linking qualitative and quantitative data.
useWhen: Mixed-methods studies where you want to test whether a qualitative pattern is associated with an outcome, or use survey scores to structure follow-up interviews.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting counts from small purposive samples as prevalence estimates; codes as variables carry measurement error. For population estimates, run a survey.
whyLost: UX teams count codes routinely but without design-stage planning, coding rules or joint interpretation, so the practice is common but its rigour is not.
whereToUse: Mixed-methods discovery, interview programmes linked to product analytics, survey plus follow-up interview designs.
example: A health app team codes 40 interviews for 'has a support person' and cross-tabulates with 90-day retention from analytics. The association prompts a test of a buddy feature.
sources: Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Sandelowski, M., Voils, C. I. and Knafl, G. (2009). On quantitizing. Journal of Mixed Methods Research, 3(3), 208-222.

name: Quantum Probability Models of Judgement
aka: QQ equality test for question-order effects
origin: Busemeyer and Bruza (2012); question-order test by Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin and Busemeyer (2014)
summary: Models judgements with quantum probability, where asking one question changes the answer to the next, to explain and test order and framing effects in surveys and choices.
description: Classical probability assumes that a person holds fixed opinions and a question simply reads them out, so the order of questions should not matter. In practice it does: asking about trust before satisfaction gives different answers from the reverse order. Quantum cognition treats a mental state as a set of possibilities that a question resolves, in the way a measurement changes a physical system. That framing makes specific, testable predictions. The best known is the QQ equality: for two yes/no questions asked in both orders to split samples, a particular combination of the order effects should be zero if the quantum account holds. For UX research this offers more than a curiosity. It gives a principled way to decide whether an order effect in a survey is noise, a carry-over bias you should counterbalance away, or a real feature of how people build judgements on the spot, which matters for in-product micro-surveys, onboarding questions and preference elicitation.
steps: Pick pairs of judgement questions where order could matter, such as trust and satisfaction, or price fairness and value.
Randomly assign respondents to answer each pair in one order or the other (A then B, or B then A).
For yes/no or binarised answers, tabulate the four joint outcomes for each order.
Compute the order effects and the QQ equality statistic; check whether it is close to zero.
If order effects exist and satisfy the QQ equality, treat answers as constructed in context: fix a deliberate order that matches the real product moment rather than averaging orders away.
If order effects break the equality, look for ordinary carry-over or fatigue and counterbalance.
outputs: A diagnosis of each order effect in a questionnaire, and a decision on question order grounded in a model rather than habit.
useWhen: Designing short in-product surveys, preference or consent flows, or any study where the same two judgements are asked together.
avoidWhen: Long validated scales with fixed item orders, or small samples that cannot be split by order.
whyLost: Quantum cognition grew in mathematical psychology and is written in Hilbert-space notation, so it rarely reaches survey practice even though its core test needs only split samples and a few proportions.
whereToUse: NPS and CSAT micro-surveys, pricing pages, consent dialogues, onboarding questionnaires.
example: An app asks 'Do you trust us with your data?' and 'Are you satisfied?' in random order. Satisfaction drops 9 points when trust comes first, and the QQ equality holds, so the team keeps the trust question after satisfaction to mirror when users actually think about privacy, and reports the order with the result.
sources: Busemeyer, J. & Bruza, P., Quantum Models of Cognition and Decision (2012)
reference: Busemeyer, J. R., & Bruza, P. D. (2012). Quantum Models of Cognition and Decision. Cambridge University Press. Wang, Z., Solloway, T., Shiffrin, R. M., & Busemeyer, J. R. (2014). Context effects produced by question orders reveal quantum nature of human judgments. PNAS, 111(26), 9431-9436.

name: Quasi-Empirical UX Evaluation
origin: Rex Hartson and Pardha Pyla (2012, 2019)
summary: An informal, facilitator-led session where evaluator and participant explore a design together, using tasks as props and pursuing issues as they arise, with no quantitative measures.
description: Hartson and Pyla separate rigorous empirical evaluation (benchmark tasks, quantitative targets) from quasiempirical methods, which still involve real participants, or an evaluator emulating one, but are informal: no quantitative data, no benchmark tasks, any location and frequent changes of direction. Tasks drawn from scenarios, essential use cases or task models serve as props rather than measurement instruments. The facilitator builds a partnership with the participant, prompts think-aloud, lets them explore and choose some tasks, and freely interrupts to probe reactions, unclear parts, comparisons, suggestions and typical-day use. Notes are the only raw data. Its value is speed and depth of qualitative insight during formative iteration; its weakness is dependence on facilitator skill and the absence of anything to compare across rounds.
steps: Prepare representative, frequent and mission-critical tasks plus exploratory questions.
Assign a facilitator and note-takers; consider two participants together for co-discovery.
Build rapport and frame the session as a partnership; prompt think-aloud.
Let the participant explore freely, then use tasks as props, letting them choose some.
Follow emerging threads: ask about reactions, unclear parts, comparisons, suggestions and how it would fit a typical day.
Take thorough notes as the only raw data and convert them into a problem and suggestion list straight after.
outputs: A UX problem list with suggestions, and qualitative insight into participants' reasoning.
useWhen: Early formative iteration, when the design changes fast and depth of understanding matters more than comparable measures.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need metrics or comparison against targets; use Usability Specification and UX Targets or Benchmarking.
whyLost: The label is little known, but the practice survives under names such as exploratory or informal usability sessions and 'user interviews with a prototype'.
whereToUse: Startup discovery sprints, concept prototypes, internal tools, early AI feature prototypes.
example: A team exploring an AI meeting-notes feature sits with five users, lets them poke at a prototype and repeatedly asks how it would fit their Monday stand-up, uncovering that editing summaries matters more than accuracy.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019). The UX Book, 2nd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, section 24.5.2.

name: Quasi-Simplex Test-Retest Reliability for Panel Data
origin: Coleman (1964, 1968); David Heise (1969); Duane Alwin (2007)
summary: Estimating the reliability of a single survey item from three or more panel waves while allowing the underlying true score to change between waves.
description: Two-wave test-retest correlations confuse unreliability with real change. The quasi-simplex model separates them with three or more waves: each observed answer is a true score plus random error, and each true score depends on the previous wave's true score (a lag-1 Markov process). With three waves the model is identified by assuming equal reliabilities or equal error variances across waves; with four or more, fit can be tested. Waves must be far enough apart that earlier answers are not remembered. The result is a reliability estimate for a single item, which cross-sectional methods such as Cronbach's alpha cannot give. Assumptions matter: change must follow the lag-1 pattern, errors must be uncorrelated, and memory effects inflate estimates.
steps: Ask the same item, worded identically, in three or more waves spaced far enough apart to prevent recall of earlier answers.
Specify a model in which each wave's answer equals a true score plus random error, and each true score is a function of the previous one.
Identify the model by constraining reliabilities or error variances to be equal across waves.
Fit it in structural equation modelling software; with four or more waves, test model fit.
Report the item's reliability and compare items or formats.
outputs: Reliability estimates for single items, separate from estimates of true change.
useWhen: Longitudinal trackers and panels that rely on single-item measures (satisfaction, NPS, trust) and need to know how much wave-to-wave movement is noise.
avoidWhen: Two-wave data or multi-item scales measured once, where alpha or omega apply. Avoid when waves are close enough for memory effects.
whyLost: UX panels rarely keep identical items over three or more waves on the same people, and the model is published in sociological methodology.
whereToUse: Longitudinal satisfaction panels, diary or ESM studies with repeated single items, customer trust trackers.
example: A neobank tracks single-item trust quarterly on the same 3,000 customers. A quasi-simplex model over four waves estimates item reliability at 0.62, showing that quarter-on-quarter movements under about five points are within noise.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Alwin, D. F. (2016). Survey data quality and measurement precision. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 527-557). London: SAGE.

name: Question Ordering and Order (Context) Effect Check
origin: Don Dillman, 2000, drawing on Schuman and Presser (1981), Schwarz (1996) and Sangster (1993)
summary: Rules for sequencing a questionnaire like a conversation, plus a review of adjacent items for documented order effects such as assimilation, contrast and evenhandedness.
description: A questionnaire is read as a conversation: abrupt topic switches make the sponsor seem not to listen and produce top-of-the-head answers. Dillman orders topics by salience to the respondent, matching the theme promised in the invitation, places objectionable items last, sequences within topics chronologically with descriptive items before evaluative ones, and groups items that share a response format. The first question gets special care: it should apply to everyone, be easy and interesting, and visibly connect to the stated purpose. The rigorous part is a check of adjacent opinion items for five documented effects: norm of evenhandedness, anchoring, carryover (addition), subtraction, and summary items answered after specific ones. A classic split ballot moved agreement with letting communist reporters into the US from 37% to 73% purely by order, and such effects appear in self-administered surveys too.
steps: Group questions by topic and order topics from most to least salient, matching the purpose stated in the invitation.
Place objectionable or sensitive items (income, health, law-breaking, politics) near the end.
Within each topic, ask in chronological and logical order, with descriptive items before evaluative ones, and group items that share response categories.

Choose a first question that applies to everyone, is easy and interesting and clearly connected to the purpose; avoid demographics, open-ended items and ranking tasks first. If screening is needed, make it the first question.
Review every adjacent pair of opinion items for evenhandedness, anchoring, carryover, subtraction and general-after-specific effects.
Where an effect is suspected, separate the items, put general before specific questions, or randomise order across forms and compare.
Record order-sensitive pairs so later waves keep the same order.
outputs: An ordered questionnaire, a chosen first question and a list of order-sensitive item pairs with the mitigation applied.
useWhen: Building a new survey or tracker, adding items to an existing one, or comparing results across versions whose order differed.
avoidWhen: Single-question intercepts where there is no sequence to manage. Do not move key items such as income or satisfaction to the front to protect their response rate; it backfires.
whyLost: UX survey practice treats order as a layout matter and rarely runs split-ballot checks; tool-level randomisation is used as a blanket fix without considering which pairs actually interact.
whereToUse: Satisfaction trackers that ask about specific features and overall satisfaction, NPS surveys followed by reasons, pricing and preference surveys.
example: A SaaS tracker asks about five specific frustrations and then overall satisfaction, depressing the overall score through a specific-before-general effect. The team moves the overall item first, keeps the order fixed across quarters and tests the alternative order on a 10% split.
reference: Dillman, D. A. (2007). Mail and Internet Surveys: The Tailored Design Method (2nd ed., 2007 update). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons.

name: Questionnaire Pilot Testing
origin: Standard survey practice; Gratton and Jones (2010) list its functions and recommend repeated piloting until the design is settled.
summary: Running a small-scale version of a survey under real conditions before launch to check wording, order, timing, administration and analysis.
description: A pilot survey is a small administration of the full questionnaire before the main survey. Gratton and Jones give it five jobs: checking that wording is clear and unambiguous to the intended respondents; checking that the sequence is logical; estimating completion time; testing the whole administration process from distribution to receipt of responses; and doing a dry run of the analysis by entering the pilot data and trying to answer the research question with it. The last is the step most often skipped, and it is where researchers discover that a question cannot support the comparison they need. The pilot should run in conditions as close to the main survey as possible and with a similar group (if the main sample includes children, so must the pilot). After changes, the questionnaire is piloted again until no further changes are needed. It differs from cognitive interviewing, which probes how individuals understand items one by one; a pilot tests the instrument and the fielding pipeline end to end. For UX teams launching in-product or email surveys, a pilot to a small random slice catches broken logic, unclear items and unusable data before the whole user base is surveyed once and cannot be asked again.
steps: Prepare the questionnaire, invitation and delivery mechanism exactly as they will be used.
Field it to a small group similar to the target sample, in conditions as close as possible to the main survey (for example a small random slice of users).
Record completion times, drop-off points and any questions respondents skip, query or misread; optionally ask pilot respondents to comment on the design.
Enter or export the pilot data and run the planned analysis to confirm the data can answer the research question.
Revise wording, order, response options, routing and administration based on what you find.
Repilot after changes and repeat until no further changes are needed, then launch.
outputs: A revised questionnaire, estimated completion time, a tested delivery and data pipeline, and a draft analysis template.
useWhen: Before any survey that will go to a large or hard-to-reach sample, uses routing logic, or feeds a decision.
avoidWhen: It is a quick throwaway poll with no consequence, or the instrument is a validated standard scale used unchanged (though the delivery still benefits from a pilot).
whyLost: Survey tools make launching so fast that teams skip the pilot or reduce it to a colleague clicking through; the analysis dry run in particular has largely disappeared from UX practice.
whereToUse: In-app and email surveys, onboarding questionnaires, diary-study entry forms, benchmark surveys, recruitment screeners.
example: Before emailing a feature-satisfaction survey to 50,000 users, a researcher sends it to a random 200. Completion averages twice the estimate, a matrix question has high drop-off on mobile and the dry-run analysis shows that the usage-frequency categories overlap. All three are fixed and a second pilot of 200 confirms the changes before full launch.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Queueing Theory and Little's Law
origin: Agner Krarup Erlang (1909, telephone traffic); John Little (1961, L = lambda W); Kendall's notation (1953)
summary: Models arrivals, service times and capacity to predict waiting times and backlog, using Little's law (items in system = arrival rate x time in system).
description: Wherever users wait, for support agents, approvals, deliveries, moderation or AI responses, queueing theory predicts how waits behave. Little's law holds for any stable system: the average number in the system equals arrival rate times average time in system. Models like M/M/c (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, c servers) give waiting time distributions; Kingman's formula shows waits explode as utilisation approaches 100% and grow with variability. These insights correct common intuitions (e.g. that adding small capacity barely matters) and allow designers to reason about perceived waiting, prioritisation, triage and self-service deflection quantitatively.
steps: Map the waiting system: arrivals, queues, servers (people, machines, models), priorities and abandonment.
Measure arrival rates, service time distributions and current waits from logs.
Check Little's law against observed data to validate measurement.
Fit an appropriate model (M/M/c, M/G/1, Erlang C with abandonment) or simulate.
Explore scenarios: staffing, deflection, priority rules, variability reduction.
Combine with perceived-wait research to design communication (position in queue, estimates).
outputs: Queue models, predicted waits under scenarios, utilisation targets and design implications for waiting experiences.
useWhen: Any service with waiting: support, onboarding approvals, claims, deliveries, AI rate limits, content review.
avoidWhen: Experiences without capacity constraints or waiting.
whyLost: Operations research is owned by ops and engineering; UX focuses on wait screens rather than wait dynamics.
whereToUse: Customer support, telehealth, KYC review queues, food delivery, AI inference capacity planning.
example: A telehealth service runs at 92% clinician utilisation with waits of 40 minutes. Kingman's formula shows that cutting service time variability via structured intake would reduce waits more than hiring one extra clinician.
sources: Little, A proof for the queuing formula L = lambda W (1961), Operations Research
reference: Little, J. D. C. (1961). Operations Research, 9(3), 383-387.

name: Quick uncertainty rules of thumb (square-root rule, rule of three)
aka: Square-root rule of thumb for count and survey data
Quick and dirty variability estimate for proportions
Rule of Three for zero observed events
origin: Square-root rule: Alan Dix's teaching heuristic from the binomial variance; rule of three: widely known zero-numerator bound
summary: Back-of-envelope error bounds: about twice the square root of a count for percentages, and 3/n as the 95% upper bound when an event never occurred in n trials.
description: Two quick rules give rough uncertainty without software. Dix's square-root rule converts a percentage to a count and takes about twice its square root as an approximate 95% margin; for a large majority apply it to those who did not choose the option, and near 50% use 1.5 times the square root. Dividing by sample size gives a percentage band. Both simplify the binomial variance. The rule of three handles zero events, where the usual interval collapses because its standard error is zero: solving (1 - p)^n = 0.05 gives an upper 95% bound of about 3/n, with 6/n giving roughly 99.75%. Both assume independent trials with a common probability. Neither corrects for biased samples, self-selection or leading wording; as Dix notes, a precise estimate from a biased sample is a good estimate of the wrong thing.
steps: Convert the percentage to a count of people (for example 10% of 1,000 is 100).
For a small proportion take the square root of that count and double it; for a large majority do the same on the count who did not choose the option; near 50% multiply the square root by 1.5.
Divide the resulting count margin by the sample size to give an approximate 95% band in percentage points.
For zero observed events in n independent trials, set the lower limit at 0 and the upper 95% limit at 3/n (about 6/n for 99.75%).
Compare the bound with the decision threshold, such as an acceptable error or defect rate.
Before trusting either rule, check independence, sample fairness, self-selection and question wording.
outputs: An approximate 95% range for a count or percentage, or a one-sided upper bound for an event that never occurred.
useWhen: Sanity-checking survey percentages, usability findings or zero-failure results in meetings, or deciding whether a difference is worth formal testing.
avoidWhen: Final reporting or small samples near the extremes (use adjusted-Wald or exact intervals). Dependent observations, such as repeated attempts by the same user, or non-random samples invalidate both rules.
whyLost: Calculators and software made quick mental rules seem unnecessary, yet teams still report percentages and 'zero errors' without any sense of their uncertainty.
whereToUse: Stakeholder reviews of survey results, small usability tests with no observed failures, safety and error-rate claims, quick readouts of A/B dashboards.
example: A team reports that none of 12 participants made a payment error. The rule of three gives an upper bound of 3/12 = 25%, so the test cannot rule out a one-in-four error rate. A survey finding that 50% of 2,000 prefer a feature carries about +/-2.5 points.
sources: Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Dix, A. (2020). Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data. Synthesis Lectures on Human-Centered Informatics #44. Morgan & Claypool.

name: QUIS (Questionnaire for User Interaction Satisfaction)
origin: Chin, Diehl & Norman (1988), Human-Computer Interaction Lab, University of Maryland
summary: The first published standardised usability questionnaire, rating specific interface factors such as screen, terminology, learning and system capabilities on 9-point bipolar scales.
description: Created by Shneiderman's Human-Computer Interaction Lab at Maryland, the QUIS measures satisfaction with specific parts of an interface rather than giving a single score. Version 7 has a demographic section, overall reactions on six scales, and hierarchically organised sections for nine interface factors: screen, terminology and system feedback, learning, system capabilities, technical manuals, online tutorials, multimedia, teleconferencing and software installation. Items use 9-point bipolar scales (for example, messages on screen: confusing to clear) with an N/A option. A short form has 41 items and a long form 122; most teams use only the sections that apply. Chin and colleagues reported an overall reliability of 0.94 for the 27-item short form and showed it separated liked and disliked systems. It requires a paid licence.
steps: License the QUIS (student, academic or commercial fee) and pick the sections relevant to your product.
Administer it after participants have used the system enough to judge each factor.
Score each item 1 to 9, allowing N/A, and average items within each section.
Compare section means across versions or products to find the weakest interface factors.
Pair with task data so low-scoring factors can be traced to observed problems.
outputs: Satisfaction scores for overall reaction and each interface factor.
useWhen: You need diagnostic, factor-by-factor satisfaction data on desktop or enterprise software and can license the instrument.
avoidWhen: You need a short, free instrument or comparison to modern norms (use SUS or UMUX-Lite).
whyLost: SUS was free and ten items long, so it displaced the licensed, much longer QUIS; its factor list also reflects 1980s software (manuals, teleconferencing).
whereToUse: Legacy enterprise systems, government software procurement, academic HCI replications.
example: A hospital records system scores well on screen layout but poorly on terminology and system feedback, so the team rewrites messages and labels before redesigning screens.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Chin, J. P., Diehl, V. A. & Norman, K. L. (1988). Development of an instrument measuring user satisfaction of the human-computer interface. CHI 88.

name: Quota Sampling
origin: Market research and polling practice; described by Veal and Darcy mainly for street surveys
summary: Interviewers fill pre-set quotas of people in each category, such as age and sex, in the proportions known to exist in the population.
description: Quota sampling gives interviewers a predetermined number of different types of people to interview, for example by age, sex or occupation, so that the final sample matches the population on those characteristics. Veal and Darcy present it as the usual answer to the problems of street surveys, where the people passing a given spot at a given time are not representative of the wider population. The proportions in each category must be known in advance, for example from the census or, for some sport tourism activities, from booking data. If the completed sample is still out of line on key characteristics, weighting can correct it further. Where nothing is known about the population, quota sampling cannot be used. Selection within each quota cell is left to the interviewer, so it is not a probability sample, and bias can enter on characteristics that are not controlled. In UX, quotas are the normal way recruiters balance study participants by segment, platform or experience level; the book's emphasis on using known population figures for the quotas, rather than arbitrary equal splits, is the part UX often misses.
steps: Decide which characteristics most affect the answers and are known for the population.
Obtain population proportions for those characteristics from census, analytics or booking data.
Set quota targets for each category, or combinations of categories, in proportion to the population.
Brief interviewers or recruiters to fill each quota and stop when it is full.
Monitor fill rates during fieldwork and adjust effort to hard-to-reach cells.
Compare the final sample with the population on other characteristics and weight if needed.
Report the method as non-probability and avoid presenting margins of error as exact.
outputs: A sample that matches the population on the controlled characteristics, with records of quota fill and any weighting applied.
useWhen: No sampling frame exists or probability sampling is too costly, but key population proportions are known.
avoidWhen: Population proportions are unknown, or precise, defensible population estimates with confidence intervals are required.
whyLost: It survived: UX recruiting screeners routinely use quotas, though often set as equal splits rather than population proportions.
whereToUse: Street and intercept research, panel surveys, participant recruitment for usability and concept testing, market sizing surveys.
example: For a survey of potential users of a city bike-share app, recruiters fill quotas of age group and gender matching the city's census profile, then weight slightly by car ownership, which was over-represented among people stopped near car parks.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: R-Indicators for Nonresponse Representativeness
aka: Coefficient of variation of response propensities
origin: Barry Schouten and colleagues, RISQ project (Statistics Netherlands)
summary: Summarising how representative a respondent set is from the variation in estimated response propensities, and using partial indicators to locate which groups drive it.
description: Response rates say little about bias. R-indicators measure representativeness directly: using auxiliary variables known for respondents and nonrespondents alike, response propensities are estimated, and R = 1 - 2 x SD of the propensities. R of 1 means every unit was equally likely to respond on those variables. The coefficient of variation of propensities gives an upper bound on nonresponse bias for estimates related to the auxiliaries. Partial R-indicators, unconditional and conditional, at variable and category level, show which groups contribute most to the lack of representativeness. These feed adaptive fieldwork (which groups to chase) and the choice of weighting variables. The indicator is only as good as its auxiliary variables, and a low R does not prove bias in any given estimate.
steps: Assemble auxiliary variables available for both respondents and nonrespondents (from the frame, account data or logs).
Estimate each sampled unit's response propensity with a logistic model.
Compute R = 1 - 2 x standard deviation of propensities, and the coefficient of variation as a bias bound.
Compute unconditional and conditional partial R-indicators by variable and category.
Use the partial indicators to target fieldwork at under-represented groups and to choose weighting variables; track R across waves.
outputs: An R-indicator, a coefficient of variation bias bound and partial indicators by group.
useWhen: Any survey drawn from a user database or CRM where rich account or behavioural data exist for nonrespondents, especially trackers compared over time.
avoidWhen: Samples with no auxiliary information on nonrespondents, such as open web links. Do not report R as proof that a given estimate is unbiased.
whyLost: UX teams report response rate as the quality signal even when they hold rich log data on nonrespondents that would allow a far better indicator.
whereToUse: In-product and email surveys of known users, B2B account surveys with firmographic data, panel waves.
example: A video platform surveys 20,000 sampled users with full usage data. R is 0.78, and partial indicators show the gap is driven by low-activity and mobile-only users, so those groups receive a reminder in-app and weighting uses activity tier and device.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Bethlehem, J. and Schouten, B. (2016). Nonresponse error: detection and correction. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 558-578). London: SAGE.

name: Radial Category Analysis
aka: Radial category analysis (of a category's members or a term's senses)
origin: Adapted for UX from George Lakoff (1987), building on Dixon (1982), Brugman (1981) and Lindner (1981)
summary: Model a category, or all the senses of one term, as a central case plus extensions linked to it by named, independently justified principles, exposing why members belong.
description: A radial category has a central subcategory and conventional variants motivated by the centre but not predictable by rule, so they must be learned. The analysis collects every member of a category or every use of a term, identifies the central member or sense, and for each non-central item finds the link that motivates it: a shared domain of experience, a belief, an image-schema transformation, metonymy or metaphor. Each link type must be justified by other cases, not invented for one item. Chains (A to B to C) and unexplained exceptions are recorded. Lakoff's examples include the Dyirbal classifier balan, the Japanese classifier hon and the many senses of 'over'. For UX, the same structure explains why an existing navigation category or overloaded label holds members users cannot predict, and which links break first.
steps: Collect all members of the category, or all uses of the term in content, logs or interviews, with example contexts.
Identify the central member or sense, usually concrete and basic-level, using centrality ratings where feasible.
For each non-central item, name the link that motivates it: experiential domain, belief, image-schema transformation, metonymy or metaphor.
Require each link type to be supported by other cases rather than invented for a single item.
Record chains of links and list exceptions that no link explains.
Use contrastive sentences or tasks to separate senses of an ambiguous term.
Check the network against users' own explanations and against where users fail to predict membership, then decide which chains to keep, split or relabel.
outputs: A radial network diagram showing the centre, extensions, link types, chains and exceptions, plus labelling or restructuring decisions.
useWhen: When a navigation category, product taxonomy or overloaded label (for example 'Account', 'Home', 'Plans') has accumulated members users cannot predict, and you need to understand the chains that brought them there.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you only need to know what users expect under a label; Card Sorting or Tree Testing is faster. Motivation explains but does not predict membership, so do not treat the network as a rule for placing new items without testing.
whyLost: It remains a cognitive linguistics method; IA borrowed prototype and basic-level ideas but not the analysis of chaining and motivated extension.
whereToUse: Mature taxonomies and mega-menus, overloaded feature names, conversational AI intent sets, cross-cultural localisation of category labels.
example: A telecom site's 'Plans' section holds phone plans, insurance, roaming add-ons and device trade-in. Radial analysis shows insurance entered via 'monthly charge', trade-in via 'upgrade', and roaming via 'allowance', so users looking for trade-in fail; the team splits off an 'Upgrade' category along that chain.
reference: Lakoff, G. (1987). Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things: What Categories Reveal about the Mind. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.

name: Rainbow Spreadsheet
origin: Tomer Sharon at Google (Sharon, 2016); GDS variant (Fu, 2019)
summary: Observers log behaviours in one shared, colour-coded grid of observations by participant, so patterns across sessions are visible at a glance and the sheet becomes the report.
description: The rainbow spreadsheet makes usability analysis a team activity. Rows are observations; there is one coloured column per participant, so issues seen by many people show as long coloured rows. Expected observations are pre-entered from the protocol, never double-barrelled, and new ones are added during sessions. The whole team watches sessions or recordings together and edits one sheet, noting only what participants do or say; short debriefs after each session merge duplicates and remove conclusions. A GDS variant lists the team's assumptions per task and marks each participant green or red for whether they behaved as assumed. After the last session the team discusses why things happened and agrees about ten actions, and a summary sheet makes the workbook the report.
steps: Finalise the protocol and copy the template, with one column per participant plus notes.
Pre-enter expected observations or the team's assumptions per task, one per row and never double-barrelled.
Watch sessions or recordings together; each observer marks the participant's cell (or green/red against an assumption) and adds notes on what was done or said.
After each session, debrief briefly: merge duplicate rows and remove interpretations or solutions.
After the last session, compare sheets and discuss why the patterns occurred.
Agree about ten action items and add a summary sheet at the front of the workbook, published as the report.
outputs: A colour-coded observation-by-participant matrix with metrics, participant details, and a summary of findings and actions.
useWhen: Fast-paced, small-sample usability tests in agile teams where stakeholders observe and a separate report would be wasted effort.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on pre-entered rows alone, since observers miss events outside them; do not use it for deep interpretive studies or quantitative benchmarks.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, collaborative and fits sprint cadences.
whereToUse: Agile product teams, government digital services, prototype testing rounds, design sprints.
example: Five participants attempt three travel booking tasks. The sheet shows four of five misreading the 'to' date field, and the team agrees the fix before the next sprint without writing a report.
reference: Sharon, T. (2016). Validating Product Ideas Through Lean User Research. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media, ch. 6.

name: RAMP Model for Intrinsic Gamification
origin: Andrzej Marczewski, 2013; drawing on Deci & Ryan's self-determination theory
summary: Designs and audits engagement features against four intrinsic motivators (relatedness, autonomy, mastery, purpose) instead of relying on points and badges.
description: RAMP organises gamification around four intrinsic motivators derived from self-determination theory and Pink's synthesis: relatedness (social connection), autonomy (meaningful choice), mastery (growing competence) and purpose (contribution to something meaningful). Rather than adding extrinsic mechanics such as points, the designer audits a product for each motivator, identifies which are absent for each user type, and designs features that satisfy them, with extrinsic rewards used sparingly and informationally. The approach guards against the overjustification effect, where external rewards reduce intrinsic interest. It becomes rigorous when paired with user-type analysis, validated motivation measures (e.g. intrinsic motivation inventories) and experiments that test whether engagement changes are sustained beyond novelty.
steps: Audit every reward/engagement mechanic in the product against RAMP: Relatedness (does this mechanic connect users to others, or is it purely individual?), Autonomy (does this mechanic constrain or enable choice?), Mastery (does this mechanic provide feedback on growing competence?), Purpose (does this mechanic connect to a meaningful goal?).
Mechanics scoring 0 on all four dimensions are likely extrinsic-only — predict motivation crowding out over time.
outputs: A RAMP audit of current features, motivator gaps per user type, intrinsic-motivation design concepts, and measures to test their effect.
useWhen: Enterprise software, learning, health or habit products where sustained voluntary engagement matters and extrinsic rewards risk crowding out motivation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when engagement is not a legitimate goal (manipulative contexts), or when tasks are mandatory and should simply be made efficient; avoid untested claims, so pair with experiments.
whyLost: Gamification became synonymous with points, badges and leaderboards; motivation-theory-based design was lost in the hype and backlash.
whereToUse: Enterprise software engagement design, health behavior change apps, learning product design, community platform design.
example: A compliance-training platform audits its badges with RAMP and finds no autonomy or purpose; adding choice of learning path and stories about prevented incidents increases voluntary completion.
reference: Kumar J & Herger M (2013) Gamification at Work: Designing Engaging Business Software. Interaction Design Foundation

name: Random Forest Key Driver Analysis
origin: Leo Breiman (2001); conditional variable importance by Carolin Strobl et al. (2007-2008)
summary: Uses random forests to estimate which experience attributes most strongly predict an outcome like satisfaction or churn, with careful importance measures.
description: Key driver analysis asks which attributes (speed, support, reliability, ease) matter most for an overall outcome. Multiple regression struggles with correlated attributes and nonlinearity. Random forests capture interactions and nonlinear effects, and provide variable importance. However, default impurity-based importance is biased toward variables with many categories, and permutation importance is biased under correlation; conditional permutation importance or SHAP values with care, plus partial dependence plots, are needed. Drivers are predictive, not causal, and should be presented as such. Many dashboards show 'drivers' from naive correlations or default importances, the vestigial form.
steps: Collect outcome measures and candidate attributes (survey ratings, behavioural metrics) for a large sample (e.g. 500+).
Fit a random forest with tuned parameters and evaluate out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
Compute conditional permutation importance or SHAP-based importance, and compare with a relative weights or dominance analysis.
Examine partial dependence and accumulated local effects plots to see shape (thresholds, saturation).
Check stability with bootstrapped importance rankings.
Present drivers as predictive associations, then test top drivers causally where possible.
outputs: Stable importance rankings, response-shape plots and predictive accuracy metrics.
useWhen: Prioritising experience attributes from survey and behavioural data with many correlated predictors.
avoidWhen: Small samples, or when causal effects are required; use experiments or causal methods.
whyLost: Dashboards adopted 'key drivers' as a feature, often with biased importance measures and causal language.
whereToUse: NPS and CSAT programmes, churn analysis, app store review analysis, B2B relationship surveys.
example: A telco's driver analysis shows network reliability dominates satisfaction only below a threshold of 2 outages a month; above that, billing clarity matters most, so investment is targeted by segment.
sources: Strobl et al., Conditional variable importance for random forests (2008), BMC Bioinformatics
Empowering Qualitative Researchers with Quantitative Techniques (Scharff, 2024)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
reference: Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32.

name: Randomisation unit selection
origin: Deng, Lu and Litz (2017); Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020)
summary: Choose whether to randomise by page, session, user, device, account or cluster by weighing experience consistency, which metrics must be valid, and interference between units.
description: The unit an experiment randomises determines what it can measure. Finer units (pageview, session) add statistical power but break when a feature or metric spans units, or when users notice an inconsistent experience; coarser units (user, account, tenant, cluster) keep experiences consistent and support user-level and long-term metrics. The randomisation unit should be equal to or coarser than the analysis unit; when coarser, variance must use the delta method or bootstrap and per-user contributions may need capping. Signed-in IDs suit cross-device and long-term work; cookies or device IDs suit flows that cross sign-in; IP addresses are reserved for infrastructure tests because their sizes vary wildly. In enterprise products, advertising and social networks, randomising tenants, advertisers or friend clusters may be needed to avoid interference.
steps: List candidate units: pageview, session, device or cookie, signed-in user, account or tenant, cluster.
Ask whether users would notice inconsistency if their experience changed between units; if so, move to a coarser unit.
List the metrics that must be valid (for example sessions per user needs at least user-level randomisation) and match the unit to them.
Check for carryover between units and interference through shared accounts, marketplaces or social ties; consider cluster randomisation if present.
Choose the ID type by scope and longevity (signed-in ID for cross-device and long-term, cookie for pre-sign-in flows, IP only for infrastructure).
Plan the variance method that matches the unit (delta method or bootstrap when the analysis unit is finer than the randomisation unit).
outputs: A chosen randomisation unit and ID type with written justification and a matching variance method.
useWhen: Designing any online experiment, especially in B2B SaaS, marketplaces, social products, search and multi-device products.
avoidWhen: It is never wrong to make the choice explicitly, but where interference dominates (two-sided marketplaces), go further to switchback or cluster-randomised designs.
whyLost: Experimentation platforms default to user or cookie IDs, so the choice is rarely made deliberately, and UX researchers seldom see the analysis consequences.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS with shared workspaces, search engines, marketplaces, social networks and multi-device consumer apps.
example: A collaborative whiteboard tests a new comment panel. Randomising by user would show colleagues on the same board different interfaces, so the team randomises by workspace and uses the delta method for user-level metrics.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Beyond t Test and ANOVA (Yu et al., 2022)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, ch. 14.

name: Randomised Complete Block Design (RCBD)
origin: Ronald Fisher and Frank Yates, Rothamsted, 1920s-1930s (Yates 1933, 1935)
summary: Group units into homogeneous blocks, run every treatment once in each block with fresh randomisation, and remove block-to-block variation from the error.
description: Blocking is Fisher's principle of local control: compare treatments within sets of units that are alike, so nuisance variation between sets does not blur the comparison. An RCBD has b blocks of t homogeneous units, each treatment appearing once per block and randomised independently within each block. Blocks may be non-specific (days, batches, recruitment waves) or intrinsic (sites, devices, suppliers). Analysis is a two-way ANOVA of blocks plus treatments, but blocks are not F-tested because they were not randomised. Relative efficiency against a completely randomised design is estimated from the block and error mean squares; Hinkelmann and Kempthorne suggest blocking is worth repeating only if it exceeds about 125 percent. Missing values can be estimated with Yates' formula at the cost of one error df each. The generalised randomised block design runs each treatment more than once per block, allowing a valid test of block-by-treatment interaction.
steps: Identify a nuisance source of variation (device, day, site, recruitment wave) and form blocks of t units as alike as possible, or rt units for a generalised design.
Form blocks before randomising, then randomise treatments to units separately within each block.
Analyse with a two-way ANOVA of blocks plus treatments and do not F-test the blocks.
Check for nonadditivity with Tukey's one-df test and transform the response if needed.
Estimate relative efficiency against a completely randomised design from MS(blocks) and MS(error); keep blocking in future studies if it exceeds about 125 percent.
If values are missing, estimate them with Yates' formula or covariance and reduce the error df by one for each.
If block-by-treatment interaction is expected, use a generalised design with each treatment repeated within each block.
outputs: An ANOVA with block and treatment rows, treatment means and contrasts, and an estimate of the efficiency gained by blocking.
useWhen: Comparing designs when a known nuisance factor (device type, test day, moderator, market) would otherwise inflate error, and every variant can be run within each block.
avoidWhen: Blocks too small to hold all variants (use Incomplete Block Designs); two crossed nuisance factors (Latin Square and Williams Counterbalancing); or when block-by-treatment interaction is itself expected but each treatment appears only once per block.
whyLost: Blocking is taught in every design-of-experiments course and alive in agriculture and engineering, but UX experiments are usually completely randomised and nuisance factors are handled, if at all, by post-hoc segmentation.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks run across days or labs, multi-market tests, device-stratified experiments, moderated studies with several moderators.
example: A team compares three onboarding flows across four recruitment waves of 30 participants, randomising flows within each wave. The wave effect is large, and relative efficiency of 160 percent shows blocking cut the needed sample substantially.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Hinkelmann, K., & Kempthorne, O. (2008). Design and Analysis of Experiments, Volume 1: Introduction to Experimental Design (2nd ed.). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 277-299, 314-327.

name: Randomised Response Technique
origin: Stanley Warner, 1965
