summary: Uses a private randomising device to let respondents answer sensitive questions truthfully, recovering population prevalence while protecting individuals.
description: When asked directly about sensitive behaviour, people under-report. In randomised response, each respondent privately uses a randomiser (e.g. a die) that decides whether they answer the sensitive question truthfully or give a forced answer. The researcher never knows which applied, but because the probabilities are known, the prevalence can be estimated. Variants include Warner's original, forced response and unrelated question designs. Meta-analyses show RRT yields more valid prevalence estimates than direct questions in many contexts, though comprehension matters. For UX, it measures sensitive behaviours like password sharing, account sharing, policy violations, cheating or risky use.
steps: Choose the sensitive question and the RRT variant (forced response is easiest to explain).
Set randomisation probabilities (e.g. 75% answer truthfully, 25% forced 'yes' or 'no').
Implement an online randomiser that respondents trust (e.g. a birthday-based rule or visible die) and explain protection clearly.
Include comprehension checks; consider a direct-question control group for comparison.
Estimate prevalence and its standard error using the design formulas, accounting for the larger variance.
Size the sample accordingly (RRT needs several times the sample of direct questioning).
outputs: Privacy-protected prevalence estimates with confidence intervals and comparison to direct questions.
useWhen: Estimating prevalence of sensitive, stigmatised or rule-breaking behaviours relevant to design.
avoidWhen: Individual-level analysis is needed, or samples are small.
whyLost: It needs larger samples and careful explanation; UX surveys rarely handle sensitive behaviours with special designs.
whereToUse: Account sharing, security practices, misuse of AI tools at work, health behaviours, financial distress.
example: A streaming service estimates password sharing. Direct questions yield 18%, a forced response design yields 34%, giving a more accurate basis for policy and UX design.
sources: Warner, Randomized response: A survey technique for eliminating evasive answer bias (1965), JASA
Lensvelt-Mulders et al., Meta-analysis of randomized response research (2005), Sociological Methods & Research
Blair, Imai & Zhou, Design and analysis of the randomized response technique (2015), JASA
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)

name: Randomised Triangle (Odd-One-Out) Discrimination Test
donor: Sensory science and design of experiments
origin: Sensory triangle test from brewing and food science; set beside Fisher's lady tasting tea and adapted to clinical comparison by Hinkelmann and Kempthorne (2008)
summary: A blind test in which judges pick the odd one of three specimens; randomisation fixes chance success at one third, and repeated trials are tested against the binomial.
description: The triangle test answers a question that precedes any preference test: can people perceive a difference at all? Each trial presents three specimens, two of version A and one of B (or the reverse), with the odd specimen and the order chosen at random. The judge, blind to the allocation, names the odd one using a protocol fixed in advance. Because of the randomisation, the probability of a correct pick under no discrimination is exactly 1/3 whatever other differences exist between specimens. A single trial carries little evidence, so the design is repeated across many trials or judges and the number correct is referred to the binomial with p = 1/3. Repetition, not a larger set within one trial, is how sensitivity is gained. Its rigour rests entirely on the randomisation being carried out properly.
steps: Prepare three specimens per trial: two of version A and one of version B, balancing across trials which version is doubled.
Randomise which specimen is the odd one and the order of presentation for every trial.
Keep the judge blind and have them name the odd one using a response protocol fixed in advance (forced choice, no 'cannot tell').
Score each trial correct or incorrect.
Repeat over many trials or judges; as a rough guide, around 30 or more judgements are needed to detect moderate discriminability.
Refer the number correct to the binomial distribution with p = 1/3 to obtain a one-sided p-value.
outputs: The count of correct odd-one-out identifications and a binomial p-value for whether a perceptible difference exists.
useWhen: Checking whether users can perceive a latency change, colour tweak, haptic pattern, audio compression or image quality reduction before investing in a preference or A/B test.
avoidWhen: When the question is which version people prefer or how large the perceived difference is (use Preference Test or Psychophysical Threshold Methods (JND)), or when specimens cannot be presented in close succession under controlled conditions.
whyLost: It is standard in sensory and food science but UX teams usually jump straight to preference or A/B testing, never confirming that the difference is perceptible.
whereToUse: Performance budgets, media compression, haptics and audio branding, accessibility contrast changes, cost-saving substitutions in hardware.
example: A video platform wants to lower bitrate by 15 percent. Forty viewers each see three clips, two at one bitrate and one at the other in random order; 16 correct picks against an expected 13.3 gives p = 0.27, so the saving goes ahead with a guardrail metric.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
reference: Hinkelmann, K., & Kempthorne, O. (2008). Design and Analysis of Experiments, Volume 1: Introduction to Experimental Design (2nd ed.). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons. pp. 139-142.

name: Rank-Ordered (Exploded) Logit
origin: Luce and Suppes (1965); applied by Beggs, Cardell and Hausman (1981) and Chapman and Staelin (1982)
summary: Model a respondent's full ranking of options as a sequence of logit choices, first from all options and then from those remaining, to estimate attribute utilities from ranking questions.
description: When respondents rank alternatives rather than choose one, the probability of the full ranking under logit is the product of successive choices: the top option chosen from all, the second from those left, and so on. Each ranking of J alternatives is 'exploded' into J - 1 pseudo-observations, with already-ranked options removed from each later choice set, and estimated with standard logit software. This uses all the information in a ranking rather than only the first choice. Because a person's pseudo-observations share their tastes, Train recommends a mixed logit estimated as panel data; with probit, rankings become utility-difference inequalities simulated by GHK. The product form depends on independent extreme-value errors, so lower ranks, which respondents give less carefully, can bias estimates if treated as equally informative.
steps: Collect rankings of alternatives described by attributes, or a choose-then-choose-again sequence.
Explode each ranking of J alternatives into J - 1 pseudo-observations, repeating the explanatory variables.
For each pseudo-observation remove alternatives already ranked higher and code the next-ranked one as chosen.
Estimate an ordinary conditional logit on the pseudo-observations.
Prefer a mixed logit that treats each person's pseudo-observations as a panel so their correlation is modelled.
Check whether lower ranks behave consistently with top ranks, for example by fitting the top two ranks only and comparing.
outputs: Attribute utility weights and preference shares that use the full ranking from each respondent.
useWhen: When surveys or studies already collect rankings of feature bundles, plans or designs and you want attribute-level utilities rather than average ranks.
avoidWhen: Avoid when respondents rank many items carelessly; MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) or choice tasks give cleaner data. If you only need a group ordering, rank-based nonparametric summaries suffice. For designed attribute trade-offs use Conjoint Analysis.
whyLost: It sits in econometrics and marketing science; UX ranking questions are usually summarised by mean rank.
whereToUse: Pricing and packaging research, feature prioritisation surveys, ranking-based concept tests.
example: A streaming service asks 800 users to rank four plan bundles differing in price, ads and downloads. An exploded mixed logit shows downloads are worth more than ad removal to families, which mean ranks had hidden.
reference: Beggs, S., Cardell, S. and Hausman, J. (1981). Assessing the potential demand for electric cars. Journal of Econometrics, 17(1), 1-19; Train, K. E. (2009). Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation (2nd ed.). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

name: Rapid Affinity Building (2-Day Sprint Version)
origin: Karen Holtzblatt, Jessamyn Burns Wendell and Shelley Wood (Rapid Contextual Design, 2005)
summary: A compressed but disciplined team affinity process: individual interpretation notes from field sessions are built bottom-up into a two-level hierarchy within a few hours.
description: The affinity diagram in Contextual Design is a bottom-up, team synthesis of interpretation notes from contextual interviews, grouped by similarity of meaning rather than predefined categories, and labelled in the user's voice. The full version uses four levels and hundreds of notes. Holtzblatt's rapid version preserves the core discipline for time-boxed projects: each researcher conducts one or two contextual inquiry sessions, writes 50-100 interpretation notes per session in a team interpretation meeting, and the team builds the affinity in about four hours with a two-level hierarchy. Rules still apply: no pre-set categories, groups of no more than about four to six notes, labels written as first-person user statements, and walking the wall to generate design ideas. Popular sticky-note clustering keeps the look but loses these rules.
steps: Preparation: Each researcher conducts 1–2 contextual inquiry sessions. From each session, create 50–100 data notes — one idea, observation, or quote per note. Physical sticky notes or digital equivalents.

Day 1, Hours 1–4 — Individual sorting: Each researcher silently sorts their notes into groups, labelling each group with a description that captures the shared meaning. No discussion during this phase.
Day 1, Hours 4–6 — Team merge: Teams combine overlapping groups. Negotiate on group labels. Every note must belong to exactly one group.
Day 1, Hours 6–8 — Second-level labels: Create higher-level labels over grouped sets. These are your themes.
Day 2, Hours 1–4 — Design insights: For each theme, generate design insights: what does this theme tell us about what users need? Convert insights to design opportunities.
outputs: Interpretation notes, a two-level affinity wall with user-voice labels, walked-wall design ideas and prioritised insights.
useWhen: Time-boxed discovery sprints with field data, small teams needing shared understanding quickly, and synthesising 6-12 sessions.
avoidWhen: When large volumes of transcripts need systematic coding and audit trails (use framework analysis or thematic analysis), or when there is no field data, only opinions.
whyLost: Affinity mapping became generic sticky-note grouping, often with top-down categories and no interpretation sessions, so Holtzblatt's rules were lost even as the name spread.
whereToUse: Agile UX programs, design sprints, any context where full Beyer-Holtzblatt affinity is not feasible.
example: After eight contextual interviews with pharmacists, four researchers write 520 notes and build a two-level affinity in an afternoon. A cluster labelled 'I don't trust the stock count, so I check the shelf' redirects the inventory feature.
sources: Rapid Contextual Design — Morgan Kaufmann (Holtzblatt et al.)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 34 — Framework Analysis & Systematic Qualitative Synthesis
reference: Holtzblatt K, Wendell JB & Wood S (2005) Rapid Contextual Design: A How-To Guide to Key Techniques for User-Centered Design. Morgan Kaufmann

name: Rapid Contextual Design variants
origin: Holtzblatt, Wendell and Wood (2005), adapting Beyer and Holtzblatt's Contextual Design (1998); agile variant with LANDesk (Beyer, Holtzblatt and Baker, 2004)
summary: Cut-down Contextual Design processes for a two-person team, chosen by project type, running from one-week field sprints to six to ten week projects feeding agile development.
description: Rapid CD defines named variants by which Contextual Design steps they keep. Lightning Fast (one to four weeks, four to twelve users) runs contextual interviews with interpretation sessions capturing affinity notes only, builds and walks an affinity, then produces quick recommendations or a vision. Lightning Fast + (four to eight weeks) adds a first-cut interface and two or three rounds of paper prototype interviews. Focused Rapid CD (six to ten weeks, eight to twelve users) adds sequence models, consolidation and storyboards, and suits new products and coherent tasks. The agile variant runs a two-person UI track one iteration ahead of developers: consolidated sequences guide user stories and each iteration's interfaces are paper-tested before coding. Discipline comes from planning rules: interpret every interview within 48 hours, start with two interviews, and chunk larger scopes into a series of short projects.
steps: Check scope: one to four clearly defined job roles; otherwise chunk the work by work group, department or geography into sequential short projects.

Pick the variant: Lightning Fast for quick fixes and market characterisation, Lightning Fast + for simple fixes, web pages and reporting interfaces, Focused Rapid CD for new products and coherent tasks, or the agile variant for XP or Scrum teams.
Staff a two-person cross-functional core team, set up visits two to four weeks ahead, and write a day-by-day schedule.
Run contextual interviews (at least three people per role) and interpret each within 48 hours, capturing affinity notes and, for Focused or agile variants, sequences.
Build the affinity in one day with two to four helpers (about 60 to 80 notes per person), consolidate sequences where used, and walk the wall with the wider team.
Finish with recommendations grouped by user impact or a vision; for Lightning Fast + or Focused, add an interface and two or three rounds of paper mock-up interviews with three to four users each.
In the agile variant, write user stories guided by sequences, paper-test each iteration's interfaces one iteration ahead, and test running code with customers every second or third iteration.
Hold weekly pluses and minuses on the process and adjust.
outputs: Affinity diagram, key issues and recommendations or vision; paper-tested prototypes; consolidated sequences and storyboards; prioritised user stories with tested UIs per iteration.
useWhen: A small team needs field-grounded requirements on a tight schedule, or wants contextual data to drive an agile backlog.
avoidWhen: Avoid when scope spans many roles or a whole business process; no method can redesign a multi-role process in two weeks, so use full Contextual Design or chunk the work. Lightning Fast produces no task analysis and no tested design, and an on-site customer representative cannot substitute for field data.
whyLost: The practice of short field sprints survives under names such as lean research and discovery sprints, while the named variants, their planning rules and sequence models are largely forgotten.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS discovery, internal tools, agile product teams wanting a dual-track discovery rhythm, and short consultancy engagements.
example: A two-person team at an HR software firm runs Lightning Fast with six payroll administrators in one week: interviews each morning, interpretation each afternoon, affinity on Thursday and recommendations on Friday. The top issue, re-keying data between systems, goes straight into the next quarter's roadmap.
reference: Holtzblatt, K., Wendell, J. B. & Wood, S. (2005). Rapid Contextual Design: A How-to Guide to Key Techniques for User-Centered Design. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Rapid ethnography
donor: Sociology (CSCW ethnography); applied anthropology; epidemiology; programme evaluation
origin: Hughes, King, Rodden and Andersen (1994); Millen (2000); Beebe (2001) rapid assessment; Patton (1987) rapid reconnaissance
summary: Time-compressed team fieldwork that trades duration for focus, multiple informants and several data sources, to inform design or urgent decisions in days or weeks.
description: Traditional ethnography is prolonged, while design wants results quickly. Hughes et al. distinguished four uses in systems design: re-examining earlier studies, quick and dirty studies giving an informed overview, concurrent ethnography running alongside development and shifting focus as design evolves, and evaluative ethnography checking decisions already made. From anthropology and epidemiology, rapid assessment sends a multidisciplinary team to work intensively for a fixed short period, using snowball sampling of knowledgeable informants and combining interviews, focus groups, observation and document or media scanning, then synthesising fast for decision makers. Rigour comes not from time in the field but from a narrow focus, a team, triangulation of sources, key informants and iterative analysis while still on site.
steps: Choose the use by design stage, time available, access and existing data: re-examination, quick and dirty, concurrent or evaluative.
Review earlier studies of similar settings before fieldwork.
Form a small multidisciplinary team and define a narrow set of urgent questions.
Use snowball sampling to reach knowledgeable key informants quickly.
Work intensively for a short fixed period (for example ten days per site), combining interviews, observation, focus groups and document or media scanning.
Analyse daily as a team and refocus the next day's fieldwork on gaps.
Synthesise quickly for decision makers; in concurrent mode, feed findings into each development iteration.
outputs: A rapid situational description, an issue list for action, a stream of findings into iterative design, or an assessment of design decisions against practice.
useWhen: Decisions cannot wait for months of fieldwork but need grounding in real practice, or when ethnography must run alongside development.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the question concerns deep meaning, long cycles or rare events; speed trades away depth, so use longitudinal fieldwork. The term reconnaissance has military connotations some stakeholders dislike.
whyLost: Short field visits are common in UX, but the rigour that made rapid methods credible (teams, key informants, triangulation, daily analysis) is often dropped, leaving a single researcher's quick visit.
whereToUse: Discovery sprints, crisis or regulatory deadlines, new market entry, service redesign in public sector and health, and agile teams wanting concurrent fieldwork.
example: A health app team entering a new country sends a designer, researcher and clinician for ten days. Daily debriefs and snowball-sampled pharmacists and community health workers reveal that medication is bought in daily doses, reshaping the reminder feature.
sources: Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
reference: Hughes, J., King, V., Rodden, T. & Andersen, H. (1994). Moving out from the control room: ethnography in system design. CSCW '94; Millen, D. R. (2000). Rapid ethnography: time deepening strategies for HCI field research. DIS 2000.

name: Rapid User Mental Modeling (RUMM)
origin: Rashmi Sinha (Uzanto), early 2000s; sidebar in Pruitt and Adlin (2006)
summary: A quantitative pipeline that derives personas and an information architecture together from online free listing, importance ratings, principal components analysis and per-persona card sorts.
description: RUMM links audience segmentation and information architecture in one data flow. An online free-listing survey asks what people want from the site, merged with stakeholders' list of critical content. Respondents rate the importance of the combined items, and principal components analysis of the ratings groups respondents into clusters that become primary and secondary personas, defined by what content matters to them. An open card sort is then cluster-analysed separately for each persona group to give a mental model per persona. The architecture follows the primary persona's model while giving secondary personas good entry points, and a closed card sort verifies it. Its strength is that personas and structure are derived from the same respondents, so the IA is traceable to segment needs.
steps: Run an online free-listing survey asking what people want from the product, and merge results with a stakeholder list of critical content.
Have respondents rate the importance of each combined content item.
Run principal components analysis on the ratings to group respondents into clusters, and write primary and secondary personas from them.
Run an open card sort and cluster-analyse it separately for each persona group.
Design the information architecture from the primary persona's model, adding entry points for secondary personas.
Verify the structure with a closed card sort or tree test (the original used about 120 respondents).
outputs: Data-backed persona clusters, per-persona content hierarchies and a validated information architecture.
useWhen: A content-heavy site serves distinct audiences whose content priorities differ, and you want personas and structure grounded in the same data.
avoidWhen: Avoid with only a few dozen raters, since clusters will be unstable; and avoid when personas must capture behaviour or goals beyond content priorities. Use latent class analysis or behavioural segmentation with larger samples.
whyLost: It was promoted by a small consultancy and tool vendor and was not maintained after that; teams adopted card sorting and personas as separate activities.
whereToUse: University, government and membership sites, intranets, documentation portals and large content platforms with distinct audiences.
example: A university site collects 300 free lists and importance ratings, which separate prospective students from current students and staff. Per-group card sorts show prospective students group by course, not faculty, so admissions content gets its own course-first entry point.
reference: Pruitt, J. & Adlin, T. (2006). The Persona Lifecycle: Keeping People in Mind Throughout Product Design. Morgan Kaufmann (sidebar by Rashmi Sinha).

name: RAS-based alert design
origin: Reticular activating system described by Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949; arousal-performance relation by Yerkes and Dodson, 1908; applied to alarm design in human factors
summary: Designs alerts around the brain's arousal system, using onset, novelty and modality to raise arousal enough to capture attention without tipping users into startle or overload.
description: The reticular activating system in the brainstem regulates arousal and wakefulness, and responds strongly to abrupt onsets, novelty and changes in stimulation; it habituates to repeated, predictable stimuli. Alert design informed by this works on two levels. First, it uses features that reliably drive arousal: abrupt onset, change from background, auditory or haptic channels during visual work, and novelty. Second, it manages habituation and the inverted-U arousal-performance curve: too frequent or too intense alerts lead to tuning out or startle, which degrades performance. The approach is mostly a design rationale rather than a measured protocol, but it can be made rigorous by testing response latencies, habituation curves across repeated exposures and physiological arousal markers such as skin conductance.
steps: Classify alerts by urgency (for example three levels) and estimate how often each fires per hour in real use.
Assign arousal features by urgency: abrupt onset and cross-modal cues for high urgency, gentle onset and single-channel cues for low urgency.
Limit high-urgency alert frequency; habituation becomes significant when a stimulus repeats frequently without consequence, so review any high-urgency alert firing more than a few times per hour.
Avoid startle: keep auditory onset rise times above roughly 20-30 ms and levels within about 15-25 dB above ambient.
Test with 10-15 participants across repeated exposures, measuring response latency per exposure to detect habituation, and optionally skin conductance responses.
Adjust alert variation, frequency or escalation to sustain response without startle.
outputs: An urgency-to-arousal feature mapping, habituation curves, response latency data and a revised alert scheme.
useWhen: When alerts are ignored over time (habituation), when alerts must interrupt deep focus, or when startle responses cause errors.
avoidWhen: When the issue is false-alarm rates or threshold setting; use ROC analysis. For simple notification copy, use content testing.
whyLost: The neuroscience is well known but rarely translated into concrete UX alert guidance, and 'RAS' is often cited loosely in pop psychology, which deters rigorous use.
whereToUse: Clinical alarms, driver drowsiness alerts, aviation warnings, security operations, and wearable notifications.
example: Nurses respond to a pump occlusion alarm in 4 s on first exposure but 19 s by the tenth in a shift. Varying the sound pattern by escalation stage and adding a haptic pulse to the nurse's badge holds response near 6 s across exposures.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Moruzzi, G. & Magoun, H. W. (1949). Brain stem reticular formation and activation of the EEG. Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology, 1, 455-473.

name: RCT design for UX
origin: Ronald Fisher, 1925-1935; first modern clinical RCT (streptomycin) by the MRC, 1948
summary: Randomly assigns users or participants to design conditions so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the design, with power, metrics and analysis set in advance.
description: An RCT is the reference design for causal claims: randomisation balances known and unknown confounders in expectation, so outcome differences estimate the effect of the intervention. A/B testing is its online form, but UX practice often strips out the discipline that makes it rigorous: pre-specified primary metric, sample size from a power calculation, a fixed stopping rule, checks for sample ratio mismatch, guardrail metrics and a pre-registered analysis plan. Fisher's principles of randomisation, replication and blocking still apply, along with clinical-trial ideas such as intention-to-treat analysis and CONSORT-style reporting. Lab RCTs comparing prototypes, with counterbalancing and within-subject designs, are the small-sample sibling of online tests.
steps: Write a hypothesis, one primary metric, guardrail metrics and the minimum detectable effect that would change the decision.
Compute sample size for alpha 0.05 and power 0.8 (or 0.9 for high stakes), accounting for variance and the unit of randomisation.
Choose the randomisation unit (user, account, session, region) to avoid interference and contamination between arms.
Pre-register the analysis plan, including stopping rule, segments and handling of outliers.
Run an A/A test or check sample ratio mismatch (chi-squared p below 0.001 signals a fault) before reading results.
Run for the full planned duration and at least one full weekly cycle; avoid peeking unless using a sequential method.
Analyse by intention-to-treat, report effect size with confidence intervals and guardrail results, and document the decision.
outputs: An unbiased effect estimate with confidence interval on a pre-specified metric, guardrail checks, and a documented ship or no-ship decision.
useWhen: When a design change can be randomised and you need to know whether it causes a meaningful change in behaviour or outcomes.
avoidWhen: Avoid when traffic is too low for the minimum detectable effect, when randomisation is unethical or illegal, or when strong network effects cause interference; use quasi-experiments or switchback designs instead.
whyLost: A/B testing is ubiquitous but often reduced to dashboard-watching, peeking and multiple metric fishing, so the trial discipline that gives it causal force has eroded.
whereToUse: Product experimentation in e-commerce, SaaS, fintech and health apps; lab comparisons of prototypes; pricing and onboarding tests.
example: A banking app pre-registers a test of a simplified transfer flow with completion rate as the primary metric and error rate as a guardrail. With 40,000 users per arm it detects a 1.5-point lift and confirms errors did not rise.
sources: Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Scott Maxwell & Harold Delaney)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 47 — Experimental Design — From A/B to Quasi-Experiments
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020) Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press.

name: Re-expression with the Ladder of Powers
origin: Adapted for UX from John W. Tukey, Exploratory Data Analysis (1977)
summary: Choose a power, root, log or folded expression for amounts, counts or fractions so batches become symmetric with similar spreads and curved relationships straighten.
description: Tukey's re-expression family replaces fixed habits (always log task times) with a data-driven choice. Expressions form a ladder: squares, raw, square roots, logs (the zeroth power), negative reciprocal roots, negative reciprocals. For several batches, plotting log spread against log median gives a tilt: near 1/2 points to roots, near 1 to logs, and each step down the ladder lowers the tilt by about 1/2; aim for no tilt. For a curved scatter, three well-spaced points and the bulging rule ('move on the ladder as the bulge points') choose expressions of y and x that straighten it. Counted fractions get their own folded scales: start the counts to avoid 0 and 1, then use froots or flogs, which are zero at 50 percent and treat 'are' and 'aren't' symmetrically; differences of flogs in a 2 x 2 table express disproportion. Comparison is then made by differences on a well-chosen scale.
steps: Classify the data as amounts, counts, balances or counted fractions; start counts with zeros (add a constant) before taking logs, and start fractions as (count + 1/6) / (total + 1/3).
For several batches, compute the median and hinges of each, then plot log H-spread against log median and read the tilt.
Move down the ladder (raw, roots, logs, reciprocals) until the tilt is close to zero, recomputing for typical points at each end.
For a curved relationship, pick three representative points, compare the two segment slopes, and move y and/or x along the ladder in the direction of the bulge until the slopes agree.
For proportions, re-express on a folded scale (froot or flog) and compare groups by differences on that scale.
Check the result with midsummaries, displays and residual plots, and use parallel data sets to guide the choice where available.
outputs: A chosen expression for each variable, batches with comparable spreads, straightened relationships with simple line fits, and residuals for further analysis.
useWhen: Comparing skewed UX metrics across segments (task times, session counts, revenue per user), straightening dose-response style curves, or comparing completion or conversion proportions near 0 or 100 percent.
avoidWhen: When a model already handles the distribution (generalised linear models, survival models), or when variables vary by only a few percent, where re-expression cannot remove curvature. Straightness is a convenience, not a natural law.
whyLost: UX statistics adopted a single fixed transform (log task times) and model-based methods; Tukey's hand-guided EDA techniques were not taught in practitioner courses.
whereToUse: Benchmark dashboards comparing segments, A/B diagnostics with skewed metrics, survey proportions by country or cohort, performance-to-satisfaction curves.
example: Median checkout times for six device segments show spread rising with level; the spread-level tilt is 0.9 raw, 0.45 for roots and 0.05 for logs, so logs are used. Completion rates of 96 to 99 percent are compared as flogs, revealing a gap the raw percentages hid.
sources: Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
reference: Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory Data Analysis. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley.

name: Re-Invention Measurement Against Core Elements
origin: Charters and Pellegrin (1972); Eveland, Rogers and Klepper (1977); Rice and Rogers (1980); Kelly et al. (2000) on core elements; synthesised by Everett Rogers
summary: Breaks an innovation into elements and measures, for each adopter, how far their implementation departs from the core version, separating harmful loss from useful adaptation.
description: Re-invention is the degree to which users change an innovation during adoption and implementation; its opposite is fidelity. Diffusion research measures it by first defining the innovation's elements and its core or main-line version, then, for each adopter observed at implementation rather than at stated intent, coding each element as kept, modified, added or dropped. Re-invention is expressed as departure from the core, with core and peripheral elements distinguished, and then related to rate of adoption and sustainability. Findings are consistent: re-invention is common (for example 56% of schools in one network implemented only selected parts), it speeds adoption and raises sustainability, but adopters over-report it and some is mere renaming. The key judgement is whether a change removes a core element that makes the innovation work.
steps: Measure adoption at the implementation stage, not as intention.
Break the innovation into elements and define its core version, with an evidence-based view of which elements are essential.
For each adopter, code each element as kept, modified, added or dropped, verifying self-reports against observation or artefacts.
Compute a departure-from-core score, separating core from peripheral elements and excluding pure renaming.
Relate re-invention to adoption rate, outcomes and sustainability.
Feed commonly changed elements back into design, making useful adaptations official and protecting core elements.
outputs: A re-invention score per adopter, a list of commonly changed elements, and evidence on which adaptations help or harm.
useWhen: Rolling out configurable products, design systems, programmes or workflows across many teams or organisations that adapt them.
avoidWhen: For single-user consumer features without adopter organisations; use log-based feature-usage analysis instead. Self-reports over-state re-invention and pseudo-re-invention inflates scores.
whyLost: It belongs to diffusion and implementation science; UX tends to treat user adaptation as workaround rather than measuring it systematically.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS configuration, design system adoption, health and education programmes, internal tool rollouts.
example: A design-system team decomposes its form pattern into eight elements and audits 40 product teams; 60% drop inline validation (a core element) while many add a helpful progress indicator, so validation is made default and the indicator is adopted officially.
reference: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). New York: Free Press, ch. 5.

name: Reaction time distribution analysis
origin: Luce, Response Times, 1986; ex-Gaussian modelling, Ratcliff, 1979
summary: Analyses the full shape of response-time distributions, not just means, to reveal slow tails, lapses and distinct processes that averages conceal.
description: Response times are positively skewed: most responses cluster near a mode with a long right tail. Means are pulled by the tail and medians ignore it, yet the tail often carries the safety-relevant information, such as occasional very slow responses to alerts. RT distribution analysis fits models such as the ex-Gaussian (a Gaussian component mu, sigma plus an exponential tail tau) or log-normal, or examines quantiles and cumulative distribution functions across conditions. A design change that shifts mu speeds routine responses, whereas one that reduces tau eliminates lapses. Rigour comes from enough trials per participant (ideally 100+ for ex-Gaussian fits), proper outlier handling decided in advance, and comparing quantiles rather than only means.
steps: Collect trial-level response times, ideally 50-100+ trials per participant per condition, with timestamps accurate to about 10 ms.
Pre-register outlier rules (for example exclude anticipations under 150 ms) instead of trimming by standard deviations after the fact.
Plot histograms, quantile (vincentised) plots and cumulative distributions per condition.
Fit ex-Gaussian or log-normal models per participant and condition, reporting mu, sigma and tau or log-scale parameters.
Compare conditions at 10th, 50th, 90th and 99th percentiles, and compare tau to detect differences in lapses.
Translate findings into design implications: tail problems suggest attention or alerting issues, central shifts suggest perceptual or motor issues.
outputs: RT distribution plots, fitted parameters per condition, percentile comparisons, and an interpretation separating routine speed from lapses.
useWhen: When response timing matters, especially for alerts and safety tasks, or when means show no difference but users report occasional failures.
avoidWhen: When you have only a few trials per participant or only aggregate timings; use median task times with confidence intervals (Sauro and Lewis) instead.
whyLost: Standard in cognitive psychology, but UX reports mean task time; the distributional tools sit in R packages unfamiliar to practitioners.
whereToUse: Alert response, emergency stops, gaming, assistive technology, and performance benchmarks of AI agents with humans in the loop.
example: Two alert designs produce near-identical mean response times of 1.4 s, but the ex-Gaussian tau is 900 ms in the old design versus 300 ms in the new one: the new design removes the rare 4-6 s lapses that matter most in surgery.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
Card, S., Moran, T. & Newell, A., The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983) and GOMS/KLM literature
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 4 — Time, Rhythm & the Three Timescales of Experience
reference: Luce, R. D. (1986). Response Times: Their Role in Inferring Elementary Mental Organization. Oxford University Press.

name: Readability Analysis
origin: Rudolf Flesch (1948); Robert Gunning (1952); Kincaid et al. for the US Navy (1975)
summary: Desk measurement of text complexity using formulas such as Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning Fog, combined with plain-language checks, to flag content too hard for its audience.
description: Readability analysis estimates how hard a text is to read from surface features: sentence length, word length, syllable counts and proportion of complex words. Formulas such as Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog, SMOG and Coleman-Liau convert these into scores or reading grade levels. In UX it is a fast triage tool for large content estates, legal and health information, and AI-generated text. Used rigorously, it is a screening measure, not a verdict: formulas ignore vocabulary familiarity, layout, structure and the reader's domain knowledge, and can be gamed by chopping sentences. Good practice sets a target grade for the audience (often age 9-11 reading level for public services), applies a consistent formula across the corpus, and pairs scores with plain-language heuristics and readability testing with real users.
steps: Define the target audience and a target reading level (for example UK reading age 9 or US grade 8 for general public content).
Extract the content to plain text, removing navigation and boilerplate so scores reflect the actual body copy.
Compute at least two formulas consistently (for example Flesch-Kincaid Grade and SMOG) for every page or string set.
Flag pages more than two grades above target and inspect them against plain-language checks: jargon, passive voice, nominalisations, sentence length over 25 words.
Rewrite flagged content and re-score, without simply fragmenting sentences to game the formula.
Validate the highest-risk rewritten content with readability testing on target users.
outputs: Readability scores per page, a ranked list of content above target, and plain-language rewrite guidance.
useWhen: Auditing large volumes of content, health, legal, financial or government information, and checking AI-generated responses at scale.
avoidWhen: When you need to know whether specific users actually understand content (use readability testing or cloze tests), or for very short UI strings where formulas are unreliable.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for health, government, and any product serving general populations.
whereToUse: Health products; government services; financial products; any public-facing content.
example: An insurer scores 400 policy explanation pages and finds the median at US grade 14. Rewriting the 30 most-visited pages to grade 8 and testing with customers halves calls asking what 'excess' means.
sources: Flesch, A new readability yardstick (Journal of Applied Psychology, 1948)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
reference: Flesch R (1948) A new readability yardstick. Journal of Applied Psychology 32(3):221-233

name: Readability Testing
origin: Cloze procedure by Wilson Taylor (1953); user-testing of medicine leaflets by Sless and Wiseman (1994), mandated in EU from 2005
summary: Testing whether real readers can find and understand content, using cloze tests, comprehension questions and think-aloud reading, with pass thresholds rather than formula scores.
description: Readability testing measures comprehension directly with target readers, in contrast to readability formulas that only estimate difficulty. Techniques include the cloze test (every fifth or sixth word deleted, readers fill gaps, 60% or more correct indicates adequate comprehension), comprehension questions requiring readers to locate and explain key points, paraphrase tasks, and think-aloud reading. European medicines regulation formalised a rigorous version: 20 participants in rounds of ten, with a criterion that 90% must find each key piece of information and 90% of those must understand it. In UX the method is vestigial: it survives as informal 'does this make sense?' checks, losing the explicit thresholds, the find-versus-understand distinction and the iterative rounds that made it reliable.
steps: Identify 10-15 key points the content must convey (actions, risks, eligibility, deadlines).
Write neutral questions for each point that require locating and explaining it, not just recognising wording.
Test with target readers in rounds of about 10, recording whether each point was found and whether it was understood correctly.
Optionally run a cloze test on key passages, deleting every fifth word and scoring exact or acceptable answers, with 60% as the comprehension threshold.
Apply a criterion such as 90% of participants finding and 90% of those understanding each key point; revise content that falls short.
Retest revised content with a fresh round until all key points meet the criterion.
outputs: Find and understand rates per key point, cloze scores, identified misreadings and revised content that meets the threshold.
useWhen: High-stakes content where misunderstanding causes harm or cost: medicine information, consent forms, financial terms, benefits guidance, AI disclosures.
avoidWhen: When you only need a rapid triage of a large corpus (use readability analysis) or when the content is short interface microcopy (use comprehension testing within UX writing research).
whyLost: Vestigial: Rarely done rigorously; replaced by expert-led readability analysis in most contexts.
whereToUse: Health literacy; legal/financial documents; safety instructions.
example: A pension provider tests its retirement options letter with 20 savers. Only 55% understand that taking a lump sum is irreversible, so the letter is restructured with a decision box and passes 90/90 in round two.
sources: Sless & Wiseman, Writing About Medicines for People (1994)
Taylor, 'Cloze procedure': A new tool for measuring readability (1953), Journalism Quarterly
Bormuth, Cloze test readability: Criterion reference scores (1968), Journal of Educational Measurement
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Taylor WL (1953) Cloze procedure: A new tool for measuring readability. Journalism Quarterly 30(4):415-433

name: Reading-Time Paradigms
aka: Reading-time paradigms (self-paced reading, given-new comprehension time)
Self-paced reading with region-by-region reading times
origin: Just, Carpenter and Woolley (1982) self-paced reading; Haviland and Clark (1974) given-new comprehension time
summary: Readers reveal text segment by segment or press when they understand, and logged times per region locate exactly where comprehension slows.
description: In self-paced reading, text is revealed one word or phrase at a time with each key press (or, in Zwaan and Taylor's variant, each small knob turn), and the latency for each region is logged; garden-path sentences slow at the point of reanalysis, and mismatches with a previously seen picture slow reading by about 50 ms. In the given-new paradigm, participants see sentence pairs and press as soon as they understand the second; comprehension is faster when its given information was stated in the first sentence than when it must be inferred, which tests the given-new contract between writer and reader. The rigour comes from matched conditions differing only in the critical region, many items and participants, comprehension questions to check reading, and comparison of region times rather than whole-text times. For UX, the paradigms can locate where policies, error messages or AI answers make readers stall.
steps: Write matched text versions that differ only in a critical region, such as two wordings of a fee clause or error message.
Divide each text into regions with the critical region at a known position.
Reveal one region per key press, or show sentence pairs and record when the participant signals understanding, logging each latency.
Add comprehension questions after a proportion of items to check genuine reading.
Use enough items and participants (typically dozens of each) and counterbalance versions across participants.
Compare region reading times across conditions with mixed-effects models, treating participants and items as random effects.
outputs: Reading time per region per condition, comprehension accuracy, and the location and size of processing difficulty.
useWhen: You need to compare wordings precisely and locate where readers struggle in critical text such as consent forms, fees, warnings or generated answers.
avoidWhen: You need natural reading behaviour or overall preference; segment-by-segment reading is unnatural and noisy. Use eye-tracked reading, readability testing or comprehension tests instead.
whyLost: It is a psycholinguistic lab paradigm needing many items and statistical modelling; UX content testing relies on readability formulas and comprehension questions.
whereToUse: Legal and financial disclosures, health information, error and warning messages, onboarding copy and LLM-generated explanations.
example: A subscription service compares two wordings of a cancellation-fee clause in a self-paced reading test with 60 participants. Readers stall on 'pro-rated remainder' in one version, so the team rewrites it in plain terms.
reference: Just, M. A., Carpenter, P. A., & Woolley, J. D. (1982). Paradigms and processes in reading comprehension. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 111(2), 228-238; Haviland, S. E., & Clark, H. H. (1974). What's new? Acquiring new information as a process in comprehension. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13, 512-521.

name: Reading-time studies of frame shifts and scenario effects
aka: Text-level reading-time studies of frame and scenario effects
origin: Rumelhart, 1980; Garrod and Sanford, 1980s; Coulson and Kutas, 1998
summary: Timing how long readers take on matched text versions that fit or overturn an evoked frame, to measure the processing cost of reinterpretation.
description: These paradigms compare reading times (or ERPs) for text versions that either fit or overturn the frame a reader has built. Coulson and Kutas took one-line jokes, removed the final word and normed the fragments on a cloze task; the top completion reveals the default frame, and its probability splits fragments into high (over 40 per cent) and low constraint. Each fragment receives a joke ending and a frame-congruent ending matched on cloze probability (about 3.6 per cent each). Self-paced reading showed longer final-word times for joke endings, but only under high constraint; the ERP version found larger N400s. A non-humorous frame-shift variant added about 100 ms on the shift word. Earlier text-level studies (Rumelhart; Garrod and Sanford's scenario titles; Pickering and Traxler's garden paths) timed matched story versions between groups, corrected for baseline speed. Matching on cloze is what makes the contrast rigorous.
steps: Collect items in which a single word or sentence forces reinterpretation of earlier content.
Remove the critical word and norm the fragments on a cloze task with a separate sample of about 20-40 people.
Split fragments into high and low constraint by the top completion's cloze probability (for example above 40 per cent).
Write a reinterpretation ending and a frame-congruent ending matched on cloze probability.
Present text word by word (self-paced, eye-tracked, or fixed rate with EEG) with comprehension probes, counterbalancing versions across lists.
Correct for baseline reading speed and compare critical-word reading time or N400 by ending type and constraint.
Analyse separately by whether the reinterpretation was understood, using probe accuracy.
outputs: Reading-time or ERP differences attributable to reinterpretation, by context constraint and comprehension.
useWhen: You need to measure whether copy, notifications or conversational AI responses force costly reinterpretation, for example a message that turns out to mean something other than first assumed.
avoidWhen: You only need comprehension or preference outcomes; a readability or comprehension test is cheaper. Effects depend on constraint and comprehension; unmatched cloze probability invalidates comparisons. Jokes are a special stimulus set.
whyLost: It requires psycholinguistic norming and timing infrastructure and is published in linguistics and ERP literature, far from UX writing practice.
whereToUse: UX writing for high-stakes messages, error and consent copy, chatbot turn design, legal and financial disclosures, onboarding narratives.
example: A banking app compares two versions of a notice: one where 'pending' is redefined late in the sentence and one that defines it first. Eye-tracked reading shows a 150 ms regression cost on the late version, so the definition moves forward.
reference: Coulson, S. (2001). Semantic Leaps: Frame-Shifting and Conceptual Blending in Meaning Construction. Cambridge University Press; Coulson, S., & Kutas, M. (1998). Frame-shifting and sentential integration. UCSD technical report.

name: Real User Monitoring (RUM) of Page Load Time
origin: Web performance engineering practice, as described by Lara Hogan (2014); no originator credited
summary: Collect load times from real visitors, segment them by location, network and device, report median and 95th percentile, and track them over time to find and explain regressions.
description: Synthetic tests measure a page in controlled conditions; real user monitoring captures timings from actual page views, so it shows the speed people really experience. The team identifies its major pages (home, top landing pages, checkout and other high-traffic areas), segments their load times by geography, network type and device, and reports both the median and the 95th percentile, which captures the slowest 5 percent of views and mostly reflects slow connections and devices. Gaps between segments and pages are explained and used to prioritise fixes. Results are tracked week over week and quarter over quarter, with the reason for each change logged in a report or wiki, dashboards marking performance budgets, and alerts to page owners when timings move. Because averages hide the tail, percentiles are essential; Google Analytics-style averages are not enough.
steps: Choose a RUM tool that records timings from real page views and reports percentiles.
Identify the major pages: home, top landing pages, checkout and other high-traffic areas.
Segment load time by geographic location, network type and device.
Report median and 95th percentile load time for each page and segment.
Compare segments and pages, isolate causes of gaps (including experiment variants) and prioritise fixes.
Track week over week and quarter over quarter, logging why each change happened, with dashboards showing budget lines and alerts to page owners.
outputs: Segmented load-time distributions, trend charts, and a performance change log or periodic report.
useWhen: Understanding how fast a live product feels for different audiences, catching regressions after releases or experiments, and setting performance budgets.
avoidWhen: Before launch or for controlled comparisons of design options (use synthetic or perceived-performance testing); when the question is how speed affects behaviour causally (use Feature-removal and latency-injection tests).
whyLost: It is mainstream in performance engineering and SRE but often sits outside UX teams, who rarely connect percentile load data to experience research.
whereToUse: E-commerce checkout, media and news sites, emerging-market audiences on slow networks, mobile web, design-system weight decisions.
example: A retailer's 95th-percentile home page load rises from 6 to 9 seconds in a quarter. Segmenting shows the rise is confined to Android users in one experiment variant with a heavy carousel, which is cut.
reference: Hogan, L. C. (2014). Designing for Performance: Weighing Aesthetics and Speed. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 118-123.

name: Real-Time Safety Monitoring with Hot Questions
origin: Kirtley, 2022; Jacobson et al., 2020; Nock et al., 2021
summary: Before collecting real-time self-reports on risky states, decide whether, how and by whom you will intervene when responses cross a threshold, and tell participants exactly what is monitored.
description: Remote real-time studies can reveal risk (suicidal ideation, abuse, acute distress) while data are still arriving. Hot questions are items whose responses beyond a threshold alert the team, for example ideation above 5 on a 1-10 scale. Thresholds are hard to set because people differ (consistently high, low or variable), so they should be co-designed with people with lived experience. Interventions range from automatic pop-ups with support details to staff reviewing responses twice a day and calling back within 24 hours. Responsibility can sit with trained staff, a named study clinician or the participant's own clinician, whose details are collected at onboarding. Anonymous designs cannot intervene, so they must give extensive support information instead. The protocol, thresholds, monitoring frequency and actions are written into consent materials. No threshold is portable across studies, and the monitoring load must be staffed.
steps: Decide whether the study will intervene at all and under what conditions.
Define hot questions and thresholds, co-designed with people with lived experience.
Choose the intervention: automatic support pop-up, scheduled review with call-back, or both.
Assign responsibility: trained staff, a study clinician or the participant's own clinician, collecting contact details at onboarding.
State monitoring frequency, thresholds and actions in consent materials and the participant briefing.
Staff and train for the monitoring load, and log every alert and action.
outputs: A written safety protocol with thresholds, escalation path, responsibilities and an alert log.
useWhen: Diary, ESM or longitudinal remote studies touching mental health, safety, finance stress, abuse or other topics where a response could signal risk.
avoidWhen: Studies with no risk-relevant content; over-monitoring burdens participants and can undermine candour. Do not promise intervention you cannot staff.
whyLost: UX ethics review focuses on consent and data protection, and real-time remote collection on sensitive states is relatively new to product teams.
whereToUse: Mental-health and wellbeing apps, fintech debt research, safety features in social platforms, and AI companion studies.
example: A debt-advice app runs a two-week diary study. An item on hopelessness above 8 triggers an in-app panel with helpline details and a researcher review within 24 hours, as stated in the consent form.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Realist Evaluation
origin: Ray Pawson and Nick Tilley (1997)
summary: Explain what works, for whom, in what circumstances and why, by building and testing context-mechanism-outcome configurations rather than average effects.
description: Realist evaluation rejects the idea that a programme has a single, uniform effect. Programmes work by triggering mechanisms, changes in participants' reasoning and resources, and those mechanisms fire only in certain contexts. The evaluator therefore states candidate programme theories as context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) configurations, collects mixed data on contexts, mechanisms and outcome patterns, and refines the configurations through iterative testing. The 'realist interview' teaches the theory to stakeholders and invites them to confirm or correct it. Findings are expressed as refined middle-range theories that can transfer to other settings, not as a verdict that the programme works. The approach suits qualitative case work and heterogeneous outcomes. Its difficulty is that mechanisms are not directly observable and are easily confused with programme components.
steps: Elicit initial programme theories from documents and stakeholders, and state them as context-mechanism-outcome configurations.
Decide which contexts, mechanisms and outcomes need data, and choose mixed sources such as logs, surveys, interviews and observation.
Collect data across contrasting contexts and subgroups, using realist interviews to test the theories with stakeholders.
Look for outcome patterns that differ by context and explain them with mechanisms.
Refine, confirm or discard each CMO configuration and repeat with new data as needed.
Report refined configurations stating what works, for whom, in what circumstances and why.
outputs: Refined programme theory as a set of context-mechanism-outcome configurations with supporting evidence.
useWhen: An intervention or feature works for some users and not others, average effects mislead, and you need to know why and where it will transfer.
avoidWhen: When you only need to know whether an effect exists; use A/B Testing or RCT design for UX. Avoid if the team cannot articulate any programme theory to test.
whyLost: It is strong in health and social policy evaluation, but product teams use segmentation and heterogeneous-effect analysis without the explanatory mechanism logic.
whereToUse: Behaviour-change and health apps, onboarding programmes, enterprise rollouts, AI features with uneven adoption, policy-driven digital services.
example: A coaching feature raises retention overall but not among shift workers; realist interviews and log data show the mechanism (accountability to a scheduled coach) only fires where users have predictable hours, so the team designs an asynchronous variant.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Pawson, R. and Tilley, N. (1997). Realistic Evaluation. London: SAGE.

name: Reality Mapping
origin: Tamara Adlin and Holly Jamesen, 2006
summary: A facilitated session with subject-matter experts that builds a colour-coded sticky-note flow of one end-to-end goal, exposing steps, questions, hand-offs and persona material.
description: With one or two experts and a note-taker for two to three hours, the facilitator writes a goal as the title and lays blue step notes left to right on a roll of paper, adding green comments, yellow questions and pink design ideas beneath each step. Digressions are parked as yellow questions so the flow keeps moving. Further sessions extend and join maps; clusters of yellow notes show unexplored or complex areas. Symbols mark phases, artefacts, problem areas and deep dives, branches show decisions, and layers show disagreement between practitioners or hand-offs between roles. Teams then analyse maps for repetition, complexity and hand-offs, read them aloud from a persona's viewpoint, stop mapping when experiences repeat, and harvest roles, goals and real anecdotes for personas. It sits alongside Contextual Design sequence models and CARD, and today survives largely as generic sticky-note journey or process mapping.
steps: Plan which goals to map; recruit one or two experts per session plus a note-taker; book two to three hours and a roll of white paper.
Open with a short script, write the goal as the title and lay blue step notes left to right as the expert describes the process.
Add green comments, yellow questions and pink design ideas beneath each step, parking digressions as yellow notes.
Run further sessions with other participants, extending and joining maps and marking new notes after each session.
Add symbols for phases, artefacts and problem areas, branches for decisions, layers for disagreements or role hand-offs, and a legend.
Analyse for repetition, complexity, hand-offs and clusters of questions; read the map aloud as a persona and stop when experiences repeat.
Harvest roles, goals and anecdotes for personas, remove real names and critical remarks, then digitise and keep the maps.
outputs: Paper and digital Reality Maps, open question lists, persona material and a basis for later design maps.
useWhen: You need a shared, detailed picture of a complex end-to-end process quickly, from experts, as input to personas, requirements or redesign.
avoidWhen: You need to observe actual practice rather than experts' accounts, or the process is simple; use contextual inquiry or journey mapping instead. Do not aim for completeness.
whyLost: Its specific notation and persona-harvesting steps were absorbed into generic journey and process mapping workshops, and the name was forgotten.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflows, legal and compliance processes, education services, internal tools and service redesigns.
example: A legal tech team maps a law firm's e-discovery process with two paralegals over two sessions. Yellow-note clusters around privilege review and a hand-off layer between lawyers and vendors define the first research and design priorities.
reference: Adlin, T., & Jamesen, H. (2006). Reality and design maps. In J. Pruitt & T. Adlin, The Persona Lifecycle, pp. 557-601. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Reality Matrix Worksheet
aka: Reality matrix (players, factors, channels and contexts)
origin: Abby Covert, How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)
summary: A scoping matrix of users, contexts, players and channels, with sentence prompts on time, resources, skills, politics and ethics, that maps a project's real limits.
description: Covert's reality matrix is a sense-making worksheet for the start of an information architecture or design project. It lists players (current and potential users, stakeholders, competitors, distractors and the roles you play yourself), completes factor sentences ('I only have ___', 'I know how to ___ but not ___ yet', 'Others want this work to say ___'), and identifies the channels that carry information and the contexts users are in. Channels and contexts intersect: many channels can serve one context and one channel many. Laid out as a matrix, every empty box is an unanswered question, which keeps discussion on track. Admitting hopes and fears alongside it exposes limits, and the completed matrix shows which further diagrams to make and for whom.
steps: List players: current users, potential users, stakeholders, competitors, distractors, and the roles you play yourself.
Complete the factor sentences on time, resources, skills, environment, personality, politics, ethics and integrity.
Identify the channels users prefer and the contexts they are in (rushed, on slow Wi-Fi, browsing for fun or completing a task).
Draw a matrix of users against contexts, players and channels and fill every box, alone or in a group.
Write down hopes and fears for the project to expose constraints.
Use the gaps and patterns to decide which diagrams, research or artefacts to make next and who will use them.
outputs: A completed matrix of players, factors, channels and contexts, and a list of next artefacts and open questions.
useWhen: Use it when a project feels messy and under-scoped, to make constraints and audiences explicit before choosing research or IA work.
avoidWhen: The contexts and channels entered are assumptions; verify them with Contextual Inquiry or a Diary Study, and map stakeholders' influence properly with Stakeholder Mapping.
whyLost: It is a brief worksheet in a self-published book for non-specialists, with no published layout or evaluation, so it rarely appears in formal UX practice.
whereToUse: Content and IA projects, small-team websites, internal tools, and onboarding new team members to a messy domain.
example: A council website lead fills the matrix and finds that 'resident on a phone at a bus stop' has no channel at all besides a PDF. That empty box becomes the first research question.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert, 2014)
reference: Covert, A. (2014). How to Make Sense of Any Mess: Information Architecture for Everybody. CreateSpace.

name: Recommendation Tracking and Research Impact Scorecard
aka: Recommendation status tracking and research scorecard
origin: Usability practice (Baxter, Courage and Caine, 2015)
summary: Record the team's decision and reason for every research recommendation, check later whether accepted items shipped, and roll results into a per-product scorecard.
description: Recommendations are often agreed in a readout and then forgotten. This method adds a status column to the recommendations table, captures a decision (accept, reject, investigate further) and a reason for each at a prioritisation meeting, asks teams to cite research as the source in requirements, and revisits after release to record what shipped. Results roll up into a scorecard showing which products received research support, how often, and how much was acted on. It answers complaints by showing whether earlier recommendations were implemented (for example 12 of 15 accepted but only 5 shipped) and gives executives an at-a-glance view of research impact.
steps: Add a status and reason column to every study's recommendations table.
At the prioritisation meeting, record a decision (accept, reject, investigate) and a reason for each recommendation.
Ask the team to cite the research as the source when recommendations enter requirements or tickets.
After each release, record which accepted recommendations actually shipped.
Summarise per product in a scorecard (studies run, recommendations made, accepted, shipped) and review it periodically with leadership.
outputs: A recommendation status log and a per-product research impact scorecard.
useWhen: A research team needs to show impact, explain persistent usability complaints, or manage a backlog of research findings across several products.
avoidWhen: The culture would experience it as policing, or in small start-ups where everyone already knows what shipped. External consultants may lose access after the contract.
whyLost: Research ops has grown, but most teams track insights in repositories rather than tracking decisions on recommendations through to release.
whereToUse: In-house research teams in mid-to-large organisations, research operations, design-system governance.
example: Customer complaints about checkout persist. The scorecard shows the team accepted 12 of 15 checkout recommendations but shipped only 5, redirecting the conversation from new research to delivery.
reference: Baxter, K., Courage, C., & Caine, K. (2015). Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Research Methods (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 469-472.

name: Reconstructed Cohort Flow Analysis
aka: Reconstructed cohort flow analysis (promotion, repetition and drop-out rates)
origin: UNESCO educational statistics, reconstructed cohort (student flow) model
summary: Estimates stage-to-stage promotion, repetition and drop-out rates from two aggregate snapshots, then simulates a notional cohort to show completion, time taken and where people leave.
description: Education planners needed to know how pupils move through grades when individual records were unreliable. Three approaches were compared: the true cohort method (follow real individuals: accurate but slow and record-dependent), the apparent cohort method (compare a stage's count with the next stage a period later, treating all loss as drop-out and ignoring repetition) and the reconstructed cohort method. The reconstructed method uses counts by stage for two consecutive periods plus the number repeating each stage in the second period to derive promotion, repetition and drop-out rates for every stage. A notional cohort of 1,000 is then simulated through the cycle under explicit assumptions, giving completers, leavers by stage, average time to complete and a coefficient of efficiency (ideal time divided by time actually spent). For products, the stages become levels, course modules, certification steps or plan tiers where users can progress, repeat or leave.
steps: Assemble counts of users at each ordered stage at time t and t+1, plus the number at each stage in t+1 who were already there in t (repeaters).

For each stage compute the repetition rate (repeaters in t+1 over count in t), the promotion rate (count in the next stage in t+1 minus its repeaters, over count in t) and the drop-out rate as the remainder.
State the assumptions: no new entrants except the cohort, a fixed maximum number of repeats, constant rates across the cycle, and the same rates for repeaters and first-timers.
Simulate a notional cohort of 1,000 through the stages to obtain completers, leavers by stage, average time to completion and the coefficient of efficiency.
Check the data for over-counted stages, new entrants confused with repeaters and missing periods, each of which biases the rates in a known direction.
Where individual logs exist, validate the reconstructed rates against a true cohort sample.
outputs: Flow diagram of promotion, repetition and drop-out by stage; simulated completion and drop-out of a 1,000-member cohort; average time to complete; coefficient of efficiency.
useWhen: Only aggregate stage counts are available (partner data, privacy-limited analytics, legacy reports) and you need flow rates through ordered stages that users can repeat.
avoidWhen: Individual-level transition logs exist (use Markov chain funnel modelling or true cohort analysis); stages are not ordered or users can skip freely; rates change sharply between periods. Confusing repeaters with new entrants understates repetition and overstates drop-out.
whyLost: It lives in education-planning manuals; product teams with full event logs rarely need it, and those with only aggregates seldom know it exists.
whereToUse: Online courses and certification paths, game level progression, subscription tier movement, partner-reported programme data, public-sector services reporting only monthly snapshots.
example: A language-learning app's partner schools report only monthly counts of learners per level and how many stayed at the same level. Reconstructing flows shows level 3 has a 35% repetition rate and the simulated cohort takes 40% longer than the ideal path, so the team redesigns the level 3 assessment.
reference: Singh, K. (2007). Quantitative Social Research Methods. New Delhi: Sage Publications.

name: Record Linkage
origin: Ivan Fellegi and Alan Sunter (1969); William Winkler; Schnell et al. (2009) for Bloom filter encoding
summary: Identifying the same person or unit across a survey and other datasets with error-tolerant deterministic or probabilistic matching, including privacy-preserving encrypted linkage.
description: Linking survey answers to administrative, account or behavioural records multiplies their value, but identifiers are messy. Record linkage first obtains consent, then preprocesses identifiers (encodings, name variants, date formats, addresses, missing codes). Because comparing every pair is infeasible, pairs are blocked on several keys in turn. Similarity is computed per field (Jaro-Winkler for names), and the Fellegi-Sunter framework turns agreement patterns into match weights, with an upper threshold for links, a lower one for non-links and clerical review between them. Privacy-preserving variants use a trusted third party or encode identifiers in Bloom filters so matching occurs without exposing raw data. Practical warnings: consent to linkage ranges from 24 to 89 per cent across surveys, non-consent and missed matches are not random, and preprocessing and approvals take far longer than the linking itself.
steps: Obtain informed consent to link and agree governance and approvals.
Preprocess identifiers: standardise encodings, names, dates, addresses and missing codes.
Block candidate pairs on several keys in turn to limit comparisons.
Compute field similarities (for example Jaro-Winkler for names, exact for dates).
Classify pairs with probabilistic weights and upper and lower thresholds; send the grey zone to clerical review.
For sensitive data, link through a trusted third party or with encrypted Bloom filter encodings.
Report match rates, consent rates and how linked cases differ from unlinked ones.
outputs: A linked dataset with match quality indicators, consent and match rates, and an assessment of linkage bias.
useWhen: Joining survey or research data to account, CRM, support or log data where no clean shared identifier exists, or merging research repositories.
avoidWhen: When a reliable unique identifier already exists and consent is in place; a direct join suffices. Do not link without explicit consent and legal basis.
whyLost: Product teams join on user IDs and assume linkage is trivial; probabilistic and privacy-preserving methods are known in health and official statistics but rarely in UX.
whereToUse: Linking survey panels to product analytics, joining research participant records across tools, healthcare and public-sector services with fragmented identifiers.
example: A health app runs an anonymous web survey and wants to relate answers to in-app engagement. Consenting respondents give email and birth date, which are encoded as Bloom filters by a third party and matched to account records, with match quality and consent bias reported.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Schnell, R. (2016). Record linkage. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 662-669). London: SAGE.

name: Recurrence Quantification Analysis
origin: Jean-Pierre Eckmann, Sylvie Oliffson Kamphorst and David Ruelle (1987, recurrence plots); Joseph Zbilut and Charles Webber (1992, RQA)
summary: Quantifies how often and in what structure a behavioural time series revisits similar states, measuring determinism, stability and coordination.
description: A recurrence plot marks every pair of time points at which a system's state is similar. RQA quantifies the plot: recurrence rate, determinism (proportion of recurrent points forming diagonal lines, indicating repeated sequences), laminarity (vertical lines, indicating stuck states), entropy of line lengths and trapping time. Cross-recurrence quantification compares two time series, such as two collaborators or a user and an agent, to measure coordination and leading/following. RQA works on short, nonstationary, noisy data where classical methods fail, and has been applied in psychology to movement, eye gaze and conversation. For UX it offers measures of routine, rigidity and coordination in interaction streams.
steps: Choose the behavioural time series (e.g. action categories, cursor positions, gaze, speech features).
For continuous data, choose embedding dimension and delay (false nearest neighbours, mutual information); for categorical data use direct matching.
Set the radius threshold to achieve a target recurrence rate (e.g. 2-5%).
Compute RQA measures: recurrence rate, determinism, laminarity, trapping time, entropy.
Compare measures across conditions, users or time, with surrogate data tests to check against randomness.
Use cross-recurrence for dyads (e.g. human-AI turn-taking) to measure coordination and lag.
outputs: Recurrence plots and RQA metrics describing routine, rigidity and coordination, with surrogate comparisons.
useWhen: Analysing dynamics of interaction (habits, getting stuck, coordination) in rich time series.
avoidWhen: When simple frequency or funnel metrics answer the question, or with very sparse data.
whyLost: It is a physics and cognitive science technique with little exposure outside nonlinear dynamics.
whereToUse: Collaborative tools, conversational AI dialogue rhythm, games, habit formation in apps, VR movement.
example: Cross-recurrence of typing activity between pair programmers using an AI assistant shows lower coordination than human-only pairs, prompting design of shared AI suggestion views.
