(3) Compute prediction accuracy. < 70% accuracy on a label's composed meaning = the composition is non-transparent. Redesign: either break the composition or make components more predictable.
outputs: An inventory of interface terms and constructions, a compositionality audit, inconsistencies that break systematic inference, and a revised controlled vocabulary.
useWhen: Command languages, query builders, rules and automation editors, developer tools and complex settings where users must combine concepts productively.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a purely theoretical exercise; for most products a terminology audit plus usability testing is sufficient and the philosophical framework is unnecessary.
whyLost: Language-of-thought theory influenced early cognitive HCI but fell from favour as cognitive science moved towards embodied and connectionist accounts.
whereToUse: Feature naming, error message design, onboarding language, design system naming conventions.
example: An automation builder uses 'when', 'if' and 'trigger' inconsistently; an audit enforces a compositional grammar ('When [event], if [condition], then [action]') and rule creation errors fall in testing.
reference: Fodor JA (1975) The Language of Thought. Harvard University Press

name: Representational State Transition Analysis
aka: Handover analysis across artifacts and people
origin: Edwin Hutchins (1995); Zhang and Norman (1994) on representational effects
summary: Traces how a piece of information is transformed as it moves across media and people, identifying each representational state and the transitions where errors and delays enter.
description: Within distributed cognition, Hutchins analysed computation as the propagation of representational states across media: for example, an air traffic instruction moves from speech to a handwritten strip, to a position on a board, to a pilot's action. Each transition re-represents the information and can add, lose or distort it. Zhang and Norman showed that how information is represented, internally or externally, changes task difficulty. The method follows a specific information item end to end, recording every state (medium, format, location, who holds it) and every transformation (who performs it, with what tool, what can go wrong). The resulting diagram exposes error-prone transcriptions, redundant states and missing feedback, and helps decide which transitions a new system should eliminate, automate or preserve.
steps: For any information flow in a system: document the sequence of representational states the information passes through.
For each transition: what transformation is performed?
By whom or what?
What could go wrong?
What information is lost or added in the transformation?
Build the representational state transition diagram.
Identify the transitions with lowest redundancy and highest consequence — these are the design priorities.
outputs: Representational state transition diagram for key information items, inventory of transformations with error risks, and redesign options that remove or support transitions.
useWhen: Clinical handovers, order entry, logistics, finance operations and any workflow where information is re-keyed, re-written or verbally relayed across people and systems.
avoidWhen: For individual, single-medium tasks with no handoffs; use GOMS or usability testing.
whyLost: It was embedded in Hutchins' theoretical work rather than packaged as a method, and lighter process maps replaced it in practice.
whereToUse: Medical record UX, legal document workflow design, any multi-step information processing system, financial transaction UX.
example: A surgical team's implant information travels from surgeon's speech to a console, a nurse's tablet and a billing system. Mapping seven representational states reveals two manual transcriptions with error risk, which barcode scanning removes.
sources: Zhang & Norman, Representations in distributed cognitive tasks (Cognitive Science, 1994)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 14 — Distributed Cognition & Cognitive Ecosystems
Hutchins, E., Cognition in the Wild (1995)
Clark, A., Being There: Putting Brain, Body, and World Together Again (1997)
reference: Hutchins E (1995) Cognition in the Wild. MIT Press

name: Representative Task Design (Brunswik)
donor: Ecological psychology and sport expertise research
origin: Egon Brunswik (1956), developed by Hammond and Stewart (2001); applied to sport by Davids, Araújo and colleagues; described in Chapter 10 of the Handbook
summary: Designs study tasks by sampling the real environmental conditions and the natural correlations between cues, not just the participants, so findings generalise to real use.
description: Brunswik argued that psychological processes adapt behaviour to environments, so experiments must sample environmental conditions as carefully as they sample participants. Representative design is often confused with ecological validity. It requires the conditions of a study task to match the conditions in which the behaviour normally works, including the natural intercorrelations among cues (Brunswik's 'ecological intercorrelation'). If a lab task breaks those links, for example by removing an information source that normally co-occurs with another, people may use different strategies than they do in real life. Davids and colleagues use this to argue that the lab-versus-field split matters less than whether key organismic, task and environmental constraints are kept. The Handbook gives examples in which small changes to task constraints, such as batting against a bowling machine instead of a real bowler, changed batters' timing and coordination. For UX the principle turns into a design audit for usability tests and experiments: sample realistic data, devices, interruptions and time pressures, keep the cues users normally combine, and check that the response asked for matches what users really do.
steps: Describe the target use situation: the information sources users combine, typical interruptions, devices, data and time pressures.
List the cues and constraints in the planned study task and mark which have been removed, simplified or decoupled.
Sample a range of realistic situations (data sets, scenarios, contexts) rather than one idealised task.
Keep natural correlations between cues, for example realistic messy data rather than clean demo data.
Match the response mode to real behaviour (acting, not only saying what one would do).
Where full representativeness is not possible, document the departures and treat them as threats to generalisation.
outputs: A task design, and a documented audit of how well the study task represents real use conditions and where it departs from them.
useWhen: Planning usability tests, experiments or benchmarks whose results must generalise to messy real-world use, especially for expert or time-critical tasks.
avoidWhen: You deliberately want an isolated, controlled test of one perceptual or motor parameter.
whyLost: UX inherited the lab-versus-field distinction and the term ecological validity, but not Brunswik's procedure for sampling situations and cue structures.
whereToUse: Benchmark usability studies, dashboard and monitoring tools, decision-support systems, automotive and aviation interfaces, AI-assisted workflows.
example: A team testing a fraud-review tool notices its lab scenarios use clean, single-signal cases. Following representative design, they sample 40 real anonymised cases with the usual mix of conflicting signals and add queue time pressure; experts' strategies and error patterns change markedly from the pilot.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Davids, K., Araújo, D., Button, C. and Renshaw, I. (2007) 'Degenerate brains, indeterminate behavior, and representative tasks: implications for experimental design in sport psychology research', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 10.

name: Representativeness Heuristic Audit
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1972-1974; UX application via prediction-before-interaction testing
summary: Asks users to predict what interface elements will do before using them, measuring where judgements based on resemblance to familiar patterns produce mistaken expectations.
description: The representativeness heuristic describes how people judge likelihood by similarity to a prototype rather than by base rates or underlying logic. Applied to interfaces, users judge what a control does, or whether a feature will work, by how much it resembles patterns they already know. When an element looks like a familiar pattern but behaves differently, users form confident but wrong expectations, producing mistake-type errors (wrong intention) rather than slips. The audit makes this measurable: participants predict an element's behaviour before interacting, and the gap between prediction and actual behaviour is coded. Elements with high prediction-gap rates are flagged as misleading prototypes. Rigour comes from collecting predictions before any exposure, using a coding scheme for gap size, and setting explicit flag thresholds such as more than 30% of participants with a substantial gap.
steps: Present users with interface elements, ask them to predict behavior before interaction.
Code gap between prediction and actual behavior.
Flag elements where > 30% of participants show prediction gap > 50%.
outputs: Prediction-gap rates per interface element, list of misleading prototype matches, and redesign or relabelling recommendations.
useWhen: Testing icons, novel controls, look-alike components, and features borrowed from other products where users may import wrong expectations.
avoidWhen: When elements are entirely novel with no plausible prototype, or when you need to observe real usage over time (use usability testing or analytics).
whyLost: It sits in judgement and decision-making research and reached UX only as a general bias name; the operational protocol of eliciting predictions before interaction and scoring the gap was never standardised in UX toolkits.
whereToUse: Icon design audits, affordance testing, affordance labeling research.
example: A trading app uses a toggle that resembles an on/off switch to choose between market and limit orders. In a prediction audit, 46% of participants expect it to enable or disable trading, so it is replaced by a labelled segmented control.
sources: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Science, 1974)
Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974 paper) (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
reference: Kahneman D, Slovic P & Tversky A (Eds.) (1982) Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Cambridge University Press

name: Request Intake Triage Matrix (Engagement Levels)
aka: UX engagement model: support-level assessment for project requests
Strategic importance by UX importance grid
Full, partial and consulting support model
Innovation by impact prioritisation of requests
donor: Management and organisational practice; data science practice
origin: Lund (2011), adapting a table by Tjeerd Hoeck (Microsoft Windows design); Nolis and Robinson (2020)
summary: Rate each incoming request on two judged axes and assign each quadrant a defined handling or service level, from full support to none.
description: Both versions answer the recurring question of how a team decides what help to give. Lund's engagement model rates a request for UX support on strategic importance (from big-bet executive commitments down to temporary tools) and on how important the user experience is to success (from experience-central or error-critical down to incremental changes), each with descriptive anchors. Cells map to A full support (about 6 to 10% of project budget), B partial support (about 3 to 6%), C consulting and reviews, and D no direct support beyond guidelines. The value lies in negotiating the ratings with the requester. Nolis and Robinson sort analytic requests by impact and novelty: nurture innovative and impactful work, take on impactful routine work, avoid novelty without impact, and challenge or automate work that is neither.
steps: List incoming requests, including quick asks, long-term projects and self-originated ideas.
Ask the requester about business goals, sponsorship and what decision the work would change.
Rate each request on the first axis (strategic importance, or whether any result would change a decision) using written anchors.
Rate it on the second axis (importance of the user experience, or whether the work is new) using written anchors.
Locate the quadrant and propose its handling: full, partial, consulting or no support; or nurture, take on, avoid, or challenge and automate.
Negotiate the ratings and the service level with the requester, then agree deliverables and funding.
Review the team's portfolio balance (Lund suggests about 50 to 60% near-term project work, 20 to 30% business-critical work being sold, the rest longer-term bets).
outputs: An agreed engagement or handling level per request, defined deliverables and funding, and a portfolio view of the team's work.
useWhen: Use it when a central UX, research or analytics team receives more requests than it can serve and needs a transparent, defensible intake rule.
avoidWhen: Ratings are judgements and can be gamed; keep anchors explicit. To prioritise design problems or features rather than requests for a team's time use the Effort × impact grid or the Research Question Prioritisation Matrix.
whyLost: The idea survives as DesignOps intake, service tiers and research request forms, usually without Lund's anchored scales or the name.
whereToUse: Central design and research teams, enterprise IT, analytics centres of excellence and research operations.
example: A retailer's central research team rates a checkout redesign high on both axes and gives it full support, while an internal reporting tool scores low on UX importance and receives a consulting review and the design system guidelines.
sources: Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Lund, A. (2011). User Experience Management. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 94-98, 244-245. Nolis, J. and Robinson, E. (2020). Build a Career in Data Science. Shelter Island, NY: Manning, pp. 203-206.

name: Requirements Extraction from Research
donor: Agile software engineering and GDS service design
origin: Hartson and Pyla (2012; 2019); UK Government Digital Service Service Manual (2016)
summary: Turn analysed research into user need statements, user stories or 'shall' requirements, add extrapolated needs, organise by task, prioritise and validate with users.
description: This step converts research data into a form product and engineering teams can act on. User needs are written in users' own words as 'I need/want/expect to... so that...', optionally with role, trigger ('When...') and constraint ('Because...'); they are high level, stable and never 'done'. User stories derive from needs with actor, narrative and goal; a story without a clear goal questions the feature. Hartson and Pyla add rigour by pulling every need-bearing work-activity note, generalising narrow statements, adding extrapolation requirements for obvious unstated needs, recording implied system requirements, and for high-rigour work writing 'shall' statements with rationale under feature headings. Stories are organised under a task hierarchy to check completeness, prioritised separately (for example by MVP release), held in a backlog with acceptance criteria, and walked through with users per work role.
steps: Pull out research notes that express or imply a user need.
Write each as a need statement ('I need... so that...') in users' words, or as a role-voiced story ('As a... I want... so that...').
Generalise narrow statements and add extrapolation requirements for obvious unstated needs, recording implied system requirements.
For high-rigour projects, write 'shall' statements with rationale and notes under two-level feature headings.
Organise needs and stories under a task hierarchy or by persona, stage or theme to check completeness.
Prioritise separately, for example by MVP releases, and record them in a backlog with priority, persona, functional requirement and acceptance criteria.
Walk through the set with client representatives and users for each work role.
outputs: A user needs list, user stories or a requirements document, and a prioritised backlog with acceptance criteria.
useWhen: Handing research into delivery in agile or public-service teams, scoping an MVP, and keeping a traceable link from evidence to features.
avoidWhen: Avoid using need statements as a substitute for understanding users; they do not replace personas, mental models or journey work. Stories not grounded in research become wish lists.
whyLost: It survived because agile delivery needs backlogs, though the grounding in research data and extrapolation is often lost.
whereToUse: Government digital services, enterprise systems, regulated products needing traceability, agile product teams.
example: Field notes from benefit advisers yield the need 'I need to see a claimant's previous contacts so that I don't ask them to repeat their story'. It becomes three stories with acceptance criteria, and an extrapolated need for an audit trail is added.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019). The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience (2nd ed.). Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 10; Government Digital Service (2016). Writing user stories. GOV.UK Service Manual.

name: Requirements Traceability Matrix for UX
origin: Requirements engineering practice, 1970s-1990s; Gotel and Finkelstein (1994)
summary: Links each research finding to requirements, design decisions, implementation items and verification tests so user insights are not lost between research and development.
description: The treatise describes a once-productive exchange between UX and requirements engineering: UX contributed ethnographic methods, requirements engineers contributed formal specification, traceability matrices and verification procedures. That intersection dissolved, and UX now produces user stories, JTBD statements and journey maps rarely integrated with formal requirements, creating a gap where insights are lost in translation. A UX traceability matrix restores the link: each requirement traces backwards to evidence (study, participant, observation) and forwards to design artefacts, tickets and acceptance tests, including usability acceptance criteria. Bidirectional traceability makes it possible to see which insights were never implemented and which features lack evidence.
steps: Assign identifiers to research findings and store them in a repository.
Write requirements, including measurable usability requirements, each citing finding IDs.
Link requirements to design artefacts and backlog items.
Define verification for each requirement (usability test criterion, analytics metric).
Maintain the matrix through releases, flagging orphan findings and unsupported features.
Review coverage at release gates.
outputs: Bidirectional traceability matrix, coverage reports, list of orphan insights and unsupported features.
useWhen: Regulated or large programmes where research must demonstrably shape delivery; audit or compliance contexts.
avoidWhen: Small exploratory projects where overhead outweighs value.
whyLost: Agile replaced formal requirements with user stories, and UX and requirements engineering communities drifted apart.
whereToUse: Medical device software (IEC 62366 files), government services, fintech compliance, large enterprise programmes.
example: A medical app's matrix shows that 9 of 31 high-severity findings from formative studies have no linked requirement; three are added before the summative validation.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Gotel OCZ & Finkelstein ACW (1994) An analysis of the requirements traceability problem. ICRE
Sommerville I & Sawyer P (1997) Requirements Engineering: A Good Practice Guide
reference: Gotel OCZ & Finkelstein ACW (1994) An analysis of the requirements traceability problem. Proceedings of ICRE '94:94-101.

name: Requisite Imagination Conceptual Design Review
origin: Adamski and Westrum (2003), after Westrum (1991)
summary: A reflective design-stage review that walks a planned design through nine considerations, from task and organisation to past failures and constraints, to foresee what could go wrong.
description: Requisite imagination is the capacity to anticipate how a design might fail before it is built. Adamski and Westrum turn it into a review of nine components that can be taken in any order: the task and design intent; the organisation (culture, resources, decision-makers, customers and users); the alignment of designers' and users' worlds across expertise levels; the operational domain and its stressors; past failures and potential human error; information needs and filtering; procedures, flexibility and training; conventions, which are reviewed and challenged; and constraints. A checklist accompanies it. The authors stress that it is reflective rather than a fixed sequence, so its rigour comes from systematically covering every component and from bringing in historical failure cases, not from scoring. It differs from a pre-mortem in being organised around design dimensions rather than an imagined failed outcome.
steps: Clarify the task the design supports and the designers' intent.
Consider the organisation: culture, resources, decision-makers, customers and users.
Compare the designers' world with users' worlds at different expertise levels and surface hidden assumptions.
Describe the operational domain and its stressors, then survey past failures in similar systems and potential human errors.
Review information needs and filtering, procedures, flexibility and training.
Challenge the conventions the design relies on and review constraints.
Record each foreseeable failure mode with a proposed design change and an owner.
outputs: A list of foreseeable failure modes linked to the review component that revealed them, with proposed design changes.
useWhen: At concept and early design of safety-relevant or high-consequence systems, when the team needs structured foresight before detailed hazard analysis is possible.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it alone when reviewers lack domain knowledge, since it depends on their imagination. For quantified failure analysis use Use Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (UFMEA) or Fault Tree Analysis; for a quick team exercise around an imagined failure use Future-Oriented Diary and Pre-Mortem Protocol.
whyLost: It stayed within cognitive systems engineering handbooks; UX adopted the lighter pre-mortem instead.
whereToUse: Medical devices and clinical software, financial trading tools, automation and AI features that hand decisions to users, infrastructure dashboards.
example: Before building an insulin-dosing companion app, the team walks the nine components and, under past failures, recalls unit-confusion incidents in infusion pumps. They add explicit units to every field and a plausibility check on doses above a set range.
reference: Adamski, A. J. and Westrum, R. (2003). Requisite imagination: the fine art of anticipating what might go wrong. In E. Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (pp. 193-220). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Resampling the Whole Feature-Selection Process (Nested Resampling)
origin: Christophe Ambroise and Geoffrey McLachlan (2002), responding to Guyon et al. (2002); Varma and Simon (2006)
summary: Place every data-driven step, including predictor selection and tuning, inside an outer resampling loop so performance estimates include the optimism of the selection itself.
description: If predictors are chosen using all the training data and the chosen model is then cross-validated, the estimate ignores selection and can look perfect on pure noise. Guyon and colleagues reported 100% leave-one-out accuracy on 62 patients with 2,000 gene predictors; Ambroise and McLachlan scrambled the labels and obtained the same zero error, proving the estimate an artefact. The fix is an outer loop: in each resample, rank predictors, fit models for each subset size (tuning in an inner loop), and predict the held-back samples; aggregate across resamples to choose the subset size; only then rank and fit on the full training set. Castaldi and colleagues found 64% of published classification analyses skipped this. Scrambling labels and expecting no-information performance is a simple sanity check.
steps: Set up an outer resampling scheme, for example five repeats of 10-fold cross-validation.
Within each outer training portion, fit on all predictors, rank them, and for each candidate subset size refit (tuning with an inner resampling loop) and predict the outer held-back samples.
Aggregate held-back performance across resamples into a profile over subset sizes and record how often each predictor is selected.
Choose the subset size from that profile.
Rank predictors and fit the final model on the whole training set.
Confirm on an independent test set where possible, and rerun with scrambled labels, expecting performance at the no-information rate.
outputs: An honest performance profile over subset sizes, selection frequencies for each predictor, and a final model with a trustworthy error estimate.
useWhen: Building churn, satisfaction or behaviour models from many logged features and few users, where feature selection or tuning precedes the reported accuracy.
avoidWhen: Avoid the full procedure with very large datasets, where separate selection, tuning and validation sets are cheaper; it is computationally heavy with flexible models.
whyLost: It is known in biostatistics and careful ML practice, but product data science often reports cross-validated accuracy after selecting features on the whole dataset.
whereToUse: Churn and conversion prediction, UX metric driver models, behavioural segmentation classifiers, survey-to-behaviour models with many items.
example: A team claims 92% accuracy predicting churn from 400 usage features on 600 accounts. Repeating the analysis with selection inside the outer loop drops accuracy to 71%, and scrambled labels give 60%, the no-information rate, so the original figure was mostly selection bias.
reference: Ambroise, C. and McLachlan, G. J. (2002). Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data. PNAS, 99(10), 6562-6566; Kuhn, M. and Johnson, K. (2013). Applied Predictive Modeling. New York: Springer, pp. 500-507.

name: Research Data Management Plan and Record-Keeping
aka: Research data management plan, ownership and sharing
origin: NIH and NSF data management and sharing requirements; Kanare (1985) on laboratory notebooks; summarised by Macrina (2014)
summary: Decide and document before collection who owns the data, how it is stored, shared, retained and disposed of, and keep a dated, complete study record another researcher could reconstruct.
description: A data management plan settles ownership (who collected the data, under whose direction, and any obligation to assign it to an employer, client or funder), formats and metadata, storage and preservation, sharing and its limits (privacy, confidentiality, security, IP), roles and responsibilities including cover when people leave, retention periods and disposal. The companion record-keeping practice treats the study notebook as the core of the research record. NSF investigators judge records on completeness (all activities, not only successes), linkage to electronic files by name and location, regular supervisor review, accuracy sufficient for another researcher to reconstruct the work, and safekeeping with off-site backup. Errors are struck through once and explained, never erased; reinterpretations go in new cross-referenced entries. Electronic records need protected storage, encryption, read-only archives, time stamps or hashes and daily backup.
steps: Establish ownership of the data: who collects it, under whose direction, and any obligation to an employer, client or funder.
Describe the data to be collected, its formats and metadata standards, and where every file will live.
Specify storage, security and preservation during and after the project, including encryption of laptops and portable media and daily backup.
Specify how and when data may be shared, and the privacy, confidentiality and IP protections that limit sharing.
Assign roles for data management, including cover when key people leave, and set retention periods and disposal or archiving from legal and organisational rules.
Keep a dated study log: purpose, methods and deviations, raw observations recorded immediately, locations of off-book files, discussion and an explicit conclusion.
Never erase: strike errors with one line and explain; record decisions, correspondence and every contributor's role.
Have records reviewed regularly (weekly or monthly) and route external data requests through a designated owner.
outputs: A written data management plan, an ownership statement and a complete, dated study record.
useWhen: Studies with recordings, personal or health data, research repositories, regulated industries, academic collaborations, or any work likely to be audited or reused.
avoidWhen: Never skip it entirely, but scale it down for quick internal tests with no personal data. Avoid editorial remarks such as 'the test failed' in records; record facts.
whyLost: Mandatory in funded science and laboratories; UX teams rely on informal folders and repositories, with retention and ownership rarely decided up front.
whereToUse: Research operations, health and fintech research, AI training-data collection, agency-client work where ownership is contested.
example: Before a video diary study, a research-ops lead fixes that the client owns the recordings, raw video is deleted 90 days after the readout, transcripts are pseudonymised and every analysis file is listed by path in the study log.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Macrina, F. L. (2014). Scientific Integrity: Text and Cases in Responsible Conduct of Research (4th ed.). ASM Press, chs. 9-10.

name: Research Ethics Protocol
origin: Belmont Report, 1979; Marsh, 2018
summary: A systematic pre-study ethics review across seven checkpoints: consent, data minimisation, participant wellbeing, vulnerability, power, data storage and researcher wellbeing.
description: The research ethics protocol is a systematic review completed before a study begins, organised around seven checkpoints. Informed consent must be specific about recording, use, access and withdrawal, and treated as ongoing. Data minimisation requires justifying every data type collected. Participant wellbeing anticipates emotional, reputational or financial distress and prepares a response and signposting. Vulnerable populations (minors, people with cognitive impairment, marginalised groups) trigger enhanced safeguards. Power asymmetry examines whether relationships with the researcher or sponsor compromise voluntary participation. Data storage and anonymisation define location, access, deletion and residual re-identification risk. Researcher wellbeing plans debriefs and support for distressing fieldwork. Rigour comes from written answers to each checkpoint and review by a second person for higher-risk studies.
steps: Describe the study's purpose, participants, topics and data types in a one-page brief that the review can refer to.

Determine whether the study counts as research needing formal review (systematic investigation aimed at generalisable knowledge that involves people or their identifiable data); where an institutional review board applies, it, not the researcher, decides on exemption or expedited review.
Draft consent materials that state what will be recorded, how data will be used, who will access it and how to withdraw, and plan to reconfirm consent during sessions.

For participants who cannot read the consent form (blind, low-literacy or non-native-language participants), use oral consent with a short written form, an impartial witness and, where needed, an interpreter.

Where information is withheld for methodological reasons, apply the reasonable-person test: if the withheld information would change a reasonable person's decision to take part, disclose it or redesign the study.
Justify each data type against the research question and remove anything not strictly needed (for example, video when audio suffices).
Assess risks of distress and identify vulnerable or power-dependent participants, adding enhanced consent, signposting resources and a stop rule for sessions.
Decide in advance how to respond if a participant discloses a risk of serious harm to themselves or others (duty to warn), and tell participants the limits of confidentiality.
Define storage location, access rights, retention period (for example, delete raw recordings after 90 days) and anonymisation approach, including residual re-identification risks.
Plan researcher wellbeing support, such as debriefs after sensitive sessions and access to supervision.
Have a second person review high-risk studies, record decisions and mitigations, and revisit the protocol if the study design changes.
Apply the newspaper test: if the study would look troubling on a newspaper front page or to senior leadership, stop and consult a colleague outside your reporting line.
outputs: A completed seven-checkpoint review, consent materials, distress and escalation protocols, a data management plan, and researcher support arrangements.
useWhen: Before any study, and necessarily before research with vulnerable participants, sensitive topics, employees or customers in dependent relationships, or retained recordings.
avoidWhen: Not a replacement for formal ethics committee approval where required (academic, clinical); a lighter checklist suits low-risk anonymous studies.
whyLost: Commercial research lacks review boards; ethics is reduced to a consent form, and researcher wellbeing is rarely considered at all.
whereToUse: Health, finance, children's and social services products; research involving employees, patients or customers dependent on the sponsor; studies using recordings or AI transcription; any organisation building a research operations function.
example: Before interviewing families about a child's hospital stay, a team applies the seven checkpoints: it adds a counsellor contact, removes video recording, excludes current inpatients, and books debriefs for researchers after each session.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
Danis, M. et al., Research Ethics Consultation: A Casebook (Oxford University Press, 2012)
Macrina, F. L., Scientific Integrity: Text and Cases in Responsible Conduct of Research, 4th ed. (2014)
Athanassoulis N & Wilson J (2009) When is deception in research ethical? Clinical Ethics 4(1)
Chapman, C. & Rodden, K., Quantitative User Experience Research (Apress, 2023)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Exploring the Ethics and Psychological Impact of Deception in Psychological Research (Boynton et al., 2013)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
When is Deception in Research Ethical? (Athanassoulis & Wilson, 2009)
Guidance and Procedure: Deception or Incomplete Disclosure (UCLA OHRPP, 2020)
reference: Marsh S (2018) User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services. Kogan Page

extra.Seven Ethics Checkpoints: Informed consent: Do participants know what will be recorded, how data will be used, who will have access, and how to withdraw at any time without consequence? Consent must be ongoing — not a one-time signature. Data minimisation: Are you collecting only what you genuinely need for your research question? Every additional data point is an additional privacy risk. Document the justification for each data type collected. Participant wellbeing: Could the study cause distress — emotional, reputational, or financial? What is your protocol if distress occurs during a session? Have signposting resources ready. Vulnerable populations: Any participant under 18, with cognitive impairment, in a power-asymmetric relationship with the researcher (e.g., employee of researcher's client), or from a marginalised group requires enhanced consent procedures and additional safeguards. Power asymmetry: Is the participant in any relationship with the researcher or sponsor that could compromise genuine voluntary consent (employee, student, customer)? Document and mitigate. Data storage and anonymisation: Where will data live? Who can access it? When will it be deleted? How will you anonymise — and what re-identification risks remain even after anonymisation? Researcher wellbeing: Fieldwork on distressing topics affects researchers. Plan for debriefs, supervision, and mental health support.

name: Research Gamification (Gamified Research Instruments)
origin: Market research practice; Downes-Le Guin et al. (2012)
summary: Redesigning questionnaires, diaries or interviews with game elements to raise respondent engagement and response quality, checked against a non-gamified version.
description: Research gamification applies game mechanics and design to research instruments themselves, not to the product under study. Techniques include reframing language and structure, narratives and storylines, levels with rewards, points and badges, competition and leaderboards, puzzles and card sorts, avatars, projective scenarios ('imagine you are...') and instant feedback such as a personality type. The aim is greater motivation, longer and richer answers and fewer satisficing behaviours. The rigour lies in testing: Downes-Le Guin and colleagues fielded one questionnaire in text-only, decoratively visual, functionally visual and fully gamified versions and compared engagement and answers. Gamification can change the answers themselves, not just engagement, so effects on data must be measured rather than assumed.
steps: Select the instrument to gamify (questionnaire, diary, interview task) or design a new game-like instrument.
Identify the engagement or quality problem to solve, such as break-off, short open answers or straightlining.
Choose game elements that fit the problem (narrative, levels, points, puzzles, projective scenarios, feedback).
Redesign language, layout and flow accordingly, keeping the measured constructs unchanged.
Field the gamified and a plain version in a randomised split and compare completion, quality indicators and answer distributions.
Adopt the gamified version only where data quality improves without shifting substantive answers.
outputs: A gamified instrument, response data and evidence on its effects on engagement and answers.
useWhen: Long or repetitive instruments with engagement problems, younger audiences, diary studies needing sustained participation.
avoidWhen: Validated scales whose norms depend on standard administration, or when the game framing could bias answers on the topic studied. For evaluating gamified products use gamification research instead.
whyLost: It peaked as a market research trend around 2012; evidence of mixed effects on answers and the cost of building game-like instruments limited uptake in UX.
whereToUse: Diary and ESM studies with long durations, research with teenagers, gaming audiences, long preference elicitation tasks.
example: A gaming platform's 25-minute preference survey has 40% break-off. A version framed as a quest with levels and projective scenarios is split-tested; break-off falls to 22%, but ratings of in-game purchases rise, so that section stays in plain format.
reference: Dawson, C. (2020). A-Z of Digital Research Methods. Abingdon: Routledge.

name: Research Interviews with Children
aka: Research interviews with children (child-centred techniques, puppet interviews, thought-bubble sheets, NICHD protocol)
donor: Developmental and forensic psychology; child-computer interaction
origin: Eder (1989) and Ablow and Measelle (1993) puppet interviews; Orbach et al. (2000) NICHD Protocol; Yarosh (2009-2014); Laporte et al. (2012)
summary: A toolkit for eliciting children's own accounts: power-levelling, concrete recent stories, show-and-tell, puppets, thought-bubble sheets and the NICHD open-prompt ladder.
description: Children are separate stakeholders: Yarosh found parents' accounts of their children's experience often diverged from the children's own, so parents are not adequate proxies. Child-centred interviewing reduces the power gap (child's turf, first names, letting the child handle the recorder), asks for specific recent events rather than abstractions, and uses show-and-tell and drawing of imagined futures, analysed for words and concepts rather than designs. For young children, puppets voice contrasting self-descriptions and the child picks the one more like them; children from 3.5 years give consistent, retest-reliable answers. For classroom-scale data, short thought-bubble sheets around a picture of a device carry simple open questions. The NICHD Protocol scripts a prompt ladder: ground rules, rapport, practice narrative, free-recall invitations, cued invitations using the child's own words, wh- questions, and option-posing questions only as a last resort, which roughly triples open prompts.
steps: Prepare parental consent and age-appropriate child assent, stressing the right to skip or stop; never promise secrecy from parents.
Choose a setting where the child feels in control and keep sessions short, with breaks.
Set ground rules: it is fine to say 'I don't know', 'I don't understand' or to correct the interviewer.
Build rapport, then have the child practise describing a recent neutral event in detail with open invitations.
Ask about specific recent events with free-recall and cued invitations, moving to wh- questions only afterwards and yes/no questions only if essential.
For children under about seven, use puppets voicing contrasting statements or simple three-point scales; for groups, use five-minute thought-bubble sheets per theme.
Add show-and-tell of places and objects and a drawing task about an imagined future, listening for key words.
Interview parents separately, compare accounts, and check reliability against other reporters where measuring.
outputs: Children's own accounts and self-reports, coded short answers, and documented points where children's and parents' views diverge.
useWhen: You design for or with children and need their perspective rather than parents' or teachers' assumptions, from about age three upwards.
avoidWhen: You need precise timing or frequency reports from children under ten, or explanations from forced-choice puppet items; use observation or logging instead. Never use leading or suggestive questions.
whyLost: These techniques are mature in developmental and forensic psychology, but child UX research mostly relies on observation and informal chats with parents present.
whereToUse: Children's apps and games, education technology, family communication and safety products, youth privacy and age-appropriate design.
example: A family video-calling team interviews children of separated parents on their own turf. Their drawings of 'magic doors' reveal a wish for bedtime rituals with the distant parent, which parents never mentioned.
sources: Using Correspondence Analysis to Monitor the Persona Segmentation Process (Laporte et al., 2012)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Lamb, M. E., Malloy, L. C., Hershkowitz, I., & La Rooy, D. (2015). Children and the law. In Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 3. Wiley.

name: Research Learning Spiral (Travis)
origin: David Travis and Philip Hodgson, 2019
summary: A staged planning cycle linking objectives, research questions, method selection, fieldwork, analysis and communication, with checks at each stage that the chain still holds.
description: The research learning spiral is a planning discipline for UX studies. It moves from objectives (what decision the research must inform), to specific research questions, to choosing a method for each question, then to conducting the research, analysing data and communicating findings, after which the next turn of the spiral begins with what is now known and unknown. Its value lies in traceability: each method choice should map to a question, each question to an objective, and each finding back to a decision. Travis emphasises checking at every stage whether the previous one still holds, so studies do not drift into collecting interesting but unusable data. As a cycle it also supports cumulative learning across studies rather than one-off projects. In practice most teams skip the explicit question-to-method mapping, which is where the rigour lies.
steps: For any upcoming study: write objectives (business/design goals).
Derive research questions from objectives (what would you need to know to achieve the objective?).
Map each question to a method (not the reverse).
For each method, verify: is this the minimal-cost method that validly answers the question?
Document the objective→question→method chain before data collection begins.
outputs: Research plan with traced objectives, questions and methods, a question-by-method matrix, findings mapped to decisions, and inputs for the next research cycle.
useWhen: Planning any non-trivial study, especially multi-method programmes, and teaching teams to justify method choices.
avoidWhen: For very small, well-defined evaluative tests where the question and method are obvious; a lightweight test plan suffices.
whyLost: Planning frameworks are seen as overhead under time pressure, so teams jump from a stakeholder request to a favourite method and the traceability step is lost.
whereToUse: Research planning, study design review, stakeholder alignment. Makes research decisions traceable from objectives to findings.
example: A SaaS research lead maps the objective 'reduce trial churn' to four research questions and chooses interviews for two, funnel analysis for one and a survey for one. The matrix exposes that the planned usability test answered none of them, saving two weeks.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher — David Travis
reference: Travis D & Hodgson P (2019) Think Like a UX Researcher. CRC Press

name: Research Method Selection Frameworks
aka: Four-question research method selection with cheat sheet
UX metric selection by study scenario
donor: UX research practice and usability engineering
origin: Rachel Hinman (presence/awareness quadrants, reported 2011); Marsh (2022) after Baliani (2021); Albert and Tullis (2008, 2022) scenario-to-metric matrix
summary: Choose methods and metrics from the research question by answering a few structured questions and reading candidates off a grid, matrix or cheat sheet.
description: Method selection should start from the question, not a favourite method. Marsh's four questions ask what the research question is, which lifecycle phase applies (define, analyse, evaluate, implement), whether attitudinal or behavioural data are needed, and whether qualitative, quantitative or both; the answers point to methods on a cheat sheet. Albert and Tullis cross ten study scenarios (transactions, product comparison, frequent use, navigation, awareness, problem discovery, critical products, overall experience, subtle changes, alternative designs) with metric types to choose performance, issue, self-report, biometric and live-site metrics. Hinman's grid classes methods by whether the researcher is present and whether the participant is aware of being studied, and asks that a plan cover at least two, preferably three, quadrants so each method's intrusion is offset by another. Together they turn method choice into an explicit, reviewable step.
steps: Write the research questions and the decisions they inform.
Identify the lifecycle phase and whether the study is generative, formative or summative.
Decide whether you need attitudinal or behavioural data, qualitative or quantitative, or both, remembering attitudes usually need larger samples.
Match the study to a scenario in the Albert and Tullis matrix and read off the recommended metric types.
Place candidate methods in the presence-by-awareness grid and select a mix covering at least two quadrants.
Choose tools, sample size and analysis plan for the selected methods and metrics before collecting data.
outputs: A shortlist of methods and metrics tied to each research question, with a rationale for the mix.
useWhen: Planning any study or research roadmap, especially when stakeholders request a specific method, or when a team defaults to one method for everything.
avoidWhen: The question is already well matched to a standard method. The matrices are expert judgement, not validated tools, and quadrants with unaware participants raise consent issues.
whyLost: It survives as everyday planning practice in UX, through cheat sheets and method landscapes.
whereToUse: Research planning, research-ops playbooks, training junior researchers, roadmap-level research strategy.
example: A team asked for 'a survey' about a confusing navigation runs the four questions, realises it needs behavioural evidence on findability, and chooses tree testing plus a short diary study instead.
sources: Regression and Key Driver Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, 2021)
reference: Albert, W., & Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience: Collecting, Analyzing, and Presenting UX Metrics (3rd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 3.

name: Research Operations and Method Repository
origin: ResearchOps community, 2018 onward
summary: An organisational function maintaining method standards, research repositories, training and planning advice so methods and findings survive turnover.
description: The treatise presents research operations as critical for method-resilient organisations. A strong ResearchOps function maintains a methodological standards library (canonical protocols for complex methods), manages research repositories preserving institutional knowledge, provides training and coaching in complex methods, and advocates for methodological appropriateness in research planning. It addresses the institutional memory problem: high turnover, valuing tool proficiency over experience, and lack of knowledge management cause organisations to lose accumulated knowledge when people leave. The method library is the organisational counterpart of the treatise's proposed field-level canon.
steps: Audit current methods, artefacts and knowledge loss points.
Create canonical method protocols with quality criteria, starting with high-priority methods.
Stand up a searchable repository linking findings to evidence and studies.
Run training, coaching and peer review for complex methods.
Add method-appropriateness review to research planning.
Measure reuse, quality and onboarding time.
outputs: Method standards library, research repository, training programme, planning review process.
useWhen: Teams beyond a few researchers, high turnover, regulated environments.
avoidWhen: Very small teams, where lightweight shared documents suffice.
whyLost: Not lost: an emerging function, though often focused on recruitment logistics rather than method stewardship.
whereToUse: In-house research teams, agencies, research-heavy product organisations.
example: A ResearchOps team publishes canonical protocols for diary studies and UFMEA, and onboarding time for new researchers to run them independently falls from months to weeks.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Sharon T (2016) Validating Product Ideas Through Lean User Research
Org Design for Design Orgs (Merholz & Skinner, 2016)
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 34 (The Research Operations Function).

name: Research Plan and Proposal with Sign-off
donor: Project management in research; HCI evaluation
origin: Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015); Leavy (2017); Blandford et al. (2008) PRET A Rapporter
summary: Write a short plan for each study covering purpose, method, participants, ethics, analysis, reporting, roles and dates, then walk stakeholders through it and get sign-off.
description: The proposal is both road map and informal contract. Baxter, Courage and Caine list history and past research, objectives and scope, method and analysis, a specific participant profile, recruitment, incentives, and a named owner and date for every deliverable, and insist on a 30-minute review meeting rather than an email because sign-off disarms later attacks on participants and tasks. Leavy's templates adjust sections to the design: quantitative plans add hypotheses, validity and pilots; qualitative plans add a philosophical stance and evaluation criteria; mixed methods add a design diagram. Blandford's PRET A Rapporter organises planning by Purpose, Resources and constraints, Ethics, Techniques for data gathering, Analysis and Reporting, and pairs each planning question with a reporting question, treating study design as 'the art of the possible'.
steps: State the purpose (formative or summative, focused or exploratory) and the decisions the study informs.
List resources and constraints: time, budget, equipment, places, participants and expertise.
Describe the method, participant profile, recruitment and incentives, and attach the screener if ready.
Record ethical considerations: consent, privacy, vulnerability and benefit to participants.
Specify data gathering, analysis and quality criteria, and how and to whom findings will be reported.
Assign a named owner and date to each deliverable; allow realistic preparation time (often one to two weeks each for goals, proposal, materials and piloting).
Hold a short review meeting with everyone who prepares or uses the data, confirm objectives, data, participants, roles and dates, and record sign-off.
outputs: An agreed study plan, a signed-off scope and a deliverable tracker.
useWhen: Every study of more than a few hours, especially with several stakeholders, external recruiters or ethics review.
avoidWhen: Very fast guerrilla tests may need only a one-paragraph brief. Beware scope creep and novice underestimation of preparation time, often by half.
whyLost: It survives as standard practice through research-plan templates, though sign-off meetings and reporting plans are often skipped.
whereToUse: All UX research, agency engagements, regulated studies, academic-industry collaborations.
example: A card-sort plan for a travel app names objectives, 15 participants per segment, the screener, who buys incentives and a readout date. A 30-minute review catches that developers expected task timings, which are added to scope.
sources: User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Blandford, A., Adams, A., Attfield, S., et al. (2008). The PRET A Rapporter framework: Evaluating digital libraries from the perspective of information work. Information Processing and Management, 44, 4-21.

name: Research Question Prioritisation Matrix
origin: Erika Hall, 2013; David Travis, 2019
summary: Ranks research questions by criticality, reversibility of the resulting decision and current uncertainty, multiplying 1-5 scores to research consequential questions first.
description: This matrix ranks candidate research questions by the decisions they inform rather than by curiosity. Criticality (1-5) asks how bad the consequence of a wrong answer would be, from cosmetic mistake to product failure or harm. Reversibility (1-5) asks how hard it would be to undo a wrong decision, from a sprint-level change to something baked into architecture or regulatory compliance. Uncertainty (1-5) asks how little is currently known, from well-evidenced to pure speculation. Priority is the product of the three. Low-reversibility questions deserve disproportionate attention even at moderate uncertainty, because errors cannot be recovered. Rigour comes from scoring collaboratively with written rationales, checking 'known' claims against evidence, and rescoring as research reports.
steps: List every candidate research question from stakeholders, the backlog and assumption mapping, phrased as questions that would change a decision.
Score each question for criticality on a 1-5 scale, from cosmetic mistake (1) to product failure or user harm (5).
Score reversibility on a 1-5 scale, from easily changed within a sprint (1) to baked into architecture or regulatory compliance (5).
Score uncertainty on a 1-5 scale, from well-evidenced (1) to pure speculation (5), citing evidence for any low score.
Multiply the three scores to obtain a priority score (maximum 125) and rank the questions.
Give extra weight to questions with reversibility of 4 or 5, even where uncertainty is moderate, and agree a cut-off for what will be researched this cycle.
Select methods only for the top-ranked questions, record why lower-ranked questions are deferred, and rescore as new evidence arrives.
outputs: A scored and ranked research backlog, rationales per score, explicitly deprioritised questions, and a research plan linked to decisions.
useWhen: When research capacity is limited, when stakeholders compete for research time, and at the start of planning cycles, before selecting any method.
avoidWhen: Avoid when one urgent question already dominates or the space is so new that questions cannot yet be formulated; start with exploratory research instead.
whyLost: Teams research what is interesting or what a stakeholder asks for; the explicit scoring step feels bureaucratic and is skipped.
whereToUse: Quarterly research planning, research operations and backlog management, product strategy reviews, and regulated domains (health, finance, government) where irreversible decisions carry high cost.
example: A health platform scores 'will clinicians accept AI triage suggestions?' at 5 (criticality) × 5 (reversibility, since it is embedded in regulatory approval) × 4 (uncertainty) = 100, ahead of a colour-scheme question at 1×1×3, so research capacity goes to the triage question.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher (David Travis)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Hall E (2013) Just Enough Research. A Book Apart

extra.The Three-Axis Matrix: Criticality (1–5): If this question were answered incorrectly, how bad would the consequence be? 1 = cosmetic mistake; 5 = product failure or harm to users. Reversibility (1–5): If the decision based on this answer turns out to be wrong, how hard is it to undo? 1 = easily changed in a sprint; 5 = baked into architecture or regulatory compliance. Uncertainty (1–5): How little do you currently know? 1 = well-evidenced; 5 = pure speculation.
extra.Priority Score: Priority = Criticality × Reversibility × Uncertainty. Research the highest-scoring questions first. Questions with low reversibility deserve disproportionate attention even if uncertainty seems moderate — you cannot afford to be wrong and unable to recover. This matrix prevents the most common research failure: researching what is interesting rather than what is consequential.

name: Research Reporting and Readouts
aka: Complete report, recommendations report and executive summary
Audience and host research before a presentation
origin: UX practice (Baxter, Courage and Caine; Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed); Heath and Heath (2007); Knaflic (2015, 2020); Weinschenk (2012)
summary: Design how findings reach decision-makers: define the audience and the action wanted, write tiered reports, and present in a short readout that leads with what matters most.
description: Delivery decides whether research is used. First define the audience: list everyone who might care, narrow to whoever must act and who decides, write down and check assumptions about their goals and beliefs, and state the action as a completed sentence ('After this, you should...'). Choose a genre by use: usability report, documentary portrait for strategy, or design springboard. Write at three depths: a complete report for the archive (summary, method, participants, findings with evidence, prioritised recommendations, limitations), a recommendations list with a status column, and a one-page executive summary. Write newspaper style, most important first, and test a beta on two audience members. Present in person within days, in an hour or less: check recommendations with a key team member beforehand, open with what works, go in priority order, park implementation debates, and end with next steps.
steps: List every possible audience, then narrow to the primary one by asking who must act, what must happen now and who decides.
Write and check assumptions about that audience's goals, beliefs and likely reactions with the host or a colleague, and state the desired action as one sentence.
Choose a report genre by how stakeholders will use the research and finish the content before formatting.

Write a complete report (summary, method, participants with IDs only, findings with evidence, prioritised recommendations, limitations), then derive a recommendations list with a status column and a one-page executive summary.
Structure newspaper style with the most important finding first, and test a beta with two audience members.
Hold a readout within days of the study, under an hour: open with positive findings, present in priority order with clips and quotes, park implementation debates and record constraints.
End with agreed next steps, schedule a prioritisation meeting and store all reports in a searchable archive.
outputs: Audience profile and action statement, complete report, recommendations list, executive summary, readout slides and agreed next steps.
useWhen: Every study whose findings must change a decision, especially with mixed or senior audiences.
avoidWhen: Very small studies may need only an email or stand-up summary; full reports may not suit fast-moving teams. Never name participants, and do not hide limitations.
whyLost: It survives because communicating findings is central to UX work, though audience analysis and tiered reporting are often reduced to a slide deck.
whereToUse: In-house research teams, agencies, research repositories, executive briefings.
example: After a checkout study, the researcher narrows the audience to the payments product manager, whose action is to approve two fixes this quarter. The readout opens with what works, plays three clips and closes with a prioritisation meeting date.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
100 Things Every Presenter Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2012)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
Storytelling to Spur Action with Stakeholders (Reimer & Howley, 2023)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M., & Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience: A Practitioner's Guide to User Research (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 531-552.

name: Research through Design
origin: Zimmerman, Forlizzi and Evenson (2007); applied by Xu and MacIntyre in Chapter 9
summary: Treating the design and study of a working artefact as the means of producing knowledge, rather than only as an application of existing knowledge.
description: Research through design recognises interaction design as a form of inquiry. Instead of first establishing facts and then designing, the team designs an artefact that embodies a hypothesis or set of ideas, often drawing on several disciplines, and then studies how people use it. The artefact becomes both a contribution and a research instrument. Chapter 9 uses the approach to build NerdHerder, a colocated augmented-reality game: guidelines derived from sociological theory and from earlier AR work were embodied in design choices, and a user study with eight groups of four, recorded from multiple cameras and synchronised with game logs, showed which player behaviours the design actually triggered. The authors argue RtD suits creative design problems where problem setting and problem solving interact, as in games, because it is hard to talk about the link between interfaces and experience without having made a product that embodies it. For UX teams, RtD is a way to explore new interaction territory where users cannot describe needs in advance.
steps: Frame the inquiry: the question or theory the design will explore.
Gather knowledge from relevant disciplines and earlier work, and turn it into design intentions or guidelines.
Design and iterate a working artefact that embodies those intentions, playtesting along the way.
Study people using the artefact with rich data such as video, logs, questionnaires and interviews.
Analyse how specific design features relate to observed behaviour and experience.
Report both the artefact and the transferable insights or guidelines it produced.
outputs: A working artefact, evidence of how its design features shape behaviour, and refined design guidelines or theory.
useWhen: Exploring novel technologies or experiences where there is no existing product to study and users cannot articulate needs.
avoidWhen: The goal is to evaluate or optimise an existing product against defined requirements.
whyLost: Common in academic HCI, but product teams often see it as too open-ended and slow for delivery timelines.
whereToUse: New interaction paradigms, AR and VR, social and colocated games, speculative products, research labs.
example: A lab designs a multiplayer AR game around theory-based guidelines on shared attention and then video-records groups playing it, finding that shared physical objects became hot spots for social interaction.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Xu, Y. and MacIntyre, B. (2016). NerdHerder: designing colocated physical-digital games with sociological theories. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 9. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Research-Derived Design Principles
aka: Themes to principles to concepts to tests
origin: Template adapted from Traci Thomas; quality tests from Jared Spool; presented in Rowland et al. (2015)
summary: Translate research themes into a few concise, product-specific imperative principles, then use them to generate concepts and to judge which concepts to keep.
description: Design principles are short imperative statements that turn what research found into what the product should do. The framework runs from patterns in the data, to themes that explain why each matters and why it occurs, to a prescriptive principle, to concepts generated by asking how might we honour it, to tests asking whether a concept should go ahead. Opower's theme that people forget simple ways to save energy became 'Always lead to action', which generated a door-tag reminder and is still used in critiques. Good principles are clear, open about form, agreed and authoritative. Spool-style tests check quality: a principle should help the team say no, distinguish the product, have a plausible opposite, and be specific to this product rather than a truism such as 'be usable'.
steps: Identify patterns or themes in the research data.
For each theme, write why it matters, why it occurs and its usual consequences.
Write a prescriptive principle stating what the product should do in response; keep the set to roughly three to seven.
Test each principle: does it help say no, differentiate the product, have a plausible opposite, and apply specifically here?
Generate concepts by asking 'How might we ...' against each principle.
Evaluate concepts against every principle and drop those that fail.
Agree the principles across the organisation, use them in critiques, and revise them when new research arrives.
outputs: A short set of product-specific principles linked to research themes, plus concepts filtered against them.
useWhen: Use it after synthesis, when research needs to steer many future design decisions by many people rather than one feature.
avoidWhen: Principles cannot replace evidence on specific designs; check concepts with Usability Testing or Prototype Testing. If the research has not yet been synthesised, run Affinity Diagramming first.
whyLost: It survived because principles are a compact, reusable way to carry research into critiques and roadmaps, though many sets decay into generic truisms.
whereToUse: Design systems, multi-team platforms, connected devices, energy and health behaviour-change products, and AI product guidelines.
example: A pension app's research shows people avoid statements they fear. The principle 'Show the next step before the number' rules out a balance-first dashboard and favours an action card, which is then usability tested.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
reference: Rowland, C., Goodman, E., Charlier, M., Light, A. and Lui, A. (2015). Designing Connected Products: UX for the Consumer Internet of Things. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 199-203.

name: Researcher positionality audit
donor: Qualitative social science, feminist methodology and anthropology
origin: Reflexive turn in anthropology and feminist research (for example Haraway, 1988; Harding, 1991); formalised in qualitative methods texts by Finlay (2002) and others
summary: A structured examination of how the researcher's identity, assumptions and relationship to participants shape access, data and interpretation, documented and revisited throughout a study.
description: Interpretivist research treats the researcher as an instrument: what they notice, ask and conclude is shaped by their social position, disciplinary training, employer and relationship to participants. A researcher positionality audit makes this explicit before, during and after fieldwork. It covers identity dimensions (class, gender, caste, ethnicity, language, urban or rural background), insider or outsider status, power relative to participants, organisational interests, and prior beliefs about the outcome. Rigour comes not from a one-off statement but from linking positionality to concrete methodological decisions: who interviews whom, which language is used, which interpretations are checked with participants, and how disconfirming evidence is sought. It supports confirmability and credibility in Lincoln and Guba's terms.
steps: Before fieldwork, write a 1 to 2 page positionality memo covering identity dimensions, relationship to participants, organisational stake in the findings and your prior expectations about the answer.
For each dimension, note specific risks to access, rapport, data and interpretation, for example participants telling a company-affiliated researcher what the company wants to hear.
Translate risks into design decisions: pairing with a local co-researcher, choosing interview language, neutral introductions, and planning member checks for the interpretations most exposed to bias.
During fieldwork, add short reflexive entries after each session noting moments where your position visibly shaped the interaction.
During analysis, have a colleague with a different position review at least 3 coded transcripts and your emerging themes, and record disagreements.
Report a concise positionality statement with the mitigation steps in the final report, and note findings that should be read with particular caution.
outputs: A positionality memo, a log of reflexive entries, documented mitigation decisions, peer review notes and a concise positionality statement in the report.
useWhen: Research crosses social distance (class, culture, language, power); the researcher is employed by the product owner; findings will inform high-stakes or equity-sensitive decisions.
avoidWhen: Purely quantitative behavioural measurement where the researcher does not interact with participants; even then, consider bias in metric choice. Avoid a formulaic statement with no methodological consequences.
whyLost: It is standard in academic qualitative research but rare in industry UX, where research is framed as neutral fact-finding and reports rarely discuss who the researcher is.
whereToUse: Global and emerging-market research, healthcare and social services, research with marginalised groups, internal research with employees, AI fairness studies.
example: An urban, English-speaking researcher from the platform company studied rural health workers. The audit predicted deference and over-reporting of tablet use, so a local co-researcher conducted interviews in Kannada and the team triangulated self-reports with logs, which revealed far lower actual use.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 25 — The Philosophy of Seeing — Epistemological Foundations of Qualitative Inquiry
reference: Finlay, L. (2002). Negotiating the swamp: The opportunity and challenge of reflexivity in research practice. Qualitative Research, 2(2), 209–230.

name: Residual Burst Analysis (Noise as Emotion)
donor: Signal processing reinterpreted for affective research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Treat deviations from a user's expected rhythm as candidate emotional or cognitive events: compute residuals, flag large bursts, and validate them qualitatively instead of filtering them out.
description: In astrophysics noise is meaningless randomness; in UX, 'noise' often represents hesitation, frustration or novelty, precisely the behaviour that reveals cognition. Standard denoising therefore deletes insight. The Behavioral Spectral Framework reframes noise contextually: compute residuals between observed behaviour and the expected rhythm, flag large residual bursts as potential emotional spikes, and validate them with video, transcripts or sentiment notes. Residual energy is read as psychological arousal, and residual energy variance as emotional arousal or confusion. The practical rule is 'never filter without first interpreting'. Because the same burst can signal stress or excitement (one case user showed high-frequency bursts with positive tone), interpretation must come from narrative context, not amplitude alone.
steps: Fit the expected rhythm for each user or session (e.g. dominant Fourier bands or a smoothed baseline).
Compute residuals between observed behaviour and the expected rhythm.
Flag residual bursts that exceed a chosen threshold as candidate affective or decision-hesitation events.
Retain flagged segments rather than filtering them, and export timestamps for review.
Validate each flagged burst with qualitative artefacts (video, transcript, sentiment note) and code it.
Report residual energy variance per session alongside the qualitative codes, noting divergent cases.
outputs: A list of validated emotional or hesitation events with timestamps and residual energy statistics.
useWhen: When micro-frustration, hesitation or surprise matters and dense interaction or biometric streams exist.
avoidWhen: When qualitative validation is impossible; unvalidated residuals invite over-interpretation.
whyLost: Original technique by Vivek Gopinath.
whereToUse: Form-heavy flows, KYC and OTP steps, game and media engagement, AI conversation pacing.
example: During checkout telemetry review, residual bursts appear at the address step; video shows repeated field corrections and a sigh, coded as frustration, leading to inline validation.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). From Stars to Signals, Sections 3.3, 4.3 and B.3.

name: Resistant Smoothing of Sequences (3RSSH, Hanning, Reroughing)
origin: John W. Tukey, Exploratory Data Analysis (1977)
summary: Split a sequence into smooth and rough using repeated running medians of 3, splitting and hanning, so outliers fall into the rough and stay visible.
description: Tukey's resistant smoothers separate a series into a smooth and a rough (data minus smooth). Running medians of 3 are repeated until nothing changes (3R), so isolated spikes cannot drag the curve. End values are set with the end-value rule: the median of the end value, the next smoothed value and a one-step extrapolation. Two-point flat peaks and valleys are split and resmoothed (S), and hanning, a 1/4-1/2-1/4 running mean (H), softens the result; the usual recipe is 3RSSH. Fences on the rough flag outside points. Reroughing, or twicing, smooths the rough again and adds it back when the smooth must follow the data closely. Across a genuine break, stop at 3RSS or smooth each side separately, because smoothing across it hides the change.
steps: Choose the expression of the values (raw, logs or roots) so that variation is roughly even.
Take running medians of 3 and repeat until there is no change (3R).
Set end values with the end-value rule: median of the end value, the next smoothed value and a one-step extrapolation.
Split two-point flat peaks and valleys and resmooth twice (SS).
Apply hanning (1/4, 1/2, 1/4) if a smoother curve is wanted (H).
Compute the rough, set fences on it and flag outside points for investigation.
If the smooth must follow the data closely, smooth the rough and add it back (reroughing or twicing); do not smooth across a known break.
outputs: A smooth trend line, a rough of residuals, flagged unusual points and an optional blurred smooth for display.
useWhen: Short or spiky metric series, such as daily sign-ups, weekly NPS or support tickets, where a few outliers distort moving averages and you want to see both trend and anomalies.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need forecasts or uncertainty bands; use time-series decomposition and forecasting or Bayesian structural time series. Use change-point detection when the question is whether a break occurred.
whyLost: Moving averages and LOESS became defaults in dashboards and statistics software, and Tukey's hand-computable median smoothers were forgotten outside EDA texts.
whereToUse: Product analytics dashboards, survey tracking, incident counts, experimentation monitoring with outliers from bots or outages.
