example: A daily active users series has two outage days and one bot spike. A 7-day moving average shows three false dips and bumps, while 3RSSH gives a clean trend and the rough flags exactly the three anomalous days for annotation.
reference: Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory Data Analysis. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, ch. 7, 16.

name: Resource conflict analysis
origin: Wickens's computational multiple resource model with conflict matrix, 2002; workload models such as W/INDEX (North and Riley, 1989)
summary: Predicts interference between concurrent tasks by scoring their combined demand and their overlap on shared resources, before any user testing.
description: Resource conflict analysis turns multiple resource theory into a quantitative prediction. Each task receives a demand score, and each pair of tasks receives a conflict score based on how many resource dimensions they share (modality, code, stage, visual channel). Total interference is the sum of demand scores plus weighted conflict scores. Wickens's model and W/INDEX use a conflict matrix with values from 0 (no shared resources) to 1 (all shared). The analysis compares candidate designs, for instance whether an alert should be visual text, an icon, a tone or speech. It is analytical, so it can be done early, but results should be validated with dual-task or simulator studies. Rigour comes from transparent coding and sensitivity analysis on uncertain weights.
steps: Decompose the scenario into concurrent task pairs or time segments.
Assign each task a demand score (for example 0 for automatic, 1 for easy, 2 for difficult).
Code each task's resource profile and compute a conflict value for each pair from a conflict matrix (0 to 1, higher with more shared dimensions).
Compute total interference for each design alternative and rank them.
Run sensitivity analysis by varying uncertain demand and conflict weights by plus or minus 25%.
Validate the top-ranked design with a dual-task test or simulator study.
outputs: Conflict matrices, interference scores per design, sensitivity analysis, and a recommended allocation of information to channels.
useWhen: Early design decisions about modality allocation in multitasking environments; when user testing is expensive or unsafe.
avoidWhen: When task interactions are poorly understood or tasks are highly strategic; use observation and simulation first.
whyLost: Used in defence and aviation workload modelling tools but unknown in most UX teams, who lack both training and tooling.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, automotive HMIs, aviation, control rooms and military interfaces.
example: Comparing alert options for a robotic surgery console, visual text scores interference 2.8 against instrument control while a spoken alert scores 1.6. A simulator study confirms faster responses to spoken alerts without reduced precision.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: Wickens, C. D. (2002). Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 3(2), 159-177.

name: Resource pool mapping (visual-verbal/visual-spatial/auditory-verbal/auditory-spatial)
origin: Christopher Wickens's multiple resource theory, 1984 and 2002
summary: Maps every concurrent task demand onto Wickens's resource dimensions, modality, code and stage, to identify where tasks compete for the same mental resources.
description: Multiple resource theory holds that time-sharing performance depends on whether tasks draw on the same or different resources along dimensions: perceptual modality (visual versus auditory), processing code (spatial versus verbal), processing stage (perception and cognition versus response) and visual channel (focal versus ambient). Tasks using different resources interfere less. Resource pool mapping lists each concurrent task demand and assigns it to cells such as visual-spatial, visual-verbal, auditory-verbal and auditory-spatial, plus response channels (manual versus vocal). Overloaded cells predict interference and suggest reallocation, such as moving verbal alerts from visual text to speech when the primary task is visual-spatial. Related tools like VACP rating scales add demand levels to each channel.
steps: List the concurrent tasks and information sources a user handles in a scenario.
Assign each demand to modality (visual/auditory/tactile), code (spatial/verbal), stage (perceptual-cognitive/response) and response type (manual/vocal).
Rate demand per channel on a 0-7 scale (as in VACP) for each time segment of the scenario.
Sum demands by channel over time; flag segments where any channel exceeds about 7 or two tasks share the same modality-code cell at high load.
Propose reallocations to less-loaded channels (for example auditory-verbal alerts during visual-spatial manual work).
Validate with a dual-task or simulator study.
outputs: A channel-by-time resource demand map, flagged conflicts, and reallocation proposals.
useWhen: When users multitask in high-tempo environments; when deciding which modality to use for alerts or information.
avoidWhen: For single-task, low-tempo interfaces; resource conflicts are unlikely to matter.
whyLost: Standard in aviation and defence human factors but rarely used outside, where multitasking is treated generically.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, driving and in-vehicle systems, aviation, emergency dispatch, and AR head-mounted displays.
example: Mapping a robotic procedure shows surgeons' visual-spatial channel saturated by instrument control while alerts arrive as on-screen text (visual-verbal). Routing alerts to brief spoken messages moves them to an unused auditory-verbal channel.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: Wickens, C. D. (2002). Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 3(2), 159-177.

name: Response Style Detection and Control
origin: Baumgartner and Steenkamp (2001); Weijters and colleagues; Blasius and Thiessen (2012)
summary: Detecting and reducing systematic tendencies to choose certain response options, such as agreeing, extremes or midpoints, regardless of item content.
description: Response styles are content-independent habits of answering: acquiescence, disacquiescence, extreme responding, midpoint responding, non-differentiation and others; Roberts lists eight. They distort means, correlations and especially comparisons between cultures or segments. Detection uses either a method factor in confirmatory factor or MTMM models, IRT or latent class models, or representative indicators built from 5 to 14 heterogeneous items per style that share no content (as in RIRMACS). Style indicators can then be entered as covariates or modelled jointly with the substantive constructs. Prevention by design matters as much: item-specific response scales instead of agree-disagree, full labelling, balanced keying, fewer grids and shorter questionnaires. Corrections must be used carefully, because styles vary with content and culture and can remove real differences.
steps: Choose the styles of concern for the population and instrument (for example acquiescence, extreme, midpoint).
Design to prevent them: item-specific scales, fully labelled points, balanced positive and negative keying, fewer grids, shorter instruments.
Include 5 to 14 heterogeneous, content-unrelated items per style if using representative indicators.
Detect styles with a method factor (CFA or MTMM), IRT or latent class models, or computed style indices.
Enter style scores as covariates or model them jointly, and compare corrected and uncorrected group differences.
Report which differences survive correction.
outputs: Style scores per respondent, corrected group comparisons and design recommendations.
useWhen: Comparing attitude scores across countries, cultures, age groups or channels, and analysing agree-disagree batteries prone to acquiescence.
avoidWhen: Single-population studies using item-specific behavioural questions. Avoid blanket correction when style and substance cannot be separated.
whyLost: UX dashboards compare satisfaction across markets at face value; style correction lives in cross-cultural marketing and psychology journals.
whereToUse: Global NPS and CSAT comparisons, cross-market concept tests, B2B versus B2C segment comparisons.
example: A consumer electronics brand finds Brazilian satisfaction far above Japanese. Representative indicators show much stronger extreme responding in Brazil; after controlling for it the gap halves, and the team stops ranking country teams on raw top-box scores.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Roberts, C. (2016). Response styles in surveys. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 579-596). London: SAGE.

name: Response Surface Methodology
origin: George Box and K. B. Wilson, 1951
summary: Fits a quadratic model of an outcome over continuous design parameters to locate optimal settings, moving sequentially toward the optimum.
description: Many UX parameters are continuous: font size, animation duration, recommendation count, delay before a prompt, price. RSM treats the outcome as a surface over these parameters. It starts with first-order designs and steepest ascent to move toward improvement, then uses second-order designs such as central composite or Box-Behnken to fit curvature and find the optimum or a ridge of near-optimal settings. It also reveals trade-offs among multiple outcomes via desirability functions. This beats guessing a few discrete A/B levels and is efficient in the number of conditions.
steps: Choose 2-4 continuous factors and plausible ranges, and the outcome(s) to optimise.
Run a first-order design (e.g. 2^k factorial with centre points) and fit a linear model.
If far from optimum, move along the path of steepest ascent with a few runs.
Near the optimum, run a central composite or Box-Behnken design and fit a quadratic model.
Locate the stationary point, check if it is a maximum, minimum or saddle, and examine contour plots.
Use desirability functions for multiple outcomes and confirm the chosen setting in a validation test.
outputs: Fitted response surfaces, contour plots, optimal parameter settings and validation results.
useWhen: Tuning continuous parameters such as timing, size, density, quantity or thresholds.
avoidWhen: Categorical design choices or when interactions with context are poorly understood.
whyLost: UX thinks in discrete design variants, and engineering DoE was never taught alongside design.
whereToUse: Notification timing, autoplay delay, recommendation list length, typography for reading apps, haptic intensity.
example: A reading app tunes line height and font size with a central composite design measuring reading speed and comfort, finding an optimum at 18 px with 1.55 line height for long-form text.
sources: Box & Wilson, On the experimental attainment of optimum conditions (1951), JRSS B
Myers, Montgomery & Anderson-Cook, Response Surface Methodology (4th ed., 2016)
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Box, G. E. P., & Wilson, K. B. (1951). JRSS Series B, 13(1), 1-45.

name: Responsive and Adaptive Survey Design
origin: Robert Groves and Steven Heeringa (2006); Statistics Canada; US National Survey of Family Growth
summary: Monitoring fieldwork indicators and switching protocols in planned phases, using response propensity models, to control cost and nonresponse bias during data collection.
description: Instead of fixing one protocol and hoping for a representative result, responsive design plans phases in advance, each with indicators that trigger a switch. During fieldwork, response by subgroup, productivity, budget spent and representativeness are monitored daily, and a response propensity model is refitted from paradata and observations. When a phase reaches capacity (further effort no longer changes estimates), the team switches protocol: first chasing never-contacted or high-propensity cases, then balancing response across domains, and finally subsampling the remaining difficult cases and giving them a new, more expensive protocol such as a larger incentive. Adaptive design pre-specifies different protocols for different groups. The approach needs timely paradata and flexible field operations; the NSFG found 12 per cent of the sample consumed 37 per cent of call attempts, which is the waste it targets.
steps: Plan the phases and the indicators and thresholds that will trigger a switch between them.
Monitor response by subgroup, productivity, cost and representativeness daily.
Fit a daily response propensity model from paradata (contact history, timing, prior behaviour).
When a phase reaches capacity, switch effort: target never-contacted or high-propensity cases, then balance response rates across domains.
In a final phase, subsample the remaining hard cases and apply a new protocol such as a larger incentive or a different mode.
Weight for the subsampling and report phase-level results.
outputs: Phase reports, propensity models and a more balanced respondent set within budget.
useWhen: Large or repeated surveys with flexible contact options (email, in-app, SMS, incentives) where certain segments chronically under-respond.
avoidWhen: Short one-shot surveys without timely paradata or the ability to change protocol mid-field.
whyLost: Product survey tools send fixed reminder schedules; the propensity and phase logic belongs to government survey operations.
whereToUse: Customer trackers with skewed response, research panels, employee surveys, in-app survey programmes that can vary channel and incentive.
example: A telecom's quarterly survey over-represents long-tenure customers. After the first week the propensity model shows new prepaid customers lagging, so phase two switches them to SMS with a higher incentive, and the final phase subsamples remaining nonrespondents for a short phone interview.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Laflamme, F. and Wagner, J. (2016). Responsive and adaptive designs. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 397-408). London: SAGE.

name: Responsive Evaluation
origin: Robert Stake (1970s onwards; 2004)
summary: Evaluate a programme by organising the inquiry around the concerns and issues of those involved and affected, rather than around criteria fixed in advance.
description: Stake contrasted responsive evaluation with preordinate evaluation, which fixes objectives, criteria and instruments before seeing the programme. The responsive evaluator talks with clients, staff and audiences and observes practice to learn what issues matter to them, and lets those issues shape the evaluation focus as it proceeds. Findings take the form of rich case portrayals that respect locality and represent multiple perspectives, and generalisation is largely left to readers, who often draw the evaluative conclusions themselves. A guiding question throughout is to whom and to what the evaluation is being responsive. The approach is strong on relevance and stakeholder voice but weak on standardised comparison and use, and critics note that the label can imply other evaluators are unresponsive.
steps: Identify who is involved in and affected by the programme or service.
Elicit their concerns and issues through conversation and observation of practice.
Select the issues that will organise the evaluation and revise them as understanding grows.
Gather evidence on each issue from multiple perspectives.
Write rich case accounts organised around the issues, respecting local context.
Share drafts with stakeholders and ask explicitly to whom and to what the evaluation has been responsive.
outputs: A case portrayal of the programme organised around stakeholders' issues, with multiple perspectives represented.
useWhen: Evaluating a service or internal programme whose goals are contested or unclear, where relevance to those involved matters more than a scorecard.
avoidWhen: When you need standardised comparison or a go/no-go metric; use a benchmark or A/B Testing. Consider Utilisation-Focused Evaluation when a specific decision-maker's use is the priority.
whyLost: It is a classic of educational evaluation; UX evaluation is dominated by preordinate metrics and usability criteria.
whereToUse: Research operations and internal tools, public-sector services, education technology, community platforms.
example: Evaluating a new internal research repository, a team interviews researchers, designers and PMs first, finds the real issue is trust in tagged insights rather than search, and organises the evaluation around that.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Stake, R. E. (2004). Standards-Based and Responsive Evaluation. Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Retrieval practice (testing effect) design
origin: Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Zaromb and Roediger, 2010
summary: An experiment comparing study-test schedules, measuring delayed retention to show whether testing users on material improves learning more than restudying it.
description: Retrieval practice designs vary how often learners are tested versus re-exposed to material and measure retention after a delay. Karpicke and Roediger (2008) used 40 Swahili-English pairs; after initial study and test, one group kept studying and being tested on everything, one stopped restudying recalled pairs but kept being tested, and one kept studying but stopped being tested on recalled pairs. A week later the first two groups recalled 81 per cent and the third only 36 per cent: dropping tests hurt, dropping study did not. Zaromb and Roediger compared schedules such as SSSSSSSS, STSSSTSS and STSTSTST, with two-day recall of .17, .25 and .39. Effects appear only at a delay, and rereading or highlighting creates illusions of learning through fluency. The method is well established in education research and directly applicable to onboarding and training design.
steps: Define the material to be learned and a realistic delayed test (for example after 2-7 days).
Design study-test schedules to compare, such as all study, alternating study and test, or test-only after first recall.
Randomly assign learners to schedules and keep total exposure time equal across conditions.
Run the learning phase, logging which items are recalled in each cycle.
Administer the final test after the delay; do not rely on immediate performance.
Compare delayed retention by condition and report effect sizes; optionally collect predicted recall to show fluency illusions.
outputs: Delayed retention by schedule, learners' predictions versus actual recall, and the recommended study-test schedule.
useWhen: Designing onboarding, training, education or certification flows where long-term retention matters.
avoidWhen: Only immediate task success matters, or users will not tolerate quizzes. Effects show at a delay, so short sessions will mislead; use a learnability test for procedural skill.
whyLost: It thrives in education research but product onboarding favours tours and tooltips judged by completion rates rather than retention.
whereToUse: Edtech, language apps, compliance and safety training, enterprise software onboarding, medical device training.
example: A compliance training vendor replaces two rereading screens with short recall quizzes. A one-week follow-up shows markedly higher retention of key rules, although learners predicted the rereading version would work better.
reference: Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. Science, 319, 966-968.

name: Retrospective (Survey-Based) UX Benchmark
origin: Sauro, Benchmarking the User Experience (2018), chapter 1
summary: Benchmarks a product by surveying existing users about their past experience, without having them do tasks.
description: Sauro distinguishes two kinds of benchmark. Task-based benchmarks watch people attempt tasks. Retrospective benchmarks ask current users to recall and rate their experience with standard instruments such as SUPR-Q, SUS, UMUX-Lite and NPS, plus top-task ratings and open comments. Retrospective studies are cheap, fast, can reach hundreds of real customers and include competitors' customers, but they capture attitudes and memory rather than behaviour and cannot pinpoint task-level problems. Many programmes run a retrospective benchmark every quarter and a task-based one annually.
steps: Define the population of current users (and competitor users if comparing).
Select standardised measures and a short list of top tasks to rate.
Screen respondents for recent, real use of the product.
Field the survey and clean the data for speeders and straight-liners.
Report scores with intervals against previous waves and competitors, plus themes from verbatims.
outputs: Attitudinal UX scores over time and against competitors.
useWhen: Tracking UX quality frequently and cheaply, or when task access is impossible (logged-in products, competitors).
avoidWhen: You need to know why tasks fail; pair with a task-based study.
whyLost: Not lost, but often confused with marketing satisfaction surveys and run without standardised instruments.
whereToUse: SaaS products, consumer apps, multi-brand competitive programmes.
example: A streaming service surveys 400 subscribers each quarter; UMUX-Lite drops 6 points after a navigation change, triggering a task-based follow-up.
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapters 1 and 5.

name: Retrospective Practice History Analysis
origin: Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer (1993) with musicians; extended to sport by Starkes, Helsen, Hodges and others; retrospective interview methods by Côté and colleagues; reviewed in Chapters 7 and 8 of the Handbook
summary: Reconstructs how people at different skill levels spent their time learning, and how they rate each activity for relevance, effort and enjoyment, to find which activities build expertise.
description: The method asks people to recall, in yearly intervals, how many hours per week they spent on different practice and play activities, and to rate each activity for its relevance to improving performance, the effort it needs and its enjoyment. Ericsson's work showed that accumulated solitary practice separated elite from less skilled musicians; sport studies repeated the pattern. The Handbook describes the method's weaknesses and remedies: recall inflates estimates, especially for less skilled people, so start with the current year, cross-check against diaries, training logs and time-motion observation of actual sessions, and use quasi-longitudinal comparisons of different age groups. Côté's interview methods add play and the variety of early activities. For UX, the method can be pointed at complex products whose expert users took years to become fluent: spreadsheets, design tools, IDEs, music software, CAD, analytics platforms. Comparing the learning histories of power users and stalled users shows which activities (tutorials, real projects, imitation, community help, playful exploration) actually built skill, which informs onboarding, learning content and in-product practice features.
steps: Define skill groups using an external criterion (for example certification level, peer nomination or measured task performance).
List candidate learning activities with users, such as formal courses, tutorials, real projects, exploration, forums and pair work.
Interview or survey each person for weekly hours on each activity by year, starting with the current year and working backwards.
Have them rate each activity for relevance to getting better, effort and enjoyment.
Cross-check a subsample against diaries, product logs or observed sessions to estimate recall bias.
Compare accumulated hours and activity ratings across skill groups, looking for activities that separate them.
Translate distinguishing activities into onboarding, learning content or product features.
outputs: Activity-by-year practice profiles per user, accumulated hours by activity, and relevance-effort-enjoyment ratings that distinguish expert from less skilled users.
useWhen: A product has a long learning curve and a visible gap between expert and stalled users, and you want to know what experience paths produced expertise.
avoidWhen: The product is simple enough to master in one session, or there is no defensible external measure of skill.
whyLost: UX research mostly studies first-use and short-term learning; long-term skill development belongs to education and expertise research, and the retrospective method is labour-intensive.
whereToUse: Professional creative tools, developer tools, data and analytics software, enterprise systems, musical instruments and music software.
example: A spreadsheet vendor interviews 30 power users and 30 long-term casual users about their yearly learning activities. Power users report many more hours rebuilding colleagues' models and answering forum questions, rated high in relevance and effort; the team builds 'rebuild this model' exercises into its learning hub.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
The Science and Psychology of Music (Thompson & Olsen, 2021)
reference: Hodges, N. J., Huys, R. and Starkes, J. L. (2007) 'Methodological review and evaluation of research in expert performance in sport', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 7. Also Chapter 8 (Côté, Baker and Abernethy).

name: Revealed-Preference Valuation (Hedonic Pricing, Travel Cost and Averting Expenditure)
aka: Revealed-preference valuation from market behaviour: hedonic pricing, travel cost and averting expenditure
origin: Sherwin Rosen, 1974 (hedonic pricing); Marion Clawson and Jack Knetsch, 1966 (travel cost)
summary: Infers what people value in an unpriced attribute from what they actually pay: in product prices, in the cost of reaching a service, or in spending to avoid a harm.
description: Stated-preference methods ask people what they would pay; revealed-preference methods read value from behaviour. Hedonic pricing regresses the price of a marketed good on its attributes, so each coefficient (or derivative) is the implicit marginal price of that attribute; estimating separately by segment allows for different tastes. In a Philippines study, rents were regressed on water source, construction, rooms and lot size by income group, and only lower-income households paid a significant premium for a nearby water source. The travel cost method values a site from the money and time people spend reaching it, deriving a demand curve and consumer surplus. Averting expenditure values a harm by what people spend to avoid it, a lower bound that is valid only when the averting good is a close substitute. These methods capture use value only and assume people perceive the attribute and markets are reasonably competitive.
steps: Define the attribute to value and the observed behaviour that reflects it: listed prices, time and money spent to access a service, or spending on substitutes and workarounds.
Collect observational or survey data on prices or costs, the attributes of each option and the characteristics of users.
For hedonic pricing, regress price on attributes (often in logs) and read each coefficient as the implicit price of that attribute; estimate by segment if tastes differ.
For travel or access cost, relate frequency of use to the money and time cost of access to derive a demand curve and consumer surplus.
For averting expenditure, total the spending on substitutes that offset the harm and treat it as a lower bound on its value.
Compare with stated-preference estimates (conjoint, contingent valuation) where both exist, and explain gaps.
outputs: Implicit prices for attributes, demand curves or lower-bound values, by segment.
useWhen: Market data exist for products that bundle the attribute you care about, or users visibly spend time or money to get or avoid something, and you want value estimates grounded in behaviour rather than survey answers.
avoidWhen: The attribute is new and not yet in any market (use conjoint analysis or contingent valuation); markets are distorted by lock-in or bundling; you need non-use value. A segment-free hedonic model assumes everyone shares the same tastes; averting spending underestimates value when substitutes are imperfect.
whyLost: Product pricing research in UX relies on stated-preference tools and live price tests; the environmental-economics toolkit for observed behaviour never crossed over.
whereToUse: Pricing and packaging for devices, apps and SaaS tiers; valuing a missing capability from add-on purchases or workaround costs; marketplace listings (rentals, used goods) where attributes vary.
example: A laptop maker scrapes 4,000 competitor listings and regresses log price on screen, battery life, weight and repairability score. The implicit price of an extra hour of battery is about 2% and repairability carries no premium, so the team tests whether that is an awareness gap with users.
reference: Rosen, S. (1974). Hedonic prices and implicit markets: Product differentiation in pure competition. Journal of Political Economy, 82, 34-55.

name: Reverse Brainstorming
origin: Described as Darkside Writing by Cirucci and Pruchniewska (2022); no origin given in the book
summary: A team answers an inverted problem with ideas that would make things worse, then swaps and flips each other's dark ideas into real solutions.
description: Reverse brainstorming loosens a team that is stuck or self-censoring by asking the opposite question. Members first answer a dark version of the problem statement, such as how a social platform could spread as much misinformation as possible. Because the goal is to do harm, people write freely and often name the mechanisms that cause real failures. Each member then takes someone else's dark idea and turns it into a constructive solution to the real problem. The swap matters: it depersonalises ideas and forces a fresh angle. Cirucci and Pruchniewska warn that flips must be inventive rather than simple negations ('don't put fake news at the top'), and suggest showing examples from unrelated products first. It runs live with sticky notes or asynchronously in a shared two-column sheet.
steps: Write the real problem statement, then its flipped dark version.
Show two or three example flips from an unrelated product to model inventive rather than literal negation.
Each member writes at least one dark 'solution' in a set time (for example five minutes), on stickies or in column A of a shared sheet.
Each member takes a dark idea they did not write and writes a flipped real solution beside it (column B).
Repeat for several rounds; in the asynchronous version ask everyone to visit the sheet at least twice.
Cluster the flipped solutions and assess them for fit, feasibility and resources.
outputs: Lists of dark ideas paired with one-sentence constructive solutions, clustered for selection.
useWhen: Use it when a team's ideation is stale or polite, or when the risks of a feature need to be named before solutions are generated.
avoidWhen: It only generates options from the team's own knowledge; when you need users' perspectives use Co-design Workshops or Interviews, and when you need to judge the ideas use Prototype Testing.
whyLost: It survived because it is quick, needs no materials, works remotely, and doubles as a light risk-identification exercise.
whereToUse: Trust and safety, social media, fintech fraud flows, onboarding friction, and AI misuse scenarios.
example: A news platform team writes 'short videos teaching users to make fake posts'; a colleague flips it to 'short videos helping users spot unreliable posts', which becomes a prototype for a media-literacy prompt.
sources: UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
reference: Cirucci, A. M. and Pruchniewska, U. M. (2022). UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies: An Introduction to Contemporary Qualitative Methods. New York: Routledge, pp. 129-135.

name: Reverse Metaphor Mapping
aka: Reverse metaphor mapping to reconstruct the tacit model behind a set of positions
origin: George Lakoff, Moral Politics (1996), building on Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual metaphor theory
summary: Infer the tacit model a group reasons from by running its apparently unrelated positions backwards through a cultural metaphor, then test the model forward.
description: Lakoff could not see what linked a political group's positions on unrelated issues. He took the conventional metaphor of the nation as a family and asked what model of the family would produce each side's positions, arriving at strict father and nurturant parent models. Informants who held each worldview corrected details and pointed him to child-rearing literature that set the models out. People hold both models, applying them in different areas. The method reverses ordinary metaphor analysis: rather than mapping a known source onto a target, it reconstructs the source model from observed target positions, then tests it by predicting positions on new issues. It is reported as personal discovery without sampling or coding, so in UX it should be treated as a hypothesis generator that is then validated against behaviour and choices.
steps: Collect a group's positions or preferences across many apparently unrelated issues or features.
Identify a conventional metaphor the culture already uses for the domain (money as a household, the app as a home, the company as a family).
Ask what model of the source domain would produce each position, and state the models and their assumptions explicitly.
Check the models with informants who hold the worldview and revise them.
Derive predictions forward from each model, including for issues or features not yet observed.
Test the predictions against users' actual choices or survey responses before acting on them.
outputs: Explicit source-domain models with their assumptions, a mapping from model to positions, and testable predictions.
useWhen: Users' preferences look inconsistent and you suspect an underlying folk model, for instance in money, health, privacy or parenting products.
avoidWhen: You lack a culturally established metaphor or cannot test predictions; the risk is a just-so story. Use laddering, mental model diagrams or segmentation analysis instead.
whyLost: It is described in political linguistics books rather than methods literature, and lacks a documented sampling or coding procedure.
whereToUse: Personal finance and budgeting, health behaviour, privacy attitudes, parental controls and political or civic technology.
example: A budgeting app finds users who love envelope budgeting also reject automatic savings. Reasoning backwards through a household-budget metaphor suggests a 'cash in the kitchen jar' model, which predicts they will want visible manual transfers, and a follow-up test confirms it.
reference: Lakoff, G. (1996). Moral Politics: What Conservatives Know That Liberals Don't. University of Chicago Press.

name: Review Analysis Methodology (RVA)
origin: Ian Livingston at Ubisoft, created for Far Cry 3 and first presented at the GURSIG Summit 2013; described in chapter 4
summary: A grounded theory analysis of a stratified sample of professional reviews, coded by several researchers against focus questions, that produces a theoretical framework of how and why a product is described as it is.
description: After launch, everyone on a team reads reviews and forms opinions, usually with bias and without method. RVA turns reviews into rigorous evidence. Livingston treats professional reviewers as highly articulate expert players who also place a game in its wider cultural context. The classic study uses two to six researchers, two to four weeks, six to eight focus questions and 20 to 30 reviews sampled from the top, middle and bottom thirds of an aggregator's score range, so that a breadth of opinion is captured. Reviews are saved as plain text and open-coded with the focus questions as loose direction; after about half are coded, the team switches to selective coding with three codes per idea: focus question, conceptual label and positive or negative sentiment. Each review is memoed. Peer debriefs at roughly 25, 50, 75 and 100 per cent of coding merge codes, sort them into concepts and categories and challenge emerging theory, while negative case analysis seeks reviews that contradict it. Only after the theory is formed is a frequency count of codes and sentiment made, to communicate weight. The report answers each focus question with quotes and counts. The method transfers to app store reviews, analyst reports or expert press for any product.
steps: Plan the study: two or more researchers, six to eight focus questions and a time budget of two to four weeks.
Sample 20 to 30 reviews across the top, middle and bottom thirds of scores and save them as plain text.
Open-code the first half of the reviews, guided loosely by the focus questions, and write a memo for each.
Hold peer debriefs to merge codes, sort concepts into categories and develop the theory; then selectively code the rest with focus question, concept and sentiment codes.
Run negative case analysis to find reviews that contradict the emerging framework, until saturation.
After the theory is articulated, count codes and sentiment per category.
Report how the theory answers each focus question, supported by quotes and frequencies, with actionable implications.
outputs: A theoretical framework (concepts and categories) answering each focus question, with supporting quotes and sentiment frequencies.
useWhen: A product has launched and attracted substantial expert or user reviews, and the team needs a rigorous, shared reading of them.
avoidWhen: There are too few substantive reviews, or the team lacks qualitative coding experience and time.
whyLost: Adopted by several game studios but largely unknown outside games, where review mining tends to be automated sentiment analysis.
whereToUse: Games, consumer electronics, apps with rich store reviews, B2B products with analyst coverage.
example: An RVA of 24 reviews of an open-world game shows reviewers praise freedom but describe the late game as repetitive because outposts reuse the same layout, which informs the sequel.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 4 (Livingston).

name: Rhetorical Analysis of Interface Communication
origin: Aristotle's Rhetoric, applied to digital interfaces in technical communication studies
summary: Applies classical rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos, kairos and implied audience) to analyse how an interface persuades and instructs, and where that persuasion fails or excludes.
description: Every interface argues: it asks users to trust it, to act, to believe a claim about safety or value. Rhetorical analysis makes that argument explicit using classical categories. Ethos covers how credibility is established; pathos how emotion is invoked; logos what reasons and evidence are offered; kairos whether persuasive moves occur at the right moment. Implied-audience analysis reconstructs the user the text assumes, with their knowledge and values, and counter-audience analysis asks who that rhetoric excludes. Each finding is tied to a specific screen or message and translated into a design change. The method is rigorous when applied systematically across a defined corpus with a consistent framework, rather than as an impressionistic copy critique.
steps: Three appeals (Aristotle): Ethos (how does the interface establish credibility?), Pathos (what emotional appeals?), Logos (what rational arguments or evidence?).
Implied audience analysis: What user does this rhetoric assume? What knowledge, values, and desires does it presuppose? Is this assumption accurate for your actual user population?
Kairos — timing: Does the interface make its persuasive moves at the right moment? An appeal compelling at one moment is intrusive at another.
Counter-audience analysis: Who does this rhetoric exclude or alienate? Rhetorical analysis reveals not just who is being addressed but who is implicitly told they are not the intended audience.
Design recommendations: Each rhetorical finding should translate directly to a specific copy, flow, or design change.
outputs: A rhetorical audit of key screens and messages, an implied-audience profile, an exclusion analysis, and specific copy and sequencing recommendations.
useWhen: Persuasive moments matter: onboarding, pricing, upgrade prompts, consent, safety warnings, AI explanations, or when trust is low and you need to understand how the product argues for itself.
avoidWhen: You need evidence of actual user response; rhetorical analysis is expert desk work, so pair it with comprehension testing or A/B tests. For power and ideology questions use Critical Discourse Analysis.
whyLost: Rhetoric lives in humanities departments and its vocabulary sounds old-fashioned to product teams, who rebranded parts of it as persuasive design or UX writing without the analytical framework.
whereToUse: Pricing and paywall pages, onboarding, consent and privacy notices, health and safety messaging, fundraising, and AI assistant tone guidelines.
example: A pension app's contribution prompt relies on fear (pathos) at the moment of login (poor kairos). Rhetorical analysis suggests moving the prompt to after a balance review and adding a concrete projection (logos); the variant improves opt-ins in testing.
reference: Aristotle. Rhetoric (trans. W. Rhys Roberts). Also: Hall, E. (2018). Conversational Design. A Book Apart.

name: RICE Prioritisation Scoring
origin: Sean McBride, Intercom (2016)
summary: Score candidate ideas on reach, impact, confidence and effort so large-impact niche ideas can be weighed against modest broad ones, with evidence-backed estimates counting for more.
description: RICE extends the two-factor effort-impact sort. Reach estimates how many users or how much traffic an idea will touch in a period; impact estimates its effect on the goal metric per user; confidence is a percentage expressing how well evidence supports the reach and impact estimates; effort estimates engineering and other staff time. In Intercom's form the score is reach x impact x confidence / effort. Confidence rewards ideas backed by research or data, although, as Crumlish notes, it tames subjectivity by adding another subjective factor. The same factors work for experiment pipelines, where proposed tests are scored on potential reach, impact, effort and confidence in the hypothesis. The score's main value is communicative: it makes the reasoning behind a ranking explicit and discussable, and teams should overrule it when judgement requires and record why.
steps: List the candidate ideas, outcomes or experiments on a shared sheet.
Estimate reach as users or events affected in a fixed period (for example per quarter).
Estimate impact on the goal metric using a fixed scale (for example 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal).
Assign confidence as a percentage (for example 100, 80 or 50 percent) reflecting the evidence behind reach and impact.
Estimate effort in person-months across engineering, design and other staff.
Compute reach x impact x confidence / effort, rank the list and discuss surprises.
Overrule the score where strategy or judgement requires, and record the reason beside the item.
outputs: A ranked list of ideas or experiments with explicit, discussable estimates and recorded overrides.
useWhen: Use when a backlog holds many ideas of differing audience size and certainty, and the team needs a transparent way to rank them for a quarter.
avoidWhen: Avoid when estimates are pure guesses: gather evidence first through Customer Problem Stack Ranking or Feature Prioritisation Exercises with Users. For quick sorting, an Effort × impact grid is enough; for user-valued trade-offs use MaxDiff or Kano Analysis.
whyLost: It survived because it is simple, spreadsheet-friendly and rewards evidence, which suits data-informed product teams.
whereToUse: SaaS backlogs, growth experiment pipelines, quarterly planning, research-informed prioritisation.
example: A B2B analytics team scores twelve ideas. A niche export feature with strong interview evidence outranks a broad dashboard redesign that rests on one stakeholder's opinion (confidence 50 percent), and the team records an override to keep an accessibility fix at the top.
reference: McBride, S. (2016). RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers. Intercom blog. Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People. Rosenfeld Media, pp. 114-115, 172-178.

name: Rich Pictures (Soft Systems Methodology)
origin: Peter Checkland, 1970s to 1981 (Systems Thinking, Systems Practice)
summary: Participants draw holistic pictures of a complex situation, showing actors, structures, processes, relationships, conflicts and concerns, to externalise multiple perspectives at once.
description: Rich pictures (Checkland, Soft Systems Methodology) are hand-drawn representations of a complex situation that capture: people, structures, processes, relationships, conflicts, and atmosphere in a single visual. Unlike structured diagrams (which impose a notation), rich pictures use free-form drawing, symbols, and caricature — the goal is to capture the complexity and messiness of a real-world situation before trying to impose order on it. Applied to UX research: rich pictures make visible the systemic complexity of a product's context of use — the competing interests, power dynamics, and interdependencies that questionnaires and interviews capture only partially.
steps: Brief participants: 'Draw a picture of [the situation you want to explore]. Include the people involved, what they do, how they relate to each other, and what feels problematic or in tension. Use any symbols, stick figures, or representations that feel right. There is no wrong way to draw this.'
Non-evaluative environment: Explicitly state that drawing ability is irrelevant. The purpose is to externalise thinking, not produce artwork.

Drawing discussion: After participants complete their picture, ask them to walk you through it. 'Tell me what's happening here.' 'What does this symbol represent?' 'What's the relationship between these elements?'
Analyst interpretation: Identify recurring elements across participants' rich pictures. What structures appear in all pictures? What conflicts are depicted? What is notably absent?

Cross-participant comparison: Compare pictures from different stakeholder groups. Where do their pictures differ — what does one group see that another doesn't? These differences reveal perspective-specific constructions of the situation.
outputs: Individual or group rich pictures, participant explanations, recurring elements and conflicts across pictures, and comparisons between stakeholder groups.
useWhen: The situation is messy and ill-defined, with multiple stakeholders and conflicting views, and you need to understand the problem before defining it, as in services, organisations or ecosystems.
avoidWhen: The problem is well defined and task-level; use task analysis or usability testing. Avoid if participants are uncomfortable drawing without careful framing.
whyLost: Soft Systems Methodology remained in systems and management science, while UX developed stakeholder maps and ecosystem maps that lack SSM's emphasis on worldviews and conflict.
whereToUse: Service design and public services, internal platform strategy, healthcare pathways, multi-stakeholder B2B products, and organisational change.
example: Before redesigning a university's student support portal, staff from five departments each draw a rich picture. Comparison shows each department believes another owns 'at-risk students', explaining duplicated outreach and gaps.
sources: When Words Fail Us — Elicitation Techniques (PMC 2024)
reference: Checkland, P. & Scholes, J. (1990). Soft Systems Methodology in Action. Wiley.

name: Ridge regression and the lasso
aka: Ridge regression and the lasso (regularised regression)
origin: Ridge regression: Hoerl and Kennard (1970); lasso: Tibshirani (1996)
summary: Fits regressions that penalise large coefficients, trading a little bias for much lower variance; the lasso also shrinks weak predictors exactly to zero.
description: Instead of choosing a subset of predictors, regularised regression fits all of them while minimising the residual sum of squares plus a penalty on coefficient size: lambda times the sum of squared coefficients for ridge (L2), or of absolute coefficients for the lasso (L1). The intercept is not penalised. As lambda rises from zero (ordinary least squares) to infinity (null model), variance falls and bias rises; with many predictors relative to observations a well-chosen lambda can cut test error substantially. Because the lasso's constraint region has corners, it sets some coefficients exactly to zero, giving sparse, more interpretable models. Neither dominates: the lasso wins when few predictors matter, ridge when many have similar effects, and cross-validation decides. Predictors must be standardised because penalised estimates depend on scale. Logistic and Cox versions follow the same logic. Selected variables are one predictive set among many, not proof of which variables matter.
steps: Standardise every predictor to standard deviation one.
Choose a grid of lambda values spanning from almost no penalty to the null model.
Fit ridge or lasso at each lambda, leaving the intercept unpenalised (use logistic or Cox versions for binary or time-to-event outcomes).
Compute k-fold (typically 10-fold) or leave-one-out cross-validated error for each lambda.
Select the lambda with lowest error, or the largest lambda within one standard error of it for a sparser model.
Refit on all data at that lambda, plot coefficient paths, and report coefficients and predictive accuracy.
outputs: Coefficient paths against lambda, a cross-validation error curve, the final (for the lasso, sparse) coefficient set and predictions.
useWhen: Key driver or churn models with many correlated predictors, more survey items or behavioural features than comfortable for ordinary regression, or p close to or larger than n.
avoidWhen: The goal is causal effect estimation or inference on a pre-specified small model (use ordinary regression with diagnostics or causal methods). Lasso selections are unstable with correlated predictors; do not present them as 'the drivers'.
whyLost: It is a staple of data science but UX key driver analyses still use ordinary regression or correlation tables, often with collinear survey items.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and NPS driver models, churn prediction from feature use, text-based sentiment models, predicting task success from many interface metrics.
example: A SaaS team models renewal from 60 usage features and 20 survey items across 2,000 accounts. Ten-fold cross-validated lasso keeps 12 predictors and improves holdout accuracy over a stepwise model, while ridge shows many small onboarding effects that the lasso drops.
sources: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
reference: James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R. and Taylor, J. (2023). An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python. Cham: Springer, pp. 240-253.

name: Right-skew detection
origin: Classical descriptive statistics (Pearson's skewness measures, 1895); normality testing by Shapiro and Wilk (1965)
summary: Diagnoses whether a UX metric is positively skewed before summarising or testing it, so the right summary statistic, transformation or test is chosen.
description: Many UX metrics are right-skewed: task times, number of errors, sessions per user, revenue per user, support contacts. Applying means and parametric tests without checking shape produces misleading summaries and inflated error rates. Right-skew detection combines visual and numerical diagnostics: histograms, box plots, Q-Q plots, sample skewness and the comparison of mean and median. With small samples, formal normality tests such as Shapiro-Wilk have low power and with large samples they flag trivial departures, so visual checks and sample skewness are emphasised. The output is a decision about analysis, such as log transform, non-parametric test, bootstrap or modelling a mixture, not a test result in itself.
steps: Plot a histogram (with sensible bin widths) and a box plot of the metric, and a Q-Q plot against a normal distribution.
Compute the mean, median, sample skewness and the ratio of mean to median; skewness above about 1, or a mean noticeably above the median, indicates substantial right skew.
Inspect the right tail for outliers and check whether they are genuine (slow users) or errors (abandoned sessions, logging issues).
Check for multiple peaks that suggest mixed populations rather than simple skew.
Choose the analysis: log transform for approximately log-normal data, rank-based tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, or generalised linear models (for example gamma or negative binomial).
Document the diagnostics and the chosen approach in the analysis plan or report.
outputs: Distribution plots, skewness statistics, an outlier review and a documented choice of summary statistic and test.
useWhen: Before summarising or testing any continuous or count UX metric, especially times, counts and money.
avoidWhen: Data are already known to be bounded and symmetric, such as well-behaved composite scale scores; it remains good practice but adds little.
whyLost: Dashboard tooling summarises with averages by default, and few UX researchers routinely look at distributions before reporting.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks, product analytics dashboards, A/B test metric design, performance and latency reporting.
example: An investment platform's 'time to first trade' had a mean of 9.2 days and median of 2.1 days, with skewness of 4.3. The histogram also showed a second hump at about 20 days, triggering a bimodality check before any average was reported.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 39 — The Distribution of Human Performance — Why Averages Lie
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Sauro, J., & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience: Practical Statistics for User Research (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Risk and Time Preference Elicitation (Holt-Laury and Discounting Tasks)
origin: Charles Holt and Susan Laury (2002); delay discounting from Ainslie (1975) and Kirby and Maraković (1996); review by Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue (2002)
summary: Incentivised choice lists that measure individual risk aversion and impatience, used to segment users and predict responses to risky or delayed rewards.
description: Holt-Laury presents ten paired lotteries with increasing probability of the high payoff; the switching point between safe and risky options indexes risk aversion under expected utility. Delay discounting tasks offer choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later amounts, estimating discount rates and present bias (beta-delta models). Using real incentives for a randomly selected choice keeps answers honest. These measures predict behaviour in savings, insurance, health and subscription contexts. For UX, they explain why some users respond to annual plan discounts, loss framing or delayed rewards and others do not, and they offer validated covariates for heterogeneous treatment effects.
steps: Choose the instruments (Holt-Laury list, a delay discounting list such as Kirby's 27-item questionnaire) and incentive scheme.
Administer with clear instructions and pay one randomly chosen decision for real.
Identify switching points; flag inconsistent multiple switching for exclusion or special handling.
Estimate risk aversion (e.g. CRRA coefficient) and discount parameters (k or beta-delta) per participant.
Relate parameters to product behaviours (plan choice, savings, adherence) or use them as moderators in experiments.
Design framing or reward timing variations for segments with different preferences.
outputs: Individual risk and time preference parameters, segment distributions and links to product behaviour.
useWhen: Products involving uncertainty or delayed rewards: insurance, investing, savings, subscriptions, health adherence, loyalty programmes.
avoidWhen: When choices in the product are not plausibly shaped by risk or time preferences.
whyLost: Behavioural economics entered UX as a list of biases and nudges, not as measurement of individual preference parameters.
whereToUse: Robo-advisors, BNPL, health behaviour apps, loyalty and rewards, annual versus monthly pricing.
example: A savings app measures present bias in 1,500 users; highly present-biased users respond strongly to a commitment-device feature while others do not, so the feature is offered selectively.
sources: Holt & Laury, Risk aversion and incentive effects (2002), American Economic Review
Frederick, Loewenstein & O'Donoghue, Time discounting and time preference: A critical review (2002), Journal of Economic Literature
Kirby & Maraković, Delay-discounting probabilistic rewards (1996), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
reference: Holt, C. A., & Laury, S. K. (2002). American Economic Review, 92(5), 1644-1655.

name: Risk format comparison (frequency versus probability)
donor: Judgement and decision making; risk communication
origin: Slovic, Monahan and MacGregor (2000)
summary: Present the same risk to matched groups as a frequency or as a probability and compare their decisions, because format alone can change how people act on identical information.
description: In the classic study, forensic psychologists and psychiatrists read the same case and decided whether to discharge a patient. Told that 20 out of every 100 similar patients commit violence, 41 per cent refused discharge; told that similar patients have a 20 per cent chance, 21 per cent refused. Frequency formats seem to call up images of actual people, making risk feel more real; experts were affected as much as anyone. As a research method this is a between-subjects format experiment: hold the information constant, vary only its presentation (counts, percentages, icon arrays, verbal labels) and measure decisions, perceived risk and comprehension. In UX it applies wherever an interface states a risk, error rate or confidence level.
steps: Define the risk information and the decision or judgement it should inform.
Create equivalent versions differing only in format: frequency (20 in 100), probability (20 per cent), and optionally icon arrays or verbal labels.
Randomly assign participants to one format each, recruiting from the real audience including experts where relevant.
Measure the decision, perceived risk and a comprehension check.
Compare outcomes across formats with appropriate tests and effect sizes.
Choose the format that leads to accurate understanding and the intended level of caution, and document why.
outputs: Decisions, perceived risk and comprehension by format, and a recommended presentation.
useWhen: An interface communicates risk, likelihood, error rates or model confidence and the format could change behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the risk number is unreliable; fix the estimate first. One study is thin evidence, and the right format depends on audience and goal, so test with your own users rather than adopting a universal rule.
whyLost: It lives in judgement and decision-making and medical risk communication research; product teams pick formats by style guide rather than testing them.
whereToUse: Health and screening results, investment and insurance products, security warnings, fraud alerts, and AI confidence or reliability indicators.
example: A lending app shows applicants their chance of rejection. Testing '1 in 5 applicants like you are declined' against '20 per cent chance of decline' shows the frequency version halves applications from marginal applicants, so the team pairs it with guidance on improving eligibility.
reference: Slovic, P., Monahan, J. & MacGregor, D. G. (2000). Violence risk assessment and risk communication: the effects of using actual cases, providing instruction, and employing probability versus frequency formats. Law and Human Behavior 24(3), 271-296.

name: RITE Method
origin: Michael Medlock, Dennis Wixon and colleagues, Microsoft, 2002
summary: A usability testing approach where the team fixes the prototype as soon as a problem is clearly identified, often after one participant, then tests the fix with the next.
description: RITE was developed at Microsoft Games Studios to speed up iteration in usability testing. Instead of running all sessions on a fixed prototype and reporting at the end, the product team observes each session together, agrees on problems and fixes those with clear causes and solutions immediately, sometimes after a single participant. The next participants test the revised version, which shows whether the fix works and whether it introduced new problems. Rigour comes from having decision-makers present, explicit criteria for when to change (obvious cause, clear fix, low cost) versus wait for more data, and logging every change and its outcome across sessions. The method trades statistical comparison for learning speed and works best with prototypes that can be changed quickly.
steps: Agree a test plan, task set and decision criteria for when a problem is fixed immediately versus after more sessions.
Ensure decision-makers (designers, developers, product owner) observe every session.
Run a session, then debrief immediately to list problems and decide which to fix now.
Update the prototype before the next session for problems with clear causes and solutions.
Continue with the next participant, checking whether fixes work and new problems appear; typical studies run 6-15 participants.
Log every change, its rationale and subsequent results, and report the problem and fix trajectory.
outputs: Iterated prototype, problem and fix log across sessions, record of fixes verified by subsequent participants.
useWhen: Early prototype iteration, onboarding and tutorial flows, games, and agile sprints with tightly integrated teams.
avoidWhen: When you need benchmark metrics or statistical comparison between designs; use summative usability testing or A/B testing.
whyLost: Renamed/consolidated: Concept absorbed into lean UX and agile UX practices; rarely named distinctly.
whereToUse: Rapid prototype iteration; lean UX contexts; agile sprint cycles.
example: A tax-filing app team ran RITE on onboarding with 10 participants over two days. A misunderstood income question was reworded after participant 2 and verified by participants 3 to 6, and completion rose from 4 of 6 to 10 of 10 by the final version.
sources: Using the RITE method to improve products (Medlock et al.)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Medlock, M. C., Wixon, D., Terrano, M., Romero, R., & Fulton, B. (2002). Using the RITE method to improve products: A definition and a case study. Usability Professionals' Association conference.

name: Robust Estimation (Trimmed Means, M-Estimators, RANSAC)
aka: Robust estimation of location and scale
donor: Mathematical statistics (robust statistics); computer vision for RANSAC
origin: Adapted for UX from robust statistics: Daniell (1920), Box (1953), Tukey (1962) trimmed means, Huber (1964) M-estimators; Fischler and Bolles for RANSAC
summary: Estimate centres, spreads and fits that stay accurate when a few observations are wild: trim the extremes, use the median, down-weight outliers with M-estimators, or fit by consensus.
description: Robustness means performing well across a range of plausible distributions rather than optimally for one. Messy UX data behave like a contaminated normal: most values well behaved, a fraction from a wide distribution (abandoned tasks, bots, distracted sessions). With 5 percent contamination the median's variance is about 29 percent of the mean's, while being only slightly worse under pure normality. The k-level trimmed mean drops the k smallest and largest values; the median is the extreme case. Huber's M-estimator minimises a loss that is quadratic within a tuning constant k of the centre and linear beyond it, so small k behaves like the median and large k like the mean; the same idea gives robust regression. Simulations favour trimming about 10 to 15 percent at each end, or an M-estimator with k of 1 to 1.5 times a robust scale such as the median absolute deviation. RANSAC fits models to random small subsets and keeps the one with most inliers.
steps: Inspect the data for skew and outliers, and examine outliers as possible findings before down-weighting them.
Choose a robust location estimator: a 10 to 15 percent trimmed mean, the median, or a Huber M-estimator with k about 1 to 1.5 times the median absolute deviation.
Estimate spread robustly with the interquartile range or median absolute deviation.
For a fitted relationship, use M-estimation (iteratively reweighted least squares from a good starting fit and scale), or RANSAC when a large share of points are gross outliers.
Compare robust and ordinary estimates; a large gap signals contamination worth investigating.
Report the robust estimate with the estimator, trimming level or tuning constant stated, and use bootstrap intervals where analytic ones are unavailable.
outputs: Robust estimates of centre, spread or regression coefficients, with a comparison against ordinary estimates as a contamination signal.
useWhen: Summarising task times, time on page, session counts, latency or ratings where a few extreme values would distort the mean, especially with small usability samples or unmoderated studies.
avoidWhen: When the mean itself is the quantity of interest (total cost or revenue per user), since for skewed data robust estimators target a different quantity. When skew is systematic, re-expression or a suitable model may be better; see Log-Transformation of Task Completion Times.
whyLost: UX reporting defaulted to means or medians; trimmed means and M-estimators are taught in statistics programmes but rarely in UX courses or tools.
whereToUse: Unmoderated test benchmarks, performance dashboards, A/B metrics with heavy tails, regression on noisy behavioural data.
example: An unmoderated study of 80 participants has five task times over 20 minutes from people who left the tab. The 10 percent trimmed mean is 94 seconds against a raw mean of 151, and a Huber estimate with k = 1.5 MAD agrees with the trimmed mean.
sources: Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Huber, P. J. (1964). Robust estimation of a location parameter. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 35, 73-101.

name: ROC curve analysis for UI alerts
donor: Signal detection theory, radar engineering and clinical diagnostics
origin: Radar engineering in WWII; Peterson, Birdsall and Fox, 1954; Swets, 1988 for diagnostics
summary: Plots hit rate against false-alarm rate across alert thresholds or user confidence levels to choose the threshold that best balances misses against alarm fatigue.
description: An ROC curve shows the trade-off between true-positive and false-positive rates as a decision threshold varies. For UI alerts it can be applied at two levels: the system level (what detector threshold triggers an alert) and the human level (how users respond, using confidence ratings to trace their curve). The area under the curve (AUC) summarises discriminability independent of threshold; the optimal operating point depends on base rates and the costs of misses versus false alarms, via the slope beta = [P(noise)/P(signal)] x [(cost FA)/(value hit)]. The method makes explicit that every alert threshold is a value judgement and that high false-alarm rates degrade human trust and response, a key cause of alarm fatigue. Rigour comes from labelled ground truth and explicit cost weighting.
steps: Assemble a labelled dataset of events (true conditions versus benign) with the detector score for each, ideally at least 100 positives and 100 negatives.
Sweep thresholds and compute true- and false-positive rates at each to plot the system ROC and AUC.
Elicit stakeholder costs for misses and false alarms and the base rate, and compute the optimal operating slope.
Run a user study where participants respond to alerts and give confidence ratings on a 6-point scale; construct the human ROC from cumulative rating thresholds.

Compare the joint human-plus-system performance at candidate thresholds, noting positive predictive value; alerts with PPV below about 10-20% are associated with override rates above 90% in clinical settings.
Select the threshold, document the trade-off, and set monitoring to recompute ROC after launch as base rates drift.
outputs: System and human ROC curves, AUC values, a cost-weighted recommended threshold, PPV at that threshold, and a monitoring plan.
useWhen: When tuning alert, notification, anomaly or AI-confidence thresholds; when alarm fatigue or override rates are high; when stakeholders disagree about sensitivity.
avoidWhen: When no ground truth labels exist or events are not binary; start with log analysis of override behaviour or qualitative alarm reviews.
whyLost: ROC analysis is routine in radiology and machine learning but UX teams rarely own alert thresholds, which are left to engineers, so the human side of the curve is seldom measured.
whereToUse: Clinical decision support, security and fraud alerts, observability tools, AI confidence indicators, and push-notification strategy.
example: A fraud team sees agents override 96% of alerts. ROC analysis shows the detector runs at a threshold giving PPV of 4%; moving to a stricter point halves volume while losing 6% of true frauds, and agent override rates fall to 70% with higher hit rates on remaining alerts.
sources: Van Drongelen, W., Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent
reference: Swets, J. A. (1988). Measuring the accuracy of diagnostic systems. Science, 240(4857), 1285-1293.

name: Role-Ordered Matrix
donor: Qualitative field research and organisational sociology
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 5, section D, illustrated by how teachers, department chairs and administrators reacted to a new reading programme.
summary: A matrix whose rows are people grouped by role, ordered by distance from the work, and whose columns are research sub-questions, so views can be compared within and across roles.
description: How people see a situation depends partly on their role. The role-ordered matrix sorts data by 'role occupants'. A general question (how do people react to an innovation when they first meet it) is unbundled into sub-questions such as what is salient, how they size it up, what changes they expect and how well it fits previous practice; these become columns. Rows are individual people clustered into roles and ordered by how far they sit from the action, from direct users through department heads to central administrators, so both within-role and between-role comparisons are possible. The analyst decides who to include (direct users, those with a stake, key administrators), summarises each person's view in a phrase, and marks 'DK' where data are missing. Reading down columns, the book's analyst found teachers saw the programme as prescriptive while administrators took a big-picture view and saw no need for organisational change. For UX this is a direct way to set out how designers, product managers, engineers, support staff and customers each perceive the same feature or problem.
steps: Break the main question into three to six sub-questions to use as columns.
Decide which roles to include and list individuals as rows, grouped by role and ordered by distance from the product or work.
Search coded notes for each person and enter a short phrase or quote per cell; mark DK where data are missing or ambiguous.
Read down columns within each role, then compare across roles.
Use counting and comparison to test apparent differences, and go back to notes for reasons.
Summarise role-perspective differences and their implications.
outputs: A person-by-question grid grouped by role, and a short text on where roles agree and diverge.
useWhen: Multiple roles touch the same product or decision and misalignment between them is suspected.
avoidWhen: You have only one role or too few people per role to separate individual quirks from role effects.
whyLost: UX uses stakeholder maps and persona comparisons, which show who exists rather than laying out each role's answers to the same questions side by side.
whereToUse: Internal tools, enterprise SaaS with many personas, cross-functional alignment work, design system adoption.
example: For a new feature-flag dashboard, researchers interview four designers, five PMs, six engineers and three support leads. Columns: what stands out, what it is for, what will change in your work, fit with current practice. Engineers see it as a deployment safety tool, PMs as an experiment launcher, support leads do not know it exists (DK), which explains confused support tickets after launch.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Root Cause Analysis and the 5 Whys
origin: Sakichi Toyoda; formalised by Taiichi Ohno in the Toyota Production System (1978)
summary: Iteratively asks why a problem occurred to move from symptoms to systemic causes, ideally with evidence at each step and multiple branches.
description: The 5 Whys asks 'why' repeatedly until reaching a cause that, if fixed, prevents recurrence. In disciplined form, each answer must be verified with evidence, branches are allowed when there are several causes, and the analysis stops at a cause within the organisation's control, usually a process or design decision rather than a person. Formal RCA (as in healthcare, per The Joint Commission) adds timeline reconstruction, cause-and-effect charting and action hierarchies that favour design changes over retraining. The method is vestigial in UX: teams ask 'why' five times in a meeting with no evidence, follow a single linear chain and stop at 'user didn't read'. Restoring the evidence and branching rules makes it rigorous.
steps: State the problem precisely with measurable symptoms, scope and time window.
Reconstruct a factual timeline from logs, recordings and interviews before any causal discussion.
Ask why the problem occurred and record each candidate cause, requiring evidence (data, observation, reproduction) for every link.
Allow branching where several causes contribute, and continue each branch until reaching a controllable process or design cause, typically 3-7 levels.
Reject causes that blame individuals; reframe as 'why was this error possible and not caught'.
Select corrective actions using an action hierarchy (forcing functions and automation stronger than warnings and training) and set a verification metric.
outputs: An evidence-backed causal tree, root cause statements and corrective actions with verification metrics.
useWhen: Investigating a specific recurring problem, incident or metric drop where evidence is available.
avoidWhen: Complex sociotechnical incidents with emergent causes; use STAMP/CAST or FRAM, as linear whys oversimplify. Real effects usually have several contributing causes, so report root causes in the plural with their relative contribution rather than a single chain.
whyLost: The name survived as a workshop ritual while its evidence requirements and action hierarchy were dropped. Linear 'why' chains are easy to run in a meeting and feel conclusive.
whereToUse: Post-incident reviews, conversion drops, support ticket spikes, onboarding failures.
example: A SaaS signup completion drops 8%. A branched 5 Whys traced through logs finds two roots: a password rule change without inline feedback and a slow email verification service; both are fixed and completion recovers.
sources: Ohno, Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production (1988 English ed.)
Card, The problem with '5 whys' (2017), BMJ Quality & Safety
The Joint Commission, Framework for Root Cause Analysis and Corrective Actions
Tidwell, J., Brewer, C. & Valencia, A., Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed. (2020)
Lidwell, W., Holden, K. & Butler, J., Universal Principles of Design, 3rd ed. (2023)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
reference: Card, A. J. (2017). The problem with '5 whys'. BMJ Quality & Safety, 26(8), 671-677.

name: Rose, Thorn, Bud
origin: LUMA Institute design-thinking practice; documented in Universal Methods of Design (2019)
summary: Team members write what works (rose), what does not (thorn) and what shows promise (bud) on coloured notes, then cluster them to decide what to keep, fix and explore.
description: Rose, Thorn, Bud is a colour-coded sticky-note exercise for reviewing a product, service, experience or set of findings. Each person writes positives as roses, problems as thorns and promising but undeveloped possibilities as buds, one per note, in three colours. The notes are clustered first by category (for example a stage of the journey or a part of the product) and then by affinity within each category, so the wall shows at a glance where strengths, pain points and opportunities concentrate. It is used both in reviews and retrospectives and as a quick framing device when synthesising research notes. Its strength is speed and inclusiveness; its weakness is that it can stay superficial and opinion-based unless every note is tied to evidence.
steps: Hand out notes in three colours and define rose, thorn and bud with an example of each.
Have people work silently for 5-10 minutes, one observation per note, ideally citing the evidence (session, quote, metric) on each.
Post the notes and cluster them by category, such as journey stage or product area.
Affinity-sort within each category and name the clusters.
Discuss and decide what to keep (roses), fix (thorns) and explore (buds), assigning owners to the top items.
outputs: A clustered wall of roses, thorns and buds by category, and a short keep, fix and explore list.
useWhen: Use it for fast, inclusive reviews of an existing experience, project retrospectives, or as a first pass at sorting observations after research sessions.
