Granollers merged Nielsen's ten heuristics and Tognazzini's interaction design principles into 60 questions across 15 categories, from visibility of system state through defaults and latency reduction. Each specialist answers every question from 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree) or marks it not applicable. Per specialist, usability equals the sum of scores divided by four times the number of applicable questions; category percentages are computed the same way, and results are averaged across specialists. Low-scoring questions and categories become improvement priorities. Its appeal is comparability: sites can be ranked and tracked. Its limits are that it measures expert judgement rather than user performance, needs experienced specialists, and is still being validated.
steps: Recruit three to five experienced HCI specialists.
Have each inspect the interface independently (remote is fine) against the 60 questions.
Score each question 0 to 4 or mark it not applicable.
Per specialist compute usability % = sum of scores / (4 x (questions answered - not applicable)).
Compute category percentages, scoring an all-not-applicable category as 1.00 and an all-zero category as 0.00.
Average across specialists for the global percentage and per category.
Review low-scoring questions and categories as improvement priorities and check agreement between specialists.
outputs: Overall and per-category usability percentages per specialist and averaged, plus a list of weak guidelines.
useWhen: Comparing or tracking the inspection quality of several sites or releases, such as public-sector portals, where a single score aids communication.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the percentage as a measure of user performance; pair with Usability Testing, and use Heuristic Evaluation when problem detail matters more than a score.
whyLost: It is used mainly in Spanish and Latin American HCI research and has not spread to mainstream industry practice.
whereToUse: E-government benchmarking, procurement comparisons, design-system compliance audits.
example: Three specialists score three Peruvian e-government sites at 70%, 61% and 64%, with consistency, error messages and information overload weakest across all three.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Paz, F. (2022). Applying a new questionnaire to evaluate the usability of Peruvian e-government websites. In DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, Springer, 460-472.

name: Scree plot vs. parallel analysis
aka: Cattell's scree test vs. Horn's parallel analysis
origin: Raymond Cattell, 1966 (scree test); John Horn, 1965 (parallel analysis)
summary: Comparing the subjective scree elbow with the objective parallel analysis criterion to decide how many factors a UX questionnaire really measures.
description: Retaining too many or too few factors is the most consequential error in EFA. Cattell's scree plot charts eigenvalues in descending order and retains factors above the 'elbow', which is subjective and can be ambiguous. The Kaiser rule (eigenvalues above 1) over-extracts. Parallel analysis compares observed eigenvalues against those from many random datasets of the same size, retaining factors whose eigenvalues exceed the random 95th percentile; simulation studies (Zwick and Velicer, 1986) found it among the most accurate rules. Velicer's MAP test is a further check. Rigour comes from using parallel analysis as the primary criterion, the scree and MAP as corroboration, and examining interpretability of adjacent solutions (k minus 1 and k plus 1).
steps: Compute eigenvalues from the correlation matrix (reduced matrix for common factor analysis where possible).
Draw the scree plot and note the elbow position independently before running parallel analysis.
Run parallel analysis with at least 1,000 random datasets, retaining factors whose eigenvalues exceed the 95th percentile.
Optionally run Velicer's MAP test as a further check.
If criteria disagree, fit the k minus 1, k and k plus 1 solutions and choose based on interpretability and item loadings.
Report all criteria and the rationale for the final choice.
outputs: Overlaid scree and parallel analysis plot, agreed factor count, and documented rationale.
useWhen: Every exploratory factor analysis of UX attitude or experience items.
avoidWhen: Not needed when confirming a known structure (use CFA fit and model comparison instead).
whyLost: SPSS and many textbooks default to the Kaiser rule and scree plot; parallel analysis needs extra syntax or code, so it stayed in psychometric specialist practice.
whereToUse: Scale development for new UX constructs and checking borrowed scales in new markets.
example: For a 30-item fintech onboarding questionnaire, the scree elbow is ambiguous between 3 and 5 factors and Kaiser suggests 7. Parallel analysis retains 4, and the 4-factor solution is the most interpretable.
sources: RELIABILITY procedures; syntax automation; parallel analysis via Python plugin
Cattell, R. B. (1966) The scree test for the number of factors. Multivariate Behavioral Research
Horn, J. L. (1965) A rationale and test for the number of factors in factor analysis. Psychometrika
Zwick, W. R. & Velicer, W. F. (1986) Comparison of five rules for determining the number of components to retain. Psychological Bulletin
The Inquiry Series, C7 — SPSS for Survey Analysis — EFA, Reliability & Scale Validation
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
reference: Zwick, W. R. & Velicer, W. F. (1986) Comparison of five rules for determining the number of components to retain. Psychological Bulletin 99(3)

name: Screen-Capture Action Coding
aka: Screen-capture action coding for interface comparison
Task-step action coding of screen recordings
origin: Wang and Babaian (2020)
summary: Code every action users take per required task step from screen recordings, categorise by intent and locus, and compare action patterns between interfaces.
description: Time and accuracy show which interface wins but not why. This method decomposes each task into the steps it requires on each interface, then codes every action users took within each step from screen recordings, counting each action type once per step. Codes emerge as actions appear and are grouped by intent (for example navigate, verify, select) and by locus: whether the user acted on separate controls or directly on the data. Analysis looks at the range and frequency of actions, adoption of features over the task sequence, and choices among interchangeable actions, interpreted alongside time and accuracy. In the source study of a node-link visualisation versus a table tool across nineteen tasks, it exposed learnability, overlooked features and extra verification effort.
steps: Record screens during a comparative task study.
Decompose each task into the steps it requires on each interface.
Code every action users took within each step, counting each action type once per step, adding codes as new actions appear.
Group codes into categories by intent and by locus of interaction (controls versus direct manipulation of data).
Analyse range and frequency of actions, feature adoption over the task sequence and choices among interchangeable actions.
Interpret alongside time and accuracy data, and have a second coder check a sample for consistency.
outputs: An action code book, category frequencies per interface and per-user adoption charts.
useWhen: Formative comparison of two complex interfaces, such as data tools or editors, where you need to explain why one is faster or more accurate.
avoidWhen: Avoid for summative claims or large samples; coding is slow and partly subjective. For large-scale behaviour use Log File Analysis.
whyLost: Detailed video coding is costly, and analytics and session replay tools offer faster, if shallower, alternatives.
whereToUse: Data visualisation tools, spreadsheets and BI products, developer tools, AI copilots compared with manual workflows.
example: A BI team codes ten recordings of analysts using a chart builder and a pivot table. Pivot users perform three times as many verification actions, pointing to missing feedback.
sources: Human Interface and the Management of Information (Yamamoto & Mori, 2020)
reference: Wang, R. and Babaian, T. (2020). A detailed examination of user interactions with two different data interfaces. In HIMI 2020, LNCS 12184, Springer, 183-198.

name: Scripted Speaker Recognition Testing
origin: IVR industry practice; Cohen, Giangola and Balogh (2004)
summary: Before launch, 10 to 20 people read a fixed script of utterances to a voice system to tune timeouts and catch common misrecognitions.
description: A pre-launch check from interactive voice response practice that base recognition parameters are right before real users are exposed. A small set of speakers, typically 10 to 20, read a predetermined script covering the key utterance types: digit strings, names, domain terms and expected commands. Results are compared with the script to tune end-of-speech timeouts (phone numbers need longer pauses between digit groups) and to identify frequent misrecognitions, which are added to expected phrases or grammars. Even with cloud recognisers it catches domain-specific failures; Pearl's medical app heard 'vial' as 'vile' or 'file'. It complements rather than replaces pilot data, because scripted speech differs from spontaneous speech.
steps: Write a script covering key utterance types: digits, names, domain terms, commands and likely confusables.
Recruit 10 to 20 speakers varied in accent, age and gender, matching the target population.
Have each speaker read the script to the system in realistic acoustic conditions.
Compare recognition results with the script and tally misrecognitions by item.
Adjust end-of-speech timeouts and add misrecognised variants to expected phrases or grammars.
Re-run problem items, then proceed to pilot testing with spontaneous speech.
outputs: Tuned timeouts, an augmented key-phrase list, and a table of misrecognition rates by item.
useWhen: Before piloting a voice app, IVR or in-car voice system, especially with domain vocabulary or long digit strings.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a usability test; it measures recognition, not flow. Use Voice Interface Usability Testing for interaction quality.
whyLost: It remains standard in speech engineering and IVR vendors but rarely reaches general UX teams who rely on platform recognisers.
whereToUse: Healthcare voice apps, banking IVR, smart speakers, voice-enabled kiosks.
example: A pharmacy voice assistant runs 15 scripted speakers through drug names before pilot. Several drug names are consistently misheard, so synonyms are added and a confirmation step is designed for them.
reference: Pearl, C. (2017). Designing Voice User Interfaces. O'Reilly Media, pp. 193-194.

name: Sean Ellis product/market fit survey
origin: Sean Ellis (survey.io; Startup Growth Pyramid), around 2009
summary: Ask active users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product; 40% or more answering 'very disappointed' is taken as a signal of product/market fit.
description: Sean Ellis devised a short survey to judge whether a product is ready for accelerated growth. Its key question asks how users would feel if they could no longer use the product, typically with options very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, not disappointed and not applicable. If 40% or more answer 'very disappointed', the product is judged to have fit and the team should shift effort to growth; otherwise it should keep iterating. Croll and Yoskovitz give only the core question and threshold. Common practice adds questions on the main benefit, the type of person who would benefit most and alternatives used, and segments results to find the users for whom the product is a must-have. The 40% threshold is a heuristic from Ellis's experience across startups, not a validated cut-off, and results depend heavily on who is sampled.
steps: Define 'active users' (for example used the product at least twice in the last two weeks) and sample from them, not from all sign-ups.
Ask 'How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?' with very, somewhat and not disappointed options.
Optionally ask the main benefit, the kind of person who would benefit most, and what they would use instead.
Compute the share answering very disappointed, overall and by segment; aim for at least 40 responses per segment.
If 40% or more, treat as product/market fit and shift to growth; otherwise study the very disappointed segment and iterate towards it.
Repeat periodically and track the share over time.
outputs: A very-disappointed percentage overall and by segment, and a fit or no-fit verdict with the must-have segment identified.
useWhen: When an early-stage product team needs a quick, comparable signal of whether a core group finds the product indispensable, before scaling acquisition.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating 40% as a validated threshold or sampling all sign-ups (inflates the denominator). It says nothing about why; pair with interviews. For mature products use retention curves (Cohort Analysis).
whyLost: It survived because it is a single question with a memorable threshold that fits startup decision-making and growth playbooks.
whereToUse: Startups and new product lines, B2B SaaS pilots, internal tools seeking budget, new AI features.
example: An AI writing tool surveys 600 weekly-active users: 31% overall are very disappointed, but 52% of legal professionals are. The team narrows positioning and onboarding to legal drafting.
reference: Croll, A., & Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics: Use Data to Build a Better Startup Faster. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, p. 50.

name: Search behaviour pattern analysis
origin: Morville and Callender (2010), drawing on information retrieval and library science (pearl growing)
summary: Classify search sessions into quit, narrow, expand and pearl-growing patterns, and detect the antipatterns pogosticking and thrashing, to diagnose search design problems.
description: A shared vocabulary turns search logs and observed sessions into diagnoses. Quit: every search ends in an exit, and analytics must show whether users succeeded or gave up, especially after no-results pages. Narrow: refining after a broad first query, the second most common pattern. Expand: broadening by dropping terms, relaxing facets or browsing a thesaurus. Pearl growing: finding one good document and mining its terms and metadata for more, supported by 'find similar' features. Two antipatterns are caused by design: pogosticking, bouncing repeatedly between the results page and individual results because snippets lack information scent, and thrashing, repeating small variations of a flawed first query, an anchoring effect. Each pattern points to a design response.
steps: Collect search analytics with session identifiers and, if possible, observe or record a sample of search sessions.
Identify exits, especially after no-results pages, and estimate success versus abandonment.
Code narrowing and expanding sequences of queries, facets and filters.
Look for pearl growing: use of similar-item features or terms mined from a good result.
Flag pogosticking (repeated rapid returns from results to the results page) and thrashing (chains of near-identical reformulations).
Respond with design changes such as clearer no-results pages with spelling suggestions, partial matching, facets, richer snippets, and autocomplete built from reformulation data.
outputs: A diagnosis of where and why searchers quit, struggle or succeed, with linked design responses.
useWhen: Improving site or in-app search where logs show heavy reformulation, exits or result bouncing.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating all pogosticking as failure; some is normal sampling of results. The patterns have no standard thresholds, so pair with site search analytics metrics and usability tests.
whyLost: The vocabulary is known in search and SEO circles, but UX teams rarely code session patterns systematically.
whereToUse: E-commerce and marketplace search, documentation and help centres, enterprise search, media catalogues and AI-powered search assistants.
example: A fashion retailer finds chains like 'snekers', 'snekers white', 'snekers men' ending in exits: thrashing on a misspelling. Adding spelling correction and partial matching cuts no-result exits by a third.
reference: Morville, P. & Callender, J. (2010). Search Patterns: Design for Discovery. O'Reilly Media, pp. 52-61.

name: Search Trends and Aggregate Search Data Analysis
origin: Popularised by Seth Stephens-Davidowitz (2017); described by Preece, Sharp and Rogers (2019)
summary: Uses openly available aggregate search data, such as Google Trends, to learn indirectly what people care about, fear or do, comparing volumes across time, place and phrasings.
description: People type into search boxes what they will not admit in surveys or interviews, such as intimate health questions or financial worries. Aggregate search data therefore act as a second source on interests, anxieties and behaviour at population scale. Tools such as Google Trends return relative, normalised search interest for phrases over time and across regions; analysts compare related and opposite phrasings, seasonal patterns and regional differences, and interpret them alongside other data. The value lies in asking well-honed questions before querying, since the data answer only what is asked and query meaning is ambiguous. Values are relative indices, not counts, and low-volume terms return too little data to use.
steps: Form focused research questions before looking at any data.
Choose phrases that express the concept, including synonyms, related and opposite phrasings.
Query the tool for these phrases, setting region, time range and category to reduce ambiguity.
Compare relative volumes over time, place and phrasing, noting seasonality and news-driven spikes.
Interpret patterns alongside other data such as surveys, interviews or product analytics, stating that values are relative indices.
Record queries and settings so the analysis can be reproduced.
outputs: Relative interest over time and place for phrases, seasonal patterns and comparative insights to inform research questions.
useWhen: Desk research to size relative interest, detect seasonality, compare regions or explore sensitive topics before primary research.
avoidWhen: When terms are low volume, when you need absolute numbers, or when query meaning is ambiguous. It cannot tell you who searched or why; use interviews or surveys to explain patterns.
whyLost: It is widely used for desk research and SEO, which is why it survives, though the interpretive rigour is often thin.
whereToUse: Health and fintech discovery, content strategy, market entry, seasonal product planning.
example: Before designing a debt-help feature, a fintech team compares searches for 'payday loan' and 'debt advice' by region and month, finding January spikes in the north, and schedules interviews and in-app messaging accordingly.
sources: Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Preece, J., Sharp, H. and Rogers, Y. (2019). Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (5th ed.). Wiley, pp. 351-352; Stephens-Davidowitz, S. (2017). Everybody Lies. HarperCollins.

name: Search-and-Select Icon Recognition Test
donor: Cognitive psychology (visual search) and HCI icon research
origin: Recurring paradigm in icon research since Blankenberger and Hahn (1991); circular array after Huang (2007); Arledge (2014)
summary: Participants see a name and must click the matching icon among distractors as fast and accurately as possible, giving speed and accuracy per icon and style.
description: A speeded visual-search experiment for icons. Each trial shows a prompt word and an array of icons; the participant selects the match as quickly and accurately as possible. Accuracy and response time are the outcome variables; semantic studies stress accuracy, visual-style studies stress speed. Arledge built 20 concrete, unambiguously named icons in filled and outline styles and two polarities (80 stimuli), presented all 20 around the prompt in a randomly ordered circle, timed trials client-side in milliseconds and randomised positions to prevent position learning. Success was analysed with chi-square and time with 2x2 ANOVA and Tukey tests, overall and per icon, then icons were cross-ranked by speed and accuracy. With 1,260 participants, outline white-on-black icons were about 170 ms slower. It differs from comprehension tests, which ask what an icon means.
steps: Choose concrete icons with unambiguous names to limit semantic effects.
Create every icon in each level of the visual factors under test at consistent size and line width, checking a minimum visual angle of about 0.7 degrees.
Pre-load stimuli and time each trial from array reveal to selection; show an untimed orientation screen of all icons with names.
On each trial show the prompt word surrounded by all icons in random, evenly spaced positions; record time and correctness, and record which wrong icon was chosen.
Run hidden warm-up trials, then balanced test trials in random order so each condition appears equally often.
Remove failed tests, warm-ups and time outliers; analyse success with chi-square and time with ANOVA and post-hoc tests, overall and per icon, and check trial-order effects.
Cross-rank icons by median time and success rate to flag slow or confusable icons.
outputs: Success rate and task time per icon and style variant, significance of main effects and interactions, and a ranking of icons by speed and accuracy.
useWhen: Choosing icon styles or validating a new icon set for findability, where milliseconds matter across frequent use.
avoidWhen: Avoid when meaning is the question; use an icon comprehension or Icon simulation test. Randomised positions reduce realism for icons that normally stay put.
whyLost: It is standard in perception and icon research but rarely run in industry, where icon sets are chosen by preference or brand.
whereToUse: Design systems, toolbar and mobile tab-bar icons, automotive and medical device displays.
example: A design-system team runs an online search-and-select test with 400 staff comparing filled and outline icons. Outline icons on dark backgrounds are slowest, so dark mode switches to filled icons.
reference: Arledge, C. P. (2014). Filled-in vs. Outline Icons: The Impact of Icon Style on Usability. Master's paper, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

name: Secondary Analysis of Qualitative Data
origin: Janet Heaton, 2004 (Reworking Qualitative Data); UK Data Archive Qualidata, 1994
summary: Re-analyses existing qualitative datasets for new questions, with explicit checks for fitness for purpose, lost context, consent coverage and transparent reporting.
description: Secondary analysis of qualitative data (Heaton) involves re-using data collected for one purpose to address a different research question. Unlike secondary analysis of quantitative data (which is technically straightforward), secondary analysis of qualitative data raises specific methodological challenges: the original data was collected with different questions in mind, the relational and contextual knowledge the original researcher had is not transferred with the data, and consent for re-use may not have been obtained.
steps: Assess fitness for purpose: Is the original dataset adequate for the new research question? Consider: was data collected from appropriate participants? Were the appropriate topics covered? Was the data collected with sufficient depth?

Account for context loss: The original researcher had knowledge — of the participants, the settings, the research relationship — that is not transferred with the data. Be transparent about this gap in your analysis.

Ethical clearance for re-use: Check whether the original consent covers secondary analysis. If not, what anonymisation procedures are in place? Can re-use harm participants whose data will now be used for a different purpose?

Supplementary data collection: In many cases, secondary analysis is strengthened by collecting supplementary data (additional interviews or observations) specifically to address gaps in the original dataset.

Transparency in reporting: Report fully: the original study's purpose, the secondary analysis purpose, the time gap between collection and re-analysis, and the limitations of working with data collected by someone else.
outputs: A fitness-for-purpose assessment, consent and ethics review, re-analysis findings, identified gaps for supplementary data collection, and a transparent methods account.
useWhen: You have a research repository or past studies relevant to a new question, recruiting is costly or burdensome for participants, or you want to compare across previous studies.
avoidWhen: Original data lack context, quality or consent for re-use, or the new question needs data the original prompts never covered; run primary research instead.
whyLost: Research repositories promised re-use, but most re-use is skimming tagged highlights, without assessing context loss, consent or fitness for the new question.
whereToUse: Research repositories and research operations, meta-synthesis across studies, sensitive populations where repeat interviewing is burdensome, and quick-turnaround strategy questions.
example: A team asked about older users' attitudes to AI re-analyses 30 interviews from an earlier accessibility study. They find consent covers re-use, note the original prompts never mentioned AI, and run 5 supplementary interviews to fill the gap.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Secondary Analysis of Qualitative Data (Long-Sutehall et al., 2011)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Heaton, J. (2004). Reworking Qualitative Data. Sage.

name: SEEV Model of Visual Attention Allocation
origin: Christopher Wickens and colleagues (Wickens, Goh, Helleberg, Horrey and Talleur, 2003), building on Senders and Moray; N-SEEV by Steelman et al. (2013, 2016)
summary: Predict the share of attention each display area receives from its salience, access effort, expectancy and value, and redesign layouts so valuable sources are salient and easy to reach.
description: SEEV models where people look during supervisory monitoring. Salience is a source's physical conspicuousness. Expectancy is the expected rate of relevant change at a location, its bandwidth. Value is the importance of the information or the cost of missing it. Effort is the cost of moving eyes, head or body (or fingers, for menus) to reach it, a negative factor. Combined, the probability of attending to an area is written P(A) = S - EF + EX x V. Well-trained operators scan almost entirely by expectancy times value, an optimal pattern reflecting a calibrated mental model, while fatigue and poor mental models let effort dominate. The design rule collapses the four factors to two: make valuable sources salient, and put valuable, frequently changing sources where they cost little effort. For discrete alerts, N-SEEV adds noticing factors such as onset salience and eccentricity, with steep losses beyond about 20 degrees.
steps: List the areas of interest the user must monitor (instruments, panels, screen regions).
Rate each area's salience, expectancy (rate of relevant change), value (importance to the task) and effort (visual angle or action cost to reach it).
Combine the ratings as P(A) = S - EF + EX x V to predict the relative attention share per area.
Compare the prediction with the optimal expectancy-times-value distribution, or with eye-tracking dwell data.
Redesign so valuable sources are salient and valuable, high-bandwidth sources are low-effort to reach.
For alerts, place critical alerts within the primary field of view (about 30 degrees diameter in aviation) and use onsets.
outputs: Predicted attention share per display area, mismatches between salience or effort and value, and layout and alert placement recommendations.
useWhen: Evaluating dashboards, monitoring consoles, in-car and cockpit displays, or any layout where users must divide attention among several changing sources.
avoidWhen: It models supervisory scanning, not reading or search; effort matters little for rested experts but a lot under fatigue; alert response also depends on reliability, which SEEV omits. For observed gaze use Eye Tracking; for search tasks use Visual Search Paradigm Testing.
whyLost: It is taught in aviation and engineering psychology; UX dashboard design relies on visual hierarchy heuristics rather than computational attention models.
whereToUse: Operations and monitoring dashboards, automotive HMIs, trading screens, clinical monitors, multi-panel AI agent consoles.
example: A network operations dashboard puts the rarely changing uptime summary in the most salient top-left tile and the volatile, critical latency chart low on the right. SEEV ratings predict under-attention to latency, and swapping the tiles brings eye-tracked dwell into line with value.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Wickens, C. D., Goh, J., Helleberg, J., Horrey, W. J. and Talleur, D. A. (2003). Attentional models of multitask pilot performance using advanced display technology. Human Factors, 45(3); Wickens, C. D. and Carswell, C. M. (2021). In Salvendy, G. and Karwowski, W. (Eds.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.). Wiley, ch. 5, pp. 116-118.

name: Segment Typing Tool (Discriminant Classification of New Users)
origin: Fisher's linear discriminant (1936) applied to market segment typing
summary: Uses a few survey questions to assign any new person to an existing persona or segment.
description: Once segments or personas exist, teams need to recognise members in new studies and recruitment screeners. A typing tool uses discriminant analysis (or logistic regression) on the original segmentation data to find the smallest set of "golden questions" that predicts segment membership accurately. The resulting equations are added to screeners and surveys so every future participant can be tagged with their persona. Sauro and Lewis demonstrate it as the practical payoff of factor and cluster analysis, keeping personas alive and measurable rather than posters on the wall.
steps: Start from a segmentation study with known segment membership for each respondent.
Run stepwise discriminant analysis to find questions that best separate segments.
Check classification accuracy with holdout data or cross-validation (aim for 80% or more).
Reduce to the fewest items that keep accuracy acceptable.
Embed the items and scoring in screeners, surveys and analytics.
outputs: A short scoring tool that types new participants into personas.
useWhen: Personas or segments need to be used in recruitment, surveys and analytics.
avoidWhen: Segments were built qualitatively without data to train a classifier.
whyLost: Persona work in UX usually ends at the deliverable; the market research practice of typing tools never came across.
whereToUse: Research recruiting, product surveys, CRM tagging.
example: Six golden questions classify new respondents into five insurance personas with 84% accuracy, so every benchmark can now be reported by persona.
sources: Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
Introduction to Latent Class Modeling using Latent GOLD (Statistical Innovations, 2015)
reference: Sauro & Lewis, Factor and Discriminant Analysis training (2021).

name: SEIPS Work System Analysis
aka: SEIPS work system analysis (Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety)
origin: Smith and Carayon-Sainfort (1989); Carayon et al. (2006); SEIPS 2.0 Holden et al. (2013); SEIPS 3.0 Carayon et al. (2020)
summary: Describe a process through the work system that produces it (people, tasks, tools and technologies, physical environment, organisation) and link work system factors to process and outcome measures.
description: The work system model holds that a person performs tasks with tools and technologies in a physical environment under organisational conditions, and that problems arise from interactions among these elements rather than from any one of them. SEIPS extends it into a structure-process-outcome chain after Donabedian: work system elements shape processes, which shape outcomes for patients, staff and the organisation. SEIPS 2.0 adds patient and family work and adaptation; SEIPS 3.0 applies the model to the patient journey across care settings and home over time. Analysis proceeds by asking, for each step of a process, which people perform which tasks with which tools in which environment under which organisational conditions, then identifying barriers and facilitators. It has been used for safety events such as wrong-site surgery and for many improvement projects.
steps: Choose the process, event or journey to analyse.
List the people involved, including users, staff and family, and their relevant characteristics.
For each process step describe the tasks, tools and technologies, physical environment and organisational conditions.
Identify interactions among these elements that act as barriers or facilitators.
Link the barriers and facilitators to process performance and to outcomes for users, staff and the organisation.
Design changes at the work system level, ideally with participatory ergonomics, and re-evaluate the outcomes.
outputs: A work system map of barriers and facilitators linked to process performance and outcomes.
useWhen: When a digital product sits inside a complex work or care process and its success depends on people, environment and organisation as much as on the interface.
avoidWhen: Avoid for a single-screen usability question; use Usability Testing. For control-structure hazard analysis use STAMP / STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis), and for detailed cognitive coordination use Distributed Cognition Analysis.
whyLost: It is the dominant framework in patient-safety human factors but is little known outside healthcare.
whereToUse: Electronic health records and clinical software, telehealth and remote monitoring, caregiver apps, field-service and warehouse tools.
example: A remote blood-pressure monitoring service has poor adherence. A SEIPS map shows the cuff works but patients' home environment (no table near a socket) and the clinic's organisation (nobody owns follow-up of missed readings) are the barriers, so fixes target workflow, not the app screens.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Carayon, P., Schoofs Hundt, A., Karsh, B.-T., Gurses, A. P., Alvarado, C. J., Smith, M. and Flatley Brennan, P. (2006). Work system design for patient safety: the SEIPS model. Quality and Safety in Health Care, 15(Suppl 1), i50-i58.

name: Selective Coding and Core Category Identification
origin: Glaser & Strauss, 1967; formalised by Strauss & Corbin, 1990
summary: The final grounded theory stage: choosing one core category that integrates all others into a bounded, testable theoretical proposition.
description: Selective coding is the final stage of Grounded Theory. You identify a single core category — the central phenomenon — and relate all other categories to it. The core category must: appear frequently in the data, be connected to all other major categories, be analytic rather than descriptive, and be able to absorb variation. When you find the core category, all the categories you identified in axial coding should make sense in relation to it.
steps: Review all your categories and axial coding memos. Ask: What is the central phenomenon that everything else relates to? What is the story of this data?
Write a storyline: a descriptive narrative of the central phenomenon and its relationship to all other categories. This is typically 2–3 paragraphs.
Test the core category: does every major category connect to it? If a major category does not connect, either the core category is wrong, or that category needs more investigation.
Write the theoretical proposition: a statement of the theory generated from the data. This should be generalisable beyond your specific sample while remaining grounded in the data.
Identify what the theory does NOT explain — these are the boundaries of your theory and honest reporting requires you to state them.
outputs: A core category, a written storyline, a theoretical proposition with stated scope and boundaries, and an integrated category diagram.
useWhen: When a programme of research must yield a single explanatory model that the organisation can reuse, test and design against.
avoidWhen: When stakeholders need a list of issues or opportunities rather than a theory; when data are insufficient or not theoretically sampled. Use thematic synthesis or an affinity diagram.
whyLost: Industry timelines reward actionable findings over theory, and few UX researchers are trained to write and bound a theoretical proposition, so studies stop at themes.
whereToUse: Strategic foundational research, research-led product strategy, and academic-industry collaborations where a reusable model of user behaviour is the deliverable.
example: After axial coding of interviews about a telehealth app, the team identifies 'maintaining clinical legitimacy' as the core category linking privacy concerns, video reluctance and note-taking workarounds. The proposition guides a roadmap and a follow-up survey.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick ed.)
reference: Strauss, A. & Corbin, J. (1990). Basics of Qualitative Research. Sage.

name: Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM)
origin: Bradley and Lang (1994); listed among established GUR questionnaires in chapter 9
summary: A non-verbal pictorial scale on which people rate their emotional reaction for pleasure, arousal and dominance by choosing among cartoon figures.
description: The Self-Assessment Manikin measures three dimensions of affective reaction without words: pleasure (valence), arousal and dominance (feeling in control). Each dimension is shown as a row of manikin figures that change in expression, agitation or size, and the respondent marks the figure that matches how they feel, on a 5-point scale in the version described in the book (9-point versions are also common). Because it is quick and language-free, SAM can be repeated many times in a session, used with children or across languages, and aligned with physiological measures such as electrodermal activity, which reflect arousal but not valence. In games user research it is used to capture players' emotional reaction to specific moments, levels or trailers. For UX research it offers a fast way to measure emotional response to designs, content, sounds or notifications, and to check whether a design meant to calm or excite actually does so. Its simplicity is also its limit: it gives coarse, single-item ratings that say nothing about specific emotions or their causes.
steps: Decide which moments or stimuli will be rated and how often.
Show participants the manikin rows and explain each dimension with an example.
Present each stimulus or let participants play the segment.
Ask participants to mark one figure per dimension immediately afterwards.
Record ratings with a timestamp or segment label so they can be matched to events or physiological data.
Compare mean ratings between stimuli or conditions and discuss outliers with participants.
outputs: Pleasure, arousal and dominance ratings per stimulus or segment.
useWhen: You need quick, repeated, language-independent ratings of emotional response, possibly alongside physiological data.
avoidWhen: You need to identify specific emotions (such as frustration versus anger) or detailed reasons.
whyLost: Well established in emotion research but often overlooked in UX, which tends to use verbal satisfaction items.
whereToUse: Games, media and advertising, sound and notification design, products for children or multilingual audiences.
example: After each of six cut-scenes, playtesters mark SAM figures; a scene meant to be tense scores low on arousal, and the team re-edits its pacing.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 9. Bradley, M. M. and Lang, P. J. (1994). Measuring emotion: the Self-Assessment Manikin and the semantic differential. Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry, 25(1), 49-59.

name: Self-Compassion Scale
origin: Kristin Neff, 2003
summary: A 26-item self-report scale of how kindly people treat themselves when they fail or suffer, scored on six subscales and a total, used as an outcome for wellbeing interventions.
description: Neff's scale measures three components, each with a positive and a negative pole: self-kindness versus self-judgement, common humanity versus isolation, and mindfulness versus over-identification. The six subscales are scored with the negative poles reversed and combined into a total. Evidence summarised by Singer and Bolz: self-compassion predicts lower anxiety and depression controlling for self-criticism, predicts outcomes controlling for self-esteem (while self-esteem adds nothing once self-compassion is included) and is linked to more stable self-worth over eight months. It was the main outcome in a randomised trial of the Mindful Self-Compassion programme (24 against 27 wait-list, gains held at six months and one year) and was used alongside the 38-item Fears of Compassion Scales in another trial. A 12-item short form exists. Trait self-report may not match behaviour, and such scales can come to define the construct they measure.
steps: Decide whether self-compassion is a plausible outcome or moderator for the product or intervention.
Administer the 26 items (or the validated 12-item short form) on the original 1-5 scale.
Reverse-score the negative-pole items and compute the six subscale means and the total.
Measure before and after the intervention and at follow-up (for example six months), with a control or wait-list group where possible.
Report subscale and total changes with confidence intervals, and triangulate with behavioural or qualitative evidence.
outputs: Subscale and total self-compassion scores and their change across an intervention.
useWhen: When evaluating mental-health, coaching, mindfulness or learning products that aim to change how users respond to their own failures, or when self-criticism may moderate reactions to feedback.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a general UX measure: it is a clinical and personality construct with little relevance to most products. Self-report trait scales may not match behaviour; for momentary affect use PANAS Affect Measurement.
whyLost: It is established in clinical and positive psychology but outside most UX work; digital mental-health evaluation is the only natural bridge.
whereToUse: Digital mental-health and meditation apps, coaching and learning platforms, feedback and grading features, fitness apps with streaks.
example: A meditation app runs an eight-week trial of a self-compassion course with 400 users and a wait-list control, finding self-judgement subscale scores fall while the other subscales barely move, which guides content revision.
sources: Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Neff, K. D. (2003). The development and validation of a scale to measure self-compassion. Self and Identity, 2(3), 223-250.

name: Self-Discrepancy Listing (Actual, Ideal, Ought Selves)
aka: Self-discrepancy listing (actual, ideal and ought selves)
origin: Higgins (1987); Higgins, Bond, Klein and Strauman (1986)
summary: Ask people to list attributes of their actual, ideal and ought selves and score the gaps, which predict dejection when ideals are primed and anxiety when duties are primed.
description: Self-discrepancy theory holds that gaps between how people see themselves and who they would ideally like to be produce dejection, while gaps between the actual self and who others think they ought to be produce anxiety. In the listing procedure participants write about ten attributes each for their actual, ideal and ought selves, and discrepancy is scored by comparing the lists. In Higgins and colleagues' study, participants high in discrepancy became sadder after discussing hopes and goals (an ideal prime) and more anxious after discussing duties (an ought prime), while low-discrepancy participants barely changed. For UX, the measure offers a structured way to understand why products that frame users' goals as aspirations or obligations evoke different emotions, which is relevant to health, finance and self-improvement products.
steps: Ask participants to list about ten attributes of their actual self in the relevant domain.
Ask for ten attributes of their ideal self (who they would like to be).
Ask for ten attributes of their ought self as a significant other sees it.
Score discrepancies by matching and mismatching attributes between actual and ideal, and actual and ought lists; split into high and low discrepancy.
Optionally, in a later session, take baseline emotion ratings, prime ideal or ought concerns (or show product messaging framed each way) and rate emotions again.
Compare emotional responses by discrepancy level and prime.
outputs: Three attribute lists, ideal and ought discrepancy scores, and emotion change by prime.
useWhen: Exploring how users relate to self-improvement goals (fitness, saving, learning) and whether aspirational or obligation framing will motivate or distress particular users.
avoidWhen: Avoid in general product research without a self-improvement dimension, and take care with vulnerable users, since priming discrepancies can raise distress. For general motivation profiling use Achievement Goal Orientation and Motivational Climate Assessment.
whyLost: It stayed in personality and clinical psychology; UX motivational research uses Jobs-to-be-Done and behaviour models instead.
whereToUse: Fitness and wellbeing apps, personal finance and savings tools, language learning, weight management and health behaviour products.
example: A savings app tests two nudges, 'Become the saver you want to be' and 'You should be saving more'. Users with high ought discrepancy report more anxiety and churn intent after the second, so obligation framing is dropped for them.
reference: Higgins, E. T., Bond, R. N., Klein, R. and Strauman, T. (1986). Self-discrepancies and emotional vulnerability. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(1), 5-15.

name: Self-explicated preference measurement
origin: Compositional approach contrasted with Green's decompositional conjoint; used as ACA priors (Johnson, 1985) and in hybrid conjoint
summary: Respondents rate each attribute's levels and each attribute's importance separately, and the two are multiplied into part-worths without evaluating whole products.
description: Self-explicated measurement is the compositional alternative to conjoint analysis: instead of inferring part-worths from choices among whole profiles, respondents state them piece by piece. They rank or rate the levels within each attribute, then rate how important the difference between the best and worst level would be if products were otherwise equal. Level desirability multiplied by attribute importance gives prior part-worths. Because attributes are never traded off together, Orme's glossary says such models are not conjoint analysis. They serve as priors in Adaptive Conjoint Analysis, in hybrid methods combining priors with trade-off questions, and for imputing utilities of levels not shown in choice tasks. Orme warns that importance grids are answered in about five seconds, crowd the top of the scale, discriminate poorly and invite social desirability (understating price); dropping them from ACA improved predictions under hierarchical Bayes.
steps: Define attributes and levels, checking that attributes do not overlap (overlapping attributes are double-counted).
Have respondents rank or rate the levels within each attribute.
For each attribute ask how important the difference between its most and least preferred level is (for example on a 1-4 scale).
Multiply level desirability by attribute importance to form prior part-worths per respondent.
Optionally combine with paired comparisons or choice tasks (hybrid conjoint) or use the priors to impute utilities for levels not shown.
Check predictive validity against holdout choices before using results for decisions.
outputs: Prior part-worths and attribute importances per respondent, and predictive validity against holdout choices.
useWhen: When there are too many attributes for full conjoint, respondents are few or time is short, or priors are needed for an adaptive or hybrid conjoint design.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the sole basis for pricing or trade-off decisions: importance ratings discriminate poorly and invite social desirability. Prefer Conjoint Analysis, Discrete Choice Modeling or MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) where feasible.
whyLost: It survives inside marketing-research software and conjoint practice; in UX it appears only as naive 'rate how important each feature is' questions, without the level ratings or validation.
whereToUse: Feature prioritisation with many attributes, B2B configuration and pricing research, early concept screening.
example: A fitness-tracker team with 25 candidate attributes uses self-explicated ratings with 300 users to shortlist eight, then runs a choice-based conjoint on the eight to set the final bundle.
reference: Orme, B. K. (2010). Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis: Strategies for Product Design and Pricing Research (2nd ed.). Madison, WI: Research Publishers LLC.

name: Self-organising map
origin: Teuvo Kohonen, 1982
summary: An unsupervised neural network that arranges records on a 2-D grid preserving similarity, producing a segment map and per-variable component maps to interpret with stakeholders.
description: A self-organising map is a grid of nodes, each with a weight vector. For each record the closest node wins, and the winner and its neighbours are moved towards the record; neighbourhood size and learning rate shrink during training. The result preserves the topology of the input: similar records land on nearby nodes. Nodes can be labelled with known classes (unused nodes get a null label) so the map also classifies. Its main strength is visualisation: a cluster map plus one component map per variable lets analysts and business teams read segments together, alongside absolute and relative views. Performance degrades as dimensionality rises, and region labels are the analyst's interpretation. In UX, SOMs offer a visual alternative to k-means for exploring segments in survey or behavioural data with stakeholders.
steps: Select and standardise input variables.
Initialise a 2-D grid of nodes (for example 10 x 10 to 20 x 20) with weight vectors.
For each record find the winning node and move it and its neighbours towards the record.
Shrink neighbourhood and learning rate over training and repeat until the map is stable.
Draw the cluster map and one component map per variable; label nodes with known classes if available.
Label regions and interpret them with stakeholders in working sessions, checking robustness across random initialisations.
outputs: A 2-D segment map, per-variable component maps, and optional node labels for classification.
useWhen: You want stakeholders to explore segments visually and see how variables vary across a continuous space rather than discrete clusters.
avoidWhen: Data are very high-dimensional, or you need statistically defined segments with membership probabilities; use GMM or latent class analysis, or UMAP for visual exploration.
whyLost: It was popular in 1990s and 2000s data mining tools, then displaced by t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation and by mixture models for segmentation.
whereToUse: Customer and survey segmentation workshops, behavioural analytics exploration, marketing research.
example: A telecom research team trains a SOM on 30 survey and usage variables. In a workshop, product managers read component maps and spot a region of high data use with low satisfaction, which becomes a research priority.
reference: Kohonen, T. (1982). Self-organized formation of topologically correct feature maps. Biological Cybernetics, 43, 59-69.

name: Self-Service CX Metrics Governance
origin: Sarah Williams, Expedia Group, 2024
summary: Open continuous CX survey metrics to stakeholder self-service by mapping the data lifecycle, educating users, planning for change, and declining requests that would dilute the metrics.
description: When CX metrics from continuous intercept surveys are opened to product managers and data scientists through dashboards, researchers gain time but risk numbers being misread or misused. Williams sets out four practices. First, map the data lifecycle (generation, ingestion and storage, processing, retrieval, analysis, decision-making, archiving or deletion) and let dashboards absorb repetitive tracking so researchers can investigate why metrics move. Second, educate self-service users: interview stakeholder groups to learn what each needs to interpret the numbers, and build a durable toolkit tied to the specific tool. Third, anticipate change as metrics scale by using the lifecycle to involve the owning teams at each stage and assign responsibility. Fourth, craft an 'empowered no': decline requests whose data are short-lived or atypical, or whose education burden outweighs the tool's value, backed by evidence and offered with a compromise.
steps: Map the lifecycle of the CX metric data from survey generation to archiving and mark the repetitive analyses stakeholders could self-serve.
Build dashboards or reusable scripts for those analyses and redirect researcher time to explaining changes.
Interview each stakeholder group (for example product managers and data scientists) to find what they must understand to use the metrics correctly.
Create lasting education materials as a toolkit tied to the specific dashboard or script, including rules such as using only surveys on tested pages for A/B readouts.
Use the lifecycle to plan change management: name the team responsible at each stage and keep a channel for changes such as survey edits or naming.
Screen each new self-service request for short-lived or atypical data and education cost, and decline unsuitable ones with evidence and a compromise.
outputs: Self-service dashboards and scripts, an education toolkit, a lifecycle map with named owners, and a documented request-screening rule.
useWhen: A research or CX team runs always-on survey metrics that many stakeholders want to query directly, and misinterpretation or inconsistent definitions are starting to appear.
avoidWhen: When the metric itself has not been validated; check it first with a Metric Quality Audit or Survey scale quality audit. For broader research democratisation (interviews, testing), use Research Operations and Method Repository practices instead.
whyLost: It is an emerging practice that survives because research democratisation and self-service analytics are now common, and teams discover they need governance once metrics are misused.
whereToUse: Travel, e-commerce and SaaS companies with continuous CSAT or NPS programmes, research operations teams, experimentation platforms that report survey metrics.
example: A travel company's data scientist builds an A/B script that pulls CX scores from site-wide surveys. After the education toolkit explains that only surveys on tested pages are valid, the script is fixed, made reusable, and later automated for selected tests.
reference: Williams, S. (2024). Data Empowerment: Supporting Precision in Self-Service Customer Experience Metrics. Expedia Group. Quant UX Con 2024, conference slides, 12 June 2024.

name: SEM Reporting Checklist
aka: Communicating about latent variable models (reporting guidance)
origin: Randall Schumacker and Richard Lomax, 2004, building on Breckler (1990), Hoyle and Panter (1995), Boomsma (2000), MacCallum and Austin (2000) and Thompson (2000); Hoyle and Isherwood, 2013
summary: A stage-by-stage checklist for planning, reporting or reviewing a structural equation model so that its specification, fit, modifications and validity can be judged and replicated.
description: Reviews of published SEMs found recurring faults: a single fit index, no cross-validation, weak theoretical grounding, missing data and no consideration of rival models. The checklist responds by asking specific questions at each stage. Data preparation: population, measurement level, descriptives, multivariate normality, missing data handling (FIML or imputation), outliers, transformations, the correlation, mean and SD table, and the matrix analysed. Specification: rationale, latent variable definitions, theory for measurement and structural parts, alternative models, exploratory or confirmatory status, sample size and power, expected signs and a diagram. Identification: distinct values, free parameters, order and rank conditions. Estimation: estimator choice, convergence, Heywood cases, scaling, software version and start values. Testing: several fit indices, composite reliability, validity, invariance, unstandardised paths with standard errors and standardised values. Modification: one change at a time with justification and equivalent models. Validation: replication, split-sample cross-validation and bootstrap.
steps: Data preparation: describe the population, measurement levels, descriptives, normality, amount and handling of missing data, outliers, transformations and the matrix analysed; share data and syntax where possible.

Specification: state the rationale, latent variable definitions, theory, alternative models, exploratory or confirmatory status, sample size justification, hypotheses with expected signs, and an initial diagram.
Identification: report the number of distinct values and free parameters and how order and rank conditions are met.
Estimation: justify the estimator, and report convergence problems, Heywood cases, scaling choices, software version and R-squared values.

Testing: report at least two fit indices with their criteria, reliability and validity evidence, invariance tests where groups are compared, and unstandardised paths with standard errors or intervals alongside standardised values.
Modification and validation: document each change one at a time with its justification, consider equivalent models, show initial and final diagrams, and cross-validate on a split or new sample.
outputs: A completed checklist and a replicable SEM report or review.
useWhen: Writing up, commissioning or reviewing any SEM or CFA, including vendor-delivered driver models and academic HCI papers.
avoidWhen: Simple regressions or single-scale reliability checks, where general statistical reporting guidance suffices. The checklist does not make a weak design sound; fit remains a judgement and no single best model exists.
whyLost: UX research reporting guidance focuses on qualitative findings and readouts; quantitative model reporting is left to whoever runs the software, and stakeholders rarely ask for it.
whereToUse: Reviewing agency driver analyses, internal TAM or loyalty models, questionnaire validation reports and SEM-based academic submissions.
example: A research lead reviewing an agency's loyalty SEM finds no missing-data handling, only CFI reported, and three unexplained correlated residuals. Using the checklist she requests RMSEA and SRMR, the change log and a split-sample replication before the model guides roadmap investment.
sources: A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
reference: Schumacker, R. E., & Lomax, R. G. (2004). A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (2nd ed.). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: SEM Specification Search and Model Modification
aka: Lagrange multiplier and Wald test search
Exploratory modification of a misfitting latent variable model
origin: Edward Leamer, 1978 (specification search); Dag Sorbom, 1975 (modification indices); Peter Bentler, 1986 (Lagrange multiplier and Wald tests); Robert MacCallum, 1986
summary: A disciplined, theory-constrained search for a better-specified structural equation model, freeing or fixing one parameter at a time using diagnostics, then cross-validating the result.
description: When an SEM fits poorly the researcher may alter it, but every change risks capitalising on chance. The diagnostic tools are: significance of free parameters (to drop paths, cautiously, since significance depends on n); standardised residuals above about 1.96 or 2.58 flagging poorly reproduced covariances; modification indices (the minimum chi-square drop if a fixed parameter is freed) and expected parameter change; Lagrange multiplier tests as a multivariate forward search and Wald tests as a backward search. First localise misfit: fit a CFA with all latent variables freely correlated, and if it fits nearly as badly the problem is measurement. Measurement remedies include dropping weak indicators only if construct meaning survives, method factors or correlated residuals, or a composite single indicator. Simulation studies show automated searches rarely recover the true model, and fail entirely when the start is more than two or three parameters away, so the final model must be cross-validated.
steps: Let theory and prior research define the initial model, and list in advance which modifications would be substantively defensible.
Fit the model; then fit a CFA with all latent variables freely correlated and compare chi-squares to see whether misfit lies in measurement or structure.
Repair the measurement model first: inspect loadings, residuals and modification indices; consider method factors or correlated residuals only with a substantive reason.

In the structural model, use Wald tests or non-significant paths to consider dropping parameters, and modification indices, expected parameter change and Lagrange multiplier tests to consider freeing them.
Change one parameter at a time, rechecking several fit indices, parameter signs and the standardised residual matrix after each change.
Report the initial and final models and every change with its justification and chi-square difference.
Cross-validate the final model on a hold-out or new sample (or report ECVI) before drawing conclusions.
outputs: A respecified model with a documented change log, chi-square differences, and cross-validation evidence.
useWhen: A theoretically grounded SEM or CFA of survey data (for example a technology acceptance or satisfaction model) fits poorly and you need to diagnose and repair it without turning confirmatory work into data dredging.
avoidWhen: You have no theory to constrain changes (run exploratory factor analysis or treat the work as exploratory and replicate); the sample is too small to split for cross-validation. Never free a parameter just because its modification index is large; all-possible-models searches explode (17 optional paths give 131,072 models).
whyLost: UX survey analysts usually accept poor fit or chase modification indices in software without the cautions, and SEM training rarely covers disciplined respecification.
whereToUse: TAM and UTAUT-style adoption surveys; satisfaction driver models; validating multi-factor UX questionnaires across product lines.
example: A health app's trust-and-adoption SEM fits poorly (RMSEA .09). A freely correlated CFA fits almost as badly, so misfit lies in measurement; two reverse-worded items share a method factor. After adding it, RMSEA falls to .05, and the model replicates on the held-out half of the 1,200 respondents.
sources: A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
reference: Schumacker, R. E., & Lomax, R. G. (2004). A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (2nd ed.). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Semantic Differential
origin: Charles Osgood, George Suci and Percy Tannenbaum, 1957
summary: Rates a concept on bipolar adjective pairs to map its connotative meaning along evaluation, potency and activity dimensions.
description: Osgood's semantic differential asks people to rate a concept on seven-point scales anchored by opposite adjectives, such as good-bad, strong-weak, active-passive. Factor analyses across many concepts and cultures showed ratings consistently load on three dimensions: evaluation, potency and activity (EPA), which together form a 'semantic space'. The rigorous method selects adjective pairs relevant to the concept and representative of each dimension, randomises pole direction to avoid response sets, and uses factor analysis or the established EPA structure to score concepts and compute distances between them. In UX it is the ancestor of AttrakDiff and UEQ, but the original technique remains useful for custom brand and emotion research where no standard instrument fits, such as comparing how users perceive an AI persona against intended brand attributes. The Stapel scale is a unipolar variant: a single adjective is rated from -5 to +5 with no zero, which avoids having to find exact opposites, although the wording of the adjective can bias answers.
steps: Define the concepts to rate (e.g. product versions, brand, competitor, ideal product).
Select 12-20 relevant adjective pairs covering evaluation, potency and activity, plus domain-specific pairs, and pilot them for relevance.
Randomise the left-right position of positive poles across items.
Collect ratings from 30+ participants per concept.
Run factor analysis or score by established dimensions and compute concept profiles.
Compare profiles and distances between concepts, such as actual versus ideal product.
outputs: Concept profiles on adjective pairs, dimension scores, semantic space plots and distances between concepts.
useWhen: Brand perception, persona and tone-of-voice research, emotional response comparison and cross-cultural meaning studies.
avoidWhen: When a validated UX instrument (UEQ, AttrakDiff) already covers the constructs; use that for benchmarkable results.
whyLost: Vestigial: Original technique less used than derivative instruments (AttrakDiff, UEQ); still valid for brand/emotion research.
whereToUse: Brand perception; emotional response measurement; cross-cultural comparison.
example: A bank tested how customers perceived its new AI assistant persona. Semantic differential profiles showed it rated as friendly but weak and passive, far from the intended 'competent' brand, prompting a revised tone of voice.
sources: The Measurement of Meaning (Osgood, Suci & Tannenbaum)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Human Interface and the Management of Information (Yamamoto & Mori, 2020)
reference: Osgood, C. E., Suci, G. J., & Tannenbaum, P. H. (1957). The Measurement of Meaning. University of Illinois Press.

name: Semantic leaps analysis
origin: Seana Coulson, Semantic Leaps, 2001; Fauconnier and Turner's conceptual blending, 2002
summary: Identifies points where users must reinterpret a word, icon or metaphor by shifting frames or blending concepts, and measures whether they make the leap correctly.
description: Coulson showed that comprehension often requires frame-shifting: reanalysing meaning when new information conflicts with an initial interpretation, as in jokes and garden-path sentences. Conceptual blending describes how people combine elements of different domains into new meanings, which is how interface metaphors such as 'desktop', 'trash' or 'cloud' work. Semantic leaps analysis catalogues the frames and blends an interface relies on, identifies places where users must shift frames mid-task, and tests whether they do so correctly and at what cost. Failure points include metaphors whose source domain implies wrong behaviours and messages that require reinterpretation. Rigour comes from explicit frame mapping and from measuring reinterpretation through prediction and reading-time tasks.
steps: Inventory metaphors, icons and key terms and identify the source frame each relies on.
Map which source-domain properties are carried into the interface blend and which are not.
Identify frame-shift points, where users must abandon an initial interpretation (for example 'archive' that deletes after 30 days).
Test with 8-12 users using prediction tasks and think-aloud, noting misinterpretations and hesitation.
Optionally measure reading or decision time at shift points versus control points.
Redesign misleading metaphors or add cues that trigger the correct frame earlier, and re-test.
outputs: A frame and blend inventory, frame-shift points with failure rates, and revised metaphors or cues.
useWhen: When designing novel metaphors, naming new features, or when users misread messages that are literally accurate.
avoidWhen: For literal, conventional interfaces with established terms; compositionality or content audits suffice.
whyLost: Cognitive linguistics has rich theory but little applied tradition in UX, where metaphor choice is treated as branding.
whereToUse: AI assistants and agents, financial product naming, health apps, and novel interaction models.
example: A surgical system labels a mode 'Autopilot'. Users carry over the aviation frame, expecting the robot to hold position safely, but it only stabilises the camera. Prediction tests show 7 of 10 surgeons misread it, so the mode is renamed 'Camera steady'.
sources: Fodor, J., The Language of Thought (1975)
Lakoff, G., Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 17 — Mentalese, Compositionality & the Language of Thought
reference: Coulson, S. (2001). Semantic Leaps: Frame-Shifting and Conceptual Blending in Meaning Construction. Cambridge University Press.

name: Semiotic Analysis
origin: Charles Sanders Peirce and Ferdinand de Saussure, late 19th/early 20th century; semiotic engineering by Clarisse de Souza, 2005
summary: Analyses icons, labels and visual language as signs, classifying how they signify (icon, index, symbol) and testing whether intended meanings reach users.
description: Semiotics studies how signs carry meaning. Peirce classified signs by their relation to what they stand for: icons resemble it, indexes are causally or physically connected to it, and symbols depend on learned convention. Saussure separated the signifier from the signified and showed meaning arises from difference within a system. Semiotic engineering (de Souza) treats the whole interface as a message from designer to user. As a method, analysts inventory signs, classify each, document intended meaning and cultural dependencies, and then test interpretation with users through comprehension and matching tasks. Rigour comes from explicit classification, considering the sign system as a whole (are distinctions consistent?), and empirical checking across cultural groups, since symbolic signs carry least transferable meaning.
steps: Inventory the signs in scope: icons, labels, colours, sounds and metaphors.
Classify each as icon, index or symbol and record its intended meaning.
Analyse the sign system for consistency and contrast, flagging signs whose meaning depends on unlearned conventions.
Run comprehension tests with 15-30 users per audience segment, asking them to name the meaning of signs out of context and in context.
Score comprehension (ISO 9186 suggests 66-85% correct as acceptance thresholds for public symbols).
Redesign signs that fail, preferring iconic or indexical forms or adding labels, and re-test.
outputs: Sign inventory with classifications, system consistency analysis, comprehension scores by audience, redesign recommendations.
useWhen: Icon sets, visual languages, international and cross-cultural products, and accessibility reviews of non-text cues.
avoidWhen: When labels are textual and the issue is information architecture; use card sorting or tree testing.
whyLost: Siloed: Academic foundation; icon and visual language work applies semiotic principles but rarely names them.
whereToUse: Icon design; visual language systems; cross-cultural UX; accessibility.
example: A global health app used a floppy-disk icon for saving records. Comprehension testing in Kenya and India found under 40% recognition among younger health workers; replacing it with a labelled checkmark raised recognition above 90%.
sources: The Semiotic Engineering of Human-Computer Interaction (Clarisse de Souza)
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: de Souza, C. S. (2005). The Semiotic Engineering of Human-Computer Interaction. MIT Press.

name: Semiotic Analysis of Interfaces
origin: Charles S. Peirce (1867-1914); Ferdinand de Saussure (1916); Roland Barthes (1957-1972)
summary: Diagnoses icon, label and visual-language failures as breakdowns at iconic, indexical, symbolic, connotative or mythic levels of signification.
description: Peirce's trichotomy distinguishes icons (resemble their referent), indexes (causally connected to it) and symbols (conventional). Saussure contributes the signifier/signified dyad; Barthes adds denotation, connotation and myth (naturalised ideology). The treatise argues every UI element is a sign: the floppy disk icon is now a symbol, functioning through convention rather than resemblance. Analysing icon failures semiotically asks whether the failure is iconic (does not look like its referent), indexical (no causal link to the function) or symbolic (convention not established in this user population), and the diagnosis changes the design response. Connotative analysis reveals cultural meanings that differ across markets. In HCI it was developed further as semiotic engineering by de Souza.
steps: Inventory signs in scope: icons, labels, colours, layout conventions, sounds.
For each, record intended referent and classify the sign relation (icon, index, symbol).
Test comprehension with target users (for example open-ended icon naming) across cultures.
Classify failures by semiotic level and analyse connotations and myths.
Redesign signs according to the failing level (resemblance, causal cue, or convention-building).
Re-test comprehension and document the visual language rules.
outputs: Sign inventory with semiotic classification, comprehension results, redesign rationale, visual-language guidelines.
useWhen: Icon and visual language design, cross-cultural products, error and status communication.
avoidWhen: Problems driven by flow or performance rather than meaning.
whyLost: Semiotics remained an academic and media-studies discipline, and de Souza's semiotic engineering stayed within HCI research; practitioners treated icon choice as visual design rather than sign analysis.
whereToUse: Design systems, global apps, AI status indicators, automotive symbols, medical device labelling.
example: A 'sparkle' icon for AI features is recognised by 80% of US users but 30% of users in another market; analysis shows it functions purely symbolically, so a text label is added until the convention establishes.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Eco U (1976) A Theory of Semiotics
de Souza CS (2005) The Semiotic Engineering of Human-Computer Interaction
The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure
reference: de Souza CS (2005) The Semiotic Engineering of Human-Computer Interaction. MIT Press.

name: Sensed-Task and Supported-Task Analysis
aka: Sensed-task / supported-task analysis for low-intention interaction
Sensed-task and supported-task modelling for low-intention interaction
donor: Ubiquitous computing; formal methods in HCI
origin: Alan Dix, incidental interaction, 2002-2017; influenced by Benford et al.'s expected-sensed-desired framework, 2005
summary: Model the activity a sensor observes and the task the system helps with, then match intervention desirability to sensing reliability to choose sensors, thresholds and fixes.
description: For systems that act on things people do for other purposes (lights that come on as a door opens, a sign that updates when a cafe opens), Dix separates the sensed task, the user's own activity as observed by sensors or logs, from the supported task the system aids. The supported task is annotated step by step with how wanted an intervention is (++ to --, with a special mark for safety issues). The sensed task is annotated with available or addable sensors and how likely each sensed state is to match reality. A state diagram grouped by what sensors can distinguish shows likely and unlikely transitions. The analysis aims to get critical cases right and others good enough, and finds states that are both wrong and likely, which are then made less likely or more noticeable.
steps: Describe the supported task and the sensed task (scenario, HTA or CTT) and model the states of relevant objects.
Annotate each supported-task step with desirability of intervention (++, +, -, --, safety) and classify requirements as absolute, strong or nice to have.
Annotate the sensed task with existing and addable sensors and the likelihood that each sensed state matches the real state.
Draw system states grouped by what sensors can distinguish, marking likely and unlikely transitions and where intervention is wanted.
Match desirability against reliability: make critical cases correct, allow leeway elsewhere, and add timers or sensors where states cannot be told apart.
List states that are both wrong and likely, and redesign to make them less likely or more noticeable.
Review privacy on the sensed task and explanation on the supported task.
outputs: Annotated task models, an annotated state diagram, sensor and threshold choices, and a list of likely failure states with fixes.
useWhen: Designing sensor-driven, context-aware or automation features (smart home, wearables, implicit logging, proactive assistants) where the system acts without explicit commands.
avoidWhen: Explicit command-driven interfaces. It does not cover opaque ML inference well and its likelihoods are qualitative; for quantified risk use Use Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (UFMEA).
whyLost: It is recent and published in formal-methods handbooks; in practice such reasoning stays in designers' heads rather than being written down.
whereToUse: Smart-home automation, automotive comfort features, presence detection, fitness trackers, and AI assistants that act on inferred context.
example: A smart office light switches off when occupancy sensors miss a still worker. The analysis marks 'occupied but sensed empty' as wrong and likely, so the team adds a longer timeout and a gentle dim warning before switching off.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
