Validation studies by Stanton and colleagues found SHERPA among the most accurate and reliable error-prediction methods, with sensitivity comparable to empirical testing at a fraction of the cost. It is structured, repeatable and teachable, which is exactly what ad hoc 'error state' design lacks. The five behaviour types and their error-mode lists are the later, widely taught form of SHERPA. Embrey's 1986 original instead classified each task segment by Rasmussen's skill-, rule- and knowledge-based processing, searched for psychological error mechanisms, recovery points, coupled failures and task disturbances, recorded procedure, training and equipment remedies on a Human Error Analysis form, and could quantify error probabilities with SLIM-MAUD through the SARAH software before a before-and-after quality assurance check.
steps: Complete an HTA of the task to the level of individual operations.
Classify each bottom-level step into one of the five SHERPA behaviour types.
Apply the corresponding error modes to each step and record every credible error with a description.
For each error, note the consequence, whether and how it can be recovered, probability (low, medium, high) and criticality (critical or not).
Propose remedial strategies under equipment, training, procedures and organisational headings.
Where possible, validate predictions against observed errors in testing and calculate hit rate and false-alarm rate.
outputs: A SHERPA table of predicted errors with consequences, recovery, probability, criticality and remedies; optional validation statistics.
useWhen: You need to predict user errors before building or testing, for a well-defined procedural task such as configuration, checkout, dosing or setup.
avoidWhen: Highly creative or open-ended tasks without a stable procedure; use contextual inquiry or critical incident technique.
whyLost: SHERPA is taught in ergonomics degrees and used in aviation, rail and nuclear, but UX programmes rarely teach HTA-based predictive analysis. Product teams default to finding errors empirically.
whereToUse: Device setup flows, B2B configuration wizards, kiosk and point-of-sale, medical and in-car interfaces.
example: Before launching a smart thermostat app, a researcher runs SHERPA on schedule setup and predicts a high-probability 'wrong value selected' error on the AM/PM toggle; testing confirms it and the toggle becomes a 24-hour picker with preview.
sources: Stanton et al., Human Factors Methods: A Practical Guide for Engineering and Design (2013)
Stanton & Stevenage, Learning to predict human error (1998), Ergonomics
SHERPA: A Systematic Human Error Reduction and Prediction Approach (Embrey, 1986)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Embrey, D. E. (1986). SHERPA: A systematic human error reduction and prediction approach. International Meeting on Advances in Nuclear Power Systems.

name: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules (Empirical Application)
origin: Ben Shneiderman, Designing the User Interface (1986)
summary: Inspects an interface against Shneiderman's eight golden rules using their empirical rationale and measurable criteria, rather than as a superficial checklist.
description: Shneiderman's eight golden rules (strive for consistency, enable shortcuts for frequent users, offer informative feedback, design dialogues to yield closure, prevent errors, permit easy reversal of actions, keep users in control, reduce short-term memory load) were derived from experimental HCI work and are well known. In practice they survive as a poster-level checklist, with little attention to how compliance should be judged or what evidence each rule rests on. The empirical application reinstates that rigour: each rule is turned into observable criteria (for example, undo available for every destructive action, feedback within 1 second for frequent actions, no more than about four items to hold in memory across screens), evaluators inspect independently, and violations are linked to observed or predicted user costs. Findings are rated for severity and, where possible, verified through usability testing.
steps: Apply each rule as an evaluable hypothesis, not a heuristic: for Rule 6 (easy reversal), measure: what % of participant error-recovery attempts succeed on first try?
For Rule 8 (memory load), measure active recall requirements per screen.
Build a measurement instrument (1–5 per rule with evidence citation) rather than a yes/no checklist.
outputs: Rule-by-rule compliance assessment with operational criteria, violation list with severity and evidence, and targeted test hypotheses.
useWhen: Expert reviews of desktop and enterprise software, design system governance, and early checks before usability testing.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for testing with users, or for domains where the rules conflict with specialised needs (for example safety-critical confirmations); use domain-specific heuristics there.
whyLost: The rules became so familiar that teams cite them without operationalising them, and Nielsen's heuristics became the default inspection set, so the empirical grounding behind each rule was forgotten.
whereToUse: Evidence-based heuristic evaluation, design system specification, accessibility and compliance auditing. Connects Nielsen's heuristics back to their empirical origins.
example: Reviewing a hospital EHR's order-entry screen against the eight rules, three evaluators find no undo for cancelled orders and a requirement to remember a patient ID across four screens. Both are confirmed in sessions with nurses and prioritised for fixing.
sources: Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines — Ben Shneiderman
Designing the User Interface (Ben Shneiderman & Catherine Plaisant)
Heuristic Evaluation of User Interfaces: Exploration and Evaluation (Ó Broin, 2011)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Shneiderman B & Plaisant C (2010) Designing the User Interface: Strategies for Effective Human-Computer Interaction. 5th ed. Addison-Wesley

name: Shortest path mapping
origin: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, 1959; applied to hypertext navigation in 1990s structural analysis
summary: Computes the minimum number of steps from entry points to each key destination and compares it with the paths users actually take, revealing structural distance and detours.
description: Shortest path mapping applies Dijkstra's or breadth-first search algorithms to a navigation graph to compute the minimal step count between any two nodes, particularly from common entry points to priority tasks. Weighted versions use estimated interaction cost per edge (for example KLM time) rather than raw clicks. Comparing structural shortest paths with observed paths from logs gives a 'lostness' or path efficiency ratio: Smith's lostness measure combines total nodes visited, unique nodes visited and the minimum required. The method separates structural problems (destinations genuinely far away) from wayfinding problems (short paths exist but users do not find them). It is rigorous when the graph is complete and the cost model is explicit.
steps: Build the navigation graph and define entry points and priority destinations from task analysis.
Compute shortest path lengths (or weighted costs) from each entry point to each destination.
Extract observed paths from logs or tests for the same tasks.
Compute path efficiency (optimal/observed) and Smith's lostness L = sqrt((N/S - 1)^2 + (R/N - 1)^2); treat L above about 0.4 as lost.
Classify each problem as structural (long optimal path) or wayfinding (short optimal path, inefficient observed path).
Fix structural problems with new links or shortcuts and wayfinding problems with labels, scent or signposting; re-measure.
outputs: A matrix of optimal path lengths, observed path efficiency and lostness per task, and a classification of structural versus wayfinding issues.
useWhen: When users take long routes to important tasks; when prioritising shortcuts; when evaluating navigation redesigns.
avoidWhen: When tasks are search-led or exploratory without defined destinations; use search log analysis or diary studies.
whyLost: Click-count rules ('three-click rule') replaced measured path analysis in practice, and lostness metrics stayed in academic papers.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial menus, enterprise apps, government services, help centres, and mobile apps with deep navigation.
example: In a hospital scheduling tool the optimal path to 'reschedule' is 3 steps, but observed paths average 9 with lostness of 0.55. The problem is wayfinding, so the team relabels and surfaces the action rather than restructuring.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 7 — Graph Theory & the Architecture of Information
reference: Smith, P. A. (1996). Towards a practical measure of hypertext usability. Interacting with Computers, 8(4), 365-381.

name: Sign Test, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank and Friedman Tests
aka: Wilcoxon T test for two related samples
Friedman's rank test for correlated samples
origin: Frank Wilcoxon (1945) signed-rank test; Milton Friedman (1937) rank test; the sign test dates to John Arbuthnot (1710)
summary: Nonparametric tests for paired or repeated measures: signs or signed ranks of differences for two conditions, and rank-based Friedman test for three or more.
description: These tests compare related measurements without assuming normality. The sign test marks each paired difference, or each value against a hypothesised median, as plus or minus and tests the count of pluses against a binomial distribution; it can also estimate the median. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test adds magnitude: take differences, drop zeros, rank absolute differences (averaging ranks for ties), sum the ranks of positive differences and compare with its permutation distribution, or report a standardised Z for larger samples. The Friedman test ranks conditions within each participant and is the nonparametric counterpart of one-way within-subjects ANOVA for three or more conditions. In UX they suit within-subjects comparisons of ordinal ratings or skewed times, which the Mann-Whitney test, built for independent samples, does not cover.
steps: Confirm the design is paired or repeated (the same participants under each condition) and choose the test: sign test for direction only, Wilcoxon signed-rank for two conditions, Friedman for three or more.
Compute each participant's difference between conditions, or rank conditions within each participant for Friedman.
Sign test: count positive differences, drop zeros, and get a p-value from the binomial distribution with p = 0.5.
Wilcoxon: rank the absolute non-zero differences, average tied ranks, sum the ranks of positive differences, and compare with exact tables or the normal approximation (report Z).

Friedman: sum ranks per condition and compare the statistic with a chi-square distribution with k - 1 degrees of freedom; follow a significant result with pairwise Wilcoxon tests and a multiple-comparison correction.
Report the median difference or a confidence interval for it, not just the p-value; ignore ties unless a result narrowly misses significance with several ties.
outputs: Test statistics (sign count, T or Z, Friedman chi-square), p-values and median-difference estimates for within-subjects comparisons.
useWhen: Within-subjects comparisons of two or more designs on ordinal ratings, skewed task times or small samples where normality is doubtful.
avoidWhen: Avoid for independent groups (use Mann-Whitney U) or when data are roughly normal and you want more power (use paired t-tests or repeated-measures ANOVA). For binary paired outcomes use McNemar's test.
whyLost: They are standard teaching material and available in all statistics packages, though UX teams often default to t-tests on ordinal data instead.
whereToUse: Within-subjects usability comparisons, preference ratings across prototypes, before-and-after redesign studies with the same panel.
example: Twelve participants rate three onboarding variants on a seven-point ease scale. A Friedman test shows a difference (chi-square = 9.5, p = .009), and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests locate it between variants A and C.
reference: Wilcoxon, F. (1945). Individual comparisons by ranking methods. Biometrics Bulletin, 1(6), 80-83; Friedman, M. (1937). The use of ranks to avoid the assumption of normality implicit in the analysis of variance. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 32, 675-701.

name: Signal Detection Theory
origin: Peterson, Birdsall & Fox, 1954; Tanner & Swets, 1954; Green & Swets, 1966
summary: Separates a person's ability to discriminate signal from noise (sensitivity, d') from their tendency to respond 'yes' (criterion), clarifying whether failures are perceptual or strategic.
description: Signal detection theory models decisions under uncertainty where a person must distinguish signals from noise, such as a real alert among false alarms, a phishing email among legitimate ones or an anomaly in a chart. Every response falls into one of four outcomes: hit, miss, false alarm or correct rejection. From hit and false alarm rates, SDT estimates sensitivity (d'), the ability to discriminate, independently of the response criterion, which reflects bias toward saying yes or no. This shows whether a design improves perception or merely shifts caution, and supports ROC analysis. In UX, it suits alert design, security warnings, content moderation and AI-assisted decision tasks. Rigour comes from designed trial sets with known ground truth, enough trials per condition (often 50 or more), and reporting both d' and criterion.
steps: Define the detection task, the signal and the noise, with known ground truth for each trial.
Build a trial set with a realistic or controlled base rate of signals, with 50 or more trials per condition.
Run participants through trials, recording yes or no responses and optionally confidence ratings.
Compute hit and false alarm rates per participant and condition, applying corrections for extreme rates.
Calculate d' and criterion (c or beta), and ROC curves if confidence ratings were collected.
Compare designs on sensitivity and bias, and consider the costs of misses versus false alarms.
Translate results into alert thresholds, interface design or training.
outputs: Hit and false alarm rates, sensitivity (d') and criterion estimates, ROC curves and recommendations on thresholds and design.
useWhen: For alert and notification design, phishing and security warnings, anomaly detection in dashboards, content moderation and human-AI decision tasks.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there is no ground truth for signal and noise, or for open-ended tasks; use usability testing or observation.
whyLost: Latent: SDT is foundational in perception psychology and widely used in radiology, aviation and security research, but UX teams rarely use it to separate sensitivity from bias in detection tasks, relying instead on simple accuracy.
whereToUse: Alert/notification design; error detection research; accessibility studies.
example: A hospital tests two sepsis alert designs with 30 nurses on 80 patient cases. The new design increases d' from 1.1 to 1.8 without shifting criterion, showing better discrimination rather than more cautious clicking.
sources: Detection Theory: A User's Guide (Macmillan & Creelman)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Green DM & Swets JA (1966) Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics
Macmillan NA & Creelman CD (2005) Detection Theory: A User's Guide. 2nd ed
Wickens CD et al. (2015) Engineering Psychology and Human Performance
Principles of Neural Science (Kandel et al., 2021)
reference: Green, D. M. & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley; Macmillan, N. A. & Creelman, C. D. (2005). Detection Theory: A User's Guide (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Signalling Game Analysis
origin: Michael Spence (1973, job market signalling); Amotz Zahavi (1975, handicap principle); Crawford and Sobel (1982, cheap talk)
summary: Analyses whether signals in a product (badges, reviews, verification, credentials) can credibly separate high-quality from low-quality senders, given their costs.
description: In a signalling game, a sender with private information (e.g. seller quality) chooses a signal, and a receiver infers type and acts. A separating equilibrium exists only if the signal is costlier for low types than high types; otherwise low types mimic and the signal becomes uninformative (pooling). Cheap talk, costless signals, is credible only when interests align. This explains why 'verified' badges, review counts or certifications succeed or fail, and why designs that make signals cheap destroy their value. Rigorous analysis models types, costs and incentives, then tests predictions with behavioural data or experiments.
steps: Identify the information asymmetry: who knows what about quality, honesty or intent.
List available signals and estimate their cost to high and low types (money, effort, risk, time).
Determine whether the single-crossing condition holds and whether separating, pooling or semi-separating outcomes are expected.
Check empirical data: do signals predict outcomes (ecological validity) and do receivers rely on them?
Redesign signals to restore differential cost (e.g. verification tied to accountability, history-based badges).
Test with field experiments or lab games, monitoring for gaming over time.
outputs: A signalling model of the product's trust system, predicted equilibria, signal validity evidence and redesign proposals.
useWhen: Designing trust, reputation, credentials, verification or quality signals in marketplaces and social platforms.
avoidWhen: Contexts without meaningful information asymmetry.
whyLost: Game-theoretic modelling is unfamiliar in UX, which designs badges by convention rather than incentive analysis.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, dating apps, freelance platforms, social verification, AI-generated content labels.
example: A freelance platform's 'Top Rated' badge pools as inflated ratings make it cheap to obtain. Tying it to repeat-client rate, costlier for low-quality freelancers to fake, restores its predictive value for client satisfaction.
sources: Spence, Job market signaling (1973), Quarterly Journal of Economics
Connelly et al., Signaling theory: A review and assessment (2011), Journal of Management
Crawford & Sobel, Strategic information transmission (1982), Econometrica
reference: Spence, M. (1973). Quarterly Journal of Economics, 87(3), 355-374.

name: SIL Method (systematic integration of solution elements)
aka: SIL method (systematic integration of problem elements)
origin: Helmut Schlicksupp, Battelle Institute Frankfurt, late 1970s
summary: Members each draft a detailed solution alone, then present them in turn while the group names each one's strengths and merges them step by step into one solution.
description: SIL (from the German for successive integration of solution elements) is a convergent ideation format for complex problems with few feasible solutions, such as industrial or product design tasks. An interdisciplinary group of six to eight frames the problem precisely; each member then drafts a detailed solution alone, which avoids the production blocking and anchoring of open brainstorming. The first two solutions are presented and discussed for their strengths only, and the group builds an integrated solution from both. Each further solution is presented, its strengths identified and folded into the growing combined concept. The session takes two to three hours and demands more of participants and moderator than brainstorming, but produces mature solutions that the whole group feels it owns. It combines the individual work of brainwriting with the group discussion of brainstorming, and it is closer to synthesis than to idea generation.
steps: Frame the problem precisely with six to eight people from different specialisms.
Give each participant 20-30 minutes to draft a solution alone, in as much detail as possible (sketches welcome).
Participant 1 presents; the group discusses and records only its strengths.
Participant 2 presents; the group records its strengths.
The group builds an integrated solution from the strengths of both.
Each further solution is presented, its strengths identified and integrated into the combined solution.
End with one or more comprehensive integrated concepts and record which elements came from which draft.
outputs: One or more integrated solution concepts with a record of the source of each element.
useWhen: Use when a cross-functional team must converge on one workable concept for a complex problem and each member brings specialist knowledge.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the goal is many divergent ideas (use Brainstorming or Design Studio) or when the problem is not yet understood (run Contextual Inquiry first). The integrated concept is untested; follow with Prototype Testing. Expect two to three hours and a skilled moderator.
whyLost: It remains known in German-language innovation management but never crossed into mainstream UX, where Design Studio and the Design Sprint's sketch-and-vote play a similar role.
whereToUse: Hardware and industrial product design, complex B2B workflows, service redesigns needing cross-disciplinary agreement.
example: Six specialists each sketch a medication-dispenser concept. Discussing strengths only, the group combines one draft's tamper-proof refill with another's large-display reminder and a third's carer notification into a single concept for prototyping.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Gaubinger, K., Rabl, M., Swan, S. and Werani, T. (2015). Innovation and Product Management. Berlin: Springer, section 6.4.2.6 (crediting Schlicksupp).

name: Silhouette scores and gap statistic validation
origin: Rousseeuw, 1987; Everitt et al., 2011
summary: Evaluates whether user segments from cluster analysis are real, stable and useful using internal indices, resampling stability and external validation, not just visual inspection.
description: Cluster algorithms always return clusters, whether or not the data contain meaningful groups. Cluster validation tests whether a segmentation reflects real structure. Internal validity uses indices such as the silhouette coefficient, Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin to compare solutions; the gap statistic compares clustering against a null reference. Stability is assessed by bootstrapping or subsampling and measuring agreement between solutions (e.g. Jaccard coefficients or adjusted Rand index). External validity checks whether clusters differ on variables not used to create them, such as retention or revenue, and whether they make sense qualitatively. Rigour comes from pre-specifying the candidate range of clusters, standardising variables appropriately, and reporting weak structure honestly.
steps: Cluster validation protocol:
Run clustering for k = 2..10.
(2) For each k, compute: silhouette score (higher is better, range -1 to 1; good clusters > 0.5), Calinski-Harabasz index (higher is better), Davies-Bouldin index (lower is better).
(3) Plot all three indices vs. k. Identify the k where the silhouette score peaks or the 'elbow' in CH/DB indices.
(4) Also compute gap statistic (compares within-cluster dispersion to random data).
(5) Report: which k did you choose, and why? Include all validation metrics.
outputs: Silhouette and other validity indices across solutions, stability estimates under resampling, external validation against outcomes, and a justified number of clusters.
useWhen: Any behavioural or attitudinal segmentation that will inform personas, targeting or strategy.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting clusters from data with no cluster structure; if validity indices are uniformly weak, use continuous dimensions or latent class models instead.
whyLost: Segmentation is commonly run with k-means and a scatterplot; validation methods remain in statistics and data mining texts.
whereToUse: Persona research validation, card sort analysis, behavioral segmentation, any UX analysis using clustering.
example: A fitness app's six-cluster segmentation shows an average silhouette of 0.18 and clusters that reshuffle under bootstrap; a three-cluster solution is stable (Jaccard above 0.85) and predicts retention, so it is adopted.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Tibshirani, Walther & Hastie (2001) Estimating the number of clusters via the gap statistic
The Inquiry Series, Ch 51 — Behavioral Clustering & Probabilistic Segmentation
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Cluster Analysis: Basic Concepts and Algorithms (Tan et al., 2006)
Selecting a Clustering Algorithm (HyPersona) (Ditton et al., 2022)
Building Actionable Personas Using Machine Learning Techniques (Farrukh et al., 2022)
A Comparative Analysis of Persona Clustering Methods (Brickey et al., 2010)
Identifying Behavioral Personas with Cluster Analysis (Lenk, 2022)
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
reference: Rousseeuw PJ (1987) Silhouettes: A graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis. Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 20:53-65

name: Similarity-informed preference tree analysis
origin: Amos Tversky and Shmuel Sattath, 1979
summary: Build a tree from similarity ratings, fit branch lengths to paired-choice data, and test whether it beats the constant-ratio model, capturing that similar options compete more with each other.
description: A preference tree is elimination by aspects restricted to aspects that nest in a tree, which cuts the parameters to at most 2n - 2. It captures the similarity effect that simple logit or constant-ratio models miss: adding an option takes share mainly from options similar to it. A trinary inequality on paired-choice odds tests the tree structure; across celebrities, political parties and academic disciplines, 78 to 96 percent of triples met it, and the tree fitted far better than the constant-ratio model. Trees built from similarity ratings and from choices largely agreed. The root does not matter for similarity but does for preference, so alternative roots are compared. The method gives a transparent, testable model of substitution among options.
steps: Collect pairwise similarity ratings and paired choices (and, if possible, choices from triples) for the same set of options.
Build a tree from the similarity data, for example with an additive tree algorithm such as ADDTREE.
Fit branch lengths to choice probabilities by maximum likelihood, trying alternative roots.
Compare fit with the constant-ratio (logit) model using a likelihood-ratio test.
Report the share of triples that meet the trinary inequality.
Use the fitted tree to predict shares when options are added or removed.
outputs: A preference tree, fit statistics against the constant-ratio model, and predicted shares for new option sets.
useWhen: Predicting cannibalisation when adding a plan, product or feature tier, or explaining why share shifts are concentrated among similar options.
avoidWhen: Avoid with few paired choices or when aspects do not nest; for large attribute-based designs use nested logit or discrete choice modelling.
whyLost: Nested and mixed logit models in econometrics absorbed the idea, and the original tree-fitting procedure fell out of use outside mathematical psychology.
whereToUse: Subscription plan line-ups, product range planning, marketplace category design, feature tier decisions.
example: Six subscription plans: the tree puts two family plans on one branch, predicting that a new family plan will take share mainly from them, where a logit simulator would spread losses across all plans.
sources: Tversky, A., & Sattath, S. (1979). Preference trees. Psychological Review, 86
reference: Tversky, A., & Sattath, S. (1979). Preference trees. Psychological Review, 86, 542-573.

name: Simpson's paradox and composition-shift check
origin: Simpson (1951); experimentation pitfall described by Crook, Frasca, Kohavi and Longbotham (2009); UX metric example by Chapman and Rodden (2023)
summary: Before trusting a pooled A/B result or metric trend, checks whether segment shares differ between arms or over time and whether within-segment effects point the other way.
description: A pooled comparison can reverse within every segment when segments are mixed in different proportions. In Crook and colleagues' A/B example, browsers were sampled at different rates, so treatment won overall but lost in every browser. In Chapman and Rodden's tracking example, pooled customer satisfaction fell about 1.5 points a year, yet the US was flat and Germany rising; the decline came from Germany, with lower ratings, making up a growing share of respondents. The check lists segments that could relate to both allocation or sampling and the outcome, compares their shares across arms or periods, estimates effects within segments, and fits models with segment main effects and segment-by-time or segment-by-treatment interactions. If composition changed, report stratified or reweighted estimates. Only stratify on variables fixed before treatment, and limit slicing to avoid false positives.
steps: List segments that could affect both allocation or sampling and the outcome: browser, platform, country, plan, acquisition channel, period.
Check that the treatment share is equal across segments and periods (a sample ratio check), or plot each segment's share of respondents over time for tracked metrics.
Compute the effect or trend within each main segment as well as overall, with confidence intervals.
Fit a model with segment main effects and segment-by-treatment or segment-by-time interactions.
If within-segment results disagree with the pooled result, report stratified or reweighted estimates and explain the composition shift.
Fix allocation or sampling so future runs keep segment shares constant, and use qualitative data to judge whether segment level differences are real or scale-use effects.
outputs: Segment-level effects or trends, composition charts, and a corrected interpretation of the headline result.
useWhen: Traffic allocation changed mid-test, features were ramped by platform, panels drift in country or device mix, or a headline metric moves without any product change.
avoidWhen: Slicing into many post hoc segments invites false positives; stratify only on pre-treatment variables chosen in advance. For a formal causal decomposition of change, use regression or reweighting models.
whyLost: It survived: sample ratio mismatch checks and mix-shift analysis are standard in mature experimentation and analytics teams, though often skipped in smaller UX survey programmes.
whereToUse: A/B testing platforms, satisfaction and NPS tracking, global products with shifting market mix, funnel metrics across device types.
example: A tracked CSAT score drops three points over two years. Splitting by country shows no decline anywhere; the share of respondents from a market that habitually rates lower has doubled, so the team reweights the series and stops a planned redesign.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Chapman, C. and Rodden, K. (2023). Quantitative User Experience Research: Informing Product Decisions by Understanding Users at Scale. Berkeley, CA: Apress, pp. 151-157; Crook, T., Frasca, B., Kohavi, R. and Longbotham, R. (2009), as cited in Shneiderman et al. (2018), Box 5.4.

name: Simulated-Data Check of an Analysis Plan
aka: Simulate data with known structure, then analyse it
Synthetic data validation of an analysis
origin: Presented by Chris Chapman and Elea McDonnell Feit (2015; 2nd ed. 2019) as standard practice among R analysts
summary: Before analysing real data, generate a synthetic data set with structure you set yourself, run the planned analysis on it, and check that it recovers what you built in.
description: Chapman and Feit simulate data before nearly every analysis and argue the habit is valuable in itself. When you created the data, you know what the analysis should find, so you can confirm the code and model work before trusting them on real data, and you can change the simulation to see how results respond. Their examples include survey data with latent satisfaction mapped to 5-point items and non-response, segments defined by a parameter table, satisfaction drivers with a halo effect, factor and structural models from published loadings, and choice-based conjoint responses from known part-worths. The same approach doubles as design planning: varying sample size, number of questions or attributes shows the precision a budget will buy, and designs can be compared by the width of prediction intervals. Recovery shows the method works, not that the model fits reality.
steps: Write down the planned analysis and the expected structure: variables, types, segments, relationships and effect sizes.
Keep the data definition (names, distributions, segment sizes, parameter tables) separate from the generating code so it is easy to change, and set a random seed.

Generate each variable from its distribution, building in the intended relationships, latent factors or part-worths, then convert latent scores to scale points and add floor, ceiling and non-response effects.
Run the planned analysis on the synthetic data.
Compare estimates with the known parameters (coefficients, loadings, segment membership, part-worths).
Vary sample size, number of items or tasks and effect sizes, rerun, and fix the study design that gives adequate precision.
Run the same code on the real data once collected.
outputs: A reusable synthetic data set, verified analysis code and estimates of the precision a planned sample and design will give.
useWhen: Before fielding a survey, conjoint, segmentation or experiment whose analysis is non-trivial, to catch coding errors and size the study.
avoidWhen: It cannot show that the model is right for the world, only that the pipeline works under your assumptions; for checking model fit to real data use Predictive Model Validation, and for simple power calculations Statistical power analysis may suffice.
whyLost: It is a habit of statistically trained analysts, rarely written down as a method, so UX quant work seldom includes it.
whereToUse: Conjoint and MaxDiff studies, driver analysis surveys, segmentation, structural equation models, experiment analysis pipelines.
example: Before a pricing conjoint, a researcher simulates 200 respondents with known part-worths answering 15 choice tasks. The hierarchical model recovers them well, but refitting with 25 respondents shows standard errors too wide, so the sample is kept at 200.
sources: R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
reference: Chapman, C. and Feit, E. M. (2019). R for Marketing Research and Analytics (2nd ed.). Cham: Springer, ch. 3-5, 7, 10, 13.

name: Simulation Heuristic for Task Difficulty Prediction
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1982
summary: Measures how easily users can mentally simulate completing a task before attempting it, using that perceived simulation ease to predict reluctance, abandonment and perceived usability.
description: The simulation heuristic holds that people judge how likely or hard something is by how easily they can construct a mental simulation of it. In UX terms, before acting, users imagine the steps a task will require; if the simulation is hard to run because steps are unclear, numerous or unfamiliar, they judge the task difficult and may avoid it, regardless of actual difficulty. The method collects pre-task ratings of expected difficulty and asks users to narrate the steps they expect, then compares these with post-task ratings and actual performance. Large gaps show where interfaces fail to support simulation (hidden steps, no progress cues) or where they look harder than they are. It complements single ease questions by separating expectation from experience.
steps: Ask users to mentally simulate the task and rate simulation ease (1–7).
Correlate with actual completion rates (target r > 0.65).
Low-simulation-ease screens are redesign candidates.
outputs: Pre-task expected difficulty ratings, narrated expected step sequences, expectation-versus-experience gaps, and design cues to improve task previewability.
useWhen: Flows with high abandonment before starting (applications, set-up, migrations), onboarding, and features users avoid because they appear complex.
avoidWhen: When users already know the task well, since simulation differences vanish with expertise; use performance measures instead.
whyLost: It remained a theoretical heuristic in decision research; UX adopted post-task ease questions but not the pre-task simulation measure that explains avoidance.
whereToUse: Pre-test difficulty prediction, cognitive walkthrough grounding.
example: A tax-filing service asks users to describe the steps they expect before starting a self-employment return; most imagine 20 or more steps and rate it 2 out of 7. Adding a 'what you'll need, about 15 minutes, 4 sections' preview raises starts by 22%.
sources: Kahneman & Tversky, The simulation heuristic (in Judgment Under Uncertainty, 1982)
reference: Kahneman D & Tversky A (1982) The simulation heuristic. In Kahneman D, Slovic P & Tversky A (Eds.) Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Cambridge University Press

name: Simulation Sickness Testing in VR
donor: Military simulator research and human factors
origin: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire by Kennedy et al. (1993); testing guidance for VR games by Ben Lewis-Evans (Epic Games) in chapter 30
summary: A set of practices for detecting simulation sickness in VR: expert review against known provoking factors, sampling of susceptible participants with the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire, larger samples and safety procedures.
description: Simulation sickness can cause eyestrain, headaches, postural instability, sweating, disorientation, nausea and vomiting. Lewis-Evans stresses that it is an individual, physiological issue affecting a significant minority, so the usual five-participant usability sample cannot detect or rule it out. He recommends three responses when large samples are not affordable. First, expert analysis against known causes: unstable frame rate or latency (he cites at least 90 frames per second and under 20 milliseconds latency), motion blur, flicker, rolling motion or moving horizons, camera movement the player does not control, zooming, low or very high camera height, artificial acceleration (vection), situations that would cause sickness in real life, and UI placed so that it demands large head or eye movements. Second, recruit vulnerable people, for example by screening with the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire and recruiting across the risk range, and including older people and those who rarely play first-person games. Third, over-recruit by at least ten per cent because some participants will stop. He adds safety and ethics checks: safe space, quick headset removal, full payment if people stop, consent wording, a recovery area, travel home, and breaks for observers watching VR footage.
steps: Review the build against known provoking factors (frame rate, latency, vection, camera control, flicker, UI placement).
Screen candidates with the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire or sickness history and recruit across the susceptibility range, including older and less experienced players.
Over-recruit by at least ten per cent and prepare a safe test space, recovery area and consent wording.
Brief participants that they can stop at any time with full payment and agree a fast way to communicate.
Run sessions, monitoring for symptoms and recording when and where they appear.
Administer the SSQ after exposure and relate symptoms to game events and settings.
Report sickness triggers and comfort options to the team.
outputs: A list of sickness-provoking features, symptom scores by participant and condition, and recommended comfort settings.
useWhen: Testing VR or other immersive and first-person experiences with artificial motion.
avoidWhen: The product involves no simulated motion or head-mounted display.
whyLost: The SSQ is standard in simulator human factors, but product UX teams often test VR with small usability samples that miss sickness.
whereToUse: VR games and training, AR headsets, first-person games, driving and flight simulators, 360-degree video.
example: Screening with the SSQ, a team recruits ten susceptible players; four report nausea during a forced camera turn in a cut-scene, which is replaced with a fade.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 30 (Lewis-Evans). Kennedy, R. S., Lane, N. E., Berbaum, K. S. and Lilienthal, M. G. (1993). Simulator Sickness Questionnaire: an enhanced method for quantifying simulator sickness. International Journal of Aviation Psychology, 3(3), 203-220.

name: Simulation-Based Power Analysis for Intensive Longitudinal Designs
aka: Simulation-based power analysis for ESM designs
Monte Carlo power for multilevel intensive longitudinal designs
Monte Carlo power analysis for intensive longitudinal designs
origin: Bolger and Laurenceau, 2013 (Mplus Monte Carlo); Lafit et al., 2021 (PowerAnalysisIL)
summary: Choose the number of participants and prompts for a diary or ESM study by simulating many datasets from a multilevel model and counting how often the effect is detected.
description: Analytic power formulas exist only for simple multilevel questions. The simulation approach generates synthetic datasets from a hypothesised population model, fits the model to each, and takes power as the share of significant results. PowerAnalysisIL, an R Shiny app, covers 11 common ESM models with AR(1) level-1 errors, including group mean differences, random-slope effects, cross-level interactions and autoregressive effects; Bolger and Laurenceau do the same with Mplus MONTECARLO for five diary models, with at least 1,000 replications. Parameter values come from the literature, a pilot or a previous study fitted by REML. Outputs are power curves over participants and time points, with bias, standard errors and coverage. Two lessons recur: adding participants usually buys more power than adding days, and random slopes reduce power for the average slope. The exercise forces researchers to state every variance component, which is useful in itself.
steps: Specify the multilevel model for the hypothesis, including AR(1) errors.
Get parameter values (fixed effects, variance components, autocorrelation) from literature, a pilot or prior data fitted with REML.
Choose candidate numbers of participants and time points, using expected completed prompts, not scheduled ones.
Run 1,000 or more Monte Carlo replicates per design, estimating run time first.
Read power curves, bias and coverage for each design.
Choose the design that reaches target power (typically 80%) within feasibility and burden limits.
outputs: Power curves by number of participants and time points, with bias and coverage, and a justified design choice.
useWhen: Planning a quantitative diary, ESM or repeated in-app survey study whose main analysis is multilevel.
avoidWhen: Qualitative diary studies, or single-level designs where standard power analysis suffices. Basic tools assume equal spacing and no missing data; extend to three levels or continuous time where needed.
whyLost: UX diary studies are usually sized by convention (10 to 15 participants), and simulation-based multilevel power analysis is a specialist skill.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX benchmarks, health and wellbeing app studies, and in-product pulse surveys feeding effect estimates.
example: A team plans to compare daily frustration between two onboarding variants over 14 days. Simulation shows 30 users per group gives 55% power while 60 per group gives 85%, and doubling days instead adds little, so it recruits more users for fewer days.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Single Ease Question (SEQ) Benchmarking
origin: Sauro & Dumas, 2009
summary: A single seven-point post-task question on difficulty, benchmarked against published norms to compare tasks, designs and releases quickly.
description: The Single Ease Question asks, immediately after each task, 'Overall, how difficult or easy was this task to complete?' on a seven-point scale from very difficult to very easy. Sauro and Dumas found it performed as well as or better than more complex post-task instruments while taking seconds to administer. Its real value emerges when scores are interpreted against norms (the historical average is roughly 5.5) and reported with confidence intervals, enabling meaningful comparison between tasks, designs and releases. Low scores flag tasks for diagnostic follow-up, and pairing SEQ with completion and time data reveals mismatches between perceived and actual difficulty. Rigour lies in consistent wording, administration timing and sample sizes adequate for the precision required.
steps: Administer SEQ immediately after each task (before the next task begins — memory decay is rapid).
Score: 1=Very Difficult, 7=Very Easy.
Compute: mean SEQ per task, % scoring 5–7 (top box).
Benchmarks (from Sauro's database): > 5.5 mean = good; < 4.5 = poor.
Correlate SEQ with task completion: expect r ≈ 0.5–0.7 between success and SEQ.
Discrepancies (high success + low SEQ) reveal effortful completion.
outputs: Mean SEQ per task with confidence intervals, comparison against the normative average (about 5.5), task difficulty rankings and trends across releases.
useWhen: Moderated or unmoderated usability tests needing a lightweight, validated, comparable measure of perceived task difficulty.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the only measure (pair with success and time), when tasks are too short or trivial to rate, or when you need diagnostic detail; use follow-up probes or interviews for the why.
whyLost: The SEQ itself survived because it is cheap; what was lost is benchmarking against norms and confidence intervals, so scores are often reported raw and uninterpreted.
whereToUse: Usability testing task evaluation, iterative design comparison, longitudinal benchmarking.
example: A SaaS team runs SEQ after six tasks; 'export a report' averages 3.9 (95% CI 3.3 to 4.5), well below the 5.5 norm, so it is prioritised even though its completion rate looked acceptable.
sources: Measuring the User Experience — Tullis & Albert
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
reference: Sauro J & Dumas JS (2009) Comparison of three one-question, post-task usability questionnaires. CHI 2009

name: Single Usability Metric (SUM)
origin: Sauro & Kindlund (2005), CHI
summary: Combines completion, time, errors and satisfaction for a task into one standardised usability score.
description: Stakeholders want one number; usability has several. SUM standardises each task metric against a specification limit and averages them. Completion is already a proportion. Task time is converted to the probability of finishing under a target time (using a z-score of log times). Errors become the proportion of error opportunities avoided. Post-task satisfaction is converted to the probability of exceeding a target rating. The result is a percentage between 0 and 100 per task, with a confidence interval, that can be rolled up across tasks. Principal components work by Sauro and Kindlund showed the four metrics share enough variance to justify combining them, while still being worth inspecting separately.
steps: Collect completion, time, errors (with error opportunities) and a post-task rating for each task.
Set specification limits: a target time (for example from expert times or goals) and a target satisfaction score.
Convert each metric to a percentage: success rate; proportion under target time; proportion of opportunities error-free; proportion above satisfaction target.
Average the percentages per task, compute an interval, and average across tasks for a product-level SUM.
Report SUM with the component metrics so a low score can be diagnosed.
outputs: A 0 to 100% usability score per task and per product, with drill-down to components.
useWhen: Executive dashboards, benchmarks over releases, competitive comparisons.
avoidWhen: Formative work where diagnosis matters more than a score, or when error data was not collected.
whyLost: It requires collecting four metrics consistently and setting spec limits, which most teams skip in favour of SUS alone.
whereToUse: Benchmark programmes, procurement comparisons, enterprise software scorecards.
example: A travel site's "change booking" task scores SUM 54% against a competitor's 78%, driven mostly by time, which focuses the redesign on the number of steps.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J. & Kindlund, E. (2005). A method to standardize usability metrics into a single score. CHI 2005.

name: Single-Subject Experimental Design
origin: B.F. Skinner tradition; Barlow & Hersen, 1984
summary: Establishes causal effects within individual users by repeatedly measuring behaviour across baseline and intervention phases (e.g. ABAB, multiple baseline).
description: Single-subject experimental designs establish causality at the level of the individual by repeatedly measuring a behaviour and systematically introducing and withdrawing an intervention. In an ABAB reversal design, baseline (A) and intervention (B) phases alternate; in a multiple-baseline design, the intervention is introduced at staggered times across participants, behaviours or settings. If behaviour changes reliably each time the intervention is applied, alternative explanations become implausible. In UX this suits accessibility work, highly individual users and behaviour-change features. Rigour comes from stable baselines (at least three to five data points per phase), visual analysis of level, trend and variability, non-overlap effect sizes, randomisation of phase starts where possible, and replication across participants.
steps: AB design for UX behavior change:
Baseline phase (A): measure the target behavior (e.g., task completion time, error rate) across multiple sessions without the design change.
(2) Treatment phase (B): introduce the design change. Continue measuring.
(3) Analysis: plot the data. Visual inspection: is there a change in level (immediate shift), trend (gradual change), and/or variability at the phase change point?
(4) ABAB extension: withdraw the treatment (return to A) and reintroduce (B). Reversal of the behavior confirms the causal effect of the design change.
outputs: Phase-by-phase time series per participant, visual analysis of level, trend and variability, effect sizes such as Tau-U, and replication across participants.
useWhen: Accessibility and assistive technology studies, rare or highly individual users, and behaviour change features where group averages hide individual responses.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need population-level estimates or when effects cannot be reversed or staggered; use randomised experiments instead.
whyLost: UX experimentation is equated with A/B tests on large samples; within-person experimental logic stayed in behaviour analysis and clinical research.
whereToUse: Accessibility UX testing for individual users, assistive technology evaluation, personalized interface adaptation research.
example: An assistive app for a user with motor impairments alternates switch-scanning and predictive layout modes over four phases; entry speed rises each time predictive mode returns, confirming a causal effect for her.
sources: Research Methods in Applied Behavior Analysis — (various)
The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
reference: Cooper JO, Heron TE & Heward WL (2020) Applied Behavior Analysis. 3rd ed. Pearson

name: SIR Transmission Models for Dark Pattern Spread
origin: Kermack and McKendrick (1927); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Models products as susceptible, infected (adopted a pattern) or recovered (abandoned it) to describe and project the spread of dark patterns across an industry.
description: Compartmental models track population flows between states governed by transmission and recovery rates. The treatise adapts SIR to design ecosystems: 'susceptible' products have not adopted a pattern, 'infected' have adopted it, and 'recovered/resistant' adopted then abandoned it under regulatory or reputational pressure. Transmission depends on how easily a pattern can be identified and copied and on competitive pressures incentivising adoption. Fitting the model to adoption timelines estimates parameters, projects spread and simulates interventions (raising recovery via regulation, lowering transmission via standards). Extensions include SIS (re-adoption) and network-based models. Rigour requires careful adoption data, e.g. from web crawls and archives.
steps: Define the pattern and population of products (for example top 1,000 subscription apps).
Build an adoption timeline from crawls, archives and audits.
Fit SIR (or SIS/SEIR) parameters for transmission and recovery rates.
Estimate R0 and check fit against observed curves.
Simulate interventions such as regulation increasing recovery rate.
Report projections with uncertainty and update as data arrive.
outputs: Fitted transmission and recovery rates, R0, adoption projections, intervention simulations.
useWhen: Industry-level analysis of pattern spread, regulatory planning, standards strategy.
avoidWhen: Single-product analysis or when adoption data are unavailable.
whyLost: Epidemic modelling never applied to design; UX lacked cross-product adoption data.
whereToUse: Regulators, consumer advocacy, research on dark patterns, design-system ecosystems.
example: Fitting SIR to 'confirmshaming' adoption across 800 retail sites gives R0 of about 2.3; simulations show a disclosure rule halving transmission would cap prevalence near 15%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kermack WO & McKendrick AG (1927) A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proc R Soc A 115
Anderson RM & May RM (1991) Infectious Diseases of Humans
Mathur A et al. (2019) Dark patterns at scale. CSCW
reference: Kermack WO & McKendrick AG (1927) A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A 115:700-721.

name: Site search analytics
donor: Information architecture; information retrieval; web analytics
origin: Rosenfeld, Search Analytics for Your Site (2011); Jansen (2006) search log analysis method
summary: Analyse the queries people type into a site's search to learn their vocabulary, find what they cannot find, and fix labels, content and results, starting with the most frequent queries.
description: Search queries are users' own words for what they want and could not reach by browsing. Query frequency usually follows a power law, so a small head of phrases accounts for much of all searching and is optimised first. Core metrics are zero-result rate, click-through, refinement and search exits; reading top queries reveals acronyms, jargon, product names and mismatches with navigation labels. Actions include adding synonyms and preferred terms, renaming labels, writing missing content and curating Best Bets for top queries. Comparing internal queries with external search-engine queries exposes SEO and IA gaps. More rigorous variants categorise queries into need-based groups with weighted conversion metrics, or follow Jansen's three stages: collection, cleaning (removing corrupt records, separating page requests from new queries, choosing a session cut-off) and analysis at term, query and session levels.
steps: Ensure search logging captures query, timestamp, session or user identifier, result count and clicks, and arrange regular access.
Export a representative period, clean corrupted records, and separate results-page requests from new queries; choose a session cut-off (studies use 5 to 120 minutes).
Rank unique queries by frequency with cumulative percentages, grouping misspellings and variants.
Compute zero-result, click-through, refinement and exit rates for the head queries.
Read the top queries for vocabulary, acronyms and label mismatches; optionally categorise queries by need and attach weighted conversion metrics per category.
Act: add synonyms, rename labels, create or fix content, and set Best Bets for top queries; compare internal with external queries for SEO gaps.
Report key metrics monthly on one page and repeat the analysis regularly; use interviews or usability tests to explain anomalies.
outputs: A frequency-ranked query list, zero-result and high-result diagnoses, candidate labels and synonyms, Best Bets targets, category-level metrics and a monthly report.
useWhen: A product has site or in-app search and you want low-cost, continuous evidence of what users seek and fail to find.
avoidWhen: Avoid using it alone to explain why users search or whether they succeeded; logs show terms, not intent. Pair with contextual inquiry or usability tests. Users enter short, misspelt queries, sessions are approximated by IP or cookie, and stored queries raise privacy issues.
whyLost: It survives because every search box produces logs, analytics tools report them, and the return on fixing top queries is quick and visible.
whereToUse: E-commerce, documentation and help centres, intranets, government and university sites, marketplaces and in-app search.
example: A university's top queries show 'parking' near the top with zero results and 'timetable' landing on an outdated page. The team adds a parking page, maps 'timetable' as a synonym for 'class schedule' and sets Best Bets for the top 20 queries.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Rosenfeld, L. (2011). Search Analytics for Your Site: Conversations with Your Customers. Rosenfeld Media; Jansen, B. J. (2006). Search log analysis: what it is, what's been done, how to do it. Library and Information Science Research 28(3), 407-432.

name: Site Visit Fieldwork
origin: Long-standing practice in evaluation research (e.g. Herriott and Firestone, 1983); described as a formal fieldwork procedure by Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016)
summary: Short, scheduled visits of a few days, often by a small team, to many comparable settings so that cross-site patterns can be found, at the cost of the depth of participant observation.
description: Yin presents site visits as the form fieldwork usually takes in policy, organisational and evaluation studies, and as a procedure in its own right rather than a weak form of ethnography. A typical visit lasts only a few days and may use two or more fieldworkers who split interviews and events. Each setting is studied more shallowly than in participant observation, but a dozen or more settings can be covered, so the method suits studies whose main questions concern cross-site patterns; repeat visits add a time perspective. Because time is short, visits follow a pre-arranged schedule and agenda. Yin is explicit about the costs: hosts help set the schedule and may stage it, interviews in a booked meeting room lose the serendipity of seeing people's own workplaces, and a host who accompanies the visitor may alter what others say. Visitors should agree in advance when they will go unaccompanied. Team visits need common training, a shared protocol and rules for joint interviewing, and they allow cross-checking between fieldworkers. For UX, this is the disciplined version of the B2B customer visit programme.
steps: Define the cross-site questions and choose a set of comparable sites, with repeat visits if change over time matters
Prepare a shared protocol and train all team members so fieldwork is consistent
Negotiate a schedule and agenda with each site, noting which parts the host arranged
Agree in advance when the team will interview or observe without the host present
During the visit, split events and interviews between team members and seek informal observation beyond the agenda
Debrief nightly as a team, cross-check what each person saw and heard, and note staged or idealised elements
Write a site report against the protocol, then compare sites to identify patterns
outputs: Per-site reports structured by the protocol, team cross-check notes, and a cross-site comparison of patterns.
useWhen: Many organisational customers or locations must be compared within limited time, such as B2B, healthcare, retail or field-service products.
avoidWhen: The question needs deep understanding of everyday practice in one setting over time; use participant observation or longer ethnography.
whyLost: UX inherited contextual inquiry and ethnography as its models of fieldwork, while customer visits were left to sales and account teams without method; the evaluation-research literature on site visits rarely reached design.
whereToUse: Enterprise software, clinical and lab systems, retail and logistics operations, franchise or branch networks.
example: A two-person team visits eight warehouses over a month, two days each, to understand why a picking app is adopted unevenly. They note that at three sites the manager scheduled only top performers for interviews, ask to spend time on the floor unaccompanied, and find a cross-site pattern linked to shift handover practice.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People (Weinschenk, 2011)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Situated Action Analysis
origin: Lucy Suchman, 1987
summary: Studies how people improvise action moment by moment in response to circumstances, rather than following plans, to expose where systems assume scripted behaviour.
description: Lucy Suchman's study of users struggling with a Xerox copier's expert help system showed that plans are resources for action, not programmes that determine it. People act in response to the unfolding situation, repairing misunderstandings as they go. Situated action analysis applies this through close video-based interaction analysis of real use: researchers record people using a system, transcribe talk and action in fine detail, and examine how users interpret the system's responses and how the system fails to grasp the user's situation. Rigour comes from detailed sequential transcripts, attention to repair and breakdown episodes, and collaborative data sessions where interpretations are challenged against the record. The method is a corrective to task models and flowcharts and is especially pertinent to conversational and agentic AI systems that infer user intent.
steps: Select real or realistic use situations where the system must interpret user intent.
Video-record 6-12 sessions capturing screen, speech and body, ideally in the actual setting.
Transcribe selected episodes sequentially, aligning user actions, talk and system responses.
Identify breakdowns and repairs where user and system understanding diverge.
Hold group data sessions to interpret episodes and test alternative readings against the recording.
Derive design implications for feedback, repair mechanisms and flexibility versus scripted flows.
outputs: Annotated interaction transcripts, catalogue of breakdown and repair patterns, design implications for system responsiveness.
useWhen: Conversational UI, AI assistants, help systems and workflow tools that assume users follow predefined plans.
avoidWhen: When you need quantitative performance data or quick evaluative findings; use usability testing or analytics.
whyLost: Siloed: Theoretical foundation for contextual and field research methods; rarely referenced directly in practice.
whereToUse: Research design philosophy; conversational UI; adaptive/responsive system design.
example: An AI coding assistant assumed users wanted complete solutions. Situated analysis of recorded sessions showed developers repeatedly interrupted to redirect partial outputs, leading the team to design for incremental, interruptible suggestions.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Suchman L (1987) Plans and Situated Actions: The Problem of Human-Machine Communication
The SAGE Handbook of Visual Research Methods (Margolis & Pauwels, 2011)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Suchman, L. A. (1987). Plans and Situated Actions: The Problem of Human-Machine Communication. Cambridge University Press.

name: Situated Knowledge and Positionality in Cross-Cultural Research
origin: Donna Haraway, 1988; Nicholas Dirks, 2001
summary: Examines how the researcher's culture, power and categories shape what is observed in cross-cultural research, so findings are not imported assumptions dressed as data.
description: Drawing on Haraway's notion of situated knowledges and on historical work such as Dirks's account of how colonial administration produced the categories it claimed to observe, this method asks researchers to treat their own categories as artefacts of position and power. Before and during cross-cultural research, the team documents where its concepts come from (bank forms, Western personas, prior markets), examines how its identity and sponsorship shape what participants say, and invites local partners to challenge interpretations. Findings are then labelled as emic (participants' own framings) or etic (researcher frameworks). Rigour comes from making these steps explicit and auditable, so that apparent 'user needs' are not simply the team's assumptions reflected back by participants eager to please a powerful outsider.
steps: Positionality audit for any product with global or cross-cultural reach:
Who designed the categories? What cultural context do they come from?
(2) What categories are mandatory vs. optional? Mandatory categories impose the designer's framework on users.
(3) What is missing — what social realities cannot be expressed in the current category system?
(4) Conduct research with users from the non-dominant cultural context to identify category impositions.
outputs: A positionality statement, an inventory of imported categories, local-partner critique notes and revised findings that distinguish emic from etic interpretations.
useWhen: Research in cultures, regions or communities different from the team's own, especially in the Global South, with marginalised groups, or where categories such as caste, kinship or gender organise life.
avoidWhen: Not needed as a heavyweight exercise for studies within the team's own context and with low cultural distance; a lightweight reflexivity journal is enough there.
whyLost: It belongs to anthropology's internal critique of colonial knowledge production; UX imported ethnography's techniques for speed but not its epistemological self-scrutiny.
whereToUse: International product design, gender/identity category design, government digital services, any product serving culturally diverse populations.
example: A payments team from Bengaluru designing for rural Bihar audits its personas and finds that 'household head' was imported from bank forms; local co-researchers show that purchase decisions are distributed across women's self-help groups.
sources: Castes of Mind — Nicholas B. Dirks
reference: Haraway D (1988) Situated knowledges: The science question in feminism and the privilege of partial perspective. Feminist Studies 14(3):575-599

name: Situation Awareness Measurement (SAGAT)
origin: Mica Endsley, 1988; theory in Endsley (1995)
summary: Freezes a simulation at random points, blanks the display and asks users queries about what is happening, objectively measuring perception, comprehension and projection.
description: Endsley defined situation awareness at three levels: perception of elements (Level 1), comprehension of their meaning (Level 2) and projection of future status (Level 3). SAGAT measures it objectively by pausing a realistic simulation at unpredictable moments, hiding all displays and administering queries derived from a goal-directed task analysis of SA requirements. Answers are scored against ground truth from the simulation. Because the freezes are random and queries numerous, users cannot anticipate them, and the scores reflect what they genuinely hold in mind. SAGAT reveals whether a dashboard actually supports understanding and anticipation, which preference ratings and task completion cannot.
steps: Conduct a goal-directed task analysis to list SA requirements at levels 1, 2 and 3 for the user's goals.
Build a realistic, scripted simulation or high-fidelity prototype with ground truth for every queried element.
Plan 3-6 freezes per session at random times, avoiding the first 3-5 minutes, each lasting up to about 2 minutes.
At each freeze, blank the display and administer a random subset of queries; record answers.
Score answers against ground truth per level and per requirement; compare designs with within-subject designs where possible.
Identify requirements with low accuracy and redesign displays to support them; retest.
outputs: SA accuracy scores by level and requirement, comparisons between design alternatives, and a list of poorly supported SA requirements.
useWhen: Dashboards, monitoring tools and operational interfaces where users must understand and anticipate changing situations.
avoidWhen: Static or transactional interfaces; use comprehension testing or usability testing. Avoid where a realistic simulation cannot be built.
whyLost: It needs simulation infrastructure and ground truth, which product teams rarely build. UX substitutes subjective dashboard satisfaction ratings.
whereToUse: Observability dashboards, trading terminals, fleet management, clinical monitoring, autonomous vehicle takeover interfaces.
example: A fleet operations dashboard is compared in a replayed day of data. With SAGAT, dispatchers using the new map view answer projection queries ('which vehicle will be late next?') correctly 71% of the time versus 44% on the list view.
sources: Endsley, Toward a theory of situation awareness in dynamic systems (1995), Human Factors
Endsley, Measurement of situation awareness in dynamic systems (1995), Human Factors
Endsley & Jones, Designing for Situation Awareness (2nd ed., 2011)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Endsley, M. R. (1995). Measurement of situation awareness in dynamic systems. Human Factors, 37(1), 65-84.

name: Situational Analysis
aka: Grounded theory after the postmodern turn
origin: Adele E. Clarke, 2005 (Situational Analysis: Grounded Theory After the Postmodern Turn)
summary: Extends grounded theory by mapping a whole situation, including human and nonhuman elements, social worlds, arenas and discursive positions, through situational, social-worlds and positional maps.
description: Situational Analysis (Adele Clarke, 2005) extends Grounded Theory by mapping the full situation — including nonhuman elements, discourses, and structural conditions — rather than focusing only on human actors and their meanings. It produces three types of maps: situational maps (all elements), social worlds/arenas maps (collective actors and their negotiations), and positional maps (discursive positions on key debates). Applied to UX: it reveals all the stakeholders, artefacts, and competing discourses shaping the product situation, not just the individual user's experience.
steps: Messy situational map: Brainstorm every element in the situation — human actors, nonhuman elements (artefacts, technologies, infrastructure), implicitly implied elements, symbolic elements, discursive constructs, political/economic factors. Put every element on the map regardless of apparent importance.
Ordered situational map: Organise the messy map into categories: individual human, collective human, discursive, nonhuman, political/economic, temporal/historical, spatial/geographic.
Social worlds/arenas map: Identify the collective actors (social worlds — those sharing a particular commitment or practice) and the arenas (sites of ongoing negotiation between those worlds).

Positional map: For each major controversy or debate in the situation: map out the positions that are taken. Each position occupies a location on axes defined by the key dimensions of the debate. This reveals which positions are represented, which are absent, and which might be silenced.
outputs: Messy and ordered situational maps, a social worlds and arenas map, positional maps of contested issues including unoccupied positions, and analytic memos.
useWhen: The problem space is complex and contested, involving many stakeholders, institutions, technologies, regulations and discourses, as in health systems, platforms or public services.
avoidWhen: You need to understand a single user group's task experience or have little time; use contextual inquiry or thematic analysis. For a lighter systems view, use Rich Pictures.
whyLost: It is a sophisticated sociological extension of grounded theory that UX rarely encounters, and its maps resemble stakeholder maps enough that its analytic depth is overlooked.
whereToUse: Healthcare and public service ecosystems, platform governance, AI policy and adoption, multi-sided marketplaces, and strategy research in regulated domains.
example: Exploring adoption of AI triage in GP surgeries, a team builds situational maps including regulators, clinical guidelines, liability discourse and legacy systems. The positional map reveals no actor voicing patient choice, an unoccupied position that shapes the service design.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
reference: Clarke, A. E. (2005). Situational Analysis: Grounded Theory After the Postmodern Turn. Sage.

name: Situational Motivation Scale (SIMS)
aka: Situational intrinsic and extrinsic motivation measure
origin: Guay, Vallerand and Blanchard (2000), within Vallerand's hierarchical model of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation; reviewed by Vallerand in Chapter 3 of the Handbook
summary: A short questionnaire, given straight after an activity, that measures why the person was doing it at that moment: intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, external regulation or amotivation.
description: Vallerand's hierarchical model separates motivation at three levels: global (personality), contextual (a life domain such as sport or work) and situational (a specific activity at a given moment). The Situational Motivation Scale measures the situational level. It asks why the person is currently engaged in the activity and scores four types: intrinsic motivation, identified regulation (doing it because it is valued), external regulation (doing it because of rewards or pressure) and amotivation. It has 16 items, and an introjected subscale is available. The scale was kept short so that it can be used in lab and field settings without overloading people. The Handbook reports studies showing that rewards, competition, feedback and choice change situational motivation, mostly through perceived competence, autonomy and relatedness. Contextual scales such as the Sport Motivation Scale measure the domain level, so both levels can be tracked over time. For UX the SIMS can show whether a feature, streak, badge or nudge shifts users from intrinsic or identified reasons towards external regulation, which predicts weaker persistence.
steps: Adapt the item stem to the task (for example 'Why are you currently doing this lesson?') and keep the four subscales intact.
Administer immediately after the task or session.
Score each subscale and, if wanted, a self-determination index weighting intrinsic and identified against external and amotivation.
Compare variants in an experiment, for example with and without a reward mechanic.
Repeat over sessions, and optionally add a contextual-level measure, to see whether situational changes build up.
Relate motivation profiles to retention or voluntary use in logs.
outputs: Subscale scores for intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, external regulation and amotivation per participant and condition.
useWhen: You are testing gamification, incentives, reminders or feedback designs and want to know what kind of motivation they create, not only how much use.
avoidWhen: Use is mandatory and the reason for it is not in question, or you can only ask one question.
whyLost: UX teams usually measure engagement through behaviour or satisfaction; self-determination theory is popular in gamification writing but its validated state measures have not crossed over.
whereToUse: Learning and language apps, fitness and health apps, gamified enterprise tools, onboarding flows, habit and productivity products.
example: A language app A/B tests a streak counter. Day-7 retention rises slightly, but SIMS scores show more external regulation and less intrinsic motivation in the streak group; the team tests a progress-mastery view instead before rolling out.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Vallerand, R. J. (2007) 'Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in sport and physical activity: a review and a look at the future', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 3.

name: Six Minds Contextual Interview and Analysis
origin: John Whalen, Design for How People Think (2019)
summary: Observe and interview people in context, then code every observation into six cognitive lenses and compare across participants to find segments and per-lens design issues.
description: Whalen treats an experience as several cognitive processes at once and reduces them to six: vision and attention, wayfinding, memory, language, decision making, and emotion.
