Fieldwork is a contextual interview: about 90-minute sessions in the participant's real setting, 8-12 people per user group, with the researcher sitting at roughly 90 degrees to see where the participant looks, probing what they look for, where they think they are, what past experience shapes expectations, which words they use, how they frame the decision, and what they hope for and fear. Analysis puts observations and quotes on notes, arranges them by participant, sorts them into six columns, and looks across participants within each lens for shared patterns, preferring groupings that hold across several lenses. Notes are filed by meaning, not by surface wording.
steps: Define user groups by role or lifestyle and recruit about 8-12 per group (24-40 overall for segmentation).
Run about 90-minute sessions in the participant's setting with one to three researchers, sitting at about 90 degrees to see gaze, and record unobtrusively.
Observe artefacts, interruptions and related tasks; use participants' words, ask why, and never demonstrate or teach.
Probe each lens: what they look for, where they think they are, what experiences shape expectations, what words mean, how they frame decisions, what they hope for and fear.
Write bite-sized quotes and observed actions on notes, arrange them by participant, then sort them into six columns, filing each by its most design-relevant component.
Look across participants within each lens for shared patterns, test each pattern against all data, and prefer groupings that hold across several lenses.
Write a psychographic profile per segment and route per-lens findings to the relevant specialists.
outputs: Six-column coded findings per participant, per-lens design issues, and psychographic audience segments.
useWhen: Discovery for complex decisions or journeys where perception, navigation, vocabulary, decision framing and emotion all matter, such as finance or e-commerce.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating the six minds as validated cognitive categories; they are a simplification with expected overlap. For narrow usability questions, standard testing is quicker.
whyLost: It is a recent consultancy framework known through one book and rarely run with its full fieldwork and sorting protocol.
whereToUse: Financial products, e-commerce and comparison journeys, enterprise tools with complex decisions, content and terminology work.
example: A credit-card team interviews 30 applicants at home and sorts observations into six lenses. A 'fearful and unsure' segment appears consistently in the emotion and decision columns, leading to a reassurance-first application flow.
reference: Whalen, J. (2019). Design for How People Think: Using Brain Science to Build Better Products. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Skill Acquisition Curve Design
origin: Kathy Sierra, 2015; drawing on Ericsson's deliberate practice
summary: Designs products around the user's progression to competence, mapping where users get stuck on the skill curve and reducing cognitive load to move them through it.
description: Kathy Sierra argues that users do not want better products so much as to be better at what the product enables. Skill acquisition curve design maps the progression from novice to competent user, identifying the 'suck zone' where effort is high and capability low and where most users abandon. Design interventions reduce cognitive resource drain, provide high-quality examples that train perception, structure deliberate practice with small chunks and immediate feedback, and show users progress in the skill rather than in the product. The method becomes rigorous when progression is operationalised with behavioural markers of competence, time-to-competence is measured across cohorts, and interviews explain why users stall at specific points.
steps: Map the target skill: what does 'expert user' look like? What do they know/do/feel that novices don't? Build a skill progression map: novice → competent → proficient → expert. For each stage, identify:
the beliefs that distinguish this stage,
the knowledge required,
the ability (can do it under real conditions). Design each product feature to move users up this map, not to make the product itself easier.
outputs: A skill progression map, identified 'suck zones' and drop-off points, perceptual and practice exercises, and metrics of time-to-competence.
useWhen: Complex tools (creative software, analytics, developer tools) where retention depends on users becoming capable, and onboarding beyond first-run tutorials.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple, single-use products where competence is immediate; then optimise for efficiency instead.
whyLost: Teams optimise for feature adoption and engagement metrics rather than user competence; Sierra's framing remained popular reading, not a practised method.
whereToUse: Professional tool design, learning product design, any product where user competence is the value proposition.
example: A data-visualisation SaaS maps how users progress from importing data to building dashboards, finds a plateau at calculated fields, and adds worked examples that halve time-to-first-dashboard.
sources: Badass: Making Users Awesome — Kathy Sierra
reference: Sierra K (2015) Badass: Making Users Awesome. O'Reilly Media

name: Skill-Rule-Knowledge Analysis
origin: Jens Rasmussen, 1983
summary: Classifies the cognitive control level a task demands (skill, rule or knowledge based) to predict error types and design displays that support each level.
description: Rasmussen's SRK framework distinguishes three levels of cognitive control. Skill-based behaviour is automatic and driven by perceptual signals; rule-based behaviour applies stored if-then rules triggered by recognised signs; knowledge-based behaviour is effortful reasoning about symbols and models in novel situations. Each level has characteristic errors and needs different interface support: skill-based tasks need direct manipulation and consistent spatial mappings; rule-based tasks need clear cues that match rules; knowledge-based tasks need representations of the system's functional structure. As a method, researchers analyse tasks and incidents to determine which level is in use at each step, often through observation and cognitive interviews, and then check that the interface supports that level. It underpins ecological interface design and Reason's GEMS error model.
steps: Decompose the task into steps using observation and interviews with experienced and novice users.
Classify each step as skill, rule or knowledge based by the cues used and the degree of deliberation.
Map known or observed errors to SRK levels (e.g. slips at skill level, misapplied rules, knowledge-based mistakes).
Assess whether the interface provides signals, signs or symbols appropriate to each level.
Redesign to support the right level, for example functional displays for knowledge-based fault diagnosis.
Test performance under both routine and novel scenarios to confirm support at each level.
outputs: SRK-classified task model, error-level mapping, interface support gaps and design recommendations.
useWhen: Expert and safety-critical tools where users shift between routine operation and novel problem solving, such as control rooms and clinical systems.
avoidWhen: Simple consumer tasks performed infrequently; standard task analysis or usability testing suffice.
whyLost: Extinct in UX: Academic cognitive engineering framework; rarely applied in practice.
whereToUse: Expert system design; safety-critical task design; error-prediction for cognitive states.
example: A network operations centre tool supported routine alarms well but outages required knowledge-based diagnosis. SRK analysis showed no view of service dependencies; adding a functional topology view reduced time to diagnose novel faults.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Information Processing and Human-Machine Interaction (Jens Rasmussen)
SHERPA: A Systematic Human Error Reduction and Prediction Approach (Embrey, 1986)
reference: Rasmussen, J. (1983). Skills, rules, and knowledge; signals, signs, and symbols, and other distinctions in human performance models. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC-13(3), 257-266.

name: Slice-Based Evaluation of ML Models
origin: Slice Finder by Chung, Kraska, Polyzotis, Tae and Whang (2019); popularised in production ML by Chip Huyen (2022)
summary: Evaluate a model separately on meaningful subsets of data to catch hidden subgroup failures, weak critical slices and Simpson's paradox reversals.
description: Overall metrics can hide a model that performs badly on a minority or more critical subgroup, and aggregation can reverse comparisons. Huyen's example: model A scores 98% and 80% on two groups (96.2% overall) and model B 95% on both, so A looks better overall but fails the second group. Slices come from three sources: domain heuristics (mobile versus desktop, browser, location, new versus returning users), error analysis by reading misclassified examples for patterns, and automated slice finders that generate candidates by beam search, clustering or decision trees, then prune and rank them. Each critical slice needs enough correctly labelled evaluation data. Slicing can also expose problems that are not about the model at all, such as poor results on mobile traced to a half-hidden button on small screens.
steps: Identify candidate slices from domain knowledge, including user groups, devices, locales and high-stakes cases.
Read misclassified examples to spot patterns that suggest further slices.
Optionally run an automated slice finder to generate, prune and rank slices by error and size.
Collect enough correctly labelled evaluation data for each critical slice.
Report performance per slice alongside the overall figure, and check for Simpson's paradox reversals between models.
Choose or improve models using sliced results, and investigate non-model causes such as interface problems.
outputs: Per-slice performance tables, a ranked list of weak or critical slices, and model selection decisions informed by them.
useWhen: Evaluating recommendation, search ranking, speech, vision or LLM features before launch and after model updates, especially where user groups differ in language, device or accessibility needs.
avoidWhen: Avoid slicing so finely that slices have too little labelled data to estimate performance; correct for multiple comparisons. For aggregate model quality use standard classifier evaluation.
whyLost: It is established in ML engineering and fairness work, but UX researchers seldom join model evaluation, so subgroup failures surface only as complaints.
whereToUse: AI assistants, speech recognition across accents, content moderation, credit and fraud models, health triage tools.
example: A voice assistant's intent model scores 94% overall, but slicing by accent shows 78% for Scottish English speakers. Error analysis finds a cluster of misheard place names, and the team adds targeted training data before a regional launch.
reference: Chung, Y., Kraska, T., Polyzotis, N., Tae, K. H. and Whang, S. E. (2019). Slice Finder: Automated data slicing for model validation. IEEE ICDE; Huyen, C. (2022). Designing Machine Learning Systems. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly, pp. 185-188.

name: SLIM (Success Likelihood Index Methodology)
origin: David Embrey (1986); AHP-weighted variant by Park and Lee (2008); ANP variant by De Ambroggi and Trucco (2011)
summary: Experts weight and rate performance-shaping factors for each task; the weighted Success Likelihood Index is calibrated to human error probabilities using anchor tasks.
description: SLIM is an expert-judgement human reliability analysis method. It assumes the probability of error on a task depends on the combined effect of performance-shaping factors (PSFs) such as time pressure, training or interface quality, which domain experts can identify and rate. Experts derive an independent set of PSFs, weight them (weights sum to 1) and rate each task on each PSF from 1 to 9, with higher values better. The weighted sum is the Success Likelihood Index. A log-linear calibration fitted to two or more reference tasks of known error probability turns SLIs into human error probabilities, with uncertainty bounds and checks of agreement between judges. It was the first HRA method to derive error probability from context, and it is fairly easy to run, but it gives little guidance on choosing PSFs, experts and anchors. AHP and ANP have been combined with it to set weights and handle PSF dependence.
steps: Define the tasks to assess and assemble a panel of domain experts.
Derive a set of independent PSFs that explain most variation in success likelihood.
Rank the PSFs and assign normalised weights summing to 1, directly or with AHP or ANP.
Rate each task on each PSF from 1 (worst, for example high time pressure) to 9 (best).
Compute SLI as the sum of weight times rating for each task.
Calibrate with log(HEP) = a x SLI + b fitted to at least two anchor tasks with known error probabilities, and convert each SLI.
Compute uncertainty bounds and check consistency between judges before using the estimates.
outputs: Human error probability estimates per task and the PSFs that most reduce success likelihood.
useWhen: Comparing error likelihood of tasks or design options in safety-critical interfaces where error data are scarce but experts are available.
avoidWhen: Avoid when no credible anchor tasks exist, since validity rests on them, or when PSFs are clearly interdependent; for task-step error prediction use THERP, and for qualitative error identification use SHERPA or Use FMEA.
whyLost: It is used in nuclear, chemical and offshore safety assessment, but UX teams rarely need quantified error probabilities and lack calibration data.
whereToUse: Medical device use-related risk analysis, control-room and aviation interfaces, comparing alarm or confirmation designs in high-stakes fintech operations.
example: For an infusion pump redesign, nurses and engineers rate programming tasks on six PSFs. Calibrated against two tasks with known incident rates, the dose-entry task has the highest estimated error probability, driven mainly by display legibility, which becomes the redesign priority.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
SHERPA: A Systematic Human Error Reduction and Prediction Approach (Embrey, 1986)
reference: Embrey, D. E. (1986). SLIM-MAUD: A computer-based technique for human reliability assessment. International Journal of Quality & Reliability Management; summarised in Salvendy, G. and Karwowski, W. (Eds.) (2021). Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.). Wiley, ch. 20, p. 547.

name: Small Multiples
origin: Edward Tufte, 1983/1990; Cleveland's trellis displays, 1990s
summary: Shows the same chart repeated across segments, conditions or time periods on a shared scale, so differences can be compared at a glance.
description: Small multiples, popularised by Edward Tufte, are series of small charts using identical design, axes and scales, each showing a different slice of the data: a segment, condition, location or time period. Because the design is constant, the eye reads the structure once and then attends only to differences, enabling rapid comparison across many groups without the tangle of overlaid lines. In UX research they suit comparing metrics across variants, markets, platforms or cohorts, and revealing which segment departs from the pattern. Rigour comes from a shared scale (or explicitly flagged exceptions), meaningful ordering of panels (by magnitude or logic rather than alphabet), minimal non-data ink, and clear labelling so each panel can be identified instantly.
steps: Identify any UX analysis with multiple conditions (users × tasks, designs × demographic groups, time points).
Convert: replace a single multi-series chart with N small charts, one per condition, at the same scale.
Arrange in a logical grid (e.g., 3 designs × 4 user segments = 12 small charts).
The visual structure makes differences and similarities immediately apparent.
Data-ink ratio: maximize by removing all repeated axes.
outputs: A grid of comparable charts with shared axes, visible segment differences and outliers, and a compact comparative view for reports and dashboards.
useWhen: Comparing a metric across many segments, variants, platforms, markets or periods, such as funnel shapes by country or task times by design variant.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there are only two series (overlay them), when panels need different scales to be readable, or when the audience needs a single headline; then highlight one comparison.
whyLost: Default dashboard tools favour single overloaded charts with many coloured lines; faceting requires deliberate design and is rarely taught to researchers.
whereToUse: Usability study findings visualization, longitudinal data presentation, A/B test result communication, segmentation analysis.
example: An e-commerce team plots checkout funnel drop-off for twelve markets as small multiples on a common scale; Brazil's panel alone shows a cliff at the address step, traced to postcode validation.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Tufte ER (1990) Envisioning Information. Graphics Press

name: SMEQ (Subjective Mental Effort Question)
origin: Zijlstra & van Doorn (1985), Delft University of Technology; online slider version by Sauro & Dumas (2009)
summary: A single post-task rating of mental effort on a 0 to 150 scale with calibrated verbal anchors, one of the most sensitive post-task measures.
description: The SMEQ is a vertical scale from 0 to 150 with nine verbal labels from "not at all hard to do" just above 0 to "tremendously hard to do" just above 110. The labels were placed by psychometric calibration rather than at equal intervals. On paper, participants draw a line across the 150 mm scale; online, they use a slider. Sauro and Dumas (2009) found it correlated 0.94 with the SEQ and strongly with completion time, completion rate and errors, and in their comparison it was at least as sensitive as the SEQ with small samples. It is free and works well when you want a finer-grained measure of task difficulty than a 7-point item.
steps: Present the SMEQ scale immediately after each task.
Ask participants to mark or slide to the level of mental effort the task required.
Record the value from 0 to 150.
Compare task means with confidence intervals, as for any continuous measure.
Look at tasks with high effort but successful completion: they are hidden friction.
outputs: A fine-grained mental-effort score per task.
useWhen: Comparing tasks or designs where small differences in difficulty matter.
avoidWhen: Survey contexts where a slider or drawn line is awkward; the SEQ is simpler.
whyLost: The SEQ is easier to explain and administer, and the SMEQ's Dutch work-psychology roots are little known in UX.
whereToUse: Lab and unmoderated task-based studies, cognitive load comparisons.
example: Two checkout designs have identical completion rates, but SMEQ effort falls from 62 to 35, showing the new design is easier even though both work.
reference: Sauro, J. & Dumas, J. (2009). Comparison of three one-question, post-task usability questionnaires. CHI 2009.

name: Snowball and Respondent-Driven Sampling
origin: Snowball sampling from Leo Goodman, 1961; respondent-driven sampling by Douglas Heckathorn, 1997
summary: Recruiting hard-to-reach participants through referrals from existing participants, with RDS adding coupons and chain tracking to correct network bias.
description: Snowball sampling uses participants' social networks to reach populations with no sampling frame: specialists, stigmatised groups, informal workers or small professional communities. Each participant refers one or two others who meet criteria. Its weakness is homophily: chains reproduce the characteristics of the seeds, producing homogeneous samples. Heckathorn's respondent-driven sampling formalises the process for HIV research among hidden populations, issuing a limited number of coupons per participant, tracking recruitment chains, recording network size, and using these to weight estimates so that, with long enough chains, results become less dependent on seeds. In qualitative UX the main safeguard is monitoring diversity after early interviews and introducing new seeds from other parts of the network.
steps: Recruit an initial seed participant who meets criteria and is known to others in the target population.
After each interview, ask for 1–2 referrals. Get permission to use their name.
RDS extension: Give each participant 2–3 formal recruitment coupons. Track chains. RDS attempts to correct network bias mathematically.
Monitor for homophily: After 5–7 interviews, check whether the sample is inadvertently homogeneous. If so, introduce new seeds from different network parts.
outputs: A recruited sample of hard-to-reach participants, referral chain maps, homophily checks, and, for RDS, network-size data for weighting.
useWhen: Populations without accessible lists or panels: niche professionals, informal economy workers, rare conditions, or communities wary of outsiders.
avoidWhen: When panels or customer lists can reach the population directly, or when independence of cases matters for statistical claims; use direct or probability sampling.
whyLost: Snowball referral is used informally, but RDS chain tracking and bias correction remain in public health research.
whereToUse: Gig and informal worker tools, rare disease patient apps, specialised B2B roles, security researchers, and emerging-market financial services.
example: Recruiting mobile money agents in rural Uganda, researchers start with three seeds in different districts and give each participant two coupons. After seven interviews they notice all agents share one distributor and add new seeds elsewhere.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Respondent-Driven Sampling: A New Approach to the Study of Hidden Populations (Heckathorn)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Heckathorn, D. D. (1997). Respondent-driven sampling: A new approach to the study of hidden populations. Social Problems, 44(2), 174-199.

name: SNR Interface Evaluation Framework
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Measures interface clarity as the share of essential elements on screen (element SNR) and the share of attention they receive (behavioural SNR), with thresholds linked to errors and success.
description: The framework defines signal as elements that directly support task completion (primary label, key button, required field) and noise as elements that distract, mislead or are irrelevant. Element SNR = signal elements / total visible actionable or reading elements; behavioural SNR = dwell on signal / total dwell, from eye-tracking, click heatmaps or cursor dwell. Low SNR correlates with misroutes and mistakes and often elevates slips and lapses, so auditing SNR before and after a redesign predicts whether clutter reduction will lower errors. Target bars are element SNR ≥ 0.60 and behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70. SNR also appears as a covariate in Cox models (HR 0.92 per +0.10) and as a multiplier in the Deviation Utility model, where a new form's utility is scaled by how legibly it presents its value. Rigour depends on a consistent signal inventory and counting rules across variants.
steps: Define a signal inventory: the essential elements for the focal task.
Count signal versus total visible actionable or reading elements per key screen, using the same counting rules for every variant (e.g. Alerts before: 9/20 = 0.45).
Collect attention data (eye-tracking or cursor dwell) and compute behavioural SNR (e.g. 35.1s / 60.3s = 0.58).
Compare against bars of element SNR ≥ 0.60 and behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70.
Pair SNR with error taxonomy and task outcomes in a side-by-side table (success, misroutes, coded errors).
Redesign to remove non-essential links and promote primary labels, then re-compute both SNRs (after: 12/18 = 0.67; 36.4s / 47.9s = 0.76).
Report SNR deltas alongside success, misroutes and coded errors.
outputs: Element and behavioural SNR baselines and deltas per screen, linked to success and error rates.
useWhen: When clutter, competing links or low salience of primary actions is suspected, and as a quick clarity metric stakeholders understand.
avoidWhen: When the problem is conceptual (wrong labels or mental model mismatch) rather than salience; use tree testing and mental-model interviews.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath (the 'SNR Interface Evaluation Framework'); signal-to-noise thinking exists in information design but is rarely quantified in UX.
whereToUse: Dashboards, fintech home screens, settings pages, enterprise consoles, AI product surfaces with many controls.
example: A redesign of a trading app's alerts screen raises element SNR from 0.45 to 0.67 and behavioural SNR from 0.58 to 0.76, while Mistake-coded errors on the navigation step fall from 39 to 18 per 100 sessions.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (Edward Tufte)
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy, Appendix A.2 and A.4.

name: SNR measurement
origin: Communications engineering, early 20th century; formalised in Shannon's channel capacity theorem, 1948
summary: Quantifies the ratio of task-relevant signal to irrelevant noise in a display, alert stream or notification channel, to show where meaning is being drowned.
description: In engineering, SNR is signal power divided by noise power, often in decibels (10 log10 S/N). Applied to interfaces it takes two forms. Physical SNR measures, for example, alarm loudness above ambient noise or luminance contrast of a target against its background. Informational SNR measures the proportion of actionable to non-actionable items in a stream: actionable alerts over total alerts, task-relevant pixels over total pixels, or relevant results over results shown. Both connect to Shannon's capacity theorem, which shows the information a channel can carry rises with log(1 + S/N). The method is rigorous when signal and noise are defined operationally before counting, and when measurements are taken in realistic conditions rather than in a quiet lab.
steps: Define what counts as signal (actionable, task-relevant) and noise (irrelevant, redundant, non-actionable) for the channel in scope.
For physical channels, measure levels in situ: alarm SPL versus ambient noise (aim for at least 10 dB above ambient), or luminance contrast (WCAG minimum 4.5:1 for text).
For informational channels, sample at least one representative week of alerts, notifications or results and code each item as signal or noise using two coders; target Cohen's kappa of 0.7 or higher.
Compute SNR per channel and per user role, and in decibels where useful.
Identify the largest noise contributors (Pareto: often 20% of alert types produce 80% of noise).
Remove, batch or demote noise sources and recompute SNR after the change.
outputs: SNR values per channel and role, a Pareto list of noise sources, and a before/after comparison.
useWhen: When users complain of overload or alarm fatigue; when dashboards or feeds feel cluttered; when evaluating notification strategy or search result quality.
avoidWhen: When the issue is discriminability between two similar signals rather than signal versus noise; use d' or ROC analysis instead.
whyLost: UX uses 'signal to noise' as a metaphor but rarely measures it; operationalising signal and noise requires explicit coding that teams skip.
whereToUse: Clinical alarms, observability and DevOps alerting, enterprise notifications, news feeds, AI assistant verbosity, and search results.
example: A surgical console shows 42 status messages per hour of which coders judge 5 actionable, an informational SNR of 0.13. Suppressing routine confirmations and batching device chatter raises it to 0.6, and surgeons' response time to genuine warnings falls by a third.
sources: Van Drongelen, W., Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent
reference: Shannon, C. E. (1949). Communication in the presence of noise. Proceedings of the IRE, 37(1), 10-21.

name: Social Impact Statement
donor: Public policy and environmental impact assessment
origin: Ben Shneiderman and Anne Rose, 1996
summary: An early, short, reviewable document stating a new system's goals, stakeholders, benefits, risks and safeguards, reviewed and enforced by a panel.
description: Modelled on environmental impact statements, the social impact statement makes anticipated impacts of a system public while change is still cheap. Shneiderman and Rose's outline has about twenty headings in three groups: describing the system (goals, stakeholders, benefits); addressing concerns (barriers, job changes and layoffs, security and privacy, accountability for misuse and failure, bias, individual rights against social benefit, centralisation, democratic principles, diverse access, keeping what works); and outlining the development process (schedule, decision process, stakeholder involvement, training, backups, migration and success measures). It is written early by a team that can include end users and managers, kept short enough for affected people to read, and submitted to a review panel such as a regulator, professional body or union that holds hearings, requests changes and later checks that actions match stated intentions.
steps: Decide whether the system's reach justifies a statement, for example public services, regulated industries or large workforces.
Draft it before schedule, requirements and budget are fixed, with a team that includes end users and managers.
Cover the system description, stakeholder benefits, concerns (jobs, privacy, accountability, bias, access, rights) and the development and migration plan with success measures.
Keep it short and readable for the people affected.
Submit it to a review panel and to affected groups; hold hearings and invite citizen or employee input.
Revise as requested, adopt it, and have the panel audit later that actions matched the stated intentions.
outputs: A reviewed impact statement, a list of stakeholder concerns with agreed mitigations, and success measures.
useWhen: Planning systems that affect many people's rights, jobs or access, especially government, workplace and AI decision systems.
avoidWhen: For small, low-stakes products where effort would be disproportionate, or where no panel can enforce it, since it then becomes paperwork. It can also raise fears or force compromises. For narrower ethics checks use Value-Sensitive Design or CHECk Ethical Checklists.
whyLost: No regulator required it, so it stayed a proposal in HCI textbooks; algorithmic and data protection impact assessments now partly fill the gap under other names.
whereToUse: Public digital services, AI and algorithmic decision systems, workplace monitoring tools, health records.
example: Before building an automated benefits eligibility tool, a government team drafts a social impact statement covering error appeals, caseworker de-skilling and accessibility, and a citizen panel requests a human review route before procurement.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Shneiderman, B. and Rose, A. (1996). Social impact statements: engaging public participation in information technology design. Proc. CQL '96, ACM, 90-96.

name: Social Media and Digital Trace Data Analysis
donor: Internet research and computational social science
origin: Internet research tradition from the late 1990s; formalised in social media research methods in the 2010s
summary: Systematically samples and codes naturally occurring online communication such as reviews, forums, social posts and tickets, as unprompted evidence of user experience.
description: Users constantly describe their experience without being asked: in app store reviews, Reddit threads, community forums, social posts and support tickets. This data avoids researcher reactivity but brings its own biases, since vocal, extreme and platform-specific users dominate. Rigorous analysis starts with an ethical assessment (public versus semi-public spaces, identifiability, platform terms), then defines a sampling strategy, such as purposive sampling of extreme cases or stratified random sampling across time and rating. Posts are coded in their conversational context, because a reply means little without the thread. Findings are treated as hypotheses about the experience and triangulated with primary research, never as population estimates.
steps: Ethical framework first: Is this data public or semi-public? Are users identifiable? Apply the Public Benefit / No Harm test.
Sampling strategy: For large corpora: purposive sampling (extreme negative reviews, specific terms). For small corpora: total population analysis.
Qualitative coding: Apply thematic analysis or content analysis. Code for: expressed needs, frustrations, workarounds, emotional valence, social context.
Context preservation: Always code text in its conversational context — a sentence means something different in a heated complaint thread than in a first review.
Triangulate with primary research: Social media data reveals unprompted opinions but lacks context. Always triangulate with interviews or observations.
outputs: A documented corpus and sampling frame, coded themes in context, representative excerpts (anonymised), trend patterns over time, and hypotheses for primary research.
useWhen: You need fast, low-cost insight into real complaints and language, want to track reaction to a release, or are researching a domain where recruiting is hard but online discussion is rich.
avoidWhen: You need representative prevalence estimates or insight into silent or non-online users; use surveys or field research. Avoid when data involves vulnerable communities without careful ethical review.
whyLost: It survived and grew because data is abundant and cheap and social listening tools industrialised it, though the sampling and context discipline is often skipped.
whereToUse: App store and marketplace products, release monitoring, competitor research, community-driven products, and health or finance topics with active online communities.
example: After a banking app redesign, a researcher samples 400 one- and two-star reviews stratified by week and codes them in context. Complaints about 'missing' features turn out to be about relocated navigation, which follow-up usability tests confirm.
sources: Advances in Longitudinal HCI Research (Karapanos et al., 2021)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
Research on the Construction of Personas Model Based on K-Means Clustering Algorithm (Quan et al., 2015)
UX Methodology Study by Data Analysis (Lee & Park, 2021)
reference: Sloan, L. & Quan-Haase, A. (eds.) (2017). The SAGE Handbook of Social Media Research Methods. Sage.

name: Social Network Analysis (SNA) for Collaborative Tool UX
origin: Jacob Moreno (1934, sociometry); Wasserman and Faust (1994)
summary: Maps who interacts with whom through a product to find bottlenecks, structural holes and how features diffuse across an organisation.
description: SNA models actors as nodes and interactions as edges, computing measures such as degree centrality, betweenness centrality (how often a node lies on paths between others), clustering coefficients and structural holes (gaps a node bridges). The treatise's transfer: map how information and decisions flow through a team using a collaborative tool. Which users are structural bottlenecks? Where are structural holes the design fails to bridge? Which features are adopted in clusters but not diffused? Network analysis reveals organisational topology to which individual-level UX research is blind. Data can come from product logs (mentions, shares, comments) or surveys, and ethics and privacy require care.
steps: Define actors and the relation of interest (messages, shares, approvals, mentions).
Extract edges from logs or collect via survey with consent and privacy safeguards.
Build the network and compute centrality, clustering and community structure.
Identify bottlenecks, isolates, bridges and feature adoption clusters.
Interview selected nodes (bridges, isolates) to interpret structure.
Design interventions (routing, visibility, shared spaces) and re-measure the network.
outputs: Network maps, centrality metrics, community and diffusion analysis, design interventions.
useWhen: Collaboration, communication and enterprise tools; design system or feature adoption across teams.
avoidWhen: Single-user products, or when interaction data cannot be collected ethically.
whyLost: Network science sits in sociology and data science; UX research focuses on individuals.
whereToUse: Slack-like tools, document collaboration, enterprise approvals, design system adoption studies.
example: SNA of approval flows in a procurement tool shows one finance manager on 64% of paths; adding delegation rules cuts median approval time from 4 days to 1.5.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Wasserman S & Faust K (1994) Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications
Borgatti SP et al. (2009) Network analysis in the social sciences. Science 323:892-895
reference: Wasserman S & Faust K (1994) Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications. Cambridge University Press.

name: Social Representations Research
origin: Serge Moscovici (1961); Herzlich (1973); Jodelet (1991); Duveen and Lloyd; Flick (2006); Foster (2007)
summary: Compare how different groups know and talk about an object, using triangulated interviews, focus groups, observation and media analysis to map shared everyday knowledge.
description: Social representations are the shared, everyday knowledge through which groups make an unfamiliar object familiar, as in Moscovici's study of how psychoanalysis was understood in French society. Research examines their content, their social distribution across groups, and their development: microgenesis in interaction, sociogenesis through media and ontogenesis in individuals. Qualitative designs are comparative, sampling groups expected to differ, and use sensitising concepts and triangulation: episodic interviews that combine narratives with question-answer sequences for knowledge, focus groups for interaction, ethnography for practices and taken-for-granted elements, and media or online analysis for sociogenesis. A ten-step design guide anchors the approach. A key lesson is that what people say may differ from what they do: in Jodelet's village study, residents denied that mental illness was contagious yet washed lodgers' crockery separately.
steps: Identify an issue and develop a research question about how an object is understood.
Define the object whose representations will be studied.
Decide who carries the representations: groups expected to differ, or documents and media.
Build a comparative design across those groups and sample their members.
Choose methods for each aspect: episodic interviews for knowledge, observation for practices, focus groups for interaction, media analysis for sociogenesis.
Analyse in a way that keeps the social representations stance, comparing content and structure across groups.
Write up emphasising differences between groups and contradictions between talk and practice.
Reflect on your own relation to the issue and the people studied.
outputs: Typologies of representations of an object, their distribution across groups, and contradictions between talk and practice.
useWhen: Launching or explaining a new technology or concept (AI, crypto, telehealth) whose meaning varies between groups and shapes adoption.
avoidWhen: Individual mental models of how an interface works; use mental model interviews. For quick attitude measurement across groups use a survey.
whyLost: It is a European social psychology tradition, little known in Anglo-American HCI, which framed similar questions as attitudes or mental models.
whereToUse: Emerging technologies, health and risk communication, financial products, cross-cultural market entry, public-sector digital services.
example: A telehealth provider compares how retirees, young parents and GPs represent 'seeing a doctor online' through episodic interviews, focus groups and press coverage, finding retirees anchor it to call-centre triage, which explains low uptake.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
reference: Flick, U. and Foster, J. 'Social representations', in Willig, C. and Stainton Rogers, W. (eds.) (2008) The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology. London: SAGE.

name: Social-Domain Criterion-Judgement Interview
aka: Domain criterion-judgement interview with neutral-faced scenario drawings
origin: Elliot Turiel (1983), with Nucci (1981) and Smetana (1981); emotion attribution after Arsenio (1988)
summary: Participants judge single-domain acts against criteria (wrong without a rule, if authority allowed it, elsewhere) to reveal whether they treat a norm as moral, conventional or personal.
description: Social domain theory holds that people distinguish moral matters (harm, fairness, rights), conventional matters (manners, dress, forms of address) and personal matters (choice of friends, recreation). Participants hear brief scenarios, each involving only one domain, and judge the act's acceptability. Criterion questions then ask whether it would still be wrong if there were no rule, if an authority permitted it, if everyone agreed, or if another culture accepted it, and how serious it is. Justifications are coded as harm, welfare, fairness, rights, convention or personal choice. Moral judgements prove non-contingent across many cultures, from age three, while conventional ones are contingent. A variant uses neutral-faced drawings and asks how the actor, recipient and observer feel. For UX, the method shows whether users treat a product norm (data sharing, community rules, AI behaviour) as a matter of ethics, etiquette or personal choice.
steps: Write short scenarios, each involving only one domain, since mixed-domain acts confound judgements.
Ask whether the act is acceptable and how serious it is.
Ask the criterion questions: wrong without a rule, wrong if an authority allowed it, wrong if everyone agreed, wrong in another place or culture.
For emotion attribution, show neutral-faced drawings and ask how each party feels.
Ask for justifications and code them (harm, fairness, rights, convention, personal choice) with two coders.
Compare judgement patterns across domains, scenarios and participant groups.
outputs: Domain classification of judgements, justification codes and contingency profiles per scenario and group.
useWhen: You need to know whether users regard a rule or behaviour as a moral issue, a convention or a personal choice, for example in community guidelines, privacy or AI conduct.
avoidWhen: Your scenarios inevitably mix domains, or you need behavioural prediction; use vignette surveys or field observation instead.
whyLost: It is a standard paradigm in moral development research that never crossed into UX, where ethics research relies on attitude surveys.
whereToUse: Trust and safety policy, community moderation rules, privacy defaults, AI assistant behaviour and cross-cultural products.
example: A social platform asks users whether reposting a friend's photo without asking would be wrong if the platform allowed it. Most say yes, treating it as a moral harm rather than etiquette, which supports a consent prompt rather than a settings toggle.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
reference: Turiel, E. (1983). The Development of Social Knowledge: Morality and Convention. Cambridge University Press.

name: Socio-organisational Church-Turing analysis
aka: Process, data, placeholders and triggers analysis
origin: Alan Dix (trigger analysis papers, 1990s to 2000s); summarised in Dix et al. (2022)
summary: Analyse an organisation as if it were a computer, locating where its processes, data, current progress (placeholders) and triggers are held, physically and digitally.
description: If organisations process information, they must contain the same structural elements as a computer: a program (formal and unwritten processes), data (files, databases and knowledge in people's heads), a program counter or placeholder (how the organisation knows where it is in each piece of work) and initiative (the interrupts and triggers that start the next step). Placeholders are often physical, such as a half-completed form on a desk or a tick on a printed list. The night-time question asks how work resumes in the morning after everyone has gone home. Digitisation commonly removes physical placeholders and triggers without replacing them, which is why new systems silently drop work. The lens shares vocabulary with distributed cognition but focuses on state and initiative.
steps: Identify the formal written processes and the unwritten ones staff simply know.
Locate data held physically, digitally and only in people's heads.
For each piece of work, ask how the organisation knows where it is: to-do lists, ticks, the location of documents, flags in systems.
Ask the night-time question: how does work restart in the morning after everyone has left?
Identify what triggers each next step: arrival of a document, a time, a message, a person noticing.
Note risks where staff departure or digitisation would remove a placeholder or trigger, and design explicit replacements.
outputs: A map of process, data, state and initiative across people, paper and systems, with a list of fragile placeholders and triggers.
useWhen: Digitising a paper or informal process, replacing a legacy system, or diagnosing why work gets lost between steps.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a full model of organisational behaviour; organisations are distributed and not lock-step. For detailed cognitive work use distributed cognition analysis or work modelling.
whyLost: It appears mainly in Dix's own writing and has no packaged procedure or tooling, so it is rarely operationalised.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflow and case-management systems, public-sector digitisation, healthcare handovers and back-office automation.
example: An insurer replacing paper claim files finds that adjusters knew a claim was waiting by the folder sitting in a specific tray. The new system lacked any equivalent cue, so the team adds an explicit awaiting-action queue with time-based triggers.
reference: Dix, A., Gill, S., Ramduny-Ellis, D. & Hare, J. (2022). TouchIT: Understanding Design in a Physical-Digital World. Oxford University Press, pp. 120-123.

name: Socio-Technical Walkthrough
origin: Thomas Herrmann (SeeMe notation and STWT); extended by Kacmaz, Herrmann and Jelonek (2020)
summary: Facilitated workshops in which stakeholders build and review a semi-structured socio-technical process diagram step by step, answering prepared questions at each activity.
description: The socio-technical walkthrough lets stakeholders with no modelling background create and inspect process models of work together. A facilitator prepares a starting diagram in the SeeMe notation, which represents activities, roles and entities and deliberately allows vagueness and incompleteness. In the workshop the facilitator explains the notation, walks through the process step by step and asks prepared questions at each activity, such as what information or tool support it needs, inserting answers into the live diagram so all perspectives are combined. Unresolved disagreements are represented as vague or incomplete elements rather than forced to closure. Diagrams are refined over several workshops until stakeholders accept them, and the method reveals hidden problems and redundancies. Kacmaz et al. added a converter from SeeMe to BPMN for wider audiences.
steps: Prepare an initial SeeMe diagram of the process, or reuse the result of a previous workshop.
Prepare a question set for each activity, for example needed information, tools, responsibilities and exceptions.
Explain the notation briefly to participants at the start of the workshop.
Walk through the diagram step by step, asking the prepared questions and inserting contributions into the diagram as they arise.
Represent unresolved disagreements with vague or incomplete elements and note them for follow-up.
Repeat in further workshops until stakeholders accept the model; optionally convert it to BPMN for developers and managers.
outputs: An agreed socio-technical process model showing activities, roles and entities, plus a list of problems, redundancies and open issues.
useWhen: Introducing or redesigning collaborative systems where work processes, roles and tools must be negotiated among stakeholders.
avoidWhen: When the facilitator cannot manage conflict or keep up with a constantly changing diagram, or when the process is simple. For observed work practice rather than negotiated models use Contextual Inquiry or Process Mining.
whyLost: It is tied to a German CSCW research group and a niche notation, so it never spread beyond socio-technical systems research.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflow tools, healthcare and public administration process redesign, ERP and case management rollouts.
example: A council introducing digital planning applications runs three walkthroughs with clerks, inspectors and supervisors; at the quality-control step, questions reveal that inspectors re-key data from a separate system, which becomes a priority integration.
sources: Human Interface and the Management of Information (Yamamoto & Mori, 2020)
reference: Kacmaz, U., Herrmann, T. and Jelonek, M. (2020). SeeMe2BPMN: extending the socio-technical walkthrough with BPMN. In Yamamoto, S. and Mori, H. (eds) HIMI 2020, Part I, LNCS 12184. Springer, pp. 72-84.

name: Sociocognitive Pathology Analysis
aka: Generic tasks, discourse patterns and power-trust analysis
origin: Alistair Sutcliffe, in Hollnagel (2003), ch. 23
summary: Anticipate sociotechnical failure by walking checklists of cognitive, communication and social pathologies over task, discourse and power-trust models, turning each risk into a requirement.
description: Sutcliffe's method models a work system at three levels and applies a checklist of known pathologies to each. Work is described with scenarios and reusable generic task templates; cognitive pathologies, organised by skill, rule and knowledge levels, are checked against each task and countermeasures are added as requirements. Communication is modelled with discourse patterns and checked for communication pathologies such as missing acknowledgement. Finally, power and trust relationships between agents are modelled in an i*-style dependency view and checked for social pathologies. The same models are then used to compare alternative designs, for example different allocations of roles between people and automation. Its strength is breadth: it brings human error, communication breakdown and organisational politics into one requirements exercise, though the pathology lists are judgement aids, not validated predictors.
steps: Model the work with scenarios and generic task templates.
Apply the cognitive pathology checklist (skill, rule and knowledge levels) to each task and record countermeasures as requirements.
Model communication between agents with discourse patterns and apply the communication pathology checklist.
Model power and trust dependencies between agents and apply the social pathology checklist.
Attach failure-point warnings and countermeasures to the requirements specification.
Use the models to compare alternative designs or role allocations.
outputs: Requirements annotated with failure-point warnings and countermeasures; comparison of design alternatives on anticipated pathologies.
useWhen: Requirements work for socio-technical systems where human error, coordination and organisational trust can all cause failure, such as control rooms, clinical workflows or human-AI teaming.
avoidWhen: The checklists are not predictive models; for quantified error risk use THERP or CREAM, and for single-user error prediction use SHERPA.
whyLost: It sits between requirements engineering and human factors and never had tool support or training outside academic HCI, so practitioners use separate error and stakeholder methods instead.
whereToUse: Clinical decision support, operations centres, AI-assisted moderation or triage teams, enterprise workflow redesign.
example: For an AI triage assistant in a hospital call centre, the analysis flags a rule-level pathology (habitual acceptance of suggestions), a discourse gap (no read-back of escalations) and a trust problem (nurses distrusting a system owned by IT), each turned into a requirement.
reference: Sutcliffe, A. (2003). In Hollnagel, E. (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum, ch. 23, pp. 549-576.

name: Sociometric Badge Sensing
aka: Sociometric badge sensing of team interaction
Social signal sensing with wearable sensors
origin: Alex Pentland's group, MIT Media Lab (Olguín et al., 2008-2009), later commercialised by Humanyze
summary: Team members wear ID-sized sensors recording speech activity, movement, face-to-face contact and proximity, from which interaction features are computed and related to team activity.
description: Sociometric badges contain a microphone, infrared sensor, Bluetooth detector and accelerometer, capturing speech activity (not content), body motion, face-to-face interaction and proximity. From these streams researchers compute interaction features: turn-taking (speech within 10 seconds of another segment), successful and unsuccessful interruptions, a contribution index ((speaking - listening)/(speaking + listening)), and rotating leadership from changes in betweenness centrality. In a design-thinking study, 18 people in four teams wore badges during working hours over a four-week sprint, gave daily self-reports of time in each activity mode, and a support vector machine predicted the mode from badge features with leave-one-out cross-validation. The approach turns team collaboration into measurable behaviour without observers. Limits include small samples, vendor-processed data of uncertain accuracy, specific hardware and significant privacy and consent obligations.
steps: Agree purpose, consent and data governance with all participants, including what is recorded (speech activity, not content).
Issue badges to be worn during working hours, excluding breaks, over the study period.
Collect ground truth with short daily questionnaires, such as percentage of time in each activity mode.
Process raw data into speech, motion and proximity measures.
Compute interaction features such as turns, interruptions, contribution index and rotating leadership.
Train and validate classifiers (for example an RBF SVM with leave-one-out cross-validation against a random baseline), or relate features to outcomes.
Interpret differences in features by mode or team with qualitative follow-up.
outputs: Interaction feature time series per person and team, network measures, and predictive models of team context or activity.
useWhen: You study co-located collaboration, meetings or workplace interaction at scale and need behavioural measures without continuous observers.
avoidWhen: Trust or consent is fragile, the team is remote, or a few observed sessions would do; use ethnographic observation or interaction logs instead.
whyLost: It moved into people analytics and computational social science; privacy concerns and specific hardware kept it out of UX research.
whereToUse: Collaboration and meeting tools, hybrid workplace design, design-team process research and hospital or control-room teamwork.
example: A collaboration software company badges two product teams for three weeks. Unsuccessful interruptions double in hybrid meetings, informing a 'raise hand' queue for in-room participants.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Pentland, A. (2008). Honest Signals: How They Shape Our World. MIT Press; Kohl, S., Graus, M., & Lemmink, J. G. A. M. (2022). Context is key: Mining social signals for automatic task detection in design thinking meetings. DUXU 2022, LNCS 13321, pp. 12-27. Springer.

name: Sociometric nomination and rating
aka: Sociometric nomination and rating (acceptance, rejection, perceived popularity)
Sociometric nomination and rating with photo boards for young children
origin: Jacob Moreno, 1934 (sociograms); Asher et al., 1979 (rating scales for young children); Bukowski, Cillessen and colleagues
summary: Members of a bounded group nominate or rate one another on liking, friendship, popularity or roles, and the counts are scored into acceptance, rejection, status classes and networks.
description: Sociometry asks members of a bounded group (class, team, community) about each other. Friendship nominations, checked for reciprocity, give mutual friendships. Like and dislike nominations yield social preference (liked minus disliked) and impact (liked plus disliked) scores and five status classes: popular, rejected, neglected, controversial and average. A rating variant has everyone rate every member 1-5. Perceived popularity uses most and least popular nominations, corrected for group size. Role nominations (such as the Revised Class Play) capture behavioural reputation. Preschoolers are trained on a 3-point scale and point to photos. Reliability rises with participation; reputation nominations stay reliable at lower participation than liking nominations. Unlimited nominations and short, randomised lists avoid alphabetical bias. Nearly the whole group must consent, because nominated non-consenters cannot be used, and reputations lag behaviour change.
steps: Define the bounded group and secure consent from nearly all members, with ethical approval for peer judgements.
Give each member a roster or photo board in randomised order; for young children, train them on a 3-point scale first.
Collect nominations (friends, liked, disliked, most and least popular, behavioural roles), allowing unlimited nominations in large groups, or collect 1-5 ratings of every member.
Count nominations received and check reciprocity for mutual friendships.
Derive preference and impact scores, classify status, and compute perceived popularity corrected for group size.
Combine with network analysis to describe group structure and how it changes over time.
outputs: Per-person acceptance, rejection, preference, impact, popularity and mutual-friend counts; status classes; a nomination network.
useWhen: When a product serves a bounded social group (classroom, team, community) and you need to understand its social structure, isolation or influence before designing collaborative or social features.
avoidWhen: Avoid where consent from nearly the whole group is impossible, or where negative nominations could harm members; consider positive-only nominations or Social Network Analysis (SNA) for Collaborative Tool UX from logs.
whyLost: It remains central in developmental and educational psychology, but UX rarely studies bounded groups directly and ethics review of peer judgements is demanding.
whereToUse: Classroom and edtech tools, team collaboration software, community platforms, workplace social features, multiplayer games.
example: Before launching group projects in a classroom app, a research team runs positive-only nominations in 12 classes and finds 9% of pupils receive none; the app's grouping algorithm is changed to avoid isolating them.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
reference: Moreno, J. L. (1934). Who Shall Survive? A New Approach to the Problem of Human Interrelations. Washington, DC: Nervous and Mental Disease Publishing; Rubin, K. H., Bukowski, W. M., & Bowker, J. C. (2015). Children in peer groups. In Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 4, pp. 175-222.

name: Solomon Four-Group Design
aka: Pre-experimental and quasi-experimental designs (Campbell and Stanley)
origin: Richard Solomon, 1949
summary: Combines pretest-posttest and posttest-only groups to estimate an intervention's effect and whether the pretest itself changed responses.
description: Campbell and Stanley classified designs by how well they rule out alternative explanations. Pre-experimental designs (one-shot case study, one-group pretest-posttest, static-group comparison) are weakest: a before-after comparison faces history, maturation, regression to the mean, testing, instrumentation, cyclical change, attrition and chance, and a paired t-test only addresses chance. True experiments add random assignment and control groups (pretest-posttest control, Solomon four-group, posttest-only). Quasi-experiments use natural groups (non-equivalent control group, time-series, multiple time-series). Embellishments strengthen weak designs: a pre-pretest giving a dry-run with no treatment, and a non-equivalent dependent variable affected by the same threats but not the treatment. Non-equivalent groups can be analysed with change scores, ANCOVA, matching or propensity scores, all vulnerable to unmeasured differences. In UX, 'before and after' studies are common but the threat vocabulary is usually missing.
steps: Define the intervention, the pretest and posttest measures.
Randomly assign participants to the four groups, balancing group sizes.
Administer pretests to groups 1 and 2 only; deliver the intervention to groups 1 and 3.
Administer posttests to all groups under identical conditions.
Analyse posttest scores with a 2x2 ANOVA (treatment x pretest) and check the interaction for sensitisation.
Use pretest data from groups 1 and 2 for gain analysis only if no sensitisation is found.
outputs: Estimates of treatment effect, pretest effect and pretest-by-treatment interaction.
useWhen: Evaluating interventions on attitudes, awareness or knowledge where pretesting may prime participants.
avoidWhen: Behavioural outcomes unaffected by measurement, or when sample size cannot support four groups.
whyLost: UX teams run before-after comparisons constantly, but the design typology and named threats are taught in social science, not UX, so the rigour is lost.
whereToUse: Security awareness features, privacy dashboards, financial literacy tools, AI explanation evaluations.
example: Evaluating a privacy dashboard, the team finds that pretested participants reported much higher awareness gains than posttest-only participants: the pretest itself explained half of the apparent effect.
sources: Solomon, An extension of control group design (1949), Psychological Bulletin
Campbell & Stanley, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Research (1966)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Solomon, R. L. (1949). An extension of control group design. Psychological Bulletin, 46(2), 137-150.

name: Solution Prototype (design-hacked key-experience prototype)
origin: Jaime Levy (2015), earlier called the five-screen MVP
summary: Build the fewest realistic-looking screens showing the key experiences, the value-proposition outcome and pricing, by collaging screens from other products into a linear prototype for interviews.
description: Customers struggle to read wireframes, so Levy's solution prototype looks real without being pixel-perfect or coded. Its screen framework is fixed: a setup screen (landing page or dashboard), one to three screens each for the first and second key experiences, a screen showing the result of a successful value-proposition transaction, and a pricing screen (or sample ads if ad-funded). Screens are design-hacked by mashing up images from competitors, influential products and stock imagery, pasted into a presentation tool and exported as a PDF that participants swipe through on a tablet. Before testing, each screen is reality-checked against the Business Model Canvas's key partners, activities and resources: where does inventory or supply come from, can a total price actually be generated. The prototype is then used in guerrilla interviews and adjusted between sessions. It is a learning tool, not a deliverable for developers.
steps: Outline the screens from the storyboard: setup, key experience 1, key experience 2, value-proposition result, pricing.
Collage each screen from existing products and stock images so it looks real (typically five to eight screens).
Assemble the screens in a presentation tool and export a linear PDF for a tablet.
Write feasibility questions for each screen against key partners, activities and resources.
Test in short guerrilla interviews with target customers, letting them swipe and talk.
Adjust screens between sessions and retest with a few more customers until the value proposition and price are understood.
outputs: A linear, clickless realistic prototype (PDF) and a list of business-model feasibility questions.
useWhen: Use when testing whether a new product concept and its price make sense to customers before any design system or code exists.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the question is detailed usability of an interaction; build an interactive prototype and run Usability Testing. A collage borrowed from rivals can bias reactions towards their brand. For demand evidence use Fake door, painted door and smoke tests.
whyLost: It survived because realistic, quickly assembled prototypes became standard in lean and sprint practice, where the Design Sprint's assembled prototype plays the same role.
whereToUse: Start-up concept validation, marketplace and platform ideas, new business lines, pitch preparation.
example: A team testing 'Airbnb for weddings' builds eight screens from Airbnb listings, a TV-package style bundle screen and a booking screen borrowed from a retailer. After a couple asks how to book a venue tour, a tour-booking screen is added for the next sessions.
reference: Levy, J. (2015). UX Strategy: How to Devise Innovative Digital Products that People Want. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 159-174.

name: Sound Design Review Checklist
aka: Sound interaction and contextual review checklist
origin: Amber Case and Aaron Day (2018)
summary: Inspection checklists that review every product sound for purpose, trigger, urgency, context, missed-notification backup, inclusion and real-world listening conditions.
description: Products accumulate beeps, chimes and spoken prompts that are rarely reviewed as a system. Case and Day offer two checklists. At design time each sound, taken from an audio map of product states, is checked for purpose (is sound needed at all), trigger, information and urgency, the product's location relative to the user, what happens if the notification is missed and whether another sense backs it up, whether it can interrupt others or play at the wrong time, durability when heard many times a day, and inclusivity. After contextual testing a final checklist groups faults under Sound (distortion, pitch, volume, cannot be turned off), Time (ill-timed, mismatched with the interface, duration, frequency), Attention (urgency, no reason, interrupts others), Inclusion, and Conditions such as noisy places, other rooms, transit or poor connectivity.
steps: Build an audio map listing every product state that produces or could produce sound.
For each state, answer the design-time questions: purpose, trigger, information and urgency, location, missed-notification backup, context, durability and inclusivity.
Test sounds in real conditions: quiet and loud places, another room, in transit, in a bag, at night, with poor connectivity.
Test durability by playing each sound repeatedly over a full day.
Run the final checklist under Sound, Time, Attention, Inclusion and Conditions and record failures per state.
Feed failures into redesign of sounds, settings (adjust, change, turn off) or modality.
outputs: A list of sound faults per product state and settings requirements for adjusting, changing or turning sounds off.
useWhen: Designing or auditing products with notifications, alarms, earcons or voice prompts, from apps to appliances.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for listening tests when perceived quality matters; use the MUSHRA Listening Test or Psychoacoustic Principles in Audio UX Design.
whyLost: Sound is rarely owned by UX teams, so systematic sound review stays with specialist sound designers.
whereToUse: Smart home devices, medical and fitness wearables, cars, payment terminals, messaging apps.
example: A smart-oven team audits its 11 sounds. The 'preheated' chime cannot be heard from the next room and has no visual or phone backup, so a push notification is added.
reference: Case, A. and Day, A. (2018). Designing with Sound: Fundamentals for Products and Services. O'Reilly Media, pp. 132-134, 185-186.

name: Source-monitoring test
origin: Marcia K. Johnson and colleagues (source-monitoring framework), 1993
summary: A recognition test that asks not only whether an item was encountered but where it came from, measuring source accuracy and misattribution separately from familiarity.
description: Source monitoring is the set of processes by which people attribute the origin of remembered information. Typical confusions include imagined versus perceived, intended versus done, heard about versus witnessed, and one channel or time versus another. In the standard test, participants study items in two formats (for example pictures and words). At test they see words naming items previously shown as pictures, words previously shown as words, and new words. In the source condition they must say where each item came from; in the old/new condition they only judge familiarity. Comparing the two isolates source judgement from recognition, and Johnson's work shows more prefrontal activity for source decisions. Children, older adults and people with prefrontal damage make more source errors. For UX it measures whether users can tell which channel, agent or person told them something, which matters for trust and attribution.
steps: Present study items from two or more sources or formats, such as an AI assistant versus a human agent, or email versus in-app.
At test, show items from each source plus new items in random order.
In the source condition, ask participants to identify the source of each item.
In a comparison condition, ask only whether the item is old or new.
Compute recognition accuracy and source accuracy, and tabulate confusions in a source-by-response matrix.
Compare source accuracy across designs, for example with and without source labels or avatars.
outputs: Old/new accuracy, source accuracy, and the pattern of source confusions.
useWhen: Users receive information from several channels or agents and you must know whether they can attribute it correctly, for example AI versus human advice or official versus user-generated content.
avoidWhen: Only overall recall matters; use free recall and recognition testing. The book gives no scoring formula, so define it in advance.
whyLost: It remains a cognitive and forensic memory paradigm; UX studies of provenance tend to ask users directly about trust rather than testing source memory.
whereToUse: AI disclosure and labelling, multichannel customer service, news and social feeds, health information, notification channels.
example: A telehealth service tests whether patients remember which advice came from the chatbot and which from the clinician. Source accuracy is near chance without avatars and much higher with distinct visual styles, informing the redesign.
reference: Johnson, M. K., Hashtroudi, S., & Lindsay, D. S. (1993). Source monitoring. Psychological Bulletin, 114, 3-28.

name: Space syntax analysis
origin: Bill Hillier and colleagues, Bartlett School of Architecture, University College London, from the 1970s
summary: Represent a building or street layout as a graph of lines of sight and compute each space's integration (centrality by turnings) to predict where people move, gather and get lost.
description: Space syntax holds that the human sense of distance in a city or building follows lines of sight and turnings, not straight-line or travel-time distance. The layout is divided into convex spaces, covered by the fewest and longest axial lines (guided by isovists), and the intersections are converted into a graph. Each line's mean depth (turnings to all others) gives its integration value: more integrated spaces are more central. Centrality maps correlate closely with movement and with the density of shops and meeting places; Berlin analysed with and without the Wall anticipated how busy areas shifted after reunification. Buildings are analysed the same way to site meeting rooms and coffee areas. In HCI it has been used to understand mobile use in physical space (Cityware), to build intelligible virtual information spaces (Tower), and to compare integration with disaster risks residents recorded on walks. Without validation against observed data it is 'pretty pictures'.
steps: Obtain an accurate plan of the street network or building and divide it into convex spaces.
Draw the fewest, longest axial lines that cover all convex spaces.
Convert line intersections into a graph and count turnings between lines.
Compute mean depth and integration (centrality) for each line, globally and locally (for example radius 3).
Colour the map by integration value.
Validate against observed data such as pedestrian counts, shop density, logged locations or resident-recorded factors.
Use the validated model to predict the effects of layout changes or to design intelligible physical or virtual spaces.
outputs: Integration and connectivity values per line or space, centrality maps, and validated predictions of movement and activity.
useWhen: When designing or evaluating physical or virtual spaces where wayfinding, footfall or encounter matters: stores, hospitals, campuses, transit, location-based services or navigable 3D environments.
avoidWhen: Avoid for abstract information architectures without spatial navigation (use Topological Analysis of Information Spaces or tree testing). Do not present unvalidated centrality maps as evidence.
whyLost: It is a mature, software-supported practice in architecture and urban planning, but UX works mostly on screens and seldom models physical layouts.
whereToUse: Retail and venue design, hospital and airport wayfinding, location-based apps, smart-building services, VR and metaverse spaces, emergency evacuation planning.
example: A hospital wayfinding app team maps corridors with axial analysis and finds the outpatient clinic sits in the least integrated zone. Combined with logs of 'lost' help requests, this justifies extra signage and in-app turn prompts there.
sources: Human Interface and the Management of Information (Yamamoto & Mori, 2020)
reference: Hillier, B., & Hanson, J. (1984). The Social Logic of Space. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press; Hillier, B. (1999). Space is the Machine. Cambridge University Press.

name: Spacing effect test (distributed vs massed practice)
donor: Cognitive psychology of learning and memory
origin: Ebbinghaus (1885); Bahrick and Phelps (1987); Cepeda et al. (2006, 2009)
summary: Hold total study or exposure constant, vary whether it is crammed together or spread over separated sessions, and test long-term retention to choose a learning schedule.
description: The spacing effect is one of the most robust findings in memory research: the same amount of study spread over separated sessions produces better long-term retention than the same study crammed together. Bahrick and Phelps found Spanish vocabulary learned with spaced sessions was better recalled eight years later, and Cepeda and colleagues showed the optimal gap grows with the retention interval, so for long-term recall spacing should ideally be weeks or months. Explanations include consolidation and encoding variability. The test is simple: hold total exposure constant, randomly assign massed versus distributed schedules, and measure recall after a retention interval, ideally long. In product design it informs onboarding, training, spaced-repetition learning and even advertising frequency, where Appleton-Knapp and colleagues found spaced ads remembered better.
steps: Define what must be learned or remembered (feature knowledge, vocabulary, procedures) and how recall will be tested.
Hold total study or exposure constant across conditions.
Randomly assign participants to massed (crammed) or distributed (spaced) schedules, optionally with several gap lengths.
Test recall or task performance after a retention interval, ideally long (weeks rather than minutes).
Compare retention by schedule and gap, and choose the schedule that matches the needed retention interval.
outputs: Retention by schedule and delay, and a recommended spacing interval.
useWhen: Designing onboarding sequences, training programmes, learning apps, feature education or reminder cadences where long-term retention matters.
avoidWhen: When only immediate performance matters (massed practice can look better in the short term) or when retention cannot be measured later; use a usability test of immediate learnability instead.
whyLost: It is well established in cognitive psychology and education, but UX onboarding is usually evaluated on immediate completion, not delayed retention.
whereToUse: Language and skills apps, enterprise software training, health self-management education, safety-critical procedure training.
example: A medical device company trains nurses on a new infusion pump. One group gets a two-hour session; another gets four 30-minute sessions over two weeks. At six weeks the spaced group makes half as many programming errors in a simulation.
reference: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T. and Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380.

name: spaCy NLP Pipeline for Qualitative Research
origin: spaCy library by Matthew Honnibal & Ines Montani (Explosion), 2015 onward
summary: Using spaCy pipelines for entity recognition, dependency patterns and sentiment to extract and aggregate linguistic evidence across large transcript corpora.
description: Natural language processing can surface patterns across hundreds of transcripts that human readers would miss or take weeks to find.
