sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, ch. 15; Hertzum, M., Bansler, J. P., Havn, E. and Simonsen, J. (2012). Pilot implementation: learning from field tests in IS development. Communications of the AIS, 30, 313-328.

name: Staged-choice (agenda) effect test
origin: Tversky and Sattath (1979)
summary: Give random groups the same options with different staged agendas (which options are grouped first) and compare final choice shares to measure how navigation structure steers choice.
description: When choices are made in stages (category first, then item), the grouping can change the outcome. Tversky and Sattath used triples where two options were similar and one dissimilar. Half the participants first chose between the similar pair and the odd option (an agenda matching the similarity structure); half chose between a pair that split the similar options. The incompatible agenda raised the share of the weaker similar option and lowered the dissimilar one; theory says choice is invariant to the agenda only when the agenda matches users' preference tree, and a worked example moves a nearly dominated option from almost zero to 0.22. In interfaces, filters, category trees and comparison steps are agendas, so this test shows whether information architecture is steering what users end up choosing.
steps: Choose three options with a known similarity structure, checking similarity with user ratings rather than team assumptions.
Create a compatible agenda (the similar pair grouped together first) and an incompatible one (a pair that splits the similar options).
Randomly assign participants and record the final choice after both stages; keep stage labels neutral so they carry no information.
Compare final choice shares between agendas, and compute a within-person index if each person completes several triples (the original used 10 triples per person and about 100 participants).
Redesign category or filter structures whose agenda shifts shares away from what users choose under a compatible agenda.
outputs: Final choice shares by agenda and the size of the agenda effect.
useWhen: Designing category navigation, filters, plan selectors or staged configurators where the order and grouping of decisions might steer the final choice.
avoidWhen: Single-stage choices shown all at once; use decoy or joint-separate evaluation tests instead.
whyLost: It is a theoretical decision paradigm; UX evaluates navigation for findability, not for its influence on which option is chosen.
whereToUse: E-commerce category filters, insurance and telecom plan selectors, car and laptop configurators, AI model pickers.
example: A laptop retailer tests 'size first' versus 'price tier first' navigation for the same three models. Size-first shifts 15% of choices toward a weaker small model, so the team reconsiders which filter leads.
reference: Tversky, A. and Sattath, S. (1979). Preference trees. Psychological Review, 86(6), 542-573.

name: Staged-Event Recall with Misleading-Question Suggestibility Test
aka: Staged-event eyewitness recall with a misleading-question suggestibility test
origin: Ceci and Bruck; Poole and Lindsay (1990s)
summary: Participants recall a staged event via general prompts, then specific and sometimes misleading questions, so accuracy and suggestibility can be compared by prompt type and age.
description: An experimental paradigm from eyewitness research. Participants, usually children, witness a staged, filmed or real event. They are then interviewed first with general free-recall prompts, then specific questions, and in the experimental condition misleading questions that presuppose false details. Responses are scored as correct, incorrect or 'don't know'. Findings are consistent: free recall grows with age and is mostly accurate, specific cues add errors, preschoolers are most suggestible, age gaps widen after delays of over a month, and permission to say 'I don't know' plus accuracy incentives reduce error. For UX, the paradigm is a way to calibrate interview and retrospective protocols: by staging a known product episode you can measure how much your question style, rather than the participant's memory, produces the account.
steps: Stage or show a known event with a documented ground truth, such as a scripted product interaction or video.
After a set delay, interview participants first with general free-recall prompts.
Follow with specific questions about details.
In the experimental condition, introduce misleading questions that presuppose false details; keep a control condition without them.
Score each response as correct, incorrect or 'don't know' against the ground truth.
Compare accuracy by prompt type, condition, age group and delay, and test whether 'I don't know' permission reduces error.
outputs: Accuracy and suggestibility rates by prompt type, age and delay; evidence on which interview prompts distort recall.
useWhen: You rely heavily on retrospective accounts (children, incident reports, retrospective think-aloud) and need to know how much your questioning style contaminates them.
avoidWhen: You want insight into users' needs or experiences; this is a methodological calibration experiment, not a discovery method. Use open interviews or observation instead.
whyLost: It is a forensic memory paradigm with no direct product question attached, so UX never adopted it even to check its own interview practice.
whereToUse: Validating interview protocols for children, incident and safety reporting, retrospective usability studies and customer support investigations.
example: A research team stages a short banking app session with 30 participants, then interviews half with neutral prompts and half with leading questions about an error message that never appeared. A third of the leading-question group 'remembers' it, prompting a rewrite of the team's interview guide.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
reference: Ceci, S. J., & Bruck, M. (1993). Suggestibility of the child witness: A historical review and synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 113(3), 403-439.

name: Staged-World Field Studies with Cognitive Process Tracing
aka: Staged-world field studies with process tracing
origin: David Woods (2003), after Hollnagel, Pedersen and Rasmussen (1981)
summary: Study how teams handle demanding work by staging realistic simulated scenarios with inserted probes, then tracing their cognitive process through layered protocols compared across teams and scenarios.
description: Woods places staged worlds between natural observation, where critical events are rare, and spartan laboratory tasks, which strip away what matters. The researcher models what matters in the field, designs scenarios with an explicit mapping between the target situation and the test, and inserts probes such as complicating events or new prototypes, which serve as instruments of discovery rather than products under test. Data from several sources are collated into a base protocol per team, then re-described in the study's concepts as a formal protocol that keeps interpretation separate from observation. Protocols are contrasted across teams, probes and scenarios, and integrated with other studies into functional accounts of how the system copes. This process tracing is the cognitive engineering method, not the political-science technique of the same name.
steps: Define the cognitive-system questions (for example how anomalies are noticed or how work is handed over), avoiding superficial labels.
Map the target situation to the test: problem space, scenario design and which situations to sample.
Build the scenario with artefacts and procedures that externalise cognitive activity, and insert probes such as complicating events or a prototype.
Map canonical expected behaviour so surprises can be recognised.
Run scenarios with teams, collecting several data sources (video, logs, talk, artefacts).
Collate a base protocol per team, then re-describe it as a formal protocol in the study's concepts.
Contrast protocols across teams, probes and scenarios, and integrate with converging studies into a functional account.
outputs: Base and formal protocols per team, cross-scenario contrasts and a functional account of how the work system copes with the probed demands.
useWhen: When the events that matter (incidents, escalations, rare failures) are too infrequent to observe naturally and you need to see how real teams reason through them, including how a new tool changes that.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need controlled causal comparisons; scenario contrasts are not experiments. For everyday work use Contextual Inquiry; for individual decision recall use the Critical Incident Technique or Stimulated Recall Interview.
whyLost: It needs domain modelling, simulation set-up and expert analysts, so it stayed in control-room, aviation and military cognitive engineering.
whereToUse: Security operations centres, site reliability on-call, clinical and emergency dispatch, trading desks, AI copilots for operators.
example: A cloud provider stages a realistic outage scenario for four on-call teams, inserting a misleading alert and a new AI incident summary as probes. Formal protocols show teams anchoring on the AI summary's first hypothesis, which reshapes how the summary presents uncertainty.
reference: Woods, D. D. (2003). Discovering how distributed cognitive systems work. In E. Hollnagel (Ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (pp. 37-53). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Stages-of-Action Gulf Analysis
aka: Seven Stages of Action Gulf Analysis
Gulf of execution and gulf of evaluation analysis
origin: Donald Norman, 1986 (revised 2013); failure points from Polson and Lewis, 1990
summary: Walk each user goal through Norman's seven stages of action to locate where the gulfs of execution and evaluation are widest and derive design fixes.
description: Norman's action cycle has seven stages: form the goal, form the intention (plan), specify the action, perform it, perceive the system state, interpret it and compare it with the goal. Mismatches between what users intend and what the interface allows form the gulf of execution; mismatches between how the system shows its state and what users expect form the gulf of evaluation. As an analysis, each important goal gets a table with one column per stage, filled by answering Norman's questions (What do I want? What are the alternatives? What can I do now? How do I do it? What happened? What does it mean? Is this okay?). Each boundary is checked against four failure points from Polson and Lewis: inadequate goal, object not found, action not known, and missing or misleading feedback. A scope check then asks which stages before and after the product's current coverage it should support.
steps: List the users' main goals and pick representative tasks, stating each goal in the user's terms.
For each goal build a table with columns Goal, Plan, Specify, Perform, Perceive, Interpret, Compare and answer Norman's question for each stage.
At each step check the four failure points: inadequate goal, interface object not found, action not known, feedback missing or misleading.
Classify each problem as a gulf of execution or evaluation and identify the features that widen or narrow it.
Check problems against visibility, conceptual model, mapping and feedback, and derive design rules or features that remove whole iterations of the cycle.
Widen the frame by listing stages of the user's activity before and after the product's scope, and decide whether to support them.
Summarise all goals in one table to compare tools or versions, then confirm the main gulfs with usability testing.
outputs: Per-goal seven-stage tables, a list of execution and evaluation gulfs, violated principles, design rules and candidate scope extensions.
useWhen: Early analytic evaluation of task flows, diagnosing why users stall, comparing tools for expert work, and checking whether a product covers enough of the user's wider activity.
avoidWhen: When you need measured problem frequency or severity (use Usability Testing). Real users skip and revisit stages, so do not treat the sequence as strict; for novice learnability use Cognitive Walkthrough.
whyLost: The gulf vocabulary is widely quoted but the stage-by-stage table and failure-point checks are rarely carried out, leaving a slogan rather than a procedure.
whereToUse: Checkout and onboarding flows, professional tools such as IDEs and analytics dashboards, AI features where system state is hard to perceive, and scoping new product areas.
example: Analysing an AI writing assistant, a team finds a wide gulf of evaluation: users cannot tell whether a suggestion used their document context. Adding a visible source indicator narrows it, and the scope check prompts a sharing feature at the end of the cycle.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Norman, D.A. (1986) Cognitive engineering. In Norman, D.A. and Draper, S.W. (eds) User Centered System Design. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Staggered-adoption DiD and event study
aka: Event study with leads and lags
origin: Goodman-Bacon (2021); Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021); Sun and Abraham (2021); Cengiz et al. (2019)
summary: When units adopt a change at different times, estimate effects with event-study leads and lags and cohort-specific estimators that never use already-treated units as controls.
description: Products roll out to markets, accounts or teams at different dates, inviting difference-in-differences with two-way fixed effects. With staggered timing and effects that change over time, that pooled estimate is a weighted average of all 2x2 comparisons, including later-treated versus already-treated units, which can bias it or even flip its sign. The Goodman-Bacon decomposition shows each 2x2 estimate and its weight. The event study regresses outcomes on lead and lag indicators relative to each unit's adoption date, plotting pre-trends and dynamic effects; flat leads are reassuring but neither necessary nor sufficient for parallel trends. Heterogeneity-robust estimators (Callaway and Sant'Anna group-time ATTs, Sun and Abraham's interaction-weighted event study, stacked DiD) compare each cohort only with never- or not-yet-treated units and then aggregate with explicit weights.
steps: Identify adoption cohorts by first treatment date and a clean control set of never-treated or not-yet-treated units.
Estimate the static two-way fixed-effects DiD as a baseline and run the Goodman-Bacon decomposition to see each 2x2 comparison and its weight; check the weight on late-versus-early comparisons.
Define event time relative to each unit's adoption and estimate leads and lags, omitting one pre-period as reference, with standard errors clustered by unit.
Plot coefficients with 95% intervals; inspect leads for pre-trends and lags for dynamic effects, and repeat for first-stage outcomes such as exposure or take-up.
Estimate cohort-by-period effects against clean controls (Callaway-Sant'Anna, Sun-Abraham or stacked DiD), optionally reweighting on covariates.
Aggregate into overall or event-time summaries with explicit weights and compare with the naive estimate.
outputs: Event-study plots, a decomposition table of 2x2 estimates and weights, and group-time and aggregated treatment effects.
useWhen: A feature, policy or redesign was rolled out to markets, accounts, stores or teams at different times and no randomised control exists.
avoidWhen: When all units adopt at once (use standard DiD or interrupted time series), when there are no never- or not-yet-treated units, or when you can randomise the rollout instead.
whyLost: These estimators are recent econometrics (2019-2021) and product analytics still applies pooled DiD or simple before-after comparisons to staggered rollouts.
whereToUse: Country-by-country launches, enterprise account rollouts, retail store pilots, regional pricing changes and policy changes across platforms.
example: A delivery app launched in-app tipping city by city over eight months. Pooled DiD shows +6% courier retention, but the event study and Callaway-Sant'Anna estimates show the effect grows from 2% to 9% over six months, and the pooled estimate was distorted by early cities used as controls.
reference: Callaway, B. and Sant'Anna, P. H. C. (2021). Difference-in-differences with multiple time periods. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 200-230; Goodman-Bacon, A. (2021). Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 254-277.

name: Staircase elicitation of upper and lower probability
origin: Tversky and Koehler, 1994 (support theory), drawing on Wallsten and colleagues
summary: Respondents mark each value on a probability ladder as too low, about right or too high; the boundaries give lower and upper probabilities, exposing how vague a belief is.
description: Point probability estimates hide how uncertain people are about their own judgement. In the staircase procedure, respondents see probability values from 0 to 1 in steps and place each in a verbal category from 'clearly too low' to 'clearly too high'. The lowest value not marked clearly too low is the lower probability and the highest not marked clearly too high is the upper probability; the interval width measures vagueness without asking for probabilities of probabilities. Tversky and Koehler used it with football fans to test whether interval judgements behave as lower-probability theory requires. Lower and upper judgements for complementary events were complementary (summing to about 1.02), but they violated additivity in the way support theory predicts, so intervals are subadditive just like point judgements. Category wording affects the bounds and long ladders tire respondents.
steps: State the event precisely and prepare a ladder of probability values in steps (for example every .05).
For each value ask the respondent to tick one category: clearly too low, probably too low, about right, probably too high, clearly too high.
Take the lowest value not marked clearly too low as the lower bound and the highest not marked clearly too high as the upper bound.
Ask the same for the complementary event and check that lower and upper bounds are roughly complementary (sum near 1).
Report interval widths per respondent and event as a measure of vagueness, alongside any point estimate.
outputs: Lower and upper probabilities per respondent and event, interval widths and a complementarity check.
useWhen: When forecasts or risk judgements from experts or stakeholders feed decisions and you need to see disagreement in confidence, not just in point estimates.
avoidWhen: Avoid with many events (respondent fatigue) or naive respondents who struggle with probability ladders; use Words of Estimative Probability or simple confidence ratings. Intervals are still subadditive, so do not treat them as coherent.
whyLost: It stayed in decision-theory experiments; UX and product forecasting collect single-number estimates or none.
whereToUse: Roadmap and launch forecasting, risk workshops, expert elicitation for Bayesian priors, AI model evaluation confidence.
example: Asked how likely a feature is to ship this quarter, two product managers both say .6, but the staircase gives .4-.8 for one and .55-.6 for the other, prompting a discussion of the first manager's uncertainties.
reference: Tversky, A., & Koehler, D. J. (1994). Support theory: A nonextensional representation of subjective probability. Psychological Review, 101(4), 547-567; reprinted in Tversky, A. (2004). Preference, Belief, and Similarity (E. Shafir, Ed.). MIT Press.

name: Stakeholder and Requirements Trade-off Matrices
origin: Alistair Sutcliffe, drawing on Chung (1993), Yu (1993) and House of Quality; Sarah Kaplan, The 360° Corporation (2019)
summary: Tabulate goals or business-model levers against each stakeholder group's priorities and quality criteria to expose shared goals, conflicts and who wins or loses before negotiating.
description: Two traditions make trade-offs between stakeholders explicit. In requirements engineering, Sutcliffe lists goals gathered separately from each stakeholder group as matrix rows; each group's priority is marked with one to three ticks, neutral or conflict marks, and further columns record associations with non-functional criteria such as accuracy, security and usability. The matrix shows how few goals are shared and where conflicts lie, so they can be negotiated in a facilitated workshop. In business strategy, Kaplan decomposes how a firm makes money into an ROIC tree of revenue and cost drivers, asks for each lever which stakeholders it helps or harms, names externalities, and sets measures and targets, complemented by direct engagement with affected stakeholders and critics. Both turn vague tension into a concrete, discussable table.
steps: Gather goals separately from each stakeholder group, or decompose the business model into value drivers (revenue, cost and capital levers).
List the goals or levers as rows of a matrix.
For each stakeholder group, mark priority (one to three ticks), neutral (-) or conflict (--); for levers, mark who gains and who bears costs.
Add columns for quality criteria (security, accuracy, usability) or impact measures, and mark associations.
Identify shared goals, conflicting goals and externalities, and set measures and targets for the main impacts.
Bring affected stakeholders, including critics, into a facilitated session to negotiate conflicts, explaining the effect of contested goals.
outputs: A shared matrix of goals or levers, stakeholder priorities, conflicts, quality-criteria implications and impact measures.
useWhen: Use it when stakeholder groups want different things from a system, or when a product's business model may be quietly trading one group's interests against another's.
avoidWhen: It structures stakeholders' stated positions; to understand end users' needs and harms directly use Interviews or Ethnographic Research. For weighted multi-criteria decisions use Analytic Hierarchy Process, and for mapping influence use Stakeholder Mapping.
whyLost: Requirements matrices remained in requirements engineering and strategy courses; UX teams rarely own trade-off negotiation explicitly.
whereToUse: Enterprise and public-sector systems with competing user groups, health data platforms, marketplaces and gig platforms, and responsible-AI reviews.
example: A clinical analytics tool's goals are tabulated for researchers and public-health analysts: 'prevent analysis errors' is marked conflict by analysts until its accuracy benefit is shown. A gig-platform team's lever analysis shows driver earnings bear the cost of faster delivery promises.
reference: Sutcliffe, A.G. (2013) Requirements Engineering from an HCI Perspective. In Soegaard, M. and Dam, R.F. (eds) The Encyclopedia of Human-Computer Interaction, 2nd edn, ch. 13; Kaplan, S. (2019). The 360° Corporation: From Stakeholder Trade-offs to Transformation. Stanford, CA: Stanford Business Books.

name: Stakeholder Interview Protocol (Organisational Research)
origin: Erika Hall, 2013
summary: Structured interviews with internal stakeholders to surface goals, constraints, politics, assumptions and success criteria that will shape a product and its research.
description: Organisational research applies interview rigour to the people inside the organisation who will build, fund, sell, support or regulate a product. A protocol covers each stakeholder's role, goals, definition of success, constraints (technical, legal, budgetary), assumptions about users, past attempts, and fears. Interviews are conducted one-to-one so that political dynamics do not suppress dissent, and they are synthesised like user research: themes, conflicts and assumptions are documented and shared back. The method reveals the real decision environment the work sits in, prevents late surprises, and builds stakeholders' ownership of later findings. Rigour comes from a consistent guide, sampling across functions and levels, and separating stakeholder beliefs about users from evidence.
steps: Stakeholder interview protocol (30 min):
'What does success look like in 6 months?'
'What would make this project fail?'
'What assumptions are you making about users that haven't been validated?'
'What constraints — technical, business, political — will shape what we can build?'
'Who else should I talk to?' Synthesize: identify assumption conflicts between stakeholders before user research begins.
outputs: Stakeholder map, documented goals and constraints, assumption list, conflicting definitions of success, and a shared problem statement.
useWhen: Project kick-off, entering a new organisation or domain, when stakeholders disagree, or before user research to understand what decisions the research must serve.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating stakeholder views as evidence about users; validate with user research. Avoid when the project scope is tiny and stakeholders are already aligned.
whyLost: Stakeholder interviews are done informally as kick-off chats, without protocol, synthesis or documentation, so organisational constraints surface late as surprises.
whereToUse: Project kickoff, design brief construction, cross-functional alignment, product discovery.
example: Before redesigning a hospital's referral portal, the researcher interviews eight stakeholders and discovers that legal requires a signature step the product owner planned to remove, reshaping the brief.
sources: Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld & Morville, 2006)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Hall E (2013) Just Enough Research. A Book Apart

name: Stakeholder Mapping
origin: Edward Freeman, stakeholder theory (1984); power-interest grid by Mendelow (1981)
summary: Identifying everyone who affects or is affected by a product or study and mapping their interests, influence and relationships to plan research, engagement and design.
description: Stakeholder mapping makes the social system around a product explicit. It identifies internal stakeholders (sponsors, teams, decision-makers) and external ones (users, customers, regulators, partners, indirect stakeholders), then characterises each by interest, influence, attitude and relationships. Common representations include the power-interest grid, onion diagrams placing stakeholders in rings around the product, and relationship maps showing flows of value, information and conflict. A systems-thinking variant maps each stakeholder's perspective on the same problem, revealing why the problem looks different from each position. Rigour comes from grounding the map in interviews rather than assumptions, including indirect and dissenting stakeholders, documenting each placement's rationale, and revisiting the map as the project changes. It informs who to recruit, who must be involved in decisions and where research findings will meet resistance.
steps: Brainstorm all individuals and groups who affect or are affected by the product, including indirect stakeholders and regulators.
Interview or survey a selection of stakeholders to learn their goals, concerns, decision rights and view of the problem.
Place each stakeholder on a power-interest grid or onion diagram, noting the evidence for each placement.
Draw relationships between stakeholders: flows of money, information, authority and conflict.
Capture each key stakeholder's perspective on the problem and where perspectives diverge.
Derive an engagement plan (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor) and a research recruitment plan, and revisit the map at each project phase.
outputs: Stakeholder inventory, power-interest grid or onion map, relationship diagram, perspective comparison and engagement plan.
useWhen: Starting a project in a complex organisation or ecosystem, planning research recruitment and communication, and designing services with many parties.
avoidWhen: When the product context is simple and stakeholders are already well known; avoid treating the map as a substitute for user research.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential project planning tool; helps manage political dynamics of design.
whereToUse: Service design; complex enterprise products; public sector; any multi-stakeholder context.
example: A hospital theatre-scheduling project maps surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses, porters, bed managers and patients. Perspective mapping shows each defines 'delay' differently, so research is planned to capture a shared timeline from all six viewpoints.
sources: Freeman, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach (1984)
This Is Service Design Doing (Stickdorn et al.)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
Org Design for Design Orgs (Merholz & Skinner, 2016)
reference: Freeman RE (1984) Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. Pitman

name: Stakeholder Request Handling and Management
aka: Ask why before yes or no
Stakeholder management for data and research teams
Four tenets of working with stakeholders
origin: Crumlish (2022), with Matt LeMay's counterpoint and Ellen Chisa's four roadmap inputs; Nolis and Robinson (2020)
summary: A structured way to respond to stakeholder requests by asking why and making trade-offs explicit, backed by a steady communication cadence with the people who commission work.
description: Requests come from customers, sales, executives, engineers and designers, and none can simply be brushed off. Crumlish's protocol responds to a roadmap request without negating its value: thank the requester, ask what problem it solves and what alternatives were considered, review current priorities and their link to strategy and OKRs, ask which agreed commitment should give way, and compare evidence. If overruled, define success metrics and later report both the outcome and the cost of dropped work. LeMay warns against falling in love with 'no'; the aim is to ask why first. Nolis and Robinson add four tenets for ongoing relationships: learn each stakeholder's goals, communicate constantly on a fixed weekly or fortnightly cadence, keep deliverables consistent in structure and storage, and build rapport.
steps: Thank the stakeholder and ask what problem or opportunity the request addresses, the expected outcome, the risk of not doing it and the alternatives considered.
Offer to research the problem space further where the request is not yet understood.
Review the current Now priorities with them and show how each connects to strategy and OKRs.
Ask which agreed commitment should be set aside to make room, noting that any change must be re-reviewed by all stakeholders, and ask for supporting data while having your own ready.
If overruled, define success metrics for the new item, measure its impact and later report the outcome and the cost of the dropped priorities.
For ongoing work, learn each stakeholder's goals and likely reactions to results, and bring in a senior colleague when delivering bad news.

Hold a recurring weekly or fortnightly meeting, send roughly weekly updates, and standardise deliverables (objective and data first, conclusions and next steps last, one format and one storage place).
outputs: Documented decisions with explicit trade-offs, success metrics for overruled items, a communication cadence and a standard deliverable template.
useWhen: Use it when research, design or analytics teams face a stream of ad hoc requests that threaten agreed priorities, or when stakeholders feel uninformed.
avoidWhen: It manages requests rather than understanding stakeholders' needs; for that use the Stakeholder Interview Protocol (Organisational Research) or Stakeholder Mapping. For responses to critique of designs use Design Review Stakeholder Handling. Saying no can become a habit that hides useful information.
whyLost: It survives because every product, design and research team has to protect priorities, and the practice is widely taught in product management.
whereToUse: Product roadmaps, research and analytics request queues, design teams embedded in sales-led B2B companies.
example: A sales director asks a B2B SaaS team to build a custom export for one prospect. The PM asks what problem it solves, shows the current priorities, and agrees to ship it only with a success metric; the later report shows low use and the cost to the delayed onboarding work.
sources: Build a Career in Data Science (Nolis & Robinson, 2020)
reference: Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People. Rosenfeld Media, pp. 157, 182-184. Nolis, J. and Robinson, E. (2020). Build a Career in Data Science. Shelter Island, NY: Manning, ch. 12.

name: Stakeholder Research Exposure Tracking (Exposure Hours, Team Engagement Score)
aka: Research exposure quota with a public dashboard
origin: Leisa Reichelt at GOV.UK (exposure quota); Bill Albert and Josh Rosenberg (2017), Team Engagement Score
summary: Set and track a minimum amount of user research each team member observes, and score how engaged product teams are during studies.
description: Teams that watch users make better decisions, so this method measures exposure directly. At GOV.UK everyone on a team had to observe at least two hours of user research every six weeks; 'have you done your two hours?' became common currency, and a public dashboard showed sessions run and the share of the team who had observed one recently. Albert and Rosenberg's Team Engagement Score combines three ratios into a 0 to 1 score: commitment (sessions observed over sessions observable), prioritisation (sessions observed in person over sessions observable in person) and involvement (the moderator's rating of the team's questions and feedback). Tracked across studies and teams, the measures show where research is being consumed and where it is being ignored.
steps: Set an exposure quota, for example at least two hours of observed research per person every six weeks.
Log who observes each session, and whether in person or remotely.
For each study compute commitment (sessions observed / observable) and prioritisation (in-person observed / observable in person).
Have the moderator rate team involvement during and after sessions on a fixed scale.
Combine into a 0-1 engagement score and publish exposure and engagement on a simple dashboard.
Review trends with team leads and follow up with teams that fall below the quota.
outputs: Per-person exposure hours, per-study or per-team engagement scores and a public dashboard.
useWhen: Building a research culture, demonstrating research reach, or diagnosing why findings are ignored by particular teams.
avoidWhen: The organisation would treat it as surveillance or a box-ticking target. The exact TES combination rule and rating scale are in the original presentation, so define your own consistently.
whyLost: The exposure-hours idea is widely cited but seldom measured, and TES remained a conference proposal.
whereToUse: Government digital services, in-house research teams, research-ops maturity programmes.
example: A SaaS research team publishes monthly exposure figures: 70 per cent of designers but only 20 per cent of engineers met the quota, so sessions are moved to engineering stand-up slots.
reference: Albert, B., & Rosenberg, J. (2017). Introducing a new UX maturity metric: Team Engagement Score (TES) during usability testing. UXPA International Conference, Toronto.

name: Stakeholder Workshops
origin: Stephanie Marsh, User Research (2018; 2nd edn 2022), drawing on Pickering (2015) and Gamestorming (2010)
summary: Structured, activity-based sessions with people who have a stake in a project to align on scope, assumptions, requirements, priorities and early designs.
description: Stakeholder workshops gather decision makers, information holders, people with influence and implementers to do activities together, not to hold a committee meeting. In one session they can produce scope, objectives, priorities, assumptions, risks, draft proto-personas and sketches that would take weeks of interviews, and group dynamics surface disagreements that individual conversations hide. Marsh distinguishes kick-off, milestone or engagement, requirements, design, co-design and content workshops. Good practice: review existing research and interview key stakeholders beforehand; about twelve participants; an agenda and goals shared with the invitation; roughly three hours with breaks; two or three facilitators; no phones; visible instructions and outputs; a structure of welcome, what we know, warm-up, diverge-then-converge activities and an uplifting summary; mixed-role groups; and everything photographed. Assumptions and proto-personas produced must be validated by later research.
steps: Set the goal and choose the workshop type (kick-off, milestone, requirements, design, co-design or content).
Review existing research, learn the domain, and interview key stakeholders before or after the session.
Invite about twelve people: decision makers, information holders, people with clout and implementers; share the agenda and any pre-work with the invitation.
Plan about three hours of timed activities with breaks, two or three facilitators, no phones, and visible instructions.
Run it as welcome, what we know so far, warm-up, core diverge-then-converge activities and an uplifting summary, mixing individual, small-group and whole-group work.
Bring disputes back to user needs and capture every output with photographs and a note-taker.
Write up agreed outputs and plan research to validate assumptions and proto-personas.
outputs: Agreed scope and objectives, priorities, assumption and risk lists, proto-personas, sketches and photographed artefacts.
useWhen: Use it at project start, at strategic turning points and at milestones, whenever multidisciplinary input and shared ownership are needed quickly.
avoidWhen: Workshops are not focus groups or group usability tests; gather user data with Interviews or Usability Testing. When users themselves should design, run Co-design Workshops.
whyLost: It survived because cross-functional alignment is a constant need and workshops are faster and more binding than serial meetings.
whereToUse: Government digital services, agency engagements, enterprise platforms, and any multi-team product start.
example: A government benefits service runs a three-hour kick-off with policy, operations and digital leads. Clashing assumptions about who applies become a list of research questions and three proto-personas tested in the following month.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Marsh, S. (2022). User Research: Improve Product and Service Design and Enhance Your UX Research. 2nd edn. London: Kogan Page, pp. 192-201.

name: STAMP / STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis)
origin: Nancy Leveson, 2004 (STAMP); 2011-2018 (STPA handbook)
summary: Models the system as control loops and identifies unsafe control actions, including normally correct user actions that become hazardous in particular system states.
description: STAMP treats safety as a control problem rather than a chain of component failures. STPA identifies losses and hazards, models the control structure (controllers, control actions, feedback), then finds unsafe control actions: actions provided when hazardous, not provided when needed, provided too early or late, or stopped too soon. It traces causal scenarios, including flawed process models in controllers' minds. Crucially, hazards can arise from normal operation in unexpected contexts, without failures. The treatise's transfer: a UX-level STPA identifies situations where a normally correct user action becomes hazardous (submit is safe when validation passes, unsafe when validation has silently failed), producing requirements task analysis misses. Rated MEDIUM priority (feasibility two stars, impact five).
steps: Define losses and system-level hazards with stakeholders.
Model the control structure, including the human operator, interface, automation and feedback.
For each control action, identify the four types of unsafe control action in relevant system states.
Identify causal scenarios, especially mismatches between the user's mental model and system state.
Derive interface and feedback requirements that prevent or mitigate scenarios.
Verify requirements in simulation or usability testing with hazard-oriented scenarios.
outputs: Control structure diagram, unsafe control action table, causal scenarios, safety-driven UX requirements.
useWhen: Safety-critical or high-stakes interfaces with automation, and AI agents taking real-world actions.
avoidWhen: Low-consequence consumer features where the analysis overhead is unjustified.
whyLost: It originated in aerospace and system safety engineering and is taught in engineering schools, not design programmes. Its diagrams look like engineering artefacts, so UX researchers rarely encounter it.
whereToUse: Medical device UX, autonomous driving handovers, industrial control, AI agents executing payments or code.
example: STPA on an AI agent that can send payments finds an unsafe control action: the user approves a batch while the agent's payee list has silently changed. The design adds a diff of changed payees before approval.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Leveson NG (2004) A new accident model for engineering safer systems. Safety Science 42(4):237-270
Leveson NG (2011) Engineering a Safer World
Leveson NG & Thomas JP (2018) STPA Handbook
Leveson, Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety (2011)
reference: Leveson NG (2011) Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety. MIT Press.

name: Standard Gamble and Time Trade-Off Utility Elicitation
origin: von Neumann-Morgenstern utility theory (1944); time trade-off by George Torrance, Warren Thomas and David Sackett (1972); review by Torrance (1986)
summary: Measures how much people value a state (e.g. living with a product limitation) by the risk or time they would trade to avoid it, yielding cardinal utilities.
description: Health economists needed utilities for health states to compute QALYs. In the standard gamble, people choose between a certain state and a gamble with probability p of the best outcome and 1 - p of the worst; the indifference p is the state's utility. In the time trade-off, people choose between t years in the state and fewer years in full health; the ratio gives the utility. These methods produce cardinal, interpersonally comparable values, with known biases (loss aversion in SG, time preference in TTO). Adapted to UX, they quantify the burden of persistent problems such as accessibility barriers, chronic friction or unreliable service, beyond satisfaction ratings.
steps: Describe the states clearly with vignettes, including the best and worst anchors.
Use a structured iterative procedure (e.g. ping-pong or titration) to find indifference points.
Train respondents with practice items and include consistency checks.
Compute utilities per respondent and aggregate with confidence intervals.
Compare utilities across states or segments and convert into burden metrics (e.g. utility loss times prevalence).
Validate against behavioural data such as switching or abandonment.
outputs: Cardinal utilities for states, burden estimates and segment comparisons.
useWhen: Quantifying the burden of persistent conditions or service states to prioritise investment, especially accessibility and reliability.
avoidWhen: Transient micro-frictions where trade-offs would be meaningless to participants.
whyLost: It belongs to health economics; UX measures satisfaction rather than utilities.
whereToUse: Digital health, accessibility, assistive technology, reliability of essential services, public sector services.
example: Screen-reader users complete TTO tasks about living with an inaccessible banking app; the mean utility of 0.82 versus 0.97 for the accessible version quantifies burden for a business case.
sources: Torrance, Measurement of health state utilities for economic appraisal (1986), Journal of Health Economics
Drummond et al., Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes (4th ed., 2015)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Torrance, G. W. (1986). Journal of Health Economics, 5(1), 1-30.

name: Standing recruitment pipeline
origin: Teresa Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits (2021); research operations practice and in-house participant panels from the 2010s
summary: Sets up an always-running system that recruits, screens and schedules participants weekly, so continuous discovery interviews happen without bespoke recruiting each time.
description: Continuous discovery depends on talking to customers every week, which fails if each round needs a new recruiting effort taking 2 to 3 weeks. A standing recruitment pipeline automates the path: in-product or email intercepts invite users, a short screener captures attributes, qualified participants self-schedule into reserved slots, and incentives are paid automatically. Torres recommends at least one customer interview per week per product trio. A good pipeline also manages the panel: tracking participation to avoid over-using the same people, balancing segments, and handling consent and data retention. Rigour comes from monitoring sample composition against the user base, so convenience does not slowly skew the voices teams hear towards the most engaged users.
steps: Define the segments and attributes you need to hear from regularly, and set quotas so that no single segment exceeds an agreed share of interviews, for example 40%.
Implement a recruiting trigger, such as an in-product intercept to a sampled share of users, an email to a random sample or a support follow-up, with a 3 to 6 question screener.
Connect the screener to self-scheduling for reserved weekly slots and automated reminders and incentive payment.
Maintain a panel database recording consent, attributes, participation dates and a cool-off rule (for example no more than one study per participant every 3 months).
Review composition monthly against the active user base, and adjust sampling to correct skew towards highly engaged or vocal users.
Track pipeline health: show rate (aim for 70% or more), time from invite to interview and weekly interviews completed per team.
outputs: A running recruitment system, a consented panel with attributes and participation history, weekly interview slots filled, and composition and health metrics.
useWhen: Teams practise continuous discovery or frequent evaluative testing; recruitment delays are blocking research; you need steady access to specific segments.
avoidWhen: Research needs hard-to-reach non-users or highly specific populations that intercepts cannot reach (use specialist recruiters or field recruitment), or regulatory constraints forbid contacting users this way.
whyLost: It survived because continuous discovery and research operations became mainstream; the vulnerability is sample bias, since pipelines over-represent engaged, digitally confident users.
whereToUse: SaaS and fintech products, marketplaces, consumer apps, internal platforms, any team practising weekly customer interviews.
example: A fintech team building a Savings feature added an in-app intercept to 2% of weekly active users, screening for savings habits and income type. They held three interviews a week, fed their opportunity solution tree, and adjusted sampling when informal-income users fell below their 25% quota.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Torres, T. (2021). Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products that Create Customer Value and Business Value. Product Talk LLC.

name: Standing Youth Tester Panel
origin: NMSU Learning Games Lab (Chamberlin and colleagues, 2012 to 2016), described in Chapter 3
summary: An ongoing programme that keeps a trained group of target users on site so that developers can run short formative tests at any point in development.
description: The Learning Games Lab solved the hardest part of frequent testing, getting access to target users, by running year-round 'think tanks' for young people. Youth consultants spend their days on engaging activities such as coding, animation and game design, and are pulled into 1 to 2 hour test sessions whenever a developer needs them. They are trained to review games, building a shared vocabulary for genre, challenge and flow so that feedback goes beyond 'it was boring'. Several methods run side by side: one-on-one interactions for early prototypes where a reviewer can explain missing parts, one-on-two observations where one reviewer silently watches two players, short focus groups to prime topics, a video closet, and written blogging. Developers act as testers so they see problems first-hand, while a testing manager observes the testers themselves to note leading questions and bias. Straight after each session the testers compare notes, agree what they saw, and the manager records a testers' consensus and recommendations in a testing journal for that project. The model trades some independence for speed, empathy and continuous access.
steps: Recruit a cohort of target users for a recurring programme, with consent covering ongoing testing and recording.
Run a daily programme of worthwhile activities and train participants in a shared vocabulary for reviewing products.
Before each test, agree specific questions and methods with the developers and note them in the testing journal.
Run the session with a mix of methods, for example one-on-two observation plus a short group discussion and individual reflections.
Have a testing manager observe the testers and note their questions and biases.
Immediately afterwards, hold a debrief where testers reconcile observations and agree recommendations.
Record the version tested, objectives, findings and testers' consensus in the journal and track changes across versions.
outputs: A testing journal per project with findings, consensus recommendations and version history, plus a pool of trained users available on demand.
useWhen: A studio or product team builds many products for a specific audience and needs frequent formative feedback throughout development.
avoidWhen: You need independent, unbiased summative evidence, or cannot sustain the space, staff and programme costs.
whyLost: It needs dedicated space, a teacher or coordinator and institutional support; most teams instead recruit fresh participants per study or use online panels.
whereToUse: Educational games, children's media, studios serving a narrow audience, in-house research labs.
example: A studio making maths games keeps a summer think tank of middle-school students; when a ratio game build is ready, two developers each watch two students play while a testing manager notes the developers' prompts, and within an hour the consensus that the fail condition is unclear is in the journal.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Chamberlin, B., Trespalacios, J. H., Muise, A. S. and Garza, M. C. (2016). User testing in the Learning Games Lab: getting valuable feedback through frequent formative evaluation. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 3. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Start-List Coding with a Structured Codebook and Check-Coding
origin: Matthew Miles and A. Michael Huberman, 1984; expanded 1994
summary: Build a provisional code list from the framework and questions before fieldwork, define each code operationally, and keep it reliable through repeated check-coding as it evolves.
description: For Miles and Huberman 'coding is analysis'. They distinguish descriptive, interpretive and pattern codes and prefer a start list made before fieldwork from the conceptual framework, research questions and key variables: a dozen to 60 codes grouped under conceptual families, each with an operational definition and a mnemonic name rather than a number. Two coders code the same pages and compute agreement as agreements divided by agreements plus disagreements, expecting about 70% at first and aiming for about 90%. Each coder also re-codes early pages days later to check self-consistency. The codebook is then revised as codes decay, swell or emerge, while keeping a governing structure. Notes from each contact are coded before the next visit, so analysis steers later fieldwork. A flat alphabetical 'ragbag' list, or more than two coding days per contact day, signals trouble.
steps: Derive a start list of a dozen to 60 codes under a few conceptual families, keyed to research questions, on one sheet.
Write an operational definition for each code and give it a mnemonic name, not a number.
Apply the list to the first field notes or transcripts and examine fit.
Check-code: two people code the same 5-10 pages; compute agreements / (agreements + disagreements), expecting about 70% at first and aiming for 90%.
Have each coder re-code early pages a few days later to check self-consistency.
Revise the codebook: drop decaying codes, split swollen ones, add emergent ones, and keep the family structure.
Code each contact's material before the next field contact, and repeat check-coding about two-thirds of the way through.
outputs: A versioned codebook with definitions, coded material, and agreement figures at the start and midpoint.
useWhen: Team-based qualitative studies, especially multi-site or longitudinal ones, where codes must mean the same thing to several analysts and analysis should steer later sessions.
avoidWhen: Fully inductive studies aiming at new theory (use open coding); when a formal reliability statistic is required, report kappa or Krippendorff's alpha rather than simple percentage agreement.
whyLost: UX synthesis is often done as affinity clustering on sticky notes, so the operationally defined codebook and the check-coding loop are dropped while the word 'coding' survives.
whereToUse: Large interview programmes, repositories with shared tags, and studies where several researchers or AI-assisted coders must apply a common scheme.
example: A banking research team starts with 30 codes under 'trust', 'effort' and 'control' for a study of open-banking consent. Two researchers reach 72% agreement on the first eight pages, tighten three definitions, and reach 88% at the midpoint check.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Startle Eyeblink EMG
aka: Startle eyeblink EMG and prepulse inhibition
origin: Peter Lang, Margaret Bradley and Bruce Cuthbert (1990s)
summary: The size of the eyeblink to a sudden noise, measured by EMG, indexes a person's current emotional state: unpleasant states enlarge it and pleasant ones shrink it.
description: Electrodes over the orbicularis oculi muscle below the eye record the blink reflex to an abrupt, usually acoustic, probe. The startle is modulated by emotional state: viewing negative material normally potentiates the blink and positive material attenuates it, giving a valence measure that does not depend on self-report and is hard to fake. States are induced by threat or safety cues, rated pictures, film clips or facial expressions. A related measure, prepulse inhibition, uses a weak 60-85 dB prepulse 60-300 ms before the probe, which reduces the blink and indexes early sensory gating. Divergence between startle and self-ratings is itself informative. Probes are aversive and disruptive, so the method suits short, controlled exposures rather than continuous interaction, and results must be read alongside self-report.
steps: Attach EMG electrodes below the eye over the orbicularis oculi.
Present emotional or neutral material, such as product images, clips or interface states, in randomised blocks.
Deliver occasional unpredictable acoustic startle probes during viewing, optionally preceded by prepulses.
Score blink magnitude for each probe and standardise within participant.
Compare blink magnitude across conditions and against self-reported valence.
outputs: Startle magnitude by condition as a valence index, prepulse inhibition percentages, and divergence from self-report.
useWhen: You need an implicit, hard-to-fake index of valence for short controlled exposures, for example where self-report is biased by social desirability.
avoidWhen: Participants are interacting continuously, or aversive probes are unacceptable; use facial EMG, skin conductance or self-report scales instead.
whyLost: Aversive probes and specialist EMG set-up suit psychophysiology labs, not product research, and facial EMG offers a gentler valence measure.
whereToUse: Advertising and packaging, health warnings, horror and immersive game content, and sensitive-topic messaging.
example: A public health team tests three smoking-warning designs with 30 smokers. Startle potentiation is greatest for the graphic image even though self-ratings are similar, supporting its use.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Lang, P. J., Bradley, M. M., & Cuthbert, B. N. (1990). Emotion, attention, and the startle reflex. Psychological Review, 97(3), 377-395.

name: Startup Metric Frameworks (AARRR, Lean Analytics Stages, OMTM)
origin: Dave McClure, 'Startup Metrics for Pirates' (2007); Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz (2013)
summary: Maps the customer lifecycle into stages, identifies which stage the product is in, and focuses the team on one metric for that stage until its gate is passed.
description: Three linked frameworks structure what to measure when. McClure's Pirate Metrics split the lifecycle into Acquisition (attention), Activation (first good experience, sign-up, onboarding), Retention (return use, actives, churn), Revenue (conversion, lifetime value) and Referral (invites, viral coefficient), with conversion measured between stages to find the weakest step; the order is not strict. Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics stages (Empathy, Stickiness, Virality, Revenue, Scale) define where a business is, with gate questions per stage and a table crossing six business models with stages to give the key question and metric. The One Metric That Matters is the single metric for the current stage, with a target from the business model or baselines, shown to everyone; when it is good enough, another metric 'bulges' and becomes the next focus.
steps: Define what Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue and Referral mean for your product and assign metrics to each.
Measure conversion between stages to find the weakest step.
Write down the Lean Analytics stage you think you are in, then honestly check the gate questions for each earlier stage.
Use your business model and stage to choose the One Metric That Matters, the one answering the riskiest question.
Set a target for it from the business model or baselines, display it to the whole team and run experiments to move it.
When the gate is passed, see which other metric has worsened and choose the next focal metric; keep capturing other data throughout.
outputs: A stage-by-stage metric map, current stage and gate status, and one focal metric with value and target.
useWhen: Early-stage or new products deciding what to measure and focus on, and teams needing a shared lifecycle vocabulary.
avoidWhen: When used as a substitute for understanding users: AARRR says where users drop but not why, users do not always move in order, and founders overestimate their stage. Pair with qualitative research; for experience quality metrics use HEART Framework.
whyLost: It survived because it is simple and memorable, though it is often reduced to dashboards without the stage gates or single-metric discipline.
whereToUse: Startups, new product lines, consumer apps, SaaS growth teams.
example: A language-learning app maps AARRR and finds activation (completing the first lesson) at 22% is the weakest step; it declares itself in the Stickiness stage and makes day-7 retention its One Metric That Matters with a 30% target.
reference: Croll, A. and Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics: Use Data to Build a Better Startup Faster. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media; McClure, D. (2007). Startup Metrics for Pirates: AARRR! Presentation.

name: State space grids
origin: Lewis, Lamey and Douglas (1999); Granic, Hollenstein, Dishion and Patterson (2003); Hollenstein (2013)
summary: Plots a person's or pair's moment-to-moment path through a grid of two coded behaviour dimensions to find attractor states and how they change.
description: Two ordinal or categorical variables coded continuously over a real-time episode define a grid; for example five levels of distress by five levels of gaze give 25 cells. Each coded moment is a point, and the trajectory is drawn cell to cell. The method borrows from dynamic systems theory: cells where behaviour settles repeatedly and returns quickly after leaving are attractors. Attractor strength is quantified by visit frequency, time spent, return latency after leaving, and the probability of falling back. For dyads, each axis is one partner's behaviour, so the grid shows joint states such as mutual engagement or escalating conflict. Grids built at successive waves reveal reorganisation over development or learning, and overall measures such as dispersion across cells index flexibility. The approach is visual and descriptive but depends on reliable, time-locked coding.
steps: Choose two coded dimensions, one per partner for a dyad (user and assistant, two collaborators) or two for an individual (affect and engagement).
Code the recording in time-locked units (for example every second or every event) with inter-rater reliability checked.
Plot the trajectory through the grid, cell by cell.
Quantify attractors by visit counts, duration, return latency and transition probabilities, and compute dispersion across cells.
Repeat at later sessions or waves and compare grids to find reorganisation.
outputs: State space grids, attractor statistics, dispersion measures and comparisons across sessions or groups.
useWhen: Studying moment-to-moment interaction dynamics, such as user frustration and system feedback, conversational exchanges with an AI agent, or collaborative work, where recurring joint states matter.
avoidWhen: Coding cannot be made reliable and time-locked, or the question concerns aggregate outcomes rather than dynamics. For many sequences and event types, lag sequential analysis or hidden Markov models scale better.
whyLost: It is confined to developmental and family-interaction research, and its coding burden has kept it out of UX video analysis.
whereToUse: Conversational AI evaluation, co-located and remote collaboration tools, games, tutoring systems, parent-child technology use.
example: Researchers code user frustration (four levels) and chatbot repair strategy (four types) every turn in 60 support conversations. Grids show a strong attractor at 'high frustration plus scripted apology' that users rarely leave, while 'clarifying question' paths return quickly to low frustration.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Witherington, D. C. (2015). Dynamic systems in developmental science. In R. M. Lerner, W. F. Overton and P. C. M. Molenaar (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 1 (pp. 63-112). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: State transition diagrams
origin: Finite automata from the 1950s; state transition networks for dialogue design by Parnas (1969) and Wasserman; statecharts by David Harel, 1987
summary: Models an interface as states and the user or system events that move between them, making modes, dead ends and missing transitions visible and checkable.
description: A state transition diagram represents each distinct interface state as a node and each event (tap, timeout, error, sensor input) as a labelled edge. Harel's statecharts extend this with hierarchy, concurrency and history, making large systems tractable. The rigorous version is complete: every state has a defined response to every event, including error and timeout events. Analysis then reveals hidden modes, states with no exit, events with no handler and inconsistent responses to the same event in different states. Modern UX uses flow diagrams that look similar but usually show happy paths only, which is why the method is vestigial. The tabular form, a state-event matrix, is the best completeness check.
steps: Enumerate states, including transient and error states, from the design, code or observation.
Enumerate events: user actions, system responses, timeouts, errors and external inputs.
Build a state-event matrix and fill every cell with the resulting state or an explicit 'ignored'; empty cells are specification gaps.
Draw the diagram, using statechart hierarchy for nested modes and concurrent regions for parallel subsystems.
Check for states without exits, unreachable states, mode ambiguity (same display, different states) and inconsistent responses to the same event.
Review with engineers and domain experts and convert into test cases for every transition.
outputs: A complete state-event matrix, a statechart, a list of gaps and mode hazards, and transition-level test cases.
useWhen: When designing complex modes, multi-step workflows, device interfaces, or conversational flows; when bugs cluster around unexpected states.
avoidWhen: For content-heavy, largely stateless experiences; use content audits or IA methods instead.
whyLost: Statecharts remain common in engineering (XState, embedded systems), but UX replaced them with happy-path flow diagrams, keeping the look and losing completeness.
whereToUse: Medical devices, checkout and payment flows, onboarding, IoT devices, voice and chat assistants, and AI agent tool loops.
example: A state-event matrix for a payments flow reveals 17 empty cells, including what happens when the bank times out after 3D Secure succeeds. Defining that transition prevents duplicate charges that were generating support tickets.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Harel, D. (1987). Statecharts: A visual formalism for complex systems. Science of Computer Programming, 8(3), 231-274.

name: Statistical Claim Credibility Check
aka: Critiquing reported survey and poll results
origin: Deborah Rumsey (2003), within the statistical literacy movement
summary: A structured checklist for deciding whether a statistic, survey result or study finding reported by someone else is trustworthy enough to act on.
description: Most statistical abuse is not bad arithmetic but subtle exaggeration, so the consumer must ask who produced a figure, what type of statistic it is, how the data were gathered and what was left out. Rumsey's checks cover arithmetic consistency (percentages totalling 100), missing or tiny sample sizes, raw counts used where rates are needed, distorted charts, non-random and self-selected samples, low response rates, leading questions, absent margins of error (which cover sampling error only, not bias), causal claims from observational data, selective reporting of one significant result among many, and anecdotes. Her example of crime totals rising while the rate per 100,000 fell shows how two sides can both cite correct figures. For UX, the checklist applies to vendor benchmarks, industry reports, stakeholder slides and internal dashboards before they drive decisions.
steps: Identify who produced the statistic and whether they have an interest in the result.
Check the arithmetic: percentages that should total 100 do, counts add to the total and fractions match percentages.
Find the sample size and number of actual respondents; treat results with no n or a tiny n as unreliable.
Check that the statistic fits the question, using rates rather than counts when the base changes.
Examine charts for honest scales, starting points, equal intervals and no 3-D distortion.
Check how the sample was chosen and the response rate, and read the actual question wording for leading phrasing.
Look for a margin of error, and if a causal claim is made, check whether it comes from a randomised experiment or an observational study with confounders.
Ask how many analyses were run and whether data were dropped; wait for independent confirmation of surprising findings.
outputs: A judgement on whether the claim can be trusted and a list of questions to put to its source.
useWhen: Before acting on third-party statistics, vendor or industry reports, stakeholder claims or dashboards, or when reviewing a colleague's survey results.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for a full methodological review of your own studies; use the Threats-to-Validity Audit (Shadish, Cook and Campbell) or Total Survey Error Framework for those.
whyLost: Statistical literacy is taught in school and introductory courses but is rarely applied as an explicit checklist in UX reviews.
whereToUse: Research operations and review of industry benchmarks, AI-generated summaries of data, executive dashboards, competitor claims.
example: A vendor claims its chatbot 'cut support contacts by 40 per cent'. The check shows the figure is a raw count over a period when active users fell by a third and that no comparison group was used, so the team asks for contacts per active user against a holdout.
reference: Rumsey, D. (2003). Statistics For Dummies. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, chapters 2, 20 and 21.

name: Statistical power analysis
origin: Neyman and Pearson (1933); popularised in behavioural science by Jacob Cohen, Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (1962; 1988)
summary: Determines the probability that a study will detect an effect of a given size, used to plan sample sizes or to judge what a completed study could have found.
description: Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a specified true effect exists, equal to 1 minus the Type II error rate. It depends on effect size, sample size, alpha, variability and design. Cohen found that psychology studies in the 1960s had a median power of only about 0.46 for medium effects, and underpowered research remains common, producing both missed effects and exaggerated estimates among significant results (the winner's curse). A priori power analysis sets sample size before data collection, typically targeting 80% or 90% power for the smallest effect of interest. Sensitivity analysis asks what effect a fixed sample could detect. Post-hoc 'observed power' is uninformative and should not be used. Rigour comes from basing the effect size on decision relevance or credible prior evidence rather than optimism.
steps: Define the primary outcome, test and design (for example two-proportion test, two independent groups).
Set the smallest effect size of interest from business relevance or prior evidence, such as a 2 percentage point uplift from a 10% baseline.
Choose alpha (usually 0.05, two-sided) and target power (usually 0.80, or 0.90 for important decisions).
Compute the required sample with appropriate software, adjusting for expected attrition, clustering or multiple comparisons.
If the available sample is fixed, run a sensitivity analysis to state the minimum detectable effect and decide whether the study is worth running.
Document the calculation in the pre-registration or analysis plan, and do not compute observed power after the fact.
outputs: Required sample sizes or minimum detectable effects, documented assumptions, and a go or no-go decision on study feasibility.
useWhen: Planning any confirmatory quantitative study, A/B test or survey comparison, and assessing whether completed null results are informative.
avoidWhen: Exploratory or qualitative studies where hypothesis testing is not the goal; use saturation or problem-discovery models for sample planning instead.
whyLost: Experimentation platforms embed sample size calculators, but UX researchers often run studies with convenient samples and skip power, or compute meaningless post-hoc power.
whereToUse: A/B tests, quantitative usability benchmarks, survey segment comparisons, unmoderated studies, pricing tests.
example: Before testing a Trust Badge, a team set the smallest meaningful uplift at 1.5 points on a 12% sign-up rate. At alpha 0.05 and 80% power, the two-proportion calculation required about 7,700 users per arm, so the test was scheduled for 3 weeks instead of the planned 5 days.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 1 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2008)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
Dangerous Statistical Mistakes in UX & Human Factors Research (carousel, n.d.)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Maxwell et al., 2018)
Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R (Chihara & Hesterberg, 2011)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella, 2010)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)

name: Statistical Process Control (Control Charts)
origin: Walter Shewhart, Bell Labs, 1924-1931; Western Electric rules (1956); promoted by W. Edwards Deming
summary: Plots a metric with statistically derived control limits to separate routine (common-cause) variation from signals of special causes that warrant investigation.
description: Shewhart's insight was that every process varies, and reacting to every fluctuation (tampering) makes things worse. Control charts set limits at about three sigma from the centre line, estimated from the process's own short-term variation (e.g. moving ranges in XmR charts). Points outside the limits, or patterns such as eight consecutive points on one side (Western Electric or Nelson rules), signal special causes. Healthcare quality improvement adopted SPC widely. For UX metrics programmes, SPC stops teams from narrating random week-to-week variation and directs attention to genuine signals, and run charts show whether improvements produced real process change.
steps: Choose a metric measured regularly (e.g. weekly task success, daily error rate) and the right chart type (XmR, p-chart, u-chart).
Establish a baseline period of at least 20-25 points to compute centre line and control limits.
Plot ongoing data and apply detection rules (beyond limits, runs, trends).
Investigate signals for special causes; do not react to points within limits.
After a deliberate process change, recalculate limits for the new phase.
Report charts instead of week-over-week percentage changes.
outputs: Control charts with limits, identified special-cause signals and documented process phases.
useWhen: Ongoing UX or service metrics reviewed regularly, especially where teams overreact to fluctuations.
avoidWhen: One-off comparisons or experiments; use appropriate experimental statistics.
whyLost: Manufacturing quality methods never entered digital product culture, which prefers dashboards and percentage changes.
whereToUse: Experience metric reviews, support quality, content quality, AI output quality monitoring, accessibility regressions.
example: A weekly CSAT dip prompts a war room. An XmR chart shows the dip is within control limits; two weeks later a genuine signal (8 points below centre) leads to a real cause, a shipping partner change.
sources: Shewhart, Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product (1931)
Wheeler, Understanding Variation: The Key to Managing Chaos (2nd ed., 2000)
Provost & Murray, The Health Care Data Guide (2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Applied Statistics and Probability for Engineers: Student Solutions Manual (Montgomery & Runger, 2002)
reference: Wheeler, D. J. (2000). Understanding Variation. SPC Press.

name: Statistical test selection by design
aka: Significance test selection by experimental design
Test selection by question and data type
Choosing a test for comparing means
origin: Textbook decision charts; Lazar, Feng and Hochheiser after Rosenthal and Rosnow (2008); Goss-Sampson (2020)
summary: Chooses a statistical test from the research question, the design (between, within or split-plot), the number of factors and conditions, the outcome's data type and assumptions.
description: Test selection is a decision procedure rather than a test. The question type (comparison with a norm, relationship, prediction, two or more independent or related groups, interactions) is crossed with the design and the outcome's level of measurement. For continuous outcomes meeting parametric assumptions: independent-samples t for two between groups, one-way ANOVA for three or more, factorial ANOVA for several factors; paired t and repeated-measures ANOVA for within designs; split-plot ANOVA for mixed designs. When assumptions fail (independent errors, equal variances, normal errors, interval scale) the alternatives are Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal-Wallis and Friedman. Nominal outcomes go to chi-square, McNemar for paired proportions, or logistic regression for prediction. The rigour lies in fixing the design and analysis before data collection, using one-tailed tests only for directional hypotheses, and remembering that nonparametric tests lose power and still carry assumptions.
steps: State the question type: difference from a norm, relationship, prediction, difference between independent groups, between related measures, or interaction.
Identify the design (between-group, within-group or split-plot), the number of independent variables and the number of conditions for each.
Identify the outcome's data type: continuous, ordinal or nominal.
For continuous outcomes, check independence, homogeneity of variance and normality of residuals.
Read off the parametric test or its nonparametric or categorical alternative from the decision chart, and pre-register the choice where possible.
Lay out the data as the software requires and report the statistic with degrees of freedom, p value and an effect size with confidence interval.
outputs: A justified choice of test and a correctly reported result.
useWhen: Planning the analysis of any comparative usability study, survey comparison or experiment, ideally before data collection.
