avoidWhen: Complex data with repeated trials, nesting or missing cells are better served by mixed-effects or Bayesian models than by a flowchart choice. The chart does not replace thinking about effect sizes and practical significance.
whyLost: It survived as the standard teaching device in HCI and UX statistics; the risk is mechanical use that ignores design subtleties.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks, A/B test readouts, survey comparisons, academic HCI studies, research ops analysis templates.
example: A text-entry study compares standard keyboard, word prediction and dictation (within participants) on transcription and composition tasks. The chart points to a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA; because error rates are skewed counts, the team uses Friedman tests for errors and the ANOVA for speed.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. and Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 75-99.

name: Statistical Tolerance Intervals
origin: Engineering statistics tradition (Wilks, 1941; Wald and Wolfowitz, 1946)
summary: An interval, mean plus or minus k standard deviations, expected to contain a chosen share of individual values with a chosen confidence, unlike a confidence interval for the mean.
description: A tolerance interval answers a question UX metrics often imply but rarely ask: within what range do most individual users fall? It is computed as the sample mean plus or minus k times the sample standard deviation, where k comes from tables for the chosen coverage (for example 99 percent of values), confidence (for example 95 percent) and sample size. A one-sided lower bound, mean minus k s, is used when a quantity must stay above a minimum, and an upper bound when it must stay below a maximum. Montgomery and Runger stress the contrast with neighbouring intervals: a confidence interval covers the mean, a prediction interval covers the next single observation, and a tolerance interval covers a stated share of the population. Tolerance intervals are far wider than confidence intervals, especially at small n, and the standard factors assume normally distributed data.
steps: Choose the coverage proportion (for example 90 or 99 percent of individual values) and the confidence level (for example 95 percent).
Compute the sample mean and standard deviation and note n, transforming skewed measures such as task time (for example by logging) to approximate normality.
Look up the tolerance factor k for that coverage, confidence and n in a two-sided or one-sided table, or compute it with software.
Report mean minus k s to mean plus k s, or a one-sided bound, back-transforming if needed.
Interpret it as the range expected to contain the chosen share of individual users, not the mean.
outputs: A two-sided tolerance interval or one-sided tolerance bound for individual values.
useWhen: Setting or checking requirements about individual users rather than averages, such as 'at least 90 percent of users complete enrolment within three minutes', or specifying latency and performance budgets.
avoidWhen: For uncertainty about an average use Confidence Intervals for Task Time (Log-Transformed and Median) or Bootstrap methods for confidence intervals; with clearly non-normal data use nonparametric tolerance limits, which need larger samples.
whyLost: UX statistics teaching stops at confidence intervals for means and proportions, and tolerance intervals stayed in manufacturing quality control.
whereToUse: Medical device and accessibility performance requirements, service-level targets for task time, performance budgets, benchmark specifications.
example: Enrolment times from 40 users are logged; mean 4.6 and s 0.35 on the log scale with a one-sided k of 1.73 for 90 percent coverage and 95 percent confidence give an upper bound of about 182 seconds, so the three-minute requirement is not yet met for nine in ten users.
sources: Applied Statistics and Probability for Engineers: Student Solutions Manual (Montgomery & Runger, 2002)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Montgomery, D. C. and Runger, G. C. (2003). Applied Statistics and Probability for Engineers (3rd ed.). Wiley, section 8-7.

name: Steering Law
origin: Johnny Accot and Shumin Zhai, 1997, extending Rashevsky (1959) and Drury (1971)
summary: Predicts the time to move a pointer or finger through a constrained path from the path's length and width, for designing cascading menus, sliders and gesture tunnels.
description: The steering law generalises Fitts' law from point targets to paths. For a straight tunnel of length A and width W, movement time T = a + b(A/W); for a curved path it is the integral of ds/W(s) along the path. Movement time thus grows linearly with the path's index of difficulty, not logarithmically as in Fitts' law, so narrow tunnels are disproportionately costly. It applies to hierarchical cascading menus, drag-to-reorder, sliders, scroll scrubbing, drawing tools and gesture paths. Rigour comes from empirically fitting a and b for the device and population, since constants differ greatly between mouse, touch, stylus and gloved hands, and from checking model fit (R squared above 0.9 is typical in well-controlled studies).
steps: Identify interactions where the user must keep a pointer within a bounded path (cascading menus, sliders, drag lanes, gesture corridors).
Measure path length A and width W (or W as a function of position for curved or variable paths) in physical units on the target device.
Calculate index of difficulty ID = A/W, or the integral form for curved paths.
Fit constants a and b from a calibration study: 10-16 participants, at least 5 ID levels, 10+ trials each, logging movement time and path exits.
Predict movement time and exit-error likelihood for candidate designs and compare variants.
Redesign high-ID paths (for example widen tunnels, add hover delay or diagonal tolerance to cascading menus) and verify with a follow-up timing test.
outputs: Fitted steering constants for the device, predicted movement times per design, error rates per ID level, and design recommendations for tunnel widths.
useWhen: When designing cascading or mega menus, sliders, drag-and-drop lanes, swipe gestures, drawing tools or any constrained-path interaction, especially with gloves or on small screens.
avoidWhen: When targets are discrete points (use Fitts' law) or when cognitive choice time dominates motor time (use Hick-Hyman or KLM).
whyLost: HCI researchers know it well but practitioners cite only Fitts' law; the steering law needs calibration studies and its insights are usually rediscovered ad hoc through menu tolerance hacks.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial touch consoles, mega menus in e-commerce, mobile sliders, VR ray-cast menus, and sketching tools.
example: A surgical console's cascading menu requires dragging through a 6 mm-wide submenu corridor with sterile gloves. Steering-law calibration predicts 1.8 s and 22% path exits; widening the corridor to 14 mm and adding a 300 ms intent delay cuts both by more than half.
sources: Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
The Inquiry Series, Ch 3 — The Ballistics of the Human Body — Fitts' Law & Motor Control
reference: Accot, J. & Zhai, S. (1997). Beyond Fitts' law: models for trajectory-based HCI tasks. Proceedings of CHI '97, 295-302.

name: Stein's two-stage fixed-width confidence interval
aka: Stein's two-stage procedure for a fixed-width confidence interval
origin: Charles Stein (1945, 1949), drawing on Dantzig (1940), Mahalanobis (1940) and Wald (1947)
summary: Uses a pilot sample's variance and a t quantile to decide how many more observations guarantee a confidence interval of preset width with at least the stated coverage.
description: With a fixed sample size and unknown variance, the width of a t interval is random and can be large; Dantzig proved in 1940 that no fixed-n procedure can guarantee both a chosen width and coverage. Stein's solution is double sampling. A pilot of m observations estimates the variance S squared. The total sample size N is the larger of m and the smallest integer at least t(m-1, alpha/2) squared times S squared divided by d squared, where d is the desired half-width. After collecting the remaining N - m observations, the interval is the overall mean plus or minus d, with coverage guaranteed to be at least 1 - alpha for every parameter value. The price is oversampling: in simulation, average N exceeded the optimal size by about 100% with m = 5 and about 33% with m = 10, so a larger pilot is more efficient. A bounded-risk variant keeps the mean squared error below a set bound.
steps: Fix the desired half-width d (for example +/-5 seconds on mean task time) and the confidence level 1 - alpha.
Choose a pilot size m of at least 2, preferably 10 or more to limit oversampling, and collect the pilot observations.
Compute the pilot sample variance S squared.
Compute N as the larger of m and the smallest integer at least t(m-1, alpha/2)^2 x S^2 / d^2.
If N exceeds m, collect N - m further observations; otherwise stop.
Report the mean of all N observations plus or minus d as the interval.
outputs: A final sample size and an interval of exactly the preset width with guaranteed coverage.
useWhen: A benchmark must report a metric to a contractually or decision-defined precision, such as mean task time within +/-5 seconds, and the variance is unknown before the study.
avoidWhen: Observations are strongly non-normal (log-transform task times first or use bootstrap-based planning), recruitment cannot be extended after a pilot, or a pilot of only a few cases would cause heavy oversampling.
whyLost: Sequential and two-stage designs remained in statistical theory and quality control; UX sample sizes are set by convention or one-off power calculations.
whereToUse: Summative usability benchmarks, regulated or procurement usability testing, performance baselines for competitive comparisons.
example: A bank needs mean time to complete a transfer within +/-4 seconds at 95% confidence. A pilot of 10 users gives S = 15 seconds, so N = ceiling(2.262^2 x 225 / 16) = 72; the team recruits 62 more participants and reports the mean +/-4 seconds.
reference: Stein, C. (1945). A two sample test for a linear hypothesis whose power is independent of the variance. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 16, 243-258.

name: Stereotype Threat Framing and Demographic-Item Placement
origin: Steele and Aronson (1995); Walton and Cohen (2003); Schmader, Johns and Forbes (2008)
summary: A study-design check that avoids framing tasks as tests of ability and places demographic questions after performance tasks, so that stereotype threat does not depress some participants' results.
description: Performance can fall when a negative stereotype about one's group becomes relevant. Steele and Aronson gave identical verbal items described either as diagnostic of ability or as a problem-solving exercise; Black students did worse only under the diagnostic framing, and asking students to state their race before a test also lowered their scores. Similar effects appear for women in mathematics, older adults with technology, low-income children and White men told they would be compared with Asian men. Causes include vigilance, thought suppression and anxiety. For UX studies the implication is concrete: usability tasks described as tests, and demographic questions placed first, can depress performance for groups facing stereotypes such as older adults with technology, and so distort comparisons between groups. The check fixes wording and order, and where it matters treats framing as an experimental factor.
steps: Identify groups in the sample that a relevant ability stereotype targets (for example older adults and technology, women and mathematics).
Describe tasks as tests of the product, not the participant, avoiding words such as 'test of your ability'.
Place demographic and self-rated expertise questions after performance tasks.
Where group comparisons matter, manipulate framing or item order as a factor and compare performance by group.
Consider mitigations such as brief affirmation or explaining that the study evaluates the design.
Report framing and item order with the results.
outputs: Task wording and question-order decisions, and where tested, performance by framing condition and group.
useWhen: Usability tests, benchmarks or skills assessments that compare performance across age, gender, ethnicity or other groups subject to ability stereotypes.
avoidWhen: Do not treat it as the only cause of group differences; effect sizes vary and replications have been mixed. For wider participant-reactivity issues use Demand Characteristics and Experimenter Effects Control.
whyLost: Moderators routinely say 'we are testing the product, not you', but the evidence on demographic placement and framing is rarely applied deliberately.
whereToUse: Accessibility and older-adult studies, financial and digital literacy research, educational products, AI tool performance studies across groups.
example: A benchmark comparing digital banking task success between under-40s and over-65s moves age and self-rated tech skill questions to the end and reframes the session as evaluating the app. The age gap in success narrows by several points, changing the team's estimate of how much redesign older users need.
reference: Steele, C. M. and Aronson, J. (1995). Stereotype threat and the intellectual test performance of African Americans. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(5), 797-811.

name: Stevens' scales (nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio)
origin: S. S. Stevens, 'On the Theory of Scales of Measurement', 1946
summary: Classifies every measure by its scale type, nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, to determine which transformations, summaries and statistical tests are legitimate.
description: Stevens defined four levels of measurement by the transformations that preserve their meaning: nominal (categories; any one-to-one relabelling), ordinal (order; any monotonic transformation), interval (equal differences; linear transformations) and ratio (true zero; multiplication by a constant). Each level permits different statistics: mode for nominal, median and percentiles for ordinal, mean and standard deviation for interval, and ratios and geometric means for ratio. UX regularly breaks these rules, for instance averaging single Likert items as if interval, or claiming that task time 'doubled' satisfaction. The debate about treating multi-item rating scales as interval is legitimate and well studied, but it should be a reasoned choice. Applying Stevens' scales is the first step of any measurement plan.
steps: List every variable in the study, from task success to satisfaction ratings to time.
Classify each by scale type and record the justification (for example task time is ratio; a single 5-point item is ordinal; a validated multi-item scale such as SUS is commonly treated as interval).
Specify permissible summaries and tests per variable before collecting data (for example median and Mann-Whitney for ordinal items).
Check transformations and composite scores for legitimacy, for example not summing nominal codes.
Where you treat ordinal data as interval, state the assumption and run a sensitivity analysis with an ordinal method.
Review the reporting plan so claims match scale properties (no ratios on interval data).
outputs: A variable-by-scale table with permissible statistics and claims, and an analysis plan consistent with measurement levels.
useWhen: At the start of any quantitative study, when designing surveys or metrics, and when reviewing dashboards or research reports for statistical errors.
avoidWhen: It is never wrong to classify, but avoid rigid application that forbids defensible practices such as treating summed multi-item scales as interval; consult measurement models such as Rasch for stronger claims.
whyLost: Taught in introductory statistics but rarely applied in UX practice, where tooling defaults to means for every number.
whereToUse: Survey programmes, UX metrics and dashboards, A/B test reporting, and benchmarking studies.
example: A product team reports 'satisfaction rose 25%' from a mean single-item rating of 3.2 to 4.0. Classifying the item as ordinal, the researcher re-reports the change as a shift in the proportion rating 4 or 5 from 38% to 71%, with a valid test.
sources: Dix, A., Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data (2020)
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Leavy, P., Research Design: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed Methods, Arts-Based, and Community-Based Participatory Research Approaches (2017)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 8 — Measurement Theory — Before You Measure Anything
Stevens, S. S. (1946) On the theory of scales of measurement. Science
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
reference: Stevens, S. S. (1946). On the theory of scales of measurement. Science, 103(2684), 677-680.

name: Stimulated Recall Interview
origin: Benjamin Bloom, 1953 (stimulated recall of classroom thinking)
summary: Replaying recordings of a participant's own session to cue detailed retrospective accounts of what they were thinking at specific moments.
description: Stimulated recall separates doing from explaining. The participant first works naturally, unburdened by concurrent think-aloud, while screen, audio and optionally eye-tracking are recorded. Soon afterwards, ideally within 24 hours, the researcher plays back the recording and pauses at pre-selected moments such as hesitations, errors or unusual actions, asking what the participant was thinking, trying to do and expecting. Because the recording shows behaviour, probing targets cognition: decisions, expectations and interpretations of feedback. Analysis maps cognitive events onto behavioural events, and mismatches between what participants believed they were doing and what the recording shows are the richest data. It avoids reactivity of concurrent verbalisation, at the cost of some reconstruction risk that increases with delay.
steps: Record the participant's work session (screen and audio, optionally eye tracking); the recording is stimulus material, not data to be analysed on its own.

Immediately afterwards or within 24 hours, play back the recording and pause at pre-selected moments such as hesitations, errors or unusual actions, asking 'What were you thinking here?', 'What were you trying to do at this point?' and 'What did you expect to happen?'
Probe for thoughts about decisions, expectations and interpretations rather than descriptions of actions, which the recording already shows.

Variant (post-experience eye-tracked protocol, PEEP; Ball, Eger, Stevens and Dodd, 2006): replay the eye-tracking recording and pause at timestamps noted during the session; this reduces reliance on memory but is labour-intensive and limits the number of tasks.

Code for cognitive processes such as error detection, goal clarification, interpretation of feedback and decision points, map them to behavioural events in the recording, and treat mismatches between what participants thought they were doing and what the recording shows as the richest data.
outputs: Time-aligned behaviour and cognition records, coded decision points, and documented mismatches between intent and action.
useWhen: Fast, high-workload or expert tasks where think-aloud would disrupt performance (trading, clinical work, gaming, driving), or when eye-tracking data need explanation.
avoidWhen: When recall delay will be long or the task trivial; use concurrent think-aloud or a simple post-task interview.
whyLost: Retrospective think-aloud is known in usability, but the structured cueing and cognitive coding from education research are rarely applied.
whereToUse: Expert tools, safety-critical interfaces, eye-tracking studies, games, and AI-assisted decision tools where users evaluate model outputs quickly.
example: Radiologists review scans with an AI triage overlay while recorded. Replaying moments where they ignored the AI flag reveals that they distrust its confidence colour scale, not the model itself.
sources: Thought Processes in Lectures and Discussions (Bloom)
Marsh, S., User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (2018) (PEEP, after Ball, Eger, Stevens & Dodd, 2006)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
Qualitative Methods in Information Retrieval Research (Fidel, 1993)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Bloom, B. S. (1953). Thought processes in lectures and discussions. Journal of General Education, 7(3), 160-169.

name: Stochastic transitivity test
aka: Stochastic transitivity test for multi-attribute choices
origin: Amos Tversky, 1969
summary: Build personal option sets around each person's threshold for negligible differences, then run replicated paired choices to test whether preferences cycle.
description: Tversky built options in which one attribute improved slightly as another worsened, such as gambles where the chance of winning rose as the payoff fell, shown as pie slices. People who ignored small probability differences chose by payoff on adjacent pairs but by probability on the extreme pair, producing cycles. After a screening session, eight participants took five weekly sessions with fillers and real play; weak stochastic transitivity was rejected for five. A second study used applicant profiles, estimated each person's threshold and built personal sets; intransitive triples occurred at about the rate a lexicographic semiorder predicts. Nobody noticed their own cycles. The test is rigorous because it is per person, replicated and compared against a random-responding baseline.
steps: Choose two attributes with a trade-off and design options in small steps along both.
Run a screening session with adjacent and extreme pairs plus filler pairs to identify people who use a lexicographic rule.
Estimate each person's threshold for treating a difference as negligible.
Build individual option sets around that threshold.
Collect replicated paired choices over several sessions (the original used five weekly sessions).
Test weak stochastic transitivity per person by likelihood ratio, comparing with the rate expected from random responding.
outputs: Per-person tests of weak stochastic transitivity and of a lexicographic semiorder, with rates of intransitive triples.
useWhen: Investigating whether incremental upsells, tiered options or side-by-side comparison layouts lead users into choices they would reject in a direct comparison.
avoidWhen: Avoid when only one session is possible, since many replications are needed; for one-off preference measurement use paired comparison scaling.
whyLost: It is a demanding decision-theory test with no product framing, and UX rarely checks the consistency of individual preferences.
whereToUse: Upsell and add-on flows, plan comparison tables, e-commerce comparison tools, configurators.
example: Add-on bundles are priced in small steps: each step looks negligible, so users drift up one tier at a time, yet prefer the base plan over the top tier when they are compared directly.
sources: Tversky, A. (1969). Intransitivity of preferences. Psychological Review, 76
reference: Tversky, A. (1969). Intransitivity of preferences. Psychological Review, 76, 31-48.

name: Story Collages
origin: Dan Hill at Arup smart-city workshops; term coined in Rowland et al. (2015)
summary: One-page montages of real photographs, rough renderings and annotations that place a future product or service in everyday context to provoke discussion.
description: Story collages are early, semi-realistic single-page visualisations that montage photographs of real places with quick renderings and generic interfaces, annotated so that viewers have to read them. They show how products, services, environments and people relate in a future situation, rather than detailing any one screen. Used as pivots for conversation in generative workshops, they are printed as posters; Arup's teams deliberately included flawed or debatable concepts to invite critique. Mixing photographic and sketchy styles signals that the scene is everyday and plausible yet unfinished and open to change. Their value lies in how cheaply they make an abstract system concrete enough to argue about, and the risk lies in over-investing in any single polished image.
steps: Choose the key forms, relationships and interactions the concept needs to show.
Montage real photographs of the setting with rough renderings and generic interface elements.
Annotate each collage so it must be read, naming actors, data and moments.
Include some deliberately flawed or debatable concepts alongside promising ones.
Print the collages as posters and use them to prompt discussion in workshops.
Record which elements people embrace, question or reject, and iterate.
outputs: Poster-sized concept collages and recorded reactions: aspirations, concerns, and selected and rejected concept elements.
useWhen: Use them early in connected-product, service or smart-environment projects, when stakeholders or residents need something concrete to react to before any prototype exists.
avoidWhen: Reactions to posters are not evidence of use; once a direction is chosen, test with Experience Prototyping or Prototype Testing. When participants should build the futures themselves, use Co-design Workshops.
whyLost: The technique stayed in urban, service and IoT design consultancies; mainstream product teams move straight to wireframes or concept videos.
whereToUse: Smart cities, mobility services, IoT ecosystems, healthcare facilities and public consultations.
example: A council's shared-bike garage concept is shown as a day and night collage. Residents question who can see entry logs, and the team removes camera-based access before prototyping.
reference: Rowland, C., Goodman, E., Charlier, M., Light, A. and Lui, A. (2015). Designing Connected Products: UX for the Consumer Internet of Things. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 582-586.

name: Storyboarding
origin: Disney story sketches (1930s); HCI practice by Beyer and Holtzblatt (1998), Truong, Hayes and Abowd (2006) and Buxton (2007)
summary: Sketch a short sequence of frames showing people, context and a product in use, to explore a design, ground it in research data and communicate it.
description: A storyboard is a sequence of sketched frames showing a person using a product or service in context: screens, physical actions, thoughts, other people, places and devices. In Contextual Design, storyboards are drawn from consolidated field models and the vision, one per main task and situation, starting with a happy path and then variants for problems in the data, and each is checked against that data before structural design. Hartson and Pyla stress the transitions between frames, where interruptions and decisions live. Truong, Hayes and Abowd found that three to six panels, minimal text, and simple figures work best; polish implies certainty. Group variants have teams sketch a persona's story across six to ten captioned panels, or an ideal future state, and present it to the room.
steps: Decide the purpose: thinking tool (whose story, which goal) or communication tool (existing problem, impact of an issue, or desired experience).
Pick one task, persona and scenario per storyboard, drawn from research data where available.
Plan three to six panels (six to ten for group persona stories) and how time passes between them.
Sketch each frame with setting, actions, screens, thoughts and speech; draw transitions that show what causes each change; stick figures are enough.
Draw a happy path first, then variants for problems and difficult situations found in the data.
Review each storyboard against the research data and with the team, critiquing gaps and assumptions.
Use storyboards in user feedback sessions or speed dating, or feed them into structural design and user stories.
outputs: Sets of storyboards per task or persona, issues spotted in transitions, and input to information structure, prototypes and user stories.
useWhen: Use it once you understand users' tasks and contexts and need to imagine and agree how a new design will fit them, or to communicate a desired experience to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: A storyboard shows an intended experience, not a tested one; evaluate with Prototype Testing or Usability Testing. For capturing what users currently do, use Contextual Inquiry or Journey Mapping.
whyLost: It survived because it is cheap, universal and bridges research and design, though the Contextual Design discipline of grounding each frame in consolidated data is often dropped.
whereToUse: Multi-device and offline-heavy services, hardware and IoT, healthcare pathways, AI agent behaviour, and pitching concepts.
example: A rail operator storyboards a commuter rebooking a missed train across platform, phone and ticket barrier. The transition frame 'barrier rejects old ticket' shows the gap, and the team adds barrier-readable rebooking.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Truong, K.N., Hayes, G.R. and Abowd, G.D. (2006). Storyboarding: an empirical determination of best practices and effective guidelines. Proceedings of DIS 2006; Holtzblatt, K. and Beyer, H. (2014). Contextual Design: Evolved. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool, pp. 54, 61-64.

name: Strange Loop Analysis of Recursive Interactions
origin: Douglas Hofstadter, 1979
summary: Identifies recursive and self-referential patterns in interactions, where system outputs become inputs to user behaviour and back, producing emergent or paradoxical effects.
description: Hofstadter described strange loops as hierarchies in which moving through levels eventually returns to the starting point, producing self-reference and emergent phenomena such as the self. In interaction design, analogous loops arise when system outputs shape user behaviour, which in turn reshapes the system: personalisation that narrows what users see and therefore what they choose, interfaces that configure themselves, or AI assistants trained on user responses to their own outputs. Strange loop analysis traces these recursive structures across levels (individual action, model state, interface presentation), looks for runaway amplification, self-fulfilling predictions and paradoxes, and designs interventions such as exploration, transparency or level separation. Rigour comes from tracing loops with log evidence rather than metaphor.
steps: Strange loop audit for complex interfaces:
List all elements whose function is to change other elements.
(2) For each: trace the chain — if the user follows this element's effect, do they end up back at the starting point unexpectedly?
(3) Identify all recursive paths in the navigation graph (using graph theory: cycles in the navigation directed graph).
(4) For each cycle: is the recursion intentional (breadcrumb navigation) or accidental (confusing settings interdependence)?
outputs: Maps of recursive loops between user behaviour and system response, identified runaway or paradoxical loops, and design interventions to stabilise or exploit them.
useWhen: Recommender systems, personalisation, social feeds, AI assistants that learn from users, and settings screens that configure the interface itself.
avoidWhen: Avoid for linear, stateless tasks where no feedback exists; for operational loop modelling use system dynamics or causal loop diagrams.
whyLost: Hofstadter's ideas inspired 1980s cognitive science and AI but were never turned into an HCI method; systems thinking tools took over loop analysis.
whereToUse: Complex settings and preferences UX, navigation audit, information architecture quality review, developer tool UX.
example: A music app finds users' 'skip' behaviour trains the recommender to narrow choices, which increases skipping; the loop analysis leads to a deliberate exploration slot that breaks the spiral.
reference: Hofstadter DR (1979) Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books

name: Strange loop audit
origin: Concept of the strange loop from Douglas Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach, 1979; operationalised for navigation by combining with graph cycle detection
summary: Finds paths where navigation or system logic loops back on itself, so that users moving 'forward' or 'up' end where they started, often without realising it.
description: Hofstadter's strange loop is a hierarchy that, by moving consistently in one direction, returns to its starting level. In interfaces this appears as settings that link to help that links back to settings, 'back' that re-opens the dialog it closed, error recovery that leads to the step that caused the error, or authentication flows that bounce between login and verification. Such loops are invisible locally, because each step is sensible, but trap users globally. The audit models the navigation and recovery structure as a directed graph, detects cycles with algorithms such as Tarjan's strongly connected components, then classifies each cycle as intentional (hub-and-spoke returns) or pathological (no exit towards the goal). Rigour comes from including error, timeout and back-stack behaviour in the graph.
steps: Map navigation and recovery behaviour as a directed graph, including back, cancel, errors, timeouts and deep links.
Run cycle detection (Tarjan's or Johnson's algorithm) to list strongly connected components and elementary cycles.
For each cycle, check whether at least one exit edge leads closer to the user's goal or a safe state; flag cycles with none as pathological.
Validate flagged loops against session logs, looking for repeated sequences (for example the same 3-screen sequence occurring 3 or more times in a session).
Observe 5-8 users on flagged tasks to confirm whether they recognise the loop and how they escape.
Redesign to break the loop with an explicit exit, state preservation or escalation path, and re-run cycle detection.
outputs: A list of detected cycles with classification, log evidence of loop frequency, user observations, and loop-breaking design changes.
useWhen: When users report going round in circles; in recovery, authentication, settings and support flows; in complex modal systems where back-stack behaviour is unclear.
avoidWhen: For simple linear flows with no back-links; a cognitive walkthrough suffices. For general IA findability, use IA graph analysis.
whyLost: Hofstadter's idea is well known as philosophy but was never turned into a practical audit; loops are found anecdotally in testing rather than systematically.
whereToUse: Account recovery and authentication, customer support and chatbot flows, surgical and industrial menus, and multi-step government services.
example: Session logs show 6% of users of a banking app cycling through 'Verify identity', 'Help' and 'Contact us', which links back to verification. The audit confirms no exit edge; adding a callback request breaks the loop and cuts abandoned recoveries by 40%.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 6 — Strange Loops, Recursive Failures & Navigation Traps
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books.

name: Strategy and Value Proposition Canvases
donor: Business strategy and business model design
origin: Strategy canvas: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne (Blue Ocean Strategy, 2005); Value Proposition Canvas: Alexander Osterwalder and Strategyzer; experience-based variant: Jim Kalbach (2016)
summary: Two canvases: a strategy canvas plotting how you and rivals perform on factors customers value, and a value proposition canvas matching customer jobs, pains and gains to an offering.
description: The strategy canvas lists factors of competition along the horizontal axis and relative performance from low to high on the vertical, with one value curve per organisation; differentiation shows where curves diverge, and blue ocean logic seeks trade-offs that make rivals irrelevant. Kalbach's experience-based variant uses journey phases (become aware, purchase, use, renew, get support) as the factors, giving an experience view of competition. The value proposition canvas has a customer profile (jobs to be done, pains, gains) and a value map (products and services, pain relievers, gain creators); where relievers and creators answer real pains and gains there is potential fit. Both are only as good as their inputs: factors, ratings, jobs and pains should come from research such as journey maps or mental model diagrams, and the fit they suggest must be validated with the market.
steps: Determine the factors customers value (or the journey phases) using research such as alignment diagrams or interviews.
Choose a limited set of competitors, ideally three and no more than four.
Rate each competitor on each factor on a relative low-to-high scale, backed by evidence such as surveys where possible, and plot the value curves.
Look for divergence, over-served factors and trade-offs that could differentiate.
For the value proposition canvas, fill in the customer profile (jobs, pains, gains) from research.
Fill in the value map (products and services, pain relievers, gain creators) and map relievers to pains and creators to gains.
List the assumed fits as hypotheses and validate them with customers before committing.
outputs: A strategy canvas with value curves, and a value proposition canvas showing fit and gaps, plus hypotheses to test.
useWhen: Use them when connecting research to positioning and offer design: deciding where to differentiate, or checking that a proposed offering answers documented jobs, pains and gains.
avoidWhen: Canvases filled from opinion are assumptions; collect jobs and pains through Jobs-to-be-Done Research or Interviews, and quantify factor importance with Kano Analysis or Competitive UX Benchmarking.
whyLost: Both survived because they are simple, visual and speak the language of business stakeholders, giving UX research a direct route into strategy.
whereToUse: Start-ups, new propositions in banking and insurance, SaaS packaging, and service portfolio reviews.
example: A neobank plots itself and three rivals across onboarding, everyday spending, support and switching; its curve dips at support. The value proposition canvas links the pain 'stuck with no human' to a callback feature to validate.
reference: Kim, W.C. and Mauborgne, R. (2005). Blue Ocean Strategy. Boston, MA: Harvard Business School Press; Kalbach, J. (2016). Mapping Experiences. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 65-73.

name: Strategy and Vision Documents
aka: Strategy and vision documents (diagnosis, guiding policies, actions; vision components)
Creating a technical vision or strategy document
Strategy kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions)
origin: Strategy kernel from Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy/Bad Strategy (2011); vision format from Will Larson (2019); creation process from Tanya Reilly (2022)
summary: Two written artefacts for aligning many teams: a strategy for one challenge (diagnosis, guiding policies, actions) and an aspirational vision for an area, produced through interviews and pre-alignment.
description: When an organisation outgrows direct oversight, written strategy and vision documents align teams better than meetings. A strategy addresses one challenge with Rumelt's kernel: a diagnosis that honestly names factors and constraints (including organisational ones), guiding policies that state the approach and its trade-offs, and coherent actions that follow. A vision describes a future in which today's trade-offs no longer conflict, written far enough ahead that details illustrate rather than constrain: a one or two sentence statement, a value proposition starting from users, the capabilities needed, constraints solved and remaining, references and a one-page narrative. Reilly's process adds an executive sponsor, a core group of two to four, broad interviews, decisions recorded with trade-offs, rough consensus with a pre-agreed tiebreaker, nemawashi (one-to-one pre-alignment before any meeting) and a memorable story. Drafts are tested on readers until confusion is minimal.
steps: Check that a document is needed; if teams are already aligned, use a lighter artefact.
Join any existing effort, secure an executive sponsor and form a core group of two to four with a weekly time commitment.
Agree scope and document type (strategy for a specific challenge, vision for an area) with the sponsor.
Interview widely, gather ideas without judgement, and write the diagnosis or the vision's value proposition starting from users.
Identify the few key decisions, decide each with recorded trade-offs, and draft guiding policies and actions (or capabilities and constraints for a vision).
Pre-align stakeholders one to one (nemawashi), test drafts on several readers, and record unresolved disagreements in the text.
Launch with executive endorsement and an official home, write a one-page narrative or slogan, and refresh yearly.
outputs: An endorsed strategy document per challenge or vision document per area, plus a narrative, slogan or deck.
useWhen: Use when several teams (product, design, research, engineering) need a shared direction that outlasts individual projects, or when a design or research organisation needs its own strategy.
avoidWhen: Avoid when teams are already aligned, or when the diagnosis rests on assumptions about users nobody has checked; ground it first with Jobs-to-be-Done Research or Contextual Inquiry. Overlapping visions are worse than none.
whyLost: It survived because written strategy and vision documents are standard in scaling technology companies, and Rumelt's kernel gives a clear structure.
whereToUse: Design and research team strategy, platform and design system direction, product line visions, AI adoption strategies.
example: A research lead writes a strategy for the challenge 'findings are not reused'. The diagnosis names scattered repositories; guiding policies favour one repository over team autonomy; actions include tagging standards and quarterly synthesis. Nemawashi with three product directors secures endorsement before the review meeting.
reference: Rumelt, R. (2011). Good Strategy/Bad Strategy. New York: Crown Business. Larson, W. (2019). An Elegant Puzzle: Systems of Engineering Management. San Francisco: Stripe Press. Reilly, T. (2022). The Staff Engineer's Path. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 69-113.

name: Strategy of Elaboration for Ruling Out Threats to Validity
origin: Charles S. Reichardt, 2000 and 2006, building on Donald Campbell's design elaboration and pattern matching
summary: When a named threat could bias an effect estimate, adds a second, contrasting estimate whose mix of effect and threat differs, and compares the two to separate them.
description: Any effect estimate equals the treatment effect plus the effect of whatever threats are present. Reichardt's elaboration strategy designs a second estimate to pull them apart. In estimate-and-subtract, the second estimate contains only the threat (for example a comparison series affected by the same history but not the treatment), so subtracting it removes the threat. In vary-the-size-of-the-treatment-effect, the second estimate contains the same threat but a different amount of effect; the effect is demonstrated to the extent the estimates differ. In vary-the-size-of-the-threat, the second contains the same effect but a different, ideally opposite, amount of threat; the threat is ruled out to the extent the estimates agree. The second estimate can come from different recipients, times, settings or outcome measures, the same four factors that underpin Reichardt's principle of parallelism. This is distinct from Lazarsfeld's elaboration model, which introduces control variables into cross-tabulations to interpret an association.
steps: Name the specific threat (history, seasonality, selection, instrumentation) that could bias the first estimate.
Choose the source of a second estimate: different users, a different time, a different setting or market, or a different outcome measure.
Arrange that the second estimate contains only the threat, a different amount of treatment effect, or a different and ideally opposite amount of the threat.
Compute both estimates using the same procedure.
Subtract (estimate-and-subtract) or compare the sizes of the estimates to separate the treatment effect from the threat.
Repeat for each other plausible threat and report which were ruled out, bounded or left open.
outputs: An effect estimate with named threats ruled out or bounded, and a documented rationale for each contrasting estimate.
useWhen: Before-after launches, staged rollouts and observational comparisons where randomisation is not possible and specific threats such as seasonality, concurrent campaigns or self-selection are plausible.
avoidWhen: A randomised experiment is feasible (run it); the threat cannot be named concretely. Each elaboration addresses only the threat it was built for, and its assumptions about how the threat behaves in the second estimate must hold.
whyLost: UX teams use validity-threat checklists to list threats but rarely design specific comparisons to rule each one out; the strategy is known mainly in programme-evaluation methodology.
whereToUse: Release impact analysis, regional or platform-staggered launches, policy or pricing changes, and evaluations of service redesigns in public sector and health.
example: A checkout redesign launched on Android only coincides with a holiday sale. The team estimates the change on Android (effect plus sale) and on iOS over the same weeks (sale only), and subtracts; a second check on a metric the redesign cannot affect, such as wishlist adds, shows the sale's effect is similar on both platforms.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
reference: Reichardt, C. S. (2009). Quasi-experimental design. In R. E. Millsap & A. Maydeu-Olivares (Eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (pp. 46-71). London: SAGE.

name: Stratified 2x2 Analysis (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel and Breslow-Day)
origin: Nathan Mantel and William Haenszel, 1959; Norman Breslow and Nicholas Day, 1980
summary: Tests and estimates the association between a binary exposure and a binary outcome while holding a stratifying variable constant, and checks whether the association is the same in every stratum.
description: When a 2x2 association (exposed to a feature or not, succeeded or not) could be confounded or modified by a third variable such as device or tenure, the data are split into one 2x2 table per stratum and analysed with three tests in sequence. The Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test asks whether exposure and outcome are conditionally independent across strata. The Mantel-Haenszel estimator pools the stratum odds ratios into one adjusted odds ratio with a confidence interval. The Breslow-Day test checks whether the odds ratio is homogeneous across strata; if it is not, the strata show effect modification and stratum-specific odds ratios should be reported instead of the pooled one. This is the epidemiologist's standard guard against Simpson's paradox, where a pooled table shows an association that disappears or reverses within every stratum because the strata differ in size and baseline rate.
steps: Cross-tabulate the binary exposure by the binary outcome separately within each level of the control variable.
Run the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test of conditional independence across the strata.
Estimate the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio and its 95% confidence interval as the adjusted strength of association.
Run the Breslow-Day test of homogeneity of odds ratios across strata.
If odds ratios are heterogeneous, report stratum-specific odds ratios and treat the stratifier as an effect modifier rather than pooling.
Compare the adjusted odds ratio with the crude (pooled-table) odds ratio to show how much the stratifier changed the picture.
outputs: Stratum tables, CMH chi-square and p value, pooled odds ratio with interval, Breslow-Day homogeneity result, crude versus adjusted comparison.
useWhen: Observational or quasi-experimental comparisons of a binary outcome where a categorical variable (device, region, new versus returning users, plan) differs between exposed and unexposed groups and could confound or modify the effect.
avoidWhen: Many or continuous confounders (use logistic regression or propensity methods); a properly randomised experiment where strata are balanced; very sparse strata with zero cells (use exact conditional methods). Do not report the pooled odds ratio when Breslow-Day shows clear heterogeneity.
whyLost: Product analytics teams usually jump from a single cross-tab to regression or ignore stratification altogether, so the simple stratified epidemiological workflow is rarely taught in UX.
whereToUse: Feature adoption versus retention by device or tenure; support-article exposure versus resolution by issue type; checking dashboard metrics for Simpson's paradox before a launch decision.
example: Users who saw a new onboarding checklist convert at a higher rate overall, but most of them are on desktop. Stratifying by device, the CMH test is still significant and the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio falls from 1.8 to 1.3; Breslow-Day is non-significant, so the smaller pooled effect is reported.
sources: An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (Agresti, 1996)
reference: Mantel, N., & Haenszel, W. (1959). Statistical aspects of the analysis of data from retrospective studies of disease. Journal of the National Cancer Institute, 22, 719-748.

name: Strauss-Corbin Analytic Tools
aka: Analysis of a word, phrase or sentence
origin: Anselm Strauss and Juliet Corbin (1990; 1998); far-out comparison after E. C. Hughes
summary: Five devices for opening up qualitative data: typed questioning, theoretical comparison, word analysis, the flip-flop and waving the red flag at absolutes.
description: Strauss and Corbin offer a set of analytic tools to break an analyst out of descriptive ruts and expose assumptions. Questioning uses typed questions: sensitising (what is going on, who are the actors), theoretical (how concepts relate, what if), practical and structural (where to sample next, what is underdeveloped), and guiding interview questions that sharpen over time. Theoretical comparison takes a puzzling concept and compares it with something close in or far out from experience or literature, listing that object's properties to look for in the data. Word analysis lists every possible meaning of one striking word and checks which holds. The flip-flop turns a concept to its opposite or extreme to reveal properties. Waving the red flag treats 'always', 'never' and 'everyone knows' as signals to seek conditions and variation. None of their outputs are data.
steps: When examining data, ask sensitising questions about what is happening and how actors define it, then theoretical questions about how concepts relate.
When an incident's meaning is unclear, choose a close-in or far-out comparison object, list its properties and dimensions, and look for those properties in your data.
Pick a striking word or phrase, list all its possible meanings, and search the document and other interviews for which meaning holds.
Flip an emergent concept to its opposite or extreme, derive properties, and consider sampling the opposite group (for example non-users).
Treat absolutes such as 'never' or 'everyone knows', or your own instant acceptance, as a red flag: ask under what conditions, how the state is maintained and when it breaks.
Use the outputs to revise interview guides and decide where to sample next, never as findings in themselves.
outputs: Candidate properties and dimensions, refined interview questions, sampling leads, and surfaced assumptions.
useWhen: Early and middle stages of qualitative analysis when coding has stalled, categories are thin, or the team shares the participants' assumptions.
avoidWhen: Avoid applying comparison properties directly to data or treating question lists as a checklist. If properties are already evident in the data, the tools are unnecessary.
whyLost: They are taught only within grounded theory; UX synthesis rarely includes explicit devices for challenging the analyst's own reading.
whereToUse: Discovery research, synthesis workshops that keep reaching obvious themes, research on familiar domains where teams 'go native'.
example: Participants say they 'never' share banking passwords. Waving the red flag leads the team to ask about emergencies and carers, uncovering routine sharing with family members that the security design had ignored.
reference: Strauss, A. and Corbin, J. (1998). Basics of Qualitative Research: Techniques and Procedures for Developing Grounded Theory (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage, pp. 73-99.

name: Strength-versus-weight evidence weighting experiment
origin: Dale Griffin and Amos Tversky, 1992
summary: Vary evidence strength (how extreme) and weight (sample size, reliability) independently and regress judgements on both, showing whether people neglect how much evidence there is.
description: Evidence has strength, such as the proportion of heads or the average star rating, and weight, such as the number of tosses or reviews. A normative judge weights both appropriately; people overweight strength. In the coin-bias study, 12 combinations of proportion and sample size (3 to 33 tosses) were judged with an accuracy prize; strength outweighed weight for 30 of 35 respondents, with a median ratio of about 2 to 1. The result is overconfidence when strength is high and weight low, and underconfidence when weight is high and strength low. Regressing the log odds of each judgement on log strength and log weight per person quantifies the imbalance. Within-subjects designs draw attention to the varied cue, so between-subjects arms show more neglect.
steps: Choose the two cues, for example average rating (strength) and number of reviews (weight).
Build a factorial set that decorrelates them.
Ask for a probability, confidence or choice per stimulus, ideally with an accuracy incentive.
Compute the normative answer where one exists.
Regress judgement log odds on log strength and log weight per person and compare coefficients.
Plot calibration by weight level and confirm key effects in between-subjects arms.
outputs: Relative weights of strength and weight per person, calibration curves by sample size, and zones of over- and underconfidence.
useWhen: Designing how ratings, review counts, confidence scores or sample sizes are displayed, and testing whether users account for how much evidence lies behind a number.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on within-subjects designs alone, and remember results depend on cue ranges; for general calibration use Brier score analysis.
whyLost: It is a decision-science paradigm; UX tests rating displays for preference or click-through, not for whether judgements are calibrated.
whereToUse: Review and rating displays, marketplaces, A/B test dashboards for non-statisticians, AI confidence indicators.
example: Listings cross 4.2 versus 4.8 stars with 12 versus 900 reviews. Purchase intent follows the stars and barely moves with review count, so the team tests a display that shrinks low-count ratings towards the category mean.
sources: Griffin, D., & Tversky, A. (1992). The weighing of evidence and the determinants of confidence. Cognitive Psychology, 24
reference: Griffin, D., & Tversky, A. (1992). The weighing of evidence and the determinants of confidence. Cognitive Psychology, 24, 411-435.

name: Stroop interference task
origin: J. Ridley Stroop, 1935
summary: Naming the ink colour of conflicting colour words takes longer than naming colour patches; the extra time measures interference from an automatic, competing response.
description: Participants name as fast as possible the ink colour of colour patches (baseline) and of colour words printed in a conflicting ink, such as RED in blue. The extra time or errors on conflicting words is the Stroop effect: reading is so practised that it runs automatically and produces a competing response, making the task a standard index of executive attention and conflict control. The effect depends on the irrelevant dimension being overlearned. Hartley (1993) compared the standard display with a separated variant (a black word beside a coloured rectangle) and found older adults differed from young ones only on the standard display, suggesting an age deficit in selecting between task operations rather than locations. The Cohen, Dunbar and McClelland PDP model represents attention as task units biasing word and colour pathways. In UX, Stroop logic predicts interference when labels, colours or icons conflict.
steps: Build congruent, neutral (patches or non-colour words) and incongruent stimuli.
Present items singly on screen with randomised order, or as timed lists, recording vocal or key responses.
Collect at least 20-30 trials per condition per participant, after practice.
Compute interference as incongruent minus neutral reaction time, and errors per condition.
For interface variants, replace colour words with interface conflicts (for example a red 'Confirm' button or a mismatched icon and label).
Compare interference across designs or user groups, such as young and older adults.
outputs: Interference cost in milliseconds and error rates by condition and group.
useWhen: You suspect conflicting cues (colour versus label, icon versus text, position versus meaning) are slowing users or causing errors, or you need a measure of executive control as a covariate.
avoidWhen: The 'automatic' dimension is not overlearned by your users; self-timed demonstrations are only illustrative. For general error diagnosis use usability testing or error analysis.
whyLost: It is ubiquitous in psychology and neuropsychology but treated in UX as a textbook curiosity rather than a test of interface conflicts.
whereToUse: Colour-coded status systems, destructive-action buttons, traffic-light dashboards, medical device displays, localisation where colour meanings differ.
example: A trading app finds that a red 'Buy' button for a short position slows confirmations. A Stroop-style test shows 120 ms interference and more errors, leading to neutral colours for action buttons.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
reference: Stroop, J. R. (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 18, 643-662.

name: Structural Dimensional Analysis of Mental Representation (SDA-M)
donor: Action theory in sport psychology and cognitive science
origin: Lander and Lange (1996); adapted for movement and action representation by Thomas Schack (2002); described by Schack and Hackfort in Chapter 15 of the Handbook
summary: Uses a repeated anchored split task, hierarchical clustering and invariance tests to map how people mentally group the steps of a skilled action and compare that structure with experts or with the task's functional structure.
description: SDA-M measures how a set of action elements (basic action concepts, such as the sub-movements of a tennis serve) is organised in long-term memory. It has four steps. First, a split procedure: one element is shown as a fixed anchor and the participant judges, for every other element, whether it is functionally related to the anchor while performing the action; each resulting subset is split again until the participant stops, and every element takes a turn as anchor. This produces a distance scaling between all pairs. Second, hierarchical cluster analysis turns the distances into a dendrogram for each person. Third, a factor analysis with cluster-oriented rotation identifies dimensions. Fourth, invariance analysis tests whether structures differ within and between groups, or from a reference structure. In the Handbook, expert tennis players' structures matched the biomechanical phases of the serve while non-players' did not. For UX the same procedure can map how users mentally structure multi-step workflows, gesture sequences or procedures, and show where novices' structures diverge from the intended workflow model or from experts.
steps: With experts, define 8 to 15 elements of the workflow or action, each with a short label and image or screenshot.
Familiarise participants with all elements.
Run the split procedure: present each element in turn as an anchor and have participants mark the others as related or unrelated, then split each subset again until they stop.
Compute pairwise distances and run hierarchical cluster analysis for each participant and group.
Use invariance analysis to compare individuals, groups and a reference structure such as the designer's intended model.
Interpret where novice clusters break from expert or intended structure, and target those points in onboarding or interface grouping.
outputs: Individual and group dendrograms of how workflow elements are mentally grouped, with statistical comparisons between groups and against a reference structure.
useWhen: You need to know how users mentally organise a procedural workflow or skilled interaction sequence, especially to compare novices with experts.
avoidWhen: The question is about navigation labels or content categories, where card sorting and tree testing are simpler, or the workflow has only a few steps.
whyLost: It was developed and published mainly in German sport and movement science, and needs specialised analysis software and statistics.
whereToUse: Professional workflows in creative, medical, industrial and developer tools; gesture vocabularies; procedural training products.
example: A surgical robotics team defines 12 steps of instrument docking. Experienced surgeons cluster the steps into three phases matching the system's design, while trainees lump calibration with draping; the team redesigns the docking screen to separate those phases visually.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Schack, T. and Hackfort, D. (2007) 'Action-theory approach to applied sport psychology', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 15.

name: Structural Equation Mixture Modelling (Factor Mixture, Growth Mixture and Regime-Switching Models)
origin: Bengt Muthen and Kerby Shedden, 1999; Gerhard Arminger and colleagues; Conor Dolan, Brenda Jansen and Han van der Maas, 2004 (switching)
summary: Assumes users are a mixture of unobserved subgroups, each with its own factor, growth or structural model, and estimates class sizes, class-specific models and, over time, switching between classes.
description: SEM assumes respondents come from one population. If unobserved subgroups exist whose constructs or trajectories behave differently, estimates become uninterpretable. When membership is known, multiple-group, multilevel or MIMIC models suffice; when it is not, SEM mixture modelling treats each latent class as multivariate normal with its own SEM-structured means and covariances, optionally predicting class membership from covariates. Factor mixture models let classes differ in factor means or loadings; growth mixture models let them follow different trajectories; regime-switching models add a Markov transition model so people can move between classes over repeated measures. Mixtures can be used directly (substantive subgroups) or indirectly (to approximate non-normality or non-linearity). Choosing the number of classes is hard because the ordinary likelihood ratio test is invalid at the boundary; information criteria, bootstrap tests and the Lo-Mendell-Rubin test are used, and switching models grow quickly in complexity (three regimes over four occasions imply 81 components).
steps: Specify the within-class model (factor, growth or structural) and which parameters may differ between classes.
Fit models with one, two, three and more classes by maximum likelihood, using many random start values to avoid local maxima.
Compare solutions with BIC and AIC, bootstrap likelihood ratio or Lo-Mendell-Rubin tests, and class sizes and interpretability.
Optionally regress class membership on covariates such as acquisition channel or plan.
For repeated measures, add a Markov transition model and estimate the probability of moving between classes.
Interpret class proportions and class-specific parameters substantively, and check that classes are not artefacts of non-normal data.
outputs: Number of classes, class proportions, class-specific SEM parameters, posterior class probabilities per person and, for switching models, transition probabilities.
useWhen: You suspect user subgroups whose attitudes relate differently (different factor structures or driver models) or whose usage or satisfaction trajectories differ over time, and you have multi-item measures or repeated measures on hundreds of users.
avoidWhen: Group membership is observed (use multi-group SEM); you only need clusters on raw variables (use latent class analysis or Gaussian mixtures); samples are small. Non-normality can masquerade as classes, and the number of classes is often uncertain.
whyLost: These models require specialist software (Mplus, OpenMx) and advanced training; UX segmentation uses simpler clustering that cannot give each segment its own causal or growth model.
whereToUse: Segmenting users by onboarding trajectories, detecting groups for whom a TAM-style model works differently, identifying regime shifts in longitudinal panel or diary data.
example: A fitness app fits growth mixture models to weekly workouts over 16 weeks for 8,000 users. Three classes emerge: steady (55%), early drop (30%) and late bloomers (15%); a covariate shows late bloomers mostly joined through employer programmes, prompting a different nudge schedule for that channel.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
reference: Dolan, C. V. (2009). Structural equation mixture modeling. In R. E. Millsap & A. Maydeu-Olivares (Eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (pp. 568-591). London: SAGE.

name: Structural Equation Modeling
origin: Karl Jöreskog, 1970s (LISREL); building on Sewall Wright's path analysis, 1921
summary: Jointly estimates a measurement model of latent constructs and a structural model of paths between them, giving direct, indirect and total effects with fit indices.
description: SEM combines confirmatory factor analysis (latent constructs measured by indicators) with path models among constructs. In Vivek Gopinath's payments case (n = 520, robust ML), constructs are Trust, Fraud Risk, Slowness and Support with 3 Likert items each, plus observed Double-Checking and Adoption. Loadings range from 0.70 to 0.82 with CR 0.81–0.87 and AVE 0.57–0.69. Structural paths follow the DAG: FR → TR −0.45, SR → TR +0.31, TR → DC −0.50, DC → SL +0.42, SL → AD −0.28 and TR → AD +0.26, with indirect TR → AD ≈ +0.059 and total ≈ +0.32. Fit is reported with CFI 0.962, TLI 0.951, RMSEA 0.041 (90% CI .032–.050) and SRMR 0.037 against thresholds CFI/TLI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.06, SRMR ≤ 0.08. Interpretation rules: |β| ≈ 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large; never interpret paths without qual context. The Nash protocol uses SEM in its Prove stage.
steps: Specify the measurement model (each latent construct with its indicators).
Screen missingness (< 10% per item, FIML), check α ≥ 0.70, and run CFA, dropping loadings < 0.60 unless theory demands.
Add structural paths exactly as the DAG specifies.
Estimate with robust ML (MLR) and report CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR.
Decompose direct, indirect and total effects.
Test multi-group invariance, sensitivity to added confounders and out-of-sample stability.
Report with the template: measurement reliabilities and fit, structural effects with significance, and prescriptions.
outputs: A path diagram with standardised coefficients, fit indices, effect decomposition and reliability statistics.
useWhen: When latent constructs and mediators matter and samples are in the hundreds.
avoidWhen: With small samples, poorly understood constructs or no theory to specify paths; use EFA or qualitative work first.
whyLost: Standard in marketing science and psychology, but UX researchers seldom have training in it and default to correlations.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption in fintech, technology acceptance studies, satisfaction drivers, design adoption (ΔU) validation.
example: SEM on 520 bank customers shows trust raises tap-to-pay adoption directly (+0.26) and indirectly by reducing double-checking and perceived slowness, for a total effect of about +0.32.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (Kline)
A Beginner's Guide to Structural Equation Modeling (Schumacker & Lomax, 2004)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Quantitative Methods in Psychology (Millsap & Maydeu-Olivares, 2009)
Structural Equation Modeling: A Bayesian Approach (Lee, 2007)
Transforming UX Research with Structural Equation Modeling (Jozranjbar, n.d.)
Myths and Facts About Using SEM in UX and Human Factors Studies (carousel, n.d.)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: Kline, R. B. (2016). Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (4th ed.). Guilford Press.

name: Structural Topic Modelling
donor: Computational social science and political science
origin: Margaret Roberts, Brandon Stewart, Dustin Tingley and colleagues, 2013-2014
summary: A topic model in which document metadata (segment, date, rating) shapes topic prevalence and wording, allowing statistical comparison of themes across groups.
description: LDA discovers topics but treats documents as exchangeable. STM incorporates covariates: topic prevalence can depend on metadata (e.g. how much churned versus retained users discuss pricing) and topic content can vary by covariate (how different segments talk about the same topic). Estimates come with uncertainty, enabling regression-style inference about themes. Tools for model selection (semantic coherence and exclusivity), stability across initialisations and representative document retrieval support validation. For UX, STM links open-ended survey responses, reviews or tickets to user attributes and time, making qualitative-scale text quantitatively comparable.
steps: Assemble a corpus (survey comments, reviews, tickets) with document-level metadata.
Preprocess text carefully (stop words, lemmatisation) and document decisions.
Fit STMs for a range of K, choosing by semantic coherence, exclusivity and held-out likelihood.
Label topics by reading representative documents, ideally with two researchers independently.
Estimate covariate effects on topic prevalence with uncertainty (estimateEffect) and examine content covariate differences.
Validate key topics against human-coded samples and follow up qualitatively.
outputs: Labelled topics, covariate effects on topic prevalence, content differences and validation results.
useWhen: Large open-text datasets where you need to compare themes across segments, versions or time.
avoidWhen: Small corpora (under a few hundred documents) or when nuanced interpretation is needed; use qualitative coding.
whyLost: It is known in political science text analysis, but UX text analytics relies on sentiment and keyword tools.
whereToUse: NPS verbatims, app reviews, support tickets, community forums, open-ended survey questions.
example: An STM on 60,000 app reviews shows the 'battery drain' topic prevalence tripled after version 5.2 among Android users only, pinpointing a platform-specific regression.
sources: Roberts et al., Structural topic models for open-ended survey responses (2014), American Journal of Political Science
Roberts, Stewart & Tingley, stm: An R package for structural topic models (2019), Journal of Statistical Software
reference: Roberts, M. E., et al. (2014). American Journal of Political Science, 58(4), 1064-1082.

name: Structured analogue observation with scripted partners
aka: Structured analogue observation with scripted partners and rigged tasks
origin: Parpal and Maccoby (1985); Bierman and Welsh (2000); Underwood et al. (1999); Hubbard et al. (2002)
summary: Build a lab analogue of an everyday situation by scripting the setting, a partner's behaviour or the task, so rare behaviours occur reliably and can be compared across people.
description: Naturalistic observation is costly and misses rare, hidden or reactive behaviours such as conflict, frustration or help-seeking. Analogue observation raises their frequency by structuring one of three things: the social setting (who is present, group size, task), a partner's behaviour (a trained confederate who cheats and taunts in a rigged game, or a parent trained to respond contingently), or the task and response options (a disappointing prize, a waiting task, a rigged failure). Every participant then has the same chance to show the behaviour, allowing comparison across people and occasions. Sessions are video recorded and coded with a defined scheme, sometimes combined with physiology and video-cued self-report, as in Hubbard's rigged game. Elicited negative emotion is kept brief and mild, and participants are debriefed. For UX, it is a rigorous form of scripted-confederate or rigged-failure testing.
steps: Define the target behaviour (frustration, conflict, help-seeking, recovery) and why it is rare or hard to observe naturally.
Choose what to structure: the setting, a partner's behaviour or the task and response options.
Script and train any confederate or partner; standardise prompts, timing and the rigged events.
Record sessions on video and code behaviour with a defined scheme; add physiology or video-cued self-report where useful.
Keep elicited negative emotion brief and mild, and debrief participants fully about scripting or rigging.
Check representativeness against naturalistic data, logs or other informants.
outputs: Standardised behaviour samples comparable across participants and occasions, with coded frequencies and intensities.
useWhen: Studying how users handle rare but critical moments (system failures, disagreements in collaborative tools, interruptions, hostile co-players) that seldom occur in observable sessions.
avoidWhen: When naturalistic behaviour can be captured in logs or field studies, or when eliciting negative emotion is not ethically justified; lab behaviour can differ from home behaviour.
whyLost: It is a developmental psychology method; UX uses ad hoc 'error injection' without scripted partners, coding schemes or psychometric checks.
whereToUse: Collaborative editing and meeting tools, multiplayer games, customer service chat, AI assistants that fail, safety-critical interfaces.
example: A video-calling product tests how teams recover when a scripted confederate repeatedly talks over others. Coded sessions show participants rarely find the raise-hand feature under social pressure, leading to a more visible queue indicator.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Brownell, C. A., Lemerise, E. A., Pelphrey, K. A. and Roisman, G. I. (2015). Measuring socioemotional development. In R. M. Lerner and M. E. Lamb (eds), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 3. Wiley, pp. 11-56.

name: Structured Diary Study
origin: Time-use and diary research in sociology from the 1920s; diary methods in psychology (Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli, 2003)
summary: Participants record experiences, behaviours and thoughts at set intervals or triggering events over days to weeks, capturing real-context use over time.
description: A diary study asks participants to record their experiences with a product or behaviour at regular intervals over an extended period (typically 1 day to 6 weeks). Unlike in-person observation, diary studies capture naturally occurring experiences in their real context — including moments that would never occur in a lab (middle-of-the-night usage, failure under stress, integration with other life activities). The fundamental tradeoff: ecological validity (high) vs. data quality control (low — you cannot verify what participants report).
steps: Onboarding session: Train participants on diary completion. Show example entries. Clarify what counts as a recordable event. Emphasise completeness over literacy.
Pilot the diary: Run a 2–3 day pilot with 2–3 participants before full deployment. Identify questions that participants cannot answer, skip, or misinterpret.
Mid-study check-ins: Contact participants every 3–4 days to maintain engagement, answer questions, and identify compliance issues early.
Exit interview: After diary completion, conduct a retrospective interview using key diary entries as stimuli. Ask participants to elaborate on entries that raise questions.
outputs: Time-stamped diary entries, coded episodes and patterns over time, exit interview data, and compliance metrics.
useWhen: Behaviours that unfold over days or weeks, occur in private or mobile contexts, or are hard to observe directly, such as habits, onboarding or intermittent tasks.
avoidWhen: When you need precise interaction detail (use usability testing or analytics), or when participants cannot sustain the burden; consider experience sampling for momentary states.
whyLost: It remains active in UX, supported by dedicated tools, though pilots, check-ins and exit interviews are often trimmed.
whereToUse: Onboarding and habit formation in health, fitness and finance apps; household technology; cross-device journeys; and B2B tools used intermittently.
example: Twenty new users of a budgeting app keep a two-week diary of every money decision. Entries show they check balances before social plans, prompting a 'can I afford this?' quick view.
sources: Diary Methods: Capturing Life as It Is Lived (Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli)
reference: Bolger, N., Davis, A. & Rafaeli, E. (2003). Diary methods: Capturing life as it is lived. Annual Review of Psychology, 54, 579-616.

extra.Design Decisions: Diary format: Structured (specific questions after each episode) vs. semi-structured (open narrative + fixed fields) vs. unstructured (free description).
