Structure increases comparability; openness increases richness. For most UX research: semi-structured is optimal. Trigger timing: Event-contingent (participants record after each occurrence of the target behaviour) vs. time-contingent (participants record at fixed intervals regardless of whether the target behaviour occurred) vs. signal-contingent (random signals prompt recording — see ESM, Method 50). Entry method: App-based diaries allow multimedia (photos, audio), time-stamping, and reminders. Paper diaries allow participants with limited digital access. Choose based on population and what the medium adds to data quality. Duration: Long enough to capture the full range of the phenomenon (including infrequent critical incidents) but short enough to maintain participant compliance. Most diary studies see compliance degrade significantly after 2 weeks.

name: Structured Observation
donor: Social science and sport performance research
origin: Long-established observational method; Gratton and Jones (2010) set out planning stages and recording with a predefined checklist, illustrated by a basketball tactics coding sheet.
summary: Observing people in a real setting and recording predefined behaviours on a checklist, with sampled times and checks on observer reliability.
description: Structured observation records specific, predefined behaviours rather than everything that happens. Gratton and Jones describe four planning stages: define the variables to be observed and link them to the research objectives; decide the sample, including a sample of times and locations, not just of people; decide how the variables will be recorded (pre-printed data sheet, video or dictation); and pilot the observation before the real event. Recording usually uses a simple checklist where each action by a sampled individual is ticked against categories, as in their example of coding each basketball play as 'dribbled then shot', 'immediate pass', 'lost possession' and so on. Because it is hard to record more than one variable at a time, observers should keep the variable list short, alternate between variables in set periods, use video or use several observers, in which case inter-observer reliability must be trained and checked. Typical mistakes are trying to record too much, ignoring the observer's effect on behaviour, not sampling times or locations and relying on memory. In UX it suits counting behaviours in physical or shared settings (kiosks, retail, hospital wards, control rooms) or coding session videos, giving frequencies that complement interviews and analytics.
steps: Define the behaviours or events to record and write clear category definitions tied to your research questions.
Choose who to observe and sample times and locations (for example peak and off-peak sessions on different days).
Build a checklist or coding sheet, or a video coding scheme, keeping the number of variables manageable.
Pilot the sheet in the real setting and refine categories that are ambiguous or never used.
Train observers and, where more than one observer is used, double-code a sample to check inter-observer agreement.
Collect the data, noting context and any signs that observers are affecting behaviour.
Tally frequencies and compare across times, locations or groups, and triangulate with other data.
outputs: Frequency counts and rates of defined behaviours by time, location and group, with reliability figures and supporting field notes.
useWhen: You need to know how often behaviours actually occur in a real setting rather than what people say they do, and the behaviours can be defined in advance.
avoidWhen: You do not yet know what matters (use open field observation first) or the behaviour is private, rare or invisible.
whyLost: Digital analytics now counts on-screen behaviour automatically, so hand-coded observation survives mainly in human factors and service design work in physical settings.
whereToUse: Self-service kiosks, retail and hospitality, healthcare and control rooms, classrooms, coding of usability-session videos, physical-digital service journeys.
example: A transport operator wants to know why ticket machines cause queues. Researchers observe six stations at morning peak and midday over two weeks, ticking each customer's actions (language switch, card retry, abandons, asks staff). A second observer double-codes 20% of sessions. Card retries turn out to account for most of the delay, which interviews had not revealed.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Structured output schemas for first-order codes
origin: JSON Schema specification (from 2009); first-order and second-order concepts from Gioia, Corley and Hamilton, 2013; LLM structured outputs from 2023
summary: Defining a strict machine-readable schema for each code an AI or human coder produces, so first-order codes always carry evidence, location, rationale and confidence and can be audited.
description: First-order codes, in the Gioia tradition, stay close to participants' own language before being abstracted into second-order themes. When an LLM produces them, free-text output is hard to verify and aggregate. A structured schema forces each code record to contain fields such as segment ID, participant ID, code label in participant terms, verbatim quote span with character offsets, rationale, confidence and whether the code is new or from the codebook. The schema is validated programmatically; invalid outputs are rejected and retried. Rigour comes from schema design that encodes methodological commitments (no code without evidence), validation of quote spans against source text, and version control of the schema itself.
steps: Decide the analytic commitments the schema must enforce (e.g. every code needs a verbatim quote; codes stay in participant language).
Write a JSON Schema with required fields: segment_id, participant_id, code_label, quote, quote_start, quote_end, rationale, confidence (0-1), is_new_code.
Pass the schema to the model's structured output or tool-use feature and validate every response.
Reject and retry outputs that fail validation, up to a fixed limit (e.g. 3), then route to human review.
Verify programmatically that each quote matches the source text at the given offsets.
Version the schema and store outputs in a table ready for second-order synthesis.
outputs: A versioned schema and a validated table of first-order codes with evidence and provenance.
useWhen: Any AI-assisted or multi-coder qualitative analysis at scale where codes must be auditable and aggregated.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary for small manual analyses in a CAQDAS tool, which already links codes to text.
whyLost: Structured outputs are an engineering feature, and qualitative researchers have rarely translated their methodological rules into data contracts.
whereToUse: AI-assisted analysis pipelines, research repositories and multi-team coding programmes.
example: A health research pipeline rejects 4% of LLM coding outputs whose quotes do not match the transcript, catching paraphrased 'quotes' that would otherwise have appeared in a report as participants' words.
sources: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G. & Hamilton, A. L. (2013) Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research. Organizational Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, C12 — AI Agents for Structured Qualitative Analysis at Scale
reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G. & Hamilton, A. L. (2013) Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods 16(1)

name: Structured Session Notetaking
origin: UX practice; codified by Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015)
summary: Capture sessions with a topic-based notetaking template, agreed shorthand, a dedicated domain-aware notetaker, observer notes, and recordings kept for checking quotes.
description: Notes provide immediate data and show participants they are heard, but a moderator who acts as stenographer stops engaging. Structured notetaking separates the roles and prepares the capture. A template organised by the topics or tasks you expect gives placeholders for each, or a generic template is used for exploratory sessions. Shorthand captures the gist rather than every word. For focus groups and other demanding sessions a colleague takes notes, in the room, on a video feed or behind a mirror; they do not interrupt and should know the domain well enough to condense. Observing stakeholders take notes too. Recording lets a solo moderator focus and preserves nuance; transcription takes four to six times session length and is justified only for exact quotes, content analysis or regulated documentation.
steps: Design a notetaking template with a section for each planned topic or task, or use a generic one for exploratory sessions.
Agree shorthand codes (for example for quotes, observations, errors and ideas) across the team.
Assign a dedicated, domain-aware notetaker for demanding sessions and brief them not to interrupt.
Record audio, video and screen as needed after testing that recording does not slow the prototype; frame the camera on what matters.
Collect notes from observers and timestamp notable moments.
Use recordings to check unclear notes and quotes; transcribe only when exact wording or content analysis is required, and apply a retention policy.
outputs: Organised session notes ready for analysis, timestamped highlights, observer notes and backing recordings.
useWhen: Any moderated interview, usability test or focus group, especially with stakeholders observing or several sessions per day.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on notes alone when exact wording matters; avoid full transcription by default since it costs four to six times session length.
whyLost: It survived as everyday practice, though templates and dedicated notetakers are often dropped under time pressure.
whereToUse: Usability labs, remote research, focus groups, contextual interviews with observers.
example: For a banking app test, the notetaker uses a template with a box per task and codes 'Q' for quotes and 'E' for errors. Timestamps let the researcher pull clips for the readout within an hour.
reference: Baxter, K., Courage, C. and Caine, K. (2015). Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Research Methods (2nd ed.). Waltham, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 171-176.

name: Structuring, Checking and Preparing ESM Data
origin: Wolfgang Viechtbauer, 2022
summary: Put experience-sampling data in long format, run design and plausibility checks, apply response-delay and compliance rules, then build centred and lagged variables and plot individual series.
description: Intensive longitudinal data need preparation beyond survey cleaning. Data go in long format, one row per prompt, with subject, day, beep, scheduled time and response time. Checks: design and time variables never missing; subject-level variables constant within a person; no out-of-range values; no duplicated beeps; beep times inside their scheduled blocks; branching items consistent. Rules then handle response delay (for example a 15-minute limit), implausibly short completion times as careless responding, and a minimum response count per person, each tested with sensitivity analyses because exclusion thresholds are arbitrary. Scale scores use a missing-item rule; person means and person-mean centred values are computed; lagged variables never cross persons or nights. Individual time series and per-person slopes are plotted before modelling. Collapsing to subject level gives descriptive statistics.
steps: Arrange the data in long format with design and timing variables (subject, day, beep, scheduled and actual times).
Check design variables for missing values, subject variables for constancy, all variables for range and duplicates, beep times against blocks, and branching consistency.
Inspect response delay and completion time; exclude responses beyond the delay limit (for example 15 minutes) or implausibly fast.
Compute compliance per person; apply any minimum and test it with sensitivity analyses.
Compute scale scores with a stated missing-item rule.
Compute person means, person-mean centred values and lagged variables, setting the first beep of each day and person to missing.
Plot individual time series and per-person predictor-outcome slopes before modelling.
outputs: An analysis-ready long-format dataset, a log of checks and exclusions, and diagnostic plots.
useWhen: Any diary, ESM or repeated in-app survey dataset before analysis, especially when results will be modelled with multilevel or lagged models.
avoidWhen: One-off cross-sectional surveys; use standard survey data cleaning.
whyLost: UX diary data are often analysed qualitatively or as averages, so structured preparation for intensive longitudinal analysis is rarely taught in UX.
whereToUse: Diary studies with structured prompts, in-app pulse surveys, wearable-linked self-reports and longitudinal beta programmes.
example: A team running 8 prompts a day for 10 days finds duplicated beeps from an app retry bug and 12% of responses delayed over an hour. It excludes delayed responses, reports results with and without a 30% compliance minimum, and plots each participant's series.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Study Quality Assessment by Component Coding
aka: Judging the quality of primary research
origin: Jeffrey Valentine, 2009, building on Campbell's validity framework and Jüni et al., 1999
summary: Code individual design features of each study in a synthesis and test them as moderators of effect size, instead of applying a single summary quality score.
description: Study quality is the fit between a study's design and the inferences drawn from it, judged against internal, construct, external and statistical conclusion validity, and is distinct from relevance and from reporting quality. Valentine contrasts a priori exclusion and summary quality scales with post hoc empirical assessment. Jüni and colleagues applied 25 quality scales to 17 trials and found that conclusions flipped depending on the scale, showing such scores are arbitrary. The recommended approach uses few, evidence-based exclusion rules, a separate relevance screen, and coding of individual design components (sampling, assignment mechanism, equating variables and method, sample sizes at assignment and measurement, outcome measure and reliability) with a 'can't tell' option. Each component is then tested empirically as a moderator of effect size. For causal questions, non-randomised studies may be included and compared with randomised ones before any cautious pooling.
steps: Set only highly defensible exclusion criteria backed by evidence for the specific context.
Screen relevance separately with yes/no items.

Code design components separately: sampling, assignment mechanism, equating variables and method, sample sizes at assignment and at measurement, outcome measure and score reliability, each with a 'can't tell' option.
Distinguish what was done from how well it was reported.
Test each component as a moderator of effect size.
For causal questions, compare randomised and non-randomised studies before pooling them, and pool only cautiously.
outputs: Study-level design component codes and moderator tests showing whether design features change the pooled result.
useWhen: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of UX or HCI studies whose designs vary widely, from lab experiments to field A/B tests and surveys.
avoidWhen: Narrative overviews with too few studies for moderator tests; summarise design features descriptively instead. Do not treat reporting quality as study quality.
whyLost: UX evidence reviews rarely assess quality at all, and when they do, they use a single checklist score rather than coded components tested empirically.
whereToUse: Evidence reviews feeding design guidelines, internal meta-analyses of experiment programmes, and vendor claims assessment.
example: A meta-analysis of 40 studies on progress indicators codes assignment (randomised or not), sample size, and whether outcomes were self-reported or logged. Effects from self-reported outcomes are twice as large as from logged ones, so guidance is based on logged-outcome studies.
sources: The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
reference: Valentine, J. C. Ch. 7. In Cooper, H., Hedges, L. V., & Valentine, J. C. (Eds.) (2009). The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Russell Sage Foundation.

name: Subject-Object Interview
origin: Lisa Lahey and colleagues (1988), based on Robert Kegan's constructive-developmental theory (1982)
summary: A developmental interview in which ten cue cards prompt recent experiences, probed not for content but for the structure of how the person makes meaning.
description: Developed by Lahey and colleagues from Kegan's constructive-developmental theory, the interview gives the interviewee 15 to 20 minutes to jot notes on ten index cards, each bearing a word or phrase: angry; anxious or nervous; success; strong stand or conviction; sad; torn; moved or touched; lost something important to me; change; important to me. The interviewee then chooses which cards to talk about. The interviewer explores not what happened but the underlying principle by which the person makes sense of experience: what they can reflect on as object and what they are embedded in as subject. Transcripts are scored for developmental structure. It is a complex method that requires extensive training, but its cue-card opening is a transferable way to let participants choose emotionally salient episodes.
steps: Give the interviewee the ten cue cards and 15 to 20 minutes to note a recent experience for each.
Let the interviewee choose which cards to discuss, typically a few in about an hour.
Ask about each chosen experience, probing for how the person constructs its meaning rather than its details.
Test hypotheses about where the person's meaning-making boundary lies with follow-up probes.
Transcribe and score transcripts for developmental structure using trained raters.
outputs: Transcripts and a structural assessment of how each person makes meaning, plus participant-selected salient episodes.
useWhen: You are researching how professionals or leaders make sense of complex responsibility (for example adoption of decision-support tools) and have trained interviewers.
avoidWhen: You need practical product insight quickly or lack trained raters; use semi-structured or micro-phenomenological interviews instead.
whyLost: It requires extensive training and serves developmental assessment, so it stayed in adult development and education research.
whereToUse: Leadership and coaching products, professional decision-support tools, and education technology for adult learners.
example: A coaching platform team uses the ten cue cards to open interviews with 8 managers. Cards like 'torn' surface conflicts between team loyalty and company targets that shape which coaching prompts feel credible.
reference: Kegan, R. (1982). The Evolving Self: Problem and Process in Human Development. Harvard University Press.

name: Subjective well-being questionnaires (SWLS, SHS, ONS4)
aka: Subjective well-being questionnaires: Satisfaction with Life Scale and Subjective Happiness Scale
donor: Positive psychology; official statistics and wellbeing economics
origin: SWLS: Diener, Emmons, Larsen and Griffin, 1985; SHS: Lyubomirsky and Lepper, 1999; ONS4: Dolan, Layard and Metcalfe, 2011, for the UK Office for National Statistics
summary: Short validated measures of global wellbeing (SWLS, SHS and the ONS four 0-10 questions) used as outcomes or segmenting variables when products aim to affect how people's lives go.
description: Three short instruments dominate subjective wellbeing measurement. The Satisfaction with Life Scale asks agreement with five statements on a 7-point scale, summed; experience-sampling answers agree with it, supporting validity. The Subjective Happiness Scale has four 7-point items on general happiness, happiness relative to peers and fit to descriptions of a generally happy and unhappy person (the published scale reverse-scores item 4). The ONS four, asked of nearly 200,000 UK respondents a year, use 0-10 scales for life satisfaction, worthwhileness, happiness yesterday and anxiety yesterday; UK means were about 7.4, 7.7, 7.3 and 3.1, and the items differ enough to justify asking several. Single-item life satisfaction is answered in about five seconds and shifts with question order (a prior political or marriage question), so placement matters. 'Yesterday' items still behave partly like evaluations.
steps: Decide whether you need global evaluation (SWLS, ONS life satisfaction), chronic happiness (SHS), eudaimonic worth (ONS worthwhile) or recent affect (ONS happy and anxious yesterday).
Administer the chosen items verbatim on their original scales: SWLS five items 1-7, SHS four items 1-7, ONS4 four items 0-10.
Place them before product-specific questions and away from items that prime life domains, to limit order effects.
Score: sum SWLS (5-35); average SHS after reverse-scoring item 4; report each ONS item separately rather than combining.
Use as outcomes measured before and after use, or to split participants into happier and less happy groups, and compare with national benchmarks where samples allow.
Interpret small changes cautiously and alongside experiential measures.
outputs: Wellbeing scores per participant, benchmarks against population norms, and change over time or across groups.
useWhen: When a product claims to improve wellbeing, when you need to check that engagement gains are not costing users' wellbeing, or when wellbeing may moderate how users respond to features.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a sensitive measure of a single feature's effect; global wellbeing moves slowly and is affected by mood and question order. For momentary experience use the Experience Sampling Method or Day Reconstruction Method.
whyLost: They are standard in positive psychology and official statistics, but UX measures product satisfaction, not life satisfaction, and seldom has the long horizons needed.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing features, social media impact studies, health and finance apps, workplace tools, public-service evaluation.
example: A social app runs ONS4 quarterly alongside engagement metrics for a panel of 5,000 users. Heavy late-night users show higher 'anxious yesterday' scores, informing a wind-down feature.
reference: Diener, E., Emmons, R. A., Larsen, R. J., & Griffin, S. (1985). The Satisfaction With Life Scale. Journal of Personality Assessment, 49(1), 71-75; Lyubomirsky, S., & Lepper, H. S. (1999). A measure of subjective happiness. Social Indicators Research, 46, 137-155.

name: SUMI (Software Usability Measurement Inventory)
origin: Jurek Kirakowski, Human Factors Research Group, University College Cork (1993-1996); successor to the CUSI (1988)
summary: A 50-item questionnaire with a global usability score and five subscales (efficiency, affect, helpfulness, control, learnability), scored against a normative database.
description: The SUMI was built with unusually thorough psychometrics: 150 candidate items were cut to 75 by expert review, then to 50 by factor analysis of 139 users, and the five-factor structure was confirmed on an independent sample. Items use a three-point scale (agree, undecided, disagree) and mix positive and negative statements. A Global scale uses the 25 items that load most strongly on general usability. Its distinctive strength is standardisation: scores are converted against a reference database so 50 is average and the standard deviation is 10, making comparisons with other software meaningful. It was widely used in European ISO 9241 work and is available in 12 languages under licence (free for students).
steps: License the SUMI from the Human Factors Research Group and choose the language version.
Have at least 10 to 12 representative users complete it after real use of the software.
Submit responses for scoring against the reference database.
Read the Global score and the five subscale scores (mean 50, SD 10) with their confidence intervals.
Use item consensual analysis to find specific items where your users differ most from the norm.
outputs: Standardised global and subscale usability scores relative to a reference database.
useWhen: Comparing software against an external norm, especially in European or ISO-driven evaluations.
avoidWhen: Websites (use WAMMI or SUPR-Q) or when licensing is not possible.
whyLost: Licensing and its European academic home kept it out of the free-tool culture of North American UX practice.
whereToUse: Enterprise software procurement, public-sector systems, ISO 9241-11 conformance studies.
example: A payroll package scores 58 on Efficiency but 41 on Helpfulness, eight points below the database mean, directing effort to in-product help.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Kirakowski, J. (1996). The Software Usability Measurement Inventory: Background and usage. In Usability Evaluation in Industry.

name: Supervised text categorisation
aka: Supervised text categorisation with ranked-threshold tuning
origin: Text categorisation research of the 1990s; presented by Feldman, 2003
summary: Train classifiers on pre-tagged documents to assign categories to new text, choosing each category's threshold from ranked precision-recall trade-offs.
description: Feldman contrasts hand-written classification rules, which cost person-years of knowledge engineering, with learning from pre-tagged documents. Classifiers may give hard yes or no answers or ranked scores. Methods include naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours (k of 30-45 works well and larger k does little harm), rule learning with a loss ratio trading precision for recall, and support vector machines. One classifier is trained per category; held-out documents are scored and ranked, and a visual tool lets the user pick each category's threshold from its precision-recall curve. In the example, ten classifiers were tested on 476 documents, and a threshold of 0.829 gave 97 per cent precision and 98 per cent recall for one category. In UX the same procedure tags support tickets, reviews and open-ended survey answers at scale, now usually under labels such as automated coding or LLM classification.
steps: Define the category scheme and tag a training set, ideally with two coders and an agreement check.
Train one classifier per category (for example naive Bayes, kNN, SVM or a fine-tuned language model).
Score held-out documents and rank them per category.
Plot precision and recall against threshold and pick each cut-off by the cost of errors.
Apply to new text and route borderline cases to human review.
Re-check performance periodically against freshly tagged samples as language drifts.
outputs: Category tags per document with a chosen precision-recall balance, and per-category performance figures.
useWhen: You must tag large volumes of feedback, tickets, reviews or survey comments against an agreed scheme.
avoidWhen: Categories are not yet known; use open coding or topic modelling first. A tagged training set is required, and categorisation yields few tags per document compared with information extraction.
whyLost: The method lives on under names such as automated coding, AI tagging and LLM classification, with its threshold discipline often forgotten.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer programmes, support ticket routing, app store review analysis, open-ended survey coding.
example: A SaaS company tags 30,000 support tickets per month into 12 themes. Thresholds for 'billing' are set for high recall, with low-confidence tickets reviewed by a researcher weekly.
reference: Feldman, R. (2003). Mining text data. In N. Ye (Ed.), The Handbook of Data Mining (pp. 481-518). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates; Sebastiani, F. (2002). Machine learning in automated text categorization. ACM Computing Surveys, 34, 1-47.

name: Support vector machines
origin: Vapnik and colleagues, 1990s (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995)
summary: Classifiers that find the widest-margin boundary between classes, allowing tuned violations and kernel-based non-linear boundaries, evaluated by held-out ROC curves.
description: Support vector machines build on the maximal margin classifier, which chooses the separating hyperplane with the widest margin to the nearest training points (the support vectors). Because real classes overlap, the support vector classifier allows slack within a total violation budget C: a large budget gives a wide margin, many support vectors, low variance and high bias. Replacing inner products with a kernel (polynomial of degree d, or radial with parameter gamma) yields non-linear boundaries without computing an explicit feature space. C and kernel parameters must be tuned by cross-validation; training ROC curves flatter flexible kernels, so comparisons belong on held-out data. Multi-class problems use one-versus-one or one-versus-all schemes. Results are often close to logistic regression, which is preferred when classes overlap heavily and probabilities are needed.
steps: Code the two classes as +1 and -1 and standardise features.
Choose a kernel: linear, polynomial of degree d, or radial with parameter gamma.
Tune C (and d or gamma) by k-fold cross-validation over a grid.
Fit on training data; note that the boundary depends only on the support vectors.
Classify new cases by the sign of the fitted function and use fitted values as scores for ROC and AUC on held-out data.
For more than two classes use one-versus-one voting or one-versus-all largest score, and compare against logistic regression.
outputs: A decision boundary, support vectors, class predictions, and scores for ROC/AUC.
useWhen: You need a strong classifier for moderate-sized, high-dimensional data such as text features or behavioural vectors, and calibrated probabilities are not essential.
avoidWhen: Interpretability or probabilities matter, classes overlap heavily, or data are very large; use logistic regression, gradient boosting or neural models. Do not leave C at a default.
whyLost: Widely used in machine learning before deep learning, SVMs never became a UX method and have since been displaced by boosting and neural models in most applied work.
whereToUse: Classifying feedback text, predicting churn or task failure from behavioural features, detecting bots or anomalies in usage logs.
example: A research operations team classifies 5,000 survey comments as feature requests or bug reports using a linear SVM on TF-IDF features. Held-out AUC of 0.92 justifies automated triage with human review of uncertain cases.
sources: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (James et al., 2023)
Computer Vision: A Modern Approach (Forsyth & Ponce, 2011)
reference: Cortes, C., & Vapnik, V. (1995). Support-vector networks. Machine Learning, 20, 273-297; James, G., et al. (2023). An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python, ch. 9. Springer.

name: SUPR-Q (Standardized User Experience Percentile Rank Questionnaire)
origin: Sauro (2015); mobile app version SUPR-Qm by Sauro & Zarolia (2017)
summary: An 8-item website questionnaire measuring usability, trust, appearance and loyalty, scored as percentile ranks against hundreds of sites.
description: SUS measures perceived usability alone; websites also live or die on credibility, looks and loyalty. The SUPR-Q has eight items: two each for usability, trust (or credibility for non-commerce sites), appearance and loyalty, the last including the likelihood-to-recommend item. It was built through factor analysis and has strong reliability with only eight questions. Its distinctive feature is normative scoring: raw scores are converted to percentile ranks against a regularly updated database of websites, so a score of 75 means the site beats 75% of the benchmark. The SUPR-Qm is a 16-item Rasch-scaled version for mobile apps. Sauro recommends it over SUS for website benchmarks because it covers more of the experience in fewer items.
steps: Administer the eight items at the end of a study (or as a stand-alone survey of recent users).
Compute subscale means and the overall mean, treating the 11-point recommend item as half-weighted.
Convert to percentile ranks using the current normative database (licensed from MeasuringU).
Compare against competitors and industry averages in the same database.
Track over releases alongside task-level metrics.
outputs: Overall and subscale percentile ranks for a website or app.
useWhen: Website or app benchmarks where trust and appearance matter, and competitive comparisons.
avoidWhen: Internal tools where trust and loyalty are not meaningful, or when you cannot license the norms.
whyLost: Norms are commercial, so academic UX teaching favours free instruments like SUS and UMUX-Lite.
whereToUse: E-commerce, banking, insurance, travel and media sites; app store competitive reviews.
example: An insurer's site scores at the 82nd percentile for usability but the 31st for trust, redirecting effort toward reassurance content rather than navigation.
reference: Sauro, J. (2015). SUPR-Q: A comprehensive measure of the quality of the website user experience. Journal of Usability Studies 10(2).

name: Surrogate (driver/leading) metric derivation and validation
aka: Driver metric development and causal validation
origin: Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020); Wendel (2014); industry growth practice (Croll and Yoskovitz, 2013); surrogate endpoint concept from clinical trials (Prentice, 1989)
summary: Find early, measurable behaviours that predict a slow or off-product outcome, then validate causally that moving them moves the outcome, so experiments can be judged in days.
description: Key outcomes such as retention, purchases of a 13-week course credential, or real-world behaviour change move too slowly or happen outside the product. Teams therefore use surrogate metrics, but often stop at correlation ('seven friends in ten days'). The rigorous version has two halves. Derivation: start from the key outcome, trace the behaviours that must precede it, use qualitative research to propose candidates, set thresholds from logs (what counts as a bounce or a successful click), and write interpretable definitions. Validation: show that changing the surrogate changes the outcome, using dedicated experiments, holdback groups, historical experiment corpora with known outcomes, and external studies. For off-product outcomes, a 'data bridge' pilot measures the real outcome directly (by observation, not survey) in a random sample with a non-user baseline and models how the in-product behaviour predicts it.
steps: Start from the slow key outcome and trace the behaviours that must precede it (for example credential purchase requires course completion, which requires module completion).
Propose candidate early behaviours from qualitative research and by comparing retained with churned users.
Set thresholds from logs (such as dwell time defining a bounce, or excluding quick-backs from successful clicks) and write interpretable, hard-to-game definitions.
For off-product outcomes, run a data-bridge pilot: measure the real outcome directly in a random sample with a non-user baseline, link it to in-product behaviour and model the relationship.

Validate causally: run experiments designed to move the surrogate, check a corpus of past experiments with known outcomes, and use holdback groups to confirm that moving the surrogate moves the key outcome.
Adopt validated surrogates as experiment metrics and revalidate periodically as the product and users change.
outputs: A validated set of driver or surrogate metrics with definitions, thresholds and evidence of a causal link to the key outcome, or a model translating in-product behaviour to real-world impact.
useWhen: The key outcome is slow (retention, renewals, credentials, health outcomes) or measured outside the product, and experiments need faster, sensitive readouts.
avoidWhen: When the key outcome can be measured within the test window, or when you cannot validate the link even once; an unvalidated surrogate can optimise the wrong thing.
whyLost: Growth practice popularised 'aha moments' from correlations, keeping the name but dropping the causal validation that clinical surrogate endpoints require.
whereToUse: Subscription retention, online education, health and behaviour-change apps, marketplaces, B2B SaaS renewals.
example: A language app finds that completing three lessons on separate days in week one predicts 90-day retention. An experiment that nudges multi-day practice raises the behaviour but retention moves only half as much as predicted, so the team recalibrates the surrogate before using it.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Methods for Applying Predictive Modeling to Survey Data (Yih, 2024)
Building a Quant UXR Practice from Inception to Integration (Bakhshi, 2024)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, ch. 7; Prentice, R. L. (1989). Surrogate endpoints in clinical trials: definition and operational criteria. Statistics in Medicine, 8(4), 431-440.

name: Surrogate Time Series Testing
origin: Nonlinear dynamics literature (Theiler et al., 1992; Kaplan and Glass, 1995); as presented by van Drongelen (2018)
summary: Compare a time-series metric on real data with its distribution across surrogate series that keep chosen properties but satisfy a null hypothesis, showing whether it reflects real structure.
description: Algorithms for dimension, entropy, Lyapunov exponents, synchrony and similar metrics return a number even for random or linear data, so a value alone is no evidence of structure. Surrogate testing generates many series from the measured data that preserve some properties but are consistent with a null hypothesis, computes the metric on the real series and on every surrogate, and rejects the null if the real value falls outside the surrogate distribution. For a purely random null a random shuffle of the values suffices, which keeps the distribution but destroys all temporal order. For a stationary linear stochastic null, a Fourier transform followed by phase randomisation and inverse transform keeps the power spectrum and autocorrelation but destroys higher-order timing. Rejecting linearity makes nonlinearity plausible but does not demonstrate chaos.
steps: State the null hypothesis: a random process, or a stationary linear stochastic process.
Generate many surrogate series from the measured data (for example 99 or more): random shuffles for the first null, Fourier transform with randomised phases and inverse transform for the second.
Compute the metric of interest on the measured series and on every surrogate.
Locate the measured value in the surrogate distribution and reject the null if it lies outside (for example beyond the 2.5th or 97.5th percentile).
Report the null used, so readers know which structure the result rules out.
outputs: The metric value with a surrogate-based null distribution and a decision on the null hypothesis.
useWhen: Before interpreting complexity, entropy, recurrence or synchrony metrics on behavioural or physiological time series, such as interaction logs, scroll traces, heart rate or EEG in UX studies.
avoidWhen: It only tests the stated null; for simple group differences use ordinary tests or a Permutation Test (Resampling Significance Test). Non-stationary data need more careful surrogates.
whyLost: It belongs to physics and neuroscience signal analysis; UX studies that borrow complexity metrics usually import the metric without its null-hypothesis procedure.
whereToUse: Biometric and neuro UX studies, telemetry rhythm analysis, interpersonal synchrony in co-located use, game input dynamics.
example: A study reports higher sample entropy in mouse movements on a confusing checkout. Against 200 phase-randomised surrogates the real values sit inside the surrogate range, so the difference reflects spectral content, not nonlinear structure.
reference: Theiler, J. et al. (1992). Testing for nonlinearity in time series: the method of surrogate data. Physica D, 58; van Drongelen, W. (2018). Signal Processing for Neuroscientists (2nd ed.). London: Academic Press, pp. 575-576.

name: Survey Climate Assessment
origin: Loosveldt and Storms (2008), drawing on leverage-salience theory; European Social Survey contact forms
summary: Monitoring a population's willingness to take part in surveys through standardised response rates, recorded refusal reasons and a short attitude-to-surveys scale.
description: Survey climate is the general disposition of a population towards taking part in surveys. It is assessed through indicators computed identically over time: standardised response rates from consistent contact forms, refusal reasons recorded as paradata, and a short scale measuring opinions about surveys. Loosveldt and Storms developed a five-dimension, 23-item measure with a six-item short form (usefulness, waste of time, keeping people from important things, boring, dislike of participating, invasion of privacy), with a reported alpha of 0.82. The method's distinctive caution is that surveys about surveys are biased towards favourable views, because people who answer them like surveys more than those who do not; a mixed-mode or self-administered follow-up is used to estimate that bias.
steps: Compute response rates identically across waves and groups, using standardised outcome codes and contact records.
Record reasons for refusal and break-off as paradata.
Field the six-item opinions-about-surveys short scale at the end of a regular survey.
Use a follow-up in another mode or with nonrespondents to estimate selection bias in the attitude results.
Track the indicators by segment and over time, and relate changes to survey load and contact policy.
outputs: Trend indicators of survey climate, short-scale scores by segment and evidence on survey fatigue.
useWhen: Organisations that survey the same user base repeatedly and see falling response rates or suspect over-surveying of particular segments.
avoidWhen: Diagnosing a single survey's low response, where contact strategy and instrument review are faster. Do not treat scale scores from respondents as the view of the whole base.
whyLost: Response rates in product surveys are monitored per survey rather than as a population climate, and the attitude scale is known only in European survey methodology.
whereToUse: Companies with many teams sending in-product and email surveys, research panels, B2B customers contacted by product, success and marketing teams.
example: A marketplace sees in-app survey response fall from 9% to 4% over two years. A climate assessment shows the decline is concentrated in power sellers, whose short-scale scores flag 'waste of time', leading to a contact-frequency cap for that segment.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Loosveldt, G. and Joye, D. (2016). Defining and assessing survey climate. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 67-76). London: SAGE.

name: Survey data cleaning
origin: Meade and Craig (2012) on careless responding; Curran (2016) on detection methods
summary: Systematically screening raw survey responses for careless, fraudulent, duplicate and out-of-range data using pre-stated rules before any analysis.
description: Survey cleaning is the first and most consequential analytic step: careless responses typically make up 10-15% of online samples and can create spurious factors, inflate or deflate correlations and distort means. Rigorous cleaning uses multiple indicators: attention or instructed-response items, response time (speeders), long-string analysis (straight-lining), even-odd consistency, Mahalanobis distance for multivariate outliers, duplicate and bot detection, and open-text checks. Rules and thresholds are written before looking at results, applied in code rather than by hand, and every exclusion is counted in a flow table. In UX practice this is often reduced to deleting obviously blank rows, which is why it is vestigial.
steps: Write exclusion rules and thresholds in the analysis plan before inspecting outcomes.
Import the raw export programmatically (e.g. pyreadstat for .sav files) and keep it unchanged.
Flag speeders, commonly those completing in under one third or under half of the median duration.
Flag failed attention checks, long strings exceeding about half the items in a scale block, and multivariate outliers at Mahalanobis distance p below 0.001.
Detect duplicates and bots via IP, device fingerprint, identical open text and impossible response patterns.
Recode out-of-range values to missing, reverse-score items as specified, and document every recode.
Exclude respondents meeting pre-stated combinations of flags and report counts at each step in a flow table; run a sensitivity analysis with and without exclusions.
outputs: A cleaned dataset, a flag table per respondent, an exclusion flow table and a sensitivity check on key results.
useWhen: Every survey analysis, especially online panels, incentive-driven samples, long instruments and psychometric work such as EFA or SEM.
avoidWhen: Never skipped, but avoid aggressive post-hoc exclusions chosen after seeing results; that is a forking path. For very small qualitative screeners, a manual review suffices.
whyLost: Survey tools offer one-click exports and dashboards that hide the raw data, and UX teams rarely received training in response-quality screening.
whereToUse: Product satisfaction surveys, scale validation, segmentation studies, panel research and in-product intercepts.
example: A SaaS team running a 1,500-person panel survey flags 11% as speeders or attention-check failures. Removing them changes the leading pain point from 'pricing' to 'integration', because careless respondents had straight-lined the pricing block.
sources: Meade, A. W. & Craig, S. B. (2012) Identifying careless responses in survey data. Psychological Methods
Curran, P. G. (2016) Methods for the detection of carelessly invalid responses in survey data. JESP
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
A Practical Guide to Experience-Sampling Procedures (Conner Christensen et al., 2003)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
reference: Meade, A. W. & Craig, S. B. (2012) Identifying careless responses in survey data. Psychological Methods 17(3)

name: Survey Fieldwork Planning, Monitoring and Back-Checks
origin: AAPOR Standard Definitions; European Social Survey fieldwork specifications
summary: Writing targets and reporting rules into the fieldwork contract, monitoring progress by interviewer, verifying interviews with back-checks and acting when targets are missed.
description: When data collection is outsourced, quality depends on specifying and checking what the field team does. Targets (response rate, interviews per week, contact rules such as the ESS minimum of four in-person attempts over two weeks including an evening and a weekend) go into the call for tender. Outcomes are coded with AAPOR Standard Definitions, so response rates are calculated consistently, and rules on partial interviews, proxies and substitution are agreed. Regular reports by interviewer cover interviews, appointments, refusals, noncontacts and timing, and outcomes prone to shortcuts (looped batteries, consent items) are watched. Back-checks re-contact respondents by mail or phone to verify that interviews happened, and delivered data are checked for duplicates and inconsistencies. Agreed repercussions follow: extend fieldwork, retrain or replace interviewers. Back-checks catch only serious problems, and interviewer effects are confounded with area unless assignments are interpenetrated.
steps: Write targets into the tender: response rate, weekly interview counts, contact rules and reporting frequency.
Agree AAPOR disposition codes and rules for partial interviews, proxies and substitution.
Require regular reports by interviewer or recruiter: completes, appointments, refusals, noncontacts, ineligibles and contact timing.
Monitor outcomes prone to shortcuts, such as skipped loops, very short interviews or identical answer patterns.
Back-check a random subsample by phone or all respondents by mail soon after the interview.
Check delivered data for duplicates, speeding and inconsistencies.
Apply agreed actions when targets are missed: extend fieldwork, retrain or replace staff, prioritise low-propensity cases.
outputs: Monitoring reports, verified interviews, documented dispositions and response rates, and a record of corrective actions.
useWhen: Outsourced survey or recruitment fieldwork, agency-run interviews in emerging markets, large moderated studies run by vendors.
avoidWhen: Small in-house studies run by the researchers themselves, where direct observation replaces monitoring.
whyLost: UX increasingly uses self-serve platforms and treats vendor fieldwork as a black box; falsification checks are associated with government surveys rather than product research.
whereToUse: Multi-country vendor studies, field intercepts in retail or transport, recruitment agencies supplying participants for incentive-heavy studies.
example: A mobility company commissions 2,000 street intercepts in four cities. Daily per-interviewer reports show one interviewer completing interviews in half the median time; phone back-checks on a 10% subsample fail to confirm a third of that interviewer's cases, which are discarded and re-fielded.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Blom, A. G. (2016). Survey fieldwork. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 382-396). London: SAGE.

name: Survey Item-Type Selection (Decision Tree and Rating-Format Catalogue)
aka: Survey item-type selection decision tree and rating-scale format catalogue
origin: Jeff Sauro and James R. Lewis, MeasuringU ('4 Classes of Survey Questions'; '15 Common Rating Scales Explained')
summary: Choose each survey item's format by naming its goal first, then its construct, using a decision tree over about fifteen rating, ranking and allocation formats.
description: Sauro and Lewis classify survey questions as open-ended, closed-ended static (single or multiple choice, rating scales), closed-ended dynamic (adaptive conjoint, MaxDiff, IRT-driven) and task-based. Their catalogue of static rating formats covers linear numeric, Likert agreement, frequency, unipolar and bipolar satisfaction, performance, disconfirmation, comparative, comparative intensity, semantic differential and semantic distance, where a single adjective per row is rated from not at all to perfectly so no polar opposites are needed. Ranking and allocation formats include forced ranking, pick-some (top task) and fixed sum. A decision tree maps goals (discovery, categorical, ranking, allocation, rating, comparison) and constructs to formats, each with documented trade-offs. Format rules follow the evidence: more than three points, a neutral point, positive wording, small grids, counterbalancing. Most format variations shift means by only about 0.3-1.5%, whereas collapsing NPS to three points changed results by 22%.
steps: State the goal of each item: discovery, categorical measurement, ranking, allocation, rating or comparison.
Discovery: use an open-ended item. Categorical: single choice if options are mutually exclusive, multiple choice if not.
Ranking: forced rank for up to about ten items; pick-some or MaxDiff for more, randomising order. Allocation: fixed sum.

Rating: choose by construct: linear numeric (general), Likert-type (agreement), frequency, unipolar (none to much), bipolar (opposites), performance (adequacy or quality), disconfirmation or Kano (meeting expectations).
Comparison: comparative item for two products; comparative intensity against a named benchmark. Adjectives: semantic differential only if true opposites exist, otherwise semantic distance.
Apply format rules: 5-7 or 11 points, include a neutral point, word positively, keep grids small, counterbalance options and items; record the rationale per item.
outputs: A chosen format for each survey item with a written rationale and noted trade-offs.
useWhen: Drafting or reviewing any UX survey, especially when teams default to agreement scales for everything or need ranking, allocation or benchmark comparison.
avoidWhen: Choosing a validated standard instrument (SUS, UEQ) whose format is fixed; use it as published. For constructing a new multi-item scale use Scale construction and validation.
whyLost: It survives because survey design is routine in UX and MeasuringU's practitioner-facing evidence is widely read; the decision tree itself is less known than individual formats.
whereToUse: Product satisfaction and feature surveys, competitive benchmarks, prioritisation surveys, in-product feedback.
example: Instead of asking agreement with 'Search is fast', an e-commerce team uses a comparative intensity item rating its search against Amazon's from much worse to much better, and a semantic distance grid of five adjectives for its checkout.
reference: Sauro, J. and Lewis, J. R. (2021). Survey Design. Survey/Stats Training slide deck for Google. MeasuringU.

name: Survey linked to consented account (log) data
origin: Nov, Naaman and Ye, 2008; Kairam et al., 2016; as reported by Lazar, Feng and Hochheiser
summary: Ask attitudes and motives in a survey and, with each respondent's permission, take their actual behaviour from their account data instead of asking them to recall it.
description: Recall questions about usage (how many tags, how much spent, how often) produce guesses and recall bias; facts a computer can record should be taken from the record. This design ends the survey by asking respondents to authorise researcher access to their account, then joins logged behaviour to their answers, so attitudes can be related to real behaviour. Nov et al. invited 1,373 Flickr users, obtained 237 valid responses and took tag counts (mean 370) from accounts. A variant samples each respondent's own content, stratified by a platform attribute, and shows it inside the survey for item-level questions: Kairam et al. selected 20 photos per person across five privacy settings and showed 10, alongside aggregate data from 638,930 active users. Inclusion rules can bias the sample, and informed consent for account access must be explicit and specific.
steps: Define inclusion criteria from platform activity and check them for hidden biases (for example language or activity thresholds).
Randomly sample eligible users and send invitations.
Administer the attitude and motivation survey without asking for behaviours the logs can supply.
Ask respondents to authorise access to specified account data, explaining exactly what will be extracted and why.
Extract behavioural measures for consenting respondents and join them to survey answers under a data-protection plan.
Variant: select each respondent's own items stratified by an attribute, show a random subset in the survey and ask item-specific questions.
Compare consenters with non-consenters on available aggregate data to estimate consent bias.
outputs: A per-respondent dataset combining self-report with logged behaviour, plus an estimate of consent bias.
useWhen: When you want to relate attitudes, motives or satisfaction to actual usage, or when recall of behaviour would be unreliable.
avoidWhen: Avoid when consent cannot be obtained cleanly or the data are sensitive beyond what participants expect; then use aggregate Log File Analysis or Experience Sampling Method. Not needed if behaviour is irrelevant to the question.
whyLost: It is routine in social computing research and large product teams with data infrastructure, but most UX surveys still ask for recalled usage.
whereToUse: Platforms with account data (social, fintech, SaaS), privacy research, attitude-behaviour gap studies, satisfaction driver analysis.
example: A budgeting app surveys users about financial confidence and, with consent, links answers to six months of categorised transactions. Confidence tracks savings-rule use, not balance, informing which feature to promote.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Nov, O., Naaman, M., & Ye, C. (2008). What drives content tagging: The case of photos on Flickr. CHI 2008, 1097-1100; Lazar, J., Feng, J. H., & Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 105-107.

name: Survey paradata analysis
origin: Survey methodology; Kreuter (ed.), 2013, Improving Surveys with Paradata
summary: Analyse the by-products of answering (time per question, changed answers, back-navigation, break-offs, device and mode) to find confusing questions, mode problems and careless respondents.
description: Paradata are records of the response process rather than the responses: how long respondents spent on each question and on the whole survey, whether they changed answers or went back, where they broke off, and which device or mode they used. Survey methodologists use them to locate questions that are confusing (long dwell, many changes), surveys that are too long (break-offs), modes or devices that cause problems, and low-effort responding. Pilot timings set expected answer times, so some tools can warn respondents who answer implausibly fast, a guard against satisficing. Paradata are cheap because most online tools already capture them, but they are personal data and should be disclosed. Fast answers are a signal, not proof, of carelessness; combine with straight-lining checks and attention items before excluding anyone.
steps: Enable capture of timing, navigation, answer changes and device data in the survey tool, and disclose it in the consent text.
Set expected times per question from the pilot (for example flag responses faster than about 2 seconds per item or under one third of the median total).
Inspect break-off points and unusually long dwell times or frequent answer changes per question.
Compare paradata by mode and device (for example mobile versus desktop) to detect mode-specific problems.
Flag speeders and straight-liners for review alongside other quality checks rather than excluding automatically.
Revise problem questions and layouts in the next wave and compare paradata again.
outputs: Evidence of problem questions, mode and device effects, and flagged low-effort responses, with revisions for the next wave.
useWhen: When running online surveys at scale, piloting a questionnaire, or cleaning data where satisficing or device problems are suspected.
avoidWhen: Avoid excluding respondents on timing alone; use it with other checks (Survey data cleaning). For understanding why a question confuses, add Cognitive Interviewing for Questionnaire Design.
whyLost: It is standard in survey methodology, but UX teams seldom look past completion rate even though their tools capture the data.
whereToUse: Product and CSat surveys, unmoderated test questionnaires, panel research, mobile-first surveys.
example: In a mobile onboarding survey, paradata show a matrix question with three times the median dwell and 40% of break-offs on phones. Splitting it into single items halves break-offs.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Kreuter, F. (Ed.) (2013). Improving Surveys with Paradata: Analytic Uses of Process Information. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Survey Question Writing (Diagnostic Checks, Structures and Wording Principles)
aka: Dillman's 19 principles for writing survey questions
Interview and survey question wording checks
origin: Don Dillman, 1978 and 2000, building on Payne (1951) The Art of Asking Questions; psycholinguistic checks from Sauro and Lewis (MeasuringU)
summary: A checklist procedure for turning draft queries into questions every respondent interprets the same way, can answer accurately and is willing to answer.
description: Question writing treated as a procedure rather than a craft. Each draft item is first put through eight diagnostic checks (does it apply to everyone, do people hold a ready answer, can they recall it, will they reveal it, will categories or layout sway it, is more than one mode used). The writer then chooses a structure deliberately: open-ended for facts, closed ordered for evaluations, closed unordered for comparisons, partially closed with an 'Other' option. Nineteen wording principles follow, such as numbers instead of vague quantifiers, balanced scales, no double-barrelled or yes-means-no items, and no respondent arithmetic. Sauro and Lewis add psycholinguistic checks: avoid embedded clauses and passive voice, and watch words such as 'ever', 'should', an ambiguous 'you' and a sponsoring 'our'. Dillman's demonstration that category ranges alone moved 23% to 69% of students into a top study-time band shows why the rigour matters.
steps: List each draft query with its response choices and the decision it serves.

Ask the eight diagnostic checks of every item: universal applicability, ready-made answer, recall, willingness to reveal, motivation, influence of categories or layout, mode differences, and whether the sponsor will accept changes.

Choose the structure deliberately: open-ended with units printed after the blank for facts, closed ordered for evaluations, closed unordered for comparisons (limit rankings to a top three), or partially closed with 'Other, please specify'; split mixed items into ordered items plus one comparison item.

Apply the wording principles: simple and few words, complete sentences, numbers instead of vague quantifiers, balanced positive and negative categories, undecided placed last, both sides of the scale in the stem, mutually exclusive categories, appropriate time referents, no double-barrelled or yes-means-no items, and no percentages to calculate.
Replace check-all-that-apply lists with a yes/no or rating per option.
Run psycholinguistic checks: remove centre- and left-embedded clauses, passive voice and adjunct wh-questions, and flag watch words (ever, always, never, could, should, would, you, our).
Have colleagues review the set and pilot it with a way for respondents to flag unclear items, then revise.
outputs: A revised question set with documented structure choices and a log of the principles applied to each item.
useWhen: Drafting any self-administered UX survey, in-product questionnaire or screener, especially where results feed roadmap or benchmark decisions and items will be reused over time.
avoidWhen: Validated standard scales (SUS, UEQ) whose wording must not be changed; use a scale quality audit instead. The principles conflict (simpler words make longer questions), so do not apply them mechanically without pretesting.
whyLost: UX survey tools made authoring trivial, so items are written quickly by non-specialists and the survey-methodology checklists rarely travel with them. The principles survive as folklore ('avoid leading questions') stripped of the diagnostic sequence.
whereToUse: Product satisfaction trackers, onboarding and churn surveys, B2B customer surveys, screeners and any questionnaire that will be compared across releases.
example: A fintech team's churn survey asks 'How often do you use budgeting features?' with options rarely/sometimes/often. Applying the principles, the researcher replaces vague quantifiers with counts for the past 30 days, splits a double-barrelled 'fees and speed' item and converts a check-all list of reasons into yes/no items.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Dillman, D. A. (2007). Mail and Internet Surveys: The Tailored Design Method (2nd ed., 2007 update). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons.

name: Survey scale quality audit
origin: Classical test theory and reliability (Cronbach, 1951), construct validity (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955), survey error framework (Groves et al., Survey Methodology, 2004/2009) and cognitive interviewing (Willis, 2005)
summary: Systematically checks a survey's items and scales for wording problems, reliability, validity, response patterns and data quality before or after fielding.
description: Many UX surveys use home-made scales with untested wording, unvalidated item groupings and unknown reliability. A scale quality audit evaluates surveys through several lenses. Item wording is checked for double-barrelled, leading, ambiguous or jargon-laden items and for balanced, labelled response options. Cognitive interviews test whether respondents understand items as intended. Psychometric checks on fielded data examine internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha or, better, McDonald's omega, with about 0.70 as a common minimum), item-total correlations, factor structure, and floor and ceiling effects. Data quality checks look for straightlining, speeding and inattentive responding. Groves' total survey error framework connects these to coverage, sampling, non-response and measurement error. Rigour comes from combining qualitative pre-testing with quantitative psychometric evidence.
steps: Review each item against a checklist: one idea per item, neutral wording, no jargon, clear time frame, balanced and fully labelled response options, and consistent scale direction.
Run cognitive interviews with 5 to 15 respondents using think-aloud and verbal probes ('What does "reliable" mean to you here?') and revise problem items.
After fielding, compute item distributions and flag floor or ceiling effects, for example more than 15% of responses at either extreme.
Calculate reliability (omega or alpha, targeting 0.70 or above, and investigating values above about 0.95 for redundancy) and corrected item-total correlations (flag below 0.30).
Check structure with exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis where samples allow (often 200 or more), and test validity against related measures or behaviour.
Screen data quality: straightlining across grids, completion times below a plausible minimum (for example under one-third of the median), and failed attention checks.
Replace weak home-made scales with validated instruments where possible (for example SUS, UMUX-Lite, SUPR-Q) and document changes.
outputs: An item-level issues log, cognitive interview findings, reliability and validity statistics, data quality flags, and a revised instrument.
useWhen: Before launching a recurring or high-stakes survey, when inheriting an existing tracker, or when survey results conflict with behaviour.
avoidWhen: Using an established validated instrument unchanged with a comparable population, where a light data-quality check suffices.
whyLost: Survey tools make questionnaires easy to build, and UX teams rarely include psychometricians, so home-made scales go unvalidated for years.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and NPS trackers, relationship surveys, onboarding surveys, employee experience surveys, AI trust questionnaires.
example: A satisfaction tracker run for 6 months had a 4-item 'ease' scale with omega of 0.58 and one double-barrelled item ('fast and reliable'). Cognitive interviews showed rural respondents read 'reliable' as 'honest company'; splitting and rewording the items raised omega to 0.81.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 42 — Ordinal Logic — Treating Likert & Survey Data Correctly
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Groves, R. M., Fowler, F. J., Couper, M. P., Lepkowski, J. M., Singer, E., & Tourangeau, R. (2009). Survey Methodology (2nd ed.). Wiley; Willis, G. B. (2005). Cognitive Interviewing: A Tool for Improving Questionnaire Design. Sage.

name: Survey Weighting
origin: Standard survey statistics practice; Veal and Darcy show it with site survey and count data and in SPSS's Weight Cases procedure
summary: Gives each respondent a weight so the sample's make-up on known characteristics matches the real user population before results are reported.
description: Survey weighting corrects a sample that is known to be unbalanced. Veal and Darcy's example is a site survey where interviews were spread evenly through the day, while counts showed that more than half of users came around midday; because midday users may differ, they are under-represented. For each group, such as a time-period, the weighting factor is the number in the population divided by the number in the sample, so each interview 'grosses up' to the users it represents. The weighted sample then matches the population. They note that the true sample size has not changed, so for significance tests the factors should be rescaled so the weighted total equals the actual number of interviews. Any characteristic known for the population can be used, such as age from the census, membership records or observed gender balance. They also suggest weighting to correct for different response rates in mail surveys. For UX surveys, which often over-represent engaged or recent users, weighting against analytics data on plan, tenure, platform or activity is a cheap way to make results more representative.
steps: Identify a characteristic that matters for the results and is known for the whole user population (for example time of use, plan, platform, age group).
Tabulate the sample and the population across the categories of that characteristic.
Compute a weighting factor for each category as population number divided by sample number.
Rescale the factors so the weighted total equals the actual sample size if significance tests will be run.
Attach the weights as a variable and apply them in the analysis software.
Compare weighted and unweighted results and report both the weighting basis and any large differences.
Avoid weighting on characteristics with very small sample cells, or combine categories first.
outputs: A weight variable for each respondent and weighted estimates that better reflect the user population, with a note of the weighting basis.
useWhen: A survey sample's make-up on a known characteristic clearly differs from the population and that characteristic plausibly relates to the answers.
avoidWhen: Population figures are unreliable, sample cells are tiny so weights become extreme, or the bias lies on unmeasured characteristics that weighting cannot fix.
whyLost: UX surveys are usually treated as convenience samples and reported raw, and few UX researchers are trained in survey statistics, though analytics now make population benchmarks easy to obtain.
whereToUse: In-product surveys, NPS and satisfaction programmes, panel surveys, site and event surveys, any survey that will be generalised to a user base.
example: An app's satisfaction survey gets 70 per cent of its responses from daily users, who make up 30 per cent of the active base. Weighting by usage frequency from analytics lowers reported satisfaction from 4.3 to 3.9 and shows that occasional users drive most complaints.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: Surveys
origin: Survey research tradition, 1930s onward (e.g. Gallup, Likert 1932)
summary: Structured self-report instruments administered to samples to measure attitudes, behaviours and characteristics at scale, from satisfaction tracking to validated scales.
description: Surveys collect structured self-reported data from a sample to estimate characteristics of a population, compare groups or track change over time. In UX they range from short satisfaction and loyalty measures, such as CSAT and NPS, to validated instruments like SUS and UMUX-Lite, and bespoke attitudinal questionnaires. Their power comes from scale; their weakness comes from the many sources of error described in the total survey error framework: coverage, sampling, non-response and measurement. Rigour comes from clearly defined constructs, well-worded and pretested questions, validated scales where possible, appropriate sampling and response-rate management, attention checks, and analysis that reports uncertainty and avoids over-interpreting small differences.
steps: Define research questions, target population and the decisions the survey will inform.
Specify the constructs to measure and reuse validated items or scales where possible.
Write clear, single-barrelled, neutral questions with balanced response options.
Pretest with 5 to 10 cognitive interviews and a small pilot.
Define the sampling frame and calculate sample size for the precision needed (for example about 385 for plus or minus 5 percent at 95 percent confidence in a large population).
Field the survey with reminders, monitoring response rates and data quality.
Clean data, weight if needed, analyse with confidence intervals and report limitations.
outputs: Descriptive statistics, segment comparisons, validated scale scores, trend data and open-ended response themes.
useWhen: For measuring attitudes, satisfaction or self-reported behaviour across large populations, segment comparisons and tracking over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid for understanding why or for discovering unknown issues; use interviews. Avoid self-report for precise behaviour when logs exist; use analytics.
whyLost: Still in use: Scalable data collection; but validity requires careful design and interpretation.
whereToUse: Satisfaction tracking; large-population attitudes; longitudinal benchmarking.
example: A SaaS company surveys 2,000 admins quarterly with UMUX-Lite and three bespoke items. A drop among admins of large accounts prompts follow-up interviews about permissions management.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
B2B Web Usability Report 2015 (Huff et al., 2015)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
The User Is Always Right (Mulder & Yaar, 2007)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Groves, R. M. et al. (2009). Survey Methodology (2nd ed.). Wiley.

name: SWAT (Subjective Workload Assessment Technique)
origin: Gary Reid and Thomas Nygren, US Air Force Armstrong Laboratory, 1988
summary: Measures workload on time load, mental effort and psychological stress, scaled with each user's own conjoint-measured weighting of the three dimensions.
description: SWAT asks users to rate workload on three dimensions, each with three levels: time load, mental effort load and psychological stress load. What makes it rigorous is the scale development phase: before the task, each participant sorts 27 cards representing all combinations of levels by perceived workload, and conjoint measurement converts the sort into an interval scale from 0 to 100 unique to that person or group. Event ratings are then mapped onto this scale. SWAT thus respects individual differences in what feels demanding. It is more laborious than NASA-TLX, which displaced it, but its conjoint foundation makes it an instructive example of psychometric rigour in workload measurement.
steps: Explain the three dimensions and their three levels to participants with standard descriptors.
Run the card sort: each participant ranks all 27 combinations from lowest to highest workload.
Apply conjoint scaling to derive interval workload values; check Kendall's coefficient of concordance to decide between group and individual scales (group scale if W >= 0.75).
After each task or event, collect quick 1-2-3 ratings on the three dimensions.
Convert ratings to scaled workload scores and compare conditions or task segments.
Triangulate with performance and physiological measures.
outputs: Interval-scaled workload scores per task, with dimension contributions and individual weighting profiles.
useWhen: Comparing workload across designs when you need individually calibrated scaling or quick in-task ratings.
avoidWhen: Most product contexts; NASA-TLX or a single-item rating is quicker. The card sort is tedious for participants.
whyLost: NASA-TLX offered similar information with less setup, and the conjoint software became obsolete. It survives mainly in older military literature.
whereToUse: Comparative evaluation of control-room displays, vehicle HMIs, complex enterprise workflows.
example: A rail operator compares two dispatch screens. SWAT shows similar total workload, but stress load dominates in one design during disruptions, pointing to alarm handling as the issue.
sources: Reid & Nygren, The subjective workload assessment technique (1988), in Hancock & Meshkati (eds.), Human Mental Workload
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Reid, G. B., & Nygren, T. E. (1988). The subjective workload assessment technique. In Hancock & Meshkati (Eds.), Human Mental Workload. North-Holland.

name: Swiss Cheese Model Analysis
donor: Safety science and healthcare risk management
origin: James Reason, 1990
summary: Traces incidents through layered defences to show how latent conditions and active failures align, so design fixes target system weaknesses rather than blaming users.
