description: Reason's model represents a system's safeguards as slices of Swiss cheese, each with holes caused by active failures (unsafe acts by people at the sharp end) and latent conditions (design decisions, staffing, procedures). Harm occurs when holes in successive layers align. As a research method it structures incident analysis: for each incident or near miss, analysts reconstruct the sequence, identify every defence that should have stopped it, and classify why each failed. The resulting picture usually shows that interface design, alerts and confirmations are some of the layers, and that user error is an outcome rather than a root cause. Rigour comes from systematic reconstruction with evidence, analysing near misses as well as harms, and aggregating across incidents to find recurring holes. Frameworks such as HFACS formalise the classification.
steps: Collect incidents and near misses with supporting evidence such as logs, screenshots and interviews.
Reconstruct each event timeline from initiating action to outcome.
List every defence layer that could have intercepted it: interface constraints, confirmations, alerts, procedures, reviews.
Classify each layer's failure as an active failure or latent condition, using a scheme such as HFACS.
Aggregate across incidents to find layers that fail repeatedly.
Design fixes that strengthen recurrent weak layers or add independent ones, and monitor near-miss rates.
outputs: Incident reconstructions, defence-layer failure maps, aggregated weak-layer analysis, systemic design recommendations.
useWhen: Healthcare, aviation, fintech operations, infrastructure tools and any product where errors cause serious harm.
avoidWhen: Low-consequence consumer flows with no incident history; standard error analysis or usability testing is lighter.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives in safety engineering and healthcare; rarely applied in consumer UX.
whereToUse: Healthcare UI; aviation; financial risk systems; any safety-critical interface.
example: A trading platform analysed a fat-finger order that lost £2m. The model showed four layers failed: no unit display, a dismissible warning, a disabled limit check and no second review. Fixes targeted the latent conditions, not just the trader.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents (James Reason)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Reason, J. (2000). Human error: Models and management. BMJ, 320(7237), 768-770.

name: Switchback and Cluster-Randomised Experiments
donor: Agricultural and clinical trial design; operations research
origin: Cluster randomised trials in public health (Donner and Klar, 2000; Hayes and Moulton, 2009); switchback designs formalised by Bojinov, Simchi-Levi and Zhao (2023)
summary: Randomises at the level of time periods, regions or groups instead of users when users interfere with each other, avoiding biased estimates in networks and marketplaces.
description: User-level A/B tests assume no interference (SUTVA). In marketplaces, social networks and shared resources, treating some users changes the experience of others: discounted riders consume drivers' supply, or a feature changes group chats. Cluster randomisation assigns whole groups (cities, teams, communities) to arms; switchback designs alternate treatment and control over time windows within a region. Analysis must account for clustering (intra-cluster correlation drives the design effect) and, for switchbacks, carryover between windows. Rigorous design balances window length against carryover and the number of clusters against power.
steps: Map interference: who affects whom (shared supply, social ties, team accounts).
Choose the randomisation unit: cluster (region, team, network component) or time window (switchback).
Estimate the intra-cluster correlation and compute the design effect (1 + (m - 1) x ICC) for sample size.
For switchbacks, choose window length longer than carryover time and randomise sequences; consider burn-in periods.
Analyse with cluster-robust or mixed-effects models, or design-based estimators for switchbacks.
Compare with user-level estimates to quantify interference bias.
outputs: Unbiased treatment effect estimates under interference, design-effect calculations and interference bias estimates.
useWhen: Marketplaces, social features, collaborative tools, shared-resource systems, pricing or dispatch algorithms.
avoidWhen: Independent users with no interaction; standard user-level A/B tests are more powerful.
whyLost: Platforms default to user-level randomisation, and UX researchers rarely consider interference.
whereToUse: Ride-hailing, delivery, team collaboration tools, social apps, multiplayer games.
example: A team-chat app tests a new notification digest. Randomising by workspace instead of user shows a smaller effect, because user-level tests had treated users replying to untreated colleagues.
sources: Bojinov, Simchi-Levi & Zhao, Design and analysis of switchback experiments (2023), Management Science
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)
Mixed Models: A Flexible Approach to Correlated Data (Seltman, n.d.)
Bayesian Analysis for the Social Sciences (Jackman, 2009)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Bojinov, I., Simchi-Levi, D., & Zhao, J. (2023). Management Science, 69(7), 3759-3777.

name: SWOT Analysis for UX Strategy and Vision
aka: SWOT analysis applied to UX positioning
UX team vision, mission and strategy workshop
origin: Albert S. Humphrey (Stanford Research Institute); applied to design research by Hall (2013) and to UX team vision work by Lund (2011)
summary: Build a SWOT grid from organisational, user and competitive research, derive UX implications from it, and use it to anchor a UX vision, mission and strategy.
description: SWOT arranges internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats. Hall's version insists the grid is filled from research: organisational and stakeholder research supplies strengths and weaknesses, while user and competitive research supplies opportunities and threats. The team then names the aspects of the experience that amplify strengths and exploit opportunities, and those that mitigate weaknesses and counter threats; strengths plus opportunities define the competitive advantage to design around. Lund uses a SWOT of UX in its organisational setting as the opening move of a team vision workshop: review corporate statements and the brand promise, brainstorm vision elements from user, company and team perspectives, cluster them by affinity, and have the leader draft the vision, mission and elevator pitch for one or two review passes rather than wordsmithing in the group.
steps: Gather inputs: stakeholder and organisational research for strengths and weaknesses; user and competitive research for opportunities and threats; corporate vision, mission and brand promise.
Arrange findings in a 2 x 2 grid (internal and external by positive and negative), citing the evidence for each item.
For each cell, list the UX features or qualities that amplify strengths and opportunities or mitigate weaknesses and threats.
For a team vision, brainstorm vision elements from the perspectives of users, company, organisation and the team, probing when ideas slow.
Cluster ideas by affinity and pull representative phrases into a logical order; avoid group wordsmithing.
Have the leader draft the vision (often starting 'five years from now'), mission and elevator pitch, and bring them back for one or two review passes.
For strategy, work through roadmap initiatives listing objectives, enablers and blockers, cluster them into themes, and revisit the statements periodically.
outputs: A research-backed SWOT grid, a list of UX implications, and where used for team strategy a vision statement, mission statement, elevator pitch and strategic themes.
useWhen: Use it to position a product's experience against competitors, or to give a UX team a shared vision and strategy after a reorganisation.
avoidWhen: A SWOT filled from opinion is only a list of beliefs; ground it in Competitive UX Benchmarking, Stakeholder Interview Protocol (Organisational Research) and user research. Competitors' reasons can only be inferred from outside. Statements that are too generic will not guide choices.
whyLost: The grid survives everywhere, but it is usually filled in a meeting from assumptions, so the research grounding Hall describes has largely been lost.
whereToUse: UX strategy and positioning work, design team offsites, new-market entry, museum and public-sector digital strategy.
example: A science museum's digital team finds strong reputation and staff (strengths), design effort focused on physical exhibits (weakness), more parents planning weekend family outings (opportunity) and schools cutting field trips (threat). It prioritises a weekend family planning feature on its website.
reference: Hall, E. (2013). Just Enough Research. New York: A Book Apart. Lund, A. (2011). User Experience Management: Essential Skills for Leading Effective UX Teams. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 129-137.

name: Symbolic object-retrieval task
aka: Symbolic object-retrieval task: scale model, picture and video versions
origin: Judy DeLoache, 1987 onwards
summary: A child watches a toy hidden in a scale model, picture or video of a room, then searches the real room; correct first searches show whether the symbol is understood.
description: DeLoache's task tests whether young children understand that a symbol stands for a real space. After orientation, in which each miniature item is matched with its full-size counterpart, the experimenter hides a toy in the model and the child searches for its counterpart in the real room. Only first searches count. Retrieving the miniature afterwards checks memory and motivation. Three-year-olds succeed over 75 per cent of the time; 2.5-year-olds mostly fail. Lower similarity hurts, and the dual representation hypothesis held: younger children succeed with pictures, a model behind a window helps, prior play with the model hurts, and a 'shrinking machine' story removes the difficulty. The task has low verbal demand, a clear outcome and is motivating, which makes it adaptable to testing whether children can use maps, video or AR representations of real spaces.
steps: Build a symbol of a real space: a scale model, picture or live video feed.
Orient the child to the correspondence, matching each item to its real counterpart.
Hide a toy in the real space while showing the hiding via the symbol.
Ask the child to find the toy and record whether the first search is correct.
Check memory by having the child retrieve the miniature from the symbol.
Vary similarity, salience or medium between conditions, using at least 10-16 children per age group and condition.
outputs: Proportion of correct first searches by condition and age; evidence on which representations children can use.
useWhen: You design for young children (roughly 2-4 years) and need to know whether they can map an on-screen or physical representation onto a real space.
avoidWhen: Participants are older children or adults; the task is very sensitive to similarity and salience, and only first searches are informative. Use observational playtesting for general usability with children.
whyLost: It remains a developmental psychology paradigm; children's UX research relies on observation and adapted usability testing rather than controlled representational tasks.
whereToUse: Children's apps, educational toys, video calling for families, AR games for preschoolers, smart-home interfaces for children.
example: A toy company tests whether 3-year-olds can find a hidden prize using a tablet's live video of the playroom. Success is high with a fixed camera view and drops with a moving camera, shaping the app's default mode.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development (Goswami, 2011)
reference: DeLoache, J. S. (1987). Rapid change in the symbolic functioning of very young children. Science, 238, 1556-1557.

name: Synchronised Log and Observation Data Collection
aka: Hybrid log and observation data collection
origin: Hammontree et al. (1992); later tools such as ChronoViz (Fouse et al. 2011)
summary: Pair automated interaction logs with a time-aligned contextual channel such as video, observer notes or a survey, so each logged event can be explained.
description: Logs record what happened with precision but not why; video and observation capture goals, frustration and satisfaction but are hard to quantify. Synchronised collection keeps both, aligned on a common clock, so an analyst can jump from a log event to the matching video moment or observer note. Variants include an observer keeping a timestamped log aligned to the system log, video annotated after the session, a proxy plus instrumented browser for breadth and detail, and remote logged sessions ending with a short satisfaction survey. Clock synchronisation and tooling that displays events alongside annotations are what make it rigorous; without them, triangulation becomes anecdotal matching. It costs more than a single channel in set-up and analysis time.
steps: Choose the primary automated log and define the events it must capture.
Add at least one contextual channel: video, live observer notes or an end-of-session survey.
Synchronise clocks across streams before the session, for example with a shared start marker.
Record sessions and keep raw streams together with session identifiers.
Use software that shows log events alongside video and annotations.
Interpret events in context, coding why behaviour occurred, and quantify patterns from the log.
outputs: Time-aligned event and context records, enabling explanation of quantitative patterns.
useWhen: Studies needing both precise behavioural measures and explanations, such as complex software, browsing behaviour or field deployments.
avoidWhen: Avoid when one channel suffices; for pure behaviour at scale use Log File Analysis, for depth alone use Moderated Usability Testing.
whyLost: The academic multi-stream method lives on in product teams as session replay linked to analytics events, usually without the explicit synchronisation discipline.
whereToUse: Session replay with analytics, in-car and medical device studies, field trials of AI assistants with telemetry.
example: A CRM team records screen video and event logs in a pilot. Jumping from an unusual spike of 'undo' events to the video shows users fighting an auto-save that overwrote notes.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Lazar, J., Feng, J. H. and Hochheiser, H. (2017). Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction, 2nd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 353-354.

name: Syndromic Surveillance of User Complaints
origin: Syndromic surveillance systems after 2001 (Henning, 2004); Farrington algorithm (1996); CDC EARS algorithms
summary: Continuously monitors grouped 'syndromes' from free-text complaints and signals, using statistical aberration detection to catch emerging problems early.
description: Public health agencies monitor emergency department chief complaints, pharmacy sales and absenteeism, grouped into syndromes (e.g. respiratory, gastrointestinal), and flag unusual increases before diagnoses are confirmed. Aberration detection algorithms (Farrington, EARS C1-C3, CUSUM) compare current counts with expected baselines accounting for seasonality and day-of-week effects, controlling false alarms. For products, user complaints, support tickets, reviews and in-app feedback can be classified into syndromes (e.g. 'login trouble', 'billing confusion') with NLP, and monitored the same way. It provides early warning of emergent UX problems with explicit sensitivity and false-alarm trade-offs.
steps: Define syndromes as groups of related complaints and build a classifier (rules or ML) with validated precision.
Assemble daily or hourly counts per syndrome, with denominators (active users).
Choose an aberration detection algorithm suited to the data (Farrington for seasonal counts, EARS for short baselines).
Calibrate thresholds to an acceptable false alarm rate using historical data.
Set up alert triage: who investigates, with what playbook (e.g. outbreak investigation).
Evaluate system sensitivity and timeliness against past incidents and refine syndromes.
outputs: Syndrome definitions, monitoring dashboards, alerts with statistical basis, and system performance evaluation.
useWhen: Products with large volumes of user feedback where emerging problems must be detected quickly.
avoidWhen: Low feedback volumes where counts are too sparse for statistical detection.
whyLost: Voice-of-customer tools show sentiment dashboards without aberration statistics; public health methods are unfamiliar.
whereToUse: Support operations, app review monitoring, AI assistant feedback, marketplace disputes, health app adverse events.
example: Classifying in-app feedback into 15 syndromes, a ride app's Farrington-based system flags a 'driver can't find pickup' rise in one city two days before ticket volume becomes visible, traced to a map data update.
sources: Henning, What is syndromic surveillance? (2004), MMWR Supplement
Farrington et al., A statistical algorithm for the early detection of outbreaks of infectious disease (1996), JRSS A
Hutwagner et al., The bioterrorism preparedness and response Early Aberration Reporting System (EARS) (2003), Journal of Urban Health
reference: Farrington, C. P., et al. (1996). JRSS Series A, 159(3), 547-563.

name: Syntactic (structural) priming
origin: Branigan, Pickering and Cleland (2000), building on Bock's structural priming work
summary: A scripted confederate describes pictures in one grammatical form, and the rate at which participants reuse that form shows how speakers align with a partner's language.
description: The participant believes they are playing a picture-description game with another participant behind a screen, who is in fact a confederate reading scripted descriptions in one of two equivalent forms ('The girl gave the book to the boy' or 'The girl gave the boy the book'). The participant first selects the card matching the confederate's description, then describes a card of their own. In the original study participants reused the confederate's construction on 78 percent of trials. The paradigm shows that conversational partners align their grammar as well as their vocabulary. Because it relies on deception, debriefing is required and the scripting must not be noticed. For UX, the design transfers directly to conversational systems: the system plays the confederate, and the measure is how far its phrasing shapes users' commands and queries, which matters for intent recognition and for deliberate steering of user input.
steps: Choose a pair of equivalent constructions or phrasings (for example two command forms the system could accept).
Script the confederate, or the conversational system, to describe items using one form per prime condition.
Have the participant identify the item described, then describe or request a new item of their own.
Interleave filler trials and counterbalance prime forms across items and participants.
Code each participant utterance for which form it uses.
Compare the proportion of target forms after each prime type, and debrief participants about the scripting.
outputs: Proportion of target constructions following each prime type, showing the strength of alignment.
useWhen: You want to know how a voice or chat system's own phrasing shapes the way users phrase requests, or to steer users towards forms the system understands.
avoidWhen: Deception is unacceptable for your participants, or you need open-ended discovery of user language; use corpus analysis of real logs or conversation analysis instead.
whyLost: It is a dialogue-theory paradigm; conversational AI teams study logs and intent accuracy rather than running controlled alignment experiments.
whereToUse: Voice assistants, chatbots and LLM interfaces, command languages, search query suggestions and accessibility of spoken interfaces.
example: A voice banking assistant alternates between 'send ten pounds to Sam' and 'send Sam ten pounds' in its confirmations. Users reuse the assistant's form most of the time, so the team standardises on the form with the best recognition accuracy.
reference: Branigan, H. P., Pickering, M. J., & Cleland, A. A. (2000). Syntactic co-ordination in dialogue. Cognition, 75(2), B13-B25.

name: Synthetic Control Method
origin: Alberto Abadie and Javier Gardeazabal (2003); Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010)
summary: Builds a weighted combination of untreated units that tracks a treated unit before a change, and uses its post-change path as the counterfactual.
description: When one market, city or customer segment receives a change, synthetic control finds weights on a donor pool of untreated units so that the weighted combination matches the treated unit's pre-period outcomes and predictors. The post-period gap between treated and synthetic unit estimates the effect. Inference uses placebo tests, reapplying the method to each donor and comparing the treated unit's post/pre RMSPE ratio with the placebo distribution. It is transparent (weights are inspectable) and suited to the few-treated-unit situations common in product launches by country.
steps: Define the treated unit (e.g. a country), donor pool of untreated units, outcome and launch date.
Exclude donors exposed to similar changes or spillovers.
Choose predictors and fit weights minimising pre-period discrepancy (using e.g. the Synth or augsynth packages).
Check pre-period fit; poor fit invalidates the analysis.
Estimate post-period gaps and run in-space placebo tests on each donor, and in-time placebos on fake dates.
Report effect paths, weights and the placebo-based p-value.
outputs: Synthetic counterfactual series, effect estimates over time, donor weights and placebo inference.
useWhen: A launch affects one or a few markets, regions or enterprise customers, with comparable untreated units and long pre-periods.
avoidWhen: Many treated units with staggered adoption (use modern DiD estimators) or when the treated unit lies outside the donors' range.
whyLost: It is relatively recent and sits in econometrics; product analytics teams default to naive country comparisons.
whereToUse: Market-level launches, regional pricing, regulatory changes by country, offline marketing campaigns.
example: A food-delivery app launches a new checkout in Portugal only. A synthetic Portugal built from Spain, Italy and Greece regions shows a 3.1% order uplift, larger than any placebo gap.
sources: Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller, Synthetic control methods for comparative case studies (2010), JASA
Abadie, Using synthetic controls: Feasibility, data requirements, and methodological aspects (2021), Journal of Economic Literature
reference: Abadie, A., Diamond, A., & Hainmueller, J. (2010). JASA, 105(490), 493-505.

name: Synthetic Perceived-Performance Testing (Speed Index)
origin: Speed Index and filmstrip view are WebPagetest features (Patrick Meenan); procedure described by Lara Hogan, Designing for Performance (2014)
summary: Load pages repeatedly from controlled locations, browsers and connections, and benchmark perceived speed with Speed Index, start render and filmstrips before and after each change.
description: Synthetic tests load a page from a third-party location and device so a team sees performance outside its own fast office set-up. Hogan recommends running five tests with first and repeat views and taking the median, inspecting the request waterfall for slow or blocking requests, and recording time to first byte, start render, visually complete, fully loaded and Speed Index, the average time at which visible parts of the page appear. Filmstrips at 0.1 second intervals show what the user sees and when. Tests are repeated for each responsive breakpoint, after every large change or experiment, against a performance budget and against competitors. Side-by-side filmstrip videos from several locations make the wait tangible for stakeholders. It measures perceived load, which ties performance to experience rather than to server metrics alone.
steps: Pick the major pages and test settings: location, browser, device and connection speed representative of users.
Run five tests with first and repeat views and take the median run to avoid flukes.
Inspect the waterfall for unusually long or render-blocking requests.
Record time to first byte, start render, visually complete, fully loaded and Speed Index.
Review the filmstrip at 0.1 s intervals to see when meaningful content appears.
Repeat for each responsive breakpoint and compare results with the performance budget.
Re-run before and after every large change or experiment, and optionally compile side-by-side filmstrips against competitors for stakeholders.
outputs: Median timing metrics and Speed Index per page and setting, waterfalls, filmstrips and comparison videos.
useWhen: Setting and policing performance budgets, judging whether a design change slows perceived load, and persuading stakeholders that speed is part of the experience.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating synthetic results as what real users experience; combine with real-user monitoring and field data. To test how much speed matters to behaviour, use latency-injection experiments.
whyLost: It is routine in front-end performance engineering but rarely owned by UX researchers, who seldom report perceived speed as a UX metric.
whereToUse: E-commerce product and checkout pages, news and media sites, mobile web in low-bandwidth markets, image-heavy redesigns.
example: Before launching a hero-video homepage, a retailer runs five median tests on a mid-range Android phone over 3G. Speed Index rises from 2.9 s to 5.4 s and the filmstrip shows a blank hero for four seconds, so the team ships a poster image first.
reference: Hogan, L. C. (2014). Designing for Performance: Weighing Aesthetics and Speed. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 19-23, 113-117, 140-142.

name: Synthetic session generation at cluster boundaries
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Methods Atlas; building on generative modelling and boundary-value testing in software engineering
summary: Uses a generative model to create synthetic user sessions in the ambiguous regions between behavioural clusters, stress-testing systems on the users they are most likely to misclassify.
description: AI systems such as recommenders, risk models and adaptive interfaces tend to fail on users who sit between typical patterns. This method trains a generative model (often a VAE) on real sessions, identifies cluster boundaries in latent space (where membership probabilities are near equal), and samples or interpolates synthetic sessions there. These sessions are fed to the target system to observe outputs, measure inconsistency, and find failure modes before real users encounter them. It borrows from boundary-value analysis in software testing. Rigour requires validating that synthetic sessions are realistic, labelling them as synthetic throughout, and confirming discovered failures with real users or real logs. Synthetic sessions test systems; they do not replace user research.
steps: Train a generative model on real sessions and fit clusters in its latent space.
Identify boundary regions where the top two cluster probabilities differ by less than 0.2.
Sample or interpolate thousands of latent points in those regions and decode them into synthetic sessions (e.g. 10,000).
Validate realism by comparing synthetic sessions with real boundary users on key distributions and expert review of 30-50 samples.
Run synthetic sessions through the target system and measure outputs: recommendation stability, risk score variance, inappropriate suggestions.
Confirm high-severity failures with real user data or targeted research before acting.
outputs: A synthetic test set at behavioural boundaries, a catalogue of system failure modes and prioritised issues for confirmation.
useWhen: Before launching or updating AI recommendation, classification or personalisation systems, especially in high-stakes domains.
avoidWhen: Avoid using synthetic sessions as evidence of user needs or attitudes, or when the generative model is poorly validated; use real-user testing instead.
whyLost: It is a new combination of ML and testing practice, and most UX teams lack access to generative models of their users' behaviour.
whereToUse: Investment recommendation AI, credit and fraud models, adaptive learning platforms, health triage systems.
example: An investment platform generates 10,000 synthetic sessions between 'cautious saver' and 'active trader' archetypes. The recommendation AI suggests leveraged products to 14% of them, a failure confirmed in real logs and fixed before scale-up.
sources: Deep Learning (Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 53 — Generative Models & Synthetic User Testing
reference: Kingma, D. P. & Welling, M. (2019) An introduction to variational autoencoders. Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 12(4), 307-392.

name: System Dynamics Stock-and-Flow Modelling
origin: Jay Forrester, MIT, 1956-1961 (Industrial Dynamics); John Sterman (Business Dynamics, 2000)
summary: Builds quantitative simulations of stocks (users, trust, backlog) and flows with feedback and delays to explore long-term dynamics of products and services.
description: Causal loop diagrams show feedback qualitatively; stock-and-flow models make it quantitative. Stocks accumulate (active users, content, support backlog, trust); flows change them (sign-ups, churn, resolution); auxiliary variables and delays connect them. Simulating the model reveals non-intuitive behaviour: overshoot and collapse, tipping points, worse-before-better dynamics after interventions. Sterman's work shows that people systematically misjudge stock-flow dynamics. Rigorous practice involves calibrating to historical data, testing extreme conditions, and sensitivity analysis. For UX strategy, it shows how growth tactics, support capacity and user trust interact over months and years.
steps: Define the problem behaviour over time (reference mode), such as growth then stagnation.
Elicit a causal loop diagram with stakeholders and data, then convert to stocks, flows and delays.
Quantify relationships from data, research and expert estimates; build the model (Vensim, Stella, PySD).
Validate: reproduce historical behaviour, test extreme conditions and dimensional consistency.
Run policy experiments and sensitivity analysis on uncertain parameters.
Communicate insights with simulation runs and use them to frame research questions.
outputs: A calibrated simulation model, policy scenario results, sensitivity analysis and dynamic hypotheses.
useWhen: Strategic questions about growth, trust, quality and capacity dynamics over long horizons.
avoidWhen: Short-term tactical design questions or where data cannot support even rough calibration.
whyLost: System dynamics is taught in management schools and policy, not design; 'systems thinking' in UX usually stops at diagrams.
whereToUse: Marketplace growth, community moderation capacity, trust and safety strategy, freemium conversion, technical debt and UX debt.
example: A social platform models how moderation backlog affects user trust and posting. Simulation shows that aggressive growth campaigns produce a delayed trust collapse after 9 months unless moderation capacity scales ahead of growth.
sources: Sterman, Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World (2000)
reference: Sterman, J. D. (2000). Business Dynamics. McGraw-Hill.

name: System Usability Scale (SUS)
origin: John Brooke, 1986 (published 1996)
summary: A 10-item questionnaire producing a 0-100 perceived usability score that can be benchmarked against thousands of published studies.
description: SUS consists of ten statements rated on a five-point agreement scale, alternating positive and negative wording. Odd items contribute (score minus 1), even items (5 minus score), and the sum is multiplied by 2.5 to give 0-100. It is not a percentage: Sauro and Lewis's normative data put the average around 68, with roughly 80 or above in the top decile. SUS is reliable (alpha typically above 0.9) with small samples and is technology-agnostic. Rigour comes from administering it unchanged immediately after realistic tasks, reporting confidence intervals, converting to percentile ranks using normative data, and not treating it as diagnostic: it tells you how usable a product is perceived to be, not why. Small wording substitutions, such as 'website' for 'system', are acceptable.
steps: Administer SUS after participants complete representative tasks, before any discussion.
Use the standard ten items unchanged apart from replacing 'system' with the product name if needed.
Score each response: odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum and multiply by 2.5.
Compute the mean and 95% confidence interval; aim for at least 12-20 participants for usable precision.
Convert to a percentile rank or grade using published norms (mean about 68).
Compare with previous releases or competitors and pair with task metrics to explain scores.
outputs: SUS score per participant, mean with confidence interval, percentile rank and grade, comparisons over time or across products.
useWhen: Usability benchmarking, comparing releases or competitors, and summative evaluations needing a standard perceived usability metric.
avoidWhen: When you need diagnostic detail about problems; use usability testing observations. For in-product micro-surveys, UMUX-Lite is less burdensome.
whyLost: Still in use: Free, validated, quick; enables benchmarking and comparison across products.
whereToUse: Usability testing; benchmarking; longitudinal usability tracking.
example: A SaaS analytics product measured SUS with 20 users each quarter. The score rose from 61 (about 30th percentile) to 74 (about 70th percentile) after a navigation redesign, giving leadership a clear benchmarked improvement.
sources: SUS: A quick and dirty usability scale (John Brooke)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Brooke, J. (1996). SUS: A 'quick and dirty' usability scale. In P. W. Jordan et al. (Eds.), Usability Evaluation in Industry (pp. 189-194). Taylor & Francis.

name: Systematic Probe Schedule
origin: Joseph Dumas & Janice Redish, 1993 (A Practical Guide to Usability Testing)
summary: Pre-defining behavioural triggers and matching probe questions for usability sessions, and coding probed responses separately from spontaneous think-aloud.
description: Think-aloud sessions often drift between unstructured observation and ad hoc questioning that varies across moderators and participants. A systematic probe schedule pre-defines, for each critical task step, a behavioural trigger (a pause over three seconds, backtracking, a verbal sign of confusion) and a standard probe question. When a trigger fires, the moderator delivers the probe, and analysis keeps probed responses separate from spontaneous verbalisation. This makes moderation consistent across sessions and moderators, reduces leading, and lets the analyst compare what participants think unprompted with what they say when asked. The discipline also exposes moderator effects that otherwise contaminate usability findings.
steps: Pre-session preparation: For each critical task step in the usability test, define a behavioral trigger (e.g., "participant pauses > 3 seconds," "participant backtracks," "participant expresses confusion verbally") and a probe question ("I noticed you paused — what's going through your mind?").

During the session: When a trigger fires, deliver the associated probe. Code probes separately from spontaneous verbalizations — this separates researcher-elicited from user-generated cognition in your analysis.

Post-session analysis: Analyse spontaneous verbalizations and probe responses separately. Probe responses reveal what participants thought when asked; spontaneous verbalizations reveal what participants thought without prompting. The gap between them is informative.
outputs: A trigger-probe schedule per task, coded probe and spontaneous responses, and comparisons between the two.
useWhen: Moderated usability tests with several moderators, comparative tests where consistency matters, or high-stakes evaluations requiring defensible moderation.
avoidWhen: Exploratory or generative sessions where rigid probing would constrain discovery; use open contextual interviewing.
whyLost: Moderation is taught as an intuitive skill and discussion guides rarely specify triggers, so the systematic schedule from the early usability engineering literature faded.
whereToUse: Benchmark usability studies, medical device formative and summative testing, multi-moderator programmes, and regulated product evaluations.
example: In a multi-site test of a banking app, three moderators use the same trigger list. Probe responses show that hesitation at the transfer limit screen stems from fear of fees, consistently across sites.
sources: A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Dumas, J. S. & Redish, J. C. (1999). A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (rev. ed.). Intellect.

name: Systematic social observation and ecometrics
origin: Reiss (1971) for SSO; Raudenbush and Sampson (1999) coined ecometrics; Odgers et al. (2012) for virtual SSO
summary: Trained raters code the physical and social features of defined places with a structured checklist, combined with independent surveys and records, and reliability is assessed at the place level.
description: SSO measures places independently of the people being studied. Trained raters walk defined units such as block faces, or record them on video, coding features such as housing layout, traffic, abandoned buildings, graffiti, loitering and public drinking. Ecometrics treats the place, not the person, as the unit of measurement and applies psychometric standards to it: multiple independent reporters (for example a community survey of 15 to 30 non-participants per neighbourhood), expert surveys and administrative records, with reliability computed at the neighbourhood level. Physical disorder is captured well by observation; sporadic social disorder needs surveys. Street View allows cheaper virtual walks. The key discipline is keeping place measures separate from participants' own perceptions to avoid shared method variance.
steps: Define the unit of place (block face, block group, tract or GIS buffer) and adapt it for rural areas where block faces do not exist.
Build a structured checklist of physical and social features and train raters to agreement.
Walk or record each unit, or use Street View for virtual observation.
Run an independent community survey of about 15 to 30 non-participant respondents per unit, plus expert surveys and linked administrative records.
Compute place-level reliability across raters and respondents.
Keep place scores separate from study participants' perceptions in analysis, and repeat over time to track stability and change.
outputs: Place-level scores of physical and social disorder, resources and collective efficacy, with reliability estimates.
useWhen: The physical or social environment is a variable in your question, such as how neighbourhood context shapes use of a service, and you need a measure not coloured by users' own views.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the context can be described qualitatively for design inspiration; use field visits. It is expensive and slow to code, and mapping captures the presence rather than the quality of resources.
whyLost: It is a neighbourhood-effects method in sociology and developmental science, and UX rarely treats place as a measured variable.
whereToUse: Location-based services, delivery and mobility products, public-health and civic technology, retail site analysis and accessibility audits of urban routes.
example: A micromobility operator wants to know why scooter return compliance varies by district. Raters virtually audit 200 drop zones on Street View for pavement width, lighting and clutter, and the place scores explain more variance in bad parking than rider demographics.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 4 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Raudenbush, S. W. & Sampson, R. J. (1999). Ecometrics: toward a science of assessing ecological settings. Sociological Methodology 29, 1-41.

name: Systematic Thematic Analysis for Conceptual Model Development
donor: Marketing and management research; qualitative methodology
origin: Muhammad Naeem, Wilson Ozuem, Kerry Howell and Silvia Ranfagni, 2023, extending Braun and Clarke (2006)
summary: A six-step thematic analysis that moves from quotations to keywords, codes, themes and concepts and ends in a conceptual model, with explicit criteria checked at each step.
description: This variant of thematic analysis aims at traceability from raw data to a model rather than a list of themes. It adds a keyword step between quotation selection and coding, and two closing steps: defining concepts and building a conceptual model. Each step has a checklist the authors coin: keywords are judged on realness, richness, repetition, rationale, repartee and regal (the 6Rs); codes on being robust, reflective, resplendent, relevant, radical and righteous; themes on being reciprocal, recognisable, responsive and resourceful (the 4Rs); and concept definitions against seven quality questions. Coding can be inductive, deductive or hybrid, and the process adapts to grounded theory, ethnography, narrative or positivist designs, where the model becomes hypotheses for quantitative testing. The criteria are the authors' own and not independently validated.
steps: Transcribe and read the data, then select quotations that show strong patterns and a range of voices, consistent with your philosophical stance.
Pick keywords from those quotations and check each against the 6Rs (realness, richness, repetition, rationale, repartee, regal); note recurring participant terms already during fieldwork.
Code segments using the keywords, inductively, deductively from theory or both, and check codes against the six code criteria.
Group codes and their keywords into themes and check each against the 4Rs; split a theme whose keywords are disparate.
Define each concept with its dimensions and indicators, relate it to prior literature and test the definitions with the seven quality questions.
Build a conceptual model grounded in the findings and an underpinning theory that answers the research questions and states the contribution.
outputs: A keyword list, a coding tree from keywords to codes to themes, concept definitions and a conceptual model diagram.
useWhen: A study must end in a defensible framework or model (for example a model of trust or switching behaviour) and stakeholders or reviewers need to trace every element back to verbatims.
avoidWhen: Fast evaluative synthesis where a theme list is enough (use Thematic Analysis or affinity mapping); reflexive, interpretive work where checklists add little; and do not read theme frequency as importance.
whyLost: It was published in 2023 for academic qualitative research in management and marketing, and UX teams rarely aim for a formal conceptual model as the endpoint of synthesis.
whereToUse: Foundational research programmes, strategy frameworks, academic-industry studies and any synthesis that will feed a survey or experiment.
example: A banking team analyses 30 interviews on why customers move money to fintech apps. Keywords such as 'hidden fees' and 'instant alerts' feed codes and three themes, which are defined as concepts and assembled into a switching model that later becomes survey hypotheses.
sources: A Step-by-Step Process of Thematic Analysis to Develop a Conceptual Model in Qualitative Research (Naeem et al., 2023)
reference: Naeem, M., Ozuem, W., Howell, K., & Ranfagni, S. (2023). A step-by-step process of thematic analysis to develop a conceptual model in qualitative research. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 22, 1-18. doi:10.1177/16094069231205789

name: Systems Thinking
origin: Jay Forrester, 1950s-1960s; Peter Senge, 1990; Donella Meadows, 2008
summary: Maps feedback loops, delays and interdependencies in the system around a product to explain emergent behaviour and find leverage points rather than local fixes.
description: Systems thinking studies how the structure of a system, its stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays, produces behaviour over time. Forrester founded system dynamics at MIT; Senge popularised systems thinking for organisations; Meadows described leverage points where small changes produce large effects. In UX it treats a product as embedded in a system of users, organisations, incentives and other products. The method builds causal loop diagrams from research evidence, identifies reinforcing and balancing loops and delays, and, at higher rigour, builds stock-and-flow simulation models. Rigour comes from grounding each causal link in evidence, naming loop polarity explicitly, validating diagrams with stakeholders and data, and testing interventions against the model to anticipate unintended consequences such as growth loops undermining trust.
steps: Define the problem behaviour over time (e.g. engagement rising then collapsing).
Identify key variables from research and data and draw causal links with polarities.
Identify reinforcing and balancing loops and important delays.
Validate the diagram with stakeholders and with available quantitative data.
Identify leverage points and test interventions, optionally with a stock-and-flow simulation.
Monitor indicators for each loop after intervention.
outputs: Behaviour-over-time graphs, causal loop diagrams, identified leverage points, optional simulation model.
useWhen: Platforms, marketplaces, ecosystems, services with many stakeholders, and recurring problems that resist local fixes.
avoidWhen: Contained usability problems with clear local causes; use usability testing.
whyLost: Latent: Growing in design thinking extensions; rarely applied rigorously in product UX.
whereToUse: Platform product design; ecosystem mapping; service design; organizational design.
example: A social app's growth team mapped a reinforcing loop where notifications drove opens but also unsubscribes with a delay. The causal model showed a balancing loop eroding the user base, leading to capped notification frequency.
sources: Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
reference: Meadows, D. H. (2008). Thinking in Systems: A Primer. Chelsea Green.

name: Systems Thinking Loops in UX Analysis (DSRP)
origin: Derek Cabrera, 2006 (DSRP theory); Cabrera and Colosi (2008)
summary: Applies Cabrera's four patterns, distinctions, systems, relationships and perspectives, to map the system around a user problem so it is not reduced to a single screen or task.
description: DSRP proposes that systems thinking consists of four universal cognitive patterns, each with two elements: making Distinctions (identity and other), organising Systems (part and whole), recognising Relationships (action and reaction) and taking Perspectives (point and view). Applied to UX, a DSRP map makes explicit what is inside and outside the problem boundary, how the product is part of larger wholes (workflows, organisations, ecosystems), the causal and feedback relationships among actors and artefacts, and how the situation appears from each stakeholder's viewpoint. This counters the habit of framing problems as isolated screen issues, especially in wicked problems such as healthcare or public services. Rigour comes from deriving elements from research data, mapping relationships including feedback loops, and checking each perspective with the people who hold it.
steps: For any UX problem:
Distinctions — what is in scope (user, interface, context, organization) vs. out of scope?
(2) Systems — what are the parts and how do they nest?
(3) Relationships — what causal relationships connect parts?
(4) Perspectives — how does the problem look from each stakeholder's position? Map all four before solution generation.
outputs: DSRP map with explicit boundaries, part-whole structures, relationship and feedback loops, and perspective comparisons; reframed problem statements.
useWhen: Complex sociotechnical problems, service design, healthcare and public sector projects, and situations where fixing one screen keeps failing.
avoidWhen: For well-bounded interface problems where systemic factors are minimal; use task analysis or usability testing.
whyLost: DSRP stayed within systems education and evaluation research; UX adopted journey maps and ecosystem maps, which capture some relationships but not boundaries or perspectives systematically.
whereToUse: Wicked problem UX analysis, organizational UX research, systems design for complex products, enterprise UX.
example: A surgical scheduling tool keeps failing adoption despite usability fixes. A DSRP map shows the operating list is part of a bed-management system whose perspective was ignored, so the project shifts to integrating with bed availability.
sources: Systems Thinking Made Simple (Derek & Laura Cabrera)
PACT analysis (Dix; Benyon, Designing Interactive Systems)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
reference: Cabrera D, Colosi L & Lobdell C (2008) Systems thinking. Evaluation and Program Planning 31(3):299-310

name: T-Pattern Detection
origin: Magnus S. Magnusson (1996, 2000, 2020)
summary: Search coded event streams for recurring sequences that occur in the same order with consistent time intervals, building hierarchically into longer hidden patterns.
description: T-pattern detection searches a time-stamped or ordered event record for pairs of events A and B where B follows A within a critical interval more often than chance would predict. Detected pairs become new units, and the search repeats so that patterns nest hierarchically into longer sequences that may be invisible to observers because other events intervene. Unlike lag sequential analysis it does not require events to be adjacent, and unlike sequential pattern mining it tests interval consistency against a null model. The THEME software runs the detection, with randomisation or shuffling checks to estimate how many patterns would arise by chance. Comparing pattern sets across sessions shows how the organisation of behaviour changes over time. Settings such as minimum occurrences and significance level strongly affect results, so they must be reported, and patterns still need interpretation.
steps: Code sessions with timestamps or at least event order preserved, using a tool such as LINCE.
Check agreement between coders before analysis.
Export to THEME and set parameters (minimum occurrences, significance level, interval type); report them.
Run detection and compare against randomised or shuffled data to estimate chance patterns.
Compare detected patterns across sessions, groups or time points.
Interpret how pattern structure and complexity change, checking examples in the raw recordings.
outputs: Sets of recurring, hierarchically nested behavioural patterns with occurrence counts and their evolution across sessions.
useWhen: Rich, time-stamped behavioural or interaction data in which you suspect recurring routines that are interleaved with other activity.
avoidWhen: Simple funnels or adjacent transitions; use Lag Sequential Analysis or Sequence Alignment of Behavioural Paths. Avoid with very short or unreliably coded records.
whyLost: It developed in ethology and sport science around specialist software; UX analytics adopted frequent-sequence mining instead.
whereToUse: Interaction logs with timestamps, multimodal session coding, collaborative work, gameplay telemetry, conversational agent logs.
example: Analysing timestamped events from 30 design-tool sessions, a team finds a recurring pattern of copy, switch file, paste, undo within ten seconds, nested in longer routines, revealing a cross-file workaround the funnel data hid.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Poth, C. N. (Ed.) (2023). The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design. London: SAGE.

name: T-SNE
origin: Laurens van der Maaten & Geoffrey Hinton, 2008
summary: A non-linear method that maps high-dimensional user data to two dimensions while preserving local neighbourhoods, for visual exploration of behavioural groupings.
description: t-SNE converts pairwise distances into probabilities of being neighbours in high-dimensional space and finds a 2D layout whose neighbour probabilities match, using a heavy-tailed t-distribution to avoid crowding. It reveals local cluster structure that PCA can flatten. But its maps are easily misread: distances between clusters, cluster sizes and densities carry little meaning, results vary with the perplexity parameter and random seed, and it can produce apparent clusters from noise. Rigour means using it for exploration only, running several perplexities (e.g. 5, 30, 50) and seeds, initialising with PCA, and confirming any visual grouping with clustering and validation on the original features.
steps: Standardise features and reduce to around 30-50 dimensions with PCA to remove noise and speed computation.
Run t-SNE with perplexity values of 5, 30 and 50, PCA initialisation and at least 1,000 iterations.
Repeat with several random seeds and compare whether the same groupings recur.
Colour maps by known variables (outcomes, segments, platforms) to interpret regions.
Do not interpret inter-cluster distances or cluster sizes; confirm any apparent groups with clustering and validation on original data.
outputs: Exploratory 2D maps of the user space showing local neighbourhoods and candidate groupings for further analysis.
useWhen: Exploring high-dimensional behavioural, embedding or survey data visually to spot potential groupings or anomalies.
avoidWhen: Avoid for quantitative conclusions, for preserving global structure (use PCA or UMAP), or for very large datasets without optimised implementations.
whyLost: It is widely used in data science and ML research; within UX it appears in analytics collaborations, often misinterpreted.
whereToUse: Exploration of session embeddings, support ticket embeddings, behavioural logs in fintech and media.
example: A team maps 50,000 sessions with t-SNE and sees an isolated island of sessions. Colouring by app version shows they all come from a buggy release, prompting an error investigation rather than a new persona.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
van der Maaten & Hinton (2008) Visualizing data using t-SNE
Wattenberg, Viégas & Johnson (2016) How to use t-SNE effectively
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: van der Maaten, L. & Hinton, G. (2008) Visualizing data using t-SNE. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 9, 2579-2605.

name: t-Tests for Comparing Designs (Paired and Two-Sample)
origin: W. S. Gosset ("Student", 1908); Welch (1947)
summary: Tests whether average ratings or task times differ between two designs, for the same or different participants.
description: The t-test is the workhorse for comparing two means: SUS scores, SEQ ratings, log task times. The paired version works on each participant's difference score in within-subjects designs and gains power by removing between-person variation. The two-sample version, preferably the Welch form that does not assume equal variances, compares independent groups. Sauro and Lewis show the t-test is robust for rating scales and works at small sample sizes, which settles a long debate about whether ordinal scale data can be analysed this way. Reporting the confidence interval around the difference matters more than the p-value.
steps: Decide whether the design is within-subjects (paired) or between-subjects (two-sample).
Log-transform task times first; leave rating scales as they are.
For paired data, compute each person's difference and run a one-sample t-test on the differences against zero.
For independent groups, run Welch's t-test using each group's own variance and adjusted degrees of freedom.
Report the mean difference, its confidence interval, t, df and p.
outputs: An estimate of how much two designs differ on a continuous measure, with significance.
useWhen: Two designs or versions, one continuous outcome.
avoidWhen: More than two conditions (use ANOVA), binary outcomes (use proportion tests), or heavy outliers with tiny n (consider a permutation test).
whyLost: Not lost, but often misapplied: paired data analysed as independent, task times left raw, or Student's equal-variance form used by default.
whereToUse: Prototype comparisons, redesign evaluations, competitive benchmarks.
example: Twelve people rate two onboarding flows with the SEQ. The paired t-test shows a mean improvement of 0.9 points (95% CI 0.3 to 1.5, p = 0.008).
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
Applied Statistics and Probability for Engineers: Student Solutions Manual (Montgomery & Runger, 2002)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce et al., 2020)
reference: Sauro & Lewis (2016), Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 5.

name: Tactics for Generating Meaning
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 10, section A.
summary: A named set of 13 moves for drawing conclusions from a qualitative display, from noting patterns and counting up to building a logical chain of evidence and conceptual coherence.
description: Miles and Huberman argue that every display is worked through a flow of specific tactics, and they name them so analysts can use and report them deliberately. Ordered roughly from descriptive to explanatory, they are: (1) noting patterns and themes; (2) seeing plausibility; (3) clustering; (4) making metaphors; (5) counting; (6) making contrasts and comparisons; (7) partitioning variables; (8) subsuming particulars into the general; (9) factoring, a qualitative analogue of factor analysis; (10) noting relations between variables; (11) finding intervening variables; (12) building a logical chain of evidence; and (13) making conceptual and theoretical coherence. Each comes with cautions: patterns 'just happen' almost too quickly and need scepticism, further evidence and openness to disconfirmation; plausibility is a pointer to a conclusion worth checking, not a basis for it. The chapter shows a bottom-up path from discrete findings, to relating them, naming the pattern and finding a construct, likened to abduction. Throughout the book's displays, the tactic used at each step is flagged in bold. For UX researchers the list is a vocabulary and checklist for synthesis: it makes visible how a theme was reached and which moves (for example counting or finding intervening variables) were never tried.
steps: Lay out the data in a display (matrix, network or clustered notes).
Note patterns and clusters, and treat early plausible conclusions as pointers to check, not findings.
Count occurrences and make contrasts and comparisons across people, segments or cases.
Partition variables that turn out to be too broad, and subsume particulars into more general categories or factors.
Look for relations between variables and for intervening variables that explain them.
Build a logical chain of evidence and connect it to concepts or theory; record which tactics produced each conclusion.
outputs: Conclusions annotated with the tactics that produced them, and a fuller set of candidate explanations.
useWhen: Synthesising any qualitative dataset, particularly when you need to explain how themes were reached or to push beyond surface patterns.
avoidWhen: Used as a mechanical sequence that replaces judgement; the tactics are a toolkit, not a fixed procedure.
whyLost: UX synthesis is usually taught as affinity mapping and theme naming, without an explicit vocabulary for the analytic moves behind each insight.
whereToUse: Interview synthesis, usability findings, research reports, peer review of insights.
example: Reviewing a matrix of 18 onboarding interviews, a researcher notes a pattern (admins complain about invites), counts it (11 of 18), contrasts large and small teams, partitions 'invite problems' into SSO issues and email deliverability, and finds an intervening variable: complaints occur only where IT owns the email domain. The report notes which tactic supported each claim.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Tactics for Testing or Confirming Findings
donor: Qualitative social research methodology and the psychology of judgement
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 10, section B, drawing on Kahneman and Tversky, Nisbett and Ross, and Wax (1971) on field bias.
summary: A named set of 13 checks for qualitative conclusions, covering data quality, exceptions to patterns, and sceptical tests of explanations, framed against known judgement biases.
description: Miles and Huberman start from evidence that human judgement is biased: people find patterns in random data, overweight vivid instances and seek confirming cases. Field researchers face three archetypal biases: the holistic fallacy (seeing events as more patterned than they are), elite bias (overweighting articulate, high-status informants) and going native. They then set out 13 tactics. Data quality: (1) checking for representativeness, for example by adding cases, sampling contrasting cases and sampling randomly within the universe; (2) checking for researcher effects, both the researcher's effect on the site and the site's effect on the researcher; (3) triangulating; (4) weighting the evidence. Looking at 'unpatterns': (5) checking the meaning of outliers; (6) using extreme cases; (7) following up surprises; (8) looking for negative evidence. Testing explanations: (9) making if-then tests, stating conditional predictions and looking to see whether the 'then' holds; (10) ruling out spurious relations, where a third variable causes both A and B; (11) replicating a finding; (12) checking out rival explanations. Finally, (13) getting feedback from informants. For UX teams, whose insights often rest on a few sessions, the list works as a review checklist before findings go to a roadmap.
steps: Before finalising, list each key finding and the evidence behind it.
Check data quality: is the sample representative, could the researcher or session setup have produced it, does it triangulate, how strong is each source?
Examine outliers, extreme cases, surprises and negative evidence rather than setting them aside.
State if-then predictions from each explanation and check them against data not yet used.
Look for third variables that could explain an apparent relationship, and try replicating the finding in another segment or study.
Write down rival explanations and test them, then take the findings back to participants for feedback.
outputs: Findings each tagged with the checks they have passed, a list of rivals ruled in or out, and documented weaknesses.
useWhen: Findings will drive significant product decisions, the sample is small, or stakeholders challenge qualitative evidence.
avoidWhen: Early exploratory work where the aim is to open questions rather than confirm them, though a light pass is still useful.
whyLost: UX borrowed triangulation and member checking piecemeal but not the full, bias-grounded checklist; tight timelines discourage systematic verification.
whereToUse: Research review, insight QA, research repositories, high-stakes discovery for strategy decisions.
example: A team concludes that users abandon checkout because of shipping costs. Running the checklist, they find most quotes came from three vocal participants (elite bias), state an if-then test (if cost is the cause, free-shipping baskets should show lower abandonment in logs), find a spurious relation (expensive shipping and abandonment both rise with international orders, where address forms fail), and revise the finding.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
User-Friendly Handbook for Mixed Method Evaluations (Frechtling & Sharp, 1997)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Tactile Acuity Measurement (Two-Point Threshold, Grating Orientation)
origin: Adapted for UX from the psychophysics of touch: the classic two-point method; grating and pattern methods credited to Cholewiak and Collins (2003) and Craig and Lyle (2001, 2002)
summary: Find the finest spatial detail a person can feel at a skin site, using two-point, grating-orientation or raised-pattern judgements, to set spacing for tactile features.
description: Tactile acuity is the touch equivalent of an eye chart. In the two-point threshold, the skin is touched gently with two points, such as compass tips or a paper clip bent into a U, and the person, not looking, reports one or two; the threshold is the smallest separation felt as two. In grating acuity, a grooved surface is pressed onto the skin and the person reports its orientation; acuity is the narrowest groove spacing judged reliably, a measure less prone to response bias than 'one or two'. Acuity can also be measured with raised letters or patterns of decreasing size. Thresholds vary at least twentyfold across the body, tracking receptor density and cortical magnification: fingertips and lips are fine, the back and leg coarse. Braille's 2 by 3 dot cell shows the principle applied. For product teams the measure sets minimum spacing for raised controls, tactile icons and vibrotactile arrays on a given body site.
steps: Choose the body site that the product will contact and the method: two points, grating or raised pattern.
Prevent the participant from seeing the stimulus; have a second person apply it with consistent gentle pressure.
Present stimuli at varying separations, groove widths or pattern sizes using a threshold procedure such as a staircase or method of limits, mixing in single-point catch trials for two-point testing.
Ask 'one or two?' for points, the orientation for gratings, or the identity for patterns.
Determine the smallest separation, spacing or size reliably perceived (for example 75 percent correct) at each site.
Repeat across sites and participants and compare with the spacing planned for the design.
outputs: An acuity threshold per body site and participant group, used as a minimum spacing for tactile features.
useWhen: Designing wearables, haptic feedback arrays, tactile icons, raised or textured controls and accessible tactile labelling for a given body site and user group.
avoidWhen: Measuring vibration detection or intensity discrimination (use Psychophysical Threshold Methods (JND) with vibrotactile stimuli); when only device timing matters (use Audio-haptic synchronisation measurement).
whyLost: It is a sensory physiology and clinical neurology measure; haptic UX design usually relies on guideline values rather than measuring its own users.
whereToUse: Smartwatches and wristbands, haptic vests and VR controllers, automotive controls used without looking, Braille and tactile signage, devices for older users with reduced sensitivity.
example: A wrist-worn navigation band plans four vibration motors 15 mm apart. Two-point testing on the dorsal wrist with 20 older adults finds thresholds near 35 mm, so the design moves to three motors spaced around the wrist.
sources: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain (Bear et al., 2016)
reference: Goldstein, E. B. and Cacciamani, L. (2021). Sensation and Perception (11th ed.). Cengage Learning, pp. 362-364.

name: Taguchi Robust Design
origin: Genichi Taguchi, 1950s-1980s (Introduction to Quality Engineering, 1986)
summary: Chooses design settings that perform well across uncontrollable noise conditions, optimising signal-to-noise ratios rather than average performance.
description: Taguchi distinguished control factors (designer chooses) from noise factors (users, environments, devices the designer cannot control). Using crossed or combined arrays, experiments vary both, and robustness is measured with signal-to-noise ratios or variance models. The quality loss function quantifies that any deviation from target imposes cost, not just out-of-specification results. For UX, noise factors are everywhere: screen size, lighting, connectivity, literacy, age, assistive tech. Robust design finds layouts and parameters whose performance is stable across them, rather than optimal for the average user and poor for many.
steps: List control factors (design options) and noise factors (device, bandwidth, ambient light, user skill).
Choose an orthogonal array for control factors and a noise array or deliberate noise sampling.
Run each control combination across noise conditions and record performance.
Compute S/N ratios (e.g. larger-the-better or nominal-the-best) or model mean and variance separately.
Select settings that maximise robustness, then adjust a scaling factor to hit the target mean.
Confirm with a validation run under fresh noise conditions.
outputs: Robust control settings, S/N or variance analysis, and confirmation results.
useWhen: Products used across highly variable conditions, where consistency of experience matters as much as average.
avoidWhen: Homogeneous user populations and controlled settings; standard experiments suffice.
whyLost: Taguchi methods lived in manufacturing quality and were criticised by statisticians on analysis details; UX never adopted the robustness mindset.
whereToUse: Emerging-market apps, accessibility, outdoor and in-vehicle UIs, IoT devices, video calls under variable bandwidth.
example: A ticketing app tests QR code size and contrast across lighting and phone age conditions. The robust choice has a slightly lower best-case scan rate but halves failures in sunlight and old devices.
sources: Phadke, Quality Engineering Using Robust Design (1989)
Nair (ed.), Taguchi's parameter design: A panel discussion (1992), Technometrics
Design and Analysis of Experiments, Vol. 2 (Hinkelmann & Kempthorne, 2005)
Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
Bayesian Methods in Engineering Design Problems (Swiler, 2006)
reference: Phadke, M. S. (1989). Quality Engineering Using Robust Design. Prentice Hall.

name: Tailored Design Method
origin: Don Dillman and colleagues (Dillman, Smyth and Christian, 2009); the follow-up sequence is reproduced by Veal and Darcy for mail surveys
summary: A planned sequence of contacts, reminders and replacement questionnaires, plus attention to letter, design and incentives, to raise self-completion survey response rates.
description: Response to self-completion surveys depends on the topic, the questionnaire's length and presentation, the covering letter, the ease of reply, rewards and, above all, reminders. Veal and Darcy call well-planned follow-ups perhaps the most important tool available, and reproduce Dillman's sequence: the initial mailing with the questionnaire; a postcard reminder after about a week; a reminder letter with a second copy of the questionnaire, 'in case the original has been mislaid', after about two weeks, possibly offering a telephone interview; and a final reminder after about three weeks. Email or phone can replace post. In their example of a residents' survey, returns would have stopped at about 40 per cent, but surges after each reminder lifted the final rate to 75 per cent. Reminders require responses to be identifiable, which raises confidentiality concerns that can be eased by numbering the reply envelope rather than the questionnaire. Identification also lets researchers check representativeness and weight. For UX email and in-product surveys, which commonly send one invitation and accept a few per cent response, a planned follow-up schedule is a direct way to reduce non-response bias.
steps: Write a covering message that explains who is asking, why it matters and how answers will be used.
Design the questionnaire to look easy to complete, with clear layout and a simple way to return it.
Send the initial invitation and track who has responded with an identifier kept apart from the answers.
Send a short reminder to non-respondents after about a week.
After about two weeks send a fuller reminder with a fresh copy or link, and offer an alternative mode such as a short call.
Send a final reminder after about three weeks, then close fieldwork.
Plot daily returns, report the response rate and compare respondents with the population to judge non-response bias.
outputs: A higher and documented response rate, a returns curve showing the effect of each contact, and data for checking non-response bias.
useWhen: You run self-completion surveys by email, post or in-product messages and need results that represent the invited group.
avoidWhen: Repeated contact would breach consent, marketing rules or goodwill, or the survey is an anonymous open link where non-respondents cannot be identified.
whyLost: UX surveys are often run as quick one-shot links with tools that make sending cheap, so the craft of contact sequencing from survey methodology was rarely carried over.
whereToUse: Email surveys of customers or members, B2B account surveys, research panels, longitudinal surveys, post-service follow-ups.
example: A sports federation's member survey drew 22 per cent after the first email. Following the reminder schedule, a short reminder at day 8, a fresh link at day 15 and a final note at day 22 took the response to 51 per cent and brought in more casual members, who rated the app lower.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Dillman, D. A., Smyth, J. D. and Christian, L. M. (2009) Internet, Mail, and Mixed-Mode Surveys: The Tailored Design Method, Third edn. New York: Wiley.

name: Target Market Sizing
origin: Marketing and business planning practice; described for UX practitioners by Christian Crumlish (2022)
summary: Define a specific target market, estimate its size from desk research, and justify the share you can realistically win, avoiding the 'just 1% of a huge market' illusion.
description: Market-oriented product goals have three stages: identify and target a market, understand its needs well enough to build something that fits, and bring the solution to it. Sizing serves the first. Casting the net wide ('everybody') produces a group too heterogeneous to reach; a defined market, such as US adults aged 18-35 considering a first new car, can be targeted with tailored experiences and narratives. With the segment defined, desk research gives a rough size, and the team must argue for the percentage it can obtain and translate it into a customer count. Crumlish warns about a numeracy trap: a small percentage of a huge denominator is not easier to win than a larger percentage of a well-defined smaller market. Sizing does not show demand, so it is followed by research or demand tests.
steps: Define the target market as a specific category of potential buyers with a real problem you can solve, not 'everyone'.
Use desk research (public statistics, industry reports, competitor data) to estimate the number of people or businesses in that segment.
Estimate and justify the share you could realistically acquire and translate it into a customer count and revenue.
Check against the denominator illusion by comparing the effort to reach the target count in a broad versus a well-defined segment.
Gauge interest in the defined market with user research or a demand test, such as a smoke test, before investing.
outputs: A defined target segment, a rough market size, and a justified obtainable share and customer count.
useWhen: Early product strategy, new-market or new-segment proposals, and business cases where UX research needs to show that a user problem matters at scale.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating size as evidence of demand; follow with research or fake-door tests. In B2B, markets are small and customers are known accounts, so account-level analysis replaces population estimates.
whyLost: It is standard in product management and marketing, and it survives in UX mainly when researchers work alongside product managers on strategy.
whereToUse: Startup and new-product proposals, expansion into new countries or segments, prioritising research investment across segments.
example: A team proposes a budgeting app for 'all millennials'. Redefining the market as UK renters aged 22-30 sharing flats gives about 1.2 million people; a justified 3% share means 36,000 users, which the team then tests with a smoke-test landing page.
reference: Crumlish, C. (2022). Product Management for UX People: From Designing to Thriving in a Product World. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media, pp. 71-74.

name: Targeted tasks that provoke rare behaviour
aka: Targeted tasks that provoke rare behaviour (including demonic interventions)
origin: Dix and Brewster (1994), sonic buttons study; described in Dix (2020)
summary: Design an artificial task, with time pressure or added noise, that makes a rare error or behaviour occur often enough to compare designs statistically.
description: Some important errors are too rare to observe in a lab session. An expert slip, moving off an on-screen button before release so the action silently fails, happened about once a month in real use and never in careful short tests.
