After analysing the mechanism, researchers built a task that invites it: type a number on an on-screen keypad, confirm, then move quickly to a distant next button under time pressure. This produced up to a dozen missed errors per session even with novices, enough to show that a sonic click made every slip noticed. In the extreme demonic variant, random noise is added to pointer movement to force overshoots so recovery behaviour can be studied. The method trades ecological validity for statistical power, and generalisation rests on the analysed mechanism.
steps: Analyse the rare behaviour's mechanism step by step from incidents, logs or theory.
Design a task whose structure invites that behaviour, such as rapid sequences or distant targets.
Add load (time pressure, secondary tasks) or perturbation (random pointer noise) to raise its frequency.
Pilot until the behaviour occurs often enough per session for statistical comparison.
Run the comparison of designs on the now-frequent behaviour.
Argue generalisation from the mechanism and other evidence, and state the limits on real-use claims.
outputs: Enough occurrences of a rare event to compare conditions statistically, with evidence about detection and recovery.
useWhen: A low-frequency but costly error or edge behaviour must be compared across designs and cannot be waited for in field data.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need realistic rates of occurrence or real-use claims; artificial tasks limit ecological validity. Use field logs or incident analysis instead, and note participants may dislike demonic tasks.
whyLost: Mainstream usability testing favours realistic tasks, and the idea of deliberately provoking errors is rarely taught.
whereToUse: Payment and trading confirmations, medical device entry, touch target and gesture design, safety warnings and undo features.
example: A banking app team suspects users occasionally confirm transfers to the wrong payee. A timed task with near-identical payee names and pressure provokes the slip in one session in five, enough to show that a payee photo cuts it by half.
reference: Dix, A. (2020). Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data. Morgan & Claypool; Dix, A. & Brewster, S. (1994). Causing trouble with buttons. Ancillary Proceedings of HCI '94.

name: Task Network Modelling of Human-System Performance
aka: SAINT / Micro SAINT task network simulation
donor: Human factors engineering and systems simulation
origin: SAINT (US Air Force, 1970s) and Micro SAINT (Micro Analysis and Design); K. Ronald Laughery and Kevin Corker, 1997
summary: Represents a system's missions as a network of tasks with sampled times and error probabilities, then runs it many times to predict crew and system performance under alternative designs.
description: Task network models are built from a task analysis: each task node has a time and error distribution (for example normal or exponential, with mean and SD), a release condition that holds it until met, and effects at its beginning, launch and end that change the system state. Branching after a task can be probabilistic (a weighted random draw), tactical (the highest-value next task) or multiple (several tasks start at once). Unlike a single-pass human reliability model such as THERP, the network is run many times to give a distribution of mission time, success and errors. Meister notes such models are human constructions but valuable for studying molar variables that cannot be manipulated in real systems, such as crew size, task allocation, display formats or workload, for instance whether a destroyer could be run by 95 sailors instead of 300. Their credibility depends on validation against real performance and on the quality of time and error inputs.
steps: Study the task analysis of the real system and decompose it into mission, functions, tasks and subtasks to the depth needed.
Define the network: the relations among tasks, release conditions and branching rules (probabilistic, tactical or multiple).
Select a simulation engine (for example Micro SAINT or IMPRINT, or a general discrete-event tool).
Specify inputs: task time and error distributions, interaction rules, equipment data and operator assignments.
Run the model many times (hundreds to thousands of replications), compare outputs with performance data from the real or a similar system, and refine until they match reasonably.
Use the verified model to compare design alternatives such as crew size, automation, task allocation or procedure changes.
outputs: Probabilistic estimates of mission time, success and error rates, workload profiles and bottlenecks under each configuration.
useWhen: Comparing staffing, automation or workflow alternatives for complex operations before they exist, when real-system manipulation is impossible and task analysis data are available.
avoidWhen: Time and error inputs are unknown or guessed (the output will be no better); a simple single-user interface where KLM or GOMS estimates suffice; you need cognitive mechanism detail (use ACT-R or other cognitive architectures). Models are costly and often only partly validated.
whyLost: Models are expensive and mostly built by defence research agencies; commercial UX rarely has the task-time and error data or the budget.
whereToUse: Control rooms, emergency dispatch, clinical workflows, warehouse and logistics operations, aviation and maritime crew design, and AI automation decisions that change task allocation between people and software.
example: An emergency dispatch centre models call handling as a task network with time distributions from logs. Simulating 5,000 shifts shows that adding AI-assisted address lookup cuts mean handling time by 20 seconds but creates a queue at the supervisor review task during peak hours, so review rules are changed before rollout.
sources: Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
reference: Laughery, K. R., Jr., & Corker, K. (1997). Computer modeling and simulation. In G. Salvendy (Ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (pp. 1378-1408). New York: Wiley.

name: Task Success Coding and Error-Opportunity Rates
donor: Human reliability analysis and Six Sigma
origin: Defects-per-opportunity from Six Sigma; applied to usability by Sauro (2004 onward)
summary: Rules for scoring each task attempt as a success or failure and counting errors against the number of chances to make them.
description: Completion rates and error counts are only comparable when they are coded consistently. Sauro's guidance defines success in advance (a correct end state, ideally checkable by URL or answer), treats assisted completions as failures, and codes partial success only with explicit criteria. For errors, raw counts are misleading because a twelve-field form offers more chances to slip than a two-click task. Dividing errors by error opportunities, the places a user could reasonably go wrong, gives an error rate that can be compared across tasks and products, and the proportion of error-free attempts feeds into SUM. Published data put the average completion rate around 78% and suggest about 0.7 errors per task is typical.
steps: Write a success criterion for each task before testing, including what counts as assistance.
Code each attempt as 1 (success) or 0 (failure), never as a percentage of steps.
Define error opportunities by walking the ideal path and listing each point where a slip or mistake is possible.
Log each error with its type and step during sessions or from recordings.
Compute errors per task, error rate per opportunity and the proportion of error-free attempts.
outputs: Comparable completion and error metrics per task.
useWhen: Any summative or benchmark test where tasks or products will be compared.
avoidWhen: Purely exploratory sessions with open-ended tasks.
whyLost: Error logging is laborious and moderators rarely agree on what counts, so many reports drop errors entirely.
whereToUse: Form-heavy flows, data entry systems, medical and financial software.
example: Two checkout designs have similar raw error counts, but per opportunity the new one is 40% lower because it has twice as many fields.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 2; Sauro, How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test.

name: Task-Action Grammar
origin: Stephen Payne and Thomas Green, 1986
summary: Describes an interface's command language as a feature-based grammar so that the number of rule schemas measures consistency and predicts learnability.
description: TAG represents tasks as sets of semantic features (direction, unit, object) and writes rewrite rules mapping tasks to action sequences. A consistent language lets one rule schema with feature variables cover many tasks, for example 'move [direction] by [unit]' mapped to a key pattern. Inconsistencies show up as extra rules. The number of schemas therefore indexes how much users must learn, and family resemblance between rules predicts transfer. TAG also captures world knowledge used in mapping, such as the conventional association of 'up' with 'previous'. It is a precise way to audit consistency in command sets, keyboard shortcuts, gesture vocabularies and voice command grammars.
steps: List the simple tasks the interface supports and identify their semantic features and values.
Write task-action rules for each task, generalising into schemas with feature variables wherever mappings are systematic.
Count rule schemas and note exceptions that require special rules.
Identify mappings that rely on world knowledge or conventions and check they are culturally valid for users.
Propose a revised command set that minimises schemas, then compare learning or error rates with a small study.
Document the grammar as a design-system rule for future additions.
outputs: A TAG description, schema counts, inconsistency list and a proposed consistent command grammar.
useWhen: Designing or auditing shortcut sets, gesture vocabularies, voice command grammars, CLI syntax or API naming.
avoidWhen: GUI flows dominated by visual recognition rather than recalled commands.
whyLost: Direct manipulation reduced interest in command languages, and formal grammar notations felt academic. Voice and CLI tools have revived the need without the method.
whereToUse: Voice assistants, developer CLIs, keyboard-first productivity apps, gesture systems in VR.
example: A note-taking app has 48 shortcuts. A TAG analysis finds 19 schemas, with heading levels mapped inconsistently; a revision covering the same functions with 9 schemas cuts recall errors in testing.
sources: Payne & Green, Task-action grammars: A model of the mental representation of task languages (1986), Human-Computer Interaction
Dix, Finlay, Abowd & Beale, Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed., 2004)
reference: Payne, S. J., & Green, T. R. G. (1986). Task-action grammars. Human-Computer Interaction, 2(2), 93-133.

name: Task-Specific Self-Efficacy Scale
origin: Albert Bandura (1977, 1997, 2001); scale construction issues in sport reviewed by Feltz and Chase (1998) and by Myers and Feltz in Chapter 36 of the Handbook
summary: Asks people how certain they are that they can perform specific task-level actions, usually on a 0 to 100 scale, to measure their confidence in their own (or their team's) capability.
description: Self-efficacy is a person's belief that they can carry out the actions needed for a given task. Bandura's microanalytic approach writes items about concrete capabilities in a specific domain ('How certain are you that you can...'), rated from 'certain cannot do' through 'moderately certain can do' to 'completely certain can do', usually as 11 categories from 0 to 100. Collective efficacy applies the same idea to a team's shared capability. The Handbook gives practical guidance on building such scales. Items should tap 'can do' beliefs rather than general evaluations. Dimensionality must be shown with factor analysis rather than assumed. Rasch rating-scale analyses repeatedly show that people cannot use 10 or 11 categories consistently, so fewer categories (around four or five) often work better. For team-level measures, decide whether to aggregate individual beliefs about the team. For UX, task-specific self-efficacy scales measure users' confidence to complete key tasks before and after onboarding, a tutorial or a redesign. Self-efficacy predicts persistence and adoption and is a common outcome in health and learning products.
steps: List the concrete capabilities the product should build (for example 'set up a recurring invoice without help').
Write 'How certain are you that you can...' items, one capability each, with graded difficulty where useful.
Choose the response format, and test category functioning with a rating-scale analysis in a pilot.
Check dimensionality with factor analysis before forming composite scores.
Administer before and after onboarding, training or a design change.
Relate efficacy change to observed task success and later retention.
outputs: Task-level and composite self-efficacy scores before and after an intervention, with evidence on scale structure.
useWhen: The product's success depends on users believing they can do something new: onboarding, financial and health self-management, learning tools, complex B2B set-up.
avoidWhen: You only need satisfaction or ease ratings for a single task, or capabilities cannot be stated concretely.
whyLost: UX uses post-task ease ratings (such as SEQ) rather than forward-looking capability beliefs; efficacy scales are standard in health and education research but rarely built for products.
whereToUse: Onboarding and training flows, personal finance and health apps, developer platforms, accessibility and digital-inclusion programmes, team collaboration tools.
example: A tax software team writes eight self-efficacy items such as 'How certain are you that you can claim home-office expenses correctly?'. After a guided set-up redesign, mean efficacy rises from 45 to 70, and users with large gains are less likely to contact support.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Myers, N. D. and Feltz, D. L. (2007) 'From self-efficacy to collective efficacy in sport: transitional methodological issues', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 36.

name: Taxometric analysis
origin: Paul Meehl (1995 and earlier); applied to attachment by Fraley and Spieker (2003)
summary: Tests whether individual differences form natural categories (taxa) or a continuum before people are analysed or described as types.
description: Cluster analysis and latent class analysis will produce groups whether or not natural groups exist, and imposing categories on dimensional data loses power and predictive validity. Meehl's taxometric procedures test the question empirically. MAXCOV examines how the covariance of two indicators changes across levels of a third; MAMBAC examines mean differences above and below sliding cut points. Taxonic structure produces peaked or distinctive curves, dimensional structure flat or concave ones. Modern practice compares observed curves with curves from simulated categorical and dimensional data matched to the sample, summarised in a comparison curve fit index. Fraley and Spieker applied the procedures to infant attachment, long described in types, and found mostly continuous variation. The procedures need adequate samples, often several hundred cases, and valid indicators that separate the putative groups.
steps: Select three or more valid indicators of the construct (for example attitude or behaviour scores thought to define a user type).
Run taxometric procedures such as MAXCOV and MAMBAC on the indicators.
Simulate matched categorical and dimensional comparison data sets and compare observed curves with each, using a comparison curve fit index.
Decide whether the construct is better treated as categories or dimensions, using several procedures for consistency.
Only if categories are supported, apply clustering or latent class models; otherwise describe users on continuous dimensions.
outputs: Evidence for taxonic or dimensional structure, with curves and fit indices.
useWhen: Before building personas or segments from cluster analysis, or before reporting user 'types' such as early adopters, power users or sceptics.
avoidWhen: Small samples (below a few hundred) or weak indicators make the procedures unreliable. If segments are needed for practical targeting regardless of natural structure, state that they are pragmatic cuts.
whyLost: It is a specialist psychopathology method; UX segmentation assumes types exist and goes straight to clustering.
whereToUse: Persona and segmentation programmes, user typologies in research reports, attitudinal segmentation for AI trust or privacy.
example: Before publishing four 'privacy personas', a team runs MAMBAC and MAXCOV on 1,200 survey responses. Curves match the dimensional comparison data, so the team presents privacy concern as a continuum with scenario-based anchors rather than as four discrete types.
sources: Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Brownell, C. A., Lemerise, E. A., Pelphrey, K. A. and Roisman, G. I. (2015). Measuring socioemotional development. In R. M. Lerner and M. E. Lamb (Eds.), Handbook of Child Psychology and Developmental Science (7th ed.), Vol. 3 (pp. 11-56). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.

name: Taxonomy and Tag Audit (Consolidation and Value Review)
donor: Content strategy and information architecture practice
origin: Lisa Maria Martin (2019), reporting Eileen Webb's redesign of The Toast (2015) and a Happy Cog college programme search
summary: Audit an existing tag set or taxonomy: consolidate sprawling terms into a controlled list and check what its term relationships and orderings imply about whose knowledge is default.
description: Free tagging saves effort at first but sprawls into misspellings, near-duplicates and one-off tags that split content streams and weaken findability and measurement. The audit exports every tag with its usage count, flags unused, single-use and duplicate terms, classifies the rest by role (topic, series, author, category, joke) and merges topics into a controlled vocabulary while moving other roles into their own metadata fields. Martin pairs this with a value review: every term-to-content relationship is a judgement, so for contested terms the team lists all plausible matches, asks what the draft ordering privileges (culture, language, gender, discipline) and neutralises it, for example with relevance tiers and randomised order within each tier. The rigour comes from working from the full usage data rather than impressions, and from recording the rationale for each relationship so it can be revisited with diverse reviewers after launch.
steps: Export every tag or taxonomy term with its count of use and the content it is attached to.
Flag unused, single-use, misspelled and near-duplicate terms; in Martin's example 6,152 of 8,182 tags had been used once and over 400 never.
Classify each surviving term by role (topic, series, author, category, humour or other) and move non-topical roles into dedicated metadata fields.
Merge topical terms into a controlled list and retag the content.
List the term-to-content relationships for contested terms, note which matches the draft favours and question what that ordering implies about culture, language, gender or discipline.
Group results into relevance tiers and randomise or otherwise neutralise order within tiers where no group should be privileged.
Set up governance for proposing, adding and retiring terms, with regular editorial review and a post-launch check by diverse reviewers.
outputs: A controlled tag list, a metadata field model, relationship and ordering rules with recorded rationale, and a governance process.
useWhen: Before a redesign or search overhaul of a content-heavy site whose free tags or taxonomy have grown unmanaged, and when a taxonomy drives search or filtering results that could privilege some groups.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there is no existing vocabulary to audit; build one with Thesaurus and Controlled Vocabulary Construction (ISO 25964). For page-level inventory use a Content Audit, and for testing whether users find things under the new structure use Tree Testing.
whyLost: Survives in content strategy and IA practice as tag clean-up, though the value and bias review of relationships is rarely made explicit.
whereToUse: Publishing and media sites, knowledge bases, e-commerce product attributes, course and programme finders, internal document repositories.
example: A health information site with 5,000 free tags finds 70 per cent used once and merges them into 300 controlled topics. The value review then notices that 'women's health' surfaces only reproductive content and adds tiers so cardiac and mental-health articles appear alongside it.
reference: Martin, L. M. (2019). Everyday Information Architecture. New York: A Book Apart, pp. 101-106, 112-114.

name: Taxonomy of Loss
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Classifies how research methods disappear (extinct, vestigial, siloed, renamed, latent) and, with cause of loss, locates priority targets for recovery.
description: The treatise defines a lost method as one that (a) was once practised with regularity and rigour, (b) has largely disappeared from practice, education or discourse, and (c) retains significant value if recovered. Its taxonomy has five types: Extinct (no current practitioners; knowledge only in literature; the methodological community has dissolved), Vestigial (practised in reduced or distorted form; original intent and theory lost, leaving a surface procedure), Siloed (active in academic or specialist contexts but absent from industry), Renamed (rebranded without credit or theoretical connection to origins) and Latent (known but rarely used; infrastructure for revival exists). The extended edition adds unmigrated methods, rigorous in donor disciplines but never adopted. Appendix A crosses survival degree with cause of loss (legitimate validity failure versus illegitimate organisational pressure); high-value, low-survival methods are recovery priorities.
steps: Inventory methods used in or relevant to the organisation or field.
Check each against the three lost-method criteria.
Assign a loss type: extinct, vestigial, siloed, renamed, latent or unmigrated.
Assess the cause of loss, distinguishing validity failure from organisational pressure.
Plot methods by potential value and current survival.
Select high-value, low-survival methods for recovery.
outputs: Classified method inventory, value-by-survival map, recovery shortlist.
useWhen: Auditing a research team's toolkit, curriculum design, building method libraries.
avoidWhen: Choosing a method for a single study; use method selection guidance instead.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: ResearchOps, UX education, professional associations, research leadership strategy.
example: A research team classifies its 40 listed methods and finds 12 vestigial (including 'thematic analysis' and 'contextual inquiry'), prompting training in the full protocols.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kuhn TS (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 1 and Appendix A.

name: Teach-Back Mental Model Elicitation
donor: Clinical health literacy practice; cybernetics (Pask's conversation theory)
origin: Gordon Pask's teachback in conversation theory (1970s); clinical teach-back popularised by Dean Schillinger et al. (2003)
summary: Asks users to explain or teach how a system works in their own words, then scores the explanation against a reference model to expose mental model gaps.
description: In medicine, teach-back confirms patient understanding: the clinician asks the patient to explain the instructions back, corrects misunderstandings and repeats until correct. Pask used 'teachback' to externalise a learner's conceptual structure. As a UX method, participants explain to a confederate novice how a feature works (e.g. how their data is shared, how the AI decides), sometimes with drawing. Explanations are coded against a reference conceptual model for correct, missing and incorrect propositions, giving a quantitative mental model accuracy score. It is far more diagnostic than asking 'did that make sense?', and directly tests whether interface explanations transfer understanding.
steps: Write a reference conceptual model of the system as a list of key propositions (e.g. 10-20).
After users interact with the product or explanation, ask them to teach a novice (or the researcher playing one) how it works.
Allow drawing and probing with neutral prompts ('and then what happens?').
Code transcripts for correct, missing and incorrect propositions; compute accuracy and misconception frequency with two coders.
Identify common misconceptions and the interface elements that produce them.
Revise explanations and repeat teach-back until a target (e.g. 80% of key propositions correct) is met.
outputs: Mental model accuracy scores, a misconception inventory and links to interface causes.
useWhen: Users must understand how a system works to use it safely: privacy settings, AI behaviour, financial products, health instructions.
avoidWhen: Simple tasks where procedural success is sufficient evidence.
whyLost: UX relies on 'did that make sense' questions and task success; clinical communication methods rarely cross into design research.
whereToUse: AI assistants, privacy and data sharing, insurance and lending, medical devices, security features.
example: Users of a budgeting app teach back how 'round-ups' work; 60% wrongly believe the money leaves their account immediately. A redesigned explainer raises correct propositions from 55% to 84%.
sources: Schillinger et al., Closing the loop: physician communication with diabetic patients who have low health literacy (2003), Archives of Internal Medicine
reference: Schillinger, D., et al. (2003). Archives of Internal Medicine, 163(1), 83-90.

name: Team Error Detection, Recovery and Learning Analysis
aka: Designing systems that learn from error
origin: Edwin Hutchins (1995), extending Donald Norman's design for error
summary: For each error type, check who has access, knowledge, attention and the right perspective to detect it, then trace how it is recovered and who learns from it.
description: Hutchins argues that where systems rely on on-the-job learning, error is inevitable, so design should support not only prevention and recovery but learning. Detecting an error requires four conditions: access to the behaviour or its trace, knowledge or expectation of correct performance, attention to it, and a perspective that brings the relevant expectations to bear. Task design can force errors to show, as a third line of position on a chart makes a bad fix visible as a large triangle. Different roles have different perspectives: a plotter sees bearings as directions where the recorder sees digits. An evaluator role has access and knowledge without doing the work, at a cost in processing capacity. Corrections teach the person who erred, the detector and witnesses, so a low, reliably detected error rate can be functional for a team.
steps: List the error types observed in the team's work.
For each, identify who has access to the error or its trace.
Identify who has the knowledge to recognise it as an error.
Check whether the task design forces attention to it, for example through redundant cross-checks.
Identify which role's perspective makes the error visible.
Consider adding an evaluator role and weigh it against lost processing capacity.
Trace how errors are recovered, with or without diagnosis and instruction, and who learns: the person who erred, the detector and witnesses.
outputs: An error-detection map by error type and role, and design options for detection, recovery and learning.
useWhen: Designing team workflows and shared tools where mistakes will happen and must be caught by someone, such as review queues, clinical hand-offs, operations centres or human review of AI output.
avoidWhen: Detection costs attention, which is scarce under high workload, and feedback under time pressure is often contentless. For single-user error prediction use SHERPA; for classifying errors use Error Taxonomy (Slips, Lapses, Mistakes).
whyLost: Cognition in the Wild is read as theory, and its practical analysis of error detection was never packaged as a method outside distributed cognition research.
whereToUse: Code review and approval flows, financial operations, human-in-the-loop AI review, clinical medication checks.
example: In a content moderation team using AI pre-labels, the analysis shows reviewers have access and knowledge but no perspective on systematic label drift. A rotating auditor role that sees aggregate decisions is added, and its findings are shared with reviewers so they learn.
reference: Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, pp. 271-279.

name: Team Operating Agreement
origin: Peter Merholz and Kristin Skinner, Org Design for Design Orgs (2016)
summary: A cross-functional team drafts, over two sessions, a one-page agreement on how it will work together, including how it will use and commission research.
description: A team operating agreement is a short written statement of how a cross-functional team will interact, approach problems and escalate issues. Merholz and Skinner suggest topics including how the team integrates as one unit, a communication plan, availability of key people for working sessions, stakeholder approvals and timing, escalation and issue resolution, and assumptions about deliverables (timing, type, fidelity). Distinctively, they include how the team works with the research or insights group: access to existing insights and the timing, recruiting, protocols and field research for new studies. The agreement is built in two sessions separated by at least a day, so first ideas can settle before they are finalised. Related practices protect maker time and keep a shared terminology document.
steps: Facilitate a first session with the full team: brainstorm agreement topics without judgement, discuss them and build an affinity diagram.
Include how the team will access existing research and commission new studies (timing, recruiting, protocols, fieldwork).
Let the ideas rest for at least a day.
Reconvene to review, modify ideas and categories, and finalise the list.
Publish the agreement as a one-page document or slide alongside or within the team charter.
Revisit it when team membership or ways of working change.
outputs: A one-page operating agreement published with the team charter.
useWhen: Use it when a new cross-functional team forms, or when friction over hand-offs, approvals or research timing keeps recurring.
avoidWhen: It is an internal team practice, not a way to learn about users; for that use research methods such as Interviews. To diagnose why collaboration fails after the fact, an After-Action Review is better suited.
whyLost: Working agreements are standard in agile teams; the research-specific clauses survive mainly in design organisations with dedicated research functions.
whereToUse: Product squads, design agencies, research operations, and teams embedding researchers.
example: A new payments squad agrees that research requests need two weeks' notice for recruiting and that the researcher joins backlog refinement. Study timing complaints drop in the next quarter.
sources: Org Design for Design Orgs (Merholz & Skinner, 2016)
reference: Merholz, P. and Skinner, K. (2016). Org Design for Design Orgs: Building and Managing In-House Design Teams. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, p. 164.

name: Technological Mediation Analysis
origin: Peter-Paul Verbeek, 2006, drawing on Don Ihde (1990), Bruno Latour (1992) and James Gibson (1979)
summary: Analyses how a product invites or inhibits actions and amplifies or reduces perceptions, then removes undesirable mediation or deliberately designs in desirable mediation.
description: Because technologies shape what people do and how they perceive the world, designers are always doing ethics, implicitly or explicitly. Verbeek's mediation analysis makes this explicit. Mediation of action is examined through scripts (Latour: a ceramic cup's script is to be washed, a cardboard cup's to be thrown away), affordances and multistability, the fact that one artefact supports different uses in different contexts; designs invite or inhibit behaviour. Mediation of experience is examined through embodiment relations, where the artefact withdraws into the body like glasses, and hermeneutic relations, where it represents the world and must be read like a thermostat; each amplifies some aspects of perception and reduces others. Verbeek offers a minimum scenario (find and reduce undesirable mediation) and a second scenario (design in desirable mediation).
steps: Describe the product's script: which actions it invites and which it inhibits, and how use varies across contexts (multistability).
Describe its relation to experience: embodiment or hermeneutic, and what it amplifies or reduces in perception.
Anticipate mediations in several use contexts and for different stakeholders, including non-users.
Judge which mediations are undesirable and reduce or eliminate them (minimum scenario).
Decide which mediations are desirable and build them in (second scenario), for example aesthetics that make a target behaviour attractive.
Optionally measure the values at stake with users, for example with Schwartz's value theory, to check the intended mediation occurs.
outputs: An account of the actions and perceptions a design mediates, and documented design decisions about desirable and undesirable mediation.
useWhen: Ethical design reviews, persuasive or behaviour-shaping products, and AI or sensing systems that change how people see situations.
avoidWhen: When you need a step-by-step protocol or empirical evidence; the source presents lenses rather than a procedure. For stakeholder-value investigations use Value-Sensitive Design; for behaviour-change evaluation use experiments.
whyLost: It is philosophy-of-technology theory taught in Dutch design schools, rarely translated into a UX procedure.
whereToUse: Persuasive and wellbeing apps, recommender and AI systems, smart home devices, design ethics reviews.
example: A smart-speaker team analyses its sleep-timer feature: it invites falling asleep to news (script) and reduces awareness of time (hermeneutic). They redesign it to fade to ambient sound and show a morning summary.
reference: Verbeek, P.-P. (2006). Materializing morality: design ethics and technological mediation. Science, Technology and Human Values, 31(3), 361-380.

name: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) Questionnaires
aka: Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use scales
origin: Fred Davis (1989), MIS Quarterly
summary: Two six-item scales for perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, which together predict whether people intend to adopt a technology.
description: The TAM proposes that intention to use a technology depends on perceived usefulness (the belief it will improve performance) and perceived ease of use (the belief it will be effortless), and that intention drives actual use. Davis built two six-item scales with 7-point likely to unlikely responses. A notable finding: his original mixed-tone items produced a muddled factor structure because reversed items correlated with the wrong construct, so he removed negative items, an early warning about alternating item tone that Sauro and Lewis echo for SUS. Coefficient alpha was 0.98 for usefulness and 0.94 for ease of use. TAM is one of the most cited models in information systems research.
steps: Administer the six perceived usefulness and six perceived ease-of-use items, adapted to your product.
Optionally add items on intention to use.
Average each scale.
Model intention or actual use as a function of the two scales (regression or SEM).
Act on whichever belief is weaker as the main adoption barrier.
outputs: Scores for perceived usefulness and ease of use, and their power to predict adoption.
useWhen: Predicting or explaining adoption of new tools, especially in workplaces.
avoidWhen: You need detailed usability diagnosis rather than adoption prediction.
whyLost: It lives in information systems journals, and UX teams rarely model adoption intention.
whereToUse: Enterprise tool rollouts, AI assistants at work, health technology adoption.
example: Nurses rate a new charting tool high on ease of use but low on usefulness, explaining low adoption better than any usability finding.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
reference: Davis, F. D. (1989). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and user acceptance of information technology. MIS Quarterly 13(3).

name: Technology Probes
origin: Hilary Hutchinson and colleagues, 2003, within the probe tradition of Gaver, Dunne and Pacenti (1999)
summary: Deploys deliberately simple working technologies in people's everyday settings to learn about needs and practices and inspire design, not to evaluate the prototype.
description: Technology probes are simple, functional, open-ended technologies placed in real settings for weeks. They serve three goals at once: a social-science goal (understanding needs and practices in context), an engineering goal (field-testing a technology) and a design goal (inspiring users and researchers to think of new possibilities). Unlike usability prototypes, probes have few functions, are easy to use and are designed to be interpreted and appropriated, and usage is logged. Hutchinson et al.'s family study deployed a zoomable message board on a writable tablet and a short video capture tool across households. Unlike Cultural Probes, which are packs of provocative materials returned to designers, technology probes are working systems whose use and appropriation become data.
steps: Choose an open question about practice and build one or two simple, robust, functional prototypes embodying a new idea, with usage logging.
Recruit a small number of households or teams (often 5 to 20) and install the probes in their everyday setting.
Leave them in place for several weeks while logging use and collecting occasional check-ins.
Interview participants about use, non-use and appropriation, using logs to prompt recall.
Hold design workshops with participants to generate ideas from what was learned.
Analyse findings for needs and practices rather than prototype quality, discounting polite praise.
outputs: Understanding of needs, practices and appropriation, usage logs and design ideas.
useWhen: Exploring a new technology space where people cannot describe needs in the abstract and context of use is everything.
avoidWhen: When you need to evaluate a specific design; participants aware the researcher built the tool may be overly favourable. Use Usability Testing or field trials for evaluation.
whyLost: The idea lives on as 'field pilots', 'diary studies with a prototype' or 'research through design deployments', with the probe's exploratory purpose often forgotten.
whereToUse: Smart home, family and elder care technology, workplace collaboration tools, AI assistants.
example: A team exploring AI assistance for carers deploys a simple shared voice note device in eight households for four weeks; logs and interviews show it is used mostly for handovers between siblings, reframing the product.
sources: Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Hutchinson, H. et al. (2003). Technology probes: inspiring design for and with families. Proc. CHI 2003, 17-24.

name: Template Analysis
origin: Nigel King, 1998 onwards
summary: Develops a hierarchical coding template from a priori and data-driven codes, applies and revises it iteratively, and suits larger datasets where some themes are already anticipated.
description: Template Analysis (Nigel King) is a method of thematic analysis in which a hierarchical coding template is developed, applied to data, and iteratively revised. It is more structured than Braun & Clarke's reflexive TA (because it involves an explicit a priori template) but less constrained than framework analysis (because the template is substantially modified during analysis). It is particularly appropriate when you have some prior knowledge of the topic that should inform the template, but do not want to impose a full a priori framework on the data.
steps: Develop a priori codes: Before reading the full dataset, develop a provisional list of codes based on: your research questions, relevant existing literature, and any preliminary data. This is the initial template.

Apply the template to a subset of data: Code several transcripts using the initial template. Note: where do codes fit comfortably? Where are they inadequate, overlapping, or missing? Where does data resist being coded?
Modify the template: Revise the template based on the initial coding. Add new codes, merge overlapping ones, redefine inadequate ones, and build hierarchy (organise codes into themes and sub-themes).
Apply the revised template to the full dataset: Code all data using the revised template. Continue modifying as needed, but document all changes.
Final analysis: Use the completed template to write a thematic analysis of the full dataset. The template structure should be visible in the presentation of findings.
outputs: An initial and final hierarchical template, coded transcripts, documented template revisions, and a thematic account structured by the template.
useWhen: You have a medium to large dataset (around 15 to 60 interviews), some prior expectations or research questions to structure the analysis, and several analysts who need a shared framework.
avoidWhen: You want fully inductive theory building (use Constructivist Grounded Theory) or highly interpretive themes from a small sample (use Reflexive Thematic Analysis).
whyLost: It is well known in organisational and health psychology but rarely taught in UX, which tends to oscillate between unstructured affinity mapping and rigid tagging taxonomies.
whereToUse: Multi-researcher studies, evaluation programmes, research repositories with evolving taxonomies, and longitudinal tracking studies.
example: Three researchers analysing 40 interviews about a telehealth service start with a priori codes for access, trust and technology, test them on 6 transcripts, add a 'family as proxy user' branch, and code the remainder consistently.
sources: The Use of Template Analysis in Qualitative Psychology (King)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: King, N. & Brooks, J. M. (2017). Template Analysis for Business and Management Students. Sage.

name: Temporal and Spatial Occlusion Paradigm
origin: Introduced by Haskins (1965) for perceptual training; developed for expert-novice anticipation research by Jones and Miles (1978), Abernethy and Russell (1984, 1987), Williams and colleagues; reviewed by Hodges, Huys and Starkes and by Williams and Ward in the Handbook
summary: Cuts off or masks parts of a realistic dynamic display at chosen moments to find out when and from which cues skilled people predict what will happen next.
description: In temporal occlusion, footage of an unfolding event is filmed from the performer's viewpoint and edited so that it stops at set points (for example before, at and after a key moment); participants say what happens next. Experts' advantage at the earliest cut-off points shows how much they extract from advance cues. In spatial occlusion, specific areas (such as an opponent's arm) are masked throughout, and a drop in accuracy when a region is removed shows that the region carries information the person uses. Variants use point-light displays to strip away surface detail, occlusion goggles in live settings, and combination with eye tracking and verbal reports. The Handbook notes that expert-novice differences grow as stimuli and responses become more realistic. For UX and human factors the paradigm transfers to any dynamic display where users must anticipate: monitoring dashboards, security and video surveillance, trading screens, driving and drone interfaces, games. It tells designers which elements expert users actually rely on to see trouble coming, and whether a redesign removes or hides those cues.
steps: Record or simulate realistic sequences of the dynamic display, from the user's normal viewpoint, with known outcomes.
Define temporal cut-off points relative to key events, and spatial masks over candidate information regions.
Recruit groups differing in expertise (for example experienced operators and new hires).
Present clips in random order and ask for a prediction or decision with confidence after each.
Score accuracy and response time by cut-off point and by masked region, comparing groups.
Combine with eye tracking or retrospective verbal reports to confirm which cues are used.
Feed results into display design (keep or emphasise the predictive cues) and into training scenarios.
outputs: Accuracy curves by occlusion time and region for each expertise group, identifying the time window and display regions that carry predictive information.
useWhen: Users must anticipate events from changing displays and you want to know which cues experts use or whether a redesign preserves them.
avoidWhen: Interfaces are static forms or content pages with no unfolding events, or you cannot obtain realistic footage with known outcomes.
whyLost: It grew up in sport science labs using film and goggles; HCI took up freeze-probe situation awareness methods instead and rarely uses cue occlusion to locate information sources.
whereToUse: Network and security operations centres, air traffic and drone control, driver assistance displays, trading platforms, esports and game spectating tools.
example: A security operations product team cuts recorded incident timelines at 10, 5 and 1 minutes before an alert, and separately masks individual dashboard panels. Senior analysts predict incidents well at 10 minutes, but accuracy collapses when the connection-volume sparkline is masked, so the redesign keeps it prominent.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Williams, A. M. and Ward, P. (2007) 'Anticipation and decision making: exploring new horizons', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 9. Also Chapter 7 (Hodges, Huys and Starkes).

name: Temporal cognition mapping
origin: Allen Newell's bands of cognition, 1990; Card, Moran and Newell's response-time thresholds, 1983; Miller, 1968
summary: Maps each interaction to the cognitive timescale it lives on, perceptual, cognitive or task-level, and checks system latencies against each band's thresholds.
description: Human cognition operates in distinct time bands: perceptual fusion around 100 ms, unit cognitive operations and immediate responses around 1 s, and unit tasks around 10 s, with rational and social bands beyond. Interactions feel instantaneous, responsive or interrupting depending on which band their latency falls into, as reflected in the familiar 0.1 s, 1 s and 10 s thresholds. Temporal cognition mapping assigns each interaction to its band, measures actual system latency and user operation times, and identifies band violations: a perceptual-band action (dragging, scrolling, robotic hand-eye coordination) with 200 ms lag breaks the sense of direct causation. Rigour comes from measured, not assumed, latencies, including the 95th percentile, not just means.
steps: List the interactions in scope and assign each to its intended band: perceptual (under about 100 ms), cognitive (around 1 s), or task (around 10 s).
Measure end-to-end latency for each interaction on target hardware and network, capturing median and 95th percentile across at least 100 instances.

Flag violations: perceptual-band latency above 100 ms (and above 50 ms for direct manipulation or tracking), cognitive-band above 1 s without feedback, task-band above 10 s without progress indication.
Observe users (5-8) on flagged interactions to note behavioural signs such as repeated input, overshoot or disengagement.
Prioritise fixes by band severity and frequency, and specify feedback strategies (immediate acknowledgement, progress indicators) where latency cannot be reduced.
Re-measure after changes, reporting percentile shifts.
outputs: A timescale map of interactions, latency distributions per interaction, a list of band violations, and latency budgets per band.
useWhen: When performance or responsiveness is part of the experience problem; when setting latency budgets for engineering; for teleoperation, real-time control or streaming products.
avoidWhen: When the problem is content or comprehension rather than timing; use standard usability testing. For precise task time prediction, use KLM or GOMS.
whyLost: The 0.1/1/10 s thresholds survive as folklore, but the underlying band theory and systematic mapping were lost when performance moved to engineering teams.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, remote control and drones, gaming, collaborative editing, voice assistants and AI streaming responses.
example: A surgical robot's instrument tracking runs at 200 ms 95th-percentile latency, inside the perceptual band. Mapping shows surgeons compensate with slower, overshooting movements; engineering sets a 60 ms budget for tracking while allowing 1 s for menu actions.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
Card, S., Moran, T. & Newell, A., The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983) and GOMS/KLM literature
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 4 — Time, Rhythm & the Three Timescales of Experience
reference: Newell, A. (1990). Unified Theories of Cognition. Harvard University Press.

name: Temporal Sentiment Modeling (TSM)
donor: Affective computing and longitudinal UX research
origin: Vivek Gopinath
summary: A framework for mapping shifts in users' emotional state across a journey over time, used to inform redesign decisions in OTT products.
description: Temporal Sentiment Modeling is listed among Vivek Gopinath's selected contributions as a framework to map emotional state shifts in OTT journeys that informed redesign decisions. The source gives only this one-line definition, so the protocol below is a reconstruction consistent with the sentiment-drift and trajectory methods he documents elsewhere rather than a published specification. The underlying idea is that sentiment is a time series: the order and timing of emotional shifts across sessions and journey stages matter as much as average satisfaction, and declining sentiment can precede behavioural drop-off even while usage looks healthy. Rigour would come from repeated structured sentiment measures, alignment to journey stages, and triangulation with behavioural telemetry and quotes.
steps: Define the journey stages and time steps over which emotion will be tracked (e.g. browse, select, play, post-play across weeks).
Collect repeated sentiment measures at each step via in-product prompts, diaries or coded transcripts.
Array sentiment per user over time and identify shifts and inflection points by stage.
Cluster trajectories into patterns and align them with behavioural telemetry for the same users.
Attach quotes explaining each inflection and prioritise redesigns at stages with consistent negative shifts.
Re-measure after redesign to confirm the trajectory changed.
outputs: Sentiment trajectories by journey stage, inflection points and redesign priorities.
useWhen: When emotional experience across a journey drives retention, as in OTT and media products.
avoidWhen: When only one-off satisfaction scores are available; use a standard survey instead.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; documented in the sources only as a selected contribution.
whereToUse: OTT streaming, media, subscription products, AI companions.
example: An OTT service maps sentiment across browse, select and play stages and finds a negative shift at title selection after the second week, which informs a redesign of recommendations.
sources: Vivek Gopinath, professional research profile (Selected Contributions)
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation

name: Temporal-Operator Task Modelling (HAMSTERS, ConcurTaskTrees)
origin: Fabio Paterno, ConcurTaskTrees, 1999; HAMSTERS by Martinie, Palanque and colleagues, 2010-2014
summary: Decompose goals into a tree of typed tasks joined by formal temporal operators, so the model can be simulated and checked against the system.
description: Where hierarchical task analysis describes plans in prose, temporal-operator notations make them formal. Goals are decomposed into a tree whose leaves are typed tasks (user perceptive, cognitive or motor; interactive input or output; system; abstract), and siblings are joined by operators such as enable, concurrent, choice, disable, suspend-resume and order independence. Tasks can be iterative or optional and carry criticality, data, knowledge, devices and error types. ConcurTaskTrees adds task category and type, frequency, platform, objects and pre- and post-conditions, with one model per role plus a cooperation model for multi-user work; tasks enabled together form presentation task sets that suggest which interactions share a screen. Tools (CTTE, the HAMSTERS editor) simulate the model, and HAMSTERS can co-execute task models with Petri-net system models to find mismatches.
steps: Structure user goals and subgoals as a hierarchical tree.
Refine to typed leaf tasks: user perceptive, cognitive or motor; interactive input or output; system.
Join sibling tasks with temporal operators and mark iterative or optional tasks.
For CTT, record each task's category, type, frequency, platform, objects and pre- and post-conditions; build one model per role for multi-user work.
Add data, knowledge, device and error information where the analysis needs it.
Simulate the task model in the tool to check that valid sequences match expectations and derive presentation task sets.
Declare correspondences between interactive tasks and system inputs and outputs, then co-execute task and system models to find inconsistencies.
outputs: A formal task model tree, simulation traces, presentation task sets and a list of task-system inconsistencies.
useWhen: Safety-critical or complex interactive systems (cockpits, control rooms, medical devices), multi-role workflows, and model-based UI generation where tasks must be checked against system behaviour.
avoidWhen: Fast-moving consumer products where informal flows suffice; large models need structuring mechanisms and tool expertise. Use Hierarchical Task Analysis for lighter work.
whyLost: It needs specialist tools and formal training, so it remained in model-based UI and safety-critical engineering research rather than mainstream UX.
whereToUse: Aviation and automotive HMIs, clinical systems, industrial control, and multi-role enterprise workflows.
example: A medical infusion pump team models nurse programming in HAMSTERS and co-executes it with the pump's state model, revealing that a 'suspend' path leaves the dose screen in a state the task model never expects.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI (Weyers et al., 2017)
reference: Paterno, F. (1999) Model-Based Design and Evaluation of Interactive Applications. Berlin: Springer.

name: Terminology Voting
origin: Bloom (1987-88), reported by Nielsen (1993); motivated by Furnas et al. (1987) on verbal disagreement
summary: Choose interface terms by having users vote among a shortlist of candidate names, then verify the winners with learning and transfer tests, instead of asking users to invent names.
description: Asking users to propose names fails because of the verbal disagreement phenomenon: two people choose the same name for a concept only 7-18 per cent of the time, and even the most popular suggestion matches a minority of users. Terminology voting instead builds a shortlist of candidate names per concept from developers, usability specialists and a few users, then asks users, given brief concept descriptions, to vote. In Bloom's study of a mail-merge facility, vote winners produced fewer learning errors than technical terms (4.6 against 14.7 in a second test) and far fewer errors on a transfer test without documentation (5.8 against 23.6). The rigour lies in separating name generation from name selection and in validating the result behaviourally, since differences may vanish once the system is learned but persist in transfer.
steps: List the concepts that need names.
Generate several candidate names per concept from developers, usability specialists and a few users.
Present the shortlist to a fresh set of users with brief concept descriptions and ask each to vote for the best name.
Adopt the vote winners, keeping strong runners-up as synonyms or aliases.
Verify with a learning test and a transfer test without documentation, comparing error counts with the previous or technical terms.
outputs: A chosen vocabulary with vote counts, plus error rates in learning and transfer tests.
useWhen: Naming features, commands, menu items or navigation labels where several plausible terms exist and the cost of a poor term falls on new or occasional users.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you do not yet know what the concept is to users; first use Free Listing and Cultural Salience Analysis or Card Sorting. For checking labels in the context of a hierarchy use Tree Testing. Vote margins alone are weak evidence without the behavioural check.
whyLost: Label preference polls survive informally, but the structured shortlist-then-vote procedure with transfer testing faded after early usability engineering texts.
whereToUse: Feature naming in SaaS, settings and menu labels, AI assistant capability names, health and finance terminology for lay users.
example: A banking app must name a feature for setting money aside. The team shortlists 'Pots', 'Vaults', 'Savings goals' and 'Envelopes'; 120 users vote and 'Savings goals' wins clearly, and a transfer test shows half the errors of 'Vaults' when users must find it unaided.
reference: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering. Boston: AP Professional, pp. 124-126; Furnas, G. W., Landauer, T. K., Gomez, L. M. and Dumais, S. T. (1987). The vocabulary problem in human-system communication. Communications of the ACM, 30(11), 964-971.

name: Territory Maps
origin: Carnegie Mellon University design practice; documented in Universal Methods of Design (2019)
summary: Early in a project, each team member lists trends, themes, ideas and key people; the team combines them into one diagram of the design territory to focus research.
description: A territory map is a boundary object made at the very start of a project. Each team member first works alone, listing the trends, themes, ideas and stakeholders they think matter, with supporting stories. The team then shares and discusses these and draws a single combined diagram of the design territory and the future they envision, marking stakeholders to involve. Rather than forcing consensus, it records individual views side by side, which makes differing assumptions visible and gives the team a shared picture to steer research focus and dialogue. Because it captures what the team believes before fieldwork, it should be revisited as research arrives.
steps: Ask each member to prepare, individually, lists of trends, themes, ideas and key people, each with a supporting story.
Share contributions and discuss overlaps and differences.
Draw a combined diagram of the territory and the envisioned future, keeping distinct views visible.
Mark stakeholders and user groups to include in research.
Use the map to plan research focus and questions.
Revisit and redraw the map as findings arrive.
outputs: A territory map of themes, trends, stakeholders and vision, and a list of research priorities.
useWhen: Use it at the start of open-ended or systemic projects, when a team needs a shared frame and wants its assumptions visible before research.
avoidWhen: It reflects the team's assumptions; replace them with evidence through Ethnographic Research or Interviews. For mapping stakeholders' influence specifically, use Stakeholder Mapping.
whyLost: It stayed in design education and academic design practice and is rarely named in industry method lists.
whereToUse: Social innovation, civic and humanitarian design, new-market exploration, and student design projects.
example: A team designing a platform linking residents and refugees maps themes such as language, housing and trust, and adds faith groups as stakeholders nobody had planned to interview.
reference: Hanington, B. and Martin, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Beverly, MA: Rockport Publishers, Method 107, Territory Maps.

name: Testing Against a Benchmark (One-Sample Tests)
origin: Acceptance testing logic from industrial quality control; adapted for UX targets in Sauro & Lewis, Quantifying the User Experience ch. 4
summary: Decides whether a product beats a specific target, such as 80% completion or a SUS of 68, rather than just reporting a score.
description: Teams often set goals like "at least 75% of users complete the task" or "SUS above 68" and then eyeball whether the sample result clears the bar. A one-sample test makes the decision explicit. For completion rates with small samples, the exact (mid-p) binomial test gives the probability of seeing this many successes if the true rate were only at the benchmark. For larger samples a normal approximation works. For continuous measures such as SUS, SEQ or log task times, a one-sample t-test compares the mean to the target. Because the claim is directional (better than the goal), one-tailed tests are appropriate, and the same logic can be read off a confidence interval: the goal is met if it lies below the lower bound.
steps: State the benchmark and direction before collecting data (for example, completion > 70%).
For proportions with n under about 30, run an exact or mid-p binomial test of x successes in n trials against the benchmark p.
For larger samples, use the z test with the normal approximation.
For rating scales and log-transformed times, run a one-sample t-test of the mean against the benchmark value.
Report the one-tailed p-value alongside the confidence interval and state plainly whether the goal was met.
outputs: A yes/no decision on whether a target was met, with the confidence behind it.
useWhen: Release gates, regulated summative validation, and benchmark programmes with agreed targets.
avoidWhen: No meaningful target exists, or the goal was set after seeing the data.
whyLost: UX rarely writes targets down in advance, so there is nothing to test against, and benchmark comparisons get reduced to traffic-light colours.
whereToUse: Medical-device summative tests, enterprise procurement acceptance, OKRs that name UX metrics.
example: A banking app targets 80% success on adding a payee. Twenty-two of 25 succeed (88%); the mid-p binomial test gives p = 0.13, so the team cannot yet claim the target is beaten and extends the sample.
sources: Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Introduction to Statistics: An Excel-Based Approach (Watts, 2022)
Statistics for Marketing and Consumer Research (Mazzocchi, 2008)
Statistical Reasoning in the Behavioral Sciences (King et al., 2011)
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience, 2nd ed., chapter 4.

name: Tests for Equality of Variances (F Ratio, F-max and Bartlett)
aka: Chi-square interval for a standard deviation
origin: Classical normal-theory inference; Maurice Bartlett (1937); H. O. Hartley (F-max, 1950); Levene (1960) and Brown and Forsythe (1974) for robust alternatives
summary: Estimate and compare the variability of outcomes across conditions, treating consistency of performance as a result in its own right rather than only an assumption check.
description: Quality engineering holds that a product must be consistently near target, so variability deserves inference of its own. For one group, a chi-square interval or test bounds the standard deviation. For two groups, the ratio of sample variances is referred to the F distribution. For k groups, Hartley's F-max divides the largest variance by the smallest and compares it with tabled values; Bartlett's test compares a log-variance statistic with chi-square on k - 1 df and handles unequal group sizes. Both are highly sensitive to non-normality, so normality must be checked first, and Levene or Brown-Forsythe tests (based on absolute deviations from group means or medians) are robust alternatives. When variability is itself a response across design factors, analyse ln(s) from at least four repeats per cell. Mason and colleagues advise against using a preliminary variance test to choose between pooled and Welch t-tests; use Welch directly.
steps: Compute the sample standard deviation and size of each group.
For one group, form the chi-square interval or test for the standard deviation against a target.
For two groups, compare the variance ratio with the F distribution.
For k groups, compute F-max (largest over smallest variance) against tabled critical values with v = n - 1, or Bartlett's statistic against chi-square on k - 1 df.
Check normality first; with skewed data such as task times, use Levene or Brown-Forsythe, or analyse log-transformed values.
If variability is a design response, analyse ln(s) with at least four repeats per cell.
outputs: Intervals and tests on standard deviations, and a judgement of whether conditions differ in consistency.
useWhen: Asking whether a redesign makes performance more predictable (task time spread, error variability, latency jitter), or whether rater or device groups differ in consistency.
avoidWhen: As a gatekeeper for choosing a t-test (use Welch's t-test by default, see t-Tests for Comparing Designs (Paired and Two-Sample)); with heavy-tailed data without robust alternatives; or when the means are the only question.
whyLost: UX analysis focuses on mean differences, and variance tests appear only as assumption checks, so the quality-engineering view of consistency as an outcome rarely crosses over.
whereToUse: Task-time benchmarking, latency and performance budgets, comparing inter-rater spread, safety-critical interfaces where predictability matters.
example: Two infusion-pump interfaces have similar mean programming times, but log task times show a standard deviation ratio of 2.3 (Brown-Forsythe p = 0.004). The less variable design is chosen because outliers drive dosing errors.
sources: Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments (Mason et al., 2003)
reference: Mason, R. L., Gunst, R. F., & Hess, J. L. (2003). Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments: With Applications to Engineering and Science (2nd ed.). Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience. pp. 81-99.

name: Text Spacing and Setting for Reading Conditions (measure, leading, tracking, kerning)
aka: Measure (line length) selection with a copyfitting table
Leading selection and vertical rhythm on a baseline unit
Spacing by reading distance (letter, word and line space as one system)
Reading-condition weight compensation (reversed, backlit and small type)
Optical weight adjustment for reversed type
donor: Typography, book design and signage design
origin: Traditional book typography as codified by Robert Bringhurst (1992, v3.0 2004) and Erik Spiekermann (Stop Stealing Sheep, 1993; 4th ed. 2022)
summary: Set line length, leading, word and letter space, kerning and weight as one system for the reading situation, using characters per line, baseline multiples and polarity adjustments.
description: Typographic setting treats spacing as a system tuned to how text will be read. Line length is chosen by characters per line: about 45-75 for single-column continuous text with 66 ideal, 40-50 per column in multi-column layouts, and ragged right below about 40. Leading is the page's rhythmic unit: longer lines, darker or larger-bodied faces, sans serifs and dense capitals need more, and every heading, quotation or figure should consume a whole multiple of it so text stays on the baseline. Long reading wants settled lines and generous line space; scanning text wants short compact lines. Line space must exceed word space. Kerning fixes problem pairs and tracking is used sparingly, since wide letterspacing slows reading. Polarity and lighting change apparent weight: reversed and backlit type looks bolder, so step down a weight and open the tracking, and avoid bold at small sizes where counters fill in.
steps: Classify the reading situation: continuous long reading, scanning, signage or interface labels; polarity (dark on light or reversed); lighting and viewing distance.

Choose face and size, then set the measure to about 45-75 characters (66 ideal) for single columns or 40-50 for multiple columns; on screen, cap text containers in characters (for example a max-width around 66ch).
Choose base leading for the face and measure (routine values 10/12 to 12/15; add lead for long lines, sans serifs or dense capitals) and express all vertical spaces as multiples of it.
Set word space relative to line length and keep line space larger than word space; tighten both for short scanning lines.
Check kerning of problem pairs (V, W, Y combinations, figures before punctuation) and use tracking globally only with care.
For reversed or backlit text, step down one weight and open tracking slightly; avoid heavy weights at small sizes.
Proof in the real medium, size and lighting, and confirm legibility with users where safety or accessibility matters.
outputs: A text setting specification: size/leading x measure, spacing tokens, kerning notes, and weight and tracking per polarity.
useWhen: Use when defining typography for a design system, long-form reading product, dashboard, signage or any interface where text is the main material.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating print ranges as proof of screen readability; confirm with Readability Testing or Reading-Time Paradigms, and check contrast and resizing with an Accessibility Evaluation. Readability Analysis addresses wording, not setting.
whyLost: It survived because typography is core to visual and interface design, carried into CSS units, design tokens and accessibility guidance on line length and spacing.
whereToUse: Design systems, reading and news apps, documentation sites, e-learning, in-car and wayfinding displays, dark-mode themes.
example: A news app caps article width at 66 characters, sets 18/28 px body text with all spacing in multiples of 4 px, and for dark mode uses a lighter weight with slightly opened tracking. A reading test shows fewer line-skip regressions than the old full-width layout.
reference: Bringhurst, R. (2004). The Elements of Typographic Style (version 3.0). Point Roberts, WA: Hartley & Marks, pp. 26-41, 194-205. Spiekermann, E. (2022). Stop Stealing Sheep & Find Out How Type Works (4th ed.). Berlin: p98a.berlin, pp. 23-25, 137-153.

name: Theatre-Based Scenario Elicitation
aka: Dramatised Scenarios and Theatre in Requirements Gathering
origin: Sato and Salvador (1999, focus troupe); Brandt and Grunnet (2000); Newell et al. (2006); Syrdal et al. (2011, robot theatre)
summary: Acted scenarios of future technology use, live or filmed, are shown to potential users who discuss or role-play them to elicit requirements and reactions.
description: Drama gives non-technical audiences something concrete to react to before anything is built. Scenarios of a concept in use are scripted and performed by team members, actors or professional theatre companies, sometimes with props, video or Wizard-of-Oz robots. In the focus troupe form, short vignettes are played to a focus group and discussed one by one. Newell et al. worked with a scriptwriter to make assistive-technology scenarios with human interest, humour and tension; videos had stopping points where older people, carers and designers discussed what was happening. Brandt and Grunnet built simple dramatised scenes from home interviews and later had users role-play with a prototype. Theatre-based HRI puts actors and remote-controlled robots on stage and lets audiences question actors in character. Drama helps people imagine themselves in scenarios and helps designers empathise.
steps: Interview or observe potential users to ground the scenarios in real situations.
Script a few short scenes showing the concept in context, including moments of difficulty; use a professional writer for emotionally complex topics.
Rehearse and perform live, or film the performance with planned stopping points; use Wizard-of-Oz control for robots or devices.
After each scene, facilitate discussion of what happened, where the technology would help or annoy, and what is missing; let audiences question actors in character if useful.
Capture reactions by notes, questionnaires and interviews, comparing across scenes.
Optionally return with a prototype and ask users to role-play scenarios of use in their own setting.
outputs: Requirements, reactions to concepts in context, brainstormed ideas and design concepts, and greater designer empathy.
useWhen: Early concept work with audiences who find abstract descriptions hard, such as older adults, or for technologies like robots and ambient systems that are costly to prototype.
avoidWhen: When scenes risk overselling the concept or when acting quality and tone could drive reactions; designer-written scripts also raise the question of whose voice is represented. Validity data are scarce. For testing real interaction use Wizard of Oz Prototyping or Prototype Testing.
whyLost: It needs scripting and performance skills and preparation time, so it remained in assistive technology and HRI research rather than mainstream UX.
whereToUse: Assistive and ageing technology, social robots, voice and ambient assistants, healthcare services.
example: A travel company films three short scenes of a traveller rebooking a missed connection with a voice assistant; focus groups pause after each, revealing that people want the assistant to speak to gate staff on their behalf.
reference: Newell, A. F., Carmichael, A., Morgan, M. and Dickinson, A. (2006). Methodologies for the use of theatre in requirements gathering and usability studies. Interacting with Computers, 18, 996-1011; Sato, S. and Salvador, T. (1999). Playacting and focus troupes. Interactions, 6(5).

name: Thematic Analysis
donor: Psychology and social science qualitative research
origin: Virginia Braun & Victoria Clarke, 2006 (six-phase method); reflexive TA, 2019
summary: A systematic six-phase method for identifying, developing and reporting patterns of shared meaning (themes) across qualitative data.
description: Thematic analysis identifies, analyses and reports patterns of meaning across a qualitative dataset. Braun and Clarke's six phases are familiarisation, generating initial codes, constructing candidate themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and producing the report. It can be inductive or deductive, semantic or latent, and in its reflexive form treats the researcher's interpretation as a resource rather than bias. A theme is a pattern of shared meaning organised around a central concept, not a topic summary or a frequently mentioned word. Rigour comes from coding the whole dataset systematically, reviewing themes against both coded extracts and the full dataset, writing analytic narrative that does interpretive work beyond quotes, and documenting decisions transparently.
steps: Familiarise yourself with the data by reading transcripts in full and writing a familiarisation memo, without coding yet.
Code the entire dataset systematically, capturing everything potentially relevant, inductively or from theory.
Collate codes into candidate themes organised around a central concept and draw a thematic map.
Review themes against coded extracts and then against the whole dataset, revising until both fit.
Define and name each theme with a short analytic description of its essence and boundaries.
Write the report, weaving analytic narrative with illustrative extracts so the narrative carries the analysis.
outputs: Coded dataset, thematic map, defined and named themes with analytic narratives and supporting extracts.
useWhen: For analysing interview, diary, open-ended survey or field data when you need a flexible, defensible way to report patterns of meaning.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to build an explanatory theory of a process; use grounded theory. For counting frequencies across large text corpora, use content analysis.
whyLost: Still in use, but often only in name: Braun and Clarke's method is the dominant qualitative approach, yet in industry it is frequently reduced to sorting quotes into topic buckets, without systematic coding, theme review or analytic narrative.
whereToUse: Interview and diary data analysis; any qualitative UX research synthesis.
example: A mental health app analyses 20 interviews with lapsed users. Instead of a topic theme like 'notifications', the team develops 'the app as another obligation', which reframes reminders as permission to rest.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 34 — Framework Analysis & Systematic Qualitative Synthesis
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Braun V & Clarke V (2006) Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology 3(2):77-101
Braun V & Clarke V (2019) Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qual Res Sport Exercise Health 11(4)
Braun V & Clarke V (2022) Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide
Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide (Braun & Clarke 2022)
Reflecting on Reflexive Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke 2019)
Braun & Clarke (2006) Using thematic analysis in psychology, Qualitative Research in Psychology
A Worked Example of Braun and Clarke's Approach to Reflexive Thematic Analysis (Byrne, 2022)
Analysing and Presenting Qualitative Data (Burnard et al., 2008)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
A Step-by-Step Process of Thematic Analysis to Develop a Conceptual Model in Qualitative Research (Naeem et al., 2023)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
