example: A claims-processing team times 15 agents through 20 claims each and finds that 31% of handling time is spent re-keying policy numbers between two screens. Auto-populating the field cuts mean handling time by 48 seconds per claim.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Taylor FW (1911) The Principles of Scientific Management
Barnes RM (1980) Motion and Time Study: Design and Measurement of Work
reference: Taylor FW (1911) The Principles of Scientific Management. Harper & Brothers.

name: Time-Locked Signal Averaging with Residual-Noise Estimation
origin: Classical evoked-potential practice (Dawson, 1954, onwards); presented by van Drongelen (2018)
summary: Average many signal epochs locked to a repeated event so a small consistent response emerges from noise, and estimate how much noise remains so the average can be trusted.
description: Signal averaging recovers small responses buried in noise, such as event-related potentials in EEG or phasic pupil and skin-conductance responses. It assumes the signal is consistent across trials, its timing is known, and the noise is random, zero-mean and uncorrelated with the signal. Averaging N trials reduces residual noise variance by a factor of N, so noise amplitude falls with the square root of N. Van Drongelen gives three ways to estimate the noise left in an average: the prestimulus baseline, bootstrap averages built from random triggers, and the plus-minus average, which inverts every other trial so the signal cancels and only noise remains. Separate odd and even averages check consistency. Periodic noise such as mains hum is enhanced rather than averaged away when the stimulus rate divides evenly into 50 or 60 Hz, so intervals should be jittered.
steps: Record repeated trials, each cut as an epoch time-locked to a trigger (stimulus onset or user event).
Randomise the inter-stimulus interval or use a non-integer rate (for example 7.7 Hz rather than 10 Hz) to avoid locking to mains interference.
Average the epochs sample by sample to form the average waveform per condition.
Form separate odd-trial and even-trial averages; real components must appear in both.
Estimate residual noise from the prestimulus period, random-trigger bootstrap averages or the plus-minus average.
Compute SNR as root-mean-square of the average over that of the residual noise, and plot it against trial count to decide how many trials are enough.
outputs: Average waveforms per condition and channel, residual noise estimates and SNR against number of trials.
useWhen: Analysing EEG, pupil, EMG or skin-conductance responses to repeated, precisely timed events such as notifications, errors or stimuli in a UX study.
avoidWhen: Avoid when responses vary in latency or form from trial to trial, or events are not precisely timed; single-trial or time-frequency methods suit those. Avoid drawing conclusions from averages whose residual noise has not been estimated.
whyLost: It is standard in neurophysiology labs but UX biometric studies often rely on vendor software and report averages without noise estimates.
whereToUse: EEG and pupillometry studies of notifications and alerts, error-related responses to interface failures, attention studies in games and VR.
example: A study of error feedback in a banking app records EEG while 20 participants meet 60 scripted errors each. Plus-minus averages show the residual noise falls below a third of the error-related negativity after about 40 trials, so the remaining trials are used for the comparison between designs.
reference: van Drongelen, W. (2018). Signal Processing for Neuroscientists (2nd ed.). London: Academic Press, ch. 4.

name: Time-on-Task Measurement
aka: Completion time outlier and speeder rules
origin: Long-standing usability-testing practice, codified by Tullis and Albert
summary: Measure the time from task start to task end under defined clock rules, clean outliers and speeders, and report skew-robust summaries, time bands and threshold attainment.
description: Task time, the time elapsed between the start and end of a task, matters most for frequently repeated tasks, though faster is not always better in games or learning. Rigour lies in rules fixed before data collection: when the clock starts (participant finishes reading the task) and stops (stops interacting or clicks an answer button), whether only successful tasks count, and how outliers and speeders are removed. Because times are skewed, report the median or geometric mean alongside the mean and confidence interval. Outliers can be screened with mean plus three standard deviations or the Q3 + 1.5 IQR rule; speeders faster than the minimum expert time are removed, and online participants who speed on several tasks are dropped. Further views are time bands and the percentage of participants finishing under a threshold such as twice an expert's time.
steps: Define start and end rules before the study, such as start when the participant finishes reading and end when they click an answer button.

Collect times with a logger, video timestamps or the testing tool; ask participants to work as quickly and accurately as possible without saying they are timed, and avoid concurrent think-aloud if time is a key measure.
Decide which tasks count: all tasks if participants chose when to give up, otherwise successful tasks only.
Screen outliers (above mean + 3 SD, or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR) and speeders faster than the minimum expert time; drop participants who speed on several tasks.
Summarise per task with mean and confidence interval plus median or geometric mean; add time bands and the percentage under a threshold such as twice expert time.
Compare designs with t-tests or ANOVA on log-transformed times.
outputs: Per-task central tendency with confidence intervals, distributions by time band, percentage meeting a threshold, and a cleaned dataset.
useWhen: Benchmarking efficiency, comparing designs for frequent tasks, or checking against efficiency targets.
avoidWhen: Avoid in think-aloud formative tests where talking inflates times, and for tasks where speed is not a goal; use task success or satisfaction measures instead.
whyLost: It survived as a core usability metric, though the clock and cleaning rules are often left undefined.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflows, call-centre tools, checkout flows, clinical systems, competitive benchmarks.
example: An insurer's unmoderated benchmark of 298 people shows a mean of 115 seconds but a long tail. The IQR rule cuts at 318 seconds and an expert-time floor removes 8% as speeders before medians are compared.
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience, 3rd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 4, pp. 82-91.

name: Time-Ordered Matrix
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994), chapter 5, section C, illustrated by changes to an innovation over several years of use.
summary: A matrix with columns as successive time periods and rows as components, roles, settings or activities, used to see when changes occurred and to spot gradual drifts.
description: The time-ordered matrix is the general form of the event listing. Its columns are time periods in sequence, and its rows depend on what is being studied: components of an innovation, roles, settings, event types or activity types. In the book's example the rows were the official components of a work-experience programme plus 'other aspects' that emerged in fieldwork, and the columns were the planning period and three school years. Each cell holds a short description of a change reported and confirmed by at least one other person; a blank cell is meaningful because it shows stability. Reading across rows reveals 'drifts', such as stiffer demands, more control and increased routinisation. The analyst then returns to the notes to explain them, and can condense the matrix into a summary table that names each drift with a gerund ('tightening up') and counts mentions. The book advises choosing time periods fine enough to keep sequences apart, looking for timing, sequence and stability, and expecting about two or three hours to assemble once notes are coded. In UX this suits tracking how a feature, workaround or team practice evolves across releases or months of use.
steps: Decide the rows: product components, user roles, settings or activity types.
Choose time periods as columns, fine enough to separate the sequences that matter.
Set a decision rule for entry, for example a change counts if one other person confirms it and nobody contradicts it.
Enter brief descriptions of changes; leave cells blank where nothing changed.
Read across rows for drifts, name them, and return to the notes for explanations.
Condense into a summary table of drifts with counts and significance if the full matrix is too busy.
outputs: A period-by-component matrix of changes, a list of named drifts, and a summary table.
useWhen: You have longitudinal qualitative data (repeat interviews, diaries, release notes) and want to see what changed when.
avoidWhen: Data come from a single time point, or rows are too vague to separate changes meaningfully.
whyLost: Longitudinal UX research is rare, and when done it is usually reported as per-wave themes rather than as a single change matrix.
whereToUse: Diary studies, longitudinal adoption research, design system evolution, post-launch follow-ups.
example: Across four quarterly interviews with 12 users of a project-management tool, rows list features (boards, automations, reporting, integrations, permissions) and columns list quarters. Reading across shows a drift from personalised boards to standardised team templates and a growing use of permissions to lock fields, which the notes link to managers asserting control after a missed deadline.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Time-series decomposition and forecasting
origin: Classical decomposition; Census X-11; Holt and Winters exponential smoothing; Box and Jenkins ARIMA
summary: Separates a metric's history into trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular parts, and forecasts it by smoothing level, trend and season or by regression on its own lags.
description: A time series is modelled as trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular components, combined additively or multiplicatively. Centred moving averages over one seasonal cycle (4 quarters, 12 months, 7 days) remove seasonality and noise to reveal trend. The seasonal index method expresses each observation as a percentage of its centred moving average, takes the median per season, rescales to average 100, and divides the series by these indices to seasonally adjust it; X-11 methods allow seasonality to evolve. For forecasting, simple exponential smoothing weights the newest observation against the previous level with constant alpha; Holt-Winters adds trend (beta) and seasonal (gamma) recursions. Autoregressive models regress the series on its own lags, choosing order by testing down from a maximum; ARIMA extends this through iterative identification, estimation and checking. All methods assume past patterns continue, so structural breaks must be watched for.
steps: Plot the series and judge whether trend, seasonality, cycles and breaks are present.
Compute centred moving averages over one seasonal period to estimate the trend-cycle.
Express each observation as a percentage of its centred moving average, take the median per season, rescale to average 100, and divide the series by these seasonal indices.
Check the adjusted series for leftover seasonality; if the pattern evolves, use X-11 or STL-type decomposition.

To forecast, choose simple exponential smoothing (no trend or season), Holt-Winters (trend and season), or an AR or ARIMA model, setting smoothing constants or lag order by minimising one-step forecast errors.
Generate forecasts with intervals, compare them with holdout periods, and review them against known launches, campaigns or breaks.
outputs: Trend-cycle series, seasonal indices, a seasonally adjusted series, and forecasts with fitted parameters.
useWhen: Reading weekly or monthly product metrics, survey trackers or support volumes that have strong seasonality, and setting baselines or targets.
avoidWhen: Short series (fewer than two or three seasonal cycles), or estimating the causal effect of a launch (use interrupted time series or Bayesian structural time series). Extrapolating fixed trends through structural breaks is risky.
whyLost: Forecasting lives in finance, operations and data science; UX metrics are often read week-on-week without separating seasonality, which leads to false alarms and false wins.
whereToUse: Product analytics dashboards, NPS and CSAT tracking, support contact forecasting, retail and travel products with strong seasons.
example: A travel app's satisfaction score dips every January. Seasonal indices show a January index of 94, so the seasonally adjusted series is flat; a Holt-Winters forecast sets the expected range for next quarter, against which a new booking flow is judged.
sources: Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Newbold, P., Carlson, W. L. and Thorne, B. M. (2022). Statistics for Business and Economics (10th ed., Global Edition). Harlow: Pearson Education, pp. 689-719.

name: Time-Use Survey
donor: Sociology, official statistics and leisure studies
origin: Multinational Comparative Time-Budget Research Project in the 1960s (Szalai, 1972); earlier BBC listening studies in Britain in the 1930s; national time-use surveys described by Veal and Darcy
summary: Respondents keep a detailed diary of everything they do over one or two days, so researchers can see how time is shared between all activities.
description: A time-use or time-budget survey collects information on how people allocate their time across all activities. It is usually run as the main or a subsidiary part of a household survey: as well as answering a questionnaire, respondents complete a diary covering one or two days. They record their waking activities with starting and stopping times, where each activity took place, with whom, and sometimes whether they saw it as paid work, domestic work or leisure. Secondary activities, such as listening to music while exercising, are also recorded. Because the diary covers the whole day rather than asking about one activity, it captures activities done briefly and often, and avoids the over-reporting that direct questions can produce, though the short reference period means rarer activities are missed. Veal and Darcy note that coding and analysis are demanding, since hundreds of activities must be coded across many quarter-hour periods. For UX the method shows where a product sits within the whole of a person's day, what it competes with for time, and what people are doing at the same moment, which a product-specific diary study does not reveal.
steps: Define the population, the diary days to sample (weekdays and weekends) and the time slots, for example quarter-hours.
Design the diary with columns for main activity, secondary activity, location, who else was present and any device used.
Recruit a representative sample, usually alongside a short background questionnaire.
Ask respondents to complete the diary on the assigned days, recording as they go rather than at the end.
Code free-text activities into an activity classification, including categories relevant to your product.
Aggregate minutes per activity, participation rates and timing profiles across the day, by segment.
Interpret where the product's use fits, what it displaces or accompanies, and which time windows matter.
outputs: Coded diary data giving minutes per activity, the share of people doing each activity, time-of-day profiles and co-occurrence of main and secondary activities.
useWhen: You need to understand the whole daily context of use, competition for time or media multitasking, rather than behaviour within your product alone.
avoidWhen: The behaviour of interest is rare or irregular, the sample cannot sustain the diary burden, or you only need in-product usage, which logs provide more cheaply.
whyLost: UX diary studies focus on one product and are qualitative, and product analytics measure in-app time directly, so the whole-day, statistically coded time-budget diary remained the domain of national statistics offices and leisure researchers.
whereToUse: Media and streaming, fitness and health apps, smart home, mobile and wearable products, attention-economy research, public sector digital services.
example: A fitness app team analyses two-day time-use diaries from 400 adults and finds that the evening slot they target is dominated by television watching with a phone as a secondary activity, while short morning commutes have unused time, prompting a test of five-minute commute workouts.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Szalai, A. (ed.) (1972) The Use of Time: Daily Activities of Urban and Suburban Populations in Twelve Countries. The Hague: Mouton.

name: Timeline Method (River of Life)
origin: Participatory rural appraisal and narrative psychology traditions; timeline interviewing (Adriansen, 2012)
summary: Participants draw a timeline of their experience, marking events, turning points and emotional highs and lows, making the temporal structure of their relationship with a product or condition visible.
description: The timeline method and its variants (river of life, experience timeline, journey timeline) ask participants to construct a visual representation of their experience over time — marking significant events, turning points, high and low periods, and their emotional quality. Unlike verbal retrospective accounts (which tend to flatten temporal complexity and highlight only the most salient moments), timeline methods make the temporal structure of experience visible and discussable.
steps: Materials: Large paper, markers, stickers, printed icons, or a digital template. The format should feel generative, not constraining.
Calibration anchor: Define the time period: 'Draw your experience from when you first started using [product] to today.' Or: 'Map a typical week of [activity].'
Dual-axis variant: Horizontal axis = time. Vertical axis = intensity, satisfaction, or emotional quality. This produces a graph-like timeline that makes both sequence and experience quality visible.
Event marking: Ask participants to mark the significant events, changes, and turning points in the timeline. Each marked event becomes a prompt for narrative probing.
Group timelines: Comparing timelines across participants reveals: shared critical periods, divergent trajectories, and the relationship between life events and product experience.
outputs: Participant-drawn timelines, interview narratives, critical incidents and turning points, emotional curves, and cross-participant patterns of shared moments.
useWhen: The relationship with a product or condition unfolds over months or years, such as adoption, churn, chronic illness or financial change, and you need retrospective structure quickly.
avoidWhen: You need accurate recall of fine detail or real-time data; use a diary study or Descriptive Experience Sampling. Avoid treating drawn curves as quantitative measurements.
whyLost: It largely survives as journey mapping, but journey maps are usually built by teams for users rather than drawn by participants, losing the participant-led temporal account.
whereToUse: Subscription and retention research, onboarding to mastery journeys, chronic health management, financial life events, and B2B customer lifecycle.
example: Eleven former subscribers of a meal-kit service draw rivers of their subscription. Most show a dip at week 3 tied to repetitive recipes, not price, which shifts retention efforts to recipe variety.
reference: Adriansen, H. K. (2012). Timeline interviews: A tool for conducting life history research. Qualitative Studies, 3(1), 40-55.

name: Tool adoption zone mapping
origin: Lev Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, 1930s (published in English 1978); scaffolding by Wood, Bruner and Ross, 1976
summary: Maps which product capabilities users can master alone, which they can master with support, and which are beyond reach, to design scaffolding and staged adoption.
description: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do unaided and what they can do with guidance. Applied to tool adoption, it distinguishes three zones for each capability: independent use, use with scaffolding (help, coaching, templates, a colleague) and out of reach for now. Mapping these zones by user group shows where onboarding and support should focus and which advanced features need staged exposure. Wood, Bruner and Ross's scaffolding functions, such as reducing degrees of freedom and highlighting critical features, translate into design patterns. Rigour comes from observing actual performance at each level of support rather than relying on self-report, and from re-mapping over time as zones shift.
steps: List the product capabilities relevant to adoption, ordered by complexity.
Recruit users across experience levels (for example 3-5 per level) and observe them attempting tasks unaided.
Introduce graded prompts (hint, demonstration, step-by-step guidance) and record the least support at which each user succeeds.
Assign each capability-user pair to a zone: independent, scaffolded or out of reach.
Design scaffolding for scaffolded-zone capabilities and defer out-of-reach capabilities to later stages.
Re-map after weeks of use to track zone movement and fade scaffolding where independence is reached.
outputs: A capability-by-user zone map, the support level needed per capability, scaffolding designs, and an adoption roadmap.
useWhen: When introducing complex tools to professionals, designing onboarding and training, or planning progressive disclosure.
avoidWhen: When products are simple enough for immediate independent use; standard onboarding tests suffice.
whyLost: ZPD is central in education but rarely operationalised in UX, where onboarding is designed without measured support levels.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics training, enterprise software rollout, developer tools, AI assistants, and educational products.
example: Junior surgeons can dock the robot independently but need step prompts for instrument exchange and cannot yet use dual-console mode. The team adds guided exchange and hides dual-console mode until 20 cases.
sources: Newell, A., Unified Theories of Cognition (1990)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
reference: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in Society: The Development of Higher Psychological Processes. Harvard University Press.

name: Toolkits for User Innovation
origin: Eric von Hippel and Ralph Katz (2002); Franke and Piller (2004); Reichwald and Piller
summary: Split development into need-intensive and solution-intensive tasks and give users a toolkit to do the need-intensive design themselves within a feasible solution space.
description: Toolkits rest on the idea that information about needs and context of use is 'sticky': costly to transfer from users to producers. Rather than researching needs and designing for users, a producer partitions development into solution-information-intensive tasks it keeps and need-information-intensive tasks it hands to users, along with a kit of tools to perform them. User designs then return to the producer for manufacture. Good toolkits support trial-and-error learning, define a feasible solution space, are easy to use, offer libraries of modules, and transfer the user's design cleanly to production. Gaubinger et al. distinguish innovation toolkits, co-design toolkits (modular, like Lego) and idea-transfer toolkits. Evidence from custom watches showed willingness to pay for self-designed products about twice that for the best-selling equivalent.
steps: Analyse the development task and separate need-intensive subtasks from solution-intensive ones.
Define the feasible solution space the producer can actually make.
Build a toolkit for the need-intensive subtasks with trial-and-error feedback, modules and a usable interface.
Release it to users and let them design their own solutions.
Transfer user designs to production without loss.
Analyse the designs for patterns in heterogeneous needs and feed them into the standard range.
outputs: User-created designs, a working configurator or toolkit, and evidence of heterogeneous needs and willingness to pay.
useWhen: Use it when needs are highly heterogeneous and hard to articulate, and the product can be modularised, as in custom hardware, configurable software or mass customisation.
avoidWhen: It hands design to users rather than understanding them; when you need to learn why needs differ use Interviews or Contextual Inquiry. For small-group collaborative making, Participatory Design or PICTIVE Participatory Prototyping fit better.
whyLost: It is well established in innovation management and mass customisation but rarely framed as a UX practice, so UX teams meet it only as configurator design.
whereToUse: Product configurators, low-code builders, game modding, custom hardware, and enterprise template systems.
example: A sports brand releases a shoe configurator; analysis of 40,000 saved designs shows many wide-fit requests, which leads to a standard wide range.
sources: Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: von Hippel, E. and Katz, R. (2002). Shifting innovation to users via toolkits. Management Science, 48(7), 821-833.

name: Top Task Analysis
origin: Gerry McGovern (2010, The Stranger's Long Neck); used for benchmark task selection by Sauro
summary: Asks many users to pick their few most important tasks from a long list, revealing the small set that matters most.
description: Most products have a "long neck": a handful of tasks account for most of what users care about, followed by a long tail of trivial ones. Top task analysis compiles an exhaustive list of 50 to 100 candidate tasks from analytics, search logs, support and stakeholders, then asks a large sample to vote for their top five. Because people must choose quickly from a long randomised list, votes reflect genuine priority. The top 5 to 10 tasks typically receive about a quarter to half of all votes. Sauro uses it to choose which tasks to benchmark; McGovern uses it to focus whole organisations.
steps: Gather every candidate task from analytics, search, support tickets, competitors and stakeholders.
Consolidate into 50 to 100 clearly worded, non-overlapping tasks in users' language.
Survey a large representative sample (several hundred) asking each person to choose up to five tasks from the randomised list.
Rank tasks by vote share and plot the long-neck curve.
Use the top tasks to focus design, navigation and benchmarking, and the tail to decide what to de-emphasise.
outputs: A ranked list of the tasks that matter most, and a clear tail of those that do not.
useWhen: Large sites or products with sprawling content, before a redesign or benchmark.
avoidWhen: Small products with only a few tasks, or when you cannot reach a large sample.
whyLost: Not lost, but often replaced with stakeholder opinion or analytics page views, which measure what people do now rather than what they need.
whereToUse: Government sites, intranets, university and enterprise portals, SaaS feature prioritisation.
example: A council website surveys 1,800 residents; "pay council tax" and "report a missed bin" take 31% of votes, while 40 news and events tasks share 3%.
sources: Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: McGovern, G. (2010). The Stranger's Long Neck. A&C Black.

name: Top-Box Analysis of Rating Scales
origin: Market research dashboard practice; analysis guidance in Sauro & Lewis (2012) chapter 4
summary: Converts rating responses to the share choosing the top one or two options, then analyses that share as a proportion.
description: Dashboards often report "percent who agree" (top-two-box on a 5-point scale) rather than means. To test a claim such as "at least 75% agree", convert 4s and 5s to 1 and everything else to 0, then use the binomial methods for completion rates: a mid-p test against the benchmark and an adjusted-Wald interval. Sauro and Lewis show the trade-off clearly: converting discards intensity, so the same data that gives a 72.5% chance of meeting the goal as top-box gives 81.4% when analysed as a mean with a t-test. Top-box is easy to communicate but needs larger samples to detect changes, so analyse raw means where you can and report top-box where dashboards require it.
steps: Decide the top-box rule before analysis (for example 4 or 5 on a 5-point scale).
Convert each response to 1 or 0.
Compute the proportion with an adjusted-Wald interval.
Test against any benchmark with the mid-p binomial test for small samples.
Also report the mean and its interval so intensity is not lost.
outputs: The share of respondents in the top box(es) with an interval, and a benchmark test.
useWhen: Stakeholders or dashboards define targets as percentages of agreement.
avoidWhen: You want to detect small improvements with small samples; use means.
whyLost: Not lost, but usually reported without intervals and without acknowledging the lost information.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction dashboards, NPS-style reporting, survey summaries.
example: Ten of twelve participants agree they feel confident buying on a site (83%), but the 80% interval of 65% to 93% includes the 75% goal, so the claim is not yet supported.
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2012). Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 4.

name: Topic labelling
origin: Topic interpretation practices in computational social science (e.g. DiMaggio, Nag and Blei, 2013); automated labelling by Lau et al., 2011
summary: Giving each machine-derived topic a meaningful, defensible name by reading its top words and representative documents, ideally with multiple analysts and documented rationale.
description: Topic models output word lists and document weights, not meanings. Labelling is the interpretive step that turns them into research findings, and it is where most errors enter: labels based on top words alone can misrepresent what documents actually say. A rigorous protocol has at least two analysts read top words, distinctive words (e.g. FREX or c-TF-IDF) and 10-20 representative documents per topic, independently propose labels and short definitions, reconcile disagreements and mark topics that are incoherent or artefactual. Large language models can propose candidate labels, but analysts should verify them against documents. Labels should be descriptive rather than prematurely evaluative.
steps: For each topic, extract top words, distinctive words and the 10-20 highest-weighted documents.
Have two analysts independently write a label (2-6 words) and a one-sentence definition from the documents, not only the words.
Compare labels, discuss disagreements and record the agreed label with rationale.
Mark topics as coherent, mixed or junk (e.g. greetings, transcription artefacts) and exclude junk from reporting.
Optionally use an LLM to propose labels from the same evidence, and accept them only after analyst verification.
Publish a topic codebook with labels, definitions, example quotes and prevalence.
outputs: A topic codebook with labels, definitions, quality ratings and example quotes.
useWhen: After any topic model or clustering of UX text, before results are shared with stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Not needed if topics are only used as machine features. Avoid presenting labels as themes without interpretive analysis of their content.
whyLost: Labelling is often done hastily by one person from top words, so the interpretive rigour of qualitative coding was never carried over to computational outputs.
whereToUse: Feedback analysis programmes, research repositories and AI-assisted synthesis.
example: A topic with top words 'card, wait, week, arrive' is first labelled 'shipping delays'. Reading documents shows it concerns physical debit card delivery during onboarding, so it is relabelled 'debit card arrival wait' and routed to the onboarding team.
sources: DiMaggio, P., Nag, M. & Blei, D. (2013) Exploiting affinities between topic modeling and the sociological perspective on culture. Poetics
Lau, J. H. et al. (2011) Automatic labelling of topic models. ACL
Saldaña, J. (2021) The Coding Manual for Qualitative Researchers, 4th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C11 — Topic Modelling at Scale — LDA, BERTopic & Semantic Clustering
reference: DiMaggio, P., Nag, M. & Blei, D. (2013) Exploiting affinities between topic modeling and the sociological perspective on culture. Poetics 41(6)

name: Topics on Trial (Knowledge-to-Skill Content Pruning)
aka: Topics on Trial and Knowledge-to-Skill Mapping
Knowledge board to skills board mapping
origin: Kathy Sierra (2015)
summary: Prune what users are asked to learn by challenging every topic with Why, So what and Who cares, then cutting knowledge that maps to no needed skill.
description: Sierra argues that people filter dry, just-in-case knowledge as noise and that most manuals, onboarding and courses teach too much too early. Two linked procedures cut content back. In Topics on Trial the team plays sceptic towards every topic, fact and procedure: it asks Why? So what? Who cares? until a compelling reason emerges, and rejects the topic if none does ('it is in all the books' does not count). In knowledge-to-skill mapping the team writes Knowledge cards (things users do not know) and Skill cards (things users cannot yet do), and links each Knowledge card to a skill that is impossible without it. Unmapped knowledge either reveals a missing skill or, more often, should be removed. The same questioning chain is used to rewrite help and FAQ content so the consequence comes first.
steps: List every topic, fact and procedure that the product, onboarding or documentation expects users to learn.
Interrogate each item with Why? So what? Who cares?, and reject any item without a compelling answer.
Write a Knowledge card for each surviving item and a Skill card for each thing users must be able to do.
Map each Knowledge card to a Skill card it is strictly needed for.
For unmapped Knowledge, check whether a Skill card is missing; otherwise cut it or move it to an appendix (rare exceptions: required by others, or intrinsically enriching).
Deliver the remaining knowledge just in time, and where it must be given in advance, rewrite it to lead with the consequence.
outputs: A pruned, skill-linked knowledge set and rewritten instructional content that leads with consequences.
useWhen: Use it when onboarding, help content, training or documentation has grown bloated and the team must decide what users actually need to learn.
avoidWhen: It relies on team judgement; to find out what users genuinely struggle with use Documentation Usability Testing, Cognitive Task Analysis or observation of real use first. Do not prune safety-critical or regulatory content on this basis alone.
whyLost: It appears as a design exercise in a popular book rather than as a named method, and content decisions in product teams are rarely made this explicitly.
whereToUse: Onboarding flows, in-app help, developer documentation, enterprise training and complex B2B tools.
example: A photo-editing SaaS lists 40 onboarding topics; trial and mapping cut them to 12 tied to the first three skills new users need. A warning about layer locking is rewritten to start with 'otherwise your edits are lost'.
reference: Sierra, K. (2015) Badass: Making Users Awesome. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media. pp. 263-273.

name: Topological Analysis of Information Spaces
origin: Henri Poincaré, 1890s; topological data analysis by Carlsson, Edelsbrunner and others, 2000s
summary: Examines properties of an information or navigation space that survive deformation, such as connectedness, loops and holes, to reveal structural gaps and dead ends.
description: Topology studies properties preserved under continuous deformation: whether a space is connected, how many loops or holes it has, which regions are reachable from which. Applied to information spaces, it abstracts away from exact layout and asks about the shape of navigation: are there isolated regions, cycles that trap users, or holes where expected connections are missing? Topological data analysis extends this to high-dimensional usage data, for example finding the shape of user journeys or content similarity spaces using persistent homology or Mapper. The method is rigorous when the space is formally defined (as a graph or point cloud), topological features are computed rather than eyeballed, and features are checked for persistence across scales so that noise is not mistaken for structure.
steps: Define the space formally: a navigation graph, a content similarity space or a point cloud of user journey features.
Compute basic topological properties such as connected components and cycles.
For high-dimensional data, apply topological data analysis (e.g. Mapper or persistent homology) across scales.
Retain features that persist across a wide range of scales and discard short-lived ones as noise.
Interpret features as UX structures: isolated sections, loops, missing bridges between content clusters.
Validate interpretations with path analysis or tree testing and propose structural fixes.
outputs: Topological summary of the information space, persistence diagrams or Mapper graphs, list of disconnected regions and structural gaps.
useWhen: Large content estates, knowledge bases, VR or spatial environments, and exploratory analysis of complex journey data.
avoidWhen: Small sites or apps where a sitemap review suffices; use graph analysis or tree testing for routine IA questions.
whyLost: Latent: Academic; potential in graph-based navigation analysis and spatial computing.
whereToUse: Navigation graph analysis; VR environment design; abstract information space mapping.
example: A clinical knowledge base with 40,000 articles was analysed with Mapper on article similarity and link data. It found a cluster of paediatric dosing content with no links into the main graph, explaining why clinicians rarely reached it.
reference: Carlsson, G. (2009). Topology and data. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 46(2), 255-308.

name: Total Survey Error Framework
origin: Groves, 1989; Groves et al., 2009
summary: Audits a survey for every source of error (coverage, sampling, nonresponse, measurement, processing) rather than sampling error alone, to design and interpret UX surveys defensibly.
description: The total survey error (TSE) framework, associated with Robert Groves, decomposes the difference between a survey estimate and the true population value into distinct sources. On the representation side are coverage error (the frame misses parts of the population), sampling error, and nonresponse error; on the measurement side are validity problems, measurement error from question wording, mode and respondents, and processing error in coding and editing. Applied to UX surveys, TSE shifts attention from margin of error, which reflects only sampling, to the often larger biases from who is invited and who responds and how questions are understood. Rigour comes from auditing each source at design time, collecting paradata, and testing for bias with follow-up samples.
steps: TSE audit for any UX survey:
Coverage error — who is excluded from the sampling frame? Users who never complete tasks? Low-literacy users?
(2) Sampling error — is the sample representative of the population? Compute design effect if cluster sampling.
(3) Nonresponse error — who declines to respond? Is there a pattern?
(4) Measurement error — do items measure what they intend? (cognitive interview pre-testing).
(5) Processing error — coding/data entry errors. Estimate the magnitude of each error type and prioritize the largest.
outputs: An error-source audit, design changes to reduce the largest errors, nonresponse and coverage analyses, and honest statements of what results can support.
useWhen: Designing or interpreting any consequential UX survey: satisfaction tracking, NPS programmes, market sizing, or surveys with low response rates or convenience samples.
avoidWhen: Overkill for quick internal pulse checks with no inferential claims. Not a replacement for qualitative work when constructs are still unclear.
whyLost: UX surveys are run as quick tools; survey methodology as a discipline remains in social statistics and official statistics agencies.
whereToUse: UX survey design and analysis, benchmarking study methodology, longitudinal survey programs, NPS validity assessment.
example: A SaaS company's in-app satisfaction survey shows 82% satisfied; a TSE audit reveals coverage error (only active users see it) and nonresponse bias, and an email sample of churned users reduces the estimate to 64%.
sources: Enhancing UX Research with the Total Survey Error Framework (Das, 2024)
The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Groves RM, Fowler FJ, Couper MP, Lepkowski JM, Singer E & Tourangeau R (2009) Survey Methodology. 2nd ed. Wiley

name: Touch Input Efficiency Review
aka: Touch input efficiency review (garbage taps and form pruning)
origin: Josh Clark (2015), with examples such as Square's single-field card entry
summary: Walk a touch flow, classify each tap as quality or garbage, and remove avoidable taps, fields and typing through better list views, inference, autofill and input controls.
description: Clark argues that tap quality matters more than tap count: a quality tap yields information, completes a step or delights, while a garbage tap could have been avoided. The review walks a task on a device and records every tap, swipe and keyboard summon. Primary actions and must-know data move into list views, with detail behind progressive disclosure. Forms get the hardest scrutiny, since length is a common reason for abandoned checkouts: merge multi-field data and parse it on the server, delete unneeded fields, infer what is known (city from postcode, card type from number), collapse card details into one field, offer one-tap suggestions and autofill before the keyboard, set the input type for the right keyboard, replace long selects with type-ahead, short ones with exposed buttons and small ranges with steppers, and replace confirmation dialogs with a deliberate gesture or undo.
steps: Walk the task on a real touch device and record every tap, swipe and keyboard summon.
Classify each interaction as a quality tap (yields information, progress or delight) or a garbage tap (avoidable).
Move primary actions and key summary data into list views and push detail behind progressive disclosure.
For each form field: merge multi-part data, delete unnecessary fields, infer known answers and collapse numeric sequences such as card details.
Before each keyboard appears, offer single-tap suggestions, autofill or device data; where typing is needed, set the input type for the correct keyboard.
Replace long select menus with type-ahead, short ones with exposed options and small number ranges with steppers.
Replace OK/Cancel confirmations with a deliberate gesture or undo, and record before and after tap counts.
outputs: A shortened flow and form specification with before and after tap and field counts.
useWhen: Use when mobile checkout, sign-up or data-entry flows have high abandonment, or before shipping any touch form.
avoidWhen: Avoid optimising tap count blindly: progressive disclosure adds taps but keeps screens clear. Confirm the gains with Mobile Device Usability Testing or Funnel Analysis; for formal time predictions use the Keystroke-Level Model (KLM).
whyLost: It survived because form pruning and input optimisation have direct, measurable effects on mobile conversion.
whereToUse: Mobile checkout, sign-up, booking, banking transfers, field-data capture apps.
example: A jeweller's 40-field mobile checkout is reviewed: billing address defaults to shipping, city is inferred from postcode, card entry becomes one numeric field, and quantity becomes a stepper. Fields drop to 14 and mobile checkout completion rises.
reference: Clark, J. (2015). Designing for Touch. New York: A Book Apart, ch. 3.

name: Touch Target Fitts' Law Calibration for Mobile
origin: Paul Fitts (1954); touch extensions such as Bi, Li and Zhai's FFitts law (2013); design guidance by Josh Clark (2015)
summary: Calibrates Fitts' law for touch by measuring effective target size, finger imprecision and posture on real devices, producing evidence-based minimum target sizes and spacing.
description: Fitts' law predicts movement time from the distance to a target and its width (MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1)). On touchscreens the standard form breaks down because finger contact is imprecise and occludes the target, so effective width depends on finger pad size, posture (one thumb versus two hands), device size, grip and feedback. Bi, Li and Zhai's FFitts law adds an absolute imprecision term to the target width. Calibration studies have participants tap targets of varied size and distance on the actual device and posture, measuring time and the spread of touch points to estimate effective width and error rates. The results set minimum target sizes and spacing for a given acceptable error rate and reveal thumb-reach zones, replacing generic platform guidelines with evidence for the product's own users.
steps: Measure empirical error rates for touch targets at sizes from 5mm to 15mm in your specific product context.
Fit a logistic regression: P(error) = f(target_size, user_group).
Identify the target size at which P(error) < 0.05 for your target user group.
Compare to: Apple HIG (44pt = 7.7mm), Google Material (48dp = 9mm), WCAG 2.5.5 (24×24px minimum).
Your empirically derived minimum may differ from all guidelines.
outputs: Fitted Fitts' parameters for the device and posture, touch-point dispersion, error rate by target size, minimum size and spacing recommendations, and thumb-reach maps.
useWhen: Mobile apps with dense controls, one-handed use, older users or users with tremor, kiosks, in-car touchscreens and wearables.
avoidWhen: When platform minimums (44 pt or 48 dp) are already met with generous spacing and errors are low; standard usability testing suffices.
whyLost: Platform guidelines replaced measurement, so teams apply fixed minimum sizes without calibrating for their users, devices or postures.
whereToUse: Mobile UX design, touchscreen accessibility, wearable UX, kiosk design for diverse user populations.
example: A ride-hailing app's driver interface is used one-handed in a dashboard mount. A calibration study with 16 drivers shows a 7 mm target yields 9% errors at the top of the screen, so critical buttons are enlarged to 11 mm and moved into the thumb zone.
sources: Bi, Li & Zhai, FFitts law: Modeling finger touch with Fitts' law (CHI 2013)
Parhi, Karlson & Bederson, Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices (MobileHCI 2006)
reference: Fitts PM (1954) The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology 47(6):381-391

name: Toulmin Argument Analysis
origin: Stephen Toulmin, 1958 (The Uses of Argument)
summary: Breaks arguments into claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal, used to audit research findings and to analyse how users or AI systems justify conclusions.
description: Toulmin modelled practical arguments on legal reasoning: a Claim is supported by Grounds (data), connected by a Warrant (the inferential rule), supported by Backing, limited by a Qualifier ('probably') and open to Rebuttals (exceptions). Making each part explicit exposes hidden warrants and overclaiming. Applied to UX research reports, it audits whether insights are justified: is the warrant connecting five interviews to 'users want X' sound? Applied to product content, it evaluates how AI explanations, recommendations or persuasive content argue, and whether users can evaluate them. It is a lightweight but rigorous critique tool.
steps: Select the arguments to analyse (research insights, recommendations, AI explanations, persuasive copy).
For each, identify the claim and the grounds offered.
Make the warrant explicit: what rule licenses the move from grounds to claim?
Identify backing for the warrant, the qualifier strength and potential rebuttals.
Assess weaknesses: missing grounds, unstated or weak warrants, missing qualifiers, unaddressed rebuttals.
Revise arguments (or design explanation templates) to include explicit grounds, qualifiers and rebuttals.
outputs: Toulmin diagrams of key arguments, identified weaknesses and revised, better-qualified claims.
useWhen: Reviewing research reports and decision memos, designing AI explanations or evaluating persuasive content.
avoidWhen: Exploratory note-taking where arguments are not yet formed.
whyLost: Argumentation theory is taught in rhetoric and law; UX research critique relies on intuition about rigour.
whereToUse: Research review processes, AI explanation design, health information, financial advice interfaces.
example: A research insight claims 'Gen Z distrusts banks' from 8 interviews. Toulmin analysis reveals the warrant (these 8 represent Gen Z) lacks backing; the claim is qualified to 'participants in urban, renting households expressed...'.
sources: Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (1958; updated ed. 2003)
reference: Toulmin, S. E. (2003). The Uses of Argument (updated ed.). Cambridge University Press.

name: Trait-Overlap Graph Clustering into Personas
aka: Trait-overlap graph clustering of coded interview data
Bottom-up behavioural segmentation from affinity traits
origin: Dupree, DeVries, Berry and Lank (2016), CHI
summary: Code interviews into behavioural traits, link participants by how many traits they share, and merge highly connected participants into labelled persona segments.
description: This method derives personas bottom-up from coded qualitative data rather than from researcher intuition. In the original study, survey and interview data from 32 participants were open-coded by two coders and affinity-diagrammed into 85 traits under 24 concepts. Each participant becomes a binary vector over traits; the similarity of two participants is the dot product (number of shared traits), used as an edge weight in a graph. Clusters grow agglomeratively from highly connected participants and merge until stable with no singletons. Traits shared by too many clusters are removed and the graph reclustered so that clusters differ meaningfully. Participants are then rated on two theme attributes, here knowledge and motivation, each cluster takes its modal rating, and clusters are placed and named in that two-dimensional space, giving five segments.
steps: Collect a survey and a semi-structured interview from each participant.
Transcribe, open-code with two coders and resolve conflicts; add survey answers to the coded data.
Affinity-diagram codes into low-level traits and higher concepts.
Represent each participant as a binary vector over traits and build a graph with edge weight equal to the number of shared traits.
Cluster agglomeratively from high-connectivity participants, merging until stable with no singletons; drop traits shared by too many clusters and recluster.
Rate each participant on two theme attributes, give each cluster its modal rating, plot clusters in that space and label them descriptively.
outputs: A cluster graph with shared-trait weights, a map of traits unique to or shared between clusters, and labelled segments positioned on two attributes.
useWhen: Interview studies of about 20-50 participants where personas should be derived transparently from coded behaviour and attitudes.
avoidWhen: Avoid with very small samples or when you need population proportions; use latent class analysis or survey-based segmentation for prevalence. Tie clustering to a specific goal or community.
whyLost: It is a single academic procedure in usable security, and practitioners rarely formalise persona derivation this way.
whereToUse: Security and privacy features, fintech risk behaviour, health self-management, any persona work needing a defensible audit trail.
example: A password-manager team codes 30 interviews into 70 traits, clusters participants, and places five clusters on knowledge and motivation. A 'knowledgeable but unmotivated' segment becomes the target for low-effort defaults.
reference: Dupree, J. L., DeVries, R., Berry, D. M. and Lank, E. (2016). Privacy personas: Clustering users via attitudes and behaviors toward security practices. Proceedings of CHI 2016 (pp. 5228-5239). ACM.

name: Transcript Combing and Concept Summaries
origin: Indi Young, Mental Models (2008) and Practical Empathy (2015)
summary: Read each transcript line by line and turn every reasoning step, reaction or guiding principle into a first-person, verb-first summary with a verbatim quote, before comparing across people.
description: Combing is Indi Young's line-by-line extraction of what a person was really trying to do. In the 2008 version each phrase expressing an action, thought, feeling or philosophy becomes an atomic first-person verb+noun task with a verbatim quote, typically 60-120 per hour-long transcript; preferences, desires, facts, explanations and complaints are excluded or logged separately. In the 2015 version, which Young prefers as less product-focused, quotes are gathered into discrete concepts (one reasoning step, reaction or guiding principle) and each gets a one-sentence summary: chosen verb first, first person, present tense, emotions written as 'feel' plus an emotion, and no compound sentences. Summaries carry their quotes and participant IDs. Only after this are patterns aggregated across people, and participants with similar reasoning in a given scene form behaviour-named segments, with a different set of segments per scene.
steps: Study each person's material for at least 10 minutes before writing anything, re-listening or reading the transcript.
Highlight phrases that express a reasoning step, reaction or guiding principle; skip explanation, facts, opinions, preferences, generalisations and conjecture.
Gather quotes for each discrete concept and tag them with participant ID.
Write one summary per concept: brainstorm three or four verbs, prefer the speaker's own, first person, present tense, one sentence with the reason after the verb, emotions as 'feel' plus an emotion.
Check one summary per concept and one concept per quote; read aloud and have a colleague or the speaker check it.
Note 'fillers' you supplied and probe them in the next session.
After all sessions, aggregate summaries into patterns and group people with similar reasoning per scene into behaviour-named segments.
outputs: Per-participant concept summaries or atomic tasks with supporting quotes (often 60-120 per hour of transcript) and reasoning-based segments per scene.
useWhen: Building mental model diagrams, thinking-style segments or deep empathy with how people reason, especially for problem-space rather than product-space research.
avoidWhen: Avoid when only quick usability findings are needed; the method is slow. Do not synthesise across people while combing, and do not attach market percentages or demographic labels to segments.
whyLost: It is practised by a niche community trained in Young's approach; mainstream teams use faster affinity notes.
whereToUse: Insurance, healthcare and financial journeys, service design, and strategy work where teams need to understand purposes rather than feature preferences.
example: An insurer combs 24 interviews about car accidents into concept summaries such as 'I check whether anyone is hurt before I think about the car'. Aggregation yields segments like 'Let This Be a Lesson' and 'Downplay It' that shape claim-flow tone.
reference: Young, I. (2008). Mental Models: Aligning Design Strategy with Human Behavior. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media; Young, I. (2015). Practical Empathy. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media.

name: Transcript quality audit
donor: Speech recognition evaluation; qualitative research quality
origin: Word error rate metric from speech recognition evaluation (NIST); transcription quality concerns in qualitative methods (Poland, 1995)
summary: Systematically checking a sample of automated transcripts against human reference transcripts to quantify errors and decide whether they are fit for analysis.
description: Automated transcripts are data, and their errors propagate into coding and quotes. A transcript quality audit selects a stratified sample of recordings (covering accents, audio quality and languages), produces careful human reference transcripts for segments, and computes word error rate (WER = substitutions + deletions + insertions divided by reference words). It also checks qualitative error types that WER under-weights: hallucinated sentences during silence, mis-heard domain terms, negations dropped ('can' versus 'can't'), and mis-attributed speakers. Poland (1995) showed that even human transcription has systematic errors. Rigour comes from pre-set acceptance thresholds, stratified sampling, reporting the audit, and correcting or flagging transcripts that fail.
steps: Define acceptance criteria before auditing, e.g. WER of 10% or less and zero meaning-changing errors in quoted passages.
Draw a stratified sample of about 10% of recordings (at least 5), covering speakers, accents, languages and audio conditions.
Create human reference transcripts for 3-5 minute segments from each sampled file.
Compute WER with a tool such as jiwer after normalising case and punctuation.
Review for meaning-changing errors: negations, numbers, product and drug names, hallucinated passages and speaker swaps.
Correct failing transcripts, build a glossary or prompt for recurrent terms and re-run, and verify every quote used in reporting against audio.
outputs: A WER table by stratum, a catalogue of error types, a pass or fail decision per file and a verified quote list.
useWhen: Whenever automated transcription feeds qualitative analysis, especially for accented speech, technical domains, multiple languages or published research.
avoidWhen: Less necessary for informal internal note-taking where recordings are consulted directly; never skip it for quotes in reports.
whyLost: Teams treat transcripts from modern ASR as ground truth because they read fluently, so error rates are rarely measured.
whereToUse: Health research with medical terminology, multilingual UX research, accessibility research with atypical speech and AI-assisted analysis pipelines.
example: A fintech team's audit finds 7% WER overall but 19% for participants with strong regional accents, and two instances where 'I wouldn't trust it' was transcribed as 'I would trust it'. Those files are hand-corrected before coding.
sources: Poland, B. D. (1995) Transcription quality as an aspect of rigor in qualitative research. Qualitative Inquiry
Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft
The Inquiry Series, C9 — Whisper — Batch Transcription at Scale
reference: Poland, B. D. (1995) Transcription quality as an aspect of rigor in qualitative research. Qualitative Inquiry 1(3)

name: Transcription confidence scoring
origin: Confidence measures in ASR (Jiang, 2005, review); Whisper token log-probabilities and no-speech probabilities
summary: Using the speech model's own token probabilities and compression signals to flag low-confidence transcript segments for targeted human review.
description: Whisper exposes per-token and per-segment signals: average log-probability, no-speech probability and compression ratio (very repetitive output signals hallucination). Combining these yields a confidence score per segment so reviewers can focus effort where errors are most likely rather than auditing randomly. Rigour comes from calibrating thresholds against audited segments (checking that low-confidence segments really have higher WER), recognising that models can be confidently wrong, especially on domain terms, and marking flagged segments in the transcript so analysts treat quotes from them cautiously.
steps: Enable word or segment-level probabilities and timestamps in the transcription output.
Compute per-segment signals: average log-probability, no-speech probability and compression ratio.
Set initial flags using Whisper's own defaults (avg_logprob below -1.0, compression ratio above 2.4, no_speech_prob above 0.6).
Calibrate by auditing flagged and unflagged samples and adjusting thresholds so flagged segments have markedly higher error rates.
Mark flagged segments in transcripts and route them to human review, prioritising those in quoted or coded passages.
Report the proportion of flagged content per file as a quality indicator.
outputs: Per-segment confidence scores, flagged segments for review, calibrated thresholds and a file-level quality indicator.
useWhen: Large transcription batches where full auditing is impractical, and AI-assisted analysis pipelines that need quality gates.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating high confidence as correctness for proper nouns, numbers and negations; still verify all quotes against audio.
whyLost: Confidence signals exist in every model but are hidden by default outputs, and few UX teams know how to read them.
whereToUse: Large interview programmes, voice-of-customer call audio, multilingual research and regulated domains.
example: In a batch of 250 support call recordings, confidence scoring flags 6% of segments. Audit shows flagged segments have 31% WER versus 5% elsewhere, so review time is focused on that 6%.
sources: Radford, A. et al. (2023) Robust speech recognition via large-scale weak supervision. ICML
Jiang, H. (2005) Confidence measures for speech recognition: A survey. Speech Communication
The Inquiry Series, C9 — Whisper — Batch Transcription at Scale
reference: Jiang, H. (2005) Confidence measures for speech recognition: A survey. Speech Communication 45(4)

name: Transferability through Thick Description
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985, drawing on Geertz's thick description (1973)
summary: Providing rich setting, participant and analytic context so readers can judge whether qualitative findings apply to their own situation.
description: Transferability replaces the claim of statistical generalisation with a shared responsibility. The researcher provides thick description of the setting, participants, data collection conditions and analytic stance; the reader judges fittingness, whether their context is similar enough for findings to apply. The quality of a study is therefore partly measured by how well it enables that judgement. In practice this means describing physical and organisational context, the pressures participants face, sampling rationale, when and how each piece of data was gathered, and the analyst's framework and positionality. It counters the common failure where UX findings from one segment or market are silently assumed to apply everywhere.
steps: Describe the research setting in depth: Physical environment, organizational context, historical conditions, social relationships, time period. Not just "a rural health clinic in Kerala" but what that clinic looks like, how it operates, who works there, what pressures they face.
Describe the participants in depth: Demographic information relevant to the research question, their relationship to the phenomenon, their range of experience, and the sampling rationale.

Describe the context of data collection: When, where, with whom, under what conditions each piece of data was collected. A transcript from a one-hour interview in a private office is different data from a ten-minute conversation during a busy clinic shift.
Describe the analytical context: What theoretical and methodological framework was applied, by whom, with what background and positionality.
outputs: A context section in reports describing setting, participants, data collection conditions and analytic positionality, plus explicit statements of where findings may and may not transfer.
useWhen: When findings from one market, segment or site will be reused elsewhere, when building a research repository, or when reporting to teams in other contexts.
avoidWhen: When you need a statistical estimate of how widespread a finding is; use a survey or analytics follow-up instead.
whyLost: Short slide-based reporting strips context, and repositories store atomised insights without the conditions under which they were observed.
whereToUse: Global product research, research repositories and insight libraries, multi-country health and fintech studies, and enterprise research reused across accounts.
example: A ride-hailing team's Lagos study of cash payments includes detailed description of driver economics and connectivity. A team in Nairobi uses this context to decide which findings transfer and which need local validation.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Transformative (Participatory-Social Justice) Mixed Methods Design
origin: Donna Mertens, transformative paradigm (2007 onwards); Creswell's participatory-social justice complex design
summary: Run a mixed methods study inside a participatory or social justice frame, in revisitable phases from relationship building to use for change, so marginalised stakeholders shape and benefit from it.
description: A complex design in which core mixed methods designs are embedded within a framework that shapes the whole study: who sets questions, who is sampled, how results are used. Mertens grounds it in a transformative axiology (cultural respect, addressing inequities, reciprocity, action, relationships), an ontology of multiple socially positioned realities, and an epistemology that honours lived experience and addresses power. Six phases are linked by two-way arrows and revisited as information arrives: building relationships, analysing context including history and power, piloting with stakeholders, implementing with ongoing qualitative feedback on a quantitatively monitored intervention, determining effectiveness with mixed data, and using results for transformative purposes. Strategies borrowed from activism, such as coalition building, and planning for sustainability raise impact. It takes time and trust, and power dynamics reassert themselves unless addressed explicitly.
steps: Build relationships with affected communities and identify who must be included, especially marginalised groups.
Analyse the context, including history, regulation and power relations.
Co-design and pilot instruments or the intervention with stakeholders, deciding together how sensitive topics are approached.
Implement, using ongoing qualitative feedback to adjust an intervention monitored quantitatively.
Determine effectiveness with mixed data, disaggregated by the groups the study aims to serve.
Use results for change and plan for sustainability, revisiting earlier phases as new information arrives.
outputs: Intervention evidence, documented changes in practice or policy, and stakeholder-validated findings.
useWhen: Research on services affecting marginalised or vulnerable groups, equity audits, and products where harm or exclusion is a central concern.
avoidWhen: Routine feature optimisation where no equity question is at stake, or when the organisation cannot commit to acting on results; tokenistic participation does harm.
whyLost: UX inclusion work tends to adjust recruitment rather than share power over questions and use of results; the paradigm sits in evaluation and education research.
whereToUse: Public digital services, healthcare access, financial inclusion products, algorithmic fairness reviews, accessibility programmes.
example: A city's benefits portal team partners with disability advocacy groups, who help set questions and decide how interviews about income are approached. A quantitative uptake monitor runs alongside monthly community feedback, and findings are presented back before release decisions.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
reference: Mertens, D. M. (2018). Mixed Methods Design in Evaluation. Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Transition Design
donor: Design studies, sustainability transitions and futures
origin: Terry Irwin, Gideon Kossoff and Cameron Tonkinwise, Carnegie Mellon University, 2015
summary: A framework for designing toward long-term societal transitions by mapping wicked problems, stakeholder relations and visions, then seeding interventions at multiple scales.
description: Transition design, developed at Carnegie Mellon, addresses wicked problems such as climate, food systems and mobility that cannot be solved by single products. It combines systems thinking, futures, social practice theory and stakeholder research. The method maps the problem as a system across scales and time, maps stakeholders' concerns, fears and hopes and the relations between them, co-creates long-term visions, and then 'backcasts' to identify interventions at different scales and horizons. Rigour comes from mapping the problem's history and interconnections with evidence, including diverse stakeholders and their conflicts, and treating interventions as experiments monitored for systemic effects. For product teams it provides a way to situate features within larger transitions, for example energy behaviour or circular commerce.
steps: Map the wicked problem across scales (household to global) and over time, including its historical roots.
Identify stakeholders and map their concerns, fears, hopes and relationships, including conflicts.
Co-create a long-term future vision with stakeholders, typically 20-50 years out.
Backcast from the vision to identify milestones and intervention points at different scales.
Design and launch small, linked interventions as experiments.
Monitor systemic effects and adapt interventions over time.
outputs: Problem map, stakeholder relations map, future vision, backcasting roadmap, portfolio of interventions.
useWhen: Sustainability initiatives, public policy, energy, food and mobility products, and organisations repositioning around societal change.
avoidWhen: Contained product problems with short horizons; use service design or design thinking.
whyLost: Latent: Academic/activist context; emerging in sustainability-focused design practices.
whereToUse: Sustainability design; systems change initiatives; policy design.
example: An energy supplier used transition design to frame home electrification. Stakeholder mapping across tenants, landlords and installers led to an intervention portfolio including landlord incentives and an installer marketplace rather than just a usage app.
reference: Irwin, T. (2015). Transition design: A proposal for a new area of design practice, study, and research. Design and Culture, 7(2), 229-246.

name: Tree + Taxonomy Diagnostic Loop
aka: Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy framework
Two-phase tree test and taxonomy design
donor: Information architecture research and human error analysis
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A two-phase protocol pairing an unmoderated tree test (where findability fails) with moderated micro-sessions coded as Slip, Lapse or Mistake (why), joined in a joint display and re-tested.
description: The framework turns 'navigation was confusing' into decision-ready action. Phase A is an unmoderated tree test (N = 80–150) on a text-only IA of 2–3 levels with 8–12 randomised tasks, yielding direct and indirect success, failure, first-click accuracy, extra clicks, time to first click and misroute hotspots. Phase B is 10–15 moderated 30–40 minute think-aloud micro-sessions on the same tree and tasks, with each breakdown coded by a one-page codebook and two coders on 30–40% of sessions (κ ≥ 0.70). The glue analysis joins phases in a joint display mapping quant signal → taxonomy read → prescribed fix → effort and impact. Decision bars are set before changes (direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0, first-click ≥ 80%) and the tree test is re-run with the same tasks and similar N, plus 5–8 verification think-alouds.
steps: Detect: export the IA as plain text (depth ≤ 3), write 8–12 tasks without label leakage, and run an unmoderated tree test with 80–150 participants, logging first click, final node, path, time and backtracks.
Compute direct success, indirect success, failure (1 − direct − indirect), misroute share per node, first-click accuracy, extra clicks and time to first click.
Diagnose: run 10–15 moderated 30–40 minute think-alouds on the same tree, using prompts such as 'What do you expect to find under this label?'
Code each breakdown as Slip, Lapse or Mistake; double-code 30–40% and compute Cohen's κ, refining the codebook until κ ≥ 0.70.

Prescribe: build a joint display mapping quant signal → mechanism → fix with effort and impact ratings, using the insight pattern 'Because [quant evidence] and think-aloud revealed [mechanism], we recommend [fix] with decision bar [thresholds]'.
Decide: confirm bars set upfront (direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0, first-click ≥ 80%).
Re-test: re-run the tree test with the same tasks and similar N and 5–8 verification think-alouds to confirm the mechanism is resolved.
outputs: Tree-test dashboard, taxonomy table by step with quotes and κ, joint display with effort and impact, decision bars, and before/after comparison.
useWhen: IA redesigns, label changes and any situation where you need both where users go wrong and why.
avoidWhen: When the issue lies in visual layout or interaction mechanics rather than labels and hierarchy; use usability testing on the full UI.
whyLost: Original pairing by Vivek Gopinath; tree testing is common but rarely paired with a reliability-checked cognitive error taxonomy.
whereToUse: Fintech navigation, enterprise menus, content-heavy sites, app settings, IA migrations.
example: Creating a price alert yields 59% direct success with 31% misrouting to Notifications; think-alouds code the cause as Mistake ('Notifications sounded like app updates'); after promoting Price Alerts to top nav, direct success reaches 89% and misroutes fall to 7%.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers.

name: TREE Mixed Methods Sampling Framework
aka: Transparent, Rigorous, Ethical and Equitable sampling
origin: Corrigan and Onwuegbuzie, building on Onwuegbuzie and Collins (2007)
summary: Make mixed methods sampling decisions in a fixed order, from paradigm to purpose, sample size, relationship between samples and techniques, so they are transparent and defensible.
description: A meta-framework using a tree metaphor for sampling across strands. The roots are paradigmatic assumptions. The trunk covers the purposes of the study and of mixing, whom to study, the approach and number of phases, and sample size per strand: power analysis for quantitative strands, saturation logic for qualitative ones, tempered by heterogeneity, scope and feasibility. The limbs cross the relationship between samples (identical, parallel, nested, multilevel) with timing (concurrent, sequential) to give eight sampling designs, plus techniques chosen by the kind of generalisation sought (statistical, analytic, case-to-case). The leaves are the data. A flowchart walks the decisions in order and each choice is documented. The framework warns that commonly cited saturation figures, such as Guest et al. (2006), are context-bound rather than universal.
steps: State paradigmatic assumptions for the study.
Set the purposes of the study and of mixing methods.
Define the population and frame, and whether sampling is needed.
Choose the approach and number of phases.
Size each strand: power analysis for quantitative strands, saturation reasoning for qualitative strands, adjusted for heterogeneity and feasibility.
Choose the relationship between samples (identical, parallel, nested, multilevel) and timing (concurrent, sequential).
Choose sampling techniques by the generalisation sought and document every decision.
outputs: A documented sampling design covering every strand, its size rationale and its relationship to other strands.
useWhen: Planning mixed methods studies where the qualitative sample is drawn from, or must be compared with, a survey or analytics sample.
avoidWhen: Single-method studies with standard sampling. Do not use it to justify fixed qualitative sample sizes by citation alone.
whyLost: UX sampling decisions are made per study by convention ('five users', '400 responses'); the cross-strand reasoning lives in educational methodology.
whereToUse: Survey-then-interview programmes, B2B studies sampling accounts and users, research ops templates for study planning.
example: A neobank plans a survey of 2,000 customers followed by interviews. Using TREE, the team chooses a nested sequential design, sizes the survey by power for segment comparisons and selects 20 interviewees from extreme survey responders, documenting the analytic generalisation sought.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Mixed Methods Research Design (Poth, 2023)
Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
reference: Onwuegbuzie, A. J. and Collins, K. M. T. (2007). A typology of mixed methods sampling designs in social science research. The Qualitative Report, 12(2), 281-316.

name: Tree Testing
origin: Donna Spencer's paper-based 'card-based classification evaluation', early 2000s; popularised by online tools from 2008
summary: Participants find destinations in a text-only hierarchy, isolating whether labels and structure work, measured by direct and indirect success, first-click accuracy, extra clicks and misroutes.
description: Tree testing removes visual chrome (colours, icons, layout) and tests whether labels and hierarchy alone let people find things. Vivek Gopinath's protocol specifies trees of 2–3 levels from the current and a proposed IA, 6–12 realistic randomised tasks without label leakage, and N = 80–150 per audience segment, run unmoderated. Metrics for N attempts: direct success (correct node with no detours / N), indirect success (correct node with detours / N), failure (1 − direct − indirect), first-click accuracy, extra clicks (total minus minimum path), time to first click, and misroute share per node. Pitfalls include leaking the target label in the task, using 4+ levels, and ignoring first-click accuracy, which strongly predicts success.
