Decision bars: direct success ≥ 85%, top misroute ≤ 10%, first-click ≥ 75–80%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0.
steps: Export current and proposed IAs as plain text, keeping depth to 2–3 levels and using real labels.
Write 6–12 realistic tasks that avoid the target label (e.g. 'Set a price alert for ABC', not 'Go to Price Alerts').
Recruit 80–150 representative participants per segment and run unmoderated, randomising task order.
Log first click, final node, full path, time and backtracks per attempt.
Compute direct and indirect success, failure, first-click accuracy, extra clicks, time to first click and misroute share per node.
Compare against decision bars (direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, first-click ≥ 75%) and build a misroute heatmap.
Re-run with the same tasks and similar N after changes.
outputs: A tree-test dashboard: success rates, first-click accuracy, extra clicks, misroute heatmap and before/after comparison.
useWhen: Comparing competing IAs or label sets before visual design, or whenever findability is suspected.
avoidWhen: When problems stem from visual layout, search or content quality; use usability testing or first-click testing on real UI.
whyLost: Survived because tools made it cheap and its metrics are clear; rigour suffers when tasks leak labels or why is never explored.
whereToUse: App navigation, fintech menus, e-commerce category structures, intranets, documentation sites.
example: A trading app's current IA gives 59% direct success, 49% first-click accuracy and 31% misroutes to Notifications; the proposed IA reaches 89% direct, 74% first-click and 6% top misroute.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
UX Research Methods for Media and Communication Studies (Cirucci & Pruchniewska, 2022)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: O'Brien, D. (2009). Tree Testing. Boxes and Arrows.

name: Tree Testing and Navigation Error Taxonomy
aka: Reverse card sort with error coding
donor: Information architecture and human error research
origin: Tree testing from Donna Spencer's paper-based 'card-based classification evaluation' (2003) and Dave O'Brien's Treejack; error taxonomy layer by Vivek Gopinath
summary: Testing a text-only navigation tree with task scenarios and coding each failure as wrong branch, backtrack failure, label failure or false confidence to target fixes.
description: Tree testing isolates information architecture from visual design: participants navigate a text-only hierarchy to find where they would complete a task scenario. Standard analysis reports success, directness and time per task. Gopinath's framework adds a navigation error taxonomy so that failures point to specific remedies. Each failed task is coded as wrong branch (the top-level taxonomy misled), backtrack failure (participants could not recover), label failure (right area, but item labels did not discriminate) or false confidence (a wrong answer accepted without doubt). Full click paths and first clicks are analysed because the first click strongly predicts eventual success. The taxonomy converts success rates into a diagnosis: restructure, relabel or add recovery cues.
steps: Build the tree: Text-only representation of your IA — no visual design, no colours, no icons. This isolates IA findability from visual design quality.

Task scenarios: Write 8–12 task scenarios. Each should be answerable by finding a specific item in the tree. Scenarios must be written in participant language — not using the exact label names in the tree (this defeats the test).
Record full navigation paths: Track every node click, not just the final answer. The path is the data — correct destination via incorrect path is as informative as an incorrect destination.

Error taxonomy coding: Code each failed task by type: (a) wrong branch (participant went to entirely wrong area), (b) backtrack failure (couldn't find the way back after going wrong), (c) label failure (correct branch but couldn't identify specific item from labels), (d) false confident (reached wrong destination and didn't try again).

First-click analysis: What was the first node each participant clicked? First-click accuracy predicts overall task success with ~87% accuracy — and first-click errors reveal where the IA's top-level taxonomy fails to match users' mental model.
outputs: Task success, directness and first-click rates; coded error type distributions per task; path diagrams; and targeted IA remedies.
useWhen: Validating a new or revised navigation structure, comparing candidate trees, or diagnosing why users cannot find content.
avoidWhen: Generating categories from scratch (use open card sorting first) or evaluating visual navigation, search or page layout (use usability testing).
whyLost: Tree testing is active, but its analysis usually stops at success rates; error-type coding that links failures to fixes is this framework's contribution.
whereToUse: E-commerce navigation, help centres, banking app menus, intranets and government information sites.
example: A bank's new menu tree scores 58% success on 'dispute a card payment'. Error coding shows mostly label failures inside the correct 'Cards' branch, so items are relabelled rather than restructured, raising success to 84% in a retest.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)

name: Trend Card Ideation
donor: Design research; futures and trend forecasting
origin: Li-Jun Liu and Yi Li, Hunan University (2022); trend factors adapted from PESTLE
summary: Trend keywords mined from news, policy and design sources are printed as cards that designers combine at random to find design opportunities.
description: Trend card ideation turns trend research into a physical prompt deck. Trends are complex and interrelated, so unexpected links between cards spark ideas. Liu and Li sort keywords into six factor categories adapted from PESTLE: economy, culture, technology, society, human needs and current design. Keywords come from news and policy documents describing developments expected to matter in two to five years, and from design awards and trend reports, extracted by automatic text summarisation and word clustering (over 70 keywords). Each card shows a keyword, an image and a short introduction. The workshop runs in three stages: self-discovery (browsing and free association), explain and use (connecting two to four cards and sketching a concept on a poster canvas), and co-creation (presenting and building on ideas with critique deferred). It is aimed at novice designers, and its effectiveness had not yet been evaluated.
steps: Collect trend sources for the topic across the six factors (economy, culture, technology, society, human needs, current design).
Extract 50-80 trend keywords by summarisation and clustering, or by careful manual coding.
Make cards in six categories, each with keyword, representative image and short introduction.
Stage 1: participants browse the cards (1-3 minutes each) and freely associate them with the theme.
Stage 2: participants choose and connect 2-4 cards, think divergently for 10 minutes, then spend 30 minutes sketching a concept on a poster canvas with the cards attached.
Stage 3: present canvases and build on each other's ideas, deferring critique.
Have experts rate the ideas for quality, novelty and diversity to choose which to pursue.
outputs: A trend keyword set, a card deck, and concept sketches on canvases.
useWhen: Use it to inject external trends into ideation, especially with less experienced designers or for long-horizon concepts.
avoidWhen: Trends are not user needs; ground chosen concepts with Interviews or Contextual Inquiry. For structured foresight rather than ideation, use the Three Horizons Framework or Futures Wheel.
whyLost: It is a recent academic proposal with no published evaluation; trend decks exist in industry but this procedure has not spread.
whereToUse: Design education, innovation labs, consumer electronics, and strategic foresight sprints.
example: A home-appliance team draws 'ageing society', 'net zero' and 'subscription' cards and sketches a leased, energy-tracking washer with large controls, which then goes to interviews with older renters.
sources: DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Liu, L.-J. and Li, Y. (2022). Design Trend Analysis and Design Innovation Based on Card Heuristic Method. In: Soares, M.M., Rosenzweig, E. and Marcus, A. (eds) Design, User Experience, and Usability: UX Research, Design, and Assessment. HCII 2022, LNCS 13321. Cham: Springer, pp. 47-56. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-05897-4_4

name: Triangulation
origin: Eugene Webb et al., 1966; Norman Denzin, 1970
summary: Corroborates findings by comparing multiple data sources, methods, researchers or theories, strengthening credibility and exposing where evidence diverges.
description: Triangulation uses more than one vantage point to study the same phenomenon. Denzin distinguished four types: data triangulation (different sources, times or places), investigator triangulation (multiple researchers), theory triangulation (multiple interpretive frameworks) and methodological triangulation (different methods). The logic is that each source and method has different biases, so convergent findings are more credible, while divergence is informative and calls for explanation. In UX, it commonly combines analytics, interviews, usability tests and support data. Rigour comes from planning triangulation in advance, documenting a convergence matrix that shows which sources support, contradict or are silent on each finding, and treating contradictions as data rather than discarding inconvenient sources. It is a credibility strategy, not a guarantee of truth, because sources can share biases.
steps: List the key findings or research questions to be corroborated.
Identify independent sources, methods, researchers or theories with different biases for each.
Collect or retrieve data from each source.
Build a convergence matrix marking each finding as supported, contradicted or silent per source.
Investigate contradictions to explain them (e.g. differing populations or measurement).
Report findings with their level of corroboration and any unresolved divergence.
outputs: Convergence matrix, findings rated by corroboration strength, explanations for divergence.
useWhen: High-stakes decisions, synthesis across multiple studies, and when stakeholders question the credibility of a single study.
avoidWhen: Low-stakes, quick evaluations where a single well-chosen method suffices.
whyLost: 'We triangulated' is commonly asserted after running two methods, without a planned protocol or analysis of divergence.
whereToUse: Research synthesis; multi-study programs; mixed-method interpretation.
example: Interviews suggested users abandoned a fintech app due to fees, but analytics showed abandonment peaked before fees were shown. Triangulating with support tickets revealed confusion about identity checks, reframing the finding.
sources: Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Convergent and Discriminant Validation by the Multitrait-Multimethod Matrix (Campbell & Fiske)
The Power of Data Triangulation (Chang & Classen, 2024)
Qualitative Methods in Information Retrieval Research (Fidel, 1993)
Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation (Bamberger, 2012)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 1 (Lerner et al., 2015)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Denzin, N. K. (1978). The Research Act: A Theoretical Introduction to Sociological Methods (2nd ed.). McGraw-Hill.

name: Triggered analysis
origin: Kohavi, Longbotham et al. (2009); Deng and Hu (2015); Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020)
summary: Analyse only the users who could have been affected by an experiment's change, gaining power, then dilute the effect back to the whole population for decisions.
description: Many experiments change something only a fraction of users ever encounter, such as a checkout step or an edge case. Including everyone adds noise from unaffected users and hides real effects. Triggered analysis restricts the analysis to units who reached a point where the variants could differ, identified by targeted segment, reaching the changed step, coverage differences, or counterfactual logging of what the other variant would have shown. Trigger definitions must rely on pre-experiment state, and triggered users stay in the analysis from first trigger onward. The gain can be large: triggering on checkout starters roughly halved the users needed (from 121,600 to 64,000). For decisions, the triggered absolute delta is diluted: multiplied by the triggered count and divided by the overall total. Validity checks include an SRM test on triggered users and an A/A-like comparison of never-triggered users.
steps: Define the trigger as any point where the variants could produce different experiences, using pre-experiment state only.
Log triggers at runtime in both variants, including counterfactual outputs where the change depends on computed results.
Analyse triggered users from their first trigger onward, keeping them in for the rest of the run.
Run a sample ratio mismatch check on triggered users and an A/A-like analysis of never-triggered users, which should show no difference.
Compute the diluted overall impact: triggered absolute delta multiplied by triggered count, divided by the overall total.
If counterfactual logging is costly, run an A/A'/B design to measure its performance cost.
outputs: A higher-powered triggered result and a diluted overall effect estimate for decision making.
useWhen: Experiments whose change affects only a subset of users or sessions, such as a specific flow step, a ranking change for some queries or a feature behind a condition.
avoidWhen: When the change affects nearly everyone, or when triggers cannot be defined from pre-experiment state (triggering on attributes the treatment changes biases results).
whyLost: Most experiment tools analyse all assigned users by default, and counterfactual logging requires engineering effort UX teams rarely request.
whereToUse: Checkout and payment flows, search and recommendation changes, eligibility-gated features in SaaS and fintech.
example: A travel site changes the seat-selection step, which only 30% of visitors reach. Triggered analysis on users entering seat selection detects a 2% conversion gain within a week; diluted, it is worth 0.6% site-wide, which is the figure used in the launch decision.
sources: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al., 2020)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. and Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, ch. 20.

name: TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving)
origin: Genrich Altshuller, USSR, 1946-1985, from analysis of hundreds of thousands of patents
summary: Resolves design contradictions (improving one parameter worsens another) using inventive principles derived from patent analysis, instead of compromising.
description: Altshuller found that inventive solutions across fields resolve recurring contradictions using a limited set of principles. Technical contradictions (e.g. more security worsens ease of use) map via the contradiction matrix to suggested principles among 40 (segmentation, taking out, local quality, asymmetry, prior action, dynamics, and so on). Physical contradictions (a parameter must be both high and low) are resolved by separation in time, space, condition or scale. Further tools include ideal final result, resources analysis and trends of evolution. For UX, contradictions are everywhere (simple yet powerful, secure yet frictionless) and TRIZ offers structured ways to transcend trade-offs.
steps: State the problem and the ideal final result (the function achieved with no cost or harm).
Formulate the core contradictions explicitly: what improves and what worsens.
Translate them into TRIZ parameters or physical contradictions.
Use the contradiction matrix or separation principles to identify candidate inventive principles.
Generate concrete concepts applying each principle to the UX context.
Evaluate concepts and test the most promising with users.
outputs: Explicit contradiction statements, candidate principles, generated concepts and evaluated solutions.
useWhen: Design problems framed as trade-offs between desirable qualities.
avoidWhen: Problems that are not contradictions but simply unknown needs; do discovery research first.
whyLost: TRIZ is popular in engineering and manufacturing innovation but its matrix is mechanical-engineering flavoured and unfamiliar to designers.
whereToUse: Security versus convenience, personalisation versus privacy, feature richness versus simplicity, speed versus accuracy in AI.
example: Faced with 'stronger authentication worsens login ease', TRIZ separation in condition (principle: local quality) leads to risk-based authentication: strong checks only when signals are unusual, frictionless otherwise.
sources: Altshuller, Creativity as an Exact Science (1984)
Altshuller, 40 Principles: TRIZ Keys to Technical Innovation (1997)
Savransky, Engineering of Creativity: Introduction to TRIZ Methodology (2000)
Innovation and Product Management (Gaubinger et al., 2015)
reference: Altshuller, G. S. (1984). Creativity as an Exact Science. Gordon and Breach.

name: Trunk Test and Navigation Stress Test
origin: Keith Instone, 'Stress Test Your Site' (1997); Steve Krug, Don't Make Me Think (2000)
summary: Drop onto a random deep page and check, at a glance, whether site identity, page name, sections, local navigation, 'you are here' cues and search are evident.
description: Users increasingly arrive deep in a site from search, social links or email, never having seen the home page. Instone's stress test ignores the home page and jumps to random interior pages, asking for each whether you can tell which site and section you are in, what the parent page is, and where each link will lead. Krug's trunk test makes it perceptual: imagine being dropped on a page blindfolded, then print it and hold it at arm's length or squint, and circle six elements as fast as possible: site ID, page name, sections, local navigation, 'you are here' indicators and search. The blur matters because wayfinding elements must pop out rather than be deducible on close study. It checks bottom-up information architecture quickly but gives no scoring or sample-size rules and does not test task completion.
steps: Select several pages at random from deep in the site, ignoring the home page.
For each page, view it blurred (print at arm's length or squint) so it cannot be studied closely.
As quickly as possible, find and circle site ID, page name, primary sections, local navigation, 'you are here' indicators and search.
Ask whether you can tell which section and parent page you are in, and whether each link's destination is predictable and distinct.
Record which elements were missed or ambiguous on each page.
Repeat with a few colleagues or users unfamiliar with the site, then fix patterns that recur across pages.
outputs: A page-by-page record of which wayfinding elements can or cannot be found at a glance, plus link-predictability failures.
useWhen: Quick reviews of navigation and page templates for content-heavy sites where many visitors land on interior pages.
avoidWhen: Avoid as evidence that tasks can be completed; use Tree Testing for structure and Moderated Usability Testing for findability.
whyLost: It is widely cited from Krug's book but seldom run systematically, being treated as an illustration rather than a method.
whereToUse: Documentation sites, news, e-commerce category and product pages, intranets, help centres.
example: A SaaS documentation team trunk-tests 20 random help articles. On 15, staff cannot spot which product section they are in, so breadcrumbs and a section header are added to the template.
reference: Krug, S. (2014). Don't Make Me Think, Revisited, 3rd ed. New Riders, pp. 82-83; Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. and Arango, J. (2015). Information Architecture, 4th ed. O'Reilly Media.

name: Trust in Automation Scale (Jian et al.)
aka: Checklist for Trust between People and Automation
origin: Jiun-Yin Jian, Ann Bisantz and Colin Drury, 2000; trust calibration theory from Lee and See, 2004
summary: A 12-item empirically derived scale measuring trust and distrust in automated systems, used with reliability data to assess whether trust is calibrated.
description: Jian, Bisantz and Drury derived their scale empirically from word-elicitation and cluster studies, yielding 12 items on a 7-point scale covering deception, suspicion, harmful outcomes, confidence, integrity, dependability and familiarity. Lee and See's theory adds that trust should be calibrated: matched to the actual reliability of the automation. Rigorous use therefore pairs the scale with objective measures of system reliability and of reliance behaviour (acceptance of correct and incorrect recommendations). Over-trust appears as accepting wrong advice; under-trust as rejecting correct advice. This turns 'do users trust our AI?' into 'is their trust appropriate?', which is the question that matters.
steps: Define the automation's actual reliability on the task set, including a planned proportion of errors (e.g. 10-30%).
Administer the 12-item scale before and after exposure, and at intervals in longitudinal studies.
Log reliance behaviour: agreement with correct suggestions, agreement with incorrect suggestions, verification actions.
Compute calibration: compare trust scores and reliance rates with actual reliability; plot trust trajectories after errors.
Test design interventions such as confidence displays or explanations for their effect on calibration, not just trust level.
Report over-reliance and under-reliance rates alongside the scale score.
outputs: Trust and distrust scores, reliance rates on correct and incorrect advice, calibration plots and the effect of design changes.
useWhen: Evaluating AI recommendations, copilots, autopilot-like features or any system whose output users must accept or reject.
avoidWhen: Systems without automated recommendations; use general satisfaction or credibility measures instead.
whyLost: AI product teams measure trust as a single satisfaction-like rating to maximise, ignoring calibration. The human factors literature on reliance is rarely cited in product research.
whereToUse: LLM assistants, medical AI, fraud scoring, navigation, autonomous vehicles.
example: A radiology AI shows a confidence bar. Trust scores rise with the bar, but acceptance of incorrect AI findings also rises from 18% to 31%; the team redesigns to show uncertainty regions instead, improving calibration.
sources: Jian, Bisantz & Drury, Foundations for an empirically determined scale of trust in automated systems (2000), International Journal of Cognitive Ergonomics
Lee & See, Trust in automation: Designing for appropriate reliance (2004), Human Factors
reference: Jian, J.-Y., Bisantz, A. M., & Drury, C. G. (2000). International Journal of Cognitive Ergonomics, 4(1), 53-71.

name: TURF Analysis
origin: Media audience research (1950s-60s); product line application by Miaoulis, Free and Parsons (1990)
summary: Finds the combination of items (features, plans, content) that reaches the largest number of users at least once, rather than the individually most popular items.
description: Ranking items by popularity often picks items liked by the same people. TURF asks which portfolio of k items maximises unduplicated reach: the proportion of respondents for whom at least one item is appealing, with frequency as a secondary measure. Computation is combinatorial (exhaustive for small sets, greedy or optimisation for larger). Inputs can be survey acceptability, MaxDiff utilities with thresholds or behavioural usage. It is useful for deciding bundles, menu items, plan features or which content to commission, especially where breadth of appeal matters more than average preference.
steps: Collect per-respondent acceptability for each candidate item (binary or thresholded from MaxDiff utilities).
Define the portfolio size k or a cost constraint.
Compute reach and frequency for all combinations (or use greedy/optimised search for large sets).
Examine the incremental reach curve to see diminishing returns as k grows.
Check robustness with bootstrap resamples and segment-level reach.
Choose the portfolio balancing reach, frequency, cost and strategic fit.
outputs: Optimal portfolios with reach and frequency, incremental reach curves and segment reach.
useWhen: Selecting bundles, plan features, default content, templates or onboarding paths to maximise breadth of appeal.
avoidWhen: When intensity of preference or revenue matters more than reach; use conjoint simulations.
whyLost: It is a marketing media tool unfamiliar in product research; roadmaps prioritise by average score.
whereToUse: Template galleries, starter plans, content commissioning, notification types, food or retail assortments.
example: A presentation app chooses 8 starter templates from 40. The top 8 by popularity reach 64% of users; the TURF-optimal set reaches 86% by including two niche templates for educators and sales.
sources: Miaoulis, Free & Parsons, TURF: A new planning approach for product line extensions (1990), Marketing Research
Orme, Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (4th ed., 2019)
reference: Miaoulis, G., Free, V., & Parsons, H. (1990). TURF: A new planning approach for product line extensions. Marketing Research, 2(1), 28-40.

name: Turing test protocols
donor: Artificial intelligence and philosophy of mind
origin: Alan Turing, 1950
summary: Blinded judges exchange typed text with hidden humans and machines and decide which is which; the proportion of judges fooled measures human-likeness under a stated protocol.
description: Turing replaced 'can machines think?' with whether a computer could do well in the imitation game, in which a judge exchanging only typed text tries to tell machine from human. He left judges, duration and topics open but predicted that average interrogators would be right no more than 70 per cent of the time after five minutes. Protocols differ: the 1950 three-party parallel game versus the 1952 serial jury version, in which judges question contestants one at a time without knowing the ratio and over-call machines; the 2014 Royal Society event with five-minute paired conversations; and the Kapor-Kurzweil wager with three judges, two-hour interviews and a rank-order criterion. A small offline variant mixes machine and human texts for judges to identify. Short sessions, lay judges, evasive personas and anthropomorphism inflate pass rates, and the test measures indistinguishability, not usefulness or understanding.
steps: Define what counts as a human and a machine contestant and state the purpose (for example disclosure decisions).
Have a committee select judges and human foils, varying expertise, age and language background as required.
Run blinded typed conversations for a fixed duration, choosing parallel (one human, one machine) or serial format and stating it.
Collect a human or machine verdict per candidate and, optionally, a rank of all candidates from least to most human.
Apply a pre-stated pass criterion, for example more than 30 per cent of judges fooled after five minutes, or the Kapor-Kurzweil rule.
Report judge selection, session length, sample selection (best versus typical outputs) and identification accuracy against a human-only baseline.
outputs: Proportion of judges fooled, per-candidate verdicts, human-likeness ranks, and identification accuracy.
useWhen: You must know whether users can tell AI-generated content or agents from humans, for example to inform disclosure, impersonation risk or persona design.
avoidWhen: You want to know whether an AI is useful, accurate or trusted; indistinguishability is not quality. Short sessions and lay judges are easily fooled; use task-based evaluation, Wizard of Oz studies or conversation analysis instead.
whyLost: It became a philosophical thought experiment and publicity contest rather than a standardised protocol, though blind human-versus-AI discrimination tests are returning with generative AI.
whereToUse: AI disclosure policy, customer service bots, AI-generated content labelling, synthetic research participants, voice clones.
example: A bank runs blinded comparisons of chatbot and human support replies with 60 customers. Customers identify the bot only 55 per cent of the time, which supports a clear disclosure label rather than relying on users to notice.
sources: Handbook of the Philosophy of Science (Thagard, 2007)
reference: Turing, A. M. (1950). Computing machinery and intelligence. Mind, 59, 433-460.

name: Tversky Contrast Model (Asymmetric Similarity)
origin: Amos Tversky, 1977
summary: Measures similarity judgements in both directions to reveal which interface or concept users treat as the prototype, using Tversky's feature-matching model of common and distinctive features.
description: Tversky's contrast model treats similarity as a weighted function of common features minus each object's distinctive features, rather than a symmetric distance in a geometric space. Because the weights differ, similarity is often asymmetric: people say a variant resembles the prototype more than the prototype resembles the variant. The direction of the asymmetry reveals which item functions as the reference. Applied to UX, asking 'how similar is our app to X?' and 'how similar is X to our app?' separately reveals whether users treat a competitor, a legacy system or a familiar convention as the standard against which new designs are judged. Feature listing then identifies which shared and distinctive features drive judgements. The method was briefly used in early HCI similarity research and has largely disappeared.
steps: Present pairs of interface elements.
Ask 'does A resemble B?' then 'does B resemble A?' Measure asymmetry.
Large asymmetry reveals the prototype.
Redesign unfamiliar elements toward the prototype direction.
outputs: Directional similarity ratings, asymmetry indices, identification of the reference prototype, and weighted common and distinctive feature lists.
useWhen: Positioning a redesign against a legacy system or competitor, deciding which conventions to keep, and understanding brand or interface prototypes.
avoidWhen: When you need fine-grained usability findings or when the products are unfamiliar to participants; use card sorting or preference testing instead.
whyLost: Multidimensional scaling and later preference testing displaced feature-based similarity research in HCI, and the asymmetric-question protocol was never packaged as a UX method.
whereToUse: Mental model research, migration UX, icon family design.
example: A bank redesigning its legacy desktop banking asks customers both directions; the new design is rated as resembling the old more than the reverse. Feature listing shows the account summary table is the anchor, so it is preserved while navigation changes.
sources: Preference, Belief, and Similarity — Amos Tversky
reference: Tversky A (1977) Features of similarity. Psychological Review 84(4):327-352

name: Two-stage clickstream persona construction
aka: Two-stage clickstream persona construction (workflow clustering then multinomial mixture of users)
donor: Statistics (finite mixture models) and game analytics
origin: Zhang, Brown and Shankar, CHI 2016
summary: Cluster session clickstreams into common workflows, then fit a mixture model over each user's workflow counts to derive behavioural personas from product telemetry.
description: Telemetry events are split into per-session clickstreams, dropping those under 20 clicks. Pairwise Jaccard similarity of unique clicks feeds Ward hierarchical clustering, giving K common workflows that are labelled with experts from top clicks, length, duration and key steps. Each user's counts of each workflow are then modelled as a multinomial given a latent persona; a mixture of M multinomials is fitted by EM, and users are assigned to their most likely persona. Personas are read from workflow probability vectors and a user-by-workflow heat map, and experts compare them with legacy personas. At Platfora, 3.5 million clicks from 2,400 users yielded ten workflows and five personas. Limitations: Jaccard on unique clicks ignores order and repetition, K and M were chosen by judgement, and the personas show behaviour, not goals, so they need triangulation with interviews.
steps: Collect opt-in UI event telemetry with anonymised user identifiers.
Split events into per-session clickstreams and drop those under 20 clicks.
Compute a Jaccard distance matrix between clickstreams and run Ward hierarchical clustering; choose K workflows with the dendrogram and expert review.
Label workflows from top clicks, length, duration and key-step frequencies, dropping stray clusters such as internal testing.
Count each user's workflows, keeping users with at least five clickstreams.
Fit a mixture of M multinomials by EM and assign users to their most likely persona, checking fit statistics where possible.
Describe personas by workflow probabilities and have UX, design and product experts compare them with existing personas.
outputs: Labelled common workflows, personas defined by workflow probabilities, a user-by-persona heat map, and comparison with legacy personas.
useWhen: You have rich product telemetry for a complex tool and want personas grounded in actual workflows rather than self-report.
avoidWhen: Telemetry is thin or you need goals and motives; triangulate with interviews. Use sequence-aware measures if order matters, and fit statistics rather than judgement alone to choose K and M.
whyLost: It is a single, well-cited CHI paper; practitioners lack telemetry access or statistical support, and most behavioural personas are still assembled by hand.
whereToUse: Enterprise and analytics SaaS, creative tools, developer platforms, complex B2B products with event telemetry.
example: A BI tool clusters 40,000 sessions into nine workflows, then finds five personas, including a 'dashboard consumer' who almost never prepares data. Interviews confirm the persona and lead to a simplified viewer mode.
reference: Zhang, X., Brown, H.-F., & Shankar, A. (2016). Data-driven personas: Constructing archetypal users with clickstreams and user telemetry. Proceedings of CHI 2016, 5350-5359. https://doi.org/10.1145/2858036.2858523

name: Two-Way Cluster Rearrangement (Biclustering) of a Data Matrix
aka: Two-way cluster rearrangement of a binary matrix
origin: McCormick, Schweitzer and White (1972) bond energy algorithm; King (1980) rank order clustering; described by Romesburg (1984)
summary: Cluster the rows and the columns of the same data matrix separately, then reorder both by their tree orders to reveal blocks of objects sharing attributes.
description: A one-way cluster analysis groups either the objects or the attributes. Two-way rearrangement does both: a Q-analysis clusters the columns, an R-analysis clusters the rows, and the matrix is reordered so rows and columns follow their dendrogram orders. Blocks of 1s, or of high values, then show which objects go with which attributes, a structure that is invisible in the raw matrix even when it is small. In industrial engineering this forms machine cells for families of components; special-purpose algorithms such as bond energy and rank order clustering reach the same block form directly. The choice of similarity coefficient matters: when shared absence is meaningful, use one that counts 0-0 matches, such as simple matching.
steps: Build the matrix, for example users by features used or tasks by screens visited, coded 0/1 or quantitatively.
Choose a similarity coefficient; use one that counts 0-0 matches (simple matching) when shared absence is informative, Jaccard when it is not.
Cluster the columns (Q-analysis), for example with UPGMA, and cluster the rows (R-analysis) separately.
Reorder columns and rows into their tree orders, or apply a bond energy or rank order algorithm directly.
Read off the blocks of co-occurring rows and columns and list the exceptions that fall outside any block.
Interpret blocks as candidate segments, modules or feature bundles and check them against qualitative evidence.
outputs: A doubly rearranged matrix showing blocks, with row and column dendrograms and a list of exceptions.
useWhen: Finding which user groups use which feature sets, which tasks share which screens, or which card-sort items co-occur with which participants.
avoidWhen: Avoid for very large, noisy matrices where block structure is weak; use non-negative matrix factorisation or model-based biclustering. If only one dimension matters, ordinary cluster analysis suffices.
whyLost: Heatmaps with dendrograms are common in genomics, but UX analytics rarely reorders both dimensions deliberately to find blocks.
whereToUse: Feature usage analysis in SaaS products, modular navigation design, permission and role design, content tagging audits.
example: A team builds a matrix of 300 accounts by 40 features used in the last quarter. After two-way rearrangement, three blocks appear: reporting-heavy finance accounts, workflow-heavy operations accounts and a small integration-heavy block, which guides packaging into three plans.
reference: Romesburg, H. C. (1984). Cluster Analysis for Researchers. Belmont, CA: Lifetime Learning Publications, pp. 23-24, 160-162; King, J. R. (1980). Machine-component grouping in production flow analysis. International Journal of Production Research, 18(2), 213-232.

name: Type-2 Tobit Sample Selection Model with Heckman Two-Step Estimation
origin: James Heckman, 1976 and 1979; Type-2 Tobit terminology from Takeshi Amemiya, 1985
summary: Models whether users do something with a probit and how much they do with a regression whose errors may correlate with that decision, correcting for self-selection.
description: Many outcomes are two-stage: whether a user buys, donates or responds, then how much. The Type-2 Tobit has a probit selection equation and an amount equation observed only for participants, each with its own regressors and parameters, and correlated normal errors. Unlike the Type-1 Tobit it lets a variable push the two parts in opposite directions: older people may be more likely to donate but give less. The correlation captures self-selection: if unobserved factors that make people participate also make them spend more, a regression on participants alone is biased. Heckman's two-step estimator fits the probit, computes the inverse Mills ratio for each participant, and adds it as a regressor in the amount equation; its significance indicates selection bias. White heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors are needed in the second step, or the model can be fitted by full maximum likelihood. Identification is fragile unless some variable affects participation but not amount.
steps: Specify a selection equation (participation) and an outcome equation (amount), each with its own regressors, ideally with at least one variable that affects participation but not amount.
Step 1: estimate a probit for participation by maximum likelihood on all cases.
Compute the inverse Mills ratio for each participant from the probit index.
Step 2: regress the amount on its regressors plus the inverse Mills ratio for participants, with White standard errors, or fit both equations by full maximum likelihood.
Test the Mills ratio coefficient for selection, and check the probit (pseudo-R-squared, likelihood ratio and heteroskedasticity tests) and the amount regression.
Interpret effects on participation, conditional amount and unconditional expected amount separately, and validate by forecasting on a hold-out sample, for example ranking users by expected value.
outputs: Separate effects on participation and amount, a test for selection, and expected-value forecasts for targeting.
useWhen: Outcomes where a participation decision precedes an amount (purchase then basket size, survey response then rating, feature adoption then usage intensity) and the same unobserved factors may drive both.
avoidWhen: No credible exclusion restriction exists, so identification rests only on normality; participation and amount share all drivers and directions (a Type-1 Tobit may suffice); zeros are true non-participation unrelated to amount (a simple two-part model is easier to defend).
whyLost: Selection models are standard in labour economics and marketing science but rarely appear in UX training, where analyses of 'users who did X' quietly ignore selection.
whereToUse: Survey results that come only from responders, satisfaction ratings from users who chose to rate, upgrade amounts among upgraders, feature usage intensity among adopters, donation and in-app purchase amounts.
example: An e-commerce team wants to know whether a new recommendations carousel raises basket size. Since only buyers have baskets, a Heckman model with a buy probit (using session source as the exclusion variable) shows the carousel raises purchase probability but slightly lowers basket value among buyers, which a buyers-only regression had missed.
sources: Quantitative Models in Marketing Research (Franses & Paap, 2001)
reference: Heckman, J. J. (1979). Sample selection bias as a specification error. Econometrica, 47, 153-161.

name: Typeface Selection and Pairing
aka: Typeface selection for task, medium and text
Typeface selection for purpose, reading conditions and message
In-context typeface trial with test words and trial fonts
origin: Robert Bringhurst (The Elements of Typographic Style, ch. 6) and Erik Spiekermann (Stop Stealing Sheep); type industry practice
summary: Choose text faces by output conditions, reading task, required features and tone, check workhorse criteria, trial candidates in context, and pair families by shared inner structure.
description: Both books treat type selection as a functional decision before an aesthetic one. Bringhurst orders the checks: the medium and output conditions the face must survive, the reading task, the features the text needs (good figures, small caps, weights, other scripts), then historical and tonal fit; an inherently good face suited to long reading comes before one sympathetic to the theme. Spiekermann's workhorse checklist for forms, catalogues, signage and small screen text asks for a sturdy regular, a clearly contrasting bold, robust and distinct numerals, and economy without compression. For screens both recommend low contrast, a generous x-height, open counters and sturdy or no serifs. Candidates are compared with a test word such as Handgloves or Hamburgefons and mocked up in the real layout with foundry testers or trial fonts. Pairing starts from one complete family; added faces should share inner structure, come from superfamilies or the same designer, and be matched optically for x-height and colour.
steps: Establish the output conditions: screen resolution and rendering, or printing method and paper, and the worst reproduction the text will meet.
Define the reading task (continuous reading, reference, forms, signage or display) and list required features: figures, small caps, weights, scripts and symbols.
Shortlist faces that survive the conditions and offer the features, then check tonal and historical fit with the content.
For heavy-duty text, test the four workhorse criteria: regular weight that neither breaks up nor fills in, a bold that stands out at a glance, unambiguous numerals, and economy without compression.
Set a test word (Handgloves or Hamburgefons) and real copy in each candidate, using foundry type testers or trial fonts in the real layout and on target browsers or printers.
Prefer one complete family; if more faces are needed, choose companions with compatible structure (same designer, same historical model or a superfamily).
Match x-height and colour optically at the intended sizes, confirm the full character set, and license the chosen faces properly.
outputs: A chosen face or small typeface system with defined roles (text, display, captions, tables) and a written rationale, plus in-context mock-ups.
useWhen: Use it when setting up a brand or design system typography, designing data-dense or form-heavy interfaces, or choosing faces for multilingual products.
avoidWhen: The criteria are expert judgement; when legibility is critical, test it with Readability Testing, Glanceability Measurement or a Preference Test with users. Faces chosen only for surface theme, or many fonts mixed casually, add drag.
whyLost: It survives because typography remains central to visual and interface design, and the craft is taught through standard texts.
whereToUse: Design systems, brand refreshes, dashboards and data products, forms and fintech statements, wayfinding and multilingual apps.
example: A banking app tests three sans faces at 13 px on low-end Android phones; one has confusable 1 and 7 and a weak bold. The team picks a superfamily whose serif companion is used only for marketing headings.
reference: Bringhurst, R. (2004). The Elements of Typographic Style (version 3.0). Point Roberts, WA: Hartley & Marks, pp. 93-117, 192-193. Spiekermann, E. (2022). Stop Stealing Sheep & Find Out How Type Works (4th ed., with F. Ulrich). Berlin: p98a.berlin.

name: Typographic Design of Tables, Forms and Complex Information
aka: Content-led layout of complex information (price lists, timetables)
Design for the bulk, not the extremes
origin: Robert Bringhurst (The Elements of Typographic Style, 4.4) and Erik Spiekermann (Stop Stealing Sheep)
summary: Set tables, timetables and forms as text to be read: edit content first, design for the bulk, align figures, and separate areas with space, not boxes.
description: Both authors treat dense information as an editorial and typographic problem rather than a cramming exercise. Bringhurst's table principles: keep all text horizontal and readable, use a minimum of furniture and a maximum of information, place rules or tints only where needed and in the reading direction, leave no rule at the outer edge, add internal white space, avoid dot leaders, and align figures flush right or on the decimal with tabular figures. Spiekermann derives layout from the content: find the shortest and longest elements, design for the bulk, then treat exceptions one by one by designing round them or rewriting. For forms he advises a narrow, legible face with a good bold and readable numerals, clear separation of printed labels from fill-in areas, light fill-in lines, and white space instead of boxes and vertical rules.
steps: Edit the content and structure of the table, timetable or form before setting it; replan any table that cannot be read.
Find the shortest, longest and typical entries and design for the bulk, then handle exceptions individually by designing round them or rewriting.
Choose a narrow, legible face with a good bold and robust numerals, and keep all text horizontal at a readable size.
Align numeric columns flush right or on the decimal with tabular figures, and text columns flush left; limit the number of alignment axes.
Remove unnecessary boxes, vertical rules and dot leaders; keep only dividers running in the reading direction and use white space to group.
For forms, separate printed labels from fill-in areas, make fill-in lines light guides, and for screen forms specify the field fonts.
Test completion and error rates with users once the layout is set.
outputs: A table, timetable or form specification covering type, alignment, spacing and rules.
useWhen: Use it for data tables, comparison and pricing tables, statements, timetables and long forms in any medium.
avoidWhen: It is craft guidance, not evidence of usability; validate forms with Usability Testing and error metrics such as Task Success Coding and Error-Opportunity Rates. For charts and visual encodings use Data Visualisation Design (LATCH) instead.
whyLost: It thrives in information design and editorial typography, but UX teams usually inherit table and form styles from component libraries without this craft.
whereToUse: Fintech statements and dashboards, insurance and tax forms, travel timetables, pricing pages, admin and analytics tables.
example: A tax filing service rebuilds its income table: figures are right-aligned with tabular numerals, vertical rules and boxed cells are removed and rows are grouped by spacing. Error rates on the subsequent form step fall in a usability test.
reference: Bringhurst, R. (2004). The Elements of Typographic Style (version 3.0). Point Roberts, WA: Hartley & Marks, pp. 70-72. Spiekermann, E. (2022). Stop Stealing Sheep & Find Out How Type Works (4th ed.). Berlin: p98a.berlin, pp. 89, 165-167.

name: Typographic Hierarchy and Text Structure Mapping
aka: Text structure analysis and typographic mapping
Read the text before designing it
Typographic hierarchy with minimal means (change one parameter at a time)
Typographic hierarchy and contrast within one family
Layout by reading mode and genre
origin: Robert Bringhurst (The Elements of Typographic Style, 1.2 and 3.5, 4.2), rooted in scribal and letterpress practice; Erik Spiekermann (Stop Stealing Sheep)
summary: Analyse a text's layers, relationships and reading mode first, then express each level with the smallest consistent typographic change, usually within one family.
description: Bringhurst casts the typographer as an interpreter who must read and understand the text before designing it. Analysis maps every layer, such as chapter and section heads, subheads, quotations, notes, lists and examples, and the relations between text and images, captions and tables, so that visible relationships mirror real ones. Each layer receives a consistent, distinct and harmonious identity; heads follow a predominantly symmetrical or asymmetrical series labelled A to F, using only as many levels as the structure needs. Emphasis and levels are built by changing one variable at a time (weight, slope, case with letterspacing, or size), trying the smallest change first and reducing weight slightly as size grows. Spiekermann adds that layout should follow reading mode: linear reading, browsing with multiple entry points, consulting under poor conditions, or glance messages.
steps: Read the whole text and note its tone, tempo, logical structure and length.
Identify the reading mode: linear, browsing with multiple entry points, consulting under poor conditions, or glance.
Map every layer and level (heads, subheads, quotations, notes, lists, examples, captions, tables) and the relations between text and other elements.
Choose a predominantly symmetrical or asymmetrical heading series and label levels A, B, C and so on, using only as many as the structure needs.

Starting from the text face, size and weight, distinguish each level by changing one variable (weight, slope, small caps or caps with letterspacing, or size), trying the smallest effective change first.
When increasing size, reduce weight slightly; keep punctuation and surrounding elements in the background.
Specify the result as heading and element styles and check it against real content at real sizes.
outputs: A map of text layers and relationships and a heading and emphasis specification (A to F heads, note form, caption placement, layout for the reading mode).
useWhen: Use it when designing content-heavy screens, documentation, articles, help centres or type scales for a design system.
avoidWhen: It structures the page from the text; if the content structure itself is unclear, use Content Audit or Content Modeling for Information Architecture first, and check scanning behaviour with Eye Tracking or the Highlighter test.
whyLost: It survives as the type-scale and heading-hierarchy work in every design system, though the prior step of analysing the text is often skipped.
whereToUse: Documentation sites, news and editorial products, help centres, long-form onboarding, design-system type scales and recipe or how-to apps.
example: A medical guidance site maps its articles and finds four real heading levels but six styles in use. It rebuilds the scale using size and weight changes within one family, and moves dosage tables into a consulting layout with short step heads.
reference: Bringhurst, R. (2004). The Elements of Typographic Style (version 3.0). Point Roberts, WA: Hartley & Marks, pp. 20-24, 60, 65-67. Spiekermann, E. (2022). Stop Stealing Sheep & Find Out How Type Works (4th ed.). Berlin: p98a.berlin, pp. 81-95, 111, 123-127, 157-163.

name: Typology Construction
origin: Frake (1962) ethnoscience; Max Weber's ideal types; Lofland (1971); presented by Patton (2002)
summary: Build typologies from participants' own category systems or by crossing inductively derived dimensions, then test each type against the data and with participants.
description: Typologies, built on ideal types or illustrative endpoints, differ from exhaustive taxonomies. Indigenous typologies are distinctions people in a setting already use: the analyst identifies the labels and then the attributes that separate one from another, as when teachers sorted truants into 'chronics' and 'borderlines'. Analyst-constructed typologies make explicit patterns participants have not named, such as museum visitors classed as commuters, nomads, cafeteria types and VIPs. Logical cross-classification crosses two inductively derived dimensions into a matrix of possible types, then returns to the data to fill, describe or leave each cell empty; in one programme, crossing teachers' beliefs about intervention with where they placed responsibility produced six teacher roles. The key risks are imposing the observer's world and forcing data into cells, so typologies are tested for recognisability with participants.
steps: Collect participants' own terms and labels for kinds of people, situations or behaviour from interviews and observation.
Identify the attributes that distinguish each indigenous category.
Derive two or more dimensions inductively from the data and cross them into a matrix of logically possible types.
Return to the data to fill, describe or leave empty each cell; treat empty cells as findings.
Label the types, using participants' language where possible, and test recognisability with participants.
Use the typology to organise findings, weight reactions by type and report the distribution and consequences of types.
outputs: Indigenous and analyst-built typologies, a cross-classification matrix, and findings organised by type.
useWhen: Synthesis where people clearly differ in how they approach a situation and the team needs a small set of meaningful types, for example for personas or segment-specific design.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing data into cells to fill a matrix, or presenting types as prevalence. For statistically derived segments, use cluster or latent class analysis.
whyLost: UX teams create archetypes intuitively and rarely use participant categories or logical cross-classification explicitly.
whereToUse: Archetype and persona work, service design, education and museum experiences, B2B role analysis.
example: Crossing 'confidence with money' against 'who manages household finances' in 25 interviews yields six types for a budgeting app; one empty cell shows that confident sole managers never sought the app at all.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2002). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (3rd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: UEQ (User Experience Questionnaire)
origin: Bettina Laugwitz, Theo Held and Martin Schrepp, SAP, 2008
summary: A 26-item semantic differential measuring six UX dimensions (attractiveness, perspicuity, efficiency, dependability, stimulation, novelty) with a public benchmark dataset.
description: The UEQ was developed at SAP through a data-driven process: a large pool of word pairs was reduced by factor analysis to 26 seven-point items forming six scales. Attractiveness is an overall valence; perspicuity, efficiency and dependability capture pragmatic quality; stimulation and novelty capture hedonic quality. A free analysis spreadsheet computes scale means, reliability and comparison with a benchmark of several hundred products, classifying results from 'bad' to 'excellent'. An 8-item short form (UEQ-S) suits in-product use, and UEQ+ allows modular scales. Rigour comes from using official translations, checking item consistency to detect careless responses, reporting confidence intervals, and using the benchmark to interpret values rather than arbitrary thresholds.
steps: Choose UEQ (26 items), UEQ-S (8 items) or a UEQ+ configuration based on respondent burden and dimensions of interest.
Administer after use, using an official translation for non-English audiences.
Collect at least 20-30 responses per product or version for stable scale estimates.
Use the official analysis tool to compute scale means, confidence intervals and Cronbach's alpha, and flag inconsistent respondents.
Compare with the UEQ benchmark to classify each scale.
Track scales across releases and pair low scales with qualitative research to explain them.
outputs: Six scale scores with confidence intervals, benchmark classification, release-to-release comparisons.
useWhen: Holistic UX evaluation, comparing design alternatives or releases, and international studies needing validated translations.
avoidWhen: When only perceived usability matters and benchmark comparability with SUS is needed; or for very short in-product surveys use UMUX-Lite or UEQ-S.
whyLost: Siloed: More comprehensive than SUS; academic origin; growing adoption in Europe.
whereToUse: Holistic UX evaluation; comparing design alternatives; longitudinal UX tracking.
example: An HR software vendor ran UEQ with 60 customers before and after a redesign. Efficiency moved from 'below average' to 'good' against the benchmark, but novelty stayed low, which the team accepted for a work tool.
sources: Construction and Evaluation of a User Experience Questionnaire (Laugwitz, Held & Schrepp)
Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
reference: Laugwitz, B., Held, T., & Schrepp, M. (2008). Construction and evaluation of a user experience questionnaire. In USAB 2008, LNCS 5298 (pp. 63-76). Springer.

name: UMAP
origin: Leland McInnes, John Healy and James Melville, 2018
summary: Projects high-dimensional behavioural or text embeddings into two dimensions to visualise structure, clusters and outliers in user populations.
description: UMAP, listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix for machine learning, is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that preserves local neighbourhood structure and more global structure than t-SNE. Applied to user feature vectors, session embeddings or embedded open-text responses, it produces maps where similar users or comments sit together, revealing clusters, continua and rare groups. For UX it is an exploratory instrument: it suggests segments and edge cases to investigate qualitatively. Rigour requires caution: distances between clusters and cluster sizes are not reliably meaningful, results depend on hyperparameters (n_neighbors, min_dist), and clusters should be confirmed with a separate method (for example HDBSCAN plus stability checks).
steps: Build feature vectors per user or session, or embed text with a language model.
Scale features and choose hyperparameters; run several settings.
Project to 2D and colour by known attributes (plan, tenure, outcome).
Cluster in the embedding or original space and test stability across seeds.
Sample users from clusters and outliers for qualitative follow-up.
Document caveats about interpreting distances.
outputs: 2D behavioural maps, candidate clusters and outliers, sampling frames for qualitative work.
useWhen: Exploratory analysis of large behavioural or feedback datasets to find unexpected groups.
avoidWhen: As evidence of segment size or distance; use confirmatory clustering or modelling.
whyLost: New and ML-native; UX teams lack the data science pairing the treatise recommends.
whereToUse: Feature usage exploration, LLM conversation log exploration, survey verbatim mapping.
example: Embedding 50,000 AI assistant prompts and mapping them with UMAP reveals a dense island of spreadsheet formula requests, a use case the team had not designed for.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
McInnes L, Healy J & Melville J (2018) UMAP: Uniform manifold approximation and projection for dimension reduction. arXiv:1802.03426
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
McInnes, Healy & Melville (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for dimension reduction
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: McInnes L, Healy J & Melville J (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction. arXiv:1802.03426.

name: UMAP visualisation
origin: Leland McInnes, John Healy and James Melville, 2018
summary: Projecting high-dimensional behavioural or text-embedding features into two dimensions to see clusters and gradients among users, sessions or responses.
description: UMAP builds a weighted nearest-neighbour graph in the original feature space and finds a low-dimensional layout preserving its structure. It is faster than t-SNE and preserves more global structure, making it useful for visually inspecting behavioural segments or semantic clusters of open-text responses. Its key parameters are n_neighbors (local versus global emphasis, typically 15-50) and min_dist (how tightly points pack). Rigour comes from treating UMAP as exploratory: distances and cluster sizes in the plot are not directly interpretable, apparent clusters can be artefacts of parameters, and results vary with the random seed. Clusters should be confirmed with a model fitted in the original space and checked across several parameter settings.
steps: Prepare a standardised feature matrix or sentence embeddings and remove near-duplicate rows.
Run UMAP with default parameters (n_neighbors 15, min_dist 0.1) and a fixed random seed.
Repeat with n_neighbors of 5, 30 and 50 and at least three seeds, keeping only structure that persists.
Colour points by known variables (plan type, tenure, GMM segment, sentiment) to interpret regions.
Confirm apparent clusters with a model fitted in the original space (GMM, HDBSCAN) and report its fit statistics, not the picture.
Annotate plots with caveats that axes and distances are not meaningful.
outputs: Two-dimensional maps of users, sessions or texts, stability checks across parameters, and hypotheses about clusters to test formally.
useWhen: Exploring large behavioural or text-embedding datasets, communicating segment structure, and checking whether a clustering solution looks plausible.
avoidWhen: Avoid as evidence of cluster existence or for measuring distances between groups; use clustering with fit indices or LDA instead. For small datasets under a few hundred points, PCA is usually clearer.
whyLost: UMAP is recent and lives in bioinformatics and machine learning; UX teams rarely work with high-dimensional feature matrices directly.
whereToUse: Behavioural persona discovery, open-ended feedback mapping, AI product prompt clustering and support-ticket analysis.
example: An AI writing assistant team embeds 40,000 user prompts and projects them with UMAP. A stable region of 'formal email rewrite' prompts emerges across parameter settings and is confirmed by HDBSCAN, guiding a new template feature.
sources: McInnes, L., Healy, J. & Melville, J. (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction. arXiv:1802.03426
The Inquiry Series, C4 — Behavioural Log Analysis — From Clickstreams to Personas
reference: McInnes, L., Healy, J. & Melville, J. (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction. arXiv:1802.03426

name: UMUX (Usability Metric for User Experience)
origin: Kraig Finstad (2010), Intel
summary: A four-item questionnaire aligned with the ISO definition of usability that tracks SUS closely with less than half the items.
description: Finstad designed the UMUX to give a SUS-like score with fewer items that map to the ISO 9241-11 definition (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction). Its four 7-point items are: this system's capabilities meet my requirements; using this system is a frustrating experience; this system is easy to use; I have to spend too much time correcting things with this system. Items alternate tone. Each is recoded to 0 to 6, summed, divided by 24 and multiplied by 100. In validation with 558 users of two systems, reliability was 0.94 and correlation with SUS was 0.96. The two positive items later became the UMUX-Lite.
steps: Administer the four items on 7-point agreement scales.
Recode positive items as response minus 1 and negative items as 7 minus response.
Sum the four, divide by 24 and multiply by 100.
Compare with SUS norms, which the UMUX closely tracks.
Report means with confidence intervals.
outputs: A 0 to 100 perceived usability score comparable to SUS.
useWhen: You need a SUS-comparable score in very little survey space.
avoidWhen: You can only ask two items (use UMUX-Lite) or need diagnostic subscales.
whyLost: Not lost; it has largely been superseded by its own two-item UMUX-Lite.
whereToUse: In-product surveys, large-scale tracking, enterprise IT satisfaction.
example: An internal IT portal scores 58 on UMUX, close to its SUS of 60, letting the team switch to the shorter instrument without losing comparability.
sources: A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
reference: Finstad, K. (2010). The usability metric for user experience. Interacting with Computers 22(5).

name: UMUX-Lite
origin: James Lewis, Brian Utesch and Deborah Maher, 2013
summary: A two-item usability questionnaire (capabilities meet requirements; easy to use) that correlates strongly with SUS and suits in-product micro-surveys.
description: UMUX-Lite derives from Finstad's four-item UMUX, keeping two positively worded items: 'This system's capabilities meet my requirements' and 'This system is easy to use', rated on seven-point scales. The two items map to the usefulness and ease-of-use constructs of the Technology Acceptance Model. Lewis and colleagues showed scores correlate highly with SUS and provided a regression adjustment to place UMUX-Lite on the SUS scale, enabling comparison with SUS norms. Its brevity makes it practical for continuous in-product measurement where a full questionnaire would suppress response rates. Rigour comes from using exact wording and scale points, applying the published conversion consistently, collecting enough responses (typically hundreds in-product) and accounting for sampling bias in who responds to intercept surveys.
steps: Use the exact two items on seven-point agreement scales.
Trigger the survey at a meaningful moment, such as after task completion, and sample users randomly to reduce bias.
Compute the raw score ((sum of items minus 2) / 12 × 100).
Apply the published regression adjustment to estimate a SUS-equivalent score if comparison with SUS norms is needed.
Report means with confidence intervals and segment by user type or feature.
Track scores over time and investigate drops with qualitative follow-up.
outputs: UMUX-Lite scores (raw and SUS-equivalent), trends over time, segment comparisons.
useWhen: Continuous in-product usability measurement, high-volume intercept surveys and dashboards tracking perceived usability over time.
avoidWhen: Lab studies where SUS is just as easy to administer and gives more stable estimates with small samples, or when you need diagnostic detail.
whyLost: Still in use: Minimal friction; good for in-product surveys at scale.
whereToUse: In-product NPS/usability measurement; continuous UX monitoring.
example: A project management SaaS added UMUX-Lite after report creation, collecting 1,800 responses a month. A drop from 78 to 69 SUS-equivalent after a release pointed to the new filter panel, confirmed in follow-up interviews.
sources: UMUX-LITE: When there's no time for the SUS (Lewis, Utesch & Maher)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
A Comparison of SUS, UMUX-LITE, and UEQ-S (Schrepp et al., 2023)
Quant UX Con 2022 Proceedings (Chapman et al., 2022)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Lewis, J. R., Utesch, B. S., & Maher, D. E. (2013). UMUX-LITE: When there's no time for the SUS. Proceedings of CHI 2013, 2099-2102.

name: Uniframe Definition from Examples and Near-Misses
aka: Uniframe definition from examples and near-misses (enforce, prevent, tolerate)
origin: Adapted for UX from Marvin Minsky (1986), retelling Patrick Winston's 1970 arch-learning program; the exception principle is Minsky's
summary: Build one definition covering several examples by deciding, against near-miss contrasts, which relations to enforce, prevent or tolerate, and keep counter-examples as an explicit exceptions list.
description: A uniframe is a single description that applies to several different things. In Winston's arch example, comparing arches with near-misses shows that the top must be supported by two standing blocks (enforce), the standing blocks must not touch (prevent), and the top may be any shape (tolerate). Most differences between examples are redundant or accidental, and which features matter depends on how the definition will be used. When no single description fits, one keeps an accumulation of alternatives. Minsky's exception principle adds that a rule which nearly always works should not be patched endlessly but complemented by a list of exceptions. Adapted to UX synthesis, the procedure gives a disciplined way to define a category, persona boundary, design pattern or eligibility rule from cases, making explicit what is required, excluded and irrelevant.
steps: Collect clear examples of the category and contrasting near-misses that differ in only one or two respects.
Break each into parts with properties and relations.
Compare each example with a near-miss and record the relation that must hold (enforce).
Record relations that must not hold (prevent) and features to stay neutral about (tolerate).
Drop differences that are redundant or accidental for the definition's intended use.
If no single description fits, keep an accumulation of alternative descriptions.
When a working rule meets a counter-example, add it to an exceptions list instead of rewriting the rule.
outputs: A compact definition listing enforced, prevented and tolerated features, plus an exceptions list.
useWhen: Defining what counts as a category, pattern, segment or rule from real cases, for example what makes a transaction 'suspicious', a user 'active' or a component a 'card'.
avoidWhen: Avoid when categories are graded or overlapping by nature; use Category structure paradigms: typicality, family resemblance and basic level or Radial Category Analysis. For open-ended theme building use Selective Coding and Core Category Identification.
whyLost: It came from early AI learning research and never entered UX synthesis, which defines categories by discussion rather than contrastive cases.
whereToUse: Design system component definitions, metric and segment definitions, content moderation and fraud rules, intent definitions for conversational AI.
example: A design system team defines a 'card' from 15 examples and 6 near-misses. They enforce a single bounded object with one primary action, prevent nested cards, tolerate any media, and list the legacy promo banner as an exception rather than loosening the rule.
reference: Minsky, M. (1986). The Society of Mind. New York: Simon & Schuster, pp. 120-127; Winston, P. H. (1970). Learning Structural Descriptions from Examples. PhD thesis, MIT.

name: Universal Design Principles Review
origin: Ronald L. Mace (term); principles by a working group at the Center for Universal Design, NC State University, 1997
summary: Review a product, service or environment against the seven Universal Design principles to find where it excludes people without adaptation or specialised design.
description: Universal Design is the design of products and environments usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without adaptation or specialised design. The seven principles from NC State's Center for Universal Design are equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use. They can evaluate existing designs as well as guide new ones. The review takes each principle in turn and asks where the design fails it, for whom, and how it could change. The original publication pairs each principle with guidelines, which give the review concreteness; the encyclopaedia summary provides no rating scheme, so findings are qualitative. Classic examples include kerb cuts, low-floor buses, acoustic traffic signals and subtitles.
steps: Define the product, service or environment and its range of users, including disabilities, ages and situational limitations.
Obtain the seven principles with their published guidelines from the Center for Universal Design.
Assess the design against each principle and its guidelines, using realistic scenarios of use.
Record each failure with the principle, the affected users and the evidence.
Propose changes that improve use for all rather than adding separate accommodations.
Validate key changes with users who have relevant disabilities.
outputs: Principle-by-principle findings with affected groups and proposed design changes.
useWhen: Reviewing physical-digital products, kiosks, public services and environments for inclusive use beyond technical accessibility compliance.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a compliance check; for web conformance use Accessibility Evaluation against WCAG, and for user evidence use Assistive Technology Testing.
whyLost: It is central in architecture and industrial design, while digital UX adopted WCAG and inclusive design toolkits instead.
whereToUse: Self-service kiosks, transport ticketing, smart home devices, retail and healthcare environments.
example: A rail operator reviews ticket machines against the seven principles. Low physical effort and size and space fail for wheelchair users reaching the card reader, prompting a lower reader and a mobile alternative.
sources: The Principles of Universal Design (Center for Universal Design, NC State University, 1997)
reference: Center for Universal Design (1997). The Principles of Universal Design, Version 2.0. North Carolina State University; Stephanidis, C. (2013). Design 4 All. In The Encyclopedia of Human-Computer Interaction, 2nd ed., ch. 42.

name: Unmanaged Performance Measurement (UPM)
aka: System performance measurement in the operational environment
donor: Human factors and military systems test and evaluation
origin: David Meister, 2004, building on his activity analysis (1985) and system test practice
summary: Records how people and a system actually perform during routine operation, with no contact or manipulation, and judges that performance against mission-derived criteria.
description: Meister calls UPM the simplest and most basic objective method: the researcher records what is done, how, when, where and how well, without contacting or controlling those observed, because any contact distorts performance. The researcher's control is limited to choosing when to measure, what to record and how to analyse. It cannot test causal hypotheses, but naturally occurring contrasts (night versus day, different crews, shifts) can be compared statistically. It is the method of choice when owners forbid interference, when the system is too large to manipulate, or when the aim is to describe actual performance and find errors and error-inducing features such as poor procedures or manuals. Its strength is that relevance and validity questions largely disappear because the real system is measured. It is common in acceptance tests, military exercises, medication error counts and inspection error rates, and beta testing is an instance, though such work is rarely published.
steps: Learn the system thoroughly through task analyses, manuals, mission descriptions, observation of ongoing work and interviews with personnel.
Fix the purpose and the measurement questions.
Derive quantitative performance criteria from mission requirements; where none exist, elicit them from experts, get management agreement and link behavioural criteria to system criteria.
Write a test plan covering subsystems, criteria, observer roles, data to collect, instrumentation, measures per subsystem, amount of data per cycle and the planned analysis.
Pretest the procedures (by walkthrough if the system cannot run), then record performance unobtrusively during normal operation, with two observers cross-checking where needed.
Only after the UPM period, add interviews, rating scales or experiments; then compare performance with the criteria, describe errors and natural contrasts, and trace causes of poor performance.
outputs: Descriptive and evaluative data against criteria: amount achieved, errors, response times, personnel interactions, problem areas and error-inducing features.
useWhen: The system is live and complete, intervention is forbidden or would distort behaviour, and you need a baseline of real performance against operational goals, for example in control rooms, clinical settings or large enterprise deployments.
avoidWhen: You need to test causes (use an experiment); the system is incomplete or not operating normally; mission criteria cannot be defined. For very large systems reduce scope to essential subsystems. For simple web behaviour, product analytics may already provide the record.
whyLost: It was framed for military and industrial system tests, and UX now treats live measurement as analytics instrumentation without the criterion-setting and test-plan discipline.
whereToUse: Hospital and clinical systems, operations centres, logistics and field-service tools, enterprise software rollouts, beta programmes with defined success criteria.
