example: Before redesigning a hospital's medication administration software, a team observes four wards for two weeks without intervening, logging time per administration, workarounds and near-misses against pharmacy-defined criteria. Night shifts show twice the scan-override rate, which is traced to poor lighting at the bedside scanner.
sources: Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
reference: Meister, D. (2004). Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Unmoderated Remote Testing
origin: Remote usability testing research, late 1990s; commercial platforms such as UserTesting (2007)
summary: Participants complete tasks on their own devices without a facilitator, recording screens and think-aloud, allowing fast, larger and geographically diverse samples.
description: Unmoderated remote testing uses an online platform to deliver tasks and questions to participants who complete them on their own, in their own environment and time. Sessions may record screen, audio and face, along with task success, time and post-task ratings. Because no facilitator is needed, tests can run in hours with dozens of participants across regions. The trade-off is the loss of real-time probing and clarification, so study design must anticipate misunderstandings. Rigour comes from unambiguous task wording, clear success criteria and validation questions, screening for attentive and representative participants, piloting, and combining behavioural metrics with recordings rather than relying on self-reported success.
steps: Define tasks, success criteria and post-task questions such as the Single Ease Question.
Write self-explanatory task instructions and include validation questions to confirm success.
Set screening criteria and recruit from a panel or your own users.
Pilot with 2 to 3 participants and fix confusing instructions.
Launch with 10 to 20 participants for qualitative insight, or 30 or more for metrics.
Review recordings and exclude low-quality sessions with documented criteria.
Analyse success, time, ratings and clips, and report findings.
outputs: Task success, time and ease ratings, recordings and highlight clips, and a list of observed problems.
useWhen: For iterative validation, quick comparisons, geographically diverse users and when you need moderate samples quickly.
avoidWhen: Avoid for complex or sensitive tasks, early concepts that need explanation, or specialist users who are hard to recruit on panels; use moderated testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Speed and scale advantage; widely adopted during/after COVID-19 shift to remote.
whereToUse: Iterative design; quick validation; when geographic diversity is needed.
example: A travel booking site tests a new date picker with 30 panel participants in two days. Recordings show 40 percent select the wrong return date on mobile, prompting a fix before release.
sources: Beyond the Usability Lab (Albert, Tullis & Tedesco)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Albert, W., Tullis, T. & Tedesco, D. (2010). Beyond the Usability Lab: Conducting Large-Scale Online User Experience Studies. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Unobtrusive Measures (Physical Traces and Archives)
origin: Eugene Webb, Donald Campbell, Richard Schwartz and Lee Sechrest, 1966 (Unobtrusive Measures)
summary: Infers behaviour from traces people leave without being studied (wear, accumulations, archives, workarounds), avoiding reactivity of interviews and observation.
description: Webb and colleagues catalogued nonreactive measures: erosion (wear on floor tiles in front of exhibits indicating popularity), accretion (fingerprints on glass, notes stuck to monitors), running records (archives, logs) and episodic records. Their argument for multiple operationalism held that every method has biases, and nonreactive traces triangulate reactive self-reports. In digital UX, logs are the obvious descendant, but physical and informal traces (sticky notes with passwords, laminated cheat sheets, printouts, home-made labels on devices, worn keys) are rich, unreactive evidence of design failures and workarounds, routinely overlooked.
steps: Identify the behaviours of interest and brainstorm traces they would leave (physical, digital, documentary).
Seek access to settings and archives ethically, including consent where traces are personal.
Systematically document traces with photographs, counts and location, using a coding scheme.
Assess biases of each trace (selective survival, deposit bias) as Webb et al. recommend.
Triangulate traces with interviews and logs.
Interpret traces as evidence of needs, workarounds and design failures.
outputs: A documented trace inventory, coded counts, and triangulated interpretations of behaviour and workarounds.
useWhen: Studying real practice where self-report may be biased, or where observation would change behaviour.
avoidWhen: When traces cannot be ethically accessed or interpreted without context.
whyLost: Digital analytics absorbed the 'running records' idea, while physical trace research disappeared from UX practice.
whereToUse: Workplace software rollouts, clinical settings, kiosks and public devices, home technology, shared devices.
example: A hospital audit photographs workstations and finds 63% have handwritten notes with EHR shortcuts or login workarounds. These traces drive a redesign of the most-annotated workflows.
sources: Webb, Campbell, Schwartz & Sechrest, Unobtrusive Measures: Nonreactive Research in the Social Sciences (1966)
Lee, Unobtrusive Methods in Social Research (2000)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Conceptual Foundations of Human Factors Measurement (Meister, 2004)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
The Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2015)
reference: Webb, E. J., Campbell, D. T., Schwartz, R. D., & Sechrest, L. (1966). Unobtrusive Measures. Rand McNally.

name: Unpacking check for probability and frequency questions
origin: Tversky and Koehler, 1994; Rottenstreich and Tversky, 1997; Fox and Tversky, 1998; Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein, 1978
summary: Compare packed and unpacked versions of likelihood, frequency or value questions, because listing components inflates their total and deflates the residual 'other' category.
description: Support theory holds that judged probability attaches to descriptions of events, not events. An implicit category ('natural causes') is judged less likely than the same category listed as explicit parts, and separately judged parts sum to more than the whole. Unpacking factors of about 1.4-1.9 were found, rising with the number of components, while complementary pairs still summed to about 1. Incentives do not remove the effect and experts show it too. Rottenstreich and Tversky separated implicit subadditivity (from unpacking and availability) from explicit subadditivity (from judging components one by one). Fox and Tversky found the same in prices: parts priced to about twice the whole. For surveys, detailed option lists inflate listed items and deflate 'other', and 'how often do you have problems?' gets a smaller answer than a list of named problems. Giving examples of the residual reduces the bias.
steps: Audit likelihood, frequency and option-list questions for differences in how finely categories are partitioned.
Where totals matter, give packed and unpacked versions to random split samples, or ask for the total separately and compare with the summed parts.
Compute the unpacking factor (sum of parts divided by packed estimate) and test the difference (for example Mann-Whitney).
Collect complementary judgements as a check that the effect is not simple acquiescence.
Populate residual 'other' categories with examples and keep partitions consistent across waves and comparisons.
Report estimates with the partition used, and avoid comparing figures from differently partitioned questions.
outputs: Unpacking factors, complementarity checks and a corrected question design with consistent partitions.
useWhen: When survey or interview questions ask how often problems occur, how likely outcomes are, or how users split time or spend across categories, and the numbers will be compared or summed.
avoidWhen: Avoid over-engineering where only relative ranking matters. The effect varies with partition type and component similarity (similar parts get repacked); for overall survey error see the Total Survey Error Framework.
whyLost: Well known in decision research but rarely translated into survey design checks; UX questionnaires are written with whatever option list seems natural.
whereToUse: Problem-frequency surveys, risk and incident estimates, time-use and spend breakdowns, feature-request tallies, forecasting workshops.
example: A survey asks 'how often do you have problems with the app?' versus a list of five named problem types; the listed version yields about twice the frequency, so the team reports both and uses the packed version for trend tracking.
reference: Tversky, A., & Koehler, D. J. (1994). Support theory: A nonextensional representation of subjective probability. Psychological Review, 101(4), 547-567.

name: Unreachable state detection
origin: Reachability analysis in model checking, Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis, 1980s; applied to interactive systems by Thimbleby and Harrison
summary: Systematically explores an interface's state space to find states that cannot be reached and, conversely, critical actions that cannot be reached from some states.
description: Reachability asks two questions of a state model: can every intended state be reached from the start state, and can every critical state (home, stop, cancel, save) be reached from every other state within an acceptable number of steps? Unreachable intended states signal dead features or specification errors; states from which a critical state is unreachable are traps. Analysis uses breadth-first search on a state graph or a model checker for large or concurrent systems, and reports shortest path lengths so designers can see not just whether but how quickly safety actions can be reached. Thimbleby's work on device graphs showed many real devices fail these checks. Rigour comes from a complete model, including timeouts and errors, and from automated, not visual, checking.
steps: Build or extract a state model of the interface (from specification, code or systematic exploration).
Define the start state(s) and critical target states (stop, home, undo, save, help).
Run breadth-first search or a model checker to compute reachability from start to all states and from all states to each critical state.
Report unreachable states and states lacking a path to each critical state, plus shortest-path lengths; flag any critical action needing more than 2 steps in safety contexts.
Review findings with designers and engineers to classify each as dead design, model error or real hazard.
Fix hazards and add automated reachability checks to the build or test pipeline.
outputs: Reachability matrix, list of unreachable and trap states, path-length distribution to critical actions, and regression checks.
useWhen: When the interface has many modes or states and safety or recoverability matters; when users report getting 'stuck'.
avoidWhen: When no reasonably complete state model can be built; use exploratory usability testing and dead-end identification on observed paths.
whyLost: Reachability is a staple of formal verification but UX teams rarely have state models to run it on, so the analysis remains in engineering and academic HCI.
whereToUse: Medical devices, surgical robots, automotive infotainment, kiosks, set-up wizards, and conversational agents.
example: Breadth-first search over a 340-state infusion pump model shows Emergency Stop needs 4 presses from the drug-library edit state. Adding a global stop key reduces it to 1 from every state.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Thimbleby, H. (2007). Press On: Principles of Interaction Programming. MIT Press.

name: Uplift Modelling
origin: Nicholas Radcliffe and Patrick Surry (1999); Victor Lo, 'The true lift model' (2002)
summary: Predicts the individual-level causal effect of an intervention from randomised data, to target users who will respond because of it, not regardless of it.
description: Response models predict who will convert; uplift models predict who will convert because they were treated. Users fall into four groups: persuadables, sure things, lost causes and 'sleeping dogs' who react negatively to treatment. Using randomised treatment and control data, uplift models (two-model approach, class transformation, uplift trees, meta-learners such as T-, S- and X-learners) estimate conditional treatment effects. Evaluation uses Qini or uplift curves on held-out data, not accuracy. In UX, uplift modelling identifies who should receive nudges, onboarding help or retention offers, and who would be harmed or annoyed by them.
steps: Run a randomised experiment of the intervention with a sufficiently large control group.
Prepare pre-treatment features for each user, avoiding any post-treatment variables.
Fit uplift models (e.g. two-model baseline, X-learner, uplift random forest) with cross-validation.
Evaluate with Qini coefficient and uplift curves on holdout data, comparing to random targeting.
Identify segments with negative uplift (sleeping dogs) and examine them qualitatively.
Deploy targeting with a persistent randomised holdout to confirm incremental impact.
outputs: Individual uplift scores, Qini curves, segment profiles including negatively affected users, targeting policy.
useWhen: Deciding whom to show prompts, offers, tutorials or interventions, given randomised data.
avoidWhen: Without randomised data, or with small samples; heterogeneous effect estimates are noisy.
whyLost: It stayed in marketing analytics, and UX experimentation focuses on average effects.
whereToUse: Retention offers, onboarding nudges, notification targeting, upsell prompts, health behaviour interventions.
example: A streaming service finds its 'come back' email has positive average effect, but uplift modelling shows 18% of recipients are sleeping dogs more likely to cancel when emailed; excluding them improves net retention.
sources: Radcliffe & Surry, Real-world uplift modelling with significance-based uplift trees (2011), Stochastic Solutions white paper
Lo, The true lift model (2002), ACM SIGKDD Explorations
Künzel et al., Metalearners for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (2019), PNAS
reference: Lo, V. S. Y. (2002). The true lift model. ACM SIGKDD Explorations, 4(2), 78-86.

name: Usability Conceptualisation Sessions
origin: Heike Winschiers and Jens Fendler, Polytechnic of Namibia, 2007 (Culture-Centric Development framework)
summary: Short group workshops where local users define what usability means to them, producing locally valid quality criteria that then shape which evaluation methods are used.
description: Winschiers and Fendler argue that standard usability testing carries a double western bias: in the definition of usability and in methods built to measure it. Their sessions ask small mixed groups of users of a given system what usability and a good working environment mean to them, then which terms their software must meet to count as usable. In Namibia, frequent terms were easy, safe, comfortable, specific, reliable, right pace, goal-oriented and conducive; no group mentioned speed, learnability, memorability or error rate, and satisfaction meant beneficial, transparent, stress-free and flexible. These locally negotiated criteria open a project. Evaluation methods are then adapted to local norms, for example collective workshop evaluations, evaluators of the same ethnicity and task framing through story-telling, and an evaluation plan follows.
steps: Form small groups of three to six users of each system, mixed by gender, age, profession and ethnicity.
Ask each group to brainstorm associations with the word usability, taking care with translation.
Ask them to describe the characteristics of a good working environment.
Have the group select from both lists the terms their system must satisfy to count as usable.
Aggregate terms across groups into local quality criteria, noting frequency.
Choose and adapt evaluation methods to fit these criteria and local norms, and write an evaluation plan.
outputs: Locally negotiated usability criteria and an acculturated evaluation plan.
useWhen: Designing or evaluating systems for cultures and contexts different from those where standard usability metrics were developed.
avoidWhen: When you need comparable benchmarks across markets (use standard instruments with Cross-Cultural Survey Equivalence Testing). Data are small and early; it is unclear whether results reflect national, group or individual views, and translating 'usability' may steer answers.
whyLost: Cross-cultural HCI moved towards dimension models and localisation checklists; renegotiating the definition of usability itself was seen as academic.
whereToUse: Products for the Global South, public sector systems in multilingual countries, enterprise tools across regions, indigenous and community technology.
example: Before testing a mobile health worker app in rural Kenya, a team runs conceptualisation sessions; health workers define usability as reliable offline, respectful and not embarrassing in front of patients, so the test plan adds a patient-presence scenario.
reference: Winschiers, H. and Fendler, J. (2007). Assumptions considered harmful: the need to redefine usability. In Aykin, N. (ed.) Usability and Internationalization: HCI and Culture, LNCS 4559. Springer, pp. 452-461.

name: Usability Engineering Lifecycle (Mayhew)
origin: Deborah Mayhew, 1999
summary: Phase-gated process model integrating requirements analysis, conceptual and detailed design, evaluation and installation, with defined usability goals and deliverables.
description: Mayhew's lifecycle gave UX an engineering-level process model: a defined sequence of activities, deliverables and decision points that could integrate with software development at the rigour appropriate to safety-critical systems. Its phases cover requirements analysis (user profiles, contextual task analysis, platform constraints, general design principles, usability goals), design/testing/development across three levels (conceptual model, screen design standards, detailed UI) with iterative evaluation at each, and installation with user feedback. The treatise argues that what was lost when agile displaced it was the insistence that usability is a system requirement to be managed with the rigour of performance or reliability, especially the setting of measurable usability goals.
steps: Produce user profiles, contextual task analysis and platform capability analysis.
Set measurable qualitative and quantitative usability goals.
Design and evaluate a conceptual model through iterative testing.
Define and test screen design standards.
Develop detailed UI design and evaluate iteratively against goals.
Install, collect user feedback and feed it into the next cycle.
outputs: Usability goals, conceptual model, screen standards, evaluation reports, installation feedback.
useWhen: Large or safety-critical programmes needing explicit usability gates and goals.
avoidWhen: Fast-moving consumer products with continuous delivery, unless adapted to sprints.
whyLost: Its sequential, phase-gated structure clashed with agile, so the whole model was abandoned instead of adapted.
whereToUse: Medical device programmes, defence, public-sector digital transformation, enterprise ERP rollouts.
example: A national tax agency adapts Mayhew's usability goals into each programme increment, requiring 90% first-time completion on core filing tasks before release.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Mayhew DJ (1999) The Usability Engineering Lifecycle: A Practitioner's Handbook for User Interface Design
reference: Mayhew DJ (1999) The Usability Engineering Lifecycle. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Usability Findings Report and Recommendations
origin: Dumas, Molich and Jeffries (2004); Molich, Jeffries and Dumas (2007); ISO/IEC 25062 for summative reports
summary: Report each usability finding with location, user-and-task description, design cause, evidence, severity and a costed, specific recommendation, ranked so teams can act on it.
description: Comparative studies such as CUE-4 showed that many practitioners write findings developers cannot use. A good finding states the problem in user and task terms, not as a solution; gives its location with annotated screenshots; names the judged design cause, linked to guidelines; provides evidence of what users did and said; rates severity with reasons; and proposes a redesign, ideally bundling related problems into one fix, with cost and trade-offs. Molich and colleagues add that recommendations should be clear, specific, at the conceptual level, respectful of business and technical constraints, and solve the whole class of problem. Ranking by importance and expected effort makes managers more likely to act. Reports should be audience-tailored, jargon-free, organised by affinity for large sets, backed by short video clips and presented in person; informal numbers must not be presented as statistics. Summative reports follow the Common Industry Format.
steps: Identify the audience (team, stakeholders, management, clients) and adapt content, format and tone.
Write each problem as user, task and effect, with location (annotated screenshot) and evidence of what users did and said.
State the judged design cause with links to guidelines, and give a reasoned severity rating.
Propose specific redesigns at the conceptual level, bundling related problems and noting cost, constraints and trade-offs.
Rank recommendations by importance and expected effort, for example top priority, mid-level changes, small required fixes and next-version items.
Organise large sets by affinity, add short self-contained video clips (with consent), and keep numbers informal and anonymous.
Present in person and argue for prioritisation; use the Common Industry Format for summative tests.
outputs: A formative or summative evaluation report with ranked, evidence-backed recommendations and supporting video clips.
useWhen: After any usability test or expert review where findings must persuade developers and managers to act.
avoidWhen: Avoid long reports when the team observed sessions and a debrief suffices; use Usability Test Debrief Meeting or Screenshot Forensics. Some practitioners prefer reporting observations only, leaving solutions to designers.
whyLost: It survives as standard practice, though the discipline of separating problem, cause and solution is often lost in slide decks.
whereToUse: Agency and consultancy deliverables, regulated industries needing documented evaluation, design-system governance.
example: Instead of 'add flashing red buttons', a fintech report writes that users could not tell what to do next because they did not notice the Continue button, rates it severe, and proposes moving it above the fold at low cost.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Molich, R., Jeffries, R. and Dumas, J. S. (2007). Making usability recommendations useful and usable. Journal of Usability Studies; Dumas, J. S., Molich, R. and Jeffries, R. (2004). Describing usability problems: are we sending the right message? interactions 11(4), 24-29.

name: Usability Issue Log and Issue-Based Metrics
origin: Albert and Tullis's synthesis of reporting practice; Marsh (2018, 2022)
summary: Catalogue every usability issue from test data, merge, count and prioritise them, and report metrics such as unique issues by severity, issues per participant and percentage affected.
description: Turning raw qualitative test notes into a prioritised issue catalogue is a disciplined sequence: get to know the data, list every issue per transcript without categorising or counting, group similar issues, return to recordings to separate subtly different problems, count instances, and weigh context, because a rare issue may still be critical, especially if the moderator had to assist. The catalogue records issue number, priority, description, recommendation and cost of fixing; a journey-board variant lays issues under each step of the journey. Albert and Tullis add metrics: unique issues per iteration (24, 12, then 4 across three rounds), split by severity; mean issues per participant with confidence interval; the percentage of participants hitting each issue; issues by three to eight categories and by task; and the percentage meeting any high-severity issue. Counts depend on evaluators and tasks, so severity schemes must stay consistent across studies.
steps: Review data after each session, then list every issue or need per transcript without categorising or counting.
Group similar issues and return to recordings to decide whether differently described problems are the same; merge duplicates across participants and studies.
Log each unique issue with participants, task, category (three to eight categories) and severity using one consistent scheme.
Count instances per issue and weigh context: severity, whether help was needed, and whether a rare issue would affect others.
Prioritise in a catalogue table with issue number, priority, description, recommendation and cost of fixing, or on a journey board with one column per step.

Report unique issues per iteration by severity, issues per participant (mean and confidence interval), percentage of participants affected per issue and percentage meeting any high-severity issue; with small samples report frequencies rather than percentages.
outputs: A prioritised issue catalogue with recommendations, and charts of issue frequency by iteration, severity, category and task.
useWhen: After formative tests or across iterations, when you need a traceable record of problems and evidence that a redesign reduced them.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating counts as objective across teams or task sets because of the evaluator effect; for performance comparison use Single Usability Metric (SUM) or task metrics.
whyLost: Issue logs are standard practice; the quantitative issue metrics are less often reported but persist in benchmarking teams.
whereToUse: Iterative product development, agency reporting, regulated usability engineering files, design-system defect tracking.
example: A health-portal team logs 41 raw observations into 18 unique issues. Across three iterations unique issues drop from 18 to 7, and none of the remaining are high severity.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience, 3rd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 6, pp. 165-169; Marsh, S. (2022). User Research, 2nd ed. Kogan Page.

name: Usability Magnitude Estimation (UME)
origin: Cordes (1984); McGee (2003, 2004); from Stevens' magnitude estimation in psychophysics
summary: Asks participants to rate each task's difficulty as a ratio of a baseline task, aiming for ratio-scale usability measurement.
description: Magnitude estimation comes from psychophysics, where people judge stimulus intensity relative to a reference (twice as bright, half as loud). Applied to usability, participants first complete an easy baseline task assigned a value (for example 10), then rate each later task relative to it, so a task rated 40 is judged four times as difficult. The goal is a ratio scale, where differences and ratios are meaningful. Participants usually need training with simple stimuli such as line lengths, and analysis uses log transformation and geometric means. Sauro and Dumas (2009) found UME was harder for participants to use and less sensitive than the SEQ or SMEQ, which is why it has largely disappeared from practice.
steps: Train participants on magnitude estimation with simple stimuli such as line lengths.
Have them complete a very easy baseline task and assign it a fixed value.
After each target task, ask for a number expressing its difficulty relative to the baseline.
Log-transform each participant's ratings to remove individual scale use.
Compare tasks using geometric means.
outputs: Ratio-scale difficulty estimates per task.
useWhen: Research contexts where ratio-level perception of difficulty is the question.
avoidWhen: Routine usability testing; the SEQ is easier and more sensitive.
whyLost: Training burden and participant confusion, and comparative studies showing simpler single items work better.
whereToUse: Academic measurement research, psychophysics-inspired UX studies.
example: With a baseline icon-selection task set at 10, participants rate "export a report" at 55 on average, more than five times as difficult.
reference: McGee, M. (2003). Usability magnitude estimation. Proceedings of HFES 47.

name: Usability Problem Identification Criteria
origin: Synthesised by Hertzum (2020) from Jacobsen et al. (1998), Stone et al. (2005), Følstad et al. (2012) and Fan et al. (2019)
summary: Scan session data for eight observable signs that a usability problem occurred, from negative emotion and surprise to unnoticed omissions, overload and trust failures.
description: Defining a usability problem as 'a needed interface change' is too vague to apply consistently, which contributes to the evaluator effect. Hertzum lists eight indicators to look for in session data: negative emotion such as frustration or uncertainty, verbal or bodily; surprise; need for assistance; trying several actions and backtracking; unnoticed omission of information or steps, visible only by comparison with the correct solution; mental overload, often signalled by fewer verbalisations; violation of standards or conventions; and failure to instil trust and credibility. No universal threshold exists: smaller difficulties count on central features. Some teams require at least two users before recording a problem; with small samples, single-user problems should count. Cultural differences matter, since indirectness can hide dissatisfaction, so culturally matched evaluators help.
steps: Agree the eight indicators and a solution key per task before analysis.
Analyse each session individually, marking episodes that match any indicator, using behaviour as well as speech.
Compare task outcomes with the solution key to catch unnoticed omissions.
Judge whether each difficulty is significant given the feature's centrality.
Set a single-user rule appropriate to sample size and apply it consistently.
Account for cultural expression, ideally with culturally matched evaluators, then merge episodes across sessions into a candidate problem list.
outputs: A candidate problem list with linked evidence and the indicator that triggered each entry.
useWhen: Analysing think-aloud or observational usability sessions, especially with several analysers who need consistent detection rules.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a severity scheme; it detects problems but does not rank them. Use Severity Rating Scale (Nielsen) for ranking.
whyLost: Practitioners detect problems intuitively, so explicit detection criteria, which reduce the evaluator effect, are rarely written down.
whereToUse: Multi-analyst research teams, regulated usability engineering, cross-cultural studies, training junior researchers.
example: Two researchers analysing a pension-app test agree to log 'unnoticed omission' whenever a participant submits without the beneficiary step. This surfaces a severe problem no participant mentioned aloud.
reference: Hertzum, M. (2020). Usability Testing: A Practitioner's Guide to Evaluating the User Experience. Morgan & Claypool, pp. 64-67.

name: Usability Session Observer Protocol
origin: Steve Krug (2010); Nunnally and Farkas (2017); Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015)
summary: Fixed roles and ground rules that let stakeholders watch test sessions live without disturbing participants, capture their top problems and feed vetted questions to the moderator.
description: Watching even one user live changes stakeholders more than any report, so the protocol aims to get influential people in front of sessions while protecting data quality. Each session has a moderator and a note-taker, rotating between sessions, and no more than two researchers in the room. Observers watch from a separate room or remotely, are briefed on rules (silence, phones off, write questions down, never interrupt, expect task order to vary), and anyone listening in remote sessions is introduced. Managers of participants are excluded, because people then describe policy rather than practice. After every session each observer writes the three most serious problems they saw. A 'hall monitor' manages the observation room and relays questions; near the end the moderator collects written questions, filters out leading ones and asks the useful ones in a closing 'coffee talk'.
steps: Schedule sessions on a quiet day and invite everyone with influence on the design, with a save-the-date about two weeks ahead and reminders.
Assign a moderator and note-taker per session, rotate roles, and limit the test room to two researchers.
Set up an observation room or remote feed out of earshot, with a shared screen and good audio; record for absentees.
Brief observers: silence, phones off, write questions down, never interrupt, note quotes with timestamps; introduce all remote listeners to the participant and exclude participants' managers.
After each session, have every observer write their three most serious problems on a form.
Near the end of each session, collect observer questions, filter and reword leading ones, and ask them in a closing segment.
Have all observers attend the debrief with their lists.
outputs: Per-observer top-three problem lists, in-session answers to stakeholder questions, complete notes and stakeholders with first-hand exposure.
useWhen: Any moderated usability test or interview programme where stakeholder buy-in and team learning matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid observers in the test room unless unavoidable, and avoid letting observers draw conclusions from a single session; for distributed teams, pair recordings with Screenshot Forensics.
whyLost: It survives as standard practice in mature research teams, though remote observation has weakened the shared-room experience.
whereToUse: Product teams adopting research, sceptical engineering or executive stakeholders, remote research with chat back-channels.
example: During remote tests of a claims app, observers post questions in a private channel. The moderator rewords 'Did you find the big blue button confusing?' to 'Tell me about this screen' before asking.
reference: Krug, S. (2010). Rocket Surgery Made Easy. New Riders, pp. 90-101; Nunnally, B. and Farkas, D. (2017). UX Research. O'Reilly Media; Baxter, K., Courage, C. and Caine, K. (2015). Understanding Your Users, 2nd ed. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 161-162.

name: Usability Specification and UX Targets
aka: Comparison to goals and expert performance
origin: Whiteside, Bennett and Holtzblatt (1988); acceptance testing proposed by Shneiderman
summary: Specify measurable usability targets with worst, target and best levels before design, then test against them, iterating until targets are met or using them as contractual acceptance criteria.
description: Instead of deciding after a test which problems matter, the team writes measurable usability requirements up front. Each row of the specification table names a user class and task, an attribute (initial or long-term performance, learnability, retention, satisfaction), a measuring instrument (benchmark tasks, a questionnaire such as SUS), a metric, the current or baseline level, and worst acceptable, target and best attainable levels. Testing then reports observed results against targets, and iteration ends when targets are met, giving an explicit stopping rule. Shneiderman extends this to acceptance testing: for example at least 30 of 35 specified participants complete benchmark tasks within 30 minutes, with separate criteria for older adults, disabled users and retention after a week. Results can also be expressed as ratios to expert performance or target page visits. Targets need team commitment, piloted benchmark tasks and one-sample tests to claim attainment.
steps: Choose user classes, key tasks and the usability attributes that matter (effectiveness, efficiency, learnability, retention, satisfaction).
Define a measuring instrument and metric for each, such as benchmark-task time, completion rate, errors or a SUS score.
Measure a baseline on the existing or competing system.
Set worst acceptable, target and best attainable levels with users and developers, for example SUS worst 71, target 80, best 90, keeping about a dozen attainable targets.
For contractual use, specify participant profile, numbers, training and pass thresholds, such as 30 of 35 completing tasks within 30 minutes, plus criteria for special groups and retention.
Pilot benchmark tasks, then test and record observed results against each target, using one-sample tests and confidence intervals to claim attainment.
Redesign and retest until targets are met; express gaps as ratios to expert time or target page visits to locate the worst tasks.
outputs: A usability specification table with observed results and pass or fail status per target, benchmark task sheets, and expert-ratio or efficiency views per task.
useWhen: Procurement, regulated or high-stakes systems, redesigns with clear performance goals, and teams needing an explicit stopping criterion for iteration.
avoidWhen: Avoid in early exploratory work or when tasks are not yet known; impossible targets such as zero errors undermine it. Use Moderated Usability Testing for formative discovery.
whyLost: Goal-setting language survives in OKRs and benchmarks, but the full worst-target-best table and contractual acceptance testing faded as the field moved to qualitative, agile evaluation.
whereToUse: Government and enterprise procurement, medical device human factors, call-centre and kiosk systems, AI tools with productivity claims.
example: A ticket-kiosk project targets 2.5 minutes for a casual user to buy a ticket against a 3-minute counter baseline. Round two reaches 2.7 minutes, so the payment step is redesigned before a final acceptance test.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Whiteside, J., Bennett, J. and Holtzblatt, K. (1988). Usability engineering: our experience and evolution. In M. Helander (Ed.), Handbook of Human-Computer Interaction. Elsevier, 791-817.

name: Usability Test Debrief Meeting
origin: Steve Krug (2010); Travis and Hodgson (2019)
summary: Straight after testing, observers pool their top problems, agree a ranked list of the most serious and commit to the simplest fixes achievable before the next round.
description: The debrief turns observation into commitment. Krug runs it over about an hour at lunch, open only to people who watched sessions. Everyone reads out their three most serious problems, repeats are marked, all items go on the wall, and the group or facilitator selects and ranks the ten most serious, judged by how many users will hit each and how badly. Working down the list without skipping, the team agrees the simplest fix for each until the month's fixing resources are committed, then a short email records what was tested, what will be fixed and when the next round is. Travis and Hodgson add that the meeting should be co-chaired with the product owner, attended by decision makers, kept to about 15 minutes of talk and 45 of discussion, start with the team's own reactions, and seek consensus on problems before solutions.
steps: Circulate a short summary in advance and ensure decision makers and observers attend; co-chair with the product owner.
Explain the aim: agree the most serious problems and what will be fixed before the next round.
Start with team reactions and surprises, then have each observer read their three most serious problems, noting repeats.
Write all problems on the wall and choose the top five to ten by severity (how many users affected, how badly).
Agree consensus on problems before discussing solutions, steering opinions back to observed evidence.
Working down the ranked list without skipping, agree the simplest feasible fix for each until available resources are committed.
Send a brief email listing tasks tested, problems to fix, owners, where recordings are and the next test date.
outputs: A ranked top-problem list, a committed fix list with owners, and a short email record.
useWhen: Immediately after a round of moderated tests that the team observed, especially in iterative or monthly test cycles.
avoidWhen: Avoid if few people observed sessions; present evidence first with Screenshot Forensics or a highlights video, or document thoroughly with a Usability Findings Report and Recommendations.
whyLost: It survived as a staple of lean and discount usability practice because it converts findings into action quickly.
whereToUse: Product squads, startups, design sprints, monthly test programmes.
example: After four sessions on a pharmacy app, the team lists 23 problems, ranks the top ten and commits to fixing five within the sprint, chiefly relabelling the repeat-prescription button.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
reference: Krug, S. (2010). Rocket Surgery Made Easy. New Riders, pp. 102-109; Travis, D. and Hodgson, P. (2019). Think Like a UX Researcher. CRC Press, pp. 221-227.

name: Usability Test Task Design
aka: Task selection and ordering for usability tests
origin: Dumas and Redish (1993, 1999); Goodman, Kuniavsky and Moed (2012); Hertzum (2020)
summary: Select, write, time and order usability test tasks so they probe likely problems and matter to users, phrased as realistic goals without interface words or hints.
description: Testing samples a few tasks from many, so task choice determines what can be found. Selection draws on likely usability problems (the first criterion, by analogy with software testing that assumes bugs exist), designers' concerns, tasks hard to recover from, and new, critical or frequent tasks; an importance-times-doubt matrix (each rated 1 to 5) picks about five feature clusters for a 60 to 90 minute session. Each task becomes a short scenario in users' words, stating the goal and needed data but not the steps, with a clear end state. Early, open-ended tasks let users bring real needs; later, specific tasks with an evaluator-only solution key probe a clarified design, optionally with one unsolvable task. Time is estimated as expert time multiplied by 3 for simple tasks up to 10 for complex ones. Tasks are ordered in a natural sequence, easiest first, and piloted.
steps: List candidate tasks from likely problems, designers' concerns, hard-to-recover tasks and new, critical or frequent user tasks.
Rate candidate features 1 to 5 for importance and for design doubt, multiply, and keep the top scorers (about five clusters for a 60 to 90 minute session), each with a one-sentence question.
Write each task as a short scenario in users' language, with a lifelike motive, the needed data and a clear end state, avoiding interface terms and hints.
Use open-ended tasks when needs are unclear and specific tasks with an evaluator-only solution key when probing a clarified design; consider one unsolvable task.
Estimate time per task as expert time x 3 (simple) to x 10 (complex or data entry), sizing to roughly 5 to 10 tasks per hour.
List resources, seeded data and reset procedures per task, and order tasks in natural sequence, easiest and most important early.
Pilot the tasks, fix ambiguity, and present them in writing one at a time.
outputs: An ordered task list with scenarios, solution keys, time estimates, resource lists and traceability to the concerns each task probes.
useWhen: Planning any task-based usability test, benchmark or unmoderated study.
avoidWhen: Avoid fixed tasks when you need to learn what users would naturally do; use Contextual Inquiry or participant-generated tasks instead.
whyLost: It survives as core practice, though weak task wording that leaks interface terms remains common.
whereToUse: All usability testing contexts, especially unmoderated studies where wording cannot be clarified live.
example: A van-hire site test gives a scenario about moving a three-room flat; the solution key says a 17-foot truck is needed. Participants who choose smaller vans reveal that size guidance is missing.
sources: A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish, 1999)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
reference: Dumas, J. S. and Redish, J. C. (1999). A Practical Guide to Usability Testing, rev. ed. Intellect, pp. 159-182; Hertzum, M. (2020). Usability Testing: A Practitioner's Guide. Morgan & Claypool, pp. 38-41.

name: Usability Testing
origin: Human factors labs, 1970s to 1980s; formalised by Dumas & Redish (1993) and Rubin (1994)
summary: Representative users attempt realistic tasks while researchers observe, revealing where and why the design causes difficulty and how severe each problem is.
description: Usability testing asks representative participants to attempt realistic tasks with a product or prototype while researchers observe behaviour, record difficulties and often collect think-aloud commentary. It can be formative, finding problems to fix during design, or summative, measuring task success, time and errors against targets. The underlying idea is that observed behaviour on real tasks is more trustworthy than opinion or expert prediction. Rigour comes from realistic task scenarios with defined success criteria, recruitment that matches the target users, a neutral and consistent moderation protocol, and severity ratings that combine frequency, impact and persistence. Small formative rounds of about five users per segment find most frequent problems, while summative benchmarks need larger samples and confidence intervals.
steps: Define research questions, target user segments and success criteria for each task.
Write 5 to 8 realistic task scenarios that avoid interface vocabulary and leading cues.
Recruit participants who match the target users, typically 5 to 8 per segment for formative rounds or 20 or more for summative measurement.
Pilot the protocol with one participant and fix ambiguous tasks.
Run sessions with a consistent script, observing behaviour and recording success, time, errors and comments.
Log each problem with evidence and rate severity by frequency, impact and persistence.
Report prioritised problems with recommendations and retest after redesign.
outputs: A prioritised list of usability problems with severity ratings and evidence clips, plus task success, time-on-task and error metrics.
useWhen: When you need to know whether real users can complete key tasks and where they struggle, from early prototypes to pre-launch builds.
avoidWhen: Avoid for questions about needs, motivations or market demand; use interviews or field studies. For measuring causal impact at scale, use A/B testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Gold standard for usability validation; supported by decades of evidence and widely understood by stakeholders.
whereToUse: Pre-launch validation; iterative design cycles; redesign projects.
example: Before launching a new loan application flow, a fintech team tests it with six first-time borrowers. Four fail to find how to upload proof of income, a severity-one problem fixed and verified in a second round.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
Measuring and Improving User Experience Through Artificial Intelligence-Aided Design (Yang et al., 2020)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish, 1999)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Rubin, J. & Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of Usability Testing (2nd ed.). Wiley.

name: Usability Testing of Interface Standards
aka: Testing a design standard with designers
origin: Thovtrup and Nielsen (1991); de Souza and Bevan (1990); described in Nielsen (1993)
summary: Test whether designers can understand and apply an interface standard by having them design a toy interface with it and list the seeded violations in a sample interface.
description: Nielsen argues that an in-house interface standard is itself a product whose users are developers, and that it can have 'meta-usability' problems. Thovtrup and Nielsen used two tasks: designers build a small toy interface using the standard, and they inspect a small interface seeded with known violations and list them. Observation, optionally with thinking aloud, shows how they use the document. Toy designs are scored for conformance and violation lists are compared with an answer key to count misses and false alarms. The evidence for doing this is sobering: Mosier and Smith found 58 percent of guideline users found what they sought, designers using a draft ISO menu standard violated 11 percent of its rules, and three real products broke 7 to 12 rules of their own company standard. Developers rely on examples and checklists more than body text, so examples must be fully compliant.
steps: Recruit a few designers or developers who will actually use the standard.
Task 1: ask them to design a small toy interface using the standard, observing their use of the document, optionally with think-aloud.
Score the toy designs for conformance with each rule.
Task 2: give them a small interface seeded with a known number of violations and ask them to list every violation.
Compare their lists with the answer key, counting missed violations and legal elements wrongly flagged.
Revise the standard, especially its examples and checklists, and retest with new designers.
outputs: Conformance rates on toy designs, counts of missed and spurious violations, and observed difficulties in finding and interpreting rules.
useWhen: Before rolling out a design system, style guide, accessibility guideline or content standard, to check that its intended users can find, understand and apply the rules.
avoidWhen: It shows whether the document is usable, not whether real products will comply; follow up with Guidelines Review and Consistency Inspection of shipped work. Not suitable for public standards you cannot change.
whyLost: Interface standards moved from documents to coded component libraries, so teams test components rather than the guidance; the idea of testing the standard's own usability faded with the 1990s standards era.
whereToUse: Design system documentation, accessibility and content style guides, AI prompt and output guidelines given to product teams.
example: A fintech design system team gives four product designers a toy transfer flow to build with the documentation and a seeded screen with ten violations. Designers miss most spacing and error-message rules but flag a legal pattern shown in an out-of-date example, so the examples are rebuilt first.
reference: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering. Boston: AP Professional, pp. 233-235; Thovtrup, H. and Nielsen, J. (1991). Assessing the usability of a user interface standard. Proc. ACM CHI'91.

name: Usability Testing with Children and Teens
origin: Hanna, Risden and Alexander (1997); robotic variant by Fransen and Markopoulos (2010)
summary: Moderated usability testing adapted to children's age bands, with parental recruitment and consent, directive time-boxed prompts and child-appropriate ways of eliciting feedback.
description: Children are not small adults. Practice distinguishes age bands: 2 to 5 (show what they can do, no concurrent think-aloud, parent present), 6 to 10 (school-like tasks, think-aloud difficult), 11 to 14 (adult-like but unpredictable) and 15 to 18. Recruitment and screening go through parents, with explicit consent for video and the child's own assent, sessions after school, and plans for siblings and teen no-shows. In session, parents stay for under-9s, siblings are separated, the moderator uses directives ('Now I need you to...') rather than questions children can refuse, time-boxed prompts keep them on task, and squirming is read as fatigue. A variant delivers the facilitator's prompts through a playful robot; one study found no more problems than in-person prompting but children seemed more at ease, though they found the robot's questions harder.
steps: Define the target age band and adapt tasks, session length and materials to it.
Recruit and screen through parents, avoiding questions about school grades; obtain parental consent and the child's assent, including for video.
Schedule after school, plan for siblings, and brief parents on their role as visitors.
Keep parents present for children under about nine and separate siblings.
Use directive, time-boxed prompts rather than open questions; avoid concurrent think-aloud with young children.
Watch body language, break when restless, and consider non-verbal reporting or a robot or puppet intermediary for shy children.
Analyse problems by age band rather than pooling across ages.
outputs: Age-specific usability problem lists and observations of children's behaviour and understanding.
useWhen: Testing products for children or teenagers, including games, education and family apps.
avoidWhen: Avoid standard adult protocols with young children; for pre-verbal reporting use Problem Identification Picture Cards (PIPC), for explanation-based data use Peer Tutoring Evaluation.
whyLost: Child testing is concentrated in child-computer interaction research and specialist children's product companies.
whereToUse: Edtech, children's games and streaming, family safety features, age-assurance flows.
example: A kids' streaming app tests 6 to 8 year olds with a parent present and directive prompts. Children ignore the text-based profile picker but succeed when profiles show avatars.
reference: Hanna, L., Risden, K. and Alexander, K. (1997). Guidelines for usability testing with children. interactions; Dumas, J. S. and Loring, B. A. (2008). Moderating Usability Tests. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 149-152.

name: Usability-Based Accessibility Measurement
summary: Measure accessibility as the effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction of specified users with diverse capabilities on specified tasks and contexts, comparing by varying one factor at a time.
description: ISO 9241-11 defines usability as the extent to which specified users achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use. ISO TS 16071 defines accessibility as usability for people with the widest range of capabilities, so accessibility becomes measurable in the same way, rather than a binary pass or fail against guidelines. Accessibility is a function of user, task, context and product; valid comparison varies only one term at a time, such as the same user group, task and context on two products. Planning identifies accessibility requirements, measures and verification criteria within the context of use, which then act as design targets. The approach shows that a product can be accessible in one context and much less so in another, something conformance audits cannot reveal.
steps: Specify the user categories with the capabilities of interest, their goals, tasks and context of use, including assistive technologies.
Set quantitative accessibility goals per user category and context, such as completion rate, time and satisfaction targets.
Recruit participants from each user category and have them perform the specified tasks in the specified context.
Measure effectiveness (completion, errors), efficiency (time, effort) and satisfaction.
For comparisons, vary only one of user, task, context or product at a time.
Verify results against targets and document them, for example in a quality plan, alongside conformance audit findings.
outputs: Effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction measures per user category, task and context, relative accessibility of products, and verification against targets.
useWhen: When conformance is not enough and you need evidence that disabled users can actually achieve goals efficiently, or to compare products or versions.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a replacement for conformance testing; combine with Accessibility Evaluation. For qualitative barrier discovery use Assistive Technology Testing.
whyLost: Accessibility practice converged on WCAG conformance audits, which are cheaper and legally referenced, leaving performance-based measurement in standards documents.
whereToUse: Public-sector services, banking, healthcare portals, procurement comparisons of accessible products.
example: A bank compares two versions of its payment flow with screen-reader users: completion rises from 60% to 90% and median time halves, evidence an audit alone could not give.
sources: ISO Standard on Ergonomics (Gulliksen et al., 2001)
reference: Gulliksen, J., Harker, S. and Steger, J. (2001). The ISO Approach to the Development of Ergonomics Standards for Accessibility. CID-121, KTH Stockholm; ISO 9241-11 (1998).

name: Use Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (UFMEA)
aka: Usability Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (UFMEA)
origin: FMEA from US military reliability engineering (1949); adapted for usability by Desurvire (1992) per the treatise
summary: Enumerates every way a user could fail at each task step, rating severity, occurrence and detectability to produce a ranked, falsifiable usability risk register.
description: FMEA identifies potential failure points before they occur. UFMEA applies this to use: for each task step, analysts list possible use errors, their causes and effects, and rate severity, occurrence and detection (typically 1-10 each) to compute a risk priority number. The treatise highlights that UFMEA is one of the few UX methods producing a falsifiable risk register: predictions about where failures will occur that can be validated against later testing and field data. It is especially valuable in medical, aviation and financial products where failures matter beyond inconvenience, and it aligns with use-related risk analysis required by IEC 62366 for medical devices. Rated HIGH recovery priority.
steps: Build a task analysis (for example HTA) of the critical user workflows.
For each step, brainstorm failure modes using error taxonomies (slips, lapses, mistakes).
Record cause, effect and existing controls for every failure mode.
Rate severity, occurrence and detectability, and compute a risk priority number or use a risk matrix.
Design mitigations for the highest-risk modes and re-rate residual risk.
Validate predictions in formative testing and update the register with field data.
outputs: Ranked usability risk register, mitigation plan, residual risk ratings, validation record.
useWhen: Safety-critical, high-stakes or regulated products, and before major releases of irreversible flows.
avoidWhen: Early exploratory work where tasks are not yet defined; use contextual inquiry first.
whyLost: Seen as an engineering compliance activity, not design research, and absent from UX curricula; agile cadences discouraged upfront risk analysis.
whereToUse: Medical devices and digital therapeutics, payments and transfers, aviation and automotive HMI, AI agent actions with real-world effects.
example: A neobank applies UFMEA to international transfers; 'wrong recipient selected from autocomplete' scores highest (severity 9, occurrence 5). Adding a confirmation with recipient photo and bank name cuts misdirected transfers by 40% in pilot.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Stamatis DH (2003) Failure Mode and Effect Analysis: FMEA from Theory to Execution
IEC 62366-1 (2015) Application of usability engineering to medical devices
IEC 62366-1:2015 Medical devices: Application of usability engineering to medical devices
ISO 14971:2019 Medical devices: Application of risk management
Stamatis, Failure Mode and Effect Analysis: FMEA from Theory to Execution
reference: IEC 62366-1:2015 Medical devices: Application of usability engineering to medical devices.

name: USE Questionnaire (Usefulness, Satisfaction, and Ease of Use)
origin: Arnold Lund (1998, 2001)
summary: A free 30-item questionnaire covering usefulness, ease of use, ease of learning and satisfaction.
description: Arnold Lund developed the USE to capture four dimensions practitioners care about: usefulness, ease of use, ease of learning and satisfaction. All 30 items are positively worded and rated on 7-point agreement scales. Lund followed standard development steps (large item pool, factor analysis, coefficient alpha), but Sauro and Lewis note that the psychometric details were never published, so its reliability and validity are taken on trust. It remains popular because it is free and its subscales map directly to product questions, separating "is it useful?" from "is it easy?".
steps: Administer the 30 items after use or in a survey of current users.
Average items within each of the four subscales.
Compare subscales to see whether usefulness or usability is the weaker side.
Track subscale means across releases with confidence intervals.
outputs: Scores for usefulness, ease of use, ease of learning and satisfaction.
useWhen: You need to separate usefulness from ease of use in a free instrument.
avoidWhen: You need published reliability evidence or norms (consider TAM or SUS).
whyLost: Lack of published psychometrics kept it out of academic recommendations.
whereToUse: Product discovery surveys, early-stage tools, internal applications.
example: A data tool scores high on usefulness but low on ease of learning, so the team invests in onboarding rather than new features.
reference: Lund, A. M. (2001). Measuring usability with the USE questionnaire. STC Usability SIG Newsletter 8(2).

name: User Engagement Scale (UES)
origin: O'Brien and Toms, 2010; game adaptation by Wiebe et al.; short form by O'Brien, Cairns and Hall, 2018
summary: A 31-item questionnaire measuring engagement on six subscales (focused attention, perceived usability, aesthetics, endurability, novelty, felt involvement), with a 12-item short form.
description: O'Brien and Toms developed the User Engagement Scale from a model of engagement as a quality of experience. The original 31 items cover six subscales: Focused Attention, Perceived Usability, Aesthetics, Endurability, Novelty and Felt Involvement. It is administered after the experience on a Likert scale, and domain adaptations exist, such as Wiebe et al.'s version for games. Landa-Avila and Cruz reworded items for a VR gesture game, translated them into Spanish, administered them on a seven-point scale to 164 visitors at a technology event, and checked reliability with Cronbach's alpha, inter-subscale correlations and oblique factor analysis. Endurability, Novelty and Felt Involvement overlapped (r above 0.7) and loaded together, echoing later work that collapsed the scale to four factors in the 12-item UES-SF. Any adaptation should be revalidated.
steps: Start from the UES-SF (12 items) or the long form, or an existing domain adaptation.
Reword and, if needed, translate items for the context, keeping meaning; back-translate where possible.
Administer immediately after the experience on the original Likert scale.
Compute subscale scores and Cronbach's alpha per subscale (aim for 0.70 or more).
Inspect inter-subscale correlations and run factor analysis with oblique rotation (sample of 150 or more) to check the structure holds.
Compare subscale scores across designs or versions and triangulate with behavioural engagement data.
outputs: Subscale and total engagement scores, reliability coefficients and evidence on factor structure.
useWhen: When evaluating experiences where engagement, not only usability, is the goal: games, media, learning, search, VR and exploratory tools.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the question is efficiency or task success (use System Usability Scale (SUS) or task metrics). Do not equate high engagement with benefit; check wellbeing too. Subscales overlap, so prefer the short form.
whyLost: It is well cited in information science and HCI research but practitioners rely on behavioural engagement metrics and rarely administer it.
whereToUse: Games and VR, news and media apps, learning platforms, search interfaces, AI conversational products.
example: A VR training team gives the UES-SF to 160 trainees after two prototype scenarios. Focused attention is high for both, but aesthetic appeal differs by a full point, guiding art investment.
reference: O'Brien, H. L., & Toms, E. G. (2010). The development and evaluation of a survey to measure user engagement. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 61(1), 50-69.

name: User Environment Design (UED)
origin: Karen Holtzblatt and Hugh Beyer, Contextual Design (1990s); updated in Contextual Design: Evolved (2014)
summary: A floor-plan-like model of a product's focus areas (places), the functions in each and the links between them, derived from storyboards and kept free of UI detail.
description: The UED shows a product's structure the way an architect's floor plan shows a building: each focus area is a place that supports a coherent activity, with its purpose, the exact functions available there, an associated interaction pattern, and connections to other focus areas. It deliberately avoids committing to screens or layouts. Design alternates between story thinking (storyboards) and structural thinking (the UED): the team walks the storyboards cell by cell, pulling out what the system must do and where. Cross-device designs show device-specific focus areas so flow between devices is visible. Printed and spread on a wall, the UED lets the team check coherence across tasks, lets developers check feasibility, and resists pressure to sacrifice coherence for ease of implementation. Validated with paper prototypes in mock-up interviews, it becomes a roadmap for releases and user stories.
steps: Walk each storyboard cell by cell and note what the system must do at each step.
Define a focus area for each coherent activity, with its purpose and the functions it must provide.
Link focus areas to show how users move between them, including across devices.
Associate each focus area with an interaction design pattern, still without screen layouts.
Print and spread focus areas on a wall to check that every storyboarded task flows naturally; developers check feasibility.
Test the structure with paper prototypes in mock-up interviews with users and revise.
Use the validated UED to plan releases, write user stories and coordinate teams.
outputs: A UED diagram of focus areas, functions and links, and focus-area definitions that feed releases and user stories.
useWhen: Use it after storyboarding, when a product supports many tasks and needs a coherent structure before UI design, especially across devices or apps.
avoidWhen: The UED is a design hypothesis; neither structure nor UI is validated until tested with Prototype Testing or paper mock-up interviews. For navigation labels and hierarchy, use Card Sorting and Tree Testing.
whyLost: It stays with Contextual Design practitioners; most teams jump from journeys or story maps to wireframes and sitemaps.
whereToUse: Enterprise software suites, multi-device consumer services, clinical systems, and platform redesigns.
example: An online grocer's team walks six storyboards and defines focus areas such as 'plan the week', 'build the basket' and 'fix substitutions'. Linking them reveals that substitutions are reachable only from the receipt, so a direct path is added before wireframing.
reference: Holtzblatt, K. and Beyer, H. (2014). Contextual Design: Evolved. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool, pp. 64-67.

name: User explainability score
origin: Hoffman, Mueller, Klein & Litman, 2018 (explanation satisfaction scale); adapted in Vivek Gopinath's Methods Atlas
summary: Measures whether real users understand, trust appropriately and can act on an AI system's explanations, combining comprehension tests with validated rating scales.
description: Technical explanation methods do not guarantee that users understand anything. A user explainability score quantifies explanation quality from the user's side: comprehension (can users predict or describe why the system acted), calibration (does trust track actual model accuracy), actionability (can users change outcomes) and subjective satisfaction. Hoffman and colleagues proposed explanation satisfaction and goodness checklists, and forward-prediction tasks, where users predict what the model will do, are an objective measure. Rigour involves comparing explanation designs experimentally, measuring calibrated reliance rather than raw trust, and combining objective and subjective components into a scored index with known reliability.
steps: Define the explanation goals: understanding, calibrated trust, actionability, contestability.
Build comprehension tasks, such as forward prediction ('what will the system recommend for this profile?') and counterfactual tasks ('what would change the outcome?').
Administer a validated explanation satisfaction scale and a trust scale after exposure.
Measure reliance calibration: agreement with the AI when it is right versus when it is wrong.
Combine component scores into an index (e.g. 0-100), checking reliability of the composite.
Compare explanation designs in a between-subjects study with at least 30-50 participants per condition.
outputs: A user explainability score per explanation design, component scores, calibration measures and a comparison across designs.
useWhen: Designing or comparing AI explanations, meeting regulatory explainability expectations, or evaluating whether XAI outputs help users.
avoidWhen: Avoid using subjective satisfaction alone, or for systems where users never see explanations; use model audits instead.
whyLost: XAI evaluation research is mostly academic, and product teams ship explanations without measuring whether users understand them.
whereToUse: Investment and credit decisions, medical AI support, AI assistants, content recommendations and moderation notices.
example: An investment app tests three explanation formats for portfolio recommendations. Feature-based explanations score 71 versus 52 for generic text, and users' agreement drops appropriately on deliberately wrong recommendations, indicating better calibration.
sources: Hoffman, Mueller, Klein & Litman (2018) Metrics for explainable AI: challenges and prospects
The Inquiry Series, Ch 58 — AI Explainability & Value Alignment Audit
reference: Hoffman, R. R., Mueller, S. T., Klein, G. & Litman, J. (2018) Metrics for Explainable AI: Challenges and Prospects. arXiv:1812.04608.

name: User Profiling with User Types
origin: Hackos and Redish (1998); Mayhew (1999); presented by Baxter, Courage and Caine (2015)
summary: Describe users by the ranges and distributions of key attributes, group them into distinct user types, and classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.
description: A user profile records attributes as ranges with proportions rather than single values: demographics, job and experience, organisation size and industry, education, computer and product experience, primary and secondary tasks, domain knowledge, technology, attitudes, learning style and the criticality of errors. Early versions draw on product managers, specifications, marketing studies, support logs, competitive analysis, census data and surveys. Users include not only direct users but managers, administrators, recipients of outputs, purchasers and competitors' users, classified as primary (regular, direct), secondary (infrequent or via an intermediary) or tertiary (affected or buying). Attributes are clustered into user types with stakeholders. The profile is the base for personas, scenarios and recruitment screeners, and is revised after each study.
steps: Draft a first-guess profile from internal and published sources such as analytics, support data, market studies and census figures.
List user characteristics and record ranges and, where possible, the share of users along each range.
Identify all user categories, including indirect users, administrators, purchasers and people affected by outputs.
Classify each category as primary, secondary or tertiary.
Cluster characteristics into meaningfully different user types in an affinity session with stakeholders.
Use the profile to write personas, scenarios and recruitment screeners, and revise it after each research activity.
outputs: A user profile document with attribute distributions and a classified set of user types.
useWhen: Starting work on a product with poorly understood users, before personas or recruiting, or in B2B and enterprise products with many roles.
avoidWhen: You need narrative empathy for design; personas serve that better. Early profiles are guesses, so do not profile only expert or 'best' users, and remember experts in one part of a system may be novices elsewhere.
whyLost: It was absorbed into personas and segmentation, so the attribute-distribution profile and the primary/secondary/tertiary classification are rarely done in their own right.
whereToUse: Enterprise and B2B software, healthcare systems with many roles, public services, recruitment planning.
example: A hospital scheduling tool profiles nurses, schedulers and managers as primary, doctors as secondary and patients as tertiary, with shift patterns and experience ranges that later define recruitment quotas.
reference: Hackos, J. T., & Redish, J. C. (1998). User and Task Analysis for Interface Design. Wiley.

name: User Requirements Specification
origin: ISO/TC 159/SC 4, ISO 9241-210:2010 (replacing ISO 13407:1999)
summary: Turn user and stakeholder needs and the context of use into a testable, consistent statement of user requirements with measurable usability objectives.
description: Human-centred design, as set out in ISO 9241-210, extends requirements work into an explicit user requirements statement tied to the intended context of use and business objectives. Needs are expressed as what users must achieve, not how. The specification includes the intended context of use; requirements derived from needs and context; requirements from ergonomic and interface standards and guidelines, including accessibility; usability requirements with measurable effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction criteria for specific contexts; and organisational requirements that directly affect users. Conflicts such as speed versus accuracy are resolved and their rationale and weighting recorded. The specification must be testable, verified by stakeholders, internally consistent and kept current, because some requirements only emerge once solutions exist.
steps: Identify user and stakeholder needs in context, stated as what users must achieve rather than how.
Describe the intended context of use: users, tasks, equipment and physical and social environment.
Derive user requirements from the needs and context.
Add requirements from ergonomic, interface and accessibility standards and guidelines.
Set measurable usability objectives for specific contexts (for example the share of intended users who complete a task, a satisfaction target, a time limit).
Add organisational requirements that directly affect users, resolve conflicts and record rationale and weighting.
Check the specification is testable, verified by stakeholders and consistent, and revise it as the design evolves.
outputs: A user needs description and a user requirements specification with measurable usability criteria.
useWhen: Procured or regulated systems, safety-critical and medical products, public-sector tenders, or any project where usability must be contractually testable.
avoidWhen: Early exploratory product discovery, where needs are too uncertain to fix; use jobs-to-be-done or opportunity mapping first and specify later.
whyLost: Agile user stories replaced formal requirement statements, and measurable usability criteria are rarely written even where ISO 9241-210 is cited.
whereToUse: Medical devices, government procurement, enterprise system replacement, automotive and aviation interfaces.
example: A call-centre system tender specifies that 90 per cent of trained agents divert a call to voicemail within 10 seconds and that satisfaction scores reach an agreed threshold, both verified in acceptance testing.
reference: ISO 9241-210:2010. Ergonomics of human-system interaction, Part 210: Human-centred design for interactive systems. Geneva: ISO.

name: User Role Modelling
origin: Larry Constantine, 1995; Constantine and Lockwood, 1999
summary: Model the distinct relationships users have with a system as roles, map how roles relate, rank them and choose focal roles to design for.
description: User role modelling is Constantine and Lockwood's usage-centred alternative to personas. It starts from all actors, separates system actors from user actors, splits user actors into direct and indirect, and identifies each role a direct actor can play, naming it by its core responsibility. Each role is described by context, characteristics and criteria, often on one index card, and described by difference from other roles. A context map shows roles around the system, and for complex systems a role map records specialisation, inclusion and precedence. Roles are ranked by frequency and business importance to choose focal roles, and personas may then be written for focal roles only. Roles also guide architecture, since parts serving one role cluster together. Its strength is coverage and traceability rather than empathy.
steps: List all actors and separate system actors from user actors.
Split user actors into direct and indirect users.
Identify every role a direct actor can play and name each by its core responsibility.
Describe each role on a card by context, characteristics and criteria, emphasising how it differs from others.
Draw a context map, and for complex systems a role map with specialisation, inclusion and precedence.
Rank roles by frequency and business importance and select focal roles.
Optionally write personas for focal roles only and use role clusters to organise the architecture.
outputs: Role cards, a context map, a role map and a ranked list of focal roles.
useWhen: Enterprise, multi-sided or administrative systems with many user types, where coverage of responsibilities matters more than empathy; workshops to agree scope quickly.
