avoidWhen: When the team needs vivid empathy or behavioural segmentation (use Personas or Goal-Directed Persona Construction (Cooper's Method)). Roles lack memorability.
whyLost: Personas won the popularity contest in the 2000s; role modelling survives in agile requirements practice and usage-centred design circles.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS with admin, approver and end-user roles, marketplaces, healthcare systems and permissions design.
example: A practice-management SaaS team lists 14 roles across clinics, then ranks them and picks receptionist, clinician and practice manager as focal. Role clusters become the three main navigation areas.
reference: Constantine, L.L. and Lockwood, L.A.D. (1999) Software for Use: A Practical Guide to the Models and Methods of Usage-Centered Design. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley.

name: User Story Mapping and Opportunity Canvases
donor: Agile software development; lean product management
origin: Jeff Patton (story mapping, 2004-2007; Opportunity Canvas adapting Marty Cagan); Ash Maurya (Lean Canvas, after Osterwalder); Year One Labs (Problem-Solution Canvas)
summary: A sticky-note map of the user's story in narrative order, sliced into releases, plus canvases that judge whether an opportunity merits discovery.
description: A story map lays out the backbone of user activities across the top in narrative order, with user tasks as short verb phrases beneath each, and details, alternatives and exceptions below. Horizontal lines slice the body into releases named for target outcomes, learning experiments for a subset of users, or a development sequence that tackles risk early. Personas, goals and sketches surround it. Patton frames mapping as a conversation tool: 'scope doesn't creep; understanding grows'. Before mapping, an Opportunity Canvas lets a discovery team record, box by box, problems, users, current solutions, user value and metrics, adoption, business problem and metrics, and budget, recording assumptions where facts are missing, so the product owner can decide go, no-go or learn more. Lean startup variants are Maurya's nine-box Lean Canvas, with a test per box, and a weekly Problem-Solution Canvas of up to three problems and experiments.
steps: Hold an opportunity conversation and fill an opportunity canvas (problems, users, current solutions, user value, user metrics, adoption, business problem, business metrics, budget), marking assumptions.
Decide go, no-go or what must be learned first.
Frame the problem: who the product is for and why it is being built.
Map the big picture breadth first ('a mile wide and an inch deep'), writing each step on a card as it is told and placing cards left to right in sequence.
Explore depth: other users, alternatives and what can go wrong; sketch, prototype and test, refining the map.
Group tasks into activities to form the backbone.
Slice releases by target outcomes for specific users, and thinner slices as learning experiments.
Slice a development strategy that tackles the riskiest parts first, and review canvases and map as learning arrives.
outputs: A story map, an outcome-named release roadmap, a backlog with shared understanding, and canvases listing assumptions, metrics and go/no-go decisions.
useWhen: Use it when a team must agree scope and sequence for a product or large feature, and when deciding which opportunities merit discovery.
avoidWhen: Maps and canvases organise what the team believes; the riskiest assumptions need research, such as Interviews, Jobs-to-be-Done Research or a Prototype / Wizard-of-Oz A/B Test. For deciding between opportunities from research, an Opportunity Solution Tree is more explicit.
whyLost: Story mapping became a standard agile practice because it fixed the flat backlog's loss of narrative context; the canvases survived as lightweight, visual business framing.
whereToUse: Agile product teams, start-up discovery, B2B SaaS roadmaps, and multi-team platform planning.
example: A media company maps its CMS from 'plan coverage' to 'publish updates', slices the first release for election night, and records on an opportunity canvas that 'editors abandon live blogs' is still an assumption, triggering five editor interviews.
reference: Patton, J. with Economy, P. (2014). User Story Mapping: Discover the Whole Story, Build the Right Product. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: User-Oriented Evaluation
origin: Dahlberg and Vedung (2001); Krogstrup
summary: Evaluate a service through the eyes of its intended beneficiaries, deriving the evaluation criteria bottom-up from their needs, values and experiences.
description: A Scandinavian evaluation model for public services that starts from the people the service is meant to benefit. It is explicitly not a satisfaction survey, where the provider sets the topics and users merely score them. Instead, qualitative inquiry finds the issues users raise in their own language, and these become the criteria against which the service is assessed. The model names its own tensions: users who cannot speak for themselves, such as people with dementia; preferences that conflict with wellbeing; conflicting needs between different users; paternalism returning when evaluators speak on users' behalf; and drift into consumerism. Handling these explicitly is part of its rigour. It sits close to responsive evaluation but focuses specifically on beneficiaries rather than on all stakeholders.
steps: Define the intended beneficiaries of the service and distinguish them from other stakeholders.
Explore their experiences qualitatively in their own language through interviews, observation or proxies where needed.
Derive evaluation criteria from the concerns they raise, not from provider objectives.
Assess the service against those criteria using mixed evidence.
Make explicit how conflicting needs between users and users who cannot articulate their needs were handled.
Report criteria, assessment and the trade-offs made.
outputs: User-derived evaluation criteria and an assessment of the service against them.
useWhen: Evaluating a public or care service, or a product for a population whose priorities differ from the provider's.
avoidWhen: When criteria are fixed by regulation or contract, or you need comparable scores; use a validated satisfaction instrument. If all stakeholders' issues matter, use Responsive Evaluation.
whyLost: It is rooted in Scandinavian public administration literature, much of it not in English; UX assumes user-centredness without deriving evaluation criteria from users.
whereToUse: Public digital services, health and care products, assistive technology, libraries and education platforms.
example: Evaluating a council's adult social care portal, researchers interview carers and residents first; their criteria (not having to retell their story, knowing who to call) replace the council's task-completion KPIs as the evaluation frame.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Denzin, N. K. and Lincoln, Y. S. (Eds.) (2017). The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (5th ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Utilisation-Focused Evaluation
origin: Michael Quinn Patton (1978, 1997), from a study of how 20 federal health evaluations were used
summary: Design every aspect of an evaluation with its specific intended users, around the decisions they will make, so that the findings are actually used.
description: Patton found that evaluations were often unused, so utilisation-focused evaluation starts by identifying the primary intended users, the people who will act on the findings, and works with them to focus the questions. Methods follow from those questions rather than from the evaluator's preferred paradigm, and use is planned before data are collected. A core move is to ask users what they would do if they had the answer to each question, which prunes a long list to essential questions. The evaluator offers method options and agrees a design users find credible, so they understand and own the study, while challenging their methodological biases where needed. Findings are reported in forms users can act on, and use is followed up. It is a disciplined version of the UX instinct to 'start with the decision'.
steps: Identify the primary intended users and the decisions they face.
Generate candidate evaluation questions with them, then prioritise to a few essential ones.
For each question, ask what they would do differently with each possible answer; drop questions whose answers would change nothing.
Present method options with their trade-offs and agree a design the users find credible.
Collect and analyse data around the agreed questions.
Report in formats users can act on, facilitate interpretation with them, and follow up on actual use.
outputs: A focused evaluation design owned by its intended users, and actionable findings with a record of use.
useWhen: Research findings have a history of being ignored, stakeholders disagree on what to evaluate, or evaluation budgets must be spent on decision-relevant questions.
avoidWhen: The evaluation must be independent of those who will use it, for example for accountability; consider goal-free or external evaluation. Users may hold unhelpful methodological biases that need challenging.
whyLost: It is well known in evaluation but UX practitioners rediscover its principles informally rather than following its procedure.
whereToUse: Service evaluations, post-launch reviews, research roadmaps, measurement frameworks for product initiatives.
example: Before evaluating a new onboarding flow, a researcher asks the growth lead what she would do if activation rose, fell or stayed flat. Two of six proposed questions change nothing, so the study focuses on the remaining four.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
reference: Patton, M. Q. (1997). Utilization-Focused Evaluation: The New Century Text (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: UX Activities Overlaid on the Development Lifecycle (RACI, tollgates)
aka: UX activities overlaid on the development lifecycle (RACI, tollgates and exit criteria)
donor: Management and organisational practice; software process
origin: Arnold Lund (2011), Microsoft IT; related to the Sapient IA process framework (Svec, 2001)
summary: Map UX activities into each phase of the organisation's existing development process, assign responsibilities with a RACI, and add UX checklist items and exit criteria to each phase gate.
description: Instead of imposing a separate UX process, Lund overlays UX onto the lifecycle the organisation already runs (plan, requirements, design, build, stabilise, operate). For each phase he lists the UX activities and deliverables expected at full support: opportunity discovery, field research and modelling, personas and scenarios, vision prototypes, information architecture, UI specification, writing, prototyping and validation, accessibility and internationalisation reviews, usability testing, UX bug triage and post-launch monitoring. A RACI states who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed across business, engineering and UX. Each tollgate gains UX exit criteria: a UX contact assigned before baseline; primary scenarios validated and a UX plan at baseline; final UI specification and usability testing of primary scenarios before build ends; UX bugs triaged before deployment. The map also shows how UX deliverables feed other teams', answering what UX does and why it matters.
steps: Obtain the organisation's existing phases, gates and required deliverables.
List the UX activities and deliverables appropriate to each phase at full support.
Draw the dependencies between UX deliverables and other teams' deliverables.
Build a RACI for each activity across business, engineering and UX roles.
Add UX checklist items and measurable exit criteria to each tollgate (for example primary-scenario usability testing complete before build exit).
Publish the map, use it in project planning, and define lighter versions for partial and consulting engagements.
Update it whenever the base process changes, for example a move to agile.
outputs: A lifecycle map, a RACI table, and tollgate checklists with UX exit criteria.
useWhen: Use in organisations with formal stage-gate or enterprise delivery processes where UX work is skipped because nobody owns it or no gate checks it.
avoidWhen: Avoid imposing a full-support map on small agile teams; a light Team Operating Agreement or Sprint-Integrated Usability Evaluation fits better. The criteria check that research happened, not what it found.
whyLost: It thrives in enterprise IT and regulated industries but looks heavyweight to agile product teams, which rarely formalise UX gates.
whereToUse: Enterprise IT, regulated industries (medical devices, finance), government digital programmes, large outsourced builds.
example: A health insurer adds 'primary scenarios usability tested with at least five members' to its build-exit gate and makes the UX lead accountable. A claims portal that would have shipped untested is delayed two weeks to fix three critical findings.
reference: Lund, A. (2011). User Experience Management: Essential Skills for Leading Effective UX Teams. Burlington, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 143-147, 179-181.

name: UX Burden of Design Framework
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise); modelled on WHO/IHME Global Burden of Disease
summary: Quantifies population harm from poor UX in time lost, financial harm and quality-of-experience impairment, enabling comparison across products, patterns and industries.
description: Borrowing from the Global Burden of Disease framework developed by WHO and IHME, the treatise proposes a UX Burden of Design framework quantifying the harm caused by poor UX across populations. It addresses a gap: product metrics vary by context so there is no agreed measure of how much UX harm exists, no way to compare harm from different patterns and no metric tracking whether population UX health is improving. The framework's unit is the UXDAI (UX Disability-Adjusted Interaction). Population estimates combine behavioural analytics, structured population surveys and expert severity assessment. Like GBD, it would rank 'causes' (patterns, failure types) by burden, show trends and support priority-setting for design standards and regulation.
steps: Define the list of harm causes (patterns, failure types) and populations.
Estimate incidence or prevalence of each cause from surveillance data.
Estimate time and quality-of-experience costs and severity weights via expert and user elicitation.
Compute UXDAIs per cause, product, industry and population.
Rank causes by burden and analyse trends and distribution.
Publish with uncertainty intervals and update periodically.
outputs: Burden estimates by cause and population, rankings, trend analyses, uncertainty intervals.
useWhen: Industry or national priority-setting, regulatory agendas, large organisations comparing product harm.
avoidWhen: Small products without data to estimate incidence and severity.
whyLost: Original proposal of the treatise; no prior population-level UX burden metric existed.
whereToUse: Regulators, digital government, large platforms, research consortia, standards bodies.
example: A national digital service agency estimates that failed benefit applications account for 40% of its UXDAI burden despite 5% of traffic, redirecting investment.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Murray CJL & Lopez AD (Eds) (1996) The Global Burden of Disease
GBD 2019 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators (2020) Lancet 396
reference: Murray CJL & Lopez AD (Eds) (1996) The Global Burden of Disease. Harvard School of Public Health / WHO / World Bank.

name: UX Canon and Living Method Registry
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: A curated, periodically reviewed body of essential works and a living registry of methods linked to primary literature, to transmit methodological knowledge across generations.
description: The treatise observes that UX has no equivalent of the medical literature: knowledge is fragmented across conferences, blogs, discontinued websites and out-of-print books. A canon, as in law and medicine, would identify essential works, curate them in accessible persistent formats and integrate them into education, with periodic review. Its candidate canon includes Card, Moran and Newell (1983), Ericsson and Simon (1984), Beyer and Holtzblatt (1998), Mayhew (1999), Reason (1990), Vicente (1999), Miles and Huberman (1994), Braun and Clarke (2006), Suchman (1987), Schriver (1997) and the epidemiological literature from Bradford Hill to Hernán and Robins. Professional associations (UXPA, ACM SIGCHI, IxDA) should maintain a living method registry, historical archives and practitioner-accessible summaries.
steps: Convene a panel to nominate candidate works and methods.
Apply explicit criteria (foundational, rigorous, still useful, at risk of loss).
Curate persistent, accessible versions and practitioner summaries.
Build a living registry linking each method to primary sources and protocols.
Integrate into curricula and onboarding.
Review and update on a fixed cycle.
outputs: Canon list, living method registry, archives and summaries.
useWhen: Professional associations, educators and large research organisations preserving knowledge.
avoidWhen: Individual projects.
whyLost: Original proposal of the treatise; no body has taken stewardship.
whereToUse: UX education programmes, professional associations, ResearchOps libraries, reference sites like this one.
example: A university UX programme adopts the canon list as required reading, with each method in the registry practised in a studio assignment.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Card SK, Moran TP & Newell A (1983)
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 32 (Toward a UX Canon).

name: UX Case-Control Study
origin: Case-control design (Doll and Hill 1950); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Compares users who experienced a specific harm with matched users who did not, measuring prior exposure to design features, efficient for rare or severe outcomes.
description: A case-control study starts from outcomes: cases who experienced the outcome are compared with controls who did not, and prior exposures are measured. The treatise proposes UX case-control studies comparing users who suffered a specific harm (financial loss from a dark pattern, task failure from an accessibility barrier, medical error from a clinical interface) with matched users who did not, measuring prior exposure to design features. They are particularly valuable for rare or severe outcomes (clinical UX errors, fraud-related design harms, automotive interface accidents) where prospective cohorts would need impractically large samples. The odds ratio estimates association; rigour depends on control selection from the same source population, matching and avoiding recall bias by using logs.
steps: Define cases precisely and identify them (incident reports, complaints, logs).
Select controls from the same source population, matched on key factors (for example time, product version).
Measure prior exposure to candidate design features, preferably from logs to avoid recall bias.
Compute odds ratios with conditional logistic regression for matched designs.
Adjust for confounders and test dose-response.
Interpret with Bradford Hill criteria and confirm with experiments where possible.
outputs: Odds ratios for design exposures, adjusted estimates, candidate causal features.
useWhen: Rare, severe or delayed harms; investigating incidents and complaints.
avoidWhen: Common outcomes where experiments or cohorts are feasible; when exposures cannot be measured reliably.
whyLost: UX samples users by convenience or segment, not by outcome, and epidemiological designs are not taught.
whereToUse: Medication errors in EHRs, scam losses, misdirected payments, automotive HMI incidents.
example: Comparing 150 users who lost money to impersonation scams with 600 matched controls shows exposure to an in-app 'verified' badge lookalike in messages has an odds ratio of 4.1.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Schlesselman JJ (1982) Case-Control Studies: Design, Conduct, Analysis
Doll R & Hill AB (1950) Smoking and carcinoma of the lung. BMJ
Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology (3rd ed., 2008)
Doll & Hill, Smoking and carcinoma of the lung (1950), BMJ
Statistics for Business and Economics (Newbold et al., 2022)
reference: Schlesselman JJ (1982) Case-Control Studies: Design, Conduct, Analysis. Oxford University Press.

name: UX Cross-Sectional Survey
origin: Cross-sectional study design; listed in the treatise's UX epidemiologist's toolkit
summary: Measures exposure and outcome in a representative sample at one point in time to estimate prevalence and associations of UX harm.
description: The treatise lists cross-sectional surveys among the epidemiological toolkit that can be adapted for UX. A cross-sectional study samples a defined population at one time, measuring exposures, outcomes and covariates simultaneously. It estimates prevalence (for example the share of adults who were charged after failing to cancel a subscription in the past year) and associations (prevalence ratios by age or literacy). Its limitation is temporality: exposure and outcome are measured together, so causal direction is uncertain. Rigour depends on probability sampling or weighting, validated questions with defined recall periods and non-response adjustment. It is the cheapest population-level instrument and the basis of active surveillance waves.
steps: Define the target population and sampling frame.
Design questions with clear recall periods and validated measures.
Draw a probability or weighted sample of adequate size for subgroup estimates.
Field the survey and track response rates.
Weight results and estimate prevalence and prevalence ratios with CIs.
Report limitations regarding temporality and recall.
outputs: Prevalence estimates, subgroup prevalence ratios, weighted datasets.
useWhen: Estimating how common a UX harm or experience is in a population; baseline for surveillance.
avoidWhen: Causal questions requiring temporal order; use cohort or experimental designs.
whyLost: UX surveys sample convenient users of one product rather than populations.
whereToUse: Regulatory evidence, market-wide studies, digital inclusion research.
example: A national survey of 4,000 adults finds 17% experienced an unwanted subscription renewal in the past year, rising to 26% among those over 70.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Levin KA (2006) Study design III: cross-sectional studies. Evidence-Based Dentistry 7
Groves RM et al. (2009) Survey Methodology
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Levin KA (2006) Study design III: Cross-sectional studies. Evidence-Based Dentistry 7:24-25.

name: UX Disease Agent Classification (Types I-IV)
aka: Cognitive, IA, interaction and systemic pathogens
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Classifies UX pathogens as cognitive, information architecture, interaction pattern or systemic, each needing different prevention and treatment strategies.
description: Medicine classifies disease agents (viral, bacterial, parasitic, environmental) because each requires different control strategies. The treatise proposes four UX agent types. Type I, cognitive pathogens, exploit or overwhelm attention, working memory, decision-making under uncertainty or framing susceptibility; most dark patterns belong here and are effective because the vulnerabilities are deep and universal. Type II, information architecture pathogens, systematically prevent users finding what they need and spread through shared templates and CMSs. Type III, interaction pattern pathogens, create systematic errors through misleading affordances, uninformative feedback or invisible status, and can 'mutate' when copied into contexts lacking the features that made them safe. Type IV, systemic pathogens, are structural features of platforms or industries, the hardest to address because they are not localised.
steps: Collect candidate harmful patterns from audits, complaints and research.
Classify each by type using the mechanism of harm, not surface appearance.
Note transmission routes typical of the type (templates, libraries, incentives).
Select control strategies suited to each type (literacy for Type I, IA standards for II, pattern library fixes for III, policy for IV).
Track prevalence of each type over time.
Revise the classification as new mechanisms appear.
outputs: Classified pathogen register, type-specific control strategies, prevalence by type.
useWhen: Building pattern audits, regulatory taxonomies, design-system governance.
avoidWhen: Single-issue fixes where classification adds no decision value.
whyLost: Original to the treatise; no prior classification of UX harms by mechanism of agent.
whereToUse: Dark pattern regulation, design system governance, trust and safety, consumer advocacy.
example: A design-system team finds a toast-based undo pattern harmful when copied into irreversible payment flows; classed as a mutating Type III pathogen, it is restricted in the library guidelines.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Gray CM et al. (2018) The dark (patterns) side of UX design. CHI
Mathur A et al. (2019) Dark patterns at scale. CSCW
reference: Mathur A et al. (2019) Dark patterns at scale: findings from a crawl of 11K shopping websites. Proceedings of the ACM on HCI 3(CSCW).

name: UX Ecological Study
origin: Ecological study design; listed in the treatise's UX epidemiologist's toolkit
summary: Compares aggregate UX outcomes across groups such as countries, sectors or platforms against group-level exposures like regulation or design system adoption.
description: Ecological studies analyse groups rather than individuals, relating group-level exposures to group-level outcomes, for example complaint rates by country against consumer protection rules, or accessibility failure rates by sector against design system use. The treatise includes them in the UX epidemiologist's toolkit. They are cheap, use existing aggregate data and suit questions about policies and structures (Type IV systemic pathogens) that only vary between groups. The main pitfall is the ecological fallacy: associations at group level need not hold for individuals. Analysts must also handle confounding by other group characteristics and small numbers of groups.
steps: Define units (countries, sectors, platforms, firms) and the group-level exposure.
Gather aggregate outcome data (complaints, failure rates, audit scores).
Collect group-level confounders.
Analyse associations with regression or time-series comparisons across groups.
Interpret cautiously, noting the ecological fallacy.
Generate hypotheses for individual-level studies.
outputs: Group-level associations, hypotheses about structural determinants.
useWhen: Evaluating policies, standards or platform rules that vary between groups.
avoidWhen: Inferring individual-level effects.
whyLost: UX rarely analyses across products or jurisdictions.
whereToUse: Regulatory comparison, sector accessibility studies, design system impact across firms.
example: Across 27 countries, those requiring one-click cancellation have 40% lower subscription complaint rates per capita, motivating individual-level follow-up.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Morgenstern H (1995) Ecologic studies in epidemiology: concepts, principles, and methods. Annu Rev Public Health 16
Robinson WS (1950) Ecological correlations and the behavior of individuals. Am Sociol Rev
reference: Morgenstern H (1995) Ecologic studies in epidemiology: concepts, principles, and methods. Annual Review of Public Health 16:61-81.

name: UX Epidemiology Framework
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Studio Aghora (uxguy.in)
summary: Applies prevalence, incidence, transmission and immunity concepts to track how usability problems emerge and spread across user populations and cohorts.
description: The UX Epidemiology Framework treats usability problems as population-level phenomena rather than isolated findings from a handful of sessions. Borrowing from epidemiology, it distinguishes prevalence (the share of users currently affected by an issue), incidence (the rate of new cases over time), transmission (how issues propagate, for example through shared workflows, team settings or word of mouth) and immunity (factors such as prior experience or onboarding that protect users). Issues are defined with explicit case definitions based on observable signals in logs, support tickets or surveys, then tracked by cohort, segment and release. Its rigour comes from case definitions, denominators and cohort comparisons, which allow teams to say not just that a problem exists but how many people it affects, who is most exposed and whether a fix actually reduced new cases.
steps: Write an operational case definition for each issue using observable signals such as error events, repeated retries or ticket tags.
Define the population at risk and the denominator for each issue.
Compute prevalence and weekly incidence per cohort, segment and release.
Identify transmission routes, such as shared configurations or team invitations, that spread the issue.
Identify protective factors by comparing affected and unaffected cohorts.
Track incidence before and after fixes to estimate their effect and report results as population metrics.
outputs: Prevalence and incidence curves per issue, exposure and protective-factor profiles, and before-and-after fix effect estimates.
useWhen: For large-scale products where issues affect segments unevenly; when post-release monitoring needs population metrics rather than anecdotes.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small products without reliable logs or ticket data; use usability testing or a critical incident study instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Novel cross-disciplinary Vivek framework; treats UX problems as population-level phenomena.
whereToUse: Large-scale consumer products; tracking issue spread across user segments post-release.
example: After a mobile banking release, a 'payment stuck' case definition shows incidence tripling among Android users on older OS versions. Fixing that path halves incidence within two weeks, which the team reports as a cohort comparison.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rose G (1992) The Strategy of Preventive Medicine
Rothman KJ, Greenland S & Lash TL (2008) Modern Epidemiology. 3rd ed
reference: Gopinath, V. UX Epidemiology Framework (uxguy.in).

name: UX Health Equity Metrics
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise); drawing on health disparities measurement
summary: Systematically measures how UX harm is distributed across age, literacy, language, disability and income groups, tracking disparities over time.
description: The treatise argues a population UX health framework must include equity metrics measuring how harm is distributed across demographic groups, as health equity research documents disparities by race, income, education and age. Preliminary evidence it cites: older users experience higher task failure and dark pattern victimisation; lower education and digital literacy increase susceptibility to manipulation; non-English speakers fare worse with products not designed for their context; disabled users face near-total exclusion from parts of the ecosystem. Equity metrics quantify these disparities precisely enough to motivate and evaluate interventions, using absolute and relative measures (rate differences, rate ratios, concentration indices) and tracking them as products change.
steps: Select equity-relevant groups and collect group membership ethically (consent, privacy).
Measure UX outcomes (failure, harm, exclusion) per group from surveillance or studies.
Compute absolute (rate difference) and relative (rate ratio) disparity measures with CIs.
Use summary indices across ordered groups (for example slope or concentration index).
Track disparities over releases and after interventions.
Set equity targets and report publicly where appropriate.
outputs: Disparity measures, equity dashboards, targets and intervention evaluations.
useWhen: Public services, regulated industries, inclusive design programmes, accessibility strategy.
avoidWhen: When group data cannot be collected ethically or samples are too small for stable estimates.
whyLost: Original proposal; UX equity work is usually qualitative or compliance-based rather than measured.
whereToUse: Government services, banking, healthcare, education platforms, AI assistant quality across languages.
example: An AI assistant's task success is 88% in English and 61% in Tagalog; tracking the rate ratio quarterly drives localisation investment and the gap halves.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Braveman P (2006) Health disparities and health equity: concepts and measurement. Annu Rev Public Health 27
Harper S & Lynch J (2005) Methods for measuring cancer disparities. NCI
reference: Braveman P (2006) Health disparities and health equity: concepts and measurement. Annual Review of Public Health 27:167-194.

name: UX Herd Immunity
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: A state where enough structural protection (literacy, standards, regulation, norms) exists that harmful patterns cannot spread efficiently, pursued at individual, product and ecosystem levels.
description: Herd immunity is the indirect protection of susceptible individuals when enough of a population is immune to block sustained transmission. The treatise asks what it would take for UX pathogens to be unable to spread efficiently even without individual immunity, and defines UX herd immunity as a state of the design ecosystem in which structural factors (standards, regulation, professional norms, user literacy) make it difficult for harmful patterns to spread and persist. It sets three pathways: individual protection (user literacy so more people recognise and resist manipulation), product-level protection (raising the floor through standards and certification) and ecosystem-level protection (changing incentives and pressures that drive adoption). Threshold reasoning (1 - 1/R0) suggests how much protection is needed for a given pattern.
steps: Estimate the pattern's R0 and derive an indicative protection threshold (1 - 1/R0).
Measure current protection at individual (literacy), product (standards compliance) and ecosystem (regulation, norms) levels.
Identify the cheapest pathways to reach the threshold.
Implement combined interventions across the three levels.
Monitor effective R and prevalence.
Sustain protection as patterns mutate.
outputs: Protection threshold estimates, protection coverage measures, multi-level intervention plan.
useWhen: Ecosystem strategies against pervasive harmful patterns.
avoidWhen: Single-product problems.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Regulators, industry bodies, education programmes, platform policy teams.
example: With fake-urgency timers at R0 about 2, a consortium targets 50% protection by combining a platform policy banning fake timers with a consumer literacy campaign.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Fine P, Eames K & Heymann DL (2011) 'Herd immunity': a rough guide. Clinical Infectious Diseases 52(7)
reference: Fine P, Eames K & Heymann DL (2011) 'Herd immunity': a rough guide. Clinical Infectious Diseases 52(7):911-916.

name: UX Incidence and Prevalence Measurement
origin: Epidemiological frequency measures; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Distinguishes the rate of new UX harm events per person-time (incidence) from the proportion currently experiencing harm (prevalence), with defined denominators.
description: The treatise defines UX incidence as the rate of new harm events in a population over a defined period and UX prevalence as the proportion currently experiencing harm, point or period. The distinction matters: a short-lived confusion may have high incidence but low prevalence, while an accessibility barrier may have low incidence but persistent high prevalence. Rigorous measurement requires a case definition, a defined population at risk, person-time denominators (for example per 1,000 active user-weeks) and stratification. Rates replace raw counts that grow with traffic, and enable comparisons across products, segments and periods. Cumulative incidence and incidence density are both useful.
steps: Write the case definition for the harm event or state.
Define the population at risk and the denominator (users, sessions, person-time).
Count new cases for incidence and current cases for prevalence over the chosen period or point.
Compute rates with confidence intervals and stratify by segment.
Track over time and compare across products or versions.
Report with explicit definitions so others can replicate.
outputs: Incidence rates, prevalence proportions, stratified and trend tables.
useWhen: Any monitoring of UX harm or failure where traffic varies or comparisons are needed.
avoidWhen: When harms cannot be defined consistently; first develop a case definition qualitatively.
whyLost: Product metrics use counts and conversion ratios without epidemiological denominators.
whereToUse: Error monitoring, accessibility barriers, dark pattern exposure, AI hallucination harms.
example: A wallet app reports misdirected transfers as 1.8 per 10,000 transfer-days rather than '412 incidents', allowing fair comparison after user growth.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rothman KJ (2012) Epidemiology: An Introduction. 2nd ed
CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice (2012), Lesson 3
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
reference: Rothman KJ (2012) Epidemiology: An Introduction. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.

name: UX KPIs with Baselines and Pre-Set Success Thresholds
aka: Outcome and action metrics with pre-committed success thresholds
donor: Performance measurement; programme evaluation; web analytics
origin: Business performance management; Beasley (2013); Covert (2014); Wendel (2014); Croll and Yoskovitz (2013)
summary: Defines goal-linked UX indicators with explicit formulas, measures baselines before change, fixes success and failure thresholds in advance, and reports a few rates regularly.
description: The sources converge on one discipline. Start from intent and break it into goals with a baseline and a measure of progress; choose a few action-oriented indicators tied to business goals, stated as rates rather than counts. Wendel adds paired metrics: an outcome metric for the real-world result and an action metric for the behaviour that drives it, each written as a formula (what, how, over what period) and checked for being accurate, reliable, rapid, responsive, sensitive and cheap, preferring automatic tracking over self-report. Baselines are measured before change, since without them assumptions mislead. Success and failure thresholds, the 'line in the sand', are fixed before results arrive, with a decision written for each outcome, guarding against post-hoc spin; the same minimum effect sets sample sizes and stopping rules. Indicators are reported on a regular rhythm, typically a one-page monthly report with context and interpretation, and flags deliver data when something important happens.
steps: Restate the intended outcome and break it into specific goals; check each is tangible and able to show both success and failure.
Write an outcome metric and an action metric as explicit formulas (what, how, over what period), stated as rates rather than counts.
Check each metric for accuracy, reliability, speed, responsiveness, sensitivity and cost; avoid self-reported actions where tracking exists.
Measure baselines before any change, over a stated baseline period.
Set success and failure thresholds before measuring, from the business model, benchmarks or a trend asymptote, and write down the decision for each result; record and explain any later change.
Set flags for situations that should trigger notification, such as a sudden drop in task completion.
Report a handful of rates monthly on one page with month-on-month and year-on-year change, interpretation and follow-up, including 'all is well' or 'under watch'.
outputs: Metric definitions with formulas, baselines, pre-registered thresholds and decision rules, flags, and a regular one-page UX KPI report.
useWhen: Any redesign, launch or experiment whose success must be judged, and ongoing UX monitoring for a live product.
avoidWhen: When you need to explain why something changed; KPIs measure what, not why, and attitudes are hard to capture. Do not chase a perfect metric, and beware rates that swing with seasonality and marketing. For experience dimensions use HEART Framework; for causal effects use A/B Testing.
whyLost: KPI dashboards are common, but baselines are often missing and thresholds are set after results arrive, so the pre-commitment that made the practice rigorous is lost.
whereToUse: E-commerce, SaaS, public digital services, health behaviour change apps, design system impact tracking.
example: Before relaunching checkout, a retailer records a 68% baseline completion rate, defines success as at least 72% and failure as below 66% over 30 days, and writes the actions for each; a mid-range result triggers a planned usability study rather than a rollback debate.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert, 2014)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Wendel, S. (2014). Designing for Behavior Change. O'Reilly Media, pp. 204-208, 251-257; Croll, A. and Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics. O'Reilly Media.

name: UX Maturity Levels Assessment (Games)
origin: Graham McAllister (Player Research); chapter 5
summary: A model of eight levels (0 to 7) that rates a studio's user research practice on staff and resources, dedicated budget, breadth of methods, depth of buy-in and evidence in released products, and says what to do next.
description: McAllister's model gives studios a roadmap for improving user research. It has eight levels, from Level 0 (does not know about UX research) and Level 1 (does not do it) through a 'have a go' approach and ineffective internal UX, to effective internal UX, outsourced UX, lifecycle UX and finally organisational UX, where research runs through company culture. Levels 0 to 3 may have no benefit or even make games worse; only from Level 4 are resources sufficient to reliably improve the player experience. Five variables place a studio: staff and resources (qualified staff, real participants, dedicated space, recruitment), dedicated budget planned per project, breadth of UX across the life cycle, depth of buy-in from the top down, and evidence, meaning whether released games are well reviewed and free of UX complaints. Each variable is rated by effort (none, low, moderate, sufficient). For each level the chapter lists signs that you are there, what to do next and when you are ready to move on. The evidence variable is notable because it checks outcomes, not just investment: if games still ship with usability issues despite research, the problem lies in process, communication or trust. The model can be used by any product organisation.
steps: Gather information on research staff, facilities, recruitment and budget planning.
Map which research methods are used across the development life cycle.
Assess depth of buy-in: who reads reports and whether findings reach leadership.
Review evidence from releases, such as review comments on usability problems.
Rate each variable's effort level and match the profile to one of the eight levels.
Use the level's guidance to pick next steps and the criteria for moving up.
outputs: A maturity level with a profile across five variables and a prioritised improvement plan.
useWhen: Making the case for investment in research, planning a research team's growth, or auditing why research is not improving products.
avoidWhen: You need a precise, validated benchmark against other organisations.
whyLost: Several UX maturity models exist outside games, but this one, with its evidence variable, is little known beyond the games industry.
whereToUse: Game studios, product organisations building research teams, research operations planning.
example: A mid-sized studio rates itself at Level 3: it has an internal researcher but no per-project budget and leadership never sees reports, so it plans budgeted testing and quarterly leadership readouts.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. & Nacke, L. (eds), Games User Research (2018)
reference: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P. and Nacke, L. E. (eds) (2018). Games User Research. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Chapter 5 (McAllister).

name: UX Morbidity and Mortality Assessment
origin: Morbidity and mortality measures; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Quantifies the harm users suffer from UX pathogens (task failure, decision error, time, money, distress) and the most severe goal-destroying or physical outcomes.
description: The treatise defines UX morbidity as harm experienced through exposure to a UX pathogen, measured as task failure, decision error, wasted time, financial loss, emotional distress or other user-meaningful outcomes. UX mortality is the complete destruction of a user's ability to accomplish a goal, or in high-stakes domains (medical, legal, financial) a contribution to physical harm or death. Morbidity assessment specifies outcome measures, severity grades and measurement sources, as in the roach motel analysis (tens to hundreds of dollars per incident, frustration, trust erosion, billions at population scale). It moves UX measurement beyond business metrics toward harms that matter to users.
steps: List harm dimensions relevant to the pattern: time, money, errors, distress, trust, exclusion.
Define measurable indicators and severity grades for each.
Collect data from logs, complaints, surveys and case reviews.
Estimate per-incident morbidity distributions and the share reaching 'mortality' outcomes.
Combine with incidence to estimate total harm.
Feed into burden metrics and prioritisation.
outputs: Harm indicators, severity distributions, per-incident and population harm estimates.
useWhen: Characterising consequences of a pattern or failure for prioritisation, regulation or accountability.
avoidWhen: When only usability defects without user harm are at stake.
whyLost: UX measured satisfaction and conversion, not harm to users.
whereToUse: Subscription traps, medical device UX, financial errors, accessibility exclusion, AI misinformation.
example: Morbidity assessment of a confusing medication-refill flow finds 4% of failures lead to missed doses (graded severe), reframing it from a UX nuisance to a patient-safety issue.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Murray CJL & Lopez AD (1996) The Global Burden of Disease
reference: Gordis L (2014) Epidemiology. 5th ed. Elsevier Saunders.

name: UX Outbreak Investigation
origin: Classic outbreak investigation methodology (CDC, Epidemic Intelligence Service); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Investigates sudden rises in UX failure, complaints or a spreading pattern by case definition, person-place-time description, hypothesis testing and control measures.
description: Field epidemiology's outbreak investigation responds to an unexpected increase in disease: establish a case definition, describe the outbreak by person, place and time, develop and test hypotheses about the source, and implement and evaluate control measures. The treatise argues UX outbreaks are real: a deployed change suddenly raising failure rates, a new dark pattern spreading rapidly across an industry, or an update generating a surge of support contacts. Applying the methodology replaces ad hoc firefighting with a disciplined sequence: confirm the outbreak versus noise, define cases, build an epidemic curve, compare attack rates across exposures (versions, devices, segments), and verify that control measures end the outbreak. The roach motel and cookie consent case studies illustrate it.
steps: Verify the outbreak: compare current incidence with baseline and rule out measurement artefacts.
Write a case definition (clinical-style: who, what event, when).
Describe cases by person (segment), place (platform, region, page) and time (epidemic curve).
Generate hypotheses and test them by comparing attack rates or with a case-control comparison.
Implement control measures (rollback, hotfix, guidance) and monitor incidence.
Write a report with root cause, lessons and surveillance changes.
outputs: Case definition, epidemic curve, attack-rate tables, confirmed source, control measures and report.
useWhen: Sudden spikes in errors, complaints, abandonment or support contacts; spreading harmful patterns.
avoidWhen: Slow chronic problems better handled by cohort studies or burden estimation.
whyLost: Incident response in tech is engineering-led and focused on uptime, not user harm.
whereToUse: Post-release monitoring, support operations, trust and safety, regulators tracking pattern spread.
example: Support contacts about missing refunds triple; the epidemic curve starts at an Android release, attack rate is 9% on Android 14 vs 0.3% elsewhere, and a hotfix ends the outbreak within 48 hours.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice. 3rd ed (2012), Lesson 6
CDC, Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice (3rd ed., 2012), Lesson 6: Investigating an Outbreak
Reingold, Outbreak investigations: A perspective (1998), Emerging Infectious Diseases
reference: Gregg MB (Ed) (2008) Field Epidemiology. 3rd ed. Oxford University Press.

name: UX Pathogen Transmission Vector Analysis
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Traces how harmful patterns spread between products via design plagiarism, component libraries, industry conventions and platform pressure, to target containment.
description: The treatise identifies four vectors of UX pathogen transmission. Design plagiarism copies patterns from successful products without understanding the conditions under which they work safely. Component libraries (Bootstrap, Material and similar) transmit patterns at scale and velocity, spreading good and bad with equal efficiency. Industry conventions normalise patterns so that even harmful ones acquire 'epidemiological immunity' because users, regulators and competitors accept them. Platform pressure transmits pathogens through technical constraints, monetisation models and requirements such as app store, ad and payment rules. Vector analysis reconstructs transmission history for a pattern (as in the roach motel case: print subscriptions to late-1990s digital, then copying and startup templates) and directs containment at the vector rather than each infected product.
steps: Select a pattern and document its first known deployments.
Trace adoption over time using archives (for example Wayback Machine), design-system changelogs and industry sources.
Attribute adoptions to vectors: copying, shared components, convention, platform requirements.
Estimate each vector's contribution and speed.
Identify containment points (library maintainers, platforms, standards bodies).
Monitor post-intervention adoption.
outputs: Transmission history, vector attribution, containment targets.
useWhen: Understanding and stopping the spread of harmful or flawed patterns across an industry or organisation.
avoidWhen: One-off, product-specific defects with no spread.
whyLost: Original to the treatise; UX lacked a vocabulary for pattern contagion.
whereToUse: Design-system governance, platform policy, regulators, industry bodies.
example: A flawed date-picker spreading accessibility failures is traced to one popular component library version; a patch upstream fixes 1,400 downstream sites within months.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Mathur A et al. (2019) Dark patterns at scale. CSCW
Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed
reference: Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed. Free Press.

name: UX Randomised Controlled Trials (Clinical-Grade A/B Testing)
origin: RCT methodology (MRC streptomycin trial 1948; CONSORT 1996); adapted to digital experiments by the treatise
summary: Runs A/B tests with clinical-trial rigour: pre-specified primary outcomes including user harm, power calculations, multiplicity control, pre-registration and CONSORT-style reporting.
description: The treatise notes A/B testing is structurally equivalent to an RCT and large companies run thousands, but most are not analysed with clinical rigour: sample sizes set by convenience, outcomes restricted to business metrics, multiple testing ignored and pre-registration rare. A UX Epidemiology approach brings clinical trial methodology to digital experimentation: pre-specified primary and secondary outcomes that include user-meaningful harm measures (guardrails), power calculations based on the effect size that would be practically significant, appropriate handling of multiple testing and peeking (sequential designs), and transparent reporting following CONSORT-equivalent standards. Harm outcomes are monitored as in a data safety monitoring process.
steps: Pre-register hypothesis, primary outcome, harm outcomes and analysis plan.
Calculate sample size for the minimum practically significant effect at 80-90% power.
Randomise at the appropriate unit (user, cluster) and check sample ratio mismatch.
Monitor harm outcomes with pre-defined stopping rules; use sequential methods if peeking.
Analyse per plan with multiplicity correction; report intention-to-treat estimates.
Report CONSORT-style: flow, outcomes, harms, deviations, null results.
outputs: Pre-registered protocol, causal effect estimates with CIs, harm results, CONSORT-style report.
useWhen: Any experiment informing consequential product decisions or affecting user wellbeing or money.
avoidWhen: Very low traffic where power is impossible; use Bayesian or qualitative evidence.
whyLost: Experimentation grew from growth marketing, optimising business metrics quickly rather than rigorously.
whereToUse: Fintech, health apps, marketplaces, AI feature rollouts, notification policies.
example: A lending app pre-registers a test of a new repayment reminder with 'missed payment' as primary outcome and 'overdraft fees' as harm outcome; the variant cuts missed payments 6% without raising fees.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Schulz KF, Altman DG & Moher D (2010) CONSORT 2010 statement. BMJ 340:c332
Kohavi R, Tang D & Xu Y (2020) Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments
Friedman LM et al. (2015) Fundamentals of Clinical Trials. 5th ed
reference: Kohavi R, Tang D & Xu Y (2020) Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Cambridge University Press.

name: UX Revenue Chain
aka: Linking UX metrics to company KPIs
origin: JD Buckley and colleagues at an enterprise HCM company; Buckley and Powers (2019); built on the Service Profit Chain (Heskett, Sasser and Schlesinger, 1997)
summary: Repeat one task-based benchmark across releases and model how task success and ease drive satisfaction, learnability and NPS, and potentially revenue.
description: The UX Revenue Chain adapts the Service Profit Chain to product experience. Instead of a single ROI calculation, it builds a longitudinal dataset: the same top-task benchmark is run before a redesign and repeated after releases, at the same time of year, collecting task-level effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction alongside perceived difficulty, SUS, trust items, UMUX-Lite and NPS. Correlations and regressions identify which task metrics most strongly drive perception metrics, and the strongest paths are expressed as a chain from top-task success to ease, to satisfaction and learnability, to NPS and possibly to revenue. In the published case, task success and ease correlated most strongly with SUS, satisfaction and product NPS. The model is a hypothesis to test against business data, not a proof of causation.
steps: Select task-level metrics (success, time, ease) and overall metrics executives recognise (SUS, UMUX-Lite, trust, NPS).
Identify top tasks by free listing with internal experts (about 20) and a forced-ranking survey of users (several hundred).
Run a baseline task-based benchmark before the redesign, for example at least 25 unmoderated participants per product plus 9-12 moderated sessions with retrospective think-aloud.
Repeat the identical benchmark after each major release, at the same time of year, over at least 18 months.
Correlate and regress task metrics against perception metrics, NPS and available company KPIs.
Express the strongest paths as a chain model and test it against revenue or retention data, keeping product NPS separate from company NPS.
outputs: A longitudinal benchmark dataset and a tentative path model linking task performance to satisfaction, NPS and business KPIs.
useWhen: Enterprise or SaaS products where leadership wants evidence that experience quality moves loyalty and revenue, and the team can sustain a repeated benchmark programme.
avoidWhen: Avoid for one-off studies or small samples, and where service quality dominates NPS. Correlation along the chain is not causal evidence; use experiments or causal modelling where attribution matters.
whyLost: It requires years of identical benchmarks and access to business data; most teams settle for single ROI estimates or NPS tracking alone.
whereToUse: Enterprise HR, finance and CRM platforms; B2B SaaS with renewal revenue; any portfolio with a standing UX benchmarking programme.
example: A payroll SaaS company runs the same ten-task benchmark every spring for three years. Task ease predicts SUS and product NPS, and accounts with higher product NPS renew at higher rates, giving the design team a defensible chain to present at budget reviews.
sources: The Service Profit Chain (Heskett, Sasser & Schlesinger, 1997)
reference: Buckley, J. D. and Powers, A. (2019). Measuring the ROI of UX in an Enterprise Organization, Part 2. UXmatters; case study 11.3 in Albert, W. and Tullis, T. (2022). Measuring the User Experience (3rd ed.), pp. 292-302.

name: UX ROI and Cost-Benefit Calculation
origin: Bias and Mayhew, Cost-Justifying Usability (1994; 2nd ed. 2005); popularised for the web by Jakob Nielsen (1999)
summary: Convert measured usability differences into money by multiplying effect size by usage volume and unit cost, then compare with the cost of the work.
description: UX ROI calculation translates a measured change in task success, time on task, conversion or support contacts into annual savings or revenue. Revenue tasks use potential sales (current sales divided by current success rate) multiplied by the success-rate gain; productivity tasks use seconds saved times frequency, working days (about 220), loaded hourly cost and headcount; support cases use avoided contacts times cost per contact. Variants include pre/post content-impact logging, opportunity-cost framing for information architecture and projecting lab improvements onto live conversion rates. Rigour comes from using large-sample benchmarks, stating every assumption, attributing an explicit share to UX when other initiatives ran concurrently, giving conservative and aggressive scenarios, and checking the projection against live analytics after launch. Most practitioners now cite headline ratios instead of doing the arithmetic.
steps: Measure the difference between the old and new design (success rate, time on task, errors or conversion) in a benchmark test or a dated before/after comparison.
Choose the value categories that apply: productivity, revenue, support contacts, training, or savings from early change.
Obtain volumes and unit costs from finance and analytics: users, task frequency, working days (about 220 a year), loaded hourly rate, cost per contact, revenue per conversion.
Project the effect onto live figures, for example new live rate = live rate x (1 + relative lab improvement), and multiply by the users who have the opportunity to act.
Where another initiative ran at the same time, state an explicit share attributed to UX (for example 30%) as a discussion point.
Sum the categories, compute ROI = (gain - cost) / cost, and present conservative and aggressive scenarios with all assumptions listed.
After launch, check the projection against live data and log the result with the study plan and go-live date.
outputs: An annual savings or revenue estimate per category, an ROI percentage, a stated list of assumptions and scenarios, and a log of predicted versus observed impact.
useWhen: Justifying a design change, a research budget or a UX team to finance-minded stakeholders; sizing which problem to fix first; reporting the impact of a shipped change.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting the figure as measured fact: small-sample effects are uncertain, lab completion rates differ from live ones (for example 80% versus 63%), uncontrolled pre/post comparisons credit UX with everything, and holistic benefits such as IA quality are rarely calculable. Where causal attribution matters, run an A/B test instead.
whyLost: The arithmetic survives as slogans ('every dollar returns $10 to $100') while the disciplined version, with benchmarks, attribution shares and post-launch validation, is rarely done.
whereToUse: Internal enterprise tools, checkout and sign-up flows, support-heavy fintech and government services, and content redesigns where contact volumes or click-through are already tracked.
example: A bank's internal case-lookup screen is redesigned and a benchmark shows 15 seconds saved per lookup. With 4,000 agents doing 30 lookups a day for 220 days at a loaded $30 an hour, the team presents about $1.1m a year as the aggressive case and half that as the conservative case.
sources: Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld & Morville, 2006)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman et al., 2012)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
Think Like a UX Researcher (Travis & Hodgson, 2019)
Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Bias, R. G. and Mayhew, D. J. (2005). Cost-Justifying Usability: An Update for the Internet Age (2nd ed.). San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: UX Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
origin: Cochrane Collaboration (1993); Glass (1976) meta-analysis; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Synthesises all relevant UX studies using defined search, inclusion, quality appraisal and statistical pooling to estimate effects and explain heterogeneity.
description: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are the gold standard of evidence synthesis in medicine, giving more reliable effect estimates than single studies and identifying sources of heterogeneity. The treatise notes UX has a large research literature never systematically reviewed with epidemiological methods; existing reviews are typically narrative, without formal quality assessment or statistical pooling. Applying rigorous methods (protocol registration, comprehensive search, dual screening, risk-of-bias assessment, random-effects pooling, heterogeneity and publication-bias analysis, GRADE-style certainty ratings) would substantially improve the evidence base for design recommendations. Internally, organisations can meta-analyse their own experiments and studies.
steps: Write and register a protocol (question, PICO, inclusion criteria, outcomes).
Search databases and grey literature comprehensively; document the search.
Where the choice of database is open, pilot a random sample from each candidate database and compare qualification rates (the share of relevant records) before committing.

Screen and extract data with two independent reviewers; on large record sets, a documented shortcut is to double-screen a random sample (for example 20%) until agreement reaches Cohen's kappa above 0.8, then single-screen the remainder.
Assess risk of bias for each study.
Pool effects with random-effects meta-analysis; analyse heterogeneity and publication bias.
Grade certainty of evidence and report following PRISMA.
outputs: Pooled effect estimates, heterogeneity analysis, bias assessments, certainty ratings, PRISMA report.
useWhen: Establishing evidence for design guidelines, synthesising many internal experiments, policy evidence.
avoidWhen: Topics with very few comparable studies; use a scoping review.
whyLost: UX publishes fragmentarily and lacks evidence-synthesis training and infrastructure.
whereToUse: Design guideline development, dark pattern policy, accessibility standards, experimentation programmes.
example: A meta-analysis of 64 internal A/B tests on social proof badges finds a pooled conversion uplift of 1.2% with high heterogeneity explained by product price.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Higgins JPT et al. (Eds) (2023) Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions
Page MJ et al. (2021) The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ
Borenstein M et al. (2009) Introduction to Meta-Analysis
Page et al., The PRISMA 2020 statement (2021), BMJ
Higgins et al. (eds.), Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (2019)
Petticrew & Roberts, Systematic Reviews in the Social Sciences (2006)

Shi M, Gao J, Jiao Y & Cao N (2023) Understanding design collaboration between designers and artificial intelligence: A systematic literature review. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 7(CSCW2), Art. 368
The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
DUXU 2022: UX Research, Design, and Assessment (Soares et al., 2022)
User Experience Design Using Machine Learning (Abbas et al., 2022)
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Understanding Design Collaboration Between Designers and Artificial Intelligence (Shi et al., 2023)

name: UX Writing Research
origin: Practice emerged around 2010s product teams (Google, Dropbox); codified by Podmajersky (2019)
summary: Writing and testing interface microcopy, labels, errors and onboarding text against user comprehension, task success and voice guidelines.
description: UX writing is the craft of the words inside an interface: button labels, form hints, error messages, empty states, onboarding and notifications. As a research practice it treats copy as a testable design variable. Candidate wording is evaluated for comprehension (do people understand what will happen?), findability (do labels match users' vocabulary?), task impact (does it change completion or error rates?) and tone fit. Methods include highlighter tests, comprehension probes, five-second tests, unmoderated preference and comprehension surveys, and A/B tests on live copy. Rigour comes from grounding terminology in users' own language (from interviews, search logs and support tickets), testing against a defined voice framework, and measuring behaviour rather than asking which version people like.
steps: Collect users' own vocabulary from search logs, support tickets, reviews and interview transcripts for the flow in question.
Draft 2-4 copy alternatives for each critical string, aligned to the product's voice and tone guidelines.
Run comprehension tests: show the screen and ask participants what will happen if they tap the button or what the message means, coding answers as correct, partial or wrong.
Use highlighter tests on longer passages, asking participants to mark text that builds confidence in green and confusion in red.
Validate high-traffic strings with an A/B test on completion, error or support-contact rates.
Record winning patterns in a content style guide and string library so they are reused consistently.
outputs: Tested copy variants, comprehension scores, terminology list grounded in user language, and updated style guide entries.
useWhen: Designing flows where wording drives behaviour: sign-up, payments, errors, permissions, AI disclosures and onboarding.
avoidWhen: When problems are structural rather than verbal (fix IA or interaction first), or when you only have opinion-based preference votes with no comprehension or behavioural measure.
whyLost: Still in use: Growing recognition as distinct discipline; UX writers now common in large product teams.
whereToUse: All digital products; especially conversational UI, onboarding, and error states.
example: A fintech app's 'Settle now' button on a credit card screen confuses users; comprehension testing shows 40% expect it to pay the full balance. Renaming it 'Pay statement balance (£312)' raises correct predictions to 92% and cuts support tickets.
reference: Podmajersky T (2019) Strategic Writing for UX. O'Reilly Media

name: UXDAI (UX Disability-Adjusted Interaction)
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise); modelled on the DALY (Murray 1994)
summary: A composite unit combining time cost and quality-of-experience cost of UX failures, weighted by interaction importance and failure severity, analogous to the DALY.
description: The UXDAI is the treatise's proposed metric for the UX Burden of Design. Like the DALY, which sums years of life lost and years lived with disability weighted by severity, the UXDAI combines the time cost and quality-of-experience cost of UX failures into a single comparable unit. It weights interactions by importance to the user (a failed banking transaction weighs more than a confusing menu in an entertainment app) and by failure severity. Estimates draw on behavioural analytics (frequency and time), structured population surveys and expert severity assessment. Developing it requires a research programme: eliciting importance and severity weights, validating against user-meaningful outcomes and testing comparability across contexts.
steps: Define interaction categories and assign importance weights through user and expert elicitation.
Define failure severity grades with weights (0-1).
Measure failure frequency and time cost per category from analytics.
Compute UXDAI = sum over failures of (time cost + quality loss) x importance x severity.
Aggregate by product, pattern and population; attach uncertainty intervals.
Validate against outcomes such as complaints, churn and financial loss.
outputs: UXDAI scores by product, pattern and population; weight sets; validation results.
useWhen: Comparing harm across very different products or failure types; burden tracking.
avoidWhen: Fine-grained design decisions within one flow where direct metrics are clearer.
whyLost: Original metric proposed by the treatise; not yet operationalised or validated.
whereToUse: Regulatory impact assessment, platform-wide quality programmes, public digital services.
example: A bank computes UXDAIs: login failures generate 12,000 UXDAI per month, mainly time cost, while failed payee additions generate 9,000 with much higher severity weights, ranking both above cosmetic issues.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Murray CJL (1994) Quantifying the burden of disease: the technical basis for disability-adjusted life years. Bull WHO 72(3)
reference: Murray CJL (1994) Quantifying the burden of disease: the technical basis for disability-adjusted life years. Bulletin of the World Health Organization 72(3):429-445.

name: VAE architecture (encoder → latent space → decoder)
origin: Diederik Kingma & Max Welling, 2013; Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra, 2014
summary: A deep generative model that compresses user sessions into a smooth probabilistic latent space and can decode points in that space into realistic synthetic sessions.
description: A VAE has an encoder that maps each input (such as a session feature vector) to a distribution over a low-dimensional latent space, and a decoder that reconstructs the input from a sampled latent point. Training balances reconstruction accuracy against a KL divergence term that keeps the latent space smooth and close to a standard normal. The result is a continuous map of behaviour where nearby points are similar sessions and new samples generate plausible synthetic data. In UX research, VAEs support synthetic test data, anomaly detection (high reconstruction error) and exploration of behaviour space. Rigour includes held-out reconstruction evaluation, latent dimensionality choice, checking for posterior collapse and validating synthetic data against real distributions.
steps: Represent each session as a fixed-length feature vector, standardised, with categorical features one-hot encoded.
Define encoder and decoder networks (e.g. two hidden layers of 128-256 units) and a latent dimension of 2-16.
Train on 80% of sessions with a reconstruction plus KL loss, monitoring validation loss for overfitting, using KL annealing to avoid posterior collapse.
Evaluate reconstruction error on held-out data and inspect latent space by colouring by known attributes.
Generate synthetic samples and compare their marginal and joint distributions with real data (e.g. KS tests, correlation matrix differences).
Assess privacy risk by checking nearest-neighbour distances between synthetic and real sessions.
outputs: A trained generative model, a latent map of behaviour, reconstruction error per session and validated synthetic samples.
useWhen: When you need realistic synthetic sessions for stress-testing systems, a smooth behaviour map, or anomaly detection on complex logs.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small datasets (under several thousand sessions), when interpretable models suffice, or when synthetic data might be mistaken for real user evidence in decisions.
whyLost: VAEs belong to ML research and engineering; UX researchers seldom have the skills or mandate to train generative models.
whereToUse: Stress-testing recommendation and AI systems, privacy-preserving data sharing, anomaly detection in fintech and health apps.
example: A VAE trained on 400,000 investor sessions provides a 10-dimensional latent space. Sessions with high reconstruction error turn out to be users repeatedly retrying failed transfers, a new error pattern for research.
sources: Deep Learning (Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 53 — Generative Models & Synthetic User Testing
reference: Kingma, D. P. & Welling, M. (2013) Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. arXiv:1312.6114.

name: Validate Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 6 of the forward-thinking loop: confirm prescriptions with pre-registered A/B tests, guardrails, qualitative follow-ups and 1-, 3- and 6-month drift checks, comparing forecast to actual.
description: Validation checks whether predicted improvements happened, whether guardrails held and whether emotional engagement was sustained. It is structured as a three-layer matrix: immediate impact (A/B lift, hazard ratio; think-alouds confirming reduced hesitation), side-effects (latency, crash rates, support tickets, adjacent UX; quotes about new pain) and sustainability (longitudinal telemetry; diary reflections on trust and motivation). It also tests the mechanism, not only the metric: the evidence array is re-run to confirm the recursive loop (Mistake → extra clicks → frustration → lapse) is absent, and the QCA truth table is rebuilt on a fresh sample to confirm the old sufficient path disappears. The rule of thumb is that a validation study is not complete until it confirms improvement, passes guardrails and shows early signs of sustainability.
steps: Run a confirmatory A/B, field or prototype study with pre-registered decision bars (e.g. OTP ≥ 80%), short but adequately powered.
Re-check Cox hazard ratios in production and compare with prototype-stage results (example: HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.63–0.82).
Monitor guardrails (latency, crash rates, support tickets, adjacent task difficulty) and do not call a win if any is harmed.
Run 5–8 think-alouds or short diaries post-change to confirm the root mechanism was resolved.
Re-run the evidence array and rebuild the QCA truth table on a fresh sample to confirm the previous sufficient path no longer holds.
Track adoption stability and sentiment at 1, 3 and 6 months (e.g. OTP success 81%, completion 60%, confidence 4.3/5, action entropy 1.1 → 1.9).
Report forecast versus actual and write a concluding note mapping forecast to actual and mechanism fixed or not fixed.
outputs: Confirmatory test results versus bars, guardrail report, qualitative confirmation, longitudinal stability metrics and a forecast-versus-actual statement.
useWhen: After a prescribed fix ships or is prototyped, and whenever the team needs evidence that the win is real and durable.
avoidWhen: When the fix has not been specified with bars, or when traffic is too low for confirmatory testing; then rely on qualitative verification and monitoring.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; post-launch validation is often skipped once a test 'wins'.
whereToUse: Post-launch reviews, OTP and verification redesigns, IA migrations, retention initiatives.
example: An OTP feedback variant raises OTP success from 65% to 82% and completion from 47% to 61%, beating a Monte Carlo forecast (+11% predicted, +14% observed); three months later completion holds at 60% and action entropy rises from 1.1 to 1.9.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 6.

name: Validated Scale Construction
origin: Cronbach and Meehl (1955) construct validity; DeVellis (1991) scale development
summary: Develops multi-item measures through construct definition, item generation, expert review, piloting, factor analysis and reliability and validity testing.
description: The treatise's curriculum calls for validated scale construction and its borrowing matrix lists validated scales among clinical research methods. A rigorous process defines the construct and its boundaries, generates a large item pool, gathers expert content-validity ratings, runs cognitive interviews, pilots with a sizeable sample, conducts exploratory then confirmatory factor analysis on separate samples, tests reliability (internal consistency, test-retest) and establishes convergent, discriminant and criterion validity. UX often writes bespoke questions or borrows SUS, UMUX or others without checking fit for new contexts, which produces scores that are not comparable or not measuring what is claimed. Validated construction is the antidote.
steps: Define the construct, its dimensions and what it excludes, based on theory and qualitative research.
Generate an item pool several times larger than the final scale.
Collect expert content-validity ratings and run cognitive interviews with target users.
Pilot with 200+ respondents and run exploratory factor analysis; refine items.
Confirm structure with CFA or IRT on a new sample; test reliability and invariance.
Establish validity against related measures and behavioural criteria, then document norms.
outputs: Validated scale with factor structure, reliability, validity evidence and scoring guide.
