useWhen: Measuring constructs repeatedly or comparatively (trust, perceived control, burden).
avoidWhen: When an existing validated scale fits the construct and population; adopt and verify instead.
whyLost: Survey writing became a generalist skill; speed and bespoke questions displaced psychometric discipline.
whereToUse: AI trust measurement, digital burden in healthcare, financial wellbeing, accessibility experience.
example: A health system develops a 10-item 'portal burden' scale through 40 cognitive interviews and two survey waves; it predicts portal abandonment better than SUS.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
DeVellis RF (2016) Scale Development: Theory and Applications. 4th ed
Cronbach LJ & Meehl PE (1955) Construct validity in psychological tests. Psych Bulletin
Boateng GO et al. (2018) Best practices for developing and validating scales. Frontiers in Public Health
reference: Boateng GO et al. (2018) Best practices for developing and validating scales for health, social, and behavioral research: a primer. Frontiers in Public Health 6:149.

name: Validity/reliability as formal properties
origin: Cronbach and Meehl on construct validity, 1955; Cronbach's alpha, 1951; Messick's unified validity, 1989
summary: Treats reliability and validity as quantifiable properties of a measure, estimated with specific statistics, rather than labels claimed for a method.
description: Reliability is the consistency of a measure: internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha or McDonald's omega), test-retest stability (intraclass correlation), and inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha). Validity is the degree to which evidence supports interpreting scores as measuring the intended construct; modern psychometrics (Messick; the APA/AERA/NCME Standards) treats it as a unified argument drawing on content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables and consequences. In UX, 'validated' is often claimed for any published questionnaire regardless of the population, and bespoke surveys are used without any checks. The formal approach estimates these properties for each use, sets thresholds in advance, and reports them.
steps: Specify the intended score interpretation and use, and the population.
Estimate internal consistency (alpha or omega; 0.70 minimum for research, 0.90 for individual decisions) and, if relevant, test-retest reliability over 1-2 weeks (ICC above 0.75).
For coded data, estimate inter-rater agreement on at least 10-20% of items (kappa or Krippendorff's alpha of 0.67-0.80 or higher).
Gather structural validity evidence with factor analysis (sample of at least 150-200; CFA fit such as CFI above 0.95, RMSEA below 0.06).
Gather convergent and discriminant evidence by correlating with related and unrelated measures.
Write a validity argument summarising evidence, gaps and limits on interpretation.
outputs: Reliability coefficients, factor structure results, convergent/discriminant correlations, and a written validity argument.
useWhen: When building or adapting a questionnaire, coding scheme or metric for decisions; when using an instrument in a new population or language.
avoidWhen: For one-off formative checks where no score-based decision is made; there, a pilot and cognitive interviews may suffice.
whyLost: UX treats validity as a property of famous instruments rather than of interpretations, and lacks psychometric training, so checks are skipped.
whereToUse: Custom satisfaction and trust scales, AI evaluation rubrics, regulated usability studies, and cross-cultural research programmes.
example: A fintech team's 6-item trust scale shows alpha 0.91 but factor analysis reveals two factors: security and fairness. Splitting the scale prevents a fairness problem being masked by high security scores.
sources: Dix, A., Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data (2020)
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Leavy, P., Research Design: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed Methods, Arts-Based, and Community-Based Participatory Research Approaches (2017)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 8 — Measurement Theory — Before You Measure Anything
Research Methodology in Behavioural Sciences (Mangal & Mangal, 2013)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 2 (Lerner et al., 2015)
reference: Messick, S. (1989). Validity. In R. L. Linn (Ed.), Educational Measurement (3rd ed.). American Council on Education/Macmillan.

name: ValTEx (Valence-Telemetry Exchange)
donor: Human-AI trust research and telemetry analytics
origin: Vivek Gopinath
summary: A metric combining emotional valence with behavioural telemetry to detect drift in human-AI trust, used to steer conversational AI product strategy.
description: ValTEx is listed among Vivek Gopinath's selected contributions as a metric to detect human-AI trust drift that influenced conversational AI product strategy. The sources give only this one-line definition; the protocol below is a reconstruction consistent with his drift and DAG-SEM work rather than a published specification. The idea implied by the name is an exchange between stated or expressed valence (how users feel about the AI) and telemetry (what they do with it, such as accepting suggestions without double-checking), so that trust drift is detected when the two diverge or decline together. This parallels the Credible proxy in his drift playbook (adopting recommendations without double-checking) and the trust → double-checking path in the payments SEM.
steps: Define trust-relevant valence measures (in-conversation sentiment, short trust prompts) and trust-relevant behaviours (acceptance without edits, re-asking, verification actions).
Collect both streams per user over time.
Normalise and align the streams per session.
Track their joint trend and divergence to flag trust drift.
Probe flagged users with interviews to name the mechanism.
Feed findings into AI product decisions and re-measure after changes.
outputs: A trust-drift indicator per user or cohort and mechanism notes for flagged segments.
useWhen: When monitoring trust in conversational or agentic AI products over time.
avoidWhen: When AI interactions are too infrequent for telemetry trends; use periodic trust surveys instead.
whyLost: Original metric by Vivek Gopinath; documented in the sources only as a selected contribution.
whereToUse: Conversational AI, copilots, AI assistants in fintech and support.
example: A support copilot shows stable sentiment but rising re-ask and manual-verification rates; the divergence flags trust drift and leads to clearer source citations in answers.
sources: Vivek Gopinath, professional research profile (Selected Contributions)
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study

name: Value Alignment Audit for AI Products
origin: Brian Christian, 2020 (synthesis); Amodei et al., 2016 (concrete problems)
summary: Audits whether an AI feature's objective, training signals and behaviour match what users and affected parties actually value, surfacing proxy gaming and harms.
description: A value alignment audit examines the gap between what an AI system is optimised to do and what the people it serves actually value. Drawing on the alignment literature synthesised by Brian Christian, it inspects the objective function and proxy metrics (clicks, dwell time, thumbs-up), the training and feedback data, and observed behaviour, looking for specification gaming, reward hacking, distributional shift and disparate effects on groups. UX research contributes by eliciting users' and affected stakeholders' values, collecting reflective judgments (regret, endorsement) that differ from momentary behaviour, and testing failure cases. Rigour comes from explicit mapping of objectives to values, documented red-team scenarios, measures that capture considered preferences, and continued monitoring after launch.
steps: For any AI-optimized product feature:
Identify the objective function being maximized.
(2) Survey users: 'Is maximizing [objective] what you actually want from this product?'
Identify potential divergences: what behaviors does maximizing the objective incentivize that users would disapprove of?
(4) Measure: compare metric-optimized outcomes to user-welfare outcomes (e.g., maximize engagement vs. maximize reported satisfaction).
(5) Document divergences as ethical design debts.
outputs: A map of stated objectives versus proxy metrics, observed misalignments and failure cases, affected-stakeholder value analysis, and mitigations with monitoring metrics.
useWhen: Recommender systems, ranking, LLM assistants and automated decisions where optimisation targets (engagement, clicks, ratings) may diverge from user wellbeing or intent.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a one-off compliance tick; it needs ongoing monitoring. For deterministic, non-learning features, a standard harm or risk assessment suffices.
whyLost: Alignment work sits with ML research and policy teams; UX researchers are rarely involved in defining reward signals or evaluation metrics.
whereToUse: Recommendation system UX, social media feed design, AI assistant design, algorithmic product ethics review.
example: A news app audits its recommender and finds the click-through objective rewards outrage headlines users later say they regret; adding a post-read 'worth it?' signal to the objective reduces regret ratings.
reference: Christian B (2020) The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning and Human Values. W.W. Norton

name: Value Opportunity Analysis
origin: Jonathan Cagan and Craig Vogel, Creating Breakthrough Products (2002)
summary: Rate a product low, medium or high on seven value opportunities to compare it with competitors or through different personas and target gaps.
description: Value opportunity analysis profiles how much value a product offers across seven opportunities and their attributes: emotion, aesthetics, identity, impact, ergonomics, core technology and quality. A team rates each attribute low, medium or high and draws the result as a profile chart. The same rating can be applied to competitors, to historic market successes and failures, or from the viewpoint of different personas, so that profiles can be compared and gaps targeted in a redesign. Its value lies in widening the team's view of value beyond function and price. Its rigour depends entirely on whether the ratings are grounded in research on what users value rather than on the team's own taste.
steps: List the seven value opportunities (emotion, aesthetics, identity, impact, ergonomics, core technology, quality) and their attributes.
Ground the team in research evidence on what users value before rating.
Rate the product on each attribute as low, medium or high and chart the profile.
Rate competitors, or rate the product from the viewpoint of each persona.
Compare profiles side by side and identify opportunities where the product lags or could differentiate.
Set design targets for the chosen gaps and re-rate concepts against them.
outputs: A value opportunity profile chart per product or persona and a list of targeted gaps.
useWhen: Early product strategy and redesigns of physical or digital products, competitive positioning, and workshops where a team needs a shared vocabulary for non-functional value.
avoidWhen: Avoid as evidence of user value: ratings are subjective and easily reflect the team's taste. Use Kano analysis or conjoint-style methods when you need user-derived priorities.
whyLost: It stayed in industrial design education; UX teams use Kano, JTBD and competitive benchmarking instead.
whereToUse: Consumer hardware, connected devices, premium apps and brand-led products where emotion, identity and aesthetics matter as much as function.
example: A smart-thermostat team rates its product and two rivals and finds it high on core technology but low on identity and aesthetics. The redesign brief targets those two opportunities.
reference: Cagan, J. and Vogel, C. M. (2002). Creating Breakthrough Products: Innovation from Product Planning to Program Approval. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall.

name: Value Stream Mapping
origin: Toyota material and information flow diagrams; codified by Mike Rother and John Shook (Learning to See, 1999)
summary: Maps every step from request to delivery with process time, wait time and information flows, quantifying waste and flow efficiency.
description: Value stream mapping documents the current state of a process with standard icons, recording for each step the process time, lead time, percentage complete and accurate, and information triggers. The timeline at the bottom compares value-adding time with total lead time; flow efficiency is often below 5%. A future-state map designs out waste (the seven wastes: waiting, overprocessing, defects, motion and so on) and a plan closes the gap. It complements journey maps: journeys show what users feel, VSM shows where time and effort go across the organisation. It is especially strong for services where users wait for back-office work.
steps: Choose a value stream from the user's request to its fulfilment and walk it physically or virtually (gemba).
Record each step's process time, wait time, percentage complete and accurate, and staffing.
Map information flows and triggers (who tells whom what, how).
Draw the timeline and compute lead time, value-added time and flow efficiency.
Identify waste and design a future-state map with fewer handoffs and queues.
Create an implementation plan and measure the new lead time.
outputs: Current and future state maps, lead and process times, flow efficiency and improvement plan.
useWhen: Services where users wait on internal processes, or end-to-end experiences spanning multiple teams.
avoidWhen: Single-screen interaction design questions.
whyLost: Lean practice lives in operations and DevOps; service design developed parallel tools without time quantification.
whereToUse: Insurance claims, mortgage applications, IT service requests, hospital discharge, government permits.
example: A mortgage provider's VSM shows 21 days of lead time with only 3.5 hours of value-added work. Removing two handoffs and a re-keying step cuts lead time to 9 days, which users notice more than any interface change.
reference: Rother, M., & Shook, J. (1999). Learning to See. Lean Enterprise Institute.

name: Value-Focused Thinking
origin: Ralph Keeney, 1992 (Value-Focused Thinking: A Path to Creative Decisionmaking)
summary: Starts from stakeholders' fundamental objectives, structured into hierarchies and means-ends networks, to generate better alternatives before evaluating them.
description: Most decision making is alternative-focused: compare the options on the table. Keeney argued for starting from values: eliciting what stakeholders fundamentally care about, distinguishing fundamental objectives (ends) from means objectives, structuring them into hierarchies and means-ends networks, and then using them to create new alternatives and evaluation criteria. Elicitation uses probes such as wish lists, problems, consequences, goals and perspectives. For UX, VFT gives a rigorous way to articulate user and business objectives and to escape narrow option sets in design debates. It links naturally to laddering and means-end research.
steps: Interview stakeholders (and users) with Keeney's prompts: wish lists, problems, consequences, goals and different perspectives.
Convert statements into objectives (verb plus object, e.g. 'minimise time to resolve billing issues').
Separate fundamental from means objectives by asking 'why is that important?' and 'how could we achieve it?'.
Build a fundamental objectives hierarchy and a means-ends network.
Generate new alternatives aimed at each fundamental objective, including combinations.
Define attributes to measure each objective and use them in evaluation (e.g. MAUT).
outputs: Fundamental objectives hierarchy, means-ends network, new alternatives and evaluation attributes.
useWhen: Strategic product decisions, stuck design debates, or framing a research programme around what matters.
avoidWhen: Tactical decisions with clear objectives and a small option set.
whyLost: Decision analysis did not cross into design, which uses 'how might we' framing without value structuring.
whereToUse: Product strategy, service design, public sector digital services, AI policy design.
example: A city's parking app team, stuck between two designs, uses VFT and discovers a fundamental objective, 'reduce circling time', that neither design addresses; a new alternative, live space availability, emerges.
sources: Keeney, Value-Focused Thinking: A Path to Creative Decisionmaking (1992)
Keeney, Developing objectives and attributes (2007), in Edwards, Miles & von Winterfeldt (eds.), Advances in Decision Analysis
reference: Keeney, R. L. (1992). Value-Focused Thinking. Harvard University Press.

name: Value-Goal Statement
origin: Jon Kolko, Well-Designed (2014)
summary: A one-sentence statement of the human value a product delivers, contrasted with a named market leader: 'I help people ...; unlike [leader], our product ...'.
description: Kolko asks product managers to replace 'I am the product manager for X' with a statement of the value they help people achieve, framed against a market leader: 'I help people [human value]; unlike [leader], our product [distinctive approach]'. Value should speak to qualities like connection, respect or pride rather than features, because value is what differentiates. The statement is a working artefact for synthesising market signals from communities and technology trends, not a presentation piece, and it must be honest about current brand values, including unflattering ones. A companion prompt asks what someone can feel after using the product that they could not feel before, an emotional value proposition. The emotional facets the statement implies become differentiators for later design decisions.
steps: Gather market signals from user communities, competitors and technology trends.
Draft 'I help people [human value]; unlike [market leader], our product [distinctive approach]'.
Replace feature language with human value (connection, respect, pride, calm).
Check honesty against current brand values, including unflattering ones.
List the emotional facets the statement implies as differentiators.
Optionally restate it as an emotional value proposition: what can people feel after using it that they could not before?
outputs: A value-goal statement and a list of emotional facets for differentiation.
useWhen: Use it when a product team describes itself by features and needs a sharper, human-centred sense of what it is for relative to competitors.
avoidWhen: It is a framing exercise based on the team's reading of the market; check the value claimed with Laddering (Means-End Chain Analysis) or Jobs-to-be-Done Research, and test positioning with users before relying on it.
whyLost: Positioning statements are common in marketing, but this human-value, design-led variant from one book is rarely used by product teams.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, marketplaces, travel and hospitality, and repositioning mature products.
example: A meal-kit team writes 'I help people feel competent cooking for others; unlike the market leader, our kits teach one technique each week'. 'Competence' becomes a design criterion for recipe cards.
reference: Kolko, J. (2014). Well-Designed: How to Use Empathy to Create Products People Love. Boston, MA: Harvard Business Review Press, pp. 51-53.

name: Value-Sensitive Design
donor: Information ethics and philosophy of technology
origin: Batya Friedman, mid-1990s; tripartite methodology formalised with Peter Kahn and Alan Borning (2002)
summary: A tripartite methodology of conceptual, empirical and technical investigations that makes human values such as privacy, autonomy and fairness explicit design criteria.
description: Value-sensitive design treats values as properties that technologies support or undermine, and gives them the same methodological status as usability or performance. Its core is the tripartite investigation: conceptual work defines the values at stake and identifies direct and indirect stakeholders; empirical work measures how stakeholders understand and prioritise those values and where they conflict; technical work analyses how specific system properties support or hinder them. The investigations iterate. Distinctive tools include stakeholder analysis that includes people affected but not using the system, value scenarios, value dams and flows (thresholds where a design choice provokes strong objection), and envisioning cards for long-term effects. Rigour lies in naming value tensions explicitly, gathering stakeholder evidence rather than assuming it, and documenting the trade-offs a design resolves.
steps: Identify direct stakeholders (users) and indirect stakeholders (people affected by the system without using it).
Conduct a conceptual investigation: define each relevant value (for example privacy, autonomy, fairness, trust) and how it could be supported or harmed.
Run empirical investigations, such as interviews, value-scenario surveys or value dams and flows analysis, to learn how each stakeholder group weighs those values and where they conflict.
Conduct a technical investigation mapping specific features, defaults and data flows to the values they support or undermine.
Document value tensions explicitly and generate design alternatives that resolve or balance them.
Iterate the three investigations as the design evolves and record the value rationale for each key decision.
outputs: Stakeholder map including indirect stakeholders, value definitions, value tension register, value scenarios and design rationale linking features to values.
useWhen: Designing systems with ethical stakes: data collection, AI decision-making, surveillance, health, children's products or civic technology, especially where indirect stakeholders are affected.
avoidWhen: For narrow usability problems with no meaningful value conflict, or when the team has no authority to change data practices; then use a lighter ethics checklist and escalate.
whyLost: Latent: Academic origin; growing relevance for AI/ethics design; not yet mainstream.
whereToUse: AI product design; public sector technology; health and finance products.
example: A workplace analytics vendor applies VSD and identifies employees as indirect stakeholders of a manager dashboard. A value dams and flows survey shows individual-level keystroke metrics trigger strong objection, so the team ships only team-level aggregates with a minimum group size of eight.
sources: Value Sensitive Design: Shaping Technology with Moral Imagination (Batya Friedman & David Hendry)
reference: Friedman B & Hendry DG (2019) Value Sensitive Design: Shaping Technology with Moral Imagination. MIT Press

name: Values-Based Concept Assessment
origin: Design research practice, described by Martin and Hanington
summary: Participants rank three to five research-derived values, then place design concepts along a tape spectrum for each top value while thinking aloud, revealing why concepts appeal.
description: Rather than asking which concept people prefer, this method asks how concepts perform on values that matter to them. The team derives three to five values from prior research, such as feeling confident or staying in control. Participants rank and explain the values, which itself reveals priorities. For each top value a tape line is laid on a table or floor from most to least, and participants place concept cards along it while thinking aloud. Finally concepts are revisited without the values to discuss overall preference. The method deliberately avoids quantifying; its output is the reasoning behind placements, which shows which value each concept serves or threatens. Samples are small and the values are researcher-defined, so it is best for directional choices.
steps: Derive three to five values from prior research.
Have participants rank the values and explain their ranking.
For each top value, lay a tape spectrum from most to least.
Have participants place concept cards along the spectrum while thinking aloud.
Repeat for the other top values.
Revisit the concepts without values to discuss overall preference, then synthesise reasons by value.
outputs: Concept placements per value and participants' explanations, showing which values each concept supports or undermines.
useWhen: Choosing among early concepts in discovery or definition, when emotional and value fit matters as much as function.
avoidWhen: Avoid when values have not been grounded in research or when quantitative ranking is needed; use Q Methodology or Card-Based Value Elicitation.
whyLost: It is a design-research studio technique that never spread to mainstream concept testing, which favours surveys and preference tests.
whereToUse: Financial wellbeing, health and care products, AI assistants where trust and control matter.
example: Participants place four digital-wallet concepts along 'makes me feel confident'. A spending-limit concept sits at the top, while an auto-invest concept is placed lowest because it feels out of control.
reference: Martin, B. and Hanington, B. (2019). Universal Methods of Design, Expanded and Revised. Rockport Publishers, Method 121.

name: Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter
origin: Peter van Westendorp, 1976 (ESOMAR Congress)
summary: Four price perception questions (too cheap, cheap, expensive, too expensive) whose cumulative curves define an acceptable price range and indifference points.
description: Respondents state the price at which a product would be so cheap they would doubt its quality, a bargain, getting expensive, and too expensive to consider. Plotting cumulative distributions (reversing two) yields intersections: the point of marginal cheapness, point of marginal expensiveness, optimal price point and indifference price point, defining an acceptable range. Newton, Miller and Smith's (1993) extension adds purchase likelihood at the cheap and expensive prices to estimate trial and revenue. PSM is quick and useful early, but stated price perceptions are hypothetical; rigorous use includes context (competitor prices, value description), validity checks for illogical answers and triangulation with behavioural methods.
steps: Describe the product and its value concretely, including relevant alternatives.
Ask the four price questions in a fixed order with open numeric responses.
Remove illogical response patterns (e.g. too cheap above cheap) and outliers.
Plot the cumulative curves and compute the four intersection points and acceptable range.
Optionally add the Newton-Miller-Smith purchase likelihood questions to estimate demand and revenue curves.
Triangulate with conjoint, Gabor-Granger or BDM before setting prices.
outputs: Acceptable price range, optimal and indifference price points by segment, and optional demand estimates.
useWhen: Early-stage pricing for new products or features where no market reference exists.
avoidWhen: Final price setting or competitive categories with clear reference prices; use conjoint or experiments.
whyLost: Pricing is owned by marketing and finance, and UX research rarely engages with willingness to pay.
whereToUse: SaaS tier pricing, new subscription features, AI add-on pricing, consumer hardware.
example: Before launching an AI meeting summary add-on, a PSM survey of 800 users yields an acceptable range of $6-14 per month, with indifference at $9, informing a conjoint study around those levels.
sources: van Westendorp, NSS Price Sensitivity Meter (PSM): A new approach to study consumer perception of prices (1976), ESOMAR Congress
Newton, Miller & Smith, A market acceptance extension to traditional price sensitivity measurement (1993), AMA ART Forum
reference: van Westendorp, P. H. (1976). ESOMAR Congress Proceedings.

name: Variable-by-Variable Matrix
origin: Louis and Miles, 1990; described by Miles and Huberman, 1994
summary: Cross the ordered indicators of two main variables and enter case codes in the cells, to see which kinds of cases combine which indicators.
description: Used when a few major variables underlie many specific phenomena and you want to see how they connect without losing the specific indicators. Each variable's indicators are defined and ordered, with colleagues adjudicating the order: in the source example problem types ran from most to least tractable as columns, and 23 coping strategies were sorted into nine clusters ordered from shallow to deep as rows. Cases are ordered on an outcome and given codes. Cells hold the codes of cases where that pairing was observed, with '?' when the link is uncertain, and a case may appear several times. Pairs are entered in a cross-case analysis meeting from displays, field notes and researcher judgement, with differences settled by discussion. In the example, shallow coping appeared mostly in less successful schools and deep coping mostly in successful ones. The matrix is only as good as the indicator orderings.
steps: Define the indicators of each variable and order them, with colleague feedback.
Order the cases on an outcome and give them codes (for example by level of success).
Make one variable's indicators the rows and the other's the columns.
Enter case codes in the cells for each observed pairing, adding '?' where the link is uncertain; allow several entries per case.
Read where each group of cases falls in the matrix.
Check the patterns against case data before drawing conclusions.
outputs: A matrix of case codes showing which indicator combinations occur in which kinds of cases.
useWhen: Multi-case qualitative studies where you want to relate two families of observations, such as problems encountered and workarounds used, to an outcome.
avoidWhen: Indicators cannot be defensibly ordered, or there are too few cases to show a pattern; use a simpler checklist or effects matrix.
whyLost: Miles and Huberman's many matrix types stayed in academic qualitative research; UX synthesis rarely uses ordered indicator matrices with case codes.
whereToUse: Support and incident research, enterprise implementation studies, and comparisons of team practices across accounts.
example: For eight customer implementations, the team crosses integration problems (ordered by tractability) with responses (from workaround to vendor escalation to process redesign). Successful accounts cluster in redesign responses for hard problems, which reshapes the onboarding playbook.
sources: Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B. and Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

name: Variational Autoencoder for Behavioural Patterns
origin: Kingma & Welling, 2014
summary: Learns a compact latent space of user behaviour from session data, enabling archetype interpolation, synthetic sequences for rare segments and counterfactual exploration.
description: VAEs learn a low-dimensional latent representation of high-dimensional data, then use that latent space to generate new samples. Applied to UX: fit a VAE to behavioral session data. The latent space represents 'behavioral styles'. New points in the latent space generate synthetic but realistic behavioral sequences, enabling: (1) behavioral archetype interpolation, (2) data augmentation for rare user types, (3) counterfactual behavioral analysis.
steps: Represent each session as a fixed-length feature vector (action counts, timing statistics, error rates, navigation patterns).
Train a VAE with encoder: session → z (latent), decoder: z → session.
Visualize latent space using UMAP.
Identify distinct behavioral clusters in latent space.
Generate synthetic sessions at cluster boundaries to understand behavioral transitions.
Use for: identifying underrepresented user types, generating training data for classifiers.
outputs: A trained encoder/decoder, a low-dimensional latent map of sessions, synthetic behavioural sequences, latent-space clusters and interpolations between archetypes.
useWhen: Large event-log datasets where you want to explore the continuum of behavioural styles, augment rare user types for analysis, or probe 'what if this user behaved like that one'.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small data (under tens of thousands of sessions), when interpretability for stakeholders is paramount, or when simple clustering or sequence mining answers the question; synthetic data must never stand in for real users in evaluation.
whyLost: Deep generative modelling sits in ML engineering teams, far from UX research; UX lacks the data infrastructure and skills, and outputs are hard to explain.
whereToUse: Behavioral research with small samples of rare user types, counterfactual analysis, behavioral simulation for design evaluation.
example: An e-commerce platform encodes 2 million browsing sessions; the latent space separates 'deliberate comparers' from 'impulse finishers', and decoding points between them shows which navigation steps distinguish the two, informing a comparison-tool redesign.
sources: Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
reference: Kingma DP & Welling M (2014) Auto-encoding variational Bayes. ICLR 2014

name: Verbal Protocol Analysis
origin: Newell & Simon, 1972; Ericsson & Simon, 1980/1984
summary: Rigorous coding of think-aloud transcripts with a theory-derived scheme to identify cognitive operations, strategies and mental models, with reliability checks.
description: Verbal protocol analysis treats think-aloud transcripts as data about cognitive processes. Transcripts are segmented into units, typically one idea or utterance, and each unit is coded with a scheme derived from a cognitive model of the task, for example goal setting, information retrieval, hypothesis generation, evaluation or error recovery. Coded sequences reveal strategies, the order of operations, where knowledge is missing and how mental models guide action. This is far more than extracting quotes for themes. Rigour comes from a coding scheme defined before analysis and grounded in theory, independent double coding with inter-rater agreement (for example Cohen's kappa of 0.7 or higher), and analysis of frequencies and transitions between codes, often comparing groups such as novices and experts.
steps: Collect concurrent think-aloud data on representative tasks following Ericsson and Simon's instructions.
Transcribe verbatim and segment transcripts into utterance-level units.
Develop a coding scheme from a cognitive model of the task and pilot it on one transcript.
Have two coders independently code at least 20 percent of the data and compute inter-rater agreement, refining the scheme until kappa is at least 0.7.
Code the full dataset.
Analyse code frequencies, sequences and transitions, comparing participant groups.
Interpret findings in terms of strategies, knowledge gaps and mental models.
outputs: Coded transcripts, reliability statistics, frequency and transition analyses, and models of user strategies and knowledge gaps.
useWhen: When understanding cognitive strategies or mental model structure is critical, such as expert tools, complex decisions or expert-novice comparisons.
avoidWhen: Avoid for routine usability findings or fast cycles; use usability testing with light note-taking. Requires training in coding and statistics.
whyLost: Think-aloud survived as a usability ritual while the theory and coding procedures were dropped because they were slow and taught only in psychology.
whereToUse: Research papers; deep cognitive analysis; when understanding mental model structure is critical.
example: An investment platform codes think-aloud sessions of novice and experienced traders placing limit orders. Novices show long loops of 'checking meaning' codes around order types, while experts move straight from goal to action, guiding inline explanations.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Ericsson KA & Simon HA (1984; rev. 1993) Protocol Analysis: Verbal Reports as Data. MIT Press
Boren T & Ramey J (2000) Thinking aloud: reconciling theory and practice. IEEE Trans Prof Comm
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods (Nichols & Edlund, 2023)
Protocol Analysis: Verbal Reports as Data (Ericsson & Simon)
Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research in Psychology (Willig & Stainton Rogers, 2008)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
reference: Ericsson, K. A. & Simon, H. A. (1993). Protocol Analysis: Verbal Reports as Data (rev. ed.). MIT Press.

name: Version control (Git) for research analysis
origin: Git created by Linus Torvalds, 2005; version control in science advocated by Ram (2013)
summary: Tracking every change to analysis code, instruments and documentation as dated, attributed commits so any reported result can be traced to the exact code that produced it.
description: Version control records the full history of a project as commits, each with an author, timestamp and message. For research this provides an audit trail: which version of the cleaning script produced the figure in last quarter's deck, when an exclusion rule changed, and who changed it. Branches allow alternative analyses to be explored without destroying the main line, and tags mark the exact state used for a report. Rigour comes from small, well-described commits, tagging every delivered result, keeping data and secrets out of the repository, and reviewing changes before they reach reported outputs. It also makes analytic flexibility visible, which is a defence against undisclosed forking paths.
steps: Initialise a repository at project creation with a .gitignore that excludes data, credentials and large media.
Commit small, coherent changes with messages that state what changed and why (e.g. 'Exclude speeders under 1/3 median duration').
Commit pre-registered hypotheses and analysis plans before data collection so the timestamp is verifiable.
Explore alternative analyses on branches and merge only the analysis you will report, noting rejected alternatives.
Tag the commit used for every delivered report (e.g. v2026-q1-report) and cite the tag in the report appendix.
Use pull requests or peer review for changes to shared cleaning or scoring code.
outputs: A complete, attributable history of the analysis, tagged report states and a reviewable record of analytic decisions.
useWhen: Any analysis in code, especially long-running tracking studies, team-owned pipelines and work that will be audited or published.
avoidWhen: Not suitable for storing participant data, recordings or transcripts; use access-controlled storage with provenance logging instead.
whyLost: UX research historically lived in documents and slide decks with no code to version, and Git's learning curve deterred researchers without engineering backgrounds.
whereToUse: Research operations, quant UX, academic-industry collaborations, regulated health and finance research and AI-assisted analysis pipelines.
example: A SaaS team reports a drop in NPS. Git history shows the drop coincides with a commit that changed the exclusion rule for incomplete responses, and reverting it reveals no real change in sentiment.
sources: Ram, K. (2013) Git can facilitate greater reproducibility and increased transparency in science. Source Code for Biology and Medicine
Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Ram, K. (2013) Git can facilitate greater reproducibility and increased transparency in science. Source Code for Biology and Medicine 8(7)

name: Viable System Model Diagnosis
origin: Stafford Beer, 1972-1985 (Brain of the Firm, The Heart of Enterprise, Diagnosing the System for Organizations)
summary: Diagnoses whether an organisation or service has the five necessary systems (operations, coordination, control, intelligence, policy) to remain viable and adapt.
description: Beer's Viable System Model, based on Ashby's law of requisite variety, states that any viable system contains five subsystems: System 1 (operational units), System 2 (coordination to dampen oscillation), System 3 (control and resource allocation, with System 3* audit), System 4 (intelligence about the environment and future) and System 5 (identity and policy). These recur recursively at every level. Diagnosis maps an organisation onto the model and finds missing or weak systems and inadequate variety in communication channels. For research and design operations, VSM reveals why insights fail to reach decisions (weak System 4-3 links) or why teams oscillate (missing System 2).
steps: Define the system in focus and its purpose, and identify recursion levels.
Identify the operational units (System 1) and their environments.
Map existing mechanisms for coordination, control, audit, intelligence and policy.
Assess variety: can each channel handle the variety it must absorb or amplify (Ashby's law)?
Identify missing, weak or overloaded systems and pathologies (e.g. System 3 micromanaging System 1).
Design structural changes and information channels, and re-assess.
outputs: A VSM diagram of the organisation, diagnosed pathologies and structural recommendations.
useWhen: Diagnosing research operations, design systems governance, product organisations or complex service ecosystems.
avoidWhen: Simple teams without structural issues, or user-facing interaction design questions.
whyLost: Management cybernetics fell out of fashion after the 1970s (despite Project Cybersyn), and its terminology is dense.
whereToUse: Research operations design, insight-to-decision pipelines, multi-team platform governance, public digital services.
example: A company's research findings rarely shape roadmaps. VSM diagnosis shows research acts as System 4 but has no channel into System 3 resource allocation; a quarterly research-to-portfolio review is introduced.
sources: Beer, Brain of the Firm (2nd ed., 1981)
Beer, Diagnosing the System for Organizations (1985)
Espejo & Harnden (eds.), The Viable System Model (1989)
reference: Beer, S. (1985). Diagnosing the System for Organizations. Wiley.

name: Video Confessional Booth
donor: Reality television testimonials, adapted by a learning-games studio
origin: NMSU Learning Games Lab (Chamberlin and colleagues), described in Chapter 3
summary: A small private room with a self-operated camera where participants record their answers to a written question, alone and in their own time.
description: The video closet was inspired by the testimonials in reality television shows. A small closet holds a mounted camera and a whiteboard with one specific question written on it. The participant enters alone, thinks about the question, and starts and stops the recording with a remote control when ready. Because no researcher is present, it reduces the social pressure that shapes answers in interviews and group discussions, and it gives quieter or introverted participants a way to say things they would not say in front of peers. The Learning Games Lab found it works best in combination with other methods: participants gave richer answers after a group discussion or after writing their thoughts in a blog, because they had already organised their ideas. Videos are rarely transcribed. Instead they are used to clarify observers' notes and, above all, as vivid evidence for developers and clients, shared through an internal site. Regular use, even when nothing is being tested, helps participants become comfortable on camera. For UX teams it is a cheap way to collect candid, quotable reflections in a lab or event setting.
steps: Set up a small, quiet space with a fixed camera, a microphone and a remote or button the participant controls.
Write one clear, specific question on a board in view of the camera.
Prime participants first with another activity, such as play, a group discussion or a short written reflection.
Let each participant enter alone, think, and record their answer when ready, as many takes as they like.
Collect the clips, tag them by question, product version and participant code, and restrict access to the research and development team.
Review clips to clarify observations and select excerpts to show developers or clients.
outputs: Short, candid video answers to targeted questions, used as qualitative evidence and as clips for stakeholder communication.
useWhen: Participants may be shy in groups, you want unmoderated reflection after hands-on sessions, or you need compelling clips for stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Participants are uncomfortable being filmed, consent for video cannot be obtained, or you need probing follow-up questions.
whyLost: Most UX teams rely on moderated interviews or remote video tools and seldom build a dedicated private recording space.
whereToUse: Games and edtech labs, youth panels, on-site research events, conference or retail intercept research.
example: After a group discussion about a new maths game, each 12-year-old tester goes into the closet and answers 'What would make you want to keep playing this game?'; the developers watch several clips that all mention the confusing fail condition.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Chamberlin, B., Trespalacios, J. H., Muise, A. S. and Garza, M. C. (2016). User testing in the Learning Games Lab: getting valuable feedback through frequent formative evaluation. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 3. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Video Highlight Reels
origin: Common usability practice; described by Nunnally and Farkas (2017), Marsh (2018, 2022), Greever (2015)
summary: Edit short, labelled clips of research sessions into themed reels of about five minutes so stakeholders who did not observe see and hear users directly.
description: A highlight reel carries users' own voices and behaviour to people who did not attend sessions, which a written report cannot. Efficient production starts during sessions: observers note timestamps of striking moments so clips can be found from notes rather than by rewatching everything. Clips are kept as short as possible but with enough context, by editing or a title card naming the theme; several participants are shown per issue to show it is not a one-off; speakers are labelled by participant number; and only the most important points get video. Clips can be tagged by feature, severity and user type to build a library from which reels per audience are assembled. Reels are paired with counts or the wider data, and consent must cover internal sharing.
steps: Agree which research goals or themes the reel must serve and who will watch it.
Have observers note timestamps of notable moments during each session.
Use the notes to locate candidate clips; select those that illustrate each theme across several participants, not only the most dramatic.
Trim each clip to the shortest length that keeps context, add a title card and label participants by number.
Tag clips (feature, severity, user type) and assemble reels of about five minutes or less per theme or audience.
Check consent covers internal sharing, anonymise where possible, and present reels alongside counts and the report.
Where possible, ask decision makers who did not observe to watch two or three full sessions as well.
outputs: Short themed reels or montages, a tagged clip library, and slides pairing quotes with clips.
useWhen: Communicating usability or interview findings to stakeholders who did not observe, especially when findings are contested.
avoidWhen: Avoid using reels as evidence of frequency; a vivid participant can be over-represented. Do not share clips without consent covering that use.
whyLost: It survived because recording tools made clipping cheap and reels persuade stakeholders effectively.
whereToUse: Usability test readouts, sprint reviews, executive briefings, research repositories.
example: A three-minute reel shows five of eight participants failing to find the delivery-date field at checkout. After seeing it, the product director funds the fix that sprint.
sources: User Research: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Products and Services (Marsh, 2018)
reference: Nunnally, B. and Farkas, D. (2017). UX Research: Practical Techniques for Designing Better Products. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Video Prototyping
origin: Common interaction design practice; examples from Superflux (Anab Jain) and Cooper, in Rowland et al. (2015)
summary: Quick, rough videos that fake a product in use, through role play, props, stop-motion or paper-prototype montage, to show and test a concept before it can be built.
description: A video prototype is a short, low-budget film, shot on a phone with simple editing, that shows a concept in action. It is especially valuable for interactions that static images cannot convey: gesture, movement, timing, sound and multisensory or connected-device behaviour. The technology is faked: actors role-play with props, objects are animated in stop-motion, or paper prototypes and photos are montaged, with narration and titles to explain what is happening. Video prototypes build on storyboards and visualisations and let teams decide early whether an audience sees value in an idea. Their danger is persuasiveness: a polished video implies working technology and shows only best cases, so keeping deliberately sketchy elements signals that the concept is open to change.
steps: Select the key moments to show, from storyboards or concept visualisations.
Write a short script or storyboard of 30 seconds to 3 minutes.
Choose an aesthetic and keep some elements deliberately rough.
Fake the technology with live role play and props, stop-motion animation, or a montage of paper prototypes and photos.
Add narration and titles; edit quickly on a phone or laptop.
Show the video to stakeholders or target users and capture their reactions and questions.
outputs: Short concept videos and recorded audience reactions.
useWhen: Use it for early concepts involving movement, timing, physical or multi-device interaction, or services that unfold over time, when building even a crude prototype is costly.
avoidWhen: Viewers judge a story, not an experience; once a direction is chosen, use Experience Prototyping, Wizard of Oz Prototyping or Prototype Testing. Avoid polished videos when you need honest critique.
whyLost: It survived because phones made it trivial, and it remains the cheapest way to show behaviour over time.
whereToUse: IoT and smart home, automotive interfaces, wearables, AR and VR, AI agent behaviour, and service concepts.
example: A smart-thermostat team films a phone-propped cardboard prototype and a hidden assistant changing the display. Viewers grasp the energy-saving idea but ask who is in control, so manual override becomes a test focus.
reference: Rowland, C., Goodman, E., Charlier, M., Light, A. and Lui, A. (2015). Designing Connected Products: UX for the Consumer Internet of Things. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 588-590.

name: Video-Based Emotion Elicitation Task
aka: Video-based emotion elicitation task with post-clip affect ratings
origin: Klimecki, Leiberg, Lamm and Singer (2012); Saron and colleagues, Shamatha Project
summary: Show short clips in contrasting emotional categories and collect affect and empathy ratings after each, optionally with facial video or brain imaging, to measure emotional responses and their change.
description: A standardised set of short clips, for example documentary footage of people suffering versus everyday scenes, is shown and after each clip participants rate positive affect, negative affect and empathy, while brain activity or facial video may be recorded. Repeating the task before and after an intervention measures change: empathy training raised negative affect even to everyday clips, while compassion training raised positive affect without lowering negative affect. A variant films faces unobtrusively during intense clips, then has participants report felt emotions through cued recall using a visual storyboard of the clip, with facial video coded by FACS. Clips must be matched across sessions, and cued recall remains retrospective. For UX, the task is a template for measuring how content, or a product intervention, shifts emotional responses in a controlled, repeatable way.
steps: Select or edit short clips in contrasting categories (high versus low emotion) and match sets for repeat sessions.
Present each clip, optionally recording facial video or neural data.
Immediately after each clip, collect ratings of positive affect, negative affect and empathy, or run storyboard-cued recall of felt emotions.
Collect brief qualitative descriptions of the experience.
Repeat at each assessment point and compare change between intervention and control groups.
Relate ratings to facial or physiological data where recorded.
outputs: Per-clip affect profiles, change scores between sessions and groups, and links between ratings and facial or neural data.
useWhen: You need a repeatable emotional baseline or want to measure whether a product intervention (wellbeing app, training, content) changes emotional responses over time.
avoidWhen: You need emotional responses to your own product in use; measure in context with experience sampling or in-session ratings instead.
whyLost: It is a research-grade paradigm from affective and contemplative science, where outcomes are psychological change rather than product decisions.
whereToUse: Wellbeing and mental health apps, empathy and compassion training, content moderation wellbeing, and media and advertising tests.
example: A content moderation vendor runs a clip rating task with moderators before and after an eight-week resilience programme in its tool. Negative affect to distressing clips falls in the programme group but not in controls, supporting rollout.
sources: Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Klimecki, O. M., Leiberg, S., Lamm, C., & Singer, T. (2013). Functional neural plasticity and associated changes in positive affect after compassion training. Cerebral Cortex, 23(7), 1552-1561.

name: Video-Based HRI Studies
origin: University of Hertfordshire HRI group (Woods et al. 2006 onwards)
summary: Show participants filmed scenarios of a robot interacting with people and collect their reactions, instead of running costly live trials.
description: Live human-robot trials are expensive, slow and risky. In video-based HRI the team scripts and films a robot performing a scenario with people, often using Wizard of Oz control, and shows the videos to groups of participants, collecting reactions through questionnaires. Comparisons found live and video trials gave comparable results where a robot approached a person, but those scenarios involved little dynamic coordination. The more contingent and coordinated the interaction, the less video simulates live experience, so validity depends on the scenario. The method trades fidelity for scale and control: many viewers, identical stimuli and systematic variation of behaviours such as approach direction or speed.
steps: Script scenarios that vary the robot behaviour of interest, such as approach direction or speed.
Film the robot performing each scenario with people, using Wizard of Oz control if needed.
Show the videos to groups of participants in a controlled order.
Collect responses with questionnaires and optional discussion.
Compare responses across behaviour variants.
Validate key findings with live trials, especially for highly interactive behaviours.
outputs: Attitudes and preferences about robot behaviours from many viewers at low cost.
useWhen: Early exploration of robot or embodied-agent behaviours with low interaction contingency, when live trials are impractical.
avoidWhen: Avoid for tightly coordinated, contingent interaction; use live trials or Wizard of Oz Prototyping in person.
whyLost: It is established within HRI research but rarely used in UX outside robotics.
whereToUse: Service and delivery robots, autonomous vehicles' external signals, embodied AI assistants, video prototypes of physical products.
example: A delivery-robot company films the robot passing pedestrians at three speeds and distances. Online viewers rate the closest pass as threatening, informing default clearance before live pilots.
reference: Dautenhahn, K. (2013). Human-Robot Interaction. In The Encyclopedia of Human-Computer Interaction, 2nd ed., ch. 38

name: Video-Reflexive Ethnography
origin: Rick Iedema, Katherine Carroll and colleagues, 2000s (Visualising Health Care Practice Improvement, 2013)
summary: Records participants' real practice on video and plays selected clips back to them, individually or in groups, to surface tacit knowledge and collectively reflect on how practice could change.
description: Video-reflexive ethnography (Iedema, Carroll, Collier) involves collecting video recordings of participants in their natural practice, then showing those recordings back to participants or groups to stimulate discussion and collaborative analysis. It is particularly powerful for: accessing tacit, embodied, and procedural knowledge that participants cannot easily describe verbally; stimulating collective reflection and learning in workplace settings; and revealing what is 'seen but unnoticed' in practice.
steps: Video collection phase: Record participants in their natural practice with their knowledge and consent. Focus camera on the work activity rather than faces where possible — this shifts focus from person to practice.

Clip selection: From the recordings, select 3–6 clips of 1–3 minutes each. Select clips that illustrate: (a) typical practices, (b) moments of complexity or adaptation, (c) moments you want participants to reflect on.

Reflexive session: Play clips to participants (individually or in groups). Your role: facilitate observation, not evaluation. Opening prompt: 'What do you notice when you watch this?' Not: 'What did you do well or badly?'
Capture participant observations: What do participants see in the video that they weren't aware of during the activity? These moments of 'I didn't realise I was doing that' are your primary data.
Group reflexive sessions: Playing clips to groups generates collective reflection — participants compare practices, debate why things happened as they did, and negotiate shared understandings.
outputs: Practice video, selected clips with rationale, recorded reflexive discussions, participant-identified insights and improvement ideas, and documentation of tacit routines.
useWhen: Studying skilled or collaborative practice where people cannot describe what they do, and when you want practitioners to own the insights and change, as in clinical teams or operations.
avoidWhen: Consent to filming is not feasible or the setting is highly sensitive; use observation with field notes. For individual consumer tasks, a usability test with retrospective review is lighter.
whyLost: It developed in hospital quality improvement, and its participatory, change-oriented framing and filming logistics made it rare in commercial UX.
whereToUse: Clinical and care workflows, operations centres, retail and hospitality service, manufacturing, and teams adopting new tools or AI assistance.
example: A hospital pharmacy team watches clips of its own medication rounds. Nurses notice they repeatedly rescan wristbands because the scanner beep is inaudible, a problem none had raised in interviews, and the device team changes the feedback.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
reference: Iedema, R., Mesman, J. & Carroll, K. (2013). Visualising Health Care Practice Improvement: Innovation from Within. Radcliffe.

name: View-Like-Comment-Post (VLCP) Engagement Framework
origin: Aldous, An and Jansen (2019), ICWSM
summary: Group engagement metrics from several platforms into four levels, from private viewing to public posting, and model content factors separately at each level.
description: The VLCP framework treats engagement as a set of levels that differ in how publicly a person expresses interest: view (most private), like, comment, and post or share (most public). Because public interactions spread through electronic word of mouth, they matter more to content producers. Each platform's metrics are mapped onto the four levels so that platforms become comparable, and each level is analysed as its own outcome. Content factors such as topic, sentiment, emotion and style (question marks, exclamation marks, hashtag counts) are coded per post and modelled against each level, for example with logistic regression. The original study covered 53 news organisations across five platforms and showed that what drives engagement differs between levels and platforms.
steps: Collect posts and their interaction counts through platform APIs.
Map each platform's metrics onto the four levels: view, like, comment, post or share.
Code each post for content factors such as topic, sentiment, emotion and stylistic features.
Model each engagement level separately against the content factors, for example with logistic regression.
Compare effects across levels and across platforms.
Feed the findings into content planning and confirm promising factors with A/B tests.
outputs: Per-level engagement profiles by platform and estimates of how content factors affect each level.
useWhen: Analysing social or in-product content engagement across channels, where a single engagement number hides different kinds of response.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating platform-reported counts as precise measures; their error is unknown. Findings rarely transfer between platforms or audiences, so do not generalise without replication.
whyLost: It sits in social computing and marketing analytics research and has not been adopted as a UX engagement model.
whereToUse: Content design, community features, news and media products, creator tools, and in-app social features with view, react, comment and share actions.
example: A recipe app maps views, saves, comments and shares onto the four levels and finds that question-style titles raise comments but not shares. The content team tests title styles separately for each goal.
sources: Understanding Audiences via Analytics (Jansen et al., 2024)
reference: Aldous, K. K., An, J. and Jansen, B. J. (2019), ICWSM, as cited in Jansen, B. J. et al. (2024). Understanding Audiences, Customers, and Users via Analytics. Springer.

name: Vigilance and continuous performance tasks
donor: Human factors; attention research; cognitive psychology
origin: Mackworth (1948); adaptive-threshold CPT by MacLean, Saron and colleagues (2010)
summary: Measure how detection of rare, unpredictable targets declines over a long, monotonous watch, separating lost sensitivity from a more cautious response criterion.
description: Mackworth's clock test showed a hand stepping regularly and occasionally making an unpredictable double step that observers had to report; detection fell markedly after about half an hour. Signal detection analysis shows much of the decline is a criterion shift: observers become less willing to risk false alarms and so miss more signals. Expectations about where targets appear strongly affect efficiency, training helps a little, and only breaks counteract fatigue. A modern adaptive version flashes a line every two seconds, 10 per cent short targets, and calibrates line length for 10 to 15 minutes until each person reaches about 75 per cent accuracy, then runs 32 minutes without a break; a response-inhibition variant asks people to withhold responses to rare targets. Accuracy is analysed per time block.
steps: Choose the paradigm: a clock-like display with occasional double steps, or brief line stimuli at a fixed rate with about 10 per cent rare targets.
Optionally titrate target difficulty for 10 to 15 minutes until each participant reaches about 75 per cent accuracy.
Run a long, unbroken watch period (30 minutes or more; 32 minutes in the adaptive version) with responses to targets, or withholding for the inhibition variant.
Record hits, misses and false alarms by time block (for example eight four-minute blocks).
Analyse the decrement as signal detection sensitivity and criterion per block.
Compare conditions such as interface designs, alert formats, break schedules or automation levels.
outputs: Hit, miss and false-alarm rates per block, vigilance decrement curves, and sensitivity and criterion estimates.
useWhen: Users must monitor for rare events over long periods, as in security screening, monitoring dashboards or supervising automation, and you need to compare designs or schedules.
avoidWhen: Avoid for short, active tasks; use standard usability measures. Decrements may reflect criterion shifts rather than lost sensitivity, and improvements can reflect perceptual sharpening rather than attention.
whyLost: It is a staple of human factors and attention research, but UX rarely runs long monitoring tasks or signal detection analysis.
whereToUse: Security and fraud review tools, network and site reliability dashboards, clinical monitoring, content moderation queues and human oversight of autonomous systems.
example: A content moderation team tests whether highlighting likely violations helps reviewers on long shifts. In a 40-minute simulated queue, highlighting keeps sensitivity steady but makes reviewers more lenient on unhighlighted items, a criterion shift the team corrects with randomised audits.
sources: Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Mackworth, N. H. (1948). The breakdown of vigilance during prolonged visual search. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 1, 6-21; MacLean, K. A. et al. (2010). Intensive meditation training improves perceptual discrimination and sustained attention. Psychological Science 21(6).

name: Vignette Method and Factorial Survey
origin: Peter H. Rossi, 1970s (factorial survey approach)
summary: Presents systematically varied short scenarios and asks for judgements, revealing which factors drive decisions and attributions without asking people to explain their own reasoning.
description: People are poor at reporting which factors drive their judgements, but they judge concrete scenarios easily. The factorial survey exploits this: the researcher defines the judgement of interest and a set of dimensions (for example price, social proof, data requested, brand), generates vignettes by crossing their levels, and has each participant rate a random subset of 10 to 20. Because dimensions vary independently, multilevel regression estimates the causal weight of each factor on the judgement, controlling for respondent effects. Fractional designs keep the vignette universe manageable while preserving key effects. A short qualitative follow-up explores reasoning. Rigour comes from orthogonal design, randomisation of vignettes and order, plausible combinations, and analysis that respects the nested data structure.
steps: Define the target judgment: What decision, evaluation, or attribution are you investigating?
Identify experimental dimensions: What scenario characteristics do you want to vary? Each dimension should have 2–4 levels.
Generate vignettes by factorial combination. Use fractional factorial design for large parameter spaces.
Randomised presentation: Each participant sees 10–20 vignettes randomly selected. Rate or respond to each.
Analysis: Multilevel regression with rating as outcome and vignette characteristics as predictors. Coefficients reveal which characteristics significantly influence judgments.
Qualitative follow-up: After the rating task, interview participants about their reasoning on selected vignettes.
outputs: A vignette universe and design matrix, ratings data, multilevel model estimates of each factor's effect, interaction effects, and qualitative accounts of reasoning.
useWhen: You want to know how users weigh factors in a judgement such as trust, fairness, willingness to share data or acceptability of an AI decision, especially where direct questions would produce socially desirable answers.
avoidWhen: You can observe real behaviour with a live A/B test, or the decision depends heavily on context a short vignette cannot convey. For product attribute trade-offs with prices, conjoint analysis may be a better fit.
whyLost: It sits between survey methodology and experimental design, needs design and multilevel modelling skills, and UX borrowed conjoint from market research instead.
whereToUse: AI fairness and explainability perception, trust and safety policy, privacy and consent decisions, pricing fairness, and content moderation judgements.
example: A lender varies AI loan-denial explanations across four dimensions (reason specificity, appeal option, human review mention, tone). Across 400 respondents, offering an appeal route raises perceived fairness more than specificity does, shaping the explanation design.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
Auspurg, K. & Hinz, T. (2015) Factorial Survey Experiments
Handbook of Child Psychology Vol 3 (Lerner & Lamb, 2015)
reference: Rossi, P. H. & Nock, S. L. (eds.) (1982). Measuring Social Judgments: The Factorial Survey Approach. Sage.

name: Viral Coefficient and Viral Cycle Time
origin: David Skok; codified in Croll and Yoskovitz, Lean Analytics (2013)
summary: Compute how many new users each user brings, invitation rate times acceptance rate, and how long one invitation cycle takes, to judge viral growth.
description: The viral coefficient is the invitation rate (invites sent divided by users) multiplied by the acceptance rate (sign-ups divided by invites). A value above 1 means each cohort recruits a larger one. Cycle time, the delay between a user joining and their invitees joining, often matters more: with the same coefficient, a two-day cycle yields about 20,000 users after 20 days while a one-day cycle yields over 20 million. Croll and Yoskovitz distinguish inherent virality (the product needs other users), artificial virality (incentivised invites) and word of mouth, which behave differently and should be measured separately. The viral loop is instrumented as a funnel so that each step (prompt, send, open, accept, activate) can be diagnosed.
steps: Define the viral loop and classify it as inherent, artificial or word-of-mouth.
Count users and invitations sent in a period and compute the invitation rate.
Count sign-ups from those invitations and compute the acceptance rate.
Multiply the two rates to get the viral coefficient.
Measure cycle time from a user's sign-up to their invitees' sign-ups.
Instrument each step of the loop as a funnel and track coefficient and cycle time by cohort.
outputs: Viral coefficient, cycle time and a funnel of the invitation loop by cohort.
useWhen: Products with sharing, invitation or collaboration features where growth depends on users recruiting users.
avoidWhen: Avoid extrapolating a coefficient: invitations saturate as friend groups overlap. For adoption dynamics over a whole population, use epidemic (SIR) models.
whyLost: It lives in growth teams and startup analytics rather than UX research, although invite flows are UX problems.
whereToUse: Collaboration tools, social and messaging apps, referral programmes in fintech, multiplayer games.
example: A shared-budget app finds 2,000 users send 5,000 invites with 10% acceptance, a coefficient of 0.25 and a nine-day cycle. Usability fixes to the invite screen target the acceptance step.
reference: Croll, A. and Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics: Use Data to Build a Better Startup Faster. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Virtual environments
origin: Python virtualenv (Ian Bicking, 2007); venv in the standard library (PEP 405, 2011); conda (Anaconda, 2012)
summary: Isolating each research project's interpreter and libraries so that analyses run with known package versions and do not break when other projects update.
description: A virtual environment is a self-contained interpreter plus library set scoped to one project. Without it, upgrading pandas or scikit-learn for one study can silently change results in another, for example by altering default parameters in factor analysis or clustering. The rigour comes from one environment per project, created from a declared specification file, and from never installing packages ad hoc into the base interpreter. conda additionally manages non-Python binaries such as ffmpeg or CUDA libraries, which matters for transcription and transformer models. Combined with a lockfile, an environment lets a colleague or reviewer recreate the exact computational instrument used for an analysis months later.
steps: Create one environment per project (python -m venv .venv or conda create -n project python=3.11) at project start.
Record every dependency in a specification file (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml or environment.yml) rather than installing ad hoc.
Pin exact versions for anything that affects results (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, factor_analyzer) once analysis begins.
Never install into the base or system interpreter; activate the project environment before every session.
Rebuild the environment from the specification file on a clean machine or container at least once before reporting results.
Register the environment as a named Jupyter kernel so notebooks cannot accidentally run under a different interpreter.
outputs: A per-project environment, a committed environment specification and a named kernel for notebooks.
useWhen: Every Python-based UX analysis, especially those using statistical or machine learning libraries whose defaults change between versions.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary for no-code analysis in SPSS or spreadsheets; there, document the software version and syntax instead.
whyLost: UX researchers rarely came from software backgrounds and analysis tools were GUI-based, so environment isolation never became part of UX training.
whereToUse: Quant UX teams, research operations, transcription and NLP pipelines with heavy binary dependencies, and long-running tracking studies.
example: A health app team reruns a 2024 SUS benchmark in 2026 and gets different factor loadings. Rebuilding the original pinned environment shows the difference came from a library default change, not from users.
sources: Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Python Software Foundation (2011) PEP 405: Python Virtual Environments

name: Visual aesthetics questionnaires (classical/expressive aesthetics and VisAWI)
aka: Four-facet visual aesthetics measure (Moshagen and Thielsch)
origin: Lavie and Tractinsky, 2004; Moshagen and Thielsch, 2010
summary: Validated questionnaires that measure perceived visual aesthetics of interfaces, either as classical and expressive dimensions or as four facets: simplicity, diversity, colourfulness and craftsmanship.
description: Lavie and Tractinsky identified two dimensions of perceived website aesthetics: classical (clean, clear, orderly, symmetrical) and expressive (creative, original, sophisticated), each correlating as expected with perceived usability, pleasure and service quality. Tractinsky's chapter credits the scales as HCI's first serious attempt to measure aesthetics apart from usability, while commentators note that classical aesthetics overlaps with usability and that the item 'aesthetic' is circular. Sutcliffe extended them with symbolic and pleasure scales and found the beauty-usability halo context-dependent; van Schaik and Ling found no relation to performance. Moshagen and Thielsch proposed four facets: simplicity, diversity, colourfulness and craftsmanship, published as the 18-item VisAWI. Simplicity and diversity correlate highly with classical and expressive aesthetics, and all four facets relate to overall appeal, which makes the facets more diagnostic for design decisions.
steps: Decide whether you need a two-dimensional overview (classical and expressive) or facet diagnosis (VisAWI).
Expose participants to the interface, either briefly for first impressions or after use, keeping exposure equal across designs.
Administer the chosen item sets verbatim on their original scales, in randomised order.
Compute dimension or facet scores and check internal consistency.
Compare designs or versions and relate scores to perceived usability, trust or behavioural outcomes.
Interpret facet differences (for example low craftsmanship) as concrete design leads.
outputs: Classical and expressive scores or four facet scores per design, with links to other outcomes.
useWhen: When visual design quality is a decision variable: comparing visual directions, checking a redesign, or separating aesthetic appeal from usability in an evaluation.
avoidWhen: Avoid using classical aesthetics as a proxy for usability or performance. For quick qualitative reads use Product Reaction Cards (Microsoft Desirability Toolkit); for very brief exposure use the 5-Second Test.
whyLost: They are established in academic HCI but practitioners judge visual design by preference tests and stakeholder taste rather than validated scales.
whereToUse: Landing pages and marketing sites, visual redesigns, design-system theming, e-commerce, fintech trust cues.
example: Two visual directions for an insurance site are shown to 200 participants with the VisAWI. Direction B wins on colourfulness but loses on craftsmanship, and comments point to inconsistent icon styles, which are fixed before launch.
reference: Lavie, T., & Tractinsky, N. (2004). Assessing dimensions of perceived visual aesthetics of web sites. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 60(3), 269-298; Moshagen, M., & Thielsch, M. T. (2010). Facets of visual aesthetics. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 68(10), 689-709.

name: Visual Layout and Web Design of Self-Administered Questionnaires
donor: Survey methodology, graphic design and Gestalt psychology
origin: Jenkins and Dillman (1995, 1997); Redline and Dillman on branching; Christian, Smyth and Dillman visual design experiments; carousel format from Roberts et al. (2013)
summary: Laying out paper or web questionnaires so words and graphics together lead every respondent through each item in the intended order, reducing nonresponse, branching errors and mode differences.
description: Questionnaires speak two languages, words and graphics. The method defines a navigational path for each page or screen and uses location, size, brightness, shape, regularity and a consistent figure/ground format to keep respondents on it, with stronger visual interruptions where they must branch. Dillman gives 28 construction principles for paper (question numbers, contrast between questions and answers, vertical answer lists, consistent box placement, even scale spacing) and 23 for web and e-mail (welcome screen, first question, cross-browser testing, restrained drop-downs, no forced responses, progress indicators). Experiments show arrows, spacing, subheadings, symbols and answer box sizes change what people answer, and that forced-choice yes/no items outperform check-all boxes. A variant for item batteries, the carousel, shows one item at a time with automatic advance under a fixed stem and scale, reducing straightlining relative to grids.
