steps: Choose a conventional format and define the order in which every word and symbol on each page or screen should be read.
Make question starts consistent and prominent, print questions more strongly than answer choices, and leave more space between questions than within them.
List answer choices vertically with boxes consistently on one side; space scale points evenly and keep scale direction constant throughout.
Place instructions exactly where needed inside the question, and for skips combine two or three devices (arrows, bold skip text, an '(If yes)' lead-in, indentation of screened items).

For web versions, open with a short welcome screen, make the first question easy and fully visible, test across screen sizes and browsers, label drop-downs, avoid forcing answers and show simple progress.
Replace check-all-that-apply with forced-choice yes/no items; for long batteries consider a carousel format with a visible position bar and back navigation.
Cognitively test the layout, and where possible compare item nonresponse or straightlining against an alternative version.
outputs: Page and screen layouts with lower item nonresponse, fewer branching errors, less straightlining and smaller mode differences.
useWhen: Designing survey instruments, especially mixed-mode or mobile web surveys, long batteries, or questionnaires with skip logic.
avoidWhen: Do not treat layout as a substitute for good wording; for question content use the question-writing principles. Some web advice in the source is dated (colour palettes, modems) and should be filtered. Carousel evidence rests on few studies.
whyLost: Survey platforms impose templates, so UX teams assume layout is solved; the experimental evidence on visual design stays within survey methodology journals.
whereToUse: Mobile in-product surveys, long B2B questionnaires, mixed web and paper public-sector surveys, research panels with grid-heavy batteries.
example: A health insurer's member survey shows high straightlining on a 12-item grid on phones. The researcher rebuilds it as a carousel with a fixed stem, converts a check-all list of channels into yes/no items, and compares non-differentiation against the grid on a split sample.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Dillman, D. A. (2007). Mail and Internet Surveys: The Tailored Design Method (2nd ed., 2007 update). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons.

name: Visual lineup test for association
aka: Visual test for association (lineup of scrambled scatterplots)
origin: Buja et al. (2009), Statistical inference for exploratory data analysis and model diagnostics; presented as a teaching device by Stine and Foster
summary: Hides the real chart among charts made from randomly re-paired data; if viewers can pick out the real one, the pattern is unlikely to be chance.
description: People readily see patterns in noise. The lineup protocol turns visual inspection into a test. The real scatterplot is placed among decoy plots in which the y values have been randomly shuffled against the x values, which destroys any association while keeping each variable's distribution. If the real plot can be singled out, the association is real; if it cannot, the pattern may be imagined. With 19 decoys and one independent viewer who did not see the data, a correct pick corresponds to a significance level of 1 in 20. Stine and Foster present it as the visual analogue of chi-square, which compares an observed table with one of no association. The same idea extends to any null model: residual plots, maps or time series simulated under the null. Once association is accepted, its direction, curvature, spread and outliers are described.
steps: Draw the chart of interest, such as the outcome against a predictor or a residual plot.
Make decoy charts by shuffling y against x, or by simulating from the null model; use 19 decoys for a 5% test (the book's teaching version uses three).
Arrange real and decoy charts in a grid, in random position and without labels.
Ask one or more viewers who have not seen the real chart to pick the one that looks most different.
If the real chart is picked, accept the pattern; with several viewers, compute the probability of that many correct picks by chance.
If accepted, describe direction, curvature, variation and outliers.
outputs: A judgement, and with enough decoys a p-value, on whether an apparent pattern differs from chance.
useWhen: Exploratory analysis of research or analytics data where stakeholders read patterns into scatterplots, heatmaps or residuals, and no formal test fits the visual claim.
avoidWhen: With few decoys, a chance pick is likely; when a standard test exists and answers the question, use it as well. Viewers who have already seen the real chart are not independent judges.
whyLost: Graphical inference is established in statistics and visualisation research but has not entered UX reporting practice.
whereToUse: Analytics reviews, survey cross-tabs and correlation plots, research readouts, teaching stakeholders about chance patterns, evaluating data visualisations.
example: A product manager sees a link between session length and NPS in a scatterplot of 300 users. The analyst builds a lineup of the real plot and 19 shuffled versions; three colleagues fail to pick it out, so the claimed relationship is dropped from the report.
sources: Statistics for Business: Decision Making and Analysis (Stine & Foster, 2018)
reference: Buja, A., Cook, D., Hofmann, H., Lawrence, M., Lee, E.-K., Swayne, D. F. and Wickham, H. (2009). Statistical inference for exploratory data analysis and model diagnostics. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 367, 4361-4383.

name: Visual Search Paradigm Testing
origin: Anne Treisman and Garry Gelade, 1980 (feature integration theory); Jeremy Wolfe's Guided Search (1994)
summary: Measures response time to find a target as a function of the number of distractors, revealing whether a design element pops out or requires serial search.
description: In a visual search experiment, participants find a target among distractors while set size varies. If response time does not increase with set size (slope near 0 ms per item), the target pops out through parallel feature processing; slopes of 20-40 ms per item on target-present trials suggest serial, effortful search. Target-absent trials show how long users take to give up. Applied to UX, these slopes quantify the findability of icons, badges, alerts and status markers under realistic clutter, and test whether a design element truly guides attention as intended. It is more diagnostic than eye-tracking heatmaps because it isolates the attentional mechanism.
steps: Define the target element and distractors from the real interface (e.g. an error badge among other badges).
Create displays at several set sizes (e.g. 4, 8, 16, 32 items), with target present on half the trials.
Run participants on many trials (e.g. 200+) with randomised positions, recording response time and accuracy.
Fit linear regressions of RT on set size for present and absent trials; compute slopes and intercepts.
Compare design variants: a good salient design shows near-flat slopes and low error rates.
Confirm in the full interface context with a smaller task-based test.
outputs: Search slopes and intercepts, error rates and a classification of elements as pop-out or serial-search.
useWhen: Designing alerts, status indicators, icons and badges that must be found quickly in cluttered displays.
avoidWhen: Questions of meaning, preference or navigation strategy; use semantic or usability methods.
whyLost: Experimental psychology paradigms are rarely adapted to product questions, and teams rely on saliency heuristics or heatmaps.
whereToUse: Dashboards, monitoring displays, map pins, notification badges, inventory grids.
example: A monitoring dashboard tests three error indicators. A red outline yields a 28 ms/item slope while a red fill plus motion yields 3 ms/item, so the latter is adopted for critical alerts.
sources: Treisman & Gelade, A feature-integration theory of attention (1980), Cognitive Psychology
Wolfe, Guided Search 2.0 (1994), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
Wolfe & Horowitz, Five factors that guide attention in visual search (2017), Nature Human Behaviour
Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Handbook of the Philosophy of Science (Thagard, 2007)
reference: Treisman, A. M., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

name: Visual world paradigm
aka: Eye movements during spoken language comprehension
Visual world paradigm and eye movements during listening
origin: Tanenhaus et al., 1995; Altmann and Kamide, 1999
summary: Record where people look in a scene while they hear speech, time-locked to word onsets, to measure moment-by-moment interpretation and anticipation of spoken language.
description: Participants view a real or pictured scene while hearing instructions or sentences, and eye movements to objects are recorded word by word. In Tanenhaus et al.'s one-apple scene ('Put the apple on the towel in the box'), people looked at the empty towel on 55 per cent of trials, treating 'on the towel' as the destination; with unambiguous wording or two apples in view, such looks fell to about 10 per cent or none, showing the scene shapes parsing from the outset. Altmann and Kamide found that after 'The boy will eat...' eyes reached the cake 87 ms before the word, against 127 ms after it for 'move'. Variants show looks to sound-alike or shape-sharing objects, and eye movements towards described events even on a blank screen. Any cover task is not the measure; the time course of fixations is. Requires precise audio-gaze alignment and careful layout control.
steps: Design scenes containing a target, competitors (sound-alike, shape- or colour-sharing) and distractors, with positions counterbalanced.
Record spoken stimuli and mark word onsets precisely.
Give a cover task, such as following the instruction or judging whether the sentence fits the picture.
Record eye movements with a tracker sampling at 250 Hz or more, synchronised with audio.
Compute fixation proportions to each object in time bins (for example 20-50 ms) relative to word onsets.
Compare time courses across conditions, for example ambiguous versus unambiguous wording, using growth-curve or cluster-based analyses.
outputs: Fixation proportions over time to target, competitor and distractor objects; anticipation and ambiguity effects relative to word onsets.
useWhen: You must know how users interpret spoken prompts in real time: voice UIs, in-car instructions, guided assembly, multimodal assistants.
avoidWhen: You only need final comprehension; use comprehension or task success measures. It needs eye tracking, precise timing and controlled layouts.
whyLost: It sits in psycholinguistics, and UX eye tracking focuses on reading screens rather than on listening while looking.
whereToUse: Voice assistants, automotive voice guidance, AR and VR narration, accessible audio description, smart-speaker displays.
example: An in-car assistant says 'Turn on the left heater'. Eye tracking shows drivers first look at the left mirror control until 'heater' is heard, so the prompt is reordered to 'Heater, left side'.
reference: Tanenhaus, M. K., Spivey-Knowlton, M. J., Eberhard, K. M., & Sedivy, J. C. (1995). Integration of visual and linguistic information in spoken language comprehension. Science, 268, 1632-1634.

name: Vocabulary Breadth-and-Depth Probe
origin: Adapted for UX from educational linguistics: breadth and depth distinction (Stahl and Nagy, 2006); definitions research by Wehren et al. (1981), Snow (1990), Kurland and Snow (1997)
summary: For each target word, combine a self-rating of knowledge with sentence use, associations and a definition, revealing whether people truly know terms or only recognise them.
description: Vocabulary breadth is how many words someone knows; depth covers pronunciation and spelling, word parts, sentence frames, multiple meanings, associations and appropriate contexts. Recognition alone overstates knowledge. This probe asks, for each target word, a three-level self-rating of how well it is known, a sentence using it, as many connected words as possible in three minutes, and a definition. Definitions are judged against the formal 'An X is a Y that Z' form; they develop from personal and functional descriptions towards synonyms and category relations, and depend on schooling and reading. Comparing self-ratings with demonstrated knowledge shows where people believe they understand a term but cannot use or define it. In UX this turns terminology decisions (labels, jargon, financial and medical terms) from guesswork into measured knowledge profiles across audiences.
steps: Select the target words or terms, for example candidate interface labels or domain jargon.
Ask for a three-level self-rating of knowledge for each word (do not know, have seen it, know it well).
Ask the participant to write a sentence using the word.
Give three minutes to list associated words.
Ask for a definition of its meaning or meanings, and score it against the 'An X is a Y that Z' form.
Compare self-ratings with demonstrated knowledge across words and participant groups.
outputs: A per-word knowledge profile and the agreement between self-rated and demonstrated knowledge, by group.
useWhen: Choosing labels and terminology, writing for low-literacy or second-language audiences, or testing whether users understand domain terms (APR, deductible, two-factor) they claim to know.
avoidWhen: Testing comprehension of whole texts (use Readability Testing) or label findability (use Tree Testing). Long probes tire participants, so limit the word set.
whyLost: It comes from education and child language research; UX checks terms through findability and preference tests rather than probing depth of knowledge.
whereToUse: Fintech and insurance terminology, health literacy, government services, localisation, AI assistant vocabulary.
example: An insurer tests 'excess', 'premium' and 'no-claims bonus' with 30 customers. Most rate 'excess' as well known, but only a third can define it correctly, so the claims flow adds a plain-language explanation beside the term.
reference: Berko Gleason, J. and Bernstein Ratner, N. (Eds.). The Development of Language (10th ed.). Plural Publishing; Stahl, S. A. and Nagy, W. E. (2006). Teaching Word Meanings. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Voice and Tone Framework with Decision Matrix
origin: Mailchimp's Voice and Tone guide (Kate Kiefer Lee, 2011); research-based treatment by Erica Jorgensen (2023)
summary: Defines a constant brand voice and maps user emotional state and task type to tone settings, then tests tone choices with users rather than relying on brand intuition.
description: Voice is who the product is and stays constant; tone adapts to the situation. A decision matrix makes this operational: rows are situations defined by user emotional state (anxious, frustrated, neutral, celebrating) and task type (error, payment, onboarding, success), and cells specify tone settings along dimensions such as formal to casual, direct to empathetic, and brief to detailed, with example strings. Jorgensen emphasises testing tone with users: comprehension and perceived appropriateness surveys, A/B tests on key messages, and analysis of support contacts, because what a brand team finds charming may feel flippant to someone whose payment failed. The matrix becomes a shared decision tool for writers, designers and AI-generated content prompts.
steps: Build a tone decision matrix: rows = user emotional states (anxious, excited, frustrated, neutral, confused), columns = task types (onboarding, error recovery, success, routine action, high-stakes decision). For each cell, specify:
vocabulary register,
sentence length,
active/passive voice ratio,
use of first/second person. Validate: show content examples to users in each context and measure: does the tone match the moment?
outputs: Voice attributes, a situation-by-tone decision matrix with example strings, user test results on tone appropriateness, and guidance for writers and AI prompts.
useWhen: Products with emotionally varied moments (finance, health, insurance), content teams scaling across writers, and configuring the tone of AI assistants.
avoidWhen: For products with very narrow, uniform contexts where tone rarely varies, or before core comprehension issues are solved (fix clarity first).
whyLost: Voice and tone guides became brand documents with adjectives and examples; the situational matrix and user testing of tone were rarely carried through.
whereToUse: Microcopy design, chatbot dialogue design, error message writing, onboarding content, customer communication design.
example: An insurer's claim rejection message uses the brand's playful voice. Testing shows customers rate it as disrespectful; the matrix assigns 'anxious, bad news' situations a direct, empathetic and detailed tone, and complaint rates fall.
sources: Nicely Said (Nicole Fenton & Kate Kiefer Lee)
reference: Jorgensen E (2023) Strategic Content Design: Tools and Research Techniques for Better UX Writing. Rosenfeld Media

name: Voice Interface Usability Testing
donor: Speech technology (IVR industry); automotive human factors
origin: Practice described by Cathy Pearl (2017), drawing on Cohen, Giangola and Balogh (2004) and Larsen (2003)
summary: Usability testing adapted to speech interfaces: observation instead of think-aloud, concealed speech capability, and voice-specific measures of error type, recovery and completion.
description: Concurrent think-aloud is impossible while a participant is talking to a system, so voice testing relies on observation, recordings, facial expression and post-task questions. Test a working build after a couple of pilot participants have caught gross recognition problems, since the aim is flow, not recognition accuracy. Do not reveal that the app accepts speech unless users would know in real life; whether and when users realise they can speak is a finding. Define task completion per task in advance and also ask users whether they achieved their goal, because users may fail without minding. Count errors by type (rejection versus mismatch) and record whether and how quickly users recovered. For cars, test safely in a mock-up rig with a simulator, in a parked car, or with a back-seat Wizard playing prompts, while watching cognitive, visual and manual distraction.
steps: Prepare a working build or Wizard of Oz set-up with fake accounts or hard-coded data, and pilot with one or two participants to fix gross recognition problems.
Write goal-based tasks without command words and rotate their order.
Do not tell participants the app accepts speech unless they would know in real life.
Observe without think-aloud: speaking cues, exact utterances, hesitation, duration, expressions; step in only for crashes or high frustration.
Ask brief questions after each task and a questionnaire at the end; code completion against predefined criteria and ask whether users achieved their goal.
Count errors by type (rejection, mismatch) and recovery success and time.
For in-car use, test in a simulator rig, a parked car or with a back-seat Wizard, and record distraction; then tally, rank issues by severity and share a fix plan.
outputs: Task completion, error type and recovery counts, subjective ratings, observed phrasing, and a ranked issue list.
useWhen: Evaluating voice assistants, IVR, smart speakers, in-car voice and multimodal assistants.
avoidWhen: Avoid when recognition accuracy itself is in doubt; run Scripted Speaker Recognition Testing first. Parked-car tests do not reproduce real driving workload.
whyLost: It remains specialist practice in speech and automotive teams; general UX teams often test voice with screen-based protocols that do not fit.
whereToUse: Voice assistants, conversational AI with speech, automotive infotainment, accessibility voice control.
example: A banking voice app is tested without telling users it accepts speech. Half never try speaking, and rejection errors cluster on account nicknames, so prompts and grammar are revised.
reference: Pearl, C. (2017). Designing Voice User Interfaces: Principles of Conversational Experiences. O'Reilly Media.

name: Voiced-Reasoning Idea Walkthrough
aka: Test how well you are empathizing
origin: Indi Young, Practical Empathy (2015)
summary: Voice research participants' reasoning in the first person and walk an idea through an extended scene, to check whether it supports or frustrates what they are trying to do.
description: Young offers a set of checks on whether a team has really understood the people it listened to, and whether its ideas fit their reasoning. The core move is to take a scene from listening sessions and voice the characters' inner thoughts in the first person, as an actor would ('I don't trust the airline to sort this out, so I go to the gate agent myself...'), then walk a proposed idea or a leader's plan through that extended scene and see where it helps or frustrates. A parallel telling of the same scene without the idea, in which characters still reach their intent, isolates what the idea actually adds. Each decision is run through at least three different perspectives in a few minutes. Findings are communicated as scenes in participants' voices rather than as opinion, which keeps critique anchored in evidence.
steps: Pick an idea or plan and a scene from earlier listening sessions or interviews.
Voice the characters' thoughts and reactions in the first person through the extended scene.
Note where the idea helps, is ignored, or frustrates each character's intent.
Tell a parallel version of the scene without the idea to see what it really adds.
Repeat with at least three different perspectives (participants with different thinking styles).
Communicate results as short scenes in participants' voices, not as personal opinion.
outputs: Adjusted ideas and short first-person scenes that explain why an idea works or fails for different people.
useWhen: Use it after listening-based research, when evaluating ideas or plans against what people were trying to achieve, and to check that a team's empathy is grounded in data.
avoidWhen: It relies on the team's prior understanding; if there is no listening data, run Interviews or Listening to Think vs. Listening to React first. To evaluate a concrete interface, use Cognitive Walkthrough or Usability Testing.
whyLost: It is a loosely bounded set of exercises in one practitioner book and is overshadowed by personas and journey maps, which feel more like deliverables.
whereToUse: Service design, customer support policy, healthcare and travel disruption flows, and leadership strategy reviews.
example: An airline team voices a stranded traveller who does not trust the app, then walks an auto-rebooking idea through the scene. The parallel story shows she still queues at the desk, so the idea adds a staff-confirmed status message.
reference: Young, I. (2015). Practical Empathy: For Collaboration and Creativity in Your Work. Brooklyn, NY: Rosenfeld Media, pp. 124-128.

name: Vote-Counting Procedures
origin: Light and Smith, 1971; Hedges and Olkin, 1985; Bushman and Wang, 1996
summary: Estimate a pooled effect from the direction or significance of study results when effect sizes are unavailable, and combine it with effect sizes from fully reported studies.
description: Conventional vote counting tallies studies as significant positive, significant negative or null and declares the modal category the winner. It ignores sample size, loses power as studies accumulate, and can conclude 'no effect' when a real effect exists. The principled alternatives are the sign test (a binomial test with p = .5 on the direction of results), maximum-likelihood vote-count estimators that recover an effect size d or r and a confidence interval from the counts and sample sizes, and Bushman and Wang's combined procedure that pools vote-count estimates with effect sizes from fully reported studies. They should be used only for studies lacking the statistics needed for an effect size. They assume a fixed common effect, give no information about heterogeneity, and direction-only estimators are at best 64% as efficient as effect-size methods.
steps: Identify the studies that report only direction or significance and cannot yield an effect size.
Classify each as positive or negative in direction, or as significant positive versus not.
Apply the sign test (binomial with p = .5) to the direction counts.
Estimate the common effect by maximum likelihood from the counts and sample sizes, and form a confidence interval.
Pool the vote-count estimate with effect-size estimates from fully reported studies using the combined procedure.
Report the fixed-effect assumption and the efficiency loss alongside the result.
outputs: A pooled effect estimate with confidence interval that uses incompletely reported studies.
useWhen: Synthesising evidence where many studies, vendor reports or internal experiment write-ups give only direction or 'significant/not' rather than full statistics.
avoidWhen: Effect sizes are available for most studies; use standard meta-analysis. Never use naive tallying of significant results.
whyLost: Naive vote counting persists informally in UX ('most studies found...'), while the corrected procedures remain in meta-analysis texts.
whereToUse: Reviews of A/B test archives with incomplete records, literature reviews of HCI studies, and competitive evidence reviews.
example: Of 25 archived checkout experiments, 10 report effect sizes and 15 only 'won' or 'lost'. The team applies the sign test and the combined procedure, finding a small positive pooled effect where a naive tally of significant wins had suggested no effect.
sources: The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (Cooper et al., 2009)
reference: Bushman, B. J. & Wang, M. C. Ch. 11. In Cooper, H., Hedges, L. V., & Valentine, J. C. (Eds.) (2009). The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed.). New York: Russell Sage Foundation.

name: Walking Interview (Go-Along)
origin: Margarethe Kusenbach, 2003; Evans and Jones, 2011
summary: Interviews conducted while accompanying participants through their own environment, accessing place-specific knowledge, embodied routines and tacit spatial reasoning that a static interview misses.
description: The walking interview or go-along method (Kusenbach, 2003; Evans & Jones, 2011) involves the researcher accompanying participants as they move through their natural environment — a commute, a shopping trip, a hospital visit — while simultaneously conducting an interview. Moving through space with participants accesses knowledge that cannot be accessed in a static interview setting: how people navigate, how their environment triggers memories and associations, how place shapes experience. Applied to UX: walking interviews are particularly powerful for studies of wayfinding, mobile app use in context, digital service touchpoints across physical journeys, and the relationship between physical and digital environments.
steps: Route selection: Either participant-led (participant chooses the route) or researcher-specified (participant does a specific journey relevant to the research question). Participant-led routes reveal habitual paths and navigation strategies; researcher-specified routes enable comparison.

Interview style during movement: Questions are opportunistically timed — ask about specific elements as participants encounter them in the environment. 'What do you usually do at this point?' 'How does being here affect how you use [app]?'
Researcher participation: Walk alongside, not behind. Co-presence in the environment affects what is noticed and discussed — sharing the sensory experience changes the conversation.
Recording: Audio recording + periodic photography or video. GPS track of the route. Note timestamps at key spatial moments.

Analysis: Map the spatial trajectory alongside the interview content. Identify where conversation changed, deepened, or stalled in relation to spatial location. What places triggered what kinds of talk?
outputs: Route-linked audio and photographs, GPS traces, place-anchored themes, and maps of where experiences, frictions and decisions occur.
useWhen: Experience is tied to place and movement: commuting, shopping, wayfinding, deliveries, hospital visits, field work, or any mobile and location-based product.
avoidWhen: The experience is desk-bound or private, safety or noise makes conversation impractical, or you need comparable structured data; use contextual inquiry or a diary study.
whyLost: UX adopted the 'ride-along' informally but without the method's attention to place, route choice and spatial analysis, which stayed in geography and urban sociology.
whereToUse: Mobility and transport apps, retail and omnichannel, logistics and field-service tools, wayfinding in hospitals and airports, and location-based services.
example: Researchers go along with 8 delivery couriers on shifts. Route-linked notes show most app frustration occurs at building entrances where GPS fails, leading to courier-contributed access notes per address.
sources: When Words Fail Us — Integrative Review of Elicitation Techniques (PMC 2024)
Evans, J. & Jones, P. (2011) The walking interview, Applied Geography
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
reference: Kusenbach, M. (2003). Street phenomenology: The go-along as ethnographic research tool. Ethnography, 4(3), 455-485.

name: Wall Walk
origin: Karen Holtzblatt and Hugh Beyer, Contextual Design
summary: Participants silently read the affinity diagram and work models, posting design ideas beside the data, then the group lists issues and 'hot ideas' that feed visioning.
description: The Wall Walk opens Contextual Design's visioning workshop and is open to people who did not collect the data, including stakeholders. After an introduction to the project, process and personas, each person reads the affinity diagram from top to bottom like a story, silently and alone, writing design ideas on sticky notes and posting them next to the data they respond to; ideas grow more holistic as reading continues. The facilitator then captures a list of issues the group thinks must be addressed and a list of 'hot ideas' with potential to spark whole solutions, grouped into themes. Each work model is then introduced and read individually or in pairs, with more ideas posted and both lists extended. Ideas stay uncommitted, and the lists let people share ideas without arguing about whose is best.
steps: Introduce the project, the process and any personas.
Have each participant silently read the affinity diagram top down, posting design-idea stickies beside the data that prompts them.
Capture the group's list of issues that must be addressed.
Capture hot ideas on a flip chart and group them into themes.
Introduce each work model; participants read it individually or in pairs and post further ideas.
Extend the issues and hot-ideas lists after each model, then carry them into visioning.
outputs: Idea stickies placed on the data, an issues list, and a themed hot-ideas list.
useWhen: Use it after a rigorous affinity and modelling phase, to immerse a wider team in the data before visioning or ideation.
avoidWhen: It needs a properly built affinity first (Full Four-Level Affinity Diagram or Five-Model Work Modelling (Contextual Design)); without one, it becomes a gallery walk of opinions. To communicate findings to people who will not engage with raw data, a Research Activation Workshop is lighter.
whyLost: Gallery walks of research walls are common, but the disciplined version tied to a full affinity and models has faded with Contextual Design's decline.
whereToUse: Enterprise and B2B product discovery, service redesign, and onboarding new team members to a research corpus.
example: A procurement software team walks a 1,200-note affinity; engineers post ideas next to 'approvers work from email'. Hot ideas cluster around approving in the inbox, which becomes the vision's centrepiece.
reference: Holtzblatt, K. and Beyer, H. (2014). Contextual Design: Evolved. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool, pp. 27, 42-44.

name: WAMMI (Website Analysis and Measurement Inventory)
origin: Kirakowski & Cierlik (1998), Human Factors Research Group with Nomos Management AB
summary: A 20-item website questionnaire covering attractiveness, controllability, efficiency, helpfulness and learnability, compared with a database of hundreds of site surveys.
description: WAMMI was one of the first instruments designed specifically for websites. Its items came from opinions collected from designers, users and webmasters about good and bad web experiences, and factor analysis produced the same five-factor structure as SUMI. The original had 60 items; the current version has 20 five-point items plus a global measure. Like SUMI, global scores are standardised to a mean of 50 and SD of 10 against a reference database of more than 300 surveys, which is its main value. Sauro and Lewis note the shorter version's subscale reliabilities (around 0.63 to 0.70) are lower than ideal, so the global score is the most dependable number.
steps: Arrange permission or a commercial licence and embed the 20 items in a site intercept or post-test survey.
Collect responses from genuine visitors after they have used the site.
Score against the WAMMI reference database.
Report the global score with its interval, treating subscales as indicative.
Compare with previous waves or competitor surveys in the database.
outputs: A standardised website satisfaction score and five indicative subscales.
useWhen: You want website satisfaction scores benchmarked against an external database, especially in European projects.
avoidWhen: You need highly reliable subscales or free norms (consider SUPR-Q or UMUX-Lite).
whyLost: Commercial licensing and the rise of free, shorter instruments.
whereToUse: Public-sector and corporate websites, intranets.
example: A university site scores 46 globally, with Controllability lowest, consistent with tree test failures in its navigation.
sources: Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Kirakowski, J. & Cierlik, B. (1998). Measuring the usability of web sites. Proceedings of HFES 42.

name: Wandering Schematic Plots and Delineations
origin: John W. Tukey (1977)
summary: Slice an x-y scatter by x, take medians and hinges of y per slice, and smooth them into traces, giving a resistant picture of how y's middle and spread change.
description: Tukey's resistant display of how a distribution of y shifts with x. The batch is sliced by x, using letter-value cuts, judgement or slice sizes such as 5, 9, 17, 35. In each slice the median and hinges (quartiles) of y and the median of x are found. Parallel schematic plots put slice box plots side by side. Wandering schematic plots go further: the medians are smoothed into a median trace and the hinge differences into letter-difference traces, from which hinge traces, fences, outside points and adjacent polygons are derived. Known functions of x can be subtracted first. Delineations extend the idea to outer letter values (eighths and beyond) and combine traces with cuts into full, reduced and schematic outlines of the scatter. Because it uses medians and quartiles, a few extreme points do not distort the picture, unlike least-squares lines.
steps: Slice the batch by x, for example into slices of 5, 9, 17 or 35 points or at letter-value cuts.
In each slice find the median and hinges of y and the median of x.
Optionally draw parallel schematic plots (side-by-side box plots per slice).
Smooth the slice medians into a median trace and the hinge differences into letter-difference traces, smoothing x as well as y.
Add and subtract to obtain hinge traces, then compute fences and mark outside and far-out points.
Draw the wandering schematic plot, or extend to outer letter values for a delineation.
outputs: A resistant plot of the middle and spread of y across x, with unusual points identified.
useWhen: Exploring skewed behavioural data, such as task time or session length against account age or experience, where spread changes with x and outliers would distort a regression line.
avoidWhen: Modern quantile regression, LOESS and binned box plots do the same job with software support; prefer them unless working by hand. Care is needed matching x-hinges with y-hinges.
whyLost: It was a hand-computation technique; software made smoothing and quantile regression easy, and the vocabulary of traces and delineations dropped out of use.
whereToUse: Telemetry exploration, response-time analysis, any scatter of heavy-tailed UX metrics where variability itself matters.
example: Plotting checkout time against number of basket items for 2,000 sessions, slice medians rise gently but the upper hinge trace climbs steeply after 12 items, revealing a growing minority who struggle with large baskets.
reference: Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory Data Analysis. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, pp. 265-330.

name: Wants and Needs Analysis
aka: Wants and Needs brainstorm with top-five booklet
origin: Oracle Usability and UI group practice from 1999 (Catherine Courage and Kathy Baxter); brainstorming tips from Kelley (2001)
summary: Users of one profile brainstorm everything an ideal system would offer under strict rules, then each privately picks a Top 5, giving needs scored by the percentage choosing them.
description: A structured focus-group variant producing prioritised requirements in about an hour. One piloted question asks about an ideal system in one of three forms: information, tasks or characteristics, neither so narrow it builds in a design nor so broad it invites irrelevant answers. Four rules are posted: it is an ideal system so all ideas are valid; no designing; the moderator may ask about duplicates; the scribe writes only the moderator's paraphrase. The moderator turns design suggestions back into underlying goals. Around 40 minutes of brainstorming typically yields about 100 numbered ideas. Each participant then completes a Top 5 booklet, one item per page with the reason it matters; picks are unranked and equally weighted, countering dominant voices. Items are grouped by meaning and scored as the percentage of participants choosing them, with at least two sessions per user profile checked for consistency before pooling.
steps: With the product team, write one ideal-system question about information, tasks or characteristics and pilot it.
Recruit 8-12 users of a single profile per session and run at least two sessions per profile, with a moderator, scribe and videographer.
Post the question and the four rules, warm up and practise with a neutral example until everyone gives a valid idea.
Brainstorm for about 40 minutes, probing design suggestions back to goals while the scribe numbers each paraphrased idea; avoid round-robin turns.
Have each participant choose an unranked Top 5 in a booklet, giving the idea number, name, description and why it matters.
Within 24 hours, sort booklet pages into groups of the same meaning, counting duplicate votes from one person once.
Compute the percentage of participants choosing each group per session; check items chosen by at least half in one session appear in the other before pooling.
Report a table ordered by percentage with exemplar quotes, plus the full idea list, and feed it into the specification.
outputs: A prioritised table of wants and needs with percentages and exemplars, the complete numbered brainstorm list and affinity groups of needs.
useWhen: Early in a project you need a fast, user-generated, prioritised list of needs for a defined user profile, and can recruit groups.
avoidWhen: You need observed rather than stated needs, or users cannot imagine the domain; people do not always know what they want and obvious needs may go unmentioned. Use contextual inquiry or Kano analysis instead.
whyLost: The name survives in one textbook lineage, but practice slid into unstructured brainstorms and dot voting without the rules, booklets and percentage scoring; its reliability was never formally tested.
whereToUse: Requirements gathering for new tools, intranets and portals, B2B products and healthcare information services.
example: A hotel booking team runs two sessions with frequent travellers. Booking a room is chosen by all 20 participants, hotel information by 95% and reviews by 70%, which sets the launch scope.
reference: Courage, C., & Baxter, K. (2005). Understanding Your Users: A Practical Guide to User Requirements. Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 9.

name: Wardley Mapping
donor: Business strategy (with roots in military strategy)
origin: Simon Wardley, 2005 onward (Wardley Maps, 2016 online book)
summary: Maps the components needed to meet user needs along a value chain (visibility) and an evolution axis (genesis to commodity) to inform strategic choices.
description: A Wardley map starts with a user and their need at the top, then lists the components required to meet it, arranged vertically by visibility to the user and horizontally by evolution stage: genesis, custom-built, product (and rental), commodity (and utility). Components evolve over time under supply and demand competition, and each stage calls for different methods (exploration versus efficiency) and attitudes (pioneers, settlers, town planners). Maps reveal where to build, buy or use utilities, inertia, and opportunities for gameplay. For UX research, the map anchors strategy in user needs and shows which needs are commoditising, where differentiation lies, and where research should focus.
steps: Define the user and their need, grounded in research.
List the components required to meet the need and their dependencies (value chain).
Place components on the evolution axis using characteristics of each stage (ubiquity, certainty, market maturity).
Draw the map, then discuss movement: which components are evolving, where inertia exists.
Identify strategic options: build versus buy, where to differentiate, which gameplays apply.
Revisit and update maps as markets and research evidence change.
outputs: A Wardley map of user needs and components with evolution positions, movement and strategic options.
useWhen: Strategy discussions about where to invest, build or buy, and how technology evolution affects user experience.
avoidWhen: Interface-level design questions.
whyLost: It comes from IT strategy and is popular in tech strategy circles but rarely linked to UX research.
whereToUse: AI product strategy, platform strategy, public sector digital services, developer tools.
example: A legal-tech firm maps its contract review service. Text extraction has become a commodity (LLM APIs), while clients' need for defensible risk explanations is at genesis, so the firm reallocates design research toward explanation and audit trails.
reference: Wardley, S. (2016). Wardley Maps. Online book, published on Medium.

name: Wargaming (Matrix Games)
origin: Prussian Kriegsspiel (von Reisswitz, 1824); matrix games by Chris Engle (1988); Peter Perla, The Art of Wargaming (1990)
summary: Players representing actors (users, competitors, regulators, platform) make moves in turns, argue outcomes and adjudicate them, to explore dynamic responses to a strategy.
description: Wargames simulate a conflict or competitive situation with players taking roles and making decisions over turns under uncertainty. Matrix games are a lightweight form: each player proposes an action with reasons for and against; others counter-argue; an umpire or dice adjudicate success; the narrative evolves. This surfaces second-order effects and interactions that static analysis misses. Business wargaming adopted the format for strategy. For UX and product, wargames explore how users, competitors, bad actors, regulators and partners might react to a launch or policy, generating research questions and design requirements.
steps: Define the objective, scenario, time horizon and key actors (e.g. users segments, competitor, regulator, scammers).
Assign players to roles with briefs describing their goals, resources and constraints.
Run turns: each actor proposes an action with arguments; others counter-argue; adjudicate by umpire judgement or dice weighted by argument strength.
Record the evolving narrative, decisions and surprises.
Debrief: identify insights, vulnerabilities, and assumptions to research.
Translate insights into design changes, research questions and indicators.
outputs: Game narrative, identified second-order effects, vulnerabilities and follow-up research questions.
useWhen: Strategic launches with multiple interacting actors, policy changes, marketplaces and platforms with adversaries.
avoidWhen: Single-user usability questions or when actors have no strategic agency.
whyLost: Wargaming stayed in defence and strategy consulting; UX research seldom models multiple actors' dynamic responses.
whereToUse: Marketplace policy changes, platform API changes, content moderation, AI launches, fintech regulation responses.
example: A ride-hailing company wargames a new surge transparency policy with players as drivers, riders, a competitor and a city regulator; drivers' coordinated log-offs emerge, prompting research on driver earnings perceptions.
sources: Engle, Matrix games (1988), self-published rules; Curry & Price, Matrix Games for Modern Wargaming (2014)
reference: Perla, P. P. (1990). The Art of Wargaming. Naval Institute Press.

name: Wason selection task
aka: Wason selection task with abstract, thematic and deontic content
origin: Peter Wason, 1966; Griggs and Cox, 1982; Cheng and Holyoak, 1985; Cosmides, 1989
summary: People choose which of four cards to turn to test an if-then rule; comparing abstract and familiar versions shows how content, not logic, drives rule checking.
description: Four cards show, for example, E, K, 4 and 7, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other. Which must be turned to test 'if a vowel, then an even number'? The answer is E and 7 (p and not-q), yet in the abstract form only a small minority choose it; most choose E alone or E and 4. In a drinking-age version (beer, soda, 16 and 24 years old), most people answer correctly. Explanations include pragmatic permission schemas and cheater detection, each with evidence for and against. Variants vary content (abstract, thematic, permission), the array and order, and think-aloud protocols show people rarely notice the shared structure. The task is a sharp test of whether people seek falsifying cases when checking a conditional.
steps: Present an if-then rule and four cards representing p, not-p, q and not-q.
Ask which cards must be turned over to establish whether the rule is true or false.
Vary content between groups: abstract, thematic and permission or obligation rules, including a version in the domain of interest.
Randomise card order and counterbalance versions.
Score selections of the falsifying combination (p and not-q) and common error patterns.
Optionally collect think-aloud protocols to see how people reason about the rule.
outputs: Card-selection patterns and the proportion selecting the falsifying combination per content version.
useWhen: Studying how users or operators check conditional rules (eligibility, permissions, automation logic), or training teams to look for disconfirming evidence.
avoidWhen: Avoid predicting real rule use from the abstract version, since performance depends on content and familiarity, and some thematic effects have failed to replicate.
whyLost: It is the most studied task in reasoning research but has no packaged applied form, so it rarely leaves psychology courses.
whereToUse: Permission and access-control settings, automation and rule builders, compliance tools, research and analytics training.
example: Admins of a workflow tool are asked which records to check to verify 'if a refund exceeds $500, it needs manager approval'. Few check unapproved records, so the tool adds an automatic audit of exceptions.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition (Bly & Rumelhart, 1999)
Wason, P. C. (1968). Reasoning about a rule. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 20
reference: Wason, P. C. (1968). Reasoning about a rule. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 20, 273-281.

name: Wavelet and Cross-Spectral Coherence
origin: Coherence analysis from classical spectral theory; wavelet coherence by Torrence & Webster, 1999 and Grinsted et al., 2004
summary: Measures frequency-specific synchrony between two signals, such as user actions and system feedback or interaction density and sentiment, as an index of flow or misalignment.
description: Coherence is a frequency-resolved correlation between two time series (0 = unrelated, 1 = perfectly linearly related at that frequency); wavelet coherence localises it in time. In the Behavioral Spectral Framework, high cross-spectral coherence between click rhythm and feedback rhythm indicates flow, while low coherence implies latency, confusion or interface mismatch; phase difference measures lag. In the fintech case, coherence between interaction density and sentiment reached 0.78 during flow states and dropped to 0.35 during breakdowns. Proposed uses include synchrony between human prompts and AI agent responses, cross-modal coherence of gesture, gaze and emotion, and spectral alignment as a metric for AI-human coherence. Coherence maps are a recommended visual.
steps: Choose two aligned signals (e.g. user input rhythm and system feedback, or interaction density and sentiment).
Normalise each signal's frequency range and sampling.
Compute cross-spectral or wavelet coherence and phase difference.
Identify periods and bands of high and low coherence.
Align low-coherence periods with qualitative evidence of breakdowns.
Report coherence maps and summary values per state.
outputs: Coherence maps, phase offsets and coherence values by state.
useWhen: When studying alignment between user and system, between people, or between modalities over time.
avoidWhen: When signals are not time-aligned or are too short; coherence estimates become unstable.
whyLost: Standard in neuroscience, climatology and engineering, unexplored in UX.
whereToUse: Conversational and agentic AI, collaborative tools, multimodal biometric studies, gaming.
example: In an AI chat study, coherence between user message rhythm and assistant response timing drops during misunderstandings, prompting adaptive response timing.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Grinsted, A., Moore, J. C., & Jevrejeva, S. (2004). Application of the cross wavelet transform and wavelet coherence to geophysical time series. Nonlinear Processes in Geophysics, 11, 561–566.

name: Wayfinding
donor: Architecture, urban planning and environmental psychology
origin: Kevin Lynch, 1960 (The Image of the City); Romedi Passini, 1984 (Wayfinding in Architecture)
summary: Designs orientation and navigation cues that help people know where they are, where they have been, where they can go and how to get there in complex spaces.
description: Wayfinding originated in architecture and urban design. Kevin Lynch identified the elements people use to form mental maps of cities (paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks), and Passini framed wayfinding as spatial problem solving involving decision-making, decision execution and information processing. Applied to digital products, wayfinding concerns how users orient themselves in large information spaces and multi-step processes: identity cues, landmarks, consistent paths, breadcrumbs, progress indicators and signage at decision points. It complements information architecture by focusing on the moment-to-moment experience of moving through a structure. Rigour comes from mapping decision points, assessing each for orientation cues, testing with tasks that involve getting lost and recovering, and measuring backtracking, disorientation and path efficiency.
steps: Map the information space or process, identifying key decision points and routes.
Audit each decision point for orientation cues: location identity, landmarks, signage and progress.
Analyse behavioural data for backtracking, loops and dead ends.
Test with tasks requiring navigation across distant areas, asking participants where they are and how to return.
Design cues using Lynch's elements such as landmarks, distinct districts and consistent paths.
Retest and measure path efficiency, backtracking and self-reported disorientation.
outputs: Decision point maps, cue audits, disorientation and backtracking metrics, and wayfinding design recommendations.
useWhen: For large information spaces, complex enterprise applications, multi-step processes, documentation sites and spatial or mixed-reality interfaces.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small, shallow products where orientation is trivial; use heuristic evaluation. For the underlying structure itself, use card sorting and tree testing.
whyLost: Latent: Concept widely understood informally; systematic wayfinding design rarely applied rigorously in digital UX.
whereToUse: Complex information spaces; multi-step processes; large-scale applications.
example: A cloud console analyses logs and finds users frequently loop between services while configuring networking. Adding persistent context headers and a 'recent locations' landmark reduces backtracking by a third in testing.
sources: Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell et al., 2023)
The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (Gibson, 2015)
reference: Lynch, K. (1960). The Image of the City. MIT Press; Passini, R. (1984). Wayfinding in Architecture. Van Nostrand Reinhold.

name: Web Analytics Interpretation for UX
origin: Michael Beasley, Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (2013); Joel Marsh, UX for Beginners (2016)
summary: Read core metrics, chart shapes, page patterns, landing pages and segments to locate where behaviour departs from expectation and form hypotheses for other methods.
description: Analytics shows the 'smoke' that leads to the 'fire' of user goals. Interpretation is relative: compare a page with others of its type and with its own history, not with the site average. Core metrics are read together: sessions against users for loyalty, new versus returning share against site maturity, pageviews and time by whether the product is a task tool or an engagement product, and bounce bands (10-30% good, 70-99% poor, near zero a tracking error). Chart shapes are diagnostic: traffic graphs show trends, spikes with a cause and cycles; item or step graphs normally slide exponentially, so out-of-order bars suggest an IA mismatch, bumps suggest power users and cliffs mark barriers. Landing-page reports with referral context, and rule-based segments that isolate relevant visitors, sharpen each diagnosis.
steps: Filter out rarely viewed pages (for example under 100 views) and group the rest by template or type.
Read core metrics in combination and against the site's own history: sessions per user, new versus returning share, pageviews, time, bounce and exit rate.
Classify each chart as a traffic graph or an item/step graph and note trends, spikes, cycles, out-of-order bars, bumps and cliffs.

Sort page metrics for highest, lowest and deviation from the type average and map each pattern to candidate explanations (for example pageviews 40-50% above unique pageviews suggests a hub or pogo-sticking).
Rank landing pages by entrances, add bounce and conversion, and infer arrival intent from medium, keyword or the linking page.
Build segments that separate relevant users (by page visited, keyword category, landing page or goal), testing that they capture about 80-90% of the intended visits.
Turn each suspect page or pattern into a hypothesis and test it with usability tasks, expert review or an A/B test.
outputs: A prioritised list of suspect pages and entry points, named reusable segments, and hypotheses about causes to test with other methods.
useWhen: Choosing what to research or redesign on a live site, diagnosing a drop or spike, setting tasks for usability tests, or checking a redesign before and after.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating analytics as an explanation: time on page excludes exit pages, devices are not people, first-position items are clicked because they are seen first, and averages hide spread. Use usability testing or interviews to find the cause.
whyLost: It survived because analytics tools are ubiquitous, though many teams read dashboards without the comparative, hypothesis-forming discipline described here.
whereToUse: Content sites, e-commerce, government services, SaaS marketing sites and help centres with established analytics.
example: A childcare provider's centre pages show high entrances from paid search but a 75% bounce rate. A segment of paid-search visitors and a look at the ad copy reveal a mismatch between the ad promise and the page, which a usability test confirms.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley, 2013)
reference: Beasley, M. (2013). Practical Web Analytics for User Experience: How Analytics Can Help You Understand Your Users. Waltham, MA: Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Web credibility element-rating survey (Stanford)
aka: What makes a web site credible survey
origin: B. J. Fogg and the Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab, 1999 and 2002 waves (Fogg et al., CHI 2001)
summary: A large online survey asking how each of about 50 site elements would change a site's credibility, rated on a 7-point scale and repeated in waves to track changing norms.
description: Fogg's team brainstormed more than 300 features that might affect perceived credibility, cut them to about 50 by judgement, and piloted three times (HCI specialists, then friends and family, with up to 90 items) to remove ambiguous wording. Respondents read an introduction and rated each randomised element on how it would affect the believability of a site's information, from 'much less believable' (-3) to 'much more believable' (+3), drawing on their general web experience. The 1999 wave (about 1,400 respondents, US and Finland) was repeated in 2002 with minimal wording changes to show drift. Because large samples make nearly every difference significant, practical thresholds were set: 0.3 between items within a wave, 0.4 between waves. Factor analysis grouped items into seven factors, including real-world feel, ease of use, expertise, trustworthiness, tailoring, commercial implications and amateurism.
steps: Generate a long list of candidate elements from the literature and from inspecting many products in the domain.
Cut to about 50 items by team judgement, dropping any that self-report cannot answer well, and write each as a short concrete statement.
Pilot with expert and lay samples to remove ambiguous items and check data capture.
Field online with randomised item order; respondents rate each element's effect on credibility from -3 to +3.
Collect demographics and experience so samples can be compared across waves and countries.
Rank items by mean, set practical-significance thresholds in advance (for example 0.3 within a wave) and group items by factor or credibility dimension.
Repeat in later waves with identical wording and a stricter threshold (for example 0.4) for change.
outputs: A ranked list of elements that raise or lower credibility, factor scores, practical-significance groupings and changes over time.
useWhen: When you need a broad, cross-site picture of which interface cues users believe affect trust in a domain, and how expectations shift over years.
avoidWhen: Avoid as evidence of how users judge a specific site: respondents report general beliefs, which differ from in-context judgement. For a specific product use task-based testing with trust measures such as the Trust in Automation Scale (Jian et al.).
whyLost: The 2001 item set dated quickly as web conventions changed, and later credibility research moved to observing judgements of real sites; the survey design itself was never adopted as a reusable method.
whereToUse: Trust research for new domains (AI assistants, crypto, telehealth), cross-cultural trust cue studies, longitudinal tracking of trust conventions.
example: A health-information platform adapts the method to 40 cues for AI-generated answers (citations, clinician review badges, confidence labels) and surveys 2,000 users yearly to see which cues gain or lose weight.
reference: Fogg, B. J., Marshall, J., Laraki, O., Osipovich, A., Varma, C., Fang, N., et al. (2001). What makes web sites credible? A report on a large quantitative study. Proceedings of CHI 2001, 61-68.

name: Web Credibility Review
origin: B. J. Fogg and the Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab (2002-2003)
summary: Inspect a site or app's credibility cues against Stanford's ten guidelines and Fogg's grid of operator, content and design by presumed, reputed, surface and earned credibility.
description: Credibility is perceived trustworthiness and expertise. The Stanford Web Credibility Project found nearly half of people judged credibility mainly on visual design, and produced ten guidelines: make accuracy easy to verify, show a real organisation, highlight expertise, show honest and trustworthy people, make contact easy, look professional, be easy to use and useful, update content often, restrain promotions and avoid errors. Fogg's Web Credibility Grid crosses site elements (operator, content, design) with four credibility types: presumed (general assumptions), reputed (awards, seals, referrals), surface (first impressions) and earned (track record). Auditing each cell shows gaps and damaging cues and assigns ownership to design, content, marketing, legal or customer service. The aim is appropriate credibility, matching actual performance, not maximum credibility.
steps: Identify which credibility contexts apply, such as advice, measurements, reported system state or simulations.
Use the ten Stanford guidelines as a first-pass checklist and note shortfalls.

Draw the grid (operator, content, design by presumed, reputed, surface, earned) and list positive and negative cues in each cell, such as ads mixed with content, broken links, typos or missing contact details.
Prioritise significant errors over large but harmless ones, and check for over-claiming as well as under-claiming.
Assign each cell to the team that controls it.
Confirm key judgements with users, for example through first-impression tests, and re-audit after release since earned credibility builds over time.
outputs: A filled credibility grid and guideline checklist with gaps, damaging cues, owners and prioritised fixes.
useWhen: Health, finance, e-commerce and information sites, or AI products where trust in content or advice drives use.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating expert judgement as user perception; validate with users or the 5-Second Test. For calibrated trust in automation use Trust in Automation Scale (Jian et al.).
whyLost: The guidelines are widely cited but rarely run as a structured audit; trust work moved into brand, conversion optimisation and AI trust frameworks.
whereToUse: Health information, fintech onboarding, marketplaces, AI-generated content and advice.
example: A telehealth start-up audits its site: surface cues are strong but operator cues are missing, with no named clinicians or registration numbers, so a clinician page and regulator badges are added.
reference: Fogg, B. J. (2003). Persuasive Technology: Using Computers to Change What We Think and Do. Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 6-7.

name: Web of System Performance (WOSP) analysis
origin: Brian Whitworth with Fjermestad and Mahinda (2006) and Bañuls, Sylla and Mahinda (2008)
summary: Specify and evaluate a design against eight paired performance requirements (functionality, usability, security, extendibility, reliability, flexibility, connectivity, privacy), weighted by environment, and resolve the tensions between pairs.
description: Whitworth argues that treating non-functional requirements as second class creates a 'requirements mess'. Any system has four constituents (boundary, structure, effector, receptor), each designed to seize opportunities or reduce risks, giving eight requirements in four pairs: security and extendibility, reliability and flexibility, functionality and usability, privacy and connectivity. They are restated at hardware, software, HCI and community levels; the social version reads productivity, synergy, freedom, order, ownership, openness, transparency and privacy. On a radar web, area is overall performance, shape reflects how the environment weights each requirement, and lines across the web are tensions that tighten as systems mature (the 'version 2 paradox'). Innovation means resolving tensions, as Palm's Graffiti resolved portability against usability that defeated the Apple Newton. Each requirement maps to its own specialist analysis and test, such as usability testing, penetration testing or legitimacy analysis.
steps: Identify the system level being designed (hardware, software, HCI or community) and translate project terms into the eight requirements using a synonyms table.
State concrete requirements for each of the eight criteria (for a community, use the social set: productivity, synergy, freedom, order, ownership, openness, transparency, privacy).
Weight each requirement for the expected environment, raising security in threat-heavy settings and extendibility in opportunity-rich ones.
Assess performance on each requirement with its matching specialist analysis or test, gathering evidence such as screenshots and test results.
Draw the radar web and compare its shape with the environment's weighting.
Identify tensions where two requirements act on the same part (for example transparency against privacy) and look for designs that satisfy both rather than trading one off.
Summarise strengths, gaps and proposed resolutions, avoiding gains in one corner at the cost of overall area.
outputs: A weighted eight-requirement performance profile (radar web), evidence per requirement, and a list of design tensions with proposed resolutions.
useWhen: When framing requirements or evaluating a complex socio-technical system where quality attributes compete, such as security against usability or openness against ownership.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need a validated score; the framework gives no standard rating instrument and weights are judgement calls. For narrower trade-offs use Kano Analysis or targeted testing.
whyLost: It comes from one research programme and course text, argued partly by biological analogy; requirements engineering kept its own quality models and UX never adopted it.
whereToUse: Platform and social product strategy, security and privacy trade-off reviews, AI agent capability design, enterprise system evaluation.
example: A messaging app's roadmap pits end-to-end encryption (privacy) against cloud search (connectivity). A WOSP review frames it as a tension and leads to on-device search, satisfying both.
reference: Whitworth, B., Bañuls, V., Sylla, C., & Mahinda, E. (2008). Expanding the criteria for evaluating socio-technical software. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part A, 38(4), 777-790.

name: Web Probing and Respondent Debriefing
origin: Martin (1984) on respondent debriefing; web probing research reviewed by Willis (2016)
summary: Adding a few open probes to a fielded or pilot survey and coding the answers at scale to learn how respondents interpreted specific items.
description: Field-based probing bridges cognitive interviews and quantitative pretests. Instead of a handful of lab interviews, a few targeted open probes are embedded in a pilot or live survey and answered by hundreds of respondents. Three probe types are used: category-selection probes (why did you choose that answer), comprehension probes (what does this term mean to you) and specific probes (what did you have in mind when answering). Probes can follow the item or come in a debriefing block at the end, and are randomised across respondents so each sees only a few. Open answers are coded into interpretation themes per item, which reveal misreadings, differences between groups or languages, and the frame of reference people used. It scales well online but adds burden and break-off, and written answers are often short.
steps: Select the items of concern, such as new, translated or ambiguous questions.
Write category-selection, comprehension or specific probes for each and decide whether they follow the item or sit in an end-of-survey debrief.
Randomise probes across respondents so each answers only a few.
Field with the pilot or main sample.
Code open answers into interpretation themes per item and compare across segments or languages.
Revise items, or document interpretation differences that explain group differences.
outputs: Coded interpretation patterns per item, frequencies of misreadings and revision recommendations.
useWhen: Checking comprehension of survey items at scale, across languages or segments, or explaining puzzling answer distributions after launch.
avoidWhen: When the reason for a misreading needs follow-up questioning; use cognitive interviews. Avoid in very long surveys where added burden would raise break-off.
whyLost: UX teams know open-ended 'why?' follow-ups but rarely use probes systematically as a pretest with coding and randomisation.
whereToUse: Multilingual product surveys, new benchmark items, AI feature satisfaction items where terms such as 'accurate' or 'helpful' are interpreted differently.
example: A generative AI writing tool asks 'How accurate were the suggestions?' Embedded comprehension probes on 600 respondents show a third read 'accurate' as grammatically correct rather than factually right, so the item is split in two.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (Wolf et al., 2016)
reference: Willis, G. B. (2016). Questionnaire pretesting. In C. Wolf, D. Joye, T. W. Smith and Y. Fu (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Survey Methodology (pp. 359-381). London: SAGE.

name: Week-in-the-Life Study
origin: Practitioner hybrid of observation, diary and interview methods common in applied research
summary: An intensive week combining baseline observation, event-contingent diaries, mid-week check-in and closing interview to map weekly patterns of product use.
description: A week-in-the-life study combines several methods into a tight seven-day protocol. Day one pairs a baseline interview with an observation session in the participant's environment to catalogue artefacts and routines. Days two to five use an event-contingent diary capturing each meaningful product interaction: time, place, device, goal, outcome, emotion and workarounds. A short mid-week call maintains engagement and catches problems. A closing interview uses diary entries as stimuli to explore typical and atypical days and patterns participants notice themselves. Analysis codes entries for occasion, outcome and workarounds and builds temporal usage maps across participants, giving more depth than a diary alone and more temporal coverage than one visit.
steps: Day 1 — Onboarding + Observation: Baseline interview (15 min) + 90-min observation session in participant's natural environment. Establish baseline usage patterns and artifact catalog.

Days 2–5 — Diary: Event-contingent diary entries for every product interaction over 30 seconds. Entry fields: time, location, device, what they were trying to do, what happened, how they felt, any workarounds used.
Day 3 — Mid-week check-in: 15-minute call. Any problems with the diary? Any notable events they want to flag? This maintains engagement and surfaces early dropout risk.

Day 7 — Closing interview: 45-minute retrospective interview using the week's diary entries as stimuli. Ask about: the most typical day, the most atypical day, any patterns they notice in their own diary, anything they expected to find but didn't.

Analysis: Code diary entries for: usage occasion (context, trigger, goal), success/failure, workaround use. Map temporal patterns: is usage concentrated at particular times of day/week? Do certain tasks correlate with certain times? Build a temporal usage map across participants.
outputs: Temporal usage maps, coded diary entries, typical and atypical day profiles, and observational baselines per participant.
useWhen: Products used across a week with rhythms (workdays, weekends, routines), and when a single session would miss variation.
avoidWhen: Very infrequent behaviours (monthly bills) or tight budgets; use a longer, lighter diary or retrospective interviews.
whyLost: It survives in agencies and service design under various names, as a pragmatic bundle rather than a codified method.
whereToUse: Meal planning and grocery apps, family scheduling tools, commuting and mobility services, and productivity software.
example: Eight households take part in a week-in-the-life study of a grocery app. Temporal maps show Sunday evening planning and weekday top-ups, leading to separate 'plan' and 'quick add' modes.
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. & Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Weekly Customer Interview Cadence
origin: Teresa Torres, 2021
summary: Establishes a sustainable rhythm in which the product trio talks to at least one customer every week, supported by automated recruiting and story-based interviews.
description: Teresa Torres's continuous discovery practice asks the product trio (product manager, designer, engineer) to interview at least one customer every week. The cadence is made sustainable by automating recruitment, for example through in-product intercepts, scheduling links and standing panels, so that interviews happen without heroic effort. Interviews collect specific stories about past behaviour rather than opinions or feature requests, and each is summarised as an interview snapshot capturing opportunities, insights and memorable quotes, which feed an opportunity solution tree. The value is cumulative: small, frequent exposures keep decisions grounded and let teams notice change. Rigour depends on story-based questioning, deliberate sampling across segments, and synthesis across snapshots rather than reacting to the latest interview.
steps: Continuous interview infrastructure:
Set up a standing recruitment pipeline (not per-study recruitment).
(2) 30-minute sessions, same day each week.
(3) Interview protocol: open with 'walk me through your last week using [product]'.
(4) Focus: collect specific stories, not opinions.
(5) After each interview: add new opportunities to the tree, update evidence for existing ones.
(6) Monthly: review the tree with the product team — what opportunities have the most evidence?
outputs: A running interview cadence, interview snapshots, an evolving opportunity solution tree, and a continuously refreshed evidence base.
useWhen: Product teams practising continuous discovery who need a steady flow of customer contact rather than periodic large studies.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it alone for rigorous, sampled answers to high-stakes questions; run dedicated studies. Avoid if interviews will be leading or sales-like rather than story-based.
whyLost: The cadence is admired but rarely sustained; recruiting friction and delivery pressure cause weekly interviews to lapse into occasional calls.
whereToUse: Product teams with continuous discovery mandates, lean UX programs, startup product development, agile UX research.
example: A fintech savings team embeds an intercept in its app that books one interview a week; each interview produces a snapshot added to the opportunity tree, which shifts priorities towards irregular-income savers.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
reference: Torres T (2021) Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products that Create Customer Value and Business Value. Product Talk LLC

name: Welcome to My World
origin: Gamestorming (2010); original source unknown according to the book
summary: Pairs from different roles each draw how they imagine the other's workflow for a duty, then compare it with reality and correct it together.
description: Welcome to My World rests on the point that nobody shares your internal map of other people's work. Each participant writes one job responsibility on a note and wears it, then pairs with the person whose responsibility they know least about. Without asking questions, each draws their best picture of the other's workflow for that duty, then shows and explains it. The pair then corrects and agrees the reality, drawing on each other's sketches and noting where ease, friction and interactions with others occur. Volunteers share insights with the whole room. The gap between imagined and real workflows exposes misconceptions and hand-off problems quickly. It needs a genuine range of roles; it loses value if everyone's work is similar.
steps: Give participants flip-chart paper, markers and notes; each writes one job responsibility and sticks it on (30 seconds).
Pair each person with the colleague whose responsibility they know least.
Each draws, in 5-15 minutes and without asking questions, the other's workflow for that duty.
Each explains their drawing to their partner (about 5 minutes).
The pair spends 5-10 minutes each correcting and agreeing the reality, marking ease, friction and hand-offs.
Volunteers share drawings and insights with the room; collect the misconceptions and friction points.
outputs: Pairs of corrected workflow sketches and a list of misconceptions, friction points and hand-offs.
useWhen: Use it to build shared understanding between functions (design, engineering, sales, support) before process change or service design, or as an ice-breaker with substance.
avoidWhen: It reveals colleagues' assumptions about each other, not users' work; for users' or employees' actual work practice use Contextual Inquiry or Organisational Ethnography and Workplace Studies, and map end-to-end delivery with a service blueprint.
whyLost: It remains a facilitation game in organisational development circles and is rarely named in UX method lists.
whereToUse: Internal tools, service design back-stage work, design operations, and cross-team onboarding.
example: In a hospital digital team, a developer draws a nurse's medication round as three app taps; the nurse redraws it with six interruptions. The gap becomes the brief for a contextual inquiry on the ward.
reference: Gray, D., Brown, S. and Macanufo, J. (2010) Gamestorming: A Playbook for Innovators, Rulebreakers, and Changemakers. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, pp. 134-135.

name: Whole-Call Recording and Reconstructed Conversation Review
origin: IVR industry practice (for example Nuance); Volio Conversation Dashboard
summary: Listen to complete, randomly sampled conversations, recorded or stitched together from logged prompts and utterances, to find dialogue-level problems invisible in per-turn metrics.
description: Most voice and conversational interface analysis works per utterance: recognition accuracy, no-match rates, intent confidence. Some problems only make sense in context, such as a failure ten turns in caused by an earlier misunderstanding. IVR practice therefore recorded whole calls, system and user, for a subset of traffic.
