A cheaper alternative reconstructs each conversation by stitching logged system prompts and user utterances in order, adding barge-in timing where enabled and screen events for multimodal apps. Calls are sampled randomly so the set is neither only smooth nor only failing, across at least a week because user types vary by time of day and weekday. Tools may need building: a turn-by-turn view of what the system said, what the user said and what happened next.
steps: Record whole calls for a subset of traffic, or log prompts, utterances, barge-in timing and screen events so conversations can be reconstructed.
Randomly sample conversations across at least one full week, avoiding samples of only errors or only successes.
Anonymise audio and transcripts before review.
Listen to (and for multimodal apps, watch) each conversation turn by turn, noting where and why the dialogue goes wrong in context.
Code dialogue-level issues such as misleading prompts, error-recovery loops and abandoned goals.
Feed issues into prompt redesign, dialogue flow changes and recognition tuning, then resample to check.
outputs: A set of dialogue-level issues with example conversations, linked to tuning and redesign actions.
useWhen: Live IVR, voice assistants and chatbots where per-turn metrics look acceptable but completion or satisfaction is poor.
avoidWhen: Avoid when storage, consent or privacy rules forbid retaining full conversations; use aggregated logs instead. For pre-launch design, use Wizard of Oz testing.
whyLost: It is routine in contact-centre quality monitoring but rarely adopted by UX teams working on chatbots and LLM assistants.
whereToUse: Customer-service chatbots, voice assistants, LLM-based agents, banking and utility IVRs.
example: An LLM support agent shows good per-turn ratings, but reviewing 200 random full transcripts reveals users looping after a vague clarification question in turn three. Rewriting that prompt cuts escalations.
reference: Pearl, C. (2017). Designing Voice User Interfaces: Principles of Conversational Experiences. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media.

name: Why-What-How Experience Design
aka: Hassenzahl's Why, What and How model
origin: Marc Hassenzahl (2010), building on psychological needs research (Sheldon et al., 2001); ordering variant by Paul Hekkert
summary: Design an interactive product by first defining the experience and the psychological needs it should fulfil (Why), then the functions (What), then the sensory-motor interaction (How).
description: Hassenzahl distinguishes three levels in designing an experience through an object. The What is what people can do with the product, its functions. The How is acting through it at the operational, sensory-motor level: buttons, gestures, sounds. The Why is the motivation for use: the psychological needs, such as relatedness, competence, autonomy, stimulation or popularity, and the emotions and meaning involved; a text message may really be a love message fulfilling relatedness. Experience design starts from the Why, clarifies the needs, emotions and meaning, and only then determines functionality and the way of putting it into action, so that the three levels chime together with the Why setting the tone. Hekkert argues for the order Why, then How (interaction qualities), then What (the carrier product).
steps: Identify the activity and the experience it should become, naming the psychological needs, emotions and meaning involved (the Why).
Express the Why as an experience goal or short story of the intended moment.
Determine functionality able to create that experience (the What).
Design how the functionality is put into action at the sensory-motor level (the How).
Check that Why, What and How chime together, with the Why setting the tone.
Variant: after the Why, define intended interaction qualities (How) before choosing the product that carries them (What).
outputs: An experience goal grounded in psychological needs, with functions and interaction qualities derived from it.
useWhen: Use it when designing for meaning and wellbeing rather than efficiency alone, for example in consumer, social or reflective products.
avoidWhen: Needs are hypotheses until checked; establish which needs matter with Interviews, Experience Sampling Method or needs questionnaires, and evaluate the result with users. Experiences cannot be guaranteed, only designed for.
whyLost: It is influential in academic experience design and European design schools but rarely appears as an explicit step in product teams' processes.
whereToUse: Wellbeing and health products, social and family technology, smart home, automotive interiors, and AI companions.
example: A family photo-sharing app starts from relatedness: grandparents feeling part of daily life. That Why leads to a weekly printed digest (What) delivered with a single tap to send a reaction (How).
reference: Hassenzahl, M. (2010). Experience Design: Technology for All the Right Reasons. San Rafael, CA: Morgan & Claypool.

name: Wicked problem framing
origin: Horst Rittel and Melvin Webber, 'Dilemmas in a General Theory of Planning', 1973
summary: Frames a design challenge using Rittel and Webber's ten characteristics of wicked problems, to decide how to approach it rather than prematurely solving it.
description: Rittel and Webber described wicked problems as having no definitive formulation, no stopping rule, solutions that are better or worse rather than true or false, no immediate test of a solution, every attempt counting, no enumerable set of solutions, uniqueness, being symptoms of other problems, multiple explanations, and planners having no right to be wrong. Wicked problem framing assesses a challenge against these characteristics and selects appropriate approaches: iterative and participatory processes, multiple framings, and argumentation-based methods such as Rittel's Issue-Based Information System (IBIS). In UX, the term is widely cited as a label for 'hard problems' but rarely applied as an analysis that changes method choice, which is why it is vestigial.
steps: Write the problem statement as stakeholders currently express it.
Assess it against the ten wickedness characteristics, scoring each as absent, partial or present with evidence.
Collect alternative framings from at least 4-6 stakeholder groups, noting conflicting causal explanations.
Map issues, positions and arguments using IBIS or dialogue mapping.
Choose an approach suited to the degree of wickedness: iterative small experiments, participatory processes and explicit trade-off documentation.
Define provisional success criteria and review points rather than a single solution test.
outputs: A wickedness assessment, alternative framings, an issue map, and an approach plan with provisional success criteria.
useWhen: For complex sociotechnical challenges with conflicting stakeholders, such as healthcare systems, policy and platform governance.
avoidWhen: For tame problems with clear criteria and solutions; standard design and testing processes are more efficient.
whyLost: The label became fashionable in design thinking, but the analytical characteristics and IBIS tooling were mostly forgotten.
whereToUse: Healthcare delivery, climate and sustainability products, AI governance, public services, and organisational change.
example: Framing 'reduce OR turnaround time' reveals conflicting explanations from surgeons, nurses and managers and no clear stopping rule. The team switches from a single redesign to iterative experiments and dialogue mapping of trade-offs.
sources: PACT analysis (Dix; Benyon, Designing Interactive Systems)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
reference: Rittel, H. W. J. & Webber, M. M. (1973). Dilemmas in a general theory of planning. Policy Sciences, 4(2), 155-169.

name: Wigmore Evidence Charting
origin: John Henry Wigmore, 1913 (The Principles of Judicial Proof); revived by Terence Anderson, David Schum and William Twining (Analysis of Evidence, 2005)
summary: Charts the full chain of inferences from each piece of evidence to the ultimate conclusion, including corroborating and contradicting evidence and the credibility of sources.
description: Wigmore devised a graphical notation for analysing masses of mixed evidence in legal cases: each proposition is a node, with symbols for testimonial and circumstantial evidence, explanatory and corroborative relations, and the analyst's belief in each. The key protocol is Anderson, Schum and Twining's seven-step method: clarify standpoint, formulate ultimate probanda (what must be proved), penultimate probanda, theories of the case, list evidence (key list), construct the chart, and refine. Schum extended it to probabilistic inference networks. For research synthesis across many studies, interviews and data sources, Wigmore charts make inferential chains auditable and reveal where conclusions rest on single, weak sources.
steps: Clarify standpoint and the question the synthesis must answer.
Formulate the ultimate proposition (e.g. 'small businesses will adopt automated bookkeeping if X') and the penultimate propositions it depends on.
Compile a key list of all evidence items, noting source and credibility.
Build the chart linking evidence through intermediate inferences to propositions, marking corroboration and contradiction.
Assess the strength of each link and identify weak or single-source chains.
Refine the conclusion and target new research at the weakest links.
outputs: A Wigmore chart and key list, explicit inferential chains, strength assessments and targeted research gaps.
useWhen: High-stakes syntheses drawing on many heterogeneous sources, or where conclusions will be challenged.
avoidWhen: Simple studies with a single data source and narrow conclusions.
whyLost: Even in law the notation was considered laborious; it was never introduced to design research.
whereToUse: Strategic research synthesis, regulatory submissions (e.g. medical device usability), investigations, contested product decisions.
example: A synthesis claiming clinicians will accept AI triage is charted. The chart shows the key inference rests on a single pilot site's survey, while three interview sources contradict it; the conclusion is downgraded and a multi-site study commissioned.
sources: Anderson, Schum & Twining, Analysis of Evidence (2nd ed., 2005)
Wigmore, The Principles of Judicial Proof (1913)
Schum, The Evidential Foundations of Probabilistic Reasoning (1994)
reference: Anderson, T., Schum, D., & Twining, W. (2005). Analysis of Evidence (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

name: Willingness to Pay and Welfare Measures from Choice Models
aka: Willingness to pay from a choice model
origin: Discrete choice econometrics: log-sum consumer surplus by Williams (1977) and Small and Rosen (1981); presented by Train (2009) and, for marketing, Chapman and Feit (2019)
summary: Convert choice-model coefficients into money: attribute willingness to pay as a ratio to the price coefficient, its distribution under random coefficients, and welfare change from the log-sum.
description: Once a conjoint or discrete choice model is fitted with price as a numeric predictor, coefficients can be expressed in currency. The average willingness to pay for an attribute level is its coefficient divided by minus the price coefficient, scaled to the price unit; with time and cost coefficients the same ratio gives the value of time. With random coefficients WTP becomes a distribution: a ratio of lognormal coefficients is itself lognormal, so median and mean can differ greatly. For whole choice sets, expected consumer surplus under a logit model with income-linear utility is the log of the logit denominator (the log-sum) divided by the marginal utility of income; computing it before and after a change in alternatives or attributes gives the welfare change. Chapman and Feit warn that 'willingness to pay' is a misnomer: it is the price change at which the average respondent is indifferent, not an amount customers would actually pay, so share simulations often communicate better.
steps: Fit a choice model with price as a single numeric coefficient, checking with a likelihood ratio test that this fits as well as price coded as a factor.
For each attribute level, divide its coefficient by minus the price coefficient and multiply by the price unit to get its money equivalent relative to the base level.
If coefficients are random (mixed logit), simulate the ratio across the coefficient distributions and report median, mean and spread of WTP rather than a single value.
For a change to the choice set or its attributes, compute the log-sum divided by the marginal utility of income before and after, and take the difference as the change in expected consumer surplus.
Report results as indifference prices from stated choices, alongside market-share simulations, with uncertainty intervals.
outputs: Money values per attribute level, WTP distributions across respondents, and welfare change estimates for product or policy changes.
useWhen: Pricing features or tiers, comparing the value users place on attributes in a common unit, or estimating how much better or worse off users are after adding, removing or changing options.
avoidWhen: When price was not varied in the design or fits poorly as a linear term; for communicating with most stakeholders, prefer the Conjoint Choice Simulator; for direct elicitation of what people would pay use the Becker-DeGroot-Marschak Willingness-to-Pay Auction.
whyLost: It is routine in transport and environmental economics and pricing consultancies but rarely reaches UX research, where conjoint is reported as importance scores and shares.
whereToUse: SaaS tier design, subscription and add-on pricing, marketplace fees, removing a free feature, public-service option changes.
example: A video service's choice study gives ad-free viewing a WTP of about 3.10 a month at the mean but 1.80 at the median, because a minority value it highly. The team prices the ad-free add-on near the median and models welfare loss from removing offline downloads via the log-sum.
sources: R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chapman & Feit, 2019)
reference: Train, K. E. (2009). Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation (2nd ed.). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press; Small, K. A. and Rosen, H. S. (1981). Applied welfare economics with discrete choice models. Econometrica, 49(1), 105-130.

name: Wireflow Prototyping
aka: Horizontal, vertical, T and local prototypes
origin: Horizontal and vertical prototypes from Nielsen (1993) and Kensing and Munk-Madsen (1993); wireflows from practitioner sources; assembled by Hartson and Pyla (2019)
summary: Choose a prototype's breadth and depth for the question at hand, link wireframes into a wireflow of navigation states, and raise fidelity in planned stages.
description: Wireflow prototyping is about planning a prototype rather than just drawing one. Scope comes first: horizontal prototypes are broad and shallow (many features, little depth), vertical ones narrow and deep, T prototypes combine both, and local prototypes isolate one detail so users can settle a design deadlock. Wireflows are directed graphs of wireframes derived from state diagrams of task sequences, showing each screen state and the transitions between them. Fidelity is raised in planned levels, from sketched wireframe decks to click-through and visually high-fidelity prototypes, often from a template library. For empirical tests, Hartson and Pyla add plausible decoy objects and a 'not implemented' message, so that tasks are not unrealistically easy along a happy-path-only prototype.
steps: Decide what the prototype must answer and choose its scope: horizontal, vertical, T or local.
Draw state diagrams of the main navigation from task sequence models.
Create a wireframe for each state and link them into a wireflow showing transitions.
Raise fidelity in planned levels (sketch, wireframe, click-through, visual), reusing a template library.
Before user testing, add plausible decoy objects and a 'not implemented' message for unbuilt paths.
Refine through evaluation and repeat at the next fidelity level.
outputs: Wireflows and prototypes at a chosen scope and fidelity, ready for evaluation.
useWhen: Use it when moving from concept to testable design and you need to match prototype breadth, depth and fidelity to the questions being asked.
avoidWhen: A prototype answers nothing until tested; evaluate it with Prototype Testing or Usability Testing. If the question is information structure rather than flow, use Tree Testing.
whyLost: It survived because wireframes and flows are the everyday medium of UX design, though the explicit scope and decoy planning are less often taught.
whereToUse: Web and mobile apps, enterprise workflows, checkout and onboarding, and any design handed to engineering.
example: For a university's network-services ordering flow, the team builds a vertical prototype of 'bundle services' with decoy menu items. Testers who wander into decoys reveal that the bundle entry point is hard to find.
reference: Hartson, R. and Pyla, P. (2019). The UX Book: Agile UX Design for a Quality User Experience. 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 20.

name: Within- and Between-Person Decomposition of Time-Varying Predictors
aka: Within-subject causal process model with person-mean centring
origin: Hoffman and Stawski, 2009; Curran and Bauer, 2011; Bolger and Laurenceau, 2013; Wang and Maxwell, 2015
summary: Enter each person's mean of a time-varying predictor and each moment's deviation from it as separate predictors, to separate between-person differences from within-person associations.
description: A correlation across pooled repeated measures mixes two questions: do people who are more stressed on average feel worse, and does a person feel worse when more stressed than usual? A model with the raw predictor gives an uninterpretable blend. Adding the person mean and the person-mean centred value separates the two; they can differ in size and even sign. In the ESM handbook example the between-person slope was over three times the within-person slope, and the within estimate was about 60 times more precise. Bolger and Laurenceau's daily process model (daily conflict predicting same-day intimacy) adds control for time trend and AR(1) errors. They argue diary designs give better causal leverage than one-off surveys because measurement follows causes and effects as they change, while still ranking far below experiments. The split extends to lagged predictors and group differences at each level. Person means from few observations are unreliable.
steps: Compute each person's mean of the time-varying predictor.
Compute person-mean centred values (each moment minus the person's own mean).
Fit a mixed model with both as predictors, a random intercept and a random slope for the centred term.
Control for time trend and allow autocorrelated (AR(1)) residuals in daily or momentary data.
Interpret the centred coefficient as the within-person association and the mean coefficient as the between-person association.
Add group interactions at each level if needed, and report both effects; never infer within-person effects from cross-sectional data.
outputs: Separate within-person and between-person coefficients with their uncertainty and variance explained.
useWhen: Diary, ESM, repeated survey or logged usage data where you want to know whether changes within a person go with changes in an outcome.
avoidWhen: Cross-sectional data with one observation per person; you cannot separate levels. Both effects remain correlational.
whyLost: UX analysts typically pool repeated observations in one regression or correlation, so the distinction between 'people who' and 'moments when' is lost.
whereToUse: Daily productivity tool studies, wellbeing app research, repeated NPS or satisfaction pulses, and session-level telemetry joined to surveys.
example: Users who encounter more errors on average report lower satisfaction, but within a person, a day with more errors than usual barely lowers satisfaction. The team learns that error-prone users differ in other ways and does not overstate the effect of reducing errors.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Within- and Between-Person Reliability of Momentary Scales
aka: Reliability of within-person change: G-theory and multilevel CFA omega
Cranford et al. reliability of change
origin: Cranford et al., 2006; Shrout and Lane, 2012; Geldhof, Preacher and Zyphur, 2014; Nezlek, 2017
summary: Estimate separately how reliably a multi-item momentary scale detects change within persons and differences between persons, and check its factor structure at each level.
description: Repeated-measures scales need two reliabilities: one for between-person differences and one for within-person change. A generalisability-theory approach decomposes variance into time, person, item and their interactions, giving RC, the reliability of change; in Bolger and Laurenceau's example a four-item positive affect scale over 10 days had RC = .77. Nezlek's approach fits a three-level model (items in occasions in persons). CFA approaches compute omega at each level from a multilevel CFA or two-step within and between decompositions; the example's within-person omega was .79. Per-person CFAs can also give a distribution of reliabilities. Factor structure can differ by level (for example two factors within persons and one between), so unidimensionality and convergent and discriminant correlations are checked at each level. There is no gold standard, methods differ in handling autocorrelation, and single-item measures cannot be assessed this way.
steps: Include at least three items per key construct in the momentary questionnaire.
Fit a multilevel CFA, or two-step within and between CFAs, or a G-theory time x person x item model.
Compute omega (or RC for change and the corresponding between-person coefficient) at the within and between levels.
Check unidimensionality at each level separately.
Check convergent and discriminant correlations at each level.
Report both reliabilities with the method used, and do not reuse a between-person reliability as evidence of sensitivity to change.
outputs: Within-level and between-level reliability coefficients, and level-specific factor structures.
useWhen: Validating multi-item scales used in diaries, ESM or repeated in-product surveys, especially when you will interpret day-to-day change.
avoidWhen: Single-item measures or cross-sectional surveys; use standard reliability analysis there.
whyLost: UX teams report Cronbach's alpha from one administration even for repeated measures; multilevel reliability remains specialist psychometrics.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX metrics, wellbeing and burnout tracking in workplace tools, and repeated satisfaction pulses.
example: A team tracking daily 'AI trust' with four items finds between-person omega of .90 but within-person omega of .55. Day-to-day changes are mostly noise, so the scale is revised before using it to detect the effect of a release.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Within-case and cross-case analysis
donor: Education research, comparative sociology and case study methodology
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994); case study methodology by Robert Yin (1984 onwards); comparative logic from Ragin (1987)
summary: First builds an understanding of each case as a whole, then compares cases systematically to find patterns, configurations and explanations that hold across them.
description: Variable-oriented synthesis pools quotes across participants and loses the configuration of conditions within each case. Within-case analysis first constructs a coherent account of each case (a person, a clinic, an account), often as a case summary and display. Cross-case analysis then compares cases using strategies such as stacking comparable displays, partitioning cases by outcome, building meta-matrices, and identifying configurations of conditions associated with outcomes. Yin's replication logic treats each case like an experiment: literal replication predicts similar results, theoretical replication predicts contrasting results for predictable reasons. Rigour comes from standardising within-case write-ups so they can be compared, from case selection that supports replication logic, and from explaining every case, including deviant ones.
steps: Define the case unit (a user, household, clinic or organisation) and select cases to allow literal and theoretical replication, typically 6 to 20 cases.
For each case, write a standardised within-case summary of 2 to 4 pages and build a within-case display, such as a time-ordered matrix or causal network.
Choose cross-case dimensions from the research questions and build a meta-matrix with cases as rows and dimensions as columns.
Partition and sort cases by outcome (for example adopters versus non-adopters) and look for conditions that consistently differ between groups.
Identify configurations of conditions that co-occur with outcomes, and check each deviant case to explain or bound the pattern.
State cross-case propositions with the number of supporting and contradicting cases, and link back to within-case evidence.
outputs: Standardised case summaries and displays, a cross-case meta-matrix, outcome-partitioned comparisons and cross-case propositions with support counts.
useWhen: Studying organisations, sites or households where context matters; explaining differing outcomes such as why some clinics adopted and others did not.
avoidWhen: Cases are not meaningful units or the interest is in individual opinions across a large sample; use thematic analysis or a survey.
whyLost: It is standard in case study research and evaluation but UX synthesis usually pools participant data, losing case configurations.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise research, multi-site health and education deployments, household fintech research, organisational AI adoption.
example: A 20-participant cross-cultural study treated each clinic as a case. Cross-case analysis showed adoption occurred only where reliable power and supervisor acceptance of digital records coincided; neither condition alone was sufficient, a configuration lost in pooled themes.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage; Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). Sage. Yin, R. K. (2018). Case Study Research and Applications (6th ed.). Sage.

name: Within-Group Agreement Index (rwg)
aka: James, Demaree and Wolf agreement index
origin: James, Demaree and Wolf (1984, 1993); its use for team-level constructs in sport critically reviewed by Myers and Feltz in Chapter 36 of the Handbook
summary: Quantifies how far members of the same group agree in their ratings, compared with the spread expected if they answered at random, before or alongside averaging their answers to the group level.
description: When individuals rate a shared property, such as their team's capability or their company's experience of a product, researchers often average the ratings to get one group score. The rwg index estimates within-group agreement by comparing the observed variance of ratings with the variance expected if responses were random. With multiple parallel items, rwg(J) combines the mean observed item variance with the number of items J; values near 1 mean strong agreement and values near 0 mean agreement no better than chance. The expected variance is usually taken from a uniform distribution, (A squared minus 1) divided by 12, where A is the number of response categories. It can be adjusted when response biases such as leniency or social desirability are expected. The Handbook warns against several common practices. The often-quoted 0.70 cut-off has no clear source. Too many response categories inflate rwg. Groups should not be dropped for low agreement. Instead, rwg should be reported descriptively and used as a group-level variable in multilevel models. For UX, this matters in B2B research, where scores from several users at one customer account are averaged into an account-level satisfaction or health score.
steps: Confirm that the items measure a shared, group-level property and form one dimension.
Collect ratings from several members of each group, such as each customer account or team.
Choose the expected random variance (uniform by default, adjusted if a response bias is expected) and state the choice.
Compute rwg(J) for each group across the parallel items.
Report the distribution of rwg values rather than discarding low-agreement groups.
Use rwg as a moderator in multilevel models, or flag accounts with low agreement for qualitative follow-up.
outputs: An agreement value for each group, a transparent account of how it was computed, and group-level scores whose meaning is qualified by within-group consensus.
useWhen: You aggregate several individuals' ratings into a team, account or site score and need to know whether the average reflects a shared view.
avoidWhen: Each respondent is the unit of analysis, or groups have only one or two respondents.
whyLost: UX analytics usually averages ratings without considering group structure; agreement indices belong to organisational and multilevel research.
whereToUse: B2B account health and NPS programmes, enterprise collaboration tools, team-level surveys, multi-site clinical or retail deployments.
example: A SaaS company averages satisfaction scores from users at each customer account. rwg shows that several mid-scoring accounts have very low agreement: administrators are happy and end users are not. Customer success teams then interview both roles at those accounts.
sources: Tenenbaum, G. & Eklund, R. (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd ed. (2007)
reference: Myers, N. D. and Feltz, D. L. (2007) 'From self-efficacy to collective efficacy in sport: transitional methodological issues', in G. Tenenbaum and R. C. Eklund (eds), Handbook of Sport Psychology, 3rd edn. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. Chapter 36.

name: Within-group practice-dose analysis
aka: Within-group practice-dose analysis with a reverse-causation check
origin: Contemplative intervention trials (Pace, Negi et al.; Kok et al.; Kemeny et al.), as reported in Singer and Bolz (2013)
summary: Log how much each participant in an intervention actually engages, relate that dose to outcomes within the treated group, and check baseline measures do not predict later engagement.
description: Intervention trials often show weak group effects because many participants barely use the intervention. Dose analysis records actual practice or engagement for each person in the treated arm and tests whether more use goes with better outcomes, as a continuous relationship or a median split. In a compassion training trial there was no group effect on stress hormones, but high-practice participants recovered to baseline cortisol faster and produced less of an inflammatory marker. The key safeguard is a reverse-causation check: if baseline outcome measures do not predict later practice, self-selection becomes a less likely explanation. The association remains correlational because dose is self-selected, so it is reported alongside, not instead of, the between-group comparison. In digital products, it maps directly onto engagement with coaching, learning or health apps.
steps: Log practice or engagement per participant throughout the intervention (sessions, minutes, completed exercises).
Run the planned between-group comparison as the primary analysis.
Within the treated arm, test the dose-outcome association, continuously or with a median split.
Check that baseline outcome measures do not predict later engagement, to argue against self-selection.
Report dose-response estimates alongside the between-group result, labelling them as correlational.
outputs: Dose-response estimates within the treated group and a selection check, reported alongside the main group comparison.
useWhen: Evaluating digital health, wellbeing, learning or coaching interventions where engagement varies widely and the overall effect is diluted.
avoidWhen: When dose can be randomised (run a dose-ranging experiment instead), or when engagement is clearly driven by baseline severity or motivation that the check reveals.
whyLost: Product analytics reports engagement and outcomes separately, and the reverse-causation check from clinical trials is rarely applied.
whereToUse: Mental health and meditation apps, fitness and rehabilitation programmes, language learning, employee training platforms.
example: A sleep-coaching app trial shows no overall difference in sleep quality, but users completing four or more sessions a week improve markedly. Baseline sleep scores do not predict session counts, so the team invests in adherence features and plans a randomised dose test.
sources: Compassion: Bridging Practice and Science (Singer & Bolz, 2013)
reference: Pace, T. W. W., Negi, L. T., Adame, D. D., Cole, S. P., Sivilli, T. I., Brown, T. D., Issa, M. J. and Raison, C. L. (2009). Effect of compassion meditation on neuroendocrine, innate immune and behavioral responses to psychosocial stress. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 34(1), 87-98.

name: Within-Person Dynamics Indices (Variability, Instability, Inertia)
origin: Kuppens and colleagues; Jahng et al., 2008; Kuppens, Allen and Sheeber, 2010
summary: Summarise how a repeatedly measured state behaves within each person: how much it varies, how large its successive jumps are, and how much it carries over between moments.
description: Three per-person indices describe the dynamics of repeated momentary measures. Variability (the within-person SD) ignores order; instability, the mean squared successive difference (MSSD), measures the size of changes from one moment to the next; inertia, the lag-1 autocorrelation, measures self-predictability. A person who is fine early in the week and low later can have the same variability as one who alternates constantly, but very different instability. High inertia suggests a self-sustaining state and low inertia one driven by outside events. Very high autocorrelation can also signal oversampling, and near-zero autocorrelation undersampling. Inertia can be estimated as a random autoregressive slope in a multilevel model, controlling for time trends. Analysts should check initial elevation bias, the tendency of first reports to be higher, before interpreting. The indices correlate with each other and with the mean, and unequal spacing distorts lag-based ones.
steps: Collect enough roughly equally spaced observations per person (several dozen where possible).

Compute each person's mean and SD (variability), mean squared successive difference (instability) and lag-1 autocorrelation (inertia), or fit a multilevel autoregressive model with a random lag slope.
Exclude lags that cross nights or persons.
Check and control time trends and initial elevation of the first reports before interpreting.
Adjust for or report correlations between the indices and the person mean.
Relate the indices to person-level outcomes or segments.
outputs: Per-person dynamic profiles (mean, variability, instability, inertia) and their associations with outcomes.
useWhen: Diary or experience-sampling studies of mood, frustration, trust or effort where how a state fluctuates matters as much as its average level.
avoidWhen: Few observations per person (under about 20) or highly irregular spacing; report means and simple trajectories instead.
whyLost: UX diary data is usually summarised as averages and themes; dynamic indices are standard in affective science but have not crossed into UX analysis.
whereToUse: Wellbeing and mental-health apps, workplace tool stress studies, wearable-linked mood tracking, and long-term AI companion use.
example: In a six-week ESM study of a meditation app, two users have the same mean stress but one shows high inertia: bad mornings persist all day. The team tests a mid-day prompt targeted at high-inertia users.
sources: The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022)
reference: Myin-Germeys, I. and Kuppens, P. (Eds.) (2022). The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology: A Step-by-Step Guide to Designing, Conducting, and Analyzing ESM Studies (2nd ed.). Leuven: Center for Research on Experience Sampling and Ambulatory Methods Leuven (REAL).

name: Within-Study Comparison
aka: Within-study comparison (benchmarking observational estimators against an experiment)
origin: LaLonde (1986); Dehejia and Wahba (1999, 2002)
summary: Replace an experiment's control group with an observational comparison group and test whether observational estimators recover the known experimental effect.
description: When a randomised experiment exists, its effect is a benchmark against which observational methods can be calibrated. LaLonde took the National Supported Work job-training experiment, swapped its randomised controls for comparison groups drawn from national surveys, and applied the econometric estimators of the day. Their estimates were far off and often had the wrong sign, which pushed policy evaluation towards experiments. Dehejia and Wahba repeated the exercise with propensity scores, checking overlap, trimming controls outside the treated range and comparing covariate balance, and came close to the benchmark. The exercise tells you which observational methods and diagnostics can be trusted in a particular domain. For product teams with both A/B tests and observational analytics, it shows whether quasi-experimental estimates from logs can stand in for experiments.
steps: Obtain a randomised experiment with a credible benchmark effect, such as a past A/B test.
Build one or more non-experimental comparison groups for the treated units, for example users not exposed in a similar period or market.
Apply candidate observational estimators (regression adjustment, difference-in-differences, matching, inverse probability weighting).
Compare each estimate, and its balance and overlap diagnostics, with the experimental benchmark.
Conclude which methods and diagnostics are trustworthy for similar non-experimental questions in this product, and document the conditions.
outputs: A calibration of observational estimators against ground truth, with the diagnostics that predicted success or failure.
useWhen: A team routinely estimates feature impact from observational data and has some past experiments to calibrate against.
avoidWhen: No credible experimental benchmark exists. Conclusions depend on sample definitions and trimming and generalise only to similar settings.
whyLost: It is a methodological exercise from econometrics; product analytics teams rarely audit their observational methods against their own experiments.
whereToUse: Product analytics, marketplace and pricing teams, health services evaluation, any organisation mixing A/B tests with causal inference from logs.
example: An e-commerce analytics team reruns five past A/B tests observationally. Propensity matching recovers four effects within the experimental interval, while naive before-after comparisons overstate all five, so before-after reports are retired.
reference: LaLonde, R. J. (1986). Evaluating the econometric evaluations of training programs with experimental data. American Economic Review, 76(4), 604-620.

name: Within-Subject (1-1-1) Multilevel Mediation
aka: Multilevel mediation with random indirect effects
origin: Krull and MacKinnon, 2001; Kenny, Korchmaros and Bolger, 2003; Bauer, Preacher and Gil, 2006
summary: Test whether a within-person link from X to Y runs through a same-occasion mediator, letting each person have their own paths and adding their covariance to the indirect effect.
description: In diary data a cause, mediator and outcome can all vary from day to day within each person, and each person can have their own X-to-M (a) and M-to-Y (b) paths. The average indirect effect is then not just the product of the average a and b: it also includes the covariance between people's a and b paths, which can be a large share of the effect. Scenarios are labelled by level (2-2-1, 2-1-1, 1-1-1); this covers 1-1-1. X, M and Y are all person-mean centred so only within-person variation is analysed. The M and Y equations must be estimated jointly, either by stacking data with one M row and one Y row per occasion and selector dummies, or with multilevel SEM such as Mplus; both give the same estimates. In Bolger and Laurenceau's example the a-b covariance was over half of the mediated effect.
steps: State the X to M to Y process and check timing: X and M should precede Y within each occasion.
Person-mean centre X, M and Y so each carries only within-person variation.
Either stack the data with one M row and one Y row per occasion and dummies selecting the equation, or use multilevel SEM software.
Fit the M equation (M on X) and Y equation (Y on M and X) jointly, without intercepts, with random a, b and c-prime slopes and their covariances.
Allow separate residual variances for the M and Y rows.
Compute the average indirect effect as a times b plus the a-b covariance, and the total effect as that plus c-prime.
Test the indirect effect and the a-b covariance with Monte Carlo or bootstrap confidence intervals, and report the share mediated.
outputs: Average within-person a, b and direct effects, their between-person variances, the a-b covariance, and average indirect and total effects.
useWhen: Diary or ESM studies asking how a daily experience affects an outcome, for example whether tool friction raises evening frustration through perceived workload.
avoidWhen: Cross-sectional data or few occasions per person; use single-level mediation with caution. Effects remain correlational, and mediator measurement error biases the paths.
whyLost: Mediation in UX, when used at all, is single-level; random indirect effects need specialist multilevel or SEM skills.
whereToUse: Workplace tool wellbeing studies, learning apps, health behaviour apps and longitudinal AI assistant research.
example: Over 15 workdays, days with more failed AI suggestions bring higher perceived workload, which in turn predicts lower end-of-day satisfaction. The a-b covariance shows that developers most sensitive to failures are also those whose satisfaction depends most on workload.
reference: Bolger, N. and Laurenceau, J.-P. (2013). Intensive Longitudinal Methods: An Introduction to Diary and Experience Sampling Research. New York: Guilford Press.

name: Wizard of Oz Prototyping
donor: Human-computer interaction and speech technology research
origin: J. F. Kelley, 1983 (coined term, IBM natural-language studies); Gould, Conti and Hovanyecz listening typewriter study (1983)
summary: A hidden human operator simulates system intelligence such as speech, AI or recommendation logic, letting you test interaction concepts before the technology exists.
description: In a Wizard of Oz study the participant interacts with what appears to be a working system while a hidden 'wizard' produces the system's responses in real time. It lets teams study how people speak to, trust and recover from errors with intelligent systems before investing in models or infrastructure. Rigour depends on wizard consistency: a written response protocol, constrained response libraries, deliberate simulated error rates, and timing that mirrors realistic latency. Without these, the wizard behaves like an idealised human, inflating satisfaction and hiding the failure modes real systems produce. Ethical practice requires debriefing participants about the deception. The method is widely used for conversational, voice and generative AI concepts, and for exploring how much automation people want.
steps: Define the system capabilities to simulate and the questions to answer (vocabulary, turn-taking, trust, error recovery).
Write a wizard protocol with response rules, a library of permitted replies, target latency and a planned error rate (for example 10-20% misrecognitions).
Build a front end that routes participant input to the wizard and wizard output back to the participant without revealing a human.
Pilot with 2-3 people to train the wizard and check the illusion holds and responses stay consistent.
Run 6-12 sessions, logging all inputs, wizard responses, timings and participant reactions, with a separate observer.
Debrief participants about the simulation, then analyse utterance patterns, failure recovery and expectations to specify the real system.
outputs: Corpus of real user utterances, interaction patterns, error-recovery behaviours, capability requirements and validated conversation design.
useWhen: Early testing of conversational agents, voice interfaces, AI assistants, adaptive recommendations or any system whose intelligence is expensive to build.
avoidWhen: When the real model already exists (test it directly, since wizards hide true error profiles) or when the deception would be ethically inappropriate for the population.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for AI product research; enables testing of intelligent behavior without engineering.
whereToUse: Conversational AI; voice UI; recommendation systems; any AI feature early research.
example: A telehealth company tests an AI symptom checker by having a nurse act as the wizard behind a chat interface, constrained to a scripted library with deliberate misunderstandings. Sessions reveal patients abandon after the second clarifying question, shaping the eventual model's dialogue policy.
sources: Kelley, An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications (ACM TOIS, 1984)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kelley JF (1984) An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications. ACM TOIS 2(1)
Dahlbäck N, Jönsson A & Ahrenberg L (1993) Wizard of Oz studies: why and how. IUI
Gould JD, Conti J & Hovanyecz T (1983) Composing letters with a simulated listening typewriter. CACM 26(4)
Chatbot Research and Design: CONVERSATIONS 2022 (Følstad et al., 2023)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar et al., 2017)
Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction (Preece et al., 2019)
Designing the User Interface (Shneiderman et al., 2018)
reference: Kelley JF (1984) An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications. ACM Transactions on Information Systems 2(1):26-41

name: Wood's friction theory
donor: Social psychology (habit science and Lewinian field theory)
origin: Wendy Wood, Good Habits, Bad Habits (2019), building on Kurt Lewin's driving and restraining forces (1951)
summary: Analyses the small situational frictions, such as distance, steps and delay, that make desired behaviours harder and undesired ones easier, then redesigns friction deliberately.
description: Wood argues that behaviour is shaped more by context than by willpower, and that friction, the time, distance and effort a behaviour requires, is one of the strongest contextual forces. Lewin described behaviour as a balance of driving and restraining forces and argued that removing restraints is often more effective than adding drivers. In Wood's habit research, small changes in proximity, ease or delay produce large shifts in repeated behaviour. Friction analysis inventories frictions on the desired path and the competing path, measures them in concrete units (taps, seconds, metres, waiting time, permissions), and redesigns to lower friction for desired behaviours and raise it for undesired ones. Rigour comes from quantifying friction rather than labelling it, and from comparing both paths rather than optimising one in isolation.
steps: Define the desired behaviour and the competing behaviour users currently choose (for example digital entry versus paper register).
Walk both paths in context and list every friction point: physical distance, steps, taps, typing, waits, logins, connectivity checks, approvals and social awkwardness.
Quantify each friction in concrete units, such as time in seconds, taps, metres or failure probability, using timing from at least 5 to 10 observed repetitions.
Build a force-field table that compares total friction on each path, highlighting the restraining forces on the desired path that exceed the competing path's equivalents.
Redesign to remove the largest restraining forces on the desired path and, where ethical, add small friction to the competing path, such as removing blank paper forms from the desk.
Measure behaviour share for the desired path before and after over at least 4 weeks, since friction changes act through repetition.
outputs: A quantified friction inventory for desired and competing paths, a force-field comparison, and measured behaviour change after friction redesign.
useWhen: Users know the desired behaviour and intend it but do not do it consistently; a competing legacy behaviour is easier in context.
avoidWhen: Users lack motivation or understanding rather than ease, or friction serves safety (confirmation for irreversible actions); in those cases use motivation research or keep protective friction.
whyLost: UX uses 'friction' as loose jargon for anything annoying, detached from Wood's habit science and Lewin's force-field analysis, so friction is seldom quantified on both competing paths.
whereToUse: Digital replacement of paper processes, health adherence, savings automation, security behaviours such as MFA, sustainable choices in commerce.
example: Digital entry required unlocking a tablet, a 30-second login and a sync wait, about 70 seconds before the first field, while the paper register was open on the desk. Keeping the app session alive for the shift and caching offline cut start friction to 8 seconds and halved paper duplication.
sources: The Inquiry Series, Ch 24 — Behavior Models, Habits & the Anatomy of Non-Adoption
reference: Wood, W. (2019). Good Habits, Bad Habits: The Science of Making Positive Changes That Stick. Farrar, Straus and Giroux; Lewin, K. (1951). Field Theory in Social Science. Harper.

name: Word embeddings and semantic similarity
origin: Distributional hypothesis (Firth, 1957; Harris, 1954); word2vec by Mikolov et al., 2013; sentence embeddings (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)
summary: Represents words, sentences or documents as dense vectors where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness, enabling clustering, search and comparison of user text.
description: Embeddings encode meaning learned from large corpora, so 'can't find my money' and 'funds missing' sit close together even without shared words. Sentence and document embeddings let researchers cluster open-ended feedback, deduplicate tickets, find all comments similar to a key quote, map feedback onto existing codebooks and measure how semantically close user language is to product terminology. Rigour involves choosing a model suited to the domain and language, checking that similarity matches human judgement on a sample, being aware of biases embedded from training corpora, and avoiding treating cosine similarity thresholds as universal. Clustering embeddings should be validated by reading samples, as with any computational qualitative method.
steps: Choose an embedding model suited to the text type and languages (e.g. a multilingual sentence-transformer).
Clean the text and compute embeddings for each document or sentence.
Calibrate similarity: have researchers rate 50-100 pairs and pick thresholds that match human judgement.
Apply to the task: semantic search for quotes, clustering (e.g. UMAP plus HDBSCAN), or matching feedback to codebook definitions.
Review samples from each cluster or match set to verify meaning, and refine thresholds.
Document model version, thresholds and known biases.
outputs: Embedding vectors, calibrated similarity thresholds, semantic clusters or search results and documentation of model choices.
useWhen: Large volumes of open text where you need to find, group or map meaning beyond keyword matching.
avoidWhen: Avoid when exact terminology matters (legal or medical coding needs controlled vocabularies), with tiny corpora, or when embedding bias could distort sensitive analyses without audit.
whyLost: It survived and spread because embedding APIs became cheap and are built into research repositories and feedback tools.
whereToUse: Feedback repositories, support ticket triage, terminology research for IA, mapping AI chat logs, research repository search.
example: A research team embeds 12,000 survey comments and searches with a quote about 'fear of pressing the wrong button'. It retrieves 340 semantically similar comments, quantifying a theme from six interviews.
sources: A Practical Guide to Sentiment Analysis (Erik Cambria et al.)
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Mikolov et al. (2013) Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space
The Inquiry Series, Ch 55 — Natural Language at Scale — Computational Qualitative Analysis
Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Bishop & Bishop, 2024)
reference: Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G. & Dean, J. (2013) Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space. arXiv:1301.3781.

name: Word-of-Mouth Economics and Bad-Profits Audit
aka: Word-of-mouth economics: value of a promoter's referrals and cost of a detractor's negative comments
Bad-profits audit: identifying policies that create detractors
origin: Fred Reichheld and Bain & Company, 2006; Dell analysis with Satmetrix; Reichheld and Markey, 2011
summary: Put a money value on a promoter's referrals and a detractor's negative word of mouth, then audit and remove policies that earn revenue by creating detractors.
description: Two linked analyses from the Net Promoter system. Word-of-mouth economics values comments: new customers are asked their main reason for choosing the firm, and all customers how many positive and negative comments they made in the past year and how many positives neutralise one negative. In the Dell case, referred customers worth $210 each and about 40 million positive comments gave $5.25 per comment; promoters made about eight a year, and detractors about four negatives, each cancelling five positives. Adding spend, tenure and service-cost differences valued a promoter at $328 and a detractor at -$57. Rules of thumb: one negative neutralises three to ten positives, and 80-90% of referrals come from promoters. The bad-profits audit then finds revenue earned at customers' expense (nuisance fees, gotcha pricing, onerous contracts, misleading sales) using detractor root causes, defector interviews and employee rankings, and sets a dated removal plan that finance will defend.
steps: Ask new customers the main reason they chose the firm, and record the share citing a referral.
Ask the recommend question and count positive and negative comments made in the past year; ask how many positives neutralise one negative.
Value one positive comment as referred-customer value divided by total positive comments, and value promoters and detractors by comment counts plus spend, tenure and service-cost differences.
Collect detractor root causes and defector accounts to identify policies that create detractors.
Ask employees to rank-order the most egregious bad-profit practices and discuss them openly.
Quantify the revenue at stake against the cost of the detractors each policy creates.
Agree and publish a dated removal plan with finance sign-off.
outputs: A money value of a promoter and cost of a detractor, the size of the prize from converting detractors, and a ranked list of bad-profit policies with a removal plan.
useWhen: Making the business case for experience fixes, or challenging fees, dark patterns and contract terms that raise short-term revenue but create detractors.
avoidWhen: Products with little word of mouth or no way to link survey answers to customer value. The valuation is conservative and ignores effects on staff, bad debt and legal costs; removing fees costs short-term profit.
whyLost: NPS travelled into UX as a single score, while the economics behind it and the bad-profits critique stayed in CX consulting and finance conversations.
whereToUse: Subscription and telecoms pricing, banking fees, marketplace policies, dark-pattern reviews and retention strategy.
example: A broadband provider finds its early-termination fee generates detractors who each make about four negative comments a year. Valuing those comments against the fee revenue shows the fee loses money once lost referrals are counted, and the team removes it over two quarters.
reference: Reichheld, F., with Markey, R. (2011). The Ultimate Question 2.0: How Net Promoter Companies Thrive in a Customer-Driven World (rev. and expanded ed.). Boston: Harvard Business Review Press.

name: Words of Estimative Probability
origin: Sherman Kent, CIA, 1964; codified in ICD 203 Analytic Standards (US ODNI, 2007/2015) and the UK PHIA probability yardstick
summary: Standardises the probability phrases used in reports (e.g. 'likely' = 55-80%) so readers interpret confidence consistently.
description: Kent found that analysts and policymakers interpreted words like 'probable' and 'serious possibility' with wildly different probabilities. He proposed a fixed mapping of phrases to probability ranges. Modern intelligence standards (ICD 203, the UK Professional Head of Intelligence Assessment yardstick) require estimative language and separate statements of analytic confidence based on evidence quality. UX research reports are full of 'most users', 'many participants' and 'likely', which stakeholders interpret inconsistently. Adopting a probability yardstick and separate confidence ratings makes research claims calibrated, comparable and auditable.
steps: Adopt a yardstick, such as remote (<5%), highly unlikely (10-20%), unlikely (25-35%), realistic possibility (40-50%), likely (55-75%), highly likely (80-90%), almost certain (>95%).
Train researchers and stakeholders on the mapping with examples.
For each key finding, state an estimative judgement and a separate confidence level (low, moderate, high) based on evidence quality.
Avoid ambiguous quantifiers ('many', 'some') unless tied to counts or ranges.
Track outcomes of estimative judgements over time and assess calibration.
Include the yardstick in report templates and repositories.
outputs: Reports with standardised probability language, confidence ratings and calibration tracking.
useWhen: Communicating research findings and forecasts to decision-makers, especially in synthesis and strategy work.
avoidWhen: Purely descriptive qualitative accounts where probabilistic claims are not being made.
whyLost: UX reporting evolved from journalism and storytelling conventions, not intelligence analysis.
whereToUse: Research reports, insight repositories, launch risk assessments, competitive intelligence.
example: A research team replaces 'users will probably adopt the feature' with 'likely (55-75%) that a majority of admins enable it within 30 days; moderate confidence, based on 14 interviews and beta data'. Leadership questions become more precise.
sources: Kent, Words of estimative probability (1964), Studies in Intelligence
ODNI, Intelligence Community Directive 203: Analytic Standards (2015)
Friedman, War and Chance: Assessing Uncertainty in International Politics (2019)
reference: Kent, S. (1964). Words of estimative probability. Studies in Intelligence, 8(4), 49-65.

name: Working Backwards Press Release
origin: Amazon practice (press release first); described by Kanungo (2022)
summary: A team writes the press release for a product as if it had already launched successfully, to define users, goals and timelines before building.
description: In a working backwards workshop the team writes a press release dated on a future launch day, describing a product or feature that has succeeded and is loved by users and critics. It includes stakeholder quotes and imagined user reviews, and states what problem it solved for users and how it contributed to their success. Writing the release forces early decisions: who the target users are, what goals the product meets for them, which business objectives it serves, and when it ships. Stakeholders can course-correct strategy while it is still cheap, and a dull release is itself a signal that objectives should be rethought. Amazon's fuller PR/FAQ adds a set of frequently asked questions that probe feasibility and risks. The release is built entirely on assumptions, which then need testing with users.
steps: Gather the team and key stakeholders in a workshop and pick a plausible future launch date.
Write a headline and a first paragraph naming the target user and the benefit.
Describe the problem, the solution and how it changes users' success, in customer language.
Add a stakeholder quote and imagined user reviews from blogs or app stores.
Optionally add customer and internal FAQs probing feasibility, pricing and risks.
Review the draft for timelines, target users, user goals and business objectives, and course-correct strategy.
If the release is not exciting, rethink the objectives; otherwise list its assumptions for research.
outputs: A press release (and optional FAQ) stating target users, goals, business objectives and timeline, plus a list of assumptions to test.
useWhen: Use it at the start of a product or major feature to align a team on the customer outcome before discovery and design.
avoidWhen: It contains no user evidence; test its assumptions with Interviews, Jobs-to-be-Done Research or a Prototype / Wizard-of-Oz A/B Test before committing.
whyLost: It survived because of Amazon's visibility and because writing in the customer's voice is a cheap, sharp test of whether an idea is worth building.
whereToUse: New products and features, internal platforms, start-ups, and investment cases for research or design work.
example: A travel app team's release for 'one-tap trip rebooking' sounds flat until rewritten around a stranded traveller. The FAQ exposes that airline APIs may not allow it, and that becomes the first discovery question.
reference: Kanungo, D. (2022). UX Decoded: Think and Implement User-Centered Research Methodologies, and Expert-Led UX Best Practices. BPB Publications, ch. 1.

name: Working memory load audit
origin: Miller, 1956; Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model, 1974; Cowan's capacity estimate of about 4 chunks, 2001
summary: Counts how many items a user must hold in mind at each step of a task and flags steps exceeding working memory limits of around four chunks.
description: Working memory holds a small amount of information for active use. Miller's '7 plus or minus 2' is widely quoted, but Cowan's review places capacity nearer 4 chunks when rehearsal and grouping are prevented, and capacity falls further under stress, fatigue and interruption. A working memory load audit walks through a task step by step, listing every item the user must remember from previous screens or external sources (codes, values, goals, pending steps) and noting when each can be released. Steps where load exceeds about 3-4 items, or where items must be retained across interruptions, are flagged. Remedies include keeping information visible, carrying values forward, and checklists. The method is vestigial because '7 plus or minus 2' is cited as a rule without any actual counting.
steps: Select critical tasks and write each as a sequence of steps.
For each step, list items the user must hold in memory (not visible on screen) and mark when each enters and leaves memory.
Plot the load curve and flag steps exceeding 3-4 items, or any step requiring retention across an interruption or screen change of more than about 15-20 seconds.
Adjust capacity assumptions for context: reduce by one or more for high stress, fatigue or concurrent tasks.
Validate flagged steps with users (5-8) using think-aloud or a secondary probe task, and note memory-related errors.
Redesign to externalise information (persistent display, auto-fill, recognition over recall) and re-audit.
outputs: A step-by-step memory load curve per task, flagged overload points, observed memory errors, and externalisation recommendations.
useWhen: For multi-step workflows, crisis procedures, configuration tasks, and flows that require copying information between screens.
avoidWhen: When tasks are short or fully visible; use heuristic evaluation. For overall workload, use NASA-TLX or dual-task methods.
whyLost: Miller's number became a slogan; the actual counting procedure and newer capacity estimates were lost in practice.
whereToUse: Emergency procedures, two-factor authentication, banking transfers, surgical device setup, and AI prompt workflows.
example: A crisis procedure on a surgical robot requires remembering an error code, two instrument positions and a reset sequence across three screens, peaking at 6 items. Displaying the code and positions persistently drops peak load to 2.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
The Inquiry Series, Ch 10 — Memory — The Architecture of Knowledge
reference: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: a reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

name: Working-memory span tasks
origin: Miller, 1956; Daneman and Carpenter, 1980; Turner and Engle, 1989; Della Sala et al., 1999
summary: A family of tasks measuring working-memory capacity as the longest sequence or largest set reproduced without error, with or without concurrent processing.
description: Simple span tasks present sequences of increasing length to be reproduced in order: digit span (average five to nine; Miller 1956) and visual pattern span (grids from 2 x 2 to 5 x 6 with half the squares shaded for 3 seconds; about 9 squares on average). Complex span tasks combine processing and storage: in reading span, participants read 13- to 16-word sentences and recall the final words (span 2 to 5 in the original), which correlates with reading comprehension; operation span pairs verifying sums with remembering words. Other measures include n-back, temporal order judgement and recognition under load, sometimes with a secondary task to load the central executive. Span depends on chunking (one participant reached 79 digits after 230 hours of practice), and modern estimates of capacity are nearer four items (Cowan 2001). In UX the tasks serve as covariates or to calibrate how much an interface asks users to hold in mind.
steps: Choose the measure: simple span (digit, visual pattern) for storage, complex span (reading, operation) for capacity under processing, or n-back for updating.
Start with short sequences or small sets (for example 2-3 items) and increase by one after correct trials.
Present items at a fixed rate (for example 1 per second) and require reproduction in order.
Stop after failures at a given length (for example two of three trials) and record the longest error-free length as span.
For complex span, enforce processing accuracy (for example 85 per cent on sums) so participants cannot trade it for storage.
Use span as a covariate, stratification variable or comparison against the memory demand of an interface flow.
outputs: Span scores per participant (digits, squares, sentences, operations); n-back accuracy; correlations with task performance.
useWhen: Interfaces demand holding information across steps (codes, comparisons, multi-step forms) and you need to know the capacity of your users or explain performance variation.
avoidWhen: You want to audit an interface's memory load rather than people's capacity; use a working memory load audit. Spans vary with chunking and practice, and correlations do not show causation.
whyLost: Capacity testing is standard in psychology and neuropsychology but UX typically cites '7 plus or minus 2' rather than measuring users.
whereToUse: One-time-passcode flows, comparison shopping, clinical and older-adult products, cognitive accessibility, complex enterprise forms.
example: A pharmacy app for older adults asks users to carry a six-digit code between screens. Digit span testing in the target group averages five, so the code is auto-filled and shown persistently.
reference: Daneman, M., & Carpenter, P. A. (1980). Individual differences in working memory and reading. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 19, 450-466; Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review, 63, 81-97.

name: Workload Profile (Tsang and Velazquez)
origin: Tsang and Velazquez (1996), based on Wickens' multiple resource theory
summary: A post-task workload instrument in which people rate the share of attention a task demanded on eight multiple-resource dimensions, giving a diagnostic profile and an additive total.
description: The Workload Profile takes its dimensions from Wickens' multiple resource theory: processing stage (perceptual or central versus response), code (spatial versus verbal), input modality (visual versus auditory) and output (manual versus speech). Immediately after a task, participants rate for each of eight dimensions the proportion of attentional resources the task required, from 0 (no demand) to 1 (maximum attention). The ratings are summed into an overall score, but the main value is the profile, which shows which resource is loaded, for instance visual-spatial perception rather than verbal response. Rubio and colleagues (2004) found NASA-TLX, SWAT and the Workload Profile all valid, with the Workload Profile more sensitive and diagnostic. Its weaknesses are equal weighting of dimensions and the need to explain the resource dimensions clearly to participants.
steps: Choose the tasks, conditions or designs to compare and run each with participants.
Explain the eight resource dimensions with concrete examples before the first task.
Immediately after each task, have participants rate the proportion of attentional resources required on each dimension from 0 (none) to 1 (maximum).
Sum the eight ratings for an overall workload score and keep the per-dimension profile.
Compare totals and profiles across tasks or designs, looking for the dimension that differs most.
Counterbalance task order to limit anchoring on the preceding task.
outputs: An eight-dimension resource-demand profile per task and an additive overall workload score.
useWhen: When you need to know not just how much workload a design imposes but which channel (visual, auditory, spatial, verbal, manual, vocal) it loads, for example when adding voice or haptic output.
avoidWhen: Avoid with participants who cannot grasp the resource dimensions after explanation, or when only an overall load figure is needed; then use NASA-TLX. Post-task ratings suffer recency and anchoring effects, so pair with performance or physiological measures for high-stakes decisions.
whyLost: It remains in workload research, but UX standardised on NASA-TLX, whose name recognition and tooling crowded out more diagnostic instruments.
whereToUse: In-car and cockpit interfaces, voice and multimodal assistants, clinical monitoring displays, AR and wearable interfaces that compete for visual attention.
example: A navigation app team compares turn-by-turn guidance shown on screen with spoken guidance. Totals are similar, but the profile shows the screen version loading visual-spatial perception far more, which supports defaulting to voice while driving.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Tsang, P. S. and Velazquez, V. L. (1996). Diagnosticity and multidimensional subjective workload ratings. Ergonomics, 39(3), 358-381.

name: World Cafe
origin: Juanita Brown and David Isaacs (1995); documented in Gamestorming (2010)
summary: Small tables hold timed rounds of conversation on questions that matter, with travellers carrying ideas between tables and a final whole-room synthesis.
description: The World Café improves large-group discussion by borrowing the features of informal café conversation: small round tables, cross-pollination of ideas and questions that matter. The quick-start version seats 24-30 people at tables of four or five for three rounds of about 20 minutes. After each round one person stays as table host while the others travel to different tables as ambassadors; each new round opens with the host summarising what was left behind and travellers sharing what they bring. Participants draw and write key ideas on paper tablecloths, look for links between rounds, and note emerging patterns. A closing town-hall synthesis asks what answers appeared at different tables and how they connect. The leader's main preparation is a simple, evocative question tied to a real challenge and a hospitable room.
steps: Prepare one or more open questions tied to a real challenge, and a room with round tables, paper tablecloths and markers.
Seat 24-30 people at tables of four or five.
Run a 20-minute round on the question, with people drawing and writing key ideas on the tablecloth.
Leave one host at each table; others move to new tables as ambassadors.
Open each new round with the host's recap and the travellers' contributions; run three rounds in total.
Hold a whole-room synthesis: what answers emerged at different tables and how do they connect?
Photograph the tablecloths and write up themes.
outputs: Drawn-on tablecloths and a whole-group synthesis of themes and connections.
useWhen: Use it to involve a large stakeholder or community group in exploring a shared question, such as service visions or research priorities, in one session.
avoidWhen: It gathers views from a large group but not systematically; for representative attitudes use Surveys, and for in-depth individual perspectives Interviews. To reach consensus among experts, use the Delphi Method or Nominal Group Technique.
whyLost: It is well established in organisational development and community engagement but seldom used by product UX teams.
whereToUse: Public-sector and community consultations, healthcare service redesign, large internal strategy events, and participatory research.
example: A city transport authority hosts 30 residents and drivers on 'How might buses feel safer at night?'. Lighting and driver visibility recur across tables and are taken into a co-design phase.
reference: Brown, J. and Isaacs, D. (2005). The World Café: Shaping Our Futures Through Conversations That Matter. San Francisco, CA: Berrett-Koehler.

name: Worth-Centred Evaluation
origin: Gilbert Cockton (2006, 2008); worth maps by Cockton et al. (2009)
summary: Judge whether an interaction was worthwhile by weighing its costs against achieved benefits, mapping system attributes to outcomes, and instrumenting designed benefits and adverse outcomes directly.
description: Cockton argues that asking whether a system is usable has little value; the useful question is whether the interaction was worth it, whether achieved benefits justified the costs. Usability is redefined as a hygiene factor: the extent to which negative experiences and outcomes reduce achievable worth. Evaluation lists problems with their time and emotional costs, and positive outcomes with present and future value, then judges worth and how to raise it, which often shows that re-engineering a whole path beats fixing individual problems. Worth maps link system attributes to user experience attributes and usage outcomes, so evaluation can target elements or connections. Direct worth instrumentation places custom measures on designed benefits and anticipated adverse interactions at every critical touchpoint of the product-service ecosystem, not only the interface, and reports unexpected positives as well as problems, across stakeholders.
steps: Describe the usage episode across all devices, services and people involved.
List problems and their costs in time, frustration and rework.
List positive outcomes and experiences and their present and future value.
Judge whether benefits justified costs and how worth could be increased: reduce costs, increase value or re-engineer the path.
For planned evaluation, build a worth map linking system attributes, experience attributes and outcomes, and identify designed benefits and anticipated adverse interactions.
Instrument these directly at all critical touchpoints, including offline service points.
Report positives and unexpected benefits as well as problems, for all stakeholders.
outputs: Cost and benefit lists, a worth judgement, a worth map and custom worth measures.
useWhen: Evaluating products and services where value delivered, not just ease of use, decides success, especially across multi-channel service ecosystems.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need diagnosis of specific interface problems; use Moderated Usability Testing. Judgements are interpretive and the method is underdeveloped.
whyLost: It remained an academic position; industry absorbed similar ideas as outcome metrics and Jobs-to-be-Done without the worth-mapping apparatus.
whereToUse: Service design, subscription products, AI features whose value is uncertain, migrations and switching flows.
example: Evaluating a phone-migration service, the team records a 2.5-hour contact transfer with high frustration and modest benefit, and concludes the path needs re-engineering rather than fixing its separate screens.
reference: Cockton, G. (2006). Designing worth is worth designing. Proceedings of NordiCHI 2006, 165-174.

name: Writing as a Method of Inquiry (CAP Ethnography and Crystallisation)
origin: Laurel Richardson (1994 onwards); Richardson and St. Pierre
summary: Use writing itself, in several genres and voices, as a way of analysing material, and judge validity by crystallisation from many angles rather than triangulation.
description: Richardson argues that writing is not a final step that reports findings but a method of discovery: rewriting material in another genre reveals what the first version assumed and hid. Creative analytic practice (CAP) ethnographies include poetry, drama, readers' theatre, layered texts and writing stories. Validity is pictured not as a triangle, fixing one true point from three angles, but as a crystal, whose many facets refract different and partial views; several texts together give a crystallised account. Five criteria judge the work: substantive contribution, aesthetic merit, reflexivity, impact and expression of a reality. Practical exercises include writing groups, a writing autobiography, field notes written as practice in point of view, turning field notes into drama, and analysing the rhetoric of a mainstream article. Freedom of form does not guarantee quality, and the results can be harder to defend to some audiences.
