steps: Write a conventional analytic account of the material.
Rewrite it in another genre or voice, for example a dialogue, script or first-person account from a participant's position.
Compare what each version reveals and conceals, and note new questions it raises.
Reflect in writing on your own position as author and the rhetorical choices you made.
Assemble the versions as facets of one crystallised account.
Judge the result against substantive contribution, aesthetic merit, reflexivity, impact and expression of a reality.
outputs: Multiple texts in different genres that together give a crystallised, reflexive account.
useWhen: Synthesis feels stuck or flattened, or findings need to convey lived complexity to stakeholders rather than a list of themes.
avoidWhen: Evidence must be traceable and standardised for decisions or audits; use Writing Qualitative Findings (Evidence Standards) and Triangulation.
whyLost: It arose in interpretive sociology and is associated with literary and performative outputs that product organisations rarely request.
whereToUse: Research storytelling, persona and scenario writing, sensitive domains such as health and grief, reflexive practice within research teams.
example: After a study of carers using a medication app, a researcher writes the findings both as a report and as a short two-voice script between carer and patient; the script exposes a tension over control that the thematic report had smoothed over.
sources: The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2017)
Miles, M. & Huberman, A. M., Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook, 2nd ed. (1994)
reference: Richardson, L. and St. Pierre, E. A. 'Writing: A method of inquiry', in Denzin, N. K. and Lincoln, Y. S. (eds.) (2005). The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research (3rd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE.

name: Writing Qualitative Findings (Evidence Standards)
origin: Qualitative reporting traditions; codified in standards such as COREQ (Tong, Sainsbury & Craig, 2007) and SRQR (O'Brien et al., 2014)
summary: Standards for writing qualitative findings: lead with analytic claims, select representative verbatim quotes, state frequency honestly, report negative cases and declare the scope of claims.
description: Qualitative findings are only as credible as their write-up. These standards require each finding to lead with an analytical claim rather than a list of participant statements, with evidence beneath it. Quotes must be verbatim, representative of the pattern rather than merely vivid, and attributed with consistent pseudonyms or IDs. Frequency language is explicit and consistent ('all 12', 'most (10 of 12)', 'several (4 of 12)') rather than vague. Each major finding states its exceptions and what explains them. Every report includes a scope statement defining the population, context and time to which claims apply, and notes methodological limits. Reporting checklists such as COREQ and SRQR formalise these expectations in academic publishing. The rigour comes from making the evidential basis of every claim inspectable.
steps: Lead with the analytical claim, not the data: Never write 'Participant 3 said X.' Write: 'Users experienced the confirmation step as accusatory [theme], illustrated by Participant 3: [short quote].' Analysis leads; data supports.
Quote selection: Each quote must be (a) verbatim, (b) representative of the pattern — not the most dramatic exception, and (c) necessary.
Explicit frequency language: 'All 12 participants' vs. 'most (10/12)' vs. 'several (4/12)' vs. 'one participant.' Use numbers, not vague qualifiers.
Negative cases in the report: Every major finding should include: what the exceptions are, how many participants showed them, and what conditions seem to predict them.
Scope statement: Every report should state explicitly for what population, context, and time period the findings apply.
outputs: Findings written as evidence-backed claims, a quote selection log, consistent frequency language, negative case notes, a scope and limitations statement, and an optional reporting checklist.
useWhen: Writing any qualitative research report, especially when findings will inform significant decisions, be challenged by sceptical stakeholders, or be reused in a repository.
avoidWhen: Never skip it entirely; for quick informal shares, a lightweight version (claim, evidence, scope) still applies. Use the Decision Memo Format on top when the audience needs only the decision.
whyLost: Speed-driven reporting favours quote collages and 'users said' bullets, and most UX researchers are not trained in qualitative reporting standards from the social sciences.
whereToUse: Research reports, repository insights, executive readouts, regulated product research, and any synthesis that will be quoted out of context.
example: A researcher rewrites 'Users hate the new dashboard' as 'Most (9 of 12) operations managers could not locate overdue items, because the status filter was hidden; the 3 who succeeded had used the legacy filter.' Stakeholder debate shifts from opinion to the fix.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Tong, Sainsbury & Craig (2007) COREQ, International Journal for Quality in Health Care
Analysing and Presenting Qualitative Data (Burnard et al., 2008)
A Step-by-Step Process of Thematic Analysis to Develop a Conceptual Model in Qualitative Research (Naeem et al., 2023)
Funerals Market Study: Qualitative Research Report (Research Works Limited, 2018)
reference: O'Brien, B. C. et al. (2014). Standards for reporting qualitative research: a synthesis of recommendations. Academic Medicine, 89(9), 1245-1251.

name: XR Heuristic Evaluation and Staged XR Usability Engineering
origin: Bowman, Gabbard and Hix (2002); Gabbard and Swan (2008); synthesised by Stanney et al. in the Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (2021)
summary: Evaluate AR, VR and MR systems in stages: expert inspection against Nielsen's heuristics plus XR-specific ones, then qualitative and quantitative testing with presence, sickness and workload measures.
description: Extended reality adds problems that desktop usability methods miss: 3D selection and manipulation, multimodal output, shared physical space, presence and adverse aftereffects. The staged flow runs task analysis, expert inspection, qualitative user testing, then formative and summative quantitative studies. In inspection, three to five experts walk representative tasks and check each step against Nielsen's ten heuristics (77 percent of 672 issues in one VR application mapped to them) extended with XR heuristics: users always know their own location and spatial relations; superimposed objects are registered and persist regardless of head or camera speed; real-world size and conventions are respected; scanning and frame-of-reference transformations are minimised; spatial audio and multimodal cues support attention; there is an explicit exit; controls outside the field of view can be found; virtual clutter is limited; and tracking latency, comfort, sickness, setup and physical-space safety are considered. User testing then adds questionnaires (SUS, Presence Questionnaire, SSQ, NASA-TLX), performance and physiological measures.
steps: Analyse the target XR tasks, interactions and information needs.

Have three to five experts walk each task and check every step against Nielsen's heuristics plus the XR additions: location awareness, registration and persistence, real-world scale, frame-of-reference load, exits, out-of-view controls, clutter, comfort and sickness, setup and physical safety.
Consolidate violations, report them to the design team and redesign.
Run qualitative testing (think-aloud, interviews) to see how users perceive and approach the XR interaction.
Run formative then summative studies with task performance, XR questionnaires for presence, simulator sickness, workload and satisfaction, and where useful implicit physiological measures.
Benchmark against a real-world or non-XR equivalent of the task where possible.
outputs: A list of heuristic violations, qualitative insight into XR interaction, and benchmarks for performance, presence, sickness and satisfaction.
useWhen: Designing or reviewing VR training, AR guidance, mixed-reality collaboration or headset applications, particularly before user testing is affordable or safe.
avoidWhen: Questionnaires alone flag problems but cannot isolate causes; do not rely on inspection for sickness or presence, which need user testing (see Simulation Sickness Testing in VR). For games, Playability Heuristic Evaluation may fit better.
whyLost: XR evaluation remains largely academic and lab-based; few AR papers include user studies, and industry teams reuse desktop heuristics without the spatial additions.
whereToUse: AR maintenance and surgery guidance, VR training simulators, headset productivity apps, automotive head-up displays, retail AR try-on.
example: An AR warehouse picking app is inspected by four experts, who find labels that drift when the head turns quickly and a menu that falls outside the field of view. After fixes, a summative study compares pick rates, SSQ and NASA-TLX against handheld scanners.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (Salvendy & Karwowski, 2021)
reference: Gabbard, J. L. and Swan, J. E. (2008). Usability engineering for augmented reality. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 14(3); Stanney, K. et al. (2021), Extended reality (XR) environments, in Salvendy and Karwowski (eds), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics (5th ed.), pp. 799-803.

name: Yin's Five-Phase Analytic Cycle
origin: Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research: From Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016). Builds on Miles and Huberman's data reduction, display and conclusion drawing (1984/1994), to which the cycle is often wrongly credited.
summary: A staged qualitative analysis cycle (compile, disassemble, reassemble and array, interpret, conclude) run alongside a project so qual evidence stays auditable from first interviews to final validation.
description: Robert Yin set out this five-phase cycle in Qualitative Research from Start to Finish. Vivek Gopinath's forward-thinking playbook, which credits it to Miles & Huberman, maps each phase to a loop stage: Compiling (Stage 1: raw mental-model quotes and sketches in one sheet), Disassembling (Stages 1–2: short codes for expectations and breakdowns, taxonomy coding with reliability), Reassembling/Arraying (Stages 2 and 4: participant × episode arrays and trajectory patterns), Interpreting (Stages 3 and 5: mechanism memos mapped to prescriptions) and Concluding (Stage 6: forecast versus actual, mechanism repair, residual risks). Miles and Huberman's lasting contribution is the systematic use of data displays such as matrices and arrays; the five-phase compiling-to-concluding sequence is most closely associated with Robert K. Yin. Its rigour lies in an audit trail where every claim can be traced back through arrays and codes to raw data.
steps: Compiling: gather verbatims, sketches and notes into one structured worksheet.
Disassembling: code utterances into short, low-granularity labels or taxonomy codes, with reliability checks where codes are counted.
Reassembling/Arraying: build participant × episode or trajectory arrays and sort them to reveal patterns.
Interpreting: write mechanism memos connecting patterns to quantitative results and prescriptions.
Concluding: compare forecast with actual, judge whether the mechanism was repaired, and document residual risks for the next loop.
outputs: An auditable chain of worksheets, codes, arrays, memos and conclusions.
useWhen: Any mixed-methods programme where qualitative evidence must remain traceable across stages.
avoidWhen: Quick one-off interviews where a lightweight synthesis suffices.
whyLost: Displays and staged analysis are standard in qualitative methodology, but UX synthesis has collapsed into sticky-note clustering without an audit trail.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX programmes, mixed-methods studies, regulated domains needing traceability.
example: In a trading app programme, the team compiles mental-model quotes, codes them, arrays error episodes, writes mechanism memos and finally documents forecast versus actual, all in one traceable workbook.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). Guilford Press. See also Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). SAGE.

name: Z Notation for Interface State Specification
aka: Z schema specification of interactive systems
Z notation for formal interface specification
origin: Jean-Raymond Abrial, late 1970s; Spivey, 1989
summary: Specifies interface states and operations in set-theoretic, mathematical notation, so properties such as predictability and safety can be checked before implementation.
description: Z is a formal specification language based on set theory and first-order predicate logic, using schemas to describe system states, invariants and operations. In HCI, researchers such as Harrison and Thimbleby used Z and related notations to specify interactive systems precisely and reason about usability properties: whether every state is visible to the user, whether operations can be undone, whether modes are distinguishable, and whether the same input always produces predictable results. Writing the specification exposes ambiguities in requirements early. Rigour comes from complete state schemas, explicit invariants, and either proof or tool-supported checking of interaction properties, with results traced back to interface design decisions.
steps: Z specification process for critical UI flows:
Define the state space: all variables that constitute the interface state, their types, and their invariants.
(2) Define each operation: pre-condition (state must satisfy X before the operation), post-condition (state satisfies Y after the operation).

(3) Check for: operations that have no valid pre-condition (dead operations), states that no operation can reach (inaccessible states), state transitions that violate invariants (inconsistency). Formal verification catches entire classes of bugs before implementation.
outputs: A formal specification of states, invariants and operations, proofs or checks of interaction properties (e.g. undo, mode visibility), and a list of ambiguities resolved.
useWhen: Safety-critical interactive systems (medical devices, avionics, rail control) where mode errors and unpredictable states must be ruled out.
avoidWhen: Avoid for consumer products with fast iteration and low risk; use state diagrams, prototypes and usability testing instead.
whyLost: Formal methods in HCI flourished in the late 1980s and 1990s but required mathematical expertise and slowed iteration, so they retreated to safety-critical engineering.
whereToUse: Safety-critical interface specification, medical device UI design, financial transaction flow specification.
example: A team specifying an infusion pump's dose entry in Z discovers that two operations can leave the system in an undisplayed mode; the interface is changed to show mode at all times before any code is written.
sources: The Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI — (various)
Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
reference: Spivey JM (1992) The Z Notation: A Reference Manual. 2nd ed. Prentice Hall

name: Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET)
origin: Gerald Zaltman, Harvard Business School, early 1990s (Zaltman and Coulter, 1995; Zaltman, 1997)
summary: Participants collect images representing their thoughts and feelings about a topic, then a structured interview elicits deep metaphors and builds a consensus map.
description: ZMET assumes most thought is unconscious and image-based. A week before the interview, participants gather 8-10 images expressing their feelings about a topic. A two-hour interview uses structured steps: storytelling about each image, missed images, sorting, construct elicitation using a Kelly repertory grid triad technique, the most representative image, opposite images, sensory images, a mental map and a summary collage, often with laddering. Analysis codes constructs and connections across 20-25 interviews into a consensus map and identifies 'deep metaphors' (e.g. balance, journey, container, connection). It reveals emotional and symbolic meanings that direct questions miss.
steps: Recruit participants and instruct them to collect 8-10 images representing their thoughts and feelings about the topic.
Conduct a one-on-one interview of about two hours following the ZMET steps, including image stories and triad sorts.
Use laddering to connect attributes to consequences and values.
Have participants create a summary collage or mental map of key constructs.
Code constructs and links across interviews; build a consensus map of constructs shared by at least a third of participants.
Identify deep metaphors and translate them into design, content and brand implications.
outputs: Construct maps, consensus maps, deep metaphors and participant collages.
useWhen: Understanding emotional and symbolic meanings of a category, brand or experience for strategy and design direction.
avoidWhen: Usability questions or when quick tactical answers are needed.
whyLost: ZMET is a proprietary, trademarked process used by consultancies in marketing research, rarely taught to UX researchers.
whereToUse: Financial wellbeing, health conditions, home and family technologies, luxury and lifestyle products, AI companions.
example: A ZMET study on retirement saving reveals a dominant 'container' metaphor (protecting a fragile nest) rather than 'journey'; the app's growth-chart framing is replaced by protection and safety imagery.
sources: Zaltman, Rethinking market research: Putting people back in (1997), Journal of Marketing Research
Zaltman & Coulter, Seeing the voice of the customer: Metaphor-based advertising research (1995), Journal of Advertising Research
reference: Zaltman, G. (1997). Rethinking market research. Journal of Marketing Research, 34(4), 424-437.

name: Zero-inflated count models
origin: Diane Lambert (1992)
summary: Models counts where a zero can arise in two ways, because the process never started or because it ran and produced nothing, estimating both parts with their own predictors.
description: Many behavioural counts have more zeros than a Poisson or negative binomial allows, because some units never engage at all. A zero-inflated model is a mixture: with probability p the process is 'off' and always yields zero; otherwise counts follow a Poisson (or negative binomial) with rate lambda, which can also produce zeros. The likelihood of a zero is p plus (1 - p) times the Poisson probability of zero; a positive count has likelihood (1 - p) times its Poisson probability. Each part gets its own linear model and link, logit for p and log for lambda, and predictors may differ. The model estimates the share of structural zeros even though no individual zero can be classified. Ignoring inflation underestimates the active rate. The two parts can trade off and be weakly identified with little data, so the model should first be validated by simulating data with known values. Hurdle models are a related alternative.
steps: State the two processes and why a zero could come from either (never discovered the feature versus discovered it but did not use it this week).
Simulate data from that story with known values and confirm the model recovers them.
Fit a zero-inflated Poisson or negative binomial with separate predictors for the zero process (logit) and the count process (log), adding an exposure offset if observation time varies.
Use weakly informative priors or regularisation if the zero probability is poorly identified.
Convert both parts to natural scales: probability of a structural zero, and rate when active.
Compare with plain Poisson, negative binomial and hurdle models using predictive checks of the share of zeros.
outputs: Estimated share of structural zeros, the rate among active units, and predictor effects on each part.
useWhen: Counts of feature use, errors, purchases or support contacts per user where many users never engage, and the team needs to separate reach from intensity.
avoidWhen: Zeros are not in excess of what the count distribution predicts, or zeros arise from only one process (use a hurdle model if all zeros are structural). Small samples make the two parts hard to separate.
whyLost: Count models with mixture components are standard in ecology, epidemiology and econometrics but UX analytics usually reports means or medians of skewed counts.
whereToUse: Feature adoption analytics, error and retry counts in usability tests, purchase frequency, help-centre visits, notification interaction counts.
example: A design tool counts weekly uses of a new auto-layout feature per user: 70% are zero. A zero-inflated negative binomial shows that onboarding exposure lowers the structural-zero probability from 0.65 to 0.45 but does not change the use rate among adopters, so effort goes into discoverability.
reference: Lambert, D. (1992). Zero-inflated Poisson regression, with an application to defects in manufacturing. Technometrics, 34(1), 1-14.
